## Front matter of the volume

## Title page of the series

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the times of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated among themselves and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the very extensive editions published during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a single glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers, and in what places of their works, commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.**

**An edition exceptionally accurate and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of its type, the quality of its paper, the integrity of its text, the perfection of its correction, the variety and number alike of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent similarity throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially the fact that this collection—single, systematic, and chronological—brings together for the first time in our library six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, gathered from works pertaining to every age, place, language, and form.**

**SECOND SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for one thousand francs; the three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# General Preface

## I

It was almost always the customary practice of distinguished writers—a practice commendably introduced and religiously preserved—that when they applied their hands to publishing any work, they did not immediately begin with the proposed subject at the very threshold of the book. Instead, after first explaining the plan of their work, employing the necessary means, and setting forth the intended goal, they prefaced it with a preliminary dissertation.

So deeply has this custom taken root with the passage of time that at the present day, just as a preface is rightly expected by everyone, so its omission by a writer is rightly regarded as an injustice to everyone. Those who prepare themselves to read a work naturally desire to know what aim its author has set before himself, toward what end his study and labor are directed, and what path and means he has decided to take in order to reach his goal. Once these matters are known, readers who fear wasting their labor and time on uncertainty are better protected.

But, to speak frankly, this practice is also of the greatest benefit to the writer himself. By placing a dissertation at the beginning, he usually leads the reader, as it were by the hand, toward the appointed goal of the work and compels him to undertake the path that the writer himself has chosen for reaching it. Since the reader is not free to turn aside elsewhere, set another goal, or employ other means than those disclosed by the writer, he must pronounce judgment on the work, while those conditions remain in force, not according to his own inclination but according to the author’s purpose.

Since this is so, we too have thought it appropriate, following in the footsteps of those who have served literature well, to explain the plan of our work, announce our intention in advance, and set out the means by which we have proceeded. Thus our labor may be judged according to what we proposed for the subject before us: whether we touched the target of our undertaking well or badly, closely or distantly, truly or falsely.

## II

Accordingly, we have undertaken to publish the works of our holy Father Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia. In making this choice we were moved by more than one consideration.

For nearly a thousand years, the works of this most holy man, to whom our province owes obligations under so many titles, had been scattered here and there. We were distressed by this, and our first thought was to gather them into a single body, lest those which by good fortune have reached us should suffer the same fate as the others—which, since they were undoubtedly more numerous, we now lament, though late and uselessly, as having perished.

While working to avert this misfortune, we had another object in mind: the honor of the Father himself and the benefit of readers. Works that have not appeared worthy of esteem are not usually esteemed. Since earlier centuries inserted Paulinus’s labors only incidentally and opportunistically among the works of other Fathers, it is not surprising that some people failed to appreciate them, neglected them, and did not read them.

Moreover, since books bearing the title of Paulinus were not inscribed under his name but were circulated under another name, the author’s glory could not fail to remain hidden, even from those who would have cared to honor so great a Father. We therefore believed that we would serve the name of our writer if, after rescuing his works from ignoble dispersion, we handed them over in a properly assembled body. By separating them from the works of other, however illustrious, men, we would show that they were not destined to derive honor from association with another, as though they needed foreign support, but were born to acquire fame from themselves.

## III

While looking ahead to the author’s honor, we also looked at the same time to the benefit of readers. We believe that very few people will have such an abundance of leisure and time that, wishing to devote themselves to Paulinus’s books, they will be willing to hold one writer and then another before them with such labor.

Even if there are some who do not fear submitting themselves to this kind of inconvenience, the matter still remains difficult. The writers among whom Paulinus’s work is found are not readily accessible. Indeed, since most of them are extremely rare and are not found in smaller libraries, they would have to be acquired at no ordinary expense. But not everyone has the opportunity to visit Corinth.

Since, therefore, those who have scant resources at home undoubtedly outnumber the rest, we have tried to oblige them by presenting the works of Paulinus gathered into a single body, which would not be expensive.

## IV

Another consideration, by no means negligible, was added to all these. We live in an age to which truth is more indebted than to any that preceded it. I venture to say that scarcely any other age has found writers more devoted to bringing truth to light with greater effort than the present one.

Matters must be submitted to examination so many times; so many laws of criticism must be observed; so many criteria applied; so many collations, observations, and notes undertaken for the sake of a single truth, that even gold itself, with equal scrupulousness, might feel that it had never and nowhere been tested upon the Lydian stone.

Since it is proper and innate to strive against what is forbidden, writers have proposed to themselves greater exertions and sharper efforts precisely where truth has seemed to be enveloped in thicker darkness. Therefore, since it is clear that no branch of literary and ecclesiastical learning has suffered greater danger than in the period called the Middle Ages, we see that the more distinguished men have resolved to devote all their strength to illuminating that age.

Those dark centuries, deprived of the stricter Muses and with the spirit of more cultivated learning in exile, were shamefully disfigured by the spread of barbarism and ignorance. This would rightly be lamented from the heart, were it not that, under favorable auspices, we have discovered that matters have reached the point where the studies, vigils, and nocturnal labors of learned men draw greater light and glory from the very places once oppressed by denser gloom—and where the more repellent things of the past become more pleasing through the sweat of the present, whether one should call the former neglect or misfortune.

Since our Paulinus flourished in that blind age, his writings have offered our studies and labors—now extended almost to a decade—a field neither barren nor narrow, so that we might contribute, to the best of our ability, the clarifications required by doctrine, discipline, or history. Following the commendable practice that has now daily grown stronger, while bringing forth a medieval author we have attempted to cleanse literature of the accumulated filth of barbarism and to rescue truth from the soot of error.

You may now learn in what order and by what means this was done.

## V

Chronology is indeed a dry study, but for us it was a torch of historical truth, to be fixed by the most probable calculations, so that we could assign Paulinus’s writings to more certain years. We shall explain the reasoning behind our calculations at suitable places.

Once this had been established, we followed in arranging the works the order which we believed corresponded to each period. Thus the little book called the *Sacrosyllabus*, presented at the Council of Frankfurt in 794, accepted in the synod under the name of the Italian bishops, and sent by decree of all the Fathers to the Spanish bishops, in which the errors of Felix and Elipandus are refuted, occupies the first place.

Since the *Adversaria* of Gaspar Barthius supplied us with certain chapters which he composed to illuminate Paulinus’s *Sacrosyllabus*, we did not think they should be omitted. We therefore placed them under their respective paragraphs, adding some material of our own which we thought would bring greater light.

## VI

From the same council we append to the *Sacrosyllabus* Paulinus’s letter concerning the penance of Heistulf. It was once believed to be a work of Pope Stephen V, and Gratian inserted it under that pope’s name into the body of canon law.

In the preface which we place before the notes, we demonstrate that it is the legitimate offspring of Paulinus. Since the gloss on canon law offers some assistance in illuminating the matters presented in the letter, we also append it, inserting certain additions from our own resources.

## VII

To these is added the book of the *Exhortation to Henry, our duke of Friuli*, which was sometimes published among the works of Saint Augustine under the title *On Saving Instructions*, but has now been restored to Paulinus, its true father, by the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur.

Among them, P. Garnerius, the most recent editor of the works of Saint Basil, admits that the book *Admonition to a Spiritual Son* is not Basil’s and confesses that he does not know its author. We are astonished that no one among his own associates warned him that the greater part of it was excerpted from this work of Paulinus.

For from what our Paulinus wrote in this *Exhortation*, from chapter 20 through chapter 45, some monk perhaps cobbled together his *Admonition* and adapted it for those devoted to the ascetic life. We point this out in the notes on chapter 20 itself. We think this work of Paulinus arose before the year 795.

## VIII

We assign to the year 796 the Council of Friuli, which must unquestionably be placed among the works of Paulinus, not only because he convened it but also because he wrote it.

To the fourteen canons that follow, besides the shorter notes that illuminate particular matters as they arise, as in the other works, we have added observations. In these we especially bring into view the force of ecclesiastical discipline and set forth the origin or antiquity of certain customs and rites that have survived down to our own days.

## IX

Next follow three books against Felix, written approximately in the year 796. They were published through the work of André Duchesne, or Quercetanus, together with the works of Blessed Alcuin.

Before that edition, which appeared in Paris in 1617, they had not seen the light of day; nor, if we are not mistaken, have they done so since. For this reason we have been unable to compare variant readings, as we did in the preceding works.

Nevertheless, we have not omitted to add suitable notes for explaining the text or subject matter wherever we thought clarification was needed. Paulinus prefixed a dedicatory letter to King Charles. From its wording we thought we could determine the time when the books were published, namely the leap year 796.

In the Duchesne edition the books are published without chapter divisions and without titles. We thought it would be helpful to the reader, by separating the text into chapters and adding titles, to divide the treatment and thereby lessen the weariness that a lengthy and uninterrupted reading ordinarily produces.

Although we postponed fragments of letters until after the complete and finished works, precisely because they are fragments, we nevertheless attach to the books themselves a fragment of a certain letter concerning his books.

## X

Just as Paulinus published the *Rule of Faith* together with these three books, we immediately append it to them. It closes the works that can be assigned to a definite period—apart from the Synod of Altinum, which will be discussed below.

We make it the beginning of the *Poems*, whose date is uncertain to us, since it too is a poem. It is followed by something resembling an *Apology* for the poem itself, which must be defended against the cold and senseless accusations of petty quibblers and schoolroom wranglers.

## XI

The *Poems* therefore follow. These are several hymns of Paulinus in honor of the saints. We have shown, by adding proofs, that the second of them belongs to Paulinus, not to Elpis, the wife of Boethius.

Hymn V, concerning Saint Mark the Evangelist, is now published for the first time. It is sufficient to compare it with the others for Paulinus’s authorship to be recognized. If it had previously been known to more recent critics, they would not have raged so violently against our tradition concerning Saint Mark’s arrival in these regions.

The *Rhythmus* follows the *Poems*. This one concerns the Nativity of the Lord. We are extremely sorry that we have searched in vain until now for the *Rhythmus on the Destruction of Aquileia*, knowledge of which we derived from Georgius Cassander. From this you will see how falsely William Cave said that Paulinus’s hymns had perished.

## XII

After these we append several fragments of Paulinus’s letters. Although the time of their composition is not apparent, we have nevertheless not omitted to add conjectures indicating to which years they may be assigned.

## XIII

Finally, Paulinus’s works are closed by his letter concerning the proceedings of the Synod of Altinum. Since the synod was held in 803 and Paulinus departed this life at the beginning of 804, we place it at the end as his final work.

Part of it emerged from extremely corrupt manuscripts: its beginning and end from the Vatican manuscript through Baronius, and the complete letter through Baluze. We supply variant readings wherever this was possible. Where no other reading was available, we noted conjectures in the notes.

Wherever we find the text, we reproduce it, mindful of the law of Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, the Samian, which forbids adding anything to books or altering them, but commands that they remain as they were first written, however and by whatever skill they may have been composed. So Synesius says in his *Dion*.

The books of Paulinus are indeed corrupt, whether through the fault of copyists or scribes; and we greatly desired to compare them with manuscripts, if this had been possible. But, as P. Bernard de Montfaucon also informed us in a letter given at Paris on the seventh day before the Kalends of February 1730, Paulinus’s manuscripts are extremely rare and not easily found.

Thus, because—as the same Synesius says in the passage cited, a little farther on—“these corrupt books seem to lack a mind that presides over the eyes,” we have applied as much judgment as nature has granted us. Recognizing the ambiguous and uncertain sense, we have selected the reading that appeared more probable and more credible.

## XIV

These, then, are the works of Paulinus that had reached our hands. I need not say at length with what labor and study we obtained them; the skilled will easily conjecture it, while the unskilled, even if I told them, would not believe it.

The work that failed in its purpose through fruitless searching was greater than the work that did not fail to reach its end. Nor should the memory of those who contributed materials, lent a hand to our labor, or offered to do so fall from our hearts. Rather, as the proverb says, let us “count friendly names as the mark of a pot in the ashes.” It pleases us to list them here as an enduring testimony of our gratitude and as an act of honor.

The reader will see how far our efforts extended, so that the work might emerge complete and perfect in every respect, insofar as that lay within us.

## XV

There were two volumes without whose assistance we could not possibly have brought our collection to completion: those of Georgius Cassander and Alcuin. The former would supply the hymns, the latter the three books against Felix.

Since both were exceedingly rare, unavailable among our people, and not obtainable even for gold, because they were not offered by booksellers, they had to be requested from elsewhere.

The distinguished man Apostolo Zeno, who never ceases to serve literature well, promised that he would first lend his assistance when he was staying for several days at Udine. He fulfilled his promise by sending Cassander from Venice and granting us its use not merely as necessity required but even at our pleasure.

The other volume was brought from Milan at our request by Father Nicolaus Calsamilia of the Society of Jesus, when he came to Udine to preach the Lenten sermons again in the principal church of Udine in the year 1729. He allowed us to use it for the duration of his stay.

That period was very short for transcribing Paulinus, examining Alcuin, and extracting what served our purpose—especially since at that time we were held by more sorrowful cares. We saw our uncle Nicolaus Madrisius, well known throughout the world of learning, die before our eyes on the day before the Kalends of April, after a prolonged illness of arthritis (*ἀρθρίτιδος*).

Thirteen days later we saw our mother Venilia, descended from the Palladian family of the Olivi, taken from the living. She was a woman especially distinguished for prudence, religion, and charity toward the poor.

Since we could not withhold from them the final offices of piety, our studies were interrupted from that time onward. We later repaired the loss with doubled vigils and more strenuous effort, and at last reached the final line of our transcription—whether one should call it the sweating of labor or an excessive toil.

## XVI

These were the writers from whose nocturnal labors no small part of Paulinus’s works had to be drawn, and they had to be brought from other regions.

We had already prepared the rest, except for Hymn 1, published by Cardinal Tommasius, which P. Franciscus Berlendus, a Theatine cleric regular, sent from Venice.

While we were gathering and transcribing these materials, we did not omit to approach more distinguished men by letter. They replied with great courtesy that they would accommodate our wishes by searching their libraries and communicating anything concerning Paulinus that might come to hand.

If, in fact, little or nothing of Paulinus remains that has not reached us, we do not doubt that they would most willingly have fulfilled what they promised and honorably discharged their pledge.

The distinguished Scipio Maffei wrote from Verona that he had nowhere and never come upon any manuscript of Paulinus, although he had examined almost innumerable codices. Nevertheless, he said that he would send a letter to Milan so that the volumes of the Ambrosian Library might be examined.

We already knew from the replies of the distinguished men Joseph Saxius, librarian of the Ambrosian Library, and Ludovico Antonio Muratori that this diligence would be fruitless. The former replied that he had searched the books but found nothing; the latter, who through long experience was thoroughly familiar with the same library, answered that the inquiry would be a useless and superfluous undertaking.

We also approached at Rome our distinguished countryman Fontanini, whom we believed more than anyone else ought to care about matters relating to his native land. He replied briefly that he had nothing to provide beyond what was contained in the catalogue of the Imperial Cardinal’s library, which he himself had edited.

Nevertheless, by the help of the good God, we have published several items which he had not listed.

## XVII

Meanwhile, when we saw ourselves laboring fruitlessly in Italy, we did not restrain ourselves from traveling beyond the Alps. We approached France, Belgium, and Germany by letters, and visited men distinguished for their reputation for learning, so that they might assist the work we had begun.

Among them, P. Bernard de Montfaucon, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, courteously replied from Paris to our repeated requests. As soon as he received our letters, he searched his chests, but in vain. He warned us—as we had already said—that manuscript codices of our writer were exceedingly rare; if any concerning him should turn up, however, he would gladly inform us.

We received almost the same reply, with equal courtesy, from P. Joannes Baptista Solerius of the Society of Jesus at Antwerp. He had not hesitated to occupy his fellow scholars in examining manuscripts, of which they possessed an immense supply.

Through the help of the distinguished man Jacob Marinoni of Udine, our countryman and mathematician to His Imperial Majesty Charles VI, we sought the Vienna Library. He himself replied that nothing of Paulinus had been found in its manuscripts, although they were extremely numerous.

What more is there to say? When the most distinguished Dominicus Passioneus passed through Udine in 1731, on his way to Vienna as nuncio of the Apostolic See, we approached him. We had already learned of his courtesy not only from public report but from the testimony of our late uncle Nicolaus, who had experienced it personally at Rome; and we truly found it to be so.

When he learned of the labors we had undertaken, he promised that he would lend his hand, investigate the matter, and use his authority to compel others to search the more distinguished collections for some unpublished work of Paulinus.

He later wished to inform us by a letter sent from Vienna that he had done so, but without success.

## XVIII

This, excellent reader, is how far our efforts proceeded in order to present you with a complete work of Paulinus.

We believed above all that the means we employed to achieve our proposed goal were effective. If, after so much study, after such great efforts, and after troubling so many distinguished men almost to the point of annoyance, some unpublished work of Paulinus should come to light which ought to have been published, we shall not begrudge anyone its publication. Indeed, we shall congratulate from the heart whoever has met with better fortune than we did for the benefit of literary scholarship, being content merely to have escaped the reproach of carelessness and negligence.

We are now prepared to give an account of what we have brought forth from our modest resources.

## XIX

We have prefixed to the works of Paulinus his Life, thinking that anyone who became acquainted with the works would be pleased also to learn the author’s deeds, character, holiness, and virtues.

The material is not abundant, since the history of those times supplies no testimony, or almost none. We have arranged the subject in seventeen chapters.

From the first through the thirteenth we proceed in chronological order—that is, from his birth to the day of his death—observing the laws of criticism and chronology. In the remaining chapters we present matters that either belong to an uncertain period or may be assigned to any period.

For the most part, everything rests upon the authority of Paulinus himself, upon writers contemporary with him, and upon testimony from documents of the same age.

Whatever could not be supported by a legitimate foundation but is held only under the name of popular tradition, we have not omitted, lest anything concerning Paulinus be lacking. Nevertheless, adding no weight of our own, we leave such matters as they are, so that the prudent reader may have the certain and the uncertain before his eyes and, if he wishes, follow what appears probable to him.

## XX

We have composed several dissertations in which no negligible difficulties that may arise in Paulinus’s writings and deeds are disentangled.

The first concerns the book of the *Exhortation to Henry, Duke of Friuli*, in which Henry and his deeds are discussed at greater length.

The second concerns the Council of Friuli, in which the year, place, and number of bishops who are thought to have attended the council are established. From this it is shown how far and how widely the province of Aquileia extended at different times, and how many bishoprics it held under its jurisdiction.

The third, which we call dogmatic, investigates which earlier heresy gave rise to the Felician branch and traces it back to Nestorianism.

The fourth is historical and chronological. It arranges through time the origin, development, and destruction of the Felician heresy. To this is added a criticism of Jacob Basnage, who wrote poorly about those who wrote against the Felician heresy.

The fifth concerns the Creed of faith, especially insofar as it relates either to Paulinus, the first person in Italy to add the word *Filioque* to the Constantinopolitan Creed, or to the Church of Aquileia, which formerly possessed a distinctive creed.

The sixth concerns the Council of Altinum. It explains the reason for convening the council, the year and season in which it was held, and finally by what right Paulinus convened it at Altinum.

## XXI

The testimonies drawn from published but rarer books or from unpublished documents, which are presented either in the observations and notes added to Paulinus’s works, or in his Life, or in the dissertations that follow, compelled us to prepare an Appendix that would not be useless and would not fail to please the reader.

For the spirit of the age in which we live is to examine manuscript chests, search the repositories of antiquity, and bring forth truth extracted from archival codices.

We divide the Appendix into two parts, assigning the first to published testimonies and reserving the second for unpublished ones.

In the first we present various matters relating to Paulinus from books already published in print. These include several letters of Alcuin and certain poems excerpted from the Alcuinian edition of André Duchesne; additional letters of the same Alcuin from Mabillon’s *Analecta*; and likewise letters of the same man that touch upon the Felician heresy.

Add to these the letter of Elipandus to Felix and Felix’s confession of faith. Matters that attack the heretic defeated by Paulinus were not to be omitted.

The letter of Charlemagne concerning the victory over the Avars, addressed to Queen Fastrada, also occupies its place among these materials. Through it, the affairs and deeds of Henry, Duke of Friuli, receive considerable illumination.

We add the Litanies of Charles the Bald, in which Paulinus is invoked, as we believe, as one of the heavenly saints. Both of these materials were supplied by Baluze in the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*.

Finally, from an old Missal of the Church of Aquileia, we present a Mass for a confessor and pontiff, adapted to Paulinus as a specimen of what they called the patriarchal rite, although it is not as ancient as we would have wished.

As you see, although these items have been published, they do not easily come into everyone’s hands. Since several matters that we assert on appropriate occasions are supported by their testimony, we display them here before your eyes so that you will not have to seek them elsewhere.

## XXII

With the exception of one or two diplomas that you will already find in the historians of our country, everything that follows in the second part of the Appendix has been taken from unpublished materials.

Even those items that had already seen the light of publication, however, we have been pleased to bring forth from archives. We have polished, removed blemishes from, and corrected from manuscripts certain items among them that required revision.

## XXIII

Those who lent their helping hands in composing this Appendix must not be passed over in thankless silence. They should rather be publicly named, both so that our feeling of gratitude may appear and so that anyone who has drawn something pleasing to himself from our nocturnal labors may know to whom he must confess himself indebted.

The more secret archives of the churches of Udine, Cividale, and Aquileia were opened to us either through the courtesy of their canons—as in the case of Cividale and Udine—or their hidden material was shown to us—as in the case of Aquileia.

We give them public thanks. Among the people of Aquileia, we especially thank Count Francesco Florio, whose hand transcribed several documents presented here. Among those of Udine, we thank our cousin Count Lorenzo Asquini, through whose assistance we were able to transcribe a Roman diploma and present a number of other documents, either drawn from the archive of his chapter or extracted from the chartulary of his ancient family.

Although we obtained no document from the archive of the church of Friuli, or Cividale, we nevertheless have reason to commend both the abundance of documents with which it is most richly furnished—though they do not bear on our subject—and the generosity of its distinguished canons.

Among them was Lorenzo della Torre, a worthy nephew of the most distinguished Philip della Torre, bishop of Adria, and now a most deserving dean of the distinguished collegiate church. He very courteously admitted us to examine the inner collections and allowed us to draw certain items from the old missal peculiar to that church and certain others from the books of distributions.

From the papers of his uncle, recently praised and always deserving praise, we obtained the hymn on Saint Mark the Evangelist, which is now published for the first time. He also supplied other transcribed materials from his private chartulary.

The gentlemen Nicolaus and Fabius, brothers of Maniago; Hector of Brazaco; and D. Agricola Agricola, who preserve in their possession a considerable number of manuscript codices, supplied several documents.

We are bound by an equal obligation of gratitude to Abbot Joseph Binius, who also contributed his material, and to Father Nicolaus Minuccius of our congregation at Rome, who sent from the Vatican Library the pledge of the suffragan bishops to the holy see of Aquileia.

To all these, and to any others who in any way, by work or advice, secretly or openly, have aided our labors, we repay such thanks as we can, through this public acknowledgment of the gratitude we owe.

Nor will you, Abbot Lucius Marenzi, depart unmentioned in our poems. When we were at times suffering from a scarcity of rare books, you were so kindly available to us through the help of our mutual friend Antonio Zanoni that we could scarcely have desired a greater favor or a more prompt assistance from any other of our necessary and dear friends.

## XXIV

These, kind reader, are the matters about which we wished to inform you before you began to turn over the works of Paulinus.

If anything should occur that pleases you less—which, would that it were little, though we fear it may be much—know that you are receiving a work from a man for whom error and stumbling are innate.

Nevertheless, we trust in the candor of your heart and the integrity of your mind, that you will not judge our labors too harshly, whatever they may be. Rather, by seeking your own advantage as well, may you judge them favorably, lest, while rising with excessive severity against efforts undertaken for your sake, and sometimes looking for a knot in a reed, you acquire for yourself the name of Zoilus and petty quibbler.

If anything worthy of approval should occur—which, however, we submit blindly in every respect to the judgment and will of our holy mother, the Roman Church—give the glory not to us, reader, not to us, but to the name of God, to whom be glory now, forever, and beyond.

[Column 0017]

# Life of our holy Father Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia

## Proem

[Column 0017A]

Describing the histories of illustrious men and committing their deeds to writing, so that posterity may benefit, can win the writer as much public gratitude as it compels him to undergo danger. The outcome is entirely uncertain and precarious, since readers’ minds, for the most part divided into factions, announce their judgments—or rather their prejudices—even before the reading itself; and these are all the more formidable because they are all the less deliberate. Indeed, very few seem to approach books without some prior mental preoccupation, or without allowing themselves to be carried by a certain inborn inclination toward whatever, through a hidden sympathy, even a conformity of temperaments, and sometimes an analogy with their own actions, appeals to them more strongly by a secret mystery of nature.

Hence it happens that, amid these disturbances of the affections, the truth sought scarcely emerges or raises its head [Col. 0017B]; or, if at last it shines forth somewhat more freely, it produces hatred that will fall upon the writer’s head. If, however, any historian might seem likely to be immune from this danger, he, in my judgment, ought to be one who presented matters belonging to a decayed antiquity and made its long age known to the wise. For things that touch us more closely move us more vividly and effectively; things beyond the range of a missile do not trouble us; and things that the longest succession of ages has placed above us are believed to have almost nothing to do with us.

Therefore, since we had resolved to describe the life of Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, so that the author of the works which we are striving to bring into common use for the benefit of all might become known to the world not only through his writings but also through his deeds and virtues, we thought we should congratulate ourselves [Col. 0017C] that we were undertaking to weave a history most remote from our own age, and thus one that would remain safe and secure from the prejudices of its readers. For ten centuries have now nearly elapsed since that excellent patriarch flourished, and only a few decades are lacking before the millennium will be complete—the thousand years that have flowed from his time down to ours.

Yet just as an age separated from ours by so many centuries protects the historian from the preconceived affections of his readers, so the scarcity of information and the almost barren memory of the past among writers makes the task difficult for him. Good heavens! Who will draw from the Lethean abyss events buried beneath the weight of a thousand years and entombed under the immense mass of the centuries, shake off the decay of oblivion, and set them in the full light of day as though they were rising again from ancient, ultimate ashes? [Col. 0017D] Who will place the truth amid the darkness of a rancid age—alas, too dense and almost palpable like that of Egypt—at such midday brightness that no room for doubt remains and no scruple disturbs the reader?

I am not that man [Col. 0018A]. Although I believe that I have moved every stone to the extent of my ability and exerted all the nerves and whatever powers my little intellect and strength possess in order to attain the end proposed, I would not therefore suppose that I had achieved it in such a way that no hiding place still remained to be searched out which might conceal the truth, or that I had presented the matter so probably, so clearly, so brilliantly—in a word, so well—that it could not have been presented better.

I earnestly ask you, kind reader, to receive our efforts with an even temper and to pursue them with your favor. It will be enough if, having recognized the difficulty of the undertaking and become well acquainted with the rough path upon which I am embarking, you do not accuse me of the presumption of daring; rather, commend the efforts undertaken out of love for the truth. If one is not always granted the choice of attaining it, at least the honor of seeking it is owed to it.

# CHAPTER ONE. On the Name of Paulinus

[Col. 0018B]

## I

When you hear that a discussion is to be undertaken concerning the name of Paulinus, do not suppose that this is the sort of question which in the schools would be dismissed as superfluous and insignificant—the question, namely, of a name. What is proposed here is not such chaff. For no one has ever doubted whether our Paulinus should be given another name.

A legitimate reason for doubt does arise, however, and it is appropriate to untangle it at the very outset: namely, whether Paulinus was the second holder of this name, or the first. For approximately two hundred years earlier another man had been appointed patriarch, and historians differ in pronouncing his name: some consistently write Paulus, others Paulinus.

## II

[Col. 0018C]

Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 10, calls him Paulus: “The blessed Paul the patriarch,” he says, “presided over the city of Aquileia and its peoples,” namely, when the Lombards had descended into Italy.

Nevertheless, I cannot help wondering at the mistake of Michael Bombardus, of the Society of Jesus, who in his *Topography of the Great Kingdom of Hungary*, published at Vienna, Austria, in 1718, confuses this Paulus with our Paulinus in an enormous anachronism. For he says on page 42:

> “Moreover, Paulinus—whom the Deacon, in book II, chapter 10, prefers to call Paulus after his own name—is believed to have been especially pleasing to Charles the Great and to his teacher Alcuin Flaccus because of the sanctity of his morals, and to have been appointed to preach the faith to the Huns and Avars, whom Charles had conquered by arms.”

Paul the Deacon does not mention our Saint Paulinus even in a dream, since he does not extend his history to the period of Saint Paulinus. The passage in book II, chapter 10, which Father Bombardus cites [Col. 0018D], concerns the earlier Paulus, who has nothing in common with Charles and Alcuin, with two complete centuries intervening between them [Col. 0019A].

To return to our subject, Dandulus likewise calls him Paulus, not Paulinus, in *Chronicle*, book V, chapter 11:

> “Paulus became bishop of Aquileia in the year of Our Lord 557.”

Moreover—and this is noteworthy—in the same chapter, section 1, when he reproduces a letter of Pope Pelagius who, as will be said below, calls him Paulinus, Dandulus reads Paulus in the letter, not Paulinus:

> “We request,” Pelagius wrote to Narses, according to Dandulus, “that you send Paulus, the pseudo-bishop of Aquileia, and Honoratus, bishop of Milan, to the most merciful prince under suitable custody.” [x]

Our Baronius too, who under the year 556, number 10, cites Pelagius’s letter calling him Paulinus, says under number 16 of the same year that Paulus is explicitly named:

> “This bishop of Aquileia,” he says, “of whom we are speaking, was named Paulus; he succeeded Macedonius and occupied the see for twenty-two years.”

Blondus, and Aeneas Sylvius in his *Epitome*, drawn from Blondus’s book VIII:

> “Paulus, patriarch of Aquileia, took refuge at Grado with the sacred objects.”

Sabellicus, *On the Antiquity of Aquileia*, book IV:

> “They write that Paulus crossed over from Aquileia to Grado with the church treasury.”

In the *Lives of the Patriarchs of Aquileia*, which the distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori publishes from a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library at the end of volume IV of the *Anecdota Latina*, Paulus is named twice; and nearly all the manuscript chronicles display Paulus, not Paulinus.

As a result, when Dionysius Delfinus, patriarch in earlier years, was renewing the patriarchal palace at Udine after renovating the other buildings of his residence [Col. 0019C—and after renewing by his excellent morals the clergy, the people, and the entire diocese—the portrait of this prelate, which had previously been inscribed with the name Paulinus and was painted on the walls of the hall together with those of the other patriarchs, was replaced with the following inscription under the name Paulus:

> **PAULUS, UNDER PELAGIUS I, APPOINTED TO DEFEND THE COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON, STANDING WITH POPE VIGILIUS AND THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE, DID NOT AGREE TO THE CONDEMNATION OF THE THREE CHAPTERS; AFTER ALBOIN LATER INVADED ITALY, HE MIGRATED TO GRADO.**

[Col. 0019D]

## III

On the other hand, many ancient and modern writers pronounce him Paulinus, not Paulus.

Pelagius I, letter V to Narses:

> “This is what we ask of you, and now ask again, that you send Paulinus, the pseudo-bishop of Aquileia, and that bishop of Milan to the most merciful prince under suitable custody.”

Sigonius, book I, *On the Kingdom of Italy*:

> “Paulinus, struck senseless by fear … left Aquileia and withdrew … to the island … of Grado.”

Candidus, *Commentary on Aquileia*, book III:

> “Meanwhile Paulinus, the twenty-fourth bishop, succeeded Macedonius after his death.”

The younger Palladius, part I, book I, calls him Paulinus, not Paulus, as do Father Christian Lupus, *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter 6, question 5; Cardinal Norisius, *On the Same Fifth Synod*, chapter 9, section 1; [Col. 0020A] Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History of the Sixth Century*, chapter 3, article 1, section 3; Pagius under the year 558, number 9; and Schönleben, *Carniolan Annals*, under the year 554.

Adrian Baillet also supports this view. In his *Lives of the Saints* under 11 January, when he presents the Life of our Saint Paulinus, he calls him the second Paulinus, with no other prelate of this name preceding the one under discussion.

An ancient inscription likewise supports it. Before the restoration of the patriarchal hall at Udine, it read beneath his portrait as follows:

> **BY HIS PIOUS ADMONITIONS, BLESSED PAULINUS INDUCED NARSES, COMMANDER OF THE ROMAN ARMY, TO BEGIN RESTORING AQUILEIA AFTER THE GOTHS HAD BEEN DRIVEN FROM ITALY; KING ALBOIN, OVERCOME BY HIS PRAYERS, PREVENTED THE WHOLE PROVINCE OF AQUILEIA AND ITALY TOGETHER FROM BEING OVERTHROWN.**

[Col. 0020B]

## IV

Thus walls too are not always consistent with themselves and are sometimes forced into contradiction. The author of the chronicle reported by Muratori in the *Anecdota* cited above contradicts himself when, in the case of Poppo, he has Paulinus rather than Paulus, although earlier he had used Paulus:

> “The treasures,” he says, “which had been carried to the island of Grado by the lord Paulinus, formerly patriarch, were brought back by the said lord Poppo.”

These authorities seem preferable to the earlier ones, not only because they are more numerous but especially because they include men of the first rank; and, most importantly, because Lupus, Norisius, Pagius, and Alexander were universally regarded as more skilled in criticism. There can be no doubt that they had examined the passages of the Deacon, Dandulus, and Blondus and weighed them carefully [Col. 0020C]; yet they still called him not Paulus but Paulinus.

Indeed, the authority of the Deacon and the others will appear feeble if one keeps in view that they themselves had elsewhere fallen into error—and in this matter as well. What credence should be given to Paulus, who calls this man blessed, although he was the chief of the schismatics and obstinate in the face of repeated admonitions from the Roman pontiffs? What credence should be given to Dandulus, who fell into another error when he says that he was consecrated by Honoratus, bishop of Milan?

[Col. 0020D]

Listen to what the distinguished Horatius Blancus observes in his notes to the cited passage of Paul, number 77, especially concerning the title “blessed,” in which Paulus errs, and the consecration by Honoratus, in which Dandulus errs:

> “The title ‘blessed’ is not appropriate to Paulinus, the leader of the schismatics. They falsely report that he was consecrated by Saint Honoratus, bishop of Milan. A most careful dissertation on this matter exists among the manuscripts of the Ambrosian Library, with the result that this error, which had long prevailed, was removed from the ancient Ambrosian Breviary.”

And rightly so. For Honoratus, who held the episcopate for two years, as may be seen in the *Ancient Chronicle of the Bishops of Milan* in *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, volume I, part II, page 228, and volume IV, page 141, saw the Lombards invade Insubria and Milan during his administration. Paul the Deacon himself testifies to this in book II, chapter 24, saying that it occurred in the indiction entering its third year, corresponding to the years 569 and 570.

At the same time Paulinus died, having been appointed in the year 557, according to Dandulus himself, and having completed twelve years in the priesthood, as the same Deacon states in the same place [Col. 0021A]. How, then, could Paulus—or Paulinus—have been consecrated by Honoratus if, in the first or second year of Honoratus’s episcopate, he had already completed the twelfth year of his priesthood?

Since it is therefore evident that Paulinus was not consecrated by Honoratus, it is equally clear that Dandulus was mistaken, drawing Honoratus from his own resources and inserting him into Pelagius’s letter, which commonly reads only “that bishop of Milan.” Since the authority of the ancient writers is wavering, the credibility of the others who follow them must necessarily waver as well.

[Col. 0021B]

The annotator of Paul the Deacon in *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, at the cited passage, number 79, therefore rightly asserts that one should say Paulinus, archbishop of Aquileia, not Paulus.

## V

Yet the authority of the writers cited seems not merely to waver but entirely to collapse when one considers the letter of Pope Pelagius I. He wrote to Narses while the patriarch himself was still alive; consequently, he attained the patriarch’s true name more accurately than Paul the Deacon, who lived in a different age and was separated from the patriarch’s time by many years.

In letter 5 he calls him not Paulus but Paulinus, as may also be seen in the fragments published by Holstenius. Indeed, a considerable suspicion arises that the Deacon originally wrote Paulinus, but that copyists, through haste in writing or for the sake of abbreviation, contracted it into Paulus by using a shortened character.

For in Baronius, who elsewhere calls him Paulus, in the Cologne edition of 1624, under the year 570, number 9, I find a passage of the Deacon, book III, chapter 12—or, more accurately, chapter 25 [Col. 0021C], which reads as follows:

> “Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, after serving eleven years in the priesthood, was taken from this life and left the governance of the Church to Probino.”

It is credible that the eminent father of the *Annals of the Church* obtained a copy of Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards* that differed from the more common copies. For in this one passage it differs from the others in two respects: it calls him Paulinus and assigns eleven years to his priesthood, whereas the others give Paulus and establish twelve years for his tenure.

This conjecture receives additional confirmation from Thomasinus, *On the Discipline of the Ancient and Modern Church*, volume I, part I, book I, chapter 21. When he quotes the words of book II, chapter 8—or, for us, chapter 10 above—he reads Paulinus, omitting the title “blessed,” as follows:

> “Paulinus, patriarch, presided over the city of Aquileia and its peoples.”

Therefore, the name Paulus is not consistent in all editions of the Deacon. Let it consequently be established that this man should be called Paulinus, not Paulus.

[Col. 0021D]

[xi]

## VI

But another difficulty remains: whether our Saint Paulinus should truly be called the second of that name.

The doubt arises from the letter of Pelagius cited above. For he does not obscurely declare the ordination of the earlier Paulinus invalid and void. Thus he says:

> “We request that you send Paulinus, the pseudo-bishop of Aquileia, and that bishop of Milan to the most merciful prince under suitable custody, so that the former, who in no way can be a bishop because he was made one contrary to every canonical custom, may not ruin others as well; and so that the latter, who presumed to ordain him contrary to ancient custom, may be subjected to the punishment of the canons.”

[Col. 0022A]

Do you hear that Paulinus is called a pseudo-bishop, that is, a false bishop, and that a reason is added why he cannot be a bishop—namely, because he was made one contrary to every canonical custom? If he is not a bishop, then he should not be counted as the first of this name among the patriarchs.

The same pontiff proceeds still more forcefully in his letter to John the patrician, which is the first among Holstenius’s letters. His words are:

> “Separated from the innermost parts of the Church and cut off from the apostolic sees, he himself rather curses and does not consecrate. Therefore, he may rightly be called accursed only, not consecrated, whom the Church, recognizing him as not united with its members in unity, does not acknowledge as having been consecrated. Let us nevertheless see whether, in his ordination, they observed even the custom [Col. 0022B] of those very regions. The ancient practice was, in fact, that since, because of the distance or difficulty of the journey, it had been burdensome for them to be ordained by the apostolic see, the bishops of Milan and Aquileia should ordain one another. This was done, however, in such a way that, in the city where the bishop was to be ordained, the pontiff of the other city had to be present, so that the choice of the ordainer, and the consent of the universal Church over which he was to preside, might more easily and properly be recognized by the ordainer who was present; and he was to be ordained in his own Church, the one being advanced to the episcopate but not thereby made subject to his ordainer.”

Pelagius does not state whether these practices were actually observed. It appears that they were not observed, since he objects to them. For the pontiff would labor in vain to examine Paulinus’s ordination if it had conformed to the lawful customs of earlier times [Col. 0022C].

Thus Paulinus also seems to have sinned in this respect: the Milanese ordainer did not come to Aquileia to perform the ordination; rather, the Aquileian who was to be ordained went to the Milanese ordainer.

P. de Rubeis, *On the Aquileian Schism*, chapter 4, says that the defect in Paulinus’s ordination consisted in the absence of the assent of the Roman pontiff, and he wishes this to be the canonical custom which the mutilated and incomplete letter does not state but merely indicates.

The pontiff therefore intimates that the consecration was defective when he says below:

> “Do not assent to their ‘consecrations,’ but rather to their execrations. Nor should you think that they are, or can be called, the Church.”

[Col. 0022D]

And in the following letter to Viator and Pancratius he rejects not only their episcopate but also their priesthood:

> “You ought to abstain from the sacrifices—or rather, the sacrileges—of schismatics.”

And near the end:

> “Do not therefore, as though there were no difference between schismatics and the Church, wish indiscriminately to associate yourself with the sacrifices of both. If we are guided by the truth, what a schismatic confects is not the body of Christ.”

What Pelagius’s intention was in these sufficiently severe words—whether he truly asserted that schismatic priests do not confect the body of Christ in the Eucharist, or whether he meant that schismatics do not confect Christ’s mystical body, which is one, namely the Church, because they are not members joined in the unity of charity and obedience to the supreme head, as the context seems more probably to indicate—whether, moreover [Col. 0023A], he truly believed that Paulinus’s ordination by the bishop of Milan was invalid and void: this is a matter requiring more investigation and leisure than is available to us.

On these matters, above all, see Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae*, part III, question 64, article 9, reply to objection 2, and question 82, article 7 and following; also *Supplement*, question 38, article 2; Lessius on part III, question 64, article 9; and the other scholastic theologians.

## VII

Nevertheless, since earlier centuries recognized this Paulinus in the catalog of the bishops of Aquileia, he should not be removed from their list. Pelagius must be understood to have spoken in this exaggerated manner and, at most, to have denied the licitness of the acts, not their validity.

For, leaving aside the other matters that would have to be considered, the failure to observe the custom of earlier times in performing the consecration cannot be the reason why the episcopal consecration was invalid. What, after all, would have contributed to the validity of the consecration [Col. 0023B]: whether the person to be ordained came from Aquileia to Milan to meet the ordainer, or whether the one who was to ordain came from Milan to Aquileia to meet the person being ordained?

Pelagius himself, in the letter addressed from Holstenius’s edition to the patrician Valerian, intimates at the end that this arrangement was not always observed, since the intermediate place, namely Ravenna, had been chosen for the consecration of the bishop of Milan:

> “Your Excellency ought to recall what God accomplished through you at the time when Totila possessed Istria and Venetia as tyrant, while the Franks were also devastating everything. You did not permit a bishop of Milan to be made until you had referred the matter from there to the most merciful prince and had again learned from his letters what ought to be done; and, amid enemies raging everywhere [Col. 0023C], both the man who was to be ordained and the man who was to ordain him were brought to Ravenna by the providence of your high office.”

Therefore Paulinus, although a schismatic, should not be erased from the register of the patriarchs of Aquileia. Otherwise, since the schism continued until Pope Sergius—as Pagius proves from Bede, *Book on the Six Ages of the World*, and Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 14, and as P. de Rubeis proves after him in *Dissertation on the Aquileian Schism*, chapter 19—at least seven or eight bishops would have to be removed from the patriarchal register: Paulinus himself, Probino, Elias, Severus, John, Martianus, perhaps Fortunatus as well, and another John.

The schism seems to have ended under Peter, who preceded Serenus, to whom the pallium was given by Gregory II—a sign that Aquileia had returned to communion with the Roman Church [Col. 0023D].

But when the eminent Norisius says in *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 9, section 6:

> “All place the end of this Aquileian schism under Pope Sergius, who sat at Rome in the year 678,”

there is a typographical error caused by the transposition of the numeral: 687 should have been written. For that was the first year of Pope Sergius.

Nor does he rightly correct the others when he adds that, before Sergius, the bishops communicated under Agatho, because Agatho began his pontificate in the year 678 and, after abandoning the schism, received the bishops of Venetia and Istria into communion with the Roman Church. They attended and subscribed the Roman council of that pontiff in the year 680: Agatho, patriarch of Aquileia, and the other suffragans.

The same appears to have occurred under Martin I at the Lateran Council in 649, where Maximus of Aquileia subscribed immediately after him [Col. 0024A]. This proves that the schismatics had been joined to the unity of the Church by that time. For neither Agatho nor Maximus was an Aquileian, but rather a Gradensian patriarch, although they were called Aquileians. See de Rubeis at the cited passage.

## VIII

Since it has therefore been demonstrated that he must be called Paulinus, not Paulus, and that this man, although a schismatic, must be placed in the register of the patriarchs of Aquileia, it remains for us to say that our Saint Paulinus was the second patriarch of this name.

A patriarch, indeed: for while the first Paulinus held the see, Baronius, under the year 570, number 10; Norisius, *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 10; Sirmondus, in his *Propempticon*, cited by Norisius; Bollandus, under 8 February, in his notes to the Life of Saint Honoratus; and Christian Lupus, in his *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter 6, [Col. 0024B] say that the name arose and was first heard of in reference to the bishop of Aquileia.

Indeed, they trace its origin to the schism, as though the nobler pearl of the Aquileian tiara had been extracted from mud and filth, and the prerogative of that most illustrious title had been bestowed as the reward of iniquity.

This appeared so far removed from the truth to Philip de Turre, bishop of Adria, that he composed a dissertation furnished with very strong arguments to refute this opinion. I found it among the papers of my uncle Nicolaus Madrisius, once bound to that same bishop by a close and sacred bond of friendship. I preserve it religiously in manuscript, worth more than gold, as a noble pledge and memorial of both men [xii], although I do not deny that copies have also reached the hands of others [Col. 0024C].

For the rest, I believe that Cointius, under the year 774, number 96, expressed in a few words the more truthful origin of the patriarchal title—namely, imitation of the Greeks and Eastern peoples. He says:

> “Shortly before the arrival of the Lombards in Italy, they claimed for themselves the patriarchal name according to the custom of the Greeks and Eastern peoples.”

How firmly our men of Udine defended the honor of this dignity and title at a later time can be seen from the constancy with which they resisted the placing of the patriarchate in commendam, which they regarded as disgraceful.

For when Urban VI had granted the patriarchate in commendam to Philip of Alençon, and the chapter of Aquileia seemed willing to tolerate this, as appears from the charter in Appendix 2, number 32; and when the people of Cividale had likewise accepted the commendatory holder, as appears in the charter in the same place, number 34 [Col. 0024D], the people of Udine resisted by force of arms. On this matter, see also the charters in the same place, numbers 33, 35, and 37.

## IX

Since these matters relating to history have been introduced in connection with the name, before withdrawing from the subject at hand it will not be inappropriate to raise and settle briefly another little question of orthography: namely, whether Paulinus should be written with one *l* or Paullinus with two; and likewise whether the derivative should be Paulus or Paullus.

Christophorus Cellarius, *Latin Orthography*, latter part, under the word *Paullum*, produces several examples from inscriptions containing the doubled *l*, and adds the authorities of writers who follow the lapidary spelling [Col. 0025A]. Among them is Vossius in his *Etymologies*, who does not even treat the matter as a question. He adds that some have thought the origin should be sought in the Greek word φαῦλος (*phaulos*), meaning “base” or “worthless,” or in παῦρος (*pauros*), meaning “few” or “small.” He adduces Augustine’s testimony that the apostle of the Gentiles, when he was called Paulus, assumed a name signifying baseness and smallness.

But if you attend to the Greek root, neither φαῦλος (*phaulos*) nor παῦρος (*pauros*) doubles its medial consonant; therefore one should write Paulus, not Paullus.

The authority of the grammarian Priscian also supports this. Concerning derivative words that double *ll*, he writes:

> “One exception is Paulus, ending in *-lus*, which does not double the *l* in the diminutive. Nor is this surprising, since the diphthong *au* prevents a consonant following it from being doubled.”

Listen on this subject to Adrianus’s entirely justified complaint, and to the skill with which he rejects and crushes the authority of the stonecutters. He says in *Adversaria*, book XXX, chapter 25 [Col. 0025B]:

> “A certain orthography differing from customary usage has recently been introduced by the most learned men into all books containing names. They write Quinctus and Paullus. But although we common people are exceedingly tenacious of custom, we can scarcely approve this novelty, and we would gladly announce the birth of a new work. Yet they rely on the authority of the Capitoline inscriptions, which, I do not think, ought to carry so much weight that it should be heeded against the schools and precepts of the grammarians. For I would not believe that those stonecutters and stone engravers were good grammarians, but rather workmen more learned in their hands than in their minds … I suspect, however, that the stonecutters … entrusted the defect of their own pronunciation to the Capitoline records; for, as the ancient grammarians observe, the common people suffered [Col. 0025C] from countless forms of faulty speech. But workmen belong among the common people, not among the learned, and in their ancient inscriptions we recognize such things every day. Paulus, however, not Paullus, according to Priscian, who is a more authoritative witness in grammatical matters than any engraver.”

Therefore, lest we seem to make the stones speak, or ourselves look like stones, but instead be supported by the common judgment of learned men and adhere to reason, we shall call this holy man Paulinus, not Paullinus, the second patriarch of that name.

# CHAPTER II. Nation; Place and Time of Birth; Social Condition

## I

As for what people our Paulinus belonged to, so that the anxiety of inquiry may not trouble you excessively, I declare him Italian by nation and a native of the Forumjulian region [Col. 0025D]. There is no lack of foundations for this free assertion, so do not think it rashly made.

For Alcuin calls him Ausonian in poem 212:

> “O light of Ausonia, glory and illustrious author of your fatherland.”

Moreover, the ecclesiastical canons, which had not lost their force in Paulinus’s time, ordained that the pontiff should be chosen from the bosom of his own diocese or Church—one who, by the votes of clergy and people, was judged worthy of the honor and equal to the burden.

Leo the Great, letter 84, chapter 6, wrote to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica:

> “After the will of all the clergy and all the citizens has been examined, the best man should be chosen from among the presbyters or deacons of that same church.”

Indeed, when the other qualifications were present, regard was had for seniority in presbyteral rank, and the episcopal chair was usually granted to the man who, by seniority of priestly ordination, presided over the others among the clergy.

[Col. 0026A]

An example of this is found in Saint Felix of Nola, who refused the episcopate and yielded his place to the priest Quintus, who had preceded him in ordination by only seven days, although Felix knew that the people had called and requested him to govern.

The other Saint Paulinus, namely Paulinus of Nola, sang of this in *Natale* V:

> “He dares not grow in honor,  
> and testifies that the honor due to the elder Quintus  
> was greater, since that earlier presbyter  
> had earned the rank of his companion in honor:  
> the whole interval was seven days.”

[Col. 0026B]

In the capitulary enacted at Aachen, at the synod over which our Paulinus presided as legate of the Apostolic See—as will be said in its proper place from Baluzius, under the year 803, chapter 2—the Fathers, who professed that they were not ignorant of the sacred canons, decreed:

> “That bishops should be chosen by the election of the clergy and people, according to the statutes of the canons, from their own diocese …”

It could happen, however, that no one suitable for the dignity in question would sometimes be found in one’s own Church. In that case the canons did not forbid taking a bishop from another Church. But how rarely this was thought likely to occur may be inferred from the words of the letter of Hincmar of Reims, placed by Baluzius in the fourth order among the *Forms of Episcopal Promotions*, volume II of the *Capitularies*, page 596:

> “If, which God forbid, no cleric of your city and parish who is worthy or suitable for the highest priesthood can be found—something which we do not believe could happen—then take care to choose another from another church of our diocese, since, according to the African Council [Col. 0026C] (canon 22), permission has been granted to ordain canonically anyone who has been elected and requested without any condition.”

Since matters then stood in this way, who could persuade himself that Paulinus’s election was conducted differently from the practice followed by everyone, or that the Church of Aquileia at that time observed a different order from the other Churches?

There was no need to seek from elsewhere a bishop to be placed over a Church that at that time felt itself so abundantly supplied with clergy that, in the prologue of the Council of Forumjulium, its clergy were called “no small throng of brothers” and “a venerable assembly of priests,” with the archdeacon himself presiding.

It is therefore permissible to say that he was elected from the bosom of his own Church and was by origin and ecclesiastical order a man of that territory.

[Col. 0026D]

## II

I am not unaware that some writers, among them Ughellus, have asserted that Paulinus was Austrian by nation. Philip Labbe, of the Society of Jesus, mentions them in his *Additions to Bellarmine*, volume II, and says that, however they came by it, they have that opinion.

But if they intend the province of Germany that we now call Austria, they are entirely mistaken, since in Paulinus’s time that region, which was at least partly a portion of Upper Pannonia, had not yet acquired this name [xiii]. And although the extent of the diocese of Aquileia may perhaps have included some part of that region [Col. 0027A], neither was that region then in such an ecclesiastical condition that it could supply a bishop, nor was Aquileia so reduced that it would have had to summon a bishop from there.

The claim becomes still less credible if they mean that part of France facing the east, called Austria or Austrasia, just as the part facing the west was called Neustria; for this region lies farther from our territories than modern Austria in Germany.

To uncover the origin of this delusion is not to reveal the sources of the Nile; the cause is obvious. These writers had at some point heard Forumjulium called Austria. Hence they immediately declared Paulinus, bishop of Forumjulium, Austrian by nation.

But to call Paulinus “Austrian” in this sense is exactly the same as calling him Forumjulian, and thus to affirm and assert what they seem to deny.

Forumjulium was called Austria because, as we say in our *Dissertation on the Council of Forumjulium*, number 13, since this region lay to the east with respect to the Lombard kingdom [Col. 0027B], whose seat was at Pavia, and since the eastern quarter was called Austria, it was designated by the appellative—or, as they say, adjectival—not substantive name Austria, as though one were saying “the eastern region.”

See the *Dissertation on the Chorographic Map of Medieval Italy*, sections 8 and 9, volume X of *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, where these matters are explained more fully.

### III

There is also another consideration, though not the most decisive, by which it may be recognized that Paulinus was not an outsider but a native of the province of Forumjulium. For the speech of Forumjulium is such that, although it shares something with several languages, it differs from all of them as a whole, and thus becomes distinctive; and whoever must speak it fluently—as a bishop, the dispenser of God’s word, must—would know it especially well.

Hear Candidus, in *Commentary on Aquileia*, book III, discussing our language and his own on the occasion of the Lombards’ arrival in Italy, which occurred in the year 568:

> “He [Alboin] selected an army of diverse peoples to inhabit Forumjulium. Hence it is not surprising if the people of Forumjulium, enlarged by so many kinds of men, possess a varied and manifold language, serving Latin, French, Spanish, Illyrian, and German. Their speech is indeed weighty, and because of its peculiar accents highly suited to acquiring and pronouncing other languages. You see that the Roman language of Forumjulium has been somewhat altered by the admixture of so many barbarians; yet do not think that their customs have been so completely overturned, or that that Italian discipline has been altered.”

Ecclesiastical discipline, moreover, requires that a pastor be placed over a flock who, preaching in the common and native language, can be heard and understood not only by the learned but also by the unlearned—for he is debtor both to the wise and to the foolish. For this reason Saint Augustine, when a bishop had to be given to the people of Fussala, proposed choosing one who knew the natural and popular language of the place. Thus he says in letter 109 of the latest edition, no. 3:

> “I was seeking someone suitable and appropriate for that place—Fussala—who would be trained in the Punic language; and I had someone in mind, a priest who was ready. On his account I wrote to the holy old man who then held the primacy of Numidia, asking him to come from far away for the man’s ordination, and I obtained my request.”

In the *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 185, it is decreed:

> “No priest shall be one who does not publicly teach in the church in a language which his hearers understand.”

From all this, therefore, one may conclude the following: if, in accordance with the provisions of the canons, a bishop ought to be chosen from the bosom of the diocese and church over which a pastor is to be placed, and if Aquileia abounded in clergy, so that it had no need to seek one elsewhere; if it has been shown by those who call Paulinus “Austrian” that Austria was then the name of the province of Forumjulium; if a bishop was to be promoted who knew the language of the people, and if the speech of Forumjulium is and was such that any non-native of Forumjulium would acquire it only with difficulty and through hard labor—then it remains to be said that Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, was by nationality an Italian, and indeed a native of Forumjulium.

### IV

Among our people the matter is so firmly established that it is not even considered controversial. If any difficulty has arisen, it concerns the place of his origin and birth. For some assert that he was born at Praemariacum, others at Gajanum, and others in a village somewhere near the city of Austria.

Antonius Bellonus, in his manuscript *On the Lives of the Patriarchs of Aquileia*, supports the first view; Franciscus Palladius the second; and Joannes Candidus defends the third, saying in his *Commentary on Aquileia*, book IV:

> “Paulinus was born in a village near the city of Austria, etc.”

Indeed, neither of the two places mentioned is very far from the city. Bellonus says of the first:

> “It is established that he was born at Praemariacum, a village near the city of Austria.”

It is at most three miles distant; the other is separated by an even shorter interval.

Praemariacum is also distinguished as the birthplace of another patriarch, namely Gerardus, as Candidus has it in book V and Palladius in part I, book IV, together with an ancient inscription placed beside his image in the patriarchal palace at Udine. Besides the church of Saint Sylvester, which is the mother and head of the others, there is another church in the upper part of the village, dedicated to Saint Maurus the abbot and Saint Paulinus the patriarch. The families of the Saccavini live there, and among the natives there is a tradition that Saint Paulinus arose from one of them.

Some attribute Saint Paulinus not to the Saccavini but to the family of the Zorzenons. Yet, apart from the fact that this tradition is weaker, as I have carefully considered the matter at hand, the Saccavini especially keep a solemn memory of him every year on 11 January. Priests from the neighboring villages are invited to offer the sacrifice to God in honor of Saint Paulinus.

There still survives among the inhabitants, handed down from grandparents and great-grandparents to their children and grandchildren, the memory of a certain event said to testify to Paulinus’s holiness while he was still young. You should not take me as a guarantor or author of it, but only as a reporter of what is commonly related. I willingly offer it, so that, when clearer and more decisive evidence is lacking, you may at least recognize what is popularly alleged.

They say, then, that while he was still a young man cultivating a field, two neighboring farmers were commending Paulinus’s holiness to one another—whether sincerely or ironically, I do not know. One of them replied that he would suspect and believe in his holiness if he saw it attested by a miracle.

And behold: the young saint’s hoe, with which he was hoeing the crops, suddenly took root in the earth, grew green, swelled into buds, and sent forth flowers. When they saw this, they marked the place where the marvel had occurred by piling up two mounds of earth, which are visible even today, as a sign of the event. They still distinguish the northern part of the village from the southern: the former, because the patriarch thereafter came from it, was freed from the burden of tithes, while the latter remained subject to them.

This is still observed today: the area in which Paulinus’s descendants are found is exempt from the payment of tithes, while the other area pays them along with the rest. I offer no opinion as to whether these arrangements, which originated in that event, are now legally valid. Let others judge.

The inhabitants still point out the site of his dwelling; and the land which, as they say, he ennobled by the flowering hoe is still called the field of Saint Paulinus in the documents of notaries and surveyors. I saw a document issued at Rubignac through the hands of Joseph Noaxius, notary of Cividale, in the year 1625. It shows that from the year 1571 Commendator Julius Antonius and the Manini brothers had been proprietors of the land called Saint Paulinus, comprising approximately two fields.

### V

But if, as you see, what is said about the place of Paulinus’s birth is obscure and entirely uncertain, what concerns the time of his birth is still more obscure and hidden. If one may make a conjecture from his ordination, his birth seems to have to be placed no later than the year 747.

For the canons generally require at least thirty years of age for one to be ordained bishop, corresponding to the age of the Savior when, after receiving baptism, he manifested himself through preaching—the principal duty of bishops. This discipline was in force in Paulinus’s time. In the capitulary of the year 789, in whose composition Paulinus himself took part, as will be said in its proper place, canon 11 of the Council of Neocaesarea is commended in chapter 49. It reads:

> “In the Council of Neocaesarea: under no circumstances is a presbyter—and even less a bishop—to be ordained before his thirtieth year, because our Lord Jesus Christ did not preach before his thirtieth year.”

The same was established, with Paulinus’s participation, by canon 47 of the Council of Frankfurt in the year 794:

> “Presbyters are not to be ordained before their thirtieth year of age.”

And the Third Council of Tours, in the year 813, decrees in canon 12:

> “A presbyter must not be ordained before the lawful time, that is, before his thirtieth year of age.”

Do you see that in Paulinus’s time no one was admitted to the honor of the presbyterate before three decades of life, and with still greater justification to the episcopate? From this, therefore, it follows that, since Paulinus did not enter the episcopate before the year 776, he must at least have begun to live by the year 747, if we adhere to the stricter calculation of the canons.

If you also consider that he had already acquired a celebrated reputation and name in the art of grammar, so that he was well known at the court of King Charles, by whom he may even have been granted, in that same year 776, a privilege and a donation of property situated in the estate of Laberiana, you will not easily believe that he was only thirty years old when he was called bishop.

Add that the privilege describes him as:

> “The highly venerable man Paulinus, master of the art of grammar.”

These words not only indicate a man of advanced age but, moreover, one approaching old age—say, at least around his fiftieth year.

On these premises, one may frame the conjecture as follows: at approximately fifty years of age, Paulinus, master of the art of grammar and a highly venerable man, had not yet been appointed bishop of Aquileia. He was appointed in the year 776; therefore he was born around the year 726.

### VI

From what was said in section 4, you can easily ascertain Paulinus’s condition and status. He was born in the countryside, to rural parents, and at some time cultivated the land himself.

Palladius the Younger, book II, part 1, and Bellonus in his manuscript *Life of the Patriarchs of Aquileia* suggest this common tradition when they say that, in his election, no account was taken of nobility or blood, but only of merit. Bellonus writes of him:
