> “Paulinus was endowed with such rare piety and holiness of life that you will find very few prelates equal to him. For in choosing patriarchs, account was not always taken of lineage so much as of integrity. It is established that he was born at Praemariacum, a village near the city of Austria, and that from childhood he was there imbued with the religion befitting a Christian man; and he showed himself to all to be the kind of pastor the people of Aquileia were seeking.”

Yet he was sufficiently adorned with the distinction of nobility who excelled in virtues. For, apart from the fact that cultivating one’s own land in no way harms the dignity of one’s blood—just as it is not forbidden to clerics, as Tiraquellus teaches, *On Nobility*, chapter 32, nos. 2 and 3—and although it is true that, all other things being equal, regard should also be had to nobility in the election of a bishop, so that a nobleman may be preferred to an ignoble man, as the same Tiraquellus testifies in the same work, chapter 20, no. 17, nevertheless greater regard must be given to virtue than to blood. Petrus Ancharanus says as much in his *Consultation* 131, cited in the same place, no. 14.

Thus Paulinus deserved to be raised to the see of Aquileia not through the nobility of his blood, but rather through service to Christ and learning.

From this obscurity of origin and birth, although he had been raised to the summit of dignity and could have advanced his relatives to positions of honor—placing them by his authority over sacred offices, or by his influence with Charles, who was extremely devoted to him, over secular ones, thereby lawfully enlarging their scant possessions—he preferred to keep them hidden through love of humility. Thus even today the family of his descendants is distinguished or elevated in no way from the other native inhabitants who cultivate the countryside, and has almost entirely forgotten that it was once adorned with patriarchal insignia—insignia which elsewhere are held in such high esteem.

## CHAPTER III

### The diploma granted by Charlemagne to Paulinus the grammarian is examined

### I

Although Paulinus had been born, as has been said, into such a humble condition of birth, he had nevertheless been endowed by the good and great God with an exceptionally keen intellect. He devoted himself to the humane disciplines and, setting aside the concerns of rural business, turned himself entirely to the cultivation of his mind.

Applying himself, therefore, to liberal studies, he advanced so far that within a short time he could teach others what he had learned. It is reasonable and entirely consistent with probability to believe that, through the merit of his learning and holiness, he made his way to sacred orders, ascending through the lesser and greater degrees and observing the intervals of time established by the canons, until he was adorned with the priesthood at the age of thirty.

Indeed, it is probable not only that he had already been initiated into the priesthood when he was raised to the patriarchal see, but also that he had previously been distinguished by this office and thereby gained easier access to the courts of princes.

As the fame of his holiness and learning spread, his name reached the ears of King Charles, a man born to cultivate every excellent pursuit, who deigned to enjoy Paulinus’s conversation and company. Thus he rewarded the recognized wisdom of the most holy priest with a distinguished privilege. We shall give the document in full in Appendix II, no. 2, from a manuscript; here we shall only weigh certain points worthy of consideration.

### II

At the beginning of the diploma appear these words:

> “Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.”

These words indicate that it was issued after the Lombards had been driven out of Italy and after Charles had obtained the Roman patriciate. Pagius, under the year 755, no. 3, and Cointius, under the year 754, no. 57, and under the year 796, no. 6, hold that this dignity was conferred according to the *Annals of Metz* under the year 754.

The annalist’s words under the year 754 are:

> “Pope Stephen, according to the custom of the ancestors, anointed with sacred unction Pippin, the most pious prince, as king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans; and he crowned his two sons, Charles and Carloman, with the same honor, in a fortunate succession.”

At the beginning of the letter which the same pontiff sent through Willharius, bishop of Nomentum, to those same men, seeking their aid against Aistulf, king of the Lombards, he likewise wrote:

> “To the most excellent sons, Pippin the king and our spiritual kinsman, and likewise to the kings Charles and Carloman, and to both patricians of the Romans, Pope Stephen.”

But the title “king of the Lombards” was not used of Charles, nor was he so called in diplomas, before the year 774, when he subdued and conquered that people. The privilege was therefore issued after that time. Before then, the use of the title would have appeared premature.

### III

The diploma continues:

> “Those who faithfully serve our service are rightly raised by us through gifts.”

From this you learn not only that Paulinus had already become known to Charles, but also that, so to speak, he had rendered him personal service. For why would the text begin in this way if the man to be rewarded had shown no service to the one who was to reward him?

Would I depart from reasonable conjecture if I said that perhaps Paulinus was one of those who served the king in the teaching of the liberal arts, acting as a teacher in one of the various schools which Charles had established?

How much effort Charles expended to restore learning is evident from the letter, or constitution, concerning the establishment of schools in every bishopric and monastery, which Baluzius publishes under the capitularies for the year 788, and from what Lupus writes in letter 1 to Einhard, reported by Pithoeus in the *Glossary to the Capitularies*, volume II, page 743:

> “For, in your memory, learning, through the most renowned emperor Charles, began to be recalled and raised its head somewhat.”

Just as Gaul received Alcuin as its teacher through Charles’s efforts, so perhaps Germany received Paulinus. Indeed, Jonas of Orléans says that studies flourished again through him especially in these regions, at the beginning of book I of *On the Cult of Images against Claudius, Bishop of Turin*:

> “Not only in Germany,” he says, “was the study of letters and the love of the holy Scriptures brought into activity, but also in that same Gaul, through the most diligent zeal and most ardent desire of that memorable man [Charles], it was accomplished—with the Lord’s help among the sons entrusted to his care—that they should excel both in the discipline of the liberal arts and in the perfect understanding of the divine Scriptures.”

This manner of expression deserves consideration. For when he says that the study of letters was introduced not only in Germany but also in Gaul, he seems to suggest some distinction between Germany and Gaul—perhaps one of time, in that Charles had done earlier for Germany what he later did in Gaul; or one of the introduction of teachers and masters, in that just as he had brought them into Germany, so he had brought suitable and capable men into Gaul.

This should be noted so that it may not seem implausible to believe that, as soon as Charles had been hailed king of the Lombards and the province of Forumjulium had come under his rule, he employed Paulinus’s services to restore the more refined disciplines in neighboring Germany, which were so dear to him—that is, from the year 774—just as in later years he employed Alcuin’s services to instruct his own Gaul.

Or, if you prefer to rely on another conjecture, it may reasonably and justifiably be believed that, once our province had been subdued and removed from Lombard rule, Charles took care that its youth should be cultivated and instructed in the humane disciplines. For this reason he appointed Paulinus to the teaching office and entrusted it to him; and, so that he might carry it out more eagerly, he honored him with a diploma of donation.

For it seems certain that Paulinus was bound to Charles’s service, whether at home or elsewhere. The words are sufficiently clear:

> “If we bring to fulfillment the petitions of those who have appealed to our ears, we exercise royal custom and stir their devotion to serve us.”

### IV

A little further on the diploma reads:

> “To the highly venerable man Paulinus, master of the art of grammar.”

Here he calls him a man, and a highly venerable one. These words appear to indicate both his age and his priestly ministry, as was said in the preceding chapter, section 5.

The word “grammarian,” however, does not precisely signify one who merely knows the art of reading and writing. Such a person should rather be called a *grammatista* than a grammarian. Suetonius, *On Illustrious Grammarians*, chapter 4, says that grammarians were “at first called learned men,” and adds:

> “Some distinguish the educated man from the elementary teacher, just as the Greeks distinguish the grammarian from the *grammatista*, considering the former learned without qualification and the latter moderately educated.”

Augustine calls such men *litteriones* in book I, chapter 24 and the final chapter of *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*:

> “They should be called *litteriones* rather than men of letters, for by reading learned works they have learned to understand nothing.”

But of true grammar he himself wrote in book II of *On Order*, chapter 12:

> “Because by its very name it loudly professes itself to be the study of letters, whatever worthy matter is committed to writing necessarily belongs to it.”

Cicero writes similarly in book I of *On the Orator*:

> “Who has devoted himself entirely to this study of letters, which those called grammarians profess, without comprehending through knowledge and understanding almost the infinite force and subject matter of all those arts?”

It is therefore in this sense of a wide-ranging learning that we must interpret the term by which Paulinus is distinguished in the diploma, when he is called “master of the art of grammar.”

In later centuries, and around Paulinus’s own time, the term was understood in this sense. Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, who flourished in the year 521, calls grammar the mother and nurse of the other arts in his *Didactic Exhortation*, or *Opusculum* 7.

Peter the Deacon, writing in the year 1137, speaking of himself in the preface to book IV of the *Cassinese Chronicle*, said:

> “For I, whom the knowledge of grammarians does not adorn, do not, etc.”

Cassiodorus, who wrote much about grammar as a grammarian, was also the author of the letter which, as secretary of the Gothic king, he issued in the name of Athalaric to the Roman senate—letter 21 of book IX of the *Variae*. In it he praises grammar in the highest terms, calling it:

> “The most beautiful foundation of letters, the glorious mother of eloquence, the teacher of words, the adornment of the human race, which through the exercise of the most beautiful reading is known to help us by the counsels of the ancients.”

He also recommends to the Conscript Fathers a professor of grammar, so that he may not receive a salary diminished from that of his predecessors:

> “For this reason, Conscript Fathers, with the divine favor we grant you this care and this authority: that the successor in the school of liberal letters, whether grammarian or rhetorician, may receive the emoluments of his predecessor from those concerned, without any diminution.”

Such were Athalaric’s provisions for grammarians. Even more commendable, however, was the generosity of Cunibert, king of the Lombards, who of his own accord honored a grammarian with dignity and gifts. Paul the Deacon writes in book VI, chapter 7 of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*:

> “At that time, Felix, the uncle of Flavian, my teacher, flourished in the art of grammar. The king loved him so greatly that, among the other gifts of his generosity, he presented him with a staff decorated with silver and gold.”

It will therefore not be surprising if Charlemagne, in this diploma and donation, rewarded Paulinus, the deserving grammarian—one who not only commended grammar in other ways but also cultivated it himself beyond what the condition of a king required, and who did not shrink from the name of grammarian.

C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXIX, chapter 11, writes:

> “The name was glorious even in the latest times, since it was adopted also by the emperor Charlemagne, who, when at leisure, did nothing else but correct books, as Theganus, the chorepiscopus, records.”

### V

The diploma continues:

> “The possessions which belonged to Waldandus, formerly the son of Mimo of Laberiana, which came to our palace because he was killed in the field by our faithful men together with Rotgandus, our enemy.”

Rotgandus’s name is expressed in various ways. Baronius has *Forticausus*. The *Chronicle of Cividale*, which will be cited below, has *Rodigausus*. He is commonly called Rotgandus, and we shall likewise use the common form.

From these few words it is clear that this Waldandus, son of Mimo, followed Rotgandus’s party and rebelled against Charles; that he was consequently killed in battle; and that the goods he possessed in the estate of Laberiana were adjudicated to the royal treasury.

Two others, the brothers Rotgandus and Felix, also appear to have followed the party of Duke Rotgandus and to have been punished for it, as is shown by the diploma to be added in Appendix II, no. 7.

Rotgandus’s revolt occurred almost immediately after Charles had returned from Italy to Francia, having defeated Desiderius and subjected the Lombard kingdom. Believing that he could bind the minds of the Lombard nobles more securely to himself through benefits, Charles did not remove them from the jurisdictions over which Desiderius had formerly placed them:

> “He left the duchy of Benevento to Aragisus, the son-in-law of King Desiderius; the duchy of Spoleto to Hildebrand; and that of Forumjulium to Rotgandus, preserving toward himself the ancient feudal obligation which they had formerly maintained toward the Lombard kings,”

as Sigonius says in book IV of *On the Kingdom of Italy*.

These men, however, were encouraged by Aragisus, the former king Desiderius’s son. After the victorious Charles had taken Verona, Aragisus withdrew to Constantinople to the Greek emperor and from there began plotting disturbances to the ruin of the Franks and the restoration of the Lombard name. They attempted to throw off the Frankish yoke.

Rotgandus, bolder than the others, was the first to raise his head. Having compelled his people of Forumjulium to revolt and called the neighboring provinces to his side by word and example, he tried to restore the Lombard cause, which was already considered lost, to its former glory.

Returning from his Saxon victory, Charles received news of the rebellion. Believing that the whole matter had to be prevented at its outset, he quickly applied a remedy. “Charles sent cavalry with light armor ahead, and they killed Rotgandus in battle, with the rest fleeing in greater numbers than those who were slain,” says Paulus Aemilius in book II.

The annalists of the Franks, however, unanimously acknowledge that the victory was won by Charles himself. At least Loiselianus should be heard, since his simplicity seems to keep him closer to the truth. Under the year 775, when Rotgandus defected from the Franks—this was the year after the Lombards had been defeated—he says:

> “Charles returned to Francia and heard that Rotgandus the Lombard had broken faith with him, breaking all his oaths and wishing to rebel in Italy. Then Lord King Charles traveled through those regions with some Franks and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in a villa called Scaldistat, and the number of the years changed to 776. Then Lord King Charles celebrated Easter at the city of Tarvisium and captured the cities of Forumjulium and Tarvisium, together with the other cities that had rebelled; and he distributed them all among the Franks, and then returned to Francia with prosperity and victory.”

The Bertinian annals and all the others have nearly the same account word for word, as does the poet Saxo. They place Rotgandus’s revolt in the year 775 and his defeat, death, and Charles’s victory in the year 776.

### VI

In these disturbances Waldandus followed Rotgandus’s standard and likewise followed him to his fate. The possessions of the man killed in battle, seized in the king’s name as belonging to a traitor, were given to Paulinus, master of the art of grammar, just as the possessions of Rotgandus and his brother Felix were eventually given to Patriarch Maxentius.

What my younger Palladius—my Palladius, I mean, who was the uterine brother of my mother’s parent—relates in book II about the single combat between Rotgandus and Roland, otherwise commonly called Orlando, a close companion of Charlemagne, may seem to belong to those tales with which the life of this hero has been stuffed, supplying poets and other men of heated imagination with abundant material for invention. Nevertheless, it is not entirely without foundation.

For in a certain ancient *Chronicle of Cividale*—a fragment preserved in a manuscript book belonging to my cousins, the Counts of Asquini, which contains many ancient documents—we read:

> “Ruodgausus, the fourteenth duke of Forumjulium, forced into the duchy by King Desiderius through the cession of Rosimund, remained at Osoppo. After the Lombard kingdom had been destroyed and Desiderius with his sons had been captured by Charlemagne, king of the Franks and of Italy, and sent into Gaul, Ruodgausus, while plotting new disturbances against Charles, was driven from Osoppo by Roland, Charles’s most warlike nephew, and was stripped of the principate of all the region of Forumjulium. He was the last duke of the Lombards.”

Therefore, if Palladius has erred in this or elsewhere, he should not be followed; but wherever he has attained what is true and correct, he should be heard and followed.

Indeed, before Fontanini, in his booklet *On the Masnada*, page 41, Palladius correctly wrote *Rotgandus* where Baronius and Bollandus have *Forticausus*. Moreover, he gives the diploma in full, whereas Candidus quotes it in mutilated form, omitting these words, which contain the essence of the matter:

> “Mimo of Laberiana, whose possessions came to our palace because he was killed in the field together with Rotgandus, our enemy, by our faithful men: namely, the property at Laberiana, etc.”

Candidus carelessly passed from the first occurrence of *Labariano* to the second, thereby omitting the intervening words.

Add that he refuted another error of greater importance: Candidus had mistakenly substituted Paul the Deacon for our Saint Paulinus; and although Candidus gives the tenth year as the date of the diploma, he himself, together with the others, consistently and correctly gives the eighth. More on this below.

Do not overlook the fact that the words of the diploma prove that Rotgandus was not executed, as Palladius himself says in the same place, nor as Sigonius says in book IV of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, perhaps following Regino’s *Chronicle*, where in book II he says:

> “He ordered the captured rebel Rotgandus to be beheaded.”

The poet Saxo himself also seems to suggest this—unless one says that he is speaking poetically—when he says:

> “Hastening to Italy with them, and deservedly punishing the tyrant with death.”

But he fell in battle, as the annalists plainly indicate, and as the words of the diploma make sufficiently clear:

> “Because he was killed in the field together with Rotgandus, our enemy, by our faithful men.”

Thus Rotgandus did not pay the penalty by decapitation or by any other dishonorable form of death, but was killed in battle. Waldandus too was killed, and his confiscated goods were given to Paulinus.

### VII

One or two words in the diploma which follows deserve attention. In the inventory of Waldandus’s goods donated to Paulinus, it says:

> “The property at Laberiana.”

So the Bollandists read it, and correctly. For *causa* in the barbarous age means the same as *res*, “thing” or “property”; hence the Italian *cosa*. The Lombard Laws, book III, title IV, law 5, say:

> “Let them not presume to take away from any man his property or his labor.”

The *Capitulary on Estates*, chapter 3, says:

> “Nor shall they accept any gifts from them—not a horse, not an ox, not a cow, not a pig, not a ram, not a piglet, not a lamb, nor any other property.”

Thus *causa in Labariano* means “property at Laberiana.” Hence you see that Baronius was wrong to read *casa*, a word that means nothing in that place.

Perhaps Palladius did not understand this and substituted *villa*, “estate,” for *causa*, perhaps because he heard *casas* shortly afterward and suspected an unnecessary repetition.

He proceeds excellently from general to particular, adding:

> “With lands, houses, buildings, tenants, and slaves.”

I think it should be read *accolabus*, not *accolabiis*, as Candidus and Fontanini have it; not *accolabiis* for *et colabiis*, as Bollandus and Baronius read it; and even less as Palladius has it, *with pastures and municipal lands*.

The *Formula* 13 of book I of Marculfus sheds light on the matter. Among other things it reads:

> “We have granted lands, houses, buildings, tenants, and slaves,”

etc.

At this passage Hieronymus Bignonius, in his notes, understands the condition of slaves devoted to the cultivation of their masters’ fields. He says that examples of this occur everywhere:

> “This enumeration of goods, or rights, is inserted in all legal instruments, so that it would be futile to produce examples. The *accolae* named here are coloni, or registered tenants, who were sold together with the estates, just as examples of stewards and administrators are found in the jurists. In the Chartulary of Saint Martin: ‘With the men dwelling there, whom we have established to live according to the condition of tenant farmers.’”

Thus *accolabus* stands for *accolis*. This escaped Fontanini, who thinks that *accolabiis* refers to such slaves as though the form were *accolabius, accolabii*. In his booklet *On the Masnada*, page 41, he says:

> “The *Accoli*, or *Accolabii*, were tenants and cultivators of the land.”

At most the form is *accolavus*, plural *accolavi*. Spelmannus incorrectly forged *accolabium* to mean a rustic house inhabited by a tenant, as Du Cange says in his *Glossary*.

An *accola* is a newcomer who cultivates the land; an *incola* is one born there, according to the verse:

> “The newcomer cultivates land that is not his own; the native cultivates his own land.”

### VIII

As for what Fontanini adds there about the slaves—that they were captives taken in war, whom Waldandus, having followed Rotgandus’s standard, had captured in war and settled on his estates—the first point indeed rests on truth, for that is what the word *mancipium* signifies; and the second is certainly not contrary to truth.

But because formulas of this kind are customarily inserted in such privileges, formulas that convey a broader meaning and present a more extensive donation through inflated language, even though the person granting the privilege knew that they could never be verified in every respect and in every place—as the aforementioned Bignonius suggests in the words, “This enumeration is inserted in all legal instruments, so that it would be futile to produce examples”—it does not seem to have been inserted specifically for the goods of Waldandus donated to Paulinus, since in every legal instrument the inventory of the goods granted is described according to this formula.

### IX

The diploma continues:

> “With rural houses, farm equipment, slaves, and aldiones.”

Here I take the *casas* to be rural dwellings, since the text is speaking of country property; and I would regard *casas* as genuinely Latin, although the barbarous Latins also called the buildings of kings *casas*.

The Lombard Laws, book II, title 17, law 1, say:

> “If a gastald, or any royal administrator, after receiving and being entrusted with the royal estates or houses for administration,”

etc.

The Bavarian Law, title I, section 9, no. 5, has:

> “To stable at the lord’s houses.”

*Massaritia* means equipment, or even the estate itself furnished with equipment. It is a common word of well-known meaning among the Italians, says Du Cange.

Indeed, among our own people—among whom Lombard words perhaps became more deeply established than anywhere else—the names *masi*, *masnatae*, *massarii*, and *massariae* are still on everyone’s lips.

Since the diploma adds “slaves,” I think these are the people who frequently appear in the documents of our region as belonging to a *masnata*. Fontanini discusses their status and condition fully and learnedly in his booklet, often cited by us, *On the Masnada*.

For those dwelling on *mansi* elsewhere gave themselves the name *masi* or *masnatae*. For the manner in which these slaves were manumitted, see the documents placed in Appendix II, nos. 26, 27, and 28.

### X

The matter is not the same with the *aldiones*, who, like the [Col. 0037C] *aldii*, are freedmen, though not entirely exempt from every form of servile labor; hence they were sometimes counted among slaves. Yet the freedom, or diminution of servitude, which they obtained was received not in a church as slaves (as is clear from the charters cited shortly afterward), but by charter or at the will of their master. *Laws of the Lombards*, book II, title XXXIV, law 5:

> “If anyone shall have freed his male or female slave in a church beside the altar, henceforth free … For whoever wishes to make him an *aldius* shall not lead him into a church, unless he does it in another manner, as he wishes—whether by charter or in whatever way pleases him.”

*Aldiones* are those who were born from *aldii*. In the same work, title XII, law 8:

> “If the *aldius* of anyone takes the *aldia* of another as his wife and begets children by her … his children shall be *aldiones*.”

[Col. 0037D] This was a class of slaves very well known in Italy under the Lombards, and sufficiently widespread that royal enactments concerning it occur throughout the *Laws of the Lombards*. Among the Italians, such men were generally considered equivalent to the *fiscalini* and *liti* in Francia. Thus Charlemagne decrees concerning them in chapter 6 of the supplementary capitulary to the Lombard law, in the year 801:

> “The *aldii* and *aldianae* belonging to the public fisc shall live in Italy in the service of their masters under the same law under which the *fiscalini* and *liti* live in Francia.”

The *fiscalini* were those who cultivated and inhabited estates attached to the royal fisc. *Capitulary Concerning the Estates*, chapter 50:

> “Let the *fiscalini* who possess holdings live from them.”

And chapter 52:

> “We wish that our *fiscal* men and slaves, or free men, who dwell throughout our fiscuses or estates …”

The *liti*, or *lidi*, were burdened with a milder obligation than slaves, as may be gathered from the Ripuarian law, chapter 62, no. 1, where it says:

> “If anyone makes his slave a tributary or a *Litus* …”

—that is, if he lightens for him the yoke of servitude. The remaining matters that follow in our diploma present no great difficulty to the reader.

### XI

More than anything said thus far, however, the date and place in which the diploma was issued demand particular examination. For at the end it reads:

> “Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth year of our reign, from the city of Loreia, happily in the name of God.”

The year 776 truly was the eighth year in which Charlemagne had held the Frankish kingdom after the death of his father Pippin in 768. Hence, unless I were mindful that Baronius was human, I would be astonished that so notable an error [Col. 0038B]—as Pagius calls it at the year 802, no. 7—had crept into his *Annals*, where he refers the diploma to the year 773. Baronius writes under the year 802, no. 13:

> “Thus far, a diploma was given in the year of the Lord 773, in which Charles himself came into Italy against Desiderius, and in which it happened that the eighth year of his reign was reckoned.”

From these words it appears that Charlemagne’s arrival in Italy against Desiderius caused Baronius to go astray, since he did not notice that, although the diploma is said to have been issued in Italy, Charlemagne had made other later journeys into Italy—for example, in 776, when he descended into Friuli to suppress Rotgand’s rebellion. Moreover, the property of Waldand, who had fallen in battle with Rotgand, is assigned to Paulinus. The battle, however, did not take place until 776. [Col. 0038C] Therefore in 773 Waldand’s property had not yet been adjudicated to the fisc, so that it could not have been donated to Paulinus. Furthermore, he is called king of the Lombards only from 774 onward; the diploma therefore cannot be placed in 773 when it bears at its head the title “King of the Lombards.”

Our Baronius therefore erred in good faith, as did Bollandus, who followed him. He likewise departs from the truth when he says that 773 was the eighth year of Charlemagne’s reign, although it was only the fifth. Candidus reads not “eighth” but “tenth” (as does the manuscript that we publish in Appendix II, no. 2), but this is an error; for the Frankish annalists—namely, the Bertinian, Lambecian, and Loiselian annalists—place Charlemagne in the Spanish and Saxon wars in 778, which was the tenth year of his reign, while they say nothing at all about Italian affairs. [Col. 0038D]

Fontaninus, in his booklet *Delle Masnade*, p. 42 and following, departs from the others and wishes the chronology of Charlemagne’s reign reported in this diploma to begin not from the year in which he entered upon the Frankish kingdom, but from the year in which he acquired the Lombard kingdom in Italy. Accordingly, he assigns the diploma to 781, the year in which Charles again came into Italy, and thus could very well have granted the privilege at the city of Lorea, situated on the banks of the Adige. Thus thinks that illustrious man.

There are, however, several arguments of no little force in support of this view. First, once Charlemagne had acquired the Italian kingdom, he did not use the title of the Italian kingdom alone, but either the Frankish title alone or the Frankish and Italian titles together, as is evident to anyone who examines his diplomas. Here, however, he would call himself only king of Italy, although he was also king of Francia. Charters are indeed found dated solely by the years of the Italian kingdom; but these are not inscribed in Charlemagne’s name as the issuer of the document. Rather, they are so inscribed by Italians subject to him, who dated their acts according to the Italian kingdom, such as those of Peter, archbishop of Milan, in Puricellus, p. 21:

> “In the sixteenth and ninth years in Italy of our lords Charles and Pippin, kings in Italy, and of our holy Paulinus of the council of Friuli; in the twenty-third and fifteenth years of their principate.”

Italians writing in Italy about affairs conducted in Italy dated their charters by the Italian kingdom, without attending to the eras of other kingdoms. But this cannot be thought of a king to whom several kingdoms were subject. Just as at the head of a document he calls himself king of the Franks and Lombards, so at the end he was accustomed to date his letters from the era of the first kingdom, or of both kingdoms, never omitting the first. In our case, Charles himself, king of the Franks and Lombards, issues the diploma. Therefore the year must be reckoned from the Frankish kingdom, since that kingdom is prior and unquestionably more important, while the other is absent.

Second, these possessions are given to Paulinus before he ascended the patriarchal see. He ascended it in the present year—that is, 776, as will be shown in the following chapter—and therefore the diploma cannot have been issued in 781. Add that the diploma was issued, as will shortly be argued with probability, outside Italy. Fontaninus’s reasoning therefore collapses, since he wants the date to have been in Italy and consequently wants the years of the Italian kingdom to be counted.

Since these considerations exclude 781, while, on the other hand, the eighth year of the Frankish kingdom agrees with 776, when both the authorities of the writers and the historical events prove that the diploma was issued, one should not abandon this view without clearer grounds. [Col. 0039C]

### XII

The place itself presents no less difficulty. The diploma is said to have been issued “from the city of Loreia.” But where in the world was the city of Loreia situated? Fontaninus readily declares it to be the place now commonly called Loreo, at the mouths of the Adige. Perhaps he derived this from Cointius, who under the year 776, no. 8, says:

> “We interpret Loreia as modern Loretum on the river Adige in the Venetian duchy.”

This opinion, however, does not seem probable.

First, at no time was Loredum, or Lauretum, in the Venetian duchy regarded as worthy of the name of a city; the ancient geographers and lexicographers scarcely even touched upon the name. Second, this place is nowhere called Loreia, but Loredum, Loretum, or Lauretum. The affinity of the names is therefore not such that it can be regarded as the city from which Charles issued the diploma. It is indeed now commonly called Loreo, but this is due to the neighboring Venetians, who in their natural dialect habitually remove the penultimate consonants of participles: for example, for *andato*, *andao* or *anda*; for *avuto*, *abbuo* or *abbu*; and for *aceto*, *aseo*. Thus for *Loredo* or *Loreto* they say *Loreo*.

Third, in the time of Charlemagne Loretum either did not yet exist, or at most was a fortification of no importance. The former is asserted by Leandro Alberti, who, speaking of Transpadane Romandiola—“Romagna beyond the Po”—says:

> “Loredo, a district situated in the marshes, formerly built by Vitale Falerio, doge of Venice.”

But this man held the duchy long after Charlemagne’s time, and therefore Loredum did not yet exist. The foundation diploma seems to support this view, which the editors of the *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum* added from a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library to part VIII, chapter 9, book IX of Andrea Dandolo’s *Chronicle*. Its formula was also preserved among the people of Loredum, as is stated there at the beginning.

It is dated in the tenth year of Vitale’s duchy: from the Nativity of Christ 1094, December III, at Rialto, with the indiction-number omitted. I think that the number of the indiction is lacking, that the Greek phrase *τὸ III* (“the III”) refers to the day of the month of December, and that the number II should be added to the indiction; for in 1094 the second, not the third, indiction was in progress.

The diploma says, among other things:

> “We, Vitale Faletro … at our own expense and cost, ordered the castle called Lauretum to be built from its foundations and constructed with all its fortifications.”

And below, when granting the place for habitation:

> “To all of you, clergy, castellans, and all the others who are going to come there, and to your heirs and successors, for permanent possession … we grant the entire aforesaid castle.”

Do you see that the castle was built from its foundations and constructed at the expense of Duke Falerio? Do you hear the formula used in addressing those who had undertaken to inhabit the place, as though they were the first to migrate there? For this seems to be what is meant by “to you and to the others who are going to come there.” Nor can you say that the words “the castle which is called Lauretum” indicate that Loretum already existed. For he adds, “we ordered it to be built,” as if he were saying: “We ordered the castle to be built, which is now called Lauretum.” The name must be understood as assigned after the construction. Loredum therefore did not previously exist in such a form that Charlemagne, residing there, could have issued a diploma. [Col. 0040C]

### XIII

Yet because Dandolo himself, in the cited chapter 9 of part VIII, says:

> “This duke, Vitale, restored the fortress of Loreto, ruined by age, in the form of a castle, and entrusted it to be guarded by inhabitants, with lands and waters and many privileges of immunity,”

—and because Peter Marcellus likewise suggests this in more concise words in *Lives of the Venetian Dukes*, concerning Vitale Falerio, the thirty-second duke:

> “Falerio,” he says, “also restored Lauretum, which had collapsed through age,”

—I would not dare assert that Lauretum did not exist at all before Duke Falerio. It is enough, however, to have shown that it was such a tiny settlement that its greatest glory and distinction consisted in having been raised, in 1094, from a small and deserted fortification to the status of a castle. When you hear “fortification,” you should not imagine a citadel, but rather a little stronghold for restraining the incursions of raiders. For the fortification had not been intended for anything more substantial than a castle.

The castle, however, is said in the privilege to have been:

> “constructed for the safety of those passing through, so that the robberies which very frequently occurred there through the cunning and ambushes of many men might no longer be perpetrated.”

Who could ever persuade himself that a place of this sort could have been distinguished by the name of a city?

### XIV

A fourth argument may be added from the date. The privilege is dated the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July. This is how I read it in the manuscript of the treasury [Col. 0041A] of the holy church of Aquileia, from which you will have the diploma in Appendix II, no. 2; and this is also how it is read by Candidus, Baronius, Bollandus, Cointius, Pagius, and Fleury. Only the younger Palladius reads “of June,” followed in this by Schönleben.

It is not credible that Charles was at Loredo on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July—that is, on 17 June—or perhaps even in Italy. For the Frankish annals say that Charles, who had descended toward the end of 775, entered Italy at the beginning of 776, suppressed the revolt into which Friuli had been driven by Rotgand’s factions, and captured Tarvisium, which was governed by Rotgand’s father-in-law Stabilinius, celebrating Easter there.

The Petavian annalist records this year:

> “The lord King Charles proceeded into Italy, and after killing Hrogaand, who had rebelled against him, they besieged Stabilinius, his father-in-law, in the city of Tarvisium. After capturing him and arranging everything, he returned successfully with his men to Francia.”

The Loiselian annalist has:

> “He celebrated Easter at the city of Tarvisium, and, after capturing the cities of Friuli and Tarvisium, he returned to Francia.”

The Bertinian annalist says the same. Although it is first said that he celebrated Easter at Tarvisium and afterward that he captured the cities, it is nevertheless clear that Tarvisium had already been captured before Easter. For if he celebrated Easter there, he had already taken it. Nor does the subsequent phrase, “and after capturing the cities,” create an obstacle merely because of its barbarous phrasing; it stands for “and, after capturing the cities, he returned.”

Therefore, at Easter—that is, on 14 April, on which day Easter fell in 776—the Friulian war had already been concluded. Once the affairs of Friuli had been settled and counts had been appointed to administer the region, he immediately returned to Francia. The Saxon Poet writes under this year:

> “He ordered Frankish counts, whom he himself appointed there,  
> To guard the cities he had recovered; and as he came swiftly,  
> So swiftly he departed from there.”

Einhard agrees with this, and, according to Pagius himself, is more careful than the others on this matter in his *Annals*, where he says:

> “To suppress these disturbances Charles hastened into Italy. After killing Rotgaud, who was seeking the kingdom, and recovering without delay the cities that had defected to him, and appointing Frankish counts in them, he returned with the same speed with which he had come.”

Now reconcile, if you can, the speed of Charles’s return from the Friulian war, which had been completed at least by 13 April, with his being at the city of Loreia—that is, Loredo—on 17 June, the date on which the diploma is said to have been issued. You will never persuade yourself that he was then at Loredo. For what concern would he have had to depart from Italy if, after the war had been concluded and the affairs settled for whose sake he had descended into Friuli, he had spent more than two months, so to speak, occupied in doing nothing, turning aside here and there in order to issue a diploma at Loredo on 17 June?

### XV

For this reason, what Pagius says under the year 776, no. 4, and before him Cointius in the same year, no. 11, does not satisfy me. They say that a Saxon disturbance prevented Charles from going to Rome. Nothing could be less true. Charles had already returned to Francia when he received news of the new Saxon rebellion.

Hear the Bertinian annalist, whom the others follow:

> “He arranged the cities that had rebelled throughout the Franks, and again returned to Francia with success and victory. Then”—note the force of this *then*: a messenger arrived and said that the Saxons had rebelled—“etc.”

Below, after narrating the events of the rebellion, he indicates the place where Charles heard this news, namely Worms:

> “And when,” he says, “the lord King Charles had reached Worms, hearing all these matters”—one of which was the rebellion itself—“he convened a synod in that same city.”

From this account it is therefore clearly established that Charles had already departed from Italy when he received the news of the Saxon rebellion. These disturbances therefore did not cause him to leave Italy.

The haste of Charles’s return, however, makes at least one of two possibilities probable: either the privilege was issued earlier than it is commonly transmitted, namely on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, as Palladius and Schönleben have it—that is, 18 May—and thus the facts could be reconciled even on a straightforward reading of the words of the Nazarian annalist, which belong to this year:

> “The May Field at Worms.”

For only the month of May still remained, so that the assembly which was first summoned for March and called the March Field, but which was transferred to May and called the May Field because, as Ducange testifies, military expeditions and affairs of the kingdom were then conducted—at least at the end of the month in which it was instituted (I say “of the month in which it was instituted,” since Cointius, in the cited place, no. 10, shows that it was often held outside May although called the May Field)—could have been held, or at least begun, at Worms; or else the diploma was issued outside Italy, from which Charles had departed after the war was concluded.

Perhaps both are true: it was issued earlier and outside Italy. However the matter may stand, one must accept only with the greatest difficulty, or rather not at all, that this diploma was issued in the city of Loreia, if that is Loredum, situated amid the marshes where the Adige enters the Adriatic Sea. [Col. 0043B]

### XVI

Yet I seem to hear my reader reply: “If you exclude Loreia, what other place do you propose? The diploma was not issued nowhere.” To tell the truth, the matter is stuck here; and experience teaches me that it is easier to attack another person’s view than to defend one’s own.

Ludovicus Schönleben says in his *Annals of Carniola*, under the year 776:

> “I suspect Loreia to be Laureacum, which perhaps was already called Lorch by the Germans at that time, unless you prefer to understand Lourana in Liburnia, near Friuli.”

I do not reject the conjecture until a better one appears that is more fully satisfying. In French, Dupin now renders the name as *Lauree* in his account of Symmachus, speaking of his twelfth letter, in which he grants the pallium to the bishop of Laureacum (*Councils*, vol. V, p. 440), although he regards the letter as spurious.

But could *Laurisham* be Lorsch in German, where the monastery of Lauresham lies three leagues from Worms, where, as just stated, Charles held the May Field in this year?

I might propose Noreia, following Amasaeus, Leandro Alberti, and the elder Palladius, who say—without opposition from the lexicographers—that modern Gorizia is the Noreia of the ancients, known to Strabo, Caesar, and Pliny, with the N changed into L through the error of copyists, if at the time of Charlemagne at least the name of the city still survived. Pliny records that in his own time it had already been destroyed, book III, chapter 20:

> “They have perished,” he says, “among the Veneti, Attina and Calina; among the Carnī, Segeste and Ocra; among the Taurisci, Noreia.”

The author of the dissertation on the *Chorographic Map of Medieval Italy*—among the *Scriptores Rerum Italicarum*, vol. X, no. 73—moves every stone in order to show that modern Gorizia is not ancient Noreia. This likewise prevents us from attaching much weight to the conjecture that Loreia represents the city of Noreia. He does not, however, assign another place that could have been Noreia.

Thus we deny that Loredum was Loreia, but without producing another candidate we leave the investigation to our reader, judging it better to offer none than to present one that is doubtful or improbable.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Assumption of Saint Paulinus as Patriarch

### I

A matter of no small importance is at stake when the time, or epoch, of Paulinus’s assumption to the dignity of the Aquileian see is established. For not everyone agrees in assigning the duration of his patriarchate. Some assign him twenty-six years, others fewer, and others no more than twenty-five. Consequently, although they do not differ greatly in determining the year of his death, it cannot nevertheless be inferred from the unequal duration assigned to his patriarchate in what year he was appointed.

Moreover, the sequence of the years of the preceding patriarchs is so badly arranged in the Aquileian chronicles that one needs a Delian swimmer. This much, however, must be established as certain: by the merits of his learning [Col. 0043C] and holiness he paved his way to so celebrated a mitre; and although he lacked the advantages of birth and the distinction of blood, he earned the see for himself through wisdom, prudence, and integrity of character.

Since, however, we are dealing in conjectures concerning the date of his assumption, let us select those that seemed more probable.

### II

Callistus, the patriarch whom Ughellus says died around 770 after forty years of episcopate, is commonly succeeded by Sigualdus, or Siginaldus, the predecessor of our Paulinus. The Aquileian chronicle published by Muratorius (*Anecdota*, vol. IV, p. 240) assigns him forty-two years in the see.

If you accept this uncritically, you will have to place Paulinus’s inauguration in the following century, namely in 812. But what will happen if, with Baronius, you insert John between Callistus and Sigualdus? He is the man who, as the distinguished father of the *Annals* records under the year 772, no. 5, relying on the power of the Lombards while harassing the church of Grado, gave occasion for the embassy sent by the Venetians to Pope Stephen—and, after Stephen’s death, received by Hadrian—through the patriarch of Grado himself, the presbyter Magnus, and the tribune Constantine. Dandolo also describes this embassy in his *Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 12, part XIII. They demanded that the transgressor of his boundaries be terrified by apostolic threats and that his audacity be broken by spiritual weapons.

He is also the man—unless I doubt the authenticity of the diploma soon to be cited—who stood beside Pope Zachary when that pope had come to consecrate the chapel of Saint Peter at Lubnia. Its rights and revenues were granted to the Church of Frisinga by Arnulf through the intercession of Waldo, bishop of Frisinga, as appears from the diploma published by Ughellus’s editor among the Aquileian documents after Callistus.

Zachary died in 752. Therefore, before that time John was prominent in the Aquileian Church under the title of bishop. Yet the matter becomes still more complicated if we consider that in 762 Sigualdus had already ascended the patriarchal see, as appears from the document establishing the monasteries of Sextum and Saint Mary in Salto, dated in the sixth year of Desiderius and the third of Aldegisius, corresponding to 762. (You will have the document in the Appendix.)

From this we must correct Wolfgang Lazius, who in *Commentaries on the Roman Republic*, book XII, section 5, chapter 8, says of Paulinus:

> “He acted as Charles’s adviser when Charles established the monastery at Sextum and that at the bank of the Salto.”

For how could Paulinus have urged Charles to build monasteries at Sextum and Salto when they had already been built under his predecessor Sigualdus?

Furthermore, another diploma, dated 772, proves that it was not John but Sigualdus who occupied the patriarchal see. Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book III:

> “In the same year [772] Sigualdus, patriarch of Aquileia, was at Pavia. For there exists a diploma granted by him to the monastery of Saint Julia at Brescia, dated at Ticinum on the third day before the Ides of October, in the eleventh indiction, in the sixteenth and fourteenth years of the kings Desiderius and Aldegisius.”

Since he was of royal Lombard blood, and indeed, according to Candidus, descended from King Grimoald, he came to Ticinum, inhabited by his kinsmen and ruled by them from the royal residence, in order to visit them. He granted the privilege on 13 October in the sixteenth year of Desiderius, which was 772, counting from 757, the first year in which Desiderius began to reign after Aistulf. The date also agrees with the eleventh indiction, which, however, had not begun until the second month after his accession.

John therefore cannot be believed to have been patriarch in 772; nor should Callistus be thought to have died as late as 770, but perhaps in 760—Ughellus being at least a decade in error.

### III

I did not say by accident that John should not be believed to have been patriarch in 772, for I have never believed that he was a patriarch at all. Thus I resolve the otherwise tangled matter, with the younger Palladius holding the torch before me.

When Palladius did not find John among the patriarchs of Aquileia in the native chronicles—as indeed he is not found there—and had also seen what Baronius wrote about John’s insolence toward the people of Grado, he thought that John had not truly been patriarch but had governed in Sigualdus’s place, functioning almost as his vicar in the administration of the Aquileian Church.

Palladius’s opinion seems entirely credible to me. For in neither Arnulf’s privilege nor in Sabellicus, whom Baronius cited as his source for knowledge of this prelate, is John called patriarch; he is called only a bishop or prelate. Sigualdus says, in the passage from the monk of Saint Gall that will be cited in the following section, that he had held the episcopate for a long time. Indeed, as shown above, he held it from at least 762 until 776, as will be seen below.

Even if you subtract a full decade from the number of Callistus’s years reported by Ughellus and suppose that Callistus died not in 770 but in 760, you still find no place for John, although in 752 he stood beside Pope Zachary when the latter consecrated a church in Sclavinia. John therefore was not a patriarch, but exercised the functions of a patriarch, both under Callistus and under Sigualdus, perhaps as the chorepiscopus of both.

For chorepiscopi provided vicariate assistance to bishops, especially in rural dioceses. On this subject see Marcha, *On the Harmony of Priests and the Empire*, book III, chapter 13; Thomassin, *Ancient and New Ecclesiastical Discipline*, passim; and Ducange in the *Glossary*. They are also mentioned fairly often in the Capitularies, especially those of 828, where they are called “assistants in the ministry of bishops.”

John could therefore have served as chorepiscopus under Callistus and Sigualdus. Under Callistus, in 752, he could have attended the consecration by Pope Zachary of the church of Saint Peter at Lubnia; and under Sigualdus, perhaps while Sigualdus was absent and residing at Pavia, in 772 he could have harassed the church of Grado. He ceased from that harassment not so much because of Pope Hadrian’s admonitions as through fear. Sabellicus says in *Enneads*, book VIII, near the end:

> “For the overthrow of the Lombard kingdom occurred at that time, and the Aquileian Church depended upon its favor.”

These words suggest the year 774, when Lombard affairs went to ruin, and indicate that John was still alive.

Since, therefore, at the same time we find Callistus and John, as the events of 752 show, and Sigualdus and John, as the events of 772 and 774 show, while John is nowhere called patriarch, he is rightly struck from the list of patriarchs, since two patriarchs cannot be admitted at the same time. He should be called merely the vicar or administrator of the patriarchs, or a chorepiscopus. [Col. 0045C]

### IV

Whatever the truth may be, Sigualdus was alive on 13 October 772, as is established by the diploma issued at Ticinum in the sixteenth year of Desiderius. Ughellus’s editor, drawing from the *Cassinense Bullary*, vol. II, says that this diploma was issued in 774 among the documents of Siginaldus. This appears to be false, both from the number of years of King Desiderius—whose sixteenth year falls not in 774 but in 772—and from the events of 774. For on 13 October it was not Desiderius but Charles who was called king of the Lombards, after capturing Pavia shortly after Easter.

The monk of Saint Gall, in book II *On the Deeds of Charlemagne*, addressed to Charles the Fat, son of Louis the German, grandson of Louis the Pious, and great-grandson of Charlemagne, chapter 27, in Duchesne’s edition, vol. II, p. 133, recounts certain matters concerning the final illness of a certain patriarch of Aquileia. These must be considered here and now in their entirety:

> “He overcame the city [Pavia]. Thereafter, advancing farther, the most religious Charles came to the city of Friuli, which those who think themselves learned now call Forum Julium. It happened that at the same time the bishop of that city—or, to speak according to modern usage, the patriarch—was approaching the end of his life. When the most religious Charles hastened to visit him, so that he might designate his successor by name, the man, drawing pious sighs from the depths of his heart, said: ‘Lord, I leave to divine judgment and to your disposition an episcopate long retained without any usefulness or spiritual profit, lest, in addition to the heap of sins that I increased while alive, I should be found after death to have added something further before the inescapable and incorruptible judge.’

> “The wisest Charles received this in such a way that he judged him not undeserving of comparison with the ancient Fathers. Since the most energetic Charles of the most unenergetic Franks had remained for some time in that region, until, when the bishop died, he could substitute for him a worthy successor, on a certain feast day, after the celebration of Mass, he said to his men: ‘Lest, growing sluggish through idleness, we be brought to cowardice, let us go hunting until we catch something, and let each of us go in the same clothing in which we are now dressed.’

> “It was a rainy and cold day. Charles himself had a sheepskin coat not much more valuable than that *roccus* of Saint Martin with which, according to divine testimony, he covered his breast and, with bare arms, offered sacrifice to God. The others, however, since it was a holiday and they had just come from Pavia, to which the Venetians had recently transported all the wealth of the East from overseas, proceeded wrapped in the skins of Phoenician birds edged with silk, and in the necks, backs, and haunches of peacocks just beginning to bloom, adorned with Tyrian purple or *diacedrina* cloth. Some were wrapped in blankets, others in dormice.

> “As they traversed the woods, they were torn by tree branches, thorns, and thistles, drenched by rain, and also befouled by the blood of wild animals and the wallowing of the hides. Then the exceedingly shrewd Charles said: ‘Let none of us remove his fur coat until we go to bed, so that they may dry better upon us.’ At this command, each man, caring more for his body than for his clothing, sought out fires everywhere and tried to warm himself. Then, returning and remaining in his service until deep into the night, they were sent back to their lodgings.

> “When they began to remove those exceedingly thin skins, or even thinner cloths, the tears caused by the wrinkles and contractions made a sound that could be heard from afar, like sticks breaking in dryness. They groaned, sighed, and complained that in a single day they had lost so much money. The emperor had ordered them to present themselves before him the next day in the same skins.

> “When this had been done, and all of them were not shining in new garments but instead looked like rags in discolored and repulsive squalor, the industrious Charles said to his chamberlain: ‘Take our fur coat in your hands and bring it before us.’ When it had been brought, still perfectly intact and shining white, he took it in his hands and showed it to all who stood around, saying: ‘O most foolish of mortals, which fur coat is now more valuable and useful: this one of mine, bought for one solidus, or those of yours, bought not merely for pounds but for many talents as well?’

> “Then, with their faces bent toward the ground, they could scarcely endure his terrible rebuke. Your most religious father imitated this example not once but throughout his entire life, so that no one …”

This is as far as the narrative of the monk of Saint Gall extends. Although all of it does not pertain directly to the present matter, I have nevertheless chosen to transcribe it all, so that the glory of our homeland may be preserved in the memory of posterity: it was illuminated not only by the victories of Charlemagne but also cultivated by his devotion to peace and adorned by his noble exercises.

### V

These events, narrated by the monk of Saint Gall without naming the patriarch or indicating the time at which they occurred, can scarcely be attributed to anyone other than Sigualdus. They cannot concern Paulinus, who in 792 had a diploma from Charles, discussed in chapter 6, section 4, so that the clergy and Church of Aquileia might choose their bishop.

Here Charles asks the dying man to name his successor, and the dying patriarch entrusts the election to Charles himself. Moreover, when Paulinus died, the thirtieth year since the capture of Ticinum was already passing. These events, however, occurred immediately after that war had ended.

Add that Charles, toward the end of 803 and at the beginning of 804, when Paulinus died, did not see Italy, but celebrated the Nativity of the Lord and wintered at Aachen, as the Bertinian annals report. Therefore these matters cannot be understood of Paulinus.

They apply even less to anyone who preceded Sigualdus, because it was not another but Sigualdus himself who occupied the Aquileian see when Ticinum was conquered, and these events occurred after that conquest. Hold, therefore, that the person about whom this monk speaks was Sigualdus.

### VI

Yet it is plainly established that this did not occur in 774, the year in which Pavia was captured, because the events took place in winter, as is indicated not only by the rainy and cold day but also by the fur clothing of Charles and his palatines, which is not ordinarily worn except in the winter season.

Charles celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the end of 773 within the very rampart of the camp, as Cointius shows from the Loiselian, Bertinian, and other annalists under that year, no. 18; and he celebrated Easter in Rome in 774. After the city was captured, the annalists do not say that he traveled through Italy and the provinces of Lombard dominion. Rather, the Bertinian annalist says:

> “There, all the Lombards coming from every city of Italy submitted themselves to the rule of the glorious lord King Charles and the Franks.”

The Lambecian annalists add that he attended:

> “the dedication of the church and the translation of the body of Saint Nazarius at the monastery of Lauresham, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 774, on the Kalends of September.”

Lauresham, or Lorsch, lies in the diocese of Worms, three leagues east of the city of the same name. It is therefore futile to seek Charles in Friuli in 774, whether at the beginning or the end of the year—that is, during the winter season—in order to provide a successor for a dying bishop.

### VII

Since this is so, no other year presents itself to which these events can more probably be fitted than 776. For in the winter of that year Charles came to Friuli to punish Rotgand, who had been convicted of rebellion. He had his winter quarters there; he was the man who celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at the estate called Scaldistat toward the end of 775, as was stated in the preceding chapter, section 5; he wintered there and, after celebrating Easter at Tarvisium, returned to Gaul. [Col. 0048A] While he was staying there at the beginning of 776, the illness and collapse of Sigualdus occurred, as the monk cited above relates.

Source/review notes: The source’s compressed poetic syntax and genuine uncertainty are retained explicitly.

### VIII

You may perhaps object that the monk of Saint Gall is not of unquestionable reliability, since Henricus Canisius, the editor of his books, characterizes his *History* as sometimes sprinkled with fables. Such, however, is this account, which introduces Siguald, a Lombard and therefore bearing a hostile name, speaking so piously and religiously before Charles that Charles judged him worthy to be ranked with the foremost fathers. Nor does such great piety in the former, or such high commendation in the latter, seem open to censure. Moreover, it places these events in the year in which Pavia was captured. For it says: “He overcame the city”; and immediately adds: “Then, advancing farther . . . he came to the city of Friuli, etc.” [Col. 0048B] These events, therefore, cannot be postponed until the year 776.

Add that they occurred in winter, as has been said. If Siguald therefore died in winter, Paulinus ought likewise to have been appointed as his successor in winter, and indeed in that same year; for Charles was staying there precisely “until, when the bishop died, he should appoint a worthy successor to him.” But since in the privilege discussed in the preceding chapter Paulinus is still called a grammarian as late as May or June, and consequently had not yet been proclaimed patriarch, it is clear that these facts cannot be reconciled with the year 776, in which Charles withdrew from Italy immediately after Easter.

Furthermore, it is said below: “They had received an order from the emperor to bring them in those same skins, etc.” But Charles was not called emperor until the year [Col. 0048C] 800. These circumstances therefore do not fit the year 776.

### IX

Nevertheless, the objections are refuted and resolved as readily as they are raised. As for the truthfulness and reliability of the writer, I do not deny that he occasionally inserts something resembling a fable, but not that everything is fictitious. For the aforementioned Canisius says that “although his style is humble and lowly, and the history itself is sometimes sprinkled with fables, it nevertheless contains things deserving the memory of all posterity.” Caspar Barthius, in his *Adversaria* (book XLV, chapter 11), after arguing at greater length that this writer should not be rejected, even though he is sometimes found to be fabulous, and indeed that in many matters one should adhere to him because of the simplicity of his style, through which truth shines forth more clearly than through an affected display of words, concludes:

> “I confess that I am captivated by the simplicity of this monk, and judge his simple statements more truthful than the bombastic tragedies of others, who, when they wish to speak to us ornately, often weave riddles.”

Moreover, the title of the books presents an authority capable of inspiring confidence, for they are said to have been “written by a certain monk of Saint Gall from the reports of Adalbert the soldier, who took part in Charles’s wars against the Huns, Saxons, and Slavs, and from those of his son, the priest Werimbert.” In this account of the patriarch lying ill, I do not detect anything fabulous that should be rejected with one’s eyes closed.

### X

As for the piety of the dying Siguald and the graciousness of Charles in praising him, which may seem strange and incredible, nothing should appear strange or incredible to anyone who proceeds without rashness of judgment. [Col. 0049A] For Charles was of such greatness of spirit and goodness that he loved virtue even in an enemy. Besides, after the war against Desiderius had been concluded, he did not treat the Lombards as enemies; rather, he wished them to retain and administer by feudal right the dominions of Spoleto, Benevento, and Friuli, as they had held them from the earlier kings of their people—still less did he treat in that manner the leaders of the Church, such as Siguald the patriarch. The condition of a man even at the point of death itself persuades a sound-minded person that it is entirely plausible that he uttered the words reported.

Indeed, a man is truly quite senseless if he cannot show wisdom even in death. But Siguald was not the kind of man, in life or conduct, who had failed in the duty of a good shepherd or had not excelled in virtues worthy of a bishop. An ancient chronicle reported by Muratori in *Anecdota Latina*, volume IV, [Col. 0049B] says that he “governed his Church successfully and laudably.” An old inscription in the patriarchal palace at Udine also honors him with the title of an excellent prelate. It reads as follows:

> **SIGUALD, RELATIVE OF KING DESIDERIUS, STRIVED TO MITIGATE THE SAVAGERY OF HIS KINSMAN; BUT THE DESTRUCTION OF THE LOMBARD KINGDOM BROUGHT THE DUTIES OF THE EXCELLENT PRELATE TO AN END.**

### XI

The connection between the statements “He overcame Pavia” and “Then, advancing farther . . . he came to the city of Friuli” is likewise no obstacle to the claim that Charles came to Friuli in the year in which Ticinum was captured—that is, in 774 rather than 776. I admit that a more precise manner of expression would be desirable; nevertheless, every consideration of fairness demands that we excuse a Germanic monk who had very little command of the rules of the Latin language and lived in an age so deficient in learning, and that we more humanely pardon his disordered narration.

In any event, if you weigh the words more exactly, they indicate nothing other than that Charles went to Friuli after the capture of Pavia, without specifying when he went there. He did go to Friuli, but not in 774: he went in 776. And *exin* means the same thing to the monk of Saint Gall as “when he came”—that is, on another occasion—to Friuli. The words “advancing farther” seem to indicate not the same expedition but rather a new one. For after Ticinum had been captured [Col. 0049D] and Italy had already been claimed as his own, Charles did not then undertake further operations; only afterward did he advance farther, when he came in response to Rotgaud, who was stirring up disturbances, intending to subdue Friuli anew after it had been thrown into revolt by the duke.

This interval of time is indicated with some clarity by what is added concerning the court officials, dressed in garments brought from Pavia, to which the Venetians had transported them from the East. For it is not credible that, while the city was still either under siege or in turmoil, the Venetians had brought their merchandise there. Rather, after peace had been restored, they transported it under more favorable conditions in the following years—say, 775 or 776—and sold it to the arriving Franks.

### XII

A greater difficulty is created by the statement that these events occurred in winter, whereas it is established that Paulinus had not yet been proclaimed patriarch at that time, since in the following May or June he is still called “master of grammar” in a diploma of the year 776. I shall, however, explain this point briefly as well.

The historian of Saint Gall nowhere says that the patriarch had died, but only that he was “approaching the end of his life”; nor does he say that Charles remained at Friuli for any other reason than “until, when the bishop died, he should appoint a worthy successor to him.” From these words we can infer nothing beyond either Siguald’s old age, foretelling his imminent death, or an illness from which no recovery was expected. Concerning his actual death there is profound silence. From this it must be inferred that the death believed to be imminent did not occur at that time.

All these circumstances can be reconciled with a condition close to death, even though the man’s end may have been prolonged [Col. 0050B] for a considerable time. For the historian’s purpose it made no difference whether the man whose words, as it seemed, were worth preserving had actually died at that moment. Since, therefore, it is not established that his death followed then, it is reasonable to believe that it occurred at another time.

Accordingly, in my judgment I formulate the following sufficiently probable conjecture. Charles, who had designated Paulinus to succeed the dying Siguald because of his outstanding merits in learning and holiness, provided that Siguald had not proposed someone more suitable, saw that Siguald’s life had been prolonged beyond what he had believed would be its brief end; and meanwhile, greatly desiring to show favor to a man especially dear to him, he gave Paulinus the property of Waldandus in the village of Labaria as a gift, as though it were a pledge in advance of the dignity of the patriarchate—a dignity which, had it been vacant, he would then have conferred, but which was nevertheless to be conferred in due time.

For what Charles granted in that diploma—Charles called “emperor” by the monk, either because the Frankish kings were sometimes so called, as Baluzius notes in his annotations on the Council of Narbonne, which we discuss in our *Dissertation on the Heresy of Felix and Elipandus*, no. 27, or because the historian wrote after Charles’s assumption of the imperial dignity—what Charles, I say, granted to Paulinus was more than ought to have been granted to a grammarian, however deserving in literary matters, whom neither noble birth nor military achievements recommended. He therefore gave to a man whom he had soon decided would occupy that seat something which, once he had been installed there, would make the gift appear worthy both of the recipient and of the giver.

Thus, after June of the year 776, when Charles had already returned from Friuli to Francia, Siguald died—“at the end of the year 776,” says G. Cave, and correctly—and through Charles’s assistance Paulinus was acclaimed patriarch. In our judgment he would then occupy the see of Aquileia most gloriously for twenty-eight years.

### XIII

Ughellus and the others who say that Paulinus began his patriarchal rule in 774 are entirely mistaken. For it is established that in 776 he is called a grammarian, not a patriarch, in a diploma; and if the title had then belonged to him, it would not have been omitted.

Those who assert that he was taken from the living in 802 are indeed compelled to admit twenty-eight years of pontificate, as we do. But it will be shown in its proper place that he did not die in 802, but rather in 804; consequently, his elevation must be placed in 776, not 774.

Those who assign him only fifteen years [Col. 0051A] of episcopate, if they wish him to have died in 804, say that he ascended the chair in 789. If they say that he died in 802, they make him patriarch from 787. Neither view is true, because the chronicles from which this period of fifteen years was taken contain many errors and should not be trusted, as has been shown: they assign forty years to Callistus and forty-two to Siguald, and thus force Paulinus’s elevation to be referred to the following century.

Their compiler is also a recent writer, since he extends his register as far as Nicholas, the successor of Blessed Bertrand—that is, to the year 1350. He shows that he wrote under that later period by calling Siguald a native of Cividale, although he was of Lombard origin and perhaps born at Friuli. By using this designation, he betrays himself as a comparatively modern writer, employing a name that is not of ancient origin. Moreover, in 789 Paulinus took part in the councils of Charlemagne as a bishop, particularly in the Council of Aachen held on 23 March, as is shown in the *Dissertation on the Councils of Friuli*, no. 10.

Therefore Paulinus cannot have been proclaimed patriarch in 789, since by 23 March we find him absent as bishop of Aquileia and performing episcopal duties in the synod. Since his inauguration as patriarch can be placed neither in 774, as excessively early, nor in 787 or 789, as excessively late, we embrace the view supported by more numerous and more distinguished patrons and resting on firmer foundations: namely, that Paulinus was appointed to the see of Aquileia toward the end of 776.

This is the view of Onuphrius, in Bollandus’s *Life of Saint Paulinus*, § 1, no. 7, who, concluding that his patriarchate lasted twenty-five years, implies that he died in 801. The younger Palladius, Schonleben, and Labbe, in the additions to Bellarmine, volume II, intimate a preference for the earlier date, 774, but incline toward 776, as does Morerius in his dictionary.

Bellarmine’s register in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers* is noteworthy: by placing Paulinus’s flourishing under the year 780, it implies that he had already been a prelate for several preceding years. Hoffmann, in his *Universal Lexicon*, does not differ greatly: admitting twenty-six years in the see and assigning his death to 803, he argues that his episcopate began in 777.

M. de Fleury also appears to support this view. In volume IX, page 588 of the Paris edition of 1703, he says that Paulinus received the privilege from Charles—discussed in the preceding chapter—“on 17 June, in the eighth year of Charles, that is, in the year 776, and shortly afterward succeeded Siguald in the see of Aquileia.” Pagius agrees with this at the end of his discussion of the year 776.

Adrian Baillet (*The Lives of the Saints*, volume I, 11 January) writes:

> “He was raised there against his will in the year 776 by the authority of Charlemagne, not to reward his virtue, but to give the peoples of Carnia a good shepherd and an excellent teacher, and to provide the Church with a skillful defender against the heresies of his time.”

Cointius, under the year 776, no. 9, using the diploma issued in June of that year to Paulinus the grammarian, excludes the opinion assigning the elevation to 774 and defends Sigonius’s assertion that it occurred in 776, saying:

> “The later opinion, therefore—the opinion of Sigonius—must be preferred, and it does not conflict with the Carolingian diploma, provided that it says Paulinus was appointed to the patriarchal dignity during or after the month of June.”

### XIV

It is still permissible to offer a conjecture by which the opinion based on our chronicles may be overturned—the opinion that assigns only fifteen years to Paulinus’s tenure.

In 776, as has been shown above, Charles visited Siguald, who was believed to be near death. It is not credible that such a man, already worn out by age, to whom the aforementioned chronicles assign so many years in the chair, and who, as it is reasonable to believe, was also crushed by anxiety over the disastrous condition of his people, should nevertheless have prolonged his life for another eleven or thirteen years.

It is more credible that Siguald died in that very year 776, in which Charles had visited him in such poor condition, whether from illness or old age, and that Paulinus was appointed in his place—indeed, as the year was drawing to its close, at the season when those exhausted by prolonged illnesses or consumed by extreme age are more easily taken from the living as winter approaches.

Since we are dealing with conjectures, the more reasonable one appears to be that which supposes a man so near death to have been removed within the year, rather than one which grants him another eleven or thirteen years of life.

### XV

Whatever weight these considerations may possess, and although they are supported only by conjectures, they nevertheless add some force of probability to our view, which is the more common and more probable one: namely, that Paulinus began his patriarchate in 776.

[xxiii] **CHAPTER V. The Journeys of Saint Paulinus and the Councils in Which He Took Part from the Year 776 to the Year 791**

[Col. 0052C]

### I

Toward the end of the year 776, therefore, Paulinus—who was exceedingly dear to Charlemagne because of his learning and the merits of his virtues—was raised through his assistance to the patriarchal see, although unwilling and reluctant. Since in this office he fulfilled every duty of an excellent shepherd and surpassed the wishes and hopes of his people, his promoter judged that this most holy and learned man should shine forth not merely for the particular benefit of the Church of Aquileia, but also for the benefit of the universal Church of God, whose affairs lay so close to his heart.

Accordingly, after the province of Friuli had been added to the Frankish realm as a result of the destruction of Lombard power, and its bishop had consequently to be numbered among those subject to Carolingian rule, it came about that, whenever Charles frequently summoned assemblies—not only of the nobles and dynasts of the kingdom, but also of abbots and bishops of the dioceses subject to him—our Paulinus often traveled abroad beyond the boundaries of his province. I would not, however, dare to assert that he attended every assembly. The distance of the places and the frequency with which the assemblies were summoned, almost every year, do not support such a claim. But just as it is not credible that he attended them all, so it is not probable that he was absent from the more celebrated ones.

### II

The first assembly after Paulinus’s initiation as bishop that presents itself is the assembly of Paderborn in 777. The annalists of Bertin and Loisel call it both a synod and a public assembly.
