A considerable number of bishops may also have been present, since the Saxons, formerly violators of treaties, gave their faith and hostages, embraced the name of Christ, and countless people were cleansed in baptism.

There is no basis either for denying or affirming that Paulinus was present, since no mention is made of the bishops and the acts of the council, which the authors do not produce, provide no opening for conjecture. It is rather suggested that he was absent, both because this is called only an assembly of Franks and Saxons and because Paulinus, newly established in his see, was occupied and hindered by the new purification of his flock from coming.

### III

The synod of 779 must not be judged in the same way. Its very first canon, which concerns metropolitans, raises the suspicion that Paulinus was present. At that time the suffragan bishops of the Church of Aquileia, already divided between the Lombards on one side and the Greeks on the other, were refusing obedience to their head.

The synod therefore seems to have occurred at an opportune moment for defending the violated rights of the Church of Aquileia, perhaps having been summoned at Paulinus’s complaint. It decreed as follows:

> “Canon I. Concerning metropolitans: suffragan bishops are to be subject to them according to the canons; and whatever they recognize as requiring correction in matters pertaining to their ministry, they are to amend and correct willingly.”

Joannes Candidus provides support for this conjecture at the beginning of book IV of his *Commentaries on Aquileia*. When he first mentions Paulinus, he says:

> “Paulinus, the thirty-sixth patriarch, hastened to him [Charles], lamenting the near destruction of the Church and region of Aquileia, and, having been received most graciously, returned with most munificent privileges.”

He does not say where Paulinus hastened. But Paulinus’s concern to vindicate the rights of his Church, and his great eagerness to do so, suggest that he hastened to this assembly, the first meeting of bishops summoned after his elevation, and obtained assistance for the affairs of his Church, which had been brought to ruin.

The title of this assembly is given in the *Capitularies* and by Cointius under the year 779, no. 1:

> “In the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Charles, the most glorious king, in the month of March, a capitulary was enacted concerning how, when bishops, abbots, distinguished men [*intustribus* in Baluzius’s *Capitularies*; *illustribus* in Cointius], and counts had been gathered together in a synodal council, together with our most pious lord, they agreed, according to the will of God and for pressing causes, upon a decree.”

Sirmondus suspects that this assembly was held at Herstal, and therefore could be called the Herstal assembly, because the Frankish annalists and Einhard assert that Charles celebrated Christmas and Easter there. Easter occurred on 11 April that year, and consequently it is reasonable to believe that he remained there during the month of March.

### IV

The annalists write that in the following years—whose events we pass over only in summary, so that the sequence of time may not be interrupted—other councils were held by Charles: for example, in 780 at the sources of the Lippe, and another there likewise in 782, and in 785 at Paderborn. In none of these, however, have we found any basis for suspecting that Paulinus was present.

The same is true of the councils of Worms in 786 and 787, except insofar as the establishment of episcopal sees in Saxony, recently converted more sincerely to the faith, was at times discussed there. Anyone may form whatever opinion he wishes about Paulinus’s presence, which we neither affirm nor deny.

During this interval Charles undertook two journeys to Rome. The first was in 781, when he celebrated Easter with Pope Hadrian in the city, while he had celebrated the Christmas festivities at Pavia toward the end of the preceding year. While he was at Rome, Carolomannus was baptized by Hadrian and received by him from the font, thereby making Hadrian Charles’s co-godparent, as the pope afterward customarily called him. He was named Pippin and anointed king of Italy, just as his brother Louis was made king of Aquitaine. Hildegard had borne them to Charles—the former in 776, the latter in 778—so that the first was five years old and the second three.

When Charles was returning, Gisla, recently born to him, was baptized at Milan by Thomas, the archbishop. [Col. 0054B] Since it is clear from this that Charles crossed through Insubria on his journey out and back, it is equally clear that this journey had nothing to do with the affairs of Friuli.

He undertook another journey in 786. As winter approached, he celebrated Christmas at Florence and immediately proceeded toward Rome. He was received most graciously by Hadrian, who did not trust Aragisus and urged Charles to act against him. Charles descended into Apulia, recovered Capua and then Benevento from Aragisus, and, returning, celebrated Easter with the pope at Rome in 787.

After hearing the envoys of Tassilo, whom Tassilo had sent to Hadrian to restore, through the pope’s assistance, the concord between them that had long since been broken—and which had not even then been sought in good faith—Charles returned to his own territories. At Worms, because of the death of Hildegard, which had occurred in 783 on the eve of the Ascension, 30 April, he took Fastrada as his new wife and summoned a synod concerning matters relating to Tassilo, both those already done and those still to be done.

In the following year, 788, he convened another synod at the villa of Ingelheim. There Tassilo’s treachery was established, and a charge was brought especially concerning the Avars, whom he had summoned into partnership in the rebellion for the destruction of the Carolingian realm and who in that same year actually appeared and ravaged the regions subject to the king.

Against Tassilo, all who were present—“Franks, Bavarians, Lombards, and Saxons, or all the provincials”—pronounced judgment as against an unquestionable capital offender. But Charles’s mild disposition moderated the sentence; and when the condemned man was given the power to decide what should be done with him, he tonsured himself together with his son Theodo.

You will find all these matters treated more fully in the annalists, especially the annalist of Bertin. Since, however, this does not appear to have been concerned purely and precisely with ecclesiastical discipline, I would not dare to say anything about Paulinus’s presence.

### V

We have now reached the year 789, when Charles assembled a council at Aachen. We do not doubt that Paulinus attended it, as well as the other assemblies of that year. In the second *Dissertation on the Synod of Friuli*, no. 10, we have shown sufficiently and more than sufficiently that they were gatherings of bishops and that Paulinus was present.

Here it may be permissible to propose only this one argument, which we also revisit in the same place. At the Council of Friuli in 796 Paulinus said that in earlier years he had often attended councils summoned by Charles. If Frankfurt is excluded, you will find no council to which it is more consistent with reason to suppose that he was present than this one, which is called a general synod and in which the affairs of the Saxon Church were treated under the same convocation of bishops, if not in the same session and place, at least in the same year.

### VI

It was, as we believe, during this journey of Paulinus and his residence beyond the boundaries of his diocese that the event occurred which Ermoldus Nigellus committed to writing and celebrated in verse near the end of book I. He dedicated this book, as well as the following three, to Louis the Pious, son of King Charlemagne.

Ludovicus Antonius Muratori, who was always most deserving of well-earned praise in the republic of letters, extracted these poems from the Viennese library of the most august reigning emperor Charles VI through the assistance of the distinguished Nicolaus Garellius, prefect of that library, made them publicly available, inserted them at the beginning of volume II, second part, of *Writers of Italian Affairs*, and illustrated them with notes.

The verses must not be omitted, since Ermoldus introduces Charles addressing his son Louis, on the basis of the received account of his victory at Barcelona and the defeat inflicted on the Saracens in 801. They are as follows:

> O most illustrious offspring, whom I have always loved,  
>   
> What Patriarch Paulinus once told me,  
> I have kept in my heart.  
>   
> The report is that the kindly patriarch  
> Came to the holy see at the king’s command.  
>   
> One day, while he sat within the gracious church  
> And, astonished, sang a hymn to Christ,  
> It happened that Charles, illustrious offspring,  
> Came to his parent, strengthened by the aid  
> And entreaties of the nobles.  
>   
> As he hastened toward the altar and had gone before it,  
> Where the holy bishop was performing his worthy duties,  
> Paulinus immediately asked of his own accord  
> Who he might be; the attendant answered  
> The question he had put to him.  
>   
> When he learned that this was the king’s first-born son,  
> He fell silent; the boy continued on his way.  
>   
> At last the hero Pippin came,  
> Accompanied by a choir of high-spirited youths.  
> Paulinus, celebrating, addressed the same attendant  
> And asked him; again he prepared to report the words.  
>   
> When the prelate recognized the name  
> And remembered that he was the king’s son,  
> He immediately bowed his head,  
> And the boy went swiftly on.  
>   
> Behold, last of all came Louis;  
> He hastened to embrace the altar,  
> And, suppliant, prostrated himself upon the ground.  
>   
> Weeping long, he asked the heavenly Christ,  
> Who reigns, to bring him aid through his prayers.  
>   
> Seeing this, the holy man rose from his seat,  
> Burning to address the sacred youth with reverence.  
>   
> Earlier, when Pippin and Charles had gone away,  
> He had remained seated and had uttered no words.  
>   
> At last the king worshiped the prophet  
> With his body prostrate;  
> And Paulinus received the pious king.  
>   
> He spoke hymnic words filled with varied expression:  
> “Go,” he said, “to Charles, for your piety. Farewell.”  
>   
> When the prophet first reached the emperor’s ear,  
> He recounted all these things to him in their proper order.  
>   
> “If God appoints a king from your Frankish offspring,  
> This one will be suited to your throne.”  
>   
> The wise Charles disclosed these things to a few followers,  
> Whose cause he trusted or favored, etc.  
> [The compressed Latin is uncertain.]

Such is the account of Nigellus, deserving of close consideration.

### VII

Here Charles’s three sons are named: Charles, the eldest of them; Pippin; and Louis. Concerning the offspring of Charlemagne, we must hear Paul the Deacon in his account of the bishops of Metz:

> “He [Charles] had four sons and five daughters by his wife Hildegard. Before lawful marriage, however, he had a son named Pippin by a noble girl named Himiltrude. The names of the children whom Hildegard bore him are these. The first was called Charles, named after his father and great-grandfather. The second was likewise Pippin, sharing the name of his brother and grandfather. The third was Lodobich, who was born at the same time as Hlotarius, who died at the age of two. Of these, by God’s favor, the younger Pippin now holds the kingdom of Italy, and Lodobich that of Aquitaine.”

These three sons of Charles and Hildegard had therefore not previously been known to Paulinus, and he had not previously seen them. This was not because there had earlier been no occasion on which they were present—for we think that he had approached Charles at least in 779—but because they were still so young that they are unlikely to have been presented in the presence of prelates. Louis was one year old, Pippin three, and Charles seven.

Or, if he had seen the children then, their appearance had faded from his memory, and he did not remember them as they grew older. Nor do we believe that this occurred on the first occasion when he approached Charles. They were at such a tender age that it is in no way probable that all of them stood among the clergy and nobles of the kingdom in an episcopal gathering.

Add that this could not have occurred before 781, when Pippin, aged five, was called king of Italy—the title by which he is presented as recognizable to Paulinus when he asks who he is. For Ermoldus says:

> “When the prelate recognized the name and remembered that he was king.”

At this passage the most learned Muratori comments:

> “Rather, *regemque*: that is, having remembered that he was king of Italy, he immediately uncovered his head to him.”

Nor does it seem likely that this occurred later than the year under discussion, 789. For how could it have happened that Pippin was unknown to Paulinus, when at this time, as Pagius maintains under the year 789, no. 6, he had taken Histria and Liburnia from the Greeks and had consequently traveled through regions either belonging to us or lying near us?

Moreover, Paulinus was present at Charles’s palace that year. What, then, prevents us from believing that these events occurred in this year, when the obstacles that arise in the earlier or later years do not apply? In the earlier years, the ages of Charles’s sons, especially Louis, do not support the event; in the later years, the events by which Charles’s sons became increasingly known, together with Paulinus’s frequent visits to the court, prevent us from saying that he did not know them, as this account requires.

Add that the farther we move from this year, the farther we also move from the time at which it becomes more probable that Paulinus came to know Charles’s sons. The ages of the sons themselves support the occurrence in this year, since they seem entirely suitable for the event: Charles was seventeen, Pippin thirteen, and Louis eleven.

### VIII

I am not unaware that a prophecy concerning Louis’s elevation after his father is also attached to the *Life of Paulinus* and to Alcuin himself. The most learned Muratori was not unaware of this either, and he notes it; but he cautiously and wisely concludes:

> “Which of these writers should rather be trusted must be left to the judgment of others; perhaps both.”

What he himself proposed tentatively, however, one who weighs all the evidence need not fear to state categorically. We believe that the account Muratori presents from chapter 10, part I, page 156, of the fourth Benedictine century, is the very account that we have used. It is prefixed to the works of Alcuin, and in both places is said to have been written by a contemporary or peer.

The account that we have seen reads as follows:

> “For the great king, and now already emperor Charles, powerful through the grace of prayer and through his desire for a mutual conversation with Albinus, sought to visit the tomb of Saint Martin with his sons Charles, Pippin, and Louis. There, holding Albinus by the hand, he said secretly:
>
> “‘Master, which of these sons of mine seems to you likely to succeed me in this dignity, which God, although I am unworthy, has given me?’
>
> “But he, directing his face toward Louis, the last of them but the most distinguished in humility—a quality for which many despised him—said:
>
> “‘He will have Louis, the humble one, as an excellent successor.’
>
> “At that time Charles alone heard this. But when he saw the same kings walking through the church of Saint Stephen after the prayers, with their heads held high, while Louis walked humbly, he sat in the place where he wished to be buried and said to those standing beside him:
>
> “‘Do you see that Louis is more humble than his brothers? Certainly you will see him as his father’s most exalted successor.’
>
> “And when, after the communion of Christ’s body and blood, he administered it to them with his own hand, that same Louis, most distinguished in humility, bowed before the holy father more than the others and kissed his hand. Then the man of God said to Sigulf, who stood beside him:
>
> “‘Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted. Certainly, after his father, Francia will rejoice in having this man as emperor.’
>
> “‘We have now both seen this fulfilled and rejoice.’”

This is the account of the author of the *Life*, a contemporary—as these final words show—of Louis himself, the emperor whose future had been foretold.

When this account is compared with the preceding one, it should be clear that it is not the history of the same event but of an entirely different one. In this account Charles himself asks the question; in the other, Paulinus, without being asked, utters the prophecy. Here Charles is already emperor, as the author explicitly states: “and now already emperor Charles.”

Would one say that Paulinus did not recognize Charles’s sons before the year 800, when Charles was proclaimed emperor? I do not think so. Paulinus does not know Charles’s sons on the first occasion; Alcuin is not said to have been ignorant of any of them. Furthermore, Paulinus’s prophecy is single, simple, and spontaneous; Alcuin’s is elicited and repeated. There are therefore two events and two histories.

For Charles, having previously received the prophecy from Paulinus, also sought it from Alcuin—not because he doubted the earlier prophecy, but because he wished the second prophecy to confirm it, with another holy and blessed man also giving his support.

### IX

From this point until the year 792, it is not credible that Paulinus left the boundaries of his diocese, whether to visit the court or to attend councils. For just as the year 790 presents no war, military expedition, or journey of Charles, so it is marked by no council.

In the following year, 791, because of the movements of the Avars, against which Charles came to Regensburg in order to lead his army into Hungary, Paulinus did not abandon his Church. Rather, he must certainly have been present with counsel and assistance to protect his flock, which had been greatly frightened by the neighboring disturbances of war.

During this interval he turned his attention to restoring the affairs of the Church, reestablishing discipline, and refining the morals of the clergy and people.

## CHAPTER VI. Paulinus Travels to the Council of Regensburg. The Diploma Granted to Him There Is Examined.

### I

In the year 792, when a council had been summoned at Regensburg concerning Felix, bishop of Urgell, who was spreading adoptionism concerning Christ the Son of God, Paulinus went there. Together with the other Fathers, he willingly condemned the pestilential doctrine in a solemn ceremony.

In the fourth *Dissertation on the Heresy of Felix and Elipandus*, no. 32 and following, we have clearly demonstrated Paulinus’s presence at this assembly, as his own words indicate in book I, chapter 5, against Felix:

> “For in this contest of gymnastic disputation, it also happened that the person of our most humble insignificance was present.”

These words can be understood of no other synod at which Felix’s error was debated than this Council of Regensburg, as we demonstrate more fully in the same place.

Since Paulinus had attended this council, he obtained from Charles a privilege, which we present in full in Appendix II, no. 3. By it, the free election of future patriarchs of Aquileia was henceforth entrusted to the clergy [Col. 0058B] of the Church of Aquileia. In addition, certain exemptions from public burdens were granted to the same clerical congregation. All these matters must now be examined more carefully.

## II.

That the authority of princes sometimes intervened in the elections of bishops, and that on occasion the freedom of the electors was infringed, is sufficiently confirmed by the history of earlier times. Even in the very age of Paulinus, the first patriarch of Aquileia, the hands of princes were involved in episcopal elections, as Pope Pelagius writes to the patrician Valerian (in the letter cited above, chapter 1, no. 7): “You did not permit the bishop of Milan to be appointed until you had referred the matter from there to the most clement prince and had again learned from his written instructions what ought to be done.” The iniquity of those times made such conduct not merely tolerable but, for the most part, commendable. Nor was the Roman See itself free from the abuse of this excessively extended authority.

Since many examples of this matter occur, the single case of Pope Symmachus will suffice. It is taken from Anastasius the Librarian, in the same marginal note, no. 77. After describing the contention that arose over Symmachus’s election and was referred to Ravenna “for the judgment of King Theodoric,” he adds:

> “The clergy were again divided: some communicated with Symmachus, others with Laurentius. Then the senators Festus and Probinus sent a report to the king, and began to act so that the king might appoint a visitor for the apostolic see. Then the king appointed Peter, bishop of the city of Altinum, although the canons prohibited this.”

But in the council that was convened, Symmachus cleared himself of the charges brought against him, “and Peter of Altinum, the invader of the apostolic see, and Laurentius of Nocera were condemned, because, while Bishop Symmachus was alive, they had usurped his see.” Do you see how far the license of princes over the priests of God had proceeded?

Yet although the canons of the Fathers sometimes grant the clergy and people—though the people were united with the clergy—the power to elect bishops, as Pope Leo said to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, in letter 84, chapter 6: “When the will of all the clergy and all the citizens has been examined . . . let the best man be elected”; and although there is the example of Cornelius, of whom Cyprian writes in letter 52 of the latest edition:

> “Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and his Christ, by the testimony of nearly all the clergy, by the suffrage of the people who were then present, and by the assembly of the ancient priests and good men”;

so carefully—even, I would say, so reverently—did the Roman pontiffs themselves protect this norm of election that they would not at times permit their own authority to be involved in such matters.

Saint Gregory the Great wrote to the clergy of Milan, who were inclined toward the election of Constantine, commending the man who ought to be elected (book II, letter 29, indiction 11):

> “Nevertheless,” he added, “because the intention of my ancient deliberation is never to become involved on behalf of any person in undertaking the burdens of pastoral care, I shall support your election with prayers.”

Pope Adrian I likewise testified this about himself, and recommended it to Charlemagne in a letter listed as number 7 in volume VIII of the councils, namely letter 85 of the *Codex Carolinus*:

> “We have never been involved, nor ought we to become involved, in any election whatsoever. Nor do we wish your Excellency to undertake such a matter. But whoever has been canonically elected by the clergy, the people, and the entire populace, provided that there is nothing obstructing his sacred order, him we ordain according to the customary tradition.”

By this example and admonition—although Charles’s piety and the reverence he always showed toward the ecclesiastical hierarchy had no need of it—Charles made such progress that, if anything in this matter had hitherto been done improperly in any way, he took ample care to repair it at the Council of Aachen in 803, through the promulgation of its second canon, which reads as follows:

> “Not ignorant of the sacred canons, and wishing that the holy Church might more freely possess its honor in the name of God, we have given our ecclesiastical assent, namely, that bishops be elected from their own dioceses by the election of the clergy and people, according to the statutes of the canons, with all acceptance of persons and gifts removed, on account of the merit of their life and the gift of wisdom, so that they may be able to benefit their subjects everywhere by example and by word.”

Our Paulinus presided over the council that issued this capitulary, as legate of the apostolic see, as will be said in its proper place. Perhaps he himself was the mediator of Charles’s assent and judgment, having the common good of the churches in view. For earlier, at Regensburg, mindful of the statutes of the Fathers and of the disadvantages that follow from the intervention of lay authority in the election of ministers of the Church, he had wished to provide for his own church in the future by obtaining the privilege of which we are now speaking.

## III.

After the customary introductory formula of those times, the king speaks of the Church of Aquileia, over which “the venerable man Paulinus the patriarch presided, which was built in honor of holy Mary, the Mother of God, or of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, or of Saint Mark.””

At first sight he seems to have spoken too ambiguously, since the particles *vel* and *sive* appear to convey uncertainty. But in that age, which did not cultivate the stricter Muses, a disjunctive particle was used in place of a conjunction, as P. de Marca observes in *De Concordia sacerdotii et imperii*, book IV, chapter 5, and book VI, chapter 24. He says:

> “That word *vel* among writers of the Middle Ages is equivalent to the conjunction *et*. Thus, when you read in this canon ‘either bishops or counts,’ it must be understood as ‘both bishops and counts.’ Likewise, ‘to priests or servants of God’ means ‘and to servants of God,’ that is, abbots.”

From this you may gather which saints’ sacred honors belonged to the Church of Aquileia: namely, to the blessed Virgin Mary, Saint Peter, and Saint Mark, by whose preaching she was begotten in Christ Jesus through the Gospel.

Since you do not hear Saint Hermagoras and Saint Fortunatus, the holy martyrs, mentioned here, you may perhaps be troubled by the question whether their church was first dedicated to them only under Patriarch Poppo, since Poppo himself says in his document, published by Ughellus in volume V under Poppo:

> “I, Poppo . . . built this church and, together with several bishops, consecrated it in honor of holy Mary, the Mother of God and perpetual Virgin, and of the holy martyrs Hermagoras and Fortunatus.”

But do you not know that arguments drawn from negatives produce weaker proof? In the same Ughellus, in the same place, there is a diploma of Henry III at Regensburg in the year 1040, on the third day before the Nones of January, in which “the holy Church of Aquileia dedicated in honor of holy Mary” is mentioned; and another, issued at Augsburg in the same year, on the fourth day before the Ides of January, in which it is said to have been “built in honor of the holy martyrs Hermagoras and Fortunatus.” In the former, Saint Mary is named; in the latter, the names of the holy martyrs are named, while Mary’s is omitted.

Do not, therefore, infer from the omission of names that there was any lapse in our immemorial tradition, nor invent Poppo as its author. Rather, he confirmed what had already taken root among the people; he was not its originator.

The Martyrology inscribed with Jerome’s name, which Dacherius calls very ancient, publishing it in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, and acknowledging in his preface, together with Henri Valois, that it preceded the time of Gregory the Great, has the following entry under 12 July:

> “On the fourth day before the Ides of July: at Aquileia, Fortunatus and Armagerus.”

There is indeed an error in the date and in the name. But who does not see that under the name Armagerus our Hermagoras is indicated?

Moreover, the Martyrology of Wandalbert, likewise inserted by Dacherius in volume V of the *Spicilegium*, whose author, as he says in the preface, flourished around the year 845, has the following clearer entry for the fourth day before the Ides of July:

> “On the fourth [day of the Ides; note: ‘that is, on the Ides’], devout Aquileia honors Hermagoras,  
> The bishop who sustains the people and the city by prayers.”

Rather accuse more recent writers, who wrongly deprive us of the evangelist Mark, though he truly belongs to our Church as its parent. Do you wish a writer flourishing in the age of Paulinus as an unimpeachable witness? Consider Notker, who flourished in the ninth century and wrote his Martyrology around the year 894, as Basnage observes in volume II, part III, page 88 of Canisius’s *Antiquae Lectiones*, Amsterdam, 1725. He writes:

> “On the fourth day before the Ides of July: at Aquileia, the birth [that is, the feast] of Saint Hermagoras—or, as he is found in ancient manuscripts, Hermechora—the first bishop of that same city and disciple of Saint Mark the Evangelist. Also Fortunatus.”

The ancient manuscripts said to exist in the year 894 show that earlier centuries recognized Hermagoras as the first bishop of Aquileia and a disciple of Saint Mark.

## IV.

A little farther on we read:

> “The holy congregation itself, which there appears to lead its life under a holy order . . . shall have permission to elect a pastor over itself.”

From this you may see how strictly we said in chapter 4, section 5, that Paulinus cannot have been the patriarch to whom, when he was dying, Charles entrusted the election of his successor. Here permission to elect a pastor is granted to the congregation of clergy, with Paulinus himself intervening to secure the privilege.

Furthermore, it is implied that the clergy of Aquileia lived, as they say, a common life and under a rule. Nor do the words “appears to lead its life” convey any uncertainty. Elsewhere—if my memory does not fail—I shall say that in the writings of that period *videtur* appears to mean the same as *est*, “is.”

For just as monks observed the monastic rule, so clerics observed the clerical rule, which they also called the canonical rule and order. The former were placed under the authority of abbots, the latter under that of bishops.

In the Capitulary of Verona under Pepin, in the year 755, chapter 11, the following provision is made concerning both groups:

> “Concerning those men who say that they have tonsured themselves for God’s sake, and now possess their property or money, but are neither under the authority of a bishop nor living regularly in a monastery, it has been decided that they shall be in a monastery under a regular order, or under the authority of a bishop under a canonical order.”

Hence clerics were sometimes called *canonici*, or canons—not only because they were listed in the canon or register of the church, nor only because the church supplied them with the stipend called a *canon*, nor, preferably, for both reasons together. For clerics ordinarily did not become clerics unless they devoted themselves to the service and revenue of the church. Those who were enrolled in this register, and no others if there were any, received stipends and allowances, which Cyprian calls *sportulae* in letter 34. Hence they are called “brothers receiving allowances” by the same author in letter 66. But they were also called canons because of the canonical way of life and regular discipline that they professed.

Especially through the efforts of Charlemagne—perhaps also of Paulinus, who proposed and recommended what was already in use in his own church—the manner of such a clerical community living under a rule was urged at the assembly of Aachen, which Paulinus himself also attended, in the year 789. For chapter 71 of the Capitulary makes the following provision concerning clerics:

> “Those who enter the clerical state, which we call the canonical life, are to live in every respect canonically according to their rule, and their bishop is to govern their life, just as an abbot governs monks.”

Here, then, you have a common life, and consequently a community of clerics within the same buildings.

You will understand the arrangement of this discipline more clearly from the Council of Meaux in 845, whose canon 53 reads as follows:

> “Let the canons in the city or in monasteries, as has been established, sleep in a dormitory, eat in a refectory, and receive the necessary assistance in the infirmary; let the healthy and the sick alike be clothed canonically; let them remain in the cloisters at suitable hours; and under canonical supervision let them devote themselves to reading and to the other offices of divine instruction.
>
> “If, however, the bishop of the place lacks the means or resources to make this possible and arrange it, let the prince, according to the constitution of our lord Emperor Louis, give his assent. That is, if land belonging to the same church is found near the bishop’s residence and is possessed by another, it shall be returned to the rector of the church for the construction of cloisters for the clergy or for any other needs of the church. If it belongs to the fisc, let royal generosity bestow that land for the construction of dwellings for the servants of God. If it belongs to another house of God or to a private owner, permission shall be granted to exchange it by agreement. And if the poverty of the place is insufficient for building the necessary houses, let royal power compel those who retain property of that church as benefices to contribute toward the building.”

This was the arrangement of the clerical community around the time of Paulinus. The “holy congregation under a holy order” that the diploma mentions in the Church of Aquileia, and to which it grants free authority to elect its own pastor, was one of these communities of which we are speaking. Its clerics, because of their common life, were perhaps still called brothers in the year 1129, as appears from the charter of Azo’s donation appended in Appendix 2, no. 13.

This discipline continued in our Church for four centuries afterward, that is, in the year 1278, as is clear from the document that I shall gladly and willingly provide in Appendix 2, no. 19. In it Patriarch Raimundus, following the example, as he says, of other churches, arranges for the purchase, enlargement, and construction of buildings for the community of canons around our Church of Udine—now dedicated to the Mother of God greeted by the angel, but then sacred to Saint Ulrich the bishop.

From this document and from the document in Appendix 2, no. 20, let anyone who continues, out of envy toward our city, to deny the dignity of the chapter and canons—at least those instituted under Gregory of Montelongo, as in Appendix 2, no. 18—before the time of Saint Bertrand, who flourished around the middle of the following century, learn that he can neither speak correctly nor speak truthfully.

## V.

Among the exemptions from public burdens that Charles granted so that the clerics of the Aquileian congregation would not be oppressed by them was immunity from the *herbaticum*:

> “They shall not be required to pay the *herbaticum*.”

“*Herbaticum*, also called *herbagium*, is the right to cut grass,” according to Du Cange. Here, however, I would understand an exemption from supplying grass or hay—or, what seems more likely, from the fine, that is, the payment of money for hay and grass, which others were obliged to provide.

This is suggested by the exemptions that follow, from *mansionaticum* and *fodrum*, which were likewise granted to the same congregation under certain very honorable conditions:

> “We have granted in our charity to the aforesaid venerable man that no one among those serving the aforesaid church shall ever dare to impose or demand *mansionaticum* or *fodrum* from it at any time. Except if it should happen that we ourselves, or our beloved son Pepin, or the royal progress should come to the regions of Friuli because of enemy impediments, or to the border of Treviso: then, if necessity requires it, the men of our household may receive lodging there.”

*Mansionaticum* and *fodrum* were public burdens owed to the prince or redeemed by a substitute payment. The former consisted in preparing a place for lodging or residence. This was supplied either in kind—as in the passage in book II of the Capitularies, chapter 17: “In those places where roads and lodgings have now been arranged by our father,” and so forth—or by payment in coined money, as in chapter 11 of Charlemagne’s *Capitulare de Villis*:

> “Let no judge seize *mansionatica* . . .”

That is, let no judge demand the payments owed for assigned lodgings.

The latter, namely *fodrum* or *fodr*, denotes the provision of military supplies, which was demanded especially from Italian subjects when the Frankish kings descended into Italy to visit their kingdom. Otto of Freising, *De Rebus Gestis Friderici I Imperatoris*, book II, chapter 13, toward the end, writes:

> “For from ancient times, ever since the Roman Empire passed to the Franks and down to our own age, the custom has continued that whenever kings intend to enter Italy, they send ahead energetic men from their household, who, traveling through the individual cities and fortified towns, demand those things belonging to the royal fisc which the inhabitants call *fodrum*.”

The same author writes in chapter 23:

> “When *fodrum* was being demanded from the cities, the people of Spoleto incurred the prince’s indignation.”

Radevicus, book II, chapter 10:

> “Frederick sent messengers throughout Tuscany, the coastlands, and Campania to collect the *fodrum*.”

By this privilege, then, Charles exempted the clerics of the Church of Aquileia from these burdens, and indeed with Paulinus in view. For among the reasons expressly given for this grant, the third is:

> “So that they may recognize that we have granted and conceded everything on account of the compelling merits of Paulinus.”

## VI.

At the end, the place and date are noted as follows:

> “Done on the day before the Nones of August, in the twenty-fourth year and the nineteenth year of our reign. Executed at Regensburg in the royal palace. In God’s name, happily. Amen.”

This is the place where Charles had assembled the council concerning Felix. We assert with sufficient probability that the diploma was issued at the time of the council’s celebration.

For in the Saint-Denis chronicle, cited by Cointius under the year 792, no. 1, we read:

> “The Saxons killed the Franks on the river Alpia, near the sea, on the day before the Nones of July, a Friday.”

After this defeat, the discovery and condemnation of Pepin’s conspiracy against his father Charles follow in the Moissiac Chronicle and the Canisian manuscript. Cointius, in the same place, no. 2, writes:

> “In the Canisian manuscript and in the Moissiac Chronicle the following account immediately follows concerning Pepin, and so forth.”

The Lorsch annalist likewise says:

> “While the king was spending the summer there—that is, at Regensburg—a conspiracy was made against him by his elder son.”

Pepin was condemned as a rebel in the assembly held at Regensburg. The Moissiac Chronicle says:

> “When King Charles learned of the plot of Pepin and his accomplices, he assembled the Franks and his other faithful men at Regensburg, where the entire Christian people who were present with the king judged Pepin,” and so forth.

The Christian people who were then present there were an assembly of bishops and religious men summoned for the case of Felix. We have already shown that Paulinus attended this assembly; see Dissertation 4, *On the Heresy of Felix and Elipandus*, nos. 32 and following.

Since all these events occurred after the day before the Nones of July, and since we have here a diploma issued only one month later—that is, on the day before the Nones of August—it seems sufficiently probable that the date of the diploma was the date of the council and that it was obtained and issued on that occasion.

## VII.

The twenty-fourth year of the Frankish reign, begun in October of the year 768, is the year 792. Likewise, counting from the year 774, this was the nineteenth year of the Italian reign, if one considers that its epoch began in the months preceding the date of this diploma—perhaps April or May—from which Charles’s Italian, or Lombard, reign took its beginning.

For the nineteenth year of the Italian reign was running on the day before the Nones of August.

Fontanini, in his booklet *Delle Masnade*, page 21, unjustly accuses Mabillon of omission because, in his catalogue of the palaces of the Frankish kings, which he publishes in book IV of *De Re Diplomatica*, he omitted the palace of Regensburg, where we have seen that the diploma under discussion was issued.

The accusation is unjust and undeserved. It was not Mabillon himself but Michael the German who was the author of the work—Mabillon himself testifies that, “being prevented by illness and other matters, he transferred this task to him.” In that study Michael himself explains the matter in his own words, not Mabillon’s, as is stated there.

But Mabillon was so modest that he did not shift the error onto his associate. Instead, as though he himself had made the mistake, he thanked his accuser, as Fontanini himself relates in the book *De Vindiciis Diplomat[icis]*.

# CHAPTER VII  
## Paulinus’s deeds at the Council of Frankfurt; after his return he devotes himself to writing books and to celebrating the Council of Friuli

## I.

Since in a separate dissertation that we are presenting, *On the Heresy of Felix and Elipandus*, nos. 42 and following, we speak at greater length and in fuller detail about the Council of Frankfurt, the matters relevant to the present subject may be gathered there. Here we shall touch only on a few points.

In the year 794, when Fathers from the Franks, Aquitanians, Germans, and Italians were summoned to a synodal assembly, Paulinus came with them to Frankfurt, where Charles had celebrated Easter.

The council was not held immediately after that feast, and still less on Easter itself, as G. Cave maintains at the end of the eighth century. This is clear from Einhard’s *Annals*, where he writes:

> “At the beginning of summer, when he also held a general assembly of his people, the king assembled at the same place—Frankfurt—a council of all the bishops from all the provinces of his kingdom, to condemn the Felician heresy.”

Since Easter in the year 794 fell on 23 March, the council does not appear to have been convened on the Easter solemnity itself. Nor was it held—as the canons sometimes imply—on the third Sunday after Easter, which fell on 13 April, a date inconsistent with the beginning of summer.

But since this was not merely an assembly of bishops gathered for matters of faith, but also a *placitum*, as it was called, of the leading men of the kingdom for political affairs, it is not surprising that the canonical time was not observed with exact precision.

Add to this the distance of the episcopal sees from which the Fathers had to be summoned and the difficulty of travel while the weather was still harsh. Necessarily, therefore, the council had to find a time that, though later, was more suitable and convenient.

From the diploma to be cited below under no. 8, issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August to Anianus, abbot of the monastery of Caunes, it may be inferred that the council was convened around the end of June or the beginning of July. It was not celebrated in a single session, but, after the heresy had first been presented, the Fathers were given several days to consider the matter carefully and respond to the heresy, after which they assembled again.

Paulinus clearly indicates this in his *Sacrosyllabus* at the beginning:

> “One day,” he says, “when all were sitting together . . . at the king’s command, the letter of Elipandus was read.”

And below:

> “When a lengthy postponement of several days had been requested and granted, it was decided,” and so forth.

Since the diploma issued on 20 July was issued after the council had acted, and since the council lasted several days, it appears to have begun at least in early July or at the end of June.

## II.

G. Cave asserts that the number of bishops who attended rose to approximately three hundred. He adds that, because of the multitude of the Fathers, the council could be called universal.

Indeed, Paulinus himself calls it a plenary synod, while the continuator of the History of Paul the Deacon calls it a great council. This writer gives Paulinus first place among the Fathers, for he truly appeared to be the head and leader of the others.

In reviewing them—as Scripture does with the more courageous soldiers of David in 2 Samuel 23—he presents three men who were strong and more distinguished and eminent than the rest: Paulinus first, as the noblest among the three; then Peter of Milan; and third, Alcuin.

Speaking of the Felician heresy, he says:

> “This heresy was destroyed by the most holy men Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, and Peter, archbishop of Milan, and Alcuin, archdeacon of the island of Britain, together with the other bishops,” and so forth.

Charles himself preserves this order in his letter addressed to the Spanish bishops, together with the decrees and judgment of the council. After giving the text of the letter of Adrian, the supreme pontiff, he presents the *Sacrosyllabus*, and places third the letter of the bishops of Gaul and the others.

## III.

The *Sacrosyllabus* is a booklet in which Paulinus attacks and crushes the Felician heresy. We shall discuss it in its proper place.

Cointius, under the year 794, no. 15, says that it was written at Frankfurt while the synod was being held there. But since it is found published in two forms—as Cointius himself observes under the same year, no. 7—in one edition using the singular *censeo, decerno* (“I judge, I decree”), and in the other using the plural *censemus, decernimus* (“we judge, we decree”), I think that Paulinus, who understood very well what was to be done at Frankfurt, prepared the book at home as a private teacher before going to the council.

When the booklet was read at the council and pleased everyone, however, and when it was to be sent in the common name to the obstinate Spanish bishops by the universal sanction of the council, it was copied at Frankfurt. A suitable beginning referring to the present circumstances was added, and the plural number was substituted for the earlier singular by Paulinus himself. Thus both versions transmitted by the two editions are true.

According to one of the editions, Cointius is also correct in saying that it was written at Frankfurt: namely, it was reshaped in a new transcription to fit the character of a conciliar address.

This is suggested by the silence concerning Bishop Peter of Milan in one edition, whereas in the other his name is added and his presence indicated. While Paulinus was staying at home, he could not have known precisely which bishops would attend the council or which would assist him more than the others, and therefore he added no one’s name.

But when Peter of Milan gave him his support after the matter had been brought onto the stage, and stood out among the Italian bishops, Paulinus, grateful to his valiant fellow soldier, expressed the name of his most welcome comrade in arms in the second edition of the book.

For Peter of Milan, see Dissertation 4, no. 44.

## IV.

The aim Charles pursued through this synod was the proscription of the Felician heresy. Accordingly, the first decree, or canon, among the fifty-six enacted there, dealt with it, just as the first question proposed was the elimination of that heresy:

> “At the beginning of the capitular matters a question arose concerning the impious and abominable heresy of Elipandus, bishop of the see of Toledo, and of Felix of Urgel, and their followers, who, thinking wrongly, asserted adoption in the Son of God. All the most holy Fathers mentioned above rejected this heresy and contradicted it with one voice, and they decreed that this heresy should be utterly eradicated from the holy Church.”

The Fathers who, in words, pronounced judgment against the heresy with such unanimity likewise all subscribed, with equal unanimity, to Paulinus’s *Sacrosyllabus*, which vigorously attacked it.

Einhard writes in his *Annals*:

> “At this council the heresy in question was condemned, and a book against it was composed with the common authority of the bishops, in which they all subscribed.”

In Dissertation 4, no. 45, we have shown that this book can be none other than Paulinus’s *Sacrosyllabus*.

## V–VI.

Many matters apart from the question of the Felician heresy were also conducted. The second canon that is transmitted plainly speaks of the abolition of the Second Council of Nicaea because of the veneration of images.

We do not wish to undertake here an examination of what Catholics and modern heretics put forward concerning this question, since nowhere in his writings do we find Paulinus involved in it.

It is certainly remarkable and worthy of consideration that two matters of faith were treated at the same synod and defined in two immediately successive chapters, yet one of them was touched upon so meagerly that you do not even find it mentioned by Paulinus; and that in the letters of Charles to Adrian and of Adrian to Charles there is an equal silence about the other.

Paulinus never speaks of the question of images, but of the Felician heresy. In the letters attributed to Adrian and Charles, images are discussed, while the Felician heresy is not mentioned even in a dream.

What is the meaning of Paulinus’s silence in a matter so serious and so consonant with the subject, since he was dealing with matters of faith? And, conversely, what is the meaning of Charles’s and Adrian’s silence in a matter so evident and well known?

Since the case of Felix is not disputed and is acknowledged by everyone, whereas the other question concerning images is disputed and attacked by many, it at least becomes suspect on this account and appears less probable.

But concerning these matters, as we have said, let others judge.

## VII.

Besides the matter touching doctrine, affairs of various kinds were conducted. In the area of discipline, a penance was imposed on Heistulf.

It is greatly surprising that historians have been so barren of information that no slight memory, but virtually no memory at all, of this matter can be said to have survived. For apart from the title of the letter—which allows one to understand only the bare outline of the event, not to know the history of what happened—nothing is found in the editions of either the councils or the canons, where the letter is usually published, that leads to knowledge of the event.

The title reads as follows:

> “Here begins the letter of Paulinus, patriarch of Friuli, issued at the famous place called Frankfurt, in the great synod, against Felix the heretic, concerning Heistulf, who killed his wife on account of adultery.”

This is the entire history. If anything has nevertheless seemed worthy of clarification, I shall explain it as fully as I am able in the notes when that letter is discussed.

## VIII.

Another matter that may be counted among the more favorable ones is the diploma, or royal precept, of Charlemagne, “issued on the third day before the Kalends of August, in the twenty-sixth year and the twentieth year of his reigns, at Frankfurt in the royal palace.” Baluzius publishes it in volume II of the *Capitularies*, page 1399, in Appendix 1 of the *Acta Veterum*, no. 18.

The year of the Frankish reign and the place agree very well with this celebration of the council, except that the Italian year is actually the twenty-first, having begun in May. But perhaps you will find some other epoch for the Italian reign beginning later in May, just as, when treating the Council of Friuli together with Pagius, we found an earlier one.

For the Italian reign did not have a single fixed epoch.

The diploma itself also suggests that Anianus, abbot of Caunes, came with his monks to the council to request a favor, as Baluzius also observes in his notes on the Council of Frankfurt:

> “Let your greatness, or your usefulness, know that the venerable man Anianus, abbot of the monastery of Saint John and Saint Lawrence, which was built in the places called Exorio and Olibegio, coming to our synodal council together with the monks Continuus, Stromundus, and Lurius, fully commended himself, with all the property or possessions of his monastery that he appears at the present time to possess, and so forth.
>
> “Therefore we have given him this document for the sake of firmness, by which we command absolutely, and so forth. Likewise, we have granted him the village of Cannas, just as Milo assigned it to his monastery by his own document,” and so forth.

In Mabillon, *De Re Diplomatica*, book VI, no. 58, the wording varies somewhat and the names of the monks are absent. It reads instead:

> “With his monks, and under our protection, with all his property,” and so forth.

Perhaps the barbarous writing is the cause of the differing interpretation.

In any case, the date agrees on both sides with the place and time. Since the document says, “coming to our synodal council,” you may infer that Anianus, Continuus, Stromundus, and Lurius attended the Council of Frankfurt. For no other council was held at Frankfurt in that year apart from this one under discussion.

But since the diploma was issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, it is plainly evident that the council had already been celebrated, since the diploma mentions matters that had already followed at the council: namely, Anianus’s request on behalf of his monastery and Charles’s acknowledgment, which he subsequently confirms by the diploma now issued.

The diploma is found in Appendix 1, no. 11.

## IX.

Besides the monks just mentioned, whom the affairs of their monastery had summoned to the council, there were also those whom the affairs of the Church and of the faith had brought together. Among the foremost were the legates of the Roman pontiff, Theophylact, Stephen, and Peter of Milan.

I had suspected that Theophylact was the bishop of Todi, who in the year 787 attended the Council of Calchuth in England as Adrian’s legate, together with Gregory, bishop of Ostia. Then I came upon P. Cointius, who confirmed the suspicion under the year 796, no. 43, writing the following about the Council of Calchuth:

> “Theophylact may have governed the Church of Todi until the year of Christ 796, when Todi passed from the Greeks to the Franks. Perhaps he was none other than Bishop Theophylact, the legate of Pope Adrian, who attended the Council of Frankfurt two years earlier.”

Stephen—perhaps the bishop of Cremona—was the man whom Adrian, with the support of Charlemagne, raised to that see in the year 776, and whom he retained until the year 816.

Charles’s intervention on his behalf indicates that Stephen was among Charles’s intimates. It therefore makes it probable that Adrian, who was always seeking opportunities to win Charles’s favor, sent Stephen as a legate to the Council of Frankfurt, considering that he would be acceptable to the king.

On this matter see Ughellus under the bishops of Cremona, no. 29.

Peter of Milan has been discussed in Dissertation 4, no. 44. Let this one point be added here: Papebrochius, in the *Exegesis on the Milanese Bishops* prefixed to volume VII of the *Sanctorum Mensis Junius*, cited shortly afterward by Pagius, does not accept the privileges published by Ughellus, especially because in them Peter is called Oldradus, evidently in honor of a family of that name.

For bishops were not accustomed to use surnames in the time of Charlemagne; indeed, the common opinion holds that surnames had not yet been invented.

There is a letter bearing his name concerning the translation of the body of Saint Augustine from Sardinia to Pavia, reproduced in full by Baronius under the year 725, no. 2. Pagius, under the same year, no. 2, likewise argues that it is spurious, just as he does the privileges.

He is given the title “Hammer of the Heretics” by Charlemagne, according to Ughellus, because Peter opportunely subdued the Arian heretics, both by writing and by force of arms.

We do not dispute—far be it from us—the honor of the title or the merit implied by the name; in Dissertation 4, in the passage cited, we confirm it by the authority of Ripamonti.

We merely wonder that, when the Felician heresy had been brought to the Frankfurt anvil, the clamor of this Hammer—or, rather, Peter’s voice—was not heard.

But let us return to our Paulinus, coming back from the council and now returned.

[Col. 0068D] **X.** After the Synod of Frankfurt, and after the final funeral rites had been performed there for Queen Fastrada, the wife of Charles, who had died there and was buried at Saint Alban near the city of Mainz, the province of Friuli joyfully welcomed back its shepherd. He considered nothing more important than to devote himself to his pastoral care, to regulate the morals of the people with vigilant pastoral concern, and to shine before clergy and people as an example of every form of holiness. Yet, since these efforts did not seem sufficient for the immense ardor with which he burned to win souls, and since he wished at once to provide for the salvation of those living then and of those to come, he devoted himself to writing books, so that he might strengthen what was sound and set straight what had been distorted.

Thus the year 795 saw Paulinus writing a book of *Exhortation* [Col. 0069A] to Henry, duke of Friuli, with whom a mutual friendship, cultivated over seven years, had grown strong. Concerning him and the book addressed by Paulinus to him, consult our first Dissertation in order. In the year 796 he undertook to compile three books against Felix; these are discussed in Dissertation 4, on the heresy of Felix and Elipandus. His literary occupation, however, did not exempt him from the practice of a stricter life or from caring for the poor. “Though occupied in these matters,” says Ferrarius, writing about him in the *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy* under 11 January, “he nevertheless relaxed nothing of the austerity of his life: for he constantly pursued fasts, vigils, pious meditations, and the other spiritual exercises.” Above all, however, his zeal for ecclesiastical discipline shone forth in the celebration of the Council of Friuli [Col. 0069B], concerning which more will be said in Dissertation 2, the principal one.

How great his devotion to God was, and how ardent his charity, is attested by more than one letter of Alcuin. You will find these, together with his other letters to Paulinus, arranged in order in the Appendix. For the most part, Paulinus asked that prayers be offered to God on his behalf, placing the greatest confidence in them. But we shall discuss these matters when the subject returns to Paulinus’s relationship and intimacy with Alcuin. Meanwhile, when Alcuin himself wrote to Henry, duke of Friuli, he commended him to Paulinus—not merely as a teacher and master of the spiritual life, but as a mirror and example of Christian conduct—as is clear from Letter 94, to be inserted in Appendix 1, no. 4.

# CHAPTER VIII. Paulinus’s Apostolate among the Carantanians and Avars

[Col. 0069C]

**I.** That before the year 798 Paulinus undertook the labors of apostolic ministry among the Carantanians and Avars will become clear from what follows. It is therefore appropriate to speak of these matters here, although it is not easy or certain to assign each individual action to the particular year in which it occurred. The opinion of the writers is consistent: Paulinus sowed the seed of God’s word among the neighboring peoples of Carinthia and carried the torch of the Gospel to the Avars after they had been subdued by Charles’s arms.

Hear Ferrarius, in the work just cited: “He devoted himself to evangelical preaching, by which he converted the peoples of Carinthia and the neighboring nations to the faith of Christ. He desired martyrdom, although he did not obtain what he wished; nevertheless, he suffered many injuries and hardships at the hands of barbarians.” So too Bollandus in the *Life*, no. 16.

[Col. 0069D]

**II.** I do not deny that the Carantanians had been instructed in the doctrine of Christ and cleansed in the sacred waters long before Paulinus’s time. For in the *Life of Saint Severinus the Abbot*, called the apostle of Noricum, which Surius reproduces from Eugippius, his disciple, in volume I for January—his death having occurred on the sixth day before the Ides—another Paulinus is foretold by Saint Severinus as bishop of Teurnia.

“When the presbyter Paulinus returned to his homeland, the saying concerning him as a preacher was fulfilled. For the citizens of Tigurina, which is the metropolis of Noricum, compelled that same presbyter to assume the highest priestly office.”

In the Cologne edition of 1576, *Tigurinae* is marked with an asterisk, indicating a reading that is not certain. But, with Norisius, in the *Dissertation on the Fifth Synod*, chapter 9, § 4, do not hesitate to understand Teurnia [Col. 0070A] as the city on the Drava. For he says this about Leonicus, bishop of Tiburnia under Elias, who came to the Council of Grado:

“The chief city of Noricum was Tiburnia on the Drava, as is clear from the *Life of Saint Severinus, the Apostle of the Noricans*.”

Lazius agrees that Teurnia, or Tiburnia, was situated in Carinthia, although he now says that its site is occupied by Racstad in the territory of Salzburg; Cluverius agrees, although he wishes it to have been Villach, in the territory of the bishop of Bamberg; and Schönleben agrees, although he thinks it was the town of Solva, or Solvente, near Klagenfurt, which Ferrarius, in his *Geographical Lexicon*, places in Carinthia under the jurisdiction of the bishop of Lorch. Whichever site you accept as having been substituted by the geographers, you do not go beyond Carinthia or far from the river Drava.

Saint Severinus died in the year [Col. 0070B] 481 or thereabouts. Therefore, before that year, Carinthia was counted among the Christian provinces, and its bishop is foretold by Saint Severinus. That in the year 579 it belonged to the jurisdiction of Aquileia is indisputably attested by Leonianus, bishop of Tiburnia, who came to the Council of Grado under Elias.

That after this synod it defected from Aquileia before the year 591 is equally clear. For at a gathering—not, indeed, the council of Marano, as Schönleben thought in the *Apparatus to the Annals of Carniola*, chapter 5, § 7, no. 11, as is evident from the subscription of Augustine, bishop of Concordia, who subscribed the document cited shortly below but had subscribed neither the council of Marano nor the Council of Grado, and who is the most illustrious witness on both sides—at a gathering, I say, held at an unknown place and listed among the councils under the year 591, the provincial bishops of Aquileia complain in a document addressed to the Emperor Maurice that the Church of Tiburnia had been withdrawn from the metropolitan of Aquileia.

Whether at that time they had also defected from the faith is doubtful. For in the age of our Paulinus they were truly being drawn back to the faith. The work of Virgil of Salzburg and of his successor Arno in the conversion of the Carantanians cannot be denied from the ecclesiastical annals.

**III.** Yet do not exclude Paulinus from this province of gathering souls; it is beyond doubt that he brought distinction to this field. Aeneas Silvius, in *Europe*, chapter 20, relates the following event, which I shall not hesitate to transcribe, since it sheds considerable light upon the view just expressed:

“It is reported,” he says, “that in the year 790 after the birth of Christ the Savior, while Charles the Great was emperor, a leader of the people named Ingo prepared a great banquet for the inhabitants of the province. He admitted the peasants into his presence and ordered that they be served in golden and silver vessels, but placed the nobles and magistrates far from his sight and ordered that they be served in earthenware. When asked why he did this, he replied that those who inhabited cities and lofty palaces were not as clean as those who lived in fields and humble cottages.

“The peasants, who had received the Gospel of Christ and had been purified by the water of baptism, possessed souls that were white and bright; but the nobles and powerful, who followed the filthiness of idols, had souls that were dirty and black as pitch. Thus he arranged the banquet according to the quality of their souls. The nobles, chastened by this treatment, sought the waters of holy baptism in crowds, and within a short time, under Virgil and Arno, bishops of Juvavia, all received the faith of Christ.”

**IV.** When you hear that nobles were converted to the faith in the year 790, pause for a moment and consider the date of this conversion. Virgil had died in 784. Thus Schönleben assigns his death to 797, or to 785, as Pagius holds on the basis of the epitaph that gives Virgil nearly forty years of episcopate and which proves that he was appointed to the see of Salzburg, or Juvavia, in 746:

> He joyfully ruled the five heights of this present see  
> For almost four times ten years with his beloved brothers.

And if you believe Cointius—although, according to Pagius under the year 785, no. 11, he had not seen these verses—you will assign the year 780 to Virgil’s death.

Virgil therefore could not have baptized the Carantanians in 790. Moreover, Arno does not appear to have gone to Carinthia before the year 798, although it cannot be denied that he had earlier ascended the see of Juvavia—namely, after Virgil’s death, as Pagius holds. Since Virgil died on the fourth day before the Kalends of December in 785, Pagius thinks that Arno’s accession should be assigned to the following year, 786. Or it may have occurred after the death of Bertricus, Virgil’s successor, whom Cointius places between Virgil and Arno under the years 780 and 781. There he also admits that Brusch, Hundius, and Bucelinus established a chronology four years later. Just as they place Virgil’s death in 784 or 785, so they place Bertricus in the see in 785 or 786; and all unanimously assign him no more than one year of episcopate.

Thus Arno was bishop of Salzburg in 790. Yet we do not believe that during this interval he went to Carinthia [Col. 0071C] to bring its peoples back to the faith. For the disciple of Saint Eberhard writes as follows in the *Life of Saint Rupert*, the first bishop of Salzburg, printed by Canisius in volume III, part II, *Ancient Readings*, Amsterdam, 1725:

“Meanwhile it happened, namely in the year of the Lord’s birth 798, that Arno, already archbishop and having received the pallium from Pope Leo, while returning from Rome came beyond the Po. There he encountered a messenger of Charles carrying a letter, ordering him on that very journey to go into the regions of the Slavs, inquire into the will of that people, and preach the word of God there.

“But because he was unable to do this before he delivered the response to his embassy, he hurried to the emperor and reported to him everything that Pope Leo had commanded through him. After completing his embassy, the emperor himself ordered Archbishop Arno [Col. 0071D] to go into the regions of the Slavs, to provide for the whole region, to cultivate ecclesiastical worship according to episcopal custom, and to strengthen the peoples in faith and Christianity by preaching. Arno did so: coming there, he consecrated churches, ordained presbyters, and instructed the people by preaching. On his return he reported to the emperor that great things could be accomplished there if someone undertook the task.

“Then the emperor asked him whether he had any ecclesiastical man who could win souls for God there. He replied that he had such a man, one who would please God and could become shepherd to that people. Then, by order of the emperor, Theodoric was ordained bishop by Arno, archbishop of Juvavia. Arno himself [Col. 0072A] and Count Gerold brought him into Sclavinia and delivered him into the hands of the princes. They entrusted to that bishop the region of the Carantanians and their neighbors on the western side of the Drava, as far as the Drava flows into the river Danube, so that he might govern the people with authority, teach them through his preaching and evangelical doctrine to serve God, dedicate the churches that had been built, establish ordained presbyters, and complete all ecclesiastical ministry in those regions as the canonical order requires. He held authority over and subjection from the rulers of Juvavia, just as he did for as long as he lived.”

Cointius, no. 49, and Pagius, no. 6, both under the year 798, observe that the writer here calls Charles emperor in advance, although he was not so called until two years later.

**V.** From this account it appears certain that this was Arno’s first journey into Carinthia to sow the faith of Jesus Christ. This may be inferred especially from the words: “He taught the people by preaching, and on his return reported to the emperor that great things could be accomplished there, if someone [undertook the task].”

If he had visited Carinthia earlier, he would have observed the character of the people and would have known not merely that the task would be easy. Before he had come, on this occasion he could have awakened hope in Charles’s heart of winning souls from prior experience. Since, therefore, Arno first approached the Carantanians in 798, he did not convert them to Christ in 790.

Schönleben places Arno’s arrival in Carinthia and Theodoric’s inauguration as bishop in 788, advancing them by a decade. But he is mistaken, since the author cited expressly says that this happened in 798. Moreover, before that year Arno was not archbishop of Juvavia; he was first appointed to that see by Leo at this time, and therefore did not possess legitimate power to appoint a bishop in Carinthia.

I therefore think that from Virgil’s death until Arno’s arrival in Carinthia, Paulinus carried out the apostolate among that people. What Aeneas Sylvius relates concerning the banquet given by Ingo in 790 is assigned to the year 803 by an anonymous writer published by Canisius in volume III, part II, in the *Life of Saint Rupert*, shortly before the end, cited above. We do not deny that at that time Arno assisted the Carantanians, if not by right, at least in fact.

[Col. 0072D]

**VI.** Schönleben [XXXI] and Megiserus, whom he cites, say that a dispute arose between Paulinus and Arno concerning the province of Carinthia in this year, 798. Yet that the dispute was settled in 811 is argued by Morocutus from a diploma of Charles, in Ughellus’s account of Paulinus.

If this quarrel truly arose at that time, Paulinus certainly recognized that he had a right in the matter. That right consisted in the fact that Carinthia had formerly belonged to the diocese of Aquileia, as is clear from the cited diploma. If Paulinus therefore believed Carinthia to be part of his province, it is not surprising that he went there to instruct it; indeed, it is improbable that he did not go.

But what Schönleben and the authors whom he cites say—that in this year, 798, the dispute over boundaries between Paulinus and Arno was settled by Charles’s authority—does not seem admissible, since the diploma says that the question had been raised [Col. 0073A] between Ursus, otherwise Urbanus, Paulinus’s successor, and Arno. Nor was it settled under Ursus, but only under Maxentius, who succeeded Ursus:

“Let it be known,” says Charles, “how the venerable men Ursus, patriarch of the holy Church of Aquileia, and Arno, archbishop of the Church of Juvavia, had a considerable dispute concerning the province of Carantania, as to which of their dioceses it ought to belong.”

If Paulinus had initiated the question, the emperor would have said that the dispute had arisen not between Ursus and Arno but between Paulinus and Arno, and that it had been settled under Maxentius. Since Charles wishes to extend the origin and beginning of the dispute to its authors, as is clear to anyone examining the diploma, and does not name Paulinus but Ursus, it is Ursus, not Paulinus, who must be regarded as the instigator of the dispute.

Charles’s decision was as follows:

“We ordered the aforesaid province of Carantania to be divided between them, so that the river Drava, which runs through the middle of that province, would be the boundary of both dioceses; and that from the southern bank the portion of the province should belong to the ruler of the Church of Aquileia, while from the northern bank it should belong to the bishop of the Church of Juvavia.”

These boundaries are still observed.

Since, therefore, the dispute raised by Ursus was concluded under Maxentius in 811, it is entirely false that it was settled and buried in 798 by Charles’s authority. It seems most probable, however, that, since we see Arno ordaining bishops in Carinthia in 798, Paulinus did not extend his apostolate among the Carantanians beyond that year.

[Col. 0073C]

**VII.** That Paulinus, inflamed by the same zeal for the faith with which he had spread the word of God among the Carantanians, also spread it among the Avars is suggested by arguments of no little weight. Perhaps as early as 791 he followed the forces of Henry, duke of Friuli, when they were sent against the Avars for the advancement of Christianity. We suspect that he was the bishop of whom Charles the Great speaks in his letter to Queen Fastrada concerning the Avar victory; on this matter see Dissertation 1, nos. 15, 16, and 17.

Having found a suitable opportunity from this victory and gathering the fruits of the peace that had been won, Paulinus in the following years turned his attention to the complete conversion of the Avars. For, according to the Bertinian Annals, in 795, while Charles was staying at Hiliun on the river Elbe in order to restrain the Saxons, who had broken their treaty and rebelled again, they sent their envoys:

“Messengers arrived from Tudun, who possessed great power among the people and kingdom of the Avars. They said that Tudun himself, with his land and people, wished to surrender to the king.”

Father Melchior Inchofer, S.J., in his *Annals of the Church of Hungary* under this year, 795, suspects various reasons that moved this Tudun, or Thudinus, or Theudo—for he is called by these various names, whether he was a king, as some hold, or, as others, in my more probable opinion, a dynast of greater power among the leading men—to renounce the superstition of idols and embrace the faith of Christ. Among these reasons he includes the following:

“There was also the exhortation of certain pious priests who, from time to time, penetrated into Hungary to win souls for the kingdom of Christ.”

To count Paulinus among these men, or even to make him their leader and chief, is not at all contrary to probability. For he possessed such concern for spreading the faith and such zeal for promoting the salvation of souls that he eagerly seized every opportunity offered to him.

When you hear that envoys came rushing to Charles in 795, this indicates that in preceding years apostolic labors had been carried out in their regions by heralds of the word of God. Perhaps Paulinus, whose recorded deeds between 791 and 794, when he took part in the Synod of Frankfurt, are preserved only very sparsely, spent this three-year interval laboring in the conversion of the Avars, as well as of the Carantanians, by making excursions here and there.

[Col. 0074B]

**VIII.** Nor was the effort without results. For in 796, “Tudun, in accordance with his promise, came with a large part of the Avars to the king, who was then staying at Aachen, and surrendered himself, his people, and his homeland to the king. He and the people were baptized, and after receiving gifts of honor they returned,” as the Bertinian annalist says.

The aforementioned Father Inchofer adds:

“It must not be supposed that Theodorus, after joining the Christians and departing from Charles adorned with gifts, returned to his homeland without taking with him religious and learned companions who would establish more deeply the roots of faith in the recently converted people and instruct them in every form of solid piety. This would have been contrary to the custom and diligence of so Catholic a ruler, Charles, to whom nothing was more important than extending the kingdom of Christ by sending suitable men to cultivate it, men who would everywhere establish both religion and priesthoods.”

And upon whom could Theudo more reasonably fix his eyes than upon Paulinus, whom he knew very well would not be a stranger to his people, and of whom he knew that the seeds of their conversion had first been scattered, as we have argued?

[Col. 0074D]

**IX.** But that the eyes of the Palatine court also turned toward Paulinus, to whom this province was to be entrusted, Alcuin, Paulinus’s friend above all others, expressly teaches in Letter 112 in the Appendix [Note: [Col. 0073] See Appendix 1, no. 1, Letter 5. (*Patrologia*, volume CI).], which is to be given in full. He writes:

“In whose”—that is, God’s—“power and grace a wondrous triumph has been achieved over the people of the Avars. Their envoys, sent to our lord the king, promise peaceful submission and the faith of Christianity. Although this is truly the work of divine grace preceding them, who among the servants of God ought to withdraw from so pious and praiseworthy a labor, by which the savagery of the devil may be destroyed and the service of Christ the Lord increased? Yet the eyes of very many are fixed upon you, excellent father, to see what your venerable holiness wishes to do. For the proximity of the regions is suited to you, the distinction of wisdom is yours, the excellence of authority is sought in you, and all the qualities seem to converge in you that appear necessary for such a work.”

This was, as the saying goes, “rather to spur on one who is already running than to stir up one who is sluggish,” as Cicero once said in Book II of *On the Orator*.

[Col. 0075A]

**X.** Alcuin wrote to Charles more than once, urging him to send suitable preachers of the word of God and capable priests who might prudently administer the task entrusted to them.

His Letter 7 [Note: [Col. 0075] See Appendix 1, no. 3, Letter 2. (*Patrologia*, volume CI).] bears this heading:

“To the most excellent lord Charles, king of Germany, Gaul, and Italy, most devoted to every honor of Christ, and to the holy preachers of the word of God: Albinus, the humble little son of holy Mother Church, sends greetings of eternal glory in Christ.”

It begins as follows:

“Glory and praise be to God the Father and to our Lord Jesus Christ, because through the grace of the Holy Spirit, by means of your devotion and ministry and your holy faith and good will, he has extended the kingdom and knowledge of Christianity and has led very many peoples, far and wide, from the errors of impiety into the way of truth.”

And below:

“You subject under your scepters the peoples and nations of the Huns, once fearsome in their ancient savagery and strength, while they serve you with due honor.
