By grace going before them, he has bound their long-exceedingly proud necks beneath the yoke of the sacred faith and poured the light of truth into minds long blinded by antiquity. But now may your most wise and God-pleasing devotion provide for the new people pious preachers, honorable in conduct, instructed in knowledge of the sacred faith, and imbued with the precepts of the Gospel; men devoted also to the examples of the holy apostles [xxxii] and of the preaching of the word of God, who in the beginning of faith were accustomed to minister milk—that is, gentle teachings—to their hearers.”

And further below, after he has urged Charles not to exact payments of tithes from those neophytes, lest they be turned away from the faith they had recently received—a subject we discuss in the *Observations on Canon 14 of the Council of Friuli*, no. 8—he adds:

“This too must be considered with the greatest care: that the ministry of preaching and the sacrament of baptism be carried out in an orderly manner, lest the sacred washing of baptism in the body be of no benefit if knowledge of the catholic faith has not first preceded it in the rational soul.”

Moved by these arguments, whom could Charles have entrusted with the task more suitably than Paulinus? The entire court was awaiting his departure and preaching among the Avars, as Alcuin used to say.

Thus a recent writer, Father Michael Bombardus, S.J., in the *Topography of the Great Kingdom of Hungary*, p. 42, praises him as the apostle of Pannonia, writing:

“But since the subject of the original religion of the Hungarians arises here, I dare not pass over it without confessing that, prompted by a particular zeal toward Saint Paulinus, patriarch and, if I am not mistaken, apostle of Hungary, I am almost exceeding the limits that I recently imposed upon myself . . . Since Paulinus, on account of the holiness of his morals, was especially esteemed by Charles the Great and by his teacher Alcuin Flaccus, he is believed to have been appointed to preach the faith to the Huns and Avars, whom Charles had conquered by arms.”

[Col. 0075D]

**XI.** But since Ferrarius says that he suffered injuries and hardships from the enemies of the faith, it should be understood that although in 796 Theudo and his followers had been cleansed by baptism, a considerable part of the Huns still remained, with Caghan as their leader, stubbornly attached to the old superstition. It may have been from these people that Paulinus suffered ill-treatment.

In this year Charles ordered his son, King Pippin of Italy, to advance into Pannonia with his forces, so that he might also suppress those whom he found still resisting. He did so, bringing back to his father, who was staying at Aachen, remnants of the treasures already captured by Henry, duke of Friuli, who had gone ahead and crushed the Huns in an earlier defeat, as we explain in Dissertation 1, § 18.

While Pippin was still staying in Pannonia, responsibility for the necessary provision of ministers of salvation for the new Christian people was entrusted not to Paulinus—who already had a sufficiently extensive province and was weighed down by too heavy a burden of duties—but to Arno [Col. 0076B].

The author published by Canisius in volume III of the *Ancient Readings*, cited above but not hitherto mentioned together, after recounting the victories of Henry and Pippin under this year, 796, adds concerning Pippin:

“On his return from there, he assigned to Bishop Arno of Juvavia the care, with instruction and ecclesiastical ministry, of that part of Pannonia around the lower lake of Pelissa, beyond the river called Rapa—that is, the Arabo, commonly called the Rab—and thus as far as the river Drava, and from there to where the Drava flows into the Danube, insofar as he possessed authority; namely, the care of the people who remained from the Huns and Slavs in those regions, until the presence of his father, Charles the emperor.”

Yet you should not believe that Paulinus was altogether excluded from Pannonia, since Pannonia extended on this side of the Drava [Col. 0076C], as may be seen in Christopher Cellarius’s *Maps of Ancient Geography*, Book II, chapter 8.

What Pippin appears to have done by way of what is called a provisional arrangement—entrusting the new Church to Arno until King Charles should ratify it—was completed only in 803. The author just cited, concerning Charles’s confirmation of Pippin’s action, writes:

“In the year of the Lord 803, the Emperor Charles entered Bavaria, and in the month of October came to Salzburg. Repeating his son’s aforesaid grant, he confirmed it with authority in the presence of many of his faithful and granted that it should remain unshaken forever.”

He then commends Arno’s zeal in advancing the faith in Sclavinia—that is, Carinthia and lower Pannonia—and recounts the action of Duke Ingo, who:

“Truly invited the believing servants to table with him, and made those who ruled over them, being unbelievers, sit outside like dogs, placing bread and meat before them, together with dark vessels containing wine, so that they might take their food there. But he ordered the servants to drink from gilded cups.

“Then the leading men outside asked, ‘Why do you treat us in this way?’ He replied, ‘You are not worthy to share with those reborn in the sacred font, but must take your food outside the house like dogs.’

“After this, having been instructed in the holy faith, they ran eagerly to be baptized, and thereafter the Christian religion continued to grow.”

The anonymous author, using simpler words than Aeneas Sylvius above in no. 3, assigns Ingo’s action and the fuller conversion of the Carantanian nobles not to 790, as Sylvius does, but to this year, 803.

Therefore, since you see that Pippin entrusted Pannonia to Arno in 796 “from Lake Pelissa beyond the river called Rapa, and thus as far as the river Drava, and from there to where the Drava flows into the Danube,” a considerable part of Pannonia still remained into which Paulinus’s zeal could extend. But since we find Arno as archbishop in 798, we do not at all believe that the peace-loving Paulinus entered into a contentious dispute with him; rather, we believe that thereafter he confined himself to the Drava, both in Carinthia and in Pannonia.

[Col. 0077A]

**XII.** When Alcuin, who had the salvation of the Avar souls at heart, learned that the province of Pannonia had been entrusted to Arno, he wrote a letter—number 104—especially concerning the proper administration of baptism, so that adults might first be instructed and then washed in the sacred font:

“To the weaker age,” he says, “holy Mother Church has granted that one who is bound by another’s sin in his father’s transgression may be released through another’s profession in the mystery of baptism.”

The letter is addressed “To the sweetest brother Aquila and most holy bishop,” because it was Alcuin’s custom to address men endowed with virtue by more exalted names. Thus he was accustomed to hear Charles called David, Angilbert Homer, and Richulf Damoetas at Charles’s court.

He also wrote to King Charles in Letter 90, urging him, while Pippin was staying with him to give public thanks to God for the Avar victory, to deal with him so that the captives might be treated more gently. Otherwise, if they were pressed too harshly, they might refuse to submit their necks to the yoke of the faith, or withdraw them after having submitted them.

“My lord,” he said, “my most beloved and sweetest, and my most desired David”—thus he calls him—“your Flaccus is sad because of your illness.” Perhaps Charles was sick at that time.

And below:

“My lord, may your piety remember the captives, while your Pippin is with you in thanksgiving for the remarkable benefit that divine mercy has bestowed upon you concerning the Huns, and for the success of the enterprises that lie before you.”

Although the Avars were treated more humanely by Charles, and although Alcuin also advised indulgence concerning the burden of tithes, as we indicated above in no. 10, they nevertheless fell away from the faith of God and the king’s treaty through renewed apostasy and rebellion. Thus in 799 it was necessary once again to send forces against them, under the commanders Gerold and our Henry of Friuli, who fell in that war, as we explain more fully in Dissertation 1, no. 23.

From this one may infer what injuries Paulinus suffered from a faithless people, so that Ferrarius rightly calls him a martyr by desire, if not in fact:

“He desired martyrdom, although he did not obtain what he wished.”

# CHAPTER IX. Another Diploma of Regensburg, Said to Have Been Given to Paulinus in 801

**I.** In the year 799 the affairs of the Church in Hungary were ruined, when Henry, duke of Friuli, who had led the province’s forces there, was killed in an ambush by the inhabitants of Tarsatica.

Whether Paulinus went to Rome in 800 will be examined in the next chapter. I would not dare affirm or deny whether he was absent from the province in 801 until I obtain a copy of the privilege given by Charles to Paulinus that year “at Regensburg in the public palace.” By it Charles is said to have granted him a hospice built outside the walls of Verona by the abbot Feroce, the Church of Saint Lawrence at Boga, now commonly called Buia, a large and respectable town of our region, and another hospice, or xenodochium, “which Duke Roduald built in Friuli under the name of Saint John,” as the diploma says.

Our distinguished Fontaninus says that he possesses this diploma, extracted from the original in Aquileia in 1195, in his booklet *Delle Masnade*, p. 21. I have sought it up to now, but in vain; I have asked and knocked, with friends’ prayers and services interposed, but to no avail. If at last I am granted the opportunity of obtaining it, you will have it in the Appendix; but if not, know that I have left no stone unturned, [Col. 0078B] so as to satisfy you, reader.

Meanwhile, let this much be enough for you to know. As I write this, the distinguished Scipio Maffei comes to mind. At the end of Book XI of his *Illustrated Verona*, he teaches me that the xenodochium was built not by Feroce but by Duke Lupone. This undermines the authority of the diploma; once that authority has fallen, it follows that the loss involved in doing without it is not great.

# CHAPTER X. The Roman Diploma Preserved at Udine Is Presented and Examined

**I.** Our college of canons at Udine boasts that it possesses authentic—and, as they say, original—diplomas of two emperors: one of Charlemagne and the other of Otto III. We do not subject this claim to scrutiny, since it does not seem relevant to the present matter.

The former, however, is certainly more appropriate for testing against the Lydian stone, since many considerations here and there suggest both that it should be accepted and that it should be rejected. You will have the complete document in the Appendix [Note: [Col. 0077D] See Appendix 2, no. 5.], together with a specimen of the script in which it was written. The canons of Udine, in their courtesy, allowed it to be conveniently transcribed, so that, with an example of the writing placed before your eyes and compared with other scripts of that period, you may judge what should be said about its authenticity.

**II.** Palladius gives an extensive account of the discovery of these diplomas of Charlemagne and Otto III in Part I, Book III, p. 99. They had once been thought lost and were unexpectedly found. Here I shall transcribe a few passages from the manuscript *Lives of the Patriarchs of Aquileia* by Antonio Bellonius, a man exceptionally exact and highly deserving in antiquarian matters, which he dedicated in 1551 to Hieronymus de Monteniaco.

Accordingly, after some remarks about our Paulinus, he writes:

“When the province had suffered disasters and many hardships from the Bavarians, he went to Rome to Charles, called the Great because of his deeds, so that he might provide for the dignity, care, and security of the entire patriarchal office. The emperor, moved by compassion for the disasters, dismissed Paulinus—who had labored with the utmost care lest anything belonging to his Church perish—with new privileges added to his dignity and honor.

“He generously granted him six bishoprics in the presence of Leo III, the Roman pontiff: Concordia, Verona, Ruginum, Petina, Tarsatica, and the one established at Civitas Nova in Istria. A privilege still exists, written in Lombard letters, at the basilica of Udine. It is as authentic as it is ancient, and so completely intact everywhere that, when reading it, one does not miss even the trace of a letter.

“I took a copy from it in the more cultivated script of Udine; the people of Udine received it as a rather distinguished favor, after paying six gold pieces. Certain men with lynx-like eyes, highly honored among scribes and citizens, examined it publicly together with me and confirmed it with their signatures in complete good faith.”

Thus far the extremely diligent Bellonius.

Yet it can no longer be called so intact, since it has been stored folded rather than in a rolled form, and has been somewhat scraped at the folds and corners, so that certain words are missing. The defects in the copy to be presented [Col. 0079B] in the Appendix will become evident.

In the manuscript copy of Bellonius that I saw, *Veronensem* has been erased in such a way, and another bishopric inserted by a different hand, that one cannot know whether the reading should be *Veronensem* or *Utinensem*.

### III.

In the year 800, when Charles was declared emperor by Leo III himself on the very day of the Nativity of the Lord, Palladius asserts that Paulinus was present on behalf of his Church, and that the pope and Charles met so that the rights of the Church of Aquileia—broken by the insolence of its suffragan bishops during the Lombard regime—might be repaired and preserved intact, with apostolic and imperial authority interposed. Palladius likewise maintains that Charles fulfilled this on his part, both by writing at that time to Cadolac, successor of Duke Henry of Friuli, and entrusting to him the protection of the rights of the Church of Aquileia, [Col. 0079C] and later, in the third year of his reign, by issuing a diploma at Rome and vindicating the Church’s former splendor and rights.

To speak frankly, the first part of this assertion causes me no great difficulty: namely, Paulinus’s Roman journey and his complaint before Charles and Leo in the year 800 or 801. For I find no contradiction between the events and the chronology; indeed, I see rather what supports it and makes it probable. For there can be no doubt that at that time the rights of the Church had been brought low, that the provincial bishops—especially those of Istria, formerly subject to the Aquileian metropolitan—had refused obedience and adhered to Grado. Moreover, we have seen above in more than one place that a substantial part of Carinthia had been withdrawn from the province of Aquileia and assigned to Arno of Salzburg. What wonder, then, if Paulinus’s zeal to defend the boundaries of his Church drove him to this journey and caused him to press his most just complaints upon the mind and ears of the pope and Charles? Especially since, during the period when Charles was present at Rome—namely, from the eighth day before the Kalends of December in the year 800, according to the Lorsch annalist, or until the seventh day before the Kalends of May, according to Ademar, volume IX of the Councils, p. 228—no act of Paulinus compels us to keep him in his own province.

Rather, it becomes probable that, when Charles descended into Liburnia in the autumn of 800, exacted punishment from the people of Tarsatica for the killing of Henry inflicted in the preceding year, and from there proceeded swiftly to Rome, Paulinus joined him as a companion on the journey. For Anastasius, in his Life of Leo III, no. 774, when Leo wished to clear himself of the charges brought against him, on account of which Charles had come to Rome, says this concerning Charles:

> “He caused the archbishops, bishops, abbots, and all the nobility of the Franks and Romans to assemble in the same church of Saint Peter; and, sitting together, both the great king and the most blessed pontiff caused the most holy archbishops and abbots likewise to sit, etc.”

What prevents us from supposing that Paulinus was present among these metropolitans, especially since he had to be counted among the number of the prelates subject to the kingdom of the Franks? When the opportunity arose, it is easy to believe that he deplored the disruption of the rights of his Church and demanded a remedy.

Once these points are granted, what prevents us from proceeding further by conjecture—namely, that Charles wrote to Cadolac for the restoration of the violated right and granted Paulinus a diploma full of honor, by which he either added new bishoprics to him, perhaps in compensation for the diminished province (since he knew that the part beyond the Drava in Carinthia and Pannonia had been occupied by the archbishop of Salzburg), or subjected to him the ancient bishops who were refusing obedience? Up to this point, I perceive nothing improbable in any of these matters.

### IV.

What causes difficulty is the dating of the diploma, which runs as follows:

> “Given on the day before the Nones of August, in the third year of our reign, and in the first indiction. Acted at Rome, happily, in the name of God. Amen.”

The third year of the reign, which is the year 803, is one in which no annalist asserts that Charles was at Rome. He arrived, as was said in the preceding section, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December in the year 800; he departed on the seventh day before the Kalends of May in 801; and, according to Einhard, *Life of Charles*, no. 33, this was the last of Charles’s four Roman journeys, when he was crowned emperor. He was crowned on this occasion on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, at the end of the year 800.

Furthermore, it seems possible to infer from a diploma issued on the Ides of August that Charles remained in Francia during August of the third year of his reign. This diploma was issued to Fortunatus of Grado in the third year of Charles’s reign, when the patriarch of Grado approached him to complain about the death of his predecessor John, who had been thrown from a tower by the son of Maurice, duke of the Venetians; Ughellus presents it in [XXXIV] among the documents of Grado. For it is improbable that Charles was at Rome on 4 August, as the diploma granted to Paulinus would have it, and in Francia on the 13th of the same month and year, as the diploma granted to Fortunatus seems to indicate. I say “seems to indicate,” since in fact it does not disclose the place. Add to this that the first indiction given in the diploma does not agree with the year 803, in which the eleventh, not the first, was in progress.

### V.

On the other hand, the form of the script and the chancellor’s subscription urge that it be accepted as genuine. For the script, as will appear from the specimen to be presented in the Appendix, bears the character of the very century in which it is said to have been written—namely, the later eighth or the beginning of the ninth, as one will discover by comparison with Mabillon’s examples from that period, especially if the comparison is made with plates 23, 24, and 25 of Book V of *De Re Diplomatica*.

The chancellor’s subscription also appears entirely authentic. It is rendered by Palladius and Schönleben as follows:

> “Jo. Jacob. Du Radoni wrote and subscribed.”

This is wrong. For anyone examining the characters and letters closely, although the writing is as ancient as it is barbarous, can plainly see that it should be read:

> “Jacobus in the place of Rado.”

Rado was an abbot, “whom,” says Mabillon, *De Re Diplomatica*, Book II, chapter 11, no. 5, “it is certain was the chief chancellor of Charlemagne.” That he had a notary named Jacobus is likewise affirmed by Mabillon in the same book, the following chapter, 12, no. 4, in these words:

> “Rado, abbot of Saint-Vaast, succeeded Hitherius; he had as notaries Wigbald, Optatus, Jacobus Erkembald, and Windolaicus.”

Moreover, from plate 25 of Book V, in confirmation of our reading, one may take the example of another diploma subscribed in this way:

> “Jacob in the place of Rado.”

### VI.

Thus, since the matter stands as it does, **ἐν τριόδῳ εἰμὶ λογισμῶν**—“I am at a crossroads of reasoning,” or at least at a fork in the road—and I confess that I am wavering between the two sides.

The form of the script, together with the material on which the diploma was written—which is membranous, commonly called parchment—does not conflict with that period; indeed, it agrees with it extremely well. The scribe’s subscription is legitimate and blameless. Moreover, the sign, or monogram, is unquestionably Carolingian; even the strokes of the writing pen, which may be called *zifrae* but signify nothing and appear arbitrary, placed merely for ornament, agree so plainly with the examples exhibited by Mabillon that one need not fear declaring the writers to be, as the proverb has it, “rivals and fellow craftsmen” (**ὁμοτέχνους**).

Yet, since defects appear in the indication of place and time, and since, if anywhere, here too “a hair casts a shadow,” I do not dare, I confess, to pronounce a judgment. Let the fair-minded reader decide. The diploma is indeed handsome—but does it, as the proverb says, contain more aloe than honey?

## CHAPTER XI. Paulinus attended the Council of Aachen in 803 as legate of the Apostolic See

### I.

In the preceding chapter, no. 3, we considered it sufficiently probable that Paulinus was present at Rome at the end of the year 800 and the beginning of 801. Additional weight is given to this opinion by the fact that in 802 Paulinus was sent by Pope Leo III as legate of the Apostolic See to the Council of Aachen, over which the pope presided through his vicar.

He was therefore known to the pontiff; and, if we may conjecture, when he was at Rome it becomes probable that this commission was entrusted to him, or even that he had distinguished himself so greatly in learning and virtue that he deserved to have it entrusted to him.

Stephen Baluze informs us of this new journey of Paulinus beyond the boundaries of his own diocese, and of this distinction of honor conferred upon him in a great synod, when he gives the following title to the *Aachen Capitulary* of the year 803:

> “The Aachen Capitulary, or the First Capitulary made in the year 803, as it seems, in the great synod, when Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, held the place of the Apostolic See at Aachen.”

I shall not hesitate to transcribe here Baluze’s notes on this passage, found in volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1058. I distrust my ability to produce stronger arguments from my own resources. He writes as follows:

### II.

> “An old note added to the Rheims manuscript, which was transferred from there by Jean de Tillet into the first book of the *Capitularies*, has the following in the margin of the earlier of these Capitularies:
>
> “ ‘In the time of Pope Hadrian and of Emperor Charlemagne, when Bishop Paulinus held the place of the Apostolic See at Aachen, this Capitulary was made because men wanted [Tillet: used] to divide bishoprics and monasteries for their own use, and no bishop, abbot, or abbess would have been left with anything except enough to live like canons and monks.’
>
> “I think, however, that the copyist erred here, placing the name Hadrian incorrectly, when he ought to have written Leo. This conjecture is supported by Hincmar in letter 44, p. 765, where he says that the edict of Charles, in which the first three chapters of this Capitulary were enacted, was issued by Charles at the advice of Pope Leo:
>
> “ ‘The lord Emperor Charlemagne,’ he says, ‘sent the entire edict, together with the inquiry concerning chorepiscopi, through Archbishop Arno to Pope Leo; and, following his advice, he issued another edict concerning the non-division of ecclesiastical property and the cases of bishops, confirmed it by the authority of the Apostolic See and by his own authority, and declared that it was to be observed perpetually throughout all the metropolitan Churches of his empire.’
>
> “The same Hincmar treats of this matter, mentioning Patriarch Paulinus, in letter 29, p. 320, which was published more fully from the papers of the most celebrated man, Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, in the appendix to the Council of Douzy:
>
> “ ‘Therefore, when we speak of other memorable emperors and kings, the memory of your grandfather, the great Emperor Charles, must not be passed over. When, as usually happens, he had been deceived by the tongues of flatterers, so that he might inflict some prejudice upon the Churches with respect to their property, the bishops resisted, especially Paulinus the patriarch, as I recognize is well known to you. Charles then so fully acknowledged his error and satisfied the Church and the bishops that the confession from his own mouth was not enough for him; rather, he sent to his descendants, who were to arise from his lineage, a written record of his confession and correction, confirmed by his own hand. A part of this edict is written in your book called the *Book of Imperial Capitularies*, in chapter 77, where it says: “Because, according to the tradition of the holy fathers,” etc.’ ”

### III.

> “Furthermore, since it is written in the note of the Rheims manuscript that these acts took place in the time of Emperor Charlemagne, it is clear that they did not take place in the time of Hadrian, but in the time of Leo, when, with the Apostolic See presiding, the plan was formed to renew the empire in the person of Charles. Finally, nowhere do we find that a synod of Aachen, attended by a legation of the Apostolic See, was convened while Hadrian was alive.
>
> “But in the annals edited by Lambecius and in the chronicle of Moissac we read that Charles convened a universal synod at Aachen in October of the year 803, and that many decrees were enacted there, both concerning political matters and ecclesiastical affairs. This assembly, in my judgment, lasted for several months, being extended, that is, until the beginning of the following year.
>
> “Evidence for this is the note appended to the *Capitulary* 3 of the year 803 in the Palatine and Metz manuscripts:
>
> “ ‘This was issued at Aachen in the third year of the reign of the lord Charles Augustus, when there was a great synod there—that is, a universal one, as the annals mentioned above call it.’
>
> “Therefore, if a legation of the Apostolic See attended any synod held at Aachen under Charlemagne, it is reasonable to think that this occurred at that synod, and that Paulinus’s legation must be referred to it.”

### IV.

> “I think that the following passage from Alcuin’s letter to Charlemagne, prefixed to the books *On the Faith of the Holy Trinity*, should be understood of this same Council of Aachen:
>
> “ ‘At the time of the most celebrated assembly, when the priests of God and the preachers of the Christian people came together by imperial command.’
>
> “And shortly afterward:
>
> “ ‘It awaits the judgment of your approval [XXXV] whether this labor of mine may worthily proceed to priestly ears.’
>
> “Baronius, under the year 789, and Cellotius in his notes on Hincmar’s *Quaterniones*, p. 459, are therefore mistaken when they write that this edict was promulgated in the twentieth year of Charles’s reign. They were deceived by the fact that in the common editions of the *Capitularies*, before the marginal note of the Rheims manuscript, there is placed a note of the year in which the first seventy-two chapters of the first book of the *Capitularies* were enacted. They did not sufficiently distinguish this from the note belonging to the chapter concerning the non-division of the property of the Church.”

### V.

Thus far Baluze, whose arguments I have thought it appropriate to transcribe in his own words, so that he himself may be the advocate of his assertion. They appeared to him so effective and powerful that he did not hesitate to use them to blunt the arguments which Sirmond gathered from Hincmar’s letter 44, chapter 30—namely, that after the death of Saint Boniface no legate of the Apostolic See had been present in Gaul or Germany during the times of Pepin, Charlemagne, and Louis.

For Baluze says in Book V, chapter 45, no. 6, additional note to Peter de Marca’s *Concord of Priesthood and Empire*:

> “Nevertheless, I think it should be observed here that what is read in that letter of Hincmar—that after the death of Saint Boniface there was no legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul or Germany during the times of the emperors Pepin, Charles, and Louis, that is, for ninety years, as Sirmond says in the margin of that Hincmarian letter—does not appear to be true. For it is established that Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia, held the place of the Apostolic See before Charlemagne in the palace at Aachen.”

See the notes to the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, p. 1058.

Thus Baluze speaks, and the arguments he has brought forward appear so weighty to him [Col. 0083D] that he declares absolutely that Paulinus’s legation is established. Add that Dupin makes the same assertion without hesitation in his *Bibliotheca*, under Charlemagne, as does the recent author of the *History of the Popes*, in the section on Leo III, The Hague edition, 1732, volume I, p. 597.

### VI.

Although Father Louis Cellotius of the Society of Jesus, in his notes on Hincmar’s *Quaterniones*, refers this event to the twentieth year of Charles’s reign—a position which, as we have just seen, Baluze refutes—he nevertheless accepts the event solely on Hincmar’s authority, even though the histories are silent about it:

> “No history,” he says, “informs us that this great disturbance of affairs was corrected by Charles, while he was still king, through the counsel and vigorous urging of Patriarch Paulinus. Yet we readily believe Hincmar when he reports it, both because of the notable authority Paulinus had acquired through holiness and learning, and because he was continually in attendance upon Charles and took part in several synods convened by him. Hincmar of Rheims himself calls him ‘the patriarch of the Aquileian parish’—Hincmar, Book I *On Predestination*, letter 1, to King Charles—and declares that his writings, like those of Bede and Alcuin, should be read together with those of the more ancient fathers.”

### VII.

The Roman diploma discussed in the preceding chapter indicates that Charles stayed at Rome during August. If this is admitted, it presents no obstacle to this Council of Aachen. For just as Charles had wintered at Aachen, so he celebrated Easter there; that feast fell in that year on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, as Cointius notes under the same year, no. 15, from the Lorsch and Metz annalists. In no. 44, moreover, he gives a privilege for the monastery of Acutianum, issued at Aachen on the Ides of June in the third year of the reign, etc. Therefore Charles was still at Aachen on the Ides of June.

Afterward he went to Mainz, and perhaps later to Rome. The assembly at Aachen began, as Baluze argues above in no. 3, in October of the year 802; and since many matters were dealt with there, as is clear from the various Capitularies then issued, it was extended to the beginning of the following year, namely 803. From the year in which it ended, the Capitularies received their chronological designation and came to be called the Capitularies of the year 803.

### VIII.

The First Capitulary of that year contains seven chapters, all of which defend the discipline of the Church.

In the first, *On the Non-Division of Church Property*, Paulinus’s zeal shines forth—as appears above, no. 2, from more than one testimony, especially that of Hincmar. At his urging, Charles decreed, according to the tradition of the Fathers, that Church property, since it consists of the vows of the faithful, the price of sins, and the patrimony of the poor, should not be permitted to be divided either during his own rule or during that of his sons who wished to imitate him.

In the second, *On the Free Election of a Bishop by the Clergy and People*, you will recognize Paulinus as the author of the enactment, since the decree issued here agrees entirely with the privilege that he himself had obtained from Charles for his Church of Aquileia. See above, chapter 6, no. 4. From this we argued above, chapter 2, no. 1, that Paulinus was a native of Friuli, because the decree says:

> “Bishops are to be elected by the election of the clergy and people, according to the provisions of the canons, from their own diocese . . . . .”

In the third, it is provided that the rights, privileges, and property of the Church are to be preserved, and that one who lays waste to monasteries or usurps their property is to be regarded as a homicide and sacrilegious person.

In the fourth, the question that had arisen concerning chorepiscopi is first proposed—whether they validly exercised episcopal functions—and it is reported that, to settle the complaints, Charles sent Bishop Arno to consult Pope Leo. Leo replied that their acts were rejected by the ancient Fathers and their canons, because they were not truly bishops; consequently, all chorepiscopi were to be prohibited from exercising authority and sent into exile:

> “But all the bishops, especially those of the kingdom entrusted to us by God, treating these matters more mildly together with the same Arno, with the permission of the aforesaid apostolic, placed the aforesaid country bishops among the presbyters.”

He then appeals to the decrees of Regensburg, which had already established the same thing. We saw in chapter 6 that Paulinus attended that council in the year 792. The work may also be inferred from this fact to be his, because this entire chapter is reproduced in Book VII, chapter 260, and its compiler, Benedict the Levite, testifies in the preface prefixed to Book V that this book was composed from canons and decrees issued chiefly by Paulinus.

In the fifth, the license of the chorepiscopi is restricted, so that they may not, through the laying on of hands—which is the office of the bishop alone—confer the Holy Spirit in sacred ordinations; ordinations attempted by them are declared invalid.

In the sixth, the invalidity and nullity of the ordination of presbyters or deacons by chorepiscopi is demonstrated, and those so ordained are judged unfit for the ministry of orders and null.

Finally, in the seventh, a form of purgation is prescribed when a priest is charged with a crime. Namely, as was advised by Pope Leo and as was held by the judgments of both the Greek and Latin Fathers, an accuser is not to be admitted except according to the norm of the canons, “with the lawful number of true and good witnesses”; and a person publicly defamed is to be judged canonically, just as the matter is to be settled if the accuser has proceeded canonically with the complaint.

But if the crimes have not been proved and the accused nevertheless remains “suspect” to his bishop, or to the clergy and people, then, following the example of Pope Leo, who had twelve presbyters at his purgation—or more, if his bishop should judge it appropriate, or should perceive that their presence was necessary because of popular tumult—he is to return himself, purged, to the Church after taking an oath before the people over the four Gospels, together with other good and just men.

[Col. 0085C] This is the substance of the chapters of the Council of Aachen. If one considers the matters dealt with in them, one will discern the spirit of its presiding officer, Paulinus.

## CHAPTER XII. Paulinus convenes the Council of Altinum concerning the killing of John, patriarch of Grado

### I.

When Paulinus returned from the Council of Aachen, early in the year 803, he learned of the monstrous crime committed by John, duke of the Venetians, who at the end of the preceding year or the beginning of the present one had thrown John, patriarch of Grado, headlong from a tower.

Moved by the report of this deed, Paulinus convened a synod at Altinum, as was customary, in the third week after Easter—that is, between the 9th and the 16th of May. After the usual discussions of various matters concerning the faith, the Church, and other affairs, he also dealt with the avenging of the death of so excellent a prelate; and, having sent a letter to Emperor Charles, he determined to implore from him vengeance for the crime.

This synod and letter have been treated at greater length in Dissertation 6, to which we refer you, excellent reader, lest you should have reheated the same dish. There the place and time of the council are discussed; here we present only the event and the origin and cause of the event.

### II.

Andrea Dandolo reveals the source of the evil rather meagerly:

> “The duke John,” he says, “taking the opportunity, sent his son Maurice with a naval force to Grado to kill the patriarch John. Maurice, however, invaded the city furiously; during the invasion the patriarch was captured and severely wounded by the Venetians, and was thrown down from the highest tower of his palace to the ground, where he died. His blood remains visibly upon the stones as testimony to his death.”

This is Dandolo, *Chronicle*, Book VII, chapter 14, § 23. The writer lived until the year 1354. Therefore this sign of the bloody death must have lasted for five and a half centuries. What opportunity John the duke seized in order to stain himself with priestly blood must be sought from other sources.

### III.

That the act was not just, but utterly unjust, may be inferred from Pietro Marcello’s *Lives of the Doges of Venice*, in the section on the seventh Doge Maurice. He calls John the patriarch “a man of illustrious justice,” and asserts that John the duke and Maurice his son, “the impious son of an impious father, bound themselves to an unspeakable parricide without any just cause.”

Some attribute the cause to an abuse of power turning into tyranny; others invoke the wicked life and conduct of John the duke and his son Maurice, because John the patriarch of Grado had repeatedly rebuked them in a fatherly manner and had consequently offended their resentful minds.

### IV.

Yet a nearer and truer cause seems to be the one presented by Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, Book IV; Baronius under the year 802, no. 10; Pagi under the same year, no. 3; Ughellus, volume V of *Italia Sacra*, under the bishops of Grado, no. 15; among our own writers, the younger Palladius, Part I, Book III; more recently, Louis Schönleben in the *Annals of Carniola* under the year 802; Father Irenaeus a Cruce, a Discalced Carmelite, in *History of Trieste*, Book VII, chapter 10; and, from beyond our region, in addition to those already cited, Cointius under the year 803, no. 2.

The account is as follows. After Obelerius, bishop of Olivolo, died, Christophorus, likewise a Greek by nationality, was elected to fill the see through the agency of Duke John, in order to gratify the Greek emperor Nicephorus. Obelerius and Felix, the tribunes, took this badly and approached John, patriarch of Grado, asking him not to lay hands upon the elected man. He did so, and also excluded him from the communion of the faithful.

From this it becomes probable that, as Palladius says, the man was infected with heresy. The duke, inflamed with anger at this, ordered his son Maurice to enter Grado with a fleet and take vengeance upon the patriarch John. The cruel father’s command was carried out by his son, who was no degenerate offspring: he first had the wounded prelate lifted into a high tower and then threw him down from it.

Moved by so great a crime, Paulinus, while convening the synod at Altinum, proposed that deliberation be held concerning the appeal to Charles for vengeance upon the priestly blood that had been shed; and he carried out what had been decided.

### V.

Father Irenaeus a Cruce, in the same passage, claims to have found this history in an ancient manuscript preserved in the library of the Discalced Carmelites at Venice. He says that the reason why the Venetian tribunes bore the election of Christophorus so indignantly was that Christophorus was the brother of Longinus, who held the exarchate of Ravenna in Italy for Nicephorus.

But the good Father is gravely mistaken. First, because only one Longinus appears in the list of exarchs, and he was sent to Italy by the Emperor Justin of Constantinople in the year 567. Second, because the dignity of exarch had already been abolished by Pepin, father of Charlemagne, in the year 752, when he expelled Eutychios, the last exarch in Italy. Therefore in 803 there was no exarch whose brother the elected Christophorus could have been.

## CHAPTER XIII. The year, month, and day of Paulinus’s death are established

### I.

From what has been said thus far, you can see that Paulinus’s life extended into the year 803. I can therefore scarcely understand why it happened that among certain historians and chronologers of no mean standing his death was placed before the year 804, when the events most clearly show that he was alive until that year.

He himself convened the Council of Altinum in response to the crime of the duke of the Venetians; that crime was not committed until the end of 802 or the beginning of 803, at which time Paulinus was at Aachen and presided over the council as legate of the Apostolic See.

Since the month in which he died is held to have been January, it is necessary to place his departure to heaven in January of the following year, 804.

### II.

Those who say that he was removed from the world in earlier years must therefore be corrected. Among them is Onuphrius, in the Bollandists’ *Life of Paulinus*, § 1, no. 7. Assigning Paulinus’s accession to the see of Aquileia to the year 776 and giving him twenty-five years in the see, he is forced to say that Paulinus died in 801.

For, having been promoted to the episcopal dignity toward the end of 776, he had likewise completed the twenty-fifth year of his administration toward the end of 801. Thus either the month of his death must be moved earlier, or several months—or at least days—must be added beyond the twenty-five years of his tenure. Both alternatives, however, will shortly be seen to be false, because his episcopate continued further.

### III.

Hermannus Contractus writes under the year 802 in his *Chronicle*:

> “Paulinus, patriarch of Friuli, or Aquileia, died.”

The Annals of Fulda have the same words, both those published by Lambecius and those who followed them; so do Bellarmine, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, our Baronius, and Pagius, who on the basis of these annalists and chroniclers likewise place the event in 802.

Nevertheless, one must not omit what the Bollandists noted in the *Life of Saint Paulinus*, § 7, no. 26:

> “In the chronicle of Hermannus Contractus that we used, there is profound silence concerning the death of Paulinus.”

We too examined the work published by Pistorius among the other writers of German affairs (Frankfurt edition, 1583), and Paulinus’s name is nowhere to be seen. Let others conjecture how it happened that these words slipped into the editions of Hermannus commonly published by Henricus Canisius. It is enough here to have pointed out that the reliability of Contractus is at least wavering, and that the annalists who give the same account in the same words copied one from another without discrimination or examination.

### IV.

Some place Paulinus’s death in the following year, namely 803. The Bollandists themselves and Labbeus in his addition to Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers* seem to belong to this group. I say “seem to belong,” because they express their view with hesitation. There they write:

> “Perhaps Paulinus died at the beginning of that year”—namely, 803—“in the month of January, which, according to the reckoning of the Gauls, who begin the year at Easter, was counted as belonging to the preceding year.”

Labbeus, however, writes:

> “He died on the second day of January of the year 802, or rather of the following year.”

The question of the day will be examined below according to his opinion and rejected. But that Paulinus died in 803 is likewise disproved by his acts at the Council of Altinum, convened in that very year around the middle of May, as was said in Dissertation 6.

Since both these writers and the others agree in assigning Paulinus’s death to the month of January, it remains to transfer his death to January of the following year, 804.

### V.

Therefore Paulinus’s departure from the living must be placed in the year 804, both as a necessary consequence of the events of his life, as has just been shown, and so that you do not make light of the number and eminence of the writers who assert this [xxxvii].

First are the records of the Church of Aquileia and of Friuli, or Cividale, on which Ferrarius relies and which he himself likewise affirms. Add to him Natalis Alexander, William Cave, Fleury, and Oudinus; to these must be added the younger Palladius, who, having carried Paulinus’s acts into the year 803, is compelled to acknowledge that he died in 804. Cointius, to be cited below, holds the same opinion.

### VI.

I do not find the controversy concerning the month of Paulinus’s death difficult, unless one agrees with Onuphrius and wishes to establish exactly twenty-five years of tenure, neither fewer nor more, as the entire period of his episcopate.

For, as was said in no. 2, if Paulinus was raised to the summit of the Church of Aquileia around the end of the year 776 and occupied that see for twenty-five complete years, then he would have died around the end of 801; and it would therefore have to be said that he departed from earth to heaven not in January but in December or November.

Since, however, as has been shown, it is not probable that the year 801 should be accepted as the year of his death, the month commonly assigned to his death need not be removed either. That month is January, as has continued to be observed until now in the annual celebration of his feast.

### VII.

The matter does not proceed in the same way when one speaks of the day of his death. Philip Labbeus, in his addition to Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says:

> “He died on the second day of January.”

Ferrarius says:

> “His feast is celebrated by the Church of Aquileia on the third day before the Nones of January.”

Miraeus follows him in his *Supplement to Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 225, and Oudinus admits that he followed Miraeus.

Yet Ughellus, Cave, Fleury, Baillet, Natalis Alexander, and the Bollandists testify that he died on 11 January. The Bollandists excuse Ferrarius’s error by saying:

> “He seems to have intended to write the third day before the Ides of January.”

Hence Moreri was wrong in the *Historical Dictionary* when he said that the Bollandists placed Paulinus’s death on 2 January, since they expressly correct Ferrarius and assign his life to 11 January.

Those too are mistaken who assert that the Church of Aquileia celebrates his feast on 2 or 3 January. In fact, it celebrates it on 11 January, as is clear from the ancient orders of services called calendars.

Even at present, the clearest witnesses that his feast is solemnly observed in the diocese of Aquileia on that day are all those who are obliged to perform the canonical hours. For although, because 11 January coincides with the sixth day within the octave of Epiphany—which is regarded as more solemn than the lesser feasts throughout all the days of the octave—the day is excluded, when an opportunity is given to perform the office according to the rubrics concerning the transfer of feasts, it is recorded that the office was to be celebrated on 11 January.

The source of Labbeus’s and Ferrarius’s error will be shown below, in no. 11.

### VIII.

Add that, since I have more than once visited Cividale in order to gather from the older records preserved in its chests whatever might contribute to my purpose in publishing and illustrating the writings and acts of Saint Paulinus, although I found very little—those materials having, as they said, been scattered through the injury of time—I came across, in the archive of the distinguished college of canons of that city, a very ancient parchment book in folio, fastened with an iron chain.

This book contains a register of the anniversaries of the Church of Cividale. Under the month of January, on the 11th day, the following is written:

> “Saint Paulinus: on the eleventh, forty denarii from the parish of Saint Peter of the Slavs are given for the feast.”

In the books of distributions today it is recorded as follows:

> “On the feast of Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia and confessor, which was on the eleventh of this month, six denarii were given as honoraria.”

### IX.

Receive what various martyrologies record about Paulinus on this day, as reported by the Bollandists, § 7, no. 27:

> “They celebrate his feast on this day: the Carthusians of Cologne, in the addition to Usuard. Likewise, the feast of Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia.”

The German Martyrology has the same entry, in which Aquileia is called *Aglar*. The manuscript Martyrology of Saint Mary of Utrecht reads:

> “At Aquileia, Paulinus the patriarch.”

The manuscript Martyrology of the Monastery of Saint Martin at Trier reads:

> “At Aquileia, Paulinus the patriarch.”

Ferrarius, in his general catalogue of the saints, from the records of the Church of Cividale and Aquileia, writes:

> “At Friuli in Carnia, Saint Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia.”

And in the following no. 28 Ferrarius likewise says:

> “His feast is celebrated by the Church of Aquileia on the third day before the Nones of January.”

Here the Bollandists add:

> “This is Ferrarius, who seems to have intended to write the third day before the Ides of January.”

Perhaps someone who has read—as we have—the Martyrology of Rabanus published by Canisius in volume II of *Ancient Readings*, Part II, will be surprised not to find a commemoration of Saint Paulinus, although he finds one of Charlemagne and Alcuin.

But it must be observed that they are not commemorated there as saints. Concerning Charles, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, the entry simply reads:

> “Charles died.”

Nothing more is added. And on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, concerning Alcuin, it reads:

> “The deposition of Lord Alcuin.”

Nowhere is the title “saint” or “blessed” attached to either name.

Moreover, the matters concerning the saints of the Church of Aquileia are not recorded with great accuracy. For Rabanus evidently did not know the names of our saints, and appears to have been acquainted with Saint Hermagoras neither by name nor by dignity. Thus under 12 July he writes:

> “The fourth day before the Ides of July. At Aquileia, the feast of the holy Fortunatus and Armigerus.”

He ought to have written:

> “Of Hermagoras and Fortunatus.”

Likewise, on the sixth day before the Kalends of December he erred when he wrote:

> “At Aquileia, of Valentine, bishop,”

instead of Valerian.

### X

Cointius must not be omitted here; his words should be set out in full. For as many periods as he has, so many are the confirmations of what we previously produced from our slender resources, before we obtained Cointius’s works. Thus he writes under the year 804, no. 1 and following:

> “The fourth year of the ninth century was a mournful one for Italy, because of the deaths of Paulinus, patriarch of Forojulium, and Peter, archbishop of Milan; we have not omitted their notable struggles in defense of the Catholic faith. Paulinus died on the third day of the Ides of January, Peter on the seventh day of the Ides of May.
>
> “Concerning the year in which Paulinus happily departed to God, two opinions are current. [Col. 0090B] One is that of the annalist of Fulda, under whom the following is read for the year of our Redeemer 802: ‘Paulinus, patriarch of Forojulium, died.’ The other is that of Ferrarius, who composed the Life of Saint Paulinus from the records of Forojulium and assigned his death to the year of salvation 804. The former opinion pleased Baronius and many others. We follow the latter, after a more careful examination of the sequence of events.
>
> “For Paulinus could not have held the Council of Altinum before the year of our Redeemer 803, when account is taken of the disturbances by which Constantinople and Grado had previously been shaken. Ferdinand Ughellus—although he does not depart from Baronius—does not acknowledge Urban, who immediately succeeded Paulinus, as patriarch before the year 804 of restored salvation.”

### XI

[Col. 0090C]

> “The day of his death is also disputed. In Labbeus, Paulinus dies on 2 January; in Ferrarius, on the third day before the Nones of January; in Bollandus, on the third day before the Ides of January. Here the author cites various martyrologies, which ought to be preferred to Labbeus and Ferrarius. From this notation—II, which signifies different numbers, namely the second and the eleventh, according to the characters used by different peoples—Labbeus’s error arose. For Paulinus gave up his soul to the Creator not on the second day but on the eleventh. Ferrarius, too, mistakenly wrote the Nones instead of the Ides. For according to this Life, Paulinus departed not on the third day before the Nones, that is, 3 January, but on the third day before the Ides, that is, 11 January.”

He continues as follows concerning his burial.

### XII

> “Paulinus was buried at Forojulium, in [Col. 0090D] the major basilica, where he had held a council in the year of Christ 795.”

Here Cointius is mistaken, for he began his council in the year of Christ 796 [xxxviii], as we have demonstrated at length in the *Dissertation on the Council of Forojulium*.

> “His epitaph is reported from Alcuin as follows—you will find it in our Appendix 1, no. 2, poem 2:
>
> *Here Paulinus, praying, rests throughout all ages;*  
> *May the worthy father deign to possess this resting-place.*  
> *May no envious enemy ever pass through this temple,*  
> *Lest he suddenly separate dear friends in spirit,*  
> *Whom the love of Christ has joined as dear friends.*
>
> “We believe that these verses were written by Alcuin while Paulinus was still alive. Yet we suspect that an error has entered the first verse, and that one should read *requiescat*—‘may he rest’—rather than *requiescit*—‘he rests,’ because the following verse likewise contains an optative form, *dignetur*—‘may he deign.’ [Col. 0091A]
>
> “The friends whom the final verses praise as joined in the love of Christ and not to be separated even in burial seem to us to be none other than Paulinus and Alcuin. We know that they often fought with united minds and arms for the cause of Christ, and together triumphed over corrupt doctrines.
>
> “The meaning, therefore, of the verses transcribed above is this: May Paulinus rest here—that is, in the church of Saint Martin—and may he deem it worthy to receive burial there, so that, buried in the same basilica as Alcuin, he may await the resurrection. But events turned out otherwise. Paulinus, as stated above, was buried in the principal church of the patriarchate of Forojulium. Alcuin, however, died at Tours in that same year, on the feast of Pentecost, and was buried in the church of Saint Martin, over which he presided with the title of abbot, [Col. 0091B] by Joseph, metropolitan of Tours.”

All this Cointius presents elegantly and skillfully.

### XIII

From the conjectures that we composed concerning his origin in chapter 2, no. 5, it remains to say that he departed from earth to heaven at approximately the age of seventy-eight, after twenty-eight years in the patriarchal see.

## CHAPTER XIV. Paulinus’s Holiness

### I

Up to this point, in the Life of our Paulinus, we have arranged in their proper order everything pertaining to chronology. We must now pursue those matters that are not contained within any definite period of time but illuminated the whole course of his years. These are holiness of conduct, uprightness of life, and learning. By the former, the affections are directed toward the attainment of the good; by the latter, the intellect [Col. 0091C] toward the apprehension of the truth. From both there proceeds the form of the perfect man, whom wickedness does not corrupt and ignorance does not blind, but whom wisdom illumines and holiness renders excellent. We shall discuss Paulinus’s learning in the following chapter. Let us now continue with his uprightness and the virtues by which he obtained the title of holiness.

### II

Let us begin with that virtue which is the basis and foundation of the others, and without which it is impossible to please God—faith, I mean, in Paulinus. It shines forth so conspicuously among his other virtues, through the many labors, journeys, councils convened, and books published on its behalf, that just as faith is first of all virtues in itself, so it must be said to have held first place in the life of Paulinus.

He fought the enemies of the faith both at a distance and face to face. He brought the neighboring peoples of the Avars [Col. 0091D] and Caranthanians to faith in Christ through the ministry of preaching, and he splendidly aided regions of Spain and other peoples far distant from him, afflicted by the Felician heresy or other errors, through the convening of synods, the writing of books, and the preaching of the word of God.

On these matters we should hear Alcuin, who, as Paulinus’s intimate friend and [Col. 0091] a worthy fellow soldier and a worthy fellow soldier in the struggles undertaken for the faith, knew his energy exceedingly well. He commends it also when, in letter 112 [Note: See Appendix 1, no. 1, letter 5 (*Patrologia*, volume CI).], he asks to be informed what decision Paulinus had reached concerning the mission to the Avars, which the members of the palace and the whole court were awaiting him to undertake:

> “The eyes of very many,” he says, “look [Col. 0092A] toward you, excellent father, to learn what your venerable holiness wishes to do. For the nearness of the places suits you, the glory of wisdom is at your disposal, the excellence of authority belongs to you, and everything is present that appears necessary for such a work.
>
> “Therefore the curiosity of my lowliness desires to know the truth concerning this holy undertaking and asks the counsel of your prudence; it demands to learn what your good will has determined should be done. The work is indeed arduous, but, as Truth itself bears witness, we know that all things are possible to one who believes.
>
> “He who made a preacher out of a persecutor and raises the poor from the dungheap to sit with princes can himself draw from the arid recesses of my heart little streams of the living fountain that leaps up into eternal life. How much more can he pour from your most abundant breast rivers like those of the Gihon, flowing through the whole breadth [Col. 0092B] of the Nile-land, to fertilize flowers of many kinds?
>
> “Let your devoted son, united with you in charity, I beg you, hear through you what your fatherly providence foresees should be done. The most certain counsel of salvation must therefore be hoped for from the mouth of him in whose breast the inhabitant of the sevenfold counsel is recognized.”

### III

At that time the Felician heresy was greatly disturbing the Church of God. In addition, a certain desire for disputation concerning whether the souls of the saints ascend to heaven before the day of final judgment was causing the sacred teachers troublesome difficulty. To this was added a newly introduced method of baptism, different from the one already established through threefold immersion, a matter that was causing no small disturbance in the discipline of the Church. [Col. 0092C]

Letter 81 invites Paulinus to address these matters and compels him both to refute corrupt doctrines and to blunt pernicious innovations in discipline. After reviewing the errors, he writes:

> “With these and similar darts, drawn, as I think, from the quivers of unbelief, some who strive to wound the unity of the holy and Catholic Church and the truth of the universal faith also pollute the clearest cups of ecclesiastical faith with their most filthy dregs, and attempt once more to turn into the waters of folly the nuptial wine that Christ mercifully changed from water for the Virgin Mother—that is, the holy Church—to drink for her salvation.
>
> “But it is your task, O chosen shepherd of the flock and guardian of the gates of the city of God, who hold the key of knowledge in your powerful right hand and hide five clearest stones in your left [Col. 0092D], to crush completely, in their exceedingly proud Goliath, with a single blow of truth, the Philistines who blaspheme the army of the living God.”

A little later he adds:

> “All eyes look to you, desiring to hear something heavenly from your overflowing eloquence and awaiting through you the swift melting of the coldest hailstones of wisdom—stones that do not fear striking the summits of the wisest Solomon—by the most fervent sun of wisdom. But you, a burning and shining lamp, and so forth.”

That letter is indeed a panegyric of Paulinus’s faith and deserves to be read in full. You will find it in Appendix 1, no. 1, letter 3, together with Alcuin’s other letters to the same Paulinus.

### IV

Alcuin had wished that, for the benefit of those less skilled [Col. 0093A] in the doctrine of the faith, an easy and straightforward formula of faith might be written, one that could be committed to memory without difficulty; and he had urged King Charles that it be entrusted to someone in a province.

Paulinus fulfilled this request by writing a rule of faith in extremely plain verses, perfectly adapted to the understanding of the unlearned. In the same letter Alcuin commends both the work and its author’s faith:

> “When I reviewed,” he says, “your little book of the most sacred faith, adorned with the purity of Catholic peace, most pleasing in the beauty of its eloquence, and most firm in the truth of its meanings, I loosened all the reins of my soul into rejoicing . . . .
>
> “You have produced a work that will benefit very many and is entirely necessary for defining the Catholic faith—a work that I long desired and often urged upon the lord king: that the symbol of the Catholic faith should be gathered into a single little document, expressed in the plainest meanings and the clearest language [Col. 0093B], and distributed throughout the parishes of the various episcopal jurisdictions, to be read and committed to memory by the priests, so that, although people might speak different languages, one faith [XXXIX] might nevertheless resound everywhere.
>
> “Behold: what my humility desired, your sublimity has fulfilled. With the author of our salvation, you have an everlasting reward for this good will and, among human beings, praise for this perfect work. May your ever-burning charity fortify the camp of the eternal King on every side with unconquerable shields of faith, so that the cunning of the ancient enemy may nowhere find an entrance for its wickedness.”

### V

There is no reason to doubt that Paulinus was a just man, living by faith, according to the Apostle’s saying, supported also by hope [Col. 0093C], carried away by love of God, devoted to works of piety and religion, and wounded by love of his neighbor.

Hear from his own mouth with what energy of spirit he attacked heresies and with what confidence in God he was strengthened. At the Council of Frankfurt he said:

> “Therefore I, Paulinus, although an unworthy sinner and the least of all the servants of the Lord . . . according to the poverty of our limited understanding, taught fully by the Holy Spirit, do not fear to respond with heart, tongue, and pen against the madness of those who oppose the true faith.”

And when addressing King Charles, he wrote three books against Felix, the father of the heresy:

> “According to the understanding of my lowliness, although the limitation of my ability is obstructed by a slower intellect, I nevertheless do not refuse, with whatever kind of pen, to write what concerns me on behalf of the faith against the [Col. 0093D] objections of those who persist in an evil invention. For I know who said: ‘Open your mouth, and I will fill it.’”

This is the mark of true hope: that in proportion as a person distrusts his own power, he promises himself divine strength. Supported by this, Paulinus undertook so many dangers, endured so many injuries, completed so many journeys, performed so many labors, and swallowed so many adversities.

He sprinkled his works repeatedly with monuments of this most noble virtue, especially the *Book of Exhortation to Henry*. In chapter 10 he says:

> “What, I ask, is sufficient for the human being for whom the Creator himself is not sufficient? What more does one seek for whom his Redeemer ought to be every joy and everything?”

And in chapter 40, lifted up by expectation of the future life, he wrote:

> [Col. 0094A] “Let our heart always meditate on the heavenly promises; let us transfer all earthly things that we possess into the future dwellings of the heavenly kingdom. For we believe that, when our soul has been released from the bond of the flesh—if we have lived well and rightly before God—the choir of angels will immediately come to meet us, and the hosts of all the saints will mingle with our embraces.”

Many testimonies to this virtue, scattered throughout that book, will present themselves to the reader.

### VI

Paulinus’s love of God was extraordinary. Thus he begins his book to Henry:

> “O my brother, if you wish to know how perfect and complete righteousness it is to love God with one’s whole heart and to cling to him with one’s whole will, since he is the highest good [Col. 0094B]: to love the highest good is the highest blessedness. Whoever loves God is good; if good, then blessed also. The more ardently one loves him, the better one becomes.”

Kindled by this fire of charity, he took the greatest care to advance and spread the glory of the beloved God. He was especially moved by the life and passion of Christ the Lord, so that he seemed wholly aflame with love for him. In the cited book, chapter 21, he says:

> “Let us consider who it is who redeemed us with his precious blood, and what we owe him who redeemed us at such great cost. If we love earthly parents with such affection, although they endured labor for us only for a short time, should we not love our heavenly Father all the more, who was crucified for us?”

And below:

> “Although he grants us such great benefits, he asks nothing from us except that we love him and preserve our souls and [Col. 0094C] bodies undefiled for him, so that he may always dwell in us and we may remain in him.”

Alcuin recognized that Paulinus’s breast had truly become a dwelling place of God through charity, and he wrote to him in letter 62:

> “Your most holy heart is the promised land, flowing with the honey of wisdom and overflowing with the sweetest light of charity. In it the true and glorious Solomon has built, with the jewels of the virtues, a temple for the beauty of his habitation and majesty—a temple not destined to perish in Chaldean fire but to remain in eternal peace, in which the holy of holies is accessible to the supreme and true Pontiff, Christ alone, not once a year but forever and ever.”

### VII

From the same ardor of charity toward the Son there also blazed a flame of love for his mother, Mary ever-virgin. When, on the basis of Felix’s doctrine—which asserted that Christ, [Col. 0094D] according to the flesh, was merely the adoptive Son of God—the Virgin’s principal and most excellent title was attacked, and she was said to be only nominally, not truly, the Mother of God, Paulinus’s zeal against the blasphemous man immediately burst into flame. He applied his hand, as it were, to secure the more splendid jewel wavering in the Virgin’s diadem.

Hear a few of his words from book 1 against Felix, chapter 15:

> “If the venerable Virgin herself did not give birth to the true God and the true human being in the unity of person . . . by what right, then, does the Catholic Church, spread as one throughout the whole world, never cease to confess with free and public voice the blessed virgin Mary—her name sweet and venerable to me—as *Theotocon* (that is, ‘God-bearer’ or ‘Mother of God’)?”

[Col. 0095A] See the preceding and following passages there, written with equal zeal in defense of the Mother of God.

### VIII

He who loved God, the Son of God, and his mother so greatly likewise pursued with equal religious reverence the one whom he knew ought to be venerated no less than loved. Therefore he took such care, insofar as he was able, over everything that seemed to pertain to the worship and dignity of the Church of God that we may glory that the practices he introduced, deeply rooted and handed down to our own age, have continued.

Among these is what he established in canon 13 of the Synod of Forojulium concerning Sunday Vespers:

> “We command all Christians to venerate Sunday, when the beginning of the night has commenced—that is, on Saturday evening . . . when the signal has sounded or the hour has arrived for celebrating the evening office—with all reverence and honorable religious devotion.”

There is also the practice [Col. 0095B] mentioned by Walafrid Strabo (*On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25), namely, that Paulinus “celebrated hymns around the offering of the sacraments, whether composed by others or by himself.”

We see such practices continuing in some fashion into our own days, especially in rural churches, where curiosity for innovations has less access. We speak as we do because, in their proper place, we make particular mention of both matters.

The first canon of that council likewise confronted irreligious conduct among the ministers of the Church, lest the dignity demanded by the enactments of the ancient Fathers—in the performance of the offices of the sacred rites, in the fulfillment of the canonical hours, and in the celebration of the most holy mysteries—be destroyed:

> “First, therefore, in accordance with the ancient, divinely promulgated enactments of the Fathers, no priest of the Lord, nor anyone established under a canon, who is ignorant of or despises the canonical, indeed apostolic, definitions [Col. 0095C], should conduct himself disorderly or dishonorably in the house of God, which is the Church. Rather, while all remain in their proper order, the beauty of ecclesiastical dignity should remain inviolate.”

For this reason, so that the ministers of the Church, freed from every matter of court and military service, might hasten more freely and willingly to the temple and to the sacred actions, he persuaded Charlemagne to release clerics from military service, as is clear from fragment 1 of his letter to the king and from the words spoken at the end of the little book *Sacrosyllabus*. In this matter there is Charles’s decree among the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings* under the year 803, chapter VIII, in which he willingly grants what Paulinus had requested. [Col. 0095D]

### IX

Since Paulinus had shown himself so concerned and religiously attentive concerning divine worship, the dignity of the Church, and the edification of its ministers, with what devotion and spiritual eagerness must we believe him to have poured himself out before God in the duty of prayer?

Alcuin seemed to regard him as saturated—or rather, enriched—with the anointing of the Spirit of God. He commended himself to Paulinus’s prayers, thereby testifying that he placed the greatest confidence in them. Thus he writes in letter 113 [Col. 0096A]:

> “Although I have not written the name of my Paulinus on wax, which can be erased, I beg you not to forget your friend Albinus in your holy prayers. Store his name in some treasury of memory and bring it forth at the fitting time, when you have consecrated the bread and wine into the substance of Christ’s body and blood.”

He repeats this still more earnestly in poem 214, recalling the gift of tears with which Paulinus sprinkled his prayers and sacrifices:

> O father Paulinus, shepherd, patriarch, priest,  
> Noble part of my soul, distinguished part of my life,  
> Remember Albinus as you stand at the sacred altars,  
> And amid the sweet tears flowing over your face  
> Say: “Have mercy, O God, in your clemency, on our friend,  
> And graciously grant forgiveness for his sins,  
> That he may be permitted to praise you with the saints forever.”

That Paulinus did what Alcuin requested is demonstrated by his voluntary offering of his prayers to Henry, duke of Forojulium, immediately at the beginning of his *Exhortation* to him. He offers himself and promises that he will pray for God to set his heart ablaze with the flame of charity:

> “I strive,” he says, “to pray daily for you with an undivided desire of heart, although I am unworthy, asking him who is this good himself to make you abound in this most blessed good, dearest brother.”

What Paulinus did himself, he also urged others to do. On this subject he gave abundant commands, full of fitting and heavenly wisdom:

> ““Whatever work you undertake,” he says in the same book, chapter 28 [Col. 0096B], “first invoke God and give him thanks; and when you have completed it, do likewise. Invoke God with your whole heart, and you will find him. When you have found him, do not let him go, so that your mind may be joined to him in love.
>
> “Strive for this, my brother, throughout your life, and offer your pure prayer to Christ the Lord. Do not let the useless thoughts of this age disturb your heart, nor let your mind be carried away in different directions. Remember that you stand in God’s presence; he sees the hidden things of the heart and knows the secrets [Col. 0096C] of your mind.
>
> “Therefore attend vigilantly and constantly in God’s presence during the time of prayer, so that you may more easily escape the temptation of the devil as it approaches. For if evil and filthy thoughts of this age disturb your heart and compel you to commit some unlawful act, they will be driven from your soul by pure prayers and holy vigils.
>
> “Prayer is indeed a great fortification of the soul. Through the purest prayers, all things useful to us are granted by the Lord, and everything harmful is driven away. And, not to prolong or dwell on this matter, just as the flesh is nourished by bodily food, so the inner person is nourished and fed by divine utterances and prayers.”

These are the principles that Paulinus set forth concerning devotion to prayer.

### X

One flame of the same fire of charity [Col. 0096D] carried him toward God; another was likewise directed toward his neighbor. Alcuin composed a panegyric of Paulinus’s perfect love of God and of his brothers in these words in letter 62:

> “What is not found in such an abundant treasure of your heart? Its inhabitant is recognized as the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden; he holds the key of David, opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens, and with the key of wisdom he locks away whatever he wills in the hidden treasure of your breast.
>
> “This is the most holy ladder of dreaming Jacob, by which devout understanding commonly penetrates the secrets of heaven through the seven steps of spiritual gifts; and then, for the edification of the people subject to him, descends by the steps of fraternal love, so that he may become a teacher of the Church, sharing with Mary in divine contemplation and, with Martha, concerned with the diligent service of the guests at the Lord’s table.”

But let us hear Paulinus speaking in his own voice and bringing forth precepts of fraternal charity in the frequently cited [Col. 0097A] *Book of Exhortation*, which we shall cite frequently hereafter as well, because, since the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart, it is the richest witness to Paulinus’s virtues and an image of his soul. Thus Alcuin aptly writes of him in the cited letter:

> “I recognize you as abundantly bringing forth new things and old from the eternal treasure of charity, and as dipping your pen in the piety of brotherly faith.”

Accordingly, in chapter 22 he writes:

> “Let us have within us love of God and neighbor, because whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law; whoever, on the contrary, hates him is a murderer. Whoever loves his brother has a tranquil heart; whoever hates his brother is surrounded by a storm.
>
> “What you do not wish [Col. 0097B] to be done to you, do not desire to happen to your neighbor. If you see him conducting himself in good works, rejoice with him and regard his joy as your own; if he suffers any adversity, consider his sadness your own, and sympathize not only with the righteous but also with sinners. Never love your neighbor with a feigned heart.”

He likewise indicates the breadth of charity, which embraces everyone without exception, in chapter 66:

> “Let us do good to all human beings. I say to all—not partially, not to one or two or three, but to all human beings. For Christ suffered not only for the saints, but mounted the cross for sinners, the ungodly, and the wicked.
>
> “God gave the sun, the moon, the rain, everything that grows from the earth, and all the fruits that arise in the lands not only to the saints, but in common [Col. 0097C] to all human beings . . . so that our good works, our almsgiving, our charity, our patience, and our humility may be distributed in common to all human beings.”

If you read chapter 52, you will find similar expressions of love of neighbor.

### XI

From this twofold flame of charity arose the zeal with which he burned whenever he saw anything pertaining to the worship of God or the discipline of religion, or contributing to the salvation of his neighbors, being brought to ruin.

Thus, grieving from zeal over the ruin of his brethren, he wept as he wrote in chapter 55:

> “Why did we not say with the prophet: ‘Who will give water to our head and a fountain of tears to our eyes, that we may weep day and night over the wounded sons of our people’? What more fitting mourning, what more genuine lament, can be found than when each of us mourns and grieves over a lost soul?”

For this reason he also admonished, in weightier words, negligent and idle rulers who were sluggish in caring for souls. Part of his admonition survives in the fragment [Col. 0097D] entitled *On Rulers*:

> “First, they teach not well by their words but badly by their examples. Second, contrary to the divine will and sacred institution, they do not hesitate to remain away from their own parishes and cities—not merely for three weeks at a time (perhaps: only three weeks), but for a much longer period . . . . As a result, the worship of God is abandoned, preaching among the people is neglected, and care of those subject to them is disregarded, especially since such wandering is neither suitable to the priestly ministry nor authorized by canon law.”

### XII
