[Col. 0098A] From zeal for the honor of God and of his Church, his bride, there also proceeded that unconquerable strength by which, with steadfast courage, he defended the Church’s immunity and rights.

An example is the convocation of the Synod of Altinum. From there, fearing nothing from the neighboring Venetian leaders, he wrote a letter urging Emperor Charles not merely to avenge the crime committed against God’s priests, but to enact a law by which the immunity of ecclesiastical liberty might thereafter be more carefully observed and more religiously respected.

Hincmar also presents testimony to that priestly steadfastness of heart in his *Little Work 1*, or *The Quaternions*, and it should not be omitted here. These are the words of the bishop of Rheims:

> “When Charles had been misled by the tongues of flatterers into inflicting some prejudice upon churches concerning their own [Col. 0098B] possessions, and the bishops—especially Paulinus, the patriarch—resisted, he recognized the matter so fully and made such satisfaction to the Church and the bishops that a personal confession from his own mouth did not suffice him; rather, he sent to his successors a written statement of his confession and correction, confirmed by his own hand.”

Consult also the charters of privileges that he obtained from Charles, and you will see that, for the most part, the liberty of the Church was either preserved or restored by Charles, whom Paulinus had often approached for this reason.

### XIII

In the assessment of penance, too, Paulinus was a strict enforcer of ecclesiastical discipline, insofar as the observance of the severe custom of his age required, lest excessive indulgence on the part of those granting absolution pave the way for the commission of greater crimes.

Therefore, when [Col. 0098C] the matter of Heistulf’s penance was discussed at the Council of Frankfurt—he had killed his wife on the basis of a slight suspicion, on the report of only one and not even a reliable witness [xli]—Paulinus imposed a punishment according to the stricter canons. This appears from his letter to Heistulf, in which he addresses him in the sweetest words of charity; nevertheless, he demands from the wife-killer the payment of a very severe penalty consisting of numerous penitential works in retribution for the crime.

He did, however, offer a choice: either to withdraw into a monastery under the authority of an abbot and undergo all the arduous demands of regular observance, or, under the canon of public penance, to prolong his life by enduring prolonged mortification of the flesh and excluding himself from every pleasure.

### XIV

[Col. 0098D] What shall I say about his other virtues? Paulinus’s entire *Book of Exhortation* bears more than sufficient testimony to his prudence and discernment in practical affairs.

In this matter, the judgment of Charles himself is beyond all exception—Charles who was truly “Great,” not merely because of the prosperity of his arms and military campaigns but also because of the clarity of his mind. Having recognized Paulinus’s prudence, he summoned him to so many synods, placed him in charge of so many assemblies, and burdened him with so many responsibilities concerning Gaul, Germany, Italy, and Pannonia, yet always found him equal to the task.

Humility shines throughout his writings, when he so often calls himself [Col. 0099A] “the least of all the servants of God” (as at the Council of Altinum), or “an unworthy sinner and the least of all the servants of the Lord” (as at the Council of Frankfurt), or “a man of slower intellect and limited capacity” (as in the prefatory letter to King Charles accompanying the three books against Felix).

He held justice so dear that he appropriately warned Count Henry to guard against false piety, which sometimes recommends giving alms from ill-gotten goods. It is better, he says in chapter 31,

> “for someone to give a little from his own poverty to the needy than much from an unjust acquisition.”

You should not doubt that he was compassionate toward the poor. For in chapter 48 he says:

> “Let us honor the poor and revere Christ in them, who said: ‘As long as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me’; and we shall be sons of God and heirs of God, but fellow heirs with Christ.”

And what he urged in words he practiced in deeds. Ferrarius states in his Life that he distributed among the poor much of the wealth [Col. 0099B] with which Charles had endowed him.

His patience also shone forth, by which he endured so many adversities, especially in the labors he undertook to win unbelievers for the Church. So too did his courage, by which he magnanimously confronted the dangers of journeys, persecutions, and preaching. He also urged in words what he displayed in deeds:

> “In times of distress, flee to Christ the shepherd,”

as he says in chapter 57 of the *Exhortation*. His words concerning courage are:

> “Let no distress terrify us; let no calamity break us. The Lord is near; our shepherd is around us. What shall we fear?”

When Alcuin had encouraged him in letter 113 to undertake such labors for the faith and to endure every adversity for the gain of souls, he immediately regretted his admonition, since [Col. 0099C] it was pointless and superfluous to apply spurs to a horse already running swiftly:

> “What am I doing,” he says, “fool that I am, contrary to the philosophical proverb—carrying wood into the forest and watering rivers with trickling streams?”

### XV

Finally, the frequently cited *Book of Exhortation* is everywhere sprinkled with countless proofs of how much temperance Paulinus displayed, together with the virtues related to it: chastity, abstinence, abhorrence of pleasures and luxury, contempt for the world, and moderation of mind and feeling.

Read especially the following chapters:

- Chapter 13, *On Contempt for the World*.
- Chapter 17, *What It Means to Live According to the Flesh*.
- Chapter 25, *How Fleeting Are the Pleasures of the Flesh*.
- Chapter 34, *On the Sins of the Heart*.
- Chapter 35, *On Subduing the Flesh*.
- Chapter 36, *On Avoiding Luxury in Food*.
- Chapter 37, *On the Evils of Drunkenness*.
- Chapter 42, *On Guarding the Tongue*.
- Chapter 48, *On the Twofold Fast*.
- Chapter 64, *That the Flesh Receives the Devil*. [Col. 0099D]

From these you will learn by what spirit Paulinus was guided and with what reins of temperance he restrained the teasing, unbridled wantonness of the senses.

Above all, the final chapter of the often-praised book must be read in its entirety. It concludes with a most effective “prayer against the evils of the flesh” and sets forth what he desires for implanting the perfection of holiness in his soul:

> “Before I put off the flesh,” he says, “I shall say to my Redeemer what good I would have wished to urge the body with which I dwell to pursue. Let there not be in me, I beg you, O Lord, the desire of lust, but the love of most beautiful chastity.  
>
> “May I be slow to hear evil—I speak in the name of my soul—but eager for your word [Col. 0100A] and swift to accomplish it. May I be anxious in your fear, perfect in love, steadfast in faith, and in no way doubting in hope. May I burn with love of my neighbor; may I not be consumed by the heat of hatred or waste away in the bitterness of envy.  
>
> “Breathe into me always the holy work that I should contemplate; compel me to do it. Persuade me to love you; strengthen me to hold fast to you; guard me, lest I lose you.  
>
> “May the foot of pride not enter or rest in my dwelling, where your habitation ought to be; nor the desire of gluttony, fornication, avarice, or envy; nor anger, sadness, or empty glory.  
>
> “Give me deep humility, by which the height of the pride of the flesh that suffocates me may be healed. Give me measured abstinence, by which the excessive greed of the belly that destroys me may be restrained. Give me purity of heart, which may render me undefiled. Give me purity of spirit, because the filthy luxury of the flesh [Col. 0100B] plunges me into ruin.”

After the other virtues he requests, he says below:

> “These things I desire, O good Jesus, Savior, best Redeemer; these things I desire, which up to this point I have prayed for in supplication. These things—and these I ask—that because of the corruption of the flesh I may not perish forever, may not enter the second death, nor come into the land of forgetfulness.
>
> “May this voice of mine sound in the ears of your mercy, so that I may do your will, not that of the flesh; and may my whole mind meditate on you, delight in you, follow you, confess you, and so forth.”

These are the virtues by which true holiness is acquired, drawn from Paulinus’s writings. And we may say, friendly reader—as Saint Zeno said in his sermon *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, around the middle, if he is indeed the author:

> “From the books we have learned the virtues of the ancients, and from the virtues [Col. 0100C], the books.”

## XVI. By the practice of these and the other virtues, Paulinus became a saint. Yet since the glorious title of sanctity is usually attributed only to those whose integrity God is accustomed to attest by miracles and signs, such testimonies likewise ought not to have been lacking in Paulinus. Nearly all the historians who have made any mention of him bring forward, in explicit words, that he was renowned for miracles.

Ferrarius: “He was renowned for many miracles, by which he confirmed the doctrine he had preached.”

Bellonus, in the *Compendium of the Lives of the Patriarchs of Aquileia*: “In life he was renowned for many miracles, and in death as well.”

But in the fuller Lives, which the Milanese Palatine associates reprinted in volume XVI of the *Writers of Italian History*, we read:

> “Paulinus [Col. 0100D], who had deserved well of God and of men, died while nearly everyone was shedding tears; he was buried in the basilica at Cividale, and, finally, having become renowned for many miracles, was enrolled among the saints.”

Ughellus: “The ancient monuments of the Church of Aquileia testify that Paulinus was renowned for miracles in life and in death.”

Baronius also, under the year 802, no. 11, refers to the Aquileian records.

Bellarminus, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*: “He died, renowned for miracles.”

Labbeus, in his additions to Bellarmine: “He died, renowned for holiness and miracles during life and after death.”

Moreri, in the *Historical Dictionary*: “This great man, whom his holiness, proved by miracles, made illustrious, died, etc.”

Candidus, *Commentary on Aquileia*, book IV:

> “Paulinus was regarded as so illustrious for his virtues”—that is, for prodigies, which differ from moral virtues [Col. 0101A]: the latter constitute holiness, while the former declare it—“and for the sanctity of his life, that everyone admired him while living as though sent from heaven; and, after his death, they continue even to our own days to celebrate him frequently in that same city of Austria as a heavenly citizen.”

His ancient and more recent cult will be discussed below. For the present, I would have you know that tablets and votive offerings, as they are called, were not lacking at his altar. For in the inventory of 1566, on 8 September, from [xlii] the archive of the Church of Cividale, one reads in the vernacular:

> “One life (*vita*) and one tooth, all of silver, presented to Saint Paulinus,” etc.

# CHAPTER XV. The Doctrine of Saint Paulinus

### I

[Col. 0101B]

Ellies Dupin, carried away by French zeal, pronounces judgment on our Paulinus as though from the tripod: “His style is very simple and has nothing elevated about it.” Erasmus proceeds still more unjustly; in the *Admonition* prefixed in older editions to the book *On Saving Teachings*, or *Exhortation*, he accuses the author of the book of being uneducated. Yet he should be pardoned if, irreverently speaking of a sacred writer unknown to him, he dares such things.

Apart from both men’s opinions, the matter should be weighed more fairly. I would not deny that our Paulinus cannot readily be compared with the writers of the more fortunate age of Latin eloquence. He does not equal Cyprian’s energetic force, nor Leo’s harmony of gracefully extended periods; nor the eloquence of Chrysologus, nor Augustine’s flowers, nor Ambrose’s honeycombs, nor Jerome’s wit and graces—not to mention Tullian [Col. 0101C] eloquence, or that purity of Latin speech which we now admire as though letters had returned from exile, we who cultivate the stricter Muses. Indeed, he does not even approach them.

But from a man who flourished in an age when elegance had entirely gone into exile and was almost universally pronounced dead, while barbarism was turning everything upside down, such beauty of expression is not to be expected—or even demanded. The matter must be handled by a fairer comparison. Paulinus should not be compared with writers of other ages, but with his contemporaries and those of his own period. Since you will find that he yields first place to none of them, you may rightly call him a most learned man.

To enable you to understand how richly he was equipped with the storehouse of learning, according to the conditions of his age, I shall not hesitate to present a view [Col. 0101D] of the age of Paulinus; for the art of painting likewise strives to bring its figures out from the shadows assumed as a background into a more prominent light.

### II

Just as in the first years after the Flood a variety of languages arose at the tower of Babel from the confusion of one language, so the confusion of the one Latin language arose from a variety of languages. Italy, so often conquered by Gauls, Carthaginians, Vandals, Goths, and Lombards—Italy, the nurse and cultivator of Latin speech—was compelled to receive foreign words, and Latium was astonished to find that it no longer spoke Latin.

For just as, according to Augustine, the imperious city of Rome, victorious over the nations and their mistress, “imposed upon conquered peoples not only her yoke but also her language” (*On the City of God*, book XIX, chapter 7), so foreign nations in turn repaid the Roman Empire [Col. 0102A]. Whether it wished to or not, it was driven not merely to submit its neck to their yoke, but also to adopt their language.

Thus foreign and simultaneously barbarous words were imported into the Latin language. Fabius already lamented this in his own time, book I, chapter 5 of the *Institutes of Oratory*:

> “Foreign words,” he says, “came from nearly all nations, just as men did, and also many institutions.”

Since he testifies that this had happened in his own age, it must be believed to have happened with still greater force in later times. For this is almost the fated condition of all things: not only do they fail to remain long at the summit of perfection, but day by day they continually decline for the worse.

Thus the Latin language, after the age of Tully had raised it to the highest elegance, did not long remain there. Gradually and imperceptibly it declined; the defects [Col. 0102B] introduced into speech grew old and entrenched, and finally it lamented its own collapse into the deepest barbarism.

If any particular centuries were subject to this miserable misfortune, those nearest to the age of Paulinus suffered from this plague more than others. For, good God, what love of learning and knowledge existed in those days, when even the more conscientious bishops expected at least that their clerics could read?

The Fathers of the Council of Narbonne, in 589, decreed in canon 11:

> “From now on no bishop may ordain as deacon or presbyter anyone ignorant of letters; but those who have been ordained shall be compelled to learn.”

And lest you think that they demanded refined learning from the clergy, they reveal their meaning in the same canon when they add:

> “What place will he have in the Church of God if he has not been trained to read?”

Indeed [Col. 0102C], the ability to read was rightly desired at that time; for such was the ignorance of the Church’s ministers in delivering words to the people that the Council of Vaison, in 529, had already enacted in canon 2:

> “If a presbyter, prevented by some infirmity, is unable to preach in person, the homilies of the holy Fathers shall be read by deacons.”

### III

In the succeeding centuries the ignorance of the clergy advanced so far that in the time of Charlemagne and Paulinus parish priests were required to possess at least enough learning to teach the people the principal mysteries of the faith in the vernacular language. If they were sometimes unable even to do this, they were ordered publicly to read what had been written by someone more learned.

Hear what is decreed in book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 185:

> “It is known to all [Col. 0102D] that without faith it is impossible to please God. Therefore let there be no presbyter who does not publicly teach in the church, in a language understood by his hearers, that the faith of almighty God is to be believed simply in unity and Trinity, as well as those things which must generally be said to all concerning the avoidance of evils, the doing of good, and the judgment to come at the resurrection. But if he himself cannot clearly explain these matters in words, let him ask someone more learned to write them out for him, so that he may read them aloud clearly and those who hear may understand. And if he can do no more, let him at least admonish them with these words: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’”

Do you see from this what ignorance afflicted those centuries, when even the ability to read was lacking in men consecrated to God?

### IV

In the ninth century—namely, the very century at whose beginning Paulinus [Col. 0103A] was taken from human affairs—the ignorance of the clergy appeared no less, or scarcely any less, severe, although the vigilance of the bishops had labored earnestly to remove it, insofar as those times permitted.

From the canons of the councils of Eugenius II in 826 and Leo IV in 850, which were issued either against the ignorance of the clergy or for the restoration of literary studies, it is sufficiently clear how deeply that age was shrouded in darkness.

For in canon 4 of the Council of Eugenius, among other provisions, we read:

> “If a bishop is found to be unlearned, he shall be admonished by his own metropolitan; and thereafter priests, presbyters, deacons, and even subdeacons shall be admonished by their bishop so that they may be taught. Meanwhile, the subordinate priests and such clerics shall for a time be suspended from celebrating the divine sacrifice and from the offices, so that, once instructed, they may return to the proper [Col. 0103B] ministry. But if they cannot be taught, it shall be within the bishop’s power to judge canonically.”

Canon 34 [Col. 0103B] shows that ministers of the Church afflicted by this kind of ignorance could readily be found, since in many places there was no one capable of teaching the others:

> “From certain places,” said the Fathers of the council, “it is reported to us that neither teachers nor any provision for the study of letters can be found.”

What remedy they devised for this evil may be learned from what follows:

> “Therefore, in all bishoprics, among the subject peoples, and in other places where necessity demands it, every care and diligence shall be taken to appoint teachers and instructors who possess knowledge of letters, the liberal arts, and sacred doctrines, and who shall teach these things assiduously.”

From this you can see [Col. 0103C] how far the solicitude of the bishops extended in promoting learning. But you will understand even more clearly from Leo IV’s addition to this canon that the cultivation of humane letters was not held in very high regard, if we allow Scripture and, at most, the canons to define it:

> “Although teachers of the liberal arts,” says Leo, “as is customary, are rarely found among the parishes”—please consider that phrase, “as is customary”—“nevertheless, teachers of divine Scripture and instructors in ecclesiastical office must in no way be lacking.”

These were the commonly recognized limits of secular and sacred learning at that time.

What more is there to say? Such was the scarcity [Col. 0103D] of learned men, even in the Roman Church and at the papal court, that at the Council of Eugenius mentioned above, in 826, when no orator was available to deliver an address to the Fathers on the subject at hand, the deacon Theodore, in the pope’s name, recited and read from a written text the very preface that Pope Gregory II had placed before his synod in 721.

Compare the councils of those years, reader, and you will discover that this is so. The recent French writer, Abbot Fleury, also noted the point in *Ecclesiastical History*, volume X, page 284, Paris edition, 1704.

### V

It is therefore no wonder that, when learning and knowledge had been so savagely ruined in those centuries, the extreme barbarism of vocabulary became prevalent. Hence illustrious men have deserved well of our age by devoting their efforts to explaining foreign words and disclosing their meanings.

Henry Spelman, an English knight [Col. 0104A], and Charles du Fresne, Lord Du Cange, supported these worthy studies with their glossaries: the former encompassing the material in two parts, the latter in three volumes. Although the later part of Spelman’s work does not fully match the dignity and merit of the first, both men bound the scholars of the Middle Ages to themselves so strongly that, setting envy aside, they compel everyone to admit that without the torch of both—or at least of one, especially Du Cange—it is impossible, or scarcely possible, for anyone to enter and traverse those dark centuries without stumbling.

### VI

Since this is so, to return to our Paulinus, you should not be surprised if he too uses a phraseology and vocabulary that would not pass the touchstone of purer Latinity. Nevertheless, this does not prevent his doctrine from appearing elevated, or from rising [Col. 0104B] above the other intellects of his age.

For what else could the prudent man Paulinus have done but express himself in words accepted in his own time and compose his discourses in the more common style approved by the general taste? He had fallen upon those evil times which Sidonius had foretold when he wrote to Hesperius, book II, letter 10:

> “The multitude of the idle has grown so great that, unless a very few of you rescue the true character of the Latin tongue from the rust of everyday barbarisms, we shall soon have to lament it as abolished and dead. Thus all the purple of noble speech will be discolored through the negligence of the common people.”

If Paulinus had therefore acted otherwise than custom required, he would have incurred the same reproach with which Phavorinus, in Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book I, chapter 10, censured a certain young admirer of archaic words:

> “Curius, Fabricius, and Coruncanius [Col. 0104C] spoke in the words of their own age. But you, as though you were now speaking with the mother of Evander, use speech that has been obsolete for many years; and you do so because you wish no one to know or understand what you are saying. Live, then, according to the customs of the past, but speak in the words of the present.”

“But,” you will say, “it cannot be denied that people spoke badly at that time.” Why not? Indeed, they spoke terribly. Yet theirs was the common speech of everyone; “so much did they delight in the corruption of language,” to speak with Jerome, letter 22.

Paulinus himself saw that some sharp-nosed critic might accuse him and charge him with inelegance and barbarism. For that reason, after the verses *On the Rule of Faith*, he offers a kind of defense [Col. 0104D]. We refer you, reader, to that passage and to our notes on it.

But whoever knew how to accommodate himself to the custom of his age, and wisely conform himself to the genius of a corrupt century, who could be so foolish as to believe that, if the age had permitted otherwise, he would not have known how to adapt himself to more cultivated Latin and shape his words to a purer mode of expression?

Those, therefore, are excessively harsh exactors who demand golden words from an iron age—and those of an overly refined, not to say superstitious and unjust, palate, for whom “meals are not pleasant unless they smell of cake, and unless Apicius has seasoned them, and unless nothing has been lightly smoked by the culinary teachers of our time,” to use Jerome’s words again, letter 130 to Marcellus.

[Col. 0105A]

### VII

To establish his doctrine for you, examine what he wrote and the reasons for which he wrote it. You will discover that, truly, in his own time he was a lamp of the Gospel—not hidden under a bushel, but raised upon a lampstand in the Church of God so that he might shine before all and show the way of salvation and truth. He was also the salt by which the minds of the faithful might be preserved unharmed from the corruption of the spreading heresy of Felix.

For just as in earlier times the divine providence of the heavenly Father opposed vigorous antagonists and guardians of the faith to the new heresies and heresiarchs bursting forth from the abyss—to Arius and Macedonius, Athanasius; to Nestorius, Cyril; to Pelagius, Augustine; and to others, others—so he opposed Paulinus to Felix and Elipandus.

I admit that Paulinus was not the only one to engage these heretics, for it is clear that Etherius [Col. 0105B], bishop of Osma, an abbot named Beatus, and Alcuin also entered the arena. But since “success did not match their efforts,” as John Mariana says in *Spanish Annals*, book VII, chapter 8, one lexicographer says that Beatus “opposed himself in vain” (Hoffman, under “Etherius”); and Alcuin, not trusting his own strength, requested fellow soldiers from Charlemagne: Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia; Theodulf, bishop of Orléans; and Richbod, bishop of the Church of Trier. It remains unknown whether the last two undertook anything against these heretics.

Paulinus, therefore, was the standard-bearer in the battle and the first in rank—or, to use the more sacred phrase of divine Scripture, he was the leader of the word. When Alcuin wrote to Charlemagne in letter 8, “I alone am not sufficient for the reply [Col. 0105C],” Paulinus himself at the Council of Frankfurt, whether from greater humility or greater courage, was able to say:

> “Therefore I, Paulinus, although an unworthy sinner . . . according to the poverty of our understanding, with the Holy Spirit teaching, do not fear to respond with heart, tongue, and pen against the madness of those who are adversaries of the true faith.”

I do not deny that he asked Charlemagne to have the three books he had written against Felix delivered “into the hands of Albinus, your distinguished and most devout spokesman, and to me sweeter than all else”—thus Paulinus wrote to Charlemagne in a surviving fragment of a letter. But this was an advance sign of friendship, as the letter makes clear, and at the same time an exercise in humility.

For he did not need another’s help, having alone undertaken, on behalf of all the Fathers of Italy [Col. 0105D], the burden of replying. How highly all the Fathers of the council valued his wisdom and learning is clearly shown by their unanimous decision that the *Sacrosyllabus* composed by him should be sent, in the name of the entire council, to the bishops of Spain.

### VIII

As the unanimous judgment of the synod’s Fathers concerning Paulinus’s doctrine proceeded from an actual case involving the doctrine of faith, so an equal judgment regarding discipline emerged from another case. In the case of Heistulf, who had killed his wife after she was accused of adultery on the testimony of a single insignificant man, the judgment of Paulinus alone is cited as the penitential ruling, while the Fathers accepted as valid whatever proceeded from Paulinus’s mouth.

That his decision was consonant with the laws [Col. 0106A] of the Church and with discipline is evident from the fact that it was later received among the ecclesiastical sanctions, chapter 32, question 2, and was adopted by other bishops as a rule and model for similar cases. For Wulfad, bishop of Bourges, asked Hincmar, bishop of Reims, to send him Paulinus’s judgment concerning wife-killers, as Flodoard records in *History of Reims*, book III, chapter 21. On this matter, however, see what we have said more fully in our commentary on that letter.

### IX

John Aventinus gives illustrious testimony in the *Annals of Bavaria*, book IV, chapter 5, no. 16, that Paulinus was also skilled in the theory and practice of forensic affairs. He relates that, when Charlemagne appointed twelve leading officials to settle lawsuits, Paulinus was placed before the others for the administration of justice:

> “Charlemagne sent twelve nobles, skilled in divine law, to Italy and Rome, to investigate disputes, hear petitions, resolve cases, settle lawsuits, and administer justice. Their leader was Paulinus [Col. 0106B] of Aquileia.”

[xliv]

### X

But now, since we are considering what reputation and opinion Paulinus’s learning had won among thoughtful men around the very time when he flourished, let us bring forward some testimonies.

First, there is that of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, from his letter to Charles the Bald, which Flodoard cites in *History of Reims*, book III, chapter 15. In it Hincmar ranks Paulinus alongside the ancient Fathers and teachers of the Church listed in the Gelasian catalogue—not merely by the judgment of his own age, but also by that of the Apostolic See, expressed in the case of Felix, the condemned heretic.

He says:

> “We likewise embrace with equal reverence [Col. 0106C] the judgments of those who flourished in the Church through Catholic doctrine and holiness of conduct”—with equal reverence, that is, with that accorded to Gelasius—“such as the venerable presbyter Bede . . . and Paulinus, patriarch of the Aquileian province, of revered memory, as well as Alcuin, a religious and learned man. The Roman Apostolic See not only most graciously accepted their faith and doctrine, but also extolled them with many praises, as we find in the writings of that holy See, which our Church received from that same mother of Churches in the time of the emperor Charles of blessed memory, when a synod was held concerning the known infidelity of Felix and its acts were sent to the Roman Church, as to the summit of the Churches. Whoever reads their writings understands how worthy they are of praise and acceptance [Col. 0106D].”

But the brilliant witness of Alcuin must also be heard.

### XI

In more than one place, indeed very frequently, Alcuin extols and commends Paulinus’s doctrine, though never beyond what the man deserved. His holiness and his intimate friendship with Paulinus make it clear that he neither wished nor was able, through ignorance, to deceive anyone. Although he speaks with Paulinus himself, you should not therefore think that there is any flattery in the man. Such courtly blandishments—or malicious insinuations—are not even to be suspected in holy men.

Accordingly, in letter 62 he addresses Paulinus, who had previously written to him:

> “You have brought forth for me innumerable examples [Col. 0107A] overflowing with rare-flowing nectar from the most holy bridal chamber of your heart, so that I see more truly fulfilled in you that Aristotelian proverb: Aristotle, who continually wrote the most acute arguments of the *Peri Hermeneias*, is said to have dipped his pen in his mind. But your most holy heart is the promised land, flowing with the honey of wisdom . . . . There is the ark of wisdom and the tablets of the two Testaments; and the cherubim cover all these things in the abundance of their knowledge. From beneath their wings the divine oracles respond to the peoples, and rivers of living water leap forth for those thirsting for eternal salvation. Let the thirsty man come from the arid regions of ignorance and drink.”

This is what Alcuin wrote. Whenever he heard that anything newly invented was beginning to sprout in the field of the Church that conflicted with sound faith, the discipline of earlier times, or the tradition of the Fathers, he fled to Paulinus as to an oracle. We noted this in the preceding chapter, nos. 3 and 4, from letter 81.

For the present, from that same letter we note only the words [Col. 0107B] in which he commends Paulinus’s eloquence and learning in the works he composed either against heresies or in defense of the faith:

> “When I am permitted to behold the letters of your Blessedness, sweeter than every honeycomb, do I not seem to myself to be wandering entirely among the various flowers of paradise and, with the eager hand of my desire, plucking spiritual fruits from them? How much more, when I reread your little book on the most holy faith, adorned with the purity of Catholic peace, most delightful in the beauty of its eloquence, and most firmly grounded in the truth of its meaning, I loosen all the reins of my soul into joy. There I saw four rivers of virtues flowing from one radiant and salutary fountain of paradise, irrigating not only the meadows of Ausonian fertility but also the fields of the whole of ecclesiastical Latin. There I understood that the golden streams of spiritual meanings [Col. 0107C] abounded with the gems of scholarly urbanity.”

### XII

After the Avars had been subdued, and while the anxious mind of Charlemagne was concerned with their conversion, he fixed his eyes, together with all the nobles of his court, upon Paulinus, to whom he would entrust the task of subjecting that province to the yoke of Christ.

Alcuin’s letter urging him to undertake this office followed. We quoted part of it in the preceding chapter, no. 2, where Alcuin urges Paulinus to make himself the teacher of the people, because “in addition to the proximity of the regions and the excellence of his authority, the distinction of wisdom and everything necessary for the undertaking are united in him.”

He further commends the abundance of his learning:

> “From his most abundant heart, the rivers of Gihon [Col. 0107D] can pour forth across the whole expanse of the Nile’s countryside, to fertilize flowers of various kinds.”

He concludes by praying that the seat of divine wisdom may remain eternally in him, since it was presently seen to be so wondrously established there:

> May wisdom ever flourish eternally  
> In your breast, rich in divine gifts, holy father.

Another letter—number 113 in the sequence, but number 6 in Appendix I, no. 1—also urges him to undertake the office of preaching:

> “Cry out,” it says, “do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet. Let your throat be God’s trumpet. Preach in season and out of season. Be a cock in preaching, girded with chastity; be a ram, strongest in truth, whom no king will be able to resist. Be a lamp upon a lampstand in the house of God. Your tongue closes and opens heaven, etc.”

Writing also to Henry, duke of Friuli, Alcuin withdraws [Col. 0108A] from offering him further and more extensive instruction, because he knew that Paulinus would fulfill his duties more abundantly:

> “I might perhaps have written more to you, venerable man, concerning the practice of Christian piety,” he wrote in letter 94, “if my distinguished teacher and pious instructor in heavenly life, my Paulinus, were not present for you; from whose heart flows a fountain of living water leaping up into eternal life. Have him as the mediator of your eternal salvation, lest the foot of your conduct stumble anywhere, etc.”

### XIII

The most abundant witnesses to his doctrine are, finally, his writings [Col. 0108B]. If you consider their number and bulk, they are neither many nor large; but if you consider the importance of the subject for which they were written, you will count them among the more weighty and more distinguished works of the Fathers.

I set out their register here briefly, preserving the chronological order.

In the year of Christ 794, at the Council of Frankfurt, he presented to the Fathers, in the name of the bishops of Italy, the little book called the *Sacrosyllabus*, and published it with their approval. Charlemagne, together with the Fathers, also sent it to the bishops of Spain. At that time Paulinus likewise wrote his letter concerning the penance of Heistulf.

In 795 he wrote to Henry, duke of Friuli, the book of the *Exhortation*, in which he presents a proper method for a man entangled in secular concerns and holding public office—a method by which a layman, a magistrate, and a head of household may each take up and attain the way of salvation without stumbling.

In 796 he convened the Council of Friuli [Col. 0108C]. In an elegant discourse he explains the purpose of the council, commends the faith, expounds the Creed, and finally proposes fourteen canons for the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline.

In the same year and the following ones he composed three books against Felix, adding at the end a *Rule of Faith*, composed with the sweetness of meter so that it might attract the uneducated and be committed to memory.

We place here Paulinus’s verses and fragments of letters as works of uncertain date.

Finally, in 803 he convened the Council of Altinum. From there he sent a letter to Charlemagne, setting out the proceedings of the synod and demanding vengeance for the crime committed against the patriarch of Grado, who had been thrown from a tower by the Venetian leaders and crushed by the fall.

[Col. 0108D]

### XIV

From these facts you can see with what right and merit the Church of Friuli venerated him not only for his exceptional holiness but also for the excellence of his doctrine. It should therefore cause no surprise if, on some occasions, when reciting the canonical hours of the Church or celebrating Masses in his memory, it used the same prayer that Rome customarily used for the other Doctors of the Church:

> “O God, who appointed blessed Paulinus as a minister of eternal salvation to your people, grant, we ask, that as we had him as a teacher of life on earth, so we may always deserve to have him as an intercessor in heaven. Through our Lord, etc.”

This prayer [xlv] appears in the manuscript book marked no. 12, entitled *Book of Sacraments of the Year of Our Lord 1303*, page 229 verso, “In the Church of the City of Austria.”

# CHAPTER XVI. Paulinus’s Friendships with the More Illustrious Men of His Age

[Col. 0109A]

### I

Laelius’s statement in Cicero’s book bearing his name, or *On Friendship*, was also taught by our Paulinus. Laelius says:

> “This is my first conviction: that friendship cannot exist except among the good.”

Paulinus taught the same when, in chapter 44 of the book of the *Exhortation*, he advised his friend Henry, duke of Friuli, merely “to enjoy the company of perfect men and not to turn his ear away from their words, because they are the life and safety of the soul; but to avoid the proud and those stained by other vices, so that not even one such person should be kept in the household.”

He also put this teaching into practice when he cultivated the friendship of those who, by common judgment, were thought to surpass others in the reputation for integrity. For since the Wise Man says, “Every person will associate with one like himself” (Ecclesiasticus 13:20), and Saint Leo says, “That friendship is firm which likeness of character has joined together” (*Sermon 1 on the Fast of the Tenth Month), he cultivated only those who appeared distinguished and commendable for the uprightness of their lives.

How could it have happened that a most holy priest [Col. 0109B] formed relationships except with such men? “For what fellowship has a holy man with a dog?” says Ecclesiasticus in the same passage, verse 22.

Therefore those whom Paulinus had as friends must certainly be considered worthy of his friendship. And those who had Paulinus as their friend are sufficiently commended by that fact, since they were judged worthy of Paulinus’s friendship. Paulinus, worthy of such friends, and such friends, not unworthy of Paulinus, mutually conferred distinction upon one another.

### II

Although friendship rarely takes root [Col. 0109C] between people of unequal fortune, it is especially rare between persons of royal and private condition. Pliny, Trajan’s encomiast, gives the reason in his *Panegyric*, when he commends Trajan’s affability, by which he had bound the hearts of his subjects to himself:

> “For what friendship could there be between those among whom some seemed to themselves masters and others slaves? You drew to yourself this friendship, once driven away and wandering. You have friends because you yourself are a friend.”

Since this is truly so, it came about that Charlemagne, king of the Franks and later emperor of the Romans, who loved Paulinus, was himself also loved by Paulinus.

The marks of this mutual love are found in Paulinus’s words and Charlemagne’s actions. Paulinus mentions in more than one place the relationship that existed between himself and the king. At the Council of Friuli he admits that he had often been summoned by Charlemagne to assemblies of the Fathers and had attended them [Col. 0109D]—a great testimony to the king’s love for the man.

Indeed, this is confirmed by what he said at the Council of Frankfurt near the end of his address, or *Sacrosyllabus*, to the Fathers. He not only extolled the king with praises, as flatterers also know how to do, but went so far as to petition that the clergy be exempted from military burdens, promising that the clergy would repay this favor by fighting for him with spiritual arms:

> “Our most tranquil prince must be entreated,” he said, “so that he may fight for us against visible enemies, and we may fight for him against invisible enemies with spiritual arms.”

He repeats the same point in a certain letter [Col. 0110A], of which a fragment survives, inserting an admonition that would not displease the king because it was accompanied by a prayer for him.

Such familiarity provided the occasion for a correspondence to be established between them. Charlemagne then required Paulinus to rise against Felix and Elipandus; and Paulinus, rising against them, dedicated to Charlemagne the books in which he attacked them, adding a letter asking him to share the books with Alcuin.

All these things sufficiently show that Paulinus’s friendship with Charlemagne was the kind of friendship that can exist with kings.

### III

But it shines forth even more clearly from Charlemagne’s actions how much love he bore Paulinus and how he returned his friendship. As soon as he learned of Paulinus, who was known throughout the world merely by the name of grammarian, he gave him a pledge of his goodwill by honoring him with a royal diploma and a royal donation, which we discussed above in chapter 3.

It should therefore be no wonder that, after Paulinus had been raised [Col. 0110B] to the patriarchal see, Charlemagne enriched the Church of Aquileia with so many privileges on his account, since he was bound to him by such great affection.

Since the proof of love is the display of works, recall what we reported in chapter 4, section 4. It will then be clear what Charlemagne accomplished, and with what solicitude, in order that Paulinus might succeed the deceased Siguald in the see of Aquileia. For a considerable time he lingered in our regions with no other purpose than this: when the patriarch, whose impending death was believed to be near, had died, to summon Paulinus as quickly as possible as a new bridegroom for the widowed Church.

IV. Finally, after he had been invested with the patriarchal mitre, he pursued him with such affection and honor that, whenever matters of greater importance in the court had to be decided, he awaited Paulinus’s judgment by letter, and sometimes his presence as well. Since Charles was accustomed to keep selected men—especially among the bishops—who could assist the king with their counsel in the administration of the state, who would deny that Paulinus must be numbered among them? Let us hear what the Fathers of the council assembled at Saint Mary’s on the borders of the parish of Rheims in the year 881 said in chapter 8 about Charles’s commendable practice, when they urged Louis, son of Louis the Stammerer and son of Charles the Bald, to choose the wisest counselors after the example of his great-grandfather:

[Col. 0110C] “Finally, most beloved lord king, we turn our speech to you . . . As some of our number heard from those who were present, the emperor Charlemagne, who nobly enlarged the Frankish kingdom, ruled it successfully for forty-six years, and surpassed the Frankish kings in wisdom both in the sacred Scriptures and in ecclesiastical and human laws, never at any time permitted himself to be without three of his wisest and most distinguished counselors. Rather, in turn, by successive appointments, insofar as it was possible for them, he kept them with him; and whatever he contemplated, whether by day or by night, concerning the welfare of Holy Church and the advancement and stability of the kingdom, he recorded on those same tablets and discussed it with those same counselors whom he kept with him.” [Col. 0110D]

Among these men, who were not always at the king’s side but remained there in turn by successive appointments, we have Paulinus, who—as he himself indicates in more than one passage—presented himself at court only when summoned. For although Charles honored and loved bishops most devotedly and affectionately, he prudently refrained from calling them away from the governance of their dioceses, and in this matter was almost scrupulously conscientious. This is clear from the permission he sought from the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt to retain in his presence “for ecclesiastical interests,” besides Angilramnus, bishop of Metz, whose stay at court was already supported by the authorization of Pope Hadrian, also Hildebold, bishop of Cologne; the entire synod consented to this by unanimous vote, as is evident from the penultimate canon of the council cited above. [Col. 0111A]

Paulinus therefore cannot be counted among the bishops who remained at court as counselors; but it is worthy and just to place him among those summoned at appointed times. Indeed, several indications of this summons are inserted here and there in his life, so that he cannot in any way be removed from the number of Charles’s intimate chosen counselors, or even from the roll of his friends. [Col. 0111B]

V. The bond of friendship between Charles and Paulinus is finally and most clearly confirmed by the judgment of the Apostolic See itself, and by the decision taken by the most holy pontiff Leo III. Having perceived not only Paulinus’s skill and prudence in conducting affairs, but also the affection with which the emperor Charles regarded him, Leo entrusted him with the burden of the legation and with his own responsibilities at the council of Aachen.

The soundest principles of statecraft advise that envoys be sent to powerful rulers who have at some time earned their favor and friendship above all others. [xlvi] For what good can be expected when an envoy who is not pleasing to the prince is sent? Rather, there is every reason to fear that he may be forced to withdraw with nothing accomplished, and sometimes with matters turned for the worse, departing not only empty-handed but also without honor. [Col. 0111C]

Thus Tacitus—or rather Helvidius Priscus in Tacitus (*Histories* IV.7), arguing against Marcellus Eprius, who wanted envoys chosen by lot, while Helvidius maintained that they should be sent by selection of the senate—wisely said that “it concerned the welfare of the state, and the honor of Vespasian, that those whom the senate regarded as most innocent should go to meet him, so that they might fill the emperor’s ears with honorable discourse . . . There is no greater instrument of good government than good friends.”

The fact that Paulinus was sent to Charles with the insignia of an apostolic legation therefore shows abundantly and beyond doubt that he was pleasing both to the pontiff and exceedingly dear to the emperor. [Col. 0111D]

VI. The love with which Paulinus was honored by noblewomen seems inseparable from Charles’s friendship with him. Among these women Liutgardis stands out, the fourth of Charles’s wives. Liutgardis, taken in marriage in 794 after the death of Fastrada, who had succeeded Hildegard—taken after the repudiation of Berta, daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards—possessed a manly spirit beyond her sex. She accompanied her husband when he went hunting, cultivated refined learning, and treated its teachers with royal favor. [Col. 0112A]

Besides these virtues worthy of a queen, by which she won the affection of subject peoples, she displayed other qualities of mind that showed her to be a religious and deeply pious woman devoted to God—as Alcuin calls her in letter 79—and a truly Christian princess. Devoted to these pursuits of piety and liberal learning, she formed an intimate relationship with blessed Alcuin, who was being retained at court by her husband Charles, as can be discerned from the letters that still survive.

And because, if the saying is true anywhere, it is truest in the case of God’s servants—that saying of Plato in the *Lysis*, “Friends are made under the guidance of the divine conciliator”—a spiritual affection grew up between Liutgardis and Alcuin, so that in the affairs of her soul she depended, as they say, upon his words and nod with blind obedience. This is suggested by the title of spiritual daughter, by which he habitually addressed her when speaking of her. Thus he closes letter 21, entitled *Epitaph of Liutgardis*, addressed to Charles: [Col. 0112B]

> May she whom I wish always to live happily forever remain so,  
>   
> My dear daughter; may she, I pray, be dear to God.

VII. Since holy love is untouched by jealousy and loves to see those whom it has once judged worthy of love loved by others as well, Alcuin brought Liutgardis to Paulinus’s attention, and Paulinus to Liutgardis’s, with the fortunate result that they afterward pursued one another with mutual affection. So great was this most religious woman’s devotion of love toward Paulinus that she honored him with frequent gifts and presented his church with precious furnishings.

Thus Alcuin wrote to Paulinus in letter 95 of our Appendix 1, no. 1, letter 4: [Col. 0112C]

> From this you may know how great my eagerness was to speak with you, if the unjust distance between our lands had not prevented the opportunity for conversation. For, because of matters that arose, I placed three little notes at once in the right hand of a single distributor: one concerning my anxiety, another concerning my small gift, and a third on behalf of my daughter Liutgardis, a religious woman devoted to God. She sent two bracelets of refined gold to Your Holiness, weighing twenty-four denarii less than a full pound according to the king’s new coinage, so that you might pray for her with your priests, that divine mercy might order her days toward the salvation of her soul and the exaltation of His holy Church. Confident in your faithfulness, I urged her to do this. But you, holy father, remembering both me and her everywhere in the love of Christ, farewell.

VIII. Moreover, a friendship grew between Paulinus and Count—or Duke—Henry of Friuli such as ordinarily arises between holy men. See the truly golden book of the *Exhortation*, which we have frequently mentioned above and which we are attempting to prepare with a special dissertation. The very title of the book bears the mark of intimate friendship. Although in earlier times Henry’s name was unknown, or the work falsely bore the name of Count Julian, those who published the work—whether under an unspoken name, because the true name was unknown, or under a false one—always declared it to be addressed either to a most dear or to a most intimate friend. [Col. 0112D]

And that Henry truly was such a friend will be recognized by anyone who reads the work: from the courtesy with which he addresses the man, from the exhortations sprinkled with the most sincere charity, from the familiarity and simplicity, from the title “brother,” by which he so often addresses Henry, and from six hundred other indications. [Col. 0113A]

Hence the love and esteem that arose in Henry for Paulinus prevailed so strongly upon the count’s mind that he was moved to promote works of piety. He built the church of Saint Nicholas at Sacile and endowed it with richer estates. Although it was situated between the boundaries of the dioceses of Concordia and Ceneda, he nevertheless wished it—plainly for the sake of his Paulinus—to be henceforth subject to the Aquileian see, under privileges obtained from the Apostolic See, as we still see it today.

There is no reason to detain our reader further over these matters; we refer him instead to the first dissertation cited above, where they are treated more fully. Let these points merely be recalled to make Henry’s evident friendship toward Paulinus clear.

IX. The mediator and kindler of this mutual affection was the same Alcuin. Although, from the time when Henry had assumed the government of our province and had become known to Paulinus, the seeds of mutual charity had begun to grow into friendly intimacy, Alcuin nevertheless did not cease, when an opportunity arose, to nurture them and provide fuel for the fire. [Col. 0113B]

Accordingly, when Henry requested writings on the practice of piety, Alcuin withdrew from the task and referred him to Paulinus, writing in letter 94:

> I might perhaps have written more to you, venerable man, about the observance of Christian piety, if my distinguished teacher and pious instructor in the heavenly life, my Paulinus, were not available to you, from whose heart flows a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life. Have him as a mediator of your eternal salvation.

When Henry had returned from Avaris with a notable victory and had carried the enemy’s baggage and spoils to the king, who was then staying at Aachen, he also brought Paulinus’s letter to Alcuin. On his return to Friuli he carried Alcuin’s reply to Paulinus, as Alcuin himself indicates in his response, letter 73: [Col. 0113C]

> Having received the lines of Your Wisdom . . . through the bearer of this present little letter, and so forth.

Here it is clear that the same man was carrying the letters in both directions. In this letter Alcuin again commends Henry, the bearer of the little letter, to Paulinus with regard to the spiritual governance of his soul, and then promises fuller offices of greeting through Angilbert, who was about to set out for Rome, God willing, to carry to the basilica of Saint Peter, in the king’s name, the offerings from the spoils of the conquered Avars.

“He himself,” Alcuin said, “by the living office of his tongue, will show our needs—or his own [*pro et suas*, ‘and his own’]. Our common son Angilbert, who is going to Rome, will send you, God willing, a fuller series of our greetings.” [Col. 0113D]

Alcuin himself mentions this letter in another letter, namely 112, where toward the end he says:

> A little earlier I sent two little letters to Your Paternity: one through the holy bishop of Istria, the other through the venerable man Henry, the duke.

X. In truth, no bond of friendship can be found stronger, holier, or sweeter than that by which Paulinus and Alcuin were bound; indeed, it was so close that either of them might with greater right have said to the other what Ausonius wrote to another Paulinus in letter 24:

> Now our names were preparing  
>   
> To be enrolled among the ancient friends of a better age.

There is no need to detain you at greater length, since the matter is perfectly clear from their mutual letters. [xlvii] Although Paulinus’s letters have not survived, to the immense loss of all good men, it is nevertheless abundantly evident from Alcuin’s writings that they pursued one another through the reciprocal offices of charity.

What could be a more tender proof of friendship than what he presents in letter 62? Listen: [Col. 0114A]

> While the fiery sun rises with the star of burning Cancer—whence you may infer that this letter was written after the middle of June—and the parched earth awaits rain because of excessive and prolonged heat, so your will, thirsting in my breast for the refreshment of great love, had long desired letters from Your Blessedness. Again and again, at every moment of the hours, this utterance returned, burning within me: “When will the desired, most sweet lines of my beloved arrive? When shall I see the signs of salvation from my dearest one? When will a page of Ausonian nobility show me the prosperity of my desired friend? Shall I see whether any memory of our friendship joined in Christ remains in his heart; whether he keeps the name of his Albinus, written by the stylus of charity, hidden in the secret place of his heart, just as the most sweet name of Father Paulinus remains alive in the heart of his son, inscribed in eternal letters by perpetual affection?” [Col. 0114B]
>
> Behold, it has come; behold, the page of paternal piety has come, which I had long desired, sweeter to my palate than every honeycomb and more honorable to my eyes than all refined gold. Joyfully I received it with both hands and embraced it with my whole breast, hanging upon what it might announce to me from my Paulinus. When the seals had been broken, I opened a path with eager eyes through every line, and, recognizing in them the desired good health of the hoped-for greeting from my father, I sipped kisses from every individual letter-stroke and poured my whole self into thanksgiving to Christ God, saying: “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing, and the humbled bones will rejoice. And I who was humbled in sadness have now been exalted in joy.” [Col. 0114C]
>
> And if anything could have been added beyond the full measure of charity, I would certainly have heaped upon the former fullness of affection the abundance of a new joy. Therefore whoever has received in his heart wounds sweeter than every honeycomb from the honeyed arrow of charity knows that I am not exaggerating in the bosom of this little letter leaves of speech withered by autumnal cold. Rather, this willing right hand has drawn from the living fountain of charity, in order truly to water the flowers of love, so that I might pour the drops of my great love into your innermost being, and so forth. [Col. 0114D]

XI. What sweeter, dearer, or more delightful thing can be read in the commerce of friendship? Receive several other passages from the following letters, equally tender and sweet. In letter 81, with the longing of a burning heart, he expresses his affection for his own Paulinus:

> I seem to have some refreshment for my spirit, so that the flame of charity hidden in my heart may perhaps draw out some spark, lest all that burns within grow completely numb, when an opportune moment presents itself for me to write something to Your Charity. Why, when I am permitted to behold the letters of Your Blessedness, sweeter than every honeycomb, do I not seem to myself to move wholly among the various flowers of paradise and, with the eager hand of my desire, gather spiritual fruits from them? And so forth.

And in letter 112: [Col. 0115A]

> If I enjoyed the presence of Your Blessedness every day, would I ever then be satisfied with the sweetness flowing from your honeyed mouth? Rather, as much as my eager mind drank from the fountain of the life-giving stream, so much would its thirst increase. But now such great distances divide us from the familiarity of face-to-face conversation that scarcely can a bearer of a traveling letter [perhaps: “of the present letter”] be found. In the narrow cavern of my breast the vessel of charity boils, but it has no one to whom it may display the radiance of its splendor or serve the cooked banquet of charity, and so forth.

In letter 113 he again laments Paulinus’s absence and commends their ancient friendship:

> Bodily absence ought not to divide affection, because a friendship that can be abandoned was never true. From the time I knew you, sweetest friend, I have always loved you, and my heart entered into a covenant of friendship with your heart. Although I did not write the name of my Paulinus on wax, which can be erased, please do not forget the name of your friend Albinus in your holy prayers, and so forth. [Col. 0115B]

XII. Although Cicero’s statement is entirely true—that “the affection and friendship of human beings is disinterested” (*On the Nature of the Gods* I, near the end)—it must nevertheless not be denied that friendships are fostered by gifts, especially when gifts are weighed in the balance of reason and distributed with prudence. Thus Seneca says in letter 19:

> What then? Do benefits not create friendships? They do, if one has been permitted to choose those who will receive them, and if they have been placed appropriately rather than scattered.

Therefore God himself, who graciously deigns to receive us into friendship and never ceases to show his love through benefits, in turn asks from us works pleasing to him as witnesses of love, and our gifts. Saint Peter Chrysologus expressed this most elegantly in sermon 10 on Psalm 28:

> You see that the heavenly Father perceives love through gifts, gives affection through what is given, and proves charity through presents. [Col. 0115C]

It is therefore no wonder that Paulinus and Alcuin testified to their friendship by mutual gifts. They did not love one another for the sake of avarice; rather, each asked the other for gifts as the token of friendship.

Alcuin testifies to his joy in letter 73, since from the gifts he had received from Paulinus he knew that he had not been erased from his friend’s memory:

> Having received, he says, the lines of Your Wisdom and the gifts of your charity, I rejoiced greatly, learning of your prosperity and of your remembrance of us, which, as I humbly beseech you, may you always preserve in your holy prayers through paternal affection. [Col. 0115D]

Thus Alcuin acted with his Paulinus as Jerome had acted with Marcella, from whom he had received little gifts, and to whom he wrote in letter 20:

> So that we may console bodily absence by spiritual conversation, each does what he can: you send gifts, and we send back letters of thanks.

Do not suppose, however, that these gifts displayed anything of curiosity or vanity. From the things Paulinus had once promised Alcuin, and which Alcuin requested from Paulinus as though they had been agreed upon, you can infer what kind of gifts they were—namely, gifts altogether befitting holy men. Thus he said in letter 113:

> For a long time I have awaited the promises of your affection, namely, the protection of the life-giving cross or of other relics. Do not, I beg you, defraud me of so great a gift . . . . Do not plead the length of the journey. Charity will find wings for flying, and rivers will not overwhelm it, and so forth. [Col. 0116A]

XIII. And lest any form of love be lacking in the intimate mutual affection of these most holy men, they did not even refrain from poetry, through which they made the ardors of their most sacred charity common to one another.

There is a proverb attributed to Euripides and also cited by Plutarch (*Symposium* I, question 5, and *Erotic Dialogues*):

> Μουσικὴν ἔρως διδάσκει, κἂν τις ἄμουσος ᾖ τὸ πρίν.  
>   
> Love teaches music, even if someone was formerly without music.

This appeared most truly in Paulinus and Alcuin. Besides their various poems, their verses—which, although the age was then generally an age of iron, were not inelegant—testify that they cultivated the Muses. Their exchanges, composed in verse as dutiful expressions of friendship, leave unmistakable witnesses of this. [Col. 0116B]

Their friendship advanced so far that they sang to one another proofs of affection bound by metrical form. Since none of Paulinus’s poems survive, the truth is drawn from those of Alcuin that do survive. Thus he says in poem 212, which, together with the others concerning Paulinus, is to be found complete in Appendix 1, no. 2, poem 1:

> Dip your pens, Charity, in Christ’s deep pool,  
>   
> And fill my breast with heavenly songs,  
>   
> So that I may render worthy thanks to Paulinus.  
>   
> He who had filled our ears with honeyed Muses,  
>   
> Remembering his like-minded friend after a long time,  
>   
> Repeated in sacred songs: “Albinus, farewell.”

XIV. Let us now proceed to recognize more intimately the passion of love from his own poems. He closes this same poem as follows:

> My mind, bound in sacred chains, burns for you;  
>   
> It loves you, seeks you, embraces you, draws you to itself, and surrounds you,  
>   
> And will keep you with itself in the eternal treasury of its heart.

[ xlviii ] In poem 114 he addresses his friend with the tenderest Horatian expression—“and preserve the other half of my soul” (Horace, *Odes* I.3). This expression pleased even Saint Augustine so greatly that he adopted it for himself and commended its first author (*Confessions* IV.6.11):

> Someone aptly said of his friend, “The half of my soul.” For I felt that my soul and his soul were one soul.

Alcuin therefore, adopting the manner of the poet of Venus, begins the poem cited above: [Col. 0116D]

> O Father Paulinus, shepherd, patriarch, priest,  
>   
> Better part of my soul, illustrious part of my life.

He closes it, after praying that the saints may pray for Paulinus so that they may share in heavenly life:

> Both now and always, my dear, my dear Paulinus, farewell.  
>   
> Here we shall end the poem with bitter tears,  
>   
> But never shall we end our sacred love.

XV. Since among friends it is especially permitted to mingle some playfulness with serious matters, this was not absent from the friendship of Paulinus and Alcuin. Alcuin seems to have included something of this kind in poem 104 (Book I, poem 4), which begins:

> Carry quickly to Father Paulinus, paper, my greeting.  
>   
> Say: “Father Paulinus, sweet friend, farewell.”

“There is a little door, and a little inhabitant in the house,” and so on in what follows. These lines seem to contain something enigmatic, proposed as a playful riddle for his friend. [Col. 0117A] That Alcuin sometimes did this is demonstrated by poems 233 and 257.

XVI. Therefore, just as Paulinus and Alcuin loved one another in life, so also in death—they were not separated, I venture to say. For in the very year in which Paulinus died, Alcuin too departed from the living. Only four months intervened: Paulinus died on January 11, while Alcuin was taken from human affairs on May 19 of the year 804.

We once commended this pair of friends, so closely united with one another, in the following words:

> Not so once did Pirithous love Theseus;  
>   
> Nor did Pylades love his Orestes so;  
>   
> Nor Euryalus Nisus, nor Pollux Castor,  
>   
> Nor anyone renowned for friendship in history,  
>   
> As Albinus and Paulinus loved each other—  
>   
> They whom God had already bound together in his own love.

# CHAPTER XVII. The Memory of Paulinus’s Holiness. Ancient and Recent Cult

[Col. 0117B]

I. The title of “saint” was heard not only in the ancient Christian centuries but also among the pagans. Emperors were often given the name “holy” or “most holy,” as appears frequently in the writers of the *Historia Augusta*. Since the Church, however, began to apply this title especially to those who surpassed others in eminent virtue and the praise of a purer life, so that they could be believed to have been taken up by God among the heavenly citizens, the emperor Constantine did not allow himself to be addressed by a title otherwise in use, as Juvencus sang in Book IV, verse 811:

> Constantine is present, to whom grace is rightly due,  
>   
> For he alone among kings fears that the burden  
>   
> Of the sacred name should be imposed upon him. [Col. 0117C]

The dead were not adorned with this title unless the Church’s consensus approved their virtue. At first the Church customarily granted it only to martyrs—those deprived of blood and life for faith and for Christ—by placing their names in the canon of the saints. This was later called “canonizing” and “canonization,” although at times it was said that such persons were “vindicated.”

Optatus of Milevis (*On the Schism of the Donatists* I) speaks of a certain woman named Lucilla who, “when she set her mouth to that of I know not what dead man—although a martyr, he had not yet been vindicated—she was reproved and departed in anger with confusion.” See Baronius’s note on April 2, letter b. [Col. 0117D]

As time passed, the title “saint” was extended from martyrs to other men of proven integrity, either by public custom of the Church or by canonization carried out through a particular solemnity and rite. Moreover, canonization was either particular to a certain church or universal, proceeding from the Roman See and proposed to the entire Church throughout the world.

For a fuller discussion of these matters, see Bellarmine (*On the Church Triumphant* I.7–8). Although the solemn and universal rite of canonization began to be practiced in the Church later than canonization by custom or by the institution of lesser churches, Dominicus Macer nevertheless wrongly accuses Polydore Vergil in the entry “Canonization” of the *Hierolexicon* V, because Vergil asserted (*On the Inventors of Things* VI.8) that “the first canonization of saints was celebrated by Alexander III.” [Col. 0118A]

Vergil says nothing else in the cited passage except that “so that no one might, according to his own judgment, regard or worship this or that person as a god, Alexander III decreed that no mortal should publicly receive divine honor on earth unless he had first been entered by apostolic decree in the catalogue of the gods.”

From this one should instead infer that, although solemn papal canonization arose later than the other forms, the established and customary practice of enrolling pious men of outstanding virtue in the catalogue of the saints continued in the lesser churches down to the time of Alexander III. Alexander’s decree took care that this should not continue thereafter.

Even if the statements that Saint Suitbert was enrolled among the saints by Leo III seem weak to modern critics, solemn canonization by a Roman pontiff is nevertheless found before Alexander III. It would therefore be false to say that Alexander III was the first canonizer among the Roman pontiffs, though Vergil did not in fact say this. [Col. 0118B]

For Pope John XV solemnly placed Saint Udalricus, bishop of Augsburg, among the saints in the year 993, by a diploma issued on the third day before the Nones of February. See Pagi on that year, and there Mabillon, whom Pagi cites. Mabillon gives several canonizations of saints carried out by various pontiffs between John XV and Alexander III, and adds:

> During that interval of time—namely, from the tenth century, when the Roman pontiffs began to exercise their authority in canonizing saints, down to Alexander III—the metropolitans nevertheless retained, in a certain fashion, their ancient practice: sometimes by consenting together with the pope to the elevation and canonization of saints, and sometimes by carrying out both acts by their own authority for the sake of their own church. [Col. 0118C]

II. As for the rite by which our Paulinus was numbered among the heavenly citizens, I believe—since the memories of ancient times are entirely silent on this matter—that it was the rite most commonly observed at that time. His canonization was not proclaimed by a universal and solemn rite. Rather, the title “saint” first arose from the consent of the people and the church of Aquileia, which had seen and tested his miracles; then from the devotion of the neighboring Carantanians, whose instruction he had undertaken; and afterward his cult spread into Germany and Gaul, to which, while he was alive, he had so often given illustrious examples of proven virtue. [Col. 0118D]

The ancient martyrologies of the German and Gallic churches support this: among others, those of the Carthusians at Cologne, of Saint Mary’s at Utrecht, and of Saint Martin’s at Trier, as well as the German Martyrology itself, in which he is called “Aglar” at Aquileia. [xlix] We have reported these from Bollandus in chapter 13, no. 9, of this Life; they speak of Saint Paulinus on the third day before the Ides of January.

III. Indeed, he was honored with the title of holiness not long after his death. In the Litanies of Charles the Bald—which we shall provide in Appendix 1, no. 12—Paulinus is placed and invoked among the other saints.

For what other Paulinus could be invoked there than our own? Since the list there is clearly a catalogue of saintly confessors who were not martyrs, the invocation must refer to some Paulinus who was a confessor but not a martyr. He would have to be either Paulinus of Nola, Paulinus of York, Paulinus of Brescia, or Paulinus of Capua.

I do not think that any of these is meant here because, as will soon be said, the saints invoked are those who in some way pertain to Gaul, Germany, or Belgium, whereas none of these has such a connection. Moreover, Paulinus of Nola, who is more celebrated than the others, would have had to be placed elsewhere, at least after Saint Leo. [Col. 0119A]

It should therefore be observed that all these confessors, apart from the four doctors of the Latin Church and Saints Benedict, Leo, and Paul the Hermit, as well as the abbots Antony and Macarius—who were too famous to be omitted—are saints either of Germany or of Gaul, in a word, of the Carolingian realm.

Hilary is of Poitiers; Martin of Tours; Medard of Soissons; Germanus of Paris; another Germanus of Auxerre; a third of Besançon; Remigius of Rheims; Fortunatus, although Italian by birth, bishop of Poitiers; Anianus of Orléans; Florentinus of Strasbourg; Columbanus, although he died at Bobbio in Italy, born in Ireland but for a long time an ornament of Gaul; Clodoaldus, a priest in the territory of Paris; Amandus of Utrecht; Vedastus of Arras; Arnulphus of Metz; Landebertus of Lyon; Audoenus of Rouen; Eligius of Noyon; the two Sulpitii, one called Pius and the other Severus, both of Bourges. [Col. 0119B]

As for Severinus, who closes the catalogue of the saintly confessors, he seems to be one of those connected with Gallic affairs: either the abbot of Agaunum, the bishop of Cologne, the monk of Paris, or the bishop of Trier. Unless, perhaps, one thinks of Saint Serinus, called the apostle of Noricum, who nevertheless can also very appropriately belong among the saints of Germany. [Col. 0119C]

From the abundant catalogue of saints belonging to the Carolingian realm, it may rightly be presumed that the compilers wished to list those who touched upon this realm, not the others. The saints remembered here, therefore, are those who had some connection—by nation, dignity, or manner of life—with the kingdoms subject to Charles.

Since the churches of Germany and Gaul had been illuminated by the holiness and teaching of our Paulinus, it is highly probable that the name invoked in these Litanies is his, and not that of another Paulinus. At that time the people of Friuli were subject to the Frankish scepter; the Aquileian see was counted among the churches of the Frankish realm; and, most importantly, Paulinus’s name was then on everyone’s lips. His memory was still fresh and blessed, and the reputation of his holiness had spread throughout that age, while those who had witnessed with their own eyes the examples of his most holy life among the Germans and Franks were still alive. [Col. 0119D]

It is therefore wholly consistent with reason to believe that Charles the Bald placed in his prayers no other Paulinus to be invoked than the Aquileian, because he had no connection with the other confessors named Paulinus, not even a remote one, whereas every analogy pointed to the Aquileian: he came from a people subject to Charles; he was known at court, a connection that still endured; he had been the friend of Charles the Great, Charles’s grandfather; his life and conduct were still recently remembered; his reputation for holiness was widespread; and even miracles—by which God customarily makes his saints illustrious immediately after death—had confirmed it. [Col. 0120A]

Source/review notes: The corrupt or compressed wording of the first Peregrine inscription line is retained and identified explicitly.

### IV

What seems almost beyond all doubt to be asserted becomes still more probable from the concord, so to speak, which has existed from time immemorial between the Church of Aquileia and the Churches of Germany and Gaul. For very many saints who either flourished in those regions or were especially venerated by them are also honored in our diocese; moreover, the Church of Aquileia rejoices in having been enriched by the relics of several of them.

Among these are Saint Sigismund, king of Burgundy; Gereon and his companion martyrs of Cologne, whose relics are preserved at Aquileia [Col. 0120B]. Among them too is Saint Uldaric, bishop of Augsburg, who was once so greatly venerated in these regions that a provostship was established in his name in a district situated along the banks of the Tagliamento and named after him. It was later transferred to our church at Udine, likewise once called by Uldaric’s name—having been founded by Bertold, the patriarch and founder—and afterward designated Santa Maria Maggiore under the title of the Annunciation. With the approval of the change of title by Blessed Bertrand, patriarch, it was attached by Bertrand himself to the canons who had previously been there. All this will become clearer from the document concerning the union of this provostship, to be included in Appendix 2, no. 24.

Saint Giles, abbot of Narbonne, who flourished in the time of Clovis [Col. 0120C] and illuminated Gaul; Saint Faith, or rather Fides, virgin and martyr of Agen in Gaul; Saint Ursula and her companions, resting at Cologne; Saint Leonard of Limoges, confessor—all these are still honored in the Church and diocese of Aquileia with an annual office.

You will find many others of this kind if you examine the old Aquileian calendars, such as that prefixed to the Aquileian Breviary of 1496 and the Aquileian Missal of 1519. In one or the other of these you will find the following saints, whose memory is not now observed but who in earlier times were celebrated with a special rite: Walburga, virgin, on 25 February; Gertrude, on 7 March; Rudbert, on the 23rd of the same month; on 4 May, Saint Florian, martyr; and on the 13th of that month [Col. 0120D], Saint Gangulf, martyr. Afra and her companions are listed on 7 August. Lambert, bishop and martyr, on 17 September. To Saint Remigius, who is still celebrated today on 1 October with a semidouble office, Saint Vedast was added. On the 16th of the same month, Saint Gall, abbot; on the 25th, Saints Crispin and Crispinian, martyrs; on the 31st, Saint Wolfgang; and finally, on 16 November, Saint Othmar, abbot.

All these saints, who belong to the Churches of Germany and Gaul, were also venerated by the Church of Aquileia.
