Moreover, certain feasts common to the Churches of those regions are celebrated there, such as the feast of the Division of the Apostles on 15 July. That this feast was observed by the Germans may be inferred from Du Cange, under “Festum,” where the *Chronological Compilation* for the year 1291 states: “Rudolf, King of the Romans, died on the Division of the Apostles” [Col. 0121A]—and the feast is still celebrated today.

The feast of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, is found in the calendars of the Breviary and Missal mentioned above with an octave; today, however, it is observed only with a common double office. It was the responsibility of the patriarch of Aquileia to add feasts to the Breviary and Missal for his own diocese, as is clear from the charter in Appendix 2, no. 15, concerning the celebration of the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene.

Churches dedicated to saints of this kind are also encountered quite frequently. In the mountains there is the church of Saint Gall, abbot, where there was once an abbey and monastery, whose origin you will learn from the testament preserved in Appendix 2, no. 12. There Saint Columba is named among the heavenly saints in whose honor the temple was dedicated [Col. 0121B], just as in the Litany of Charles the Bald. Saint Columba has relics and a cult at Osoppo. On her, consult Fontanini’s little work *On Saint Columba*. Whether this is the saint presented here in both places may be left to free judgment. Certainly, in spiritual matters the church of Osoppo depends upon the Abbey of Mosac as upon its mother church, so that the latter could rightly embrace Saint Columba among its saints as one belonging to it.

Near Udine is the church of Saint Gothard, built through the assistance of Blessed Bertrand, patriarch, formerly the residence of the Camaldolese [l] hermits, as appears from the charter of the appointment of a certain brother as prior, which you will find in Appendix 2, no. 38. The church of this Gothard, bishop of Hildesheim, is visited every year on 5 May by a great gathering of the people of the province [Col. 0121C].

Besides the principal church of Udine, formerly—as has been said—dedicated to Saint Uldaric of Augsburg, there is the church of Saint Antony, abbot, under the title “Saint Antony of Vienne,” as it is called in the manuscript constitutions of Patriarch Marquard of 1381, which I possess. In Constitution 1, concerning the feasts and festivals to be celebrated, we read: “Likewise, on the feast of Saint Antony of Vienne.” This designation—which the saint acquired because his relics were once transferred from Alexandria to Constantinople, then by Gozzelin to the Allobroges, and finally to Vienne, and because, through the remarkable cures effected by his intercession of the disease called “sacred fire,” or commonly “Saint Anthony’s fire,” such a crowd of those afflicted with that plague stayed there around the basilica to seek help [Col. 0121D] that it became necessary to build a hospital, which later grew into a celebrated abbey and the head of an order—this designation, I say, although it became established in some places, nevertheless indicates the agreement that prevailed between the Churches of Gaul and our own.

In this present year 1733, as I write, Dionysius Delphinus, patriarch, after the countless monuments alike of magnificence and piety with which he adorned our city, brought the façade of this church to completion with cut marble artistically arranged up to the centre, after preparing there in his lifetime a place for his own burial. Since, then, the Church of Aquileia was bound by such a connection with the German and Gallican Churches, it is no wonder that they in turn placed the Aquileian saints among their own and recorded them in their calendars [Col. 0122A] or martyrologies, as we saw above concerning Saint Paulinus and reasonably believe to have occurred in these Litanies of Charles the Bald.

### V

Since we see that Paulinus was venerated in foreign regions in the very century in which he was transferred from this earth to the joys of paradise, it remains indubitable that he always received veneration among our own people, although testimonies for each individual century are not available.

A testimony from the twelfth century is the document of Patriarch Peregrine, issued at Cividale in the year 1139 in the chapel of Saint Paulinus; you will find it in Appendix 2, no. 14. Toward the end of that same century Peregrine was elected patriarch. He made a silver panel on which, besides certain saints of universal cult in the Church of God, Saint Paulinus also occupies a place among the saints of Cividale [Col. 0122B] and Aquileia. From it we have taken the image which we present at the front of this book.

In the Mass—which we append in Appendix 1, no. 13, as a specimen of the ancient rite of the Church of Aquileia and adapt to Saint Paulinus—we add prayers extracted from the archive of the Church of Cividale. One is taken from a manuscript entitled *Order of the Missal according to the custom of the Roman Curia, A.D. 1254*. It was not written in the same hand as the rest of that book, because the Missal was according to the custom of the Roman Curia, in which no commemoration of Saint Paulinus occurs. Perhaps, however, at that time—that is, in 1254—it was added by the clergy of Cividale for the use of their church. This demonstrates that the cult of Paulinus was in existence in the thirteenth century.

We likewise reproduce another prayer extracted from the archive of the same [Col. 0122C] church, from the book marked no. 12 and entitled *Book of Sacraments, A.D. 1303*. This is another testimony from the fourteenth century. In the calendar prefixed to it, the following is written in red letters in January, as is customary for feasts: “3 January. Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, nine lessons, double.”

Coming nearer to our own times, we first encounter a manuscript lectionary of the church of Cividale, which at least reflects the fifteenth century, before the invention of printing. For Saint Paulinus it contains four lessons from a sermon of Saint Maximus, bishop, *To the Saints*. In addition, there is the Aquileian Missal of 1519, in which, for 11 January, a Mass from the Common of Confessors and Pontiffs is prescribed; from this we extracted the Mass which we present in the Appendix [Col. 0122D]. Finally, there are the calendars published by order of Patriarch Francesco Barbaro in 1595 and 1598. In them an office for Saint Paulinus is indeed inserted, but not with the same rite in both: in the calendar of 1595 the Gospel is “Watch,” whereas in that of 1598 it is “A man going on a journey.” In our own day his feast is celebrated from the Common of Confessors and Pontiffs as the principal office.

### VI

We have also learned from a manuscript on the antiquities of Friuli by Marc-Antonio Nicolletti that in earlier times an oratory dedicated to Paulinus existed. Speaking of the patriarch’s first arrival to take possession, as they say, of the temporal jurisdiction at Cividale, just as he had taken spiritual possession at Aquileia, he writes [Col. 0123A]:

> Since the patriarch, nobly accompanied, was reaching the gate of this city—that is, Cividale—one of the noble Bojani family, carrying out the honorable duty of his ancestors, paid him homage. Carrying before him a raised sword, fitted with a white scabbard in the German fashion, he accompanied him as far as the staircase of the palace of Patriarch Callistus. In the innermost part of that palace he visited the little church dedicated to the same Paulinus, rich in the most beautiful marble and in figures executed by excellent painters. When the prayer was finished, surrounded by all the orders, he ascended to the choir of the greater church.

Here, then, you have a chapel in the patriarchal palace—called the Palace of Callistus after him who transferred the see to Cividale—dedicated to Paulinus.

The same Nicolletti, speaking of Patriarch Wolfer, the successor of Patriarch Peregrine II [Col. 0123B], who died at the beginning of the thirteenth century, and recounting the funeral rites of this Patriarch Peregrine, writes:

> The body, beneath a golden baldachin recently donated for sacred uses by the ministers of God, Corrado the dean and Pellegrino the provost, was carried from the little church of Saint Paulinus into the choir of the greater church of the City of Friuli. From there it was removed and received burial in the holy Church of Aquileia.

And below, speaking of the illness by which the same Wolfer was taken away, he has these words:

> He could scarcely move. He was carried to the little church of Saint Paulinus, where, lifted up in spirit, he sent his prayers to God; and, asking pardon for his sins, he heard Mass.

No trace of this chapel, once dedicated to Paulinus, now appears, and when the people of Cividale were questioned, they could not indicate [Col. 0123C] where it had been. While examining the archive of the Chapter of Cividale, I found a book commonly entitled *1564. Roll of Benefices, also of Altars and the Vicariate*. On page 284 were these words:

> Income of the chapel of Saints Vincent, Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, and Maxima, virgin, in the church of Santa Maria di Corte, under the right of patronage of Lord Michael Nicoletti and his brothers, possessed by the Reverend Vicar of the said church.

This church, restored, still survives. In it, as you see, Saint Paulinus was specially venerated.

In the district of Premariacco, where Paulinus is believed to have been born, as we already said above in chapter 2, there is a church shared with Saint Maurus, abbot, and called the church of Saints Maurus and Paulinus. It contains an altar dedicated to his name [Col. 0123D]. In the principal church of the same district, dedicated to Saint Sylvester, pope, among the images of the saints placed on the high altar, we also saw an image of Saint Paulinus when we visited those places in search of ancient memories useful to our subject.

We were also told there that every year on 11 January the Saccavini family celebrates the memory of Paulinus, whom it believes to have belonged to its lineage. Priests from the neighboring villages are invited to offer sacrifice to God in honor of their kinsman, and the observance is held with particular solemnity.

### VII

With regard to the relics of Saint Paulinus, which are fragrant with a wonderful odor—as Nicholas Canussius writes in his manuscript, book 2, *On the Restoration of the Homeland*, chapter 3—two calendars issued by order of Patriarch Francesco Barbaro, which we cited above, firmly assert that they are preserved at Cividale [Col. 0124A] [li]:

> “His relics,” they say, “rest on the high altar of the collegiate church of the city of Friuli.”

An old inventory of relics, dated 15 June 1584 and preserved in the Chapter archive, states:

> “The body of Saint Paulinus, which was placed on the high altar in the collegiate church of Cividale in the year 1578.”

I do not think it was brought from elsewhere; rather, what was already in the church was transferred to the high altar. Perhaps it had been there previously, or nearby, as appears from the chronicle of Julian, which will be cited shortly. Or perhaps it was removed because of some event—for example, the earthquake of 1348, when the church collapsed—and afterward restored in 1578.

In any case, [Col. 0124B] the chapter registers show that before this time smaller relics of his body had at times been kept separately in containers. In an inventory, as it is called, of the year 1407, dated 19 October, we read:

> “Likewise, another small glass reliquary, broken and gilded, in which there is also a small ivory *pissis* with relics of Saints Hermagoras and Fortunatus; and in the same reliquary there is part of the head of Saint Paulinus.”

Later registers, for example those of 1545 and 1583, dated 18 November, also mention the relics of Paulinus.

The manuscript chronicle of Julian, canon of Cividale, speaking of Gregory of Montelongo, states:

> “In the year of the Lord 1269, on the eighth day into September, at Cividale, Gregory, patriarch of Aquileia, died in the Lord. He had been patriarch for seventeen years, ten months, and sixteen days, and was buried beside the body of Saint Paulinus.”

You will find the same account in the lives of the patriarchs of Aquileia in Muratori, volume 4 [Col. 0124C] of the Latin *Anecdotes*. See also Ughelli under Gregory.

The same manuscript chronicle designates and, as it were, points with a finger to the place—namely, the high altar—in these words:

> “In the year of the Lord 1299, on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, at dawn, lightning struck the great tower of the church of Cividale and reached the third cross. It killed James the subdeacon, who was a monk, before the altar of Saint Paulinus in the choir. It should be known that it would have killed several of the lords, but they were not in the choir, because they had said Matins in the evening.”

The matter was known even outside the region. Father Philip Labbe, in his additions to Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says:

> “Paulinus,” he says, “died renowned for holiness and miracles both during his life and after death, and was buried in the greater basilica of the city of Friuli.”

Ferrarius likewise says [Col. 0124D] in his *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*:

> “At Cividale, buried in the greater basilica.”

When the canons wished to restore the high altar of the same church in 1716 and erect a new structure, the body—or rather, the more substantial relics of the body—were found in a stone chest, stored, truthfully speaking, in a most undignified manner. The urn is merely an unpolished, bare stone, hollowed out and covered only by a stone slab secured with gypsum.

In these days they have constructed a new repository in the chapel and altar situated beneath the choir. You will find below, no. 9, the document of this latest translation. We also place before your eyes here a specimen of the repository and even of the altar.

Some of Paulinus’s relics were at some time transferred to Aquileia, and the canons of Aquileia say that they are preserved there in the sacristy [Col. 0125A], perhaps the nobler portion of what is displayed today. For at one time that chapter decreed that a silver statue should be made, presumably in order to place some of Paulinus’s relics in it; we shall give the decree in Appendix 2, no. 41.

Before this, the Church of Aquileia already possessed a silver head of Saint Paulinus. We saw an inventory written on 17 May 1409 by John of Merlatis, scholastic of Aquileia and notary of the chapter, in which we read:

> “A silver head of Blessed Paulinus, with enamel letters before the breast.”

We also saw another inventory made on 30 September 1485, when the canons of Aquileia handed over [Col. 0125B] relics and other precious treasures, in the manner of a deposit to be returned, to the syndics of Cividale, who, as it says, “placed them upon their wagon and conveyed them to their city.” In that inventory, however, no mention is made of the head of Saint Paulinus, nor of those of Saints Lawrence and Sigismund, although they had been mentioned in 1409. This indicates that by then these saints’ heads—whatever the reason, God knows—no longer existed, and that consequently in 1494 it was decreed that other heads, especially that of Saint Paulinus, should be made.

At present, Aquileia possesses silver heads of Sigismund and Lawrence, but not of Paulinus.

### VIII

The final history of the reinterment of the relics of Saint Paulinus is as follows. From the year 1716, when it was removed from the high altar, the stone chest described above, in which the bones of Paulinus rested, lay in the chapel of Saint Donatus the martyr—a chapel on the right side of the choir, near the sacristy, commonly called the vestry—as though in a place not its own and, as one might say, merely provisionally, until it could find a more suitable location [Col. 0125C].

The chapel beneath the choir was selected, called the Chapel of Piety; if you call it the Confession, you will conform to the older terminology. Accordingly, through the intervention of several canons and of Lord Laurence della Torre, dean of the chapter, together with Ignatius Scuffoni, Francis Fana, surgeons, and Jerome Zanuttini, physician, on the evening of 26 January of this year, 1734, the chest was again examined and opened. The greater and nobler portion of the bodily bones was found, namely: the skull, though not complete, since part had previously been kept separately and is still preserved in a glass vessel for easier display; the upper and lower jaws, furnished with twenty-four teeth; a considerable portion of the vertebrae of the back [Col. 0125D]; the hip bones, thigh-bones, and shin-bones; besides other small fragments of bones.

I wished to be present at this discovery and had asked to be notified. But, by some fate, I was not notified; nor, even had I been present on the day before the announced reinterment, would I have been permitted to see it. As soon as the bones had been examined and a public document of the discovery had been drawn up by the notary John Baptist Pistachio, they were returned to the same stone urn in which they had previously lain. They were immediately placed in another iron chest, and this was set in the altar of the chapel beneath the choir, as stated above. It was coated with mortar and secured to the wall at the back. A stone was inserted in its rear portion which had formerly seemed to lie in the pavement south of the basilica among the other stones that, like bands, intersected the floor of the church. Through the ignorance of the craftsmen it had once been placed there among the ordinary stones after being taken from some more distinguished location [Col. 0126A].

Perhaps it had belonged to Paulinus’s ancient urn, for it bears the inscription:

> **T PAULINUS PATHA**

It should formerly have been read, as being an inscription on a tomb:

> Here rests, or lies, Paulinus the Patriarch.

The stone was broken after *requiesci* or *jace*; only the final *T* remains. This inscription was the reason why the stone was set into the wall behind the repository.

As I said, I had hoped to be present at the discovery and examination of the bones, but, disappointed in my hope, I gathered what I record here from those who were present.

The reinterment of the numerous relics of other saints in the same chapel was therefore appointed for the following day. On 28 January—the day on which the Church of Cividale customarily celebrates the office of Saint Paulinus, transferred from 11 January because of the concurrence of the octave of Epiphany—the procession and translation of the relics took place, on the Thursday after the Third Sunday after Epiphany, after Terce had been sung.

The singers went first, continually chanting the praises and hymns of the saints. The canons followed, each carrying a vessel of relics. After them came the dean carrying the head of Saint Donatus, the deacon carrying a fragment of the skull of Saint Paulinus, and the subdeacon carrying a relic of another saint. They were respectively clothed in a cope, dalmatic, and tunicle. They proceeded beneath a baldachin, preceded by thurifers and accompanied before and behind by candles and torches. The civic magistracy also followed, together with the noble Laurence Orio, provost for the most serene lord of Venice, dressed in a red garment commonly called ducal [Col. 0126C]. Proceeding from the sacristy, they circled the interior of the church and descended to the chapel beneath the high altar.

The relics were placed in a cabinet at the head of the chapel behind the altar. Those of Saint Paulinus were then exposed upon the altar, to be returned afterward, once the sacred rites had been completed, with the others. The dean celebrated solemn Mass. When it was completed, we were given a place at the epistle side to deliver an address, which you will find below.

### IX

For the present, I shall transcribe the document concerning the discovery, examination, and reinterment of the relics of Saint Paulinus and present it in the vernacular language in which it was issued. It is as follows:

> In the name of our Lord. In the year of His most holy Nativity 1734, indiction XII, on Tuesday, 26 January [Col. 0126D], at Cividale in Friuli, in the cathedral, at the foot of the altar table of the chapel of Saint Donatus, in the presence, etc. Whereas, by a decree of 17 January of the present month, it was decided in the most reverend chapter of this city to remove the urn in which the body of Saint Paulinus is enclosed and now placed upon the said venerable altar of Saint Donatus, and to place the chest in a suitable manner—that is, in another iron chest, ornamented and gilded, marked on the front with a perforated cross, bearing the inscription:
>
> **CORPUS SANCTI PAULINI PATRIARCHAE AQUILEIENSIS**
>
> **BODY OF SAINT PAULINUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA**
>
> and securely provided with a lock and key—and likewise, as has been said, to place it beneath the table of the venerable altar newly erected beneath the choir, entitled “Of Piety”; therefore [Col. 0127A] the magnificent and most reverend lords Laurence della Torre, dean; Vincent Sillani; Charles Bojani; Luke de’ Massotti; and Andrew Foramitti, theologian, all canons of this distinguished collegiate church, specially appointed to carry out the aforesaid task, having assembled here for that purpose, as in the said decree of 17 January, etc.;
>
> In executing the order that the aforesaid urn should be placed in the prescribed manner, as above, it was removed from the table of the said altar of Saint Donatus. At the foot of that table an urn of white natural stone was found, two feet four inches long, one foot five inches wide, and one foot high, with a door or cover, oval at the top and edged elsewhere, closed by two iron hasps with two strong padlocks. Upon examination at the side of the said cover, a small cross was observed, one inch long, and at the extreme end corresponding to the oval, a corded cross, eight and a half inches high and equally wide [Col. 0127B].
>
> When this urn was opened by Monsignor the dean, still dressed in a surplice—that is, when the two padlocks had been opened and the cover then removed—with the participation of the magnificent and most reverend canons named above and in the presence of the witnesses listed below, and with the very reverend Lord Dominic Franchini, vice-chancellor of the chapter for spiritual matters, and the distinguished Lord Candido Candido, chancellor of the chapter for temporal matters, also present, all attending the examination or inventory of the sacred bones by the light of two burning torches, and after they had been examined by the excellent Doctor Jerome Zanottini, physician, together with the excellent Lords Ignatius Scuffoni and Francis Fana, surgeons and practitioners in this city, they reported and declared that the following bones were found in the urn:
>
> The forehead, partly bare; part of the calvarium with the sagittal suture; the petrous bone near the ear, together with the nose; the upper jaw with nine teeth, partly molars and partly incisors; most of the lower jaw with eight teeth, three incisors and the rest molars; another small piece of the upper jaw with three molars; another similar piece with three other molars; another piece of petrous bone; five vertebrae of the neck with the atlas; an eye tooth; one vertebra of the back; the entire breastbone; one complete clavicle and part of another fragment of clavicle; the crest of the ilium with other adjacent bones; both complete ulnae, the ulna and radius of each of the two arms [Col. 0127D]; both femurs, and the tibia and fibula of the legs; and other particles of bones which cannot be identified.
>
> This having been received and recorded, the urn was again closed by the said Monsignor the dean, with the participation of the aforesaid canons, in the presence of the vice-chancellor, chancellor, and witnesses. Two lateral padlocks, one on each side, were applied, and lime was placed over the cracks around the cover. It was then reverently lifted by men, carried beneath the choir, and placed in the iron chest described above. The chest was secured with a lock and key and returned to the body of the altar entitled “Of the Blessed Virgin of Piety.”
>
> Attached to the iron chest was a small tin box [Col. 0128A], containing a document written by the magnificent and most reverend Canon Giulio Pisenti of this city, dated 29 September 1733. It recounts what he happened to see in 1716, when the said stone urn was discovered in the table of the high altar. Also included was another authenticated sheet, dated 17 December 1733, recording an examination conducted by Lord Pietro Checcia, son of the late Lord Giannantonio de Vico, with its legal authentication of the 22nd of that month. The aforesaid decree of this most reverend chapter of 17 January, drawn up in the acts of me, the notary, all in authenticated form with its legal certification, was also joined to the present documents.
>
> The cover of the iron chest was then closed with two strong clamps and afterward with a key. This key, together with the other two keys of the padlocks, remained in the hands of the said dean. An order was issued that the rear portion of the said altar should immediately be walled up, for perpetual safekeeping.
>
> [Col. 0128B] Present as witnesses to all the foregoing matters were the most illustrious Lords Brandis de Brandis; the most illustrious Lord Livio Carlo; Fabio d’Attimis, son of the most illustrious Lord Giovanni; the Reverend Doctor Antonio Stradiotti, formerly of Lord Bartholomew; the very Reverend Lord Giulio Trivisano, chaplain of this distinguished collegiate church; the excellent Doctor Gian Girolamo Grudena, formerly of Lord John Baptist; Monsignor Antonio Provisano, formerly of Vincent; Monsignor Charles Braga, formerly of Peter; Francis, Antonio, and Joseph Coceani, brothers and sons of Master Dominic; Master Paul Zanottino, formerly of Dominic; Master Andrew Rampone, formerly of Simeon; Master Philip Artesano, formerly of John Baptist; Master James Dussolino, son of Leonard; Gian Maria Zuliano, son of John Baptist; Pietro Cepellotto, formerly of Bartholomew; Master John Baptist Vicenzuto, called Casalotto, formerly of Antonio, all of this city; and Master Philip Lanteriis, formerly of Zuane, of Udine and presently in this city.
>
> The documents cited above were omitted here and placed in the iron chest beside the urn, in the tin box, etc.
>
> From his own acts, John Baptist Pistachio, public notary by Venetian authority and notary of the collegiate church of the city of Friuli, having been so requested, faithfully drew up, published, and extracted this document, and subscribed it with his own hand in testimony.
>
> **L. D. O. M. — Praise to God, best and greatest.**

### X

So that, finally, nothing concerning Paulinus may be lacking which you might otherwise be compelled to seek elsewhere, excellent reader, I shall place here two inscriptions: namely, the one which we formerly read, and the one which we now read beneath the image of Paulinus in the patriarchal hall at Udine.

The old inscription is as follows:

> **SANCTI PAULINI PRAECLARA GESTA TAM MULTA EXSTITERUNT UT AQUILEIENSIS ECCLESIA PRAETER DISCIPLINAM DEBEAT SUAM PRAECIPUE AMPLITUDINEM ILLIUS APUD CAROLUM IMPERATOREM AUCTORITATI.**
>
> So many illustrious deeds of Saint Paulinus came to pass that, besides its discipline, the Church of Aquileia owes especially its greatness to his authority with Emperor Charles.

The new inscription, proposed by Bernardino Angelo Serli, formerly prefect of the patriarchal library—which Patriarch Dionysius Delphinus, most munificent of men, had built for the public and perpetual benefit [Col. 0129A]—and now a canon of the distinguished collegiate church at Udine, was composed when the hall of the palace was restored and new paintings were made. It reads:

> **SANCTUS PAULINUS SUB ADRIANO I CONTRA HAERESIM FELICIS ET ELIPANDI CONCILIUM FOROJULIENSE CELEBRAVIT IN FRANCOFORDIENSI LIBELLUM OBTULIT SUAQUE APUD CAROLUM MAGNUM AUCTORITATE DISCIPLINA PROVINCIAM AMPLITUDINEM AQUILEIENSEM ECCLESIAM DECORAVIT.**
>
> Saint Paulinus, under Adrian I, held the Council of Friuli against the heresy of Felix and Elipandus; at Frankfurt he presented a treatise, and by his influence with Charlemagne adorned the province with discipline and the Church of Aquileia with greatness.

We have omitted the images beneath which inscriptions of this kind were written, since they were arbitrary. We do, however, reproduce and place at the front of this volume the image which, although it too may perhaps have been made according to the artist’s own fancy, nevertheless has antiquity in its favor. Since it was executed at the end of the twelfth or the beginning of the thirteenth century, we have judged it both closer to Paulinus’s age and more likely to resemble the archetype than all the more recent images [Col. 0129B].

It was taken from a silver and gilded panel on which Patriarch Peregrine II had caused various images of saints—especially of the Churches of Aquileia and Cividale—to be engraved, and which he had given as a gift to the church of Cividale, which he himself had rebuilt. The published and manuscript chronicles of Friuli, when speaking of Peregrine, mention this panel. Among them is the account which Muratori gives in volume 4 of his *Anecdotes*, under Peregrine III—although others, and more correctly, call him Peregrine II:

> “This Peregrine rebuilt the church of Cividale, which had been burned with all its books and treasures, and he made in it a silver panel.”

Other manuscripts read:

> “He made a very beautiful silver panel in the said church.”

This is the panel now seen placed on the high altar. It is three feet six inches in height, or length, and six feet in width. Beneath it Peregrine had himself represented kneeling and adoring the Virgin Mother, who occupies the central and chief place, with the following inscription and brief prayer surrounding him:

> **Sacerdos [or rather, probably, Secundus] Peregrinus patriarcha: Mater Dei, miserere mei.**
>
> Priest [or more probably, Second] Peregrine, patriarch: Mother of God, have mercy on me.

[Col. 0130A] In the upper part of the panel—which the Latins, following Vitruvius, would call the *zophorus*, and the Italians the *fregio della cornice*, the frieze of the cornice—are these verses:

> **MATER. SUME. DEI. DEUS. HUJUS. MATERIEI**  
> **PRAESTANS. PLACATA. PEREGRINO. REGNA. BEATA.**  
> **HOC. QUI. DEVOTE. CURAVIT. OPUS. FORE. PRO. TE.**  
> **EXORA. REGEM. FIRMAM. CONSCRIBERE. LEGEM.**  
> **NE. QUIS. FUSCARE. VELIT. HOC. VEL. CONTAMINARE.**
>
> O Mother, supreme glory of God, surpassing the material of this work,  
> being propitious, grant blessed realms to Peregrine.  
> For him who devoutly caused this work to be made for you,  
> entreat the King to establish a firm law,  
> so that no one may wish to deface or pollute it.  
> [The printed first line, *MATER. SUME. DEI. DEUS*, is compressed or corrupt; the translation gives its probable sense without silently regularizing the source.]

In the lower part are the following:

> **AD. LAUDEM. CHRISTI. SEDI. SEMPER. INHAEREAT. ISTI.**  
> **ARAE. SUBLIMI. FIANT. ET. IN. AETHERE. PRIMI.**  
> **HAEC. QUIBUS. EST. CURA. QUO. PERSTET. TABULA. PURA.**  
> **AST. VIOLATORES. HEREBI. SINE. FINE. DOLORES**  
> **FRIGORE. VIBRANTE. PATIANTUR.**
>
> For the praise of Christ, may those whose concern it is that this panel remain pure  
> Always cling to this seat; may they be foremost at the lofty altar and in heaven.  
> But may its violators suffer  
> The endless pains of Erebus in trembling cold.

[Col. 0130B] Now, since the silver plate is worn and broken, these words are missing from the first and second verses respectively: **AD. CHRISTI** and **ET. FIANT.** We supplied the gaps from the chapter archive of that same church, where the inscription had been preserved.

From this panel, in whose lower-left area our Paulinus is visible, we have taken his image. Let no one doubt that this is the image of no Paulinus other than the Aquileian. For, besides certain apostles and several martyrs and confessors who are venerated with universal devotion in the Church of God, the remaining figures belong entirely to the Churches of Aquileia and Friuli: Saint Donatus, whose relics are preserved in the church of Cividale; Saint Quirinus, whose relics rest at Aquileia; and Saints Hermagoras, Fortunatus, and Helavus, prelates of Aquileia [Col. 0130C]. Thus no doubt remains that the figure represented here is our Saint Paulinus, patriarch, and no other.

To form a clearer idea of the panel and conceive the arrangement of the images contained in it, take the representation from this diagram, which my cousin Henry Palladius carefully extracted from the original together with me. With his assistance, the image of Saint Paulinus at the front of this volume was likewise drawn from it [Note: [Col. 0129C] See this image on the following page]. This was done expressly on a recent separate journey undertaken to Cividale; from the names you will understand the position of the saints.

[Col. 0131]

[Col. 0133]

[liv] ### Prayer delivered on 28 January 1734 at the solemn reinterment of the relics of Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia

In the chapel beneath the choir of the principal basilica of the city of Cividale.

[Col. 0133A] **I.** How joyful this day, N. N., how auspicious, how delightful—the day which, after so many centuries have run their course, displays and brings before our eyes for veneration the precious relics of the sacred body of the illustrious confessor of God, eminent teacher of the faith, and most distinguished patriarch of our holy Aquileian Church! Blessed day, and one to be recorded with a brighter mark than all the rest upon the calendar of our lives, to which the kindly providence of the most good and great God has reserved us, so that, instructed by his wisdom, imbued with his precepts, and taught by his preaching, we might joyfully behold the instrument of that very wisdom—his body, I mean—and receive, embrace, and kiss it with exultant joy.

For who is so devoid of the feelings of gratitude that, remembering the great deeds of our holy father Paulinus, reviewing the labors he endured, and turning over his outstanding writings, by which he enlightened not only our province but almost the whole world, would not be suddenly moved to joy when, in today’s light, he sees and contemplates his revered relics and ashes, rescued from the ravages of time, surviving after so many centuries, and placed before us? I am not the man whom these things do not affect. Indeed, as I turn the past over in my mind and behold the present with my eyes, I feel myself almost carried outside myself; my heart leaps for joy, and, shaken by a kind of ecstasy, I recognize that I am swept away to dare beyond my powers.

What the present occasion demands and the solemnity of this day requires, I willingly undertake as the duty of an orator—though, I confess, unequal to the task in strength and unlikely to produce words worthy of its dignity. But in your humanity you will pardon an orator who exults in his exultation if at times he strays beyond the limits and, although he directs his arrow at a target set far above him, fails to reach it.

[Col. 0133B]

**II.** Although this is a substitute observance, [Note: [Col. 0133] See above, no. 8, what we said concerning the transfer of the office and feast of Saint Paulinus.] this is that day which was ennobled in the year 804 of our restored salvation by the passage of Paulinus to heaven, and which, annually recalling his birth into glory, is to be honored by us with a more solemn office. How appropriately, how wisely you decreed this, most renowned Forojulian Church, when you dedicated to the solemn re-entombment of his body that very day which carried him into heaven, so that, just as his spirit obtained eternal peace among the heavenly beings, his bones too might find in your bosom a rest destined to last until the end of the world.

It has always been the custom of all nations that have not wholly departed from the laws of humanity to honor the shades of their dead with rites of purity and with final gifts, as they called them—the more solemnly, the more illustrious their life or the dearer their companionship had been. [Col. 0133C] For since death is the final boundary of all things, and since we have no further common relation with those who have been taken from life, at least the duty of piety which the surviving owed them on that final occasion was, by the sacred law of humane feeling, established as something to be held in higher and more solemn honor. Your learning does not permit you to be instructed by examples concerning the funeral pomp, the magnificence of the obsequies, or the variety of rites and ceremonies by which the ancients, even the pagans, paid the due honors to their dead—sometimes crowning their funeral rites with apotheosis and their public translation among the gods.

Since these things are not unknown to you, you must admit that, through the aid of a benevolent spirit, we have been granted the opportunity to attend upon holy Paulinus, removed from earthly life for more than nine hundred years, with a new funeral—or rather triumphal—procession, and to stand present at today’s solemn re-entombment as the honored relic was placed in a newly prepared tomb.

[Col. 0133D] Yet, for such a duty to receive its proper counterpart, there ought not to have been lacking someone who would at least in some fashion praise the man from the pulpit. Undertaking this charge out of a particular devotion to the most holy prelate, I find myself placed at the same crossroads at which Chrysostom confessed that he had been placed when praising Ignatius, patriarch of Antioch, on a similar occasion:

“Shall we first praise him,” he said (*Oration on Saint Ignatius the Martyr*, vol. V), “as martyr, or apostle, or bishop? For the grace of the Spirit wove a triple, indeed a manifold, crown with which it encircled that holy head . . . And, to begin with, if it pleases you, let us begin with the praises of his episcopate.” [Col. 0134A]

Thus Chrysostom, paving the way for our praise of Paulinus.

**III.** After being rewarded with praise and distinction in the teaching of humane letters, and with the grant of the estate of Laberia through the munificence of Charlemagne, that most impartial judge of learned men, Paulinus was raised under his patronage to the patriarchal dignity. I need not detain you at length by proving with what zeal and vigilance he fulfilled the duties of his office. It is enough to observe even in passing the councils which he attended, so that his zeal, learning, and truly episcopal strength of spirit may become known.

Among the many assemblies convened by Charles in those times, scarcely one is found in which Paulinus’s presence was not desired; indeed, everywhere he held the first place, if not always by right of rank, then certainly by the merit of his learning. This was evident at the assembly of Regensburg and at that of Frankfurt, in both cases in the matter of Felix and Elipandus, Spanish bishops who held erroneous opinions concerning the person of Christ. By his spoken arguments and his brilliantly written works he defeated, crushed, and scattered them.

[Col. 0134B] But what shall I say of the synod held at Altinum, or of that which he convened in his beloved Forojulium, when the letter issued from the former and the canons promulgated by the latter, containing as many testimonies to his virtue and learning as they have periods, display the spirit of Paulinus through the mere act of reading them? In them shines his diligent care to restore ecclesiastical discipline; his ardent vigor in preserving the immunities of churches; his immense zeal in safeguarding the religious observance of feast days; his unconquerable strength and unwearied diligence in preserving the honor of marriage, the dignity of virgins in the asceteries, and the reverence due to temples, or in restoring it where it had been lost; his sharp zeal and—if I may use the words of Scripture—not merely eating but devouring zeal.

**IV.** Having become inwardly the model of the flock which he had formed through most holy instructions and preaching, he went before it on the way of God by his example, so that, even when he was silent, the life of the shepherd displayed to the subject flock what it ought to flee and what it ought to embrace through his virtues and disciplined conduct.

[Col. 0137B] He was that bishop whom Paul, writing to Timothy (1 Tim. 5) and Titus (Tit. 3), desired and described with precise detail: blameless, irreproachable, kind, prudent, holy, and just; holding fast to the faithful word that accords with the teaching, so that he might be able to exhort in sound doctrine and rebuke those who contradict it.

To show that Paulinus fulfilled these requirements, there is no time to review his individual virtues one by one. It is enough to note how tenaciously he embraced the faithful teaching concerning the incarnation of the Word of God, so that he was able, at his synod of Forojulium, to exhort his own people in sound doctrine and to rebuke the Spaniards who contradicted it.

[Col. 0137C] As for his other virtues, let us merely sample them through a few words of his friend, who encompasses in them his chief praises. This was the blessed Alcuin, whose piety and learning had made him distinguished above all others, not only at the court of Charlemagne but throughout the Christian world; thus praise of Paulinus by such a praiseworthy man may itself be regarded as a worthy praise.

“Your most holy heart” (so he sometimes addressed Paulinus in writing, Letter 62) “is a land of promise, flowing with the honey of wisdom and overflowing with the light of the sweetest charity. In it the true and glorious Solomon has built, with the gems of the virtues, a temple of beautiful habitation for his majesty. There is the ark of wisdom and the two tablets of the Testaments; and cherubim in great number cover all these things with knowledge. What is not found in so abundant a treasure of your heart, whose inhabitant is recognized as the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden?”

[Col. 0137D] And elsewhere, writing to Henry, duke of our people, with instructions concerning piety, he says that he restrained his pen from a longer letter and spared further admonitions because he could draw examples with his own eyes from Paulinus and receive his words with his ears—examples and words more effective than all the precepts he himself could offer:

“I might perhaps have written more to you, venerable man, concerning the observance of Christian piety” (he said in Letter 94), “if my eminent teacher and pious instructor in heavenly life, my Paulinus, were not present to you. From his heart flows a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life. Have him as your mediator for eternal salvation.” [Col. 0138A]

**V.** But the man whom the Aquileian Church had found to be an outstanding pontiff in episcopal office was recognized by a foreign province as an indefatigable apostle. I am not now bringing Paulinus onto the stage as he descended into the arena in frequent assemblies of Germany and Gaul against the enemies of the faith, in order to recount his apostolic crown, woven from the heresies he had crushed.

To confound and overthrow heretics is the work of a teacher; to lead pagans to knowledge of the faith is the work both of a teacher and of an apostle. The peoples of Carinthia and Hungary are the insignia of Paulinus’s apostleship: by his agency the light of the Gospel, extinguished in some places and not yet kindled in others, either shone again or began to shine in those provinces.

I do not deny that, before Paulinus’s time, the Gospel had become known to the peoples of Carinthia. But, through the misfortune of the times, barbarism of morals had so returned that a new mission of the Lord’s disciples and fresh apostles seemed altogether necessary for their conversion in Paulinus’s age.

[Col. 0138B] Inflamed with zeal to spread the faith, Paulinus gladly undertook this particular task, all the more willingly because Carinthia had from ancient times been counted as a member of the Aquileian diocese, like a limb belonging to a body. He labored so greatly and for so long in this apostolic office that, when the prelate of Juvavum had recently been raised to the archiepiscopate, the neophyte people of Carantania might be assigned to the Church of Salzburg, the new metropolitan see.

Paulinus, most devoted to peace, did not resent the separation of his province. He had proved that every spirit should praise the Lord, and he trusted that no one could take from him the apostolic distinction for which he had labored. From that time, boundaries were established at the River Drava, and they are still maintained: the land of Carantania beyond the river was assigned to the metropolitan of Salzburg, while the whole territory this side of the Drava became the field cultivated thereafter by Paulinus’s apostleship and remained under the protection and care of the patriarchs of Aquileia.

**VI.** He also devoted diligent labor to bringing the Avars into the Church of God. Alcuin suggests that the Avars, after being defeated by Charles’s arms and subdued in more than one battle by the forces of Henry, duke of Forojulium and Paulinus’s dearest friend, had received a new apostle. Writing to Paulinus concerning the victory over the Avars and the attempt that should be made to convert those peoples, Alcuin says (Letter 112):

“The eyes of very many look to you, excellent father, to see what your venerable holiness wishes to do, because the nearness of the places suits you, the distinction of wisdom is yours, the excellence of authority belongs to you, and all the qualities which appear necessary for such a work are united in you.”

This was like putting spurs to a horse and driving forward one already running. The rulers of the Hungarians had requested that a way be opened for them to embrace the faith through the mission of priests. Paulinus, becoming their leader and—as Scripture says—the duke of the word itself, penetrated those regions, to the great gain of souls and the advancement of the Church whose expansion he pursued.

[Col. 0138C] If the malignity of the times had not begrudged us clearer monuments of his apostleship, we would have seen him overthrow idols, destroy shrines, and tear out the sacred groves of superstition. Here addressing the people, there instructing the neophytes; here cultivating the untrained through catechesis, there washing catechumens in the sacred waters of purification, and elsewhere confirming those reborn of water and the Holy Spirit by the laying on of hands; building churches, raising altars, and appointing priests—we should not rashly, but truly, and with still less exaggeration, have included Paulinus among the first apostles of Pannonia, as Father P. Bombardus, S.J., does in his *Topography of Hungary*.

**VII.** Anyone who understands the nature of martyrdom and has examined Paulinus’s deeds more closely will readily persuade himself that, to episcopal distinction and apostolic glory, Paulinus finally added the crown of martyrdom. Martyrdom is not always adorned with blood, and the Church venerates among the martyrs many whose death was not sealed by blood.

[Col. 0139A] For someone to be counted among the martyrs, it is enough that, for the sake of the faith, he has suffered at the hands of the enemies of the faith some kind of punishment which demonstrates both hatred of the faith in the one who inflicts it and zeal in the one who suffers it.

Thus we venerate in the catalogue of martyrs Pontian, Marcellus, John, Silverius, and Martin, Roman pontiffs; Eusebius of Vercelli; Felix of Nola; and many others whose lives the persecutor’s sword did not take. Yet they did not lose the palm of martyrdom—as is said of Martin, bishop of Tours—because, as far as lay in them, they placed their lives in danger for the faith, and, as far as lay in the enemy, neither hatred nor violence was lacking to bring about death for the faith.

But in Paulinus’s case the matter was otherwise, by the providence of him who, at times pleased with the preparation of his servants’ minds, requires the vow but not the outcome; and, going before them with blessings of sweetness, places upon their heads the crown of martyrdom made of precious stone.

[Col. 0139B] With how much justice, then, and with what merit ought Paulinus to have a place among the martyrs, since in preaching the Gospel he not only endured so many labors, but encountered so many dangers, bore so many punishments, and swallowed so many injuries?

The treacherous Avars eventually renounced the faith they had embraced. Rebelling against God and Charles through repeated apostasy, they drove out those whom they had at first received as apostles, treating them with insults and punishments as martyrs. If it is not the punishment but the cause that makes a martyr, according to Augustine’s judgment (*Letter* 89, no. 2, and *Letter* 204, no. 4, latest edition), there is no reason to hesitate to call Paulinus a martyr, since he lacked neither the cause nor the punishment.

[Col. 0139C] Indeed, if, according to Cyprian’s judgment (*On Mortality*, Book II), martyrdom conceived in the mind is crowned, how could Paulinus not be considered worthy of the martyr’s crown, since he summoned and almost embraced martyrdom not merely in vow and ardent desire, but in reality and in fact?

Let this profane expression be forgiven on this occasion:

> And, had the fates allowed it,  
> he would have deserved to fall by my hand.  
> (*Aeneid* II, line 433.)

[Col. 0139D] Hence, to speak frankly, a certain biographer wrote of him with excessive restraint and less praise than was fitting (Ferrarius, *Catalogue of the Saints of Italy*):

“He desired martyrdom, although he did not obtain what he had vowed; nevertheless, he suffered many injuries and hardships from the barbarians.”

For how could he have failed, at least in part, to obtain the martyrdom he desired, when the same author freely admits that he suffered hardships and injuries from the barbarians out of hatred for the faith?

**VIII.** Since it has now been shown, at least in summary fashion, that Paulinus lacked neither the glory of the episcopate, nor the insignia of apostleship, nor the crown of martyrdom, my speech now turns to you, who are adorned by so great a pledge.

Behold, chosen company of the Lord’s priests, the venerable ashes of a most vigilant bishop, a most fervent apostle, and a martyr most ardent both in fact and in desire, whom the providence of the eternal Father has entrusted to your faith. Guard the deposit, and where your treasure is, there let your heart also be.

You may rightly rejoice above all others, most extensive Church of this Forojulian province, for although you were once given life along with the others by the spirit of Paulinus, now, above all others, you possess his body.

Look upon his limbs and upon what remains of his members; and, exulting with joy mingled with wonder, cry out:

This is he whom pontiffs commended and kings venerated; from whose mouth the court of great Charles hung; whose counsels Germany received; whose judgments Gaul embraced; whose mind the councils followed; whose teaching, authority, and holiness princes, peoples, and nations wondered at, feared, and honored.

[Col. 0140A] That is the golden mouth whose eloquence thundered in synods, whose tongue, interpreting eternal truth, was held authoritative. Those are the hands whose writing joints the Spanish heresy dreaded, whose formed letters those nations, although so far removed from ours, feared as though they were thunderbolts.

How beautiful were the feet of him who proclaimed peace and proclaimed good things to the regions of Carantania and the Avars! While he lived, they traversed those lands for the gain of souls; but, as though the Creator of all things, who had rested in the tabernacle of his heart, had commanded himself to dwell in this church and cast down roots among this people whom he had chosen, he was established here. He likewise rested in the sanctified city and took root among the honored people, until, when his spirit had been taken from human affairs, his dwelling became among the fullness of the saints.

[Col. 0140B] Rejoice, therefore, among yourselves, you who now venerate him in the place where his feet stood. The words which Chrysostom addressed to his Antiochenes apply especially well to you when they received from Rome the bones of Ignatius, once their bishop:

“Rome,” he said (*Homily on Saint Ignatius*, cited above, “received his blood as it streamed.”

And I say: Gaul, Germany, and Carinthia received his sweat, and perhaps Hungary received both his sweat and his blood.

“But you received his relics; you enjoyed his episcopate. They rejoiced in his apostleship and martyrdom. They saw him contending, conquering, and crowned; you possess him forever. For a short time God took him away from you, but he restored him with greater grace. You sent forth a bishop; you received an apostle and a martyr.”

Thus Chrysostom spoke to the Antiochenes; thus I speak to you, to whom these pledges have been entrusted, among whom they have been deposited and today exposed.

[Col. 0140C] Therefore, O Forojulian Church, guard your deposit!

**IX.** Guard it, I say, by which you are guarded. For if Augustine does not deny that it can benefit the dead to obtain burial among the sarcophagi of confessors of the faith and martyrs of Christ (*On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*), what protection and defense may you not expect from him at whose ashes you keep vigil, pray, meditate, and sing psalms?

How could it happen that he does not watch over you from heaven, since you watch over him in this way; that he does not protect you, since you protect him so; that he does not guard you, since you guard him so?

Believe it, and do not doubt: your Paulinus returns your devoted care to you, and, in reciprocal solicitude, preserves the one whom you preserve. For no one hates his own flesh. The spirit of Paulinus still loves these relics of his flesh deposited with you, once the vessel of the Holy Spirit who dwelt in him.

Therefore he cannot fail to love you, who preserve them; nor can he turn toward them without turning toward you, in whose hands they are. This, then, is your helmet of salvation; this is your shield, this your buckler, by which you are defended, protected, and supported.

**X.** Therefore, excellent father and most holy cultivator of the Lord’s Aquileian field, look down from heaven, see, and visit this vineyard, and perfect it (Ps. 79:15 ff.)—the vineyard planted by your right hand, watered by your sweat, cultivated by your teachings, pruned by your decrees, and warmed by the fire of your zeal and charity.

Like that evangelical farmer (Matt. 25), you surrounded it with a hedge when, through your writings, you fortified it against the heresies that might invade it. You built a tower in its midst when, with your aid, you raised the patriarchal see—endowed with many privileges by the great king and emperor Charles—to a truly tower-like height.

You dug a winepress in it when you held your celebrated synod of Forojulium, at which the wines of purer doctrine and stricter discipline, pressed out by your canons, are still daily drunk with joy of heart in our own times—the wine with which the later winepresses, that is, the councils imitating yours, overflowed.

[Col. 0141A] Perfect, then, by your intercession and prayers from heaven the vineyard which your right hand planted on earth. Look upon it, because you are its bishop; see it, because you are its father; visit it, because you are its shepherd; perfect it, because you are holy.

**XI.** But, so that you may possess perfected the vineyard which you look upon, see, and visit—the vineyard planted by your right hand—let your hand be upon the man of your right hand, upon that man, I say, who is not so much the heir of your see as of your zeal, not so much of your dignity as of your virtue: Dionysius Delphinus, patriarch, your true and undegenerate heir.

He regards your beloved vineyard with no lesser vigilance, as a bishop; sees it with love, as a father; visits it with solicitude, as a shepherd; and strives to perfect it with no less zeal, aspiring to a holiness worthy of succeeding you.

He is truly the man of your right hand, because, when he acts, you may believe that you are acting in such a way that you see yourself almost revived in him. Let your hand, therefore, be upon the man of your right hand and upon the son of man whom you established for yourself, because he works on your behalf and in your place.

I do not doubt that, through your intercession—you for whom the vineyard of the Aquileian Church was and remains so dear—he was granted to us and strengthened by a long episcopate, so that by his life, example, and teaching he might fulfill your duties. Strengthen him for us still longer, so that in our Delphinus, who strives so exactly to imitate your virtues, we may recognize you made everlasting.

**XII.** But we who have taken part in the solemn re-entombment of your sacred bones will not depart from you unless you give us life, because we have called upon your name.

For my part, I will not release you unless you bless me (Gen. 32:26); once I have received that blessing, I shall go on my way rejoicing. And I, who, while laboring to unfold your works and prepare them for public light, have already beheld your spirit, and who now, after so many centuries have passed, have venerated your body—who could restrain me from saying again:

“I have seen my Paulinus face to face, and my soul has been preserved”? (Ibid., 30.)

[Col. 0141]

[lvii] **THE SECOND LIFE OF SAINT PAULINUS**, excerpted from the more extensive manuscript of Marcus Antonius Nicoletti, preserved among the Fathers of the Society of Jesus at Graz in Styria; transcribed in January 1736 by Andrea Foramitti, canon and theologian of the distinguished Collegiate Church of the City of Austria.

[Note: [Col. 0149]

**NOTES ON THE LIFE OF SAINT PAULINUS.**

[Col. 0149D] The matters we are about to note are deliberately few, and only those which present themselves almost spontaneously for examination. We have already said that the credibility of nearly everything stated here rests with the author. But our admission of some points does not mean that we approve the rest; nor, because we reject many things, does it follow that we reject everything.]

**PREFATORY NOTICE**

[Col. 0141D] We had already laid the final hand upon our work concerning the life and writings of Saint Paulinus of Aquileia—indeed, our manuscript had already been entrusted to the printer and was entering the press—when Lord Laurentius a Turre, dean of the Forojulian chapter, informed us that at last the Life of Saint Paulinus, composed by Marcus Antonius Nicoletti, had been discovered among the Fathers of the Society of Jesus by Lord Andrea Foramitti, a canon of his church, who was residing at Graz on legal business.

We arranged for a copy to be sent to us as quickly as possible, but did not obtain it until the beginning of April of this year, 1736. I thought, excellent reader, that I was about to offer you an exceptional gift. But I would have acted badly both toward you and toward myself if I had wished to present the Life exactly as it came from its author.

[Col. 0142D] For a not careless copyist filled 134 pages of ordinary folio. From this you may infer how much irrelevant material the author has stitched together. Yet he examines no critical question, discusses no chronology, produces no councils, and presents or evaluates none of Paulinus’s writings. He invents several lengthy speeches in which he imagines not what Paulinus—or anyone else whom he introduces as speaking—actually said, but what he might have said.

Almost the entire work is occupied with such inventions. Nevertheless, I do not deny that some things worthy of reading and remembering are occasionally found here, things which you would seek elsewhere in vain. Accordingly, omitting the superfluous and freely invented speeches, we present only what concerns Paulinus and is drawn from the author’s own account, placing confidence only in those things which he testifies that he saw or read. For the rest, let him seek a guarantor for himself.

Marcus Antonius Nicoletti of Forojulium flourished in the sixteenth century and, as we noted in our final note to this Life, was still alive after the year 1578. He wrote several works on the patriarchs of Aquileia, illustrious writers, the ancient laws of the people of Forojulium, and the war fought among the Forojulians from 1360 to 1367, as well as other works circulated in manuscript among our fellow provincials.

[Col. 0143A] We had once regretted that Paulinus’s Life had not survived, since although we had earnestly desired it, we had searched for it with the greatest diligence in vain. Now, through Father Antonio Sponno of Udine, chancellor, as they call him, of the Society of Jesus at the University of Graz, we have obtained what we desired. He communicated the Life to the canons of Forojulium, and through their courtesy we readily secured permission to use it.

As I said above, we present it abridged and expressed in summary form. We have also translated it from Italian into Latin—not as interpreters of words but of meanings—in order to serve the interests of the greatest number.

**THE LIFE BEGINS**

[Col. 0143B] **I.** When the fortunes of the Lombards had been overthrown and Desiderius, their king, had been deprived of his kingdom by Charlemagne, Signoaldus, bishop or patriarch of Aquileia, who had been born in the city of Forojulium from the stock of King Grimoald, died by fate after having most holily fulfilled the pontifical office for forty-two years.

Paulinus, elected by the votes of the clergy [Note: [Col. 0149D] Paulinus was elected by the votes of the clergy and people. This is not so: for Paulinus himself obtained this power for the Aquileian clergy; therefore they did not possess it beforehand. See the diploma given to Paulinus in the council of Regensburg in the first appendix, no. 3, and what we say in chapter 6 of his Life. Nicoletti himself includes this diploma in his manuscript Life of Paulinus, yet does not notice the point.] and people, succeeded him.

**II.** Paulinus is thought to have sprung from one of the more illustrious families which King Alboin had left with Gisulf, the first duke of the Forojulians. Others assert that he came from Praemariacum, where he had possessed estates.

Even now the ruins of the buildings which he had inhabited can be seen, as well as the field in which he was staying when he received news of his election as patriarch. Holding a staff in his hand, he said: “When this piece of wood produces flowers and leaves, then I shall believe that I have been chosen as prelate.”

[Col. 0143C] Immediately it put forth flowers and leaves, its buds swelling as though with gems. At this sight he believed in the call and yielded his consent, after the assent of Pope Adrian I and the approval of King Charles had followed within a short interval.

**III.** Meanwhile Duke Rotgandus stirred up disturbances and rebelled against the king. Defeated and captured, he was punished with the ultimate penalty. Felix [Note: [Col. 0149D] Felix, brother of Rotgandus, and Joticausus. We said something about this Felix in our *Life of Paulinus*, chapter 3, no. 5, from that passage and from the diploma given to Patriarch Maxentius in the second appendix, no. 7. See whether some light can be shed on the identification of these men.] the brother of Rotgandus, Joticausus, and Guiselpertus also fell in that war, while their wives, Gorimberga, Beralda, and Brunichilda, were preserved alive.

Lupo, the son of Felix, was taken to Francia and died in prison. After paying the final honors to those who had fallen in the war, Charles proceeded toward Aquileia. He was received by the patriarch and clergy, and there received the envoys of the entire province who had come to congratulate him.

[Col. 0143D] He listened to a polished speech by Paulinus on the excellence and duty of a ruler. Charles, admiring his eloquence, gave him the estate of Laberia and afterwards freely assented to his election to the patriarchal see in the year 776. [Note: [Col. 0150D] He assented to his election in the year 776. An excellent date, which we too follow.]

**IV.** After Rotgandus had been removed, the remaining Lombards—with the exception of Ildebrand, duke of Spoleto—returned to Charles’s allegiance. When Charles visited Treviso during the Easter season, he incorporated and united the duchy of Forojulium with his kingdom, appointing counts to govern each city.

[Col. 0144A] The Forojulians, bearing this more reluctantly because they thought that depriving them of the dignity of a duke damaged the honor of their homeland, desired the former system of government. Paulinus, it is believed, presented the people’s wishes. Their request was granted: Henry was appointed duke after Rotgandus, and Carinthia and Styria—still not regenerated by the baptism of Christ—were added to the duchy of Forojulium. [Note: [Col. 0150D] Henry was appointed duke after Rotgandus. See Dissertation 1, no. 5, and what we say there concerning Duke Mercarius between Rotgandus and Henry.]

[Col. 0144B] **V.** Charles confronted a new rebellion of the Saxons and defeated them, with the Forojulians under their duke Henry providing auxiliary forces for the battles. The defeated Saxons sought pardon and baptism. Paulinus, who had come to congratulate Charles, labored greatly to strengthen them in the faith.

On his return to his own see, he cultivated Carinthia for several months through preaching and example, not without danger to his life on some occasions, and was a martyr in all but blood. He won many to Christ. He informed the apostolic see of this, first by letters and afterward in person when he went to Rome not long afterward.

[Col. 0144C] Everywhere he greeted Charles, who had returned from battle in the Pyrenees after driving out the Saracens. Kindly received by Charles, he stood, at the king’s wish, at the coronation of Charles’s son Louis as king of Aquitaine, which was performed in those days by the hands of the pontiff.

**VI.** After this Paulinus returned to his see and turned his attention to abolishing corrupt customs. At that time, in contracts, agreements, and similar documents, it was customary to state the nation of the contracting parties and witnesses; furthermore, under which law they had been born and lived—whether Roman papal law, Lombard law, or Bavarian law.

An example of this can be clearly seen more than once in the chartulary of the chapter of the city of Forojulium. One example among many will suffice, of the following kind:

“We, in the name of God, Hugo and Acella, mother and son, and Leuza, wife of the same Hugo, who have declared that we, mother and son, live according to the law of the Bavarians by our nationality, and I, Leuza herself, who have declared that by my nationality I live according to the law of the Lombards, but now, on account of my husband, I appear to live according to the law of the Bavarians, hereby promise and undertake, we, mother and son and wife, together with our heirs and co-heirs, to you, Corrado, and your heirs and co-heirs, or to whomever you shall grant the right, the houses, farmsteads, vineyards, and other property listed below.

“Mark of the hand . . . of the aforesaid Hugo and Acella, mother and son and married couple, and of Leuza, wife of the same Hugo, who requested that this deed of promise be written and who received it in Latin, as above.

“Mark of the hand . . . of Sigepotus and Govenus, living according to Bavarian law by their nationality, and of Rantulus, Sfredericus, Cazilinus, Egilus, Droponus, Ardeneus, and Varnerius, son of the late Lutonus, living according to Roman papal law by their nationality.”

[Col. 0145A] This practice, since it introduced different rites, customs, and ways of life among people and fostered disagreements and disputes, appeared to Paulinus to be a seedbed of lawsuits and controversies. For this reason he strove to eliminate it as a plague upon charity. Indeed, the custom had been abolished in his own days, though it later grew up again through the negligence of those who came after.

**VII.** Meanwhile, when the Saxons newly stirred up disturbances, they were again subdued by Charles, with the Forojulians participating in the battles under their duke Henry. Terrified by this defeat, Ildebrand, duke of Spoleto, hastened to submit to Charles, intending to beg humanely for pardon, peace, and his life.

[Col. 0145B] Passing through Forojulium, he was kindly received by his fellow Lombards and by Paulinus. Paulinus dismissed him with good wishes through his prayers and blessings. Ildebrand entered Germany and obtained from Charles what he desired and requested.

**VIII.** By decree of the pontiff, Constantine and Irene convened a council of 350 bishops at Nicaea, in which the impiety that sought to abolish the veneration of images of Christ and the saints, as well as of their relics, was buried. Paulinus therefore rejoiced beyond measure and decreed that thanks should be offered to God throughout the whole territory of his Church.

[Col. 0145C] **IX.** Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, presses arms against Charles as far as the Julian Alps, toward Tyrol. Defeated, he presents his son Theodo and twelve Bavarian nobles as hostages for his pledged faith. Liutberga urges her husband to summon the Huns against the Franks and involves him in a new rebellion. Accused and convicted of this crime, he undergoes a very mild punishment through the prince’s kindness and the intercession of Paulinus and other bishops. He himself and his son put on the monastic habit in a monastery.

Meanwhile the Huns, or Hungarians, having been summoned, arrive in two armies, devastating Bavaria with fire and sword on one side, and Carinthia and the Forum of Julius on the other. Charles, advancing from Gaul through Bavaria, and Henry, from the Forum of Julius, drive the enemies away. In a small church of Saint Pantaleon near the city of the Forum of Julius, in the time of [Col. 0145D] Nicolaus Maccheropius—

[Note: [Col. 0150D] Nicolaus Maccheropius was a mansionarius and chancellor of the chapter of the Forum of Julius from 1534 until 1574, when he died. From the notes of the archives of the chapter of the Forum of Julius.]

—a man whose poetry was as sweet in song as his name was renowned, and most skilled in antiquities,— two images were seen as witnesses of the event. They had been fashioned long ago with a crude brush but had by then been worn away through the long passage of years. In one, Paulinus, seated on his throne, was blessing an army setting out against the enemy; in the other, a battle and engagement with the enemy were depicted. Beneath them, in barbarous script, these words could be read:

**“The people of the Forum of Julius, blessed by Paulinus, overcome the Hungarians.”**

**X.** Charles, encountering new rebellions in Bavaria, reduces it to the form of a province under various governors. He also urges Virgil, bishop of Salzburg, and Paulinus of the Forum of Julius to devote themselves to the conversion of Styria and Carinthia. The former preached beyond the Save, toward Bavaria; the latter on this side, toward the region of the Forum of Julius. They persuaded only the rustic population, while the nobles rejected conversion.

The duke Ingon retained the glory of this deed. Having summoned his provincial subjects to a meal, he ordered that the rustics should be served before him with gold and silver vessels and that choice dishes should be set before them, while the nobles, kept apart from him, were given common food in earthen and wooden vessels. When the nobles asked the reason for this distinction, he replied that the rustics and common people, washed with the waters of baptism, were cleaner, while the magnates, who had refused baptism, were dirtier and more contemptible. On hearing this, they too gave their names to Christ through the bath of regeneration.

Through this work, as is believed, it came about that, as a sort of reward for Paulinus’s labors, Charles granted to the patriarchal see of Aquileia the spiritual jurisdictions—which even today it administers through its archdeacons around the Save and the Mura under canon law—and, in addition, many temporal possessions in the Forum of Julius, Istria, and Germany.

**XI.** When certain Italian forces sent against the Huns had their station at Aquileia, Aquileian affairs were being ruined by military license. Paulinus hastened directly to Retimburch, complained to Charles about the arrogance of the soldiers, and obtained from him a diploma containing the privilege of various immunities, especially exemptions from what were called *foderum* and *mansionaticum*.

[Col. 0146C] **XII.** When Paulinus had returned to his own country, a heresy that had earlier arisen in Spain raised its head. For Felix, bishop of Urgel in the Pyrenees, had asked Elipandus for a solution to the question whether Christ should be believed to be the adoptive or the natural and proper Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0150D] Felix had asked Elipandus. Not so, but the reverse. See what we say in Dissertation 4, note 18.]

Elipandus answered that he was adoptive. Paulinus refuted this blasphemy at the Council of Frankfurt, held by command of King Charles, and the Fathers of the council subscribed to his opinion. Elipandus was then captured and sent to Rome, where, in the church of Saint Peter, he confessed his error before the pontiff.

When the council had ended, the patriarch accompanied Charles to Paris, the principal seat of the kingdom, where, together with Albinus Flavus, Isuardus—

[Note: [Col. 0150D] Isuardus the monk, in place of Usuardus; nevertheless, Trithemius calls him Isuardus. He flourished not under Charlemagne but under Charles the Bald, to whom he dedicated his martyrology. This Charles was nevertheless not rarely called “the Great” by writers of the ninth century, from which the error arose among Bellarmine, Baronius, and others, who believed that Usuardus flourished under Charlemagne and in the time of our Paulinus. On this matter, see Casimir Oudin’s supplement *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Usuardus.]

—the monk, his fellow citizen Paul the Deacon, and other exceptionally learned men, he gave the University of Studies its constitution and laws.

**XIII.** After this, Charles built a temple at great expense between the Rhine and the Meuse, at a place called Aachen, from which the present city is called Aquisgranum or Aquisgrana. Paulinus sent Charles, for the glory and adornment of the temple, not only finely carved stones excavated from the ruins of Aquileia, but also relics of the saints taken from the treasuries of all the churches.

[Note: [Col. 0151A] He sends relics to Charles. Guicciardini, in his description of Belgium, says of the temple at Aachen built by Charles: “In it various relics are still displayed, brought to this town by the same emperor, partly by his authority and command, and partly also at great cost and expense.” I would not therefore deny that Paulinus too offered Charles relics taken from the treasury of Aquileia, which had always been abundantly supplied in this respect.]

Meanwhile Pope Adrian died and was succeeded by Leo III, at whose coronation Paulinus was present. After this, having returned to his own country, he summoned by letters the bishops called suffragans to a council in the church of the Forum of Julius, then—as now—dedicated to the Virgin, in the year 796.

[Note: [Col. 0151A] He summoned the bishops to a council in 796. The date is most rightly assigned; when we saw it, we rejoiced that our own opinion was supported by the authority of this writer as well.]

[Col. 0147A] **XIV.** Irring, duke of the Huns, ravages Carinthia and Styria. King Pippin of Italy sets against him Henry, duke of the Forum of Julius, with his battle lines. As Henry prepares to go out against the enemy, Paulinus blesses him and, [lix] together with the clergy, directs prayers to God for his safety; by a long address he strengthens the duke and the soldiers setting out for war.

Henry conquers and occupies Ring, the noble royal residence of the Huns. He plunders much booty, which he sends back to Charles, then residing at Aachen; Charles himself, through Angilbert, hangs part of it at Rome as an offering at the altar of the Apostles. Pippin, together with Henry, renews the war against the Huns, a new cause of conflict having arisen. While Henry pursues and besieges a considerable band of the enemy that had taken refuge at Teusate in Liburnia, he is treacherously killed by the Teusatans.

[Col. 0147B] Among fragments of a very ancient marble arch of Lombard workmanship, visible in the principal church of the city of the Forum of Julius, brief eulogies of the dukes of the Forum of Julius could still be read not many years ago. Henry’s was also among them; but through the negligence of those who ought not to have been more careless than the others, they have either been secretly removed and concealed, or broken and scattered.

Meanwhile Paulinus orders Henry’s funeral rites to be performed throughout the province by all the priests, with sacred prayers. He gives alms for the repose of Henry’s soul and, from the pulpit, commends the duke’s merits, recalling especially his charity in redeeming captives and freeing those shackled by the hands of unbelievers, for which purpose he had repeatedly spent a great quantity of gold to relieve their misery.

[Col. 0147C] **XV.** When Leo III was being badly treated by the kinsmen of his predecessor, Paschal and Campulus, Charles prepared to avenge the monstrous crime and arranged an Italian expedition. When Paulinus and the people of the Forum of Julius learned of this, they hastened to repair the sacred and secular buildings so that they might receive him with fitting honor.

His departure was delayed by intervening affairs. During this interval, the Bavarians devastated the territory of the Forum of Julius, made bolder by the removal of the duke who had protected it. Paulinus, responding to the misfortunes of his country, crossed the Alps and went to Mainz to Charles, who received him with great kindness.

Charles set out for Italy in August of the year 800, but completed the journey only in autumn. Departing somewhat from the established route, he went to Liburnia to punish the Teusatans for Henry’s death. He executed some of them and would have undertaken harsher measures had Paulinus not dissuaded him.

Meanwhile Paulinus obtained the appointment of Cadolac as duke of the Forum of Julius in Henry’s place, and magnificently received the king as he passed through Istria and the Forum of Julius. Mauritius the father and John the son, dukes of the Venetians, were also present, accompanying Charles honorably on his journey.
