Paulinus joined Charles as his companion when he went to Rome. In the case of Leo, Paulinus said much about the privilege of the first see, which is to be judged by no one. He also argued at length that the Lombards should not be completely exterminated; the pontiff and Charles embraced his support.

The prayers and supplications instituted three days before the Ascension by Mamertus, bishop of Vienne, because of the fear of earthquakes—which had violently shaken Italy in those days—were adopted by the Roman bishop. On returning to his own people, Paulinus established that they too should be performed every year.

**XVI.** While the Huns were still stirring up war, Gerard, with a band of Bavarians, crossed into their territory and put many to death, but finally fell in battle. Meanwhile, at the counsel of Paulinus and the duke Cadolac, or Cadolus, the people of the Forum of Julius hastened to confront the barbarians, blocking the Alpine passes, but in vain.

For, after laying waste Bavaria, they attacked the region of the Forum of Julius with fire and sword, sparing neither age nor sacred places. Paulinus withdrew into the city of the Forum of Julius.

[Note: [Col. 0151B] Paulinus withdrew into the city of the Forum of Julius. These words seem to suggest that the patriarchs were then residing somewhere other than the Forum of Julius. But it is not evident that the patriarchs had another place of residence from which Callistus transferred it to the Forum of Julius from Cormons.]

To divide the enemy’s forces, Charles sent his son Charles as well—this was the third year of his empire—with a picked band of soldiers into Hungary. After several skirmishes here and there, the Frank finally triumphed over the enemy and was enriched with splendid spoils. He distributed part of them among the soldiers and sent part to his father, who divided it among the poor and used it to repair the roofs of the Roman and Aquileian churches.

**XVII.** To quiet the complaints of the nobles and peoples, the Emperor Charles summoned an assembly, which they call a parliament. He summoned his sons as well: Charles from Hungary, Pippin from Italy, and Louis from Spain, and ordered them to attend the general assembly.

When Pippin withdrew from it and returned to Italy because affairs there were not sufficiently secure, he received from Charles a letter commending the preservation of the laws.

[Note: [Col. 0151B] A letter in which he commends the preservation of the laws. Our author does not possess it in full. See the whole letter in Baluze, *Capitularies*, vol. I, p. 461.]

Believing that the presence of the legislator would be more effective than words, Pippin descended into Italy and arrived at Rome. There, to protect the affairs of the churches, when the bishops had gathered more than once with the pontiff and emperor, Paulinus was present, lamenting the condition of his Church and explaining the incursions and disasters of the Hungarians.

Charles, on the advice of the pope and the bishops, granted six bishoprics to the metropolitan of Aquileia, bishoprics that had once been counted among the province of Aquileia:

“Namely, one at Concordia, another at Ceneda, a third known to have been established at the New City of Istria, a fourth at Ruginum, a fifth at Renetum, and a sixth at Tersatia.”

[Note: [Col. 0151B] One at Concordia, etc. We have reproduced the words as they appear in the diploma apud Nicoletti; concerning them, consult the copy of the diploma itself in Appendix 2 and chapter 10 of the *Life of Saint Paulinus*. Nevertheless, attribute an error to the writer’s haste if you find *Renitensi* written where *Penitensi* or *Petinensi* is intended.]

Enriched by these grants, Paulinus returned to his church, devoting the remainder of his life to works of piety and episcopal care. At least three times a year he visited the women’s monasteries under the rule of Saint Benedict. Concerning this, an old tradition handed down from ancestors and great-grandparents reports that he bestowed notable benefits upon them, especially upon the monastery of Saint Quirinus and the Greater Monastery, as it is called, of the city of the Forum of Julius, in which many of his relics are preserved to the present day.

From the neighboring provinces of Carinthia and Styria he converted many pagans to the faith through miracles and exhortations. He maintained a correspondence with William, duke of Aquitaine—

[Note: [Col. 0151B] With William, duke of Aquitaine. Do not confuse with another duke of Aquitaine of this name, famous for his remarkable conversion through the work of Saint Bernard. The man under discussion here, son of Theodoric and Aldana, was honored by Charlemagne with the title of count; after he expelled the Saracens from Occitania, he is called duke of Aquitaine.

[Col. 0152A] Nevertheless, in the year 806 he bade farewell to the world and, with the consent of his wife, withdrew into a monastery he had built. He died on 28 May 812, renowned for the fragrance of his holiness. See Baillet, *Lives of the Saints*, under 10 February, and Mabillon, fourth Benedictine century, part 1.]

—with Turpin, bishop—

[Note: [Col. 0152A] With Turpin. He is also called Tilpinus. Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book II, chapter 17, says of him: “He was taken from the monastery of Saint Denis and made bishop of Rheims; it is found that Charlemagne obtained the pallium for him from Pope Adrian.” After forty-seven years as bishop, he died and was buried at the feet of Saint Remigius. Hincmar wrote his epitaph, as is clear from its closing:

“Hincmar  
Made him a tomb and composed an inscription.”

These words are found in Flodoard, in the passage cited.]

—with Paul the Deacon, and with other distinguished men of his age.

**XVIII.** When Paulinus’s life and conduct had been such as these, it pleased Christ to call him to eternal blessedness. Struck not so much by illness as by old age, he lay ill in the patriarchal residence called the Palace of Callistus. As his poor health grew worse, he was fortified with the sacraments of the Church and, on 11 January of the year 804, rested in the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0152A] 11 January 804. Excellent. The author here has a little from the *Chronicle*, but what he has follows it exactly.]

His bones were buried with solemn ceremony in a marble tomb, not carved but plain. A fragment of it can still be seen today in the principal church, with this bare inscription:

[Note: [Col. 0152B] This inscription: “PAULINUS,” etc. It does not seem to be the same stone as the one about which we wrote in his life, chapter 17, note 8, since our stone has a T before *Paulinus* and, after *Patriarcha*, lacks the word *Aquileiensis*, which appears here.]

**PAULINUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA.**

**XIX.** He worked miracles both while alive and after death. Therefore, by decree of the supreme see, he was enrolled in the catalogue of holy confessors.

[Note: [Col. 0152B] By decree of the supreme see. We do not believe this, for the reasons given in chapter 17, notes 1 and 2 of his *Life*. If only this writer had indicated the places from which he drew these and other statements, he would have found readers more ready to believe him.]

When that day returned, his feast began to be celebrated annually throughout the entire patriarchal territory, and altars began to be dedicated to his name and honor. The succeeding patriarchs built in the same Palace of Callistus, on the left side, a vaulted chapel and an altar. Its construction was indeed barbarous, but the stone was well chosen and skillfully worked, especially the pavement, which was faced and variegated with multicolored marble.

**XX.** This chapel, which I, the present writer, saw many times and venerated devoutly before it was leveled to the ground together with the Palace of Callistus in the year 1553, was sufficiently long and of proportionate width. It projected at the head in a semicircular curve and was adorned everywhere not only with selected stones but also with very small paintings, so that observers, whether near or far, could recognize the same elegance and the artist’s careful hand, just as Giotto’s works are admired.

They are believed to have been the truest likenesses of all Paulinus’s works. Saint Elisabeth, Landgravine, was extraordinarily devoted to this holy confessor. Gregory of Montelongo, a man of most holy mind, valued Paulinus so highly that he chose his own tomb near Paulinus’s.

[Col. 0149C] His successors revered him so greatly that they regarded him as the particular patron of the patriarchate among the saints above and offered daily sacrifices of praise to God upon his altar.

Finally, the chapter of the city of the Forum of Julius regularly had a fairly lengthy eulogy of him recited in the liturgy, expressing an account of his life and deeds. It concluded its peroration in these words:

[Note: [Col. 0152B] His eulogy. This is not a eulogy of Paulinus’s life, but the second homily of Saint Maximus, bishop, on the feast of Saint Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, which is still partly read in the office for confessors and bishops in common. At the end of the entire homily, adapted to our Paulinus by inserting his name here and there as circumstances required, and divided—entire as it is—into several readings, these words are followed by: “For this reason the Lord admitted him to this our land,” and so forth. I saw the legendary, or lectionary, of the church of the city of the Forum of Julius; and I was not the only one who saw it. The matter is indeed as stated.]

**XXI.** “The Lord admitted Paulinus to this our land so that we might be formed by the examples of his deeds, and, looking toward him as toward a mirror, might shape the faces of our souls, and, like good sons, cultivate in ourselves the likeness of our father.

“Just as a great householder, wishing to paint his house with the greatest brilliance, searches out models and images to place before the eyes of a diligent painter, and the painter, carefully examining the figures and eagerly applying himself to the excellence of his art, takes up another’s work and transfers from so learned a hand to the shining wall the face and dignity of living persons, so our true God, the master of this household, in his greatest care to paint his house—that is, to adorn your souls in his Church—seems to have brought forth and displayed to this city the deeds and merits of holy Paulinus as models of living, as models of painting, to be impressed upon your hearts, calling his image back to himself all too soon.

“Accordingly, let each of you overlay the faces of your souls with the precious colors of Paulinus’s virtues. Let one take the grace and spirit of compunction; another, the purest pigment of shining chastity; that one, the pallor of abstinence; this one, the blush of spiritual modesty; that one, [lx] the ardent faith in the things of God, radiant like the brightness of gold.

“And in this way, with the spiritual limbs of his inner person joined together into one body of his people, let him pass into heaven. Let us all, according to that one image, adorn the house—that is, paint the whole Church of God. And when he sees us thinking either of the trembling of eternal judgment or of future blessedness, may he be able to take up that evangelical saying of Christ: ‘Father, I ask that where I am, they also may be with me.’

“And when at some time we are to depart from this world, may your patron, blessed Paulinus, like Abraham receive us, his own special ones, into his own seat and bosom, and on that day may the joyful shepherd recognize his sheep unharmed, with the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

**XXII.** Saint Paulinus governed the patriarchate for twenty-seven years and several months. In my own time his bones were laid to rest by the college of canons of his native city within the high altar, which stands in the choir of the principal church.

[Note: [Col. 0152C] His bones in my own time. They were placed there in the year 1578. Nicoletti therefore wrote this after that date.]

Just as a sacrifice is offered to God there daily, so Paulinus daily—indeed, with perpetual prayers—entreats God for the safety of his people.

[Col. 0151]

# 1. SAINT PAULINUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA

[Note: [Col. 0166C]

**Sacrosyllabus.** Barthius, book XLII, chapter 14; Sidonius and other writers after him call imperial letters or epistles *apices*, as is well known. Paulinus, however, calls the writings *syllables*: “so that each person might bring to his clemency through sacred syllables, on the appointed day, whatever he could more rightly perceive by the grasp of his intellect.” Nevertheless, he may seem rather to have intended collections, and for this reason the book itself is entitled *Sacrosyllabus* in the volumes of the Councils, since one document was offered on behalf of all in the year of the Lord 802 at the Synod of Altinum. This is Barthius.

Although Barthius is wrong here on more than one point—for these things occurred not in 802 but in 794, and not at the Synod of Altinum but at Frankfurt—his reasoning is not unacceptable as to why the book was called *Sacrosyllabus*: namely, because one document was offered on behalf of all.

It was given on behalf of all—I mean the bishops from the nearer parts of Italy—as Charlemagne says in his letter to Elipandus and the other bishops of Spain, included among the acts of the Council of Frankfurt: it was the common vote of the Italian prelates present at the council. Indeed, the word *syllaba* is derived from Greek συλλαμβάνω (*syllambanō*), “I comprehend,” because a syllable generally arises from the joining together of several letters. But that belongs to the grammarians.

Moreover, sometimes not only things expressed by the votes of several people but also letters sent by one person were called *syllabae*. Anastasius, in his account of Adrian (Roman edition, 1718): “The pontiff, sending with him his messengers to the aforesaid most excellent king of the Franks with apostolic syllables of admonitions, etc.” And the Second Roman Council, in 745, act 1: “In recent days you brought us the syllables of our most reverend and most holy brother Boniface, archbishop.”]

## A BOOKLET CALLED THE SACROSYLLABUS AGAINST ELIPANDUS

[Note: [Col. 0166D] Concerning the edition of this booklet in Labbe’s *Collection of Councils*, which we follow after collating it with Cardinal Aguirre, Hardouin says: “Collated by Father Sirmond of the Society of Jesus with the manuscript of Saint Mary of Rheims, donated by Hincmar, as he himself says in the copy preserved in the library of the college of that same Society.”]

Sent to the provinces of Spain by decree of the Council of Frankfurt in the year 794.

[Note: [Col. 0151C] The Basel edition of 1555 reads *Eliphandum* here and below.]

[Col. 0165]

# 8. NOTES ON THE BOOKLET CALLED THE SACROSYLLABUS. PREFACE

[Col. 0165C] Caspar Barthius, that noble Saxon and illustrious ornament of Germany—if you desire his eulogies, consult Thomas Pope-Blount in *Censura celebriorum auctorum*—who subjects almost countless authors to the touchstone and scales of criticism in those dense and crowded sixty books of his *Adversaria*, did not omit this booklet of our Saint Paulinus. He discusses it in book XLII, chapter 14, and book XLIII, chapter 11.

Believing that it would not be inappropriate to set down here what he noted about it, so that it might be available to everyone, I have done so. But since he was a man of extensive reading, though, as someone said of him, not entirely of refined judgment—

(Paul Colomes, *Opuscula*, p. 250)

—and since he passed over some things, touched others only lightly, and since even the matters he considered lack selection and orderly arrangement, something almost unavoidable for a man wishing to write much, we shall preserve the progress of Paulinus’s discourse and note whatever deserves comment, inserting Barthius’s observations where they belong and interspersing our own. We shall do so, however, in such a way that the two sets of notes can be distinguished and recognized at first sight.

The booklet called the *Sacrosyllabus* begins, salutarily composed in a Catholic style, at the council held by divine will in the suburbs of the metropolitan city of Mainz, in the region of Germany, at the celebrated place called Frankfurt, in the presence of the most clement prince, the lord Charles, glorious king, in the twenty-sixth and most fortunate year of his reign.

Accordingly, the holy and venerable council resolved that this booklet should be sent, on behalf of the faith, to the provinces of Galicia and Spain, so that harmful errors might be cut away—especially to Elipandus, bishop of the see of Toledo, in whom the entire substance of this controversy is concentrated.

[Note: [Col. 0167A]

**In the name of the Father, etc.** Thus it is prefixed in the Basel edition of 1555 by Heinrich Petrus, in the *Collection or Library of the Ancient Doctors of the Church*, vol. II, p. 1122, and in the Paris edition at the end of Alcuin, 1617. It is reasonable to believe that Paulinus began in this way and, moreover, that when he spoke these words at the council he added the sign of the cross, as we now do and as has become customary in the Church.

It was customary even among pagans to begin their prayers by invoking the gods. Virgil, book XI, verse 300:

“Having invoked the gods, the king begins from his lofty throne.”

Servius comments: “According to the ancient custom; for our ancestors began no speech without invoking the gods, as in all the speeches of Cato and Gracchus.”

Nothing was more customary among Christians than to begin their daily affairs and actions by invoking the supreme God. Cassian, *Conferences*, XXI, chapter 26: “What should I say of the first fruits which all who faithfully serve Christ are known daily to offer? For … when awakened from sleep … with the first movement of their tongue they invoke him, celebrating his name and praises together.”

Ambrose was referring to this in the hymn for Monday at matins:

“May the tongue first sing to you;  
may the ardor of the mind surround you;  
so that, in the actions that follow,  
you, Holy One, may be the beginning.”

And our Paulinus, in book 28 of the *Book of Exhortation*, admonished Count Henry in these words: “Whatever work you begin to do, first invoke God and give him thanks; and when you have completed it, do likewise.”

As for the sign of the cross, which is placed at the beginning of every action, its use is so ancient in the Church that Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27, placed among the apostolic traditions “that most common practice, to mark ourselves with the sign of the cross,” as well as “the very profession of faith by which we believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.”

Hear Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3: “At every step forward and advance, at every entrance and exit, when dressing, putting on shoes, bathing, at tables, lighting lamps, going to bed, sitting down, whatever occupation exercises us, we wear down our forehead with the sign of the cross.”

Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, verse 865, in the hymn before sleep:

“Grant that, when sleep calls  
and you seek a chaste bed,  
the sign of the cross  
may mark your forehead and the place of your heart.”

Since Christians began their actions either by invoking the supreme and triune God or by forming the sign of the life-giving cross, it gradually came about that the formation of the cross was joined to the invocation of the most holy Trinity, as Claudius de Vert says, *Explanation of the Ceremonies of the Church*, vol. I, p. 187, Paris edition of 1706; see also pp. 257 and following.

This was already the practice in Paulinus’s time. For Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, in his vernacular rule—vernacular, I say, since Father Philip Labbe, who gives Chrodegang’s own rule in the *Collection of Councils* after the Council of Aachen in 816, says that this vernacular version was pieced together by some interpolator from his rule, the capitularies of the Council of Aachen, and other sources, though it is not without the weight of authority—prescribes in chapter 14:

“When the cleric rises during the night hours for the divine office, let him first impress upon himself the sign of the holy cross through the invocation of the Holy Trinity.”

Chrodegang flourished around the year 743. It is therefore highly probable that Paulinus began his prayer with both the invocation of the Trinity and the formation of the cross.]

**IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY SPIRIT**

[Note: [Col. 0152C] Absent from Labbe and Aguirre’s *Collection of Councils*; present in the Basel edition and in the Paris edition of Alcuin, 1617.]

[Col. 0151C] **I.** With the Holy Spirit urging him, and with zeal for the Catholic faith glowing like a spark beneath his breast, a multitude of bishops assembled into one college, obeying the sacred commands, as the decree of the most tranquil and glorious King Charles, lord of the earth, passed with the greatest speed through the various provinces of his kingdom subject to his authority.

[Note: [Col. 0168A] **Most tranquil.** This is not a new title for emperors. Vegetius, addressing Valentinian, to whom he dedicates his book, says in the prologue to book II: “But your tranquility, unconquered emperor,” and so forth. Book I of the *Codex*, title “When a petition,” law “Doubtful,” addressed by Arcadius and Honorius to Remigius: “Even if petitions have been offered to our tranquility.”

Certainly, if any other person, tranquility especially becomes a king and judge: it enables him, though surrounded by external cares, nevertheless not to deviate from what is right, and, “with tranquil governance,” as Gregory says, *Moralia*, book XVIII, chapter 25, “to arrange the things around him that are less tranquil.” Let kings and judges therefore imitate him of whom it is said in Wisdom 12:18: “But you, master of strength, judge with great tranquility.”]

[Col. 0153A]

[Note: [Col. 0153D] The Basel edition reads “most glorious.”]

When all were seated one day—

[Note: [Col. 0153D] The Basel edition reads “on a certain day indeed.”]

—in the hall of the sacred palace, with priests and deacons—

[Note: [Col. 0168B] **Deacons.** Barthius, book XLII, chapter 14. Since the ancient Christian writers knew that *diaconus* was a Greek word, while the unlearned multitude, ignorant of Greek, pronounced it contrary to its origin, they too wrote *diaconem*, not *diaconum*. Thus Cyprian, in the fifth letter among the earliest Fathers: “Cyprian to the presbyters and deacon brothers.” So too the Synod of Sardica, in its letter to the Church among Hilary’s fragments published by Pithou. Simon Goulart erred in his note on Cyprian. Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book III, chapter 7: “Deacons clothed in dalmatics.” Thus Anastasius the Librarian writes to John, deacon of the city of Rome. Thus, under Charles, Paulinus of Aquileia: “And on a certain day, when all were seated in the hall of the sacred palace, with priests, deacons, and the whole clergy standing around them in the form of a circle, in the presence of the aforesaid prince a letter was brought.” This is Barthius.]

—standing around them in the form of a circle, and with the entire clergy present, a letter was brought in the presence of the aforesaid prince. It had been sent by Elipandus, author of the harmful crime, the pseudo-bishop of the see of Toledo, enclosed within the boundaries of Seville.

[Note: [Col. 0168C] **Elipandus, etc.** Why Elipandus is called the author of the crime, although Felix was the actual author, see Dissertation IV, note 47.]

When it had been read aloud by royal command, the venerable prince immediately rose from the royal seat, stood upon his dais, and spoke about the matter of the faith in a lengthy address.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] The Basel edition reads “and addressed them.”]

He added:

“What do you think? For a full year now, and ever since this madness of the plague began to swell and the ulcer of treachery to boil over more widely, a considerable error—

[Note: [Col. 0153D] The Basel edition reads “horror.”]

—has taken root in these regions, although they lie at the farthest boundaries of our kingdom. The judgment of the faith must cut it away by every possible means.”

[Note: [Col. 0153D] The Basel edition reads *ulcer*, not *ulcerous sore*.]

When a delay of several days had been requested and granted to his gentleness—

[Note: [Col. 0168C]

**A lengthy delay.** Barthius, book XLII, chapter 14. *Morosus* means difficult or causing a long delay, as we noted in Hericus of Auxerre and Terentianus Maurus. Paulinus himself says: “And when a lengthy delay of several days had been requested and granted to his gentleness,” and so forth.

Again, in book XLIV, chapter 19, where he corrects certain passages of Prudentius the Younger’s *Life of the Blessed Virgin Maura*, he says that *morose* means “for a long time.” Prudentius writes: “Before the aforesaid image of the aforementioned Savior, she prostrated herself for a long time every day in succession.” Hericus of Auxerre likewise calls spondees *morosi* in a poem, because they linger longer.

Moreover, *morosus* does not derive from *mora* (“delay”), as Barthius seems here to derive it, but from difficult manners. Nonius, *On the Difference of Words in Meaning*, under *morata*: “Morose: with contrary and perverse manners.” Cicero, *On Old Age*: “But old men are morose and anxious, irritable and difficult.”]

—it pleased his gentleness that each person should bring, [2] through sacred syllables, on the appointed day, whatever he could more rightly perceive by the grasp of his intellect, offering to his clemency the heart of his own breast as a gift of faith, conveyed by the vehicle of the stylus with lively intelligence.

But, as is the custom of heretics—to mix sad things with joyful, sweet things with bitter, and temper the cup of poison with the flavor of honey—

[Note: [Col. 0168D]

**To temper with the flavor of honey.** This is a very well-known comparison: a bitter doctrine, surrounded by fraud, is compared to a medicinal cup whose mouth has been smeared with honey, concealing its bitterness.

Paulinus himself says: “But, as is the custom of heretics—to mix sad things with joyful, sweet things with bitter, and temper the cup of poison with the flavor of honey—some passages in the same letter were found to be full of blasphemies.”

We have noted elsewhere the passages of Lucretius, Jerome, Phoebadius, and others.

**BARTHIUS**, in the passage cited.]

The passages which Barthius seems to have intended to indicate may perhaps be these; and even if they are not, they are nevertheless relevant [Col. 0169A]. Jerome, Letter 7, to Laeta:

“Poisons are not administered unless they are coated with honey; and vices do not deceive unless they are concealed beneath the appearance and shadow of virtues.”

Phaebadius, Book Against the Arians, near the beginning, concerning the faith of Valens, Ursacius, and Potamius:

“I have accepted nothing simple in this confession of faith, which at first appearance, by heretical subtlety, flatters the inexperienced, the credulous, and the unsuspecting in order to deceive them—just as honey recommends a cup of poison.”

Lucretius, Book I, line 932:

“But just as physicians, when they try to give children the bitter wormwood, first touch the rims of the cups all around with the sweet, yellow liquid of honey, so that the child’s unsuspecting age may be deceived merely as far as the lips, while meanwhile he drinks down the bitter juice of the wormwood and, deceived, is not caught, but rather, refreshed by such treatment, recovers and grows strong—so do I.”

Thus, too, heretics offer not a cup of life but of death. Paulinus also uses this comparison in Book I Against Felix, chapter 12.]

to temper with the taste of honey; yet certain things were found in the same letter that were full of blasphemies and in every respect hostile to the Catholic faith, while others, if one may say so, could be found that ought not to be rejected. But in the same cup in which a drop of poison swells and spreads, the sweetness of the honey nevertheless turns bitter.

## II

Therefore I, Paulinus, although an unworthy sinner and the last servant of all the servants [Note: [Col. 0169B]

“Last servant of the servants of the Lord.” Today “servant of the servants” is a title given to the supreme pontiff. Formerly, out of a desire for humility, any Christian bishop might adopt it for himself. Our Paulinus writes: “Therefore I, Paulinus, although an unworthy sinner and the last servant of all the servants of the Lord, etc.” Anastasius the Librarian writes: “To my lord, in all respects most holy, venerable to God, spiritual father and teacher Theodosius the presbyter, Anastasius, a lowly presbyter and monk, servant of the servants of God, sends greetings.” BARTHIUS, in the cited place.

But he is mistaken when he says that this title was given to the supreme pontiff; it is not given to him, but assumed by him for the sake of humility. Saint Gregory the Great provided the origin of the designation and the example of its lowliness, as John the Deacon testifies in his Life, Book II, chapter 1: “in order,” he says, “to rebuke the arrogant display and conduct of John, patriarch of Constantinople, who vaunted himself as universal.” Ducange, in his Glossary, under “Servant of the servants of God,” cites the same Deacon. He adds that kings, princes, and even bishops have used this title, as did Sigualtus, patriarch of Aquileia (he was the predecessor of Saint Paulinus), in the Cassinese Bullary, volume II, page 16: “Servant of the servants of the Lord.” The many others may be consulted there. Also examine the openings of the letters of Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, and you will find this title used very frequently. See also the notes of Nicolaus Serarius on Letter 2, where he discusses the matter more fully. The familiar verse is found in the Gloss, chapter “Quoties,” distinction 1, question 7:

“Rome, formerly, your servants were servants of lords;

now your lords are servants of servants.”

This may perhaps be by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, as is conjectured from Cassander’s commentary on Hymn 2 of Saint Paulinus concerning Saints Peter and Paul.]

of the Lord, bishop of Aquileia [Note: [Col. 0153D] Cardinal Aguirre: “Aquileian.”] [Note: [Col. 0169C]

“Of the Aquileian see, girded by the western shores,” that is, contained within the Italian boundaries [Col. 0169D]. For Hesperia, meaning the western region, was called Italy by the Greeks, to whom it lay in the west. Virgil, Aeneid I, line 530:

“There is a place which the Greeks call Hesperia,

an ancient land, powerful in arms and rich in soil.

The Oenotrians inhabited it; now, it is said,

their descendants have called it Italy, from the name of their leader.”

Book II, line 781:

“Coming to the land of Hesperia, where the Lydian Tiber

flows gently through rich fields and among men of valor.”

Silius Italicus, Book I, line 50, called Cannae a hill of Hesperia. Horace, Book III, Ode 6, line 294:

“The gods have inflicted many grievous evils

upon sorrowing Hesperia.”

And Book IV, Ode 5, line 237:

“O good leader, may you grant long holidays,

lest I perish.”

Since Spain also, which lies west of Italy, is called Hesperia, Spain is called “the furthest” Hesperia to distinguish it from Italy, as in Book I, Ode 36, line 819:

“Who now, safe from furthest Hesperia.”

When Paulinus says that Aquileia is girded by the Hesperian, that is, Italian, shores, he does not support those who place it within the boundaries of Illyricum, as do several Greek writers whom he cites; nevertheless, the eminent Norisius does not follow them in his Dissertation on the Fifth Synod, chapter 10. Add Sirmondus, Book I, chapter 8, and Book II, chapter 7, of the *Propemptica*. The author of the *Chronicle*, or of the ancient patriarchs of Aquileia, in volume IV of Muratori’s *Anecdotes*, speaking of Frederick the patriarch, who repelled the neighboring enemies, says:

“Restoring peace to Hesperia, which is the head of the Church,”

perhaps because Rome is in Italy. This appears more clearly in the epitaph appended there, where it says:

“He restrained the fury of Pannonia with great moderation,

and brought peace to afflicted Italy.”

Pancirolus likewise, in *A Description of the Western Empire*, chapter 58, “calls Aquileia the first city of Italy after Rome and the metropolis of Venetia, although under Augustus it was considered outside the boundaries of Venetia, as Strabo records in Book V.”]

of the see girded by the Hesperian shores [Note: [Col. 0153D] Cointius, under the year 794, no. 7, reads “by the Venetian shores”], which by God’s authority I serve, in name [Note: [Col. 0170B]

“In name, not in merit, a bishop.” Barthius, in the cited place. What Paulinus says—“in name, not in merit”—proceeds from priestly humility. Even the holiest men declared that they could not fulfill so great an office; therefore they said that they were called bishops, not that they were bishops. Thus Hincmarus, *On the Divorce of Lothair*: “Hincmarus, in name, not in merit, bishop of Reims and servant of the people of God.” Likewise in his letter to Gunthar of Cologne. Saint Bernard, in Otto of Freising, *Deeds of Frederick*, Book I, chapter 41: “Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux.” The same interpretation applies to Ivo of Chartres, Letter 12: “To the most reverend Father of Fathers, Urban, Ivo, his most faithful son, called bishop of the Carnutes.” He likewise was accustomed to write that he was the servant of the church of Chartres and not an adequate minister of it. A thousand similar examples may be found among Desiderius and his associates, Geoffrey of Vendôme, Peter of Celle, Peter Maurice of Cluny, and others, abbots and bishops. Thus far Barthius. One may add what the patriarch Gotpold wrote in his own epitaph, as it is found in the Chronicle cited and reported by Muratori:

“Here I, Gotpold, lie in this miserable monument.

Here the bishop is called such in name, not in merit.”]

not in merit a bishop, together with the most reverend and entirely worthy Peter, archbishop of the see of Milan [Note: [Col. 0153D] Absent in Basil, which reads: “together with my colleagues and brothers . . . according to the poverty of my understanding,” etc. Labbé and Aguirre write in the margin: “Read ‘of Istria,’ ‘of Venetia,’ or ‘of Istria and Hesperia,’ without distinction.”], and with all our colleagues, brothers, and fellow priests, the venerable bishops of the Catholic churches of Liguria, Austria, Hesperia, and Emilia, according to the weakness of our understanding, taught by the Holy Spirit, I do not hesitate to respond with heart, tongue, and pen against the madness of those who oppose the true faith [Col. 0153D], since the holy and universal Church is nevertheless immovably founded upon a firm rock, and the gates of hell cannot prevail against it.

Yet because she remains established in the sea of this age [Note: [Col. 0153D] Basil has *persistat*, “may she remain.” Barthius, unwillingly resisting the reading, proposes it. [Col. 0154D] See the notes.] [Col. 0154A] [Note: [Col. 0170C]

“Established in the sea of this age, she resists with difficulty the attacks of heretics,” etc. Barthius, in the cited place. But the first clause of these words is not free from error either. Write: “Established in the sea of this age, she resists with difficulty the attacks of the heretics,” etc.

Yet, with due respect to Barthius, I think nothing should be changed, but that the text should be read as it stands. What prevents the meaning from proceeding correctly, unless *aegre* (“with difficulty”) is inserted at will, *resistit* (“resists”) is read for *persistit* (“remains”), and *adversis* (“hostile”)—which is perfectly suitable as an adjective modifying “the blasts of the heretics,” as is clear also from the following epithets, “the violent storms of the faithless” and “the foaming waves of the slanderers”—is attached to the word *flatibus* rather than being freely transferred to *resistit*? For if you separate *adversis* from *flatibus*, the harmony of the sentence is destroyed.]

she is battered and shaken by the hostile blasts of heretics, the violent storms of the faithless, and the foaming waves of slanderers. Although she can be shaken, she cannot be submerged, strengthened by Christ’s right hand and guided by the apostolic helm, I nevertheless consider it necessary for all Christians and all the faithful, especially apostolic men, to fight against her enemies with the weapons of faith.

For a soldier of Christ ought not cowardly to fear the assault of an advancing war, nor, unarmed and wandering, seek hidden places of escape. Rather, girded with the weapons of his warfare, he must fearlessly pierce the breasts of attacking enemies with spiritual arrows [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Shooting arrows from the bow of the Scriptures.” Barthius writes *intorquendis* and adds: “As I have written it, these words must be read.” The correction is unnecessary: *intorquens* is equally good, indeed better, than *intorquendis*, if two commas are supplied or understood for clearer meaning—one after *jaculis*, the other after *Scripturarum*—so that the sense is: “he must pierce them with arrows, shooting those arrows from the bow of the Scriptures.”], shooting them from the bow [Note: [Col. 0154D] Barthius reads *intorquendis*. See the notes.] of the Scriptures, so that, armed with the shield of faith, he may preserve himself unharmed and wound the flanks of his enemies with sharp darts.

For before the trophy of battle, the recruit is not crowned with the triumphal wreath around his head [Note: [Col. 0154D] Basil, instead of *non plectitur*, has *complectitur*, omitting the negation; but this is wrong.] [Col. 0154B]. The truth of this is demonstrated more clearly by apostolic teaching. “There must be heresies,” says the distinguished preacher and most proven soldier from the Lord’s camp, “so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Corinthians 11:19).

For sometimes, by a lofty dispensation, it comes about that, from the very point at which wavering feet fear to fall into ruin, it is strengthened more powerfully and remains firmly unshaken; and that, from the very point at which the ancient enemy proudly boasts that he has conquered, he is overcome by divine power and, cast down, grieves that he has been defeated.

For since he knows that the structure of all virtues endures upon the foundation of faith [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Upon the foundation of faith.” Nothing is more frequent in Scripture and the Fathers than the description of faith as root and foundation. One or two testimonies will suffice on a matter so familiar. Eusebius Pamphili, Book II Against Sabellius: “Faith is the highest, chief, and first foundation and root of all works that are done.” Ambrose likewise develops the allegory of foundation and root when speaking of faith, as in Book II *On Cain and Abel*, chapter 9, where he says that faith “is the root of all things . . . and whatever you build upon this foundation alone advances toward the fruit of its work and the reward of virtue.” And in his exposition of Psalm 1: “Virtues without faith are leaves: they seem to flourish, but they cannot be useful; they are tossed by the wind because they have no foundation,” etc.], he hastens to uproot the firmness of faith itself with the hand of his wickedness, just as the Psalmist says of his followers, that is, of the evil spirits: “They say, ‘Lay it waste, lay it waste, down to its foundation’” (Psalm 136:7).

Indeed, the evil spirits boast that they have emptied the soul to no purpose down to its foundation if, by intensifying the darts of temptation, they can uproot the firmness of faith from the very foundation of the mind [Note: [Col. 0154D] Basil: “the foundation of faith.”]. They know, of course, that nothing which appears good is good unless it has been firmly rooted upon the foundation of faith.

“For without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6) [Note: [Col. 0154D] “God” is absent in Basil.]. “But God’s firm foundation stands,” bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19) [Note: [Col. 0154D] Basil: “and it has.”].

Although that enemy rages and, by the deceitfulness of his cunning, creeps in a thousand ways beyond the enclosures of the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0154D] Basil: “beyond the enclosure.”], here and there stripping off the scales of his wickedness after striking against the reefs of the Syrtis [Note: [Col. 0154D] Basil: “against these reefs.”], and then running about everywhere—at one moment, while circling about the world, secretly placing himself beside the road, so as to bite the foot of the simple passerby; at another, hanging himself high above and infecting the breasts of heretics with the poison of faithlessness, making them swollen—so that, when their vital organs have been wounded, they vomit out spiritual nourishment in disgust [Note: [Col. 0154D] Harduinus, from a manuscript, and Basil have *eorum*, “their.”] [Col. 0155A] [Note: [Col. 0155D] The word *spiritualia* is absent in the manuscript of Labbé.]. Yet because she is founded upon the firm rock, the gates of hell shall not prevail against her.

## III

Under the impulse, then, of this destructive serpent, and intoxicated by the cup of gall [Note: [Col. 0155D] Basil: “intoxicated.”], certain men whose names are not inscribed upon the white stone [Note: [Col. 0171A]

“Upon the white stone of the Lamb.” The ancients used counters to record totals of expenditures; hence “to sit at the counters” means to calculate an account. Once the account had been calculated with counters, it was then entered into the records of expenditures and receipts. Thus, in our Paulinus, *calculus* designates those very records when he says: “Under the impulse of this destructive serpent and intoxicated by the cup of gall, certain men whose names are not inscribed upon the white stone of the Lamb strive to revive an ancient heresy.” The sense is the same as if he had said “account,” and this is how the old glossator Rhapsodus Papius explains *calculus*. Thus Barthius, in the cited place.

[Col. 0171B] Yet this explanation is not convincing. I am not unaware that *calculi* were used for accounts, or for records of receipts and expenditures. Indeed, if you wish, add the *calculatores*, who were among the slaves appointed to preserve written accounts of expenditures, as Pignorius states in *On Slaves*, chapter 18. But that Paulinus did not have this meaning of *calculi* in mind is sufficiently shown by his saying “upon the white stone.” What has “white” to do with accounts of receipts and expenditures? The designation “white” is not applied to such accounts. It is better, therefore, to say that he had in mind the passage of Revelation 2:17: “To the one who conquers I will give a white stone, and upon the stone a new name written, which no one knows except the one who receives it.” Arctas sheds light on this passage: “He placed here,” he says, “the white stone because it was known to those who competed in theaters and stadiums, and it was given to the victors.”

No one even slightly acquainted with letters is unaware that the ancients used a white pebble to mark fortunate days and events, and a black one for unfortunate ones. Pliny, Book VI of the Letters, Letter 11, to Maximus: “A joyful day, one that I must mark with the whitest stone!” Persius, at the beginning of Satire II:

“Count this day, Macrinus, with a better stone,

a white day that adds passing years to you.”

Judges also cast their votes with black or white counters when acquitting or condemning. Ovid, Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*, line 41:

“It was the custom of the ancients, with white and black pebbles,

with these to condemn the accused, with those to absolve them.”

Menochius, in his excellent commentary on the passage in Revelation, embraces all these points:

“The white stone is the verdict of blessedness which Christ will pronounce upon the victors, and the eternal blessedness with which he will reward them. For among the ancients the white stone was a sign of good fortune and happiness, of acquittal in judgment; and in elections for magistrates, a white counter bearing the name of the candidate who received the votes was given.”

This is what Paulinus had in mind when he said that the names of these men were not inscribed upon the white stone of the Lamb—that is, as Revelation elsewhere says, in the Lamb’s book of life, chapter 13, verse 8: in a single word, that they would not be saved.]

of the Lamb, attempt, from a thorny stock, to revive an ancient heresy—of illustrious and powerful men, certainly, trampled down wonderfully beneath heels [printed *inculcatam* for *conculcatam*, “trampled down”] and once utterly cut down by the Catholic sickle from its roots.

They therefore assert—but with false assertions—that our Lord Jesus Christ was born from the Virgin as God’s adoptive Son, something they cannot prove by divine testimonies. In saying this, they must either suppose that he was adopted in the Virgin’s womb—which it is impious to say, because he indescribably took flesh from the blessed Virgin; he did not adopt flesh—or else confess that he was born a mere man without God, which is impious to think. Consequently, they must say that afterward [Note: [Col. 0155D] Absent in Basil.], as though he had needed adoption, he was adopted by the Father as a son.

For God, who was in him not by grace, as in other holy and pure human beings, but essentially by nature, had need of nothing. “God,” says the Apostle, “was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

How, then, could he grant us the adoption of sons if he himself required what was necessary in order to possess it? [Note: [Col. 0171D]

“He needed what was necessary.” The sentence is defective. Write: “If he himself needed it by necessary right.” Necessary right is natural kinship, which makes those born from us necessary heirs. Thus Phaedrus, Fable 54:

“He had no power at all in begetting.

Why should this be preferable, which has pity on the newborn

and freely offers sweet goodwill?

Goodness makes parents, not necessity.”

Here we do not approve Rimicius’s and Neveletus Doschius’s restoration, “birth.” The necessity of being born is owed to parents, and the provision of nourishment or food after birth follows from natural law. Ambrose, Book I *On Duties*, whose words Niccolò Rigaltius produced in his commentary on that passage of Phaedrus, says the same. In our Paulinus, *eguit* means “lacked.” If he did not possess the necessary right of paternal succession, how could he give it to us as an adoptive son? BARTHIUS.

I admit that the reading is difficult and perhaps corrupt through the negligence of a copyist or scribe, so that one should write not *non eguit* but *habuit* (“had”); unless one prefers to lay the blame upon the barbarism of the age, in which case many things must certainly be forgiven the writers of that period.

Barthius, in producing a learned annotation, makes the more difficult reading still harder to attain and accept. For how can Paulinus say: “How could he grant us the adoption of sons if he himself lacked, or needed, the necessary right, so that he might have it for himself?” If he lacked or needed the necessary right, it would follow that he was not the natural Son of God. For necessary right is founded upon natural birth, as Barthius himself says.

Moreover, what connection of words and sequence of meanings is this? “He himself lacked the necessary right to obtain adoption for himself”! Necessary right does not grant a right to adoption, because it is natural sonship itself. A natural son cannot be said to lack or need necessary right, nor adoption: not necessary right, because he is a natural son; nor adoption, because, if he is natural, he should not be adopted, and adoption does not apply to him.

The meaning of Paulinus’s words therefore seems simple and clear: “He cannot grant the adoption which he himself needs, because, if he himself needs adoption, he has nothing to give another.” This is plainly confirmed by the words immediately following: “For because he had no sin, he gave us sins” [that is, he forgave our sins]; “because he did not receive life in order to be life, but is himself essentially life, therefore he bestowed eternal life upon us.”

From these words, then, infer as follows: “Because he did not have adoption, he adopts.” Conversely: “How could he grant us the adoption of sons if he himself needed adoption in order to have it for himself?” Perhaps *necessarium* is used adverbially for *necessario*, “necessarily.”]

needed adoption in order to have it for himself? For because he had no sin, he bestowed forgiveness of sins upon us; because he did not receive life in order to be life, but is himself essentially life, therefore he bestowed eternal life upon us.

[Col. 0155C]

## IV

Let us now see what Gabriel, to whom the mystery of the hidden dispensation had been entrusted, says to the Virgin Mary concerning Christ’s incarnation. “Hail,” he says, “full of grace; the Lord is with you” (Luke 1:28). When she was troubled by his words, the angel continued: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found favor with God. Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He will be great, and he will be called the Son of the Most High” [Note: [Col. 0155D] In Basil, from “you will bear” through “he will be called” is absent.].

And when she had already believed the angel’s words and was asking how so unprecedented a thing could occur without a man, the angel immediately added: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore also the holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God.”

For he did not say, “He will be called the adoptive Son of God,” but simply “the Son of God” and “the Son of the Most High.” Nor was the angel speaking merely of the excellence of his majesty, but rather of the divinity incarnate.

Furthermore, *quod* is a pronoun of the neuter gender, and *sanctum* is likewise neuter. For he says: “The holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God.” Matthew again reports that the angel said: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 1:20).

So that you may not doubt that he was speaking of the body which he took from the inviolate Virgin, in accordance with the usage of sacred language, in which a part is put for the whole, understand by the body alone the entire human being, born from her with a rational soul [Note: [Col. 0156D] Basil: “may understand.”].

But so that no scruple of ambiguity might remain [Note: [Col. 0172B]

“Any scruple of ambiguity.” *Quilibet* in this class of writers means “anyone whatsoever.” Paulinus: “so that no scruple of ambiguity might remain . . .” A *scruple* is doubt or ambiguity. Tertullian, at the end of *To Scapula*: “For anyone who observes such endurance is struck by some scruple and is stirred to inquire what is at issue; and when he has learned it, he himself immediately follows the truth.” Hence *scruple of ambiguity* here, and “scrupulous evasions” in Justinian, Code, Book 1, *On Legacies*: “Who would employ scrupulous evasions in a matter of remission?” BARTHIUS.

Add that *scrupulus* is the diminutive of *scrupus*, concerning which Festus, letter S, says: “Scrupi are rough stones and stones separated from the track; hence we call something *scrupulous* when it contains some roughness.” From this comes the proper use of *scrupulus* for the little stone hidden in a shoe that causes distress by hurting the foot. It is then applied figuratively to matters that produce anxiety by signifying doubtful and two-sided questions; hence we say *to remove a scruple*, meaning to remove anxiety, and *to introduce a scruple*, meaning to cause anxiety. Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria*: “He asks you to remove from his mind this scruple which goads and pricks him day and night.” The same, *For Aulus Cluentius*: “A scruple and a certain doubt were then introduced into the minds of the people as to what had actually been done.”]

because he had spoken about the mystery of Christ’s incarnation [Note: [Col. 0156D] Basil: “because he spoke.”], he immediately adds a little later: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father.” He is called David’s son according to the flesh, plainly, not according to divinity.

You have, therefore, the fact that concerning the one of whom he had previously said, “The holy thing that will be born from you will be called the Son of God”—not an adoptive son, but the true Son; not an alien, but his own—he subsequently added: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1:32).

For who could be believed to have adopted him as a son, when the whole holy Trinity brought about the man Christ in the Virgin’s womb? Thus it is written, both according to the history of the first Adam and concerning the second, that is, Christ, in the mystery of prophecy: “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26).

Or, certainly, as the angel’s voice declares in this same Gospel reading: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.” Here you have the third person of the Trinity, the Holy Spirit. “And the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” In the power of the Most High the person of the Son is indicated, because he is the power of God and the wisdom of God. In the name “Most High,” the person of the Father must likewise be understood.

Let the heretics therefore say, if they can [Note: [Col. 0172D]

“Let the heretics say, if they can.” “Let the heretics say, if they can, which of these three persons adopted him, when the whole Trinity brought him about in the womb of the immaculate Virgin; and if they cannot, let them humbly submit to the salutary teachings of the Catholics.” Thus, says Barthius, these words must be arranged, since they have commonly been broken up and incorrectly separated.

The arrangement of the words is excellent, but not entirely necessary. For if you observe the parenthesis, which is skillfully placed in Cardinal Aguirre’s edition and which we also reproduce from it, every apparent confusion of the words disappears. Besides, such transpositions are found even in the best writers. Quintilian is the authority, *Institutio Oratoria*, Book IX, chapter 6: “When nothing is to be changed in the meaning and only the structure varies, it may rather be called a figure of words, as when many alter a narrative by long hyperbata.”]

(which, if they cannot, let them humbly submit to the salutary teachings of the Catholics), which of these three persons adopted him [Note: [Col. 0156D] Basil: “which.”] [Note: [Col. 0173A] “Adopted him.” Barthius, who had read *optaverit*, as it appears in Basil’s edition, writes: “*Optare* means ‘to adopt’ . . .” Papias the Master, generally not an inept interpreter of this class of authors, says: “*Optare*: to choose, desire, or make someone a son.” Thus Barthius. Certainly, “to desire” does not suit this passage. Nevertheless, *optare* can mean “to choose.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I, line 429:

“Some choose a place for a dwelling and enclose it with a furrow.”

Likewise III, line 109:

“And he chose a place for his kingdom . . .”

But to adopt, according to Hotomanus in his commentary on legal terminology, under “Adoption,” “is the same as to choose by an act of selection and to receive someone into one’s family.”], since the whole Trinity brought him about in the womb of the immaculate Virgin?

## V

Now, an adoptive son can be called such only if he is alien [Note: [Col. 0173A]

“Only if he is alien.” Paulinus gives an excellent description of adoption, one entirely consistent with the conditions required by the jurists: the person adopted must not be a true son but an alien and an outsider. To this may be added Gellius, Book V, chapter 19, describing adoption as the act “when outsiders are taken into another family and into the place of children.” Hotomanus, in the cited place: “Adoption is a lawful act by which an outsider is received into another family and into the legal position of a son under paternal authority . . . I said ‘outsider,’ meaning one who is not his own.”], by the one by whom he is said to have been adopted, and adoption is freely granted to him, since adoption is conferred not by obligation but solely by favor.

So we, at a certain time, when through sin we were sons of wrath, were alienated from God; through his own true Son, who did not need adoption, the adoption of sons was granted to us, as Paul testifies when he says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons through him” (Galatians 4:4–5).

The proper Son was born of a woman, not an adoptive son. Hence the same distinguished preacher says elsewhere: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Romans 8:32).

Therefore, when he approached the Jordan’s channel, with John as companion, whom the people supposed to be the Christ, [Note: [Col. 0173B] “So that the nature of the waters might be sanctified.” Saint Ambrose, *Commentary on Luke*, Book II, no. 83: “The Lord was baptized, therefore, not wishing to be cleansed, but to cleanse the waters, so that, washed through the flesh of Christ, which knew no sin, they might possess the right of baptism.” Saint Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration on the Holy Lights*: “Above all, so that through these things the waters of the Jordan might be sanctified, so that, just as he was spirit and flesh, so also for those who were to be baptized the succession of sanctification might be handed down in spirit and water.” Finally, to omit others, Saint Maximus, Homily 1 on the Epiphany, says that our Lord “by receiving baptism from John consecrated the streams of the Jordan and at the same time purified his own Baptist.”], and when he had immersed himself in the middle of the Jordan’s waters in order to sanctify the nature of the waters, the Father’s voice immediately thundered, saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17).

And again, when he was on the holy mountain with the disciples whom he had chosen, and Moses and Elijah were seen speaking with him, the bright paternal voice suddenly rang out through the cloud and distinguished those who were servants by grace and adoptive sons from the true and proper Son:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.”

For God the Father made known that he had been displeased with himself in Adam, who by sinning lost the dignity of a son [Note: [Col. 0157D] Basil: “thundered.”]. “I repent,” he says, “that I have made man upon the earth” (Genesis 6:6–7).

He was pleased with his only-begotten Son, because the Son had no sins of his own but bore the sins of others; never deviating from the Father’s will, he became obedient to the Father for us, even unto death, and death upon a cross. “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:8–9).

If, then, according to the heretics, he is designated by an adoptive name [Col. 0157B], as we are, pure and ungrateful human beings, how can the Apostle testify that he possesses a name above every name?

An adoptive name [Note: [Col. 0157D] Harduinus, from a manuscript, and Basil: “adoptive.”] is not above every name; it is common and is held below the measure of names.

## VI

Let us now see how the first shepherd of the Church laid the foundation of the faith [Note: [Col. 0157D] The word “first” is absent in Basil.].

When the Teacher and Lord was carefully examining the disciples to learn what people were saying about him, and they had repeated the statements of individuals in various words, those people regarded him as one or another of the adoptive sons, whose adoption was not yet present in reality, which they had received through the coming of the Mediator, but was still hidden in hope [Note: [Col. 0157D] Basil: “examined more carefully.” “They repeated.” “Whose adoption was not yet present in reality, received through the Mediator.”].

The Lord immediately added what they held more firmly in their hearts concerning him. “But you,” he said, “who do you say that I am?” Then blessed Peter, to whom not flesh and blood but the heavenly Father had revealed it, said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

Behold the faith of the blessed apostle Peter, which the heretics pass over with deaf ears perfunctorily [Note: [Col. 0173C]

“To read perfunctorily.” *Perfunctorie* means carelessly, negligently, without diligence. Petronius Arbiter: “He untied the thong from the stone and began to beat me, not perfunctorily.” Barthius cites these words in connection with this passage.

*Perfunctorie* comes from *perfungor*, but with an entirely opposite meaning. For *perfungi* means to perform a duty carefully and diligently. *Perfunctorie*, however, is said of something done carelessly, as though one were engaged in another matter. The Latin word is clear from the Petronius passage cited above, but is not easily found in Cicero. It is used fairly often by the jurists: Digest, *On Evictions*, law “Qui libertatis”; Digest, *On the Decree of the Senate concerning Silanus*, law “Propter”; Digest, *On the Decree of the Senate concerning Tertyllus*, law “Si ingenua sit mater”; finally, Digest, *On Things Done by Force or Secretly*, law “Aut qui aliter.” Ulpian says: “He will have to say it . . . neither perfunctorily nor obscurely.”

The same meaning as *perfunctorie* is found in *dicis causa*, which appears in Cicero and in the jurists. For something done *dicis causa* is done for no other reason than that it may be said to have been done. Thus money counted *dicis causa* is money counted for no purpose other than that it may be said to have been counted. Cicero, *Second Speech Against Verres*: “Nevertheless, so that he might be able to say that he had bought it, he ordered Artagatho to give some coins, merely for appearance’s sake, to those whose silver it had been.” Ulpian, Digest, *On the Decree of the Senate concerning Silanus*, law 1, “Cum aliter,” near the end: “If someone pretended that he was offering assistance, or offered it merely for form’s sake, this fiction will be of no benefit.” In the margin there: “Some wrongly read *ditis gratia* or *dictis gratiam*. It must be understood as *dicis gratia*, that is, perfunctorily and superficially.” Augustine, Book II, chapter 2, has the same. *Dicis* is conjectured by Hotomanus, under “dicis gratia,” to derive from the nominative *dex*, as *judicis* comes from *judex*.

In the very sense used by Paulinus, Saint Ambrose also uses *perfunctorie*, Book VI of the *Hexameron*, chapter 9: “But what shall I say of the nostrils, which, with their double and elongated opening, provide a kind of cavern for receiving odors, so that the smell does not pass through perfunctorily, but remains longer in the nostrils and, by their passage, feeds upon the brain and the senses?” The same writer, *On Paradise*, chapter 6: “To know is certainly not merely a superficial and perfunctory knowledge, but consists in carrying out the things that ought to be done.”]
fear to read. Peter confessed that Christ is the true Son of the living God, and you, heretic, say: “Christ is an adopted son”? Indeed, perhaps you would have raised the ear of your unbelief if he had said simply: “You are the Son of the living God.” You might, according to your custom, have fabricated a false argument and said: “He confessed him, according to him, to be the Son of God.” But since he had said with the added qualification, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” he crushed the mouths of all heretics with the fist of his faith [Col. 0174A; Basil lacks “according to your custom”]:

**He crushed them with the fist of his faith.** That which scarcely fills the measure of a fist is said to be gathered together most tightly. Prudentius, on a corpse:

> And it will have become a dry little ash,  
> the measure of a very small fist.

Thus—incorrectly; read *fidem* (“faith”), and correct the copyist’s ignorance—thus, I say, this Paulinus calls the faith concerning Christ, gathered and uttered most tightly by blessed Peter, a fist. The comparison with a blow struck upon the mouth is added. BARTHIUS, *loc. cit.*

[Col. 0174B] I would not doubt that Paulinus was looking to the contest of pugilists. For *pugiles* comes from *pugna*, and *pugna* from *pugnus*, because people first fought with these weapons supplied by nature; afterward stones, clubs, fire, and iron were employed in fighting. Lucretius, book V, verse 1286:

> The ancient weapons were hands, nails, and teeth,  
> and stones, and likewise fragments of branches from the forests,  
> and flame and fire, once they were first discovered.  
>   
> Later the power of iron and bronze was found.

On this sort of pugilistic contest, see Mercurialis, book II, chapter 9 of *De arte gymnastica*. Yet when, on Pliny’s authority, he says that boxing was invented before the Trojan period, he is mistaken. For Pliny, book XIII, chapter 11, is speaking not of athletic boxing but of writing tablets, which belong to the practice of writing. The bodily firmness and strength of limbs that pugilists were required to possess sufficiently indicate the character of this contest. Hence Plautus, in *Epidicus*, act I, scene I, verse 26, when Epidicus asks:

> How is our master’s son?

he introduces Thesprion as replying:

> Like a boxer and an athlete.

Thus, to show that Peter dispersed the deceptions of the heretics by a forceful and effective method, Paulinus asserts, using an allegory drawn from the strength of pugilists, that Peter crushed the mouths of them all with the fist of his truth and faith.]

he crushed them. For he received the name Christ from the man whom he assumed, because he was anointed in manhood. You have nothing left to say except, following your customary practice [Basil: “you do,” followed by “take from ...”], to take from the workshop of falsehood arrows smeared with poison, with which you do not blush to pierce the hearts of the simple by shooting at them false assertions. For you have acquired the brow of a harlot; you did not wish to feel shame (Jer. 3:3). Indeed, you do not fear to defraud Sacred Scripture [Col. 0157D]—Basil: “for you defraud Holy Scripture”—making light of the prohibition of the teacher of the nations, when you say: “Do not adulterate the word of God” (2 Cor. 4:2).

### VII.

But what wonder if, being foolish, you do not know how to pluck from these allegorical thickets [Col. 0174C]:

**In these thickets, which are allegorical.** Barthius, who evidently had before him the Basel edition, or perhaps one similar to it, restores what appears confused there as follows:

> “The words of the sentence in what follows must likewise be transposed and put back in this order: ‘But what wonder if, being foolish, you do not know how, with a learned hand, to pluck from a dense and shady forest, beneath the leaves of spiritual letters, the apples of spiritual fruits hanging there, when, by badly understanding the orthodox doctrine brought into the open by the holy preachers, you corrupt it?’”

Thus Barthius [Col. 0174D].

The rearrangement of the words in that corrupted edition is sufficiently elegant. But it is superfluous if, from the Labbe edition and the reading contained in Cardinal Joseph Saenz de Aguirre, you adopt the form in which it ought to be adopted.]

which are allegorical—a dense forest—and, wrapped in the shadowy riddles of its ornaments [Basil: “and you do not know how to pluck from a shady forest”; the intervening words are absent], you do not know how, with a learned hand, to pluck from beneath the leaves of letters the apples of spiritual fruits hanging there, while, by badly understanding the orthodox doctrine brought into the open by the holy preachers, you corrupt it? What sort of rashness and audacity is yours, miserable men puffed up with the arrogance of pride, that you do not blush to corrupt with perverse fables [Basil: “to corrupt. According to ...”] the very wonderful teachings of John the Evangelist, according to your senselessness and not according to sound doctrine, while you fail to understand the mystical sacraments? [Col. 0158B] [Col. 0158D: Basil: “you understand.”]

For you say that John writes in his Epistle: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 2:1); and that this word “advocate” means the same as “adopted” [Col. 0158D: Basil: “adopted”], although “advocate” is something entirely different from “adopted” [Basil omits the second “is”]. For that advocate is one who intercedes with the judge on my behalf and defends my needy case by his own protection. He may more appropriately be called propitiated than adopted, because he himself is the propitiation for our sins.

[Col. 0175A] **For when he shows our nature, etc.** B. maintains that this sentence should be read as follows:

> “For when he continually shows the Father our nature, which, having assumed it into himself, he had placed at the Father’s right hand, our Advocate, as it were by interceding, makes him propitious and gracious toward us.”

The common text is wholly corrupt. BARTHIUS.

Everything is to be approved from the Basel reading; in it the final observation is altogether necessary: in the word *efficitis*, as it is commonly read, either the final syllable *-is* must be omitted, as the better editions do, or it must be separated with Barthius.

**That advocate is one who intercedes for me, etc.** This is a beautiful description of the Advocate, whom those monstrous heretics absurdly confused with the adopted one. BARTHIUS.

Moreover, in Paulinus’s time anyone who in any way protected another’s interests was called an *advocatus*. Hence Charles the Great is called *advocatus* in various charters, as may be seen in Ducange, because he boasted that he was the defender of the holy Church. There too one will find Pope Gregory IX writing in a letter to the emperor Frederick II in these words:

> “Since the advocate of the Church ought to be understood as the same as its defender, if you neglect the office of defender, you improperly retain the name of advocate.”

It will also be evident from the charters that the Church of Aquileia had him as its advocate; we promise to discuss these at the end, from documents cited in the notes to canon 5 of the Council of Friuli.]

For when he shows the Father the nature that he assumed in himself [Basil: “having assumed it into himself”], established at the Father’s right hand, he continually manifests it to the Father and, by interceding as our advocate, makes him favorable and benevolent toward us [Col. 0158D: Basil: “you make him,” but incorrectly; *efficit is et benig.* is preferable. See the note.].

But an adopted son is one to whom nothing is owed by the adoptive father, but who is granted the relationship freely and indulgently. The son is called “adopted” abusively, not essentially, just as Moses was adopted as the son of Pharaoh’s daughter, although he was alien to her both by birth and by blood relationship [Col. 0175A]:

**Both by birth and by blood relationship.** That is, he was neither related by blood nor connected by affinity. Cassius defines blood relatives as those connected with one another by blood, as Ulpian says, *Digest*, “On those who are their own and legitimate,” book 1, section “After those who are their own.” This is obtained only through generation. Modestinus, *Digest*, “On degrees and affinities,” book 4, section “But since”:

> “Those related by affinity are the kinsmen of a husband and wife; they are so called because two kinships, which are distinct from one another, are joined through marriage, and one approaches the boundary of the other’s kinship; for affinity is formed through marriage.”

Therefore, since Moses agreed with Pharaoh’s daughter neither by blood nor, so to speak, by the boundary of blood, Paulinus very properly said that he was alien to her both by birth and by blood relationship.]

and therefore we have included this, so that it might plainly be understood that one is called adopted who had not previously been the natural son of the adopter. Consequently, the name of adoption cannot apply to the Son of God, because he was always the true Son, always Lord; and therefore, even after assuming manhood, he did not lose the title of true Son, since he never ceased to be the true Son.

But if, according to your madness, you think that “advocate” means the same as “adopted,” then confess [Basil: “God. Confess therefore ...,” omitting the intervening words]—what is worse and full of every blasphemy—two adopted sons: the Son and the Holy Spirit. For you cannot deny that the Holy Spirit is the Paraclete [Col. 0175B]:

**That the Holy Spirit is the Paraclete.** G. Budaeus, *Commentarii linguae Graecae*, p. 994: “Παρακαλῶ (*parakaleō*) also signifies ‘I intervene on behalf of another,’ as an advocate and patron. Hence the Holy Spirit is called Παράκλητος ἅγιον Πνεῦμα, ‘the Holy Spirit the Paraclete,’ as receiving the pleas of all.” Note that Paulinus here says not *Paraclitus*, as it is commonly pronounced, but *Paracletus*. Among scholars, says C. Macer in *Hierolexicon*, under “Paraclitus,” it is disputed whether one ought to say *Paraclitus* or *Paracletus*, with the *e* lengthened. For Haimon, bishop of Halberstadt, commenting on the Sunday Gospels, says that when a certain Greek came to the king’s palace while that Gospel was being read and the word *Paraclitus* was pronounced, he said that it ought to be pronounced *Paracletus*. “Nevertheless, we do not dare to change it because of customary usage.” John Baptista Thiers also attempts there to defend this custom from both prosody and the force of the Greek word, as the same Macer reports.]

For what is called *paráklētos* in Greek is called *advocatus* in Latin. You even confess—what is worse than every evil and more criminal than every impiety—two adopted sons, namely the Word and the Holy Spirit, so that you are worse than Arius and Eunomius, and worthy of a Macedonian anathema—*maranatha*—[Col. 0159A] [Col. 0175C]:

**And worthy of *maranatha* under an anathema.** Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XLIII, chapter 11. The words are corrupt. They should be written: “Worse than Arius and Eunomius and Macedonius, worthy of anathema—*maranatha*.” *Maranatha* is a formula of execration, like *anathema*. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 16:22:

> Εἴ τις οὐ φιλεῖ τὸν Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν, ἤτω ἀνάθεμα· μαράναθα.  
> “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed: Maranatha.”

Different interpreters explain it differently. The word is derived from *Samattha*, which expresses a final curse, as John Drusius notes in book VI of *Paralipomena*. The Macedonians denied that the Holy Spirit was God, as Honorius of Autun writes in his *Catalogue*. Rather, they asserted that he was a creature and servant, having corrupted by their distinction the passage in John 1, as Constantine Harmenopulus records likewise in his *Catalogue*. Hence they were called Πνευματομάχοι, “fighters against the Spirit,” as Augustine reports in *On Heresies*, chapter 52. They denied that Scripture gives an explicit testimony in which the Holy Spirit is called God; nevertheless, Leontius of Byzantium adduces several such testimonies in his fourth action, and the commentaries of the Fathers are full of them. Barthius treats all this learnedly.

On *Maranatha*, hear Jerome, letter 137 to Marcella:

> “Maranatha is more Syrian than Hebrew, although, because of the closeness of the two languages, it also has something of a Hebrew sound and is interpreted as ‘Our Lord has come.’ Thus the sense is: ‘If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed’; and, when that has been completed, let the following be added: ‘Our Lord has come.’ For it is futile to wish to contend with stubborn hatred against one whose coming is already known.”

See the rites and formulas of this excommunication in Baronius under the year A.D. 57, no. 71 and following, especially Selden, *De jure naturali et gentium juxta disciplinam Hebraeorum*, book IV, chapter 9.]

and, with Macedonius, worthy of an anathema—*maranatha*—[Col. 0159D: Barthius: “worthy of an anathema—*maranatha*—against Eunomius and Macedonius.” See note f.].

For an adopted son is called the son of one alien to him only by an affective manner of speaking. Every adoption derives the origin of its name from affection, although its etymology may not seem to convey a sound resembling that of its meaning. On both sides it has the adverb *utinam* (“would that”) elegantly inserted, as when you say: “Would that you were adopted by me as a son”; and conversely: “Would that I might deserve to be adopted by you as a son.” From the affection of love one part steals into the other [Col. 0159D: Basil: “of the agreement”], so that the affection of love corresponds in both.

But let the heretics, who are the gates of hell, consider what they have said—or rather, let them babble with their perverse mouths. Their hardened hearts, hiding places of falsehood, rage along the precipices of unbelief, always searching; and, lest they be flooded with the light of truth [Col. 0159D: Basil: “overspread”], they hasten to conceal themselves in a cave of falsehood [Col. 0159D: Basil: “in a mirror”; not an unsuitable reading. See the note from Barthius] [Col. 0176A]:

**In a cave of falsehood.** Barthius, *loc. cit.*, having read *speculum* (“mirror”) rather than *spelaeum* (“cave”) in the Basel edition or one similar to it, adds: “*Speculum* is a diminutive of *specus*, not a mirror in which someone looks at his own appearance. No other example—that is, apart from this one in Paulinus—occurs.” So he.

We used this testimony in connection with “Mirror of justice,” no. 3, when explaining in Italian the Litany of the Blessed Virgin Mary called the Litany of Loreto, which we also published for public use in the year 1725, printed in Venice by Ertz.]

They fell—alas, what grief!—under the fire of envy, and therefore were not worthy to see the sun of justice (Ps. 57:10).

### VIII.

The holy Catholic and apostolic Church, although spread throughout the whole world, is nevertheless one: the beloved, the close companion, and the dove of the Bridegroom. She shines with the beauty of sacred speech, with silvered wings; and her hind parts shine with the purity of perfect faith in the pallor of gold [Col. 0159D: Basil: “through the purity of right faith”]. She confesses the holy and ineffable Trinity in unity—indeed, rather, preserving without confusion the distinctness of the persons—, and confesses the substance to be inseparable [Col. 0160D: Basil: “substantial”].

Thus the Father is believed to be one, because he is the Father who begot the Son, coeternal with himself, without time and without any beginning; and the Son is believed to be another, because he is the Son who was begotten without beginning by the Father—not nominally, but truly; and the Holy Spirit is believed to be another, because he is the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son [Col. 0160D: Basil omits “and”].
