The Father is not one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another; rather, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparably one—not one [Col. 0176A]:

**Not one, but one thing.** A similar statement is found in Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitorium*, book I, chapter 19:

> “In the Trinity, one is one and another is another, not one thing and another. In the Savior, one thing is one thing and another, not one person and another. How is it that in the Trinity there is one and another, not one thing and another? Because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. Yet the nature of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is not different and different, but one and the same. How is it that in the Savior there is one thing and another, not one person and another? Because the substance of divinity is one and that of humanity another; yet divinity and humanity are not one person and another, but one and the same Christ, one and the same Son of God.”

Paulinus repeats similar points in book I against Felix, chapter 13.]

but one: because the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. Yet the majesty of the indescribable divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, equal, consubstantial, and coeternal, because God is one. We confess unity in essence, but proclaim Trinity in the distinction of persons.

Therefore we always believe our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, to be true God [Col. 0160D: Basil omits “God”], in the Father, with the Father, and at the Father. In the last times, for us and for our salvation, according to the decree of the hidden dispensation, he descended from heaven, from which he had never departed. He came, certainly, among his own, where he had never been absent. He was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, as the angel says: “For that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20).

Having become true man, according to what is written, “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), he remained true and almighty God in both natures, one Son of God and likewise Son of man. Human birth did not prejudice divine birth in any way. He assumed what he was not, but remained essentially what he was; he suffered neither mixture nor division. Rather, in the one person of Christ, God remains true and man remains true—not two sons, God and man, but one Son, God and man; not one Son of man and another Son of God, but one and the same Son of God and man.

Hence we greatly curse those who, with an impious mouth, grunt that he is adopted [Col. 0176B]:

**With an impious mouth they grunt.** Sounds proper to beasts are attributed to human beings who speak vainly and absurdly. Thus Arnobius, book III:

> “If the number nine gives its name to the Novensiles, Cornificius is convicted of bleating, since he attributes the power of an alien force to the gods who preside over novelty.”

This passage should not be altered. Thus Paulinus here speaks of the more impure heretics, with the simplicity of that pagan Cornificius:

> “... Hence we greatly curse those who, with an impious mouth, grunt that he is adopted” [Col. 0176C].

It is true, however, that Heraldus noted that Arnobius alludes to the name. For *vervex* (“ram”) proverbially denotes stupidity, and *cornifex*—hence *Cornificius*—could not inappropriately suggest a ram, since hardly any animal is more horned than a ram of that kind. BARTHIUS, *loc. cit.*

But Paulinus most appropriately applies the voice of pigs to the heretics. Philo of Carpathus calls them “herds of unclean animals” in his commentary on the Song of Songs, and Tertullian, book *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 41, understands the Lord’s saying in Matthew 7—namely, that pearls are not to be cast before swine—as referring to pagans and heretics.

In any case, it is not unusual for the voices of animals to be attributed to human beings. Consult Varro, who gathers many examples and testimonies, book VI—or, as others number it, book III—of *On the Latin Language*. Apuleius also notes certain expressions of human emotions in the voices of animals, book III of the *Florida*, shortly before the end.

Ausonius amusingly addresses a man with an unnatural voice, epigram 75:

> You imitate the barking of puppies and the neighing of horses;  
>   
> you liken the bleating of horned beasts  
> and wool-bearing flocks; you would say that asses bray  
> when you wish, Marcus, to imitate an Arcadian beast.  
>   
> You imitate the crowing of cocks, crows praying in their throats,  
> and every sound that such a brute possesses.  
> Although you imitate them all so truly that they are judged not to be imitations,  
> you cannot produce the sound of a human voice.

But *grunnire* (“to grunt”) is also found used with another meaning among writers of later Latin. Ducange, in his *Glossary*: “*Grunnire*: to murmur, to show indignation in the manner of a pig. Ancient Cluniac usage, chapter 106: ‘Let him begin the verse again, and let him do this as often as he realizes that the prior grunts on account of it.’”]

with his mouth: for, as we said above, no one can be called adopted unless he was previously alien to the one by whom he desires to be adopted.

How, then, can the Son of God be believed to be adopted, when, through the manhood inseparably assumed and both natures united in one person, there are not two sons—one of God and another of man—so that, as they mistakenly judge, he is the adopted son of man and the Son of God without adoption? Rather, in one person there is one and the same Son of God and man, who never abandoned the man whom he assumed—not even on the cross, when, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

Paul bears witness to this when he says: “For if they had known it, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). The Lord of glory is said to have been crucified, although only the flesh was crucified; but because the Lord of glory himself was the one who was also the Son of man who was crucified, and because he never abandoned the man whom he assumed, as has been said, he is therefore said to have been crucified.

[Col. 0177B] **For this reason, therefore.** This type of writer is especially eager to construct allegories and inflate his arguments through them. Thus our Paulinus here seems to himself to have spoken magnificently when he says:

> “For this reason, therefore, and because of the cloud of this sort of error, we hasten, with the fan of our pen, to scatter the airy shadows of the clouds from the air of the mind, so that the shining stars, drenched with the rays of the eternal sun, may be able to behold with pure eyes throughout the heavens of the Scriptures.”

These expressions are more affected than poetry can properly bear. Yet they have as their model the genius of Sidonius and, even more perhaps, of Ennodius. Those highly learned writers twisted words and style so as to separate themselves from the common people, who spoke corruptly in that age; but in doing so they fell into the opposite vice. BARTHIUS.]

[Col. 0177C] **Fashioned together by the craftsman’s hand.** Barthius, who, as in the Basel edition, reads *configulare* rather than *configurare*, as in the other editions, writes concerning this passage:

> “He elegantly used *configulare*, meaning to join together as in the work of a potter. The almighty God is frequently compared to a potter in the sacred books.”

This is evident from Jer. 18:16; Isa. 45:9; Rom. 9:20; Ps. 102:13–14; Job 10:8–9, and often elsewhere. This was not said allegorically or merely by way of comparison, but in a strict and proper sense, since Genesis 2:7 says: “The Lord God formed man from the clay of the earth”; or, as Tertullian reads it in more than one place, especially at the end of *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 5, “fashioned him.” But how aptly he applies it to the present matter in chapter 7:

> “Thus the clay was obliterated and devoured into flesh. When? When man was made into a living soul by the breath of God—namely, by a vapor suitable for scorching the clay, so to speak, into another quality, as into pottery, and thus into flesh. In the same way, a potter is able, by tempering clay with the breath of fire, to reconstitute it into a stronger material and to fashion one form from another, more suitable than the former and already of its own kind and name.”

Basil aptly observes in *Hexaemeron*, homily 11:

> “Where it says, ‘And God made man; in the image of God he made him,’ the verb ἐποίησεν (*epoiēsen*), that is, ‘made,’ is expressly used. But afterward, when the discourse concerns the substance of the body, it introduces the verb ἔπλασε (*eplase*), that is, ‘formed,’ ‘fashioned,’ or ‘molded.’ For the royal Psalmist taught that this is the distinction between making and forming in his verse: ‘Your hands made me and fashioned me.’ He made the inner and hidden man; he molded or fashioned the external man. Properly, molding or fashioning refers to clay or mud, just as making refers to the image. The flesh, therefore, was formed, but the soul was made.

> “Hence the former courtesan Thais, afterward converted through repentance to the Lord, often said: ‘You who fashioned me, have mercy on me.’ The abbot Paphnutius had prescribed this prayer for her after bringing her back to the way of virtue, as Bellovacensis narrates in the *Speculum historiale*, book XIV, chapter 77.”]

### IX.

There are also many who assert that the one person of the Mediator consists of three substances: the Word, the flesh, and the soul. Yet in a matter of faith it does not seem necessary to scatter the calculations of secular literature by a syllogistic hand in a sophistical dispute. It would be sufficient, according to the salutary teaching proclaimed by the preceding Catholic Fathers, to confess in the sincere voice of simplicity one person from both natures—the Christ who is true God and true man, namely, divine and human.

But because of those who suppose that in the dispensation of the flesh a half-complete nature, without a rational soul, was assumed, with the divine nature taking the place of the soul [Col. 0176D]:

**In place of the soul.** These are the Apollinarists. Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, writes against them in his letter to Paschal I against the Origenists, speaking of Christ:

> “He does not have an inanimate substance without a soul; for he did not have inanimate flesh, nor was God the Word in it in place of a rational soul, as the drowsy disciples of Apollinaris imagine.”

In the *Life of Blessed Damasus, Pope*, from a manuscript in the archive of the canons of Saint Peter, inserted in volume XXVII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, the condemnation of the heresy of Apollinaris is related in these words:

> “He also condemned Apollinaris, bishop of Syrian Laodicea, who asserted that the Lord assumed only a body, and not also a soul, in the dispensation. When he was pressed by the clear testimonies of the Gospel, he later changed his position, lest he seem to be completely defeated, and said that Christ did indeed have a soul, but not in that part by which it is rational; rather, he had only that part by which the body is given life. In place of the rational part, he maintained that the very Word of God was present. When this assertion reached the ears of blessed Damasus, he immediately rejected it with the following judgment: ‘If anyone should say that the Son of God, who was truly God and truly man, possessed less of either humanity or divinity, let him be judged alien from the Church.’ He also ordered this judgment to be confirmed in the holy Second Council, which was held at Constantinople by his command and authority.”]

It is against these people that Paulinus directs his words: “They suppose that a half-complete nature without a rational soul, and with the divine nature assumed in the dispensation of the flesh in place of the soul, was present.”

while the Psalmist says with an eager heart: “For behold, God helps me, and the Lord is the upholder of my soul” (Ps. 53:6).

For this reason, therefore, and because of the cloud of this sort of error, we hasten, with the fan of our pen, to scatter the airy shadows of the clouds from the air [Col. 0160D] [Col. 0160D: In Labbe, from a manuscript: “and from the air”] of the mind, so that, drenched with the ray of the eternal sun, it may be able to behold with pure eyes the stars of Scripture shining throughout the heavens.

For we are not ignorant that human nature subsists from two substances, namely, soul and flesh; but one without the other does not constitute a complete man [Col. 0160D: Basil: “constitutes”]. For what is flesh without a soul except earth? And what is a soul without flesh? Is it not spirit? [Col. 0161A] A human being consists of both, not of one alone.

Therefore, because our Redeemer assumed a perfect man into God, we confess God and man from two natures. For flesh without a soul cannot be called complete human flesh or an integral human nature.

When God had formed man from the clay of the earth, he immediately breathed into him the breath of life, as it is written: “And man became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7). Thus the one who was formed is not one person and the one into whom the breath was breathed another [Col. 0161D: Basil adds “was”], but they are one and the same.

Through the breath, therefore, the earth was animated, fashioned by the incomprehensible art and wondrous method of the supreme craftsman’s hand [Col. 0161D: Basil: *configulata*; Barthius likewise. See the note], so that it cannot be fully investigated how soul and flesh are one, constituting a perfect man, and yet how the substance of flesh and spirit is different.

For when it is written, “To you all flesh shall come” (Ps. 64:3); and again, “I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Ps. 56:4); and again, “All flesh shall see the salvation of our God” (Isa. 40:5, according to the Septuagint, as also in Luke 3:6), flesh cannot in any way see without a soul, so that it may see the salvation of God; nor can it come, so that all flesh may come to him.

### X.

Let us therefore set forth, by way of example, according to the inclination of human reason, and under the compulsion of necessity above all things, material subjects for discussion. For just as a line in plane and solid figures, and a point in quadrangular figures [Col. 0178A], although they are indivisible and cannot be divided, and therefore admirably represent the figures of dimensions, nevertheless retain within themselves the sum of the multitude of all numbers joined together; proceeding from themselves toward an infinite number and returning again into themselves toward unity [Basil: “a finite number”], they are proved to retain an indivisible measure of union.

**Point.** For Paulinus, *punctus* here means what others call *punctum* in another grammatical gender. BARTHIUS.

The word *punctum* is commonly used in the neuter gender. Nevertheless, Latin authors of no little distinction have also used *punctus, puncti*; *punctus, punctus*; *punctum, puncti*; and *puncta, punctae*. Pliny, book XXIX, chapter 6: “They say that even when a weasel’s eyes have been pierced with a point, its sight returns.” Vegetius, book I of *On Military Matters*, chapter 12: “A point driven in two inches is fatal.” Again, Pliny, book II, chapter 69: “This point of the world is the material of our glory.” Seneca, preface to book I of *Natural Questions*, uses the neuter: “This is the point that is divided by sword and fire among so many peoples”; and shortly afterward: “It is the point in which you sail, in which you wage war, in which you arrange kingdoms.”

Let us imagine [Col. 0178B].

**Let us imagine the soul in the form of the body, like a line or point in plane and solid figures.** He discusses the soul in a learned inquiry. On the soul, Claudianus Mamertus is especially elegant, as is Tertullian—although Tertullian must nevertheless be rejected together with the body which he attributes to the soul, and because he maintains that after death a soul passes from an evil life into a demon, as Honorius of Autun also writes, as do Nemesius, Cassiodorus, Gregory Thaumaturgus, and, in our own age, the Englishman Andreas Williatus. BARTHIUS.

Paulinus’s comparison is excellent, although not sufficiently clear or obvious.

> “A point is that which has no part. A line is length without breadth,”

says Euclid, book I, definitions 1 and 2. Taquet says of the point, book I of the *Elements of Geometry*:

> “A point is, as it were, the beginning of every magnitude, just as unity is the beginning of number. A line is understood to be generated by the movement of a point.”

Clavius likewise says of the point:

> “In magnitude, one must conceive of the point as what unity is in number and what an instant is in time. For these too must be conceived as indivisible.”

The meaning of Paulinus’s comparison seems to be this: just as a point, although altogether indivisible, and a line, although indivisible in breadth, nevertheless constitute and circumscribe every body and every part of a body while always preserving their own indivisibility, so the soul gives life to the whole body and to each of its parts while itself remaining undivided.

And just as every plane, solid, or quadrangular figure, when resolved, is resolved into an indivisible line and point, so the life of the body’s limbs, even though it perishes in parts, does not thereby destroy the indivisibility of the soul, to which it is ultimately reduced. The same thing can be explained by number, which returns to unity and is not divided further.

This, it seems to me, is Paulinus’s meaning. If anyone believes that he has grasped it more closely, I shall be grateful if he teaches it to one who wishes to learn without envy.
therefore the soul, in the form of the body—as a line or a point in plane, solid, and quadrangular figures—individually contains within itself the positions of all the parts of the limbs, each inserted in its own joint, so that it is both one and diverse. For if you remove the line and the point of equality [Note: [Col. 0161D] Basil places a comma thus: “the point of equality, nobility.”], the nobility of the figure degenerates. With the origin of the recumbent line impinging [Note: [Col. 0161D] Basil has *linea* (“line”).], and with the quadrature of number spread around the point, it is demonstrated, by an indissoluble division, in the privilege of line and point, which things can or cannot be separated and resolved. Thus indeed the power of the soul, since it is incorporeal and invisible, can neither be divided nor receive the clefts of divisions; yet it wondrously governs the entire mass of the body—which can be divided or separated—containing it within itself, and, diffused throughout it, gives it life by animating it; and, like a point in the middle, it individually retains its own dignity and is not resolved into an alien quality. For, as has been said, since it is incorporeal, it orders all things throughout the body in a bodily manner; and since the substance of the flesh is corporeal, through the incorporeal creature—that is, the soul—it accomplishes corporeal actions. So great is the harmony of their fellowship that they are joined to one another in such a way that the one can do nothing without the other, and the one without the other cannot fully display human nature [Note: [Col. 0161D] Basil has *unitae* (“united”) for *junctae*.] [Note: [Col. 0161D] Basil lacks *et alterum sine altero plenam non possit*.] [Note: [Col. 0161D] Basil has *constare* (“to consist”) instead of *monstrare* (“to display”). See the note.] [Note: [Col. 0178D] “To display human nature.” B., reading from the Basileian manuscript *humanam constare naturam* (“that human nature consists”), says: “Moreover, these passages concerning body and soul have been corrupted … cleanse them: ‘so that the one can do nothing without the other, human nature demonstrating this.’ For human nature teaches this, and therefore it is constituted from two.” BARTHIUS.—I do not reject the correction of the Basileian reading. But see whether the reading we present is better than Barthius’s correction.] Human nature, and for this reason it has pleased us to define human nature from both. For the incorporeal soul sees, hears, and feels through bodily eyes [Note: [Col. 0161D] Basil has *incorporeos* (“incorporeal”), but incorrectly.]; and bodily eyes are shown to see through the incorporeal soul. For if the soul departs, the eyes remaining open and the ears uncovered can neither see [Note: [Col. 0161D] Basil has *videri* (“to be seen”), equally incorrectly.] nor hear. Through the tongue the soul speaks, and the tongue speaks through the soul. For whenever the flesh is cut in any part of the body, the soul feels pain; but flesh cut into pieces [Note: [Col. 0162D] Basil has *frustra* (“in vain”), incorrectly.] without the soul can neither feel pain nor perceive. Through the flesh, indeed, the soul hungers, thirsts, and grieves, and through the soul the flesh does likewise. Can flesh without the soul be called human nature, when it is nothing other than earth? But animated earth can properly be called a complete and perfect human nature [Note: [Col. 0162D] In Labbé’s edition, Hardouin notes in the margin that the word *terra* (“earth”) is absent from the manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0162D] Basil has *perfecta* (“perfect”)—or perhaps *profecto* (“certainly”)?]. For everything imperfect loses the proper character of its name unless a supplement of perfection is more suitably added to it [Note: [Col. 0162D] Basil lacks *ei*.]. Human nature, therefore, is said to subsist from four different elements: hot, cold, moist, and dry—that is, fire, air, earth, and water. Since man subsists from these four diverse natures, ought we to profess four substances in one man? If this pleases anyone, let a fifth also be added, namely the soul, so that man consists of five, and the omnipotent Word is a sixth; and then—something more senseless than all folly and more foolish than every madness—let them declare that there are six substances in the one person of God and man, Christ [Note: [Col. 0162D] Basil has *profanius* (“more profanely”) rather than *dementius* (“more madly”).] [Note: [Col. 0162D] Basil has *substantias* (“substances”) rather than *substantiae* (“of substances”).]. [Note: [Col. 0179A] “Having been nourished by the sweetness of refreshment.” Barthius, on *depastus*, says that it means “well fed, satisfied.” And rightly so. For the preposition *de-* in compounds generally intensifies the meaning of the verb, as in *defrui*, *deperire*, and *devitare*.]

### XI

Perhaps you, whoever you are who oppose our assertion, suspect that we have forgotten that the blessed Apostle said that Christ dwells in the inner man through faith in our hearts (Ephesians 3:17). We retain this with complete devotion of mind and with complete sincerity of heart [Note: [Col. 0162D] Basil has *corde* (“with the heart”).]; and we add what we remember that the same chosen vessel, Paul, said—things that perhaps lie hidden from you while you dream [Note: [Col. 0162D] Labbé and Aguirre note *nesciente* (“while you are unaware”) in the margin.]. “May the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, so that [Note: [Col. 0162D] Basil has *aut* (“or”) rather than *ut* (“so that”).] your spirit and soul and body may be preserved blameless at the coming [Note: [Col. 0162D] Basil has *adventum* (“coming,” accusative) rather than *adventu* (“at the coming”).] of our Lord Jesus Christ.” He said three things [Note: [Col. 0178D] “He said three things: spirit, soul, and body.” This sentence of the Apostle Paul, which Paulinus explains here, is also used by either Etherius or Beatus, or by both—for the book that they composed against Elipandus of Toledo bears the names of both—in Book I: “It is not,” they say, “that the soul is one substance and the spirit another, as the soul is one substance and the flesh another; rather, the soul itself is one and the same spirit. But when a man afflicts the outward flesh through repentance, according to the Apostle (2 Corinthians 4:16), the inner soul is renewed day by day in the knowledge of God. And after it has come to know God, it is called spirit, that is, God’s contemplative servant, because it contemplates God: through the contemplative life it sees God, not in the body but in the mind. The mind is related to the soul as the head is to the body. The spirit is related to the mind as the eyes are to the head.” Paulinus likewise understands the contemplative inner man by “spirit,” when below he says: “This is the inner man, in whom Christ is believed to dwell; he retains himself inwardly through the grace of contemplation.”]—spirit, soul, and body. Is the spirit one thing and the soul another? He did not distinguish substances, but dignity. For he wants the spiritual soul and the spiritual body to be preserved at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. In this [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil lacks *hoc* (“this”).] spiritual man, who is also called the inner man, the same wondrous teacher professes that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts. For there is an animal man and there is a spiritual man—not according to substance, but according to the quality of merit. The animal man is so called from *anima* (“soul”), and the spiritual man from *spiritus* (“spirit”); in the same way that the same truthful teacher [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil has *liquidius* (“more clearly”) rather than *veridicus* (“truthful”).] clearly distinguished one from the other. “The animal man,” he says, “does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:14). This is the outer man, who pours himself outward toward the desire for external things. But the spiritual man judges all things—that is, he discerns them—and he himself is judged by no one. This, I say, is the inner man, in whom Christ is believed to dwell; he retains himself inwardly through the grace of contemplation and, nourished by the sweetness of inward refreshment, gently rests in the love of his Creator.

[Note: [Col. 0179B] “Hence our forefathers, this definition having been established.” Whatever has been established by authority is thereafter regarded as sacred. Our Paulinus says: “Hence our forefathers, this definition having been established—for whose most discerning and capacious childhood lies very far from the inertia of our sluggishness—it pleased them, with the Holy Spirit consenting, to profess without hesitation two natures in the one person of Christ.” You see how badly this most truthful statement concerning the doctrine of the former Fathers has been received. I think it should instead be written: “Hence our forefathers, this definition having been established—for whose most discerning expertise of understanding lies far and very far from the indolence of our sluggishness—it pleased them, with the Holy Spirit consenting,” and so forth. He praises three qualities in the ancient Fathers in a well-ordered manner: discernment, capacity, and expertise, which is acquired through diligence, so that in every respect he makes them greater than those of his own age. [Col. 0179C] Capacity is understanding. Claudianus Mamertus, Book I, chapter 14: “Both desire the same thing with the same will, that is, with the same spirit. Both apprehend this same thing with incorporeal capacity.” Victorinus the martyr, on the Apocalypse: “But, so far as the capacity of my understanding perceives what is being stated, since the number ten signifies the Decalogue, the number one hundred displays the crown of virginity.” BARTHIUS.]

### XII

Having thus made these preliminary observations [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil has *ita* (“thus”) rather than *itaque* (“therefore”).], let us return to what we left aside. I ask you, then, to tell me in which nature Christ Jesus, the man who is the mediator between God and human beings, deigned to hunger, thirst, and feel the pains of suffering. Why do you hesitate? You cannot deny it. It is better for you to profess that he did so according to the human nature [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil lacks *est*. Hardouin notes in the margin of Labbé that the manuscript lacks the words *melius est ut profitearis* (“it is better for you to profess”).]. For the divine nature always remains impassible, inviolable, and unchangeable [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil lacks *et*.]. It is true—entirely true—that this occurred in the human nature. I therefore want you to define more clearly what human nature is: flesh alone, soul alone, or both together, soul and flesh? For we can neither do so nor may we contradict the truth: human nature consists nonetheless of both, namely of soul and flesh. Tell me, then: did he bear the wounds of suffering in flesh alone, in soul alone, or—in the truer account—in both? Flesh without the soul feels nothing; for the soul without flesh does not hunger or thirst, nor can it be crucified, and yet it was crucified through the flesh. For he was crucified in the palms of his hands and at the extremities of his feet [Note: [Col. 0163D] Aguirre has *externis* (“outer”) rather than *extremis* (“extreme”).]. If it was not crucified together with the flesh, why did it feel pain? For flesh, as has been said, feels nothing without the soul. But if the soul feels [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil has *sensit* (“felt”) rather than *sentit* (“feels”).] pain through its relationship with the flesh, and the flesh suffers pain through the soul when it is cut, then neither flesh without the soul nor soul without the flesh can properly be called complete human nature [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil has *enim* (“for”) rather than *ergo* (“therefore”).] [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil has *Dei* (“of God”) rather than *plena* (“complete”), apparently incorrectly.]. For complete human nature consists in the connection of both, namely flesh and soul. Hence our forefathers, this definition having been established, whose most discerning expertise of understanding lies very far from the indolence of our sluggishness [Note: [Col. 0163D] Basil has *pueritia* (“childhood”), incorrectly, rather than *peritia* (“expertise”).], it pleased them, with the Holy Spirit consenting, to profess without hesitation two natures in the one person of Christ, namely divine and human; for soul and flesh are not two, but one man. He confesses the Son of God as God and man [Note: [Col. 0164D] Basil has *Dominum* (“Lord”) rather than *Deum* (“God”).] [Note: [Col. 0164D] Basil has *confitemur* (“we confess”), which appears more correct, rather than *confitetur* (“he confesses”).]. “The mediator,” says the Apostle, “between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5), who, from soul and flesh, is called not two, but one man.

### XIII

Let all the superfluous inventions of those who mutter now cease [Note: [Col. 0179C] “The inventions of those who mutter.” *Mussitare* is a frequentative formed from *mussare*. “*Mussare*,” Varro says in Book VI of *On the Latin Language*, “was so called because mute people say no more than *mu* [μῦ]; hence the same poet—Ennius—says: ‘Which is least, and which, as they say, he dares not even *mu*.’” Festus, under the letter M, quoting Ennius: “*Mussare*, to murmur. Ennius: ‘They were muttering in secret.’” In ordinary usage it means “to be silent,” as the same Ennius says: “It is not fitting for good men to be silent.” But Nonius, in *On Different Expressions*, says: “*Mussare* and *murmurare* are distinguished in that *mussare* applies to people speaking secretly and in a restrained voice, who wish something to remain concealed. Virgil, in Book X of the *Aeneid*: ‘What fortune may bring the people, they mutter to say.’ And elsewhere: ‘The sorrowful fathers weep … and mutter.’ *Murmurare*, however, is louder, approaching tumult. Virgil, in Book I of the *Georgics*: ‘The murmur of the groves grows frequent.’ [Col. 0179D] Such a sound is attributed to pythonesses, ventriloquists, and all kinds of sorcerers. Isaiah 29:4: ‘And your voice shall be like that of a python from the earth, and your speech shall mutter from the ground.’ Coelius Rhodiginus, Book VII, chapter 10, testifies that in his own time ‘there was at Rodigium a certain little woman named Jacoba, from whose belly he himself and countless others heard an exceedingly thin voice, yet one articulated and entirely intelligible whenever she wished.’ Thus poets, whenever they deal with sorceresses and diviners, almost always present the thinness of the voice and mention muttering. Virgil, *Aeneid* III.92: ‘And the prophetic tripod roars when the sanctuary is opened.’ And Book VI.492: ‘part of them to raise a faint voice.’ Ovid, *Fasti* V.456: ‘The bloody ghost of Remus seemed to stand beside the bed; and with a faint murmur to speak these words.’ But that the voices of ventriloquists, which are said to mutter, were sometimes natural and not always produced by the agency of an evil demon is shown at length by P. Augustine Calmet in his commentary on verse 7 of chapter 28 of Book I of Kings; consult it if you wish. Nor did this escape the notice of the ancients, among whom Hippocrates calls such people *engastrimythoi* (ἐγγαστρίμυθοι, “ventriloquists”). Galen, in *Explanations of the Terms Used by Hippocrates*, says: “These are people who speak with their mouths closed, because they seem to emit their voice from the belly.” Paulinus therefore quite appropriately called the voices of heretics who secretly pour forth their doctrines “the inventions of those who mutter.”]

—the calumniating objections of querulous questions, which have no relevance to the matter but rather serve to subvert the simple. Let us not be led astray by various and foreign doctrines, but let us confess with our holy Catholic and orthodox Fathers, who both received the right faith in their hearts and taught it salutarily to the sons of the Church with an inviolable mouth [Note: [Col. 0180B] “The sons of the Church.” The sons of an art or of some science are those who are, as it were, its household members and acquainted with its secrets, being devoted to it with exceptional zeal. Thus *paides iatrōn* (παῖδες ἰατρῶν, “sons of physicians”) are the disciples of Hippocrates who devoted themselves exclusively to that science. These are the people whom he himself calls *mathētēs syngamēmenous kai ōrkismenous nomō iētrikō* (μαθητὰς συγγεγραμμένους καὶ ὠρκισμένους νόμῳ ἰατρικῷ, “disciples bound by writing and sworn according to medical law”) in the Oath. Thus our most learned bishop called them “sons of the Church.” BARTHIUS.], namely, two natures in Christ, divine and human, true God and true man; in both, the proper Son of God, not an adopted son; eternal from the Father [Note: [Col. 0180B] “Eternal from the Father.” Barthius, who follows the Basileian reading *sed sempiterno* (“but eternal”), says: “*Sempiterno* marks this writer as existing before all ages and from eternity.” So he says.

“But Junianus Majus says that *sempiterne* properly signifies continuation, which does not strictly correspond to the eternity of God, which is not by continuation but is wholly simultaneous and an everlasting instant. Nevertheless, besides Paulinus, we have other authors who used this word to signify eternity. Claudianus Mamertus, Book I of *On the State of the Soul*, chapter 3: ‘But because the Divinity knew Christ’s passion eternally—for it had itself ordained it—nothing new for it to know, much less to feel, was added at the time of the passion.’ And below, in the same chapter, he takes *sempiternitas* in the sense of eternity: ‘For immutable and abiding eternity,’ he says, ‘encloses everything temporal, mobile, and changeable.’” [Col. 0180C]]

[Note: [Col. 0164D] Basil has *sed sempiterno ex Patre* (“but eternal from the Father”). So also Barthius; see the note.] born temporally from a virgin mother; consubstantial with God the Father and the Holy Spirit in his own nature, and also consubstantial with us in ours. We say “ours” with respect to the condition of the flesh, not with respect to participation in sin or misery. For he committed no sin, but bore what belonged to another, and no deceit was found in his mouth; rather, he himself bore our pains [Note: [Col. 0164D] Aguirre has *dolos* (“deceits”) rather than *dolores* (“pains”).], was wounded for our iniquities, and was crushed for our crimes: “the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed” (1 Peter 2:22 and Isaiah 53:9). But we judge that all the perverse doctrines of heretics, together with their authors and adherents, are to be struck with eternal anathema. For Elipandus and Felix, new enemies of the Church but polluted with the rancid dregs of perfidy [Note: [Col. 0164D] Basil has *fere perfidia* (“almost perfidy”). So also Barthius; see the note.] [Note: [Col. 0180C] “With the rancid dregs of perfidy.” Barthius, reading *veternosum* instead of *faece*, as in the Basileian manuscript, notes that *veternosus* means “old, ancient, aged, already rancid with age.” Papias, in his *Glossary*: “*Veternosus*, old, aged, full of years.” So also Sidonius, Book I, Letter 1, where see the notes of the most learned interpreters. In this way Barthius has grasped Paulinus’s meaning.

“But *veternosus* is one who is oppressed by deep sleep,” says Festus; and this is the proper meaning, strictly speaking. Terence, however, uses the word in a not dissimilar sense in the *Eunuch*, line 687, Act IV, Scene 9:

‘Here is an old, withered, somnolent old man.’

Donatus explains: ‘*Veternosus*, worn out by an old illness.’ Another scholiast, Peter Marsus, explains it more clearly: ‘*Veternosus* is one who suffers from illness and the infirmity of old age.’ I am convinced that Paulinus used it in the sense of ‘old,’ both because of the antithesis he establishes—‘new enemies, polluted by old perfidy’—and because the Adoptianists seemed to be restoring Nestorianism, which had already been abolished, as will be shown in the dogmatic dissertation on the heresy of Felix and Elipandus.”] [Col. 0180D] [Col. 0164C]—unless they recover from this folly and cleanse themselves through satisfaction to the true faith and through the lamentations of repentance, we decree that they be eliminated from the fellowship of Catholics by perpetual punishment as unworthy and ungrateful, and we judge them alien from the bosom of the orthodox Church [Note: [Col. 0164D] Basil has: “I decree, and I judge them alien from the bosom of the holy mother Church.”] [Note: [Col. 0164D] In Basil this entire sentence is absent, up to “Those also.”]. Nevertheless, with all the effort of our minds, we desire—and we implore the clemency of the good shepherd of immense compassion, who laid down his life for his sheep and wills that no one perish—that, abandoning the error of perfidy, they may return to the way of truth, which is Christ, with Christ himself leading them; so that, received into the bosom of Mother Church in the embrace of love, they may rest peacefully and gently in the tranquility of faith, nourished by the most abundant breasts of God’s goodness, and through this, by the grace of God who tasted death for all, may attain the joys of perpetual happiness without end.

We also decree that those who, after this most salutary definition, which a plenary synod, inspired by the Holy Spirit, unanimously and with subtle sincerity brought to a conclusion [Note: [Col. 0180D] “A plenary synod … brought to a conclusion.” Here *terminare* means “to define.” Cicero likewise uses it in *On Ends*, Book I: “Epicurus thinks the highest pleasure is bounded by the complete absence of pain.” A synod is called plenary either because the matters under discussion were defined by the votes of all the bishops present—for in law *plenary* means something that needs no addition, as Pererius says in the *Elucidarium*—or because it was an assembly of a great many bishops. There were, in fact, “about three hundred, so that it could be called the universal council of the whole West,” says G. Cave at the end of the eighth century. The great number of participants, or the fullness of the constitutions, was at that time called by the name of plenitude. In Volume I of the *Capitularies*, Appendix II, chapter 28, near the end: “Since we had neither leisure nor time nor the plenitude of our fellow priests, we postponed consideration of these matters. And in Volume II of the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, in the year 846, title VII, at Sparnacum: ‘The fullness of the capitularies contained in the fullness of synodal proceedings is set out in this way in the several places.’”] [Col. 0181A] and who have given assent to their utterly false assertions, whether secretly or publicly, should be punished by a similar sentence, while in every respect preserving the legal privilege of the supreme pontiff, our lord and Father Adrian, the most blessed pope of the first see [Note: [Col. 0181A] “While in every respect preserving the legal privilege of the supreme pontiff.” Although Theophylact and Stephen, legates of Pope Adrian, were present at the Council of Frankfurt, Paulinus nevertheless sought the authority of the Roman See and the pope in order to give validity and force to the council’s definitions. For the Church and the council are not above the pontiff; rather, the pontiff is above the council and the Church—just as the members are not above the head, nor the sheep above the shepherd, nor the bride above the bridegroom, but the head is placed above the members, the shepherd above the flock, and the bridegroom above the bride. Hear only what Pope Damasus says, together with Valerian, whom we believe to have been bishop of Aquileia, and the other advocates of the Roman bishop in the case of Auxentius; in their name a letter was sent from the Second Roman Council to the Catholic bishops established throughout the East. When they brought forward the number of bishops assembled at Rimini against the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, the pope replied: “No prejudice could arise from the number of those who assembled at Rimini, since it is established that neither the Roman bishop—whose judgment above all others ought to have been sought—nor … gave any assent to such decrees.” Sozomen also mentions this event and letter in Book VI, chapter 23.] [Note: [Col. 0181C] “According to the evangelical, apostolic, and canonical rules.” Paulinus invokes rules drawn from the Gospel and the Apostle that forbid clerics, at least indirectly, to take up arms. Add what the Lord said to Peter in Matthew 26:52: “Put your sword back into its place.” From this passage Saint Thomas argues in *Summa*, II–II, question 40, article 2: “To Peter, in the person of bishops and clerics, it is said in Matthew 26: ‘Put it back,’ and so it is not permitted for them to fight.” Saint Bernard likewise wrote to Pope Eugenius in Book IV of *On Consideration*: “Why do you again attempt to usurp the sword which you were once commanded to put into its sheath?” Among canonical decrees forbidding clerics to bear arms, which Gratian includes in Decree II, 23, question 8, the notable one is that of the Second Council of Toledo, chapter 45, under King Sisenand, concerning clerics who have taken up arms: those found guilty in this matter are to be deprived of their rank and handed over to a monastery for penance. Some editions read: “let them be handed over perpetually to penance.” The Council of Meaux, chapter 37, calls clerics who bear arms despisers of the canons. It says: “Let no one who appears to belong to the clergy take up military arms, nor let him walk armed … But if they despise this, let them be punished by the loss of their rank as despisers of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical holiness, because they cannot serve both God and the world.” This council, held in the year 845, seems to have drawn its arguments from the final words of the reasoning given by Paulinus, who said: “Let no one flatter himself that he can serve both God and the world.”] [Note: [Col. 0182B] “He must be entreated.” Barthius: “To entreat someone is a phrase used by authors of this kind.” So he says.

“And rightly so. For among the Latins it is used with the dative, as is well known. Among authors of Late Latin it has a particular meaning: to incline oneself toward someone out of respect. The Cistercian *Ancient Usages*, chapter 71, in Ducange under *supplicare*: ‘When they walk, let them proceed humbly, and with uncovered heads, bowing to one another as they meet. But if they meet the abbot, let them turn aside, bowing to him.’ The Latins also used it for ‘to adore.’ Suetonius, in his account of Augustus, chapter 93: ‘He highly praised his grandson Gaius because, passing through Judaea near Jerusalem, he had not bowed in worship.’”]

[Note: [Col. 0182C] “A reciprocal recompense.” Barthius: “That is reciprocal which is rendered in turn. If we pursue such matters too diligently, I should like to know whether our critics would then say that we had been idle; yet they themselves are inelegantly occupied when they summon our playful exercises to serious examination.” Thus Barthius concludes. See also what we have noted in the letter of the Council of Altinum, numbers 37 and 38.]

### XIV

But we, lords and most beloved brothers, following the sound doctrine of the preceding Fathers [Note: [Col. 0165C] Basil adds “of the faith.”], rejecting in every respect the ravings of foolish men, let us believe in our hearts unto righteousness and confess with our mouths unto salvation our Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God, not a merely supposed one; his proper Son in both natures [Note: [Col. 0165C] Basil lacks “in both natures.”], not an adopted son; equal and coeternal with the Father and the Holy Spirit. May he preserve his Church, acquired with his own blood, spotless and immaculate, without stain or wrinkle, and preserve our hearts with unimpaired authority in the purity of the true faith.

May the almighty and holy Trinity, through the intercessions of the blessed and glorious Mary, ever-virgin, Mother of God—through whom we were deemed worthy to receive the author of life—and of blessed Peter, the first shepherd of the Church, and of all the saints, and also through your prayers offered on our behalf, surround the Catholic, most merciful, and ever-renowned lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0165C] Basil and Aguirre have *Dominum* (“Lord”) rather than *domnum* (“lord”).] with its grace, and may it always protect and defend him with its right hand [Note: [Col. 0165C] Basil omits “and may it always protect him with its right hand.”], so that he may always do what pleases it, and so that [Note: [Col. 0166C] Basil has *et quatenus* (“and so that”).], relying on heavenly arms and supported by aid from heaven, he may cast down from heaven to earth the enemies of Christ’s name. May almighty God subject the barbarian nations to his boundless power and dominion, so that through this opportunity they may come to knowledge of the truth and recognize their true and living God, their Creator. Having been reborn in the water of baptism [Note: [Col. 0166C] Basil lacks *siquidem* (“indeed”).], may they be gathered into the bosom of Mother Church, so that what the good shepherd promised may be fulfilled when he said: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, so that [sic] there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

May peace multiply in his days, so that the holy Church may be free and secure from every disturbance of the world, with that freedom by which Christ liberated her. May the priests of the Lord be permitted, according to the evangelical, apostolic, and canonical rules, to serve the Lord simply and to serve in the Lord’s camps alone; for according to the same Lord’s word, “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24). And Paul says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2:4). Let no one flatter himself that he can serve both God and the world, because the one who testifies that this cannot be done is truth itself and cannot lie.

Hence our most tranquil prince must be entreated to fight for us against visible enemies for the love of Christ, with the Lord’s help; and we, praying for the Lord’s power, must fight for him against invisible enemies with spiritual arms, so that on that day the Son of God may render him a reciprocal recompense for his Church; so that, just as he now makes her secure amid so many worldly disturbances [Note: [Col. 0166C] Basil has *illam nunc eis* (“makes her secure for them”).], she may in turn make him a participant in the heavenly kingdom [Note: [Col. 0166C] Basil has a feminine plural form, “they,” rather than “she.”]. May he, in compassion, pardon captives; may he aid the oppressed; may he loosen the bundles that weigh them down; may he be the consolation of widows and the refreshment of the wretched; may he be lord and father, king and priest, the most moderate governor of all Christians, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0181]

## 15. LETTER OF SAINT PAULINUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA, TO HEISTULFUS

From a manuscript of Reims, collated with chapter 40 of Book VI of the *Decrees* of Burchard, bishop of the Church of Worms.

[Note: [Col. 0185]

## NOTES ON THE LETTER TO HEISTULFUS

### Preface

[Col. 0185C] This letter is not by Pope Stephen V, as Gratian says in Decree II, 33, question 2, chapter *Admonere*, but by Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia. Gratian, who is frequently mistaken in other matters, is mistaken here as well. This is also asserted by Burchard, who is older than Gratian, and indeed by Ivo himself, the collector of canons. We learned this from the observation placed at the foot of this canon in Pithou’s edition of Gratian, as well as from the note placed by Pithou at the beginning, where he says: “Rather, Paulinus, bishop of Forojulium, to Heistulfus, in Germany, in the year 794.” Morinus also noticed this, *On the Sacrament of Penance*, Book VII, chapter 7, number 10.

The Labbean edition of the Councils likewise recognizes Paulinus as the author from a manuscript of Reims, and says that the letter was issued from the Council of Frankfurt, convened against the heresy of Felix, so that there is no longer any room for doubt on this matter. This is the judgment concerning wife-killers that Hincmar, bishop of Reims, calls “the judgment of Paulinus,” and which Vulfadus, archbishop of Bourges, asked to have sent to him. Flodoard bears witness to this in his *History of Reims*, Book III, chapter 21, where he lists the distinguished men with whom Hincmar maintained an exchange of letters: “To Vulfadus,” he says, “archbishop of Bourges, concerning those who rashly kill their wives, he wrote the judgment of Paulinus, which Vulfadus had requested to be sent to him.”

This Vulfadus was the man whose ordination Hincmar rejected because it had been performed by Ebo, formerly archbishop of Reims but later deposed. Nevertheless, several Gallican councils, including the Third Council of Soissons and the Council of Troyes, approved it, as did Popes Nicholas I and Adrian II. Adrian also confirmed Vulfadus’s election as archbishop of Bourges, although the matter had not yet been fully settled by Charles the Bald. Yet this exchange of letters sufficiently proves that there was no personal hostility between them, and that their disagreement concerned opinion, not the heart; judgment, not the will.

Vulfadus wisely sought from Hincmar the judgment of Paulinus concerning wife-killers. For at that time no one surpassed Hincmar in knowledge of the sacred canons, and no one was regarded as more learned in deciding matrimonial controversies, as the single case of the divorce of Lothair and Teutberga plainly demonstrates. Thus, whatever difficulties might arise day by day in questions of law and fact, and whatever ought to be strengthened or weakened by the teaching of the ancient canons and by examples from past events, Vulfadus rightly and properly judged that he should seek from the most learned and experienced Hincmar.

Since the Glossator, as is his custom, attempts to illuminate this chapter in the Decrees, we have thought it best to provide his gloss. But because the letter is filled with passages of exceptional learning, we have judged that it should not be treated lightly, but illuminated, as occasion required, with more extensive notes, asking the reader to judge our efforts fairly and kindly. [Col. 0186D]

Here begins the letter of Paulinus, patriarch of Forojulium, issued at the celebrated place called Frankfurt, in the great synod against Felix the heretic, concerning Heistulfus, who killed his wife on account of adultery on the testimony of a single witness.

[Col. 0181D] [Note: [Col. 0186D]

“Admonere.” Gloss: Hugh presents the case as follows: “This Heistulfus killed his wife and, after her death, accused her of adultery, wishing to show that the sons he had had by her were illegitimate and therefore unworthy of their father’s succession. To support this excuse he produced a single witness, himself a murderer and an adulterer.

“First, therefore, the pope rebukes him for the death of his wife. Then he censures him on three grounds: namely, because he accused her after her death; because he did so through a single witness; and because that witness was disqualified and criminal. Afterwards he shows him what penance he ought to perform, and leaves him the choice—perhaps *option* rather than *opinion*—of whether he wishes to do penance in a monastery or outside it. Thus far the Gloss.”]

17. The Glossator proceeds and, following Gratian in good faith, asserts that the author of the letter was Pope Stephen V [Col. 0187A], who nevertheless lived twelve years and more after Paulinus; for he held the see from the year 816 to the year 817, for seven months. But apart from what we stated above in the preface, it is sufficiently clear that Gratian’s authority is unreliable from other spurious decretals as well, and especially from the one he attributes to that pontiff in *Decretum*, C. 63, c. *Quia sancta*. There it is asserted that, in the election of the Roman pontiff, the emperor’s approval—or rather his personal presence or that of his legates—ought to be taken into account. Our Baronius, under the year 816, no. 101, detected its falsity from other such fabricated decretals inserted here and there by Gratian without discrimination, especially from the two immediately following: *Cum Adrianus* and *Ego Ludovicus*. These demonstrate not only that the decree *Quia sancta* was never put into practice, but also that the Romans always enjoyed a free election of their pontiff, which did not depend upon the emperor’s discretion.

This is confirmed by the authority of Master Florus, deacon of the Church of Lyons. According to N. Alexander in *Synopsis historiae ecclesiasticae*, ninth and tenth centuries, chapter 1, article 3, Florus wrote around the year 820; and in his little book *On the Election of Bishops*, no. 6, he says:

> “In the Roman Church, down to the present day, we see that pontiffs are consecrated legitimately without inquiry of the ruler, solely by the judgment of divine disposition”—which de Marca, *Concordia sacerdotii et imperii*, book VIII, chapter 12, thinks should be added—“and by the suffrage of the faithful. And in no. 7 and following he says: ‘Therefore, although the sacred canons of the Fathers mention very many circumstances without which episcopal ordination is to be considered invalid, nothing is found inserted on this matter”—namely, the ruler’s intervention in electing the pontiff—“at all.’”

If the decree *Quia sancta* had been issued by Stephen only three years earlier, how could a canon of such recent origin have remained unknown to Florus, so that he could assert absolutely that nothing concerning this matter had been inserted in the canons of the Fathers down to his own time? The decree *Quia sancta*, therefore, is spurious and was falsely attributed to Stephen V. It is consequently unsurprising that the chapter *Admonere*, which is Paulinus’s, should likewise have been falsely attributed to that same Stephen.]

I had taken care to admonish you, with tears and much anguish of heart [Col. 0181D]—“we take care,” so Gratian reads—my son [Col. 0187C] Heistulf.

[Note: I would not dare assert who this man was. If it is permissible to conjecture, the name appears to be Lombard. For many names ending in this way are commonly found among that people: Marculfus, Landulfus, Rodulfus, Gisulfus, and similar names, which one cannot doubt were brought into Italy by northern peoples. One of Pemon’s sons, duke of Friuli, who preceded Desiderius in the Lombard kingdom, was called by this name; he greatly disturbed the period of Pope Stephen III by wars and disasters. See Baronius under the year 752 and following years; under the year 756 he records that Heistulf was removed from the living. But at about this same period one also finds another man named Heistulf in the succession of the bishops of Mainz. He is first mentioned in the capitulary of Tribur, in the year 822, at Theodonis Villa.]

Heistulf [Col. 0182D]—“Hastulf,” and so Gratian also reads—if indeed [Col. 0187C] you ought to be called a son,

[Note: “To be called a son.” The Glossator of Argenton says that he may be deprived of the name on account of his crime, according to the verse: “If you are deprived in fact, you deserve not even to have the name,” *art.* 13, q. 2, after *postquam*; also 2, q. 7, § *Quibus ergo*; 2, q. 1, *Scelus*; and *Codex*, *Defer a nullo*. Argument to the contrary: *De poenitentia*, dist. 4, *Si ex bono*, since those who were not in the Church are called sons of God. Thus the Gloss.]

Yet literally: because those who fall away from grace, according to their present state, are not called sons of God by grace, Paulinus therefore says that the homicide ought not to be called a son, as Gratian reads; or, “if you ought to be called a son,” in the form of a question, as Labbé and Pithou read. This formula, however, is sometimes used for an absolute denial or assertion, as will be clear below at the words, “if perhaps the infinite goodness of God may forgive.”]

you ought to be called a son, who have perpetrated so cruel and wretched a homicide. For you killed your wife, a part [Col. 0187D]

[Note: “A part of your body.” The Glossator gives something similar above, 31, q. 2, *De neptis*, and 27, q. 2, *Agathosa*. The argument is that one who withholds provisions from himself seems to withhold them from his wife, since the two are one body, and likewise from his children and servants; compare 50, dist. *Stud eat*, and *Digest*, *De usu et habitatione*, book 2. Thus the Gloss.]

of your body, lawfully joined to you in marriage, without cause of death and not resisting you [Col. 0183A],

[Note: “Not resisting, not lying in wait.” The Glossator supplies “especially,” since even if she had resisted or plotted against him, he would not on that account have been permitted to kill her. No argument should be drawn here from the contrary sense because of chapter 32, q. 5, *Quidquid*. Thus the Gloss.

Paulinus defends the woman on two grounds: both because she did not resist and because she did not plot against her husband. He does not use “resisting” in a sense that excludes resistance or force by which someone repels an attack—so that, if a husband attacked his wife and threatened her with death, she would in no way resist him with movements, kicks, blows, or the effort of her arms. It is entirely natural in such circumstances to protect a life placed in sudden danger. What advantage, moreover, would a woman gain from such resistance, since compared with a man she is generally not only softer but also weaker? Understand “not resisting,” therefore, as meaning not obstinate or quarrelsome, but obedient and accommodating toward her husband. By this word he excludes the woman from the number of those about whom that Terentian Gnatheo in the *Eunuch*, act IV, scene 7, verse 680, said:

> “I know the nature of women:
>
> They do not want what you want; when you do not want something, they desire it spontaneously.”

And the Satirist says, *Satires* VI, verse 242:

> “There is scarcely any case in which a woman has not
>
> stirred up a lawsuit . . .”

Hence Varius Geminus, praised by Saint Jerome in book I *Against Jovinianus*, used to say: “A bachelor is one who does not quarrel.” Paulinus also protects the woman from another accusation commonly brought against women—namely, that they plot against their husbands when they are seized by an illicit love. Saint John Chrysostom noticed this, *Homily* 49 on Matthew:

> “Such a thing is certainly lust; it makes people not merely wanton but also murderous. Nor should one doubt that women eager for adultery are prepared and armed for the slaughter of their husbands, against whom they are planning to commit an injury.”

Since this woman was neither an adulteress nor a plotter, she must accordingly be believed innocent.]

and not plotting in any way against your life [Col. 0183D]—“in any way,” and so Gratian also reads. You did not find her committing that abominable act with another man; but, stirred up by the devil and inflamed by impious fury, in the manner of a brigand you slaughtered her with your sword, more cruelly than any wild beast [“more atrocious and more cruel than any wild beast, you killed her with your sword,” according to Labbé].

And now, after her death, you add iniquity to iniquity, you shameless robber of your sons [Col. 0188D],

[Note: “Shameless robber.” The Glossator does not mean that he could deprive them of their rights. Even if a wife is killed on account of adultery, her dowry nevertheless passes to her children, according to *Authentic*, *Ut liberi matris et aviae*, § *Si de adulterio*. But you are attempting to deprive them of their mother’s comfort and protection. Although as a rule a husband profits from the dowry on account of his wife’s adultery, according to *De dote inter virum et uxorem*, chapter *Plerumque*, he does not profit from it in this case when he kills her, even if he had previously made an agreement that he would receive it; *Digest*, *Soluto matrimonio*, *Si ab hostibus*, § 3. Thus the Gloss.]

who did not spare their mother, and therefore [Col. 0183D]—“and your sons,” according to Gratian—made your sons orphans [Col. 0189A],

[Note: “You made your sons orphans.” Properly speaking, an orphan is one who lacks a father and paternal protection. Paulinus therefore seems not to have used the word strictly when he called children whose father had not died orphans. Yet apart from the fact that the word is not always taken strictly in law, and that in the law *Orphanotrophos*, *Codex*, *De episcopis et clericis*, orphans are called not specifically those lacking a father but those deprived of their parents, Heistulf’s sons were not improperly called orphans, since they were also destined to be deprived of their father. By his inhumanity he had himself departed from nature and the law of blood; what paternal duty or affection, therefore, could sons have expected from such a man, who had removed from himself and his children a part of himself—namely, his wife and, in relation to them, their mother—more cruelly than any wild beast, as Paulinus said?

If he himself, whether driven by the bite of conscience or punished by a judge with exile, had withdrawn from his country and home as an outcast and fugitive, would he not have deprived his sons of paternal comfort and protection, and truly and properly made them orphans? From the context this seems to have been Paulinus’s meaning. “You did not spare their mother,” he says, “and you made your sons orphans.” To indicate the children’s maternal bereavement, it would indeed have been sufficient to say, “you did not spare their mother.” By adding, “and you made your sons orphans,” he indicates that they would also be deprived of their father.]

you wish to impose upon her a cause of death after her death [Col. 0189B].

[Note: “You wish to impose upon her a cause of death after her death.” Since crimes are extinguished by death, 23, dist. *Quorundam*; *Codex*, *Si reus vel accusatus*, law 1; unless someone wishes to bring an action on account of property, *Codex*, the same title, final law; *Codex*, *Si pendente appellatione mors interveniat*, law 2; and *Digest*, *De rei vendicatione*. Thus the Gloss.

Paulinus accuses Heistulf of impiety because he was harassing the dead woman’s spirit by charging her with an unspeakable crime, adultery, when she could no longer defend herself or plead her case. This is a monstrous deed and a form of impiety that all nations especially abhor; for, as Horace says, *Epistles* I, 17, verse 79, death is “the final boundary of things,” and therefore closes every judgment. Here Arnobius’s statement in book I *Against the Nations* is more appropriate:

> “No innocent person ever unjustly killed is infamous, nor is he stained by the mark of any disgrace, because he suffers severe punishment not for his own merit but through the cruelty of his torturer.”]

through one homicidal and disreputable witness [Col. 0183D]—“you accuse the dead woman through a witness,” according to Gratian—although [Col. 0183D] neither according to the Gospel [Col. 0189C]

[Note: “Although neither according to the Gospel nor any divine or human law does anyone condemn or acquit a person even on the testimony of one suitable witness.” Hence the rule in 21, q. 1, *Quicunque* does not hold. Yet one person may be believed as a narrator or as an associate, as in 8, q. 3, and 86, dist. *Tanta*. Thus the Gloss.

Paulinus accuses Heistulf on two grounds: that he believed a single witness and that he believed a criminal. As to the first, he says that neither the Gospel nor any divine or human law accepts the testimony of one person alone. From the Gospel we have the Lord’s instruction in Matthew 18:16, given concerning fraternal correction: “If he does not listen to you, take with you one or two more, so that every word may stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses.” The Lord referred to Deuteronomy 17:6: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses shall he be put to death who is to be killed.” Let no one be killed on the testimony of one person speaking against him. But he referred especially to Deuteronomy 19:15: “One witness shall not stand against anyone, whatever the sin or crime may be; but every word shall stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses.”

The human statutes of the emperors agree with the Gospel and the divine law and altogether exclude a single witness. *Codex*, *De testibus*, law *Jusjurandi*, the constitution of Constantine to Julian, says:

> “We have enacted that no judge in any case should readily admit the testimony of one person; and now we expressly decree that the statement of one witness is not to be heard at all, even if he is distinguished by the honor of high office.”

The jurists likewise pronounce the same. Ulpian, *Digest*, *De quaestionibus*, law 1, says concerning criminal cases:

> “The truth of the matter is certainly not to be established by the examination of a single slave.”

And Paulus, in the same title, law 20, *Maritus*, adds more clearly:

> “The testimony of one man ought not to be admitted.” [Col. 0190A]

Hence the proverb mentioned by Rhodiginus, book VII, chapter 22: “Not even Cato should be believed on the testimony of one witness.” Therefore Q. Mucius Scaevola is highly praised by Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 1, example 11, because he would not allow even himself to be believed unless another witness were present:

> “For,” he said, “to believe someone on the testimony of one person would be a most pernicious example.”

If, then, the testimony of both a human being and a single person is weak, as Minucius said at the end of his *Octavius*, how much weaker will be the testimony of one scoundrel and a man of condemned character? Paulinus therefore rightly added with force:

> “How much more, through this most disgraceful and most wicked man, ought she neither while alive to have been condemned, nor, and so forth.”

The Twelve Tables contain these words: *Improbus intestabilisque esto*—“Let him be dishonorable and incapable of giving testimony”—that is, if he is dishonorable, he is *intestabilis*, unable to testify. Gellius, *Attic Nights* VI, 7, shows that the word must be understood in this sense when he says concerning the Vestal Tarratia:

> “The right of giving testimony is also granted to Tarratia, and she is permitted to be *testabilis*, capable of giving testimony, as the only one among all women. This is the word of the Horatian law. Its opposite is written in the Twelve Tables: ‘Let him be dishonorable and incapable of giving testimony.’”

Hence Cicero, in his speech *For M. Fonteius*, rightly addressed and instructed his judges as follows:

> “Therefore, judges, you not only may but also ought not to believe witnesses who are eager, angry, conspiratorial, and removed from religious scruple.”

For the conditions of integrity and blameless life required by Callistratus in legitimate witnesses, see *Digest*, *De testibus*, law *Testium*, and Budaeus there. Add that this man, notoriously disgraced by the particular stigma of adultery, ought altogether to have been barred from giving testimony. Those condemned for adultery have no right to give testimony in contracts or wills, as Harmenopulus says in book I, chapter 1, citing Johannes Calvinus under the word *Testatores*:

> “A person condemned for adultery who gives testimony in a will . . .”

The Greek reads: **Ὁ καταδικαθεὶς ἐπὶ μοιχεία ὁ μαρτυρεῖ ἐν διαθήκῃ**—“He who has been condemned for adultery gives testimony in a will.”]

nor does any divine or human law condemn or acquit anyone on the testimony of a single person, even if suitable [Col. 0183D]—“suitable,” according to Gratian—[“you wish to accuse the dead woman. Neither does the Gospel permit this, nor any divine or human law permit anyone to be condemned or acquitted on the testimony of one person, even if suitable,” in the same place, Col. 0183B].

How much more, through this most shameful and so utterly wicked man [Col. 0183D]—“and criminal,” according to Gratian—ought she neither while alive to have been condemned, nor could you be excused [Col. 0183D] after her death—“nor accused by you after her death,” according to Gratian. First the truth of the case ought to have been carefully investigated [Col. 0183D]—“carefully investigated,” according to Gratian—and then, if she had been found guilty [Col. 0183D]—“if that had been the case,” according to Gratian—she ought, according to the course of law, to have received the punishment of vengeance [Col. 0183D]—“to have received,” according to Gratian.

For even if it had been true, which God forbid, as that adulterer falsely asserted, after eight [Col. 0183D]—“after seven,” according to Gratian—years of penance [Col. 0190B]

[Note: “After completing penance.” The argument is that after penance has been completed and a crime purged, someone can still be accused of that crime, as in 15, q. 5, *Presbyter*; 25, dist., final chapter; *Extra*, *De schismate*, *Fraternitatis* 2; for one who bears the stain of a memorable crime, and so forth, dist. 61, *Non negamus*; and 1, q. 7, *Si quis omnem*. Through penance a person does not cease to be guilty, *Digest*, *De aedilicio edicto*, *Quis sit fugitivus*. Indeed, even after baptism someone may be accused of this, *Extra*, *De divortiis*, *Gaudemus*, at the end.

Argument to the contrary: 23, q. 4, *Si illic*; 32, q. 1, *Quod autem*, at the end; 3, and so forth, *Non erit*, and *Apud*; 50, dist. *Ferrum*; *Extra*, *De accusationibus*, *De his*; and *Digest*, *De aedilicio edicto*, *Quod ita*. I discussed this at 6, q. 1, *Qui crimen*, and chapter *Illi qui*.

But does the husband not prejudice his own case by remaining silent for seven years, since an accusation of adultery is not heard after five years, according to *Codex*, *De adulteris*, *Adulter*? Yet the rule *Quicumque* and dist. 8, *Qui contempta*; 24, q. 3, *Ecce*; and the statement “after penance has been completed” refer to a time before judgment has been pronounced, as above, the proximate q. 5, chapter *Christiana*. Thus the Gloss.

Examine the canons and laws cited here, and if any difficulty arises, resolve it lightly. We are hurrying on to other matters not explained by the Gloss.]

perhaps, after completing penance, you could have dismissed her for an approved cause if you had wished; but you ought in no way [Col. 0183D]—“nevertheless you ought not at all,” according to Gratian—to have killed her [Col. 0190D].

[Note: “You ought in no way to have killed her.” Although worldly laws—as Pope Nicholas calls them, chapter *Inter haec*, 33, q. 2—sometimes permit adulterous wives to be killed, as Cato says in his speech *On the Dowry*, cited by Gellius, book X, chapter 23:

> “If you had caught your wife in adultery, you could kill her with impunity without a trial,”

they nevertheless did not support Heistulf’s crime, since he did not kill a woman caught in the act—“not found,” as Paulinus puts it, “committing that abominable deed with another man”—but killed her at the instigation of a slanderer.

Moreover, even if this were permitted under Lombard law, it was not permitted under Roman law, as the Glossator says at the cited chapter *Inter haec*. Roman laws act more mildly: they remit the ultimate penalty to a husband who kills his wife while she is actually defecting from marital fidelity, and they do not include him under the Cornelian law on assassins, because they judge that he was carried away by an impulse of grief, as L. Gracchus says, *Codex*, *Ad legem Juliam de adulteriis*. Yet they do not acquit him with impunity, as can be seen in *Digest*, *Ad legem Juliam*, law *Si adulterium*, § *De marito uxorem occidente*, and *Digest*, *Ad legem Corneliam de sicariis*, law 1, *Lege Cornelia*.]

You ought not to have killed her. For God does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn to repentance and live. Therefore let our council please you, and do what may seem better and easier for you; have pity on your soul, lest you become your own murderer [Col. 0183D].

[Note: “Your own murderer,” that is, “you murderer.”]

Therefore, murderer, we beg you to leave this wicked age [Col. 0183D]—“therefore, we beg you to leave this evil world,” as Gratian reads—which drew you into so monstrous a deed of sin. Enter [Gratian omits *in*] [Col. 0191A]

[Note: “Enter a monastery.” From this passage it seems that, however much penance a person may be bound to complete, if he enters religious life he is no longer bound to complete it, because religious life dissolves the bond of an oath, *Extra*, *De jurejurando*, *Pervenit*. It also dissolves a vow, *Extra*, *De voto*, *Votum redemptionis Scripturae*. It likewise dissolves the bond of obedience, 19, q. 2, *Duae*.

Thus, even if a pope has imposed upon someone as penance that he go to Rome or do something of that sort, and the person enters religious life, he is not called a transgressor. A transgressor is one who abandons the greater for the lesser, as in 20, q. 3, *Propositum*, and 17, q. 1, *Qui bona*; argument to the same point in *De poenitentia*, dist. 1, § *His auctoritatibus*. Hugh concedes this.

Others say that a person remains bound to fulfill what he promised and what was imposed upon him as penance, unless the abbot dispenses him from it, 18, q. 2, chapter *Nullum*. Thus the Gloss.]

[Note: [Col. 0191B] Paulinus left Heistulf free either to enter a monastery or to perform penance at home, as is also prescribed in *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 71, for one who violates his maternal aunt’s daughter: “Let him either seek a monastery, or, if he wishes to remain outside, let him fully discharge the periods of penance according to the canons.” For the solitude of monastic life and the continence of the ascetic retreat, together with constant application to prayer and bodily discipline, were regarded as equivalent to canonical penances.

Perhaps this accounts for the establishment of houses of penance, especially for women: not only that they might be kept from relapse, but also that, enclosed in such houses, they might more conveniently perform the duties of penance. In the time of Berrold, patriarch of Udine, one such house stood at Saint Quirinus. See Appendix II, no. 17. Outside monasteries, penitents were separated from others, though for different reasons, according to the stages of penance completed or still to be completed. Some stood at the doors, some in the narthex with the catechumens, some within the portico itself, some within the church itself, and some with the other faithful, though they were not admitted to everything. They were called Weepers, Hearers, Prostrated, Standers, and Participants in the sacraments, according as they discharged the imposed penance step by step. But those bound by graver offences lay prostrate on their knees under the open sky—not in the portico, much less among the catechumens—and begged the prayers of those entering; these were called *Hiemantes* (“winterers”). The Council of Ancyra, canon 17, calls them **Χειμαζομένους**, “those exposed to winter’s storms”; Gentian Hervetus translates this *Hiemantes*. Tertullian seems to have referred to them when he said in *On Modesty*, chapter 4: “But the remaining impious frenzies of lust, directed against bodies and sexes beyond the laws of nature, we remove not only from the threshold but from every roof of the Church, because they are not offences but monstrosities.”

If penance was prolonged, this separation of penitents was supplemented by confinement in the catechumenium or diaconia, as is shown by Pope Gregory’s *Dialogues* II, cited by Baronius under the year 726: “Where anyone has sinned and confessed, instead of hanging or beheading, they place the Gospel and its cross around his neck; they cast him as into prison into the sacristies and treasury of sacred vessels; they banish him to the church’s diaconia and catechumenium; and they prescribe fasting for their bodies, vigils for their eyes, and praise for their mouths.” This being so, what substitution could be more fitting for such separation than the profession of monasticism? For monk and monastery derive from **ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀμονάζειν**, because monks lived alone and apart from others. Hence Rutilius Gallicus, *Itinerary*, book I, verse 441, says of the ascetics of the island of Capraria:

> “They call themselves monks by a Greek name,
>
> Because they wish to live alone, with no witness.”

And Saint Jerome, letter 13 to Paulinus: “If you wish to be what you are called, a monk—that is, alone—what are you doing in cities, which are surely dwellings not of solitary persons but of many?” Eusebius, bishop of Vercelli, was the first in the West to bring monks into communal and civic life, assigning them also to clerical duties. Ambrose, letter 63: “In the Church of Vercelli two things seem to be required alike of the bishop: the continence of the monastery and the discipline of the Church.
