For Eusebius of holy memory was the first in the western regions to unite things previously distinct, so that, though placed in a city, he retained monastic institutions and governed the Church with the sobriety of fasting.”

Moreover, since penitential works—fasts, vigils, and other such things—were prescribed for penitents, these too were observed in monasteries. Chrysostom testifies to this in his extensive account of the character of the monastic state, *Homily* 14 on chapter V of the First Epistle to Timothy: “Monasteries,” he says, “are truly houses of mourning, where there are ashes and haircloth, where solitude is found, where there is no laughter and no noise of worldly business, where there are fasts and the hardness of earthen beds,” and the other matters that follow, abundantly worthy of reading.

Yet even if these were absent from a monastery—and indeed they were not seldom absent, for such severity of diet as was imposed on sinners in punishment for monstrous offences was not to be prescribed indiscriminately for innocent monks—the obedience itself and the sacrifice of one’s own liberty and will, more pleasing to God than any penance, amply compensate for the prescribed penitential works. For it takes the place even of martyrdom itself, as Saint Antiochus said in *Homily* 39, *On Obedience*: “To cut away your own will is as though you were shedding your own blood; and this too is counted to a person as a sacrifice.”

Nevertheless, entrance into a monastery did not always free a person from the burden of public penance, as is shown by chapter 90 of book VI of the *Capitularies*, which says: “Whoever kills a monk or cleric shall lay aside arms and serve God in a monastery all the days of his life, never to return to the world, and shall undergo public penance for seven years.” Thus the debt of penance did not wholly cease through the profession of monasticism. But because the condition and state of a monk were more suited to bearing penitential works, the Fathers of the Church recommended it and sometimes imposed it absolutely.

“For this reason also,” says Morinus, *On Penance*, book VII, chapter 15, no. 12, “this later custom, adopted by many, seems to have arisen: that the monastic habit be assumed at the point of death, so that those who had refused to embrace penance while living might at least honor it in dying. Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, Blanche, mother of Saint Louis, and before them Burchard, count of Melun and Corbeil, did this with great humility and devotion of spirit, as our histories relate; many private persons imitated their piety and do so even now.” These are Morinus’s words. To these it seems one should add that perhaps from the same source arose the practice, often seen in Italy (perhaps elsewhere as well), and especially among our own people, that many persons—not while they are in extremis, but altogether dead and being carried out for burial—wish to be clothed in the habit of some sacred order and direct in their wills that they be buried in it; and that this is sometimes done solely from the piety of survivors.]

a monastery, humble yourself under the authority of an abbot, aided by the prayers of many brothers [“and of many brothers,” according to Gratian] [Col. 0183D]. Observe with a simple heart everything that is commanded you [the edition of Labbé adds: “by the abbot”] [Col. 0184A], if perhaps the infinite goodness of God may forgive your sins and refresh your soul before you are tormented by everlasting flames.

[Note: “If perhaps the goodness of God may forgive.” This is not stated doubtfully; indeed, it is a known form of assertion and means fully “if.” *De poenitentia*, dist. 1, *Quamobrem*. Thus the Gloss.

Paulinus uses here a scriptural phrase that is not uncommon, as in Daniel 4:24; Joel 2:14; Jonah 3:9; and Acts 8:22. Hear Ambrose, book II *On Penance*, chapter 5. Ribera improperly doubts in his commentary on Joel whether Ambrose is the author of those books, since Ambrose himself, writing about himself in Psalm 37, testifies: “Long ago I wrote two little books on penance.” The Benedictine Fathers, noting this and restoring Ambrose’s works to their proper standard, as they do with others, clearly establish that this is not spurious. They relegated another work on penance, attributed to Victor of Tunnuna, to the appendix; but this one is genuinely Ambrose’s.

I say, hear Ambrose refuting the objection raised by the Novatians from such passages, especially from Acts 8:22, by which they supported the irreversibility of sins that they imagined:

> “I do not say that Peter doubted, nor do I think that so important a matter should be strangled by the prejudice of a single word. For if they think that Peter doubted, did God also doubt? He says to the prophet Jeremiah [chapter 26, verse 2]: ‘Stand in the court of the Lord’s house, and you shall give an answer to all Judah, to those who come to worship in the house of the Lord, all the words that I have commanded you to answer them; do not remove a word: perhaps they will listen and turn back.’ Let them say, then, that God did not know what would happen. But ignorance is not expressed by that word; rather, the divine Scriptures frequently exhibit this manner of expression, because the wording is simple.

> “For the Lord also says to Ezekiel: ‘Son of man, I am sending you to the house of Israel, to those who have provoked me, they and their fathers, even to this day; and you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: If perhaps they will listen and be afraid.’ Did he not know whether they could or could not be converted? This expression, therefore, does not always belong to one who is doubting.

> “Finally, even the wise men of the world, who place all their glory in the expression of words, did not always use what we call *forte* in Latin and **τάχα** (*tacha*) in Greek to express doubt. Thus they say that the first of their poets, Homer, wrote in book III of the *Iliad*: **ἡ τάχα χήρα ἔσομαι**, that is, ‘I shall soon be a widow’; and elsewhere: **Τάχα γάρ σε κατακτανέουσιν Ἀχαιοὶ πάντες ἐφορμηθέντες**, ‘For all the Achaeans, rushing upon you, will soon kill you.’ He was not doubting that one man could easily be struck down by everyone attacking him at once.

> “But let us use examples from our own writers rather than from foreigners. In the Gospel, the Son himself says of the Father—when the Father had sent servants to his vineyard and they had killed them—that he said, Matthew 21:37: ‘I will send my most beloved son; perhaps they will fear him.’ Elsewhere the Son says in his own person, John 8:19: ‘You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would perhaps know my Father.’

> “If Peter therefore used these words, which God used without prejudice to his knowledge, why should we not understand Peter also to have used such expressions without prejudice to his faith? For he could not doubt concerning Christ’s commission, since Christ had given him authority to forgive sins.”

Thus far Ambrose. If, following Ambrose, you wish to confirm this from the foremost of the Greek poets, you may confirm it from the foremost of the Latin poets, at Virgil’s words, *Aeneid* I, verse 207:

> “Perhaps one day even this will be pleasant to remember.”

Add also Ulpian, *Digest*, *De rei vindicatione*, law *Item si*, where he takes *fortassis* and *forte* without a sense of doubt. When Paulinus therefore said, “if perhaps the goodness of God may forgive,” he was not uncertain about God’s goodness but followed the usage of the Scriptures.]

and refresh your soul before you are tormented by everlasting flames. Know with absolute certainty that this is easier and better for you [“Know with absolute certainty that this counsel is easier and more salutary: that you should mourn your sins under another’s supervision,” according to the edition of Labbé].

But if, remaining in your house, you wish to undertake public penance, or to perform it in this world [Col. 0183D]—“we exhort you to perform it as you ought, since you should not doubt that it will be worse, harder, and more burdensome for you,” according to Gratian—although you should not doubt that this will be more burdensome, harder, and worse [Col. 0193C],

[Note: “You should not doubt that it will be more burdensome.” It seemed to be a greater punishment to live among people and be deprived of human assistance than to be far from people and not experience human comfort. *Codex*, *De apostatis*, *Hi qui*. Thus the Gloss.

For, as Seneca says, *Letter* 9:

> “The sweetness of friendship is innate; and just as solitude is hateful, so the desire for companionship seeks sweetness”;

and in book IV *On Benefits*, chapter 18:

> “Take us one by one: what are we? . . . Remove society, and you will tear apart the unity of the human race by which life is sustained.”

Nothing more burdensome or distressing could happen to a human being than to be deprived of the company and fellowship of friends.

When, as is customary, I was visiting those confined in prison, I witnessed something that seemed remarkable to me at the time. Women committed to custody continually attacked one another with insults and complaints, vomiting curses in mutual quarrels as their bile swelled, so that scarcely an hour’s peace or brief rest ever arose among them. Eventually, when all the others had been acquitted and released, only one remained. When I returned, I found her inconsolable and almost bereft of hope. I asked what had happened and why she was suffering so painfully. Once the causes of their former disturbances and quarrels had been removed, she replied that she was mourning her solitude and that, in her judgment, the quarrels, disputes, and insults she had previously endured could not be compared with the present quiet and silence.

Solitude is therefore so grievous that even when accompanied by peace—the greatest of all goods—it is considered something to be avoided. Paulinus was therefore right to say [Col. 0194A] that it would be more burdensome for Heistulf to remain in the world and bid farewell to the world, preserving solitude amid the crowd and the desert in the city. This is what was demanded of Heistulf, as the Glossator indicates and as the following context makes clear.]
...you should doubt, so that we exhort you to act accordingly. All the days that you live, repent. [Note: [Col. 0184D] During which you ought to repent; and Gratian.] Do not drink wine or any fermented drink. [Note: [Col. 0194A]

Do not drink fermented drink. By “fermented drink” understand every beverage that intoxicates, as in Distinction 35, in the rubric *Drunkenness*: Gloss.

Here applies what Jerome says in Letter 2 to Nepotian, on the life of clergy: “In Hebrew,” he says, “*sicera* denotes every drink that can intoxicate, whether it is made from grain, or from the juice of fruit, or from honeycombs boiled into a sweet and barbarous drink, or from the fruit of palm trees pressed into liquid, with water thickened and colored by boiled grains.” Thus *sicera* should be understood as a generic term, as is also gathered from the *Capitulare de villis et curtis*, chapter 45, where it is decreed: “Let each judge in his jurisdiction have good craftsmen, blacksmiths . . . [Col. 0194B] makers of fermented drink—that is, those who know how to make beer, cider, perry, or any other liquid suitable for drinking.” And because penitents sometimes evaded the canons forbidding wine by using these beverages—for, as Pliny says of them in Book XIV, chapter 22, “it was discovered how even water could intoxicate”—the Fathers of the Second Council of Chalon in 813 condemned the practice, chapter 35: “So that, with these more luxurious things—meat and wine—forbidden to them, they may be seen to live by the desire for other foods or drinks.” Therefore, in the enumeration of penances, the prohibited beverages were sometimes expressly listed, lest the law be defrauded. Thus the Council of Worms in 868, chapter 30: “Let them abstain from wine, mead, and honeyed beer for three days each week.” And when penitents were being tempted to transgress, disciplinary measures were brought to bear. Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 151: “Let no priest or layman invite a penitent to drink or eat meat unless, on his behalf, he first gives one or two denarii according to the character of the penance.” Nevertheless, a little question is proposed and answered in the margin of the Gloss cited above:

“Is it permissible for him to drink milk or almond water, or to eat grapes?” H. says: “I believe so, because such things do not intoxicate.” So far as he is concerned.] 

Do not drink [Note: [Col. 0184D] “You shall drink,” and Gratian.]. Do not eat meat [Note: [Col. 0194C] Never eat meat at any time. But what of eggs, since an egg is liquid flesh, or milk, since milk is nothing but blood altered in color? We say no; and this is what the wording that follows intends, “in bread and water.” Nevertheless, it may be understood that he must do this on specified days, as on the appointed ferias. But may he use bacon? Is it forbidden under the name of meat? It seems not, by the argument of Distinction 82, *Presbyter*, where fat is permitted when eggs are permitted. Gloss.] at any time whatsoever, except on Easter and the day of the Nativity of the Lord. In bread and water and [Note: [Col. 0194C] Do penance in bread, water, and salt. This is not a new practice. Epiphanius, *Against the Arians*, heresy 75, no. 6, writing against the Aerian condemnation of Christian fasts, maintains that this rite must be traced to apostolic times: “If our authority is to be derived from the apostolic ordinance . . . why do they prescribe that for the six days of Easter”—understand, Holy Week—“nothing at all should be taken as food except bread, salt, and water?” In the *Exposition of the Faith*, no. 22, he says that one should eat *xerophagy*: “Throughout those six days of Easter, he says, the whole people have been accustomed to live on *xerophagy*, that is, dry food: namely, to take only bread with water toward evening.” Canon 50 of the Council of Laodicea extends this to the whole of Lent: “It is necessary to fast throughout Lent, eating dry foods.” The Greek reads: **Δεῖ πᾶσαν τὴν τεσσαρακοσὴν νησεύειν ξηροφαγοῦντας**, “It is necessary to fast throughout Lent, eating dry food.” Tertullian, *Against the Physicists*, chapter 1, seems to indicate that something besides bread and salt could be added to *xerophagy*, provided it was dry and without juice: “They reproach us,” he says, “because we observe our proper fasts . . . and also practice *xerophagy*, drying our food of all meat, all broth, and every juicy fruit, so that we neither eat nor drink anything of a vinous nature.” By adding *homophagy* to *xerophagy*—that is, the eating of raw foods—the monks did not think they were diminishing the fast. “Nor,” says Cassian, *On the Institutes of the Renunciants*, chapter 22, “is much care spent among them in preparing or cooking food, since they make the greatest use of *xerophagy* and *homophagy*.”

Now, when you hear of *homophagy* among monks, you should understand that it is not what Arnobius detested among the pagans in Book V of *Against the Nations*: “Let us pass over the monstrous Bacchanalia,” he said, “which have the Greek name *Omophagia*: in them, amid feigned madness . . . the entrails of bleating goats are torn apart by bloodstained mouths.” Rather, understand the eating of raw foods, such as radishes, turnips, garlic, onions, melons, cucumbers, and the stalks of other herbs or vegetables from which salads are made, or which we eat raw without any other seasoning.

What in ancient times they called *xerophagy*, in Paulinus’ period they called dry food. Bede’s *Penitential*, chapter 7, cited by Morinus, Book VII, chapter 20, no. 2: “Each week let him spend three days without wine, mead, or meat, and let him fast until evening, and eat dry food; and let him spend the three Lents always on dry food.” And from the Roman *Penitential*, cited in the same place, no. 4: “Let him fast until evening, and then be refreshed with dry food.” Further on: “Let him fast two days each week until the ninth hour, and eat dry food.”

That kind of abstinence was not unknown among pagans, as is gathered from Capitolinus, *Antoninus Pius*, chapter 13: “Before the morning visitors arrived, as an old man he ate dry bread to sustain his strength”; from Vopiscus, *Tacitus*, chapter 11: “He never ate bread except dry bread, seasoned with salt and other things.” And from Seneca, who said of himself: “Dry bread, and a meal without a table, after which there is no need to wash one’s hands.”

I am not unaware that *siccus* is sometimes used to mean “alone.” Julius Capitolinus, *Maximinus*, chapter 13: “He presented some consular men . . . in dry vehicles, others, etc.” Herodian, Book VII, chapter 3, has **μόνοις ὀχήμασιν**, “in vehicles alone,” as Politianus interprets it, “placed in vehicles without any attendants.” But it should more literally be read as **μόνοις**, “alone”; and this is what *siccis vehiculis* means, “in vehicles alone.” Since certain printers failed to understand this, they absurdly printed in Capitolinus not *siccis vehiculis*, “in dry vehicles,” but *Scythicis*, “Scythian vehicles.”

Likewise, *assum* (“roasted”) means the same as *siccum* (“dry”), namely, “alone”; and *assa*, says Nonius in the dictionary beginning with A, is “a solitary and unadorned word, not mixed with other musical expressions.” Especially relevant is what he says in the following entry: “*Assum* should be understood of dishes without the flavoring of another seasoning, just as *merum* is said of something alone.”

However *dry bread* is understood, it is the frugal food of a temperate person; but dry food is the food of the penitent, as has been demonstrated above.] Do penance with salt [Col. 0184B] [Gratian: “Do penance”] [Note: [Col. 0184D] Do penance.]. Persevere at all times in fasts, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving.

Never gird yourself with weapons. [Note: [Col. 0195C]

Never gird yourself with weapons, except by the counsel of a bishop for the defense of justice; see below, *On Penance*, Distinction 5, *Falsas*. So the Gloss.

This penalty is imposed especially on homicides. The Council, or capitulary, of Worms in 829, title 3, [Col. 0195D] chapter 3, deals specifically with wife-killers: “Whoever, after abandoning his own wife, or killing her without cause, takes another wife, shall lay aside his weapons and perform public penance.” More generally, the Council of Tribur in 895, canon 55, says: “If anyone voluntarily commits homicide, let him be excluded from entering the church for forty days, and let him eat nothing during those forty days except bread and salt, nor drink anything except pure water; let him walk barefoot; let him not wear linen garments except breeches; let him carry no secular weapons; let him use no vehicle, etc.”

These provisions agree with the statutes of Paulinus. The Fathers prescribed this for two reasons: so that penitents might display humility and so that they might avoid the opportunity to sin by shedding another’s blood. For, just as bearing a sword is a mark of honor, as Guntherus Ligurinus said in Book I of *The Deeds of Emperor Frederick*:

“. . . The sword makes men revered throughout the world,”

[Col. 0196A] so laying it aside is a sign of humility and a silent confession of the crime committed. John of Salisbury, *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, Book VI, chapter 13: “It sometimes happens that, because of his offense, a soldier is deprived of the military belt, especially when sacrileges have been committed.” And below: “Surely he deserves to lose the privilege”—the belt and sword of which he is speaking there—“who abuses the power granted to him.”

The Fathers also sought to remove the opportunity of relapsing into homicide when they commanded penitential homicides to lay aside the sword. Hence Pope Leo wrote to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, Letter 92, chapter 10: “It is wholly contrary to ecclesiastical rules, after performing penance—and therefore much more so during the performance of penance—to return to secular military service. Thus he is not free from the devil’s snares who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service.”

And the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea judged that one who resumed the military belt after conversion, having long ago laid it aside, was like a dog returning to its own vomit, and decreed that he should be punished by ten years of penance after three years spent among the hearers, chapter 11, elsewhere numbered 12. But he was not forbidden to take up arms again for the defense of justice, as is clear from the Roman synod of 1078, chapter 5: “Let him lay aside his weapons and thereafter bear them no more, except by the counsel of the bishops for the defense of justice.” Pope Nicholas permitted this especially against the enemies of the Church to a certain matricide, as stated in 33, question 2, chapter *Latorem*: “Let him take up arms only against pagans.”

Indeed, the Council of Clermont, number 21, in 1095, convened under Urban II to summon the faithful marked with the cross to recover the holy places, decreed in canon 2 that arms might be borne against unbelievers in place of any penance: “Whoever, solely out of devotion and not for the acquisition of honor or money, goes to Jerusalem to liberate the Church of God, let that journey be counted as his entire penance.”]

Never gird yourself with them, and do not presume to litigate any case anywhere. [Note: [Col. 0184D] “Nor in any place,” and Gratian.] [Note: [Col. 0196B] “Nor presume to litigate in any place.” The reason for this statement is that a public penitent must not bring his complaint before a secular tribunal to have it argued there, but must approach an ecclesiastical judgment; see above, 2, question 1, *Aliud*. Supply, therefore: unless in his own case and before ecclesiastical judges. Gloss.]

Never take a wife. [Note: [Col. 0196C]

Never take a wife. If, however, he does take one, the marriage remains valid, by the argument above, in the same place, *Quicunque*. Others say the contrary, as is noted below, in the same place, section *On Penitents*. Gloss.

The learned Morinus teaches in Book V of *On Penance*, chapters 18–24, that from the fourth century through the eighth, indeed even to the twelfth, both renunciation of military service and prohibition of marriage—or abstinence from one’s wife—continued in force; but that after this period both ceased, and that the Church dealt more mildly with penitents. If you have time, read the discussion.] 

Do not take a wife, nor have a concubine [Gratian: “Do not have a concubine”], nor commit adultery. [Note: [Col. 0184D] “Do not dare to commit it,” and Gratian.] Never bathe in a bathhouse. [Note: [Col. 0196C]

Never bathe in a bathhouse, except from necessity. *On Consecration*, Distinction 3, *Pervenit*. Gloss.

Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor*, Book III, chapter 9: “There are,” he says, “four reasons for which we go to the bath. We go either for cleanliness, for warmth, for health, or finally for pleasure. Bathing undertaken for pleasure must be rejected, for shameless pleasure must be entirely cut away. Women should bathe for cleanliness and health, but men only for health. To bathe for warmth is superfluous, since what has collapsed through cold can be restored in another way.”

But these remarks are appropriate to a well-mannered and frugal man. Hear what Diadochus, bishop, says to one striving for perfection, chapter 52, *On Spiritual Perfection*: “No one would say that going to the bath is a sin or contrary to reason; nevertheless, I say that to abstain from it for the sake of continence is manly and especially characteristic of the temperate.”

Jerome tolerated bathing in a young girl, but forbade it in an adult woman, Letter 7, *On the Education of a Daughter*: “Until the years of robust maturity, let her go to the baths if necessity requires it.” But below: “I entirely disapprove of bathing in an adult virgin, who ought to be ashamed of herself.” [Col. 0197A] The most holy Fathers rightly removed from repentant sinners those indulgences that they rejected in a virgin. Add that, as is said in Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 122: “Let penitents receive a hair shirt from the priest, as has been established everywhere.” It is superfluous, as Saint Hilarion said—and Saint Jerome records in his *Life*—“to seek cleanliness in a hair shirt.”]

[Note: [Col. 0184D] “You shall bathe,” and Gratian.] Never mingle with the feasts of those who rejoice. [Note: [Col. 0184D] “Do not mingle,” and Gratian.] In church, separated from the other Christians, place yourself humbly behind the door and its posts. [Note: [Col. 0184D] “Place yourself humbly,” Gratian.] Commend yourself submissively to the prayers of those entering and leaving. [Gratian: “Commend yourself.”]

[Note: [Col. 0197A] Abstain from communion of the sacred body, etc. Therefore it seems that the man who kills his wife sins more grievously than one who kills his mother, because a greater penance is imposed on the wife-killer than on the matricide in the chapter *Latorem*, which is below in the same question, and thus the crime is greater, by the argument of 24, question 1, *Non afferamus*, which H. concedes; for he says that one who kills himself sins more grievously than one who kills another. 23, question 5, *Si non licet*. Hence one who kills a part of his own body sins more grievously than one who kills his mother. He also proves this by the passage: “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife,” in *Extra*, *De bigamia*, *Debitum*.

Others say that one who kills his mother sins more grievously than one who kills his wife; but because people are more inclined to kill their wives, they are punished more severely for that reason, so that they may be deterred from such a crime. Hence this argument is invalid: “They are punished more severely; therefore they sin more grievously.” The same applies to notorious fornication: although many crimes are more serious, because people offend more easily and shamefully in this crime than in others, a harsher punishment is therefore prescribed for it, by the argument of 32, Distinction, section *Verum*. Gloss.]

Abstain from communion of the sacred body and blood of Christ, considering yourself unworthy throughout all the days of your life. [Note: [Col. 0197A] Abstain from communion of the sacred body and blood of the Lord throughout all the days of your life, considering yourself unworthy; and Gratian.] On the final day of your life, however, as viaticum, if you have deserved that there should be someone to administer it, we permit you to receive it, but only as a venial concession. [Col. 0184C] [Note: [Col. 0198A] “That you may receive it as a venial concession.” The argument is that the Church can forbid the body and blood of the Lord to some even at the end of life, by the argument of 27, question 1, *Impudicas*; above, 2, question 3, *Si quis episcopum aut presbyterum*; above, 13, final question, *Quaestitum est*, where it says, “according to the prescriptions of the canons.” To this belongs the fact that something belonging to a person by common law is sometimes said to be granted out of mercy and compassion, by the argument of 11, question 3, *Quoniam*, and *Digest*, *On usufruct*, *Si extraneo*, and in the other passages marked here: “For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” John. Gloss.]

There are also many other things that, in proportion to the great burden of your sin, wretched man, ought to be added to your penance, and they would be harsher and considerably more severe. But if, with God’s help, you perform and keep with a perfect heart all these things mercifully stated above, we trust in the immense clemency of God that you will obtain forgiveness of your sins; and, according to the command of the good and just shepherd, holy Church will release you on earth from this bond of sin, so that by the grace of him who acquired her with his blood, you may be released in heaven. But if you act otherwise and despise so salutary an admonition from holy Mother Church, you yourself will be your own judge, and you will remain entangled in the devil’s snare. Your blood be upon your own head. [Gratian: “Your blood”; [Note: [Col. 0198A] “Your blood,” that is, your sin. Hence the saying, “blood touched blood,” that is, sin, 44, Distinction, *Ephesiis*. John. Gloss.] and blood.]

We, estranged from your fellowship for the salvation of God’s other children, strive with every care, God assisting, to labor earnestly and to implore the Lord’s mercy more attentively each day. He is God who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

(The material that follows is fuller in Burchard, as there. LABB.) The second counsel is as follows: Lay aside your weapons and abandon all secular business. Do not eat meat or fat on any day of your life except one day of the Lord’s Resurrection, one day of Pentecost, and one day of the Nativity of the Lord. At other times, do penance in bread and water and occasionally in legumes and vegetables; persevere at all times in fasts, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving. Never drink wine, mead, or honeyed beer except on those aforementioned days. Do not take a wife, have no concubine, commit no adultery, and remain perpetually without hope of marriage. Never wash yourself in a [Col. 0186A] bathhouse; do not mount a horse; do not conduct your own case or another’s in an assembly of the faithful. Never sit at the feasts of those who rejoice. In church, separated from the other Christians, stand humbly behind the door; commend yourself submissively to the prayers of those entering and leaving. We consider you unworthy of communion of the sacred body and blood of the Lord throughout all the days of your life; at the final end of your life, as viaticum, we permit you to receive it if you have observed the counsel.

There are many other, harsher things that ought to be added to you in proportion to the weight of so great a crime. But if, with God’s help, you carry out and keep with a perfect heart all these things mercifully stated above, we trust in the immense clemency of God that you will obtain forgiveness of your sins, and that, according to the command of the good and just shepherd, holy Church will release you on earth from this bond of sin, so that by the grace of him who redeemed her with his blood, you may be released in heaven. But if you act otherwise and despise the salutary counsel of holy Mother Church, you yourself will be your own judge, and you will remain in the devil’s snare in which you are entangled; your blood shall be upon your own head. [Note: [Col. 0198A]

“We, estranged.” The argument is that the malice of subjects is not imputed to a prelate when it does not depend on him that they are not corrected, by the argument of 7, question 1, section *Cum autem*. Above, Distinction 44, *Ephesiis*; above, 44, Distinction, final chapter. Gloss.

## 22. BOOK OF EXHORTATION OF SAINT PAULINUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA, WRITTEN, AS IT SEEMS, AROUND THE YEAR 795 FOR HENRY, COUNT OR DUKE OF FRIULI, COMMONLY CALLED *ON SALUTARY INSTRUCTIONS*

Collated with several editions and illustrated with appropriate notes.

[Note: [Col. 0197C]

### PREFATORY NOTE TO THE FOLLOWING NOTES

Some of the notes that follow, gracious reader, which do not concern textual criticism, I could indeed have omitted. But since I observed that this work concerns morals and would not be useless to preachers of the word of God, especially to our fellow priests of the congregations of Saint Philip Neri, upon whom rests the burden of addressing the people—and since this book, arranged in a plainer style, can serve them as a specimen and model—I judged it not inappropriate, indeed I considered it likely to benefit them, if, when occasion offered, I supported the subject at hand with similar opinions of other holy Fathers and writers, so that they would not be forced to seek elsewhere whatever might happen to suit their purpose.

I would wish, since I am indebted to everyone, to satisfy everyone. Those who pursue textual criticism in history and discipline will find here, as elsewhere in the work, something to satisfy their desires. Let those, therefore, who cultivate the morals of others have material with which to enrich and strengthen their sermons for the edification of the rest.]

### CHAPTER I. To Love God Is Justice and Blessedness

[Col. 0197C]

O my brother, if you desire to know what the most perfect and complete justice is—although I do not know [Note: [Col. 0197] Thus the manuscripts. But the edition reads: “what justice may be.” “For justice is to love God,” etc. Thus the Benedictine Fathers note in the margin.]—it is to love God with one’s whole heart and cling to him with one’s entire will, for he is the highest good! To love the highest good is the highest blessedness. Whoever loves God is good; if he is good, therefore, [Note: [Col. 0198D] “If he is good, therefore he is blessed.” Seneca, Letter 85: “The blessed life possesses in itself a perfect and unsurpassable good; and if that is so, it is perfectly blessed . . . Do you doubt that the blessed life is the highest good? Therefore, if it possesses the highest good, it is supremely blessed.”] he is also blessed. The more ardently one loves him, the better one becomes. [Note: [Col. 0198D] “He will become better in proportion.” On this subject Augustine’s discussion is especially excellent, *On the Customs of the Catholic Church*, Book I, chapter 14: “The more widely and more fully God is proclaimed, the more ardently he is loved and cherished. When this happens, the human race proceeds by a sure and steady path toward the best and most blessed life . . . For what else is the highest good of man than that to which cleaving is supremely blessed? And that is God alone; we certainly cannot cling to him except by devotion, love, and charity.”]

I strive, dearest brother, to entreat him—who himself is this good—with daily prayers and an undivided desire of heart, though I am unworthy, so that he may make you abound in this most blessed good.

### CHAPTER II. Man’s Privileges in Creation

[Col. 0199A]

But you, dearest brother, understand that you were created by the counsel [Note: [Col. 0199C] “By the counsel of the Holy Trinity.” The author of the book *On Spirit and Soul*, customarily included among the works of Saint Augustine—whether he was Hugh of Saint Victor, as Trithemius maintains, or a certain Cistercian monk, specifically Alcher, as the Benedictine Fathers hold—was certainly later than Paulinus. Not only does he cite Boethius in chapter 37, who was later than Augustine, but comparison of the two writers shows that he had this and the following chapter of Paulinus before his eyes when he composed chapters 35 and 36. Indeed, this can be established from the very words that we append:

“Such is the dignity of the human condition that man was created not only by the word of the one commanding, as were the other works of the six days, but by the counsel of the Holy Trinity and by the work of divine majesty. Thus, from the honor of his first creation, he might understand how much he owed his Creator, since the Creator immediately granted him so great a privilege of dignity in his creation, and he might love his Creator all the more because he understood that he had been created by him in so marvelous a manner.”

Who does not see that these words proceed from the same source? What Paulinus had said individually to Henry, this writer applies generally to every human being.] of the Holy Trinity and by the work of divine majesty. From the first honor of your creation understand how much you owe your Creator, since the eternal Creator immediately granted you so great a privilege of dignity in your creation that you might love him more ardently, the more wondrously you understood yourself to have been created by him.

### CHAPTER III. How the Image of God Exists in Man

Nor is it only because you were so excellently created by the counsel of the Holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 0199D] “Nor only this,” etc. The author of the book *On Spirit and Soul*, chapter [Col. 0200C] says: “Nor indeed merely because he was so excellently created by the counsel of the Holy Trinity, but also because the Creator of all created him in his own image and likeness—something he granted to no other creature. He then returns to Paulinus’ senses and words, as will immediately become clear.] that the Creator of all created you in his own image and likeness; he granted this to no other creature except man alone. First, because by God’s gift you live and possess understanding. [Note: [Col. 0199] Thus the Venetian edition of 1551. But the Benedictine Fathers read: “He lives and possesses understanding, just as he was created in the image of his Creator.”]

Second, because you were created in the image of your Creator.

## 24. CHAPTER IV. Turning to God

[Col. 0200B]

Let spiritual knowledge be added to your mind, dearest brother, so that it may illuminate you and lead you, as I desire and pray, to eternal life. With all the affection of my heart I desire, and I beseech God, that you may always reach forward to what lies ahead until you attain the lofty crown of everlasting blessedness, and that you may not permit the nobility of your spirit—which I know to be excellent in you—to be changed from the love of Christ by any counsel of friends or any ambition for worldly desires. Do not obscure your goodness by the wickedness of others; but wherever you can, appear lovable before God and all the people. [Note: [Col. 0199] The Benedictine Fathers add: “Do not think that one who at times displeases human beings is therefore displeasing to God in all things.”]

The grace of God who assists you will not be lacking if there is in you the will to follow the holy admonition to which your good mind has so often attended in the divine Scriptures.

### CHAPTER V. He Urges Almsgiving and Works of Piety

Be, I beg you—although a layman—ready for every work of God, [Col. 0200C] compassionate toward the poor [Note: [Col. 0199] The Benedictine Fathers read: “kind toward the delinquents, compassionate toward God’s afflicted.”] and the afflicted, a comforter of those who mourn, sympathetic toward everyone’s misery, generous in almsgiving, remembering the Gospel widow’s two small coins (Luke 21:2) and the prophet’s words: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isaiah 58:7), but carefully discerning the proper distribution of alms [Note: [Col. 0201] The Benedictine Fathers read: “take care.”], so that it may be a consolation to both—the giver, that is, and the recipient.

Therefore, meditate not only on your own salvation but also on the progress and prosperity of many. Choose for yourself the best counselors. ### CHAPTER VII. True Friendship

Although the distance of place [Note: [Col. 0201] The Benedictine Fathers read: “the condition of place.”] may have carried me far away [Note: [Col. 0201C] “The distance of place may have carried me far away,” etc. It is well known that absence dissolves ordinary friendships, or at least causes them to grow cold. Propertius, Book III, verse 869, or Elegy 19 to Cynthia:

Hence Athenaeus, *Deipnosophistae*, book V, chapter 2, calls that saying “the most inhuman of all proverbs” (*Μισανθρωποτάτην τῶν παροιμιῶν*): “Those who live far away, though friends, are not friends” (*Τηλοῦ φίλοι ναί ὄντες, οὐκ εἰσὶν φίλοι*). Turpilius, in *Fragments*, verse 11, lamented that in this matter he was judged by the character of others:
