Here we may linger somewhat longer, in order to answer the accusations of certain petty quibblers. For they object to this statement of Paulinus because it is clear that true affection can at times be abandoned. Everyone who sins falls away from affection and abandons it. Yet people do sin—alas, all too often! These words are cited under Augustine’s name by Gratian, *De poenitentia*, distinction 2, chapter “Charity,” who adds: “But he does not have charity who is going to sin criminally.” No Catholic doubts that this is false, and the gloss found there is equally false. “Gratian,” says the glossator, “shows through many authorities that charity cannot be lost; for if it seems to be lost, it was not true charity.” Below, however, the same glossator attempts to explain the phrase “which can be abandoned” (*quae deseri potest*) by adding, “that is, which may be abandoned easily or without difficulty,” and the word “true” by adding, “that is, enduring and final,” or “true,” meaning “leading to life,” that is, to eternal blessedness. But, with all due respect to Gratian and the glossator, this passage should not have been cited as referring to true supernatural charity, by which we are said—and are—the friends of God through grace. It must be understood solely of human affection. This is clear to anyone who considers the text. Paulinus says to his friend, the count:

“Although the place of my change had carried me far away from you in body, yet in no way in affection, for affection that can be abandoned was never true. Therefore, by the innermost affection of friendships, let us unite ourselves as much as we can to the Lord Christ.”

Do you see what affection he is discussing? Clearly, it is the love of friendship by which, through shared pursuits and desires, good and like-minded friends strive toward union with Christ Jesus. One kind of friendship united them to Christ, and this is supernatural charity; another kind encouraged them mutually to attain Christ’s friendship and charity, and this is natural and human affection. It is of this latter affection that Paulinus must be understood to have spoken. The word “affection” (*charitas*) certainly caused some difficulty for them, since they thought that by the name of charity no love other than the supernatural love by which we love God could be intended. But pagan and secular writers commonly use the word not to signify divine love but human friendship [Col. 0202D]. Livy, Decade I, book X, chapter 17: “So great was the ardor of the soldiers, both through devotion to their commander and through hope of greater … booty, that in one day … they captured the city.” Cicero, book I, *On Ends*: “They win goodwill, and, what is most fitting for a life of peace, affection.” Indeed, where Cicero refers *charitas* to the gods, he also applies the very same word to human beings, as he does in *On the Divisions of Oratory*: “Men are moved either by affection, as for the gods, their country, and their parents; or by love, as for brothers, spouses, children, and intimates.” But these matters, to use Tully’s own words in book I of *On the Orator*, we have briefly considered as though passing by a lattice. Thus *charitas* is also said of human friendship. No one who considers attentively that Paulinus spoke of it in this sense can doubt it. He drew this statement from Jerome, who, writing to Rufinus in letter 49 about his friendship with Bonosus, concludes thus: “Charity cannot be bought. Affection has no price. Friendship that can cease was never true. Farewell in Christ.” You see that Jerome here uses *charitas* for friendship, and that it is precisely the same thing. For Jerome’s and Paulinus’s statement is identical, if you substitute Jerome’s *friendship* for Paulinus’s *charity*. Alcuin too, writing to our Paulinus in letter 113, begins thus: “Bodily absence ought not to divide affection, because friendship that can be abandoned was never true.” I do not doubt that both Paulinus and Alcuin learned this statement from Jerome, who uttered it before either of them.] which can be abandoned was never true. Therefore, by the innermost affection of friendships, let us unite ourselves as much as we can [Col. 0203A] to the Lord Christ, for he himself says: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you” (John 15:14). And again to his disciples: “I will no longer call you servants, but my friends” (ibid., 15).

## CHAPTER VIII. Friendship with God and observance of the commandments are commended.

And if we wish to earn the rewards of eternal life, let us strive with all our strength to keep his commandments. For his commandments are burdensome to those who are unwilling, but light to those who are willing [Note: [Col. 0203C] “Burdensome to those who are unwilling, light to those who are willing”—that is the same as saying “to those who love and those who do not love.” Hence Jerome, letter 22, near the end: “Nothing is difficult for those who love, and no labor is hard for one who desires … Let us also love Christ and always seek his embraces, and everything difficult will seem easy; we shall think everything long to be brief.” Augustine likewise touches on both points, *Tractate* 48, no. 1, on John: “You know that the one who loves does not labor. For every labor is burdensome to those who do not love.”], as he himself says: “For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30). And again: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2).

For the friendship of the world [Note: [Col. 0203D] “The friendship of the world is based on gain,” and so forth. Nothing is truer or more firmly established. Such friends are called in Scripture “table-companions” (Ecclesiasticus 6:12), and those “who grieve with a friend only for the sake of the belly,” as that same Sirach says, chapter 37, verses 5 and 11, are the people of whom Cicero writes in *Laelius*: “They love friends as though they were cattle, especially those from whom they hope to obtain the greatest profit.” Hence that familiar line of Ovid, *Ex Ponto*, book II, verse 202, or *Tristia*, III.8:

“The common crowd approves friendships by their usefulness.”] is based either on profit, benefits, or various honors; but the friendship of the Savior consists in loving him and one’s neighbor. Therefore, whenever we fulfill Christ’s commandments through good works, we are called Christ’s friends. He is always inviting us to his friendship, while the envious devil seeks to plunge us into hell. The Savior loves us, while the betrayer hates us; therefore, let us not neglect the Redeemer or follow the robber. Let the one who restored us to freedom be dearer to us than the one who captured us and subjected us to slavery.

Always set before the eyes of your heart the fact that neither a crowd of friends nor a multitude of relatives, neither a heap of gold and silver, nor shining gems, neither the abundance of vineyards, nor the density of crops, nor the pleasant expanse of meadows can bring any assistance to the soul [Note: [Col. 0204C] To the soul departing from the body. Such was the language of those whose words are found in Wisdom 5:8: “What did our pride profit us, or what benefit did the boasting of riches bring us?” There is also Psalm 48:18: “When he dies, he will take nothing with him, nor will his glory descend with him.” Gregory aptly says, *Moralia*, book V, chapter 11, on 1 Kings, chapter 12: “Suddenly the high things of the world collapse; beautiful things pass away; joys and prosperity vanish. For while the flattering world is seen standing amid its blossoms, sudden fortune throws it into confusion, or swift death, which overturns everything, brings it to an end.”] when it departs [Col. 0204A] from the body; rather, those who love them more mourn more [Note: [Col. 0203] The Benedictine edition; but the Venetian: “rather, those who love them mourn.”] [Note: [Col. 0204C] Those who love them more mourn more. Gregory, *Moralia*, book I, chapter 4: “Nothing is ever lost without pain unless it is possessed without love.” Augustine likewise, *Sermon on the Mount*, book I, chapter 3: “What is held with delight is not abandoned without pain.”].

Therefore, our true friend, the Lord Jesus Christ, must be loved; he will grant us present happiness [Note: [Col. 0203] The Benedictine edition reads: “will grant us happiness and the blessedness of eternal life”; the Venetian edition reads: “will grant us blessedness.”] and eternal blessedness. For our Redeemer is called “Redeemer” because he redeemed us from the captivity of the devil; “Savior,” because he saves us from our sins; “Helper,” because he helps us in times of need and in tribulation; “Protector,” because he protects us so that we may remain unharmed among our enemies; “Welcomer,” because he welcomes us into eternal dwellings.

Therefore, let us fulfill with all our strength the charity, commandments, and love of so great a friend, and preserve within us the nobility of his image. Let us always remember [Note: [Col. 0203] The Benedictine edition reads “and let us recall.”] how illustrious and exceedingly glorious our emperor and friend is. He asks no other gift from us [Col. 0204B] than a spiritual one. Let us take the greatest care we can [Note: [Col. 0204C] “Let us take the greatest care we can,” from Caesarius, sermon 52, in the appendix to volume V of Augustine’s sermons, sermon 229: “Let us labor as much as we can with his help, lest our Lord find in his temple—that is, in ourselves—anything that offends the eyes of his majesty.”], lest he find anything in us [Note: [Col. 0203] Thus the Venetian edition and the Benedictine edition; the words “in us” are absent in the latter witness.] that offends his eyes. And if perhaps, as is customary with the condition of human frailty, the evil spirit imprints some stain of negligence upon us [Note: [Col. 0203] So the Benedictine edition; the Venetian edition reads “inflicts upon us.”], let us hasten with every effort to wash it away through confession, repentance, and the fountain of tears [Note: [Col. 0203] The Benedictine edition notes in the margin that the manuscripts do not contain “and the fountain.”], lest we remain long without the embrace of our friend; for he is more ready to receive us [Note: [Col. 0203] The Benedictine edition notes in the margin that the manuscripts read “to receive us.”] than to lose us, provided only that we do not delay returning to him from day to day. For almighty God hates these two evils in all human beings [Note: [Col. 0204D] “These two evils,” namely, delaying repentance because of excessive presumption, and despair because of the absence of hope. Augustine, *Tractate* 33 on John, no. 8: “People are endangered by both things—by hoping and by despairing, through contrary circumstances and contrary emotions … What, then, does the Lord say to those endangered by both diseases? To those endangered by hope he says: ‘Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day, for his wrath will come suddenly and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you.’ What does he say to those endangered by despair? ‘On whatever day the wicked person turns, I shall forget all his iniquities.’”], namely, negligence in returning and despair of salvation.

Let these two things be far from our thoughts [Col. 0204C], and then he will be near to our souls [Col. 0205A]. Let us not, I beg you, place our confidence in earthly happiness while boasting of it; rather, let us give thanks to him who, although he wished human beings to be rational, commanded us to seek him not with pride but with humility. What greater glory, I ask, or what more exalted honor could there be for us than to be friends of that emperor who is above all emperors? And the more exalted he is in omnipotence [Note: [Col. 0205] Thus the Venetian edition; the Benedictine edition reads “in the power of omnipotence.”] and strength, the more diligent we ought to be in justice, holiness, humility, and observance [Note: [Col. 0205] Thus the Benedictine edition; the Venetian edition reads “in the observance.”] of his commandments.

## CHAPTER IX. Where holiness consists; the value of reading the Scriptures.

Holiness consists in works of justice. Justice, in turn, is fulfilled in two ways: by not doing what he has forbidden and by doing what he has commanded, according to the Prophet: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 33:15). For the entire sequence of the holy books has been written for our instruction [Note: [Col. 0205D] “Written for our instruction,” from the Apostle, Romans 15:4: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction.”]; and this, above all, resounds in our ears and repeats again and again what a person must avoid and what he must follow.

In these books your dignity [Note: [Col. 0205D] “Your dignity.” Du Cange, *Glossary*: “A title of honor by which kings are addressed—and why not princes also? See Besly on the counts of Poitiers, p. 257, and Casaubon on *Pollio*, p. 463, first edition.” From this one may also infer the distinguished rank of our Henry.] knows best how to exercise itself [Note: [Col. 0205] Thus the Benedictine edition; the Venetian edition reads “is accustomed to be exercised.”], because through them God himself, our Lord, speaks to us and shows us the affection of his pious will. Let us recognize and reflect upon the honor with which his embassy must be received by us. What if an embassy or a little written order [Note: [Col. 0205D] “Or a little written order.” I think this is the genuine reading. Embassies are usually sent by kings and princes, not by judges in lawsuits, as the Venetian and Frobenian editions read. A *little written order* (*indiculus*)—sometimes a letter, sometimes a command of a ruler, differing from a *praeceptum* only in that the latter is ordinarily accompanied by a seal, whereas the former is not, as Bignonius holds in his notes on chapter 6 of book I of Marculf’s *Formulae—*can also be issued by kings. “Nothing is more common in that age than the name *indiculus*.” See Bignonius there.] from a king came to us, would we not immediately set aside our other concerns, receive the letter with ready willingness and complete devotion, and strive to fulfill it after reading it? And indeed, the King of kings and Lord of lords, indeed our Redeemer, has deigned through the prophets and apostles to send us his letters from heaven—not to impose upon us some service necessary for himself [Col. 0206A], but to make known what can benefit us for salvation and glory [Note: [Col. 0205] Thus the Benedictine edition; the Venetian edition reads “may be commanded.” The Benedictine edition notes in the margin that a manuscript reads “he knows.”].

## CHAPTER X. Let God be our possession.

*(From Julian Pomerius—or Prosper—On the Contemplative Life, book XI, chapter 16.)* Therefore, if we take pleasure in possessing anything in this world, let us possess God, who possesses all things, with an unencumbered mind [Note: [Col. 0206D] “Therefore, if we take pleasure in possessing anything,” and so forth. That Paulinus had read the books *On the Contemplative Life* is demonstrated by the many passages inserted from this chapter through chapter 20, which were written not by Prosper, as is commonly and incorrectly believed, but by Julian Pomerius. We have Isidore of Seville as a witness in his book *On Illustrious Men*, where he says of Julian: “He also published three books on the contemplation of the future life.” More exacting critics, Du Pin and G. Cave, likewise establish Julian, not Prosper, as their author. In these matters Paulinus proceeds so cautiously and prudently, blending his own material with that of another, that it is clear to a reader who examines and compares the texts that he has not incurred the charge of plagiarism; rather, he adopted another’s offspring in such a way that they appeared to be his own. Who would blame so many holy Fathers who so gracefully and appropriately borrowed selected sayings of earlier Fathers, like a choice bouquet of flowers, to add both adornment and weight to their own writings? We refrain from presenting comparisons, lest we say what has already been said, believing that merely warning the reader is sufficient.] and let us have in him whatever we rightly and devoutly desire. But since no one possesses God except one who is possessed by him, let us ourselves become God’s possession, and God will become our possession [Note: [Col. 0205] The Benedictine edition reads “God our possessor.”]. What could be happier in the world than for someone whose emperor and redeemer becomes his own property, and for divinity itself to deign to be his inheritance? For from him we receive every fruit; in him and from him we always live. What, I ask, is sufficient for a person for whom the Creator himself is not sufficient? What more does one seek when one’s Redeemer ought to be one’s every joy and one’s all?

## CHAPTER XI. The joy of the world.

*(From the same book of Julian, chapter 13.)* Alas, how subtly that ancient enemy deceives us by beguiling us, and spreads such blindness [Note: [Col. 0205] Thus the Venetian edition; the Benedictine edition reads “and the blindness.”] before the eyes of our mind [Note: [Col. 0205] Thus the Benedictine edition; the Venetian edition reads “brings upon us.”] that we cannot distinguish the joys of this age from the joys of the eternal King! For rejoicing is indeed good; but if the person who rejoices does not rejoice in what he ought, what he rejoices in cannot be good.

The earthly soldier rejoices in having acquired honors of this passing age [Note: [Col. 0205] The Benedictine edition does not contain “having acquired.”], beautiful garments, splendid bracelets encircling his arm, and a crown placed upon his head; but such joy is not eternal—it is destined to perish. The robber also rejoices when he has carried off what he desired. The drunkard rejoices when he has found an opportunity for drinking. The adulterer rejoices when he has obtained the pleasure of enjoying a prostitute. The perjurer rejoices if he has acquired the resources of this age by swearing falsely [Note: [Col. 0205] The Venetian edition reads “the one who is perishing,” incorrectly.]. The angry man rejoices if he has carried out his anger. And there are many other examples that your good-mindedness, dearest brother, will be able to comprehend.

Although rejoicing is good, nevertheless rejoicing in these things and things of this kind is a great evil, leading [Note: [Col. 0207] The Venetian edition adds “even unto death.”] to the death of sin [Note: [Col. 0207] Thus the Venetian edition, which gives the clearer reading; the Benedictine edition reads “sin,” and adds in the margin: “*Peccatum* is referred to the verb *est*, not to *perducens*.”]. No crime whatsoever becomes so abhorrent before God as rejoicing by recalling one’s past sins, exulting over them, and continually lying in them [Note: [Col. 0207] Thus Isaiah; the Benedictine edition reads “and therefore.”] [Note: [Col. 0207] The Benedictine edition adds in the margin, from a manuscript, “in it.”]. These are the things we mentioned above: the things in which the world wants us to rejoice, so that we may perish with the lovers of this world. We must reject these joys as poisons of the devil, because they hasten to destroy not only the body but also the soul forever.

## CHAPTER XII. Joy, the weapons and riches of the spirit.

[Col. 0207B]

*(Excerpt from a chapter of the same book.)* I beg you, my brother, I beg you: strike these arrows of the devil against the rock that is Christ [Note: the source cites 1 Corinthians 10:4], take up the shield of faith (Ephesians 6:16), with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the devil; and let us rejoice in the Lord’s good things [Note: [Col. 0207] The Venetian edition omits “of the Lord”], in a pure conscience, in true confession, and in worthy repentance, in mourning and true sorrow—not sorrow according to the world, which produces death, but sorrow according to God, which produces eternal salvation (1 Corinthians 7:10).

The Apostle firmly forbids the sorrow that belongs to this world, saying: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Let every bitterness and anger and indignation and shouting and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice; and be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:31–32).

And as much as we can, let us correct our conduct with diligent care, and hasten to acquire every virtue of all good things, so that we may be able to obtain God’s piety and mercy at the proper time and rejoice unspeakably in the promise of that future kingdom. These are the weapons that arm us against the assault of the devil and commend us to God. These are the weapons that strengthen, fortify, and ennoble our friends. These weapons are with us, and, by God’s gift, they are within us [Note: [Col. 0207] The Venetian edition omits the second “are.”]. These are our true riches.

For chastity makes us chaste, justice makes us just, piety makes us pious, humility makes us humble, gentleness makes us gentle, innocence makes us innocent, simplicity makes us simple, purity makes us pure, prudence makes us prudent, temperance makes us temperate, and charity makes us dear to God and to human beings. All these good things were created by God, the good God.

## CHAPTER XIII. Contempt of the world and of the desires.

*(From Pomerius, book II, On the Contemplative Life, chapter 21, from John II.6.)* Therefore, if we wish to be in him what we ought to be, let us walk spiritually just as the holy apostle John says that he walked. What is it to walk as Christ walked, except to despise the vanity and happiness of this miserable age and not fear to suffer adversity for his name? Let us hope for what he promised and follow where he went before us.

In no way should the miserable sweetness of this age separate us from the love of Christ; nor the excuse of a wife, nor concern for children [Note: [Col. 0207] The Venetian edition reads “concern,” but adds “nor”;] nor a great heap of gold and silver, nor the delight of possessions [Note: [Col. 0207] Thus the Venetian edition; the Benedictine edition reads “the delight of possessing gold and silver.”], while the holy apostle John solemnly warns us, saying: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (1 John 2:15–16, from chapter 19 of his book [Col. 0208B]).

These are the things that expelled Adam and Eve from the paradise of delights into this miserable exile. For if the love of God had not failed them, they would never have begun to love the counsel of the deceitful serpent—indeed, they would not even have believed it. The desire of the eyes was that they wished their eyes to be opened. The ambition of the age was that they believed they could become what God is. And therefore the Apostle, wishing to warn us all against these three kinds of death, said: “Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age.”

## CHAPTER XIV. By what steps our first parents fell into sin.

*(From the same chapter, chapter 19 of Pomerius, book II.)* And so that your goodness, my brother, may understand more easily, if you please, I shall explain how those first human beings—Adam and Eve—committed so great a sin, so that the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ may grant that you always avoid it; for in those two the entire human race was condemned in its origin.

They would not have eaten from the forbidden tree unless they had desired it [Note: [Col. 0207] Thus the Venetian edition; the Benedictine edition and Pomerius at this passage read “had desired it” in both places.]; they would not have desired it unless they had been tempted; they would not have been tempted unless they had been abandoned [Note: [Col. 0207] Pomerius reads “unless they were abandoning.”]; and they would not have been abandoned by God unless they had first abandoned God themselves. Nor would they have abandoned God unless they had grown proud and damnably neglected the likeness of God in whose image they had been made. For this reason their diseased bodies contracted death, and, according to the Lord’s sentence, they are believed to have died on the very day on which the necessity of dying was judicially imposed upon them.

## CHAPTER XV. What it means to imitate Adam or Christ.

[Col. 0208D]

*(From Pomerius, book II, chapter 20.)* We said these things shortly before about the first human beings so that we might escape the example or punishment of their fall and condemnation. For although we were born carnally from Adam, we must not imitate him, but Christ our Lord, in whom we have been reborn through baptism and live.

What is it to imitate Adam except to have ourselves killed by perpetual death through carnal desires and longings? And what is it to imitate Christ except to mortify within ourselves carnal desires and longings [Note: [Col. 0209] Thus the Venetian edition; the Benedictine edition reads “to mortify carnal desires and longings within us”] and to reign happily with him who redeemed us at the price of his blood?

And if at some time we were in Adam, we all fell in him [Note: [Col. 0209] The Venetian edition reads “in him.”]; so, since we have now begun to be in Christ [Note: [Col. 0209] The Venetian edition omits “since.”], let us all rise spiritually with him. And, to say everything in brief, Adam took paradise away from us, while Christ bestowed the kingdoms of heaven and gave his body for us sinners. For Christ died [Note: [Col. 0209] Julian at this passage reads “for sin”; the other editions read “for our sin.”] for sin—not his own, but ours. Yet each one of us does not die for the sin of all, but for one sin.

## CHAPTER XVI. What it means to die to sin and to the world.

What is it to die to sin except to condemn wicked works within ourselves and flee this miserable age? Thus, like a dead person in a tomb, who by his flesh [Note: [Col. 0209] The Venetian edition omits “by his flesh.”] harms no one, acts violently toward no one, slanders no one, oppresses no one, does not envy the good, does not insult the wicked, does not serve the lust of the flesh, does not kindle thirst within himself by drinking more and more, does not burn with the flame of hatred, does not flatter the powerful and wealthy of this age [Note: [Col. 0209] The Benedictine edition notes in the margin that the printed editions add “as many do in our times.”], is not dragged about by restless curiosity, does not concern himself with the great crowd standing around him [Note: [Col. 0209] Thus the Venetian edition; the Benedictine edition reads “does not concern himself with the great crowd standing around him,” referring to chapter 9.], does not swell himself out with gold, silver, or a cloak [Note: [Col. 0209] Thus the Venetian edition; the Benedictine edition reads “cloaks,” noting in the margin that better manuscripts read “cloak.”], does not take pleasure in the greetings of the powerful or of relatives, does not weary himself over injuries, is not puffed up by pride, is not destroyed by the ambition of this age, is not shamefully tossed about by empty glory, is not inflamed by gold, bracelets, or all the false riches of this age, is not driven by the fury of mad rage, is not attracted by the stoutness and love of horses, is not made greedy by the most beautiful appearance of women, is not provoked to laughter by the words of wretched actors, is not disturbed by the quarrels of this age, is not exalted by boldness, is not delighted by the joys of this age, is not made angry by animosity, is not made suspicious by perversity, is not made verbose by vanity, is not made a mocker by malice [Note: [Col. 0209] Thus the Benedictine and Venetian editions; Pomerius has “an injurious person” in the text and “a mocker” in the margin.], and is not spun about by the fickle love of this age, making him changeable and unstable [Note: [Col. 0209] The Benedictine edition notes in the margin that the manuscripts add “makes him.”].

I have prolonged the enumeration of these and similar things so that your most affectionate brotherhood may understand that a person dead in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0209] The Benedictine edition notes in the margin that the Colbert manuscripts read “mortal.”] can neither do nor suffer the things I have mentioned. And so that we may not grow sluggish in such matters [Note: [Col. 0209] Thus the Benedictine edition; the Venetian edition reads “so that we may not be tortured.”], let us strive as much as we can, with God’s help, to mortify our bodies with their vices and desires (Galatians 5:24), and let us put on the new person, who was created according to God in the justice and holiness [Note: [Col. 0209] The Venetian edition reads “the holiness of truth.”] of truth (Ephesians 4:24).

Let us take no pleasure in human praises, willingly lend no ear to detractors, trust none of our flatterers, and not be at odds [Note: [Col. 0209] The Benedictine edition adds in the margin, in the printed editions: “with those subject to us and with our brothers.”]. Rather, let us call those whom we can to harmony, because, according to the Gospel, “Blessed are the feet that run toward peace” (perhaps from Matthew 5:9 or Romans 10:15, from Isaiah 52:7).

## CHAPTER XVII. What it means to live according to the flesh.

*(From Pomerius, book III, chapter 1.)* Let us not be carnal—that is, let us not live carnally in this age—for the Apostle says: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die” (Romans 8:13).

Therefore, the person who lives according to the flesh is the one who lives according to himself. For he is a human being, and he lives, and he lives according to himself: he goes where he wishes, sleeps when he wishes, speaks what he wishes, and to whom and where he wishes; he eats and drinks when he wishes and as much as he wishes; he laughs and engages in disgraceful amusement [Note: [Col. 0209] The Venetian edition reads “and rejoices.”] among those he wishes and when he wishes.

Finally, he seeks whatever is pleasant to his nostrils; whatever is pleasing to the touch, whatever delights the eyes, whatever is agreeable to his body, he practices and pursues as he wishes and when he wishes, because he desires everything—permitted and forbidden—according to the flesh. He delights in the most beautiful garments, riders, and weapons as he wishes and when he wishes; and thus he lives and delights not according to God but carnally, and fulfills all the desires of his flesh as he wishes and when he wishes.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Remedies for the vices.

*(From the same book, book III, chapter 3.)* Therefore, dearest brother in Christ, we must implore divine clemency so that spiritual delight may diminish carnal desires, piety may restrain anger toward cruelty within us [Note: [Col. 0209] The Venetian edition reads thus; the Benedictine edition reads “may resist.” Pomerius has “will resist cruelty.”], patience may check wickedness, chastity may conquer lust, tranquility may endure animosity, measured silence may restrain buffoonery and verbosity, spiritual diligence in vigils, prayers, and almsgiving may replace curiosity [Note: [Col. 0209] Thus the Benedictine edition and Pomerius; the Venetian edition reads “may cut off curiosity …”], sobriety may master drunkenness, gentleness may rule anger and fury, maturity may govern frivolity, true chastity may exclude lust, love of God and neighbor may curb love of the world, and profound humility may trample down boasting and pride. For humility makes human beings like the holy angels, while pride made demons out of angels.

## CHAPTER XIX. No sin exists without pride, which belongs to the devil, just as humility belongs to Christ.

[Col. 0210D]

(From the same book, Book III, chapter 2.) And to show clearly that it is itself the beginning, end, and cause of all sins: not only is pride itself sin, but no sin could, can, or ever will exist without pride. For every sin is nothing other than contempt of God, by which we despise his commandments; and nothing else persuades a human being to this except pride.

Moreover [Note: Venetian: *superbus* (“proud”).], pride and greed are so entirely one evil that neither can pride be found without greed, nor greed [Note: Venetian: *cupidus* (“greedy”); Pom has both readings.] without pride. For from pride are born heresies, schisms, slanders, envies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, disputes, resentments, ambitions, exaltation, presumption, boastfulness, loquacity, vanity, unrest, lying, perjury, and other things of this kind, which it would take too long to enumerate individually. Greed likewise makes people gluttonous, intemperate, drunken, covetous, rapacious, fornicators, adulterers, debauchers, incestuous persons, shamefully depraved persons, and guilty of countless other things [Col. 0211B], through which the devil customarily plunges the human race into ruin.

(A similar—indeed, I might say the same—account will be found in St. Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXXIV, at the end of the final chapter.)

Through pride and greed the devil says, “I will ascend into heaven” (Isaiah 14:13); Christ, in humility, says, “My soul is humbled to the earth” (Psalm 43:25). Through pride and greed the devil says, “I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:14); Christ, through humility, although he was in the form of God, “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; he humbled himself to the Father, becoming obedient unto death” (Philippians 2:6 ff.). Through pride and greed the devil says, “Above the stars of God I will exalt my throne” (Isaiah 14:13); Christ, in humility, says, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble” [Col. 0211C] “of heart” (Matthew 11:29).

The greedy and proud devil speaks through Pharaoh, saying, “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exodus 5:2); Christ, in humility, says, “If I should say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar; but I do know him, and I keep his commandments” (John 8:55).

The proud and greedy devil says, “The rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezekiel 29:9); Christ, in humility, says, “I can do nothing of myself” (John 5:36); “but my Father, remaining in me, himself does the works” [Col. 0212A] (John 14:10).

The proud and greedy devil says, “All the kingdoms of the world and their glory are mine, and I give them to whomever I wish” (Matthew 4:8). Christ, although he was rich, became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

The proud and greedy devil says, “As abandoned eggs are gathered up, so I have gathered the whole earth; and there was no one who moved a wing, opened his mouth, or chirped” (Isaiah 10:14). Christ, in humility, says, “I have become like a solitary pelican; I have kept watch and become like a solitary sparrow on the roof” (Psalm 101:7–8).

Through pride and greed the devil says, “With the sole of my feet I have dried up all the streams of the embankments” (Isaiah 37:25). Christ, in humility, says, “Can I not ask my Father, and he will provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matthew 26:53) [Col. 0212B].

And, to bring the matter finally to a conclusion, through pride and greed the devil is hurled down into hell with a great fall; Christ, through humility, is lifted up to heaven.

Therefore, dearest brother, I have described for you a few snares of the devil’s deceit and steps of holy humility, so that you may more easily teach those subject to you how and in what manner they may escape these snares and, through humility, possess the kingdom of heaven. And if we wish to complete the course of our contest and reach eternal blessedness, let us first beware of evil greed and devilish pride, and with complete humility strive to follow the footsteps of Christ. If someone serving an earthly emperor struggles to obey all his commands, how much more ought one who is to serve the heavenly Emperor to keep the heavenly commandments? [Col. 0212C]

[Note: From this chapter through chapter 45, what Paulinus has here may be found in the *Admonition to a Spiritual Son*, placed in disordered arrangement among the works of St. Basil the Great [Col. 0211D]. All agree that this admonition is not Basil’s, since they assign it to an uncertain author. Du Pin, Cave, and Oudinus add that it is only a Latin work. Indeed, it contains nothing that has the character of a Greek text, even though its title assigns it to an uncertain translator or an anonymous author, as in the Appendix to the *Codex Regularum*. Lucas Holstenius produces it in a better order, according to Oudinus. I would believe it to be the product of some more recent monk, who tries to apply to a monk and ascetic what Paulinus explains to a layman holding public office. The compiler of the work himself suggests this at the outset when he says: “For these words are mine, but they have been drawn from divine sources. I shall not instruct you in a new doctrine, but in one that I learned from my fathers.” I do not set out the conflicting passages in the notes, lest I merely repeat what has already been done. I point out only that P. Garner, the most recent editor of St. Basil’s works, has brought forward nothing certain about this matter [Col. 0212C], although in volume II, published at Paris in 1722, page 706, he lists this work under *Admonitions*. Indeed, in the preface to the same volume [Col. 0212D], section 60, he writes: “Finally, I would dare affirm that this third little work—that is, this one—is indeed not Basil’s; but by whom, or at what time, it was composed, I frankly do not know.” If he had compared it with this *Book of Exhortation*, he would have said, together with his fellow Fathers of the Benedictine Congregation, that it was Paulinus’s, or excerpted from Paulinus’s book.]

## CHAPTER XX. The spiritual and earthly soldier

My brother, my brother [Note: The Venetian edition adds here, “my dearest brother.”], rouse your soul to vigilance, and let no sleep weigh it down. An earthly soldier, wherever he is sent, is ready and prepared, and cannot excuse himself on account of a wife or children [Note: [Col. 0212D] “Nor because of a wife.” Among the Hebrews, a soldier who had married was released from military service, at least temporarily, as stated in Deuteronomy 20:7 and 1 Maccabees 3:56: “And Judas said to those who … had betrothed wives … that each should return to his house according to the law.” In the Roman army, it was sometimes forbidden to have women in the camp. Hence Propertius, Book IV, elegy 3, verse 259:

“Would that Roman camps had been open to girls:

I would have been the faithful burden of your military service.”

They wisely judged that chastity suited military service. Servius, commenting on Book III of the *Aeneid*, verse 519, “We move the camp,” says: “A camp is where a soldier has stood. It is called *castra*, as if from *casta*, ‘chaste’; or because lust was castrated there, for a woman was never present in those places.” And on Book VIII, verse 688, “And the Egyptian wife follows the crime,” he says of Antony and Cleopatra: “The crime consisted not only in the fact that a Roman took an Egyptian woman in marriage, but also in the fact that the woman followed the camp; among our ancestors this was considered a great disgrace. Hence, when Pompey was about to wage war in Lesbos, he left his wife.” Tacitus confirms the custom in *Annals*, Book XIV, chapter 27: “The veterans, unaccustomed either to contracting marriages or to raising children, left their homes bereft and without descendants.” Severus nevertheless softened this severity, as Herodian reports—and at the same time criticizes—in Book III, chapter 8: “He granted many concessions that they had never previously received. … For he permitted them to keep a woman at home. All these things seemed unlikely to make them, girded and prepared for war, well suited to military discipline.” Tertullian, who lived in the time of Severus, perhaps had this in mind when he wrote in *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 8: “Clearly, only the homes of married men are flourishing. The households of celibates, eunuchs, soldiers, and travelers without wives have perished. For are we not also soldiers, indeed of a greater discipline, since we serve so great an emperor?” These words agree with what Paulinus adds below: “Much more, the soldier of Christ, without the hindrance of this world, ought to obey his emperor, the Lord Jesus Christ.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition reads *ac* (“and”) instead of *aut* (“or”).] Much more, the soldier of Christ, without the hindrance [Col. 0213A] of this world [Note: “Without the hindrance of this world.” He aptly calls the care of wife, children, and household a hindrance. Thus the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 7:33: “He who is with a wife is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife,” which he later calls a hindrance to entreating the Lord. Or, as Chrysostom calls it in Homily 19 on this passage [Col. 0214C], a hindrance to philosophy.] ought to obey his emperor, the Lord Jesus Christ, who redeemed him with his precious blood.

You, an earthly soldier, go into battle against a visible enemy; but he does not cease fighting daily against an invisible enemy. You struggle against the enemies of your body [Note: [Col. 0213] The Venetian edition reads this way; the Benedictine edition has “to fight against the bodies of your enemy.”], using carnal weapons; his struggle, however, is against the devil, with spiritual weapons. In battle you wear an iron helmet [Note: [Col. 0214C] “An iron helmet.” Originally helmets were made from the hides of animals. In Homer, *Iliad*, Book X, verse 257, a bull’s-hide helmet is given to Diomedes: “Around his head he placed a helmet of bull’s hide.” Xenophon, Book V of the *Expedition of Cyrus the Younger*: “The Mossynoeci protected their heads with leather helmets, such as those generally used by the Paphlagonians.” Herodotus, Book VII: “The Thracians wear caps of fox-skin.”] on your head; but his helmet is Christ.

So that you may not be wounded, you are clothed in a breastplate; but he is clothed in Christ’s charity as his breastplate. You hurl spears and arrows against your enemy; he strives to direct humility and words that bring salvation against his enemy. Until you finish the battle, you do not throw away your weapons, lest you be wounded by your adversary [Col. 0213B]; he must never be unarmed, because his enemy is more cunning than yours.

Your enemy fights for a time; his enemy, for as long as he remains in the body, does not cease fighting against him. Your weapons are laborious and heavy to carry; his weapons are gentle and light. For earthly labor you receive an earthly gift [Note: [Col. 0214D] “You receive a gift.” That is, a present with which soldiers were rewarded by the emperor, just as the people received a *congiarium*. Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 7: “When the recruit was led into the Forum, he announced a *congiarium* for the people and a gift for the soldiers.”]; he, however, will receive [Note: [Col. 0213] The Benedictine edition reads “will receive”; the Venetian edition, “receives.”] a heavenly reward for spiritual labor.

You adorn your arms with the ornament of armlets [Note: [Col. 0214D] “The ornament of armlets.” Festus writes: “They think that the armlets of gold worn by military men who have received them from commanders were so called because the ancients called the shoulders together with the arms *armos*, from which weapons hanging from them were called *arma*.”]; he receives from Christ the adornment of virtues as the beauty of his soul [Note: [Col. 0213] The Venetian edition reads “you decorate”; the Benedictine edition, “you are decorated.”]. For the one who casts away the earthly pomp of this world is always awaiting a heavenly gift from Christ.

Woe to us if we reject from ourselves the gentle yoke of Christ and place upon our souls whatever is heavy and burdensome to carry—and, while loving it, fall into danger and so into death [Note: [Col. 0213] The Benedictine edition reads “fall”; the Venetian edition, “we fall.”]

## CHAPTER XXI. To promote the love of God, he recalls the benefits of creation and redemption

Therefore, dearest brother, let us consider who it is who redeemed us with his precious blood, and what we owe him who redeemed us in such great poverty. If we love our earthly parents with such affection, although they endured labor on our behalf for only a short time, should not our heavenly Father be loved much more, since he was crucified for us [Note: [Col. 0213] The Venetian edition reads “who was crucified”]?

For whatever service our parents have rendered us is his gift: before we were born, by his providence he prepared parents for us in this world, so that we might be nourished by their care [Note: [Col. 0213] In the margin of the Benedictine edition, the manuscripts of Corbie read “we were born.”], and he filled our mother’s breasts with milk from which we might be nourished. Therefore, let us love our Redeemer more than all else, for he fashioned both us and our parents with his own hands; and let us attribute all the good that is done for us daily to his mercy, not to our own strength.

Scripture commands us to love our parents as our own inmost being, provided that they do not prevent us from approaching the service of Christ [Note: [Col. 0214D] “Provided that they do not prevent us from approaching,” etc. Jerome, Letter 10 to Furia on preserving widowhood: “Honor your father, but if he does not separate you from the true Father. Know the bond of blood to last only so long as he knows his Creator.” With this intention he wrote, but more forcefully Heliodorus, Letter 1, persuading him to embrace solitude: “Remember the day of your enlistment, when you were buried with Christ in baptism and swore in the words of the sacrament that, for his name, you would spare neither father nor mother … Even if your mother shows you the breasts that nourished you, her hair scattered and her garments torn; even if your father lies in the light of day: trample over your father and fly with dry eyes to the standard of the cross. In this matter, cruelty is the only kind of piety.”]; but if they do, we owe them not even burial [Note: [Col. 0215B] “Not even burial,” etc. This comes from Luke 9:60: “Let the dead bury their dead,” which the Lord answered to the young man who wished, under the pretext of filial piety, to withdraw from following him. St. Ambrose raises and resolves the question in his commentary on Luke, Book VII: “Since we regard the duty of burying the dead as religious, how is burial even of one’s father forbidden here, unless it is so that you may understand that human matters must be placed after divine ones? The devotion is good, but the hindrance is greater.” St. Peter Chrysologus likewise says in Sermon 19: “He does not deny the service of piety, but places divine service before human affections. Hear what the disciple said: ‘Permit me first to go and bury my father.’ This should not have been first for him, but second: an earthly father must be placed after the heavenly Father.”]

Christ must be loved above our parents, because parents do not grant us what Christ grants us. He himself said in the Gospel: “Whoever loves father or mother or children or fields more than me is not worthy of me” (Matthew 10:37). The more anyone loves him, the happier and more blessed he will become.

For he loved us so greatly that he even deigned to die for us; his hands, which performed countless miracles, were fastened with nails for our redemption; to his honey-sweet mouth, from which saving teaching flowed, the ungodly offered gall as food; he who harmed no one was beaten; and he who cursed no one endured insults and curses for our sake. He endured all these things so that he might grant us eternal life.

And although he bestows such great benefits upon us, he asks nothing from us except that we love him and preserve our souls and bodies undefiled for him, so that he may always dwell in us and we may remain in him. For he does not ask gold from us [Note: [Col. 0215C] “He does not ask gold from us.” Compare Psalm 49:9: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks.” Or Isaiah 43:23: “I did not make you serve through offering, nor did I burden you with incense. You did not buy me fragrant cane with silver, nor did you satisfy me with the fat of your sacrifices.” Lucretius, otherwise an impious poet, recognized this, although he wrote much incorrectly about divinity; nevertheless he expressed this truth in Book I, verse 60:

“Powerful in its own strength, needing nothing of us.”

What God seeks, since he seeks us and not our possessions, as Paulinus says, is explained by Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, Book III, chapter 1: “God alone is in need of absolutely nothing, and he rejoices especially when he sees our minds clean in their adornment.” Lactantius said the same in other words in *Divine Institutes*, Book VI, chapter 1: “That holy and unique majesty desires nothing else from human beings except innocence alone.” See Micah 6:8.]

nor silver, nor cloaks, nor costly garments, nor armlets, nor fields, nor anything else of this kind; rather, he seeks us ourselves. He desires to rest in us. Let us therefore approach him, so that we may have eternal life.

## CHAPTER XXII. He inculcates love of one’s neighbor and devotion to concord

Let us therefore have within us love of God and of our neighbor, because whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law (Romans 13:8). But whoever, on the contrary, hates is a murderer (1 John 3:15). Whoever loves his brother has a tranquil heart [Note: [Col. 0215D] “Whoever loves his brother is at peace,” etc. Nothing is truer. Hence Cassiodorus, in *On Friendship*, chapter [on] charity, calls it “the true rest of the human mind and perfect Sabbath.” At the end of the book he exclaims: “O excellence of charity, O sweetness of love, O security, O rest, O deified Sabbath! … Who will grant that, transferred by me into the love of God and neighbor, I may sleep and rest in peace and unity between these two destinies?” This is what John Climacus in *The Ladder of Paradise*, step 8, calls “complete victory over anger, a tranquil serenity of soul amid the storms of monstrous tempests.” The truly honey-sweet Bernard possessed this quality; although the Premonstratensians accused him unjustly in Letter 252, he nevertheless wrote to their abbot near the end of the letter: “But as for me, brothers, whatever you do, I have resolved always to love you, even when I am not loved … You may loosen, or rather break, your bonds with me, but not mine with you. I will cling to you even if you do not wish it; I will cling to you even if I myself do not wish it. Long ago I bound myself with a strong bond, with sincere charity, that charity which never fails. When you are disturbed, I will be peaceful; to those who disturb me I will give place to anger, so that I may not give place to the devil. I will be overcome by quarrels, but I will conquer through service. I will give to the unwilling, add to the ungrateful, and honor those who despise me.”]

but whoever hates his brother is surrounded by a storm [Note: [Col. 0216C] “He who hates is always in turmoil.” This is also entirely true because of the discipline of opposites. “They define hatred,” says Plutarch in *On Envy and Hatred*, “as a certain affection and determination to do harm, together with the seeking of an opportunity to do so.” When anger is joined to hatred, as usually happens—for Cicero in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book IV, defines hatred as inveterate anger—it truly raises disturbances and storms in the mind. Hear Seneca, *On Anger*, Book I, chapter 1: “This emotion of anger is wholly agitated and in motion … while it harms another, heedless of itself, rushing upon the very weapons, and eagerly considering many plans of revenge. Therefore some of the wise have called anger a brief insanity.” And below: “Thus the signs of those who are angry are the same as those of madmen. Their eyes blaze and flash; a deep flush spreads across the whole face, as the blood boils up from the innermost organs; their lips tremble, their teeth are clenched, their hair bristles and rises, their breath is constrained and hissing, their twisting joints make a sound, they groan and bellow, and their speech is broken because the words are scarcely articulated; they clap their hands repeatedly, stamp the ground with their feet, and their whole body is agitated and gives signs of great anger—a face ugly and terrible to see, disfiguring and swelling with rage.” Hence Chrysostom, on Psalm 5: “To hate is grievous and excites disturbances and tumults.” And in Homily 8 on Matthew chapter 5: “Hatred is the spirit of darkness, and wherever it settles it soils the beauty of health.”]

A gentle and kindly man, even when he suffers harm, counts it as nothing [Note: [Col. 0216D] “A gentle and kindly man, even when he suffers harm, counts it as nothing.” By “harm” I mean harm inflicted by adversaries; the discussion concerns this, as is clear to anyone who considers it. Climacus speaks most aptly of this gentleness in *The Ladder of Paradise*, step 24: “It is a jutting rock against the sea of anger, which dissolves and breaks all the waves that strike it, while it itself is neither moved nor broken.” Hence Lactantius wisely criticizes Cicero in *Divine Institutes*, Book VI, chapter 18, because Cicero says that a wise man “ought to harm no one unless provoked by injury.” “How,” Lactantius says, “did he corrupt a simple and true statement by adding two words? … He said that a good man would do harm if provoked; but from this very fact he must lose the name of good man, if he does harm.” Indeed, even the pagans valued this disregard of injuries most highly, as the surest sign of perfect wisdom and virtue. Seneca exalted it as an example in Cato. “A certain man,” he says in *On Anger*, Book II, chapter 32, “struck Marcus Cato unintentionally in the bath … When the man later apologized, Cato said: ‘I do not remember having been struck.’ He thought it better not to acknowledge the blow than to avenge it.” And in *On Constancy of the Wise Man*, chapter 14, he says of this same matter: “He showed greater greatness of spirit in not acknowledging it than he would have shown in forgiving it.” This is indeed to regard as nothing the harms and injuries we suffer.], whereas an unjust man considers even a small word [Note: [Col. 0217C] “A small word.” Indeed, sometimes merely the suspicion of a word or action directed against someone kindles anger in certain minds. Seneca notes this in several places in *On Anger*, Book II, chapter 22: “The cause of anger is the opinion of an injury, which should not readily be believed … Let the ears not be easy to accusations”; and in the following chapter: “What of the fact that we are driven not only by accusations but also by suspicions, and, interpreting the faces and laughter of others for the worse, become angry with the innocent?” Chapter 24: “Suspicion and conjecture, the most deceptive provocations, must be removed from the mind. ‘He greeted me rather coldly; he did not cling to my kiss; he abruptly cut short the conversation he had begun; he did not invite me to dinner; his face seemed more averted.’ Suspicion will never lack an argument.” In Book III, chapter 2, he says: “It is not useful to see everything or hear everything. Let many injuries pass us by, most of which are not perceived by the person who does not know of them. Do you not wish to be irritable? Then do not be curious. Whoever investigates what has been said about him, whoever rummages through malicious conversations, even when they were held secretly, disturbs himself. Some interpretation leads to the point at which things appear to be injuries.” Richard of St. Victor, *On the State of the Inner Man*, treatise I, chapter 9: “It is truly astonishing, indeed pitiable, that this noble creature, created in the image of God and set above every creature, should be violently shaken from its upright state by a small word, a slight breath, the sound of a tongue, or a blow of air, and driven into a whirl like a tempest.”] spoken by his neighbor as an insult.

The person full of charity goes forward with a tranquil mind and a most serene face; the person full of hatred walks in anger. But you, dearest brother, do not cause anyone scandal by your life. (A matter that does not concern you, leave to others to handle; unless you are asked or questioned, disentangle yourself from it; judge only what is pleasing to God; and, if you cannot do otherwise, avoid the unjust judgments of others and make room for mercy.) [Note: [Col. 0217] The Benedictine edition places in the margin: “A gloss absent from the manuscripts,” but nevertheless does not remove it, as it does elsewhere in the text.]

Do not do what is useful to you, but what is pleasing to him [Note: [Col. 0217] The Venetian edition reads “to God.”]. What you do not wish to be done to you, do not wish to happen to your neighbor [Note: [Col. 0217D] “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not desire to happen to your neighbor.” This comes from the admonition in Tobit 4:16: “What you hate to have done to you by another, see that you never do to another.” This maxim pleased Alexander Severus so much that, according to Aelius Lampridius in his *Life*, chapter 51, “he often proclaimed what he had heard from certain Jews or Christians and retained; and he ordered it to be announced by a herald whenever he corrected anything: ‘What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.’ He loved this saying so greatly that he ordered it to be inscribed both in the palace and on public buildings.” The saying of Christ the Lord in Matthew 7:12 agrees with it. Jerome, Letter 10—or rather Paulinus’s letter to Celantia—writes of it: “You should choose that saying of the Gospel as a kind of concise admonition and write it above your heart, for it is spoken by the Lord’s mouth as a summary of all justice: ‘Whatever you wish people to do to you, do likewise to them.’”] (Tobit 4:16).

If you see him conducting himself in good works, rejoice with him and call his joy your own [Note: [Col. 0218C] “Make his joy your own … count his sadness as your own.” This agrees with Paul’s statement: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Romans 12:15). St. Bernard in Sermon 10 on the *Song of Songs* calls these two things—compassion and congratulation—the breasts of the bride. St. Gregory says aptly in Homily 5 on the Gospel: “A good will is to fear another’s adversity as our own and to rejoice in our neighbor’s prosperity as in our own progress; to regard another’s losses as our own and another’s gains as our own.”]; and if he suffers some adversity, count his sadness as your own [Note: [Col. 0217] The printed Benedictine editions add in the margin: “And grieve not only with the righteous but also with sinners.”]

Never love your neighbor with a feigned heart, because through such things God is provoked to anger. Whoever embraces peace prepares a dwelling for Christ in the lodging of his mind, because Christ is peace [Note: [Col. 0218C] “Christ is peace and wishes to rest in peace.” Compare the Apostle (Ephesians 2:14): “He himself is our peace.” Concerning his rest, see Psalm 75:3: “His dwelling is in peace.” Guaric, abbot, applies this in Sermon 3 on the Advent of the Lord: “When you invite Jesus,” he says, “take care not to invite the God of majesty into a filthy and unworthy lodging where even a quarrelsome wife does not allow you yourself to dwell in peace … for his dwelling is made only in peace.” Hear Jerome commenting on this passage of the psalm: “God’s dwelling is only in a soul that has peace. Therefore, let the soul that has no peace know that it is not God’s dwelling. ‘My peace I give you; my peace I leave you.’ This is the Savior’s inheritance.”], and wishes to rest in peace.

But God has utterly cursed the angry, envious, slanderous, lying, and proud person. An envious man is like a ship tossed by the waves of the sea; he is always in turmoil [Note: [Col. 0218D] “The envious person is always in agitation.” Ovid treats envy correctly and at length in *Metamorphoses*, Book II; among other passages, he sings at verse 780:

“He enjoys no sleep, awakened by watchful cares;

He sees the ungrateful, wastes away as he watches,

He gnaws at the success of others, and is himself gnawed by it.

His punishment is himself.”]

He rages pointlessly like a ravening wolf; he is held in misery, and, wasting away, is reduced to nothing; always full of fury, he becomes a partner of demons.

The peaceful person possesses a secure mind; he is wholly protected by the host of angels and filled with the fruit of joy, rejoicing and delighting in the Lord. Everything about him is ordered in peace. He drives away discord and enlightens the hidden places of his mind. He will be worthy of the fellowship of the angels and will possess forever the kingdom of eternal blessedness.

## CHAPTER XXIII. The virtues of the soul

Do not, I beg you, my brother, think that God’s commandments are fables or that they were issued by me, since they have flowed from the fountain of our Savior [Note: [Col. 0217] The Venetian edition reads “have flowed.”] [Col. 0218B]. Let no adversity or prosperity of the world break your soul away from God’s precepts and commandments or from the charity that is in Christ Jesus our Lord [Col. 0219A].

For it is the virtue [Note: [Col. 0219B] “It is the virtue of your soul.” It belongs to the soul because it is in the soul, but it comes from the gift of God—or rather, it is “the gift of God, from whom alone it can be given,” as Augustine says in *The City of God*, Book IV, chapter 20. Since “virtue was defined by the ancients as the art of living well and rightly,” as the same holy Doctor teaches in the following chapter, Paulinus here proposes to Henry a certain summary of the good life, placing it almost entirely in courage, endurance of evils, and avoidance of enticements. For, as Cicero says in *Tusculan Disputations*, Book II: “It is called virtue from *vir*, ‘man’; and the quality especially proper to a man is courage.” In the fragments of Lucilius, verse 910, certain duties of virtue are listed, almost in the manner and order in which Paulinus has given them:

“Virtue is knowing what each thing possesses.

Virtue is knowing what is right, useful, and honorable;

what is good and what is bad, likewise what is useful, shameful, and dishonorable;

virtue is knowing the limit and measure of what is to be sought;

virtue is being able to pay the price for riches.

Virtue is giving what is truly owed to honor;

being the enemy and opponent of evil men and evil morals,

but the defender of good men and good morals;

exalting such men, wishing them well, and living as their friend;

and considering the interests of one’s country first,

then those of one’s parents, and lastly one’s own.”] of your soul to love God and to hate what God does not love. It is the virtue of your soul to pursue patience and to turn away from all impatience. It is the virtue of your soul to preserve chastity both of body and of soul. It is the virtue of your soul to despise the vain glory of this world, to trample upon all perishable things, and, for love of him who redeemed you, to labor while you live in the body.

It is the virtue of your soul to cultivate humility and abhor pride. It is the virtue of your soul to restrain and suppress anger and fury. It is the virtue of your soul to turn away from all folly and embrace divine wisdom. It is the virtue of your soul to subject every pleasure of the flesh and raise your mind toward Christ.

You could therefore have obtained these virtues easily—indeed, most easily—if you had been willing to avoid concern for worldly affairs and perishable earthly things, and had placed nothing before the love of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Let him not be drawn away by any love from the endeavor to please God in all things

O my brother, love God with your whole mind, so that you may please him in all your actions. For whoever is joined in marriage hastens to please his wife (1 Corinthians 7:33); much more must the soul redeemed by Christ’s blood please Christ, its bridegroom.

For God does not wish to be loved only with words (Matthew 15:8; James 1:11, 13), but with a pure heart and righteous works, because he is the hearer and examiner not of words but of the heart (Wisdom 1:6) [Note: [Col. 0219] The Venetian edition has, without any intelligible sense: “righteous, good, not of words,” etc.].

Never, I beg you, my brother, let carnal love exclude heavenly love from you. Never, I beg you, let the sweetness of this storm-tossed and wretched world deceive you. Let no bodily beauty seduce you, lest death enter your soul through the windows of your eyes (Jeremiah 9:21).

## CHAPTER XXV. How fleeting are the delights of the flesh

Tell me, I beg you, my brother, what advantage is there in the beauty of the flesh? Is it not like grass [Note: [Col. 0219C] “Is it not like grass,” etc. This comes from Isaiah 40:6: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field”; and Job 14:2: “Man comes forth like a flower and is cut down.” David likewise says in Psalm 102:14: “Man’s days are like grass; like the flower of the field, so he will blossom.” St. Gregory gathers all these passages in *Moralia*, Book XI, chapter 26, when he says: “He comes forth like a flower who shines in the flesh; but he is cut down because he is reduced to corruption. For what are human beings born into the world except certain flowers in a field? … Life in the flesh is therefore a flower in grass. [Col. 0221B]

Do not lend [Note: [Col. 0222C]

“Do not lend your ears,” and so forth. Scripture and the Fathers frequently warn that ears should not be given to whisperers. They also provide a method by which we may resist so dangerous an evil. Sirach 28:28 says: “Hedge in thy ears with thorns, hear not a wicked tongue”—perhaps suggesting that, in listening, we should adopt a certain sternness of countenance, one that shows we resent the insolence of their tongue and that, like a thorn pricking and repelling those who try to enter where they have no right, it should prevent that tongue from insinuating itself into our ears and minds. Solomon had expressed the same thing in other words in Proverbs 25:23: “The north wind driveth away rain, and a sad countenance a backbiting tongue.”

Hence Jerome—or, more truly, Paulinus—in letter 14 to Celantia says: “Do not grant authority to detractors by agreeing with them, lest by your nodding you nourish their vice.” Chrysostom, in Homily 3 *To the People of Antioch*, shows that this is how one should act:

> Say to your neighbor: “Do you have someone whom you may praise and commend?” I open my ears to receive perfumes; but if you wish to say something bad, I close the entrance with words. ## CHAPTER XXVII. Confession of sins

All evil vices ought to be alien from us, since Christ wishes to be our inheritance. Therefore, because we are uncertain about such matters, let us humbly prostrate ourselves before the face of our merciful Father and quickly bring our sins into the open, so that our heavenly Father Himself may erase them. And when we have confessed, let us not justify ourselves in prayer, lest, like that Pharisee, we depart condemned. Let us remember that tax collector [Note: [Col. 0223]

The Venetian edition has “let us remember.”], and let us pray in such a way that we may be worthy to obtain pardon for our offenses. May the cry of our heart strike the ears of almighty God, for in a pure mind He will be appeased at the time of prayer.

## CHAPTER XXX. That he should avoid the evils of greed

For a greedy man holds his soul for sale [Note: [Col. 0226C]

“He holds his soul for sale.” From Sirach 10:9–10: “There is nothing more wicked than a covetous man . . . and there is nothing more wicked than to love money: for such a one setteth even his own soul to sale.” This is because, as Cornelius says here, “he sells his soul to the devil for gold.” Or because in Scripture the life of the body is sometimes designated by the word “soul,” as in John 15:13: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.” Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologiae* II–II, question 118, article 5, reply to objection 1, interprets the passage as follows:

> The covetous man holds his soul for sale because he exposes his soul—that is, his life—to dangers for the sake of money.

Augustine, or someone else, includes both senses in the sermon formerly numbered 25 *On the Words of the Lord*, now numbered 367 in the latest edition:

> What, I ask, is this madness of souls: to lose life, to desire death; to acquire gold, to lose heaven?]]

If he finds an opportunity to covet someone’s gold or silver, beautiful clothing, or even any woman beautiful in face, he commits murder for nothing. And just as someone pours out water upon the ground, so for him it is to pour out the blood of his neighbor [Note: [Col. 0226D]

“Just as someone pours out water upon the ground, so for him it is to pour out blood.” Psalm 78:3 says: “They have shed their blood like water, round about Jerusalem.” This comparison is frequent in Scripture, especially to signify abundance or the worthlessness of the thing poured out. This is the sense in which we should understand the Psalmist’s words in the person of the suffering Lord Christ, Psalm 22:14: “I am poured out like water.” In the first sense, the passage in Hosea 5:10 is to be understood: “I will pour out my wrath upon them like water.”].

Many souls have fallen into mortal danger because of greed, and many were stoned at the Lord’s command for this reason (Joshua 7:25). Saul became alienated from God because of avarice, and at last, expelled from the royal throne, he was killed by his enemies (1 Samuel 15). I could have said many things about many people, but a word is enough for the wise [Note: [Col. 0226D]

“A word is enough for the wise.” This is a proverbial saying. In *Phormio*, line 540, act III, scene 3, Terence has Antipho and Geta converse as follows:

> Ant. Is my father here?  
> Get. I know—but what of it?  
> Ant. Ah, a word is enough for the wise.

That is, as Donatus observes on this passage: “A brief statement, serving almost as an admonition, is enough for a wise person; this is also commonly said: a few words are enough for one who understands.”].

Our Lord and Savior wished to exclude the love of money from the hearts of the Pharisees; but because they were exceedingly greedy, they mocked the Lord’s salutary words (Matthew 15). The love of money likewise did not permit that rich man whom the Lord invited to the heavenly kingdom to enter it (Matthew 19:2). And Judas’s breast burned with the flame of avarice, so that he handed over the Lord, the giver of all good things, into the hands of the impious (Matthew 26:15). A greedy man is like hell. For however many hell devours, it never says, “It is enough.” So too, even if all treasures should flow into the greedy man, he will never be satisfied.

> The labors of many years, prayers, almsgiving, fasts, and vigils, if they end in pride, are counted as nothing before God.]

But what is done humbly is pleasing to Him. Let them be humble in all their works, because humility [Note: [Col. 0227D]

“Humility is the sublimity of the virtues,” not in dignity but in merit, because the other virtues are supported and sustained by it, so that they may be virtues. Chrysostom, Homily 30 on the Acts of the Apostles:

> Nothing is comparable to the virtue of humility. For it is the mother, root, nurse, support, and bond of good things—namely, of good works.

Abbot Guanicus of Igny, sermon on the Saturday of the second week of Lent, at the end:

> Humility is the greatest of all virtues, although it does not know itself to be a virtue. It is almost the root, seedbed, fuel, and stimulus of all of them; it is also their summit and pinnacle, their safeguard and discipline. From it they begin, through it they advance, in it they are brought to completion, and through it they are preserved. And although it grants to all of them that they may be virtues, if any one of them is lacking or less perfect, it advances through the defect of another and makes good that loss from its own resources.]

is the sublimity of the virtues; nor will anyone enter the kingdom of heaven except through humility. But the labors, prayers, almsgiving, fasts, and vigils of many years, if they end in pride, are counted as nothing before God. The humble man is pleasing to God, and carries God within himself.

We have already discussed the evil of pride little by little, but because of those subject to you I have found it necessary to include this passage, so that they may learn to raise the shield of humility against the arrows of the devil. But the proud man is hateful to God [Note: [Col. 0228C]

“The proud man is hateful to God,” in accordance with Sirach 10:7: “Pride is hateful before God and men.” Hence Prudentius in *Psychomachia*, line 333:

> Cease your grand speech: God breaks every proud man;  
> Great things fall, inflated things burst, swollen things are crushed.]

and like the devil [Note: [Col. 0228C]

“Like the devil.” “Indeed, whoever is proud is full of the demon,” says Caesarius of Arles, bishop, Homily 23. Saint Basil, bishop of Seleucia, in Oration 35, calls pride “the citadel of maladies, which is driven by the devil’s disease.”

Saint Cyprian likewise says in letter 55 that pride “is born from the spirit of Antichrist,” that is, from the devil, to whom the Lord reproaches through the prophet Isaiah 14, saying: “Thou hast said in thy heart: I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God.”]. Though the humble man may be lowly in outward appearance, he is nevertheless glorious in virtues before God. But the proud man, even if he appears handsome and distinguished in outward appearance, is nevertheless worthless in his works before God; and in his words, actions [Note: [Col. 0228D]

“And in words and actions,” and so forth. For a description of pride, see Prudentius in the passage cited. Cassian, *On the Institutes of the Coenobia*, book XII, chapter 29, vividly depicts the proud man:

> At first there is shouting in his speech, bitterness in his silence, loud and uncontrolled laughter in his joy, unreasonable sadness in his seriousness, rancor in his reply, facility in speaking, words bursting forth everywhere without any gravity of heart. He is devoid of patience, and so forth.

Concerning the proud man’s gait, Cassiodorus, *Variarum*, book VI, formula 9:

> The proud man reveals himself by his straddling steps.

Concerning his eyes, Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXXIV, chapter 17:

> Pride is judged by the eyes. Inflated by the arrogance of swelling, they look down from a kind of height; and the more they abase themselves, the higher they raise themselves. For unless pride poured itself out through the eyes as through certain windows, the Psalmist would never have said to God (Psalm 18): “Thou wilt save the humble people; and wilt bring down the eyes of the proud.” Nor, unless pride displayed itself through the eyes, would Solomon have said of the exaltation of Judea (Proverbs 30): “A generation whose eyes are lofty, and their eyelids lifted up on high.”], and face, and gait, his pride and fickleness are always recognized [Col. 0229A]. He desires always to be praised [Note: [Col. 0229C]

“He desires always to be praised, and when he does not obtain what he seeks, he commends himself in resentful silence,” as Gregory says in *On 1 Kings*, book V, chapter 14. His words are:

> It is customary for the arrogant that, when another’s tongue is silent about their praise, their own estimation is not silent. While others are silent, they shout, because they carry within their heart the heralding of their own reputation.]

by all people [Note: [Col. 0229]

The Venetian edition has “by all human beings.”], and he wants himself proclaimed for qualities from which he is alien. He does not allow himself to be subject to anyone [Note: [Col. 0229D]

“He does not allow himself to be subject to anyone, but always desires to hold first place among his equals.” Gregory likewise says, *Moralia*, book XIII, chapter 9:

> All the arrogant remember that they were created equal to all human beings, but through the pride of knowledge they disdain either to be or to believe their hearers equal to themselves. They place themselves alongside them by the condition of nature, but through the swelling of knowledge they set themselves above them. They judge themselves to have been born equal, but not to have remained equal in life.

How beautifully Bernard says in sermon 1 *On Various Matters*:

> This solitude belongs to the proud, because they consider themselves alone and desire to be thought alone. He is learned: he hates a companion. He is clever in worldly business: he would wish no one to be found like him. He has money: if he sees another becoming rich, he is tormented. He is strong or handsome: give him an equal, and he wastes away. He is solitary—but errant.

And elsewhere, namely in *On the Degrees of Humility and Pride*, degree 7, “presumption”:

> He sits first in assemblies, answers first in councils, approaches uninvited, intrudes without being sent, rearranges what has been arranged, remakes what has been done. Whatever he himself has not done or ordered, he considers neither rightly done nor beautifully arranged. He judges those who judge and prejudges those who are about to judge.]

but always desires to hold first place among his equals. Lucan sang something not unlike Paulinus’s judgment concerning the rival commanders of the Romans, Caesar and Pompey, in book I, line 125:

> Nor can Caesar now endure anyone as his superior.

Pompey as an equal.] He cannot tolerate anyone being subject to another, but always desires to hold primacy among his peers and to rise to a higher rank; and what he cannot obtain by merit, he wishes to seize by flattering [Note: [Col. 0230C] “By flattering.” Chrysostom, commenting on Paul’s words in 1 Thessalonians 2:5–6, “For neither at any time used we flattering words … nor sought we glory of men,” explains them as follows: “We did not flatter—which is characteristic of those who … wish to obtain domination.
