It cannot be said: ‘We flattered in order to obtain domination.’” Or, as Primasius says on the same passage of the Apostle: “Everyone who flatters does so either for avarice or for glory.”] [Note: [Col. 0229] Ven. adds, and Bened. notes in the margin: “Ed. by flattering superiors, slandering and envying equals, and despising the humble, he wishes to seize it.”] and by slandering [Note: [Col. 0230D] “By slandering.” Gregory, *Moralia* book XXXIII, chapter 3: “All who pursue vainglory, because they place themselves above everyone, reproach some for foolishness and others for unworthy conduct—that is, they judge some to know nothing and others not to live well.” Slander proceeds from pride; for, as Peter Damian says in book VI, letter 30: “Clearly, unless our own life shone very brightly in our eyes, the conduct of others would not displease us so greatly.”] he wishes to seize it.

And just as a ship without a helmsman is tossed about by the waves, so the proud man, unstable and frivolous, is carried about through all his actions. The humble man, however, considers himself the least of all; and, looking down with a gentle countenance [Note: [Col. 0229] Ven. has “looking at the ground.”], he appears exalted before God. When he has done everything, he says, “I am an unprofitable servant,” and declares that he has done nothing. Yet God proclaims [Note: [Col. 0230D] “God proclaims his works.” There are innumerable examples. It is enough to recall two. The deed of Mary Magdalene, who anticipated anointing Christ’s body for burial, is preached throughout the whole world, in accordance with Christ’s own prophecy (Matthew 26:13). The almsgiving of Martin is commended by the mouth of Christ, who had received it, in these words: “Martin, still a catechumen, clothed me with this garment,” as Severus relates in book I of his *Life* of Martin, no. 2. Truly, God, as Mary says, exalts the humble, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.] his works, brings them into the public eye, glorifies his deeds, exalts him, makes him renowned, and grants him the power to obtain from God what he asks for at the time of his prayers [Col. 0229B].

Humility alone obtains these and similar things from God, because it is the seat and pleasant resting-place of our Lord Jesus Christ, who says: “Upon whom shall I rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isaiah 66:2). And again: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29). Announce it, I ask, to your people, and say to them: “For God resists the proud” (James 4:6). And: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1:20). [Note: [Col. 0229] Bened. does not have this, nor does he mark anything in the margin; it appears in the Venetian edition between brackets.]

Many pretend to be gentle and patient, yet, when they find the opportunity, they become more bitter. God will judge fornicators and adulterers (Hebrews 13:4) on the day of judgment. It is written concerning perjury: “A man who swears many oaths will not escape sin, nor will the scourge depart from his house” (Ecclesiasticus 23:12). Slander is fornication of the soul. Hence the Psalmist says: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbour, him I pursued” (Psalm 100:5). The Lord detests discord, as Solomon sang, saying: “There is a seventh thing that my soul detests” (Proverbs 6:16)—that is, “the one who sows discord among brothers” (ibid. 19). [Note: [Col. 0229] Bened. does not have this, nor does he note it. It appears between brackets in the Venetian edition.]

I judge such people to resemble no one so much as the devil, who sowed discord between God and man.

### CHAPTER XXXIII. Receiving the Eucharist

[Col. 0230B]

These are the foods and drinks of death for our soul. May the piety of our Lord Jesus Christ free us from these [Note: [Col. 0229] Ven. has: “from these poisons.”], and grant us himself to eat, for he said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41). “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life in himself” (ibid. 6:54).

But before anyone receives the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, let him examine himself and, according to the Apostle’s command, “eat of that bread and drink of the cup” [Col. 0231A], because “whoever eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:28–29).

When, then, we ought to receive it [Note: [Col. 0231] Ven. has “that”], we must first have recourse to confession and repentance [Note: [Col. 0231B] “Before confession and penance, etc.” This is precisely what the Apostle commands elsewhere, in different words, in 1 Corinthians 11:28, according to the Council of Trent, session 13, chapter 7: “A person intending to communicate must be reminded of his (Paul’s) command: ‘Let a man prove himself.’ The Church’s practice declares that this examination is necessary, so that no one conscious of mortal sin, however contrite he may seem to himself, should approach the sacred Eucharist without prior sacramental confession.” This most holy practice of the Church is evident from letters 9, 10, and 11 of Saint Cyprian, as well as from other passages. Let a few excerpts from these letters suffice. In letter 9, grieving that the Eucharist had been given prematurely to the lapsed, he writes: “For although sinners in lesser sins do penance at the proper time, and according to the order of discipline come to confession, and receive the right of communion through the laying-on of the bishop’s and clergy’s hands, now, before the proper time … before penance has been done, before confession has been made … the Eucharist is given to them.” He complains of the same matter in the tenth letter, repeating it in almost the same words in the eleventh.

Bernard had this in mind in sermon 1 on the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, when he says that Bethlehem signifies “house of bread,” while Judah signifies “confession”; and he adds: “Therefore, if you receive that bread which came down from heaven and gives life to the world—that is, the Lord’s body, Jesus … you have truly become worthy of receiving the Lord, provided that confession has not been lacking.”

It is pleasing here to cite the relevant words of the two fathers Etherius and Beatus, nearly contemporaries of our Paulinus and his comrades-in-arms in the struggle they undertook against Elipandus, from book I *Against Elipandus*: “Some say: the Christian ought always to receive Communion; unless some sin intervenes, the Lord’s body should be received daily … They speak rightly, provided that they receive it with reverence, devotion, and humility. But if their sins are such that they remove them from the altar like a dead person, penance must first be performed, and only then should this saving medicine be received.”], and carefully examine all our actions. If we perceive sins within ourselves, let us hasten to wash them away through confession and true repentance, lest, like Judas the traitor, by not concealing the devil within us, we perish—prolonging and concealing our sin from day to day.

### 40. CHAPTER XXXIV. Sins of the heart must be avoided, because God sees the heart

If we have thought anything evil [Note: [Col. 0231] Ven. has “anything bad.”] or wicked [Note: [Col. 0231] Bened. adds “and concerning it.”], let us repent of it and hasten quickly [Note: [Col. 0231D] “Let us hasten to eradicate it.” On the care to be taken in driving away evil thoughts, see Cassian, book VI, chapter 13, *Institutes of the Coenobites*. Antiochus likewise warns in homily 81: “Thoughts of this kind, in their many forms, must be immediately routed and repelled at the very entrance, without delay, through the diligent practice of pious resistance and prayer.”] to erase it from our heart [Col. 0231B].

Let us not wish to say: [Note: [Col. 0232B] “Let us not wish to say: ‘This is not a serious sin.’” Chrysostom, in volume V, *On the Perils of Minor Sins*, treats this subject at length. A brief excerpt follows: “Perhaps you do not think that our thoughts pertain to God? No act is performed without a thought preceding it; no work is completed without the heart meditating upon it … Although at times we think something but do not do it, we plan it but do not carry it out, nevertheless thoughts are counted as deeds, even if they are not yet completed in action. For to think something in the heart is to do it; the body’s part is to carry out what has been thought … The heart is held guilty through thinking, even though the body appears free from the deed. The mind that conceived the thought is already guilty, although the body is free from the act it did not perform.”] “This is not a serious sin, what I thought.”

Alas, foolish people! Why do we not [Note: [Col. 0231] Ven. has “why do we not think”; alternatively, “understand.”] understand that, in the sight of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0232C] “Our thoughts are in the sight of the Lord.” There is no need to cite Scripture, which Paulinus has already produced on a matter sufficiently well known. Let us instead listen to the pagans, to whom this same truth also became clear.

Seneca says in letter 41: “God is near you, with you, within you. I tell you, Lucilius: a holy spirit sits within us, observing our evil and our good.” And in letter 83: “We must certainly live as though we were living in the sight of someone, and think as though someone could look into the innermost recesses of our breast—and someone can. For what benefit is there in concealing anything from a human being? Nothing is closed to God. He is present in our souls and intervenes in the midst of our thoughts.”

Thales too, according to Laertius, *Lives of the Philosophers*, book I, when asked whether a person acting wickedly could be hidden from the gods, replied: “Not even when he is thinking.” It is therefore no wonder that the Christian Juvencus sang in book I of the *History of the Gospel*, verse 617:

“Nothing do we say when God is absent; nothing hidden do the secret chambers of the heart conceal. God is present and sees all things.”] our thoughts, before they proceed into action, are manifest and open! For the Psalmist says: “God searches hearts and reins” (Psalm 7:10). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of men” [Note: [Col. 0231] Ven. adds: “for they are vain.”] (Psalm 93:11). And elsewhere the same Psalmist says: “You have understood my thoughts from afar; you have investigated my path and my resting-place” (Psalm 138:3).

Let us not, I ask, permit wicked thoughts within us, nor neglect them as though they were insignificant, because “the one who despises small things gradually falls away” (Ecclesiasticus 19:1). Let us not despise the serpent’s bite [Note: [Col. 0232D] “Let us not despise the serpent’s bite.” Theodore the Studite, sermon 1: “You surely know that wicked thoughts bite like serpents, injecting poison into the soul. This must be removed with every effort as soon as it arises, lest delay turn it into a difficult-to-heal ulcer.”], lest its poison be scattered through our hearts. For although poison is the serpent’s life, it is the human being’s death.

Let us cut away the thorny shoots from the field of our heart, lest they drive deep roots into us. For we know that our heart is the field of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let us cultivate it with heavenly disciplines, and let us not allow weeds to be sown in the field of so great a [Col. 0232B] ruler [Note: [Col. 0232D] “To sow weeds.” The author of the *Opus imperfectum* among Chrysostom’s works, volume II, Lyon edition of 1687, homily 13 on Matthew 6: “Wheat is the good will that God sows in the human being. The weed, however, is the evil thought that the devil has sown through the flesh.”]; rather, let us adorn it with every flower of virtue, because almighty God delights in these, as it is written in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song of Songs 2:1)—that is, “I am the beauty of the world, and the virginity of the humble.” [Note: [Col. 0231] Bened. does not have “and.”]

### CHAPTER XXXV. The flesh must be disciplined

[Col. 0233A]

And always and [Note: [Col. 0233A] “Always and always.” This repetition of the word intensifies the force of the expression, meaning “continually and without interruption.” Terence, *Eunuchus* 56, act I, scene 1:

“Therefore, while there is time, consider again and again.”

And “more and more,” as in Virgil, *Georgics* III.185:

“Then more and more to rejoice in the kindly praises of the master,” etc.

The same appears in repeated nouns, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* II.668:

“Bring the man’s arms, bring his arms.”

Statius, *Thebaid* VII.135:

“Arms, arms, the madmen seize, each his own and each unknown, without delay.”

And Jeremiah 22:29: “Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord.”

Thus “always and always” means for Paulinus “unceasingly and without any interruption.”] always our flesh must be subject to the soul and must serve its mistress like a maidservant. Let us not provide our body with unlawful strength, lest it wage war against our spirit; rather, let the flesh always be subject, so that it may obey the commands of the Holy Spirit.

Nor should we allow the maidservant to grow fat [Note: [Col. 0233B] “The maidservant, lest she despise her mistress.” This alludes to Sarah and Hagar in Genesis 16. Nicholas of Lyra understands the passage morally in this way: “By Abram may be understood any good man, having in his household—that is, within himself—Sarai, whose name means ‘my princess’; through her, therefore, right reason is signified, which ought to rule, and Hagar, the maidservant—that is, the flesh—which ought to be subjected and chastened. When Sarai says, ‘Go in to my maidservant,’ this signifies the concession made to the flesh for a reasonable cause. But because it is difficult there to maintain the proper measure, rebellion of the flesh against the spirit frequently arises from it, which is indicated when it is said that Hagar despised her mistress. But when reason announces such rebellion to the human being, he ought to subject the flesh to reason, as is indicated when Abraham replies: ‘Behold, your maidservant is in your hand,’ etc., so that she may be chastened. And if the flesh resists such chastisement, it must nevertheless be brought back to obedience to reason.”] lest she despise her mistress; rather, let her be devoted to all her commands and services.

For just as [Note: [Col. 0233D] “As reins must be placed on horses.” Saint Gregory, *Moralia* XXXI.9: “The body of every holy soul is like a horse. The soul knows how to restrain it from unlawful things by the bridle of continence and, again, to release it for the exercise of good works through the impulse of charity. Thus the holy man’s soul is expressed under the name of the rider, governing the well-subdued beast of the body.” Augustine should also be heard, as he explains this comparison at length in book *On the Benefit of Fasting*, chapter 3: “Reply to that evil counsellor, the servant of the belly, by means of this comparison and say: if you were sitting upon a beast, if you were using a horse that could throw you by its spirited movements, would you not, so that you might travel safely, take food away from the raging animal and tame by hunger what you could not control with a bridle? My flesh is my beast; I am travelling to Jerusalem; it often carries me away and tries to throw me from the road. My road, however, is Christ. Shall I not restrain it, when it is exulting, by fasting?”] horses must be fitted with bridles, so our bodies must be curbed by fasting and prayer. For just as [Note: [Col. 0233D] “Just as charioteers,” according to Virgil, at the end of *Georgics* I:

“When the four-horse chariots have burst forth from the starting-gates,

They fling themselves into the course, and while the charioteer vainly strains the reins,

He is carried along by the horses, and the chariot does not heed the reins.”] charioteers, if they loosen the reins, are dragged over precipices, so the soul, together with the body, if we do not place a bridle upon it, slips down into the precipices of hell. Let us therefore be good and well-trained charioteers of our body, so that we may proceed along the right road.

### CHAPTER XXXVI. Excess in food must be avoided

Excessive food harms not only souls but also bodies [Note: [Col. 0234B] “Food greatly harms our bodies and brings them to illness.” Hippocrates, *Aphorisms* II.17: “Wherever nourishment beyond nature enters in excessive quantity, it produces disease”—that is, wherever food is taken in more abundantly than nature permits, it causes illness.

Ecclesiasticus 37:32: “Do not be greedy in every feast, and do not pour yourself out over every food, for in many foods there will be illness.”

Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* II.1, quotes the physician Antiphanes of Delos as saying that “the variety of foods is a cause of diseases.”

Chrysostom, homily 21 on John, discusses the matter as follows: “If you ask physicians, you will find that nearly all diseases arise from this cause. A cheap, light, and simple table is the mother of health—as the physicians have called it … the parent of health. Satiety, on the contrary, they have called, by the very art of medicine, the source of diseases that cannot be cured; and this is evident. Diseases of the feet, head, eyes, and hands, paralysis, dropsy, jaundice, prolonged and acute fevers, and many illnesses of this kind are contracted through excessive gluttony. It is not possible at present to enumerate all those that arise from voracity and overindulgence.”

Philo gives the reason in *On the Creation of the World*: “An immoderate accumulation of food is deadly and poisonous, since the food taken in does not permit digestion because of its quantity, when one thing is added upon another before what came first has been digested.”

The author of the poem addressed to the senator—once thought to be Tertullian—expresses the matter well, verse 56:

“Food nourishes the body; the body is corrupted by food;

And its strength diminishes if anything is extended beyond the proper limit.”] and bring them to illness. For through excessive greed for food and immoderate drinking the strength of the stomach is usually broken [Note: [Col. 0234C] “The strength of the stomach is broken,” etc. Clement of Alexandria, in the passage cited above, calls these effects “upsets of the stomach”: “The many varieties of foods must therefore be rejected, since they produce various harms, unhealthy bodily conditions, and upsets of the stomach.”

Suetonius, *Caligula* 58, uses the expression “to make the stomach languish through feasting”: “He hesitated whether to rise for lunch, while his stomach was still languishing under the burden of the previous day’s food; at last … he went out.”

Seneca, letter 2: “It is characteristic of a queasy stomach,” he says, “to taste many things; when they are varied and different, they pollute rather than nourish.”

The same thought is expressed by two Christian poets. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* 431, hymn before meals:

“Lest the sluggish stomach burden the distended entrails with immoderate banquets.”

And Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, *Poems* I, in the *Paraenesis to Judges*, verse 415, speaking of the variety and multiplicity of foods:

“These things, though small, comfort the stomach; if there are more, they will burden it.”

Hear Horace explain how this happens, *Satires* II.2.161:

“Sweet things will turn into bile, and a sluggish phlegm

Will bring turmoil to the stomach.”] as well as an excess of blood and bile [Note: [Col. 0235A] Ven. has: “arise through bile, etc.” Bened. has: “of blood and bile, and many illnesses are contracted through an abundance of food.” Both readings seem defective; the form printed here is an emendation.] [Note: [Col. 0235B] “And bile.” “Cholera,” that is, *cholera*, says Paul of Aegina in book III of his medical work, “is an excessive disturbance of the bowels, involving diarrhea and vomiting, arising from the continual indigestion of food because of excessive swallowing or a harmful excess of fluids,” as quoted by Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings* IV.5.

Hence Ecclesiasticus 37:33: “In many foods there will be illness, and greed will approach even to cholera.” And 31:23: “Sleeplessness, cholera, and torment are for an undisciplined man.” The Greek has *aplēstos* (ἄπληστος), meaning “insatiable” or “inexhaustible.”

Seneca likewise says in letter 24: “Feasts bring indigestion,” evidently referring to excessive feasts, of which Horace says, *Satires* II.7.977:

“Indeed, feasts pursued without end grow bitter.”] and many illnesses are contracted through an abundance of food.

For just as these things are contrary to soul and body, so the remedy [Note: [Col. 0235B] “The remedy for both is the moderation of fasting.” In the prayer for the Saturday after Ash Wednesday, the Church says that “fasting was beneficially instituted for the healing of souls and bodies.”

Saint Athanasius, in *On Virginity*, treats at length the praises of fasting and the benefits that flow from it into soul and body. Among other things he says: “You see what fasting does: it heals diseases, dries up bodily fluids, drives out demons and evil thoughts, makes the mind brighter, gives a pure heart and a sanctified body.”] for both is the moderation of fasting.

Even if we cannot fast throughout the whole year, let us at least, with God’s help, avoid the pleasures of the world and the abundance of food on the most sacred days [Note: [Col. 0235C] “The most sacred days of fasting.” Augustine, letter 36 in the new edition, formerly 86: “As I read through the New Testament, I see that fasting is commanded. But on which days one ought not to fast, and on which one ought to fast, I do not find defined by the command of the Lord or the Apostles.”

The Church therefore established seasons and days of fasting. Which fasts, besides Lent and the Ember Days, had already been introduced into the pious practice of the Church in Paulinus’s time can be gathered from the capitularies of the Frankish kings, where they are frequently mentioned.

In 817, the Aachen Capitulary on the life and conduct of monks, chapter 51, decrees: “Let no one fast unless days of fasting have been established.” Baluzius adds in his notes: “The edition of the Centuriators adds: Let there be fasting on the Ember Days, as on the vigils of Saint Mary, the Annunciation, the Assumption, and the Nativity. Likewise let there be fasting on the Nativity of all the Apostles, or of Saint John the Baptist on the anniversary of his martyrdom, or on the feast of any saint in whose honour the place where the monks serve has been dedicated.”

The Ember fasts were distributed as follows, according to a homily by an unknown author preserved in the oldest manuscript of Saint Gall, which Baluzius cites in his notes on chapter 186 of book VI of the *Capitularies*: “You ought to observe four fasts in the year, that is, in the month of March, in the first week, when March begins, you ought to fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. In June, in the second week after June begins, you ought to fast on the day, etc. In September, in the third week, fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday.”

Because some of the fasts mentioned there seem to have been established for monks alone, it is useful to transcribe chapter 187 of book VI of the *Capitularies*, which prescribes three solemn fasts for the entire population, called the legitimate fasts: “Let the priests admonish the people that the three legitimate fasts of the year be observed: namely, forty days before the Nativity of the Lord, forty days before Easter, when we pay the tithes of the year, and forty days after Pentecost. Although some of these lack canonical authority, it is nevertheless fitting for all of us together to observe them by the custom of the people and the practice of our ancestors, as has been shown above. And although it is fitting to pray and abstain on all days, at these times we ought to devote ourselves more fully to fasting and penance. Besides these legitimate seasons of fasting, every Friday should be observed as a fast because of the Lord’s Passion. Saturday too is regarded by many as consecrated to fasting, because on that day Christ lay in the tomb.”

Besides these, fasts called “proclaimed fasts” were also observed. They were sometimes proclaimed by the king for a public cause, as appears from the Capitulary of 828, in the letter of Louis and Lothair included there, which says in part: “And so that all these things may succeed, we wish a general three-day fast to be proclaimed for celebration on the Monday after the Octave of Pentecost, and for it to be observed by everyone with the greatest devotion.”

They were also proclaimed by bishops, as appears frequently. That those who resisted sinned is evident from the Council of Gangra, which ordered such people to be anathematized; this is reported in book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 152, concerning a proclaimed fast. It is also evident from Rhabanus, book II, *On the Instruction of Clergy*, chapter 25, cited in Baluzius’s notes: “Those fasts too,” Rhabanus says, “which the bishop of the church commands all together to observe, whether for tribulation or thanksgiving, must be kept by everyone. For whoever neglects to observe the fasts established and commanded commits sin.”

Such was the discipline of the Church in Paulinus’s time.] so that we may not, God forbid, later, tormented in the flame [Note: [Col. 0235] Ven. has “in the torment of flame.”] [Note: [Col. 0236D] “Tormented in the flame, let us seek a drop of water.” This refers to the punishment of the rich man in Luke 16:24, who, while in torment and suffering in the flame, asked Lazarus for a drop of water, but in vain.], seek a drop of water and obtain no refreshment.

### CHAPTER XXXVII. The evils that follow drunkenness

[Col. 0236A]

Let us flee drunkenness, lest we incur the crime of debauchery, because the Apostle commands us not to become drunk with wine, “in which is debauchery” (Ephesians 5:18). For God gave us wine for the joy of the heart [Note: [Col. 0236D] “Wine for joy.” In accordance with Ecclesiasticus 31:35: “Wine was created for gladness, and not for drunkenness.” Cornelius a Lapide apparently reads it thus: “Wine was created to cheer people, not to intoxicate them.” Chrysostom writes similarly in his homily *On Gluttony and Drunkenness*: “Wine was given so that we might be cheerful, not so that we might disgrace ourselves; so that we might laugh, not so that we might be laughed at; so that we might be healthy, not so that we might become ill; so that we might strengthen bodily weakness, not so that we might overthrow the powers of the soul.”], not for drunkenness. Let us therefore drink not as much as the appetite demands, but as much as the weakness of nature requires.

Let us not, then, turn into a cause of destruction what was given for the healing [Note: [Col. 0236D] “For the healing of the body.” Ecclesiasticus, in the passage cited above, verse 37: “Sober drinking is health for soul and body.” Chrysostom, homily 1 to the people of Antioch: “Wine is the best medicine when it is taken in proper measure.” And below: “Wine was given to strengthen the weakness of the body, not to destroy the health of the soul.”

Pliny, book XXIII, chapter 1, lists some of its medicinal properties: “By wine the strength, blood, and colour of human beings are nourished … the nerves are aided … the stomach is restored, appetite for food is stimulated, concern over sadness is blunted, urine and cold are expelled, and sleep is induced. Moreover, it stops vomiting and soothes abscesses when applied externally with moist wool. Asclepiades declared that the usefulness of wine could scarcely be equalled by the power of the gods.”] of our body.

Announce, I ask, to those subject to you in your house [Col. 0237A] that many people have committed murders and [Note: [Col. 0237B] “Murders through wine.” Ecclesiasticus 31:38 and following: “Much wine drunk causes irritation, anger, and many falls … and causes wounds.” Saint Peter Chrysologus, sermon 26 on Luke 12:45, concerning the wicked servant—“and he began to beat the menservants and maidservants, and to eat and drink and become drunk”—says: “He expressly said ‘to eat, and to drink, and to become drunk, and to beat.’ Drunkenness is the mother of slaughter, the parent of quarrels, the source of fury, etc.”

Hence Proverbs 23:29 and following: “Who has woe? Whose father has woe? Who has strife? Who has pits? Who has wounds without cause? Who has redness of eyes? Is it not those who linger over wine and seek to drain the cups?”

Seneca confirms the point with examples in letter 83: “Recall,” he says, “the example of Alexander of Macedon, who stabbed Clitus, most dear and most loyal to him, during a feast,” etc. And below: “What other thing destroyed Marcus Antonius, a great man and of noble intellect, and transferred him into foreign customs and un-Roman vices, than drunkenness? … It made him cruel, when the heads of leading citizens were brought to him at dinner; when, amid the most elaborate banquets and royal luxury, he recognized the faces and hands of the proscribed, while heavy with wine yet thirsting for blood. What he did while drunk was intolerable … Cruelty generally follows drunkenness,” etc.] fornications [Note: [Col. 0237C] “And fornications”—indeed, every shameful and abominable act. Therefore the Apostle warned the Ephesians: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Ephesians 5:18).

Chrysostom, in his homily *On Gluttony and Drunkenness*: “It devises unlawful intercourse and illicit loves, and turns the mouth, eyes, nostrils, and every limb altogether into sewers of sin.” And homily 71 on Matthew 22: “Drunkenness is armed with many heads, like a Hydra: from it arise fornication, anger, softness, and shameful loves.”

Jerome expresses the same view and confirms it with examples in letter 83 to Oceanus: “Drunkenness,” he says, “belongs to buffoons and revellers; and the belly, seething with wine, quickly foams over into lust. In wine there is debauchery, in debauchery pleasure, and in pleasure immorality. Whoever lives in debauchery is a living dead man; therefore whoever becomes drunk is both dead and buried. Noah exposes his thighs after a single hour of drunkenness, although he had covered them for six hundred years in sobriety. Through drunkenness Lot, unaware, mingles incest with lust; and the man whom Sodom had not conquered, wine conquered.”

Origen says similar things in homily 5 on Genesis: “Drunkenness deceives the one whom Sodom did not deceive. He is burned by the flames of women whom the sulphurous flame did not burn.”], and have not refused death itself [Note: [Col. 0237D] “Nor did they refuse death itself”—I think this has been written in place of “escaped death.” For very few people take their own lives, whereas many die as a result of excessive drinking.

Laertius, book IV, on Arcesilaus: “He died, as Hermippus says, after drinking unmixed wine to excess.” The same author, in the same book, on Lacydes of Cyrene: “He died of paralysis, which he contracted from excessive drinking.” Athenaeus, book X of the *Deipnosophistae*, chapter 12, provides more than one example of this. It is enough to cite the case of a certain drunkard who, driven into madness by drunkenness, violently laid hands upon himself: “Cleomenes of Lacedaemon was such a man; he drank unmixed wine … and that he blinded himself with a knife because of drunkenness, Herodotus has recorded.”

Hence Sirach, Ecclesiasticus 31:30: “Wine has destroyed many.”], while others have been seized by demons through wine. Drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest [Col. 0238A] [Note: [Col. 0237A] Ven. has “manifest.”] [Note: [Col. 0238B] “Drunkenness is a most manifest demon.” Saint Bernard—or whoever else was the author of the book *On the Way of Living Well for a Sister*, chapter 25—perhaps drew from this passage of Paulinus what he wrote: “Many have been seized by demons through wine; and drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon.”

The Fathers frequently brand drunkenness with this designation. Chrysostom, homily 19 on Genesis: “Truly drunkenness is a voluntary demon, and it darkens the mind more grievously than a demon.” Peter Chrysologus, sermon 26: “Drunkenness is a flattering demon, a sweet poison, voluntary madness, an invited enemy.”

This should not, however, be understood in the sense of the Manichaeans, who said that wine was the work—or even the bile—of the devil, although they allowed grapes. Against them Augustine argues in book II of *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, no. 44, chapter 16: “What greater perversity is there than to think wine the bile of the prince of darkness, while not refraining from eating grapes? Is that bile more present in the cup than it was in the grapes?”] demon.

The drunkard thinks he is doing something excellent when he has fallen headlong into destruction. Through drunkenness he is armed [Note: [Col. 0238C] “Armed for abuse.” Philo, *On the Contemplative Life*: “When the common crowd has filled itself with wine, as though it had drunk not wine but a cup of madness … it attacks others, and like savage dogs turns rabid; then, rising up, they attack one another with bites … and fight as though in an arena or in a pankration.”

Lucretius, book III, verse 481:] for curses and abuse.

Clamor, sobbing, and quarrels increase. In the *Apophthegms*, Plutarch relates the following about Pyrrhus:

> “He had heard that certain young men had reviled him with many insults while drinking. The next day he ordered all of them to be brought before him, and first asked one of them whether they had said such things about him. ‘Indeed,’ he replied, ‘such things—and we would have said more if we had had more wine.’”

So true is what Plutarch himself adds in *Symposium*, book VIII, question 1, following the philosophical view that calls drunkenness a delirium arising from wine:

> “When uncontrolled chatter and foolishness accompany wine, the most ignorant and unpleasant conclusion follows: insults and revelry.” [Col. 0238D]

The delirium that philosophers called a change of mind our Paulinus described as follows: He then proceeds to curses and insults against his neighbors, and his mind is changed.[^c0024-1] [Col. 0239A] His tongue stammers.[^c0024-2]

[^c0024-1]: “His mind is changed.” Plato, *Laws*, book I, has the Athenian Stranger and Cleinias speak as follows: “Athenian: Does drunkenness make the senses, memory, opinion, and understanding stronger, or does it completely extinguish them, if someone is overcome by drunkenness? Cleinias: It completely extinguishes them. Athenian: He therefore returns to the condition he had as a child in his earliest years? Cleinias: Certainly. Athenian: Then he will least of all be master of himself. Cleinias: Least of all. Athenian: He will therefore be the worst. Cleinias: Very much so. Athenian: Thus, it seems, not only will an old man twice become a child, but the drunkard himself will also become one? Cleinias: That is excellently said, Stranger.” Saint Peter Chrysologus, *Sermon* 26, cited above: “Whoever has this [drunkenness] does not possess himself; whoever has this is not a human being; whoever has this does not merely commit sin but is himself sin.”

[^c0024-2]: “His tongue stammers.” Lucretius, in the passage cited: “His tongue grows sluggish.” Seneca, discussing the drunkard in Letter 83: “Add,” he says, “that lack of self-knowledge, words that are hesitant and scarcely intelligible, uncertain eyes, and so forth.” Blessed Eugenius the Younger, bishop of Toledo, describes these effects of drunkenness beautifully in poem 5 against drunkenness:

> From it trembling in the limbs, from it forgetfulness of mind,  
> And a step wavering at the knee, and deceptive vision;  
> The ears grow deaf, and at last the tongue stammers,  
> Losing eloquence, it pours forth half-formed speech. [Col. 0239C]

Saint Ambrose recognizes these effects as necessary consequences of drunkenness in *On Elijah and Fasting*, chapter 12, no. 43: “The mind,” he says, “must stagger, and the tongue stammer.” The author of *On Sobriety and Chastity*, chapter 1, in the latest edition of Augustine’s works, volume VI of the Appendix, page 227, calls “the storm of the tongue” a fruit of drunkenness: “Drunkenness,” he says, “is disturbance of the head, overturning of the senses, a storm of the tongue, a tempest of the body, and so forth.”

Such a man, when he thinks that he is drinking wine, is in fact being drunk by wine. For very many people have contracted the greatest weakness through wine and have been unable to regain their former strength,[^c0024-3] because they did not restrain the ardor of their appetite. Just as a fish, hastening with greedy jaws to swallow the bait, suddenly finds a hook inside its jaws,[^c0024-4] so the drunkard receives within himself an enemy—wine—which, once inside him, immediately drives him toward every most shameful deed.[^c0024-5] Thus a rational human being is captured like an irrational animal.[^c0024-6]

[^c0024-3]: The Venetian manuscript reads “health” instead of “strength.”

[^c0024-4]: The Venetian manuscript reads “with greedy jaws extended.”

[^c0024-5]: Benedict, in the margin, records that the better manuscripts read “death” instead of “immediately.” Gerard’s version reads: “Through wine he receives an enemy, who, dwelling within him, drives him on.” The Venetian version reads: “which, once it has entered him, immediately drives him on.”

[^c0024-6]: “Like an irrational animal.” Saint Basil, Homily 14, *On Drunkenness and Luxury*: “By depriving him through drunkenness of the light of his mind, he may be counted among irrational beasts and appear like them.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The commandments of God pertain to all Christians

But you, my brother, command all your household and those subject to you to show themselves sober, and again not to raise themselves up in pride on account of abstinence,[^c0024-7] but to do everything temperately, justly, devoutly, and religiously, according to God’s help. [Col. 0239B] For Christ shed his blood not only for us clerics but also for the whole human race destined for eternal life.[^c0024-8] The kingdom of heaven has been promised not only to us but also to all laypeople who keep his commandments with their whole heart. [Col. 0240A]

[^c0024-7]: “That they not raise themselves up in pride on account of abstinence.” To warn us to avoid seeking such praise, the Lord repeatedly gives instruction in the Gospel, so that we do not thereby lose the merit of good works before God. Such is the passage in Matthew 6:17–18, where we are warned not to imitate the conduct of hypocrites who seek praise and applause from their gauntness: “When you fast, do not become like the hypocrites with gloomy faces, for they disfigure—or, as others read, following the judgment of Paschasius Radbertus, destroy—their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting.” Saint Maximus, bishop of Turin, says the following in a homily for Ash Wednesday: “Whoever seeks human glory by displaying his fasting does not fast for God but for human beings. They disfigure their faces who, by feigned sorrow, counterfeit a devout appearance before the eyes of the people. The teacher of heavenly discipline does not wish that what is commanded to be done for religion should be done irreligiously; nor does he permit the labor of those who invoke him, for whom he prepares an eternal reward, to perish through the vice of fruitless boasting.” [Col. 0239C–D]

[^c0024-8]: “For the whole human race destined for eternal life.” Take care here not to fall into the error that Christ shed his blood only for those predestined to eternal life. At first sight Paulinus’s words may appear to suggest this, as though he were saying “for that class of human beings who are predestined.” Paulinus’s words should instead be understood in the sense of the Apostle’s statement in 1 Timothy 4:10: “Who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.” Paulinus explains himself in chapter 46: “Christ suffered not only for the saints but for sinners and ungodly people, and by his passion he recalled all to life.” [Col. 0239D–0240B]

For it is a great disgrace to the souls of laypeople who say:

> “What concern is it of mine to hear or learn the books of Scripture by reading, or even frequently to go to priests and the churches of the saints? When I become a cleric, I will do what clerics ought to do.”[^c0024-9]

Why does such a person not understand that he wishes to share equally in bread and wine, in all the good things of this earth, and in the happiness of the kingdom, while refusing to bear the yoke of Christ with equal labor? What benefit is there for such people in being exalted in one respect in this world and cast down in another—in shining with gold and precious garments on one side, while on the other being overwhelmed by the miseries of this world[^c0024-10] and the darkness of vices? [Col. 0240B]

[^c0024-9]: “Who say: What concern is it of mine to hear the books, and so forth.” In chapter 112 of book V of the *Capitularies*, public reading of the holy Scriptures in church was indeed forbidden to laypeople: “A layman ought not to recite a reading in church or say the Alleluia, but only a psalm or responses without the Alleluia.” Private reading, however, was not forbidden, still less listening; indeed, Paulinus commends this here when he rebukes those who withdraw themselves not only from reading but also from hearing the reading of the holy Scriptures, saying: “What concern is it of mine to hear or learn the books of Scripture, or even frequently to go to priests and churches?” We have, on this matter, a homily of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, Homily 20, in which he responds to such excuses, among other things, as follows: “This excuse, dearest brothers, is empty and useless. First, even if someone who does not know letters cannot read the divine reading, he can nevertheless gladly hear someone reading it. And for one who knows letters, can it really be that he cannot find books from which he can read the divine Scripture?” At the end, teaching the people how to gain fruit from his preaching—namely, by retaining in their minds something of what they have heard—he concludes his sermon as follows: “Whoever cannot retain everything should remember at least some part. Let one person say to another: ‘I heard my bishop speaking about chastity.’ Another should report: ‘I remember my bishop saying that whoever knows letters should diligently read the divine Scripture, while whoever does not know them should seek out and ask someone who ought to reread God’s commandments to him.’ Let another also say: ‘I heard my bishop saying that just as merchants who do not know letters hire literate laborers to acquire money for them, so Christians ought to seek and ask for someone—and, if necessary, even pay him—to reread the divine Scripture to them,’ and so forth.” The Venetian reading at the corresponding point has “clerics.” [Col. 0239; 0240B–D]

[^c0024-10]: The Venetian manuscript omits “of this world.”

Let there be no concern in you about the status or person of a layman,[^c0024-11] because with God there is no partiality. [Col. 0241A] The heavenly palace is equally open to laypeople who keep God’s commandments, as it is to clerics and those clothed in the monastic habit. For there is neither Jew nor Greek, neither slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all (Galatians 3:28).

[^c0024-11]: “Let there be no concern about the status of a layman.” That is, do not let it trouble you that you are not a cleric or monk but a layman dressed in lay clothing. In those times, each person’s condition was ordinarily distinguished by clothing itself. Charles the Bald, in the preface to the Assembly at Villa Collonia, *Capitularies*, volume II, page 3: “Our faithful, both those in the venerable clerical order and illustrious men established in noble lay attire.” That this differed from clerical dress is clear from chapter 3 of the Capitularies of Soissons, in the year 744 under Pepin: “And let all clerics not commit fornication, nor wear lay clothing.” Just as clothing does not make a monk, but rather an explicit or implicit religious profession, as Saint Pope Celestine says in *Opusculum* VIII, chapter 24, so lay attire and clothing, provided one’s conduct is moral and holy, bring no harm to salvation. Benedict’s marginal reading, supported by the better manuscripts, has “or that of a layman”; Gerard reads, uncertainly, “that you have received the person/status of a layman’s dress, or of a cleric.” [Col. 0240D–0241C]

Whoever is in his body is great. Insert yourself into his holy body, so that you may be a member of the noblest head. Love with your whole heart your head and the members of that head.[^c0024-12] How can one hand be hostile to another, or one foot hate another, or the remaining members fail to rejoice with their own joint? They ought to grow into a perfect man, into the increase of Christ’s body.[^c0024-13]

[^c0024-12]: “Love your head and the members of the head.” Here he suggests love of God and neighbor under the allegory of our head, which is God and Christ the Lord, and of the members, which are our neighbors. The figure is taken from the Apostle in 1 Corinthians 12, where he pursues it at length, and Chrysostom explains Paul’s teaching about the members extensively in Homilies 30–32. Peter of Blois likewise develops this same subject—namely, the mutual service by which our members provide one another with common assistance—in his treatise *On the Love of God and Neighbor*, chapter 37. He concludes as follows: “Let that law of communion which is written in our members therefore exist in us, so that one spirit may give life to us all as one body; so that through true unity of hearts we may remain in God, and God in us, until the whole body grows through the bonds and joints of its members and its structural connections into the measure of the fullness of Christ’s age.” [Col. 0241C–D]

[^c0024-13]: The better manuscripts recorded by Benedict in the margin read: “if the other members did not rejoice together.” Some have: “if the other members rejoice together, they ought to grow.” The Venetian margin alternatively reads: “into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.” [Col. 0241]

Every cleric and layperson who has been redeemed by the precious blood of Christ and washed in Christ’s baptism ought to walk humbly and persevere in the Holy Spirit. For it is of no benefit to answer that one is a Christian in words while denying it in deeds, when one is corrupt in mind and spirit.[^c0024-14] Concerning such people Truth itself says in the Gospel:

> “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7:21). [Col. 0241B]

[^c0024-14]: “To answer in words that one is a Christian while denying it in deeds.” Cyprian, writing about the truly Christian people of his own time in *On the Good of Patience*: “We who are philosophers not in words but in deeds, who do not speak great things but live them,” and so forth. [Col. 0241D]

And elsewhere the prophet rebukes them, saying:

> “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13). [Col. 0242A]

For if a city is fortified on one side but destroyed on another, it gives its enemies access to itself. And if a ship is strongly secured by its joints but has one plank pierced, it is sunk into the depths by the waves.

It is equally fitting for all laypeople, clerics, and monks to possess faith, hope, charity, and humility,[^c0024-15] to serve God with their whole heart, to make a true confession, and to perform worthy penance. For the most merciful Lord forgives those who flee to repentance.

[^c0024-15]: The Venetian manuscript omits “humility.” [Col. 0241]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The dangers of delayed repentance

But lest we become so secure about the Lord’s mercy[^c0024-16] that we add sins to sins, let us not say:

[^c0024-16]: “So that we add sins to sins.” This teaching is already given in Ecclesiasticus 5:5: “Do not be without fear concerning an absolved sin, and do not add sin upon sin. And do not say, ‘The Lord’s mercy is great; he will have mercy on the multitude of my sins,’ for mercy and wrath quickly come from him, and his wrath rests upon sinners. Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you.” [Col. 0241D–0242C]

> “While the strength of our bodily age remains, let us indulge our desires, and finally let us repent of our evils in old age.”[^c0024-17][^c0024-18]

[^c0024-17]: “While the strength of our bodily age remains.” This corresponds to the words of the foolish and impious in Wisdom 2:6: “Let us use creation as in youth, quickly.” So too the foolish pagan poets, among them Horace, *Odes* I.9, lines 13–15:

> Do not scorn, while you are young,  
> sweet love or the dances,  
> while morose old age is absent from your green youth.

And Seneca’s Nurse, speaking to Hippolytus in the tragedy, line 443:

> Enjoy your age; it flees with swift movement.  
> Now the heart is pliable; now Venus is pleasing to the young.

Ovid likewise, *Amores* III.65:

> Use your age; age slips away with swift foot.  
> Nor does the good follow so readily as the first good did. [Col. 0242C–D]

[^c0024-18]: “And finally let us repent of our evils in old age.” Saint Caesarius of Arles, Homily 13: “But someone says, ‘When I reach old age, then I will flee to the remedies of repentance.’ Why does human frailty presume this about itself, when it does not possess even one day of its life in its own power?” [Col. 0242D]

For the Lord is kind and merciful and will no longer remember our crimes.[^c0024-19]

[^c0024-19]: “The Lord is kind and merciful.” Saint Chrysostom, Homily 22 on 2 Corinthians 11: “You say, ‘I do not rely on uncertain outcomes but on God’s kindness.’ God is indeed kind and merciful; I myself know this well. Yet this kind one nevertheless removed from the world even those whom I mentioned.” [Col. 0242D]

Let us not, I beg you, think in this way, because it is the height of folly to do so,[^c0024-20] since it is impious for anyone to wish to ask such permission from God,[^c0024-21] the beginning of which is separation from God for the person who thinks these things. For impious thoughts separate us from God (Wisdom 1:3). [Col. 0243A]

[^c0024-20]: “It is folly to think this.” Salvian, book I, which he entitled *To Timothy*: “He does not rest upon good hopes who sins throughout life for the sole purpose of redeeming the mass of his sins in death.” And below: “To promise something in so late a cure is reckless.” Seneca also recognized this folly in *On the Brevity of Life*, chapter 4: “Are you not ashamed,” he says, “to reserve for the remnants of life what you should have reserved for yourself, and to devote to a sound mind only that time which can be applied to nothing? How late it is to begin living when one must stop! What such foolish forgetfulness of mortality it is to defer sound counsels until one’s fiftieth or sixtieth year, and then wish to begin life from the point to which few have made their way!” [Col. 0242D–0243D]

[^c0024-21]: “It is impious to ask for such permission.” Chrysostom, Homily 22 on 2 Corinthians, cited above: “Take care not to say, ‘There will be a time when I must return to a better way of life.’ These words greatly provoke God to anger. Give thanks to God that he has not snatched you away in the midst of your sins; do not ask that another period be allotted to you for living shamefully.” The Venetian manuscript reads: “whose beginning is to separate us from God; therefore, I say,” with the intervening words absent. [Col. 0243D]

Therefore, I say, let us not think such things, since we do not know on what day we shall die. No human being knows the day of his departure.[^c0024-22] Not everyone dies in old age, but people leave this world at different ages.[^c0024-24] Whatever actions a person is found engaged in, by those same actions he will be judged when his soul leaves the body. For the Psalmist says:

> “No one in the underworld will confess to you” (Psalm 6:6).

[^c0024-22]: “No human being knows the day of his departure.” Who is unaware of this? Ecclesiastes 9:12: “A person does not know his end.” And the Lord in the Gospel, Matthew 24:42: “You do not know at what hour your Lord will come.” And Luke 12:40: “At an hour when you do not expect him, the Son of Man will come.” Explaining these words with reference to death, Guarric, abbot, Sermon 3 on the Advent, says: “Our final day, whose coming is absolutely certain to us, is entirely uncertain in regard to when, where, or from what direction it will come to us—except that, as has been said before us, for the old it is at the doors, while for the young it lies in ambush.” So too the philosophers and poets. Juncus, in Stobaeus, Sermon 116, *On Praise of Old Age*: “Death’s departure is common to all, and no law concerning it, nor any definite time, has been prescribed by the gods.” Statius, *Silvae* II.224:

> Wretched are we, for whom it is uncertain  
> whence the final day comes, and what the end of life will be. [Col. 0243D–0244D]

[^c0024-24]: “Not everyone dies in old age, but people depart this world at different ages.” Saint Basil, Homily on Saint Julitta the Martyr: “God has assigned to each soul its own condition and measure of life here, and has prescribed different limits for different persons’ departure from here. For he has appointed one to remain longer in the flesh, but has decreed that another be released more quickly from bodily bonds.” [Col. 0241D–0244C]

Therefore let us hasten to turn to repentance. Let the final day always be before our eyes. When we rise at dawn, let us not assume that we shall reach evening; and when we lay our limbs down in bed, let us not rely on the coming of the daylight.[^c0024-23] In this way we shall also be able very easily to restrain our body from vices and evil desires.

[^c0024-23]: “Let us not rely on the coming of the daylight.” Horace, *Odes* IV.7, lines 17–18:

> Who knows whether the gods above will add  
> tomorrow’s hours to today’s total?

And Seneca, *Thyestes*, line 617:

> No one has possessed the gods as favorable  
> that he can promise himself tomorrow.

The Venetian manuscript omits “in this way.” It also omits “evil.” [Col. 0243B–0244D]

## CHAPTER XL. The joys of the future life

Let our heart always meditate on the heavenly promises. Let us transfer all earthly things that we possess into the future dwelling places of the heavenly kingdom, so that when we have advanced there,[^c0024-25] we may enjoy heavenly goods. [Col. 0243]

[^c0024-25]: The Venetian manuscript reads “when we have prospered” instead of “when we have advanced.”

For we believe that when our soul has been released from the bond of the flesh, if we have lived well and rightly before God, a choir of angels will immediately come to meet us; the hosts of all the saints will mingle in our embraces,[^c0024-26] and they will lead us to adore the true Judge.

[^c0024-26]: Benedict reads “will be mingled.” [Col. 0243]

If, while we live in the body, we do what is pleasing to God, as I have said, then peace and complete security will surround us. We shall no longer fear the fiery darts of the devil, nor any enemy who desires to pierce our souls,[^c0024-27] nor iron, nor fire, nor the torturer’s savage face, nor hunger, nor thirst, nor any bodily illness. [Col. 0243C–0244A]

[^c0024-27]: Benedict records in the margin, from a second hand in the Colbert manuscript, “to slaughter.” The Venetian manuscript has “to pierce,” with a wordplay on the danger.

The flesh will no longer oppose the spirit, and we shall fear no danger. But when we have cast off the burden of the flesh, then the Holy Spirit will grant us a dwelling in heaven—he who shortly before had been given a dwelling by us within the lodging of our body. We shall await with joy and gladness the day of the future judgment, on which the souls of individuals will receive the rewards due for their actions.

## CHAPTER XLI. The punishments of the condemned

On the other hand, sinners and the impious will repent,[^c0024-28] but in vain. Robbers and the greedy, the proud and adulterers, the angry and covetous, slanderers and perjurers will weep most bitterly, but they will not obtain forgiveness for their evils. [Col. 0243]

[^c0024-28]: The Venetian manuscript reads: “But the sinners and impious will perish. Then the rapacious, and so forth, will weep in vain, because of their evils, and so forth.” [Col. 0243]

All who have followed the pleasures of their flesh will be held in the greatest mourning; those who have served vices and passions will remain in everlasting sorrow and groaning. And when all these are assigned to the fires of Gehenna for their crimes and wicked deeds, we, if we have pleased God while we are in this body, will receive everlasting rewards with the saints. [Col. 0244B]

Therefore let us despise everything that is vain and fleeting, so that, through Christ’s mercy, we may deserve to attain such great glory.

## CHAPTER XLII. Guarding the tongue

Let us always turn away from vices and strive toward virtues. Let no superfluous words proceed from our mouth, because we shall have to give an account for idle words on the day of judgment. [Col. 0244C]

Let us not accustom our tongue to curse anyone, since it was created to bless and praise God.[^c0024-29] [Col. 0244D] Nor should we accustom ourselves to the worst habits in any action of ours, or even in our thoughts, because a habit that has been prolonged and strengthened cannot be avoided or driven out without great effort.[^c0024-30] [Col. 0245A]

[^c0024-29]: “It was created to bless God.” Chrysostom teaches the same in a sermon *On Faith, the Law of Nature, and the Holy Spirit*, volume III: “He gave it a tongue with which to speak, praise God, sing divine things, and interpret the beauty of nature.” The same author, Oration 17 on Ephesians 5: “You have a tongue, not to attack people with comic insults, but to give thanks to God.” The Venetian manuscript reads: “It was created, because it is a habit,” with the intervening material absent. [Col. 0244D–0245C]

[^c0024-30]: “A habit is not driven out without considerable effort.” Saint Basil, Homily on Psalm 1: “A vicious habit,” he says, “usually gives souls a disposition that scarcely ever ceases and is extremely difficult to move.” He adds that “in these matters, as in many others, habit changes and passes into nature,” a point he repeats in his response to Question 7 in the *Longer Rules*: “Habit, strengthened by age, usually acquires the force of nature.” Hence Gregory, book XI of the *Moralia*, chapter 5, calls evil habit a prison, from which the person held inside cannot escape: “Often some people desire to leave their evil actions, but because they are weighed down by the burden of those same actions, confined in the prison of evil habit, they cannot escape from themselves.” Augustine, taught by experience, compares it to a chain by which he felt bound and from which he could not free himself, however much he wished. He explains this in *Confessions* VIII.5:

> “My enemy held my will, and from it he had made a chain for me and bound me. For from a perverse will came lust; and while lust is served, habit was formed; and when habit is not resisted, necessity was formed. Joined together like links, which is why I called it a chain, a harsh slavery held me bound. But the new will that had begun to exist in me, by which I might serve you freely, was not yet strong enough to overcome the former will, strengthened by age.” [Col. 0245C–D]

## CHAPTER XLIII. Perfection is demonstrated not by years but by contrition

Let us be infants in wickedness and mature men in understanding (1 Corinthians 14:20).[^c0024-31] In some respects let us show ourselves old, and in others young. For it belongs to little ones to play, but to the perfect to mourn.[^c0024-32] Present mourning produces everlasting joy.[^c0024-33]

[^c0024-31]: “Let us be infants in wickedness.” According to Paul in 1 Corinthians 14:20: “Brothers, do not become children in understanding; rather, be infants in wickedness, but mature in understanding.” Chrysostom comments: “What does it mean to be little children or infants in wickedness or vice? Not even to know what vice is. He wanted them to be both men and children: children in vice, but men in prudence. For in this way a person will also be a man if he is a little child. But so long as he is not little in vice, he will not be a man either.” This is the point of what follows: in some things to be children, in others to be old. Old in prudence, children in wickedness. The Venetian manuscript reads “for little children … for mature men.” [Col. 0245D–0246B]

[^c0024-32]: “Little children play, but the perfect mourn.” In fragments circulated under the name of Cornelius Gallus, verse 115:

> A child exults in lightness, old age in gravity;  
> Joy suits the young man, a sorrowful brow the old. [Col. 0246B–C]

[^c0024-33]: “Mourning produces everlasting joy.” According to Matthew 5:5: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted.” Augustine says in *Sermon on the Mount* I.1: “They will be comforted by the Holy Spirit, so that, having lost temporal things, they may enjoy eternal joy.” Our Chromatius likewise says: “It is not without reason that the Lord promises holy mourners the consolation of eternal rejoicing.” And below: “The Lord compensates this kind of mourning with the consolation of perpetual joy.” So he says in his sermon on Matthew 5. [Col. 0246C–D]

Everything that is immoderate brings about the dissolution of the soul and makes it negligent toward God’s commandments. Such a person cannot easily recall his sins to mind; and, forgetting them, he does not urge himself to repentance, and thus little by little he falls away from every good thing. Where immoderate vices and evil desires exist, contrition of heart will gain no entrance. But where there are tears, there the spiritual fire is kindled, illuminating the hidden places of the mind.[^c0024-34]

[^c0024-34]: “Where there are tears, there the spiritual fire is kindled.” Hence Saint Macarius the Elder, Homily 25, on the power of tears and divine fire, presents Mary weeping and adds: “For this reason that divine fire illuminates souls.” [Col. 0246C–D]

Let no love of the world separate us from the love of Christ. Let all our thoughts strive toward the rewards of the future life and meditate on heavenly things.

This is your glory; this is the perfection of the course of your struggle. A person is called perfect not because he is perfect in age but because he is perfect in understanding. A childish age harms no one if the mind is perfect; nor will old age benefit anyone if he is childish in mind or understanding.[^c0024-35]

[^c0024-35]: The Venetian manuscript reads “a childish age harms no one,” and, for the following phrase, “in mind or understanding.” It also reads “his heart” and “was raised up” where the text has “heart” and “was chosen.” [Col. 0245]

David, although he was a boy, was perfect and had his heart and mind fixed upon the Lord. For this reason he was chosen and raised to be king. Saul, although he was advanced in age, because he possessed malicious wickedness within himself, was expelled from the royal height.

But our Lord and Savior is crucified by the elders, while upon entering Jerusalem he is praised by little children. Likewise, if a tree has been fruitless for many years, it is cut down; but if it is young and fruitful, it is cultivated so that it may produce still more abundant fruit.

I use these comparisons so that neither a young person nor an old person in your household may trust in his salvation or even in his deeds, but that “whoever boasts should boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31). [Col. 0246A–B]

## CHAPTER XLIV. Loving the company of the good and fleeing that of the wicked

Enjoy the company of perfect men,[^c0024-36] do not turn your ear away from their words, and let your soul delight in their counsel. For the words of people who fear God are words of life, and they bring safety of soul to those who gladly hear and attend to them.

[^c0024-36]: “Enjoy the company of the perfect.” Isaac the Syrian, priest, also gave this advice in *On Contempt of the World*, chapter 13: “Approach the righteous, and through them you will draw near to God. Associate with those who possess humility, and you will learn their ways. If merely seeing them is beneficial, how much more their teaching?” Basil the Emperor gives the same advice to his son Leo in his letter to his son, chapter 7: “Associate constantly with physicians of souls, so that you may be healthy in soul. From them you will be able to learn what things you ought to seek and what to avoid, with which people you should become familiar and from whose company you should recoil, and how your whole life ought to be ordered so that you do not fall into frequent illnesses.” Hence Seneca, Letter 11 to Lucilius: “We should choose some good man and always keep him before our eyes, so that we may live as though he were watching us and act as though he saw us.” So greatly can the company of good people help. [Col. 0246D–0247A]

Just as the rising sun drives away darkness, so the teaching of the saints drives darkness from our senses.[^c0024-37][^c0024-38]

[^c0024-37]: Benedict’s edition omits “for” (*enim*). [Col. 0247]

[^c0024-38]: The Venetian manuscript reads “drives the darkness of life away.”

Avoid, I beg you, proud, envious, slanderous, lying, and perjured men, as well as those who neglect themselves and their salvation,[^c0024-39] who are dead to virtues and delight in their own pleasures so that they may be deprived of divine joys.[^c0024-40]

[^c0024-39]: Benedict’s text does not contain “themselves” (*seipsos*). [Col. 0247]

[^c0024-40]: “Avoid proud men, and so forth.” Why? Because the Wise Man says, Ecclesiasticus 13:1: “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it; and whoever associates with a proud person will put on pride”—and likewise envy, detraction, and the other vices, should he associate with the envious, slanderers, or persons polluted by any other vice. Paulinus feared this even from one person. Seneca also notes it in Letter 7: “One example of luxury or greed has done much harm. A self-indulgent companion gradually weakens and softens one; a wealthy neighbour excites desire; a malicious companion rubs his rust upon even a candid and simple person.” [Col. 0247C]

I do not say that you should have even one such person in your household; wherever you hear that such people are found, avoid them. Let there be no association or intimacy between you and such people,[^c0024-41] and do not wish to converse with them unless, by the Lord’s mercy, you are able to recall them from their error.

[^c0024-41]: Benedict has: “Let there be no intercourse or familiarity with persons of that kind.” [Col. 0247B]

For often an entire flock is polluted by one diseased sheep.[^c0024-42] A small portion of gall turns great sweetness into bitterness.[^c0024-43]

[^c0024-42]: “One diseased sheep pollutes the whole flock.” Juvenal, book I, Satire 2, line 219:

> This contagion has given the stain,  
> and will give it to many more; just as an entire flock in the fields  
> falls from the mange of one sheep, and swine from scab. [Col. 0247C]

[^c0024-43]: “A small portion of gall turns great sweetness into bitterness.” Saint Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 21, uses a similar example: “A small vice,” he says, “can more quickly and abundantly impart itself to someone than even the most plentiful virtues can be shared sparingly. A little wormwood quickly imparts its bitterness to honey; honey, even if twice as great, cannot pour its sweetness into wormwood.” [Col. 0247C–D]

If such a person appears to you distinguished and noble in his appearance, and speaks sweet words to you,[^c0024-44] yet acts toward you in ways contrary to his words, his conduct does you more harm than his outward form pleases you. For a person is judged not by words but by virtues.

[^c0024-44]: “If he is noble and speaks sweet words, he does greater harm.” Such are those of whom Saint Cyprian says in *On the Spectacles*, not far from the beginning: “There is no shortage of flattering and indulgent defenders of vices who lend authority to vices.” Seneca reproached his fellow citizens for attributing human vices to their gods in order to derive permission to sin from them. Thus, in *On the Brevity of Life*, chapter 16: “What else is it to inflame our vices than to inscribe gods as their authors and to grant the disease an excuse for license through the dignity of its example?” Such is the noble person in Paulinus who speaks sweet words but acts in contrary ways. The Venetian manuscript omits “to you” in both places. [Col. 0247D–0248C]

## CHAPTER XLV. Patience, repentance, and right intention are especially commended in prayer
So may you too be approved before God, and willingly suffer everything for the love of Christ. When bodily tribulations befall you, let your spirit not be broken, lest the fleeting things of this age soften the vigor of your patience. [Note: In the Benedictine edition’s margin: in the manuscripts the word *tribulationibus* (“tribulations”) is absent.] [Note: The Venetian edition reads: “nor the vigor of your patience. Let not the fleeting things of this age soften you.”] Rather fear God if you have drawn back from your purpose; and when you realize that you are liable to sins, do not be ashamed to turn to repentance, because whoever repents here will not repent at the last.

In all your actions and thoughts, seek to please God, and do not strive to please anyone else except for the building up of the soul. In every work that you intend to do, think of God first. If what you are thinking is according to God, examine it carefully; and if it is right before God, carry it through. But if it is found to be contrary, cut it away from your soul. Do everything with the counsel of the wise, so that your works and your steps may be directed according to the Lord’s will. In every prayer and supplication, ask that the Lord’s will, not your own, be done in you. According to the Apostle’s command, “we ought to pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17), and to “lift holy hands to God without anger or dispute” (1 Timothy 2:8). [Note: The Venetian edition adds “and of the Lord.”]

## CHAPTER XLVI. Beneficence toward all is proposed after the example of God and Christ Jesus

The Lord is merciful, and he grants mercy to those who hope in him. He did not need mercy, since he had no sin, created the angels, and appointed the archangels over them; rather, he gave alms so that we might obtain mercy from him. [Note: The Benedictine edition reads *eleemosinas*, “alms,” in the plural.] [Note: “He gave alms.” The meaning is ambiguous. It is nevertheless explained by what follows: “so that we might obtain mercy from him, he gave alms”—that is, he commanded almsgiving, in order to make us, through our alms, participants in the kingdom of heaven. It is as though he had said: so that by acts of mercy we might merit his mercy, he gave the command to give alms—not for himself, who had no need, but for us, supplying what we lack through his mercy. If, however, one considers what precedes—namely, “The Lord is merciful, and grants mercy”—then *he gave alms* appears to mean the same as *he granted mercy*, the Greek word by which we call a gift given, or to be given, to a poor person being taken for its Latin equivalent, *mercy*. [Note: In this sense the Greeks themselves sometimes used the word *eleēmosynē* (“almsgiving”) to indicate mercy, although among them mercy is ordinarily called ἕλεος (*heleos*), not ἐλεημοσύνη (*eleēmosynē*). Thus Callimachus, *Hymn to Delos*, line 151:

> . . . μὴ σύγ’ ἐμεῖο πάθῃ κακὸν ἕνεκα, τῆς δὲ  
> Ἀντ’ ἐλεημοσύνης . . .

“Do not suffer any evil on my account, in return for that mercy.”

Or, finally, *he gave alms* may bear this meaning: he gave the means by which almsgiving could be performed, namely money, bread, and clothing. In that case *alms* should more correctly be read in the plural, as the Benedictines do. For everything that we give to the poor belongs to God and has been given to us by him. Hear Augustine, near the end of his exposition of Psalm 95: “From whose possession do you give, unless from his? If you were giving from your own, it would be generosity; when you give from his, it is repayment. For what do you have that you have not received?” And elsewhere, in Psalm 147, section 13: “God wishes to have distributed from what he has given. For what do you give that he has not given? . . . Or, I do not say to God, but to anyone at all, do you give something from your own? You give from his possession, who commands you to give.” From these interpretations, reader, choose whichever seems more convenient to you, whatever one most pleases you. Whichever you embrace, I think you will not depart very far from Paulinus’s meaning.]

Almsgiving was not necessary for him whose are all the kingdoms of heaven, who established dominions, principalities, virtues, and powers; but so that he might make us participants in the kingdom of heaven through our alms.

The Lord is patient and peaceful, so that by his patience and peace he might reconcile to God the whole world, which lay in wickedness (1 John 5:19). And if we wish to reach God, let us also be patient and peaceful, without anger or dispute. Let us do good to all people. [Note: “Let us do good to all” means not to one or two alone. Precisely because they are human beings, they are our neighbors; and our neighbors are to be loved. Augustine, *Letter* 155, in the new edition, section 14, after saying that neighbors are to be loved, says that neighbors are to be understood “not by blood relationship, but by the fellowship of reason, a fellowship that embraces all human beings.” He then adds a profane but highly pertinent example. He continues: “Hence that Comic poet [Terence, *The Self-Tormentor*, act 1, scene 1], when one old man said to another, ‘Have you so much leisure from your own affairs that you concern yourself with matters that do not concern you?’ had the other reply: ‘I am a human being; I consider nothing human alien to me.’ They say that the whole theater, filled with foolish and uneducated people, applauded this sentiment. For the fellowship of human friendship touched everyone’s feelings so naturally that no human being there failed to feel that he was the neighbor of every other human being.” A similar statement is attributed by Stobaeus, *Sermons* 37, to Aristotle: when reproached by someone for having given money to a worthless man who asked for it, he said that he had given it “not to the man, but to humanity.” And in Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book 9, chapter 2, Herodes Atticus says of a wicked man asking for money: “Let us give this fellow some money, whatever sort of person he is—as human beings, not for the man as such.” Such philosophers understood that even if those who asked were, through their vices, less than human, they ought nevertheless to give because they were of the same nature, because they were human beings.]

I mean good to all, not selectively: not to one, or two, or three, but to all human beings. For Christ suffered not only for the holy, but for sinners and the ungodly and the wicked he mounted the cross; and by his passion he recalled us all to life.

God gave the sun, the moon, the rain, all things that grow from the earth, and all the fruits that arise upon the earth not only to the holy, but in common to all human beings. [Note: “He gave those things in common to all.” Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book 3: “Does God not supply equally to all—the sun’s generative heat, the seasons of night, winds, rains, crops—to good and evil, just and unjust” (thus according to the reading of Fulvius Ursinus), “free and enslaved, poor and rich?” St. Eucherius, *Paraenesis to Valerian*, shortly before the end: “Behold, as we see, divine generosity has granted to all alike the common use of the most cherished light. The godly and the ungodly alike are permitted to look upon the common sun; toward all, creation preserves its service through kindly offices; possession of this world is indiscriminately shared by the good and the wicked.” St. Ambrose, book 5 on chapter 6 of Luke, concerning the woes of the wicked, near the end: “The kindness of God extends widely: he sends rain upon the ungrateful, and the fruitful earth does not refuse its produce to the wicked. The same sun of the world illuminates sacrilegious and religious alike.” Prudentius discusses this argument at length in book 2 *Against Symmachus*. Seneca also noted it, *On Benefits*, book 4, chapter 26: “If you imitate the gods, give benefits even to the ungrateful. For the sun rises also upon criminals, and the seas lie open to pirates.”]

He makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matthew 5:45). [Note: The source has “Matthew 5:96,” evidently an obvious numerical error.] Therefore he gave those things to all human beings in common, so that our goodness, our almsgiving, our charity, our patience, and our humility might be distributed in common to all human beings. As long as we are in this world, let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith (Galatians 6:10); and let us pray for our enemies and repay evil with good.

49

## CHAPTER XLVII. The rewards and labors of the righteous

Let us honor the poor and receive Christ in them, who said: “As long as you did it for one of the least of these my brothers, you did it for me” (Matthew 25:40). Then we shall be sons of God, heirs of God, and coheirs with Christ (Romans 8:17), and we shall be participants in his kingdom, where we shall never grow old and never die; where there is nothing belonging to human nature, nor any pain, nor sadness after joy, nor the light of the sun, nor that of the moon, nor the radiance of the stars. [Note: Thus the Venetian edition; but the Benedictine edition reads, “where we shall not die and shall not grow old,” and adds in the margin: “where there is no human nature,” that is, “frail and wretched.”] [Note: “Where there is no human nature.” We have preferred the reading of the Venetian and Basel Frobenian editions as the clearer one. The reading printed by the Benedictine Fathers seemed obscure even to them, and they attempt to explain it in the margin as “that is, frail and wretched.” Yet it is false to say that human nature will not be there. “Where there is nothing of human nature” is more conveniently understood, namely, where there is nothing characteristic of human nature, such as suffering and dying; this appears to be explained by the following words, “nor any pain nor sadness.” Indeed, to suffer something can mean nothing other than to die.
