Thus in Paul, *Digest*, “On Deposit,” law 1, *Publia Moevia*: “If anything human should happen to me, you shall restore [the deposit] to my son”; this means the same as “if I should die.” Cicero himself, in the *Philippics*: “If anything should happen to me in human fashion” (although many things seemed to threaten me beyond nature and even beyond fate), “I would leave this day’s speech as a witness to the Republic of my constant devotion to it.” These words mean nothing other than: “If it should happen that I died.”]

But our Lord Jesus Christ will be light, health, life, charity, peace, joy, and every good thing for all who believe in him. There is the land of the living, which the Prophet had sung, saying: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13). That is, he signified that he would see the heavenly reward [Note: The Venetian edition reads “that he would see”; the Benedictine edition, on the basis of manuscripts, reads “signified himself to see.” They note in the margin: “Perhaps, ‘of the living.’”] and live and reign with Christ forever, where no night comes upon us, the day will never end, poverty will not be seen, and desire will not appear, but there will be perpetual joy and everlasting gladness.

These are the promises made to the righteous, and these are the promises for which they labored, hastened, and did not cease to run in good works as long as they lived in this world: in fasts and almsgiving, in chastity, continence, patience, endurance, gentleness, goodwill, much labor, prayers, persecutions, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and many vigils for the love of Christ; and in every way they avoided useless vigils.

Vigils are useless when someone keeps watch over many shameful thoughts, or in order to do something contrary, or to perpetrate a crime. The righteous avoided such vigils [Note: The Venetian edition has this reading; the Benedictine edition omits *justi*, “the righteous.”] and undertook holy vigils. [Note: “They undertook holy vigils.” It is well known that the Church had the practice of vigils, in which the faithful gathered at night to sing divine praises. The rite appears to be of very ancient origin, as is indicated by the words of those Christians whom Pliny questioned about their religion. He wrote to Trajan, book 10, letter 100: “They affirmed that the whole of their guilt or error was this: that they were accustomed to meet on a fixed day before dawn and to sing responsively a hymn to Christ as to a god.” This rite may have been introduced into the churches as a correction of pagan vigils, so that an existing custom might be turned toward something better rather than newly invented. For Plautus’s *The Pot of Gold*, line 60, in the prologue, shows that vigils of Ceres were celebrated. These vigils were held on the night preceding some solemn festival; in time they passed into fasts on the preceding day. John Baptist Mantuanus gives the reason in *Fasti*, book 2, concerning the change of vigils into fasts:

> This too I shall add, for the place is most worthy of notice:  
> what our ancestors used to keep watch for in temples,  
> enduring guard-duty in order to receive the solemn  
> festivals that followed in the morning—this custom a new age removed.  
> For since night is usually an occasion for crime, and those who intend  
> to commit deeds observe the time,  
> it seemed wiser to fast through the day that precedes  
> and to sleep through the night in a closed chamber.

Nevertheless, it is probable that Paulinus did not refer precisely to these vigils here, but rather to those which anyone secluded from others and shut within his own chamber might establish by devoting himself to prayer and reading. Such were the vigils of which John Climacus says in *The Ladder of Paradise*, step 20: “There are some who, during evening and nocturnal watches, stripped and freed from every concern for visible things, stretch pure hands toward God in prayer. Others present themselves to God in those same watches through the singing of psalms. Others remain awake over the reading of sacred things. Others, weaker in mind but active in work, nobly struggle against sleep. Others seek to bring themselves to compunction through constant consideration of death.” Yet do not think that Climacus means monks alone; for he adds that only “the second group follows the monastic manner of praying.” From this you see that vigils were also appropriate for non-monks. In commending them, St. Peter Chrysologus gives this reason, sermon 24: “because in truth, to keep watch more is to live more.” But the scholiast on Climacus, at the same place, scholion 4, says: “Take care not to spend your vigils on empty stories or wicked thoughts. For it is better to sleep than to keep watch over empty conversations and thoughts.” Paulinus says that the righteous avoided such vigils.]

Such people trampled upon the present world in order to gain the kingdom that is to come. They did not receive here the promises or the miserable riches of this world, which, when people use them badly, lead them to hell. Leaving this present homeland, they sent the gaze of their souls ahead to the heavenly city, whose architect and founder is God. They avoided sin in word, deed, thought, sight, laughter, movement, the nodding of the eyes, the hands, the feet, anger, quarrel, fury, dissension, vainglory, pride, arrogance, and greed, guarding their bodies and their souls.

50

## CHAPTER XLVIII. The twofold fast—of soul and body—and food

For they fasted with a twofold fast, that is, the fast of body and soul: abstaining from anger, fury, slander, blasphemy, and quarrel. For, as we stated above, these are the deadly foods of the soul, which feed it toward evil and kill it with everlasting death.

Again, these are foods of both body and soul: gluttony, sleepiness, fornication, drunkenness, complacency, sensual pleasure, and murder. These are foods of both body and soul, which feed the body but kill and burden the soul. [Note: The Benedictine edition adds *et gravant*, “and burden.”] Let us avoid such foods; let us desire instead the heavenly foods that draw and lead us toward heaven: divine wisdom, strong faith in Christ, kindness, goodwill, patience, humility, virtue, and divine gladness.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Having set forth the reward of those who do good, he terrifies by describing the punishments prepared for the wicked

Let good and excellent words proceed from our mouths, seasoned with divine salt for the building up of those who hear. Let us always meditate in our minds and fulfill in our deeds the love of God and neighbor, on which the whole law and the prophets depend (Matthew 22:40). These are Christ’s commandments, which he orders us to carry out. If we carry them out, we shall share in his kingdom and reign with him; but if we do not carry them out, he too will not give us his kingdom. If we deny him, he too will deny us. If we do not believe, he will remain faithful [Note: The Venetian edition reads *permanet*, “remains,” rather than *permanebit*, “will remain.”], because every unbeliever acts unfaithfully: for it is a human fault to believe everything, and it is also a fault to believe nothing. [Note: “It is also a fault.” Seneca, *Letters*, 3: “Both are faults: believing everyone and believing no one.”] [Note: The printed editions of the Benedictines add here in the margin: “and always saying the greatest evils about an enemy, although, if his words toward us are harsh, he perhaps nevertheless remembers that he is a Christian and weeps over himself as guilty before God. Slanderous words, however, always say evil things about an enemy; but if you speak good things, you immediately put him to shame. For such words never produce concord, but discord: they throw wood into the fire.” The Venetian edition has this passage within brackets.]

With the greatest care and vigilance we must see to it that on the day of judgment we do not hear from Christ, the judge of all, what sinners will hear: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:41). For Gehenna has truly been prepared for the devil, and not for all human beings, provided that we have not done the devil’s works. Woe to those for whom have been prepared the pain of worms, the burning of flame, thirst without relief, [Note: “Without relief” is used instead of *extinction*. Pliny, book 7, chapter 7: “The smell from the extinguishing of lamps.”] weeping, and the gnashing of teeth; tears of the eyes; outer darkness without light; unending punishment; where there is no honor or recognition of one’s neighbor, but continual pain and groaning; where death is desired but not granted; where there is no honor for elder or king, nor is a master over a slave; where a mother does not love her son or daughter, nor a son honor his father; where every evil, every indignation, stench, and bitterness abounds.

The righteous feared these things and fled from them. I ask, plead, and again and again entreat you, dearest brother, that we too love and fear God and flee these things, because our soul’s death is everlasting if we persevere in them.

## CHAPTER L. Three worst things here; an equal number of best things

There are three things in this world worse than every evil: the soul of a sinner persevering in sin, which is blacker than a raven; [Note: “Which is blacker than a raven.” Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 17: “Guilt is dark and feeds upon the dead like a raven.” Augustine, *Annotations on Job*, chapter 38, verse 41: “The black ones—the ravens—therefore signify sinners not yet whitened by the remission of sins.” Bruno of Asti, commentary on Genesis, chapter 8: “For what does the raven signify if not sinners?” Some Greek Fathers, however, assert that the devil himself is signified by the raven’s blackness. Thus Chrysostom, sermon on Pentecost, concerning the Holy Spirit: “The devil, who is truly a black and dark raven, was expelled from the ark of the Church and drowned in the waters of baptism.” And Anastasius Sinaita, book 1 of the *Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexameron*: “When the dark raven Satan had been drowned and perished”—understand, in the waters of baptism of which he is speaking—“and so forth.” The devil, moreover, is the head of sinners.] the evil angels who seize it; and hell, to which it is led. For nothing is worse than these three.

The same soul, terrified by fear of the future judgment and looking upon its corruption, says: “My scars have become foul and putrid because of my foolishness” (Psalm 37:6). Again, there are three things in this world better than all others: the soul of a holy person persevering in good works, which is more beautiful than the sun; [Note: “Which is more beautiful than the sun.” This comparison is not uncommon in Scripture. Judges 5:31: “But those who love you, let them shine as the sun at its rising.” Ecclesiasticus 27:12: “A wise man remains in wisdom like the sun.” See Cornelius a Lapide for eight analogies between the sun and the righteous in this passage. Add the Lord’s statement in the Gospel, Matthew 13:43, concerning the righteous who have persevered in good works, as Paulinus says here, and who will obtain glory: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”] the holy angels who receive it; and paradise, to which it is led, together with the expectation of the heavenly kingdom. Nothing in this world is better than these three.

For the holy angels delight the soul with spiritual song, as the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the one whom you have chosen and taken to yourself, O Lord; he shall dwell in your tents. We shall be filled with the good things of your house. Holy is your temple, wonderful in righteousness” (Psalm 64:5–6). Let us meditate on these things, dearest brother.

## CHAPTER LI. He teaches us to beware of every sin, explains the purpose of Christ’s redemption, and urges us to labor in good time

Let us hold these things firmly in our minds and guard ourselves from every sin and iniquity—in word, deed, thought, hands, feet, sight, and hearing—and let us guard our body and soul. For Christ our Lord, who is God and the Son of God, descended from heaven to earth in order to carry us with him from earth to heaven. For us sinners he mounted the cross, so that he might free us from the devil’s torment. [Note: “So that he might free us from torment.” *Cruciatus* derives from *crux*, “cross,” as is clear from Terence, *The Eunuch*, line 382, act 2, scene 3:

> “And those crosses,  
> and the things that always torment us in every way.”

Thus Paulinus’s antithesis is especially apt.]

He received punishment from his enemies so that he might free us from everlasting punishment. He accepted death so that he might rescue us from death. He rose from the dead so that we might rise in soul and body on the great day of judgment. Therefore, while we have time, let us labor, and with God’s help let us always strive to do good works that please God, lest, suddenly overtaken by the day of death, we seek time for repentance and be unable to find it. [Note: “Lest we be suddenly overtaken.” This is part of the responsory that is now said after the fourth lesson on the First Sunday of Lent and on the Tuesday and Friday of that same week: “Let us amend for the better what we have sinned through ignorance,” and so forth. Whether Paulinus borrowed the words from the responsory, or the author of the responsory from Paulinus, is uncertain. For whatever Agobard may say in *On the Correction of the Antiphonary* and in his book *Against Amalarius*, the Church, as Walahfrid Strabo testifies, customarily and commendably borrowed sentences in its prayers even from the Fathers and other approved writers, *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 25. Amalarius writes of this responsory in *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, chapter 35: “It seemed right to me that the responsories concerning fasting should be written in such a way that the first would be: ‘Let us amend for the better what we have sinned through ignorance,’ and so forth; for it is especially suitable to the season of Lent and to repentance.” It was, after all, the Church’s custom to conform its prayers to the mysteries. Alcuin, *Poem* 3:

> We shall bring forth hymns and psalms and responsories  
> suited to the festivals beneath the vaulted roof.

When Amalarius wrote this, Paulinus had already written his work. Nevertheless, I would not dare to assert that Amalarius excerpted it from the passage of Paulinus before us, since Amalarius says that what he discusses was not newly invented, but better arranged.]

While we are in this present time, we must sow; for in its proper time—that is, after death, or on the day of judgment—we shall reap what we ought to possess in eternal life. [Note: The Benedictine edition reads *debemus*, “what we ought to have,” rather than *debeamus*, “what we should have.”] Let us therefore labor in this way and bear one another’s burdens. For where the head has gone before, the other members will follow. [Note: The Venetian edition reads *sunt*, “are,” rather than *erunt*, “will be.”]

## CHAPTER LII. Concerning faith, hope, and especially mutual charity
Let us hold fast, as has already been inserted above, to right faith, sure hope, and perfect charity, because faith is, as it were, our perception, and charity as it were our health. Faith believes, charity acts, hope strengthens. And although different members have different functions, if all the members are nevertheless held together by the unity of charity, then they will deserve to follow the head.

[Note: “Faith is as it were our perception, and charity as it were our health.” These and the final words of the preceding chapter, together with several passages occurring below in this very chapter, are found in Sermon 105 among those rejected as works of Saint Augustine and placed in the Appendix. Read especially sections 4 and 5 of that sermon, and you will find several points agreeing with this chapter of Paulinus. That these sermons are not Augustine’s is certain here. Whether they are by Caesarius, bishop of Arles, whose various sermons were at times attributed to Augustine, the Benedictine editors of Augustine’s works hesitate to decide. They prefix to the sermon this title from the manuscripts: “Extracts from Augustine’s books: how true and perfect love is to be preserved, and concerning the love of the members, how all the members serve when a thorn is trodden upon.” The editors add: “The extracts reproduce the sense, not the words, and perhaps are by Caesarius.”

There is no denying that Caesarius appropriated much from Augustine. Yet they note that the passages in this sermon which belong to Augustine were taken from the Expositions on the Psalms. They show that the passages agreeing with our Paulinus were taken from no place in Augustine or any other writer. Therefore the passages found near the end of sections 4 and 5, which agree with Paulinus’s statements, belong to Caesarius or to another author.

But since this Sermon 105 is inserted among Caesarius’s works neither in the works published by Baluze nor in volume 27 of the Library of the Fathers, where it is added as a supplement to the sixth century, what prevents us from suspecting that the sermon was composed by some later person from sayings of Augustine and also of Paulinus? For this book of exhortation was long believed to be Augustine’s; indeed, even in the ninth century, at whose beginning Paulinus had already died, “we see this work taken away from Paulinus,” say the Benedictine Fathers, “so that it might be attributed to Augustine. For there exists at Thérouanne, if we are not mistaken, a copy eight hundred years old bearing this title, written by the first hand on the front of the book: ‘The Book of Exhortation of Saint Augustine to a Certain Count, Most Dear to Him.’” Thus write the exceptionally exact Benedictine Fathers in the notice prefixed to the book in volume 6 of the works of Saint Augustine. In the preface to volume 5, which contains Augustine’s sermons, the Fathers themselves do not deny that some sermons were taken from later Fathers, including contemporaries of Paulinus such as Alcuin, and even from later writers such as Ivo of Chartres. Perhaps, therefore, this passage under discussion was drawn from this passage of Paulinus rather than from the spurious sermon, which was drawn from Paulinus.]

Our head is in heaven, and Truth itself, our Lord Jesus Christ, says of his faithful: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my servant be” (John 12:26).

Let us beware—indeed, let us beware in every way—that through envy, hatred, slander, anger, or quarrelling we may not be severed from our head, Jesus Christ. Whatever evil our neighbor has endured for the love of Christ, let us share in it with charitable affection; and whatever good someone else has received, let us rejoice as though we ourselves had received it, and give thanks on behalf of the one who received it.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads “and quarrelling.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “the righteous, for the love of Christ and of our neighbor.” The Benedictine editors add: “ourselves and our neighbors.” Both readings are faulty: first, because neighbors are not necessarily righteous; second, because “ourselves” has no connection with “have endured,” and compassion for ourselves is not what is being urged.]

Behold, as we have said, someone suffers tribulation or loss in this world, or is punished for his sins, or, by order of the imperial dignity, is thrust into prison; someone grieves at the death of parents or friends. If we grieve for him, we belong within the body of the Church; if we do not grieve, we have already been severed from the body.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads “as we have already said.” The Benedictine edition reads: “for his sins he is shut up in prison at the command of the imperial eminence.”]

[Note: *Imperiali sublimitate* (“by imperial eminence”) is an honorific title. Nicholas I, in Letter 30 to Charles the Bald, near its beginning and end, writes: “Moreover, we ask that your eminence, etc.” Since, as Festus says under S, “*sublime* is said from the upper threshold, because it is above us,” the word was applied to those elevated above others in nobility. Thus Salvian, *On the Government of God*, IV, used *dignitas sublimium* for the rank of nobles; Statius used *sublime genus* in *Silvae* III.440 and *Thebaid* X.219, as did Claudian in *On the Fourth Consulship of Honorius* 217, all indicating nobility. We also learn from *Code of Justinian*, *On Judges* 16, that tribunals, judges’ seats, judges themselves, and those set over the settlement of lawsuits bore the title *sublimissimi*: “Established from the general forms of your most exalted seat, etc.” In *On Appeals* one reads “the most exalted master of offices,” and in the following law “the most exalted judges.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition adds within brackets: “and we sympathize as much as we can.”]

[Note: The printed editions and the Venetian edition add within brackets: “But, alas, sometimes we pretend to be strict, cast the material into the flame, and, once the fire has been kindled, flee.”]

Charity, which gathers together and gives life to all the members of the Church, immediately cuts us off from the body if it sees us rejoicing at another’s ruin.

[Note: The Benedictine edition reads “gathers together” (*colligit*) rather than “may gather together” (*colligat*).]

Perhaps, then, we do not grieve over the ruin of our neighbors because we have been severed from the body. For if we were there, without doubt we would grieve.

[Note: The Venetian edition adds: “but lie in wait for him.”]

Let us consider, dearest brother, and attend carefully to this: a member suffers only so long as it remains joined to the body;

[Note: “Brother” is absent from the Venetian edition.] but if it has been cut off, it can neither suffer nor feel. When a hand or some other member has been cut off from the body, even if the whole body is then divided into many parts, that hand feels nothing, since it has already been separated from the fellowship of the other members. Such is every Christian who not only does not grieve at another’s loss, affliction, or even death, but—what is worse—perhaps even rejoices.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “mocks and rejoices.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “therefore he does not have the affection of charity in his heart, because he is already alienated from the body.”]

And because he is already alienated from the body, he does not retain the affection of charity in his heart, although the Apostle commands: “Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep, having the same mind toward one another” (Romans 12:15–16).

And Solomon very clearly warns us not to rejoice at the ruin of our brothers (Proverbs 17:5).

[Note: The printed editions and the Venetian edition add within brackets: “Wretchedly, we rejoice and mock at the ruin of our enemies; and if he does not fall, we wish him to fall in revenge against us. But let us pray to God.”]

But we, dearest brother, if we wish to preserve true and perfect charity, should strive to love all people as ourselves. Since Christ is our head, may we deserve to be his members; and when Christ, our glory, appears, may we also, through the harmony of charity—that is, through love of God and neighbor—deserve to appear with him in glory as his true and perfect members, without any deceitful malice or envy, loving all people as ourselves.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “so that, by his help, we may strive to love all people as ourselves,” and reads “and through love” for “through the harmony of charity.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition omits “in the Gospel.”]

For he himself says in the Gospel: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). Love of neighbor does no evil (Romans 13:10).

O dearest brother, if our Lord and Savior, who had no sin, deigns to love us sinners with such affection and such love that he testifies that he himself suffers what we suffer, why do we, who are not without sin and who can redeem our sins through charity, not love him with equally perfect love, since he loved us so greatly that he even handed over his only Son to death for us sinners?

[Note: The Venetian edition omits “dearest.” The Benedictine edition reads *tantum* (“so much”) where the Venetian and the present text read *tanto* (“with so great a love”), agreeing with the preceding *amore* (“love”).]

[Note: The Benedictine and Venetian editions both have: “and who can redeem our sins through charity.” The Venetian edition places these words in brackets.]

And since he has shown such kindness and mercy toward us, let us be watchful lest we lose the good he gave us, and the sacrament of our baptism, in which we swore to renounce the devil, his pomps, and all sins.

[Note: The Benedictine edition has in the margin, according to the manuscripts, “in which.”]

And if after baptism we transgress in some sin, the merciful God has given us a second baptism—that is, a fountain of tears—and has appointed penance for us because of our frailty.

[Note: The Venetian edition adds within brackets: “we take care to cleanse ourselves with the tears of penance, because he is merciful.”]

Therefore we must confess our confessions truthfully and perform worthy fruits of penance; that is, in accordance with the command of the Lord and the counsel of a priest who fears God, we must not repeat past sins.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “that is, we must not repeat past sins.”]

That priest, as a wise and perfect physician, must first know how to heal his own sins and then wipe away and heal the wounds of others, without making them public.

[Note: The Benedictine edition has: “according to the command of the God-fearing priest.”]

If we can, let us seek out and follow such men, and with them undertake counsel for our salvation,

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “Let us seek them out and follow them.”] so that we may not lose the heavenly inheritance which the Lord prepared for us from the beginning of the world, if we serve him in righteousness, holiness, purity of heart, and sincere charity, crying out with the Apostle:

“Who will separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or persecution, or distress, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Romans 8:35).

[Note: The Venetian edition omits “or persecution, or famine.”]

And the rest that follows, as it is said: “Neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, nor any creature will be able to separate us from the charity of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38).

[Note: The Venetian edition has “it was said, moreover.”]

It was also said of the primitive Church that “they had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32) in the Lord, and that they had one will and one refusal, because the charity of Christ had joined them together as one.

## CHAPTER LIII. The Opinions of Wicked Men, and Again Concerning Almsgiving from One’s Own Property

By contrast, the carnal and those who love this world separate and divide themselves from one another, provoking among themselves scandals, quarrels, anger, fights, dissensions, murders, perjuries, thefts, robberies, and everything that this world loves. Each one takes delight in saying in his heart:

[Note: The Benedictine editions omit “this world.”]

“I will do what I wish and what I can; I will fulfill my thoughts and bodily pleasures. My plans are supported either by my own friends or by powerful relatives. I have gold; silver abounds. I have servants and maidservants, fields and many possessions of this world, cloaks and costly garments, from which I can redeem myself. I will fulfill my will. God will give me time for life and repentance.”

[Note: The Venetian edition adds within brackets: “I have my Lord as my friend and defender; no one opposes me. In the meantime, I will do what I can.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition reads *implebo* (“I shall fulfill”) for *impleam* (“let me fulfill”).]

[Note: Later, the Venetian edition likewise reads *adimplebo* (“I shall fulfill”) for *adimpleam* (“let me fulfill”).]

[Note: The Venetian edition adds within brackets: “I will oppress whom I wish and support whom I wish.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition adds within brackets: “My eloquence surpasses everyone’s; whom should I fear?”]

Alas, why do we not fear what the Gospel thunders forth, saying: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and whose will those things be which you have prepared?” (Luke 12:20).

[Note: “Let us recognize that we are human, so that we may not grow so proud.” The argument for humility is the recognition of our humanity. “Why does earth and ashes grow proud?” says the Wise Man (Sirach 10:9). Augustine, Tractate 25 on John, section 15: “What is said of the proud mortal, girded with the clothing of flesh, weighed down by a corruptible body, and yet lifting himself up and forgetting with what skin he is clothed? What does Scripture say to him? ‘Why does earth and ashes grow proud?’ Why does he grow proud? Let him say why he grows proud.” And in the following section: “Why are you proud, man? … God became man; you, man, recognize that you are man. Your entire humility consists in recognizing yourself.”

We also learn from chapter 33 of Tertullian’s Apology that the memory of human nature is set before the mind to restrain arrogance: “Even while triumphing in that most lofty chariot, he is reminded that he is a man. For someone behind him whispers: ‘Look behind you; remember that you are a man.’ And certainly he rejoices all the more in shining with such glory, so that the reminder of his condition becomes necessary to him.”]

Let us recognize that we are human, and let us not become so proud against God and our neighbor that we carry out our evil desires and put God aside.

[Note: The Venetian edition has “and not so.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition has “and” instead of “so that.”]

Let us not strive, by means of gifts, to turn the Lord’s good will toward our evil wills, while neglecting to correct our perverse will according to the Lord’s ever-righteous will.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “while we neglect to correct ourselves and our perverse will.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition omits “God.”]

But wherever it pleases us, we wish to avenge our injuries, saying: “I will commit murder, perjury, adultery, fornication, and afterward I will give the Lord my ransom.”

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “and we do not spare our brother,” saying: “I will take revenge on my brother or my father; I will commit murder.”]

Why do we not understand that, when we sin so boldly, thinking that God can be appeased by gifts, we provoke him much more to anger than to mercy?

[Note: Thinking that God can be appeased by gifts: Sirach 7:11 says, “Do not say: God will regard the multitude of my gifts, and, when I offer gifts to God Most High, he will receive them.” See also chapters 34 and 35 of the same book, where Sirach brings together much relevant matter. From this judge how ineptly and falsely Ovid wrote in *The Art of Love* III.633:

“Believe me, gifts win both men and gods;
Jupiter himself is appeased by your gifts.”]

[Note: “We provoke him more to anger than to mercy,” as is clear from the Lord’s words in Isaiah 1:11 and following, Jeremiah 6:20, and Amos 5:21–22. Among these are the words spoken through Isaiah: “What are your many sacrifices to me? I am full … Incense is an abomination to me … these things have become burdensome to me.”]

For God takes no pleasure in gold or silver, nor does he ask anything else from us than that our souls be presented clean in his sight.

[Note: God does not delight in gold or silver offered by sinners, because he has no need of gold or silver. For the Lord of hosts says: “The silver is mine, and the gold is mine” (Haggai 2:9). And Ezekiel 7:19 says: “They will throw their silver into the streets, and their gold will be treated as refuse.” “Their silver and their gold will not be able to deliver them on the day of the Lord’s wrath.”]

For he does not involve himself in the counsels of sinners, but continually admonishes us for our salvation and gives saving counsel, because he is himself the counselor of our salvation, as the prophet says: “His name will be called Wonderful, Counselor” (Isaiah 9:6).

And again it was said of him in the Psalm: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked” (Psalm 1:1). And again, because there is no injustice in him (Romans 9:14).

Perhaps even the almsgiving which we think we are performing for our benefit, whether from the estates of the dead or from the plunder of the poor, appears to be almsgiving in name, but not in deed: one person is unjustly clothed while another is unjustly stripped; one is unjustly fed while another is unjustly tormented by hunger.

[Note: “From the estates of the dead”: the reading is uncertain, or perhaps it should be “from the plunder,” as the Venetian, Frobenian, and other editions have it. In that case the passage would seem to concern the alms of plunderers, with “of the dead” meaning “of those who have been killed,” as in the case of robbers on the road.

Or perhaps “from estates,” as the Benedictine Fathers read it. In that case it should be understood as referring to estates unjustly acquired. For who could doubt that it is most pleasing to God to give alms from possessions obtained by a just title? We have retained this reading because the first meaning is found in the words that follow, “in the plunder of the poor.” Here it seems necessary to exhaust the whole subject, so that everyone may understand that things unjustly acquired, whether by fraud and deceit or by force, if given as alms, appear to be alms in name but not in deed.]

God does not ask these things of us. I dare to say it: almighty God hates them.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “Hear the prophet, who says.”]

Hear what he says through the prophet: “Whoever offers sacrifice from plunder, or from the substance of the poor, is like one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father” (Sirach 34:24).

“He says, ‘I will not accept these things from your hands; for your hands are full of blood’” (Isaiah 1:15).

[Note: The Venetian edition has: “God says.”]

And another prophet says: “The bread of the needy is the life of the poor; whoever deprives him of it is a man of blood” (Sirach 34:25).

Let us refuse to give unjust alms, since we wish to give just and spiritual alms. Let us give from honest labors, not from plunder,

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “Let us strive to give just, spiritual alms.”] whether from an increase of crops or from dishonest business, lest many sacrileges perhaps be committed in this way, or—even worse—blood be shed because of greed or drunkenness, and the voices of those afflicted by much labor cry out against us to God.

[Note: The Benedictine edition has in the margin, according to the manuscripts: “more serious sacrileges may occur.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition has: “because of greed or drunkenness.”]

Therefore the Psalmist says: “He who has not given his money at interest, nor accepted gifts against the innocent” (Psalm 14:5), and the other things stated above in the same psalm, which can make the hearer, the believer, and the one who fears, blessed and cautious.

[Note: The Venetian edition has: “The Psalmist says.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition adds: “and the believer and the one who fears.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition adds: “and the same.”]

As the same psalm concludes: “Whoever does these things will never be moved” (ibid.).

## CHAPTER LIV. Christian Happiness Is Not of This World; Therefore One Must Not Cling to It, but to God

Since the Creator of all things announces and teaches such things and others like them to his rational creature, let us believe that the Creator loves what he created; that he persecutes no one unless the person himself persecutes himself; that he withdraws from no human being unless the human being first withdraws from him; and that he hates not the nature he placed in us, but the vice we have contracted.

[Note: The Venetian edition reads: “We believe that the Creator who loves what he has created persecutes no one, etc.” It also has an unclear abbreviated variant: “nor nature—not in us—or vice.”]

[Note: “He withdraws from no one unless the person withdraws from him.” 2 Chronicles 12:5: “You have forsaken me, and I have forsaken you”; and 15:2: “If you forsake him, he will forsake you.” Augustine, Confessions 4.9: “No one loses you except the one who leaves you.” See also chapter 11 of that book and chapter 2 of the following book. He repeats the same point in City of God 13.15: “The soul’s life, which is God to it, was not abandoned so that it might abandon him; rather, it abandoned him so that it might be abandoned.”]

[Note: The Venetian edition adds “God.”]

Nor does it benefit us—indeed, it harms us—to have been redeemed by the blood of Christ and voluntarily to be subject to the devil.

[Note: “It does not benefit us; rather, it harms us,” etc. Consult John 15:22 and 24, Hebrews 6:4 and following, and 10:26 and following. Salvian, On the Government of God, book 4, addresses Christians who received redemption through the blood of Christ in baptism as follows: “We, who are called Christians and Catholics, if we do anything similar to the impurity of the barbarians, sin more grievously. For under the profession of the holy name we sin more atrociously. Where the privilege is higher, the guilt is greater; the very religion which we profess accuses our errors.” He has much else of this kind in the same book, though not so relevant to our subject as these words of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, Homily 4: “Crimes are repeated with grave condemnation after they have been redeemed by the blood of Christ. It is an inexcusable evil for a servant to be stained by sins after the death of our Redeemer, the Lord.”]

Therefore let us think and think again that we did not become Christians for earthly happiness, nor do we worship Christ for the riches of this world or for this life, as the Apostle says: “If in this life only we have hope in the Lord, we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Corinthians 15:19).

[Note: The Venetian edition has “in Christ.”]

Christ taught us not to love gold by teaching us to despise the gifts offered to him; not to fear hunger, by fasting for forty days; not to dread nakedness, by forbidding his disciples to have anything except one tunic; not to fear tribulations, by enduring everything himself; and not to fear death, by accepting death himself.

And after teaching us all these things, he went before us not only in word but also by example. May this burn in our hearts; may the fire of the Holy Spirit make this flame within us, so that we may follow his footsteps, not desire to remain in this world, and perish with this world.

Alas, how wretched we are if we refuse to believe this and do not withdraw our minds from the love of this age, while we cannot possess these things forever and lose those things through false security!

What will we do? What shall we undertake? We must mourn if we lose the promised kingdom, and if it is suddenly said to us: “You lovers of the world, come out to meet the bridegroom, and come to the one whom you do not wish to see because you have put his commandments aside.”

For you will see the very wounds which he bore in his body for you.

[Note: The Venetian edition adds “he himself.”]

What then, grieving and groaning, shall we say? And what shall we answer when our deeds justly demand retribution from us, since we have often heard and neglected what the Psalmist sang:

“What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115:12).

[Note: The Venetian edition has: “We hear and neglect.”]

[Note: The Psalmist sang this. What does it mean? How does it connect with what precedes? I think Paulinus’s meaning is this. He had said: “You will see the wounds which Christ bore for you.” Since we did not respond to his love as we ought, nor listen to the Psalmist commanding us to render to the Lord for all that he rendered to us—namely, to accept some cup of suffering for him—he therefore says that we heard and neglected.

Salvian, On the Government of God, book 4, supplies something similar: “What, then, do we render for all these things, or rather what ought we to render? First, that which the most blessed prophet testifies that he both owes and will repay, saying: ‘What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.’ The first repayment, therefore, is that we return death for death … The second is that, if we do not pay the debt by death, we pay it at least by love.”]

Let us hold firmly that the hope of good things is not placed in this world, although what appears to be worldly hope exists; it turns into bitterness, and the world itself offers its lovers a bitter drink.

[Note: The Venetian edition has “human or worldly hope.”]

And Truth itself addresses them, saying: “Where is what you loved? Where is what you considered so important?”

## CHAPTER LV. How Greatly the Loss of Souls Must Be Mourned

O my brother, are our flesh made of iron, so that they do not tremble? Is our perception made of adamant, so that it does not grow gentle, or even wake up, at such words of God?

[Note: The Venetian edition has “does not wake up at all.”]

Why do we not say with the prophet: “Who will give water to our head and a fountain of tears to our eyes, so that we may weep day and night for the wounded children of our people” (Jeremiah 9:1)?

[Note: The Venetian edition has: “and so that we do not weep.”]

The eyes of those who consider not only the deaths of bodies but also the deaths of Christian souls fail from weeping.

What mourning is more fitting, what lament more certain, than when each one of us grieves and sorrows over a lost soul with the Apostle, who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

[Note: The Benedictine edition supplies in the margin: “than.”]

And again, in another place, moved by compassion for the love of his neighbors, he says: “I could wish that I myself were accursed, separated from Christ, for the sake of my brothers” (Romans 9:3).

[Note: The Venetian edition has “in Christ,” but places “from” in the margin.]

Let us learn in so great an Apostle of Christ to burn with so great a charity of Christ, since he knew that God “did not spare his only Son, but handed him over for us all” (Romans 8:32).

He says “for us all.” Therefore no layperson, no cleric, and no consecrated virgin should neglect the salvation of their souls, since it is evident that the price of such great blood was poured out for us.

## CHAPTER LVI. Seizing the Time of Mercy through Timely Conversion
Therefore, let all of us who remain upon the earth acknowledge our sins, lest we perish with the impious, while we do not quickly appease the Judge by worthy satisfaction.

[Note: [Col. 0261] Benedictus does not have *the Judge*. The Venetian edition reads *we appease*.]

How swiftly did the man who said, “I have acknowledged my sin, and I have not concealed my iniquity. I said: I will declare my iniquity against the Lord” (Psalm 31:5), appease his anger! He promises that he will declare it, and it is already forgiven him.

[Note: [Col. 0263] Benedictus, in the margin, reads as follows: “A gloss inserted into the text, which is lacking in our manuscripts; we place it, as they do, within brackets.” The Venetian edition does not do so.]

Consider, my brother, a great matter! He said, “I will declare,” not “I have declared”; and you have forgiven, because by that very fact that he said, “I will declare,” he showed that he had not yet declared it with his mouth, but had declared it in his heart. To say this very thing—“I will declare”—is to declare it; therefore you also forgave the iniquity of my heart. My voice was not yet in my mouth; therefore my confession had not yet reached my lips. I had said, “I will declare my iniquity against myself,” yet God heard the voice of my heart. My voice was not yet in my mouth, but God’s ear was already in my heart. And what followed? “And you forgave the iniquity of my heart.”

God is always ready to forgive our sins, provided that we do not delay in returning to him. For if we delay, let us fear lest he inflict his wrath upon us,

[Note: [Col. 0263] Benedictus, in the margin: “The manuscripts read *upon us*.”]

because he has indeed predestined some to punishment,

[Note: [Col. 0263] “He predestined some to punishment.” Theologians today might perhaps be greatly troubled if the word *predestination* happened to escape them while they were speaking of the reprobate. For the usage of the schools has introduced this distinction: predestination is spoken of only with reference to those elected to glory, who themselves are called the predestined; whereas the reprobate are called foreknown. Saint Thomas certainly says of predestination (*Summa theologica* II-II, question 174, article 1, response): “It concerns the good alone.”

“But the Fathers of earlier times were certainly not troubled by this scruple. For that decree which they call the sentence by which, once guilt has been posited—that is, sin and final impenitence, by which a person dies as God’s enemy—God condemns the person, they call predestination to punishment.

“Listen to Augustine in more than one passage. In *Tractate 48 on John*, section 4: ‘How did he say to these people, “You are not of my sheep”? Because he saw that they had been predestined to eternal destruction.’ And below, section 6: ‘What can the wolf do? What can the thief and robber do? They destroy only those who have been predestined to destruction.’ In *Tractate 107*, section 7, concerning Judas: ‘The betrayer of Christ was called the son of perdition, predestined to perdition.’ Likewise, in *Tractate 3*, section 5, on the words ‘The world did not know you,’ he says: ‘For that world, predestined to condemnation, rightly did not know you.’

“Saint Fulgentius also calls the wicked ‘predestined to punishment’ in Book I to Monimus, chapter 13. I gladly transcribe his words, because by offering the reason and explanation for this kind of predestination he can remove every scruple, even from the most delicate mind. He says:

“‘He was able, as he willed, to predestine some to glory and some to punishment. But those whom he predestined to glory, he predestined to righteousness. Those whom he predestined to punishment, however, he did not predestine to guilt.’

“That our Paulinus must be understood in this sense is clear from his own words. For he says: ‘If we delay, let us fear lest he inflict his wrath,’ and he adds the reason for fearing: ‘because he has predestined some to punishment.’ Thus the cause of some persons’ predestination to punishment is the postponement of conversion and the hardened wickedness of sinning. Therefore, if we delay, this is what must be feared. This is the force of the word *because* (*quia*); otherwise, why would he have inserted that causal expression?

“Moreover, just as predestination to punishment depends upon the evil works of human beings, so conversion and works of righteousness depend upon God’s grace alone. Therefore he adds: ‘and to some he granted a great benefit,’ which he explains by the examples that follow.

“Fulgentius expresses the same point in other words in the passage cited: ‘In the saints God crowns the righteousness which he himself freely bestowed, freely preserved, and freely brought to perfection. But the wicked he will condemn for the impiety or injustice which he himself did not produce in them. In the former he glorifies his own works; in the latter he condemns works that are not his own.’

“In the ninth century the monk Gottschalk uttered an evil doctrine concerning predestination. Under the name of predestination to punishment he included necessity, as though guilt itself followed from predestination. He stirred up a very thorny and perilous controversy and compelled the Fathers of that age, as the saying goes, to walk along an outstretched rope.

“If you wish to know the origin and development of the error, and the history of those who opposed and defended it, consult, besides the writers of that period, Rabanus, Hincmar of Rheims, Florus, and Prudentius of Troyes; among more recent writers, consult Du Pin, *Ecclesiastical Bibliotheca*, century VII, chapter 2, and G. Cave, on Gottschalk.”]

to punishment,

[Note: [Col. 0263] The Venetian edition adds: “to punishment, and yet not unjustly”; the remaining text is lacking.]

and he has indeed granted a great benefit to some—not unjustly, but according to his profound judgment. For Cain completed the murder,

[Note: [Col. 0263] The Venetian edition reads: “the fratricide.”]

while Job, though wounded, became God’s friend, and Abel, innocent, was killed by his brother. Yet Job did not endure his torment for long; nor did he grant Ananias a place in which to obtain forgiveness; nor did he abandon Paul, struck with a blow, whom by his grace he made strong; nor did he receive Judas when he repented; nor did he abandon Peter when he wept; nor did he regard Saul when he repented; nor did he despise David when he confessed.

[Col. 0264A]

[Note: [Col. 0263] Benedictus notes in the margin that these words are not found in the manuscripts.]

Thus, in his profound judgment, the pious and merciful Lord separates the vessels of wrath from the vessels of mercy. Oh, if only we would consider wretched Judas, once a perfect vessel,

[Note: [Col. 0263] The Venetian edition adds *and in*.]

but led into perdition! He could not bear the new wine of the Holy Spirit;

[Note: [Col. 0263] The Venetian edition reads *drink* instead of *bear*.]

when he received it, he immediately burst, and, entirely broken, he became useful for nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0263] Benedictus, in the margin: “The manuscripts read: ‘when he had received it’; and shortly afterward: ‘and, entirely broken.’”]

Fearing these things, let us turn back; and let us turn back while there is time.

[Note: [Col. 0263] The Venetian edition does not repeat “and let us turn back.”]

For the Psalmist says: “Seek the Lord while there is time, and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Psalm 104:4). It is indeed time for us to be restored. And if we have been broken by some sin, we have the almighty God as potter and craftsman. Let us believe that he is able to restore what has been lost, since he created all things whole. For he himself says: “As clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand” (Jeremiah 18:6).

[Note: [Col. 0264] In Benedictus, “in the hand” is absent.]

Therefore let us humble ourselves beneath the hand of almighty God, so that he may exalt us at the time of visitation (1 Peter 5:6). Let us consider that we stand in the sight of God; let us acknowledge what we are; let us acknowledge that we are earth and ashes, since the prophet also speaks against us: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Sirach 10:9).

And if we do not acknowledge this, we vainly wish to raise our necks, since God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6). “Comfort the humble,” says your God; “comfort those who are fainthearted; take courage, and now do not fear. Behold, your God will render judgment; he himself will come and save us” (Isaiah 35:4).

The Lord is near: “Be anxious about nothing” (Philippians 4:5–6).

[Col. 0265A]

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Venetian edition reads “you” instead of “us.”]

Let not the unhappiness of the world terrify us.

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Venetian edition adds here: “nor the wickedness of unjust rulers.”]

For if all the saints of God had feared this worldly unhappiness, they would not possess perpetual happiness. If the happiness of this world, which passes away, is loved, perpetual happiness is not found here. But if perpetual happiness is sought, then, since it is not found here, let us press toward perpetual happiness, where we have our homeland and our parents. Let us endure with the greatest patience all things in this world for the name of Christ.

What, I ask, is there to endure in comparison with what is promised to us?

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Venetian edition reads: “What, then, I ask, is there to endure?”]

The Apostle says: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18).

## CHAPTER LVII. In times of distress, to flee for refuge to Christ the Shepherd

[Col. 0265B]

Therefore let no distress terrify us, and let no calamity break us. The Lord is near,

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Venetian edition adds: “and our shepherd.”]

our shepherd is near us—what shall we fear? And if we are afraid, let us cry out to our shepherd, so that he may hear us. Let us cry out in contrition of heart, saying: “I have gone astray like a sheep that has perished; seek your servant, Lord” (Psalm 118:176).

Let us cry out and say: “Deliver my soul from the sword, O God,”

[Note: [Col. 0265] In Benedictus, “O God” is absent.]

“and my only one from the hand of the dog; save me from the lion’s mouth” (Psalm 21:21). Let us cry out and say: “Flight has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Psalm 141:5).

“Shall I look to the left? Behold, the devil roars like a wolf and growls like a lion. Behold, there is a wolf; a dog barks against it.” I cried out to you, Lord; I said: “You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living” (ibid., 6). Deliver me

[Note: [Col. 0265] In Benedictus, “me” is absent.]

from the hands of my enemies and of those who persecute me.

Will our good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep, abandon us to wander any longer, or to be torn apart and devoured by wild beasts, if we cry out to him? Indeed, leaving the ninety-nine in the desert,

[Note: [Col. 0265] In Benedictus, “in the desert” is absent here and shortly afterward.]

he went to seek the one lost sheep. He did not go merely because he heard it crying out, but before it cried out. For the Evangelist says: “Leaving the ninety-nine in the desert, he went to seek the one sheep that had perished” (Luke 15:4 and following). When he found it, exhausted and weary, he placed it upon his shoulders and carried it back to the flock.

The shepherd deigned to carry it back to the flock upon his shoulders and, by his mercy, to call it back from its wandering. But since the Lord carried this sheep back to the flock after placing it upon his own shoulders,

[Col. 0265D]

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Venetian edition reads “his” instead of “his own.”]

how great is the gratitude we owe for his mercy, since he so humbled and bent himself down toward us?

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Venetian edition has: “he bent himself down, carries, and so forth.”]

He carries and refreshes; he rules and guards.

## CHAPTER LVIII. The shepherd’s aid is sought against the devil

[Col. 0266A]

We beseech you,

[Note: [Col. 0265] Benedictus does not have “you.”]

good Lord, supreme and excellent shepherd: do not let the sheep perish. Fulfill the office of the supreme shepherd; pursue the lion

[Note: [Col. 0265D] “The lion that snatched the sheep from your flock.” These words and those that follow indicate the Felician heresy, as does the following chapter, as we have shown in the first dissertation, which is appended below, near its end.]

that snatched the sheep from your flock. Let the lion be killed, and let the sheep be rescued from his jaws; for you are the shepherd of the sheep.

Our powerful King, crush Satan beneath our feet. And now, Lord, our shepherd,

[Note: [Col. 0265] In the Venetian edition, “our” is absent here.]

our king, so many sheep are daily snatched from your flock—and why

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Venetian edition reads: “Why are you silent? Why are you so utterly silent?”]

are you so utterly silent? Answer: why are you silent? Behold, your sheep are being dragged away over various precipices, and your enemies, who hate you, raise their heads against you—and you are silent?

O Lord God, why are you silent for so long? Concerning this the Lord cries out and says through the prophet: “I have been silent, I have been silent” (Isaiah 42:14), but I will not always be silent: my hand will execute judgment.

Therefore, Lord Jesus, our shepherd and our king, take up your weapons and advance, so that you may fight against our adversary, the lion, who goes about seeking to devour us (1 Peter 5:8). Be for us, Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0265] Benedictus does not have “Lord.”]

a tower of strength against the face of the enemy (Psalm 60:4). We ask—and we ask with the greatest insistence—that you deliver us. For the world is placed in the power of evil (1 John 5:19).

Deliver us, Lord God,

[Note: [Col. 0265] The Venetian edition reads: “our God.”]

For the will of our Father is, as the Gospel says, that not one of his little ones should perish (Matthew 18:14), and that we should not perish or be torn away from the right path.

## CHAPTER LIX. The works of darkness and the weapons of light

[Col. 0266D]

Let us lay aside the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light (Romans 13:12). When the darkness of night has been driven away and the shadows

[Col. 0267A]

of darkness have been scattered,

[Note: [Col. 0267] Benedictus, in the margin: “The manuscripts read ‘roots.’”]

let the ray of the true light shine in our hearts.

At night let us perform not the works of night but the works of day, because we have been called children of God. Let not the sense of our minds grow numb through the pleasure of sleep; let not our souls be deceived by various fantasies; let not rest incline our bodies, weighed down by the warmth of their bedding, into deep torpor. Rather, by keeping watch, praying, fasting, and singing psalms, let us fight against the adversary, the devil; let us feel the great light poured into our hearts, and let us carry out the works of day in the night.

For what should we do in the dark night of this age except drive away the devil and introduce Christ? What should we do in the blindness of this night except take captive the captor and follow the liberator? What should we do in the night except shake the devil’s darkness from our hearts and draw in the true light? What should we do in the night except uproot pride and introduce humility? What should we do in the night except drive from us the prince of all vices and receive the fountain of every good?

Let us receive him, dearest brother; let us receive him, so that we may also be received by him and see what good things have been prepared for us by him who calls us daily. Let us receive his easy yoke and his gentle burden, for he lightens the burden of our sins.

[Note: [Col. 0267] The Venetian edition reads “reveals” instead of “lightens,” incorrectly.]

Let us lay aside the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light (Romans 13:12). For what is it to lay aside the works of darkness except to renounce the devil’s pomp and his angels?

[Col. 0267C]

And what is it for us to put on the weapons of light,

[Note: [Col. 0267] The Venetian edition reads “to be clothed.”]

except to believe in God the almighty Father, who enlightened every person coming into this world, and who also

[Note: [Col. 0267] The Venetian edition reads: “who said this.”]

said: “While you have the light, believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light” (John 12:35)?

## CHAPTER LX. What the devil is toward us and what he has been

Against them Augustine argues at length in *Tractate 42 on John*, sections 12 and 13. Here are a few excerpts:

“Some people thought from these words that the devil had a father, and they asked who the devil’s father was. This is the detestable error of the Manichaeans.”

A little later:

“The Lord called the devil the father of falsehood. … For not everyone who lies is the father of his own falsehood. If you received a falsehood from someone else and spoke it, you certainly lied by uttering the falsehood, but you are not the father of that falsehood, because you received it from another. But the devil was a liar from himself; he himself generated his falsehood and heard it from no one. Just as God the Father generated the Son, the truth, so the fallen devil generated falsehood as a kind of son. … Now recall the Lord’s words: ‘When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from what is his own, because he is a liar and its father.’ He is both a liar and the father of falsehood.”

Add that just as God is called Truth, so the devil is called falsehood, as Paulinus says here; indeed, he himself is falsehood.]

[Note: [Col. 0269] In Benedictus, “of the world” is absent.]

and his angels, when the Judge comes, then, as the Evangelist says, he will be handed over as a debtor to the exactor; and the exactor will thrust the debtor into prison. “Amen, I say to you,” says the Lord, “he will not come out from there until he repays the last penny” (Matthew 5:26).

Divine Scripture therefore commends the whole human race, as poor and small, to God, saying: “To you the poor man is left; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Psalm 9 according to the Hebrews, 10, verse 14). And, indicating his adversary, it continues: “Crush the arm of the sinner and of the wicked” (ibid., 15).

May our Lord Jesus Christ, pious and merciful, be present and show some mercy to this orphan

[Col. 0270B]

[Note: [Col. 0269] The Venetian edition reads: “to this poor man and orphan.”]

and poor man.

[Note: [Col. 0270D] “Orphan and poor man.” Paulinus understands the human race as “the orphan and poor man,” as is evident. Saint Augustine, however, in his commentary on this Psalm, understands the orphan as “one for whom the world through which he was born according to the flesh has died, and who can now say, ‘The world has been crucified to me and I to the world.’”

“But in writing on another Psalm, namely Psalm 145, section 18, he declares this of everyone: ‘In a certain sense we are all orphans, while the Father is absent—not dead. For according to human usage one becomes an orphan when one’s father dies. … Yet, as long as we are in the body and dwell in the place of pilgrimage, our Father is absent, and to him we cry: “Our Father, who are in heaven.”’”]

because he suffers a crafty and most savage adversary, and the orphan is already failing in his own case.

[Note: [Col. 0269] The Venetian edition reads: “even the orphan is failing in his own case.”]

Therefore his adversary hastens to deceive him by wicked arts. Be present, Lord Jesus Christ, as an able defender of the orphan. Stand in the case

[Note: [Col. 0270D] “Stand in his case.” Here “to stand” means to be on someone’s side and favor him. It is used in this sense also in Scripture. “God is said to stand,” says Saint Eucherius, *Formularies*, chapter 1, “when he patiently sustains us, his weak creature, toward repentance and conversion.” Saint Gregory likewise says in *Homily 29 on the Gospels*: “To stand is the action of one who fights or helps.”]

of the one for whom you commanded

[Note: [Col. 0269] The Venetian edition has in the margin: “another reading: ‘whom you knew.’”]

the sons of men to judge rightly. Lift up your arm, and crush the arm of the sinner and the wicked.

You know exceedingly well the case of this poor man and orphan—that is, the case of the human race—which is owed from a paternal

[Note: [Col. 0271C] “The case that is owed from a paternal written obligation.” Paulinus learned this magnificent expression from Paul, who writes concerning Christ in Colossians 2:14: “Blotting out the written obligation that stood against us.”

Chrysostom, in the same place, says: “Nowhere has he spoken so magnificently.” A *chirographum* is a security written or signed by someone’s own hand, and more specifically a document in which someone has written that he owes money. This is the definition given by Hotoman, John Calvin, and other jurists. Chrysostom agrees when he says in the work cited: “It is a written obligation when someone is liable for a debt.”

Juvenal also alludes to this in Book V, line 795, the final satire:

“The debtor or borrower goes on without repaying the money,
speaking empty written obligations on an empty tablet.”

Written obligations were extinguished when payment had been made by the debtor to the creditor. Once payment had rendered the written obligation void, it was said by Ulpian in the law *Solutione*, in the *Digest* title *Ad exhibendum*. Since debts pass to children or heirs, when the written obligations of the deceased were returned, they had to be returned to the children or heirs as well, as is clear from Julian, *Digest*, title *De legatis* I, law *Hujusmodi*, paragraph “If so.”

On these matters, if you wish, consult the jurists, especially B. Brissonius, *Formularies*, Book VI.

Paulinus understood the force of this word extremely well. Thus, explaining almost juridically what he had said, he adds: “He was found guilty and is held bound by the adversary.” Paulinus rightly says that the human race is held by a paternal written obligation—that is, by the obligation by which Adam was held. Chrysostom says of this in the passage cited:

“‘The devil held the written obligation which God made with Adam when he said: “On the day you eat from the tree, you will die.” The devil therefore held this written obligation, but Christ did not give it to us; rather, he tore it up himself. This is indeed the act of one who gladly forgives.’”]

written obligation. He has been found guilty and is held bound by the adversary. There is no other way in which we can be helped except through your counsel and most necessary

[Note: [Col. 0271] The Venetian edition reads: “Thus: ‘counsel and necessary assistance of the Judge of the case; defend us, because you are powerful, Lord.’”]

assistance. Judge our case; defend us, because you are powerful.

## CHAPTER LXII. The demon as accuser in judgment
O my dearest brother, how blessed is the soul that has so powerful a defender! Therefore let each one of us now keep watch, lest on the day of judgment the devil recognize his own rags in us and begin to hold as a guilty defendant the one whom Christ in his grace wished to set free [Note: [Col. 0271] Venice has *liberare*, “to set free.”]. Let those who refuse correction after receiving grace, and return again to their former pleasures [Note: [Col. 0271] Benedictine edition: *voluntates*, “desires.”], not flatter themselves evilly. For the day of judgment is awaited: that most equitable Judge will be present, who will accept no powerful person’s influence, and whose palace no bishop, abbot, or count [Note: [Col. 0272C] “Nor count.” Why did he list a count among secular dignities while passing over the others in silence? Clearly because he was writing to Count Henry. For although the names “count” and “duke” differed, they were often confused, as we shall say in the first dissertation, § 6. The Benedictine Fathers also observed this in the admonition prefixed to this book. He could indeed have named other lay dignities; but he could not omit the count, since he was writing to a count. Since, while omitting the others, he retains this one, there is no doubt that the man to whom he was writing was a count.] will be able to corrupt with gold and silver. All souls will stand present, so that each may give an account according to what he did in the body [Note: [Col. 0271] Venice: “according to what he did in the body.”], whether good or evil. For the adversary, the devil, will be present, and the words of our profession will be recited [Note: [Col. 0272C] “The words of our profession” will be recited. Augustine indicates such a profession in *On the Creed for Catechumens*, book IV, chapter 1, addressing them as follows: “You professed that you renounced this one”—namely, the devil, the enemy—“and in that profession you said, not to men but to God and his angels, who recorded it: ‘I renounce.’ From this angelic record these words of our profession will be recited.” Hence Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* I, on Baptism: “Do not fail to understand that whatever you say, especially at that fearful hour [of baptism], is written in the hidden books of God, so that if afterward you commit anything contrary to those declarations, you may be judged as a transgressor.”], and he will bring before our face [Note: [Col. 0272D] “He will bring before our face,” and so forth. Chrysostom likewise used this figurative expression in *Homily 20 on Genesis*: “If we forestall our adversary—I mean the devil—who on that day will stand before our face . . . and we ourselves become our own accusers, we shall move the Lord to such great mercy that . . .” See something similar in Peter of Celle, *On the Loaves*, chapter 15.] everything we did, and on what day we sinned, and in what place, and what good work we ought then to have done [Col. 0271C] [Note: [Col. 0271] Benedictine edition: *deberemus*, “we ought to have done.”]. And if we are found to be such people [Col. 0272A], that adversary will exult in the presence of the most merciful Judge, loudly declaring that he is superior to us, and bringing such a case before such a Judge.

For the devil himself will then have this to say:

“Most equitable Judge, judge that this man belongs to me because of guilt, since he refused to belong to you through grace. He is yours by nature; he is mine through misery. He is yours because of your Passion; he is mine because of my persuasion. He disobeyed you; he obeyed me. From you he received the robe of immortality; from me this ragged tunic in which he is clothed [Note: [Col. 0271] Venice: *vestem*, “garment.”]. He lost your garment; he has arrived here wearing mine. What was immodesty doing with him, what intemperance, what greed, what anger, what pride, and what of the rest of my members? He abandoned you; he fled for refuge to me. I see my sisters accompanying him.

“For what reason was he doing all that [Note: [Col. 0271] Benedictine edition reads this way; the printed editions and Venice have: ‘What then? For this reason he did everything,’ with *quia loco quid* apparently in place of the word *quid*.]? What was he arguing about with pride? What was he raging about with anger? He stored up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. Most equitable Judge, judge, I say [Note: [Col. 0271] Benedictine edition: *inquit*, “he says.”], because righteousness and judgment are the preparation of your throne (Psalm 88:14). Judge that he belongs to me and must be condemned with me.

“I recognize that all these things he has brought here belong to me. He wished to be mine and coveted what was mine; he must be punished with me, because the one whom you deigned to free at so great a price afterward willingly chose to bind himself to me.”

Alas, alas, dearest brother! Will such a man be able to open his mouth, when he will be found there to be such that he is justly assigned to go with the devil?

## 60. CHAPTER LXIII. How Dangerous Relapse Is

Let us see what we are doing; let us see from whom and how we may be freed; and let us beware lest we receive the grace of God in vain [Note: [Col. 0273] Benedictine edition: *suscepissemus*, “we had received.”]. Rather, with an undivided heart and perfect faith, let us renounce and reject the devil’s ruinous inheritance [Note: [Col. 0273] Benedictine edition: *diabolicam*, “devilish.”], lest we remain orphans and poor.

Let the terrifying sentence of the blessed Apostle, uttered with terrible force, be read aloud in our midst, so that it may make both our hearts and our bodies tremble. For he says:

“If we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, no sacrifice for sins is left, but a certain terrifying expectation of judgment and the fury of a fire that will consume the adversaries. Anyone who rejected the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you suppose, will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as defiled the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified [Note: [Col. 0273] Thus in Venice and in the Apostle’s text; Benedictine edition has *sanctificati estis*, “by which you were sanctified,” as also below.], and insulted the Spirit of grace? For we know who said, ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay’ [Note: [Col. 0273] “I will repay” (*ego reddam*).]. And again, ‘For the Lord will judge his people.’ For it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10:25 and following).

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore do not surrender your confidence, which has a great reward. For you need patience, so that, having done the will of God, you may receive the promise. For yet a very little while [Note: [Col. 0273] Thus in Venice and in the Apostle’s text; Benedictine edition lacks *modicum*, “a little.”], and ‘the one who is to come will come and will not delay,’ to repay each according to his work” (ibid., 35).

For these words flowed not from me but from the one himself who said: “Do you seek proof of Christ speaking in me?” (2 Corinthians 13:3). Let us extend the gaze of our heart’s eye [Note: [Col. 0273] Venice adds *nostri*, “of our heart’s eye.”], and let us see; let us also lend the ear of our heart to perceive and investigate the Apostle’s terrifying sentence. Let us cleanse the eye [Note: [Col. 0273] Venice: *oculos*, “eyes.”] of our heart—or rather, let the very light that we desire to see cleanse our heart, and, through his mercy, let it be cleansed from the darkness of sins. For he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

Let this labor of ours not be fruitless unto destruction, but fruitful unto salvation. Let us run while we have the light, lest darkness overtake us (John 12:35). And again the Apostle exhorts us most earnestly, saying:

“Lift up the hands that hang down and the feeble knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray but rather be healed. Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see [Col. 0274A] God. See to it that no one falls short of the grace of God, and that no root of bitterness springing up may cause trouble, and through it the many be defiled” (Hebrews 12:12 and following).

And shortly afterward:

“See that you do not refuse him who speaks. For if those who refused him who spoke on earth did not escape when they disobeyed the divine word, much more shall we not escape if we turn away from him who speaks to us from heaven [Note: [Col. 0273] The Benedictine marginal note says: “Thus the manuscripts; the Vulgate has *avertimus*, ‘we turn away’; the Greek has ἀποστρεφόμενος, ‘turning away.’ The printed edition has *advertimus*, ‘we heed’; Venice in the text has *advertimus*, and in the margin: ‘others, *avertimus*.’”], whose voice then shook the earth, but now he has promised, saying: ‘Yet once more I shall shake not only the earth but also heaven’” (ibid., 25 and following).

But when he says “yet once more,” he declares the removal of the movable things as things made, so that the things that are immovable may remain. Therefore, receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us have grace, by which we may serve God acceptably, with fear and reverence. For our God is a consuming fire [Col. 0274B], and he will consume the adversaries.

Let us approach him before we are consumed by him, asking him to burn our heart and our kidneys. And again: “For you have tested us, O God; you have examined us by fire, as silver is examined” (Psalm 65:10). For it is entirely clear that if we are not burned by him here, there we shall be consumed like adversaries.

The Apostle says: “Let no one deceive himself; let no one mislead himself with empty words, because whatever a person sows, that he will also reap” (Ephesians 5:6; Galatians 6:8). Let us not speak one thing with our tongue and another with our heart, lest we be Judas and Herodians [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Judas and Herodians.” In rightly bringing forward the examples of Judas and the Herodians as men double-minded, Paulinus explains them as follows. Judas calls the Lord “Rabbi” and kisses him, saying, “Hail, Rabbi,” while in deed he was betraying him, as in Matthew 26:50. The Herodians, on the other hand, tried to entrap him in his speech, as in Matthew 22:16, saying: “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God in truth,” and so forth. He immediately explains this by adding: “Some in destruction, others in confession, as Judas; some in confession, others in dissimulation, as the Herodians.”]—some in betrayal [Note: [Col. 0273] Benedictine marginal note: “The Colbertine manuscripts have: ‘some unto perdition, into confusion, into dissimulation.’ Another edition (Venice) has: ‘some unto perdition, into confusion, into dissimulation.’”], others in confession, others in dissimulation, but others [Note: [Col. 0273] Venice omits *alii*, “others,” here.] in the humility of truth.

Therefore, with a true heart, let us hasten toward the fullness of faith, having our hearts sprinkled [Note: [Col. 0274D] “Having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience”: this is how the Benedictine Fathers and the Venetian edition read. I suspect, however, that the text should read not *aspers i* (“sprinkled”) but *abstersi* (“wiped clean”). To sprinkle is not properly to cleanse, whereas *abstergere* means to wipe away.] from an evil conscience. Let us hold fast the unwavering confession of our hope, and let us not abandon the beginning of good works, as is the custom of some; but let us encourage one another, and all the more as we see the day of judgment approaching [Note: [Col. 0273] Venice omits *et*, “and.”].

## 61. CHAPTER LXIV. A Description of the Evils of the Flesh from Scripture, and a Denunciation of Them

Let us trample down the pride of our flesh, for it is the flesh that destroys the soul and brings complete pride; and, as the Apostle says, whoever sows in the flesh will also reap corruption from the flesh (Galatians 6:8).

It is the flesh that receives the devil. For the devil sows his seeds in our flesh—that is, murder, fornication, desire, lust, anger, quarrelling, drunkenness, pride, theft, and every evil suggestion. The Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the spirits of this air [Note: [Col. 0275] Benedictine edition: *carnis*, “of the flesh.” Venice: *aeris*, “of the air.” We choose the latter because it is less distant from the Apostle’s text.]” [Note: [Col. 0275C] “Against the spirits of this air.” He does not reproduce the Apostle’s words in full, but rather his meaning. I am not unaware that demons may derive their names from the vices to which they incite us and be called the spirit of the sin to which they provoke a person—for example, the spirit of greed, envy, and so forth. John Climacus indeed calls this, in *The Ladder of Paradise*, the “spirit of lust,” a demon promoting the works of the flesh; and the author of the *Imperfect Work*, homily 15, called it “the spirit of the flesh.” Yet such an interpretation cannot be accepted here, so that the reading would be “the spirit of the flesh,” as the Benedictine Fathers read it.
