Apart from the fact that the antithesis seems to destroy itself and that “spirit of the flesh” is a faulty construction, the Apostle’s passage plainly indicates that Paulinus should read *aeris*, “of the air,” not *carnis*, “of the flesh.” For he says that our struggle is against “the rulers of the darkness of this world” and “spiritual wickedness in heavenly places,” implying that demons inhabit the air surrounding us. Among others who said this was Honorius of Autun, who writes in book I, chapter 53, of *The Image of the World*: “In this air demons dwell, awaiting the day of judgment in torment. From it they take bodies when they appear to human beings.” This reasoning persuaded me that the Venetian reading should be retained above the others: it has *aeris*, not *carnis*. See Saint Augustine, sermon 222, latest edition.], “against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12).

He speaks of the devil, who is an evil spirit [Note: [Col. 0275D] “He is an evil spirit.” In Scripture the demon is often addressed by this name. Above, in the notes to chapter 60 of this book, we also cited Chrysostom’s words, in which he calls him *malum profectum* (“an evil development”). Yet do not suppose that I mean he was evil by nature. God created him good; he made himself evil. Saint Cyril of Jerusalem says in the Second Catechesis for the Illuminated: “He sinned, not receiving vice by a necessity of nature . . . but, created good, he became the devil by his own will.”], and is not seen. That most wicked spirit himself was cast down from heaven with his angels. Of them it is said in the Apocalypse: “Behold, the accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them day and night; and they conquered him because of the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 12:10).

Of him the Apostle says: “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan, to strike me. For this I pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7 and following).

Again, he himself says: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin that is in my members” (Romans 7:23). Again he says: “With my mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (ibid., 25). And again: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ” (Romans 8:1).

It is the flesh that receives the devil, and the devil has the flesh in his power, not the soul. Therefore the Apostle says: “There was given to me a thorn in my flesh”; he does not say, “in my soul” [Note: [Col. 0275] Venice omits *meae*, “my.”], but “an angel of Satan in my flesh.”

Finally, Job was tempted in the flesh by the devil, when the Lord said: “And power was given to him by the Lord over his possessions and over his flesh” (Job 1:12) [Note: [Col. 0275] Venice omits *in carne*, “over his flesh.”]. And again: “I will give him into your power, except for his soul” (Job 2:6).

“For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do whatever you wish” (Galatians 5:17) [Note: [Col. 0275] Benedictine edition: *ea*, “those things.”].

The flesh is a wretched beast [Note: [Col. 0276C] “The flesh is a wretched beast.” Philip the Solitary vividly depicts the savage impulses of the flesh in book II, chapter 1, of *The Christian Mirror*. Here are a few passages from the dialogue there between soul and flesh:

“**Soul:** As a sow throws itself into the mud, defiles itself, and rolls about in it with pleasure, so you, foolish and destructive to me, behave. Like the foulest pig, you are stained with carnal desires and utterly pollute me . . .

“**Flesh:** Why do you speak in this way, mistress, when you hold power over me? Like a rider, you turn me, your horse, wherever you wish . . .

“**Soul:** You do not speak truth, nor what the matter really is. You behave instead like a wild, unmanageable horse that rejects the reins, kicks, and strikes; biting the bit and running over steep places, it drags its rider, neighs, strikes the ground with its hoof, and, when it begins to rage, throws the rider—even one who is firm and holding the reins—from the saddle, which is the worst thing, and hurls him headlong. This is how matters now stand between us. You have a wooden mouth and, like a horse neighing against the reins, you cannot easily be led or turned; rather, you try to lead, drag, and tyrannically treat me.”], which burdens the soul. The Apostle says: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:9).

Again, our Lord Jesus Christ, the Truth himself, says of himself: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew 26:41).

For our flesh always wishes to be powerful in evil; but in abstinence—that is, in fasting, vigils, prayers, and good works—it pretends to be weak [Note: [Col. 0276D] “The flesh powerful in evil . . . weak in abstinence.” Cornelius aptly understands the flesh by the “lying rich man” in Ecclesiasticus 25:4. He says: “The rich man who lies is the flesh, because it lies when it says that it cannot undertake the labors of virtue, although, if it wished, it could undertake them. For example, when it says that it cannot fast because of lack of strength, it lies; for it has strength to fornicate. Why, then, should it not have strength to fast? It has strength to serve the world and endure many great labors for it; why should it not have strength to serve God?”].

It is our flesh that plunges us into a pit. The Apostle says: “Put to death your members that are upon the earth,” namely, fornication, uncleanness, anger, quarrelling, and the other things that follow (Colossians 3:6). And again: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13:14).

Therefore let us put our flesh to death through abstinence, fasting, vigils, and prayers, lest it bring the devil upon you with evil desires [Note: [Col. 0275] Venice: “in fasts, prayers, and vigils.”].

The flesh, moreover, has been given to us as a war against the soul. If it is put to death, it brings life; if it is nourished, it prepares itself for war against the soul. But I praise the one who is able to exercise power over his flesh [Note: [Col. 0276D] “Who is able to exercise power over his flesh.” Paulus, in the Digest, *On the Meaning of Words*, law *Potestatis*, says: “The word ‘power’ has several meanings: in the person of magistrates, command; in the person of children, paternal authority; in the person of a slave, ownership.” The flesh has the status of a slave, while the soul has that of a master. Therefore the one is to be praised who knows how to exercise power and command over his flesh and does not allow it to cast off the yoke of servitude.].

While we fear the weakness of our flesh, we neglect the salvation of our soul.

O wretched soul [Note: [Col. 0277] Venice: “our wretched soul.”], what do you say, you whom the flesh so heavily burdens? Solomon says: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15). And again he repeats: “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

Woe, woe to the wretched soul whom the flesh persecutes! Our flesh fights against the soul every day, and we must fight against the flesh every day, as the Apostle commands: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Romans 8:13).

The flesh desires and displays every evil suggestion; the flesh desires every evil; the flesh urges wrongdoing; the flesh provokes anger; the flesh provokes murder; the flesh provokes adultery and quarrelling; the flesh introduces drunkenness; the flesh carries every evil desire of this world; and the flesh desires every evil.

O flesh, cruel beast, what have you, what do you burden the soul for—an soul that would have desired nothing except to serve God, had it not been joined to you, its enemy? But you, wretched flesh, not only kill yourself, you also kill the soul [Note: [Col. 0277] Venice: *necas*, “you kill.”]. Your own destruction is not enough for you; you still wish to plunge the soul into hell [Note: [Col. 0277] Benedictine edition: *demergi*, “to be plunged.”].

Woe to you, soul, that have received the flesh as an adversary, which neither enters itself nor permits you to enter [Note: [Col. 0277C] “It neither enters itself nor permits you to enter,” and so forth. It does not enter—not because it will not rise again, but because, as the Apostle says, “flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:50). What this Apostle understands by “flesh” here may be learned from Chrysostom, homily 42 on the passage, and from it one may grasp Paulinus’s meaning. He says: “So that you may learn that evil actions do not introduce anyone into the kingdom; and for this reason he added, ‘nor will corruption possess incorruption.’ That is, vice does not possess glory.” To say, therefore, that “the flesh does not enter and does not permit entry into the kingdom” means nothing other than that the works of the flesh—that is, sins—do not enter and do not permit entry. For who could be so foolish as to say that this material flesh, namely our body, will not enter the kingdom of God, when we confess the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life? Just as below he says that the flesh does not escape punishment when the soul suffers in hell, namely because of the works of the flesh that have been committed, so here the soul, once blessed, should not be excluded from the kingdom.], into the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0277] Venice: *intrare*, “to enter.”]!

O evil flesh, what do you seek, what do you desire? You do not wish to endure labor? You do not wish, though restless, to come to rest? You suffocate the soul so that, in a reversal of roles, you may be the mistress and it the servant.

I ask you: why do you burden the soul, which is not troublesome to you? Nor will you escape punishment while it suffers hell; for it cannot be judged on the day of judgment without you. Why do you not consent to our spirit and soul, as the Gospel exhorts you, saying:

“Be reconciled with your adversary while you are with him on the way”—that is, in this world—“lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge”—that is, Christ—“and the judge hand you over to the officers”—that is, the evil angels—“and the officers cast you into prison”—that is, into hell. You will not come out from there until you have paid the last penny” (Matthew 5:25–26), that is, the smallest sin [Note: [Col. 0277] Benedictine edition omits *et*, “and.”].

## CHAPTER LXV. Another Accumulation of the Evils of the Flesh

What are you [Note: [Col. 0277] Benedictine marginal note: the manuscripts have *quis*, “who.” Venice reads: “What are you? What do you provide for us?”], and what do you provide for us except harm to our soul? Whoever nourishes you nourishes you in order to do evil [Note: [Col. 0277D] “Whoever nourishes you nourishes you in order to do evil.” Hence Saint Leander wrote to his sister Florentina in chapter 15 of his Rule: “It is a harsh condition to nourish that against which you fight, and so feed one’s own flesh as to find it rebellious . . . What can flesh nourished on flesh do except burst forth into lust and cruelly ravage the wretched soul with the violence of luxury? . . . But if by abstinence we scarcely restrain the weakened body from the law of sin that dwells in our members, what will she do [Col. 0278C] who so overwhelms the soil of her flesh that it can produce thorns and thistles for her?”]. For the soul does not sin except through the flesh [Note: [Col. 0278C] “The soul does not sin except through the flesh.” Certainly actions that require external powers in order to be performed must be performed through the flesh. There is no difficulty in this. The greater difficulty concerns merely inward actions and consequently merely inward sins: namely, whether the soul can sin—or, likewise, do good, since the same reasoning applies, for example, to a good or evil thought—without the mediation of the senses.

Yet Saint Thomas teaches, in Part I, question 83, article 7, and often elsewhere: “It is impossible for the intellect, in the condition of the present life, in which it is joined to a passible body, to understand anything actually except by turning toward phantasms.” Since phantasms depend upon bodily senses and organs, as is evident, the intellect’s cognition must depend upon the senses. The will, by which sin—or indeed any good or evil—is performed, follows the direction of the intellect because it is blind; consequently, since the intellect is illuminated through phantasms, the will also depends upon the body’s organs and senses.

From this teaching two axioms have been formed, familiar in the speech of the schools: “The will does not move toward what is unknown,” and “Nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the sense.” Therefore the good or evil performed by the soul depends upon the flesh. Philip the Solitary explains the same matter in simpler teaching in book II, chapter 1, of *The Christian Mirror*; see that work.].

As it is written: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:4).

Someone may say [Note: [Col. 0277] Benedictine edition omits *aliquis*, “someone.”]: “How can the soul sin, when it is not seen? What can it fear, when it itself is not held?” The flesh itself sins, and it burdens the soul; and the soul, overcome by the flesh, consents to the flesh in sins.

For the flesh is headlong toward lust, shameless toward wantonness, constant in luxury, immodest toward fornication, placing crime upon crime every day [Note: [Col. 0277] Venice: *supponens*, “adding beneath.”], sin upon sins. It does not cease joining worse things to the worst; cruel in its will, vain and foolish, always inclined to evil, excusable [Note: [Col. 0278D] “Excusable with respect to the good,” that is, presenting an excuse. Here the word is active, not passive, as such verbal forms generally are in Latin. This is to be attributed more to the vice of the age than to Paulinus.] toward the good, and extremely lazy [Col. 0279A]; swift toward death, slow toward life; hating the works of light and loving darkness above all [Note: [Col. 0279D] “Loving darkness above all.” This word too has an unusual meaning: it is equivalent to Paulinus saying “most dear.” Unless perhaps one understands that the flesh itself is exceedingly fond of darkness, just as it hates the works of light.].

For it loves to fall and neglects to rise; salvation is bitter to it, and destruction sweet. It is always falling from evil into worse, and from worse into the worst [Note: [Col. 0279D] “Falling into the worst,” in place of “into worse things.” Superlatives are sometimes used in the manner of comparatives. Seneca wrote in Letter 108: “Yet in such a way that I may now preserve the abstinence of those whose abstinence I interrupted; and indeed be nearer to continence.” He should have said “nearer,” but he used the superlative *proximior*—from *proximus*, “nearest”—as though it were a comparative.]. It is restless and impatient, surrounding the soul with the flames of hell; thrusting itself among the shoots of desire and greed, vanity and arrogance, anger and impatience, and the other vices [Note: [Col. 0279] The Benedictine marginal note says: “Thus the manuscripts; perhaps it should be read: ‘excessive and dishonorable,’ or, as in the manuscripts of Theodore, by a second hand, ‘it sinks itself into excess and dishonor.’ We choose this reading because it seemed less obscure. Venice reads: ‘the excesses of vices’; the dishonorable things sink themselves down.”], it lowers itself into excess and dishonor, withdrawing itself from heavenly things and delighting in earthly things. It abandons truth, hastens to drink in vanity and words of falsehood.

And what more? Just as a moth devours wool and fire consumes wood, hay, and straw, so rebellious and pampered flesh consumes and burns up the soul [Note: [Col. 0280D] “As a moth . . . as fire,” and so forth. Job 13:28: “I am to be consumed like a garment that the moth eats.” On this passage Saint Gregory writes, *Moral Commentary* XI, chapter 25: “Like a moth, temptation consumes the flesh as a garment from which it came.” Concerning fire, Job 31:12 says: “It is a fire that consumes unto destruction and roots out all produce.” There Saint Gregory writes, *Moral Commentary* XXXI, chapter 9: “If the flesh rules the soul in perverse order, the fire of lust burns up everything that has been brought forth well.”].

What do you say to these things, soul? What do you answer to them?

“I shall say to my Redeemer,” it replies, “before I am stripped of the flesh, what I ought to answer to these things, and to what good I would have wished to incite the body that I inhabit.”

## CHAPTER LXVI. The Soul’s Prayer to God against the Evils of the Flesh
Do not let lustful desire be in me, I beseech you, Lord, but love of the most beautiful chastity. Let me be slow to hear evil, but quick to hear your word and hasten to accomplish it [Note: [Col. 0279] Benedictus in the margin: the Colbert manuscript has “eager.”]. Let me be solicitous in your fear, perfect in love, steadfast in faith, and in no way doubting in hope. Let me burn with love of my neighbor; let me not be consumed by the heat of hatred or waste away through the pallor of envy.

Breathe into me always the work that is holy, so that I may think of it; compel me to do it. Persuade me [Note: [Col. 0279] In the Venetian manuscript, “me” is absent.] to love you; strengthen me [Col. 0279C] so that I may hold fast to you; guard me, lest I lose you. Let not the foot of pride enter or rest in my dwelling, where your habitation ought to be; nor gluttony’s desire, fornication or avarice, envy or anger, sadness or vainglory [Note: [Col. 0279] The Venetian manuscript reads: “nor gluttony, nor desire, nor fornication, nor avarice, nor envy, nor anger, nor sadness, nor …”].

But from you I ask profound humility, who said: “Upon whom shall I rest, if not upon the humble and quiet one?” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0279] In the Venetian manuscript, “and so forth” is absent.] (Isaiah LXVI, 2). Give me profound humility, by which the height of the flesh may be bent down—the pride that suffocates me [Note: [Col. 0279] The Venetian manuscript has: “the pride of the flesh.”]. Give me measured abstinence, by which the excessive gluttony of the belly, which destroys me, may be restrained. Give me purity of heart, which may render me undefiled. Give me cleanness of spirit, because the unclean lust of the flesh drags me down. Give me hands [Note: [Col. 0279] Benedictus: “give the will to be lavish.”] generous in distributing alms, so that grasping avarice may be rejected. Give me the love of charity, by which the zeal of envy may be extinguished. Grant the patience of endurance, through which cruel anger, that beast, may be overcome and brought to an end. Grant the hope of everlasting joy, by which the bitterness of sadness may be soothed.

Make my mind glorify itself inwardly in you for a good work, so that the boasting of vainglory may not proceed outward from me. Grant me also to maintain justice, greatness of spirit, and self-control in all things; and make me [Note: [Col. 0279] Thus the Venetian manuscript; Benedictus has: “make simplicity be prudent with me.”] prudent with simplicity, so that I may live a blessed life sincerely and flee evil prudently [Col. 0280B] [Note: [Col. 0279] Benedictus: “flee back from it”]; and so that I may be able to understand the fraudulent and deceptive cunning of the devil, lest he deceive me under the appearance of good [Note: [Col. 0279] The printed editions add here: “and lest I be deceived by anyone, or deceive anyone.” The Venetian manuscript places these words in brackets.], and may be able rationally to distinguish and foresee what good I should do and what evil I should avoid.

After this, make me gentle, kindly, peaceable, meek, without pretense, in harmony with all good people, steadfastly vigorous in vigils, fasts, and prayers. Grant also that in gentleness I may attain silence through measured speech [Note: [Col. 0279] The Venetian manuscript has two readings here in the text: “Grant me also, in gentleness, to attain silence through measured speech.” Another reading in the margin is: “Grant me also, in gentleness, speech that is not pretended but measured, so that …”], so that I may say what is fitting and be silent about what ought not to be said—or whatever else you may deem worthy to confer through the fruit of the virtues.

Grant that I may preserve for you an undefiled faith without any error, and that my works may be worthy in accordance with the faith [Note: [Col. 0279] Benedictus in the margin: the Colbert manuscript has “worthy,” feminine agreement.], so that I may not pollute right faith by wicked conduct; and that I may not deny by evil living you whom I confess by believing; and that I may not offend by negligent works you whom I follow with vigorous faith in action [Col. 0279] [Note: [Col. 0279] The Venetian manuscript reads: “whom I follow in action, and by negligence.”].

Make me, while living according to a holy purpose [Note: [Col. 0279] The Venetian manuscript has “to live,” rather than “living”], pursue justice, love mercy, cherish truth, reject falsehood, and neither think nor speak anything false [Note: [Col. 0279] The Venetian manuscript adds: “Make me ceaselessly …”]; fear you without ceasing, love you, cherish you, keep your commandments, preserve peace with everyone without deceit [Note: The printed editions and the Venetian manuscript add, in parentheses: “not oppress subjects; regard myself as a sinner before all others”], call those who are at odds to harmony without pretense, offer sincere charity to all, scandalize no one, prefer myself to no one, but judge myself inferior to everyone; show reverence and fear not on account of fear of the powerful, but because of the Most High; offer obedience to elders and charity to equals [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript adds: “without despising equals.” The printed editions and the Venetian manuscript add: “offer no resistance in anything to Christian rulers and powerful persons, but obey them in all things.”]; show the younger the grace of timely affection [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript and the printed editions read: “show paternal affection.”]; bear with equanimity the burdens or dangers of brothers [Note: [Col. 0281] Here too they add: “love a friend as my own soul, love my neighbor as myself.”]; benefit all together and harm no one; injure no one, oppose no one, slander no one, place a stumbling block before no one, judge no one, disparage no one, wrong no one, criticize no one’s life, investigate no one’s path, but be concerned only about myself; never repay evil with evil; be neither mindful nor avenging of my injuries, but overcome malice by every form of goodness; prepare a blessing for one who curses; love enemy and friend [Col. 0281B]; endure the insults and reproaches of those who are angry, and not return them [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript reads: “not return injuries, but quickly forget my offenses and forgive”]; quickly forget injuries, forgive my offender, and always be ready to grant pardon.

Do not covet what belongs to others, nor take it on any pretext; but mercifully distribute my own to those who have nothing. [Note: Thus the Venetian manuscript; Benedictus reads: “distribute: for the sake of him who redeemed me, keep the hungry person, and then refresh him.”] For your sake, who redeemed me, keep the stranger and the traveler, refresh the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, gather in the guest, clothe the naked, visit the sick, seek out the imprisoned [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript has “the incarcerated”], console the sad, show compassion to the afflicted and grieving, provide necessities to the one who has none, divide food and clothing with the needy, embrace the native, cherish the member of my household, love the foreigner, redeem the captive, receive the stranger [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript has “support the stranger”], protect the orphan and the fatherless, assist the widow, help the oppressed, [Col. 0281C] provide aid to the forsaken, “break the bonds of wickedness” (Isaiah LVIII, 6); and whatever other instructions your commandments declare, believe and hear diligently, investigate ardently, know wisely, practice promptly, fulfill eagerly, and always remain humble before you:

so that I may rise and not be cast down; be lifted up and not collapse; ascend and not descend. For the flesh with which I dwell always wants to lead me into sin; it wants to be crowned with me, but not to fight alongside me. I suffer no worse enemy than my body, in which I dwell [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript has “in which I live.”]. For it is like a destructive lion in my house (Ecclesiasticus IV, 35), tearing me apart everywhere with its poisonous bite and consuming me.

[Col. 0282A] Therefore, drawing long sighs, I shall cry out: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God. Through whom? Through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII, 24–25).

These are the things I desire, good Jesus, Savior [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript reads: “Savior, good Redeemer: these things which I have prayed for up to this point, I beseech you; these things I ask, because by your most precious …”], excellent Redeemer, which up to this point I have asked in prayer; these, these I beseech, because I have been redeemed by your most precious blood: that because of the corruption of the flesh I may not perish forever, may not come into the second death, nor into the land of oblivion.

Let this voice of mine sound in the ears of your mercy, so that I may do your will, not that of the flesh; and let all my mind meditate upon you, delight in you [Note: [Col. 0281] Benedictus has “and rejoice”], follow you, and confess you, because your mercy is eternal in redeeming me [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript has: “because you have redeemed me in your eternal mercy”], and in your mercy I, lost through the sins [Col. 0282B] of my youth, have come back to life [Note: [Col. 0281] Benedictus notes in the margin: the printed editions and the manuscript of Victor insert: “and I rose from the dead, because you separated me from the sins of my adolescence”]. I did penance before you because you preserved for me a time of conversion; considering my sins, I was pierced with remorse, and through your inspiration I did penance before you.

From that time onward, joyful, I now and always give you countless thanks, because, so that I might find you, you first sought me; so that I might return to you, you compelled me; so that I might be chastised, you looked upon me like a merciful Father [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript adds: “as a shepherd and father”]; so that I might confess, you acted; so that, recognizing myself, I might weep, you gave me the gift.

“Place my tears in your sight, O Lord” (Psalm LV, 9), and let my prayer reach you in heaven. Be present, I beg you, and help me; receive me, commending myself to you, into your hands, delivering me from the mouth of the fiercest dragon and from the hand of the most terrible hell.

When you have received me and taken me from the midst of the shadow of death, indeed lead me onto the path of light, into the brightest land of the living. Place me in the safest folds of your flocks, because you are the good shepherd who seeks and brings back the lost sheep [Note: [Col. 0281] Thus the Venetian manuscript; Benedictus has: “you bring back the lost one, and the one found sick and languishing you save”; they omit “sheep”], protects and saves the one who has been found, heals and cherishes the sick.

And you are the merciful Lord, who do not let those who hope in you be put to shame, do not abandon those who seek you, and do not reject those who return to you, but receive them with rejoicing and praise and grant them to reign eternally in everlasting blessedness together with your saints and elect. For with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit you have one deity, glory, might, [Note: [Col. 0281] The Venetian manuscript has “and dominion”], dominion, and power, forever and ever. Amen.

## [COUNCIL OF FORUM JULII]

[Col. 0283]

65 COUNCIL OF FORUM JULII, convened by SAINT PAULINUS concerning the MOST HOLY TRINITY AND THE INCARNATION OF THE DIVINE WORD, under Pope LEO III, in the year of the Lord 796 and the twenty-third of CHARLES THE GREAT, in Italy; and the fifteenth of PEPIN, his son.

I. Our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever over all the heavens and over the whole earth, King of kings and Lord of lords, whose kingdom is everlasting, who is God, blessed above all forever. From the hand of his most abundant goodness, the unconquered princes, Lord Charles and Pepin, having received the royal scepters as a gift of his piety, are shown, with his aid, to govern their affairs prosperously.

II. Therefore, in the twenty-third year of their most fortunate rule, a brotherly company of certain bishops, summoned by fifteen canonical letters [Note: [Col. 0283C] Coinkius, in his Annals under the year 795, reads “and in the fifteenth year,” and consequently disrupts the chronology. [Col. 0284C] The fifteen canonical letters must be understood as having been sent to the same number of bishops of the province of Aquileia. HARD.], reverently assembled in the municipality of Forum Julii, the metropolitan city of Aquileia.

When all had taken their seats, as customary, in the prepared places, and a considerable throng of brothers in agreement stood around them in the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin and Mother of God, first offering to God upon the altar of the heart a sacrifice of praise and burning the offering of prayer upon the altar of the breast with the fire of charity; after the apostolic and Gospel reading, and after spiritual hymns had been healthfully tasted in advance, while the public doors had not yet been opened more fully and the gathered crowd of the people still remained outside the doors, the archdeacon summoned them, and through the entrance of a more private door they were admitted into the venerable priestly assembly, briefly and in silence. Paulinus, servant of Christ and of the Lord, shortly afterward began to speak in these words:

66 III. No priest, gentlemen, who has carefully and intelligently examined the sacred rules of the venerable canons can have any doubt that a council ought to be held twice a year in each province (Council of Nicaea, canon 5; Distinction 18), namely in the city and the metropolis, at whatever suitable place the metropolitan of that region may decide and the order of time may more conveniently dictate, for the necessary care of ecclesiastical dignity.

Indeed, because of the influx of matters requiring action and the confused business that more frequently arises from the thorny pricks of lawsuits, and consequently because the green shoots of the wheat harvest of the Lord’s field are still, so to speak, swelling with ears of spiritual fruit within the sheath of the straw, not yet sending forth golden ears into yellowing stalks, while the bundles of sterile weeds have not yet been tied together in one bundle with flaming cords and handed over as food to avenging flames, they are nevertheless striving to smother them under the shade of the little branches of falsehood [Note: [Col. 0284A] Perhaps “to suffocate.”].

IV. For this reason, it has been judged necessary, through the efforts of many venerable brothers who have been appointed to cultivate with the utmost care the field of the court of the heavenly patron, that such fruits, and others of this kind growing luxuriantly from a pestilential shoot, should be cut off at the root, so that, trimmed by the sickles of the tongue, they may wither; and that, by the authority of judgment, the little branches of wickedness may be cut away more often, until at last the very substance of the roots, corrupted by the infusion of poison, is entirely torn out.

But why the session of the revered council has not been held for so many successive periods, according to what was decreed in this venerable seat, over which, by God’s appointment—not through my merits but by a freely bestowed office—I acknowledge that I preside, I do not doubt that your most sincere charity knows.

For because of the wicked, who are accustomed to break in, and because of worldly disturbances, and because of the wars of battle that threatened us and did not cease to rage all around the circuit of our borders with roaring ferocity, this magnificent work may certainly be judged to have been interrupted for a time. Nevertheless, truthful assertions will not allow it to be considered entirely interrupted.

For whenever we were summoned by the revered commands of the princes, and at the general and most celebrated assembly of the venerable Fathers in synod, my most humble presence—since it has often happened that I was present—was, as I think, not hidden from your minds; nor do I doubt that it was often plainly visible to your eyes.

But now, with divine mercy assisting, the pride of the savage barbarians having been worn down—their necks, lifted up in arrogance, having been crushed—and with aid from heaven supporting us in every respect, the most peaceful peace having already been restored to the earth through the abundant grace from above, and the royal commands breathing somewhat more freely, we judged it supremely necessary, and hastened, to gather your most beloved brotherhood into one college, in accordance with the inviolable decrees of the ancient canons.

Thus, bound together by an unbreakable bond of charity, and humbly entreating him who graciously promised his faithful that he would be present in their midst wherever two or three were gathered together in his name, under his presence, though unworthy, yet established as his servants, let us begin at once—with him as the author, the consummator of our struggle, and the perfecter of our works, or rather, I should say, the perfecter of his works rather than ours, since all things are his and from his hand we freely receive everything.

For it is written: “He has accomplished all our works for us” (Isaiah XXVI, 12).

Let us carefully examine whether there are any things that are ineffective and persist in an excessive condition, which ought to be firmly restrained by the sacred laws; let us correct the past, establish the present by supporting it, and avoid the future by taking precautions.

V. But since, in order to construct the fabric of this spiritual building, the foundations of faith must first be laid more deeply and inserted in every way into that unbending foundation of which Paul says, “For no one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians III, 11), the construction of this foundation must be supported by a hand laid in disorder [the reading is uncertain].

That heralding voice cries out in the Song of Love, in whose chamber these foundations are laid more deeply: “Ordered in me by love,” it says (Song of Songs II, 4). And long beforehand it was promised by a prophetic oracle: “I will lay your stones in order; I will found you upon sapphire” (Isaiah LIV, 11).

Through sapphire, which by imitation represents ethereal beauty, the mystery of faith is not inappropriately shown to be very closely analogous.

VI. Therefore, it first seemed to me, the least of all the Lord’s servants, that the very text of the Creed, salutarily published by the holy Fathers, should be extended at the front of the first order like a straight line, step by step under an even rule, within and without the mass of the foundation of this spiritual building.

Thus, with the entire structure of our work aligned according to the measure of that straight rule, balanced here and there by the plumb line of catholic faith, growing more correctly toward higher things, and measured on either wall by equal cords of disputation, the summit of perfection may be supported by truthful assertions in the highest art of knowledge.

While the equal, three-chambered structure of this invisible building endures, supported beneath by four arches of virtues placed on either side, let the golden beauty of its ornaments now be suspended more pleasingly upon a triple and purple cord that is not easily broken.

67 VII. After the inviolable definition of the Creed—which, as was said, must in every way be inserted by me, and which was once wonderfully set forth by the venerable bishops through the revelation of the Holy Spirit—namely, by the three hundred and eighteen who were at Nicaea in Bithynia, and by the one hundred and fifty who were at Constantinople, I profess that I have promised to speak in clearer language about the mystery of the holy and wondrous Trinity.

Avoiding entirely the rhetorical ornaments of sophistical language, and abandoning the inextricable conclusions of introductory arguments, I desire to give a simple account for simple minds, and a clearer one, insofar as human weakness permits—or certainly, insofar as the holy Trinity itself deigns to reveal itself, to make it fragrant through a more cultivated understanding than through style.

Because of the various errors of heretics and the differing suspicions of certain simple people, I do not consent to compose or teach another faith, but only that faith which all sincere ages have received as handed down by the holy Fathers.

For I know that certain synodal documents have decreed, in order to refute new and manifold heresies—especially on account of the fraudulent and fabricated, not faith but rather faithlessness, of the pestilential and deceitful men Nestorius and Eutyches—that no one may teach or compose the Creed of another faith.

But far be it from us, and far from every faithful heart, to compose or teach another Creed or faith, or one different from what they established.

Rather, according to their meaning, we have decided to hand down for exposition those things which, because of the brevity of the truth, are understood less than they ought to be by simple or uneducated people; and we have committed it to memory and retained the very text of the Creed, so that, according to the Apostle, the man of God may be equipped and ready for every good work, and for resisting unsound faith.

For he himself says: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews XI, 6). Elsewhere it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah VII, 11, according to the Septuagint). That wondrous teacher himself forbids us to be led astray by varied and foreign teachings (Hebrews XIII, 9), while nevertheless teaching that sound doctrine must be preached to the faithful in every way.

Indeed, in the matter of faith, it is not adding or taking away anything from what the holy Fathers rightly and salutarily promulgated to think correctly according to their meaning and to complete, by exposition, their subtle understanding. Rather, to add or take away is to think something different, through crafty evasion, contrary to their sacred meaning; it is to compose a perverse doctrine in confused language, and thus, with impious mouth, to chatter boastfully rather than presume to teach.

For the venerable work composed concerning the holy faith by many catholic men and worshipers of the churches of God is read in various words and resounds through dissimilar pens, yet it is shown to breathe forth, in harmony, the same meaning and the same understanding of the mind in one testimony of inviolate faith.

For if the venerable sequence of the Nicene Creed is reviewed, nothing else concerning the Holy Spirit can be found promulgated in it except this: “And in the Holy Spirit,” they say.

What, then, does it mean to say, “and in the Holy Spirit”? How should their very brief confession be understood except so as to make plainly intelligible the religious devotion of their minds’ integral faith—that they believed in the Holy Spirit, just as in the Father and in the Son—in the same way as was later confessed by the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers, who bore witness that the faith of the Council of Nicaea should remain inviolate forever?

Nevertheless, as though explaining their meaning, they supplemented it by confessing that they believed in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father, to be worshiped and glorified with the Father and the Son.

For these things and what follows are not contained in the sacred doctrine of the Nicene Creed. But afterward, because of those heretics who whispered that the Holy Spirit belonged to the Father alone and proceeded from the Father alone, this was added: “Who proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Yet these holy Fathers are not to be blamed, as though they had added something to or taken something away from the faith of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, because they did not think differently in opposition to their meaning; rather, they strove to supplement their immaculate understanding with sound teaching.

The one hundred and fifty therefore learned, when they inserted “proceeding from the Father,” that the only-begotten Son himself had promised his disciples, as the Evangelist testifies, concerning his Spirit: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father—he will glorify me” (John XV).

## VIII.

For those later readers who added, “who proceeds from the Father and the Son” [Col. 0287B] (John XVI), had indeed read this very truth rebuking Philip in the Gospel: “Philip,” he says, “who sees me sees my Father also. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John XIV, 9–10). If, therefore, as he himself testifies, the Father is inseparably and substantially in the Son, and the Son in the Father, how can it be believed that the Holy Spirit, consubstantial with the Father and the Son, does not always proceed essentially and inseparably from the Father and the Son?

Who, I ask, is this who says to his disciples, after breathing upon them, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John XX, 22)? Who, I say, is the one who promised him to them? Is it not the only-begotten Son, who is in the Father, and the Father in him? “Unless I depart, the Paraclete will not come; but when I have been taken up, I will send him to you” [Col. 0287C] (John XVI, 7). And again: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance everything that I have said to you” (John XIV, 26).

For it has often been unhesitatingly defined by us and by our elders that the works of the Holy Trinity are always inseparable. The Holy Spirit is believed to proceed from the Son in that same respect in which there is no doubt that he proceeds from the Father. But we can establish this more effectively if the account of the deed accomplished through the apostles is brought forward.

Through the most trustworthy proofs of history, which are called the Acts of the Apostles, we have learned, as the evangelist Luke bears witness, that when Peter was preaching in Judea and nearly three thousand believers were cut to the heart, they said to Peter and the other apostles: “What shall we do, brothers?” [Col. 0287D] (Acts II, 37). We have learned that Peter answered them on his own behalf and on behalf of all: “Repent,” he said, “and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins.”

And again, summoned by the centurion Cornelius, a just man who feared God, after he had opened his mouth he preached many things to them about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. “And while he was still speaking, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who had heard the word” (Acts X, 44). A little later it is immediately added that Peter said: “Can anyone forbid water, so that these who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have may not be baptized?” And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

But the teacher and instructor of the nations, laboring with the most vigilant care in faith and truth for all the churches, when he was discussing John’s baptism, said that “John indeed baptized the people with a baptism of repentance into the one who was to come after him, that is, into Jesus” (Acts XIX, 4).

Moreover, when many Samaritans had believed Philip as he evangelized concerning the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus, men and women were baptized—undoubtedly in the name of Jesus Christ (Acts VIII, 12).

If, therefore, all these people, who were baptized as believers in the name of Jesus Christ when the holy apostles preached, and the holy Church remains inviolably founded upon that rock which blessed Peter confessed to be his—not through flesh and blood, but through the revelation of the Father who is in heaven—and if the whole Church is ruled and governed by that faith, and if it was said especially to him as the first shepherd, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew XVI, 18), where, I ask, is that rule of the Trinity which the Lord, after his resurrection, entrusted generally to his apostles, whose leadership that same blessed apostle Peter held?

“Go,” he says, “teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0288B] (Matthew XXVIII, 19). Why does the Master command baptism in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, while the disciples command that people be baptized only in the name of Jesus? Did Truth itself teach one thing and the disciples of Truth another, or did they hand down another form of teaching to the churches? Far from it. No one of sound mind is so foolish; no one enslaved to such insane madness would dare even to entertain these thoughts.

But let us see how both are true and holy, both the shared good and the indivisible mystery. The sacrament, therefore, of the Holy Trinity, which the Master and Lord wished to reveal by naming three persons but in one name—this the disciples of the same Truth deserved, through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, to understand in one person of the Trinity, that is, in the person of the Son, as the whole and holy Trinity essentially.

For, as has been said repeatedly, the works of the Trinity are always inseparable. Where the Father is, there inseparably are the Son and the Holy Spirit; and where the Son is, there ineffably are the Father and the Holy Spirit; and where the Holy Spirit is, there incomprehensibly are the Father and the Son.

Although the disciples had heard the Lord and Master command, because of the mystery of the Trinity, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0288D] (Matthew XXVIII, 19), they had certainly also heard him, while he was present and showing them the unity of nature, say: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30); and again: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 10); and again: “The Father, who remains in me, himself performs the works” (ibid.).

They also perceived with their inward eyes that Word consubstantial with the Father and the Holy Spirit, who was in the beginning, was with God, and through whom all things were made (John I). They knew that he always remained inseparably in the Father, always with the Father, always beside the Father.

Therefore Philip deservedly had to be rebuked, since perhaps he was seeking the Father somewhere else or something greater when he said: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John XIV, 8 ff.). The Lord immediately answered him, as if reproving him: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father also. Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?”

Concerning the Holy Spirit, to show that he is his own and the Father’s, he says: “The Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, will glorify me” (John XV, 26, and XVI, 14). For he who proceeds from the Father is certainly the Father’s Spirit; and he who is the Spirit of Truth is likewise his own Spirit, for he himself says of himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV, 6).

Hence, through Isaiah, he testifies that he is the Father’s Spirit when he speaks on account of the humanity he assumed [perhaps: “Hence this Spirit of the Father testifies through Isaiah”]: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me” [Col. 0289B] (Isaiah LXI, 1); and again: “The Lord sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah XLVIII, 16). And because the Spirit is his own, he himself promised through Joel, saying: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel II, 28, and Acts II, 17).

How fittingly, therefore, did the Lord, in his profound and ineffable wisdom, wish to display the mystery of the Trinity personally, saying, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit,” and, in order to demonstrate the essentially inseparable unity of the indivisible Godhead, precede this with the words “in the name.” For he did not say “in the names,” as though there were many, but “in the name,” because God is threefold and one. He distinguished not nature, but person.

How happily, indeed, did the apostles also teach that the whole holy and ineffable Trinity is to be understood in the name of Jesus, that is, of the Savior! How did the catholic and holy Fathers, established firmly in this stability of faith, profess that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father! How gloriously also do those who confess that he proceeds from the Father and the Son proclaim this!

From this it is clearly given to be understood that the eternal and omnipotent wisdom of God, which wondrously never ceases to educate the infancy of our understanding, condescends to speak of itself in sacred language in order to make known that it is the triune and one God. At one time it speaks distinctly for the sake of distinction; at another it speaks indistinctly because of the consubstantial unity of the indivisible Godhead.

For if it always spoke indistinctly, it would conceal the mystery of the Trinity; but if it always spoke distinctly, it would certainly hide the excellence of the inseparable Godhead. Through the sacred pages of the Testaments it wonderfully teaches both, so that we may understand and believe in our hearts for righteousness, and confess with our mouths for salvation, the triune and one God (Romans X, 10).

Therefore, although the Divinity—the triune and one God—is ineffable, it is not unknowable. The Creator ought indeed to be known by his rational creature. Hence the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father (John I, 18), speaks in the Gospel to the Father: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII, 3).

Elsewhere, speaking prophetically in advance, he testifies, saying: “All shall know me, from the least to the greatest” (Jeremiah XXXI, 34). Hence the chosen vessel, thundering reproachfully against those who are ignorant of God, says: “Whoever is ignorant will be ignored” [Col. 0290A] (I Corinthians XIV, 38).

He is indeed ineffable, because no one can discover how great God is or what he is; and not only human nature, but not even the subtle and incorporeal angelic nature, can investigate with the keenness of any intelligence that supreme, incomprehensible, and unbounded essence of divinity in its fullness [perhaps: completely; Latin *penitus*].

For even though angels, perpetually attending the fountain of knowledge, know all things, they cannot measure the fountain of knowledge itself—how great it is, since it admits no beginning and is enclosed by no end. Yet “great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Psalm CXLVI, 5).

They know of him, without doubt, only as much as he deigns to reveal of himself to them. Nevertheless, he is knowable to them insofar as they can more fully receive him according to their nature; and to us, surely, in a mirror and in an enigma (I Corinthians XIII, 12), so long as we walk by faith and not by sight (II Corinthians V, 7), according to the measure of our nature and insofar as the weakness of our capacity can perceive him in summary fashion.

But in sacred language, or in the instrument of faith, to add or subtract is to understand wrongly and to think otherwise than the sacraments of the mysteries, wonderfully arranged by the Holy Spirit through the pen of the tongues of holy men, stand. These men, inspired by the same Holy Spirit, strove to inscribe them upon the sacred pages of books.

Such is the custom of heretics, who, neglecting the meaning, manner, and character of speech of divine Scripture, corrupted by the ancient serpent, heap up for themselves, according to their desires, irreconcilable tumults of questions [Col. 0290C]. Therefore, having dipped their rusty pen into the vat of falsehood, they boast that they are composing their own, yet perverse, doctrine.

Rather, they endeavor to misuse foreign and diverse teachings rather than ecclesiastical and spiritual ones; as opponents of truth, they scorn the commandment of the Law [Note: [Col. 0289] We removed the point that had previously stood there and obscured the sense.] (Leviticus XXI), by which it is mystically prescribed that a priest should take a wife once, from his own tribe and from his own lineage, or a virgin from that same Christian religious teaching with which he was once instructed, from which he received the Christian name of which he boasts, and through which he recognizes himself as regenerated by water into the purity of immaculate faith, so that he may embrace, as it were, a virgin—not corrupted by heretical pollution—in the love of that faith, in order to beget from it offspring for the continuation of the catholic faith.

But deceived by these things, and utterly imitating Zimri (Numbers XXV), they burned with adulterous intercourse. His name, worked out in the vernacular of another language and interpreted from its own sense, is said to mean “violent outpouring” or “my song.” Deceived by the beauty of an Ammonite prostitute, he sought her, just as these people delight in the beauty of shining eloquence while frothing excessively with the violent outpouring of perverse doctrine.

Phinehas, the priest of the Lord, whose name, translated according to its own derivation, resounds in the Latin mouth as “the oracle of the mouth” or “he rested,” struck him through with an avenging dagger in the genitals and killed him together with his adulteress.

For ecclesiastical discipline, after one or two admonitions, casts the heretical man out of the bosom of the Church (Titus III, 10) and destroys him with the eternal javelin of anathema, together with his condemned and violated heresy.

Indeed, in accordance with the interpretation of his name, he had caused the anger, indignation, and fury of the Lord to rest—the anger that had already gone forth to destroy the people in vengeance for their insolence [Col. 0291A].

For just as that slippery serpent corrupted Eve in the paradise of delights by his cunning (Genesis III, 4), infecting her mind with the poison of falsehood and inciting her not to believe the truth but rather to assent to falsehood, when by wrongly interpreting the commandment he persuaded her to transgress it, so now the crafty serpent, in this paradise of the holy Church, which overflows with spiritual delights, always seeks to pour the poison of wickedness into the hearts of heretics, so that, intoxicated by the cup of falsehood and wandering with faltering steps through the winding paths of error [perhaps: “roaming abroad,” *evagantes*], they may be unable to find the fountain of truth.

Hence Paul, cautiously expressing his concern about certain people, says: “For I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted, lest you believe the truth” (II Corinthians XI, 3).

In this way the unhappy Arius, stuffed with the poison of this serpent, attempted to add to or subtract from the holy Gospel. With a conscience whose itching ear had been cauterized, he had heard the voice of the Mediator thunder forth and had read superficially that, according to his humanity, he said: “I am going to the Father, because the Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28).

Accordingly, someone is convicted of having added to this when, with polluted understanding and impious mouth, he inferred from his own reasoning: “He did not fear falsely to assert that he is lesser and later than the Father not only according to human nature, but also according to divinity.” He will never be able to prove that he has read this in the holy Gospels, or anywhere at all in the sequence of the divine Testaments.

And he is accused of having subtracted from the reading of the holy Gospel when, with an ear deaf and hardened like that of an asp (Psalm LVII, 5), he disdained to hear the same only-begotten Son of God say: “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

Here too he seems to have subtracted, but to have imprudently added something to himself there, to his own destruction, without in any way prejudicing the divine oracles [Note: [Col. 0291D] Something appears to be missing here. HARD].

But the holy and venerable sacraments of the Gospel will remain inviolate throughout all ages.

## IX.

Any catholic teacher who thinks rightly, explaining through a manifold discourse how, according to what was more gloriously set forth beforehand by the Lord, he is lesser according to his humanity but equal to the Father according to his divinity, is not to be accused of adding or subtracting; rather, he ought irreproachably to be proclaimed to have supplied an explanation of the mysteries affirmed by the holy Gospel.

Many darts of objections of this kind and similar ones, hurled from the bow of the tongue, could have been found—darts that would silence the pierced breasts of hostile slanderers, infected with a grievous wound. But, for the sake of brevity, we have now and again decided to refrain from drawing these matters out with the pen.

For in the Apocalypse the apostle John, under the title of a single book, bore witness concerning the entire sequence of both Testaments, saying: “If anyone adds to these things,” he says, “God will add to him all the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of this prophecy, God will take away his portion from the book of life and from the holy city” (Apocalypse, final chapter, 18–19).

## X.

Nevertheless, this avenging punishment does not strike the holy preachers of the Church. We praise them for having beneficially explained the book of the Apocalypse itself, and each chapter of Scripture, by expounding them individually in the varied style of their discussions; and we believe that for this they will receive an eternal reward.

For the Lord and Master himself, the Mediator between God and human beings, multiplied the distinguished expressions of the words in many parables that he himself had proposed, explaining them with the honeyed mouth of divinity. He opened the understanding of the two who were walking on the road, and, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself (Luke XXIV, 27).

Nor is the blessed apostle to be blamed, who explained the enigmas of the Law through the manifold words of his discussions. This far we have proceeded on account of those who cannot discern with sufficient precision what it means to add to or subtract from sacred language.

Now that these matters have been set out in this way, let us no longer delay in finally repaying in full, with a complete pen, the obligation of our promised undertaking.

## XI.

In the matter of faith, we promised to argue against those who, entangled in various errors, do not think rightly about the mystery of the Trinity. Specifically, against those who doubt the distinction of the persons; who think that the Father himself is the Son himself; who falsely claim that the Son is inferior and later than the Father; and who confess three principles.

But we, together with the holy Fathers, confess one principle: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For it is written: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power” (Psalm CIX, 3). This is not a beginning that begins, or something like an initial beginning, but a beginning that precedes all things.

For the Father never was not; that is, the paternal name was never absent, because he always was and is Father. And the Son never was not; that is, the name of Son was never absent, because he always was and is Son, without beginning.

In every respect we oppose the Patripassians, who dared to make his divinity speechless. Likewise, we do not yield to those who appear to divide the one Christ, the Son of God, into two sons, while they attempt to assert that he is natural and adoptive, although he is one and the same Son of God and of humanity, to whom the Prophet says: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm CI, 28).

But we shall make these matters clearer if, as we have said above, we proceed in this order through the text of the creed itself and what follows. We beseech you, brothers, and earnestly implore you with brotherly affection, that from this point through the passage where the divine essence of the Only-begotten is read in these words—“in which he reigns in unity and in Trinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit”—you take care to retain these matters in your memory, writing them not on parchment or dead skins but on the fleshy tablets of your hearts.

## 71. THE CREED OF FAITH

## XII.

I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.

And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, born from the Father before all ages: God from God, light from light, true God from true God; begotten, not made; consubstantial with the Father, through whom all things were made.

For us human beings and for our salvation he descended from heaven, and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, and became human.

He was also crucified for us under Pontius Pilate; he suffered and was buried, and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures [Col. 0293B]. He ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. And he will come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, and his kingdom will have no end.

And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, who proceeds from the Father and the Son; who together with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified; who spoke through the Prophets.

And in one holy, catholic, and apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the forgiveness of sins. And I await the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the age to come. Amen.

## XIII.

I confess the holy, perfect, inseparable, ineffable, and true Trinity—that is, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—as indivisible in the unity of nature, because God is triune and one.

He is triune through the distinction of persons [Col. 0293C], but one through the inseparable substance of the Godhead. We therefore believe that these three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—are not merely imaginary or conjectural, but true, subsisting, coeternal, coequal, and consubstantial.

For the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, and that of the Holy Spirit another. Yet the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one God.

For the true God, the Father, is truly and properly Father, who timelessly and without beginning begot from himself—that is, from his own substance—a true Son, coeternal, consubstantial, and coequal with himself.

And the Son is true God, truly and properly Son, who was begotten from the Father before all ages, timelessly and without any beginning: light from light, true God from true God [Col. 0293D].

The Father was never without the Son, nor the Son without the Father. For the Father is, was, and always will be Father; and the Son is, was, and always will be Son. The Father never was not, because the Son never was not. For the Father is always the one who begot a Son equal to himself; and the Son is always the one begotten equal to the Father.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is true God, truly and properly the Holy Spirit: not begotten, nor created, but proceeding timelessly and inseparably from the Father and the Son. He is always, was, and will be consubstantial, coeternal, and equal to the Father and the Son.

The Father or the Son was never without the Holy Spirit, nor was the Holy Spirit ever without the Father and the Son. Therefore the works of the Trinity are always inseparable, and in the holy Trinity there is nothing diverse, dissimilar, or unequal [Col. 0294A]: nothing naturally divided, nothing personally confused; nothing greater or less; nothing earlier or later; nothing inferior or superior; but one and equal power, equal and eternal glory, and coeternal and consubstantial majesty.

For the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are essentially one. Therefore God is one; but the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not one with respect to the distinction of persons.

The true Father is properly Father and is not the Son; the true Son is properly Son and is not the Father. The Holy Spirit also is properly the Holy Spirit and is not personally the Father or the Son, but proceeds from both; and yet they are not three gods, but one God.

In this holy Trinity, nothing should be thought—God forbid—to be visible, bodily, tangible, or comprehensible [Col. 0294B]. For the almighty Holy Trinity, invisible, incorporeal, intangible, incomprehensible, uncircumscribed, infinite, immeasurable, and eternal, governs all things by its will and command.

Although the eye of the Lord, or his arm or right hand, and other such things, are read of, we must understand them with the complete and upright faith that they indicate not the position of limbs or bodily mass, but the effect of the supreme and ineffable divine power.

Because he sees all things, penetrates all things, and everything is naked and open before him, he is said to have eyes. Because by his power he created, rules, protects, and defends us, he is said to have an arm or a right hand, and similarly in other cases.

Of this ineffable Trinity, only the person of the Word of God—that is, the Son—descended from heaven in the final days, for us and for our salvation, according to the purpose and free decision of the hidden dispensation; yet he had never departed from there.

He was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and became true human from Mary, ever-virgin, and he remains true God. Human and temporal birth did not harm his divine and timeless birth; rather, in the one person of Christ Jesus there is a true Son of God and a true son of humanity.

There is not one son of humanity and another Son of God, but one and the same Son of God and of humanity, true God and true human in both natures, divine and human.

He is not the supposed Son of God, but the true Son; not an adopted son, but his proper Son, because on account of the human being he assumed he was never alienated from the Father [Col. 0294D].

For he alone was born as a human without sin, since he alone was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the immaculate virgin as the new human. He is consubstantial with God the Father in his own—that is, divine—nature; and consubstantial with his mother, without the stain of sin, in our—that is, human—nature.

Therefore in both natures we confess him to be the proper, not adopted, Son of God, because, with the human being assumed, he is inseparably and without confusion one and the same Son of God and of humanity.

He is natural Son to the Father according to divinity, natural son to his mother according to humanity, yet proper to the Father in both respects. For, as has been said, there are not two sons, one of God and another of humanity, but one Christ Jesus, because of the one person, Son of God and of humanity, true God and true human, in a rational soul and true flesh [Col. 0295A].

He is perfect human according to humanity and perfect God according to divinity. In the same nature—that is, the human nature he assumed from the Virgin—he endured human weaknesses, but not the frailty of sinning. In that nature he deigned to grow through the stages of time, to hunger, thirst, and grow weary, and to endure insults and reproaches.

In that nature he deigned to be scourged, to undergo the gibbet of the cross, to receive the lance in his side, to be pierced with nails, and to taste gall and vinegar. In that nature he deigned to die, to be buried, to descend to the underworld, to rise again on the third day, and to associate with his disciples. After the triumph of victorious glory, by ascending above all the heavens he exalted that same human nature above all the angels and placed it at the right hand of the Father.

In that same nature he will come again to judge the living and the dead, and the age by fire, repaying each according to his works: eternal punishment to the impious, but eternal life to the righteous.

That divine, ineffable nature, in which God is equal to the Father and the Holy Spirit, remains impassible, unchangeable, unalterable, present everywhere, and always almighty. In it he reigns in unity and in Trinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## XIV.

We wish, therefore, all the priests of God and every rank of the Church to learn and retain in memory this most sincere purity of the catholic faith with the greatest devotion and without any defect, distinctly and attentively, so that not even one jot is omitted or added, and to leave it to their successors to learn.

If anyone has previously been able to do this with more vigilant understanding, we praise and encourage him. But if anyone, dull through a weak intellect, was previously unable to do so, nevertheless, at the next anniversary gathering and revolving session of this venerable council, if, with the Lord’s help, we deserve to be present before your eyes while life accompanies us, may the love of your God-beloved fraternity retain this in memory as it has been said.

Indeed, in the presence of our humility, let it be able diligently to review it; otherwise, reckon that you will scarcely escape the ecclesiastical rods.

## XV.

Moreover, let every Christian of every age, sex, and condition know the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart: men, women, young people, old people, servants, free persons, boys, married people, and unmarried girls. For without this blessing no one will be able to receive a portion in the kingdom of heaven.

But whoever observes these things and guards himself from evil works will be safe in the present age and will rejoice together with the angels in the age to come.

## XVI.

Dearest ones, we are not instituting new rules, nor are we greedily pursuing superfluous inventions of things. Rather, after reviewing the pages of the sacred canons of the Fathers, and embracing with the utmost reverent devotion those matters that were well arranged and beneficially promulgated by them and remain established as though by a sword’s edge, we have judged it worthwhile to renew them in a more recent style [Col. 0296A].

Thus, following the example of the clean animal that chews the cud and divides its hooves (Leviticus IX, 3), recalling to the throat of memory the food already swallowed, we may, as it were, chew again through the study of sacred reading the spiritual nourishment long since consumed, and pour it more finely and clearly into the stomach of the mind.

Thus, satisfied with the gentle banquet of delights, we may be encouraged in every way to render thanks to the heavenly Giver, from whose kindly hand we have received all things as a free gift.

He, in order to lead us after the guilt of discord back to the grace of the Father and to his own grace by the cord of charity, though he was equal to the Father in the form of God, emptied himself for us, taking the form of a servant (Philippians II, 6–7), and deigned to become the mediator between God and us. By his bruise we have been wonderfully healed from the wound of death inflicted by the devil (I Peter II, 24).

## 73. CHAPTERS

### I.

First, in accordance with the ancient divinely issued decrees of the Fathers, we have determined that no priest of the Lord, nor anyone placed under a canon, who is ignorant of or scorns the canonical, indeed apostolic, definitions, should conduct himself disorderly or dishonorably in the house of God, which is the Church. Rather, with all remaining in their proper order, let the beauty of ecclesiastical decorum remain inviolate.

With the greatest care and vigilant attention, we have determined to prevent this above all: that no one subject to canonical authority should dare, fraudulously deceived by the price of money, to sell or buy the gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0296C], lest anyone be permitted, for the sake of a required payment, to advance someone into any sacred degree of the ecclesiastical order.

With the ear of an open heart, let him always fear and understand [perhaps more congruously, “understand,” *intelligat*] that most clear word of the Lord: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew X, 8).

The first shepherd of the Church took care to cut away this pestilential Simoniac heresy completely with the sword of anathema at its very, so to speak, original root of avarice (Acts VIII, 18 ff.).

### II.

The life of the shepherd should stand far above that of the subject flock, since the voice of the good shepherd uniquely says to them: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew V, 14); and again: “You are the salt of the earth” (ibid., 13); and again: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (ibid., 16).

From this it can be understood how far the shepherd ought to differ from the flock, since the Lord wished to call these people human beings, but those people more than human beings—that is, the light of human beings.

If, therefore, we are the light of the world, we must shine without any mixture of cloudy hypocrisy. And if we are the salt of the earth, we must likewise season earthly minds with the flavor of wisdom through the word of preaching.

### III.

It was likewise decided that, soberly, devoutly, and chastely, in accordance with the Apostle, we should flee the favor of shameful profit—not in revelries and drunkenness, nor should we become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery (Titus II, 12; Romans I, 13; Ephesians III, 18).

Truth itself, generally giving a command in the Gospel, declares this, saying: “Beware of gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this age” (Luke XXI, 34).

Therefore it is authoritatively established in the ecclesiastical canon that one must either cease from such indulgence in vice or, if one persists, risk the loss of honor. We confess that we are accomplices and supporters of the framers of that avenging judgment.

### IV.

In accordance with the venerable definition of the Council of Nicaea (Canon 5), no one should tolerate women introduced into the household living with him in his own house, or live privately with them [Col. 0297B].

Although it may be read that some women free from suspicion of impropriety were treated more leniently in this matter, we have nevertheless now deemed it necessary to prohibit all such arrangements entirely, since experience has taught us that under the cover of those women others have obtained a freer approach to such men, with disastrous consequences.

We do not, however, forbid anyone to do good to poor persons related to him by right of kinship; rather, we encourage it, since good must be done to everyone. But let such women remain separated from them, living in their own dwellings.

### V.

No one should be permitted to conduct secular business beyond the proper measure. For the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Timothy II, 4).

Therefore it is useful to examine more carefully whose soldiers we rejoice to be. And because we serve in the camps of the Lord, we are compelled to consider attentively with what weapons, equipped against so great an adversary, we are able to enter into the battles of combat and fight, so that, freed from every impediment of the present age, standing fearlessly in the front line, we may deserve to receive, after the palm of victory, the crown of triumphant glory from that King who triumphed over our ancient enemy.

## 74. VI.

It was likewise decided that no one established under an ecclesiastical canon should dare, swollen with the pride of arrogance, to presume at any time to abuse those worldly dignities that secular men or earthly princes customarily exercise—namely, hunting^a, secular songs^b, or loose and immoderate merriment, lyres and pipes, and similar amusements—because of an outpouring of empty pleasure.

Unless, perhaps, he takes delight in hymns and spiritual songs, using those worthily and honorably composed from the volumes of the sacred Scriptures^c [Col. 0297D]. From these, therefore, we not only do not forbid abstention, but by a tolerant concession even permit such a choice.

### VII.

It was likewise decided that no bishop should dare to condemn a presbyter, deacon, or archimandrite to loss of honor^b without consulting this venerable see [Col. 0298A]. If anyone thereafter attempts rashly to usurp what has been forbidden, he will have no doubt about the danger to his own honor.

### VIII.

Concerning those who attempt to join themselves in marriage to persons related to them by close blood relationship: because a very severe and exceedingly harsh judicial sentence concerning this matter, carefully formulated by the ancient Fathers in the old canon, continues to stand under the scourge of penance as its punishment, we have therefore thought it right, foreseeing the danger of so great a crime, to define the matter more carefully and prudently. Accordingly, no one may contract a marriage secretly and hastily, lest, through the negligence of error or—what is worse—instigated by diabolical desire, illicit unions should be celebrated. Rather, after betrothal agreements have been made, and after some interval of delay, the matter must be investigated with diligent care by neighbors or elders of that place who may know the genealogical line of both parties, namely the bridegroom and the bride. This must also be done with the knowledge of the priest of that congregation, so that no distress of separation may subsequently arise.

If everything is carried out in this order, and the matter has been established without fraud by witnesses, but it later happens either that the parties themselves remember what they had at first professed not to know, or that they are found, through the testimony of other truthful persons, to stand within a degree of consanguinity in which relatives are customarily separated, then they shall indeed be separated from one another and perform penance; and, if possible, both shall remain unmarried.
