But if they cannot persist in this on account of incontinence or—what is more honorable—because of their love for children, they may indeed enter a second marriage. We say this by way of indulgence, not by way of command (1 Cor. 7:6). Nevertheless, they will be more blessed if they remain in this state, according to our counsel.

The children born from such a marriage shall be regarded as legitimate for the purpose of receiving the inheritance of the deceased. But those who do not observe all these provisions, which have been briefly set down above for the salvation of the soul and the frugality of life, and who presume to contract secret or forbidden marriages, and are found to be close relatives, shall themselves also be separated and shall remain throughout all the days of their lives in lamenting penance. Neither the man nor the woman shall ever proceed to a second marriage; they shall be judged excluded from the grace of communion; and the children born from so incestuous a union shall be regarded as illegitimate and shall be unable to acquire any part of their parents’ property.

### IX.

Furthermore, taking every precaution, we have decreed that this must be prohibited: no one may presume to join a boy or girl in marriage before the years of puberty, that is, before the proper age, nor may anyone join persons of unequal age; rather, they must be of the same age and mutually consenting. We have often heard that great ruin of souls has resulted from such marital contracts, and that fornications have been committed of a kind not found even among the nations (1 Cor. 5:1).

Thus, for example, when a boy has reached adulthood while the girl is still a child, or conversely when the girl is of mature age while the boy is still tender in years, the husband’s female relative and mother-in-law may be discovered committing adultery, and through the girl the boy’s brother or father may become entangled and perish in the guilt of so great a sin. Therefore, whoever thereafter presumes to undertake these forbidden unions shall be excluded from all ecclesiastical fellowship and shall not be exempt from public courts either.

### 75. X.

It has also been decided that, when the marital bond has been dissolved on account of fornication, a husband may not, so long as the adulterous woman lives, marry another wife, even if she is herself an adulteress. Nor may the adulteress, who must pay the gravest penalties or endure the torment of penance, take another husband, either while the husband whom she did not blush to defraud is living or after he has died.

For although it is read in the sacred Gospel pages that the Lord said that a man may dismiss his wife on the sole ground of fornication, it is not nevertheless read that He granted permission to join himself in marriage to another woman while she was living; rather, it is undoubtedly prohibited in every way. For He says: “Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another commits adultery; and whoever marries the dismissed woman commits adultery” (Matt. 19:9).

Accordingly, we have thought it right to define the matter so that, in accordance with the same Lord’s honey-sweet saying, no one may presume to violate these prohibitions. But since an ambiguous expression occurs in the middle—namely, “except on account of fornication”—one may reasonably ask whether it refers only to the permission to dismiss a wife, so that the meaning is “whoever dismisses his wife except on account of fornication,” or whether it also refers to both parts of the statement, that is, to taking another woman while the first is alive, as though He had said: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another, except on account of fornication, commits adultery.”

For this reason we carefully commissioned the commentary of the most learned man, blessed Jerome, to be examined, eagerly hastening to learn how that most renowned teacher was shown to have understood these sacred words of the Lord, in accordance with the subtler capacity of his intellect. When we carefully investigated his meaning, it nevertheless became immediately clear that the phrase concerned only the permission to dismiss a wife. For when the holy man, following his usual practice, briefly passed over the exposition of this chapter, he says among other things, shortly afterward:

> “And because it could happen,” he says, “that someone might bring an accusation against an innocent woman and, on account of a second marriage, charge the former wife with a crime, he is commanded to dismiss his first wife in such a way that he does not have a second wife while the first is alive.”  
> *(Jerome, Commentary on Matthew, book III.)*

A man ought not to imitate the evil of an adulterous wife and, if she has divided the two—or rather the one flesh—into three through the fissures of fornication, divide it into four. Hence it is plainly understood that, so long as the adulterous woman lives, a husband may not, and cannot do so with impunity, contract a second marriage.

### XI.

It has also been decided concerning women of every condition—namely, girls or widows—who voluntarily promise a resolve to preserve virginity or continence and have been dedicated to God, and who, as a sign of continence, have put on a black garment, as though religious women, in accordance with the ancient custom of these regions: even if they have not been consecrated by a priest, we nevertheless command that they persevere perpetually in this resolve.

But if afterward they either corrupt themselves secretly or marry publicly, they shall indeed be subjected to bodily punishment by a fitting secular judgment, separated from one another, and perform penance throughout all the days of their lives; and they shall be deprived of communion in the body and blood of Christ. Unless perhaps the bishop, having learned of their penance and finding it worthy, may, with more humane foresight, grant them the grace of communion. At the end of their lives, however, they shall not be deprived of the more mercifully granted viaticum.

Above all, this prohibition must be guarded in these matters in every way: no one may permit the persons mentioned above to change their habit—that is, their clothing—without the knowledge of their bishop.

### XII.

[Col. 0300B]

With this decree fixed inviolate, we have rightly determined that the monasteries of girls who live under the rule of discipline must be enclosed by more strongly secured gates, and that no entrance for men may be open to them, except perhaps when the greatest necessity compels it.

Nor may priests or deacons, or anyone from the clergy, or even an archimandrite, grant himself permission to enter them under the pretext of visitation or preaching without the permission of the bishop of the city. Indeed, even the bishop must not think that he may enter there freely without his priests or clerics, as propriety and decency require.

But if either the bishop himself or any religious person, free from illicit suspicion and adorned by the gravity of his conduct, should be judged worthy—by the bishop’s permission and admonition, for the purpose of exhortation or edification concerning the salvation of the soul—to visit these places dedicated to God, this must be done only with suitable witnesses, lest, through careless presumption, the angelic order of Holy Church be defamed.

At no time may an abbess or any nun, with Satan transforming himself into an angel of light and suggesting to them that they go for the sake of prayer, have permission to travel to Rome or to visit other venerable places. No one is so witless or foolish as not to know how irreligious and reprehensible it is for women to associate with men because of the necessities of travel.

If, after this definition of this reverend council, anyone attempts with rash audacity to violate what has been established by common voice and for the sake of salvation, he shall be restrained by canonical punishments: either he shall be fined by excommunication according to the measure and character of his fault, or, punished by the bond of anathema, he shall be bound, or, stripped of his own dignity, he shall be torn away from the bosom of the Church as guilty. These are the avenging punishments of the canons, from which no transgressor of the sacred law will be able to depart immune, unless perhaps, through the healing intervention of penance, he merits obtaining pardon.

### XIII.

We command all Christians to venerate the Lord’s Day with every reverence and devout religious observance from the beginning of the night—that is, from Saturday evening, which gives way to the dawn of the first Sabbath—when the signal has sounded or when it is time for the evening office to be celebrated; this is not on account of the honor of the final Sabbath, but of that holy night of the first Sabbath, that is, the Lord’s Day.

They must first of all abstain from every sin and from every carnal work, even from relations with their own spouses, and from every earthly work; they must devote themselves to nothing else except prayer; they must hasten to church with the greatest devotion of mind; every tumult of lawsuits must cease; and with charity and love they must bless God the Father, praise with all the depths of their hearts the only-begotten Son of God, who sanctified this day through His glorious resurrection, and sing a hymn to the Holy Spirit, who blessed it through His wonderful coming, when He descended upon the blessed apostles in tongues of fire (Acts 2:3).

Moreover, it is believed that on this same most sacred day nearly all the gifts of the charisms were bestowed upon the world. On this day, after His resurrection, the Lord breathed the Holy Spirit upon His disciples for the remission of sins (John 20:22). On this day, in the desert, the Lord fed five thousand people with five loaves (Matt. 14:20). On this day manna first rained from heaven in the wilderness (Exod. 16:13), and many other spiritual gifts were manifested on this day, all of which would take too long to list individually.

For this is the Lord’s “delightful Sabbath” (Isa. 58:13), concerning which Scripture says: “Whoever performs servile work on it—that is, the work of sin—shall be put to death” (Exod. 35:2). If it were speaking of that Sabbath which the Jews celebrate, the last day of the week, which our peasants also observe, it would have said merely “Sabbath,” and would by no means have added “delightful” and “my.” But because it wished to distinguish between that Sabbath and this one, which is the Lord’s Day, it therefore added “my,” as though it said: “Mine, not yours; delightful, not defiled by your observances.” For this reason it must be honored and celebrated by us with every reverence.

The other principal festivals likewise must be honored and observed with reverence. Those festivals that the priest proclaims in church must be observed in every way.

We, however, who are called priests, ought to instruct the people subject to us by preaching the words of every good thing and by doing what we teach through our example: in charity, chastity, humility, continence, moderation, vigils, fasting and prayer, religious devotion, almsgiving, hospitality insofar as our strength permits, speech seasoned with the salt of wisdom, moderation in eating and drinking, holy conduct, simplicity of heart, and every good work. Thus we should live piously and justly while awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (Titus 2:12–13), who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

### XIV.

Concerning tithes and firstfruits—while, of course, preserving the mystical sacramental meanings of allegorical matters—I do not think anything better can be taught than what is written in the prophet Malachi, where the Lord says:

> “Bring the whole tithe into my storehouse, so that there may be food in my house, and test me in this, says the Lord: whether I will not open for you the floodgates of heaven and pour out a blessing upon you in abundance; I will rebuke the devourer for your sake, and he shall not destroy the fruit of your land, nor shall your vine be barren in the field, says the Lord of hosts; and all nations shall call you blessed” (Malachi 3:10 ff.).

But because the indignation and anger of God remain over the nation or people who do not fulfill this command of the Lord with their whole heart and good will, He had already said above:

> “Will a man pierce God?” He says, “yet you pierce me; and you have said: ‘In what way do we pierce you?’ In tithes and firstfruits. You are cursed with want, and you pierce me, the whole nation” (ibid., vv. 8–9).

Therefore, who would not offer to God with an eager and joyful heart, so that he might deserve that blessing of which He says, “I will pour out my blessing upon you in abundance”? Or who would not fear and tremble at the curse that He threatens against those unwilling to offer: “You are cursed, and you have afflicted me, the whole nation”?

And if perhaps you do not believe us or despise us because we are human beings, then believe the Lord Himself, who cannot lie, who promised both a curse in this age and in the age to come to those unwilling to obey His commands, and a blessing, abundance, and salvation of soul and body in the present age and in the future to those who obey His commands in good will.

God does not demand from you what you do not possess, nor does He weigh how much you give. But, according to what you possess, give to the Lord from His gifts, with a simple heart, not from what is truly your own. For everything that we are, live by, and possess (Acts 17:28) belongs to Him, and we have received it from the hand of His goodness. He considers with what mind, not how much, you offer in sacrifice to Him, who is able to grant a hundredfold in the present age and eternal life in the future. He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and forever, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0301]

## OBSERVATIONS AND NOTES

### NOTES OF SEVERINUS BINIUS ON THE TITLE OF THE COUNCIL

[Col. 0301D]

**a Council.** On the occasion by which this synod was convened in Italy under Paulinus’s authority, Paulinus himself gives information in the speech that he delivered to the council Fathers, in these words:

> “Now, with divine clemency helping us, since the arrogance of the savage barbarians has been crushed and their necks, raised in pride, bowed down, and since assistance has been supplied from heaven in every way, the most tranquil peace has now been restored to the lands through the altogether heavenly gift of grace, and royal commands have for a little while allowed us to breathe again, we have thought it necessary, hastening with the greatest urgency, to gather your most beloved fraternity into one fellowship, in accordance with the inviolable decrees of the ancient canons.”

Paulinus said this to the synod while, in the preceding passages, he was excusing himself for the interruption of council meetings caused by the disturbances of war and frequent journeys.

**b Forojulian.** So called from Forojulium, which, according to the acts of this council, was a municipality of the province of Aquileia and in modern times is subject to the Venetians. Formerly Aquileia was a distinguished city there, destroyed by Attila, king of the Huns, just as about two hundred years later Forum Julii was overthrown by the Avar king.

**c By Paulinus.** Wilfrid Strabo, who flourished under Louis, son of Charlemagne, writes the following about Paulinus in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25:

> “It is indeed reported that Paulinus, patriarch of Forojulium, often, and especially in private Masses, celebrated hymns composed either by others or by himself around the offering of the sacraments.”

That he was distinguished in holiness and learning, and that he took a very large part in the synods convened under Charlemagne—so much so that he could not possess the care of his own province to the extent he desired—is shown by the acts of the council.

**d In the matter of the most holy Trinity.** At this time two different heresies were ravaging the Church: one concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, the other concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Regarding the Holy Spirit, the question was whether He proceeded from the Father alone or simultaneously from the Father and the Son. Paulinus most learnedly settled this ancient controversy against heresies repeatedly condemned beforehand, showing that the Father and the Son are one principle of the procession of the Holy Spirit, and that it therefore appeared impious and blasphemous to stir up new errors against the doctrine received by the universal Church in the time of Saint Leo the Great.

Regarding the incarnation of the divine Word, Elipandus, bishop of Toledo in Spain, and with him Felix, bishop of Urgell—the man by whom he had been led astray and whom he himself had led astray [the antecedents are uncertain]—asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ should, according to His divine nature, be called the natural Son of God, but that according to His humanity the same Son should be called the adopted Son of God. Since this doctrine asserted two Sons of God and thus revived Nestorianism, which had long before been condemned, Paulinus most solidly refuted, rejected, and condemned it by reciting the creeds of Nicaea and Constantinople.

Finally, in this same synod, after the treatment of the dogmatic controversies had been completed, fourteen canons relating to ecclesiastical discipline were enacted.

**e In the year of the Lord 791.** This year of the Lord coincides with the twenty-third year of Charlemagne, which is placed at the beginning of the synodal acts.

Thus far Binius. All these matters will become clearer from our dissertation on the Council of Forojulium. In the meantime, we append our notes on the remainder of the council.

## NOTES OF THE COLLECTOR

### § II.

[Col. 0303D]

**a Seated according to custom.** In the Council of Forojulium Paulinus preserved the order prescribed by the Fourth Council of Toledo. For that synod decrees in canon 4:

> “At the first hour of the day, before sunrise, let everyone be expelled from the church; after the doors have been secured, let doorkeepers stand at one door, through which the priests ought to enter; and let all the bishops assemble and enter together, taking their seats according to the dates of their ordination. After all the bishops have entered and taken their seats, let the priests whom the matter has shown should enter be summoned, and so forth.”

Here one sees that the remaining priests are summoned after the bishops have taken their seats. It is also clear, on consideration, that Paulinus did this. Shortly afterward he adds:

**b He was admitted through the entrance of the more private door, the archdeacon summoning him to the brief of the priestly assembly.** What does *intromitti ad brevem*—“to be admitted to the brief”—mean? I think it signifies “from a list,” or “according to a list.” Since the archdeacon summoned them, as stated here, and read from a list the names of those to be admitted, I believe that they were admitted *ad brevem*, that is, according to the order of the register from which they were summoned.

For *breve* or *brevis* sometimes meant a register of any matter. The *Capitularies*, book III, chapter 82, says: “Let not only the benefices of the bishops but also those of our treasury be entered in the *Breve*.” This word was also used by later, less barbarous centuries. Flavius Vopiscus, in *Aurelian*, chapter 36, says: “Mnestheus wrote out a brief of names and read the brief to each person whose name it contained.” Lampridius, in *Alexander Severus*, chapter 21, says: “He knew his soldiers everywhere so well that in his chamber he kept briefs containing both the number and the terms of service of the soldiers.”

He says “the archdeacon summoning,” because this was the duty of deacons. Saint Athanasius, *Apology II*, says:

> “With what face do they dare to call such an assembly a synod, where a registrar introduced those arriving on behalf of the church’s deacons?”

### § III.

[Col. 0304B]

**a Nevertheless to choke.** Writers of later Latin use *nihilominus* for “and already,” as Paulinus does here and other writers do elsewhere. Sedulius, in his letter to Macedonius on book V of the *Paschal Work*, says:

> “Let them know that Origen, most skilled in divine law, nevertheless adapted almost everything he discussed to three editions,”

that is, “also to three editions.” Thus *nihilominus suffugare* means “also to choke.”

But *suffugare* is not Latin. Du Cange, citing this passage of the council in his *Glossary*, says: “The word seems to have been used for *suffundere*, ‘to spread over,’ or certainly for *offuscare*, ‘to darken.’” I suspect, however, that *suffugare* has crept in for *suffocare*, with an allusion to seed choked by thorns, concerning which Luke 8:7 says: “And another fell among thorns, and when the thorns sprang up with it, they choked it.” See also the note in book I against Felix, chapter 4, letter a.

### § IV.

**a In the smoke of pride.** *Τύφος* (*typhos*) means “smoke.” It is frequently used for arrogance and elevation of spirit. Augustine, in book XI, chapter 33, of *The City of God*, uses the word without the addition “of pride,” but nevertheless allegorically, as smoke figuratively representing pride.

That the meaning of this foreign word was known to everyone at that time, and indeed that it was in common use, is clear from how frequently it occurs in Augustine: for example, in *Confessions*, book III, chapter 3; likewise book XIII, chapter 25; letter 93, chapter 6, in the latest Venetian edition of 1729, formerly letter 48; and letter 187, chapter 21, formerly letter 57.

We also see it used by Arnobius several times without qualification, especially in book II:

> “If the elevation of mind and the *typhos*, as it is called by the Greeks, did not stand in the way,”

and four more times in the same book. Augustine and Arnobius therefore use *typhos* for pride.

Paulinus, however, says “the smoke of pride” to give the word greater force, as also in book II against Felix, chapter 6:

> “Whose boastfulness does the smoke of pride inflate in you?”

Gregory the Great speaks in the same way in letter 23, book VI, writing to Cyriacus, bishop of Constantinople:

> “For true charity is then shown, if there is no schism among us through the smoke of pride.”

**b And persisting in an abnormal condition.** That is, continuing outside the norm and proper order. For *enormis* means “outside the norm.” See the following note.

### § VI.

**a As though forming a straight line according to the little rule.** This is allegorical, but an allegory drawn quite properly from a rule, as shortly afterward: “made equal according to the little rule of that straightness.”

For a *norma*—an invention, if Pliny is to be trusted, of Theodorus of Samos, like the level—is a craftsman’s and architect’s instrument consisting of two rules joined at a right angle, by which we test whether angles correspond, just as heights are tested by the plumb line and lengths by the ruler. Vitruvius, book VIII, chapter 3, says:

> “Lengths are to be tested by ruler and line, heights by the plumb line, and angles by the norm; it is commonly called a *squadra*.”

The metaphorical use of the word is more frequent than its proper use, as is also the case with *regula*. A rule or norm may commonly mean any order, formula, precept, or direction for acting, studying, praying, writing, or living.

Pliny the Younger, book IX, letter 26, called Demosthenes the norm and rule of an orator, as though he were saying “the true and proper model of an orator.” Hence *abnormis*, “without a norm,” and *enormis*, “outside the norm.”

In particular, the institutions of monks were called rules and norms by writers of Middle and Late Latin. The charter of Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, from the year 770, says:

> “He gathered together a crowd of monks living their lives under the holy norm.”

The poem *On the Origin of the Frankish People* says:

> “Here he establishes, under the revered law, the decrees of Father Benedict, and renews the legal ordinances of the ancient norm.”

See Du Cange.

Paulinus here uses the diminutive *normula*, “little norm,” and *normulatim*, “according to the little norm,” just as in book I, chapter 37, against Felix, where he means a formula or rule of religion but at the same time explains the function of a norm measuring the straightness of sides, saying:

> “While the simple and sincere principle of faith extends the straightness of both sides according to the little norm of its religion, bending it nowhere at all through deceptive error.”

**b While the three-chambered structure remains, let the golden ornament of the decorations be suspended.** Paulinus seems to have referred to an ancient custom by which chambers—so called from their curved form, according to Nonius, *On the Proper Meaning of Words*—were also gilded. Aurelian, considering this excessive luxury, was planning to abolish it. Vopiscus, in *Aurelian*, chapter 46, says:

> “He intended that gold should be placed neither in chambers nor …”

### § VII.

**a Trappings of words.** *Phalerae* were originally ornaments for horses, as Pliny suggests concerning certain gems, book XXXVII, chapter 12:

> “Of such great size that they made hanging ornaments for the horses of kings as trappings.”

The word was then transferred to denote the adornment of human beings. Livy, book IX, first decade, final chapter, says:

> “The election of Flavius was held in such disgrace that many of the nobles laid aside their gold rings and trappings.”

Hence the word was allegorically transferred to signify the ornaments of speech. On this matter, see the notes on chapter 3 of book I against Felix.

**b In certain synodal leaves.** Saint Athanasius, in his letter to Antioch concerning the decree of the Council of Sardica in the year 37, says:

> “Although certain men wished to attribute some things to the Council of Nicaea as though they had been lacking, and vigorously insisted upon this, the holy synod assembled at Sardica nevertheless took it indignantly and decreed that nothing further should be written concerning the faith; and they declared that they were content with the faith of Nicaea.”

The Fathers of the Council of Constantinople in the year 381, although they had added something to the Nicene Creed in order to repel the new heresies of Macedonius and others, nevertheless profess that they had changed nothing and established no new formula. Canon 1 says:

> “The faith of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers who assembled at Nicaea must not be abolished, but must remain firm and stable, and every heresy must be anathematized,”

and so forth.

The Council of Ephesus in the year 431 also established this by a decree inserted in action 6:

> “The holy synod has decreed that no one may propose, write, or compose another faith besides that defined by the holy Fathers who were gathered at Nicaea with the Holy Spirit.”

**c A work composed from the faith of very many men.** Besides the Apostolic Creed, we have the Nicene, the Constantinopolitan, and the Aquileian Creeds, as well as the one published under the name of Saint Athanasius. There also exists the creed of Saint Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, and of Peregrinus, bishop of Lauriacum in Germany, along with any others there may be: although they resound in different words, as Paulinus says here, they retain the same meaning in harmony.

### § VIII.

[Col. 0306A]

**a For often by us and our forebears.** Here Paulinus hints that he had previously discussed the mystery of the Trinity and the common operation of the divine persons. None of that work has been able to reach us because of the ravages of time; only longing and grief over the common loss remain.

When he adds “and our forebears,” he may perhaps be referring to Saint Chromatius, once his predecessor in the see of Aquileia. Near the end of his *Tractate on “I Ought to Be Baptized by You,”* Chromatius says:

> “Neither can the Father be understood without the Son, nor the Son without the Holy Spirit.”

God is known, as the Apostle says in Romans 1:20, through the things that have been made. Therefore the divine persons are inseparable.

Augustine develops and explains this argument above all in *Tractate XX on John*, section 3:

> “The Catholic faith, established by the Spirit of God in His saints, holds this against every heretical perversity: the works of the Father and the Son are inseparable.”

And below:

> “The Catholic faith does not say that God the Father did one thing and the Son another, but that what the Father did, the Son also did, and the Holy Spirit also did.”

He repeats this in *Tractate XCV*, section 1, and *Tractate C*, section 3.

Cyril of Alexandria, in his *Apology to the Orientals against the Ninth Anathema*, wrote:

> “Accordingly, that the Holy Trinity is of the same substance, the same power, and the same operation, we have not learned from your discourse, but have instead been taught by the sacred Scriptures.”

**b He does not cease to educate the infancy of our understanding.** “Infancy” means weakness or smallness; or rather, he alludes to 1 Peter 2:2: “Like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit.”

**c Nor even the subtle angelic nature.** Subtlety is a gift not of the spirit but of the glorified body. Paulinus nevertheless uses the word here in the sense in which Wisdom 7:22 says of the spirit of understanding that it is “holy, unique, manifold, subtle,” and verse 23 says that it “can enter into all spirits,” being “intelligent, pure, subtle.”

Or, as Emmanuel Sa observes, according to the Greek, “pure, most subtle,” so that the words refer to angelic spirits. Many Latins read the passage in this way. Cornelius says here:

> “It is as though he were saying that the Holy Spirit comprehends—that is, perfects—intelligible spirits: ‘pure’ referring to the first hierarchy, ‘subtle’ to the second, and ‘most subtle’ to the third.”

This is summarized by Cornelius a Lapide, whom Saint Gregory Nazianzen supports in Oration 37:

> “Penetrating through all pure, exceedingly subtle intellectual spirits—that is, through the angelic hosts, as I think.”

**d With a rust-colored stylus dipped in ink.** In these two words Paulinus touches upon several matters: first, the material of the stylus, which was once and originally iron. Job 19:23 says:

> “Who will grant me that my words may be written … that they may be engraved in a book with an iron stylus?”

Althelmus, *Heptastichon*, book I, on letters, says:

> “We are born from iron, and again we die by iron,”

because one end was pointed, with which writing was made in wax, while the other was blunt, with which what had been written was erased at the writer’s discretion.

Hence Symphosius, *Riddles*, no. 1, “The Stylus”:

> “Flat at the top, but I am not flat below;  
> I turn in the hand at either end, performing different tasks;  
> One part recalls whatever the other part has done.”

But *rust-colored* signifies not only the material but also, allegorically, the obscurity, perversity, and wickedness of speech. For the color rust is often taken as black and ominous. Virgil, *Georgics*, book I, verse 467:

> “When he covered his shining head with dark rust.”

And in the *Aeneid*, book VI, verse 303, concerning Charon:

> “And he carries the bodies in his rust-colored boat.”

That is, “black and gloomy,” as Servius says there.

Everyone knows that *stylus* is also used for the speech itself that is written with a stylus. Thus for Paulinus a rust-colored stylus is the same as a bad stylus, one that had written badly through the fault of the writer. Compare Cicero, *Speech on the Response of the Haruspices*:

> “When Sextus Clodius had written the other crimes with an impure stylus,”

and so forth.

When Paulinus says that the stylus was dipped into the dye-vat of falsehood, he passes from one manner of writing to another. Properly speaking, the stylus used for engraving wax tablets was not dipped in ink. A reed pen, however, like a bird’s feather today, is dipped into the inkpot, that is, the inkwell.

The usage must nevertheless be excused, since it has precedent. Suetonius writes of Augustus, chapter 85:

> “He began a tragedy with great enthusiasm, but when his stylus did not succeed he destroyed it. When his friends asked what Ajax was doing, he replied that his Ajax had fallen upon a sponge.”

Here the stylus is also used in reference to a manner of writing in which a sponge erases the writing—obviously a kind of writing that uses ink, such as writing with reeds, rushes, or feathers. See the notes in book II, chapter 1, against Felix, and below in § 16.

**e For vengeance upon the wanton.** That is, upon the wanton and fornicator, concerning whom Paulinus speaks from Numbers, chapter 25.

*Petulcus* is an adjective. Virgil, *Georgics*, book IV, verse 10:

> “Nor may the sheep and wanton kids  
> Trample upon the flowers.”

Servius comments on this passage:

> “Wanton: lewd, exuberant; and they are called *petulci* from *petere*, ‘to seek or assail.’ Hence we also call prostitutes *petulcae*, ‘wanton.’”

### § XI

**a They dared to cut out the tongue.** Properly, *elinguare* means “to pull out the tongue.” Plautus, *The Pot of Gold*, act I, scene 4, verse 269:

> “By Hercules, if I do not have you tongue-less from the roots.”

But Paulinus uses the verb with a new meaning, “to speak against” or “to slander,” as though, just as from *loquela* (“speech”) we have *loquor* (“I speak”) and hence *obloquor* (“I speak against”), so from *lingua* (“tongue”) we have *linguo* and *elinguo*.

**b And we invoke blessings upon you with brotherly affection.** Paulinus was addressing the bishops of the province; for that reason he uses this word, which was especially customary among bishops as a term of honor.

The title of Augustine’s letter 186 in the latest edition reads:

> “To the most blessed lord and brother Paulinus, whom one must embrace with genuine affection in the depths of Christ, more desirable than can be expressed, Alypius and Augustine.”

Letter 45 similarly begins:

> “Alypius and Augustine send greetings in the Lord to their most genuine, beloved, and praiseworthy brothers in Christ, Paulinus and Therasia.”

The word was sometimes used of non-bishops as well, as Augustine himself uses it when writing to Jerome in letter 92, within the body of the letter:

> “What I did not do by reproving your genuine affection.”

### § XIII

**a And if “the eye of the Lord” is read, and so forth.** We frequently see human limbs and emotions attributed to God in Scripture. But for how these things should be understood spiritually, besides what Paulinus gives here, consult John Cassian, *Institutes of the Coenobites*, book VIII, chapters 3 and 4; Cassiodorus, *On the Soul*, chapter 19; Saint Gregory the Great, *Moralia*, book XX, chapter 23; and above all Saint Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, *Book of Formulae*, chapters 1 and 2, since he goes through all the limbs and human passions individually and explains them with reference to God.

### § XIV
### a. Ecclesiastical Ferulae

“Ferula” here signifies the punishment inflicted with *ferulae*. A *ferula* is a shrub or herb that grows so tall and becomes so hard that it resembles wood. Pliny, Book XIII, chapter 22: “No shrub is lighter; for that reason, when carried, it more readily provides old age with the use of walking sticks.” For the same reason it was also employed by schoolmasters in keeping boys under discipline. Martial, *Apophoreta*, epigram 80, whose heading is “Ferulae”:

> Hated exceedingly by boys, and pleasing to teachers,  
> We are bright woods, a gift from Prometheus.

The *ferulae* subsequently became insignia of rank—not only of abbots and bishops, but also of popes and emperors. Charles du Fresne, Seigneur du Cange, in his *Dissertation on the Coinage of the Later Age*, marginal note 21, writes:

> What earlier Latin and Byzantine writers called the *labarum*, they called the *nárthēx* (νάρθηξ), or *ferula*; for it was likewise an emblem carried by emperors, as it plainly appears to have been, although afterward it did not retain altogether the same form and shape.

And below:

> Codinus writes (*On Offices*, chapter 17, no. 37) that it was customary, whenever the emperor carried the *stemma*, for him to hold a cross in his right hand and a *nárthēx* (νάρθηξ) in his left. Symeon of Thessalonica, however, states that emperors carried the *ferula* as a symbol of the power granted to them to chastise subject peoples.

This is what Du Cange says concerning the emperors’ *ferula*. Concerning the papal *ferula*, the passage in Liutprand, Book VI, chapter 11 of his *History*, near the end, is sufficient. After the following words—“The antipope Benedict took off the pallium, which, together with the pontifical *ferula* that he carried in his hand, he returned to Pope Leo”—the account continues: “That pope broke the *ferula* and showed the broken pieces to the people.”

The *ferula* in the hand of a bishop or abbot is the same as the pastoral staff or crozier, as Honorius of Autun teaches in Book I of *The Gem of the Soul*, chapter 217, whose title is “On the Episcopal Staff.” He says:

> The staff—which is also called the pastoral rod, *capuita*, *ferula*, and *pedum*, and so forth.

Concerning abbots, Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino, bears witness in Leo of Ostia’s *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book III, chapter 65. When he was asked to receive the new pontiff for election in his monastery at Monte Cassino, just as he had once received Gregory, “he most willingly promised to do so, and by the *ferula* that he carried in his hand he invested them in his pledge concerning this matter.”

In the Church of Milan during the time of Ambrose, as Landulf the Elder reports in Book I, chapter 8 of his *History of Milan*, when the orders of ministers had been divided into ten classes, an equal number of superiors “carried daily in their hands *ferulae* decorated above and below with leather, to show their offices or rank, so that each might correct and amend his subordinates with rod and staff.” Nor was this custom pointless or introduced merely for display. The same Landulf writes, in Book II, chapter 35, that:

> If one of them behaved improperly by singing, reading, or standing, or by muttering and chattering with another in the choir, he either corrected himself of the fault in which he was offending, or, once his undergarment had been pulled up in the sacristy, he was corrected with rods by the archdeacon, whether he wished it or not.

The *Rule of the Monks*, no. 11, and the author of the *Life of Saint Woltan* likewise teach that offending monks were customarily punished, as Du Cange notes in his *Glossary*. Paulinus therefore very appropriately called the punishments inflicted by the Church, figuratively, “ecclesiastical *ferulae*.”

### § XV

#### a. “Let everyone know the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart.”

What he had said in the preceding section about the rule of faith being retained by heart and impressed upon posterity—that is, upon sons and grandsons—he repeats here concerning the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Whether this was the cause, or certainly at least an example, of the following decree issued not long afterward, namely in the year 813, the Council of Mainz, canon 45, also recorded among the *Capitularies*, Book V, chapter 161, decreed as follows:

> Let priests always urge the Christian people to learn the Creed, which is the seal of faith, and the Lord’s Prayer; and we wish those who neglect to learn these things to receive a fitting discipline [the text reads *sic*], whether by fasting or by some other punishment. Therefore it is right that they send their sons to school, either to monasteries or outside them to priests, so that they may properly learn the Catholic faith and the Lord’s Prayer, and may be able to teach others at home. Whoever cannot otherwise do so should learn it in his own language.

Theodulf likewise says in his capitulary, chapter 22:

> The faithful must be admonished, he says, so that all alike, from the least to the greatest, may learn the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed. They must also be told that upon these two statements rests the whole foundation of the Christian faith; and unless someone retains these two statements by heart, believes them with all his heart, and repeats them very frequently in prayer, he cannot be a Catholic.

### § XVI

#### a. “Published with a salutary pen-point.”

A *mucro* in a writing instrument is the sharp part with which letters were written by cutting them into wax tablets. Pignorius, *Commentary on Slaves*, chapter 15:

> They wrote with the point: they scraped away what had been written on the surface.

This is indicated by a verse of Prudentius’ *Peristephanon*, or *The Crowns*, verse 2136, in the passion of Saint Cassian the Martyr:

> From there others brandish iron points and goads,  
> With the part by which writing is made in ploughed furrows,  
> And by which the cut letters are erased and the smooth surface  
> Is made bright again, renewed.

Hence the word was used for the writing instrument itself, as a part standing for the whole. Columella, Book X, *On Garden Cultivation*, toward the middle:

> 80 … Just as the letter next to the first  
> Is traced in wax by the point of the learned teacher.

Paulinus himself, in Book II, chapter 1, against Felix, called the point of the reed—or of the pens made from reeds that served the writer’s use—the “point of the reed.” See above, § X, letter d.

# NOTES ON THE CANONS OF THE COUNCIL

## PREFACE

There are two things that draw human beings away from the supreme truth and the supreme good: error and malice. By these the intellect and the will are injured; hence it comes about that we do not understand the truth, or understand it wrongly, and that we do not love the good, or love it wrongly. From this arise confusion, darkness, ignorance, and falsehood in the intellect; and depravity, corruption, and perversity of conduct in the will.

After these wounds have been inflicted upon the soul through sin, divine mercy confronts them with two remedies, namely faith and charity. God communicates faith through his written or orally handed-down word; charity, either through the eternal law impressed by God’s finger upon each person’s heart, or through his Decalogue and commandments.

The Church imitates this heavenly ordering in her councils, namely through dogmas and canons. Through the former she confronts error; through the latter, the corruption of morals. On the one hand, by anathema she drives away heresies opposed to the truth of doctrine; on the other, through discipline she commends honorable conduct and corrects and chastises what is wrong. In this way she guards, with care for the faith, the deposit of faith and commandments that she received from Christ.

Accordingly, our Paulinus, following the example of other councils, after defending the faith that had been attacked by errors in an extended and elegant discourse, and adding the Creed and an exposition of the faith, established fourteen canons in his synod for strengthening and invigorating discipline in his province—whether for restoring, preserving, or increasing it.

Since matters concerning discipline are subject to variation, depending as they do upon the circumstances of times and places, which themselves change, whereas the dogmas of faith are immutable, we have resolved to examine more carefully and elucidate with the following observations whatever each canon presents as worthy of attention for a fuller knowledge of ancient customs and discipline.

# OBSERVATION ON CANON I

### I

Paulinus begins, as is fitting, with divine matters, namely by barring the simoniacal plague from the Church. This is the purpose of this decree, which appears to be a complete exposition of the rule or canon whose establishment Paulinus himself took part in at the Council of Aachen, seven years before he held this assembly at Friuli, namely in the year 789.

In his first capitulary, no. 21, we read:

> In the Council of Chalcedon [the text above has *sup.*], it is decreed that no bishop or anyone from the clergy may be ordained for money, because both parties are to be deposed—the one who ordains and the one who is ordained—as well as the intermediary between them. The same matter is found in the canons of the Apostles. The prince of the Apostles himself already condemned this heresy terribly in the person of Simon Magus.

How necessary it was for the Fathers and councils to oppose this evil with all their strength is clear from the fact that this plague was spreading widely throughout Gaul, Germany, and Italy around the time of Paulinus.

Gregory the Great, therefore, wrote to Virgilius, bishop of Arles, in Book IV, letter 51, in the month of August, in the thirteenth indiction, which fell in the year 595:

> I have learned from the reports of certain people that in the regions of Gaul and Germany no one reaches holy orders without making a payment.

After condemning also the wicked custom then prevailing there—namely, the immediate ordination of laymen as priests and bishops—he adds:

> Therefore it is necessary that Your Fraternity strive to admonish our most excellent son, King Childebert, so that he may utterly remove the stain of this sin from his kingdom.

### II

In the following century, indeed in Paulinus’ own lifetime, Pope Hadrian I wrote to Charlemagne that he did not cease preaching the Lord’s commandments against the simoniacal ordinations of clerics, which were then defiling Italy, especially Tuscany and the territory of Ravenna.

There is an extant letter in volume VIII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, 1729, p. 534, where it is numbered 7; in the *Caroline Code* it is numbered 85:

> Since we bear pastoral care for all the Churches, we do not cease preaching the divine commandments concerning the offense of consecration that is committed in the regions of Italy and Tuscany through the simoniacal heresy. Nevertheless, in many places it is not prevented; indeed, as your messengers, it is said, have reported, it is customarily practiced in the Church of Ravenna as well. Hence it is evident that much money is alienated through such an abominable payment.

After Hadrian’s death and the succession of Leo III in his place, that same Charlemagne, writing to Leo through Abbot Angelbert in the *Memorandum of Matters to Be Handled with the Pontiff*, which is included among the *Capitularies* under the year 796, also emphasizes the following:

> Earnestly persuading him concerning the overthrow of the simoniacal heresy, which in many places grievously stains the holy body of the Church.

Indeed, since the Council of Verneuil, held under Pippin in the year 755, chapter 24, decrees:

> No one should approach an ecclesiastical office or rank through money, because it appears to be the simoniacal heresy.

[Note: “Appears” in place of “is,” a phrase frequently encountered in those times.]

It plainly demonstrates that those times were suffering from this plague.

### III

In the following century as well, Paschasius Ratbert, abbot of Corbie, who died on 26 April 851, wrote in Book IX of his *Exposition on Matthew* concerning Gaul, which was still infected with this disease. On the passage, “He drove out all those who were buying and selling in the temple,” he writes:

> The simoniacal heresy has often been attacked in Gaul, but never overcome, because both those who buy what belongs to their own churches and those who sell it have become robbers. Although this heresy could indeed be condemned, it has so far not been overcome because, just as a robber is so called from hiding, so these people very often act secretly, or at least so boldly—although shamelessly—that no one dares oppose them. This deed, to speak frankly, is felt and lamented throughout all Gaul today.

From these statements, then, infer how consistent with reason it was that Paulinus should oppose, in the first canon of his council, a disease that was creeping inwardly and secretly.

# NOTES ON CANON I

### a. “Established under the canon.”

Du Cange, under “Canon,” that is, “under ecclesiastical rule.” The First Council of Nicaea, canon 16:

> Whoever are altogether numbered among the canon.

In Greek: **ἐν τῷ κανόνι ἐξεταζόμενοι**, “those examined or enrolled in the canon.”

The word *canon* is not always understood in only one way. At times it indicates a distinction from the laws and statutes of secular princes, as is clear from the law *Privileges*, title “Concerning Churches,” where we read:

> All pragmatic sanctions that are contrary to the ecclesiastical canons, etc.

Here sanctions are distinguished from canons, and conversely.

At the Council of Aachen in 789, chapter 71:

> Those who enter the clerical state—which we call the canonical life—we wish to live canonically.

### b. “Indeed, apostolic as well.”

Either because simony is prohibited in the canons called apostolic, or because Peter, the head of the Apostles, condemned it in Simon himself, as Paulinus adds there in these words:

> For the first pastor of the Church took care to cut away this deadly simoniacal heresy at its very original root of greed, so to speak, with the sword of anathema.

# OBSERVATION ON CANON II

### I

In imitation of what Saint Gregory the Great said concerning salt in homilies 7 and 13 on the Gospels, Paulinus likewise speaks here of salt and light.

The words of Gregory’s seventh homily are:

> We must continually consider what is said to the holy Apostles, and through the Apostles to us: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew 5:13). If, then, we are salt, we ought to season the minds of the faithful … For we are not the salt of the earth if we do not season the hearts of those who hear us. Indeed, the person who does not withhold the word of preaching truly gives this seasoning to his neighbor.

Concerning light, in another homily:

> We hold burning lamps in our hands when, through good works, we show our neighbors examples of light. Concerning these works the Lord says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (ibid., verse 16).

This is also reinforced by canon 70 of the Council of Aachen in 789:

> We also ask Your Holiness that the ministers of the altar … have a good and commendable life and conduct, as the Lord himself commands in the Gospel: “Let your light shine,” etc., so that many may be drawn to the service of God by their good conduct.

## OBSERVATION ON CANON III

### I

What Paulinus adds at the end of this canon or chapter is altogether noteworthy. He says:

> Hence it is also authoritatively established and decided in the ecclesiastical canon that people must either cease from such indulgence in vice or, if they persist, must risk the loss of their rank. We confess that we are partners and supporters of those who dictated this avenging sentence.

For a long time I remained uncertain which canon this was, whose partner and supporter Paulinus confesses himself to be, until after prolonged investigation I thought I had grasped the matter.

### II

It is, in my opinion, the canon inserted in Book VII of the *Capitularies*, no. 218. There we read:

> It has been decreed that priests, deacons, and the other clerics must altogether avoid drunkenness, which is the fuel and nurse of all vices. Therefore, concerning anyone who is shown to have been drunk, we decree that, as the order permits, he either be removed from communion for a period of forty days or be subjected to corporal punishment.

The same decree is repeated under no. 270.

It should be known, however—as we also point out elsewhere—that the last three books of the *Capitularies*, namely the fifth, sixth, and seventh, were collected by Benedict the Levite. Concerning the third book that he himself collected, which is seventh in order, he writes in the preface:

> In the third little book, certain chapters collected here and there from the canons by Bishop Paulinus, Master Albinus, and others, at the command of the unconquered prince Charles, have been inserted.

We believe that this canon concerning drunken clerics is one of the Paulinian chapters.

### III

The year in which this canon was issued, or the assembly at which it was issued, is not indicated there. For although the margin of that text adds, “Second Capitulary, year 803, chapter 5,” nothing of the kind appears in the cited capitulary or in any capitulary of that year.

It is, however, quite probable that it was issued in the year 789, at the assembly of Aachen. At that time this vice was spreading far and wide, especially among the ministers of the churches, as may be gathered from the *Capitulary of Admonition*, the fifth of the works that Baluzius calls “of uncertain date.” Yet in volume II, p. 1075, he says in his notes concerning it:

> These chapters of the *Capitulary of Admonition* were formerly published by Jean Cordes as though they were those of Jesse, bishop of Amiens. They are not Jesse’s, however, but Charlemagne’s, and, in my opinion, were given to the royal envoys.

Charlemagne had sent his envoys to reform ecclesiastical morals from the assembly at Aachen in the year 789, as is clear from Charles’ preface. These statements, therefore, seem to refer to that time.

In chapter 2 of the *Capitulary of Admonition* we read:

> Secondly, that the priests themselves should show the peoples subject to them such conduct as may be imitated, namely, as the Apostle said, in chastity and sobriety; that they should not serve gluttony and the desires of this age; and that what they admonish others to observe, they should display in themselves.

In chapter 4 this evil is explained more fully:

> Fourthly, that the priests themselves should withdraw from feasting and drinking, as the Apostle admonishes, since certain of them spend time drinking with some of their neighbors until midnight and even beyond, although they appear religious and holy. For some remain there and then return to their churches satiated or drunk, and neither by day nor by night is the service of God performed in the church entrusted to them [the text has *persolvitur vel persolvunt*, “is performed” or “they perform it”]. Some even sleep in the very place to which they have gone for the banquet.

All these circumstances, then, must be referred to the Council of Aachen in 789. We have shown that Paulinus took part in that council—and indeed in all the assemblies held that year—and that he applied a strong hand to the reform of morals, in Dissertation II, no. 10, and in the *Life of Paulinus*, chapter 5, no. 5. They sufficiently explain why Paulinus said here that he had been a partner and supporter of those who issued the sentence.

# NOTES ON CANON III

### a. “From such indulgence in this vice”

This is a hypallage, meaning “from such vice of indulgence,” a construction frequent in Scripture, as in “the odor of sweetness,” meaning “the sweetness of the odor,” and in Ecclesiasticus 4:1: “Do not withhold alms from the poor,” meaning “Do not defraud the poor of almsgiving.”

### b. “Of those who dictated the sentence”

The substantive *dictatorum* derives from *dictator*. To *dictare* is to teach something that another person takes down in writing, as Du Cange shows from Juvenal’s *Satire* VIII, using a passage from Britannicus. Accordingly, a *dictator* is someone who transmits what he teaches or says in such a way that another person records it.

But *dictator* sometimes also means “writer.” Lucifer of Cagliari, in Book *On the Necessity of Dying for the Son of God*, addressing the emperor Constantius, says:

> Sometimes you yourself, since you consider yourself learned and possess, as you think, a marked number of writers, etc.

A little below he says:

> You and your assistants in letters.

It is therefore beyond doubt that *dictatores* is used for “writers,” and *dictares* for “to write.” Zeno, in the law *Dictantibus*, title “Concerning Wills,” plainly uses *dictantes* for “writers”:

> In making wills … whatever … the testator may wish to leave, there is no reason for doubt. Nor is he prohibited from leaving it to witnesses …

Pauline therefore says that he was an associate of those who dictated, or wrote, the sentence.

### c. “We are partners”

The word *complex* has an uncertain meaning, for it is often used and understood in a bad sense, but also in a good one. Isidore, Book X of the *Etymologies*, writes:

> A partner is one who is joined to another in a single sin or crime, for evil; but it is never said for good.

Arnobius, however, in Book III *Against the Pagans*, says that Varro claimed the names of certain gods were unknown. He reports that the Etruscans called them *complices*:

> Varro believes that those who are within and in the innermost recesses of heaven are the gods whom we speak of, although their number and names are unknown. The Etruscans call and name them *consentes* and *complices*, because they arise together and set together.

Desiderius Heraldus, in his *Observations* on this passage, says:

> I have read nothing concerning these *complice* gods. At one time I thought that this was a gloss in the passage, as though some ignorant person had wished to interpret *consentes* as *complices*, as if they were conscious partners in the same crime … But what Arnobius adds—that they arise together and set together—seems to confirm the reading, so that they are *complices*, as being joined together and bound by the closest ties.

It may therefore be inferred from this that *complex* does not always imply partnership in crime, but may indiscriminately signify association and connection. In this sense Paulinus says that he was a *complex*, that is, united and joined to those who dictated or wrote the sentence against drunkards.

# OBSERVATION ON CANON IV

### I

Here Paulinus establishes two matters. The first concerns abolishing the cohabitation of clerics with women of any kind. The second concerns relieving relatives oppressed by beggary and poverty, but in such a way that female relatives are in no way received into the home.

He introduces this second matter only incidentally, lest clerics, because they are forbidden to live even with female relatives, should entirely neglect their care and violate charity under the pretext of propriety. The Apostle says in 1 Timothy 5:8:

> If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

On this passage Chrysostom should be consulted. Among other things, he also presses Isaiah 58:7 as a command of the Lord. Where our Vulgate reads, “And do not despise your own flesh,” he reads, “Do not despise the members of your household.”

The Council of Nantes, canon 3, teaches how clerics should provide for such persons:

> If anyone has among them a person suffering such necessity that the support of a priest is required, let him have a house in a village or town far from the priest’s residence, and there let him provide whatever is necessary.

### II

The principal purpose of this canon, then, is the moral integrity of the ecclesiastical order. For this reason, when Philip Briet speaks of this Council of Friuli under the year 791, he calls Paulinus “the most vigorous defender of discipline and chastity among clerics.”

It did not seem sufficient to Paulinus, taught by experience, that the Council of Nicaea had decreed that:

> No one among the clergy may have an introduced woman in his house, except only his mother, sister, or aunt, or those persons alone who entirely avoid suspicion.

For notes on this canon—third or fourth, depending on how the canons are variously numbered—see Severinus Binius, and the Arabic version with the notes of Francis Turrianus, S.J.

Perhaps Paulinus had before him the teaching and example of Saint Augustine. Possidius writes in the *Life of Augustine*, chapter 26:

> No woman ever lived in his house or remained there—not even his full sister, who, serving God as a widow, presided over the female servants of God for a long time until the day of her death. Nor did his uncle’s daughters or his brother’s daughters, who likewise served God, remain there—persons whom the councils of holy bishops placed among the exceptions. He used to say that although no evil suspicion could arise concerning a sister or nieces living with him, nevertheless those persons could not remain with him without other necessary women also being present; and since other women would enter from outside to visit them, this could give rise to offense or scandal among those of lower rank. Those who happened to remain with a bishop or any cleric might be ruined by human temptations because of all the women living or visiting together there, or at least be shamefully defamed by the evil suspicions of men.

### III

John of Salisbury, bishop of Chartres, had this action and statement of Augustine before his eyes when he wrote letter 68 to someone whose name is not given but who, from the context of the letter, seems to have been the bishop of Lincoln. This person had consulted him about a certain Renier, whom he had written was living with his former mistress under the appearance of paternal service.

Salisbury replied as follows:

> Although many canons have not wished a mother, sister, grandmother, maternal aunt, nieces, household servants, or persons joined by the affection of the first degree to be regarded with suspicion because of cohabitation, blessed Augustine nevertheless does not approve of a cleric living even with his sister, because sometimes women who are not sisters live with sisters, and, as the pagan poet says:
>
> “The name of kinship may conceal the guilt.”

### IV

The fathers of the Third Council of Braga were troubled by the same reasonable scruple. They permitted clerics to live with their mothers alone, excluding even sisters:

> We decree with complete authority that no priest, or any other member of the clergy, may presume to associate privately with any woman without honorable and suitable testimony, except his mother alone—not only with foreign women, but not even with sisters or relatives. Otherwise, once freed by the permission to have sisters or female relatives, he might become too familiar with them for the perpetration of crime.

### V

In fact, the depravity of human filth eventually grew so far that the sacred bonds of kinship were violated by hostile acts of fornication, and the rights of family and blood were polluted by sacrilegious defilement among God’s clerics.

This was why certain councils, like Paulinus here, entirely prohibited the companionship of even closely related women with those serving the Church and altar.

Thus the Council of Nantes, praised above, says in the same canon 3:

> Nor should he have those whom the canons permit—because, at the instigation of the devil, crimes are frequently committed even with them, or even with their attendants—namely, his mother, aunt, or sister.

The Council of Mainz likewise considered this matter in 813, canon 10:

> We decree that clerics must be altogether forbidden to have women in their homes. Although the sacred canons permit certain female persons to live together with clerics in one house, nevertheless—and this is greatly to be lamented—we have often heard that many crimes have been committed through this permission, to such an extent that certain priests, sleeping with their own sisters, fathered children by them. Therefore this holy synod has decreed that no priest may permit any woman to remain with him in his own house, so that every occasion for evil suspicion or wrongdoing may be completely removed.

### VI

In this matter the sagacity of our most holy patriarch Philip Neri was ingenious and therefore should not be passed over. A certain young man, acting on the advice of Father Angelo Velli, had come to him and, more freely than was proper—but not out of vice—had been playing with his sister without feeling any scruple about it.

The holy old man asked him what discipline he was studying. When he replied, “Logic,” Philip said:

> Beware, my son, lest the devil, being an accomplished logician, teach you a bad abstraction, so that in your games and jokes you eventually say “a woman” and not “a sister.”

This is related in his *Life*, taken from Father James Bacci, Book II, chapter 7, no. 12.

Human wickedness sometimes advances to such a degree. It is therefore no wonder that our Paulinus prohibited the clerics of his province from cohabitation and companionship with any woman whatsoever.

# NOTES ON CANON IV

### a. “Introduced women”

Women whose common residence with clerics is prohibited by the councils are often called *subintroductae mulieres*, “introduced women.”

The First Council of Nicaea, canon 3, to which Paulinus referred, decrees:

> No one at all among those in the clergy may have an introduced woman in his house.

At the First Roman Council under Pope Zacharias, canon 2:

> Priests or deacons must in no way dare to have introduced women with them.

Likewise, at another Roman Council in the time of Nicholas II, in 1059, canon 3:

> No one should hear Mass from a priest whom he knows certainly to have either a concubine or an introduced woman.

Likewise at Rouen in 1072, under Alexander II, canon 15:

> Archdeacons must not be permitted to have either a concubine or a mistress.

The Councils of Carthage I, canon 3; Ilerda, canon 15; Braga III, canon 5; and the law *He Who Is Probable*, title “Concerning Bishops and Clerics,” call these women *extraneae*, “outsiders.” See Ludovico Antonio Muratori’s discussion of the *Synisacti* and *Agapetae* among the *Greek Anecdotes*, p. 218.

# OBSERVATION ON CANON V

### I

The points Paulinus proposes here are clear and self-evident, and entirely consonant with what had been proposed at the assembly of Aachen in 789—which he himself attended—from the Council of Chalcedon and from the decrees of Pope Leo.

In chapter 22 it reads:

> Likewise, in that same council—namely, the Council of Chalcedon mentioned above—within the two chapters below, and also in the decrees of Pope Leo, it was decreed that neither monks, clerics, nor priests should engage in secular business.

Saint Pope Celestine V briefly explains what secular business is forbidden to clerics, in *Opusculum* VIII, part V, section 3, chapter 19:

> Secular businesses, such as buying and selling, leasing, renting, guardianship, administration, commerce, litigation, and the practice of all mechanical arts, including shoemaking, weaving, and similar occupations, are forbidden to all clerics and religious. Hence Jerome says: “Flee the cleric who engages in commerce as a kind of plague—one who changes from poor to rich and from obscure to glorious.”

# NOTES ON CANON V

### a. “We serve in the Lord’s army”

The metaphor of military service is frequently applied to the duties of the clergy. Peter of Blois, archdeacon of Bath, writes in letter 6:

> You complain that I waste my days uselessly, although I could have been fruitful for many in the scholars’ camp. Good master! These are God’s camps in which we live, and you should know that here there is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven.

Paul often mentions military service when speaking of the clerical office. Thus, in 2 Timothy 2:3:

> Work as a good soldier of Christ.

And:

> No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business.

Also in 1 Timothy 1:18:

> I commend this instruction to you, my son Timothy … so that you may serve as a good soldier in them.

And in 2 Corinthians 10:3–4:

> Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh, for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, etc.

Augustine likewise writes in letter 60, formerly numbered 76:

> If deserters from monasteries are chosen for the military service of the clergy …

In the Gallican churches, some members of the prebendary clergy bore the title “soldier.” A charter of King Philip of France, dated September 1307, teaches us, in Du Cange under “Ecclesiastical Soldiers,” that the Church of Lyon had ten such men. It reads:

> To these military offices we and our successors, the kings of the Franks, shall appoint clerics who are prudent men and distinguished in knowledge of letters.

And below:

> We wish these three soldiers to be our faithful and familiar clerics.

Do not confuse these men with the advocates of the churches. We know that the latter were sometimes genuinely soldiers, so that they might defend the rights of the churches not only by word and writing but also by arms against the power of invaders.

The Church of Aquileia once had its own advocate, as is clear from the charter produced by Ughellus under Patriarch Ulrich, and from the testament of Chacellinus, founder of the monastery of Saint Gall. In that document, concerning the advocacy of Aquileia, Henry, perhaps duke of Carinthia, is mentioned as having granted the Church of Aquileia an estate in Carinthia. The testament will be found in Appendix II, no. 12. We also provide an inscription relevant to this matter there, no. 16. See also the document of Patriarch Peregrine I, no. 14.

### b. “Fearless in the front line”

Vegetius, *On Military Matters*, Book III, chapter 14:

> An “array” is an army drawn up in formation … The rule of formation is that trained and veteran soldiers should be placed in the first rank; formerly they were called the *principes*.

From this the metaphor is derived by which those who, because of the dignity of their position, ought to go before others by their example are said to stand “in the front line.” Seneca, *On the Constancy of the Wise Person*, chapter 19:

> The more honorable someone is in birth, reputation, or property, the more courageously he should conduct himself, remembering that those of the highest rank stand in the front line.

## OBSERVATION ON CANON VI

### I

In this canon Paulinus continues to regulate the life of the clergy. First, he removes them from illicit matters and from things incompatible with the clerical state; then he shows how they ought to conduct themselves in matters that are lawful and appropriate to that state.

Here he seems to have summarized what is set out more fully in canon 452 of Book VII of the *Capitularies*. We have already noted above that the canons of that book were compiled from the works of Paulinus.

In that canon we read:

> By the law of the Fathers, clerics are admonished that, set apart from ordinary life, they abstain from the pleasures of the world; that they do not attend spectacles or pomps; that they avoid public banquets … that they do not walk with wandering eyes, an unrestrained tongue, or an immodest and haughty bearing, but display modesty and shamefastness of mind through simple clothing and gait. Let them also utterly abhor obscenity of speech, just as of conduct … Finally, let them devote themselves continually to exercise in doctrine, readings, psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.

For the great severity with which all these things were forbidden to clerics in the time of Charlemagne, which was also Paulinus’ time, see Thomassin, *On Ancient and Modern Ecclesiastical Discipline*, volume III, Book III, chapter 45. We shall indicate in the notes that follow that the specific matters prohibited here by Paulinus were excerpted from capitularies issued around his time.

## Notes on Canon VI

**a. “In hunting.”** In the capitulary of Carloman, in the year 742, chapter 2: “We forbid all servants of God to hunt or roam through the forests with dogs. Likewise, they are not to keep hawks or falcons.” Likewise, in the capitulary of Soissons under Pippin, in the year 744, chapter 3: “All clerics … are neither to keep dogs for hunting nor to carry hawks.” Likewise, in the first capitulary of Charlemagne, in the year 769, chapter 3: “We forbid all servants of God to hunt or roam through the forests with dogs, and to keep hawks or falcons.”

Although provision had thus been made against this clerical wandering in pursuit of game, it nevertheless required a new censure to cut it off, so that those who, when placed in positions of dignity, practiced it with greater scandal to their subjects might also be restrained. Accordingly, in the third capitulary of the year 789, at which Paulinus was present, chapter 15, we read that the following was decreed: “Let bishops, abbots, and abbesses have neither packs of dogs nor falcons nor hawks nor jesters.”

Women who held precedence over others had also been seized by this kind of enthusiasm, so that it was necessary to restrain them as well. *Cupla* is formed by syncope from *copula*. Concerning it, Ovid, *Tristia*, book V, poem 9, verse 508:

> And as the harsh leash holds back the dog,  
> as it vainly struggles after the tracks of a frightened hind.

And in the *Metamorphoses*, book VII, verse 767:

> The leash is removed from the dogs …

**b. “Or in secular songs, etc.”** In the capitulary of the year 802, chapter 23: “Let priests carefully ensure that the clerics whom they have with them live canonically, and that they do not indulge in empty games, secular banquets, songs, or luxurious behavior, but live chastely and soberly.” Likewise, in the fourth addition to the capitularies, chapter 66: “Scurrilous clerics and those who joke with obscene words are to be removed from office”; and in the following chapter, 67: “Clerics who sing during meals are to be restrained by the severity of the aforesaid sentence.”

**c. “From the books of Sacred Scripture, etc.”** Here Paulinus proves that divine praises should be drawn from Scripture; he does not, however, deny that other songs, even if not taken from Scripture, may also be sung. For he himself “frequently, and especially at private Masses, celebrated hymns composed either by himself or by others,” says Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 25.

Nevertheless, it appears that this practice was not approved by everyone at that time. For, almost as though offering an excuse for what had been done, he immediately adds: “I would indeed believe that a man of such great and extensive learning acted neither without authority nor without the weight of reason.” See what we say in the preface to Paulinus’s hymns, no. 1, and especially weigh the authority favorable to Paulinus cited there, no. 1, from canon 13 of the Fourth Council of Toledo.

Agobard, bishop of Lyon, however, in his little work *On Divine Psalmody*, and in another *On the Correction of the Antiphonary*, strives with all his strength to expel from the Church every hymn or song not drawn from the source of Scripture. In the first work, among other things, he says:

> In the temple of God and before the divine altar, let only the melody of divine utterances be celebrated.

He concludes the other work as follows:

> In honor of divine praise, let us sing—not human but divine and spiritual psalms, hymns, and songs, in accordance with the Apostle. For other things are sought in vain where these are known to be sufficient and more than sufficient.

Yet he wished to be excessively strict in this matter, contrary to what Scripture forbids in Ecclesiastes 7:17. As Brietius says under the year 831: “Agobard of Lyon, since he wished to admit nothing besides the words of Scripture, pursued the matter more scrupulously than accurately.”

## Observation on Canon VII

**I.** In this canon Paulinus restrains bishops who, in more serious cases, strike ministers of lower rank with a sentence of condemnation. Consistent with this is what is found in book VII of the *Capitularies*, perhaps written by Paulinus himself, chapter 102: “The canons of the African province, and likewise the decrees of Nicaea, have entrusted clerics of lower rank, and even bishops themselves, most explicitly to their metropolitans.”

Sometimes the deliberation of a provincial synod was also required. In the same work, chapter 109: “If any cases or disputes arise among laymen, or among clerics of either higher or lower rank, it has been decided that the dispute shall be settled according to the Council of Nicaea, after all the bishops of that province have been assembled.”

Indeed, even in lesser cases, where no loss of honor was involved—that is, deposition—the bishop was not permitted to hear and decide the case alone. *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 358: “It has been decided that one bishop shall not claim jurisdiction for himself.” And the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 23, decreed: “Let a bishop hear no one’s case without the presence of his clergy; otherwise the bishop’s sentence shall be invalid unless confirmed by the presence of the clergy.”

Anastasius, in the life of Pope Nicholas I, no. 596, in the Roman edition of 1718, lists among the reasons that moved the pontiff to order that the deacon Pepon, deposed by Bishop Pandulf, be restored to his office, first “because he had been judged without a fixed number of bishops.”

## Notes on Canon VII

**a. “Or an archimandrite.”** In Greek, Ἀρχιμανδρίτης (*archimandritēs*), approximately “prince of the *mandra*.” It is a title of abbots, just as *archimandritissa* is a title of abbesses. (*Capitularies*, book II, chapter 29: “a monastery of both monks and holy women, having an archimandrite or an archimandritess.”)

See our notes on chapter 2 of book I *Against Felix*, at the words “far from the *mandriles*.” Du Cange shows that the term was sometimes applied to bishops in his *Glossary*, especially from a charter of the year 990, in which Dagobert, archbishop of Bourges, styles himself “archimandrite of the first holy see of the Church of Bourges”; and from the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble, where Amblard of Lyon is called an archimandrite.

Macer, in the *Hierolexicon*, also attempts to prove that an archbishop was sometimes called by this name, from Novel 5 of Justinian, in these words: “Let the beloved bishops and archimandrites of God prohibit this.” Yet the passage of Justinian’s novella appears to concern abbots, not archbishops. First, if it referred to archbishops, it would place archimandrites before bishops. Second, it is speaking there of monks wandering without cause from one monastery to another. For it reads as follows:

> Such a life is indeed a wandering life, and in no way close to monastic discipline, nor to a steadfast and persevering spirit; rather, it bears the judgment of a vagrant, always seeking one thing after another. For this reason also, let the God-beloved bishops and those called archimandrites, preserving monastic propriety according to the sacred rules, prohibit it.

**b. “At the loss of honor,” and below, “concerning the danger to his honor.”** Here *honor* is to be understood as ecclesiastical rank or order. Thus Cyprian, letter 34, in Baluzius’s edition, speaking of the priestly order, says: “You should already know that we designated for them the honor of the presbyterate.” And in letter 65: “The deacon of whom you write must repent of his boldness and acknowledge the honor of the priest.” And below: “If he further exasperates and provokes you by his insults, you will exercise over him the authority of your honor.”
