In the Fourth Council of Arles, canon 1, we find the expression “the honor of the clergy.” Hence Charlemagne, in the charter dividing the Frankish kingdom, which is *Capitularies* I, from the year 806, calls ecclesiastical persons “honored men” in chapter 7: “Let every sinful man … flee either to holy places or to honored men.”

Therefore, loss or danger to one’s honor means deposition, or at least what we now call suspension from office or benefice, even if only threatened.

## 84. Observation on Canon VIII

**I.** Paulinus confronts clandestine marriages in this canon, together with the evils that necessarily arise from marriages contracted in this way. “The holy Church of God,” says the Council of Trent, session 24, *On Reform*, chapter 1, “has always detested and prohibited clandestine marriages for the most just reasons.”

For Paulinus, the reason for the prohibition is that, when marriages are celebrated secretly, the degrees of consanguinity or affinity that may exist between the betrothed cannot easily be detected. Paulinus pursues this matter at length.

It should be noted, however, that he does not call these marriages invalid because they are clandestine, but merely illicit, because they pave the way for marriages that were genuinely invalid even in his time—namely, those contracted between relatives by blood or affinity. Marriages were regarded as invalid merely because they were clandestine only after the Council of Trent.

On this matter, see Lancellotus, *Institutes of Canon Law*, title 13, *On Clandestine Betrothals*, and the Gloss there; especially John Solerius, who, speaking of the French, writes:

> Among us there are three forms of clandestine marriage. The first occurs when children under paternal authority contract marriage without the consent of their parents, or minors without the consent of their guardians or curators when their parents are absent. The second occurs when the proclamations are omitted. The third occurs when the marriage is not celebrated before the parish priest and witnesses.

**II.** This recent author, Solerius, taught these things on the basis of the customs of earlier times. For the capitularies of the Frankish kings assume that the obedience owed to parents extended even to the contracting of marriage, and that for its validity their judgment and authority, at least manifested by their presence, were necessarily required.

Thus, in the treatise or book of the Salic law, written at Charlemagne’s command in the year 798, title 70: “If anyone seeks another man’s daughter in marriage, in the presence of his own parents and the girl’s parents,” etc. See there that marriages are treated as contracted only with the parents acting as arbiters.

Moreover, letter 2, circulated under the name of Evaristus in the *Decretals*, although falsely attributed, bears witness to the same point that we are now making. It reads:

> We have likewise received and handed down the rule that a wife should be lawfully joined to her husband. For a marriage is not legitimate—as we have received from the Fathers and found handed down by the holy apostles and their successors—unless the woman is sought from those who appear to exercise authority over her and by whom she is guarded, and unless she is betrothed by her parents or nearest relatives.

The collector Pseudo-Isidore compiled this in the ninth century, that is, shortly after the time of Paulinus. Therefore, even if this letter is not by Evaristus, it nevertheless proves that the custom was already accepted and put into practice in Paulinus’s time.

**III.** As for the proclamations that were to precede marriage, in Paulinus’s time the examination of the elders of the locality served the same purpose. He himself said:

> After the betrothal agreements have been made, with some interval of delay, the neighbors or elders of that place should also be diligently consulted—those who might know the genealogical line of both parties, namely the bridegroom and the bride.

Pope Nicholas I, who died in the year 867, gave a somewhat similar answer to the Bulgarians’ inquiries, chapter 3:

> Our people, both men and women, after the betrothal—which consists in the promised pledge of future marriage and which is celebrated with the consent of those who contract it and of those under whose authority they are—and after the bridegroom has betrothed the bride by giving her a ring marked with the pledge of faith, and has handed over to her, before invited guests from both sides, the dowry agreed upon by both parties, together with a written agreement containing this arrangement, are brought together for the marriage covenant, either immediately or at a suitable time, so that no such act is rashly undertaken before the time defined by law.

Hence Lancellotus, *Institutes of Canon Law*, title 14, *On Clandestine Betrothals*, says:

> When marriages are to be contracted, they should be publicly announced by the priest at a suitable appointed time, within which anyone who wishes and is able may bring forward a legitimate impediment; and the priest himself should investigate whether any impediment stands in the way of the future marriage.

This is what it means for marriages to be celebrated publicly: they are so proclaimed that they may come to anyone’s knowledge, and thus any impediments that exist may be brought to light.

This was established even before Paulinus’s time. For in Pippin’s capitulary of the year 755, chapter 15, it is decreed “that all laymen, both noble and ignoble, should celebrate public weddings.”

**IV.** The principal reason why clandestine marriages have always been disapproved is the absence of the priest, who, by the authority of the Church, ratifies what the betrothed have contracted with each other.

Whether the priest’s presence and blessing constitute the sacrament, or whether they merely confer the weight of the Church’s authority upon a contract celebrated through the mutual consent of the betrothed and the express mutual giving of their bodies—on this point ancient and modern theologians contend with one another.

Although the more common opinion is that the presence of the parish priest is not necessary for the making of the sacrament, but that the sacrament is made through the mutual consent of the betrothed, we have nevertheless always favored the opinion of those who say that the Lord entrusted the making of all the sacraments to priests, not laymen, with baptism alone excepted because of its necessity.

But let them look to that themselves; our concern is with our subject. Paulinus certainly required the intervention of a priest. For he says:

> It must in no way take place without the knowledge of the priest.

In the letter cited above, once marked with the name of Evaristus, we read:

> At the proper time, let her be blessed by the priest in priestly fashion, as is customary, with prayers and offerings … and let her be solemnly received, so that good offspring may be born.

**V.** What is said here, “so that good offspring may be born,” is explained at greater length in book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 179. It is worth transcribing at length, because it fits this canon very well:

> It has been decreed that public weddings are to be celebrated by those who wish to marry, because often in marriages contracted secretly grave sins increase and accumulate, both among the spouses of others and among relatives, or in adulterous unions—and, what is worse to say, among blood relatives. From such unions the offspring are commonly born blind, lame, hunchbacked, or squinting, or otherwise marked with disgraceful blemishes. Everyone must take care that this does not happen henceforth.
>
> First, however, the priest in whose parish the wedding is to take place must be approached, and the marriage must be celebrated in the church before the people. There the priest, together with the people, must inquire whether she is a relative or not, or another man’s wife, or betrothed, or an adulteress. And if he finds everything lawful and honorable, then, with the counsel and blessing of the priest and after consultation with other good men, he must betroth her and lawfully provide her dowry.

**VI.** As you see, the Fathers and councils were concerned through these enactments with the reverence and dignity owed to blood relationship. For it has always seemed disgraceful for those already united by blood to mingle their seed.

Therefore the Lord forbids this through Moses in Leviticus 18:6:

> No man shall approach his near blood relative to uncover her nakedness.

At one time the prohibition extended even to the seventh degree, as is clear from *Decretum* 35, questions 1 and 2, chapter *Nullum* and chapter *Progeniem*, concerning consanguinity; and in book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 130, we read:

> Christians are not to enter into marriage on account of their blood relationship up to the seventh degree.

But in canon 32 of the Council of Worms, in the year 868, the marriages of blood relatives are prohibited without a specified limit, until the passage of time has erased the memory of kinship:

> In the union of the faithful, we do not define the number of generations, but establish this: no Christian may take a wife from his own consanguinity or kinship so long as the generation is remembered, known, or retained in memory.

Finally, for the gravest reasons, the Church judged it expedient to restrict the prohibition to the fourth generation only, as Innocent III decreed at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, chapter 50:

> It should not be judged reprehensible, said the pontiff, if human statutes are sometimes changed according to the variation of times, especially when urgent necessity or evident usefulness demands it.

And below:

> Henceforth the prohibition of conjugal union shall not extend beyond the fourth degree of consanguinity and affinity, since in the more distant degrees such a prohibition can no longer be generally observed without serious loss.

And further below:

> Since, therefore, the prohibition of conjugal union has now been restricted to the fourth degree, we wish it to remain so perpetually, notwithstanding the constitutions formerly issued on this matter either by others or by us.

**VII.** Bishops granted dispensations within these prohibited degrees only for the gravest reasons. Indeed, as Hildebert, first bishop of Le Mans and later bishop of Tours, who flourished around the year 1125, writes of himself in letter 34, when Gautier of Mayenne requested a dispensation so that he might give his daughter in marriage to the count of Mortain in order to extinguish the war that had broken out between them, Hildebert judged that the request should be denied:

> To one seeking consent, I announced refusal, allowing no consideration of a dispensation to permit relatives or persons related by affinity to contract the prohibited bonds of marriage.

Pope Paschal II, as may be gathered from Ivo’s letter 69, cited by Baronius under the year 1104, no. 3, granted a dispensation to Philip I, king of France, who was entangled in love with Bertrada:

> We assembled at Bléneau … The king and his consort also came together, and, according to your command, after touching the most holy Gospels, they were prepared to swear off absolutely every practice of carnal union … until your dispensation … The manner of the dispensation, however, has displeased none of the wise … And since we say this by way of suggestion, not instruction, the substance of our suggestion is that you accommodate yourself to human weakness as far as you can without endangering his salvation, etc.

Ivo wrote this to Paschal, at the same time indicating how greatly the Church recoiled from dispensations.

**VIII.** What Thomasinus says about this dispensation of Paschal with Philip is difficult to accept. In *Ancient and Modern Ecclesiastical Discipline*, book II, book III, chapter 29, no. 10, he writes:

> The first dispensation of this kind is thought to have been granted by Paschal II to Philip I, king of France, who had married Bertrada.

And shortly afterward:

> After Pope Paschal opened the door to dispensing in the degrees of kinship, dispensations of this kind multiplied afterward in a remarkable way.

Paschal was not the first dispenser, nor did he himself open the door to dispensations. When Gregory the Great was asked by Augustine, bishop of the English, in question 6 of book XII of the *Register*, at the end, “Up to what generation should the faithful be joined in marriage with their relatives?” he replied:

> The faithful may lawfully be joined in the third or fourth generation. But from what we call the second generation they must abstain entirely.

Do you not see Gregory already dispensing among the English for the third and fourth generations? On this matter, when interpreted by Felix of Sicily, he wrote back—as though wishing to justify himself—in the same book XII, letter 31:

> As for what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English people, your foster son, as you recall, concerning unions between blood relatives, know that I wrote specifically to him and to the English people, who had recently come to the faith, lest they withdraw in fear from the good work they had begun because of excessively harsh measures; I did not write this generally for others. Hence the entire Roman city has been my witness. Nor did I commit these things to writing for them with the intention that, once they had become firmly rooted and established in the faith, if they were found within their own consanguinity they should not be separated, or that they should be joined within the line of affinity, that is, up to the seventh generation.

What he adduces as a justification was an argument for a legitimate dispensation.

The other Gregory likewise judged that a dispensation should be granted to the Germans in the fifth degree. In letter 13 to Bishop Boniface he answered in the first chapter:

> First, therefore, it was asked in which generation the marriage of relatives might be contracted. We say that, so long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity, they ought indeed not to enter into this union. But because moderation, especially among such a barbarous people, is more pleasing than strict severity, it must be permitted that they be joined after the fourth generation.

Paschal II therefore was not the first to grant a dispensation, nor did he open the door to dispensations in marriage, as Thomasinus claims; the first and second Gregory preceded him by their example.

**IX.** Although the Church sometimes showed herself more lenient and indulgent in granting dispensations within these degrees of kinship, for the public good of peace or for other grave reasons, nevertheless, to make it known to everyone that she strongly rejected such concessions, and to remove entirely, as far as possible, any scandal that might have arisen in the minds of the weak, she was accustomed not to confer the favor without imposing some form of penance.

A notable example is the marriage of Otto, king of Germany, which Otto of Saint Blaise reports in his *Chronicle*, chapter 51. Innocent III agreed that, in order to reconcile the minds of subjects who were excessively divided by partisan loyalties—some favoring Philip, others Otto—Otto might marry the daughter of Philip, who had been killed the previous year, although she was related to him.

“For Otto’s father had been the uncle of Frederick the emperor, Philip’s father,” says the aforementioned chronicler. Nevertheless, he imposed penance. The same author continues:

> When the king had devoutly consented to this, the abbot of Morimond, of the Cistercian order, arose, assuming the person of all the other abbots and cloistered members of both orders, namely the Cluniac and the Cistercian. By apostolic authority he imposed upon the monastic order the penance for this offense, to be committed by dispensation in this marriage contrary to the custom of the Church. Through this he imposed penance upon the king, requiring him to be, as far as possible, a defender of monasteries and churches, to preside over widows and orphans with just judgment, to build a monastery of the Cistercian order on his own land, and thereafter to assist the Church of Jerusalem in person. The king obeyed all these commands, etc.

For it was an ancient practice of the Church to impose canonical penance even for acts that lacked genuine guilt but nevertheless presented to human eyes the appearance of guilt.

Thus, in *Decretum* 50, chapter *Clerico*, Urban II requires a cleric to remain perpetually in penance who had killed a boy by accidentally throwing a stone, without fault.

Likewise, in *De Consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter *Si per ebrietatem*, a person who vomited the Eucharist because of nausea rather than drunkenness is ordered to do penance for seven days.

In the same way Paulinus makes even those who are found to have contracted marriage in good faith and without fault liable to penance if consanguinity is subsequently discovered, in addition to separation:

> Let them indeed be separated from one another and do penance.

It should also be noted here that the burden of performing canonical penance was imposed upon monks, who could easily perform what the king himself might perform only with difficulty or not at all, and thus redeem the king by substituting other works more appropriate to royal dignity.

**X.** When this practice, which they called the redemption of penances, began to be introduced, stricter Fathers disapproved of it, as may be seen from canon 27 of the Second Council of Clofesho in England, in the year 747. There the penance of a certain rich man is condemned because he claimed that his offense had been sufficiently expiated “through the psalmody, fasting, and almsgiving of others.”

On the redemption of penances, see Morinus, *On Penance*, book X, chapter 17, and Du Cange, *Glossary*, under “Redemptions of Penances.” There you will find that a penance redeemed by money distributed to the poor was called *deargentata*, according to Guigo, *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, no. 20.

## Notes on Canon VIII

**a. “In the ancient canon.”** Either the nineteenth among those attributed to the Apostles, or the third chapter of the decrees of the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, especially chapter 5 at the end, where the penalty of excommunication is imposed upon those who contracted marriage contrary to the decrees cited in the preceding chapters:

> Whoever contradicts in this way the law enacted in this book, the assembly of the holy disciples and this holy synod strike him with anathema and wound him with the sword of a curse.

Perhaps the Council of Agde in the year 506 was referring to this when, after establishing penalties for those who contracted such marriages in canon 61, it added:

> We prohibit this in the present time in such a way that we do not dissolve what has hitherto been established.

**b. “Let the children of such a marriage be considered legitimate.”** Among jurists this marriage is called putative, namely when “blood relatives, unaware of the impediment, contract marriage within a prohibited degree. For once the impediment is discovered, the marriage has already been dissolved,” according to Zasius, *Institutes, On Actions*, cited by John Calvin, *Legal Lexicon*.

Concerning offspring born from such a marriage, Saint Pope Celestine V says in his *Opusculum* VIII, chapter 24, the same as Paulinus here. See also chapter *Cum inter virum* in Gregory’s *Decretals*, book IV, title 17, *Who Are Legitimate Sons*:

> We decree, says Alexander III, that the children whom they had before the divorce, and those who were conceived before the sentence was pronounced, shall be considered no less legitimate, and shall succeed to their father’s property by hereditary right.

**c. “Under the lament of penance.”** Chapter *Hi ergo*, 27, question 1, canon 13: “And during their lifetime let them afflict themselves severely in the lamentations of penance.” Likewise Pope Siricius, letter 1 to Himerius, chapter 6: “Lamenting such a great crime with continual mourning.”

**d. “Let the children who … be regarded as wicked.”** That is, illegitimate. Celestine, in the passage cited:

> But after both have learned this—that is, that they are related by blood or affinity—the children who are born are illegitimate.

The book of the Salic law, title 14, *On Free Persons*, chapter 16, says of such spouses:

> Even if they have had children, they shall not be regarded as legitimate heirs, but shall be marked with infamy.

Augustine, too, in question 6 on Leviticus, concerning Leviticus 20:20, “Whoever lies with his kinswoman has uncovered the nakedness of his kin; they shall die without children,” writes:

> But what does “they shall die without children” mean, since children born from such unions existed in the past and are still born today? Is it to be understood that God’s law established that whoever is born from them is not to be counted as a child—that is, that he should succeed to nothing belonging to his parents by any legal right?

## Observation on Canon IX

**I.** This canon is reproduced almost word for word among the Lombard Laws of Charlemagne, no. 145, by the Palatine collectors, *Writers of Italian Affairs*, volume I, part II, page 3, perhaps at Paulinus’s suggestion. Here he disapproves of several things because several disadvantages follow from such marriages.

First, he disapproves of marriages before puberty; second, even if contracted after puberty, he disapproves of those contracted between persons of unequal age. In addition to suitability of age, he requires freedom of consent. We shall treat each point in a separate observation.

**II.** Paulinus discusses at length the disadvantages produced by marriages contracted before puberty, and the temptations and dangers to which such marriages are exposed through the absence of continence. To a prudent man, acquainted with human affairs, it can be clear that in issuing this canon Paulinus did not act more scrupulously than the precarious nature of the matter required.

The reasonable fear is supported by what Innocent III recounts in his letter to the archbishop of Magdeburg, in Gregory’s *Decretals*, book IV, title 13, chapter *Veniens* 2:

> E., a layman, came to the apostolic see and explained to us that, when he was still a child, he had sworn that he would marry a certain girl as soon as she reached the lawful age. The girl’s father, after the guarantee of such an arrangement had been secured by obligations binding both sides, received him into his own house and raised him together with the girl. Then, through prolonged association, he joined himself carnally to the girl’s sister. Finally, overcome by the insistence of his friends, he took as his wife the girl whom he had sworn to marry. After the wedding had been celebrated, whenever opportunity presented itself, he had relations with both of them.

For, as Lucretius says in book IV, verse 1276:

> Habit cultivates love.

Since the dangers are so great in marriages involving the immature, such unions are disapproved not only here by our Paulinus and by ecclesiastical canons, as may be seen in Gregory’s *Decretals*, *On Betrothing the Immature*, book IV, title 2, especially chapters *Puberes*, *Attestationes*, and *Ex litteris*, but also by civil laws, which may be consulted in Tiraquellus, *On the Laws of Marriage*, law VI, gloss 1, part VI.

Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 11, says:

> Even the pagans observe the proper time, assigning the rights of nature to the appropriate ages. For they send females to their occupations from the age of twelve, but males from two years later, determining puberty by age, not by betrothals or marriages.

Justinian also established this as the age at which puberty is to be judged, in the *Code*, *When a Guardian Ceases to Be One*, final law:

> Just as females are judged fully pubescent after completing twelve years, so males are to be considered pubescent after passing fourteen years, without the indecent examination of the body.

**III.** Difference of age, however, is not free from disadvantage even between persons who have reached puberty, especially if a young man is joined to an old woman, or a young girl to a man of advanced age.

Leonidas, in the Greek *Anthology*, book II, chapter 9, epigram 4, cleverly sharpens his style against Philenus, who as a young man had married an old woman and later, as an old man, had married a young girl:

> Philenus married an old woman when he was young; when old, a girl of twelve; Cyprian Venus was never timely.  
>
> For then he remained childless, sowing in unfruitful ground; now, having married a bride “for others” [as printed], he is deprived of both.

The author's Latin metrical rendering may be translated as follows:

> Young, Philenus married an old woman; old, he married a twelve-year-old girl:  
> Propitious Venus was nowhere to be found.  
> Then he lacked children, because he had married a barren woman; now,  
> When he takes a bride for others, he lacks them both.

Theognis also pursues the same point in a witty allegory in another epigram, which runs as follows:

> A young woman is not of one mind with an old man;  
>
> For, like a ship, she does not obey the rudder.  
>
> Having broken her moorings, she has no anchor and often, by night, reaches another harbor.

At Stobaeus, series 71, *That the Age of Both Parties Should Be Considered in Marriage*, you will find an interpretation. The author's Latin metrical rendering may be translated as follows:

> A young bride does not suit you, old man;  
> For you will scarcely steer her by the helm, like a ship.  
> When the ropes are broken, an anchor will not hold her fast,  
> And often by night she seeks another shore.

**IV.** After Paulinus had condemned marriages involving the immature and those of unequal age, he wishes the betrothed to be of similar age and mutually consenting.

The first point must be understood not to mean that both parties must be exactly the same in age and years, but that each must be of an age proper and suitable for bearing the burden of marriage, with due regard to the man and the girl, so that their ages may be judged proportionate.

For the age suitable to marriage for each party, see the opinions of the philosophers in the Tiraquellus cited above, from no. 39 to the end. At no. 46 he says very prudently:

> We do not wish equality of age in spouses to be understood so that they must be in every respect the same age, but so that they cease to be capable of begetting at approximately the same age and time. Aristotle thinks that this happens only if the male precedes the female by twenty years, more or less.

**V.** Paulinus added that those entering marriage must be mutually consenting. It not rarely happens that parents, wishing to increase their family or wealth through their children’s marriages, or to make the family illustrious by nobility, compel their children into marriages toward which they feel little inclination. Hence many evils and even scandals often arise.

There must therefore be free and spontaneous consent on both sides, which is the form and constitutive basis of the contract. This freedom is obstructed not only by force or grave fear, which completely destroys consent, but also by deceit and fraud, by which inexperienced and easily deceived youth is more than once ensnared.

Marriage is a contract, and at times it was even instituted under a form resembling sale and purchase. Sale and purchase, indeed every contract, is completed by the mutual consent of the parties. Hence of the marriage contract it is said in *Decretum* 30, question 2, canon 2:

> Where there is not the consent of both parties, there is no marriage.

But consent cannot exist where violence or fraud has intervened. Concerning violence or coercion, there are several canons in Gregory’s *Decretals*, book IV, title 1, *On Betrothals and Marriage*, especially chapter 14, where we read:

> Since consent has no place where fear or coercion intervenes, wherever the consent of each party is required, every occasion for coercion must be removed. Marriage, however, is contracted by consent alone.

## Notes on Canon IX

**a. “Before the age.”** This is a formula not uncommon among legislators. In the Lombard Laws, book VI, of Liutprand, law 76, in *Writers of Italian Affairs*, volume I, part II, page 77:

> If, after the death of his father or grandfather, a boy remains below the age, and any woman presumes to join herself to him before that boy completes fourteen years … the union itself shall be invalid.

There the Estense manuscript has “below the age,” which is better. It means nothing other than “below the age of puberty.” Those who had completed the years of puberty are said to have been “within the age.”

The Theodosian Code, book III, title *On Betrothals*:

> If property has been given at the time of the wedding to future spouses who are below the age …

Tertullian, in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 12, calls this “the authority of age.”

### Note on Canon IX

**b. Nor be exempt from public judgments.** “Public judgment” was set against ecclesiastical judgment. It meant the same as the sentence of lay magistrates. *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 16: “That all should administer justice, both public and ecclesiastical.” Book VI, chapter 107: “That bishops should admonish public judges.” Book VII, chapter 153: “That no one should dare accuse a bishop before public judges.” Bignonius, in his notes on book I, chapter 3, of the *Formulas of Marculf*, says:

> “For some time I thought that ‘public’ was used in distinction from ‘private,’ so that those were public who belonged to the king and administered royal justice, whereas private judges were those who pronounced law in the place of private lords. Although this interpretation did not seem irrelevant, I nevertheless changed my opinion when another, and—unless I am mistaken—more accurate interpretation occurred to me. For in the capitularies of Charlemagne, a public judge is opposed to an ecclesiastical judge.”

### Observation on Canon X

**I.** No Catholic has called the teaching of this canon into question. It is evangelical and has been sufficiently, indeed abundantly, confirmed by the testimonies of the holy Fathers, as may be seen in Gratian, *Decretum*, cause 32, question 7, especially in Augustine and Jerome. For all purposes, let the first canon suffice, which is Augustine’s, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 7:

> “When divorce has intervened, that marital bond is not abolished, so that they remain spouses even when separated; and they commit adultery with those to whom they are joined after their repudiation.”

Tertullian likewise asserted this in book *On Monogamy*, chapter 9, saying:

> “For us, even if we repudiate our wives, it is not even permitted to marry.”

**II.** The capitularies of the Frankish kings are entirely consonant with the ecclesiastical canons. Thus, in the synod of King Pippin at Soissons in 744, chapter 9:

> “Likewise we decree that … while the husband is alive, no one may take his wife, nor may a woman, while her husband is alive, take another man.”

And book VI, chapter 87:

> “If anyone has expelled his own wife, lawfully joined to him in marriage, then, if he rightly wishes to be a Christian, he shall not join himself to anyone else, but shall either remain as he is or be reconciled to his own wife.”

Moreover, book VII, chapter 73:

> “Those who, after a repudiation had intervened, joined themselves to another marriage are plainly adulterers on both sides. Those who, while their wife was alive, hastened to another union, even though the marriage might appear to have been dissolved, cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers; indeed, the persons to whom they are joined are also shown to be adulterers.”

See also the same book, chapter 382.

### Notes on Canon X

**a. She must undergo the torment of penance.** What sort of penance was imposed on such a woman in Paulinus’s time, although Paulinus does not say here, may nevertheless be inferred from the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 382:

> “Let her do penance for seven years, three on bread and water; during the remaining four, it shall be at the priest’s discretion how he judges her capable of bearing it, and abstinence from food shall accordingly be imposed upon her.”

Jerome offers a celebrated example of this penance in his letter 30 to Oceanus, praising Fabiola, who, after leaving her first husband—an admittedly vicious and wicked man—married another with considerable imprudence:

> “Fabiola, because she had persuaded herself and believed that she had lawfully dismissed her husband, and did not know the force of the Gospel, in which all justification for marrying is taken away from women while their husbands are alive, avoided many wounds of the devil but, through carelessness, received one wound. But why do I linger over things abolished and ancient, seeking to excuse a fault whose penance she herself confessed? Who would believe that, after the death of her second husband, having come to her senses, she would publicly confess her error and, with the whole city of Rome looking on, stand before Easter in the basilica once belonging to the Lateran, in the order of penitents, while the bishop, priests, and all the people wept with her; that she would appear with disheveled hair, a pallid face, unwashed hands, and a filthy neck? … She disclosed her wound to everyone, and weeping Rome saw the scar upon her discolored body. Her sides were ungirded, her head uncovered, her mouth closed. She did not enter the church of the Lord, but sat outside the camp, separated with Mary the sister of Moses, so that the priest who had expelled her might himself call her back,” and so forth.

**b. Not even after the other’s death.** A person may not, nor is it legally possible, while the spouse is alive, to join another marriage, even when the separation has occurred on account of fornication. But whoever gave the cause for the separation was compelled, as punishment for violating the marriage bed and marital fidelity, to abstain thereafter from every marriage even after the other spouse’s death. This is what Paulinus indicates by the words “not even after death.”

In the penitential books of the ancients, one may find that the power to enter marriage was removed on account of various crimes; see Morinus, *On Penance*, book V, chapter 21 and following. For confirmation of this matter, it is worth transcribing one or two canons from the age of Paulinus.

At the Council of Compiègne in 757, canon 8:

> “If a man has a legitimate wife and his brother has committed adultery with her, that brother and that woman who committed the adultery shall, as long as they live, never have a marriage.”

In book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 381:

> “If two brothers have fornicated with one woman, each unaware of the other’s fornication, as soon as the adultery becomes known, the one who has her as his wife shall dismiss her. After doing penance, he may, if the wife has died, be joined to another; while she is alive, he may not. But she can never be taken in marriage by another, and, subjected to perpetual penance, she shall receive the grace of communion until the end of her life.”

**c. An ambiguous statement is inserted.** In former times some people, including Catholics, doubted whether the marriage bond was dissolved on account of one spouse’s adultery, as is clear from Gratian, cause 32, question 7, chapter 17; likewise from Photius’s ninth canon, title XIII, chapter 4, *On Those Who Divorce*, and from the scholion cited by Balsamon.

I pass over the laws of the Christian emperors that supported this opinion, as may be seen in the *Theodosian Code*, under *On Repudiations*. The Third Council of Aachen, convened in 862, permitted Lothair, king of the Franks, after rejecting his lawful wife Theutberga on account of fornication, to take Waldrada as his wife. The bishops of that assembly tried to prove, by many arguments and authorities, that their judgment had been lawfully issued; but Pope Nicholas later excommunicated all of them.

The Greeks still maintain that marriage is dissolved even with respect to the bond itself. On this matter Saint Basil, in letter 2 to Amphilochius, chapter 21, says:

> “Τούτων δὲ ὁ λόγος οὐ ῥάδιος, ἡ δὲ συνήθεια οὔτω κεκράτηκε”

that is:

> “The account of these matters is by no means easy, but custom has prevailed in this way.”

Yet Eugene IV and the whole Western Church openly disapprove this custom—or rather abuse—in the Council of Florence. See the Venetian edition of Labbe’s *Collection*, volume XVIII, page 535 and following.

Nevertheless, the most eminent Fathers of the Church—Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, and others—always held the contrary view (see Gratian at the place cited above), and so did the Church itself. Most recently, the Council of Trent removed every occasion for doubt in session XXIV, canon 7, *On the Sacrament of Marriage*, where it defined as follows:

> “If anyone says that the Church is in error when she has taught—and therefore it must be said that this has always been the Church’s teaching—and teaches, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic doctrine, that the marriage bond cannot be dissolved on account of the adultery of one spouse; that neither spouse, nor even the innocent spouse who did not give cause for the adultery, can contract another marriage while the other spouse is alive; that the man who dismisses an adulterous wife and marries another commits adultery, and likewise the woman who dismisses an adulterous husband and marries another—let him be anathema.”

### Observation on Canon XI

**I.** This canon concerns two classes of women who profess continence. The first consists of those who, after receiving from the bishop the consecrated veil and making solemn vows in his hands, were to spend their lives in an asceterium or monastery. The second consists of those who, without any solemnity of vows, professed chastity in their own homes, adopting only a dark garment as a sign of continence.

The institution of the latter is older than that of the former. For just as Antony the Egyptian is commonly believed to have established monasteries for men, so his sister is believed to have established those for women, which did not flourish until around the middle of the fourth century. Thomasinus, *On the Old and New Discipline of the Church*, part I, book III, chapter 44, believes that there is no room for doubt on this point, on the basis of Athanasius’s own words.

But let Athanasius’s words in the *Life of Antony* be considered:

> “Ἔχαιρεν οὐν καὶ αὐτὸς, βλέπων τήν τε . . . ἀδελφὴν γηράσασαν ἐν παρθενίᾳ, καθηγμένην τε καὶ αὐτὴν ἄλλων παρθένων.”

Thomasinus translates them:

> “Antony, seeing also his sister, now an aged virgin and teacher of other girls, rejoiced with extraordinary exultation.”

It seems to us that they can be translated more briefly and more literally:

> “He too therefore rejoiced, seeing his sister … having grown old in virginity and having become the teacher—or, if you prefer, the instructress—of other virgins.”

From these words nothing can be inferred except that Saint Antony’s sister was placed over the others for the education or instruction of girls; not that she was the teacher and founder of the monastic life for women. For, as is clear from the same author of the *Life of Antony*, when Antony was eighteen or twenty years old and first renounced the world, he considered what he should do with his very young sister and entrusted her to a monastery of virgins to be nourished and educated. The text says:

> “Τὴν δ` ἀδελφὴν παραδεδόμενος γνωρίμοις καὶ πιστοῖς παρθένοις, δούς τε αὐτὴν εἰς παρθενῶνα ἀνατρέφεσται”

that is:

> “Entrusting his sister to known and faithful virgins, he gave her to a monastery to be brought up.”

Therefore the monastery that received Antony’s sister cannot have been established and founded by her.

**II.** This nevertheless proves that an ancient custom existed in the Church of God, instituted almost from its beginnings, of professing virginity either in a monastery or outside one. This is clear from Acts of the Apostles, chapter 21, verse 9, where Philip the deacon’s daughters are mentioned:

> “He had four virgin daughters who prophesied.”

The same must be said of widows who professed continence, on the basis of more than one passage of the Apostle, such as 1 Timothy 5:

> “Honor widows who are truly widows,”

and below, verse 9:

> “Let a widow be enrolled who is not less than sixty years old.”

Thus they came to acquire a particular rank in the ecclesiastical hierarchy, as may be gathered from Saint Ignatius the Martyr’s letter 7 to the Tarsians:

> “Hold in honor those who live in virginity as the priests of Christ; and widows who remain in chastity as the altar of God.”

And in letter 10 to the Smyrnaeans:

> “I greet … those who live in perpetual virginity, and the widows.”

Tertullian likewise includes virgins and widows when listing, in a certain gradation, the various states of the Church, in book *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 3:

> “What then if a bishop, a deacon, a widow, a virgin, a teacher, or even a martyr should fall away from the rule? Will heresies therefore seem to possess the truth?”

These women lived at home, since asceteria had not yet been introduced.

**III.** At times the Church supported these women—whether virgins or widows—with its alms. There is especially ancient testimony concerning widows in Acts of the Apostles 6:1, when the Greeks murmured against the Hebrews because their widows were being neglected in the daily ministry. This gave the apostles the occasion to entrust their care to seven deacons.

The Church kept a register of them, whether virgins or widows, so that it might provide assistance to all accurately and at the proper time. The Church under Chrysostom’s care supported an enormous number. He wrote in homily 67 on Matthew:

> “Consider with yourself how many widows and how many virgins the Church assists every day. Their number, already entered in the register, has reached three thousand.”

Sozomen records that on one occasion this support was provided from the public treasury by a law of Constantine the Great, book V, chapter 5. Julian not only repealed that law but also

> “ordered that those virgins and widows who, because of poverty, had been enrolled among the clergy should be required to repay what they had previously received from the public treasury.”

**IV.** Since such widows saw that it was to their advantage to display public signs of widowhood, because they would then receive more generous alms, it sometimes happened that immediately after their husband’s death they assumed the status of widows, but later abandoned it after changing their minds.

Accordingly, a law of the Lombards issued through Liutprand (*Lombard Laws*, book II, title VI, law 1) provided that a wife should not impose the widow’s veil upon herself before a year had elapsed after her husband’s funeral. But because more fervent women considered this delay too burdensome, they asked Charlemagne and obtained permission that those driven by a more ardent spirit to assume the veil of widowly continence might freely and without penalty embrace the widowed state:

> “Concerning women whom the Lombard law forbids, after their husbands’ death, to change into the religious dress or receive the veil before the expiration of a year: they asked for our permission that, as soon as divine mercy should inspire them, they might receive it without harm. We, however, considering that in the past many women, because of this delay, had been carried off and transferred to another party within that same period, have accepted their petition as just and grant that it be done accordingly.”

Nevertheless, the bishops thought that a limit should be imposed in this matter, so that women would not make their vows within thirty days, while the heat of grief was still raging, creating confusion and overturning sound judgment; nor should they receive the veil without the bishop’s authorization.

The Aachen capitulary of 816, under Louis the Pious, chapter 21:

> “Concerning women who lose their husbands, it is our judgment that they should not, as hitherto, veil themselves indiscriminately, but should wait thirty days after their husband’s death. After the thirtieth day, they should choose what they ought to choose on the advice of their bishop; or, if the bishop is absent, on the advice of their other religious priests and of their relatives and friends.”

**V.** Yet because poverty repeatedly opened a way into this devotion—for the sake of relieving poverty, widows assumed the veil so that they might be admitted to the service of the church, where they could obtain a supply of income or alms—and because ecclesiastical administration consequently suffered no slight inconveniences, the Sixth Council of Paris wisely addressed such abuses in the following canon:

> “We have discovered that certain women, especially those who are very poor in worldly goods, impose a veil upon themselves without the consent of the priests, for the purpose of becoming, under the pretext of this veil, watchwomen and administrators of churches. Each bishop shall take care that this rash veiling does not occur in his parish. Since we have learned that in many places such veiled women have become a snare to priests, we prohibit any priest from presuming to admit such persons into the basilicas entrusted to him for this kind of service.”

**VI.** If virgins, and those closely associated with them—that is, widows (for Blessed Bruno, bishop of Würzburg, interprets Psalm 44:16 in this way: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you”)—had abandoned their purpose of virgin or widowly continence, whether by attempting marriage or by corrupting themselves secretly, as Paulinus says, they paid the penalty of strict discipline, as is clear from the canon under discussion.

Entirely consonant with it is what is read in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 338:

> “Concerning widows and girls who, in their own homes, whether by their parents’ decision or by their own, have changed their clothing into the religious habit, and afterward have believed that they should join themselves in marriage contrary to the institutions of the Fathers or the commands of the canons: let both parties be suspended from communion until they correct what they have unlawfully done. If they neglect to correct it, let them be permanently separated from communion and from the fellowship of all Christians.”

Gratian cites this canon in the second part of the *Decretum*, cause 27, question 1, chapter 7, under the name of the Fourth Council of Toledo. But neither we, nor the earlier commentator on Gratian’s passage, have found these words: “It is not found in the councils of Toledo.” It is, however, in book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 338.

### Notes on Canon XI

**a. Of whatever condition.** Paulinus includes everyone, whether noble or humble. The Sixth Council of Paris, however, deals more humanely with noblewomen who, after losing their husbands, take the veil. It exhorts them, without commanding them, that after the thirty days following their husband’s funeral they should

> “either marry, or, if they should rather request to be consecrated to God, be admonished and instructed to submit themselves to God’s service not in their own homes but in monasteries, under the direction of a spiritual mother.”

**b. Voluntarily making the promise.** Yet the *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 180, commands even those who received the veil unwillingly to remain in that state:

> “In whatever manner a woman, with her husband’s canonical permission, or after his death, has received the holy veil upon her head, whether willingly or unwillingly, she must remain in it altogether and must not remove it.”

This seems excessively harsh. The synod at Verberie in 762, under Pippin, proceeds more equitably, canon 4:

> “Whatever the manner in which a woman has received the veil, she shall remain in it unless someone veiled her while she was unwilling or protesting. Nevertheless, she should be exhorted to remain with her veil if she wishes. If a priest has veiled her while she was unwilling and protesting, he shall lose his rank on this account. If a woman presumes to veil herself without her husband’s agreement, it shall be in her husband’s power whether she remains in it or not.”

From this one may infer that sometimes married women themselves professed continence with the consent of their husbands.

But if a widow claimed that she had received the veil only temporarily, intending to pass from it to a second marriage once the period had ended, she was not believed and was compelled to preserve her purpose. The Council of Tibur in 895, canon 25:

> “We judge that if a woman has voluntarily placed a veil upon herself, even though it was not consecrated, and has offered an oblation to God in the church among the veiled women, she must henceforth retain the habit of holiness, whether she wishes it or not—even if she wishes to confirm by oath that she placed the veil upon herself on such terms and for such a reason that she would later be able to remove it.”

**c. They have been emancipated to God.** Festus, under the letter E, says:

> “‘Emancipated’ is understood in two ways: either those who have gone out from their father’s power, or those who become subject to the ownership of others.”

Hence the Plautine Pistoclerus, *Bacchides*, verse 69:

> “Now I emancipate myself to you as a woman.  
> I am yours.”

Paulinus uses the word in this sense.

**d. A black garment, etc.** From what has been said it is sufficiently clear that these women had a distinctive garment, which was sometimes called the garment of holy Mary. Liutprand, in the *Lombard Laws*, book III, title XXXVII, law 1:

> “Concerning those women who … although they have not been consecrated by a priest, it has seemed right to us … that those who bear such a sign upon themselves—that is, the veil or garment of holy Mary, Mother of God—however they have taken it upon themselves, should afterward in no way presume to return to secular life or to a secular habit.”

The following law says the same, and is entirely consonant with the Paulinian canon. It is therefore probable that the words “as was the ancient custom in these regions” are to be understood of the whole Lombard dominion. Unless one prefers to say that it was an ancient custom of the region, introduced before the Lombard invasion and later transferred into Lombard law.

The color of the garments was black, also called *pullus*. From this one may understand what sort of clothing the ancients used in mourning. *Pullae* garments were likewise those of people of the lowest rank.

Lampridius, in *Commodus*, chapter 16:

> “He himself used to preside at funerals in dark clothing,” and so forth.

Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 44, describing the separation of the common people from the nobles in the theater:

> “He enacted that no wearer of dark clothing should sit in the middle section.”

Calpurnius, *Eclogue* VII, verse 702, on public spectacles:

> “We came to the seats where a crowd watched among the women’s chairs  
> in a filthy dark garment.”

And verse 754:

> “Oh, if only we did not wear rustic clothing!  
> I would have seen the gods more closely; but my poverty,  
> My squalor, dark-clad poverty, and a brooch  
> Fastened with a hooked clasp stood in my way.”

Rightly, therefore, this sort of garment, suited to mourning and humility, was adopted by women who had renounced worldly pleasures and pomp, whether they were virgins or widows. Hence Vincent of Lérins, very aptly, in the *Commonitory*, book I, chapter 6, calls widows whom heretics had driven from their purpose *depullatae*, “stripped of their dark garments”:

> “Then wives whose marriage had been violated, widows stripped of their dark garments, virgins profaned,” and so forth.

Among the Spaniards, the Fourth Council of Toledo, held under King Sisenand in the Spanish era 671—that is, in 633—assigned widows and virgins a distinctive dress whose color displayed penance. According to Garsias, in the following canon, widows wore a white veil:

> “From this I think that the secular widows of Spain even now wear a long and white veil as a covering for the head, as a sign of their ancient profession of widowhood.”

But in the Spanish era 694—that is, in 656—the Tenth Council of Toledo, likewise held under Recceswinth, assigned these women not white but black or purple clothing, and specifically of a single color:

> “Let the garment be free from varieties of color and differences of parts … But henceforth, so that nothing may be called into doubt, let her cover her head with a mantle of purple or black color.”

I do not think “purple” should be understood as the color produced by human artifice. Purple, the insignia of magistrates and nursemaid of worldly pomp, as Tertullian says in *On the Crown*, chapter 14, is not suitable for widows who bear the burden of their humility. Rather, the reference is to a color approaching purple, that is, reddish, which was praised in Baetican wool because nature itself supplied the dye, as Tertullian likewise says in *On the Pallium*, chapter 3.

Pliny, book VIII, chapter 48, attributes reddish—or even scarlet—wool to Asia just as to Baetica:

> “Spain possesses especially fine black wool. Pollentia, near the Alps, has gray wool. Asia has reddish wool, which it calls scarlet; Baetica has it as well.”

It is therefore probable that the Fathers of the Council of Toledo, by “a mantle of purple color,” understood a veil of naturally purple or reddish color, such as nature imparted to the wool of Spain, and especially of Baetica.

That outside our province, too, and in the centuries following Paulinus, a black veil was imposed on those professing widowly continence is proved by the visions of Flotilda, which du Chesne included in volume II of the *Historical Writers of France*, page 625:

> “Likewise she saw herself in a certain pleasant place, with a black veil upon her head. When she asked about this, she heard that she ought to become a nun.”

That widows were called *nuns* is attested by Saint Jerome, letter 22 to Eustochium:

> “And because, having experienced the rule of husbands, they prefer the freedom of widowhood, they are called chaste women and nuns.”

For fuller discussions of such veils, see Baronius in his notes on the *Martyrology*, May 7, letter C, and Paulus Aringhi, *Subterranean Rome*, book IV, chapter 37, section 23—two distinguished lights of our congregation. Nor should Fontanini’s discussion of Saint Columba be omitted.

**e. By secular judgment.** This is distinguished from ecclesiastical judgment. See what we noted on canon 9, letter b, concerning public judgments. “Secular” (*mundanum*) meant the same as worldly or profane. In the Aachen capitulary of 816, under Louis the Pious, laws issued by the prince are called secular laws, just as those made by bishops are called ecclesiastical laws.

Thus Ansegisus, abbot, in the preface to book III of the *Capitularies*, states that in his first two books he had transcribed the ecclesiastical chapters of Charlemagne and Louis, but in the third he had gathered together those pertaining to secular law.

Likewise Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, verse 81, called the profane palace worldly:

> “The ruler of the worldly palace ordered me to go to the altar.”

**f. To change her garment.** This means the same as, after abandoning a profane garment, to assume the clothing of some profession—for example, of continence or penance.

Book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 338, has the title: *Concerning women who have changed their clothing into the religious habit in their own homes, and what should be done if afterward they choose sexual intercourse.* As is clear from the context, “they have changed” means the same as “they have assumed.”

Concerning penitents, book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 116:

> “If she lets down her hair or changes her habit, let him lay hands upon her.”

**g. Without the knowledge of her own bishop.** The prohibition against virgins or widows being veiled without consulting the bishop is found in book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 172. Its chapters are at least partly the work of Paulinus, and the Sixth Council of Paris may perhaps have derived its own canons—chapters 40 and 41, consonant with this enactment—from it.

Here *conscientia* means knowledge, awareness, or cognizance. Innocent I, letter 2 to Victricius, chapter 1:

> “Let no one dare to ordain a bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan.”

Phoebadius uses the word in this sense in his book *Against the Arians*, not far from the beginning, when he says that heresy can be brought into the public consciousness. Considering this passage in his *Adversaria*, book XXIX, chapter 1, Barthius confirms it with an example from Vegola—whose name, corrupted by the barbarians, he calls Vegetius—in *On Boundaries*:

> “If slaves act for their master, they will be changed for the worse; but if it happens with the master’s knowledge, the household will be uprooted more quickly.”

Cicero likewise uses this word in the same sense in book II of *On Ends*:

> “When the consciousness of other people is removed, nothing is so shameful that a person would not seem likely to do it for the sake of pleasure.”

### Observation on Canon XII

**I.** This canon establishes three things:

1. That the enclosures of nuns are to be guarded.
2. That they may not, under the pretext of devotion, go to Rome or to other places.
3. That penalties are established for transgressors.

**II.** Regarding the first point: Boniface VIII, in the chapter *Periculoso*, in the sixth book of the *Decretals*, book III, *On the Status of Religious Persons*, title 16, strictly prohibits laymen from approaching the enclosures of nuns and nuns from leaving their enclosures:

> “We decree that all nuns, individually and collectively, present and future, whatever their religion or order, wherever in the world they may be, must henceforth remain perpetually enclosed in their monasteries, so that none of them may thereafter have the power to leave the monasteries themselves, and so that no dishonorable person whatsoever—and not even an honorable person—may have entry or access to them.”

This was the first statute issued under a command of perpetual enclosure for nuns, as Francisco Pellizarius says, *Treatise on Nuns*, chapter 5, section 1, question 2. It was confirmed by the Council of Trent, session XXV, chapter 5, *On Religious Orders and Nuns*, by Saint Pius V through the constitution *Circa pastoralis*, and by Gregory XIII through another constitution, *Deo sacris*.

From this it appears that only in the fourteenth century were the enclosures of nuns universally closed under a binding command, and that access to those places of women dedicated to God was forbidden to laymen.

**III.** Yet although this had not previously been established by a universal decree, particular councils and Fathers had already introduced it in many provinces, sometimes by conciliar decision and sometimes by command, as part of the discipline of their own dioceses.

Apart from what we have in this canon of Paulinus, there are several enactments in the capitularies of the Frankish kings, issued around the time of Paulinus, concerning the matter itself. It is worthwhile to transcribe some of them, so that it may be clear that the statute of the Council of Forum Julii was neither without precedent nor without subsequent imitation.

Under Pippin, therefore, the synod of Verneuil in 755, canon 6, decreed:

> “We decree that no abbess … shall have permission to leave the monastery, except when compelled by hostile circumstances. But when the lord king orders one of those abbesses to come to him, she may come once a year with the consent of the bishop in whose parish she is, provided that he has ordered her to come and necessity requires it. She must not stay elsewhere at all—not in villages nor in other places—except only for as long as she can travel and return as quickly as possible. Before leaving her monastery, she shall first send her messenger to the lord king. If the king orders her to come, she shall come; otherwise she shall remain in the monastery until such time as he may regulate this matter more fully according to the canons. Likewise, those nuns shall not leave the monastery,” and so forth.

In capitulary 3 of 789, which, as we say in Paulinus’s *Life*, chapter 5, number 5, Paulinus attended, chapter 3 states:

> “Let no abbess presume to leave the monastery without our command, nor permit those subject to her to do so; and let their enclosures be securely fortified.”

In capitulary 1 of 802, chapter 20:

> “Let the abbess, together with her nuns, unanimously and diligently keep themselves within the enclosure, and let no one presume to go outside the enclosure.”

**IV.** These statutes had been established so that devout women would not leave their monasteries. But equal care was taken to prevent men from approaching their enclosures.

Book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 272, provides:

> “Only men of tested character and mature age shall be permitted to enter a monastery of girls, and then only for whatever needs or services they may have. As for clerics who enter to celebrate Masses, once the service has been completed they shall hasten to return. Otherwise, neither a cleric nor a young monk shall have any access to the community of girls, unless a paternal or fraternal relationship is proved to justify admitting him.”

The same is ordered in the capitulary issued at Salz in 804, chapter 5, with only this qualification:

> “Subject to the needs of the monastery, according to canonical institution and in accordance with what the bishop of that parish shall have arranged there.”

The following chapters, 6 and 7, also prohibit keeping girls in the monastery, except those who are to be admitted there for the purpose of undertaking the regular life. The admission of boys, even when related by blood, is entirely forbidden.

The Sixth Council of Paris, book I, chapter 46, prohibits not only entry but also access to monasteries and conversation with nuns by clerics or monks, except for preaching or hearing sacramental confession, and even then only with the bishop’s permission:

> “If a sermon is to be preached, it shall take place in a suitable place before everyone. If reason requires conversation with one of the nuns, it shall take place nowhere except in an appointed place, that is, in the audience hall, in the presence of religious men and women.”

And below:

> “If nuns wish to confess their sins to priests, they shall do so only in the church before the holy altar, with witnesses standing not far away. If illness prevents the confession from taking place in the church, it shall be made in whatever house is suitable, but likewise only with witnesses standing not far away.”

Such was the discipline of the Church concerning women’s monasteries in the age of Paulinus.

**V.** Paulinus had prohibited devout women from leaving their monasteries, and he expressly and specifically prohibited pilgrimage to Rome, as well as every other pilgrimage undertaken for the sake of piety.

At that time, pilgrimages undertaken from religious devotion had become so widespread that bishops had to impose limits upon those whom either the care of others—as in the case of parish priests—or the obligations of their own state—as in the case of monks, and even more so nuns—ought to have kept in place.

Thus the councils of that period frequently contain statutes against monks who wandered about, called *gyrovagi* in capitulary II of 789, chapter 1, and against clerics who, neglecting their asceteria and churches, undertook pilgrimages.

In particular, at the synod of Verneuil under Pippin in 755, the bishops prohibited monks from making a pilgrimage to Rome without consulting their abbots. Canon 10 states:

> “Let monks who truly live according to the rule not be permitted to wander to the Roman See or elsewhere, unless they are carrying out the obedience of their abbot.”

At the Second Council of Chalon in 813, chapters 44 and 45, it was decreed concerning priests and other clerics:

> “We have decided that it must be entirely prohibited for them to go to Rome or Tours without the permission of their bishop. For there is great error on the part of certain people who imprudently travel through Rome, Tours, and certain other places under the pretext of prayer.”

The same Fathers who made this provision concerning clerics also decreed at the same council concerning nuns, chapter 57:

> “An abbess who has a monastery in a city shall by no means leave the monastery except with the permission of her bishop.”

Chapter 62:

> “Nuns shall by no means leave the monastery, unless perhaps their abbess sends them because of some pressing necessity. Those who have neither male nor female servants to conduct business shall come as far as the monastery gate and conduct their business there before witnesses.”

Chapter 64:

> “A gatekeeper shall be chosen only if she is mature in age, has a good reputation, and leads a life worthy of approval.”

### NOTES ON CANON XI

#### VI.

Saint Jerome discusses at length the dangers to pilgrims and the damage to souls caused by pilgrimages in Letter 13 to Paulinus. He disapproves of such excursions by monks, even to the holy places of Jerusalem, where he himself was then living and directly witnessed the evils he was trying to avert.

> “If the places of the cross and resurrection were not in that exceedingly famous city, in which there are a court, a military palace, prostitutes, mimes, buffoons, and everything that is usually found in other cities—or if it were frequented only by crowds of monks—such a dwelling would truly be desirable for all monks. But now it is the height of folly to renounce the world, leave one’s homeland, abandon the cities, profess oneself a monk, and live more dangerously among larger populations than one would have lived in one’s homeland. People converge here from the whole world; the city is full of every kind of person; and there is such a throng of both sexes that what you were fleeing from elsewhere only in part, here you are compelled to endure in its entirety.”

These considerations, which troubled Jerome and which he used to deter Paulinus, as a monk, from pilgrimage to Jerusalem, are much more compelling when the matter concerns nuns. Accordingly, Gregory of Nyssa also forbids monks and virgins access to the holy places in his letter or short treatise, as Baronius most prudently interprets it under the year of Christ 386, no. 39, and Bellarmine, *Controversies*, vol. II, book III, *On the Veneration of the Saints*, chapter 8, against the Magdeburg Centuriators, who seize upon this letter as an opportunity to condemn the pious Catholic devotion of visiting the holy places.

> “In that discourse,” says Bellarmine, “pilgrimage to Jerusalem is not condemned absolutely, but is condemned in certain persons, namely monks and nuns; for only such persons are being discussed in that passage.”

Alternatively, as du Pin and G. Cave maintain—although Cave certainly does not stand with the Catholics—the bad conduct of the inhabitants of Jerusalem caused Gregory to disapprove of a journey that had otherwise been undertaken in a holy manner.

> “He visited Jerusalem,” says Cave, “and contemplated the holy places with a pious mind. But offended by the vices and dissensions of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, he suddenly withdrew; indeed, shortly afterward he wrote a letter against those who visited Jerusalem for the sake of piety.”

This testimony, extracted from an opponent, incidentally demonstrates the bad faith of the Magdeburg Centuriators.

#### VII.

Finally, Paulinus proceeds to the penalties for those who violate this most salutary decree, namely:

> “Either let the offender be punished by excommunication according to the measure and character of the fault; or, punished by the bond of anathema, let him be bound; or, stripped of his own honor by loss of rank, let the guilty person be removed from the bosom of the Church.”

Three kinds of penalties are noted here. Although they do not seem very different from one another, we learn from various sources that they were nevertheless distinct. For in the Second Council of Tours, held in 587, canon 24, it is said of a certain transgressor that he should die not only excommunicated but also anathematized.

Therefore, by excommunication—which may seem capable of being confused with anathema— I understand only what is called minor excommunication, which truly differs from anathema; by anathema, major and proper excommunication; and by loss of honor, suspension or deposition from office.

At present our theologians recognize only one kind of minor excommunication, incurred by anyone who communicates with a person under major excommunication. Formerly, however, as Morinus observes, *On the Sacrament of Penance*, book VI, chapter 25, no. 11, it was incurred in ten cases according to Sylvester, nine according to Antoninus, and eight according to Innocent and Henriquez. Since it is now incurred in only one case, it has only one degree and produces only one effect, namely, to deprive a person of what is called passive participation in the sacraments.

In antiquity, however, it admitted various degrees, which Morinus lists in the same place, no. 13, in these words:

> “In brief, I shall say that among the ancients the forms or degrees of minor excommunication were exceedingly common. The first excommunicated or excluded the sinner from participation in the Eucharist alone; the second, more severe than the first, excluded him from the Eucharist and from the prayers of the Church or of the faithful; the third added to these two degrees expulsion or excommunication from the prayers made over catechumens and penitents lying prostrate; the fourth excommunicated or excluded them from every entrance into the church. Or, what amounts to the same thing, there were four degrees of those excommunicated with minor excommunication: the standing, the prostrate, the hearers, and the weepers.”

I therefore think that Paulinus had one of these degrees in mind when he decreed that the transgressor of his canon should be excommunicated. This seems sufficiently clear from his own words. Since this penalty could be either milder or more severe, as we have just seen, he himself said: “The offender is to be punished by excommunication according to the measure and character of the fault.”

#### VIII.

Anathema is an indication of a graver fault and is called major excommunication: the most dreadful of all thunderbolts, not to be hurled without serious cause. This is established in the capitulary of Charles the Bald, from the year 846, title VI, chapter 56, in words that also demonstrate the difference between anathema and the excommunication explained above:

> “Let no bishop deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a certain and manifest cause of sin. But let anathema be imposed on no one without the consent of the archbishop or of the fellow bishops, and only after evangelical admonition has been given, except where canonical authority teaches otherwise. For anathema is the condemnation of eternal death, and it ought to be imposed only for a mortal crime and upon one who could not otherwise be corrected.”

At the Synod of Verneuil, held in 755, canon 9 explains more fully what benefits are denied to one whom the Church has judged deserving of this censure:

> “And so that you may know what the form of this excommunication is: he must not enter the church, nor eat or drink with any Christian; no one may accept his gifts or offer him a kiss; he must not join in prayer or greet anyone, until he has been reconciled by the bishop.”

If you wish to know the causes, rites, ceremonies, and form of absolution associated with this excommunication among the Hebrews, see Selden, *On Natural and Gentile Law according to Hebrew Discipline*, book IV, chapter 8 and following.

Paulinus wished to bind with this penalty only those who had added obstinacy to their transgression. Extreme remedies are to be applied only to extreme evils.

#### IX.

Suspension or deposition, which are here designated by the name “loss of honor,” imply lighter penalties and a correspondingly lighter degree of guilt. How this loss of honor is to be understood has already been explained above in the note on canon 7 of this council.

#### X.

One point remains to be noted at the end: these censures—whether of excommunication, anathema, or loss of honor—were not imposed by Paulinus and the Synod of Friuli in such a way as to bind the offender automatically by the fact itself, but under threat of a condemnation still to be imposed. That is, they were not *latae sententiae*—to use the formula of the scholastic theologians and canonists—but *ferendae sententiae*, as is shown by the terms “let him be restrained,” “punished,” “bound,” and “removed.”

The Sixth Council of Paris, book I, chapter 46, however, appears to have punished those who approached the ascesoriae of devout women—monks and clerics—with excommunication *latae sententiae*:

> “We decree that the person who transgresses this definition of ours is excommunicated.”

Let Van Espen consider, since in part III of *Ecclesiastical Law*, title XI, chapter 6, no. 19, he asserts that excommunication *latae sententiae* was unknown for ten centuries, whether this case is of that kind.

### NOTES ON CANON XII

#### a. “Whom the seriousness of their character adorns.”

By this phrase—which is genuinely Latin and excellent—the author excludes young men, ephebes, and beardless youths, to whom levity or inconstancy is attributed. Cicero says in *On Old Age*:

> “I, as a young man, loved Quintus Maximus, the man who recovered Tarentum, when he was an old man, as though he were my equal; for in that man seriousness was tempered by courtesy.”

And below:

> “To each period of life its appropriate season has been assigned. For just as weakness belongs to children, impetuosity to young men, and seriousness to mature age that has already acquired stability, so the maturity of old age possesses something natural.”

#### b. “The angelic order.”

Virgins. Ambrose, book I, *On Virgins*:

> “No one should wonder if those who are joined to the Lord of the angels are compared with angels.”

Cyprian, *On the Conduct of Virgins*, near the end:

> “As you persevere in chastity and virginity, you are equal to the angels of God.”

Chrysostom, *On Virginity*, chapter 79:

> “In what respect, I ask, did Elijah, Elisha, and John—the true lovers of virginity—differ from the angels? In none, except that they were constituted of mortal nature.”

See also the same author, book III of *On the Priesthood*, near the end, and chapter 12 of the same author’s *On Virgins*.

Saint Peter Chrysologus, sermon 143:

> “Virginity is always akin to the angels. To live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not earthly life but heavenly life. And if you wish to know, acquiring angelic glory is greater than possessing it: to be an angel is a matter of blessedness; to be a virgin, of virtue. For virginity obtains by strength what an angel possesses by nature. Thus the angel and the virgin perform a divine, not a human, office.”

Saint Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, Oration 3:

> “Indeed, virginity is marvelous, as though akin to the angels, as though a companion of the heavenly powers, as though an associate of incorporeal natures.”

And so say all the other Fathers with one voice. Yet Cyril of Jerusalem comes especially close to the Pauline expression. In *Catechetical Lecture* IV, section “On the Body,” he calls the order of virgins in the Church “the order of virgins who lead a life equal to that of the angels.”

#### c. “To go to Rome.”

He names Roman pilgrimage specifically, while mentioning other pilgrimages generally, because Rome surpassed the others. In later centuries the name came to designate any pilgrimage and any pilgrim.

John of Salisbury, *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, book VI, chapter 1:

> “Who can count how many among us the license of these men, stripping people of their possessions under the guise of religion or some other pretext, has made not so much Rome-bound pilgrims and travelers as exiles?”

The Lateran Council of 1122, under Callistus II, canon 16:

> “If anyone attempts to seize Rome-bound pilgrims, pilgrims, or those visiting the thresholds of the apostles or the shrines of other saints, let him be deprived of Christian communion.”

Here it is evident that *Romipetae* does not mean precisely those who go to Rome to the thresholds of the apostles, from whom they are rather distinguished, but all those who travel for any religious reason. They were also called *Romei*.

Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, in *The Life of Saint Gerald, Count of Aurillac*, book II, chapter 17:

> “At the time when the *Romei* are accustomed to pass through.”

And chapter 23:

> “Near the suburb of Saint Martin, where the *Romei* are accustomed to camp.”

Hence Tuscan writers often call pilgrims *Romei*, and pilgrimage *romeggio*. Jacobus Passaranti, *Mirror of True Penitence*, distinction 5, chapter 4, section 2:

> “The other case concerns the *Romei* and the pilgrims, and the merchants who go to various countries and places.”

He repeats this there more than once. Giovanni Villani, book VI, chapter 92:

> “A *Romeo* arrived at his court, returning from Saint James.”

Matteo Villani, book I, chapter 56:

> “The pilgrim went on pilgrimage.”

And in the *Ancient Novellas*:

> “A citizen of Bari went on pilgrimage.”

### OBSERVATION ON CANON XIII

#### I.

In this canon Paulinus explains the excellence of the Lord’s Day and the manner in which it and the other feast days are to be honored.

Saint Ignatius, *Letter 7 to the Magnesians*, calls it “the queen and mistress of all days”; Saint Gaudentius, *Treatise III to the Newly Baptized*, “the birthday of the world’s restoration,” and in *Treatise X*, “the first day of the age”; Sophronius, *Oration I on the Nativity of the Lord*, “the mistress of days”; Theodore the Studite, sermon 11, “the day of peace”; Saint Chrysostom, *Homily 5 on the Resurrection*, “the Lord’s Day, the day of light, the day of bread, the royal day”; and in his homily *On Almsgiving from the Letter to the Corinthians*, “the birthday of the whole human race.” These titles are drawn from the mystery of the resurrection.

“For all Sundays are the eighth days of this feast,” says Durandus, *Rationale*, book VI, chapter 86, no. 6—perhaps drawing on Saint Leo, sermon 10 *On Lent*, who says of the Lord’s resurrection:

> “Through it the dignity of all solemn celebrations is consecrated in the Church of God.”

The Church substituted this day for the Jewish Sabbath. Saint Athanasius gives the reason in his book *On the Sabbath and Circumcision*:

> “The Sabbath was the end of the first creation; the Lord’s Day, however, was the beginning of the second creation, on which he renewed and restored the old man.
