Therefore, just as in former times he wished the Sabbath day to be observed as a memorial of the former things, so we venerate the Lord’s Day as a memorial of the beginning of the second restoration.”

#### II.

For this reason the Church always customarily spends this day joyfully, removing every penitential practice that would be inappropriate on a feast day.

Epiphanius, *On the Exposition of the Faith*, no. 22:

> “The Catholic Church has decreed that all Sundays be festive and joyful … and it celebrates no fasts.”

Against the errors of Eustathius, bishop of Sebaste, and his followers, who prescribed fasting on this day, stands canon 13 of the Council of Gangra:

> “If anyone … fasts on the Lord’s Day, let him be anathema.”

Against the Manichaeans, see Augustine’s Letter 36, latest edition, especially chapter 12; nor should one omit Saint Ignatius’s Letter 5 to the Philippians, where he compares those who fast with the killers of Christ.

Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 3:

> “We consider it unlawful to fast on the Lord’s Day or to worship while kneeling.”

The reason, says Abbot Theonas in Cassian, *Conferences* XXI, chapter 20, is that “the elders handed down that we should stand more upright out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection.” Saint Nilus similarly wrote to Ursacius in Letter 112:

> “On Sunday we pray standing, prefiguring the upright state of the future age of blessedness. On other days we bend our knees, signifying the fall of the human race through sin. By rising from our knees we indicate that Christ’s resurrection has been communicated to us and is soon to be brought to completion on the Lord’s Day.”

#### III.

This day is endowed with many privileges by both divine and human law. By divine law, all those things that were once attributed to the Sabbath have been conferred upon it—those things that can be established from Scripture.

It would also be too lengthy a task to list all the provisions made by the laws of the Church in the canons. Anyone may consult *On Consecration*, distinction 3 in its entirety, especially canons 1, 4, 9, 10, 12, 14, and 15.

It is no wonder that God, who commands this, and his bride the Church, which must preserve the honor of the bridegroom, have made this day of the greatest importance. Consider instead what secular lawmakers established concerning it.

Honorius and Theodosius wrote to Caecilianus, as recorded in the Theodosian Code, book IX, title 2, *On the Custody of Prisoners*, law 3:

> “On every Sunday the judges are to see the prisoners brought out from their prison custody; they are to inquire whether humane treatment is being denied to those confined because of corrupt prison guards. They are to have food supplied to those who have none … and those persons are to be taken to the bath under reliable guard.”

Related to this is Constantine’s decree in the same Code, book II, title 8, *On Holidays*, law 1:

> “Just as it seemed utterly unworthy that they should celebrate the day of the sun—that is, the Lord’s Day—of its worship while occupied with quarrelsome disputes in harmful conflicts between parties, so it is pleasing and welcome that on that day the things most earnestly desired should be fulfilled. Therefore, on the feast day all are to have permission to emancipate and manumit, and legal proceedings concerning these matters are not to be prohibited.”

That it is utterly unworthy to occupy the Lord’s Day with lawsuits and quarrels was also prohibited by many others, as will become clear in the notes.

#### IV.

In the meantime Paulinus proposes the manner of honoring this day and the other feast days: namely, that, besides refraining from the works of the servitude of sin and of the flesh, as well as from lawsuits and legal proceedings, people should devote themselves to divine matters, especially to hearing the word of God proclaimed to the people by pastors.

That this practice was observed from the very beginnings of the Church is evident from the Acts of the Apostles. The preaching of Moses, which took place every Sabbath in the synagogues, was transferred—according to Acts 13, 14, and 15—to the first day of the week, that is, the Lord’s Day, for the proclamation of the Gospel, as is demonstrated by chapter 20:7:

> “On the first day of the week, when we had gathered together to break bread, Paul was speaking with them.”

The rite appears still more clearly in Saint Justin Martyr’s *Second Apology* to Antoninus Pius, shortly before the end:

> “On the day called Sunday, all who live in the towns or in the countryside gather together in one place, and the memoirs of the apostles or the writings of the prophets are read, as long as the time permits. Then, when the reader has ceased, the presider gives an instruction, admonishing and exhorting the people to imitate these beautiful things.”

This is commended in the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book VI, chapter 205:

> “It has pleased us that the faithful should all honor the Lord’s Day with reverence … and that on that holy day they should not, as is customary, devote themselves to empty tales or conversations, songs, or dances, standing at crossroads and in the streets. Instead, they should go to a priest or to some wise and good person and make use of their preaching and good instruction concerning the things that pertain to the soul.”

### NOTES ON CANON XIII

#### a. “At the beginning of the night,” that is, on Saturday evening.

What had been said about the Sabbath in Leviticus 23:32—

> “From evening to evening you shall celebrate your Sabbaths”—

was transferred to the observance of the Lord’s Day.

Capitulary 1, from the year 789, chapter 15, based on canon 29 of the Council of Laodicea:

> “Let the Lord’s Day be observed from evening to evening.”

The same is found in the Council of Frankfurt, held in 794, canon 21.

Miracles confirm that this was a legitimate practice, according to Gregory of Tours, book III of *The Miracles of Saint Martin*, chapter 31. He relates that a woman of Angers, having disregarded the pious custom, was punished by paralysis of her right hand:

> “Because,” he says, “on Saturday after sunset, which belonged to the night of the Lord’s Day, she wished to prepare bread.”

In chapter 56 he adds a similar story about another woman who baked bread in an oven on Saturday evening.

Anastasius of Sinai gives the mystical reason for the precept in *Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexaemeron*, book I, concerning the first day of creation:

> “Evening comes first, and then day. Hence it was established by law that the Lord’s day should begin with evening, because from obscure death we proceeded to the light of the resurrection.”

#### b. “Which dawns on the first day of the week.”

This is from Matthew 28:1:

> “But in the evening of the Sabbath, as it dawned toward the first day of the week.”

Saint Augustine, Letter 36, chapter 12:

> “The day of the Lord’s resurrection is called by Matthew the first day of the week, but by the other three [Evangelists] the first day of the week; it is clearly the day that was later called the Lord’s Day.”

See also Selden, *On Natural and Gentile Law according to Hebrew Discipline*, book III, chapter 17.

#### c. “When the signal has sounded.”

Suppose that this means the sound of a bell, which the capitulary of 789, book III, chapter 18, calls *cloca*, a French word.

It seems to have been the same as the signal for Vespers. For in most of the old manuscript statutes concerning the artisans of the city of Paris, the chief provision is that they should not work “on Saturday from the last stroke of Vespers sounded in the parish,” where certain of those trades were located. See Du Cange, under *Dominica*.

The opposite, however, is suggested by a custom that still survives in our regions. In some churches, especially in villages, on the day before a feast, even when Vespers are not celebrated there or announced by the sound of bells, the church bells are usually rung about an hour before sunset as a sign of the impending feast of the following day. This signal is still called in Latin *vigiliae*, according to the ancient rite of vigils.

Indeed, some uneducated people still regard it as religiously improper not to cease from every kind of work when they hear it. Paulinus himself, however, condemns the practice of taking the entire Saturday off as a kind of learned Jewish superstition, even among his own country people, as is evident from the words of this canon below:

> “But if he were speaking of that Sabbath which the Jews celebrate, which is the last day of the week, and which our country people also observe,” etc.

#### d. “First of all, to abstain from every sin.”

The servile work prohibited on a feast day in Numbers 28:18 may also be called sin, since the Lord says in John 8:34:

> “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

Paulinus himself interprets the work of sin as servile below.

Moral theologians debate whether committing a sin on a feast day constitutes a new sin arising from the circumstance of sacred time. See de Lugo, *On the Sacrament of Penance*, disputation 16, section 12, no. 55 and following, and Diana, part I, treatise VII, *On Aggravating Circumstances*, resolution 32. They more probably deny that it is at least a mortal sin.

That this was Paulinus’s view is clear from the following note.

#### e. “Even from one’s own spouses.”

Saint Augustine, sermon 244 *On Time* in the old edition—or rather Saint Caesarius, in the appendix to volume V of Saint Augustine’s sermons, sermon 292 in the latest edition—warns the people that whenever a solemnity is celebrated in the Church and they wish to receive Christ’s sacraments, they should not have intercourse with their wives.

To those who object that this is a slight sin, he replies:

> “Nor do we say that it is a capital sin.”

Saint Gregory, in his tenth response to Augustine, says the same and adds:

> “Nor, in saying these things, do we consider marriage itself to be a fault.”

This is also the common teaching of moral theologians. Therefore, if failure to abstain from marital relations on a feast day is no sin at all, or at most only a slight sin, and yet Paulinus forbids both sinning on a feast day and having intercourse with one’s spouse under the same formula, it remains to be said that Paulinus did not prohibit either act under pain of grave guilt.

#### f. “And from every earthly work.”

What kinds of work are forbidden on a feast day is sufficiently known from the practice of the faithful. Works relating especially to cultivation of the earth are appropriately called “earthly” here.

The First Capitularies of Aachen, from the year 789, chapter 79, lists at least some such works:

> “Men are not to perform rural labor: neither are they to work in cultivating vineyards, plowing fields, reaping, cutting hay, or making hedges; nor are they to grub in the woods, cut down trees, or work in the quarries; nor are they to build houses, work in gardens, assemble at pleas, or engage in hunting. Three kinds of cart work may be done on the Lord’s Day: hostile military carts, carts carrying provisions, or, if necessary, the transportation of anyone’s body to the grave. Likewise, women are not to perform textile work, cut out garments, sew, or make embroidered work with a needle; nor may they comb wool, strike wood, wash clothes in public, or shear sheep. In every way the honor and rest of the Lord’s Day are to be preserved.”

Similar provisions are found throughout the capitularies.

The pagan Tibullus himself, in book II, elegy 1, lines 5 and following, indicated that a feast day ought equally to be free from bodily and earthly labor:

> Let the earth rest on the sacred day; let the plowman rest;  
> Let harsh labor cease, with the plow suspended.  
> The oxen are released from the yoke and now ought to stand  
> At the full mangers, their heads crowned.  
> Let everything be devoted to God; let no woman dare  
> To place her wool-working hand upon the distaff.  
> You too, I order to keep far away; depart from the altars,  
> You whom Venus brought joy on the previous night.

#### g. “When all the tumult of lawsuits has ceased.”

The Theodosian Code, title VIII, *On Holidays*, law 2, includes the day of the sun among the days of rest. In book VIII, title III, *On Executors and Legal Actions*, it says:

> “On the day of the sun, which our ancestors rightly decreed to be the Lord’s Day, let all proceedings of every kind of litigation, business, and legal assembly cease. Let no one demand a public or private debt, nor voluntarily admit any accusation of quarrels. And let the person who departs from the institution or rite of holy religion be judged not merely infamous but sacrilegious.”

I believe the text should be corrected here, since it is wrongly read as *religionis instincto ritu vel deflexerit*; it should read as above.

Add the passage of Ulpian, *Digest*, *On Holidays and Adjournments*, law 6:

> “If judgment has been given on holidays, the law provides that there shall be no judgment on those days,”

that is, it is to be regarded as not adjudicated and void.

See also, in volume I of the *Capitularies*, page 9, the order of King Guntram from the year 555; *Capitularies*, book V, chapter 153, and book VI, chapter 318; as well as the Lombard Laws, book II, title 50, law 2.

Ovid also notes the same point concerning a feast day in book I of the *Fasti*, line 73:

> Let ears be free from lawsuits, and let insane  
> Quarrels immediately be absent; hostile crowd, postpone your work.

#### h. “Almost all the gifts of grace.”

To the gifts listed by Paulinus may be added those mentioned by Augustine, sermon 251 *On Time*, or rather by Alcuin, *On the Divine Office*, chapter 7, in the appendix to volume V of Augustine’s sermons, sermon 280 in the latest edition:

> “It is the first day of the age; on it the elements of the world were formed; on it the angels were created.”

Saint Leo, Letter 81 to Dioscorus, chapter 1:

> “On this day the apostles take up the trumpet for preaching to all nations and receive the sacrament of regeneration to be brought to the whole world.”

Canon 8, among the nine canons added to the Sixth Synod—which, although they are not by that synod, as Surius warns there, are nevertheless received as pious—adds:

> “On it he deigned to be born; on it the star shone upon the Magi; on it he fed five thousand people with five loaves and two fish; on it he received baptism in the Jordan from John.”

#### i. “It would take too long to list them all individually.”

Saint Augustine, or whoever else wrote sermon 136 *On Time*—sermon 159 in the latest edition, in volume V of the appendix—says:

> “The day would fail me if I wished to explain the whole sacramental meaning of this day.”

Saint Leo, in the passage cited above:

> “It has been consecrated by such great mysteries of divine dispensations that whatever has been established with particular distinction by the Lord was accomplished in the dignity of this day … so that we may know that the mysteries of priestly blessings are to be celebrated on that day on which all gifts of grace were bestowed.”

#### j. “The other principal festivals.”

It is useful to extract from the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*, book VI, chapter 189, which festivals were customarily celebrated at that time:

> “Let the priests announce these principal festivals, so that they may be observed as Sabbaths, like Sundays: the Nativity of the Lord, four days, beginning on the eighth day before the Kalends of January; the Circumcision of the Lord, one day, on the Kalends of January; the Epiphany, one day, on the eighth day before the Ides of January; the Purification of Saint Mary, one day, on the ninth day of February; Easter, three days after the Lord’s Day through the octave of Easter; the Ascension of the Lord, one day; the nativity of Saint John the Baptist, one day, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July; the passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, one day, on the third day before the Kalends of July; the Assumption of Saint Mary, one day, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September; the passing of Saint Martin, one day, on the third day before the Ides of November; the passion of Saint Andrew the Apostle, one day, on the second day before the Kalends of December.”¹

In the Aachen capitulary of the year 717, chapter 46, the feasts of Saint Stephen, Saint John the Evangelist, and the Holy Innocents are explicitly added after the Nativity of the Lord, as are, in general, the feasts of the blessed apostles and, specifically, the nativity of Saint Lawrence.

Likewise, the *Capitularies*, book I, chapter 158, adds the nativity of every saint whose honor is specially celebrated in any parish; the Greater Litany is added in book I, chapter 158; and book II, chapter 35, adds Pentecost, as at Easter, the dedication of Saint Michael, and the nativity of Saint Remigius. At the end it adds:

> “And we decree that those festivals of martyrs and confessors are to be observed whose holy bodies rest in each parish.”

#### k. “And those feasts that the priests announce in the church.”

The priests are commanded to announce the feasts by the Council of Lyons, *On Consecration*, distinction 3, canon 1:

> “It must be announced to the laity so that they may know the times of rest throughout the year.”

The time and manner of this announcement are given in the same distinction, canon 25, from canon 9 of the Council of Braga: namely, “each priest is to write them down briefly in his own church and, when the day of the Lord’s Nativity arrives, announce them before the people after the Gospel reading.”

This is now done at the Epiphany, according to the Fourth Council of Orléans, canon 1, and the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 4; the form is found in the Roman Pontifical.

In our own days and regions, according to the synods of 1660 under John Cardinal Delfino, chapter 2, section 4, and under Dionysius, his nephew and patriarch, every Sunday the feasts occurring during the following week are announced to the people. A similar practice had already been observed in the Church of Aquileia around the middle of the thirteenth century, as is evident from the Gospel book of that period.

That the patriarchs of Aquileia sometimes established new and solemn offices of the saints is evident from the charter to be placed in appendix II, no. 15.

### OBSERVATION ON CANON XIV

#### I.

A tithe is so called because one part is separated from ten. Firstfruits are what is first gathered from any produce. The Lord once granted these to priests and Levites in return for their priestly office and for the ministry by which they served in the tabernacle of the covenant, as stated in Numbers 18:8 and 21.

Perhaps the Gentiles derived this custom from the Hebrews. Among them Camillus is said to have vowed a tenth of the spoils to Apollo, according to Livy, decade 1, book V, chapter 23.

#### II.

Those who assert that tithes were introduced into the Church only shortly before the time of Charlemagne appear to be speaking complete nonsense. For the Second Council of Mâcon, held in 585, canon 5, says of the laws concerning tithes:

> “The Christian community preserved these laws inviolate for a long time … Therefore we establish and decree that the ancient custom be restored by the faithful, and that all the people bring tithes for those serving in ecclesiastical rites.”

The same is also evident from Saint Augustine, sermon 219 *On Time* in the old edition, or rather from Saint Caesarius of Arles, a sixth-century writer, in the appendix to volume V of Augustine’s sermons, sermon 277 in the latest edition, where he discusses tithes at greater length.

#### III.

Devotion to giving tithes and firstfruits at one time progressed so far that the faithful thought they ought to be given not only from the fruits of the earth but also from every other income obtained through any kind of industry.

“From military service, from business, from craftsmanship, give tithes,” Caesarius said in the passage cited above. Abbot Antiochus, homily 120, also required monks to tithe the alms they received:

> “Monks, above all, ought to offer firstfruits and tithes to God … from those things distributed to them through the generosity of others, or from the profits resulting from the work of their hands.”

#### IV.

But since those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and those who serve at the altar share in what comes from the altar, as the Apostle explains at length in 1 Corinthians 9:13, priests may rightly convert the income from tithes to their own use—but not all of it.

The division of tithes is established in the capitulary of the bishops from the year 801, chapter 7:

> “The priests themselves are to receive the people’s tithes, keep written records of the names of all who give them, and divide them before witnesses according to canonical authority. They are to choose the first part for the adornment of the church, and distribute the second for the use of the poor or pilgrims … while the priests alone are to reserve the third part for themselves.”

Walafrid Strabo gives a slightly different division of tithes in *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 27:

> “According to the canons, four parts are to be made from the offerings of the faithful: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth for the repair of the churches.”

#### V.

Paulinus promotes the payment of tithes by advancing an argument from divine generosity toward those who obey and by presenting the threat of punishment against the disobedient, in words spoken by the Lord through Malachi, which Caesarius also uses in the sermon cited above.

The Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt, held in 794, among whom Paulinus himself was present, commanded tithes in canon 25 and added:

> “For we have learned by experience that in the year when that severe famine broke out, empty granaries, devoured by demons, boiled over, and voices of reproach were heard.”

That year was 779, as Sirmond proves in his notes on the council from the decree of supplication issued in that year. The decree shows that the people were then suffering from a severe famine.

#### VI.

It is not surprising that princes who care about the welfare of the people should inflict heavier penalties on transgressors.

The capitulary of Metz, chapter 4:

> “Whoever has not done this shall lose the property itself.”

The capitulary of Worms, from the year 829, chapter 5:

> “Let him know that he will lose the benefice from which this ninth and tithe ought to have been paid.”

Nor was it permissible to give or withhold the tithes or ninths of the produce to whichever church one pleased, but only to the church to which they were legally owed. Therefore, in the following chapter:

> “Whoever removes the tithe from the church to which it ought to be given by right and, presumptuously, whether because of gifts, friendship, or any other reason, gives it to another church, is to be compelled by the count or by our envoy to restore the amount of the same tithe together with its legal penalty,”

that is, together with the fine established by law.

#### VII.

The bishops, however, did not proceed with the strictness of the princes’ laws in collecting tithes, since they devoted themselves to the gentleness appropriate to their vocation.

Among the capitularies of Herard, archbishop of Tours, no. 132, we read:

> “Let no priest receive tithes with litigation and quarrelling, but through preaching and admonition.”

Earlier, namely in chapter 42:

> “Those who do not give tithes are not to be compelled by swords or oaths, but are to be corrected ecclesiastically.”

VIII. Hence, lest—once the censures of the Church had been set aside and secular authority summoned to take part—an occasion for scandal should arise among the little ones, or lest any prejudice against matters of faith should be thought imminent, the more religious Fathers preferred to abstain from exacting the tithe rather than expose the matter to such dangers. Therefore Alcuin advised Charles, in Letter 7, when he was congratulating him on the victory over the Avars, to refrain from exacting tithes, lest he create some impediment to the growth of faith in the minds of the neophytes, who were not yet adequately prepared; they would comply more willingly once they had matured in faith:

> “Your most holy piety should foresee, by wise counsel, whether it is better at the beginning of faith to impose upon peoples the yoke of tithes [Col. 0341C] . . . We know that the tithing of our substance is very good. But it is better to lose it than to lose the faith. Yet we, born, nourished, and instructed in the Catholic faith, scarcely consent to tithe our substance fully. How much less will tender faith, an infantile spirit, and an avaricious mind consent to their generosity? Once faith has been strengthened and the Christian way of life confirmed, then, as though they were mature men, stronger precepts should be given—precepts from which a mind grown old in Christian religion would not recoil.”

## NOTES ON CANON XIV

**a.** “While preserving the mystical meanings of allegorical matters.” The principal allegory of tithes, which derives from the deed of Abraham, who gave tithes to Melchizedek (Gen. XIV, 20), is treated at length by Chrysostom, Oration 13 on Chapter VII of the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Apostle too discusses mystically the excellence of Christ’s priesthood. Radulphus of Flavigny, however, has the following brief statement in Book XX on Leviticus, chapter 7:

> “The number ten contains the fullness of its number; and just as counting begins from one, so it is completed in the tenth. Therefore, when the Lord testifies that both the firstborn and the tithes are his, he teaches us mystically that from him comes whatever enables us to rise toward the good, and from him also comes our perseverance to the end. This is what the Psalmist likewise declares, saying: ‘His mercy shall go before me, and your mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.’”

If you desire another, tropological interpretation, see Ribera on Malachi III, no. 39 and following; and it is the same passage of the prophet that Paulinus cites.

**b.** “From their own gifts, not from yours.” Augustine—or, more truly, Caesarius—in the previously cited Sermon 219 on the seasons:

> “Hear this, ungrateful humanity. You know that everything you receive belongs to God, and yet do you not return it from what belongs to the Creator of all things? . . . He does not demand from you something of your own that you should return.”

The Council of Trosly, in the year 909, canon 6:

> “By giving them faithfully [the tithes], they contribute nothing to God . . . but return what is his.”

**94 c.** “Because everything that we are, live, and possess, etc.” He takes this from Paul’s statement in Acts XVII, 28: “For in him we live and move and exist.” The Apostle confirms this from Aratus, in the *Phaenomena*: “For we are indeed his offspring.” Hence Arnobius, Book I *Against the Pagans*:

> “Do we not owe to this God the very first thing—that we exist, that we are called human beings? . . . Do we not owe to him the fact that we walk, breathe, and live; that the very power of living comes to us from him and makes us exist and move with animal motion?”

**d.** “With what intention, not how much.” This is a familiar saying among ascetics: “God does not regard how much, but of what kind.” Eusebius—or whoever commonly circulated under the name of Eusebius of Emesa—praises, in more than one place, namely in the homily for Ash Wednesday and in the homily *On the Confessor*, the saying of a certain Christian sage:

> “Hence, as a certain wise man says: One must not consider chiefly what someone does, but with what intention he does it.”

To this corresponds Chrysostom’s statement in Homily 3, near the end, on Chapter I of the First Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “For God is accustomed to determine crowns not from the outcome of the things rightly done, but from the mind of those who do them rightly.”

Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, expresses this more closely, and yet more vigorously, in Letter 62:

> “God considers not what you offer, but how you offer it.”

These, then, seemed worth observing and noting in the canons of the Council of Friuli, celebrated by Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia.

[Col. 0343]

## 95. SAINT PAULINUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA

[Note: **Against Felix, etc.** No one who reads this work will deny that it is vigorous and well suited to its subject. The one thing to be wished for would be that its author had flourished in a century more favorable to letters. For I do not deny that at times the force of the argument is somewhat blunted by an undigested mass of words, and the meaning so entangled that the passage must often be read again before we can fully grasp the writer’s thought. Yet, as has been said elsewhere, allowance must be made, and the style of an Iron Age must not be required to equal that of the Golden Age.

A fair and discerning reader can meet this difficulty in two ways: either by imagining himself born in Paulinus’s century, or by imagining that Paulinus’s phrasing and style flourish in his own century. This is not a chimerical remedy, even though it is imaginary. In our memory, allegories, metaphors, and other figurative expressions had intruded so monstrously into the Etruscan language that those who spoke from the rostra were considered worthless unless courts, marketplaces, academies, and even sacred temples resounded with such monstrous figures, with words of sesquipedalian length exploded from swelling mouths. Now, through the help of good genius, the style has been restored as though by a right of return, and everyone sings in a purer manner, the old style having been expelled. Yet at that time only the one who spoke in that way seemed wise; purity was displeasing.

Think the same way about Latin. In Paulinus’s age, those who seemed learned generally spoke and wrote in sermons as the contemporary authors show. Moreover, the barbarous vocabulary and the poorly constructed syntax, scarcely conforming to the rules of pure Latin grammar, sometimes delay the reader. Therefore we thought it worthwhile to confront this difficulty with our observations and notes. Without touching Paulinus’s phrasing—for it is a religious duty neither to add even the smallest note to the writings of the ancient Fathers nor to remove one—we shall attempt to explain obscure words, clarify meanings confused by defective orthography, examine the passages cited from Scripture or the Fathers, and indicate the sources from which they were drawn.

We have also addressed the inconvenience that usually arises from an extended and uninterrupted reading by adding headings and numbering the chapters, something lacking in Andrea du Chesne’s first edition of Paulinus. Use our work, kind reader, if you wish; if not, set it aside. You will still have Paulinus whole and pure.]

## THREE BOOKS AGAINST FELIX, BISHOP OF URGELL

Drawn from the library of the most distinguished Putean brothers, the sons of Claudius V., a celebrated Parisian senator [Note: **Drawn out.** By André du Chesne, and published in the *Works of Alcuin*, Paris, 1617, Additional volume, column 1761], and illustrated with observations and notes; they appear to have been written in the year 796.

## LETTER OF SAINT PAULINUS TO KING CHARLES CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOKS

[Col. 0343A] To the most glorious lord Charles, more gloriously distinguished by triumphal crowns granted by the Lord, most vigorous cultivator of the orthodox faith, exalted by the height of royal majesty: Paulinus, though unworthy, servant of the servants of God, little door of the Catholic and holy See of Aquileia [Col. 0344A].

[Note: **Little door of the See of Aquileia.** *Valvae*, words used in Latin only in the plural, are gates consisting of two hinged and folding parts. Those standing at them were called *Valvasores* by writers on feudal matters; Balbus also calls them barons. See Jean Claveau, *Legal Lexicon*, under this word.

Perhaps Paulinus wished to call himself this because he himself, like a door securely barred, kept heresy from entering the Church of Aquileia; or because, like a vigilant doorkeeper, he kept watch at the gates. For sometimes the office itself of porter was called a “door,” as may be gathered from the privilege granted to the monastery of Arras at the Council of Vermer, around the year 866: “He appointed [him] to the gate of Verneuil,” that is, to the office itself of monastic porter, as du Cange records in his *Glossary*, from this and other authorities cited there.

He may also have called himself a “little door” as an expression of humility. Unless one prefers to suppose that he said he had been placed as a guardian at the gates, not *valviculam* (“little door”) but *valvicolam* (“gate-dweller”), just as we say *ruricola* for one who lives in the countryside, *coelicola* for one who dwells in heaven, and *terricola* for one who dwells on earth, and similar formations.

When he adds “in the red sprinkling of blood,” he either alludes to the blood of the lamb with which the Hebrews’ doors were marked, and which the destroying angel of Egypt revered and passed over, as in Exodus XII, 7; or to the blood of the covenant with which Moses sprinkled the people (Exod. XXIV, 8), and with which he also sprinkled the book, as in Hebrews IX, 19. Thus he seems to indicate that the Church of Aquileia—or his book, by which he confronted the heretics—was protected by the sprinkling of the blood of Christ, the Lamb of God; that is, fortified by the grace of Christ. Or finally, by this sprinkling of blood he prays for the king’s salvation, namely, that eternal salvation which has been obtained for us through the merits of Christ’s blood.]

He wishes salvation in the crimson sprinkling of purer, precious blood [Note: **Of richer blood.** That is, purer and more genuine. *Merum* is what is unmixed and pure—in a word, what has nothing added to it. Terence, in the *Phormio*: “He has nothing except pure hope”; Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book II: “Behold, Socrates has arisen, the teacher of them all, from whose school, as from the Trojan horse, the pure leaders came forth.” These passages are found in Nonius under the letter M.

The same is true of *meracus*, from which undiluted wine is called *meracum*. Horace, Book II of the *Epistles*, verse 407, Epistle 2:

> “He drove out the disease with hellebore, and the bile with unmixed wine.”

Cicero too, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book III, calls purer wine *meracius*:

> “If a physician knew that a sick man who had been ordered to drink wine would drink it unmixed and immediately die, he would be greatly at fault.”

Paulinus therefore calls the blood “richer,” just as Lucretius, Book I, verse 260, calls milk *merum*:

> “The new offspring  
> Plays in pure milk, its young mind struck with wonder.”

That is, it was to say that salvation was obtained from pure, unmixed blood—that is, from Christ alone—for, as the Apostle Peter says in Acts IV, 12: “There is salvation in no other.” And in his First Epistle I, 18: “You were not redeemed with perishable gold or silver, but with the precious blood of Christ, like that of an unblemished lamb.”]



[Col. 0345A] When I had reverently examined the sacred syllables of your reverend writings and reread them repeatedly, as the sweetness of their flavor required, their savor became nourishment in my mouth, like sweet honey [Note: **In my mouth like sweet honey.** Ezekiel XXXIII: “I ate it, and it became in my mouth like sweet honey.” See also Revelation X, 10], and like somewhat dark, honeyed drops from a honeycomb dripping with sweetness there [Note: **Of a honeycomb dripping with flowing sweetness.** Perhaps *ibifluus*, a compound from the local adverb *ibi* (“there”) and *fluo* (“flow”), as in *mellifluus* (“honey-flowing”) and *imbrifluus* (“rain-flowing”); or perhaps one should read *hyblifluus*. Honey from Hybla was famous and proverbial.] poured into my throat [Note: **Drops of honeyed, somewhat darkened sweetness.** For *subfuscae*. Honey and its drops are not truly dark, but somewhat dark in color, or tending toward dark. Thus one says *subacidus* (“somewhat sour”), *subgravis* (“somewhat heavy”), *subniger* (“somewhat black”), and *subflavus* (“somewhat yellow”), meaning moderately sour, heavy, black, yellow, and so forth], the taste of sweetness undoubtedly took possession of my entire self, insofar as this was fitting.

But when the harsh clamor of the perfidious sect of Felix—or rather of unhappy and perverse supporter of a dogma—was carried through the empty air, it did not cease to strike the ears of my humility [Note: **Did not cease to strike the ears.** Here *multare* means “to beat,” “to strike,” and, if you wish, even “to wound.” Terence uses it in the last sense in the *Adelphoe*, Act I, Scene II, verse 90:

> “He beat the master himself and the whole household,
> and did not kill them.”

“Wounding the ears” is a common expression. Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*, verse 1434:

> “What heavenly sound strikes our ears?”

And verse 1441:

> “Whence does the sound strike my trembling ears?”],

my flesh immediately turned to bitterness, and the vital organs of my breathing inner parts stiffened as though poisoned drink had been poured into them. Thus I immediately grew pale, my inward man’s lung having been corrupted. The roseate glow of beauty suffused over the face I behold in a wonderful manner declares that, once the pestilent bout of bile-vomiting bitterness has been cast off, the capacious receptacles of my stomach [Col. 0345B] [Note: **Receptacles of the stomach capable of receiving it.** For *capacia*. Something is *capabile* if it can be received, just as something is *capax* if it can contain. Du Cange shows in his *Glossary*, among other examples, that this word was sometimes used with its meaning reversed, citing this authority of Paulinus], have been cooled in a marvelous manner, as the blush of beauty suffused over my face, which I have contemplated, makes clear.

Therefore, once the liver of my mind had been cleansed by being sprinkled with a bundle of hyssop [Note: **The liver sprinkled with a bundle of hyssop.** For *asperso*. He alludes to Hebrews IX, 19: “Having sprinkled the people with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop”], and once a cataplasm of scarlet wool entwined around cedar wood had been applied with a brush [Note: **With a brush used as a cataplasm.** *Cataplasma*, says Gorræus, cited by N. Stephanus, *Thesaurus Linguae Graecae*, vol. III, col. 351, is “a soft medicine of moderate consistency, used to repel, concoct, digest, resolve, loosen, evacuate, cleanse, warm, dry, and relieve pain.” Thicker and drier preparations are called *emplastra* and waxed plasters; more liquid ones are called *synchysmata* and ointments. A medicine is something applied by smearing it on. Hence *cataplasmare* means “to smear on.” The Interpreter uses this word at Isaiah LVIII, 21: “And Isaiah ordered them to take a mass of figs and apply it as a poultice to the ulcer, and it was healed.”

John the monk also used the word, as du Cange reports in Book II of the *Life of Saint Odo, Abbot of Cluny*, and in an allegory not unlike that of our Paulinus: “By these and similar examples he poulticed the wound of my mind and depravity.”

A *peniculum*, or *penicillum*, is “that with which wounds are packed, either so that they do not close or so that they may be opened further; such brushes are made from scraps of linen, elder pith, or sponge.” Pliny: “Then the open wound with a brush.” Celsus: “Next, small brushes are to be inserted.” Thus in the *Thesaurus Linguae Latinae*.

We commonly call this a *taste*, and perhaps it is the same as the *turundae* that Cato calls them in *On Agriculture*, chapter 157: “If there is a fistula, push in a plug; if it will not receive the plug, dilute it.”

Unless, perhaps, *cataplasmato peniculo* means a brush dipped in a poultice. It is called *peniculum* from *penis*, “tail,” because it is made from the end of tails, as Festus explains under the word *penem*. Wounds are commonly treated more gently with such brushes or sponges smeared with oil and ointment. This interpretation seems more consistent with Paulinus, who joins the poulticed brush to scarlet wool entwined around wood.]

I shall offer him, as an act of charity, a golden cup shining with yellow radiance—not that Babylonian cup (Rev. XVII, 4–5) from which all nations have been given to drink, but the one in the Lord’s hand, full of pure wine mingled with mixture, which is poured from this into that, whose dregs have not been emptied (Ps. LXXIV, 8–9).

And although all the sinners of the earth drink from it, for some it is a taste of life leading to life, and for others a taste of death leading to death (II Cor. II, 16). There is no death in it, but life. Yet death and life are in the mouth of the one who drinks from it, according to the disposition and religious faith with which one drinks.

If, therefore, someone, with a holy mind and transparent sincerity of Catholic faith, drinks from it, he lives with life and shall not die [Note: **“He lives with life and shall not die.”** Ezekiel’s passage reads *vita vivet* (“the living one shall live”), which agrees with the following *non morietur* (“he shall not die”). Here, and below, Paulinus always has *vita vivit* (“he lives with life”). Perhaps this is because the one who lives by the life of faith, who believes rightly, shall not die an everlasting death, according to the Gospel saying: “Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved”—which, however, must be understood on the condition that he maintains faith through works] (Ezek. XVIII, 21).

But if someone, with a darkened mind and enslaved to the error of perfidy, drinks from it, he shall die by death and shall not live (ibid. 13). For the morsel bestowed by the Lord’s hand was not death, nor was it infected with the violence of Satan’s deadly power; rather, it was active in the soul of the betrayer. For from the same source from which Judas suffered the intolerable punishments of eternal death (John XIII, 27), the blessed Apostles, who by faith were worthy to receive a portion of bread from the Lord’s hand, obtained the joy of eternal life and possess without end the reward of the heavenly kingdom.

Finally, when any Catholic, with the Lord’s hand bestowing it, has drunk from the cup of sacred Scripture with right faith, devoted mind, and sound understanding, and has believed that our Lord Jesus Christ is true God and the true Son of God, truly begotten from the true God, and truly human, truly born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; that he is one and the same God and man, one and the same Son of God and Son of man, one from both natures and one in both natures, not two Gods, and not two but one Son of God—he lives with life and shall not die.

“If you believe in your heart,” says the Apostle, “that the Lord Jesus Christ is God, and confess with your mouth that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved” (Rom. X, 9).

But whoever drinks from this cup of Scripture with a treacherous mouth, an evil heart, and a perverse mind, and dares, like this heretic, to chatter with a perfidious voice that our Lord Jesus Christ, because of the great mystery of piety, is a titular God and an adoptive son—that person shall die by death and does not live.

[Col. 0347B] Therefore, urged by the most salutary commands of your venerable writings, I do not refuse, according to the understanding of my insignificance—even though the capacity of my slower intellect stands in the way—to write, in whatever style I can, what concerns me in the cause of the faith against the objections of this pestilential and perverse doctrine. For I know who said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX, 9).

Finally, probable judgments concerning these matters compel the suspicion that, at some future time, either by the man himself, if his life continues, or through his accomplices, if he has been removed from this light by the just judgment of God, he will attempt to plant again the shoot of this poisonous stock in a rejuvenated, branch-bearing shrub (IV Kings IV, 16).

Accordingly, since the fault of my slow delay in responding necessarily arose from an intervening cause, the hope of obtaining pardon for this neglect will waver in one who asks for it, disappointed by the torpor of delay [Note: **“The hope will not be shaken.”** This is equivalent to “the hope will be shaken.” But do not let such stylistic defects delay you: for Paulinus was concerned with being understood, not with the rules of Latin].

Therefore, taking precautions for the future, I thought it not inappropriate to meet, one by one, the things inserted in any of his writings that appear contrary to the rule of Catholic faith, both with testimonies from Scripture and with arguments based solely and reasonably on the limits of human capacity. If anything in them has been stated correctly, let it remain strengthened by our assertions. Excepting those matters which either seem to have no importance or do not appear to belong more suitably to this subject and therefore did not readily offer themselves for treatment by our refuting style.

Finally, although not with precious hands—for they are not clean from the filth of sin—but nevertheless with precious gifts drawn from the sacred treasures of Scripture, I have judged it best to offer before the manger of my Lord, with a full and supplicating heart, these three little books [Note: **To offer the gift of three books before the manger of my Lord.** He alludes to the three gifts offered to the Lord by the Magi (Matt. II, 11)], according to what is prescribed by the Lord’s law: “You shall not appear three times a year empty before the Lord your God” (Deut. XVI, 16).

Therefore I deemed it unworthy to appear three times in this year—which figuratively signifies the whole period of the present life—empty before my Lord. By this year I mean, to speak more plainly, the year of my conscience, which is reckoned as revolving through the four returning seasons by means of the four cardinal virtues: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice.

For through the five outward senses of the body, which when multiplied together complete the sum of the number ten [Perhaps: “the sum”], and to which two are added—namely, the substance of soul and body—the number twelve is produced. It is as though, through the twelve lunar divisions of the months, the moon repeatedly unfolds its returning courses.

To these are also added the three principal effects of natural moral life: heart, soul, and mind, as in the saying: “with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Mark XII, 30). Through these, one hundred multiplied by three depicts the figure of the number three hundred.

To these are joined the six distinctions of the ages [Note: **Six distinctions of the ages.** Not everyone agrees. Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 14, says that Varro thought the stages of life divided equally into five, each except the last lasting fifteen years.

Macrobius, in the *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, takes seven. For in Book I, chapter 6, he says: “This is the number, namely seven, which causes a human being to be conceived, formed, born, live, be nourished, pass through all the stages of life into old age, and altogether continue in existence.”

Philo the Jew, in *On the Creation of the World*, says that Hippocrates likewise makes seven stages of human life. Solon makes ten, and Philo there quotes his elegy containing this division.

Saint Ambrose, Letter 44, Class I, in the latest edition, following Hippocrates’ view, concludes in favor of a sevenfold division: “There is therefore an infant, a child, an adolescent, a young man, a man, a veteran, and an old man.”

Galen, cited by Caelius Rhodiginus in *Ancient Readings*, Book XIX, chapter 21, establishes four ages altogether: “the young, the vigorous, the middle-aged, and the old.” This is also Pythagoras’ view, as reported by Laërtius, Book VIII.

Servius Tullius, as Gellius recounts from Tubero in *Attic Nights*, Book X, chapter 28, recognized only three ages: children up to the seventeenth year; juniors from the seventeenth year to the forty-sixth; and seniors beyond that.

Aristotle in *Rhetoric*, Book II, chapter 15, text 1, does not differ, saying: “The ages are youth, vigor” (so Sigonius translates it; Majoragius has “adolescence” and “middle age), “and old age.”

From these examples you can see that there is no single opinion concerning the division of the ages of our life. Paulinus’s division seems the best of all. It neither exceeds nor falls short; the divisions above and below this number seem to suffer from one or the other defect.]

—that is, infancy, childhood, and so forth—which, multiplied six times by ten, forms the sum of the number sixty [Perhaps here too: “the sum”].

Into these are inserted, in successive degrees, the distinct qualities of moral life belonging to various rational thoughts, such as hope, faith, charity, and similar things. Their quantity, multiplied as though by the reckoning of many days, rises, as it were, into the height of our year of three hundred sixty-six days [Note: **“The height of our year of three hundred sixty-six days.”** The number of days in a year is ordinarily only 365, with the addition of five hours and forty-nine minutes. This addition of hours gave rise to the leap year, which has 366 days. These facts are sufficiently familiar to anyone even slightly acquainted with the reckoning of time.

Thus, when someone asks how many days a year contains, the ordinary answer should be 365, not 366, since it has that number only every fourth year, when it is a leap year.

Since this is so, how could our Paulinus—who certainly was not ignorant of these matters—mention the days of the year more than once in this letter and always speak of 366 days? I confess that I was briefly troubled by the novelty of the matter. But since I was convinced that Paulinus could not have erred through ignorance, especially in so familiar a matter, I finally concluded that the only possible explanation was that Paulinus wrote this letter in a leap year and stated the number of days with reference to the year in which he was writing.

Once this conjecture is accepted—which I trust no one will reject—it seems possible to establish with certainty the year in which the letter was given. That year was 796, which agrees perfectly with the other circumstances. For these books were undoubtedly written after the Council of Frankfurt in 794 and before the year 799, as will be said in the dissertation on the Felician heresy. No other leap year occurred between these limits except 796. Therefore the letter must be held to have been written in that year.]

This is perhaps the crown of the perfection of the year to which the Psalmist recalls that God has given and continues to give blessing: “You will bless the crown of the year with your goodness” (Ps. LXIV, 12).

For the crown of the year is the perfection of completed righteousness. This crown of perfection belongs not to the one who wills or runs, but to God’s goodness and mercy (Rom. IX, 16). Therefore the fields of God—that is, the minds of the humble elect—will be filled with abundance not from themselves, but from the goodness of the merciful God.

In this year, then, the mercy of divine goodness bestowing abundant plenty, so that I might not appear empty before the Lord three times, I hasten to store three books in the treasury of the sanctuary with a faithful hand, books produced, though in an uncultivated style, in the name of the Holy Trinity.

This, then, is how I think this year should be understood morally. Allegorically, however, it is understood as being given by our Redeemer in a more excellent and sacred manner [Perhaps: “more holy and more sacred”]. In it, the twelve Apostles are like the twelve months, and all his elect are like the sum of many days, contained through this sacred number—namely 366—as though joined together in a single body.

He himself is signified by the one who declares through the prophet Isaiah concerning himself:

> “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of redemption of our God” (Isa. LXI, 1–2).

Amen.

## 99. SAINT PAULINUS, BOOK ONE AGAINST FELIX

[Col. 0349]

### CHAPTER ONE. He sets forth the lamentations of the grieving Church.

Our voice—the voice of one and the same chanting dove (Song II, 10) and of her chosen mother, rejoicing and grieving—has been heard in the land in renowned proclamation:

> “But now he has exalted my head above my enemies” (Ps. XXVI, 6);

and:

> “But now those younger in age mock me, whose fathers I did not deem worthy to place among the dogs of my flock” (Job XXX, 1).

At another time, when she was surrounded on every side by various anxieties because of the afflictions of her tender offspring, she recalls the days of her youth (Ezek. XVI, 22), when, having brought forth over her kinsman, she rejoiced more securely with an eager heart.

By the service of a voice expressing desire, from the secret breaths, as it were, flowing from the innermost parts, the abundant conversations of her mouth have poured down to the middle of the neck (Isa. XXX, 28). Against this no contrary objection can resist the undeniable saying:

And thus, in the manner of a torrent of honey and butter, she sets forth through words of prayer the oracle of her prolonged recollection:

> “Who will grant me that I might be as in the former months, according to the days when God guarded me? When his lamp shone over my head, and by his light I walked in darkness? As I was in the days of my youth, when God was secretly in my tabernacle? When the Almighty was with me, and my children were all around me?” (Job XXIX, 2 and following).

Having reviewed these and similar prosperous favors with a heart full of gratitude and rejoicing, she immediately turns to lamentations over her dangers:

> “But now,” she says, “those younger in age mock me, whose fathers I did not deem worthy to place among the dogs of my flock; whose hand-strength was of no account to me, and who were considered unworthy even of life; barren through poverty and hunger, they gnawed in the wilderness, filthy with calamity and misery; they ate the herbs of the earth and the bark of trees, and the root of junipers was their food. But now I have become the subject of their song and have become their byword,” and so forth (Job XXX, 1 and following).

### CHAPTER II. The heretics, enemies of the Church, are sons of the devil.

Who are these young men of a hundred years who indulge themselves? (Isa. LXV, 20.) “O most beautiful among women, who are these?” O sole one of your mother! (Song VI, 8.)

A dove because of the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit; beautiful in blood; made white in the washing; a sister in the bond of charity; a close companion in the fellowship of assumed nature; sweet in the delights of Scripture.

Who are these who cannot escape the curse of the child of a hundred years? Whom, with such confidence in unrestricted authority, have you judged unworthy to be companions of the simple dogs of your flock?

That the holy dogs of your flock are the most sacred dogs of a certain group of your fathers [Alternative reading: “their fathers”], for whom sons were born to you (Ps. XLIV, 17), we have learned by prophetic utterance. For this kind of ten-stringed Psalter of David resounds:

> “The tongue of your dogs from your enemies, from him. The processions of my God have been seen” (Ps. LXVII, 24–25).

[Col. 0351A] These, then, are the most famous dogs [Note: **“These most famous dogs.”** Paulinus seems to have taken this allegory of dogs from Saint Gregory, *Morals*, Book XX, chapter 9, where he explains the passage from Job that Paulinus cited: “Whose fathers I did not deem worthy to place among the dogs of my flock.”], whose processions of God have been seen. It is certainly beyond doubt that they perform the shepherd’s office toward the sheepfolds in a wonderful manner: the rage of savage beasts, with holy—if one may say so—[far] from the sheepfolds [sentence fragment in the supplied text] [Note: **“Far from the sheepfolds.”** Just as *ovile* is derived from *ovis* (“sheep”), so Paulinus derives *mandrile* from *mandra*, an otherwise uncommon word. The Latins use *mandra* for a group of pack animals. Martial, Book V, epigram 23, verse 202:

> “And scarcely is one able to overcome the long troops of mules.”

The word was also sometimes used for the stable in which animals were shut up. H. Stephanus, *Thesaurus Linguae Graecae*, vol. IV, col. 1413:

> “Μάνδρα (*mandra*) is a stable or enclosed enclosure, a fenced place in which animals are shut up at night. For Hesychius, μάνδρας are σηκοὶ βοῶν καὶ ἵππων ἕρκη, that is, enclosures of oxen and horses, and also φραγμοί, fences; besides, ὕλας, woods. It is interpreted not only as a stable or sheepfold, but also as a cave; likewise as a place where wine presses are located and grapes are squeezed. The word μάνδρευμα is also found for a sheepfold.”

The Latins used it for an enclosure. In the game of *latrunculi*, the enclosure in which the pieces were held shut was called a *mandra*, as Lucan suggests in his little poem to Calpurnius Piso, speaking of this game, especially verse 191:

> “So that, swift, it may burst forth from the broken ranks of the enclosure.”

From this you will understand Martial, Book VII, epigram 71, verse 550:

> “So may you conquer both Novius and Publius,
> shut up in enclosures with the glass robber.”

From *mandra* came *mandritae*, the name for monks, and *archimandritae*, the name for abbots presiding over them, because at the beginning monks were shut up in caves or enclosed places as though in a *mandra*. Du Cange shows from several sources that a monastery was sometimes called a *mandra*, especially from Alcuin’s Book II, *On the Life of Saint Willibrord*:

> “Therefore this vigilant man encircles the sheepfolds with this protection.”]

For these deserved names, to enlarge Christ’s fold. Not far removed from this derivation is what Budaeus has in the same place, namely, that monasteries were called *mandrae*, “from the flock of monks, over which abbots preside as shepherds over a *mandra*, that is, a sheepfold.” The archimandrites are mentioned in canon 7 of the Council of Fréjus convened by Paulinus. [Note: If you wish to see anything further of this kind, consult the notes there, letter a.] They do not fear restraining the flocks of such men by their barking.

But who are the fathers of those rebellious young men whom you were ashamed to associate with the venerable dogs of your flock? We are still asking; and, as we ask, the intention of finding them is already revealing itself. Were not the ancient heresiarchs the furious fathers of these pestilential young detractors of yours—Arius, namely, Macedonius, Sabellius, Eunomius, Nestorius, Eutyches, together with their followers, whom the fixed and authoritative denunciation of the Catholic faith judged, with deserved censures, to be alien from the fellowship of your venerable dogs? They themselves, without doubt, and these sons of darkness were propagated from their accursed offspring.

Indeed, we may learn all the sooner from the friends of the bridegroom—“who stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29)—from what root this most wicked and pestilential offspring derives its kind. “Brood,” he says, “of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke 3:7.) By a transferred use of the word, he intended the parent and the offspring to be designated, the one by “viper,” the other by “brood.” Thus, through the pattern of this likeness, it might plainly be understood that from a poisonous root—a shrub of thorny tamarisk—there had grown a sorcerous offspring.

[Note: A poisonous shrub has emerged from the tamarisk. The allegory fits excellently. “For,” says Pliny, *Natural History* 13.21, “we call tamarisks unlucky trees … which, when brought into a house, are said to cause difficult births and miserable deaths.” Hence Strabo, concerning the Magi of Persia, *Geography* 15: “They utter imprecations,” he says, “while holding a bundle of slender tamarisk rods.” Indeed, in Jeremiah 17:5–6, the sinner exposed to divine curses is described thus: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, and makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. For he shall be like a tamarisk in the desert.” It is a plant of ill omen, since Nicander in the third book of the *Theriaca*, line 612, calls it πανάκαρπος, “utterly fruitless”:

> Καὶ μυρίκης λάζεο νέον πανακαρπέα θάμνον.

“And take the newly grown, utterly fruitless tamarisk shrub.” For whom else could these words more suitably apply than to the sort of men whom Paulinus attacks here?]

Perhaps Scripture records the iniquity of such forebears as being visited upon their children to the third and fourth generation. Such men, certainly—and the order of truthful reasoning permits no doubt—are called their sons because of their pestilential imitation of their faithless fathers. I would therefore regard them as the sons of such fathers more appropriately than as their carnal sons.

“ The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20). For this reason Truth itself reproaches the Jews in the Gospel—those who had degenerated from the original nobility of their ancestor—as diabolical sons, with honeyed speech. For he says: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8:44). He makes the reason for saying this still clearer when he immediately adds: “And you wish to do the works of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning” (ibid.).

From these words it is made clearer than daylight that he did not wish them to be called sons of the devil naturally, [Note: “Not naturally.” As the Archontics dreamed, who said that the devil “approached Eve and had intercourse with her just as a man ordinarily does with a woman, and from her begot Cain and Abel.” Against them, see the holy Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 40.] nor as though they had been created by him, [Note: “Nor as though created by him.” As the Manichaeans maintained; Augustine frequently refutes their madness, especially in *Tractate* 42 on John, section 10.] nor even by adoption, [Note: “Nor even by adoption.” Since adoption is an act of love—whence Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists* 2.3: “For no one is absurdly said to have begotten, not by flesh but by love, one whom he has adopted as a son”—and since the devil pursues human beings not with love but with hatred, those whom he makes his own he treats as slaves, not as sons.] but because they imitated [Note: “But because they imitated the cunning of diabolical deceit.” Augustine, *Tractate* 42 on John, section 10: “Whence are the Jews sons of the devil? By imitating, not by being born.”] the tricks of diabolical deceit, he rightly wished them to be called sons of the devil. [Note: “He wished them to be called.” Should one read *voluisse* instead?]

## CHAPTER III. The Church triumphs over the heretics.

[Col. 0353A]

Was not the devil the father of the most wretched Arius and his associates, who, by an adulterous embrace, poured the poisonous seed of faithlessness into the womb of their corrupted minds through a pestilential coupling? And so, conceived and formed from so secret an intercourse, the son of perdition emerged; as though from a mother’s womb, with a most shameless tongue acting as midwife, there proceeded offspring destined to be handed over to the fires of eternal Gehenna. In precisely the same way he begot sons like himself, destined to be punished by a similar vengeance.

And because the Catholic faith has decreed that all who are entangled in their errors are to be struck by the same curse of condemnation by which they were struck—unless the remedy of repentance intervenes—the deception of the father’s iniquity is, as it were, transmitted to the children by hereditary right down to the third and fourth generation. This passage concerning the third and fourth generation may also be explained otherwise, with a more elaborate adornment demanded by the subtlety of an acute intellect. [Note:]

[Col. 0353C]

“An adorned theme.” Terence’s Dorio in *Phormio* 3.2, line 498, said:

> Are you so thoughtless and shameless, Phaedria,  
> That you lead me on with adorned words …?

Donatus explains: “With adorned words, that is, honorable and embellished words.” See what we have said elsewhere, namely in the notes on the Council of Fréjus, section 7, letter a.

Throughout nearly this entire work, the following spelling practice is observed: in compound words, the component particles from which they are formed are kept intact. This comes closer to ancient orthography. For, except in a few cases where harsh combinations required a change for the sake of euphony, writers almost always observed this practice, as is especially clear from coins and inscriptions. But consult the grammarians on these matters; one warning must suffice.]

Yet since, because of the wars of the enemies threatening us, we are hastening as quickly as possible to spiritual arms—lest, while we wander into trivialities, the enemy ranks suddenly and unexpectedly shatter the Church’s gates by a headlong attack—we have therefore decreed, with the most diligent care, that, while the armed soldier is at hand, the duties of the watches should be distinguished only by a fourfold alternation.

Thus, during the morning watch, the hand of Moses, raised at God’s command, together with the Lord’s rod which had represented the victorious banners of the cross, may overturn the wheels of the chariots, and by divine power violently engulf their horsemen and riders amid the waves of the Red Sea (Exodus 14:24 ff.). Let the prophetess Miriam therefore take up the tambourine. Although, in her reviling of Moses, the man of God, she had represented the envious Synagogue, in this place she nevertheless bore the figure of the holy Church. Let her immediately break into a voice of praise—not, as though exhorting to battle, making a trumpet resound with broken blasts, but beginning with grateful lips the song of victory, while other women sing along:

> Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified;  
> he has cast horse and rider into the sea.  
> He has become my helper and protector for salvation.  
> (Exodus 15:20–21.)

## CHAPTER IV. The heretics are serpents.

[Col. 0354A]

After the Egyptians had been submerged in the Red Sea—where not only the hosts of sinners beneath the baptismal waters, but also, not inappropriately, the extinguished communities of heretics may be understood [perhaps: “may be understood” in the plural, *dantur*]—behold, as we depart and have already crossed the Red Sea, a poisonous throng of serpents meets us in the vast wilderness of the world. They will burst forth from the pestilential eggs of those men, which they have abandoned in the nest of faithlessness.

Of these eggs Isaiah says: “They have broken the eggs of asps, and they weave spiders’ webs. Whoever eats of their eggs will die, and what has been warmed has burst forth [alternative: “will burst forth,” *erumpet*] as a basilisk” (Isaiah 59:5). But so that we may not fear such serpent poisons, as we look upon the bronze serpent that Moses raised up (Numbers 21:9), the same prophet also consoles us: through the infancy of a singularly born child, he records the extinguished blasts of the deadly venom of an asp or basilisk.

“The infant at the breast,” he says, “shall play over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand into the den of the basilisk. They shall not kill, nor shall they harm, on all my holy mountain” (Isaiah 11:8). To this child another prophet says: “You shall walk upon the asp and the basilisk, and you shall trample the lion and the dragon” (Psalm 90:13). Hence elsewhere the trumpet of prophetic song resounds concerning the same one: “His spirit adorned the heavens, and by his hand the twisting serpent was brought forth” (Job 26:13).

But who this wondrous infant is who plays over the hole of the asp and puts his hand into the den of the basilisk, I learned from the angel announcing the signs of his birth to the shepherds: “You will find,” he says, “an infant wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger” (Luke 2:12). And the multitude of the heavenly host sing with a harmonious voice, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to men of good will” (ibid. 14).

And since it is certain that, on the whole mountain of the Lord—which [perhaps: “who”] is the Church of the living God—the blasts of these pestilences cannot do harm, the greatest care must be taken lest, as they wander through the open country, they be found by those who are stifled by them. [Note: “Be found by those who are stifled.” The sense is obscure. Nevertheless, I think it means this: care must be taken lest the faithful be found wandering through the open country by those who suffocate the faithful. [Col. 0354C] Moreover, *offocentur* may perhaps be read instead of *offucentur*. *Offucare*, according to Festus, means “to give water into the throat for swallowing,” which does not fit the present passage. *Offocare*, however, like *suffocare*, is derived from *fauces*, “throat,” and has a similar meaning. Florus, book 2, chapter 2: “When they had offered their throats to one another to be strangled.” Augustine also uses the word in *Confessions* 5.2: “But those bodily masses, which oppressed me as I contemplated them, seized me and, in a way, suffocated me, so that, gasping beneath them, I could not breathe into the clear and simple air of your truth.” The word seems suitably applied to serpents, since Virgil likewise describes Laocoön as so tightly bound by snakes that he was suffocated, *Aeneid* 2.218:

> Twice they encircled his middle, twice their scaly coils  
> were wrapped around his neck; they tower above him with head  
> and lofty necks.

Thus, in Paulinus, *offucare* appears to mean the same as *offocare*, or *suffocare*, as we learn can also be said of serpents from Virgil’s example.]

For this reason, I think it necessary to lead them all back to the mountains, lest, wandering among the precipices of the deep valleys, they suffer harm from an unexpected assault, as though from a robber rushing upon them.

## CHAPTER V. He complains of Felix, the breaker of his pledged treaty, concerning the councils attended by Charlemagne and Paulinus himself.

[Col. 0355A]

102 Having arranged these matters, we thought it worthwhile to pass from the genus to the species and to return from the fellowship of the general community to the privilege of one’s particular right. Let us therefore attack—supported in every respect by divine assistance—this shameless man, whom the quality of the matters at issue proves, by certain and effective evidence, to have been long ago defeated by the contest of the arena. [Note: “The shameless man whom the contest of the arena, etc.” The sentence is quite corrupt. The reading was *inscio visum*, which the first editor noticed and replaced in the margin with *inscium*. Likewise, for *qui devictus* he restored *quem devictum*. Here too *palaestri certamini* seems to require correction to *palaestrae certamini* or *palaestrico certamini*. Otherwise he aptly calls the debate held with Felix a contest of the wrestling-ground, since *palaestra* signifies not only the place where athletes and boxers exercise themselves, but also the place where philosophers debate. Vitruvius testifies to this in book 5, chapter 2: “In three porticoes are established spacious exedrae with seats, in which philosophers, rhetoricians, and others devoted to study may sit and debate.” Among rhetoricians, too, the middle style of speech—between the excessively vigorous and the excessively slack—was metaphorically called *palaestric*. Hence Cicero, in the *Brutus*, or *On Famous Orators*, praising Demetrius of Phalerum for this style of speaking, says: “Phalereus succeeded those old men as a young man, very learned indeed in all these matters, but trained not so much in arms as in the wrestling-ground.” Not in arms—that is, not vehement and forceful in speaking, like soldiers who fight in earnest, but smooth and gentle, like wrestlers, whose contests are generally playful and taste of oil rather than blood. Therefore Cicero likewise says in *On the Orator* 1.7: “There is a certain polished and lively style of words, but it belongs more to the wrestling-ground and oil than to this civic crowd and forum.” Paulinus therefore most aptly called the debate held in the council a contest of the wrestling-ground, conducted with words drenched in the oil of charity rather than with weapons wet with blood.]

But now, by reckless daring, and—who knows at whose instigation [alternative reading: *intinctu*]—he attempts to revive and renew the wars. [Col. 0355B] Moreover, forgetting the treaty of the oath [Note: “Forgetting the treaty of the oath, etc.” Twice, or rather three times, by the time Paulinus wrote this, Felix had been convicted and condemned for his error. First, at the assembly of Regensburg in 792, which we say Paulinus attended in the dissertation *On the Heresy of Felix and Elipandus*, section 32; there Felix himself rejected the opinion condemned by the Fathers. Then at Rome, where he had been sent by the Regensburg assembly through Abbot Angilbert in the same year to Pope Hadrian; there he condemned the condemned heresy. Third, at the Council of Frankfurt in 794, which Paulinus likewise attended, the heresy was condemned for the third time, as the Frankish annalists unanimously acknowledge. Paulinus therefore rightly complains of Felix as a breaker of his pledged word, since he himself had once been present as guarantor—and, so to speak, mediator—of the oath Felix had given, as he testifies here. This proves, first, that Paulinus attended the preceding councils concerning Felix; second, that Charlemagne himself was present; and third, that these books were written after 794 and published by Paulinus. But these matters will be discussed more fully in their proper place, namely in the dissertation *On the Heresy of Felix and Elipandus*. For now, it is enough merely to mention them.]

—the oath by which he had bound himself to God, surrounded by bright throngs of thousands of angels. Nor, I think, was the multitude of the human army absent from this spectacle. [Note: “This spectacle.” For *spectaculo*, just as *exspectabilis* occurs for *spectabilis*, and *exspectare* for *spectare*, frequently among writers of the later age—that is, approximately Paulinus’s own period—cited by Du Cange in his *Glossary*, under *exspectabilis* and *exspectare*.]

Especially since this sort of controversy was being debated in the presence of the venerable prince. For, touching the most holy Gospels, he protested under oath that, as the strictness of the most sincere faith at that time required, the obscure chatter of the dispute having been silenced in suppressed silence, he would never thereafter [perhaps: do anything, *quidquam*] reopen the question by any contrary effort, under any title whatsoever; rather, he promised that he would remain perpetually and unchangeably in the rule of faith to which he had assented.

In this conflict of gymnastic debate, it also happened that our most humble insignificance was personally present. Alas! How terrible is what is said! The treaty struck with God, which did not pass unpunished when invalidated, is alleged, with the fraudulent presumption of human audacity, to have been dissolved.

But these matters must be reserved for the judgment of God.

## CHAPTER VI. He attacks Felix as a deserter from battle and as lukewarm, to be vomited out.

[Col. 0356A]

When the pact of this so venerable and ratified agreement had been broken, the wicked warrior hastens to return to the battlefield, although the Lord’s power stands in his way. I wonder with what face. For if, having received military pay in the Lord’s camp, he was being trained for arms as a tested athlete, marked with the insignia of the king, he ought not to have turned his back upon those fighting against him, so that he would not be proclaimed famous either as free because of the hiding place of flight, trembling among the bushes, or as brave because he persisted in battle. [Note: “So that he would not rather be free in the hiding place of flight, etc.” In my judgment the sentence is exceedingly obscure, unless *ut* means *quod*, or *quippe qui*. He ought not to have turned his back, so that—that is, since or because—he would be described neither as free because of flight nor as brave because he persisted. In short, he would become famous neither for the freedom achieved by flight nor for courage shown by resistance: not the former, because he was captured; not the latter, because he yielded. This seems to be Paulinus’s meaning, although the following sentence is nearly equally involved. But, he says, events occurred in such a way that he could neither flee nor resist bravely; instead, captured by his adversaries, he confessed himself bound by his own judgment and voluntary surrender. This, I think, is Paulinus’s meaning. If anyone offers a clearer and more certain interpretation, I shall gladly follow it. For the rest, I am Davus, not Oedipus.]

From this it became clear, not without reason, that the affair had occurred in such a way that he, girded with arms but perhaps deprived of the protection of flight, was captured by his pursuers and did not fear to submit himself to the judgment of the triumphant victors by a surrender that made him subject to their authority. [Note: “By a surrender that made him subject.” Does this indicate the act by which he confessed himself bound, and is it equivalent to *deditione*, “by surrender”? Or does *ditione capabili* refer to the Fathers, to whose laws, judgment, and power—or rather to whose experienced, known, and exercised authority—he did not hesitate to submit himself? Cicero likewise says in *On the Agrarian Law*, speech 2: “By this provision, Quirites, I declare that all peoples, nations, provinces, and kingdoms have been entrusted and surrendered to the authority, judgment, and power of the decemvirs.”]

Forgetful of the command of the King, the Lord of Sabaoth, who says: “Be strong in war.” Moreover, he ought to have relied upon the marvelous exhortations of a renowned leader among the Lord’s soldiers in a certain strong camp—exhortations with which, amid battles, he used to rouse the phalanxes of armies, crested, that is, with helmets of faith:

> Who will separate us from the love of Christ?  
> Tribulation? Or distress? Or famine?  
> (Romans 8:35.)

And shortly afterward:

> For I am certain that neither life nor death …  
> (ibid. 38.)

After several intervening words, he concludes in summary:

> Nor will any creature be able to separate us from the love of God,  
> which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.  
> (ibid. 39.)
