If, then, perfect love was at that time burning more fervently in the heart of his mind, it ought not to have grown cold at all. But if fear grew cold [perhaps: “through fear,” *timore*], then surely he did not possess perfect love, which casts out fear. “Perfect love,” John says, “casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Finally, it may be asked to which of the three classes of human beings this man, diminished in brain, is to be assigned. [Note: “This man, diminished in brain.” The phrase “to diminish the head or brain” is common among comic writers, Plautus and Terence, but means “to break down” or “shatter.” See the former in *Mostellaria*, line 275; the latter in *Eunuchus*, line 671, and *Adelphoe*, line 573, where it reads:

> Your brain will certainly be shattered by now.

Since the head is believed to be the seat of the soul, and the brain is in the head, and since, as Pliny says in *Natural History* 11.37, “Here they have the citadel of the senses, here the highest summit, here the government of the mind,” the container is often taken figuratively for the contained, and we use “brain” and “head” for “mind.” Thus “diminished in brain” means lacking in mind—in short, mentally deficient.]

Clearly, the third class: the lukewarm. If these things are so, he ought therefore to have been vomited from the mouth of the Lord. For it is written: “Would that you were hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth” (Revelation 3:15–16).

Rejected, therefore, from the stomach of the holy and universal Church because of the nausea of his lukewarmness, let him go with his followers into the wilderness. Let them gnaw the withered grasses of the earth and the bark of trees amid calamity and misery; let the root of juniper be their food.

For if the holy Catholic Church once disdained to place their fathers with the dogs of her flock, how much less does she consent to place their sons with them, when she knows that they are offspring and hereditary successors to their parents’ faithlessness? [Note: “She does not consent to place them, whom, etc.” The sentence seems incomplete unless one supplies: “She does not consent to place the sons where she disdained to place their fathers.” The meaning would be: If the Church disdained to place the fathers of the heretics with the dogs of her flock, how much less does she consent to place the heretics themselves there, since she knows them to be, by hereditary right, the successors of their parents’ faithlessness?]

## CHAPTER VII. Felix is to be struck down like Goliath by a stone and consumed like the Hydra by fire.

[Col. 0358A]

Let us therefore choose five very clear stones from the torrent. Casting one of them from a sling, let us pierce the shameless forehead of this swollen Goliath’s gigantic boastfulness (1 Samuel 17 and following), striking it with a blow as sharp as lightning and cutting down the double wrinkle of faithlessness. [Note: “Cut down by the double wrinkle of faithlessness.” Wrinkles on the forehead, especially those projecting above the eyebrows, indicate pride. But why “double”? Perhaps because Felix attempted to divide the unity of faith and to assert two sons or two gods, as Paulinus adds shortly afterward. Thus the wrinkle of faithlessness seems to be double.]

[Note: “The shameless forehead.” That is, reckless. Someone reckless and guided by no sense of shame is sometimes called shameless. Plautus, *Rudens*, line 397:

> Oh, shameless deed!  
> How free she must be, to demand to serve.]

Thus, struck by the wound of one stone, let him perish—he who attempts to divide the unity of the faith and, in schismatic striving, endeavors to grasp the one Lord Jesus Christ as two sons or two gods.

And so, struck down by his own sword’s point, with a Davidic hand wondrously cutting him, may he no longer be able in any way to remember [possibly: “revive,” instead of “remember”]. [Note: “May he be able to remember.” From the preceding and following context, it is obvious that an error has crept in and that *revivisci* should be restored; nevertheless, the proper form should be *reviviscere*, as we noted conjecturally in the text.]

But if, after the fabulous manner of the Hydras, he mocks us with a monstrous creature whose necks, after its three-forked heads have been cut off by the sword, have again resumed their hissing in greater number, and thus boasts that he has advanced more successfully through a loss that has, as it were, revived from its own destruction, let a fire therefore be applied to him, kindled by divine and inextinguishable flame.

[Note: “With heads cut off by a three-forked sword.” It should not be *trisulcibus*, but *trisulcis* should be read. Yet what then? The difficulty still remains. Why “three-forked heads”? I therefore think another error must also be removed, by reading *trisculco ferro*. For Naucrates says that the Hydra had seven heads, Zenodotus nine, and Heraclides fifty, as reported by Natalis Comes in book 7, chapter 1; no one says it had only three. Perhaps it is called “three-forked” because the Felician heresy had already been proscribed three times. The text also suggests [perhaps: *trisulco*] in place of *trisulcibus*.]

Thus, let the scorched veins of their rebellious marrow no longer possess the monstrous power to produce a prodigious offspring through any further infusion of infecting poison.

## CHAPTER VIII. Felix, departing from the judgment of the Fathers, follows Arius at one time and Nestorius at another.

But since defenders of the truth must nevertheless avoid the trap of falsehood with every precaution, I therefore bear witness on his behalf: for, in most cases, he seems to publish the sequence of his profession with sufficiently sound and sensible meaning, in a style that is not very degenerate.

One thing, at least, seems beyond doubt: as long as he follows the footsteps of the preceding Fathers and does not turn aside from the road trodden by their steps of right faith, he is recognized as walking with a composed gait. But whenever he boldly returns to his own opinion, he is immediately seen to wander astray through the winding paths of falling rocks, covered by the thickest darkness of excited ignorance.

Thus, at one time he strikes against the rocks of falsehoods that he had previously avoided [alternative reading: “deified falsehoods,” *deitatis falsitatum*], [Note: “The rocks of falsehoods that he had avoided.” I think this should be read in this way. The meaning is that he strikes against the rocks from which he had previously kept away. Both the preceding and following context support this conjecture. If anyone thinks otherwise, I do not object.] and at another he is seen to move about amid the precipices broken open by madness. At one time he embraces Arius, who meets him; at another he follows Nestorius, who goes before him, with errant steps.

Immediately he attempts to destroy, by a perverse effort, the things which shortly before he had boasted of building through laborious struggle. Accordingly, insofar as can presently be understood, he is convicted of having placed his foundation upon the husks of rolling gravel, not upon a firm rock. [Note: “Upon the husks of rolling gravel.” Festus: “*Gluma* is the husk of barley, so called because the grain is stripped from it; hence an animal is also called *glubi*, because its hide is removed.” Varro, *On Agriculture* 1.48: “The *gluma* is the husk of the grain. The awn, thin and long like a needle, projects from the *gluma*. Thus the *gluma* is the grain’s sheath and the awn its tip. The awn and grain are known to almost everyone; the *gluma* to few. … The word seems to derive its origin from *glubere*, because the grain is stripped from that husk.” Aldhelm, *On Virginity* 9, uses not *gluma* but *glumula*: “Although some customarily assign to the martyrs the sheaves of hundredfold fruit sprouting abundantly in the Gospel fields and producing the little husks of grain-bearing ears.” But what has this to do with gravel? Nothing at all. Here, I confess, the water stopped and I found myself unequal to resolving the knot, until the timely thought occurred to me that some error, through the carelessness of copyists or scribes, might have entered the text, and that *grumos* should be read instead of *glumas*. The similarity of the words seems to have caused the mistake. Let the reader weigh and judge. If, as I suspect, *grumos* rather than *glumas* should be written, the meaning is obvious. Festus: “A *grumus* is a small gathering of earth, smaller than a hill.” Nonius: “A *grumus* is called a field, and is so named from a heap.” Columella, *On Agriculture* 2.18, explaining how sown earth was formerly to be leveled to the flat and even surface of meadows, says: “Then we shall break up the clods with hoes, level them with the harrow drawn over them, and scatter the *grumi* that harrows usually make when they are dragged across the furrow.” With this understood, Paulinus aptly spoke of the *grumi* of rolling gravel. He wished to reproach Felix’s foolishness by means of his own stupidity, according to Matthew 7:24: “He built his house not upon rock but upon sand; and the rain descended, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they struck that house; and it fell, and great was its ruin.”]

Therefore, when the rains poured down and the winds drove against it, the suspended building, battered by them, collapsed. Indeed, he thought that he possessed instruments of song, like David (Amos 6:5), and therefore boasted that he had scattered Solomon’s radiant golden apples upon silver couches (Proverbs 25:11).

And although they had been secretly stolen from the Lord’s treasury, they were nevertheless mixed with another kind of metal by the worst sort of adulteration, [Note: “Mixed with another kind of metal by the worst adulteration.” I am aware that a *caupo* is one who sells food and drink for profit, and that *cauponari* means to seek profit by the trade of a tavern keeper. In the fragments of Ennius, line 256, those who seek gain from war are called *cauponantes*:

> I ask neither gold nor payment from you,  
> nor that you should traffic in war, but wage war,  
> let us both value life by iron, not gold.

Nevertheless, I think Paulinus uses the word in another sense, namely from the adulteration of wine with water, which tavern keepers very often practice to defraud buyers. Hence I believe *pessimo cauponatu*, “by the worst adulteration,” should be read rather than *pessimo cauponato*. The meaning is that the golden apples—that is, doctrines—which Felix took from the Lord’s treasury, that is, from Scripture, he adulterated by the worst practice of tavern keepers, mixing them with other metals—that is, his own errors—just as tavern keepers increase and adulterate wine by mixing in water. There is a passage in Tertullian, *On the Soul* 3, where the word is used with a similar intention. Speaking of the errors that pagan philosophy, the parent of heresies in this matter, had introduced concerning the origin of the soul—errors already foretold by the Apostle—he says: “For even then the Apostle foresaw the shaking of truth by philosophy. At Athens, having experienced that city given to talk, and having sampled all the traffickers in wisdom and eloquence there, he conceived that warning proclamation. Thus, too, concerning the soul, through philosophized doctrines, some deny immortality, mixing the waters of men with wine, while others affirm something more than immortality.”]

and, covered with dark rust, they caused it to lose the splendor of its beauty.

For Saul too is read among the prophets (1 Samuel 10:11–12), but Scripture does not designate Saul as a prophet in the same way as David. Afflicted by a possessing disease, he was more lightly relieved of the stupor of madness by the sweet melody of David’s lyre, whose three strings produced harmonious lines (1 Samuel 16:23). In one way, and altogether differently, manna of nectar-like sweetness sweetened the most delightful taste in the mouth of Moses and Aaron; in another way, of course, it nauseated in the throat of Dathan and Abiram as well. [That is, it created nausea.]

As for which of the two this problem of the present figure has been cast toward, let the prudent reader seek to derive it with evident understanding. [Note: “This problem of the present figure.” The sense is obscure, unless one prefers to read *conjectum* instead of *conjecta*, with the meaning “a problem cast forth,” that is, a problem proposed. Or *conjecta* may be a substantive: Du Cange notes that *conjectus* and *conjecta* were used for a symbol; it would then mean “the symbol of this figure.” But, to tell the truth, *symbolum* was then understood in the sense of a contribution collected from several people who paid money. Or finally, it may be equivalent to *conjectura*, “conjecture.” As to which of the two—Moses or Dathan—the conjecture or problem of this figure can be applied, let the discerning reader decide.]

## CHAPTER IX. Felix, inconsistent with himself, calls Jesus Christ at one time the true God and Son of God, at another an adoptive and titular god.

[Col. 0360B] But since it was stated above that certain things were rightly pronounced by him, yet shortly afterward were perversely corrupted by the same man, this can be demonstrated from the very comments with which he had recently arranged those matters in an elaborate fashion [Note: [Col. 0360B] *Approbare*? Perhaps *approbari* should be read.] Justly, then, God permitting this by his judgment, so that one who had voluntarily withdrawn from the truth of the holy Church by embracing opinions contrary to the orthodox faith might deservedly become inconsistent with himself, punishment for his sin requiring it. For he confesses that he believes the Lord Jesus Christ to be true God and true man: from the very conception in the virginal womb, inseparably assumed by the Word of God in the unity of person, without any confusion or change of either nature, one and the same Son of God and man; not one Son of God and another of man, but one and the same Son of God and man; not two sons, nor two gods, and other such things. In accordance with the rule of the Catholic faith, he presents a sufficiently clear and extended discourse.

How, then, does he immediately forget, under the impulse of some persuasive inspiration, who he had been a little earlier—suddenly forgetful, as though in the derangement of an insane mind, of what he had said? When a cause of contention is brought against him, though he had shortly before supplied testimony in its favor, he contradicts it by angrily hurling opposing darts of words. And what was thought to be a clear oracle assigned to the right faith, as though it were the work of another’s conscience and not his own, he shortly afterward, in his frenzy, more harshly repudiates.

For he says: “But if, as you maintain, a man assumed by the Son of God was immediately from the conception in the virginal womb conceived as God and born as true God, how does the Son himself prophetically say of himself: ‘And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself’ (Isa. XLIX, 5)? And again,” he says, “by what authority is the man of the Lord proclaimed by you to have been conceived from his mother’s womb as true God, and born as true God, when by nature he is true man and in all things subject to God?”

What more is needed? Through arguments of various kinds he hastens to carry the matter to the point where, with a ruined mind, he defines him as both the adoptive Son of God and God by appellation: as though he were a mere ordinary man, to whom the privilege of faith is freely granted, and to whom, through the bath of regeneration, power is given by that same Son of God, so that by a gratuitous gift he may be both an adoptive Son of God and, through divine grace preceding him, become God by appellation through advancement in religion.

From the language of such trivial [*frivolae*] disputation it is therefore perceived more clearly than daylight that he has resolved the mystery of the single person into a duality of number and, by separating the plural number, is convicted of cutting apart the unity of the divine name. Although, even when these matters are so severely established, he often attempts to defend himself verbally behind the shield of falsehood. “I do not divide the persons,” he says; “I distinguish the natures completely.”

But while he tries to excuse himself from this charge, he can nevertheless be refuted by his own comments, since he does this repeatedly. Accordingly, he is declared, by the sanction of a just judgment and with all ambiguity of doubt removed, guilty of two crimes—of the deed, namely, and of falsehood. Thus, insofar as it can be understood and the evidence of the circumstances makes clear, he does not strive to resist the charges brought against him out of zeal for the truth, but, compelled by fear, endeavors to excuse his purpose as one of necessity [Col. 0362A]: lest perhaps he be cast forth from the womb of the most holy mother Church, like an abortive child, before the dawn of light.

## CHAPTER X. Paulinus does not intend to examine Felix’s heart and intention, but his words.

Now, regarding what I acknowledge having passed over in speech that was almost biting, I declared that I had assigned to him—not out of zeal for truth, but under the compulsion of necessity—those things that he had pronounced well. In the meantime, I did not introduce this as though the matter were certainly established, but because the character of his conjectural [variant: argumentative] disputation persuaded me to think so.

For the intimate secrets of thought belong to God alone to scrutinize. He is the searcher of the kidneys and hearts and the discerner of thoughts. [Col. 0362B] It is ours to see what is in the face; but both what is in the face and what is in the heart belong to God. Nevertheless, since through the door of the mouth, when the key of the tongue unlocks it, whatever secrets lie hidden within are often disclosed publicly, it may reasonably be judged that things which are plainly visible externally may be compelled to undergo examination on a subtle scale by human intelligence, though they are entangled in ambiguous circumstances.

Let us therefore set aside the hidden secrets of thoughts and inner recesses, and now listen to what pours through the open gates of the ears into the inner chamber of our mind.

## CHAPTER XI. He teaches that Felix thinks wrongly about God and speaks still worse, dividing the Son into a proper and an adoptive son.

Accordingly, with utterly shameless expression, he does not fear to divide the one and the same Son of God into two designations—proper and adoptive, true God and God by appellation—boldly disputing with a dissident [Note: [Col. 0361D] *Audacter dissiganti*. I find this verb taught by neither the highest, middle, nor lowest Latin. Perhaps it is a scribal error for *litiganti* (“contending”), *investiganti* (“investigating”), *dissidenti* (“dissenting”), or something similar. I would prefer *dissidenti*, since it comes closest to the corrupted word and more closely suits Paulinus’s meaning, as he reproaches Felix for dividing Christ into an adoptive and a proper son.] mind about God, paying no heed to how dangerous and terrible it is even to think unworthily about God, and how much more indecent it is to dispute carelessly about him.

For it is written: “Do not seek things higher than you, and do not investigate things stronger than you; but always consider what God has commanded you” (Eccles. III, 22). Hence, concerning one who is more moderately restrained and one who is more unrestrainedly headlong, it is written again: “He who presses the breasts hard to extract milk squeezes out butter; and he who squeezes violently extracts blood” (Prov. XXX, 33).

Finally, the very Wisdom of God the Father, as we are more solemnly instructed by the teachings of the Gospels, after patiently enduring the intolerable insults of the blaspheming Jews, did not judge that the testimony of truth should be suppressed in silence [variant: *supremi*, “of the highest”]. For he says: “I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me” (John VIII, 49).

Again the Jews reviled the Lord, as is most truly declared by the illustrious proclamations of the Gospels, receiving through their itching ears the sound issuing from his honey-sweet mouth [Note: [Col. 0362D] *From his honey-sweet mouth through an itching ear*. The first editor of these books entered in the margin *f. melliflua* or *mellifluum*, that is, either “through a honey-sweet ear” or “a honey-sweet hearing.” Nothing, however, needs to be changed. The construction is indeed a transposition not easily approved, but the sense remains complete: “with an itching ear receiving the sound from his honey-sweet mouth.”]: “I have done many good works for you; for which work do you stone me?” They replied, “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because, although you are a man, you make yourself God” (John X, 32–33).

Therefore the same Evangelist immediately supplies the reason why the Jews wished to kill him, when he adds: “For this reason,” he says, “the Jews were seeking to kill him, because he said that he was the Son of God, making himself equal with God” (John V, 18). [Note: [Col. 0363D] “For this reason, he says, the Jews.” Here Paulinus does not quote the words, at least not exactly, but their sense, which is found in John, chapter V, verse 18. The words themselves are: “For this reason, therefore, the Jews were seeking to kill him, because he not only broke the sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God.” Thus the reason is not supplied immediately—that is, in the same chapter X previously cited. Rather, the reason for the contemplated killing is found in chapter V. Nevertheless, the intention of the Jews is the same in both places.]

## CHAPTER XII. Felix, like the Jews and Arius, introduces division in the person and confusion in the natures of the Son of God; Paulinus rejects this.

Moreover, since this man—an old-womanish fable of the law concerning whom we are speaking, if indeed he should be called a man, since he acts not manfully but feebly—does not hesitate to profane the Lord Jesus Christ by the most foolish assertions, on the ground that he is not the true Son of God and true God, because we believe and proclaim that a true man was ineffably assumed by the person of the Word of God in the fullness of complete human nature, he is without doubt marked as differing in no respect from Jewish perfidy.

For although he uses different words, he does not employ a different perversity of a guilty heart. The Jew says: “Although you are a man, you make yourself God.” The heretic, when thoroughly refuted, says: “Since he is man and subject to God, he cannot be believed to be true God and the true Son of God.”

Although at times he professes Christ to be, as though by division, true God and the true Son of God in one respect, and in another respect an adoptive son and God by appellation, he is judged rather to have been compelled by fear than overcome by love of truth, as the account of the matter’s character makes clear. [Col. 0363C] He mixes a little honey into cups already filled with well-worn poison [variant: *triti*, “of worn-out poison”], so that the deadly sweetness may deceptively beguile the drinker’s throat with its feigned pleasant taste—a man in every respect an imitator of the paternal tradition and a devotee of a most false doctrine.

For Arius, from whose destructive root or origin this man plainly seems to have sprung [the verb is missing; perhaps “to have descended”], while maintaining that the Son of God was an adoptive son and a creature, nevertheless, to deceive the minds of the simple, pretended to attribute to him something like an exceptional distinction: as more excellent—not creator—he preferred him to all creatures [Note: [Col. 0363D] “More excellent, not creator.” He alludes to Arius’s teaching, which Arius himself sets forth in his letter to Alexander, preserved in Epiphanius, *Heresy* 69, no. 7, where he calls the Son “a perfect creature of God, but not like any of created things; likewise a product, but not like one of the rest.” This suggests that perhaps the first hand read: “he preferred an excellent creature to all creatures.”].

But since Christ is one, the Son of God and man, and unity is not cut into parts—for one cannot in any way be divided, and personal union has never admitted separation by any possibility of reason, since human nature is united inseparably with divine nature in an indescribable manner, and in such an incomparable consideration that it is known only to the ineffable Trinity, according as the peace of God surpasses all understanding—human nature has been conjoined in such a way that neither confusion nor division of the natures can ever be suspected.

Rather, with the property of each nature preserved, without their being poured into or infused into one another [Note: [Col. 0364D] “Without being poured into or infused into one another,” that is, not poured into and not infused into one another—namely, neither the nature of God into man nor that of man into God. The addition of the particle *in* very often has negative force.], in the one person of God and man, God is never believed without the man whom he deigned to assume from the very conception in the virginal womb; nor man without God, who, from the very conception in the virginal womb, is most truly proclaimed to have been assumed into God, the Holy Spirit’s grace making it fruitful.

Thus both God, because of the man he assumed, and man, because of the God who assumed him, are, from both and in both, true God and true man: one and the same Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and man, and true God. In his name every knee of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth is bent, and every tongue, in accordance with the apostolic trumpet, confesses that he is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. II, 10–11).

## CHAPTER XIII. Although he is one thing insofar as he is God and another insofar as he is man, Christ is not another and another, but always God-man.

When, therefore, I say “true God and true man,” I do not define two persons, one of God and one of man, but confess both—God and man—in the one person of God. Finally, Christ God is not one, and Christ man another [Note: [Col. 0364D] “Christ God is not one, etc.” He says the same in *Sacrosyllabus*, § 8; see there note a, and what we cite from Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory* 1, chapter 19.]. There is plainly one thing insofar as he is God and another insofar as he is man; but Christ is not one and man another, as has been said.

The former statement concerns the distinction of the natures; the latter concerns the unity of the person. For just as, in the mystery of the holy Trinity, the distinction of three persons [Note: [Col. 0364D] “The distinction of three persons.” It seems that it should have been written *in the distinction of three persons*, since what follows is “in the inseparable majesty of one and the same essential glory.” Or, if *discretio* is retained, *inseparable majesty* should be restored. One or the other must necessarily be corrected for the sense to be coherent.] and the inseparable majesty of one and the same essential glory do not lead us to believe in three gods, but one God, so conversely, in the dispensation of the pious and great mystery of the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, the true distinction of two natures and the truthful confession of one person instruct the rule of apostolic faith and sincerely urge the heart to believe unto righteousness, and safely impel the mouth to confess unto salvation (Rom. X, 10)—not two sons, or two gods, or two Christs, but one and the same Christ Jesus, true and only-begotten Son of God, from both natures and in both natures, true and almighty God.

For it must be understood that Christ was not first conceived or born as an ordinary and mere man, and that God afterward dwelt in him as in one of the prophets, by a gift of grace. Rather, in the very conception by the Holy Spirit, with the blessed womb of the inviolate Virgin supplying the true material of flesh [Note: [Col. 0365C] “The blessed womb … supplying.” Grammarians would prefer *with blessed womb and supplying* in the case they call the ablative absolute. This is nevertheless characteristic of Paulinus. So too at the beginning of the following chapter XV and elsewhere.], he was ineffably assumed by the Word of God through birth at the beginning of conception. From that moment, man began to be one person with God; he was, is, and will always be the only-begotten Son of God and true God.

Since true man has been essentially assumed by the true Son of God and true God in the unity of person, though without confusion, he is true Son of God and true God, and is believed and worshiped without any groping uncertainty [Col. 0365B] [Note: [Col. 0365D] “Without groping uncertainty.” *Palpatione* or *palpitatione*? Either works well. One who doubts, being moved in different directions, seems to palpitate. Seneca, *Hercules Oetaeus*, lines 708–709, act III:

“And the stunned heart leaps,  
and the fearful liver trembles and throbs in the veins.”

Moreover, one who doubts sometimes gropes. Thus Isaac gropes for Jacob, doubting whether he is Jacob or Esau (Gen. XXVII, 22). Likewise the Lord Jesus, to remove every doubt among the disciples concerning the truth of his resurrection, said (Luke XXIV, 39): “Touch and see.” Hence the phrase *ψηλαφεῖν ἐν τῷ σκότῳ* entered proverbial usage—that is, “to grope with the hand in darkness.” Erasmus, *Adagia* III, cent. VII, no. 59: “Those are said to investigate a matter by obscure conjectures.” Examples occur in Aristophanes’ *Peace* and Plato’s *Phaedo*.]

For it was not man, who did not yet exist, who assumed God; rather, the eternal God graciously assumed man in time, making him uniquely his own.

## CHAPTER XIV. The Word was not changed into flesh; it underwent neither division nor commingling.

The Word of God, therefore, which became flesh (John I, 14)—that is, became man—was not changed into flesh. Rather, the flesh ineffably assumed by the Word of God was made, in conception, the proper flesh of the Word of God: united to the divine nature in so great a fellowship that it is believed to remain forever in the unity of personal union, neither divided nor mingled.

For it is written: “What God has joined together, let no man separate” (Matt. XIX, 26). God, indeed, inseparably joined human nature to himself in the bridal chamber of the virginal womb. From it he came forth like a bridegroom and rejoiced like a giant to run his course (Ps. XVIII, 6); but the heretic, through an impious separation, strives to tear it away from its insertion into that unity.

Man, therefore, ought to advance into God, because he greatly needed advancement. It was not fitting that God should diminish in man, since he received no increase of perfection and suffers no diminution whatsoever, but always remains what he is. To him the Prophet says: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI, 28). And again: “He who is sent me to you”; and: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14).

For in the dispensation of the pious and great mystery, the person of God did not assume the person of man; rather, the eternal person of the Word, one namely of the Trinity, according to the fact that he emptied himself, assumed in time the form of a servant—that is, human nature. Nor did confusion of one person arise from the diversity of persons; rather, while the distinct truth of both natures remained, an undivided and unconfused essential fellowship was effected in the union of the person.

## CHAPTER XV. Paulinus proves from the Apostle that Christ is Son of God and man; otherwise Mary must be called a mother by appellation, though she truly bore the most high God.

[Col. 0366B]

With these matters established [for “these matters being so”], the force of apostolic reasoning can also be more effectively supported by arguments of this kind. “Have this mind among yourselves,” he says, “which was also in Christ Jesus. Though he was in the form of God, he did not consider being equal with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. II, 5ff.).

In the name of Christ Jesus, therefore, the person of the only-begotten is indicated; in the form of God and the form of a servant, the properties of both natures are described. For if, not within the virgin’s womb, as this heretic foolishly claims [for *dissipit*, read *desipit*], the only-begotten Son of God—eternal from the Father, temporal [Col. 0366C] from his mother—built himself a house, that is, truly clothed himself with human nature, while remaining the unchangeable God that he was; if he did not come forth from the womb of the undefiled Virgin mother like a bridegroom from his chamber; and if that venerable Virgin did not give birth to true God and true man in the unity of one person, so that Christ God is not one and Christ man another, but one and the same, as has often been repeated, God-man; and if he is not himself the temple and himself the inhabitant of the temple, as this old man, with his gray hair emptied of sense, raves in his frenzy [Note: [Col. 0365D] “This old man raves more furiously with his sense emptied by gray hair.” Felix was therefore mature in age. Paulinus is not merely reproaching him for gray hair, which can also occur in vigorous men, but for hoary old age, to which mental and intellectual decay is commonly attributed, since nothing is more frequent in old men. Hence Paulinus aptly says “with his gray hair emptied”: *exinanire* means to make empty or evacuate, which is well said of an old man with an empty and vacant brain. Paulinus writes *delerare*, not *delirare*, though with the same meaning, and he is not without authority for it. Nonius consistently writes *delerare* in *De proprietate sermonum* and supplies examples confirming the same point. He says that *delerare* means “to depart from the straight.” A *lera* is a straight trench dug to protect fields and into which the moisture of the earth runs. Pomponius, Lucilius, and Plautus support this usage; in Plautus’ *Amphitryon* occurs the expression: “The wife is raving.” But if we investigate the matter from Greek roots, *λῆρος* means nonsense or folly, whence also ravings; it is not an agricultural term as in Latin, and is written with eta, not iota. Thus, if derived from Greek, it should be written *delerare*. Yet when Latins write *delirare*—“and farmers call *lirae* the ridges when the land is plowed so that, between two more widely spaced furrows, the central mound provides dry ground for the grain,” as Columella says, *De re rustica* II, chapter 4; and “oxen are said to *lirare* when, with boards attached to the plowshare, they both cover the sown grain in the ridges and cut furrows through which rainwater may run down,” as Marcus Varro says, *De re rustica* I, 29, from the Aldine edition of 1533—the reading of Nonius becomes doubtful. In any case, both those who write *delerare* and those who write *delirare* use the word figuratively, Greek and Latin alike, for going mad; they apply it especially to old men whose minds have been impaired by age. Plutarch, *On the Education of Children*, shortly before the end, reporting the words of flatterers who corrupt young men, says among other things: “Why should you care less for your father? He is a senile fool.” In Greek, *κρονολῆρος*, which in ordinary language would be rendered “an aged fool.” Cicero, *De oratore* II: “This Carthaginian is said to have replied, not in the best Greek but nevertheless freely, that he had often seen many senile old men, but had never seen anyone more senile than Phormio.” And so do the others. Paulinus therefore rightly reproves Felix as senile and foolish, like an old man bereft of sense.]

—or if the birth from the Virgin is not the glorious manifestation of the divine name which the Apostle calls a great mystery of piety (I Tim. III, 16)—how, then, does the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world as one, never cease publicly and freely to confess the blessed Virgin Mary—sweet and venerable is that name to me—as *Theotokos*, that is, “Mother of God”?

If, therefore, a mother truly bore from her womb not the true God but God only by appellation, as this man of insane mind froths forth from his throat falsehoods, namely, that same one who was begotten before the morning star from the Father’s womb—that is, from the Father’s essence—without beginning, always remaining what he was, how will the blessed Virgin be confessed by the most truthful mouth of all Catholics to be the true Mother of God?

The heretics must acknowledge her as a mother by appellation if they suppose that the mother of the offspring is a mother by appellation. But the Catholic and apostolic faith has confessed, does confess, and will confess throughout eternal perpetuity the true God, the true man who was born, and the true Mother of God who gave birth: God and man, not two but one true and proper Son of God; not two but one true God, Jesus Christ our Lord.

The blessed Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, also exclaimed: “And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” (Luke I, 45). For truly the venerable Virgin is both servant and mother of the Lord, since the God of all flesh who created her himself deigned to be born from her.

For she herself said to the angel: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it happen to me according to your word” (ibid., 38). The angel foretold that she would be the mother of the Son of the Most High [Col. 0367C]; she humbly confessed herself to be the handmaid of the Son of the Most High.

David’s proclamation is also shown, not inappropriately, to agree with this angelic oracle. “Mother Zion,” he says, “declares: ‘A man and a man was born, or was made, in her; and the Most High himself founded her’” (Ps. LXXXVI, 5, from the Septuagint). It is the same one, not another, who was made in her from the seed of David according to the flesh; it is the same one whom the Most High founded forever.

The angel, finally, mentions the Son of the Most High; the prophet likewise mentions the Most High himself. For just as the Father is proclaimed God and the Son God, so the Father Most High and the Son Most High are proclaimed. Thus the Old and New Testaments harmonize with one another, because the same Holy Spirit is the author of both.

## CHAPTER XVI. By comparing the testimonies of John and Paul, he says that Christ’s glory belongs truly to the Son of God, not to one who is God merely by appellation.

Let that beloved disciple, therefore, be summoned who uniquely drew streams of knowledge from that very fountain of wisdom when he reclined upon the breast of the Savior at the banquet of the supper. Having been satisfied by the refreshment of the fullness [sic: perhaps *plenitudine*, “with fullness”] of divine savor, he caused the streams of his teaching to overflow through evangelical instruction over the whole world. Finally, directing the eye of faith toward contemplation of the height of divinity, let him say what existed in the beginning, or where it was, or what it was.

“In the beginning,” he says, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John I, 1ff.).

Let him also add what this Word, which was God and is God, deigned to become for us. “And the Word,” he says, “became flesh and dwelt among us.” That is, God became man, while remaining eternally what he was.

Let him continue and declare in what glory the Word made flesh remained: “And we saw,” he says, “his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.”

Contemplating Christ Jesus exalted in this glory, the marvelous teacher says: “Let every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II, 11). The Evangelist testifies that the Word made flesh, full of grace and truth, possessed the same glory that the only-begotten Son, coeternal with the Father, had from the Father before the world was made. God is taught to be full of grace and truth, and man likewise full.

How, then, O heretic, do you dare, in the deadly sleep of a dream, to imagine that the Word made flesh—that is, God made man—possessed another glory, namely, that of an adoptive son and a god by appellation, when so great an Apostle gloried in having seen his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth?

John the Baptist also bears witness to this fullness, saying: “And from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace, because the law was not made through Moses but given; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John I, 16).

110 ## CHAPTER XVII. He accuses Felix of corrupting a passage of the Apostle; he teaches that Christ suffered, was buried, and so forth, in his own flesh.

When the outstanding preacher Paul contemplated this fullness of divinity in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ, he did not conceal it. For he says: “In him all things were established in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers [Col. 0368D]; all things were created through him and in him, and he is before all things, and all things hold together in him” (Col. I, 16).

And shortly afterward: “Because in him he was pleased to make all the fullness dwell bodily, and through him to reconcile all things in him, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things in heaven or the things on earth” (ibid., 19).

I remember, as I think, having read that you inserted this apostolic testimony in your comments [Note: [Col. 0369D] “That you inserted the apostolic testimony.” Although in the passage cited, Colossians I, 19, the Apostle says only, “Because in him he was pleased to make all the fullness dwell,” nevertheless, in the following chapter, II, verse 9, he expressly says: “For in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” That these are the Apostle’s words, and not those of the earlier passage, which Felix had mutilated and to which Paulinus refers, is manifestly proved by this statement of Paulinus [Col. 0370D]: “In him you profess that the Apostle said that all the fullness of divinity dwells.” The words “fullness of divinity” do not belong to the earlier passage but to the later one, in which the Apostle adds “bodily,” fraudulently omitted by Felix; hence Paulinus rightly rebukes him.], but you have clearly not abandoned your customary cunning.

For you admit that the Apostle said that all the fullness of divinity dwells in him, but you have not hesitated, with the knife of your perfidy, to cut out the words “dwells bodily in him,” as though the Apostle had carelessly added “bodily” unnecessarily.

Was that vessel of election, in whom Christ was speaking, ignorant of why he added “bodily”? Far be it. The point is not that any Catholic of sound mind would foolishly imagine anything bodily or tangible in that invisible, intangible, and incomprehensible nature of divinity. Rather, it is that the ineffable nature of divinity truly deigned to clothe itself with human nature, and through this human body, which it assumed, made that nature its own.

Thus the one who, according to himself—that is, insofar as he is divine—cannot at all be seen, touched, subjected, suffer, die, or undergo anything else of this kind, is instructed by apostolic teachings to be capable, in his own flesh and through the veil of a bodily garment—that is, the mystery of the Incarnation—of being seen as invisible, of suffering as impassible, and of dying as immortal. For the flesh assumed by the Word is the proper flesh of the Word.

The first shepherd of the Church says: “Christ having suffered in the flesh” (I Pet. IV, 1)—in the flesh, certainly, not with the divinity suffering together with the flesh, since the divinity is in every respect beyond suffering.

But because the flesh that suffered was the proper flesh of the Word, the one whose proper flesh is said to have suffered and died is himself said to have suffered and died. After the mystery of the assumption, his impassible and unchangeable divinity is never proclaimed to have been separated from that flesh.

Accordingly, Christ Jesus is truly declared, according to the Scriptures, to have suffered, died, been buried, and risen again. This is what the Apostle Paul subsequently handed down to all the churches, and what the unalterable creed of the venerable Council of Nicaea, the well-known rule of all Catholics, proclaims.

For it confesses that the true man, the only-begotten Son of God, made and born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary—whom it confesses to have been begotten from the Father before all ages, not made—was that same one who, for us and for our salvation, was crucified under Pontius Pilate, suffered and was buried, rose alive from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, and also sits at the right hand of God the Father, and will come with glory to judge the living and the dead [perhaps “there is an omission of *ad* before *judicandos*”].

For he who remains impassible and immortal in his divinity is believed to have suffered, died, and been buried in his humanity. “For although he was dead,” says the Apostle, “through our weakness, he lives through the power of God” (II Cor. XIII, 4–5).

## CHAPTER XVIII. Christ suffered by his will, not by necessity.

He endured all these things, therefore, through the proper voluntary power of his pious condescension, not compelled by necessity. Long beforehand he professes this to the Father through the Prophet, saying: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII, 8). And again: “I willed to do your will, my God” (Ps. XXXIX, 9).

Because you willed it, O Lord Jesus Christ, you did all these things; for since you are almighty God, no word is difficult for you. For to will and to be able are the same for you. Concerning you, I profess that I have read this written: “The power to do all that you will is at your disposal,” says a certain wise man (Wis. XII, 18).

The eloquent prophet David also sang of you, saying: “All that the Lord willed, he did in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the abysses” (Ps. CXXXIV, 6).

We firmly retain, relying on the foundation of inviolate faith, that all the patriarchs, prophets, evangelists, apostles, and every Catholic man, filled with your holy [Spirit?; Note: [Col. 0370D] “Perhaps ‘Spirit’ is missing.” Moreover, it should have said “the patriarchs, prophets, etc., filled with the Spirit.”] from the beginning of the world, have borne witness to the truth concerning you. Their combined support must likewise strengthen the conversations of our disputations.

For, to pass over much—indeed, an infinite amount—concerning these matters, since your beloved disciple declares that the world itself could not contain the books that would have to be written about you (John XXI, 25), I shall therefore insert into this work, though with a sluggish pen, a few things from many, in accordance with the poverty of my understanding, granted freely by you, namely those which appear suited to the character of the present undertaking.

## CHAPTER XIX. Testimonies from the Psalms and the Prophets that Christ is not divided into one who is God by appellation and one who is proper.

David, therefore, chief among the prophets, performing the office of the Father’s voice—for you, the Son, coeternal with the eternal Father, were ineffably begotten before the ages and without beginning—says:

> “With you is dominion on the day of your power, in the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109:3).

And because you yourself, according to the economy of the incarnation you assumed, deigned to become for us priest, offering, and victim in an aroma pleasing to God, he immediately added:

> “The Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (ibid., 4).

But because you did not refuse to drink, in passing, the cup of death for the salvation of the world, a little later he continues:

> “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head” (ibid., 7).

Hence, elsewhere, the same Prophet thus thunders concerning this great sacrament of divine mercy:

> “The mother of Zion says: A man, and a man was born in her; and the Most High himself founded her forever” (Psalm 86:5, from the Septuagint).

A man, I say, and the Most High: for you are true God and true man, one and the same person—not another, merely titular God, and an adopted son, as the heretics are not afraid impiously to profane with their mouths.

I also hear, unworthy though I am, according to the mystery of the incarnation, your honey-sweet voice happily resounding through the mouth of the same Prophet:

> “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7).

And that you spoke of that birth which you wished to have from your mother is most clearly demonstrated by the preceding and following circumstances. Your Paul also, explaining you to the Jews according to the Scriptures, set forth the matter when he hastened to adduce the testimony of this psalm. For he says:

> “And we announce to you the promise made to our fathers, because God has fulfilled this for our children, raising Jesus, as it is written in the second psalm: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’” (Acts 13:32–33). [The text has *eam*, “the promise”; alternatively *ea*.]

For by this you are believed to have been raised—that is, because you deigned to be born of the holy Virgin. [Perhaps *per* (“through”) is missing from the text.]

Finally, the prophet Isaiah, who is deservedly called by the name of evangelist—not proclaiming, as in prophecy, a mysterious allegory wrapped in shadowy leaves, but publishing an oracle radiant with evident clarity, almost identical with the words of the Gospel—says:

> “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14).

And he took care to assert the name with its interpretation of its dignity when he immediately added:

> “And his name shall be called Emmanuel,” which means, “God with us” (Matthew 1:22). [The text has *vi*, “by the force”; alternatively *vim*.]

[Note: “And his name shall be called,” together with the interpretation, he took care to assert. Isaiah’s passage does not contain anything except, “His name shall be called Emmanuel.” The interpretation, however, belongs to Matthew 1:23, where he adduces Isaiah’s passage and adds the interpretation. This resulted in the passage being attributed to Isaiah and Paulinus. Yet, lest you seize upon this as an occasion for accusing Paulinus, Jerome’s judgment forbids it in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 7, where he says: “In many testimonies which the evangelists or apostles took from the ancient books, one must carefully observe that they did not follow the order of the words, but the sense.” Add to Jerome the judgment of Cardinal John Bona, who says this in the preface to his work On Divine Psalmody: “I do not scrupulously follow the words, provided that the meaning remains intact. For the apostles too, when quoting the Old Testament, sometimes interrupt passages in the middle and combine one passage from several, as Pope Adrian I observes in Letter 3; Leo of Castro in his commentary on Isaiah chapters 8 and 9; and Francisco Ribera on Hosea chapter 13, section 33. Moreover, Isaiah himself, in the following chapter, verse 10, teaches that this is the true and legitimate interpretation; so does Saint Matthew, who, in the passage cited, has this interpretation in the margin. Thus Paulinus’s otherwise powerful argument is in no way weakened.”]

The interpretation of this name does not express its force according to its proper meaning as “titular God,” but “God with us.” And again the same prophet says:

> “A child is born to us, a son is given to us; and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God” (Isaiah 9:7).

Here too, behold, he is “Mighty God,” not a titular god, according to the most wicked ravings of the heretics.

And as though the same prophet were speaking face to face with the incarnate Wisdom of God the Father, he says:

> “Truly, you are God, and there is no other besides you; for you are God in hiding, and we did not know it” (Isaiah 45:14–15).

[Note: “He was speaking face to face.” In 2 John 12, “mouth to mouth,” and likewise in 3 John 14, “we shall speak mouth to mouth,” this expression signifies nothing other than the mutual presence of those conversing, as Father Cornelius notes in this passage. Paulinus, wishing to express the same thing, said “face to face.” For the eyes perceive the presence of things more than the other senses. Hence Plautus speaks of “seeing hands,” meaning hands that grasp gifts actually present; this passed into a proverb, as Erasmus records in Adagia, 1.8.31: “Plautus called them ‘seeing hands’ because they want promises to be displayed in reality, not promised in words. For they have eyes with which they see what is presented, but no ears with which they hear promises.” Thus, explaining the following proverb from Plautus’s Pseudolus—“Buy oil on credit, by Hercules; sell it on the day when it is seen”—he says: “That is, buy without present money, on an agreement for a future day; resell for money present at hand.” Paulinus therefore indicates the prophet’s intimate presence with God when he says that he spoke “face to face.”]

For God was hidden because the invisible divinity was concealed beneath the veil of flesh.

Hence Jeremiah says:

> “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him, who discovered every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. Afterward he was seen on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36 and following; see the note).

[Note: Jeremiah says, “This is our God,” and so forth. This passage is not from Jeremiah, but from Baruch 3:36 and following. Yet because Baruch was Jeremiah’s scribe and wrote in his name, the Fathers often attribute what belongs to Baruch to Jeremiah. Bellarmine notes this in book 1 of On the Word of God, chapter 8. Among others, Chrysostom, in volume 5, in his Demonstration that Christ Is God, adduces this very passage from Baruch under the authority and name of Jeremiah: “That God, existing as God, was to become man, Jeremiah says: ‘This is our God,’ and so forth.” Augustine likewise cites this passage in City of God, book 18, chapter 33, and adds: “Some attribute this testimony not to Jeremiah but to his scribe, who was called Baruch; but it is commonly regarded as Jeremiah’s.” Paulinus likewise retained the familiar and more widely recognized name. See what was done concerning this matter at the Council of Trent in Cardinal Pallavicini’s history, book 6, chapter 11, section 14.]

You yourself also testified, saying:

> “I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6).

> “By myself I have sworn: Every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall confess” (Isaiah 45:23–24).

This heretic does not humbly bend the knee of faith so that, with an orthodox tongue, he may devoutly confess you to be true God and the true Son of God. Although, by placing before himself a kind of veil of argument, he attempts to deceive Catholic minds, as though he were offering something plausible, when he is conjecturing that you, the one true and omnipotent God, should be divided, for the sake of the great sacrament of divine mercy, into two gods—namely, a true God and a titular god—and into a true son and an adopted son.

[Note: “A true God and an adopted son.” Since throughout the preceding discussion he contrasts a titular god with the true God, and an adopted son with the true Son, here too one should perhaps read “a true son and an adopted son” instead of “a true God and an adopted son.”]

[Note: “He is conjecturing that he should divide.” Perhaps the reading is *conicitur*—“is conjectured”—or *convincitur*—“is convicted”; unless one prefers *conatur*—“he attempts.”]

With a deaf ear he gives a hearing to what was said: “I am God, and I do not change.” [The text may read *surda auris*, “of a deaf ear.”]

[Note: “He does not apply those ears.” The expression “to apply voices and hands” for “to threaten” and “to lay hands upon” is found in Tacitus, Annals 3.36. The verb is not very suitable for application to ears. I therefore think it is used here for *intendit*, “he directs” or “applies.”]

He does not direct those ears toward hearing the mysteries of the ineffable sacraments—ears which you, as the Evangelist taught us, sought when you poured forth in parables things hidden from the foundation of the world, saying:

> “Let anyone who has ears to hear, hear” (Matthew 13:35, 43).

## CHAPTER XX. Christ is one in one way from the Father and in another way from his mother, but is not another person.

Why, unhappy man, do you not hear what is said to you: “I am God, and I do not change; nor is there any other besides me”? Why has the cunning of empty glory deceived you, so that you suppose that, because you hold the true God to be one and the same Christ Jesus our Lord from the Father, but a titular god from his mother, you cannot be restrained by judicial punishment from advancing your doctrine? As though the one who is from the Father were one person and the one who is from the mother another, when one and the same true God and true Son of God is, both before the ages and without beginning, from the Father, and at the end of the ages is not another but the same person from the virgin mother—as you yourself seem to bear fruit in a harvest of sound faith, before the good seed is snatched from the field of your heart.

[Note: “So that you suppose that you cannot voluntarily be restrained by judicial punishment,” and so forth. The meaning is obscure, since there seems to be an error in the wording. Perhaps one should read, “that you cannot be restrained by judicial punishment.” The period would then be more intelligible, though otherwise entangled and excessively obscure: “so that you suppose that you cannot be restrained, or forbidden, by the judgment of the Church from pouring forth your doctrine, because you confess the true God,” and so forth. Or perhaps the text means, “so that you suppose that you cannot voluntarily restrain judicial punishment,” in place of “judicial punishment,” that is, that the judgment of the Church cannot prevent or forbid you from doing so, because of the fact that, and so forth. The former seems to be the intended meaning.]

He is believed to have been born in one way from the Father and in another way—but not as another person—from his mother. From the Father, of a simple nature: one from one, true God from true God. From his mother, from both natures, divine and human: true God and true man. Not God and man as two sons or two gods, but one God and man, true God and man.

For the assumption of a temporal nature did not prejudice that eternal and divine nature, so as either to divide him into two sons, a proper son and an adopted son, as you attempt to establish [the text reads *coniceris*, perhaps *conaris*, “you attempt”]; or to sever him from the one—namely, from the union of the person; or to change him into another, that is, into a titular god, so that your open and intolerable throat, like an open tomb, was not ashamed to breathe forth such stench.

## 113 CHAPTER XXI. He reproaches Felix for his long-standing obstinacy.

Awaken at last, if you are not utterly dead, and wake from the sleep of unbelief after being struck by such a tumultuous cry. How long will you continue to snore through your nostrils, stupefied by the bear-like sleep of perfidy?

[Note: “You will not cease to snore through your nostrils like a bear.” To snore is to emit rattling sounds while asleep, something done only by those sleeping deeply. Plautus says, “While he sleeps, he snores.” Cicero, in book 2 of the Academic Questions, entitled Lucullus, has Carneades say: “You may snore for all I care, not merely rest”—that is, not merely remain at rest, but sleep, and indeed sleep until you snore and snort. Since this occurs through the nostrils, from which the snoring sound comes, Juvenal clearly indicates it in Satire 1.57:

> “Learned even to snore through an alert nose beside the cup.”

Paulinus therefore properly said “to snore through the nostrils.” As for why he says “bear-like,” the reason is that bears withdraw in winter and hide themselves in caves. “For the first fourteen days they are oppressed by such deep sleep that they cannot be awakened even by wounds. Then they grow fat in a remarkable way through torpor,” as Pliny writes in Natural History 8.36. Hence Juvenal, describing the disturbances of the city caused especially by the shouting of muleteers and drivers, who roused and urged on animals either kicking or slow to move, and saying that sleep was driven from the eyes even of those accustomed to sleep most deeply, like bears among land animals and seals among sea creatures, wrote:

> “And the insults of the standing mule-yard  
> snatch sleep from the bear and from the sea-calves.”

See John Britannicus on this passage.]

For winter has already passed, the rain has gone away and departed. Come out now from the dark cavern of the deep:

> “The flowers have appeared on the earth; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song of Songs 2:11–12).

The raven has gone away to dwell among ruins; the dove has now returned to the ark on silvered wings, carrying a branch of green olive (Genesis 8:11). Remember that evening returns, lest, while you are weighed down by the sleep of perfidy and are reluctant to rise, the dove enter the ark and, with the door shut outside, you begin to wander after the raven.

Why do you not perceive? Or, if you do perceive, do you remain stupefied, shaken by excessive terror? How terribly the thunders of the prophets resound so that you may awaken! Amid the flying and dripping clouds of the advancing air, they do not cease to roar with the most tremendous tumult; and on the spiritual hinge of the heavens of Scripture, upon which they turn, they shrill with melodious harmonies and sing sweet songs in a deep-voiced melody!

Or perhaps, with your eyes corrupted by the harmful smoke and your eyelids therefore blinking, you are unable to look up at the bow depicted in the cloud on the day of rain (Ezekiel 1:28)? And, as the lightning bolts of the Gospels run about, with clouds suffused by flashing rays, are you granted no ability to see?

[Note: “With blinking eyelids.” Might the reading here too be *palpitantibus*, “with throbbing eyelids,” as above in chapter 13b? For when smoke clouds the eyes, they wink and twitch, and the eyelids truly throb. Some derive *palpebrae* (“eyelids”) from *palpitare*, because they are almost always tremulous; others from *palpare*, that is, feeling or testing the objects before them. For they were given “as a kind of rampart for sight, and a projecting defense against animals that come in the way and other things that accidentally strike,” says Pliny, Natural History 11.3. “Varro preferred to say *palpebras* with t. Favorinus, however, said it with b. Some call the cheeks *palpetras*; but *palpebras* are the hairs themselves.” Servius on the Art of Grammar, in Junianus Maius, s.v. *Palpetrae*. But let these observations be made on the occasion offered.]

You therefore differ not at all from a dead man, if it can soon be proved by your own indications that all these things being said appear senseless to you. You could easily have been taught, if you had not refused to lend a willing ear.

## CHAPTER XXII. He rebukes the yawning Felix, who ignorantly and carelessly confuses “assumed” and “adopted.”

[Col. 0375A]

“Adopted,” as it seems to you, is not the same as “assumed,” or “attached,” or the other expressions of this kind that are read in your disordered style.

[Note: “Arranged in a disordered style.” No Latin author of either the Golden or the Silver Age teaches me this word. The Greeks merely suggest its meaning. For *στρέμμα* means something twisted or contorted. Thus what we call dislocated limbs are called *στρέμματα* by Dioscorides, as Budaeus testifies in his commentary on the Greek Language, column 760 in my edition, and as H. Stephanus records in the Greek Thesaurus, volume 3, column 1079 in my edition: “Marcellus notes on that passage of Dioscorides that things called dislocated in Latin are *στρέμματα* in Greek, the name being formed from twisting, since bones displaced from their proper position impede, with pain, their natural movements in that part.” Thus “a disordered style” appears to mean, in our Paulinus, perhaps not unfamiliar with Greek speech, a style that is contorted and outside the norm.]

Moreover, I ask whether “assumed” is one and the same as “taken up” or “adopted.” How then can one understand the statement of the Evangelist that the devil took up the Lord and placed him in the holy city or upon a high mountain (Matthew 4:5, 8)?

If you are still asleep, you do not perceive it; if you were awake, perhaps you would notice that it cannot be understood, nor does any possibility permit us to suppose, that that cunning serpent, who had approached him intending to tempt him and, if possible, deceive him, took him up as an adopted son and placed him in the holy city or upon a high mountain.

[Note: The text reads this way, but one should perhaps read “intending to tempt and deceive” or “to be tempted and deceived.”]

Likewise, because “attached” is not the same as “adopted,” we learn this from the Lord’s words when he discussed the same ancient enemy with blessed Job. For when the Lord mystically distinguished that head of all the reprobate and all the reprobate as his various members, and indicated by his power that he had broken that proud neck, he immediately added:

> “He who made him applied his sword” (Job 40:14),

that is, by the command of his power he restrained his malicious capacity to do harm.

Can the statement “he applied him” be understood to mean “he adopted him,” when that one will never return to forgiveness or, as though through the grace of adoption, be restored to the lot of sons? [For *redintegraturus*, perhaps read *reingressurus*, “about to re-enter,” or *redintegrandus*, “to be restored.”]

Who could be sunk into so great an abyss of laziness as, being out of his mind, to dare even to entertain such thoughts? Why, I ask, do you not carefully consider what you say, and neglect to weigh attentively about whom you are speaking?

Or do you not know that every animal which does not ruminate or divide the hoof is declared unclean by the law of the Lord (Leviticus 11:26)? In ruminating and in the distinction of the divided hoof, subtle weighing of the mind and discernment of a considered quality are understood. [Perhaps *distinctione*, “in the distinction,” should replace *distinctionem*.]

For Scripture does not admonish us without reason:

> “A time to keep silence, and a time to speak” (Ecclesiastes 3:7).

That man speaks wisely afterward who first knows how to be silent wisely.

Many testimonies of the Scriptures, heaped together in your little book of faith, are examined with a curious gaze, so that through them the greatness of your wisdom might reveal itself. But, on the contrary, this enabled us to learn how far it lay dissolved in the depths, distant from the height of true wisdom.

## CHAPTER XXIII. He refutes Felix’s error concerning the difference between an advocate and a mediator.

There is no ambiguity in your having placed there the testimony of the apostle John’s confession in this form:

> “That we may know the true God and may be in his true Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20).

Since he himself also said:

> “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (ibid. 2:1),

you say that “advocate” is the same as “mediator,” and therefore you claim that he cannot be believed to be the true God.

You have rightly lied against your own head.

> “Behold, the angel of the Lord cuts you in two” (Daniel 13:55, 59).

An advocate, therefore, is not the same as a mediator. A mediator is the same as a reconciler. The meaning of “mediator” is announced together with the interpretation of its effect. A mediator is so called because he is in the middle between two hostile parties, in order to reconcile both into one.

Our Redeemer, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, graciously deigned to become such for us between God and us, so that we, who by sinning had become estranged from participation in God’s love, might through him be reconciled to harmony with divine love and, by his blood, deserve to be restored, as Paul teaches:

> “When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, and saved by his blood” (Romans 5:10);

and:

> “He erased the bond of the decree that was against us, which was contrary to us, and removed it from the midst, fastening it to the cross. He stripped principalities and powers, and led them confidently in triumph, publicly triumphing over them in himself” (Colossians 2:14).

Finally, Paul was not the mediator but the faithful ambassador of the mediator:

> “We act as ambassadors for Christ,” he says; “be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20).

An advocate is one who now intercedes for those who have been reconciled, just as our Redeemer does when he displays to God the Father the human nature in the unity of the person of God and man. For this is what it means to intercede with God the Father for us.

John declares not merely that he intercedes, but that he himself is also the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:2).

But if, as your opinion maintains, an advocate is the same as a mediator, and if, because he is an advocate, he is not believed to be the true God, what then do you think about the Holy Spirit, who is not believed to have been incarnate, yet is himself called the Paraclete—that is, the advocate?

The one term is pronounced in Greek, the other in Latin. Thus you have it in the Gospel:

> “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 14:16).

By saying “another,” he clearly designates both himself and the Holy Spirit as the Paraclete—that is, the advocate. Nor are you granted any opportunity to answer by asserting that the Holy Spirit, who was not incarnate, is called an advocate according to the assumption of flesh.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Holy Spirit, although the Paraclete, that is, the advocate, is nevertheless God.

[Col. 0377A]

If, then, you deny that Christ Jesus is true God and the true Son of God because he is our advocate and intercedes for the sins of sinners, I ask what you presume to determine concerning the Holy Spirit, who is also our advocate and was not incarnate: whether he is true God or not.

For Paul also testifies that he intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings. He says:

> “The Holy Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Romans 8:26).

But if the one who pleads is also an advocate, then according to your madness true God is not to be worshiped. You, following the sect of Macedonius, deny that the Holy Spirit is true God.

[Note: “Following the sect of Macedonius.” John Cassian briefly relates and refutes the heresy of Macedonius in book 1 of On the Incarnation of the Lord, chapter 2: “Macedonius, blaspheming against the Holy Spirit with an irreparable impiety, although he said that the Father and the Son were of the same substance, nevertheless called the Holy Spirit a creature and thus became guilty against the whole divinity, because nothing can be harmed in the Trinity without injury to the whole Trinity.” The Fathers rose up against him, especially Saint Athanasius in two dialogues and in two books—or letters—on the Holy Spirit to Serapion, bishop. Saint Epiphanius likewise, in heresy 124, under the name *Πνευματομάχων*, that is, “those who fight against the Spirit,” attacks the Macedonians. Against them there are also the condemnations and anathemas of the Second Council of Constantinople in the year 381.]

But if you thought rightly concerning the Son, you would certainly also understand rightly concerning the Holy Spirit. For the Son of God voluntarily accepted everything for us, not for himself, in divine mercy. Therefore the assumption of human nature, which he truly bore in the flesh, detracts nothing from the divine majesty. He also strengthened the weakness of our nature by the power of his divinity.

For just as the fact that the Holy Spirit is called an advocate and is said to plead for us does not prevent him from being true God, so likewise nothing prevents our Savior, God Christ Jesus, who deigned to become our advocate and mediator, from being true God and the proper Son of God. [The text reads *nil contradicitur*; perhaps *nil contradicit*.]

Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit is true God, and since that ineffable essence of divinity remains entirely beyond suffering and change, who could doubt that it cannot ever receive a groan of disturbed emotion? Why, then, did the apostle Paul teach, as was related above, that he pleads for us with inexpressible groanings?

But because, as was also said before us, he has suffused minds with the illumination of his grace, he likewise makes them groan and plead:

[Note: “As was also said before us.” Especially by Augustine, Letter 130 in the latest Benedictine edition, formerly Letter 121, chapter 15, section 28: “For it is said that he intercedes for the saints because he makes the saints intercede.” And in Letter 104, formerly 115, section 16: “What does ‘he intercedes’ mean except that he makes us intercede?” Gregory the Great likewise says in Moralia 2.22: “He is said to plead because, plainly, those whom he fills he makes pleading.” See, if desired, Fulgentius in fragment 5 from book 2 Against Fabian; also Remigius and Primasius in their exposition of the cited passage of the Epistle to the Romans, all of whom preceded Paulinus in age, so that he rightly said, “as was said before us.”]

[Note: “Those who plead.” I emend *postolantes* and *postolare* in this way. In the Duchesne edition, which we are using, the reading was formerly *postolantes* and *postolare*; not because the reading should be retained as a product of the barbarism of the age, but because, since *postulare* is consistently read throughout this chapter, there is no reason why the spelling should be changed in this one place.]

He is said to plead with inexpressible groanings because he causes us both to plead and to groan. He causes this because, by his gift, grace merits that it come to be.

## CHAPTER XXV. Christ Jesus the Redeemer, not redeemed; the Savior, not saved; the Liberator, not liberated.

Finally, because, driven by the obstinacy of such a stubborn mind, you do not cease somehow to affirm an adopted son of God, listen, then, in what way you may attribute this name to him without guilt.

Jesus Christ, the Son of almighty God, our almighty Lord, redeemed us by the price of his blood. He is therefore rightly proclaimed by the voices of all the redeemed as the true Redeemer.

He, I say, was not redeemed, because he was never captive. We, however, were redeemed because we were captives, sold under sin (Romans 7:14), bound by the bond of the decree which he himself removed from the midst, erasing with his blood what the blood of no other redeemed person could erase:

> “He fastened it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14),

publicly triumphing over them in himself.

Likewise, he is the Savior because he saved us, although we were lost. Thus one of those who had perished confidently asks that he be sought and saved by him:

> “I have gone astray like a sheep that was lost; seek your servant, Lord” (Psalm 118:176).

He was not saved but Savior, because he had never perished. For he himself says of himself:

> “The Son of Man came to seek and save what had perished” (Luke 19:10).

Do not insult him with the Jews who mocked him:

> “He saved others,” they say; “he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42).

Since he certainly saved others, he had no need to be saved by another. He says:

> “My own arm has helped me” (Isaiah 63:5).

He is the Liberator, not liberated, because he was never a slave of sin.

> “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin,” he says (John 8:34).

We, on the other hand, were liberated: oppressed beneath the yoke of sin, we had become slaves of demonic dominion, while the prince of this world and ruler of these darknesses claimed jurisdiction over us by tyrannical power.

For the yoke of sin:

> “was made rotten by the presence of the oil” (Isaiah 10:27),

when our Redeemer breathed upon the disciples and said:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John 20:22–23).

Finally, he asserted that he was the Liberator when he said:

> “If the Son sets you free, you are truly free” (John 8:36).

## 116 CHAPTER XXVI. Jesus is the adopter, not adopted; we, however, are adopted.

In this way, as we have stated above, he may properly and without any unjust accusation be proclaimed not as the adopted one but as the adopter, although this name is not worn smooth by customary usage and is perhaps therefore precious because it is rare.

It is certain that he was not adopted but rather the adopter, because he was never estranged through sin; he was never at all a son of wrath, conceived in iniquities, nor did his mother give birth to him in sins (Psalm 50:7). The Virgin mother, having conceived him from the Holy Spirit, truly gave birth to one God and man in both natures.

We, therefore, are the adopted ones. The bond of sin demanded it, and by right of the devil’s fraud we were held captive, standing far removed as strangers from the fellowship and dominion of our Creator. Conceived in iniquities through the intercourse of corrupted nature and cast from the womb of our mother in sins, we were sons of wrath.

He, not an adopted but the proper Son of God, sent by the Father in the fullness of time, born of a woman, made under the law (Galatians 4:4), graciously deigned to bestow upon us the grace of adoption through the washing of regeneration.

But, as the Evangelist says:

> “As many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12).

Therefore he is the adopter, just as he is Savior, Liberator, and Redeemer—not adopted, because he was neither saved, nor liberated, nor redeemed.

We, certainly, are the adopted, saved, liberated, and redeemed [the preceding text appears to require *adoptati*, “adopted”]; he is entirely the Savior, Liberator, Redeemer, and adopter, who saved, liberated, redeemed, and adopted us into the lot of the sons of God, so that we, who by debt were sons of wrath—that is, of the devil—might by his gracious gift deserve through his grace to become sons of God.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Although Christ is not adopted, he is nevertheless man.

You object:
