> “Whoever denies,” you say, “that he is an adopted son of God according to his humanity must necessarily deny that he was a true man.”

Why, I ask, do you not blush to think this, wearing such a wrinkled brow?

[Note: Perhaps one should read, “wearing a wrinkled brow.”]

Why, in such foolishness, are you not ashamed to speak of the one Christ as God and man, when the adopted son ought to be called one who is merely human—one who is counted by the name of adoption not by merit but by the gift of grace?

He is not one person consisting, together with God, of both natures, as is our Lord Jesus Christ, who, from the moment he began according to his humanity to exist after being conceived of the Holy Spirit in the Virgin’s womb, remains eternal God and man.

When I confess that he was not redeemed but the Redeemer, not saved but the Savior, do you suppose that I deny him to be man? I confess, I say, that he is a true man; but, proclaiming him true God, I worship him with reverence.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. When Christ prayed in the Scriptures to be saved, redeemed, and liberated, he was speaking not for himself but for us: the head spoke for the members.

You add still another argument, because windy words have no end (Job 16:3): that the members cannot possess anything except what has previously occurred in the head.

You would say this correctly if you had learned more religiously, with the subtle discrimination and cautious hand of faith, to distinguish what you say: what is assigned to the head alone; what is referred to the members alone; and what is common to both.

In our head, therefore, there occurred beforehand the legal circumcision, the offering of sacrifices, the observance of the Paschal feast, and the sacrifice of the lamb, when the typological Passover was celebrated as a mystery on Thursday. None of these things passes literally to his members in any way; they are derived typologically.

No one should be disturbed because we have testified that our Lord, the Son of God, was not saved, liberated, or redeemed, but the Savior, Liberator, and Redeemer of all, on the ground that he himself, through the mouth of all the prophets, pleads to be saved, liberated, and redeemed.

But he who was born not for himself but for us, as the angel testifies:

> “Today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke 2:11),

and as the prophetic statement says:

> “A child is born to us; a son is given to us” (Isaiah 9:6),

and in other passages of this kind—he who suffered, died, and was buried not for himself or on his own behalf but for us, and rose again according to the evangelical and apostolic voices, as Peter says:

> “Christ suffered for us” (1 Peter 2:21),

and as Paul repeats very often:

> “The love of Christ urges us, because if one died for all, then all died; and he died for all so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose for them” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).

He did not pray for himself or on his own behalf, because, as has often been made clear, he was not born for himself, nor did he suffer or die for himself. Rather, he prayed for them—that is, for his members—for whom he endured all these things by voluntary condescension and the highest power.

What is surprising if he wished, with infinite mercy [*pietate*, “by mercy”; alternative *pietas*, “mercy”], to pray for them—that is, for his consubstantial members—with human feeling and a human voice, since for them he also deigned to be born, suffer, die, be buried, and rise again through the successive stages of human growth?

This was no disgrace to the excellence of the divine majesty, which, in a marvelous and ineffable manner, received all these things while remaining impassible and immortal in the height of its honor, the divinity remaining unchanged.

For since he alone prayed not for himself or on his own behalf—because no necessity compelled this—but for us, whose misery was burdened by the extremity of necessity, this is most clearly demonstrated by the Gospel’s manifest testimony concerning our same Redeemer.

## 117 CHAPTER XXIX. Christ troubled himself when he wished; the voice of the Father glorifying him and his prayer to the Father were both made not for his own benefit but for those standing around him.

[Col. 0380D]

Therefore, being close to the Passion, he took upon himself the feeling of human weakness and troubled himself—not, as the heretics chatter, with the disgrace of fear, but as a sign of his power. “Now,” he says, “my soul is troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name” (John 12:27 ff.). Immediately the response of the Father’s thunderous voice is heard: “I have glorified it,” he says, “and I will glorify it again.” As the astonished crowd, struck with wonder and bewilderment, received the sound of that blessed voice and was exalted by the marks of his dignity, various suspicions [perhaps: *suspicio*, “suspicion”] turned over in different minds: whether thunder had sounded or an angel had spoken to him from heaven. At once Truth itself deigned to make public, with its own mouth, what was truer: “This voice has come not for me, but for you” (John 12:30). And again: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him. If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately” (ibid. 13:31–32).

“In himself,” certainly, because the power of divinity, which inseparably united him to itself in his own person, exalted him as true God and true Son of God. Thus the Apostle Peter says: “Let the whole house of Israel know with certainty that God has made this Jesus both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36). God, plainly, made him Lord, the Christ of God. That is, the whole fullness of divinity, which, according to Paul’s statement, was pleased to dwell bodily in him (Colossians 2:9): for God deigned to become man, according to the saying, “The Word became flesh.” God made the man Christ the Christ of God—not by a changeable conversion, or by alteration, or by a transfusion of natures, but by the dignity of one person, since the person of God deigned to assume human nature into himself.

[Note: “Or by alteration” (*vel immutabilitate*). For Paulinus, *immutabilitas* has the same sense as *mutabilitas*, just as *immuto* means the same as *muto*. Although *immutabilis* and *immutabilitas* do not have the same sense as *mutabilis* and *mutabilitas* among writers of approved Latin, Paulinus derived from *immuto* not only the word but also its meaning, as the context makes clear.]

The statement that the Lord made known in his prayer before Lazarus had yet been raised also serves to strengthen this point. [The text reads *Lazarum*; perhaps: *resuscitato Lazaro*, “the Lazarus who had been raised.”]

[Note: “The Lord made known.” That is, he “made known” in the active sense, although by its nature the word has a neuter-passive meaning. Nevertheless, I find it used in this sense not infrequently by writers of the later period. Marculfus, *Formulae*, book I, chapter 36: “He made known to us that they had purchased [it] from various men . . .,” that is, “he signified.” Saint Agobard, in his *Book on the Insolence of the Jews*, addressing the emperor Louis the Pious: “I entrust myself to your goodness and patience, giving myself over to dangers and making known to you what it would be harmful to keep silent”; *making known* means “signifying.” In a letter, or consultation, to the palace nobles concerning the baptism of Jewish slaves, he uses the same word again: “Some things which I do not think ought to be kept silent I make known to your prudence,” that is, “I signify, I make known.”]

“Father,” he said, “I thank you because you always hear me; but I said this for the sake of the crowd standing around, so that they may know that you sent me” (John 11:41–42). Here too he testifies that he prayed for no other reason than for the sake of the people standing nearby. He prayed as a true man for human beings, but with the mark of power, not with the dishonor of necessity. For everything that the incarnate Wisdom and Power of God wonderfully did in speech, action, posture, movement, sitting, rising, and walking was either an example, or instruction, or mystery—or all of these together.

## CHAPTER XXX. Scriptures Corrupted by Felix: Christ Prayed Not for Himself but for Us, Just as He Was Born, Died, and Was Buried Not for Himself but for Us

You, therefore, are not ashamed, with your bile-spitting throat, to explain that he is not true God and true Son of God because, while keeping vigil in prayer, he necessarily prayed not only for others but also for himself—taking an apostolic testimony that is sufficiently clear and plain, but, according to the sense of your faithlessness, sufficiently badly and obscurely corrupted. Surely, with the Apostle Peter’s astonishment, the voice of Paul too, praising wisdom, is heard against you in this manner?

“Our beloved brother Paul,” he says, “according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, as he does in all his letters when he speaks about these matters. In them there are some things difficult to understand, which wicked people endeavor to distort according to their own understanding, as they do the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:15–16; partly according to the wording, partly according to the sense).

You will not be able by any argument to deny that you inserted the guilt of so obscene a sacrilege into the letters you recently published, just as you will also be unable to dispute the truth of this testimony. Moreover, if he prayed to himself or for himself, then he was born, suffered, died, and was buried for himself; for himself also he poured out his own blood. Thus he had nothing more than a mere man, if he prayed for himself under the compulsion of necessity.

This is also what you argue: that, according to the flesh, he was certainly not—as he himself testifies through the Prophet (Psalm 87:5)—“free among the dead”; nor was he born exempt from that mass of perdition and law of sin. May divine mercy turn away from every heart the suspicion of such a thing. If he did all these things for himself and not for us, as truth itself shows, then only the Word made flesh—that is, God made man—performed them. Where, then, are the inviolable prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic utterances that cry out and declare that Christ was born, suffered, died, was buried, and was raised from the dead for us, along with the other statements of this kind, which the Son of God, coming in the flesh, deigned to accomplish through even the stages of infancy, from the very cradles, so to speak, of his beginnings?

He remained wholly in the Virgin’s womb, wholly in the bosom of the eternal and coeternal Father; the very same one lay wholly amid the narrow confines of the manger, while wholly reigning upon the Father’s throne. It was he himself, and no other, who deigned to be nourished on earth by virgin milk—the one who wonderfully fed the holy angels in heaven.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Christ Did Not Pray from Necessity: Felix’s Misunderstanding of Paul

Therefore, while keeping vigil in prayer, he alone prayed to God for all, because he alone had come to die for all (Luke 6:12). No—no, he had absolutely no need to pray for himself, since he had never been entangled by any bond of necessity, as any ordinary one of the elect might be.

[Note: “No, not for himself.” The repetition of the negative particle does not affirm here, but denies more emphatically, as in Terence, *Phormio* 5.304, act 2, scene 1: “No, no, it will not turn out this way; it cannot.” Donatus says that the negation is strengthened by frequent repetition.] He, having been assumed essentially by the Word made flesh and remaining a true man, deserved to be so exalted into God that, by the power of divinity, there naturally remained for him an elevation of glory comparable to it: never at all to be able to sin—he who “committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth” (1 Peter 2:22).

Nor, although it was possible for him to suffer or die because he willed it, did he have the ability to suffer or die in any other way or at any other time. Rather, in whatever manner and at whatever time he pleased, by his own power, he deigned to suffer or die.

You, however, attempt to support the assertions of your false conjectural objections with the remembered testimony of Paul, because in the Epistle entitled *To the Hebrews* he wrote concerning the Mediator of God and human beings that, “in the days of his flesh, he offered prayers and supplications with tears and loud cries for himself to the one who was able to save him from death” (Hebrews 5:7; more according to the sense than the wording). You do not understand that one can collect one thing from another and grasp the force of a statement—which you are unable to comprehend from a single passage—by intelligently comparing many similar passages.

Suppose you think you have made a great beginning by carefully building a wall, of whatever kind, from the Tower of Hananel as far as the Corner Gate (Jeremiah 31:38). Do you perhaps think it should be considered of little importance if, beyond the threshold of the gate, you exceed the rule of measurement? It is plainly no less dangerous to exceed the boundaries of the final measurement—as is the case at the beginning—than to cast the stones of a foundation’s structure beyond its proper measure.

[Note: “To exceed the boundaries of the final measurement,” as at the beginning. This appears to be Paulinus’s meaning: that it is equally dangerous to err at the boundary and to err at the beginning. Paulinus, drawing an allegory from architecture, says that to exceed the boundaries of the final—or ultimate—measurement is no different a danger from exceeding the beginning, that is, the foundation, when masses of stone are thrown beyond the measure. In the edition of Duchesne, the margin suggests *funalis*, “of the measuring cord.” This seems to allude to the cord by which fields were once measured and enclosed by boundaries. Scripture frequently mentions this: Amos 7:17, “Your land shall be measured with a cord”; Psalm 77:54, “He divided their land among them by lot, by the cord of inheritance.” Likewise Psalm 15:6, “The cords have fallen to me in pleasant places,” meaning, according to the Psalmist, that land measured by cords and lines had fallen to his lot, in pleasant or fertile fields, as Jerome explains. See P. Lorme on this passage.

Yet since, in the second part of the comparison, he is speaking of the foundations of a house to be built, the first part also seems to be understood from the rules of the same craft—namely, cords, lines, and plumb-lines, by which architects draw straight lengths and heights. Vitruvius, book 7, chapter 3, requires lengths to be aligned by the line and heights by the plumb-line. It is dangerous to deviate from the line and plumb-line and to exceed their boundaries, as Paulinus aptly says.]

Moreover, that you have closed the entrance to yourself for entering through the Corner Gate can be proved by sure indications: the ornamented excess of your words testifies that you have exceeded the measure of the rule.

Remember that the one who, through David, is called the Cornerstone (Psalm 117:22) is himself prophesied through Jeremiah as the Corner Gate (Jeremiah 31:38). In the preceding passages the Apostle is read to have discussed these matters at sufficient length—indeed, from the very beginning of his Epistle. Omitting the customary title of greeting at its head, he begins the elements of his discourse as follows:

“Long ago, in many portions and in many ways, God spoke to the fathers through the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom also he made the ages. He is the radiance of his glory and the figure of his substance, sustaining all things by the word of his power. Having made purification for sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, having become as much superior to the angels as the name he inherited is more excellent than theirs” (Hebrews 1:1 ff.).

## CHAPTER XXXII. Paul Asserts That Christ Is Not an Adopted Son but the Proper Son, Not a Merely Nominal Son but True God: In Scripture He Is Recognized by the Father as the True Son and, Conversely, the Father by the Son as the True Father; He Calls the Father “My Father,” Not “Our Father”

It is worthwhile to observe carefully in these apostolic words how the remarkable teacher distinguished the properties of both natures, and, contemplating more profoundly the person of the Only-Begotten and true God, placed him indifferently in both natures. He neither duplicates him through the privilege of adoption nor alters him through the disgrace of a merely nominal designation. Rather, he proclaims one and the same Lord Jesus Christ to be the true Son of God and true God, begotten from the Father before the ages without beginning, and temporally born from a virgin mother at the end of the ages.

When he asserts that God formerly spoke to the fathers through the prophets in many ways, and finally in the Son, he more clearly signifies both things: he proclaims the glory of the eternal divinity of the coeternal Word of the Father and announces beforehand the sacrament of the ineffable mystery of the assumed flesh. For the Father formerly spoke through his Word—that is, through the Only-Begotten—and in these last days he spoke to us in that same Son, that is, through the incarnate Wisdom of God. As the same Son testifies through Isaiah, both on account of what he spoke formerly in many ways and on account of what he spoke in himself in the last days: “Behold, I myself, the one who was speaking, am here” (Isaiah 52:6).

Again, through the same prophet, the Holy Spirit did not keep silent about him: “Eye to eye they shall see when the Lord restores Zion” (ibid. 52:8). The incarnate Truth itself, free from every stain of deception and wholly unable to lie, bears witness to the truth about itself, saying: “Behold, I am here, the one who was speaking.” And: “I am the Lord, and I do not change” (Malachi 3:6).

But through the mouths of heretics the lying spirit attempts to assert that, through the dispensation of the incarnation, the property of the Only-Begotten has been doubled into a duality of names—namely, a proper and an adoptive name—and that the unity of the indivisible Godhead exists in the plural number.

[Note: Something seems to be missing here, perhaps “when,” “or,” or “nevertheless, the Son.”]

He is also read to have been called singularly and specially by the Father’s own voice, and through the mouth of the saints, with a possessive pronoun; and he himself is clearly found to have invoked the Father with that same pronoun and with singular particularity, as we can learn from the sacramental writings of the prophets, the Gospels, and the apostles. Thus: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17); and again: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Psalm 2:7). And again through the Prophet: “I will be a Father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (1 Chronicles 17:13). Elsewhere: “He will call upon me: You are my Father” (Psalm 88:27). And again: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 11:3), and similar passages.

That the Son always distinctly called the Father his own can be demonstrated by numerous testimonies of Scripture. Through Mary Magdalene he declares to the disciples: “I am ascending to my Father and your Father” (John 20:17). Elsewhere: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:17). And: “Philip, whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9). Again: “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (ibid. 14:16).

Nowhere is he read to have said “our Father,” but either “my Father,” or simply “Father,” without the addition of “our,” as in: “I am going to the Father” (John 16), and: “The Father, who remains in me, himself does the works” (John 14:20). And: “The Spirit who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26), and the rest.

Scripture, however, has always taken care to commend the calling of the elect by the Father, or their invocation of the Father, in the plural number. No one who willingly undertakes to possess knowledge of Scripture with particular diligence is unaware that these things are more truly so.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. How Israel Is to Be Understood as God’s Firstborn, and Why Christ Taught Us to Say in Prayer “Our Father,” Not “My Father”

No one ought to be disturbed as though it could appear contrary to our assertion that in the sacred history we read that God commanded Pharaoh through his servant Moses, saying: “Israel is my firstborn son. Let my firstborn son go, so that he may sacrifice to me” (Exodus 4:22–23).

Although the ordinances of this command are written in the singular, they nevertheless require, in every respect, a plural interpretation. “Israel is my firstborn son” does not seem to be understood individually of any one of the elect; rather, it is certain that it refers to the entire multitude of the children of Israel, just as terms such as “people,” “assembly,” “crowd,” and the like do. We avoid pursuing these matters at length here, restraining the pen from an extended discussion in this work.

[Note: “In this work.” What does *in procinctu* mean? In Latin, *in procinctu* means that something is done quickly and readily. Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, book 1, elegy 8, line 9:

“And the more kindly you may judge our little books,
you will read these poems, composed in haste.”

That is, composed readily and with speed. Thus, for Paulinus, “to avoid pursuing [the matter] *in procinctu*” may mean that he does not wish to pursue it quickly and readily, and therefore restrains or suspends his pen. Or should we read *in procincto*, meaning that Paulinus does not wish, while handling these matters, to linger over work that is ready or prepared? Those who set out on a journey in haste gird themselves. See Tobit 5:5 and Isaiah 5:26–27. Yet because *procinctus* among medieval writers means the same as *ambitus*, commonly “enclosure,” as can be seen in Du Cange’s *Glossary*, I do not know whether Paulinus’s *in procinctu hoc opere* means what would more clearly have been expressed as *in ambitu huius operis*, “within the compass of this work.” Whatever the case, it is clear that he means nothing other than that he does not wish to speak at greater length about these matters.]

Nor can the following rightly be objected by any disputant of slower understanding. When the Lord Jesus was asked by his disciples to deign to instruct them in a rule of prayer, and warned them how to pray, he inclined a benevolent ear to their prayers and said:

“When you pray, pray in this way: Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9; Luke 11:2).

Perhaps someone may attempt to oppose our definitions on the grounds that, when the Lord says “our Father,” he indicates by the common term “our” that he has the name of Father in common with the others, failing to understand the force of the statement and the order of the words.

For he does not say indiscriminately, “When we pray,” but distinctly, “When you pray, say: Our Father.” He taught us not to presume, each one of us, to appropriate the dignity of the special privilege that belongs to the one and only Son of God by using the name of Father, but to say by a common designation, “Our Father,” as adopted sons and not natural sons.

It belongs uniquely to him alone to invoke the name of the eternal Father in a singular manner: he who, having become the Son of Man, could remain the one and same eternal Son of God and therefore immutable. Let this preliminary statement concerning these matters suffice.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The Text “God Was with Him,” Misunderstood by Felix, Explained by Paulinus, Who Teaches from Numerous Scriptural Passages That Christ Is the True Son of God

Now let the point of our pen turn again and again against you, who, in such arrogant pride, attempt to raise yourself so high that you seek to tear away the firm foundation of the faith of Peter, the chief of the apostles and first shepherd of the Church—a foundation which believers do not hesitate to affirm that he established firmly upon the solid rock, which is Christ.

When you appropriate his testimony, which is found in the book called the *Acts of the Apostles*, observers plainly see that it has been inserted into your syllables. The whole passage, set out in this way, runs before the reader’s eyes:

“Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power, who went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with him” (Acts 10:38)—that is, “in him.”

The Holy Spirit spoke these words through the mouth of the Apostle Peter. But you, stirred up by an evil spirit which is drawn out through the organ of your laboriously cultivated throat, added from your own error that Jesus of Nazareth is not true God because Peter taught, “God was with him,” and did not say, “God was himself.”

“God was with him,” that is, “in him”: Peter confessed this—not as God is with any one of the elect by a gift of grace, but in a more excellent manner with him, because God and man were essentially in one person, according to the statement that the whole fullness of divinity dwells in him bodily.

“God was with him,” not in the manner in which he was with nominal gods, to whom the word of God came or into whose hands the word of the Lord had been placed, but singularly and inseparably with him. In an ineffable manner, the word of God was not spoken to him; rather, the Word became flesh—that is, God became man.

When he says “with him,” he introduces a distinction of natures; he does not distinguish a duality of persons.

[Note: The alternative reading is *cum*, and something seems to be missing, perhaps “to say” or “to assert that Peter …”]

Why, then, are you not ashamed, possessed by the madness of such great impiety, to claim that Peter denied that Jesus Christ is true God—the very one from whom, to speak more excellently, for the glory of his purest confession of faith, he immediately received a corresponding blessing as his reward?

When differing opinions about the Son of Man were held by the disciples on the basis of what various people thought—some saying that he was John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets, that is, one of the nominal or adoptive gods—the Lord, the one and same Son of God and man, indignantly endured such humble and contemptible declarations.

The Lord did not wish, by favoring such faith, to confer the support of rewards upon a confession that did not hesitate to make him equal with servants. Peter was waiting until the Lord’s question to the disciples had run its course. Although he was first in the order of the apostles, he remained silent for a long time because the Lord deigned to discover not only what the one for whom Peter alone was to answer thought, but also what people thought about the Son of Man.

But when he had inquired what they themselves, whose hearts he knew, had decided about him, Peter at once, one speaking for all, preserving in every respect the order of his primacy according to the united and indissoluble bond of charity, said:

“You are the Christ,” he said, “the Son of the living God.”

Immediately, with no delay whatsoever, he won the glorious reward of blessedness from the Lord:

“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah,” he said, “for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I say to you that you are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church,” and the other statements of this kind that follow (Matthew 16:16 ff.).

Should we believe that Peter learned by revelation from the Father that Christ was adoptive? Or did he attain such a summit of blessedness and such an astonishing authority for confessing a merely nominal God or an adoptive son, so that he became the arbiter of binding and loosing and, in a special sense, the doorkeeper of the heavenly court?

Who could say such things with a shameless tongue? Who, being of sound mind, would not fear to review the secrets of impenetrable hearts through passing thoughts?

The heretic, foaming from his deceitful throat, conjectures—struck by an eternal anathema—that Christ Jesus is not true God. But Peter, with a consecrated heart and blessed lips, proclaims the Lord of all with a honey-sounding voice:

“The Word,” he says, “sent to the children of Israel, announcing peace through Jesus Christ—he is Lord of all” (Acts 10:36).

Certainly, the one who is Lord of all is beyond doubt also true God.

The accursed heretic, with a sacrilegious mouth full of faithlessness, [the printed reading *delerat* is uncertain; perhaps *delirat*, “raves”] calls Christ Jesus adoptive and not the proper Son of God.

[Note: In the edition of Du Chesne, the margin reads *delirat*, “raves.” I would judge the word to be neuter, but the sense requires *declarat*, “declares.”]

Peter, with his sweet-flowing mouth, blessedly confesses the Son of God:

“The God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” he says, “has glorified his Son Jesus” (Acts 3:13).

And again: “God, having raised up his Son, sent him first to you, blessing you through his words” (ibid. 3:26).

Luke records Paul’s testimony in the same canonical book:

“Immediately,” he says, “he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, that he is the Son of God.” And shortly afterward: “Saul grew stronger and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus, affirming that this is the Christ” (Acts 9:20, 22).

## CHAPTER XXXV. Other Christs Are Merely Nominal; Jesus Christ Is the Proper One: The Apostle Says That He Suffered in the Flesh, Not with the Flesh

It may therefore be asked how it is appropriate to understand Luke’s emphatic assertion that Paul affirmed, “This is the Christ,” since many others who were anointed with the oil of anointing are often read to have been called christs. The answer is that the others are nominal christs.

The one whom Paul affirms, however, is by nature the true Christ, the Son of God. The others were mere human beings, conceived and born in iniquities, and anointed with Christ’s chrism. But the one whom Paul proclaims was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and the glorious Virgin Mary; Christ was formed essentially in the womb. He was never not Christ, because, anointed above his companions by the Holy Spirit, he was undoubtedly made Christ as God essentially at the very conception in the Virgin’s womb.

“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”—that is, in Christ, whose members we are. And therefore he dwelt among us because he was in Christ, who deigned to assume the form of a servant, since in him the whole fullness of divinity was pleased to dwell bodily.

In no other merely nominal Christ is the whole fullness of divinity read to have dwelt. Nor is it found written of any of them: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Paul, disputing with the Jews, affirmed this true Christ as God, saying, “This is the Christ.” The Apostle Peter agrees with him in his Epistle, although in different words and with no different meaning:

“Christ, having suffered in the flesh” (1 Peter 4:1)—that is, Christ God suffered in the flesh, not with the flesh, nor as suffering together with the flesh.

For Christ God is beyond suffering. It is read, in accordance with Paul’s words, that he was crucified, died, and was buried “according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4), but only in the flesh. Christ God, together with the flesh, is believed neither to have been crucified, nor to have died, nor to have been buried.

For, impassible in what belongs to himself, he deigned to suffer in what belongs to us; remaining immortal, he willed to die, and was pleased to be buried in a tomb.

This is the meaning of what the same remarkable teacher teaches elsewhere, namely, that Christ Jesus deigned to suffer and die only in the flesh, and not with the flesh:

“For even if he died because of our weakness,” he says, “yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Corinthians 13:4).

## CHAPTER XXXVI. He Shows from the Scriptures That Christ Is True God

Behold Peter and Paul, those two shining lamps of the world, confess that the one born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary is Lord of all, Son of God, uniquely the true Christ, and above all God, blessed forever.

[Note: “Two shining lamps of the world.” Paulinus himself, in his hymn for the feast of these apostles, line 7, calls them “lamps radiant with light,” using similar wording and meaning in both places.]

John, than whom no one born of women was greater, confessed him to be the true Son of God, saying: “I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1:34). He even pointed him out with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (ibid. 1:29). If the one who deigned to become a lamb were not true God, the man who was more than a prophet would never have testified that he takes away the sin of the world.

John, Christ’s table-companion, also proclaims him to be that true Son of God, true God, and eternal life (John 10:27).

[Note: “John, Christ’s table-companion.” The Evangelist John acquired this name from the place at table where Christ deigned to have him recline at the Last Supper, when he rested upon Christ’s breast; the Fathers say that from there he drew the streams of the Gospel. Ambrose, dealing with a similar question against the Arians, says of John in *On the Incarnation*, chapter 4, section 29:

“Peter says, ‘You are the Son of God’; he does not say, ‘You are a creature.’ John said this. If you still do not believe because you have not understood the mystery of the one reclining above Wisdom, Peter repeated it. Christ commended both: the one by judgment, the other by mystery. For he added this so that you might read that John reclined upon Christ’s breast and understand that his head, in which lies the chief seat of all the senses, was filled with a certain secret wisdom.”

Chrysostom, *Homily 4 on the Incomprehensibility of God*: “Who says this? . . . John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast and drew his sacred streams from that divine fountain.”

Augustine, *Tractate 36 on John*: “How no one else spoke of the Lord’s divinity—he was belching forth what he had drunk. For it was not without reason that this very Gospel relates that he was reclining at the table upon the Lord’s breast. From that breast he drank in secret; but what he drank in secret he poured forth publicly.”

Paulinus therefore rightly calls John Christ’s table-companion, since, in agreement with the Fathers, he drew the fountain of truth from that reclining.]

Thomas touched the marks of the nails in Christ’s body, examined the open side pierced by the lance, and immediately cried out that he was both his Lord and his God.

The very Son of the eternal Father is shown by the astonishing proclamation of the Father’s voice, through a twofold declaration—on the holy mountain and above the bank of the Jordan:

“This is my beloved Son,” he said, “in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 3:17; 17:5).

He taught the disciples to believe that he is God, saying: “You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14:1). He did not say, “Believe me,” but “Believe in me.”

[Note: “Believe me” and “believe in me” are different. Eusebius Gallicanus, *Homily 2 on the Creed*: “It is one thing to believe that God exists and another to believe in God. Even the devil is found to believe that God exists; but no one is proved to believe in God unless he has piously hoped in him.”]

For “believe me” is a common expression and can apply to any creature. But “believe in me” is the honor owed to the confession of the one true God. “Do you believe in God?” he says, because one must believe in no other than the one and only God. “And believe in me,” namely, because I too am God.

[Note: “And believe in me,” certainly because I too am God. Augustine, *Tractate 67 on John*, section 1, explains and confirms Paulinus’s statement as follows: “It follows that, if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me. This would not follow if Christ were not God.”]

Not many gods, but one and the same God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Again, through the same Evangelist, he says: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). The words “and Jesus Christ whom you sent” are understood to mean that they should believe Jesus Christ whom he sent to be the only true God.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. He Rebukes Felix for the Division He Attempts into Four Persons in Christ, Whom He Nevertheless Proves to Be Inseparable

The illustrious oracles of so many lordly men proclaim this true God. The almighty Father also marked his beloved Son.

[Note: “Lordly men.” He calls both Johns—John the Baptist and John the Evangelist—*heriles viri*, that is, “men belonging to the Lord,” by the force of the word. They were so closely joined to Christ both by kinship and by knowledge that, more than others, they seemed worthy to be called by the names of sons or brothers. *Herilis* means one who belongs to a lord, but especially a lord’s son was designated by this term, as a lesser lord. Terence, *Phormio*, line 40:

“For I hear that his lord’s son has taken a wife,”

and in *The Eunuch*, line 289:

“But I see that the younger lord’s son is coming here.”

Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, line 1939, in the hymn concerning Saint Fructuosus, calls the prefect’s daughter a *herilis filiolla*, “a little daughter of the lord.” Medieval writers revived this use of the word, as Du Cange shows in his *Glossary*, applying it to the sons and brothers of kings. The Greeks call such persons δεσποσύνους, as though “lesser lords” or “little lords.” But who could be more deserving of this designation than those who were joined to Christ by the merits and knowledge of their virtues, not to mention by blood, as these men were—especially John? Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 1, chapter 7, says that Christ’s relatives according to the flesh were called δεσποσύμους, or δεσποτίκους, as Nicephorus reports from Africanus, book 1, chapter 11; that is, “lordly,” or “little lords,” and *heriles*, because of the kinship of race that existed between them and the Savior.]

But you, unhappy man, have attributed nothing more to him than to a mere human being. You call him a merely nominal God and an optional son while, with an impious sneer, you—
You mock with an impious snort. There is more than one way of mocking. For sometimes they pretended to strike the back of the person mocked, with their fingers gathered together into a point like a stork’s beak; or, placing their hands beside their temples and extending their fingers, they imitated an ass’s ears; or, thrusting out their tongue like a dog parched with thirst and stretching their lips apart, they distorted their mouth against the one whom they wished to ridicule—yet always from behind, so that they would not be seen. [Col. 0391B] Persius describes all these practices in Satire 1, verse 72, addressing Janus, whom he sees from behind:

[Col. 0391C]

> O Janus, whom from behind no stork pecks,
>
> Nor does a mobile hand, imitating white ears,
>
> Nor does any tongue pant as much as an Apulian dog thirsts.
>
> You, O patrician blood, for whom it is lawful to live,
>
> Meet the mockeries directed at your unseen back.

See Britannicus, or rather the pseudo-Britannicus, Cornutus, and the others at this passage. Strictly speaking, however, *subsannare* means to insult by distending the nostrils and opening the mouth in a kind of mimetic gesture. Juvenal, Satire 6, verse 306:

> Go now, and wonder with what mockery Tullia
>
> sniffs the air, and what she says to the famous Maura,
>
> when Maura passes by the ancient altar of chastity.

Here Britannicus writes: “A *sanna* is a derision produced by distortion of the mouth and nose.” Ascensius writes: “With what mockery she sniffs the air,” that is, “with what nasal sound Tullia eagerly inhales and draws air through her nostrils.” This agrees with what Caelius Rhodiginus noted at the end of Book XV, chapter 22: “Among Cratinus, *sanna* indicates a fool. Hence, I think, the verb *sannare*, frequent among the Latins, also arose, although grammarians suppose that it was derived from the sound of the nostrils.” Paulinus therefore spoke strictly when he accused Felix of mocking through the nostrils.]

When you mock, [Col. 0391A] what else are you doing than paying to any one of the elect a common honor which you ought rather to have displayed uniquely and more excellently from the wings [Note: [Col. 0391D] “Whom you ought uniquely to have shown the glory of power more excellently from the wings.” I confess that I do not know what it means to “show the glory of power from the wings.” In a human being, wings are the hollow place beneath the arms. They are also called armpits—indeed, *axillae* comes from *alae*, “wings.” Cicero writes in *De Oratore*: “Words are often contracted, not for the sake of usage, but for the ears. For how did our *axilla* become *ala*, unless through the avoidance of a more cumbersome letter? The same custom has removed that letter from *maxillae*, and so forth, by the elegant usage of Latin speech.” The arms depend upon the armpits, but the wings depend upon both, and both serve exertion and effort. But does “from the wings of power” mean the same as with the whole effort and exertion of the arms and wings? Or rather, does “from the wings of power” mean that, with all the powers of intellect and eloquence as wings, one should carry his glory even to the stars? Let the learned reader decide.] of power? But since you know that for this reason Arius was condemned by the holy Fathers with an eternal anathema, you therefore strive to defraud the catholic faith with a laborious [Note: [Col. 0392C] “You will labor with a laborious objection.” *Satages* is used for *satagis*, as the context proves. But the substitution of *e* for *i* is frequently found in Paulinus, as is shown by *intellegens*, *intellegentia*, *neglegens*, *neglegentia*, and similar forms, instead of *intelligens*, *intelligentia*, *negligens*, and *negligentia*, which occur throughout. But what is a “laborious objection”? Is it used for *lugubri*, “mournful,” because the objection tended toward an injury to the faith? Or does *lucubri* mean an objection composed by lamplight? For *lucubrum* sometimes means a lamp. “*Lucubrum*,” says Macer in the *Hierologicon*, “a word found in the most ancient manuscript glossary among the works of Alcuin, preserved at the monastery of Saint Andrew of Avignon, means a lamp.” Du Cange, however, has not *lucubrum* but *lucibrum*, which the French explain as “a light or candle for keeping vigil at night.” In Greek it is *φανός* (*phanos*). Isidore writes: “It is called *lucubrum* because it gives light in darkness. It is a small fire usually made from fine tow and wax.” See also Salmasius on Solinus. [Col. 0392D] Thus for Paulinus “with a laborious objection” means the same as “with an objection laboriously composed,” that is, constructed by the dim light of a lamp. Unless one prefers to understand it as follows: since lamps of this kind become black and sooty from the smoke of a burning wick, “with a laborious objection” may mean “with a black, sooty, obscure objection,” and so forth.] objection; and while you pretend to repel the viperous hisses with an itching [Note: [Col. 0392D] “To repel with an itching ear.” Properly, *prurire* means to burn with a desire to scratch the ears, teeth, head, and so forth; that is, to suffer an impatient irritation which one seeks to remove by scratching. Hence *prurio*, as though *peruror*, “I am burned.” To relieve the irritation that affects the ears or teeth, the toothpick and ear-pick were invented. Martial writes of these in *Apophoreta* 23:

> If your ear teems with a troublesome itch,
>
> We offer weapons suited to such desires.

Paulinus therefore speaks precisely when he says that Felix seems to repel the sound with an itching ear—that is, with an ear that cannot endure and drives away from itself the hisses of evil doctrine.] little ear, you are condemned to death by the deadly breath of an asp and a basilisk. For you strive, with a dissecting heart (see chapter 11, note a), to divide the one and same Christ, the Son of God, into parts. For when, possessed by the fury of madness, you deprive the true God and the true Son of God of speech (see note a in §11 of the Council of Forojulium), what else are you hastening to introduce than four persons? Although you deny that you assert this even nominally, nevertheless you are shown to have established it by the propositions you have presented. Since our Redeemer is truly proclaimed as one and the same Son of God and of man from both natures—namely, the divine and the human—it therefore seems correct to you to confess two and two: the true and the proper [perhaps, in the accusative, *verum, proprium*], that is, the titular and the adoptive; as though one Christ were pure God, that is, true, and another pure man, like any one of the elect, that is, titular God—hence the proper son from the one, and the adoptive son from the other. Yet the simple and sincere rule of faith extends the straight line of its religious norm in every direction without bending at all through error on either side [the reading is *utrinque*; alternatively *utrique*, and perhaps *utriusque* should be read]. For in one way he is from the Father, because before all ages and without beginning, invisible and incorporeal, he was born from the coeternal Begetter; in another way, certainly, he is from his mother, because at a definite time the Word, having become flesh, was bodily born as God and man. It is not one who existed before the ages and another who appeared in time, but one and the same, from both natures and in both natures. Once the terms “titular God” and “adoptive son” have been entirely removed [the text has *nuncupativo Dei*, perhaps for *nuncupativi … adoptivi*], he remains in every respect one true God and true Son of God, both before and after the Virgin’s birth.

For one cannot be divided. Therefore you are not permitted to believe that he is true in one part and not true in another; nor can the twofold distinction of the natures be separated within the one person, which has come together ineffably. The Holy Spirit bears witness to this when he speaks through Scripture: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6). For God joined to himself, in his bridal chamber, in the unity of person—that is, in the inviolate womb of the blessed Virgin—the human nature, without confusion, or [for *et*] inseparably. This inseparable union of the natures, the united communion of the divine and human, you strive to split with a bloody hand. And although you make a futile attempt, you will not achieve the result you seek.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Martha, the thief, the centurion, and Gabriel confess Christ to be the true Son of God; Felix calls him adoptive.

[Col. 0393A]

You are therefore guilty of the sole undertaking of such an obscene intention [Note: [Col. 0393D] “Such an obscene intention.” The etymology of the word varies. Priscian, Book IX, near the end, says: “*Obscenus* comes from *obs* and *canere*, or from *coenum*, or from *ἀπὸ τοῦ κυνός*—‘from *kyōn*, dog’—whence also *inquinare*, ‘to defile.’ Others derive it from *κοινόν*, which in Greek means ‘common,’ because something is, as it were, polluted by common and worn-out usage, in accordance with the language of Scripture, Mark 7:2 and Acts 10:14, where the unclean is called ‘common.’ Varro, Book VI—or, according to others, Book III—of *De Lingua Latina*, says: ‘That which is disgraceful is obscene, that which ought not to be spoken openly except on the stage.’ Nonius, under the words beginning with O, writes: ‘Obscene means unclean … and also avoidable,’” which he confirms with examples taken from Virgil. He adds: “*Obscene* also signifies accursed,” which he proves by the authority of Accius and Lucilius. I would think that Paulinus used *obscena voluntas*, “obscene intention,” in this last sense, insofar as Felix’s intention impelled him to vomit curses against the Son of God. Hence the words are both accursed and obscene, because he had suggested accursed and obscene words against Christ. Nevertheless, I do not deny that *obscene intention*, that is, unclean intention, may be understood as arising from the blasphemies he uttered.] and, unless you repent of this crime, you will be held before the sight of the eternal Judge. Did not holy women confess him to be the true Son of God? When Martha was asked by him whether she believed that he was the life and resurrection of the dead, she answered: “I have believed, Lord, that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who has come into this world” (John 11:27). In what sense did he come, when through the power of his divinity he was wholly present everywhere? Yet he came into this world through the Virgin’s womb. And Martha confessed him who, by virtue of what he is from the Father, had nowhere to come from, yet nevertheless came through the Virgin’s womb, to be the Son of the living God.

Perhaps the centurion—not yet having washed his hands of blood—was of stronger faith than you, to say nothing of the thief as Christ’s confessor: when the Son of God had been crucified in the flesh, he struck his breast and said: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Matt. 28:54). He confessed the true Christ hanging on the cross to be the Son of God; you assert that the one already seated at the Father’s right hand is adoptive.

For the archangel Gabriel had proclaimed Christ, lying in the manger, as Lord and Savior and as joy for all the people, saying: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, which will be for all the people, because today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:10–11). Yet you, with a ruined heart, confess him who now reigns with the Father on the throne of his majesty to be titular God. [Col. 0393C]

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The Scriptures contain neither a titular God nor an adoptive son, but, on the contrary, the true God and the proper Son.

I ask, then, who that teacher of error was—one who had never been a disciple of truth—from whom you learned that Christ was titular God and an adoptive son. For in the sacred books, through the teaching of the Holy Spirit, his name is found inserted otherwise. Thus David says: “His name shall endure before the sun, and his throne before the moon” (Ps. 71:17, 45).

Isaiah, foremost among the prophets, foretold the one who deigned to be born of a virgin, together with the interpretation of his name: “And his name,” he says, “shall be called Emmanuel,” which is interpreted as “God with us” (Isa. 7:14; 8:10; Matt. 1:23; see note a in chapter 19 of this book). “God with us” likewise accords with the words: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), that is, “God with us.” Again: “And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God” (Isa. 9:6). And again: “Your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, shall be called God of the whole earth” (Isa. 54:5).

David, moreover, does not prophetically urge every nation to clap its hands and sing with a voice of exultation to some titular god, but to the true God and great King who is above all gods: “For God is the Most High, terrible, and a great King over all gods” (Ps. 46:3). And because he had foretold the Word made flesh, he makes this clearer when shortly afterward he adds: “God has ascended amid rejoicing, and the Lord with the sound of the trumpet” (ibid. 6). And: “He who ascends above the setting sun, the Lord is his name” (Ps. 67:6). And below: “The Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory” (Ps. 23:10). A similar statement is sung by Moses in a triumphal hymn: “The Lord is like a warrior; Almighty is his name” (Exod. 15:3).

Zechariah says: “Behold, a man; Orient is his name” (Zech. 6:12). The angel says to Joseph: “And you shall call his name Jesus” (Matt. 1:21), that is, “Savior.” Again, the same angel says to the blessed Virgin: “The holy one who will be born from you,” he says, “shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). And again: “He shall be called the Son of the Most High” (ibid. 32).

The evangelical Zechariah also foretold him as both Lord and Most High: “And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High; for you will go before the face of the Lord to prepare his ways” (Luke 1:76). Nathanael professes him in this way: “Rabbi,” he says, “you are the Son of the living God; you are the King of Israel” (John 1:49). Luke writes: “And his name was called Jesus, as he had been named by the angel before he was conceived in the womb” (Luke 2:21). Peter says: “He is Lord of all” (Acts 10:36). Paul confesses him to be God blessed above all, forever (Rom. 9:5).

## CHAPTER XL. Emmanuel, Jesus, Redeemer, and Christ are the names of the Son of God in Scripture—not titular God and not adoptive son.

I plainly do not know who imposed upon him the name “titular” or “adoptive.” For if all the pages of both Testaments are examined, these two terms, referring to him, will nowhere be found there, because they do not deserve to be ascribed to the Son of God.

The names revealed to us through angels, prophets, and holy apostles, however, fit the Son of God most suitably [Possibly: “fit suitably”]. Emmanuel, because he is “God with us”; Jesus, because he is the Savior of all; Redeemer, because he redeemed us, captives, at the price of his blood; Christ, because he was anointed more secretly in the Virgin’s womb—that is, he was born from the Holy Spirit.

That conception itself was likewise a spiritual and invisible anointing, although he was more openly anointed on the banks of the Jordan by the Holy Spirit, who descended upon him in the form of a dove. The latter is proclaimed the more manifest anointing; the former the more hidden. He is Lord because every creature in heaven and on earth serves him. And because he was more secretly imbued in the Virgin’s womb by the breath of the Holy Spirit, he was born Christ—that is, “Anointed One”—as we are taught more explicitly by the angelic oracle: “Today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord, in the city of David” (Luke 2:11).

## CHAPTER XLI. What “titular God” means, and why it does not apply to Christ.

Come, then, with every fuel of envy extinguished—for envy immediately burns more fiercely the coals of disputes—let us now see with the simple eye of the mind whether these two terms have been more appropriately attributed to Christ, the only-begotten Son of God.

That one is called titular God who, although he is a mere man and is not one person with the true God, as Christ is, is called “God” only by an accidental gift of grace. He earns the title of this honor from the gratuitous gift of the giver at some point, because he did not essentially possess it always, so as to be God. To call someone *nuncupare* is to designate him by an intended or conventional expression. Therefore, one who was not always God, but to whom the privilege of imitation was at some point added so that he might be God, can undoubtedly be called not true God but titular God.

Christ, however, who was never not God and man—for from the moment he was assumed by the true God in the unity of person, he has always remained true God and man—although he is one thing in respect of that by which he is God and another in respect of that by which he is man, is nevertheless one God and man in both. He was never at any time conceived or born as a mere man; rather, because he was conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and virginal flesh, from his very conception, or ineffable birth, the true God and man proceeded forth.

How, then, is he not always and wholly true God, who was never without the true God, neither conceived nor born? Nor was the title of titular God ever added to him, so that he might become titular God, since the true man was deemed worthy to be born in the unity of person with the true God. Christ was never a person belonging to anyone other than the true God.

## CHAPTER XLII. By an example and comparison he shows that one person cannot possess two designations, adoptive and proper.

How, then, can one person exhibit two gods? Or how can the property of one person receive diversity through the unequal designation of a duality of sons? Although it is established that one man consists of two different natures—for this reason Paul speaks of the inner and outer man (Rom. 7:22)—John the Baptist, nevertheless, one and the same inner and outer man, would not properly be called one son of his father Zechariah according to the inner man, that is, the spirit, and an adoptive son according to the outer man, that is, the fleshly body.

For the one John is proclaimed to be the proper and true son of the one Zechariah. But if Zechariah had gratuitously substituted James son of Alphaeus—namely, the son of another father—in the place of a son by the privilege of adoption, then, because of the distinction of their persons, the two, John and James, could truthfully be called sons, one proper and the other adoptive.

If the capacity of human possibility had allowed it—so that John, remaining what he was, could become inseparably one with James in a union of person, while the two natural properties remained distinct and the personal union of individuality could not for any reason be severed—then perhaps the one person formed from John and James could have been called both an adoptive and a true son. But although John and James can, through a fellowship of love, be one heart and one soul, they can never naturally become one through a unity of person. John therefore always remains, in every other respect, nothing but the true son of Zechariah.

Although whatever is drawn from human affairs as an example is undoubtedly unworthy of being applied to divine worship, nevertheless, insofar as the reasoning of a comparison requires [perhaps *exigit* for *exerit*], invisible things may be compared with visible things, and sublime things with humble things. When our Redeemer declared himself figuratively to be the true vine, his disciples the branches, and his Father the cultivator, he certainly raised the glory of the divine mystery to a higher level through earthly things (John 15). Strengthened, therefore, by the proclamation of so great and so divine an authority, I do not think that anything rashly introduced can harm the figure of the example set forth above.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Adoption applies to us, not to Christ.

Christ, therefore, the only-begotten Son of the eternal Begetter, who, from the very—more accurately, ineffable—conception in the Virgin’s womb, was received into the person of the Son of God, and who, together with God, became one person without confusion and also without division, is one and the same true Son of God and man [Note: [Col. 0395D] The verb *est*, “is,” seems to be missing], a person undivided according to the dispensation of the flesh but distinguished according to nature.

According to the divine majesty of ineffable glory, he is inseparably one in essence with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but distinguished in person; always the only-begotten and true Son of God [Note: [Col. 0395D] Here too *est*, “is,” or *permanet*, “remains,” seems to be missing], with the title “adoptive” entirely and absolutely excluded.

For the designation of adoption does not suitably or validly apply to Christ Jesus, to whom no disgrace of alienation ever occurred. Since adoption is a name that is a benefit to me and to all the redeemed [Note: [Col. 0395D] It seems that the text should have said “to all the redeemed,” because *mihi*, “to me,” precedes it], nevertheless the regular principle of catholic faith does not permit it to be more suitably ascribed to the one who is both God and man. For through this same Son of God and man, the one who comes from the mass of perdition through hereditary descent, conceived in iniquity and born in sin, and who is consequently an outsider with respect to the privilege of his father’s dignity, must attain the benefit of regeneration [Note: [Col. 0396D] Perhaps *bonum*, “benefit,” should be supplied, referring back to the preceding phrase].

Before the time when adoption would take place, such a person existed as a son of wrath. But no order recognized by sound faith demonstrates that Christ Jesus ought to be believed to be an adoptive son. He alone, uniquely conceived and born from the Holy Spirit, came forth from the Virgin’s womb without sin, God and man. He was never a son of wrath, so that through a gift of grace he might become the Son of God by a process of adoption. From the moment the Word became flesh and Christ the man began to be one person with God, he has always remained, one from both, the true and only-begotten Son of God.

## CHAPTER XLIV. He argues from the fact that God makes sons of wrath adoptive sons through baptism: Felix must either have said that Christ was a son of wrath or must not call him adoptive through baptism; Christ did not need baptism but sanctified it for us by receiving it.

[Col. 0397B]

Would you not justly condemn yourself by your own mouth, unless you are afraid promptly to contradict your own assertions [Note: [Col. 0397C] “You will not hesitate.” The sentence is obscure and tangled, as are several others in this chapter, partly because of the barbarity of the style and partly because of the carelessness of copyists. I make some corrections, while noting in brackets the differing reading that the reader may still prefer. I sometimes add a simple conjecture for the reader to follow at will. In this sentence, which was read as “Would you not justly condemn yourself, if you will not hesitate to contradict your assertions as soon as possible?” *nisi* should apparently be read, that is, “unless you contradict your assertions,” and so forth. For if he does not hesitate to contradict his own assertions, there will no longer be anything for which he can be condemned by himself. He will condemn himself to the extent that he hesitates to contradict himself, and will be caught in the snare of his own mouth. Consider what follows, and you will approve the conjecture.]? For your own writings betray you by reporting: “Through the sacrament of baptism, which nevertheless comes to their aid, those who are sons of wrath become sons of God through the grace of adoption.”

Either, then, you will be convicted as guilty of the crime of falsehood if you attempt to resist the claim that all, as you have said, are originally sons of wrath who become sons of God through the grace of adoption; or, if you do not refrain from proclaiming Jesus Christ, one God and man, to be an adoptive son, you must assert that he was originally a son of wrath, as though he were a mere man, conceived in iniquities, with an impious mouth and a heart full of curses. Then, with confused language, assign to him the name of adoption, so that, with all the heresies of all the heresiarchs [Note: [Col. 0397D] “So that all the heresiarchs’ heresies,” and so forth. The sentence is obscure. I would express this clause as follows: “when all the heresies of the heresiarchs have been gathered together and reduced to one, no judge would be sufficient to assess them, nor would any other sect’s crime, even halfway, suffice for comparison.” The meaning would be that Felix’s heresy contains the wickedness of all the leaders of heresy—as was shown above in chapter 8, where he is understood to side with Arius and Nestorius, and in chapter 24, with Macedonius—and therefore cannot be evaluated by any arbiter or judge, indeed not even by comparison with half the crime and wickedness of any other heresy. Let the reader judge whether I have grasped Paulinus’s meaning.] collected and heaped together, no arbiter would be sufficient to assess it, nor could it be compared with the crime of any other sect, even in part, though it be uttered in a novel sound by an old and purulent palate.

An incurable [Note: [Col. 0397D] “An incurable pestilence of a deadly cancer devastates you by creeping.” The meaning is ambiguous, since one does not recognize the nominative governing *devastat*. Read either “an incurable cancer of a deadly pestilence,” or “an incurable pestilence of a deadly cancer,” or “an incurable, deadly cancer.” For *cancer* is nominative, not *canceris*, and is masculine in gender, although some have taken it as neuter, deceived by the following passage of Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.826:

> And as an incurable evil, the cancer is accustomed to creep widely.

The word *immedicabile* is joined to *malum*, “evil,” and is added by apposition to *cancer*. Paulinus here has in mind the Apostle’s words, 2 Timothy 2:17: “Their speech spreads like a cancer.” Saint Julian of Toledo likewise says at the beginning of Book I *Against the Jews*: “They presume to argue with cancerous words.”] pestilence of a deadly cancer devastates you by creeping, when you reckon the only-begotten Son of God to have two births after the Virgin’s birth, in this way:

“he,” you say [the text perhaps reads *inquam* or *inquis*], “contains within himself, according to the man, these two generations: the first, which is according to the flesh, and the second, spiritual, which comes through adoption. The first he assumed by being born from the Virgin; the second he inaugurated [Note: [Col. 0398C] “Which he inaugurated in the laver.” The verb *initiare* has more than one meaning. Sometimes it means to imbue with sacred rites, sometimes to dedicate; strictly speaking, however, it means to begin, and *initium* means a beginning or origin. The other meanings derive from this. We call those who are imbued with sacred rites *initiated* because those who are initiated begin to be admitted to rites to which they were previously not admitted. Cicero likewise derives the initiation of sacred rites from a beginning in Book II of *De Legibus*, when he says: “Athens seems to have brought nothing better into human life than those mysteries by which we were cultivated into humanity and softened from a rustic and savage life; and, as they are called initiations, so in truth we have recognized them as beginnings of life.” Thus Paulinus uses *initiare* here for “to begin.” Felix had asserted that Christ possessed another birth, which he inaugurated in the laver; Paulinus replies that catholic faith recognizes only two births in Christ: one from the Father without beginning and the other from the mother, not a third inaugurated in baptism. Therefore you should suspect no mystery, still less profanity, in the word, even though it was uttered by Felix, especially since Du Cange shows that *initiare* was used by later Latin writers for “to begin” in many instances.] in the laver by rising from the dead.”

Catholic faith confesses one birth from the Father before all ages and proclaims another from the mother at the end of the age. But it rejects in every way, according to the rule of the Church, the third birth that you assert was inaugurated in baptism. For although you maintain that there are two generations—one from the Virgin, the second inaugurated in baptism—you are shown to have forgotten that ineffably glorious birth from the Father’s womb before the morning star.

Moreover, eager to introduce two generations in addition to that one, you foam them out with a poison-flowing mouth. Of these, you assert one from the Virgin through a wondrous birth, and the other from the sacrament of the laver. You do not shrink from strangling yourself in that snare of falsehood, because you attempt to assert a third birth precisely in order to make it seem that he needed to be regenerated through baptism—as though he were originally a son of wrath, who was not conceived and born from the Holy Spirit like Christ, but, conceived in iniquity from the seed of a corrupted nature, exists as such.

Therefore the snares of your hidden faithlessness, twisted through its winding folds, are more clearly exposed, because, deprived of sound judgment, you think Jesus Christ the man to be an adoptive Son through empty-flourishing speech [Note: [Col. 0399C] “The meaning of *vaniflavo*.” I thought an error had crept in and that *vaniflavo* had been substituted for *vanifluo*, “empty and flowing.” But I hesitated when I found in Ambrose Calepinus, in the Venice edition of 1533, that the etymology might be derived from *flare*, “to blow.” He says under *flaveo*, from which *flavus* derives: “*Flaveo*, I shine and produce the color of gold; this is a color not unlike flame, or from *flare*, because metals that have been blown have that color.” If this derivation is accepted, Paulinus’s meaning is no longer impenetrable: in reproaching Felix’s “empty-flourishing” judgment, he understands it as empty and vain, like dust blown by the wind from the face of the earth. If one instead wishes *flavus* to mean elegant and beautiful—for people who are fair-haired appear beautiful, and Turnebus says in *Adversaria* XXII.7 that *flavus* came to mean “beautiful” for this reason, as in Catullus’s epigram to a door:

> The blond honey runs along in a gentle stream.

And the learned Hesychius likewise interprets the Greek word *ξανθόν* (*xanthon*) as both “blond” and “beautiful—then Paulinus’s meaning may be that Felix’s style luxuriates in a certain beauty and elegance, but is entirely vain and worthy of contempt.] as though it were necessary for him to be born again, both from his mother and from the womb of the font, like other human beings who are baptized for the remission of sins—even if they are not guilty of personal wrongdoing, as infants are not, yet they are subject to original crimes transmitted from the mass of perdition.

“Unless someone is born again from water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” according to the declaration of the Lord’s preaching (John 3:5). Yet he did not say to Nicodemus, “We must be born again,” but excluded himself [Note: [Col. 0399D] “But he excluded himself.” Properly, *exceptare* is the frequentative of *capio*, “to take,” as in Virgil’s passage concerning mares impregnated by the wind, *Georgics* III.273:

> All turned toward Zephyr, they stand on the high cliffs
>
> and catch the light breezes.

Caesar also uses it in this sense in *The Gallic War*, Book VII, no. 189: “Lucius Fabius … having found three of his own soldiers and been lifted up by them, climbed the wall. Then, catching them one by one, he lifted them onto the wall.” Paulinus, however, uses *exceptavit* here for *excepit*, “took.” For *excipere* is as though *extra capere*, “to take outside,” and he perhaps formed *exceptare* from the adverb *excepto*, which Du Cange shows to have been frequently used in later Latin. Hence Festus writes under the letter E: “From *excipere*, *excipuum*, that which is excepted, just as *praecipuum* is that which is taken first.”] himself, for whom it was not necessary to be born again. “You,” he says, “must be born again” (ibid. 7).

For just as he is truly believed to have been born, suffered, died, and been buried—not for himself or on his own behalf, but for us—so he deigned to dedicate the sacrament of baptism not for himself or on his own behalf, but for us. For if it had not pleased him to sanctify the waters of the Jordan by his baptism, the nature of water could never have possessed the power to regenerate.

Thus, when John asked to be baptized by him first, saying, “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (Matt. 3:14), he immediately heard from the Lord: “Let it be so for now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid. 15). John therefore, by his own baptism, could not sanctify the nature of water, nor could he confer upon it, through the washing of his body, the effect of regeneration for the remission of sins, as did the washing of his Lord.

For that reason John ought not to have been baptized first, before the precious waves of the Lord’s Jordan had flowed over the limbs of their Creator [Possibly: “before they had washed the limbs”]. The sanctification of the waters had to be supplied through the fulfillment of righteousness. Once the Lord had been baptized, John—[Possibly: “the Jordan”—]sanctified by the baptism of that same Lord, thereby acquired the power [The text has *vim valuit*; “had the power” is intended] to bring the sublime things of heaven into effect.

## CHAPTER XLV. The Apostles, baptizing and performing miracles in the name of Jesus, prove that he is God.

If, then, Jesus of Nazareth were not himself the true God, as your impiety maintains, Peter and Paul—who were regarded as the pillars of the Church—would certainly never have administered, in the name of Jesus, the sacrament of baptism for the remission of sins, a sacrament belonging in name to no one but the true God alone. For the multitude of believers, instructed according to the rule of faith and imbued with the Lord’s promulgated commandments, was not prevented by contrary words from being commanded to be baptized in the name of Jesus by those who had been instructed through the gift of divine graces. Luke attests this, thus writing with the truthful evangelical pen the words of Peter and Paul. For, after the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon the believers, he records Peter’s speech as follows:

“Then Peter answered: ‘Can anyone forbid water, so that these people should not be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit?’ And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus” (Acts 10:47–48).

But when Paul had affirmed from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Christ, and had received the answer from those who had believed that they had been baptized with John’s baptism, he said:

“John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him—that is, in Jesus.” When they heard this, “they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 19:4–5).

And again in the same book:

“When they had believed Philip as he proclaimed the kingdom of God, men and women were baptized in the name of Jesus Christ” (Acts 8:12).

I marvel that, with the wrinkles of shamelessness carved into your brow, you do not hesitate to defame Peter and Paul, those two splendid lights of heaven,[^c0042-1] by conjecturing that they kept silent about Jesus of Nazareth being the true God, as though, in your madness, they had thought him a merely titular god.

[^c0042-1]: See the notes on *Hymn* 2, “On the Nativity of the Apostles,” verse 8.

And if he himself were not the true God, Peter and John would certainly never have said to the man lame from his mother’s womb, in the name of Jesus the Nazarene: “Rise and walk” (Acts 3:6). Nor would they have said:

“Let it be known to all of you that in the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified, this man stands before you healthy. And there is salvation, he says, in no one else; for there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:10).

And to a certain man lying on a bed, paralyzed, he said:

“Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose (Acts 9:34).

## CHAPTER XLVI  
### Jesus is the author of life, life itself, and the resurrection; therefore he is not a titular god but the true God

If, then, he himself were not the true God, how could that same chief of the apostles elsewhere have confessed him, on his own authority, to be the author of life? For he boldly rebukes the Jews’ unbelief, saying:

“But you asked for a murderous man to be given to you, while you killed the author of life, whom God raised from the dead” (Acts 3:14–15).

Do you not say that Christ Jesus, who was killed, is always living, and that the one whom God raised is not the true God? Yet Peter proclaims him the author of life. No one can be called or believed to be the author of life among titular gods unless he is the true God—just as our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, bears witness about himself. “I am,” he says, “the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). And again: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

Tell me, I beg you, tell me; do not be reluctant to speak the truth: where do you remember having read that some other titular god said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”? And truly I know that you have never read it, nor will you ever read it.

Why, then, do you not correct yourself and turn to the way, along which you do not cease wandering in weariness of error? Why do you not embrace the truth? How long will you follow the father of lies, deceived by a false error? Why, desiring it, do you not long to grasp life? How long will you not be ashamed to be the follower[^c0042-2] of death and to be its author?

[^c0042-2]: *Sequipedam* means “a follower” (*pedisequus*). This is an old Latin word. Plautus uses it in *The Braggart Soldier* 1028, act 4, scene 2: “I am your attendant.” Terence uses it in *The Girl from Andros* 120, act 1, scene 1: “I approach the attendants.”

Medieval Latin writers frequently used the word. Anastasius the Librarian, in *On Zachariah*, p. n., margin 214, Roman edition of 1718: “But, trusting in Christ’s help, he boldly went out from the city of Ravenna, entered the borders of the Lombards, and became a *sequipes* to his own messengers.” In *On Stephen III*, no. 248: “Pippin, king of the Franks, also his *sequipes*, etc.” And in *On Hadrian I*, no. 305: “Therefore I shall also strive to send my messengers as your *sequipes*.” The Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 3: “We likewise prohibit this concerning close female relatives at improper times, lest, under the parental license granted to them, the life or reputation of those women should be polluted by the *sequipes* mentioned.” John of Salisbury uses not *sequipes* but *sequipeda*, as our Paulinus does, in book 1, chapter 13, of *The Frivolities of Courtiers*: “A dog is a most convenient *sequipeda*.” And in book 3, chapter 6: “For who are they who are surrounded by the company of *sequipedae*?” The word was occasionally used by imitation by the Second Council of Tours, canon 22: “We have learned that some are followers of the ancient error, who celebrate the Kalends of January.” Paulinus uses it here in the same way.

Hence I suspect an error in the printed reading when I read: “How long will you not be ashamed to be the author of death’s *sequipeda*?” If *sequipeda* is feminine, it cannot be “author.” For an author is one who goes before; a *sequipeda* is one who follows and imitates. Therefore I conjecture that we should not read *auctorem* (“author”), but *auctoris* (“of the author”), that is, of death, who is the devil.

For by clinging to it, you will become food for everlasting Gehenna.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### Paul understands the passages that repeatedly say that the Lord is God as declaring that Jesus Christ is God

Thus the heretic, drunk with the cup of viperous poison wickedly swallowed,[^c0042-3] denies with his throat that Jesus of Nazareth is the true God. But Peter, filled with the sweetness of the Holy Spirit, confesses with sanctified lips that he is Lord of all.
