And that the Lord of all is himself God is very clearly and truthfully declared in the celebrated prophecy of the Psalmist:

“Enter into his presence with exultation; know that the Lord himself is God” (Psalm 99:2–3).

For “the fool has said in his heart: ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13:1). The most wise Solomon, imbued with prophetic inspiration, likewise declares in an extended sequence of prayer:

“So that all the peoples of the earth may know that the Lord himself is God” (1 Kings 8:60).

And there is also the statement of the patriarch Jacob:

“If I return safely,” he says, “to my father’s house, the Lord shall be my God; and this stone, which I have set up as a pillar …” (Genesis 28:21–22).

This is demonstrated still more clearly elsewhere in the aforesaid book of Kings, under the form of a conditional proposal, when Elijah prophetically challenged the prophets of Belial. When nothing worthy had been accomplished by those invoking their gods, the prophet Elijah immediately purified the structure of the altar,[^c0042-4] invoked the everlasting name of the omnipotent Lord God of heaven, and placed the sacrifice of an ox upon the altar. After it had been drenched three times with leaping streams of water, divine fire consumed it at once with blazing flames. When the truth of so remarkable an event had been revealed by the clear report of the miracle, the people, astonished and prostrate upon the ground, immediately repeated the same expression and proclaimed the profession of right faith:

“The Lord himself is God!” (1 Kings 18:39).

[^c0042-3]: “Drunk with the cup having been swallowed,” that is, “made exceedingly drunk.” The prefix *de-* intensifies the meaning of the verb, as we explained, following Bortius, in the notes on §11, letter b, of *Sacrosyllabus*. See there.

[^c0042-4]: “The structure of the altar.” Paulinus here used an ancient word. Festus says that the ancients called the structures of all things *struices*. The expression occurs in Plautus, *The Two Menaechmuses* 112, act 1, scene 1: “He arranges such great pastry structures.” Thus, for Paulinus, *purificata altaris struice* means “the structure of the altar having been purified,” that is, the pile of wood from which the altar had been constructed.

It is certainly judged beyond doubt that this profession of faith accords fittingly with the profession expressed earlier, as in the sacred history concerning the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh. When they were being severely rebuked by the delegation of the Israelites, whose leader was Phinehas, the priest of the Lord, they were accused because they had constructed an altar of extraordinary size, lest it appear that they had deliberately built it for the worship of the gods of the nations.

All these matters require the proofs of allegorical interpretation; but we restrain the point of our pen by raising it somewhat higher, lest the reader’s mind grow weary of the lengthy sequence of discussion already reviewed.

After the two and a half tribes had been vehemently reproached, Scripture reports that they replied firmly in these words:

“The strongest God, the Lord, the strongest God, the Lord—he himself knows whether we built this altar with a rebellious purpose, and not rather with this thought and intention: that it should be a witness between your sons and our sons, lest your sons should say tomorrow to our sons, ‘You have no share or inheritance in the Lord God of Israel’” (Joshua 22:22ff.).

Extending the following words in a connected sequence, Scripture carries the matter to the boundary where the judgment examining the final clause of their unviolated faith[^c0042-5] is displayed, when it immediately adds:

“And the sons of Reuben and Gad called the altar ‘Our Witness,’ saying that the Lord himself is God” (ibid. 34).

[^c0042-5]: The reading may be “of their violated faith” (*violatae*) or “of their unviolated faith” (*inviolatae*).

Behold: the beginning of their reply expressly indicates not just any god, but “the strongest God, the Lord.” Behold also the conclusion of their statement: “Our witness declares that the Lord himself is God.”

I do not think that this witness belongs only to these particular tribes; rather, as is customary in sacred language, which often puts the part for the whole, it must unquestionably be understood as the general testimony of both Testaments. For all the pages of Scripture publicly confess both Christ Jesus, the strongest God and Lord, the Son of God, and that the true Lord is God.[^c0042-6] This is the one most illustrious testimony of all divine doctrines.

[^c0042-6]: “That the Lord is the true God.” Throughout this chapter Paulinus argues that Christ is understood by the name “Lord,” and that he is called “Lord” in an eminent sense, according to Psalm 109:1: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit …,” which Jesus himself understands as referring to him (Matthew 22:44).

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
### He explains the passage of Isaiah concerning Jesus, who, although human and from the earth, is nevertheless the true God by the unity of person, not a titular god

Moreover, you ought at least to have read continually, engraved upon the tablet of your heart in a wave of divine liquid, that most important prophecy of Isaiah’s sincere faith—which you thought better to insert into the page of your discussion with the blackness of ink:

“He who is blessed upon the earth shall be blessed in God, amen. And he who swears upon the earth shall swear by God, amen” (Isaiah 65:16).

But what does it profit to honor him with your lips when your heart suddenly departs from him? It is characteristic of fear to confess with the voice and to contradict in conduct [perhaps “with the heart” or “in the mind”]. This profession is one of weariness rather than love, since it does not arise from the root of truth.

You have certainly read the exposition of this chapter, composed by our predecessors in Catholic style—but with the mouth, not with the heart. For they confessed that the true God dwelt in the substance of our flesh, which he took from the virgin, and taught that we should believe that the same one, from the womb, is the one God, the true Son of God.

But you, with sacrilegious mouth, will assert that the true God is a dweller, while you will make the titular god the one who is inhabited. On this account you are rightly accused of introducing two gods, a true god and a titular god, although from two natures there is one and true God.

And if one and true God did not remain from and in both natures—divine, that is, and human, earthly in other words—distinct in substance but undivided in person, the same prophet would certainly not have said, with a sworn affirmation:

“He who swears upon the earth swears by God, amen.”

For *amen* is a word of oath. Although it is transferred from Hebrew into Latin speech as “truly” or “faithfully,” it more mysteriously announces the power of an ineffable sacrament than the translator’s tongue can effectively express the full propriety of the sounding word.

Beautifully, then, he says: “He who swears upon the earth shall swear by God, amen.” For the true God who deigned to assume the earth of our flesh did not, through the dispensation of the great and holy sacrament, divide himself into two gods—a true and a titular god, an adoptive or [perhaps “and,” with “son” apparently missing] proper Son—but, remaining the true God and the proper Son, is believed to be one and the same true God from both.

And although by lying evasions you strive, under the appearance of an excuse, to deny that you assert two gods, you are nevertheless refuted by the very objections expressed in your own words, since you persist in forcing two pairs of relational terms upon one person. For “true” and “titular” are two terms; “proper” and “adoptive” likewise signify two. They produce the reality of two persons, not merely in superficial sound but in substantial fact.

## CHAPTER XLIX  
### The altar of earth, to which ascent by steps is forbidden, is Christ in the Incarnation, though the person is not multiplied

One person, then, cannot by any rational expedient be both true and titular, both the proper son of one begetter and an adoptive son. You will not be able to diminish yourself through such a fantasy of subtlety that, with both feet wavering, you may safely escape more cleverly from the horns upon which you have stumbled.

For “he who swears upon the earth swears by God, amen.” Hence elsewhere the divine voice says to Moses:

“You shall make an altar of earth for me” (Exodus 20:24).

Regarding this altar, the Lord’s law expressly forbids ascending by steps:

“You shall not go up by steps to my altar” (ibid. 26).

The altar of earth is the flesh of Christ, taken from the virgin. To make an altar of earth is to place one’s hope in the incarnation of the Mediator, who is truly to be trusted.

Ascending by steps is forbidden because steps imply inequality and an increase in numerical quantity. Through this the Holy Spirit signifies that, in the excellence of the holy and ineffable Trinity, no inequality or diversity is to be suspected. And in the sacrament of the Word of God the Father incarnate, through which the one and same Son of God deigned to become the Son of man, no numerical quantity has been supplied through a diversity of persons.

We have furthermore judged it worthwhile, sufficiently clear, and worthy of every reverence to insert into this work that remarkable and most solemn testimony of the Son of God and man—namely, our Redeemer Jesus Christ—which he deigned to pour forth concerning himself with the sweetness of his honeyed mouth, as the eye of the reverent reader beholds it in the Gospel of John.

No one at all who recognizes that he has fixed the solidity of sincere faith upon the firm rock that is Christ is unaware that this single testimony is sufficient to overturn the foundation of this heresy’s material unbelief:

“No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

And again:

“When you see the Son of man ascending where he was before” (John 6:63).

In these words of the Lord, if I may put it so, the beauty of orthodox faith shines forth with an utterly clear radiance of inviolable brilliance.[^c0042-9]

[^c0042-9]: The text reads *quamspicui*, evidently for *quam perspicui*, “of very great clarity.”

## CHAPTER L  
### The Word became flesh, yet not another son; rather, he remained the same one who existed before. Jesus was never merely an earthly human being, for he was always also heavenly

In this way, by declaring with the voice of divinity that he was one and the same Son of God and man, he taught plainly that the Son of man had descended from heaven and ascended where he had previously been. For the Son of God, who was always coeternal, himself deigned at a definite time to become the Son of man.[^c0042-10] He became what he had not been—that is, man—for “the Word became flesh.”

[^c0042-10]: “To become” appears to be missing from the text.

Yet another Son, who had not existed before, was not made. He who always was, is, and will be—the only-begotten Son, always the Son of God—was so on earth that he was never absent from heaven. In an ineffable and marvelous manner he came into the virgin’s womb, while never departing from the Father’s bosom.

Moreover, solely through his condescension, by that which he became as man, he was able to be subject to his parents while always remaining that same Lord of the angels, wholly present everywhere—in heaven, that is, and on earth.

Thus it is more fittingly and correctly understood that the Son of man descended from heaven and ascended where he had previously been, because the Son of God, who descended from heaven and was in heaven while he spoke on earth, is altogether one and the same Son of man.

The most high wisdom of God the Father—and [perhaps another epithet is missing after *atque*]—wished to instruct us by a kindly forewarning, so that, without any ambiguity of doubt and without any hesitant fumbling of scruple, we might understand with certainty that [the printed *non semper* perhaps stands for *nonnunquam*] the mystery of the Incarnation had not changed into two gods or two sons, as heretics seem to rave; nor into a true God in part and a non-true God in part; nor into a proper Son at one time and a non-proper Son at another.

Rather, he deigned to declare that he is always the true God and the proper Son of God, both before and after the virgin’s childbirth, while nevertheless indicating the truth of human flesh through the mystery of the assumption.

And since the distinctiveness of each nature remains unconfused in the one person of the Son of God and man, in a perpetual and inseparable communion under inviolable right, the clear order of reason frequently shows that he did not hesitate to confess this.

When, therefore, he teaches that the Son of man descended from heaven and asserts that the same one ascended where he had previously been, he plainly wished to demonstrate himself as true God, true man, the proper Son of God, and the Son of man.

Guided by this rule, [the Apostle or Paul seems to be missing here][^c0042-11] first proclaims the first man earthly, from the earth, and the second heavenly, from heaven (1 Corinthians 15:47).

[^c0042-11]: Something is missing here, perhaps “the Apostle” or “Paul.”

This does not mean that the man should be believed to have descended from heaven before, after being assumed into God, he ascended into heaven.[^c0042-12] Rather, the God who descended from heaven, while remaining the true God through the sacrament of the Incarnation, also became truly man. They are not personally two—God, that is, and man—but one and the same God-man in the unity of person.

[^c0042-12]: The text has *homo* (“man”), where *hominem* is grammatically required in the accusative construction.

For this reason the Apostle truthfully teaches that the second man is heavenly and from heaven, since the earthly man became heavenly through the human nature essentially assumed by the heavenly God.

The second man, then—that is, Christ Jesus—is from heaven because the heavenly and earthly became one God and man. He is therefore no longer earthly, since through the heavenly one he became heavenly in the very conception of the womb.

And although he possesses the reality of an earthly body, he was never so earthly that he was not always also heavenly. For he was never first created as a mere human being and afterward transformed into God; rather, when he was conceived by the Holy Spirit in the virgin’s womb, God and man emerged together: one God-man from two natures, not one God and another man, although he is God by one property and man by another. Yet he is one and the same heavenly God-man from heaven.

## CHAPTER LI  
### Jesus, who descended, ascended where he had previously been; for he is the Son of God, less than the Father according to human nature, yet the Son was not less, even though he was human; therefore as man he inherited the name above every name

### [Col. 0406D]

The herald’s cry, therefore, does not differ from the judgment of its judge. For what the Lord testified—that the Son of man descended from heaven and ascended where he had previously been—his Apostle confesses, namely, that the second man is heavenly and from heaven.

I do not deny that I have read this passage of the Lord’s address inserted in your *pittacia*,[^c0042-13] and that, in accordance with your customary insolence, I recognized it as arranged according to the understanding of your puffed-up knowledge.

[^c0042-13]: “Inserted in your *pittacia*.” Greek *πιττάκιον* means writing tablets or boards made by casting pitch, for inscribing upon. See H. Stephanus, *Thesaurus Linguae Graecae*, vol. 3, col. 332, letter G, and Du Cange, *Glossarium*. The word also has other meanings. Sometimes it signifies a piece of cloth, leather, or a similar material. The Gibeonites, according to Joshua 9:5, had very old sandals sewn with *pittacia* as a sign of their age, in order to deceive Joshua and the people of God. John of Genoa, in Du Cange under “Peciatus” and “Repeciatus,” says that “a *pittacium* is that piece of leather sewn into a repaired sole … hence *pictaciatus*, that is, repaired.” Salmasius likewise derives the word from *pitacium*, supported by William Brito, book 2 of *Philippis*, where, concerning a military tunic, he writes:

> Thus struck through it is visible, thus cut up by little  
> patches it hangs.

Moreover, *pittacia* were sheets, otherwise called briefs or short documents, on which names or titles of things were written. These tablets, smeared with pitch or maltha, were then attached to jars, amphorae, and other vessels to indicate the quality, origin, age, and so forth of wine, oil, and similar products. Petronius, *Satyricon*, p. 26 in my edition: “At once glass amphorae were brought in, carefully plastered with gypsum; on their necks labels were attached with this title: Falernian. Opimian. One hundred years old.”

Likewise, the documents commonly called memoranda, to be presented to the emperor, which were to be brief, were called *pittacia*, as appears in Lampridius, *Alexander Severus*, chapter 21: “He also made notes about those to be promoted and read through all the memoranda.” See Macri, *Hierolexicon*.

Thus the word also came to designate little sheets or pages on which we write something briefly for the sake of memory, to be inserted more fully into a larger work or book. In this way Saint Eulogius, bishop of Toledo, relates in his final letter that he had arranged the acts of the martyrs he had collected, for the composition of a book entitled *Memorial of the Saints*, on sheets and *pittacia*. He writes to Alvarus:

> When the work was already nearly finished, and a raging official order sent me into dreadful prisons, while my household was thrown into confusion by the sudden incursion of the guards, I supposed that what had been arranged on various sheets and *pittacia* had been scattered in different directions.

The handing over of *pittacia* also became a sign of the conferment of dignity, as is clear from Pope Hadrian II’s letter to Charles the Bald, cited by Baronius under the year 871, no. 79, where the pontiff says:

> Finally, we establish your aforementioned legate as cardinal metropolitan and archbishop of the province of Tours by staff, *pittacium*, and ring.

Perhaps conferment by *pittacium* is the same as the investiture called investiture by notes or by a book; see Du Cange under “Investiture by …” and related entries.

In summary, from the same source: “Papias: *petacia*, *petaciola*, a small piece of paper; elsewhere: *pitacium* or *pitaciola*, a little membrane-letter. Isidore’s Glosses: *Pictacium*, a short and small letter; *pictaciuncula*, a small membrane.”

Here note in passing the varying spelling of this word, which differs in nearly every example cited: some write *pittacium* with double *t*, others with one, others *pictacium*, others *petacium*. Finally, determine what Paulinus understood by Felix’s *pittacia*.

Why do you not inspect with the eyes of sincere light and with a much greater contemplative gaze the wheel within the wheel—that is, the two Testaments joined together—so that you divide the Old from the New by a treacherous calculation, namely, into the true God and the titular god?[^c0042-14]

[^c0042-14]: “With the eyes of contemplation, inspect, etc.” The first editor notes in the margin: “Something seems to be missing here,” which is certain. I add that what survives is also mutilated and corrupt. Nevertheless, I think it can be supplemented somewhat as follows: “Why do you not inspect with the eye of sincere light and with a much greater contemplative gaze the wheel within the wheel—that is, the two Testaments joined together?” Paulinus perhaps alludes here to Ezekiel 1:16: “As though it were a wheel within a wheel.” The rest of the period that follows requires a Delian swimmer—that is, an exceptionally skillful interpreter.

The Catholic faith does not permit itself, under any circumstances, to offer the breaches of open ears to the hearing of such an impious assertion. For both before the mystery of the Incarnation and after the sacrament of the assumption, the one and same proper and true Son of God always remains the true God.

In the form of God he is equal to the Father; in the form of a servant he is less than the Father. Not another, but one and the same, both equal and less. It is not the Son who is less, but the human nature, which is inferior.

He is equal because he is one with the Father; less because he is one with his mother. Is it not the same one, and no other, who says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28)?

One is from the Father without a mother; one and the same is from the mother without a father. Moreover, the Apostle recalls that the one established as heir of all things by what he is from his mother is that same one whom, by what he is from the Father, he confesses to be the radiance of glory and the exact representation of his substance. And he affirms that the one born from the virgin was made so much superior to the angels as the name he inherited is more excellent than theirs.

The language of inheritance and being made pertains to the human form, not the divine. And what that more excellent and distinctive name is is explained by the Apostle when he immediately adds:

“To which of the angels did he ever say: ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again: ‘I will be his Father, and he will be my Son.’”

And again:

“To which of the angels did he ever say: ‘Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet’?” (Hebrews 1:5, 13).

This is the distinction of name that he mentioned earlier: the angels are servants, but he is the Son of the Most High and Almighty God the Father.

The angels, finally, expressly receive the designation “angels” from the office of their ministry. Hence they are called by the common name “angels”; but they are not to be thought to have received the name above every name, as Christ Jesus inherited the name above every name.

The name above every name is God, the true Son of God. But we leave these matters to be treated in their proper place.

## CHAPTER LII  
### David and Paul confess Christ as God without the addition “titular,” and as the Son of God without the addition “adoptive”

The Apostle declares that he inherited the name more excellent than every name according to the fact that he deigned temporally to become the Son of man. For, in what he is from the Father, he did not inherit the Son’s name in time—the name he always possessed by nature, begotten from the Father without any beginning.

But you, heretic, why are you not ashamed to assign to him in any fashion the common name “adoptive” and “titular,” when this name is below, and not above, every name?

For if he who was born as the firstborn from the virgin were not the true God, David would certainly never have compelled the angels to adore him, as though by an exhortation intended to incite them, saying:

“Let all his angels adore him” (Psalm 46:8).

And because the prophet foretold the Word made flesh, that chief teacher explains it when he subsequently presents this passage of the psalm:

“And when he again introduces the firstborn into the world, he says: ‘Let all the angels of God adore him’” (Hebrews 1:6).

You yourself also affirm that he is firstborn from his mother, and for that reason you proclaim him not the true God but a titular god. Yet angels are believed to adore not just anyone but the true God.

The eminent preacher continues in the same epistle:

“To the angels he says: ‘He makes his angels spirits.’ But to the Son: ‘Your throne, O God, is forever and ever.’ And shortly afterward: ‘God, your God, has anointed you with oil beyond your companions’” (ibid. 7–9).

Behold: the one whom he asserted had been introduced into the world as the firstborn through the dispensation of the great and holy sacrament, that same one he taught through the prophetic oracle to have been adored by the angels.

The prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, unquestionably spoke to that very one:

“Your throne, O God, is forever and ever”; and, “Your God has anointed you.”

The prophet and the Apostle, therefore, confess both God—without the addition “titular”—and the Son—without the addition “adoptive.” For the person of the only-begotten, through the assumption of flesh, received neither increase nor diminution, neither change nor mixture; rather, it remained what it was, namely, the true God and true Son of God, and without any loss to itself assumed what it was not.

He is truly God, whose throne remains forever and ever, and he is testified by the same prophet to have been anointed by the true God. The true God, therefore, was anointed by the true God—not, as you customarily mutter in your foolish, senile manner with your obscure throat, that a titular god was anointed by the true God—but the true God is believed to have been anointed by the true God, unquestionably in the form of a servant.

Christ Jesus, then, the true God, had the form of another kind, in which he could be anointed by the true God; yet he did not have the person of another son, through which he could be divided into another. For it was not the person of the only-begotten but only the diversity of natures that received distinction in this sacrament of the Incarnation.

For he is always the true and only-begotten Son, and always the true God, blessed above all forever. According to what the Word was in the beginning with God, and according to what the Word became when it was made flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1, 14), the rule of inviolate faith proclaims him most sincerely throughout the entire expanse of heaven and adores him with devout affection.

Hence the statement in the song of love, where the bride sings in bridal melody:

“My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands” (Song of Songs 5:10).

He is white according to what he was—the Word in the beginning; ruddy according to what he became—the Word made flesh and dwelling among us.

By [perhaps something is missing, e.g. *quod fuit*] the crimson rose-garden of the four-part cross, sprinkled with the precious purple of blood, the beloved of the bride likewise shone ruddy. To him Isaiah says:

“Why is your garment red, and your clothing like that of one who treads the winepress?” (Isaiah 63:2).

## CHAPTER LIII  
### Christ is from the fathers according to the flesh; according to divinity, from God the Father: true God, not titular, whom the Catholic faith does not acknowledge. The proper and only-begotten Son of one Father
Paul is therefore shown, by the pen with which he wrote to the Romans, to teach as follows [Col. 0410A]: “Their fathers, and from whom Christ is descended according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5). According to the flesh he is indeed descended from the fathers, and according to his divinity, without flesh, from God the Father; yet he confesses him to be one and the same Christ Jesus, God over all, blessed forever. For he was not merely a man descended from the fathers, like any of the prophets, who may be reckoned by the title of adopted sons and titular gods; rather, from the immaculate womb of the blessed Virgin, who had descended from the holy stock of those preceding fathers, God and man was truly born, coming forth like a bridegroom from his bridal chamber.

Concerning him the apostle John, bearing witness in his epistle, writes: “We know,” he says, “that the Son of God has come, and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). That Jesus Christ is the true Son of God and true God is proclaimed by John, Paul, and all the declarations of Scripture: he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; he suffered, was crucified, died, and was buried for us; on the third day he rose again, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God, and is to come with glory to judge the living and the dead.

[Note: At [Col. 0409D] *judicare* (“to judge”), so it is noted in Du Chesne’s edition in the margin; but the phrase is characteristic of Paulinus, as also in this same book, chapter 17.]

Who, then, is that Christ whom you, heretic, attempt to assert is a titular god and an adopted son? The Catholic faith nevertheless knows nothing of him, and it scorns in every way to know him together with you. Keep for yourself and your followers another Christ, who was not born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, a titular god; but we have, shall have, and in the age to come shall possess the true God and only-begotten Son of God, Christ Jesus our Lord, who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity, now and always, throughout all ages, world without end. Amen.

He gave himself for us, to redeem us from every iniquity (Titus 2:14); and the Father, wishing to commend his love toward us more abundantly, did not spare him, but handed him over for us all. The Apostle confesses him to be his own Son, not an adopted son: “God did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32). Elsewhere the evangelist John likewise testifies: “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the salvation of the world” (John 3:16). He gave his only-begotten Son, not an adopted son.

I say that you are granted no sophistical means by which, even if you attempt to fly with oars and wings—not of doves but of ostriches—you may refer two relative names belonging to one Son to the person of one Father. Observe what I have said: you cannot ascribe “son and son,” which is relative to something—that is, “own” and “adopted”—to one progenitor. For since there is one God the almighty Father, and he has begotten for himself one coeternal almighty Son, by what possible order could one who is born of one progenitor be understood as both his own and his adopted son? No order of possibility ever permits this.

This is especially so since these things are said of the Son of God, who, eternally begotten from the eternal Father, in a wondrous manner assumed a second birth in time for our sake, so that, because he willed to become man’s Son, he might nevertheless remain the very same unchangeable Son of God. Yet it is not two sons, one of God and one of man, who are worshiped, but one and the same Son of God and man.

## CHAPTER LIV. The Apostle testifies that Christ is the Son of God, and the Father himself at the Jordan.

So greatly, then, has the great mystery of piety—which was manifested in the flesh (1 Tim. 3:16)—become cheap in your eyes that, because the true God and true Son of God is proclaimed in apostolic praises to have become high priest for us in order to drain away the sins of many, you deny him through your false arguments. Yet the blessed Apostle himself, having searched out the secrets of the third heaven, confesses him both as high priest or priest and as the Son of God. For he says: “We have, therefore, a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God” (Heb. 4:14).

And again: “No one takes the honor upon himself, but he who is called by God, as Aaron was. So also Christ did not glorify himself, but he who said to him, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you.’ As he also says in another place, ‘You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek’” (Heb. 5:4–6). If, then, you disregard the testimony of the Apostle who bears witness, may the ineffable sweetness of the Father’s words concerning his own Son, I beg you, not be repugnant to you.

For through the prophet, according to the fact that the Word became flesh, he says: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7). And, thundering from heaven with a voice over the channel of the Jordan, and also on the holy mountain, he testifies: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 3:17; 17:5).

Hence John the Baptist, hearer of the testimony of so great an eternal Father, having confessed the good confession before many witnesses, says: “He who sent me to baptize in water himself said to me, ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one.’ And I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God” (John 1:33–34). Paul also testifies: “He transferred us,” he says, “into the kingdom of the Son of his love.”

## CHAPTER LV. His reply to the objections of Felix: showing that Christ, God and man, is the only-begotten Son in the unity of one person.

Against all this, you are recognized as having found one point of contradiction with a scrupulous mind. “According to his divinity,” you say, “he is to be believed to be true God and the true Son of God.” This is good, and by this part of your statement you share in our confession—provided that you had remained in this sincere profession of goodness. But when, shortly afterward, on account of the dispensation of the incarnation of the ineffable mystery, you do not cease with reckless lips to blaspheme him as a titular god and an adopted son, you stand deprived of participation in our faith.

When, therefore, you endeavor with a lawyer’s mouth to establish this—

[Note: “With a lawyer’s mouth you will establish.” *Astrues* is used in place of *astrue*, with *e* frequently employed by the copyist for *i*, as noted elsewhere. But what does “with a lawyer’s mouth” mean? That is, a crafty, deceitful, evasive one. See Du Cange, *Glossarium*: “*Causidicatio*, evasion, excuse …” Julius I, in his letter to the Orientals, says: “It is clearly apparent that this lawyerly pleading belongs to men who do not sufficiently trust themselves.” Lawyers frequently plead their cases because they conceal, and sometimes even stifle, the truth with circumlocutions and verbal entanglements, to the loss and misfortune of their clients, whom they plunder. Hence Apuleius, *The Golden Ass*, book X: “He calls them toga-clad vultures.” “For it is their very common practice to act dishonestly, betray defendants, sell their advocacy, and flay men with bloody rapacity,” says Caelius Rhodiginus, book VIII, chapter 18.

Hear also a few passages from Peter of Blois, letter 25, which is wholly devoted to this subject and extremely worthy of reading. He attacks such men, whom he himself calls “officials”: “The business of the officials, whose number you have joined, is today to confuse laws, stir up lawsuits, rescind settlements, impose delays; suppress truth, encourage falsehood, pursue profit, sell equity, gape after exactions, contrive deceptions … Verbal plotters and hunters of syllables set snares and traps for the capture of money. They interpret laws according to their pleasure, and according to their will now reject them, now admit them; they corrupt well-spoken arguments, overturn wisely alleged points, and so forth.”

Thus Quintilian rightly distinguishes the orator from the lawyer, although he had already said that only a good man could become a good orator; in the lawyer he argues that certain vices are present which he cannot tolerate in the perfect orator. He says, *Institutes of Oratory*, book XII, chapter 1: “Shall we bestow upon a betrayer, a deserter, a colluder, that sacred name of orator? … For we are not establishing some kind of forensic employment, nor a mercenary voice, nor—to spare harsher words—a merely serviceable advocate in lawsuits, whom the common people finally call a lawyer; but a man outstanding by the nature of his intellect, and so forth.”

Thus Paulinus judges that in a lawyer’s mouth—“lawyer” being used adjectivally here, or *causidici* perhaps being restored—there are wickedness, deceit, fraud, and treachery; and that Felix had such a mouth.]

—you are nevertheless proved to be attempting to sever the unity of the indivisible person. There is certainly no duality in the person of the Only-begotten, but a distinction of natures. The name “Only-begotten” remains eternal both before the ages, from the Father, and after the Virgin’s birth, from the mother. The person of the Only-begotten assumed the substance of another kind, not the designation of another son, because “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb. 13:8)—that is, he remains unchangeably what he was, what he is, and what he is to come: the Almighty.

Although he was in the form of God, he assumed the form of a servant, that is, the nature of man. The distinction is doubled not in persons but in natures. The same remained what he was: the only-begotten Son of God. He is “Only-begotten” because he is one.

Who, I ask you, do you suppose, among Catholic Christians would confess Christ Jesus as true God and true Son of God if he were merely an isolated man and did not remain truly, inseparably God and man in the unity of one person? The assumed man did not remove, diminish, or change the fullness of divinity; rather, through the fullness of divinity dwelling bodily in Christ, the man Christ Jesus was exalted into God, so that the same one is God and man, Son of God and man, while the proper character of each nature remains preserved and the natures remain unconfused.

Your heart has also been weighed down on this occasion, so that, after the fruit of your faith has been emptied by all your inventions, however slight it may be, the prophetic lament uttered by the voice of prophecy might be fulfilled in you: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the beetle ate; and what the beetle left, the rust consumed” (Joel 1:4).

Attend to what follows. “Awake,” he adds, “you drunkards, and weep.” Rather, you have increased the weight of your sin by a leaden talent—

[Note: “A talent of lead.” *Talentum* is commonly used for a definite numerical quantity of gold, silver, and similar substances. Thus the Attic, Babylonian, Euboean, Hebrew, Egyptian, and other talents were said to contain a fixed number of minas or drachmas; Budaeus discusses these extensively in his books *On the As*. Georgius Agricola also treats them in *On Measures and Weights*.

Sometimes, however, it was used for a weight, as appears from Vitruvius, book X, chapter 21, at the end, where, concerning the tortoise of Agetor of Byzantium, he says: “One hundred men operated it; it had a weight of four thousand talents, which amounts to four hundred and eighty thousand pounds.” Indeed, the Greek Τάλαντον (*tálanton*) is sometimes itself a weight; hence Ταλαντόω means “I weigh,” just as ἀντιτάλαντον means “of equal weight” or “making an equal balance.” Therefore a talent of lead is an enormous weight of lead.]

—in such a way that you are not ashamed to say that Christ Jesus, bound by the necessity of weakness, had to pray as quickly as possible for himself, and therefore argue that he cannot be believed to be the true God because he had to pray even for himself. I do not deny that I have discussed these matters more fully above, according to the measure of my limited understanding, as he himself, of whom we speak, graciously enabled me to do.

## CHAPTER LVI. Paul’s passage explained: Christ, insofar as he is God, raised himself; insofar as he is man, he was raised—yet the one who raises and the one who is raised are not different.

This testimony of Paul, then, brought forward, so to speak, in your own words, teaches through the prophetic oracle assumed concerning the Lord Jesus Christ: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.” He adds: “In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, he was heard because of his reverence.”

And because he prayed neither for himself nor on his own behalf, but, as we have said above, for us and on our behalf—for whom he deigned to be born and to die—the scriptural declarations supporting our earlier assertion have been set forth above with the clearest testimonies. But the reasoning concerning him who was able to save him from death, by which perhaps you were hanging in the noose of error and, because you had not rejected it, tightening the knot of the loop still more firmly, has not yet been fully set forth by the sharp point of our pen; necessity rather than parsimony has required this restraint.

Now, however, let us explain what it means that he was able to save him from death. Nothing else, I think, is meant, nor is it taught to be understood otherwise, than that he was able to raise him from the dead. For “to save from death” is equivalent to “to confess that he raises from death.”

And because the works of the Trinity are always inseparable, just as the whole Trinity worked the man Christ in the Virgin’s womb, so the whole Trinity is acknowledged to have raised him from the dead out of the tomb. That the Father raised him, Paul writes to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Gal. 1:1).

And since he himself raised his body from the tomb, this is taught by his own divine testimony when he said to the Jews: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). The Evangelist indicates what temple he meant when he adds: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.” Likewise: “For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life, and I take it up again. I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:17–18). It should be noted that he laid down and took up his life again by power, not by necessity.

And again: “When I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee,” and similar passages (Matt. 26:32). That God raised him is proclaimed by countless oracles of both Testaments. Thus the Apostle says: “If you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus Christ and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Rom. 10:9). Elsewhere: “When they had completed everything that had been written about him, they took him down from the tree and placed him in a tomb. But God raised him from the dead” (Acts 13:29–30).

And because the Holy Spirit is God, the whole Trinity—both the Father, the Son himself, and the Holy Spirit—raised him from the tomb. But the Son who raised him is not one and the Son who was raised another. Although there is a difference—that is, between the divine and the human—there is nevertheless one Son, both raising and raised. By power and will he laid down his life for us, not for himself; by power or will, because his will and the Father’s will are one, he prayed for us, not for himself, “in the days of his flesh,” offering prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death.

He offered himself to God as a sacrifice for us, as a pleasing fragrance; for us he saved himself from death, that is, he raised himself from the dead. Hence the Apostle, aptly adding a sentence corresponding piece by piece to this passage, explained what he meant when he immediately continued: “Although he was the Son of God, he learned obedience from the things that he suffered” (Heb. 5:8). According to Paul’s statement, the Son of God suffered; from the things he suffered he learned obedience, and he was raised from the dead. The impassible one suffered; the immortal one died; the one who is always living was raised. He is the same and not another.

“The one who descended,” says the Teacher of the Gentiles, “is himself also the one who ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things” (Eph. 4:10). Since the same one is both dead and always living, this is placed more clearly before the eyes of the reader in the Apocalypse, when he did not shrink from declaring concerning himself to his servant John, placing his right hand upon him: “Do not fear; I am the first and the last, that is, Α and Ω, the living one, and I was dead. And behold, I am living forever and ever” (Rev. 1:17; 22:13).

## CHAPTER LVII. Christ’s sitting at the right hand of the Father proves that he is not a titular god but the true God, and not an adopted son but his own Son.

Receive, then, this clear testimony of the blessed Paul: “The Law appoints men as priests who have weakness, but the word of the oath, which came after the Law, appoints the Son, perfected forever” (Heb. 7:28). Observe how the Apostle distinguishes between God and man, and between them and mere men.

A little later he says: “We have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens” (Heb. 8:1). Behold, Paul testifies that this high priest—whom you, drowsy with the sleep of treachery, invent as a titular god and adopted son—sits in the heavens at the right hand of the throne of Majesty as the Son perfected forever.

And he is said not merely to sit but expressly to sit together with the Father. Of what madness, I ask you, do you miserably strip yourself, stunned by impious stupor, so that you expose both sides openly to be pierced by the horns of a syllogism, leaving yourself no way to escape the venom you have worked out in winding folds?

For you are accused of falsely proclaiming with your tongue one Christ to be both a titular and true God, both an adopted and true Son; nevertheless, you are charged with introducing four persons, although God rejoices in the distinction of persons only in the number three and receives, in the mystery, the unity of an inseparable essence.

Who could doubt that “titular and true,” “own and adopted,” designate not natural but personal names? Does it seem to you Catholic and good that two gods and two sons should sit in the heavens at the Father’s right hand? Or—what is more treacherous than every treachery and more wicked than every wickedness—have you dared with a most criminal mouth to babble that you will distinguish the triune and one God by a fourfold division?

Moreover, it is not written, “Sit, you plural,” but “Sit,” singular. For the number three cannot be divided in any way; nevertheless, the three are one, because the Holy Trinity remains inseparable. But the number four permits itself to be cut in half without any contradiction; hence it is alien to the ineffable mystery of the Trinity.

[Note: “But the number four.” This is the number about which the Pythagoreans make remarkable claims. For the present subject, consider what Macrobius writes in *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 5: it is the number that is both generated and generates. For this number four “is born from two and generates eight … The Pythagoreans called this number—eight—justice, because it is the first of all numbers to be resolved into evenly even numbers, that is, twice four, and because the division itself is likewise resolved into evenly even numbers, twice two. It is also constructed according to the same proportion, namely, twice two twice.” This is what Paulinus means when he says that four allows itself to be cut through the middle.]

In the meantime, because it is the base of a square—

[Note: “Because it is the base of a square.” Plutarch, *On the Generation of the Soul from the Timaeus*: “That tetractys, or quaternity, so highly praised by the Pythagoreans—namely, the number 36—has this remarkable property: it is composed of the first four even numbers and the first four odd numbers.” The first four even numbers are 2, 4, 6, and 8; the first four odd numbers are 1, 3, 5, and 7. If you add them together, you obtain 36, and thus you have a square whose base is four, as Paulinus says.]

—it contains the figure of a more sacred mystery—

[Note: “It contains the figure of a mystery.” If one listens to pagan theologians, just as three is assigned to the heavenly gods, so four is assigned to the gods below and to their mysteries and sacred rites. See Lutatianus on Statius, book V, line 86: “Four times he thundered through the clear sky,” and also the solemn oath of the Pythagoreans, which Macrobius records in *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 6. “The Pythagoreans venerated the quaternary, which they call τετρακτύς (*tetraktýs*), among their secret things as belonging almost to the perfection of the soul, so greatly that they made it the religious object of an oath:

> Οὐ μὰ τὸν ἡμετέρᾳ ψυχῇ παραδόντα τετρακτυν

That is: “No, by him who gave our soul the number four.”

But I add matters still more sacred: the name of God, τετραγράμματον (*tetragrámmaton*), that is, “expressed in four letters,” and indeed in vowels, among the Hebrews.

Nor should Ambrose’s passage be omitted, *On the Incarnation*, chapter 7, where, treating the same argument as Paulinus, he excludes a quaternity of persons from the Trinity. He says: “Nor do I fear that I may seem to introduce a tetrad: we truly worship only the Trinity, who assert this. For I do not divide Christ when I distinguish the substance of his flesh and divinity; rather, I proclaim one Christ with the Father and the Spirit of God. I shall show that those introduce a tetrad more readily who say that the flesh of the one Christ is of the same substance as his divinity.”]

—but it is wholly excluded from fellowship with the Trinity. Therefore there is one who sits at the right hand of the Father: Christ Jesus our Lord, true God and true Son of God, begotten from the Father’s womb before Lucifer and, in time, from the Virgin’s womb.

This is clearly declared by the brilliant oracle of the evangelist Mark: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sat at the right hand of God” (Mark 16:19). Why are you not confounded to confess the Lord Jesus Christ, sitting at the right hand of the Father, to be a titular god and adopted son, when the Father said to no other titular god, “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1), but only to the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ?

He lives and reigns as God with the same almighty God the Father and the Holy Spirit in perfect Trinity throughout all ages, world without end. Amen.

[Col. 0416C] Having taken, therefore, from the final part of the book the concluding sentence of the evangelist Mark, as a sweet-sounding testimony, this little book is now at last closed at the boundary of its ending.

**138 BOOK TWO**

[Col. 0417]

## CHAPTER I. Jesus was predestined as the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, as Paul says—not by adoption, as the heretics claim.

[Col. 0417A]

I shall therefore begin the beginning of the second book from the opening of the epistles of the blessed Apostle, that eminent teacher of the world, so that, supported by the thread of the words of the disputation—

[Note: “With the shuttle of disputation.” Among the instruments of the art of weaving, Ovid mentions the shuttle and describes its use together with the other implements in *Metamorphoses*, book VI, line 55:

> The warp is fastened to the loom; the reed separates the threads;  
> The weft is inserted among the sharpened shuttles,  
> Which the fingers guide, drawing it between the warp threads.  
> The teeth of the inserted comb strike when beaten.

For by what other instrument than the small shuttle—that is, the shuttle proper—is the weft inserted? Lucretius also lists other instruments of this art, including shuttles, in book V, line 1366:

> The heddle and spindles, the shuttles, and the sounding reeds.

Thus Paulinus uses the shuttle, heddle, comb, warp, thread, separation, and weaving allegorically, in order to begin and weave another web of disputation against Felix.

Such allegory is not uncommon among writers when some action or speech is being discussed. Isaiah 25:7: “He will destroy on this mountain the face of the covering cast over all peoples, and the web which he has woven over all nations.” And again, 30:1: “Woe to the rebellious children, who take counsel but not from me, and weave a web, but not by my spirit.”

Plautus, *Bacchides*, line 326, act II, scene 3:

> This web that I have begun is not altogether badly started for this business.

The elegance of this expression was also used more than once by the Etruscan poets. Torquato Tasso, *Jerusalem Delivered*, canto IV, stanza 24:

> I wove the web which I now show you begun,  
> A bold performer of an ancient song.

And Francesco Petrarch, in the ode beginning “I was thinking,” final stanza, compares the course of his life to a web:

> For while deliberating, I have already turned upon the beam  
> A great part of my brief web.

The response of Narses is also relevant here. When Sophia recalled him from Italy and, because he was a eunuch, sent him among the women to spin flax and wool, he replied that “he would weave for her such a web as she herself, while she lived, would not be able to lay aside.” He fulfilled this by bringing the Lombards into Italy, as Paul the Deacon testifies in *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapter 5. Our Baronius, however, does not agree with him under the year 567, number 11; from Corippus he proves that Narses was not then staying in Italy but had already been recalled to Constantinople and was held in great honor. Seek clarification of the matter in P. Pagi’s *Critica*, which brings forward three Narseses.

But not to abandon the thread of our web, scarcely anything occurs more frequently than the allegory of the web and weaving when writing is being discussed, so that *texere* (“to weave”), *textus* (“woven,” “text”), and similar expressions are used no less of speaking than of weaving. Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, book IX, letter 21: “We are accustomed to weave our letters in everyday words.”

Likewise, when speaking of the doctrines of certain ancient philosophers, Francesco Petrarch, in the work entitled *Triumph of Fame*, chapter 3, near the end, writes:

> Then, with a great beam and a marvelous spindle,  
> I saw Chrysippus weave a fine web,

and shortly afterward:

> And to shape his beautiful conception,  
> Cleanthes wove his noble web.

Therefore Paulinus, using this allegory—]

—that, taught by the shuttle of his teaching and supported by its aids, I may be able to distinguish the threads of the disputation, and, having taken up the comb of sincere faith, may not grow sluggish in weaving the very flowing threads inserted in the typological heddle, after examining heavenly indications.

Paul says: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined as the Son of God” (Rom. 1:1ff.).

He is unquestionably said to have been predestined according to that by which he is proclaimed to have been made from the seed of David according to the flesh. Tell me, I ask you, O Teacher of the Gentiles, who cared not only for the Roman Church but for all the churches, and who learned through the revelation of Jesus Christ (Gal. 1:1, 11–12)—the one who spoke in you whatever you taught—do you think that the Word made flesh was predestined as the Son of God by adoption, like any of the elect, who nevertheless, being propagated from the mass of perdition, become children of light through the bath of regeneration, with his grace itself going before them?

Or rather, just as the glory of his singular birth is proclaimed in an outstanding way, so is the dignity of the Son taught in a singular and wondrous manner? “He was predestined as the Son of God,” you say. By what means, I ask, explain this more clearly. Perhaps by adoption? Far from it. By no means by adoption. For the heretics do not fear to mutter this with excessive boldness.

Therefore he was predestined as the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, through the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord.

You have greatly, greatly consoled me, blessed Apostle Paul. Through this, I confess, my flesh has blossomed again, and this is my refreshment. For he was predestined as the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, not in adoption, because the power of the Most High overshadowed the blessed Virgin, and the Holy Spirit, making the inviolable maternal womb fruitful, sanctified it. Therefore what was born from her, being holy, was called the Son of God.

Because the Holy Spirit filled the Virgin’s womb, the power of the Most High overshadowed her, and the Word became flesh, he was called the Son not by the common title of adoption but uniquely by the name proper to the Most High. For it is not by the point of a reed—

[Note: “For it is not by the point of a reed.” Why does Paulinus here exclude the reed, an entirely innocent instrument of writing and an indifferent instrument of truth and falsehood? Perhaps because it is a sign of some profane matter. Among writers it is frequently used of writing that tends toward vanity and fiction. If you wish, add that reeds were held in esteem by the people of Cnidus, sacred to Venus, or by Egypt, corrupted in customs and flowing with luxury, although superior in use, yet infamous in origin.

Hear Pliny, book XVI, chapter 36: “Reeds serve the purposes of paper; Egyptian reeds especially, by a certain kinship with papyrus, though those of Cnidus are considered better.” At the beginning of his *Metamorphoses*, Apuleius says in Milesian style that he is composing little tales and soothing the ears:

> Provided only that, with your wit, you do not disdain  
> To look upon Egyptian papyrus inscribed  
> With the Nile’s reed.

Ausonius presents the letters, which he calls the daughters of Cadmus after their inventor, on Egyptian papyrus, but with Cnidian reed:

> The black daughters of Cadmus,  
> The white page of Melon,  
> The marks of the dark cuttlefish,  
> And the Cnidian knots he produced.

And in line 279, letter 7:

> May the furrow of the Cnidian reed  
> No longer crawl through the paths of the split-footed reed;  
> May you be painted upon a dry page  
> Beneath the black letters, the children of Cadmus, and so forth.

Thus, because the reed carried a profane and fictitious odor, Paulinus perhaps excludes the point of the reed and opposes truth to it by saying: “It is not written by the point of a reed deceitfully, but truthfully: ‘The Word became flesh’”—that is, “This is not a little tale of poets written with a reed.”

Unless perhaps an error has crept in and the reading should be: “Not by the point of a reed deceitfully, but truthfully.” If you reject these conjectures, I yield and willingly confess that I have not grasped Paulinus’s meaning.]

—nor deceptively, but truthfully, is it written: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us”—

[Col. 0419A]—that is, God became man.

He is therefore believed to have been made from the seed of David according to the flesh; but through divine generation—that is, from the substance of the Father—he remains eternally God, neither made nor predestined, but begotten.

## CHAPTER II. Paul and Ezekiel prove through their testimony that Christ is God over all.

Behold two wondrous witnesses of truth, agreeing wonderfully with one another: one the prince of the heavenly army, the other the commander of the Lord’s terrifying camps, clothed with the helmet of faith and the breastplate of righteousness, fortified with heavenly weapons, advancing into battle as a teacher in order to pierce the opposing breasts of the enemy with spiritual arrows.

By the testimony of these most truthful heralds—

[Note: “Most truthful heralds.” See the note on book I, chapter 37.]

—and of countless other holy witnesses who bear testimony, it is proved that he was not predestined by the prerogative of adoption, but in power according to the Spirit of sanctification: because, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary, he remains true God and true man, one and the same in both, and truly the Son of God.

Finally, you, vessel of election, were caught up to the heights of the third heaven so that you might hear what you ought to know. The archangel Gabriel was sent from the highest point—

[Note: “Sent from the highest point, if one may say so, from the seventh hinge of heaven.” Correct the possible scribal error as follows: “sent from the highest point, namely from the hinge of the seventh heaven,” so that it means “from the highest hinge of heaven, namely the seventh,” which is the highest.

Concerning the number seven of the heavens, by which especially the spheres of the planets are included, see Basil, *Homilies on the Hexaemeron*, homily 3; Ambrose likewise, *On the Hexaemeron*, book II, chapter 2, number 6; and especially Thomas Aquinas, *Summa theologica*, part I, question 88, article 4. From Rabanus on Genesis 1, he adopts a different system but nevertheless acknowledges no different number of heavens.

He says “from the highest hinge of the seventh heaven,” not “from the seventh heaven,” so that he might be understood as sent from the empyrean and the royal dwelling of the blessed, which is above all the heavens. David speaks of it in Psalm 113:16: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord,” and in Psalm 148:4: “Praise him, heavens of heavens.”]

—if it is permissible to say so, from the hinge of the seventh heaven, so that with angelic tongue he might joyfully proclaim the joy of the world.

The heretics have altogether descended to the deepest abyss [for *millissimum*, a corrupt reading]—

[Note: “To the deepest.” Here too there is an error: perhaps *millissimum* has been written for *vilissimum* (“most base”), or rather—although it is barbarous Latin—for *humillissimum* (“lowest,” that is, deepest), improperly placed. Depth belongs to the abyss. For, according to Festus, “The Greeks call *barathrum* a precipitous place from which one cannot emerge; it is derived from the word βαθύς (*bathýs*), ‘deep.’” Hence Virgil, *Aeneid*, book III, line 421, concerning the chasms of Charybdis:

> And deep within the abyss, three times in its whirlpool, it drew down the mighty … ]

“The wave swallows [him] into the abyss.”] Into the hidden and precipitous depth of the infernal abyss; and yet they do not hesitate, with their tongue quivering in a serpent’s hiss, to contradict your venerable teachings. And although you profess that there you heard secret words which it was not lawful for a human being to utter [Col. 0419C], there, divinely instructed, you had nevertheless learned that Christ Jesus our Lord was predestined to be the Son of God, not by adoption but in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification [Col. 0420A]. Nor did you contemplate God as merely titular, as that heretic foolishly claims, but as the true and supremely blessed God, in the greatness of revelation. You took care to transmit this quite clearly in your venerable letter to the Romans:

“Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5).

He who is the only Son from one coeternal Father, begotten not according to the flesh, and yet one and the same who is descended from the fathers according to the flesh, is proclaimed God over all, blessed forever. The one whom Paul calls the blessed God over all, the prophet Ezekiel declares to be the exalted God. For he says:

“And I heard,” he says, “behind me a sound like the sound of many waters, like the voice of the exalted God” (Ezek. 1:24).

Behold Christ Jesus, whom that same vessel of election, caught up into the heights of contemplation above every power and virtue and every name that is named either in this age or in the age to come, had seen exalted. That same prophet saw him, in the likeness of a son of man, above the firmament of crystal—that is, above all the angelic powers—gazing upon him with the prophet’s attentive eye. “And above the firmament,” he says, “was the likeness of a son of man” (Ezek. 1:22, 26).

[Note: [Col. 0420D] “The prophet had seen him with a careful gaze through the cup.” Why “through the cup”? Here too an error has crept in, which in my judgment should be corrected by restoring *oculo* (“with the eye”) in place of *poculo* (“through the cup”), so that the meaning is: “he had seen him with the prophet’s eye and with attentive gaze”—that is, not merely with an eye illuminated by heavenly light, as the eyes of prophets are, but with the very act of vision carefully applied, that is, with the faculty of seeing itself diligently directed toward seeing.]

## CHAPTER III. He refutes Felix’s false understanding of Paul: “God was in Christ”; for, according to Paul himself, since he was in the form of God, he was true God.

[Col. 0420C] Since, then, you had taught, O remarkable teacher, while you were the Christ-bearing instrument of him who spoke through you in harmonious and heavenly-sounding speech, and while his holy Spirit sang together with you—the Spirit through whom the world had been reconciled to God—that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (1 Cor. 5:19), this heretic, fortified with the weapons of impiety, does not cease to contradict the truth that Christ is true God with a most false assertion. He conjectures, to your discredit, that you said “God was in Christ,” and did not say “God was Christ.”

As in other cases, he is not ashamed to distort this testimony of Scripture in his customary manner, as though one God were in Christ and another were Christ the man, in whom God was present, although Christ Jesus is one: God and man. There is one thing according to what he is God, and another according to what he is man, as has often been repeated; but Christ God is not one and Christ man another. One and the same is Christ, God [Col. 0421B] and man.

“God,” you say, “was in Christ,” because Christ was essentially God and man, since in him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell bodily—that is, to put it more explicitly, in a divine manner. Because God was the one who assumed, and man the one who was assumed, Christ Jesus remained true God and naturally became true man.

This heretic, therefore, had read with deaf ears the gifts of charity which you earnestly strove to commend to the Philippians, so that each might seek not his own interests but those of another:

“Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:5–6).

I ask you, therefore, O heretic who oppose the truth: if Christ Jesus [true God seems to be missing] were not true God, how, according to the Apostle, can Christ be understood to be in the form of God? For being in the form of God means nothing other than being in the nature of God. And again, taking the form of a servant means assuming the nature of man.

If, then, according to apostolic teaching, Christ Jesus was in the form of God—that is, in the nature of God—why should he not naturally be true God? And if, while he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant, namely, the nature of man, why should he not naturally be true man? From both natures, therefore—divine, certainly, and human—Christ Jesus is believed, without any doubt [see Book I, chapter 13, col. 365, note b], to be true God and true man.

## CHAPTER IV. He explains by a common example that Christ, in assuming the form of a servant, did not lose the name of true Son, nor change it into an adopted or titular son.

[Col. 0421D]

You are no longer permitted to flee from this into the hiding place of your faithlessness. The pit of your lie has plainly been exposed, in which you, a trembling fugitive, were accustomed to dwell.

The Apostle therefore cries out with truthful voice that Christ Jesus, while he was in the form of God, did not consider it robbery to be equal with God. It was certainly not robbery; rather, by nature, Christ Jesus, the only-begotten God and truly the Son of God, remains equal to God [Col. 0422A].

If, then, Christ Jesus, as we are instructed by apostolic teachings, was not a robber but naturally equal to God, I ask: who is that Christ in whom God was, and whom your objections deny to be true God? A titular god cannot be equal to the true God.

Christ Jesus our Lord, therefore, in whom, according to Paul’s word, God was, was himself also Christ God [141]. The Apostle declares Christ Jesus to be in the form of God. How can he not naturally be true God, who is truthfully proclaimed by the Apostle to be in the form of God?

And since, being in the form of God and equal to God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, why should he not naturally be true man? If I ask the Apostle who it was who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, he replies: Christ Jesus, who did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.

By power, therefore, or by will—not compelled by necessity—Christ Jesus, remaining in the form of God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant. By power also he deigned, in the form of a servant, to become lower than the Father. For it was he himself, and no other, Christ Jesus, the true Son of God, who remains lower in the form of a servant and equal to the Father in the form of God.

Whatever is done by power or by will brings no dishonor to the powerful, nor diminishes the honor of the willing.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] “Whatever is done by power or by will brings no dishonor to the powerful, nor diminishes the honor of the willing.” I do not understand the words, although I seem to grasp the sense from what follows. Whatever is done by power or by will brings no dishonor or loss of honor, properly speaking, to the powerful or willing. Consider what precedes and follows, and I think you will admit that this was Paulinus’s meaning. The words, however, seem to require some sort of correction, perhaps as follows: “Whatever is done by power or by will brings no dishonor to the powerful or dishonor to the willing,” that is, it neither dishonors the powerful nor is dishonorable to the willing.]

For if, to speak in human terms, the son of some king, overcome by the merciful compassion of his affection, should embrace his servant, rushing to kiss him by his own authority or even by his personal choice; or if he should not disdain to clothe himself in the servant’s garment; or, moved by mercy, should wish to carry a sick man home on his own shoulders; and if, although he was master, he should not disdain to care for him in turn as though he were a servant—would the master be thought, because of these acts of indulgence, to have lost the privilege of mastery, or to have lost, diminished, or weakened his former power [Col. 0422C] and dignity?

[Note: [Col. 0422D] “Or diminished.” *Minutare*, says Du Cange, means “to break into small pieces.” Thomas Walsingham uses it, p. 267.] Or, because he had bestowed the benefit of servile service, would he have brought an injury of deformity upon his lordship? Or, because he had put on the servant’s garment, would he have ceased to be the one whose true son he was—the son of a king?

Certainly not. He remained what he had been: the true son of the king.

When all this had been accomplished, he did not lose the name of true son, nor change it into an adopted son, nor alter it into a titular son.

If, then, reason does not deny that a human being can accomplish this without detriment to his mastery—and to whom are all things not possible?—how much more can God, who has done whatever he wished (Ps. 134:6), for whom nothing is difficult or impossible, as no sound-minded person doubts, and for whom to be able is the same as to will?

For he possesses the power to do everything he wills (Wis. 12:18). Otherwise he would not be omnipotent, if he lacked the ability to do what he willed.

He who emptied himself by his own power—or, to speak more clearly [variant: “more dearly”], through the gracious kindness of his compassion—taking the form of a servant, and by that same power or voluntary condescension of compassion humbled himself, did so neither unwillingly nor under compulsion. Rather, he mercifully humbled himself for us: compassionate for the impious, merciful for the wretched, gracious for criminals [variant: “for the wicked”], and becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8).

[Note: [Col. 0423D] Read: “May our Redeemer, the king, the Lord Sabaoth … have exercised.” Thus it appears in the margin of Du Chesne’s edition.]

The unshakable faith of all the redeemed, in a sincere confession, declares that our Redeemer, the king, the Lord Sabaoth, and the Son of the true King, having become man in himself, performed all these things.

For in that he does not disdain to bestow kisses upon an unworthy servant, according to the servant’s own desire—she who cried out, “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1); and in that he did not refuse to assume the servant’s garment, that is, the veil of the incarnation, in accordance with the sigh of the one who longed for him, who prayed with the sweetness of a heart full of desire, saying, “Receive me according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame because of my hope” (Ps. 118:116), and, “The Lord is the protector of my soul” (Ps. 53:6); indeed, in that he did not shrink from serving a sick and almost dead servant, but mercifully deigned to bestow upon him the remedies of attentive service—

[Note: [Col. 0423D] “He did not shrink from bestowing remedies of attentive service.” The sense is: he did not shrink from bestowing remedies, namely, the service of attendance. *Obsequela* means compliant service, and *obsequela famulatus* means compliant servitude. Thus Plautus, *Asinaria* 1.1, verse 73:

“Every parent, Libanus, to his children,  
who listened to me, will now show obedience.”]

—he did not delay, in indescribable compassion, to lavish countless benefits, to such an extent that he did not disdain to carry the man, wounded in every part and left half-alive, upon his own shoulders to the house of healing. Once healed, he deigned to receive him with glory triumphant beneath the royal roof of the palace of his throne [Col. 0423C].

That healing salvation was needed by the man who anxiously pleaded from the depths of his heart, “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak; heal me, Lord” (Ps. 6:3); and likewise by the one who said, “Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise” (Jer. 17:14).

## CHAPTER V. The name above every name and every bending of the knee belong not to a titular god but to the true God; therefore Jesus is God, since these things belong to him.

What follows in the Apostle’s words must likewise be explained. “Therefore,” he says, “God highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Phil. 2:9–10) [Col. 0423D].

The name above every name belongs to the one true God alone and to the true Son of God. A titular or adoptive name, however, is not above but beneath. Common names are contained in both categories.

You assert that he is a titular god and an adopted son, as your writings testify, who became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. The Apostle, that truthful teacher, explains that he was exalted because of the death of the cross and that he possesses the name which is above every name, when he immediately adds: “So that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” [Col. 0424A].

To whom, I ask, does every knee bend except the true God? He himself testifies through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be one after me; for every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess” (Isa. 43:10; 45:24).

He who through Isaiah declared himself to be the one exalted God before all things and after all things, supreme over all, and to whom he confessed that every knee would bend—Paul plainly asserts that this very one, namely Christ Jesus, has the name above every name, and indicates that every knee is to bend at his name.

And he who through that same prophet declares that every tongue will confess—this same Paul, the great herald of that thunderous voice, explained that every tongue should confess that Christ is in the glory of God the Father [Col. 0424B].

Tell me, I beg you—if indeed you are so enveloped in the cloud of such a great error and so surrendered to the stupor of such madness that you are not ashamed to profane with your babbling lips the matters on which you speak so feebly—to which titular gods or adopted sons does every knee bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth? Or which of them does every tongue confess to be in the glory of God the Father?

And when, failing to find another whom you could seek, you could find none except Christ Jesus, true God and the true only-begotten Son of God, then, I beg you, repent of your past evil, so that at last you may recover your senses from the devil’s snare, by which you are seen to be held captive in a cave [Col. 0424C]—with a sincere eye of Catholic faith.

[Note: [Col. 0424D] Could this be a diminutive derived from *specus* (“cave”)? See what we said, following Bartholomew, in the note on *Sacrosyllabum*, section 7, letter g.]

Christ Jesus, therefore, is in the glory of God the Father. The glory of a titular god and an adopted son is one thing; the glory of the true God and true Son of God is something far more excellent. This glory is shared by him with God the Father and with the Holy Spirit.

God exalted him and bestowed on him the name which is above every name: namely, the name of power and divinity, which dwelt bodily in Christ in all its fullness and still dwells in him. No other is said to possess the whole fullness of divinity dwelling bodily except Christ Jesus alone, who is the true and only-begotten Son of God.

## CHAPTER VI. No one in Scripture is called the Son of God except Christ; he explains: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven.”

[Col. 0424D]

To support more readily and vigorously the matters under discussion, no argument appears to me more suitable than this: throughout the pages of both Testaments, the Holy Spirit, with great care, taught what must be observed in order to distinguish between the God-man and ordinary human beings, and between the true God and the titular god, and between the proper Son and the adopted son.

For if the entire sequence of these sacred writings is reviewed, nowhere in them will it easily be found that any other of the elect is called the Son of God in the singular number. Nor is any one of them found to have invoked God the Father in the singular number, except Christ Jesus alone, the only-begotten Son of God the almighty Father [Col. 0425A].

From the bosom of allegories, then, let the dignity of this solitary privilege emerge [Col. 0425B], when they are lifted by the spirit of life which breathes in them from the earth. Their wheel, with its spokes fixed in order into the hubs [Col. 0425B], carries the winged creatures upward and downward—

[Note: [Col. 0425B] “With spokes fixed into the hubs,” that is, with spokes fixed into the hubs. A *modiolus* is the wooden part of a wheel into which the spokes are inserted and from which they extend toward the wheel’s circumference.
