Pliny, speaking of certain marine creatures resembling wheels, says in Book 9, chapter 4: “There also appear creatures called wheels because of their resemblance, divided by four spokes, with their hubs enclosed on either side by two eyes.”

I admit that in a water-lifting wheel, Vitruvius, in Book 10, chapters 9 and 10, also calls *modioli* the wooden vessels or receptacles coated with pitch or wax, placed at the ends of the wheel’s paddles to catch water and raise it higher when the wheel is turned around by the river. But in that case the spokes are not inserted into the hubs; rather, the hubs themselves are attached to the spokes. Paulinus must therefore be understood to mean the former kind of hubs.]

[Note: [Col. 0425C] “Winged creatures.” Strictly speaking, *pinnata* means “winged,” for in birds *pinnae* are the larger and harder feathers used for flight, whereas *plumae* are the smaller and softer feathers. Apuleius, *The Golden Ass*, Book 3: “The soft downy feathers stand out, and the strong little flight feathers grow.” Beroaldus comments on this passage: “He skillfully and meaningfully separated and distinguished the little flight feathers from the down. The *pinnae* are harder, while the little feathers are softer and more delicate; moreover, the down is on the inside and the flight feathers on the outside.”

Because these creatures had feathers only for flying, not plumage for covering, Paulinus properly called them *pinnata*, “winged.”]

—with the force of the gleaming wings’ oarlike movement—

[Note: [Col. 0425D] “With the force of the gleaming wings’ oarlike movement.” For the various meanings and etymology of *flaveo*, see what we said in the notes to Book 1, chapter 44. To call birds’ wings oars, as one calls the oars of ships wings, is a common enough metaphor among writers. Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.304:

“He flies through the great air  
with the rowing of his wings, and swiftly reached the shores of Libya.”

And in Book 6, verse 18, concerning Daedalus:

“First restored to these lands, Phoebus, he dedicated to you  
the rowing of his wings and built enormous temples.”

Lucretius, Book 6, verse 737:

“When the flying creatures have reached those regions,  
they forget the rowing of their feathers and slacken their sails.”

Ovid too, *Metamorphoses* 5.558:

“You wished to be able to stand upon the waves  
on the oars of your wings, and you found the gods gracious;  
you saw your limbs suddenly become golden with feathers.”

Just as this poet said *flavescere pennis*, “to become golden with feathers,” so, I believe, Paulinus used *flaventium alarum impetu*, “with the force of the golden wings,” in the same sense.]

—sometimes hastening to carry them to the heights, sometimes lowering them to the depths with wings let down; now touching the earth, now beating the air. At times, too, little globes are seen flaming as though exploded by sparks scattered from the stars.

[Note: [Col. 0426B] “Little globes are seen flaming as though exploded by sparks scattered from the stars.” I have not found *glovellus* in the lexicons of classical, medieval, or late Latin, nor in any other sacred or ordinary lexicon. I therefore believe that the word was coined in Paulinus’s time and that it is the same as *globulus*. The consonants B and V are very closely related, so that one readily passes into the other. The Basques, who pronounce B as V, gave Julius Caesar Scaliger an argument for his wit when, in an epigram, he wrote that among them *vivere* and *bibere* were the same word.

In my opinion, therefore, *glovellus* is the same as *globellus*, that is, *globulus*, “little globe.” Cicero, *On Divination* 1, confirms that fires falling from heaven and traveling through the air can be called globes. Speaking of certain monstrous omens, he says: “And globes were observed in the sky.”

I would not, however, have you think that Paulinus believed those fires to fall from the substance and body of the stars, as is commonly believed and said. He is speaking from the allegorical prophecy of Ezekiel, chapter 1. That this was the popular opinion is attested by poets, who speak according to popular belief. Virgil, *Georgics* 1.365:

“Often too, when a windstorm threatens,  
you will see stars slipping headlong from the sky.”

Tasso, canto 9, stanza 62, verse 7:

“Thus, cleaving the liquid expanse,  
a star is wont to fall into the bosom of the great mother.”

But although poets are granted indulgence, such a view cannot be allowed to a philosopher. Hence Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book 1, chapter 1: “It is utterly foolish,” he says, “to think either that stars fall, or leap across the sky, or that anything is taken away from or scraped off them; for if that were so, they would by now have disappeared.” Ammianus Marcellinus, Book 25, speaking of phenomena of this kind regarded as omens under Julian, says: “Anyone who believes that bodies can fall from heaven is rightly judged impious and mad.” He then proceeds to assert natural causes, which you may consult if you wish—but I fear they will not please you once you have seen them.]

When the wheels of the writer are raised, then, his meaning must also be raised; every precaution must be taken lest it grow sluggish. And when the wheels are lowered, one must consider how the meaning should be lowered, lest lofty matters be written in a mean style or humble matters in an excessive one [Col. 0426A].

This is because the glorious and venerable marvels of the sweetness of the Lord are examined by the sharp edge of your eloquent but base explanatory style.

[Note: [Col. 0426D] Something seems to be missing, perhaps *deturpata* (“distorted”), *male explanata* (“badly explained”), or something similar; or else *diserti* should be read as *diserta*.]

“Sometimes,” you say, “things which certainly pertain only to God’s divinity, not to his humanity, are referred to that same humanity, as in the Gospel of John: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven.’”

And you added: “Since it is plainly evident that the Son of man did not descend from heaven, nor was he there before he was born on earth …”

Although this can be refuted by no inadequate human argument, why do you strive to oppose the inviolable words of his will? What arrogance inflates you, so that you do not fear to resist the Son of God with pestilential words?

[Note: [Col. 0426D] “The swelling of arrogance.” See the Notes on the Council of Friuli, section 4, letter a.]

He himself said: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven.” And as though those asking him who had descended were awaiting his answer, he replied: “The Son of man who is in heaven.” He himself testifies that the Son of man descended from heaven, that he was then in heaven while he spoke on earth, and that he would ascend to where he had previously been [Col. 0427A].

But you, sacrilegiously resisting these most evident statements, have falsely claimed that he neither descended nor was then in heaven, nor ascended to where he had previously been—that is, to heaven.

Thus you seem to fabricate the notion that this venerable and sacred declaration of the Lord was spoken figuratively, as it is customary for sacred language, in appropriate and definite places, to signify a part by the whole, or the whole by a part.

But since, through a negligent and unjust treatment, you forced the language into service for this kind of expression, your understanding, plainly crippled by the poverty of its ignorance, has also led you to misunderstand more rationally the manner of this same figure of speech. For that reason, you introduced there this irregular rule of expression [Col. 0427B], although there is no avenue of defense where no place is granted for introducing it.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] “This irregular rule of expression.” The whole sentence seems quite confused, and I would not dare to alter it in any way, lest I depart from Paulinus’s meaning. In brief, and in a single word, I think his meaning was this: there is no place here for figurative or tropological language, as Felix wished.

As for *inhormiter*, or *inormiter*, this is not a new word derived from *inormis*, which means “without a norm,” just as *abnormis* means “departing from a norm” and *enormis* means “outside the norm.” See the notes on the Council of Friuli, section 6, letter a. In the verses appended to Letter 69 of Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, the word occurs more than once, showing that it was commonly used around Paulinus’s time. In the first poem it appears as follows:

“Formless elements  
are shaken beneath the ether,  
and shapeless forms  
are made in the vaulted chamber of heaven.”

And below, in the second poem:

“Like beautiful ornaments  
displayed beneath the folds of veils,  
so they carried  
the distinguished relics  
of certain saints  
in irregular fashion.”

And in the third poem:

“Whatever is spoken sublimely,  
the rising prolixity  
of this song  
opposes irregularly,  
and its vastness resists.”]

This twofold character of figurative expression is distinguished, as we taught above, by the familiar manner of speech in which a part is placed for the whole human being—for example, “All flesh shall see the salvation of our God” (Luke 3:6)—or, conversely, when only the soul is mentioned, as is observed in the Mosaic style: “Jacob went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Gen. 46:27; Deut. 10:22), and, “That soul shall perish from the assembly of the children of Israel” (Exod. 12:19).

The proper mode of understanding this expression must be recognized where a person is not expressly introduced, but the difference of natures is distinguished. For in this passage he taught not about the distinction of natural qualities but about the unity of the person of the only-begotten Son of God and man.

## CHAPTER VII. He continues to explain what is meant by “the Son of man who is in heaven.”

When he says, “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven,” and adds, “the Son of man who is in heaven,” he makes it known with the clearest manifestation of truth that the Son of man is himself the Son of God who descended from heaven.

He assumed from the Virgin a form of another kind—that is, another nature—not the person of another son. For he is not another according to the fact that he is the Son of man. There is, however, something else according to the fact that he is man; yet God and man are one Son of God and man.

One nature, namely that of man, was only on earth; the other, namely the divine nature, was everywhere, in heaven and on earth. Thus what was twofold—divine and human—could be in one respect in heaven and everywhere, and in another respect only on earth.

Yet he who was one—the Son, namely, of God and man—could not fail to be wholly everywhere, both in heaven and on earth. He is wholly everywhere because he is one and omnipotent God, one and the same Son of the omnipotent God and of man.

The human nature did not descend from heaven, nor was it there before it ascended bodily into heaven after being assumed by God. But the Son of man, because he is one and the same Son of God, descended from heaven, from which he had never departed; and he was in heaven while he spoke on earth. He came to earth, where he was, and was to ascend into heaven according to what he is as man; and he ascended there where he had previously been according to what he is as God [Col. 0428B].

These are the Lord’s words: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven.”

But you, with reckless boldness, strive to contradict the truth, asserting that the Son of man did not descend from heaven and was not there before he was born on earth, but claiming that only the Son of God descended from heaven.

The truth is one thing; the lie has produced another.

## CHAPTER VIII. From Felix’s confession he proves that Felix admits two sons.

Perhaps you ought to have been asked by us who this Son of man is who, according to your madness, did not descend from heaven and was not there before he was born on earth. But I thought it better to resist your lie than to hear a falsehood from you.

Know, then, that by what you have said you are strangled in the snares of two heresies. For when you assert that the Son of man—that is, Christ—did not descend from heaven, but only the Son of God, you are plainly hastening, by saying this, to introduce two sons: one, Christ the Son of God, and the other, Christ the Son of man [Col. 0428C].

And where is that declaration—or what evil spirit, do you think, so suddenly snatched it from your heart—which shortly before you professed with your lips, though not sincerely?

“No,” you say, “there are not two gods or two sons. Far from it; there is one Son of God and man.”

Very well, then: how do you confess one son at one time and two sons now? For you said that the Son of man did not descend from heaven, but only the Son of God. You plainly proclaim two: one who descended from heaven, namely the Son of God, and another who did not descend, namely the Son of man.

The Lord Jesus Christ, to show that he is one and the same—the one who descended and was in heaven while he spoke on earth—said: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of man who is in heaven” [Col. 0428D].

When, therefore, he confessed himself to be the Son of man, he certainly did not deny himself to be the Son of God.

## CHAPTER IX. He accuses Felix of the error of saying that the Son of man, who is the Son of God, Jesus, was not in heaven before he was born on earth. He might excuse the error, but he doubts Felix’s repentance.

[145] Behold, you hang upon a dry stake, pierced by the noose of yet another snare. For you have prepared another for yourself, whose chain you had firmly fastened by tightening it with your own hands.

You have heaped iniquity upon iniquity, so that you said that the Son of man, although he is himself the eternal Son of God, was not in heaven before he was born on earth [Col. 0429B].

By saying this, what else are you hastening to assert, in the worst possible way, than that he began with the Virgin’s childbirth?

For when the only-begotten Son of God and man was born from the Virgin, he was wholly in his Mother’s womb, yet he preserved his whole self in the coeternal bosom of the Father.

Before, therefore, he was born on earth, he was always in heaven. The human nature was not in heaven before it was born on earth—that is, before it was man. But the Son, because he is one and the same Son of God and man, was always in heaven and on earth.

His glorious voice is also always heard saying: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Alas, alas! What a dangerous gulf, opening in two great chasms, lies before you, with its twin pits [Col. 0430A]!

For if you persist in that obstinacy of faithlessness by which you seem to assert two sons, you will soon be dragged down into the depths below. But if, because there is one Son of God and man, you should acknowledge that this one Son was not in heaven before he was born on earth, you will immediately be led, without any delay, to the precipices of the infernal abyss.

I think that one remedy of indulgence may benefit you: recover your senses from this folly and repent of your past evil. Perhaps it is more fitting to attribute this to weakness of judgment than to arrogance. For the fault which the quality of pride does not accuse is pardonable.

But since we are not yet certain of the lamentations of your conversion—

[Note: [Col. 0429B] “But since we are still not certain of the laments of your conversion.” From this it may be gathered that these books were composed by Paulinus after he attended the Council of Frankfurt. At that council it was certain that Felix had returned to his vomit, since the council had been held on his account after he had departed from the synods of Regensburg and Rome and resumed his heresy. But because he was reported to persist in it, Paulinus adds that he suspects not the resumption of the heresy, which was evident, but rather the hardness of his heart through obstinacy and stubbornness. From this it follows that, with probable conjecture, we may judge these books to have been completed around the year 796.]

—and since we are altogether suspicious of the stubborn hardness of your heart, it remains for us to pursue what follows with the warmth of a fervent faith.

## CHAPTER X. He reproaches Felix’s inconsistency: at one time calling the Son God, at another denying it; asserting that the true God dwells in a titular god and that the proper son dwells in an adopted son. From the Gospel he proves that the Son of man is the Son of God.

Although you often seem to speak correctly, we do not deny it; but because you are not seen to persevere in that same goodness, we grieve.

For at times you appear, in a sincere profession, to proclaim him as God and the Son of God; but immediately you return to the behavior of some crafty animal whose imitation you had been following—

[Note: [Col. 0429C] “An imitator of some crafty animal.” What sort of animal this is, he indicates immediately by adding: “If you sought a hiding place in flight like a hedgehog, and sought a hole in the rock in the manner of a hare.”

These two animals, whose cleverness Paulinus seems to locate in their habit of fleeing to rocky caves and grottoes, are understood interchangeably by commentators in Psalm 103:18, where the Vulgate reads, “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs,” while Jerome, in Letter 8, translated it, “The rock is a refuge for hares,” adding: “Many read ‘hedgehogs’ instead. The hedgehog is a small and timid animal.”

Arnobius the Younger likewise joins hedgehogs with hares in his commentary on the same psalm: “There is the rock,” he says, “providing refuge either for the young of hedgehogs … or for hares, because both hares flee dogs and hedgehogs.”

Chrysostom does not differ from them in this passage of the same psalm. He reads, as Jerome does, “The rock is a refuge for hares,” and adds: “By rocks he means caves and dens, to which hares and terrestrial hedgehogs flee.”

A little later he says that Symmachus translated the word as “hares and hedgehogs.”

The animal is called by various names, as we have said, following Plutarch, *On the Cleverness of Animals*, where he says that they are called *echinoi*, *erinacei*, and *ericii*. Sometimes you will find the word written with an aspiration at the beginning, sometimes without one, as is clear from the authors cited.

But *her* or *er* is also used for *herinacius*, as by Plautus, who does not separate it from the hare in *The Captives* 1.2, verse 193:]

“Go now, hunt the hare; now you have the hedgehog.” [Col. 0430B] Olympius Nemesianus likewise writes in *Cynegetica*, verse 57:

[Col. 0430C] “And the hedgehog enclosed within the folds of its spiny body.”

Some also identify the porcupine (*histrix* or *hystrix*) with the hedgehog, or at least, as Pliny says in Book VIII, chapter 35, regard it as “of the hedgehog kind; but the porcupine has longer quills, and when it stretches its skin, they are missiles.” Hence Calpurnius Siculus writes in *Eclogue* 8, verse 595:

“Then came the bristly porcupine, more spiny than a shaggy beard.”

In *Eclogue* 2, verse 176, because chestnut coverings are spiny, he also calls them hedgehogs:

“And as many chestnuts, when the green hedgehogs burst open  
with the ripe nuts in the November sun.”

Aldrovandi, in *On Fish*, Book IV, chapter 17, following Rondeletius, also cites a certain fish of the orb-fish kind, which “because it has several sharp points arising from its spines, has acquired the name *echinatus* (‘hedgehog-like’) or *muricatus* (‘spiny’). Some not improperly call the porcupine a hedgehog because of its spines.”

Likewise, according to Lorinus on the cited Psalm, there are those “who wish the islands called Echinades to have been so named because of the abundance of hedgehogs, or because their ground is rough and thorny, like that of hedgehogs.” [Col. 0430D]

But to return to the cunning of the hedgehog, Caelius Rhodiginus says in *Ancient Readings*, Book XII, chapter 18, that “the hedgehog is an animal distinguished by cleverness; for this reason Nauplius, because of his excessively crafty nature, called Sycophus a hedgehog. It is also called *echinus* and *acanthochoetus,” that is, by a name derived from its spines.

We also learn of its intelligence from Ambrose, in *Hexameron*, Book VI, chapter 4. He says:

“The hedgehog, foreseeing what is to come, prepares two breathing passages for itself, so that, when it has realized that the north wind will blow, it blocks the northern one. When it has learned that the clouds of the air are being cleared by the south wind, it moves to the northern side, so that it may avoid the opposing and harmful blasts.”

This is what concerns the hedgehog. We omit the hare, since it is a familiar and harmless animal. You will pardon me, reader, if the discussion seems to have strayed too far from its purpose. The mind must sometimes be refreshed, lest it collapse, overcome by excessive toil; besides, when many things are set before us, there is always something that may be removed.

[Col. 0431A] You hasten to return to the cavern of error.

[Col. 0431A] How much better it would have been for you to seek a hiding place from flight, like a hedgehog or a hare, in a hole in the rock; and the rock, apostolic language declares, is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4).

For immediately, forgetful of your most pure confession of faith, you strive with anxious breath to reproach him as God merely by designation and as Son merely by adoption. You are seen groping in the dense darkness of so impenetrable a cloud, enveloped in smoke, that you assert the true God to dwell in a God who is God only by designation, and the proper Son to dwell in a Son who is son only by adoption.

From this you are rightly accused of cutting apart the union of the undivided person and the duality of the distinct natures into four distinctions—an assertion so intolerable to Catholic ears that they never allow any open passage through which it may enter.

If the Son of Man—that is, Jesus Christ, who was born [Col. 0431B] of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary—were not true God and true Son of God, Matthew, Mark, and Luke would never have declared with one voice to his disciples that he would come in great power and majesty.

“But when the Son of Man comes,” Matthew says, “in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit upon the throne of his majesty, and all the nations will be gathered before him” (Matt. 25:31–32).

Who, then, is believed to sit upon the throne of majesty except the true God? Or certainly, whoever is said to come in his own majesty is undoubtedly taught to be true God.

If the Son of Man, although he is himself the Son of God, is not true God according to heretical perversity, how is he foretold as sending his angels from the four corners of the earth and gathering [Col. 0431C] his elect? He said “his angels,” because everything that the Father has belongs to him.

Or how does the Son of Man possess authority on earth, as he himself testified, to forgive sins, if he is not the true Son of God? For it belongs to the true God alone to have authority to release sins (Matt. 9:6).

Or how will the coming of the Son of Man be “as lightning comes from the east and appears as far as the west” (Matt. 24:27), if he is a son merely by designation [or by adoption?]? Is it fitting for anyone else to have such a coming except the true God, to whom it is said: “To you praise is due, O God, in Zion, and to you vows will be paid in Jerusalem” (Ps. 64:2)?

Or how, if he is an adopted son, does the one who does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood not possess eternal life?

“He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood,” he says, “has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:55–56).

The power of raising up on the last day remains with no one except the true God. Flesh and blood can indeed be referred to the human nature by which he is the Son of Man, not to the divine nature. Yet if that Son of Man, whose flesh and blood these are, were not true God because he is one and the same Son of God and of man, his flesh and blood would in no way grant eternal life to those who eat and drink them.

Therefore the evangelist John also says: “The blood of his Son cleanses us from every sin” (1 John 1:7).

Whose flesh and blood gives life to those who eat and drink it, except that of the Son of Man, whom God the Father has sealed, who is the true and almighty Son of God?

For us also the living bread descended from heaven, and it gives life to the world; whoever eats of it will not die forever. For he himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51).

Thus the living bread descended from heaven while remaining always in heaven; so also the Son of Man descended from heaven, yet because he was one and the same as the Son of God, he never abandoned heaven.

## 147. CHAPTER XI. From the testimonies of John the Baptist and the Apocalypse he demonstrates that the Lamb of God is the Son of God.

Moreover, he deigned to become a lamb for us. John the Baptist pointed him out with his finger, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29).

Concerning him, the evangelist John testified that in the Apocalypse he heard a new song being sung:

“The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fell before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls.”

A little later:

“Worthy are you,” they said, “to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood.”

And further:

“Then I saw and heard the voice of many angels around the throne, and of the living creatures and the elders. Their number was thousands of thousands, saying with a loud voice: Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power, and divinity, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing.

“And every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and those in the sea and all that is in it, I heard saying: To him who sits upon the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and power forever and ever” (Rev. 5:8ff.).

Behold: all the angels, the living creatures, the elders, and every creature confess that the Lamb who was slain is to receive power and divinity. Yet the Son of Man has become so worthless in your eyes that you are not ashamed to profess him a God merely by designation and an adopted son?

## CHAPTER XII. He accuses Felix of lying when he says that Scripture asserts that the Son of Man, not the Son of God, was handed over for us. He reproaches his faulty understanding of the name “servant,” which is equivalent to “Son of Man.”

You, then, said—not I—that throughout the entire body of the Gospel it was always the son of man who was handed over, not the Son of God.

But I say that you lied, and that this very lie falls upon your own head. Perhaps with deaf ears you read in John’s Gospel that the Son of God himself said to Nicodemus:

“God so loved the world,” he said, “that he gave his only-begotten Son” (John 3:16).

He gave the only-begotten Son, not an adopted son—that is, he handed him over. For what is “to give” other than “to hand over”? What the Lord is said to have given, his apostle declared to have been handed over:

“He did not spare his own Son,” he says, “but handed him over for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

The Lord likewise foretold at one time that the Son of Man and at another that he himself would be handed over:

“One of the Twelve,” he said, “who dips his hand with me in the dish, he will hand me over into the hands of the ungodly” (Mark 14:20, 41).

And again:

“Woe to that man by whom I am handed over” (Matt. 26:24; Mark 14:21).

You say that the handing over, and the other evils that he endured for us, were a more atrocious insult to him; or at least that it is more insulting to ascribe or confess in him the name of servant than that of adopted son.

Yet everything that the highest piety endured for us, whether through power or through condescension, and endured willingly in humiliation, is embraced more gloriously and more laudably by every sound and upright heart.

It is very strange, however, that you repeat the term “servant” so frequently in your little writings, when he was called a servant for no other reason than that he was human. As for what Paul writes concerning him—“Although he was in the form of God, he took the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7)—this can be understood in no other way than as the form of a human being, just as he is called the son of a maidservant because he is the Son of Man.

The same insult is present in the name “servant” as in the term “man.” But because the man—that is, the servant—was glorified into God while the entire glory of his divinity remained complete within him, he himself says:

“Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him” (John 13:31).

Paul likewise recounts the great mystery of piety: “manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16).

Finally, the one who said through his prophet, “Grant power to your servant, and save the son of your maidservant” (Ps. 85:13), confesses through his own mouth that he is no longer the son of a maidservant, but always the Son of Man.

He is not a servant in any other sense, as you seem to mutter, except because he is human. He deigned to become a servant—that is, he deigned to become human—who became a servant for the sake of useless servants while remaining the eternal Lord of the angels and of every creature.

He lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, God in the perfect Trinity, forever and ever. Amen.

Let the final clause conclude this second book as follows:

## 148. THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0433]

## CHAPTER I. The testimonies of John the Baptist and John the Evangelist concerning the divinity of Christ Jesus.

[Col. 0433B]

Let John and John, namely the Baptist and the Evangelist, therefore begin to weave the sequence of this third book in evangelical style.

Let John the Baptist point out with his finger the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world—the one who came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him (John 1).

Let the evangelist John teach where, when, and how this occurred, so that the authoritative judgment of orthodox faith may be more clearly instructed, not by the ingenuity of human invention, but under the most sincere guidance of divine inspiration. [Col. 0433C]

John indeed bore witness, saying:

“I baptize in water. But there stands among you one whom you do not know. He is the one who is to come after me, who was made before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie.”

“These things,” the Evangelist says, “took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.”

The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said:

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

And John bore witness again, saying:

“I saw the Spirit descending like a dove from heaven, and it remained upon him. I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’ And I saw and bore witness that this is the Son of God.”

The next day John was standing there again, with two of his disciples. Looking upon Jesus as he walked, he said:

“Behold the Lamb of God” (John 1:26ff.).

And again:

“He must increase, but I must decrease. He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. He who comes from heaven is above all. What he has seen and heard, this he bears witness to” (John 3:30ff.).

## CHAPTER II. Jesus alone is the true Son, because the Father was pleased in him; the others, since they are from the mass of perdition and he was not pleased in them, are not true sons but adopted sons.

Behold, then, where, when, and how John articulately points out the Lamb of God, who is the Son of Man; and by confessing the same Lamb and Son of Man, he confessed him to be the true Son of God.

[Note: [Col. 0433D] “He articulately points out the Lamb of God.” He says “articulately” either because John pointed out Jesus distinctly and openly, whereas the other prophets indicated him only through figures and enigmas. What is said clearly and plainly is said to have been shown articulately. Cicero writes in Book I of *On the Laws*: “What was formerly discussed at length and freely is now stated distinctly and articulately.” Or he says this because John pointed him out as though indicating him with a finger. Concerning John, Paul the Deacon sang: “Another light of our Aquileian Church.”

“You appear as one pointing out him who removes the world’s sin”;  and the joints—which are the smaller limbs—are properly found in the fingers. To point someone out with a finger means to make him clearly known and conspicuous. Hence Horace, Book IV, Ode 3, verse 122:

“I am pointed out by the finger of passers-by.”]

He confesses that he has been taught by him—or rather, by the mystery of the Holy Trinity—more than a prophet, since the one who sent John to baptize in water taught him that the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit is the true Son of God, upon whom the Holy Spirit descended and remained: namely, Christ Jesus, whom John proclaimed by pointing him out as the Lamb of God both before and after the baptism.

Let heretics, too, lulled into insensibility by the falsehood of their own lie, erase the God merely by designation and the adopted Son.

For the Holy Spirit singled out that Lamb—namely Christ—and distinguished him in the form of a dove. The Father’s voice, however, identified not just any adopted son, but the beloved one in whom he testified that he was pleased:

“This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17).

And on the holy mountain it was added: “Listen to him” (Matt. 17:5), so that the Lord might be revealed both to John amid the waters of the Jordan and to Moses and Elijah on the summit of the mountain.

Without doubt, the eye of the Father’s vision perceived in his adopted sons—although they were elect, they were still merely human beings—something in which he was displeased. For once human nature had been corrupted at its very root, it could not be free from the stain of sin.

But in the only-begotten Son alone, because he was God and human being, the Father confessed with his own voice that he was pleased. The majesty of divinity did not need testimony concerning the cause of its good pleasure; rather, testimony had to be given to human nature.

After human nature had been corrupted and ruined in paradise through the serpent’s cunning, the woman’s consent, and the husband’s transgression, none of the adopted sons thereafter came into being without having drawn something from the mass of perdition, something on account of which his creator would be displeased with him.

But in the only-begotten Son of God alone, as has already been stated, who is not an adopted but a true Son, human substance was assumed in such a way that it possessed the truth of its lineage while knowing nothing at all of the cause of sin.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the beloved Son of God the Father: Scripture, misunderstood by Felix, in which Christ sometimes speaks as the head from his members and the members sometimes speak from Christ the head.

The almighty Father therefore elegantly says:

“This is my beloved Son,” who was made human in such a singular manner, while remaining God, that I wished you to recognize from the testimony of my voice that I was pleased in him alone.

The language of love and good pleasure indicates the fullness of charity. Yet this heretic, with his followers, asserts that Christ Jesus the Son of God, in whom the Father was pleased, in whom all the sweetness of the Father’s love and the entire fullness of divinity dwells, did not know the day of judgment because he deigned to become human; he declares that he is not good essentially; he derogates from him by saying that he did not come to do his own will; he maintains that it is not his to grant the kingdom of heaven; and similar claims.

He gathers these statements together from the sacred pages of the Gospels—testimonies indeed properly uttered through the Holy Spirit, but wickedly distorted by him through an evil spirit—paying little attention to the fact that, since our Redeemer is the head of all the elect and all the elect are his members, the head often appears to speak with a human voice on behalf of his members, as though speaking about himself.

So it is with the saying:

“You saw me hungry and thirsty,” and the rest.

When they responded in amazement, asking when they had seen him hungry or thirsty, he immediately explained what he had said by adding:

“As long as you did it to one of these least ones,” he said, “you did it to me” (Matt. 25:37ff.).

He secretly said that he had been hungry and thirsty. Since he is the truth, he could not have lied. Yet he made this known not properly concerning his own person, which is Christ, but concerning his members, as though he had spoken about himself.

And what is surprising if the head speaks on behalf of his members as though about himself, when his members sometimes appear to speak about him as though about themselves, just as the utterances of the prophets testify?

“They pierced,” says the Psalmist—one of Christ’s members—“my hands and my feet.”

And again:

“They divided my garments among themselves” (Ps. 21:18–19).

And:

“They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22).

The Prophet did not first say, “Thus says the Lord: ‘They pierced my hands and my feet.’” Rather, he began as though speaking about himself, saying: “They pierced my hands and my feet.” Yet it was not his own hands and feet that were pierced; thus the statement must be understood both historically, as concerning him, and figurally.

Therefore our Redeemer assumed for us, not for himself, a nature of another kind, namely human nature, through which a human voice could speak with human feeling, and through which he could hunger, thirst, grow weary, suffer, be crucified, die, and be buried. All these things are entirely foreign to his own—that is, his divine—nature.

This is why, hanging upon the cross, he is read as having called upon the Father on behalf of his members as though on behalf of himself:

“My God, my God,” he said, “why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34).

He knew that he had never been forsaken by the Father, with whom he had one counsel: that he should be crucified for the salvation of the world.

## CHAPTER IV. He refutes Felix’s claim that, because Jesus was God merely by designation, it was not his will to suffer or die, and that he therefore prayed for the cup to be taken from him.

For this reason, before the Passion, at the very moment, so to speak, of his betrayal, he prayed—not for himself but for his members, for whom he had come to suffer; he became sorrowful [Note: [Col. 0435D] “He became sorrowful unto death.” A later age used *tristare* in the sense “to make sorrowful.” William Brito, Book X of *Philippiad*, writes:

“... he made the fields sorrowful with an undeserved funeral”; and in Book II:

“... and he had made the world sorrowful with a mournful funeral.”

Paulinus, however, used *tristasse* to mean “to have become sorrowful himself,” or more accurately, “to be sorrowful.”] unto death, became distressed, and, as the Evangelist makes known, prayed that the Father’s will, not his own, might be done. [Note: [Col. 0436D] “The Evangelist makes known,” meaning “he makes known” or “makes clear.” See the note on chapter 29 of Book I.]

Although this heretic diminishes him, claiming that because he was human he prayed, out of fear, for the cup of suffering to be taken from him, and that because he was human and God only by designation, it was not his will to suffer or die, but only the Father’s.

Indeed, in a disgraceful statement he voiced the same motive of fear, saying:

“According to the substance of his humanity, he did not come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him; and in his Passion he implored the Father, saying: ‘Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me’” (Matt. 26:39).

“He could have implored.” [Note: [Col. 0437D] Paulinus rightly censures Felix because he dared to say that Jesus “implored” that the cup might pass from him. *Efflagitare* is not the word of one who obeys and submits, but rather of one who seeks to draw another’s will toward his own. As Paulinus elegantly says, *efflagitare* does not belong to the effect of a simple prayer; rather, it means either to extort from another, through persistent questioning, what one seeks, or to investigate what one does not know with an ardent eagerness for inquiry.

Hence some, not incorrectly, derive *flagitare* from *flamma*, “flame,” so that it means to seek something vehemently and with a kind of inward inflammation. Cicero distinguishes *flagitare* from *postulare* in more than one place, separating the greater from the lesser. In the First Speech for Publius Quintius he writes:

“On these matters I do not need to say what Publius Quintius wishes me to recall, although the case demands it; nevertheless, because it demands it but does not insist upon it, I shall pass it over.”

And in Letter IX, 8:

“Even if someone has displayed a gift, no one ordinarily insists upon it from him—not even the people—unless stirred up. Yet I am moved by expectation of your promise to remind you, not to demand it. I have sent you four reminders, not overly modest ... whom I fear may perhaps demand it. I myself instructed them to ask.”

*Efflagitare* increases the force still further and intensifies the demand, as in the line concerning Turnus in *Aeneid* XII, verse 759:

“... and he demands the famous sword.”

Pauline therefore rightly expunges and rejects *efflagitare* as a word improperly and irrelevantly used by Felix.]

He could have said this, as though he had stated something new, since *efflagitare* does not belong to the effect of a simple prayer, but rather means either to extort what is sought from another through persistent questioning, or to investigate what is unknown with an ardent [Note: [Col. 0438D] “With an ardent eagerness for inquiry.” If the reading here is not corrupt, I think *flavo* has been written in place of *flagranti*, with the same meaning for Paulinus as “ardent” and “flaming eagerness.” For *flavus* is the color of burning and blazing fire, that is, of flame. See the note on chapter 44 of Book I.] eagerness for inquiry.

But if, according to heretical perversity, he did not willingly endure the Passion, where is what he had long before vowed to the Father through the prophet:

“I will willingly sacrifice to you” (Ps. 53:8)?

And again:

“To do your will, my God, I desired” (Ps. 39:9).

Should we suppose that what he had previously promised was emptied of its force by fear when he was already near the Passion? Far be it from us. Truth is entirely alien to every kind of falsehood.

Let us hear the prophecy of Isaiah:

“He was offered,” he says, “because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53:7).

Paul cries out that he himself handed himself over for us:

“Walk in love, just as Christ loved us and handed himself over for us” (Eph. 5:2).

And again:

“He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2:20).

## CHAPTER V. He demonstrates that Christ underwent the Passion willingly, and that he prayed and sweated in the garden for his own and as an example.

How, then, could he pray that the cup of suffering should pass from him without being drunk, as though it were the Father’s will and not his own that it should be drunk, when he did not refuse to hand himself over in order to drink it?

When Peter resisted, overcome by a carnal love that would not let him drink it, he said:

“Do you not want me to drink the cup that the Father has given me?” (John 18:11).

“How then will the Scriptures of the prophets be fulfilled, that it must happen in this way?” (Matt. 26:54).

Since he knew that what was necessary was necessary not for himself but for us, and that he himself had become human in order to accomplish it, is he perhaps believed to have accomplished it unwillingly? What madman, or person possessed by such frenzied insanity, would dare even to think this?

Moreover, many days before, he had foretold to his disciples that the Son of Man must be handed over into the hands of sinful people, to be mocked, spat upon, scourged, and crucified, and that he would rise again on the third day.

Peter, refusing to accept this and already satiated with the sweetness of excessive love, immediately opposed it with this reply:

“Far be it from you, Lord; may God be gracious to you. This shall not happen to you.”

At once, because of this, he heard the Lord rebuke him:

“Get behind me, Satan, because you are a stumbling block to me; for you do not understand the things of God, but the things of human beings” (Matt. 16:22–23).

How, then, did he not willingly endure what he had long before and most earnestly commended to his disciples as necessary? Or how can it reasonably be understood that he exercised unwillingness concerning this very matter, when he is known to have rebuked the disciple who was unwilling, correcting him with a reprimand, so that the sentence of punishment imposed upon him by the name “Satan” might demonstrate this also?

For he himself reports concerning himself:

“For this reason the Father loves me, because I lay down my life for my sheep. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me” (John 10:17ff.).

Certainly, the one who lays down and takes up his life by his own power is not the merciful steward of fear or unwillingness, but of willingness and authority.

As has often been stated, the Son of God did not shrink from assuming human nature so that, in his goodness, he might not disdain to be touched by human feeling.

That he becomes sorrowful, mourns, fears, and is distressed more openly demonstrates the truth of human flesh, and through this gives strength to our weakness. The inviolable Power could not be made weak by compulsion, except insofar as, by a more excellent voluntary exercise of power, it pleased him to become weak for us.

He is certainly not alien from his own will. He is the co-eternal and proper Son. He always had one common counsel with the Father: that he should be crucified for the salvation of the world.

But in words, example, and teaching he deigned to become consubstantial with his own. Therefore, at the time of his Passion, he wished to establish the rule of prayer in this form [Col. 0438C] so that his members—that is, his elect, of whom he himself is the principal head—when placed in distress, might remain vigorous in prayer, united through submission to God’s will, and strong in the power of the struggle.

They were to be certain in every circumstance that they had not been abandoned by divine consolation amid adversity and prosperity, even though they might sometimes seem to be deserted, when the power of their persecutors is exercised against their flesh even unto death. They may therefore imagine themselves to have been overcome, but divine consolations are by no means withdrawn from them, since a glorious crown is granted to them, purple with the triumphs of martyrdom.

For this reason our same Redeemer, who had no need whatsoever of another’s help, at the very moment, so to speak, of his betrayal, when he entered into agony and prayed at greater length, allowed angels to strengthen him for our consolation.

No necessity compelled him to do so; rather, by this example he wished all his members and his holy martyrs, when placed in any tribulation and abandoned among the hands of executioners, entirely deprived of every human consolation, to remain, as though in agony, more tenaciously and devoutly suspended in hope upon the help of God alone.

For this reason the evangelist does not report without purpose that, in place of the drops of sweat from the body of our one and same Consoler—since it is certain that it is not at all natural for human beings to sweat blood—drops of blood fell and trickled down to the ground.

Through the earth upon which it flowed, he wished to bring forth the earthly members of the blessed martyrs; and through the purple drops, the crimson trickling blood of Christ painted those same members of the holy martyrs purple.

## CHAPTER VI. He addresses Jesus in order to understand what it means that he descended from heaven not to do his own will but the will of the Father who sent him.

He also argues from that passage of the Gospel that he was not acting according to his own will, where he speaks concerning himself:

“Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out, because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of my Father who sent me” (John 6:37ff.).

If, according to the most shameless opinion of this heretic’s folly, it was not your will, Lord Jesus Christ, even according to that by which you deigned to become human, to save everything that the Father gave you and not to cast it out, but only the Father’s will—where is what you yourself deigned elsewhere to foretell, you who cannot lie?

“The Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10).

Where is what one of your prophets, through your gift, proclaimed to the Father about you with the joyful heart of a divine song’s sweet melody?

“You granted him the desire of his soul; you did not deprive him of the request of his lips” (Ps. 20:3).

Behold: the prophetic utterance declares that the Father granted you not merely the effect of an ordinary will, but of desire—indeed, of desire filled with the full sweetness of joy—so that you might save and not cast out everything that the sweetness of the Father’s love is said to have given you. [Note: [Col. 0439D] “But of desire, because indeed...” I believe the meaning of this otherwise rather obscure sentence to be as follows: the prophetic utterance declares that the Father granted you not merely some affection of the will, but also desire—indeed, desire filled with sweetness, with the fullness of delight—the desire, I say, to save and not cast out everything that the sweetness of the Father’s love is said to have given you. Let the reader judge whether I have reached the intended point.]

And that this was foretold of the Word made flesh, whom you wished to crown with the glory of triumph through the sacrament of the completed Passion, the following sequence of the prophetic account demonstrates, when it immediately adds:

“For you went before him with the blessing of sweetness; you placed upon his head a crown of precious stone” (ibid., 4).

Moreover, the great increase of your mercy in such abundant kindness is clearly taught, inasmuch as your evangelist describes you as having wept, moved by human feeling of heart, over the entrance into the city of Jerusalem, which you had chosen. [Note: [Col. 0439D] “Moved by human feeling of heart.” Grammar requires *tactum*, not *tactus*, because *tactus* would refer to the one who wept. The evangelist describes you as having wept, moved by human feeling of heart; this is what should have been written. Yet the saint and theologian is not to be flogged by grammarians.]

For this reason he introduces the counsel of one who pities: like a hen, he says, you wished to gather her children beneath the wings of your mercy, though she refused.

If it was not contrary to your will to receive the Passion as quickly as possible, why did you present yourself to your persecutors at night, exposing yourself to betrayal, so that when they replied that they were looking for Jesus of Nazareth, you said:

“I am he. If, therefore, you are looking for me, let these men go” (John 18:8).

But because the voice of your mercy is heard in your Gospel saying:

“I came down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of the Father who sent me” (John 6:38),

teach me, I beg you, merciful Lord God and uniquely good teacher, instructor in sincere faith, how, by your gracious gift, it may be understood both that you descended from heaven and that you did not do your own will.

You know that I am very much afraid of thinking about you otherwise than is worthy of you and pleasing to you. Therefore, by a free gift, grant me what no ability of venerable life can merit, so that I may think rightly and may fittingly express with a faithful mouth what I have conceived.

For you said:

“Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11). [Note: [Col. 0439D] “Open the doorway.” The Vulgate has: “Open your mouth wide.” The error therefore seems to have entered because someone read *ostium tuum*, “your doorway,” instead of *os tuum*, “your mouth,” in an old copy of Scripture, and consequently wrote *ostium*.]

## CHAPTER VII. He continues addressing Jesus, teaching the distinction of persons between the Father and the Son, not of wills, since the Father and the Son have one will.

[Col. 0440C]

Therefore I cannot agree with those who say that you, insofar as you also deigned to become human, existed in some way with a will alien to the unity of the Father. I believe, Lord, that you were never truly human in such a way that you were not always also true God. Since, then, you are one person, God and human, I cannot see how you could fail to have one will with the Father—while, of course, preserving the distinct property of each of the two natural wills.

[Note: “While preserving, of course, the distinct property of each of the two natural wills.” Nothing could be more appropriate than this qualification. For to posit a single will in Christ is the condemned error of the Monothelites, condemned at the Sixth Ecumenical Council, together with the originator of the heresy, Sergius, and his fellow errorists Paul, Cyrus, and others. When Paulinus says that Christ has one will with the Father, he might at first sight seem to posit a single will in Christ. But when he adds, “while preserving the distinct property of each of the two natural wills,” he most clearly shows that he admits two wills in Christ according to the two natures. By “one” with the Father, he understands the divine will.]

But because you descended from heaven not for yourself or on your own account, but for us and on our account; because you were born of a virgin through the dispensation of the flesh; and because everything that you did and taught, whatever you deigned to speak with a human voice, you did, taught, and spoke not for yourself or on your own account, but for us and on our account; and because you are the Wisdom of God the almighty Father—in what you said, that you came not to do your own will but the Father’s, you deigned to indicate both things to us: it was at once a privilege of teaching bestowed upon us and a demonstration of example.

When you say, “I came down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of the Father who sent me,” you more openly declared the distinction of the persons, since the Father is truly Father and you are truly Son. Your will is neither yours alone nor another will, but is common and one with the Father. For you yourself taught that you neither existed nor came from yourself but from the Father and out of the Father, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not two or three principles but one principle. Just as you do not exist from yourself but from the Father, so your will is neither another will nor from elsewhere, but one and the same will, and from the Father. In this, then, you demonstrate more clearly than light that you are one with the Father, when you teach that you have with the Father not another will but one will.

## CHAPTER VIII. By the similarity of the speech and teaching that belong to Christ and the Father, he confirms what precedes.

It is evident that elsewhere, through the same evangelist, you said something similar: “The word that you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s, who sent me” (John 14:24); and again: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me, the Father’s” (John 7:16).

As, then, it is made possible to understand that the word heard is not yours but the Father’s—because you are the only-begotten Word of God the Father, and are not from elsewhere but from the Father, and are not yours but the Father’s, because you are the only-begotten Son of God the Father—and as your teaching is not yours separately but the Father’s, because yours and the Father’s teaching are not different but one and the same, so your will is not one will of yours and another of the Father, but one and the same will, yours and the Father’s.

[Note: See similar passages in Saint Augustine, *Tractate 29 on John*, near the beginning.]

## 153. CHAPTER IX. He teaches that Christ descended from heaven as an example of humility and obedience, not to do his own will but the Father’s.

Since these matters stand thus, let us now see, as you teach us, what kind of mirror of the example of humility and obedience you set before us to contemplate when you said that you did not do your own will but the Father’s. For you give the reason why you spoke in this way. You say: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6:37 and following).

And when, as though questioned, you explain why you do not cast him out, you add: “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me, the Father’s.” For this reason you descended: that is, by emptying yourself and assuming the form of a servant, you bent down the excellence of the divine height, so that by example and admonition you might train your members—namely, your elect—to do not their own will but God’s will.

You knew, surely, that Lucifer, who rose like the morning star, was cast out of the palace of heaven because of his pride, when he followed his own will. You knew, certainly, that the first-formed human beings, at the serpent’s persuasion, were cast out from the joys of paradise because they made their own will and transgressed the commandment of their Creator through pride.

Therefore you descended from heaven not to teach human beings to do, through pride, their own will—the will by which they were cast out of paradise—but to teach them always to do God’s will through humility, by which they may remain within, that is, in eternal blessedness, without end.

To teach that you did not do your own will was to teach that no one should do his own will, but God’s. To cast out was what the devil achieved by persuading the first-formed human beings to do their own will, not God’s. Not to cast out was to command your elect, Lord Jesus Christ, to do the will of your Father, not their own.

I have learned that through another of your evangelists you also taught the rule of this doctrine. So that those redeemed by your precious blood would not seek the boastful arrogance of pride from the devil, the inventor of every evil, but would learn from you, the giver of every good, to retain the gentleness of humility in the bosom of the mind with the mildest devotion, you gave this warning: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

That is the rest which the first human being, deceived by the cunning of the crafty serpent in paradise, had lost through pride and by following his own will.

## CHAPTER X. The will to save human beings, which is in the Father, is also in the Son. And how the saying “No one is good except God alone” is to be understood.

Let us now hear what follows from the connection of these words, as your sweetly sounding mouth says: “This is the will of my Father who sent me: that I should lose nothing of everything he has given me, but should raise it up on the last day” (John 6:39 and following).

Continue, Lord, teacher essentially good, and explain what the Father’s will is concerning the one who has seen the Son and believes in him. “That everyone,” you say, “who sees the Son and believes in him may have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”

Who, then, could be so insane and senseless that he would not believe that, even insofar as you are human—because, as a rational soul and kind mind, you are gentle and humble in heart—it was unquestionably your will to save and raise up on the last day everything that the Father gave you, indeed everything that he drew to you?

Destroy, I beg you, Lord Jesus Christ, God, with your most powerful right hand the wall of the Babylonian city, set upon the chaff of shifting sands,

[Note: **154 “Heaps of sand.”** See what was said in the note on Book I, chapter 8.]

in which the she-lamia, with her breast exposed, weans her young on poisonous milk.

[Note: **“In which the lamia, with her breast exposed.”** He is referring to Jeremiah’s Lamentations 4:3: “Even the lamias expose their breasts; they nurse their young.” For some, *lamiae* are female sorcerers or witches and striges, or prostitutes. See Rhodiginus, Book XXIX, chapter 5. For others they are fish, called *carcharias* dogs; concerning these, see Aristotle, *History of Animals*, Book V, chapter 5; Pliny, Book IX, chapter 24; Petrus Gyllius, *On the Names of Fish*, chapter 99; and especially Ulysses Aldrovandus, *On Fish*, Book III, chapters 32 and 63. Yet neither interpretation seems to fit Jeremiah’s meaning. The passage cannot properly be explained of female lamias, since they do not nurse young animals; for “young” refers to the offspring of beasts. Nor can it be explained of fish-lamias, since the carcharias dog does not belong to the class of whales and therefore has no breasts, as Aldrovandus demonstrates at greater length in the places cited.

The Hebrew text of Jeremiah at this place has *tannin*, that is, “dragons”; so also do the Chaldean and the Septuagint, although the Syriac and Arabic interpret it as “wild dog.”

“Therefore,” says Menochius, “the meaning is that even savage beasts have not lacked maternal affection toward their offspring, whereas the mothers of the Jerusalemites have lacked it.”

Paschasius Ratbertus, however, interprets the passage in Jeremiah according to the mind of our Paulinus, in Book IV on the Lamentations of Jeremiah. He says:

“But the Church of Christ also laments the crafty perversity of hypocrites and heretics through the lamias: they bear a human face, but through impiety they carry bestial hearts. They expose the breast when they freely preach their error; they nurse their young when they teach the immature souls of their wicked followers perverse doctrines and, by nourishing them evilly, conform them to impiety, and so forth.”]

and make Zion prosper in your good favor, so that the wall of Jerusalem may be built, firmly set upon the rock, in which thousands of angels shall lead choirs, singing psalms in honey-sweet harmonies. Uproot the thorns and thistles that the accursed earth has produced, and plant fresh olive trees and vine-clad vineyards, enclosed on the earth you have blessed by lilies white as milk and purple roses, when you turned back the captivity of Jacob.

This lamia’s young is surely nourished on poisonous milk: with sacrilegious mouth it asserts that you are not essentially good because of the sacrament of your piety. For when a certain person craftily questioned you, confessing you as a good teacher as though you were merely a human being, although the rule of right faith required him to profess you true God and human being, it says that you replied: “No one is good except God alone” (Luke 18:19).

It tries to tear you away from fellowship with God alone—because you deigned to become human—to such an extent that, insofar as you are human, you are not essentially but only nominally good, like any ordinary human being who is not one person with God, as you alone are believed to be. Nor, it claims, are you naturally good, since every human being is born from the mass of a corrupted substance, but becomes good through the gift of grace granted by you.

But you, who were born from the Holy Spirit as a true human being, were never merely a human being. In the very spiritual conception itself you were believed to be God: always God and human being.

## CHAPTER XI. He shows that Christ did not deny himself to be good, but answered “No one is good except God” to one who believed himself to be merely a good human being.

This heretic, therefore, with his poisoned lips, must confess that the Holy Spirit is not essentially good if he refuses to grant that you, who were truly born from the Holy Spirit and the virgin as a human being, are uniquely and essentially good.

For you did not deny that you were good when you said, “No one is good except God alone,” because you, who are Christ, are, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, while preserving the distinct property of the three persons, the one and only good God.

You did not say, “I am not good,” since elsewhere you professed: “I am the good shepherd” (John 11:11). And again: “Is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matthew 20:15).

Nor did you reject the title of teacher, since at the supper with your disciples you commendably explained the reason for this name, saying: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am” (John 13:13).

Therefore, as the hearer of the thoughts and intentions of the heart—which properly belongs to God alone—you answered not according to the sound of the hypocritical scribe’s words but according to his cry [read *audientis*, “hearer”]. Rebuking his faithlessness, you condemned the cunning written on the tablet of his heart; you did not reject the honor of the title “teacher” when it was used sincerely.

And since he called you not God and human being but merely a human being under the title of teacher, although he ought truly to have confessed you as God and human being, you declared that such a person was not essentially good as the teacher whom he had confessed—namely, a good but merely human teacher.

“Why,” you say, “do you call me good? No one is good except God alone.” As though you were saying: “Why do you call me a good human being, when I am God and human being? I say that no one is essentially good in the way you imagine me to be merely a good human being.”

Accordingly, if he wished to have life, you taught him to return to the commandments of the Law, so that by reading them he might learn how the first promulgation of the Law in the mystery of the Trinity would demonstrate that you are true God, and that you were to be loved not with a feigned heart—as by this hypocrite who thought himself learned in the Law—but, as it is written there, “with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength.”

## CHAPTER XII. How the Son is said to be ignorant of the day of judgment, although judgment belongs to him. Paulinus modestly refrains from resolving the controversy, although τὸ *Filius* (“the Son”) is not found in the cited sentence in the authentic copies of his church or in Jerome and Ambrose.

In the same way, on account of the mystery of the Incarnation, he maintains that you, the Son of God, are ignorant of the day of judgment, although the day of judgment is plainly and properly ascribed to the Son of Man.

“As lightning,” you say, “comes out from the east and appears as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matthew 24:27). And again: “Then they will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (ibid., 30). And again: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty” (Matthew 25:37).

But because in the authentic ancient copies of the Gospels that were in our possession and were kept in the archive of our holy church, the word “Son” could not be found inserted in that same Gospel passage, and because two men most distinguished and thoroughly learned in sacred eloquence—namely, the blessed Jerome and Ambrose—

[Note: **Jerome.** Jerome’s passage is in his commentary on Matthew 24, volume 26 of Migne’s *Patrologia*, column 181: “In certain Latin codices there has been added, ‘nor the Son,’ although this is not found written in the Greek copies, especially those of Adamantius and Pierius. But because it is read in some copies, it seems that it should be inserted. Arius and Eunomius rejoice, as though the ignorance of the teacher were the glory of the disciples.” Thus Jerome.

If Adamantius is no one other than Origen, who was called Adamantius, I confess that I do not understand how Jerome can assert that the addition “nor the Son” was not written in Adamantius’s Greek copies, since Origen, in his thirtieth homily on Matthew 24, Paris edition of 1520, expressly has “nor the Son.”

Here are his words: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, except the Father alone.” I give the Latin version, since the Greek copies are not at hand; yet you should not suppose that those words are absent from them. For Origen goes on to explain this difficulty at length: how the statement in Matthew that the Son does not know the day of judgment is to be understood. He would certainly not do so unless he had written it in the Greek copies that he published.]

and Ambrose—

[Note: **Ambrose.** The passage of Ambrose cited by Paulinus is Book V of *On the Faith*, chapter 16, no. 193, volume 16 of Migne’s *Patrologia*, column 688:

“‘It is written,’ they say—the Arians—‘Concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone.’ First, the ancient Greek codices do not contain the words, ‘nor does the Son know’; yet it is no wonder that those who falsified the divine Scriptures also falsified this. But the reason why it appears to have been added is revealed when it is referred to the interpretation of so great a sacrilege.”

Thus Ambrose.]

both affirm with one accord—having plainly read the ancient Greek codices—that the name of the Son was not found in that Gospel passage. Hence it may reasonably seem that the word was added far from the truth and superfluously.

For if it had been proclaimed by the evangelist’s renowned pen, the name of the Son would never have been placed after the angels, as it is found written in certain more recent volumes: “Concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son” (Mark 13:32).

The order is inverted: the Son after the angels, the Lord after servants, the Creator after the creature. Therefore I do not think it inappropriate to suspend the thread of argument concerning matters whose shifting uncertainty of truth requires the writer to hesitate in every way.

## CHAPTER XIII. He refers the question concerning the mother of the sons of Zebedee to Hilary and Ambrose.

Concerning the request of the woman’s devotion—namely, the mother of the sons of Zebedee, who pleaded that her two sons might deserve to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in the kingdom of Christ (Matthew 20:20 and following)—and concerning the Lord’s answer that granting this seat of such exalted dignity was not his to give; and concerning the subjection of the Son, when he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father: I recall that I read in ancient doctors, men exceptionally accomplished in divine matters, namely Hilary of Pictavium—

[Note: **Hilary of Pictavium**, supply “bishop of that see.” As we have noted elsewhere, Paulinus here also used *e* for *i*, saying *Helarium* for *Hilarius* and *Pectavin.* for *Pictavien.* The passage explained at length by Hilary is 1 Corinthians 15:28, not, as Paulinus indicates somewhat hesitantly, Book X, but Book XI of *On the Trinity*.

Saint Jerome refers Amandus to this book in Letter 147, where he had proposed a similar question to himself concerning the Apostle’s passage:

“I am amazed that you wished to ask this of me, when Saint Hilary, bishop of Pictavium, completed Book XI against the Arians with this question and its solution. Nevertheless, let us say at least a few things. The whole difficulty here is why the Son is said to be subject to the Father . . . Christ is subject to the Father in those who are faithful, because all believers—indeed, the whole human race—are regarded as members of his body. But in those who are unbelieving, namely Jews, Gentiles, and heretics, he is said to be unsubdued, because part of his members is not subject to faith.

At the end of the world, however, when all the members have seen Christ reigning—that is, his body—they too will be subjected to Christ, that is, to his body, so that the whole body of Christ may be subjected to God and the Father, so that God may be all in all.”

I have chosen to present this exposition of Saint Paul from Jerome because it agrees entirely with the one Paulinus gives in chapters 16 and 17. Hilary should be consulted especially at numbers 8, 30, 35 through 44, volume X of Migne’s *Patrologia*, columns 404–428, in the cited Book XI.]

and Ambrose, bishop of the see of Milan—

[Note: **Ambrose of the see of Milan.** The passage cited by Paulinus is Book V of *On the Faith*, chapter 5, numbers 55 through 68, volume XVI of Migne’s *Patrologia*, columns 660–663, where Ambrose discusses the request of the mother of the sons of Zebedee. Note, however, that in the same book, chapter 13 and following, numbers 154 through 188, Ambrose goes on to explain the Apostle’s passage concerning the subjection of the Son. Thus Paulinus has two testimonies, even in Ambrose alone.]

—in the fifth volume addressed to Gratian Augustus, written in clear style to refute utterly the madness of Arian faithlessness, and I recall that these distinguished men labored with great effort over a broad sequence of argument to explain the matter with an adequate little instrument of reasoning (*glovello*). [Note: *Glovello*. See the note on Book II, chapter 6.] One of them explained the mother’s request, while the other discussed the Son’s subjection in an extensive work.

Therefore I judged it more useful, and not inappropriate, to moderate my pen of definition by referring to them as well, though not exhaustively, and to proceed more briefly. And because the nature of the necessity demands that I not pass over the matter through complete negligence—especially since this man, composed of a half-sized portion of brain,

[Note: **“Composed of a half-sized portion of brain.”** An excellent circumlocution. Pliny, in Book XI, chapter 37, says that a man’s brain is larger than a woman’s, and adds: “It is the seat of the mind.” Hence a deficiency in the proper portion of the brain is regarded as evidence of madness and stupidity. Coelius Rhodiginus, Book XV, chapter 23, says from Galen that “the ruling power of the soul is situated in the brain, while the manly and irascible power is situated in the heart,” and adds: “We commonly hear it said, more or less in this way, when we hear a foolish man: he has no brain; and of a timid and faint-hearted man: he has no heart.”]

as is his custom, tries to drag down to earth, by the hand of argument, the soaring theoretical reflections of sacred eloquence—

[Note: **“The soaring theoretical reflections of sacred eloquence.”** *Theoricas* may perhaps have been written for *theoreticas*. Could this have happened through the fault of copyists? Here *theoriae* means meditations and contemplations of Scripture, from Greek θεωρός, “one who contemplates.” Budé says that θεωρία properly means the inspection and spectacle of divine things. Among the Areopagite writers it signifies contemplation through spiritual understanding. See Henri Estienne, *Thesaurus of the Greek Language*, under θεωρία.

He says “soaring” perhaps by allusion to Zechariah 5:1: “A flying scroll.”]

—I shall therefore take up the sequence of the same scriptural passage, touching it briefly and summarily, as the order of the present time permits, without lingering over it.

## CHAPTER XIV. He explains in two ways that it is not Christ’s prerogative to give the kingdom to the sons of Zebedee, but to those for whom it has been prepared by the Father.

From the fact that, when the mother of the sons of Zebedee requested the distinction of a seat on the right and left, the Lord answered not the mother but the sons, no objection of contradiction stands in the way. It is plainly indicated that the mother, overcome by maternal affection, approached the Lord on behalf of her sons at their prompting, when he says: “You do not know what you are asking,” and immediately adds: “Can you drink the cup that I am about to drink?” When they answered, “We can,” the Lord at once said: “You will indeed drink my cup; but to sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you, but belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father” (Matthew 20:22 and following).

It should be noted that when the Lord said, “To sit at my right or at my left is not mine to give you,” the reason for the impossibility implied by the Lord’s objection is made clear by the preceding statement: namely, that they did not know what they were asking.

Nothing, therefore, is difficult for God; rather, the nature of the request creates difficulty for the petitioner, depending on whether the request is made rightly or wrongly. If rightly: “Whatever you ask in my name, I will do” (John 14:13). But if wrongly: “It is not mine to give you.”

Observe also that the Lord did not give the reason in a general statement—“It is not mine to give to anyone at all”—but expressly referred it to “you.” It is as though he plainly said: “It is not mine to give it to you, who do not know what you have asked.”

For in the request of these two brothers lies the summary of nearly all who ask wrongly. Moreover, when he said, “It is not mine to give you,” he did not conclude his statement with that ending, since he immediately added: “But it belongs to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.”

He did not say, “It belongs to those to whom the Father gives it,” but rather, “It is mine to give to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” It is not mine to give to those who ask wrongly; it is mine to give to those to whom my Father reveals it, as he revealed it to Peter so that he might confess Christ as the Son of the living God—and it was mine to give him the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

Likewise, he opened Isaiah’s ear so that Isaiah might hear what the Lord God was saying within him, and thus proclaim through prophetic prediction that a virgin would conceive in the womb and bear a son, whose name would be Emmanuel (Isaiah 7:14).

To those whose minds the Father prepares so that they may ask rightly, it belongs to the Son to give the kingdom of heaven. For he himself said: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). And: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

Can the woman who asks that one son sit at the left be thought to have asked rightly? At the left, surely, the goats—that is, the reprobate—are to be placed.
