The request would have been right if she had asked that both sons stand at the right, or sit upon the twelve thrones from which the twelve tribes of Israel are to be judged.

The passage may also, not implausibly, be understood in this way: “It is not mine to give you,” because the mother of the sons of Zebedee, at that time a rival of Mary Magdalene, had not yet seen the Lord ascend to the Father (John 20:17). That is, she believed him to be not equal to the Father in the height of divinity but merely human, and the Lord adapted the wording of his answer to the intention of her heart:

“Because you still confess me as human and not yet as God, it is not mine—that is, it is not a matter of human power, in which only the human nature is human—to give it. But for me, who am God and human being, it is a matter of supreme power to give it to those for whom it has been prepared by my Father, that is, to those who ask rightly.”

## CHAPTER XV. He raises from the Apostle the difficulty of how Christ is or is to be subjected to the Father.

For this reason, then, this babbler will assert that Jesus Christ our Lord is not true God but subject to the true God in perpetual subjection, because Paul writes to the Corinthians:

“When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father, and all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:24 and following).

I ask, then: if all things have not yet been subjected to him, and the Son himself will then be subjected to him when all things have been subjected to him, if the depth of this lofty statement is to be understood simply according to what the ears hear and judge, rather than in a higher and more sacred sense, how is that same Son, one and the same in both forms, divine and human, now believed to sit at the Father’s right hand in subjection?

Or is he not to sit in subjection? The Apostle cries: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him.” “Then” clearly designates a future time.

I therefore wish to be taught how this is to be understood: if he is to be subjected then, that is, in the future, when death has been swallowed up in victory, how must he now be believed to be subject—or not subject? But if he is subject, how does Paul proclaim that he is to be subjected in the future: “Then, when all things have been subjected to him, he will be subjected”?

And if he is not subject now, because the Teacher of the Gentiles asserts that he will be subjected then, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father and all things have been subjected to him, what reason requires that the one who is now not subject should then be subjected?

Could it be that, in the one person who possesses the form of a servant together with the form of God, while every suspicion of quaternity nevertheless ceases in the mystery of the Trinity, he does not now sit at the Father’s right hand, so that he might then be taught to resume the form of a servant by which he could then be subjected to the Father? Far be it from us.

One and the same Son remains, in both natures, eternal now and then, unchangeable God and equal to the Father.

## CHAPTER XVI. He addresses the Apostle concerning his meaning in the difficulty proposed.

Since this heretic has fallen silent and no place for a reply has been left to him at all, I shall swiftly seize him and, striking hard at his bombastic throat,

[Note: **“Of his bombastic throat.”** I think *bumbosae* stands for *bombosae*. *Bombus* is a harsh or hoarse sound, such as that of trumpets or horns. Perinus, *Satires* I.114:

> They filled the grim horns with Mamillonean blasts.

Catullus, line 1502, *The Marriage of Peleus and Thetis*:

> Many blew their horns with hoarse blasts.

Adelmus likewise, in *On the Praise of Virginity*, chapter 10, used *bombosa* for “bellowing”:

> At whose birth—the birth of Elisha—a golden four-footed creature is described as echoing at Gilgal with the bellow of a booming voice, signifying the fall into idolatry and the ceremonies of images, which must be rejected.

The word has been chosen to suggest pride and arrogance, as is clear from Venantius Fortunatus, *Life of Saint Martin*, Book IV, in these verses:

> Rash judge, puffed up with the deeds of his life,  
> Boasting emptily of intolerable bombast.]

squeeze its gullet

[Note: **“I shall crush his gullet.”** I believe Paulinus wrote *gurgustionem* for *gurgulionem*. The context shows that he intended the part through which the breath passes inside the neck, from the throat toward the lungs: the tracheal artery, also called the windpipe, together with the throat.

Or, if you prefer, following Thomas Bartholinus, *Anatomy Reformed*, Book III, chapter 12, it is the uvula itself, which others have called *gargareon*, *gurgulio*, or “the column.” In general, however, it means the throat. Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book II, chapter 3: “The goat has softer hair, especially white hair, a short mane and neck, and a gurgulio longer than its neck.”

*Curculio* is also often pronounced with *c* in place of *g*. Hence gluttons and parasites, who are accustomed to devote themselves especially to the throat, were called *curculiones*, as Plautus testifies, having made *Curculio* the title of a comedy.

But let us return to the matter. Paulinus not undeservedly says that he will crush the gullet of Felix, who babbles and loudly proclaims many empty things about the adoption of Christ Jesus as Son of God—that is, he will compress his throat so that he can no longer spew out such nonsense.]

with a syllogistic hand, so that whatever he attempts to vomit as the venom of faithlessness against others through his destructive mouth may, melted down and poured back into himself, cause the vital powers of his wounded inner organs to waste away.

Tell me, then, I beg you, blessed Apostle Paul; I want to learn more carefully from you what you said. What does this mean that you say: “When all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will also be subjected to him who subjected all things to him”?

Why did you expressly make the time of subjection future, if it is appropriate to refer this specifically to the person of the Son, that is, Jesus Christ? It is as though he were subject then and not now.

I do not understand what you said unless the cloudiness of my dull [*obtunsae*; read *obtusae*] understanding is flooded with the ray of divine light.

Or perhaps, so that it might be understood more reverently, you had not forgotten the heavenly voice, heard twice as it called: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). From this you had learned that the one whom you were able to persecute while you were placed on earth was already reigning in the heavenly palace.

But rather, on account of his body, that is, on account of his elect, he complained that he was being persecuted by you: those whom you thought you were leading bound to Jerusalem by the authority of letters.

Strengthened, perhaps, by consideration of this saying, you taught more correctly according to the rule of the Lord’s statement that “then the Son himself,” that is, his body—namely, his elect, of whom he himself is the almighty head—would be subjected to him who subjected all things to him, so that God might be all in all.

Finally, you first said: “For we do not yet see all things subjected to him.” But when all things have been subjected to him, then the Son himself will be subjected to him.

And I ask this: how could you say that all things are not subject to him, when elsewhere, through the testimony of the prophetic Spirit, you explained: “You have subjected all things beneath his feet”?

“In that he subjected all things to him,” you say, “he left nothing that was not subject.” Yet now you say: “We do not yet see all things subjected to him,” showing that all things are to be subjected to him in the future.

What is this? It is most remarkable: “nothing that was not subject,” and yet “not all things subject.”

## 158. CHAPTER XVII. The proposed solution to the difficulty: all things are subjected to Christ through the power of his divinity; all things are to be subjected through the obedience of his servants. And then God will be all in all.

Be present, I beg you, Holy Spirit; reveal the ear of my mind, so that, taught by you, I may hear what you mean by the fact that you have deigned to speak in this way through your Apostle: “nothing not subjected,” and “all things subjected.” By your generosity I shall now say what I understand. I consider the former to concern power, the latter obedience.

For I understand that nothing is not subjected through the power of divinity. But I observe that not all things are subjected to him through the obedience of his servants. Although his elect are subject to him insofar as human capacity permits, they are nevertheless not subject to him through obedience, while they remain in this mortal body, in such a way that God may be all things in them all. “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15).

But when this mortal has put on immortality, and this corruptible has put on incorruption, and death has been swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:15, 53, 54), and he has handed over the kingdom—that is, his elect, among whom he had reigned by governing them through the gift of grace—to God the Father, that is, when he has led them to the knowledge and contemplation of the Father’s glory, then all things will be subject to him. For there will be nothing perverse in his members through which, by resisting in the corruption of carnal struggle, all things would not be subject to him.

Then the Son himself also—that is, his body, namely his elect—will be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all things in all. Nothing else will then be necessary for them, once they have been stripped of every wretched misery of carnal desire; rather, God alone will be all things in them all. The Apostle plainly gives the reason why the Son himself is subjected to him: “so that,” he says, “God may be all things in all.” This, I say, is the reason for the subjection: that God may be all things in all. For God is all things in all through the subjection of the Son—that is, of his body, which consists of his elect.

They never at all exist in disagreement with the harmony of the Holy Trinity through the weakness of the flesh, as they do in the present evil age; nor are they ever alienated from the sweetness of his love. Rather, God alone will be all things in them: namely, the love of God alone, ineffable and always enduring in the desire of their souls. This is what it means for God to be all things in all.

## CHAPTER XVIII. He begins to cite the judgments of the doctors, first showing that Peter and Paul the apostles were misunderstood by Felix.

With these matters thus arranged, let us now come, proceeding along the straight paths of our style, to the preachers of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church and the cultivators of orthodox faith. Let us see, certainly, of what faith the preachers were imbued with heavenly mysteries: of two Christs or of one; of a named Christ who is God, or of the true Christ who is God; of an adoptive Christ, the Son of God, or of the proper and true Christ, the Son of God.

For this heretic either asserts that they preached two Christs who are gods—one named, and therefore an adoptive son, and the other true—or that they preached one Christ who is God in two ways, true in one respect and not true in another.

The Apostle took great pains to rebuke the Corinthians, who were attempting to divide one Christ. But why be surprised if he does not hesitate, with rash audacity, to defame the disciples, when, with the contracted brow of treachery, he was not ashamed boldly to accuse the very teachers of the Church, Peter and Paul?

Since the first shepherd of the Church, as we stated much earlier, professed that Jesus of Nazareth had healed all who were oppressed by the devil, and added, “because God was with him”—that is, in him—this heretic says that he did not say, “God himself was he,” but “God was with him” (Acts 10:38).

“If he himself had been God,” he says, “so great an Apostle would never have said, ‘God was with him,’ but ‘he himself was God.’” And because Paul writes to the Corinthians, “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19), here too, he says, Paul did not say, “Christ was God,” but “God was in Christ.”

The character of this statement, wrapped in the stupefaction of what sort of delusional madness, is not concealed from the prudent reader. It is as though one God were in Christ and another were the human Christ. Yet he is shown by what he has said to have implied precisely this, although Christ is one and the same, God and man. Though the divine and human are different, through which he is God and man, Jesus Christ is nevertheless one God-man.

This heretic does not subject his own thought to apostolic understanding according to the grace of the Holy Spirit through which the apostles spoke; rather, according to his own perversity, he has attempted to corrupt the holy apostolic meaning with his treacherous understanding.

Since faith arises from what is done—that is, so that what is believed may be brought about—and so that faith may not be dead without the effect of acquisition:

> **[Note: “So that faith may not be dead without the effect of acquisition.”** *Capio* is a legal term belonging to jurists, also called *usucapio*, expressing the manner of acquisition, namely through use. According to Modestinus, *usucapio* is defined in the Digest, *On Usurpation and Usucaption*, book 3, as “the acquisition of ownership through the continuation of possession for the period defined by law.” The law establishes this period as longer and more extended for immovable property, and shorter and more restricted for movable property. Hence, among some writers, the prescription of immovables is also called *capio*, while *usucapio* properly applies to movables; it too is defined as the acquisition of a thing through use. See John Calvin, *Legal Dictionary*, under both *Capio* and *Usucapio*.

> Paulinus appears to have this legal effect of *capio* in view, and to intend the following: just as acquisition arises from use, and prolonged use is a sign of something acquired, so the sign of possessed faith is the practice of faith displayed through obedience to the commandments. When the effect of this acquisition is absent—and it is absent when the practice of faith is absent—faith is dead.]**

This man, however, thinks that the advantage of the profession of faith consists merely in words.

For when he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources, not considering how very different it is for God to dwell in his elect through the gift of grace—departing from them at times, when he wills, by a profound dispensation, although he cannot at any time be absent, being everywhere always present through the power of his divinity—and how differently he dwells essentially in Christ Jesus, from whom he never departs, because he is one God and man.

In those men, as though impure, he dwells after the grace of adoption; but in that man, from the very mystery of conception, he dwells inseparably united to the man in one person. In that man, namely, who was never not God; who never began to be man in such a way that he had not always been God and man. From the moment he began to be man, he remains the eternal God.

## CHAPTER XIX. He argues that Felix made improper use of Hilary’s meaning, which he explains.

Moreover, when it is said, “God was with him,” and “God was in Christ,” the distinction of natures is certainly indicated by this; the indivisible name of the one God is not split apart.

What do you think, heretic? Do you suppose that you can lightly regard and leave unpunished so great a crime of the most wicked sacrilege? You accuse Peter, the keeper of the keys of the kingdom of heaven; you disparage Paul, the teacher of all the Churches. Let the evangelists and prophets, whose inviolable oracles you were not ashamed to mutilate, themselves avenge their cause against you.

Why do you not cease to tear apart Hilary, of blessed memory, bishop of the see of Poitiers, the conqueror of the elder and perverse heresiarch Auxentius? After the exile that he suffered under Arius, why do you now threaten him with another? In the discussion of his twelve books, in which he utterly opposes those who attempt to assert Christ as the adoptive Son of God, they take testimony from sacred history concerning the voice of the Father. Because it speaks of the chosen people of the Hebrews, from their ancestry, as though of any one man who was called by the grace of adoption into the lot of sons, saying, “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. 4:22), you do not cease to slander Hilary by claiming that he taught Christ to be adoptive.

For you say that, in book twelve, he states that love and will are found in the adoptive son. You say this, not Hilary. Then you set down Hilary’s words, but not according to that doctor’s meaning:

> “For where there is birth,” he says, “there is my beloved Son. But where there is election from the nations, and adoption [or: adoptive sonship] through the will, there is my firstborn son” (Book XII *On the Trinity*, no. 15).

In these words, it seems to you that Hilary divided one Christ in your manner, so that in one respect he is the beloved Son of the Father, and in another respect the firstborn—not beloved, but a son through adoption. Yet Hilary was carefully distinguishing the generation of the one born from God the Father, under the name “beloved,” from what is called adoption. By the designation “firstborn” in this passage, he wished to indicate the calling of that people, made before all the nations through the grace of adoption, under the title “son.”

## CHAPTER XX. He brings forward various statements of Hilary in support of his Catholic position.

After the argument concerning this matter has been set out at greater length, he says:

> “For although [Note: ‘For although,’ and so forth. Paulinus seems to have attended to Hilary’s meaning rather than his words; or else the copies available to us lack the material cited by Paulinus. The former explanation is more probable than the latter. How could it happen that no copy survives containing these words, when manuscripts have nevertheless been examined with such care in our own age? Hilary’s words, according to the edition of the Fathers by the Benedictines, are as follows:
>
> “For although ‘my firstborn’ is written concerning him, there is nevertheless a very great difference between ‘my beloved son’ and ‘my firstborn son.’ Where there is birth, there is my beloved son; but where there is election from the nations and adoption through the will, there is my firstborn son. Here, what is his own belongs to the firstborn; there, what is his own belongs to the son. In birth, the son is first his own and thus beloved; in election, the son is first the firstborn and thereafter his own, so that for the son Israel, adopted from all the peoples, what belongs to him is that he is firstborn, whereas for the one born from God alone it is manifest that what belongs to him is that he is son.
>
> “From this you may infer that Paulinus attended to Hilary’s meaning rather than his words, as he sometimes does in what follows, something we have noted in the margin.”]**

> “my firstborn,” that is, that people of whom it is written, nevertheless differs greatly and extensively from “my beloved Son” and “my firstborn Son.” For “my beloved Son” is so naturally; but “my firstborn Son” is also that Israelite people, through election and voluntary adoption.”

Behold how, while discussing quite adequately the privilege of the term “adoption,” gratuitously bestowed upon the Israelite people, he removed it from the designation of the true God. Yet you construct a completely false argument by claiming that he taught otherwise.

For no one who has taken care to read those books attentively is unaware that, having removed the “named” God and the adoptive proper son, he professed Christ in the books published for the defense of the faith to be true God and true Son of God.

In the seventh volume of his work, among other statements, he says as follows (Book VII *On the Trinity*, no. 9):

> “For the Word that became flesh is nothing other than God. No suspicion remains here of a designation either assigned or assumed.”

And shortly afterward:

> “What place is there here for adoption, or for the indulgence of a name?”

And in book eight:

> “Christ cannot be anything different from what God is. Therefore Christ is God.”

And again:

> “If Christ is your Lord by the nature of God, you have the Holy Spirit. But if this Lord is so by an adoptive name, then, deprived of the Holy Spirit, you are animated by the spirit of error.”

He says in the same place:

> “Christ, God from God, is wholly himself what God is.”

And in book nine:

> “Therefore God, the Only-Begotten, was born human from the Virgin.”

Again, in the same book:

> “Nor, after the human being, is the whole human being not in God: the whole is God.”

Again, there:

> “I ask, therefore, what could disturb the understanding so that Christ would not be true God?”

And again, in book ten:

> “Thus Christ Jesus, the human being, is the Only-Begotten God through flesh and Word; as he is the Son of man, so also he is the Son of God.”

In the same book ten he says:

> “The apostolic faith knows birth in Christ, but does not know a beginning; it knows the dispensation, but does not know division. It does not tolerate Jesus Christ in such a way that Jesus is not himself Christ, nor does it distinguish the Son of man from the Son of God. It neither believes Christ to be other than Jesus, nor preaches Jesus as other than Christ.”

> **[Note: In book ten, no. 52, I read as follows: “The faith of the Church, imbued with apostolic teachings, knows,” and so forth. Paulinus also collected the remaining material only in summary.]**

And in book eleven:

> “He who does not know God born does not know Christ God.”

Again, in the same book:

> “For in himself God glorified him, that is, in the nature in which he is God [or: in which God is what he is], so that God may be all things in all.”

Let these statements suffice concerning this matter.

## CHAPTER XXI. He cites and explains the authority of Ambrose; he accuses Felix of corrupting Ambrose’s reading.

The blessed Ambrose, conqueror of the elder and perverse heresiarch Auxentius, and now—though after his death, and though another in person but not another in treachery—the combatant against a younger one, in his commentary and exposition of the Gospel of Luke, truly confesses him, that is, Christ, to be the proper Son of God.

He recalls that the Father said to him—that is, to Christ himself—through the Psalmist:

> “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7).

Nor is an opportunity given you to refute this in your customary manner, as though the saying referred only to his divine generation before the ages, although it could not improperly be understood of that generation. Nevertheless, from the surrounding circumstances both preceding and following, it is more correctly understood as having been foretold of the second birth, which he was not unwilling to assume temporally for our sake.

For the words, “But I have been established as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain,” and “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations” (ibid. 2:6, 8), and what follows, are plainly and undoubtedly seen to belong to the great mystery of piety that appeared in the world through the dispensation of the flesh.

“Who,” Ambrose says, “is that proper Son of God except the one to whom it was said, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’?” (Book III of the *Exposition of Luke*, no. 9.)

Behold, I hear the holy Ambrose, the truest witness of Jesus Christ the Lord yesterday, today, and forever, and an advocate in agreement with our faith—the man whom you perversely supposed to be a supporter of your most false testimony—confessing that the very same one is the proper Son of God, to whom the Father is said to have spoken before all the ages: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

And at the end of the ages the Lord says:

> “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

For “today” signifies time within time; “before” precedes all times, although every time must be reckoned as “today” for God alone.

In the sixth book *On the Incarnation of the Lord* (chap. 5, no. 35), because Christ is the true Son, he says:

> **[Note: “In the sixth book *On the Incarnation of the Lord*.” I cannot determine with certainty why our Paulinus called this work the sixth book of *On the Incarnation*, since it is commonly regarded as a single book and is placed separately by other writers. It may nevertheless be conjectured that the reason was that, in former times—and perhaps in Paulinus’s copy—it was added as a sixth book to the five books entitled *On the Faith*.
>
> “Since the subject matter is one and the same both in the books *On the Faith* and in the treatise *On the Incarnation*, and in both places Ambrose discusses the divinity of the incarnate God, which he strives to defend and vindicate against the same enemies, chiefly the Arians, it is plausible that certain scribes did what we conjecture and counted *On the Incarnation* as a sixth book among the books *On the Faith*.
>
> “Moreover, Ambrose himself suggests the sequence and connection of the books in the words found in this very book *On the Incarnation*, chapter 7, no. 62 and following:
>
> “‘I could pursue the matter at greater length, but I fear that these things may seem to some either superfluous or prolix. For perhaps someone may say: “Did you not promise, in those five books you wrote, to bring your discussion of the divinity of the Father and the Son to a conclusion?” But what am I to do, when new questions are being sown every day? The promise is not passed over; rather, the objection binds me. For how can an answer have an end if there is no limit to the objection? And yet I had promised above that I would complete my response concerning the divinity of the Father and the Son; in this book, however, a fuller treatment, as was fitting, has been given of the mystery of the Lord’s Incarnation,’ and so forth.
>
> “Do you see how Ambrose himself recognizes this book as if it were the sixth?”]**

> “This is the general faith against all heresies: that Christ is the Son of God, eternal from the Father, and born from the Virgin.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Although God was always eternal, he assumed the mysteries of the Incarnation, undivided but one, because one is both, and one in each—that is, in divinity and in body.”

Again, in the same work (chap. 7, no. 71), using words almost as though they were the Lord’s own:

> “God, therefore, before the flesh, God in the flesh, assumed the perfection of human nature.”

Again, in the same work:

> “When we venerate in him the image of God and the cross, do we divide him?”

But that testimony of the same venerable doctor, which is known to have been inserted in your writings, seemed to you especially useful to your stubborn objection, since you never cease to claim Christ as the adoptive Son of God. He said:

> “For by our very usage he is an adoptive son and a true Son.”

You, however, corruptly set it down in your customary manner:

> “For he himself,” you say, “by our usage is an adoptive son.”

You wrote *ipse* (“he himself”) instead of *ipso* (“by the very”), as though, deceived by old-womanish absurdities, you thought that this man had spoken of Christ in that way.

Yet in the discussion in which he took pains to publish this chapter, no mention is found of any privilege of choice, as though he had fanned it with the little fan of his tongue:

> **[Note: *Linguae flavello*, “with the little fan of the tongue,” is written instead of *flabello*, with *b* changed into the consonant *v*, as is often seen. It is an instrument used to produce a current of air. Terence, *Eunuchus* 5.594:
>
> “‘Take this fan, and fan him with it in this way.’
>
> “This was the duty of maidservants, whom Plautus calls *flabelliferae* (‘fan-bearers’) in *Trinummus* 254. See concerning them Laurentius Pignorius, *Commentary on Slaves*, chapter 20. The same service was performed for Paula, the mother of Eustochium, when she was dying; Jerome praises Eustochium for it in the epitaph of Paula:
>
> “‘She herself sits beside the little bed, holds the fan,
>
> “‘and anticipates the duties of all the maidservants.’
>
> “But Cicero too uses it metaphorically, as Paulinus does, in *Against Flaccus*: ‘That assembly was so bereft of the nobles that Meandrius was the leader of leaders, and by his tongue, as though by a fan, that assembly of needy men was then stirred into sedition.’]**

Rather, he was resisting those who contradicted themselves and conjectured that the term “nature,” inserted in the sacred writings in connection with the designation of God, could nowhere be found. Accordingly, after he had heaped up many proofs from divine matters—proofs by which they had been refuted with a clarity brighter than daylight, and which were more than sufficiently decisive—he also wished to close the mouths of the treacherous with arguments drawn merely from ordinary usage of speech.

He says:

> “By our very usage he is an adoptive son and a true Son. We do not say that an adoptive son is a son by nature; rather, we say that the one who is a true son is a son by nature. Therefore,” he says, “we have proved by divine reading that nature and substance are divine” (*On the Sacrament of the Incarnation of the Lord*, chap. 8, nos. 87–88).

## CHAPTER XXII. He adduces Jerome in support of his position.

The blessed Jerome, of most happy memory and renowned for his admirable life, distinguished by his clear command of various languages, plainly demonstrates in the sacred writings of his works that, whenever he undertook to discuss the matter of orthodox faith, he always taught Jesus Christ our Lord to be both true God and the true Son of God.

In the first book of his commentaries, entitled *On the Gospel of the Evangelist Matthew*, he unfolds the text by setting down the words of the evangelist’s concise expression:

> “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham” (Matt. 1:1).

And shortly afterward:

> “He began with the carnal, so that through the human being we might begin to learn God” (*Commentary on Matthew*, book I, chapter 1).

What does “through the human being to learn God” mean except that we are to understand Christ Jesus to be not merely a pure human being, but, just as he is a true human being, also a true God, one and the same?

In the same volume he says:

> “But if the Savior proclaims the same things that John the Baptist had proclaimed beforehand, he shows himself to be the Son of the same God of whom John was the prophet.”

Again, in the same work:

> “The scribes,” he says, “because they thought he was a human being, accuse him of blasphemy. But the Lord, seeing their thoughts, shows himself to be God, who is able to know the hidden things of the heart” (ibid., chapter 4).

And because, according to Paul’s saying, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily in him,” this man of famous subtlety understood, with notable admiration, that when the crowd had been driven from his Father’s house by the blows of the whip, “something fiery and star-like shone from his eyes, and the majesty of his divinity flashed forth in his face.”

Again he says:

> “This too must be considered: that the centurion, before the cross, in the very scandal of the Passion, truly confesses him to be the Son of God, while Arius preaches a creature in the Church” (Book III, chapter 21).

But you, unhappy man, confess him to be a named and adoptive son, not true God and the true Son of God.

## CHAPTER XXIII. He brings forward testimonies from the books of Augustine.

Finally, the doctor Augustine, of blessed memory and admirable teaching, did not deceive the diligent reader: in his first and second books *On Predestination*, just as in all his little works he taught that Christ Jesus is true God and the true Son of God, so he concluded with these words:

> “Did not the very human being, through the Word acting and assuming him, begin to be the only Son of God from the moment he began to exist? Was not the only Son of God born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary?” (chapter 15, no. 30).

In the second book:

> “Faithful is the one who believes and confesses in him the true human nature, namely ours, although, through God the Word receiving it in a singular manner, it was exalted into the one Son of God, so that the one who received and that which he received might be one person in the Trinity” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 67).

> **[Note: “In the second book.” The words of Augustine cited here by Paulinus occur in the book *On the Gift of Perseverance*, as we faithfully place in the margin. Why it is called the second book *On Predestination*, as it is here and in our Paulinus, see the preliminary notice prefixed to this work, volume X of the *Patrologia*, column 993.]**

In the epistle entitled *To Peter*, in which he specifically set forth the most sincere sequence of the rule of Catholic faith, he says among other things:

> “Born from the Father, God the Word was born from his mother as the Word made flesh. Therefore one and the same is God the Son of God, born before the ages and born in the age, and both births belong to one Son of God. Indeed, the same God-man came forth from the womb of his mother; the same God-man, having been made so, lay in the tomb; and the same God-man, having been made so, rose from the dead on the third day” (Fulgentius, *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 2, nos. 10–11).

> **[Note: “In the epistle entitled *To Peter*.” This and the statements that follow are not Augustine’s but Fulgentius’s, as we accurately note in parentheses. The book or epistle *On Faith to Peter* is attributed to Fulgentius.
>
> “Nevertheless, among the ancients the opinion that it was Augustine’s prevailed so strongly that it is commonly listed among his works, both in manuscripts and in printed editions; it is therefore not surprising that Paulinus regarded it as Augustine’s work. See the Benedictine notice prefixed to this work in the appendix, volume VI of Augustine’s works, and volume XL of the *Patrologia*. See also John Molanus, preface to the works of Fulgentius, section 6, and Bellarmine’s observation *On Ecclesiastical Writers* in volume III of Augustine.
>
> “As for the claim that Ratramnus—or Bertramus, the monk of Corbie—in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* cites the work under Fulgentius’s name, this is not especially compelling, since Ratramnus lived some years after Paulinus and flourished, according to Trithemius, in the time of Lothair, around the year 830. Therefore, if the matter were to be decided solely by the authority of the ancients, greater credence should be given to the older writer Paulinus than to Ratramnus. But we are not disputing this point. It is enough for us that Paulinus, following the common opinion, may reasonably be excused.]**

Now attend to what is said, if any portion of rational understanding remains in you. Do you not say that the human being Christ Jesus, received by the Word of God, was not God from the very origin of the virginal womb, both conceived and born, and therefore is treacherously erased—or, rather, insanely asserted by you to be believed—not as a true but as an adoptive son?

The blessed Augustine, a truthful preacher, asserts:

> “From the moment he began to exist”—without doubt in the Virgin’s womb—“he began to be the only Son of God.”

The words “he began to exist” are not understood according to what he is as God, but according to what he temporally wished to become as man. And Augustine proclaims that the man who began to exist, who had always been God, is the one Son of God, not an adoptive son. For “one” or “only-begotten” is shown to be a term of proper identity, not of adoption.

In the same aforementioned epistle (no. 16) he says:

> “By what words can the singular excellence of that flesh be explained, whose person is divine from the very moment of its conception? For the Word became flesh in such a way that he was one person with his flesh, the Only-Begotten and eternal God, himself conceived through the conception of his own flesh.”

And shortly afterward (no. 17):

> “The Only-Begotten God, when he was conceived, conceived the reality of flesh from the Virgin. This is the reason that God was made the son of the Virgin Mary, and the Virgin Mary became the mother of the Only-Begotten God.”

You call the son of man—that is, the son of the Virgin—a named God and an adoptive son; Augustine, however, calls him the Only-Begotten God.

Again, in the same work (chapter 9, no. 52):

> “The Father alone is the one who said, ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’; the Son alone is the one over whom the voice of the Father alone sounded, when the Only-Begotten God was baptized in the Jordan according to the flesh.”

Behold, Augustine confesses that the one who was baptized in the Jordan according to the flesh, over whom the Father’s voice thundered and upon whom the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove, is the Only-Begotten God.

You assert that Augustine said that an adoptive son was baptized in the Jordan, over whom the voice of the Father sounded as “the Son.”

Again, in the little book of his faith entitled *Against All Heresies*:

> **[Note: “In the little book of his faith, entitled *Against All Heresies*.” I have gone through the entire list of Augustine’s works, both the Leuven edition and the most recent Paris edition of the Benedictine Fathers, yet I have found neither among the genuine nor among the spurious works of this holy Father any epistle, treatise, or book entitled *The Little Book of Faith*, or *Against All Heresies*.
>
> “Nor does Possidius mention such a work in his catalogue of Augustine’s writings. Whose work it is remains unknown to me. It has the character of Fulgentius, but I do not find these words in Fulgentius. Perhaps he intended to present the meaning rather than the words; and indeed you will find other statements not unlike them in Fulgentius, so that, since the preceding and following material belongs to Fulgentius’s *On Faith to Peter*, it may reasonably be conjectured that the author wished to write according to the mind of Fulgentius—or of the supposed Augustine.
>
> “He calls it ‘his little book of faith’ because it is in fact entitled *On Faith*. And because the doctrines of faith that it explains strike almost all heresies, it is said to be entitled *Against All Heresies*—that is, ‘against all heresies’—rather than merely ‘written against all heresies.’]**

> “The Father is the one whose voice was heard from heaven: ‘This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him.’ The Son is the one who says: ‘I came forth from God and came from God.’ The Paraclete is the one of whom the Son says: ‘Unless I go, the Paraclete will not come.’”

I do not know which Augustine it is who says that the Father’s voice sounded over an adoptive son; but I am ashamed to recognize that Augustine with you. This is the Augustine accepted by the man who is renowned throughout the breadth of the world in matters divine.

Again (Fulgentius, *On Faith to Peter*, chapter 17, no. 60):

> “God the Word did not assume the person of a human being; the person of divinity assumed the temporal substance of flesh. Therefore there is one Christ, the Word made flesh, who according to the flesh is from the patriarchs, God blessed above all forever.”

Again, in the same work (no. 61):

> “You hold most firmly, and in no way doubt, that it was not flesh without divinity that was conceived in the Virgin’s womb; rather, before it was assumed through the taking up of its flesh, it was conceived as belonging to him.”

Nothing stronger or more sacred can be explained concerning the mystery of the Incarnation of the Only-Begotten.

That the Lord Christ Jesus himself is true God, the same excellent doctor stated in his exposition of the third psalm (no. 3):

> “He too whom the Word of God so assumed that he became God together with it calls God his glory.”

In the treatise on the twenty-ninth psalm you find the following:

> “Know that the Lord himself is God.”

“Who,” he says, “does not know that the Lord himself is God? Let that Lord not seem contemptible to you. You crucified him, scourged him, smeared him with spittle, crowned him with thorns, and so forth; you stationed guards at the tomb: he himself is God. Know that the Lord himself is God.”

Elsewhere, too, he is said to have made such a little song of David’s hymn resound:

> **[Note: *Carminis odola*, “a little song of the hymn,” perhaps stands for *odula*, that is, a small ode, a song or little melody, from the Greek ᾠδή. But, I admit, *odola concrepasse* (“to make the little song resound”) fits poorly. Unless you prefer to write *odolla* with a double *l*, as though he intended to refer to that cave often mentioned in Scripture into which David frequently withdrew and hid, and to say allegorically that he made the *odolla* resound because David sang psalms there, and the cave of the *odolla* resounded with that song. The former explanation is perhaps clearer and therefore more likely.]**

> “Let us weep,” he sang, “before the Lord who made us, for he is the Lord our God” (Ps. 94:6–7).

And also:

> “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; the Lord God has shone upon us” (Ps. 117:26–27).

In the book called by the Greek title *Enchiridion*, or entitled in Greek style, he taught among many other things that Christ Jesus has always been the one and true Son of God from the moment he began to exist, as follows (chapter 36):

> “Certainly, from the moment he began to be human, he began to be nothing other than the Son of God, and this one and only Son; and because of the Word, which became flesh by assuming him, he is certainly God.”

When he says, “and this one and only Son, and certainly God,” he will crush your foolish babbling with a Catholic fist. Yet you do not cease to insist that the man who was made God is a named God and an adoptive son.

> **[Note: *Non desinis summare*—“you do not cease to *summare*”—is probably written instead of *adhortari*, “to exhort.” Du Cange, in the *Glossary*, gives *summare* the meanings “to admonish” and “to exhort,” from the French *sommer*. Gerard Machet, bishop of Castres, writes in letter 352: “I admonished his father, exhorting and commending him, so that he might urge his son to enter the college.” Thus *non desinis summare* means for Paulinus: “you do not cease to exhort and insist that it be believed,” and so you irritate him with your foolish speech, deserving to have your mouth crushed with a fist.]**

And shortly afterward (chapter 38):

> “The human being, however, born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, possessing both substances—divine and human—is the one Son of God the almighty Father.”

One Son in both substances, not an adoptive son, according to Augustine.

And because, contrary to your stupidity, he would not have needed another beginning of birth through baptism, he says that the human race cannot be absolved from the law of sin “except through the one mediator of God and human beings, who alone could be born in such a way that he did not need to be born again” (ibid., chapter 48).

You assert that he underwent two temporal generations, one from the Virgin and another in baptism; Augustine taught that he did not need to be reborn through baptism.

Again, elsewhere (*Tractate 78 on John*, no. 3):

> “For just as one human being is rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and man. Accordingly, Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh.”

This man says, “Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh”; yet you censure the Apostle Paul for saying that God dwelt in Christ, rather than confessing that Christ was God.

Again, in his seventh sermon, when the Gospel according to John was being expounded, because Christ is the one Son of God and not an adoptive son, he says:

> “It was necessary that he should baptize who is the one Son of God, and not an adopted one. Adopted sons are ministers of the one Son. The one Son possesses the authority; the adopted possess the ministry” (*On John*, tractate 7, no. 4).

## CHAPTER XXIV. He teaches that Felix’s heresy has already been struck down by the anathema of Pope Damasus. He adduces certain passages of Athanasius altered by Felix and explains how they should be understood.

Blessed, therefore, was Pope Damasus, who in that letter which he had addressed to Paulinus, bishop of the see of Antioch, thundered forth the following words, linking them to what preceded:

> “The Catholic Church anathematizes those also who confess two sons in the Savior—that is, one before the incarnation and another after the assumption of flesh from the virgin—and who do not confess the same one to be the Son of God both before and afterward.”

By the thunderbolt of this anathema your head, too, is struck—your head, which with treacherous tongue confesses a true Son before the incarnation, but an adoptive son after the incarnation. For “true” and “adoptive” are two, not one, Son.

That Athanasius, a man of outstanding nobility and a distinguished guardian of the right faith—namely, the bishop of the see of Alexandria—argued at length for the cause of the faith in the letter entitled *To Bishop Epictetus*, and did so in a brilliant style, is not, I think, concealed from our modest intellect. I do not deny having noticed that you inserted a reference to it in your little work—whatever its quality, it is nevertheless not sound in faith. And since I recall reading there a chapter well written by him, but not well reported by you, I thought it not inappropriate to append these words:

> “These things,” he says, “were not done by adoption, perish the thought, as some have supposed; but as the truth is: when the Savior had become man, the salvation of the whole man was accomplished. For if, according to them, the Word was in the body by adoption—and what is said by adoption is an appearance—then salvation itself would also be reckoned merely apparent.”

[Note: “These things,” he says, “were not done by adoption.” This Athanasian passage is not free from difficulty. Peter Nannius’s translation in the Cologne edition of 1686, vol. I, p. 587, reads: “These things, however, were not effected fictitiously—far be it—as some supposed; but so that, truly and through the true Savior who became man, the salvation of the whole man might be brought about. For if, in their opinion, the Word was in the body fictitiously and only in appearance, and if what is done fictitiously is imaginary, it follows—and is easy to grasp—that human salvation and resurrection are matters of opinion and appearance.” Here there is not even a word about adoption. The version cited by our Paulinus is more compressed; moreover, it uses the word “adoption” more than once. Consider the Greek: “These things did not occur by adoption, perish the thought, as some again supposed; rather, truly and in reality, when the Savior became man, the salvation of the whole man occurred. For if, according to them, the Word was in the body by adoption, and what is said to be by adoption is an appearance, then the so-called salvation and resurrection of human beings will likewise be found to be merely apparent,” etc.

Our literal translation of this text is: “These things were not done by adoption, perish the thought, as some, on the contrary, supposed; but altogether and truly, when the Savior became man, the salvation of the whole man was accomplished. For if, according to them, the Word was in the body by adoption—and what is called adoption is an appearance—then the so-called salvation and resurrection of human beings will be found to be apparent.” Paulinus’s version comes closer to this nearly literal translation than Nannius’s, for Nannius uses paraphrase and circumlocution.

Yet I confess that I am troubled by a scruple arising from the context. I know that *thesis* (the word on which the difficulty turns) is not infrequently understood as adoption. Henri Estienne, in the *Thesaurus Linguae Graecae*, vol. III, cols. 1474–75, says: “Thus *thesis* is said of something which is not so by nature, when, as Appian uses it (according to Budaeus), it is taken for *huiothesia* [adoption]; for to appoint sons (*thesthai huious*) and to adopt (*huiothetein*) belongs to one to whom nature has given no children, but who admits and adopts strangers into his family.” Budaeus himself, in his commentary on the Greek language, col. 240, understands *thesthai paida* as “to adopt a child.”

But Athanasius’s text is not speaking precisely of the adoption of the Son of God, Christ Jesus, but of the reality of his body. He goes on to prove, from the Lord’s own words uttered in the Passion, “Why do you strike me?” and from what he said after the Resurrection when he showed his wounds to the disciples, “Handle me and see,” words preceding and following those quoted by Paulinus, that the body of Christ Jesus was not phantasmal but real and true. Thus *thesis* here does not properly mean adoption. Nevertheless, since Felix was abusing this passage of Athanasius, as Paulinus shows, Paulinus proceeds appropriately in employing the reading “adoption” and attacking his adversary with his own weapons. Further, in the course of the chapter Paulinus most aptly infers from Athanasius that these things occurred not in the body of an adopted son, but of the true Son. Yet Paulinus himself had observed Athanasius’s variant, double reading when he said, “Although in our manuscripts they may be found written otherwise.”]

You added this from your own teaching:

> “And here what better could he have said, when he abolished adoption not from the body in which the Word was, but from the Word himself?”

I, however, say that he spoke better because he taught that salvation was accomplished not always by adoption, but in truth, when the Savior became man. And what could be worse and more wicked in you than to assert that the Word dwelt not in his own body—which, assumed from the virgin, he made essentially his own—but in an adoptive body?

I should like to know—but not from you—what he means when he says, “These things were not done by adoption,” and adds, “Perish the thought.” You say that this was spoken according to his divinity. What, I ask you, do these things have to do with the divinity of the Word? He did not say, “This was done,” so that the statement might be understood as referring to the Word. For “these things” is expressed in the plural, whereas “Word” is a singular noun. Why do you not first carefully and moderately consider what it is, and, more rightly, the true utterances of the Word? [Note: Something appears to be missing here; what is missing is not easy to conjecture.]

Why do you not, in greater secrecy, invoke the Holy Spirit and speak with him, and then, by the gift of his grace, bring forth in public, as though released from bondage, the salutary utterance conceived after your tongue’s veil—formerly bound in silence—has been loosened by the infusion of divine dew? Do you not know that every vessel lacking a covering or fastening is taught by the Lord’s law to be unclean without question (Num. 19:15)?

Therefore, “these things were not done by adoption,” because, once every necessity for adoption had ceased in the Son of God, our weaknesses were made strong through the sacrament of the incarnate Mediator, earthly things were made heavenly, and carnal things passed over into spiritual things. For many matters had already, in a certain sense, been set forth by him above, to which he added: “But these things were done.”

Finally, he was discussing how he referred to himself whatever his human body truly assumed as the Word’s own body suffered: how the impassible one could suffer, the immortal one die, the tireless one grow weary, and the one who could not be buried be buried in his own body, and other things of the same kind. And therefore he adds:

> “These things were not done by adoption, perish the thought.”

Although in our manuscripts they may be found written otherwise.

The same author, in his *Book of Faith* (book 9), where he argues against the heretics in alternating speeches, almost in dialogue, adds the following after many other points:

> “The Only-Begotten was incarnate,” he says, “through that secret mystery which he himself knows. It is ours to believe; it is his to know. And so God the Word himself, receiving the whole of what belongs to man, became man; and the man assumed, receiving the whole of what belongs to God, could not be anything other than God.”

If, then, God the Word, by receiving the whole of what belongs to man, is man, and the man assumed, by receiving the whole of what belongs to God, is God, where, I ask you, will the term “denominative God” or “adoptive son” be able in this mystery to claim any privilege for itself?

## CHAPTER XXV. He examines and praises the teaching of Cyril of Alexandria.

Cyril, likewise bishop of that see, says the following in the letter sent to Nestorius, among other things (Letter 8, or Council of Ephesus, part 1, chapter 8):

> “For a common man was not born from the holy virgin, and only afterward did the Word dwell in him; rather, in the very womb and virginal uterus he united himself with the flesh and endured a bodily generation, making his own birth the birth of his flesh.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Not because it had fallen into corruption—perish the thought—but because his body rose, do we confess one Christ and Lord. We do not worship a man together with the Word, for his body is not alien to the Word, since it also sits with him beside the Father.”

But when you suppose that Christ is not the true God but subject to the true God, you seem divisibly to imagine two Christs instead of one. Blessed Cyril, author of the third council, confessed not two Christs—one exalted and the other subordinate—but one and the same Christ, God and man.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Testimonies of Pope Leo.

Therefore venerable Pope Leo, a remarkable defender of the orthodox faith, in a volume filled with the truth of sincere faith, which he sent to Flavian, bishop of the city of Constantinople, because of the Eutychian impiety, explains among many other things that Jesus Christ is true God in the true nature of man, not merely denominatively:

> “In the complete and perfect nature of a true man,” he says, “true God was born, wholly in what was his own and wholly in what was ours” (Letter 10 to Flavian, chapter 3).

Although you falsely assert that in a certain letter he supported the view that adoption preceded in the head—that is, in Christ—nevertheless, from the very connection of the words placed before and after that chapter, it may plainly and unmistakably be seen that this is not so.

The same author, explaining Peter’s faith in certain synodal letters, says:

> “‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ This means,” he says, “that you who truly are the Son of man are also truly the Son of the living God. You, I say, are true in deity, true in flesh; and, with the distinct properties of each nature preserved, you are one on both sides” (Letter 15, to the Ephesine synod, part 2).

The same author says in the homily called *On the Lord’s Nativity*:

> “Accordingly, he who in the form of God made man became man in the form of a servant. Yet in both cases he is God, because of the power of the one who assumes; in both cases he is man, because of the humility of the one assumed” (Sermon 3, chapter 2).

And because there is not one inhabitant and another habitation, as you assert when you speak from your own position—and because you have falsely claimed that holy Cyril taught this—in the same homily he says:

> “Nor was the creature assumed into fellowship with its Creator in such a way that he was the inhabitant and it the habitation; rather, it was so that one nature was joined to the other. And although one is that which is assumed and another that which assumes, nevertheless the diversity of both came together in such unity that the Son is one and the same” (chapter 1).

## CHAPTER XXVII. He pursues at length the authorities of Pope Gregory.

Blessed Pope Gregory, of sweet memory, melodious in speech, outstanding in the beauty of his eloquence, renowned for the moderation of his words, most pleasing in the distinction of his holiness, and radiant with the purity of his faith, in the broad and celebrated series of his writings—although he speaks of the Lord in scattered passages—confessed with apostolic voice that Jesus Christ is true God and the true and same Son of God, having abolished every proclamation of denominative or adoptive status in him (Moralia, book 4, chapter 11, no. 18; book 35, chapter 14, no. 24; and *Exposition of Psalm 5*, no. 1).

Yet you tried to defile the beauty of that man with the vomit of your madness, reporting that he taught Christ and the Church to be one person. This is indeed true, because it is his own statement—but not in the sense you previously introduced. Elsewhere, however, you added what is yours: “one man and one flesh,” and you assert that Paul taught Christ and the Church to be one man (Eph. 5:23–32).

From this you seem to destroy the assertion that Christ is essentially a person, if Christ and the Church are one man and indeed one flesh. You would have been more tolerable if you had added more meaningfully, “as one man,” because of the diversity of the many members belonging to one head. Therefore Christ and the Church are not, according to you, one man and one flesh, but “as one man.”

Yet you deliberately fabricate and confess “one man and one flesh” so that, through perverse citations, you might separate the one God-man, Christ, from the Church. For it is one thing—and it is understood in a very different way—to say, according to Paul’s words, that Christ and the Church are typologically one person, head and body; and another thing to say that the Word made flesh—that is, God made man—is one person, Christ, with God, and consequently that Christ is truly God.

Nor should that statement which you have woven into your own inventions from apostolic teaching—“we are members of his body, from his flesh and from his bones” (ibid. 30)—properly be referred, as you strive to refer it, to that body or that flesh which the Word made flesh assumed and truly made his own body and his own flesh.

It may instead be understood figuratively of his elect, either because of both sexes or, certainly, because of the diversity of their merits, so that some may appropriately be called “flesh” because of the softness of their weakness and their more delicate sex, while others may be called “bone” because of the strength of their fortitude. Of them, of course, the voice of the Church says through the Psalmist:

> “Your eyes saw my unfinished work, and in your book all shall be written” (Ps. 138:16).

And again:

> “The Lord has blessed all who fear him, the small together with the great” (Ps. 113:13).

Finally, that remarkable teacher, in the first volume of the *Moralia*, confessed among other things that Jesus Christ is the Son of God not through the prerogative bestowed by adoption but in truth:

> “He surpasses all who are born to God in faith,” he says, “because adoption does not exalt him as it does the others; rather, the nature of his divinity exalts him” (chapter 18, no. 26).

Behold this holy man, correct in faith and full of God: he declares that Christ, born from the virgin as God and man, was exalted as the Son of God not like other mere men through the gift of adoption granted to them, but through the nature of his divinity.

You undertake to divide the one Christ into two persons, so that the one born from the virgin may be adoptive, while the one from God is believed to be the proper Son of God. Yet, from God the Father and from a human mother, there is one Christ, not by adoption but the proper Son of God.

As your writings show, it seems to you that this distinguished man, in this passage, discussed only the generation that is from the Father. I therefore ask: of what “others” does he speak when he says that adoption does not exalt him like the others, if he was not discussing the true man Christ? Why did he furnish his comparison with men, as though with a material mirror in which it might be examined, saying, “Adoption does not exalt him like the others”? Such a comparison cannot ordinarily be introduced unless the others belong to the same genus as the one with whom they are compared.

It is clearly inappropriate, and no rational order can conceal the absurdity, if, when the subject under discussion is man, a likeness of another genus—namely, “others”—is introduced. For example, if one were to say: “The first man was not begotten or born, but was made from the clay of the earth; the other men, however, were both begotten and born from the two sexes.” It would not accord with fitting and salutary fairness, nor would ordinary usage permit one to tune the measure of speech so as pleasantly to delight the ears by introducing, after mention of a man who was not born but created, other horses or oxen as born or begotten. They would have to be other men.

Similarly, after mention of an angel, “other men,” and after mention of man, “other angels,” cannot appropriately be inserted; rational order shows that each thing must be joined to its own genus. Without this addition, however—that is, without the word “others”—after mention of an angel, men, and after men, angels, may without absurdity be inserted into sacred writings and permitted in ordinary speech. [Note: Should the text read *et trito*, “and with well-worn usage,” or *non sine trito*, “not without well-worn usage”?]

Therefore, when he says, “Adoption does not exalt him like the others,” the implicit meaning is, “Adoption does not exalt him like other men,” because Christ is man, and Christ is not merely man, but is always God and man.

For this reason adoption did not exalt him as it exalts other men; rather, the nature of his divinity exalted him as the Son of God, because the one who remains the eternal Only-Begotten of the Only-Begotten Father was never not the Son of God.

He was never, like other men, merely man, so that the privilege of sonship might be granted to him as a benefit of adoption. Rather, the Word of God made flesh—who, without compromising the proper character of either nature, assumed him essentially into his own person, not as he assumes other men through the gift of grace—made it possible through this wondrous mystery for the eternal Son from the Father and the temporal Son from his mother to be one and the same true Son of God and man.

Hence the same preacher explained the matter most truthfully in the eighteenth book of this work:

> “For it is one thing for men who are born to receive the grace of adoption, and another for one man, uniquely, through the power of divinity, to proceed as God from the very conception” (chapter 52, no. 85).

And shortly afterward:

> “The same one existed before the ages from the Father without a mother; the same one, at the end of the ages, from a mother without a father. The same one is the temple of the Creator; the same one is the Creator of the temple.”

Again, in the twenty-seventh book:

> “Our Redeemer is man without sin, Son without adoption” (chapter 1, no. 3).

Behold: after first calling him man without sin, he confessed him to be Son without adoption.

Elsewhere, concerning certain people, he says:

> “For although they do not live according to the Lord’s commandments, they nevertheless acknowledge that God is Lord, because in the truth of the flesh they understand the form of deity, as it is said through the Prophet: ‘Know that the Lord himself is God’” (book 23, chapter 2).

You seem to assert that because, through John and Paul, he is taught to be our advocate, he should therefore not be proclaimed the true Son of God. But this distinguished teacher unhesitatingly professed him to be the Only-Begotten Son of God in the twenty-second book of the *Moralia*:

> “For to intercede with the Only-Begotten Son of God on behalf of man is to show himself to the coeternal Father as man; and to have pleaded with him for human nature is to have assumed that same nature into the height of his divinity” (chapter 17).

No one can be called “Only-Begotten” unless he is the true Son. Either accuse me, therefore, together with blessed Gregory and your supporters, or, abandoning the treachery of their wicked promises, believe with me in blessed Gregory.

In the eighth homily of his exposition of Ezekiel he says:

> “Paul, wishing to distinguish the denominative name of God from the essential one, spoke of our Redeemer, saying: ‘Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever.’”

And shortly afterward:

> “He showed that this one is not merely God, but God over all.”

The same author says in the thirteenth homily:

> “Our Redeemer was made not only man above men, but man even above angels” (book 2, homily 1, no. 4).

In his evangelical homilies, whenever and wherever the reasoning of faith required it, he consistently and everywhere confessed the one true Son of God, the same one from both natures and in both natures. Thus, in the tenth homily, the reader’s eye is not cheated of a passage engraved in brilliant style as though by a plough:

> “Consider, brothers,” he says, “what today’s solemnity concerning the coming of the Holy Spirit is after the incarnation of the Only-Begotten Son. In that event God, by creating in himself, assumed man; in this event men were made by the adoption of God” (book 2, homily 30, no. 9).

The same author says:

> “At that time many could be called ‘Jesus,’ but not substantially—only denominatively” (book 2, homily 21, no. 4).

You have, therefore, that God became man naturally. You have, moreover, that Jesus must be proclaimed Jesus not denominatively but essentially. Since God naturally became man, and Jesus is to be believed essentially Jesus, why do you act so foolishly that you pay so little attention to the danger into which your objection falls, so that you are not ashamed to heap, as an insult, the term “denominative” or “adoptive” Jesus upon God who was naturally made man?

Woe, woe to you, unless through a good confession you truly return to knowledge of your author.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. He explains the authority of Fulgentius.

The venerable Fulgentius, resplendent with the radiant brilliance of his eloquence, says in the third book of the work entitled *On the Sacrament of the Lord’s Passion* (chapter 12)—because the apostle Peter teaches that our Redeemer is the author of life, and therefore is to be believed without hesitation to be true God, not merely denominatively—among many other things:

> “From the moment, therefore, that the God who is the author of life assumed man in the unity of his person, from that moment that man obtained the name of life. Just as, from the moment when the Son of God assumed man in the virginal womb, the one who is simultaneously God and man began to be called the Son of God, when the angel said to Mary: ‘The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you. Therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.’”

And likewise:

> “He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Christ is called not only the Son of God according to the fact that he was born from a human being; that man is also called God because he was assumed by God.”

It is enough to have made these points sufficiently clear.

Now, in the confession of good and sincere faith—that Christ Jesus is the true God and true man, the Only-Begotten of God the Father; that he is one and the same, the proper Son of God and the same proper Son of man—all the marks of denominative or adoptive status have been entirely abolished from him, though they are granted to us. The sequence of this third book remains more tightly concluded under the following final title:

## PAULINUS’S CONFESSION AND THANKSGIVING TO GOD FOR THE WORK COMPLETED

Grant me, I beg you, Lord Jesus Christ, forgiveness as I, a sinner, approach you with the wholehearted devotion of one presuming upon your mercy. Compelled by necessity and according to the strength of my understanding—which you have granted me—I acknowledge that I have labored with unusual diligence in my responses on behalf of the Catholic faith; yet I do not excuse myself from having tried even to desire what exceeded my strength.

Nevertheless, I had nothing that I had not received from you, and I received absolutely nothing that was not yours. Everything that is excellent is yours, Lord, and I confess that I received it from the hand of your goodness. Everything good and excellent is unquestionably understood to be yours; and whatever is seen to be perverse and unworthy is likewise without doubt to be reckoned mine.

Why should everything I seem to possess not be yours, when I myself am not my own and am not the possessor of my own rights? I am your creation, though an unprofitable little servant, because after the misery of captivity you redeemed me at a great price: for when the power of the sweetness of your mercy demanded a strong exertion, you did not shrink from pouring out your blood for me as the price.

Moreover, if anyone may judge or suppose that something useful has been offered in the character of this undertaking, I have not thereby been granted the opportunity for boasting; rather, all forms of thanksgiving must be offered to you, Lord, the giver of every good. Whatever useless or foolish things are seen to have been inserted here must unquestionably be attributed to my stupidity.

For these things cannot fail to appear blameworthy if they are weighed more finely in the balance of your examination. But I ask you to restrain your anger because of my repentance, and to spare these imperfect things from the scrutiny of your judgment—though even perfect things cannot appear irreproachable to you. [Note: Either *reprehensibilia* (“blameworthy”) should be read, or *irreprehensibilia* (“irreproachable”) should be read with the *non* removed.]

My confidence of hope, therefore, is more firmly and tenaciously preserved in the bosom of my unviolated faith, because, if I have erred, I do not recall having gone astray through obstinate treachery. Rather, if a cloud of ignorance intervened in technical knowledge, or if I was frustrated by the plainness and economy of unpolished speech, I do not entirely excuse myself from having failed.

Forgive me, therefore, infinite Goodness, boundless Fountain of compassion, abyss of mercy without any prescribed limit, Jesus Christ, Lord God, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit live and reign as God in perfect Trinity throughout all the ages and beyond, forever and ever. Amen.

## FRAGMENT OF A LETTER OF PAULINUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA, TO CHARLEMAGNE, CONCERNING THE BOOKS HE WROTE AGAINST BISHOP FELIX

These special libations of my prayers, stirred by the purest devotion of my heart, I hasten to pour forth uniquely in the presence of the orthodox ruler and lord of the land. Thus, whatever little gift this may be—not precious, certainly, but nevertheless a gift—may be conveyed as quickly as possible, under the pressure of your revered commands, into the hands of that most reverend man, most accomplished and distinguished in divine matters, namely Albinus, your foremost religious orator, and for me, above all the most delightful honey of your flowering favor.

I do not know whether I might at some time be able, in another volume, to offer this gathered material to his inviolate charity with my own strength. Not because he needs these things, but so that through them it may be understood more clearly how the sweetness of my love, filled with affection and friendship toward him, may continually and quickly grow sweetly flavorful in my heart.

## 169. THE POEMS OF SAINT PAULINUS

## A POEM ON THE RULE OF FAITH

### NOTES ON THE POEM ON THE RULE OF FAITH

### Prefatory Note

Those who intend to transmit the precepts of any discipline often like to set them out in verse, so that they may be more easily committed to memory and retained. Aristotle teaches that even laws were sometimes sung among the Agathyrsi so that they would not be consigned to oblivion (*Problems*, section 19, no. 28). The pleasure produced by the harmony of meter and the elegance of poetry attracts people, by a certain sweet compulsion, to learn what has been transmitted.

There is scarcely any discipline whose chief precepts, at least, someone has not adorned with verse. Alcuin, knowing well how useful it would be to everyone, but especially to those less instructed in matters of faith, if someone carefully embraced the rule of faith in verse and published it for the people, had repeatedly and often urged King Charles to entrust this task to one of the more learned men.

When he saw that Charles had, according to Alcuin’s desire, communicated to him not only the three books against Felix but also the requested rule of faith arranged according to the laws of meter—as is clear from the fragment quoted above—he could not long restrain himself from congratulating Paulinus. He wrote him a letter, numbered 81 in the sequence of the published letters, in which he says among other things:

> “You have produced a work that will benefit very many and is exceedingly necessary for the exposition of the Catholic faith—a work I long desired, and about which I advised the lord king: that the symbol of the Catholic faith should be gathered into a single little document, in the clearest meanings and most brilliant language, and distributed throughout the parishes of each episcopal jurisdiction for all priests to read and commit to memory, so that, although they might speak different languages, one faith might nevertheless resound everywhere.”

Thus far Alcuin. We, for our part, have made and recorded several observations on this *Rule of Faith*.

You, almighty Father, who govern the world with light,

and you, Son of God, who set the stars of heaven in motion,

and you, sacred Spirit, ruler and author of all things,

the eternal and triune God, I reverently confess as one;

[5] with my lips I confess, but with a full heart I believe.

In you I believe, Father, with whom the one Offspring, God,

reigns; and the almighty Father, with whom the one Offspring, God,

reigns. Therefore, not three Gods—perish the thought—but one

God I believe in my heart, and with my lips I do not cease to confess:

[10] he who is always supreme, always perfect, always exalted,

himself alone, powerful, triune, persists as one.

Finally, I distinguish the persons by a threefold number,

but I do not allow the nature to be divided in any way.

In the Godhead, indeed, a simple essence subsists;

[15] but in the Trinity a threefold subsistence remains.

[Note on verse 16: “Not this one to be the Father,” etc. By the demonstrative words “this one” and “this,” in the following verse, Paulinus wishes to indicate the distinction of the persons in the Trinity and the unity of nature. “Not this one to be the Father,” he says, “the offspring whom I believe thunderously,” that is, the Father is not the Son, nor the Son the Father; but “this is the Father which the Offspring is,” that is, the Father and the Son are of the same nature. This is clearer from the two following verses concerning the Holy Spirit:

> “And the one who is Begetter and Begotten is not this Spirit;
> 
> but this which the Begetter and Begotten is, this Spirit is.”

What is similar appears in book 1 *Against Felix*, chapter 13, and in the *Sacrosyllabus*, section 8. See the notes there. Comparable are the words I add from Augustine, *Tractate 45 on John*, no. 5:

> “Arius says, ‘The Father is one thing, the Son another.’ He would speak correctly if he said ‘another person,’ not ‘another thing.’”

Thus, conversely, Paulinus says: “This is the Father which the Son is”; “this is not the Father who is the Son.”]

Not this one to be the Father, the offspring whom I believe thundering,

but this to be the Father, the supreme Offspring whom I adore.

[Col. 0468C]

And the one who is Begetter and Begotten is not this Spirit;

but this which the Begetter and Begotten is, this Spirit is.

[20] I believe the Son of God, begotten of the holy virgin,

born of the sacred Spirit; with faithful tongue I sing him,

who, at a fixed time, created all time,

who governs the shining stars of the dew-bearing heaven,

who created sea and earth and sky, the greatest

[25] regions of the fourfold world, mountains and hills;

[Note on verse 26: “Who closes the boundaries of ether and earth with his fist.” This is taken from Isaiah 40:12: “Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the heavens with a span? Who has enclosed the mass of the earth with three fingers, and weighed the mountains in a balance, and the hills on scales?”

He used *cludit* instead of *claudit* (“closes”). This has an archaic flavor, although it is used by excellent writers. Columella, book 12, chapter 44: “Then, after spreading out the ropes, they close the tree.” Pliny, book 33, chapter 1: “He enclosed certain gems in gold.” And shortly afterward: “Others enclose poisons beneath gems.” Juvenal, book 3, satire 7, verse 26:

> “Or close them, and pierce through the booklets laid out, with the moth.”

Martial, book 11, epigram 92:

> “But death hastened to close the path of the flattering voice.”

And many others in various places. Just as Paulinus here substituted *cludit* for *claudit*, so below, in the *Apology for His Poem*, he says *clusas uvas* for *clausas* (“closed grapes”).]

Who closes the boundaries of ether and earth with his fist,

with three joints, with vast limits, he balances the globe,

and measures broad Olympus with his palm.

He precedes the ages, who made all the ages.

[30] This one, when he had been dipped in the Jordan’s wave,

the almighty Father at once declared from on high,

[Col. 0468D]

while the Holy Spirit descended from heaven

in the form of a white dove,

with John the Baptist himself ministering with great devotion,

to be his beloved, own, gracious, sweet, thunderous Offspring—

[35] his own Begotten—from his holy mouth.

[Note on verse 36: “When a splendid cloud encircled the flower-bearing mountain peak.” This is from Matthew 17:1 and following, where the history of the Lord’s Transfiguration is recounted.

Although the Alps properly are the mountains that fortify Italy, as Petrarch says:

> “the beautiful land,
> 
> which the Apennine divides, and the sea and Alps surround,”

nevertheless the word is sometimes used for any lofty mountain. Servius, commenting on Virgil, *Georgics* 3.474, “Then let him know the airy Alps,” says:
