> “In the language of the Gauls, lofty mountains are called Alps.”

The Pyrenees mountains in particular are called Alps by Venantius Fortunatus, book 6, poem 2, verse 89:

> “Through powerful winters and the Alpine Pyrenees.”

See also book 6, poem 7, verse 210, and book 10, poem 22, verse 13.

Paulinus therefore appropriately called Mount Tabor—where, as is believed, the sublime miracle of the Transfiguration took place—an Alpine peak, and indeed a flower-bearing one. For Adrichomius says in *The Tribe of Zebulun*, no. 95:

> “It is exceedingly healthy because of the climate of heaven; everywhere it is completely planted with vines, olives, various shrubs, and fruit-bearing trees; it is continually moist with dew; it is always green with the foliage of trees and many-colored grasses, and most fragrant with the sweet scent of every kind of flower. In brief, the whole mountain is devoted to delighting the eyes and refreshing the souls. For this reason Christ the Lord rightly chose it both for prayer and for his Transfiguration.”]

When a splendid cloud encircled the flower-bearing mountain peak,

and he stood in the highest place, on the summit of the secluded mountain,

with three disciples and two servants,

Jesus, the unique glory of heaven’s high throne,

[40] his face shone more beautifully than a ray of the sun;

his garment radiated whiteness like the brightness of snow, and behold,

a mighty voice of God thundered from the serene cloud,

pouring through the empty air and spreading through the tender breezes,

and with honeyed words it uttered such joys:

[45] “This is my one beloved Son,” it said;

“listen to him.” This was given as a wondrous sign:

that Christ, God and man, is true and exalted,

that he, the Son of God, was born from the holy virgin.

[Note on verse 49: Perhaps Peter is taught by this utterance not to equate men with God or servants with the Lord. Cornelius à Lapide, commenting on Matthew 17:4, says:

> “Peter, intoxicated by the sweetness of this vision and wishing to prolong it, spoke incongruously, as though deprived of reason; he wandered in mind and, as it were, babbled. This happened first because he equated Moses and Elijah with Christ.”

This is repeatedly condemned in the Book of Job, and especially in chapter 22, verse 2: “Can man be compared with God, even when he is perfect in knowledge?”]

Hence he is reproved: perhaps Peter is taught by this utterance:

[50] not to equate men with God, nor servants with the Lord.

[Col. 0469B] [Note: [Col. 0473B] Verse 51. “The necks of the chelydros.” He has used a species for the genus, understanding the devil, who in Scripture and the Fathers is called by the names “serpent” and “snake.” Properly, however, chelydroi are aquatic tortoises. H. Stephanus, *Thesaurus*, vol. IV, col. 464B: “Χέλυδρος is the same as if one said χέλυς ἕνυδρος, ‘aquatic tortoise,’ a tortoise dwelling in water.” Nicander, in the *Theriaca*, vv. 411 ff., takes it for a serpent, which he calls δρύϊνος, because it sometimes lives in the hollow of oaks. Virgil refers to it in *Georgics* II, v. 214:

> And the rough tufa, and the chalk eaten away by black chelydroi.

And in book III, v. 414:

> Learn also to kindle fragrant cedarwood in the stalls  
> and to drive on the heavy chelydroi with Galbanum’s odor.

On this passage Servius says: “They are called chelydroi, as it were chersydroi, because they dwell in water and on land; for χέρσος means ‘land,’ and ὕδωρ ‘water.’” But that chersydroi and chelydroi are not the same is shown by Nicander, who discusses chersydroi at vv. 359 ff. and later chelydroi as wholly distinct from them; and by Lucan, who in book IX of the *Pharsalia*, v. 712, distinguishes them most clearly when he says:

> And the chersydros, born to inhabit the fields  
> of the uncertain Syrtes, and the chelydroi dragged along the smoking road.

On the serpent—that is, the devil—see the note on Hymn 3, v. 26.]

This is the true faith that breaks the necks of the chelydros;

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Verse 52. “This conquers the world.” 1 John 5:4: “This is the victory that conquers the world, our faith.”]

This conquers the world and removes the crimes of sin;

By this Peter opens the thresholds of heaven,

Unlocking the golden ranks for the heavenly realms,

[55] And sends them into the countryside, drawing forth for them the joys of snow-white life.

He bids the tender lambs, newly born with white fleece,

Graze, Jordan, beside your fields, surrounded by roses,

Beside green fields and myrtle groves,

[60] And, trusting in the flowering pastures where lilies mingle with roses,

To crop a thousand things with their ruminating mouths.

There the painted meadows glow red with saffron flowers;

Never do they wither from cold, nor dry up beneath the sun’s rays;

[65] Never do they fade, touched by icy frosts,

[Col. 0469C] Nor, drenched with rains and soaked through, do they decay;

But, Paradise, they always breathe forth the fragrant odors

They display a grove sparkling with leafy strength,

But retains pomegranates mixed among its leaves,

Which always drip liquid juices from their bark;

They pour forth sweet flavors in the manner of those who chew.

It flows toward the spring of leaping water,

[75] Which pours forth living streams, and from one source

Sends out divided dews,

Leads the bleating sheep, white and equal, along four rivers,

And compels them to drink, so that they may never, with foaming mouths,

[Col. 0469D] Thirstily seek the streams of another spring.

[80] I judge that all supporters of wicked doctrine,

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Verse 81. “With Paul’s doubled anathema.” Paul says in Galatians 1:8–9: “Even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you anything other than what we preached to you, let him be accursed. As we said before, so now I say again: if anyone preaches to you anything other than what you received, let him be accursed.” Here we have Paul’s doubled anathema. Paulinus expresses a similar judgment: “If even an angel should teach otherwise than what Gabriel foretold, and Peter and Paul taught, and the four evangelists confessed with one voice, he must be struck by the thunderbolt of this doubled anathema.”]

The liars whom Paul, the teacher of the world, condemns

With his doubled anathema—perhaps to frighten the rebellious Galatians—

Or whoever, girded in a saffron robe,

An angel, hurling through the lofty air,

[85] Speaks in a resounding voice and proclaims something else

Than what Gabriel, the messenger of the lofty King, foretold,

[Note: [Col. 0473D] Verse 87. “Which Paul’s reed writes.” That characters were once incised with a stylus on waxed tablets is evident from Luke 1:63, concerning Zechariah: “And asking for a writing tablet, he wrote.” The Greek for “writing tablet” is πινακίδιον, meaning a waxed tablet, on which people formerly wrote with a stylus, sometimes of iron—called a *graphium*, from the Greek γραφεῖον—as was also the case with the *graphiarium*, the case in which it was stored so that it would not prick the person carrying it, as Martial testifies in *Apophoreta*, epigram 21; sometimes with a bone stylus, as we learn from the sole surviving verse of Atta:

> Let us turn the plowshare into wax and plow with the bone point …

This manner of writing remained in use even in later centuries, as is clear from the martyrdom of Saint Cassian, concerning whom Prudentius writes in *Peristephanon*, v. 2136:

> Then others brandish goads and iron points,  
> on the side with which writing is made in furrowed lines.

For they were handed over to be stabbed by the boys whom he had taught, and this they accomplished with iron styli. Yet I would not deny that Paul wrote with a reed or pen, since this kind of writing was also known to the ancients, as is clear from Psalm 44:2: “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe.” John, Paul’s contemporary, mentions ink and a pen in his second and third epistles. Paul himself also implies this in 2 Corinthians 3:3, when he says: “You are a letter of Christ, delivered by us and written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God.” Ink, however, was used only by those who wrote with a pen or reed, since bird feathers had not yet been introduced; from that ancient writing instrument the name remained, and even today an ink vessel is called a *calamarium*. Thus Paulinus could not improperly say of Paul writing: “Which Paul’s reed writes.”]

Which Peter taught, which Paul’s reed writes,

Which the four leaders confess with a shared voice,

[Note: [Col. 0474B] Verse 89. “He will be struck by the blow of the biblical thunderbolt.” What is *bibici*? Could it mean “violent,” from Greek βία, “force” or “violence”? For in Du Cange, *bibix* in Papias means “battle.” Or should *biblici* be read, because he derived the judgment of anathema from the Bible, that is, from Scripture—specifically Paul’s Epistle to the Galatians? Or should *bifidi* rather be restored, because Paul hurls anathema twice against the obstinate, as Paulinus said above, “with Paul’s doubled anathema”? Let the reader weigh and choose.]

He will be struck by the blow of the *bibici* thunderbolt.

[90] [Note: [Col. 0474C] Verse 90. “Cerinthus, the beginning and entire head of every evil and impiety.” Why is Cerinthus called the beginning and head of evil, since he is not listed first among the heresiarchs but eighth by Irenaeus, book I, chapter 25; by Epiphanius, book I, heresy 8; and by Philaster, *On Heresies*, no. 8? Because the seeds of the Felician doctrine lay hidden in the Cerinthian teaching. Tertullian says of Cerinthus in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 48: “He proposes that Christ was born from Joseph’s seed, maintaining that he was merely a human being without divinity.” Irenaeus adds in the same passage that Cerinthus taught that Christ was distinct from Jesus: “For he taught that Christ descended upon him after baptism in the form of a dove, and then proclaimed the unknown Father and performed miracles; but at the end Christ again flew away from Jesus, and Jesus suffered and rose again, while Christ remained impassible, being spiritual.” You see how the impious doctrine of Cerinthus anticipated Felix’s teaching, which divided Christ, as Paulinus shows in more than one place, especially from chapter 9 of book I against him. Thus Paulinus rightly calls Cerinthus the head and beginning of all evil, as does Cyril of Jerusalem in *Mystagogical Catechesis* VI, “the Lerna of evils”—Λέρνη κακῶν, “the Lerna of evils,” according to the proverb.]

Cerinthus, the beginning and head of every evil, every impiety,

[Note: [Col. 0474D] Verse 91. “He is carried, burned, into avenging flames.” Should *fomis* be read as *foveis*, with an allusion to the abyss of Gehenna and hell? Or is *fomis* used for *fomes*, meaning fuel and nourishment for avenging flames? *Fomes* properly means any material suitable for feeding fire. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, v. 178:

> First Achates struck a spark from the flint,  
> caught the fire in leaves, gave dry fuel around it,  
> and snatched up the flame in the tinder.

Servius says there: “*Fomites* are splinters shaken from trees when they are cut.” But Opilius, quoted by Festus, thinks that vines already scorched are called *fomites*. Salmasius notes in his commentary on Solinus, p. 181, that the word is derived from mushrooms, “because mushrooms were used as tinder and were called fuel. Hence among later Greek physicians ἵσμαι—that is, ‘fuel’—properly denotes mushrooms growing on trees, because they provided tinder.” Cerinthus, therefore, is carried into avenging flames like the fuel of the fire of Gehenna.]

He is burned and carried into avenging flames as their fuel.

[Note: [Col. 0475A] Verse 92. “Unhappy Ebion, in every respect not unlike him.” Philaster says: “Ebion, a disciple of Cerinthus, erring similarly to him in many respects, believed that our Savior was a human being carnally born from Joseph, and said that there was no divinity in him.” Saint Jerome says in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, concerning Saint John the Evangelist: “He wrote his Gospel last of all, at the request of the bishops of Asia, against Cerinthus and the other heretics, and especially against the doctrine of the Ebionites, which was then arising. They asserted that Christ had not existed before Mary; and therefore John was compelled to proclaim his divine birth.” Thus Paulinus very properly says that Ebion was not unlike Cerinthus.]

Unhappy Ebion, in every respect not unlike him,

[Col. 0470A] Lies in impiety, beneath the wound of punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0475A] Verse 94. “Arius dug the pit into which the traitor himself fell.” What pit did Arius dig, and into which did he also fall? The very Scriptures, by which he was convicted and condemned—the Scriptures that he corrupted and mutilated. Hear Chrysostom in his sermon against the heretics: “As soon as Arius is summoned to speak from the Scriptures, he begins … For what does he say? ‘The Lord,’ he says, ‘declares in the Gospel: I have come down from heaven not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me, the Father.’ You see,’ he says, ‘that he is the Father’s minister? You see how he is subject to him? … O Arius, why are you silent? Say what follows … Though you remain silent, I shall cry out with the Gospel: ‘And this is the will of the Father, that they should believe in him whom he sent.’” Thus Chrysostom demonstrates that Arius fell into the pit of the Scriptures that he had prepared. Sedulius, moreover, seems to have supplied Paulinus with something, when he says near the end of book I of the *Paschal Poem*:

> Unhappy Arius, who, trying to bend  
> the straight path through crooked byways,  
> fell into a dark pit,  
> plunged down into the depths of the foul abyss;  
> now empty of sense, and at the time of his deserved punishment  
> empty also of entrails, his belly having been poured out.]

Arius dug the pit into which the traitor himself

[95] Fell; condemned to eternal night, he wastes away.

[Note: [Col. 0475C] Verse 96. “Eunomius hung himself by a noose on high.” Saint Isidore of Pelusium, book I, letter 246, notes this distinction between the heresy of Arius and that of Eunomius: “The former shamelessly dared to assert that the Son of God was something made; the latter impiously affirmed that he was a servant.” Whether Eunomius actually killed himself by a noose is uncertain. For those who wrote about his death—Sozomen, book VII, chapter 17; Nicephorus Callistus, book XII, chapter 19; and Nicetas Choniates, *Treasury of Orthodox Faith*, book V, chapter 35—say nothing more than that he died after returning from exile and received burial in his homeland. Callistus adds in book XIII, chapter 1: “It is reported that through the agency of the prefect Eutropius all of Eunomius’s writings were publicly burned. His corpse, however, was taken from its tomb, carried away, and thrown into Dacoris of Tyana.” If he had ended his life by a noose, our Father Thomas Bozius, in *On the Signs of the Church*, sign 96, which concerns “the inglorious and unhappy deaths of heresiarchs,” would not have omitted it. Hence I think Paulinus is speaking allegorically, as he himself suggests in verse 98, where he says of the same man: “He struck his own forearm with the dart of treachery.”]

Eunomius hung himself by a noose on high;

He burst apart in the midst and sought the depths of the pitch-black abyss;

He struck his own forearm with the dart of treachery.

[Note: [Col. 0475D] Verse 99. “Nestorius, etc.” Concerning him and Arius, see more fully the dogmatic dissertation on the Felician heresy. For the present, take this account from Evagrius, book I, chapter 7: “Near the outermost regions of the Thebaid, moving from one place to another and striking the ground, he met an end of life worthy of his former life; and in the very manner of his death he was shown to be another Arius. In this it is plainly evident and may be recognized almost as certain what reward is prepared for impious blasphemy against Christ. For both Arius and Nestorius blasphemed him in similar fashion, the one by calling him a creature, the other by considering him to be a human being.” At the end of the chapter he adds: “I myself received from a certain writer this account of the manner of his death: namely, that his tongue was eaten away by worms, and that he passed from the miseries of this life to more grievous punishments, inflicted by God’s just judgment and everlasting.”]

Nestorius, madman, descended to the Stygian shades,

[100] [Note: [Col. 0476A] Verse 100. “Like a cancer, the Macedonian doctrines creep as a pestilence.” On the comparison with a cancer, see what was said in book I against Felix, chapter 44, letter d (col. 397). On Macedonius, see the same work, chapter 24, letter a (col. 377). How skillfully Paulinus said that the pestilence of the Macedonian error creeps may be gathered from Sozomen, book VII, chapter 2: “Some bishops,” he says, “of that sect—the Macedonian—invaded the churches from which they had been excluded under Valens. After assembling at Antioch in Caria, they decreed that the Son should be called not ὁμοούσιος, that is, ‘consubstantial,’ but ὀμοιούσιος, that is, ‘of similar substance to the Father,’ as they had previously called him.” Thus they were not merely injurious toward the Holy Spirit, whose divinity they denied and whose denial was their chief error; they were also blasphemous toward the Son, whose consubstantiality with the Father they denied, introducing only a likeness of substance to the Father.]

Like a cancer, the Macedonian doctrines creep as a pestilence,

[Note: [Col. 0476A] Verse 101. “For these things Macedonius, burned, burns in a cauldron,” that is, in hell. Origen, in homily 2 on Psalm 37, understands a cauldron or cooking-pot as the punishments of the future life: “If,” he says, “we are still flesh here, we shall be thrown into those cauldrons which will be kindled with wood, hay, or straw—that is, with our works, which we have placed upon Christ’s foundation.” Saint Eucherius, *Spiritual Formulae*, chapter 8, says: “In Scripture, the cauldron is the boiling of tribulation.” Saint Gregory the Great, *Dialogues* IV, chapter 30, recounting a vision of the condemned Theodoric reported by a servant of God, makes him say: “Theodoric is dead; for yesterday, at the ninth hour, stripped of his belt and shoes, with his hands bound, he was thrown between Pope John and the patrician Symmachus into this nearby cauldron of Vulcan.”]

For these things Macedonius, burned, burns in a cauldron.

[Note: [Col. 0476B] Verse 102. “Unhappy Eutyches, etc.” You have the primary error of Eutyches from his own mouth in Nicephorus Callistus, book XIV, chapter 47, and in Theodoret, *Dialogues*, dialogue 2, *Polymorphus*. But hear Demetrius, metropolitan of Cyzicus, writing concerning the Jacobite heresy: “Before the union—that is, the incarnation of Christ—Eutyches said that there were two natures which came together in the union, namely divinity and humanity. But after the union he taught that both natures had been mixed into one, as if someone had mixed wine with water, so that a certain mixture, confusion, and alteration of both natures had resulted.” Paulinus perhaps therefore used the image of drinking to explain his error, as follows.]

Unhappy Eutyches, utterly impious in every respect,

[Note: [Col. 0476C] Verse 103. “He drank the trampled poisons”—understand: evils. Gaius, *On the Meaning of Words*, 236, says: “By this term everything is included which, when applied to a nature, changes the nature to which it is applied.” These words fit perfectly the Eutychian doctrine, which altered the nature of Christ, the Son of God. He says “trampled” either because these doctrines had been crushed and proscribed by several councils—see Baronius from the year 446 to 452 and volume V of the Councils—and because the whole world had condemned them, as Pope Leo writes in letter 70; or because Eutyches revived the trampled errors of ancient heretics, which had already been condemned many times. Hence Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables* IV, at the end, calls Eutyches wretched because he “made the heresy of Valentinus, which had long ago withered, sprout again.” We call things “trampled” when they are common and on everyone’s lips.]

He drank the trampled poisons that he himself mixed together.

[Note: [Col. 0476D] Verse 104. “That pestilential Manes, whom error wholly possesses.” Manes, or Manichaeus, does not derive his name from madness and barbarity, as Titus of Bostra says at the beginning of book I against the Manichaeans, although the word sounds that way in Greek. It is a Persian name that he gave himself in order to conceal the servile condition in which he was born. This happened because, when he had taken refuge with the widow of a certain Therebinthus—the disciple of Scythianus, the author of the books of Manichaean doctrine—not only was he received by her, but later he was made heir both to her money and to her books, whereas previously he had been called Cubricus. In Persian, *Manes* means “homily”; he assumed this name so that among the Persians he might appear and be regarded as a good disputant. “But by divine providence,” says Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6, “it happened that, unwillingly, he accused himself: while he thought to honor himself in Persia, among the Greeks he called himself by the name of madness.” Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History* I, chapter 17, recounts some of his ravings. Among other things: “He does not wish Christ to have been born; he said that Christ was a phantom; he abolishes the Law and the Prophets; he calls himself the Paraclete.” How truly and properly Paulinus said of him, “whom error wholly possesses,” may be learned from Saint Leo, sermon 5 on the fast of the tenth month: “Although the devil holds the chief place in every kind of perversity, he nevertheless built for himself a citadel in the madness of the Manichaeans, and found in them a very spacious palace in which he might display himself more exultantly. There he possessed not merely one kind of depravity, but, in general, a mixture of all errors and impieties. Whatever is profane among the pagans, whatever is carnal and blind among the Jews, whatever is illicit in the secrets of magical art, and whatever is sacrilegious and blasphemous in all heresies—this flowed together into them, as into a kind of sewer, with the confluence of every impurity.” And below: “Therefore, dearly beloved, reject these men, utterly detestable and pestilential in every respect, completely from your friendship.” Leo calls the Manichaeans pestilential, just as Paulinus here calls their father Manes pestilential.]

That pestilential Manes, whom error wholly possesses,

[105] [Note: [Col. 0477B] 173 Verse 105. “He endlessly melts the smoke of sulfurous Gehenna.” *Conflare* is often used of the melting of metals. Suetonius, *Augustus* 52: “He melted down all the silver statues once erected to him.” And chapter 71: “After Alexandria was captured … he soon melted down all the golden vessels used most frequently.” But it is also used for blowing into something. Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 11: “Philiscus painted a workshop with a boy blowing the fire.” Paulinus uses it in this sense when he says that Manes melts the smoke of Gehenna. Therefore restore *fumus* in place of *fumum*, and *sulphoreae* in place of *sulphureae*.]

He endlessly blows forth the smoke of sulfurous Gehenna.

[Note: [Col. 0477B] Verse 106. “No differently, with his terrible and filthy mouth, Sabellius, etc.” Cassian says, *On the Incarnation of the Lord* I, chapter 2: “While Sabellius maintained that there was no distinction between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, he mixed together the sacred and ineffable Trinity, as far as he was able, in blasphemous confusion.” In opposition to him stands Arius, who separated even the nature itself, as Amphilochius, bishop of Iconium, aptly says in his letter to Seleucus, translated by Joachim Zechner, v. 206:

> For the one mingles the hypostases of the persons;  
> the other, in impiety, again divides the substance.

Saint Fulgentius, *On the Faith of the Incarnation of the Son of God*, addressed to Scarila, says: “The only-begotten God alone possesses both births as his own: one from the truth of the divine nature, the other from the grace of the humanity assumed.” Since Sabellius admitted only one person in the Godhead, he attributed the incarnation, birth, passion, and death to the entire Trinity. Hence the heretics were called Patripassians, because, following Sabellius, they imagined that the Father also had suffered.]

No differently, with his terrible and filthy mouth, Sabellius,

[Note: [Col. 0477C] Verse 107. “Burned by the wave of fiery-mouthed Cocytus, he will groan.” *Gemet* is very apt, for Cocytus is derived from ἀκωκύω, meaning “I weep, groan, lament.” Hence Claudian places beside it a fountain of tears, *On the Baptism*, book I, v. 86:

> And Cocytus sat beside the compressed fountain of tears.

Paulinus says “burned by the wave” because they imagined the waters to be sulfurous. As for Paulinus’s contraction of the middle syllables in *blasphemus* and *Cocyti*, do not condemn it unless you have read the defense he offers concerning this matter.]

The blasphemer, burned by the wave of fiery-mouthed Cocytus, will groan.

[Col. 0470B] [Note: [Col. 0478A] Verse 108. “For these and all the others, etc.” Here Paulinus expressly attacks those heretics who held erroneous opinions concerning the mystery of the incarnation and the divinity of Christ, as will be clear to anyone who considers their errors individually. He did this for very good reason, since at that time he understood that Felix’s impious doctrine—blaspheming the mystery of the incarnation and the divinity of Jesus Christ, and dividing our Lord into a proper Son of God and an adoptive son—had to be opposed in every way. He did not, however, preserve the chronological order, since he was attacking doctrines, not composing a chronicle, nor arranging the periods in sequence.]

For these and all the others who, with confused hearts,

Resist the sacred commands of the exalted Name;

[110] Who with deceitful mouths assail the King Sabaoth,

And, driven by foaming lips, wickedly deny

That the Lord Christ was born of a holy virgin,

From the Holy Spirit, both king and man and God,

They strive to attack him, barking in vain exertion—

[115] I decree that they be torn away from the holy womb,

Cut off with the knife of faith from the body

Of Mother Church—the faith that Peter and Paul teach,

That the world sings together, and that the ancient prophets

Clearly proclaimed long ago.

[Note: [Col. 0478A] Verse 119. “Catholic and holy men, etc.” That is, the 318 Fathers who attended the Council of Nicaea, whose decrees of faith he declares that he embraces with wondrous humility of spirit and obedience.]

Catholic and holy men, blessed Fathers,

[120] [Col. 0470C] Three hundred and eighteen in number, and all worshipers indeed

Of the harmonious faith of the eternal Judge—

I embrace them, happily clasping them in peaceful arms.

170 No terror from them, no treacherous avenger,

Will be able to cut me off with a blood-dripping sword:

[125] No oblivion will be able to remove their renown

From my heart or erase it by any compact.

[Note: [Col. 0478A] Verse 127. “No longer beneath tablets, etc.” He alludes to what is found in Scripture, Proverbs 6:3 and also 2 Corinthians 3:3.]

No longer shall I carve on tablets cut from hard rock,

With the furrowed incisions of a chisel’s point,

Nor paint with a pen dipped in black ink;

[130] Rather, beneath the casket of my heart I shall write

With a stylus infused by the gently dripping fountain

From the radiant summit of heaven; after me I leave

Monuments written for those to come. Gladly I do not refrain from setting them forth

[Col. 0470D] In compact verse, yet with the broad channel of my mind,

[135] As I embrace the two streams of sweetness poured forth by the command

Which the holy Lord uttered with his mouth.

[Note: [Col. 0478B] Verse 137. “I offer the first to God; I return the second to my colleague.” He passes from faith to charity, whose two commandments he sets forth under the allegory of two streams, one of which he gives to God and the other returns to his colleague, that is, his neighbor. Although the term “colleagues” includes, as Ulpian says, “those who possess the same authority,” and therefore indicates an office or duty to which several people are appointed, it is sometimes used of any associate, and *collegium* may also mean a natural association. Thus Pliny, *Natural History* X, chapter 17: “The hawk assists the owls in a certain fellowship of nature and shares the war.” Fellowship requires a complete harmony of minds, such as marriage itself nearly demands. Hence Apuleius, *Golden Ass* II: “This is so stable and sacred a fellowship that you might take it for marriage.” And Claudius Rutilius Namatianus, *Itinerary* I, v. 17, speaking of the Roman Senate, says:

> Such as through the heavenly axes  
> of the world’s summit we believe to be the marriage  
> of the supreme God.

Or, as Barthius reads in his *Observations* and *Adversaria* XXII, chapter 17, *summis Diis*, “of the highest gods”; and he adds: “It should be noted that *connubium* denotes the closest union, a council, or a fellowship, as though indissoluble.”]

I offer the first to God; I return the second to my colleague,

Conquered in my pure heart by the love of charity,

With joyful face and cheerful mind,

[140] I shall always offer sincere thanks in harmonious speech

To you, supreme Father, God of highest power;

And to you, Son of God, the world’s only hope;

To you, life-giving Spirit, fearsome and terrible majesty,

Fountain of charity, sweet love above all honey,

[145] Light and source of goodness, pure inspirer of love;

[Note: [Col. 0478C] Verse 146. “You do not know where you go or whence you come, etc.” From John 3:8: “The Spirit breathes where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes,” etc. Although many, following Cornelius, Sa, and Menochius, understand this passage more appropriately of the spirit—that is, the wind—from which Christ drew the comparison to the Holy Spirit, some understand the entire passage of the Holy Spirit. Among them is Gregory, *Morals* XXVII, chapter 13: “The voice of the Spirit coming upon us, which insinuates itself into the ears of the heart, is not investigated even by the mind that has been enlightened by it. For invisible power cannot be weighed: by what channels it flows into us, by what means it comes to us, or by what means it departs. Hence John rightly says: ‘The Spirit breathes where it wills,’ etc. To hear the voice of the Spirit is to rise, through the force of inward compunction, into love of the invisible Creator. But no one knows where it comes from, because it is not known through the mouths of preachers by what opportunities it pours itself upon us. And no one knows where it goes, because when many hear one sermon, it cannot be known whom it abandons and rejects, or whose heart it enters and in whom it rests.” This agrees with what Paulinus adds here.]

You, whose destination and origin are unknown,

Who fill the whole earth and breathe forever where you will.

Behold, your voice is heard; with silent cry

It sounds in the ear of the heart, with no resounding blow.

[150] [Col. 0472A] To the Father and to God the Begotten, let glory be given,

And to the Holy Spirit, God, throughout all the ages.

## APOLOGY OF SAINT PAULINUS FOR HIS POEM

[Note: [Col. 0477]

## NOTES ON SAINT PAULINUS’S APOLOGY FOR HIS POEM

### PREFATORY NOTE

[Col. 0477D] From this *Apology for his poem*, prudent reader, you will clearly perceive that Paulinus was not unaware how far his age stood from the purity of the Latin language. He would not have composed this defense of his verses if he had believed that he had expressed everything correctly. But because he wished to accommodate himself to the practice of his age and not depart from the phrases then in common use, he preferred to follow customary and popular speech rather than withdraw from ordinary usage with the stigma of singularity and to the detriment of his readers. Charity and zeal for the salvation of others, especially the uneducated, would not otherwise have allowed him to speak as he did. For when someone wishes to set forth the rule of faith and the standard of belief, it is worthwhile to speak in a manner more easily understood by everyone. It remains for us to add a few notes to this *Apology* for a deeper understanding of it.]

[Col. 0471]

[Col. 0471A] But you, my dearest brother, whoever you may be who have deigned to read these little verses, I beg you, in a spirit of devotion, if you should find written in them either a short syllable in place of a long, or a long in place of a short, or a common syllable in place of a natural one, or a natural in place of a common, or one foot in place of another, or one metrical figure in place of another, or one trope in place of another, or unmarked caesuras of clauses cut away by the hand of negligence, or an ill-considered point inserted in a colon, or unequal divisions of commas,

[Note: [Col. 0479A] “Or uncultivated melodies of euphony.” Concerning euphony, Quintilian says in book I, chapter 5: Paulinus made *melos* declinable, although among the Latins it is properly indeclinable. He did not do so, however, without a prior example. Venantius Fortunatus—not Lactantius, as was once wrongly believed—declined *melos* in book III of his poem *On the Resurrection*, v. 32, when he said:

> Hence the nightingale attunes its instruments to its reeds,  
> and the breeze becomes sweeter from the echoed melody.]

or uncultivated melodies of euphony, or if anything of this kind can be found, you should inspect them in these verses,

[Note: [Col. 0479A] “And you see the little courtesan Carmenta becoming indignant.” [Col. 0479B] He mocks the rules of profane poets, as though they were wanton because of their excessive elegance. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* I, testifies that Carmenta was so called from *carmen*: “Evander, the son of Mercury and of a certain Arcadian nymph whom the Greeks call Themis, led a colony from the Arcadian city Pallantium. Since she was filled with divine power, the writers of Roman antiquities call her Carmenta in their native language; the name of the nymph means ‘prophetic,’ derived from *carmen* according to Roman etymology.” Concerning her, see Livy, first decade, book I, chapter 7, who attributes the introduction of letters into Italy to Evander, the son of Carmentis. Paulinus therefore alludes to her, the patroness entrusted with songs.]

and perhaps for that reason you see the little courtesan Carmenta becoming indignant,

[Note: [Col. 0479B] “And putting her hand to the rod.” On the *ferula*, see the note on the Council of Forum Julii, § 14, letter a.]

and putting her hand to the rod: do not let fear of anything of this kind disturb you; but gird your loins like a man and bravely stand up to her in defense of my littleness. With fearless voice, tell that little fox that, caring nothing for her blazing and furious outbursts of indignation, I shall bend the neck of her pride, reduced as it is to mud. And, though I have been ashamed to say it, and though it will embarrass me to report it, I shall not conceal it,

[Note: [Col. 0479B] “Like a Lycisca barking loudly and long behind the reed-beds.” Paulinus seems to have had in mind the following passage of Virgil, *Eclogue* III, v. 17:

[Col. 0479C]

> I did not see you, most wicked one of Damon,  
> catching the goat in ambush,  
> while Lycisca barked loudly?  
> And when I cried, “Where is he rushing off to now?”]

Tityrus, drive the flock together: you were hiding behind the thickets.”] The recollection of that little she-wolf, barking far behind the thickets, moves the feelings of my mind [Col. 0472A]. But you, driven by zeal for truth, after completely extinguishing to the ashes every spark of envy, supply, with the pen of charity, whatever is lacking; prune away superfluities with the knife of sweetness; and strive to straighten what is crooked in affection with a little rule. Take great care, moreover, lest the line, perhaps carelessly extended too freely, be forced by a violent, straight stroke into a deformed curvature from its proper state of rectitude. Consider most earnestly,

[Note: [Col. 0479C] “Lest at some time you regret having cut off, together with the sacraments, even the little buds of the vine-shoots.” An allegorical expression, but not obscure. What a bud is on a vine you will learn from Pliny, Book XVII, chapter 21: “On the vine, he says, it is called a bud when it has produced a tuft there; before it produces one, it is an eye in a hollow.” Augustine, Sermon 10 on the Saints—or rather Caesarius, or whoever else it was, Sermon 220 in the Appendix, volume V—says allegorically, though differently, that the innocent children killed by Herod may rightly be called shoots: “The flowers of the martyrs, which sprang up amid the very winter of unbelief like the first bursting-forth gems of the Church, were blighted by a frost of persecution.” We also learn from Tertullian, Apology, chapter 50, that adult martyrs were called “shoot-martyrs,” because they were burned with branches. “Although,” he says, “you now call us ‘shoot-martyrs’ and ‘half-axle-martyrs’ [others: ‘half-ass-martyrs’], because we are bound to a stake half an axle [others: ‘half an as’] in length and burned amid a mass of branches.”]

lest at some time you regret having cut off, together with the shoots, even the little buds of the vine. Do not, I beg you, despise

[Note: [Col. 0480A] “The springtime husks.” Among writers on agriculture and natural history, *folliculi* properly means the husks in which grains themselves and ears are contained. Columella, *On Agriculture*, Book II, chapter 8: “The spelt has a firm husk in which it is contained.” Seneca, Letter 124, or the last letter: “The tender ear emerges from its husk.” In grapes it is the skin with which the grape is covered and which contains its moisture. Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book I, chapter 54: “The clusters of grapes that have been trodden, together with their stalks and skins, are to be placed beneath the press, so that if they retain any must, it may be squeezed into the same vat.” See also Pliny, Book XII, chapter 43. None of this, however, suits Paulinus’s meaning, since he is expressly speaking of shoots not yet emerging from the vine. I therefore think that for Paulinus *folliculi* means the tubercles from which a bud emerges—the “eyes” which, as we saw above from Pliny, he calls them; in Greek, however, they are called ὀφθαλμούς, “eyes,” as is clear from what follows.]

the springtime husks, not yet bursting into flowers,

[Note: [Col. 0480B] “Which conceal enclosed clusters of grapes.” *Clusas* stands for *clausas*, as in the poem *On the Rule of Faith*, verse 26, where *cludit* stands for *clausit*. See the notes there. *Botrion* is a Greek diminutive from *botrus*, “cluster.” Palladius, February, title 33: “So that various little clusters may grow.”]

which conceal the enclosed buds of grape-clusters, destined in due season to produce grapes. Nor should you disdain the wheat-tops of the ears, which, armed with sharp awns that prick the stalks with sluggish effort, appear to wave.

[Col. 0472B] Remember what sweetness of flavor is concealed in the ear, and what edible sweetness the yellow grains keep stored in their case. For these do not pass into the human mouths of those who eat them unless both

[Note: [Col. 0480B] “The grape first by feet or teeth.” He omits the winepress, by which wines are expressed, called ληνός in Greek; hence Bacchus, that is, “the one belonging to the winepress,” says Probus in his note on verse 7 of Book II of Virgil’s *Georgics*, where the poet mentions the pressing of grapes by foot:

> Come here, father Lenaeus, and with me  
> Dip your legs, stripped of their boots,  
> In the fresh must.

And Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book II, verse 29:

> Autumn too stood there, stained with trodden grapes.

Since in Paulinus’s time grapes were perhaps more frequently pressed by feet, as is now done, than by winepresses, he mentions that method rather than the latter.]

the grape is crushed first by feet or teeth, and the ears of grain

[Note: [Col. 0480C] “Or by a wagon, etc.” Although there are four methods of threshing grain and beating out the kernels—by wagon, by the feet of animals, by a threshing-sledge or drag, and by staffs—he mentions only the first and last. The first is referred to in Isaiah 25:10: “Moab shall be threshed beneath him, as straw is threshed in a wagon.” The last seems to be referred to in Judges 6:11, concerning Gideon, when he was beating out and winnowing grain. Cyril of Alexandria discusses the third and second methods in his commentary on Isaiah 41:15: “I have made you like a new threshing wagon fitted with serrated teeth.” “The sons of the Egyptians,” he says, “bring sheaves from the fields to the threshing-floor; then, binding them to oxen and driving them around, they crush the ears beneath their hooves and separate the wheat from the chaff. Others, using wagons and wheels like threshing-sledges—for these are the *tribula*, which are dragged like wagons, as Varro explains in *On Agriculture*, Book I, chapter 55—try to accomplish the same thing.”]

are crushed, struck either by the wheel of a wagon as it passes over them or by flails.

[Col. 0479]

[Note: [Col. 0479D]

Hymns—Greek ὕμνος, Latin *celebratio*, “celebration”—are any praise of God celebrated with song. Hence the definition of Remigius in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 5, should be embraced: “*Hymnus* in Greek, rendered in Latin speech, means the praise of God. If it is composed but not sung, it is not a hymn. If it is composed and sung but not in praise of God, it is not a hymn. But if it is composed and sung in praise of God, then it is a hymn.” Who, moreover, does not know that the pagans also sang hymns in praise of their gods? On these matters see J. Caesar Scaliger, *Poetics*, Book I, chapters 9 and 45, and Book III, chapters 12 and 13.

In the Church of Christ, hymns began to be sung from its infancy, with our Savior Jesus Christ providing the model when, after rising from the supper, he went out to the garden after singing a hymn (Matthew 26:30). Paul likewise repeatedly admonishes the newly converted Ephesians (Ephesians 5:19) and Colossians (Colossians 3:16) to sing the praises of God and give thanks to the Lord with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. The Jewish philosopher Philo himself records that this was also practiced among the ascetics of Alexandria, in his book *On the Contemplative Life*.

Ignatius, third bishop of the Church of Antioch after Peter, having heard angels praise the Trinity antiphonally, was the first to institute the singing of hymns and psalms in alternating choirs, according to Socrates, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 8: “This tradition,” he says, “has been received in all the churches.” In the West, the first to introduce this custom was Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, as Isidore writes in Book I, chapter 6, *On the Offices*, concerning hymns. Later, in the church of Milan, Ambrose did so; from him other hymns commonly acquired the name “Ambrosian,” as is gathered from canon 13 of the Second Council of Tours: “Although we have Ambrosian hymns in the canon, nevertheless, since among the others there are some worthy of being sung according to a proper form, we wish gladly to embrace them.”

But because some people, more superstitious than was fitting, rejected the hymns of Hilary or Ambrose, wishing to allow in the Church only those taken from Sacred Scripture, the Fourth Council of Toledo, in the year 671 of the Spanish era—that is, A.D. 634—canon 13, condemns their excessive scrupulousness or audacity. It commends and admits hymns composed in honor of the saints by Hilary, Ambrose, and other prudent men, because it does not reject the hymn composed by men, “Glory be to the Father, etc.”; indeed, the Church accepts it by common usage, and all the faithful embrace it. See what we say in the note to canon 6 of the Council of Friuli, letter e.

Having premised these general remarks on hymns, let us now approach our Paulinus more closely. Walafrid Strabo, *On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 15, bears this testimony concerning him: “Moreover, metrical and rhythmic hymns are sung in the Ambrosian offices. Some have also been accustomed to use them occasionally during the solemnities of Mass, because of the compunction that is increased by their harmonious sweetness. It is indeed reported that Paulinus, patriarch of Friuli, often, and especially in private Masses around the offering of the sacramental elements, celebrated hymns composed either by others or by himself. I, for my part, would believe that so great and learned a man did this neither without authority nor without sound reason.”

In the missal of the ancient Aquileian rite, the sequences, as they are called, which were to be sung after the Epistles and were composed in rhythmic verse, occur very frequently. An example of this will be the Mass which we shall present in Appendix 1, no. 13, concerning Saint Paulinus; perhaps the rite originated with him and continued for a long time, namely until 1519, when the missal from which the Mass will be presented was published. If only we had found some older copy! We could then satisfy the wish of the blessed Pierre Lebrun, priest of the French Oratory, who in volume II, page 220, of the Paris edition of *Explication de la messe*, etc., desired to know the rite called patriarchal, whose traces Ughelli detected in the church of Como, a suffragan church of Aquileia, down to the year 1590. Nevertheless, it will be considerably older than the missal which the church of Como displayed in that year, when it saw the patriarchal rite abolished under Clement VIII and gradually embraced the Roman rite, although the latter did not differ greatly from the former. How this happened Lebrun discusses more fully in the same place. See Appendix 2, no. 44, for the attempt to restore it at Aquileia and its eventual disappearance.

We have no doubt that the hymns presented by us are Paulinus’s, whatever Father Cave may say in contradiction: “The sacred hymns which Walafrid Strabo reports Paulinus to have composed have perished.” But the hymns themselves which we present plainly prove this false; and they also expose the omission not only of Father Fabricius but likewise of Albert Fabricius, who instituted a section on works omitted by Georgius in Book IV, chapter 2, of his *Latin Library*, when listing the Latin sacred poets of the Middle Ages. For they omitted Paulinus, although they remembered Paul the Deacon, Alcuin, and others of the same or approximately the same period.

Polycarp Leyser also omitted Paulinus, as can be seen in the supplement to the same Albert Fabricius’s edition, Venice 1728. He should not have been omitted by one preparing a corpus of the Latin sacred poets of the Middle Ages, as the prospectus placed there, page 262, volume II of Albert Fabricius’s *Latin Library*, indicates. These writers treat the matter rather superficially and failed to notice the collection of hymns assembled by Georgius Cassander, in which he presents more than one hymn under the name of Paulinus.

The weight of William Cave’s authority will become clear below, when Hymn 2 is vindicated for Paulinus. We have also drawn out one or two hymns from the eminent Joseph Maria Thomasius, adding another concerning Saint Mark from the papers of the most illustrious Filippo della Torre, bishop of Adria; its subject, form, and style persuade us that it is Paulinus’s. We have undertaken to illuminate them with observations and notes, as we do with the others. You, prudent reader, make use of our labor, and I ask you to judge our watchful efforts fairly and favorably.]

## 175. The Hymns and Rhythmic Poems of Saint Paulinus

### Hymn I

[Note: [Col. 0479D] Concerning the Roman Chair. What is meant by the name “Roman Chair” is well known. See Baronius under the year 45, no. 1, and in the notes for January 18 in the martyrology. From the more ancient breviaries it is established that the feast is of ancient institution. Hence Offmann is mistaken in the universal lexicon, under “Chair,” when he says that the feast of Saint Peter’s Chair at Rome was instituted by Gregory XIII at the request of Antonio Caraffa in 1576, and cites Dominicus Macer as his authority in the *Hierolexicon*, under “Apostolic Gestatorial Chair.” He is mistaken in both places and sufficiently shows that he has little concern for the affairs of the Roman Church, which he treats perfunctorily. For in the passage cited under “Chair,” etc., Macer does not mention this matter; nor, when he does mention it under “Chair,” does he speak of its first institution. He says only this: “The Feast of Peter’s Chair at Rome, on January 18, in the year 1576, Gregory XIII, at the request of Cardinal Antonio Caraffa, established so that it might be observed as a feast of obligation.” Do you see whether Gregory first instituted the feast, or whether he ordered that what had been instituted in antiquity should be observed as obligatory? Certainly Gavantus shows that in earlier years—namely, in 1558—the feast was restored by Paul IV, volume II, section 7, chapter 3, *On the January Feasts*, no. 18. It therefore existed long before, but through a decline of devotion and the injuries of the times had ceased to be celebrated. Indeed, in the Aquileian missal of 1519 there is no Mass for the Roman Chair, but only one for the Antiochene Chair on February 22, with the Gospel “If your brother sins against you,” from Matthew 18:15–22 inclusive.]

Concerning the Roman Chair of Saint Peter.

[Col. 0479D]

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Verse 1. “O Peter, rock of the Church.” From Matthew 16:18: “You are Peter,” etc. Hence Chrysostom, *Homily 9 on Repentance*: “When I say Peter, I name the indestructible rock—not himself; the immovable foundation, the great apostle, first of the disciples, first called, first obedient.”]

O Peter, rock of the Church,

By this blessed name,

[Col. 0480D]

[Note: [Col. 0482D] Verse 3. “By which Peter is [called] rock from Christ,” etc. Augustine, *Tractate 124 on John*, no. 5: “For the rock is not named from Peter, but Peter from the rock. Just as Christ is not named from Christian, but Christian from Christ. For this reason the Lord says, ‘Upon this rock I will build my Church,’ because Peter had said, ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God.’ ‘Upon this rock,’ therefore, he says, ‘which you have confessed, I will build my Church.’ For the rock was Christ; upon that foundation Peter himself also was built.”]

By which Peter is a rock from Christ:

[4] Christ is not a rock from Peter.

You are Peter, the first

Confessor of God's faith,

[Col. 0481A]

[Note: [Col. 0483A] Verse 7. “Now remaining first among the members, because you were called Cephas.” Cephas, from the Greek κεφαλή, which means “head,” was not derived by Paulinus alone, nor was he the first to do so. Optatus of Milevis, long before him, wrote thus in Book II *Against Parmenianus*: “Therefore you cannot deny that you know that in the city of Rome the episcopal chair was first conferred upon Peter, in which Peter, the head of all the apostles, sat; hence he was also called Cephas.”

Although this interpretation is not legitimate—for Cephas derives from a Syriac, not a Greek, word, and Peter and *petra* are said to mean “rock,” since *cepha* is “rock” in Syriac, as a Lapide says on Matthew 16:18—Baronius nevertheless supports it by the example of other Fathers, under the year of Christ 21, no. 27, who explained Hebrew or Syriac words through Greek etymology.

But since such appellations are used to defend the primacy in the Church of Peter and his successors, the Roman pontiffs—a doctrine that greatly torments and vexes heretical innovators, especially those who take arms against the Roman Church on the basis of Augustine’s interpretation of “rock”—be sure not to omit what Bellarmine wrote explicitly in more than one place in his book *Controversies on the Roman Pontiff*, especially Book I, chapter 10, and Augustine himself in Book I of the *Retractations*, chapter 21. There, from Ambrose’s hymn, “By this very rock of the Church, while singing, he wiped away his guilt,” Augustine recognizes Peter as the rock and foundation of the Church established by Christ, although more than once he understood Christ himself as the rock. Yet he does not retract his earlier judgment concerning Peter himself, but concludes: “Let the reader choose which of these opinions is the more probable.”]

Now remaining first among the members,

[Note: [Col. 0483C] Verse 10. “In the City you were consecrated,” in place of “you attained.” For Peter did not receive episcopal authority, as did the other apostles, and pontifical primacy throughout the whole Church above the other apostles, only at that time, but earlier, and indeed from Christ the Lord. But since *consecrare* can sometimes mean “to ordain” and “to lay on hands”—an act called χειροτονία in Greek, commonly performed when someone is to assume an episcopal see—the antecedent is here placed for the consequent. Add that χειροτονία is sometimes used for the election itself, or the reception of someone as bishop, as Macer explains from Zonaras in the *Hierolexicon*, under “Chirotonia”: “Sometimes it is taken for the election itself, as Zonaras noted, saying: Formerly the election itself was also called *chirotonia*; because, Macer adds, clergy and people used to raise their hands in the election of a bishop, so that in this way the votes of those participating could more easily be counted without confusion, as the same author reports.”

That custom of raising hands in judgments for the purpose of delivering a sentence continued in these regions down to the time of Marquard, the patriarch, as is clear from the charter which Ughelli prints corruptly under Marquard; we shall provide a corrected version in Appendix 2, no. 31. He was therefore here consecrated as one received into the episcopate and placed upon the throne, as is clear from the following verse, where it is said:]

In the City you were consecrated;

[Note: [Col. 0484A] Verse 11. “In which, ascending the noble chair, you are raised up to the throne.” I would not wish, as many modern writers do—whether they always judge legitimately and truly is for them to decide—that, whenever they hear the word “chair,” they immediately condemn the event and prefer legend to history, as though episcopal ornaments such as the chair, pastoral staff, mitre, and the rest ought to be excluded from the apostolic age to such an extent that, whenever they are found in a writer, he must at least be declared suspect and sometimes even apocryphal.

Baronius demonstrates at length in his notes on the Martyrology for January 18 not only that Peter sat upon a genuine chair, but also that the very genuine wooden chair on which he first sat at Rome is preserved in the Vatican basilica. He confirms the matter with the remarkable example of the episcopal seat of James, the brother of the Lord and first bishop of Jerusalem, preserved after the destruction of that city until the time of Constantine. Eusebius writes of it in Book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 14: “The chair of the apostle James, preserved to this time, is held in very great honor by the bishops who have succeeded one another there.”

Our own Paulus Aringus likewise writes of this real, not allegorical, chair of Peter preserved in the Vatican basilica, in *Subterranean Rome*, volume I, Book II, chapter 7, no. 14 and following. Adrian Baillet, a recent French writer, does not entirely disapprove—remarkable!—the authenticity of Peter’s Roman chair, but refers the matter to Baronius as the more immediate investigator. See him under January 18, volume I. Francesco Maria Febei writes in his book *On the Identity of the Roman Chair* that it was placed at length upon the altar of the Vatican basilica by Alexander VII.]
