[Note: [Col. 0484C]

Hymn II, which has been denied to Paulinus and attributed by the Vulpian brothers to Elpis, the wife of Boethius, must here be restored to its rightful parent. The Vulpian brothers, therefore, in their edition of the books of Severinus Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*, which they produced at Padua in 1721, do not wish the two hymns they published at the end of that work to be Paulinus’s, but Elpis’s.

First, because G. Cave said of Paulinus: “The sacred hymns which Walafrid Strabo reports Paulinus to have composed have perished.” Second, because Lilius Gregorius Giraldus wrote in *On the History of Poetry*, dialogue V: “Boethius’s wife Elpis is celebrated by our writers not only for her moral character but also for her learning, especially in poetry. Certainly there exist hymns to the apostles in a style of expression that is not commonplace: ‘Golden light’ and ‘Happy throughout the whole world,’ which our writers consistently assert to be hers.”

But, with due respect to the Vulpian brothers, whom I nevertheless highly esteem and even love for their exceptional learning and scholarship, the authorities cited do not press us very hard. Gabriel Cave’s assertion collapses of itself, since we present several hymns by Paulinus, and it would be utterly rash to deny that all of them are Paulinus’s, especially since Cardinal Thomasius—eminent not only in sacred purple but also in excellence of learning and integrity—supplies some, while others come from Georgius Cassander, whom Cave must have failed to know.

Nor should Lilius’s opinion, who is presented as the most ancient witness of all on this matter, be valued so highly that we must depart from the judgment of the very learned and scholarly Thomasius, whose memory is blessed in the Church of God. He asserts that the hymn *Felix per omnes*, the only one disputed with the Vulpians, is Paulinus’s. Since Giraldus’s authority extends no further than his own lifetime—he was born in 1479—and no witness earlier than him is produced, his testimony must be regarded as quite recent and therefore rather slight.

Those writers who followed Giraldus either kept silent about Elpis or spoke hesitantly, saying that the hymns are believed to be hers. Thus the entire position which the Vulpians call the common opinion reduces itself to Giraldus alone. But since Cardinal Thomasius drew what he published from the oldest manuscripts, he would never have inscribed the hymn *Felix per omnes* with Paulinus’s name unless he had been supported by the authority of ancient monuments.

What then? Who would dare assert that Thomasius, a most diligent man, failed to see Giraldus or to weigh his authority? He could easily have had at hand a manuscript that surpassed Giraldus in age and authority. The argument should therefore run as follows. Thomasius, a man of discerning judgment who knows how to detect truth in ancient monuments, publishes a hymn under Paulinus’s name; but it is now clear from the careful edition of Paulinus of Nola’s works prepared by Jean-Baptiste Le Brun, Paris, 1685, that it is not by Paulinus of Nola. Therefore it is by another Paulinus. But no other hymn-writer of this name appears besides Paulinus of Aquileia; therefore it must be assigned to Paulinus of Aquileia.

Apart from the authority of so great a man, the hymn is sufficiently proved to be Paulinus’s by its style, subject matter, form, division of the verses, and comparison with similar expressions. Compare the style of the first hymn, *Aurea luce*, which is attributed to Elpis, with the other, *Felix per omnes*, which we, with Cardinal Thomasius, say is Paulinus’s: you will plainly find Elpis much more “Latin,” so to speak, than Paulinus, in whom you will undoubtedly find a more barbarous style.

Compare their subject matter, form, and division of verses. The first proceeds in quatrains, the second in five-line stanzas, as is usually the case, although both are in iambic trimeters. Moreover, the comparison with olive trees occurs in both. In the first we read: “Two olive trees, of one devotion”; in the second: “These are the two olive trees before the Lord.” This reasonably arouses suspicion that the two poems are the offspring of two parents. For Elpis would seem to have reheated the same dish if, writing on the same subject, she had used the same division of verses and the same comparisons. A prudent writer would have avoided this fault by varying at least one element—either the subject matter, the comparisons, or the type of poem. It is therefore rightly said that the two hymns were composed not by one author but by two, and that one imitated the other.

Add that the phrases and thoughts of the second hymn correspond almost word for word to Paulinus’s phrasing and ideas used elsewhere. For in Book I against Felix, chapter 36, he says: “Behold Peter and Paul, plainly the two shining candelabra of the world.” And in chapter 14 of the same book: “You do not hesitate to defame Peter and Paul, the two splendid lights of heaven.” Now compare the hymn, and you will find the same expressions there. For it reads:

> These are the two olive trees before the Lord,  
> And the two candelabra shining with light:  
> The two splendid lights of heaven.

Nothing is more like an egg than an egg, or milk than milk. The rules of criticism establish that the stronger proofs of the genuineness of any work are those drawn from within it, including, among other things, conformity of vocabulary, agreement of ideas, similarity of phrasing, and still more, identity.

To confess the truth, I observe that certain words, adopted by the Fathers through peculiar and frequent usage, enable one who reads them immediately to divine the author. For example, whenever I hear in a breviary a homily or sermon containing the word *districtus*, *districtio*, *districtius*, or similar forms, Gregory the Great immediately presents himself to my mind. There are certain formulas of words to which, I know not by what fate, we cling even unwillingly; they are like the identifying marks of our works. When you see these here in our Paulinus, nothing should prevent you from assigning to Paulinus the hymn *Felix per omnes*, which is in dispute.

Georgius Cassander himself, long before Joseph Maria Thomasius, reported this hymn in his work published at Paris in 1616, page 265, without naming Paulinus, but also without naming Elpis—something he would not have omitted had it been established that the hymn was hers.

Incidentally, I am astonished that G. Cave says not a word about this poetess and composer of sacred hymns, nor does Du Pin. The former, although he mentions her, does not even dream of recalling hymns composed by her; the latter does not name her at all. Du Pin, however, does not even name her, whereas Sixtus of Siena, Bellarmine, and Oudin do. I note this so that you may see how little weight this woman carries with those who catalogue ecclesiastical writers.

I have also seen part of this hymn in a manuscript breviary of the Aquileian Church. Paulinus’s name is not attached to it, but neither is the name of any other author, as is likewise the case with the other hymns. The stanza “Blessed Peter” occurs on the feast of Saint Peter in Chains. On the feast of the Chair, however, there is “Whatever the bonds,” together with the concluding stanza, “Glory to God.” Cardinal Thomasius places these three stanzas together under the Roman Chair. Whatever may be the order in which the stanzas are arranged, I have no doubt that Paulinus is the author of this hymn.]

### Hymn II

[Note: [Col. 0484D] On the Birthday of the Holy Apostles. Chrysologus, Sermon 129: “When you hear ‘the birthday of the saints,’ beloved, do not think that this means the day on which they are born on earth from flesh, but from earth into heaven, from labor into rest, etc.”

The anniversary of any memorable event is likewise called a birthday by sacred and secular writers. Paschasius the abbot called Maundy Thursday, the day of the Lord’s Supper, “the birthday of the chalice,” in his book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, chapter 2. Saint Leo the pope called the day on which he ascended the supreme chair of the Church “the birthday of our servitude,” in Sermon 3 on the anniversary of his accession. Arnobius mentions the birthday of the earth and of the powers of heaven in Book VII. Rome and Constantinople have their birthdays in the Theodosian Code, Book II, “All Days.” Pliny places the birthday of Rome on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, in Book XVIII, chapter 26. Cicero indicates the birthday of colonies; in Book IV of his letters to Atticus, letter 1, he mentions the birthday of the colony of Brundisium on the Nones of August. Emperors likewise have birthdays, as Capitolinus records in his life of Pertinax, chapter 15, and Spartianus in his life of Hadrian, chapter 4, where he records the birthday of Hadrian’s adoption, that is, when he was adopted by Trajan. I also find a birthday of a return and of a voyage: the former in Cicero, Book III of his letters to Atticus, letter 20; the latter in Vegetius, Book IV of *On Military Affairs*, chapter 39.

Thus the annual feast-day of the saints of the Church is also called a birthday, as here, that of the apostles Peter and Paul.]

On the Birthday of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Verse 1. “Happy throughout the whole world’s festive regions.” Concerning this feast, whose celebration had gradually grown cold among the Greeks but was later restored to its former solemnity, see the notes on the Martyrology for June 29. Chrysostom, Homily 26 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, says of the feasts of these apostles: “Days known and manifest, since they are celebrated as feasts throughout the whole world.” Saint Leo, Sermon 1 on their birthday, says: “Today’s solemnity has deserved reverence throughout the whole world.”

He says “regions” while circumscribing the entire world by its cardinal directions: the two poles, sunrise, and sunset. Thus Statius, Book I of the *Thebaid*, verse 156:

> Ah, wretched men! What if the crime were so great  
> That either boundary of the poles were sought—  
> The one which the sun, released, looks upon from the eastern  
> Hinge, and the one toward which he declines at the Iberian harbor?]

Happy throughout the whole world’s festive regions,

The feast of the apostles joyfully surpasses all:

Of blessed Peter and most holy Paul,

Whom Christ consecrated with life-giving blood;

[5] He appointed them princes of the churches.

[Note: [Col. 0487A] Verse 6. “These are the two olive trees before the Lord.” He alludes to Zechariah 4:12: “What are the two olive trees on the right and on the left of the lampstand?” Verse 15: “And he said: These are the two sons of oil, who stand before the Ruler of the whole earth.” Cornelius interprets this passage of Saints Peter and Paul, and before him Guarric, abbot, in his sermon on the nativity of the Apostles Peter and Paul: “Let others interpret it,” he says, “as they wish or are able . . . yet, without prejudice to a better understanding, I think Peter and Paul can not unreasonably be understood: indeed, it may seem absurd for anyone today to wish to interpret it otherwise . . . for although it may be applied to others, I think it corresponds more particularly to these men—whether to what the prophet sees as two olive trees around the lampstand, or to what the angel describes as two sons of the oil of splendor.” Nevertheless, it seems more probable that the likenesses in this and the following strophes were drawn from Revelation 11:4. For there it says: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth.” And verse 6: “These have power to shut the sky so that it may not rain.” Although these words are commonly understood literally of Enoch and Elijah, they can nevertheless appropriately be applied to the holy Apostles, as Paulinus does here and in Book I, chapters 36 and 45, Against Felix. From this agreement of the likenesses you may therefore have no doubt about the author of both the hymn and the book, as was said in the prefatory vindications to these notes.]

These are the two olive trees before the Lord,

[Col. 0486A] [Note: [Col. 0487C] Verse 7. “Lampstands radiant with light.” As he had said in Book I, Against Felix, chapter 36: “Two lampstands, shining lights of the world.”]

And lampstands radiant with light:

[Note: [Col. 0487C] Verse 8. “The two splendid lights of heaven.” Just as he had said in Book I, Against Felix, chapter 45: “The two splendid lights of heaven.”]

The two splendid lights of heaven,

They powerfully loosen the bonds of sins;

[10] They open Olympus’ gates to the faithful.

[Col. 0487A] They have heavenly power to close

The seats by their utterance, and to open the shining

Thresholds of the heavenly realm above the stars:

[Note: [Col. 0487C] Verse 14. “Their tongues have become the keys of heaven.” Concerning Peter’s tongue, Guarric the abbot says in his second sermon on the nativity of Peter and Paul: “For whom should heaven be believed to have been more accessible than to the very gatekeeper, whose tongue has become the key of heaven?” And Saint Maximus, in his first homily on the same Apostles: “For the keys of heaven are Peter’s tongue.” How Paul’s tongue too is a key of heaven, the same author explains in his fifth homily on this feast: “For to Peter, as to a good steward, he gave the key of the heavenly kingdom. To Paul, as a capable teacher, he entrusted the task of ecclesiastical instruction—namely, that those whom the one should educate for salvation, the other should receive into rest; and that for those whose hearts Paul opened by the teaching of words, Peter should open the kingdoms of heaven to their souls. For Paul too, in a certain way, received from Christ the key of knowledge . . . Thus both received keys from the Lord: the one of knowledge, the other of power.”]

Their tongues have become the keys of heaven.

[15] [Note: [Col. 0487D] Verse 15. “They drive away phantoms beyond the boundaries of the world.” You may understand demons themselves. Cyril says in Book VI Against Julian: “After Christ shone upon the world, all that tyranny of the demons was consumed, and, like a stage filled with childish games and foolish trifles, the deception was dissolved.” Thus we translate the Greek words μειρακιωδῶν ἀθυρμάτων, “of childish games”; because the passage speaks of a stage, this seemed more appropriate than the reading in the edition of Ezekiel Spanheim, “teeming with childish rattles.” Oecolampadius likewise translated it “with childish games.” Demons, therefore, sometimes assume fictitious but nevertheless dreadful faces in order to frighten and undermine those whom they attack, just as happens in theaters with masked actors. Aldhelm calls these theatrical phantoms and fictitious faces maschae in his poem On the Eight Capital Vices, not far from the end; hence the Italian maschera later arose:

“So too the crested face of masks departs,

When the bold soldier does not fear phantom or mask.”

You also find everywhere among the Platonists that demons were called larvas, especially in Augustine, City of God, Book IX, chapter 11. Thus you may understand larvas—that is, demons—as what Peter and Paul drive beyond the boundaries of the world, when they dispersed the darkness of idolatry from the world enlightened by the truth of the Gospel and abolished the worship of demons. Moreover, you may understand by larvas those afflictions which Scripture calls “sendings” by evil angels, by which especially those who are called ἐνεργούμενοι, ἐγγαστρίμυτοι—“possessed,” “ventriloquists,” maniacs, and haunted persons—are afflicted. Such persons were very well known to the ancients, who frequently joined them with the cerriti. Nonius, letter C: “The cerriti and larvati are mentally unwell, their souls troubled either by the wrath of Ceres or by the attacks of phantoms.” Plautus, Menaechmi, act V, scene IV, verse 885:

“What disease did you say it was? Tell me, old man.

Is that man haunted or possessed? Let me know.”

That the Apostles freed people of this sort, possessed or oppressed by demons, is too well known to require proof. Read the Acts of the Apostles.]

They drive away phantoms beyond the boundaries of the world.

[Note: [Col. 0488B] Verse 16. “Blessed Peter, the snares of chains.” In an old manuscript Breviary which I saw, this strophe occurs in the feast of Saint Peter in Chains; therefore this verse should be understood of the real chains with which Peter was bound, not of the metaphorical chains from which he frees sinners by authority given from heaven. Baronius discusses these iron chains of Peter at length in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, August 1; these words of his deserve particular notice: “So that, since he possesses the chief power in the Church of binding and loosing the chains of others, his own chains too should be honored by all the faithful.” Thus, since Paulinus had regard both to the literal and the metaphorical kinds of chains in this and the following strophe, the Church also has regard to both when it sings:

“Peter, at God’s command, loose the chains of earth,

You who make the heavenly kingdoms open to the blessed.”]

Blessed Peter wondrously broke

The snares of chains at Christ’s command.

[Col. 0488A] Guardian of the fold and teacher of the Church,

Shepherd of the flock and keeper of the sheep,

[20] He wards off the savage fury of wolves.

Whatever he binds with chains upon earth

Shall be firmly bound among the stars;

And whatever he looses on earth by his judgment

Shall be loosed beneath the vault of heaven.

[25] [Col. 0489A] At the end of the world he shall be Judge of the age.

[Note: [Col. 0488C] Verse 26. “Paul, not unequal to him.” Not unequal in chains, nor unequal in the power of absolving from sins or binding. Chrysostom, in his eighth homily on the Epistle to the Ephesians, which is almost entirely devoted to praising Paul’s chains, addresses the jailer thus: “What do you say? They received power to open the heavens, and would they not open a prison? They loosed those who were bound by demons, and would an iron chain overcome them? He who, though bound, loosed souls—could he not loose his own body? He who shattered the bonds of demons, would he not loose the fastening of iron?”]

Paul, not unequal to him, teacher of the nations,

Most sacred temple of election,

[Note: [Col. 0488D] Verse 28. “Equal in death, sharing the crown.” He earned this equality through equal merits. Guarric the abbot says in his second sermon on the nativity of the Apostles: “These two Apostles, brothers in faith, alike in devotion, equal in merit and virtue, united in charity, were joined also in their very passion and death. For just as they loved one another in life, so they were not separated in death.” Saint Leo the Great, Sermon 1 on their nativity, chapter 7: “Concerning whose merits and virtues . . . we ought to think nothing different or distinct, because election made them equal, labor alike, and the end made them equals.”]

Equal in death, sharing the crown.

Both lamps and glory of the Church,

[30] They flash throughout the radiant world.

[Note: [Col. 0489B] Verse 31. “O happy Rome,” etc. Saint Leo discusses at length, in the same sermon, Rome’s blessedness after being subjected to Christ through the Apostles. Tertullian, On the Prescription Against Heretics, chapter 36: “How happy is that Church of Rome, into which the Apostles poured all their teaching together with their own blood.” And Book IV Against Marcion, chapter 5: “Let the Romans also sound forth, to whom Peter and Paul left the Gospel sealed even by their own blood.”]

O happy Rome, which has been made purple

By the precious blood of such great leaders!

[Note: [Col. 0489B] Verse 33. “You surpass all the beauty of the world.” Saint Chrysostom, in his final homily on the Epistle to the Romans, concerning Paul’s death, which he suffered at Rome: “Hence this city too has become more illustrious than all the others.” Paulinus therefore rightly said that Rome surpasses all the beauty of the world, not through its own praise or merit, but through the power and death of the holy Apostles. He did not mean this in the sense in which the malicious Cassander chatters in his note on this hymn, citing verses of Hildebert. His hatred of the Roman Church is sufficiently clear from that note.]

You surpass all the beauty of the world,

Not through your own praise, but through the merits of the saints,

[35] Whom you slaughtered with blood-stained swords.

Therefore, now, you glorious martyrs,

[Note: [Col. 0489C] Verse 37. “Paul, lily of the world.” At about the time when Paulinus was composing his hymns, Pope Adrian I wrote to the bishops of Spain in the case of Felix and Elipandus, the heretics, and, bringing Paul’s teaching against them, said: “For Paul, the lily of the world . . . calls him Lord, not servant.” Everyone can see that Adrian borrowed this distinctive designation from Paulinus, or Paulinus from Adrian, so that from this fact alone one may conjecture that the hymn is not by Elpis, who did not live until Adrian’s time, but by Paulinus, who was contemporary with that pontiff and, under his, so to speak, banners, fought most energetically against the heretics.]

Blessed Peter, Paul, lily of the world,

Triumphant soldiers of the heavenly court,

By your gracious prayers protect us from every evil;

[40] Carry us above the ether.

Glory to God through endless ages;

To you, Son, be honor and dominion;

Honor and power to the holy Spirit.

May there be undivided salvation for the Trinity

[45] Through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## HYMN III. On the Resurrection of the Lord

[Col. 0490A]

The golden world shines with every light,

[Note: [Col. 0489D] Verse 2. “The ether, drenched,” etc. He alludes to that angelic food, manna, with which God fed the children of Israel in the desert after leading them out of Egypt; that departure was a figure of the Lord’s passion and resurrection and a shadow of our Pasch. Exodus 16:13 and following. He said “to bedew” for “to send down.” The word is Latin, but Paulinus rendered it barbarously when, speaking as grammarians do, he made an active verb from a neuter one.]

The drenched ether rains down sweetness,

The stars, with their joyful lights,

Encircle the whole heaven in radiant splendor,

[5] [Note: [Col. 0489D] Verse 5. “The air distills.” From Psalm 67:10: “The heavens distilled before the face of God at Sinai.”]

The air distills drops of balsam.

Sunset, sunrise, Aquilo, North Wind,

Earth and sea, the bounds of Ocean,

Broad poles and hinges of heaven, rejoice,

Fountains of waters, flowing rivers,

[10] Rejoice, plains and mountain peaks.

Behold, the Lord has risen from the underworld;

He returned victorious, having conquered death;

He plundered wicked Tartarus,

[Col. 0490B] [Note: [Col. 0489D] Verse 14. “He broke the barriers of Gehenna.” Adrichomius gives a fuller account of what Gehenna was and where it was in his Description of Jerusalem, no. 186; there he also discusses at length the sacrifices offered there to the idol Moloch and the origin of the name Tophet. The word is used figuratively for hell in more than one place in the Gospel. Paulinus says here the same thing, in other words, as the Church says in the fourth responsorial lesson of the office of Holy Saturday: “Today our Savior shattered alike the gates and bars of death, destroyed the barriers of hell, and overthrew the powers of the devil.” Likewise: “And by his rose-flowing blood he washed away the record of death,” from the Epistle to the Colossians 2:14. He called the blood rosifluus, “rose-flowing,” because of its rose-like color, an expression not uncommon among writers of that age. Paulinus likewise says in his letter On the Acts at the Synod of Altinum: “In the rosy blood of Christ Jesus.” Pope Adrian I similarly says at the beginning of his letter to the bishops of Spain against Elipandus: “Pope Adrian, etc., sends greetings to the churches presiding in the rosy blood of Christ.”]

He broke the barriers of Gehenna, and the record

[15] Of death he washed away with rose-flowing blood.

[Note: [Col. 0490C] Verse 16. “The sun, the bright form of the world’s light.” Schema, Greek σχῆμα, is a word of more than one meaning. Sometimes it means clothing or a garment, and this is its more proper sense. Herodian, Book I, chapter 9: ἀνὴρ φιλοσόφου φέρων σχῆμα, that is, “a man wearing a philosopher’s garment,” or, as Politian translated it, “someone in a philosopher’s dress.” Plautus uses the same word in the same sense in Amphitryon, verse 132, in the prologue:

“Now do not wonder at this attire of mine,

Because I have come here thus in a slave’s garb.”

He uses the word in the feminine gender, as Suetonius does in Caligula, chapter 43: “So that no one should lack a model of the prescribed dress when producing a work” (others read, incorrectly, “of the requested scene”). Here, however, it means not clothing but the body’s bearing and gesture, which is another meaning of the word, as in Euripides’ Medea:

Ὦ φιλτάτη χείρ φίλτατον δέ μοὶ στόμα  
Καὶ σχῆμα, καὶ πρόσωπον εὐγενὲς τέκνων

That is:

“O dearest hand, and to me most dear mouth,

And form, and noble face of my children.”

Just as species has many meanings in Latin, sometimes denoting beauty, so σχῆμα does in Greek. In this sense Paulinus perhaps called the sun the “form of the world,” whose light makes the world appear beautiful. This is suggested by another reading placed in brackets: “The sun, the form of the world, the ruddy glory of heaven.”]

The sun, the bright form of the world’s light [Alternative: The sun, the world’s form, the ruddy glory of heaven]

[Note: [Col. 0490D] Verse 17. “It illumined the whole age at midday,” etc. Deluxit, “illumined,” must be retained, not delusit, “deceived.” He refers to the darkness that fell over the whole earth from the sixth hour to the ninth at the death of Christ the Lord. Concerning this portent, Sedulius writes elegantly and in a similar style in Book V, chapter 16, of his Paschal Work: “Meanwhile, suddenly the whole world was darkened, oppressed by the darkness of sudden blindness and drenched by a mournful mass of clouds; it celebrated funeral days as though at a burial. But the sun, withdrawn behind hidden rays, lay concealed beneath a dreadful cloak and stained the world with the mourning of an alien night.”]

It illumined [Alternative: deceived] the whole age at midday;

It covered the lamps of the spheres with blackness.

[Col. 0491A] Heaven melts, terrified by dreadful night,

[20] The whole world languished beneath the darkness,

[Note: [Col. 0491C] Verse 21. “The fields were terrified.” Is the alternative reading placed in brackets, aura, better? Unless perhaps arva means “earth,” and the neuter verb has been used with active force, so that expavit means “made afraid.” I more readily accept the latter. He proceeds to describe the terror and trembling of earth and sea. On this and the other portents that occurred at Christ’s death and are mentioned here by Paulinus, see Sedulius in the cited passage and the following chapter.]

The fields were terrified [F.: the air], the seas trembled:

The veil of the temple was soon torn down the middle;

Then the split rocks opened;

Many bodies of the righteous had risen

[25] From the tombs, those who had long been sleeping.

[Note: [Col. 0491C] Verse 26. “When the serpent saw the sacrifice slaughtered in the evening.” He alludes either to the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb, which took place among the Hebrews in the evening of Passover, Exodus 12:6; Deuteronomy 16:6, or to the rite established by the Lord in Exodus 29:38–39, of sacrificing a lamb each day morning and evening. In both cases the sacrifice of the Savior, to be performed on the altar of the cross, was prefigured, as Paulinus indicates in this and the following strophe. Nothing is more frequent or better known than the designation of the demon by the names serpent, snake, and basilisk, so there is no need to linger over a very familiar matter. From the time when, taking the form of a serpent—or, if you prefer Augustine’s view, in On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, Book XI, chapters 27 and 29, using a real serpent as an organ and instrument—he deceived Eve, he has borne this name through the ages.]

When the serpent saw, sacrificed in the evening,

The holy sacrifice of the gracious body,

Which in the morning filled heaven with fragrances,

Wounded by great grief, he shrieked,

[30] Struck by the wound of the gentle Lamb.

He saw upon the sacred altar of the cross the victim,

The flood of blood, a liquid flowing from his holy side,

Which washed away the world’s sins,

And the deep joys of paradise granted to the thief;

[35] With his neck crushed, he [the serpent] hisses.

The blessed day shone forth after the sorrowful Sabbaths,

Illuminated by serene light,

[Note: [Col. 0491D] Verse 38. “Which alone is preferred to all days.” To make the meter proceed harmoniously with the rest, the second syllable of diebus must be contracted. The assertion itself is entirely true. “This day,” says Sedulius in Book V, chapter 20, of his Paschal Work, “which, by the glory of the eternal King and by the trophy of his resurrection, he has also illumined, he judged worthy to retain primacy among all days with religion.” Venantius, Book III, poem 9, on this day:

“Greetings, festal day, venerable through every age,

On which God conquered hell and holds the stars.

The year’s nobility, the months’ glory, gracious splendor of days,

The radiance of hours,” etc.

The author of Sermon 1 on the Resurrection, elsewhere listed among Augustine’s sermons as Sermon 136 on Time, now in volume V of the appendix, no. 159: “It seems to me that this day is brighter than all other days . . . Just as Mary, the mother of the Lord, holds primacy among all women, so among all other days this is the mother of all days.” Chrysostom, Homily 5, On the Resurrection: “Today’s day has shone more joyfully than all the days of the year.” Do you see how the Fathers place this day before the others, as Paulinus says here? See also what we said in the observations and notes on canon 13 of the Council of Forum Julii.]

Which alone is preferred to all days,

On which the Redeemer rose from the dead,

[40] After conquering the proud ruler of the world.

Mary Magdalene came on the Sabbath;

The other Mary came at dawn

To the tomb, carrying spices,

So that very early they might soothe the most sacred body

[45] Of Christ with fragrant chrism.

[Col. 0492A] Behold, the angel of the Lord, radiant beyond measure,

Sitting in white garments beside the rolled-away stone,

Refreshes them with these words:

[Note: [Col. 0492C] Verse 49. “Why do you, among the stars, seek the living with the dead?” If you prefer the alternative reading, “Why do you women seek the living with the dead?” it will conform more closely to Luke 24:5; and indeed Christ, God and man, had not yet ascended above the stars to reign.]

“Why do you [women] seek among the stars the living with the dead?

[50] He has risen himself, as he said.

Behold the place where the Lord was laid:

Go, tell his disciples:

He has risen and gone to Galilee,

He has destroyed him who previously possessed

[55] The dominion of death, as he had foretold.”

[Note: [Col. 0492C] Verse 56. “Let hostile death,” etc., from 1 Corinthians 15:26. Anastasius Sinaita, Prayer 5, On the Resurrection: “The death of Christ became life for the dead. He who can wisely heal even incurable diseases cures opposites with opposites; and when the mystery of death was completed, and death, which held power in the body, had itself been destroyed,” etc. Saint Peter Chrysologus, Sermon 74: “Death is condemned, death which, rushing upon the guilty, collided with the Judge; having ruled over servants, it raged against the Lord; raging against human beings, it sprang upon God. Rightly, then, the law of Tartarus perishes, the rights of hell are removed, the power of death is taken away, and in punishment for its rashness it raised the dead,” etc. Venantius Fortunatus expresses this beautifully and appropriately in Book III, poem 9, addressing the risen Christ:

“You snatch an innumerable people from the prison of death,

And then the author of their freedom enters.

The savage beast anxiously spews out the people it had swallowed,

And the Lamb draws the sheep away from the wolf’s throat.”]

Let hostile death grieve that it has perished.

Dead Life seizes the kingdom of death;

Death shall no longer rule over him;

He restored the lost sheep to the fold;

[60] On the cross he renewed the whole world.

To you, God the Father, be praise and glory;

To the Crucified, honor and dominion;

And to the holy Spirit likewise, power.

May there be undivided strength for the Trinity

[65] Through all the ages of ages.

181 ## HYMN IV. [Note: [Col. 0492D] On Saint Simeon. This hymn, drawn from the account in Luke 2:22–28, is for the feast that we now call the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary and celebrate on February 2. For its institution and origin, consult Baronius in his notes on the Roman Martyrology for that day. [Col. 0493B] This feast was introduced into the Church not in place of the Lupercalia or Saturnalia, as Baronius says here and in the Annals, but in place of the Ambarvalia, as the brothers Macri argue at length in their Hierolexicon, under the word Hypante. Yet they too must be corrected, since they confuse Ambarvaia with Amburbalia or Amburbium. “Ambarvale,” says Servius in his note on Virgil’s Eclogue 3, verse 77, “is called the sacrifice in which a victim circles the fields . . . just as Amburbale or Amburvium is called the sacrifice in which a victim circles and surrounds the city.” Of the former Virgil, Georgics I, verse 344:

“Three times let the fortunate victim circle the new crops.”

Of the latter Lucan, Pharsalia I, verse 592:

“Then he orders the entire city, trembling with citizens,

To be circled, and the walls purified with a festal rite,

With the long pomerium encircling the outermost boundaries.”

Since this month, called February either from Februus, that is, Pluto, to whom it was sacred, or from the goddess Februa, who presided over purifications and sacrifices and expiations instituted to appease the Manes, was the month in which the city was purified every fifth year after the census had been completed and the people reviewed—hence lustrum is also used for a period of five years—and the amburbial sacrifice was offered, the Church, as it has customarily sanctified other profane rites, sanctified this observance and instituted the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary, together with the circling or procession with candles to be performed on that day. Thus Saint Eligius, bishop of Noyon, says in his third homily near the end, and Saint Ildephonsus in his eleventh sermon, one of twelve on Blessed Mary. From these authorities you may infer that the litany or procession of this day was instituted elsewhere before it was instituted at Rome by Pope Sergius. Anastasius, volume I, marginal no. 164: “He decreed that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Nativity and Dormition of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, and of Saint Simeon—which the Greeks call Hypante—a litany should always go out from Saint Adrian’s, and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s.” Sergius died in the first year of the eighth century, that is, in 701; Ildephonsus in 677; and Eligius in 665, and both of the latter mention litanies. Just as those who regard Sergius as the originator of the solemnity must be corrected by Ildephonsus and Eligius, so Baluzius must be corrected by what Sergius did. In his notes on the Frankish Capitularies, Book II, chapter 35—which reports canon 36 of the Council of Mainz, held in 813, concerning feasts—Baluzius says of this feast: “This alone of Saint Mary’s feasts was formerly celebrated in the Church. Later the Assumption was added, then the Conception, Presentation, Annunciation, and Visitation,” etc. If τὸ olim, “formerly,” indicates—as it seems and is reasonable to believe—the period under discussion, namely the feasts established at the Council of Mainz in 813, he is mistaken, since Sergius, more than one hundred and ten years before the Council of Mainz, mentions the Nativity, Dormition, and also the Annunciation, just as he mentions this feast under the name of Saint Simeon, as our Paulinus does and others also did. Baronius lists them in his note on February 2, where he shows that this feast has been called by many names.]

On Saint Simeon.

The bright day of gracious light shines forth,

After the virgin girl’s golden delivery,

When the Son, sent from the heavenly dwelling

By the Father, willed to be born as a man,

[5] [Note: [Col. 0494C] Verse 5. “The offspring of the lofty name remained the same.” That is, although he became human, he nevertheless remained and was called the Son of the Most High, as in Luke 1:32, etc.]

The offspring of the lofty name remained the same.

Subject to the sacred ceremonies of the Law,

[Col. 0493A] He who rules the radiant angelic ranks

From the Father’s citadel deigned to be subject

To every Mosaic statute,

[10] And founded heaven, earth, and the seas.

When the fortieth day after the girl’s delivery

[Note: [Col. 0494C] Verse 12. “According to the law of the Lord,” Exodus 13:2; Leviticus 12:2; Numbers 8:16.]

Had been fulfilled according to the law of the Lord,

The virgin Mary then carried the holy child Jesus

In her consecrated arms into the temple courts,

[15] The only-begotten Son of the dread Father.

The blessed mother bore God beneath the veil of flesh

Upon her most chaste shoulders;

She impressed sweet, brief kisses beneath her lips

Upon the mouth of the true God and man,

[20] At whose command all things were created.

[Note: [Col. 0494C] Verse 21. “They brought two bright little dove-chicks with milky down,” from Luke 2:24 and Leviticus 12:8. Paulinus uses diminutive forms both for the beauty of the poem and in keeping with the subject’s nature: diminutive words commonly express our feelings, especially love, as is particularly evident in Plautus, who often says corculum for cor, “heart,” and uses other expressions of this sort. Do not too quickly object to Paulinus’ phrase “bright little ones with milky down,” as though it were a fault of synonymy. Candidum, “bright,” is not properly identical with album, “white,” for which he used lacteum, “milky.” Servius very aptly notes the distinction in his commentary on Georgics III, verse 82: “To be bright,” he says, “is one thing—that is, to be suffused with a certain shining light; to be white is another, since it lies close to pallor.” Thus candidulos pullos means “slightly shining little ones,” while lacteolis plumulis means “slightly pale,” resembling the color of milk, which is especially pleasing and, so to speak, conveys a certain loveliness and gentle delight to the viewer. Thus Catullus, verse 801, in the epigram to Camelius:

“Now milk-white girls hold you.”

]

They brought two bright little dove-chicks

[Col. 0493B] With milky down;

They offered in the temple a pair of turtledoves for him,

As the sanction of the Law prescribed,

[25] [Note: [Col. 0494D] Verse 25. “Such as they might consecrate as thoroughly burned offerings.” See the rite in Leviticus, chapter 1.]

Such as they might consecrate as thoroughly burned offerings.

A priest of God, humble and most gentle,

An upright man and excellent old man, was in the city:

The blessed Simeon, filled with heaven-flowing

[Col. 0494A] And holy inspiration,

[30] Hastened into the sacred court at God’s prompting.

For long before he had received this response,

Taught by the Holy Spirit: that he could not be released

From the bond of death from his body

Until, while alive, he had seen Christ the Lord,

[35] Whom the Father sent from his lofty dwelling.

Therefore he received the child in his hands;

He gave thanks to the heavenly Father;

Holding him in his arms, he blessed the Lord,

Full of love and the sweetness of his heart,

[40] Adding these words in a lofty utterance:

“Release your servant now, Lord, I beg you,

In peace; for I have been deemed worthy

To see your salvation with my eyes,

Which you prepared in your singular mercy

[45] Before the face of your peoples.

A light of the nations, shining in [their] eyes [printed *fulgente*, “shining,” ablative singular; variant *fulgensque*, “and shining,” nominative singular],

The glory of the people of Israel’s offspring:

This one is appointed for the fall of scandal,

And for the salvation of Jacob, the golden stock,

[50] [Note: [Col. 0494D] Verse 50. “Until the secrets of hearts conceal themselves,” that is, until they are hidden. Palliare means “to cover” or “conceal,” a metaphorical transfer from the pallium, the cloak by which we are covered. Yet, as scholars note, it is generally used in a negative sense. John Calvin, Legal Lexicon: “Palliare, a metaphorically derived verb, signifies ‘to cover an ugly deed’; thus it is used in the chapter Nisi specialis, in the Extravagantes, under the title De usu pallii.” C. Barthius also notes this in Adversaria, Book XLIV, chapter 21: “Palliare something means to veil or cover it, and it is generally used in a bad sense. The old writer of the Life of Saint Frodobert: ‘He began carefully to investigate whether that simplicity sprang from the innermost source of purity, or whether, as is familiar to some, a treacherous mind was concealing itself under feigned innocence.’ Philip the priest, in his Prolegomena to Job: ‘These three friends of Job therefore represent, as I have said, those who inwardly are enemies of Christ but are cloaked under the name of Christianity.’” He says that the secrets of hearts would one day conceal themselves because at some point—namely, at the death of Christ Jesus—they were destined to be revealed, as in Luke 2:35: “so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.”]

Until the secrets of hearts conceal themselves.

[Col. 0495A] Behold, holy Mother, a sword’s blow

Will pass through your soul;

Mary kept the lofty mysteries beneath her breast,

Joyfully pondering the words,

[55] Faithfully believing the heavenly declarations.

Glory to the Father of Jesus of the great name,

And to you, Son, only-begotten of the Father,

God, power, and strength above the ether,

To the holy Paraclete through every age,

[60] Infinite praise, honor, and dominion.

Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0495C] I found this hymn among the papers of the illustrious bishop of Adria; his nephew, Lorenzo della Torre, most courteously shared it with me. As soon as I read it, I immediately recognized Paulinus as its author. Its style, the form of its verses, and the order of its strophes prove this plainly. At the foot of the hymn and the sheet these words had been written in Italian: “This is the hymn extracted from two very ancient codices, one of which is in my possession.” By these words he indicates that the hymn had been recovered from two very ancient codices.]

## HYMN V. On Saint Mark the Evangelist

Now throughout the whole age the light shines forth,

That light of the Father, which shines from the throne.

[Col. 0495B] [Note: [Col. 0495D] Verse 3. “Which is the source, origin, splendor of golden light.” Splendorem was read, in my opinion incorrectly, instead of splendor. Although the latter is irregular, since the poem always proceeds in twelve syllables and this line would otherwise have thirteen, the sense—which, unless the passage is corrected, is sufficiently obscure—led me to restore splendor.]

Which is the source, origin, splendor of golden light,

And always possesses unfailing light;

[5] It clears the sky, driving away the world’s darkness.

From the sacred radiance of this light

The blessed Mark, evangelical teacher,

Received a gracious ray within his breast,

Made a lamp after the likeness of so great a light,

[10] Burning, he drove away the age’s darkness.

[Note: [Col. 0495D] Verse 11. “One of seven little white columns.” He seems to allude to Proverbs 7:1, where Wisdom has hewn seven columns, and to Song of Songs 3:10, where it is said of Solomon, who was a figure of Christ Jesus: “He made its columns of silver.” Who does not know that the Apostles and disciples of Christ are frequently called columns? See the interpreters on Psalm 74:4: “I have strengthened its columns.” Menochius says in his note on that passage that “seven” columns cut out by Wisdom means many columns. Thus Saint Mark is called by Paulinus one of the many columns by which the house of God’s wisdom, which is Christ’s Church, is established. Hence a little later he says of the same man: “He supports the foundations of the lofty structure.”]

One of the seven little white columns;

[Note: [Col. 0496C] Verse 12. “One of the seven golden lampstands.” From Revelation 1:12–13.]

One of the seven golden lampstands,

And he encircles the whole world with a bright star;

He stands beneath the roof of the Churches,

[15] He supports the foundations of the lofty structure.

[Note: [Col. 0496C] Verse 16. “What the holy prophet Ezekiel once saw,” etc. He alludes to the visions of Ezekiel 1:10 and John’s Apocalypse 4:7, in which the four living creatures set before them on every side constitute the symbols of the Evangelists. Saint Mark is commonly understood by interpreters in the figure of the lion. The matter is well known. Anastasius Sinaita, however, in his Anagogical Contemplations on the Hexaemeron, Book IV, recognizes Mark in the ox. Apart from the fact that this view is almost unique, he is also mistaken in both the argument and the reason he gives for it: “The Church possesses Mark,” he says, “who appeared like an ox among the six-winged living creatures, because he began his Gospel with sacrifices.” But he is wrong, because it is not Mark but Luke who begins his account with the sacrifice of Zechariah, and therefore the ox is assigned to him. Mark, however, begins with John’s preaching in the desert, where, like a lion roaring in the forest, he began: “Prepare the way of the Lord”; therefore he is compared with the lion. He calls John the one reclining with Christ because of what we say in our notes on chapter 36 of Book I Against Felix.]

What the holy prophet Ezekiel once saw,

The most joyous living creature, typologically

Are they not real shadows, rather than fictitious ones? ## HYMN VI. On the Dedication of a Church

[Note: [Col. 0497C] On the Dedication of a Church. For the origin of this rite, see what Gratian, in *De Consecratione*, distinction 1, chapters 2 and 17, has taken from Pope Felix. He refers the rite to the construction of the tabernacle, completed at the Lord’s command through Moses, and to the dedication of Solomon’s temple—matters which Paulinus does not leave unmentioned in this hymn, indeed he alludes to them. An explanation of the rites of dedication may be found throughout the writers on ecclesiastical ceremonies.

Each year the memory of the dedication itself is celebrated; in the Gospel of John 10:22 it is called the *Encaenia*. On that passage see Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate 48, no. 2. Gregory, *Homily 14 on the Gospels*, indicates with how much joy Christians used to observe these annual solemnities: “Certainly, if somewhere the people were celebrating a fair, and if we hastened together to the dedication of some church when the solemnity had been announced, we would all hurry to be found there, and each would strive to take part. 184 He would consider himself afflicted by a grave loss if he did not see the solemnity of the common joy.” From these words it may be inferred that, already in Gregory’s own time, the celebration had begun to degenerate from spiritual into worldly joy, since he mentions together both the frequency of fairs and of church dedications: an indication of the creeping profanation that later centuries greatly increased, until people indulged more freely in revelry at banquets held near the churches. This displeased the Church so much that the Council of Chalon, around the year 650, prohibited it and directed in canon 19 that “the priests of the place must forbid and keep such things away from the precincts of the basilicas, their porticoes, and even the atria themselves.”

Saint Paulinus of Nola, in *Natale* 9 of Saint Felix—that is, poem 24—does not approve this custom, although he excuses it on account of the simplicity of the offenders:

“Would that they celebrated these joys with sound intentions,
And did not mingle their cups with the holy thresholds!

. . . . Yet I think such joys should be forgiven to the humble,
Who pursue these pleasures at their little feasts:
For error has crept into their untutored minds,
And simplicity, unaware of so great a fault,
Falls through piety, wrongly believing
That the saints rejoice at their tombs,
Drenched and breathing out the scent of wine.”

The evidence of such merriment increased so greatly in our region that, lest quarrels, disputes, and murders—as commonly happens—should follow amid the drinking, and lest any questions that arose should remain unsettled, custody of the celebration was entrusted to a certain magnate. This later passed into what they call the right of investiture, and the right of guarding the feast was established. Sanctions enacted under Patriarch Marquard at the castle of Saint Vitus in the year 1381 speak of it; I possess them in manuscripts of that period, written in the original script, on page 58. See also the documents in Appendix 2, nos. 29 and 40.]

[Col. 0497B] Fragrant with the scent of precious balsam
[5] Mingled with spices.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] V. 6. From 2 Chronicles VI, 19 and 2. V. 16, from Exodus XL, 32. V. 21, from 2 Chronicles VII, 1 and 2. V. 26, ibid. VI, 28 and VII, 13. V. 38, from John I, 29.] May your open eyes, Lord, always be

[Col. 0497C] To flood the walls of this hall

[20] [Col. 0498A] With its presence.

May the luminous mist, once famous,

[25] Enrich this house with an everlasting gift.

[35] [Col. 0498B] The endless joys of everlasting life.

Jesus, only Son of the Father, Creator of all things,
You who save the world with purple blood,
You alone who take away the deadly sins,
Deign, by your gratuitous gift,

[40] [Note: [Col. 0498D] On verse 40, *ruricolas*, “dwellers in the countryside.” Is this instead *terricolas*, “earth-dwellers”? Or is it because the temple was perhaps being dedicated in the countryside, and he composed the hymn for the benefit of country people?] To send the country-dwellers to the stars of heaven.

## RHYTHM: On the Nativity of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0498D]

I would discuss the nature of rhythms at greater length if the distinguished Scipio Maffei had not nearly exhausted the entire subject in a special dissertation on historical diplomatics, published at Mantua in 1727 on the occasion of a certain *Rhythm on the Praises of Verona*, to which I gladly refer our reader.

Since, however, some may perhaps think that Paulinus did not observe metrical laws, or that he spoke too much in the popular manner, I wish to note only this point as worthy of observation—a point which I have found no one who has written on the subject to have noticed: namely, that rhythm differs from meter, and does not follow the laws of meter. Maurus Terentianus briefly expressed this distinction in book *On Meters*, verse 54:

“For meter confines feet and fixed measures;
A measured law of times contains rhythm.”

Horace suggests that Pindaric dithyrambs were of this kind in book IV of the *Odes*, ode 2, verse 50, where he says:

“Or through daring dithyrambs he rolls forth
New words, and is borne along
With measures freed from law.”

On this passage the grammarian Acron writes: “He called these dithyrambs daring because they are more vehement than other rhythms. . . . ‘And is borne along with measures freed from law’: with measures by which rhythm, relating to sound, is held together, not with those relating to the law of verses, as Virgil says of a corresponding poem: ‘I remember the measures, if only I could retain the words.’ Therefore in this case the law of feet is not followed, but that of syllables. . . . Or he said ‘freed from law’ because in this meter it is permitted to vary, and not to remain in the same meter.”

Quintilian should also be consulted, book IX, chapter 4, where this point above all should be noted: “Rhythms, that is, measures, consist in the duration of times; meters also consist in order. Therefore the former seems to be a matter of quantity, the latter of quality.”

We have also thought it worth observing that, since rhythms are released from the stricter law of poems, they were employed with a freer inspiration as being more suitable for popular songs, especially those accompanied by dancing and bodily movement. Such pieces are called *ballistea* by Vopiscus in *Aurelian*, chapter 6, from the Greek βάλλειν, meaning “to throw” or “to hurl,” from which comes βαλλίζειν, “to dance,” and perhaps the vernacular *ballare*, since dancers repeatedly throw about their limbs, especially their hands.

Propertius, book IV, verse 678, in the elegy concerning Cynthia and the dragon, says:

“And the dwarf, himself briefly bent into his own limbs,
Threw his maimed hands toward the hollow pipes.”

Hear Vopiscus in the same passage: “Theoclius, a writer of the Caesarean age, 186 reports that Aurelian killed forty-eight men with his own hand in one day during the Sarmatian war, and on many different days more than nine hundred and fifty—so much so that boys even composed *ballistea* and little dances about Aurelian, which they performed in military fashion on feast days:

‘A thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand,
We beheaded.
One man—a thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand,
We beheaded.
A thousand, a thousand, may he live,
Who killed a thousand, a thousand.
No one has as much wine
As the blood he poured out.’

I see that these verses are utterly frivolous; but since the author mentioned above inserted them in Latin in his writings exactly as they are, I did not think they should be omitted.”

Thus Vopiscus. In the following chapter he adds that, after the Franks who were ravaging Gaul had been checked near Mainz, a new song was composed about him:

“A thousand Franks, a thousand Sarmatians,
We killed at one time;
A thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand, a thousand Persians
We seek.”

You will find something similar, like a *ballistium*, in Scripture at 1 Samuel 18:6–7. When David returned after striking down the Philistine, the women came out from all the towns of Israel, singing and leading dances to meet King Saul, with tambourines of joy and sistrums; and the women, playing, sang:

“Saul has struck down his thousand,
And David his ten thousand.”

Thus Paulinus composed a rhythm, not a meter, and perhaps shaped it for use by uneducated people, adapting it to their understanding in a very plain and popular style.

To this rhythm on the Nativity of the Lord, which Georgius Cassander gives in his *Works*, page 201, Paris edition of 1616, he appends the following note. It is as follows:

“Paulinus. I have found several hymns and verses of this kind written in certain little books under the name of Paulinus. But it is readily evident that they do not belong to that Paulinus of Nola, celebrated in the age of Jerome and Ambrose, who consistently observed the law of meter in his verses. Rather, they seem to belong to another Paulinus, much later in time, who was bishop of Aquileia under Charlemagne and who wrote, in the name of the cities of lower Italy, a letter against Felix, bishop of Urgel, and Elephandus, bishop of Toledo, and lamented the destruction of that city in precisely the same kind of rhythm in which this hymn is composed. It begins:

‘To mourn your ashes, Aquileia,
No tears are sufficient for me:
Words fail; grief has taken away
The sense of my bitter heart.’

It is entirely apparent that both poems proceeded from the same author. Yet I am uncertain whether these verses should be attributed to Paulinus, bishop of Aquileia, or to Paul the Deacon of the church of Aquileia. For in a manuscript book, some poems of this kind bore simply the name Paulinus, as does the present hymn, while others bore the name of Paul the Deacon, as does this lament for the destruction of Aquileia. Nevertheless, I am inclined to think that these and similar rhythms belong rather to Bishop Paulinus than to Paul the Deacon, because the hymn on Saint John beginning ‘That they may sing with unrestrained voices,’ which everyone without dispute attributes to Paul the Deacon, is less compatible with the composition of these hymns and seems to display a different author.”

Thus far Cassander. His highly probable conjecture is supported by the *Register of the Works of Paul the Deacon*, which Peter the Deacon likewise presents in *Cassinensian Illustrious Men*, chapter 8. There is no mention there of a poem on the destruction of Aquileia, just as no trace of it appears in the note on the same chapter by Giovanni Battista Mari, who carefully lists what Peter had omitted, as may be seen in *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, volume VI, page 17.

Nevertheless, we moved almost every stone in our efforts to obtain this rhythm, which we think belongs to Paulinus, in complete form so that it could be added to the preceding work—but in vain. We approached by letter, either directly or through friends, the prefects or learned men of the more celebrated libraries of Italy, France, Belgium, and Austria. They replied with great courtesy, but acknowledged that the Paulinian rhythm was unknown to them, promising that in future they would search their archives with greater diligence. So far, however, nothing has been supplied to us.

Add another loss to this one. Among the works of Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, Paris edition of 1693, column 1214, a certain rhythm is included which, to tell the truth, has the style and phrasing of Paulinus; there it is said to be preserved in the library of Cardinal Ottoboni. We omitted no effort to locate this manuscript, since the matter was entrusted to Father Nicolaus Minuccius, a priest of the Roman Oratory, who is as devoted to letters by his own nature as he is attached to me by his kindness; but all the labor proved fruitless.

I thought that I might draw some light from the Benedictine Fathers of the Congregation of Saint Maur in Paris. In the end I discovered that I had tried to cut through an isthmus. For when asked, Father Bernard de Montfaucon replied on the tenth day before the Kalends of March 1733:

“Concerning the rhythm circulated under Hilary’s name, which you think belongs to Paulinus, I cannot give you any information. More than twelve years ago our associate D. Pierre Coutant died; he had worked diligently on editing Hilary. But where his writings and archives went, I do not know, nor is it easy to learn from others.”

I am greatly astonished that relics of such venerable antiquity should have been so easily destroyed or lost in this age, when they are valued against gold.

Nevertheless, receive what I find there, the beginning and the end—and even the notice that precedes it. It states that this hymn was composed to be sung in the evening, because Hilary says that he sent his daughter Abra a hymn to be sung in the morning—that is, at daybreak—and one in the evening, in the letter prefixed there, near its end, in these words:

“Meanwhile I have sent you a morning hymn and an evening hymn, so that you may always remember me.”

Thus it reads there:

“In a manuscript formerly belonging to Cardinal Sirlet, then to the Altemps Library, and now to Cardinal Ottoboni, this hymn follows another [this one is the morning hymn and begins ‘Giver of splendid light’], a longer hymn which may be considered the evening hymn mentioned in the preceding letter to Abra. Certainly it is very suitable for evening. It begins from the stars and is a kind of general confession of a soul which laments that it has been assailed by the vices of lust, pride, envy, discord, vainglory, gluttony, and exultant joy, and which, relying on God’s mercy alone and on Christ’s merits, asks forgiveness.

Moreover, it bears the mark of the age of the Arian heresy in that, while professing a faithful spirit, it expressly detests Arius and Sabellius, adding no other heretic except perhaps Simon Magus, to complete the verses. Yet the diction does not seem worthy of Hilary. Throughout, the measure of the verses is determined by the number of syllables rather than by feet. And although, if this hymn were to be sung by a daughter, the language ought to be feminine in gender, it is masculine everywhere. From the beginning and the end, let the reader judge what should be thought of the remainder of the hymn.”

**Beginning**

“To the bright stars of heaven I am not worthy
To raise my unhappy eyes,
Pressed down by the heavy weight of sins:
Spare the redeemed.

I neglected to do the good I ought to have done;
I committed shameful crimes without end;
I perpetrated wickedness bounded by no limit:
Come to my aid, O Christ.”

**End**

[Col. 0502D]

“Modulating a hymn with a faithful throat,
I reject Arius and barking Sabellius;
Never have I assented, whispering in the ear,
To Simon’s grunting.

And I have been zealous with the zeal of Christ’s name;
For the holy Church, my mother,
Has nourished me with Catholic milk
At her sacred breast
Throughout all time.”

This is what is found there. If anyone should happen to encounter the remaining portions of these rhythms, which have escaped us, or should discover that they exist somewhere in complete form, we earnestly and sincerely desire that he make them public, lamenting our own loss, and we repeatedly and fervently beg him to do so.

We offer no other notes on the rhythm concerning the Nativity; it is sufficiently clear in itself. We do, however, wish to warn the reader that in verse 71 something appears to be missing; perhaps the word is *dicunt*, “they say.” Moreover, in verse 79, perhaps *perdocente*, “instructing,” should be read rather than *perducente*, “leading.”]

Today the heavenly host first sang,
Glory to God in the highest.

[Col. 0498C] The peace of angels truly descended upon earth
[Col. 0499A] In their voices.

Today the heavens became honey-sweet;

## 187. FRAGMENTS OF THE LETTERS OF SAINT PAULINUS (C)*

## FIRST LETTER. PAULINUS TO KING CHARLES

[Note: [Col. 0503D] Stephen Baluze presents this fragment of a certain letter of Paulinus in volume I of his *Miscellanea*, page 362, Paris edition of 1678, from an old manuscript codex belonging to the distinguished Aymo of Campo, a predecessor at Orléans.

Some statements in it agree word for word with those added at the end of the little book *Sacrosyllabus*, presented at the Council of Frankfurt. Hence it seems probable that the letter was written around that time. But because Baluze, in the *Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks*, reports a petition of the people to the emperor that bishops should not be harassed by enemies—that is, that they should not be compelled to march to the army—and that they wished the same arrangement to be maintained for priests, while Charles granted it, using these words: “Instructed by apostolic authority and by the admonition of many holy bishops . . . correcting ourselves . . . we desire that no priest go to war,” we suspect that Paulinus was one of those admonishing bishops through this letter. We also suspect that Charles, in correcting himself, was referring to the earlier admonition proposed by Paulinus at the Council of Frankfurt, to which he perhaps did not promptly assent, and that the letter was therefore written around this time.

We think the date of this petition—where, incidentally, according to the observation of D. Borjon as reported in *Journal des savants*, volume III, year 1683, article 157, Charles the Great was for the first time honored with the title “majesty,” previously bestowed on no prince—was the year 800. Although Baluze places the people’s petition under the eighth capitulary of the year 803, this is because Charles had previously promised that he would confirm at a fuller synod what he had already granted; this he did in 803. The petition of the people, however, had already been made, as is clear from Charles’s first response, in which he both grants what is being asked for in the meantime and refers the confirmation of what he grants to a fuller synod. That synod was the Council of Worms of 803, under whose name Baluze records the concession confirmed in that year.

In the *Councils of Gaul*, volume II, cited by Thomassinus in *The Old and New Discipline of the Church*, part III, book I, chapter 40, it is assigned to the year 800. Therefore Paulinus’s admonition perhaps appeared in that year, and before Charles was called emperor, since the letter is addressed to him as king.] [Col. 0503D]

I warn and earnestly entreat you, most devout prince, by him who said to his disciples and apostles, whose unworthy representatives we are, “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew VI:24), and “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X): that you, with the Lord’s assistance, may fight on our behalf against visible enemies for the love of Christ, while we, praying to the Lord for you against invisible enemies, fight with spiritual weapons;

and that the priests of the Lord may be permitted, in accordance with evangelical, apostolic, and canonical rules, simply to serve and fight for the Lord in the Lord’s own camps alone, since, according to the same Lord’s words, “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24), and Paul says, “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2:4).

Let no one flatter himself that he can serve both God and the world, because the one who testifies that this cannot be done is Truth itself and cannot lie.

## SECOND LETTER. THE SAME AUTHOR AS ABOVE, ON RULERS

[Note: [Col. 0505B]

We suspect that this letter was written by Paulinus shortly before the Council of Frankfurt and perhaps presented to the council, serving as a kind of complaint addressed to those to whom it was directed—namely, Charles and the bishops of the council. It appears to have achieved the desired effect, since several provisions were enacted in the council’s canons according to Paulinus’s wishes and intention.

What prompts us to believe that it preceded the council, or at least did not follow it, is Baluze’s observation. In the preface to book I of his *Miscellanea*, he states: “These fragments seemed so important to the ancients that they were copied into the Gallican synods of those times and into the capitularies of the Frankish kings.” Here one sees that Paulinus did not borrow his opinions from the Gallican synods; rather, the Gallican synods borrowed their opinions from Paulinus.

Since at the Council of Frankfurt, which must be counted among the Gallican councils, opinions are sometimes inserted in Paulinus’s very words, as will soon be evident, it follows that the council’s canons, the letters, and the writings containing those opinions must necessarily have preceded it.

There are two principal abuses that Paulinus attacks and attempts to uproot: the misuse of ecclesiastical revenues and the failure of personal residence.

Concerning the first he complains in these words:

“Ecclesiastical possessions, which are called the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor, by which the faithful, inflamed with the ardor of faith and desiring the remedy of their souls and the heavenly homeland, enriched the holy Church so that the Church of God might be adorned by them, the soldiers of Christ nourished, the poor refreshed, and captives redeemed when circumstances required it—those who seize them, not as shepherds but as plunderers, do not hesitate to spend them on military service and worldly vanity against divine law.”

As Baluze notes in the margin, this passage is also found in book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 77, and almost word for word in book I of the Council of Aachen of 816, chapter 116. Compare, I ask, the cited passage of the council with Paulinus’s words, and you will see that the Fathers constructed their canon from his very words, so pleased were they with his judgment.

For if one removes the words, “Ecclesiastical possessions are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor”—which are not Paulinus’s, but Prosper’s, or more accurately Julianus Pomerius’s, book II of *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 9, and which are also inserted in the spurious decretal letter of Pope Urban I, chapter 2—the remaining words of the Council of Aachen’s canon continue up to *redimerentur*, “might be redeemed.”

The uses to which Paulinus asserted that the goods of the Church ought to be put, and which the Council of Aachen consequently affirmed—namely, the adornment of the church, the support of the soldiers of the faith, the relief of the poor, and the redemption of captives—were recognized as an ancient institution, since they are mentioned by the earlier Fathers of the Church.

Tertullian, in chapter 39 of his *Apology*, speaking of the collections of his own time and their use, says:

“Each person contributes a modest sum on a monthly day, or whenever he wishes—if indeed he wishes, and if he is able. For no one is compelled, but contributes voluntarily. These are, as it were, deposits of piety; for from them funds are not spent on banquets, drinking, or thankless gluttony, but on feeding and burying the needy, on supporting boys and girls who lack resources and parents, and likewise on aged householders, shipwreck victims, and those who are confined in the mines, on islands, or in prisons, provided that they have become wards of the confession of their faith for the sake of God’s sect.”

Saint Ambrose also, writing to the emperor Valentinian in letter 18, class 1, of the latest edition, attacks the detractors of the Church by showing for what purposes the gifts of the faithful were expended:

“Church property,” he says, “is the support of the needy. Let them count how many captives the temples have redeemed, what nourishment they have provided to the poor, and to how many exiles they have supplied the means of living.”

But on this matter we should hear Saint Agobard, who recalls both the ancient canonical decrees and the practice of his own times in his book *On the Administration of Ecclesiastical Goods*, especially no. 19, where he says:

“The sacred canons established a method for administering ecclesiastical possessions: namely, that they should be spent on feeding the needy, supporting the clergy, repairing buildings, and supplying the needs of the rulers, as the examples of the saints commend. There is no doubt that this practice was maintained until very recent times.”

These last words seem to indicate that Agobard was referring to constitutions enacted either in councils or in capitularies during the time of Charlemagne and Paulinus, whose publication Paulinus perhaps urged through this admonition in order to preserve the ancient canons.

For Papirius Masson, in his prefaces to Agobard, observed that Agobard was “born in the golden age of Charlemagne, nourished by the illustrious and most learned Apollini, flourishing in the silver age of Louis, and extinguished amid the iron struggles of Louis’s sons at Saintes.” Remembering, then, the recent constitutions enacted by Charles, or by Charles’s authority and under his auspices, and promoted by Paulinus, Agobard could very appropriately say that the proper method of preserving the ancient canons concerning the administration of ecclesiastical possessions had been maintained “until 189 very recent times.”

The Council of Frankfurt did indeed establish several provisions on this matter, especially in canons 27, 42, and 49.

[Col. 0507B] As for the other subject of Paulinus’s complaint—namely, those who refused to remain in their own parishes—compare the canons of the Council of Frankfurt [Col. 0507C] with Paulinus’s complaint, and you will immediately recognize where they came from.

Paulinus was distressed that they “teach well by no words, but badly by their example.”

The council addressed this evil in canon 30:

“That each bishop should teach and instruct well, so that worthy men may always be found in the house of God who can canonically be elected.”

Moreover, for the requirement that they teach well by words, see canons 34 and 54; and for the requirement that they not teach badly by their example, see canons 20, 35, and 37.

Paulinus also complained that, “against the divine will, sacred institution, and apostolic and canonical authority, they were not absent from the Church entrusted to them for merely three weeks at most, but for a much longer time, abandoning their own sees and peoples, without shame.”

Following the pattern of the complaint, the council established in canon 7:

“That a bishop should not move from city to city, but should care for his own Church; likewise, a priest and a deacon should canonically remain in his own Church.”

And again, more specifically, in canon 42:

“That no bishop should lose his own see by frequenting another place, or dare to remain on his own properties for more than three weeks.”

He further complained about neglected preaching; and the council orders in canon 34:

“That the Catholic faith of the holy Trinity, the Lord’s Prayer, and the creed of the faith be preached and handed down.”

He complained about the abandonment of divine worship; and the council decreed in canon 22:

“That the Lord’s Day be observed from evening until evening.”

In short, at least for the greater part, the provisions enacted by the council appear to have been excerpted from Paulinus’s admonition.

But above all it must be noted that, at the end of this fragment, Paulinus says that it had been determined by the Councils of Sardica and Africa how many weeks a bishop might be absent from his church, and when and for what reasons he should go to and remain at the royal palace. Since, however, from canon 56 of the Council of Frankfurt one sees that Charlemagne was concerned that the synod should grant him permission to keep Bishop Hildebald with him, just as, after seeking permission from the pope, he retained Archbishop Angilram, it may be clearly evident that Paulinus’s complaint instilled a scruple in Charlemagne, prompting him to say and request such things from the council. Add that Benedict the Levite teaches us in the preface to the three later books of the *Capitularies* that Paulinus himself, together with Alcuin, collected several chapters at Charlemagne’s direction, which were subsequently inserted into the capitularies. With still greater justice, therefore, we should believe that the canons of Frankfurt themselves were Paulinus’s work, since he took part in the synod and almost presided over it. Since they correspond to his memorandum, this is a sign that, by the authority of the Fathers, he applied a remedy where he had previously exposed the sore.]

The first point is that they teach badly, not by their words but by their examples [Col. 0506A]. Second, contrary to the divine will, the sacred institution, and apostolic and canonical authority, they are not ashamed to remain away—not merely for at least three weeks, but for a long time—from the churches entrusted to them, abandoning their own sees and congregations, setting aside divine counsel and authority, and likewise setting aside preaching, instruction, correction, the assignment of the Spirit the Paraclete, the consecration of the sacred holy chrism, and every sacred institution. They do not fear to roam about indiscriminately—not casually, but like plunderers and armed soldiers—in order to stir up and provoke those who shed blood and commit many crimes. Those who ought to govern God’s people and the Church entrusted to them by praying, teaching, and preaching, and ought to appease God’s clemency toward the human race [188], instead, by acting wickedly, as we have said, do not cease to increase the discipline, vengeance, and anger of divine judgment. Thus is fulfilled what prophecy threatens through the Holy Spirit: “As is the people, so also is the priest” (Isaiah XV).

They do not hesitate to seize the goods of the Church—which are called the offerings of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor—goods with which the faithful, inflamed by the ardor of faith and love of Christ, enriched the holy Church for the salvation of their souls and their longing for the heavenly homeland, so that through them the Church of God might be adorned, the soldiers of Christ nourished, the poor refreshed, and captives redeemed when circumstances required—and to spend them, not as shepherds but as brigands, on military service and worldly vanity, contrary to divine law. Hence it can very easily be inferred that they love earthly things more than heavenly ones and fear mortal men more than the Lord, since it is written: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V). And again the apostles say: “It is not right for us to abandon the word of God and serve tables” (Acts VI).

For this reason, neither on the principal festivals and solemnities of the year, nor even during the days of Lenten observance—which are consecrated to salvation and penitence and ought to be spent with great devotion, when we should watch especially assiduously and attentively over the care of souls—do we deserve to remain in our own parishes and cities. Consequently, the worship of God is abandoned, preaching among the congregations and care of those subject to us are neglected, especially since such roaming is neither compatible with the priestly ministry nor sanctioned by canonical authority.

For it is read in the Council of Sardica, chapter 15, that a bishop ought not to be absent from his church for more than three weeks. In chapter 8 of the same council it was established when and for what reasons bishops should go to the palace. It is read in the African Council, chapter 62, that a universal council should be held only from necessity. Likewise, in the same council: bishops should not be detained for too long at a council. It is also read in ecclesiastical history that, when Julian wished to bring about the abandonment of the Christian religion, he hastened to distract and detain the bishops of the churches away from their cities, so that through their absence the Church might be dissolved; and, since there would be no one to teach them, the peoples would for a long time suffer the loss of remembrance of their own religion.

## EPISTLE III. THE SAME AUTHOR TO CHARLES THE EMPEROR

[Note: [Col. 0508C] This letter, or fragment of a letter, bears at its beginning the address “to Charles the emperor,” sufficiently suggesting thereby that it was written after 25 December 800, when Charles was crowned at Rome by Leo III and hailed by the people as emperor. If, however, the admonitions, indeed even the wording, of the letter are weighed more carefully, it seems to indicate not obscurely that it was delivered at the very time of the imperial inauguration.
