For since Paulinus well knew that he was exceedingly dear to Charles, he appears here, on the basis of their intimacy, to suggest certain things suited to a newly made emperor and to instruct him rightly in exercising his new government, so that he would not cease to increase the dignity of the holy Church—which in temporal affairs is likewise imperial dignity and majesty—with virtues worthy of an emperor. Although he had always previously done this, it is nevertheless clear that after receiving the august diadem Charles performed the duty more diligently, from what Dungalus, a deacon and monk of Saint-Denis in Paris, later wrote in his letter concerning the eclipse of the year 810. Dacherius publishes it in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 156, and Thomasinus mentions it in *Vetus et Nova Ecclesiae Disciplina*, part II, book I, chapter 100, no. 7. Among other things it contains the following:

“Charles, who is regarded equally by all as the foremost teacher of all good works, virtues, and honorable disciplines, and as the perfect exemplar: for rulers, in governing their subjects; for soldiers, in exercising their military service lawfully; for clerics, in rightly observing the rite of the universal Christian religion; for philosophers and scholars, in philosophizing and acquiring wisdom honorably concerning human matters, and in thinking and believing reverently and orthodoxly concerning divine matters.”

These are practically all the qualities that Paulinus desires in Charles in his letter.]

It is expedient for you, venerable prince, to train bishops in the investigation of the sacred Scriptures and in sound and sober doctrine; the entire clergy in discipline; philosophers in knowledge of divine and human matters; monks in religious observance; and everyone generally in holiness. Train leading men in counsel, judges in justice, soldiers in the practice of arms, prelates in humility, subjects in obedience, and everyone generally in prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, peace, and harmony.

With these and similar qualities, excellent man, and with God favorable to you, do not cease to increase the dignity of the holy Church, so that in the administration of ecclesiastical or civil affairs you may be energetic and overflowing with the fountain of wisdom, and may triumph through the display of virtue.

## EPISTLE IV. PAULINUS, AS IT SEEMS, TO POPE LEO III

[Note: [Col. 0509C]

We came upon this letter, or fragment of a letter, when we were going through volume IV of Stephen Baluzius’s *Miscellanea*, where it is presented on p. 412 under this title: “From a letter of Paulinus to Leo the patriarch.” The name Paulinus immediately prompted us to re-examine the letter, and, by comparing its style with Paulinus’s other works, we detected a considerable—indeed, very great—similarity, as anyone making the comparison can see.

Since more than one error had crept into the course of the letter, we thought that one had also crept into the title, and that it ought to have been written: “From a letter of Paulinus the patriarch to Leo.” We suppose that this reversal—*hysteron proteron* (ὕστερον πρότερον, “later-before”)—was caused by the ignorance or haste of the copyist. Moreover, we compared all the Paulinuses of any repute whom we could find among ecclesiastical writers, men distinguished by patriarchal dignity, among the Latins—for it cannot be doubted that this letter is the work of a Latin writer—who lived in the times when pontiffs named Leo occupied the Roman see. We found no one to whom this writing could be assigned except our own Paulinus, who flourished in the time of Pope Leo III. Paulinus himself also indicates his dignity in the body of the letter when he calls him the supreme pontiff: “And let them offer him, as is fitting for so great and supreme a pontiff, the honor due . . .”

The supreme pontiff is the pope, who may also be called patriarch, as the chief of the Fathers of the whole Church; and in fact the Roman patriarch is often found so called. This may perhaps please some people more and seem more probable than the error of transposition which, as we said above, we thought was present in the writing. Whatever the case may be, although the letter seems to us assignable to no one other than Paulinus, we put this forward modestly and add “as it seems,” lest we have to deal with those who readily seek a knot in a bulrush.

If we have correctly grasped its purpose, this letter appears to have been written in the case of Felix, bishop of Urgell, against whom Paulinus himself had written several times. Felix was the one who, like a wandering sheep from the embrace of the Church, and like that wounded man lying between Jerusalem and Jericho, needed to be brought back and healed. He was a member cut off from the body of the Church, whom Paulinus was striving, through Leo’s gentleness and charity, once again to incorporate and unite with the other members.

Since Leo had convened a council in 799 concerning Felix, fragments of whose three sessions still survive, we think that this letter was written before that time, and perhaps that through it the pope was moved to convene the synod and to move the final stone, so that the unhappy man might come to his senses.

It will be clear to the reader that not a few errors have crept into the transcription of the letter. Lacking the manuscripts, we thought it better to leave them uncorrected than to produce something based on our own judgment.]

[Col. 0509B] For it must be understood that both the man who, descending from Jerusalem—that is, withdrawing from the peaceful contemplation of the holy Church—and the one who is said to have been expelled from the walls of paradise—that is, who went out separated from the sheepfold of the Church and the fellowship of the brethren—and every member that has been cut off from the body—that is, separated from the unity of the Church—unless, through penitence and worthy satisfaction, he ascends by the gift of the grace of almighty God to Jerusalem, namely, raises himself to the contemplation of peace, and returns to the sheepfold he had abandoned, that is, being bound again by the bond of charity, is received into the bosom of the Church and inserted into the body from which he was cut off, namely, into unity, and is reconciled and joined to the brethren, can be saved—just as you, in your exceptional [190], holier, and more profound understanding, know well—must not flatter himself in any way through falsehood, deceived by fraud.

Woe, then, to them, unless the highest mercy comes benignly to their aid through a gracious example: mercy that compassionately assists the half-dead man left on the road, the wandering and lost little sheep, and the precious member cut off from the body, with the purple of blood.

May your serenity therefore deign to pour wine and oil over these wounds and this injury of sin. Having sprinkled them, apply gently the soothing remedies of instruction; and, with the medicinal hand, bind and fill the fractures with the little bands of charity, so that, carried upon the beast of your patience, they may be brought to the inn of the Church. May you rejoice to report the care shown by your blessedness—and thereby, being uniquely likened to the good shepherd, carrying the wandering sheep upon your shoulders—to its own fold, namely, to the bosom of Mother Church.

Indeed, hasten in every way, imitating the Apostle Paul, to unite the members separated from the body to the supreme and unique Head through the unity of faith and the harmony of charity; so that, when peace has been restored to all through your diligence, they may offer him, as is fitting for so great and supreme a pontiff, the fruits of due honor and obedience; may fear the Lord; and, like a father, love him with the great sweetness of devoted affection. May your kindness and tranquility, cherishing them as your own sons, govern them under perpetual protection; and may the eternal Judge deign to grant you the heavenly kingdoms as the reward of a worthy recompense.

[Col. 0511]

# 191 LETTER OF SAINT PAULINUS TO CHARLEMAGNE CONCERNING THE PROCEEDINGS OF THE SYNOD CELEBRATED AT ALTINUM IN THE YEAR 803

[Note: [Col. 0515]

## NOTES ON THE LETTER CONCERNING THE SYNOD OF ALTINUM. PREFATORY NOTICE

[Col. 0515B] If any work seems to require comparison with some old manuscript, this one certainly requires it more than any other. Baronius published the beginning and end of the letter from a very corrupt Vatican manuscript. Baluzius, from the papers of Sirmond, gives the complete letter in volume VII of the *Miscellanea*, p. 6, but it is equally full of errors. We have selected what seemed the better reading at the beginning and end of the letter, since these portions could at least be compared in some fashion with the printed editions. What we have from the middle solely from Baluzius’s edition we present untouched, merely pointing out in the notes the barbarous and sometimes meaningless expressions, while always fearing that we might easily stray from the goal of truth.]

[Col. 0511A] I. To the Catholic and ever-renowned triumphant lord Charles, crowned by divine clemency and emperor [Note: [Col. 0515B] “Emperor.” So the Vatican manuscript cited by Baronius under the year 802, no. 7, and in the Council editions of Labbe. Baluzius has “king.”], Paulinus, the least of all servants [Note: [Col. 0515B] “Servant of servants,” in agreement. “Servant” is lacking in Baluzius.], with concordant and equal devotion, together with our brethren and fellow priests [Note: [Col. 0515C] “And with our fellow priests.” Baluzius has “and fellow priests.”], in the rosy blood of Christ Jesus, offer multiplied eternal greetings in a humble, supplicatory, and harmonious voice.

II. Since the sacred and vigorous admonitions of the canons of our fathers [Note: [Col. 0515C] “Of the paternal canons.” Baluzius has “of the paternal canons,” feminine; the present reading is masculine.] strongly urge this, and your—as truth resounds—honeyed and health-giving syllables sprinkle it [Note: [Col. 0515D] “And your . . . syllables.” The Frankish kings often urge bishops in their capitularies to convene synods. The first capitulary of Carloman, 742, chapter 1, orders one to be held once a year; the capitulary of Verneuil under Pippin, 755, chapter 4, twice a year; likewise the Council of Aachen under Charlemagne in 789, chapter 13, orders bishops to assemble for a synod. Paulinus was referring to these.], we have thought it worthwhile humbly to announce, under the name of the king, to the most tranquil ears of your serenity, in these humble notes—however uncultivated their letters—that, by God’s authorization, a council was held at Altinum in this see, in which I serve, unworthy as I am, with unworthy service [Note: [Col. 0515C] “To announce.” Baluzius has “to weaken.”].

[Col. 0511B] For neither is it lawful in justice, nor can any sanction of rational form, arranged by whatever teachable pen, be regarded as clearly established unless it has been more thoroughly examined by judicial decision and, after the manner of silver, purified from its harsh rust by a sevenfold refining in the fire. Then, supported by the judgment of many, it may rightly appear venerable when inserted into the sacred pages. Otherwise, as I think, it will be able to be considered credible only according to the personal judgment of the writer.

III. When, in accordance with the agreement, the priestly assembly had been canonically summoned and had gathered together in religious devotion, it is immediately established that they unanimously investigated, with the greatest possible speed and the keenest subtlety, every matter of active business, as the most solemn order of that religious council declares [Note: [Col. 0515D] “As the order of the council declares.” The First Council of Auvergne, 535, canon 1, established that general cases should be treated first and particular cases afterward. Paulinus does this here, first defining common matters of faith and the Church, then proposing that the murder of the patriarch of Grado be avenged. This canon is inserted in book VII of the *Capitularies*, chapter 264.]: namely, the cause of orthodox faith; the condition and beautiful dignity of the ecclesiastical summit; the ruinous loss of every kind of property; every necessary petition of those who murmured; all matters about which one could complain justly and rightly; and the presentation of whose plaintive dispute, worn down by the knotty allegation of lawsuits, nevertheless desired to be resolved and disentangled by priestly judgment.

IV. In accordance with the very limited capacity of our humble smallness and our exceedingly slight and, as was fitting, inadequate understanding—not as it would have been worthy and fitting according to consummate perfection, nor as the scrutiny of so great a government required—but insofar as the highest clemency, graciously consenting, deigned freely to bestow upon us undeserving men, we attempted to explain, as the nature of the matter more fully demanded, the complaints concerning each of the unavoidable affairs.

Since these matters, in accordance with the accustomed practice of our will—which is not unknown to your glory [Note: [Col. 0516B] “Of our will, not unknown.” He has said “not unknown” more modestly [194] instead of “sufficiently known.” The meaning is otherwise sometimes the same, as in Virgil, *Georgics* II.129:

“They mingled herbs and words not harmless.”

And in *Aeneid* XI.27, concerning Pallas:

“Whom the dark day, though not lacking in valor,

Carried away and plunged into bitter death.”

This is equivalent to “words not harmful,” and to one endowed with valor.]—as we stated at the beginning of this letter, we have decided to leave them to the free judgment of your authority, reserving them nevertheless for your decision. Thus, weighed on the subtle and moderate balance of your judgment, if they should be found to be of no importance because the scale of your moderation has relaxed too far on the unfavorable side, let them be abolished and quietly suppressed by the judgment of your authority. If, however, with the balance held evenly, they can perhaps be approved as possessing some usefulness, let them, strengthened by your assistance, vigorously grow firm.

V. But if, as a mere pruning, the foliage of wandering branches [Note: [Col. 0516B] “The fruit-bearing foliage of the branches.” This period seems inaccessible because of the barbarous expressions and awkward transposition of words. I do not understand *fruticantem* here; should one read *fructicas* or *fruticantium*?] requires a pruning hook, let it be done only so that, after the defective shoots have been cut back at the trunk and, so to speak, burned in the furnace of your wisdom, they may be reduced to ashes of the smoke-producing kitchen [Note: [Col. 0516B] “To the ashes of the smoky kitchen.” I think this means the same as *fulina*. “A *fulina* is a kitchen, from the soot with which kitchens are stained,” says Isidore, cited by Du Cange.]. Thus, once they have been expelled, may the vineyards of our poverty, partly pruned and pure, suspended on a honey-flowing, jewel-like vine, redden with the rich abundance of grapes by some proper right [Note: [Col. 0516C] “May it redden by a proper right.” It is impossible to determine what this means, unless there is a corruption, as I suspect.].

Therefore, once it has been made known to the nations . . . [lacuna] . . . may a new Falernian wine of sound doctrine turn golden in cups, with the *triones* [uncertain] pressed in little bags by the weight of ingenuity in the winepress of minds. When it has been healthfully drained to the bottom, may the sorrowing hearts, renewed [192] with the sweetness of its flavor, immediately be filled with joy and shine with gladness. This refers to that drinking of wine of which the Psalmist sang figuratively, saying: “Bread,” he says, “strengthens the heart of man, and wine gladdens it” (Psalm CIII.15); and again: “They shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delights” (Psalm XXXV.9) [Note: [Col. 0516C] “Of delights,” according to the Hebrew, as in Bruno of Würzburg here.].

VI. For behold, having crossed the bed of the balsam-bearing Jordan [Note: [Col. 0516C] “The balsam-bearers having crossed the channel of the Jordan.” *Balsigeri* is an unknown word. Could it mean *balsamigeri Jordanis*, “the balsam-bearing Jordan,” since balsam grows in Judea, through which the river Jordan flows? Hence Statius, *Silvae* I.5.213, says:

“Palestinian and Hebrew liquids.”

He is alluding to those who were entrusted by Moses with exploring the land of promise, as in Numbers XIII; as a sign of the land’s fertility, they carried back pomegranates, figs, and a cluster of grapes with its vine on a pole. Hence the suspicion arises whether by *balsigeri* these bearers of fruit—and perhaps also of the balsam that grows in Judea—might be meant. Let the reader judge.], and having entered the land of promise while following Jesus as leader, we immediately undertook to plant fruitful trees, compelled by the command [Note: [Col. 0516D] “Compelled by the command.” Leviticus XIX.23.], which is likewise read as having been set forth in figurative proclamation.

Accordingly, in the first, second, and third year, we refused to touch or taste the first fruits of those trees, which we had been forbidden to gather; nor did we think that any of them should be desired even with the greatest longing, deceived by greedy fraud, with the tip of the tongue licking them [Note: [Col. 0517A] “With the tip of the tongue licking.” Perhaps “touching with the tongue.”]. Soon we saw that their foreskins ought more honorably to be cut away with the knife of discernment, and we judged that, wrapped in the thinnest leaves of words, they should remain untouched, lest, dissolved in exceedingly wanton softness and flowing with the tender delicacy of excessive pride, and not at all drenched with the juice of humility, they should, with the taste of ripe sweetness [Note: [Col. 0517A] “With the taste of ripe sweetness, juicy.” Perhaps *succidua*, “about to fall,” since he is speaking of fruits whose ripening has been delayed and which are not yet *succidua*, that is, near to falling.], provoke the eater’s throat more toward the vomit of pride than, sweetly softened by the grace of nourishment, gently delight the receptacles of the stomach.

But now, since the legal permission to eat of their fruits has been granted in this year [Note: [Col. 0517A] “Now, however, legal permission to eat their fruits has been granted this year, Moses’ pen restraining in every respect”—that is, yielding, favoring, or consenting. Du Cange teaches through numerous examples and authorities in his *Glossary* that *cohibere* is often used in this sense. Since Paulinus had once adopted the Levitical legal precept concerning not eating the fruits of trees in order to explain the delay in celebrating the council, he continues the allegory by using the words of the precept. Hence he says that permission has been legally granted, with Moses consenting, as though he were simply saying: “There is now nothing to delay the celebration of the council.”], I judge that it is not inappropriate if I desire to eat of them more eagerly with a humble and simple palate. “Who plants a vineyard,” says the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0517B] “Who plants,” and so forth, from 1 Corinthians IX.7. Baluzius has *plantivit*, but this is an error, perhaps of the printer.], “and does not eat of its fruit” (1 Corinthians IX.7)? And who feeds a flock or presses the udders and, deprived of the sweetness of milk, wasting away in fasting, becomes dried up in the stomach?

VII. But we thought it much better to bring all these things together in one bundle and carry them, as a dish of our style, before your serene countenances, so that, by the judgment of your discernment, the sharp fruits—still not translucent with mature juice—might not be plucked by hand alone or, so to speak, shaken down by the golden-sounding rod of judgment, hidden among the syllables of those passing by, and trampled underfoot in the orchards [Note: [Col. 0517B] “In the orchards,” for *frutetis* or *fruticetis*.].

But whatever fruits may be found, if indeed they can be found, drenched by the sun’s rays and driving away gold with their beauty upon the bark [Note: [Col. 0517B] “They drive away gold with beauty upon the bark.” It may be that the clearer reading is *fuant decora in cortice*, “may they be beautiful upon the bark,” for *sint decora* or *fuerint*. Ancient Latins occasionally used *fuat* for *sit* or *fuerit*. Virgil, *Aeneid* X.113:

“Whether Trojan or Rutulian he be, I shall make no distinction.”

Servius explains this passage: “*Fuat*, that is, *fuerit*; a defective verb of the future tense.”] and plucked with a rational finger, painted with multicolored little palms [Note: [Col. 0517B] “Painted with multicolored little palms.” A species is used for the genus: *palmulae* are dates, or *dactyli*. Varro, *De re rustica* I.67: “The walnut, the date, and the Sabine fig: the sooner you bring them out, the more pleasantly you will use them; for with age the fig becomes paler, the date thicker, and the nut drier.”], may they be returned to your judgment, fragrant in baskets, for the use of those who will enjoy them—even if they are not worthy of the noble, they may perhaps be necessarily reserved for the poor.

For I know that your boys are highly accomplished men, skilled in and energetic practitioners of this art. Through their splendid labor and the graceful charm of their words, they—who, having exercised the ingenuity of a clever pen of the tongue, are not ignorant of dipping the pen into the tincture of the mind [Note: [Col. 0517C] “In the tincture of the mind, not ignorant of dipping.” The negative is redundant. He uses *tinctum* for a vessel of ink or for the ink itself, which medieval writers called *tinctum* or *tincta*. Lucifer of Cagliari, *On Dying for the Son of God*: “Remember how many he has cast down through the steep descent of a single stroke of your signature.” That is, a single signature, made with tincture or ink. Among the Spaniards *tincta* still means ink; see Du Cange’s *Glossary*. Paulinus is here repaying the services of the men whom Charles kept at his court, perhaps Alcuin, who had written to him in Letter 62: “I see that the Aristotelian proverb is more truly fulfilled in you, since, writing the exceedingly acute arguments of the *Perihermeniae*, you are said to have dipped your pen into your mind.” Thus he acknowledges that they know how to dip the pen of the tongue into the tincture of the mind.], will be able, in every respect according to your great-sounding commands, both to correct errors and more carefully to separate the wheat flour from the tares of vices. They are held by royal hands, however, more moderately than that golden and royal pruning hook [Note: [Col. 0517C] “Who are held by royal hands more moderately than by that golden and royal pruning hook.” I confess that I do not grasp the meaning of the words [Col. 0517D]. I suspect that something is missing. Perhaps he intended to suggest that King Charles himself possesses the pruning hook—that is, wisdom—by which he could correct errors without another’s assistance. But this is conjecture.]

[Col. 0513C] VIII. Without doubt they themselves also carry their own pruning hooks, sharpened with finely toothed files, suspended from girding bands and carried in shoulder straps [Note: [Col. 0517D] “They carry them suspended from girding bands in shoulder straps.” Supply “pruning hooks.” Here *cinctoriis* should be taken adjectivally and seems to belong with *strophiis*, so that they may be distinguished from the *strophium*, the crown placed on the head, as in Pliny, *Natural History* XXI.2. Since weapons are carried suspended from a belt, he called the shoulder straps *strophia cinctoria*. Properly, a *strophium* is a woman’s breast-band. Nonius, concerning kinds of clothing: “A *strophium* is a short band that restrains the maidenly movement of the breasts.” Theodulf of Orléans therefore used it properly in *Carmina* III.1.106, speaking of Charles’s daughters:

“One wears a milk-white breast-band, another a red one.”

Nevertheless, it is sometimes used of men. Turpilius, cited by Nonius, chapter 14, no. 8: “Woe is me, what shall I do? An unfortunate letter fell from me between the roads, between the tunic and the breast-band where I had placed it.” So too Paul the Deacon in his hymn concerning John the Baptist:

“The camel offered a harsh covering

For his sacred limbs, a double-toothed breast-band.”

The verb “pruning hooks” must be understood here although it is not expressed, because just above he had spoken of the royal pruning hook. He now passes from the agricultural pruning hook to the military sickle, for soldiers too are given sickles. Claudian, *On the Consulship of Stilicho* I.110:

“Neither did the Gelonian men drive them back with sickles,

Nor the Getae with bows, nor the Sarmatian with his spear.”

G. Barthius explains: “The Gelonian sickle: a curved sword customary among that people.”]

Although they are not without weapons of war, being equipped with threefold coats of mail [Note: [Col. 0518A] “With threefold coats of mail,” for *triformibus* or *trilicibus*. A *trilix* is a well-known coat of mail, from Virgil, *Aeneid* III.467:

“A coat of mail fastened with hooks and triple-woven with gold.”

And VII.639:

“A coat of mail triple-woven with gold is put on.”

Adrian Turnebus, *Adversaria* XXIX.35: “Coats of mail are apparently called *trilices* because, although they were joined together with iron hooks or scales, they were also furnished with three threads running through them.”] and equipped with crested helmets, they advance to war, most learned men that they are.

I know that one of them is among the thirty nobles [Note: [Col. 0518B] “I know that one of them is among the thirty nobles,” and so forth. Here he alludes to David’s mighty men, as related in 2 Samuel XXIII, designating the learned men who were associated with King Charles. It is not probable that by this allusion he intended to refer to exactly thirty learned men living at court who surpassed the others. Rather, as we said above in the note at letter *l*, just as the passage of Scripture concerning the five years to be observed before eating the fruit of trees did not indicate a chronological period to which Paulinus referred, but merely a delay in the celebration of the council, so here the Scripture concerning David’s outstanding soldiers does not imply a similar number of learned men whom these surpassed. It seems only to indicate that they surpassed the others, learned and cultivated though they were, whatever their number. I think Alcuin held the most prominent place among them; perhaps Richbodus and Theodulf, bishops to whom Alcuin wished to send his books together with Paulinus, as the most learned among the king’s companions, should be added. Nor should Angilram and Hildebald, bishops whose assistance Charles himself had testified that he needed at the Council of Frankfurt, canon 55, be omitted.], another most renowned among the three, and a leader above the three most celebrated; also three other exceedingly brave young men, by whose flashing spears the enemies of the Church, the Philistines—that is, evil spirits or heretics—may be driven back here and there in bloody slaughter, and the camps cut down.

These are the bravest leaders of the camps and also the wisest cultivators of the Lord’s vineyard. I do not wish them to pursue me with all their strength, but, overlooking the faults of my merits, to extend to me the hand of indulgence. For it is not a great boast, nor will the garland of a triumph be judged to be the crown of a victorious recruit, if it has been reddened with the blood of an unarmed little frog.

IX. But if giants attempt to break in upon me in their violent attack, I beseech you, venerable prince, for the sake of mercy exemplified in me [Note: [Col. 0518C] “By example.” Perhaps *extemplo*, “immediately”?], do not hesitate to extend your wings, spread far and wide, and, by this shield of kindness held before me and the darts prepared by your lips, do not allow me to be trampled by their violent feet.

And if one of them, boasting that he carries Hercules’ club beneath his strong shoulder [Note: [Col. 0518C] “Boasting that he carries Hercules with a strong club beneath his shoulder.” It seems that one should read: “the Herculean club beneath his strong shoulder.”], should come step by step, secretly or openly, and wickedly attempt to strike and shatter the brain of my head with a blow violently driven into it [Col. 0514A], so that, inflamed by mocking taunts, he might begin, foaming with his companions and with spittle poured [195] between his teeth [Note: [Col. 0518C] “Foaming with spittle poured between his teeth.” *Salibo* is used for *saliva*, “spittle.” Du Cange’s *Glossary*: “*Salibum* for *saliva* in the Alamannic Law, title 64, §2, in Herold’s edition.” Baluzius, however, in the second capitulary of Dagobert, or the Alamannic Law, title 63, §2, has *salivam*.], eagerly to curl his mocking laughter at the collision caused by this work [Note: [Col. 0518D] “To curl his laughter.” *Cachinnum*, “laughter,” should be read instead of *cacinnum*. He says that laughter is “curled,” indicating the movement of the mouth that occurs in laughing. Strictly, he should have said “to curl the gape.” The gape is opened and moved apart when someone gives himself over to laughter. Horace, book I of the *Satires*, verse 950, or satire X, verse 7:

“Therefore it is not enough to stretch the laughing mouth.”

Laughter poured forth, by which the gape and face are twisted, is a *cachinnus*, the loud laugh itself, or the action while it occurs. Ovid, *The Art of Love* III.287:]

There is one who distorts faces with a perverse guffaw. ]; let Banaias [Note: [Col. 0518D] Benaiah son of Jehoiada, David’s confidential chamberlain, with a staff, who might wrest a club from a man. In II Kings XXIII, vv. 20, 21, 22, and 23, it is read: “Benaiah son of Jehoiada [Col. 0519A], when he had gone down with a staff to an Egyptian man, forcibly wrested the spear from the Egyptian’s hand and killed him with his own spear. These things Benaiah son of Jehoiada did; he too was named among the three mighty men; and David made him his confidential chamberlain.” If anyone among Charles’s courtiers is perhaps indicated by this Scripture, I would believe him to have been Angilbert, abbot of Centula, who was one of Charlemagne’s confidential advisers, as is clear from the letter, or memorandum, addressed to him when he was sent to Rome in 796 to Pope Leo III. For it is inscribed: “Charles, by the grace of God king and defender of the holy Church, greets Homer, his confidential chamberlain.” Behold David’s chamberlain. For Charles was called David by his own people, just as Angilbert was called Homer and Richulf Damoetas.] son of Jehoiada, David’s secret chamberlain, hasten to him immediately with the utmost speed—he who, with a staff, can wrest the club from the man’s hand—not, however, for his final and fatal destruction, so that, with confidence in his strength lost and dried up, he may be reduced to despair [Note: “Quo circo.” Or perhaps *quo circa*, that is, “for which reason confidence may be dried up,” meaning emptied out, so that the sense would be, “for which reason he may not be driven to despair.” But I still would not dare claim that I have grasped the legitimate sense.], but rather that, limb by limb, he may be bound by the bond of charity and the loop of humility to three or thirty very strong men.

### X.

Nevertheless, as we stated above in the persuasive voice of our pen, overcome by love of almighty God and compelled by concern for the advancement and honor of your holy mother Church, command us through your sacred words to make more clearly known whatever pleases or displeases you—or even if you judge nothing at all worthy of approval [Note: “Propalate.” Here *propalari* (“to be made known”) would apparently have been intended.]. Nor did we wish to pass this over, but rather preferred in every respect to learn the gentleness of your sincerity, since we have seen it right and proper to send the statutes of this council—not as general statutes, but as local or even particular ones—to the provincial bishops of this see and those in agreement with them [Note: The statutes of the council are not called “general” as opposed to “local,” etc., because they concerned only the discipline of its own province. Hence one may conclude that the council was provincial. See the dissertation on the Synod of Altinum, no. 21. These statutes have perished.], provided that they have been credibly strengthened by the authority of you and your faithful, or provided that your reaping sickle, bent within its circle, should allow some or even very many of them to escape unharmed [Note: “Should allow them to escape.” The sense is obscure. These and the following highly involved words seem to mean: “We have thought it right to send these statutes to you. If they are strengthened and confirmed by the authority of you and your people, or at least admitted and not cut away, so that, as it were, they have escaped correction and, supported by that authority, deserve to return to us, marked with the venerable sign of your indulgence”—yet we still leave it to each person’s discretion to reject what displeases him or embrace what pleases him.], and should deserve to return joyfully to the hands of our humility, which are girded with prosperous delight and swift favor of gladness, marked with the venerable sign of your indulgence [Col. 0514C]—not indeed [lacuna] for those to whom they might be agreeable, nor constrained for those to whom they might be displeasing—we nevertheless offer them, freely corrected, leaving each person the discretion to reject or embrace them. For we do not thrust the cups of this little draught unbidden into the throat of one who is disgusted, nor do we hastily snatch from the open mouth of one who eagerly buries [Note: “Nor of one who eagerly buries.” *Humare* means “to bury.” I therefore suspect the sense to be: “We do not withdraw the cups from the throat of one who buries wine,” that is, one who seems to bury it; thus he intensifies the eagerness of drinking, in accordance with Psalm 5:11: “Their throat is an open grave.”] full cups filled with the dew of Lyaeus, excepting, naturally, those to whom these wine-filled cups must in every way be offered through the service of our mouth, at opportune and inopportune times, as duty requires [Note: “Excepting these, naturally, to whom …” I think *excussis* is used for *exceptis* and carries the same meaning, so that the sense is: “We compel no one, whether disgusted or eagerly taking them, to accept these things—except those to whom we owe the duties of our mouth,” that is, those subject to us, residing in our province, whose salvation the Apostle commands us to care for by preaching at opportune and inopportune times.].

### XI.

As for the priests who have been subjected to wounds and left half alive, or certainly slain by the agents of the devil while a diabolical fury raged, the judgment will belong not to me but to your decision. I recall having read, in the height of your authority and in a certain judicial memorandum previously salutarily set forth by the holy Fathers of old [Note: “In a certain judicial memorandum, previously set forth by the holy Fathers of old … reserved.” I would not venture to assert which book he calls “judicial.” For there is not just one work among the Fathers—or rather among the councils—from which the defense of the Church and vengeance are commended to princes and kings. See Marca, *De Concordia sacerdotii et imperii*, book II, chapters 10 and 12. Nevertheless, we suspect that this memorandum was Paulinus’s own *Sacrosyllabum*, presented at the Council of Frankfurt and approved by the vote of the holy Fathers assembled there; this will become clearer from the following note. I say “I remember having read” that it was reserved because what he had previously prepared was read by him at the council, as we stated in Dissertation 4, no. 42, and in the *Life of Paulinus*, chapter 7, no. 3. The Fathers approved what had been read.], that it was reserved. For what reason they did this, I know with certainty has not escaped—and does not escape—the sacred memories of you [Note: “For what reason they did this has not escaped your …” In Baluzius these words, “they did this,” are absent.]. For they judged that no one else could avenge the holy Church for the injuries inflicted upon it with such power and royal severity, seeking from him in return the corresponding care [Note: “Seeking from him the corresponding care …” *Expetens* should be *expetentem* if it refers to the Church, or *expetentes* if it refers to the Fathers. At the end of Paulinus’s *Sacrosyllabum*, in the name of the Fathers of Frankfurt, he argued as follows: “Therefore our most tranquil prince must be entreated that he, with the Lord’s assistance, fight on our behalf against visible enemies for the love of Christ, while we, praying for him to the Lord’s power, fight on his behalf against invisible enemies with spiritual arms, so that on that day the Son of God may repay him with a reciprocal offering for His Church, so that, just as he now renders her secure amid so many worldly tumults, so she may make him a participant in the heavenly kingdom. May he mercifully forgive captives, assist the oppressed,” and so forth. Compare this with the words here: “Just as she [the Church], both in the present evil age, continually protects him with holy prayers, and amid wars never ceases to crown him with spiritual triumphs, and implores that he be made a participant in the heavenly kingdom by beseeching divine clemency, so he, having obtained princely power, should never cease to defend her valiantly from her enemies and to avenge her upon them by a sentence of punitive attack.” From this comparison one may reasonably infer that Paulinus was referring to his *Sacrosyllabum*. Hence he adds, “For what reason they did this”—that is, the Fathers of Frankfurt, by approving our petition—“I know has not escaped your memories,” because certain statutes were established according to the pattern of that petition, so that there is no doubt that the request made by Paulinus in the name of the Fathers was committed to royal and public records. The present matter, concerning the vindication of the Church that has suffered injury, agrees with it; hence he rightly renews the memory of the earlier memorandum.] from him [Note: *Vicissitudinis*; Baluzius reads *necessitudinis*.]—so that, just as she [Note: *Eum*; Baluzius reads *cum*.] protects him in this present evil age with holy prayers continually [Note: Baluzius has: “in this evil age she continually protects him with holy prayers”; the words are absent from the Vatican manuscript.], never ceases to crown him amid spiritual battles with triumphs, and prays that he may become a participant in the heavenly kingdom by imploring divine clemency, so he, having obtained princely power, may both valiantly defend her from her enemies and never cease to avenge her upon them by a sentence of punitive attack. Let, therefore, the excellence of your kindness not disdain to undertake watchful care for her in this matter [Note: *Eam*; Baluzius reads *eum*.], remembering in every respect that you have been reborn from the womb of the sacred font, far more happily nourished by the sweetness of the milk of faith than you were previously generated, though well, from your mother’s womb, and nursed at her bodily breasts [Note: “Weaned from the breasts,” used for “nursed,” as stated in book III *Against Felix*, chapter 10, in the notes.].

### XII.

Let there therefore proceed, if it pleases you, throughout the broadly extended monarchy of your kingdom, a retribution in the form of a decretal sentence—one that no oblivion may ever erase under any impulse of opposition urged against the truth or hostile to justice [Note: *Quam*: so Baluzius and the Vatican manuscript; the collection of Labbé, cited by Baronius, reads *quae*. “Under any impulse that may urge.” Thus the Vatican manuscript has *quaelibet urgente instinctio*; Baluzius, *quaelibet urgente instincto*.]. For the savage phantoms of this crime have prevailed greatly throughout all the churches of the world because of the neglect of discipline [Note: *Praevaluere*: Baluzius reads *praevalure*.]. It is therefore for the judgment of your teaching to cut away this pest of a destructive disease by every means, and to uproot it completely with a most powerful yet instructive hand, so that the holy Church, assisted by your protection, may be free and unstained by human blood—she who has been dyed purple by the precious blood of Christ. Therefore, happily retained within her embrace, may you always enjoy prosperity in this life, safe and glorious, and rejoice in eternal blessedness, happy through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God in perfect Trinity throughout all ages of ages [Note: Baluzius reads *omnium*]. Amen.

[Col. 0519]

## DISSERTATIONS ON THE WORKS OF PAULINUS

### FIRST DISSERTATION ON THE BOOK OF EXHORTATION TO HENRY, DUKE OF FRIOUL

196 [Col. 0519D]

### I.

Let immense thanksgivings be rendered to our God, who has preserved us for good times, in which truth, sought through the labor of so many learned men, raises its head more successfully than ever before and triumphs more fully over falsehood as well as ignorance.

This book was almost from its infancy taken away from its true parent and, by a most fortunate misattribution, assigned to the great light of the Church, St. Augustine: a work sufficiently commended by the fact that it could have appeared not unworthy of so great an author. I do not deny that it displays neither Augustine’s style, nor his thought, nor his eloquence; add also that the date does not at all agree. Yet, as barbarism increased and the age of Paulinus was almost everywhere deprived of the elegance of Latin, it was enough for a work not to be entirely commonplace for it to be regarded as a marvel. But concerning the outlook of this age and Paulinus’s eloquence, see what is said in chapter 15, beginning at no. 2, of the *Life of Paulinus*. For the present, it is enough to observe that earlier generations regarded this book as belonging to so remote a period that they thought it could not improperly be associated with Augustine’s own works [Col. 0520D].

Whatever Erasmus might object in his criticism prefixed to the book in the old editions—“That its author was unlettered, and that it is the height of impudence to attribute the work to Augustine”—the author was not unlettered, as will be clear from this and from his other works, as well as from the testimony of others. Nor did Gratian fear this charge of supreme impudence when he cites him under Augustine’s name in *On Penance*, distinction 2, chapter “Charity”; nor did the Master of the Sentences, book III, distinction 31, A; nor did the highly learned and otherwise exceptionally skilled brothers Pithou in ancient monuments. Rather, they reinforce the attribution, since, after citing the canon as Augustine’s, they add: “perhaps written in Africa around the year 420.” The Fathers of the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur have placed the entire republic of letters under an obligation to them. By examining the records of earlier ages—a task they continue to perform for the greatest benefit of scholarship—they publish the books of the holy Fathers as accurately corrected as possible and distinguish genuine works from spurious ones.

These Fathers therefore assign this work to Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia, as his true and authentic offspring, “on the authority of a certain manuscript of excellent quality,” as they themselves say in the notice prefixed to their edition of Augustine, “and of a very ancient manuscript written in the Colbert Library, apparently, in their judgment, in Paulinus’s own age. It bears the following title: ‘The sermon of blessed Paulinus, bishop of Friuli, wishing peace and prosperity, health and everlasting joy in the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior, to a certain friend serving in the world.’”

Nor did those who wrote about ecclesiastical writers after their Augustinian edition call this into doubt; indeed, they add weight to the assertion. Thus William Cave, in *Historia litteraria scriptorum ecclesiasticorum*, under Paulinus, and Casimir Oudin, in his supplement to Bellarmine’s *De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, who states that he saw more than one manuscript copy of this work, in these words: “I add, on the reliable evidence of the manuscript copies I have seen, that the same Paulinus, bishop of Friuli, is the author of the book or little work *On Salutary Instructions*, which appears among the works of the divine Augustine.” Élie du Pin likewise lists this very work among Paulinus’s writings in volume VI of his *New Ecclesiastical Library*.

In volume III, however, when reviewing Augustine’s works, he had attributed it not to our Paulinus of Friuli, but to a certain Paul, bishop of Fréjus in Gaul, commonly called Fréjus; there he said that this Paul lived toward the end of the ninth century. Yet, although he ought to have remembered him as an ecclesiastical writer known to him, he does not mention him at all when discussing the writers of the ninth century. I would indeed wonder that an otherwise diligent man could fail to be consistent with himself, unless I clearly understood that such lapses occur humanly to those who write much and therefore ought humanly to be forgiven.

We know this, and we both ask and grant this pardon in turn. Perhaps, however, after examining the matter more carefully, he corrected the error of volume III in what he wrote in volume VI. Let it therefore stand as certain that the book belongs to Paulinus, Patriarch of Aquileia [Col. 0521C].

With this established, we shall examine somewhat more fully the author and the person to whom the book was written, and more briefly the work’s subject and form, as well as the place and time of its composition. The matter is plainly obscure and can be rendered more probable only through the illumination of sounder conjectures.

### II.

Concerning the author of the book, there is nothing else worth investigating here except whether this work was written by Paulinus before he was raised to the episcopate or after he had been elevated to the episcopal see. G. Cave, who makes a practice of assigning Paulinus’s more important works to the years in which they were produced, does not even mention this book.

Some may think that it was written before his elevation to the episcopate, because he always, or almost always, calls the person to whom he writes “brother.” The designation of brotherhood seems unsuitable for a bishop in relation to a layman, which was the status of the man to whom Paulinus was writing. For “brotherhood” indicates a certain equality between those who call one another brothers, even if in the spiritual sense. Moreover, the manner and style of the writing itself suggest the same conclusion. He writes with such courtesy and familiarity that no greater intimacy could be expected even between blood brothers. If Paulinus had already been a bishop when he wrote, he would have addressed his recipient as a son rather than a brother and would have proceeded in a more weighty style.

### III.

Despite these considerations, I believe that the work was written by a bishop, for the following reasons.

First, it is certain that the author was not a layman. This is clear from chapter 5, where he says: “Be, I beg you, though a layman, ready for every work of God.” He would not have said this if he too had been a layman and no distinction of status had existed between the writer and the person to whom he wrote. Erasmus himself noticed this in his criticism, saying: “The writer of this little book implies that he was a cleric.”

But it is not probable that a simple cleric, or even a priest, would have proceeded with such confidence and familiarity as to call a man occupying a position of dignity “brother” and, as the phrase goes, address him face to face. This is still less likely since, as they say, Paulinus was not of illustrious but humble birth. It is therefore scarcely credible that a man of the lowest condition should have cultivated friendships with palatines, counts, and dukes because of his social standing [Col. 0522A].

It remains, then, to say that he was a bishop when he wrote, and that the dignity of the episcopal see introduced a certain equality, so that there is nothing extraordinary in a bishop addressing a count and duke as brother and closest friend, employing terms that fostered mutual affection while setting aside the appellation “son,” which would have expressed reverential respect.

Second, the Benedictine Fathers, in their preliminary notice, reinforce the title “to a certain count” from the fact that he writes in chapter 62: “No bishop, abbot, or count will be able to corrupt the palace of this Judge [Christ] with gold and silver,” as though the writer were alluding there to the rank of the count to whom he was writing. By the same reasoning, the dignity of the bishop who wrote may be inferred from this passage.

Third, in the notice cited above, these same Fathers say that the Colbert manuscript was written in Paulinus’s own age. Why, then, does it identify him as “bishop of Friuli,” unless a bishop had written it? [Col. 0522B]

Alcuin wrote a letter to Duke Aeric, whom we shall show below, in section 6, to be the very man to whom Paulinus had sent this book; in that letter he directs Aeric to Paulinus for instruction. Henry, or Aeric—for they are the same person, and although authors vary somewhat in the name, they agree concerning his deeds and identity—does not seem to have become known to Paulinus until after the killing of Rotgand, or Rothgand, formerly Duke of Friuli. Rotgand was put to death for the rebellion he had raised against Charlemagne in the year 776, as the Frankish annalists unanimously report. Indeed, Henry may have become known still later, when Charlemagne himself appointed him to the dukedom of Friuli.

This appointment did not occur immediately after Rotgand’s death, if we believe Paulus Aemilius, who, writing to Charlemagne about the matter, says: “The king first entrusted the prefecture of Friuli to Frankish counts; afterward he created Henry, a Frank, Duke of Friuli.” Yet he made him duke nearly a decade later. By that time, however—already from the year 776, as will become clear in chapter 4 of the *Life of Paulinus*—Paulinus had ascended the see of Aquileia. It follows, then, that the book was written by Paulinus already as a bishop.

### IV.

We must now discuss the person to whom the book was written. In nearly all manuscript and printed copies, the book is addressed to a certain count. Some have “to Count Julian,” and this is the title under which Gratian cites it in *On Penance*, distinction 2, chapter “If Anyone.” The brothers Pithou do not hesitate over this in their edition of the decretals; nor does Trithemius, who says: “It is called Augustine’s letter to Count Julian; under this title it also occupied a place among Augustine’s letters in the first edition of the Amerbach brothers,” as the Benedictine Fathers testify in the notice cited above.

They add: “Indeed, in almost all the other manuscript copies of the book which we have found, including the Theodoric manuscript—which, unless we are mistaken, is an eight-hundred-year-old copy and bears this title written by the first hand at the beginning of the book, ‘The Book of Exhortation of Saint Augustine to a Certain Count, His Most Dear Friend’—all later copies are marked ‘to a certain count, his most intimate friend.’ But the name of Count Julian is written at the end of the book in scarcely one or two manuscripts.”

The name Julian, therefore, should not hold us back. Just as an error was made in the author’s name, so an error could have been made in the name of the person to whom the book was written. We must first discuss the dignity of the count and afterward the identity of the count.

### V.

As for the etymology of *comes*, a count is one who joins himself to another or travels together with another. Thus, in the administration of public affairs, because men come together and unite, agreements and associations are called *conventiones* and *coitiones*, while assemblies and electoral meetings are called *conventus* and *comitia*. John of Salisbury, letter 263: “Who does not know that counts are so called from participation in companionship,” and so forth.

In former times, boys who had not yet reached puberty were entrusted to them for protection. Hence Virgil’s words in *Aeneid* V, verse 545, concerning Aeneas:

> He calls Epitides to himself as guardian and companion of the young Iulus.

Cicero states in the Fourth Speech against Verres that those who were assigned by the Roman Senate as companions to magistrates in the performance of their offices were also called counts: “Those favorite companions of yours were your hands,” namely, when he extorted money from the peoples; and below: “If we wish to be thought innocent, we must show not only that we ourselves abstain, but also that our companions do so.”

Under the emperors, those who belonged to the emperor’s court and retinue were called counts because they belonged to his *comitatus*. Lampridius, *Life of Severus*, chapter 15: “He purged both his palace and his entire retinue, casting out from the service of the court all disreputable and infamous persons.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVIII, chapter 10: “Maximinus was summoned to the emperor’s retinue.”

Constantine the Great distinguished various grades of counts at court, assigning them to reward the differing merits of his subjects, as Eusebius writes in book IV, chapter 1, of *The Life of Constantine*: “He placed some of the counts in the first order, others in the second, and still others in the third. By this arrangement, almost countless others attained the most distinguished honors. For, wishing to bestow honors upon very many people, the emperor devised various grades of rank.”

Following the model of this Constantinian division of the honor of the *comitatus*, other forms arose over time under kings in the provinces removed from the Roman Empire. Those whom the prince admitted at court to share in the government were called palatine counts; those placed in charge of administering a province were called provincial counts. “Those who hold this office in the palace are palatines; those who hold it in the provinces are provincials,” says John of Salisbury in the letter cited above.

For various formulas of appointment as count for a particular office, see Cassiodorus, book VII of the *Variae*. Individual counts were ordinarily appointed to civil administration in each city. Yet Venantius, in book IV of *The Life of Saint Martin*, represents Avitianus, governor of Tours, whom he calls a judge, as follows:

> Then Avitianus’s sick wife was made the judge’s companion;

A little later he depicts him as count of the people of Tours:

> When Count Avitianus was acting in a state of swelling pride,  
> he approached Tours, supported by a terrifying office.

Counts were regarded as subordinate to a duke, a magistrate of higher rank. For a duke was in charge of several cities. Gregory of Tours teaches this briefly in book IX of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 7:

> “When Ennodius was administering the dukedom of the cities of Tours and Poitiers, he also received authority over the towns of Juliacum and Béarn. But when the counts of the cities of Tours and Poitiers went to King Childebert, they obtained from him that Ennodius be removed from their midst.”

Venantius himself, in book X, poem 19, predicted Sigoald’s promotion from the countship to the dukedom, as from a lower to a higher degree of dignity:

> May King Childebert, as you grow, compel you to rise:  
> he who now gives you the gifts of a count, may he give you the gifts of a duke.

There is no time to investigate how these temporary dignities migrated into feudal tenure, nor does it concern the present matter [Col. 0523D]. Returning now to our subject, we learn from Sigonius, book IV of *On the Kingdom of Italy*, that after Charlemagne defeated Desiderius, king of the Lombards, in 774, he “allowed Rotgand to retain the dukedom of Friuli, preserving toward him the ancient feudal right that had formerly existed toward the kings of the Lombards.”

But when Rotgand rebelled in 775 and was killed, Charlemagne “attached the dukedom of Friuli to the kingdom and gave the individual cities to counts for administration.” Cointius and Pagius, both under the year 776—the former at no. 6, the latter at no. 3—assert from letter 57 of the *Carolingian Code* that Marcarius was placed over these counts as duke.

Charlemagne’s affairs in Friuli did not long prosper under these officials. “The province was again reduced to the form of a dukedom, the counts were removed, and Henry was appointed duke.” This is from Sigonius, who thinks that it happened, with considerable probability, around the year 787, in order to suppress the Avars, who had already begun stirring up disturbances. From that year, therefore, Henry was constituted duke.

### VI.

He, then, is the very dear friend of Paulinus, the count to whom Paulinus dedicates the book. This is shown clearly enough by the letter cited above in section 3 of this dissertation. A few passages may be extracted from it for the present purpose.

“Perhaps I would have written more to you, venerable man Henry,” says Albinus, “about the practice of Christian piety, if my distinguished teacher, pious instructor in heavenly life, Paulinus, were not present to you—a man from whose heart flows a fountain of living water springing up into eternal life. Have him as the mediator of your eternal salvation, so that your foot may not stumble anywhere, but, running along the straight path, may by divine grace be worthy to reach the harbor of perpetual life.”

Who would not understand from these words that Paulinus fulfilled for Henry what Alcuin desired, through this book of exhortation filled with such salutary instructions? Moreover, Paulinus was present to Henry, duke or count, to offer counsel concerning the practice of Christian piety, as a distinguished teacher, a pious instructor in heavenly life [Col. 0524B], and a mediator of eternal salvation.

These counsels concerning Christian piety and these instructions concerning eternal salvation are found in Paulinus’s work addressed to his most intimate friend. Why, then, should we wander uncertainly in search of another count besides Henry, especially when, for the greater part of his episcopate—that is, for nearly twelve years—Paulinus could not have been available to any other duke or count?

Not to a count, because the counts had already been abolished in the year 787, when Henry himself was placed in charge of the province of Friuli. Not to a duke, because during this period he alone was duke. Nor is there any difficulty in the fact that Henry was called and regarded as a duke while Paulinus’s book is addressed to a count, since “count” and “duke” are very often used for one another and confused.

To give an example from the dignity of the dukedom of Friuli itself, Rotgand, who preceded Henry in this office, is called both duke and count by the poet Saxo, book V of the *Annals of the Deeds of Charlemagne*:

> For Charlemagne appointed him  
> duke and count over the people of Friuli.

I possess a manuscript copy taken from an old text, which, judging from its script, appears to belong to the thirteenth century. We shall provide a specimen of it in Appendix 2. In it, King Berengar calls the province of Friuli not a dukedom or a march, as he sometimes does, but a countship. Henry, therefore, is both Duke and Count of Friuli, and he is the count to whom Paulinus, as to a friend, directs this book of exhortation.

### VII.

It will not be burdensome to say something about Henry’s person, since we have already mentioned certain matters concerning his dignity. Most people call him Henry; some call him Eric, others Erich, and others Aeric, the variation apparently arising from the accent of national pronunciation.

He was regarded as a Frank by nationality. But I would not have you understand by “France” the boundaries within which the country now ruled by the Frankish king Louis XV is contained. Charlemagne’s kingdom extended far and wide through the regions now called the provinces of the Empire and of Germany, or Alemannia. Indeed, it reached and included Illyricum itself, as Otto of Freising says in book VI, chapter 17, of his *Chronicle*:

> “In the time of Charlemagne,” he says, “the whole of Gaul—that is, Celtic Gaul, Belgic Gaul, and Lugdunensian Gaul—and all of Germany, from the Rhine as far as Illyricum, constituted the boundary of the Frankish kingdom. Then, after the kingdom had been divided among the sons of sons, one part was called the eastern kingdom and the other the western; nevertheless, both were called the kingdom of the Franks.”

If, after the division, it retained the designation “Frankish,” then all the more before the division, when it was called the kingdom of the Franks under the scepter of Charlemagne, who ruled over so many regions [Col. 0524D].

Thus Henry is called a Frank, not precisely because he came from modern France, but either because he came from some province subject to the Frankish kingdom, or, more probably, because he came from Franconia itself, which was once considered no insignificant part of the eastern Frankish kingdom.

We think this is the part of Germany that Saint Jerome describes in the *Life of Saint Hilarion* in these words:

> “A candidate of the emperor Constantius, with reddish hair and the whiteness of his body indicating his province—his people, situated between the Saxons and the Alemanni, are not so extensive as they are powerful; among historians they are called Germany, but now France—[he] sought, and so forth.”

Baudrand places the boundaries of Franconia to the north at Saxony and Thuringia, and to the south at part of Bavaria and Swabia, which the Swabians—known as Alemanni—are known to have inhabited. Hence the proximity of the provinces had already produced a confusion of names, so that later an Alemannian could equally be called a Frank, and a Frank an Alemannian.

### VIII.

Henry, therefore—whether you call him a Frank or an Alemannian—was appointed sole duke over the affairs of Friuli. The lesser counts who, under Duke Marcarius, had governed after Rothgand’s revolt had been removed.

The Avars provided the cause for this change. Around the year 787 they were summoned by Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, at the instigation of his wife Luitperta, daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards. She was contemplating vengeance for her father, who had been expelled from his kingdom and deprived of his authority by Charlemagne. The Avars then began to harass the Frankish dominion. This may be gathered from the *Annals of Bertin* under the years 787 and 788.

It therefore happened that, in order to protect the affairs of Friuli, a count with full authority in war and peace was sent there. The province, threatened by the imminent dangers of disaster, would confront them after being divided into many smaller countships; but, once gathered under a single head, it could be restored with little difficulty.

Henry, a man distinguished for military and political ability, was ordered to shoulder this burden. Since he was thoroughly imbued with Christian and religious morals, it seems that, before hastening his departure from Charlemagne’s court, he visited Alcuin, a man distinguished for piety and learning, perhaps to request counsels for eternal salvation so that he might carry out the undertaking he had assumed without offending God, and to commend himself to Alcuin’s prayers so as to obtain heavenly assistance.

This may be inferred without difficulty from Albinus’s letter 94, addressed to Aeric himself:

> “I am sufficiently pleased,” he says, “with your attention to sacred reading and your conduct of pious humility, in which you did not disdain to visit familiarly the little dwelling of my lowliness. Therefore we give thanks for your kindness and earnestly pray God for your safety, that by the power of His great mercy He may everywhere make the right hand of your strength victorious against the adversaries of His holy name, and mercifully protect you from every adversity of diabolical deceit and from all the snares of your enemies. May He deign to govern you in prosperity and protect you in adversity, since you most diligently fulfill, insofar as human frailty permits, His most holy will in observing His commandments. Perhaps I would have written more to you, venerable man, concerning the practice of Christian piety, if my distinguished teacher, pious instructor in heavenly life, Paulinus, were not present to you,”

and so forth, as quoted above.

This letter appears to have been written immediately after Duke Henry’s arrival in Friuli, that is, in the year 787. At that time Alcuin was living in France, from which Henry had departed shortly before. Alcuin returned to England in 790, and about three years later returned to France, as may be gathered from his preface to the book *Against Elipandus*, together with the account of the learned Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, volume IX, under the year 792, pages 590 and following.

You see, then, the bonds of association by which Henry was connected with men distinguished for holiness and wisdom. He was otherwise a layman, a courtier, and a soldier; from this you may easily infer his piety, strength of mind, and virtue.

### IX

Once the province had been reached, conformity in piety and morals very quickly kindled mutual affection between these otherwise opposing men. How greatly Paulinus bound Henry to himself through the fellowship of sacred friendship, and how greatly he made him zealous in the works of God—not merely energetic in protecting churches, but also a generous donor in enriching them—is evident from the foundation and endowment of the church of Saint Nicholas at Sacile. For Henry himself, [Col. 0526A] to whom a sufficiently extensive province had been entrusted, founded the parish church of Sacile, endowed it with estates, and, although it lay between the boundaries of the dioceses of Ceneda and Concordia, obtained from the Roman see that it should be subject to Patriarch Paulinus and his successors at Aquileia. This is shown by a charter of Patriarch Berthold, issued at Aquileia in 1249, which Patriarch Paganus cites in 1328 at Udine, at the request of the parish priest of Sacile named Sigibaldinus. We publish it from the archives of the city of Udine in Appendix 2, no. 23. For now, let us transcribe a few passages:

> “In those times, when the illustrious Duke Henry of blessed memory, who, although born of the noble stock of the Alemanni, then ruled these regions around the river Livenza, founded at Sacile, for the remedy of his soul, the aforesaid church in honor of the blessed Nicholas (spelled “Nycholay”), glorious confessor and bishop,” between the boundaries of the dioceses of Concordia and Ceneda. He hoped at that time, and thereafter for as long as life should last, to build there a praiseworthy town or fortress, [Col. 0526B] which would add glory to his name and increase the magnificence of his greatness.”

Further on, after recounting the exemption obtained from the bishops of Concordia and Ceneda and listing the estates with which he enriched that church as its endowment, he adds:

> “Thus (spelled “Hys”), the same illustrious Duke Henry, mentioned above, endowed the aforesaid church of Saint Nicholas at Sacile with the aforesaid estates, possessions, territorial serfs, and quarter-tenants, and, together with all its exemptions, honors, and rights, and with all its possessions, subjected it by the authority of the supreme pontiff to the Church of Aquileia, along with certain other churches, as the aforesaid privileges of both him and us freely and fully declare.”

### X

The Henry mentioned in this charter can be no other than our Henry, of whom we are now speaking. The other two—for only three men of this name are found among the dukes of Friuli—barely set foot in the province and possessed the duchy more in name than in fact. One was the brother of Otto, duke of Bavaria. In 952, according to Sigonius, book VI, he received the duchy or march of Friuli from his brother. Otto, says Sigonius, “having received Berengar and his son Adalbert into his allegiance, left them the kingdom, except for the Veronese and Friulian marches, which he said he had assigned to his brother Henry, duke of Bavaria.” Sigonius makes this same Henry die in 955. In the intervening period, however, he records no action of his in the province; indeed, he shows that Henry did not even maintain a station there, being occupied and distracted by foreign wars.

Of the other, who is listed last in the catalogue of the dukes of Friuli, he records only this: “After his brother Henry died, Otto granted Bavaria to Henry’s son.” Perhaps, because the duchy of Friuli had already been entrusted to the father, who was then duke of Bavaria, he thought that the son had succeeded his father in this Friulian duchy as well. In any event, this man is unknown by name among our native historians, much less is he listed in [Col. 0526D] the catalogue of the dukes of Friuli.

Since, therefore, what Berthold presents in his charter cannot apply to the later Henrys, it must be understood of the earlier one. Nor is it an obstacle that the document calls him of Alemannian stock, whereas other historians call him a Frank, since it has already been shown sufficiently and abundantly that the terms “Frank” and “Alemannian” could be used interchangeably, Alemannia at that time comprehending in name and in fact the more distinguished provinces of Germany and Francia, such as Franconia. Nor should you think him one of the Henrys who were dukes of Carantania. Although the advocacy of the Church of Aquileia had been entrusted to them, as is clearly shown by the testament of Cacellinus, founder of the monastery of Mosacum, in Appendix 2, no. 12, they nevertheless did not rule in these regions around the river Livenza, as Berthold says of our Henry.

### XI

Henry stood out no less for military courage and energetic spirit than for religion and piety. [Col. 0527A] You have already heard from Berthold’s charter of his intention to add to the foundation of the church of Saint Nicholas at Sacile another distinguished work, namely, “to build a praiseworthy town or fortress, which would add glory to his name and increase the magnificence of his greatness.” He does not appear to have accomplished this, perhaps because death overtook him. For if he had completed what he had planned, Berthold would have reported it as an accomplished fact, not as a project.

The man’s greatness of spirit nevertheless shines forth from this intention alone, just as it shone forth in later centuries in Patriarch Raymond, who intended to establish a territory or marketplace to be called Raymond’s Milan, as appears from a charter in Appendix 2, no. 22. He too was unable to carry out the plan or bring it to its desired completion.

### XII

Henry’s excellence, however, shone more brilliantly in military affairs on the occasion of the Avarian war. We have already touched upon the origin of the war. At the urging of Luitperga, daughter of Desiderius, formerly king of the Lombards, her husband Tassilo, duke of Bavaria, summoned the Huns against Charles, with whom he had entered into an alliance. Hear from the Saxon Poet the beginning of this war under the year 788:

> **199** But the Huns, a harsh people devoted to warfare,  
> Striving to fulfill the promises made to the aforesaid duke  
> (That is, Tassilo.)  
> Began, with two armies drawn up,  
> To invade certain borders of the Frankish kingdom.  
> One army had penetrated the regions of Italy,  
> And the enemy had come to the very borders  
> Of that city to which, illustrious Julius, you gave the name of Forum.  
> The other army entered Bavaria,  
> But in vain: for all its effort was fruitless,  
> And, defeated, both armies were forced to withdraw from the field.

He rightly asserts that the war began in this year, 788, and does not conflict with Einhard in the *Life of Charles*, who says that it was completed in its eighth year:

> “The greatest of all the wars undertaken by him, apart from the Saxon war, followed this one—namely, the war undertaken against the Avars or Huns. He conducted it with greater determination than the others and with a far greater deployment of resources. He himself made only one expedition into Pannonia, for that was the province inhabited by this people at that time. He entrusted the completion of all the others to his son Pepin and to the prefects of the provinces, as well as to counts and envoys. When these operations had been carried out with the greatest vigor, the war was finally completed in its eighth year.”

But Einhard’s uncertainty appears in his reckoning of the years. If you count the beginning of the eighth year from 788, you arrive at 796. Since the baptism of the Avars occurred in that very year, according to the unanimous testimony of all the annalists, that year seems to mark the end of the Avarian war. Yet because war was also waged against the perjured Avars after 796, down to 799, when our Henry died, Einhard seems to count the years from 791, when Charles himself first and on only one occasion personally directed the war.

### XIII

In this year, namely 791, although the preceding year had offered hope that the war might be brought to an end through the reciprocal dispatch of envoys—both of Huns to Charles and of Charles to the Huns—as Cointius notes from the Lorsch annalist under 788, no. 16, and 790, no. 1, the war flared up again when a dispute arose concerning the boundaries of the two realms. Hear the cited annalist:

> “In this year (790) the king undertook no expedition, but, residing in Worms, both received the envoys of the Huns and in turn sent his own to their princes. The matter under discussion was the frontier between their kingdoms, and the places where it ought to lie. This contention and dispute was the seed and origin of the war that was afterward waged with the Huns.”

Thus, in 791, the Avarian war broke out again, and Charles conducted it personally. So report the Lambach, Bertin, and Loisel annals, Hermannus Contractus, and the others. The Saxon Poet likewise assigns the same war to this year, speaking of Charles:

> After a hundred volumes of years had passed in their course,  
> Seven having been completed and about ten more besides,  
> When nine times ten years had elapsed since God became man,  
> He undertook this first campaign against the Huns.

[Col. 0528A] “First”—that is, the first conducted by him personally. For the same poet also records earlier wars with the Avars, as we have seen, and further wars followed, although several years intervened between them.

### XIV

For you, reader, we assemble an account of this war from various annalists.

The Lorsch Annals:

> “When spring had passed and the beginning of summer had arrived, the king set out from Worms for Bavaria, intending to repay the Huns for their deeds and to make war upon them as soon as he could.”

The Loisel Annals:

> “From there, having set out on his journey, he proceeded toward the regions of Bavaria and went to Regensburg. There he joined his army. After the council of the Franks, Saxons, and Frisians had been held, they decided that, because of the great wickedness and intolerable offenses which the Avars had committed against the holy Church and the Christian people, and because they had been unable to obtain justice through envoys, they should, with God’s help, carry out the plan of marching into the regions of the Avars already mentioned. They proceeded toward the river Enns. [Col. 0528B] There they ordered litanies to be performed for three days and, celebrating the solemnities of Mass, sought God’s consolation for the safety of the army, the assistance of our Lord Jesus Christ, and victory over the Avars.”

The Bertin Annals add that Charles led his forces along the Danube, one army marching along the left bank and the other along the right. When the Avars saw this, and were further struck with terror from heaven, they turned their backs and fled.

> “Thus they proceeded as far as the river called the Rába, and from there the two armies returned home by both banks, glorifying the Lord for so great a victory.”

The Canisian manuscript, cited by Cointius under 791, no. 1, adds:

> “The army which his son Pepin sent from Italy entered Illyricum and from there Pannonia, and likewise ravaged and burned that land, just as King Charles had done with his army where he himself was present. When King Charles saw that no one from the Avar side dared to resist him or his men, he then went around that land for fifty-two days, burning and devastating it, carrying away booty without measure or number, and leading away an immeasurable multitude of captives, women, and children. On this journey Angilram, archbishop of the Church of Metz, died, and Bishop Simpert also died there.”

The Lorsch Annals conclude:

> “This expedition was carried out without any loss of property, except that such a pestilence among the horses arose in the army which the king led that scarcely a tenth part of those many thousands of horses is said to have remained. When he had dismissed his forces and arrived at the city of Reginum, now called Regensburg, he settled there to winter and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord there.”

Here, in passing, note the death of Angilram from the manuscript of Saint Symphorian of Metz, cited by Cointius under 791, no. 6. It occurred “on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, at a place called Asnagahunc Cunisberg.” At that time, therefore, Charles’s armies had already withdrawn from enemy territory, and the journey mentioned by the Canisian manuscript was their return.

### XV

The date of this victory is made no clearer by any source than by the letter Charles sent to his wife Fastrada, whom he had left at Regensburg awaiting the outcome of the war. I shall quote part of it:

> “The envoy of our beloved son Pepin, [name omitted], informed us of his health and that of the apostolic lord … He further reported to us how the divisions which we previously ordered to proceed from Italy into the regions of the Avars and to take up station on those frontiers entered their territory on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, engaged them in battle, and Almighty God, in his mercy, granted them victory. They killed so great a number of those Avars, as they say, that no greater slaughter of the Avars had been made for many days. They stripped the rampart and remained there that night, or until the third hour of the following day. After taking the spoils, they returned in peace.
