They captured one hundred and fifty of those Avars alive and kept them, so that our command might determine what should be done with them. The faithful of God and of us who carried this out were that bishop, that duke, and those counts. The illustrious duke of Histria, as was reported to us, performed well there with his men. Our vassals were those men. With the Lord’s help, we performed a litany for three days, beginning on the Nones of September, which fell on Monday, then Tuesday and Wednesday, and so forth.”

### XVI

There can be no doubt that this letter is to be understood of the Avarian victory of this year. For from 791 until 794, when Fastrada died, you will find no other expedition against the Avars, as all the annalists unanimously affirm. Moreover, the first day of the litanies, which was a Monday, properly falls on 5 September, as Pagius, no. 2, and Cointius, no. 5, observe for this year.

The matter was not completed in a single operation. For as early as the tenth day before the Kalends of September—that is, 23 August—the divisions which Charles had recalled from Italy and Pepin had sent forward entered the territory of the Avars, engaged them in battle, and, with God granting victory, carried the day, as Charles himself testifies in this letter. Charles himself then continued the war from the Nones of September onward and harassed the enemy for fifty-two days, as we have seen from the Canisian manuscript.

Thus Charles’s stay in Avarian territory seems to have continued until around the end of October, or somewhat less, since Angilram died “on the seventh day before the Kalends of November,” that is, 25 October, at Cunisberg, “on the very journey”—namely, while they were returning. Perhaps he was then with the Saxons and Frisians, who, “through the Bohemians, as they had been ordered, returned home,” as the Lorsch Annals say.

When he reached Cunisberg, which we suppose to have been Königsberg, the illustrious city of Ducal Prussia, a part of Poland (Baudrand), he ended his final day. Therefore, before 25 October, if not the whole army, at least the portion in which Angilram was serving, had already withdrawn and was returning home.

### XVII

Although the ancient annalists make no mention either of Henry or of the Friulian army, one may confidently say that he was present. What other divisions—that is, armies—which Charles ordered to proceed from Italy were nearer to the borders of the Avars than the Friulian forces? Or which others could have entered Illyricum and penetrated into Pannonia more conveniently and quickly? And who else could have been their commander than Henry, who governed the entire province?

Indeed, we believe that he is the man whom Charles praises without naming in these words:

> “The duke of Histria, as was reported to us, performed well there with his men.”

Cointius, under this year, no. 161, shows from Einhard that Histria had been taken from the Greeks in 789 by Pepin, and Schönleben, under 800, observes that it was assigned to the duke of Friuli, together with inland Dalmatia, Liburnia, Croatia, Slavonia, Carniola, Lower Styria, and part of Carinthia as far as the Drava.

He is called “the duke of Histria” either because Histria sometimes designated all Venetia, as we suggested in Dissertation 2, no. 19, or because the region of Histria was nearer to the Avars than the other regions which Henry governed in Italy.

If you were to say that the bishop whose name, like those of the others, is not given in the letter was Paulinus, you would not find me a hostile opponent. I know that bishops followed armies at this time: we have just seen that Angilram and Simpert were present on this expedition. Moreover, the religious purpose of the war and the proximity of the places make the conjecture probable.

Let us now return to our Henry.

### XVIII

The interruption in the Avarian war lasted until 796. For in the preceding year, 795, while Charles was occupied with the Saxon war, “at a place called Lunis there came envoys of Tudun, who held great power among the Avarian people and kingdom. They said that Tudun himself, with his land and people, wished to surrender to the king and, under his direction, receive the Christian faith.” So report the Loisel Annals, in agreement with the others.

If from this you do not understand that Hunia was being afflicted by civil war, you will recognize it more clearly from the events of the following year, 796. Henry seized the opportunity presented by these dissensions and attacked them. “Having sent soldiers with Wonomir the Slav, he plundered the Ring of the Avar people, long undisturbed in former times, while their princes, exhausted by civil war, were fighting among themselves”—there you have the Avars divided against one another, one of whose leading men, Tudun, had defected to Charles in the previous year after promising to receive baptism with his people—“and, after the Chagan or Viguro had been overcome by internal slaughter and killed by his own men, he sent to King Charles at the palace of Aachen the treasure collected by the ancient kings over the course of many centuries.”

Thus the cited annals. They regard Rhingum as a prince and dynast among the Avars. But the Saxon Poet shows in this year, 796, that it was a place, not a man, when he says:

> For the royal seat of the Huns was plundered,  
> Which they call Rhingum. Duke Henry had captured it that year.

### XIX

Einhard, however, says in his annals that Henry did not send the Avarian booty but brought it:

> “In the same year, Duke Hericus of Friuli, after the royal seat of the Huns called Rhingum had been plundered, brought a large part of the treasure from Pannonia to the king.”

That he brought it, rather than sent it, is made probable by Alcuin’s Letter 112 to Paulinus, written in this very year, when the Avars had been defeated, in which Alcuin urges Paulinus to promote their conversion by his preaching. At its conclusion he adds:

> “A short while ago I sent two little letters to Your Paternity: one through the holy bishop of Histria, the other through the venerable man Aeric, the duke.”

Returning to Friuli, therefore, Henry brought the letter mentioned here to Paulinus from the delivery of the Avarian booty to the palace at Aachen, where Alcuin may then have been staying with the king. Perhaps it was the letter in which Angilbert, who was going to Rome, was mentioned.

From the letter itself one may gather that Henry had first carried Paulinus’s letter to Alcuin—perhaps Paulinus was then living with him in the camp—and that Alcuin, in turn, wrote back to Paulinus through the returning Henry, commended the bearer to Paulinus’s spiritual guidance, and added that Angilbert was going to Rome. Here are some words from the letter:

> “Having received the lines of your wisdom and the gifts of your charity through the bearer of this present little letter—for observe that the same man carries and returns it—I rejoiced greatly … The bearer of these letters, now present, is commended to your assistance and protection in support of our petition. He will reveal to you by the living service of his tongue our needs or his own; and Angilbert, our common son, going to Rome, will, God willing, convey to you a fuller account of our greeting.”

But more about Angilbert’s journey below. Paulinus and the council in which he took part will also be discussed elsewhere.

### XX

The Avarian affair was not completed in a single operation that year. Perhaps Tudun, shaken by this first defeat and setting out from there for King Charles in order to fulfill the promise of receiving baptism which he had made through envoys the previous year, was followed by many Avars. They were received by Charles with great kindness, cleansed through baptism, and enriched with royal gifts before returning home.

Meanwhile, after sending his son, King Pepin of Italy, into Pannonia with an army to hold in check the peoples newly subdued, Charles himself, while encamped in Saxony, received two embassies from the Avarian regions.

> “One said that the Chagan had come to meet him with the other nobles, whom the Avars had appointed for themselves after the former leaders had been killed. The other said that Pepin was seated with his army at Rhingum.”

So report the Loisel Annals, which add:

> “The lord king then traversed Saxony with his entire army and returned to Gaul. At the palace of Aachen he joyfully saw his son Pepin returning from Pannonia and bringing back the remaining part of the treasure. There he celebrated both the Nativity of the Lord and Easter.”

Of this same war Einhard writes in the *Life of Charles*:

> “No war against the Franks can be recalled within human memory by which they were more enriched and increased in wealth.”

Henry was not present at this second expedition entrusted by his father to Pepin. Charles ordered him “to depart”—that is, from Aachen, where he had first arrived carrying the spoils of the enemy, as stated above—“and return to Italy, lest anything new should arise in that region during Pepin’s absence,” as P. Aemilius says in book II.

Angilbert was appointed to carry to Rome, in Charles’s name, the greater part of the spoils which Henry had taken from the Avars and had dedicated to the Roman churches for offering. Angilbert was known to the pope, for in 792 he had brought Felix from the Council of Regensburg to Pope Adrian.

### XXI

While Angilbert was preparing to hasten his pilgrimage, news spread of the death of Pope Adrian. According to Anastasius, he died on the seventh day before the Kalends of January and was buried as the previous year, 795, was drawing to a close.

From this we may infer that the Avarian war, first completed by Henry, whose spoils were now being prepared for shipment to Rome through Angilbert, may have begun in the final months of 795, although it is commonly assigned to 796, at the beginning of which it was completed.

Thus once again the persons involved change, and the letter and embassy previously directed to Adrian are redirected to Leo III. Charles himself acknowledges this in the letter with which he replied to Leo’s letter, by which Leo, according to custom, had informed Charles of his elevation to the chair of Peter. Among other things, Charles says:

> “We have sent to Your Holiness Angilbert, a personal member of our household,” whom previously, as we promised through the religious men Campolus and Anastasius, we had arranged to send to our most blessed father, your predecessor. But, as we have stated, while all the gifts were ready, his journey was suddenly delayed by the mournful news of our father’s death. Now, however, made happier by the succession of Your Holiness, we are striving to accomplish in you what we desired to do with that pious father.”

Charles furnished Angilbert with a private and familiar memorandum and instructed him concerning what was to be done with Leo. It bears this title: *Admonition to Pope Leo*. It is addressed to “Homer, the confidential adviser,” the name by which Angilbert is designated. Charles’s court used such names, drawn from learned literature, when addressing men distinguished by some appearance of virtue. Thus Alcuin called Charles “David,” and Richulf “Demosthenes.”

### XXII

Armed with these instructions and laden with the Avarian spoils intended as a gift for Leo, Angilbert undertook the journey to Italy. On the way he visited Paulinus and delivered Alcuin’s letter to him.

This is established by the treatise of Paul Petavius on Nithard, grandson of Charlemagne, which Duchesne included in volume II of the *Writers of Frankish Affairs*:

> “At that time Angilbert also carried Alcuin’s letters to Leo III and to Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia.”

A marginal note there adds:

> “These are numbers 27 and 59 in the printed copies, but in the manuscript of the best quality, 72 and 73.”

I do not deny that Alcuin’s Letter 72, addressed to Leo, is the one mentioned here. At its conclusion it mentions Angilbert as the bearer of the letter:

> “This dearest son of mine, Angilbert, is able to disclose to you our humble devotion toward the apostolic see.”

But I would not venture to say the same of Letter 73, which was indeed addressed to Paulinus but apparently not delivered by Angilbert. Rather, it seems to have been delivered by another man who had carried a different letter to Paulinus and who, as we conjectured above in section 19, may have been Henry.

For it appears to have been written before Angilbert’s arrival, since it refers to his Roman journey not as imminent but as something that would occur later. We believe instead that the letter carried by Angilbert was Letter 112, in which Alcuin mentions the submission of the Avars and their embassy to the king:

> “By the power and grace of God,” he says, “a wondrous triumph has been won over the people of the Avars. Their envoys, sent to the lord king, promise peaceful submission and the Christian faith.”

[Col. 0531D] That this occurred in the year 796, after the first victory over the Avars achieved by Henry, is unanimously attested by the annalists.

### XXIII

But when the faith of the Avars began to waver, and indeed some of them returned to their ancestral rites—perjurers and covenant-breakers against God and humanity—Gerold of Bavaria and Henry of Friuli were killed in 799 by a monstrous act of treachery while they were bringing forces to recall the rebels to obedience to God and the king.

The Bertin Annals state:

> “In the same year (799) the Avarian people defected from the faith which they had promised, and Henry, duke of Friuli, was overwhelmed by the ambushes of the townsmen near Tarsatica, a city of Liburnia, after he had achieved so many successful undertakings; and Gerold, count and prefect of Bavaria, fell in a battle fought against the Avars.”

That this disaster occurred on the Kalends of September appears from the epitaph of Gerold, which Henry Canisius presents in volume II, part 2, of the *Church Antiquities*, page 73, Amsterdam edition of 1725, from an unknown poet. It reads:

> Beneath this mound the limbs of mighty Gerold are preserved;  
> He enlarged the rights of this place and strengthened them with all his power.  
> He was slain by the Pannonians for the peace of the true Church,  
> And fell by the savage sword on the Kalends of September.  
> He gave his soul to the stars. Faithful Saxo  
> Carried his limbs away, brought them back here,  
> And here closed them in worthy honor.

Palladius the Younger, book II, writes that Henry, returning from the battle and intending to take revenge on the troublesome Liburnians and Histrians, was deceived by the treachery of the people of Tarsatica. They promised to hand over the fortress if he entered at night with a small escort, after the gates had been secretly opened.

When he entered the city with a chosen band of soldiers, the townsmen closed the gates behind him, took up arms, and wounded them all mortally. They also hurled a vast quantity of stones and roof tiles, leaving the dead and buried in a single assault.

Let the credibility of this account rest with its author; I would not make myself guarantor of such claims, since no ancient writer supports them. The event itself, however, is certain, and the treachery and death are beyond doubt.

The following year Charles avenged it when, as Aemilius writes at the beginning of book III, “as he passed through Venetia, he avenged it: the authors of the crime were executed by the sword.” Such was the end that Henry met—certainly he did not deserve to perish in this way.

But a few further points remain concerning the book addressed to him.

### XXIV

If one considers the subject matter, it is indeed appropriate to a man who, although a layman, was devoted to the perfection of life. The author draws several things especially from the storehouse of the ancient Fathers, including Julian, but adapts them so prudently to the subject that he does not make them appear to be his own. He also produces other material from himself which seemed not unworthy of being attributed to Basil the Great, as we note in chapter 20.

As for the form, however, the order is not consistently maintained and the method is neglected. This may easily be pardoned in an age less cultivated. Nor was it done without reason. For when uniformity of order repeatedly produces weariness in a reader, variety itself, by contrast, gives pleasure, and the reader is drawn into the work because it does not fatigue the mind.

Moreover, the work was written for a man burdened with cares, who had no leisure to devote himself to extended reading. It was quite enough if he were able to read one or two chapters in a day. If, therefore, you consider the condition of the man to whom it was written, you will praise this somewhat tumultuous arrangement of the material, as I may call it, and admire the prudence of the director; and you will recognize that what appears to lack order is in fact ordered.

Say the same concerning the style. Paulinus knew how to be abundant and how to be concise. One should therefore commend a man who, when speaking in the assemblies of councils, raises his discourse to a dignity appropriate to the person and subject under discussion, but who, when dealing privately with an individual, proceeds on foot, keeps his language plain, and yet does not advance in a base or sordid manner.

### XXV

The words of chapter 7 seem to indicate the place and time of writing:

> “Although a change of place has carried me far from you in body, and so forth.”

They show not that he was absent when he wrote, but that he had been absent and had moreover returned, as is clear upon consideration. He was absent when he attended the councils at Aachen in 789, Regensburg in 792, and Frankfurt in 794, as appears from his Life. We nevertheless believe that he is referring here rather to his most recent absence, since the friendship had already been cultivated for seven years, as the book itself suggests.

Moreover, in chapters 58 and 59 of this book he seems to allude to the heresy of Felix, recently condemned at that council, when he says to the Lord:

> “Pursue the lion who has snatched a sheep from your flock, and, after the darkness of night has been driven away and the shadows of darkness dispersed, and so forth.”

All these things correspond to the heresy recently proscribed.

[Col. 0533A] We therefore think that Paulinus, already a bishop, wrote, for Duke or Count Henry, about the year 795, on his return home, a book of exhortation appropriate in subject matter and prudent in form and style.

# SECOND DISSERTATION ON THE COUNCIL OF FRIULI

[Col. 0533]

### I

Although our Paulinus attended many of the councils convened during the time and at the command of Charlemagne, and held the first place in nearly all of them, we shall refrain from discussing them individually. This is both because they have been treated here and there as occasion arose, and because they were not the work of Paulinus alone, so that we would otherwise be compelled to produce a separate dissertation on them. We are endeavoring not only to bring his works into the public light but also, insofar as has been granted to us, to illuminate them through our labor and study.

The case is different with the Council of Friuli. At that council Paulinus not only held the primacy, as was fitting, in his own metropolitan church, but also summoned the bishops of the province by the authority of the prince; he delivered an extended and elegant address, proposed a statement of faith, and presented canons to be observed. In short, he, and no one else, convened, held, and completed the council. It is therefore proper that we treat the affairs of this synod in a separate dissertation.

So that we do not waste time on superfluities or abuse the reader’s patience, we shall speak only of the time and place of the council and, in addition, of the bishops who assembled and of their churches subject to the metropolitan see of Aquileia. If any passage in the text seemed to require a particular comment or explanation, we have already dealt with it in its proper place through notes and observations.

### II

Before the address delivered by Paulinus at this synod there is placed a kind of preface. I would call it the work of the scribe who recorded the acts of the Council, were it not that the style, entirely consistent with the rest of the address, identifies Paulinus as the author.

[Col. 0533C] In it are found the following words, which constitute the principal—and almost the sole—subject of this dissertation:

> “In the most felicitous year of their rule, the twenty-third and the fifteenth, a brotherly company of certain bishops, summoned by canonical formulas, gathered together in the municipality of Friuli.”

There you have the indicated time, place, and bishops. But they are only apparently indicated. For neither the time nor the place, nor the number of bishops and their churches, is free from controversy and difficulty. It must therefore be investigated more carefully in what year of Christ the twenty-third year of Charlemagne and the fifteenth year of Pepin coincided, what place is meant by the name Friuli, and finally how many bishops assembled and from which churches they came.

### III

When we first discuss the date, a considerable difficulty arises from the words just cited:

> “In the twenty-third year of their rule and the fifteenth, summoned by canonical formulas, and so forth.”

These words [Col. 0533D] have grievously tormented the ingenuity of critical chronologers. Baronius, under 791, no. 3, assigns the fifteenth year to Pepin’s reign, but this cannot agree with the year 791 of Jesus Christ, in which he says that the synod was convened.

For Pepin had been proclaimed king of Italy in 781, when he was baptized at Easter in Rome by Pope Adrian. From that year until 791, not fifteen but only ten years had elapsed, and the eleventh year began on 15 April, the date on which Easter fell in 781.

### IV.

Cointius, *Annales Francorum Ecclesiastici*, vol. VI, under the year 795, no. 8, follows the reckoning of the years of Charles’s reign from the year 768—that is, when, after his father Pepin died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, he assumed the kingdom of Gaul on the seventh day before the Ides of that same month. He thinks that the number of his regnal years should be corrected, so that instead of 23 the twenty-seventh year should be read; thus the council would fall in the year of Christ 795, which, from 15 April onward, was the fifteenth year of Pepin’s reign.

His reason for introducing this correction into the chronicle is as follows: Since the heresy of Felix is said in the Council of Frankfurt to have been condemned for the third time—first “at Regensburg, then at Rome, thirdly at Frankfurt”—and since they place the Synod of Forojulium, in which Felix was likewise condemned, after the Council of Frankfurt, which is known to have been held in the year of Christ 794. [Col. 0534A]

Yet neither the correction is convincing nor does the argument compel it. Not the former, first, because this seems to have been asserted without evidence. Why should the number 23, the years of Charles, be corrected, when it is expressed in such explicit words, accepted and maintained by everyone, and why should it not rather be the year of Pepin that is corrected, with 11 substituted for 15? Nor does the argument for the correction compel us. The formal and legitimate proscription of Felix’s heresy was indeed issued for the third time at Frankfurt; but that occurrence should not be counted in the same reckoning as what was done incidentally against it at the Council of Forojulium, without explicitly naming the heretic. For Felix’s doctrine could have been rejected at the Council of Forojulium—and in fact it was rejected—without thereby removing the number of the three formal condemnations or separating our synod from the year 791, in which Baron and others believe it was held. Cointius, therefore, did not reach the correct conclusion.

### V.

Hardouin, in the notes appended by the Venetian editors to the Forojulian Synod in vol. IX of Labbe’s collection, p. 31, does not understand the number of years to be contained in the numeral notation XV, or 15—which is written everywhere in this form and nowhere spelled out as *quindecim* or *decimo quinto*—that the aforementioned authors attach to Pepin’s reign. Rather, he takes it to be the number of bishops summoned to the synod.

Thus Hardouin writes, against the Cointius just cited, concerning the phrase “and 15 canonical syllables”: “Cointius, in his *Annals* under the year 895” (correcting the error that slipped in through the printers’ carelessness, and restoring 795), “read *et quintodecimo*, ‘and in the fifteenth,’ and consequently disturbed the chronology.” So Hardouin.

What should be thought about the number of bishops will be explained below. Meanwhile, attention must be paid to the words “in the year of their rule,” by which the years of both rulers, not of only one, are presented in the reckoning and chronology. Therefore, that 15 must necessarily be referred to the years of Pepin. The words, then, cannot be understood as referring to the summons itself.

### VI.

Having rejected these opinions, we ought apparently to adopt that of P. Pagi, who places the synod in the year 796. In his critique of Baronius under the year 791, no. 6, he observes that the fifteenth year of Pepin, king of Italy, and likewise the twenty-third year of Charles’s Italian reign coincide in the year 796.

Pepin was indeed baptized at Rome by Pope Adrian in the year 781, when Easter fell on 15 April, and was called king of Italy. His fifteenth year therefore began on 15 April 795 and ended on 15 April of the following year, 796. But from the year 774, on 26 May, when Pavia was captured and King Desiderius was carried away to Francia, Charles was called king of Italy, and the twenty-third year of his Italian reign began.

It is true that, with matters proceeding in this way, we do not yet obtain a perfect correspondence between the years of the two kings: Pepin’s fifteenth regnal year ended on 15 April, whereas Charles’s twenty-third regnal year had not yet begun on that day, since it did not begin until 26 May. But only one epoch should not be considered in reckoning the years of Charles’s Italian reign. One epoch begins on 26 May, when Ticinum was captured and Desiderius was driven from the throne; the other begins with the victories won over the Lombard enemies before 15 April.

To prevent this from seeming to be asserted without evidence, Pagi observes that Adrian called Charles king of the Lombards before the capture of Pavia, in a letter numbered 55 in the *Caroline Letters*. He notes that the letter was carried to Gaufridus, who was returning to the camp situated near Pavia for the siege of the city, under the year 774, no. 9—and therefore before the city itself had been captured. Moreover, under the same year, no. 10, from a charter concerning the ninths and tithes and the restoration of the churches of the diocese of Le Mans, subscribed as follows—“Given in the month of April, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the second year, by Christ’s favor, of our glorious empire, and in the thirty-fourth year of our reign in Francia and the twenty-ninth in Italy”—he shows that on 23 April 802, Charles had already reached the twenty-ninth year of his Italian reign in the second year of his imperial rule.

Therefore, Charles’s Italian reign must at some point have begun before 26 May. This is Pagi’s argument.

### VII.

Yet this epoch can be investigated even more precisely from the dates of other charters. In the latest editor of Ughelli, among the documents concerning Concordia, there is a charter issued at Frankfurt to Peter, bishop of Concordia, on the day before the Nones of April in the year 802, marked as the thirty-fourth year in Francia and the twenty-ninth in Italy. From this one may infer that by 4 April 774 Charles had already begun to be called king of Italy.

Keep this point in mind. In the same Ughelli, among the documents concerning Ceneda, another charter is produced, likewise issued at Frankfurt, on the day before the Kalends of April, in the twenty-sixth and twentieth years of the reign; that year corresponds to the year of Christ 794. Since the date of that document establishes the point, the twentieth year of the Italian reign cannot have been complete on that day. If it had been complete, it would already have been the twenty-first; but if Charles’s twentieth year of Italian reign was not complete on 31 March and the twenty-ninth year had already begun on 4 April, it is necessary to place its beginning between 31 March and 4 April.

Pagi did not investigate precisely on which day it should be considered to have begun. He merely says that “since, according to Anastasius, Charles subdued various cities before the capture of Pavia, he began to call himself king of Italy from the part of Lombardy that had been conquered.”

It seems probable to us, however, that Charles did not assume the title of king of the Lombards by arbitrary usurpation, but that in the year 774, when he was going to Rome after leaving the siege of Pavia and after several cities belonging to the Lombard dominion had already been captured—although Ticinum and Verona had not yet been taken, as the distinguished Scipione Maffei shows in *Verona Illustrata*, part I, book XI, from a document numbered 9, which he prints at the end and which is dated to the “eighteenth and fifteenth year of Desiderius and Adelchis, by indiction XII, in the month of April,” a year which, according to Maffei himself, corresponds to the year of Christ 774—Adrian, who had received him with great courtesy, conferred upon him the title “king of the Lombards.”

The letter numbered 55 above cited itself suggests this. In it the pope calls him king of the Lombards and mentions both his arrival at Rome and his return to the siege of Ticinum in these words:

“From that time, from the day on which you departed from this Roman city for those regions, every day, even at every moment and hour, our priests have not ceased to cry out to our God on your behalf…”

The time of his arrival at Rome is recorded by Anastasius as having been on Holy Saturday. His stay there continued at least until the following Wednesday; for the Librarian says that on that day he confirmed before the pontiff the donation made to Pope Stephen and added other gifts to those already given.

Observe also that on Easter Monday, at the solemn celebration of Mass in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, the pontiff had praises offered to him. Praises, or acclamations, were public ceremonies performed especially for rulers when they were inaugurated, consisting of prayers for life, happiness, and victory, as Du Cange explains at length in the *Glossary*, under the word *Laus*.

It is therefore entirely consistent with reason that in these praises the people, by their acclamation, bestowed upon a ruler who had rendered such great services to the Roman Church the title “king of the Lombards”; and the pontiff himself did not hesitate to confirm it when writing to him.

In the year 774, when these events took place at Rome, Easter fell on 3 April. From this time, therefore, the epoch of the years of Charles’s Italian reign sometimes began to be reckoned.

Since this is so, Charles’s twenty-third year of Italian reign, beginning in 796, coincides with the ending of Pepin’s fifteenth year of Italian reign. The interval between 3 or 4 April and 15 April was therefore the period not only of the coinciding twenty-third year of Charles and fifteenth year of Pepin, but also of Paulinus’s Council of Forojulium.

For Paulinus, when dating his council, followed Italian usage. Among the Italians, as Mabillon observes in *De Re Diplomatica*, book II, chapter 26, § 2, no. 12, under Pepin, son of Charles the Great, a double epoch was sometimes given. Thus, in Puricellus, p. 21, a charter of Archbishop Peter concerning the Ambrosian Basilica concludes: “In the sixteenth and ninth year in Italy of our lords Charles and Pepin, kings.”

So our Paulinus inscribed and celebrated his council in the twenty-third and fifteenth years of their reign.

### VIII.

The authority of Georgius Pilonus can support this view. In his *History of Belluno*, book II, he places this Pauline synod in no other year than 796, and adds that the practice of convening synods, which had been interrupted for various reasons, was then resumed. This agrees with what Paulinus said at the council.

Yet Pilonus is mistaken when he asserts that the council was convened at Aquileia and that all the bishops, the suffragans—so called because the patriarch was elected by their votes—were present. None of this is correct: the synod was convened not at Aquileia but at Forojulium; not all the bishops were present, as will be explained below; nor were the suffragans called by that name because they cast votes in the election of the patriarch, since he was elected not by the bishops of the province but either by the ruler or by the clergy of the church.

For the reason why they are called suffragans, see Du Cange in the *Glossary*.

Our Palladius also reports that in this year a synod was convened by Paulinus, and indeed immediately after the victory over the Avars achieved by Henry. But he too is mistaken when he says that this was a different synod from the one he assigns to the year 790. It is the very same synod, not another; it was celebrated not in 790, when no synod was held, but in 796.

### IX.

To the chronological arguments just drawn upon, by which our opinion is supported, one may add no slight confirmation from Paulinus’s own words. Compare what he said at the council with the events of that time, and you will find that they fit no other year better than 796.

He says as follows:

“Because of the impending wars of battle, which with roaring ferocity did not cease to assail us on every side throughout the circuit of our borders, the temporary interruption of this magnificent work”—that is, the council—“can undoubtedly be approved.”

For the origin, progress, and renewal of the Avar war, to which Paulinus chiefly refers here, see Dissertation 1 on the book addressed to Henry, beginning at no. 12 and following.

Thus, through alternating battles and victories, the king’s poorly pacified affairs deprived Paulinus of the opportunity to assemble the council until the year 796. The Avar war, renewed in 795 and brought to an end by Henry’s victory at the beginning of the following year, 796, gave Paulinus the occasion to address the assembly of the Fathers in these words:

“But now, with divine clemency lending aid, the pride of the fierce barbarians has indeed been crushed, their uplifted necks brought low, peace has been restored to the lands, and royal commands are breathing again for a little while; we therefore judged it most necessary, hastening with the utmost speed, to gather your fraternity into one college.”

Note the words “now that their necks have been crushed.” They indicate that not much time had elapsed between the victory itself and the convocation of the council. This is shown even more clearly by the words “hastening with the utmost speed.”

To hasten with the utmost speed means to exert one’s final strength so that what we wish to be done may be accomplished quickly, without any intervening delay, insofar as the nature of the business prudently permits.

Paulinus therefore assembled the council at the first opportunity presented to him. Immediately after Easter—which, as in 774, also fell on 3 April in 796—he held his synod, in the interval extending to 15 April, the day on which Pepin’s sixteenth year began. If one may venture a conjecture, it was perhaps assembled and completed on the tenth, the Sunday *in Albis*.

### X.

Paulinus further added, in excuse for the interruption of the councils, that he had in some measure made up for it by attending synods convened by Charles whenever summoned.

“Nevertheless,” he said, “it will not be possible to judge by truthful assertions that it was entirely interrupted. For whenever, summoned by the revered commands of our rulers, I have been present in the general and most celebrated synod of the venerable Fathers with the humblest presence of my smallness—for it has often happened that I was there—it has not, as I think, been hidden from your minds, nor do I doubt that it has on several occasions been abundantly evident to your eyes.”

By these words he was referring to various assemblies previously convened, among which was the Council of Aachen in 789. That it was an assembly of many bishops is clear from Baluze’s notes on it in vol. II of the *Capitularies* and from King Charles’s own preface, in which, addressing the bishops, he said:

“Therefore it pleased us to ask your diligence, O shepherds of the churches of God, that with vigilant care, etc.”

But consider the words that follow:

“We have also appended certain chapters from canonical institutions that seemed more necessary.”

These chapters, compiled from canonical institutions, were the work of Paulinus and Alcuin, as Benedict the Levite explicitly asserts in the preface to book V of the *Capitularies of the Frankish Kings*. Speaking of book VII in the sequence—which is book III among those collected by Benedict himself—he says:

“Third, in the little book … certain chapters collected from the canons by Bishop Paulinus and Master Albinus, together with the other teachers, at the command of the most invincible prince Charles, have been inserted in scattered form, and after certain interpolations there follow other matters suitable to the monastic rule.”

The capitulary of Aachen from the year 789 is thoroughly filled with the canons of ancient councils and Fathers. Moreover, chapters for monks were inserted in it, so that there can be no doubt that these are, at least in part, the same chapters which Benedict the Levite identifies as the work of Paulinus.

If you wish, compare with these the chapters of the Council of Aachen in the seventh book of the *Capitularies*, and you will find many that correspond exactly.

Since several capitularies are recorded under the same year 789 and several edicts are found issued on different days, it is easy to believe that Paulinus took part in preparing them. He said in the words quoted above that “it often happened that I was present with the humblest presence of my smallness.”

### XI.

Above all the councils to which he was referring in these words was the most celebrated Council of Frankfurt, which he singularly calls “the general and most celebrated synod of the venerable Fathers.” He could quite properly assert that he had not been absent from it, since he stood out so prominently in his speech and in its proceedings that no one could have failed to notice him.

This Council of Frankfurt, convened in 794, is the synod Paulinus is discussing. It plainly proves that the Council of Forojulium was later than that year and therefore belongs to the year 796.

This concludes the question of the date.

### XII.

As for the place, Paulinus’s words make it perfectly clear that it was Forumjulium:

“The company of certain bishops came together at the town of Forumjulium, [of] the metropolitan see of Aquileia…”

For a long time, however, there was controversy over what and where this Forumjulium was. Among our own people, the ancient rivalry between the people of Udine and those of Cividale divided the authors into opposing parties, each city competing for the glory of the name and each relying on its own arguments to claim the precedence of ancient honor.

I would prefer to leave the matter, as it has hitherto stood, undecided, rather than incur the indignation either of my own countrymen or of the people of Cividale, whose nobility I otherwise esteem and whose goodwill I honor.

Nevertheless, let what is now commonly called Cividale, or Cividale of Austria, be Forumjulium. For recent authors generally hold this view—authors who have no interest in whether one city or the other prevails, but only in reporting what is more truthful. We commend them and strive to imitate them, making friendly truth our chief concern.

### XIII.

The alteration of the name nevertheless causes some difficulty. Why and when was Forumjulium called Cividale, and Cividale of Austria?

Candidus, in book III, shortly before the end, derives the origin of the name “Cividale of Austria” from the following story:

“Rosimund, the wife of King Liutprand, descended from the princes of Austria, withdrew to the seat of Forojulium after her husband had died, at the urging of Hirprand. There, observing the noble character of the citizens in difficult deliberations, she bestowed the whole administration upon them, seeking to spend the remainder of her life without anxiety. Therefore, by decree of the senate, for the memory of posterity, it was decided that, with the name of the town changed, it should be called Cividale of Austria.”

But this has the flavor of an old wives’ tale, which men of more discerning taste, once they catch its scent, should blow away.

Fontanini comes closer in his booklet *Delle Masnade*, when he says that the city was called Cividale of Austria because the eastern region or district was called Austria; and in relation to Ticinum, the royal city of the Lombards, Forumjulium truly lay in that position. He adds, by way of example, that the part of Gaul extending toward the east was likewise called Austria or Austrasia.

Thus the name was changed on account of the Lombards, and, as Fontanini says in the same work, p. 23, the usage continued into the memory of our ancestors.

Yet, leaving aside this origin of the name, why did Paulinus, who assembled the council after the Lombards had been expelled from Forojulium, call it not Cividale of Austria but Forumjulium? It would be unjust to attribute to Paulinus, who lived there, forgetfulness of a new nomenclature introduced only shortly before by the people expelled from that place.

Whatever may be the truth concerning the change of name, there is no reason for further concern about it. Let the people of Cividale, if they wish, possess the wise glory of old age, and let it benefit them. Let the matter only be resolved with an even balance, and let judgment proceed discreetly with equal steps on both sides, so that, while we silently concede to them the greater antiquity, they may acknowledge that our present claims are stronger.

### XIV.

Within Forojulium itself, Paulinus selected for the assembly a church dedicated to the blessed Virgin Mary.

It is evident that this was not the church which today holds the principal place in the city and is adorned with a distinguished college of canons, although it is honored under the title of the Assumption of the Virgin Mary into heaven. Its construction is not sufficiently ancient to establish this, and the charter of the erection of the church of Cividale—which I would produce, if my uncle Nicolaus Madrisius had not already given it to the editor of Ughelli, who inserted it under Patriarch Gotofredus—shows that it was not built before 1191 and was dedicated to Saint Donatus.

In truth, even that church is not the same one that was then erected from the alms of the faithful, especially those listed in the cited charter. It is another church of still more recent construction, built by the canons in 1494, as is clear from the charter in Appendix 2, no. 42.

Indeed, in 1283, a document written by Nicolaus, notary of Cividale, is dated as follows: “Done at Cividale of Austria, before the doors of the major church of Saint Donatus.”

There is in the city a church called Saint Mary in Curia, which is seen not far from the palace called that of Callistus. When Callistus transferred the patriarchal see from Cormons to Forojulium, he left his name to the patriarchal buildings that he had erected.

Perhaps Paulinus, who succeeded Callistus with only Siguald intervening, held the council more conveniently in the nearby church. Or, if you prefer, it may have been held in the church of Saint Mary in the Valley of the Maidens, belonging to the monastery already built in the forest under Patriarch Siguald and, if the report is true, transferred at the time of Paulinus to Forojulium by Louis and Lothar and later granted to Patriarch Maxentius, as the charters in Appendix 2, nos. 1 and 8, show.

On the eastern side of the city, across the bridge over the Natisone River—formerly a wooden bridge and now a stone bridge of exceptional construction, erected in 1441, as appears from charter 204 in Appendix 2, no. 39—there is another church dedicated to the Virgin Mother.

I would not venture to assert that this church already existed then or that it was selected for the synod.

I believe that the church which housed the council was the one that held the principal place in the city and was dedicated to the Virgin Mary. Perhaps one of its doors, near the altar of Saint Donatus, was called the Door of Saint Donatus.

### XV.

We now come to the third question proposed: how many bishops, and of which churches, assembled at the Pauline synod.

The province of Aquileia was once exceedingly extensive. It stretched from the Adda as far as Pannonia, including Noricum and the inlets of the Adriatic Sea—that is, both maritime and inland Venetia, Istria, and Liburnia.

Here is a catalogue of the thirty-three bishoprics which, at various times and according to various authorities, we have learned were subject to the see of Aquileia:

1. Juliensis  
2. Altinensis  
3. Opiterginus  
4. Acilanus  
5. Sacillanus  
6. Maranensis  
7. Aemonensis  
8. Scarabantiensis  
9. Cellianus  
10. Sabionensis  
11. Petoviensis  
12. Tiburniensis  
13. Beconensis  
14. Augustanus  
15. Aventiensis  
16. Vejentanus  
17. Cittanovanus  
18. Justinopolitanus  
19. Tergestinus  
20. Petinensis  
21. Polensis  
22. Parentinus  
23. Mantuanus  
24. Concordiensis  
25. Cenetensis  
26. Vicentinus  
27. Tridentinus  
28. Feltrensis  
29. Veronensis  
30. Patavinus  
31. Tarvisinus  
32. Bellunensis  
33. Comensis.

Let us append a brief account of each.

### XVI.

#### 1. The Bishopric of Juliensis

The bishopric of Juliensis is mentioned in the Synod of Grado under Elias, patriarch of Aquileia, in the year 579. At that time Maxentius was bishop of the town of Julium Carnicum, now commonly called Zuglio, whose name is still preserved by a few remains of the ancient city among the settlements of the Carnic mountains.

Take care, however, not to assign the bishops of this place to one of our own cities, as our countrymen—whether the people of Udine or of Cividale—often do, through a most pleasant error of mind, assigning them now to one city and now to the other as love of country carries them, but always incorrectly.

Thus those too are mistaken who believe that they rely on truth when the patriarch Marino Grimani says in the privilege granted to the people of Cividale on 18 December 1524, when he first visited their church and presented them with the pontifical cope:

“It was fitting that, just as your republic once stripped itself of its own bishopric for the adornment of our patriarchate, so we too, in memory of so great a matter, should be stripped by a mutual added compensation of our chief garment, for your sake.”

The good bishop was imposed upon by the claim that Cividale of Austria had at some time divested itself of episcopal dignity for the sake of the patriarchate, although it had never been adorned with its own bishop, as the eminent Norisius shows from Paul the Deacon in *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 9, § 4.

Likewise, Philip of the Tower, a native of the city and bishop of Adria, writes in his dissertation *On the Colony of Forojulium* that the city did not strip itself of a bishopric for the sake of the patriarchal see, but that Amator had been expelled by Patriarch Callistus. Amator was not the proper bishop of Forojulium, but of Julium Carnicum; he was living temporarily at Forojulium with the permission of the Lombard dukes. After him no bishop of Juliensis is found.

The stripping of the cope, however, and its presentation have a different origin from that claimed by the people of Cividale. When the newly appointed patriarch visited the metropolitan church of Aquileia itself, the ministers of the church stripped him of the cope, as is clear from the charter that we produce in Appendix 2, no. 25.

The rites of the church of Aquileia passed over with the patriarch to the church of Forojulium. One such rite was the recitation on the day of the Purification of the names of the patriarchs in the church of Cividale, a practice that had been observed in Aquileia on the same day. The ritual manuscript of that church prescribes the following after the antiphon “Today the blessed Virgin…”:

“When this has been completed, the names of the patriarchs are recited.”

Augustine Gradonicus, as will be clear from the charter to be included in Appendix 2, no. 45, in the time of our ancestors gave his pastoral staff to the chapter of the church of Udine. This was indeed a more distinguished gift than a cope, which is sometimes granted to other and lesser ecclesiastical dignities. Yet who among the people of Udine ever dreamed that such a gift signified an abolished episcopal dignity of Udine, removed for the sake of the patriarchal see?

Our patriarchs, when they visited their see at Aquileia, which had been transferred to the church of Udine, used to grant the people of Udine the mule on which they had ridden there, together with its trappings, saddle, and gilded spurs. You will learn from the charter in Appendix 2, no. 43, to be inserted there, that Marino Grimani himself did this—not as a sign of any ancient dignity, but only as a token and testimony of honor and affection.

This was an old custom, which can be found in Ughelli under Walterus, when a dispute arose concerning the patriarch’s horse between Alardinus de Capite Pontis and the canons of Verona. The horse of the patriarch of Aquileia, who had first arrived at Verona, was adjudged to them on 3 March 1207.

Consider the matter of the cope with the people of Cividale in the same way. But let us return to the road from which love of truth, not the itch of contention, has led us somewhat astray.

### XVII.

#### 2. The Bishopric of Altinensis

The bishop of Altinensis was Peter under the same Elias, and he also took part in the Synod of Grado. You will find a fuller account of him and of Altinum in the dissertation on the Synod of Altinum, especially no. 18.

#### 3. The Bishopric of Opiterginus

Some improperly confuse Opiterginus with the bishopric of Ceneda, as though the latter had arisen from the destruction of the former.

For under Elias, Marcianus of Opitergium, or Opitergia, and Vindemius of Ceneda are found subscribed to the same Council of Grado. In the year 680, when Agatho held the see of Peter, both Ursinus of Ceneda and Benenatus of Opitergium subscribed at the Roman council.

Therefore one did not arise from the decline of the other, since it is plainly evident that both flourished at the same time. But consult also what we shall say below, no. 25, under Ceneda.

#### 4. The Bishopric of Acilanus

The bishopric of Acilanus is mentioned in a charter of Otto, which the Venetian editor of Ughelli publishes among the bishops of Treviso. In that charter, in the year 968, Otto grants to Rozo, also called Roccio, bishop, “the castle of Asilo, with the church built in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary, which once seemed to have been the head and seat of the bishopric of that place.” Here, as the note on diplomatic terminology indicates, *erat* (“was”) should be read in place of *videbatur* (“seemed to be”), through a change and misuse of the verb.

The bishopric of Azolum, or Acilum, is mentioned as a suffragan of the metropolitan of Aquileia in the Synod of Mantua, where Arthemius of Azolum appears in the penultimate place. Before that, in the council of Marano, Agnellus of Azilium is found, as the more reliable reading has it—not “of Sacillum.”

#### 5. The Bishopric of Sacillanus

Ughelli confuses Sacillanus with Acilanus in his preface to the patriarchs of Aquileia, and says that the subscription of Sacillanus is found in the synodical letter of Pope Agatho concerning the Sixth Synod.

I do not find his subscription there, however, nor does P. de Rubeis find it in his note on the Council of Mantua, no. 10. Nor do I find it in the code of the Apostolic Treasury or in the Roman provincial list, where it had been claimed that mention was made of a bishop of Sacillanus. Neither Charles of Saint Paul nor Lucas Holstenius, who had already examined these records, found it there.

#### 6. The Bishopric of Maranensis

Palladius thinks that there was at some time a bishop of Maranensis from the Synod of Marano held under Patriarch Severus, but he does not state on what evidence or by what reasoning.

The Donatus who subscribed to the Lateran Council under Martin I was not, as the distinguished Father de Rubeis observes in his dissertation *On the Aquileian Schism*, chapter 12, a bishop of Marranum in Forojulium, but a bishop of Marianum in Corsica.

#### 7. The Bishopric of Aemonensis

Aemonensis is the same as the bishopric of Labacum, as Schonleben holds in the *Annals of Carniola*. Its bishop Patritius, called Peter by others, subscribed to the Council of Grado.

Apart from him, I find no bishop of Aemonensis or Labacum down to the year 1000, the point to which Schonleben brings his work.

Indeed, from Ughelli’s list of the suffragans of the metropolitan see of Aquileia, I find that an episcopal see at Labacum was established only by Pius II in 1461 and placed under the patriarch of Aquileia. But only six years later, at the request of the Emperor Frederick, it was removed from the jurisdiction of Aquileia by Paul II and immediately subjected to the Roman see.

All these bishoprics either had never existed, did not yet exist, had ceased to exist, lacked a bishop, or had been transferred to another see in Paulinus’s time.

## XVIII. In Noricum

8. I find the bishopric of Scarabantia, whose bishop Vigilius signs the council of Elias. Scarabantia, now called Sapringh or Zapprinum, according to Ferrarius following Lazio, lies eight German miles east of Vienna and was perhaps destroyed by the Avars in the year 789 or thereafter. For under the year 791 the Bertinian annalist says:

“Because of the excessive and intolerable wickedness which the Avars had committed against the holy Church and the Christian people,”

Charles proceeded into their territory and, at the river Arrabo, commonly called the Rab, beside which Scarabantia was situated according to Cellarius, defeated them. Thus what the Avars suffered from Charles in 791 was vengeance for the evils they had perpetrated against the Church in the preceding year; during that disturbance this see was either extinguished or suppressed.

9. Bishop John of Celia signs the same council of Grado in eighth place. Celeia, or, as Aeneas Sylvius has it in *History of Europe*, chapter 21, and as it is commonly pronounced, Cilia, was once a city of no little distinction, as the inscribed stones frequently found there testify. It perhaps also suffered the disasters inflicted by the Avars, and was at different times subject to the metropolitan of Aquileia, that of Lauriacum, and finally that of Salzburg. It now lacks a bishop.

10. The bishopric of Sabiona was honored by Saint Ingenuinus, whose name occurs in the councils of Grado and Marano. Morocutus, in his additions to Ughellus under Fortunatianus, the tenth bishop among the Aquileians, makes him the founder of this see in the year 550. He then conjectures that Sabiona was withdrawn from Aquileia on the occasion of the dispute that arose between the patriarch of Aquileia and the archbishop of Salzburg, when Charlemagne established the boundary between the two provinces and, with Sabiona destroyed, supplied Brixen to Salzburg.

This substitution could not have taken place before 798, when the church of Juvavum, or Salzburg, was raised by Leo III to an archbishopric, with Arno appointed as its first archbishop. Yet in 807 the name of Sabiona still survived; for in that year Enricus, or Einricus, bishop of Sabiona, attended the council of Salzburg under Arno.

Perhaps, therefore, Sabiona experienced the changing fortunes of other churches. Once subject to the metropolitan of Aquileia, it was left without a bishop after a long period of troubles and, on the occasion of the new archiepiscopal see, was placed under Salzburg when the recently appointed bishop Alimus was created; Enricus succeeded him about 807.

11. That Marcus and Valens were bishops of Petovium is clear from the council of Aquileia in 381 under Valerian, a celebrated council attended by Saint Ambrose and many men distinguished for learning and holiness. I would not venture to assert who held the episcopal see at Petovium—called both Petovium and Petavio—after these men and Virgilius, or Bergullus, who attended the council of Elias.

12. Leomanus, bishop of Tiburnia, attended the council of Grado. Candidus, among the other absurdities with which he stuffs his little work, also asserts in book IV that the church of Tiburnia now belongs to the territory of Trieste. What could be farther from the truth? Who would extend the extremely narrow diocese of Trieste as far as the Drava? Or, because he found Ternovo within the territory of Trieste, did he, misled by the similarity of the names, suppose it to be Teurnia, or Tiburnia?

Joseph Mota erred still more grievously in his dissertation *On Metropolitan Jurisdiction*. He neither understood Candidus’s meaning when he said, on the authority of Candidus, that the bishopric of Tiburnia later became that of Trieste, nor was it later made Triestine, nor did Candidus say this. He said only that the diocese of Tiburnia was then Triestine—that is, that the church or bishopric of Tiburnia then belonged to the territory of Trieste or was included in the diocese of Trieste—not that the Triestine see now existed in place of the Tiburnian one.

For each church gave its own bishop at the same time under Elias: Tiburnia gave Leomanus, and Trieste gave Severus. This church of Tiburnia, together with that of Beconia and that of Augusta, had already been withdrawn from the metropolitan of Aquileia in 591. Hence the schismatic bishops of the province of Aquileia complain in their petition to the emperor Maurice that the metropolitan right of the Aquileian church—namely, the right of ordaining bishops in the subject sees—had begun to be torn away “some years before,” and that “in three churches of our council, namely Beconia, Tiburnia, and Augusta, the bishops of Gaul had appointed priests.”

I think this Augusta was none other than Augusta Vindelicorum, since it was almost contiguous with the province of Friuli. This may be inferred from chapters 21 and following of the *Life of Saint Magnus*, written by Theodore of Campedon and printed among Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, volume I, page 666, Amsterdam edition of 1725, through the efforts of Basnage. He says that the work is filled with fables, especially in its chronology; in geographical matters, however, it is not to be rejected.

There Saint Magnus visits the bishop “Wichtpertus of the holy church of Augusta Vindelicorum,” to whom he says that he was “sent by the Lord to a place called Fauces, where the proper sources of the Julian Alps are found.”

15. Bishop Aaron of Aventia, or Avoritia, signs the council of Grado under Elias. Was he the bishop of the city which Cellarius calls Avendo among the Iapydes?

16. Let it be Vejentia, under which title Andreas, bishop of Vejentia in the province of Istria, signs the letters of Pope Agatho at the Roman council of 680. Geographers place it in Liburnia on the Flanatic Gulf and call it Vegium. See Cellarius.

Although in Paulinus’s time the bishops of Istria did not recognize the metropolitan of Aquileia but rather that of Grado, they are nevertheless counted both before and afterward, as they are today, among the province of Aquileia. Therefore those who, under Agatho, the patriarch of Aquileia—that is, of Grado—sign the Roman council of Pope Agatho as bishops of the province of Histria were formerly subject to the see of old Aquileia.

17. Cittanova, however, is a bishopric that only recently came to be called Aemonensis—that is, after the year 1000, according to Ughellus. Nevertheless, Cointius lists it among the sees of Istria under the name Aemonicensis in the year 774, no. 110, and under the name Oemonensis in 795, no. 25. Palladius thinks that the bishopric of Marano was transferred here; Schonleben thinks it was the Aemonian, that is, the Labacensian. I think neither is correct; rather, I would infer that the bishopric and city were of more recent origin from the name itself, which truly means “new city.”

18. Justinopolis, otherwise the island of Aegida, famous—if we believe the legends—for the landing of the Argonauts, received its name from the auspices of Justin, under whom it was restored, as a stone inscription attests, according to Reinesius, although he makes little of it.

Schonleben, against Ughellus, wishes Saint Nazarius to be counted as its first bishop, if not in the actual succession, at least in the catalogue, under the year 524. In the year 756, however, John appears; according to Ughellus, he was ordained that year by Vitellianus, the patriarch of Grado. But Ughellus made a harmless chronological mistake here, placing Vitellianus’s ordination at Grado only in the following year, 757.

After John, Senator was ordained by Vitellianus himself before 766, since in that year the patriarch of Grado died. Whether Senator survived until Paulinus’s time is irrelevant, since he would not have attended the council as an Istrian.

19. Severus of Trieste attended the council of Elias, and Gaudentius attended the Roman council of Pope Agatho as bishop of Istria—the name by which the entire province was then known, as is well established.

20. Ughellus and Cointius call the bishop of Petina also Pucinensis. I am surprised. Petina lies across the whole extent of Istria from Pucinum, situated between Aquileia and Trieste, a place famous not as an episcopal see but even for its old wines. Martianus appears at the council of Grado under Elias as bishop of Petina, not of Pucinum.

21. Adrian, bishop of Pola, signs the same council, and Cyriacus signs the letters of Pope Agatho at the Roman council.

22. John, bishop of Parentium, attended the synod of Elias. He must be placed before Euphrasius, which Ughellus did not do. For Euphrasius was still alive in 796, the sixteenth year of Constantine, son of Irene, as is clear from a document published by Ughellus’s editor among the records of Parentium. John, however, who attended the council of Grado in 579, preceded Euphrasius by more than two centuries.

## XX. Let us now proceed from the coast of Istria to inland Venetia

23. The bishopric of Mantua was established by Leo III in the year of our Paulinus’s death, namely 804. Ughellus deals briefly with the matter in volume I of his *Mantuans*:

“When Leo III, having learned of the discovery in 804 of the sponge soaked with Christ’s blood, formerly buried by Longinus, came to Mantua and with his own eyes examined the truth of this admirable relic, then for the first time”—note: *for the first time*—“he granted Mantua episcopal dignity and wished its bishop to be a suffragan of the patriarch of Aquileia. Leo’s decree retained its force until Pope Nicholas V, who in 1453 exempted the church of Mantua from the jurisdiction of Aquileia and subjected it immediately to the Roman see.”

24. The famous bishop of Concordia attended both councils: the council of Grado under Elias and that of Marano under the patriarch Severus. Cardinal Norisius, who could read *Concordiensis* in the Barberini manuscript and in Dandolo, because he read *Coelicanae*, changes it to *Caelinanae* and accumulates many arguments—rather unconvincing, in my judgment—about the bishop of Concordia’s journey to Caelina, now Maniago.

According to a document produced by Ughellus’s editor at the suggestion of Hieronymus David, a distinguished Venetian citizen, Charlemagne, in the thirty-fourth year of the Frankish kingdom, that is, in the year 802, received Peter the bishop and his church of Concordia under imperial protection. If Peter had visited his see in 796, he ought to have attended Paulinus’s council.

25. We have already said that Cenetia was distinct from Opitergium. Among other arguments which Father Bernard de Rubeis adduces in his dissertation on the Aquileian schism to weaken the council of Grado under Elias, he also alleges in chapter 11 that *Vindemius* should be read as *Cessensis*, not *Cenetensis*, because there was an island called Cissa in Istria.

He infers from the words of Paul the Deacon that Vindemius was an Istrian bishop, since Paul says that Severus was brought from Ravenna by Smaragdus with three bishops from Istria, namely John of Parentium, Severus, and Vindemius. But it is clear from the Roman council under Agatho that all the bishops of the province of Aquileia were called bishops of Istria. There Ursinus of Cenetia clearly appears under the patriarch Agatho, together with the bishops of the inland sees, such as Patavium and Opitergium, all of whom are called bishops of Istria.

This father seems, in attacking the council of Grado—which until now had not been called into question—to be attempting to establish and strengthen the acts of the council of Mantua, recently brought to light through his efforts, in which the claims of Grado are depressed and those of the church of Aquileia, through the agency of its patriarch Maxentius, are exalted. Whether he did both things lawfully, let others judge.

Dulcissimus, not Valentinus, as Ughellus thought in his account of Cenetia, obtained a privilege from Charles dated in the twenty-sixth and twentieth years of his reign, a year corresponding to A.D. 794. In it we read:

“And where”—that is, “at the fortress of the Cenetians”—“the venerable man Dulcissimus, bishop, presides.”

I think he was one of those who ought to have attended Paulinus’s council.

26. Ughellus says that the bishopric of Vicenza was established by Saint Prosdocimus, and that he was “the first bishop of Vicenza after he had shed distinction upon Aquileia, Patavium, and other cities.” But he is inconsistent with himself, since in his account of Aquileia he writes that Saint Mark and Saint Hermagoras, not Saint Prosdocimus, were its founders, and in his account of Patavium he says that Saint Prosdocimus was established by Saint Peter as “the first bishop of the people of Patavium,” not of Vicenza.

Ughellus himself places Bishop Henry of Vicenza in the time of Patriarch Elias, although Henry did not attend the council of Grado, “lest he should appear to be a participant in its error,” that is, in the schism formed at Aquileia. But Horontius, Henry’s successor, fell into the pit Henry had dug when he took the side of Severus at the conciliabulum of Marano and joined the assembly of schismatics who appealed from Pope Gregory to the emperor Maurice, signing the petition of appeal.

From the year 701 until 813 Peter appears, and afterward Reginald. Reginald attended the consecration of the church of Saint George at Verona, performed at the request of Rotaldus, bishop of Verona, by Maxentius, patriarch of Aquileia. He could have occupied the chair of Vicenza seventeen years earlier and attended Paulinus’s council.

## XXI. Tridentum

27. Ughellus states that the bishopric of Tridentum received the faith from Saint Hermagoras. The distinguished Joannes Benedictus Gentilottus, in his notes on Ughellus, observes that particular inscriptions in the cathedral choir, dedicated to him and to Saint Fortunatus, his companion in faith and martyrdom, were placed there for the sole purpose of bearing witness to this.

Abundantius, the eighteenth bishop of Tridentum, signs in seventh place at the council of Aquileia in 381 under Saint Valerian. Agnellus, the twenty-fifth, signs at the council of Grado under Elias and at that of Marano under the patriarch Severus.

After him and down to Hildegarius, who is listed as the forty-fourth, Ughellus enumerates bishops without any chronological indication. He assigns only the year 802 to Hildegarius; before him stands Amator, and above Amator, Clementianus. It is probable that one of these three attended Paulinus’s council.

28. Feltria, as commonly happens among neighboring peoples, is continually seen as a rival of the adjoining city of Belluno. Thus, in 1204, to settle the complaints of both flocks under one shepherd, a settlement had to be accepted by which Torrentinus, bishop of Feltria, and Anselmus, bishop of Belluno, agreed, with the authority of Innocent III, that upon the death of the first of them, the other would hold both churches under a single pastoral government. This arrangement lasted until 1462, under Pope Pius II.

Yet even after peace had been secured, the churches returned to their original separation under two shepherds. After Anselmus’s death, Torrentinus, adorned with the title of bishop of both churches, is named as a witness to a donation made by Wolcherus, patriarch of Aquileia, to the monastery of Saint Nicholas on the shore, namely:

“Tunilinus”—so it reads there—“bishop of Belluno and Feltria.”

Fonteius, the first bishop of Feltria whom we encounter, attended both the council of Grado and the conciliabulum of Marano. In Charlemagne’s time Endrighettus occupied the see; according to Pilonus, he is mentioned from 769 through 781. Whether he was still alive fifteen years later and attended the council of Friuli in 796 is uncertain.

After him, until the year 826, when Amatus is recorded and inserted into the council of Mantua, no other bishop appears.

## XXII. Verona

29. If any bishopric depends upon the see of Aquileia, it is that of Verona. Solacius attended the council of Grado under Elias, and Junior attended that of Marano. Rotaldus, who succeeded Aeginus after Aldo—one of these two occupied the chair of Verona at the time of Paulinus’s council—was summoned by the patriarch Maxentius to the consecration of the church of Saint George. According to the diploma produced by Ughellus in his account of Verona, Rotaldus exempted the chapter from the authority of future bishops of Verona and subjected it immediately to the patriarch.

The diploma, however, is considerably defective in its chronological notes. It is dated to the forty-first year of Charles and the first year of Bernard, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth indiction. Ughellus’s annotator wishes this to be the year 814. But in 814 Charles was no longer alive in September; he had died before the fortieth year of his Italian reign began, on January 28, namely the fifth day before the Kalends of February.

If it was dated in 813, as Ughellus wishes, it still cannot be the first year of Bernard, who is called king after the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October—that is, in the following month, November, of the same year 813. The Roman, or papal, sixth indiction corresponds to 813, but the Caesarean, or Constantinopolitan, indiction had already moved into the seventh.

Whatever may be true of the diploma, the present subjection is in fact certain.

## XXIII. Padua

30. The bishopric of Padua is sufficiently recognized as a suffragan of the metropolitan of Aquileia in Paulus, who signs the letters of Pope Agatho as bishop of the province of Istria—for this was then the name of the Aquileian province, as has been said—and in Dominicus, who is included in the council of Mantua under the name “of the province of Venetia” as bishop of Padua.

The subjection which the bishops of Padua owed to the see of Aquileia in the thirteenth century appears from the document of 1296 that is to be appended below in Appendix 2, no. 21. But not only in the thirteenth century, and not only in the church of Padua; rather, already in the eleventh century, indeed in Paulinus’s own time, the manner in which all the suffragan bishops conducted themselves toward their metropolitan when they first entered upon their sees will become clear from other formulas of subjection which newly ordained bishops professed on that occasion. These will be found in Appendix 2, nos. 6 and 11.

Luitardus succeeded Rodoni in 793, as may be inferred from Ursatus, who assigns Rodon the year 780 and gives him thirteen years in the see, as reported by Ughellus. Filling the see from 793 until about 809, Luitardus could and ought to have attended Paulinus’s council at Friuli.

31. The church of Treviso presented Russius, or Rusticus, at the council of Marano. Felix succeeded Rusticus, and signed the petition addressed to Maurice in the case of Severus.

Therefore those of our writers must be corrected who thought that the petition had been composed at the council of Marano itself: Felix, who subscribed the petition, did not attend that council, but Rusticus did.

Ughellus places Bishop Fortunatus in the year 799. He also says that Fortunatus received Leo III as a guest when Leo was returning from Gaul, and adds that under this bishop, in 780, a monastery was founded in the diocese of Treviso by Count Gerard, who bequeathed his property to the monastery of Nonantola. Fortunatus, therefore, could have attended Paulinus’s council, and perhaps did attend it.

32. Belluno, at the conciliabulum of Marano and in the petition addressed to Maurice, supplied Laurence as its signatory. Ughellus places Ayroldus under the year 781; after him Odelbertus appears in the council of Mantua in 827. Ayroldus’s tenure therefore falls perfectly within the time of Paulinus’s council, and consequently he himself may have attended it.

33. The church of Como reveals its dependence upon Aquileia even through its singing. The chant, of which we gave some indication in the preface to the notes on Paulinus’s hymns, was preserved for a long time by this see because it had developed from the rite of the patriarchal church of Aquileia; it is therefore called “patriarchal.”

Peter was appointed bishop of Como in 776. Born in Gaul, he obtained the appointment through the support of Charlemagne, from whom he secured a privilege for his church at Regensburg in 803. In 818, the year of his death, Louis the Pious granted another privilege at Como, at Saint Peter’s. From this you can see that this bishop could very well have attended Paulinus’s council.

## XXIV

From these facts it may be concluded that, although the province of Aquileia was so extensive, it nevertheless had few bishops whom it could send to the council of Friuli in 796.

Cointius, under the year 795, no. 25, says the following about these bishops:

“Sixteen suffragan sees were subject to the patriarch of Friuli: Concordia, Vicenza, Padua, Treviso, Cenetia, Feltria, Belluno, Como, Verona, Tridentum, Trieste, Justinopolis, Oemonia, Parentium, Petina or Pucinum, and Pola . . . From the bishops we have mentioned, it is clear that at the time when Patriarch Paulinus summoned the council of Friuli, Bodon”—for Rodon, though he had already died—“was seated at Padua, Fortunatus at Treviso, Aeginus at Verona, Peter at Como, Amator at Tridentum, and Dominicus at Parentium. But the names of the other bishops who then governed the dioceses of Concordia, Vicenza, Cenetia, Feltria, Belluno, Trieste, Justinopolis, Oemonia, Petina, and Pola are unknown.”

We do not accept this conclusion. For if one subtracts the twenty-three bishoprics which either never existed, such as Marano and Sacile; or had ceased to exist, such as Julium, Opitergium, Scarabantia, Pelinnus, Petovium, Aventia, and Vejentia; or had migrated into another province, such as Altinum, Sabiona, Tiburnia, Augusta, and Beconia; or did not yet exist, such as Mantua and Cittanova;

if one subtracts the Istrian bishoprics—Trieste, Justinopolis, Parentium, Petina, and Pola—which had obeyed Grado from the division of the metropolitan see into Aquileia and Grado, although Istria had been conquered by Pepin and taken from the Greeks in 789, according to Cointius, and whose sees were moreover at that time almost all deprived of their pastors;

if one subtracts the bishoprics whose episcopal succession is known to have been interrupted for a long time, especially during that period, such as Acileia and Oemonia, or Labacum;

only ten remain which could probably, doubtfully, or certainly have attended the council.

Probably: Peter of Concordia, Dulcissimus of Cenetia, and Reginald of Vicenza.

Doubtfully—that is, one or the other of two bishops, since it is uncertain who occupied the chair in 796: at Tridentum, Amator or Hildegarius; at Feltria, Endrighettus or Amatus; at Verona, Aldo or Aeginus.

Certainly: Luitardus of Padua, Fortunatus of Treviso, Ayroldus of Belluno, and Peter of Como.

How aptly Paulinus, perhaps hinting at this number of ten, called this group “the messmates of certain bishops”! For Vegetius, in *On Military Affairs*, book II, chapter 13, says:

“A mess-unit consisted of ten soldiers living under one tent, with one decanus, as if in command, who was called the head of the mess-unit.”

# THIRD DISSERTATION ON THE HERESY OF FELIX AND ELIPANDUS: A DOGMATIC DISSERTATION

## I

Father Mabillon, in his treatise *On Monastic Studies*, near the end of the work, lists the principal difficulties which still seem to require fuller explanation in the reading of councils, the Fathers, and ecclesiastical history as arranged according to the succession of the centuries. Among these, at the end of the eighth century, he includes the following:

“Were Felix and Elipandus, whose heresy was condemned at the council of Frankfurt, Nestorians?”

Since we have undertaken, to the best of our ability, to illuminate this question through the works of Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, who rose against them with all his strength, we cannot leave it untouched. Indeed, if we undertook such a task while avoiding the greatest difficulty—namely, exposing the manifest poison of the Felician heresy—we would rightly be reproached.

Accordingly, we have decided to bring forward the doctrines of related heresies, so that the kindred wickedness of the Felician heresy may appear more clearly and so that the reader may recognize which of them it most closely resembles.

## II

Lest the reader’s mind be wearied by a lengthy survey of the heresies that had some relationship or similarity to the Felician heresy, we shall pass over those which seemed most closely connected with one another.

Paulinus himself gives them an indication when, in book I, chapter 8, he reproaches Felix for an opinion that leaned at one time toward the Arian and at another toward the Nestorian position. I do not deny that he sometimes also hurled the ravings of Macedonius in his face, when in chapter 24 of the same book he showed him to be a blasphemer against the Holy Spirit in these words:

“For, following the sect of Macedonius, you deny that the Holy Spirit is truly God.”

Yet Felix’s principal error did not turn upon this point.
