Since Christ is called our advocate, and since from the other Paraclete promised in the Gospel Felix argues that Jesus himself is also a Paraclete—that is, an advocate—he concludes that Jesus should not be regarded as God, since he had undertaken the role of advocate. Paulinus therefore properly follows up by asking what Felix thinks about the divinity of the Spirit, who likewise is an advocate: whether, with Macedonius, he attacks the divinity of the Spirit because the Spirit is an advocate, just as he removes Christ’s divinity because Christ too is an advocate.

In any event, the Felician heresy has either nothing or very little in common with the Macedonian heresy, since the latter rose against the Holy Spirit, whereas the former rose against the Son. We must therefore examine whether Felix’s opinion approached more closely the insane doctrines of Nestorius or those of Arius.

## III

Arius taught that the Son was a creature and not God equal to the Father. Felix approaches Arius when he calls Christ the adopted Son of God, not the proper Son, and a titular or nominal God, not true God. For if he is neither true God nor the proper Son, what remains for him to be but a mere creature?

Nestorius, who favored the presbyter Anastasius, who taught that the Virgin Mary should not be called Θεοτόκος—that is, *Deipara*, “the God-bearer,” or “Mother of God”—accordingly posited two persons in Christ, just as there are two natures: one person because he was God, and another because he was man.

Felix follows him when he says that, according to his humanity, Christ is not the true Son of God but only an adopted son. Thus he removes the person of the Son of God from Christ’s humanity and substitutes the person of the son of man, who is adopted.

He also approaches another error of Nestorius, who said that the Word dwelt in the humanity as in a temple, thereby abolishing the ineffable mystery of the incarnation and the theandric works of Christ. Felix likewise, by asserting that Christ according to the flesh was not the proper Son of God, seems to admit the divinity of the Word in the flesh, but not hypostatically and personally united with the flesh. Consequently he removes and eliminates the theandric works by which Christ redeemed us, since they belonged simultaneously and truly to the one Son of God and man.

## IV

But to approach more closely the difficulty proposed, it seems sufficiently clear that the Felician heresy was not properly a germ of Arian origin, strictly speaking. Arius did not locate inequality precisely in Christ’s humanity, nor did he make the Son lesser than the Father because of the assumption of flesh. Rather, even before the mystery of the incarnation, he asserted this very inferiority of the Son to the Father.

Let us seek his confession from his own mouth. He wrote a profession of his faith in a letter to Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, which Saint Epiphanius quotes in *Heresy* 69, no. 7. Among other statements relevant to our subject, Arius inserts the following:

“We believe in one God, alone unbegotten, alone eternal, alone without beginning . . . who before everlasting times begot the only-begotten Son, through whom he created the ages and all other things. We say that he begot him in reality, not merely in appearance, and that by his own will he established him as a subsisting being, such that he could neither be turned nor changed: a perfect creature of God, but not like any one of created things; likewise an offspring, but not like one among the rest.

“Not as Valentinus, or Sabellius, or Hieracas, or others taught, but, as we have said, created by God’s will before all times and ages in order to live and exist, we confess that he received his being from the Father. Thus, in that same creation, the Father bestowed upon him glory and splendor . . . .

“Therefore there are three hypostases: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. And indeed, since God is the cause of all things, he alone among all is without a beginning. But the Son, begotten timelessly by the Father and created and established before the ages, did not exist before he was begotten. Rather, begotten timelessly and before all things, he alone was produced by the Father alone.

“For he is neither eternal nor coeternal, nor unbegotten with the Father. Nor did he exist with the Father, as some assert concerning things that are related to something else, establishing two unbegotten principles. Rather, as unity and principle of all things, God exists before all things. Therefore he is also prior to Christ himself, as we have learned from you, when you preached this in the midst of the Church.

“Accordingly, since the Son received from God the capacity to exist, and also life, glory, splendor, and all the other things bestowed upon him, God is his principle in this respect. For God is prior to him and his principle, being his God, who existed before him and from whom he also proceeded.

“But if we understand such expressions as ‘from the womb’ and ‘I came forth from the Father and have come’ in the sense in which some understand them—as implying consubstantiality, a part, or an emission—the Father will be composite, divisible, and changeable; indeed, in their opinion, God, who is free from body, will be a body and will suffer the things appropriate to a body.

“We wish you well, etc.”

Thus Arius wrote in the letter cited, in the translation of Dionysius Petavius.

## V

In this letter we may note several points by which the Arian poison is revealed.

1. Arius calls God alone unbegotten and alone eternal, thereby excluding the Son’s coeternity.

2. He says that the Son was begotten before everlasting times, but not from eternity; shortly afterward he calls him not begotten but a perfect creature of God, created before times and ages. He says also that in this creation the Son received from the Father his existence, so that he might live, together with glory and splendor. All these statements plainly present the Son as inferior and make him lesser than the Father.

3. He admits three hypostases: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Yet he seems immediately to confine divinity to the Father alone when he adds:

“And indeed, since God is the cause of all things, he alone among all is without a beginning. But the Son, begotten timelessly by the Father and created and established before the ages, did not exist before he was begotten.”

These final words conceal an immense blasphemy, for they imply that the Son was at some time not begotten. Arius did not say that the Son was begotten in time; but since he did not say that he was begotten from eternity and always, he devised an intermediate expression by saying that he was begotten before all times, yet not eternal or coeternal, nor unbegotten with the Father. He thus mixed truth with falsehood.

For it is true that he is not unbegotten with the Father: he was begotten by the Father. But it is false that he is not eternal and coeternal with the Father, since, having been begotten from eternity by the Father, he is coeternal with the one who begets him.

4. Because the Son receives his existence from the Father, Arius infers that the Father is prior to the Son as the Son’s God:

“For he is prior to him and his principle, being his God, who existed before him.”

Thus he establishes the Son as lesser than the Father.

Not understanding consubstantiality, Arius asserts that composition is necessarily found in the Father. Indeed, he says that the Father must be attributed a body, presenting this absurdity as an objection so that he need not admit a truth he cannot comprehend.

All these statements, as you see, attack and attempt to overthrow the Son’s equality with the Father absolutely, not merely according to the dispensation of the assumed human flesh.

## VI

But the mind of the arch-heretic may be exposed still more clearly from other points of Arian doctrine, and it may be seen whether he truly rose against the Son’s divinity or rather proved the Son to be lesser because of the humanity he assumed.

Arius blasphemed when he said and taught that Christ’s body was without a soul. Hear Saint Epiphanius speaking of the Arians in *Heresy* 69, no. 19:

“They further deny that he was endowed with a human soul. They construct their argument with deliberate purpose so that they may acknowledge that he received true flesh from the Virgin Mary and the other things proper to man, with the exception of a soul.”

In a collection by an unknown author, published by Canisius in volume V of *Ancient Readings* and now found in volume XIII of the *Maxima Bibliotheca Patrum*, translated by Francisco Turrianus, several formulas of faith of two Arians are produced in which they profess that Christ did not assume a soul.

Eudoxius, in his book *On the Incarnation*, says:

“We believe in one sole true God and Father . . . and in one Lord Jesus Christ . . . incarnate, not made human, for he did not assume a human soul, but became flesh.”

And Lucius of Alexandria, in his sermon *On Easter*, says:

“Why,” he asks, “was a soul necessary, so that a man who had progressed together with God might be worshiped? Therefore John cries, ‘The Word became flesh,’ meaning that he was compounded with flesh, not with a soul.”

The Church counters this error in the Creed, saying not only “and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit of the Virgin Mary,” but also adding, “and was made man.”

Why, then, did the Arians strive so insistently to expel the soul from Christ? Clearly, so that, since the flesh was vivified by the Word, who according to their view supplied the role of the soul, and since Christ endured in that flesh every kind of degradation and extreme suffering, they could attribute these weaknesses to the Word who vivified the flesh and thus prove the Word himself inferior and the Son lesser than the Father.

Saint Epiphanius continues:

“Clearly, when you hear of hunger, thirst, labors, journeys, sweat, sleep, and anger, and say that he experienced these things because of the human nature he assumed, they can immediately object that the flesh could not perform these things by itself unless it were endowed with a soul. And this is indeed rightly said to them.

“What, then, they ask, is the meaning of saying that his divinity needed all these things? Once they have said that his divinity was in need, they may declare him a stranger and alien to the essence and nature of the Father.”

Leontius of Byzantium, a monk, expresses the point more clearly, though more briefly, in book III of *On the Sects*, or *Scholium*, near the end:

“The Arian doctrine taught that Christ’s body was without a soul, so that we might attribute such humble expressions—of pain, weakness, weariness, and the like—not to a man but to the Son of God; and according to their opinion the Son might thereby be discovered to be lesser than the Father.”

There is where the deceitful tongues of the Arians were aiming. They paved the way from one blasphemy to a greater blasphemy. They denied a soul to Christ, the Son of God, so that they could also deny his divinity as equal to the Father’s. As Saint Hilary aptly says in book XI of *On the Trinity*, no. 6:

“They seize upon the dispensation of the assumed body as an insult to the divinity, and they derive grounds for impiety from the mystery of our salvation.”

## VII

All these points, as you see, tend toward proving that the Son of God was inferior to the Father even before the mystery of the Incarnation. Our Felix of Urgel, however, did not deny the divinity of the Son of God, nor did he posit inequality among the divine persons; he merely posited adoption in Christ’s humanity and proclaimed him, insofar as he was man, an adopted son of God and a “nominal” god.

Let Felix himself be heard condemning his former errors—whether sincerely or feignedly will become clear in the following dissertation, no. 74—in his confession of faith addressed to the priests and clergy of the Church of Urgel:

> “We profess that henceforth we in no way believe or preach the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God, or a merely nominal designation (*nuncupatio*) in his humanity.” [Col. 0549B]

Let Elipandus also be heard, his companion in the same perfidy, in the letter he sent to Felix. Speaking there of Albinus, as will be discussed in the following dissertation, no. 36, he says:

> “He does not believe in the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God, which the holy Fathers and we ourselves believe to exist solely in the form of human servitude, not in the glory or substance of the divine nature.”

He professes the same in his confession of faith, which his doctrinal opponents Eterius and Beatus quote, and which we reproduce in the same dissertation, no. 12:

> “Whoever does not confess Jesus Christ as adopted in his humanity and in no way adopted in his divinity is both a heretic and must be exterminated.”

He considered himself so far removed from Arius’s teaching that, in more than one letter addressed to Alcuin, he did not hesitate to proclaim Alcuin a new Arius. What exactly, or in what fit of madness, moved him to do this, I would not dare assert with certainty. It seems possible to infer from his words that he believed Alcuin, because he did not admit adoption in Christ’s flesh or humanity [Col. 0549C], admitted it in his divinity.

For he objects to Alcuin that he and the holy Fathers, as he imagined, posited adoption “solely in the form of human servitude, not in the glory or substance of the divine nature,” as though adoption necessarily had to be posited in Christ, and as though the difference between himself and Alcuin were that he recognized adoption in the flesh, whereas Alcuin recognized it in the substance of divinity.

In truth, however, it seems more probable that he produced this accusation from an itch to insult than from any plausible or apparent argument. For he was a genuinely delirious old man—he had entered his eighty-second year when he wrote this—and was not proposing to Alcuin anything that could be opposed with even a semblance of rational argument. He was saying these things merely to spew out the poison with which his diseased inner organs were swollen.

## VIII

[Col. 0549D] I would not, nevertheless, deny that there was some agreement between the teaching of Arius and that of Felix or Elipandus, since Arius himself at times misuses the term “adoption” when speaking of the Son of God.

This is evident from Epiphanius, Heresy 69, no. 18, where he teaches that Arius called the Son of God the Word, as he called the others sons of God. He says:

> “But if the Son is called the Word only in the sense in which all the others have been called sons of God, he will differ in no respect from the others. Why, then, is he worshiped as God? For all those also to whom that name of adoption applied would, in the opinion of those who worshiped him, have had to be worshiped, since they are called sons of God.”

This resemblance, whatever its extent, was noted both by Paulinus in his writings against Felix and by Alcuin in his writings against Elipandus. The former says in Book I, chapter 12:

> “Arius, from whose branch-bearing” [supply: “root”] “this man plainly seems to have descended, when he firmly maintained that the Son of God was adopted and a creature, and so forth.”

The latter says in Book I against Elipandus:

> “Do you not affirm that adoption exists in the same person whom Arius once, with detestable impiety, asserted to be adopted?”

Yet this resemblance existed in name only, not in reality. Felix said that Christ—that is, the Son of God already incarnate—was, according to his divinity, truly the Son of God, but according to his humanity merely an adopted son. [Col. 0550A] Arius, however, calling the Son “adopted” while abstracting from the Incarnation, as the schools say, spoke absolutely of the Son as adopted.

I am not unaware that in Book II against Elipandus Alcuin openly charged him with following Arian blasphemies because he had called the Son of God adopted in the man. Alcuin says:

> “And thus,” you say, “the Son of God is called adopted together with the man, and the son of man is called adopted together with the Word. In all other respects your unbelieving mind and impious judgment erred only concerning Christ’s humanity; but now you have advanced from impiety to the most atrocious impiety, saying that the Son of God is adopted together with the man, and immediately repeating the same notion in perverse alternation, you said: ‘The son of man is called adopted together with the Word.’ What could be said or imagined more wicked, more impious, than that the Son of God—that is, the Word of God—should be called adopted together with the man he assumed? Perhaps you thought that you were dividing Christ, with Nestorius, into two persons, one the proper son and the other the adopted son. In wishing to avoid this snare, you have fallen into the prison of Arian perversity.” [Col. 0550B]

Nevertheless, I still do not recognize in these teachings of Felix and Elipandus a specifically Arian offspring, because Arius called the Son adopted without any reference to the mystery of the Incarnation or to the humanity assumed—something Felix and Elipandus never taught. Elipandus called the Son of God adopted merely because he had assumed a man.

**209**

## IX

If Arius sometimes appropriated passages of the Gospel or of another Scripture that speak of Christ—such as “The Father is greater than I,” and others of that sort—it is clear that he did so to suggest that Christ was inferior to the Father, not according to his humanity, as the texts speak and ought to be understood, but according to his divinity.

Hilary says very well in Book IX of *On the Trinity*, no. 5:

> “Hence heretics have an opportunity to deceive the simple and ignorant, so that they falsely claim that what was spoken by him according to man was spoken according to the weakness of the divine nature.” [Col. 0550C]

Elipandus and Felix, however, did not misuse Scripture as Arius did to suggest a difference in excellence and dignity among the divine persons. They merely dreamed up the dogma of adoption from the humanity assumed by the Word.

## X

Since the Felician heresy has almost nothing in common with the Arian, let us see whether it approaches the teaching of Nestorius more closely. Many men, both ancient and recent, and men of the highest authority, have thought that it did approach Nestorianism and was imbued with it.

Among the ancients, the first is Paulinus himself. In Book I against Felix he says of him:

> “Now he embraces Arius when he encounters him; now he follows Nestorius, who went before him, with wandering steps.”

By these words Paulinus seems to indicate that he believed Felix to be a disciple of Nestorius, whom he follows as his precursor, rather than of Arius, whom he embraces only when he happens to encounter him on an occasion that has arisen.

2. Alcuin, in Book I against Felix, says:

> “Just as Nestorian impiety divides Christ into two persons on account of the two natures . . . so your ignorant rashness divides him into two sons, one proper and the other adopted . . . You cannot in any way, while thinking thus, escape the impiety of Nestorian teaching.” [Col. 0550D]

And in Book I against Elipandus:

> “Without any doubt you divide him [Christ], with Nestorius, into two sons and into two persons, through propriety and adoption.”

The same author says in the same work:

> “If you strive to avoid this blasphemy of Arius, you immediately fall into the snare of Nestorius, dividing Christ into two persons, one proper and the other adopted.”

And in Book IV against the same opponent:

> “There is no doubt that you are entangled with Nestorius . . . This alone remains as a remedy for you: that you . . . abandon the unbelief of that Nestorius and your own, which unquestionably proceeded from the impiety of a single root . . . But so that you may know that we divide Christ into neither two persons with Nestorius nor two persons according to your unbelief, and so forth.”

3. The Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt, in their letter to the bishops of Spain, no. 22, reproach Felix and Elipandus as follows:

> “Was not your same heresy formerly refuted and condemned in Nestorius by the universal holy Church?” [Col. 0551A]

4. Jonas of Orléans, near the beginning of Book I of *On the Cult of Images*, speaking against Claudius, bishop of Turin, of the Council of Frankfurt and of the heresy of Felix condemned there, says:

> “For by the command of that same ruler [Charlemagne], they assembled together, with the authority of the holy Roman Church also brought to bear, and condemned Felix himself; indeed, together with the author of his error, Nestorius, whom he imitated, they consigned him to perpetual anathema.”

5. Agobard, bishop of Lyons, in his book against Felix, and especially in no. 7, asserts in more than one passage that Felix was a Nestorian. He says:

> “Fearing the mixture of Eutyches, he fell into the division of Nestorius. But since we have said that the man of whom we are speaking fell into Nestorius’s most wicked division, I think it appropriate to set forth here the opinions of Nestorius before we proceed to examine this man’s statements, so that the prudent reader may recognize how harmoniously Felix thought with Nestorius.”

These, then, are the witnesses among the ancients. [Col. 0551B]

## XI

Among the more recent writers, the first is Papirius Masson, who writes in his synopsis of the first volume of Agobard:

> “A certain bishop of Urgel . . . revived from the underworld the seeds of the Nestorian sect, long since extinguished by the light of the Gospel.”

2. John Mariana of the Society of Jesus, in Book VII, chapter 8, of his *History of Spain*, speaking of Felix and Elipandus, says:

> “The opinions of Nestorius, long ago suppressed by the diligence of the Council of Ephesus, were revived by these men as sparks of an ancient fire, when they affirmed that Christ, insofar as he is certainly man, is by adoption the Son of God, contrary to law, contrary to auspices, contrary to all divine and human writings and religious traditions.”

3. Our Baronius, under the year 794, no. 1, speaking of this kind of adoption, says:

> “For although the holy Catholic Church of God had nothing concerning these matters about which it could even slightly doubt—since the Ecumenical Council of Ephesus had most fully defined what was to be believed concerning them when it condemned Nestorius, and so forth.”

[Col. 0551C]

4. Severinus Binius, in his note on the Council of Frankfurt, letter c, speaking of Elipandus, says:

> “He was reviving Nestorianism, which had already been suppressed.”

5. Denis Petau, *On the Incarnation*, Book I, chapter 22, whose title is:

> “On the Felician Heresy, Which Was an Offshoot of the Nestorian.”

6. Natalis Alexander, who in century VIII, dissertation 5, lays down this proposition:

> “Felix and Elipandus consequently defended the Nestorian heresy concerning two persons in Christ.”

7. Philip Brichus, under the year 794, speaking of the Council of Frankfurt, celebrated in the case of Felix of Urgel and Elipandus of Toledo, says of them:

> “The former had taken up again the sect of Nestorius, which he had renounced.”

8. Germonius, in the appendix to *Disputation 2 on the Art of Distinguishing Charters*, chapter 2:

> “That man [Felix] was renewing the Nestorian heresy.”

9. Christian Lupus, *Dissertation on the Seventh Synod*, chapter 16:

> “He calls the pure and unmitigated Nestorianism revived by Felix and Elipandus.”

But leaving aside the others, this is, in a word, the common opinion of recent and ancient writers alike.

[Col. 0551D]

## XII

Authorities must, however, be supplemented by arguments. The principal argument—indeed, I would almost say the only one—is that Felix and Elipandus, by their doctrine of adoption, necessarily posited in Christ not only two sons but also two persons. That this has the character of the Nestorian heresy is evident.

That they posited two sons, or divided one into the adopter and the adopted, is clearly established by Paulinus himself in the *Sacrosyllabus*, nos. 4 and 5, where he says:

> “Let the heretics say which of the three persons adopted him [Christ], since the whole Trinity wrought him in the womb of the immaculate Virgin. Moreover, no one can be called adopted unless he is alien to the one by whom he is said to have been adopted.”

From this Paulinus wished to infer that, since the Trinity adopted him, and the Son of God exists within the Trinity, the Son himself was also the adopter. Since the adopter and the adopted are not one and the same, they established in Christ two sons, one the adopter and the other the adopted.

Paulinus objects to them even more clearly in no. 8:

> “Not two sons, one of God and the other of man, so that, as they mistakenly judge, the son of man might be adopted and the Son of God without adoption.” [Col. 0552A]

And in Book I against Felix, chapter 11:

> “In the two terms ‘proper’ and ‘adopted,’ and ‘true’ and ‘nominal’ God, he does not fear to divide the one and same Son of God.”

If they admitted two sons, they necessarily admitted two persons as well. Saint Thomas teaches in the third part, question 23, article 4, *corpus*, that:

> “Filiation properly belongs to a hypostasis or person, not to a nature, because filiation is a personal property.”

Paulinus himself noticed this when, in Book I, chapter 37, he reproaches Felix for deriving a duplication of persons from the division into son and son:

> “You are attempting to divide the one Christ. For while at one time you call him true God and the true Son of God” [supply from what follows: “at another time nominal God and adopted son”], “what else are you hastening to introduce than four persons?” [The text has *elinguas*, “you speak tongue-tied,” apparently for “you assert”; see the notes.]

That is, four persons in the mystery of the Trinity, because he was compelled to posit two sons and consequently two persons in the divided or duplicated Son, thereby establishing a quaternity of persons. [Col. 0552B] But to posit two persons in Christ is the proscribed dogma of Nestorius.

Therefore, to use the words of our John the Baptist Conventatus, *Oration II on the Second Birth of the Son of God*, chapter 16, section 109:

> “Felix and Elipandus were the final offspring of Nestorius.”

The reason follows from the same source:

> “Because Christ was cut into two sons and two persons, since ‘son’ signifies a person; and the same Son of God cannot be both natural and adopted.”

## XIII

From this Paulinus rightly inferred that, if Christ is according to his humanity a nominal God and an adopted son, the Virgin Mary ought not to be called his mother *Theotokos* (Θεοτόκος), that is, “Mother of God,” since she did not give birth to God but only to a man; and thus one would be driven into the well-known error of Nestorius.

[Col. 0552C]

He says in Book I against Felix, chapter 15:

> “If the venerable Virgin herself did not give birth to true God and true man in the unity of the person . . . how does the Catholic Church, one throughout the whole world, continue openly and publicly to confess the blessed Virgin Mary with the sweet and venerable name *Theotokos*, that is, ‘Mother of God’? If, therefore, this madman, of deranged mind, spews forth from his throat the utterly false claim that a nominal God, and not a true God, was born from the womb of a true mother, how will the blessed Virgin be confessed by the most truthful mouth of all Catholics as the true Mother of God? The heretics must necessarily admit that she is a nominal mother, if they are to think that the mother of the offspring is nominal.”

## XIV

Although this position is supported by authority and reason, Gabriel Vásquez, in volume I of his commentary on the third part of Saint Thomas, question 23, disputation 89, chapter 8, attempts to overthrow it by several arguments and to show that Felix and Elipandus should not be called Nestorians.

1. Elipandus asks Charlemagne for the judgment of a council approving his opinion concerning Christ’s adoption. He would have been utterly foolish and deranged if he had asked a Catholic king, through an orthodox council, to have a Nestorian dogma confirmed. **210**

2. The Fathers of Frankfurt call Elipandus’s opinion “new”; they would not have called it this if it had been Nestorian.

3. If Felix and Elipandus had held anything in common with Nestorius, they ought to have been refuted by Scriptural passages proving the unity of Christ’s person, as was done against Nestorius. For the arguments brought against them tend only to establish that they necessarily had to posit two persons, not that they had actually posited them.

4. Since Elipandus asserts servitude in Christ just as he asserts adoption, if he understood servitude as belonging to the person, Pope Adrian, who wrote against him, would have answered as he answered Nestorius: that Christ could be called a servant not according to his person but according to his human nature, because he assumed a nature belonging to a servile condition.

Adrian does not answer in this way, however, but proceeds allegorically by explaining the matter. Why? Because he saw that Elipandus would then have inferred that adoption, just like servitude, had to be admitted in the human nature. But if Elipandus had posited adoption in the human nature, and not in the person, just as he posited servitude there [Col. 0553A], he would not have been a Nestorian.

Natalis Alexander omitted this fourth point, although he answers the others. Vásquez also adds and magnifies Elipandus’s words about Christ, whom Elipandus calls “conjoined in one and the same person.” He then adds, as though Elipandus had explained his own mind plainly and without any disguise, and as though his explanation had to be accepted with one’s eyes closed:

> “Let our theologians, then, cease inventing evasions and attributing to Elipandus the manifest error of Nestorius, since he explicitly confesses one person of God and man, since he proclaims Christ the natural Son of God in the divine nature, and since he declares two natures in one person—all of which Nestorius never conceded.” [Col. 0552D]

## XV

Natalis Alexander responds to these objections in century VIII, dissertation 5.

To the first: Elipandus did not advance the dogma of Nestorius in explicit words, but through evasions and disguised arguments. Hence:

> “It is not surprising that they asked Charles for the judgment of a council, because either they did not understand that the manner in which they explained and defended their error actually fell into the heresy of Nestorius, or they hoped—as is not unusual among heretics—that by their pretense they would deceive the synod and draw others over to their side.” [Col. 0553B]

Ignorance, as the proverb says, produces and reinforces boldness.

To the second, Alexander says that the error was called “new” with respect to its manner of explanation, not with respect to the matter itself. Thus Paulinus, shortly before the end of the *Sacrosyllabus*, calls them:

> “New enemies, but stained with the age-old dregs of perfidy.”

For this reason Agobard, at the beginning of Book I against Felix, calls it:

> “A new—indeed, a revived from the old—heresy.”

We call it “new” and “revived,” or “renewed,” in the same sense. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 288, of the rising sun:

> “Or when the East sprinkles the lands with a new sun.”

And *Georgics* III, verse 437, of the renewed serpent:

> “When, having laid aside its slough, it is new and gleaming with youth.”

The sun and the serpent are not different from those that existed before, but are the same as previously. So too with this heresy.

To the third, Natalis Alexander says it is false that Felix and Elipandus were not confronted with Scriptural passages proving the unity of Christ’s person.

> “For the council’s letter to the bishops of Spain is filled with testimonies of this kind, as is evident to anyone who reads it. If Vásquez had paid attention to it, he would not have denied this so confidently.” [Col. 0553C]

Nor does it follow that Nestorianism was absent merely because they said that they did not duplicate the persons; given their doctrine, the persons would in fact have had to be duplicated. The Fathers who opposed them rightly compelled them to acknowledge this absurdity, although the heretics themselves, abhorring the name of Nestorians, recoiled from it.

As for the fourth objection, which is drawn from the manner in which Pope Adrian responded—not by interpreting the Scriptural passages concerning Christ’s servitude according to the servile condition of his humanity, as had formerly been done in the case of Nestorius, lest Elipandus infer that adoption too belonged to the humanity, but by understanding those passages mystically and allegorically—I say that Adrian did not fear this consequence.

For although the Scriptures are applied allegorically to Christ, Adrian nevertheless refers the allegories not to the nature but to the person. He says in his letter to the bishops of Spain:

> “All these things, revealed both prophetically according to the letter and mystically, designate the person of our Mediator.” [Col. 0553D]

The person of the Word, which suffered and was crucified in the human nature, also bore the image of servitude. He himself says of himself in Matthew 20:28:

> “I did not come to be served but to serve,”

and in Luke 22:27:

> “I am among you as one who serves.”

For he displayed and demonstrated through acts and duties of servitude the form of a servant that he received in assuming flesh, Philippians 2:7. Since these acts belong to supposita, as the schools say, they must also be attributed to the person.

But this does not prove that he truly had a servile person in relation to the Father, as Elipandus claimed; nor does servitude and adoption proceed in the same way. Servitude can belong to Christ allegorically on account of acts of servitude. Although these acts proceed from the person, they do not alter the person or establish him as inferior in his being. [Col. 0554A] He did this through condescension, not through condition.

Adoption, however, can exist only in a person other than the proper son; therefore it would presuppose a filiation distinct from the proper filiation, and consequently two filiations—one natural and the other adoptive. Elipandus could not therefore infer adoption from the notion of servitude, which was arbitrary and represented Christ as a servant only figuratively, not in reality. Adoption affects not the acts of the person but the person himself and his essential condition.

The natural Son of God could, without any change in his condition, present himself as a servant and perform acts of servitude. Since he performed them, he was represented under the allegory of servitude. But he could not present himself as adopted, since he was natural, as Saint Thomas says in the third part, question 23, article 4, *corpus*:

> “The filiation of adoption is a participated likeness of natural filiation. But something is not said to be received participatively when it is said of itself. Therefore Christ, who is the natural Son of God, can in no way be called an adopted son.” [Col. 0554B]

This is Saint Thomas’s teaching. In the same third part, question 20, article 6, throughout, and especially in the response to objection 2, he does not hesitate to assert, in the sense explained, that Christ is a servant and subject to the Father on account of the servile condition of the assumed nature.

## XVI

Since Vásquez more than once appeals to Elipandus’s testimony and quotes his words in which he says that there is one person in Christ, not two as with Nestorius, our Paulinus noticed the deception and exposed the fraud. Speaking of his associate in wickedness, Felix, he says in Book I, chapter 9:

> “‘I do not divide the persons; I distinguish the natures completely.’ But although he tries to excuse himself from this charge, and nevertheless does it repeatedly, he can still be convicted from his own inventions—guilty of two crimes, the deed and the lie, and so forth.”

It is as though he were saying: the mentality of these men is deceitful. Wishing to avoid the mark of heresy, they disguise their cauterized consciences with the allurements of words, and, so that they may deceive the unwary, they appear to recoil from any division of the persons in Christ, while nevertheless striving with all their strength to introduce that division into their doctrine. [Col. 0554C]

Eterius and Beatus demonstrate this from Elipandus’s words in his confession of faith. Immediately after saying that Christ is:

> “conjoined in one and the same person of God and man, and clothed in the garment of flesh,”

he adds:

> “For it was not through the one born of the Virgin that he created visible and invisible things, but through the one who is not [a son] by adoption but by generation, not by grace but by nature.”

While explaining the words of 1 John 4:1, “Every spirit that dissolves Jesus is not from God,” they say:

> “What does it mean to dissolve Jesus except to proclaim God separately and man separately? He undoubtedly dissolves Jesus who says to the people: ‘Did he create visible and invisible things through the one who was born of the Virgin, or through the one who created all things not by adoption but by generation, not by grace but by nature?’”

And below:

> “One son of the Virgin is sufficient for us, who bears the name Jesus. We have no need of those of yours whom you call ‘this one’ and ‘that one.’”

They show that by “that one” and “this one” Elipandus designated a plurality of persons.

Alcuin also noted this in his response to the same Elipandus:

> “How do you not understand from these words of yours that you affirm two persons in Christ, when you say ‘to him’ and ‘to that one’? As though one were he who was begotten of God the Father and another he who was made from the Virgin Mother, although the Evangelist says: ‘And the Word became flesh.’” [Col. 0554D]

The words of heretics, therefore, must not be judged at first glance; their entire doctrine must be weighed, just as was done in the case of Nestorius. The author of the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, Olympiad 333, year 1, discussing the Councils of Constantinople and Ephesus, which condemned Nestorius and Theodore—men who wished persons to be understood under the name of natures—says:

> “Nor is it surprising if the writer of the impious letters used the name of natures. Heretics are accustomed, in order to impose upon simpler people, to use words piously employed by the orthodox, and to transfer their pious and correct understanding and explanation to their own perfidy or impiety . . . Thus the first Synod of Ephesus, presided over by Coelestine and Cyril of holy memory, did not accept Nestorius, who asserted two natures and one person but denied their union according to hypostasis; indeed, it condemned him.” [Col. 0555A]

Just as it did Nestorius no good to assert one person—since, by denying the hypostatic union and in reality introducing two hypostases, he was condemned by the council and the Fathers—so Felix and Elipandus could not be believed when they sometimes asserted unity of person in Christ but in fact established, through adoption, one person distinct from another.

## XVII

From these considerations arises a question examined by Suárez in volume I of his commentary on the third part of Saint Thomas, question 23, article 4, disputation 49, section 2: namely, whether it is a matter of faith that Christ, insofar as he is man, is not an adopted son.

He first answers that, speaking absolutely, it is a matter of faith that Christ is not adopted but natural. Second, he adds that if the phrase “insofar as” designates the suppositum, it is also a matter of faith that he is not adopted.

Third, he adds:

> “Finally, if in that proposition the phrase ‘insofar as’ is taken properly and specifically, although it is entirely true that Christ, insofar as he is man, is not an adopted son, I do not nevertheless judge this to be a matter of faith. Rather, it is so certain that the contrary is not at all probable or plausible. The reason is that, although the Council [of Frankfurt] and the other testimonies strongly support this truth, they do not explicitly define it in this sense; especially since all the histories that speak of the Council of Frankfurt teach that it was convened against Elipandus’s error, which they say was the same as Nestorius’s error . . . Therefore that error does not seem to have been directly condemned except insofar as it introduced a created person into Christ; the remaining points, which depend upon scholastic disputation, do not seem to have been defined.” [Col. 0555B]

If, therefore, the Council of Frankfurt condemned adoption only in the Nestorian sense—insofar as it introduced a created person into Christ—it is clear that Felix and Elipandus, who asserted such adoption, were Nestorians.

## XVIII

Before we place the final hand upon this dissertation, however, it is worthwhile to vindicate certain holy Fathers from the slander of these heretics. With brazen confidence, the heretics claimed that those Fathers supported them and attempted to impose upon the Fathers of Frankfurt the assertion that their doctrine of adoption had proceeded from the mouths of these Fathers.

The Fathers of Frankfurt interpret the opinions of certain writers—namely, Hilary, Augustine, and Jerome—in their letter to the bishops of Spain. They explain the sounder meaning that the obstinate ignorance of the heretics had attached to those opinions. But when they come to the authorities of the Spanish Fathers, such as Eugenius, Ildefonsus, and Julianus, they neither explain nor interpret them; rather, they punish them with a harsher censure.

Thus they say in the cited letter, no. 7:

> “The following also appears in your little book: ‘Likewise, our predecessors Eugenius, Ildefonsus, and Julianus, bishops of the see of Toledo, said the following in their own teachings, in the Mass of the Lord’s Supper: “Who, through the passion of the adopted man, while he did not spare his own body.” Likewise, in the Mass of the Ascension of the Lord: “Today our Savior, after the adoption of the flesh, returned to the seat of divinity.”’ And other passages that you have set forth from the sayings of your ancestors, so that it may be evident what sort of ancestors you have, and so that everyone may know from where you have been handed over into the hands of unbelievers. See there also what follows, which is harsher still.” [Col. 0555D]

## XIX

But who is so inexperienced in human affairs that he would fail to recognize the malice of heretics who corrupt the writings of the Fathers? In this very case, Alcuin, in Book II against Elipandus, points out that Felix had corrupted a passage of Hilary.

The passage was in Book II of *On the Trinity*:

> “Thus the dignity of power is not admitted, while the humility of the flesh is adored.”

Felix substituted *adoptatur*, “is adopted,” for *adoratur*, “is adored.” Hence Alcuin says:

> “In this passage the same Father Hilary most certainly discusses the adoration of the Magi, not the paternal adoption that you most perversely attempt to assert in this passage.”

This is confirmed by Hincmar’s account in the preface to his book *On Predestination against Gottschalk*:

> “And as we learned from the account of those who took part in the council, when the lord Charles of divine memory discovered that Felix, the wretched bishop of the city of Urgel, had been proved and condemned as a heretic by synodal decree, he also found him convicted of this: after corrupting with bribes the junior librarian of the palace at Aachen, he had scraped the book of blessed Hilary, and where it was written, ‘Because in the Son of God the humility of the flesh is adored,’ he omitted the words and wrote instead, ‘The humility of the flesh is adopted.’” [Col. 0556A]

See Germanus, who treats this event at length in the appendix to *Disputation 2 on the Art of Distinguishing Charters*, chapter 2, pages 396 and following, Paris edition, 1706.

## XX

Since this is so, it becomes highly credible that those holy Fathers originally wrote *assumpti* or *assumptionem*—“of the assumed [man]” or “the assumption”—where the heretics read *adoptivi* or *adoptionem*, “of the adopted [man]” or “adoption,” and that through malicious corruption they substituted the word favorable to themselves.

This most reasonable conjecture is supported by an observation of Father Vásquez. In the third part of Saint Thomas, disputation 89, question 23, chapter 15, he notes:

> “Now in the Gothic Masses—for it was from such Masses that the authorities were taken, as is apparent from what was cited above—whether printed copies or manuscript copies, which still exist and are kept in the Church of Toledo, nothing of this kind is found. Therefore they were either falsely cited, or similar prayers have been expunged. I would believe either that they never existed, or that Ildefonsus and Julianus were not their authors, but that they were falsely attributed to them by someone. For the author of the Gothic Masses was Isidore, who explicitly asserts that Christ is not adopted but natural in both natures; Ildefonsus makes the same assertion.” [Col. 0556B]

## XXI

Since the Fathers of Frankfurt particularly attack this Ildefonsus, when explaining the words, “This is my beloved Son,” they say:

> “It is better to believe the testimony of God the Father concerning his Son than that of your Ildefonsus, who composed for you such prayers in the solemn celebration of the Mass as the universal and holy Church of God does not possess. Nor do we think that you are heard in those prayers . . . and your Ildefonsus named Christ ‘adopted’ in his prayers, whereas our Pope Gregory of the Roman See, the most distinguished teacher throughout the world, did not hesitate in his prayers always to call him ‘the only-begotten.’” [Col. 0556C]

[Col. 0556D] It is therefore worthwhile to produce some passages from Ildefonsus, so that his own words may show whether he truly admitted adoption in Christ Jesus, the Son of God, as the heretics alleged.

In Book *On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary*, chapter 4, he writes:

> “And thus, in the unity of the person, the same is the Word as is flesh, and the same is man as is God.”

A little farther on:

> “Therefore adoption did not make him, as it made the others, a son of God; rather, the nature of divinity exalted him as God’s proper Son. He was never conceived or born as a mere man, as the other infants are born, so that a prerogative of sonship might be bestowed upon him by the grace of adoption or by the effort of virtues. Rather, because the Word of God became flesh, he assumed man into himself without a human person, so that Christ in his entirety might be God’s proper Son—not being reborn by a gift of grace like the others, but with the propriety of both natures preserved.”

What could be had more fully or more clearly for excluding adoption from Christ? Ildefonsus drew this doctrine almost word for word from Gregory the Great, *Morals*, Book I, chapter 7, near the end, where Gregory says:

> “He surpasses all who are born to God in faith, because adoption did not exalt him as it did the others; rather, the nature of divinity exalted him.”

Paulinus himself cites these words of Gregory in his own defense, in Book III against Felix, chapter 27.

XXII. But how inopportunely—and I might almost say perversely—the Fathers of Frankfurt, deceived by the report of the heretics, accused the faith of the Spanish bishops Eugenius, Ildefonsus, and Julianus is demonstrated by the Eleventh Council of Toledo, held in the Spanish era 713, that is, in A.D. 675, in the very century in which the aforesaid bishops flourished: the first around the year 646, the second around 657, and the third around 680, when they adorned the Church by their writings and most holy examples.

For in their confession of faith the Fathers of Toledo said:

> “This one also, the Son of God, is Son by nature, not by adoption.”

And below:

> “In this Son of God we believe there to be two natures, one divine and the other human, which the one person of Christ so united in himself that neither divinity can ever be separated from humanity, nor humanity from divinity. Hence Christ is perfect God and perfect man in the unity of one person. Yet, because we have said that there are two natures in Christ, we shall not thereby assert that there are two persons in him, lest a quaternity seem—God forbid!—to be added to the Trinity. For God the Word did not receive the person of a man, but his nature; and into his eternal divine person he received the temporal substance of flesh.”

Such was the faith of the Church of Spain in the age of Eugenius, Ildefonsus, and Julianus. The Fathers of Frankfurt did not subject their doctrine, corrupted by impostors, to examination; it is therefore no wonder if, in a matter of fact rather than of law, they appeared to have exceeded the proper limits of censure.

> “This error can also intrude into ecumenical councils and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, and it has sometimes happened, as all theologians, together with Cardinal Bellarmine and Baronius, acknowledge,”

says Cardinal de Aguirre in his letter *On the Method of the Work*, prefixed to volume III of his collection of the councils of Spain, no. 12, speaking of this very case.

**212 DISSERTATION FOUR. A HISTORICAL-CHRONOLOGICAL DISSERTATION ON THE HERESY OF FELIX AND ELIPANDUS**

[Col. 0557]

[Col. 0557B] **I.** Since it can easily be discerned from the works of our holy Father Paulinus that his principal concern was to uproot the heresy of the Adoptians completely and radically from the field of the supreme master of the household, and that he labored with unremitting effort against Elipandus and Felix, the sowers of this error, it seemed right—and, we trust, not unwelcome to our readers—that, having dealt in the preceding dissertation with the doctrine that may be called an appendage of the Nestorian error, we should now treat historically of its authors and bring into view the origin, progress, condemnation, and destruction of their heresy, assigning everything to its proper time.

Thus, when the audacity and insolence of the enemies have been exposed, the virtue of the victor shines forth more brilliantly. Paulinus was not attacking men of dull intellect, whose defeat would have brought him neither labor nor glory; rather, they raised their crests and lifted their horns, becoming more audacious even in disaster. Hence Paulinus often had to join battle, both in person and in writing, from a distance and at close quarters, [Col. 0557C] until at last, by the happy outcome of events, when he departed this life he left the heresy either wholly extinguished or drawing only its final breaths somewhere. But now we must come to the subject itself.

**II.** From the beginning of the eighth century, the Moors, having crossed the Strait of Cádiz, oppressed Spain, conquered by war, under a terrible slavery. For in the year 711 after the birth of Christ they were summoned by Julian, governor of Tingis, against Roderic—Roderic, successor of Vitiza, whom Roderic himself had also blinded—in revenge for the outrage Roderic had inflicted upon Julian’s daughter; perhaps they were also invited by Vitiza’s sons, who were then living in exile with Julian. Under the command of Tariq, they occupied Mount Abila; from the Arabic expression *Gabal-Tariq*, that is, “Tariq’s mountain,” the moderns subsequently called it Gibraltar, or Gibilterra. In the following year they sent forces, sufficient to aid Tariq, under Musa, governor of Armenia, to Seville. Finally, in the year 713, after Roderic, the last of the Visigothic kings, had been killed, they took possession of the rule of Spain, establishing the seat of their empire at Córdoba.

In the years immediately afterward, Pelagius—whom some regard as a kinsman of Roderic—was acclaimed king by the Christians who had withdrawn into the mountains of Asturias to escape Moorish slavery. Rising against the Moors, he laid the first foundations of the kingdoms of León and Oviedo. From these kingdoms the enemies of the Christian name saw their foes repeatedly emerge at appointed times to restrain their advances and efforts, until, after being routed and defeated many times and driven back within the boundaries of the kingdom of Granada alone, even that kingdom, held for more than eight centuries, finally yielded in 1492 to Ferdinand and Isabella.

With everything thrown into confusion by Moorish incursions and dominion, especially the doctrines and mysteries of religion, this is hardly surprising. For when bishops neglected their pastoral duties in order to look after themselves, and the contagion of ignorance and wickedness spread from the neighboring mixture of Arabs, what could more easily follow than that the Lord’s flock should first become emaciated and then be overtaken by a deadly pestilence? Hence many maintain that, from the Muhammadan sect, [Col. 0558B] the seeds of the heresy of the Adoptians were cast, sprang up, and matured—to the injury of Christ.

**III.** This will not seem implausible to anyone who considers the beginnings of Mohammedanism and the Qur’an, which Peter the Venerable, ninth abbot of Cluny, recounts in book IV, letter 17, when he says:

> “Sergius, a monk and follower of the heretic Nestorius, expelled from the Church, joined Muhammad and supplied what was lacking in him [Muhammad]. He explained the sacred Scriptures, both of the Old and New Testaments, according to the understanding of his master, who denied that our Savior was God; he interpreted them partly as it seemed right to him, and, while attempting to turn him away from idolatry, made him a Nestorian Christian.”

For what else was the infamous heresy of the Adoptians than a shoot of Nestorianism, as was shown in the preceding dissertation? Nicolaus Antonius also seems to acknowledge that this was the origin of the error in Spain, in *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, volume I, book VI, chapter 2, no. 25, in these words:

> “When this century was drawing to its close”—he is speaking of the eighth—“a new error, born from the ignorance of the Spanish people groaning under the Saracen yoke, infected the purer age of Christianity, in which the faith of that period was flourishing, concerning the person of Christ the Lord . . . . . . Felix, bishop of Urgell, and Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, were the foundation and occasion of the evil. For, deceived perhaps by the contagion infecting those who were already under its influence, or by the blasphemies of the neighboring Muhammadans, neither of them was ashamed to call and teach Jesus to be the adoptive Son of God.”

**IV.** Although the root of this infamous shoot appears to have sprouted only at that time, to speak the truth, earlier centuries also heard the term “adoption” wrongly applied to Christ Jesus. For Bonosus, who preceded Nestorius and in a sense anticipated his heresy, uttered the designation “adoptive” at some point near the end of the fourth century, as is clear from the condemnation of the wicked doctrine made in the year 389 at the Council of Capua—Baronius and Labbe’s councils place it in that year.

Bonosus, bishop of Nussitania in Dacia, followed, as Sirmond conjectures in his notes on letter 3 of Avitus, bishop of Vienne, and in canon 17 of the Second Council of Arles, the party of Photinus, who denied that Christ was God and proclaimed him merely a man. He taught that Christ was the adoptive, not the proper, Son of God, as is reported from Isidore, book VIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5, in *Gratian’s Decree* 24, question 3, canon 39.

Isidore himself bears witness to this in his book *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, writing as follows concerning Justinian, bishop of Valencia, who flourished under Theudis, king of the Visigoths—that is, around the middle of the sixth century:

> “Justinian wrote a book of Responses. . . . The second of these is against the Bonosians, who say that Christ is adoptive and not the proper Son.”

Elipandus, however, says in his letter, which Etherius and Beatus inserted in book I against him, that Bonosus had held a different view from his own:

> “Bonosus,” he says, “believed that he was adoptive from his mother, and not properly begotten from the Father before the ages.”

Thus Bonosus altogether denied that Christ was God, since he removed his eternal generation from the Father before the ages. Elipandus claimed that he himself did nothing of the kind, as will appear below.

Moreover, we do not doubt that these were the very heretics whom, around this time—that is, about the year 420—our Chromatius, another most distinguished light of the Church of Aquileia, attacked in the fragment on the words, “I ought to be baptized by you.” For, commenting on the words “This is my Son,” spoken by the Father concerning Christ, he says:

> “His own, certainly, not by the adoption of grace, nor through the status of a creature, as the heretics wish, but by the propriety of his kind and the truth of his nature.”

**V.** It is credible that Theodiscus, who succeeded Saint Isidore in the see of Seville, transferred the term “adoption,” which had been applied to Christ Jesus by Easterners, to the Westerners. Concerning him, Lucas of Tuy, in Baronius under the year 636, no. 9, says:

> “Theodiscus, a Greek by nationality, succeeded the most blessed Isidore . . . . He was found to be unfaithful and proved to be erroneous in the articles of faith, and was degraded from the archiepiscopal dignity by a synod. For he asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, was not one God, but rather adoptive. Having thus been deprived of the honor of the priesthood, he went over to the Arabs, joined himself to the sect of the false prophet Muhammad, and taught many detestable things under the emperor Heraclius.”

After Theodiscus had been deposed, the plague of this error did not spread further at that time. But, nourished by the related malice of the Muhammadans, like an evil seed committed to the earth, it appeared again after nearly a century and a half, and through Felix and Elipandus recovered life and strength.

**VI.** Those who believe that the error was reborn only in the year 792, perhaps led by the fact that they read in the annals of the Franks that the first mention of this heresy occurred in that year, are mistaken. Natalis Alexander appears to have fallen into this trap, carried away by the authority of Einhard. In the *Synopsis of Ecclesiastical History*, eighth century, chapter 2, article 3, section 1, he says:

> “In the year of Christ 792, Felix, a Spaniard by nationality . . . not only declared the Son of God to be adoptive according to his humanity, but also most obstinately defended this corrupt opinion in books written to Elipandus, the bishop, as Einhard reports in his annals under the year 792.”

Indeed, not only Einhard but also the other annalists say nothing about the heresy before this year. Yet it is absolutely certain that it originated earlier. For Etherius and Beatus, beginning their book, address Elipandus as follows:

> “We read the letter of your prudence, in the present year 213, secretly sent—not to us, but to the abbot Fidelis—in October, under seal, in the Spanish era 823. We heard by report that it had arrived, but we did not see it until the sixth day before the Kalends of December. And when we went to our brother Fidelis, not compelled by that letter, but led by the recent devotion of the religious lady Abosinda, we heard that the little book against us and our faith had been publicly circulated throughout all Asturias.”

If, therefore, in the Spanish era 823, which corresponds to A.D. 785, Elipandus was already rising against the opponents of his doctrine, with a little book against them already circulated throughout all Asturias, it is clear that the heresy had arisen before the year 792.

That the Frankish annalists began to mention it only in that year is not surprising, since nothing was done against it until that year, under the auspices of Charlemagne—namely, the calling of the Council of Regensburg. They are not speaking precisely of the heresy as beginning then, but of its being condemned for the first time then. This is not obscurely gathered from the Loiselian Annals, which state under the year 792:

> “The Felician heresy, formerly heard of, was first condemned at Regensburg.”

Do you hear of a heresy first condemned which had been heard of previously? *Primitus* here means “formerly.”

**VII.** Even Natalis Alexander himself is compelled to acknowledge that its origin preceded the year 792, on the basis of words spoken by Paulinus at the Council of Friuli, in which, according to Alexander, he condemned the Felician madness in the year 791. [Col. 0560A] For if Paulinus opposed the heresy in 791, who would be so foolish as to say that it arose only in the following year, 792?

> “The first synod against the Felician heresy,” says Natalis, “was convened at Friuli, which is a town of the province of Aquileia, by Paulinus of Aquileia in the year of salvation 791, the twenty-third year of Charlemagne.”

So he says in the cited work, section 11. In the preceding section, however, he appears to have taught that Felix did not raise it until the year 792. Nevertheless, it has been more fully demonstrated in our second dissertation that the Council of Friuli must be assigned not to 791 but to 796.

**VIII.** Father Antonius Pagi attempts to establish the date when the Felician heresy arose—namely, not before the year 783—from the fact that Pope Hadrian had written in the preceding year to Bishop Aegila that he should protect the churches from various errors which had crept into Spain, without mentioning the Felician heresy, which he would not have omitted had it already raised its head. Cointius holds the same opinion, and Pagi derived his view from him.

> “In the preceding year”—that is, 781, says Cointius under the year 782, no. 21—“Charles became Hadrian’s fellow godparent,” and in the following year—namely, 783—we shall deal with the death of Peter, bishop of Pavia.”

These letters mention Hadrian as Charles’s godfather and Peter as bishop of Pavia. Therefore, he concludes, the letter to Aegila, which is found in Codex Carolinus 95, belongs to the year 782. And below:

> “In the same letter Hadrian attacks many errors that had arisen against the Catholic faith in the regions of Spain; yet he makes no mention of the Felician heresy. From this silence you may infer that it began to be heard of only later.”

So Cointius.

**IX.** Yet, in my judgment, this very fact seems to imply not that the heresy was arising in 783, but that it had arisen somewhat earlier. For Hadrian admonishes Bishop Aegila to protect the orthodox faith in the year 782, according to Pagi and Cointius, without the Felician heresy being openly identified—although they say that Hadrian himself attacked it by name in the following year, 783, in another letter, which we too shall discuss below in section 14. From this they seem to infer that the heresy began to sprout in that very year, 783.

But surely it will seem astonishing to anyone that, in the very year in which it emerged, the Roman pontiff, separated from the Spaniards by so great a distance, should have learned of the heresy both in fact and by name, and should have learned of it and attacked it at the same time. It seems more probable that in the preceding year the pontiff sensed the stench of some unsound doctrine and wrote about it, as the saying goes, in an exploratory manner, to Bishop Aegila; then, having perceived it more clearly in the following year, he rejected it in an explicit and carefully worded letter.

Hence, even if Pagi’s conclusion is admitted—that the letter of Hadrian in Codex Carolinus 97, by which this heresy is rejected, should be assigned to the year 783—it still does not follow that the heresy arose in that same year. Rather, it had probably been conceived and brought forth in earlier years.

**X.** In this year, 783, Silo died. He was the husband of Abosinda—or Abdosinda, or Adosinda, for her name is rendered in all these ways—the daughter of Alfonso the Catholic. He had ruled in Asturias and León for eight years, according to some accounts, and nine according to others. Elipandus made every effort to win this widow over to his side, thinking that the spread of his poison would be greatly advanced if he administered it through a woman powerful and distinguished by authority and religious virtue.

After performing the final duties of piety toward her husband, she had bid farewell to the pomps of the world and withdrawn into a convent, as is related by the author of the *Life of Saint Beatus*, to be cited below in section 22, and by Baronius under the year 783, no. 5.

Hear John Mariana, *Annals of Spain*, book VII, chapter 8:

> “Elipandus wrote to the bishops of the Asturians and Galicians, relying upon the authority that he possessed over other churches, an authority both special and supreme; and, in particular, he attempted to lead Adosinda, the widow of King Silo, into deception. She, as was necessary, refused to pronounce judgment in the controversy, declaring that the decision did not belong to her own judgment; and, being a most holy and prudent woman, referred the entire matter to the bishops and priests, among whom was Beatus the presbyter and Etherius, bishop of Osma.”

This appeal to Adosinda seems to have been attempted by Elipandus around the beginning of the year 786. For Etherius and Beatus appear, at the urging of that same former queen, now a religious woman, to have gone to Fidelis the abbot. From Etherius’s words, which will shortly be quoted, one may suspect that Elipandus used Fidelis in attempting to subvert Adosinda, so that those present could discuss face-to-face and orally the controversy over which Elipandus was trying to win her.

This is gathered from the beginning of book I of Etherius and Beatus, whose words we quoted above in section 4. From them it may be inferred that, if these men encountered the letters written by Elipandus and sent to Abbot Fidelis in October 785, receiving them on the sixth day before the Kalends of December, at the urging of Adosinda, it is sufficiently clear that she was not approached until about this time. For it is entirely credible that, as soon as the matter had begun to be discussed with her, she would have referred it to the bishops and priests.

**XI.** Here, however, Elipandus’s letter to Abbot Fidelis must be included, as Etherius and Beatus present it in book I; from it several matters worthy of knowledge may be inferred. They introduce it as follows:

> “Elipandus says: Whoever does not confess Jesus Christ to be adoptive in respect of his humanity and in no way adoptive in respect of his divinity is both a heretic and must be exterminated. Remove the evil from your land. They do not ask me questions, but seek to teach, because they are servants of Antichrist. I have therefore sent this letter of the lord Bishop Ascaricus to your fraternity, dearest Fidelis, so that you may recognize how great is the humility reigning among the servants of Christ and how great is the pride reigning among the servants of Antichrist.”

**XII.** “When the lord Ascaricus wished to write these things to me, not with the authority of one giving instruction, but with the desire of one asking questions, just as true humility taught him, these men, however, now saying the contrary, now treating me as though I were ignorant of what is right, did not wish to ask questions but to teach. Therefore God knows that, although they had written insolently [the margin notes: ‘the passage is mutilated’], if they had spoken the truth I ought gratefully to have obeyed, remembering what is written: ‘If something is revealed to a younger man, the elder should keep silent’ [1 Cor. 14:30]. And again: ‘He is nearest to God who knows how to keep silent with reason.’ [In the margin this is attributed to Cato.] For it has never been heard that the people of Lebanon should have taught the people of Toledo.

It is known to the whole people that, from the very beginning of the faith, this see has shone with holy teachings, and that nothing schismatic has ever issued from it. And now a single diseased sheep seeks to become our teacher. Yet he did not wish to bring these matters to the ears of our other brothers before this evil had been cut out by the roots there where it arose. For it will be a disgrace to me if this evil is heard of within the territory of Toledo [the margin reads: ‘within the dominion of Toledo’].

What I and my other brothers in Seville have judged for so long, and what, with God’s help, we have condemned both in the Paschal celebrations and in the other errors of the Migetians—now they, on the contrary, find grounds on which to accuse us. Yet if the matter is handled lukewarmly and is not corrected by you, I shall bring it to the attention of the brothers; and it will be disgraceful for you if they reproach you for it.”

**XIII.** “Let your fraternity instruct the youth of our brother Etherius, who was brought up on milk and has not yet been led to the strength of perfect understanding; for he held conference not with the best teachers but with ignorant and schismatic men, namely Felix and Beatus Antiphrasius [the margin explains that Elipandus called Beatus by this name through *antiphrasis*, as is also clear from Charlemagne’s letter to Elipandus], his equals in virtue and peers in error.

Bonosus and Beatus were condemned for the same error. The former believed that Christ was adoptive from his mother and not properly begotten from the Father before the ages, and not temporally adoptive from his mother. Whom shall I regard as like him except Faustus the Manichaean? Faustus condemned the patriarchs and prophets; [the printed text has: “214”] this man condemns the ancient and modern teachers.

I beg you, inflamed by the fervor of faith, to be so fervent in your zeal that you remove the aforesaid error from your midst, so that, just as through his servants the Lord uprooted the Migetian heresy from the boundaries of Baetica, so through you he may completely tear the Beatian heresy from the territory of the Asturians.

But because I have heard that the forerunner of Antichrist has appeared among you, announcing that he has already been born, I ask you to inquire of him where, how, or when that lying spirit of the prophets was born—the spirit that speaks in him—and report the answer to us.”

Thus Elipandus apparently wrote from Toledo to Abbot Fidelis in the Spanish era 823.

**XIV.** I am astonished that Baronius under the year 783, no. 7; Vasquez, volume I, on the Third Part of Saint Thomas, disputation 89, chapter 1; and Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, eighth century, chapter 2, article 3, section 3, assert that this letter was written in the year 783. If one subtracts thirty-eight years from the Spanish era, as one must when seeking the corresponding Christian year in the Spanish era 823, it falls not in 783 but in 785. Pagi also noticed this under the year 783, no. 9.

In this letter Elipandus mentions the Council of Seville, which he himself had convened to suppress the errors of Migetius, who, besides teaching several other absurdities, had gone astray concerning the celebration of Easter. In the cited passage Pagi supposes that Elipandus was prompted by the letter of Pope Hadrian found in Codex Carolinus 97, with this title:

> “Copy of a letter of Pope Hadrian, addressed to all the bishops residing throughout Spain, but especially to Elipandus and Ascaricus and those agreeing with them, concerning the heresy or blasphemy by which they call the Son of God adoptive, rebuking them on many points by the authority of the holy Fathers. Also concerning the Paschal feast, etc.”

This is the letter mentioned above in section 9, which Pagi and Cointius assign to the year 783. Pagi also places in that year the Council of Seville mentioned by Elipandus; on his authority it is listed under the same year in the Venetian collection of the councils of Labbe, under the title “Council of Spain.”

Given these facts, it is clear that the letter to Fidelis was written not in 783, as Baronius, Vasquez, and Natalis maintain, but later—namely, in 785. For in it he speaks of the Migetian error concerning Easter as having already been judged and extinguished, specifically at the synod convened in the year 783.

**XV.** “Among those whom Elipandus drew over to his side were Ascaricus, bishop of Braga, and Abbot Fidelis, to whom he first revealed the secrets of his sect, writing to him in October of the Spanish era 823, or A.D. 785.”

So Pagi says verbatim. His statement appears to contain an error, or rather a contradiction. For how can it be true that Elipandus first revealed the secrets of his sect to Abbot Fidelis in a letter written in 785, when Pagi himself says there that Hadrian’s letter, by which the Spanish bishops were warned about the error of the Adoptians, was sent in 783? In that same letter the Roman pontiff mentions Ascaricus as a man stained by the same pitch.

It was therefore Ascaricus, rather than Fidelis, who first imbibed Elipandus’s poison. [Col. 0562D] Pagi adds in the same place:

> “Having convened an assembly of the provincial bishops, Elipandus promptly suppressed the Migetians, who had gone astray concerning the date of Easter, as he boasts in his letter to Abbot Fidelis; yet he did not cease to publish his own error, which he had received from Felix.”

If Elipandus had been equally zealous from the year 773 both in suppressing the Migetian error and in publishing his own heresy, as Pagi indicates in the words quoted, how could he have whispered his error into Abbot Fidelis’s ears for the first time only in 785?

From such zeal in disseminating the error, Elipandus might appear to someone to have been the author of the wicked doctrine. I do not think so; rather, I regard Felix as its author, since Elipandus had received the error from him, as Pagi said above. But how this happened I shall explain shortly, after first making a few observations about the condition of both men.

**XVI.** Elipandus—whom some call Elifandus, others Eliphandus, and others render differently according to the varying accent of their nations—must be considered younger than Felix if we consider the order of their studies. For he seems to have depended upon Felix’s teaching as upon the words of a master; according to Einhard in the annals under the year 792, he consulted Felix concerning the question of Adoption.

But if we consider age, I would not dare to assert that he was younger. For in the year 792, when Felix was living at Rome and had been sent by Charles to Hadrian through Angilbert in order to renounce his heresy, following the condemnation of that heresy at the Council of Regensburg, as will be seen below in section 34, Elipandus was eighty-two years old. Thus Elipandus wrote to Felix, who was staying at Rome:

> “Inform me, you who have been stationed at Rome.”

And below:

> “But know that, already in decrepit old age, I entered my eighty-second year on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.”

It follows that he must have been born in the year 710, on July 25. It seems difficult to make Felix older than this. For Felix was still alive in the year 814, around which time, as will be established from Agobard in section 76, he died both in life and in wickedness; he would therefore have had to live beyond his hundredth year. Yet it is not credible that a man over ninety years of age was summoned to and attended the Council of Aachen, as Felix himself did in 799, as will be said in section 71 and following.

**XVII.** “Some suspect that Felix was a Gaul by nationality because of the proximity of the regions and because Frankish arms had penetrated that part of Spain in earlier years,” says John Mariana, book VII, chapter 8. But Einhard clearly declares under the year 792 that he was a Spaniard:

> “Urgell,” he says, “is a city situated on the ridge of the Pyrenees, whose bishop, named Felix, was a Spaniard by nationality, etc.”

For the location of the city of Urgell, consult Ferrarius and Baudrand, who place it in Catalonia at the foot of the Pyrenean mountains, and wonder that Ortelius located it in Aragon.

Papirius Masson appears to have followed Ortelius’s error in the synopsis prefixed to the works of Agobard, where he says:

> “Under the rule of the emperors Charles the Great and Louis, a certain bishop of Origella in Aragon emerged from the highest peaks of the Pyrenees.”

Papirius adds another error from his own store. Origella is not on the peaks, but rather at the foot of the Pyrenees, as the geographers cited above maintain.

He is likewise mistaken when he adds there concerning this bishop:

> “He was first rebuked and convicted by Elipandus”—he himself writes “Helipandus”—“the bishop of Toledo.”

For all ancient and modern authorities agree that Felix was not rebuked by Elipandus; rather, when Felix had at some point renounced the heresy—if indeed he ever truly renounced it—he returned to his vomit at Elipandus’s persuasion, as will be said below.

Mariana, in the cited passage, writes that Elipandus was descended from an ancient Gothic family. Thus the matter stood between these bishops.

**XVIII.** Before the year 783, as we believe on the basis of the argument given above, Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, consulted Felix, likewise a bishop, “by letter, asking what he ought to think concerning the humanity of the Savior, our God and Lord Jesus Christ—whether, according to that by which he is man, he should be believed and called the proper or adoptive Son of God. Felix, very rashly and thoughtlessly, and contrary to the ancient doctrine of the Catholic Church, not only declared him adoptive, but also most obstinately endeavored to defend the depravity of his error in books written to the aforesaid bishop.”

These are Einhard’s words under the year 792 in the annals, where he records the first origin of this heresy.

The Saxon Poet, however, in book III of his *Annals*, under the year 792, suggests that Felix had already administered his poison to the people and spread his erroneous doctrine among the masses before Elipandus consulted him by letter. For he sings:

> High above the lofty ridges of the Pyrenean mountain  
> stands the city of Urgell, whose bishop  
> was Felix by name. Here he undertook to establish  
> a wicked heresy and taught doctrines  
> contrary to holy faith,  
> asserting that, since the Lord Christ had deigned  
> to become man by assuming a body,  
> he was not thereby the proper Son,  
> but the adoptive Son of the Almighty.

Do you not see him deliberately teaching the heresy? He then inserts Elipandus’s consultation in these words:

[Col. 0564A]

> And to the Toledan bishop Elipandus  
> he gave this answer, consulted by him  
> concerning so great a matter;  
> and he took every care, with all the zeal and skill he could command,  
> to defend his doctrine in writing with a little book.
