Jonas of Orléans also asserts this no less clearly at the beginning of book I of *On the Worship of Images*, where he demonstrates that it was not Felix who joined Elipandus, but Elipandus who joined Felix as the author of the error:

> “There emerged from Spain, in the time of the holy-memory, most pious and invincible emperor Charles, a certain Felix by name, but unhappy in his deeds, bishop of the city of Urgell. Having joined Eliphantus”—this writer spells the name thus—“the bishop of the city of Toledo, to his most wicked error, he dared to preach that, according to his humanity, Christ was not the proper Son of God but the adoptive Son.”

Therefore, with the utmost justice, although Pagi wishes to maintain under the year 783, no. 9, that Elipandus had previously been imbued with this doctrine, we assert that Felix was the true parent of the pestilence which writers commonly recognize under the name of the Felician, not the Elipandian, heresy.

Felix himself hints at this in his confession of faith, in these words spoken about himself:

> “Through whom contention has continued in the Church of God until now.”

**215 XIX.** Yet although the movement first proceeded from one man, both subsequently acquired supporters. Hear from Jonas of Orléans about the zeal and solicitude of both in spreading the tares of evil doctrine:

> “By this poisonous doctrine the two of them infected a large part of Spain. Then, wishing to appear to imitate the deeds of Christ’s apostles, they each separately sought to imbue different provinces with the same doctrine. Eliphantus sought Asturias and Galicia; I remember having once seen his disciples among the Asturians . . . . Felix, after administering the same poisonous draught to many in Septimania, wished, insofar as it lay within his power, to administer it also to Gaul and Germany. But, with divine grace assisting, his error was unable to find any place in Gaul or Germany.”

**XX.** Among the disciples whom Elipandus acquired through this solicitude were those already mentioned above: Ascaricus, bishop of Braga, and Abbot Fidelis, through whom he perhaps attempted the Catholic mind of Adosinda, once a queen and then a religious woman, though unsuccessfully, as stated above.

Some men of Córdoba were added to their number, as is gathered from Elipandus’s letter to Felix, in which he says:

> “I sent your letter to the brothers at Córdoba who think rightly about God, and they wrote many things to me that I ought to have sent for your assistance. But I sent these same things to Master Albinus, Beatus Antiphrasius, to read.”

**XXI.** Although Felix did not enjoy equal success in propagating the error, since Gaul and Germany were sufficiently and more than sufficiently fortified by the vigilance of the bishops and Charlemagne, he nevertheless eventually produced an unhappy offspring: namely, Claudius of Turin, a Spaniard by nationality, who later carried the evil outside Spain.

Writing against him, Jonas says:

> “Under the rule of Louis, the son of Charlemagne, the same Felix was reborn in a certain disciple of his named Claudius—just as, to use the words of blessed Jerome, Euphorbus was reborn in Pythagoras.”

And below:

> “This man, then, of whom we are speaking, arising from the same Spain and adhering from early youth to the discipleship of the same Felix, served for some time in the palace of that most glorious, serene, and beloved-of-God emperor in the office of presbyter. But, so that he might provide for the benefit of others through the teaching of evangelical preaching, which seemed to be present in him in a marked degree, by the clemency of that most pious prince he was appointed bishop of the church of Turin.”

And farther below:

> “It was not without reason, but by a certain prophecy, as is believed, that he received the name Claudius. For although he does not appear openly to follow the error of his master . . . nevertheless, because he limps in his attempt to oppose ecclesiastical authority, he rightly bears the name Claudius and is justly enrolled among those concerning whom the Psalmist says: ‘The children of strangers have lied to me; the children of strangers have grown old and have limped from their paths.’”

But Claudius not only limped; he also fell. He asserted that the images of the saints ought altogether to be removed and eliminated. In this matter Jonas himself also limped: although he argued against Claudius that images should be preserved for the edification and example of the faithful, he nevertheless strove to abolish all worship and veneration of them.

But enough has now been said about Claudius, Felix’s disciple, and Jonas, his opponent. Let us return to our subject.

## XXII

Those who were especially alarmed by the insane doctrine were Beatus, a priest and abbot, and his disciple Etherius, later bishop of Osma, as is recorded by Alcuin in Book I *Against Felix*: “As for your statement,” he says, “that a certain abbot Beatus and his disciple Etherius were the first to oppose this sect of yours, we praise them for having attempted to defend the truth.” Since, however, it is characteristic of heretics to stain the doctrine of those who attack their errors, Felix and Elipandus slandered Beatus and Etherius, alleging that, like Eutyches, they confused the two natures in Christ—just as a drop of liquid scattered into the ocean is confused, mixed, and united with seawater. Theodoret remembers this comparison in *Dialogue 2*, entitled *The Inconfused*. Alcuin therefore added: “But if it is true that you said they confuse Christ’s two natures into one, like wine and water, we by no means agree with this; rather, if it is true, we judge them highly blameworthy in this respect.”

Here, incidentally, note Alcuin’s prudence: still unaware of the truth, and therefore hesitant to assent to the accusation brought against them, he twice expressed the qualification, “if it is true,” thereby keeping their doctrine intact. Concerning Beatus, take the following from his *Life*, written by a certain Spaniard of a later age and reported by Mabillon in the appendix to the fourth Benedictine century. Pagius cites it under the year 783, no. 11, adding that among the Asturians he is venerated as a saint under the common name San Bieco:

“But when,” says the author of the *Life*, “the dispute over the Felician depravity had subsided, the holy man Beatus became the constant spiritual guide of Adosinda, wife of King Silo, who, because of the tyranny of Mauregatus, had put on the sacred habit, and did so for the remedy of her soul. Eventually he withdrew to the Valley of Cava—called Valcabado by the Spaniards, not far from Saldaña, a town in the diocese of León—devoting himself to prayers, fasts, and the study of Sacred Scripture. On the mysteries of the Apocalypse he composed a book in remarkable order. Finally, renowned for miracles, he commended his spirit to the Lord whom he had served in peaceful sleep, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, in the year of our Lord 798.”

## XXIII

Elipandus was displeased to hear that Beatus and Etherius had risen against his opinion. He complained about them to Abbot Fidelis in a letter dated in the Spanish era 823—that is, A.D. 785, as stated above. One may admire in this letter the man’s confidence: he praises Ascarius, bishop of Braga, most highly because Ascarius had consulted him in this matter; he rebukes Beatus and Etherius for having acted otherwise; and he expresses indignation that men who ought to have requested instruction from the see of Toledo, as though from the teacher of all the others, should rise up with reckless audacity against their own mother.

He admits that opposition had been directed against him—an opposition which he does not hesitate to call the “Beatian heresy”—and declares that he would no longer communicate with the other brethren, lest, as he said, he bring shame and disgrace upon himself if the Toledans appeared to be taught by Libanenses, among whom Beatus lived in Asturias. In reality, however, he was putting forward a screen for his malice. More truthfully he would have said that he feared that, through Beatus’s opposition, the perfidy of his doctrine would be exposed and, once exposed, execrated by everyone.

## XXIV

The plague, however, did not remain hidden for long. Only three years after Elipandus’s complaints, the Council of Narbonne was assembled against the Felician heresy. Guillelmus Catellus, in Book V of *On Daniel, Archbishop of Narbonne*, first published this council, as Cointius testifies in the passage cited below; afterward it was published by Stephanus Baluzius in his additions to chapter 25 of Book VI of Peter de Marca’s *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*. Here we give only the beginning, since it is more relevant to our subject than the rest:

“The Council of Narbonne was held in the year 788. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 788, in the twelfth indiction, while the most glorious Lord Emperor Charles was reigning in the twenty-third year of his reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, when, because of many and various ecclesiastical matters, especially because of the pestiferous doctrine of Felix, bishop of the see of Urgell, we had assembled at the city of Narbonne at the warning conveyed in letters from the lord apostolic Adrian and from the lord emperor through his envoy named Desiderius, etc.”

Apart from this, reader, you will find absolutely nothing else concerning Felix’s heresy. His name appears only in the thirteenth place among the subscriptions, as follows: “I, Felix, bishop of the see of Urgell, have subscribed.”

## XXV

There are some who detect several flaws in the dating of this council; among them is Pagius, under the year 788, no. 11. They say:

1. There is an error in the date, because Charles’s twenty-third year did not fall in A.D. 788.

2. The indiction is inconsistent, since the year then current was not the twelfth but only the eleventh.

3. Charles is called emperor, although he did not obtain the empire until A.D. 800.

4. The Frankish annals show that the Felician heresy was first condemned at Regensburg in A.D. 792; this could not be true if it had first been proscribed at Narbonne in A.D. 788.

5. Felix’s own subscription appears implausible in a case involving his condemnation.

6. Certain bishops, such as the bishop of Barcelona, are said to have subscribed to the council, although it is difficult to believe that the Barcelonans—so tenacious of their rights and so unwilling to defer in any matter to the Frankish name—were present.

## XXVI

These objections, however, do not seem sufficiently weighty to deprive the council of all authority and condemn it outright as a falsification and illegitimate fabrication. For Baluzius, by the common judgment of all scholars and by Pagius’s own admission, “highly experienced in the study of ancient manuscripts, asserts that he transcribed it from a manuscript which was either nearly contemporary with Charles or not far removed from his age.” He himself saw the objections that could be raised and met them appropriately, as may be seen in his notes on the council itself.

As to the first objection, before Pepin, the father of Charlemagne, died, his kingdom was divided among his sons at Worms in A.D. 763 or 764. Aquitaine, Septimania, and that part of Spain then subject to the Franks were assigned to Charles; he was consequently called king at that time. Thus there would be only a one-year discrepancy in reconciling A.D. 788 with the twenty-third year of King Charles.

Cointius, in his annals under the year 791, no. 11, does not reject the council but notes certain defects, such as the fact that at that time they were not accustomed to add either the year of the Incarnation or the indiction. “Both of these chronological markers,” he says, “must therefore be dismissed as later additions.” Since Charles was not given the title of emperor until later, he adds: “But whoever inserted the year of the Lord’s Incarnation and the indiction easily called him emperor whom he ought to have called king.”

Cointius, observing here that Charles acquired the Frankish kingdom only after his father’s death, places the council not in A.D. 788 but in A.D. 791, the year corresponding to the twenty-third year of Charles’s Frankish reign.

The first explanation of the difficulty nevertheless seems preferable, since the assigned twelfth indiction—for neither the indiction nor the year of the Incarnation creates any difficulty for Baluzius—differs less from the eleventh, which truly belongs to A.D. 788, than from the fourteenth, which would have to be assigned to A.D. 791. If there is an error in the indiction, a copyist could easily have introduced it through carelessness, writing 12 instead of 11 by adding a small stroke. The response to the second objection is therefore also apparent.

## XXVII

Baluzius deals at greater length with the third objection, showing most clearly that the title “emperor” was often given to the kings of the Franks even though they had not yet received the imperial diadem. Thus, in a charter of Maurengy, Pepin is called: “Executed at the monastery of Flavigny in the seventeenth year of Pepin the emperor.”

To the fourth objection it may be answered that the Felician heresy was indeed first condemned at the Council of Regensburg—first, that is, by name and solemnly. But what prevents us from asserting that it was also dealt with at the Council of Narbonne, especially since nothing is said there about its condemnation? Perhaps it was merely discussed at that time, without any definitive judgment being made.

This is apparent from what survives of that council. Apart from the words quoted above, nothing further is added concerning the Felician heresy; instead, the text quickly passes to the question of the boundaries between the dioceses of Narbonne and Elne. Hence it is not surprising that Felix’s subscription should be found there: in a case concerning boundaries, he could quite properly cast a vote and express an opinion. This also supplies the answer to the fifth objection.

As to the sixth, although the Barcelonans may have tolerated no Frankish subjection in civil affairs, it is not implausible that they attended in matters of faith and the churches—especially since the heading of the acts says that the synod was convened “at the warning conveyed by letters from the lord apostolic Adrian.” Add what Cointius noted under the year 791, no. 13: at that time “Urgell was subject to the metropolitan church of Narbonne.” Provincial bishops, although subject to another power in temporal matters, could surely have attended the Council of Narbonne when summoned by the metropolitan and urged by the supreme pontiff.

## XXVIII

Felix therefore withdrew from the Council of Narbonne no better than he had entered it. Perhaps because his madness had been discussed but not yet proscribed, he became more insolent and did not cease disseminating his pestiferous doctrine among the people. As the disease spread and gained strength from day to day, its evil odor reached even the regions of Germany, so far removed from Spain, and struck the purer nostrils there.

As the contagion continued to spread for a considerable time, the Church was compelled, with a strong hand reinforced by princely authority, not merely to cauterize the wound with a salutary remedy but also to cut it out from the root with the public sword of anathema. Accordingly, in A.D. 792, a synod was convened at Regensburg, where the heresy was first struck with an ecclesiastical sentence. I say “first” because its condemnation was issued under its proper name. How this occurred, you may now hear.

## XXIX

After the Avars had first been subdued in August by Henry, duke of Friuli, and then harassed by Charles, Charles wintered at Regensburg. There, toward the end of the year 791, he celebrated Christmas, and in the following year, 792, Easter. So report the Annals of Lorsch and the others.

During this interval, or around that time—for as summer approached, the Saxons, breaking their treaties and rebelling against God and the king, were provoking the Franks to war rather than to peaceful undertakings, as the Chronicle of Moissac relates—Charles convened a synod in the same city.

At it, consideration was given to a conspiracy formed against Charles by his son Pepin, born of Hilmintrude, according to Cointius under the year 792, no. 5; but according to Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, “born of a concubine: handsome in face, but disfigured by a hump.” The Annals of Lorsch record for this year: “A conspiracy against the king by his son Pepin was discovered and suppressed.”

This Pepin, the son of Hilmintrude, was different from Pepin, the son of Queen Hildegard and king of Italy. Riccobald of Ferrara is therefore not to be followed. At the beginning of Book IX of the *Historians of Italy*, page 109, he confuses these two Pepins and makes Pepin, the rebel against his father, king of Italy. This is false.

With the advice of the nobles and bishops, Charles inflicted no other punishment on his rebellious son than to have him confined in a monastery and tonsured before the altar, as the author of the Chronicle of Moissac relates.

The Frankish annalists agree that Felix was summoned—or rather brought—to the council to give an account of his doctrine. The synod was entirely justified in demanding an account of the faith from Felix, since, with the authority of the Roman pontiff, it was about to condemn the accused after hearing him. A monk of the monastery of Angoulême writes: “He celebrated Christmas and Easter at Regensburg. There he held a synod, and first the Felician heresy was condemned with the authority of Pope Adrian.”

The Fathers did not proceed tumultuously to launch the thunderbolt of anathema without examining the matter. Felix himself was given whatever opportunity the case required to present, defend, and confirm his arguments in support of the proscribed doctrine. This is gathered from Einhard’s annals under the year 792:

“Felix was brought to the royal palace, where the king was then residing at Regensburg, a city of Bavaria in which he had wintered. There, after a council of bishops had been assembled, he was heard and convicted of error,” and so forth.

The Saxon Poet gives a corresponding account:

> From there he was led to the court of the Catholic prince  
>   
> (Regino likewise was wintering then in the city).  
>   
> Before many bishops and the crowded synod  
>   
> He was heard, and convicted of having taught  
>   
> A wicked error, and so forth.

## XXX

Severinus Binius, in note a on the Council of Regensburg, thinks that Jonas, bishop of Orléans, referred to this synod at the beginning of his book *On the Worship of Images*, where he writes:

“By command of that same prince, Charles, they—the bishops—were gathered together, and with the authority also of the holy Roman Church they condemned the same Felix; indeed, together with the author of his error, Nestorius, whom he imitated, they consigned him to perpetual anathema.”

I believe, however, that these words must be understood of the Council of Frankfurt. For a little earlier the same Jonas says of such heretics:

“And because, in accordance with the apostolic command, they had already been admonished three times to desist from that same preaching of theirs, yet they remained in the same error, they were to be avoided as heretics.”

The three ecclesiastical admonitions, however, had been completed only at the Council of Frankfurt, where the Frankish annalists unanimously affirm that the heresy was condemned for the third time.

Moreover, Jonas appears to be speaking of the decisive and final action taken by Charles against Felix. Immediately after the words quoted above he adds:

“But after the orthodox prince Charles had been removed from human affairs, his glorious son Louis, etc.”

By these words he seems to indicate that this condemnation was the one after which no intervening event occurred before Charles’s death. If the final censure was not issued at Frankfurt, it was even less likely to have been issued at Regensburg.

## XXXI

Alcuin, in Book I *Against Elipandus*, speaks of this Regensburg assembly more clearly than Jonas:

“Before I came to Francia at the command of that same most wise king Charles”—he came, or rather returned, from England, to which he had departed in A.D. 790, as stated in Dissertation 1, § 8, either at the end of this year or the beginning of the next, as Cointius prefers under the year 793, no. 17—“this same sect of your error was debated, while that glorious prince presided, in the celebrated place called Regensburg, with Felix, whom you are accustomed to praise greatly, at that time the defender of your party; and by the synodal authority of the priests of Christ, who had gathered from different parts of the Christian empire, it was condemned with eternal anathema.”

At this council Felix detested his heresy, as the Fulda Annals relate in these words:

“The Felician heresy was first condemned at Regensburg, with its author himself denying it.”

## XXXII

But because Felix returned like a dog to his vomit and again embraced what he had renounced, our Paulinus, in Book I, chapter 5, reproaches him for his inconsistency in faith and for violating the oath that he had solemnly given at this assembly after touching the Gospels and pronouncing the prescribed words. Hear Paulinus, who, as we infer from this, was present at the council and describes the matter:

“Let us approach this man, insensible to shame, whom the character of his deeds proves by reliable and certain evidence to have long since succumbed in the contest of the arena. Now, however, by reckless daring, and we do not know at whose prompting, he attempts to renew and restore battles that had died away. Moreover, he has forgotten the covenant of the oath which he had made with God, amid the shining companies of thousands of angels surrounding him on every side.

“Nor, as I think, was the multitude of the human army absent from this spectacle, especially since a controversy of this kind was being debated in the presence of the venerable prince. For after touching the holy Gospels, he protested under oath that, when the judgment of the most sincere faith at that time demanded it, the obscure chatter of disputation had fallen silent under forced restraint: never thereafter, under any title whatsoever, would he revive the question by any contrary effort; rather, he pledged that he would remain forever unchanged in the rule of faith to which he had consented.

“In this conflict of gymnastic disputation it also happened that I, the least and most humble of all, was personally present.”

## XXXIII

These final words most plainly demonstrate, leaving no room for doubt, that Paulinus was present at this council, since they cannot be understood of any other. They do not refer to the Council of Frankfurt, because although Paulinus and Charles were present there, Felix was not, as you will see below, no. 47, when we return to the Council of Frankfurt and to our Paulinus’s *Sacrosyllabus*. Felix therefore did not reject his perfidy at Frankfurt, as is stated here.

Nor do they refer to the Roman council, because, as will shortly be shown under no. 35, although Felix abjured his error there before Pope Adrian, Paulinus was not present. Paulinus says here that he was present when the controversy was debated in the presence of the venerable prince—that is, Charles—who himself was not present at the Roman council.

Finally, they do not refer to the Council of Aachen of A.D. 799, because it is certain that Paulinus wrote these words and cast them in Felix’s face before the year of the Aachen council, namely in A.D. 796. This is clear from the dedicatory letter prefixed to the three books addressed to Charles—the first of which contains the material now before us—against Felix, as we observed in the notes to that work.

Moreover, in this same year Paulinus obtained a privilege from Charles at Regensburg, as is related more fully in chapter 6 of his *Life*. It is therefore clearer than midday that Paulinus was present at this synod of Regensburg.

## XXXIV

After Felix had abjured his perfidy at that Bavarian synod, he was brought to Rome by command of Charles, under the escort of Angilbert, so that before the chair of Peter—which is the pillar and foundation of truth—he might publicly confess his error and Pope Adrian himself might receive the pledge of his repentance.

The Fulda Annals state:

“Moreover, he was brought by Abbot Engilbert into the presence of Adrian the apostolic, and after making a confession he again condemned it”—that is, his heresy.

The Annals of Lorsch and the others report the same under the year 792.

Here the Fulda annalist calls Angilbert an abbot. Cointius, under the same year 792, no. 22, and under the year 796, nos. 139 and following, attempts to show that he was neither abbot nor priest before A.D. 796, claiming that only in that year did he become a tonsured monk at the monastery of Centula. There is no time to examine every detail in order to settle the dispute, since for our purposes it is enough to identify the person. Anyone who wishes to investigate his status may consult, besides Cointius in the cited passage, the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, fourth century, under the year 814, and should not omit Angilbert’s life for February 18 in Adrian Baillet.

## XXXV

After leaving Regensburg, Felix arrived in Rome under Angilbert’s guidance and was received kindly by the excellent shepherd as a wandering sheep. Yet, as the enormity of his error demanded, he did not escape imprisonment. While in prison he composed a document renouncing his error, which he presented to Adrian and to the Fathers of the Roman council, whom the pope had convened for this purpose in the basilica of Saint Peter.

This is taught us by the words of Leo III at another Roman council in A.D. 799, session 2:

“Under our predecessor of holy memory, the lord Pope Adrian, this most wretched heretic, the unhappy bishop Felix, having been sent by the lord Charles, the most illustrious great king, was instructed by that same blessed pontiff. In prison he composed that orthodox document, anathematizing and affirming, among other things, that the Son of God was in no way adoptive, as he had said, but that I confess our Lord Jesus Christ to be the proper and true Son of God.

“Therefore, placing his orthodox document upon the sacred mysteries of God in our patriarchal church, he swore that he would hold and confess this doctrine. Again, placing the same orthodox document upon the body of blessed Peter the apostle in his confession, he likewise swore there that he would never dare to call him adoptive, but that he held and confessed him to be the proper and beloved Son of God.

“Afterward, having transgressed the law of the Most High God and fleeing to pagans who shared his views, he became perjured.”

All this is from Pope Leo III. After this public retraction of his error, Felix was released and sent back to his own country. Einhard writes in his annals: “When this had been done, he returned to his own city.”

The Saxon poet, under the year 792, describes the event with equal accuracy and elegance for the circumstances of the time:

> … after this he was sent to gracious Adrian,  
>   
> Who at that time was bishop of the apostolic see.  
>   
> In his presence, corrected in blessed Peter’s church,  
>   
> Before the holy and renowned assembly of pontiffs,  
>   
> Felix condemned the sect of perfidy  
>   
> Which he had unhappily originated,  
>   
> And earned the right to return  
>   
> To retain once more the honor of his own see.

What was defined at this Roman council, and what Adrian replied on several occasions when Charlemagne questioned him about the matter, he collected into a single letter or document and sent to the bishops of Spain against Elipandus. Charles mentions it in his letter to Elipandus, sent from the Council of Frankfurt together with the synodal letter of the council and the *Sacrosyllabus* of our Paulinus. All these documents are found in the acts of the Council of Frankfurt:

“First, what the lord apostolic, together with the holy Roman Church and the bishops living throughout those regions, and with the Catholic teachers, held concerning this matter, we established in a single document.”

## XXXVI

At about this time Alcuin opportunely returned from England to Francia after an absence of nearly three years. It was the period when Felix, having been sent back to his own church, displayed signs of the simulated conversion and feigned renunciation of error that he had made at Regensburg and Rome.

The unfortunate man mocked God and the Church. In truth, he had never abandoned the perverse doctrine in his heart, as he himself admits in his confession of faith at the Council of Aachen, when he appeared to have been converted. He said:

“We have returned with our whole heart, not with any simulation or veil of falsehood, as formerly.”

By this he implied that on the earlier occasion he had been converted deceitfully.

Indeed, while still living in Rome, he sent a letter to Elipandus, whose reply clearly exposes his perfidy. In replying to Felix, Elipandus wrote in a letter that we have already quoted in parts several times:

“Lord Felix, I inform you that I received your written message at the end of July, and at the end of August I likewise wrote to you.”

A little later he adds:

“Let me know how you fare, you who are stationed in Rome. I received your letter, which had somehow descended to me from heaven, at the end of July, and with outstretched arms I gave immense thanks to my God, who made me rejoice in your conversation.”

And further:

“I sent your letter to the brethren at Córdoba who think rightly about God, and who wrote many things to me which I ought to send to your aid. But I sent it to the heresiarch Beatus, the Antiphrasius of Albinus the teacher, so that he might read it. You, however, send that writing on behalf of your faithful and glorious prince before it comes to that son of perdition, Albinus, who does not believe in the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God, etc.”

## XXXVII

This letter was plainly written after the one sent in August to which it refers, that is, toward the end of A.D. 792 or the beginning of the following year, 793. It clearly shows how falsely Felix had renounced his doctrine, whether at Regensburg or at Rome, since he maintained such an exchange of letters with Elipandus and expected such assistance from him.

It also shows how much both of them feared Albinus’s learning. They took such care that their writings should not fall into his hands.

Although, as we have said, Alcuin had returned to Gaul around this time, he was nevertheless not ignorant of the sequence of the Spanish error. Before his departure from Gaul, approximately in A.D. 790, rumor of the evil doctrine had already spread widely. This may be gathered from his eighth letter to Charlemagne, in which, speaking of a certain booklet by Felix, he says:

“Recently a booklet was sent to me by Felix the unhappy. Out of curiosity, as I hurried through a few pages of it, I found worse heresies—or rather more blasphemies—than I had previously read in his writings.”

Alcuin therefore already knew Felix’s doctrine from earlier years, having read his writings before this.

## XXXVIII

Felix had obtained the occasion for publishing this booklet from a letter by Alcuin himself. Soon after returning to Gaul, Alcuin learned that Felix had deserted the conversion he had simulated at Rome as soon as he reached Urgell. In a spirit of charity and peace, Alcuin therefore attempted by that letter to recall him to the path of salvation.

Hear Alcuin himself in Book I *Against Felix*, which begins as follows:

“I previously wrote a letter”—namely, the letter that furnished the occasion for publishing the booklet—“to Bishop Felix with the pen of charity, not with the goad of contention; out of concern for fraternal salvation, not in the style of biting criticism; wishing to correct him in the love of Christ, since he was known to be departing from the unity of Catholic peace because of the novelty of a certain name.

“But, as I recognize, the aforesaid Felix did not receive my little letter with that charitable duty or humble courtesy with which the person who reads my letter attentively and with a pious regard for me will recognize that I wrote it. For this same Felix immediately wished to send us a booklet”—the booklet written on the occasion of the letter—“not concise in epistolary brevity but extended in a lengthy sequence of discourses.”

## XXXIX

You rightly admire, reader, Alcuin’s modesty. Admire also his humility: he did not rely on his own strength but requested that Charles provide him with assistants. Thus he says in his eighth letter:

“The response to this book, or rather to this error, must be examined with great diligence and with the assistance of many helpers. I alone am not sufficient to answer it. Let your holy piety provide suitable assistants for so arduous and necessary a task, so that this impious heresy may be utterly extinguished.”

In another letter he specifically requested, besides Pope Adrian, that our Paulinus also be consulted and undertake the task of writing against Felix:

“Concerning the booklet of the unhappy man—not a teacher but a subverter—I am very pleased that your most holy will and devotion have taken care to provide a response in defense of the Catholic faith. But I ask, if it pleases your piety, that a copy of this booklet be sent to the lord apostolic, and another to Paulinus the patriarch, likewise to the bishops Richbod and Theodulf, teachers and masters, so that each may answer on his own behalf.

“Your Flaccus is laboring with you to give an account of the Catholic faith. Let him merely be given enough time to examine calmly and diligently, with his students, the opinions of the Fathers and what each one would say concerning the propositions that the aforesaid subverter set forth in his booklet.”

## XL

Meanwhile, the booklet addressed to Alcuin had not merely reached Charles’s hands; as Alcuin had requested, it had also been sent to Paulinus and Adrian, and perhaps it provided them with the occasion to respond clearly and at length.

While Felix was struggling in these controversies, his wicked fellow soldier Elipandus opportunely rushed to his aid, like a sacred battle formation (*ἱερὸς λόχος*, “sacred battalion”) bringing reinforcements. Some claim that Felix had been corrupted by Elipandus, but this is incorrect: Felix had never truly been converted, as has been said; rather, he had been strengthened in his perfidy.

Elipandus sent letters to Charles requesting that he deign to order that what he and his associate had written, according to the opinions of the holy Fathers, concerning the adoption of the Son of God be read aloud to them and heard calmly. They asked that the opinion not of one or another person but of many be sought before their doctrine was rejected. They further requested that Charles himself sit as judge in an assembly of teachers.

They added that Charles should beware of Beatus, whom they called “Antiphrasius,” the defender of the Catholic party, lest what Isidore had said once happened to Constantine happen to him.

All this is evident from Charlemagne’s reply, which he sent to them from the Council of Frankfurt. Nor were they satisfied with addressing Charles by letter alone; they also assailed the ears of other bishops with letters of this kind. They did not ask, as they ought to have done, to be instructed, but displayed the arrogance of those who intended to instruct.

This is clear from Charles’s letter, which states:

“You took care to send letters about your faith to these regions: general letters to the most holy priestly ears, and particular ones to us. In the sequence of these letters it was not sufficiently clear whether you intended to teach us as though by the authority of a master, or desired to learn from us in the humility of discipleship.”

And further:

“We did as you requested. Having gathered ecclesiastical teachers and leaders of the Christian people from every direction, and while we all sat together in a peaceful chorus of unanimity, we ordered that the same booklet be read from beginning to end, through the distinctions of each proposition and by means of questions and answers, according to each person’s preference.”

And further still:

“We found written in your letter the following kind of entreaty: ‘We ask you, by him who stretched out innocent hands upon the cross for you …, that you yourself sit as judge.’ Behold, fulfilling your requests, I sat as both hearer and judge in the assembly of priests.”

A little later:

“You proposed to me the example of the Emperor Constantine, whose beginning, you say, blessed Isidore praised and whose end he lamented. You kindly urge me to take care that the same thing not happen to me through a certain Beatus whom you have called Antiphrasius. By the mercy of divine grace, I also strive to guard against this, etc.”

From these words of Charles’s reply it is perfectly clear what Elipandus and Felix had requested. Charles’s gentleness satisfied their wishes fully enough by convening the Council of Frankfurt at the beginning of the summer of A.D. 794.

## XLI

In the time of Charlemagne, Frankfurt had not yet grown to the size in which it is seen today. It received its name in his own age from the crossing made there by his army advancing against the Saxons. Gunther the Ligurinian, in Book I *On the Deeds of Frederick*, writes:

> … for the Teutonic inhabitant called it  
>   
> Franconefurt. In Latin speech we may call it  
>   
> The ford of the Franks, because Charles is believed  
>   
> To have attacked the rebellious Saxons,  
>   
> Excessively fierce and untamed,  
>   
> And to have crossed the broadest streams of the swift Main  
>   
> At an unknown ford, leading his troops  
>   
> Through the middle of the river without a bridge.  
>   
> Hence the name remained attached to the place.

Today the site is especially famous for its fairs and imperial assemblies, particularly for the inauguration of emperors.

At this place, where Charles had already celebrated Easter and where the assemblies of the kingdom were to be held, he decided to convene a council of bishops concerning the faith. Accordingly, after letters had been sent throughout the provinces of Gaul, Britain, and Italy—as he himself testifies in the letter quoted above to Elipandus—he summoned the bishops.

After consulting especially with Pope Adrian, Adrian sent legates, Theophylact and Stephen, who were to represent the presence and authority of the apostolic see at the synod.

## XLII

What role our Paulinus played at this council may be gathered from his *Sacrosyllabus*. Cointius, under the year 794, no. 7, observes that it was first published in two forms:

“It was issued in two ways: first, as Paulinus wrote it against the letter of Elipandus; afterward, as it was sent by the bishops of Italy to the provinces of Spain by decree of the Council of Frankfurt. The former edition is found after the works of Alcuin published by André Duchesne and in the libraries of the Fathers; the latter is found in the collections of councils.

“There is little difference between the two. In one, Paulinus occasionally uses the singular—‘I decree,’ ‘I judge’; in the other, he always uses the plural—‘we decree,’ ‘we judge.’ The chief difference occurs at the beginning of the work,” where, to summarize, Paulinus does not include Peter, bishop of Milan, in the first version, but does include him in the second.

In every other respect, the booklet was judged worthy by the council to be sent in the name of the bishops of Italy to the churches of Spain with synodal authority.

The continuator of Paul the Deacon’s history, published by Marquard Freher and printed by Duchesne in volume II, brings Paulinus, Peter of Milan, and Alcuin onto the stage above all others. Because of the dignity and number of the bishops—about three hundred, according to Baronius under the year 794, no. 1—he calls this synod “great,” while Paulinus calls it “plenary.” The continuator writes:

“This heresy was destroyed by the most holy men Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, and Peter, archbishop of Milan, or by Alcuin, archdeacon of the island of Britain, together with the other bishops, through assertions from Sacred Scripture; and they decreed that he should be called proper, not adoptive.”

Charlemagne also preserves the same order in his letter, so that after Pope Adrian’s document he immediately reviews Paulinus’s work, and in third place the book of the bishops of Germany, Gaul, Aquitaine, and Britain.

[Col. 0573B] **XLIII.** You will find the acts and canons of this council in Labbe’s collection of councils. But we owe the sequence of the acts and the order in which they were conducted—especially at the beginning—to our Paulinus, who must be heard throughout from the opening of his *Sacrosyllabus*. He writes:

> “With the Holy Spirit urging him, and the zeal of the Catholic faith burning spark-like in the breast of the most merciful, tranquil, and glorious King Charles, while his imperial decree was swiftly passing through the various provinces subject to the jurisdiction of his kingdom, a multitude of bishops, obeying the sacred commands, assembled together in one college. One day, while all were seated in the hall of the sacred palace, with the priests, deacons, and the entire clergy standing around in the form of a circle, a letter was brought, sent by Elipandus, the author of a harmful crime, the pseudo-bishop of the See of Toledo, enclosed within the boundary of Seville. When it had been read aloud at the king’s command, the venerable prince immediately rose from his royal seat, stood [Col. 0573C] upon his step, and spoke at length concerning the cause of the faith. He added:
>
> “‘What do you think? For a full year now, and ever since the madness of this plague began to swell and the ulcer of perfidy to boil forth more widely, no small error has taken root in these regions, although they lie at the farthest boundaries of our kingdom. The judgment of the faith must necessarily cut it out in every way.’
>
> “When a lengthy postponement of several days had been requested and granted, his gentleness approved that each person should bring forward, on the appointed day, whatever he might be able to perceive more correctly by the capacity of his intellect, and should present to his clemency, in sacred words, the offering of his heart, carrying it vividly in the vessel of his mind … 219 Therefore I, Paulinus … together with the most reverend and wholly honorable Peter, archbishop of the See of Milan, and all our colleagues, brothers, and fellow priests—the venerable prelates of the Catholic churches of Liguria, Austria, Hesperia (others read ‘Istria, Venetia,’ with Cointius, who nevertheless notes in the margin, ‘Austria, Hesperia’), and Emilia—… I do not hesitate to respond [Col. 0573D].”

**XLIV.** Among Paulinus’s fellow soldiers, Peter, the prelate of Milan, is listed as a kind of standard-bearer, as you see. He was surnamed Oldradus (for the basis of this, see *Life of Paulinus*, chapter 6, no. 9). From Ughellus’s account of the bishops of Milan, we learn that he had been one of the more distinguished Milanese and had served as Pope Adrian’s secretary.

In the year 772, according to Cointius, in that year, no. 35, he was sent into Gaul to convey the pope’s complaints concerning Desiderius, who was insulting Rome. In order to escape Desiderius’s plots, he took the sea route and, arriving at Marseilles, then went to the king, who was residing at Theodonis Villa in 773. The king promised that he would bring aid to the pope. Thus Cointius reports from the *Lorsch Annals*.

In 783 he was appointed archbishop of Milan. In 784 he added monks to the order of canons to serve the church, after constructing buildings and appointing Benedict abbot of the Ambrosian monastery, as Tristan Calco likewise asserts. He took part in the Council of Frankfurt, as we have seen, [Col. 0574A] and wrote several works mentioned by Ughellus.

He conducted himself so energetically against the disseminators of false doctrine that Charles bestowed upon him the glorious title “hammer of heretics,” as Ripamonti reports in *Decade* 1, book IX, cited by Cointius under the year 804. According to Ughellus, Peter died on 9 May of that year. Here is Ripamonti’s eulogy of Peter:

> “After establishing the patrimony of the Church of Milan and founding a monastery worthy of such resources and of the name of Ambrose himself, Peter labored with no less diligence to establish the morals of the people and to remove and heal whatever vice had crept into religion. So great was his hatred of corrupt doctrines that Charles the Great called him the hammer of heretics.”

But let this suffice concerning Peter of Milan.

**XLV.** The booklet called the *Sacrosyllabus*, therefore, which Paulinus presented at the council and which was read aloud before everyone, was approved by the Fathers. According to its standard they established the first canon, which is as follows:

> “At the beginning of the chapters there arose the matter of the impious and unspeakable heresy of Elipandus, bishop of the See of Toledo, and of Felix of Urgell, together with their followers, who, thinking wrongly, asserted adoption in the Son of God. All the most holy Fathers mentioned above rejected this and opposed it with one voice, and they decreed that this heresy must be utterly eradicated from the holy Church.”

Eginhard, speaking of this matter in his *Annals*, writes:

> “At this council the heresy in question was condemned, and a book was composed against it by the common authority of the bishops, in which they all subscribed.”

I do not see what that book could have been other than this work of Paulinus. The most diligent annalist distinguishes the condemnation of the heresy from the book written against it. He says: “The heresy was condemned, and a book was composed against it, in which all subscribed”—so that you should not perhaps suppose that the bishops’ subscription applied only to the anathema above.

Therefore, in addition to the common assent given to the sentence of anathema, it follows from Eginhard’s words and those of other annalists who report the same thing that a common subscription was made to Paulinus’s booklet. It was judged worthy, by the vote and in the name of all, to be sent to the bishops of Spain with the authority of the council.

This is made perfectly clear by the title of the book, which runs as follows:

> “Booklet of the bishops of Italy against Elipandus, sent by decree of the council to the provinces of Spain. Here begins the *Sacrosyllabus*, a salutary booklet composed in Catholic style, at the council held by divine will in the suburbs of the city of Mainz, in the region of Germany, at the celebrated place called Frankfurt, in the presence of the most merciful prince, Lord Charles, glorious king, in the twenty-sixth and most fortunate year of his reign. Therefore it pleased the holy and venerable council that this booklet, concerning the cause of the faith, should be sent to the provinces of Gaul and Spain for the removal of pernicious errors, and especially to Elipandus, bishop of the See of Toledo, in whom the entire substance of the questions at issue in this matter is found.”

**XLVI.** I am not unaware that another synodical letter of the bishops of Gaul, Germany, and Aquitaine was sent to the Spanish bishops; it is placed after Paulinus’s booklet in the acts of the Council of Frankfurt. I am unaware, however, that it was sent in the common name and by decree of the council, since this is not stated in its title, which is as follows:

> “Synodical letter of the council, sent by the bishops of Gaul and Germany to the bishops of Spain. The holy synod and the venerable Fathers in Christ, together with all the bishops of Germany, Gaul, and Aquitaine, and the entire clergy of Catholic peace, send greeting in the Lord God and in his true and proper Son, Jesus Christ, of eternal blessedness, to the bishops of Spain and to all others there who bear the name of Christians.”

Do you see the difference between the titles? This letter was sent—we do not deny that; the other was decreed to be sent by common assent, which is the more honorable status. For who does not see that what Eginhard says—that all the Fathers subscribed—applies more fittingly to Paulinus’s book than to this letter, even though it is synodical? He is speaking of the book itself, not of the letter.

Thus Paulinus was worthy of the honor [Col. 0575A] with which the Council of Frankfurt wished to honor him. Receive all this briefly from the Saxon poet under the year 794:

> In order to tear from the sacred field of the Lord  
> the dire seeds of the poisonous sect,  
> which Felix had wickedly scattered with unhappy daring,  
> the Catholic prince summoned bishops from every side  
> to celebrate the aforesaid synod at the royal court.  
>
> Stephen was also present, together with Theophylact.  
> Both were bishops and legates of the Roman See,  
> whom holy Pope Adrian, sending them,  
> had duly commanded to represent him there.  
>
> Then all together, with a general decree,  
> condemned this heresy; and a booklet was written  
> against it, which that assembly of bishops approved,  
> and all of them likewise subscribed to it.

**XLVII.** This was the third solemn, juridical, canonical, and legitimate proscription of the Felician heresy—of the Felician heresy, I say. For although Elipandus is expressly named at the Council of Frankfurt, this was because he himself had challenged the council by his letters to settle the question, while stubbornly adhering to Felix’s doctrine.

Yet, although struck by the third thunderbolt, the heresy was not thereby extinguished; the efforts and strength it displayed afterward bear witness to this. I am therefore surprised that Aventinus wrote in book IV of the *Bavarian Annals*:

> “There, for the third time, the Felician and Elipandian heresy concerning the adoption of the Son of God was condemned. All the priests subscribed. When Elipandus recognized his error, pardon was granted to him, and likewise to Felix. Their dignity was preserved.”

For nothing concerning their dignity was there decided, and neither of them repented thereafter or returned to sound judgment, as the subsequent acts demonstrate. Moreover, they themselves were not present there to obtain pardon or preservation of dignity, as is clear from the letters issued by this council, which show that the persons to whom they were sent were absent.

**XLVIII.** King Charles, who had convened the council, therefore, accommodating Elipandus, who requested a more careful examination of his doctrine, sent him what had been defined there [Col. 0575C]. He also added Pope Adrian’s letter, which Cointius, under the year 793, no. 15 and following, supposes Adrian sent to Charles, to be delivered to Elipandus, as a response to the false doctrine proceeding from the Roman council and derived from Elipandus’s letter, which Charles had transmitted to the pope.

He further sent Paulinus’s booklet in the name of the bishops of Italy, though with the authority of the entire council, and the synodical letter of the bishops of Germany, Gaul, Aquitaine, and Britain. Nor did he disdain to send, in his own name, another letter in which he addressed both men with truly paternal charity and tried to lead them back to the way of truth:

> “In fourth place,” he says, “I have appended my own agreement with the decrees and Catholic statutes of the most holy Fathers mentioned above, just as you yourselves requested in your letter, which you specifically assigned to my name.”

He concludes it as follows:

> “Return to the pious bosom of Mother Church. May she cherish and nourish you until you come to perfect manhood and to the fullness of the body [Col. 0575D] of Christ. Consider us fellow workers for your salvation and helpers of Catholic peace, and may our fellowship be in Christ Jesus our Lord.”

Here too you see that these bishops were not present at the council.

**XLIX.** There can be no doubt that the acts of the council became known to Pope Adrian, since he had presided through his legates, Theophylact and Stephen.

At this time Charles again sent Angilbert to Rome concerning the matter of images, as can be gathered from Adrian’s reply to Charles, which our Baronius quotes in sections under the year 795, no. 32 and following:

> “We have received from your most merciful, exalted royal power your faithful servant and familiar, namely Engelbert, abbot and minister of the chapel … He presented to us a capitulary against the synod held at Nicaea concerning the erection of sacred images.”

Cointius rejects Charles’s letter concerning images, Adrian’s reply, and Hincmar’s authority on this matter, treating the former as spurious and the latter as weak. He also objects to the error of giving Angilbert the title “abbot” [Col. 0576A], since he maintains that Angilbert was clothed as a monk only in 796. See him, if you wish, under the year 794, no. 26 and following. Yet, under no. 108, he does not hesitate to accept Angilbert’s journey to Rome, because Alcuin’s letter 63, addressed to Adrian and serving as a letter of recommendation for Angilbert, cannot be assigned to another year, as he himself demonstrates.

Among other things, the letter says:

> “The most distinguished envoy of my lord king, indeed my own son Angilbert, is being sent to the most blessed paternity of your supreme authority … We have found him to be exceptionally faithful to all his friends, and especially to you, as is truly fitting, most holy Father. He used very frequently to recount your goodness to our lord king in laudatory words, in the presence of many witnesses.”

These words clearly show that the pope and Angilbert knew one another, namely from the journey of the preceding year, 792, on which he had brought Felix to Rome.

Whether the things that various writers report concerning the second chapter of this Council of Frankfurt, on images, are genuine and legitimate is not ours to decide. Nothing concerning the Felician heresy is mentioned in these letters of Charles and Adrian. What then? Does this silence concerning a doctrine that was handled no less, and perhaps more diligently, than the doctrine concerning the veneration of images not add weight to the suspicion of those who think that these letters should be dismissed as spurious? See what we say in the *Life of Paulinus*, chapter 7, no. 6.

**L.** Charles, however, with his letter filled with every courtesy, was, as the saying goes, singing to deaf ears, and the Fathers accomplished nothing through their admonitions and commands. We learn this from Leo III, who says the following in the Roman council of 799, session 2:

> “Nor did he fear that venerable and orthodox council—the council of Frankfurt—which was held in the presence of the radiant and orthodox Lord Charles the Great concerning this matter and contained sufficient right faith; hurling the same Felix, together with his followers, into the bonds of anathema, they condemned him if he persisted in error. And when he heard of your council, he returned, like a dog, to his vomit, to the mire of filth, as you heard through his blasphemous booklet, which he sent to the venerable Albinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin; he descended into worse barking than before.”

This booklet of Felix to Albinus, of which Leo speaks, was written, as his words make clear, after the Council of Frankfurt. It is therefore different from the one mentioned above, no. 38, which was written after Felix’s departure from Rome, when he resumed the weapons that he had falsely laid down—or rather, which he had never laid down—and again attacked the faith despite his pledged word. But more will be said about this booklet below.

**LI.** Before this—indeed, immediately after the Council of Frankfurt, in which Alcuin had held first place, or something close to it—he appears to have written to Elipandus, because Elipandus himself had challenged Charles by letters to convene the council. He wrote a letter full of love, so that both Elipandus and his companion in perfidy, Felix, might return to a sounder mind.

It is useful to quote part of this letter. It is a notable proof of charity and an example of truly fraternal correction:

> “To the venerable Father Elipandus, a bishop beloved in the charity of Christ, Albinus the levite, son of ecclesiastical peace, sends greetings. The perfection of fraternal charity rejoices to gather many friends into the bosom of peaceful unity, and regards it as a kind of loss to itself if it does not strive to commend itself more widely to men of renowned name and praised piety, so that there may be spiritual unanimity in true love, even though there is some bodily separation from sight.”

And later:

> “Nor is my dispute with you, excellent Father, in this little page of my insignificance a lofty controversy. It is a humble supplication, earnestly begging you to strive, with the whole intention of your mind, to attain apostolic doctrine in Catholic unity and peace, and to be a standard-bearer for the people entrusted to you, leading them toward the prosperity of eternal blessedness. Do not permit any new names to be inserted into the traditions of the Fathers, etc.”

At the end of the letter [Col. 0577A]:

> “But I earnestly beseech you all together, most sacred lights of Spain, at the conclusion of this letter, to deign to remember us in your holy prayers.”

**LII.** As we said in the preceding section, we believe that this letter was written immediately after the council, which was held at the beginning of summer, as Eginhard testifies. Elipandus received it at the end of July, as is clear from his reply, which plainly and abundantly reveals the spirit by which its author was moved. He writes:

> “To the most reverend brother Albinus, a deacon—not a minister of Christ, but, by antiphrasis, a disciple of the foulest Beatus, born in the lands of Austria in the time of the glorious prince, a new Arius, opposed to the doctrines of the holy and venerable Fathers Ambrose, Augustine, Isidore, and Jerome: if he turns from the error of his way, eternal salvation from the Lord; if he refuses, eternal condemnation. We received your letter, deviating from the path of right faith, dreadful in its sulfurous brightness, written in superstitious language, as we were rereading it at the end of July [Col. 0577B].”

The rest is composed in the same style. We refrain from quoting it, lest we stir the bile and stomach of the reader.

To the delirious old man Elipandus, however, Alcuin replied with Christian gentleness but vigorous force in two books, adding two others on the Incarnation of Christ; these four works are directed against Elipandus. They appeared later, as will be said below, no. 66.

**LIII.** Against Felix, however, who had written the booklet mentioned above in no. 50, Alcuin composed seven books. They were sometimes circulated under Paulinus’s name, but Alcuin himself testifies that they were his own work in book I against Elipandus:

> “I replied to Felix’s booklet with seven little books of our devotion, and refuted all the doctrines of his depravity. They were read and approved in the presence of King Charles and the priests of Christ.”

For Alcuin had wished, indeed had requested, that his books be examined before they appeared publicly. Just as he had once displayed humility by asking that fellow soldiers be assigned to him for battle with Felix, so now, by presenting another example of the same humble spirit, he requested that Charles himself review his studies.

When they had been reviewed and approved, he promised to send them to the brothers living in Gothia—that is, the part of Gaul extending toward Spain, which was formerly occupied by the Goths and took its name from them, namely the regions of Narbonne and Toulouse and those included in Occitania, now commonly called Languedoc, as if *Landet Got*, “land of the Goths.” He says this in the letter to be quoted when we discuss below, no. 64, Benedict, abbot and companion of Laidradus.

On this matter there is a letter of his published by Baluze in volume IV of the *Miscellanea*. Among other things, it says:

> “I had this booklet present at the disputation that was conducted in your venerable presence with Felix. But because it has not yet been read before your wisdom, nor approved by you, for whom it was especially laborious, I judged it inappropriate to bring it before public ears [Col. 0577D]. Now let your authority decide what it wishes to be done with it. I ask only that it not be discarded or brought into public view under any circumstances before it has been read in its entirety and examined by the familiar associates of your authority.”

When Charles had done this, Alcuin thanked him in letter 15:

> “We give thanks to your venerable piety for having, according to the command of your instruction, caused the booklet sent to you to be read aloud to your wise ears, and for having caused its errors to be noted and sent it back for correction, although it could have been corrected better by you, etc.”

**LIV.** These events did not occur until 799, when Alcuin debated with Felix before King Charles at Aachen. This is gathered from the words of the earlier letter:

> “I had this booklet present at the disputation that was conducted in your venerable presence with Felix.”

For Alcuin debated before the king and with Felix only at Aachen. At the preceding councils, when one was present, the other was absent. Thus, in 792, Felix was present at Regensburg, while Alcuin was absent, being in England at that time. In 794, Alcuin took part at Frankfurt, while Felix was absent, as was shown above, no. 47. Therefore these words must be understood of the Council of Aachen in 799.

As Alcuin had requested, Charles sent his books back to the author after submitting them to the examination of learned men, so that they might be purged of certain blemishes. After they had been corrected, Alcuin sent them again to Charles, preceded by a preface preserved by Baluze in the cited volume IV of the *Miscellanea*. Its title is:

> “Alcuin’s preface to Charles the Great concerning the seven books against Felix.”

It begins as follows:

> “I have sent to your most holy authority, my lord David, these five loaves and two fish, consecrated together in the number seven and brought forth from the purse of apostolic faith, etc.”

From this G. Cave reasonably argues when he asserts that Alcuin composed these seven books against Felix in 798. Since the author says that he had them ready in 799, the year in which he debated with Felix before the king, it necessarily seems that they had been completed at least in the preceding year [Col. 0578B].

**LV.** It was not enough for Felix to pour forth his perfidy in a single booklet; he also composed a dialogue with a Saracen. Charles wished to see it and asked Alcuin about it. Alcuin replied in letter 15:

> “I have neither seen Felix’s disputation with the Saracen, nor has it been found among us. Indeed, I had not previously even heard his name. Nevertheless, when I made a more careful inquiry as to whether anyone among our people had heard of it, I was told that it might be found with Laidradus, bishop of Lyons. Therefore I promptly sent our envoy to the aforesaid bishop, in case he might be able to find it there, so that it could be sent to your presence as quickly as possible.”

Pope Leo III appears to indicate the subject of this disputation, or dialogue, when he speaks of Felix in the second session of the Roman synod:

> “Afterward, having transgressed the law of the Most High God, he fled to like-minded pagans and became perjured.”

Since the pagans, or Saracens, with whom he agreed and with whom he held dialogues were his companions in thought, he should hardly be believed to have written anything good in the dialogue.

**LVI.** In the meantime, before Alcuin took up the task of blunting Felix’s books, Paulinus had already undertaken the attack on the heresy. Alcuin congratulates him in letter 81, entitled:

> “To Paulinus the patriarch: Concerning certain Spanish heresies.”

In it he greatly praises Paulinus, who had already done what Alcuin himself had desired: namely, around the year 796, writing “three books against Felix” and adding a *Rule of Faith* composed in verse. This had long been one of Alcuin’s wishes; for that reason he had also urged the king to order it to be done especially for the benefit of the less educated and the unlearned.

He seems to understand these three books together with the *Rule of Faith* as four parts of a work, since he compares Paulinus’s four-part work with the four rivers of the earthly paradise. Read the letter; I shall not hesitate to quote a little from its conclusion:

> “Therefore, venerable Father, most learned athlete, and sweetest teacher, let us always remain fellow soldiers in the camp of Christ, fighting in one battle line beneath the banner of the holy cross, with united aid and strength, so that through us he who cannot be conquered may conquer his adversaries. Now again the ancient serpent, crushed from the thickets of the Spanish countryside and from the caves of poisonous perfidy, is trying to raise his head—not with the club of Hercules but with the evangelical club, that is, the anathema of the Council of Frankfurt—and to mix new poisons of cursing into the former cups of wickedness, etc.”

**LVII.** Paulinus had already been urged by the king’s letters to oppose the renewed plague, as he himself testifies in the dedication prefixed to his three books to Charles:

> “Therefore, urged by the most salutary commands of your venerable letters, I do not refuse, according to the understanding of my insignificance, although the limitations of my ability are hindered by a sluggish intellect, to write, in whatever style I can, what concerns me concerning the cause of the faith against the objections of pernicious and evil invention.”

These Fathers—Paulinus and Alcuin, I mean—were distinguished equally in doctrine and holiness. Just as one encouraged the other to undertake the struggle against the enemies of the Church, so each competed with the other in humility.

For just as Alcuin wanted his writings to be submitted to Paulinus’s examination, so Paulinus urged Charles in a certain letter, of which a fragment still survives, to obtain Alcuin’s judgment before his book enjoyed the light of public circulation. He requested:

> “That this little gift of ours, although not precious, whatever it may be, should be brought, at your venerable command, into the hands of the most reverend and most learned man in divine matters, the distinguished Albinus, the eminent spokesman of supreme religion, your envoy, and for me sweeter than all the honey of the blond bees.”

**LVIII.** Paulinus published these books in 796, as we can gather clearly enough from the leap year, whose mystical interpretation he develops in the dedication itself, since that year was indeed seven hundred ninety-six.

But in this year he did not attack the Felician heresy only through these writings. He also attacked it by the synodical proscription of the heresy issued at his own Council of Friuli, which was held after the feast of Easter in that same year, as we demonstrated fully in our second dissertation.

This requires us to pause for a while. P. Pagi, under the year 791, no. 5 and following, advances—although with another purpose—an argument that could deprive Paulinus and his council of the honor of condemning the Felician heresy unless it is refuted. He says that the council defined only generally against opponents of the mystery of the Incarnation, not specifically against Felix.

If this is admitted, Paulinus and his council would have had no part in condemning Felix and his unsound doctrine, if, as Pagi says, the council had dealt only generally

> “with those who, entangled in various errors, held incorrect opinions concerning the mystery of the Trinity, especially concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, and, moreover, against those who seemed to divide the one Christ, the Son of God, into two sons, when they attempted to affirm him to be natural and adoptive,”

as Paulinus says in his *Oration*. By these words, Pagi says, Paulinus shows that this council was not assembled against Felix of Urgell, but generally against Ebionites, Nestorians, and other heretics who sinned against the sacred mystery of the Incarnation [Col. 0579C].

**LIX.** Yet Paulinus’s text, as quoted by Pagi, proves—and, in my judgment, proves with complete clarity—not merely that Felix’s doctrine was condemned in general, but that it was condemned specifically. This is also confirmed by the events of those times.

Two principal heresies were then troubling the Church: one in the East, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit among the Greeks; the other in the West, concerning the adoption of Christ, the Son of God, among the Spaniards. Paulinus rose against both and proscribed and condemned both.

For just as it cannot be said that only the opponents of the mystery of the Trinity were condemned in general when those who held incorrect views particularly concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit were condemned, so it cannot be said that only the opponents of the mystery of the Incarnation were condemned in general when Paulinus expressly condemns those who attempt to divide Christ, the Son of God, into two sons, natural and adoptive.

We do not say that the council was convened precisely against Felix, any more than it was convened against the Greek *pneumatomachoi*—the “fighters against the Spirit.” We say, rather, that both heresies were condemned in it: the one sufficiently circumscribed as Felix’s, even though Felix’s name was not mentioned.

A council need not be convened for one purpose and no other in order for it to be said truly and properly to have proscribed a particular error. Otherwise it would not be possible to say that the censure and condemnation of the Felician heresy proceeded from the Synod of Frankfurt or from the Council of Regensburg, something no one has yet claimed. For those councils were not assembled solely for the business of condemnation: in the former, the conspiracy of Pippin against his father was treated; in the latter, many other matters were discussed.

Thus the Council of Friuli, even if it is not said to have been convened for the condemnation of Felix, nevertheless properly and truly proscribed the Felician heresy under the name of those who asserted adoption in the incarnate Son of God. But let us continue along the path we have begun.

**LX.** The works recorded thus far, over which Paulinus and Alcuin labored, encompass a period of four years: from 796, inclusive, when Paulinus’s books together with the *Rule of Faith* appeared, to 799, by which time Alcuin had completed his own works.

Yet all their efforts seemed fruitless, and these Fathers appeared to have wasted their labor and oil. Charles, however, did not lose courage in recalling the wanderers to the way of salvation. He moved a new stone, so to speak, by ordering the Council of Urgell, judging that the serpent would more easily be killed if it were attacked in its own lair. He also urged Leo III to convene another council at Rome.

**LXI.** Cointius rightly observes under the year 799, no. 16, that this Roman council was held not in the thirty-second year of Charles’s reign, as Labbe thought, but in the thirty-first:

> “In this year,” says the cited annalist, “Charles completed the thirty-first year of his reign and entered the thirty-second on the eighth day before the Kalends of October.”

For at the end of April, Leo, because of the disturbances stirred up against him and the injuries inflicted upon him by Paschasius and Campulus, kinsmen of his predecessor Adrian, on 25 April during the greater litanies, departed from Rome and set out for Gaul to go to Charles. He remained away from the city until the feast of the holy apostle Andrew, that is, until the day before the Kalends of December. On this matter consult Anastasius under the same heading.

Since, moreover, in the thirty-third year of Charles’s reign, according to Alcuin, whom we shall cite below in no. 74, Felix, in that synod, renouncing his perfidy, also mentioned a Roman synod already held under Leo, at which Felix was neither summoned nor present—whatever Berninius may write to the contrary in *History of Heresies*, ninth century, chapter 1—for Felix’s profession of faith was made not at Rome, as Berninius thinks, but at Aachen, as will appear below—it follows that this council could not have been convened [Col. 0580C] except before Leo’s arrival in Gaul, and therefore before 25 April.

Accordingly, at the beginning of 799, in the thirty-first year of Charles’s reign, Pope Leo summoned fifty-seven bishops in the basilica of Saint Peter; they again proscribed the Felician heresy.

The occasion of the assembly was the booklet mentioned above, as Leo states in session 2 of the council, and as Felix confessed in the profession of faith made at Aachen:

> “By the authority of the synod,” he says, “which was recently assembled at Rome for this purpose, at the command of our glorious and most pious lord Charles, against my letter, which I had formerly—not recently, as Pagius has it—written to the venerable man Albinus, abbot of the Church of Tours. In that synod, with Leo the apostolic present and the other bishops, fifty-seven in number, seated with him, and many priests and deacons together with them in the house of the most blessed apostle Peter … they rejected our aforesaid opinions.”

But they did not merely reject them; unless Felix repented, they bound him with the bond of anathema. For Leo says in session 3:

> “Let Felix, bishop of the Church of Urgell, be anathema if he refuses to turn away from his heretical doctrine, in which he dared to assert the Son of God to be adoptive.”

Concerning this synod, the continuator of Paul the Deacon writes:

> “Against this heresy Pope Leo III convened a synod at Rome and condemned it forever with many testimonies from the Gospels and the holy Fathers.”

**LXII.** Not long afterward, after the council at Rome had been conducted, Leo III, who had been badly treated there, as stated above, went to Charles, who was residing at Paderborn because of the Saxon disturbances.

After communicating the matter to Leo—as it is proper to believe—the king sent a group of bishops and an abbot to Urgell, so that, after a council had been held there, they might recall Felix to his senses. The mission was entrusted to Laidradus, bishop of Lyons, who, taking with him as companions Nefridius, bishop of Narbonne, Benedict the abbot, and other men of the same rank, set out for Urgell in that very year.

All this is gathered from Alcuin, who dedicated his books against Elipandus to these most holy men. He apparently wanted them to have in their hands a brief outline and summary of the books, as will be said below in no. 66, for the comfort of their journey, as he says in the preface, so that they might be fortified by the doctrines contained in them against their adversaries, and especially against the letter that Elipandus had published long before and addressed to him.

Pagi, under the year 799, no. 13, and under the year 800, no. 18, together with Cointius under the year 799, no. 30, distinguish two journeys of these bishops into Spain. They maintain that the books against Elipandus were given to them only in 800 and reserve them for the second expedition.

Let it be granted that they returned to Spain on a twofold journey. Nevertheless, after Felix’s conversion at Aachen in 799, we do not think that either journey was undertaken that year. How the matter actually stood will soon become clear, in no. 65, after we have first said a little about Laidradus, Nefridius, and Benedict.

**LXIII.** Laidradus, who held first place among his companions [Col. 0581B] and appeared to be the leader in speech, was a man as distinguished in piety as in learning. Some of his works survive; concerning them, consult the writers of the *Ecclesiastical Library*. Theodulf states that he was of Norican origin in the *Paraenesis to the Judges*, verse 119, speaking of him before Charles promoted him to the See of Lyons:

> Norius fathered this man; and you, Lyons, shall have him as your future …

You hope for a pontiff through the aid of religion. In the same place we are told that, together with the same Theodulf, he carried out the lord’s mission through the province of Narbonensis. Cointius places his election as archbishop in 798 and his ordination in the following year, at 798, nos. 10 and 11. With Laidradus were associated Nefridius, who had succeeded Daniel, the archbishop of Narbonne mentioned above in no. 24, in the see of that same church not long before this year, and Benedict, abbot of Aniane. The latter, because of the vow by which he had bound himself when, while his brother was in danger in the river Ticino, he extended a hand to him and himself was brought into mortal danger after following the victorious arms of Charlemagne, which drove the Lombards from Italy in 774 [Col. 0581C], became a monk at the age of twenty-three in the monastery of Saint-Sequanus. But when he was elected abbot in 780, lest he should be compelled to accept the honor, he withdrew to his homeland, that is, to Gothia or Septimania, and there, on his paternal estates, built a monastery beside the river Anianus. He began the work with a small cell, but it later grew into an immense complex. There his generosity toward those oppressed by famine shone forth in 793, when, besides the grain wisely reserved for the brothers until the new harvests, he fed and supported a huge multitude of poor people from every direction who that year were suffering from want. He became especially dear to Alcuin through his zeal in defending his homeland against the errors of Felix, which had invaded Septimania; from these errors he rescued not only people from the common populace but also the bishops of the church, often engaging them in disputation. We have given this briefly; Cointius, in the years mentioned above, treats it at greater length from Smaragdus, the author of the Life of Benedict, who died at the age of seventy [Col. 0581D] in 821.

### LXIV

This, then, is the man through whom Alcuin, replying “to all the abbots, sons, and brothers who are in the regions of Gothia,” says that he had already sent a little book, which would serve as a consolation in the controversies of that time. “We have sent it,” he says, “through the blessed Benedict to you, for the consolation and confirmation of the Catholic faith.” He adds: “But at present we have a greater work in hand because of other matters which we have read in the little book of the venerable Felix; and, God willing, we are sending that work to you” (for *we shall send it*) “after it has been read and approved by our bishops and by our lord the king.” And below: “All these things you will read more fully . . . in the same little book, which we now have in hand.”
