From these words that double journey which Pagius and Cointius established above in no. 62 may seemingly be reconciled as follows: the first took place before Alcuin published the books against Felix of which he is speaking here, and on that first occasion he sent the little book through Abbot Benedict, so that it might be a consolation to them. [Col. 0582A] The second took place in 799, when Benedict again traveled to Urgell together with Laidradus.

### LXV

In the preface to the books against Elipandus, addressing the envoys and the men who were setting out, Alcuin speaks of this twofold journey. “With the aid of divine goodness,” he says, “you formerly endeavored to dispel this cloudy sect of impiety with the clear light of virtue, and, with Christ granting it, you also completed in large part the work of preaching that had been begun.”

These words seem applicable to the earlier journey, on which, through Abbot Benedict—one of the apostolic men—he sent the little book mentioned above, approximately at the time when he was writing the books against Felix, namely in 797 or 798. The following words, however, are more probably to be understood of the second mission in this year, 799:

“We have heard that, at the command of the glorious prince and most devoted king Charles in every good work, you are again going to undertake the venerable work of that most holy preaching.”

Thus the two journeys are clear. [Col. 0582B] He then continues concerning the second:

“Therefore I have undertaken the labor of a few days for the consolation of your most holy journey, so that you might have in your hands pious and extremely necessary replies to a certain letter addressed in my name by Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, lest the minds of some people should be stained by reading that letter, since we have heard that the same letter reached the hands of others before it was returned to us, to whom it had been sent.”

We believe that the letter mentioned here is the one which, at an earlier time, after the conclusion of the Council of Frankfurt, was written to Alcuin and which we reviewed above in no. 52.

### LXVI

Alcuin therefore composed a response to this letter, and perhaps to similar letters of Elipandus equally overflowing with rancor, and enclosed it in four books. Pagius and Cointius date these books to the year 800—and we do not dissent—because in the first of them he mentions Felix as already converted and restored to the right path, and therefore they must have been written after the Council of Aachen in 799.

Pagius and Cointius think that these books are the ones which Alcuin here calls “pious and necessary [Col. 0582C] replies,” sent to the men proceeding to Urgell. Since the books mention Felix as already converted in 799, they infer that the journey must be assigned to the following year, 800. But because a journey to Urgell after Felix’s conversion may appear superfluous—since his conversion was the reason for undertaking it—we think that these “pious and necessary replies,” which Alcuin calls the labor of a few days, were a work different from the four books in which Felix’s conversion is mentioned. In this we disagree with Pagius and Cointius, who include those books under the name of the replies.

For we suspect that some brief writing was produced, composed through the labor of a few days: perhaps a summary and synopsis of the arguments and responses by which, as I may put it, objections arising on the spot could be answered extemporaneously. For the four books, written as a formal work, ought not to be called the work of a few days, since they could not have been completed through the labor of only a few days. We believe that he composed those four [Col. 0582D] books with more suitable study and time, and that, since they were completed after Felix’s conversion, he could mention that conversion in them. Although they are inscribed to and offered to the same bishops, it is not necessary to say that they were the same writing with which, when the men were setting out for Urgell, he presented them.

### LXVII

But even if you continue to argue that these books against Elipandus are included under the name of the replies sent to Laidradus and his companions—a position which I certainly do not concede—it still does not follow that the second journey of Laidradus and his companions took place in 800, the year in which the books said to have been published after Felix’s conversion appeared.

Consider these words from the preface:

“I think that your piety rejoices in reading these books, of which I have spoken above, because I was rejoicing to dedicate the whole work to your name and to send it first of all to you for examination and correction, content only with the judgment of your authority and holiness. Nor do I wish these little letters of my devotion to proceed into public [Col. 0583A] ears unless they have first been examined by the judgment of your authority and confirmed by the reading of the brotherly congregation. I consider it sufficient for them to be examined by the judgment of those whose love I have chosen to labor for in a singular way.”

From these words it is clear that he had first sent the books to be examined and confirmed by the reading of the congregation—namely, Laidradus and his companions—before they emerged into public view. He could therefore have sent them a work merely sketched and outlined in its first lines while Laidradus and his companions were setting out, intending later to publish it after it had been examined and approved at a more convenient time. This is what he did in 800, inserting, when he put the final hand to the work, the fact that Felix’s conversion had already taken place, and dedicating the work to the aforementioned men with a newly added preface, after the work had been completed through sustained labor.

### LXVIII

But another doubt arises from these books of Alcuin against Elipandus. At their end he mentions two letters: one from Elipandus to Felix, [Col. 0583B] and one from Felix to his own people concerning his conversion. He says that he added to the books “the letter of Elipandus to Felix, formerly the defender of that sect but now, by God’s gift, a preacher of the Christian faith.” Of the other letter he writes: “We have taken care to append the letter concerning his [Felix’s] conversion to the Catholic faith.”

Pagius adds that it is certain that both letters were sent toward the end of this year, 799. But although I do not deny that the second letter was written by Felix to his people concerning his repentance, I do not think the same of the first, that is, of Elipandus’s letter to Felix. In it we read: “Inform me, you who have been placed in Rome.” Until it has been shown that Felix was in Rome in this year under discussion, namely 799, so that these words could truthfully have been written to him, we must not depart from the perfectly clear words of Elipandus. They allow no other interpretation than that which the words themselves present at first sight.

Hence, since in 792 we find Felix brought to Rome by Abbot Angilbert, we cannot remove the letter from that year. For it is not established that Felix was in Rome in any other year. [Col. 0583C]

### LXIX

But certain difficulties are drawn from Alcuin himself, and they must be answered. At the end of the books addressed to Elipandus, he says that he added “the letter of that Elipandus to Felix, formerly the defender of that sect but now the preacher of the Christian faith.” [Col. 0583C] Moreover, the letter bears the heading: “To Felix, recently converted.”

Add also these words of Alcuin, placed likewise at the end:

“The origin of this perfidy proceeded especially from the city of Córdoba, as can be understood from that letter of Elipandus to the aforesaid Felix, when he considered the same Felix still bound by the chains of his error.”

From all this it seems that the letter was sent after Felix’s conversion, and therefore not in 792, as we maintain, but, as Pagius holds, in 799.

Yet the answer is readily available. Alcuin could not have spoken otherwise at that time, if Felix had in fact been converted by the time Alcuin completed his books. There is therefore nothing surprising in his saying “formerly a defender of the heresy, now a preacher of the faith.” The meaning is: Elipandus wrote to Felix when Felix was formerly a defender of his sect, but now, at the time when I am writing this, he is a preacher of the faith. What could be clearer?

The letter is indeed headed “To Felix, recently converted,” but the heading was not written by Elipandus. This is clear from the context, in which Felix is reproved as though he were still entangled in errors. For Elipandus speaks with him about a shared heresy that had not been renounced but rather was still being fostered.

The heading was therefore perhaps added by Alcuin. When he brought forward the rancid letter of Elipandus on the occasion of Felix’s conversion, he entitled it on the basis of a fact that had recently occurred, and therefore wrote “recently converted,” because he wished to indicate the conversion of the preceding year, 799, while he himself was transcribing and publishing the letter in 800.

Furthermore, the word “still” in Alcuin’s later statement refers to the time when Elipandus’s letter was written, at which time Felix really was still bound by errors. The meaning is: Elipandus wrote to Felix at the time when he considered him still bound, as he truly was, although he was later released. [Col. 0583D] [Col. 0584A]

### LXX

Nor should you think it objectionable that Alcuin placed the letters at the end of the books written—or at least published—against Elipandus only in 800. They are not offspring of the same author as the books. He could have added a letter written some time earlier to his books of a later period, without its following that the letter belonged to the same period as the books.

Moreover, the order of the letters, especially in Alcuin, in which they are arranged according to the dignity of the persons rather than according to time, should not be taken into account. For, as Brietius observed at the year of Christ 139, “the order which is generally found in the writings of the holy Fathers belongs to the scribes, from whom you will usually expect in vain anything beyond the letters themselves.”

Finally, perhaps you will object that Alcuin sometimes calls the city of Aachen “another Rome,” or “the second Rome.” Granted; what follows from that? “Therefore,” you say, “when Elipandus says, ‘Inform me, you who have been placed in Rome,’ he must be understood to mean the city of Aachen, and Felix as being there in 799.”

This is certainly an excessively subtle and elaborate interpretation. I do not think that anyone, unless led by a preconceived opinion, could suppose that when Rome is mentioned in this letter of Elipandus, any city other than the true Rome—the leading city of the world and of Italy—is meant. But enough of this. Let us now proceed to Felix laboring in the assembly at Urgell. [Col. 0584B]

### LXXI

When Laidradus, therefore, reached Urgell with Nefridius and Benedict, his two companions on the journey, he convened a synod and proscribed the heresy, but reserved the heresiarch Felix for the hope of conversion. The Fathers acted humanely with the obstinate old man: they treated the wound gently and promised that, if he approached Charles and was kindly received and patiently heard by him, he need only come forward and say in person what had to be said.

We have all this not only from Marca, whom we shall cite shortly, but also from Felix’s own words at the beginning of his confession presented [Col. 0584C] at the Council of Aachen. We owe our knowledge of this synod to Peter de Marca, whose words Baluzius transcribes from book III of Marca’s *Hispania* in his notes on Agobard’s book against Felix, chapter 18. Cointius also cites him at the year 799, no. 30:

“Charles also ordered a synod of Urgell to be held on this matter by Laidradus, bishop of Lyon, Nefridius of Narbonne, Benedict the abbot, and the bishops and abbots of the province of Gothia, so that they might overcome Felix’s obstinacy through gentle conversations.”

This is Marca’s account. Yet, as Pagius notes at 799, no. 13, he incorrectly assigns the Council of Urgell to 794, whereas it should not be removed from this year, 799, as Cointius also maintains in the cited passage.

Felix therefore yielded the field of disputation to Laidradus, and toward the end of this year, 799, in the thirty-second year of Charles’s Frankish reign, he came to the council. There he found everything confirmed that had been promised to him, as he himself confesses at the beginning of his confession of faith in these words:

“After I had been brought into the presence of our lord, the most pious and glorious King Charles, and presented before him, we received permission from him—just as the venerable lord Laidracus” (read *Laidradus*) “the bishop had promised us at Urgell—to present in his presence, before the bishops whom the arrangement of our glorious prince had caused to assemble before him, the opinions which we believed, from the books of the saints, that we held concerning the adoption of the flesh in the Son of God, or concerning its being named in his humanity.” [Col. 0584D]

### LXXII

Aachen was the place of the assembly. The city took its name from its waters, endowed with medicinal properties, and was therefore also called the Aquensian city.

A hymn sacred to the holy Charles the Great:

> Aquensian city, royal city,  
> Seat of the principal kingdom,  
> First court of kings.

For in it, by the decree of Charles the Great, [Col. 0585A] the empire began with the first bestowal of the diadem. Because of the church dedicated to the Virgin Mother, it is called Aix-la-Chapelle by the French. Some have fancied that it was built by a certain Granus, the brother of Nero. Its inhabitants, according to Guicciardini in part II of his description of Flanders, acknowledge Charles as either the founder or at least the restorer of the city, which had once been destroyed by Attila. Charles, attracted by its temperate climate, the pleasantness of its location, and especially the healthfulness of its warm waters, chose it as a more permanent residence for himself. He endowed it with privileges, increased it with buildings, and omitted nothing that might make his goodwill toward the city evident.

### LXXIII

In this city, therefore, which he loved so dearly, Charles assembled the bishops. In their presence and in his own, Felix was brought forward and, at the king’s command, willingly or unwillingly entered into disputation with Alcuin. For Felix, fearing the learning of his opponent, would have avoided the encounter.

The anonymous author of the *Life of Alcuin* writes:

“Calling together Albinus, his teacher at Tours, and wretched Felix, the promoter of this heresy from the regions of Spain, [Col. 0585B] he assembled a great synod of bishops in the imperial palace at Aachen. Sitting in their midst, he ordered Felix, although strongly resisting, to engage reasonably in disputation with the most learned Albinus concerning the nature of the Son of God according to the flesh.

“Then how great was the silence of the bishops at that time! How clear and unconquerable was Charles’s confession and defense of the faith, together with the authority of his teacher! But Felix, fleeing through many hiding places, was pierced by numerous darts from Alcuin, so that he almost completed all the cities of Israel until the Son of Man should come. For from the second day of the week until the seventh, little else was done.

“Finally, when his stupidity had been exposed to everyone and his heresy had been refuted by all with apostolic authority, the disgrace remained hidden from him alone, until he sorrowfully read the words of the martyr Cyril sent to him by Albinus:

> ‘That nature which has been corrupted through the devil has been exalted above the angels because of Christ’s triumph and has been gathered to the right hand of the Father.’

“When he had read this statement, he testified with his voice and with abundant tears that at last he had recognized how he had acted impiously.” [Col. 0585C]

Felix himself also confesses the same in his confession of faith, made public on this occasion.

### LXXIV

Alcuin briefly reports the same thing in book I against Elipandus. He adds that Felix came to the council with a group of disciples, who were themselves also converted:

“In the thirty-second year of the aforesaid glorious prince, Felix, summoned, came willingly to the palace at Aachen. There, in the presence of the lord king and his nobles, or priests of God, he was heard rationally and convicted truthfully. Giving glory to God and confessing the true faith, he returned to the peace of Catholic unanimity with his disciples who were present with him at that time.”

To those who were not present he sent a letter in which he inserted his profession of faith. Although the title contains the name of bishop, you should know that it was not written by his own hand but by another’s; for he had been driven from his see, as he himself implies in the body of the letter:

“In God’s name, Felix, formerly an unworthy bishop.” [Col. 0585D]

Ado, in the sixth age of his chronicle, further says that Felix was sent into exile and remained at Lyon until his death.

### LXXV

Although Felix was thought to have returned to his senses, Alcuin did not cease trying to recall Elipandus, his companion in wickedness, to a better path. In the books addressed to Elipandus he even set before him Felix’s example:

“I urge you, venerable father,” he says in book I, “to follow the humility of Felix together with your disciples.”

For he thought that Felix had at least then truly converted. Thus in the same book he added:

“I . . . . . have, through God’s mercy, made Felix, formerly a partner in your error, Catholic.”

But Felix’s conversion was feigned, or at least it did not last; consequently, he is commonly reported to have died in the odor of eternal death. Ado, in the cited passage, says: “They report that he died in that very error of his.” [Col. 0586B]

Hear the history of the matter from Agobard. At the beginning of the reign of Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, when Laidradus was resigning the bishopric of Lyon [Col. 0586A] and choosing the better part in the monastery of Soissons, as the chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny reports, Agobard entered that same church. Thus he writes in book I against Felix’s doctrine, no. 1:

“After the death of that Felix, who had once been bishop in the see of Urgell, we found a certain document issued by him in the form of questions and answers. When we read and examined it, we perceived that the man had carefully and deceitfully restored, as far as he could, the whole depravity of his doctrine in which he had formerly been exposed and convicted, and on account of which he had been deposed from the honor of the episcopate. Although afterward he suppressed certain words which he had previously uttered rashly, he nevertheless added certain things that he had retained at that time.

“When I had criticized this document as best I could according to the truth of the faith, or had published it for criticism, some of the brothers, as I learned, took offense. Not from perversity of mind, as I think, but from simplicity of understanding, they believed that I had done this not out of zeal for the faith but out of jealous hostility.”

The reason why some took offense at this was the reputation for holiness that the hypocrite had acquired for himself, as Agobard indicates in no. 2:

“Those who, imprudently admiring the life of the aforesaid Felix, think that everything he said must be approved do not know that faith is not to be measured by a man’s life, but that life is to be tested by the faith.”

### LXXVI

But it is clear not only from the document itself, composed perhaps at the end of his life, that he had returned to madness; even earlier, although he had been placed in exile, he was not afraid to spread his errors publicly.

Agobard, no. 5:

“While he was still vigorous, he tried to persuade certain people of things that ought not to be approved. At one point, as I have said, he began to teach certain people to believe that our Lord Jesus Christ, according to the flesh, truly did not know the tomb of Lazarus, the day of judgment, and so forth.

“When I learned of this, I approached him in the presence of those whom he was persuading in this way and asked him whether he really thought so. When he attempted to affirm it, I rebuked him and denounced his wicked statements. I showed the others, as best I could, with what vigilance they should reject these things and in what sense they ought to understand those passages of Scripture. [Col. 0586C] I also sent Felix for reading passages taken from the holy Fathers which contradicted his blasphemies.

“After reading them, he promised that he would apply every diligence to his own correction. For this reason I dismissed him quietly and did not think it necessary to publish his blasphemies abroad, since it was not my concern.”

And in no. 6:

“After his death, however, I learned from certain faithful brothers who had heard it from him that he had said that the Son of God the Father ought in no way to be called one who suffered or was crucified, but rather that a man assumed by him [lacuna].

“Felix repeatedly acted in this way because he in no way consented to think, nor could he persuade himself to believe, that in the one Lord Jesus Christ there had been a substantial union of two natures and that God the Word had been united according to subsistence to the flesh.”

### LXXVII

From these words of Agobard it may be inferred that Felix was still alive approximately around 815. [Col. 0586D] At that time, when Laidradus had resigned the bishopric of Lyon, Agobard occupied his place; and, if G. Cave is to be trusted, from 813 onward he had undertaken the duties of chorepiscopus as Laidradus’s assistant.

When Agobard says that he did not publish Felix’s errors because it was not his concern, he implies that he was not yet bishop or chorepiscopus. Otherwise it would have been his duty to expose and even proscribe the evil he had discovered, for the protection of others.

By saying that he found the document after Felix’s death, without mentioning Laidradus—whose duty it would have been to suppress the evil and cast it out by a solemn anathema, and who knew Felix’s affairs extremely well, since he had been entrusted with summoning Felix from the see of Urgell, as stated above—it becomes perfectly clear that Agobard himself governed the church of Lyon when Felix died.

It was therefore around this time that Felix at last breathed out his black soul. [Col. 0587A]

### LXXVIII

It is not known what end Elipandus met. Some do not hesitate to assert, and wish others to believe, that he embraced the heresy of the Adoptionists not through his own wickedness but solely through Felix’s deceit; that he did not defend the error obstinately or persist in it for long; but that, brought back to his senses by the letters of Adrian and King Charles, he abandoned his previously wandering mind after convening a council at Toledo, detested the evil doctrine in the synod with tears of repentance, continued thereafter in a commendable manner of life, and closed his final day with the kiss of the Lord in 810.

See John Tamayo de Salazar in the *Hispanic Martyrology*.

To establish the truth of this account, they produce a letter of Ascaricus, bishop of Braga, to Elipandus, which mentions this synod and his repentance. They further rely on the testimonies of Julian and Luitprand in their chronicles. The latter speaks of Elipandus under the Spanish era 820, or the year of the Lord 782, as follows:

“Elipandus the archdeacon succeeds Cixila, bishop of Toledo, in the patriarchal see of Toledo, in place of Cixila his teacher. In the year 810 he presides. Through the evil persuasion of Felix, bishop of Urgell, his teacher, he falls into the foul error concerning the adoption of Christ; but through the letters of Pope Adrian and of Charlemagne, son of Pippin, king of the Franks, he returned [Col. 0587B] to the mind and true understanding of the Church.”

Under the Spanish era 848, or the year of the Lord 810, he speaks as follows concerning Elipandus’s death:

“In this year, when Elipandus, archbishop of Toledo, a prudent and humble man, fervent in zeal for the Catholic faith, had died a holy death, his archdeacon Gumesindus was appointed in his place. He himself was buried amid the tears of the poor and widows in the secretarium of the church of Saint Justa. His successor and disciple Gumesindus placed a funerary poem over him in the Gothic manner.”

### LXXIX

But who is unaware that the works of these writers are filled with absurdities? They are accordingly either counted among the pseudo-historians or rejected by more sensible people as interpreters of the tales of old women.

Hear what Nicolaus Antonius of Seville, a jurist, wrote on this subject in his posthumous work, the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, published by order of D. Joseph Saenz de Aguirre, cardinal, a man outstanding equally in dignity and learning and sharp-nosed in detecting [Col. 0587C] errors scattered through the writings of authors.

This Spanish bibliographer, in volume I, book VI, chapter 2, no. 42 and following, writes:

“We have said that there are many pseudo-historians who, in treating the Toledan bishop Elipandus, or magnifying his repentance and recounting his affairs, write on these matters—namely Julian and Luitprand. We shall give here some material from them to show the vanity of these authors.

“Julian the archdeacon says (in his chronicle, no. 395) that Elipandus was a citizen of Toledo under the archbishop Cixila, at the time when Charlemagne was in Toledo, and that he married Galiana, daughter of Galafre, king of that city, from whom, as certain authors say, the emperor Louis the Pious was born.

“This is the learning of the great Julian, at which our people marvel: Julian alone strives against all the ancients and wishes it to be believed. Nothing is more certain than that Louis was begotten by King Charles from his Swabian wife Hildegard, and is said to lie near her tomb at Metz, at Saint Arnulf; and nothing is farther from the truth than that Charles was ever in Toledo or married Galiana.

“For this latter story is one of the old-woman’s tales that have rashly burst into some of our histories, and wiser men rightly reject it. Julian then embellished Elipandus’s deeds, saying that he was a citizen of Toledo but of Gothic stock (*Grachorum*, we believe, was printed corruptly), and that, deceived by Felix and Vincentius, he wrote about the adoption of Christ to Charlemagne, who was his closest friend. I wish there were some trace of this friendship in the letter of Charles addressed to him.

“Under Elipandus he reports that the Mozarabs suffered most grievously under the yoke of the Saracens. Yet shortly afterward—something that would have been difficult to achieve in profound peace and among prosperous Christians—Elipandus is said to have held a council of many bishops in that same city of Toledo. This was at the very time when the same Julian says elsewhere (no. 402) that the Mozarabs suffered most grievously after being provoked by the injuries of the Saracens, because of which some were forced to flee to Asturias and others to Gaul.

“To attack Julian with his own weapon, Luitprand, whom Julian pretends was a man of that age and who wholly conspires with him, speaks of these same years as containing the council and says: ‘Afterward, Julian himself says that Gumesindus, his archdeacon, and Lupus, son of Andreas Ficulneus, and others were sent to Charlemagne with Elipandus’s embassy and letters.’”

### LXXX

In the following sections he continues to demonstrate many fabulous and empty claims in Julian, as well as the spurious material that he reported and produced concerning Ascaricus and concerning the council of Toledo attributed to Elipandus.

He continues:

“That Elipandus repented at this council, solemnly assembled with the Moors watching and consenting—this is the difficulty for us. I know that mention is made of this Council of Toledo in the acts, or Life, of Saint Beatus, which John Tamayo says he derived from the legendary of the church of Astorga, and which the most distinguished compilers of the great work inserted from him in the Acts of the Saints on 19 February.

“But it was John Tamayo’s custom—one of perverse judgment and abominable audacity—to insert into genuine acts of the legendaries and breviaries the inventions of the pseudo-chronicles to which he adhered, as though they were of the same texture and authority as those ecclesiastical records that preserved the ancient traditions of our people.

“I judge that all the following must be counted among the things produced by Tamayo’s hand: what is said, as we have mentioned, concerning the presence of Heterius and Beatus at the Council of Frankfurt; what is said here concerning a second Council of Toledo, drawn from Luitprand and Julian; and likewise the claim that Felix was a Gaul by ancestry, whereas, according to the testimony of Einhard—to whom we ought to give greater credence than to Tamayo—he was a Spaniard.

“Mabillon, arriving at this point with his customary acumen, saw the difficulty, setting Einhard against this supposed Gallic homeland of Felix and noting that John Mariana did not dare to assert it. . . . Yet he did not justly attack them as though all Spaniards adored these fables, in these words:

“‘The Spaniards are amusing: those rogues whom they possess, they assign to the Franks or Gauls; but those whom they regard as more distinguished, they claim for themselves, as is evident from many examples in the *Hispanic Martyrology*.’

“This writing deserves to hear this and still sharper criticism, but not all Spaniards agree with him. Indeed, we are ashamed whenever we take it into our hands, and we earnestly desire that a true martyrology of Spain, replacing this work of Tamayo’s—defiled by countless fictions and in which [Col. 0588C] truth is mixed with falsehood—be supplied by some man who loves truth and the good name of our nation.

“As for the claim that Elipandus died after almost thirty years in the episcopate—that is what Julian finally taught his admirers—he does not depart from Luitprand’s reckoning.”

Thus he speaks, teaching sufficiently and more than sufficiently with what credibility the claims produced on behalf of Elipandus by these authors should be received. [Col. 0588D]

### LXXXI

Nevertheless, the matter of the time of Elipandus’s age and death remains obscure. Garsias de Loaysa, prefacing his *Collection of the Councils of Spain* with a chronology of the Toledan bishops, places Elipandus approximately in 784. He assigns his successor Gumesindus to 820, and therefore attributes thirty-six years to the preceding episcopate. [Col. 0589A]

It would follow from this that Elipandus, who in 792 was eighty-two years old according to our view—based on the letter written while Felix was living in Rome in 792—would have had to live until the age of 118, which seems impossibly long.

I think, however, that Loaysa is speaking of the period around which these bishops flourished, not precisely of the year in which they entered the episcopate. For it is clear from what was said above in no. 14 that Elipandus had already been installed in the Toledan see in 783. In that year he received, as a bishop, the letters of Pope Adrian warning him about the novelty of the doctrine and the error concerning the feast of Easter; and, as metropolitan bishop, he convened the Council of Seville in that same year and for that reason.

It therefore seems more probable that he was appointed bishop in 780. If you assign approximately thirty years to his episcopate, as Julian and Luitprand do—or the authors hiding under their names—and with Nicolaus Antonius of Seville, the jurist praised above, not disapproving that reckoning, you will place his death in 809. Thus the end of his life, which we said above in no. 16 began in 710, would fall around his ninety-ninth year, more or less.

### LXXXII

It is probable from the fact that Garsias de Loaysa did not precisely assign in his chronology the year in which the Toledan bishops were installed in the episcopal see that, when speaking of Elipandus, he writes as follows:

“In the year of the Lord 784, Elipandus, infected with heresy, was condemned at the Council of Frankfurt.”

It could have happened that, for the year 794—in which he was actually condemned at the Council of Frankfurt—the number 784 was inserted through carelessness. This could have occurred more easily because he uses Arabic numerals, and he may have written 784 instead of 794.

If you admit this, it is now clear that he designated not the precise year of their creation as bishops but the period around which the bishops flourished.

Add that nowhere was he sufficiently exact in his enumeration of the Toledan bishops. For, discussing [Col. 0589B] the primacy of the church of Toledo in his account of Gundemar’s decree, he lists them from his annals as follows:

“While the Saracens ruled, the following succeeded in this order: Cixila, Peter Pulcher, Sunicredus, Concordius, Elipandus, Westremirus, Saint Eulogius, elected, Gumesindus, Bonitus, and so forth.”

Yet in his chronology he places Gumesindus immediately after Elipandus, and in section 4 of the same dissertation he again places Westremirus next to Elipandus.

It is worth quoting some of his words here. [Col. 0590A] From them, although the author is a Spaniard writing on behalf of his own people, the character of Elipandus’s life and teaching becomes evident; and he is more worthy of trust than Tamayo and other such men who make glorious claims:

“Peter Pulcher had Elipandus as his successor after several others. He fulfilled the great responsibility entrusted to him not merely negligently but most wickedly. For, through frequent association with the Moors, he was far removed from the prosperity of those times in which sound ecclesiastical teaching flourished; and because he had not applied himself very carefully to the sacred writings, he arrogantly and ignorantly stumbled into the heresy concerning the adoption of Christ our Savior.

“This heresy was later condemned by the Council of Frankfurt. When he attempted by letters to persuade certain bishops and cities of Spain of his impiety, he was rejected by the elegant writings of Heterius, bishop of Oxama, and Beatus the presbyter. These men, thoroughly learned in the sacred writings, produced distinguished works against Elipandus.

“After Elipandus was removed, the Toledan see was entrusted to Westremirus, an outstanding and excellent bishop.”

LXXXIII. These, excellent reader, are the matters I had to set forth concerning the heresy of Felix and Elipandus. From them you may understand the origin, progress, and destruction of the error, as well as the life, character, and end of its authors. I arranged everything, as far as I could, according to the laws of chronology and criticism. From this you may also infer how great were the holiness and learning of the writers who fought against such men, and especially of our Paulinus. Although he was farther removed than the others from the Spaniards, he did not fear his enemies, as he himself says, either from a distance in writing or at close quarters in debate; rather, he was to be feared by them. He attacked and repelled them, assailed and conquered them, struck them down, crushed them, destroyed them—in a word, he triumphed.

## 226. CHRONOLOGICAL EXCERPT FROM THE HISTORICAL DISSERTATION ON THE HERESY OF FELIX AND ELIPANDUS

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589C] **Year 389.** Bonosus, teaching the adoption of Christ, is condemned at the Council of Capua, no. 4.

**420.** Saint Chromatius of Aquileia writes against the Adoptianists, no. 4.

**636.** Theodiscus brings the name and error of adoption from Greece into Spain, no. 5.

**710.** Elipandus is born on 25 July, no. 16.

**711.** The Moors cross the sea and occupy Ceuta, no. 2.

**712.** The Moors occupy Seville, no. 2.

**713.** After killing Roderic, the Moors establish the seat of the kingdom of Granada, no. 2.

**763.** Pippin, residing at Worms, divides the kingdom among his sons, no. 26.

**772.** Peter Oldradus of Milan is sent by Hadrian into Gaul to Charlemagne, no. 44.

**773.** Peter approaches the king, who is residing at Thionville, [Col. 0589D] no. 44.

**774.** Benedict serves under Charles at Pavia. He then becomes a monk of Saint-Sequanus, no. 63.

**780.** Benedict flees lest he be made abbot, no. 63. — Elipandus is made bishop of Toledo, no. 80.

**781.** Charlemagne becomes Hadrian’s compater, no. 8.

**782.** Hadrian admonishes Aegila, a Spanish bishop, to safeguard the faith, no. 8. — Around this year the Felician heresy arises, no. 9.

**783.** Peter of Pavia dies, no. 9. — Peter Oldradus is made bishop of Milan, no. 44. — Silo, husband of Adosinda and king of Asturias, dies, no. 10. — Hadrian writes to the Spanish bishops, no. 14.

**784.** Peter of Milan adds monks to the canons; he makes Benedict abbot of the Ambrosian monastery, no. 45.

**785.** Etherius and Beatus rise up against Elipandus, no. 23. — Elipandus writes to Abbot Fidelis in October, no. 10.

[Col. 0590C] **786.** Elipandus endeavors to subvert Adosinda, no. 10.

**788.** The Council of Narbonne is held on 27 June, no. 24.

**790.** Alcuin returns to England, no. 31.

**791.** The Avars are subjected to Charles through Henry, duke of Friuli, no. 29.

**792.** The Council of Regensburg is held against Felix, with Paulinus present, no. 29. — Felix is led to Rome by Angilbert, no. 34. — Elipandus writes to Felix residing at Rome, no. 36.

**793.** Alcuin returns to Gaul around the beginning of this year, no. 31. — After establishing a monastery by the Aniane River, Benedict feeds the poor oppressed by famine, no. 63.

**794.** The Council of Frankfurt is celebrated at the beginning of summer, no. 61. — Alcuin writes to Elipandus immediately after the council, no. 51. — Elipandus replies after receiving Alcuin’s letter around the end of July, no. 52. — Angilbert again travels to Rome.

**796.** Paulinus publishes three books against Felix, nos. 33 and 58. — He celebrates the Council of Friuli, no. 58.

**797 or thereafter.** Alcuin writes Book VII against Felix, no. 54.

**798.** Saint Beatus dies a martyr on 21 April, no. 22. — Laidradus is elected bishop of Lyon, no. 63.

**799.** His ordination, no. 63. — The Roman Council is held under Leo III before 25 April. — On that day he is badly treated by rebels during the Greater Litanies. He then proceeds to Gaul to Charlemagne. — He returns to Rome on 30 November, nos. 61 and following. — The Synod of Urgel is convened by Laidradus and his associates against Felix, no. 71. — The Council of Aachen is held toward the end of the year, no. 73.

**800.** Alcuin completes and publishes Book IV against Elipandus, no. 66.

[Col. 0591A] **804.** Peter of Milan dies on 9 May, no. 44.

**809.** Elipandus dies, no. 81.

**813.** Agobardus is Laidradus’s chorepiscopus, no. 76.

[Col. 0592A] **815.** He becomes bishop of Lyon; around this time Felix dies under him, nos. 76 and following.

**821.** Benedict, abbot of Aniane, dies, no. 63.

# OBSERVATION ON JACOB BASNAGE’S HISTORICAL OBSERVATIONS CONCERNING THE FELICIAN HERESY AND THE BOOKS OF ETHERIUS AND BEATUS

[Col. 0591]

[Col. 0591A] We had already put the finishing hand to our historical dissertation on the heresy of Felix and Elipandus when, while reading the second volume of the *Ancient Lessons* of Henry Canisius, Amsterdam edition of 1725, we came across, on page 284, Jacob Basnage’s observations on the Felician heresy, which Etherius and Beatus had undertaken to attack in their books. We read through each of them eagerly, yet found nothing that caused us to regret our own labor. Rather, certain matters appeared that deserved observation and required filing and polishing, since they injure the truth and disparage the reputation of very holy writers. We therefore decided to gather our strength and examine his observations, striking out whatever he says against the truth. As we carry this out briefly, may the fair-minded reader receive our labor kindly—not from an itch to contradict, but from love of truth.

**I.** In section 1, under the year 783, Basnage, following Pagi, argues from a letter of Pope Hadrian addressed to the Spanish bishop Aegila that the Felician heresy arose then, and dates the letters to the year 732. This is perhaps a printer’s error, and the year 782 should be restored. We believe the heresy arose somewhat earlier, as we explain in our dissertation, no. 9, for the reason given there: namely, it is scarcely credible that in the very year in which the heresy arose it became known to the Roman pontiff, so far removed from the center of Spain, was subjected to examination, and had its doctrine attacked. Basnage uses this argument to show, against Cardinal de Aguirre [this is not Cardinal de Aguirre, but Nicolaus Antonius’s *Bibliotheca Hispana*, from which this material was taken], that Elipandus could not in that year have complained to Abbot Fidelis about Etherius and Beatus, both because they had not yet written anything against him and because an error so recently born could scarcely have become known. But if an error born in Spain can scarcely be known in Spain in the year of its birth, how could it have been refuted in Rome in that same year? Therefore the year 783 is not the birth-year of the Felician heresy, but one of the earlier years is.

**II.** In section 2 Basnage writes several things worthy of observation. Because Mabillon had refuted certain Spaniards who asserted that Felix was a Gaul by birth, he said: “The Spaniards are amusing: if they have any scoundrels, they assign them to the Gauls, but the more distinguished saints they have, they claim for themselves.” Basnage adds: “Let the most celebrated man pardon these words! First, Felix was not a scoundrel, since he was distinguished by purity of morals and zeal for the faith. Concerning his character, Alcuin says this, although he was extremely hostile to him: ‘We read in the letters of blessed Felix—namely, of a man outstanding in religious life and distinguished for holiness—that he wished to love and preach the Catholic faith and the unity of the Church, without which no one can please God.’ Alcuin charges him with the guilt of error, but praises his religious life and conspicuous holiness, and calls him not a scoundrel but blessed. His zeal for the faith is evident, since he defended the truth in writing against the Saracens then ravaging Spain and persecuting both the Church and the bishops—a work which Charlemagne diligently sought and earnestly requested from Alcuin himself. Finally, Felix could be called a Gaul because of the proximity of the regions, and because the arms of the Gauls had penetrated that part of Spain in earlier years.” Thus Basnage.

**III.** Do not be surprised, excellent reader, that Basnage so openly acts as patron of a heretic so often condemned, for

> “The cicada is friendly to the cicada,  
> and the ant to the ant.”

But observe how unlawfully he attacks Mabillon. Mabillon does not allow Felix to have been a Gaul, and rightly so. Although Urgel at that time belonged to the dominion of the Franks, it does not follow that Felix was a Gaul, since it is not established that he was Urgellitan by origin and birth. Einhard declares him to have been a Spaniard: “Urgel is a city situated on the ridge of the Pyrenees, whose bishop, named Felix, was Spanish by nation, etc.” Thus he writes in his *Annals* under the year 792. The testimony of this author, rather than that of Tamayo, must be followed; Nicolaus Antonius, himself a Spaniard of Seville and author of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, cited in our dissertation, no. 79, asserts and affirms as much. Felix could therefore be counted among those subject to the Frankish dominion without thereby deserving to be called a Gaul, since a contemporary author expressly says that he was a Spaniard.

Basnage praises Felix’s zeal from a writing in which, as he says, Felix defended the truth against the Saracens. Who revealed this to Basnage? Felix composed a dialogue with a Saracen. Charlemagne had wished to see it. He inquired about it from Alcuin, and Alcuin from Laidradus. But what was debated in it is everywhere passed over in deep silence. We know that Leo III, in the second act of the Roman synod, calls Felix a renegade among pagans akin to him. One who regarded the pagans, or Saracens, as his kindred does not appear to have defended the truth of the Church against them with all the strength he ought to have shown.

Basnage is also distressed that Mabillon calls Felix a scoundrel, although Alcuin calls him blessed and an outstanding man of religious life and holiness. But what of it? Could Mabillon not call Felix a scoundrel when Basnage himself, in the same paragraph, repeatedly declares that Felix, condemned for his error, falsely performed repentance? Who forbids anyone to call a liar, perjurer, oath-breaker, and covenant-violator a scoundrel? The writers of those times were certainly not troubled by this scruple. Jonas of Orléans, in Book I of *On the Worship of Images*, says that Felix was “in name Felix, but in fact unhappy.” Attacking Claudius of Turin, bishop and disciple of Felix, he calls him Euphorbius reborn as Pythagoras, and, using Jerome’s words, lashes him as the worst father reborn in a worse son. Our Paulinus, in Book I against Felix, chapter 5, calls him a man ignorant of shame; there he also throws in his face that he was a profaner of oaths and violator of the sacred religious pledge, and rebukes him as a perjurer. Moreover, in chapter 11 he calls him, with the most shameless front, a man equal to the Jews and Arius, and a character from an old wives’ tale; in chapters 12 and 21 he addresses him thus: “How long, drunk with the cup of treachery, will you not cease to snore with a bear-like nose?” And you will find countless other expressions of this kind scattered through the three books he wrote against him.

What fault, then, did Mabillon commit if he called a man of this sort a scoundrel, when the holiest men of his own time so justly traduced him? But if Alcuin called him blessed, what then? I am surprised that Basnage, otherwise very learned, did not know that the title “blessed” was honorific, as Du Cange teaches at length in his *Glossary*, under “Beatitudo,” where he shows not only that in the present age the title was reserved to the Roman pontiff, but also that in an earlier period it was sometimes common to other bishops and even to laymen. Here Brissonius must be heard, *On Formulae*, Book III, p. 323, Frankfurt edition, 1592. After collecting various formulas of this kind, he concludes: “In these examples, I briefly call attention to the solemn words used in addressing archbishops, namely, ‘your blessedness’—ἡ σὴ μακαριότης.”

Moreover, when Alcuin calls Felix outstanding in religious life and distinguished for holiness, this was said as an honor and was a courtesy by which he thought it preferable to soothe the proud spirits of the heresiarchs. Add that, since Felix had not yet appeared obstinate and stubborn in teaching his heresy, Alcuin ought to handle him gently, lest, if he had not spared him harsher words, Felix’s heart should become hardened. But what is the point of all this? The man’s character is evident. A heretic would not want another heretic to be traduced; hence Basnage defends his cause. The lid is worthy of the pot.

**IV.** But, good God, who can understand this man’s disposition? You have heard, excellent reader, Basnage exalting Alcuin because he called Felix blessed and a man distinguished for holiness. Read a few lines of the same paragraph, and you will find Basnage attacking and treating most severely Alcuin when he praises Elipandus.

“‘Elipandus,’ Basnage writes, ‘excelled in learning.’” In commendation of him he then adds Alcuin’s words addressed to Elipandus: “For you are a most holy prelate, a city set upon a mountain, which cannot in any way be hidden; its wall must by no means be pierced anywhere by the treacherous tunnels of any perfidy, etc.” Basnage adds: “Wonder, reader, at the character of this theologian flattering Elipandus, although he believed him to be in error: he applies to him, at least in a profane style, the words of Christ, upon which the stability of the whole Church is founded. Elipandus, then, if Alcuin is to be believed, was a city set upon a mountain that could not in any way be hidden. Now extract from Christ’s own words the splendid stability of the Church, which will remain in the same conviction to the very end of the ages, since Elipandus, while in error, is that city set upon a mountain which could neither be hidden nor pierced.”

**V.** Who could hear this without restraining his anger? You will not read so many periods as the lies you will encounter.

First, Alcuin does not praise the man because he believed him to be in error. He praises him on account of the eminence of his dignity and the holiness of his episcopate, which in itself is worthy of praise because it is most holy and excellent. There is therefore no reason to marvel at the character of a theologian flattering Elipandus.

Second, when Alcuin says that Elipandus is a city set upon a mountain that cannot be hidden, he says nothing other than what the Church says very frequently when it applies the words of the Gospel, Matthew 5:14, to holy teachers: “You are the light of the world. A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house.” These words, which the Lord spoke concerning his apostles, and which the Church applies to the successors of the apostles, imply nothing other than that apostolic men ought to shine before others by their teaching and example of virtue. Just as a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, so those who in the Church are placed above others by reason of ministry or dignity cannot be hidden, since their life and teaching must be visible to others as an example. Those who light a lamp—that is, those who cause such men to stand out—do not put it under a bushel; that is, they do not establish them in such a way that they lead a hidden life, but one that shines before all who are in the house, raised up as upon a lampstand.

This is the obvious and genuine meaning of the passage in Matthew. It is not to be understood of the Church and the congregation of the faithful, as Basnage understands it in order to attack Catholics with biting sarcasm for defending the stability of the Church. These are not the words, Basnage, upon which the stability of the whole Church is founded. Rather, we derive the splendid stability of the Church, which will remain in the same conviction to the very end of the ages, from other words of Christ: “Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20). There are many other testimonies by which the stability of the Church is supported; but since this is not the place for controversies and they are known to nearly everyone, we shall refrain from adducing them.

Third, when Basnage reports Alcuin’s words, he twists them as follows: “Since Elipandus, while in error, is that city set upon a mountain which could neither be hidden nor pierced.” Alcuin did not say this. But we have stumbled upon a liar who has forgotten what he himself said. Basnage had recited Alcuin’s words, which from his own mouth are as follows: “Whose wall must by no means be pierced anywhere by the treacherous tunnels of any perfidy.” A little farther on, repeating and commenting on them, he says that according to Alcuin Elipandus was a city “which can neither be hidden nor pierced.”

Alcuin said “must not,” Basnage; he did not say “cannot.” The Catholic Church cannot be pierced, just as it cannot be hidden. Elipandus, as bishop and prelate of the Church, indeed cannot be hidden; but because he can be pierced, Alcuin, reminding him of the duty of his office, says: “whose wall must by no means be pierced by the tunnels of perfidy.”

**VI.** In the same paragraph, after reporting the errors by which Spain was infected and mentioning Pope Hadrian’s letter attacking them, Basnage adds: “There is one thing we find astonishing: amid such a flood of evils and errors, the slightest theological mistakes concerning the celebration of Easter and the expression ‘adoptive son’ attracted so many and such severe censures, while greater errors concerning predestination and free will, and impurity of morals, were spared.”

How are those to be regarded as slight theological mistakes by which the heresy of the Quartodecimans was encouraged and the divinity of Jesus Christ attacked? The ancient Church did not regard errors concerning the feast of Easter as slight mistakes; it once pursued them with the greatest severity.

Basnage himself there laments that “the nobles and the people of Spain, each according to his own pleasure, ordered his life as he wished, and, since no one prohibited it, each person formed his own opinions about divine matters according to his own will and judgment—which is a great calamity.” He admits that forming opinions about divine matters according to one’s own will and judgment is a great calamity, yet calls the theological mistakes that produced this great calamity slight mistakes? I cannot understand the man.

**VII.** In section 3 Basnage attacks Mariana and Cardinal de Aguirre, who think that the errors of Felix and Elipandus may perhaps have originated from contamination by the blaspheming Mahometans living nearby, as follows:

“But what intercourse could there have been with the most savage Saracens? Or what fusion of faith could there have been among bishops otherwise most distinguished for defending the faith? And by what means could the doctrine of an adoptive son have been drawn from the Mahometans, when in those times it had so often been condemned as heretical, though by no means as Saracenic—for formerly, as the councils themselves expressly said, they spared no words? Finally, we have already noted that Felix wrote against the Saracens.”

Nearly every word is a lie.

First, this opinion does not belong to Cardinal de Aguirre, but to Nicolaus Antonius of Seville, who writes it in the *Bibliotheca Hispana*—although we do not deny that the work was published with the assistance of Cardinal de Aguirre. Basnage’s quotation of his words has also been quoted by us in the *Historical Dissertation on the Heresy of Felix and Elipandus*, no. 3.

Second, by using the word “perhaps,” Nicolaus presents his statement as an opinion. Basnage, looking for a knot in a rush, attacks it as though it were an absolute assertion.

Third, he wonders what intercourse there could have been between the Spaniards and the Saracens. For more than eight centuries the Moors and Saracens ruled the Spaniards: from the year 711, when they entered Spain, until 1492, when they were expelled from Spain under King Ferdinand. And he asks what intercourse there could have been between Spaniards and Saracens for more than seven hundred years?

Fourth, are Felix and Elipandus, as condemned heretics, bishops distinguished for defending the faith, Basnage?

Fifth, by what means could the doctrine of an adoptive son have been drawn from the Mahometans? Basnage appears to be a new man in the doctrine of the Mahometans. Peter the Venerable, ninth abbot of Cluny, could have instructed him. In Book IV, Letter 17, Peter says that Sergius, a monk and follower of Nestorius, joined to Muhammad, made Muhammad a Christian Nestorian according to his master’s understanding—namely, that the monk denied that our Savior was God. The more common opinion is that the Felician heresy was a shoot of the Nestorian error, as we showed in our dogmatic dissertation on the heresy of Felix.

Sixth, Basnage says that the doctrine of an adoptive son had in those times been condemned several times as heretical. I wish he would show what those times were in which it had then been repeatedly condemned as heretical. I am not unaware that before Nestorius Bonosus taught that Christ was adoptive from his mother and in a certain sense anticipated Nestorius. This heresy was condemned at the Council of Capua in 389; our Chromatius refuted it on one occasion in 420 in explicit, though brief, terms. But this was not properly the Felician heresy, as Elipandus himself admits, because Bonosus asserted only that Christ was adoptive from his mother, not from the Father, from whom he was begotten before the ages.

How, then, could Basnage say that it had been repeatedly condemned in those times, when he is investigating the time in which it arose? The origin is being examined in relation to those times; therefore it was not repeatedly condemned in those times. It was indeed condemned repeatedly, but not in those times—in later times.

Seventh, Basnage has already noted above that Felix wrote against the Saracens. We have already said above: where did Basnage learn this, when Leo III, calling Felix akin to the Saracens, gives grounds for arguing that he wrote not for the Saracens, but certainly not wholly for the truth of the Church?

**VIII.** Basnage says in the same place:

“He who does not allow himself to be carried away by even deeply rooted prejudices denies the Nestorianism in Felix’s doctrine, which most people, Marca not excepted, hold to be contained in it, as we have shown in the dissertation cited above. Why? Because the heretics themselves deny it. Elipandus confesses not two persons with Nestorius, but one; and although he calls the Son adoptive according to his humanity, the number of persons in the Trinity was not increased, and the actions of the entire time belonged to one person.”

After presenting this as Elipandus’s genuine doctrine, Basnage adds:

“What, then, was the nature of the error, for whose condemnation Charlemagne, Pope Hadrian, and the other doctors stirred up not merely such commotion but so many councils, while other errors were spared? We frankly admit that it was purely a logomachy, of the kind that often occurs among theologians. The bishop of Toledo reasoned far too subtly and, if I am not mistaken, was quibbling over a very slight point concerning the word ‘adoptive.’ For the hypostatic union of divinity with humanity, which formed one person, conferred such eminence that it had no need of adoption . . . . . The controversy over the expression ‘adoptive son’ was therefore exceedingly slight, since it concerned only his humanity.”

These are Basnage’s words, with a few omissions.

I shall not explain here at greater length with what justification and by what right most people assert that Nestorianism is contained in Felix’s doctrine. See our dogmatic dissertation on the heresy of Felix and Elipandus, beginning at no. 10 and following.

What Basnage says here to diminish the weight of the controversy is futile and foolish. Felix and his followers did indeed deny that they divided the persons, but they established a doctrine that necessarily asserted a division of persons. See the same dissertation, beginning at no. 14 and following.

Hear also Paulinus against Felix, Book I, chapter 9:

> “Felix says, ‘I do not divide the persons; I distinguish the natures completely.’ But when he tries to excuse himself from this charge, and nevertheless does it more and more frequently, he can still be convicted from his own inventions, being guilty of two crimes, deed and falsehood, etc.”

And Alcuin, in his reply to Elipandus:

> “How do you not understand from these words of yours that you affirm two persons in Christ, when you say ‘to him’ and ‘to that one’? As though one were he who was begotten from God the Father and another he who was born from the virgin mother, whereas the Evangelist says, ‘The Word became flesh.’”

Nestorius, too, said that he did not deny two natures and one person, while nevertheless denying the hypostatic union; consequently, he necessarily presupposed two persons. He was condemned by Celestine and Cyril, and by the councils convened through them, as we showed in the same place.

We must not, therefore, trust heretics—and even less Basnage, who, with utter confidence, declares that the doctrine which deprived our Savior of the sonship of God, made him, like the rest, in need of adoption, and caused Nestorianism to revive, was a very slight controversy of mere wordplay concerning the expression “adoptive.”

**IX.** In section 4, writing about Beatus, Etherius’s companion in attacking the Felician heresy, Basnage asserts that Beatus was a religious man who renounced the world and his brother and put on the monastic habit in order to find other brothers in the cloister. He proves that Alcuin called him an abbot, not a commendatory abbot—for this practice was not customary among the Visigoths—but a true monk. He commends Beatus for being endowed with a talent more ready for writing than for speaking, and for having written not only against Elipandus but also a commentary on the Apocalypse, which has not yet been published. He readily and repeatedly admits that the people of Asturias venerate him under the corrupted name San Bieco as one of the heavenly beings.

But when Basnage offers so many praises of Beatus and shortly afterward seizes upon insults hurled at him by Elipandus as an opportunity to disparage him, may we not rightly marvel at the critical judgment and inconsistency of our censor? In writing to Alcuin, Elipandus poured forth dreadful insults against Alcuin and Beatus. Speaking of Beatus, he says:

> “Beatus only by antiphrasis [‘Blessed’ in the opposite sense], disciple of Antichrist, stinking with the uncleanness of the flesh, and, estranged from the altar of Christ, a pseudo-Christ and false prophet.”

What does Basnage do with these words taken from Elipandus’s mouth? He moves every stone to make the accusations seem credible. Hear him:

“But we have a special observation to make concerning Beatus,” he says, “who was stinking—or rather most foul—with the uncleanness of the flesh, and who, because of the impurity of his morals, was estranged from the altar of God. Is it likely that the bishop of Toledo, an eyewitness, a contemporary writer, and a fellow countryman, would have written such things to Alcuin, Beatus’s zealous defender, who could very easily have branded him with the mark of slander if they had been false? Does the most celebrated Marca repel this charge? He merely notes in passing that these words are full of anger and slander. Elipandus does not merely reproach Beatus everywhere for foul morals; when he says that Beatus was estranged from the altar of God, this could have happened only by a public sentence depriving him of the priestly office. To this foul man Elipandus opposed Felix, whom we know to have been outstanding in charity from his earliest age, chaste, and adorned with good morals—Felix whom you pursue while he hides in the mountains, caves, and hollows of the earth.”

What need was there, I ask, for Marca to repel these charges with greater force than by saying that the words were full of anger and slander? This is the most appropriate response of all.

Do Elipandus’s statements about Felix become credible merely because he praises Felix as outstanding in charity, chaste, and adorned with good morals—Felix whom we know as an exceedingly obstinate heretic and perjurer, repeatedly condemned by the holiest Fathers in several councils? Certainly not. Therefore the statements he spewed from his shameless mouth about Beatus are not credible either.

Alcuin did not refute them. What of it? He also did not refute the curses hurled at himself. This silence was a mark of virtue; it did not serve as a confession, as Basnage maliciously tries to imply.

**X.** These were the matters, apart from certain minor details, that we had to criticize in Basnage’s observations. Far be it from us to take pleasure in stirring up anyone’s ashes. But when we saw the truth and innocence of the holiest teachers so disgracefully traduced, and the errors of heretics condemned by the Church defended so openly and shamelessly, zeal and charity compelled us to rise with shield and spear, to champion the cause of the innocent, and to refute the lies for the warning of others.

If our style appears sharper than is customary with us, let him remember Terentianus’s words in the prologue to the *Phormio*, V.20:

[Col. 0598A]

> “Here he wished to answer, not to provoke.”

> “Had he contended with the blessed, he would have heard good things.”

# FIFTH DISSERTATION: ON THE CREED

[Col. 0597]

[Col. 0597A] The Greek word σύμβολον (*symbolon*) has an exceedingly broad range of meaning. It is used for an indication or sign of anything whatsoever; hence military, hospitality, theatrical, and convivial tokens were also called *symbola*. Among Christian Fathers, however, its meaning is narrowed to indicate that rule in which the sum of the faith is contained.

Thus our Paulinus, at the Council of Friuli, following the ancient usage of the word, proposes that the creed be committed to memory:

> “Let every Christian,” he says, “know the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart.”

A little earlier he had commended the Nicene, or Constantinopolitan, Creed, which he had presented at the synod with certain clarifications, and had likewise proposed that it be committed to memory by the clergy, granting a full year to those whose understanding was duller. It was therefore commanded that at the council’s annual session they should be able to recite what they had learned without omitting even a letter.

Since certain matters arise in the history of the Creed that touch the Church of Aquileia more closely, we thought it not inappropriate, beginning at the beginning, as they say, first to compose a concise history of the Creed of the faith in the universal Church; then to descend to the Creed of our own church; and, if we should learn anything relevant to our Paulinus, to insert it at the proper point.

**II.** To begin with the contemporary writers of our holy Paulinus, hear from Book I of Etherius and Beatus, which they wrote against Elipandus, why the rule of faith is called the Creed:

> “Symbolon in Greek means ‘indication’ and ‘contribution’ in Latin. It is called an indication because it indicates in whom we ought to believe—namely, in the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. . . . It is called a contribution because several people contribute something into one whole. . . . For our elders say that after the Ascension of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the apostles composed this Creed, a brief indication of their preaching, by bringing together into one what they believed, so that, when they departed from one another geographically, nothing diverse or discordant would be preached to those who were being invited to the faith of Christ.”

Rufinus had written nearly the same thing before them in his *Exposition of the Creed*, no. 2. It should nevertheless be noted that a contribution in which each person puts forward something of his own—for example, in organizing a dinner—is more properly called *symbola* than *symbolon*.

**III.** It has been peacefully handed down as a tradition that the Creed proceeded from the apostles, so that many have wondered that the matter has been called into doubt in our own times. Elias du Pin, in volume I of his *Ecclesiastical Library*, p. 9, vigorously defends the novelty of his opinion, but not with impunity. The distinguished monk Dom Matthieu Petitdidier rises against the Dupinian position with all his strength and successfully proves that one must not depart from ecclesiastical tradition, which recognizes the Creed as the work of the apostles.

He confirms this by citing statements of the holy Fathers. Although they do not expressly discuss the manner in which the Creed was put together, they nevertheless speak in such a way that there can be no doubt that it was composed by the apostles. From this he concludes that he is exceedingly surprised that Du Pin could say that Rufinus was the first and only writer of the fifth century to believe that the apostles were the authors of the Creed.

Du Pin replies; Petitdidier answers in volume II. If you have the time and inclination, read it. It is enough for you to know that the question was raised, so that you would not follow the opinion of a recent author blindly, without knowing that it had been refuted by a more recent author and that the ancient position—that the Creed originated with the apostles—had been preserved intact.

Do not omit Natalis Alexander either, who in century I, dissertation 12, on the Creed, defends at length the truth of the tradition affirming that the Creed was composed by the apostles.

## IV

This work of the apostles, then—the Creed, I mean—the Catholic Church has always embraced and revered. In the earlier centuries, when it was being attacked on every side by persecutors, lest it be forced to expose its holy things to dogs, it was accustomed to transmit it orally, not in writing. Hence it is not surprising that it is scarcely found among the ancient Fathers, since they took the greatest care that such writing should not fall into profane hands.

Rufinus, *Exposition of the Creed*, no. 2:

> “For this reason they handed it down as something not to be written on sheets of paper or parchment, but to be retained in the heart, so that it might be certain that no one had learned these things from reading—a form of instruction that sometimes reaches even unbelievers—but rather that it would be enough to have learned them from the tradition of the apostles.”

Jerome had this in mind in Letter 61, arguing against the errors of John of Jerusalem, when he said:

> “In the Creed of our faith and hope, which is said to have been handed down by the apostles—not written on paper and with ink, but on the fleshy tablets of the heart—after the confession of the Trinity and the unity of the Church, the whole mystery of Christian doctrine is brought to its conclusion in the resurrection of the flesh.”

Accordingly, you will find no more extended statement of the Creed in the holy Fathers of the first centuries than this one of Jerome, except for Tertullian, who in *On the Veiling of Virgins* indicates some, though not all, of the articles, and these in sufficiently condensed form:

> “The rule of faith is altogether one, alone immovable and irreformable: namely, that we believe in one only God, the almighty Creator of the world, and in his Son Jesus Christ, born of the virgin Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised from the dead on the third day, received into heaven, now seated at the right hand of the Father, destined to come to judge the living and the dead, also through the resurrection of the flesh.”

Moreover, Saint Augustine himself observed this precaution. Thus, in *On the Creed to the Catechumens*, book I, chapter 1, he warned the catechumens:

> “No one writes down the Creed so that it may be read; but, so that forgetfulness may not perhaps erase what careful instruction has handed down, let your memory be your book for reciting it.”

Saint Peter Chrysologus said the same to his own hearers in Sermon 58, which is the second sermon *On the Creed*:

> “Since, then, you are about to receive the Creed . . . prepare your breasts, not paper; sharpen your understanding, not your pen; and write down what you hear not with ink, but with the Spirit who ministers.”

He immediately adds the reason:

> “So that no profane judge, no dishonest examiner, may discover what he could tear to pieces, and what was given for the salvation of one who confesses and believes may not become the ruin of one who despises and does not understand.”

For the same reason Sozomen testifies in book I, chapter 19, that pious and friendly men had advised him not to insert the Nicene Creed in his history, although he had intended to do so, because such mysteries

> “ought to be both spoken and heard only by priests and bishops.”

He approved their advice, since it was likely that some who had not been initiated into the mysteries would read the book through.

## V

Until the time of the Nicene Council, then, from which the Creed emerged in a new form, the Church embraced that apostolic Creed, with very few additions, omissions, or alterations in certain churches—perhaps so that a doctrine attacked by heretics might be impressed more deeply. This nevertheless did not prevent the apostolic Creed from both being called and being regarded as apostolic.

Rufinus noticed this when he said, in the work cited above, no. 3:

> “I think it should not inconveniently be pointed out that in different churches there are certain words added to those found in this text. In the Church of the city of Rome, however, this is not found to have occurred, which I think is because no heresy originated there . . . But in other places, as far as can be understood, certain additions appear to have been made on account of some heretics, so that the meaning of novel teaching might be excluded.”

## VI

But when Arius had vomited forth his poisonous blasphemies against the consubstantiality of the Son of God, the Nicene Council judged that a new Creed should be composed in explicit words, to confront that abominable heresy.

Perhaps someone will think that Hermogenes was its author, on the basis of Letter 82 of Saint Basil to Patrophilus, because Basil says there:

> “Hermogenes, the enemy of the rejected opinion of Arius, as is clear from the faith which was first proclaimed at Nicaea by that man, and so forth.”

In Letter 74 he also calls him bishop of Caesarea. But since, according to Saint Athanasius’ letter to the solitaries, the Arians themselves said not of Hermogenes but of Hosius:

> “He composed the formula of faith at the Council of Nicaea,”

and since it was not Hermogenes but Leontius who was bishop of Caesarea and who attended and subscribed to the Nicene Council, Baronius says under the year 325, no. 33:

> “It is thought that Saint Basil—something human—had a lapse of memory when he says that Hermogenes, the successor of Leontius, sat with the Fathers at the Council of Nicaea.”

Hosius, therefore, is believed to have been the author of the Nicene Creed. Although Hermias Sozomen took care to avoid reporting it in his history, lest it reach profane hands, as stated above, nevertheless, once the faith had been sufficiently established and disseminated, the Fathers and pious men in the Church no longer fearing its profanation began to promulgate it publicly, both orally and in writing, so that they also decreed that it should be sung during the synaxis, as will soon be shown.

But when a new plague of heresy was spreading, something was added to the Nicene Creed at the Council of Constantinople, in order to confront the recent errors. Yet the old name was sometimes retained, and you will find that what was called the Constantinopolitan Creed was also called Nicene by many, especially by the Master of the Sentences, book I, distinction 11.

According to Nicephorus Callistus, book XII, chapter 13, the addition was the work of Gregory of Nyssa, who inserted what concerns the Holy Spirit:

> “They also added to the holy Creed of the Nicene faith the glory of the Holy Spirit, since he is like and equal to the Father and the Son, with Gregory of Nyssa supplying what was lacking in it.”

Pope Damasus, approving the acts of the council presented to him by the Fathers—as may be seen in the letters which the same Callistus reports in the cited work, chapters 16 and 17—may therefore have been the reason why he was eventually believed to have been the author of the Creed sung at Mass.

Durandus states this in *Rationale*, book IV, chapter 25:

> “The Nicene Creed, namely, ‘I believe in one God,’ Pope Damasus instituted to be sung aloud at Mass, by agreement with the universal synod celebrated at Constantinople.”

But it will become clear below that the origin of this singing was different.

## VII

Meanwhile, the Constantinopolitan Creed acquired such great authority among the churches of the world, and especially among the Roman Church, which is the head and mother of the others, and gained such veneration for itself, that it was regarded as sacrilegious either to add even a letter to it or to diminish it.

For when, in the course of time, *Filioque* was added, to indicate against the new heresies of the Greeks and others that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son no less than from the Father, the Roman Church did not admit the addition—not condemning the novelty of the expression, but venerating the antiquity of the earlier formula.

The occasion for the addition in the West was the error of the Priscillianists. The councils of Spain, rising against it, established a formula of faith, which you will find after the First Council of Toledo in the edition of García de Loaysa. Do not, however, suppose that it was composed by that council, since the council was celebrated in the Spanish era 438, that is, in the year of Christ 400, while the title of that rule mentions Pope Leo I, who occupied Peter’s chair from 440 to 461.

It therefore belongs to another council that has perished, says Loaysa; and Pagius asserts elsewhere that it was celebrated at another place during the time of Pope Leo, namely in the year 447, as Baronius had suspected. See Pagius under the year 405, no. 16.

The Spanish confession reads as follows:

> “We believe, etc. . . . that the Paraclete Spirit also exists, who is neither the Father himself nor the Son, but proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Saint Leo, writing to Turibius, bishop of Astorga, Letter 93, chapter 1, concerning the errors of the Priscillianists, said:

> “In the first chapter, therefore, it is demonstrated how impiously they think about the divine Trinity: they assert that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person, as though the same God were now named Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit, and as though the one who begot, the one who was begotten, and the one who proceeded from both were not distinct.”

Do you see that the Spanish Fathers used Leo’s very words? You may rightly therefore believe that, since the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Son as well was asserted so clearly in the confession of faith, the Spaniards had derived it from Leo himself.

## VIII

From Spain the Creed, enlarged by these four syllables, passed into Gaul:

> “In what year is uncertain,” says Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, century IV, dissertation 37, article 3. “Perhaps at the Council of Gentilly, which was celebrated in the year 727 in the presence of King Pippin, where a dispute took place between the Latins and the Greeks concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit.”

But this council was celebrated not in 727 but in 767, according to Ado, who says explicitly:
