> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 767, a synod was held, and a question was debated between the Greeks and Romans concerning the Trinity, and whether the Holy Spirit, just as he proceeds from the Father, also proceeds from the Son.”

Moreover, Pippin, under whose reign the Council of Gentilly is said to have been celebrated, is not called king until the year 752, according to Pagius, following the annalists. Thus the synod was held not in 727 but in 767.

Even before this time, however, the Gauls seem to have admitted the addition. Gregory of Tours, who died in 594, says at the beginning of book I of his *History of the Franks*:

> “I believe that the Holy Spirit proceeded from the Father and the Son.”

He gives this account of his faith before beginning his history, lest he be considered less Catholic.

What the Gallican Church had already received was therefore also received by the other provinces subject to the Frankish king. When Gaul and Germany were already confessing with one voice that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, Italy too embraced the addition.

The first Italian who is encountered as using this formula is our Paulinus. In the Creed which he presented at the Council of Forum Julii in 796, he says explicitly:

> “who proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Indeed, this was something that had to be done anew. For that synod dealt equally with the errors attacking the Incarnation of the Son of God and the procession of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, in the declaration which he added after the Creed, inserting it as though placing food already chewed into the mouth, he says:

> “The Holy Spirit is true God; truly and properly he is the Holy Spirit, and he is not personally the Father or the Son, but proceeds from both.”

## IX

There is no one so unfamiliar with ecclesiastical history that he does not know how many disturbances the Greeks, who fostered this error, raised over the matter.

What is especially astonishing, however, is that the Greeks themselves were often caught by the Westerners corrupting the writings of the Fathers, writings that were genuinely Greek in faith.

Binius already observed in his notes on the Roman Council convened under Pope Agatho in 680 that the four syllables *Filioque* had been removed from the profession of faith in the synodal letter sent by the Roman Fathers to the Council of Constantinople. He says:

> “The Greek impostors corrupted it [the synodal letter], and where it once read, ‘We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son,’ they erased the name *Filioque*.”

Julian the cardinal also noticed this corruption, when it was brought against them at the Council of Florence, following Manuel Calecas.

The result was that they were called falsifiers of the Scriptures. To use the words of the chronicler Briet under the year 780:

> “When it had been written in the profession of faith that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, the Greeks disgracefully erased the name of the Son: they were readily believed to be corrupters of books.”

Nor were the Greeks accused of falsehood and adulterine corruption on that occasion alone.

When Pope Zacharias translated the *Dialogues* of Pope Gregory the Great into Greek, John the Deacon, the writer of Gregory’s Life, says in chapter 75 that they had tampered with the text and erased the name of the Son:

> “Zacharias, bishop of the holy Roman Church, highly learned in the Greek and Latin languages, translated these books into Greek during the time of the Emperor Constantine, nearly 175 years later, and circulated them among the Eastern churches; although the clever perversity of the Greeks, in the passage concerning the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, scraped away the name of the Son on its own initiative and removed it.”

The passage is found in the corrupted version of Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 38, or the final chapter. Gregory’s Latin words are:

> “For since it is certain that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son, etc.”

In Greek it reads:

> **Φανερὸν οὖν ὑπάρχει, ὅτι τὸ Παράκλητον Πνεῦμα ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς προέρχεται, δὲ ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ διαμένει.**

This is translated:

> “It is therefore plainly evident that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds from the Father and remains in the Son.”

Who does not see the corruption of the text? Who does not recognize the Greek sponge erasing it, and the Greek hand substituting a new meaning and new words?

Basnage himself does not deny this, but, as a man who seizes every opportunity to attack the Roman Church, he takes this occasion to accuse Pope Zacharias. In his observations on Gregory the Great’s *Dialogues* and the fragments from them inserted in Henry Canisius’ *Ancient Readings*, volume II, part I, page 88, Amsterdam edition, 1725, he rants as follows:

> “It is worthy of observation that Pope Zacharias, occupying the same Roman see and rendering the Latin of Gregory I into Greek, completely altered the opinion of his predecessor. For Gregory wrote these words (*Dialogues*, book II, chapter 38): ‘For since it is certain that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son’; whereas in Zacharias’ Greek it reads: ‘It is plainly evident that the Paraclete proceeds from the Father and remains in the Son.’ Thus Zacharias embraced the opinion of the Greeks concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father alone; and, what is even more astonishing, he adorned the opinion of his fellow-countrymen with Gregory’s name and attributed it to Gregory contrary to Gregory’s intention. What faith can even heavenly beings, as they are called, have in men if they can impose upon such sluggish readers in this way?”

A fine fellow is Basnage, who judges the text from its fringe!

We know the man to whom the saying applies:

> **Οὗτος ἄν θεῶν ἀγορᾷ δυσφημήσει**  
> “This man would speak ill even in the assembly of the gods.”

Which of the gods descended to tell Basnage that the Greek who corrupted Gregory’s text was Zacharias himself, its translator?

John the Deacon, who flourished in the century after Zacharias, asserts that the translation was Zacharias’, not that Gregory’s text was corrupted by Zacharias.

Moreover, Anastasius, in the Roman edition of his account of Zacharias, 1718, marginal no. 219, gives this testimony concerning the most holy pontiff:

> “This most blessed man, in accordance with ecclesiastical rite and the orthodox pledge of his faith, sent a synodal letter to the Church of Constantinople, and at the same time directed another petition to the most serene Emperor Constantine.”

How can Zacharias be believed to have corrupted Gregory’s text on an article of faith, in order to please his fellow countrymen among the Greeks, when he sent a synodal letter to those very Greeks of Constantinople and to their emperor in accordance with the orthodox pledge of his faith?

But let us leave the man, sometimes intoxicated without wine.

## X

In the year 809, John, a monk in Jerusalem, revived the question of the procession of the Holy Spirit. This controversy, brought into the West, was the reason that Emperor Charlemagne, coming from the Ardennes to Aachen in November, convened a synod, about which Ado and the other Frankish annalists agree unanimously.

Let Bertinianus speak for all under the year 809:

> “The emperor, returning from the Ardennes to Aachen in the month of November, held a council concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. A certain John, a monk in Jerusalem, first raised this question. To settle it, Berengar, bishop of Worms, and Adalard, abbot of the monastery of Corbie, were sent to Rome to Pope Leo.”

Baronius, under the year 809, no. 53, says that the matter concerned not the procession of the Holy Spirit but whether the *Filioque* had rightly and legitimately been added to the Creed by the Spaniards, Gauls, and Germans.

Indeed, what Berengar and Adalard did and said with Leo III—as reported by Smaragdus the abbot and at length by Baronius—concerns whether they had erred in singing the Creed with the addition *Filioque*, with Leo’s assent and approval.

But the agreement of all the writers sufficiently proves that the matter truly concerned the procession of the Holy Spirit, a question raised by the Jerusalem monk who had nothing to do with the syllables added to the Creed by the Westerners.

This is suggested by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, who in the preface to his *Collection of the Sentences of the Ancient Fathers on the Procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son*, addressed to Emperor Charles, says in verse 26:

> “And you will lay your hand upon the matter which that Spirit makes fruitful,  
> The matter concerning which the dispute began in your time.”

The issue, then, was not precisely the addition, but the procession itself, which, as has been shown, had already been discussed in the East and in Spain.

After receiving Charlemagne’s embassy from the Council of Aachen—celebrated in November, with the arrival of the envoys in Rome falling in the following year, 810—Pope Leo acted at length to persuade the legates that, although it was entirely true that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and this must be held as Catholic faith, nevertheless nothing should be added to the Creed, since many other mysteries that are unquestionably matters of faith were not inserted in the Creed.

See the acts of this matter in Baronius.

Leo therefore concluded that care should be taken that the Creed not be sung with the addition. The example should begin at the royal palace: the addition *Filioque* should be omitted there wherever its use had been introduced; the other churches would more easily follow the royal example.

Meanwhile, Leo, extremely devoted to ancient rites, erected two silver shields, as it were two supports or defenses, one inscribed in Latin and the other in Greek with the Creed without the addition.

Anastasius, in his account of Leo III, no. 410, says:

> “He [Leo], out of love for and caution on behalf of the orthodox faith, had two silver shields made, as stated above—that is, in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter—each inscribed with the Creed, one in Greek letters and the other in Latin, hanging on the right and left above the entrance to the body of the church; together they weighed ninety-four pounds and six ounces.”

In the basilica of Saint Paul he erected another, concerning which the same Librarian says, no. 411:

> “He also had a shield of the purest silver made above the entrance to the body of the church, on which he had the Creed of the orthodox faith written; it weighed thirty-two pounds.”

Such is Anastasius’ account of Leo.

## XI

But what Leo had done out of veneration for the practice of the ancient Church was brought forward in that same century by Photius, the leader of the schismatics, as proof of his own error.

The matter proceeded as follows. Before the year 883, the patriarch of Aquileia communicated by letter with Photius of Constantinople. Baronius, narrating the history under that year, names no one. It is plausible, however, that the man was Walpert, who held the see at least until 884 and was succeeded by Frederick.

It seems more plausible to the younger Palladius, in *History of Forum Julii*, part I, book III, that he was called Gradensis, though sometimes Aquileian, because the patriarchs of Grado had greater and easier communion and familiarity with the Greeks than did the Aquileians, who had formerly been devoted to the Lombards and were then devoted to the Western empire.

Thus readily do we shake the dirt from our own bosom and throw it upon a neighbor and associate. If anything appeared here that brought honor to our people, I fear that my Palladius would have credited the Gradians with it.

Among these men I find no one who did not flourish in praiseworthy life and integrity during this period. From Ughelli’s account of the patriarchs of Grado, from 854 to 897, no one appears who did not maintain communion with the Roman See, as is clearly established by the reception of the pallium or by summonses to councils.

It seems serious and harsh to condemn our Walpert as responsible for this error, since his communion with the Roman pontiff is established by a letter of Pope John VIII, letter 48, indiction 10, which falls in the year 877, as appears from the preceding and following letters. It was addressed to John of Ravenna, Ansbert of Milan, and Vaipert—that is, Walpert—archbishop of Aquileia. It may be seen in the *Councils*, volume XI, Venice edition, 1730.

Lupus preceded Walpert, and Lupus was preceded by Hindelmar, who held the see in 857, as is clear from a diploma of Louis II, which the supplementer to Ughelli, at the suggestion of the distinguished Apostolo Zeno, presents, dated in the fifth indiction, which falls in the year 857, the tenth year of Louis’ reign. Yet these details do not agree among themselves.

The year 858 is marked as the fifth indiction, but it is Louis’ second year. Louis’ tenth year, however, is 866, marked by the fourteenth indiction. Perhaps the two first characters, X and I, were omitted in the notation of the indiction.

They extend Hindelmar’s tenure to the twenty-first year, so that his death would fall in 877, the year in which Walpert received the letter from Pope John. Between Hindelmar and Walpert they place Lupus, whose period in the see cannot be determined if all these details are accepted.

If you refuse to believe that the letter to Photius was written by Hindelmar because its date is too late, or by Walpert because he had communicated with the Roman Church, or by Frederick because he was later, and therefore refuse to believe that any of these men was a schismatic, as Baronius says, consider whether Lupus—an episcopal figure of neither great duration nor renown—could bear this mark, and whether, in name as well as in fact, he may have been a wolf in Christ’s fold.

Whoever he was, then, he wrote to Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, a schismatic to a schismatic and a traitor to a traitor, says Baronius.

He wrote because, appearing to be the only Latin who held this opinion, he sought assistance from the Greeks. Photius did not fail to answer the request. He sent back a lengthy letter, cunning as well as eloquent, in which, by praising both the sender and the bearer who delivered the letter, by exalting his own opinion and depressing the opposing one, by misrepresenting the Fathers, misinterpreting the synods, and, in almost everything, lying, he attempted to uproot orthodox doctrine completely and confirm the patriarch of Aquileia in error.

Here are a few words. The title reads:

> “Of Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, to the archbishop of Aquileia, that is, of Venetia, concerning those who affirm with blasphemous mouth that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son.”

The letter continues:

> “The letters of Your Beatitude delivered to us first revealed your mind, which is according to God, and also the affection of your spirit, which is great and exalted and surpasses the condition of ordinary men. Then we admired the man who brought them to us . . . It has reached our ears that certain Westerners introduce by a new dogma that the divine and most holy Spirit proceeds not only from God the Father but also from the Son. This is in no way to be tolerated.”

After Photius had loudly and boastfully asserted that the patriarchal sees supported him, he maliciously brought forward even Leo the Great, who, in condemning Eutyches and Nestorius, said that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father but not from the Son. He added:

> “Likewise the younger Leo, who imitated not only his name but also his faith . . . so that our immaculate doctrine of faith might in no way be corrupted by a barbarous tongue, he handed down the glorification and celebration of the Holy Trinity in the Greek language to the Westerners. And he not only arranged for this to be done by word and command, but also inscribed it on certain supports, constructed as shields and erected as columns, and, setting them up in full view of all, placed them at the doors of the Church.”

Thus Photius turned to the service of his own cause what the prudent Leo III had done at that time.

## XII

It is difficult to establish the period when the addition *Filioque*, inserted into the Creed in the course of time, was finally received by the Roman Church; nor is it yet known who was its first author.

Manuel Calecas, in book IV *Against the Greeks*, says that some made Damasus its author:

> “They say that after the First Council a certain heresy arose which applied the name of Son to the Father. In Greek it was called **υἱοπατρία** (*huiopatria*), and it declared that the Son was the Father of the Holy Spirit, while the Spirit himself was the Father’s grandson. Therefore Damasus, who was then bishop of Rome, convened a council and added to the Creed that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son, opposing those who said that he was born from the Son. For one who proceeds from the Father through the Son and is said to proceed from the Father and the Son cannot have been generated from the Son.”

But to Alexius Aristenus, who likewise makes Damasus the author of the addition, Natalis Alexander replies in *Ecclesiastical History*, century IV, dissertation 37, article 3: Theodoret, who reports Damasus’ synodal letter, does not mention this matter; surely he would not have omitted it if Damasus had been the first to receive the addition.

As for the fact that the words *Filioque* are found in the Creed circulated under Damasus’ name among Jerome’s works, this is to be regarded as worthless, since all the more learned agree that the Creed is not Damasus’. For how could it have happened that, if Damasus had decreed that *Filioque* be added to the Creed, Leo III, several centuries later, would have so harshly rejected the addition made by the Spaniards and Franks and defended the Creed so stubbornly without it?

Bellarminus, *Controversies*, volume I, book II, chapters 21 and 29, *On Christ*, assigns the time of the addition to the sixth century. He says:

> “The Greeks were not unaware that the addition had been made, yet they remained silent for approximately three hundred years and did not create a schism, as is evident, because the addition was made around the year 600.”

He had prefaced this with:

> “For Hormisdas, in his letter to the Emperor Justin, explicitly wrote that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

Against this assertion of Bellarminus the same response applies: Leo III would not have been displeased by the addition if one of his predecessors had established it.

Moreover, in that letter of Hormisdas—letter 79, volume V of the Venice edition of the *Councils*—he does not speak precisely of the Creed but of the mystery of the Trinity. Speaking of the Holy Spirit, he adds:

> “It is known that it is proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son within the one substance of the Godhead.”

The fact that this truth is repeatedly affirmed by the Fathers does not therefore allow one to infer that the addition had also been admitted into the Creed.

## XIII

If conjecture is permitted in this matter, it becomes highly probable that, not by the decree of any general council or Roman pontiff, but around the time of Nicholas I, when the particular churches had long since received the addition, it was introduced into the Creed of the Roman Church as well because the new and more aggressive schism of the Greeks demanded it, and was confirmed by reception rather than by any decree.

Or, if you prefer, perhaps a lesser council—such as that of Forum Julii, which first added it to the Creed in Italy in 796—or a national council—such as that of Aachen in 809, at which the Greeks complained that they had not been summoned and which therefore was not plenary—added the particle *Filioque*.

Once usage itself had approved the novelty and the pontiff had ratified it, some perhaps believed, though incorrectly, that it had been confirmed by some formal decree of the pontiff and a general synod.

Saint Thomas seems to hold this view in *Summa theologica*, I, question 36, article 2, reply to objection 2:

> “When the error of certain persons arose, it was expressly stated, in a certain council convened in the Western regions, by the authority of the Roman pontiff, by whose authority the ancient councils also used to be convened and confirmed.”

The words “in a certain council” do not seem to indicate a general council. A general council is not of such slight importance that it is ordinarily designated merely as “a certain council.”

What the Angelic Doctor adds—that it was stated by the authority of the Roman pontiff—indicates nothing other than that the authority of the Roman pontiff was added to strengthen what had been done by the council.

For by bringing forward as an example the ancient councils confirmed by the pontiff, Saint Thomas indicates that the particle *Filioque* was not inserted precisely by the pontiff’s command, but was inserted by the Fathers and approved by the pontiff when he confirmed the council.

This conjecture is confirmed by the complaint of the Greeks themselves, mentioned in that Constantinopolitan treatise written by the Friars Preachers in Constantinople itself in 1252. Peter Stevartius publishes it among the observations and notes on the works of Calecas, collected from various Greek sources, at the end of the works of Manuel Calecas.

There it reads:

> “The second cause of the division [of the Greeks from the Latins] was that they were not summoned to the Ultramontane Council, when the expression *Filioque* was added.”

It was therefore not a general council. Perhaps this Ultramontane Council was the Council of Aachen in 809, as stated above.

## XIV

Dionysius Petavius, *Theological Dogmatics*, volume II, *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapter 2, no. 4, conjectures from the encyclical of Photius, which will be cited shortly, that either under Nicholas I or around his time the syllables *Filioque* were added to the Creed.

Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, century IV, dissertation 37, article 3, also seems to hold this view. If the question concerns the period, there is almost nothing that can be brought against it, since the circumstances of that time suggest it, and the very words of Photius, which will soon be produced, point in the same direction.

But that Nicholas I himself was the author of the addition in the Roman Church is denied with sufficient probability by our Baronius under the year 883, no. 35:

> “If this had been so,” he says, “Photius would have railed more vehemently against Pope Nicholas himself, who had introduced it into the Creed. But although in two letters he attacks the Roman Church with the utmost bitterness, he never taunts him with having inserted it into the Nicene Creed.”

Among the words of Photius in his encyclical letter addressed to the Alexandrian and the other patriarchal sees of the East—which contains enormous calumnies and falsehoods, and is cited by Petavius and Natalis Alexander—the following bear upon our subject:

> “O the devices of the evil demon! They most foolishly proclaim that the Holy Spirit proceeds not from the Father alone but also from the Son.”

Baronius gives the entire letter under the year 863, no. 34, from the translation of Frederick Metius, who, in Baronius’ words,

> “translated it into Latin with the greatest diligence, comparing the Vallicellian manuscript with that of the Greek College, and labored greatly in examining them.”

He translates the passage as follows:

> “O the arts of the evil demon! They newly teach that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son.”

Two words resolve the difficulty, if Metius’ translation is accepted. For if Photius is attacking errors that, as an impostor claimed, had recently been introduced by the Latins themselves, and if he is speaking of the addition *Filioque* made to the Creed, it becomes most evident that the word had been added at about this time.

The Greek text in Petavius, at the cited place, reads:

> **Ὢ τῆς τοῦ πονηροῦ μηχανημάτων· τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον οὐκ ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς μόνον, ἀλλὰ γε καὶ ἐκ τοῦ Υἱοῦ πορεύεσθαι κενολογήσαντες.**

Strictly speaking, **κενολογήσαντες**, written with epsilon, means “speaking vainly.” But if it is written with the diphthong **αι**, namely **καινολογήσαντες**, it must be interpreted as “speaking new things.”

For **κενόν** means “vain,” whereas **καινόν** means “new.”

What Photius wrote is uncertain. The similarity of the words could easily have led copyists to take one for the other. The second reading, however, seems more probable, and it should be interpreted as “speaking new things,” because Photius accused the Latins of novelty in doctrines and rites.

Whatever the case concerning the spelling of the word, Photius intended to accuse the addition of novelty. From this accusation it may be inferred that around this time the Roman Church added the word *Filioque* to the Creed.

### XV

But when did the Creed begin to be sung in the synaxis [Col. 0606A]? Caranza, in the *Summary of the Councils*, at the end of the canon of the First Council of Carthage, puts forward Pope Mark, successor of Sylvester, as the author of this practice. Durandus confirms this in Book IV, chapter 25, when he first says that it was “instituted by Damasus to be openly sung 233,” and then adds: “Although Pope Mark had also first decreed that it be sung in a loud voice.” Among more recent writers, Dominicus Macer holds this view in his *Hierolexicon*, under “Creed.”

Yet, in my judgment, it is in no way probable that the Roman pontiffs were the authors of a rite which they themselves did not admit in their own Church, and that only belatedly they received and approved a custom already practiced elsewhere. The Creed is found in the liturgies of the Eastern churches from ancient times. In the books circulated under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, and specifically in *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 3, part II, by the name of the hymn of praise and confession preceding the placing of the holy bread and the chalice of blessing upon the altar, the Scholiast of Stavelot understands the Creed of faith. If this is correct, it must be understood of the Apostles’ Creed, which is older than all the others [Col. 0606B].

In the Liturgy of Saint Basil the Great, in the third litany, this rubric is appended: “Deacon: Let us attend and sing the Creed. And everyone sings the Creed, with the archdeacon beginning.” Basil’s Creed, if it is not the Apostles’ Creed, can be nothing other than the simple Nicene Creed. For the Constantinopolitan Creed did not emerge until the Council of Constantinople in 381. Basil, however, died in 379, on the first of January.

Something different must nevertheless be said about the Creed contained in the liturgy commonly attributed to Saint John Chrysostom. Since Chrysostom came to the see of Constantinople in 398, that is, after the Council of Constantinople had been held, it is reasonable to believe that he used no other Creed than the one recently issued by that council. This becomes still clearer from a comparison of the Creeds: in Chrysostom’s Creed one finds “maker of heaven and earth,” words added by the Constantinopolitan council and absent from the Nicene Creed.

Even if one maintains that the Creed was added to these later liturgies in the centuries of their authors, it is nevertheless proved that the Eastern churches preceded ours in this matter. For Theodore the Reader, in Book II of his *Collectanea*, and Nicephorus Callistus, whom he follows, in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book XVI, chapter 35, say that Timothy was the author of the practice of singing the Creed in the synaxis:

> “Timothy, at the request of his friends”—these are the Reader’s words—“arranged that the Creed of the faith of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers should be recited at every synaxis, namely to rebuke Macedonius, as though he had not accepted this Creed, whereas previously it had been recited only once a year, namely on Good Friday, during the time of the Lord’s Passion, when the bishop catechized.”

This Timothy died in the year 511. Others, however, in the aforementioned Nicephorus, Book XV, chapter 28, include among the innovations of Peter the Fuller the following:

> “That the holy Creed, which previously had been recited only once, on the great and holy day of Good Friday, should be sung at every synaxis and gathering of the church.”

[Col. 0606D] Cardinal Bona, in *Liturgical Matters*, Book II, chapter 8, no. 2, attempts to reconcile these opinions as follows:

> “But perhaps the former”—Peter the Fuller, who flourished in the time of Zeno, that is, toward the end of the fourth century, and died before Timothy—“introduced this custom in the Church of Antioch; the latter”—Timothy—in the Church of Constantinople. Later the Spaniards were the first among the Latins to adopt it.”

### XVI

P. le Brun explains the spread of this rite in the West at greater length in volume II, dissertation 5, *On the Hispanic or Mozarabic Liturgy*, article 1. He investigates a more remote source, but it is not worth pausing here to disclose it. It is enough to know that at the Third Council of Toledo, assembled under Pope Pelagius II by order of King Reccared, on the eighth day before the Ides of May in the Hispanic era 627, the Fathers of the council proposed that the Eastern churches should be imitated in this matter.

The second chapter reads as follows:

> “Out of reverence for the most holy faith, and in order to strengthen the weak minds of human beings, the holy synod, with the counsel of our most devout and glorious lord King Reccared [Col. 0607A], has decreed that in all the churches of Spain and Galicia, according to the practice of the Eastern churches and of the Council of Constantinople—that is, of the one hundred and fifty bishops—the Creed of faith shall be recited, so that before the Lord’s Prayer is said it may be sung aloud by the people.”

P. le Brun reads not “by the people” but “to the people.” We consider this the purer and more genuine reading.

In accordance with the decree of this chapter, Cardinal Ximenes inserted the Creed into the Mozarabic liturgy, to be recited before Communion. The prescription there reads:

> “The priest shall raise the body of Christ so that it may be seen by the people, and the choir shall say the Creed, two by two, namely: ‘We believe in one God,’ etc.”

After this the priest breaks the Eucharist. The same is found in the liturgy used by Saint Leander, except that there the priest breaks the Eucharist not afterward but while the Creed is being sung.

### XVII

Just as the Creed with the addition *Filioque* passed from the Spaniards to the Gauls, then to the Germans, and then to our own Carnic or Forum-Julian peoples, neighbors of the Germans, so the practice of singing the Creed at Mass migrated from Spain into these provinces. It is difficult to assign the time when this began.

Walafrid Strabo, who flourished shortly after Charlemagne, says in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 22:

> “Among the Gauls and Germans, after the deposition of Felix the heretic, condemned under the glorious Charles, ruler of the Franks, the same Creed began to be recited more widely and more frequently in the offices of the Mass.”

If it is said to have been done more widely and more frequently afterward, it is clear that it had already been done previously, though more restrictively and less often.

The Gauls did not do this without consulting the Roman pontiff, as appears from the dialogue between the envoys of Charlemagne, sent from the Council of Aachen in 809, and Leo III, which Baronius reports under that year, nos. 54 and following. In no. 60 he says that Charlemagne’s envoys spoke to Leo as follows:

> “Was it not by your authority that permission was given in the Church to sing the Creed? [Col. 0607C] Did this practice of singing proceed from us to this place? …  
> **The Pope:** I gave permission to sing it, but not to add anything by singing it, etc.”

The Franks, therefore, were not themselves the first to introduce the rite. They received it from elsewhere, namely from Spain, and used it only after obtaining permission from the Roman pontiff. Since Leo admits that he granted this permission, he could not have granted it before the year 795, when he is said to have become pope, and therefore not before the Council of Frankfurt in 794, at which the Felician heresy was condemned.

Since that condemnation was the reason for singing the Creed more frequently, as has just been said with Strabo, it seems that one should conclude that at the beginning of Leo’s pontificate the Creed began to be sung more frequently at Mass.

Although in 809 Leo exerted every effort with Charlemagne’s legates to remove the rite from the Gallican Church, because he himself strongly detested the novelty of the addition *Filioque*, and urged that it be omitted in the royal chapel so that the other churches might more quickly unlearn what they might have learned from the example of the royal chapel, his effort nevertheless proved fruitless. For in that same century the rite spread everywhere and was accepted by all the Gallican churches, so that bishops issued statutes for its observance.

Such is the statute of Herard, bishop of Tours, issued as no. 16 among the capitularies delivered at a synod in 858, in the sixth indiction, in the third year of his episcopate, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June:

> “Concerning the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed: let everyone know them by heart; and let the *Gloria Patri*, the *Sanctus*, the *Credulity*, and the *Kyrie eleison* be sung reverently by all. Likewise, let the Psalms be sung distinctly by the clergy. And let priests not begin the Secret before the *Sanctus* has ended, and let them sing the *Sanctus* with the people.”

Apart from the opening words, everything else plainly seems to concern the Mass. The Creed that he calls for memorization is the Apostles’ Creed. By “Credulity” he understands the Nicene or Constantinopolitan Creed, to be sung at the Mass about which he is speaking.

That the “Credulity” itself is the Creed is also gathered from Charlemagne’s general letter to the archbishops of the Frankish kingdom, in volume I of the *Capitularies*, p. 483. There he distinguishes it from the Apostles’ Creed, namely the Nicene Creed. He says that he wishes to know how the priests teach the people:

> “Concerning the Creed, what its interpretation is according to the Latins; concerning the Credulity, how one ought to believe in God the Father almighty, and in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Spirit … [Col. 0608A] the Holy, the holy catholic Church, and the rest that follows in the same Creed.”

He has two Creeds: the first is the Apostles’ Creed; the other, which he calls the “Credulity,” is the Nicene or Constantinopolitan Creed itself.

### XVIII

Finally, the Roman Church adopted the practice of singing the Creed at Mass in 1014, under Benedict VIII, at the insistence of the most holy Emperor Henry. The account is given by Berno, abbot of Reichenau (Augia Major, or Augia Dives), who was present at the events.

In his short work *On Certain Matters Concerning the Mass*, chapter 2, speaking of the angelic hymn *Gloria in excelsis*, which some did not sing because the Romans sang it very rarely, he adds:

> “For if we are forbidden to sing that angelic hymn on feast days because Roman priests are not accustomed to sing it, we may in the same way remain silent about the Creed after the Gospel, which the Romans until these times, in the memory of the divine Emperor Henry, had in no way sung. But when they were asked by him why they acted in this way, I heard them, while I was present, give this answer: namely, that the Roman Church had never been infected by any filth of heresy, etc. … But the lord emperor did not desist until, with the agreement of all, he persuaded the lord Benedict the Apostolic that they should sing it at the public Mass. Whether they still observe this custom, however, we cannot affirm, because we do not know it with certainty.”

Berno wrote this after the year 1024, when Saint Henry died, and before the year 1048, when Berno himself died. The events, however, occurred earlier, namely in 1014, when the emperor was staying at Rome, intending to receive the imperial crown from the pontiff.

From this year, therefore, the Creed began to be sung in the Roman rite, whereas previously it had not been. Accordingly, Alcuin, Amalarius, Rabanus, Remigius, and all who wrote before this time about the order of the Roman Mass do not mention it. Nor does any trace of it appear in the ancient sacramentaries, if one accepts the observation of the eminent Cardinal John Bona, who noted this in *Liturgical Matters*, Book II, chapter 8, no. 2.

### XIX

But now let us draw in our sails and turn our discourse to the Aquileian Creed:

> “And indeed, now at the very end of my labor,  
> I draw in my sails and hasten to turn my prow toward land.”

This Creed is none other than the Apostles’ Creed, apart from a few words that are varied, added, or omitted. Take it in its fairly pure form from Rufinus, a priest of the Church of Aquileia, and compare it with the common form; you will see how much addition, omission, or alteration has been inserted. It is as follows:

> “I believe in God the Father almighty, invisible and impassible; [Col. 0608D] and in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord; who was born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary; crucified under Pontius Pilate and buried, he descended to the lower regions; on the third day he rose from the dead; he ascended into heaven; he sits at the right hand of the Father; from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. The holy Church. The remission of sins. The resurrection of this flesh.”

This is the Aquileian Creed in Rufinus, as published after the works of Cyprian by Stephanus Baluzius—that is, by a certain Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, who completed the work begun by Baluzius.

Du Pin, in his recension of the Aquileian Creed, differs from this in several places. He attributes the reading “I believe in God,” etc., to scribal error and restores “I believe in God” with the accusative, etc. Rufinus’s annotator defends his reading from three manuscript codices. When Pamelius restores the accusative in the examples of other Creeds found in Jerome and Augustine, he replies:

> “Pamelius’s arguments prove that in most Creeds one usually says ‘I believe in God’; but they by no means prove that this was also the reading in the Creed of the Church of Aquileia. Indeed, the more usual the accusative was in the Creeds, the less probable it is that scribes, whether through carelessness or deliberately, would have placed the ablative in this Creed. It is not at all surprising, however, if, when they found the ablative, they inserted the accusative, offended by its novelty. Therefore, the codices in which one reads ‘I believe in God,’ etc., and ‘in Christ,’ and ‘in the Holy Spirit,’ seem to me to preserve more accurately the custom of the Church of Aquileia than those that use the accusative.

> “This manner of pronouncing the Creed does not seem to have been adopted by this Church without a council; rather, it was adopted so that the distinction of the three divine persons might be clearer from the articles that follow: ‘the holy Church,’ etc.”

Indeed, in our Rufinus the verb “I believe” is not repeated before “the holy Church,” as it is repeated in Du Pin. From this one may infer the reason for the ablative used with the persons of the Trinity: in these we believe *in* them, in distinction from the accusative, by which the faith is expressed through which we believe that the Church exists. Rufinus suggests this in the cited work, no. 36, as does Venantius Fortunatus at the beginning of Book XI.

### XX

Three noteworthy features are added to this Creed, in the first, fourth, and final articles.

The first reads: “I believe in God the Father almighty, invisible and impassible.” This is omitted by Du Pin, yet Rufinus gives the reason for the addition in *Exposition of the Apostles’ Creed*, §§ 4–5, in these words:

> “It should be known that these two expressions are not found in the Creed of the Roman Church. Among us, however, they are evidently added because of the heresy of Sabellius, specifically that which our people call Patripassianism—that is, the doctrine that says either that the Father himself was born from the Virgin and became visible, or that he suffered in the flesh. Therefore, in order to exclude such impiety concerning the Father, our predecessors seem to have added these words and called the Father invisible and impassible.”

Yet one finds this addition in the Creed of the Eastern churches as well, inserted for the same reason.

### XXI

The article “He descended to the lower regions” seems peculiar to the Aquileian Creed, since it is found nowhere in the other Creeds except the common form, “He descended into hell.”

Rufinus says in § 18:

> “It should be known that the words ‘He descended to the lower regions’ are not added in the Creed of the Roman Church, nor are they found in the churches of the East. Nevertheless, the force of the expression seems to be the same in the statement that he was buried.”

Because it is absent from the other Creeds, most commentators omit its explanation when expounding the Creed. Those who have undertaken to explain it—Richard the Hermit and Bruno, bishop of Würzburg—have drawn their words not from the common form, “He descended into hell,” but from the Aquileian form, “He descended to the lower regions.”

Venantius Fortunatus, who knew the Aquileian Creed very well, being close to it in both birthplace and origin, has “He descended into hell.” He explains it as follows:

> “By descending into hell he suffered no injury, because he did so out of mercy, as a king entering a prison—not so that he himself might be held, but so that the guilty might be released.”

The reason for its absence from the other Creeds is given, if one believes Macer in his *Hierolexicon*, under “Creed,” as follows: no one had yet arisen who doubted its truth, and no heretic had attacked this doctrine.

Bellarminus, indeed, in volume I, Book IV, chapter 6, concerning Christ’s soul, admits that:

> “This clause, ‘He descended into hell,’ is now found everywhere. It is likewise read in Luther’s larger and smaller Catechisms, and also in those of Calvin, Brenz, and others. The Centuriators likewise read it in Century I, Book II, chapter 4, as does Peter Martyr in his short work *On the Creed*. Indeed, Calvin, in Book II of the *Institutes*, chapter 16, § 8, says that this article should be counted among the principal ones.”

But in this matter Calvin should be viewed with suspicion, for the following verse is proverbial:

> Λόγον παρ’ ἐχθροῦ μὴ ποτ’ ἡγήσῃ φίλον  
> “Never consider an enemy’s words friendly.”

Calvin magnifies the article concerning Christ’s descent into hell in order to establish his wicked and impious doctrine about Christ’s torments in hell and the punishments of the damned [Col. 0610A].

Although this article had no heretical opponents, it nevertheless did not lack an opponent, whether genuine or apparent, as Petavius testifies in *On the Incarnation*, Book XIII, chapter 15. He means Erasmus, who, discussing this article, says, according to Petavius:

> “Recently he expressed an opinion insufficiently fair to the Catholic confession, and showed himself inclined toward it.”

After Petavius had cited in chapters 16 and 17 innumerable—indeed, one might almost say countless—testimonies of both Greek and Latin Fathers establishing the truth of this article, he attacks and reproves Erasmus in chapter 18. Although Erasmus does not openly oppose the doctrine, he speaks of it less reverently than one ought to speak of an article of faith.

It is worthwhile to present some selected passages from Petavius, by whom Erasmus is deservedly chastised:

> “Nor should Erasmus be heard, when in chapter 4 of his *Catechism*, concerning the clause of the Creed ‘He descended to the lower regions,’ he brings the matter to the point that, although he does not think this clause ought to be entirely rejected, nor rashly condemned because of the authority of the Church, he nevertheless refuses to admit with sufficient certainty that it was added to the Creed, as he suspects. At this point he heaps together many absurdities, plainly deserving of no light correction.

> “The first is that he says Cyprian declared that this article is not found in the Roman Creed, nor is it added in the churches of the East. The Cyprian whom he names there is not Cyprian but Rufinus, as no one with even a little learning today is unaware. This error might have been excused in another writer, whom we might suppose to have merely skimmed that little work, excerpting the passage from among Cyprian’s works without reading the rest. But this excuse has no place in the case of Erasmus, who published Cyprian and carefully revised him. Who, then, would not be astonished at the man’s ἀπροσεξίαν—his lack of attention—and thoughtlessness, not to use a harsher term, when he failed to notice how many things in that treatise could have alerted anyone who was not completely dull that it was not Cyprian’s work but that of another, much later in age? …

> “Likewise, he names the Church of Aquileia, in which he asserts that he was initiated by baptism. Surely this alone could have taught any stupid person that the work was not Cyprian’s.”

Petavius proceeds to refute the remaining trifles of this contentious critic. See him there; there is no time to review everything.

### XXII

The final article of the Aquileian Creed reads: “The resurrection of this flesh.” When this was said, the hand touched the forehead with the sign of the cross, as was and is customary among the devout. Thus it was the flesh that was touched, and in this flesh, not in another, each person professed that he would rise.

After Rufinus had collected various testimonies from Scripture to establish the truth of the resurrection of the flesh, especially from the Book of Job, no. 45, he continues:

> “Consider how consonant the addition of the word ‘this’ is with all the passages we mentioned from examples in the divine books. For what else is indicated in the words of Job that we explained above, when he says, ‘He will raise up my skin, which now endures this,’ that is, which suffers these torments? Does he not plainly say that the resurrection of this flesh is to come—of this flesh, I mean, which now endures the anguish of tribulations and temptations?”

He says something similar in Book I of the *Invectives*, near the beginning. After saying that thirty years earlier he had entered the monastery, been regenerated through baptism, and received the seal of faith from the holy men Chromatius, then a priest, Jovinus, the archdeacon, and Eusebius, deacon of Saint Valerian, he adds:

> “For greater certainty in the matter … I disclose the principal mystery of our Church … The holy Church of Aquileia, foreseeing by the Spirit of God the future accusations against us, when it hands down the resurrection of the flesh adds a syllable of a single pronoun. In place of what the others say, ‘the resurrection of the flesh,’ we say, ‘the resurrection of this flesh,’ so that, touching the forehead with the sign at the end of the Creed, as is customary, and confessing with the mouth the resurrection of this flesh—namely, the flesh that we touch—we may close every avenue for the accusations of every poisonous tongue against us.”

Rufinus was addressing an objection that could be brought against him because he stood for Origen, who removed the distinction of sex in those who are raised. But his labor was fruitless, for Saint Jerome exposed the device in *Apology II against Rufinus*:

> “I do not ask about what you write, namely, that the same flesh in which we live will rise again, with no member amputated and no part of the body cut away—for these are your own words. But I ask what Origen denies: whether bodies will be raised in the same sex in which they died … You ought either to have said this or denied it.”

Here one may also cite Gregory, *Moral Commentary*, Book XIV, chapter 29, on the words of Job, “And again I shall be clothed with my skin.” He reports that Eutychius of Constantinople, who denied the true resurrection of bodies, was so thoroughly confuted by him that, when dying, he held the skin of his hand and said: “I confess that we shall all rise in this flesh.”

### XXIII

These, then, are the additions in the Aquileian Creed. The principal omissions are “the communion of saints” and “eternal life.”

The first, although it is not inserted, is understood in the word “Church.” Accordingly, it is rather an exposition of that article than a distinct article of faith, as we are taught in the *Roman Catechism*, section 24.

“Eternal life” is absent not only from the Aquileian Creed but also from the Eastern and Roman Creeds—the latter being truly Apostolic—and is found only in the common form.

Saint Jerome, in Letter 61, against the errors of John of Jerusalem, says:

> “After the confession of the Trinity and the unity of the Church, the entire mystery of Christian doctrine is brought to a close by the resurrection of the flesh.”

But eternal life is included in the resurrection of the flesh, as Rufinus suggests in the cited passage, no. 45:

> “Therefore the body that will rise from the dead will be incorruptible and immortal, not only that of the righteous but also that of sinners.”

And if the body, then also the soul, through which the body will live eternally.

# SIXTH DISSERTATION. ON THE ALTINUM CREED

[Col. 0611]

### I

Father Antonius Pagi, in the *Baronian Criticism*, under the year 802 of Christ, no. 5, has these words:

> “Baluzius promises in the Preface to Book I of the *Miscellanea* that he will publish the complete letter of Saint Paulinus written to Charlemagne concerning the events that took place at the Council of Altinum.”

By these words he clearly indicates that he had not seen it. Indeed, he could not have seen it complete, since he died at Aix-en-Provence in 1699, on the Nones of June, whereas the letters did not appear among Baluzius’s *Miscellanea* until 1715. In volume VII, Baluzius himself publishes the letter promised in volume I, complete, from the papers of the distinguished man Jacques Sirmond, on page 6. From this source we too have drawn it and placed it in its proper position among the works of Paulinus.

Baronius, under the year 802, nos. 7 and following, and the collectors of the councils give the beginning and end of the letter. We corrected, from the Vatican manuscript used by Baronius—although he admits that it is quite faulty—and from the Councils in the Labbe edition, the errors with which the Baluzius edition abounds.

Since the Vatican manuscript is incomplete, however, it was possible to correct only the beginning and end of the letter. For the remaining portions, we extend our notes and observations by conjecture, so that some light may shine upon an otherwise none-too-clear discourse. Paulinus’s style, if ever at any other time, is here entangled in a definite abundance—or, rather, jumble—of words, and displays an even more inflated phrasing than appears in his other writings. The corrupted taste of the age demanded this, and he himself pursued elaborate expressions, so that the letter might appear worthy of a prince and of a royal court.

Three matters concerning it call for more subtle examination and greater precision: namely, what the principal or immediate cause of the council mentioned in the letter was, apart from the common causes; in what year and season the council was convened; and finally, by what right it was convened at Altinum.

### II

As one begins to examine the intimate cause for convening the Council of Altinum, the opinion of Father Bernardo Maria de Rubeis, a most learned man, immediately presents itself at the outset. Since, as we shall show below, we are compelled by clear arguments to dissent from him, we must not only report his view but also refute it wherever necessary. We do not doubt that a man so devoted to truth will accept this fairly and in good faith.

In his dissertation *On the Aquileian Schism*, chapter 21, he does not accept the crime committed by Mauritius, son of the duke of Venice, against John of Grado, which is commonly regarded—if not as the sole cause, at least as the principal cause—of the council, as we said in the *Life of Saint Paulinus*, chapter 12, no. 4. Instead, he says that the words of the letter that disclose the crime must be referred to the injuries inflicted upon Pope Leo III at Rome by Paschal and Campulus during the litanies on 25 April 799, and that the council was celebrated later in the same year [Col. 0612B].

He says:

> “It is wrongly said that the monstrous crime mentioned by Paulinus concerned the Venetians, who deprived the bishop of Grado of his life. Rather, it must be understood of what was attempted at Rome against the most holy pontiff Leo III.”

And in the following section:

> “This occurred in the year 799, as the writers commonly reckon. From this it is inferred that Paulinus held the Council of Altinum in the same year. Anastasius specifies the day on which the great sacrilege was committed, when Leo, following his customary practice, proceeded in the litanies that everyone calls the greater litanies: namely, 25 April. During these days, in the paschal season, Paulinus celebrated his customary synod at Altinum, and reported the notorious criminal deed to King Charles for punishment.”

### III

The arguments themselves by which he was led to this opinion must be examined.

1. The reason is that Charlemagne is never called emperor in the letter, but only king. He was called emperor in the year 800, before the murder of the bishop of Grado had occurred. If, therefore, the death of the patriarch of Grado had not yet occurred, it could not have been the reason for convening the council.

2. Because, just as Anastasius says that Leo was left half-dead by his attackers, Paulinus likewise says that priests were left half-dead.

3. The chronological period Paulinus had in mind when he alludes to the law of Leviticus 19:23—concerning the prohibition against eating the fruit of fruit-bearing trees from the first year of planting through the fifth—suggests an interruption of synods, namely from the Council of Frankfurt in 794 to the Council of Altinum in 799. In the year 799, however, the crime occurred not against the patriarch of Grado but against the Roman pontiff. Therefore, Paulinus’s letter and synod concern the latter crime, not the former.

These are the principal arguments, or conjectures, of P. de Rubeis.

### IV

To the first it may be answered, first, that the Vatican manuscript reads “to the emperor.” Pagi approves this reading under the year 802, no. 4.

Moreover, the argument from the designation “king” or “emperor” proves nothing and necessarily establishes nothing. For just as Charles was called emperor several times before he was acclaimed emperor, as Baluzius himself teaches in his notes on the Council of Narbonne—and as we observed in dissertation 4, no. 27, and as may be seen under “Emperor” in Du Cange—so there can be no doubt that after receiving the imperial diadem he could still be called king.

Thus, in a diploma granted to Fortunatus of Grado in the third year of his empire, Charles himself says: “The greatest fortification of our kingdom,” not “of our empire,” etc.; and toward the end: “to pray continually for the stability of our kingdom before the mercy of the Lord.”

Nor does he use “empire” here. It is worth noting what Cointius says under the year 803, no. 58 [Col. 0613A]:

> “In the same decree”—speaking of this diploma granted to Fortunatus—“Charles gives the third year of his empire as the chronological date, but in the body of the diploma he wishes the mercy of the Lord to be invoked not for the stability of his empire but for that of his kingdom. The reason why he does not mention the empire in both places may be given as follows. The name ‘empire’ is highly honorific, but it denotes no territory—not even a village. Therefore, when Charles records the time at which he issues the decree, he notes the year of his empire; but when he speaks of his territories, he represents them not by the term ‘empire’ but by the term ‘kingdom.’”

Thus Paulinus, who convenes the council in the territory of King Charles, calls him king, perhaps moved by the same consideration.

### V

As for the second argument, concerning the conformity of the words found in Anastasius and Paulinus—namely, “half-alive”—did Father de Rubeis omit certain words by chance, or because they in no way favored his opinion, even though he touched upon the neighboring passage?

The text reads:

> “As for the priests, whether they were left half-alive after wounds had been inflicted upon them, or certainly were killed by his satellites while the devilish fury was raging, judgment will belong not to me but to your definition.”

He omitted “killed,” although he says that it is “most probable that not one pontiff alone but also other priests who opposed themselves to wicked men were beaten with clubs and suffered wounds, while others were killed.”

In Leo’s case, however, no one was killed. And whether it is highly probable that priests opposed themselves and were therefore killed, hear Anastasius in *Leo III*, marginal no. 369:

> “Armed men secretly gathered against him”—Leo—“to slaughter him without any reverence, with Paschal standing at his head and Campulus at his feet, according to their wicked plan. When this had been done”—note these words—“all the people who were around him, namely the unarmed people prepared for the service of God, terrified by fear of weapons, turned to flight.”

In what follows, you will find no one injured by blows by the pontiff’s persecutors, much less put to death, in Anastasius.

The account of Leo reported by Anastasius, therefore, does not agree with Paulinus’s exposition, which asserts that priests were left half-alive after wounds had been inflicted upon them, or—“or” having the same force as “and,” as anyone familiar with the usage of that age knows well—were certainly killed by his satellites through diabolical fury.

Father de Rubeis therefore seeks in vain to support his opinion by the similarity of the words. Rather, the difference of the words supports our opinion, which we shall present below.

### VI

The third argument, or conjecture, drawn from legal symbolism has little force. What does the number of years during which Paulinus was supposed to convene councils in his own province have to do with the Council of Frankfurt? Although he attended that council, it was not convened by him, so that he could eat fruit from a vineyard planted by himself, as though he were entitled to do so under the law. Whatever Paulinus did there could not be attributed to himself, since the plant belongs to the soil. Consequently, he could not count Frankfurt among his own councils and calculate from its celebration the number of intervening years according to the example of the Mosaic law.

If Paulinus alluded to this mystical number and referred to the councils that had been omitted, it seems more probable that, as the saying goes, he calculated the time with a broad brush and designated the Council of Forum Julii. From the year 796 to the year 803, when we believe that the Council of Altinum was celebrated, a full seven years elapsed. This not only equals but exceeds the mystical number of years mentioned in the law so often cited.

The matter should not, however, be pressed to the ultimate precision of comparisons. It was enough for the mystical number of five years to be included in some fashion, as it is included within seven years.

If this does not satisfy you, and you say that we are taking the five-year period too broadly, we reply that it is not established that the Council of Frankfurt belonged to Paulinus, so that, when speaking of his own councils and stopping within the allegory of trees planted by himself, he would establish the epoch of five years.

What we think should be understood about this mystical number was stated in the notes. Meanwhile, a few further objections must be considered. [Col. 0614A]

### VII

P. de Rubeis, concerning the day on which Leo was ill-treated at Rome, writes as follows: “Anastasius specifies the day . . . namely, 25 April. On these days”—note these words—“during the Easter season, Paulinus, as was customary, celebrated his synod at Altinum, and reported the infamous crime to King Charles for punishment.”

We do not deny that the synod was summoned according to custom, indeed at the time prescribed by the canons. This is what Paulinus says: “At the prompting of the canonical documents, the council was held at Altinum.” For Paulinus convened it not precisely to punish some particular crime, but for the customary business transacted in synods—namely, matters of faith, discipline, and similar affairs—as will become clear below. It was therefore an ordinary synod, as P. de Rubeis himself seems to imply by the words, “during the Easter season, as was customary.” For the canons, establishing two annual gatherings of synods, order one to be held on the Ides of October and the other during the week of the third Sunday after Easter. Thus the First Council of Nicaea, canon 5, and the First Council of Antioch, canon 20. [Col. 0614B]

P. de Rubeis himself does not assign the Altinum synod to October, since he says that it was held during the Easter season. In the year 799, however, when Easter fell on the day before the Kalends of April, that is, 31 March, the third Sunday after Easter must be placed on 21 April. It was during the Thursday of that week, namely 25 April, that Leo’s misfortune occurred. Therefore Paulinus, celebrating his customary council at Altinum during that week according to the canonical prescription, could not have learned of the event and, on behalf of the bishops of his province, written to Charles to urge him to punish the crime.

If you say that the council was held during the following weeks, I ask whether you mean that it was held ordinarily or extraordinarily. If ordinarily, it was no longer “according to custom.” For the custom, in accordance with the canons, was to hold councils in the third week after Easter. If extraordinarily, since no reason appears for summoning it extraordinarily other than the ill-treatment of the priests, apart from the ordinary matters transacted in every council, surely it cannot be said to have been assembled before Leo’s misfortune became known. [Col. 0614C]

But it could not have become known before May had already begun, approximately on the seventh or eighth day. From that date, therefore, the synod could at most have been summoned. The feast of Pentecost, however, fell on 19 May, when it is most probable that the provincial bishops were dismissed to their own churches for that solemnity. Thus, within approximately eleven days, the cause becomes known, the synod is summoned, assembled, and conducted? Who could digest that? If you extend the time still further, we are already proceeding beyond the Easter season, and yet it is said: “On these days, during the Easter season, the council was celebrated.”

### VIII

But the dispute with P. de Rubeis must now be settled. Although, for the sake of investigating the truth, there may be disagreement in opinion between us, there can be no hostility or contention. For, as the saying went:

[Col. 0614D]

> It has always been permitted for two people  
> to think differently about the same matters  
> while friendship remains unharmed.

Thus, when Paulinus writes to Charles about priests who had been beaten, left half-dead, and killed by agents, he may have had both crimes in view—namely, the Roman and the Gradan crime. Seeing the savagery that wicked men had exercised against Leo III in 799 renewed against John, patriarch of Grado, at the beginning of 802 or 803, he directed complaints from the council of Altinum to the emperor Charles, so that he might extend helping hands to the suffering Church. By saying that priests had been left half-dead, he alluded to Leo, who had been wounded by wicked Romans; by mentioning priests killed, he alluded to John of Grado, who had been thrown headlong from a tower and cruelly deprived of life.

This seems possible to infer from the words of the letter, when he urges Charles to issue a judgment that would restrain such rash, impious, and unbridled men in the future and prevent them from acting throughout the broad dominion of his kingdoms. “Let there go forth,” he says, “if it pleases you, throughout the whole monarchy spread far and wide across your kingdom, the punishment of a decretal judgment concerning this matter, which no forgetfulness ever hostile to truth and opposed to justice . . . could erase or abolish. For, through neglect of discipline, the savage manifestations of this crime have prevailed throughout all parts of the Churches of the world.” [Col. 0615A]

This mode of expression, if properly understood, indicates that Paulinus did not seize upon merely one criminal act as an occasion for calling Charles to vengeance. Rather, observing that priests were wounded at Rome, killed at Grado, and that the evil—which he calls a plague—was spreading and raging, growing worse day by day, he urged the emperor to remove, by a law enacted against them, the freedom of wicked men who raged against Christ’s ministers to continue their madness throughout his kingdoms.

[Col. 0615B]

Let us therefore agree on this point. Let P. de Rubeis grant that Paulinus referred in his letter to the crime committed against Pope Leo; and let him grant us that, by his words, Paulinus also intended the killing of John of Grado—one having been left half-dead, the other killed.

### IX

Since Paulinus did not refer in his words solely and precisely to the misfortune of Pope Leo, as has been clearly proved, and since no other crime of this kind occurring around that time and relevant to Paulinus appears in the histories except the death of John of Grado, we stand with those who believe that the killing of the patriarch of Grado gave Paulinus grounds for complaining about priests who had been wounded and killed, and for writing from the council of Altinum to Charles and urging him to avenge that crime.

For this reason the synod must necessarily be removed from the year 799, since the event at Grado had not yet occurred. The council of Altinum is commonly assigned to the year 802. But to understand that it could not have been held in that year, recall what we have already said in the *Life of Saint Paulinus*, chapter 12, numbers 1 and 2, about the election of Christopher as bishop of Olivolo, in favor of the emperor Nicephorus of Constantinople. John of Grado did not admit him to consecration, although the Venetian tribunes were insisting, and from this arose the cause that led to the killing of the patriarch of Grado.

Nicephorus’s accession to the empire—or, more accurately, his usurpation after the deposition of Irene, the mother of Constantine—occurred in indiction 11, on 31 October 802, a Monday, according to Petavius, *Rationarium Temporum*, part I, book VIII, chapter 6; Brietius, book IX, chapter 1, decade 1; Baronius, under the year 802, no. 1; and Pagius, same year, no. 2. As Pagius notes there, the year 802, according to the Alexandrian reckoning, began on 1 September 795. Paul the Deacon seems to have followed this computation in his *History*, book XXIII:

> “In the following year”—that is, the fifth year of the reign of Irene, who recovered the empire, as he himself writes there, in the year 791 from the Lord’s Incarnation—“which is the first year of Nicephorus, on the day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction, at the fourth hour of the night, which dawns on Monday, the same Nicephorus, while he was patrician and chief logothete, stirred up a tyranny against the most devout Irene.” [Col. 0615C]

Therefore Nicephorus ruled from the Kalends of November 802.

But how could all the following events have occurred in the mere two months remaining in that year: the news of Nicephorus’s accession reaching Venice; the announcement or discovery of his desire concerning the election of Christopher; the election of Christopher as bishop of Olivolo in his favor; the Venetian tribunes’ approach to John, patriarch of Grado, asking him to accept the election; the rejection of the elected bishop; the preparation of the Venetian fleet; the patriarch’s fall and death; the assembly of the council of Altinum; and the drafting of the synodal letter? To complete all this, nearly a year is consumed—indeed, scarcely would a whole year be sufficient.

### X

Those who place Paulinus’s death in 802 failed to notice this accession of Nicephorus, in whose favor the bishop of Olivolo was elected by the Venetians. What an anachronism it would be to establish that Paulinus died on 11 January 802 and then describe him as convening the council of Altinum after the Kalends of November of that same year! [Col. 0615D]

In his *Life*, chapter 11, we show that he went as legate to the council of Aachen toward the end of this year. From this you may see how rightly we have removed Paulinus’s death from the year 802, just as we are compelled to remove it from 803, so that the council of Altinum may find its proper date.

Cointius saw and wrote about this chronological argument before us. We, however, had considered and written it before seeing Cointius; when we transcribed our own work, we happened merely to come upon his. He therefore places the celebration of the council of Altinum in 803—and, in our judgment, he is not mistaken. Since he failed to specify the time of year in which the synod took place, we now undertake to demonstrate it.

### XI

Above, in section 8, we accepted what Father de Rubeis had said: that the assembly of the bishops at Altinum had taken place during the Easter season, according to custom. Accordingly, we place it within the third week after Easter, and readily concede this point, although we disagree about the year. [Col. 0616A]

For Paulinus knew the decrees of the canons and Fathers, which in the same section we cited from the First Council of Nicaea, canon 5, and the First Council of Antioch, canon 20, and especially what Pope Saint Leo had written to Anastasius, bishop of Thessalonica, in Letter 84, chapter 7:

> “Concerning episcopal councils, we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers wisely ordained: namely, that two assemblies should be held each year, at which judgment may be rendered concerning all the complaints that ordinarily arise among the various orders of the Church. But if, perchance, a case should arise among those who preside concerning greater sins—God forbid—which cannot be settled by a provincial examination, your metropolitan will take care to inform your Fraternity about the nature of the whole matter; and if, when the parties are present, it is not settled by your judgment, whatever it may be must be transferred to our judgment.”

This is not only something that seems naturally to be conceded; it is also evident from Paulinus’s own words at the council of Forumjulium, where he said:

> “A council ought to be held twice each year in every province, namely in the city and metropolis, or in any suitable place, according to the judgment of the metropolitan of that region.” [Col. 0616B]

Moreover, at the council of Frankfurt, which Paulinus attended and which could not have escaped his notice, it was decreed in canon 6:

> “If there is any matter that the metropolitan bishop cannot correct or pacify, then the accusers, together with the accused, should come with letters from the metropolitan, so that we may learn the truth of the matter.” [Col. 0616C]

This is virtually identical in meaning with what Leo had prescribed for the bishop of Thessalonica.

### XII

From these provisions, which Paulinus knew well, we infer the time of year in which the council was held—namely, between 9 and 16 May. For in 803 Easter fell on 16 April. The third week after Easter therefore included 9 and 16 May.

Since two periods are assigned as the principal times for celebrating councils—the Ides of October and the third week after Easter—one of these must certainly have been observed by Paulinus. Although a complaint about the killing inflicted upon the bishop of Grado is presented, the other matters transacted at the council show that the bishops’ gathering was an ordinary one and was assembled according to the canonical prescription. [Col. 0616D]

Listen to Paulinus’s account:

> “And when, in accordance with the agreement, the priestly assembly had gathered together in religious devotion, compelled by the canonical formulas, it is immediately agreed unanimously . . . as the solemn order of that religious council itself declares, concerning every kind of active business, concerning the cause of the orthodox faith, concerning the condition and dignity of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, concerning the ruinous loss of possessions, and concerning whatever complaints may be brought forward and which they desired to have resolved.” [Col. 0617A]

This was not, therefore, one of those synods that, being held outside the established time, propose only the particular matter for the sake of which they are assembled. Rather, it was one of those customarily summoned during one of the two appointed periods.

Furthermore, that council was not convened in October is plainly demonstrated not only by what was said above about its having been summoned during the Easter season, but also by what follows shortly.

### XIII

The misfortune of John, patriarch of Grado, occurred toward the end of 802 or the beginning of 803. For before the Kalends of November 802, when Nicephorus began to reign, and when Christopher of Olivolo is said to have been elected in his favor but was not admitted by the metropolitan of Grado, and the patriarch was consequently cast headlong to his death, we must not say that the council was convened.

Nor can it have occurred after 21 March 803, when it is clear that Fortunatus, having succeeded John, his kinsman, in the see of Grado, received the privilege and pallium from Leo III. At this time, namely from October 802 until the beginning of 803, the synod of Aachen was being celebrated, with Paulinus present as legate of the Apostolic See, as we state in his *Life*, chapter 11. Paulinus was therefore absent when John was killed.

Paulinus’s complaint, and that of the Fathers of Altinum, would have seemed untimely to Charles if it had been delayed until the middle of the following October, since it could appropriately have been brought forward from the synod convened during the Easter season. [Col. 0617B]

### XIV

Pagius, under the year 802, no. 5, argues that the council of Altinum had been held earlier because the pallium was given to Fortunatus of Grado on 21 March. He writes:

> “The council of Altinum . . . cannot be removed from this year [802], since Paulinus, as I shall immediately demonstrate”—whether validly, will be considered in its proper place—“departed to God in this year, and Leo III sent the pallium in March of the following Christian year to the successor of John, patriarch of Grado.” [Col. 0617C]

You see that Pagius argues from the pallium’s being given on 21 March that the council had previously been held—namely, in the year 802, as he himself thinks. But that year has already been excluded.

I see no necessity for placing the council before the bestowal of the pallium. I willingly and readily grant that the pallium was given to Fortunatus, the successor of John, on 21 March 803. What then? Does it follow that the synod of Altinum could not have been held later in that same year 803? That does not follow.

For the succession of Fortunatus to the see of Grado, and the conferral of the pallium, did not deprive Paulinus of the right to convene a council and implore Charles to exact vengeance. Indeed, it seems most probable that Fortunatus, having received the pallium in 803 and proceeding to Gaul to Charles “to inflame him against the dukes of the Venetians, who were embracing the cause of Nicephorus with greater zeal than was fitting,” as Sigonius says—and perhaps intending to demand vengeance for the killing of his uncle and for the injuries inflicted upon the Church of Grado—brought with him the council’s letter. [Col. 0617D]

He did not depart before the council’s celebration, as is indicated by the period extending from the middle of May to the middle of August, when he obtained a privilege from Charles on the Ides. A period of three months provides a reasonable proportion for the journey and the completion of the business.

Above, we have seen that Leo in his letter, and Charles at the council of Frankfurt, determined that if any serious crime were committed which a council could not remedy, it should be referred to them. Who could doubt that a crime committed against a bishop was among the most serious? Therefore, just as no one could more fairly have directed complaints to Charles than Paulinus and the council convened by him, whose church was adjacent to that of Grado and had once been united with it, so no one else could more justly have brought the complaints and the council’s letter to Charles than Fortunatus, who was related by blood to the murdered bishop and was the legitimately elected successor to his see.

Accept, then, this argument, if you please: Paulinus convenes the council in obedience to the canons, and especially to the formulas expressed by Charles at the council of Frankfurt; the Frankish canon establishes that matters which cannot be corrected by a council are to be brought by the accuser to the king with letters from the metropolitan; the deed of the duke of the Venetians could not be corrected or avenged by the council; the metropolitan Paulinus gives letters of accusation in the name of the council; Fortunatus of Grado proceeds to Charles to obtain protection for his church, as has been shown above. [Col. 0618A]

What, then, prevents us from saying that Fortunatus himself delivered Paulinus’s letter and that of the council of Altinum to the emperor Charles? The year does not prevent it, since it has been demonstrated above that the council was held in 803, the year in which Fortunatus went to Gaul. Nor does the month, since the council was held before he went to Gaul, around the middle of May, as has also been shown. Neither the time nor the sequence of events presents an obstacle.

### XV

Here, as though at a central point between the question of time and that of place, we must examine the criticism that Baluzius appends to Paulinus’s letter, since he appears to attack both its date and its location at once. He writes:

> “Baronius, and others after him, referred this letter to the year 802 on insufficient conjectures. I, however, think that it should be connected with the council of Altinum, or Forumjulium, which Paulinus the patriarch celebrated several years before Charlemagne became emperor.
