This, unless I am mistaken, is supported by the beginning and the end of the letter, where the patriarch asks the prince to confirm the matters established in that synod. Add that at the end of this letter, in the Vatican Codex, it is written: ‘Synod of Forumjulium.’ A synod held at Altinum is rightly called Forumjulian, because it was held in the diocese of Forumjulium. The letter should therefore be placed at the beginning of the proceedings, as was done in the First Council of Orléans and in several others, as we noted in the preface to Council V, section 17.” [Col. 0618B]

These are Baluzius’s words. Consider them point by point.

“Baronius, and others after him, referred this letter to the year 802 on insufficient conjectures.” See carefully what we said in sections 9 and 10, where we demonstrated that the council, and consequently the letter, cannot be assigned to 802 on any grounds.

“I, however, think that it should be connected with the council of Altinum.” All the writers whom I have seen, and whom we cited in the *Life of Saint Paulinus*, chapter 12, no. 4, rightly acknowledge and admit this.

“Or Forumjulium, which Paulinus the patriarch celebrated several years before Charlemagne became emperor.” Incorrectly—indeed, falsely. For, my dear Baluzius, the council of Altinum is not the same as the council of Forumjulium. [Col. 0618C]

“Add that at the end of this letter, in the Vatican Codex, it is written: ‘Synod of Forumjulium.’ A synod held at Altinum is rightly called Forumjulian, because it was held in the diocese of Forumjulium.” So be it. What follows from this? The synod of Altinum must still be distinguished from that of Forumjulium.

For Forumjulium may mean either the city or town—which Paulinus calls a *municipium*—or the province. The council called Forumjulian was celebrated in the town of Forumjulium; the council held at Altinum, which lay in the province of Forumjulium, was called Altinian. The Altinian assembly and the Forumjulian assembly are therefore not the same.

Moreover, the distinction is plainly evident from the matters treated in each place. At Altinum the subject was the priests killed in the disaster at Grado; at Forumjulium there is not even a word about this matter, because the disaster had not yet occurred. The council of Forumjulium is therefore one thing, and the council of Altinum another, although the latter is sometimes also called Forumjulian because it was held in the province of Forumjulium. [Col. 0618D]

### XVI

Finally, the location of the council must not be passed over without examination, since it raises an argument for doubt both in law and in fact.

By what right did Paulinus convene a council at Altinum, when the see of Altinum had already been transferred to Torcello and had become subject to the jurisdiction of the metropolitan of Grado? This will be the legal question.

How, when Altinum had suffered the same destruction at the hands of Attila’s forces as Aquileia, Concordia, and the other cities situated on the mainland, could Paulinus have held a council in a deserted city that had been reduced to solitude for many centuries? This will be the question of fact.

Before resolving both questions, accept a few observations about Altinum.

### XVII

Altinum was once a distinguished city, mentioned by Pliny in book III, chapters 16 and 18, and by Strabo in book V, where he says:

> “Altinum lies in a marsh and has a situation like Ravenna. It is fertile and famous for the fleeces of its sheep.”

Martial, in *Apophoreta*, epigram 155, gives only two regions of Italy precedence over it in the abundance of their wool:

[Col. 0619A]

> Apulia is renowned for first-rate fleeces, Parma for second-rate;  
> the sheep of Altinum is praised third.

It was rich in delights and so distinguished for the pleasantness of its location that, according to the same witness, he wished to spend his old age there. Thus, in book IV, epigram 25:

> Altinum’s shores rival the villas of Baiae,  
> and its forest knows the pyre of Phaethon;  
>   
> and the loveliest of the Dryads, the sole maiden wedded to the Antenorean Faun,  
> lived beside the Euganean lakes.  
>   
> And you, fortunate Aquileia, beside the Ledaean Timavus,  
> where Cyllarus drank the seven waters:  
>   
> you shall be the harbor and resting-place of my old age,  
> if our leisure may be subject to its own authority.

Altinum once had an episcopal see, over which Heliodorus presided in the time of Saint Jerome. Writing to him Letter 3, a consolatory letter on the death of Nepotianus, his nephew through his sister, Jerome describes that region while, in a sense, describing Nepotianus’s character:

> “His manner of dress, following the custom of the province, was notable neither for elegance nor for squalor. Although he burned daily either to go to the monasteries of Egypt, or to visit the communities of Mesopotamia, or at least to occupy himself in the solitude of the Dalmatian islands, which are separated from Altinum by only a narrow strait, he did not dare abandon his uncle, the bishop.”

He then continues by describing Nepotianus as destined to succeed his uncle there:

> “You were seeking a nephew; the Church, a priest. Your successor went before you. What you were, he deserved, in the judgment of all, to become after you. Thus from a single household emerged the dignity of a double episcopate: in one case there is rejoicing that he held it; in the other, grief that he was taken away before he could hold it.”

The Church of Aquileia had produced this distinguished offspring, for at that time, under Saint Valerian, it was a fruitful mother of men renowned for piety and learning. Concerning its clergy, among whom Heliodorus was considered second only to Valerian, Saint Jerome wrote in his *Chronicle*:

> “The clergy of Aquileia are regarded as a choir of the blessed.”

But let us return to our subject.

### XVIII

I would call Heliodorus himself as witness that the episcopal see of Altinum had once been subject to the metropolitan of Aquileia. Under Valerian, who presided over the council convened at Aquileia in the time of Pope Damasus in the year 381, in the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius, Heliodorus took part and is listed in the sixteenth place. I would do so unless I suspected that someone might object that this was not a provincial synod, since Ambrose of Milan and many bishops from Gaul, including canonical bishops, were present.

The councils of later times remove the difficulty entirely. For in 579, under Elias, metropolitan of Aquileia, in the matter of the transfer of the see of Aquileia to the island of Grado—after it had so often been driven out by the Huns, Goths, and Lombards—we find subscribed in fifth place “Peter, bishop of the holy Church of Altinum.” He also subscribed the conciliabulum of Marano among those who received Severus. [Col. 0619A]

I am astonished that Thomasinus, *On the Old and New Discipline of the Church*, part I, book I, chapter 21, was so mistaken as to replace “Altinensis” with “Utinensis,” when in Paul the Deacon, whom he cites in book III, chapter 12—which is actually chapter 27—the distinct words “Peter of Altinum” are plainly read. [Col. 0619B]

But since the see of Altinum had already been transferred to Torcello in Paulinus’s time, by what right could Paulinus convene a council in that church, since his see belonged not to the province of Aquileia but, for more than a century, to Grado? This is the first legal doubt proposed.

### XIX

To settle it briefly, it should be known that, as soon as the see of Aquileia, compelled at one point to abandon its ancient location, withdrew to the island of Grado, it was divided into two sees. The Lombards established John in the Church of Aquileia by election of the clergy and people, while the people of Grado supplied themselves with Candidianus.

From this arose discord and a dispute that greatly afflicted these churches over time: the patriarchs of old and new Aquileia—for Grado was called New Aquileia—were supported respectively by the Lombards in the case of the old see, and by the Exarch and the pontiff in the case of the new.

When Serenus, patriarch of Aquileia, invaded the rights of Grado, Pope Gregory II wrote him a letter of reprimand, which Baronius reproduces under this year, no. 4. He wrote another to the people of Grado and its suffragans, and to Marcellus, duke of Venice, declaring that he was defending the rights of that church.

Baronius also adds, from a letter of Leo IX reproduced there, what both Gregory II and Gregory III had once done to restrain the bishops of Aquileia, who could scarcely tolerate anything being done for the benefit of Grado. [Col. 0619C]

He further reproduces another letter of Gregory III, the immediate successor of Gregory II, in which he rebukes Callistus, who had succeeded Severus, and compels him to restore what he had usurped from the monastery of Saint Mary on the island of Barbiana, which belonged to the Church of Grado. Indeed, “Callistus,” says Dandulus in his *Chronicle*, book VII, chapter 3, page 10, “having received the papal admonitions and returned to his senses, restored the islands he had invaded to the Church of Grado.” [Col. 0619D]

In later years new disputes arose, and through the efforts of Maxentius, at the council of Mantua—unless one doubts its authenticity—the affairs of the Church of Aquileia were repaired in 826. We omit what subsequently occurred in this matter in the following centuries, lest we move too far from Paulinus, who is our subject. [Col. 0620A]

### XX

In the period between Callistus and Maxentius, Siguald, Paulinus, and Ursus, or Urbanus, appear. Under the last of these, the dispute that Maxentius had extinguished arose again between the bishops of the sees of Aquileia and Juvavum, or Salzburg, as we state in the *Life of Paulinus*, chapter 8, no. 6. Under the first of them, namely Siguald, the spirit of contention is discerned, whose chorepiscopus John, as we argue with considerable probability in the *Life*, chapter 4, numbers 2 and 3, caused trouble for the Church of Grado.

Thus, as you see, while others were seized by a desire for dissension, Paulinus stood between them. Under him, we believe that no such disturbances arose, because this man of God and lover of peace would have abhorred such controversies to the point of nausea, since they were generally raised more for the scandal than for the edification of the faithful.

The character of this peaceful man, and his mind bound to the other bishops by the bond of charity, can be discerned from the very letter that supplies the subject of this dissertation. He begins:

> “To Charles, etc. Paulinus, the least of all servants, a servant with concordant and equal devotion together with our brothers and fellow priests, etc.”

And below:

> “with the provincial bishops of this see and the bishops who are in agreement with them.”

But the very matter dealt with at Altinum—namely, the convocation of the synod and the letter sent to Charles to avenge the killing of the patriarch of Grado—provides the most probable, if not evident, indication that at that time no disputes existed between the two sees.

### XXI

Paulinus therefore adhered to the ancient sanctions, which, from the very division into two patriarchates, had been such that:

[Col. 0620D]

> “All the bishops who had their sees on the mainland of Venetia, which was under Lombard rule, obeyed Aquileia; whereas those who held the estuaries and Istria, subject to the emperor of the East, obeyed Grado.”

So writes Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book II; and Ughellus in the preface to the patriarchs of Grado.

Since Altinum was situated not in the estuaries but on the mainland, specifically near the left mouths of the river Sile—as is confirmed by the remains still encountered among the ruins and thickets by those traveling to Venice, and as Leander Alberti testifies in his *Description of Italy*, in the district of Treviso, and Cellarius in *Ancient Geography*, book II, chapter 9—it is plainly established that Paulinus then had the right to convene a council in that same Church, since it was subject to him as a church situated on the mainland. [Col. 0620B]

This also seems to be drawn from his words. For in his letter to Charles he said:

> “We have considered it worthwhile to inform Your Serenity’s ears that a council was held at Altinum in this see which, by God’s authority, I serve.”

Do you see how he includes Altinum within the “see”—that is, within the province over which he presided as metropolitan and which, by God’s authority, he served? [Col. A]

Below, he asserts that the acts were “not general, but local, or even particular, statutes, with the provincial bishops of this see and the bishops who are in agreement with them.”

One should not imagine a provincial council being held outside the province with provincial bishops.

As for what the distinguished Fleury says, *Ecclesiastical History*, volume X, book XLV, no. 24—that Altinum was once episcopal but then depended upon another see—understand it to mean that it was governed by another bishop, perhaps the bishop of Treviso or Concordia, both of them belonging to the province of Aquileia; it did not, however, depend upon another see, that is, upon another metropolitan.

Cointius correctly writes under the year 803, no. 10:

> “From the fact that Paulinus celebrated a council at Altinum, it is clear that that town did not then belong to the bishopric of Torcello, which was subject to the patriarch of Grado, but to that of Concordia, which was subject to the patriarch of Aquileia.”

Pagius transferred this word for word, as he often does, under the year 802, no. 4. [Col. 0621B]

### XXII

But the question of fact remains to be resolved: did Paulinus really convene a council at Altinum, which had been destroyed several centuries earlier?

When Saint Niceas was seated in the see of Aquileia—he had been invested with that dignity in 454, according to Dandulus, *Chronicle*, book V, chapter 5, page 1—Attila captured and devastated Aquileia. From there he proceeded to Concordia and Altinum, leveled them to the ground with equal ferocity, and ravaged the region.

The inhabitants of Concordia and Altinum prudently withdrew to the estuaries. The former settled at Caorle, while the latter were allowed to inhabit Torcello and the neighboring islands.

Nevertheless, the episcopal see was not transferred to Torcello immediately, but only in 608. At that time Rotharis, king of the Lombards, eager to unite with the rest of his kingdom the two provinces that remained under the Roman Empire—namely, the Cottian Alps and Opitergium with their dependencies as far as Treviso—engaged the Romans in battle at the Scultenna. Having been victorious and having compelled Opitergium to surrender, he brought about a cessation of the war between the exarchs and his own people that lasted until the time of Liutprand. [Col. 0621C]

Following the example of the ancient Venetians, and at the urging of their bishop Saint Magnus, the people of Opitergium founded Eraclea on the sea, naming it after the emperor then ruling, Heraclius. When country people, together with their livestock, joined themselves to them and the new city could not accommodate everyone, they added Equilium not far away.

These facts are taken from Sigonius, who adds:

> “When this had been observed, Paul, bishop of Altinum, transferred his see to Torcello, and Paul of Padua transferred his Catholic see to Malamocco; and all these arrangements were confirmed by the authority of Pope Severinus.” [Col. 0622A]

But according to Dandulus, *Chronicle*, book VI, chapter 7, page 11, the privilege was obtained not by Paul, who survived at Torcello for only one month, but by his successor Mauricius:

> “for the confirmation of his church at Torcello, from Pope Severinus, with the consent of the Patriarch and the commendation of the people.”

Here, then, is the transfer of the see of Altinum to Torcello and, consequently, its migration from Lombard territory and the province of Aquileia to Venetian territory and the diocese of Grado. Nevertheless, the name of the see was still retained. For at the Roman council under Pope Agatho in 680, the ninety-fifth subscriber is:

> “Paul, the least bishop of the holy Church of Altinum, province of Istria,”

by which name the coastal and inland regions of Venetia were designated.

We observe something similar in the patriarchate of Aquileia, which is found to have been called first Gradan, later Forumjulian and Utinian, and also Aquileian, because of the various transfers of the see. The difference, however, is that the patriarch used the title Forumjulian or Utinian [Col. 0622B] without ever losing the name Aquileian.

The see of Altinum, on the other hand, came in time to be called Torcellan in such a way that it eventually lost the title Altinian and the name of the see was abolished.

### XXIII

In any event, it is clearly inferred that in Paulinus’s time some shadow of the former city still stood, perhaps restored to some extent from the remains left by earlier disasters. For Dandulus, book VIII, chapter 5, pages 19–20, mentions the monastery of Altinum, concerning the appointment of whose abbot a dispute arose between the duke and the patriarch of Venice in the time of Charles the Bald, who assumed the empire in 876—that is, seventy-three years after the council held there by Paulinus.

Moreover, in the *Chronicle* of Raphayni Caresini, Venetian chancellor, contained in *Rerum Italicarum Scriptores*, volume XII, column 499, a charter of the emperor Frederick is recited. It was issued at Venice in indiction 10, on 3 August, in the year 1177 from the Lord’s Incarnation. Among its witnesses were Henry, patriarch of Venice, and another patriarch of Aquileia, whom you will learn from another charter appended to this one [Col. 0622C], of the same year and indiction, to have been Ulrich. In that charter Altinum is repeatedly mentioned, especially the monastery of Saint Stephen, “which is of Altinum”; the parish of Altinum is also mentioned there.

If, therefore, even in times so distant from Paulinus’s, you still find a church and monastery at Altinum, you understand that it is futile to object to the destruction of Altinum in order to deny that Paulinus held a council there.

This has been said against those who imagined that the synod was held not in some church at Altinum but in the church of Torcello, which had replaced the see of Altinum.

## Appendices to the Works of Blessed Paulinus

[Col. 0621]

### Preliminary Notice
[Col. 0621D] Since, in elucidating Paulinus’s works, it has not infrequently been necessary—sometimes by notes, sometimes by observations, sometimes by dissertations—to adduce certain material in support of the truth of what was being said, it seemed not beside the point to present in fuller form matters which had merely been touched upon, as it were by sampling and tasting with the tips, as they say, of the lips, so that what is inferred might appear clearer and truer from the context. We have done this all the more willingly because we think it will be more agreeable to the reader. For we publish only those things whose discovery is more difficult: some are still unpublished, while many others have indeed been published, but are contained in books not commonly available. It was fairer to present them here than to send the reader elsewhere, usually on a futile and unprofitable journey. This Appendix will therefore be twofold: one part will consist of published materials, though rare ones and those more closely connected with Paulinus’s affairs; the other, for the most part, of unpublished materials relating to Aquileian affairs. Some documents, although it is clear that they were published elsewhere, are nevertheless placed among the unpublished, not only so that the sequence of the documents may remain unbroken, but also because, having been newly examined and corrected against manuscript copies, they rightly seem to be counted among the unpublished. Since almost nothing nowadays is valued unless it is supported by some document of deeper antiquity, we have judged that we ought to accommodate ourselves to the spirit of the age. We earnestly ask you, reader, to regard our efforts with fairness and goodwill.

[Col. 0623]

## FIRST APPENDIX. PUBLISHED ANCIENT DOCUMENTS

Under this title, in the first section, the most learned Madrisius reprinted numerous letters of blessed Alcuin, ten of them addressed to Saint Paulinus and an equal number to Charlemagne. These are followed by the Letter of Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, and the Confession of Faith of Felix of Urgell. In the same appendix eight further letters of blessed Alcuin to various persons are subsequently listed, together with Charlemagne’s letter to Queen Fastrada and a grant for the monastery of Caunes. But we have already published all these among the works of Charlemagne and Elipandus, in volumes XCVI or XCVIII of this Patrology, or will shortly publish them in our edition of the Works of blessed Alcuin. We have therefore judged the repetition of these letters superfluous and wished to inform readers why they have been omitted. EDITOR.

### II. [Note: [Col. 0625] Items common to the Roman Missal are omitted or merely indicated.] MASS OF SAINT PAULINUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA

Extracted from the Missal of the Church of Aquileia, printed in 1519, as an example of the rite of that church.

[Col. 0625B]

### ENTRANCE CHANT

“Let your priests, O Lord, be clothed with righteousness, and let your saints rejoice; for the sake of David your servant, do not turn away the face of your anointed.”

Psalm: “Remember, O Lord, David and all his meekness.”

“Glory to God in the highest,” etc., as in the Roman rite. “Lord Jesus Christ, only-begotten Son, most high,” or “and Holy Spirit.” “Lord God,” etc., as in the Roman rite. But concerning blessed Mary, as follows:

“Lord Jesus Christ, only-begotten Son: spirit and gracious advocate of orphans. Lord God, Lamb of God, Son of the Father: firstborn of Mary, virgin mother. You who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. You who take away the sins of the world, receive our prayer to the glory of Mary. You who sit at the right hand of the Father, have mercy on us. For you alone are holy, sanctifying Mary. You alone are Lord, governing Mary. You alone are Most High, crowning Mary, Jesus Christ, [Col. 0625C] with the Holy Spirit, in the glory of God the Father. Amen.”

### PRAYER

Grant, we ask, almighty God, that we may be aided by the merits of your blessed confessor and bishop Paulinus, whose votive solemnity we celebrate. Through our Lord, etc.

In the Church of the city of Austria, however, in a manuscript book marked no. 12, entitled *Book of Sacraments*, dated 1304, on page 299 verso, the following prayer for Saint Paulinus occurs:

“O God, who appointed blessed Paulinus as a minister of eternal salvation for your people: grant, we ask, that we may always deserve to have in heaven as intercessor him whom we had as a teacher of life on earth. Through the Lord, etc.”

We found this also in other manuscript Missals and Breviaries of the same church. In another book entitled *Order of the Missal according to the custom of the Roman Curia*, dated 1254—as appears after the months—the following prayer for Saint Paulinus is written in a hand [Col. 0625D] not entirely corresponding to the rest of the Missal, but more recent, though not belonging to the present age:

“O God, who willed your clergy and people to be governed by the episcopate of your confessor Paulinus: grant that through his continual intercession we may fear no adversity, attain victory, and obtain eternal life. Through the Lord, etc.”

It should be noted, however, that the Church of the city of Austria has a special Missal, distinct from that of Aquileia and following its own customs, some of which it still preserves today.

### READING FROM THE BOOK OF WISDOM

“Behold the great priest, who in his life supported the house and in his days strengthened the temple. He also founded the height of the temple: a double building, and the lofty walls of the temple. In his days wells of water poured forth, and they were filled like a sea beyond measure. He cared for his people and delivered them from destruction. He prevailed in enlarging the city; he attained glory in the conduct of the people and enlarged the entrance of the house and the court. Like the morning star amid the clouds, and like the full moon in his days, he shines. And like the sun shining forth, so did he shine in the temple of God. Like a radiant bow among clouds of glory, and like a rose in springtime. Like lilies beside flowing water, and like incense emitting a sweet fragrance.”

Gradual: “Behold the great priest, who in his days pleased God.”

Verse: “No one was found like him to preserve the law of the Most High.”

Alleluia. Verse: “I have found David,” etc.; or: “The Lord chose you for himself as priest among his people.” Alleluia.

For the praises of the Savior, so that the humble mind may be stirred.

To celebrate the Father’s such great glory, the choir jubilates [Col. 0626C] with worthy praise, and the people answer with joyful voices.

Let us all say, bending low: let the flock of so great a Peter join its Shepherd, and with prayers and poured-out tears let us cry:

### GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

At that time the Lord Jesus said this parable to his disciples: “A certain man going abroad,” etc., as in the Roman rite. In the Civitas Missal, however, the Gospel is: “Watch.” Offertory: “I have found David,” as in the Roman rite.

### SECRET

May the annual solemnity of your confessor and bishop Saint Paulinus, O Lord, [Col. 0626D] we ask, render us acceptable to your goodness, so that through these devout services of reconciliation it may obtain for us the gifts of your grace. Through our Lord.

The Preface and Canon are as in the Roman rite. Nevertheless, the words “and our bishop N.” and “for our king N.” are added in the Canon.

Communion: “Blessed is that servant,” as in the Roman rite.

Prayer after Communion, which we call the *Completa*: “O God, who reward the souls of the faithful, grant that through the prayers of your confessor and bishop Saint Paulinus, whose venerable feast we celebrate, we may obtain forgiveness. Through our Lord.”

The rest is as in the Roman rite. The dismissal of the people, however, apart from “Go, the Mass is ended,” or “Let us bless the Lord”—which are also Roman usages—was performed in two forms in the Church of Aquileia. On the feast of a major double rank it was as follows:

[Col. 0627A]

“Go, blessed and chosen ones, into the way of peace: for you an offering has been sent to God the Father.”

On the greater solemnities of the blessed Virgin Mary, it was as follows:

“Go, blessed and chosen ones, into the way of peace: for you the Son of Mary has been sent as an offering.”

### III. [Note: [Col. 0627D] From the Himmerod manuscript, written about 500 years ago, in Martène’s *Amplissima Collectio*.] PAULINUS’S PREFACE INVITING US TO THE JOYS OF REPENTANCE

The most just order and most correct form of repentance is this: that it should begin with tears and end in joy, so that by such an example it may be recognized that what is written is true: “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.” This occurs when the penitent’s most devout intention toward repentance sighs, because, groaning continually with sighs out of a feeling of divine mercy, the hardness dissolved in the wound of his heart awakens all the senses of his inner being, so that they cry out to the Lord [Col. 0627B] with the strength of their inward voice. The sighs of his breast come together, and one sigh follows another; the murmuring of his groans resounds in the Lord’s ears, if perhaps he may at some time deign to hear them.

Nor does the penitent do only this. In addition, loosening the reins of his eyes and pouring forth abundant waters, his eyelids pour out streams of tears; the channels of the veins of his head run without ceasing, until the offenses of all his crimes have been washed away and every impurity of iniquity cleansed. Then his mouth is filled with the words of the truest confession, in which the Lord delights, and he hastens mercifully to spare and does not delay granting forgiveness, saying, as it were: “Man, your sins are forgiven you.”

To this most merciful consolation and to so kind and loving a forgiver—indeed, cleanser—of sins, the heart of the penitent, flooded with unspeakable joy, says, so to speak:

“I have sinned, Lord, and have grievously offended; beyond measure I have multiplied my crimes. For this reason my tribulations have spread like a cedar, tormenting my conscience all day long. For my faults, Lord, are not slight, nor is the heap of my sins small. Therefore I cannot remain silent; hence my many groans, and my mind is most sorrowful amid the great upheaval of its distress. But, refreshed by consideration of your great and innumerable mercies, Lord, and by your gift, I see myself, wretched as I am, gradually rising from the stain of so great a danger.

“I confess, Lord, that your goodness lifts me to hope for pardon, so that, hesitating in nothing concerning faith, I may ask forgiveness and not die but live. Therefore, returning to the one who has power over my wounds—to you, my Lord—I bend my knees before you, and with earnest prayer, together with confession of repentance, [Col. 0627C] I implore you, giving glory to your name in frequent praise and blessing.

“My Lord and God, I glorify you in all things. Remaining steadfast, you taught my foolishness and softened my heart, until, though unwilling, I heard your voices crying out for so long, and, converted, followed you. I too, Lord, recognized; I too understood the sound of your cry. Rebuking myself, I was converted and did penance before you, as this day proves.

“Therefore, to your praise and my consolation, I would sing prophetic words to you: ‘You chastised me, Lord, and I was instructed, like an untamed little worm. For after you converted me and I did penance, and after you showed me, I struck my thigh; I was converted and blushed with shame.’ I remembered you, my Lord, because through your mercy my soul came back to life and rose from the dead.

“Therefore I have become a man of good hope, because you waited for me and endured me in my former wantonness. Considering this, I was pierced with remorse and did penance. From now on, joyful, I shall always render you countless thanks, imploring you with all my inward being and commending myself to you with complete devotion. For, that I might find you, you sought me; that I might return, you compelled me; that I might confess, you brought it about; and that, recognizing myself, I might mourn, you gave me the gift. For you are the God whom no one loses except through deception, whom no one seeks unless admonished, whom no one finds unless purified. For you are good; for your mercy endures forever; for you alone are God, and besides you there is no God. You are the God of Israel, God the Savior of all ages. Amen.”

This is the fitting order of penitents, and in this way repentance becomes fruitful: from mourning it gives birth to joy, from negligence it brings forgiveness, and from labor it brings rest. It begins, as has been shown, with tears and ends in joy, as stated above.

Accordingly, once the more careful procedure has been set out, anyone who hastens either to confess sins or to undertake penance may perhaps quite appropriately be approached in the following manner by the person who is to teach or instruct him, through questioning or examination:

“Do you wish to confess your sins?”

If he answers, “I do,” then one should continue as follows:

“First, you must understand in this matter that you will need to proceed simply and purely. You must not, in regard to those sins which perhaps appear shameful or disgraceful before human eyes or ears, put forward any pretense or try to make those sins respectable by disguising them. Rather, you ought to confess with sorrow and shame those things which, because of their enormity or disgrace, deserve accusation or detestation, instead of keeping silent about them out of human embarrassment.”

They begin [Note: [Col. 0627D] This entire book of Paulinus consists of various excerpts from the holy Fathers on repentance, especially Saints Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, Gregory, [Col. 0628D] Chrysostom, Ephrem, and others, and it cites no author later than Saint Isidore. From this you may conclude that the author is neither Paulinus of Nola nor Paulinus of Périgueux, who are said to have written on repentance, since they lived before most of the authors whom he cites.] the salutary admonitions of Paulinus, excerpted from treatises [Col. 0628D] of the holy Fathers.

[Col. 0627]

## 255 SECOND APPENDIX. UNPUBLISHED ANCIENT DOCUMENTS (C)

### INTRODUCTORY NOTICE

We call this appendix one of unpublished documents, not because everything presented here has never previously seen the light of publication, but because most of it has not been published, while some items, although published at some time, are here presented after being newly corrected against manuscript copies.

Of the following document, which we place first, we obtained two copies. One came from the writings of the monastery of Saint Mary in the Valley of the city of Austria, called the Greater Monastery; the other was supplied by the distinguished men Peter Anthony, the father, and Nicholas and Fabius, his sons, counts of Maniago. They possess a select and abundant series of ancient documents, as extensive as a private individual in our province could possess, and they communicate it to men of letters not merely without envy but willingly and readily.

Since we owe both the present and several of the documents and charters that follow to their courtesy, we have wished to make this public acknowledgment as a token of gratitude. But since both copies are not only full of numerous errors but differ enormously from one another in several places, we were inclined to publish neither, since the genuine and authentic text could not be recognized owing to the absence of the original copies. Nevertheless, because both agree in their account of Patriarch Siguald, from whom it is especially useful for our affairs to reckon the epoch, we omit neither. Let the reader choose whichever seems more agreeable to him. It is enough for us that the period of Siguald and the chronology reckoned from it not be overturned.

Both copies will therefore be placed opposite one another, exactly as they were communicated to us. For purposes of distinction, we shall call one the Civitas copy and the other the Maniago copy.

### I. THE CIVITAS COPY

Year 762, from the charters of the Greater Monastery of Civitas.

[Col. 0629A] [Note: [Col. 0629] In Migne, the Civitas copy and the Maniago copy are printed in parallel.]

A copy of a certain privilege concerning the foundation of several monasteries in the territory of Friuli, transcribed by me, Bernardinus of Amel, coadjutor in the chancery of the abbey of Sexto, exactly as I found it, without adding, changing, or correcting anything.

This privilege was granted in the year of the Lord six hundred and sixty-second [for seven hundred and sixty-second].

For a long time it has been implanted in our minds that the singular monastery of the founders should be declared and all the praises of their merits recounted, so that we ourselves may grow in the Lord with greater zeal and may be able to provide others with a pattern for imitation. For the Apostle testifies that, in general, the whole foundation and progress is the Lord Christ, saying: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ.”

Therefore, when these things are founded in the hidden places of the human mind, all vices immediately give way, and all corruptions of the flesh melt like wax placed upon fire. Likewise temptations and all the devil’s deceits are immediately extinguished, nor can he resist any longer when the power that had taken possession has found no place [to remain], because Satan rules in a human being only as long as he recognizes the instruments of his possession. But when the enemy’s disturbances have been driven from a Christian, he begins to be God’s temple, and the Holy Spirit enters rejoicing as into a most beautiful dwelling.

Therefore we, the brothers Erfo, Zaneto, and Marcus, though still living as laymen, under divine inspiration of grace, built two monasteries in the territory of Friuli: one in a place called Sexto, in honor of Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, and of the blessed John the Baptist and Peter, apostle of Christ. We decreed that brothers should live there under the regular yoke in God’s service.

We built another monastery on the bank called Salto, in honor of the saints Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, John the Baptist, and Peter, apostle of Christ. There our lady and mother Piltruda, together with the women gathered around her, was to live in monastic habit.

But because, hearing that divine prophetic voice in the forty-fourth Psalm in which God speaks to the human soul—“Hear, O daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house”—we followed this voice, left our land and kindred, and decided to live in the regions of Tuscany, and because our men and the brothers whom we left in the monastery did not refrain from troubling these monasteries already mentioned, since we had held them under our power, we therefore, Erfo and Marcus, although unworthy abbots, provided by this present document that all our possessions should be administered or disposed of in the monasteries mentioned above and that our gifts should be determined.

First of all, in the monastery at Ripa Salto, where our lady and mother is known to be, together with the other nuns, we give and grant our estate, where the monastery founded by us stands, with all its agricultural work: arable lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, and small holdings; also the halves of Casteneto in Ausemano, the remaining halves of which we gave to the monastery at Sexto; likewise half of the mill at Palatiolo, and half of the aforesaid monastery of men. Yet, so long as our lady and mother lives, the entire grain shall remain under her control; but from now on they shall divide the ordinary grain equally.

After her death, they shall jointly possess everything belonging to that mill: the monastery of the nuns shall have the half belonging to us of the mountain at Carnea, and the monastery at Sexto the other half. Whether they wish to pasture jointly or divide the property shall be in their power.

As for the farmhouses, we specify by name those which are to belong to the monastery of the girls: farmhouses at Sogiaco, farmhouses at Magretas, farmhouses in the Greater Field, farmhouses at Maras, farmhouses at Fara beside the Tower, farmhouses at Ardeliaco, farmhouses at Mattiarlo, farmhouses at the Two Basilicas, farmhouses at Aureliano, farmhouses at Avenianico, farmhouses at Gratialeo, farmhouses at Carnea in the village of Ampetio, and the houses of John at Mattiarlo.

Thus we grant from the income which they must pay annually: farmhouses at Ramacieto; the lands, vineyards, or meadows which we possess at Daunino; whatever we appear to possess at Coloniola; and the vineyard at Grobagnas, held by the son and grandsons of Antonius.

We also add our estate at Medegia with all its appurtenances, and likewise the houses at Cisiario. According to what their charters contain, they shall deliver one hundred amphorae of wine annually to the monastery of the girls; whatever remains we grant to our monastery at Sexto.

They shall make hay at Mariano and work the mill at Palatiolo as they have been accustomed to do. They shall likewise possess the woods at Vento and Comariola. The monasteries of the girls shall pasture their animals at the Port of the Synod-house, which lies nearby, without any obstruction and with the authority of the aforesaid monastery.

In the monastery of the men at Sexto we wish our gifts to include everything between the rivers Tagliamento and Livenza which is recognized as belonging to our authority between those rivers: whether the estate at Sexto, where we built that monastery; or the estate at Laurentia with the oratory of the Lord Savior, which is located there; or the estate at San Focato with its houses, estates, fields, [Col. 0631C] meadows, vineyards, woods, small holdings, mountains, living waters, pastures, and marshes; likewise mills, and all movable and immovable property which is recognized as belonging by our right to the estates listed above between those rivers.

Likewise, the farmhouses in the village of Macerano in Veronese territory; also the houses at Belluno, in the Conel judicial district, across the Tagliamento; a house at Ramussello with all its appurtenances; and whatever appears to belong to us at Saleto or anywhere there from the property of my wife.

Accordingly, I, Erfo, made a *vegaria* [term uncertain] from it. If, over and above that *vegaria*, anything should be there according to its assessment, the abbot who is in office at the time shall devote it to almsgiving, Masses, or psalmody each year.

We also grant what was previously assigned to that monastery: houses at Carnos in Vinearetum, our house at Mariano with all its appurtenances, half of Casteneto in Ausemano, half of the mill at Palatiolo as defined above, and the mountain at Carnea which belongs to us. The monasteries shall possess equal halves of all these things.

As for our male and female servants, Aldiones and Aldionae of either sex, we have released them all as free persons and have drawn up their charters of freedom. Likewise, we have made provision concerning their household dependants and those who had already been declared free to them; and we wish and decree that none of them shall make any imposition, but shall act as their charters prescribe.

The abbot, or his successors, who is appointed in due order at the monastery at Sexto, shall live regularly with those monks. He shall also govern and administer the monastery of the women at Salto, or at the Synod-house.

The abbot and the monks entrusted to him must live according to the rule, and from now on neither they nor the monastery shall be reduced under the power of us or our heirs. The monastery of the men shall remain independent, except that, when an abbot dies, the monks shall do what has customarily been ordered.

If they agree together upon one person and unite in one concord, or, God forbid, choose an evil head for themselves, then the bishop of the See of Aquileia shall bring them back to one agreement and appoint the better man from among those monks as abbot.

The abbot himself, with the consent of the bishop of the See of Aquileia, shall humbly appoint an abbess, namely the woman whom the united community, or the better part of it, has chosen, so that great reward may come to them and they may persevere in God’s service without the devil’s bite.

For none of them, male or female, shall have license to impose anything upon the others, nor to receive anything from them, nor to send his own message or issue any command, either in the monastery or in the monastery’s property, unless the bishop has been invited by the abbot or abbess. If, God forbid, the community should neglect to live according to the rule, the bishop shall admonish them as much as may be fitting and helpful.

If they despise this, then, after being corrected again and again, they shall be compelled under his authority. If, contrary to our hope, they should fall into worse behavior, the monastery itself shall then be changed into a synod-house, governed and administered by the abbot together with the consent of the bishop of the See of Aquileia, as we stated above concerning the monastery of the girls.

No one else shall inflict any injury upon these properties, monks, or nuns.

But you, Lord Siguald, who are the present bishop and are recognized as worthy of God, we adjure by the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and by blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, not to permit any violence against them or against the women, nor to commit such violence yourself. Rather, let this charter remain perpetually firm, written under anathema, so that your successors may take greater care and a great reward may increase for you.

But if you despise doing this, fear the Lord with his angels.

We asked the monk Amspert to write this charter made for us.

This was done at the monastery of all the holy apostles, situated at Nonantula in the territory of Modena, in the sixth and third years of our lords King Desiderius and King Adelchis, on the third of May, in the fifteenth indiction. [Note: [Col. 0633D] In both copies there is an error in the chronological notation: in the Maniago copy because the notation is not supplied, and in the Civitas copy because it is incorrect. Read here: “In year 6 and on the 3rd.” This agrees with the year 762 and with indiction 15. See what is said in the Life of Saint Paulinus, chapter 4, no. 2.]

+ I, therefore, an unworthy monk, wrote this charter made by me with my own hand and asked that it be subscribed.

+ I, Marcus, an unworthy abbot, consenting to this, wrote it with my own hand.

+ I, Anto, an unworthy monk, wrote it with my own hand.

+ I, Victorianus the sinner, wrote this charter with my own hand.

+ I, Silvester, called an unworthy abbot, at the request of Erfo, wrote this charter with my own hand.

+ I, Guidulfus, an unworthy monk of the holy apostles, at the request of Erfo and by order of Lord Silvester the abbot, wrote this charter with my own hand.

+ I, Ursus, although an unworthy priest and monk of Christ and of the archangel Michael, at the request of Erfo, wrote this charter with my own hand.

+ I, Beatus, an unworthy deacon of the saints and apostles, at the request of Erfo, wrote it with my own hand.

+ I, Theophilus, an unworthy monk of the saints, at the request of Erfo and by order of Lord Silvester the abbot, wrote this charter of ours with my own hand.

+ I, Anselm, although an unworthy monk of all the holy apostles, at the request of Erfo, now abbot, and by order of Lord Silvester the abbot, wrote this little charter of donation and settlement for the monastery of the monks at Sexto. Another charter of equal tenor and meaning, which they are to have for the monastery of the monks at Salto, was likewise written; and there are also the remaining charters, one written for the presbyter Ursus and another for the deacon Beatus, making four in all. This one was delivered to the monastery at Sexto; another was delivered to the monastery of the women at Salto; the third to the monastery of Lord Victorianus the abbot, the monastery of the holy archangel Michael; the fourth to the monastery of Lord Erfo in Tuscany, so that without any further fraud these venerable places may remain perpetually secure.

Here ends. Thanks be to God. Amen. Pray for us, all saints.

### I. THE MANIAGO COPY

In the charters of the counts of Maniago, from the archive of the abbey of Sexto, pages 19 and 203.

[Col. 0630A]

Foundation and endowment of the monastery and abbey of Saint Mary of Sexto in Friuli, in the year of the Lord 770.

It has long been impressed upon our minds that the singular excellence of monks should be extolled, and the praises of all their merits recounted, so that we ourselves may grow more earnestly in the Lord, and may be able to serve as a model for others; and that, for all in general, the whole foundation and progress should be the Lord Christ, as the Apostle [Col. 0630B] bears witness, saying: “No one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ.” Once these things have been established within the secret places of the human mind, all vices immediately give way, and all the corruptions of the flesh melt like wax placed upon fire. Hence the temptations of men and all the wiles of the devil are straightaway extinguished; nor can he resist any longer where he finds no place in which to possess those whom he has conquered, because Satan rules in the light only so long as he recognizes the instruments of his possession. When the enemy’s forces have been driven away from the Christian, he begins to be God’s temple, and the Holy Spirit, rejoicing as in a most beautiful dwelling, enters him.

Therefore we, the brothers Herto, Anto, and Marcus, formerly established in the lay state, by the inspiration of divine grace built two monasteries in the territory of Friuli: one in the place called Sexto, in honor of Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, and of the blessed John the Baptist and Peter, apostle of Christ; and we had determined to live there with the brothers under the yoke of the Rule in God’s service. [Col. 0630C] We also built another monastery at Rippa, which is called Salto, in honor of Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, John the Baptist, and Peter, apostle of Christ, where our lady and mother Geltruda was to dwell with the women gathered there, wearing the monastic habit. But since we heard that prophetic divine utterance in the forty-fourth Psalm, where God speaks to the human soul: “Hear, O daughter, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house,” we followed this utterance, departed from our land and kindred, and resolved to live in the regions of Tuscany.

But since, regarding these aforesaid monasteries, no one should fail to restrain himself from troubling our men or our brothers whom we left in the monastery, on the grounds that we had held them in our power, we, Herto and Marcus, although unworthy abbots, have therefore provided through this present document that all our possessions should be adjudicated, administered, and assigned by our gift in the aforesaid monasteries.

First of all, in the monastery at Rippa Salto, where our lady mother is known to be with the other monks, we give and grant our estate, where that monastery was founded by us, with all its cultivation, arable lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, astalaria, and one-half of the castle of Ausimano, the other half of which we gave to the monastery of Sexto. We have likewise granted one-half of the mill at Palaciolo, and one-half to the aforesaid monastery of men. Nevertheless, so long as our lady and mother [Col. 0632A] lives, the whole of the grain shall remain at her disposal. The grain of the peasants, however, shall henceforth be divided equally. After her departure, everything from that mill shall be held jointly by them. The monastery of nuns shall have one-half of the mountain at Carnea, which belonged to us, and the monastery at Sexto the other half; whether they wish to pasture jointly or divide it, that shall be in their power.

As for the farmhouses, we decree that those belonging to the monastery of the girls shall be named: the farmhouses at Logiaco, the farmhouses at Macretas, the farmhouses in the Major Field, the farmhouses at Avora, the farmhouses at Tara beside the Tunion, the farmhouses at Adeliaco, the farmhouses at Maitiuculo, the farmhouses at the two basilicas, the farmhouses at Aureliano, the farmhouses at Aviniaco, the farmhouses at Gratiolaco, the farmhouses at Carnia Anvico Ampitio, and the farmhouses of John and Martiolo.

Thus we grant to you, at the proper time, the revenues that the farmhouses at Remacetto and Trans ought to pay annually, and the vineyards or meadows that we possess [Col. 0632B] at Dauvino, and whatever we are seen to possess at Coloniola, and the vineyard at Brombagiis, which the sons or grandsons of Budon hold. We also add our estate at Medeja with all its appurtenances, and likewise the farmhouses at Cisiano, according to the terms and conditions contained in their charter.

One hundred amphorae of wine shall be conveyed to that monastery of the girls; whatever remains beyond this we grant annually to the monastery at Sexto. Let them make hay at Marciano and at the mill at Palatiolo, as they have been accustomed to do. They shall likewise have the woods at Vetreto and Carnariola. Let the monastery of the girls pasture its pigs at Porci of the Senodochium, which is situated nearby, without any charge, together with the pigs of the aforesaid monastery.

Finally, in the monastery of men at Sexto, we wish it to possess the domain between the river Tagliamento and the river Livenza, and whatever between them is known to have come under our power: whether the estate at Sexto, where we built that monastery; or the estate at Laurentiaca, with the oratory of the Lord and Savior situated there; or the estate [Col. 0632C] at San Focato, with houses, estates, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, astalaria, mountains, streams, pastures, and marshes, as well as mills; or movable and immovable property, whatever is known to belong to the aforesaid estates or to our right between those rivers.

Likewise, the farmhouses and smallholdings in the village of Mariano, in the territory of Verona; the farmhouses at Belluno, in the district of Ceneda; and, across the river Tagliamento, the estate at Ramussello with all its appurtenances, as well as Saletto and the Marshes, and whatever is there—all of which came from my wife.

The estates at Rippa Fracta, the estates at Bivero, the estates at Azano, the estates at Pissettana with all their appurtenances, the estates at Silo with an oratory, the estates at Blessaga with a cell; the estate of Villa; the estate of Aquae, which is called Hedago: on one side it extends along the Lemida, and on the other as far as the ditch of the Savonari and Coibula; the estate of Anone; the estate at Sacco; the estate at Crispinaga with its castle; the estate of Veruo, of Mulinego, and of Lutrano; the estate of Salto with a cell; the estate of Ribaria; the estate of Porpirio. [Col. 0632D] The estate of the village of Leonum with the cell of Saint Florian; the estate of Medeja; and whatever appears to belong to our right between the flowing waters—that is, between the Tagliamento and the Livenza—as far as the Hungarian road is seen, and the marshes of the sea, and whatever belongs to royal authority, together with every domain that can be spoken of or named.

In addition, our estate at Mariano with all its appurtenances.

We have set free all our male and female servants, aldiones and aldionae, of either sex, and have made charters of their freedom. Likewise, concerning their wages, and concerning those who had previously been free, we have made charters for them. We wish and decree that none of them should impose anything upon them, but that they should act according to what their charters contain.

The abbot, or his successors, who shall in due course be appointed [Col. 0634A] in that monastery at Sexto, shall live regularly with those monks, ordering and arranging matters for the monastery of women at Salto and for the Senodochium, with that abbot governing and administering them. The abbot and the monks entrusted to him shall live regularly, and henceforth shall not be reduced under the power of us or our heirs. Rather, he himself shall always preside over the monastery of men, except when the abbot has died, as is customary by God’s command. Then, if the monks do not unanimously agree together upon one person, or—God forbid—choose an evil head for themselves, the pontiff of the see of Aquileia shall restore them to agreement and appoint the better of those monks as abbot.

The abbot himself, with the consent of the pontiff of the see of Aquileia, shall humbly appoint the abbess; and this shall be done when all do not choose unanimously, or when the majority, being the better, makes the choice, so that great reward may thereby come to them, and they may remain in God’s service without the devil’s bite.

He shall have no other license over them or over the women to impose anything, nor to have a reception for himself, nor his own missus, nor to issue any command [Col. 0634B], either in the monastery or concerning the monastery, unless the pontiff has been invited by the abbot or abbess. And if—God forbid—the community neglects to live according to the Rule, the pontiff himself shall admonish them to live as is fitting. If they despise this, after being corrected they shall again and again be constrained under due warning.

But if—something we do not wish—they should go further and those in the same monastery should have no monastic observance at all, then the monastery itself shall be changed into a senodochium, with that abbot governing it together with the consent of the pontiff of the see of Aquileia, as we said above concerning the monastery of the girls. He shall inflict no further injury upon its possessions, monks, or nuns.

But you, who are now the pontiff and are recognized as worthy of God, Lord Sigoald the patriarch, we adjure by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and by blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, not to permit any violence to be inflicted upon them or upon the women, nor to inflict it yourself. May this charter, written under anathema, remain perpetually firm [Col. 0634C], so that your successors may take greater care and a great reward may accrue to them. But if you neglect to do this, fear [God] with his angels.

We asked Anspert the notary to write this charter made by us.

This was enacted at the monastery of All the Holy Apostles, situated at Nonantula in the territory of Modena. In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 760, in the fourteenth indiction, during the reign of our lords Desiderius and Adelchis, kings, on the third day entering the month of May.

[Note: [Col. 0633D] In both copies there is an error in the chronological notices: in the Maniacense because the notice is not supplied, and in the Civitatense because it is incorrect. Read here: “year 6 and 3.” This agrees with the year 762 and with indiction 15. See what is said in the Life of Saint Paulinus, chapter 4, no. 2.]

I, Herto, unworthy abbot, wrote this charter with my own hand, and asked the following to subscribe.

I, Marcus, unworthy abbot, consenting to this, wrote with my own hand.

I, Anto, unworthy abbot, wrote with my own hand.

I, Victorianus, sinful abbot, wrote with my own hand.

I, Silvester, an unworthy abbot, called and requested by Herto, wrote this charter with my own hand.

I, Gandulfus, abbot, requested by Herto, wrote with my own hand.

[Col. 0634D] I, Ursus, although an unworthy abbot of the Archangel Michael, requested by Herto, wrote this charter with my own hand.

I, Beatus, unworthy abbot of the Holy Apostles, requested by Herto, wrote with my own hand.

I, Theophilus, sinful abbot, requested, wrote with my own hand.

I, Ansbertus, notary of the royal court, requested by Herto, illustrious abbot, and by order of the most illustrious lords Anto and Marcus, wrote this charter of donation and settlement for the monastery of monks at Sexto, and at the same time another charter of equal tenor and agreement, which they ought to have in the monastery of monks at Salto. Thus two other charters were also written, one for the aforesaid Urtone and the other for the deacon Beatus, making four in all. This one was delivered to the monastery at Sexto, and another was delivered to the monastery of women at Salto. The third was delivered to the monastery of Lord Victorianus the abbot, [Col. 0635] in the monastery of the holy archangel Michael; the fourth, indeed, to the monastery of Lord Herto at Tuxia, so that those venerable places may endure perpetually without any fraud. Explicit. Thanks be to God. Amen. All the saints, pray for us.

## II. DIPLOMA OF CHARLEMAGNE TO PAULINUS THE GRAMMARIAN

[Col. 0635A]

Charles, etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Charlemagne, Patrologia, volume XCVII, column 957.

## III. DIPLOMA OF CHARLEMAGNE TO PAULINUS THE PATRIARCH, FOR PRESERVING THE FREEDOM OF THE AQUILEIAN CLERGY IN THE ELECTION OF PATRIARCHS

Charles, by the grace of God, etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Charlemagne, Patrologia, volume XCVIII, column 1447.

## IV.

Here should be inserted the diploma of Charlemagne to Paulinus, issued at Regensburg in the year 801, by which he subjects to him a hospice constructed by Feroce, abbot of Verona. [Col. 0635B] Fontaninus discusses it in his booklet *Delle Masnade*, page 21, and says that he possesses there a copy extracted from the original at Aquileia in the year 1195. But since we have hitherto labored in vain to obtain access to it, we cannot produce it.

We nevertheless judged that the absence of such a diploma should not be considered a serious deficiency in our collection, since the marquis Scipione Maffei teaches us, near the end of book XI of *Verona Illustrata*, that this hospice was constructed not by Feroce the abbot, but by Duke Lupo and his wife Ermilenda:

> “The monastery, or hospice, of Saint Mary, which the blessed Lupo, duke, built with his wife Ermilenda.”

These are the words of a certain judgment of the year 845, recovered by Maffei himself from the archive of that monastery. Therefore, since it is rejected by the Veronese as a forgery, we too do not regret lacking it.

## V. DIPLOMA OF CHARLEMAGNE TO PAULINUS THE PATRIARCH

[Col. 0635C]

Charles, by the grace of God, etc. For the remainder, see volume and column as above, column 1448.

## VI. [Note: [Col. 0635D] In manuscript codex 1322 of the Vatican Library, where the canons of the Council of Chalcedon are found, this formula appears at the end, page 280 and following.] OATH OF THE BISHOPS TO THE HOLY SEE OF AQUILEIA

[Note: [Col. 0635D] This charter was communicated, with his customary kindness, by the distinguished Lord Laurentius a Turri, dean of the chapter of the city of Austria. It had been found, as I believe, among the papers of his most illustrious uncle, Philippus a Turri, once bishop of Adria, a man who rendered outstanding service to letters; perhaps he had copied it in Rome and brought it from Rome to his homeland.

Observe, however, that the chronological notices do not agree with the ninth indiction. That is the year 801, which is the twenty-eighth, not the twenty-ninth, year of Charles, and the twenty-first, or at least twentieth, year of Pippin’s Italian reign. Moreover, ten years do not intervene between the eras of Charles and Pippin, but always seven: namely, from the year 764, when Charles’s Italian reign begins, to the year 781, when Pippin’s Italian reign begins, in both cases in April.

Another copy was sent by our most learned Father Nicolaus Minuccius, obtained from the Vatican through the assistance of the distinguished abbot Polidoro. We publicly offer them our thanks, since they provided us with the means of comparison and of selecting the reading we judged the more accurate.]

The precepts of the Doctor of the law of the world testify that a bishop ought to be irreproachable, that he should have a good reputation even among those outside, and that he should be ready for every good work. But it appears highly reprehensible, disgracefully notorious, and obscurely of ill repute if anyone is accused, both within and without, as guilty of perjury—so that the tongue which ought to proclaim the truth, which is the Lord Christ, whether in the venerable solemnities of the Mass, or in the pages of both Testaments, or in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, or even in daily speech with the clearest devotion, has first been polluted [Col. 0635D] by the most wicked foulness of lying.

Accordingly, the bishops of the first see must consider this with the utmost care and avoid it attentively with the whole intention of their minds: lest, perhaps, inflamed by the zeal of inconsiderate pride, they drive those whom [Col. 0636A] they hasten to raise to the rank of the sacred order into the pit of falsehood, from which they ought by every means to keep them from falling, and quickly force them headlong into the inescapable snares of an oath. For this reason, leaving aside these bonds of sin—into which anyone may become entangled if he does not take care where he sets the steps of his mind, and from which, without doubt, no one can be torn away without harm to his soul—I, the bishop who am now to be ordained, therefore testify, having touched the sacred Gospels before the Lord and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead and his coming, that I shall religiously swear according to the formula which I have learned the Apostle Paul, the teacher of the nations, to have used—not according to another formula but according to that one—to preserve inviolably in my heart, and, whenever necessity requires, to preach sincerely to my hearers according to the capacity of my understanding, the rule of the Catholic faith as defined by the Council of Nicaea and as the volume of blessed Pope Leo declares, namely according to the strength of my understanding and insofar as, with the Lord’s help, I shall be able.

I also promise [Col. 0636B] to preserve, with a full and inviolate heart, according to my ability, measure, and the quality of my strength; according to what the order of time dictates and the capacity of my understanding supplies; the statutes of the canons beneficially established by orthodox prelates, insofar as they do not oppose the holy faith and have not been abolished in the bosom of the Church through disuse.

And this, therefore, I promise under the proclamation of this oath alone: because, according to canonical documents, I ought not to be promoted to the priestly dignity without examination. [The copy of Lord a Turri does not have the word “not.”] For this reason, apart from those sins which are not hidden but manifest—such as homicide, theft, false testimony, and similar offenses, which I omit to swear concerning because they can be proved—I declare myself free from those matters in which hidden sins are concealed and which are read as expressly named: namely, from the impious plague of simony, condemned nonetheless by the Church’s first shepherd, and known to every canonical man; from the leprosy [Col. 0636C] of the most abominable crime, which is undoubtedly called the sin of the Sodomites; from the filthy crime concerning quadrupeds; and from the accursed intercourse with another man’s wife, or at least from the corruption of a virgin dedicated to the Lord. Let this suffice concerning these matters.

Concerning other affairs of various kinds, I do not make this promise under oath, but by the sole binding force of writing, under the title of this charter, I submit myself to ecclesiastical correction; and, what is more, I judge my own honor to be exposed to the loss of its dignity. This shall apply if, in other matters concerning which I may appear to be accused, I should be proved truly and rashly to have committed an offense, and should be unable to defend myself by showing that I acted under the compulsion of necessity, with the intention of avoiding an offense.

If, when summoned to a synod, I should refuse to come, entirely abandoning the proper excuse and puffed up with boastfulness; if, according to the quality of my strength and the measure of my understanding, I should prove disobedient to the bishop of the first see, that is, to my metropolitan; and if I should not obey with sincere affection, as is fitting, his most salutary [Col. 0636D] commands—which are not contrary to right faith or canonical institutions and do not turn aside from the path of truth—whether they have been issued orally or expressed in sacred letters; [Col. 0637A] and if I should not refuse, with a whole heart, to receive his messengers honorably and offer them the services of hospitality.

In ecclesiastical duties, in the diligent celebration of Masses, in psalms, hymns, and modulated spiritual songs, in the lighting of the candlesticks, and in the burning of incense at the appointed hours, I promise to be most diligently attentive and dutiful. In ecclesiastical property, whether movable, immovable, or self-moving, I promise to act carefully, according as the strength of my understanding provides me with the ability to carry things out.

Accordingly, unless the force of temporal powers is brought against me so that, under imposed necessity, I am unwillingly compelled to depart from the straight path, I do not refuse to govern or administer according to the canonical rules. But if, through the proof of truth, I should show myself blameworthy through negligence in the affairs mentioned above, I judge myself liable to the punishment set forth earlier.

I subscribed this promise below with my own hand and admonished and requested those who would subscribe it [Col. 0637B], and I have now presented it to you, thrice-blessed Patriarch Paulinus.

In the year of our lords Charles and Pippin, his son, most excellent kings, 29 and 19, under the ninth indiction, prosperously.

## VII. DIPLOMA OF CHARLEMAGNE TO MAXENTIUS THE PATRIARCH, FOR THE RESTORATION OF THE AQUILEIAN CHURCH

Charles, most serene, etc. For the remainder, see among the Works of Blessed Charlemagne, *Patrologia*, volume XCVIII, column 1449.

## VIII. [Note: [Col. 0637D] Year 829, from the charters of the monastery of Major Civitas, cited above, page 203.] DIPLOMA OF THE EMPERORS LOUIS AND LOTHAIR FOR THE MONASTERY OF SAINT MARY IN THE VALLEY OF THE CITY OF AUSTRIA, TO MAXENTIUS THE PATRIARCH

In the name of the Lord and our Redeemer Jesus Christ, Louis and Lothair, by divine providence emperors Augusti.

[Col. 0637C] If by the gift of our generosity we contribute some assistance to places dedicated to God, we clearly believe that this will undoubtedly benefit the stability of our empire and the advantage of our souls. Therefore let the knowledge of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, know that Maxentius, patriarch of the Church of Aquileia, coming into the presence of [our eminence; *nostri* is missing] and humbly imploring our clemency with the prayers at his disposal, asked that we hand over to the aforesaid mother church of Saint Mark the Evangelist and Saint Hermagoras, martyr and bishop, where by God’s authority that patriarch presides, the monastery of girls called Saint Mary, situated beside the basilica of Saint John and constructed within the walls of the city of Friuli, in the place called Valley.

Let everyone’s diligence know that we have done so. Therefore, for the sake of firmness, we ordered these imperial letters of ours to be made for the aforesaid mother church, by which we command and order [Col. 0637D] that the aforesaid monastery of girls, with the possessions and people lawfully and legally belonging to it at the present time, shall henceforth and forever remain under the right and power of the aforesaid church and its rulers.

Thus, namely, the rulers and ministers of the aforesaid church shall enjoy complete freedom in all matters to order and administer canonically whatever they may wish for its benefit and advancement, and to do whatever they choose. And so that this grant of our authority may be held more firmly and preserved more effectively for future times, we have signed it below with our own hands and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Louis, most serene emperor.

Sign of Lothair, most glorious Augustus.

Durandus, deacon, acting by request in the place of Federicus.

[Note: [Col. 0637D] In the chronological notices of this diploma, which we obtained from the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Mary in the Valley, now commonly called the Major Monastery of the City of Austria, it should be observed that the eras of these rulers must be reckoned as follows: Louis’s from the year 813, when, while his father Charlemagne was still alive and governing, he was hailed emperor at Aachen in an assembly of nobles and bishops held there; and Lothair’s not from the year 817, when he was admitted by his father Louis into partnership in the empire, but from the year 821, when he confirmed what he had done in the aforesaid year 817 and presented it to the nobles of the kingdom.

See Baronius and Pagi, discussing these years from the older annalists. The date of this diploma therefore falls in the year 829. From this you may infer that Patriarch Maxentius continued in his see and life until this year.]

Given on the third day before the Ides of November, in the seventeenth year, Christ being propitious, of Lord Louis, most serene emperor, and the ninth of Lothair Augustus.

Enacted at the royal palace of Nijmegen, prosperously in the name of God.

261

## IX. [Note: [Col. 0638D] Year 921. There is a charter in the possession of Lord Francesco de Masottis, cited above, page 197.] DIPLOMA OF BERENGAR, EMPEROR, FOR THE CASTLE OF PUZIOL, IN FAVOR OF FREDERICK, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA

In the name of the eternal God, Berengar, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus.

[Col. 0638B] Let the knowledge of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, and of our own people, know that Grimald, glorious marquis and our beloved faithful servant, humbly entreated our clemency that we should deign to grant to a certain Frederick, our most faithful patriarch, a certain castle belonging to our imperial jurisdiction, called Puziol, situated and adjoining in the county of Friuli, with all its dependencies and appurtenances, together with the judicial rights, jurisdictions, and properties belonging to that castle throughout its circuit [Col. 0638C], on every side as far as the distance of one lawful mile extends, just as it anciently and now lawfully and reasonably belonged to that county.

We confirm to him all the instruments of his charters that have been lost through fire, negligence, or the incursion of pagans, and whatever the patriarch Frederick has lawfully and legally acquired, or has inherited through his father’s or mother’s side, or has rightly devolved upon him by hereditary right from his parents, and in which he is seen to have been lawfully and legally invested, whether by charters or without charters, forever.

Inclining to his prayers, we grant and bestow upon the aforesaid patriarch Frederick the aforesaid castle belonging to our imperial jurisdiction, called Puziol, situated and adjoining in the county of Friuli, with all its dependencies, together with the judicial rights, jurisdictions, and properties belonging to that castle throughout its circuit, on every side as far as the distance of one lawful mile extends, just as it anciently and now lawfully and reasonably belonged to that county; and we delegate it to be transferred entirely from our right and dominion into his right and dominion.

We confirm to him all the instruments of his charters that have been lost through fire, negligence, or the incursion of pagans, and whatever the patriarch Frederick has lawfully and legally acquired, or has inherited through his father’s or mother’s side, or has rightly devolved upon him by hereditary right from his parents, and in which he is seen to have been lawfully and legally invested, whether by charters or without charters, forever [Col. 0638D], together with houses, lands, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, willow plantations, sown lands, waters and watercourses, fisheries, male and female servants, aldiones and aldianae, mountains, valleys, marshes, plains, and everything lawfully and legally belonging to it.

For having, holding, and firmly [Col. 0639A] possessing it, both the said Frederick, illustrious patriarch of the holy Church of Aquileia, and all his successors, without contradiction from any authority whatsoever.

If anyone should attempt to infringe or violate this precept of our authority and grant, let him know that he shall pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid illustrious patriarch Frederick.

And so that this may be believed more truly and observed more carefully, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it to be marked below with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Lord Berengar, most pious emperor Augustus.

John, bishop and chancellor, acting in the place of Ardengus, bishop and archchancellor, reviewed this.

[Note: [Col. 0639C] There is an error in the chronological notice of the reign. Berengar was elected king in the year 888, in the month of March, as Pagi argues from the date of constitution 45 of the Cassinese Bullary, under this year, no. 2. Therefore the year 821, in the month of October, is the thirty-fourth year of his reign. But the copyist misread and wrote V for X in the Roman numerals, and omitted I. Unless perhaps the era should be reckoned from the year 894, when, after Guido had been driven out with the assistance of Arnulf, Berengar recovered Pavia and the kingdom. See Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, book VI.

The year of the empire, omitted by the copyist, is the seventh. For he is called emperor in the year 915, as Pagi observes under that year, no. 3, from the date of the constitution in the Cassinese Bullary for the monastery of Saint Julia at Brescia; and this appears more clearly from the following diploma.

The tenth indiction agrees with the year 921 if one follows the Constantinopolitan indiction from the Kalends of September, or the Constantinian or Caesarean indiction from the eighth day before the Kalends of October. If one prefers the Roman indiction, an I is missing before X, for in the year 921 the Roman indiction was actually the ninth. [Col. 0639D]

The patriarch Frederick mentioned here may be the one whom Ughelli lists as no. 44 among the Aquileians, who ascended the patriarchal throne of Aquileia in the year 883 or 884 and, according to Candidus and the old Aquileian chronicle reported by Muratori in the *Latin Anecdotes*, volume IV, held it for fifty-three years.

The credibility of this diploma is supported by another diploma that we read in Ughelli under Walterus. It was issued by the same patriarch in the year of the Lord 1210, indiction 14, on the sixth day before the Ides of November at Flumisellum, by which he handed over to the Church of Aquileia the parish of Puzol and the revenues arising from it, especially so that expenses might be made for the ornaments of the temple and the beauty of the house of God. If, therefore, the patriarch handed Puziol over to the Church of Aquileia, it had already been handed over and granted to that patriarch himself, presumably by Berengar.]

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of October, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 821, in the twenty-eighth year of the most pious king Lord Berengar, and in the seventh year of his empire, indiction 10.

Enacted at Pavia, prosperously in the name of Christ. Amen.

## X. [Note: [Col. 0639D] Year 921. From the charters of Count Hector de Brazzano, cited above.] DIPLOMA OF BERENGAR, EMPEROR, FOR THE CASTLE OF SAVORNIANO, IN FAVOR OF PETER, PRIEST OF AQUILEIA

[Col. 0639B]

In the name of the Lord, the eternal God, Berengar, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus.

Let the knowledge of all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, and of our own people, know that Grimald, glorious marquis and our beloved faithful servant, humbly entreated our clemency that we should deign, by this authority, to grant to a certain priest of the holy Church of Aquileia named Peter permission to confirm and fortify his own castle, called Saburniano, constructed on his own property, with battlements, defenses, *bertistae*, and ditches.
