Inclining to his prayers, by this precept of our grant we have given the aforesaid priest Peter permission and authority to confirm and fortify his castle at Saburniano with battlements, defenses, *bertistae*, and ditches: commanding and absolutely ordering that no duke, marquis, count, viscount, sculdasius, gastald, dean, or any person, great or small, entering that castle, inflict any dispute or annoyance upon it.

Let no one there hold a public judicial assembly or impose a lodging obligation by authority; rather, let the aforesaid priest be permitted to possess his castle under secure right forever, without any public disturbance or contradiction. Above all, we decree and command that the men of that priest who reside on his properties shall not attend any public judicial assembly, except in the presence of the marquis who is in office at the time, three times a year.

If anyone attempts to infringe this precept of our grant, let him know that he shall pay fifty pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid priest and his heirs, or to whomever he himself has given it or permitted to possess it.

And so that this may be believed more truly and observed more carefully, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it to be marked below with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Berengar, most serene emperor Augustus.

262 John, bishop and chancellor, acting in the place of Ardengus, bishop and archchancellor, reviewed this.

[Note: [Col. 0639D] This diploma and the preceding one belong to the same year, namely 921. Observe here that, in expressing [Col. 0640C] five hundred years, the numeral V was used in place of D, as though the writer intended five centuries to be read together with the four other centuries expressed by the letter C; the total thus produces nine hundred years.

The twenty-eighth year of the reign is also given here. Its era must be reckoned not from the year 888, when he was first called king, but from the year 894, when he was restored to the kingdom with Arnulf’s assistance, as we noted concerning the preceding diploma.

The seventh year of the empire agrees perfectly with the year 921. The month is not supplied, but the inserted indiction 10 shows that the diploma was issued after the Kalends of September or after the eighth day before the Kalends of October. For the Constantinopolitan or Caesarean indiction had begun its tenth from those dates, while the Roman indiction remained ninth until the end of the year.

But the assertion made by some that the priest Peter mentioned here was the patriarch of Aquileia is incorrect, for no patriarch named Peter appears in the list of Aquileian patriarchs at that time.]

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 921, in the twenty-eighth year of King Berengar, and in the seventh year of his empire, indiction 10.

Enacted at Verona, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

### XI. [Note: [Col. 0640D] We have seen these formulas at the end of a certain Gospel Book of the Church of Aquileia, excellently written on parchment and, especially on its first pages, in letters of gold. We think it is the book that was presented to bishops when they swore their oaths and placed before them. The conclusion, “So may God help me,” is everywhere similar and customary. The oath of Archbishop Hincmar at the Synod of Pontigon, among the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, volume II of the *Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks*, title L, §4, closes as follows: “So may God help me, and these holy pledges.” Since each formula is written in a hand different from the others, we believe that each was written by the hand of the bishop who swore it. Perhaps, because the back of the last sheet had been filled by the three oaths made by Poppo, Eberard, the bishop of Mantua, while swearing his oath, wrote his formula in the blank space that remained at the end of the Gospel passages terminating on the front of the last sheet, so that it should properly be placed after the others. This belongs to the year 1045, when, as Ughellus records, [Col. 0641C] in volume I, under Mantua, Marcianus was appointed to that see. Astulfus, bishop of Vicenza, was present in 1046, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, at the Council of Pavia, as is clear from a charter cited by Ughellus under Verona, where the question concerns the immediate precedence of the bishop of Verona after the patriarch of Aquileia, on the occasion of the Council of Pavia, at which Patriarch Eberardus attended with this Astulfus among the other bishops. But because Conrad the Emperor is named in the pledge, and he died in 1039, it is evident that it was given before that year. Moreover, because it is written before the formulas of Pola and Concordia, which were given, as will soon be said, around the year 1027, we believe it was made before them, and [Col. 0641D] we think there is an error in Ughellus, who places Theobaldus as bishop of Vicenza in 1037 before Astulfus, and before Theobaldus, in 1046, Lambertus, and before him another Theobaldus. Either there was only one Theobaldus, whom Astulfus succeeded around 1024, or Astulfus must be placed before Lambertus and the other Theobaldus. The latter cannot be admitted, because we have Astulfus as bishop in 1046. Therefore there is only one Theobaldus, whom Astulfus succeeded. Ughellus himself, by saying “they say” and “they report,” indicates that he did not place much confidence in his own list. John of Pola subscribed in 1031 to the document of the consecration of the Church of Aquileia under Poppo, in which that year is said to be Conrad’s fifth, reckoned from his coronation at Rome in 1027. Thus this promise falls between 1027 and 1031, in which the Emperor Conrad is mentioned. Robert of Concordia is the man who, in 1031, is included in the donation of Patriarch Poppo, by which he established the number of priests whom he calls brothers for the service of the Church of Aquileia; Poppo completed that donation with the counsel of Robert and the others named there. In the Concordian records under Ughellus it is said that Rudbertus subscribed this donation. In the Aquileian records under Poppo he does not appear among the subscribers, but he is found in the body of the document as one consulted. He, like John of Pola, ought therefore to have made his promise after 1026 and before 1031, for the same reason.]

## FORMULAS OF THE PROMISE OF FIDELITY

Made to the Patriarchs of Aquileia by future suffragan bishops.

1. *(Around the year 1015.)* I, Marcianus, future bishop of the holy Church of Mantua [printed *Mantunae* for *Mantuanae*], promise and pledge that I shall be faithful and obedient to the holy Church of Aquileia, and to you, Lord Patriarch Heverardus, and to your successors according to my order, saving my fidelity to King Henry. So may God help me, and these four holy Gospels.

2. *(Around the year 1024.)* I, Artulfus, future bishop of the Church of Vicenza, promise and pledge to be faithful and obedient to the holy Church of Aquileia, and to you, Lord Patriarch Poppo, and to your successors according to my order, saving my fidelity to Conrad the Emperor and to his son Henry. So may God help me, and these four holy Gospels.

3. *(Around the year 1027.)* I, John, future bishop of the holy Church of Pola, promise and pledge that I shall be faithful and obedient to the holy Church of Aquileia, and to you, Lord Patriarch Poppo, and to your successors according to my order, saving my fidelity to Conrad the Emperor and to his son Henry. So may God help me, and these four holy Gospels.

4. *(Around the year 1027.)* I, Ruodbertus, future bishop of the holy Church of Concordia, promise and pledge that I shall be faithful and obedient to the holy Church of Aquileia, and to you, Lord Patriarch Poppo, and to your successors according to my order, saving my fidelity to Conrad the Emperor and to his son Henry. So may God help me, and these four holy Gospels.

### XII. [Note: [Col. 0642C] From two manuscript copies, one shown to us by Mr. Agricola and the other by Mr. Joseph Binius, both nevertheless extracted from the archive of the monastery of Mosacum, whose church is called that of Saint Gall—the former by Bernardinus, son of the late John Andreussius, the chancellor of the monastery of Mosacum, and the latter by Albertus, son of the late Bernardinus Andreussius—we produce this instrument. Although it is said to have been enacted in 1072, when Singefredus was patriarch, the intention of the donor was not fulfilled either by Henry, who is called patriarch in 1077, or by Frederick, who died in 1084 or 1085, but only under Udalricus, or Voldaricus, who was appointed patriarch in 1086 and held the see until 1119. Under him, in 1118, the church of Mosacum was dedicated; a document of its dedication is found, from the same Joseph Binius, in Ughellus under Voldaricus. It is noteworthy that almost the same saints are listed there as are named in this instrument; and Andreas, bishop of Civitas Nova, who is a witness here, is the consecrator of the church in that document. Thus he remained bishop of Civitas Nova for more than forty-six years.]

## DOCUMENT OF THE DONATION OF COUNT CANCELLINUS

For the foundation of the abbey and monastery of Mosnicum or Mosacum.

“The good man brings forth good from the good treasure of his heart.” Therefore let it be known to all the faithful of Christ, present and future, how Count Cancellinus openly and without any contradiction handed over his allod to Patriarch Frederick, earnestly requesting that he establish divine service on that estate. Because Patriarch Frederick, prevented by death, could not fulfill this, his successor Patriarch Udalricus happily completed it. Since he built this place in honor of the holy and undivided Trinity, of the holy cross, of holy Mary the Mother of God, of Saint John the Baptist, Saint John the Evangelist, and the holy apostles Andrew, Bartholomew, and Matthew; likewise of the holy martyrs Blaise, Cantius, Cantianus, Chrysogonus, Tatianus, Germanus, Gervasius, and Protasius; and of the blessed confessors Martin and Saint Gall the Great, Othmar; and also of the holy virgins Cecilia, Margaret, and Columba, he endowed it with the allod of the aforesaid count.

These, then, are the properties which Count Cancellinus offered to the Lord as a sweet-smelling sacrifice, and which Patriarch Udalricus, as a faithful and prudent servant set over the household of the Lord, permanently attached to this church.

First, whatever the aforesaid count possessed in this place, with all its appurtenances, at Upper and Lower Valach—twenty-three *mansi*—and Mount Sartum as far as Mount Habilis, together with everything belonging to these, he dedicated and granted to this monastery. In addition, whatever he possessed and held as his own at Mariani and at one mountain called Lanachs, and at Fustrech.

At Adelarium, eleven *mansi*, in the place called Fortis. He likewise established the lake called Ingan, just as he himself had possessed it, with every right, possession, and appurtenance, as permanently fixed and immovable for this place. At Bellunum he transferred eight *mansi*.

Moreover, the same patriarch, considering that he who sows in blessings will reap from blessings eternal life, also enlarged and magnificently endowed this place by appropriately adding to its portion. In the village called Plaguths, 263 fifty *mansi*; at Walchen, fourteen *mansi*; at Colles, sixteen *mansi*; at Salcanum, ten; at Udine, one; at Basilianum, eleven *mansi*; in the village called Impons, eleven; in Versegna, one; in the forest of Schint; in the village of Caum, one for raising pigs, and for the common benefit of the villages of Plaguths and Ingan. At Castellanum, sixteen *mansi*; at Bagnaric, three *mansi*; [Col. 0642C] at Aventio, one; and in Istria he confirmed as given to this church the place called Portus, with everything belonging to it. He also gave two mills situated at Lecina, as well as the tithes from Furnich and from certain other villages in the parish of Saint Mary of [Note: [Col. 0644D] Year 1139. From the new archive of the city of Udine, at the end of the book of instruments of the year 1543 by Antonius Bellonus, cited pages 50 and 82.] [Col. 0643A] Villach, and in the parish of Saint John of Gilsitis; these he had held for his own use, together with the tithes near the place of Vinchirese and two fishing *mansi*, and he gave and established them for this place.

He also joined three parishes to the properties mentioned above: one, namely, that of Clausach; another, that of Ingan, with the whole right of the parish and of the Christian court; and the third, that of Corto, without the right of the Christian court.

Likewise, he gave, assigned, and subjected to this monastery the hospital at Clansa and the hospital at Aquileia, both ordered and built by the same patriarch, with everything pertaining to them, in such a way that they should be governed by the abbot of that place, and that everything formerly administered for the benefit of the poor on the basis of the two prebends established there daily should be arranged entirely for the use of those fellow brothers.

But if anyone, which God forbid, should presume to take away or diminish anything of all that has thus been granted to the church, may he be blotted out from the book of the living, condemned by the eternal Judge and all his saints, and burned with Judas the traitor in everlasting punishment.

In addition, he gave the church one area in Carinthia called Erro, which Duke Henry had given to the patriarch for the Aquileian advocacy, together with its fisheries and everything belonging to the same court, and the crossing at Ponbenvelch, which he specifically assigned for the clothing of the brothers.

The witnesses to this matter are Andreas, bishop of Civitas Nova; Abbot Gaudentius of Sirriach; Abbot Robonus of Saint Udalricus; among the eight Aquileian chaplains, the archdeacon Sefridus and Walpertus; Cuono, provost of Austria; and Wolfredus, Hilprandus, and Benedictus, archpriests. Among the laymen: John, son of Hecho; Lupoldus, son of Pobo; John, Aquileian vice-dominus; Hiltepoldus, steward; Gotfredus; Germanus; Cuono, steward of Rocca; Hermannus; Bedinus; Riccarius; Sigibotto; Udalricus; Cheamordus; Udalricus Stolich; Hilipoldus; John Bertaldus Pericchio; [Col. 0643C] Bertaldus of Gemona and his brothers; Pericho Duringus; Articus; and many other clerics and laymen.

This was enacted in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1072, on the fourth day before the Ides of November, in the twelfth indiction.

I, Udalricus, Patriarch of Aquileia, have subscribed with my own hand; and, so that it might afterward remain valid, we ordered this charter to be marked with our seal.

### XIII. [Note: [Col. 0643D] Year 1129. From the archive of the Church of Aquileia, cited page XXVI.]

## DONATION OF AZO AND HIS WIFE MACTILDA TO THE CANONS OF THE CHURCH OF AQUILEIA

A brief record. How I, Azo of Azmurgen, together with my wife Mactilda, for the salvation of our souls and of those of our parents, gave our court in perpetuity [lacuna], situated with all its appurtenances, and two *massaritiae*, one in the village called Bicinis and the other in Clavenzano, upon the altar of holy Mary the Mother of God, for the use of the brothers [lacuna]. We made this donation in such a way: that my wife and I should hold and possess it without rent until my death. But if my wife should outlive me, she should have the usufruct during her life from the brothers for a small rent; after her death, however, everything that we gave to those brothers should remain free and undisturbed, without any contradiction. This was enacted at Aquileia in the year 1129 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [lacuna] on the Ides of March, in the seventh indiction, when there was no Patriarch of Aquileia.

The witnesses to this matter are Count Poppo of Celsa; Meginardus of Suarcemburg; Pellegrinus; Franciscus; Carolus; Fridericus; and Hermenardus of Saint Stephen; Roduldus; Venerius; Dranosa; Marinus; Vvernerus; Arpo; Baron; and Henry; Bertoldus [Note: [Col. 0643D] Although this charter does not name the Canons of Aquileia, do not doubt that it belongs to them: they placed it among the documents of their rights, from which we extracted it. It is dated, as stated, when there was no Patriarch of Aquileia, because, according to Baronius, Sigonius, and Dandulus, Ughellus says that in 1128 Gerardus of Premariaco—or, as others read, Richardus of Primerio—the patriarch, was deposed by Honorius II together with the Patriarch of Grado, John, because they were found to be the authors of the schism and, evidently, supporters of Conrad. In the interval between Gerardus’s deposition and the accession of Pellegrinus in 1130, when Engelbertus, dean of the Church of Bamberg, was elected patriarch but was not accepted by the people of Aquileia, Azo and his wife Mactilda drew up this charter of donation for the brothers, that is, the Canons of Aquileia. See Ughellus under Aquileia.]

### XIV. DOCUMENT OF THE EXCHANGE OF THE RIGHTS OF THE ADVOCACY OF AQUILEIA

Confirmed by the authority of Pellegrinus I, Patriarch of Aquileia.

The examples of the ancient Fathers instruct us to assent to the just petitions of those who serve in the Church of God. By assenting with the paternal grace of compassion and the zeal of brotherly [lacuna] affection, let us diligently strive to provide them with counsel and assistance in their new undertakings. Therefore I, Pellegrinus, by the grace of God Patriarch of the holy Church of Aquileia, wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful, present and future, how our beloved brother Hatturicus, provost of Saint Stephen, often came to us and tearfully complained that the collectors of the advocate Minghinardus were continually and intolerably harassing the peasants of his church with unjust and excessive exactions through their malice and wickedness, and burdening them with such varied severity that many, stripped of their possessions, had departed and left their houses empty; and unless we should quickly assist them by our authority, the remaining peasants would be forced to do the same. Moved by paternal pity for their afflictions and needs, and sympathizing with them in fraternal affection, we did not delay in advising and assisting them for the time being; and, as necessity pressed, we resolved to free them from such great oppression.

Accordingly, summoning the advocate Menghinardus and his son Henry, partner in the same advocacy, we explained to them the complaint made to us, and under the assurance of our grace and authority we asked and commanded them to forbid their collectors to do such things, and to be willing in every way to heed our admonitions and commands, obey our requests, and reprimand and restrain their unjust judges from the wickedness which they were practicing against the poor peasants. Hattuvicus, provost of Saint Stephen, unable to endure the affliction of his peasants and the destruction of the goods of his church, after consulting with his brothers and his other faithful men, proposed, with the goods of the Church of Saint Stephen and by our permission and authority, to transfer [lacuna] from the aforesaid advocate M. and his son H. (printed *filiaque eius H.*) in two villages, namely Praedemano and Terenzano, and also in Carnia [lacuna], but in the remaining goods of the church by stable [lacuna] and perpetual right. To bring this about with God’s help, he did not cease laboring tirelessly, both personally and through everyone he could enlist. Finally, by God’s will, who always grants the wishes of his faithful [Col. 0644D] [lacuna], an agreement was made between them [lacuna]: that the aforesaid H. [Hattuvicus] should give the advocate Menghinardus and his son Henry twenty-four *massaritiae* from the estates of his church, which had been granted as benefices by his predecessors—four of them at Praedemano, two at Terenzano, four in the foothills, six in Carnia, and eight at San Daniele—together with the toll at the market of San Daniele, and, in addition, twenty marks of silver, on the condition that the advocate M., the father, and his son H. should renounce into our hands the court and every right of advocacy which they appeared to possess in the aforesaid properties, namely at Praedemano, Terenzano, and in Carnia (for they had no such rights in the other estates of the church), and transfer and convey them with us into the right and possession of that church.

When this agreement had finally been made, they came into our presence, reported all the foregoing to us in order, and sought our assent to these arrangements. The advocate M. and his son H. therefore renounced into our hands the court and every benefit of the advocacy which they had in the aforesaid village of the Church of Saint Stephen, and asked that it be donated to that church, as stated above. The father and son, for their part, received from us through these agreements the twenty-four *mansi* established in the places prescribed above and the toll at San Daniele.

Therefore, as we stated at the beginning, considering the affliction of the poor and wishing to rescue them from such violence, and also caring in every respect for the benefit of the church and of the brothers serving in it, we transfer and grant to the right and ownership of that church the court of the advocacy, with the full extent and justice that ought to be exercised in the aforesaid properties which the Church of Saint Stephen is seen to hold or possess, or which it may at any time thereafter acquire or redeem; and we grant and confirm it to be possessed in perpetuity, under the anathema of almighty God and of ourselves. We decree that from now on no advocate, nor any person, small or great, shall presume to hold court in the goods of the aforesaid church, or to inflict violence or any molestation; but that the provost who presides over that church at the time shall strive, as best he can, faithfully to minister these things to the brothers. So that this may be believed more firmly and guarded inviolably by all, we ordered this charter of our donation to be written, and, subscribing with our own hand, invited the other clerics and laymen who were present to subscribe likewise; and so we ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Enacted at Civitas Austria in Friuli, in the chapel of Saint Paulinus, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1134.

Sign of Patriarch Pellegrinus.

Sign of Bishop Berturicus.

Sign of Archdeacon Vudalticus.

### XV. [Note: [Col. 0645D] Year 1180. From the Archive of the Church of Aquileia, through Count Franciscus Florio, canon of that church, cited pages XLIX, 93, and 205.]

## STATUTE OF VOLDARICUS, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA

[Note: [Col. 0645D] This charter, which we mentioned in the final note on canon 13 of the Council of Friuli, presents Voldaricus the patriarch; you should know that he is different from Voldaricus, the executor of Count Cancellinus’s will, reported above under number 11. See Ughellus.]

For the celebration of the solemn feast of Saint Mary Magdalene in the Church of Aquileia.

Voldaricus, by the grace of God Patriarch of the holy Church of Aquileia and legate of the Apostolic See, to his beloved brothers in Christ, Liuprandus the dean and the other canons of the same church, present and future, forever.

If we readily and kindly admit the just and honorable petitions of those whose faithfulness and steadfastness toward the holy Church of Aquileia and toward our person have been demonstrated by manifold experience, we both make them more fervent in their devotion to us and, by this example, encourage the minds of others who observe it to undertake the service of the Church of Aquileia in the hope of a worthy reward. [Col. 0646A] Therefore, yielding to the petitions of our dearest brother and chaplain, and your fellow canon, Master Romulus, whose abundant and most pleasing merits have shown his faithfulness toward us and our church, petitions which he humbly and devoutly presented to us, we establish and decree by the privilege of this present document that you should henceforth celebrate carefully and solemnly, with the office of nine readings, the feast of Blessed Mary Magdalene, whom our brother Master Romulus has chosen as his special patron, as is customary, although until now it has not been accustomed to be solemnly celebrated in our church.

Although this feast was not part of the ancient custom of our church, matters concerning the veneration of God’s saints, and especially the observances devoted to the most blessed Mary Magdalene, are nevertheless worthy of being established and accepted with fitting and proper devotion. Even if we should not call her more excellent than the other citizens of heaven, she was nevertheless the first herald of the Lord’s resurrection, and through the examples of her conversion and repentance she gives us, who are weighed down by the burden of sins, the strongest indications of divine clemency.

At the request also of the aforesaid Master Romulus, we confer, donate, and secure by this present privilege, for you to hold and possess by right of ownership, the stall in the forum of Aquileia which he held and possessed from us and which Bertlottus the Venetian currently holds through him. Its rent is one mark of sixteen Frisach denarii. Thus, on the aforesaid feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, you shall have the full service from the said rent, and whatever remains shall be spent for the common benefit on the anniversary of his death.

So that you may believe this to be true, and so that it may remain firm and undisturbed for all time, with no successor of ours permitted to alter or disturb it, we ordered this document to be written and marked with the impression of our seal. The witnesses are Girardus of Padua [lacuna]; Jonathan of Concordia and John, bishop of Emonia; Herremannus [lacuna], the elected bishop; Master Dominicus and Reginhardus, chaplains; Herremannus, treasurer of Aquileia; [Col. 0646C] Bertholdus of Albo; and many others.

Enacted at Padua in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1180, in the thirteenth indiction, on the third day of April.

I, Chunradus, the lord patriarch’s chaplain, wrote and delivered this charter by his command.

### XVI. [Note: [Col. 0645D] Year 1196. From the Archive of the Church of Aquileia, where a copy of the stone inscription is preserved, although it cannot now be read conveniently because it has been worn away. Cited page 82.]

## INSCRIPTION OF THE COURT OF THE ADVOCACY

In the portico of the Church of Aquileia.

Let it be known to all Christ’s faithful how I, Duke Henry, for the sake of my soul and that of my wife Luicarda, gave the entire court of the canonical advocacy to this church, to Saint Mary and to these brothers, in the presence of clerics and laymen, with Lord Patriarch Vodolricus commending and confirming it; namely, on the condition that every year, on the feast of All Saints, an excellent service should faithfully be administered to these canons by their provost during my lifetime, and that Christ’s poor should be fed; but after my death, everything stated above should be fulfilled on the anniversary of my death.

In the year of the Lord 1196, in the fourteenth indiction, on the eighth day of the month beginning October. I, Vilelmus, notary of the sacred palace, in the city of Aquileia, before the doors of the major church, wrote this privilege at the request of the parties, exactly as I found it in the original, adding nothing and taking nothing away.

[Note: [Col. 0646D] These things were indeed transcribed by the notary in 1196, but they appear to have been enacted before the year 1072. For the cession by Duke Henry and Patriarch Vadolricus is mentioned in the will of Count Cancellinus above, under no. XII.]

### XVII. [Note: [Col. 0647D] Year 1242. Charter extracted from Book I, folio 203. It is in the Archive of the Chapter of Udine, in the possession of Count Laurentius Asquinus, canon. Cited page 18.]

## EXEMPTION OF THE CHAPEL OF SAINT QUIRINUS

Where converted women were housed, from subjection to the parish priest of Udine, by Bertoldus, Patriarch of Aquileia.

[Col. 0647A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. In the year of the Lord 1242, in the fifteenth indiction, on the eighth day before the end of July.

As the sacred page testifies, whoever releases handmaids from the debt of servitude deserves that his own debt be released by the supreme Judge; and prudent men have also established that whatever someone wishes to remain more firmly established should be set forth beforehand in the evidence of his writings. Therefore let those now living and those who come after know that we, Pertoldus, by the grace of God Patriarch of the holy See of Aquileia, wish it to be known to all to whom this document shall come that, with our consent and will, the chapel of Saint Quirinus of Udine, where the converted women reside, shall henceforth neither belong nor be subject to the parish of Udine, except that it shall be bound to pay it one pound of wax annually; and that henceforth no parish priest, vicar, or priest of Udine shall have any lordship over the aforesaid chapel, except the person whom we and our successors shall appoint there, in our place and name, to serve God.

If at any time any parish priest, vicar, or priest residing in Udine, or any other temporal or spiritual person, should attempt to act against the foregoing, let him know that he has incurred the indignation of God and all the saints, and of us and our successors. Therefore, so that no accusation may later arise that might attempt to weaken the gift we have made, we wish to confirm this document by the subscription of witnesses and by the authority of our seal. The witnesses to this matter were Vuilhelmus, dean of Aquileia; Jacobus, archpriest; Vvolricus of Cucanea; John of Roncas; Naus of Mels; Bonacontus; and others.

[Col. 0647C]

Enacted at Udine, in the Church of Saint Mary.

I, Martinus, notary of the sacred palace, wrote and authenticated this by the command of the aforesaid Lord Pertoldus, Patriarch of Aquileia.

### XVIII. [Note: [Col. 0647D] Year 1263. Charter in the possession of Count Laurentius Asquinus. Cited page XXVI.]

## THE RIGHTS OF THE ARCHDEACONATE OF AQUILEIA

Reformed by Gregorius of Monte Longo, Patriarch of Aquileia.

In the name of Christ. Amen. In the year from the birth of Christ 1263, in the seventh indiction, at Civitas Austria, in the patriarchal antechamber, on 15 December; in the presence of Lords Arnardus, bishop of Pedena; Transimundus of Anagni, the lord pope’s chaplain; Brother Leonardus, lector of the Friars Preachers; Jacobus, son of Master Cettonellus of Civitas; Sclavus of Campo, chaplain of Lord Gregorius, by the grace of God Patriarch of Aquileia; John of Cucanea; Master Ascanio the physician, formerly of Perugia; Lord Rufinus of Ponto of Piacenza; witnesses called and requested for this matter; and many others.

The Reverend Father and Lord Gregorius, by the grace of God Patriarch of the holy See of Aquileia, put forward the following ordinance or statute, namely:

Our beloved son John, archdeacon of Aquileia, voluntarily and freely resigned into our hands, in the presence of me, the undersigned notary, and the aforesaid witnesses, certain rights and customs which he was known to have concerning the appointment or maintenance of sworn officials in his archdeaconate for the purpose of reporting offenses; as well as another right which he claimed in law to possess over a certain quantity of grain owed to him by the inhabitants of the boroughs and market of Udine. A legal dispute had been brought by that same archdeacon against those inhabitants concerning this matter. He resigned these rights so that we might dispose of them according to the law and the useful condition of the land, at our discretion.

Therefore, for greater clarity concerning the matter, with the same archdeacon present and consenting, we judged, decreed, and ordained as follows: that the same archdeacon and his successors henceforth should neither appoint nor maintain any sworn official in any place. We also wish and ordain that the quantity of grain which the archdeacon claimed was owed to him by the inhabitants of the boroughs and market of Udine should in no way be exacted from them by that archdeacon or his successors; nor should those inhabitants henceforth be bound to pay it to him, since we have decided to retain all the foregoing for ourselves and our church.

We further establish and command that the archdeacon of Aquileia who shall hold office at the time, whether personally or through a procurator or vicar if he wishes, shall henceforth receive no report or conduct any inquiry based merely on hearsay. In the case of manifest offenses belonging to the ecclesiastical court, which come to him, his procurator, or his vicar through accusation or complaint, they may and must hear the case, judge it, and impose the customary penalty. As for the other rights [Note: [Col. 0647D] Something appears to be missing.] and customs of the archdeaconate, both those due to the archdeacon or his vicar in connection with visitations and procurations, and the demand and receipt of a certain quantity of grain owed to him by certain persons of his archdeaconate [lacuna].

Moreover, we reserve to him in full the right to demand and receive money from the parishes—the money called the Easter money, or archdeaconate money—and other money in all places and penalties in which, and from those from whom, the archdeacon has been accustomed or ought by custom or law to receive or possess it; and, in general, all the rights which the archdeacon or his predecessors have held by custom or law, insofar as they have not been taken from them by a special privilege.

Several considerations moved us to make the foregoing ordinance. Above all, however, it was the removal of numerous scandals and the evident wickedness of the sworn officials. For, as we learned with certainty, those sworn officials, seeking not the things of God but their own interests, through premeditated malice reported innocent men as guilty while leaving the guilty unreported through favor or affection, and also because of illicit agreements. Consequently, as a result of their reports, innocent men were condemned; or, even if they did not incur a legal penalty, they nevertheless incurred disgrace in fact. This aroused serious scandals among our subjects. In addition, since the petitions and pleas of our beloved petitioners, the community of Udine [something is missing, perhaps “were brought forward”], together with the considerable benefit of our church and of that place, urged us, we decree that certain canons be appointed in the aforesaid place of Udine.

We wish, ordain, and establish that, when the canons to be instituted by us have been appointed, they shall receive and possess one half of the revenues of the former vacant parish and of the church now called Saint Vorlicus of Udine.

[Note: [Col. 0648D] The alienation of the revenues of the Church of Saint Udalricus, which Gregorius instituted here for the benefit of the Archdeaconate of Aquileia, was rescinded by Patriarch Blessed Bertrandus. See the document below, no. 25, concerning the union of the provostship of Saint Udalricus with the common table of the Chapter of Udine.]

Since we also observe that, as a result of our aforesaid ordinance, the Archdeacon of Aquileia suffers no small loss in annual revenues, and considering that the other revenues of the archdeaconate were and are meager and scant, we have decided to assign to that archdeacon, for himself and his successors, as compensation for the revenues withdrawn, the other half of the revenues of the aforesaid former vacant parish and of the aforesaid Church of Saint Vorlicus. From this moment we invest the same archdeacon, with our own hand, with one half of the aforesaid revenues.

Moreover, we henceforth wish and establish that the appointment and restoration of chaplains, lower priests, and clerics in the aforesaid church called Saint Vorlicus shall belong to the Archdeacon of Aquileia who holds office at the time. We establish and command that no one shall henceforth be buried, baptized, or receive other sacraments in the church situated in the castle of Udine, which was formerly the parish church; nor shall the people solemnly gather there for divine worship. Instead, everyone shall be buried and baptized at the lower church now called Saint Vorlicus, and shall gather there for divine worship and receive the ecclesiastical sacraments. We wish and ordain that this same church, which was formerly the parish church, be entirely subject to the church called Saint Vorlicus of Udine, as a chapel to its mother church.

For the clarity of this matter and for public and lasting validity, the aforesaid Lord Gregorius, Patriarch of Aquileia, caused this present instrument to be drawn up and strengthened with the protection of his pendant seal.

### XIX. [Note: [Col. 0649D] Year 1278, from the archive of the Chapter of Udine.]

## STATUTE

Issued by Lord Raimundus, Patriarch of Aquileia, for the purchase of houses for the common life of the canons of Udine.

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year 1278 from the Nativity of the same Lord, indiction 6, at Udine, in the patriarch’s residence, on the third day of February. Present were Brother Humilis of the Order of Friars Minor, and Master Martin of Crema, parish priest of the parish of Flambrio, chaplains of the reverend lord, by the grace of God, patriarch of Aquileia; Lord Lippo Capon, a Florentine merchant; Rolando of Sant’Angelo, doorkeeper; and Burla of Milan, household servants of the said patriarch—witnesses summoned and requested for this purpose—and many others.

The reverend father and lord Raimundus, by the grace of God patriarch of the holy Aquileian see, diligently concerned for the condition, growth, and honor of the church of Saint Vorlicus at Udine, and wishing that the canons of that church should have houses in which they could live, as is the case in other churches possessing chapters, ordered, in the presence and with the consent of Lords Naticlerus, custodian; Leo, priest; Henxuttus of Attens; Matthew of Carate; and Frainus of Milan, acting on their own behalf and on behalf of the other canons of the said church who were absent, that the following be established, ordered, and observed inviolably.

One half of all the revenues of the aforesaid church of Saint Vorlicus, by whatever name they may be assessed—whether they belong to the archdeacon of Aquileia or to the aforesaid canons—shall be placed in safekeeping, to be preserved by two of the canons of the said church, chosen by agreement and consensus among those canons. These two canons shall use the revenues to purchase land adjoining the land that the canons themselves possess near the said church of Saint Vorlicus, and shall have houses built according to the advice of the aforesaid patriarch and canons, so that the same canons may live there conveniently.

The two canons shall nevertheless be required, whenever they are summoned before the said patriarch and canons, to render a complete account of these revenues. This statute shall remain firm and inviolable until the completion of the said houses.

Likewise, the same patriarch, in the presence and with the consent of the aforesaid canons, acting on their own behalf and on behalf of the absent canons, established and ordered that the following be observed perpetually and inviolably in the aforesaid church of Saint Vorlicus: the daily offerings of that church shall be distributed and given equally among the canons of the church who are present in it on the days when the offerings are made.

The custodian who now holds office, and whoever shall hold it in the future, shall, as the senior and more eminent among the said canons, whenever he is present, receive and retain from these offerings as much as two of the canons who are present would receive. All and each of the aforesaid canons of the church of Saint Vorlicus shall obey the custodian who now holds office, and whoever shall hold it in the future, in lawful and honorable matters.

The custodian shall also be required to seek and obtain the advice and consent of the aforesaid canons who are able conveniently to attend the useful deliberations of the church.

If, moreover, the said custodian or any of the aforesaid canons should be ill but present in the territory of Udine, he shall nevertheless receive his share of the aforesaid offerings as one of the other canons present, according to what has been stated above. If he is outside the aforesaid territory of Udine, he shall receive nothing whatever from those offerings.

In witness of this matter, the aforesaid lord Raimundus, patriarch, caused this instrument to be strengthened by the protection of his pendant seal.

I, Joannes of Lupico, public notary of the Holy Roman Empire, was present at all the foregoing and, having been requested, wrote it, reducing it to public form.

[Note: From this charter you can see how badly those conjecture who assert that the chapter of Udine was instituted only by Blessed Bertrand, the patriarch, since it clearly shows that it existed before Raimundus.]

## XX. [Note: 1289. In Count Lorenzo Asquino, cited above, p. XXVI, ch. 2.] The Right of the Church of Udine Asserted against the Archdeacon of Aquileia

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year 1289 from the Nativity of the same Lord, indiction 2, on the ninth day of July. Present were Lords Augustine, dean of Saint Felix of Aquileia; Lazarus, archpriest or vicar of the venerable lord, the archdeacon of Aquileia; Christopher of Udine, parish priest of Luzinico; witnesses; and others.

Lord Jacobus, custodian of the major church of Udine, appearing before the venerable lord Servillion of Villalta, archdeacon of Aquileia, presented the following statement:

“My lord archdeacon, today you are summoning the clergy of your archdeaconry to celebrate a synod in the major church of Udine, without having summoned either me or the chapter, although you have no business there. For I, the church, and the chapter of Udine belong immediately to the lord patriarch of Aquileia; nor has such a right ever belonged to your predecessor. Therefore, in my own name and in the name of the church and chapter of Udine, please conduct yourself in this matter in such a way that this act may not prejudice our church or us, nor create any future prejudice for us through such a summons.”

When this statement had been made, the said lord archdeacon replied that he knew well, and also acknowledged, that he had no authority to act in the major church of Udine or over the clergy of that church. He nevertheless requested this as a special favor, because a synod could be summoned more conveniently in the church of Udine, owing to the suitability of the place and its position in the middle of the territory.

The custodian therefore granted the request, unwilling that this should create any future prejudice for himself, the church of Udine, or the chapter.

Done at Udine, in the house of Lord Nicolaus of Lady Palma.

I, Nicolaus of Udine, notary by imperial authority, was present at all the foregoing and, having been requested, wrote it.

## XXI. [Note: 1296. From the old archive of the city of Udine, cited above, p. 206, ch. 2.] Oath of Fealty Presented by Stephen Jordani, a Paduan Canon, in the Name of John, Bishop of Padua, to Raimundus, Patriarch of Aquileia

In the year 1296, indiction 9, at Udine, in the castle, in the chapel of the major palace of the lord patriarch of Aquileia, on Monday the 12th, toward the end of August. Present were Lord Nicolaus Dalfino of Venice, archdeacon of Pola; Lords Philipponus della Torre of Aquileia and Beccacius of Padua, canons; Brother Bonettus of Civitate of the Order of Friars Minor; Lord Folcherus, parish priest of Wrazlau; and Lord Bonus of Labereta, chaplains of the reverend father and lord, the reverend patriarch of Aquileia by the grace of God—witnesses summoned and requested for this purpose—and many others.

The noble and prudent man Lord Stephen, son of Lord Jordan of Rome, a Paduan canon and chaplain of the lord pope, constituted as messenger and procurator of the venerable father Lord Brother John, by divine permission bishop of Padua, for the matters contained in the procuratorial instrument set out below, appeared in the presence of the reverend father and lord Raimundus, by the grace of God patriarch of the holy Aquileian see. On behalf of the said lord bishop and the church of Padua, he presented and delivered to the patriarch a certain procuratorial instrument, whose wording, word for word, is known to be as follows:

Know all who shall inspect this present public instrument that, since we, Brother John, by divine permission bishop of Padua, are occupied with various affairs of our Paduan church, because of which we cannot at present conveniently be absent from that church of ours at Padua, nor can we personally approach the venerable father, the lord patriarch of Aquileia, as we are bound by law to do, we make, constitute, and appoint the prudent man Lord Stephen, son of Lord Jordan of Rome, a Paduan canon, chaplain of the lord pope, our kinsman and beloved companion, who is present and accepts the office, as our procurator and special messenger.

He shall appear in our name and in the name of our church of Padua before the venerable father, the aforesaid lord patriarch of Aquileia; he shall swear to him, in the name of the church of Aquileia, the oath owed to him according to the canonical sanctions; and he shall visit the church of Aquileia in the manner required by law and approved custom.

In our name and in the name of the church of Padua, we promise the undersigned public notary, acting on behalf of all whom it concerns, to hold as valid and firm whatever is done by this procurator in the matters set out above.

In witness of this matter, we have caused this instrument to be made by the undersigned notary, [lacuna], and, for greater security, strengthened by the protection of our seal.

Done at Padua, in our palace, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1296, indiction 9, on 15 August. Present were Masters Ricicherus, canon of Parenzo and vicar; Johannes Cio of Rome, chamberlain; and Jacobus of Actara, notary, members of our household, as witnesses.

And I, Manfredus, son of Thomas of Osimo, public notary by imperial authority and now notary of the lord bishop, was present at all the foregoing and, by his command, wrote and published it and affixed my customary sign.

When this procuratorial instrument had been read before the aforesaid lord patriarch, the said Lord Stephen, in the name of the procurator and on behalf of the aforesaid lord Brother John, bishop of Padua, swore the oath of fealty to the aforesaid Lord Raimundus, patriarch of Aquileia, in these words:

“I, Stephen, son of Lord Jordan of Rome, a Paduan canon and chaplain of the lord pope, procurator and special messenger of the venerable father and lord John, by the grace of God bishop of Padua, for the matters contained in the procuratorial instrument set out above, swear in his soul, in the name and stead of that lord Brother John, bishop of Padua, that from this hour forward the said Lord Brother John, bishop of Padua, shall be faithful and obedient to Blessed Hermagoras, to the holy church of Aquileia, and to the reverend father and lord, his lord Raimundus, patriarch of Aquileia, and to his canonically succeeding successors.

“He shall never knowingly participate by counsel, consent, or deed in anything by which they might lose life or limb, or be taken in an evil captivity. He shall disclose to no one any counsel which [lacuna], whether personally or through his messengers or letters, may come to him to their detriment.

“He shall assist them in retaining and defending the patriarchate of Aquileia and its regalia against every person, saving the rights of his own order. He shall treat honorably, both when going and returning, the legates and messengers of the lord patriarch and of the church of Aquileia, and shall aid them in their necessities.

“When summoned to a synod, he shall come unless prevented by a canonical impediment. Every year he shall visit the threshold of the church of Aquileia, either personally or through his messenger, unless he is released from this obligation by permission of the said lord patriarch.

“He shall not sell, give away, pledge, enfeoff anew, or otherwise alienate the possessions belonging to the table of his Paduan church without consulting the lord patriarch of Aquileia.

“So may God help me and the same lord bishop of Padua, and these holy Gospels of God.”

For this matter, the aforesaid Lord Brother John, bishop of Padua, caused this present instrument to be strengthened by the protection of his pendant seal.

I, Joannes of Lupico, public notary of the Holy Roman Empire, was present at all the foregoing and, by order of the aforesaid Lord Raimundus, patriarch, wrote it, reducing it to public form.

## XXII. [Note: 1297. From the old archive of the city of Udine, cited above, p. 198.] Designation of a Territory or Market, to Be Called “Mediolanum Raimundi”

In 1297, indiction 10, in a certain field belonging to the younger Raynerussius of Scarelius of Gemona, which lies a short distance from the mountain on which there used to be a certain castle called Grossembeh, beside the public road leading to the hospital of Collibus of Gemona. On Tuesday the 10th, toward the end of May. Present were the noble men Lords Muscha of Lature, marquis of Istria; Mathias and Adelgher, brothers of Gemona; Lord Albertinus of Reponio, scholastic of the church of Aquileia; and Master Fulcherus of Wrazlau and Nicolaus of Gorizia, parish priests of parishes and chaplains of Lord Raimundus, by the grace of God patriarch of Aquileia; Lord Milanus of Paona, inhabitant of the castle of Udine; Stephanus Vilich; and Pizulus, son of the late Lord Ottolinus of Portis of Gemona—witnesses summoned for this purpose—and many others.

The reverend father and lord Raimundus, by the grace of God patriarch of the holy Aquileian see, holding his right hand upon a certain staff, at whose top a certain iron cross was fixed, and standing in the aforesaid field, said:

“For the honor of God, of the glorious Virgin Mary, his mother, and of the blessed martyrs Hermagoras and Fortunatus, our patrons; for the honor, status, and exaltation of ourselves and of the church of Aquileia; and for the benefit of all our subjects and of the said church of Aquileia, we have fixed, and order to be fixed, this staff bearing the sign of the holy cross in this field, as a sign that, with the Lord’s gift, we intend to construct here, and cause to be constructed, a town and market of ours in the name of the church of Aquileia. We wish and decree that it be called Mediolanum Raimundi.”

And he caused the aforesaid staff with the cross to be fixed in the aforesaid field.

[Note: The intended work never reached completion, since no trace of the undertaking appears between Gemona and the hospital of Collibus. Nevertheless, even attempting great things is a great praise. Ughellus mentions this matter in his account of Aquileia under Raimundus, as does Palladius, part I, book VII.]

I, Joannes of Lupico, public notary of the Holy Roman Empire, was present at all the foregoing and, by order of the aforesaid Lord Raimundus, patriarch, wrote it, reducing it to public form.

## XXIII. [Note: 1328. In the archive of the old city of Udine, cited above, p. 198.] Foundation of the Church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile

Paganus, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See, patriarch of the holy Aquileian see, to all who shall inspect the present document, eternal greeting in the Lord.

We wish it to be known to all of you that, wishing to respond to petitions, after seeing and carefully examining on every side a certain privilege of Bertoldus, of good memory, patriarch of Aquileia, bearing his undamaged wax seal pendant, which was presented to us by our beloved son Sygebaldinus, parish priest of the church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile, we ordered that it be transcribed and renewed, at the request and humble supplication of the same parish priest, by the hand of our undersigned notary.

We wish, decree, and establish that this transcript or copy shall have the same force, validity, and authority in every respect as the aforesaid original is known to possess, even if that original should never again appear in the future.

We further decree that the same Sygebaldinus, parish priest, and his successors shall possess from us the same authority to restrain, by ecclesiastical censure and after canonical warning, those who detain the rights and possessions of the said church, as well as violators of those rights and possessions, or those who contradict or rebel against them—an authority which our predecessor is known once to have granted by that privilege to Bonus, parish priest of the same church, and to his successors.

Its wording is as follows:

[Note: As you see, one charter is inserted into another, and one document into another. Bertoldus held the see before Paganus, as is clear to anyone who reads the text, although Paganus is mentioned first; for he was renewing the instrument of the foundation made by Bertoldus. We use the authority of this document in Dissertation 1, where we discussed Henry, no. 9.]

Bertoldus, by the grace of God patriarch of the holy Aquileian see, to his beloved son Bonus, parish priest of the church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile, greeting and blessing in the Lord.

Your prudence has frequently and earnestly petitioned us that, through our writings strengthened by the protection of our seal, by which the knowledge of the truth might be clearly evident to you, your successors, and others in the future, we should deign to make you secure, certifying in those writings—according to the position we hold and as our rights declare—that the aforesaid church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile, which with all its rights belongs immediately to the church of Aquileia and to us, especially because it is situated there between the dioceses of Concordia and Ceneda, ought to have its own people and cemetery, be a baptismal church, and enjoy the liberty of exemption.

Moreover, since it is not established through public documents with what rights and possessions the said church, of which you are parish priest and shepherd, was endowed in ancient times, you have humbly and earnestly petitioned us that, at least from the knowledge contained in certain privileges of the church of Aquileia, in which mention is made of these matters, we should deign through the same writings of ours to make you more fully certain in this regard, lest, through the absence of such documents, our church of Sacile should suffer loss or any detriment concerning some of its rights and possessions.

We, therefore, kindly yielding to your devout petitions, which we commend highly in the Lord, wish you, your successors, and all who shall inspect these letters to know clearly, by the tenor of the present document, what we have learned through certain privileges of ours.

At the time when the illustrious Duke Henry, of blessed memory, although he was of German descent, born of noble stock, ruled in these regions around the river Livenza, he founded the aforesaid church at Sacile, between the boundaries of the dioceses of Concordia and Ceneda, for the salvation of his soul and in honor of the blessed Nicholas, glorious confessor and bishop. He hoped at that time, and for as long as life should last thereafter, to construct there a praiseworthy town or fortified settlement that would add glory and increase to his name and magnificence.

At that time he appears to have obtained from the Roman Curia, by special favor, as is evident from our aforesaid privileges, that, notwithstanding the privileges and jurisdictions of the dioceses of Concordia and Ceneda, the said church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile should be a baptismal church, possess a cemetery, and freely have subject to it a people within and outside the fortifications and enclosures of that place at Sacile, and within the surrounding and adjoining village, as far as the fortifications and enclosures of the said place and the neighboring village could then and thereafter encompass.

The aforesaid dioceses of Concordia and Ceneda shall nevertheless have no authority in any matter; rather, the church itself shall be wholly exempt from both bishoprics, together with all its rights and possessions.

Thus our aforesaid privileges appear to testify and assert that, when the same magnificent Duke Henry founded the aforesaid church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile, he then, for the remission of his sins, freely gave, donated, and transferred to it an estate measuring three fields, on which he built that church, together with a certain territory not far from it beside the bank of the Livenza, along with all the quarter-shares that thereafter, in succeeding times, should arise by the Lord’s gift from newly cleared land in certain woods and from other cultivated and worked lands newly brought into use within the boundary and district of Sacile.

Likewise, there was a certain tract of land toward the mountains on the upper side, near a stream called Orzale. There were also certain estates in a place called Viganorum and within its boundary and district. On the lower side, beside the river Livenza, two leagues from the same church, he gave it another tract of land. In the district and boundary of Canipe, he gave it yet another tract of land, together with certain estates and serfs dwelling there.

Thus, having endowed the aforesaid church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile with the aforesaid estates, possessions, territories, serfs, and quarter-shares, the same illustrious Duke Henry, with all its exemptions, honors, and rights and all its possessions, subjected it to the church of Aquileia by authority of the supreme pontiff, together with certain other churches, as his and our aforesaid privileges report fully and precisely.

Therefore, so that our writings may more fully satisfy your conscience and that of your successors in this matter, we wish the church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile to enjoy and freely use, now and forever, the aforesaid exemptions, honors, jurisdictions, and possessions, together with all its rights, both by virtue of the aforesaid privileges of the holy church of Aquileia and by ancient prescriptive right, while preserving the honors owed in these matters to the church of Aquileia, to which, as stated, that same magnificent man subjected the church of Sacile.

Furthermore, by the present document we entrust and command you, and through you your successors, both on our behalf and on behalf of our successors, to maintain and vigorously defend the aforesaid exemptions with their honors and all the rights and jurisdictions of the said church of Saint Nicholas of Sacile. You shall fearlessly restrain, by our authority and after due warning through ecclesiastical censure, those who detain its rights and possessions, as well as the violators of the said rights and possessions of the parish, and those who contradict or rebel against them.

In witness of this matter and for stable security, we grant these present letters to you and your successors, strengthened by the protection of our pendant seal.

Given at Aquileia in 1249, on the second day of November, indiction 7.

Given and enacted at Udine, in our patriarchal palace, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1328, indiction 11, on the thirteenth day of May. Present were the venerable men Lords Brother John, abbot of the monastery of Rosazzo, and Peter Mora, rector of the church of [lacuna] in the diocese of Milan; [lacuna], canon of Aquileia; Eusebius of Romagnano; Brother Bernard, monk of Catevah of Milan, chaplain of the aforesaid lord patriarch; Odoricus and Franciscus Nassutti, notaries of Udine; the priest Tadeus, parish priest of the parish of Cerchinis; Franciscus of Manzano; and Guillelmus, son of Master Gualdus, of the city, as witnesses, together with others specially summoned and requested for this purpose.

I, Gubertinus, son of the late Ressonandus of Novate in the diocese of Milan, public notary by imperial authority and scribe of the said lord patriarch, saw and carefully examined, together with the same lord patriarch and the witnesses written above, the aforesaid privilege, which, as stated above, was suspect in no part. By order of the same lord patriarch, I copied it, renewed it, and reduced it to this public form; and, having been requested, I subscribed it at its end by affixing my sign.

## XXIV. [Note: 1334. From the archive of the chapter of the city of Udine, cited above, p. XLIX, ch. 2.] Transfer of the Provostship of Saint Odorlicus to the Church of Saint Mary Major of Udine

Bertrandus, by the grace of God and of the Apostolic See, patriarch of the holy Aquileian see. For perpetual remembrance of the matter.

Among our other cares, this one especially presses upon our mind: that in our churches entrusted to our direction and established in distinguished places, divine worship should increase as the population has increased.

Some time ago, Pope Innocent IV, of pious memory, granted apostolic letters to our predecessor, the patriarch of Aquileia, without specifying his personal name, in the following form:

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother [lacuna], patriarch of Aquileia, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, as you stated when you appeared before us, our beloved sons [lacuna], provost and chapter of the church of Saint Odorlicus, wish to transfer that church, because it is situated in an unsafe place, to a secure place—namely, the castle of Udine, fully subject to you in spiritual and temporal matters—and since you wish to enlarge that provostship, we, inclined by your devout petitions, grant you by the authority of the present document full power to attach to that provostship the parish of the same castle.

Let no one, therefore, be permitted to violate this page of our grant or rashly oppose it. Whoever should presume to attempt this shall know that he will incur the indignation of almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul.

Given at Lyons, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the third year of our pontificate.

[Note: As you see, this was not the original institution of the chapter of Udine, as some idle persons have wrongly supposed, but the transfer of the provostship to a chapter that already existed.]

Since, therefore, the affairs that overwhelmed the aforesaid predecessor of ours and his other successors, who held office down to our time, prevented any of them from bringing this matter to completion, we, although at the beginning of our promotion the flood of those same affairs made us no less overwhelmed in the church of Aquileia entrusted to us, were moved by the frequent exhortations of clergy and people to begin attending to the aforesaid union or annexation.

After careful deliberation on the matter with our beloved sons, our canons, and the chapter of our aforesaid church of Aquileia, and with their advice and consent, we erect by ordinary authority the parish or mother church of Saint Odorlicus of the said territory of Udine, in our diocese—now commonly called under the name of Saint Mary, and henceforth decreed to be called so—into a collegiate church, where, by the favor of divine grace, the multitude of the faithful has increased; and we decree that it shall remain collegiate forever.

By the same ordinary authority, and also by the aforesaid apostolic authority with which we are invested in this matter, we incorporate, attach, and unite to it the provostship of the church of Saint Odorlicus near Tolmino in our diocese, or that church itself with all its rights and appurtenances. Because the place where it is situated is unsafe, we transfer it from that place and decree that it shall henceforth remain transferred.

We establish and ordain that the same collegiate church of Saint Mary of Udine, newly erected by us as stated above, with the addition of the said provostship and the matters added to it below, shall henceforth be governed, after the title of custodian—who formerly held the chief position in it—has been abolished, by a dean who shall be head of the chapter and shall receive a double portion from the revenues.

The present custodian, Franciscus, shall nevertheless remain a canon for as long as he lives, so that during his lifetime he shall receive his prebend and the other things he was accustomed to receive, with the double portion.

The man who now holds the aforesaid provostship of Saint Odorlicus near Tolmino, namely Franciscus della Torre, shall, with the title of provost changed, be dean of the aforesaid church of Saint Mary of Udine. All the canons of the aforesaid provostship shall henceforth be canons of the aforesaid church of Saint Mary.

Both Franciscus, the dean, and the canons of the said provostship shall, for as long as they live, receive the fruits of their canonries and prebends, which they hold in the aforesaid provostship, with the same completeness with which they have hitherto received them, together with their customary honors and jurisdictions.

When they resign or die, the prebends of the said Franciscus, provost, and of the canons who resign or die shall pass to the collegiate church of Udine and be assigned to their successors, but only after those prebends have first been equalized with the prebends that previously existed in the said church of Udine.

Furthermore, since the necessary offices are lacking in the same church of Udine, without which it cannot exist honorably or suitably—namely, the sacristy and also the cantor’s office—we, after considering everything that must be considered in such matters and after careful investigation, attach and unite, by ordinary authority and with the advice and consent of the said chapter and our canons, to the church of Udine the parish or church of Saint John the Evangelist of Variano in our diocese, which likewise belongs to our jurisdiction and in which there are a parish priest and a cleric.

We newly appoint the same parish priest, under a changed title, as sacristan, and the cleric as cantor of the same church of Udine, so that the sacristan and cantor shall have and receive the fruits and revenues of that parish as they have hitherto received them.

To ensure that we do not appear to neglect the care of the people or other spiritual matters, either in that parish or in the aforesaid church of Saint Odorlicus near Tolmino, we decree and ordain that in each of them there shall be one perpetual vicar, namely a priest who shall be appointed and removed there by us and our successors whenever this is appropriate.

The other titular priests, or priests of the daughter churches of the said parish and church, shall retain their former rights; we reserve to ourselves and to our successors their appointment and removal.

Moreover, since it has come to our attention that Gregory, of blessed memory, our predecessor, for certain causes that were neither just nor reasonable, withdrew half the revenues of the aforesaid church of Saint Mary of Udine—which at that time was called the parish of Saint Odorlicus—from that church and its ministers without observing any legal formality, and assigned that half to the archdeacon of Aquileia who then held office and to his successors, we wish to provide for the indemnity of the aforesaid church and to increase the honors and revenues of this distinguished and populous place as a mother church.

Therefore, with the advice and consent of our aforesaid chapter, we annul that assignment, which had proceeded in fact but not in law. We recall to the right and ownership of the same church of Udine the said half of the revenues, which the archdeacon of Aquileia has hitherto unjustly claimed for himself by virtue of the aforesaid assignment, whatever goods or rights it may be found to consist of.

We decree that from the fruits and proceeds of that half there shall be formed two equal portions. One shall be divided among the dean and resident canons who have nevertheless attended the divine offices, for their daily distributions.

From the other, four prebends shall be established for four canons: namely, Tristano, son of Fedricus of Savorgnano; Nicolaus Gabrielis, son of the late Henriginus of Pistoia, of Cremona; Franciscus Missotti of Meduno; and Raymundinus Jacobini of Paona, clerics of Udine. From this moment we newly constitute and create these men canons there, in addition to the customary number, and assign them the aforesaid prebends.

Furthermore, we establish and decree that whenever the dignity of dean in the aforesaid church of Udine becomes vacant, the election of the dean shall belong to the chapter of that church, while reserving to ourselves in every respect the confirmation of the elected dean.

Moreover, whenever the dean or any canon of the aforesaid church of Udine dies, the fruits and proceeds of the first year after his death shall be reserved in full, as though he were alive and attending the divine offices, for an anniversary to be celebrated by the chapter in that church alone. From those revenues, certain possessions shall be purchased, the rents and proceeds of which shall every year be faithfully divided among the dean and the canons attending the anniversary.

In testimony of all these matters, we have ordered these present letters, or public instrument, to be written and published by the undersigned notary Petrus Joannes of Baono and secured with our pendant seal.

Dated and enacted in the aforesaid church of Udine, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1334, indiction 2. Present were the venerable and distinguished men: Lord Brother John, abbot of the monastery of Rosazzo; Lord Brother Gibert, abbot of the monastery of Moggio in the aforesaid diocese of Aquileia [Col. 0658A]; Lord William, dean of Aquileia; Lord Guido of Manzano, dean of the church of Saint Mary of Cividale in the aforesaid diocese; Lord Brother Albertino, custos of the convent of the Order of Friars Minor at Udine; Brother Paul of Mantua, of the same convent; and Brothers Artrusio of Brazzacco, prior, and Gregory, lector, of the convent of the Order of Friars Preachers at Udine; as well as Lords William Majorani, doctor of decrees, and Gerald Regis, prior of Sauman in the diocese of Città di Castello; William of Salvagnaco, rector of the church of Able in the diocese of Toulouse; and William Bertrandi, rector of the church of Saint Martin of Monte Equino, chaplains of that lord patriarch; Lord Morando of Porcia, canon of Aquileia; and Lords Odorico of Cucanea, Hector of Savorgnano, and William of Grusimpach, knights; likewise Gerard, son of the said Lord Odorico of Cucanea; Frederick of Savorgnano; Hermann and Henry, brothers of Carnea; Philippusio and Thomas, brothers and residents of the city of Udine [Col. 0658B]; Odorico, notary of Udine; Master Francis of Udine, professor of grammar; Masters Bonaventure and Manino, physicians of Udine; and many others, both clerics and laymen, in a great multitude, specially summoned and requested to attend the foregoing proceedings. On the twenty-third day of December, in the aforesaid year of the Lord’s Nativity and indiction.

And I, Peter, son of John of Roano, a cleric of Treviso, public notary by apostolic and imperial authority, was present at all these proceedings and at each of them, together with the aforesaid witnesses and many others; and at the mandate of the aforesaid reverend father, the lord patriarch, and at his request, I wrote them down, reduced them to this public form, and authenticated them with my customary sign, in testimony of the foregoing.

S. N.

## 270. XXV. [Note: [Col. 0657D] Year 1351. There is a charter in the possession of D. Agricola Agricola, cited, p. 204, col. 1.]

### CHARTER OF THE ARRIVAL OF NICOLAS, PATRIARCH, At his first arrival at the see of Aquileia

[Col. 0658C]

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of his Nativity 1351, on Saturday, the twenty-first day of May, indiction 4.

All the canons, mansionaries, chaplains, and clerics of the church of Aquileia having been assembled in one chapter, and a procession having been made with the cross and banners as far as the All Saints’ Gate, we went to meet the lord patriarch named below at that gate. In this procession were the reverend fathers Lords John Aemon, bishop; Albert; the abbot of Saint Prosper of Reggio; and Guido, abbot of Moggio. Of the canons there were present Lords William, dean; Oduin of Bergamo; Gambinus of Roddan; Conrad Ambrose; Francis; and Beltramolus of Laturre; William, Matthew, Maffeo, James, and John of Cãr., canons. Of the mansionaries there were Simoninus, Henry, Bassanus, James, Mazochus, Liberalis, [Col. 0658D] Dondinus, Johanninus Lanzelotus, Zanetus, and James of Cividale, and others.

When they had reached the church, the lord patriarch dismounted from his horse onto a designated stone. After he had entered the church and knelt in the middle of it, the lord dean gave the blessing. After the blessing, the monks removed the cloak with which he was clothed. Then the lord dean, together with the canons, led him to the seat, and there installed that reverend father and lord in Christ, Lord N., patriarch of the holy see of Aquileia, in the seat. The lord patriarch then received all the canons present to the kiss of peace, and there remained seated while the *Te Deum laudamus* was sung; then he entered upon the patriarchate.

S. N. [Note: [Col. 0657D] This authentic subscription appears at the end of the protocol for all the acts inserted there. The initial letter N. of the name, together with the chronological indication of the year, identifies without dispute the patriarch Nicolas, successor of Blessed Bertrand. [Col. 0658D]]

[Col. 0659A] I, James, son of the late Ture, a cleric of the City of Austria, of Aquileia, wrote, signed, and abbreviated the aforesaid notes and abbreviations in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1351, indiction 4, with my own hand and with my customary sign and appended name, having been requested to do so and having been present with the witnesses named wherever they occur.

## XXVI. [Note: [Col. 0659D] Year 1351. From the archive of the old city of Udine, cited, p. XVII, col. 1.]

### MANUMISSION OF A CERTAIN SLAVE Committed by testament

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of his Nativity 1351, indiction 4, on the fourteenth day of April. In the church of Aquileia. Present were the priest Nicolussius, parish priest of Aquileia; Lancelotto of Cucanea, mansionary of Aquileia; John, son of the late Lamfranchino of Udine; and others.

The venerable man Lord Gambinus of Roddan, canon of Aquileia, in the name and on behalf of the aforesaid church of Aquileia, presented Leonard, son of the late Lazarino of Villalta, [Col. 0659B] upon the altar of Saint Mary of Aquileia. There Leonard produced a certain public instrument attesting to his manumission, of the following tenor:

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of the same Lord 1348, indiction 1, on the first day of October, at Udine, in the house that formerly belonged to Galdenerius in the Upper Borough of Udine. Present were Lord Priest Francis of Mugla, chaplain in Colloredo; the noblemen Lords Vicard of Colloredo, Nicolussius, son of the late Lord Frederick of Villalta, John, son of Lord Francis of Villalta, Clizogo, son of Lord Bernard of Colloredo, Johanninus called Testera of Fagagna, Bruno of the city residing at Villalta, Machoro of Castelnuovo, son of the late Lempse, and Arnosto of Colloredo, witnesses; and many others specially summoned and requested for this purpose by the testator named below.

The nobleman Lord Nicolussius of Villalta, son of the late Lord Odoric of the aforesaid place, sound by God’s grace [Col. 0659C] in mind, sense, and understanding, although weakened in body, not wishing to die intestate, arranged to make a disposition of all his possessions and goods, movable and immovable, present and future, by this present nuncupative testament, without writing, in the following manner.

First, he chose burial for his body at the church of Saint Mary Magdalene of Villalta. To that church, for the sake of his soul, he bequeathed forty Aquileian denarii for the present year.

Among other things that he bequeathed in his last testament, he bequeathed, willed, ordered, and left to the church of Saint Mary of Aquileia, for the sake of his soul, Leonard, son of the late Lazarino of Villalta, with the intention of manumitting him. He completely manumitted him, together with his heirs thereafter born from him, both male and female, with all his peculium; and he absolved and freed him and his descendants, as stated, from every bond of servitude. Thus, from now on, he may and shall be able, as a free man may, to make a testament, sell, pledge, donate, buy, receive, contract, and perform freely all other acts, both individually and collectively, in court and outside court, which any lawful and free person may perform.

He also bequeathed to the aforesaid Leonard three fields, which the said testator had acquired for the purpose of giving and assigning them to Leonard, situated in the territory of Villalta, so that he might do with those fields whatever he wished.

With respect to all his other movable and immovable goods, rights, actions, and claims, he instituted and wished to be his universal heir the nobleman Lord Maynard of Villalta, son of the late Lord Henry of the aforesaid place.

He wished this to be his last will and his last testament, and he wished it, and it, to have validity by the law of a testament and of a last will. If it could not have validity by the law of a testament, let it at least have validity by the law of codicils, or of any other last will, and by whatever law and in whatever manner it could have the greater validity and force.

And I, Guirgelminus of Fagagna, notary by imperial authority, was present at all these proceedings and, having been requested, wrote them down.

These things having been done, the said Lord Gambinus led the same Leonard three times by the hand around the aforesaid altar. I, the notary, also administered to him the oath of observing fidelity and loyalty toward the lord patriarch and the church of Aquileia, as is customary, performing the other acts customarily performed as a sign of liberty and manumission.

## XXVII. [Note: [Col. 0660D] Year 1351. Same source, cited, p. XVII, col. 1.]

### ANOTHER MANUMISSION Of a man belonging to a *masnata*

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of his Nativity 1351, indiction 4, on the seventeenth day of November. In the church of Aquileia, near the altar of Saint Mary of Aquileia [Col. 0660B]. Present were Leonard, son of Missius, cleric; Priest John of Bergamo, prebendary in the said church; Francis, son of the late Saracenus, notary of Aquileia; and others.

Constantine, son of the late Frederick of Castilirio, residing at Budrio, in the name and on behalf of his said father, all his heirs and his brothers, as a messenger specially appointed for this purpose by his father, the late Frederick, presented Martin, son of the late Vincentius of Ronchis near Palmanova, formerly their man belonging to the *masnata*.
