The same late Frederick had manumitted him and freely given him to the church of Saint Mary Major of Aquileia, upon the altar of Saint Mary Major of Aquileia, and had given him to that church together with all his present and future heirs, all his military or quasi-military peculium, and all his present and future movable and immovable goods.

Thus from now on he may make, buy, sell, make a testament or codicil, contract, [Col. 0660C] agree, and perform all other acts, individually and collectively, as a free man of the church of Aquileia. From now on neither the lord patriarch nor the chapter, nor any other person or persons who might at the time be rectors of the church of Aquileia, may or shall subject him again to the aforesaid condition of servitude.

Martin, having duly taken the oath of fidelity, as a sign of liberty, presented and left upon the aforesaid altar one new denarius of Aquileian currency, and performed the other acts customary in such matters.

With every improvement, etc.

## 271. XXVIII. [Note: [Col. 0660D] Year 1352. Same source, cited, p. XVII, col. 1.]

### DECLARATION OF LIBERTY And solemn declaration of the manumitted persons whose manumission was being challenged

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of his Nativity [Col. 0660D] 1352, indiction 5, on the twelfth day of July. Present were Priest James the Florentine and Anzelotto of Cucanea, mansionaries of Aquileia; the aforesaid Priest Gabriel; and others.

Joseph, sworn messenger of the patriarchal court of Lord Nicolas, patriarch of Aquileia, by commission and mandate of Lord James Maroel of Lucca, vicar of the said lord patriarch, presented upon the altar of Saint Mary of Aquileia Margaret called Muyans, and Indryna and Catherine, sisters and daughters of the said Margaret, and John, their brother, as is customary (as above). There he exhibited a letter of the following tenor:

“James Maroel of Lucca, general vicar in Istria of our lord patriarch, marquis, etc., sends greetings.

“Since Margaret called Muyans of Saint Margaret, together with three sons and an equal number of daughters, before us, acting in this matter as commissioner of our lord, Lord Patriarch of Aquileia, have been released by award and sentence from every cloud of servitude and [confirmed in] the liberty which Fradonus of Brazacco sought to challenge, we request your honesty that you proclaim and make known the aforesaid Margaret, her sons, and her daughters in your churches, when a multitude of the people is present, as free persons, like the other persons of the church of Aquileia.

“Dated at Udine, 10 June, indiction 5, to the honorable priests Henry and Francis, chaplains of the parish of Saint Margaret, and to each of them.”

S. N. And I, James, son of the late Ture, notary, [Note: [Col. 0661D] Since these three documents are issued by the same notary James, we have transcribed them under this single subscription.] wrote and abbreviated the aforesaid notes, and authenticated them with my customary sign and name in the presence of those concerned.

## XXIX. [Note: [Col. 0661D] Year 1358. From the charters of Gubertinus the notary in the Archive of the Old City of Udine, cited, p. 184, col. 2.]

### STATUTE Against one disturbing the right to guard the festival

[Col. 0661B]

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of his Nativity 1358, indiction 11, on the twenty-seventh day of December. Present were the reverend father in Christ, Lord Brother Bartholomew, by the grace of God bishop of Caorle; the venerable and wise man Lord Benevenutus of Udine, dean of Cividale and doctor of decrees; and the noble knight Lord Francis of Savorgnano, marquis of Istria, witnesses, together with others.

The most reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord Nicolas, by the grace of God patriarch of the holy see of Aquileia, stated and protested that Rizardus of Castello had fallen back under the penalties and sentences of treason and confiscation of all his goods according to the agreements made with him by the same lord patriarch when he restored him to his favor.

This was because, contumaciously, violently, and obstinately, against the commands and prohibitions of the same lord patriarch, he had recently guarded, and was guarding, the festival and market of Saint Peregrine with armed force. He had expelled the vice-marshal of the same lord patriarch and his companions from the lodging at which they had stayed in Gonars, having been sent to guard that festival and market in the name of the same lord patriarch, without prejudice to the aforesaid Rizardus and the chapter of Aquileia, each of whom asserts that the guardianship of the said festival and market belongs to him.

Enacted at Aquileia, in the patriarchal palace.

## 273. XXXI. [Note: [Col. 0663D] Year 1367. The charter is in the possession of D. Agricola Agricola, cited, p. 176.]

### OF URBAN V [Note: [Col. 0663D] The pontiff Urban who issues the rescript was the fifth of that name. He was raised to the papacy on 28 October 1362 and, in the year of Christ 1367, was entering the fifth year of his pontificate. He left Avignon to visit Rome on the last day of April of that year, and, arriving at Marseille, departed from there on 20 May. On 4 June he reached Corneto, and on 9 June Viterbo, where he remained until 26 October. The stages of this journey may be seen in the account of Urban’s life by our Odorico Raynaldo in the annals under the year 1367. Thus, while he was staying at Viterbo, he issued this rescript on 20 July. Ughelli is mistaken in claiming that it was issued in 1364. He is not mistaken, however, in saying that it was issued to Marquard, since in fact no one other than Marquard was then called patriarch of Aquileia; and from 23 August 1364 until after 23 September 1381, the day on which his constitutions are dated, he held the patriarchate. But an enormous anachronism has crept into Ughelli when he says that Marquard was not patriarch of Aquileia before 23 August, while asserting that the rescript was issued to him on 20 July. Although this rescript was published by Ughelli, we reproduce it here from a manuscript because it differs in several places from Ughelli’s version, as will be evident to anyone who compares them.]

### RESCRIPT OF URBAN V, SUPREME PONTIFF, TO MARQUARD, PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA Concerning the correction of abuse in the rendering of judgments

[Note: [Col. 0664D] We found it so entitled: “Copy of the rescript held by the lord patriarch, sealed.”]

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother . . . . . [Col. 0665A] patriarch of Aquileia, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Recently it has come to our hearing that in the city of Aquileia, Udine, Cividale, Gemona, Venzone, Marano, Monfalcone, Sacile, San Vito, Meduno, and certain other places, lands, castles, *gastaldiates* [Ughelli: Castellenii], and towns of the homeland of Friuli in the diocese of Aquileia, subject to your temporal jurisdiction, there has taken root, in the criminal and civil temporal forum, a certain abusive custom—which ought rather to be called a corruption—very greatly subversive of the proper administration of justice.

This is because in the aforesaid courts, whether in commands, admonitions, interlocutory and definitive sentences, or in any other judicial acts whatsoever [variant: “other acts whatsoever”], the patriarch who is in office and his officials cannot (*non possunt*; variant *non possit*) examine, hear, define, conclude, or perform other judicial acts after considered and mature deliberation. Rather, they can do so only insofar as, at that very moment, the persons present, or the greater part of those present, indiscriminately and without distinction—whether noble or ignoble, learned or unlearned, artisans or persons of any other condition, dignity, or status, even if they were not summoned by the patriarch or his officials presiding in court but came of their own accord or by chance, at the times [variant: “from temporal causes”] when the same patriarch and his officials happened to sit [variant: “were contained”] in the place of judgment to administer justice—after an act has been performed by the parties or their advocates or procurators (*ipsarum*, variant *ipsorum*), and after everything that those parties wished to say or allege at that moment concerning the article of the case upon which they happened to litigate at the term appointed for them [variant: *pluribus*], has been narrated [Note: [Col. 0666D] A comma, otherwise necessary, is lacking, so that the sense is: “and after the matter, that is, the case as it was conducted, and after everything has been narrated, then, etc.”], are called upon by the patriarch or his officials, almost as by a herald summoning the persons present, to state what appears according to law in the foregoing acts or judicial articles.

Then, at that very moment, without any further deliberation, whatever the case or business brought before the court may have been [*deducta*, variant *deducto*], the patriarch and his officials are bound [variant: “are bound summarily”] to publish and pronounce judgment precisely and wholly as the persons present, or the greater part of them, have said and judged [summarily]. It is shown, by the separate and successive raising and counting [variant: indication] of their fingers, which of the aforesaid [variant: “said”] persons present, giving judgment as above [variant: summarily], constitutes the greater part. As a result, rashly and without suitable deliberation, and often through the fraud of the parties and of the persons present or assembling [variant: “the persons present assembling”] in the aforesaid place and at the aforesaid time of judgment, judicial acts, interlocutory and definitive sentences [variant: “the interlocutory pronouncement and judgment”], and commands are improperly promulgated at the instigation of friends, relatives [variant: “presence”], or certain powerful litigants.

Therefore, considering that a custom opposed to canonical institutions ought to have no force, and that a sentence issued by a judge who is not the proper judge has no validity, so that both you and your aforesaid officials may issue sentences in the cases of your subjects after the merits of those cases have become clear to you and to them, as the order of reason requires, notwithstanding the aforesaid custom, by the authority of these presents we grant your fraternity the faculty to do so.

Given at Viterbo, 20 July. In the fifth year of our pontificate.

## XXXII. [Note: [Col. 0666D] Year 1381. There is a charter on parchment in the possession of D. A. Agricola, cited, p. XII.]

### CHARTER OF THE PRESENTATION Of the apostolic letters of Pope Urban VI to the chapter of Aquileia, in favor of Philip of Alençon, designated commendatory patriarch of Aquileia

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of his Nativity 1381, indiction 4, on the third day of August.

Enacted in the land of Sacile, in the diocese of Aquileia, in the sacristy of the church or parish church of Saint Nicholas, in the presence of the noble and powerful men Lords Andrew, knight and marquis of Cavalcabò of Cremona, doctor of laws; Jacomutio and John Furlan, counts [Col. 0666B] of Porcia; and Zifridino de la Turre, witnesses, together with many others specially summoned and requested for the matters written below.

There, on the aforesaid day and at the aforesaid place, in the morning after mass, the chapter of the Church of Aquileia was summoned and assembled by the venerable men Lords Frederick, count of Porcia; John the younger of la Turre; and Ottobonus of Ceneda, canons of the said Church of Aquileia. They possessed the faculty, commission, and authority to summon and assemble the chapter for the matters below to be undertaken and completed, granted to them by the venerable man Lord John of Spiritellis of the city of Belluno, vice-dean, the canons, and the chapter of Aquileia. This grant of faculty, commission, and authority is attested by a public instrument written by the hand of John Lancellotus of Cucanea, notary and cleric of the diocese of Aquileia, under the aforesaid year and indiction, and dated on the penultimate day of July, which I, the undersigned notary, saw and read.

In that chapter were present the venerable men Lords Frederick, [Col. 0666C] John, and Ottobonus aforesaid; John the elder, son of the late Phebusinus of la Turre; Thomasinus of Pontirollis of Forlì; Odoricus of Ragogn a; Antonius of Ronchis; and John, both of Udine; Bartholomew of Bobbio; and Honofrius . . . . . of Reggio, prebendary canons of the Church of Aquileia, summoned and assembled to the chapter as stated above. There, all and each of the aforesaid publicly declared and confessed that they had been summoned to the chapter for the aforesaid day, place, and hour and were present.

Before the aforesaid lords, the canons, and the chapter, assembled in chapter as stated above, appeared the venerable man Master Hugh of Hernorst, master of arts and bachelor of theology, dean of the church of the Holy Apostles of Cologne, acting as procurator and in the name of his principal, the most reverend father in Christ and most serene prince Lord Philip of Alençon, by divine mercy cardinal bishop of Sabina of the holy Roman Church, appointed by our most holy father in Christ and lord, our lord Pope Urban VI, by divine providence, administrator of the patriarchal Church of Aquileia in both spiritual and temporal matters, and possessing a full commission of administration.

The same Lord Hugh possessed a full, legitimate, and [Col. 0667A] sufficient mandate for the matters written below and certain others, as is attested by the said mandate or procuration, contained in a public instrument written by the hand of Giles of Doullens of Rouen, public notary by apostolic and imperial authority, in 1381, indiction 4, on the second day of May, in the fourth year of the pontificate of the most holy father in Christ and lord, our lord Pope Urban VI, by divine providence. I, the undersigned notary, saw and read this instrument.

He exhibited and presented to the same lords, the canons, and the chapter the aforesaid apostolic letters of our said lord the pope, intact and unharmed, neither erased nor cancelled, neither corrupted nor in any part suspect, but wholly free from every defect and suspicion. They were sealed in the manner of the Roman Curia with the true leaden bull of the same lord pope hanging from a cord of hemp, and had been drawn up concerning the commission of administration of the aforesaid patriarchal Church of Aquileia. The tenor of these letters follows word for word and is as follows:

Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to our venerable brother Philip, bishop of Sabina, appointed by the apostolic see administrator in spiritual and temporal matters of the church of Aquileia, greetings and apostolic blessing.

Presiding over the universal government of the Church, though with inadequate merits, by the Lord’s disposition, we earnestly consider how we may direct, as far as is granted to us from above, all the churches of the world and their pastors in a manner salutary for their condition. But a more intense concern presses upon us: that we should provide a salutary remedy for those churches which are deprived of their pastors, lest those churches suffer loss in spiritual and temporal matters, as the need of the churches and the quality of the times require.

Previously, while Marquard of good memory, patriarch of Aquileia, presided over the government of the church of Aquileia, desiring, when it should happen to become vacant, to place over that church through the providence of the Apostolic See a useful and suitable person, we judged that the provision, ordering, and disposition of that church should on that occasion be specially reserved to ourselves, decreeing from that time that anything otherwise attempted concerning these matters by anyone, knowingly or unknowingly, under any authority whatsoever, would be null and void.

Afterward, when the same church became vacant through the death of Marquard, patriarch, who paid the debt of nature outside the Roman Curia, we, moved by certain reasonable causes, judged that the church should be retained in our hands until we should otherwise order concerning it.

Therefore, wishing to provide the said church with a useful and suitable governor according to our heart, through whom that church might be usefully ruled and salubriously governed, and hoping that you may be exceedingly useful and fruitful to that church, and that you will know how and be able to defend that church manfully against the efforts of the wicked, we, with the counsel of our brothers, by apostolic authority, appoint and deputize you as administrator of that church, now vacant, and of all its rights and appurtenances, until our pleasure, both in spiritual and temporal matters. We entrust to you fully and freely the care, governance, government, and administration of the same church of Aquileia in spiritual and temporal matters; the alienation, however, of the church’s immovable goods and precious movable goods is entirely forbidden to you.

We wish, moreover, that, once the due and customary burdens of that church have been supported, you may freely dispose, during the continuance of this pleasure, of the remaining fruits, revenues, and income belonging to the patriarchal table of Aquileia, just as the patriarchs of Aquileia who held office at the time could or even ought to have disposed of them.

Accordingly, by apostolic letters we command your fraternity that, during the continuance of this pleasure, you diligently, faithfully, and prudently exercise the aforesaid care, governance, government, and administration, either personally or through another or others, so that the church of Aquileia may rejoice that it has been entrusted to a useful and fruitful governor; and that, besides the reward of eternal recompense and the praise of human renown—which you will thereby deserve—you may merit to obtain more abundantly from us and from the said See our blessing and grace.

Given at Rome, at Saint Peter’s, on the third day before the Ides of February, in the third year of our pontificate.

The aforesaid canonical lords and chapter reverently and humbly received these apostolic letters, offering themselves ready reverently and humbly to carry out the apostolic commands in all matters in which they would be able to do so.

[Note: What outcome the granting of the patriarchate in commendam, as it is called, produced is clear from the histories of our affairs. Indeed, the people of Udine, who stood up for the honor of the patriarchal see, stubbornly refused to obey, so that they rose with every severity against their own people who had at some time gone to Cividale, fearing that they might favor the cardinal who had taken refuge among the people of Cividale. Moreover, the seeds of a fiercer war were sown between the two cities. Everything is evident from the following two charters, one drawn from the annals of the city of Udine, the other taken from the archives of Cividale.]

[Col. 0668B] S.N. And I, Alexander, notary of Ser Bartholomeus, notary of Ceneda, public notary by apostolic and imperial authority, was present, together with the aforesaid witnesses, at the presentation and reception of the apostolic letters and at all the other matters written above, while they were being conducted and done as stated. At their request and solicitation I wrote them with my own hand and reduced them to this public form, and I affixed my customary sign and name as faith and testimony of all the foregoing.

### XXXIII

[Note: Year 1381. From the archives of Cividale, Udine, cited on page XII.]

**CHARTER OF THE RECALL FROM CIVIDALE OF TWO CITIZENS OF UDINE, SO THAT THEY SHOULD NOT FOLLOW THE PARTY OF THE COMMENDATORY PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA**

In the council of the magnificent city of Udine, on 8 October 1381.

All those appointed concerning the war and, in the public assembly, to administer justice against all offenders [the printed *arva* is uncertain]—Ser Fantus Arcoloniani and Odoricus, notary, son of the late Andrea of Udine—remain in Cividale and secretly follow the lord cardinal who holds the patriarchate of Aquileia in commendam. The commune of Udine, wishing to preserve the status and liberty of the church of Aquileia and of the province of Friuli, since the church of Aquileia has never before been granted in commendam to any person, and since this residence by the same Ser Fantus and Odoricus appears to be undertaken especially against the honor and status of the land of Udine and of the council, caused a warning to be given to the said Ser Fantus and Odoricus: namely, that within fifteen days they must come to Udine to remain and dwell there, just as they had remained before the lord cardinal came to Cividale. If they did not come, they were to understand that judgment would be rendered against them according to the decision of the council of the land of Udine, condemning the same Ser Fantus and Odoricus for not appearing, not coming, and not wishing to comply with the commands of the council, thereby scorning the council.

From the annals of the magnificent city of Udine. Ferandus Ornianus, chancellor. 28 January 1734.

### XXXIV

[Note: Year 1382. This is a charter preserved by Co. Laurentius Alquinus, cited on page XII.]

**CHARTER OF THE CONSULTATION GIVEN BY THE COMMUNITY OF CIVIDALE CONCERNING PHILIP OF ALENÇON, COMMENDATORY PATRIARCH OF AQUILEIA, AGAINST THE PEOPLE OF UDINE**

1388. On Friday, 7 February, in Cividale, in the council chamber, in a full council, according to custom, etc.

Concerning the fact that our lord, Lord Philip of Alençon, bishop of Sabina, cardinal, and patriarch of Aquileia, requested that the commune of Cividale give him advice concerning the method and course by which he should proceed against the people of Udine and their allies, who refused to obey him as their own lord, as they ought and are bound to do; likewise, how he should proceed after gentleness and kindness had proved entirely ineffective in bringing them back to due obedience: it was deliberated and decided that advice should be given to our said lord on behalf of the commune, namely, that he should petition our lord the pope to send his processes against the people of Udine and the others refusing to obey our aforesaid lord patriarch and cardinal, with the penalties that the Roman Curia would know how to impose; and that our lord patriarch himself should ask and persuade the prelates, nobles, and communes who presently obey him to send their envoys to our lord the pope concerning this matter.

The commune intends and wishes willingly to do from its side whatever it can; and that our said lord should use the papal processes, and also war on both sides if that should prove necessary. Before proceeding to war, however, he should diligently investigate his strength and what he is able to do, both from his own faithful supporters and from his friends. Once his strength has been weighed, there should then be a new action and a new council.

Furthermore, the patriarch himself should be told to disclose his action to his other faithful supporters and seek advice from them, just as he had sought advice from the commune concerning the course and method to be followed against the people of Udine.

It was further decided that if our aforesaid lord should ask how many men or what assistance the commune wished to provide for service in the war, a general answer, and not a particular one, should be given. Meanwhile, those appointed should inquire how much assistance the commune could provide, and then report to the council; after that, there should be a new council, etc.

I, Marcus Antonius Nicolettus, citizen and vice-chancellor of the city of Friuli, faithfully copied these decisions from the large volume of decisions of the magnificent community of the city, which is in my possession, and subscribed my name in testimony, etc.

### XXXV

[Note: Year 1382. From the archive of the city of Udine, cited on page XII.]

**LETTER OF THE KING OF JERUSALEM AND SICILY, ADDRESSED TO THE PEOPLE OF UDINE IN FAVOR OF THE CARDINAL OF ALENÇON**

[Note: On the reverse: “To the noble and prudent men and to the commune of the city of Udine, our most dear and devoted friends.”]

Most noble and most dear devoted men,

Since we cherish with sincere affection the most reverend father in Christ, Lord the patriarch, by the grace of God bishop of Sabina and cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, called of Alençon, our most dear kinsman, for worthy reasons of consideration—so that we may promote his honors and advantages and willingly avoid any harmful losses—we therefore request and exhort your devotion that, considering that the virtue of obedience is described as the greatest gift of the human condition, just as disobedience is detested by all, you should desist from every act of disobedience and opposition toward the said lord cardinal, and willingly attend and obey him and his officials as lord of that city, as it is alleged, in those matters in which you are reasonably bound and obliged to do so. This will be to your benefit and advantage, and we shall regard it as a particular service to us.

Given at Naples under our secret ring, on 14 May, in the fifth indiction.

[Note: This charter does not state the year, but the fifth indiction reveals the year 1382. No other indiction of this number occurs during the administration of Philip of Alençon. For, while the people of Udine and their allies constantly refused obedience to the commendatory of their patriarchate—whose rights they always guarded as the apple of their eye, and still defend with all their strength insofar as they can—he returned to Rome without having accomplished his purpose, after his arrival had provoked a persistent and fierce war in the province of Friuli. That war was finally extinguished only after six years, chiefly through the efforts of Queen Elisabeth of Hungary, who acted through her ambassadors, and with the support of the Venetians. See among our native historians Candidus . . . . . . This is that Elisabeth who at that time sent the people of Udine a letter full of honor. I shall not hesitate to publish it, even if it concerns another matter.]

After the date we add that whatever favor or assistance, or perhaps opposition, you may have rendered to the same lord cardinal, we shall regard as having been done personally to us.

Charles, king of Jerusalem and Sicily.

### XXXVI

[Note: Year 1383. From the archive of the city of Udine.]

**LETTER OF ELISABETH, QUEEN OF HUNGARY, TO THE CITIZENS OF UDINE**

[Note: On the reverse: “To the noble and wise men, the governors and councillors of the city of Udine, our most dear friends.”]

[Col. 0670B]

We, Elisabeth, by the grace of God queen of Hungary, Poland, Dalmatia, etc., amicably and affectionately exhort you, wise and noble men of the government, councillors of the city of Udine, our friends, that you permit the illustrious prince, Lord Leopold, duke of Austria, our most dear brother, as he travels with his armed force toward the regions of Italy, to pass peacefully through the territories of your dominions; and that, out of regard for our request, you cause the necessary provisions to be supplied to him and to his aforesaid troops for their money, thereby showing us a favor pleasing to us in the matters aforesaid.

Given at Kemphe, on the seventh day of October, in the year of Our Lord 1383.

### XXXVII

[Note: Year 1384. From the archive of the city of Udine, cited on page XII.]

**COMPLAINT OF THE COMMUNE OF FLORENCE AGAINST THE PEOPLE OF UDINE**

[Note: On the reverse: “To the noble men, the captain, council, and commune of the city of Udine, our most dear friends.”]

[Col. 0670C]

Most dear friends,

For some time we have heard that, as we believe, having been misled by evil suggestions because of the disagreement which you have with our most reverend father, the patriarch of Aquileia, you have publicly sold many movable and immovable goods belonging to John, son of the late Castrone de Bardi, our most beloved citizen, and to his brothers, on the ground that he adheres to the supporters of the aforesaid lord patriarch. When we heard this, we were astonished for many reasons.

For the fact that he followed your father and true bishop ought not to have been imputed to him as a fault or any crime. Therefore, please cause such goods—both those belonging to him and those belonging to his brothers—which, as we see, were taken away without just cause, to be restored; and if any have been consumed, let due compensation be made for them.

Since the said John and his brothers are our citizens, we cannot deny them their due justice in so manifest an injury.

[Note: From this it may be inferred with what determination our city fought for the right of the patriarchal residence, which the aforementioned commendatory patriarch had transferred elsewhere.]

Given at Florence, on 18 February, in the seventh indiction, 1384.

The priors of the guilds and the standard-bearer of justice of the people and commune of Florence.

### XXXVIII

[Note: Year 1423. From the original on parchment in the possession of D. Agricola Agricola, cited on page L.]

**APPOINTMENT BY A PRIOR OF CAMALDOLI TO THE GOVERNMENT OF THE MONASTERY OF SAINT GOTTARD NEAR UDINE**

[Col. 0671A]

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year of His Nativity 1423, in the first indiction, on the eighth day of September. Done in the church of the sacred Camaldolese hermitage, in the presence of the venerable religious lords Jacob of Seravalle of the diocese of Arezzo, chamberlain of the said Camaldolese house; Lord Benedict Baldi of the said city of Arezzo; and Bernard, son of the late Damian of Rimini, monks of the said order, witnesses called, present, and requested for this purpose.

Let it be clearly evident to all who inspect this public instrument that, since the monastery of Saint Gottard near Udine, in the diocese of Aquileia, was vacant through the promotion of Lord Luca of Germany, the immediate prior of that place, to the monastery of Saint Mary of Orbivio in the diocese of Padua, and since it was at present deprived of its customary and proper governor, etc., the chapter of the hermits of the aforesaid sacred hermitage was assembled in the said church at the sound of the board, as is customary.

Present were Lords and venerable brothers Caspar Major of Germany, Jerome the sacristan, John the recluse of Bologna, and Placidus of Sotera, hermit monks of that place, who constituted the greater part of the said chapter.

The most reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord Benedict, prior of the often-mentioned sacred Camaldolese hermitage and general of the whole order, after mature counsel and deliberation concerning the reform of the said place of Saint Gottard, and unwilling that the monastery of Saint Gottard should suffer loss in spiritual or temporal matters through lack of a rector, for the honor of God, of blessed Mary, the glorious mother of Christ, of blessed Gottard, in whose name the said monastery was founded, and of the other saints and the entire heavenly court; for reverence toward Holy Mother Church and the most holy father in Christ and lord, Lord Martin, pope V, its general and universal pastor; for the honor of the sacred Camaldolese hermitage and of the whole order; and for the peaceful and perfect condition of the aforesaid monastery, directed his mind’s attention to Lord Angelus Ciera of Venice, a fellow monk of Saint Michael of Murano, expressly professed in the aforesaid order, of legitimate age, born of legitimate parents, ordained to the priesthood, and distinguished in knowledge and character.

With the said Lord Angelus present before the prior and the hermits, he instituted and appointed that same Lord Angelus as prior, rector, and administrator of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Gottard of Udine, in every manner, right, and form that he could most fully and suitably employ. He entrusted to the said Lord Angelus, as prior, the spiritual and temporal care and administration of the aforesaid monastery, in the place and name of the chapter of the hermitage, fully until the pleasure of the said prior and chapter of the hermitage alone.

Lord Angelus, kneeling before the aforesaid Camaldolese prior, humbly accepted the appointment made in his regard. In consideration of the administration of the aforesaid monastery, he promised that prior manual obedience and reverence, and took an oath of fidelity, touching the hand of the said general.

He swore to the said Camaldolese prior, who received the oath in the place and name of his canonically entering successors, that from this hour onward he would always be faithful, obedient, and subject in all matters which, according to God and his ability, with a clear conscience, he could undertake. He would receive and treat the said prior, the hermits, the household of the aforesaid hermitage, their messengers and those of the hermits, the Camaldolese house, and the other members of the aforesaid order reverently, kindly, and charitably, whether coming, returning, or remaining, according to his knowledge and the resources of the monastery entrusted to him.

Any sound and faithful counsel requested of him by the prior, or by his messengers or letters, or by another person holding his place and office in the Camaldolese hermitage or order, he would give to them and to each of them, according to the discretion granted to him by God, in every respect.

Any secret entrusted to him by the same prior, his messengers, or his letters, or by anyone acting in his place, whether in the hermitage or elsewhere in the Camaldolese order, he would never disclose to anyone in a manner harmful or injurious to the person of the prior, to his office, status, or honor, or to the hermitage, the Camaldolese house, or the aforesaid order.

He would not participate in any counsel or undertaking by which the said prior of Camaldoli, or any hermit monk, lay brother, servant, or messenger of the same hermitage or Camaldolese house, might unjustly lose life or limb; nor would he permit the said prior of Camaldoli or any of those persons to suffer any real or personal injustice, injury, or loss. If he learned that anyone was plotting or attempting the contrary, he would prevent and hinder it insofar as he could and as it was permitted.

He would defend, maintain, and preserve, according to his strength, the immunities, liberties, rights, and honors of the hermitage and of the Camaldolese house, and of the monastery of Saint Gottard entrusted to him, against all persons, insofar as God supplied him the means, his ability allowed, and the resources of his monastery permitted, while preserving the continuing honor of his order.

He would pay, without exception, within the established terms, the collections and taxes which the aforesaid order might impose upon him and others; and he would pay the census which he freely or by right ought to pay to the hermitage and the aforesaid order.

When summoned to a synod or to a general or particular chapter by the same prior or by his representative in the hermitage or order, he would come unless prevented by some canonical impediment.

Furthermore, he would not again enfeoff the immovable goods of the said monastery of Saint Gottard, nor alienate them, nor make any contract concerning the lands or church of that monastery to their detriment. He would not alienate, sell, pawn, or pledge the instruments, privileges, or any other precious objects, nor contract any debt, except in the case of very great and unavoidable necessity, or evident utility to the monastery, or for a sum specified in the constitutions of the aforesaid order, and then only with the special permission of the said Camaldolese prior.

Thus he said: “So may God help me,” touching the holy Gospels of God.

Thereafter and immediately, the said Camaldolese prior received the aforesaid Lord Angelus, prior of the aforesaid monastery, to the kiss of peace and, by his ring, invested him in person with the said priory.

We commission our brothers, namely, the lords priors of Saint Matthew [perhaps Saint Michael] of Murano or of Saint John of the Giudecca of the same order, each individually, to induct the aforesaid Lord Angelus, prior, or his legitimate procurator acting in his name, or anyone substituted by him or by them, into corporal possession of the aforesaid monastery, and to defend him after his induction.

They are to restrain contradicters and rebels by ecclesiastical censure in our place, invoking for this purpose, if necessary, the aid and secular arm.

In testimony of all these matters, we ordered our customary seal to be affixed by attachment of our office, as a precaution, and we also caused the matter to be registered.

S.N. I, John, called Lord, formerly son of Jacob of the Borough of the Holy Sepulchre, notary and ordinary judge by apostolic and imperial authority, and also scribe of the aforesaid general prior, was present while the foregoing matters were being conducted; and, requested to write, I wrote and published it. Therefore I subscribed it and affixed my customary sign.

### XXXIX

[Note: Year 1441. From the charter in the possession of D. Laurentius della Torre, cited on page 204.]

**CHARTER OF AN AGREEMENT FOR THE CONSTRUCTION OF A STONE BRIDGE OVER THE NATISONE AT CIVIDALE, CONTRACTED BETWEEN THE MAGNIFICENT COMMUNITY OF CIVIDALE ON THE ONE HAND AND MASTER JAMES, SON OF THE LATE MARTIN DAGURO OF BISSONE IN THE DIOCESE OF COMO, ON LAKE LUGANO, CONCERNING THE DEMOLITION OF THE WOODEN BRIDGE AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF A STONE ONE**

JESUS CHRIST.

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year from the Nativity of the same Lord Jesus Christ 1441, in the fourth indiction, on the eleventh day of December. Done in the council chamber of the commune of Cividale in the diocese of Aquileia, in the presence of the venerable man Lord Mark of Crivelli, canon of Cividale; the reverend priest Nicholas, son of the late Matthew Tresoldi of Giustins, residing in the borough of the bridge; the noble man John Daniel, son of the late John Pizul of Meduno; the prudent man Lord Nontin of the said Cividale; and the provident men James, son of the late Ser Nedonus of Formentini, and Hermacora Cerdone, son of Bortulutius, of the borough of the Broxana Gate, witnesses specially called and requested for this purpose.

There, the noble and circumspect men Ser Francis of Claricini, Ser George Cont, son of the late Ser Bernard, of the borough of the bridge, and Ser Tanus, son of the late Ser Philip of Coti, citizens of Cividale, appointed in full council and public assembly to carry out the matters written below, having for this purpose a special and full commission from the aforesaid magnificent community of Cividale, and acting in the place and name of that magnificent community and for it on the one hand, considered that the work and building described below would serve not only as an ornament and decoration of Cividale itself but also for the common praise and the increased utility of its republic.

They considered the frequent costs and expenses by which the aforesaid magnificent community was often accustomed to be burdened and charged in repairing the wooden bridge described below, called the Major Bridge. Wishing at last to be relieved of such frequent and almost daily expenses, and having repeatedly held mature and diligent deliberation on the matter, they recognized that it was much better and more useful to have the said Major Bridge once built, constructed, founded, made, and fashioned so strongly and securely that it would probably last for perpetual times, rather than to maintain and possess the decaying wooden bridge.

Thus, acting and contracting in the place and name of the aforesaid magnificent community and for that community on the one hand; and the provident man Master James, son of the late Martin Daguro of Bissone in the diocese of Como on Lake Lugano, for himself and in the place and name of his associates and master craftsmen whom he wished to have and employ with him to complete the bridge or building and work described below, and for those associates, master craftsmen, and assistants, for whom he promised to obtain ratification under the obligation of all his goods, on the other hand, they mutually and unanimously reached the following compositions, agreements, promises, covenants, and obligations under solemn stipulation and contract.

First, it was agreed, covenanted, promised, and established by solemn stipulation, in the names stated and between the said parties, that the aforesaid Master James should, must, and be bound, as he solemnly promised, agreed, and obligated himself before the aforesaid deputies, who requested and stipulated in the place and name of the community, to cause to be constructed, founded, fashioned, and built, and to complete and finish in its entirety, the Major Bridge of Cividale, situated over the water of the Natisone, of stone, as wide as could be made, with one double arch extending from one side to the other, with all necessary and suitable foundations and frameworks of every kind, whether of timber or wood, iron, or squared and pointed stones on the sides.

The said bridge was also to be raised at the sides with battlements honorably made of squared and pointed stones.

If it pleased the magnificent community of Cividale, to which the choice belonged, the aforesaid Master James and his fellow craftsmen and assistants whom he would take with him were to build, make, and construct the said bridge with two arches resting upon the central pier which presently exists, and with another arch extending over those two arches from one side to the other—for example, from the side toward the bridge borough as far as the side toward the city—with frameworks and battlements as above.

Thus the community was free to choose whether it wished the bridge to be made with two arches or with three, as stated above.

The following was also agreed: one drawbridge was to be made upon the said bridge near the tower, on the city side or toward the city, with a sufficient barbican or ravelin.

The said Master James was to find, excavate, and work all and every stone necessary, sufficient, and suitable, of whatever kind and condition, for the construction and completion both of the bridge itself and of its foundations. He was to complete, finish, and work the entire bridge at his own cost and expense, sufficiently, faithfully, in good faith, and without fraud, so that, in the judgment of all good master builders, the bridge would be and ought to be good and sufficiently constructed, made, and worked, and would probably last forever, as such a work and building required, both in its foundations, bindings, and frameworks and in its arches, as stated above.

Conversely, the aforesaid lords deputies, acting in the place and name of the community and for that community, for which they promised ratification and solemnly obligated themselves, promised to pay, give, and count out to the aforesaid Master James, for the completion and full accomplishment of all the matters written above, 1,525 gold ducats. The aforesaid community was to give and disburse these to Master James from time to time as he worked and as necessity required.

From those 1,525 ducats, Master James was to accept in payment as much wine and grain as would suffice for the expenses of his operations, at the price at which they were sold in the market, and at which he could obtain the wine and grain from other persons.

It was further agreed, promised, covenanted, and established under solemn stipulation between the said parties that the aforesaid Master James should have the entire wooden bridge presently existing, together with all its ironwork and everything else belonging or pertaining to that bridge; and that he might dispose of the said bridge as he pleased, since the said wooden bridge would have to be removed.

It was further agreed, promised, and established under solemn stipulation between the said parties that the aforesaid community should provide and cause to be transported, at the expense of the community, the lime and sand necessary for constructing the said bridge.

The aforesaid community was also to transport, at its own cost and expense, all the prepared stones excavated by Master James himself and any others found by Master James for the construction of the said bridge.

It was agreed, covenanted, and promised between the said parties that the aforesaid community should seek or obtain a license [lacuna] without harm or expense to Master James himself, from all who possessed quarries or places in which stones were available and could be excavated under the administration and lordship of the community, so that Master James could obtain and excavate whatever stones were necessary, without, however, harming other persons.

It was agreed between the said parties that the aforesaid Master James should have, and was to have, all the framework that he would place and make for constructing and building the said bridge, and that he could remove that framework from the bridge at the proper place and time and without damage to the bridge.

The aforesaid community was to act in good faith and show due diligence in finding two *sarthiae*, or two thick ropes, though at the expense of Master James himself, and in obtaining permission from the most serene lordship of Venice to export them from the city of Venice, if permission could be obtained.

It was agreed, covenanted, and promised that the aforesaid community should find for Master James, without payment by him, a house with four furnished beds, in which Master James and his associates could lodge.

It was agreed between the parties that, if Master James found the timber necessary for the frameworks and other requirements of the work, the aforesaid magnificent community would be bound to have it transported by its subjects, at the honest cost and expense of Master James himself and for a fair and reasonable price to be paid by him.

Finally and lastly, lest the work should be delayed by the slowness and difficulty of transporting timber and other things necessary for the construction of the said bridge, it was agreed, covenanted, and promised between the parties that the aforesaid community should keep ready, at its own cost and expense, at least two large carts, which are called *currus matti*.

All the aforesaid agreements, promises, and obligations were solemnly promised by the aforesaid lords deputies, in the place and name of the aforesaid magnificent community and for that community, with the obligation of all the movable and immovable goods of the community, present and future, on the one hand; and by the aforesaid Master James, for himself and for his fellow master craftsmen whom he would take with him, and for whom he promised ratification, with the obligation of all his movable and immovable goods, present and future, on the other hand.

They also mutually promised, by solemn stipulation and contract, to make good all losses, interest, and legal and extrajudicial expenses, one party to the other and the other to the one, to hold, maintain, observe in good faith and without fraud, and fully perform all the foregoing as firm, ratified, and accepted; never to contradict or act contrary to them, under a penalty of double the matter concerning which a dispute or action might arise. Whether that penalty were paid or not, the foregoing agreements would nevertheless remain valid.

The parties requested me to draw up a public instrument concerning all and each of the foregoing matters, with all my [lacuna] and the advice of a learned man.

Published and delivered to Master James.

### XL

[Note: Year 1461. From a charter in the possession of Co. Raymund of Arcano, cited on page 184.]

**CONVEYANCE AND DONATION OF CERTAIN RIGHTS, INCLUDING THE RIGHT TO OBSERVE THE FESTIVAL**

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year from the Nativity of the same Lord 1461, in the ninth indiction, on the nineteenth day of February. Done in the town of San Daniele, in the diocese of Aquileia, under the great loggia of the commune, in the presence of the provident men Ser Colla, stipendary, son of the late Augustine of Naples, man-at-arms of the magnificent Lord Christopher Folentin; Ser Leonardo Naso, son of the late Gabriel of Pithianis of San Daniele; and Ser Thomas, son of the late nobleman Ser Frederick of Lower Varmo, witnesses present, specially called, and requested for this purpose.

There, the noble co-heirs of the aforesaid Arcano, namely Sir Joannes Antonius, son of the late nobleman Sir Rizzardus de Arcano, acting on his own behalf and as agent in the name of the noble Sir Joanninus, his paternal uncle—as he said was evidenced by the hand of me, the undersigned notary—and also Sir Antonius, son of the late nobleman Gabriel of the same place, by way of a pure, genuine, free, simple, and irrevocable gift between living persons, gave, ceded, transferred, and assigned to the distinguished young Sir Simon Buccinatus, son of the nobleman Sir Christophorus de Strasoldo, present there and accepting for himself and his heirs, all and every one of their co-heirs’ rights and legal actions, real and personal, beneficial and direct, tacit and express, which they have, had, or might have in the village and dependencies of the village of Campolongo della Strada, by reason of the jurisdiction or *garritus* belonging and pertaining to those co-heirs in the same village and its dependencies—namely, the right to guard and announce the festivals held there, to exact profits, fines, and condemnations, and to do and exercise all other things which are recognized, or could be recognized, as belonging and pertaining fully by right or custom to those co-heirs.

They appointed the same Sir Simon as assignee and procurator, as though in his own proper matter, and placed him in their position, so that the aforesaid Sir Simon, the assignee, in his own name and by his own beneficial and direct, tacit and express actions, might and should be able to act, sue, plead exceptions, reply, obtain judgment, and defend himself against anyone and everyone on the aforesaid matters, and to say, do, and exercise all other things just as the aforesaid co-heirs could and might have done and exercised before this cession and transfer.

The aforesaid co-heirs and cedants, in the names stated above, also promised, on their own behalf and that of their heirs and successors, binding all their movable and immovable property, present and future, and undertaking restitution of all damages and legal and extrajudicial expenses, solemnly to bind themselves to the aforesaid Sir Simon, the assignee, stipulating for himself and his heirs, or for anyone to whom he might wish his right to be transferred, to hold, maintain, observe, and fulfill perpetually as firm, valid, and acceptable the aforesaid cession, gift, and transfer, and everything contained in this instrument, and not to act, say, or proceed contrary to them, either personally or through another or others, for any legal or factual reason or cause, nor to revoke the gift on any ground or through ingratitude.

This was stipulated and promised under a penalty of double the value of the matter concerning which a dispute or question should arise, not less than five solidi in each clause of this contract. Whether or not the penalty was paid, the present instrument and everything contained in it were nevertheless to possess full force and perpetual validity, etc.

I faithfully extracted the foregoing from the former notes of Master Jacobus Pithianus, citizen and notary of San Daniele, as I found them in his own hand. I, Jacobus Justa, public notary by imperial authority of the same place, have subscribed and signed this in witness, etc.

## XLI. Decree of the Chapter of Aquileia concerning the making of silver heads of certain saints, especially Saint Paulinus

*[Note: A.D. 1494. From the Aquileian Archive, cited work, p. LI.]*

[Col. 0677A]

Sunday, 13 July 1494.

After dinner the chapter assembled in the residence of the reverend lord Doymus, dean. Present at the chapter were the lord dean himself, Filippus, Franciscus, Ottus, Thomeus, Jacobus de Montegnaco, Petrus, Bod., Daniel, and Richardus, all canons, etc.

There, the aforesaid lords—the dean, the canons, and the chapter—determined and deliberated that silver heads of Saints Paulinus, Laurentius, and Sigismundus ought to be constructed and made; and that at least the head of Saint Paulinus should be made in the present year, that is, by the next Easter, and thereafter the others should be undertaken as soon as they could be made.

And just as it had previously been determined that the chapel of Saint Cancianus should be constructed beneath the enclosed choir in the aforesaid church, it was deliberated today that construction should begin in the present year. The matter was entrusted to the reverend lord Doymus, dean and chamberlain, and to Lord Richard, his colleague, for execution, etc.

## XLII. Document concerning the construction of the principal church of the city of Austria

*[Note: A.D. 1494. Charter in the possession of Lord Laurentius a Turre, dean of the chapter of Cividale, cited work, p. 203.]*

Agreement between the reverend lord Hieronymus de Nordys, dean of the collegiate church of Saint Mary of Cividale, Lords Bernardus Cont, Daniel de Puppis, and Laurentius, canons acting in the name of the reverend chapter, together with the distinguished Sir Federicus de Formentinis, gastald of Cividale, and Sir Guarnerius de Manzano, overseers of the territory of Cividale on behalf of the community, on the one side, and Master Albertus de Monte and Master Franciscus, his nephew, on the other.

In the name of Christ, amen. In the year 1494 from the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, indiction 12, on the fifth day of April, in Cividale in the diocese of Aquileia, in the square, in the presence of—

There the reverend lord Hieronymus de Nordys, dean of the collegiate church of Saint Mary of Cividale; Lord Daniel de Puppis and Lord Laurentius, deputies for the reverend chapter of Cividale; and Lord Bernardus Cont, acting as canon and for the benefit of the chapter; together with the distinguished Lord Federicus de Formentinis, gastald, and Guarnerius de Manzano, procurator of the land of Cividale; Lord Philippus de Portis, master builder; and Nicolaus Zani, deputies appointed for this purpose; and the distinguished doctors Lords Ermanus de Claricinis and Bartholomeus de Nordys, acting as counselors and consulted by all the aforesaid deputies on one side; and the prudent man Master Albertus a Monte of Padua on the other—having assembled concerning the construction of the principal church of Cividale, reached the following agreements and contracts.

The said Master Albertus promised and undertook to construct and build all and every one of the walls to the necessary height, with their faces, which are to rise above the columns placed on the side of the patriarchal court, entirely at his own cost and expense, [lacuna], the aforesaid deputies supplying Master Albertus with all necessary preparations and materials required for the said construction and building.

He likewise promised and undertook to make and raise all the framework necessary for that construction, the aforesaid deputies similarly supplying everything necessary for the framework.

The said Master Albertus was not, however, required to provide anything except manual labor. The aforesaid deputies, in the names stated above, promised and undertook to give and pay Master Albertus as his remuneration at the rate of seven and a half pounds for each *passus*, measured according to the Venetian measure.

It was nevertheless agreed that Master Albertus should work on the walls according to the width already begun, which is visible above the first columns at the entrance of the church and also above the other walls on which it would be necessary to build. The deputies were also required to pay and satisfy Master Albertus for the empty spaces between the wall faces, according to the custom of all builders.

They further agreed that Master Albertus should accept wine and grain for his remuneration at the current price, as needed for himself and his workers.

They agreed that, for the period during which he remained at the construction of the church, Master Albertus should have one house with two beds and more according to his needs.

The deputies promised to provide all necessary ropes, as well as the necessary constructed wheels and buckets, though Master Albertus was required to adapt them for use in the work.

Master Albertus agreed to accept the necessary laborers from within as part of his remuneration; those who were to serve on the upper side were to remain under his direction.

## XLIII. Description of the first arrival of Lord Marino Grimani at the patriarchal see of the city of Udine

*[Note: A.D. 1524. From the Archive of the city of Udine, cited work, p. 204.]*

[Col. 0678C]

In the name of God, amen. In the year of the Lord 1524, indiction 12, on Monday, the last day of October, at the seventeenth hour.

The most reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord Marino Grimani, by divine providence patriarch of the most holy Aquileian Church, entered this distinguished city of Udine happily, seated upon a magnificent mule. He was accompanied by a very large body of the city’s infantry and cavalry, and by the excellent Lord Andrea Fosculus, governor of the entire patria, who had come to meet him with the praetorian cohort on the raised plain upon the bank of the Torrent Cormor.

A cavalry force led by Lord Taddeus Vulpianus, knight of the Golden Spur and commander of the light cavalry of the illustrious Venetian Senate, went before him. The entire clergy of the city, together with that of Aquileia, proceeded in supplication as far as the Poscolli Gate. There, a youth standing in nymph-like dress recited a finely composed ode; the patriarch, preceded by his cross-bearer, then entered the city.

Immediately at the gate, the magnificent and distinguished citizens Lords Bartholomaeus Brugnus and Joannes Candidus stood at either rein in the name of the public community of Udine, as the patriarch sat beneath a canopy—or, as it is commonly called, a baldachin. Hieronymus Sanctoninus and Franciscus Maninus stood behind him; these two were jurisconsults distinguished by golden chains hanging from their necks.

Sebastianus Monteniacus, Antonius Maninus, Joannes Luchatellus, and Laurentius Sacchia carried the canopy. All were outstanding ambassadors of the city of Udine, appointed to accompany the most reverend prelate as far as Portus [lacuna] Gruarius. They wore close-fitting garments and, as people commonly say, were adorned with velvet. Following them came, two by two, the magnificent governor and the most reverend bishops: Lords Joannes Argentinus of Concordia, Joannes Grimanus of Ceneda, Daniel Rubeus of Caorle, Paulus Burgascius of Nîmes, and Jacobus Nordius of Urbino.

After proceeding through Poscolli Street and both the new and old squares, the patriarch dismounted from the mule at the gate of the cemetery of the city’s principal church, opposite the Candidian alley, in order to enter the church itself.

The magnificent ambassadors of the city, in the presence of the aforesaid most reverend bishops and of many other horsemen and foot soldiers, received the mule, which was adorned with purple and gilded trappings valued at two hundred gold pieces, with the patriarch’s consent. Then, proceeding on foot in the same order in which they had come, they led it to the stone steps of the palace of the republic. Sanctoninus and Maninus carried the gilded episcopal spurs in their hands, while a crowd of infantry accompanied and acclaimed the empty saddle through the old and new squares.

When Lords Bartholomaeus Brugnus, Hieronymus Sanctoninus, and Antonius Maninus, the ambassadors, had ascended the steps together with the members of the council of seven, where Lords Joannes Baptista Tursius, Gabriel Pavonius, and Daniel Baldanus, their colleagues, were also present, the jurisconsult Lord Joannes Candidus addressed them as follows:

> “Magnificent and most distinguished lords and deputies, this is the mount with the adornments of the most reverend lord patriarch. By the privilege of this magnificent city, on the occasion of his solemn first entry today, he has given it to us, your ambassadors, as the true metropolitans of the new Aquileia, the city of Udine, according to the custom of the city at the first entry of its bishops. Accepting it on those terms, we have brought it before your magnificences and now consign it to you, so that you may dispose of it as you please.”

To him Lord Bartholomaeus Brugnus, one of the seven men, replied in the name of all, in these words:

> “Magnificent ambassadors, we thank your magnificences countless times for the most worthy services performed by you in this magnificent embassy, for which this magnificent city will take due account. We accept the mule presented to us in the name of this magnificent republic, which will decide what is to be done with it.”

When these matters had been completed, the mule, still adorned with the same trappings, was led by heralds acting on the orders of the seven men to the horse stable in the nearby house of Lord Sebastianus Monteniacus.

At the request of those seven men, I, Franciscus Stayner, registered notary of Udine, recorded all these matters for the perpetual memory of the event. The delivery of the mule took place in the presence of the magnificent Lord Alexander Rauber, son of Lord Andreas the knight and vice-dean of Carinthia; the nobleman, the late Gabriel de Zucco; Lord Nisidorus Sanctorius of Spilimbergo, professor of grammar; Sir Martinus, son of Sir Donadinus de Salardis of Bergamo; Sir Antonius Toninus of Venzone; and Sir Antonius of Trent, residing at Udine in the Aquileian quarter, together with a great multitude of the common infantry. They were witnesses, summoned and called aloud by me, the undersigned notary, etc.

I, the same Franciscus Stayner, son of the late Sir Jacobus Stayner of Udine, public notary by imperial authority, was present at the foregoing, wrote it down at the request of the parties, and published it in my own hand, etc.

## XLIV. Extracts from the acts of the Chapter of Aquileia, showing how an attempt was made to restore the ecclesiastical rite called patriarchal

*[Note: A.D. 1585. From the Archive of the Chapter of Aquileia, cited work, p. 176.]*

[Col. 0679D]

### Questions of the illustrious and most reverend lord, the apostolic visitor, Caesar de Nores, bishop of Poreč, to the reverend chapter of Aquileia

Under Friday, 8 February 1585; from the manuscript book of the acts of the reverend chapter from 1580 to 1586, pp. 184 ff.

**Question 7.** Whether daily distributions have been established and whether they have been distinctly assigned for each hour.

**Answer.** By the most ancient custom, the resident canons are accustomed to earn each day, for as long as the course of the *canipa* lasts, four loaves of bread and four *zasiae* of wine—that is, two for Mass and two for Vespers—and likewise wine in the same quantity. Also, two hens and three pounds of cheese each week, and likewise oats and millet together, from the day of Saint Hermagoras until the day of Saint Paulinus, whose feast is celebrated on 11 January, approximately sixteen *staria*; finally, one *starium* of rye and beans for the course as above, etc.

**Question 9.** Whether in the celebration of Mass the provisions established by the holy council in session 22, in the chapter “On the Things to Be Observed and Avoided in the Celebration of Mass,” are observed.

**Answer.** They observe the aforesaid decree as diligently as they can. It is nevertheless true that, according to Aquileian usage, on certain days they use altar vestments different from those used, and in a different manner, by the Roman Church.

**Question 11.** Whether they sing in the choir, what office they recite, and whether they celebrate according to the rite of the Church or according to Roman custom.

**Answer.** Six richly endowed canonical prebends were divided, by the authority of Pope Innocent IV, into twelve mansionaries, to whom the duty of singing and reciting the divine office in choir was attached. They sing and recite the office according to the usage of Aquileia. The canons, however, say the Roman office. Masses in the church are celebrated by some according to Aquileian usage, and by others according to the Roman. Omitting the rest, etc.

### Saturday, 9 February 1585, after dinner

All the aforesaid lords canons assembled, etc.

Because the illustrious and most reverend apostolic visitor had admonished them and raised the matter of saying one single divine office in choir and outside the choir, both by all the reverend canons and by the mansionaries, a resolution was proposed that everyone should continue to sing the office in choir according to the rite of the holy Aquileian Church, as it had hitherto been observed.

Outside the choir, however, by dispensation, the office was to be said according to the Roman rite until such time as new books and breviaries according to the patriarchal rite were revised and printed. This was to take place within two years. From that moment onward, and with effect from then, a petition was to be made to the illustrious patriarch that he order the new patriarchal breviaries to be corrected and printed. The votes having all been taken, the resolution was adopted.

### Page 189. Monday, the 18th of the aforesaid month and year

The chapter assembled after Vespers in the usual chapter house. Present were the reverend lords Theupolus, dean; Carlevariis, Canussius, Ronchonus, Franciscus, Frumentinus, Sbroyavacca, Tritossius, and Andreutius, all prebendary and resident canons, constituting the full chapter.

There the constitutions of the aforesaid lord visitor were read by the distinguished Lord Othelius, syndic, and were carefully considered in turn. They are as follows.

[Col. 0680D]

### Ordinances, or decrees, made by the illustrious and most reverend father in Christ, the lord Caesar de Nores, bishop of Poreč and apostolic visitor, during the visitation of the holy patriarchal church of Aquileia

### Visitation of the holy patriarchal Church of Saints Hermagoras and Fortunatus of Aquileia

**I.** This holy patriarchal church has rites of divine worship different from those of the holy Roman Church, as well as its own Breviary and Missal. Nevertheless, during the visitation it was discovered that the same manner and formula were not observed in the celebration of divine worship.

The mansionaries and a very few other clerics sing or recite both canonical hours in choir according to the formula of the Aquileian Breviary. The canons and the remaining clergy of the same church, however, privately recite the office according to the Roman rite and Breviary, even in the choir itself; and only the conventual Masses are celebrated according to the patriarchal rite, while the others are celebrated according to Roman custom and rite, even from the Roman Missal by the priests.

Thus, in the same church, and indeed in one and the same choir, a differing worship is offered to God by the same ministers of the church, as though they were plowing with an ox and an ass.

Since this is recognized as contrary to the sacred decrees of the canons, to the authority of the holy Fathers, and also to the statutes of this very church, which have repeatedly and clearly laid down provisions on this matter; since it brings considerable disorder to the church, in which everything ought to be done in due order as in the house of God; since it produces profound ignorance among the clergy concerning the ceremonies and rites of their own church, and causes offense and scandal even in the minds of the devout—the most reverend lord visitor decreed and declared that all, both canons and mansionaries and the other ministers of that church bound to the duties of the choir, should observe one and the same order or rite of singing in choir and in the church, namely the Aquileian rite.

Those who act otherwise, in addition to the loss of fruits and daily distributions and the other penalties imposed by the sacred canons, apostolic sanctions, and the statutes of the church itself, are also to be punished severely at the discretion of the illustrious lord patriarch, unless within two months of the publication of this decree they obtain from our most holy lord and from his holy Apostolic See a dispensation or another remedy. The rest omitted, etc.

### Udine, Friday, 4 October 1585

The chapter assembled after Vespers in the house where the reverend lord P. Theupolus, dean, lived, etc.

Moreover, the aforesaid lords unanimously and deliberately agreed to visit the reverend lord bishop of Cattaro, patriarchal vicar, at the patriarchal residence where he was then staying. In his hands they returned and delivered letters from the illustrious and most reverend Lord Cardinal de Sans, sent from Rome, etc.

Present were Sir Franciscus of Brescia, steward of the aforesaid lord dean, and Sir Joannes Busina of San Daniele, servant of the aforesaid patriarchal vicar, as witnesses, etc.

The letters were then read aloud there, by order of the same lord vicar, by the distinguished Botana, vice-chancellor of the patriarchal court, in the presence and hearing of the aforesaid lords dean and canons, and were formally communicated to them, as appears in the record of the same distinguished Botana, etc.

What follows is the text of the letters mentioned above.

> “To the very reverend lord, as to a brother, the bishop of Cattaro, vicar of Aquileia.
>
> “Very reverend lord, as to a brother,
>
> “The chapter of Aquileia, through two canon procurators sent here expressly several months ago, has brought before this sacred congregation certain points against some decrees of the lord bishop of Poreč, apostolic visitor in that patriarchate.
>
> “Although the decrees were made holily and on good and holy grounds by that prelate, whose prudence and goodness, joined with zeal for the service of blessed God, are very well known, nevertheless these illustrious lords of mine, after hearing the said procurators several times, and after examining the said decrees very carefully, having given them mature consideration and having weighed with diligent reflection the conditions of the times and of the region, and for other good and just reasons, have moderated and resolved the matter as set out here. I send this to Your Reverence annotated beneath the same points submitted by the chapter.
>
> “1. In the first decree he obliges the clergy to say the office according to the Aquileian rite. It is presently impossible to carry this out, since there are no longer any Aquileian breviaries in that territory, nor can any be found anywhere for sale. The few that exist are in the possession of the old mansionaries, without an index, foliation, or rubrics, since none has been printed for a hundred years.
>
> “Therefore, Your Illustrious Lordships are petitioned to grant us the favor that, outside the choir, the Roman offices may legitimately be recited, until sufficient Breviaries can be provided.
>
> “**Answer.** It is a holy and appropriate thing that the rite of that very ancient and approved church should be observed, and that all should conform to the same office. The chapter should therefore obtain Breviaries of that rite. It can do so readily, since a small number have recently been printed at Como. If this cannot otherwise be done, let the lord patriarch arrange for them to be printed at his own expense within two years; meanwhile, outside the choir only, let it be lawful to say the Roman office. The rest omitted, etc.
>
> “Your Reverence should therefore publish these decisions to the said chapter, employing the appropriate remedies so that they may be put into effect in the manner in which they have been moderated.
>
> “Your Reverence must likewise take every care that the other decrees made by the said apostolic visitor be fully executed according to his holy intention. This is what these illustrious lords of mine desire, since the labors and exertions expended in that visitation would have been wasted if the decrees were not carried out as they ought to be.
>
> “While I trust that Your Reverence will act accordingly out of your piety, since all this is for the service of blessed God and of those souls, I remain, with heartfelt offers of service, praying the Lord to grant you his holy grace.”

*[Note: This did not take effect. For the rite is now abolished.]*

> “From Rome, 10 September 1535.
>
> “Your very reverend lordship’s,
>
> “As a brother,
>
> “Cardinal de Sans.”

## XLV. Gift of the pastoral staff by the patriarch of Aquileia, Lord Augustinus Gradonicus, to the chapter of Udine

*[Note: A.D. 1629. From the Archive of the Chapter of Udine; a charter in the possession of Count Laurentius Asquinus, canon of Udine, cited work, p. 204.]*

Monday, 25 December, on which the feast of the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, 1629.

The illustrious and most reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord Augustinus Gradonicus, patriarch of Aquileia, was present in the collegiate church of Saint Mary Major of the city of Udine, which was filled with people. While Vespers were being sung with solemn rite, after the first Psalm had ended, he ordered me, the chancellor, to come to the patriarchal seat, where his illustrious lordship stood dressed in pontifical vestments. The very reverend lords dean and canons of the same church, clothed in their customary sacred vestments, were seated on either side.

He summoned me so that I might record how his illustrious lordship, on this solemn feast on which Christ the Lord deigned to be born of the blessed Virgin Mary, wishing to give the very reverend chapter of the same church some sign of the love with which he cherished it and to show clearly his special affection, donated to that very reverend chapter his silver pastoral staff, which was present there and which he used on the greater solemnities, so that it might be preserved perpetually among the chapter’s precious objects as a sign of such special affection—though always for the use of his illustrious lordship and of future patriarchs.

Concerning these matters I, the public notary and chancellor, was requested to draw up this present public instrument.

Done in the place stated above, in the presence of many people, including the very reverend Mario Zerbo, canon of Feltre; the reverend lords Thomas Colloredo and Mario Turso, members of his illustrious lordship’s household; and others, etc.

From the notes of the late distinguished Lord Bernardinus Amutius, collegiate notary of this city and also patriarchal chancellor of Aquileia, Gaspar Gazoldius, notary of the Apostolic and patriarchal chancellery of Aquileia, extracted the foregoing instrument of donation in his own hand and, having been requested to do so, subscribed it in witness.

Udine, 9 April 1661.

## XLVI. Verses of Paulinus concerning Duke Hericus

*[Note: In Pez, Thesaurus Anecdotorum, from manuscript 76 of Saint Martial of Limoges, now in the Royal Library.]*

[Col. 0683]

*[Note: The poems are divided in this manner in the manuscript.]*

### Timavus, weep with me

You nine rocks, you rivers

overflowing through nine

springs.

The wave of the Ionian sea

swallows these rocks;

Hister, Sava,

Tisza,

*[Note: Tissa, a fortress between Cephaletum and Amestratum. Silius, Book IV, line 268.]*

the Maruvium’s guilt?

*[Note: Marruvium, now Morée, a fortress of inner Abruzzo near the river Liris, five miles from Lake Fucinus. Virgil writes of it in Book VII of the *Aeneid*.]*

The Natissa, the Corea,

the whirlpools of the Isoncius.

*[Note: The Isoncius is a river of the Carni; it rises in Carniola and, enlarged by several streams and by the river Natiso, flows into the territory of Trieste.]*

Mourn for me

the sweet name of Hericus:

Sirmium, Solla,

the land of Aquileia,

Forum Julium,

the rural lands of Carmo,

*[Note: Carmo is a place in Messenia, and a temple of Apollo in Laconia; in Achaea it is a river, and in the Peloponnese a mountain.]*

the cliffs of Osopium,

*[Note: Osopium, a city of the Carni.]*

the ridges of the Cetenenses,

the Nastensian soil,

let them weep, and Albenga.

*[Note: Albergaunus, commonly Albenga in Liguria.]*

Nor should you, city,

whose territory he came from,

cease to mourn:

a wealthy silver city,

you have lost in deep

and grievous groaning

a famous citizen,

born of noble stock

and illustrious blood.

In barbarian speech

you are called Strasburg,

because you once lost

that celebrated name;

I have restored it to you,

a name sweet as honey,

for the love of your dear friend,

who was nourished on milk

beside the river Quirnea.

Generous in gifts

to the churches,

a father to the poor,

a support to the wretched;

the supreme consolation

of widows,

and dear beyond measure

to many priests;

powerful in arms,

subtle in intellect.

He subdued the most savage

barbarian peoples,

whom the Drauvus encircles,

whom the Danube shuts away,

whom the Maeotian marshes

conceal among their reeds;

whom the wave

of the salt-flowing sea

confines within the Pontus,

and against whom

the boundary of Dalmatia stands.

The towers of Strato,

*[Note: The Tower of Strato seems to be Caesarea of Palestine.]*

the beginning of the frontier,

know Mount Hymettus;

he who separates from himself

the axis of Stracia

gives one boundary back

to the South,

another to the North,

and stretches toward the gates

called Caspian.

The Libyan shore,

where the seas overflow,

and the Laurentian mountain

of the enemy, as you are called,

may no rain, dew,

or shower ever descend upon you.

May flowers not bloom,

nor the earth produce

purple blossoms.

May the soil not yield

wheat-bearing fruits.

May no elm support

a vine with jeweled foliage,

nor grapes hang

from its branches.

May the fig tree remain green

on its ever-dry trunk.

May the bramble not bear

pomegranates filled with seeds,

nor the chestnut tree

its rounded fruit.

Where the man of the front line fell in battle,

with his shield shattered,

his sword reddened with blood,

his spear at its point

resounding back [reading uncertain],

his body pierced

by arrows,

and crushed, it is said,

by stones hurled from slings.

Alas, how harsh

and how grievous was the news

that, on that day,

spread forth to be lamented.

For a dreadful cry,

worthy of tears,

arose through the streets,

and grief, through words,

made known his death

[lacuna].

Mothers, husbands,

boys, young women,

masters, slaves,

every sex and tender age,

the illustrious multitude

of priests,

will strike their breasts

with their fists,

tear their hair,

and howl together.

Eternal God,

who, from the dust of the earth,

fashioned our first parents

in your image,

through whom we all die,

you sent your beloved Son,

through whom we all

live wondrously.

By whose purple blood

we have been redeemed,

whose sacred flesh

we receive,

grant, I beg you,

to your little servant Hericus,

[the phrase *melliflua* is grammatically uncertain in this fragment],

the joys of Paradise,

now and forever,

through the boundless ages.

*[The Saxon Poet.]*
