[Col. 0683]

# Five Books of the Saxon Poet’s Annals Concerning the Deeds of Blessed Charlemagne

*[Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica.]*
The unique surviving manuscript of our poet, formerly brought into the library of the Julia at Helmstedt from the monastery in the territory of Hildesheim, as is attested by an inscription of the twelfth century on its first page—“the book of Saint Adrian at Lamspring”—was first printed at Helmstedt in 1596, in quarto, by Reinerus Reineccius. In his edition he improved the text where it had been corrupted in several places, restored years that had occasionally been omitted, made the division of the books clearer, and returned to their proper places passages that had been wrongly inserted under the year 781 in the manuscript.

Chesnius, vol. II, p. 136, and Kulpis, vol. IV, p. 3, followed Reineccius’s authority. No one before Leibniz suspected that he had sometimes departed from the manuscript’s true reading; but when that great man was preparing to publish the poet anew in volume I of the *Brunsvicensian Writers*, he verified the matter by consulting the manuscript itself. Accordingly, he not infrequently supplied the true reading beneath the Reineccian text and added very few notes. I have retained those that seemed relevant, identifying them by the author’s name.

Bouquet’s fifth edition surpasses the others in this respect: the manuscript readings brought forward by Leibniz were inserted into the text, as was proper, and the verses were numbered. Since we were planning another edition to be included in the *Monumenta*, our Ebert, with his customary kindness, sent us the manuscript itself; therefore I thought the text should be restored according to it.

It is a parchment quarto. Its first fifty-five leaves contain our work; the remainder contains the *Passion of Saint Adalbert* and the books of the priest Juvencus on the *Life of Christ*, all written in the same eleventh-century hand. There are twenty-five verses per page. In several places the scribe himself corrected the text (1), and in others a second contemporary hand corrected it (2); I have recorded both readings. The sole exception is that, when the second hand more often supplied a better division of the words, I judged that the earlier reading, which made no sense, should not be reproduced.

Although few, and neglected by the editors, I judged that the glosses written either in Latin or in the dialect of our Lower Saxony would be no less welcome to students of these matters than the ancient letter *d*, which occurs four times in the words *adernam* under the year 778, *ferdi* under the year 782, *padarbrunnon* under the year 799, and *hludouicus* in book V. Since these glosses were added by the second hand, everyone will agree that this feature was not introduced through some error, but is a survival of the old autograph; for the same letter can also be found in diplomas issued in 986 by Otto II, the Saxon emperor, in writing the place-name *nordana*.

In establishing the text, therefore, I followed this principle: to read the traces of the manuscript reverently, while nevertheless, in a few places—and those unquestionably corrupted through the scribe’s fault—either accepting the conjectures of Reineccius or Leibniz, or assigning something to my own judgment if a suitable emendation occurred to me. In this matter, since the *Annals of Einhard*, which our poet follows almost exactly, together with metrical considerations, generally prevented error, I nevertheless had to allow something to the poet’s century. I did not indiscriminately remove everything that conflicted with ancient rules; following the example of others, such as Nigellus, I admitted that elision before the letter *h* should sometimes not be permitted.

Only a few notes were needed, since the *Annals of Einhard* and the *Life of Charles* far surpass this work in the abundance and importance of their commentary. The great lacuna in the second book, however, can scarcely be filled without another manuscript. I have nevertheless indicated without difficulty how many verses are missing.

Leibniz had already observed that the thirty verses which are rightly assigned in the editions to the year 783 are placed in the manuscript between the twelfth verse of the year 781 and the first verse of 782, without any indication of a division between the years. Since so serious an error could have arisen only through the transposition of the leaf on which the verses were written, and since it could not have occurred in the surviving manuscript, whose individual leaves contain fifty verses, it necessarily follows that each leaf of the autograph contained thirty verses.

Hence it immediately becomes clear that, in the middle of the year 782—which now, with the superscription counted as a verse, contains only eighty-nine verses—one verse has fallen out. As to where it was lost, since everything else is very well connected, one would have little doubt: after the thirty-fourth verse, the name of Worad, the third of the Frankish commanders mentioned by the poet, is missing.

Leibniz indicated two other lacunae. No one, taking the arrangement of Einhard’s *Annals* into account, will deny that many verses are missing after the twelfth verse of 781 and before the first verse of 783. There it is permissible to conjecture that either one or two leaves have fallen out, and here that one leaf is missing. Thus, besides the twelve verses that survive under the year 781, I assign thirty or sixty additional verses; under the year 783, however, not thirty but twenty-seven, since, with the superscription counted as the twenty-eighth verse, the remaining two still belong to the preceding year, in which the poet had not yet expressed the words of the *Annals* concerning the retreat into winter quarters, where Charles celebrated Christmas and, as usual, Easter. I therefore believe that I have detected this fourth lacuna.

There is scarcely anything else that needs to be mentioned. The fact that adverbs are often written with a final tailed *e* is no more unusual than the interchange of the letters *e*, *oe*, and *ae*.

That the poet lived under the reign of Arnulf is proved by the verses in book V: “We ask, Arnulf,” and “Now, nevertheless, under Arnulf.” The whole work shows that he was a Saxon and a cleric, perhaps a monk. It cannot at all be inferred from the verses for the year 777—“whom they call Pathalbrunnon”—that he lived at Paderborn. Still less would I oppose those who, because of the place where the manuscript was preserved in the twelfth century, wish to count him among the people of Lamspring. For the monastery of Lamspring had already been founded in 872 and confirmed in the following year by King Louis.

Except in a very few passages, where he himself, an honest and trustworthy observer, reports what he had seen and heard, the author’s entire account depends on Einhard’s *Annals* and *Life of Charles*. His usefulness for the history of the emperor is therefore almost nonexistent; but as an outstanding monument of the beginning of literary culture among the Saxons, he will always be held in high esteem by our countrymen.

# THE LIFE OF CHARLES

[Col. 0685D]

After the Savior of the world deigned to be born of the Virgin

and clothed himself in the limbs of our body,

the wheel of time rolled out seven hundred years.

And ten times seven years, with almost one more completed,

had passed when, by divine right, the monarchy of the Frankish kingdom

was given to the great Charles.

For his brother Carloman had died

near the end of the present year.

And Charles, arriving at the estate called Carbonata,

had there received all the chief nobles and powerful men

of his brother’s former realm,

who did not hesitate to submit themselves to such a lord;

except for only a few, whom perhaps their great love

for their former lord, together with his wife

and children, had caused to remain with him.

Accompanied by these, she went to Italy,

hoping that she might be able to live a peaceful life

under the protection of King Desiderius.

King Charles, meanwhile, celebrated Christmas

at Attigny, as well as the festival of Easter.

## Year 772 [printed 722]. Indiction 9

After the bishop of the Roman see, Paul, had died,

Adrian succeeded him in the pontificate.

And King Charles, having gathered the Frankish nobles

at Worms, summoned them to a general council.

With them he resolved to attack the Saxons in war; [Note: From Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, chapter 7.]

for the land of the Saxons lies next to the Franks toward the north,

and, scarcely divided by any definite boundary,

the territories of the two peoples adjoin one another.

But the closer they were in neighboring territory,

the more discord separated them in spirit.

For throughout the bordering fields they were accustomed

to engage continually in slaughter, fires, and plunder.

The Saxons, fierce by nature and hard of heart,

had not yet deigned to bear Christ’s gentle yoke;

they had been thoroughly subdued by demonic error.

But the Franks, worshipers of Christ, had long possessed

the Catholic faith and already ruled over many peoples

throughout the world. Supported everywhere,

and especially by the power of God, whom they rightly worshiped,

they were surely able to overcome this one nation.

The Saxons were not even united under a single king,

so that they might defend themselves together through military practice.

Instead, the whole people was divided in various ways:

there were almost as many leaders as districts,

as though the limbs of a single body

had been torn apart here and there.

Their general division, however, makes three peoples,

by which Saxony once flourished.

Their names remain; their ancient valor has departed.

The people who live in the western part

are called Westphalians; their boundary is not far

from the river Rhine. The Osterliudi inhabit

the region toward the rising sun; [Note: Reineccius and Leibniz: “the Osterlingi inhabit.”]

some call them by another name, Ostphalians.

Their borders adjoin those of the faithless Slavic people,

who harass them.

Between the peoples already named, in the central region,

live the Angarii, the third Saxon people.

Their territory borders Frankish lands to the south

and is joined to the Ocean toward the north.

Charles therefore resolved to subdue this nation.

Without delay, attacking it with all the power of the Franks,

he laid waste to a wide area with sword and fire.

By great force he captured a strongly fortified castle,

made secure by nature and strengthened by human hands,

which the barbarian tongue calls Eresburg.

The same people also worshiped an image

which they called Irminsul. Its structure was like a column; [Note: The manuscript has *factura similis*, “structure like”; the text transposes this to *similis factura*, “like [a column] in structure.” Reineccius’s conjecture *factura simulque columna*, “structure and column alike,” was rejected; Leibniz repaired the passage merely by transposing the words.]

it was at once a work of no small size and of beauty.

After destroying it, the king himself remained

for three days in the nearby camp.

Then, because summer’s heat continued for a long time

and the sky remained clear, the fields burned,

and there was no moisture even in the springs.

The streams were parched and covered with much dust. [Note: First hand: *qualebant*, a defective form beside *squalebant*, “were parched.”]

Thirst, increased by the heat, now severely wearied

the royal camp. But the power of the Almighty intervened,

for it pleased him that the profane shrine should rightly be overturned.

At midday, suddenly, through the hollow bed

of a certain torrent that lay close by,

a sufficient stream of water burst forth for the army. [Note: Second hand: “it pleased him.” The older reading can no longer be recovered.]

After accomplishing these things, when the king had reached

the river Weser and received twelve hostages

from that people, he returned home in great prosperity.

## Year 773. Indiction 10

Pope Adrian, sending messengers,

sought to obtain the aid of the great Charles

against the Lombards, whose king at that time

was Desiderius; for the wicked violence

of this people was oppressing the Romans severely.

Since the greater part of the whole kingdom of Italy

was then subject to him, and through those lands—

namely, hostile territory—the Roman bishop

could not safely send anyone who might travel

by a direct route to the Frankish lands, [Note: Reineccius: “safely.”]

he caused a legate named Peter to board a ship at Rome.

Thus, wandering around the sea by a long circuit

and traversing its waves, he avoided the dangerous route.

Often the fury of the Ocean and the storm of the sea

seem safer in this way than the minds of men,

which turbulent anger stirs up.

Peter, therefore, sent from the city of Rome,

went by sea to Marseilles and then, passing over

a long journey, reached the renowned King Charles

at a place called Theodone.

He devoutly begged him to defend

the Church of Peter, whose supreme key-bearer

could grant him the greatest rewards in the heavenly court.

He also begged him to come to the aid of the pope’s anxiety

and of the Roman people, who had suffered innumerable evils,

for whom, after God, the sole hope of preserving

their liberty and their lives remained in him.

When the king heard these things,

he immediately turned the whole matter over

in his anxious mind and judged that it was entirely just

and pleasing to God that he himself should be

the defender of the apostolic see with all his strength.

At once he gathered from throughout his kingdom

an army of immense strength, drawn from various peoples.

Leading it with him, he reached the city of Genoa,

which the river Rhône passes with swift current.

He then resolved to invade the Lombards

with a twofold campaign. He divided his people

and ordered one part, under Duke Bernard,

to go over the Mons Jovis—

an old error gave it that name—

while the king himself led the other part

by way of Mont Cenis.

After crossing the dreadful Alps,

the two armies rushed like a whirlwind

into the fields of Ausonia,

laying waste far and wide the wealthy kingdom.

A great fear now struck all the Franks.

For Desiderius, who had first prepared for war,

hoping in vain that he could resist Charles,

was put to flight by terror before any battle

had taken place. Charles besieged him at Ticinum,

now called Pavia, after drawing up the royal army

in camps on every side.

Though he attempted many stratagems

throughout the entire winter,

he could not break through the city walls by force of arms.

## Year 774. Indiction 11

While these events were taking place in the Italian regions, [Note: That is, “shores.”]

the Saxons, daring to invade the neighboring territories of the Franks,

plundered the district called Hesse

and simultaneously ravaged it with flames and weapons.

The king’s distant expedition encouraged them,

for they believed that the time had come

to avenge the losses which they had previously suffered

at his hands and which had been very great.

When they had advanced as far as the place called Fritzlar,

they wished to commit to the flames a church

which Boniface, the martyr and bishop beloved by Christ,

had consecrated there for eternity.

While they were vainly attempting to complete

this impious crime, a great terror suddenly seized them

from God, and compelled them, trembling,

to retreat in shameful flight to their homeland—

those whom neither enemies nor weapons had driven away.

But the king, having stationed his legions

to press the people of Ticinum by continuous siege and war, [Note: The manuscript’s *Ticinensum* is a genitive plural; Reineccius: *Ticinensum*.]

went to Rome to visit the holy places for prayer.

There, having offered supplications from his heart,

he returned to Ticinum, which, wearied by the long struggle,

had now lost all strength to resist.

When this most famous city surrendered to the Franks,

it became an example for all the others.

For immediately all the cities of the same kingdom

surrendered themselves unanimously to Charles,

and he decided that the kingdom had now been subdued

by right, insofar as circumstances permitted.

Eager to return to his ancestral seats,

he hastened his journey, taking with him

the aforementioned king of Italy,

whom he had recently conquered by arms.

Here you may behold the mockery of human affairs,

how the wheel of this life turns in differing courses.

Yesterday Desiderius flourished

with the royal diadem; behold, today he is poor,

a captive, and an exile.

His son, called Adalgis by name,

though great hope for the Lombards rested in him,

lost confidence in his country’s fortunes

and withdrew from there to Constantine,

who ruled the scepter of the Greeks.

Made patrician by him, as a distinguished gift,

he remained in that honor until the end of his life.

When King Charles was returning,

before his swift arrival was yet known to the Saxons,

he caused a threefold army to be sent into their territories.

It afflicted them with many slaughters

and plundered many places;

then, laying waste a great number of regions,

it returned victorious with rich spoils.

## Year 775. Indiction 12

While the king was spending the winter

at a place called Quierzy, a royal estate,

he summoned there the Frankish nobles

and the entire senate. After lengthy deliberation

about the matters that needed to be undertaken,

and about the various concerns of the commonwealth,

he is said above all to have adopted this plan:

that war should continually be imposed upon the Saxons,

whom he had found forgetful of every pledge and treaty,

unwilling ever to rest under peace.

He therefore resolved that they should be granted no rest

until, abandoning their pagan rites and worship,

they became worshipers of Christ or were destroyed forever.

O blessed piety of God, who wills the whole human race

to be saved! For he knew that the hearts of this people

could not otherwise be softened, so that their hard neck

might learn to bend its native rigidity

and submit to Christ’s gentle yoke.

For this reason he gave them such a teacher

and master of the faith—namely, the renowned Charles—

who would subdue by war those whom he could not master

by reason, and thus compel them to be saved,

even against their will.

This plan, divinely inspired in his heart,

was accompanied by vigorous deeds.

For all the leaders and the chosen youth together

hastened to the village of Düren,

where, at the king’s command, a general assembly

of the people was held.

Then, after crossing the great river Rhine,

Charles entered the Saxon territories as an enemy.

First he captured the fortress of Sigiburg;

from there he went to Eresburg,

the city which we have said was captured.

But so that it could not serve as a defense for the Franks,

the inhabitants destroyed it.

At length he fortified it again

and stationed his legions there.

From there he advanced quickly to the river Weser.

Near the mountain called Brunsberg,

a large crowd came to meet him, wishing to resist

him so that he could not cross the river.

But this attempt failed.

Struck down in the very first engagement,

they fled, and the sword had laid innumerable men low

on that day.

From there Charles moved into the regions

held by the Osterliudi. [Note: Reineccius: “Osterlingi.”]

He encamped beside the river

which is now called the Ocker.

Then a certain man named Hessi,

one of the leading men of that people,

came humbly to meet him.

All the people of that district likewise came forward,

and, after giving the hostages that Charles had demanded,

they pledged by the greatest oaths

to keep faith with the king.

When all this had been done in due order,

he returned to the district called Bucki.

There the leaders of the Angarii came to meet him

with their people. In the same manner,

while they all obeyed the royal commands,

they confirmed by oaths that they would remain faithful.

The victorious king immediately prepared to return.

Meanwhile, a part of the king’s armies remained

near the Weser. The place itself is called Hlidbeki,

where they had likewise established a camp.

But success had made them dangerously secure.

The king’s power had terrified all his enemies,

and at that time no one dared to resist him.

Consequently, caution in the camp had grown lax,

so that they could be harmed by the excessive treachery

of the Saxons.

The sun was descending from the highest point of the sky

and had already begun to approach the evening hours.

Some men then went out from the camp

to bring fodder for the horses from a distance,

and soon returned together.

A certain Saxon band mingled with them,

pretending in mind to be allies and faithful companions.

Each man then attached himself blandly

to a new friend, while a savage enemy

lay concealed beneath the name.

By adding service to their lying words,

they increased the confidence placed in them.

All worked together for the common purpose;

some carried the load of green hay on both sides.

Thus the deceitful men entered the Frankish camp.

What they could not accomplish by force,

they achieved by craft. But the saying is ancient:

“Fraud or valor—who would ask which in an enemy?”

The Saxons attacked the Franks,

who were sunk in sleep, and fiercely carried out

a great slaughter.

At last, when the numbness of sleep had been shaken off,

some men seized their weapons and began

to resist courageously.

Then, with the battle in some measure withdrawn—

in accordance with the agreement dictated

by such an emergency—the enemy quickly retreated.

When the king heard this, he hastened there,

and, pursuing the backs of the fugitives

with sufficient speed, struck down many

of the authors of this crime.

From there he came to the Westphalians.

After receiving at once the hostages whom they had surrendered,

he departed. France received the returning king

with rejoicing.

## Year 776. Indiction 13

As the prince hastened his journey homeward,

he learned that in the Italian regions there was a tyrant

named Hrodgaud, who, attempting fresh schemes

and dissatisfied with the honor which the king had given him,

wanted to subject to himself the whole breadth

of the kingdom of Italy.

For Charles had appointed him duke and count

over the people of Friuli when he first

returned victorious from the Lombards

with his famous standards.

Ungrateful for this gift, he wickedly stirred up

the people of many cities and caused them

to revolt to him, spurning Charles’s rightful rule.

To suppress these movements, Charles delayed no longer.

He swiftly summoned, by command, the vigorous forces

he needed; with them he hastened to Italy,

and justly punished the tyrant with death.

He ordered the Frankish counts whom he had appointed

in the cities to preserve those he had recovered,

and, as soon as he arrived, he quickly withdrew again.

Hardly had he crossed the Alpine peaks

near to heaven when sad news met him:

Eresburg, the city which he had once captured

and entrusted to his soldiers for defense,

had been stormed by the Saxons,

and its garrison had been violently expelled.

Then the same people attempted to attack

the other fortress, Sigiburg, with much effort. [Note: Manuscript: “Siburg”; Reineccius: “Sigeburg.” I emended “Sigiburg” from Einhard’s *Annals* and the verse for year 775, “First he captured Sigiburg,” etc.]

They did not succeed in overcoming it,

although they wished to drive the king’s legions from it.

But while the Saxon people were pressing the battle,

they were surrounded from behind and put to flight,

as those stationed inside simultaneously burst out

and easily struck down the unsuspecting enemy

with a broad assault. [Note: Reineccius: *internis*, “those inside.”]

When this report first reached Charles’s ears,

he ordered a gathering of nobles to be held

in the city of Worms and resolved to brook no delay

before the faithless people paid the penalty

for so great a crime.

Therefore, having gathered his armies from every direction,

the king with swift effort forestalled all the enemy’s attempts

to defend themselves.

When he reached the sources of the river Lippe,

he found numerous bands of that people gathered there,

humbly begging pardon because they had not kept

the promises made the previous year.

But when merciful Charles forgave them,

and many promised that they wished to believe

in the Lord Christ and abandon the worship of idols,

he ordered them to be cleansed in the waters

of sacred baptism.

He again received their promises to preserve faithfulness,

strengthened by the delivery of hostages whom he himself selected.

He fortified Eresburg once more with strong defenses,

and, beside the river which we previously called the Lippe,

he built another fortress and filled both with chosen soldiers.

Then, returning again to the Gallic fields,

he spent the winter in a palace

which the barbarian tongue called Heristal.

## Year 777. Indiction 14

When the mild season of new spring was approaching

and the harsh winter had already passed,

King Charles came to Nijmegen

and celebrated the solemn rites of Easter there. [Note: Gloss: “Niumagan.”]

Since he always regarded the Saxons with suspicion, [Note: Gloss: “doubtful.”]

and did not doubt that, in order to preserve their liberty,

they would employ every kind of stratagem

within their power, and that, unless continually oppressed

by the burden of war, they would break the treaties

frequently concluded with him,

he again led the strongest forces into their homeland.

He announced that he wished to hold there

a general assembly with his leaders.

A place was chosen for this great council,

which they call Paderborn.

The people themselves have no other place

more distinguished by natural dignity:

it abounds in especially notable,

clear, and numerous springs,

and from them derives its ancient name

in the language of the barbarians.

At that time there was only a village there;

now it shines as the most renowned seat

of a pontifical church.

When Charles arrived, he found that almost all

the leaders, the people, and the entire senate

of the Saxons had assembled,

except that a certain Widukind had fled from there,

fearing the king.

For, conscious of his own bold deed

and many offenses, he had gone to Sigfrid,

who ruled the Danes.

The other leaders, gathered there with the people, [Note: Reineccius: *gregata*, “gathered” (feminine singular).]

all humbly begged pardon and peace.

They had submitted to the king on this condition:

that, if they dared afterward to violate his decrees,

they would lose both their former liberty

and their homeland, after the whole burden

of their earlier crimes had been forgiven.

A great crowd among them then professed

that it wished to believe in Christ

and received the saving bath of baptism.

But feigned faith soon emerged from their deceitful mouths;

the events that followed made this clear to many.

At that time a certain Saracen had arrived there,

whose native name was Ibinalarbi (*Ibn al-Arabi*).

With not a few companions and fellow citizens,

who accompanied him as he left the territory of Spain,

he surrendered himself to Charles,

together with the cities over which

the Saracen king had formerly appointed him.

After leaving the Saxon region at last,

he made for the Frankish kingdoms.

Afterward, Aquitaine received the renowned King Charles

for the celebration of Easter.

## Year 778. Indiction 15

Since the aforementioned Saracen encouraged him

to hope, not without reason, that he could subject

certain Spanish cities to himself,

Charles began to lead his great forces

over the lofty mountains of the Vascones.

After crossing the first ridges of the Pyrenees,

he came to Pamplona, which is said

to be a famous fortress of the Navarrese,

and captured it by force of arms.

Crossing the ford of the famous river Ebro,

he entered a distinguished city of that region,

named after Caesar Augustus.

Nevertheless, after receiving the hostages

whom the aforementioned Ibn al-Arabi,

together with loyal and distinguished men

of his own people, had given him,

he withdrew from there.

Returning to Pamplona, he cast its walls

down to the ground, lest it should perhaps rebel.

When he had returned through the inner passes

of the Pyrenees and, with his exhausted soldiers,

was crossing the narrow paths,

the Vascones dared to set an ambush

for him on the mountain’s highest summit

and attempted a new battle.

Finally, attacking the rear of the royal army,

they first struck the soldiers down

with missiles from the high hills.

Although the Franks were superior in arms and spirit,

the narrowness of the place made them inferior

and put them at a disadvantage.

The king had already gone ahead,

while the slower part of the army remained behind,

delayed by the need to transport the baggage.

A panic arose among the armies.

In the sudden tumult, they were thrown into confusion,

and the victorious and wicked band of brigands

carried off enormous booty and killed many.

For some of the royal attendants fell,

those to whom the royal treasure had been entrusted;

the plunderers enriched themselves

with their splendid spoils.

After this deed, the enemy fled through the trackless

and vast forests of the mountain.

They hastened away, [Note: Reineccius emended: “They quicken their flight.”]

for they knew the hidden places of the deep forest valleys.

The fugitives escaped detection,

and the approaching night rescued them

so that no vengeance could follow.

Since so great a crime therefore remained unpunished,

it drew gloomy clouds over the royal mind,

which many previous successes had made serene.

Moreover, thinking that they had found

a suitable opportunity to avenge the many losses

inflicted on them by the Franks,

because the king was absent,

the Saxons marched in hostile force

to the bank of the Rhine.

Unable by any means to cross it,

they nevertheless dared to lay waste

with great ferocity the Frankish lands

lying on the same side from which they had come,

from the walls of the city now called Deutz

until the place where the same Rhine meets the Moselle,

which bears along its banks the springs of Lyaeus. [Note: Printed *Musella Liei*; Reineccius: *Mosella Liaei*. *Liei*, or *Lyaei*, means “of Bacchus, of wine.”]

All the villages they could attack

they committed to the flames.

Their anger did not spare even the churches,

and there was no limit to the slaughter of human beings.

Their savage fury made no distinction

of sex, age, or any condition;

everything was consumed either by the sword

or by devouring fire.

From this it is clear that they did this

not for the sake of plunder,

but to inflict some vengeance on the Franks.

The king learned of this when he returned

from the Spanish regions.

He immediately ordered the eastern Franks

and the Alamanni to bring arms against the Saxons.

When they pursued the Saxons as they were already

returning to their homeland,

they attacked them resolutely near the river Ader,

at a place called Baddanfeld.

By the judgment of God, who rightly wished

to condemn such great crimes committed

by that people, the Saxons were cut down

in so great a slaughter that only a few

survived from their enormous army.

## Year 779. Indiction 1

In the new spring, while traveling through

the former lands of Gaul as necessity required,

Charles came to the village called Wirciniacum. [Note: Reineccius: “Werciniacum.”]

There the duke of Spoleto, named Hildibrand,

came to meet him.

Bearing precious gifts, he was sent back

to his own lands with sufficiently great honor.

But the king, intent on invading the lands

of the Saxons, soon crossed the Rhine.

The people themselves, trusting in the vain hope

that they could resist him, had come to meet him

with arms likewise taken up,

having gathered at a place called Bocholt.

But when they began to clash in battle,

they immediately turned their backs,

terrified by the great number of the Franks.

Charles then received the Westphalians

into submission.

Advancing from there, he reached the river Weser

and remained for several days in an established camp.

He compelled the Angarii and Ostphalians,

who came to him to confirm the faith

which they had promised—pledging that they would

be subject to him and faithful in spirit—

by taking hostages and administering oaths.

[Note: Reineccius read this verse as the first verse of the following year.]

After accomplishing these things,

the king returned to the city of Worms.

## Year 780. Indiction 2

Moving from there at the proper season,

he hastened again with his army into the Saxon region.

First he went to Eresburg; afterward, where the river Lippe

has its sources, he is said to have remained

for several days in camp,

making extensive preparations.

From there, taking the eastern road,

he came to the river Ocker.

A very large crowd of that same people,

obeying his command, had come to meet him there,

and, pretending to believe in Christ,

received baptism.

Proceeding quickly from there,

he established his camp where the great river Elbe

joins the Ora. [Note: First hand: *ora*; second hand: *horas*; Reineccius: *Hora*.]

For the affairs [Note: Manuscript: *rex* (“king”); Reineccius emended: *res* (“affairs”).] of the Saxons he wished to settle,

and also those of the Slavs,

whom the river Elbe divides in the middle.

The Saxons live on this side;

on the farther bank remains the pagan people

of the Slavs.

After arranging everything properly

for the circumstances of the time,

he finally resolved to return to his ancestral seats.

Since he always burned with a special love

for Peter, the most illustrious of the apostles,

he decided to seek the holy threshold of Rome,

intending to fulfill his vows and prayers to God.

Hastening quickly, and taking his wife

and children with him,

he reached the city of Ticinum,

where he celebrated the festival of Christmas.

Here, then, at the end of the first decade

of the years of Charles, after he had begun

to be sole king of the Franks,

I have decided to bring the first little book

to an end, so that rest may provide solace

to my slight powers.

# THE FIRST BOOK OF THE ANNALS OF THE DEEDS OF CHARLES THE GREAT ENDS. THE SECOND BEGINS.

[Col. 0695]

After seven hundred and eighty years had passed

since Christ was born of the Virgin,

this first year follows, in which the pious King Charles,

under the guidance of the Lord for the second time,

visited the Roman citadels.

Then Adrian, the apostolic bishop already mentioned,

received him joyfully with great honor.

The Roman people likewise came together

in unified rejoicing to meet him,

as their defender and giver of liberty,

and returned thanks.

While Charles was present there

for the solemn rites of Easter,

that same venerable bishop washed in the life-giving font

Pippin, his son, by name. [Note: In the manuscript, the verses printed below under the year 783 immediately follow here: “Gloria certabat” through “Salvavit mundum, voto celebraverat almo.” After these come the verses beginning “Exoriens aestas ubi primum,” and so forth. This transposition was made through the copyist’s error; Reineccius corrected it with a skillful hand and restored the events to their proper order according to the *Annals*, as they are printed here. Nevertheless, some material seems to be missing at this point in our poet. —Leibniz.]

[lacuna]

(Thirty or sixty verses are missing here.)

## Year 782. Indiction 4

As soon as the advancing summer had clothed

the lands in beautiful grass,

and the army could suitably be led out,

because the tender herbs had supplied

sweet fodder of blossoming hay for the animals,

the renowned king, supported by countless peoples

and distinguished soldiers, came again

into the Saxon region.

At the sources of the river called the Lippe,

he ordered a general assembly of the nobles

to be held.

There he arranged many affairs of the kingdom.

He heard envoys from Sigfrid,

king of the Danes,

and those whom the Hun leaders Iugurgus

and Caganus had likewise sent to him

to seek peace,

and wisely dismissed them after giving his replies. [Note: Leibniz: “he approached.”]

Afterward the great king crossed the Rhine

and withdrew into the Gallic fields.

Meanwhile, Widukind, who had been an exile

from the borders of his former homeland

and had sought the aid of the Northmen,

returned and, stirred by vain hope,

urged the Saxons to attempt to break

the treaty concluded with the Franks.

He summoned many of the people to arms

and caused a new war to arise.

The people of the Slavs, also called Sorabi,

suddenly and boldly burst forth with arms taken up.

They ravaged the Saxon lands neighboring them

and the fertile, grain-bearing fields of the Thuringians,

who inhabit the central lands and plains of the Sorabi,

lying between the rivers.

From one side flows the river called the Saale;

from the other the Elbe runs more broadly.

When Charles learned of the deeds of the Slavs,

he immediately judged that their boldness

must be restrained and the enemy driven

from the borders of his kingdom.

Therefore he summoned to himself

three palatine princes,

one of whom was the chamberlain of King Adalgis,

while the other, Geilo, was count of the stable. [Note: Manuscript: “Gilo.” On the authority of Einhard’s *Annals*, Reineccius correctly read “Geilo.”]

[lacuna] [Note: It is clear from the three preceding verses and from Einhard’s *Annals* that a verse containing the name of Worad, the palatine count, is missing here; there is no lacuna in the manuscript.]

He ordered these men to be commanders of the armies.

He commanded them to march against the Slavs

with forces gathered from the eastern region

of the Franks.

He also ordered the Saxons, whom he commanded

to obey him, to provide assistance to those leaders.

But when the envoys had begun to lead their columns through their territory—for they had been ordered to invade the Slavs by a direct route—the great defeat of the aforementioned people immediately became known to them.

For this reason they turned aside from the route they had begun, at first wishing, confident in their numbers, to overthrow the Saxons in battle. This undertaking, begun with excessive carelessness and equal arrogance, was brought to completion amid the grievous slaughter of the Franks.

For when the commanders learned that Widukind, accompanied by a great multitude, had prepared himself for battle and had placed his camp beside Mount Suntal, they hastened there at once with hostile standards, expecting that they would go to plunder rather than to battle, since the king himself, after attacking that land each year, had first exhausted its strength [Note: R. and L. read *exhauserat* (“had exhausted”) instead of *exhauserit* (“will have exhausted”).]

They had forgotten both the customs and the character of the people, which, the more it is oppressed by war, strives with such varied cunning and deceit, and, once defeated, does not know how to remain at rest, always preparing renewed attempts at vengeance.

Therefore, while the palatine commanders were hastening toward them, the Saxons, drawn up in a sufficiently long battle line, came out to meet them before the camp. There a savage battle immediately began, pouring forth enormous bloodshed. The Frankish nobles were slain in a cruel massacre; Adalgisus and Geillo were likewise killed, the king’s envoys. Four distinguished counts were also killed there, together with twenty other honored and noble men, who perished in the disaster.

[Col. 0697B] But the remainder of the people was consumed in that battle, so that only a very small band, fleeing to the lofty mountain nearby, reached it and escaped the enemy by hiding in the woods.

A sad messenger reported all this to the king. He hastily gathered his armies together and immediately came to the Saxon plain.

When the leading men of that people approached him, asserting that they had certainly not committed that deed, and the king sought the authors of the act, they all cried out that Widukind was guilty of this crime, together with those whom he had allied to himself at his own urging.

Yet he could not be handed over, because after the battles he had gone again to the land of the Northmen.

Four thousand five hundred men of the remaining people, who at his urging had waged so grave a war against the Franks, were indeed handed over to death. The king beheaded them all on a single day beside the river Aller, at the place called Ferdi.

Having exacted this vengeance there, the most illustrious of kings returned to his own estate called Theodone [Note: After this verse, two or three other verses are missing, which would have expressed the final sentence of Einhard’s Annals.]

[lacuna]

[lacuna]

Year 783. Indiction 5.

[lacuna]

(Twenty-six or twenty-seven verses are missing here.)

[He] was contending lest his accustomed glory should perish.

The other, now judging that no hope of safety remained, rushed upon the sword in defense of his ancient liberty.

But at last Charles, victorious by divine favor, after countless men had been slain, drove the survivors into flight.

A few days had passed when he learned that war had again broken out among that people.

For, clearly, in the region of the Westphalians, many having gathered on the bank of a river called the Hase, men possessing more courage than strength were again daring to engage in open battle, though they had been defeated so many times [Note: *Confligere habentes* (“having to fight”) has been repeated from the preceding verse in witness 1 (witness 2 reads *habentis*, “of one having”). I believe that Leibniz’s conjecture cannot be accepted for the sake of the construction, which would run as follows: “Clearly, with many gathered … they dared again to engage in battle, who had been so often defeated in open battle.” I have therefore supplied *aperta* (“open”); let others judge differently.]

As the king planned to march against them and reviewed his allies, he discovered that many more had fallen in the earlier battle, and that many wounded men had happened to be taken in.

But suddenly a new army from the Franks arrived for him. When all his legions had been increased, he hastened to destroy the rebels.

While that excellent and prudent commander had prepared everything, Fortune, as she is accustomed to do, followed valor.

The Saxons were again defeated and driven far away; a great number of captives was carried off.

From there the victorious king entered the eastern regions, laying everything waste with sword and fire as far as he came to the river called the Elbe.

After this he returned to his homeland. Then the wife called Fastrada, daughter of Count Radolf, born of noble stock, was joined to the royal marriage bed.

At that time he had spent the winter months at Eresburg and had celebrated with pious devotion the days on which the Redeemer, by his birth and death, saved the world.

Year 784. Indiction 6.

The mighty hero, wishing at last to complete the war that had been waged for so long against the Saxon people, led their numerous thousands of men chosen throughout the land.

First crossing the waters of the Rhine [Note: The manuscript reads *trans* (“across”); Reineccius conjectured *transcendens* (“crossing over”), while I have conjectured *transgressus* (“having crossed”).], he laid waste to the villages of the Westphalian region and came to the Weser, at the place called Uculbi.

From there he made his way through the fields of the Thuringians and the Saxon plains touched by the neighboring rivers, the Elbe and the Saale. He inspected many estates there and handed them over to the flames, until he reached the place known by the ancient name Scannigi.

From there, returning to Wormatia, he went into the city.

Meanwhile the king’s son, equal to his father in disposition and mind and bearing the same name, was commanding the ancestral armies. In the Westphalian district called Dreini, he encountered bands of that same people prepared for war and immediately defeated them in a cavalry engagement. Victorious, he came to his father in the city mentioned above.

The father, immediately accompanied by a strong force, made for the fields and encamped beside the river Ambra, where there is a fortress called Skideronsburg [Note: Witness 1 reads *considerat* (“he considers”) instead of *consederat* (“he had encamped”).]

After solemn vows had been performed in the camp there on the Nativity of the Lord, he marched to the mouth of the Warne, where it flows into the Weser. There was no longer any opportunity to go farther north, as he desired.

The harshness of winter hindered him, as did the course of incessant rains, which was flooding everything violently. For this reason he withdrew and settled in the city of Eresburg.

Year 785. Indiction 7.

Since he had decided to remain there with his retinue for the remaining days of the winter cold, he summoned his own family there with his wife.

With them, after leaving a faithful and secure garrison, he took along young men vigorous in spirit and strength. He roamed through all the fields of that broad region, as well as its various towns, and mingled everything together with flames, plunder, and savage slaughter, wishing by such devastation to crush the spirit of those whom he had often found rebellious.

When at last that mournful winter, fatal to him and to that people, had ended, and the spring breeze, breathing joyfully, adorned the fields with flowers, a general assembly was held at Paderborn.

After the illustrious king had completed it according to solemn custom, he hastened by a swift route to a district which the barbarian language calls Berdango [Note: A word is omitted; it was added by a second hand at the end of the verse.]

There he learned that the aforementioned Widukind and Abbo, who belonged to the leading families of their people, were hiding in their native territory, mindful of their crimes. Their land was enclosed on the northern side by the broad Elbe, near the borders of the Danish territory.

First sending envoys from among the citizens themselves, he urged them at last to bend their necks to him and entrust themselves to his faith, promising pardon for what they had done and rewards as well.

But their consciences, aware of their great guilt, hesitated over these promises until their hope of safety was strengthened by the hostages whom they had requested and sent.

When a certain Amulwin, a native servant of the court, had brought them, both men hastened at once to the king, who had by chance then returned to his own estate called Attiniacus.

There they were washed in the water of holy baptism and at last remained faithful to the king; from that time the people themselves rested for several years.

Meanwhile certain wicked men conspired to commit a dreadful deed with criminal intent, either killing the king with the sword or murdering him by some other means.

Hardradus, then count of this region, had been the instigator of the crime. But when the savage faction was exposed by reliable information, it was immediately subdued and came to an end, although it had been very great and had arisen with extreme violence.

The supremely prudent king ordered some of its authors to be deprived of their sight and the rest condemned to exile. Yet his clemency awarded none of them a punishment worthy of so great a crime.

Year 786. Indiction 8.

By order of the great Charles and the sacred council, an army set out toward the western regions to subdue the Bretons, who were then in rebellion.

Their former homeland had been the fertile island of Britain. They had lived there for a long time, but when the Angles wished to seek new settlements for themselves, and the fierce Saxons invaded it at the same time, the old inhabitants, expelled, immediately withdrew.

Most of them, fleeing, crossed the sea and at last occupied, at Gaul’s outermost bounds, the fields nearest the ocean waves. They remain in those lands to this day, giving the soil an indication of their former homeland through its name.

This people, after being overcome by the princes of the Franks, regularly paid tribute, though unwillingly.

When, in the time of that lord, it attempted to disregard his commands, Duke Audulf, sent there with many thousands of men, quickly restrained it by his valor and thoroughly subdued the fierce hearts of the rebellious people.

Then, with the King of Kings, Christ, assisting by his mercy, Charles having organized his kingdom and peace having been granted throughout the world, he decided to set out for Rome and also to bring the remaining part of Italy under his authority. Its capital and greatest portion had already been conquered, Desiderius having been captured and the Lombards subdued.

Only the duchy of the Beneventan region was not subject to him; at that time Duke Aragisus ruled it.

Burning with eagerness to attack him, Charles set out for those regions and hastened his journey. Neither the icy winter, already pressing upon the customary months, nor the terrifying road that had to be climbed across the Alps could delay him. On the mountain summits, rocks covered with black clouds and perpetual snow rise toward the stars.

After crossing them, he entered the Italian cities. Among them was one called Florence, where, venerating the flower of the Virgin’s birth, he had humbly celebrated the holy garden of Christ.

From there he strove to reach Rome quickly.

While he spent a short time there dealing with the preparations for the war he had undertaken, Aragisus, wishing to drive him away with gold when he could not do so with iron, sent through his own son the greatest gifts possible, humbly requesting peace.

But the king, thinking that he ought to proceed otherwise with the matters he had begun, advanced into the region where fertile Campania spreads its broad fields and settled in the city of Capua, intending to wage war immediately unless the aforementioned duke had prudently taken thought for himself.

For first he shut himself securely within the city of Salerno. Then, through envoys, he surrendered both his sons to the king, the elder called Rumoldus and the other Grimoldus, and promised that he himself and all his people would remain subject to the king’s commands with faithful hearts.

When these things had been offered, Charles’s ardor subsided. Fearing God above all, lest he thereafter be held guilty of having shed Christian blood, he refrained from war and no longer cared to storm the duke, who was in hiding.

The elder son was returned to the duke, while the younger was detained as a hostage with the king. The entire Beneventan people also did not delay in surrendering themselves; they gave eleven hostages, confirmed this treaty of submission, and swore by oaths that they would serve the Franks, the lords of the world [Note: From Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.282], forever.

Then he returned joyfully to Rome and there, with a glad heart, celebrated the greatest joys of the Easter festival.

Year 787. Indiction 9.

While the king was still staying in the Roman city, Tassilo sent envoys to the blessed Adrian, the supreme pontiff. One of them was Bishop Arnus, and the other was an abbot named Hunricus. They earnestly requested that he serve as mediator and guarantor of peace and good faith between himself and Charles [Note: *Sequester* (“guarantor,” “mediator”). Gloss: *grieduuard*.]

The apostolic bishop considered it proper that concord and peace, restored from the holy see of Peter, should give rest to leaders and peoples. He earnestly asked the king to lay aside all resentment in his heart.

When the king kindly agreed, the pope began to inquire of the duke’s envoys by what terms the present agreement was to be secured.

The envoys confessed that nothing of this sort had been entrusted to them, but that they had been instructed only to report to their lord the king’s answers and those of the apostolic bishop.

Therefore the sacred pope rejected them as bearers of deceitful and fraudulent instructions, and even declared that they should be condemned by a dreadful anathema if they attempted to break the pledge of faith previously promised, which they had wished to make with Charles.

Thus, leaving the peace negotiations unfinished, they returned to their homeland.

After these events, the king returned joyfully to the region of the Franks. Then he assembled a general council of his nobles within the walls of Worms and there resolved to learn by certain proof whether the aforementioned Tassilo wished to keep the faith he had sworn and remain subject to him.

For this reason he brought all the peoples of his kingdom to very strong camps, arranging them in three divisions and deploying them against the Bavarians, so that their great armies might terrify them. For the Christian king wished to overcome the people’s arrogance by terror rather than by the shedding of blood.

Pippin, the king’s son, went there with many troops, supported by Italian legions, and led his armies through the valley of Trent.

The eastern Francia that he had sent to this war, together with the Saxons who were then following the royal standards as ordered, armed themselves and went to a place called Pheringa, near the banks of the great Danube, which in ancient times was called the Hister.

The king himself placed his camp above the Lech, which is a fixed boundary between the Bavarians and the Alamanni, near the borders of the city of Augsburg.

Accompanied by a powerful force, he wished to overthrow with the sword the Noric kingdom held by Tassilo. When the duke saw himself surrounded on every side [Note: *Circumsessum* (“surrounded”). Gloss: *bisetenne*.], he humbly approached the king’s feet and begged for his life and pardon with devoted prayers.

Because the king was naturally very mild, he spared him when he saw him utterly defeated and humbled.

Nevertheless, the ancient treaties of the Bavarians were renewed. The people were compelled by oaths to promise perpetual loyalty or submission.

Moreover, a twelfth hostage was handed over to the king [Note: *Obses* (“hostage”). Gloss: *gisl*.]

Afterward he returned and spent the entire winter at Ingulenheim, where the royal residence shines.

Year 788. Indiction 10.

When the king had ordered an assembly of his nobles to be held at that same estate according to their solemn custom, Tassilo was also present there with the others.

His former people, whom he himself had governed, accused him of great crimes and of the guilt of high treason, and justly stirred the king’s anger against him.

First they charged that, neglecting the treaty of submission in which he had sworn that he would remain subject and faithful in heart, he had repeatedly incited the Huns by gifts and persistent entreaties, and had thereby made them enemies of the Franks, so that they wished to devastate their borders violently with arms and challenge Charles to war.

His wife Leutberga had persuaded him to do this. Because she was the daughter of King Desiderius, she had remained hostile to the Franks after her father’s exile. Carrying the flames of womanly hatred in her heart, she sought by wicked counsel to send peoples into the greatest dangers, without caring how much human blood was shed or how many thousands perished on either side, so long as she could inflict the burdens and losses of war upon the Franks and avenge her father by such means.

Many other charges were also brought against him by word and deed, clearly demonstrating that faith had been violated and that, having rejected the treaty, Tassilo had plotted against the king.

He himself neither began to deny any of these things nor could deny them. Convicted of the offense, he was condemned to death. So it deservedly happened to anyone who had followed a woman’s counsel.

But the king’s mercy immediately absolved the condemned man, withdrawing him from the very threshold of death, making him a monk, and ordering him to observe the monastic rule.

His son, a young man named Theodo, had likewise followed his father’s deeds [Note: Or should we read *fata* (“fate”)? Certainly nowhere do we find that Theodo was also accused of treason. If *facta* (“deeds”) is retained, it must be understood that he chose the clerical life.] and had taken up the leisure of the contemplative life.

But the Huns, a people harsh and devoted to war, wishing to fulfill what had been promised to the aforementioned duke, began, after preparing two armies, to invade certain borders of the Frankish kingdom.

One army entered the regions of Italy and reached the borders of the city to which Forum Julii had given its illustrious name.

The other army invaded Bavaria, but in vain: all its effort was fruitless, and, defeated, it withdrew from both places.

At this same time the noble Constantine ruled the empire of the Greeks. Splendid in birth, he had succeeded as heir to the august fathers to whom he was bound by descent.

The previous year he had sent envoys to ask Charles to accept him as a son-in-law and to join his daughter to himself in a marriage alliance. But, as usual, the Greeks were fickle; the frustrated hope of the petitioners stirred them to anger.

Accordingly, his court gave the emperor this advice: he should not allow to go unavenged the fact that King Charles had refused to grant him the embraces of the maiden whom supreme power scarcely allowed any mortal to equal.

For this reason he issued an imperial command to Theodore, the prefect whose office was to administer the Sicilian regions, joining several commanders to him, and ordered him to lay waste immediately the neighboring borders of the Frankish kingdom, thus arranging to kindle the beginnings of a general war.

But when the Greek leaders, following his orders, had approached the western shore with a powerful fleet in order to devastate the villages and cities of the Beneventan region with sword and devouring flame, Charles’s commanders, whose task it was to defend those places, met them.

Grimoldus was foremost among them, having been made duke that year in place of his deceased father Aragisus. Hildibrandus, ruler of Spoleto, was also hastening to conduct this war with many troops.

When widespread report announced that new enemies, powerful in wealth and numbers and unknown in language, had arrived after crossing the vast expanse of sea, he urged men from several Italian cities to bring arms against them with united forces, so that they might protect themselves by repelling the raiders.

The whole of Calabria, shaken by this movement, is said scarcely ever to have witnessed such a similar tumult [Note: Witness 1: *similes spectatu multus*; witness 2: *similes suspecta tumultus*. I believe that I have restored the true reading by repeating only the final syllable of *specta*.]

There the battle was joined on both sides. With immense zeal, the just side won the trophy.

The Achaean cohort gave way; the phalanxes of the Danaans turned their backs. For although the Greek people has always been vigorous in speech, it is usually sluggish in hand, very ready to provoke wars but not at all competent to conduct them well.

Thus Charles’s victorious men returned faithfully, after killing countless enemies. Filling their camps with much booty and a multitude of captives, they gained a great triumph without serious loss.

Then King Charles went to the region of Bavaria and, arranging the whole land with all its borders, entrusted it to suitable governors.

Returning to Aachen, the magnificent palace that he himself had founded, he celebrated there with the greatest joy the feast of the Nativity of the Lord and also the holy Easter.

Year 789. Indiction 11.

There is a people of the Slavs called by the name Wilti. It possesses fields near the farthest shores, where Germany joins its boundaries to the ocean.

For a long time this people had been extremely hostile to the Franks. It persecuted with hatred the neighboring Slavic peoples, whether subject to the Franks or joined to them by treaty, and often oppressed them by war.

The renowned ruler could not tolerate this for long. Taking with him various peoples and a large army, he sought to penetrate the insolent nation.

As he proceeded through the lands of the Saxons, he had to cross the very broad river Elbe.

There, after setting up a vast camp on the bank, he undertook a great work and completed it swiftly. He spread a very large double bridge across the waters and fortified both ends with a rampart, also placing a garrison there, lest anyone, after his return, should be able to block the road laid across the high river by breaking its fragile wooden framework.

Afterward he invaded the lands of the Wiltzi after crossing the river [Note: R. reads *multorum* (“of many”) instead of *Wiltorum*.]. As he laid them waste with sword and fire, he suddenly subdued their barbarian arrogance through terror.

Finally, when the Wiltzi saw that the Frankish camp was filled with many peoples, although they were a very strong nation and powerful in number, they avoided battle in every way and immediately surrendered to the king.

Above all, King Dragawitus, whom noble birth and more mature age distinguished above the others, did so. For when the king approached his city, Dragawitus himself had gone out to meet him with all his people, surrendering himself to Charles’s authority.

Thus that people, together with its commanders and nobles, also promised with faithful hearts that it would serve all its Frankish lords, giving oaths of allegiance.

Then the king received the hostages whom he himself had ordered and, after subduing the people in this manner, returned by the route along which he had come to the aforementioned river.

With a fortunate journey he returned, brought his own legions back across the bridge, and himself spent the winter at Worms.

Year 790. Indiction 12.

Here, Muse, now reveal Charles’s new period of repose.

This was the first year after he had begun to reign in which he did not set out for distant lands with his own soldiers, either to crush various enemies or to undertake other causes and affairs.

When at last he was permitted to remain at Worms, he received envoys from the Huns and sent his own envoys to them. For a very grave dispute stirred a cruel conflict between these peoples, as they debated with immense zeal where the fixed boundaries of their kingdoms ought to be established according to ancient right.

This was also the origin of the war which the Franks are known to have waged against the Huns at a later time.

But the king, unwilling to lie idle even for a short time in leisure, always vigorous in disposition, undertook a naval journey along the river Main.

He ascended it until he came near the walls of the great palace residence called Salt, situated near the source of the Saale. A still-modest stream of this river encircles the palace itself there, scarcely raising a hoarse murmur as it moves over the echoing stones.

After arranging affairs there, he returned by the favorable current and made for Worms. While he remained there through the winter season, a fire suddenly consumed the royal buildings that had been constructed there, destroying them completely during the night.

There he had celebrated the sacred feasts of the birth and passion of the Redeemer and had spent the beginning of spring, waiting for the earth to be clothed in grass, for the forests to put forth leaves, and for the various peoples and nations from different regions to be summoned suitably to war beneath a clear sky and in the sunshine.

For he wished once again to undertake a battle and exchange brief repose for arduous labor.

THE SECOND BOOK OF THE ANNALS OF THE DEEDS OF CHARLES THE GREAT ENDS HERE. THE THIRD BEGINS.

[Col. 0705]

The sun had begun to pass above the golden horns of heavenly Taurus and to enter the bright Laconian quarters of the sky; the shadows, shortened by the cold nights, and the pleasant breeze of the lengthened day gave Charles, whose mind was always flourishing in study and vigorous, a welcome season in which he could use his strength and lead his troops out to war.

After the course of seven hundred years and, in addition, approximately nine times ten years had elapsed since God was born human, he undertook this first campaign against the Huns.

He did not think he should delay in repaying them the treatment they deserved; the ancient cause of hatred finally demanded this.

For while that people flourished, ruling countless others whom it had subdued by arms, they had often been accustomed to inflict harm upon the Franks [Note: From Gregory of Tours, *Ecclesiastical History* II.6.]

Thus the ancients commonly relate that long ago, raging in a monstrous massacre, they utterly devastated the lands of the Franks and gave everything—the towns, fields, homes, cities, monasteries, and estates—to devouring flames.

For the enemy’s fury wished not to spare even sacred buildings, and scarcely one church remained in that kingdom: the church of Stephen, fittingly built within the walls of Metz; he is regarded as the first martyr.

For several successive years the Huns thus attacked the Franks, until their king Attila, so often the victor over many peoples, was thrust beneath Tartarus by a woman’s hand [Note: The poet confuses the deaths of Alboin and Attila. Compare Jordanes, *History of the Goths*, ch. 49.]

For they say that, when he was weighed down by wine and sleep, while deep night was bringing rest to every kind of living creature [Note: *Suggereret* (“was bringing,” “was supplying”). Gloss: *scunde*.], his savage wife, driving sleepless shadows onward under the stimulus of hatred, killed the king with a dreadful act of audacity.

Yet she avenged the death of her own father by this crime.

After this, as though the affairs of the Huns had fallen under a gloomy omen, their power retreated and thereafter they did not enjoy their former prosperity.

In ancient times they had oppressed the Franks—then pagans, afterward Christians [Note: It is universally agreed that the Franks were pagans in Attila’s time and that the Huns were distinct from the Avars.]—while God chastised those dear to him in his customary merciful manner.

Thus the memory of the fathers’ slaughter remained engraved upon the hearts of their descendants, preserving memorials of their ancient anger.

Moreover, a new dispute arising from the causes already mentioned stirred Charles’s mind, so that he might attack them with all the strength of the Franks.

Immediately, by imperial decree, an enormous army was brought forth from all the peoples subject to him, and the strongest supply of every resource required for conducting so great a war was prepared with watchful care and diligence.

But because he had brought forth too many troops, he divided them into separate groups and in this way strove to penetrate Pannonia, which the savage people of the Huns occupied and which lay at a great distance by land.

Then he entrusted one part of the people to Count Theodoric and Magenfrid, the foremost commanders at that time, and ordered them to hasten their journey along the northern bank of the Danube.

He himself advanced through the fields of the southern shore, accompanied by countless thousands and a powerful army.

The river carried provisions for all the forces in the middle of them, filled with the king’s splendid fleet, whose protection was entrusted chiefly to the Bavarians.

He ordered the Bavarians themselves to descend in boats with the favorable current.

Thus the king came to the river Enns, which separates the Bavarians and the Huns in the middle.

After placing his camp beside it in the green meadows, they unanimously decided to spend three days in humble prayer and to seek with all their hearts the assistance of Christ, King of Kings, so that in his mercy he might approve what they had begun and grant prosperity in everything to so many peoples who had set out for so distant a land, fortified by the sign of faith, and so that the battle against the impious gentiles might be successfully fought.

Then, moving the camp, he carried the aforementioned war against the people. He immediately destroyed its fortifications after driving out their garrisons. One of them was skirted by the Cambus, a river of no small size; another fortification had been surrounded by a very large rampart on the mountain called Cumberg.

After both had been destroyed with a strong force and leveled to the ground, he laid waste far and wide the enemy’s lands with sword and fire. At last he came to the mouth of the Raba, where it is carried into the waters of the Danube, and there, placing his weary soldiers in quarters, he gave them a short time to rest.

When the greater part of broad Pannonia had thus been stripped of its wealth and handed over to the flames, the victorious king led his people back unharmed.

This entire expedition had plainly been successful against the enemy, and no misfortune occurred in it, except that so great a plague consumed the legion led by the king with a dreadful disease that they say scarcely a tenth part of all those thousands could be brought back free of the disaster.

The king came to Reginum, now called Regensburg, and there celebrated the joys of Christ’s Nativity and Easter with a devout and faithful heart.

Year 792. Indiction 14.

Above the lofty ridges of the Pyrenees stands the city of Urgell, whose bishop was named Felix.

Here he attempted to establish a wicked heresy and taught doctrines contrary to the holy faith, asserting that because Christ the Lord had taken on a body and deigned to become human, he was not by this very fact the proper Son, but was the adopted Son of the Almighty.

When consulted about so grave a matter by Helipandus, bishop of Toledo, he gave this answer and took every possible care and employed every skill to defend his doctrine in written booklets.

From there he was brought to the court of the Catholic ruler—Charles was then wintering in Reginum [Note: *Regino*. Gloss: that is, Regensburg.]

There he was heard by many bishops and a numerous synod. Convicted of having taught a wicked error, he was afterward sent to the blessed Adrian, who at that time was bishop of the apostolic see.

In his presence, corrected in the church of blessed Peter and before the holy and renowned council of bishops, Felix condemned the sect of perfidy that he himself had earlier and unhappily originated, and earned permission to return to retain once more the honor of his own see.

But while the king was spending the summer season in the Bavarian regions, he nearly encountered the greatest dangers, had not divine mercy resisted human attempts and overthrown their savage plots.

Horror fills the minds of those who recall such attempts: how nearly the bright light of the Franks was extinguished, and how wicked men could even conceive such a crime.

For they strove by every means to deliver Charles to death. Hence a conspiracy is said to have been wickedly formed among the Frankish nobles.

Its principal author was a man sprung from the king’s maternal blood [Note: The manuscript reads *materno* (“maternal”). Leibniz: “Should we read *nativo* (‘natural’)? For he means Pippin, Charles’s natural son.” But the word is sound, with the construction proceeding as follows: “especially the king’s offspring, degenerate in maternal blood, but more so in the wickedness of his morals than in his birth.”], but more degenerate in the wickedness of his morals than in his birth.

This madman presented himself as the author of the crime.

Yet neither the king had deserved such hatred nor could the enemy justly complain of him; rather, the savage queen Fastrada, carrying a cruel swelling of spirit, was responsible.

An ugly noose of death hanged some of the conspirators, while the king spared only his own son and ordered him tonsured and purified of the contemplated crime according to the monastic rule.

While remaining in the Bavarian region, the prince was intent on building a bridge for naval operations across the Danube, for use in the war he had formerly undertaken against the savage Huns.

There he also celebrated the Nativity of the Lord, a festival especially renowned because of its triumph, by which he likewise conquered death and the author of death.

Year 793. Indiction 15.

When the king had decided to complete the war he had begun and invade the Huns again, he learned that the legions commanded by Duke Theodoric had been destroyed in the Frisian district called Hriustru.

They had perished through the treacherous ambushes of the Saxons, having been captured near the banks of the beautiful Weser.

Therefore, concealing the misfortune of so great a disaster, he abandoned the journey by which he had planned to go to Pannonia and engage the Huns in battle.

Meanwhile, men who brought him this information advised him that, between the rivers, one of which is called the Radantia and the other the Alcmona, if a canal were prepared through the earth so large that, reaching both rivers, it touched their waters and could carry floating vessels, a swift passage could be made from the Danube to the Rhine and navigation by boats would be easy.

For the Radantia is known to mingle with the Main, and the Main with the Rhine [Note: Reineccius reads: “There it joins the Main, here the Rhine.”]; the Alcmona flows into the raging waters of the Danube.

Trusting this advice, the prince himself sought out the place that he believed suitable for the work. After many thousands of laborers had been brought there, he spent nearly the entire autumn in fruitless effort.

Nevertheless, a canal two thousand paces long was dug and extended, and it lay open at a width of three hundred feet. But the work could not be completed at all, because continuous rain interfered too greatly and the natural moisture had dissolved the earth.

Whatever had been dug out by the day’s labor flowed back into the ground again during the night. As the mud continually increased across the sodden fields and the canal nowhere acquired a firm bank, a vast marsh, seeking the bottom, flowed through the slippery soil, and thick mud settled in the deep pits.

Although he persisted in the work he had begun, at last, recalled by grim news, he abandoned it. For it was reported that the entire Saxon people had suddenly rebelled again and begun a war.

Moreover, the Saracens had inflicted very great losses, laying waste certain borders of the kingdom with the sword. They finally returned after killing the Frankish commanders, carrying away booty and a splendid triumph.

Then the king, moved by these adversities, returned from there to the Franks. He devoutly celebrated the joys of Christ’s Nativity near the bright waters of the Main, at the place illustrious by the name and merits of the blessed martyr Kilian. He also honored the holy Easter with great devotion at Frankfurt.

Year 794. Indiction 1.

The Catholic prince, wishing to uproot from the sacred field of the Lord the accursed seeds of the poisonous sect that Felix had wickedly scattered by an unhappy attempt, summoned bishops from everywhere and held the aforementioned synod at the palace.

Stephen too was present together with Theophylact:

For each was a legate of the bishop of the Roman see, whom the holy pope Hadrian, sending them, had duly instructed to represent him there.

Then all, together with the general decree, condemned this heresy, and a written statement against it was drawn up; that body of bishops had confirmed it, and all had likewise subscribed to it.

[Col. 0709B] Moreover, not many years earlier, the Greek emperor—Constantine by name, and his mother called Irene—had caused a synod to be held in Constantinople. They decreed that it should be called the Seventh, or General, Council; but this council likewise recognized that it was not worthy of such a title and judged it to be disregarded as superfluous.

At that time Fastrada, the king’s wife, had departed this life, receiving her final day. He had her body buried with great honor in the splendid church of the martyr Alban, which shines joined to the walls of the city of Mainz.

After Charles had accomplished all these things in due order, he once more brought arms against the treaty-breaking Saxons.

[Col. 0709C] He had resolved to subdue them with two armies, equipped alike with terror and steel, so that this one people might quickly succumb to two wars, of which it would scarcely have been able to endure even one.

The king’s forces hastened from the southern region, laying waste far and wide the wretched lands of the Saxons. His son Charles had crossed the waters of the Rhine, accompanied by a picked body of young men, and attacked the rebels from the western region.

A great and well-deserved terror immediately seized them. Although they had assembled across the open fields of the great plain of Sinothfeld and were prepared to fight a battle, their courage collapsed through fear, nor did they have any hope of resisting the Franks, whom they saw supported by the armies of so many peoples and impossible to defeat.

[Col. 0709D] At once, abandoning the contest of war, they submitted to the king and confirmed this treaty of surrender by oaths and by giving hostages.

He returned to Aachen—thus is the royal residence illustriously named, and it is also called Aquensis—and there, according to his custom, celebrated the holy season in which our substance was united to God and the death of the Redeemer restored the whole world.

### Year 795. Indiction 2.

Since the rebellious people of the Saxons had become exceedingly suspect, having so often broken their treaty and refusing to rest under the king’s just rule, the most powerful ruler decided not to grant them any breathing-space or opportunity for rebellion,

[Col. 0710A] but once more, laying waste their land with hostile intent, he finally pitched his camp near its furthest boundary, where a notable village stands called Bardonwich. He had ordered the nobles of the Slavs, bound to him by treaty, to come to him there.

While he was waiting there for their arrival, as chance would have it, he learned that one of them had been killed. He was the king of the Abodrites, Witzun by name. While coming, as he had been ordered, to visit the king, he had fallen into an ambush previously prepared for him by the Saxons, because they knew him to be loyal to the Franks.

Therefore, moved in spirit by the bitter goads of anger, he ordered the fields and villages of that same region to be ravaged far and wide with sword and fire.

[Col. 0710B] Then one of the leading men of the Huns, named Tudun, came there by a long route. He declared that he wished to submit to the king and to believe in Christ the Lord with a devoted heart.

After this Charles had returned to the palace at Aachen and there celebrated the previously mentioned festivals as a suppliant.

### Year 796. Indiction 3.

In this year Hadrian, a bishop raised to the lofty summit of the apostolic see, departed this life. After him Leo attained the supreme pontificate. At once he sent to Charles the keys by which the confession of Saint Peter is preserved, together with the banners of the city of Rome and suitable gifts.
