He also urged him with pious prayers to send some of his own leading men,

[Col. 0710C] and to subject the Roman people to him, compelling them to promise, by solemn oaths, to preserve this treaty of faith.

Angilbert was sent for this purpose. He had governed as abbot the church splendidly adorned by the body of Saint Richarius, and he likewise carried there royal gifts, which the king had devoutly sent to Saint Peter.

For the royal palace of the Huns had been stripped of its treasures—the place they call Hringum. The commander Erich had captured it in this year and had transported from there many kinds of treasure to the king, treasures which the Huns had accumulated in ancient times by repeatedly plundering innumerable peoples.

The greatest abundance of these was then sent to Rome; the king’s lavish hand enriched all the remaining leading men and ministers of the palace with very great gifts.

[Col. 0710D] After these events the king again invaded the regions of the Saxons, laying waste far and wide; then, returning victorious, he remained at Aachen during the winter.

Meanwhile Pippin, duke of Italy and royal offspring, together with the Bavarian legions assigned to him, had made war upon the Huns, as his father had ordered. With them he fought successful battles across the river Tizsa, and after all the enemies had been put to flight, the entire royal palace of the Huns was leveled to the ground by the Franks—the place we mentioned earlier as Hringum.

At that time nearly all the treasures of that people, whose quantity was immense, and all the riches of their former kings were plundered; these are said to have been shamefully amassed over many years by plundering holy sanctuaries in diverse lands.

[Col. 0711A] After these things had been taken away, Pippin, victorious and entitled to so splendid a triumph, came to his father in the palace, bringing him the treasures of the plundered kingdom, as well as the spoils of the leaders and the captured banners.

The aforementioned Tudun had also come there with him. He strove to confirm his promises by his own faithfulness, and, receiving baptism together with his whole company, he also pledged by oaths that he would remain subject and loyal to the Franks forever.

But after he returned, changing his promises and his faith, he paid the penalty for his treachery a short time later.

Meanwhile the king had celebrated there, with solemn vows, the seasons sanctified by Christ’s birth and death.

[Col. 0711B] ### Year 797. Indiction 4.

While summer, shining in its beautiful rising, was resplendent, a Saracen named Zatus came to the king and handed over to him the city he had won, called Barcelona. For, built on the Spanish frontier and compelled by varied circumstances, it had at one time belonged to the Saracens and at another been subject to the Franks; finally, through the aforementioned commander, who had likewise voluntarily entrusted himself and the city to Charles, it became subject thereafter to Frankish rule.

From there he sent his son, named Louis, then king of the Aquitanians, to besiege Huesca, as a certain Spanish city is called.

He himself once more brought arms against the Saxons, lest they should perhaps dare again to raise their stubborn necks. He laid waste all their outermost territories, those enclosed by the Elbe and those where the famous waters of the Weser mingle their spreading stream with the salty waves of the ocean.

When he returned to Aachen, Abdallah, son of the king of the Moors, came devotedly to meet him. His name was Abdella. After the merciful king had received him there, he summoned his council and devised a prudent plan for bringing the Saxon wars at last to an end, remaining in that region throughout the coming winter.

Therefore, taking with him immediately his entire retinue, he pitched camp on the bank of the Weser and ordered the place to be called Heristal; it still bears that name. He divided among the peoples he had brought with him the land itself,

[Col. 0711D] and compelled the native inhabitants, though unwilling, to give them winter quarters and supplies for all.

Pippin came to him there from Italy; Louis, returning from the Spanish regions; and envoys of the Huns, as well as those of Alfonso, king of Asturias, came to Charles from lands so far away, bearing the greatest possible gifts.

From there each royal son was dismissed to his own kingdom. He also sent Abdella with Louis, after first having him escorted back to his homeland, and entrusted him to those whom he himself had then chosen and whose loyalty he did not hesitate to trust.

The king, however, remaining in the land of the Saxons,

[Col. 0712A] celebrated the most holy festivals in the aforesaid place, in which Christ came forth clothed in a body and, dying, laid down his flesh, while rising again he took it up.

### Year 798. Indiction 5.

At the beginning of spring a certain Saxon people committed a horrible crime. They dwell separately north of the Elbe, which encloses them toward the south, extending toward the northern pole. In their native speech we call them Northalbingians.

When the king sent envoys there to administer justice according to the law, an impious, treaty-breaking faction of the people slaughtered them.

And when Godescalc, likewise an envoy of the king, had been sent a few days earlier to the kingdom of the Danes, whose ruler was named Sigifrid, he was intercepted by the Huns while returning at that very time. They had been the authors of this revolt,

[Col. 0712B] and yet he had suffered death for no crime.

Moved by this, the king hastened to the river Weser and established his camp at a place called Munda. As the most just avenger of the envoys’ deaths, he gave free rein to his anger against the deserters, ordering that their land be widely ravaged by troops scattered throughout it.

Then the savage soldier raged everywhere; everywhere blood moistened the fields like streams, and everywhere a dreadful slaughter increased: wounds, death, mourning, shouting, flight, flames, and plunder filled everything, until the Elbe, advancing with its deep waters, restrained the armies from going farther.

But when the Northalbingians saw that those whom they had sent had been killed with impunity—the royal camp of Charles had not crossed the river—they decided to add great audacity to their undertaking. Finally they began, with all their strength, to harass the Abodrites, who at that time were subject to the Franks and bound to them by treaty.

But the Abodrite duke Thrasco, having learned of this movement, brought his forces against them. In the battle joined at the place called Suentana, he struck down four thousand of the enemy and compelled the defeated survivors to return amid enormous losses.

When the king had returned to the palace at Aachen, he received envoys sent from Constantinople. Irene had sent them to him on her own affairs, bearing prayers and gifts, for Constantine, who had been born of her,

[Col. 0712D] had been deposed by the Greeks from the throne of the kingdom because of his immense moral depravity, and, deprived of his sight, had paid a heavy penalty for his wickedness.

One of those sent was Michael, and the other was the priest Theophilus. At their request it was finally arranged, through the king’s great mercy, that Sisinnius, once captured in war, should be released and permitted to return to his homeland. He was the brother of the aforesaid bishop of the city, which shines as the noble capital of the Greek empire.

After these men had also been dismissed, envoys came from the Spanish lands of King Alfonso. They brought great gifts to Charles, renewing the ancient treaty which had always united those kings in friendship. He kindly bestowed great gifts upon them when he received them and sent them joyfully back to their homeland with such honor.

[Col. 0713A] In this year, it is said, the Balearic Islands were invaded; one of them is called Majorca, while the other bears the name Minorca in the older language. Moorish pirates had devastated these islands.

The king celebrated in the aforesaid palace the season in which the Creator of heaven and earth chose to be born, in which death was the death of death and he wounded hell, and in which, rising from death, he restored life to us.

### Year 799. Indiction 6.

Oh, what lamentable wickedness mortal hearts repeatedly conceive! How, submerged in the precipitous depths of depravity, they fear neither laws nor justice and blindly slip into deeds of dreadful horror.

[Col. 0713B] This year bears witness, a year in which an outrage unworthy of report stained the Roman city with savage crime. For Leo, the holy bishop venerable throughout the world, suffered terrible punishments at the hands of his own citizens.

We had believed that the sufferings of the righteous had ceased, since the cruel torturers had long ago been condemned to the fire of Gehenna—those whom immense worldly power had made arrogant while they held the scepters of empire.

Now, in times of peace, executioners born of criminal enterprises filled Rome with the blood of martyrs slain in similar fashion, although they were far inferior in lawful authority but equally savage in mind.

They committed such a great crime in our own times, when, with a public cessation of business proclaimed, the faithful people ought to have chastised itself, fulfilling public vows together with prayers,

[Col. 0713C] and likewise to have cleansed its own offenses.

Then, wishing to celebrate the mysteries of Christ for all those entrusted to him, the bishop proceeded on horseback in solemn fashion from the Lateran palace. He went to your sacred threshold, Laurence the martyr, where a metal bed now enhances the glory of the church and offers most celebrated memorials of your virtue, since, placed upon burning coals, you scorned the flames, his body burning, he burned yet more deeply within with love for Christ.

But not even such merit of yours could calm the hostile fury, so that, while the supreme bishop was hastening to seek your holy aid, they prepared both ambushes and torments for him.

As he hurried on his way, surrounded by an evil crowd and enduring cruel hands, he lost the light of his eyes, which were gouged out; the torturer also cut out his tongue and then left him lying naked outside, half-dead and stained with much blood. Afterward he was taken to the monastery of the martyr Erasmus—its perpetrators had ordered this to be done—and was kept there under the pretense of being treated.

[Col. 0713D] [Note: R. Orci. I have corrected Reineccius’s faulty punctuation at this point by removing the period after *Romam* and placing the other after *feroces*.]

Until Wingisus, duke of Spoleto, learning how matters had unfolded, came in haste to Rome. During the night he lifted the holy bishop over the wall and escorted him away with the proper honors.

[Note: [Col. 0714D] R., *Winigisus*.]

By God’s mercy, after a short time he recovered both the sight he had lost and the power of speech: either because the torturer, hurrying and trembling at his wicked deeds, fearing that crowds gathering would not tolerate such acts but would wish to defend their pope, had not carried out his cruel work as fully as he intended; or—and this is more credible—because the Redeemer, renewing the ancient miracles through the merit of the great Peter, had granted that his successor should be healed.

When Wingisus reported these events to Charles, the king, reminded of the man’s uprightness and of his supreme reverence for the order of the apostolic see, ordered that the glorious bishop should come to him, escorted with honor.

He himself nevertheless continued his journey, as he had decided, entering the lands of the Saxons. After establishing his camp at Paderborn with a large army,

[Col. 0714B] he waited there for a considerable time for the arrival of the supreme bishop.

Charles also, the king’s son, sent by his father to the borders of that people, proceeded along the region through which the Elbe flows in a broad course. He was to arrange certain affairs with the Wiltzi and Abodrites and to receive some Saxons who had already chosen to entrust themselves to the king’s allegiance from those regions.

While the younger Charles was delayed there, accomplishing all these matters quite successfully, and while the great king, moved by paternal affection, watched for the return of his son, the apostolic bishop arrived, having already penetrated almost to the farthest reaches of the world. To him the journey had seemed short, because the sight of Charles had repaid all the hardships he had previously endured,

[Col. 0714C] from whom he had long confidently believed that worthy consolation for all his troubles would rightly be granted to him.

For as soon as he learned that the bishop was approaching, Charles himself went to meet him at the place of the aforementioned camp, accompanied by many thousands of people.

He received the pontiff, the representative of Peter, to whom it is permitted by his word to close and open heaven, and who occupied the apostolic see, with magnificent and reverent honor.

After spending several joyful days there, the bishop explained each of his affairs to the king and easily recognized his willingness to grant everything he piously wished to request. He therefore entrusted him to the leading men of the Franks, who were to escort him back honorably. Fulfilling the orders,

[Col. 0714D] they entered Rome together and restored everything to the pontiff, so that he might retain the rights of governing the apostolic see and its rightful honors.

After the pope’s departure the king remained for a short time in the same place, when suddenly a sad messenger brought him news of the death of two leading men, whom the greatest valor had made illustrious.

One was the count of Bavaria, named Gerold. While attempting to defend the people of Christ and resisting the savage Huns in war, he ended his fragile life and took up eternal life.

[Col. 0715A] The other had been duke of the Italian frontier. His name was Erich. After fighting very many battles and repeatedly winning triumphs over the enemy, he had undertaken to attack the city of the Liburnians, Tarsatica; but the citizens of that place, whom they had always known to be unconquerable by force, killed him by trickery and deceit.

Then Charles, having arranged all matters concerning the Saxons with firm discipline as much as the time allowed, proceeded to the palace at Aachen.

There Count Wido, to whom the regions of Brittany had been entrusted, brought him the weapons of the leaders, each inscribed with its owner’s name. They had established these as a sign of their surrender, compelled as they were to serve the Franks.

For that count, together with many of his companions, had this year thoroughly traversed the whole land, subduing its fierce hearts by the great terror of war.

The Bretons would already have been permanently subjected to Frankish rule if the treacherous hearts of that faithless people had not changed their promises and their loyalty.

At that time, too, a Saracen called Azan sent Charles the keys of the city over which he ruled, Oca—thus the barbarian tongue named it—and, sending great gifts at the same time, promised to surrender it if a suitable opportunity should arise.

Then a monk sent from the city of Jerusalem, having crossed an immense distance of land and sea, brought the king a gift more precious than all gold. A pious patriarch had sent holy relics of the place where Christ, having been buried in the flesh,

[Col. 0715C] rose again after conquering death, and where an angel sent from the heights of heaven proclaimed these joys to the world.

The king also celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in the palace already mentioned. Thereafter, when the monk wished to return, he released him and joined to him as companion Zacharias, who was a priest of the royal palace.

Through him he sent great gifts to the holy places,

[Note: [Col. 0715D] From Einhard, *Life*, chapter 27.]

and to the men there who were leading lives of poverty and enduring the world’s evils in Christ’s name.

### Year 800. Indiction 7.

When the months of March had completed their middle course, and Phoebus, the beginning of the whole world and of the year, was thundering as he trod the signs of the heavenly Ram, spring returned, driving away the harshness of winter, adorning the forests with leaves and the meadows with green grass, giving birds their voices and lengthening the days.

Then Charles, the outstanding glory of the world and the bright light of the present age, emerged from the palace at Aachen and surveyed the shore of the ocean, whose name is Gallic. There he equipped a fleet upon the sea itself, which the Northmen pirates had made hostile.

[Note: [Col. 0715] *Pyrate*. Gloss: *ashmen* (“ship-men”); in Adam of Bremen, chapter 212, *ascomanni*.]

[Col. 0716A] By then that excessively harmful people had become a great danger to the kingdom of the Franks.

In the monastery where the body of Saint Richarius rests, he joyfully celebrated the solemn rites of Easter.

Then, proceeding along the route he had begun, he reached the city of Tours and, seeking your aid as a suppliant, visited the tomb of your most holy Martin, who shines forth as a confessor radiant with apostolic virtue.

There the sad illness of his wife compelled him to delay. She had ended her final hours of life there, a woman praiseworthy in every respect for her character and manner of life; her name was Liutgard.

After duly attending to the funeral and completing the burial with fitting dignity, he himself returned to Mainz. At the beginning of August, having gathered his leading men from everywhere, he held a general assembly there.

[Col. 0716B] He then announced that a journey into Italy was to be undertaken by the many peoples whom he had decided to take with him there, a plan he had postponed for only a short time.

Accompanied by a picked force, he set out and sought the splendid walls of famous Ravenna.

After spending no more than seven days there, he sent King Pippin with a large army to the towns of the land of Benevento, while he himself proceeded devotedly toward the Roman strongholds.

At Nomentum Pope Leo, the consecrated pontiff, came to meet him. He received him with great joy and reverence, recognizing him as the sole defender he had formerly possessed.

After they had exchanged sweet words and shared a meal there, the supreme bishop went ahead of the king to the city.

On the following day, when the solemn and festive dawn rose, offering joy to the Romans on the day when so great a king was to be received by them, the pope gathered all his bishops and clergy.

Taking them with him, he came to the threshold of the great basilica of Saint Peter, the supreme apostle, and stood on the steps of the church, surrounded by the sacred choir.

He received Charles as he approached, singing sweet melodies of praise and rendering thanks to God with his whole heart for having given the Church such a ruler and defender—one for whom that age knew no mortal equal, either in strength of virtue or in devotion to every good work.

Such honor and such glory of the Franks accompanied the king, together with the great rejoicing of the Roman people,

[Col. 0716D] as he entered the church of the great Peter with a pure heart, shedding tears and humbly imploring the holy aid of so great a patron.

By then the growing harshness of winter, at the time of the icy solstice, finally compelled them to provide the soldiers with their desired winter rest there.

## HERE BEGINS BOOK IV OF THE ANNALS ON THE DEEDS OF CHARLEMAGNE THE EMPEROR

[Col. 0715]

[Col. 0715D] The festive day of heaven, equally most renowned on earth, had shone forth: the birth from the Virgin and the coming of Christ,

[Col. 0716D] eight hundred years after he had first proceeded forth, the Lord clothed in the veil of servile form.

[Col. 0717A] And now Rome had heaped every joy upon that great Nativity through the presence of King Charles.

When the solemn rites of the Mass were about to begin, he proceeded into the great hall which contains the body of Peter, venerable throughout the world, to whom Christ himself gave the keys of heaven.

After the king had raised himself from before the sacred limbs with a faithful heart and poured-out prayers, Pope Leo placed a crown upon his head.

At once the people cried out together; the sacred church resounded with immense jubilation, and the voice of the people rose to heaven as the Roman people sang with one accord:

“Glory to Augustus Charles the Great, bringer of peace, deservedly holding the scepters of the Roman Empire; prosperity, kingdom, peace, life, and triumph!”

After these praises had been spoken, the supreme bishop venerated him in the manner that long-standing custom prescribed for ancient princes. His title of Patrician was set aside—the title by which he had previously been called—and he deserved thereafter to be called Augustus, the pious prince of the empire.

After a few days had passed, Charles had previously ordered the men by whom the holy bishop had suffered so many disasters in the preceding year to be brought before his tribunal and undergo legal judgment.

Because their crime compelled judgment under Roman maiestas, he condemned them all, as they deserved, to capital punishment. But, although they were unworthy, at the intervention of the merciful bishop he granted them their lives; nevertheless, so great a crime would not remain unpunished, and he sent them all into exile.

[Col. 0717C] After spending the Easter festivals at Rome, he departed and proceeded to the city of Spoleto.

At the time when Augustus was staying there, when the final night of April enveloped the second hour in excessive darkness, the earth suddenly trembled, terrified by a tremendous movement. It produced dreadful and exceedingly fearful sounds; the wrath of heaven disturbed its stable repose, violently shaking the innermost organs of the world hidden beneath the earth’s great mass.

When a stormy whirlwind had penetrated the hidden caverns and the places of the veins concealed beneath the earth’s deep bosom, and found nowhere any open fissure through which the force of the wind might burst out, it generated certain waves amid the fields.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The manuscript reads *penetranset*, easily corrected; R. instead reads “the whirlwind penetrating.”]

[Col. 0717D] At home the terror was even greater than upon any body of water during a shipwreck, as each person fled beneath his trembling roof, fearing the sudden collapse of the buildings.

All the walls resounded at once with a dreadful uproar, as hanging sails shriek when ruffled by the wind,

[Col. 0718A] or as servants shake out cloths that had become soiled with fine dust, vigorously beating them in turn.

You might have seen all the walls trembling in no other way.

Yet this terror struck all Italy with particular force. It overturned many of its cities and tore mountains from their deepest roots.

Then at Rome the beams of the venerable church fell—the church which the apostle Paul adorns with his own relics.

Neither Gaul nor Germany was free from so great a disaster. In the regions around the Rhine, many places were violently shaken by the exceedingly terrifying movement.

Mugings were also heard from the high mountains, dreadful sounds and various roars were echoed, and a very great plague of disease began to spread.

After returning from the regions of Spoleto, Charles came back to Ticinum, now called Pavia. Leaving the borders of Italy, Augustus sought the residence at Aachen and remained there quietly during this year.

He sent envoys throughout every part of his kingdom,

[Note: [Col. 0717D] From Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 29, but it may also have derived from another source, for example the *Annals of Lorsch* under the year 802.]

[Col. 0718B] instructing them, with impartial administration of the laws, to dispense justice and settle various disputes, to restore civil right to the good, and to terrify the wicked. He had also ordered the divine laws and the pious laws of the world to be applied and renewed in due order.

### Year 802. Indiction 9.

In this year an elephant was first brought from distant regions, a wondrous spectacle for the kingdom of the Franks. The prince of the Persians, Aaron, gave Charles this elephant; Aaron was also the ruler to whom all the East, except India, had been subject.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] From Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 16.]

He had voluntarily taken care to bind himself to Charles’s friendship by a firm treaty and considered him alone, above all the kings of that age, worthy to receive generous gifts as a mark of exceptional honor.

For he repeatedly sent him gems, gold, garments, spices, and the other riches of the East, and granted that the holy place of Jerusalem should always belong to Charles’s own jurisdiction.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] The entire account of the events of the year 803, according to the poet, derives from Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 7. Einhard, however, states that peace was agreed only after the transfer of the Saxons; since that took place in 804, it is clear that the pacification of Saxony should be assigned to that year rather than to the year in which our author places it, and that it was not completed at the location he gives. [Col. 0718D] For in 804 Charles, returning from Saxony to Cologne and Aachen, did not reach the palace at Salz on his journey. Nor is the one piece of evidence that might be brought forward—the heading of the capitulary of the manuscript of Metz concerning Salz (Baluze, *Capitularia*, ed. Chiniac, vol. I, p. 415, II, 1063)—sufficient to establish the contrary by its phrase “in the fourth year at Salz,” since everyone knows that at this period the authority of Einhard’s *Annals* was exceptionally great and virtually unique among writers. The error may have arisen because the poet read in Einhard’s *Annals* that another peace, namely one with the emperor of Constantinople, was concluded at Salz in the year 803.]

### Year 803. Indiction 10.

This noble year finally brought to an end the long struggles of war between the Saxons and the Franks by a firm treaty of perpetual peace.

The pious Augustus had come to the place called Salz. There, with all the nobility of the Saxons assembled, they jointly established these terms of peace:

[Col. 0718D] They were to abandon completely every pagan observance and ritual, by which they had previously been deceived into worshiping through demonic art, and thereafter submit themselves to the Catholic faith and serve Christ God forever.

But, according to the unanimous decision of all, they were not to pay any census or tribute at all to the Frankish kings.

[Col. 0719A] They were to offer only the tithes established by divine law and strive to obey the bishops and likewise their clergy, who taught the sacred doctrines, the faith pleasing to the Lord, and the life that accords with it.

Then, under the judges whom the king had appointed over them,

[Note: [Col. 0719D] “Judges,” that is, counts.]

and under his envoys,

[Note: [Col. 0719D] “Envoys,” that is, royal missi.]

the Saxons were permitted to use their ancestral laws and enjoy the honor of freedom.

Finally, they were joined to the Franks by this treaty, so that they might become one people and nation in harmony and always obey one king equally.

If this seems doubtful to anyone, let him read for himself the book written about the life of Charles, which the famous, truthful, and exceptionally prudent narrator among the Franks, Einhard by name, composed.

[Col. 0719B] Under these conditions of peace they swore that they would remain faithful to Charles, to his sons, and to the line of his descendants throughout the ages.

Their efforts to continue the war, which they had prolonged so harshly for thirty-three years, were brought to an end more by the king’s mercy and generosity than by terror.

For whenever anyone had entrusted himself to his exceptional faith by rejecting profane rites, he enriched him with resources and adorned him with extensive honors.

The poor Saxons first came to know an abundance of the goods that wealthy Gaul produces when the king granted estates to many of them there, from which they could receive costly clothing,

[Col. 0719C] heaps of silver, and the sweet-flowing waters of Liei.

When he had enticed their leading men with these gifts, he crushed all the rest who were subject to him by force of arms. Having tested his character in many ways, they learned that his mercy was as sweet as his anger was terrifying, and they resolved in faithful observance to preserve the aforesaid treaty forever. They are shown not to have altered it thereafter.

### Year 804. Indiction 11.

The apostolic bishop Leo departed from the city of Rome, led by his fervent love for Augustus. Because of the affairs of the Church, for which he saw that imperial protection was necessary, he again undertook to visit the lands of the Franks, traveling a long distance.

As soon as he had crossed the terrifying Alps, almost all Gaul learned through swift rumor that so great a man had arrived. Augustus immediately heard the news with joy and went to meet him at the city of Reims. After receiving him with sufficiently worthy honor, he led him to the residence called Carisiacum.

There they duly celebrated the festivals of the Lord’s Nativity. From there they sought the walls of the beautiful palace at Aachen and together gloriously celebrated the holy season in which, when the star showed the way, the Magi were deemed worthy to recognize the rising on earth of the true light.

After the conversation for which the revered bishop had come had been completed, the illustrious king offered him gifts worthy alike of the giver and the recipient, since one was unquestionably the most distinguished of the bishops and the other of the kings of that age.

After these events the bishop returned to his own city. There they were separated in body alone, remaining forever joined in the pious love of their minds.

### Year 805. Indiction 12.

A nation of Slavs, exceedingly fierce in its devotion to war, whom they call Bohemians, had provoked the Franks with insolent frivolity and aroused Charles’s anger.

Against them his son and namesake was sent with many thousands. He engaged them in war with skilful valor and completed it as victor with a swift conclusion.

### Year 806. Indiction 13.

[Col. 0720B] When the pious Augustus, supported by the protection of the Lord, preserved all the boundaries of so great an empire under legitimate and orderly governance and established peaceful conditions everywhere, he carefully considered how to remove the causes of disputes which he saw might in the future generate division among the faithful people.

Therefore, lest a division of the ancestral kingdom should arise among his sons after some dispute, he himself assigned definite portions to each, as he wished.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] From the Charter of the Division of the Empire.]

He had added all Bavaria to Pippin, king of Italy; likewise, he assigned him Burgundy insofar as it lies between the lofty Alps at their lower extremity, together with a few districts of the Alamanni.

But to Charles he granted the remaining Alamanni, and subjected the Saxons and Frisians to him,

[Col. 0720C] together with a large part of Gaul, extending as far as it is enclosed by the broad waters of the ocean.

He arranged that this Charles should succeed him in the Frankish kingdom, if the Lord did not otherwise will it.

Almost all Burgundy, however, was placed under the scepter of the pious king Louis, who was to hold the empire by right thereafter. All Aquitaine, which had previously been entrusted to him, was likewise assigned to him as his own kingdom, to be governed under stable rule.

Then he adjured them all and earnestly entreated them, warning them to preserve faithfulness and not to despise peace, lest anyone, transgressing his proper boundary, should cause quarrels and war and become forever guilty, as deserved, of the bloodshed of the Christian people.

Instead, they were to act among themselves so that the due harmony joining brotherly minds might remain firm.

[Col. 0720D] Thereafter the emperor himself remained at his residence in Aachen and no longer undertook his customary military activities or went to wage war against any enemies.

There was no need for it, nor did his age permit him to renew the labors by which he had already been exhausted. Advancing heavily, and growing from moment to moment, old age made his strength decline.

### Year 807. Indiction 14.

The king of the Saracen people, exceedingly savage and a grave threat throughout the world by land and sea,

[Col. 0721A] nevertheless honored Augustus with splendid gifts. He also sent him a marvelous present: a tent made by every kind of art, larger and more beautiful than all the others.

If tradition is accustomed to report anything true about the ancients, one might wonder where such great quantities of canvas could have been gathered, or in what fertile fields such a crop of flax had grown, or where suitable material for so great a work could have been obtained. Only thousands of men could have erected such a mass.

The fabric wall, attached to lofty columns, enclosed a broad area of ground. Even arrows shot with great force could not surpass the summit of the roof in flight.

Inside were beautiful dwellings of many kinds, so that anyone emerging would not have thought that these were movable sails, but rather the walls of a noble palace.

Meanwhile the Northman duke called Alfden submitted himself to Augustus, accompanied by a large crowd, and strove to make his loyalty perpetual.

### Year 808. Indiction 15.

There are certain Slavs called by the name Lini. Against them the younger Charles set out, sent by his father.

The broad Elbe did not hinder his journey; rather, after the Frankish legions had crossed the waters of that river, under favorable auspices he led the aforementioned forces against the enemy,
And brought back victorious standards to his rejoicing father.

## Year 809. Indiction 1

Peace throughout the present year had gladdened

[Col. 0721C] all the frontiers of the empire, but certain grievous things had befallen many lands: for a pestilence more savage than any enemy destroyed every kind of livestock. For when shepherds drove out their herds and flocks, lively, into the green meadows in the morning, scarcely the smallest remnant returned home in the evening, sick, bearing the dreadful signs of the plague in emaciation and approaching death. But the greater number lay across the open fields, breathing out their sweet lives upon the green grass.

Now the pastures stank with the bodies lying there; even the mangers, once emptied, could scarcely be cleansed with much labor. And those who, seeing an animal about to die, chose rather to slaughter it with the sword, immediately revealed the poison congealed throughout its body as it dripped from the wound.

[Col. 0721D] The Noric district is said to have suffered this especially, together with the neighboring regions.

Moreover, at this time the vines became barren. They gave no return for the labor expended upon them; the hope of the eager farmer was frustrated when he saw the vineyards, swelling with no offspring of their own, and the useless tree growing wild in vain. Though the vine-shoot spread out, the leaf-covered branch did not conceal any grapes, and the broad vineyard stood empty of fruit.

Thus, in many parts of the kingdom, Bacchic cups perished in an unusual disaster. Surely, although much time still lay ahead, this most grievous event was already foreshadowing the mourning that would come upon the world when Augustus departed from the earth.

## Year 810. Indiction 2

Pippin, king of Italy, once the illustrious light of the Franks, while leading a joyful life in the splendor of his age, vigorous alike in the bloom of youth and in the beauty of mind, endowed with distinguished virtue and supreme glory, and possessing at that time every prosperity of the deceptive world, ended his life through a bitter illness.

His death was premature and his life delightful; therefore, his funeral left his father, and all the Franks, with excessive groaning and mourning.

## Year 811. Indiction 3

Again, just as the Almighty often teaches those dear to him through scourges, so that he may grant them the joys of eternal life, the venerable power of heavenly judgment doubled all the mourning of the preceding year for Augustus,

[Col. 0722B] taking from his body another son and commanding him to end the turmoil of mortal life.

He had been his father’s namesake, and not in name alone: in the nobility of his mind and the uprightness of his character, and in every kind of virtue, he reflected his father. If he had deserved to enjoy France under such a ruler—

Augustus, the pious, had in this same year entrusted the Italian kingdom to Bernhard; for this son of Pippin had rightly succeeded his father as heir.

## Year 812. Indiction 4

From the distant regions of the earth came a very great embassy sent by the princes of the Greeks. Augustus was asked by them to grant peace; moved by their pious prayers, which he knew would greatly benefit both kingdoms, he immediately and graciously consented.

[Col. 0722C] Then both parties promptly strengthened the treaty between them by swearing to maintain faith and peace.

## Year 813. Indiction 5

By now a grave illness and old age together had taken from Augustus’s wasting body its customary strength. He saw that he could no longer bear the excessive burden of the cares by which so great a commonwealth had to be governed and preserved; instead, in the final declining period of his life, he saw that only the leisure of peaceful repose was desirable, so that he might strive to procure rest and forgiveness for his departing soul.

Therefore, he gathered solemnly from every quarter all the dukes, leading men, and magistrates for a general assembly. With the counsel of all, he handed over to his son Hludowic the entire authority to govern

[Col. 0722D] the empire, designated him as his father’s successor by placing upon him the diadem of the kingdom, and ordered that he himself, now made partner in all his dignity, should likewise be called Augustus.

When all the council received this with sufficiently magnificent approval, they understood in every way that it was useful to the kingdom. Hence Charles’s majesty shone forth increased, and concord was established for future times, since a single head now stood over all, shown to the peoples as one whom they should follow with united mind.

From this arose great fear among foreign peoples. It gave them no hope that Charles would soon die, by whose death the condition and most upright order of the Frankish kingdom might be diminished. Never before had so illustrious a prince left its government as the one who now took it up, whom they would rightly regard as his father’s equal in virtue. There was no doubt that, through arms and with gentle wisdom as his guide, he would rule all the kingdoms that had been subdued.

Thus once the great king and prophet, instructed in heavenly songs by the divine breath as the lyre’s melody sounded, now accustomed his fingers to harps and sounding strings, now his hands to sword-hilts and weapons. After he had subjected countless nations and enemies to his triumphs, mature in merit and in years, while still alive he commanded that his son, his own Hebrew Solomon, should enjoy the honor of the whole kingdom.

So our Charles, who had in turn been accustomed to wage battles, overthrow even demonic rites, strengthen the Catholic faith, and condemn perverse sects, so that hearts everywhere might sound in harmony with heavenly teaching in praise of Christ, left a kingdom greatly enlarged by wars to a prudent son who loved peace; one who would quietly take up the good things acquired through his father’s labor and exercise the teachings of divine worship.

While these things were taking place, you could see joys mingled everywhere with sadness. For although what had been accomplished in due order and with pious reason rightly pleased many, the bitter goads of grief nevertheless troubled everyone inwardly all the more, because the moment was approaching when the death owed by every flesh would snatch the beloved Charles from their eyes. Illness and age together compelled this.

[Col. 0723C] And, as usually happens, whenever some good thing is lost, grief itself then makes its usefulness and value appear more clearly: so then the uprightness of his character, his supreme strength of mind, and Charles’s piety, clinging to the minds of all, had become more fully apparent, when they saw that they were destined to lack such a prince forever.

Grave anxieties gnawed at the hearts of many wise men, who already feared that the affairs of the Franks would fall into a worse state and that many disasters would come after the death of so great a prince.

As a longer day ends, its shadow falls; and the sun, hastening to dip itself in the ocean’s waters, proceeds to its setting and covers its light-giving face with rust-colored pallor, mottled with dark stains, giving signs of the stormy night that follows—although the moon, advancing along the same path, can render the world somewhat bright beneath its full disk—

[Col. 0724B] so then the prudent perceived that storms of war were in store, and rightly mourned the ruin of the Frankish kingdom when Charles should die.

Meanwhile the assembly of the people was dissolved, and the nobles who had been present, returning by a long road to their own homes, already imagined that this would be their last sight of their beloved lord [Note: [Col. 0723C] It is not clear that a hiatus should be removed.]. They gave an inward groan and, with their faces pale and oppressed by sorrow, offered a sign of their grieving hearts.

Many kept their faces composed, while pretending to be cheerful so that the new Augustus would find nothing suspicious in them; yet, although they wished to smile, tears moistened their faces amid false joys that were nevertheless real.

At that time the Aachen palace was not filled, as usual, with the sound of rejoicing; nowhere was a musical voice heard. Each spoke to his companion scarcely even in a sad murmur, silently revealing what he carried in his heart, while grief imposed lamenting silence upon many.

## THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE ANNALS OF THE DEEDS OF CHARLES THE GREAT ENDS; THE FIFTH BEGINS, ON HIS LIFE AND DEATH

[Col. 0723]

[Col. 0723C] Now sing a mournful song, wounded Muses, for this year is worthy of many tears.

Behold: through forty-three preceding years, what but prosperity was said of Charles?

When his annual deeds, marked by varied triumphs, were set down in a joyful style, that pleased us. But now the order of events, and the time, admonish us to commemorate the death of so great a man.

Here the true elegies lament; there is no need to invent anything sad, for the event itself possesses its own emotions. Who, remembering what he was, would not groan and grieve excessively that such glory is now absent from the world?

But since this one thing consoles the faithful—those whose beloved [Note: [Col. 0723D] Rein. and Leibn.: *carus*] ones death has perhaps taken away may confidently believe that, because of their righteous deeds, they are happily participants in the heavenly kingdom—for this reason I gladly sing the merit by which we now rightly believe that he lives with Christ.

Such a great subject is attacked by a barbarous tongue, too bold for the powers of my feeble talent;

[Col. 0724D] but great love, the author of this present poem, does not allow me, ignorant though I am of speech, to remain silent.

For I am always aflame with love for Charles, and I am also a perpetual debtor of service to him. He had caused our people to know the light of faith, when the darkness of unbelief had been cast aside.

How long he fought, how many dangers he endured, with what heavy sweat and vigilant zeal! Almost all the peoples of Europe, participants in so great a work, remember this to the present day.

Indeed, he had gathered all the strength of his kingdom so that he might draw us away from demonic worship. Finally, who could soften savage barbarism by the persuasive address of exhorting doctrine?

[Col. 0725A] For this reason the merciful God worked through Charles what at that time could not otherwise have been accomplished. Employing a twofold method, he persuaded the stony hearts of the Saxons to submit to the Lord: now terrifying them by war, now attracting them with gifts—there magnanimous, here also munificent.

Nor did he cease before all Saxony together, casting away its idols, had become faithful.

What thanks, then, can we all now render him, or what can each person offer according to his own measure? If some small spark of the art of writing illuminates my mind, and if some slight knowledge enlightens me, will it not rightly offer praises of Charles, through whom I deserved to obtain such a good?

Our parents had known not merely the precepts of faith,

[Col. 0725B] but had been utterly ignorant of all letters. Through Charles, the honor of this faith and, together with it, the hope of eternal life have recently been given to us.

Therefore, O God, fountain and source of every kind of good, grant us first to speak worthy praises to you. Grant us, O guide of our spirit, to unfold in him some part of your gift, you who, merciful Christ, piously providing for the salvation of many, had granted that he should become such a man.

For, pitying the condition of our nature after the serpent’s deceit had corrupted it, you had bestowed frequent consolations upon the human race through illustrious men pleasing to you, making the strong govern the weak,

[Col. 0725C] the learned instruct the foolish, so that their light might drive away the darkness of the latter, recalling the wandering and restoring them to the way; so that those standing might raise up the fallen, and the virtue of the pious might be an example and aid to the wretched.

From the beginning of the world you had always given such men, fit to save others. First came the sacred order of the patriarchs, then the lawgiver and the chorus of prophets sent for this purpose.

They also once furnished, among various nations, an example of righteousness worthy of imitation, with you as witness. But who would be surprised that you cared for servants through servants, even if the gift were extraordinary, when you, the Lord of the world, did more—indeed, suffered the greatest things for the least of your servants?

[Col. 0725D] For the unjust, the just; for the guilty, the innocent—you had handed over your soul to its own death. So great was your concern, Redeemer, for our salvation, lest your image should be utterly lost.

Therefore let all created things sing praises to you, and let the underworld, the fields, and the heavens bend the knee. For even when your grace had completed so great a work, it did not cease; without it every human being perishes. Rather, after this, the same care for winning all people was displayed to the nations through the elect.

The sound of the apostolic mouth traveled through the whole earth; words thundered to the furthest regions,

[Col. 0726A] to which the almighty Spirit, sent down from the heavenly citadel, gave fiery tongues.

O how many minds, cleansed of the filth of guilt, he made ardent with love for you! Afterwards, many others like them followed, of the same order and honor of virtue, who by examples and sacred teaching together restored many souls to their heavenly homeland.

Why should I recall how many suffered torture and death for you and thereby won others? Constancy of spirit moved some to believe these things, and visible miracles moved others to believe in you, their giver.

In a thousand ways, O God, your great mercy saves nations through holy and excellent men. Nor do you make kings exempt from this gift,

[Col. 0726B] while through them you correct and teach souls. In our own times, how many people was King Charles, by your gift, the cause of supreme salvation?

He was admirably suited to believe and to regulate morals, and able piously to transform faithless hearts.

[Note: [Col. 0725D] From Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, chapter 2.]

If I should now attempt to disclose his distinguished lineage, I would be compelled to write a catalogue of kings. But this is unnecessary: his lofty rank did not make him distinguished; rather, he himself added distinction to the highest lineage.

Born of the renowned, he shone more renowned still, and he proved stronger than unconquered fathers. It is already well known that common songs celebrate his grandfathers and ancestors with great praises; they sing of Pippins, Charleses, Hludowics, and Theoderics,

[Col. 0726C] and chant of Carlomanns and Hlothars. But how much more he accomplished than all of them, the following account of the present work will tell.

Let me mention one equal to him from so great a stock, whom the Church of Christ proclaims a saint: namely Arnulf, who was once prince of the Franks and afterwards a very distinguished bishop.

Led by love of God, he had despised all the things of the world that delight the eyes and attract the mind, preferring to hand on the divine laws rather than those of the world, and to be God’s servant rather than the people’s lord.

Now he rejoices in heaven, displaying to earth miracles and glorious signs of his lofty merit; from there he protects and cherishes the entire succession of our lords—his own stock.

[Col. 0726D] Therefore, we ask that, among all your descendants, your namesake Arnulf may be your especial care. Make Christ the guiding author of the reigning ruler, for whom the Church has such great need:

the just king, her sole defender amid the many disasters by which she is now being crushed.

From that holy prince, therefore, a noble line has ruled over us to this day. Into it descended the blessing of holy Jacob, which he himself, revealing what was to come, gave to Judah, so that the scepter-bearing branch would not fail from his stock, but a long succession of leaders would remain from it.

Thus, chosen by God, this stock has remained for a long time in the kingdom, and may it long remain; from it no one should wonder that Charles was born as a king strong and full of piety.

As outward virtue and strength adorned his ancestors, so the love of religion adorned him sufficiently; and the greater the worldly glory that came to him, the more humble was his mind before God.

But whatever nature at birth had bestowed upon him for good [Note: [Col. 0727D] Compare Einhard’s *Life of Charles*, chapter 15.], he increased through constant practice, always intent upon steadfastly carrying out affairs and arranging them with firm counsel.

Therefore no one was more successful than he in war, nor more moderate in time of peace. And the flourishing and noble kingdom that he had received, he made twice as broad and better.

[Col. 0727B] Thus he is known to have surpassed his unconquered ancestors, and by this achievement to have been much more distinguished. One man subdued more lands and peoples than the entire succession of earlier kings had conquered.

Earlier rulers reigned between the Rhine and the Loire; to the north the ocean had been their boundary, while the Balearic shores, and the Alps covered with perpetual snow, marked the southern limit. They had already held the eastern Franks, the Alamanni, and the Bavarians; they had also ruled the Frisians and the Thuringians. The kingdom of Charles’s fathers had extended this far.

After his father Pippin’s death, he ruled it with his brother

[Col. 0727C] Carloman, each enjoying his own allotted share. While the latter continually caused him quarrels and disputes, Charles endured much with patience, so that many found it astonishing that no one had ever seen him stirred to anger, even by serious causes.

After Carloman had died when two years had passed, the kingdom was rightfully given to Charles alone.

He enlarged it first by conquering the peoples of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0727D] Compare the same work, chapter 15.] and at the same time subjecting the Basque people. He overcame all the passes of the Pyrenees, until his empire stretched as far as the river Ebro.

Then he subjected all the regions of Italy—who could name them in an exact number? Italy, as is said, extends for more than a thousand miles in length.

To these he added the Saxons, together with the part of Germany that was not inconsiderable,

[Col. 0727D] and subjected them to his empire. This region exceeds Francia by twice as much in breadth and by almost an equal extent in length.

He also conquered both Pannonias, together with countless neighboring cities; the fields of the Liburnians, or those called by the river Hister; and he subjected Dalmatia and Dacia.

He compelled more peoples of the Slavs to pay tribute to him than anyone could count.

The wars by which he achieved these things were already recounted, with the earlier events marked out, by the four books of the annals. Now I shall report his pursuits, character, domestic habits, bodily appearance, and dress.

[Col. 0728A] Whoever knows these things will no longer wonder why everything turned out so favorably for him abroad.

Since it is proper for everyone to know and remember this about a human being, let me briefly remind the reader of it also.

Let every ruler hear this, and everyone who wishes to receive rewards for praiseworthy deeds: the root of outward actions lies within; a man’s mind and character openly produce his deeds.

He who is habitually steadfast and suitably prudent at home often accomplishes honorable deeds abroad. Dominating his vices within himself and strong in reason, he allows no outward things to harm him.

Whether acting or suffering bravely in all things, glory will come to him according to the merits of his mind. But whoever is sluggish in mind and does not correct his character within himself is rightly destined for outward disgrace.

So a kingdom terrifies all external enemies when it preserves peace and justice within itself; but, on the contrary, if crime and discord stain it, it makes eager plunderers rejoice in its ruin.

Therefore, because Charles followed the laws of reason at home, great glory accompanied him abroad.

By becoming accustomed to virtue, he was able to excel and to endure all his dangers through prudence. And because he made peace within through justice, he rescued his kingdom from external disasters.

He himself was instructed in every honorable art [Note: [Col. 0728D] Compare Einhard, the same work, chapter 25, and passim in the following chapters to the end of the book.], and he honored their teachers magnificently.

[Col. 0728C] From a certain old deacon named Peter he first took care to learn grammar.

From Alcuin’s teaching he gained knowledge of the art of rhetoric and of what is called dialectic. This man, also a deacon of high rank and very learned, had come from the English and was Saxon by race.

From him especially Charles studied the whole system and law of the course of the stars [Note: [Col. 0728D] The manuscript reads *Sidereos*; Rein’s emendation should be retained.].

As the most just judge in legal cases, he heard them frequently and brought lawsuits to an end. In speech he was sufficiently sweet, eloquent, and abundant; he was distinguished not only in his native language, but was also accustomed often to speak in Latin, and was not entirely ignorant of Greek.

[Col. 0728D] He understood it better than he was able to express its idioms in his own voice.

He had read the statements of Holy Scripture diligently, as well as the books composed by the holy Fathers. He had often listened with affection to the books which Augustine wrote concerning the blessed citizens of heaven.

He attempted to write, for he used to carry writing tablets with him in small books. He kept them beside his pillow at his royal bed and never allowed them to be absent from him. Amid so many cares and the business of so great a kingdom, the king exercised his mind in these studies.

[Col. 0729A] His keen intelligence shone greatly, and so did the excellent balance of all his impulses. He was never excessively joyful, never overly relaxed, never excessively sad or severe; he was neither indulgent toward human vices nor turbulent with anger.

He punished the guilty with just reasoning. He preferred this to be done through fear rather than death, except when the dreadful wickedness of the deed compelled it.

O what integrity, what steadfast order shone forth in all his character! Strong in adversity and cautious in prosperity, he maintained the path of perpetual moderation.

Only when death took from him his sons Pippin and Charles did he grieve excessively for that reason. He also wept and lamented greatly over the death of Rhuottrudis, who was the eldest of his remaining daughters.

[Col. 0729B] The wealthy kingdoms of the Greeks also mourned her, because they were not worthy to possess such a mistress.

For she had been the bride of Constantine, who ruled the scepter of that ever-noble empire. Illustrious Constantinople, from the stock of our Charles, had hoped to become more noble.

Such were the misfortunes that had befallen the king among the pledges born to him, all of them sufficiently distinguished.

Then steadfastness contended with piety; in Charles neither virtue was slight. The former commanded him to endure all circumstances with dignity, while the latter reminded him of his beloved offspring. The former shone in his magnanimous virtue, but the latter

[Col. 0729C] burned no less, filled with pious love. Piety toward his own overcame him in their deaths and compelled the king to shed abundant tears.

He also wept over the death of his Roman friend, the pontiff Adrian by name. For, as in other matters, so in friendship his excellent character is rightly praised: he admitted friendships cautiously but firmly, and once he had established them, he preserved them through an everlasting bond.

Thus, by his deeds and by his name among his friends, he increased the glory of his kingdom among foreign kings and peoples.

One of these was a man called Hadefonsus, who was king of Asturias and Galicia. When he sent messengers and gifts to Charles, he ordered them to say that he was Charles’s own man.

[Col. 0729D] The kings of the Scots called him their lord and testified in letters sent to him that they were his subjects and servants; their immense affection shines forth in their address.

The prince of the Persians was bound to him by exceptional love; his name was Aaron. Charles’s favor was dear to him above that of all kings and princes of that time. When the Augustuses of the Greeks voluntarily sought it, he deigned to enter into a peace treaty with them.

Therefore Leo, Nicephorus, and Michael frequently arranged to send their envoys to him.

We exceed the boundaries while describing his friends; Charles himself must rather be shown by our style.

He had made himself utterly unacquainted with idleness through frequent hunting and riding.

[Col. 0730A] Scarcely could icy winter deprive him of military habits and martial activities.

Moreover, he was accustomed to practice hunting, an art in which no one was then more skilled. Natural hot springs provided him with exceedingly pleasant baths.

For this reason he chose Aachen as his residence, where a very abundant supply of such water flows. There he remained continually during the final years of his life, making delightful baths more densely adorned with great splendor.

He had his sons, nobles, and the whole company that served as guardians of his body bathe with him. For the spacious convenience of that same bath was able to accommodate more than a hundred men.

[Col. 0730B] His body was suitably strong and large; his gait was firm, and he was vigorous and agile. He was remarkably tall, with a proper proportion—for he was seven of his own feet in height.

The crown of his head was round, his neck thick, and his nose somewhat larger than average. His eyes shone broadly, his face was cheerful, his voice sufficiently clear, and his hair beautifully gray.

He wore his native dress and always rejected foreign clothing, although he himself was handsome.

Only twice at Rome, when the highest bishops earnestly requested it, did he wear a long tunic. On those occasions he also took up a handsome cloak and Roman-style coverings for his feet.

He wore royal dress with all its splendor only when a very sacred day was being celebrated, or whenever envoys arrived bearing messages from distant peoples and rulers.

Then a golden brooch fastened his gold-woven garment; gems of various kinds adorned his feet. He wore a diadem decorated with green emeralds, and his sword glittered with rays of jasper.

[Col. 0730C] On the other days he differed little in dress from the customary attire of the nobles or the people.

Always cheerful in good health, he had reached almost the final years of his life. He preserved his health by taking a moderate diet and consuming only what he felt was wholesome for him.

If, however, he suffered some minor ailment, as happened with advancing age,

[Col. 0730D] he did not admit physicians, since he disliked them, preferring to do everything according to his own judgment.

Among other vices he especially hated that one by which many cups overturn the state of the mind. Hence he drank wine and every other drink sparingly; yet he found it somewhat difficult to abstain from food.

For he could scarcely endure fasting with his body, and sometimes complained that it was harmful to him.

He was accustomed to hold banquets for a large number of people, but only on the principal feast days. Four courses regularly supplied the dinner, apart from what the labor of the hunters brought in.

The roasted meat that they used to serve on long spits was more pleasing to him than any other food.

[Col. 0731A] A reader was never absent while he dined, and at intervals he listened to some entertainment. He regularly had the deeds of the ancients and of pious kings read aloud to him.

His mind, always devoted to great plans, allowed him little sleep; and the constant meditation that revolved around magnificent undertakings made him wakeful amid many cares.

For this reason, it is said that he rose from his bed four times or more during the night, having driven away all sleep.

O how greatly the commonwealth grew through those cares, and how flourishing the empire remained under his preservation! For he foresaw well by what means and in what manner access might be opened into the kingdom by various enemies.

He fortified the Gallic and German shores where the rivers enter the ocean,

[Col. 0731B] and the places where the sea separates Europe from the southern lands and divides the territories with its waters, where it receives swift rivers from the regions of Gaul or from parts of great Italy.

At every harbor and port he established stations and made them altogether inaccessible to enemies.

Thus, while he lived, the Moors did him no harm, nor was there then any fear of the Northmen, except for Centumcellae—for so the Etruscan city is called—which was then ravaged by the Moors, and for the serious damage inflicted upon a small island of the Frisians by the Northmen’s raids.

Woe to you, woe to France, lacking a defender of such a kind! You lie exposed to savage peoples ravaging you everywhere; once fortunate, you are now exceedingly wretched.

For your enemies rejoice in your tears and are continually enriched by your spoils. The thousands of your slain and the captive multitude of your people are greater in number than the sand of the sea.

For when Charles died, all your glory and honor gradually fled from you and perished with him.

Now, however, you rejoice under Arnulf, a ruler worthy of praise, who resembles so great a great-grandfather in character. Magnanimous, merciful, and ready for labor,

[Col. 0731C] he restores the fallen empire through vigilant effort, moves the arms of the Franks with their ancient valor, and calls the idle men back to arms.

But the immense mass that collapsed long ago does not permit itself to be restored suddenly. May he who gave him such abundant virtue grant him life; then he will be for us a great cause of salvation.

As for the things that remain to be said of Charles, Muses, sing them briefly in swift song.

Although he was so renowned for enlarging the kingdom and was intent in spirit upon continuous wars, he nevertheless adorned it with varied works and had created immense glory and beautiful buildings, magnificent to behold.

Among these, the basilica of the Aachen residence, wonderfully built, is rightly praised above all. He took care to make it for the perpetual praise of you, pious Christ, and of your holy mother.

The place where he built the palace is called Ingelheim;

[Col. 0732A] our age has seen none at all equal to it. Whoever undertakes to describe their manifold magnificence will weave far too long a work.

Rome supplied marble columns for them, and beautiful Ravenna gave certain outstanding ones. From so distant a region, France was able, through his power, to bring you this adornment.

Moreover, he constructed a bridge over the waters of the Rhine, providing great convenience to the city of Mainz. There the river is five hundred paces wide, so that you may understand the magnitude of the work.

And, what will amaze you still more, he had immense hills strengthened in a straight line amid the waves. He placed foundations beneath them on which bases could be set, and from these he built a high roadway.

[Col. 0732B] This work, toward the end of his life, was entirely consumed suddenly by devouring fire.

When he wished to repair it and make a stone bridge there, where a wooden one had previously been built, alas, he was prevented by death, and the work remained unfinished; so too it will always remain.

Nevertheless, monuments of his virtue endure forever: mounds standing amid the vast waters. For masses of stone and earth piled up there rise with lofty peaks above the river, and a row of embankments, spaced at equal intervals, measures the broad back of the sea with a graceful line.

He also founded very many temples to be dedicated to the Lord, adorning them at his own expense. What had previously fallen into ruin through neglect or long passage of time, he repaired anew throughout his kingdom.

For he was a devoted lover of holy religion and a follower of the Catholic faith. In his time he extinguished the heresies that arose, as we said earlier in the preceding books.

He entered the church diligently at the appointed hours, pouring out devoted prayers night and day. He arranged all its ministry, together with its vestments and vessels, with lavish adornment.

For as a true worshiper of God, he never wished to place anything before holy service to him.

Though he held an earthly kingdom, he burned much more intensely and eagerly with love for the heavenly one. He took care to purchase it for himself through constant gifts, merciful above all and generous to the needy.

[Col. 0732D] No one, it is said, loved foreigners more than he, and no one received them with equal care. His piety had almost exceeded proper measure in this, if anyone can do too much in such a matter,

since not only was the royal crowd of strangers a burden upon his palace, but it was already a burden upon the whole empire. He himself, pious as he was, compensated for the expense of these things by the joyful contemplation of eternal reward.

Attracted by this reputation, the poor came to him from every region of the world. Yet he did not think it enough to practice the work of free generosity in his own kingdom; through envoys he frequently sent gifts to poor Christians in foreign kingdoms.

[Col. 0733A] Those whom Egypt and the city called by the name of Alexandria held in poverty, he helped with resources. Africa and Carthage experienced his generosity, and Syria found him abundantly liberal.

To Jerusalem, and to the other places that remain sanctified by Christ’s bodily deeds, he frequently sent considerable weights of gold and silver to be distributed to needy believers.

With the gentile kings situated across the sea he established and strengthened friendships for this purpose: that their faithful subjects might receive refreshment from them.

Above the other holy places, however, love of the Roman see especially clung to his mind. Revering holy Peter, who stands as the bearer of the keys of heaven and the first of the apostolic choir,

[Col. 0733B] he often sent the greatest gifts to his church and bestowed countless treasures. Throughout the whole time of his reign, he cared for nothing more and had no greater concern than that the Roman see, supported by his protection, should remain powerful in its ancient nobility.

Yet he himself had reached that place only four times, wishing to fulfill vows and prayers with a devout mind.

His final arrival occurred because the condition of the Church was then disturbed: Pope Leo had been expelled and had suffered torture at the hands of his own citizens.

[Col. 0733C] He determined to restore to the harbor of peaceful tranquility that state which had undergone the supreme dangers of a shipwreck and been harassed by sedition in the city, remaining there for almost the whole winter.

At that time he received the imperial crown there, in the manner that we described earlier in the fourth book.

Yet he accepted it unwillingly, compelled by the pope and by the many prayers of the Roman people. If he had foreseen the bishop’s intention, he would have withdrawn entirely from the Church.

Indeed, he himself had sworn this publicly before many, although that day was very solemn.

You may see why this had displeased him so much: the custom was one that other kings desired.

After this, he lived happily for approximately thirteen years in imperial dignity. During them he corrected the ancient laws, ordering that what had been discordant should be brought into unity.

He also newly added what he judged appropriate—few in number, but very useful—and collected the laws of all the peoples of his kingdom, making several books from them.

He also ordered the poems that recount the wars of ancient kings, barbarian songs, to be written down in letters.

Then, with all the keen powers of his intellect, he began to translate grammar into his own language. This would be a difficult task even for philosophers: to compel an art of this kind into barbarian speech.

Neither the greatest demands of the kingdom nor advancing age then recalled him from such studies.

He was thoroughly familiar with the annual reckoning,

[Col. 0734A] which he examined with a sufficiently vigilant mind. He recorded the risings, courses, and settings of the stars; no point of the zodiac escaped him.

He himself composed names in the language of the Franks for the twelve winds and for the twelve months. Previously, they had called the months by Latin names and partly by names in their own language; but they had known how to express only the names of the four winds in their own speech.

When you see how much he labored in these arts, would you not suppose that scarcely any wars were waged by him? Yet if you count his wars and triumphs, the kingdoms and peoples subjected by arms, you may wonder when he found leisure even for a little reading or for any opportunity to learn.

[Col. 0734B] As I delay bringing the labor of this work to an end, while I tremble to speak of Charles’s death, let it be mournful and sad for us; nevertheless, the order of the narrative requires it, and it is pleasing to us not to conceal it.

Indeed, sweet tears often comfort mourners, and lament itself is accustomed to become a kind of consolation through its own grieving.

His son Hludowic, by his father’s command, became heir and partner of his kingdom—for he had ordered him, after receiving the diadem, to be called Augustus and to govern the empire with him.

Then, himself exhausted by illness and age alike, he set out toward the entrance into another life.

He nevertheless set out from the palace at Aachen to hunt,

when autumn was already midway past.

From there, returning, he betook himself to the aforementioned palace,

[Col. 0734C] intending then to winter in that place.

But as the month of January, so named, came on,

it suddenly afflicted him with sharp fevers.

He abstained from food, since he was accustomed immediately to drive away illnesses in this way,

or at least to bear them more lightly.

But when pain in his side followed, it made it beyond doubt that

the time of his death had arrived.

After he had lain ill for six days, the seventh

proved to be his last in this life.

Having then received the venerable body of Christ,

he deserved to be joined to the citizens of heaven.

He lies buried in the church that he himself founded there;

no one can relate with what grief.

After eight hundred years from the birth of Christ

this was the fourteenth year;

[Col. 0734D] he died on the fifth day before the Kalends

of the month in which King Numa established the Februa.

There had been many portents of his approaching end,

and prodigies appropriate to so great an event.

Finally, an eclipse of the sun and moon occurred frequently

three years in succession beforehand.

For seven days a dark color was seen upon the sun,

staining the face that gives light;

a portico of immense size suddenly collapsed,

diminishing all the beauty of the palace already mentioned;

and the bridge over the Rhine, which he had built in ten years,

flames consumed completely in three hours:

for except what the flowing river carried away from the fire,

not even a small splinter remained.

[Col. 0735A] The old man himself, preparing to wage his final wars

against Godefrid, king of the Danes,

was traveling through our country with his army

and went out to the camp at daybreak.

For then the sun, approaching the upper regions,

was spreading a clear light through the pale sky.

Suddenly, seen by everyone, a fiery apparition of a star

was observed to fall from heaven

and to draw a flaming torch through the air in a long flight,

until it itself fell into the left-hand region.

His horse, upon which he was riding away, startled by this,

struck him heavily in a headlong accident;

finally, the clasp of his royal cloak was broken,

and at the same time the belt of his sword was torn,

while the weapon that he happened to be carrying fell from his hand

and, against his will, was hurled a long distance.

Moreover, a tremor in the palace at Aachen foretold this,

terrifying everyone with unusual movements,

and the palace of the king marked it by the frequent creaking of its ceilings

and by the basilica struck by lightning.

Within it, a shining inscription ran around the circuit,

proclaiming who had built so great a church for the Lord;

for this reason Charles, the prince,

had been commemorated in the sequence of the final verse.

But the letters in which PRINCEPS was written—marvelous to relate—

entirely disappeared of their own accord,

leaving no trace of themselves,

not many months before his death.

Because some power unknown to all had done this,

this omen brought sadness to many.

[Col. 0735C] The world, rightly terrified by these signs,

mourned him, for it was destined to have no equal after him.

Nor among the ancient commanders or kings

did anyone shine forth more illustriously than he in every respect:

the Romans, over many commanders and through many years,

had scarcely subjected the peoples of Italy to themselves;

this one man, in a very short span of time,

conquered and subjected the whole land as its master;

add to this the many peoples of Europe whom he conquered,

whose names the Romans had not known.

Therefore, as you read of the marvelous deeds of Charles,

cease admiring the histories of antiquity.

Neither Decius, nor the Scipios, nor Camillus himself,

nor Cato, nor Caesar was greater than he;

neither Pompey, nor the Fabian clan,

who likewise died for their country,

is preferred to him on merit.

Perhaps their earthly glory was equal to his,

but now the heavenly Charles possesses the summit of honor.

There he is distinguished by the honor of Davidic valor,

together with Constantine and Theodosius;

there he rejoices that he conquered the ancient enemy,

rescuing many from his snares;

there the thousands of spirits saved through him

rejoice with him by your gift, O Christ.

Who could count how many souls he restored to the Lord

when he brought the Saxon peoples to faith?

[Col. 0736B] How many churches now shine where the ancients worshiped shrines,

how many monasteries have been built?

For as many praises are offered in them, and as many vows

the faithful render to you, so many rewards, O Christ, will you give to Charles.

And when the final day of the great judgment comes,

on which you will repay every person what he has deserved,

O how joyful he will be, presenting the talents entrusted to him,

multiplied by great profit!

Then, as the matter itself shows, no one can rightly be nearer than he to the apostolic companies.

For when Peter comes forth attended by the Jewish host that had believed through his teaching,

Paul will lead the nations of the whole world, saved through his preaching—if it is permissible to say so—[Note: [Col. 0735] The codex has *totius*; I added *-que* for metrical reasons. Leibniz thought that perhaps *liceat* should be read.]

Andrew will lead after him the Achaean peoples,

[Col. 0736C] John will bring forth the churches of Asia;

Matthew will bring the Ethiopians, made white through baptism,

and Thomas will lead the flocks of the Indians to the stars.

Then the rejoicing company of the Saxons will follow Charles,

to the glory of everlasting joy.

O would that I might follow, even last, among all those

of our people who will have been saved!

O Christ, if only you would transfer me, a kid, from the left,

so that in your mercy you might join me to the sheep on your right,

where I may sing to you not mortal songs,

but be able to utter everlasting praise! Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 809. Saint Simpert, Abbot of Murbach.

[Col. 0737]

## Historical Notice on Saint Simpert

(From Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis.*)

Sindpert or Simpert, abbot of Murbach and bishop. Gabriel Bucelinus and Charles le Cointe, in the *Annals of the Franks*, remove him from the succession of abbots of Murbach; Mabillon, however, restores him.

Not everything concerning his episcopate has until now been clear. Mabillon says that his see is unknown. The authors of the *Literary History of France*, vol. IV, p. 362, say that he was bishop of Augsburg and died in 809. Eccard, more accurately, in *Frankish Affairs* XXV, 46–47, asserts from various documents that he was bishop of Regensburg and died in 791.

Mabillon published his very brief Encyclical Letter, *Annals*, p. 418, together with another letter of greeting. Bernhard Pez published the regular statutes of the monastery of Murbach in vol. II of the *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, p. 72.

[Col. 0737]
