## The Regular Statutes of Saint Simpert for the Monastery of Murbach

(From Pez, *Treasury of New Anecdotes*, vol. II.)

[Col. 0737A] In the name of the Lord, amen. Let all who shall inspect this present public instrument know that it contains a copy or transcript of the regular statutes and ceremonies written below, promulgated and likewise observed in the time of Saint Simpert, bishop of Augsburg and abbot of the monastery of Murbach. In the year 1500 from the Nativity and Incarnation of the Lord, in the third indiction, on the first day of the month of May, at the eighth hour of that day, or approximately before midday, in the chapter house of the monastery of Murbach, while the most serene prince and lord, Lord Maximilian, King of the Romans, was happily reigning, there personally appeared in the presence of me, the public notary, and of the witnesses written below, specially summoned and requested for this purpose, the reverend, honorable, [Col. 0737B] and religious men, Lord Walther of Wiltsperg, abbot; Leonhard of Reichenstain, dean; and the chapter, or convent, of the church or imperial monastery of Saint Leodegarius at Murbach, directly subject to the Roman Church, of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Basel. They proposed and affirmed it to be true that, in the year and indiction stated above, on the first day of April, because of the evident and urgent needs of the said monastery of Murbach, and also because of the royal summons issued to the aforesaid abbot to attend the diet of the princes of the Holy Empire appointed at Augsburg, with the certain knowledge and express will of the monastery’s ministeriales, they had sent to Augsburg [Col. 0738A] the venerable and distinguished man Brother John Naburg, professor of sacred theology and doctor of decrees, a monk of the aforesaid monastery and provost of the church of the Blessed Virgin at Murbach. For the honor of Saint Simpert and of the abbot, he visited the monastery of Saint Ulrich at Augsburg, of the same order, and, as he himself asserted, was received there with a cheerful expression of humility. During their conversation, the abbot of Saint Ulrich and certain other Fathers, possessing the regular instruction of Saint Simpert—as was fitting—and wishing to enhance the honor due to him, humbly entreated the aforementioned doctor and monk to have the regular institutions observed in Saint Simpert’s time and promulgated by him copied and transferred, and to obtain this from the abbot of Murbach.

[Col. 0738B] Therefore the aforesaid reverend, honorable, and religious men—the lord abbot, dean, and convent of the aforementioned monastery of Murbach—wishing to comply with these pious requests and not fail truth, and desiring, for God’s sake, to propagate the magnificent glory of Saint Simpert’s life and reputation, he who is glorious among his saints, showed, presented, and delivered to me, the undersigned notary, the statutes and ceremonies of Saint Simpert, teaching an unblemished life and the edification of pious ears, written on one old small roll or parchment document, authentic, sound, complete, unharmed, and with no letters erased or decayed. They then earnestly requested me, in the presence of the undersigned witnesses, [Col. 0739A] to copy and reduce to public form for the abbot and convent of Saint Ulrich at Augsburg, where Saint Simpert is known to have been buried, that same roll of regular statutes and ceremonies, so that these authentic copies might be accepted and believed before any persons whatsoever, of whatever status or [Cod., *status sui*, “their own status”] preeminence.

We received that roll or parchment document, written in an ancient script; I saw it and copied and transcribed it word for word, and had it copied, after making the proper collation with the document myself, adding or changing nothing that would alter the substance of the fact or vary its meaning. I then read aloud, clearly and intelligibly, before the attending witnesses, the very parchment or roll containing the regular statutes of Saint Simpert, word for word, and in their presence, so that it contained the text that follows.

Regular decrees of the holy synod celebrated in France by order of Charles the Great, patrician and king of the Romans, disclosed to the brothers of the monastery of Murbach, by word and writing, for their remembrance, through Simpert, abbot of that place and bishop of Augsburg, who personally attended the synod.

For your remembrance, dearest brothers, we have decided to recall in writing those matters which were arranged there in words and chapters, making a kind of recapitulation and seeking in them what was useful according to possibility and necessity. For some things there were put forward according to the authority of the Rule, while others were put forward by usage and custom; and this custom, if it has not been corrupted by some fault, may be retained blamelessly as regular law.

First, it was announced in the first chapter that, when the abbots had returned to their own places, they should reread the Rule, examining it point by point, and fulfill it. We have done this in our examination of the words, according to the measure of our understanding. But this fulfillment is not to be placed within a period of time, as that interpretation was, but throughout the course of our entire life, in two ways: either by fulfilling, with the Lord’s help, our promise; or, if seized by sins we have become transgressors of the holy Rule, by correcting ourselves through regular discipline.

Second, that those who are able should learn the Rule by heart. [Col. 0739D] Here we thought it should be added that, when it is said to be recited from memory, it should be interpreted by the appointed *dictatores*, who remain apart. We have ordered certain men to commit the whole Rule to memory in sequence; they are listed in our catalogue, and their number rises to thirty-six. To others we have assigned ten chapters from the same Rule to learn; they too are known to be listed in the same way, unless age or impaired sight prevents them from learning. At least these men can recite the chapters from memory with the book closed. Those who cannot go through this either in full or in part should penetrate and store in their minds the meaning of what is heard from each section; they should not doubt that they are partners with the others if they prove by their conduct what they have heard. It must also be added that no brother [Col. 0740A] should be left without being occupied at the appointed time in some meditation on divine reading. For example, after the scholars have committed the psalms, canticles, and hymns to memory, the Rule should be entrusted to them after the text of the Rule; meanwhile, they should proceed, while their teachers listen, by reading the history of divine authority and its interpreters, as well as the Conferences of the Fathers and their lives. After they have been adequately trained in these matters, they should turn to the art of letters and to spiritual flowers. Those who have been converted from secular dress and lack knowledge of letters should, after acquiring that knowledge, not cease learning the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, then the penitential psalms, and afterward the remaining psalms, for as long as life and strength permit.

[Col. 0740B] Third, that all should perform the office of Saint Benedict. This chapter should be observed by those who have hitherto lived under the monastic habit using the office of the Roman Church. But we, who from almost our cradles have been taught by our ancestors and have lived in the same arrangement, must supply through correction whatever negligence has omitted from our minds. That is, all the canonical hours, both the nocturnal vigils and the daytime hours, except Compline, should conclude with antiphons. The weekly servers, reading in the refectory, should recite in the church the readings appropriate to each canonical hour and commit them to memory in sequence. Likewise, the readings from the prophets that are to be sung at the nocturnal office during summer should be proclaimed in the choir throughout the three canonical hours—that is, at Nocturns, at the morning assembly, and at Vespers—without interruption. The psalms should be sung in order, without any haste, with the divisions into verses observed. The prayers recited by the priest should be said by that same priest up to the division of the verses, and thereafter the congregation should respond with what follows. Psalm 50 should be said without confusion or precipitous haste, with the choirs alternating. *Kyrie eleison*—“Lord, have mercy”—should be sung together in its proper order while all stand. Those things added to the regular distribution of the psalms from the usage of the Roman Church, and not practiced in certain monasteries, we have judged should still be retained by us until, after consultation with better authorities, they are either abandoned or confirmed as more certainly to be held.

[Col. 0740D] Fourth, that abbots should be common to their monks in eating, drinking, sleeping, and all other matters. In this matter I wish to use the authority of the Rule, which is not prejudiced by the censure of any new constitution. For whether through common food or through individual abstinence, anyone may be sullied by popular rumor; and this is known to have been done in the case of the Savior and his precursor. But just as we have exposed the weaknesses of our bodies in the assembly of the brothers—not so much by yielding to the allurements of the appetite as by attending to the needs of the body—so we wish to arrange our food under the Lord’s moderation, so that it may sustain us for useful things and not harm us for adverse ones.

[Col. 0741A] Fifth, that the brothers should labor in the kitchen, bakery, and other occupations proper to their crafts with their own hands, and wash their clothing. In washing clothes, the ancient custom should be retained: those who can do it themselves should do so; but for those who fail through old age or infirmity, their needs should be met through the care of the superior, with assistance from others. As for footwear and clothing to be sewn, our present arrangement should still be maintained, so that those who can do this themselves should do it; but for those whom the impossibility described above prevents, the superior and chamberlain should provide for their needs, so that they are not forced to seek assistance from others inside or outside. Meanwhile, while these matters are being arranged, fullers, tailors, and shoemakers should be instructed—not externally, as until now, but internally—to do for brothers in need what is required. This provision is to remain in force until the next Kalends of September. In the work of cooking and baking, all should assist in common, both the weekly servers and all the others; our novices and postulants assigned for this purpose should serve as their assistants until, within the period stated above, brothers are selected for this work, who, after the appointed annual periods have passed, will perform it in rotation, assisted, as until now, by the support of all the others.

[Col. 0741B] Sixth, concerning the manner in which vigils are to be observed: as it is contained in that capitulary, it is sufficient for us that the work of the vigils always end with daybreak, unless it should happen that we rise earlier, when the weakness of our bodies must be refreshed by sleep.

Seventh, that everyone abstain from birds at all times, except in cases of illness, although the authority of the Rule does not forbid this but leaves it, as it were, to the discretion of each person whether to eat or abstain. The holy Fathers decreed in the aforementioned synod that, since the choice had been left to us, we should adopt the discipline of the more religious life; and by their command they confirmed that monks should at all times be restrained from such food by the rein of abstinence, except in the necessity stated above.

In the eighth and ninth chapters, in which the washing of feet during Lent and on the Lord’s Supper is described, the matter can easily be observed if the abbot is present. If he is not, the superior who acts in his place should fulfill both his position and his office.

Tenth: that abbots should not frequently travel around the estates [Col. 0741D] except for a reason of necessity, nor entrust them to the brothers to guard. Here, would that the infrequency of our visits did not cause harm. For we never make frequent rounds among the estates because another obstacle tires us through our occupations, since, amid the affairs of the episcopate and the arrangements of the palace, we have no freedom to look after our possessions. But God is witness, who knows the heart, that I remain attached to earthly occupations not willingly but unwillingly; may he sometimes release us from Caesar’s taxes, to which we are subject, so that at times we may more securely perform the things that belong to God. As for the brothers who have been occupied outside in various ministries, when the change is to be made in mid-August, let them return to the monastery from their cells or estates; this cannot be done at all earlier, because of their knowledge of the places over which they preside. Meanwhile, good administrators must be appointed to provide for the aforementioned places in the future.

Eleventh: that apples and lettuces should not be eaten unless another food is being taken with them. This was immediately put into effect.

Twelfth: that no fixed time for bloodletting should be prescribed; it should be permitted only when necessity demands it. Here it should be added that those who undergo bloodletting alone should be restored with Lenten food; but those who have drunk a potion for specified or named illnesses should be restored with the eating of birds. Therefore, the birds that customarily came annually from our estates should be reserved for this purpose; but consideration must be given to how those things which came from our people as assessed tribute [Cod., *exacte*, “exactly”] may be more usefully converted to the brothers’ needs.

Thirteenth: that the washing of feet (*mandatum*) should take place after supper, which we likewise did before.

Fourteenth: what has been said about the number of garments or shoes, and about the distribution of ointment and soap, should continue to be observed as we have hitherto observed it: garments should be provided to those in need, with the old ones returned at once; whatever remains over should be returned to the prior, for the consolation of the poor. Prepared leather should be given to the brothers for a year, as before, until shoemakers are maintained. Then shoes should be provided, as was decreed in the synod. The practice of shaving, which used to take place in mid-Lent, should be postponed to Holy Saturday [Col. 0742C] of Easter.

In the sixteenth and seventeenth chapters nothing needs to be added, because what has been observed by us before will continue to be observed.

In the eighteenth chapter, where a prison is ordered to be made in such a way that a fire can be lit in it, let the one we have had until now suffice until the more necessary buildings that were consumed by fire have been restored.

In the nineteenth chapter, concerning the singing of the Alleluia, let it be omitted in agreement with the Roman Church during Septuagesima, as was defined in that same synod.

In the twentieth chapter, concerning the reception of novices, let it be done as the Rule teaches. Their tonsure and change of clothing should take place after they have confirmed their promise. Concerning priests or scholars who are to be received, we have no command of the synod; therefore let their reception be conducted according to the Rule, insofar as possibility permits, until a clearer decree concerning this is heard.

In the twenty-first chapter the use of the bath is entirely forbidden, except for those whom the necessity of illness compels. Therefore, considering the weakness of the sick, we permit bathing in tubs until the beginning of Lent. Meanwhile, an ample supply of bathing tubs should be made under the direction of the superior and cellarer, in which the brothers may wash individually, not communally, whenever necessity demands, after first receiving a blessing, offering one another assistance without access by outsiders. In this postponement [Col. 0743A] let us not, God forbid, be transgressors of the synod; rather, having made this concession, let us proceed until the necessity has been provided for, so that what is unlawful may be brought about with greater caution.

In the twenty-second chapter it is commanded that the abbot should not dine with guests at the gate; this is something we have never practiced. In the audience room, however, where the abbot is accustomed to read and to converse alternately or together with brothers and guests, we have very rarely eaten with guests. Unless this practice is more certainly forbidden, we wish to retain it. This room is situated at the boundary of the cloister and the monastery gate, so that it can receive brothers for conversation without hindrance from the guests, and guests without the brothers.

In the twenty-third chapter: guests who have permission to enter the refectory should be served suitably; the abbot, however, should be content with the brothers’ food. This will easily be observed, so that both the abbot and the guests may be served suitably. The brothers should also rejoice somewhat at the arrival of brothers and relax the reins of abstinence.

The twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth chapters, which set out the food of the reader and the refreshment of the ministers, were immediately observed.

The final two chapters, concerning the prohibition of kissing women and the prohibition against monks being beaten naked, refer to practices that have never existed among us and, with the Lord’s help, never will. All care should be taken to avoid spiritual fatherhood and motherhood, lest any monk presume upon them for any reason, because in truth [Col. 0743C] they are not beneficial to their souls and are wholly foreign to their purpose. With the chapters that were recently enacted in their synod and recapitulated by us now completed, some matters remain that the monastic school observes in practice, according to whose examples we are to be instructed.

They observe two rules of silence, one nocturnal and the other diurnal. The nocturnal silence extends from the evening conference until the verse of the chapter; the daytime silence extends from the verse of the chapter until the aforementioned evening conference. During the nocturnal silence, permission to speak is entirely forbidden. During the daytime silence, however, when one addresses another, or a junior asks something of an elder, a quiet and humble conversation takes place without any loudness of voice, using very few and reasonable words. No time is allowed for them to stand, sit, or walk together, except for the sake of learning or working together; rather, they should spend all the hours of the day either in reading or in manual labor.

The interval that occurs between the work of God and the hour of refreshment they spend either praying or reading, except when someone must go to attend to a bodily need. Wherever the glory of the Holy Trinity is sounded, whether in the oratory or in any other place, if they are standing, they prostrate themselves almost to the ground until the Holy Trinity has been proclaimed. If they are sitting, they rise from the ground and, by rising and bowing, render glory to the Holy Trinity.

[Col. 0744A] When juniors meet their elders, they humble their bodies by bending the knee and ask for a blessing. When they enter any house where an assembly of brothers ought to be, they kneel and, with their right hand extended humbly, ask for a blessing. In greeting guests they likewise kneel and lower their right hand to the ground.

When it is time for reading, they never dare sit without their reading books; each one, having his own reading-book, commits it to memory [Cod., *suam meis memoris*; corrupt]. Whatever this means, and however such persons may also be made by us, must be ordered by us. The practice of swearing is entirely absent among them, since the evangelical command forbids it to all Christians—how much more to those who, in the Christian name, have also renounced the world.

Those among them who are scholars follow the usage of Latin rather than rustic speech. In such conversation, too, knowledge of the Scriptures is sometimes penetrated more deeply than through reading; the practice of dictation is learned, and the mind is sharpened for learning.

We have discovered these and other similar practices, which do not now come to mind, in the way of life of the aforementioned coenobites. By imperial authority he has decreed that monks throughout all the monasteries of his kingdom should be instructed according to their examples, so that the things performed by authority of the Rule, and those performed by the invention of customs, may be practiced in one uniform manner. Therefore I think it necessary, if it pleases your affection, that, having been warned beforehand about these matters, you should strive in all of them to be instructed, so that, cultivated in good and honorable customs, you may be praiseworthy not only before God but also before human beings [lacuna] may be able to recall the others to humility and thanksgiving. Meanwhile, one or two men should be appointed and sent to each of these monasteries to observe the life and conduct of its members, so that they may make us more certain in all the matters in which we perhaps falter; they may also be examples of good conduct to those whom they visit, and bring back to us, without weeds mixed in, the wheat to be stored in the granaries.

Concerning all these matters individually, the reverend, honorable, and religious men, Lord Walther of Wiltsperg, abbot; Leonard of Reichenstain, dean; and the chapter or convent of the imperial monastery of Murbach [Col. 0744D] requested that one or more public instruments be made for them by me, the undersigned public notary, as many as should be necessary.

These acts were performed in the year, indiction, day, month, and time of the aforementioned Maximilian, King of the Romans, in the place and at the hour stated above, in the presence of the honorable lord and of the discreet men John Ortt, priest and chaplain of Murbach, and Richard Muling and John of Wertheim, lay literate inhabitants of the same place in the diocese of Basel, witnesses specially summoned and requested for the matters stated above.

And I, William of Hohenhem, etc., a married layman, public notary of Constance by sacred imperial authority, because I was present together with the aforementioned witnesses at the presentation, reception, request, copying, and reading aloud of the aforesaid ancient parchment roll or charter of the statutes and regular ceremonies observed in the time of Saint Simpert, as well as at all the other matters stated above, when they were performed and carried out as described, and because I saw and heard each of those things being done, have therefore faithfully written out this present public instrument of the copy, [Col. 0746A] subscribed, published, and reduced it to this public form, and, having been asked and requested, signed it with my customary sign and name as confirmation and testimony of all and each of the matters. Nevertheless, so that the truth might shine forth more clearly and full faith be given, the reverend and ever-venerable Lord Walther, the aforementioned abbot of Murbach, caused and ordered this present public instrument of the copy to be authenticated by the attachment of his seal.

[Col. 0745]

## The Encyclical Letter of Saint Simpert

(From Mabillon, *Analecta*, p. 418.)

[Col. 0745B] To the most reverend noble mother of a household, illustrious lady: Sindbert, called by the gift of God bishop and abbot of the monastery of Murbach, sends eternal salvation in the Lord.

Furthermore, let your honey-sweet Charity know that your brother, so-and-so by name, has departed from this light [Col. 0746B] to Christ, as we believe. For this reason we earnestly beseech your goodness to act for his soul with psalms, Masses, and vigils, as you are commanded (sic) to do, as your great goodness has been accustomed to do. We wish you good health.

[Col. 0745]

## The Same Author’s Brief Note to a Bishop

(Mabillon, same work.)

[Col. 0745B] To the most reverend lord bishop, illustrious lord: Sindbert, [Col. 0745C] called by the grace of God bishop and abbot of the monastery [Col. 0746B] of Murbach, together with the brothers, sends eternal salvation in Christ [Col. 0746C] Jesus our Lord, etc., as above.

## In the Year of the Lord 809. Saint Ludger, Bishop of Mimigardeford.

[Col. 0745]

## Historical Notice on Saint Ludger

(From Mabillon, *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century.)

[Col. 0745C] 1. Liudger or Ludger, also called Luidger or Luidiger, the first bishop of Mimigernaford, now Münster, of the Church among the Westphalians or western [Col. 0745D] Saxons, who are neighbors of the Frisians and Ripuarian Franks, has been celebrated by many writers. Altfrid was the first, as I believe, to undertake writing something about the life of Saint Father Liudger. Altfrid succeeded Liudger after Gerfrid and ceased to live in 849. He wrote “so that such venerable examples of his might benefit many for their edification,” considering it wrong “that the virtues of so great a man should remain hidden.” These words of his preface sufficiently indicate that no one before him had accomplished this. Altfrid’s work, contained in two books, was first published in the Bollandist volume for March, together with learned commentaries. An anonymous monk of Werden likewise treated the subject again in two books, occasionally adding matters that differ somewhat from Altfrid’s account. Christoph Brower recovered the writing of this author from the Fulda manuscripts; Brower believed that Othelgrim, Liudger’s companion, was its author. In fact, the author of this Life wrote after the year 864, as is clear from Book II, chapter 26. A third Life, also consisting of two little books and compiled from the two earlier ones, was published by Surius in the first edition of his work; for the third editors of the Surian collection substituted Brower’s version in its place. The fourth [Col. 0746D] is in verse. It was composed by the monks of Werden in the form of a litany, at the command of Abbot Bernard, around the year 1140, and was published in part in the Bollandist volume for March. Brower adds another Life composed by the monk Uffing at the beginning of the tenth century; perhaps this is none other than the metrical eulogy of Liudger likewise published by the Bollandists, who also testify that they had read another work by a more recent author. It seemed worthwhile to present here the first and second of these Lives, both because each has an author almost contemporary with Liudger and because Brower’s version contains certain things not found in Altfrid’s. The composer of the Werden litany says that the first writers of Liudger’s Life were “Othelgrim, his disciple; Altfrid, bishop of Münster; and Uffing, a monk of Werden.” The second Life appears to attribute the work to Othelgrim as its principal author, although it was published somewhat later than Othelgrim’s lifetime would permit.

2. Besides these authors, quite a few others discuss him: Dithmar, bishop of Merseburg, in his *Chronicle*; John of Leiden in the *Belgian Chronicle*; John Beka [Col. 0747A] in the bishops of Utrecht; Cincinnius in a separate little book; and other more recent writers, besides John Trithemius, Wion, and others among our own authors.

3. Various miracles immediately after Liudger’s death declared his holiness. Over his tomb, placed outside the basilica at Werden, his brother Hildegrim, bishop of Halberstadt, erected an oratory, which Hildebold, archbishop of Cologne, dedicated in honor of Saint Stephen, according to the testimony of Walafrid Strabo. The following verses were inscribed in the church of the monastery called Rura:

This temple is celebrated as dedicated in honor of Stephen,

together with James, the brother of our Lord.

Through the prayers of these men, received by the mercy of Christ,

may we attain the rich gifts of the supreme Good.

Hildigrim built it; Hadabald, archbishop, [fragment]

He sanctified it: a sure honor remains for both. The people of Werden began to celebrate his feast day around the middle of the ninth century, as did the inhabitants of the surrounding region, [Col. 0747B] as is clear from Book II, chapters 8 and 9, of the Second Life. Finally, in the time of Adalwig, abbot of Werden, around the year of the Lord 1075, the body of Saint Liudger was transferred from the crypt of the oratory of Saint Stephen into the larger basilica of the Werden monastery. There it rests behind the high altar of the choir in a precious shrine, raised upon two magnificent marble columns, as the Reverend Father Gregory, prior of Werden, attested to me in a letter. He also adds that the most illustrious Christoph Bernhard, bishop of Münster, recently obtained with difficulty from the people of Werden two small portions of the sacred body—namely, two bones from the spine and one from a finger.

Liudger is commemorated by the Martyrologies, the Roman, Benedictine, and nearly all the other more recent ones. The Saxon Chronicle, in a manuscript, records the following about him: “In the year 809 Saint Liuder departed to the heavenly realms; together with his brother Hildegrim, bishop of Halberstadt, he imposed the yoke of Christ upon the savage Saxon people.” Thus he should rightly be called the apostle of the Saxons, as should Saints Willehad and Anskar. [Col. 0747C] In a certain brief chronicle of the monastery of Utrecht, Liudger is called “the chaplain of Charlemagne.”

### 4.

Whether Liudger was a monk is questioned, after Albert Crantz, by Brower and subsequently by the Bollandist associates. Crantz does not prove that he was a monk, both because Liudger did not abstain from eating meat and because he laid aside the monastic habit. Brower inclines to the view that he was a monk. The Bollandists say that the holy man was rightly honored by the Benedictines even if he had not worn the monastic habit—which in fact he did wear—“since he so loved and adorned their order, and lived as a monk for two and a half years among monks in their principal monastery.”

Before all these writers, “a certain man,” as Paulus Langius, a disciple of Johannes Trithemius, says in the Chronicle of Zeitz, “who recently compiled an epitome from the deeds of the bishops of the Church of Münster, endeavors at the beginning of his little work, by empty sophistries, to show that the holy Liudger, the first bishop of that Church, was not a monk of our order. But,” he says, “he desires in vain to deny what is demonstrably established.” Nevertheless, the reason Paulus gives—that “in that age the prelates of Churches were commonly chosen from monasteries”—does not sufficiently prove the point.

Altfrid settles the controversy in Book I, no. 27, of the later Life, writing as follows: “Because he had not made a promise to observe the monastic rule, he ceased to wear the cowl; nevertheless, he continued to wear next to his flesh until the end of his life the garment of haircloth, which could more easily be concealed. At certain times he did not refuse to eat meat.” The people of Werden report nearly the same thing in their rhythmic Litany:

> After a prudent council had been held with his sons,  
> they permitted him to live among them,  
> to take the cowl, but not to promise  
> its regular observance.

I think the matter stood as follows. Liudger “received the tonsure in the monastery at Utrecht,” where I have shown, in the Life of Saint Gregory, abbot of Utrecht, Part II of the third century, that monks of our order, or at least canons observing our rule, were then present. Later he was educated at York under Alcuin as his teacher; afterward he was “all the more worthy and acceptable to Father Gregory and the others, the more distinguished he was in monastic learning.” Finally he went to Monte Cassino, where he remained for two and a half years under the abbot Theodemar, his kinsman. I think he received the monastic garments there; but afterward, when he became a bishop, he laid aside the cowl and sometimes ate meat, since he had not made the solemn profession of the rule, while nevertheless retaining the hairshirt, which at that time was almost perpetually worn by our monks.

### 5.

Three matters must be observed in this connection. First, monks who were promoted to the episcopate retained their monastic garments, and therefore also the cowl. On this subject there is the final canon of the Roman council under Pope Hadrian II, or of the Eighth Synod, which forbids “monks appointed to the episcopate to lay aside the monastic habit.” We also read in the Life of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, that Pope Eugene III always slept “with the cowl.”

Second, it is worth noting that these same monks who became bishops also abstained from meat, as they had done in the monastery. This is relevant to what Pardulus, bishop of Laon, a former monk of Saint-Denis, wrote to Hincmar, bishop of Reims. He forbids a man recovering from illness “to abstain from bacon or quadrupeds until his health has been restored; and then let him return to the dry, wretched, and more austere monastic foods.”

Finally, observe that some men in those times assumed monastic garments and retained them for a long period both inside and outside the monastery, without making a solemn profession of vows. A later example is provided for us by Wadislaus, son of Casimir, duke of Evinac, who remained for several years as a lay brother in the monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon, “without having made any regular promise,” as Pope Clement V testifies in a letter written to him, preserved in volume VII of the *Spicilegium*. Nevertheless, the Synod of Aachen in 817 decreed in chapter 34 that a novice “should neither be tonsured nor change his former clothing before he promises obedience.” For it was the belief of the ancients, even before Liudger’s time, that receiving the habit made a man liable to the vows. I would therefore certainly believe that Liudger bound himself by vows, were I not restrained by the weighty authority of the writer Altfrid.

### 6.

Liudger built three monasteries. One was for clerics “serving Christ under the canonical rule,” according to Altfrid, Book I, no. 20. It was situated at Mimigardeford, a city that in the eleventh century was called *Monasterium* from that monastery, and hence the bishop was called the bishop of Münster. The second was at Werden, on the river Ruhr, among the Westphalians. The third was near Helmstedt in the duchy of Brunswick. The latter two were monasteries of monks of the Order of Saint Benedict.

### 7.

The first of these appears to have been founded at Werden, or Werdin, taking its name also from the river Ruhr flowing past it. It was situated in the forest of Wideburg, adjoining the diocese of Cologne. Liudger cleared the place divinely indicated to him and selected for himself the place granted to our monks, as a retreat during life and a burial place after death.

He dedicated a church there in honor of the Savior and of blessed Mary. From Pope Hadrian he had obtained relics of both—namely, some of the blood of the Lord Christ and some of the milk of the Mother of God. We determine the year in which the monastery’s foundations were laid both from the Surian Life, Book I, chapter 18, where Liudger is said to have learned that God had destined the place for this purpose and to have gone there “about nine years before the episcopate assigned to him,” thus in the year 793; and from the letters and documents of the monastery, which the Bollandist associates carefully investigated.

The first donation recorded as having been made “to the priest Liudger for the relics of the holy Savior and Saint Mary” is that of a certain Amulric, “executed in the seventeenth year of the reign of our most religious lord, King Charles, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April,” [Col. 0749A] that is, in the year 795. In the following year another donation is found, that of Theganbald to Liudger the abbot, along with several others bearing the same inscription. This shows that some monks were already present there and that Liudger presided over them.

The monastery was later called that of the holy Savior and Saint Liudger, because of the renown of the holy man buried there. Hence the writers of the Surian Life, in its prologue, are also called, after Altfrid, “the brothers dwelling in the monastery of the holy Savior and Saint Liudger.” Jacobus Gerardus Vossius incorrectly interpreted these words in his book *On Latin Historians* as referring to the monastery of the holy Savior at Utrecht. This monastery still exists under the Bursfeld Congregation.

### 8.

The monastery at Helmstedt in the duchy of Brunswick also continues to exist. It was named after its founder Saint Liudger and is commonly called the Monastery of Saint Ludger. Liudger built it “on his paternal inheritance,” as a kind of place of refuge where he could periodically refresh himself when exhausted by the labor of preaching.

Dithmar, bishop of Merseburg, mentions this monastery in Book IV of his *Chronicle*. In Heinrich Meibomius, following the *Annals* of Widukind, there is a diploma of the emperor Otto the Great by which he grants certain tithes to the monks of that place at the request of Bernard, bishop of Halberstadt. The abbey lies in his diocese, midway along the road between Brunswick and Magdeburg, in the suburb of Helmstedt.

### 9.

The place where the episcopal city of Münster is now situated was formerly called Mimigerneford, Mimigarneford, and Mimigarnevord. There Charlemagne established an episcopal see, whose first prefect was Liudger. This occurred in the year 802, as the Bollandist associates deduce from various documents in which Liudger is called abbot down to the thirty-third year of Charlemagne, which fell in the year 801.

The holy man founded a church in that place, and “a monastery of those serving Christ under the canonical rule,” as Altfrid writes in Book I, no. 20. From that monastery the place acquired its name and renown in the tenth century.

I think that from the beginning there was a mixed congregation of canons and monks. It is most likely that the clerics wore “canonical dress” and “lived under a monastic rule,” as Adam reports was the case at Bremen. I further infer that monks were present from the beginning, either alone or at least mixed with the canons, not only from Liudger’s favorable disposition toward our order, but also from Altfrid’s testimony. In Book II, chapter 12, he calls Hildrad “our monk and deacon,” that is, a deacon of the Church of Mimigardeford.

In his prologue, Altfrid likewise praises Thiatbald, Liudger’s “priest,” whom the Browerian author sufficiently suggests was a monk of the monastery at Werden in Book II, chapter 27.

The people of Werden sing the following in their rhythmic Litany concerning the condition of these three monasteries:

> He also founded three places together,  
> equal in number to the places and peoples.  
> Werden and Helmstedt he founded for monks  
> from his own property or inheritance,  
> and the episcopal seat called Münster.  
> And he is said to have founded other places as well:
>
> He also founded ancient little cloisters,  
> here for men who had entered religious life, there for women.

### 10.

From what has been said thus far, the sequence of Liudger’s life can be arranged as follows. Around the year 758, he was entrusted to Gregory, abbot of Utrecht, and tonsured by him. Later he crossed to England to attend Alcuin’s school, after the death of Egbert, archbishop of York, which occurred in 766. He then became a deacon and returned to Utrecht.

Afterward, around the year 772, he again returned to England; after two years he came back to Abbot Gregory, who died around the year 776. In that same year Albric was ordained bishop as Gregory’s successor. Liudger was a priest and preached the word of God among the Frisians for approximately seven years.

In 784, when the storm of Witikind’s persecution against the Christians was raging, Liudger went to Rome. After obtaining relics from Pope Hadrian, he withdrew to Monte Cassino, where he remained for two and a half years.

In 787 Charlemagne appointed him to convert the Frisians. He sought a suitable place for founding a monastery and laid its foundations at Werden around the year 795. He became bishop in 802 and died on the seventh day before the Kalends of April in the year 809 according to the more recent reckoning—that is, at the end of the preceding year according to the older reckoning.

### 11.

As for his writings, he composed a book on the lives of his venerable teachers, namely Gregory and Albric. In that book, “he wrote in elegant language the beginnings of Saint Boniface’s arrival and ordination, which had been omitted in another little work on the Life of Boniface,” as Altfrid says in Book II, no. 6.

Apart from that little book, it is uncertain whether he left anything else in writing. For the letter concerning the canonization, as it is called, of Saint Suidbert, and other writings of the same kind attributed to Liudger, have been proved spurious in the *Eulogy of Saint Suidbert*, Part I of the third century.

[Note: We searched in vain for this letter in Surius, *Acts of the Saints*, volume I, March, page 81, and elsewhere, where Fabricius indicates that it exists, *Bibliotheca Latina medii et infimi aevi*, volume IV, page 277. It has therefore remained unknown and undiscovered by us. EDIT.]

In any case, Liudger, “although he did not know all languages, nevertheless did not lack knowledge of the Germanic and Latin languages—to name no others—that is, of the barbarian and Roman tongues,” as we read in the Surian Life.

[Col. 0749]

# LIFE OF SAINT GREGORY, ABBOT AND RECTOR OF THE CHURCH OF UTRECHT ON THE RHINE, BY SAINT LIUDGER, BISHOP OF MIMIGARDEFORD, A DISCIPLE OF GREGORY HIMSELF

*(From Mabillon, in the same place.)*

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0749D]

### 1.

That the Life of Saint Gregory, abbot and administrator of the Church of Utrecht on the Rhine, was written by Saint Liudger, bishop of Mimigardeford and Gregory’s disciple, is taught above all by Bishop Altfrid in the Acts of Saint Liudger:

> “Saint Liudger,” he says, “was by no means uneducated in the sacred Scriptures, as is clearly proved in the book he composed on the lives of his venerable teachers, namely Gregory and Albric. He also himself wrote in elegant language the beginnings of Saint Boniface’s arrival and ordination, which had been omitted in another little work”—namely, that of Saint Willibald.

Saint Liudger carries all this out in the book that follows. Christoph Brower published it in 1619 and supplied it with notes; several fragments of the book had already been published by Nicolaus Serarius in Book IV of his *History of Mainz*. [Col. 0751A] Johannes de Beka and Willem Heda summarize Gregory’s deeds in their *History of Utrecht*, and Johannes Gerbrandus does so in Book VI of the *Chronicle of the Netherlands*.

### 2.

A considerable number of arguments persuade us that Gregory was a monk and the Father, or abbot, of monks, although the Life that follows contains no mention of a monastic profession. As a young man, uneducated and unskilled in letters, he attached himself to Saint Boniface and appears to have been instructed in monastic matters, either in the company of Boniface and his fellow monks, or in the monastery of Ohrdruf, which Saint Boniface is said to have built first, or in that of Fritzlar.

For boys were educated in the monasteries founded by Boniface, as is clear from Letter 17, in which he orders that after the death of Wigbert, abbot of Fritzlar, “Wigbert the priest and Megingoz the deacon shall be teachers of the children.”

Certainly Gregory was abbot and Father of the monks in the Church of Utrecht, whom he himself instructed and formed. Thus the author of the book on the Life of Saint Liudger, in Brower, chapter 6, says that Gregory “educated Liudger with paternal care in the monastery of the monks.”

The following passage of Altfrid in the same Life also pertains to this:

> “They”—that is, Liudger’s parents—“commended him to the venerable man Gregory, disciple and successor of Saint Boniface the martyr, for the Lord to nurture. Gregory willingly received him, and, having recognized the boy’s intelligence, diligently instructed him. Thus Liudger grew, advancing in the fear of the Lord; and, having laid aside secular clothing”—these words deserve notice—“he devoted himself entirely in the monastery at Utrecht to the study of spiritual learning. Hence he was all the more worthy and acceptable to Father Gregory and the others, the more distinguished he was in monastic learning.”

He had not yet acquired these monastic studies at Monte Cassino while Gregory was alive, but in the monastery at Utrecht.

Nor do the ancient charters of the Frankish princes in favor of the same Church, reported by Johannes de Beka and Willem Heda, allow us to doubt that monks first existed in the Church of Utrecht, founded by Saint Willibrord. Although these documents have been interpolated in some places, they should certainly not be regarded as suspect in those passages where the monks of the Church of Utrecht are mentioned. For monks have given way to canons there for many centuries, and it cannot be suspected that the charters were fabricated by the canons in favor of the monks.

Nevertheless, Brower doubts “whether something similar existed in the Church of Utrecht to what is read of Saint Anskar, bishop of Bremen, who established a congregation of holy men at Bremen. As Adam recorded, they used canonical dress but lived according to a monastic rule, in a kind of mixed and intermediate arrangement.”

But Adam of Bremen nowhere calls the clerics of Bremen monks, as the Utrecht men are called, but “canons.” Certainly Johannes a Leidis, in Book IV, chapter 4, of the *Chronicle of the Netherlands*, when reporting a diploma of Charlemagne for the Church of Utrecht, explicitly uses both names: monks and canons.

### 3.

Gregory, moreover, was never a bishop or archbishop, contrary to the opinion of the Utrecht writers Johannes de Beka and Willem Heda; he was only a priest and abbot. For Saint Liudger, in the later Life, no. 20, calls Gregory, when he was seized by his final illness, “my abbot and teacher.”

Altfrid and other writers agree in the Acts of Saint Liudger. “For,” says Altfrid, “the same Gregory had not been ordained to the episcopal rank, but remained in the rank of the priesthood.”

And the Anonymous author in Brower writes:

> “They commended Liudger to a certain Gregory, a man of great merits, who, both disciple and successor of Saint Boniface the martyr, presided over the see of Utrecht as a priest in place of the bishop.”

Relevant here is a letter of Lullus, bishop of Mainz, addressed to Gregory, “honored with the twofold dignity of the priesthood and the abbacy.” In it Lullus, although “younger in age,” gives excellent admonitions to Gregory, whom he calls his “dear colleague and devout teacher.” Among these admonitions is the following:

> “In this temporal authority and earthly dominion which, by God’s authorization, you now exercise, always remember the Lord’s saying: ‘My kingdom is not of this world,’” and so forth.

[Note: See this letter among the works of Lullus of Mainz, *Patrologia Latina*, volume XCVI, column 821.]

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

### 1.

The precepts of the sacred Scriptures admonish us to love the Lord with our whole heart, and to love our neighbor as ourselves; and they teach us to regard as our neighbors in truth those who devote themselves more to spiritual than to carnal things and do not cease to prepare themselves by pious works for the promises made to them until the final day. They are not vainly exalted by carnal descent, but are made fruitful and advance through spiritual rebirth.

Although this charity is to be shown to all members of the household of the Catholic faith, which works through love, it is especially to be shown to our holy Fathers and superiors, as the holy Apostle exhorts us, saying:

> “I ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you, preside over you in the Lord, and admonish you; hold them in the greatest love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves” (1 Thess. 5).

What is this recognition by which we are commanded to know our superiors more than others, except that while they are alive we should sincerely render them the honor and obedience due to them, and that their pious and beneficial examples, after their death, should not merely never depart from our memory, but that we should also continually repeat and spread them in our speech for the edification of others?

Thus may what the same Apostle elsewhere exhorts us to do concerning those spiritual Fathers of ours truly be accomplished:

> “Considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith” (Heb. 13).

In this way, while in our present mortality we retain their footsteps and examples both in mind and in action, we may deserve, according to the saying of the Gospel (Matt. 25), to enter with them into the joy of our Lord in the future immortality.

When, by Christ’s freely given grace, we have entered into everlasting happiness, no one will take it from us forever. For we were created for this at the beginning by the pious purpose of the Creator, and after the fall of the first man into death we were recalled to the same destiny by the merciful visitation of our Redeemer. We shall reach it on the day of final necessity, if in the days of this mortal life we follow the exhortations of our spiritual Fathers and God himself is always for us the greatest cause of rejoicing.

Therefore, since, as I have said, the testimonies of Holy Scripture clearly teach that honor is rightly to be paid to spiritual Fathers and that after the Lord’s commands nothing is to be preferred to their orders, I shall now briefly explain why I have prefaced this little introduction. With Christ’s grace granting it and the merits of the man himself assisting, I begin to write a few things about his innumerable benefits.

## THE LIFE BEGINS

### 2.

This account concerns my lord Gregory, my abbot and teacher from childhood. He was born of a noble Frankish family [Note: They say that he was from Trier. His father was Alberic, mentioned below in no. 3. In the will of Adela, abbess of Pfalzel, reported above under the year 734 (*Patrologia Latina*, volume LXXXVII), Alberic is called Adela’s son; Adela, in turn, is called the daughter of King Dagobert, specifically of the Austrasian king, as Henschenius interprets it. Certainly in no. 3 Addula is called the mother of Albric and grandmother of Gregory. Furthermore, Willem Heda, in his *History of Utrecht*, says that Gregory’s mother was Saint Wastrada, buried in the church at Susteren in the diocese of Liège; her feast is celebrated on the twelfth day before the Kalends of August. Gregory’s brothers are mentioned below in no. 13.]

He adorned and surpassed the nobility of the world by the nobility of his character and by the evidence of his wisdom. This spiritual nobility and prudence he acquired from Saint Boniface the martyr, archbishop, and his teacher. In the days of the most noble Frankish prince, King Charles, that illustrious star came from Britain and the English people to Francia. Under Carloman and Pippin, the most glorious sons of that same King Charles, he spread the rays of his virtue and preaching like a shining sun in holiness. While still alive in the body, he refreshed nearly all the kingdoms with the richest nourishment of his teaching and improved them both in faith and in life.

After his passage from this world through holy martyrdom, he caused those same Frankish kingdoms, through the chosen seeds of his disciples, to bear fruit and advance as an example of the Lord’s seed, continuing to do so to this day. Among them blessed Gregory was found to be a pillar of the Church of God. During the reign of the most religious King Pippin, he succeeded his teacher and was sent as a preacher to the people of the Frisians. In this way blessed Gregory began to attach himself to that teacher, the martyr Boniface, and to enter his discipleship.

### 3.

When the chosen martyr of God, Boniface, had completed thirteen years of preaching in Frisia [Note: This number cannot stand unless the years are counted from Saint Boniface’s first departure for Frisia. For during his second journey he stayed in Frisia for only three years before going to Thuringia, as is clear from his Acts.], during which, as a poor evangelist and almost solitary man, he had carried out his holy ministry in three places on the southern side of Lake Almere [Note: That is, the gulf of the German Sea between the present-day Batavians and Frisians, into which the eastern channel of the Rhine flows together with the IJssel near the city of Kampen. The inhabitants call this lake the Southern Sea].

The names of those places were as follows. The first was called Wyrda [Note: Werda, now the island of Kaiserswerth, on the Rhine midway between Cologne and Wesel, adorned with the relics of Saint Suidbert, must be distinguished from the town of Vorda, likewise situated on the Rhine in the territory of the Batavians], on the bank of the Rhine, where he lived for seven years. The second was called Attingohem, beside the river Vecht [Note: The river Vecht flows into Lake Flevo not far from the town of Vollenhove; that lake separates the Frisians from the Batavians], where he lived for three years. There he first began to have a disciple named Gembert. The third place was called Felisa, which was nearer to the peoples and pagans; he likewise remained there for three years.

After these thirteen years, then, when, warned by God, he had begun to travel through the eastern regions of the Franks, to the Hessians and eastern Thuringians, for the purpose of winning peoples for God, he arrived at Pfalzel [Note: In the aforementioned will, Adela is said to have received the place called Pfalzel from Pippin, the mayor of the palace, by an exchange, and there to have founded a monastery in honor of the Virgin Mary and the apostles Peter and Paul. In it she gathered “a community of nuns living under the discipline and rule of Saint Benedict.” The place, about three thousand paces north of the city, now enlarged by fortifications, passed to a college of canons], a monastery of virgins near the city of Trier on the bank of the Moselle. At that time it was governed by an abbess named Addula, a highly religious woman who feared God.

When she saw the pilgrim and needy athlete of God, she joyfully received him into her hospitality, fulfilling the Lord’s admonition: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. 25). When that holy traveler Boniface had celebrated the mysteries of the Mass according to his usual custom—for he was accustomed to do so almost every day—he and the handmaid of God, the abbess Addula, sat down to table with her household.

At that holy meal they began to seek something more than food: the consolation of sacred Scripture, by which the faith of those listening might be kindled and their hope and love renewed toward God, who desires all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth. A reader was then sought, and the chosen boy Gregory was found. At that time he had recently returned from school and the court, still wearing secular clothing, and was about fourteen or fifteen years old. By God’s prompting he came to his grandmother—that is, to Addula, the abbess who feared God and was the mother of his father Albric, mentioned above.

A book was given to him. After receiving the blessing, he began to read, and, according to his age, read through it well. The teacher, recognizing the boy’s perceptive mind and good character, began to praise him moderately after he had finished reading, saying:

> “You read well, my son, if you understand what you read.”

But he was still wise as a little child and spoke as a little child, and professed that he knew what he was reading.

> “Tell me,” he said, “how do you understand what you read?”

The boy repeated his reading from the beginning, wishing to read it as before. The holy teacher delayed him for a little and said:

> “Not in this way, my son, do I ask you to tell me your reading. Explain to me what you read according to the character of your own language and the natural speech of your parents.”

Confronted in this way, he confessed that he could not do so. Saint Boniface then said:

> “Do you want me to tell you, my son?”

“Yes,” he replied.

Then blessed Boniface said:

> “Repeat your reading from the beginning and read it distinctly.”

When he did so, the holy teacher began, and in a clear voice started to preach to the mother and to the entire household.

### 4.

The source from which that preaching proceeded is made clear by the conversion of Gregory, the gifted and perceptive boy. It did not flow from human eloquence, which often deceives for a time, but from the grace of the Holy Spirit, according to the promise of the Gospel, flowing from the teacher’s heart like a river of living water (John 7).

It penetrated the prudent and teachable heart of the boy Gregory with such power and speed that, after a single exhortation and sermon by the teacher whom he had until then not known, he forgot both his parents and his homeland. At the very moment when the holy teacher had finished his sermon, unwilling to be separated from him any longer, he went to his grandmother, the venerable abbess Addula, and said that he wished to travel with the man and enter his discipleship in order to learn the divine books.

But she, bound by natural affection, immediately rejected him and absolutely refused to allow this, since she did not know the man or where he was going. Yet, as it is written, “Many waters cannot quench love” (Song 8). The boy Gregory remained firm in his purpose and said to his grandmother Addula:

> “If you do not wish to give me a horse so that I can ride with him, I will undoubtedly go with him on foot.”

Thus they disputed with one another for a long time over the unknown journey. At last the love of the chosen boy Gregory prevailed, and, as was fitting, spiritual affection conquered natural love.

When the handmaid of God Addula, who was a prudent woman, saw that the boy’s mind was immovable, she gave him servants and horses and allowed him to go [Note: This occurred in the year of Christ 722, when Boniface, leaving Willibrord in Frisia, turned to the Hessians and Thuringians. Gregory had already passed his fourteenth year and therefore was born in the year 708] with the holy teacher in the work which they completed together up to his holy martyrdom.

You understand, pious and prudent reader, whom the chosen boy Gregory followed in this action, when, without consulting his parents or any of his relatives, and despite the resistance of the grandmother who was present, he was so suddenly transformed. It seems to me that the same spirit was then at work in this boy that inflamed the apostles of Christ and the stewards of God’s mysteries to leave their nets and their father at the Lord’s single call and follow the Redeemer.

Therefore, scorning his parents and homeland and leaving behind everything that could flatter the mind of an adolescent in a carnal way, blessed Gregory, according to the saying of the Psalmist (Ps. 16), followed the difficult paths for the sake of the words of God’s lips.

For it was difficult and very harsh that someone who had been raised in his father’s house amid great wealth, amusements, and luxuries should follow one poor and wandering man, not knowing where he was going; and that he should obey him so completely that, like a deaf man, he would not listen to any other people, whether powerful men of the world or his own parents, provided only that he obeyed that man’s commands in everything.

Who could estimate how great was the authority already shining in the future martyr Boniface, which moved the boy’s heart to such a sudden change? Or what ardor of love inflamed the young man’s mind to obey an unknown teacher, so that, suddenly forgetting himself, he followed Christ’s poor man, destitute of every worldly possession?

This was not accomplished by love of gold or silver, nor by desire for estates or proud boasting, none of which played any part. It was accomplished by the supreme craftsman, the one and same Spirit of God, who works all things in everyone, distributing to each as he wills.

### 5.

Then the chosen men of God, traveling along the desired road, came to Thuringia. There, both for their greater good and to prove the steadfastness and endurance of their minds, they found the people in such extreme poverty that scarcely anyone there had enough to live on unless he gathered a little from far away to sustain his want for a short time.

For the entire region, situated on the frontier of rebellious pagans, had at that time been burned and devastated by an enemy army. Yet this poverty could in no way frighten the ministers of Christ or cause them to withdraw from announcing to the people the whole counsel of God.

Following the apostolic example (1 Cor. 4), they began to labor with their own hands for the things necessary both for themselves and for those who were with them. They remained firmly with that people in its trials and, preaching throughout the surrounding region, invited them to the heavenly kingdoms.

Persevering in these efforts, they had, according to the pattern of the primitive Church, “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). And every day God increased the number of those who were saved and joined to them.

### 6.

Then the fame of the holy teacher and future martyr Boniface began to spread throughout all the eastern kingdoms of the Franks. The chosen young man Gregory also began to advance in his discipleship, in age and wisdom, and became so dear to his teacher that Boniface loved him as an only son and already had him as a faithful helper in every good work.

This great progress of God’s chosen men was not initiated through wealth and worldly pleasures, nor through security and the prosperity of mortal life, but amid hunger, nakedness, and many hardships.

In all these circumstances they were compelled to live by the work of their hands; and sometimes, because they feared death from the persecution of the nearby pagans, they had to flee together with the people into a city. There they lived for many days on scanty bread and amid hardship, until the citizens, having gathered a crowd, drove the pagans away again with greater force.

Since this struggle took place in countless villages between pagans and Christians, a large part of those regions had consequently been reduced to desolation on both sides.

In such a fierce and dangerous contest in those days, amid the great struggle and confusion of the warring peoples, the chosen shepherd Boniface was never able to cease guarding and instructing his flock. Rather, the more frequently and violently he saw the wolves’ rage threatening, the more steadfast and ready he became to lay down his life for his sheep.

Likewise his faithful disciple Gregory, an indefatigable helper in the work of God, remained with his teacher in guarding and educating Christ’s flock, having become a second shepherd.

### 7

These things continued in this way until, through the grace of Christ, the Christian hand triumphed and full peace was restored to the churches of God. They grew and advanced more and more in the Lord’s work, as can be seen even now by those who consider those regions.

But what shall we wretched, sluggish, and inert men say amid the peace of the Church of God? We who, always seeking our own advantages rather than the gains of the flock, scarcely ever utter even one bark of the smallest word in guarding the sheep against the fury of wolves; who, as I have said, are sluggish and drowsy in guarding the flock when the Church is at peace, but excessively energetic and watchful in pursuing carnal profits.

Those, however, of whom we speak, amid such great turmoil and the struggles of war, not only remained with pure hearts in the innermost and chaste guardianship of themselves, but also, in the profit of the flock and the instruction of their disciples, were expanded by such a blessing of God and multiplied through divine assistance and their own vigilance. [Col. 0757B]

### 8

Then the foremost and more prudent men of the Franks, who were able to know and understand God’s chosen martyr Boniface, together with his disciples, the venerable Gregory and his companions, in the great power of their works and the strength of their perseverance, began day by day to offer them more diligently what was theirs, and did not conceal from the elder king of the Franks, Charles, their praise of such blessedness and concord.

The king himself also began to wish to see the man of God, and ordered him to come to him. When he arrived, however, the king did not immediately receive him at the outset with the honor due to him, but delayed him for an appropriate reason: there were certain false teachers and flatterers who tried to obscure and obstruct the reputation of the holy man and his disciples before the king. [Col. 0757C]

> **Note:** Nevertheless, that Charles favored Boniface and admitted him into his presence is established by a letter of Charles himself, which is number 32 among the Bonifacian letters, addressed to bishops, dukes, counts, vicars, household officials, and other nobles of the Frankish kingdom, beginning as follows: “You should know how the apostolic man, Bishop Boniface, our Father in Christ, came to us and represented to us that we ought to receive him under our protection or defense,” and so forth. This, however, must also be attributed to the commendatory letters of Pope Gregory to Charles. [Col. 0758D]

Nevertheless, from that day the love and honor accorded to the man of God and his disciples increased among all who desired to know and investigate inwardly their faith and manner of life; and, in accordance with the Gospel’s saying, “Wisdom is justified by her children” (Luke 7:35).

God’s chosen men returned again to their own work and, remaining without hesitation in what they had begun, continued in Thuringia and Hesse, where at that time their teaching was especially necessary because of the proximity of the pagans and the uneducated populace. There they began to accept from those who offered them, for the love of God and the salvation of their souls, modest estates and territories; to build churches in them; and in this work also, as in their preaching, to make great progress with God’s blessing.

Among these places were one in Thuringia called Erpesford, and another in Hesse called Frideshlar, together with several others which God’s chosen men founded and cultivated through divine worship. Then the estates grew in wealth, the number of disciples increased, and their work advanced in power.

The blessed young man Gregory also grew with his master in every excellence of work and in the beauty of divine wisdom, according to the model of his master, from whom he had learned. Thus, in all these matters, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying (Psalm 83), he who gave God’s chosen ones the law in the power of their works also gave a blessing in the multiplication and advancement of their disciples. And so they went from strength to strength, progressing and increasing each day in every good work.

### 9

Meanwhile, while these things were being carried out by God’s chosen man Boniface and his disciples, the religious sons Carlmannus and Pippin succeeded their father Charles in the kingdom, their father having paid the debt owed by all flesh and departed from this world.

Then, because through Christ’s grace the pious sons who succeeded their father in the kingdom had been granted greater relief from wars on every side than their father had enjoyed, they began, with God’s inspiration, to seek more earnestly and improve the religious observances of their kingdom. Blessed Boniface, the future martyr, and his disciples began to hear of this; they began to approach the palace more frequently than before, to speak with the kings, and to preach the people of God within the palace itself, according to the grace given them by God.

They came into such favor with the kings mentioned above and with the entire Frankish people that all, with one voice, declared and agreed that blessed Boniface was most worthy of the episcopate and of every honor—except for those false teachers and flatterers whom I mentioned earlier. [Col. 0758B]

> **Note:** Perhaps Clement and Aldebert, the worst of heretics, are meant; they are discussed in the Acts of Saint Boniface, unless the author also refers below to bishops. Or perhaps Virgilius is intended, whom Boniface accused before Zacharias of having usurped an episcopate, as appears from Book II of Othlo, chapter 9; and Clement claimed to be a bishop, in the same work, chapter 4. The Roman council mentioned there, and the council of Soissons in which Aldebert and Clement were condemned in the year 744, are relevant here. [Col. 0758D]

These men had at times even plotted to kill him, but the Lord his protector did not allow him to fall into their malevolent hands until he had announced, in accordance with the Psalmist’s saying (Psalm 70), God’s arm and power to the generation that was to come.

They alone, therefore, began to contradict and slander him as much as they could, asserting that he was not worthy of the episcopate because he was a foreigner. At that time laymen of sounder judgment than the clergy were so clearly aware that God’s wisdom and grace were in this man that the more those utterly wicked men—I will not call them bishops, since that name was undeservedly given to them—tried to disparage him, the more he was loved by everyone and raised up in praise, until they came to a dispute before the kings and before the entire senate of the Frankish people.

But why should I speak of that dispute which they then held against one another: those utterly wicked men, whom I do not wish to name, on one side; and Saint Boniface on the other, with his disciples Gregory and his companions? The adversaries departed from there confounded and refuted by the entire senate and by the kings themselves, while Saint Boniface, the future martyr, reached the point at which, without anyone’s opposition and by the unanimous voice of all, he was chosen for the most exalted rank of the episcopate, and the kings entrusted to him the metropolitan Church of Mainz to oversee and govern. [Col. 0759A]

> **Note:** We have shown in the Life of Saint Boniface, in Book II of Othlo, chapter 7, that this occurred in the year 745 or the following year. [Col. 0759D]

From that day, how brightly his wisdom shone throughout the entire Frankish kingdom, and how many synods he later established with the religious kings for the correction of the people, should not be related only in this little work, since he shone like the sun in the temple of God and by his preaching and examples dispelled all the clouds of unbelief and heretical perversity. For all these matters are fully and clearly revealed in the little book written about his passion.

### 10

In all these matters he was greatly assisted by his chosen disciples, who, after their master, became the most illustrious preachers and pillars of the Church of God. Each of them illumined his own city and region by his example, like Lucifer rising in the morning.

Through his teaching, blessed Gregory illumined Traiectum [Utrecht], an ancient city, and the famous settlement Dorstad, [Col. 0759B]

> **Note:** It is now a town situated on the bank of the Rhine, at the place where the Lecca flows out of the old Rhine, here called Lagbeki. For *Beech* or *Bach* means “river” in the Germanic languages and can be prefixed to *Lecca* or *Legga*, as Browerus correctly observes. [Col. 0759D]

together with that part of Frisia which at that time was reckoned under the name of Christianity. He continued as far as the western bank of the river called Lagbeki, where the boundary lay between the Christian Frisians and the pagans, throughout all the days of King Pippin.

Lullus inhabited Mainz, the metropolitan city, together with the greater part of the Christian Frisians who belonged to the parish of that city.

Megingodus, a venerable father and shepherd of the flock entrusted to him, seasoned and guarded the city of Würzburg with its surrounding territories in his portion with the salt of his wisdom and teaching.

Willibaldus, God’s chosen bishop, improved and guarded in a similar way the bishopric called Hehstedi, [Col. 0759C]

> **Note:** Others call it Eichstätt. Read the Acts of Saint Willibald and of the other men named here in their proper places. [Col. 0759D]

in the part of Bavaria nearest to us; and likewise in the Nordgau, like a pious father, he raised it from its foundations, improved it, and guarded it.

Nor did the brother of the aforementioned Willibaldus, named Winnibaldus, a priest greatly loved by my master, blessed Gregory, fail to illumine his own place and region in holiness and prosperity. After his death, he showed even more through miracles what he had done while alive.

But the venerable abbot Sturmi, one of that company of God’s chosen men, made such progress in his wilderness after the martyrdom of his holy master that the forest of Bocauna bears witness to it. Previously it had been entirely uncultivated and deserted; now, from east to west and from north to south, it is filled with churches of God and chosen shoots of monks. [Col. 0759D]

Sturmi the abbot also merited from God and from his holy master this privilege above his fellow disciples: that he should be worthy to possess and establish the very place which the holy master had chosen for the burial of his body, [Col. 0760A] and to receive there his holy martyred body; and that he should advance and glorify that place so greatly that, before his departure from this world, he became father and teacher to approximately four hundred monks, apart from the *pulsantes* [Col. 0760B]

> **Note:** That is, novices. See Haeften, Book IV, treatise 2, inquiry 1, on the Rule of Saint Benedict. [Col. 0759D] Nevertheless, Adelard, abbot of Corbie, calls the canonical clerics of the monastery *pulsantes* in Book I, chapter 3, of the *Statuta*. [Col. 0760D]

and other lesser persons, whose number in that monastery, situated beside the river Fulda, was very large.

Two of those chosen men of God, Wigbertus and Burghardus, departed from the world before their master. But they are not without the palm of their election, since they were worthy to precede their master into the heavenly kingdoms; and in their own regions they are regarded and honored as God’s saints by all who were able to know their life and virtue with God.

You see, thoughtful and diligent reader, how many gifts of grace were present in one man, [Col. 0760B] and what that poor man, who had once been solitary in the regions of Frisia, accomplished during the period of his manifestation for the fruitfulness of the Church of God.

Yet he could not accomplish these things by himself. Rather, in accordance with the Apostle, “the grace of God with him” accomplished and established all these things (1 Corinthians 15:10). Since, therefore, I have strayed a little from the intended course of my narrative for the sake of giving a common account of the disciples of the holy master Boniface, I shall now return to the point from which I digressed.

### 11

Then blessed Boniface, the future martyr, with the consent of the religious kings and of the entire senate of the Frankish people, was sent to Rome to be ordained to the episcopal rank by Pope Gregory III. [Col. 0760C]

> **Note:** There are two errors here. Boniface was ordained bishop not by Gregory III but by his predecessor, who had the same name; nor did Boniface first receive his name at his episcopal ordination. Both points are established by the Acts of Saint Boniface. Certainly the author also relates some other events out of order, such as the refutation of the pseudo-priests above, in section 9, which took place long after Boniface’s ordination. [Col. 0760D]

There, together with the episcopal blessing and rank, the apostolic pontiff gave him the name already known and spread among everyone—Boniface—because of the eloquence of his tongue and the grace of his lips granted him by God. Previously he had been known by the name Winfrid.

Thus the holy man, adorned both with rank and with a name, prostrated himself before all the clergy and household of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and before Pope Gregory himself. He prayed that, for God’s sake and for the love of Saint Peter, all the clergy who were present would immediately bend their knees for him in that very church with humble devotion, and that all would unanimously pray to the Lord and invite blessed Peter to be the intercessor and helper of his prayer, so that he might be worthy to bring his days to a good and pleasing conclusion before God.

All of them, inspired by God, unanimously bowed with the greatest devotion before the relics of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and fulfilled his request, pouring forth before God the sacred prayer of both shepherd and flock. How powerful that prayer was before almighty God, in harmony with his holy merits, is attested by his accomplished martyrdom in the days of his old age, when his bodily weakness was then extreme and, placed in decrepit age, he could no longer remain alive in this world for long.

Behold how the wise architect and chosen pontiff of God, Boniface, built his house not upon the shifting sand of human counsel and proud obstinacy, but upon the most secure rock of divine counsel and apostolic humility. Therefore, when the rivers of human adversity and turmoil came, and the winds of diabolical temptation and cunning blew and struck his house, they could not move it, because, according to the Lord’s saying, it had been founded upon the firm rock, and that rock was Christ.

Our intercessor and most certain patron before God now considered and reflected upon the danger and misery in which human weakness has been placed. He did not place his trust in himself, as the proud of the opposing party do; rather, he turned to apostolic humility and the sons of God, and established his hope upon the abundance of divine mercy and the Church of God’s devout supplication.

For so too the apostles of Christ, and their successors and coheirs in the kingdom of God, aided without interruption by the prayer of the Church of God in all their labor and tribulation, were able to accomplish everything that the Lord had commanded them.
