Therefore, you prelates and preachers of the people of God, adorned in this world with the same honor and equal rank, look upon this, understand it, and take the example of a righteous man, so that when you have been called by God and chosen by the Church of God, and approach the episcopal rank and holy governance without being blinded by gifts, you may shape yourselves according to his model and bear fruit that will remain unto eternal life. [Col. 0761C]

### 12

On that journey also, while the holy martyr Boniface was raised at Rome, as has been said above, to the sacred rank, blessed Gregory, my teacher, remained the tireless companion of his chosen master, entering, departing, and traveling at his command, as he had always been accustomed to do in every good work.

Not only did he fulfill on that journey the merit of humility and obedience, as is fitting for younger men to submit to their elders and superiors in all things; but, with the Lord’s generosity, he also acquired there several volumes of the Holy Scriptures and brought them home, at no small cost of labor, for his own advancement and that of his disciples.

With his master’s consent he also brought back with him two boys of the English people for his discipleship, namely Marchelmus [Col. 0761D]

> **Note:** This is Marchelmus, the companion and disciple of Saint Suidbert, to whom spurious writings about Saint Suidbert are attributed under the name Marcellinus. [Col. 0761]

and Marcuvinus. Of the elder, Marchelmus, a most religious and holy man, I shall say something more fully in its proper place, as God grants.

Then the blessed company—the holy master and his chosen disciples—commended to God and his saints both by their own merits and by the intercession of all the clergy and household of Saint Peter, returned home, growing and advancing from that day in every good work. Teaching and instructing in the way of God, in which they themselves walked, they seasoned not only the people and nobles of the Franks but also the religious kings themselves with no small measure of the salt of divine wisdom.

Thus, with the agreement and unanimity of the kings and of the entire people throughout the Frankish kingdom, the losses of the devil began each day to increase, while the gains of the Church of God increased; heretical perversities ceased to appear; the Catholic faith shone brightly in all things; and pure and undefiled religion became resplendent far and wide.

### 13

But since up to this point I have attempted, in a general and mixed account, to commend in writing for the benefit of my hearers and the example of those to come a few things, drawn from many, concerning the holy conduct of the holy master and martyr Boniface and, at other times, of blessed Gregory, his chosen disciple, I shall henceforth not neglect to disclose more particularly a few of blessed Gregory’s deeds and virtues, together with the teachings of his saving preaching, by which I was permitted to be instructed, unworthy though I am, and which I was privileged to witness from childhood.

First, I think it worthy of mention that he carried out an evangelical work of great significance: through marvelous charity and an example beneficial to posterity, he fulfilled the remission and forgiveness of enemies.

He had brothers who were noble and distinguished, born of his father, and other brothers born of his mother who were younger in age and strength according to the dignity of this world; they were necessarily subject to the service of their elders.

It happened that some of the elder brothers, honored by the king, were sent to distant regions of Gaul. Their younger brothers were obliged to follow them there and remain with them.

After some time had passed, when they wished to visit their parents and homeland, and having received permission from their superiors, two brothers born of the same mother as my teacher Gregory began to travel and set out on the road they had chosen, so that they might reach Francia, that is, their native land.

As they traveled, however, more confident than was proper in youthful boldness, they were surrounded in a certain forest by the cruel hands of robbers and killed. This grievous news could not immediately be concealed from their masters, who in those days possessed considerable authority in those places.

When they heard it, they sent their agents in every direction to seek out and arrest those robbers and executioners. They were found, seized, bound, [Col. 0762D] and immediately brought in.

Although they were considered deserving of every punishment and of death by the most cruel execution, their captors nevertheless, out of reverence and love for their brother Lord Gregory, thought that they might offer him some consolation after the death of his loved ones if they brought the murderers and killers into his jurisdiction and presence, so that, as a satisfaction and mitigation of his grief, he might order them to be killed in whatever manner he wished.

And so they did: they ordered two of them to be brought before him, thinking only in a carnal way, according to the foolish wisdom of this world, which does not know how mercifully to spare enemies.

But Gregory, being a spiritual man, taught by the Lord Jesus Christ and his holy Gospel, in which he had learned the command, “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:44–45), received them spiritually and gratefully. He considered both his own eternal salvation and the absolution of the brothers’ killers.

As an example beneficial to posterity, he ordered them to be released, bathed, clothed in clean garments, and refreshed with food. Then, when they had been brought before him, he commanded them, saying:

“Go in peace; and take care that you do not commit such evil again, lest something worse happen to you.”

He ordered them to be escorted away in peace, admonishing them with paternal charity to guard themselves carefully from their other relatives.

What shall we insignificant and weak men say in response to this? We are unable to endure even the injury of the smallest word without retaliation whenever the opportunity is available. When we learn such things about the perfect, let us consider where our weakness lies prostrate; for it has never conceived anything of this kind even in thought. It is more fitting to weep than to say anything.

Perhaps our tears will obtain pardon for us from the merciful Judge, God, since we cannot place our confidence in our merits.

### 14

Nor must this matter be concealed in silence: I learned it from the account of the venerable man Marchelmus, whom I mentioned above. After the martyrdom of the holy master, through whose grace in Christ and merit of holiness all the neighboring nations were illumined, blessed Gregory also received authority from Stephen, the bishop of the apostolic see, and from the illustrious and religious King Pippin to sow the word of God in Frisia.

There the first holy Willibrord, called an archbishop, began the foundations of the Christian faith in the conversion of that people, together with his disciples.

Then, when he had grown old in God’s work, had established the bishopric at the place called Traiectum, also known as Wiltaburg, and had departed from this light to the Lord, the same archbishop and martyr, Saint Boniface, succeeded him. I myself saw him with my own eyes: white-haired and decrepit with age, yet full of virtues and merits of life.

At that time blessed Gregory, my teacher, had been nurtured from early youth in his discipleship, as I mentioned above. He succeeded him as the pious heir, pastor, and preacher of that people of the Frisians, ordained by the Lord and by the aforementioned rulers of the Church of God. [Col. 0763C]

> **Note:** He was not, however, ordained bishop, as is clear both from the Acts of Saint Boniface and from the preliminary observations to this Life. [Col. 0763D]

With the same charity and firmness of faith as his predecessors—namely Saint Willibrord, archbishop and confessor, and Boniface, martyr and archbishop—he illumined the people with generous and honey-sweet instruction, together with his chorepiscopus and assistant Alubertus, [Col. 0763D]

> **Note:** You will read more about Alubertus, Gregory’s chorepiscopus in the pastoral care entrusted to him at Traiectum, in the Acts of Saint Liudger below. [Col. 0764D]

who came from Britain and the English people and was distinguished by great merits of life. With the same goodwill, according to his strength, he diligently strove to acquire for the Lord the gains of souls.

### 15

No one who wishes to weigh the merit of that chosen man’s life and investigate the most precious treasure of his wisdom doubts that blessed Gregory was enriched by God with this manifold blessing in his disciples.

Therefore it also seems worthy of remembrance how, by living a common life together with his disciples, he educated and loved them as a father educates his children, and how he was joined to each one by so strong a bond of charity that he not only proclaimed from his mouth, for the edification of his hearers, that holy and illustrious apostolic testimony concerning the calling and election of all nations, which is known to have been spoken by the blessed apostle Peter—“In every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10:35)—but also demonstrated through work and truth that all should imitate it.

His disciples were not gathered from any one nation, but assembled from the flowers of all the neighboring peoples. They were illumined by such familiarity, gentleness, and spiritual joy that it became clearer than daylight that they had been born and united from one spiritual father and from the mother of all, charity.

Some of them were of noble Frankish stock; some of the religious people of the English; some of the new planting of God begun in our own days among the Frisians and Saxons; others of the Bavarians and Suebi, or of whatever nation and people God had sent them from. I am the least of them, a small and weak pupil.

To all these men, gathered from every direction as if into one sheepfold, the pious father and shepherd Gregory provided and bestowed, with equal devotion, both the spiritual nourishment of divine teachings and words and bodily food. Inspired by God, he burned with such love and care for his disciples that scarcely a day passed when, sitting down early in the morning with paternal concern, he did not offer each person who came to him the cup of life according to that person’s request and water him with the word of God.

### 16

Many of his disciples were also so noble and endowed with such ability and knowledge of God that they were called to, and attained, the citadel of the episcopate. [Col. 0764D]

> **Note:** Altfrið also attests this in the Life of Saint Liudger, section 8; Liudger himself must be counted among them.

Many others, though equally instructed and disciplined and not raised to so high a rank, were nevertheless not insignificant in merit but outstanding in knowledge and love of God.

It seems worthwhile and worthy that, in whatever way I can, I should not conceal the testimony of each of them or the signs of their charity, but relate them in their proper places.

For the present, however, I shall attempt to set forth a few things from the many concerning blessed Gregory, with which I had begun, for the advancement of my hearers; for I fear being guilty of sin if, concerning things known to me and so beneficial, I do not begin to relate at least some small part.

### 17

That venerable man was, in accordance with the saying of Wisdom, one who did not pursue gold or place his hope in treasures of money. Therefore his goods were established in God, and the Church of the saints proclaims his almsgiving.

He certainly knew what was written, and knew it through work and truth, not through empty speech: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). For this reason he feared it and guarded against it in all things as though it were a monstrous precipice and pit of hell.

Just as those greedy for money and avaricious men, who hold their souls for sale, fear betraying and losing their earthly profits, so that holy man feared lest, by hiding and preserving such things, he should lose heavenly ones.

Therefore, whenever any gold or silver came into his possession, he immediately took care to spend it and distribute it to the poor, so that, as an evangelical man, he might obey the Gospel’s command and store up treasures for himself in heaven, “where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal” (Matthew 6:20).

And because he placed all his hope so firmly and readily in heavenly things, nothing that seemed pleasurable in the earthly and perishable world could harm or ensnare him.

O venerable and chosen man, gentle and devout, always intent upon heavenly things and little concerned with the perishable and earthly—something he showed both in his clothing and in his conduct! Superstition concerning clothing and food found no place in him, nor boasting or detraction. He was always content with the same simple clothing and food as the others. From this purity of tongue and life it became evident outwardly how fully his heart was inwardly filled with love of purity.

Through his simple use of clothing and food, he showed his hearers by example what he taught in words from the commandments of God and his saints. For he had read what the blessed apostle Peter admonished: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Peter 3:3); and from his fellow apostle Paul he had learned that “the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).

What should I say about his drinking? He exercised such moderation in it that scarcely ever, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying, did he use “a little wine” (1 Timothy 5:23) unless it was mixed with water.

He fulfilled this apostolic saying not only in himself but also constantly and forcefully admonished all those subject to him never to fall into the evil of drunkenness, but to avoid and shun it as though it were a pit of hell.

In his preaching, concerning the destruction of every vice and the building up of virtues, he frequently used that prophetic saying: “I have appointed you to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and to plant” (Jeremiah 1:10). He wished all his hearers to understand by this saying that the beauty of virtues and the edifice of good works never rise unless the stain and impurity of vices are destroyed.

He also very frequently used, at the conclusion of his preaching, that glorious apostolic testimony, worthy of all praise, to arouse love of God and neighbor and desire for the heavenly kingdom: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9).

The devout preacher knew that, through these two testimonies—the prophetic and the apostolic—much was imparted to attentive hearers through the hidden gift of the Holy Spirit, who had filled both the prophet and the apostle. For this reason he used this oracle and exhortation to virtue so diligently in his heavenly preaching. [Col. 0766A]

### 18

Since above, through one testimony concerning his conduct, many marks of good works have been displayed—namely, how religiously the man of God Gregory fulfilled, according to the Lord’s prayer, the command concerning forgiveness—I would also like to relate how he behaved in his daily life toward all his detractors, who sometimes disparaged him, provoked by their own vices.

He did not shrink from or hate them as detractors, but always loved and approached them as friends and helpers. In accordance with the Psalmist’s saying (Psalm 37), he behaved kindly toward them as though he were deaf and did not hear them, and as though he were mute and did not open his mouth, refusing them nothing that he ought to offer friends.

From where could this have come to him, except through the gift of heavenly grace and the purity of his extraordinary mind—that he was able to become as forgetful of injuries as a little child, yet so tenacious of virtues?

The Lord’s arrow of speech not only touched the ears of his body but truly penetrated and illumined the ears of his heart. In the Gospel, when he called a little child to himself, he admonished his still inexperienced apostles, and with them the whole human race, concerning how they ought to enter the way of the kingdom of heaven, saying: “Amen, I say to you, unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3).

He practiced this continually, not only once, with his familiars and with strangers alike, except where the strictness of discipline and correction among his subjects required otherwise.

Because this man was so humble and patient that, for divine love, he was both willing and able to endure with equanimity things so contemptible and unworthy of his person, something occurred which was known to almost everyone who knew him in his days: nearly all who refused to show such a great man the honor due to him were struck by divine vengeance and brought to knowledge of themselves, though compelled and unwilling.

Thus it was openly made clear to those who wished to understand that he was strongly protected inwardly under divine guardianship, although at times before the eyes of proud men he appeared to endure unworthy insults.

Whoever pays attention to this and imitates it will gain no small benefit for entering the kingdom of heaven, since all who went before along that same road suffered such things, in accordance with the saying and example of the apostles, who went away from the presence of the council rejoicing because they had been flogged, saying that “through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts 5:41; cf. Acts 14:22).

19. But because the work of almsgiving has been ordained by the Lord and our Redeemer among the greatest virtues, and because all the sacred Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments praise and glorify this saving work, a few things should be brought forward concerning the generous giving of alms by Blessed Gregory, as a memorial for posterity and an example for imitation. For that man flourished in many other virtues, but he was always especially devoted to the sacred purification achieved through almsgiving, to such an extent that he never wished to keep for himself any gold or silver beyond what the Church’s necessary ministries required. [Col. 0767A] He was also considered generous and open-handed with his other possessions, showing the same kindness, and was always helpful and compassionate toward Christ’s poor. From them he wished to reserve nothing for himself except his daily food and simple clothing, placing all his hope rather in the dreadful examination of judgment than in the present accumulation of the world’s treasures and riches.

Therefore he could so readily give away everything he had for the love of Christ, from whose mouth and example he had learned to do precisely these things: “Give as alms what remains for you; and behold, everything will be clean for you” (Luke XI). He considered that the holy Fathers of the Old Testament, endowed by God with the same faith and charity and hoping for the same eternal reward, had always been solicitous for the fruitful works of almsgiving. Hence in the Psalm the holy Prophet set devotion to this work as a testimony of blessedness, saying: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him” (Psalm XL). Another prophet also sings and says laudably of this same holy work: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus III). The Lord himself, for this work, raises up and exalts his saints on the dreadful day with his grace and everlasting blessing, saying: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world; for I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you clothed me,” and so forth (Matthew XXV).

By understanding and penetrating such things from both Testaments, in which he was most learned, Blessed Gregory turned the law into deeds. He was always a doer of God’s law, not a forgetful hearer. [Col. 0767C] Come, soldiers of Christ: listen, understand, and take up the exceedingly upright and noble examples of this Father, so that, while you still live in the body and behold and love these things, God’s grace may increase in you also, granting remedies for our wounds, just as the adornments of such great virtues increased in him.

20. As my blessed abbot and teacher Gregory advanced through such achievements and merits of life, continually growing toward what was better, and reached nearly seventy years of age, beloved by God as well as by all people, the day arrived on which the Lord wished to raise his soldier, through further improvement, to higher things and to bestow upon him the rewards of recompense owed to his merits and fruitful works.

Accordingly, he was afflicted by a bodily illness in his left side, which physicians call paralysis. As this illness increased and grew heavier day by day, God, according to the testimony of Scripture, scourged his son during this pilgrimage (Hebrews XII), the one whom he was soon to receive into the homeland of the heavenly dwellings. For he was seized by that illness three years before his death.

His weakness, however, was such that at first he could scarcely walk, or be led by the hand for the benefit of himself [Col. 0768A] and his subjects, or speak about matters pertaining to edification. Yet he did not forget to do this. As he had always been accustomed to do, he did not cease to hand on to his hearers books of divine law and exhortations concerning eternal salvation. Indeed, during the same illness he gave several books to my fellow disciples and superiors; and to me, the little Ludger, he gave a book of Saint Augustine, which he himself called the *Enchiridion*, that is, the *Manual*.

21. By acting in this way, blessed Gregory, the holy man, never ceasing even in his illness to advance in the spiritual succession of his achievements, increased day by day in the wisdom of a sound mind, although his body was weak, for what would benefit him and his own toward entering the kingdom of heaven and attaining everlasting joy.

At last, in the third year after the beginning of his illness, purified by the exhaustion of his body as gold that has passed through fire, he reached the point where, wherever it was necessary, he had to be carried in the hands of his disciples. Yet even then the venerable man never ceased from the work of God. He continually had either the divine books read before him or, as an exercise for his mind, the Psalms sung in devotion to heavenly things. Thus, when his feeble bodily limbs had been brought to their final weakness and had to be supported constantly by a bed, they became white and shining like milk or white wool, so that those who saw him might recognize the great purity in which his spirit was held inwardly before the eyes of God.

Then his friends and relatives of both sexes who were present there began to complain and grieve, both over his approaching departure and over the delayed arrival of his chosen son Albricus, in whom the hope of the entire household rested. [Col. 0768C] At that time he was occupied in royal service in Italy, and no one knew when he would come. [Note: That is, the hope of Gregory’s own stock and lineage, from which Albricus sprang as Gregory’s successor in the entrusted care of the people of Utrecht, and as bishop, as appears from the Acts of Saint Ludger, where Albricus is called Gregory’s nephew.]

Hearing this, Gregory, the Father beloved by God, began to sympathize with those who mourned: secure concerning himself, but anxious about his son. He consoled them and, as he had often done when sound in body during ordinary conversations, brought forward and spoke that prophetic saying: “Do not be afraid. I shall not depart,” he said, “before he himself comes.”

How truly he had foreseen this in spirit was proved by the outcome. For three or four days before his departure, his long-awaited and chosen son Albricus arrived unexpectedly, without anyone knowing it except the spiritual Father, who had foretold his arrival long beforehand. [Col. 0768D]

22. During those three or four successive days they occupied themselves with the common good and the welfare of the entire household, discussing with one another whatever they desired with sound understanding. Then came his final day in this mortality, destined for entrance into the kingdom and everlasting salvation.

His disciples surrounded him, wishing to keep their Father with them longer, although he was weak, and saying to one another in their desire: “He is not dying today; he is not dying today.”

But he, gathering whatever strength he could, said: “Today I wish to have permission.” Having said this, he ordered his disciples to carry him before the oratory of Saint Saviour [Col. 0769A] and to open the door. There, after praying and receiving communion of the sacred body and blood of the Lord, he gazed toward the altar, his mind intent upon heavenly things, and departed to the Lord, whom he had served with a sincere heart for so long. [Col. 0770A]

[Note: In the seventy-third year of his age—that is, since, having been seized by paralysis at the age of seventy, he lived on for three years, as stated in section 20—and in the year 781 of Christ. For, since he began to associate with Boniface in the fifteenth year of his age, this occurred in the year 722, according to the indications noted in section 4. Molanus assigns the day in the *Additions to Usuard*, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. In the Leodiensian Annals cited by Willem Heda, Gregory is said to have been buried with his mother, Saint Wastrade, in the Susteren monastery of noble Benedictine virgins in the diocese of Liège. John of Beka contradicts this in his account of Alberic, where he asserts that Alberic was buried with Gregory in the church of Saint Saviour, which at that time was the principal church of Utrecht, according to what is said in the Observations on the Life of Saint Willibrord. Certainly, above he is said to have given up his last breath in the oratory of Saint Saviour.]

by the grace of the same Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.

# APPENDIX

[Col. 0769]

## THE ACTS OR LIFE OF SAINT LUDGER, BY ALTFRID, BISHOP OF MÜNSTER

(*In Leibnitz, Writers on the Affairs of Brunswick.*)

## TABLE OF CHAPTERS

[Col. 0769B]

Concerning the persecution of Wursingus. Concerning his expulsion. How Radbod attempted to recall him. Concerning the death of Pippin. Concerning the death of Wursingus. [Col. 0769C] Concerning the birth of Liafburga. How Liafburga was rescued from the danger of death. Concerning the birth of Saint Ludger. Concerning his diligence. Concerning the arrival of Alubert and how he returned across the sea together with Ludger. How Saint Ludger again sought the lands beyond the sea. How Saint Ludger returned to his homeland. Concerning the arrival of Saint Liafuvinus. Concerning the death of Saint Liafuvinus. How Saint Ludger destroyed idols in Frisia. Concerning the ordination of Albricus and Saint Ludger. How the governance of peoples was revealed to Saint Ludger. How Saint Ludger taught in East Frisia. Verses of Joseph to Saint Ludger . . . (The remainder of this table is missing.)

## AUTHOR’S PROLOGUE

### 1

Altfrid, bishop by the grace of God, to his beloved brothers [Col. 0769D] and monks serving the Lord in Christ in the monastery of Saint Saviour and of the holy Father Ludger.

I granted your request because I could deny nothing to your charity. You therefore asked repeatedly that I undertake to write something about the Life of the holy Father Ludger, so that his examples, so worthy of reverence, might benefit many toward edification.

Although I knew myself unequal to this diligent task, weak both in knowledge and in learning, I nevertheless applied my mind to writing it, compelled by charity, because I considered it wrong that the virtues of so great a man should remain hidden. As the voice of blessed Gregory, in his investigation of the sacred word, says: “There are some whom examples kindle to love of the heavenly homeland more than exhortations do.”

Examples of the Fathers generally provide a double assistance to the mind. I am also unable to comprehend fully the examples and deeds of Saint Ludger because I learned them not by sight but by hearsay, from those who had known him from childhood: namely, his brother Hildigrim, the bishop, and his nephew Gerfrid, the bishop, [Col. 0770C] as well as his sister, the religious woman Herburga, and also his venerable priests Alubert, Atingus, and Thiatbald.

Accordingly, after passing over through negligence many virtues and signs that the Lord worked through him, I have caused only those things to be written in this little book which, together with you, I either observed with my own eyes or certainly learned to have taken place.

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE

### 2

As I set out to write the Life of Saint Ludger, I judged it right to begin farther back, so that I might unfold from what parents he was born in this world.

In the days of Radbod, king of the Frisians, there was a certain nobleman among that people named Wursingus, by surname Ado. Although he did not yet know the faith of the Holy Trinity, he was nevertheless a helper of the poor, a defender of the oppressed, and also just in judgment.

Because that people at that time was blinded by the error of unbelief, many suffered many injustices from the king and his officials. For the same king had killed some by ambush, possessed their inheritances, and nevertheless continued to claim their inheritances for himself.

But the man mentioned above did not hold back from defending the truth before the king and his nobles. In judging justly and embracing the truth, he respected no person. Consequently, it happened that he suffered great plots from the cruel king, who ordered him to be secretly killed and his possessions taken away. One of the king’s counsellors immediately took care to report this deadly plan to him, because he was loved by many.

### 3

[Col. 0771A] Then Wursingus fled secretly with his wife Adalgarda, his one son Nothgrimus, and a few members of his household, and reached the Frankish duke named Grimoldus.

[Note: This Grimoldus was a duke, son of Pippin, mayor of the palace, and died in the year 714.]

The duke received him kindly. Wursingus lived in the Frankish region and, having been instructed in the Catholic faith, received the grace of baptism together with his wife, his son, and the rest of his household.

After the death of the duke mentioned above, the individual Frankish dukes retained the venerable Wursingus among them, honoring him with benefices. During his exile his wife bore him another son, named Thiatgrimus, and nine daughters; she then died peacefully. Six of her daughters likewise passed away in virginity.

The father therefore raised and preserved his two sons and the three daughters who remained, in the fear of the Lord, and kept his chastity for the rest of his life. [Col. 0771B]

### 4

After these events, King Radbod began to fall ill with the illness of which he also died. For six continuous years before the day of his death he gradually endured suffering. His kingdom began to decline, while the kingdom of the Franks grew by expansion.

When he became ill, he sent to the aforementioned Wursingus, asking him to return to him in order to receive his inheritance. He also promised to give him many other things if he wished to keep peace with him.

But the Catholic man did not yield to his requests. Radbod sent to him again, asking that, if he himself did not wish to come, at least he should send his son, and swore that he would give him whatever he had promised.

Overcome, therefore, by the king’s pleas, Wursingus sent his younger son to him. Radbod received him kindly, arranged for him to live honorably with him, and restored his father’s inheritance to him. The father himself, however, lived in the Frankish region with his elder son and daughters until the king’s death.

[Note: This occurred in the year 719.]

It happened that Pippin, duke of the Franks, departed from this life, and his son Charles gained his father’s kingdom. He added many peoples to the Frankish realm, including Frisia, after Radbod had been destroyed, adding it to his paternal empire with the glory of triumph. At that time Saint Willibrord was established among that people as its preacher, and an episcopal see had been assigned at the fortress of Utrecht, as is written in the little book on the Life of Willibrord himself.

Charles therefore gave the aforementioned Wursingus a benefice on the border of the Frisians and sent him to his homeland to strengthen the faith. When he arrived and received his own inheritance, he lived in a place called Suabsna.

[Note: In the metrical Life it is called Sualisna; in the Budic manuscript, Suahsna, as the Antwerp Fathers note.]

It lay near Utrecht. He began to assist Saint Willibrord, together with his sons and relatives, in whatever ways he could. Saint Willibrord loved him greatly because he was a good man, full of faith, acceptable to the whole people, and observant of chastity.

### 5

Nothgrimus, his elder son, likewise took a faithful wife, and his three daughters were joined in marriage with the fear of the Lord. While their father was still alive, that family had great intimacy with Saint Willibrord and also with Saint Boniface, who after him shone forth as a serene teacher in those regions, until he was crowned with martyrdom for the faith of Christ and gave up his spirit in the district called Astrache, in a place called Doccinga, as writings about him also attest.

After the death of their father, Thiatgrimus, the younger son of the aforementioned Wursingus, took a wife named Liafburga (Hafburch), the daughter of a certain Nothrad and Adelburga. This Adelburga had previously entrusted two of her brothers to Saint Willibrord, of whom we spoke above, to be brought up for the Lord. The elder was called Wullibrat, the younger Thyatbrat. [Col. 0772B] They were the first of all the Frisian people to undertake the clerical office. The elder died in the rank of levite; the younger did not attain that rank but departed from this life in his youth.

### 6

When the aforementioned Liafburga was born, she had a pagan grandmother, namely her father’s mother, who had entirely renounced the Catholic faith. This woman—whose name should not be mentioned—was driven into a rage,

[Note: The Antwerp and Benedictine editions read “into fury.”]

because the wife mentioned above had given birth only to daughters and had no living son. She sent executioners to snatch the newborn daughter from her mother’s lap and kill her before she could suck her mother’s milk. For it was the custom of the pagans that, if they wished to kill a son or daughter, they would kill the child without earthly food.

The executioners, as they had been ordered, seized her and carried her away. One of them bore her to a bucket filled with water, wishing to drown her in it and end her life. But by a wondrous gift of the Almighty it happened that the girl, who had not yet sucked at her mother’s breasts, stretched out both arms and seized the rim of the bucket with both hands, resisting so that she would not be submerged.

We believe that this strength in so tender a girl was brought about by divine predestination, because from her two bishops were to descend, namely Saint Ludger and Hildigrim.

During this remarkable struggle, in accordance with the merciful disposition of God, a neighboring woman arrived. Moved by pity, she rescued the girl from the hand of the aforementioned servant, ran with her to her own house, and, closing the door behind her, reached a room where there was honey. She put some of that honey into the infant’s mouth, and the child immediately swallowed it.

Meanwhile the executioners came to carry out their mistress’s commands. That furious woman ruled the whole household of her son. The woman who had snatched away the infant went out to meet the executioners and told them that the girl had eaten honey. At the same time she showed them the child still licking her lips; for this reason, according to the custom of the Gentiles, it was unlawful to kill her.

The executioners then left her, and the woman who had rescued her secretly nourished her, putting milk into her mouth through a horn. The mother also secretly sent a wet nurse to her, bringing whatever was necessary, until that savage woman mentioned above ended her life. Only then did the mother take back her daughter to raise her.

But let this suffice concerning these matters.

### 7

Now that we have begun to speak of Saint Ludger, it is pleasing to repeat a true account of him.

[Note: The Antwerp and Benedictine editions read *iterum* (“again”).]

When his father Thiatgrimus had returned from a certain journey, his mother was pregnant and carrying in her womb the future bishop, being close to giving birth. On hearing that her husband was coming, she hurried toward him in immoderate joy, struck her foot, and fell. A stake pierced her side, and she was carried away as dead, so that no one thought that she could be restored either to her present life or to the son whom she carried in her womb.

But through the mercy of divine kindness her spirit came back to life, and she was properly healed. Nor did any mark of injury appear on the boy, who was born a few days later.

When he was baptized, he received the name Ludger. As soon as he was able to walk and speak, he began to collect little skins and tree bark.

[Note: The ancients called these materials “papyrus.” Mabillon.]

We customarily use such things for lamps. Whatever of this sort he could find, he sewed together from his collections, as if making little books, while other boys played. When he found some liquid, he imitated scribes and brought his nurse what looked like useful books to keep. Whenever someone asked him, “What did you do today?” he said that he had spent the whole day either arranging books, writing, or even reading. When he was asked again, “Who taught you?” he replied, “God taught me.”

While still a child, he meditated on what he later devotedly fulfilled.

### 8

[Col. 0773C] After this, having grown through greater grace, he asked his parents to entrust him to some man of God for instruction. Since they were kind, they glorified God when they saw the young man’s intention and entrusted him to the venerable Gregory, disciple and successor of Saint Boniface the martyr, to be brought up for the Lord. Gregory gladly received him and, discovering the boy’s intelligence, diligently instructed him.

Ludger therefore grew, advancing in the fear of God. After laying aside secular clothing, he withdrew to the monastery at Triectum (Utrecht) to study the spiritual art.

There were also in Gregory’s school other noble and prudent fellow students. Some later became bishops, while others became teachers of churches in the lower orders. [Col. 0773D] Among them Ludger was held in great affection because he was a man of remarkable gentleness, with a cheerful countenance, though not quick to laughter, and because in all his actions he embraced prudence together with moderation.

He was a constant meditator on divine Scripture, especially on what pertained to the praise of God and to Catholic teaching. For this reason he was loved by his venerable teacher like an only son.

### 9

[Col. 0774A] Meanwhile a certain man named Alubret came from the land of the English to Abbot Gregory, wishing, with the Lord’s help, to benefit the people of that region by teaching, for they were still inexperienced in the faith.

[Note: Benedict reads Aluberth. The Budic manuscript, praised by the Antwerp Fathers, reads Adelbertus.]

Abbot Gregory received him gladly. Discovering that he was a good and learned man, he urged him to become a bishop. Gregory himself had not been ordained to the episcopal rank but had persevered in the rank of priest.

The prudent man replied: “So that you may know that I crossed over here with the permission and counsel of my bishop, send faithful brothers with me to the land from which I came, to my bishop, so that I and they may be ordained by him. In this way I agree.”

Abbot Gregory gladly heard this. He sent him, together with Ludger and another brother more advanced in age, named Sigibod, to the bishop of whom Alubert had spoken. That bishop ordained Alubert bishop, Sigibod priest, and Ludger deacon, and they remained there for one year.

Alcuin was also teaching in that place at the time. Later, in the time of Charles, he exercised his teaching office at Tours

[Note: The Antwerp and Benedictine editions read “in the time of the younger Charles, at Tours.” By “the younger Charles” is meant Charles the Great, reckoning from his grandfather Charles Martel.]

and in Francia. Ludger immediately attached himself to him, drawing in spiritual doctrines.

[Note: Supply from the Antwerp and Benedictine editions: “diligently.”]

. . . After the completion of a year, those who had been sent returned, and under the Lord’s guidance came to Abbot Gregory. He received them kindly and rejoiced greatly at their arrival. Alubert remained with him, laboring together in the work of the Lord.

### 10

Saint Ludger, therefore, wishing to fill himself with the sweetness of the honeycomb he had tasted,

[Note: In the Life of Ludger by Surius another explanation is given: namely, that when Ludger, then a deacon, stumbled over a certain word while reading the Gospel before Gregory, and Gregory corrected him, he resolved to return to Alcuin’s school, considering himself unworthy of the diaconal rank if he could not read correctly.]

asked Abbot Gregory for permission to return to Master Alcuin. Gregory took this hard and tried to prevent it, but he did not wish to distress the petitioner and began to restrain him with gentle words.

When he saw that he could not turn him from his intention by any objections, he summoned Ludger’s father and asked him to try to recall him from the journey he had begun. But the diligent levite remained steadfastly committed to his resolve.

Then Ludger’s parents and Gregory, eventually overcome by his pleas, sent him to the aforementioned teacher in the city of York in England, supplying him with what he needed on the way. The illustrious teacher Alcuin received him with great joy.

Once received, Ludger was loved by everyone in the customary manner because he was adorned with good morals and holy studies. He remained there for three years and six months, advancing in the study of doctrine.

He wished to remain longer in that holy study, but the opportunity was not granted. For when the citizens of that place went out to war against their enemies, it happened that the son of a certain count of that province was killed in a quarrel by a Frisian merchant. For this reason the Frisians hastened to leave the region of the English, fearing the anger of the murdered young man’s relatives.

Then Alcuin, compelled by necessity, sent Ludger with the aforementioned merchants. He also sent with him his deacon named Putul,

[Note: The Antwerp and Benedictine editions read: “He sent Ludger with the aforementioned merchants; he also sent with him his deacon, named Putul, fearing,” and so forth.]

fearing that, in his love of learning, Ludger might enter another city of that region and suffer some ambush in retaliation for the young man mentioned above. For he said that he would rather die than allow his beloved son to suffer any deadly harm.

Thus sent away, Ludger reached his homeland on a prosperous journey, well instructed and possessing an ample supply of books. He was then so much more worthy and acceptable to Father Gregory and the others as he was more distinguished in monastic learning.

The deacon who had come with him, in accordance with Alcuin’s arrangement, went to Rome, intending to return. Later he also came with Alcuin to Gaul in the rank of priest.

### 11

[Col. 0775B] While these things were taking place, a certain holy and learned priest of English descent, named Liafuvinus, came to Abbot Gregory. He said that the Lord had terrifyingly commanded him through a threefold admonition to benefit the people in teaching on the border of the Franks and Saxons, beside the river Isla. He asked Gregory to order that he be led to that place and to the river named for him by the Lord.

Gregory, because that place belonged to his parish, decided kindly to send him there, giving thanks to the supreme Shepherd because he was visiting his flock. He also sent with him Marchelm, a servant of God of English descent who had been instructed from childhood in holy morals by Saint Willibrord the bishop, so that he might place him over the people.

The priest Liafuvinus was received by a certain matron named Averhilda. Together with the other faithful, he sowed teachings of salvation and watered the meadows of their minds. They built an oratory for him on the western bank of the aforementioned river, in a place called Hulpa.

### 12

After this they also built a church for him on the eastern bank of the same river, in a place called Daventre. When the people flocked to it because of the holy man’s teaching, the Saxons, who at that time were darkened by pagan rites, were driven into a fury. Gathering an army, they expelled the Christians from those places and burned the church with fire.

Then the man of God Liafuvinus returned to Abbot Gregory and awaited consolation from the Lord. When the disturbance had subsided and the raiders had returned to their own homes, the man of God rebuilt the church that had been burned. In the customary way he did not cease to impart teachings of salvation to the flock, until he returned his beloved soul to the supreme Shepherd. He died and was buried in that same church.

### 13

After the death of Saint Liafuvinus, the impious Saxons again devastated that place and set the church on fire. For three days they searched for his body but could not find it.

Abbot Gregory also departed to the Lord.

[Note: The Antwerp Fathers have demonstrated that Abbot Gregory died in the year 776.]

His nephew Albricus took over the pastoral care. He loved the venerable Ludger with great affection and addressed him as follows:

“Now, because you are my dearest brother, I ask you to fulfill my desire. The place where the holy priest of the Lord, Liafuvinus, whom you knew, labored in the Lord’s work until death, and where his sacred body is covered by burial, has been reduced to desolation. Therefore I ask you to undertake its restoration and to rebuild a church over the saint’s body.”

### 14

The servant of God Ludger obeyed the commands of his teacher. He searched for the saint’s body in the place mentioned above but did not find it. Nevertheless, within the area where he thought it lay, he began to construct a church.

When he had laid the foundations and was attempting to raise the walls, the priest of the Lord Liafuvinus appeared to him in a dream and said:

“Dearest brother Ludger, you have done well in restoring God’s temple, long ago destroyed by the Gentiles. But you will find my body, which you sought, buried beneath the southern wall that you have raised.”

In the morning, after completing the praises of the Lord, Ludger found the saint’s body in the place indicated to him in the vision. He gathered a multitude and had the foundations of that building moved to the southern side; thus he enclosed the tomb of the man of God within the church.

The church was completed and consecrated, and thereafter was never polluted by the Gentiles. In that place, however, through his servant Liafuvinus, the Lord continues to perform many miracles to the present day. There is also now a monastery of canons serving the Lord.

### 15

After this Albricus sent Ludger, together with other servants of God, to destroy the shrines of the gods and the various forms of idolatrous worship among the Frisian people. They fulfilled the command and brought back a great treasure that they had found in the sanctuaries.

[Note: The Antwerp and Benedictine editions read “to him.”]

The emperor Charles received two parts of it, while he ordered Albricus to take the third part for his own uses.

When Albricus had received the episcopal rank at Cologne, he also had Ludger receive the rank of priest with him. He appointed him teacher of the church in the district called Ostrache (that is, Ostergau), in the place where Saint Boniface was crowned with martyrdom.

The same Albricus divided the year into four assignments, so that at the monastery in Utrecht, taking precedence over the other superiors, he himself would preside over the brothers during the spring for three months in the study of doctrine and holy conduct. After him, during the summer, the priest Adalger would serve as his substitute for three months; after him, the priest Ludger for three months; and then, in winter, the priest Thiatbrat for three months.

### 16

Accordingly, during the period of his assigned turn, after the psalmody and prayers that he had always loved, Ludger was accustomed to give his limbs rest at night in the upper room of the church of Saint Saviour, which Saint Willibrord had built.

One night the venerable Abbot Gregory appeared to him in a vision and said: “Brother Ludger, follow me.”

As Ludger followed him, Gregory climbed to a higher place and threw down before him, piece by piece, what looked like membranes and parts of clothing. He said: “Gather these into heaps.”

When Ludger had gathered them into three mounds, Gregory said to him: “Distribute these well in the work of the Lord, and I will give you enough.” He then marked him with the sign of the cross and departed.

When morning came, Ludger reported the dream to the monastery’s superior, named Haldon, and to the holy custodian of the church, Marchelm, whom I mentioned above. Marchelm immediately began to explain what the outcome of events proved, saying:

“The three mounds that you gathered represent the governance of three peoples, over whom you must still preside by pastoral rule.”

Ludger replied: “Would that in the place entrusted to me I might accomplish some fruit for the Lord.”

Here too, concerning how Ludger carried out his desired ministry of evangelization among the Frisian people, and how the seeds of heavenly life sprang up most abundantly in the fields of many hearts at his preaching, with grace watering them like dew, the peoples of that region remain witnesses to this day: for he recalled them from their ancient error to the recognition of truth. The churches that he built in the various places are also witnesses, as are the communities serving God that he gathered together in certain places.

### 17

A certain disciple of Alcuin also bore witness to him, committing the following words to heroic verse:

Brother, sweeter through the love of God than every kinsman,  
And rightly more precious even than blood relations themselves,

Beloved Ludger, may Christ’s grace save you:  
Live, bright pillar of your Frisian people,

A priest worthy of praise in the western regions of the world,  
Learned, prudent in speech, and profound in mind;

You adorn your rank by your merits and your noble conduct.  
And, behold, though a boy, you serve the aged with humble heart;

You act as a brother toward all your peers in age,  
And as a father you offer life’s instruction to the young.

As you grow toward what is better, remember me, priest,  
And in your prayers, I ask, commend to the Thunderer

This poet who has praised you in his songs—  
To whom, for such a poem, as a generous man,

Give the gift of a polished staff. Perhaps this little payment  
Is fitting for the modest poet. Farewell, happy without end.

[Note: In the editions of the Life of Saint Ludger prepared by the Antwerp and Benedictine Fathers, the following verses are distinguished from the preceding ones, and before the verse “This outstanding Father,” and so forth, they found the following title: “Verses of Alcuin on the church of Ludger.” This title also seems to belong before them. For Joseph’s earlier poem ends with the words “Farewell, happy without end.” A new poem begins with the words “This outstanding Father,” and so forth.]

This outstanding Father, Boniface, through his noble merits,  
Together with his companions poured forth a stream of blood,

Receiving the renowned crowns of sacred martyrdom.  
A blessed land, exceedingly rich in the blood of saints,

From here the victorious soldier flies across to heaven’s rewards,  
Leaving his final footprints upon these grassy mounds.

Therefore, kneeling suppliantly, I urge:  
Whoever you are who read, press kisses upon these lands.

May great hope be yours [perhaps: “will be”] that your tears, supported by these patrons, may ascend to heaven from here. [Note: [Col. 0778D] In declining Latin, *diaconibus* is also often used for *diaconis* (“deacons”).]

Thus that blood remains more precious than all gold [Note: [Col. 0778D] Others read *hic* (“here”) for *manet* (“remains”); perhaps *manat* (“flows”)],  
and here the limbs, drenched with heavenly dew, lie at rest.

Paul the teacher assists from one side, Boniface from the other,  
when this hall is known to have been dedicated to them together.

**18.** While the man of God Ludgerus was persisting for nearly seven years in the work of teaching in that region, Wutukind, the Saxon duke, a root of wickedness, rose up—until then the Saxons had been pagans—overthrew the Frisians from the way of God, burned their churches, expelled the servants of God, and compelled the Frisians as far as the river Fleo to abandon the Christian faith and sacrifice to idols according to the custom of their former error. Bishop Albricus also departed to the Lord amid that very perverse upheaval.

Then Ludgerus, compelled by necessity, abandoned those parts. Having arranged the company of his disciples, he took two of them with him, namely Hildigrimus, his brother, and Gerberius, surnamed Castus, and went to Rome [Note: This took place around the year 783]. From there he proceeded to the monastery of Saint Benedict in the Beneventan kingdom, and, remaining there in holy conduct, learned the rule of that holy Father Benedict. For he desired to build, from his own inheritance, a monastery of monks; this was afterward granted, with the Lord’s help, at the place called Werthina.

**19.** After two years and six months, therefore, he returned to his homeland, and his fame reached the ears of the glorious prince Charles, who appointed him teacher among the Frisians on the eastern side of the river Labeki [Note: Commonly called the Lauwers by Cornelius Kempius, *Description of Frisia*, book I, chapter 6; by others, the Lavica], over five districts, whose names are these [Note: In the Antwerp and Benedictine editions these districts are called Hugmerthi, Hunulga, Fivilga, Emilga, and Fedirilga]: Hugmerchi, Hunusga, Fuulga, Emisga, and Fedirga, as well as one island called Bant.

With diligent care he strove to supply the streams of the Lord’s teaching to the flock entrusted to him, to destroy the pagan shrines, and to wash away all the filth of their former error. He also took care to carry the rivers of instruction farther. On the emperor’s advice he crossed over at the frontier between the Frisians and the Danes to an island called Foseteslant after the name of their false god Fosete [Note: The Antwerp editors believe this island to have been the one which Tacitus called the Sacred Grove, although Tacitus mentions there not the god Fosete but the goddess Hertha, and it is more credible that he meant Rügen. Adam of Bremen, book IV of his *History*, says that Foseteslant is the same as the island of Farria, “which lies hidden at the mouth of the river Elbe, far within its recess; otherwise called Hetligelant, that is, ‘holy land.’”].

As they approached it by ship, he held a cross in his hand and poured forth prayers and praises to the Lord. Those who were in the ship saw a dark mist issuing from that same ship; when it departed, great serenity remained over the island. Then the man of God said: “Do you see how, by God’s mercy, the enemy who had previously occupied this island with darkness has been driven away?”

When they reached the island, they destroyed all the shrines of Fosete that had been built there, and constructed churches of Christ in their place. As he imbued the inhabitants of that land with the faith of Christ, he baptized them with invocation of the holy Trinity in a spring that bubbled up there, in which Saint Willibrord had previously baptized people. No one had earlier dared to draw water from that spring except in silence.

He also took from the font Landricus, the son of one of their princes, and, having instructed him in sacred letters, ordained him priest. For many years he presided over the Frisian people in the work of teaching. Then again, through the activity of the Evil One, a great night of unbelief arose among the eastern Frisians, whose leaders were Maluinno (Malumno) and Eilrat [Note: The Antwerp and Benedictine editions read: “of this evil, Huno and Cilrac,” etc.]. Churches were burned and the servants of God driven away. But when the sun of justice shone forth, the darkness of radiant error was dispersed, so that after a year had passed Saint Ludgerus, together with his companions, did not cease confidently to supply that people, according to the ancient custom, with the nourishment of faith, and, with the Lord’s help, they persevered in the faith they had then received.

**20.** Meanwhile, by the dispensation of the merciful God, the Saxons were converted to the Lord, and King Charles appointed that same man of God, Ludgerus, shepherd over the eastern part of Saxony. The principal seat of his diocese was at the place called Mimigernefor (below, Minigerneford) [Note: The Antwerp and Benedictine editions read: “The principal seat is in the district of Sudergoe, at a place whose name is Mimigerneford,” etc. It is now Münster.]. There he honorably built a monastery for those serving the Lord under the canonical rule.

Thus, according to his customary practice, he diligently and eagerly sought to benefit the untrained Saxon peoples through teaching; having uprooted the thorns of idolatry, he carefully sowed the word of God everywhere, built churches, and appointed priests in each of them—men whom he himself had nurtured as fellow-workers in the word of God.

He therefore desired to assist many peoples in the work of evangelization that he had begun; yet he humbly wished to avoid the episcopal rank. For that reason he frequently asked his disciples whether one of them might receive the episcopal order in his place. When Bishop Hildibald urged him to be ordained bishop, he replied with that apostolic saying: “A bishop must be blameless.” But Ludgerus, being humble and most devoted to the man of God, said with a sigh: “This has by no means been fulfilled in me.”

At last, overcome by everyone’s consent and compelled rather by God’s disposition, he agreed, lest he seem to oppose the counsel of many—or rather, the will of God.

**21.** Having therefore received the sacred episcopal order, he supplied the Saxon flock entrusted to him with the teachings of salvation in great abundance, with all prudence and moderation, until, by the Lord’s generosity, he led them to perfect faith.

He likewise presided with episcopal governance over those five districts in Frisia whom he had brought from paganism to recognition of the true and indivisible Trinity, since previously they had had no bishop. His successors also treated both places as one diocese. King Charles gave him, in the kingdom of the Franks, in the district of Brachante (Bracbante), at the place called Locus, the monastery of Saint Peter to govern, together with all its adjoining churches and villages [Note: Other manuscripts read Lotus or Lotusa. Commonly Leuze, a town in Hainaut between Ath and Tournai.].

Then the dream which the man of God Marchelmus had earlier interpreted for him was fulfilled: the gathering of three hills, signifying the governance of three peoples.

# BOOK TWO

**1.** Although the ministry of evangelical preaching and the illumination of many hearts through miraculous works and displays of signs ought to be placed first, nevertheless, in honor of the Lord who grants them, we have committed to writing what we remember to have been done by that holy man.

When he had come to a certain village in Frisia called Helewirt for the sake of evangelizing, a matron named Mensuit received him into her house. While he was reclining there with his disciples, behold, a blind man named Bernlef was brought in. He was greatly loved by his neighbors because he was affable and knew how to recite in song the deeds of the ancients and the battles of kings. But he had been struck by continuous blindness for three years, so that no light, not even the faintest vision, remained to him.

The man of God looked at him with a cheerful expression and asked whether he wished to receive penance from him. After Bernlef had promised this, Ludgerus ordered him to come to him the next day.

On the following day the same blind man met the man of God as he was riding. The servant of God took hold of his horse’s bridle, led him away from the crowd, and imposed penance upon him after he had confessed his sins. Then he made the sign of the holy cross over his eyes, held out his hand before him, and asked whether he could see anything.

With great joy Bernlef said that he could see the man’s hand. “Then,” said Ludgerus, “give thanks to almighty God.”

As they spoke together about the Catholic faith, they came to a village called Vuerthen [Alternative forms: Werfhem, Wersheim, Imerfhem]. Ludgerus asked whether Bernlef could see it itself. Immediately he named it and declared that he could clearly see its trees and all its buildings.

Ludgerus said: “Give thanks to almighty God, who has enlightened you.”

When they came to a village called Wiscuuirt [Alternative forms: Usquurd, Vuscuurdis, Vosgurd, Wuscurdus], where an oratory had been built, he made Bernlef pray with him and give thanks to God. He bound him by an oath not to tell anyone, before the day of his death, how he had been enlightened.

Bernlef fulfilled the command of the man of God. For several days he acted as though he were still blind and used another person’s guidance; but after Ludgerus’s death he declared how he had been enlightened.

**2.** During the second expulsion of the servants of God from Frisia, of which we have already spoken above, the holy man Ludgerus ordered that this same Bernlef—because he was loved by many—go from house to house and persuade the matrons to have their dying infants baptized. They were to baptize the infants by dipping them in, or pouring over them, water simply blessed in the name of the Lord, with invocation of the holy Trinity.

Obeying his orders gladly, Bernlef baptized eighteen infants during that upheaval. All of them died soon after they had been baptized, except two whom blessed Ludgerus, when peace returned, confirmed with the holy anointing of chrism.

Wherever Bernlef found the man of God, he learned the Psalms from him, and he remained in the illumination he had received until, old and full of days, he died in peace.

When his wife, weeping, asked him as he lay dying how she would be able to live after him, he replied: “If I can obtain anything from the Lord, after my death you will not remain alive in this world for long.” When she heard this response while still healthy and unharmed, she followed him in death on the fifteenth day.

**3.** On another occasion, when blessed Ludgerus was beside the sea at a place called Werdina, where he had built a church for himself from his paternal inheritance, he saw a terrifying dream. Relating it to his sister Herburga, he said:

“I saw in a dream what seemed to be the sun fleeing over the sea from the northern regions, with most dreadful clouds following it. As it fled and faded, it passed beyond us, so that once it had withdrawn it could no longer be seen by us; and the darkness that had followed it covered all these coastal places.

“After a very long time, the sun returned, smaller and paler than it had been before, and drove the darkness across the sea.”

As he said this, he drenched his face abundantly with tears. When his sister saw him weeping, she too wept and said: “What does this dream mean?”

He replied: “Great persecutions and continuing wars will come from the Northmen, together with immense devastations, so that, because their sins demand it, these pleasant coastal regions will be left almost uninhabitable. Afterward, with God’s favor, peace will be restored to the Church, and the most severe plague that has lain upon these regions will be turned back upon the Northmen themselves.”

She said with a sigh: “Would that the Lord might deign to take me from this world before these things come upon us.”

“It will not be so,” he replied. “These things will occur in your days; but I shall not see that plague in this body.”

The truth of this prophecy has therefore been proved in the times of his sister and of ourselves.

For throughout all the days in which that servant of God lived in this world, peace was joyfully present everywhere, so that no one thought any disturbance from the Northmen could come upon these regions. But after his death we suffered almost innumerable evils year after year from the exceedingly harsh people of the Northmen [Antwerp and Benedictine editions: “the most savage people of the Northmen”].

Churches were burned, monasteries destroyed, and estates abandoned by their inhabitants, to such an extent that, because their sins demanded it, the coastal regions previously filled with crowds of people were almost reduced to a wilderness.

But we hope that the sun of justice, which departed and withdrew because of our sins, will return, and, according to the prophecy of the man of God, that peace will return to the Church.

**4.** That same man of God also came to a place called Bilurbike [Antwerp and Benedictine editions: Billurbeki], to a church. There a certain woman, who had been joined to a man in an unlawful marriage, wishing to lessen his severity, sent him honey as though for a blessing. But he refused to accept such a gift, scorning it.

Some young men among his disciples, however, desiring the honey, took it and secretly placed it behind the altar in the church. When the man of God approached that altar to celebrate Mass and opened his mouth for the prayers, the earthen vessel containing the honey of disobedience immediately cracked into pieces, and the honey was scattered. They gathered it up and threw it outside.

The soldier of Christ did not cease until he had destroyed that unlawful marriage; he also expelled from the homeland the man who had dared to perpetrate it.

**5.** When he had come to his church in Frisia for the sake of teaching, near the river Lade, he asked the fishermen of that place, who were accustomed to bring him fish, to bring him a sturgeon that they had caught.

They replied that the season in which such fish could be caught had long since passed—for winter was near. With a cheerful expression he said to them: “Go, sons; do what I have said. God is able at every season to grant his servants what they desire.”

Compelled by the prayers of the man of God, they began, according to their custom, to draw their net through the waters. Suddenly, raising their eyes, they saw a great bird descending from heaven before them. As they fixed their gaze intently upon it, one said to the other: “It truly resembles a fish.”

While they wondered and were terrified, the figure of the fish—or bird—fell before them into the water. When they reached the place, a fish of extraordinary size entered their net. It was the fish called a sturgeon [Note: Commonly *sior*. Among the ancient Saxons, as among northerners today, *stor* means “great”; among the English, *store* means “abundance”], which the man of God had desired.

They caught it and brought it to the man of God, recounting the miracles that had occurred. He said to them: “Let us give thanks to almighty God, who gives food to all flesh.”

He also warned them not to presume to say that this had happened because of anyone’s holiness or merits.

**6.** Saint Ludgerus was by no means unlearned in the sacred Scriptures, as is clearly proved in the book he composed on the life of his venerable teachers, Gregory and Albricus. He also wrote, in elegant language, the beginnings of Saint Boniface’s arrival and ordination, which had been omitted in another little work.

He did not neglect, on each morning, to give lessons to his disciples personally, and whatever he found prescribed in the sacred books he diligently strove to observe and teach. He was therefore careful never to make a vain name for himself, and for that reason, following the Apostle, he desired to do all things with moderation.

Because he had not made the monastic promise of observance, he ceased to wear the monastic cowl. Yet he wore next to his flesh, until the end of his life, a garment of haircloth, which could more easily be concealed.

He did not refuse to eat meat at appointed times; nevertheless, none of his disciples ever saw him satisfied with food or drink. When, according to his custom, he invited poor and rich alike to dine with him, he did not cease pouring the teachings of eternal life into their hearts, so that they departed more satisfied with spiritual than bodily delights.

Thus he was a father to the needy and one who despised himself. Following the Apostle, he took care to adapt himself to everyone so that he might benefit everyone.

He earnestly desired to visit the Northmen for the sake of teaching them, but King Charles gave no consent whatever.

**7.** When almighty God had determined to repay his pious labors with an everlasting reward, he was afflicted for some time before his death by bodily illness.

Even while sick, however, he occupied his mind most intensely, according to his customary practice, with holy works: either listening to sacred readings, singing the Psalms, or engaging in any other spiritual activity. He did not allow his mind to grow lukewarm by being loosened from heavenly contemplation, and almost every day, although sick in body, he celebrated the mysteries of the Mass with an unfatigued spirit.

On the very Sunday before he was to depart from this world to the Lord during the following night, he preached publicly in his two churches, as though bidding farewell to all entrusted to him. In the morning he preached at the place called Coasfelt, while a priest was singing Mass; and around the third hour, at the place called Billurbike, where, as we related above, he had himself fallen ill in body but was strong in the fervor of charity, he devoutly celebrated the final solemn Mass.

There, during the following night, with his disciples attending him, he surrendered his soul, beloved of the Lord.

At the very hour of his departure, the Lord deigned to show a sign of his mercy. Gerfridus, his nephew and successor in the priesthood, had hurried there that same night with the brothers in order to visit him. When only a little of the journey remained, they saw before them a great light, as though a fire rising upward, which drove away all the darkness of that dreadful night.

Immediately understanding from this sign that the holy and venerable man had died, they completed the remaining road with great speed. They found him already dead and, carefully making inquiries, learned that at the very moment when the light had appeared to them, that constant watcher and lover of the true light had departed to the Lord.

**8.** The disciples therefore, remembering how that priest of the Lord had arranged while still alive that his body should be buried at the place called Werthina—where, on his own inheritance, he had built a church as a dwelling for monks in honor of the holy Savior, the holy Mother of God, and Saint Peter, prince of the apostles—sought to carry out his wishes.

But when the people of that place, mindful of his holy merits, resisted vehemently, they took counsel and carried his body to the monastery he had built, called Mimigerneford, about which we have already spoken. They left it buried in the church of Saint Mary until the venerable bishop of the church of Cadola, Hildigrimus by name, brother of that man of God and instructed by him, could act with the glorious King Charles so that, by the king’s command—or rather by God’s decree—the holy body might be buried at the place where Ludgerus had decided while alive: outside the church, on the eastern side, as he had ordered.

For he had never agreed that a human body should be buried in his consecrated church.

He died in the year 809 of the Lord’s incarnation, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April [March 26], and on the thirty-second day after his holy death, that is, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [April 26], he was buried at the same place, wonderfully fragrant.

# BOOK THREE

**1.** By the divine gift of mercy, just as he desired while alive to benefit many, so after his death his holy merits do not cease to assist some who remain far away, some who travel to his tomb, and others who remain there or return home from it. Of these, we relate those that come to memory.

There was a certain man named Irmingerus in the district of Nortgo, who had served that same holy Ludgerus in his youth. It happened that he lost the light of his eyes and remained blind for thirteen continuous years.

One night the holy man appeared to him in a vision and called him by his own name, saying: “Irmenger, are you awake?”

When he said that he was awake, Ludgerus touched his face and said: “Just as the color in this place appears different from the rest, tell your master Dindoni to have you brought to my church at Werthina, which I built there for the Lord, where my body also lies covered by burial. There, if the Lord grants it, you will receive the light of your eyes.”

After receiving this admonition, Irmingerus told his master what message he had received from the holy man. He also showed him the mark that Ludgerus had placed upon his face. In accordance with the man of God’s words, it remained different from the rest of his skin throughout all the days of his life.

His master then went joyfully with his wife to that place and took Irmingerus with him. There they found Bishop Gerfridus, Saint Ludgerus’s nephew and successor, together with the brothers and monks.

When they recounted what had happened, they had Irmingerus lie that night in the church mentioned above. After he had prayed and kept vigil, he immediately received the light of his eyes through God’s grace, according to the words of the man of God.

That same night, around cockcrow, a certain paralyzed woman was suddenly restored to bodily health before the tomb of the man of God. She departed unharmed, glorifying God, who had deigned to heal her so quickly through his servant.

**2.** In the district of Suderge [Alternative form: Sudergoe], a matron named Sigiburch had a tenant named Reinoldus. His wife lay prostrate under a long illness and had almost despaired of bodily recovery.

One night, while her exhausted limbs slipped into sleep amid painful sighs, she saw in a dream someone standing beside her and saying: “Speak with Bishop Ludgerus.”

As she afterward used to relate, although neither heavily asleep nor fully awake, she saw him standing with his face turned toward the east. Since she did not dare address him, he turned his face toward her and said: “I have tested your patience. Have patience, and the Lord will heal you.”

When the vision ended, her body received such strength that the memory of her former illness was almost removed from her. At daybreak she arose joyfully and recounted the manner of her restoration. Her husband and sons, together with the household, rejoiced with her and blessed God.

From then on she was accustomed to visit Saint Ludgerus’s tomb with thanksgiving. Later it was revealed to her that she had not been washed in sacred baptism; when the truth of this revelation was established, she received the grace of baptism.

**3.** Another man named Berthricus, a tenant in the same district of our priest Igon, a disciple of Saint Ludgerus, had a young daughter deprived of strength by paralysis and pains.

When he heard of the saint’s fame, he was inflamed with hope for the girl’s recovery, took to the road, and hurried to bring her to the saint’s sacred tomb. As they were traveling there, she said to her brother, who was carrying her ahead of him on horseback upon a saddlecloth, that she felt no pain anywhere in her body.

Then she added: “Put me down and let me walk.”

When they had done so, she stood with a healthy body and walked. She leaped up and ran, rejoicing greatly as she walked.

When they saw this, they glorified God. Reaching the place mentioned above, they recounted the miracles that had occurred on the journey and at the same time showed that she bore no mark of injury.

After completing their prayer and thanksgiving, they returned joyfully to their own home.

**4.** It happened to one of our deacons, a monk named Hildiradus, while he was still a teacher in the monastery of the man of God, that during a long illness his nerves contracted and his knee bent, so that his lower leg was joined to his thigh. After the rest of his body had been healed following a long period of suffering, that leg remained bent as it had been.

For many days he used a staff to support himself while walking. His father, named Sigibertus and already a monk at that time, had begun to consider whether the contraction of his son’s nerves might be relaxed through some medical treatment.

Behold, the priest of the Lord Ludgerus appeared in a vision to that student, wearing priestly vestments and a *cidaris* (priestly head-dress) on his head, and said: “See that, because of what you suffer, you do not presume to seek bodily medicine anywhere. For if you do this, you will receive no healing from that remedy.” He likewise rebuked him for his frivolity and childish fickleness, and departed.

When morning came, Hildiradus recounted what he had seen. That same day, after the evening praises had been completed, he entered the house of the sick where the holy man had appeared to him in a vision the previous night. In the presence of the brothers who were there, he suddenly fell to the ground. His leg was straightened without pain, and the sound of the nerves in his knee could be heard as though dry branches were breaking there.

He immediately rose up healthy, feeling none of his former weakness, and, exulting with the brothers, gave praise to God. From then on he strove, in accordance with the man of God’s word, to correct his life more carefully.
