**5.** A girl named Modswith had lost the light of her eyes and remained without light for twelve months, unable even to enjoy the faintest vision.

Her father and mother heard of the fame of Saint Ludgerus and of the many things the Lord did through him for the consolation of the sick. After completing their journey, they brought her to the church mentioned above. Having obtained permission, they spent the night in prayer before the tomb of the distinguished confessor, together with their blind daughter.

When morning came, the girl said that she could now see her own hands. Thus, by the Lord’s generosity, the light gradually increased, so that before she had returned home she could see clearly. She retained throughout her life the gift, free from deception.

**6.** Another girl afflicted by a mute demon was brought to the church mentioned above. As soon as she entered, the unclean spirit immediately departed from her, and she who had been mute began to speak.

She asked her mother how she had come there and said that she was hungry. When her mother recounted to her in order the misery of her affliction, the girl prostrated herself before the tomb of the athlete of God, giving thanks to the Lord and Savior, who had deigned through his servant to free her from such cruel pollution. Having accepted penance for her deeds, she departed unharmed.

**7.** It happened that a certain young man named Heliduvin contracted paralysis and lay on a bed for many days, deprived of the use of all his limbs. His left leg contracted and adhered to his thigh; likewise, his right arm contracted and withered. The remaining limbs, as we have said, remained useless to him, and he was also accustomed to emit a miserable sound, a sign of pain, when he was carried outside.

After suffering this for a long time, he addressed his sister, who sympathized with his pains more than anyone else, and said: “I have heard of Saint Ludgerus, and how God has deigned through him to grant health to the sick at the place where his holy limbs lie buried. Have me carried outside also and placed facing the road that leads there, so that I may vow to serve him if the Lord should deign to grant me health through his merits.”

When this had been done, that very night, by divine grace, his pain ceased and all the functions of his body were restored to him, except for one leg, which remained as it had been, contracted.

After giving thanks, he asked his master to order that he be taken to the place mentioned above. When his master delayed, the man driven by necessity, supporting his weak side with a staff, reached the aforesaid tomb.

After he had spent five nights there, the feast of Saint Ludgerus arrived. That night, while he had laid his limbs down to sleep in the portico before the basilica’s door, beneath which the holy priest’s tomb had been received, the same man of God appeared to him in a vision, accompanied by a great light and attended by clerics. He touched his limbs and departed, leaving him asleep.

When he awoke at the signal for the nocturnal vigils, he rose healthy. Forgetting his staff and his former weakness, he entered the church joyfully and unharmed with the others.

After prayer, returning to his senses, he recounted all that had happened to him. When the celebration of the Lord’s work was completed, he went out and fixed his staff at the entrance of the basilica, at the place where he had been healed, as a sign of the cure.

Nor did he forget his earlier vow: he redeemed himself from his temporal master and fulfilled his vow of servitude.

**8.** A certain woman was brought from Saxony to the same place, blind. While the solemn Mass was being celebrated before the tomb of the servant of God, she suddenly received the light at the hour of the Gospel reading. After giving thanks, she returned unharmed to her home.

**9.** A certain young man in Frisia named Osbrat was afflicted by a mute demon. His father led him through each of the churches in the hope that he might be healed. But when he could be healed in none of them, his father, inspired from heaven, finally brought him to the church mentioned above after completing a long journey.

Having obtained permission from the custodians, he remained there during the night in prayer before the tomb of Christ’s priest Ludgerus, keeping that same son with him, deprived of understanding and speech.

When the demon had been expelled through God’s mercy, complete health of speech and understanding was granted to him.

A neighbor of the same Osbrat, who was paralyzed, was also brought to that church. Immediately receiving complete restoration, she returned to her homeland on her own feet, giving thanks to the Lord her Savior, who had deigned through his servant to restore so swiftly her body, deprived of the use of all its limbs.

**10.** In the district of Borathra, a certain tenant named Follit [Antwerp and Benedictine editions: Folcbad] had a blind son named Gerbaldus. Although the boy had been taken through many holy places, he received no healing.

At last, prompted by the gracious Lord, the fame of Saint Ludgerus came to mind; the boy’s parents, rejoicing in hope, immediately led him outside and placed him facing the road that led to the church where that priest of the Lord rested bodily. They vowed to bring him to the sacred tomb with offerings.

After making this vow, they entered the house. Suddenly the boy wiped his right eye, opened it, and was immediately able to see. He wiped the other, and when it too opened, he likewise received sight. Crying out with joy, he said that he could see clearly.

When they recognized this, his parents and the household were filled with immense joy and blessed God, who had deigned through his servant to grant the boy health so suddenly.

They fulfilled their promise and brought him to the church mentioned above. With an offering of thanksgiving, they showed that he had no mark of injury in his eyes.

**11.** A certain girl was being brought there whom a long illness and continual pain had made paralyzed. She was also accustomed continually to clutch her head with her arms, and an immense pain had settled upon her, so that a sound like a hissing could be heard from her brain.

When she was laid down in the new crypt, not yet completed, to pray to God at Ludgerus’s tomb, by the wonderful grace of almighty God she immediately rose, cured of every bodily weakness, and departed unharmed, blessing God.

**12.** A certain man from Saxony at a place called Vuerthina [Antwerp and Benedictine editions: Werina] became deaf through a trial, so that he could perceive no sound whatsoever with his ears.

After he had been entirely deprived of the use of his ears for a long time, he was finally led by hope of recovery to the tomb of the servant of God, Ludgerus. When the signals for the nocturnal vigils sounded, his ears were suddenly opened, and he said that he could clearly hear the sound of the bells and the monks singing the Psalms. Thus, immediately receiving the restoration of his hearing, he returned home glorifying God.

**13.** At one time a column of light also protected the very church beneath which the tomb of that servant of God had been received. It stood there during the night, extending upward as far as heaven and visible to those keeping watch outside. The sound of bells was also frequently heard there, although no human hand touched them; rather, the hidden knowledge of the Godhead brought it about.

**14.** A certain blind man [Note: The Antwerp edition and Benedictines read: “A certain blind man named Eilwold, from the place called Amaloh.” Browerus notes in the margin that this place is commonly called Almelo] was brought to the tomb of the servant of God Ludgerus. While he lay prostrate there in prayer, he suddenly received light from the Lord.

**15.** Another blind man named Richbertus was brought to the same holy tomb. There, quickly illuminated by the Lord’s mercy, he gave thanks to God and returned home healthy.

16. Our monk Adalvardus is accustomed to affirm what happened at the time when the custody of the same church of Saint Ludger had been entrusted to him. He relates that one day, as evening was approaching, when he was going to the same church to replenish the lamp that always used to burn there, he saw the ancient enemy standing beside the corner of the church, where his little bed had been placed inside. The apparition was utterly black and terrifying. At the sight, the monk mentioned above made the sign of the holy cross over himself and, as he says, stood for a long time fearlessly looking at the same demon. When the devil saw the monk’s great confidence, he raised such a loud and tremendous noise that the wall of the church and his bed, which had been placed inside, seemed to be shattered into tiny pieces. Then the monk cried out: “Saint Ludger, help!” As soon as he had invoked and pronounced the name of the man of God, by the Lord’s assent the same devil was suddenly bound and dragged toward the west. With what violence he was being pulled, he showed by shrieking and uttering pitiable cries. The monk, meanwhile, found the lamp that he had left there a little earlier, and saw that his bed and the whole building remained intact. He still heard the demon’s voice shrieking in the western part.

17. A certain woman, who for a long time had been deprived of the use of her limbs and lay in bed, breathing out sighs accompanied by pitiable cries, was eventually carried with great joy and effort to the aforementioned tomb of the man of God Ludger. There, by God’s favor, she quickly recovered the former health of her limbs; rejoicing and exulting, and praising God, she returned home on her own feet.

18. Then, instigated by the Evil One, a certain young man named Adam killed his brother Henry in a quarrel. For this crime, by judgment of Bishop Jonas, he was scourged and thrown into prison, where he lay for a year. Then, with iron placed around his arms and middle, after a very strict fast had been imposed on him, barefoot and without linen clothing, he was sent into exile.

In the fourth year of his exile, before the tomb of Gertrude, the iron fell from his left arm. Then, after the course of another year, while he was in Rome, in the very crypt of Saint Peter, the iron with which he was girded likewise fell away. When he was again traveling toward Rome, it happened that he was overcome there by a severe illness. When his life had been despaired of during that sickness, someone in the appearance of a priest appeared to him in a vision and said: “Rise, go and seek the tomb of Saint Ludger, formerly bishop of the Saxons and Frisians; there, through the Lord’s mercy, you will recover health by his merits.”

When the vision was over, he was immediately released from the illness by which he had been afflicted. Nevertheless, the iron still tightly constricted his right arm as before; the flesh and sinews had wasted away, and the very bone itself was so tightly encircled by the same iron that all the fingers of that right hand except the thumb and index finger remained weak and stiff. The aforementioned wretched man was young, and therefore, as the time of his fetters passed, his flesh and bones grew, increasing his pain.

When he related the dream in the morning, many people were immediately found there in Rome who had seen the same Saint Ludger in the flesh and knew his holy works well. When they had informed the young man of the road by which he should go there and of the location of the venerable tomb, he completed the journey and reached the aforementioned tomb of Saint Ludger at the time when the monks there were celebrating the morning praises of the Lord. The iron that encircled his right arm suddenly burst apart and was thrown a considerable distance away by the power of the Lord.

19. [Note: Antwerp and the Benedictines: “In the Ripuarii, near the entrance to the Hamarithi forest, there is a village called Budica, in which there was a certain woman,” etc.]

A certain woman was weak, and her right arm, through the action of illness, was immovable; while her hand remained bent, the nails were pressed firmly into her palm. After she had suffered this for a long time, the fame of the aforementioned man of God came to her mind. Led by hope of healing, she hurried to his tomb; but before she arrived there, on the journey itself the Lord suddenly granted her complete bodily health on account of the holy man’s merits. Nevertheless, after completing the journey, she reached the same tomb, healthy and exultant, with offerings, praising the Savior; and thus she returned unharmed to her home.

20. A certain tenant of the venerable Count Cobbo had a young son named Warmund, whom an evil spirit invaded and began to torment so violently that his life was brought to the point of despair. His mother carefully sought to report this by messenger to her mistress, namely Cobbo’s wife. She immediately sent word to her, saying: “If the boy is still alive, have him carried out quickly and place him facing the road that leads to the tomb of Saint Ludger. I believe that he will be healed through the merits of that man of God.”

Accordingly, while the mother was fulfilling her vow for the half-dead boy according to her mistress’s command, immediately, in that same place and at that same moment, the demon was expelled and he received complete health. Then, in accordance with the vow that had been made, his mother led him healthy to the aforementioned tomb of the man of God, and he returned healthy.

[Note: Antwerp and the Benedictines: “He returned healthy and, by the Lord’s gift, remained in the health he had received.” With these words ends the Life of Saint Ludger published by the Antwerp editors and the Benedictines. What follows in our copy is either by a continuator or by Altfrid himself; it is also found, in nearly the same words, in the Acts of an anonymous contemporary Frisian, edited by Brower from a Fulda manuscript.]

21. Yet although Ludger wished to conceal all works of this kind, he did not entirely succeed, since God revealed them. There is a village in Saxony, in the district of Suderge, called Alna.

[Note: Cincinnius, in the title, chapter 24, calls it Alen.]

When he came there while visiting his parishes, one day, as he was sitting at table, a poor man was heard outside crying out and anxiously begging that the bishop would deign to look upon a blind man. The deacon whose duty this was hurried out, supposing him to be one of the poor people who had come to ask for alms. Taking bread and food, he offered them to him. The man refused to accept them, saying that something else was necessary for him. Drink was brought. He replied that he did not want that either, and that he had not come to ask for alms, but to be admitted before the bishop so that he might help a blind man.

The deacon, however, not understanding what he had requested, dismissed him and returned to the house. But the man, left outside, continued shouting for a long time. At last Ludger looked around and said to the deacon: “Why do you wish to disregard for so long what you hear?” He replied: “I brought him food and drink, but he cares for none of these things.” “Give him a coin,” the bishop said. When this had been done and was nevertheless rejected, the bishop ordered him to be brought in to him.

When he had been admitted, he said to him: “What is wrong, brother? What do you seek?” The man replied: “Make me see, I beg you, for the love of God.” “You shall see,” said Ludger, “for the love of God.”

And, wonderfully, although he had not said this as a command but had merely replied in similar words, astonished at the request, the man immediately saw. Ordered to approach the table, he ate and drank more joyfully, and went away on his way.

22. The most truthful men among his disciples used to report that once, while he was traveling to the count’s court and was passing through the province called Hesse, a dead man had come back to life through his prayers. This man had been condemned to death for the theft of horses belonging to Duke Widekind of the Saxons, so that he was to be tied to a stake in a field and killed by javelins and stones thrown at him.

[Note: Therefore Widekind possessed estates in the territory of the Hesse, at a place called Budenfeld.]

When this had been done, his lifeless body was left in the field. Ludger came by the place, and, learning that the man had been a Christian, sent to Witikind and obtained permission to bury the body. He then ordered the limbs of the entire body, which had been torn apart, to be gathered in a cloak and carried into his tent, until a grave could be prepared for burying the body.

When the time came for the body to be carried out of the tent and placed in the grave, with the bishop standing by, he said: “Take him out of the grave, for there is a spirit in him.” When he had been lifted up, he began to breathe. He was carried back into the tent and revived with drink. The bishop ordered his wounds to be bound, and in a short time he recovered.

A stone cross still stands in that place, erected by the inhabitants as a memorial of this miracle. Because the man was called Buddo, that field has been called Buddonuelt from his name down to the present day.

23. There is a town in Saxony known to many, called Meppea. When the holy bishop was traveling toward Frisia and came near it, he saw not far from the road an assembly of common people gathered on a Sunday. He turned aside, wishing to learn the reason for such a gathering on that day, and saw on a hill, which they had surrounded, that preparations were being made to hang a certain criminal.

He approached and addressed them gently, asking them to hand the man over to him. Or, if it was necessary that he be killed, he asked that they not do it on that day, but rather gather at the church to hear Mass. When he could obtain none of this from the peasants—and they even insulted the cleric with abusive words because the place did not belong to his parish—he scarcely managed to obtain permission to speak with the man briefly about repentance.

This was done. The bishop departed, and the man was hanged on the gallows. But in the evening of that day, when the bishop had traveled six miles from that place and was staying in a village called Aschandorp, the man whom they had hanged a little earlier came and fell at the bishop’s feet.

As everyone marveled and asked what had happened to him, he explained the matter as follows: “When the bishop had departed from there and I was being hauled up onto the gallows, I saw two men riding beside the bishop and conversing with him along the road for some time. Then, shortly afterward, one of them hurried back and placed something beneath me as I hung. Standing firmly upon it, I felt no torment, until those who had hanged me had dispersed and, as the sun was declining, that same man took me down.”

He ordered the man, once released, to follow the bishop’s route as quickly as possible and to give thanks to the holy bishop for the life granted him, which the bishop himself had obtained for him from the Lord while being despised by foolish men. He added that he had no way of knowing how he himself had traversed so great a distance in an instant after the man of God.

Venerable men among his disciples also report many other wonderful things done or said by blessed Ludger. To set them all down would perhaps be an excessive length.

24. Moreover, he diligently sought a place where the monastery that he had once decided to build in honor of the holy relics he had received from the Apostolic See could be constructed, having learned of the desolation of the maritime regions. Two places seemed suitable for building monasteries: one at Witmundi, beside the river Isla,

[Note: A place still known on maps, one league from the city of Sutphen.]

and the other called Ad Cruces, beside the river Arnapa.

[Note: This river is commonly called the Erfft and Erpe; it flows past various towns of the Julia region and empties into the Rhine between Cologne and Doesburg.]

But by devoted fasts and prayers he asked that the will of divine foreknowledge concerning these matters be shown to him. Accordingly, when he came in winter to the place beside the river Arnapa that we have said he had chosen, he ordered a wooden cross to be erected there. Then, alone before the cross, amid deep snow, severe cold, and the long night, he prolonged his vigils in prayer until daylight.

Afterward, by divine revelation, he learned that a monastery could not be established there, but that God had foreseen a place in a certain woodland beside the river Rura for the foundation of a monastery. Therefore, when he reported what he had learned divinely to his companions on the road, he hurried to the place promised by God. After speaking with its owner, he acquired the place in exchange for other land.

Later, when he had been freed from various occupations and was able to find a suitable time for this undertaking, he set out again for that same place, taking with him those whom he knew to be necessary for the work.

25. There was there a certain *sarculum*,

[Note: Surius translates it as “woodland.” The Antwerp editors suspect that *sartulum* should be read, as a diminutive of the Germanic word *sart*, pronounced *hart* in Upper German, signifying not simply a forest but a forest almost impassable because of the density of its undergrowth, such as the place described here.]

completely enclosed on every side by the shade of trees and the density of the forest. After pitching their tents there, they planned at first light to cut down the trees and clear the site for the buildings, if any possibility were offered.

Yet this seemed altogether impossible to them. Therefore, seeking to turn the blessed man completely from his intention, they said that it seemed utterly incredible that the place could ever be made habitable, since the density of the trees and the covering of the branches hid even the sky itself.

But he placed his hope in the Lord and said: “What is impossible for human beings is possible for God.”

When night came and they had risen earlier for the nocturnal vigils, after completing the office they returned to bed. When he thought that everyone was now asleep, he quietly rose, left the tent, and withdrew a little for the sake of prayer. But one of his companions, a cleric named Thiatbat, kept watch at that same hour and immediately followed him outside. The man of God soon noticed this, paused briefly as though to inspect the hour, then entered the tent and came out again. The same cleric whom we mentioned followed him.

Thus, on the second occasion as well, his prayer having been interrupted, he ordered the cleric to return to his bed and not rise before daylight. He too returned to bed, in order to evade the cleric’s curiosity.

After waiting for some time and supposing that no one was keeping watch, he rose a third time. Going out, he devoted himself to prayer beneath a certain tree. But when the aforementioned cleric, contrary to the command of authority, did not dare to follow him and was determined to discover what he intended to do, he lifted the flap of the tent beside his bed and saw him engaged in prayer. The night was exceedingly bright with moon and stars.

After he had prayed for a very long time and had learned through the spirit that he had been heard by God, he returned to the tent, supposing that everyone was unaware. Immediately the clear sky that had prevailed changed: the stars were obscured, and a violent storm followed as winds arose from different directions. Ancient trees fell all around, and, despite the great fear of everyone, the very elements served the servant of God.

When they arose at daybreak, they saw that the forest had been torn up here and there, providing ample space for founding the monastery, while the trees lying scattered about supplied enough timber for construction. Therefore, when day had become bright, Saint Ludger urged his men to continue the remaining work and began jokingly to ask them whether they still thought they would see the sky from that place.

26. In the morning, of the trees that we have said had fallen there, only one remained standing. Beneath it the man of God had prayed during the same night. Now, with a little seat placed beneath it in broad daylight, he encouraged his men to work.

There, one of his clerics named Odilgrimus came to him from the journey on which he had been sent. During the conversation they had with one another, Ludger asked him what he thought of the place and whether he considered it suitable for a community of monks.

But when the cleric saw that his face was brighter than usual, he said: “In your face I see that this work has not been begun without God’s will. This place, long ago chosen by God, will be most suitable for divine service.”

Pleased by this reply, Ludger said: “Give thanks, because, speaking according to my will, you have shown the good will that a human being alone can show; but the outcome rests in God’s power. I want you to know this, though while I live I do not wish you to make it public to others: I shall await the day of judgment in this place, and here, where I now sit, I shall have my monument.”

Thus the cleric carefully observed the tree for as long as it stood there. But afterward, when it was cut down for use by the church being built toward its western side, he secretly buried a stone in that place as a marker. Later, when a grave was being dug there for the saint, the stone was unearthed.

27. Whenever he was in difficulties or anxious while dealing with important matters, he was accustomed to begin immediately in this way: he instructed a priest to celebrate Masses, ordered religious men or women to fast, invited the poor and needy, and thus commended himself to the Lord in all his steps.

He promptly distributed all the revenue collected from his hereditary property or from the bishopric. He took care of nothing beyond what was strictly necessary for more confined buildings [F.: more august buildings] or for elaborate appurtenances. Therefore, when some of the king’s princes accused him of stripping the bishopric, saying that he neither provided suitable dignity for the buildings nor ornaments of precious metal appropriate to the churches, the most glorious emperor summoned him to his presence.

When Ludger arrived and had been given lodging at the palace, the emperor sent a chamberlain to him early in the morning and ordered him to come to an interview. At that time, however, the bishop was occupied, as usual, with psalms and prayers. He told the chamberlain to go ahead and said that he would follow as soon as the divine office had been completed.

When messengers came a second and a third time and he was not moved from the work he had begun, his accusers rejoiced that they had found an opportunity and added this conduct to their charges against him.

But when he came before the emperor after completing the psalmody, the emperor said: “Why, bishop, have you received our command so reluctantly, that, summoned by so many messengers, you disdained to come immediately?”

Ludger replied: “Because I believed that God ought to be placed before you, O king, and before all human beings. You yourself commanded this of me when you entrusted me with episcopal care. Therefore, although summoned by your messengers, I judged it improper to interrupt the service of the Almighty. But as soon as the divine service was completed, I came more readily at the king’s command.”

The excellent emperor revered this answer and said: “Thank you, bishop, for I now find you to be just as I formerly judged you. Some people have maliciously interpreted your good works to me, but henceforth I shall hold them in less favor, and I promise that I shall no longer accept anyone’s words against you.”

28. Since mention has been made of his sacred duties, they relate that, when the man of God stood at the divine office, he remained with ineffable fear and a fixed mind.

Once, while he was traveling, a bed was prepared for him near a hearth. At night, as he stood beside the bed singing the morning praises with the clerics, smoke rose from the embers covered with ashes and blew into his face. He stood motionless in mind and body, as though he felt nothing.

One of the clerics, wishing to remove this discomfort, bent his knee, uncovered the coals, and, blowing upon them, revived the smoldering fire. In the morning Ludger summoned the cleric and questioned him distinctly—

[Note: Perhaps *districte*, “strictly.”]

—asking why he had acted so thoughtlessly that, abandoning the sacred hymns, he had bent down instead to tend the fire. He imposed on him a penance of several days and taught the clerics that, when attending the divine office, they must drive away every distracting thought and, as far as the fickleness of the human heart permits, think of nothing else.

29. [Note: What appears in this chapter from this point to the end is not found in any printed copy of the life or miracles of Saint Ludger known to date.]

Thus, concerning the holy passing of the most blessed man, we see that we ought not so much to grieve as to rejoice. We ought to give thanks that God granted such a man to our times: one equal to the saints of earlier ages, incomparable among the people of this age, and set before posterity as an example for imitation.

We ought to give thanks that he caused us to have him as a patron from being a shepherd. For although we trust that all the saints are our patrons, we may nevertheless reasonably hope that he protects us, unworthy though we are, with a special patronage.

How powerful his patronage is with God is testified by the healings of the sick, whom he assists in various necessities. Therefore we do not mourn him as dead, but pray that, as one living, he may help us by the assistance of his prayers.

O truly blessed man and most worthy of every praise, not undeservedly to be compared with angels, prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, and virgins: with the angels, in purity and contemplation of heavenly things; with the prophets, in knowledge of future events; with the apostles, in succession to pastoral care and imitation of preaching; with the martyrs, in chastisement of the flesh and desire for martyrdom; with the confessors, in confessing the divine name before kings and princes; with virgins, in purity of body and mind alike.

Who would not venerate his holiness? Who would not marvel at the working of his miracles? Who would not admire his humility in concealing his signs? These things are greater than the dryness of our tongue can adequately express.

He has no need of the praise of our speech, for he is renowned among mortals for such prodigies and glorified in heaven among the angels and the choirs of all the saints. There, now joined to Christ, may he intercede for us, his servants, and for those who serve him, with Christ himself, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0795]

## Extract from the Rhythmic Litanies Containing the Life of Saint Ludger, Written at Werden: On the Foundation of the Monastery at Helmstedt by Saint Ludger

(From Leibniz, in the same place.)

### From Litany I

[Col. 0795C]

Moreover, he founded three places together,

In number of places as well as of peoples:

He founded Werden and Helmstedt for monks,

From property or hereditary possession,

And the bishopric called the monastery, etc.

### From Litany II

So that he was always diligent to give

A lesson every morning to many disciples.

Instructing and training them himself,

He led them through honorable conduct to honors.

Of these, very many became bishops;

As did his first brother Hildegrim,

Who had formerly been bishop in a certain Church—

Bishop of Châlons, under Rheims—

[Col. 0796C]

Where, while he lived and governed what had been entrusted to him,

And saw that his brother Ludger prospered in converting

The peoples whom he had won from paganism to Christ,

He himself, plainly warned by divine providence,

Committed himself to the people of North Thuringia,

Using the aid and hospitality of his brother,

Who remained in the place called Helmstedt.

There, arranging the holiest seeds

Of the Gospels, they cast them into

The hearts of the North Thuringians,

Until the grace of God

Made fruit grow there, reaching to heaven.

The bishopric is still a testimony,

Where that same Hildegrim began his see;

Although his body is buried at Werden,

He is nevertheless the patron of Halberstadt. Amen.

[Col. 0795]

## Werden Cartulary

(From Leibniz, in the same place.)

[Col. 0795D] **In the name of the Holy Trinity begins the Book of Charters of the Exchange with Folcbert at Widuberg.**

### 1. Exchange with Folcbert

I wish it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Ludger the priest, purchased for a fixed price a small portion of an inheritance from Theganbald, a freeborn and noble man, in the village called Fislacu (Fislack), namely that Hova which is called Alfgedine-Hova, with complete rights, whether in forest, pasture, and paths, or in the use and courses of the waters.

All these things I, Ludger the priest, purchased from the aforesaid noble Frank Theganbald, and for several years possessed and worked it as much as I could. Now, however, I gave the same Hova, with all the arable land in it, whatever had ever been plowed there, to Folcbert in exchange for that Roth which is called Widuberg, between two streams: namely between the Diapanbeci and another on the west, extending to the river Rura.

Except that I, Ludger, retained for myself the lordship belonging to that Hova—whether in forest, waters, pasture, or clearing—with all its rights, reserving it to my own legal possession. In this arrangement I received that Roth from Folcbert, my neighbor, in exchange for the arable land of the aforesaid Hova, so that I might possess it forever by hereditary right and devote it to the eternal uses of the Church of God and its servants.

I shall have free and firm power over all of it, whether during my lifetime or after my death, to do whatever I decide will be useful from it, provided that it pertains to and advances its productive use.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs or those claiming through my heirs, or any opposing person, should attempt by an unjust effort to act against this charter of exchange or wish to violate it, may he immediately incur the wrath of the heavenly God, be separated from the fellowship of the holy angels, and be excluded from entry into all churches until he has corrected his wicked presumption.

Moreover, let him be fined by the treasury and compelled to pay two pounds of gold and ten pounds’ weight of silver. Thus may he be unable to vindicate what he claims, while this exchange, supported by stipulation, shall remain firm and unaltered forever.

This was publicly enacted in the twenty-first year of the glorious and religious second King Charles, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, at the place called Diapanbeci on the bank of the Rura, before the witnesses and those who placed their hands, whose names are written below. I have recorded the time, day, and place at which these things were done. I, Thiatbald, humble priest, wrote and subscribed this at the request of the parties.

Sign of Folcbert, who requested that this charter be made and confirmed it with his own hand. Sign of Regenberth. Sign of Alfdagi. Sign of Bonno. Sign of Fridubald. Sign of Hluduwin. Sign of Giffud. Sign of Bornger. Sign of Hildirad. Sign of Borbin. Sign of Luidric. Sign of Walafrid.

### Donation of Hludwin to Werden

2. I wish it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Hludwin, in the name of God, son of the late Thiather, for the remedy of my soul and for eternal recompense, donated all my share of the inheritance at the place called Werden to the relics of Saint Savior and to the venerable man Ludger, abbot, who is accustomed always to carry those relics with him.

This consists of the land between two streams that rise on the mountain and flow into the river Rura. One is called Diapanbeci; the other lies on the eastern side, without a specific name, extending from the arable land to the river Rura. I wish this donation to remain perpetual and unaltered at any time.

The venerable abbot Ludger himself shall hold and possess this donation—which is known to have formerly been my clearing—together and in full with the land there that already appears to have been cultivated, throughout all time, for the uses of the Church of God. He shall have free and firm power over it, against me and all my heirs, to do whatever he wishes with it and to place it in whatever person’s hands he decides, while he yet lives, so that after his death that person may cultivate it and devote it to the benefit of the Church of God.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs, or any opposing person, should attempt to act against this donation, may he immediately incur the wrath of the heavenly God and be anathematized from the fellowship of all churches. Moreover, let him be compelled to pay to the Lord’s treasury five pounds of gold and ten pounds’ weight of silver.

Thus may he be unable to vindicate what he claims, while this donation, supported by stipulation, shall remain firm and unaltered forever.

This was publicly enacted in the twenty-first year of the reign of the most religious King Charles, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, before those who placed their hands, at the place called Diapanbeci or Werden, whose names are recorded below. I have recorded the day, place, and time at which I wrote this. I, Thiatbald, humble priest, wrote and subscribed this at the request of the parties.

Sign of Hludwin, who carried out this donation with the dominant hand and confirmed it below with his own hand.

Sign of Reginbert. Sign of Thiathald. Sign of Thiathor. Sign of Frithurad. Sign of Frithubald. Sign of Frithubrand. Sign of Reginbald. Sign of Theganrad.

### Donation of Oodhelm to Witmund

3. Since everyone lives in the present age, each person ought to consider and weigh how to acquire life and everlasting reward after death. Therefore I, Oodhelm, son of the late Oodwerc, for the remedy of my soul and for eternal recompense, donated part of my inheritance, which came to me by hereditary right under the law: namely three Hovas in three places, whose names are as follows.

One Hova is at Okinni in the district of Isla; another is at Manheri, namely Selihova, in the district of Northuanti; the third is at Hasungun in the same district.

What I have just named I donated to the relics of the holy Savior established at Witmund and into the hands of Ludger the priest. I wish the donation to remain perpetual and never thereafter to be altered, but that the guardians of the same church may possess all these things with unimpaired integrity for its perpetual uses.

Only this condition applies: during our lifetimes, I and my beloved wife Theodlinda may hold these properties in usufruct as a benefice of the same church, namely that each year we must give one solidus for the church lights at the Nativity of the Lord.

After our departure from this life, the properties themselves, improved and with all their integrity, shall pass into the lordship of the aforementioned church. Its lawful administrators shall have free and firm power against all persons to do with them whatever they wish for the church’s benefit.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs or those claiming through my heirs, instigated by the devil, should attempt to act against this donation or wish to violate it, may he immediately incur the wrath of the heavenly God, be separated from the fellowship of the holy angels, and be excluded from entry into all churches until he has corrected his wicked presumption.

Moreover, let him be compelled to pay to the Lord’s treasury two pounds of gold and ten pounds’ weight of silver. Thus may he be unable to vindicate what he claims, while this donation, supported by stipulation, shall remain firm and unaltered forever.

This was publicly enacted at the place itself called Witmund, in the twenty-first year of the reign of the most religious King Charles, on the fifth day before the Ides of June. I have recorded the day, time, and place at which this was written. I, Thiatbald, humble priest, wrote and subscribed this at the request of the parties.

Sign of Oodhelm, who requested that this charter of donation be made and confirmed it with his own hand. Sign of Hildign. Sign of Meginulf. Sign of Ludger. Sign of Meginung. Sign of Gerwin. Sign of Marcric. Sign of Thathumer. Sign of Gerhard.

### Donation of Imma

4. I wish it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Imma, donated part of my inheritance to the church of the holy Savior, which has been built in the district of the Ripuarii, at the place called Werden, on the river Rura.

That is, I donated in the district of Sutrachi, in the village called Aldgreposhem, land for twenty and a half animals; and in another village, land for fifteen animals, which is called Kompingwerva in that same district; and in a third village, land for twelve animals, which is called Inwostarburon in the district of Westrachi.

I wish this donation to remain perpetual, and I confirm it with the readiest will. I have transferred it from my power into their power, so that from this day forward they may have free and firm power against all persons to hold, possess, exchange, and do whatever they wish with it.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself afterward, or any of my heirs, or any opposing person, should wish to act against this donation made by me, or attempt to violate or alter it, may he immediately incur the wrath of Almighty God and become a stranger to the thresholds of the saints. Let the present donation remain firm, supported by stipulation.

This was enacted at the monastery of Werden on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the sixth year of the reign of Lord King Louis, in the eighth indiction. I, Thiathard, humble deacon, wrote and subscribed this at the request of the parties.

Sign of Imma, who made this donation and confirmed it with his own hand. These are the witnesses and hearers:

Sign of Rembert. Sign of Erpolf. Sign of Aldhard. Sign of Wichard. Sign of Snclger. Sign of Erbald. Sign of Iti. Sign of Sigiward. Sign of Heio.

### Donation of Henry beside the Rura
[Col. 0799B] **5.** While each person lives in the present age, he ought to consider and provide how he may save his soul and find eternal refreshment for himself after the temporal and mortal life of this world. Therefore, having weighed this in my heart and revolved it in frequent meditation, I, Henry, have given, for the remedy of my soul and for eternal recompense, to the relics of Saint Saviour and of Saint Mary ever-virgin, and into the hands of the presbyter Ludger, who cared for those same relics, a portion of my inheritance and of my own labor: namely, the whole tract enclosed in the forest called Hoissi, on the northern bank of the River Rura, which I formerly enclosed there between the mountain and that river, together with my share in the same forest.

In like manner I have given the fishing-right in the Rura, together with the pastures, roads, and watercourses belonging thereto, which can be cultivated and improved in that place. All these things I have given to the relics named above and into the hands of the aforesaid presbyter, and I wish them to be given in perpetuity [Col. 0799C] and never thereafter altered through any passage of time. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the Church of God, as my alms, the aforesaid presbyter Ludger shall possess, hold, cultivate, and make fruitful all these things by hereditary right; and he shall have free and most secure authority from me and from everyone to entrust and give them after his death to whomever he shall determine and recognize to be useful.

But if anyone, stirred up by the devil—which I nevertheless do not believe will happen—whether I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs or acting on behalf of my heirs, or any outsider, should attempt to act against this gift or deliberately and resolutely propose to violate it, let him first incur the wrath of the heavenly God, be separated from the fellowship of the holy angels, and be excluded from entry into all churches until he corrects himself from his wicked presumption. Moreover, under compulsion, let him pay to the royal fisc two pounds of gold and ten weights of silver. And thus, whatever he claims, let him be unable to recover; but let this gift remain firm and unalterable forever, supported by legal stipulation. [Col. 0799D]

It was publicly enacted in the reign of our most devout lord, King Charles, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, in the villa called Hlopanheldi, before the witnesses and manumissors whose names are written below. And so that this testament of gift might endure more firmly forever, I have recorded the time, day, and place in which it was made. I, Thiatbaldus, humble presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

Sign of Henry, who completed this gift and confirmed it with his own hand. Sign of Hriatthruda, his wife, consenting and confirming. Sign of Aeaeric, his son, doing the same. Sign of Bernger, confirming below. Sign of Alberct, cleric. Sign of Hluduwind. Sign of Theganbald. Sign of Guntfrid. Sign of Oodfinn. Sign of Hildibert. Sign of Wimberct. Sign of Cassus, deacon. Sign of Raafrid. Sign of Landbert.

**Gift of Ludger.**

**6.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Ludger, son of the late Hrodger, for the remedy of my soul and for eternal recompense, have given to the relics of Saint Saviour and of Saint Mary ever-virgin, and into the hands of the presbyter Ludger, who cared for those same relics, my share of the inheritance: namely, everything that came to me by hereditary right according to law in the villa called Bidningahem and in another called Thornspye, whether arable land, meadows, or pastures, and my entire share with me in the forest called Huistarbant, except for one portion in the meadow called Blidgeryngmad, which I have reserved for my needs.

I have given all the rest to the relics named above and into the hands of the aforesaid presbyter, in its entirety, in the little estates mentioned earlier, whether arable land, meadows and pastures, fisheries, watercourses, and common roads belonging to those estates. I wish all these things to be given in perpetuity and never thereafter altered at any time; rather, for the perpetual uses of the Church of God, the aforesaid presbyter Ludger shall possess them by hereditary right.

But if anyone, stirred up by the devil—whether I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs or acting on behalf of my heirs, or any outsider—should attempt to act against this gift or resolve with fixed and deliberate intention to violate it, let him first incur the wrath of the heavenly God, be separated from the fellowship of the holy angels, and be excluded from the thresholds of all churches until he corrects himself from his wicked presumption. And thus, whatever he claims, let him be unable to recover; but let this gift remain firm and unalterable forever, supported by legal stipulation.

It was publicly enacted at the place called Adosumnis (Rocroort), in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of our most devout lord, King Charles, on the day of the Kalends, the eighth day before the Ides of June, before the witnesses and manumissors whose names are written below. And so that this testament of gift might be held more firmly forever, I have recorded the day, time, and place [Col. 0800C] in which these things were done. I, Thiatbaldus, humble presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

Sign of Ludger, who made this gift as his alms and confirmed it below with his own hand.

Sign of Bernsuida, consenting. Sign of Gerwal. Sign of Welfric. Sign of Bago. Sign of Hrodbert. Sign of Wigbald. Sign of Borhtric. Sign of Fefinger. Sign of Wilbald. Sign of Helmric. Sign of Luidberth. Sign of Meginbald. Sign of Bernhard. Sign of Hiddon. Sign of Hrafaugrim. Sign of Weringer. Sign of Folcrad. Sign of Raadger.

**Gift of Folchard, Reginald, and Gerhard, etc., at Withmundi.**

**7.** We desire it to be known to all, present and future, how we, the heirs, co-sharers, and kinsmen named Reginald, Folchard, Gerhard, Wifel, and Helmberth, have given our hereditary land at Withmundi to Ludger, presbyter and abbot, in order to build a church upon it, on the northern side of that field which Ludger himself received from Count Wrachar, who made the gift. We wish it to be given in perpetuity and never altered at any time; rather, for the perpetual uses and benefit of the Church of God, the aforesaid presbyter shall have from us and from everyone free and most secure authority to do with it while alive whatever he wishes, or after his death to give it to whomever he decides, for cultivation and production in the Church of God.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—whether we ourselves, God forbid, or any of our heirs or acting on behalf of our heirs, should attempt to act against this gift or, stirred up by the devil, wish to violate it, let him first incur the wrath of the heavenly God, be separated from the fellowship of the holy angels, and be excluded from entry into all churches until he corrects himself from his wicked presumption. Moreover, under compulsion, let him pay to the royal fisc two pounds of gold and ten weights of silver, [Col. 0801A] and thus let him be unable to recover whatever he claims; but let this gift remain firm and unalterable forever, supported by legal stipulation.

It was publicly enacted at the very place called Withmundi, in the thirty-second year of the reign of the most devout King Charles, on the thirteenth day of October. I have recorded the day, place, and time when these things were written. I, Thiatbaldus, humble presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

These are the witnesses and hearers:

Sign of Folchard, Gerhard, Wifel, and Helmberth, who completed this gift and confirmed it with their own hands. Sign of Hildiger. Sign of Oodhelm. Sign of Meginung. Sign of Walfrid. Sign of Werinberth. Sign of Hrodbert. Sign of Ludger. Sign of Werinhard. Sign of Engilbert.

**Gift of Hrodulf at Englandi.**

**8.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Hrodulf, son of the late Wibald, have given to the relics of Saint Saviour and of Saint Mary ever-virgin, and into the hands of Ludger the abbot, a portion of my inheritance in the county of Folum (Velow), in the villa called Englandi: namely, one enclosed homestead and a twelfth part of the forest called Braclog, with the pastures and full lordship which has been found by legal right to belong to that homestead.

I have given all these things as my alms to the relics named above and into the hands of the aforesaid abbot, and I wish them to be given in perpetuity and never thereafter altered through any passage of time. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the Church of God, the abbot Ludger shall have free and most secure authority from me and from everyone to do with them whatever he wishes, supported by legal stipulation.

It was publicly enacted at the place called Wigtmundi, at the church of Saint Saviour, in the thirty-third year of the reign of our most devout lord King Charles, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, before the witnesses and manumissors whose names are written below. And so that this testament of gift [Col. 0801C] might endure more firmly forever, I have recorded the time, day, and place in which it was written. I, Thiatbaldus, presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

Sign of Hrodulf, who completed this gift with dominant hand and confirmed it below.

Sign of Hildiger. Sign of Ludger. Sign of Eurwin. Sign of Ludger. Sign of Meginberth. Sign of Engilberth. Sign of Oodhelm. Sign of Germund.

**Gift of Hirping.**

**9.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Hirping, son of the late [lacuna], having received a price from Ludger the abbot, sold him one vineyard in the villa called Bacheim, which villa also lies on the bank of the river called Melenbach (Melem near Bonn), and I firmly transferred it to him. I wish it to be given in perpetuity and never altered at any time; rather, for his perpetual uses and those of the Church of God after his death, he shall have from me and from everyone free and most secure authority to do with it whatever he wishes, supported by legal stipulation.

It was publicly enacted in Saxony, where we were then on campaign, at the place called Minmithum (Minden), in the thirtieth year of the reign of our most devout lord King Charles, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, before the witnesses and manumissors whose names are written below. And so that this testament might be held more firmly, I have recorded the day, time, and place in which it was written. I, Thiatbaldus, presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

Sign of Hirping, who made this gift and confirmed it with his own hand. Sign of Hildibrand. Sign of Bernger. Sign of Hugbald. Sign of Gundhold. Sign of Bernger. Sign of Wanberth. Sign of Hathubald.

**Gift of Ludger and Hiddon.**

**10.** I, Ludger, son of the late Hrodger, and I, Hiddon, son of the late Herewin, desire it to be known to all, present and future, how we have given a portion of our own inheritance to Ludger the bishop, for the remedy of our souls and for eternal recompense, in the villa called Thornspic (Dornspick), in these two places: Quarsingseli and Borugtanseotan. Whatever we had there, whether by hereditary right, by enclosure, or by any other acquisition, all this we have given in its entirety to Ludger the bishop as our alms, and we wish it to be given in perpetuity and never altered at any time. Rather, for his perpetual uses and for the benefit of the Church of God, he shall have from us and from everyone free and most secure authority to do with it whatever he wishes.

It was publicly enacted, supported by legal stipulation, in the villa called Bidingahem, in the thirty-seventh year of the reign of the glorious Emperor Charles, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, before the witnesses and manumitters whose names are written below. And so that this gift might endure more firmly [Col. 0802B] forever, I have recorded the day and place in which these things were written. I, Thiatbaldus, presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

Sign of Ludger, who completed this gift with dominant hand and recorded it below.

Sign of Hiddon, likewise making the gift and confirming it below. Sign of Marchard. Sign of Baior. Sign of Holmeric. Sign of Hengilbald. Sign of Luidberth. Sign of Wilbald. Sign of Folcrad. Sign of Reginger. Sign of Lodoc. Sign of Gerbert. Sign of Thiatbald.

**Gift of Eforwin and his parents.**

**11.** While each person lives in the present age and appears to possess this mortal life in the body, he ought to consider and foresee how he may acquire for himself in the future state and in an everlasting dwelling some remedy and salvation for his soul in the heavens. Therefore it pleased us, co-heirs and co-sharers in one patrimony, named Erfurwin, Hildirad, and Irminwin, at the request of Ludger the presbyter, to give to the relics of Saint Saviour—which Ludger himself always carries with him—and into the hands of that same presbyter, as our alms, a portion of our inheritance; and this we did as follows:

In our own inheritance and lordship, in the forest called Hoissi, we gave that tract which Ludger himself desired to enclose there, and which Hildirad enclosed together with him in our name and assigned to the aforesaid relics of Saint Saviour. In like manner we gave into the hands of that same presbyter a certain lordship in the same forest adjoining the tract mentioned above.

This enclosure which we have given, beside those enclosures which Henry and Hluduwin formerly gave, some years ago, to the same relics and to Ludger himself, is contiguous and joined to them from the top to the end. This is the gift which we have given as our alms, and we wish it to be given in perpetuity and never thereafter altered. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the Church of God, the presbyter who received it shall have from us and from everyone free and most secure authority to do with it whatever he wishes for the benefit of the Church of God. [Col. 0802D]

It was publicly enacted, supported by legal stipulation, at the very place called Diapanbeci, in the thirty-second year of the reign of the glorious King Charles, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October. I have recorded the day, place, and time when these things were written. I, Thiatbaldus, presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

These are the witnesses and hearers:

Sign of Evurwin, who requested that this gift be made and confirmed it with his own hand.

Sign of Irminwin. Sign of Heribald. Sign of Hildirad. Sign of Anolon. Sign of Efurhard. Sign of Thiatfrid.

**Gift of Amulric at the Cross near Arnapa.**

**12.** While each person lives in the present age, he ought to consider and foresee how he may save his soul and find eternal refreshment for himself after the temporal and mortal life of this world. Therefore, having weighed this in my heart and revolved it in frequent meditation, I, Amulric, have given, for the remedy of my soul and for eternal recompense, to the relics of Saint Saviour and of Saint Mary ever-virgin, and into the hands of the presbyter Ludger, who cared for those same relics, a portion of my inheritance: namely, the very place called Ad-Crucem, with the meadows lying there on the bank of the River Arnapa, where formerly my grandfather Irminfrid had a dwelling with two fields, which are separated not far from that same place; and a lordship in the forest called Sitrath, with pastures, roads, waters, and fisheries that can be cultivated and improved in that place.

I have given all these things to the relics named above and into the hands of the aforesaid presbyter, and I wish them to be given in perpetuity and never thereafter altered through any passage of time. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the Church of God, the aforesaid presbyter Ludger shall possess, hold, cultivate, and make fruitful all these things as my alms; and he shall have free and most secure authority by hereditary right, from me and from everyone, to entrust and give them after his death to whomever he determines and recognizes to be useful. [Col. 0803B]

It was publicly enacted, supported by legal stipulation, in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our most devout lord King Charles, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the villa called Hrodberhtinga-Hova, before the witnesses and manumissors whose names are written below. And so that this testament of gift might endure more firmly forever, I have recorded the time, day, and place in which it was written. I, Thiatbaldus, presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

Sign of Amulric, who completed this gift and confirmed it with his own hand. Sign of Helmberth. Sign of Goduberth. Sign of Folcberth. Sign of Hrundulf. Sign of Eoric. Sign of Hildifrid. Sign of Duodo. Sign of Friduric. Sign of Alfger. Sign of Guntberth.

**Gift of Theganbald.**

[Col. 0803C] **13.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Theganbald, son of the late Hrodbald, have given a portion of my inheritance to Ludger the abbot in the villa called Fislacu, beside the bank of the River Rura: namely, the entire Hova called Alfating-Hova, with pastures, roads, and watercourses, and Seara in the forest beside the boundary of the full Hova.

I have given all these things, as stated above, as my alms and that of my wife Regintruda, to Ludger the abbot, and I wish them to be given in perpetuity and never altered at any time. Rather, for his perpetual uses and the benefit of the Church of God, Ludger the abbot himself shall possess the aforesaid Hova with complete integrity by hereditary right, and shall have from me and from everyone free and most secure authority to do with it whatever he wishes.

It was publicly enacted, supported by legal stipulation, in the twenty-eighth year of the reign of our most devout lord King Charles, on the second day before the Kalends of April, at the place called Ad-Crucem, in the county of Nivansheim, on the bank of the River Arnapa. It was confirmed by the hand of Bernger, my nephew, to whom I myself gave authority for this purpose, in the very villa named above, namely Fisclacu, where the same Hova lies, before the witnesses and manumissors whose names are written below. And so that this testament of gift might endure more firmly forever, I have recorded the time, day, and place in which it was written. I, Thiatbaldus, presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

Sign of Bernger, who, having received authority from Theganbald, completed this testament and confirmed it with his own hand.

Sign of Hrodrich. Sign of Hildirad. Sign of Reginberth. Sign of Bernhard. Sign of Berwin. Sign of Hlotwin. Sign of Waldmar. Sign of Eforwin. Sign of Benno. Sign of Alfnand. Sign of Herebald.

**Gift of Hiddon and his wife Madalgard.**

**14.** Let it be known to all, present and future, how I, Hiddon, son of the late Heriwin, for the remedy of my soul and for the remedy of my wife Madalgard, have given a portion of our inheritance to Bishop Ludger in these places: first, in Quarsingsoli, Bertanscotam, Bochurssi, and Tolgud. In Quarsingsoli, everything that we had there in our enclosure; in Bertanscotam, everything; in Bochurssi, half of what we had there; and in Tolgud, a third part of what was ours.

We have given all these things and wish them to be given in perpetuity and never altered at any time. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the Church of God and his own benefit, Ludger the bishop shall have authority to do with them whatever he wishes, and shall have free and most secure authority from us and from everyone forever.

This gift was publicly enacted, supported by legal stipulation, in the thirty-ninth year of the reign of the most devout Emperor Charles, on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the villa called Bidningahem, before the witnesses and manumitters whose names are written below. And so that this gift might be held more firmly [Col. 0804B] forever, I have recorded the day, place, and time when it was completed and written. I, Thiatbaldus, presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

Sign of Hiddon, who carried out this gift with dominant hand and confirmed it below.

Sign of Ludger. Sign of Berather. Sign of Marchard. Sign of Liudberth. Sign of Wilbald. Sign of Folcberth. Sign of Folcrad. Sign of Gerberth. Sign of Holmric. Sign of Hildiward.

**Gift of Wolf.**

**15.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Wolf, and my brother Reinbrat, together with my sisters Osbirin and Meinbirin, have given a portion of our inheritance: namely, at Saginandum, twenty pigs and eight day-works of cultivated and uncultivated land, with all appurtenances.

We have given these things for the remedy of our souls and of the soul of our mother to the church of the Saviour, which was built at the place called Werthina, in the county of Riporum, on the River Rura. We confirm this with our own hands, and let this present gift remain firm.

Enacted at the monastery of Werithina in the twentieth year of the reign of the lord Emperor Hluduwic, in the first indiction.

Sign of Wolf, who made this gift. Sign of Meinbirin, his sister. Sign of Osbirin, his sister. Sign of Reginberth, his brother, who likewise made this gift. Sign of Gundhard. Sign of Heribald. Sign of Bonno. Sign of Irminnoth. Sign of Berhar. Sign of Hildibald. I, Hrodbaldus, humble presbyter, wrote and subscribed it at their request.

**Gift of Fridric, Hildibert, and Altperct at Ripo.**

**16.** We, Frithuric, Hildibert, and Altprect, desire it to be known to all, present and future, how, for the remedy of our souls, we have given to the relics of Saint Saviour, Saint Mary, and Saint Peter, which are deposited in the county of the Ripuarian people, at the place called Werithina on the River Rura. We wish it to be given in perpetuity and have confirmed it with the readiest goodwill.

This [lacuna] our property in the county mentioned above, in one place where Frithuric and Hildibert, brothers, by common agreement gave, at the boundary belonging to Hrotberhtinga-Hova, three day-works of arable land. It is bounded on both sides by royal land; on one end by the land of Hildigrim, and on the other end by the land of Saint Peter.

In another place the aforesaid brothers gave, at the boundary belonging to Weldi, three day-works of arable land. It is bounded on both sides and at one end by the land of Frithuric; at the other end, by the land of Dodun within this boundary. What we have given by common agreement shall, after this day, benefit those relics as an increase.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—should later arise, whether we ourselves or any of our heirs, and attempt to act against this gift or try to violate it, let him pay to you, together with the associated fisc, a fine of one pound of gold and five weights of silver, under compulsion; and let him be unable to recover whatever he claims. Rather, let this present gift remain firm, supported by legal stipulation. [Col. 0805A]

Enacted at Ad-Crucem, where it was written, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the fifth year while the lord Emperor Hludowic was ruling.

These are the witnesses and hearers:

Sign of Altbert, Frideric, and Hildibert, who requested that this gift be made and confirmed. Sign of Ercanfrid. Sign of Alfger. Sign of Gerwin. Sign of Widrad. Sign of Hildimar. Sign of Hludubret. Sign of Heriulf. Sign of Ausgor. Sign of Hildigrim the bishop. Sign of Hirminger. Sign of Ausger. I, Adalgerus, deacon, wrote and subscribed it at their request.

**Sale of Friduric.**

**17.** In Christ, to Brother Hildegrim, bishop and purchaser, I, Friduric, seller.

It is established that I have sold to you, and thus I have sold, my own property situated in the county of Nivenhem, in the villa of Hrodbertinga-Hova on the River Gilibech: namely, two day-works of land. On one side they have the land of Saint Andrew; on the other side, the land of the purchaser himself. On one end, the land of Friduric; on the other end, water.

I have transferred them to you perpetually for possession, and I have received from you the price as we agreed and settled between us, namely six solidi, so that after this day you shall have free and most secure authority in every respect to have, hold, sell, or do whatever you wish with them.

It was publicly enacted, supported by legal stipulation, at the place called Ad-Crucem, where it was written, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourth year of the reign of the lord Emperor Hludowic.

These are the witnesses and hearers:

Sign of Friduric, who requested that this gift be made. Sign of Hildibert, who delivered possession. Sign of Grimald, vicar. Sign of Dado. Sign of Heriulf. Sign of Widrad. Sign of Benno. Sign of Heridac. Sign of Hagor. Sign of Adolric. Sign of Brun. Sign of Hodilard. I, Adalgerus, deacon, wrote and subscribed it at his request.

**Gift of Count Hrotstein.**

**18.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Hrotsten, have given a portion of my inheritance to the church of Saint Saviour, which is built in the county of the Ripuarian people, at the place called Werthina, on the River Rura: namely, one unfree woman belonging to my right, named Hildisuit. I wish her to be given in perpetuity, and I wish this present gift to remain firm at all times, supported by legal stipulation.

Enacted at the monastery of Werthina, written on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, in the first year of the reign of the lord Emperor Hludowic, in the fifth indiction. I, Hildiwardus, chancellor, wrote and subscribed it.

**Gift of Abbo at Lopanheldi.**

**19.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Abbo, son of the late Gerrard, have given my inheritance to the church of Saint Saviour, which is built in the county of Riporum, at the place called Werithina on the River Rura: namely, two manses in the aforesaid county, in the villa called Lopanheldi, on the bank of the aforesaid river, both in lands and in forests, as well as in meadows, pastures, waters, and watercourses, with all appurtenances; and the following unfree persons: Wiva, Sigifrid, Radgis, Rattruut, and Frithuric.

I wish these things to be given in perpetuity, and I confirm them with the readiest goodwill. I have also received from the custodians of the aforesaid church the price as we agreed and settled between us, namely twenty-four pounds, and I have transferred them from my authority to theirs, so that after this day they shall have free and most secure authority in every respect to have, hold, possess, exchange, or do whatever they wish with them, supported by legal stipulation.

Enacted at the monastery of Werithina, where it was written, on the Nones before the Kalends of November [as printed; date uncertain], in the twenty-first year while the lord Emperor Hludowic was ruling.

[Col. 0806A] These are the names of the witnesses who saw and heard this:

**Gift of Folcrada.**

**20.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Folcrada, full sister of the late Hemming the exactor, have given one field by hereditary right to Ludger the abbot, having received a price of suitable valuation, beside the Arnapa, near the dwelling called Ad-Crucem.

I wish it to be given in perpetuity and never thereafter altered at any time. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the Church of God, the aforesaid abbot shall possess that field by hereditary right and cause it to bear fruit throughout his life; and he shall have free and most secure authority from me and from everyone to entrust and give it for possession after his death to whomever he wishes.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs, should attempt to act against this gift and resolve to violate it, let him be excluded from entry into all churches and pay five pounds of silver to the royal fisc, and thus let the matter lie without effective action. Let this gift remain firm, supported by legal stipulation.

It was publicly enacted at the very place called Ad-Crucem, before the witnesses and manumissors whose names are written below.

I wish it to be given in perpetuity and have confirmed it with my own hand; and let this present gift remain firm, supported by legal stipulation.

**Gift of Hildirad at Wenaswalda.**

[Col. 0807A]

**23.** Let it be known to all, present and future, how I, Hildirad, son of the late [lacuna], for the remedy of my soul and as an inheritance, have enclosed a tract from the stream called Burgbeki (Bornebeck) to the stream that runs on the western side of Widuberg (Wynberg), giving it to the relics of Saint Saviour and of Saint Mary ever-virgin, and with complete integrity as far as the bank of the Rura, except for that portion which Faecbert formerly began to clear in the nearby corner between the Rura and Widuberg.

Therefore I have given this designated enclosure, in its entirety, as my alms to the relics named above and into the authority of Ludger the abbot, and I wish it to be given in perpetuity and never thereafter altered through any passage of time. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the Church of God, the aforesaid abbot Ludger shall have free and most secure authority by hereditary right, from me and from everyone, to do with it whatever he wishes.

But if anyone, stirred up by the devil—which I nevertheless do not believe will happen—whether I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs or acting on behalf of my heirs, or any other person, should attempt to act against this gift or wish with fixed and deliberate intention to violate it, let him first incur the wrath of the heavenly God and be separated from the fellowship of the holy angels if he does not quickly correct himself from his most wicked presumption. Moreover, under compulsion, let him pay to the royal fisc two pounds of gold and ten weights of silver, and thus let him be unable to recover whatever he claims; but let this gift remain firm and unalterable forever, supported by legal stipulation. [Col. 0807C]

It was publicly enacted at the place called Diapanbeci, on the bank of the Rura, at the relics of Saint Saviour and Saint Mary, in the thirty-third year of the reign of our most devout lord King Charles, on the Kalends of May, before the witnesses and manumissors whose names are written below. And so that this testament might endure more firmly forever, he recorded the time, day, and place in which it was written.

Sign of Hildirad, who completed this gift with dominant hand and confirmed it below.

**Gift of Sigihard.**

**24.** I desire it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Sigihard, have given a portion of my inheritance lying in the villa of Fisclaco, in the county of Ruricgao: namely, I have given a full *jormal* [or *jornal*] of land to the relics of Saint Saviour, which are deposited at the place called Werthina, in the county of Ruricgoa, in the duchy of the Ripuarian people, where the bishops Hildigrim and Gerfrid appear to preside as administrators.

I have given this for the remedy of my soul and for a good eternal recompense, so that from this present day the administrators of that church may have, hold, and possess it; and whatever they wish to do with it, let them have free authority in every respect to do whatever they choose, supported by legal stipulation.

It was publicly enacted on the third day before the Ides of September, in the sixth year while our lord Hludowic, most glorious king and emperor, was reigning.

Sign of Sigihard, who requested that this gift be made and confirmed. Sign of Reginbrat. Sign of Hrodhard. Sign of Ohtric. Sign of Bonno. Sign of Erkinger. Sign of Erimbrot. Sign of Alfric. Sign of Odbold. Sign of Alvold.

I, Liudberth, deacon, wrote and subscribed it.

**Charter concerning the exchange of Bishop Gerfrid and Frithuard at Hesangi and Castorp, and at Werina.**
### 25.

No one is seen to diminish his own estate by accepting in exchange whatever is received as an increase; therefore it was agreed and settled between Bishop Gerfrid and Frithuard that they should exchange their lands wherever the circumstances required. And so they did.

Accordingly, the aforesaid Frithuard gives to the above-mentioned [Col. 0808A] Bishop Gerfrid, in exchange, his land in the village called Hesingi, in the district of the Riparii, on the river Rura: namely, half a mansus, with meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, possessions, and livestock. In return, Bishop Gerfrid gave the above-mentioned Frithuard half a mansus—that is, land alone—in the district of Bortergo, in the village called Castorp. And in return for the pastures and forests which Frithuard gave, Bishop Gerfrid gave twenty furlongs in the district of Dreginni, in the village called Werina.

Therefore they asked that letters written in a single form be drawn up and confirmed between them, so that each might have, hold, and possess whatever he had received from his equal, and might have full and entirely secure power to do with it whatever he wished. And if any of our heirs should wish to violate this exchange, let him render an account of it before the sight of God on the day of judgment, and in this world let him pay one hundred pounds of refined gold and two hundred [pounds] of silver.

[Col. 0808B]

Executed at the place called Billarbeci, on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, during the reign of the Emperor Hludowic, in the twenty-first year.

The mark of Frithuard, who asked that this conveyance be made and confirmed with his own hand.

The mark of Reginhard. The mark of Walger. The mark of Bruni. The mark of Bovo. The mark of Berning. The mark of Reginfrid. The mark of Hildibald. The mark of Herico. The mark of Egon.

I, Regiharius, unworthy priest, wrote and subscribed.

Executed at the monastery of Werithina, where this document was written, on the tenth day before the Kalends of November, during the reign of the lord Emperor Hludowic, in the first indiction.

### Of Holtseara at Witi

30. A brief account of that pasture which we possess on both sides of the Rura, at Hosi and at Wagnoswald.

First, at Hosi, Heinric gave enough for nine pigs. At Hrotinga (Ratingen), Willibald and his niece sold enough for sixty pigs. Aluric sold us his inheritance at Lapanheldi (Lopenhelt); there it amounts to enough for eighty pigs. Gerfrid has enough in the same village for thirty pigs. Alfnant conveyed to us enough for twenty pigs. At Menedinna, Gerala sold us enough for fifteen pigs. At Witi, Evurwin conveyed, for the salvation of his soul, enough for twenty pigs. In the same village, Evuco and Hildirad and their co-heirs conveyed enough for thirty pigs. Othilulf at Hratuga (Ratingen) conveyed to us pasture for ten pigs.

To that land belongs what we purchased at Witi from Meinhard, who had Huntion’s sister as his wife: pasture for twenty-five pigs. From Eribald we purchased pasture for thirty pigs. At Wagnoswald we possess, at Fisclaco, everything belonging there to one mansus, and from another mansus one third part. In the same village Hrodhard conveyed enough for five pigs; Hludowin, enough for five pigs; and in the same village Huntio gave enough for five pigs. Thiathold and Thruthger conveyed pastures for twenty pigs at Witi.

### Conveyance of Gundvin and Adelbold

31. In Christ, to Father Hildigrim, bishop and purchaser: Gundvin and Adelbold, sellers.

It is established that we sold to you, and so we did sell, one small enclosure in the district of Bunnengdo (Bonna), in the village of Melenchen (Melheim). This enclosure measures 120 feet in length and 56 feet in width. On one end it borders the Caballaricia road, and on the other end the Rigo; on one side, the heirs of that property.

We received from you the price agreed and settled between us, namely twenty solidi, so that after this day you may have the property itself by right, with full and entirely secure power to have, hold, give, and do whatever you wish with it, with the stipulation appended.

Executed at the Rura, before the basilica of Saint Saviour, where it was written, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the twelfth year of the rule of the lord Charles, most glorious emperor.
