### Conveyance of Amulric at the Cross on the bank of the Arnapa

37. While each person lives in this present age, he ought to consider and foresee how he may save his soul and find eternal refreshment after the temporal and mortal life of this world. I, Amulric, having weighed this in my mind and turned it over in frequent meditation, conveyed, for [Col. 0811D] the salvation of my soul and for eternal recompense, to the relics of Saint Saviour and of Saint Mary, ever Virgin, and into the hands of the priest Ludger, who was entrusted with those same relics, a portion of my inheritance: namely, the very place called “At the Cross,” with the meadows adjoining it on the bank of the river Arnapa, where formerly my grandfather Irminfrid had a dwelling, together with two fields situated not far from that place.

I conveyed this to the aforesaid relics of the aforementioned priest. I wish it to remain conveyed forever and never thereafter to be altered in any passage of time. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the church of God, as my alms, let the aforesaid priest Ludger possess, hold, cultivate, and make fruitful all these things mentioned above; and let him have full and entirely secure power, from me and from everyone, by hereditary right, to entrust and convey them after his death to whomever he determines and perceives to be useful.

But if anyone, instigated by the devil—which I do not believe will happen—or if I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs, or any outsider should attempt to act against this conveyance or wish to violate it with fixed and deliberate intention, let him first incur the anger of the heavenly God and be separated from the fellowship of the holy angels, unless he promptly corrects himself from his wicked presumption. Moreover, let him be compelled to pay two pounds of gold and ten pounds in weight of silver to the lord’s fisc, and in such a way that he may not prevail in claiming back what he demands. Let this conveyance nevertheless remain firm and unalterable forever, with the stipulation appended.

It was publicly executed in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord, the most religious King Charles, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the village called Hrodbertinga Hova, before the witnesses and sureties whose names are noted below. And so that this testament of conveyance might endure more securely forever, I recorded the time, day, and place at which it was written.

The mark of Amulric, who completed this conveyance [Col. 0812B] and confirmed it with his own hand. The mark of Godobert. The mark of Aeoric. The mark of Frithuric. The mark of Folcbert. The mark of Hildifrid. The mark of Alfger. The mark of Helmbert. The mark of Hruodulf. The mark of Duoden. The mark of Gundbert.

I, Thiatbald, humble priest, wrote and subscribed at the request.

### Conveyance of Eric and Ermenfrid at Arnapa

38. We wish it to be known to all, present and future, how we, Eric and Ermenfrid, conveyed to Bishop Hildigrim two parts of that forest which lies [Col. 0812C] on the river Arnapa, at the place called “At the Cross.” Everything belonging to those two parts we give and convey in full and entire ownership, to be possessed forever.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—if hereafter we ourselves, or any of our heirs, should wish to act against this conveyance or attempt to violate it, let him be compelled to pay you, together with the associated fisc, two pounds of gold and five pounds in weight of silver; and let this present conveyance remain firm at all times, with the stipulation appended.

Executed at the Rura, before the basilica of Saint Saviour, where it was written in the third year of the empire of our lord Emperor Hludowic.

These are the witnesses who saw that Eric and Ermenfrid conveyed, for thirty solidi, two parts of that forest at Arnapa which had belonged to Amulric and Theadrada; Theadrada herself had previously had a third part and a fifth part conveyed to her.

Namely, I conveyed one bivang in the forest of Waneswalde, between two rivers, the Podrebeci and the Farnthrapa, with all its appurtenances—that is, lands, forests, [Col. 0813A] pastures, waters and watercourses.

### Sale of Gunthard and Athilwin

41. In Christ, to Father Altfrid, bishop by the grace of God, purchaser: I, Gunthard, and Athilwin, sellers.

It is established that we sold to you, and so we did sell, namely our enclosed tract in the forest called Witerowald. Your men, together with us, went around this enclosure and secured it with new boundary marks. We received from you the price agreed between us, namely three pounds, on this condition: that after this day the enclosure itself should belong to your own monastery, which is called Werthina; and that from this day you should have free and entirely secure power to do whatever you wish with it.

But if anyone—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt to violate this deed of sale, let him incur the anger of God and be excluded from the thresholds of the saints, and let this sale remain firm, with the stipulation appended.

Executed at the monastery of Werithina, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 848, during the reign of Hludowic the Younger, in his ninth year, in the eleventh indiction, on Friday.

These are the witnesses who heard and saw this.

I, Liudbald, humble levite, wrote and subscribed at the request.

### Conveyance of Huntio

42. I wish it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Huntio, son of the late Egilbern, conveyed my possessions to the church of Saint Saviour, which was built in the district of Ruriggo, at the place called Werthina on the river Rura.

Namely, one jornal of land in the village called Wisi, and with it half of the forest—whatever came to me in that village by paternal right. I wish it to remain conveyed forever and confirm it with the readiest will, so that after this day the custodians of that church may have permission to hold, possess, exchange, or do whatever they may wish with it, and may have full and entirely secure power in every respect, with the stipulation appended.

Executed at the monastery of Werthina, where it was written, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh year, during the reign of the lord Emperor Hludowic.

45. In Christ, to brother Hildigrim, bishop and purchaser: I, Widrad, seller.

It is established that I sold to you, and so I did sell, my own property in the district of Nivense, in the territory of Welde: four jornales, bordered on both sides by the land of Frithurie. On one end, Lantbert’s land; on the other end, the land of the purchaser himself.

I conveyed it to you forever for possession, and I received from you the price agreed and settled between us, namely six solidi, so that after this day you may have full and entirely secure power to have, hold, sell, and do whatever you wish with it, with the stipulation appended.

Executed at the place called “At the Cross,” where it was written, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the fourth year of the reign of the lord Emperor Hludowic.

### Conveyance of Ludger in Suiftarbant, or in Seuwald and Berelsi

46. I wish it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Ludger, son of the late Hrodger, conveyed to my friend, the priest Ludger, for the salvation of my soul and for eternal recompense, half of my inheritance which came to me by paternal right and hereditary law in Berilsi and within the boundaries belonging there—that is, from the Emese as far as the aforesaid place.

I also conveyed to him half of my inheritance in the forest called Seuwald or Suifterbant, except for the fields which had previously been cleared there by our fathers or by our men. I conveyed the remaining half to the priest Ludger in the territory already mentioned and in the forest named above, with complete integrity.

I wish it to remain conveyed forever and never at any time to be altered. Rather, let the priest Ludger possess all these things by hereditary right, and, after his death, let him commend them by hereditary right to whomever he wishes for the benefit of our souls, with the stipulation appended.

This conveyance was publicly executed in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of the most religious King Charles, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, in the village called Bidmingehusum, before the [Col. 0815A] witnesses and sureties whose names are noted below.

The mark of Ludger, who completed this conveyance and confirmed it with his own hand. The mark of Bernsuide. The mark of Wilfrid, priest. The mark of Fledrad. The mark of Folcleb. The mark of Thiadulf. The mark of Wendilbald. The mark of Wigbald. The mark of Wilbald. The mark of Isinbald. The mark of Racddeg. Likewise, the mark of Reginhard. The mark of Hildigrim, deacon.

### Conveyance of Oodhelm

47. I wish it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Oodhelm, son of the late [lacuna], conveyed, for the salvation of my soul and for eternal recompense, one third of my inheritance to the relics of Saint Saviour and of the other saints, which were established by Abbot Ludger at Withmundi.

I wish it to remain conveyed forever and never thereafter to be altered, but on this condition: as long as I live in this mortal life, that share shall belong to me, to be increased through proper service and not diminished. After my death, however, it shall pass in full integrity and right to the aforesaid relics and to the servants of God who are found to guard them lawfully.

This third part of my inheritance consists of three locations: in the district of Hisloi, in the village called Ocanni, one hova, for which my *liti* render service; in the district of Northluianti, in the village called Huleri, a second hova; and in the same district a third hova, in the village called Manheri. Also, one sixth part of a fourth hova in the village called Hrenneri. That sixth portion of the hova, while I am alive, likewise goes to the uses of the aforesaid relics, together with the enclosed tracts in the forest which are marked out beside the Hisla.

I convey and transfer all these things to the aforesaid relics and to the uses of the servants of God who are seen properly to administer those holy relics, so that, with everything belonging to them, they may look to that place and serve it forever, as stated and decreed above, in complete integrity.

It was publicly executed with the stipulation appended at the place called Withmundi, in the twenty-ninth year of the reign of the lord, most devout King Charles, on the third day before the Kalends of July, before the witnesses and sureties whose names are noted below. And so that this testament might endure more securely, I recorded the day, time, and place at which it was written.

The mark of Oodhelm, who completed this conveyance and confirmed it below.

The mark of Hildigar. The mark of Bernhard. The mark of Hildibert. The mark of Judon. The mark of Buton. The mark of Meginlev. The mark of Bernher. The mark of Meginbert. The mark of Germund.

### Conveyance of Wracharius in Suiftarbant, or in Seuwald

48. I wish it to be known to all, present and future, how I, Wracharius, son of the late Brunhar, conveyed to the priest Ludger, for the salvation of my soul, land belonging to me by right of ownership in the district of Hisloae, in the village called Withmundi. Namely, all that land which my *litus* Landulf inhabited and rendered service on, and one field which Hildiger, a free man, formerly held from me as a benefice, together with everything belonging to that land: forests, meadows, pastures, roads, waters and watercourses, and fishing rights.

I except one small enclosure in the same village, in compensation for which I conveyed the field mentioned above. I conveyed all these things, in full integrity, for eternal recompense, to the aforementioned priest Ludger. I wish them to remain conveyed forever and never thereafter to be altered. Rather, for the perpetual uses of the church of God, let the aforesaid priest possess that land by his own right, cultivate it, and cause it to bear fruit as our alms; and let him have full and entirely secure power, from me and from everyone, to entrust it after his death to whomever he wishes and foresees will be useful to us.

It was publicly executed with the stipulation appended in the twenty-seventh year of the reign of our lord, the most religious King Charles, on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the village called Brunnum, before the witnesses and sureties whose names are noted below. And so that this testimony of conveyance might endure more securely forever, I recorded the time, day, and place at which it was written.

The mark of Wracharius, who completed this conveyance with his own hand and confirmed it below.

### Charter concerning the forest at Arnapa

50. We, Eric and Erminfrid, wish it to be known to all, present and future, how, moved by the fear of God and for the salvation of our souls and eternal recompense, by this donation we give to the relics of Saint Saviour and to Bishop Hildigrim two parts of that forest which lies [Col. 0816C] on the river Arnapa in the district of Nivenen, together with whatever our father Amalric left us as an inheritance.

Also, in two other places, [we give] arable land: one before the eastern gate, the other near the forest itself. Between those two places there are ten jornales in all. We give and convey the whole of it, in full, forever for possession.

And so that this present donation may remain firm at all times, it was publicly executed with the stipulation appended in the third year of the empire of our lord, the most glorious Emperor Hludowic.

### Conveyance of Bado
51. **Exchange of land of the holy Savior and of Duadung.**

52. No one appears to lessen his own possessions when, in return, he receives something in increase. Therefore it was agreed and settled between Meinhard, advocate of the monastery of the holy Savior at Werthina, and also a man named Thiadung, that they should exchange among themselves their lands wherever a suitable place occurred; and so they did. Accordingly, the aforesaid Meinhard gave to the above-written Thiadung, in exchange, on the land of the holy Savior at Giffriding, a hova, eight jornales, and one pound with five solidi. Likewise, the aforesaid Thiadung gave in return to the above-written Meinhard, in exchange, his land—whatever he had there—beside the estate of the holy Savior above the river Hosapa. Therefore they requested that two documents, written in one and the same form, be made and confirmed between them, so that each might have, hold, and possess what he had received from his father, or might have free and most secure power in every respect to do with it whatever he wished. Enacted at the place called Wertina, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, while Lord Hlothar was reigning, in the first year, indiction 4.

I, Thiathard, an unworthy subdeacon, wrote and subscribed at their request.

The sign of Thiadung and Wracard, who transferred this property beside the Hosapa. The sign of our advocate Meinhard. The sign of Benno. The sign of Gunthard. The sign of Genic. The sign of Bernher. The sign of Wlfeni. The sign of Helmbrat. The sign of Irminfrid. The sign of Lotrad. The sign of Wolfrid. The sign of Nithard.

**Lease of Helmbald.**

53. Since it is not unknown to all his neighbors how Helmbald, son of Heribald, transferred to the relics of the holy Savior, and into the hands of Abbot Ludger, as his alms, that holding which Helmbald himself, in his hereditary property and in common with his nearest relatives, had legally enclosed and cleared through his own labor and the help of his friends—namely, at the place called Widapa, in the villa of Salchem—he afterward requested that he should receive half of that holding as a benefice for the days of his life and that of his son, under usufruct, namely, on payment of one-half solidus each year at the Lord’s Easter for the aforesaid relics, which are to be placed at that same site for the purchase of lights.

And so I, the humble Abbot Ludger, did this: I granted him that half of the holding on the condition that, during the days of his life and that of his son, they should improve it; and that the properties belonging to the same holding, without any alienation or opposition, should after their death return improved to the aforesaid relics, and thereafter be used for the benefit of the servants of God who, by God’s grant, deserve to administer and guard those relics.

This lease was publicly enacted at the very place called Widapa, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the thirty-third year of the glorious King Charles. I, Ludger, abbot, subscribed.

The sign of Jerusalem, priest. The sign of Hardger, cleric. The sign of Wlger, cleric. The sign of Guntbert, cleric. The sign of Bocco, cleric. The sign of Gerfrid, cleric.

I, Wambert, cleric, subscribed.

**Transfer of Sigiwin at Hrotbertinga-Hova.**

54. I wish it to be made known to the present and also to future generations how I, Sigiwin, son of the late Gislbert, transferred to the priest Ludger, in return for his price, a portion of my inheritance: namely, at Hrotbertinga Hova, one small courtstead with three fields in the same villa, together with watersheds, paths, common pastures, and I gave him power over the forest called Sitroth and over another forest called Huvil. All these things I, Sigiwin, transferred according to law to the above-named priest Ludger; and I wish them to remain transferred forever and never at any time be altered. Rather, he shall have from me and from everyone hereditary right and power to do with them whatever he wishes and to give them after his death to whomever he wishes. This was publicly enacted with a stipulation attached, in the villa called Widugises Hova, in the thirty-fifth year of the reign of our lord, the glorious King Charles, on the second day before the Kalends of July, before the witnesses and those who gave their consent, whose names are noted below.

I have recorded the day, time, and place at which these things were written. The sign of Sigiwin, who requested that this testament be made and confirmed it with his own hand. The sign of Hildifrid. The sign of Theodbert. The sign of Raadher. The sign of Meinhard. The sign of Folcher. The sign of Wigbert. The sign of Boldher. The sign of Notric.

I, Werinbard, priest, wrote and subscribed at his request.

**Transfer of Raadald.**

55. I, Raadald, transferred as my alms to the church which Abbot Ludger established at Withmundi every part of my small inheritance—that is, both at Holmissi and at Withmundi, whatever I appeared to possess there, whether land or woodland. I transferred it all in its entirety to the aforesaid church; and I wish it to remain transferred forever and never afterward be altered.

The sign of Meginung. The sign of Walda. The sign of Gerbald. The sign of Bosuc. The sign of Werbert. The sign of Atalgot. The sign of Alfgrim. The sign of Frithuward, priest.

**Transfer of Folcbert.**

56. I wish it to be made known to all, present and future, how I, Folcbrat, having given a small portion of my hereditary land belonging to my own right in the villa called Bilici, purchased from Theganbald, a freeborn and noble man, in the villa called Fisclacu, that parcel called Rothum, which is named Widuberg. I, Folcbrat, purchased this Rothum from the aforesaid noble Frank Theganbald, possessed it for several years, and worked it as I was able.

Now, however, I gave the same Rothum, in arable land—whatever in it had ever been plowed—to the priest Ludger, in its entirety, in exchange for the arable land of that hova called Alfgeding-Hova. On this condition I received that hova from the priest Ludger, my neighbor, in exchange for the arable land of the aforesaid Rothum: that I should possess it forever by hereditary right and convert it to the proper uses of my inheritance, or should have free and most secure power to do whatever I might decide would be useful with it, whether during my lifetime or, after my death, only insofar as it belonged to and contributed to usufruct.

But if anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, God forbid, or any of my heirs or those claiming through my heirs, or any opposing person, should attempt by an unjust effort to challenge this charter of exchange or wish to violate it, may he immediately incur the wrath of the heavenly God, be separated from the fellowship of the holy angels, and be excluded from entry into all churches until he has corrected himself from his wicked presumption. Moreover, may he be fined by the treasury and compelled to pay two pounds of gold and ten pounds’ weight of silver, and thus be unable to vindicate what he claims, while this exchange remains firm and unaltered forever, secured by stipulation.

This was publicly enacted in the thirty-first year of the glorious and religious King Charles II, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March, at the place called Diapanbeci, on the bank of the Bura, before the witnesses and those who gave their consent, whose names are noted below.

I have recorded the time, day, and place at which this was enacted. The sign of the priest Ludger: he requested that this charter be made and confirmed it with his own hand.

The sign of Bernger. The sign of Alfdag. The sign of Hildirad. The sign of Berwin. The sign of Gisfrid. The sign of Benno. The sign of Liudric. The sign of Walafrid.

**Transfer of Theodgrim the deacon.**

57. I wish it to be made known to all, present and future, how I, Theodgrim, son of the late Aldgrim, transferred all my inheritance, which Ricfrid transferred to me, for the remedy of my soul and for eternal recompense, to the monastery built in honor of the holy Savior at the place called Werthina, in the district of the Ripuarian people beside the river Rura, where Bishop Hildigrim appears to preside.

I transferred the aforesaid property in the villa called Arlo, in the district of Threant, with complete integrity—that is, one church, lands, dependents, houses, buildings, woods, waters, and watercourses. I transfer and reconfirm the whole and entire property. Thus I transferred it, and I wish it to remain transferred forever and never at any time be altered. Rather, the custodians of the same church named above shall have from me and from everyone free and most secure power to do with it for the perpetual uses of that church whatever they may wish.

This was publicly enacted with a stipulation attached, in the seventh year of the glorious and religious king and emperor Hludowic, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July. This transfer was made at the place called Mimigernaford, before the witnesses and those who gave their consent, whose names are noted below.

I have recorded the day, time, and place at which these things were written.

The sign of Theodgrim, who requested that this transfer be made and confirmed it with his own hand.

The sign of Liudolf. The sign of Aldger. The sign of Aldbert. The sign of Ado. The sign of Adaldung. The sign of Eburger. The sign of Folcbrat. The sign of Erpulf. The sign of Thancher. The sign of Thead. The sign of Osger. The sign of Bavo. The sign of Hildold. The sign of Egilhard. The sign of Waldrich. The sign of Marcward. The sign of Marcrad. The sign of Vab. The sign of Herimod.

I, Werinhard, priest, wrote and subscribed.

**Transfer of Betto at Holtheim.**

58. I wish it to be made known to all, present and future, how I, Betto, son of the late N . . ., transferred a portion of my inheritance to Abbot Ludger, having received the price by mutual agreement, in the district of Nivanheim, in the villa called Holtheim: namely, a courtstead with its appurtenances, one rod and a small meadow, from one jornal of arable land, together with everything else that legally belongs to that courtstead—that is, pastures, paths, rights of water use, and lordship over the woods belonging to the aforesaid villa, with full grazing rights according to the measure of that courtstead.

I, Betto, transferred all the things named above in their entirety to Abbot Ludger, and I wish them to remain transferred forever and never afterward be altered. Rather, he shall have from me and from everyone free and most secure power to do with them for the perpetual uses of the church of God whatever he wishes. This was publicly enacted with a stipulation attached at the place called Ad Crucem, in the thirty-third year of the reign of the most religious King Charles, on the sixth day before the Nones of May. I have recorded the day, time, and place at which these things were written.

The sign of Betto, who completed this transfer and confirmed it with his own hand.

The sign of Landbert. The sign of Horulf. The sign of Erlulf. The sign of Folcher. The sign of . . . The sign of Hrotulf. The sign of Folcbert. The sign of Milo.

And I, Thiatbald, priest, wrote and subscribed.

**Transfer of Andger at Volum.**

59. I wish it to be made known to all, present and future, how I, Andger, through the hands of Wolfhram, sold one third of my inheritance and distributed it to the poor; I transferred the remaining two parts to the church of the holy Savior, which is built in the district of the Ripuarian people, at the place called Werthina beside the river Rura, on the condition that my wife should have, for all the days of her life, half of the inheritance which I transferred to the aforesaid church as a precarious holding—namely, one third of my inheritance—and that after her death it should pass to the aforesaid church for the remedy of my soul. I wish it to remain transferred forever, and I wish this present transfer to remain firm forever.

Enacted at the monastery of Werthina, on the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the fifth year of the reign of Lord King Hlothar, indiction 7.

I, Thiathard, deacon, wrote and subscribed at his request. The sign of Andger, who made this transfer. The sign of Wolfhram. The sign of Folcbert. The sign of Meinhard. The sign of Aldbert. The sign of Wolf. The sign of Theatrad. The sign of Sigibald. The sign of Gerbald. The sign of Frithubald. The sign of Reginbald. The sign of Bomher. The sign of Waldher. The sign of Meinrad.

**Transfer of Willeburg.**

60. To Hildigrim, brother in Christ and purchaser, I, Willeburg, seller. It is established that I have sold to you, and so I have sold, my property in the district of Ruraegawa, in the villa called Menithima: namely, six jornales of arable land, land and woodland. I received from you the price, as we mutually agreed and settled, so that from this day forward you should have free and most secure power in every respect to hold, possess, give, sell, or do whatever you wish with the aforesaid properties.

This was publicly enacted with a stipulation attached, in the villa called Werithina, at the place . . . . . beside the river Rura, where it was raised, and before the witnesses or those who gave their consent, on the sixth day . . . while our lord Charles the emperor was ruling.

The seal of Willeburg, who requested that this transfer be made.

Sale of Friddric from Arnapa. — 68. Transfer of Sigibald and his wife at Hoangi. — 69. Transfer of Rumfrid from the district of the Ripuarians. — 70. Transfer of Heribrat. — 71. **IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 804. JOSEPH, ALCUIN’S DISCIPLE.**

[Col. 0821]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON JOSEPH

*(From Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict)*

I think it worthwhile to bring together here certain observations concerning Joseph, found in published and manuscript books. Alcuin says that Joseph was in good health in his letter to Colcu (letter 3); but in letter 173, addressed to his beloved son Joseph, he expresses sympathy for his illness. In letter 180 he begs Bishop Remigius to pray for the soul of Joseph, his disciple; Joseph therefore died before his teacher.

I once wondered whether this was the same Joseb whom Charlemagne wished to place over some monastery, as we read in the letter of Abbot Theodemar to King Charles, or whether he was Joshua, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent at Vultur num. I have no doubt, however, that he is the Joseph who, at Alcuin’s command, abridged Jerome’s Commentary on the prophet Isaiah. Until now this work of Joseph’s has remained unknown.

[Note: Nevertheless, Mabillon, in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, no. 12 of the *Eulogy of Blessed Alcuin*, transcribed several verses placed before and after the abridgment of the Commentaries of Saint Jerome on Isaiah. EDITOR.]

[Col. 0821]

# JOSEPH’S POEM TO SAINT LUDGER

*(See this poem in the Acts, or Life of Saint Ludger, column 777 of this volume.)*

[Col. 0821]

# VERSES OF JOSEPH PLACED BEFORE AND AFTER HIS EPITOME OF THE COMMENTARIES OF BLESSED JEROME ON ISAIAH

*(From Mabillon, at the place cited.) (C)*

At the beginning of the epitome:

Who could unfold for the reader in brief words

the mysteries of Isaiah, handling and examining everything?

Saint Jerome, employing lengthy treatises,

wisely explained him through great circumlocutions.

From his immense books I shall attempt to extract

what may briefly lay bare the prophet’s meaning.

Thus it pleases Albinus that we undertake such labor.

At the end of the same epitome:

Jerome instructed me, at the beginning of his final little book,

that whoever found the text of Isaiah itself too long

should excerpt all the books,

and bind their vast meanings in brief words.

Therefore, obeying your commands, dearest one,

I have dedicated these things, collected concisely, to you, Albinus.

Would that these things often make you mindful of me.

As you read them, loving Father, pray earnestly for us,

and say more than once: “May the Lord preserve Joseph.”

These words too I return to you from my whole heart.

Dear master, hail; may the Lord save you everywhere.

Then Joseph continues in prose:

As briefly as I could, I have devotedly excerpted from Jerome’s diffuse treatise on Isaiah, dearest master Albinus, just as you commanded. For you instructed me to follow throughout only what was absolutely necessary for the meaning and the path of the Hebrew truth, and to avoid the uncertain and confused tracks of other interpreters and treatises.

You wished this to be done, as I think, for two reasons: either so that the labor of reading long books might be lightened for weary and lukewarm readers, or so that for men of intelligence and ardent spirit a readier and shorter way of seeking the truth might be provided.

But if anyone despises this work because it is shorter and therefore more obscure—for brevity is often accompanied by obscurity—let him hasten with uplifted head to the source from which we drew these things; and if this little stream is not enough for him, he can [be satisfied] from above, where the river overflows its banks.

But you, beloved master, in return for our labor, grant us the grace of your blessing and prayer, so that, as we knock at the mercy of our Redeemer, he may not despise us, but, in view of his great mercy toward many, may regard in us also the work of his hands; and, once the waves of this age have been overcome and the nets of our [sins] broken, may the merciful Lord Jesus lead us to the harbor of an undisturbed life.

**IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 809. FARDULF, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS.**

[Col. 0823]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON FARDULF

*(From Gallia Christiana, vol. VII)*

Fardulf was a Lombard by birth. After Pavia was captured, Charlemagne brought him to Francia, and he became dear to the king because he had exposed the conspiracy of Pippin, Charlemagne’s son by his concubine Himiltrude. Therefore, after Abbot Maginarius died, Charles entrusted him with the governance of the monastery of Saint-Denis. To show himself in turn grateful to Charles, Fardulf arranged for a building adjoining the monastery to be constructed in the style of the ancient royal palaces, where the prince, whenever he came there, might lodge with his companions.

Fardulf himself attests this in verses reported by Chesnius in volume II of the *History of the Frankish Writers*, p. 645. There one may also read of an oratory built by him for the blessed John the Baptist, in fulfillment of a vow which Fardulf says he made at the beginning of his exile, in the following verses. Alcuin likewise praises him (*poem* 117) for a ciborium made by him in the church of Dionysius.

An old manuscript of Saint-Denis records that Fardulf was taken by Charles into the retinue of counts on the military expeditions against the Saxons, in these words:

“While Charlemagne was directing the war against the Saxons with marvelous skill by his personal presence, it happened that Fardulf, abbot of Saint-Denis, was among the others who had been summoned from every direction and had gathered to bear the burden of the battle and suppress the boldness of that people. He had been ordered to carry with him the sacred relics of the blessed martyrs, and he had appointed clerical guardians who traveled with him so that, by succeeding one another in turn, the proper reverence might be shown to them.”

Fardulf was also among the *missi dominici*, to whom Charlemagne assigned various provinces of the kingdom to visit, so that they might ensure that both ecclesiastical and civil laws, when neglected, were observed, administer justice, and report back to him about each matter.

In 797, the thirtieth year of Charles, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, he experienced the generosity of Count Theudald; in 799, of Gisela, Charlemagne’s sister; and in 805, of the noble Hasbanian Nevelongus (*History of Saint-Denis*, nos. 64, 65, and 66). Fardulf is believed to have died the following year, 806, on 22 December. Our Felibianus extracted his epitaph, as follows, from a manuscript in the library of the eminent Cardinal Ottoboni and appended it to his *History of Saint-Denis*:

A worshiper of the Church, a generous compassionate benefactor of the needy,

Fardulf was; here he lies in this tomb.

In this house of God, by his famous name,

he deserved to be raised up through eternal praises and prayers.

[Col. 0823]

# FARDULF’S POEMS

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories, vol. V)*

## I. Verses inscribed on the buildings of Saint-Denis

Reader, as you behold the roof, bring forth the inscription:

Fardulf built this for his own Charles.

Once, while he followed the scepter

of his own people, fate carried him along adverse paths.

Yet here he preserved the honor owed to his lords,

although these were the kingdom’s furthest bounds.

At last, through the fortunate arms of Charles the ruler,

he yielded, and fortune turned his course for the better.

While he preserved for this king

the gifts of his loyalty,

the lofty king Charles granted him many gifts.

Among them, the peaceful Charles allowed him,

to become rector of the church of Saint-Denis.

This prudent man built this house for his benefactor,

so that he himself might rejoice there with his servants.

May the warlike prince offer joy

to his servants, whom the bonds of loyalty unite.

Yet after the manner of the ancient forefathers

he ordered the roofs to rise; the houses shine with the king’s honor,

so that whenever he surveys the splendid palaces of the kingdom,

he may remember Fardulf’s servants.

[Note: What he says concerning his loyalty to Charles should be compared with Pippin’s conspiracy, which Fardulf exposed, as both the Dionysian Annals indicate and Einhard explicitly records in his *Chronicle* under the year 792. Sirmondus. — Fardulf died in 806 or the following year.]

## II. Other verses of Fardulf

For you, O forerunner of the Lord, Fardulf built

this rich hall, adorned with divine worship,

returning to you the vows which, suppliant, he once vowed,

when he first began to experience the hardships of exile.

Charles, the most excellent hero, approved these words,

whom Christ, through your merits, wished to render a gracious servant to himself, and increased with great honors.

Now the power of fulfilling his vow has been granted to him.

## III. Other verses of the same man

Now, therefore, while the opportunity to speak is granted us,

may the name of his friendship increase everywhere,

and may the constant vow grow within his bold heart,

a vow that will add to him a long life in the world.

It also adds an eternal palm through abundant rewards,

which the everlasting God will preserve for him in his citadel.

**IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 809. DAGULF.**

[Col. 0825]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON DAGULF

*(From Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis)*

Dagulf wrote in his own hand a Psalter inscribed in letters of gold, which Charlemagne presented as a gift to Pope Hadrian I. Dagulf dedicated to Charlemagne this eighteen-line poem, which Lambecius published from that codex, brought into the imperial library, in volume II, p. 266.

*The codex which Fabricius here cites through Lambecius was once inspected and examined by me when I visited the Vienna library. It contains not only a Psalter, but also biblical canticles. At the beginning it has certain general material about the psalms, such as their origin and prophecy. I am entirely uncertain whether Dagulf was their author. In addition, there is read there, under the name of Saint Jerome, that exposition of the Catholic faith which the distinguished Vallarsius included among Jerome’s apocrypha in his edition of Jerome’s works, vol. I.*

[Col. 0825]

# DAGULF’S EIGHTEEN-LINE POEM

He dedicates his Psalter, written in letters of gold, to Charlemagne.

Behold, golden lettering paints David’s songs;

it has taught such melody to adorn them so well.

Golden words resound; they promise golden kingdoms,

and sing of a good that will endure without end.

These things deservedly are embellished on ivory tablets,

which an ingenious hand has carved wondrously.

There the Psalter’s first origin is displayed,

and the learned-speaking king himself sings in the choir.

And the beauty, once removed from the thorns,

has returned through the man’s vigilant devotion—

what it formerly had been.

Golden offspring, brighter than gleaming gold,

Charles, our radiance and the lofty love of the people,

pious king, wise leader, distinguished in virtue and arms,

to whom belongs all that is seemly, whatever pleases in the world,

receive the labor of your humble servant Dagulf,

and read it kindly with your learned mouth.

Thus may your scepters be adorned through many triumphs,

and at last may you be joined to the Davidic choir.

**IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD 714. SAINT ANGILBERT, ABBOT OF CENTULA.**

[Col. 0825]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON SAINT ANGILBERT

*(From Mabillon, Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict)*

## I. The rationale of this eulogy; writers of the life of Saint Angilbert

1. Although two ancient authors attempted to rescue the deeds of the blessed Angilbert from the darkness of oblivion, neither succeeded in doing so fully and completely. And since much in their works is either omitted, obscure, or doubtful, it seemed worthwhile first to set out here the testimonies of the ancients concerning Angilbert and compare them at the same time, so that the historical truth about him might become clearer. Since these matters cannot conveniently be contained within a brief space of observations or notes, I thought it preferable to arrange them in a historical eulogy, which I append here in the manner of a commentary.

2. There are two principal authors who wrote about the life of Saint Angilbert. One is Hariulf, first a monk of Centula and later the third abbot of Aldenburg, as I read in his manuscript epitaph. He published a *Chronicle of the Abbey of Centula* in four books toward the end of the eleventh century, a truly outstanding monument of good antiquity. It is extant in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*. His entire second book concerns Abbot Angilbert; he describes two translations of Angilbert in books three and four.

The other writer of the *Life* is, I think, Anscher, abbot of Centula. John Bolland published this author’s work in mutilated form in his February volume, with excellent commentaries, repeatedly praising it under the name of Hariulf—not so much on his own judgment as on the conjecture of Paul Petavius and William Peiratus. I, however, think it should rather be attributed to Anscher. Here is the basis of my conjecture.

It is not likely that Hariulf wrote the life of Saint Angilbert twice. At that time Anscher published three books on the miracles of the holy man, which are appended to the later *Life* in manuscript codices. The books on the miracles are dedicated to Radulf, archbishop of Rheims; the book on the life is dedicated to someone else, whom he addresses by the title of “Majesty”—which I interpret as referring to the Roman pontiff.

The author asks him how Angilbert “ought to be treated: whether, as has hitherto been done, his memory should be retained among the faithful dead, or whether, according to the Scripture which says, ‘The memory of the righteous is with praises,’ his anniversary day should solemnly be celebrated among the number of the saints. And so that your wisdom may not be unaware,” he says, “of how this same man, while placed in this life, devoted himself to the Lord’s commands, we have gathered his deeds from the histories of the Franks and various short historical works and offer them to Your Majesty, so that from these you may know that he is not declared by the Lord through miracles without reason, but rather in accordance with his merit.”

These things, therefore, were written while Angilbert was performing miracles. This began in the year 1110, according to Anscher, in the book on those miracles, which is evidently the work of this author. Anscher wished to obtain Angilbert’s canonization, as it is called. For that reason he offered the book on the miracles to the archbishop of Rheims and the book on the life to the supreme pontiff, whom he addresses as “Majesty.” By that time such matters concerning the canonization of saints had begun to be referred to the pope, to be completed with the advice and permission of the metropolitan and bishop, as appears from the history of the elevation of the body of Saint Bertin, abbot, in part I of the third section of the century.

Finally, if Anscher, the abbot, personally offered the book on the miracles to the archbishop of Rheims, he certainly employed no other author to compose the book on the life, which was to be offered to the pope. Add that Hariulf writes with greater discernment and judgment than the author who composed the other *Life*, whom in what follows I shall call Anscher.

Before Hariulf and Anscher, Angilbert’s deeds had been mentioned in an old book on the abbots of the monastery of Centula, now lost, which Abbot Gervin of Gorze discovered, as Hariulf testifies.

3. Besides these authors, John of Capella, a monk of Centula, also deals with Saint Angilbert in his *Chronicle of Centula*, which he composed “with the permission of Abbot Eustace in the year of the Lord 1492”; so too do Paul Petavius in his *Syntagma on Nithard*, William Peiratus in *On the Chapel of the Kings of France*, chapter 30; our Menardus in book II of his *Observations on the Martyrology*; Jacobus Malbrancus in book II of *On the Morini*; and Ignatius Josephus in book II of his *History of Abbavilla*.

## II. Angilbert’s two names, his parents and homeland, and his education

4. Angilbert—or Anghilbert, or Engilbert—also known by the additional name Homer, arose from a distinguished Frankish family of palace officials. His noble lineage is demonstrated both by his singular intimacy with Charlemagne, by his union with Berta, Charlemagne’s daughter, and finally by the eminent public offices which he held.

The names of both his parents are unknown. This alone survives for us concerning his other relatives, as written by his son Nithard in book IV of his *History*, where he says of Angilbert:

“This man was born at that time from a family that was not unknown. Madhelgaudus, Richardus, and this man were of one stock, and were rightly held in high esteem by Charles the Great.”

This seems to me to be the Madelgaud who, together with Bishop Magenard, was sent in the second year of Charlemagne and assigned “in the Cenomanian, Hoxonian [or Hoxiensian],” and other neighboring districts of Neustria. Richard, however, was the count who, together with Willebert of Rouen, in the year 795, in the book on the *Life of Louis Augustus*.

From these facts one may conjecture that Angilbert was of Neustrian origin.

As I said, his additional name was Homer; Alcuin, Theodulf, and others repeatedly praise him under this name. Walafrid Strabo gave the same designation to Grimoald, chaplain of Louis Augustus, in a poem preserved by Henry Canisius on p. 622 of volume VI.

5. We read in a letter of Pope Hadrian to Charles concerning the Second Council of Nicaea, or concerning images, that Angilbert was educated at Charles’s court. In it the pontiff praises “Engilbert, who, as he says, was raised in your palace almost from the very beginnings of infancy.”

Anscher writes that Angilbert lived at the court of King Pippin, “involved in palace and royal affairs.” I would rather place this at Charles’s court, as Hadrian’s words sufficiently suggest. For while Pippin was reigning, Angilbert was not of an age at which he could have handled palace business. Certainly Alcuin habitually calls him his son, for no other reason than that he himself was much older than Angilbert. This would not be so if Angilbert, during Pippin’s rule, had already been a grown man qualified to conduct public affairs.

## III. His union with Berta: whether after receiving priestly orders, and who their children were.

### 6. It is related in the later Life of Angilbert that Berta, daughter of Charlemagne, captivated by love for Angilbert, persuaded her father to allow her to marry him, and obtained this permission.

This passage greatly perplexed John Bollandus. That exceptionally perceptive man observed that no mention of such a marriage occurs among earlier writers before the time of Hariulf, who lived scarcely three hundred years after Angilbert. He observed that Berta, Charlemagne’s daughter, born third—that is, after Pippin and Rotrude—to Hildegard, who was betrothed to Charlemagne only in the year 772, could scarcely have been marriageable before the year 792, by which time Angilbert was already a monk at Centula. He observed, I say, that Angilbert is repeatedly praised by Alcuin, and sometimes also by Pope Hadrian, Einhard, and even King Charles, yet is nowhere called Charlemagne’s son-in-law.

Furthermore, according to Einhard’s testimony in his *Life of Charlemagne*, Charles loved his daughters so deeply “that he would not give any of them in marriage, either to one of his own people or to a foreigner; rather, he kept them all with him in his household until his death, saying that he could not do without their companionship. For this reason, although otherwise fortunate, he experienced the malignity of adverse fortune; yet he concealed it so completely that it seemed as though no suspicion or report of any disgrace concerning them had ever arisen.”

Yet, on the other hand, Nithard—whose testimony it would be impious to reject—states of Angilbert that “from Berchta, daughter of that same great king, he fathered me and my brother Harnid.” Bollandus, I say, noted these points and pressed them modestly, declaring that he did not wish to overturn the tradition of the people of Centula or refute the *Life of Saint Angilbert*, nor indeed to suspect anything disgraceful concerning the royal maiden or the distinguished courtier and priest; he wished only to set out the matters that troubled his mind.

These questions certainly present considerable difficulty. I shall pass over the other points, which can easily be resolved. Einhard’s testimony, that of a serious man and eyewitness to events, can scarcely be explained satisfactorily unless one says either that, if Charles gave one of his daughters in marriage to one of his own men, he did not allow her to move into her husband’s household but kept her with him, or that Angilbert was united with Berta not by a solemn but by a secret marriage.

For every suspicion of an illicit union seems to be dispelled by Angilbert’s constant and uninterrupted intimacy and friendship with Charles, by his untarnished reputation and standing among all men, and by the distinguished embassies and other notable offices entrusted to him. It is scarcely possible to persuade oneself that Charles, a prudent and wise man, could have concealed disgrace brought upon his daughter and yet have bestowed so much honor and friendship upon a man who had inflicted such a stain upon his family.

Finally, if Einhard’s own wife was Imma, a daughter of Charles, married with Charles’s approval—as many considerations certainly suggest—who would be surprised that Einhard makes no mention of Angilbert’s marriage to Berta, when he did not even count his own wife among Charles’s daughters? “The story,” you will say, “comes from the chronicler of Lorsch.” Yet Einhard clearly calls Lothar, son of Louis Augustus, his nephew when he says in Letter 34, addressed to Lothar: “Therefore I have thought it necessary to admonish your nephewship, so that, through the prudence granted you by God, you may guard against your danger.” If Lothar was Einhard’s nephew, then he was so because of his wife, who consequently must have been Charles’s daughter. And yet, as I have said, Einhard nowhere counts his wife Imma—which is what he himself calls her in his letters—among Charles’s daughters. Why, then, should it be surprising if he omitted Angilbert’s marriage to Berta, while omitting his own?

Nor do the remaining doubts proposed by Bollandus stand in the way. Rotrude, Charles’s eldest daughter, was betrothed to Constantine, emperor of the Greeks, in the year 781, as is recorded in the oldest Frankish Annals. Why could Berta, who followed her immediately in age, not have been betrothed to Angilbert some years later? Certainly their mother Hildegard had married Charles before the year 770.

“But in what year,” you ask, “did Berta marry Angilbert?” I think this happened scarcely before the year 787. About that time, when Charles the Younger, son of Charlemagne, sought in marriage the daughter of Offa, king of the Mercians, Offa refused to agree “unless Berta, daughter of Charlemagne, were given in marriage to his son,” as we read in the published text of chapter 15 of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*.

Although Charles refused Berta to Offa, I nevertheless infer from this that she had not yet been united to Angilbert—or at least that Offa did not know of it. Finally, in Hadrian’s letter to Charlemagne, it was perhaps inappropriate to call Angilbert the king’s son-in-law, because of the inequality of their status. And Alcuin’s letters to Angilbert were addressed either before he was married or after he had become a monk and abbot. These matters I offer with due caution, since the ground is uncertain.

### 7. The author of the later Life creates another difficulty when he says that Angilbert married Berta after he had already become a priest.

Yet this author’s opinion is not so weighty that we should spend a long time examining it. Since the matter is unheard of, contrary to the sacred canons, and was written by no one until three hundred years later—and was indeed passed over by Hariulf, the author of the earlier Life, who was the more authoritative witness—it is only fair to clear Charles of this charge. Charles was exceedingly devoted to the canons, as is evident both from his letter to Pope Leo, in which he urges him to observe the canons, and from his letter to Offa, king of the English, to whom he refers back the Scottish priest for judgment because he was said to be guilty of violating Lenten abstinence:

“Let him,” he says, “be judged there from which he arose. For there also the purity of God’s holy Church in morals, firmness in faith, and uprightness in conduct must be observed according to canonical sanction, so that she may be one, perfect, and immaculate.”

How much less would he have tolerated a priest rushing into marriage—something that the Greeks themselves were never permitted to do after receiving the clerical rank!

Yet I seem to see the reason why the author mentioned above fell into error. He read that Angilbert had been Charles’s chaplain. He did not suppose that this dignity had been conferred upon him after his monastic profession—a state that removes men from worldly affairs, and especially Angilbert, who had renounced royal marriage and the other honors of the palace. He therefore judged that Angilbert had been chaplain, and consequently a priest, before contracting marriage. Thus, with Berta his wife approving and accompanying him, he withdrew to Centula as a married man.

What should be thought about this matter I shall explain in the following chapter.

### 8. What children Angilbert had by his wife is reported by Nithard, the son of both of them, in Book IV of his *History*, where he writes of Angilbert: “From the daughter of that same great king, named Berchta, he fathered Harnid, my brother, and me, Nithard.” These and other words of Nithard are quoted by Abbot Anscher, author of the later *Life of Angilbert*.

Some add a third to these two sons of Angilbert, namely Harduin, who, with good reason, seems to others to have been the same person as Harnid, called Harduin through a scribal error.

## IV. Offices before entering the monastery; withdrawal into the monastery; doubt concerning Berta’s religious life

### 9. It will be useful to explain here what offices Angilbert held as a layman at court.

It is certain from Alcuin’s Letter 144 that he was “first officer of the palace” of King Pippin and, if we believe Hariulf and Anscher, also “duke of Maritime Francia.”

I do not agree with Petavius and Bollandus, who think that Alcuin’s letter should be understood not of Pippin, king of Italy and son of Charlemagne, but of Pippin, Charlemagne’s father. They argue this first because, when Pippin the elder was reigning, Alcuin had not yet left school, since he did not become head of the schools at York until after the death of Egbert, bishop of York—which occurred in 766, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, scarcely two full years before Pippin’s death.

They argue, secondly, that if Angilbert had already been mature enough, during the reign of King Pippin, for the highest office at court, he would have been older than, or at least no younger than, Alcuin, who nevertheless calls him “son” in this letter and in others.

Finally, the letter seems to have been addressed to Angilbert while he was in Italy, since Alcuin commends to him the bearer of the letter—namely Folrad, the priest mentioned also in the following letter—who was setting out for Rome, and asks that the relics of the saints be sent to him through him.

The heading and opening of the letter are as follows:

> To his faithful friend and venerable Angelbert, the humble deacon Albinus sends greetings. Remembering the friendship agreed between us, I have ventured to send you this letter, asking that you kindly receive its bearer and pray that the lord King Pippin assist him on the roads of his pilgrimage.

And below:

> Moreover, dearest brother, I most earnestly beg you to arrange to send me—or at least some of—the very sweet and greatly needed gifts, namely relics of the saints.

At the end:

> May you flourish, my son, crowned with the virtues,

and so forth.

The title of the letter likewise reads: “To Angelbert, first officer of the palace of King Pippin.”

This friendship between Alcuin and Angilbert seems to have been “agreed” only after Alcuin’s arrival in Gaul. We shall say below in Alcuin’s Life [Note: See volume CII of *Patrologia*.] that Alcuin stayed in Gaul at least twice: first from the year 780 for several years, during which he remained with Charles, and then from the year 793 for the remainder of his life.

On his first visit he formed a familiar friendship at court with Angilbert, whom Charles appointed first officer of the palace of his son Pippin, crowned king in Italy in 781—that is, his chief counselor. Angilbert held this office for several years; Adalhard, later abbot of Corbie, was appointed as his successor.

That Angilbert was in Italy while Alcuin was in Gaul, at the time when Charles was occupied with the Saxon expedition, is clear from Alcuin’s letter to Damoeta, in which he writes:

> I remain at home almost as though bereft of my sons. Damoeta has gone to Saxony, Homer to Italy, and Candidus to Britain.

The reason for Damoeta’s departure to Saxony is indicated by the preceding words:

> I am greatly concerned about your journey and your expedition against the enemy, because many dangers commonly arise in such undertakings.

At the end he prays that God may bring David “his beloved one, and all of you victorious, back to your homeland with joy.”

David is to be understood as Charlemagne, Homer as Angilbert, and Damoeta as Ricolfus. Ricolfus was still a deacon at that time, not yet archbishop of Mainz, an office in which he succeeded Lullus in the year 787.

This expedition took place in the year 792 or in one of the two following years, when Charles marched into Saxony with his army. Therefore, at that time Angilbert was staying not in Gaul but in Italy, specifically at the court of King Pippin.

### 10. Angilbert is also called “duke of Maritime Francia” by Hariulf and Anscher.

By “Maritime Francia” they understand the county of Boulogne and the other districts bordering the British Ocean. The interpolator of the *Life of Saint Richarius* extends the duchy of Maritime Francia “from the River Scheldt to the Seine.”

Anscher adds that, at that time, the Danes who had poured into that coast were conquered by Angilbert through divine intervention and destroyed in a massacre, after he had made a vow “to put on the monastic habit immediately after the victory.”

The old Frankish Annals are silent about this Danish incursion. If Angilbert’s victory is indeed historical, it occurred after his return from Italy, around the year 787, by which time he had already been united with Berta.

### 11. Then, around the year 790, he withdrew to the monastery of Centula, where, after the customary probation, he became a monk under Abbot Symphorianus.

Anscher gives two reasons for this withdrawal: illness and the victory over the Danes.

Angilbert had two advisers who urged this withdrawal, namely Alcuin and Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, as Alcuin himself makes clear in his letter to Antonius—for Antonius was another name of Adalhard. Alcuin saw that Homer, or Angilbert, took pleasure in theatrical entertainments, and he grieved that his pupil should engage in something contrary to the strictness of Christian devotion.

Alcuin rebuked Angilbert on this matter and asked that, if he hesitated, Adalhard should admonish him again. Alcuin’s words in Letter 107 are these:

> I fear that Homer may grow angry with the page that forbids spectacles and diabolical fictions, which all Holy Scripture forbids, to such an extent that I read that Saint Augustine said: “The man who brings actors, mimes, and dancers into his house does not know what a great multitude of unclean spirits follows them.” But far be it from the Christian household that the devil should have power there. Long ago I wrote to you about these things, desiring the salvation of my dearest son with all the affection of my heart, and wishing that through you there might be accomplished what I recognized could not be accomplished through me. Let your affection, dearest son, rejoice in the service of God and in the salvation of your brother, so that your reward of merits may increase through the progress of others.

From this we understand what pious men of that age thought about those theatrical spectacles, which they could not tolerate even in a courtier. Homer yielded to the pious admonitions of Alcuin and Adalhard and renounced these entertainments and the world. Compare section 29 below.

### 12. Whether Berta withdrew with her husband to Centula, as Anscher relates, must be examined here.

Anscher should be heard in chapter 4 of the *Life*:

> Thus Angilbert, departing from the king, returned to Centula. Scorning the height of pompous dignity, he first of all placed his most noble betrothed, Berta, consecrated by the sacred veil, in a suitable place within the same monastery of Centula, where she devoted herself with great fervor to sacred vigils, devout fasts, and divine songs. When this had been done, Angilbert prostrated himself alone among the company of the monks and, bathed in tears, humbly begged that he might deserve to receive the habit of the sacred life, and so forth.

John de Capella says more briefly in his *Chronicle of Centula*:

> Saint Angilbert, with the consent of his wife and of Charlemagne, became a religious at the monastery of Centula; and Berta his wife became a nun and recluse in the same monastery.

Hariulf says nothing about Berta’s withdrawal.

It is certainly established from Book I of the *Miracles of Saint Richarius*, chapter 16, that consecrated women who had taken the veil lived either in buildings attached to monasteries—which was common in other monasteries at that time—or at least in private houses. There we read of a certain married woman who had been deprived of her eyesight:

> She begged her husband to leave her and grant her permission to place the veil upon her head, declaring that she had been instructed in a vision to receive, in the monastery of Saint Richarius at Saint Mary’s, the veil for her head in the manner of nuns. She humbly asked that from then on he support her by alms. When he heard this, he consented. She was brought by her own people to the basilica of Saint Mary, as she had requested, and received the aforesaid habit. But when she returned that same day, and so forth.

And in Book II, chapter 4, concerning a crippled woman who, after recovering her health, “to this day,” as the ninth-century author says, “frequently visits that woman’s place of prayer [perhaps ‘oratory’], wearing a veil upon her head in the manner of nuns.”

Three points must be observed in these passages: those women had vowed chastity; they had received the veil in the manner of consecrated women; and most of them lived in their own private houses, like devout women whom Herard, bishop of Tours, in chapter 37 of his capitulary, forbids to cast off the veil “even if they have changed their clothing in their own houses.”

Such women sometimes also lived in royal palaces. One was Hundrudis, an English matron, to whom Alcuin addresses Letter 89 in these terms:

> To Hundruda, a woman devoted to God,

whom he admonishes “so that, in the king’s palace, the devotion of a regular life may be seen in her conduct.”

It is therefore not surprising if Berta, even if she professed this form of life at Centula, sometimes returned to her father’s palace. Yet it is surprising if, while wearing the religious veil, she could retain worldly pomp.

Nevertheless, in a certain poem about Charlemagne’s arrival to see Pope Leo, attributed to Alcuin, the author, describing the king’s entire retinue, sings of Berta after Rotrude:

> Next among them Berta, accompanied by many maidens,  
> With manly voice, spirit, bearing, and bright countenance,  
> She bears a face, manners, eyes, and a heart that imitate her father.  
> Her noble head is encircled by a golden diadem.  
> Golden threads mingle with her snowy hair.  
> She wears precious marten-fur around her milk-white neck.  
> Her costly garment is adorned with varied jewels  
> And gleams with the abundant brilliance of ordered gems.  
> Plates of gold are set with chrysoprase stones upon her coverings.

This is far removed from the habit of a religious woman: instead of a veil, a diadem is assigned to her; instead of the modest clothing of a devout woman, she is given the entire array of feminine finery appropriate to royal offspring.

Gisla, or Gisala, the third daughter of Charles, also took part in this procession, although she was already a nun. Yet the same poet describes her adornment very differently in these and other verses:

> After them Gisala follows, gleaming with brightness,  
> Accompanied by a maidenly choir; the golden child shines.  
> The woman glitters beneath a melocine garment;  
> Soft veils gleam with purple threads.

Here are the insignia of a nun: a maidenly retinue, veils or a veil gleaming with “purple threads,” although the *flammeum* had once belonged to brides. There is no mention of a golden diadem, small jewels, gems, or garments decorated with gold plates—the ornaments with which Berta is said to have been adorned.

Moreover, this occurred toward the end of the year 800, nearly a decade after Angilbert had withdrawn to Centula. The verses of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, addressed to Charles in Book III, poem 1, could also be brought into this discussion, since he describes Berta in almost the same way in the year 796. Whether these things can apply to a devout and secluded woman I leave others to judge.

Einhard states in his *Life of Charles* that only four of Charles’s children—namely Charles, Pippin, and Rotrude—died before their father. Berta therefore survived him. Her death is recorded in the Dionysian and Argentolian Necrologies in these words:

> On the fifth day before the Ides of March: Berta, daughter of the emperor Charles, who gave the upper court.

Perhaps she withdrew to Centula after her father’s death, when Louis Augustus ordered Charles’s daughters to leave the palace because of their ill repute. According to Nithard, Louis “repeatedly ordered them to depart for their monasteries.”

## V. The priesthood, the abbacy, and the embassies

### 13. It may be doubtful whether Angilbert was a priest.

Although Pope Hadrian calls him “minister of the royal chapel,” he should not therefore immediately be regarded as having been a priest, whether one interprets Hadrian’s letter as referring to the chief chaplain or to a chaplain of the second rank.

Hincmar is a witness on this point in his *Treatise on the Order of the Palace*, chapter 14, drawn from the work of Adalhard, abbot of Corbie. Speaking there of the *apocrisiarius*, he says among other things:

> Sometimes the Apostolic See was served in this office by bishops, but sometimes by deacons. . . . In these regions beyond the Alps, after Louis, converted to Christ by the preaching of blessed Remigius, had come into being, holy bishops, through successive reigns, visiting the palace from their sees at the appropriate time, took turns arranging this administration. From the time of Pippin and Charles, however, this office was sometimes carried out by priests, sometimes by bishops, by royal will and episcopal consent; [sometimes] by deacons or priests rather than by bishops.

As he adds in chapter 16, the *apocrisiarius* was the person “whom our people call chaplain or guardian of the palace,” who “governed the entire palace clergy under his care and direction.”

It is therefore not correct to infer from the dignity of chaplain that Angilbert was a priest, since at that time some chaplains were merely deacons.

Nor can this be inferred from his abbatial dignity, for Paschasius Radbertus, abbot of Corbie, and many other abbots were not of priestly rank. Finally, in Alcuin’s letters, where Angilbert is frequently mentioned, he is never called a priest, although Alcuin usually makes a point of using that title.

Even if the holy man was a priest, it should not be concluded that he had been promoted to that rank before his monastic profession, whatever Anscher may say to the contrary. Anscher perhaps assumed—although it is not true—that no one could be the king’s chaplain unless he were a priest.

### 14. After Abbot Symphorianus died, Angilbert assumed the dignity with the common consent of the monks and the approval of King Charles.

I think this happened in the year 793, approximately three years after he entered the monastery. I infer this from the fact that, in the embassy to Rome which he undertook in 792 in order to bring Felix of Urgell, convicted of heresy at Regensburg, “into the presence of Pope Hadrian,” he is not yet called abbot but simply Angilbert. In another embassy to Hadrian in the year 794, however, Hadrian calls him “Abbot Engilbert.”

### 15. I find that this distinguished man undertook three Roman embassies, all of them after he had become a monk.

The first concerned Felix in the year 792, as has already been said. The Loiselian Annals under that year state:

> The Felician heresy was first heard and condemned at Regensburg; Angilbert brought him into the presence of Hadrian the Apostolic.

The same is stated in the *Life of Charles* by an unknown author and in another work by a monk of Angoulême; Regino in his *Chronicle* agrees with them word for word.

The second embassy took place in the year 794. After Charles held the council at Frankfurt, he sent to Pope Hadrian through Angilbert four books written against the seventh synod concerning the veneration of images. Hadrian replied to Charles through Angilbert, writing:

> Moreover, from your most merciful, exalted royal power we have received your faithful familiar, namely Engilbert, abbot and minister of the chapel, who has been brought up in your palace almost from the earliest beginnings of infancy and has been admitted to all your counsels. Therefore, just as he is received by you in all familiarity, so he was to be received and honorably treated by us. Accordingly, because of the immense love we bear toward your honey-sweet royal excellence, when you sent him we received him with an immense sweetness of love, welcoming him as he wished and in whatever manner he wished. He spoke to us with great familiarity, and we received him with a receptive and kindly ear, as though your bodily excellence itself were speaking to us through him; we therefore trusted his counsel more patiently, for the advancement of our holy Roman Church and the exaltation of your power protected by God. Among other matters, he presented to us a capitulary against the synod held at Nicaea for the erection of sacred images. Therefore, because of our honey-sweet royal affection for you, we have given a response to each chapter.

From this it is clear what standing the venerable abbot enjoyed with Charlemagne. When Angilbert departed for Rome, Alcuin gave him letters of recommendation to Pope Hadrian in his own name; they are found in Chesne’s collection as Letter 63.

Concerning the third embassy Einhard writes:

> In the year 796, after Hadrian had died at Rome, Leo assumed the pontificate. He immediately sent the king through his legates the keys of the confession of Saint Peter and the standard of the city of Rome, together with other gifts. He also asked him to send one of his nobles to Rome, who would bind the Roman people to his allegiance and subjection by oaths. For this purpose Engilbert, abbot of the monastery of Saint Richarius, was sent. Through him he also sent to Saint Peter a large part of the treasure which Duke Eric of Friuli, after plundering the royal residence of the Huns called the Ring, had brought to the king from Pannonia in that same year.

The same account is found in other Frankish Annals.

What Charles instructed him to do in Rome beyond these matters is explained by Alcuin’s letter [Note: Among the Letters of Charlemagne, *Patrologia* vol. XCVIII, col. 909, Letter 9.], delivered in Charles’s name to Homer the chamberlain. It contains these words:

> Under the guidance of divine mercy, and with its favor bringing you safely once more to our lord the Apostolic Father, admonish him carefully concerning every aspect of the uprightness of his life, and especially concerning the holy observance of the canons and the pious governance of God’s holy Church, according to the opportunity afforded by your conversation and the harmony of his mind.

A man must have been exceptionally eloquent, learned, and wise if so important a commission was entrusted to him by the wisest of kings, to be conveyed to the supreme shepherd of the Church.

Charles likewise writes in Letter 84 to Pope Leo:

> We have sent to Your Holiness Angilbert, the personal familiar of your familiarity, whom earlier, as we promised through the religious men Campolus and Anastasius, we arranged to send to our most blessed Father, your predecessor. . . . We entrusted him with everything that seemed either desirable to us or necessary for you, so that through mutual discussion you might determine whatever was understood to be necessary for the exaltation of God’s holy Church, the preservation of your honor, or the stability of our patriciate.

No one could have been entrusted with a more honorable mission.

Alcuin also placed in his hands Letter 92, addressed to his dearest son Homer, concerning the relics of the saints, as well as Letters 72 and 73, addressed to Pope Leo and Paulinus, patriarch of Friuli; in these he calls Angilbert his dearest son.

The following passage of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, in Book III, poem 1, addressed to Charles, should be understood as referring to this embassy. Speaking of the recently brought treasures of the Huns and the recent conversion of that people to the Christian faith, he writes of Angilbert, absent from court because of his embassy:

> I would sing sweet music to you, sweet Homer, if you were not absent;  
> But since you are absent, my Muse is silent here.

## VI. Palatine offices and dignities after entering the monastery

### 16. We have already discussed above what dignities Angilbert held before entering the monastery. We must now explain those he held as monk and abbot.

Charles calls him *auricularius* and *manualis* in the letters just mentioned. Hadrian calls him minister of the royal chapel and says that he was admitted to all Charles’s counsels. Anscher finally calls him *silentiarius*.

### 17. There is no mention of an *auricularius* in the *Book on the Order of the Palace*, whose fragment Hincmar reports from Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, in his *Treatise* 14.

I think this dignity belonged to the number of those counselors who, as Hincmar testifies in chapter 31 of the same treatise, “discussed privately and familiarly with the king both the condition of the kingdom and the personal affairs of each individual.” These are what we now call counselors and secretaries of state.

Thus Angilbert belonged to Charles’s innermost circle of confidential advisers and counselors. Matters of particular secrecy were entrusted to him in the king’s ear, from which he was perhaps called *auricularius*.

### 18. Since, as Hincmar relates in that passage, the rule among such counselors was “that whatever they had discussed among themselves, no one was to disclose without their consent to any member of his household or to anyone else,” they could consequently be called *silentiarii*, the title Anscher gives to Angilbert.

It is plausible, however, that Anscher was the first to give this title to Angilbert, perhaps without any authority, in imitation of the Greeks, among whom the dignity of *silentiarius* was held in high esteem.

On this subject one should read the note of Charles Fresnius, a man of extensive learning, on the history of John Cinnamus. He observes that among many Greek writers *silence* and *silentiarius*—Greek *σιλέντιον*—are used for a discussion or conference, and even for the place where a conference takes place. Such is the expression in the commonly circulated Anastasius, in his Life of Pope Stephen III, “in the silence of blessed Peter the apostle,” as found in the various readings of the royal edition, where *silence* seems to mean what elsewhere is called the church secretary’s office.

He also observes that the dignity of the *silentiarii* was so illustrious that at the Council of Chalcedon, in the first session, they are given the epithet *θαυμασιωτάτων*, “most admirable”; and that Pope Damasus, in his letter to Acholius, testifies that nothing could be added “to the merit of Rusticus, since he possesses the prerogative of his office, for he was silentiarius of Augustus Gratian.”

But, as I have said, this title of dignity was especially common among the Greeks, and Anscher seems to have given it to Angilbert in imitation of them. I think that by this name he intended here to signify the dignity of *auricularius*, or supreme counselor.

### 19. In Charles’s letter to Leo, Angilbert is called “the hand-bearer of your familiarity.”

He was evidently a secretary, or secretary of letters, namely of the letters that Charles wrote to the Roman pontiffs and other great men. Alcuin’s epigram 184 to Charles belongs here:

> For your servant Homer came to us,  
> Bringing joyful messages, David, from your lips.

And at the end:

> I have sent this young man back again through your kindness,  
> So that he may serve you in song, in heart, and by hand.

Do not suppose, however, that he was supreme chancellor, for no diplomas are known to have been signed and authenticated in his name. In chapter 7 of the later *Life*, Anscher notes that “the golden instruments of the royal notary” were deposited at Centula by Angilbert; Angilbert had doubtless once used them.

### 20. Finally, according to Pope Hadrian, Angilbert was “minister of the royal chapel,” that is, chief of the chaplains or archchaplain, as Anscher, and after him William Peiratus, Paul Petavius, and Sancta Marthani, interpret the title.

The Bollandists deny that he was archchaplain. They think that he was one of the royal chaplains, but not the chief. Their reasons are that Alcuin and others nowhere call him by this title, and that Angilram, bishop of Metz, succeeded Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis, in the office of archchaplain; Hildebold, bishop of Cologne, succeeded Angilram, as is clear from Hincmar’s *Treatise* 14, and Hildebold retained this dignity after Angilbert’s death.

Nothing certain can be established from Hincmar’s testimony. Hincmar’s purpose was not to provide a complete and exact list of the archchaplains, but merely to offer examples of those who held this office in the time of Pippin, Charles, and Louis.

That his list is neither complete nor exact is clear from the fact that Hincmar writes in chapter 14 that, under Pippin and Charles, this dignity was sometimes administered by deacons; yet among the examples given in the following chapter he names no deacon.

Certainly, if Angilbert was minister of the royal chapel, as is established by Hadrian’s letter, it is highly probable that he was not one of the lower-ranking chaplains but the chief. This is suggested both by the great honor he enjoyed with King Charles and by the embassies that belonged to this dignity, which Angilbert undertook frequently.

Finally, to explain my own opinion on this matter, I think that at that time the dignity of archchaplain was divided into two offices: an honorary office, concerned with undertaking embassies, and an ordinary office, concerned with governing the palace clergy and managing ecclesiastical affairs.

The former was granted to Angilbert, the latter to Hildebold, archbishop of Cologne.
