Thus someone would always be present to conduct legal business, govern the palace clergy, and bless the food of the royal table—for Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, assigns this duty to the archchaplain in Book III, poem 1, in these verses:

> Let the bishop stand by, rejoicing in spirit and kindly in face,  
> Bearing blessed lips and a devout heart.  
> Let sincere faith, the dignity of so great an office,  
> And an innocent breast commend him to you, King Christ.  
> Let him stand ready to bless the king’s drink and food;  
> Whatever the king wishes to consume, he will bless.

Charles certainly wanted both Angilram and Hildebold to remain constantly at the palace, as is clear from canon 56 of the Council of Frankfurt:

> The lord king also said at the same synod that he had obtained permission from the Apostolic See, from Bishop Hadrian, to keep Archbishop Angilram constantly in his palace because of ecclesiastical necessities. He asked the same synod that, just as he had kept Angilram, so he ought also to keep Hildebold.

Thus Hildebold managed ecclesiastical affairs at the palace after Angilram, while Angilbert handled the embassies. Both were archchaplains: the former ordinary, the latter honorary.

These are my conjectures, which I submit to the judgment of learned men.

## VII. The restoration of the monastery of Centula, charters, and revenues
### 21. Whether the Monastery of Centula Owes More to Richarius, Its Founder, Than to Angilbert, Its Restorer and Enlarger, Can Scarcely Be Determined

How much splendor and adornment he added to this place is demonstrated by the document [Col. 0836C] and by the poems which he composed on this subject, which I shall present below from Hariulf and Anscher. For three basilicas were erected there, with continuous access to them through a triangular cloister or dormitory; in them perpetual and unceasing psalmody, after the manner of the Acaemetes—they call it “unceasing praise”—was celebrated. In these basilicas were many altars and an immense abundance of sacred relics and ornaments: all of these Angilbert either contributed himself or obtained through the generosity of Charles.

He appears to have undertaken the monastery’s new construction from the year 793, when he was made abbot. The dedication of the greater church took place, as I conjecture, after his third embassy from Italy, in the year 801, and was performed by twelve bishops. The bodies of the saints Richarius, Caidoc, and Fricorius, otherwise called Adrian, were transferred into precious reliquaries, which he adorned with verses. Finally, so that nothing might be lacking from his devotion to Richarius, he arranged for his Life to be polished in a more elegant style by Alcuin, at the command of Charles Augustus, who, as Einhard records in the *Annals*, “celebrated Easter of the year 800 at Saint Richarius.” All these undertakings he began and completed both out of devout piety toward God and from his exceptional devotion toward Saint Richarius.

### 22–23

After this, the holy man obtained from Charlemagne that the monastery of Forest, [Forestmonstier], built at the place where Saint Richarius had completed the final days of his life, should be separated from Centula and again be permanently subjected to it. We learn this from a manuscript fragment appended to a copy of the chronicle of Hariulf, together with Charles’s diploma, in the following form:

> “After the memorable Angilbert, therefore, had rebuilt the place with the utmost diligence of heart, and had adorned not only its interior but also its exterior with great splendor, and when, after everything had been properly completed, he had ceased laboring on the rebuilding of the place, he approached Lord Charles the Great, king, and asked him to confirm by his royal authority that the cell of Forest, which Saint Richarius had first inhabited and built, and which the Lord glorified with many great signs of miracles on account of the merits of that same saint, should perpetually belong to the abbot of Centula. And he, who was most ready to bestow much greater gifts upon this beloved man, already venerable on account of his holiness, most willingly granted this request also. Nor was he content with a simple concession: he ordered a royal document to be drawn up and preserved for the knowledge of posterity, and it is still kept intact in our archives.”

(See this charter in *Patrologia*, vol. XCVII, col. 986.)

### 24

In the year 800, Charles, as Einhard and others testify, “celebrated Holy Easter at Saint Richarius. From there, traveling again along the seacoast, he came to the city of Rouen. After crossing the river Seine, he proceeded to Tours, to Saint Martin, for the sake of prayer. He stayed there several days because of the unfavorable health of his wife Liutgard, who died and was buried there; from there, through Orléans and Paris, he returned to Aachen. At the beginning of August, coming to Mainz, he held a general assembly there and announced an expedition to Italy; toward the end of the year he set out for Rome.”

Angilbert accompanied him on his journey to Rome, as Petavius writes, and obtained from Pope Leo III, by privilege, that the abbot alone should have ecclesiastical jurisdiction over all the estates of Centula (I reproduce Petavius’s words), and that the bishop of the see of Amiens should have no power to appoint churches or clergy of that place. This was done “at the suggestion” (these are the words of the privilege, according to Petavius) “of our brother and fellow bishop Jesse, bishop of Amiens, and likewise of Abbot Angilbert, who communicated this to us in the presence of our glorious and most excellent son Charles, whom, by God’s authority, we have today consecrated Augustus for the defense and advancement of the holy universal Church,” and so forth. There is also mention there of the monastery of Centula, “recently restored,” as he says, and brought back to a noble condition.

This is Petavius’s account, to which he adds in the margin:

> “The privilege was written, examined, and subscribed by Zacharias, regionary deacon and regionary of the holy and apostolic Roman Church, and librarian of the holy and apostolic Roman Church, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the ninth indiction.”

I reproduce this here in Petavius’s words because I have not been able to see such a privilege myself. John of Capella is mistaken in thinking that on that day and in that year the “privilege of the mitre, sandals, ring, and other pontifical ornaments” was also granted to Angilbert and his successors. Such privileges were not yet granted to abbots in that age, a matter on which, God willing, I shall speak more fully elsewhere.

Certainly, if the use of sandals and other pontifical ornaments had belonged to the abbot of Centula in the eleventh century, Pope Leo IX would not have offered them to Abbot Gervinus when he had summoned him to Rome, “ordering Gervinus to use these sandals”; nor would Hariulf, in book IV, chapter 27 of his *Chronicle*, have said that “the venerable abbot refused those ornaments out of humility.”

### 25

The size of the revenues of the monastery of Centula at that time is shown by the “description of the treasure and possessions, or vassals, of Saint Richarius” composed by Hericus, abbot after Angilbert. A large part of it is found in Hariulf, book III, chapter 3. Yet Hariulf omitted two things: namely, the enumeration of the villages dependent upon the monastery, which John of Capella lists, and the income from the town of Centula, the total of which I reproduce here from a manuscript codex and from John Bollandus.

> “In Centula itself there are two thousand five hundred dwellings of laymen. Each one pays twelve denarii, four chickens, and thirty eggs. They must always perform the service of the lord abbot and the brothers wherever it is necessary.
>
> “There are four mills, from which are rendered six hundred modii of mixed grain [John of Capella: 120 modii of grain], eight pigs, and twelve geese [Bollandus: cows]. From the weekly market, forty solidi; from the weekly transport service, twenty solidi.
>
> “There are thirteen ovens, each of which yields annually ten solidi and three hundred loaves, and at the Litanies thirty *flatones* each [Capella: *flanni* or tarts]. The care of souls at the portico of Saint Michael is supported by the brothers’ alms and is worth five hundred solidi annually.
>
> “The burial of the poor and of strangers at Novavilla, at Saint Albinus, yields one hundred solidi annually at the gate of the nobles, to be distributed as alms. The abbot’s daily alms amount to five solidi: three hundred daily poor, one hundred and fifty widows, and sixty clerics.
>
> “Each manor pays annually one sextarius of wheat, likewise one of oats and one of beans. From marriages, twenty pounds annually. From the court judgment of foreigners, sixty-eight pounds annually.
>
> “Also there is a merchants’ quarter, which every year supplies one cloak worth one hundred solidi. The quarter of the smiths pays all the ironwork; it is worth three pounds annually. The quarter of the shield-makers supplies, makes, and sews all the coverings of books; it is worth thirty solidi.
>
> “The quarter of the saddlers provides saddles for the abbot and the brothers living there. The quarter of the bakers supplies one hundred loaves per week. The quarter of the servants is entirely free. The quarter of the shoemakers supplies all the footwear of the servants and cooks.
>
> “The quarter of the butchers pays fifteen sextarii of lard every year. The quarter of the fullers supplies all the felt to the brothers. The quarter of the furriers prepares and sews all the brothers’ skins.
>
> “The quarter of the vintners pays sixteen sextarii of wine and one of oil per week. The quarter of the tavern-keepers supplies thirty sextarii of beer each day.
>
> “The quarter of the soldiers numbers one hundred and ten; each one always supplies a horse, shield, sword, lance, and the other weapons.
>
> “The chapel of the nobles pays twelve pounds of incense and frankincense every year. The four chapels of the common people each pay one hundred pounds of wax and three of incense.
>
> “The offering at the tomb of Saint Richarius is worth two hundred marks every week, or three hundred pounds, apart from other gifts.”

### 26

Thus far extends this outstanding monument of antiquity, which I thought should be reprinted here for the benefit of our readers. In addition, John of Capella lists one hundred and two villages belonging to the same monastery “by way of advocacy,” with their rents and revenues, apart from “one hundred and seventeen villages or towns not described, possessed by as many soldiers as fiefs from the said church. Each of these men was bound to serve the lord abbot and the convent in arms and on solemn occasions, and especially to lodge at his own expense during the feasts of the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and the solemnities of Saint Richarius, together with his household, and whenever they were summoned.”

Even today, under our congregation, the monastery continues to exist, not without some remnant of its former dignity; and the town of Centula also continues to exist. Yet both have declined greatly from their ancient condition.

## VIII. Angilbert’s Remaining Deeds, Writings by Him and Addressed to Him

### 27

Of Angilbert’s remaining deeds we know only that he subscribed Charlemagne’s testament, composed in the year 811, after the bishops and abbots Fridugisus and Adalungus: “Engilbertus.”

### 28

As for his writings, although it is plausible that he wrote many things, nothing has been preserved for us concerning him except the document he himself composed about the restoration of his monastery, together with certain verses quoted above, to be quoted below, and those presented by Andreas Chesnius in volume II of his *History of the Franks*, p. 646.

### 29

Several letters of Alcuin addressed to him survive, some in Alcuin’s name and some in Charlemagne’s—namely, letters 27, 42, 83, and 92. He is praised in letters 15, 60, 63, 65, 72, 73, 84, and 93; likewise in poems 184, 201, 221, 222, and 270, and in the preface to the *Life of Saint Richarius*.

Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, also composed a poem addressed to Angilbert; it is the third poem of book III. Jacob Sirmond’s judgment concerning it is as follows:

> “This entire poem of Theodulf is filled with changes of names, which perhaps could be understood by those who heard them; now they appear inexplicable.”

In this passage Theodulf attacks a certain poet whom Angilbert admitted to his table—a man who intruded improperly among the good Muses and polluted them, while silencing everyone more learned than himself. The poem begins with these verses:

> What are swans doing while crows resound such things,  
> and many songs clatter throughout my halls?  
> Now the deceitful, guilty magpie imitates human speech;  
> scorning the birds, he sits at the sacred dishes.  
> The parrot imitates various Muses with its voice,  
> defiling your Muses, poet Homer.  
> The diver and Black, a fisherman in the waters of the Liger,  
> now habitually dwell in the forests of Briga.

He repeatedly calls this poet “Crow” and “Corvinian,” after his black color. Against him he introduces a certain hostile Scot in this way:

> A little Scot, girded with a sharp sword, watches you,  
> so that he may pierce your breast, Corvinian.  
> He does not fear crows, nor would he spare any bird,  
> if only he hoped that Damoetas were far away.  
> Our Scot is not pious, Damoetas the poet.  
> The wanton game is turned from the mouth into mourning.

This Damoetas is none other than Ricolfus, or Riculfus, whom Theodulf again praises in book III, also called Macarius. He was first a palatine deacon and later archbishop of Mainz after Lullus. An epigram of Alcuin, number 258, survives addressed to him, containing these verses:

> These gifts I have vowed to you, Macarius, shepherd:  
> may you be blessed forever with Christ and the saints.  
> Remember Albinus, and may Christ’s grace remember you;  
> and you, my Black one, become white in God.

And below:

> As I commanded you, instruct our men of Berg;  
> and let whoever pleases you learn together with you.

From this it is plausible that this Black man was himself the Crow or Corvinian whom Theodulf attacks. He was then living among the men of Briga or Berg, repeatedly slipping into the court and into Angilbert’s dining hall—Angilbert perhaps still being a layman and, as stated above in section 11, excessively devoted to amusements.

Or perhaps this Black and Corvinian was the Scot Clement the Scot, whom Charles is said to have retained in Francia for the purpose of teaching, according to book I of the monk of Saint Gall. In any case, I would prefer to read *Bergenses* here, as in Alcuin, rather than *Brigenses* in Theodulf. By this name, if I am not mistaken, are meant the monks of Berg, the monastery of Saint Peter in the district of the Meuse, on the river Roer, which joins the waters of the Meuse at Roermond. This monastery is called Berg by Browerus in book VIII of his *Annals of Trier*, where it is said that King Lothar donated the place to Hunger, bishop of Utrecht, in the third year of his reign.

Enough conjectures—and perhaps more than enough.

## IX. His Death and Burial, Translations, Canonization, Feasts, and Relics; His Successors

### 30

The holy man died in the year 814, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, twenty-two days after Charlemagne. As death approached, “acting with great humility,” says Hariulf, “of which he had been a steadfast guardian, he ordered that he be buried before the doors of the church. His burial place is so close to the entrance of the church that no one can enter the basilica without treading upon the holy tomb of his body.”

### 31

Various epitaphs of his are reported. Hariulf reports one consisting of four verses, which “were read around his tomb.” Anscherus gives another, which he calls a “bronze epitaph,” that is, one inscribed on a bronze plate. I read a third in Alcuin, poem 116:

> All that you see renewed with the highest adornment,  
> the sacred temple, both within and without,  
> Angilbert, rejoicing, has now made through fatherly love  
> for the saints and for God everlasting,  
> sparing none of his own resources; for whatever he possessed,  
> he has already given to the Church in generous devotion.
>
> And you, servant of God, as you come … from there, traveler,  
> pass through these beautiful places of the monastery,  
> and with devout heart toward Christ behold the churches of God,  
> behold their varied splendor through the work of piety.
>
> Always say great praises to Christ with your lips,  
> who willed his servant to accomplish such things.
>
> And say: “Grant heavenly rest, Christ, to your servant,  
> who made these beautiful things in your name.
>
> “And you, servants of God, always intercede for him,  
> so that Christ may preserve his servant everywhere.  
> May he forgive his sins and grant him eternal salvation.”

If this epitaph was composed by Alcuin after Angilbert’s death, as it seems to have been, Alcuin survived Angilbert.

### 32

Hariulf and Anscherus commemorate two translations of Angilbert’s body: one performed by Abbot Ribbodo in the twenty-eighth year after his death; the other by Gervinus, also an abbot, in the eleventh century.

### 33

At what time Angilbert was enrolled among the saints, and when his memory first began to be celebrated in the divine offices, must be investigated. I think both occurred in the year 1110, when Abbot Anscherus, for this purpose, offered Pope Paschal a book on the Life of Angilbert and another on his miracles to Ralph, archbishop of Rheims, so that they might enroll him in the canon of the saints and order that he be honored with a liturgical feast.

That this was indeed Anscherus’s intention in describing Angilbert’s deeds is clear from a fragment of the preface to the book he composed on his Life. There he says that he did this so that it might be known “how this cultivator of righteousness ought to be treated: whether, as has been done until now, his memory should be kept among the faithful dead, or whether, according to the Scripture which says, ‘The memory of the righteous is with praises,’ his anniversary day should solemnly be celebrated among the company of the saints.”

Thus, until then—that is, up to Anscherus’s time—Angilbert’s memory was kept among the faithful dead, with suffrages offered for him, as Gervinus had ordered after his body was discovered. For previously the men of Centula did not commemorate the day of his death, because they were unaware of him, according to Hariulf.

### 34

After that time, by the consent and decree, as I suppose, of Pope Paschal II, the feast of Saint Angilbert’s death was celebrated, as was likewise the feast of his translation. In an ancient calendar of solemnities that “properly belong to Centula,” written four hundred years ago, I find the following concerning Saint Angilbert:

> “The twelfth day before the Kalends of March: deposition of Saint Angilbert, abbot and founder.”

He was a restorer, but also a second founder.

> “On the Nones of November: first translation of Saint Angilbert, abbot.”

This is certainly the translation carried out by Abbot Ribbodo, which Nithard mentions in book IV of his *History*. No mention is made in the aforementioned calendar of solemnities of the other translation, whose author was Gervinus.

### 35

Who succeeded Angilbert as abbot is disputed among the authors. Hariulf substitutes for him his son Nithard, “whom he had fathered by the king’s daughter Berta.” Paul Petavius proves this to be false in his *Syntagma of Nithard*, on the grounds that Nithard, in the thirtieth year after his father’s death—that is, in the year 844, when he composed his *History*—had not yet departed this life.

By this argument Petavius also refutes the author of Anscherus’s second Life, who places Nithard after Abbot Ribbodo, who died in the aforementioned year, and makes Louis succeed Ribbodo, and Nithard succeed Louis. This is also what he was taught by the following ancient marginal note copied into a manuscript of Hariulf:

> “After Lord Louis, Lord Nithard is said to have been appointed [in charge]. And because at that time a severe persecution of the pagans was pressing upon them, he also undertook the county of the maritime [Francia].”

Finally, Petavius conjectures that Nithard was killed in war in the year 853, when the Danes and Suevi—whom the Germans call Northmen, that is, Northerners—had left the boundaries of their habitation and for twenty years had been afflicting the entire seacoast with fires, plunder, and every form of cruelty.

Perhaps someone will doubt whether Nithard was abbot of the monastery of Centula because he is omitted from a certain poem composed by Abbot Angelramnus of Centula about his predecessors, one hundred years before Hariulf. Hear Hariulf in book IV, chapter 17, where he is discussing Angelramnus:

> “That same honorable man, taking thought for posterity, wrote a metrical catalogue of the fathers of this holy place—not indeed designating all of them, but mentioning only those whose names seemed to be indicated by charters or any little written notices, or were specifically identified by the Life of Saint Richarius. (What follows is absent from the printed editions.) He wrote as follows:
>
> “I write the names of the abbots  
> of the monastery of Centula,  
> who come to mind—  
> although they are not in order.  
>
> “Above all, our excellent shepherd  
> Richarius, born in this village,  
> is placed first in the register.  
> Ocioaldus follows.  
>
> “The magnificent Angelbertus;  
> Guitmarus, a most holy man;  
> Helisachar and Aldricus.  
> Hericus is added to them,  
>
> “and Hludoguicus, also royal;  
> Herbertus, Symphorianus,  
> Ruodulfus, Karlomannus.  
> With Guelfo and Hedenoldus,  
>
> “Gerbertus and Fulchericus.  
> After Ingelardus, therefore,  
> Angelramnus is entered,  
> imitator of the order of the saints  
>
> “and devoted to letters.
>
> “This, indeed, was the honorable Angelramnus.”

Although this catalogue is not exact, it nevertheless provides grounds for doubting Nithard’s abbatial dignity. Yet Hariulf meets this doubt in book IV, chapter 17, where, after several remarks, he concludes:

> “These, then, are the names of the abbots that are found less fully in Lord Angelramnus’s writing but more fully in ours: namely, Lord Nithard, Lord Ribbodo, and also Helgaudus and Coschinus. The first two were found in the codex brought from Gorze, while the third was found in the parchment books of our school. For concerning Lord Coschinus, several things are written at the monastery of Jumièges, from which it is proved that this same man was abbot both of our place and of that one.”

## On the Restoration of the Monastery of Centula

*(In Mabillon, at the same place.)*

I, Angilbert, considering and examining with the most diligent investigation and devotion of mind how, with the agreement of my brothers and of all the faithful of the holy Church and of all other good men, I might wish, with the Lord’s assistance, to rebuild for the better this holy place, which, though unworthy, had been entrusted to me by almighty God and by my most excellent lord Charles, most serene Augustus [Note: From this it is clear that this document was composed by Angilbert after the year 800, at the end of which Charles Augustus was named and crowned at Rome on Christmas Day], so that the monks and other servants residing there, and likewise our successors who will succeed us through the various periods of time, might be able to serve God and more attentively implore the mercy of that same God for me and for the aforesaid lord, and so that what we have done might become an everlasting consolation to them, and that what we who labored for the love of God have done might, through their prayers, bring us an eternal reward—insofar as reason permitted and our ability provided, though not as much as we wished but as much as circumstances allowed, we took care to labor, as is declared below.

Since, therefore, every people of the faithful ought to confess, venerate, and worship in mind the most holy and inseparable Trinity, and ought firmly to believe according to the rule of this faith, in the name of almighty God we endeavored, with the Lord’s cooperation and with the assistance of the aforesaid lord Augustus, to establish in this holy place three principal churches with their appurtenant buildings.

The first and chief is in honor of Saint Savior and Saint Richarius; the second in honor of the holy mother and perpetual virgin Mary and of the holy apostles; the third, in the brothers’ cloister, in honor of Saint Benedict the abbot and of the other holy abbots of the rule. These churches were also dedicated in wondrous order by twelve venerable holy bishops, whose names we have judged should be appended to this little work for their veneration and remembrance.

They are: Megimhardus, venerable archbishop of the see of the Church of Rouen; Georgius [Note: Of these bishops, apart from Megimhardus, the only ones certainly known to me are Pleon of Noyon, Theodoinus of Thérouanne, Hildiguardus or Hildoaldus of Arras and Cambrai. Among the others, I do not know whether Georgius was bishop of Amiens, and Benedictus bishop of Angers. Gerfridus seems to me to be the man praised by Alcuin in poem 50, where he is remembered as having been consecrated bishop in a certain church of the blessed Mary, perhaps at Laon. The succession and period of governance of the bishops of that see, specifically those who lived in the eighth and ninth centuries, ought to be corrected from two letters of Hincmar of Rheims, recently published in volume VIII of the Labbean edition of the Councils.], Absalon, Gerfridus, Pleon, Hildiguardus, Theodoinus, [Col. 0842D] Ydelmarus [Read: Hidelmarus], Benedictus, and Kellanus, most illustrious bishops; and John and Passivus, legates of the holy Roman Church of God, most noble prelates.

The altar of Saint Savior, on which his relics and those of the holy Innocents who suffered for him have been placed; the altar of Saint Richarius, on which are the relics of the holy mother Mary and of that same Saint Richarius; the altar of Saint Peter, on which are his relics and those of Saint Paul and Saint Clement; the altar of Saint John the Baptist, on which are his relics and those of Zachariah, his father; the altar of Saint Stephen, on which are his relics and those of Simeon, who received the Lord into his arms; the altar of Saint Quentin, on which are his relics and those of the saints Crispinus and Crispinianus; the altar of the holy Cross, on which are relics of its wood; the altar of Saint Dionysius, on which are his relics and those of Rusticus and Eleutherius; the altar of Saint Maurice, on which are his relics and those of Exsuperius and Candidus; the altar of Saint Laurence, on which are his relics and those of Sebastian and Valerian; and the altar of Saint Martin, on which are his relics and those of Remigius, Vedastus, Medardus, Gualaricus, Lupus, Servatius, Germanus, and Eligius—

in the church of Saint Benedict, the altar of that saint, on which are his relics and those of Anthony and Columbanus; the altar of Saint Jerome, on which are his relics and those of Ephrem and Aequitius [Note: John of Capella has “the bones of Saint Jerome and some of Saint Wulfran”]; and the altar of Saint Gregory, on which are his relics and those of Eusebius and Isidore—

were duly and diligently consecrated to the Lord with great joy by those same distinguished men already mentioned, on the day of the Kalends of January.

In the church of the blessed Virgin Mary, the altar of the Blessed Virgin herself, on which are deposited her relics and those of Saints Felicitas, Perpetua, Agatha, Agnes, Lucy, Cecilia, Anastasia, Gertrude, and Petronilla; the altar of Saint Paul, on which are his relics and those of Barnabas and Timothy; the altar of Saint Thomas, on which are his relics and those of Ambrose and Sulpicius; the altar of Saint Philip, on which are his relics and those of Sylvester and Leo; the altar of Saint Andrew, on which are his relics and those of George and Alexander; the altar of Saint James, on which are his relics and those of Sixtus and Apollinaris; the altar of blessed John the Evangelist, on which are his relics and those of Linus and Cletus; the altar of Saint Bartholomew, on which are his relics and those of Ignatius and Polycarp; the altar of Saint Simon, on which are his relics and those of Cosmas and Damian; the altar of Saint Matthew, on which are his relics and those of Mark and Luke; the altar of Saint Thaddeus, on which are his relics and those of Nazarius and Vitalis; the altar of Saint James, the brother of the Lord, on which are his relics and those of Gervasius and Protasius; and the altar of Saint Matthias, on which are his relics and those of Hilary and Augustine—

were dedicated with the highest honor on the sixth day before the Ides of September, on the most sacred Nativity of the Virgin, by the venerable bishops Georgius, Absalon, Pleon, and Gerfridus.

Likewise, the altar of the blessed archangel Gabriel, situated at the southern gate, was consecrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on the Annunciation of Saint Mary; that of Michael, situated at the western gate, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, by Hildegualdus, a venerable bishop; and that of Raphael, situated at the northern gate, on the second day before the Nones of September, in honor of those archangels and of all the heavenly Powers, by Jesse [Note: He was bishop of Amiens, who took part in Charlemagne’s coronation at Rome on Christmas Day in the year 800. It is therefore uncertain whether Georgius, who was present at the dedication of the church of the blessed Mary on the sixth day before the Ides of September of that same year, as it appears, was the same person as Gregorius, bishop of Amiens, Jesse’s predecessor], a most worthy and religious bishop.

With the same Lord cooperating, we also took care to rebuild from the foundations all the remaining walls of the monastery that are seen today, as they are seen, and, so that its inhabitants might attend the solemn Masses there and take delight in serving almighty God, we made certain that the place was firmly enclosed by a wall, with his assistance.

When we saw that the churches prescribed above had been founded by prudent deliberation in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, of his glorious mother, and of all his saints, as has been written above, we were inflamed by a great desire and an excessive ardor of love to obtain, according to our ability and through the mercy of that same Lord, a portion of the relics of those saints with which to adorn those holy churches of God.

Therefore, with all our strength and with the whole intention of our mind, we strove to determine how, through the help of almighty God and the assistance of my glorious lord, the great emperor, we might gather from various parts of the whole of Christendom relics of as many kinds and as great a number as possible, and from where they had been brought, and place them in this holy site, as is evident below.

First, from the holy Roman Church, through the generosity of Hadrian, of blessed memory, supreme pontiff, and after him of the venerable Pope Leo; from Constantinople and Jerusalem, brought to us through legates sent there by my lord; then from Italy, Germany, Burgundy, and Gaul, sent to us by the most holy fathers, namely patriarchs, archbishops, bishops, and abbots; and also from the sacred palace, where they had been gathered over time by earlier kings and afterward especially by our aforesaid lord. Through his almsgiving we were worthy to receive a portion of all these and to store it fittingly in this holy place.

Of those relics whose identities we knew with certainty, and concerning which we received written attestations from the aforesaid holy men, we did not neglect to insert all their names in this little work, so that by us and by all our successors who in time will succeed to this holy place and wish to know these things, the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—through whom these things, though we are unworthy, and all other good things have been granted to us—might always and everywhere be glorified, for he is blessed forever.

But concerning the other relics, whose names were uncertain to us, although we received them from those same holy fathers, we wrote nothing. As for the remaining relics, we arranged, as we had decided, to record their names in the following order. First we followed the relics of the Lord and our Savior, of his glorious mother, of the holy apostles, and of the other martyrs; afterward those of the confessors, and likewise those of the holy virgins and women devoted to continence.

Of the wood of the Lord; of his garment; of his sandals; of his manger; of his sponge; of the Jordan where he was baptized; of the rock where he sat when he fed five thousand men; of the bread which he distributed to his disciples; of the Temple of the Lord; of the candle that was lit at his Nativity; of the Mount of Olives where he prayed; of his table; of the mountain where he was transfigured; of the pillar where he was scourged; of the bonds with which he was bound; of the rock on which he mounted the cross; of the nails with which he was crucified; of the place of Calvary; of the morsel where gall and vinegar were mixed; of the rock upon which blood dripped from his side; of the Lord’s tomb; of the stone rolled away from the entrance of the tomb; and also of the tomb of the Innocents who suffered for him; of Mount Horeb; and of the wood of the three tabernacles.

Of the milk of Saint Mary; of her hair; of her garment; of her mantle. Of the beard of Saint Peter; of his sandals; of his chasuble; and of his table. Of the table of Saint Paul; of his stole; of the block in which he was confined. Of the cross of Saint Andrew. Of the manna of Saint John the Evangelist. Of the relics of the apostles James, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon, Thaddeus, Matthias, Barnabas, and Timothy. Of the bones of Zachariah, father of Saint John the Baptist. The relics of blessed Simeon, who received the Lord into his arms. Of the hair of blessed John the Baptist; of his blood; of his garment.

Of the ribs of Saint Stephen; of the stone with which he was stoned; of the grill of Saint Laurence. A finger of Saint Apollinaris; of the sponge of Saint Symphorianus; and of the garment of his mother. Relics of Saints Pancratius, Vigihi, Sisinnius, Martyrius, Pamphilus, the holy Gemini, Fabianus, Valerius, Pergentinus, Cosmas, Damian, Anastasius, George, Alexander, Cassianus, Magnus, Vitalis, Nazarius, Nabor, Celsus, Gervasius, Protasius, Innocent, Laurence, Tiburtius, Valerian, Hippolytus, Christopher, Felix, Maurice, Candidus, Exsuperius, Victor, Innocentius, Benignus, Dionysius, Rusticus, Eleutherius, Cornelius, Leodegarius, Sixtus, Firminus, Saturninus, Quentin, Valentinus, Marcellus, Lucianus, Crispinus, and Crispinianus; and bones of the forty martyrs, and blood of many others.

Of Saints Hilary, Martin, Germanus, Medardus, Audoenus, Eligius, Amandus, Lupus, Aventinus, Sulpicius, Remigius, Maurilius, Albinus, Servatius, Jerome, Aequitius, Ephrem, Gregory, Augustine, Leo, Sylvester, [Col. 0845D] Felix, Isidore, Donatus, Benedict, Columbanus, Isaac, Vincent, Anthony, Paulinus, Fortunatus, Simplicianus, Gualaricus, and Vedastus. Relics from the bodies of the saints, which Pope Paulinus deposited [that is, the bishop or patriarch of Aquileia]. Relics of Saint Megimboldus, Priscus, Eugenius, Fronto, Fidelis, Asterius, Simplicianus, Faxidus, Astogius, Gislarius, Speratus, Robertus, Galemerus, and Osqualdus [perhaps Oswald].

Of Felicitas, Perpetua, Agatha, Eugenia, Thecla, Cecilia, Petronilla, Euphemia, Fausta, Euphrasia, Aldegundis, Columba, Felicula, and Scholastica.

Up to this point, concerning the certain relics of the saints, whose names we received with certainty from the holy fathers who bestowed them upon us, we have separately listed the martyrs and the confessors. From this point onward, because we did not find the names of the other saints—whether martyrs or confessors—we have written nothing further.

Having thus honorably and suitably stored these relics, as was written somewhat earlier, we prepared with great care, in the name of the holy Trinity, a larger reliquary adorned with gold and gems [Col. 0846B]. In it we placed part of the relics listed above. Together with them, out of reverence for those saints whose relics appeared to be stored in it, we endeavored to place it beneath the crypt of the holy Savior [Note: [Col. 0845D] This reliquary was called that of Saint Prima, as John of the Chapel testifies when he speaks of Hugh of Chevincourt, the thirty-third abbot: “This Hugh of Chevincourt,” he says, “visited the feretory which we call that of Saint Prima—that is, of the primitive foundation of the Church Militant—because in it rest very many bodies of saints: Peter, Paul, John the Baptist, and other confessors and holy virgins.” Prima was likewise the name given to the monastery of Corbie in the Life of Saint Adalhard.]. As for the relics of the other saints listed above, we divided them among thirteen other smaller reliquaries, most honorably prepared with gold, silver, and precious gems, which, together with those same relics, we were deemed worthy, by the Lord’s gift, to receive from the venerable Fathers mentioned so often. We arranged for them to be placed upon the beam that we set in the arch before the altar of blessed Richarius [Note: [Col. 0845D] John of the Chapel counts thirteen gold and silver reliquaries [Col. 0846D] which Angilbert placed upon a single silver altar dedicated in honor of blessed Mary.]. Thus, in every respect as is fitting, the praise of God and the veneration of all his saints might always be adored, honored, and revered in this holy place.

[Col. 0846C] Once the altars had been arranged for the veneration of the saints named above, and had been reverently adorned with their relics, as stated above, by our humble efforts, we began carefully to consider how we might also adorn them, for the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ and in honor of all the saints in whose honor they had been consecrated, with works of the craftsman’s art in gold, silver, and gems, from the gifts of God and the generosity of my great lord and his most noble offspring, as well as from the other good and free persons whose gifts had been bestowed upon me; and, wherever suitable places existed, how we might set canopies above them. Accordingly, with the same Lord’s assistance, we endeavored to do so as best we could.

In the church of the holy Savior and of holy Richarius, eleven altars were constructed; two canopies [Note: [Col. 0846D] What a *ciborium* is, I have explained at length in the preface to the second century, no. 47: namely, a turreted shrine supported on four or eight columns, customarily set over altars and the tombs of saints. Charlemagne, in the capitulary of 789, commands that *fecuaria* or ceilings be made over altars. Now *ciborium* means κιβοτὸς (“chest”) or a pyx in which the body of Christ the Lord is kept.]; and two lecterns prepared with gold, silver, and marble. In the church of the holy Mother of God, Mary, and of the holy apostles, thirteen altars were constructed; one canopy and one very finely prepared lectern. In the church of Saint Benedict, three altars were prepared [Col. 0847A]. In the churches of the holy angels Gabriel, Michael, and Raphael, three altars were made, making thirty altars in all; also three canopies and three lecterns.

As for the other vessels and furnishings, these churches possess: seventeen items prepared with gold and silver; two golden crowns; six silver lamps; twelve copper vessels decorated with gold and silver; three golden apples; two golden chalices with patens; one large golden chalice with figures and a paten; twelve other silver chalices with their patens; and ten silver offertory plates.

At the head of Saint Richarius: one panel prepared with gold and silver; two larger doors prepared with gold and silver; two other smaller doors; two other little doors similarly prepared; one golden belt; one excellent silver inkstand prepared with gold [Col. 0847B]; one knife prepared with gold and pearls; one ivory codex most finely prepared with gold, silver, and pearls; one gold-prepared purse [Note: [Col. 0847D] That is, a bag or little pouch. Audoen, Book I of the Life of Saint Eligius, chapter 10: “Whenever he stole from him a golden armlet or a purse adorned with gold and gems, it was only so that he might assist the poor.”]; and four silver censers prepared with gold.

Thirteen silver-gilt hanaps; one large silver basin with silver figures; one silver bocularis [commonly *bocar*, a kind of flask]; two silver pitchers with their aquamaniles; one silver tube and one ivory one; two silver buckets; one golden key; one silver bell; thirteen crowns with lights; six columns before the altar of Saint Richarius prepared with gold and silver; three smaller beams with their arches prepared with silver; three bell towers prepared with gold; fifteen excellent bells [small bells or rattles], with their fifteen rings [Note: [Col. 0847D] Adrevaldus, in *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 26, calls the bells’ arm-rings hanging from ropes [Col. 0848D].]; three smaller bells; six bronze images; one ivory image; two candelabra prepared with gold; and seven doors prepared with gold.

Moreover, we gave there seventy-eight excellent hangings; two hundred copes; twenty-four silk dalmatics; six Roman albs with their amices, prepared with gold; two hundred sixty linen albs; thirty chasubles of *pallium*; ten of purple; six of *storax*; one of fish; fifteen of *platta*; and five of *cendatum*. Five stoles prepared with gold; ten maniples of *pallium* prepared with gold; five cushions of *pallium*; and five cloaks of *pallium*.

Of books: one Gospel book written in gold, wonderfully prepared with silver covers, gold, and precious stones; one other complete Gospel book. Of other books, two hundred volumes [Col. 0847D].

In addition, there were very many ornaments for construction and various uses, made of lead, glass, marble, and other materials, as well as other implements whose enumeration and fuller description would take too long. At that time, however, these were valued by the faithful of God and of Saint Richarius—who had labored with you in the service of God—as being worth fifteen thousand pounds, or even more.

When these and other things had been elegantly arranged, as the Lord enabled us, and the churches had been adorned with the various relics of the saints named above [Col. 0848A], we began to consider with devoted care how, by the Lord’s gift, we might attain this end: that, just as these churches shine honorably before human eyes in their marble buildings and other ornaments, so we might also be pleasing to almighty Christ through the praises of God, through various teachings, and through spiritual songs.

Therefore, with God’s help, we established three hundred monks who were to live regularly in this holy place, desiring and ordering that, if not more, a community of this number should be maintained forever. We also appointed one hundred boys to be educated in the schools, under the same habit and with the same food [Note: [Col. 0848D] It is clear from this place and from others that oblates used the same habit and the same food.]. They were to assist the brothers in psalmody and singing, the brothers being divided into three choirs.

Thus, the choir of the holy Savior was to have one hundred monks together with thirty-four boys; the choir of Saint Richarius was perpetually to have one hundred monks and thirty-three boys; and the choir singing before the holy Passion was likewise to have one hundred monks together with thirty-three boys.

The three choirs were to resound in the divine praises in such a way that all of them together would sing all the canonical hours in common. When these had been properly completed, one third of each choir was to leave the church and attend for a time to bodily needs or other duties, returning again after a fixed interval to celebrate the offices of divine praise.

In each choir, this was also to be continually observed: that an equal number of priests, levites, and members of the other sacred orders should be maintained. Likewise, an equal division of singers and readers was to be arranged, so that one choir would not be burdened by the other. Indeed, all, united in one mind, were continually to offer the sacrifice of praise to almighty God for the salvation of my glorious lord, Augustus Charles, and for the stability of his kingdom, with constant devotion.

When the morning or evening office had been completed, all the choirs were immediately and orderly to assemble before the holy Passion, with only ten psalmists remaining in each choir. Then, passing through the gate of Saint Gabriel and through the hall [commonly *salle*, a hall] of the lord abbot, they were to proceed, singing, through the western part of the cloister to Saint Mary. There, after prayer had been offered according to the time, they were to return to Saint Benedict, situated on the eastern side of the cloister. From there they were to enter by the steps of the arches to Saint Maurice; then, entering the basilica of Saint Richarius, they were to return to their respective choirs.

We also order with the greatest devotion that no day pass without the singing of holy Masses—namely, that, if not more, at least thirty Masses be celebrated daily by the brothers of the various choirs at the various altars, apart from the two conventual Masses, which are celebrated most solemnly in the morning and at midday [Col. 0849A]. At these, daily remembrance is to be made of the most holy Pope Adrian and of my glorious lord, Augustus Charles, his wife, and his offspring, so that, in accordance with the Apostle’s command, we may continually offer to our Savior God supplications and prayers of thanksgiving for kings and for all who are set in high positions [Col. 0850A].

[Col. 0849]

## Certain Rubrical Statutes

*(In Mabillon, in the same place.)*

[. . .] What majesty and reverence were observed there in the celebration of the divine offices is shown to us by one or two examples, which it is useful to present here from an old codex, formerly Petau’s, then belonging to the most serene queen of Sweden, and now in the Ottobonian Library.

In that codex, Abbot Angilbert is said to have ordered that on the most holy day of Easter and on the Nativity of the Lord, the brothers and all the others who had gathered in the church of the Savior for Mass should receive communion in that same church. While the brothers and the other clergy were receiving communion from the priest who had sung Mass that day, two other priests, together with two deacons and an equal number of subdeacons, were to be present: one priest was to give communion to the men and the other to the women there, so that clergy and people, having received communion together, might together hear the blessing and the conclusion of the Mass.

After this, the two priests—one at one door and the other at the other—were to give communion to the boys descending from the upper ambulatories or porticoes. Then each priest, with his ministers, standing at the far end, perhaps at the step of the altar [Col. 0849C], was to give communion to those who had not come forward to receive it at the places mentioned above. To ensure that this was properly done, the same abbot had ordered that on those two feasts four priests, and the same number of deacons and subdeacons, should assist the priest celebrating the solemn Mass.

This concerns the first rite.

The second concerns the greater litanies. For their more solemn celebration, the crosses and processions of seven neighboring churches were required to come to Saint Richarius. When they had arrived there, they all stood together in the paradise, or atrium, of the church before the holy Nativity. After prayer had been offered, they remained there in orderly fashion, with the men divided off on the north and the women on the south, awaiting the brothers and the schola—that is, the boys—as they came out of the church of Saint Richarius [Col. 0850A].

First, the person carrying the vessel of holy water proceeded through the gate of Saint Michael; then came three others, each carrying a censer. Next came seven crosses, followed by the large reliquary of the basilica of the holy Savior, positioned between three priests, one on either side, who carried the smaller reliquaries [Col. 0850B]. After them came, in groups of seven each, the deacons, subdeacons, acolytes, exorcists, readers, and doorkeepers. Then came the remaining monks, seven by seven, lest, if they proceeded in groups of two or three, they fill a mile’s distance.

All these were followed by seven boys, each with a small flame or torch. After them came noble men, seven by seven, chosen by the provost or dean; the more distinguished women followed in the same order. After all these came seven crosses from the churches outside the monastery. They were followed by boys and girls skilled in singing, who sang the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and other such texts. Then came the more honorable men and women from those churches. At the very end came the mixed crowd of the sick and elderly, who likewise proceeded on foot in groups of seven [Col. 0850C]. Those who could not walk because of infirmity followed on horseback.

When everything had been arranged in this way, the procession proceeded through the middle of the monastery, then along the public road, and, passing through the southern gate, returned by circling the wall and entering through the northern gate.

During these greater litanies, after antiphons, psalms, and other things of that kind, three creeds were sung—the Apostles’ Creed, the Constantinopolitan Creed, and that of Saint Athanasius—followed by the Lord’s Prayer. After the general litany, the brothers with the boys’ schola sang litanies, first the Gallican, second the Italian, and third the Roman. Finally, the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* followed, and afterward the solemn Mass at the holy Savior.

[Col. 0849]

## Poems of Saint Angilbert

### I. Abbot Angilbert to Saints Richarius and Eligius

[Note: [Col. 0849D] In Quercetanus’s edition, no. 177; it was also published by Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part 1, in the Life of Saint Angilbert, p. 101. Angilbert was no stranger to the art of poetry, and perhaps for that reason he earned from Alcuin the name “Homer.” Therefore there is no reason why this poem should not be attributed to the person who speaks in it.]

*(In Frobenius’s edition of the works of Blessed Alcuin.)*

Behold your little servant, illustrious shepherd Richarius:

This little dwelling he has built for you, Father.

Ever shall I be *honoris* [F.: *honorus*, “honorable”], through a great love of devotion,

Everywhere truly your devoted worshiper [Al.: “yours”].

You first bore me, wretched as I was, from the waves of the world

Into a gracious bosom, Christ granting it to you.

You nourished my tender [Note: [Col. 0851D] “Tender” is not to be understood with reference to age, but to spiritual life, which must be nourished at the beginning with the sacred milk of heavenly doctrine, as Paul says to the Corinthians. MAB.] mouth

With the sacred milk of salvation, forming it through excellent songs.

Therefore, best of Fathers, I love you with all my vows,

And I desire that you also may always love me.

Complete what you began in me with a kindly mind,

And restore your servant to his Lord as your own.

You also, holy priest Eligius,

Assist me by your prayers through the merits of your virtues.

You now have great power in the heavenly seat through him

Who granted you the ability to accomplish so much on earth.

O holy Fathers, O most brilliant lights of the world,

Hope of life and forgiveness, you are my sure salvation.

Here, prostrate at your feet, drenched in bitter tears,

I lament the sins of my life.

Often striking my guilty breast violently with my fists,

I confess my sins to the merciful Lord [Col. 0851B].

Be gentle patrons to me now in my misery:

I beg you, seek pardon for my sins.

I believe that great praise, glory, and reward await you:

That your little servant may not perish in death.

Whoever reads this inscription, say, I pray, to Angilbert:

“Christ, remember your poor and wretched servant.”

May this house be blessed through you, Christ, we pray,

So that your gifts may come here to your servants.

### II. Poem inscribed inside the tower of Saint Richarius in the monastery of Centula

Almighty Lord, who governs the heights and the depths,

Powerful in majesty, God always and everywhere,

Look down from your throne, glory of the saints above,

And grant help to your servants, good King.

Grant peace to rulers and salvation to their subjects.

Drive away the threats of the enemy and restrain savage wars.

May these shining heights of the temple which I, Angilbert,

Have established be pleasing to you, O God.

Grant Augustus Charles, by whose strength I completed this work,

The great joys of your empire.

And to everyone who here strikes the highest ears with prayers,

Grant, O God, that their prayers may always attain fulfillment.

### III. Poem depicted on the pavement of the church of Saint Richarius

I, humble abbot Angilbert, had this pavement constructed,

Led by love of God,

So that after my death Christ, my life and salvation,

Might deign to grant me holy rest.

### IV. Poem to Pippin

*(From Duchesne, *Writers of Frankish History*.)*

And now, Pippin, ruler from the shores of the West,

You are here to increase the great joys of your father Charles.

For just as Phoebus rises from the eastern stars,

So you yourself shine as an ornament among the western peoples.

Your father and your family rejoice that, long awaited,

You are at last coming from the cold Alps.

With so great a prince, the people, clergy, altar, and priest

Gather in great joy at your arrival.

For as greatly as you have delayed, striving to create postponements,

So strongly did love shine forth in your father’s anxious heart.

And the farther the joys delay the mind,

The more powerfully the image of the absent offspring pleases.

This is what your brother Charles is doing: he is consumed

By love for his outstanding brother.

He delays, and loses himself in reasons for delaying,

On difficult and uncertain roads.

Sighs rise, and he frustrates the messengers he has sent as they go,

Thinking negligence to be whatever can cause absence.

Chlodowih, though held by the same love,

Comforts him, speaking more gently of his brother’s actions.

“Spare yourself, brother,” he says; “stop complaining.

Our beloved companion will come, I believe.

For while I was enjoying the rewards of the present night,

The image of my outstanding brother stood before me [Col. 0852B].

It played with me through embraces and very great joys.

As it departed, it said: ‘I bring every good thing.

Know that soon I shall be present before your beloved eyes,

And tell my Charles these things that have happened.

For before the horns of the waxing moon are filled,

When you are my companion, I shall give you faithful kisses.’”

Now, by God’s gift, we no longer see dreams unbidden,

But I, Angilbert, see the fruits of the dream.

For I embrace you, victorious, in the fields of Langres,

Having scarcely been able to mingle words with pious words.

Your father’s love troubled you; both loves burn me:

His constant love, and now your profound love.

Long-awaited one, grant—please—the petitioner a little time,

So that you may hear many words in a few words [Col. 0852C].

May you be happy, accustomed as you are to renewing our grief,

For by departing quickly you renew our wounds.

May he who rules all things, the highest and the lowest, be with you;

May he lead you safely across the waters and along the road.

May you go safely, defended by Christ’s protection,

So that the embrace of your revered parent may receive you.

If divine protection guards you two through the years,

May you be blessed by its gift, protected from every evil.

O why was I not worthy then to behold the king’s face,

When he gave pure kisses as he embraced you?

When Charles, thirsting for you, and Chlodowih, the anxious hero,

Could scarcely hide the uncertain laughter in their hearts,

What will Chrodthrudis do, what will Berta and the royal household,

Awaiting you, be able to say, bearing such joys?

What do Gis [F.: Gisla] and Teodrada, together with their offspring,

Discuss concerning all the other things your royal love brings about?

What does Gisla, the outstanding and most beautiful bride of the mighty Thunderer,

What does Luitgard, rejoicing, gain from the King’s love?

What does Hildibald, preeminent in the rank of prophet,

And what do dukes, counts, boys, and old men do?

A profound love burns them all with sacred bonds,

And they keep their eyes fixed upon your faces.

May these joys of peace remain for the father and his brothers;

May these blessed festivities remain for the good Franks.

May Christ, the ruler from the stars, strengthen this kingdom,

So that the offspring may flourish and the father himself may prosper.

May your brother Charles love you, and may you love him who loves you:

Bind Chlodowih to yourselves with a twofold devoted love.

He himself will repay your love with affection;

Thus learn together to love your own father.

### V. Epitaph of Saint Chaidoc the Confessor

*(In Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum of the Order of Saint Benedict*.)*

Beneath this mass lies Chaidoc, rightly a priest:

Scotland gave him birth; Gallic soil covers him.

Here, rejoicing, he followed the commandments of the Lord Christ;

Blessed in mind, he despised his native riches.

From this there grew for him an abundance a hundredfold,

And he reaps rich rewards from the heavenly soil.

Trusting in piety as his guide,

Angilbert composed for him both a poem and a tomb.

### VI. Epitaph of Fricor, or Adrian

*(In Mabillon, in the same place.)*

He who is seen buried in an earthly body

Now joyfully possesses heavenly joys according to his merits.

This was Fricor, associated with Chaidoc,

Whom Centula rejoices to have received as its own.

Strong in virtue, he despised the prosperity of the world,

And now great glory is revealed to him who lives.

When it pleased God, he sought the kingdom of heaven;

Now he shines in Angilbert’s poem. Amen.

## In the Year of Our Lord 816: Leidrad, Bishop of Lyon

[Col. 0853]

## Historical Notice on Leidrad

*(From Galland, *Ancient Library of the Fathers*, volume XIII.)*

[Col. 0853B] Leidrad, by nationality a Noric [Note: [Col. 0853B] Theodulf of Orléans, *Paraenesis to the Judges*.], and, as some seem to think, a very close associate of Charlemagne, even his librarian, obtained the see of Lyon after Hilduin, the nephew of Ado [Note: [Col. 0853B] Hugh, in the *Chronicle*.], from the year 799 to 813.

During this period the bones of blessed Cyprian were brought to Lyon and placed in the principal church, together with the heads of the holy martyrs Pantaleon and Speratus of Scillium [Note: [Col. 0853B] Ado, *Martyrology*, eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.]. He built many churches, founded monasteries, restored chant in the church of Lyon, and performed other duties of a good and diligent shepherd, despite poor bodily health [Note: [Col. 0854B] Compare his first letter below.].

At Charlemagne’s command he returned to Spain to strengthen the people against the teaching of Felix [Col. 0854B]. At the beginning of Louis’s reign he withdrew to the monastery of Soissons, in whose place Agobard was appointed [Note: [Col. 0854B] Ado and Hugh, in the passage cited.]. These facts may be found in Agobard’s work in the Baluze edition.

There survives from his works a book on the sacrament of baptism, together with a letter on the same subject to the emperor, which Mabillon published in his *Analecta* and from which we too have taken it. In addition, there are two letters, which are read at the end of Baluze’s Agobard. We have arranged to reprint both of them from that edition.

Leidrad scarcely completed a year in the monastery of Soissons, where he died.

[Col. 0853]

## Leidrad’s Book on the Sacrament of Baptism to the Emperor Charlemagne

[Col. 0853C]

To the most Christian and most glorious lord Charles, emperor, most fortunate Augustus.

You have deigned to command us [Note: [Col. 0853] Indeed, also the other bishops, as is clear from the letter to Odilbert, in Mabillon, *Annals*, volume I, p. 21.] to make known to you, either through our writings or in person, how we and our suffragans teach and instruct the priests of God and the people entrusted to us concerning the sacrament of baptism and the other rites celebrated in connection with baptism. You also ask whether we ourselves observe what we preach.

All these matters, just as they are difficult and arduous to understand, are likewise intricate and involved to explain—especially for us, whom the smallness of our intellect constrains and the greatness of the subject so overwhelms that we are more likely to shrink back than to lift it up. But because he has commanded who can neither be evaded by excuse nor disregarded by silence, the work must be undertaken, and, according to the measure of our strength, what we understand must be explained concerning what is to be received and observed in the sacrament of regeneration.

Whatever we put forward contrary to what is fitting is not the result of presumption but of timidity, because we are answering one whose question we do not dare to leave unanswered. We offer our knowledge to him who is more accustomed to teach than to rebuke, whose rebuke is most health-giving—a rebuke by which each person is instructed rather than confounded—and whose teaching mercifully invites everyone into fellowship with his word, while unjustly frightening no one away.

Relying, therefore, on the favor of your most steadfast modesty, we explain, insofar as we can approach these matters, though we may be able to speak of them with little dignity, what we understand you to have commanded us, drawing chiefly upon the words of the holy Fathers taken from various short works.

Before we come to the other matters, we wish to set forth a few things that were prefigured from the beginning of the world as pertaining to the power of baptism, and to arrange the mysteries of the second birth—or rather, the first birth in Christ—and afterward to treat the remaining matters, especially since you say that you wish to know how we teach and instruct the people and the priests.

## Chapter I. The Symbolic Meanings of Holy Baptism

[Col. 0855B]

The world was still unformed. The sun did not yet shine red, the moon did not yet grow pale, and the stars did not yet glitter. Matter, disordered and invisible, lay oppressed by the vastness of the abysses and by hideous darkness. The Spirit of God alone was borne over the waters like a charioteer, and gave birth to the world as it was coming into being, in the figure of baptism.

A firmament is constructed midway between heaven and earth. According to the etymology of the Hebrew language, heaven—that is, *Samaim*—derives its name from the waters, and the waters that are above the heavens are separated for the praises of the Lord. Hence, in Ezekiel, crystal is seen stretched out above the cherubim—that is, waters compacted and made denser.

The first living thing emerges from the waters, and lifts the faithful, winged creatures from earth to heaven [Col. 0855C]. Humanity is fashioned, and amid the hands of God the mysteries of the waters are present.

Paradise is planted in Eden, and one spring is divided into four sources. Later, according to the vision of the prophet Ezekiel, it flows out from the temple and travels toward the rising sun, giving life to bitter and dead waters.

The world sins, and is not cleansed without a flood of waters. Immediately the dove of the Holy Spirit, after the most dreadful bird had been driven away, flies down to Noah—as to Christ in the Jordan—and announces peace to the world with a branch of refreshment and light.

Pharaoh, unwilling for the people of the Lord to leave Egypt with his army, is drowned as a type of baptism. In the Psalms, his destruction is described: “You strengthened the sea by your power; you crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters” (Psalm 73:13) [Col. 0855D].

Hence the little snakes and scorpions pursue all that is dry. The mystery of the cross is changed upon the altar, and the seventy palms of the apostles are watered by the sweetened streams of the Law.

Abraham and Isaac dig wells; the foreigners oppose them; the city of Beersheba, named from the oath, and the kingdom of Solomon derive their names from springs. Rebecca is found at a well; Rachel is greeted with the kiss of the Supplanter because of the waters; Moses rescues the daughters of the priest of Midian from harm at an opened well.

“The voice of the Lord is over the waters.” “The Lord is over many waters.” “The Lord makes the flood dwell.” His teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep that have come up from the washing, all of them bearing twins, and none is barren among them [Col. 0856A].

Micah prophesies concerning the grace of baptism: “He will have compassion on us; he will plunge our iniquities beneath the waters, and he will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea” (Micah 7:19).

Ezekiel says: “For I will take you from among the nations, and gather you from all the lands, and pour clean water over you, and you shall be cleansed from all your iniquities” (Ezekiel 36:24–25).

After his baptism, and after the waters of the Jordan had been sanctified by his washing, the Savior himself performs his first sign from water. He who had begun with water ended in water. His side is pierced by a lance, and the mysteries both of baptism and of martyrdom are poured forth.

After his resurrection, he sends his disciples into the whole world and says to them: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” And again: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved” [Col. 0856B].

From that time, therefore, the apostles began to teach and baptize, while the nations began to believe and be baptized. Thus the person who is to be baptized is first taught to believe—that is, instructed in the faith. For this is what it means to be a catechumen: to be instructed. *Catechize* means “to instruct.”

Thus the children of Israel were instructed by Moses concerning the sacrifice of the lamb and its blood before they came to the Red Sea. Hence the person to whom God first speaks through a priest, as through Moses, is called a catechumen—that is, “one who hears.” For they say that *catechumen* can be interpreted as both “instructed” and “hearing.”

First they are exorcized; then they receive salt and are anointed. “To exorcize” is said in Greek; in Latin it means “to adjure” or “to rebuke.”

For through sin we fell in the first man, and all came into the inheritance of death. We are filled with fears and errors because of the sin with which we are born. Therefore even infants are breathed upon and exorcized, so that the hostile power of the devil, which deceived humanity in order to possess human beings, may be driven away from them.

It is not God’s creature in infants, therefore, that is exorcized or breathed upon, but the one under whose power all are born with sin. For he is the prince of sinners.

Exorcism is a word of rebuke and adjuration directed against the unclean spirit on behalf of the possessed or of catechumens [Note: [Col. 0855D] From this it is clear what power is conferred upon exorcists at their ordination, namely, the power to lay hands upon the possessed. [Col. 0856D] Compare Berardus, *Canons* 11, 15, and 20, distinction 23, part I, chapter 15, section 4.]. Through it, the devil’s most wicked power and long-established malice, or his violating attack, is expelled and driven away from them.

This was signified by that lunatic whom the Lord Jesus rebuked, and the demon departed from him. Therefore the devil’s power is exorcized and breathed upon in them, so that they may renounce him; and, having been rescued from the power of darkness, they may be transferred through the sacrament of baptism into the kingdom of their Lord [Col. 0856D].

Salt was instituted by the Fathers to be given to catechumens in the rite for this reason: that by tasting it they might receive the seasoning of wisdom and not lose the savor of Christ; that they might not be foolish and look backward, like Lot’s wife, who was turned into a pillar of salt; and that by its sign those who renounce the world, its deeds, and its desires through faith might be seasoned, no longer remembering their former affections or returning to the allurements of the age.

Therefore the command of the Law was that every sacrifice should be seasoned by the addition of salt, as the lawgiver says: “You shall not remove the salt of the covenant from the sacrifice of the Lord.” For this reason the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Every victim shall be salted with salt.” And elsewhere: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves.”

Some believe that among certain pagans there was also an ancient custom by which those who promised loyalty to kings would eat sworn or consecrated salt in the presence of the very kings to whom they promised their allegiance. Hence it is written in the Book of Ezra that the Samaritan officials, when writing to the king of the Persians concerning their accusation of the Jews, said: “We remember the salt which we ate in the palace” (1 Esdras 4:14) [Col. 0857A].

There is certainly a distinction between catechumens and competentes [Note: [Col. 0857D] Compare the letter of Jesse of Amiens.]. Catechumens are those who first come from paganism and, desiring to believe in Christ, hear the word of faith, but are not yet called believers.

Competentes, however, are those who, after instruction in the faith and after a life of self-restraint, hasten to receive the grace of Christ. Therefore they are called *competentes*, that is, “those seeking the grace of Christ.”

The former ask and receive; they are catechized and instructed in the instruction of the sacraments. To the latter the saving Creed is handed over as a reminder of the faith and a sign of holy confession, so that, instructed by it, they may recognize how they ought now to present themselves for the grace of Christ.

This entire action, which is celebrated over catechumens and competentes, is called by some “scrutiny.” We think this is for no other reason than that it derives from “scrutinizing,” in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “God, who scrutinizes hearts and kidneys.” For there the hearts of believers and doubters were scrutinized by the priests, so that they might understand who was already rightly to be admitted to baptism and who was still to be deferred.

In accordance with this, the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Search the Scriptures.”

## Chapter II. Concerning the Touching of the Nostrils and Ears: For What Reason, According to Ecclesiastical Tradition, It Is Performed by All Catholic Priests of Christ
The entry of faith and of all holy teaching is admitted into the mind through the ears, and understanding arises from hearing. For no one can know the sacraments of faith unless he hears one preaching, as the blessed Apostle affirms when he says: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of God.” Rightly, therefore, the organs of his senses are sanctified, [Col. 0857D] without which faith cannot reach the mind.

It must nevertheless be understood that different practices concerning this matter are observed in different regions. Some touch the ears and nostrils of catechumens with holy oil; others with spittle; others without spittle or oil; and still others touch the mouth with oil, following the Lord’s example. Thus it is written in the Gospel concerning the deaf and mute man: “He put his fingers into his ears.”

But whether by the touch of oil or otherwise, the ears are sanctified so that those who are coming to baptism may keep their ears undefiled by every evil and shameful word, as it is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclus. 28:28). And again: “Apply your heart to discipline, [Col. 0858A] and prepare your ear for words of wisdom” (Ecclus. 2:2). The sanctification of the ears therefore signifies that the faithful should turn away from and flee all speech outside the discipline of Christ, as though contradicting his teaching, and should devote themselves solely to hearing the words of God, because they have consecrated their hearing to Christ’s utterances.

The nostrils likewise are sanctified by a similar touch, so that those who come to baptism may be admonished to preserve the sacrament of so great a mystery inviolate and entire until death: so long as they draw the breath of this life through their nostrils, they must not depart from the worship and service of Christ our Lord. Hence the holy man Job also says: “As long as my breath remains in me, and the spirit of God is in my nostrils, my lips shall not speak iniquity, nor shall my tongue utter deceit.”

But an even subtler meaning is signified by this sanctification of the nostrils. That touch summons the faithful to spiritual perception of fragrance, so that they may be able to sense Christ—not with bodily, but with mental faculties—with inestimable sweetness, and say to him: “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:3). The Apostle commends this fragrance to Christians when he says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of him in every place, because we are the good fragrance of Christ to God.” The faithful must therefore live in such a way that the sweetest fragrance from the holiness of their lives may rise to God.

The catechumens are also now anointed on the chest and between the shoulders with exorcised oil when they renounce Satan and his works and pomps. We believe that this is done [Col. 0858C] so that the dwelling-place of the heart may be marked both before and behind; by this sign, the devil, the author of faithlessness, may be driven away, and Christ, the giver of faith and charity, may enter. For the human heart is the seat of error and vices when possessed by the devil; but it becomes the dwelling-place of faith, hope, and charity when defended and illumined by Christ. As it is written: “From the heart come evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders.” And: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart.” The hearts of the catechumens are therefore rightly anointed in their renunciation of the devil, so that he may depart from them together with all his works and pomps.

## CHAPTER III. On the renunciation of Satan, and on what his works and pomps are

Renunciation is abdication and rejection. And when we say, “Do you renounce Satan?” what else do we say but, “Do you resist the devil?” as the Apostle says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you”; and, “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.” The devil must be resisted, his works must be despised, and his pomps must be renounced, so that he may find no means by which to dominate us but may be excluded from the hearts of the catechumens, so that the house of conscience may be cleansed. The house is cleansed so that Christ, entering it, may find it clean. In this profession of renunciation, the words “I renounce” are spoken not to human beings but to God and to his angels, who record them. Renunciation must be made not only with words but also with conduct, not merely with the sound of the tongue but with the action of life. [Col. 0859A] After a person has expelled the worst invader by renouncing the devil, let him introduce the best possessor.

There is, however, a distinction between works and pomps. The works of the devil are the profane rites offered to idols, and then murder, theft, robbery, fraud, perjury, adultery, enmities, dissensions, anger, quarrels, divisions, and other things of this kind. The pomps of the devil include spectacles, insane pleasures, shameless jesting, and the various plagues of envious dispositions. Thus we know that the ancient Fathers preached to the faithful concerning the avoidance of the devil’s pomps:

“Why does the devil set before us the madness of spectacles and the snare of entertainments and shameful pleasures, except to capture by these delights those whom he had lost? Flee, beloved, flee the spectacles; [Col. 0859B] flee the most shameful arenas of the devil, lest the bonds of the evil one hold you. Is someone a lover of the circus? What pleasure is there in seeing charioteers competing in the circus, crowds panting with insane fury, or anyone breaking the horse of his opponent who is ahead? All that pleasure consists in shouting, ‘He has won!’ in the theaters. It is a stain upon morals to learn shameful things and hear indecent ones. That chorus and song of the pantomime entice the ear, but they conquer a healthy disposition.”

The pomps of the devil are all illicit desires that disfigure rather than adorn the soul, such as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the ambitions of the world. To the desire of the flesh belong enticements and pleasures; to the desire of the eyes, the frivolity of spectacles; to worldly ambition, insane pride: there is an inflated smoke by which a person placed in some position of power fails to recognize that he is a human being when he judges another human being. Whoever therefore wishes to conquer these three things should conquer the things that are in the world; and through them he also conquers the one who, by persuading through pride, deceived the world.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Creed

*Symbolum* is Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “sign” or “contribution,” that is, something which many contribute into one. The apostles did this in these words, each contributing into one whole what he understood. It is called a sign or token because at that time many pretended to be apostles of Christ, naming Christ indeed but not proclaiming him with true faith. Therefore they established the Creed as a sign by which the one who truly preached Christ according to the apostolic rules might be recognized. For when the apostles were about to depart to evangelize among the nations, they established this as the sign or token of their preaching. It contains the confession of the Trinity, the unity of the Church, and the entire confession of Christian doctrine. The apostles did not leave this Creed of our faith written in ink on paper, but on the fleshly tablets of the heart.

## CHAPTER V. On belief
