After the Apostles’ Creed, the most certain faith, which the teachers of the Churches have handed down, is this: one must profess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one invisible God, of one essence, power, and eternity, so that, while the distinct property of each Person is preserved, the Trinity is neither divided substantially nor confused altogether personally. One must also confess the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeding from the Father and the Son. The Son proceeds from the Father by being born, whereas the Holy Spirit proceeds without being born. We also believe that the Son himself assumed humanity from the Virgin without sin, so that he might mercifully restore, by his own will, the one whom he had created by goodness alone and who had fallen of his own accord. We believe that he was truly crucified, rose on the third day, and ascended into heaven with that same flesh glorified. In that flesh he is expected to come for the judgment of the living and the dead. And we believe that in the divine and human substance Christ possesses one Person, which he did not divide by the integrity of both substances, just as he did not confuse the two substances by the unity of the Person.

After Christ’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection, the Creed commends the holy Catholic Church. For once God has been demonstrated, his temple also must be demonstrated: the Church, holy, one, true, and catholic, warring against all heresies and never conquered. All heresies have gone out from it, like useless branches cut off from the vine; but it remains in its root, in its vine, and in its charity, and the gates of hell shall not overcome it.

We believe in the forgiveness of sins. Without this faith, [Col. 0860C] if anyone approaches baptism, he closes the door of pardon against himself. Holy baptism completely wipes away all offenses, both original and personal, whether committed, thought, known, or unknown; all are forgiven. He who made all things renews the human being; he who does not seek merits grants pardon for offenses. Grace anticipates even infancy itself, so that those who had previously been held captive by the devil in Adam may be free through Christ. Baptism was instituted for all sins. For lesser sins, without which we cannot exist, the Lord’s Prayer was instituted. We are washed once by baptism and washed daily by prayer. For crimes, however, or certain monstrous deeds—that is, mortal sins—those who have committed them must perform penance, and for these it is necessary that they be separated from the body of Christ. Thus sins are forgiven in the Church in three ways: in baptism, in prayer, and in the greater humility of penance. Nevertheless, God does not forgive sins except to the baptized.

We also believe in the resurrection of the flesh, which has already occurred in Christ, so that the body may also hope for what has occurred in the Head. This is the whole hope of our faith: that we shall rise again. The good will rise, and the evil will rise; the good so that they may enjoy eternal blessedness, the evil so that they may be punished with everlasting fire.

We believe in eternal life, in which the incorruptible will be equal to the angels of God, so that they may live with them in eternal life, in one immortality and an everlasting homeland. In that homeland, Christ himself will be our eternal life. But who could explain in words what that good is which God has promised to his saints? [Col. 0861A] Nevertheless, we can more easily say what will not be there in that eternal life than what will be there. Death will not be there, nor mourning, weariness, sickness, hunger, thirst, heat, corruption, want, distress, or sadness. Regarding these matters, therefore, about which we question catechumens when they are baptized, we believe in this way, and after baptism we preach to them in this way.

## CHAPTER VI. On baptism

*Baptismus* is Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “immersion.” It is called immersion because there a person is changed for the better by the spirit of grace and becomes something altogether different from what he was. Previously we were foul through the deformity of sins; in the immersion itself we are made beautiful by the whitening of virtues. Through baptism the human body [Perhaps: spirit] is restored to the former condition of that first human being before sin—but not in such a way that he may live carelessly after baptism. For he is brought into contests to fight against the devil, the prince of vices, in the arena of this world, where “we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4:9). An immense multitude of people watches both sides—that is, Christ’s and the devil’s—struggling.

There are two covenants of believers. The first covenant is that in which a person renounces the devil, his pomps, and his entire way of life. The second covenant is that in which he professes his belief in God the almighty Father, in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the [Col. 0861C] Holy Spirit. But this is not the end of the victory. The faithful bring these covenants before the angelic court, where the names of those who profess them are recorded in the book of life, not by any human being but by a higher power from heaven. Then the recruits of God and soldiers of Christ receive the weapons of the sacraments, so that they may wage war against the devil. Their strongest defense, however, is Christ himself, whom they have put on in baptism, as the Apostle says: “You who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” Whoever wishes to conquer by his hand must prove strong in good works; let him plant his feet firmly and not let his steps waver, so that he may achieve victory.

There are therefore also two kinds of baptism. The first baptism washes away the filth of sins through the bath of regeneration; the second is that by which someone is baptized in his own blood through martyrdom. Christ was baptized with this baptism, so that in this matter also, as in others, he might give believers an example, as the Apostle says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example.” Concerning this baptism the Lord himself says: “I have a baptism with which I must be baptized, and how I am constrained until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12:50). He said to the sons of Zebedee: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink, and be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” (Mark 10:38).

The baptism of water is that water which, at the time of the Passion, flowed from Christ’s side; and there is no other element that cleanses everything in this world and gives life to all things. Therefore, when we are baptized into Christ, [Col. 0862A] through him we are reborn, so that, purified, we may be given life. This font is the source of all glories; this font is an image of the eternal font. That water not only washes away filth but also frees the soul from sins.

It is sanctified through the consecration of the word. Remove the word, however, and what is water except water?

> “[Col. 0861D] The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament.”
>
> [Note: Saying of St. Augustine, *Tractate 80 on John*.]

The power of the word cleanses us through water. For the Apostle says: “Let us draw near to God with a true heart in the fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our body washed with pure water.”

It must be understood that the order and practice of baptizing differed at different times; nevertheless, there has always been one faith and one baptism. John baptized in one way, the Lord himself in another, and the apostles before the Savior’s Passion [Col. 0862B] in another—before blood and water flowed from his side—and afterward in another, once it had been said to them: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

The Apostle also calls those who departed from Egypt fathers who were baptized: “I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea.” And indeed, after departing from Egypt, they were led by a strong hand and an outstretched arm. When they came to the Red Sea, Moses, the servant of God, went before them carrying the staff he had received from the Lord. He struck the waters, and immediately the waves were forced into a heap, and the billow, driven back upon itself, bent over; the liquid gained solidity, and the bed of the sea dried into dust. Some entered [Col. 0862C] to be saved, others to be punished. The one element of the waters, at the command of the author of all creation, judged both groups and separated the godly from the ungodly.

Moses bore the figure of the Lord Christ: in the staff we recognize the cross; we understand the Red Sea as the baptism of Christ reddened by blood; and the king of Egypt and his people as the devil, the author of sins, together with all his ministers. Baptism, however, is an image of Christ’s death and burial, as the Apostle testifies: “Do you not know, brothers, that all who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as he was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be so in the likeness of his resurrection, knowing this: that our old person was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin. For whoever has died has been justified from sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ.”

Some have understood that a threefold immersion is performed out of reverence for the Trinity; others, because of the sacrament of the three-day burial. But when the blessed Pope Gregory was questioned by someone about threefold and single immersion, he replied as follows:

> “Concerning the threefold immersion of baptism, nothing truer can be answered than what you yourselves have understood, because, where there is one faith, a diversity of custom does no harm to the ministry of the holy Church. When we immerse three times, we signify the sacrament of the three-day burial, so that, when the infant is brought out of the waters three times, the resurrection of the three-day period may be expressed. But if someone should also understand it as being done out of reverence for the supreme Trinity, this in no way prevents immersing the one being baptized once in the waters. Since there is one substance in three subsistences, it cannot in any way be reprehensible to immerse an infant in baptism either three times or once, since in the three immersions the Trinity of the Persons can be signified, and in the single immersion the unity of the divinity can be represented.”

> [Note: It was Leander of Seville; to him is addressed Letter 4 of Book I.]

Although, according to the Apostle, we are baptized into Christ’s death, if baptism is administered at the solemnity of regeneration with any Person of the Trinity omitted, nothing is accomplished unless the whole Trinity is invoked. For the rite of baptism is sanctified only in the one name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Baptism belongs not to a human being but to Christ. Therefore it makes no difference whether a heretic or a believer performs the baptism, because the sacrament is so holy that it is not polluted even when administered by a murderer. A heretic indeed possesses Christ’s baptism; but because he is outside the unity of the faith, it benefits him nothing. Once he has entered into that unity, however, the baptism that he possessed outside, to his condemnation, immediately begins to benefit him for salvation. Heretics possess baptism as a deserter possesses his military mark; yet if the deserter himself is corrected and begins to serve again, no one dares change his mark.

## CHAPTER VII. On the sacred anointing

After the bath we are anointed, so that we may be reckoned among those who bear Christ’s name. For *chrisma* is interpreted as “anointing,” just as *Christus* means “anointed”; through this anointing we become a royal race.

In the Old Testament not only kings and priests were anointed, but also the tabernacle of the testimony, which was established at the Lord’s command, was sanctified with sacred anointing. The Lord said to Moses: “You shall surround the court with curtains and its entrance; and, taking the oil of anointing, you shall anoint the tabernacle with its vessels, so that they may be sanctified; the altar of burnt offering and all its vessels, the basin and its base—you shall consecrate all of them with the oil of anointing, so that they may be holy of holies.” Not only the altar but also all the vessels are consecrated with oil, because all the members of the Church are made Christian through the chrism.

The priests also—that is, Aaron and his sons—were first washed with water, as a figure of baptism, and afterward anointed, as the Lord says to Moses: “You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and, after washing them with water, you shall clothe them in the holy garments, so that they may minister to me, and their anointing may advance them to an everlasting priesthood” (Exod. 40:13). In these words it must be especially noted that this typological anointing advances them to an everlasting priesthood, which is that of Christ and the Church. For that Levitical priesthood cannot in any way be called everlasting, because, when the truth came, the figure ceased.

Concerning this ointment which advances to an everlasting priesthood, the Psalmist also says: “Like ointment on the head that runs down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.” The anointing that was truly fulfilled in Christ and is daily completed in his members therefore had its figure in that anointing of which we read in the Old Testament:

“Samuel took a flask of oil and poured it over his head—that is, Saul’s—and kissed him and said: ‘Behold, the Lord has anointed you as prince over his inheritance.’” And again: “Samuel therefore took the horn of oil and anointed him—that is, David—in the midst of his brothers; and the spirit of the Lord was directed into David from that day and thereafter” (1 Sam. 16:13).

In these words also it must be noted that after the anointing—or rather, through the anointing—the spirit of the Lord is directed into David, just as we believe that in the Church the Holy Spirit is given through the anointing of chrism and the laying on of hands. For just as the forgiveness of sins is given in baptism, so through anointing the sanctification of the Spirit is bestowed. This also applies to the former discipline by which people used to be anointed for priesthood and kingship: although it is performed bodily, it produces a spiritual effect. So too in the grace of baptism, the visible act is that we are immersed in water, but the spiritual effect is that we are cleansed from sins. For this reason they are called sacraments: beneath the covering of bodily things, divine power works the salvation of those same sacraments more secretly.

The reason why priests are permitted to anoint the heads of the baptized with chrism—provided that it has been consecrated by a bishop—but are not permitted to sign the forehead, which belongs to bishops alone when they bestow the Holy Spirit, is that although priests too are priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. That this belongs to bishops alone is shown not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by the reading from the Acts of the Apostles, which states that the apostles Peter and John were sent to Samaria to confer the Holy Spirit upon those who had already been baptized. It is also said of them: “They prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit.” From this it is shown that we can receive the Holy Spirit but cannot give him; rather, we invoke the Lord so that he may be given. For this reason the laying on of hands is performed, so that through prayer and blessing the Holy Spirit may be summoned; and then the Paraclete willingly descends from the Father upon bodies that have been cleansed, blessed, and anointed.

Some people commonly ask why the laying on of hands must afterward be performed, since the baptismal font cannot be sanctified at all without the Holy Spirit, and forgiveness of sins is not granted without him. It must be understood that the Holy Spirit is given in many ways, not only in baptism but also after baptism. For we believe that the apostles themselves received the Holy Spirit in baptism, so that their sins might be forgiven, whether inherited through origin [Note: The apostles did not possess original sin when they were baptized. The meaning, therefore, is that a Spirit of such a kind was given to them as could forgive every kind of sin.] or committed by the will. [Col. 0865A] Again, after the Lord’s resurrection, while the Lord himself was still present on earth, they received the Holy Spirit so that they might have the power either to forgive or to retain the sins of others. As it is written: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.”

Third, they received the Holy Spirit when the Lord was already seated in heaven, so that they might possess various gifts in the same Spirit: the grace of healings, the working of miracles, prophecy, discernment of spirits, kinds of tongues, and interpretation of utterances. We believe that the Holy Spirit is given not only for the reception of these sublime gifts but also for every good work. “For all who are led by the Spirit of God,” says the Apostle, “these are sons of God.”

Thus forgiveness of sins occurs in baptism, while in the laying on of hands gifts of powers are conferred, as the Apostle Peter says: “Let each of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you shall receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

The blessed Augustine explains the difference between baptism and chrism by saying:

> “When infants are exorcized, they are, as it were, ground like grain; when they are baptized, they are moistened; when they are chrismed, they are baked.”  
>
> A beautiful comparison! When they are ground through exorcism, they are snatched from the power of the devil; when they are moistened through baptism, they are cleansed from the filth of sins; when they are baked through chrism, they are illumined and strengthened by the grace of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER VIII. On white garments

[Col. 0865C]

The baptized are clothed in white garments so that, by the outward appearance of the external person, they may also display the renewal and cleansing of the inner person. Whoever is transferred from the power of darkness into the kingdom of light and glory naturally uses white garments, following the example not only of Jesus son of Jehozadak but also of Jesus the Son of God. For what was prefigured in Jesus son of Jehozadak was to be fulfilled in Jesus the Son of God.

The prophet Zechariah says: “And Jesus was clothed in filthy garments and stood before the angel. The angel answered and said to those who stood before him: ‘Take the filthy garments away from him.’ And he said to him: ‘Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I have clothed you in festal garments’; and he said: ‘Put a clean turban upon his head.’ And they clothed him in garments” (Zech. 3:4–5).

Although these things have been fulfilled in part in the Lord Jesus Christ, they are fulfilled more fully each day in his members. In a certain sense the Lord too was clothed in filthy garments, because, although he committed no sin, he was made sin for us; he himself bore our weaknesses and suffered for us. Yet because there was no iniquity in him to be taken away, but he was wounded for our iniquities, filthy garments are taken away from us when our sins are erased, so that, rising again in him, we may hear after baptism: “Behold, I have clothed you in festal garments.” And that which is said in the Song of Songs—“Who is this who ascends, made white?”—is likewise fulfilled in us. After we have been anointed on the head, what is said is as though fulfilled in us: “Put a clean turban upon his head, and they clothed him in garments.” Thus we may hear: “Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

Whoever escapes the darkness of Egypt through baptism and becomes a member of Christ is rightly clothed in white garments, because Christ’s flesh too was buried wrapped in a clean linen cloth. Whoever rises from death with Christ through passage across the sacred font is rightly clothed in white, because the holy angels who witnessed his resurrection appeared in white garments.

The white garments of the baptized carry three meanings. One concerns the past, accomplished through the renewal of baptism. Another concerns the present, which is manifested through the brightness of virtues, as it is written: “Let your garments always be white.” Concerning these garments it is said again: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments, lest he walk naked.” The third concerns the future, which is hoped for in eternal life through the brightness of immortality.

Hence the Apostle John says that he saw an innumerable multitude standing before the throne in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, and that one of the elders asked him: “Who are these clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?” He heard from him: “These are those who have come out of the great tribulation and have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.” Because of these whitenings of the reborn, the Prophet says that the sons of Zion are “whiter than milk, more ruddy than precious ivory” (Lam. 4:7). And the Lord commands John to write to the angel of Laodicea: “I advise you to buy from me gold refined in the fire, so that you may become rich, and to be clothed in white garments” (Rev. 3:18).

The twenty-four elders are also said to sit upon twenty-four thrones, clothed all around in white garments, with golden crowns on their heads. And this is promised commonly to all who conquer: “The one who conquers will be clothed in white garments.”

## CHAPTER IX. On the Lord’s body and blood

Those renewed through baptism ought to be brought to the Lord’s table, so that, receiving the bread which strengthens the human heart and the wine which gladdens it, they may say with the Psalmist: “He led me out beside the waters of refreshment; there he restored my soul.” And shortly afterward: “You have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me.”

The one who said, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven,” also said: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” The whole force of this statement is that without the body and blood of the Son of Man they cannot have life. The Lord says again: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.” By “the life of the world” human beings are signified, since by being born they come into this world. Therefore Christ’s flesh was given for the life of human beings; unless they eat it, they will not have eternal life.

The blessed Augustine says in one place:

> [Note: *Exposition begun on the Epistle to the Romans*, no. 13.]
>
> “[Col. 0865D] Punic Christians very appropriately call baptism nothing other than ‘salvation,’ and the sacrament of Christ’s body nothing other than ‘life.’ Why? Because, as I think, they hold to an ancient and apostolic tradition by which the Churches maintain that Christ is incorporated into them through baptism and participation in the Lord’s table, and that without these they can attain neither the kingdom of God nor salvation and eternal life. Scripture also testifies to this. For what else do those who call baptism by the name ‘salvation’ maintain than what was said: ‘He saved us through the bath of regeneration’? And what else do those who call the sacrament of the Lord’s table ‘life’ maintain than what was said: ‘The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world’? The same Lord says in the Gospel: ‘For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.’”

> [Note: Augustine, *Tractate 26 on John*.]

> “Since people desire food and drink so that they may neither hunger nor thirst, this is truly provided only by that food and drink which makes those who receive it immortal and incorruptible—provided, however, that those who receive it first fulfill what follows: ‘Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.’ For this is truly to eat that food and drink that drink: to remain in Christ and to have him remain in oneself. Consequently, whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, undoubtedly neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood,”

even if he eats and drinks the sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment. For the sacrament is one thing, and the power of the sacrament another. Salvation and eternal life are not externally present in the sacrament, since unbelievers too can receive it; but inwardly it cannot be received in the power of the sacrament, which is received only by those who are truly devout and faithful, imitators of God as beloved children, and who walk in love, just as Christ loved us.

This bread, which gives life to the world, was signified by the manna on which the children of Israel were fed in the desert, concerning which the Lord said to the Jews: “Your fathers ate manna in the desert, and they died” (John 6:59). Since it is clear that the Lord was not speaking of bodily death, by which we too die, even though we have eaten the bread that descended from heaven, but of the death of the soul, why is it said that those who ate the manna died? Did Moses and the other holy people who were there also die? Rather, he calls those dead who received the sacrament without the power of the sacrament.

That the power of the sacrament is inward, invisibly providing cleansing, sanctification, and life—as do the water of baptism, the anointing of chrism, and the body and blood of the Lord—no believer is unaware. From this it is understood that even those ancient Fathers who are said to have been baptized in the cloud and in the sea were saved, cleansed, and sanctified through the power of the sacraments. Therefore no one ought to feel secure merely because he has received the sacraments, unless he inwardly possesses and guards their invisible power.

We say all these things in this manner because, unless we explain them, how shall we teach the people entrusted to us?

## CHAPTER X. On infants and those who cannot answer for themselves

[Col. 0868A]

The custom of the Church is, and the teachers hand down, that we celebrate the mysteries of baptism for infants with precisely the same sacramental words as for adults. Hence, when the priest administers the same sacraments, he does not ask one person on behalf of another—that is, an adult on behalf of a child—whether he renounces the devil or believes in God; rather, he asks the very one who is to be baptized, saying, “Do you renounce?” or, “Do you believe?” The person who receives the child does not answer, as one person for another, “He renounces” or “He believes,” but “I renounce” or “I believe.” The reason is that infants can be called both penitents and faithful.

Accordingly, to some who deny this, the Fathers are found to have replied as follows: If penitents should not be called penitents because they do not possess the understanding of repentance, then neither should they be called believers, since they likewise do not possess the understanding of belief. But if they are rightly called believers because, through the words of those who carry them, they in some manner profess the faith, why are they not also first regarded as penitents, when through those same words of their sponsors they are shown to renounce the devil and this world?

All this takes place in hope, through the power of the sacrament and of the divine grace that the Lord bestowed upon the Church when they are baptized, on account of the power and celebration of so great a sacrament, although they themselves do not perform with heart and mouth what pertains to believing and confessing. Nevertheless, they are counted among the number of believers.

It happens to many that, with a Catholic mind and heart not estranged from the unity of peace, when some necessity of imminent death presses upon them, they fall among heretics and receive from them Christ’s baptism without sharing their perversity; and whether they die or are delivered, they by no means remain among those to whom they had never turned in heart. How, then, can it happen that what one person perniciously administers another receives beneficially, unless it is because the sacrament is judged according to the faith of those who receive it, not according to the faith of the one who gives it?

For this reason, those born deaf or mute are found either among Catholics or among heretics. And although the Apostle says, “How will they believe unless they have heard?” and again, “So faith comes from hearing,” nevertheless, in a wondrous manner—whether they are deaf, mute, or infants—they are joined to the number of the faithful through the hearts and mouths of those who offer and receive them.

## CHAPTER XI. On the discipline of living and teaching

[Col. 0868D]

As for what is asked of us—namely, that we should likewise say whether we ourselves observe what we preach—we have not known until now, and still do not know, whether a person can claim that he observes the divine commandments. For although every day we strive to attain continence of life, every day we sin either through forgetfulness, or through being overtaken unawares, or through weakness, or, what is worse, through the will; how can we profess the things that we do willingly, when we do not even understand the things that we do unwillingly? As it is written: “Who understands his offenses?”

Even though it is said, “O God, I have recounted my life to you,” we think that we can say this concerning our crimes, but not concerning our other actions, as it is written: “I said, ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord.’” How, then, can we observe in ourselves what we preach, when we sin every day? And sin is iniquity, as the Apostle confirms when he says: “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity, and sin is iniquity.”

Therefore we practice iniquity; and if we practice iniquity, we do not walk in the ways of the Lord, as the Psalmist says: “For those who practice iniquity have not walked in his ways.” Since these things are so, what better can we say about keeping the commandments—that is, about how we ourselves observe what we preach—than what the same Psalmist says: “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your statutes!”

For who can fulfill what is commanded to us: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” and again, “Love your enemies,” except the one whose heart the Lord has enlarged by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit in love, so that he can say to him: “I have run the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart”?

The Lord sets before us very solemnly in the Gospel the pattern of humility and simplicity, saying: “Unless you turn and become like little children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” In accordance with this, the Apostle also commands: “Do not become children in understanding, but be infants in wickedness.”

But who can attain such perfection of innocence, except the one whom such abundant gratuitous kindness from God has preceded that he can say from the depths of his inmost being: “I have loved, because the Lord has heard the voice of my prayer, because he has inclined his ear to me”?

And shortly afterward: “The Lord preserves the little ones; I was humbled, and he delivered me.” Then, secure, he says: “Return, my soul, to your rest.”

The teachers of the Church say that the divine commandments are the mirror of the soul, so that each faithful person, looking at himself in it, may detect in himself either the ugliness of vices or the beauty of virtues. Therefore the Psalmist says: “Then I shall not be put to shame, when I have looked upon all your commandments.” The implied meaning is: “If you direct my ways toward keeping your statutes.”

But which of us, without this shame, can sing:

> “Lord, our Lord, if I have done this,”  
> if there is iniquity in my hands,  
> if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil,  
> then may I rightly fall empty before my enemies”?

From this shame, then, the Lord wishes to raise us to joy when he says: “Blessed are you when people curse you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you falsely for my sake; rejoice and exult.” And elsewhere: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.”

Whoever can fulfill this from the depths of his heart will not be put to shame when he looks upon all God’s commandments as in a mirror. For the Apostle John says: “Whoever says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar.” And again: “Whoever says that he remains in him ought to walk as he walked.”

What else, then, should we do in these circumstances except, groaning, say:

> “Let not the tempest of water overwhelm me,  
> nor let the deep swallow me,  
> nor let the pit close its mouth over me.  
> Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind;  
> according to the multitude of your mercies, look upon me.”

Thus, as the Apostle mentioned above teaches: “Whoever does not love his brothers remains in death.” But what kind of love we ought to have for our brothers, he himself shows shortly afterward, saying: “By this we know the love of God: that he laid down his life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.” And again: “Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.”

But because we cannot fulfill this supreme love, and because, by not loving our brothers in this way, we remain in death, terrified by fear we cry out to the Almighty:

> “My soul has clung to the pavement;  
> give me life according to your word.”

And:

> “Lord, if you are willing, you can save me.”

There are, moreover, in the divine commandments still higher and more difficult precepts to fulfill. But if, because we cannot fulfill them, we do not preach them to others, there will, as we think, be a double evil. We must not doubt that among the people entrusted to our oversight there are some who have become vessels of divine mercy, in whom God displays the riches of his goodness. He is accustomed even to bring forth splendid pearls from a dungheap, fit to adorn the heavenly city; for their sake the Scriptures must not be silenced.

The teachers know that there is no condition among human beings, no rank, no age, and no intellect from which people do not perish—and from which they are not saved unto life. This takes place by the judgment of justice and the gratuitous mercy of God, who humbles one and exalts another, because “there is in his hand a cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, and he inclines it from this side to that.”

Therefore the Scriptures must be preached, the Gospel must resound, and both the terrors of threats and the consolations of encouragement must be proclaimed. For within the ecclesiastical people there are also hard-hearted persons, for whom the thunder and hail of God’s words are beneficial: they strike them first and afterward water them. There are also gentle people, for whom only the mild and peaceful word of God is suitable.

For we live in this world so that, always solicitous, we may never cease saying to God:

> “My soul has thirsted for you;  
> how greatly my flesh longs for you,  
> in a desert land,  
> and pathless and waterless.”

Our souls are vessels. Therefore, as we ask and seek, we must lift them up to God and say:

> “My soul is like land without water for you.”

Behold, in accordance with the smallness of our understanding, we have briefly answered what was asked, indicating how we teach our people and how we ourselves observe what we teach.

Now, most steadfast and most glorious emperor, ever blessed, excellent and august, we offer you the greatest thanks: by your devout concern you awaken us as though we were sleeping, shake off the sluggishness of our minds, and summon us to holy exercise, as though, together with the prophet, you were saying to the holy Church—for whose defense the Lord Jesus Christ deigns to preserve you:

> “Shake yourself free from the dust;  
> rise up; sit, Jerusalem.”

May the King of kings and Lord of lords deign to lead you, as her most beloved member, to share in her everlasting glory, transferring you from kingdom to kingdom.

[Col. 0871]

# LEIDRAD’S LETTERS

## FIRST LETTER. [Note: [Col. 0871D] From Baluze, first letter.] TO CHARLES THE GREAT, EMPEROR

[Col. 0871A]

Leidrad, bishop of Lyon, sends greetings to the most exalted Emperor Charles.

Our lord, steadfast and holy emperor, I beseech the clemency of your Highness to hear this brief little petition of mine with your most serene countenance, so that what is inserted here may become known to your most devout wisdom, and that the purpose of my request may be remembered by your generous clemency.

Long ago you wished to appoint me, the least of your servants, to govern the Church of Lyon, although I was unequal and unworthy of this office. But you, who do not consider the merits of men but your customary clemency, dealt with me as your ineffable piety desired, although there was no merit of mine; and you deigned to admonish me to undertake the care of this responsibility, so that the negligences known to have been committed in the aforesaid Church might be corrected and those yet to be committed avoided.

For that Church was deficient in many respects, both inwardly and outwardly, in its offices as well as in its buildings and other ecclesiastical services. Hear, then, what I, your most humble little servant, have accomplished there since my arrival with God’s assistance and yours.

For, as the almighty Lord, who examines consciences, is my witness, I do not disclose to you what I am about to say with the intention of thereby deserving an increase in my possessions, nor have I formed any such thought in my mind that it might provide me an opportunity for acquisition. Nor am I making this suggestion because I expect to remain long in this world, since, owing to my weakness, I daily suspect that my departure from human affairs is near and am constantly mindful of death.

I therefore make these things known so that, when they have been presented to your most gracious ears and kindly examined, whatever I have done well and according to your will may not, after my departure, fail or perish.

[Col. 0871D]

Finally, after I had undertaken the aforesaid Church in accordance with your command, I acted with every diligence according to the strength of my smallness, so that I might have clerics trained for the offices, as, with God’s favor, I now seem to possess them in large part. Therefore it pleased your piety to grant my request and restore to me the revenues that had belonged of old to the Church of Lyon.

Through these revenues, with God’s help and with your reward and approval, the order of psalmody has been restored in the Church of Lyon, so that, according to our ability and in conformity with the rite of the sacred Palace, everything required for the fulfillment of the divine office may appear to be performed in every respect.

For I have schools of singers, many of whom are so well trained that they can train others as well. In addition, I have schools of readers—not only readers who are exercised in the readings of the offices, but also those who may gain the fruit of spiritual understanding through meditation on the divine books. Some of them can attain, at least in part, a spiritual understanding of the Gospel book. Many, moreover, have attained a spiritual understanding of the book of the prophets. Likewise, they have attained an understanding of the books of Solomon, of the books of the Psalms, and also of Job.

I have also worked, as far as I could, at having books written in the same Church. Likewise, I have provided vestments for the priests and liturgical furnishings.

I have not ceased, insofar as I was able, to restore the churches. Thus I newly roofed the principal church of that city, which is dedicated to Saint John the Baptist, and partly rebuilt its walls. Likewise, I restored anew the roof of the church of Saint Stephen. I also rebuilt the church of Saint Nicetius from the ground up, and likewise the church of Saint Mary.

In addition to restoring monasteries, I also restored episcopal houses, among them one that had already been almost destroyed and which I roofed. I also built another house with an upper story and doubled its size; I prepared this for you, so that, if your arrival in those regions should occur, you could be received there.

I also built a cloister for the clerics, in which they are now known to dwell together under one roof. In the same city I restored other churches: one dedicated to Saint Eulalia, where there had been a monastery for girls, and one dedicated to Saint George, which I newly roofed and whose walls I partly rebuilt from their foundations. Another house dedicated to Saint Paul was also newly roofed.

I also restored from their foundations both the church and house of the monastery for girls dedicated to Saint Peter, where the body of the holy martyr Annemundus is buried. The holy martyr and bishop himself had established it. There now appear to live thirty-two religious women, living according to the rule.

I likewise restored the royal monastery of Barbara Island—situated in the middle of the River Saône, formerly dedicated in honor of Saint Andrew the Apostle and all the apostles, but now apparently newly founded in honor of Saint Martin at the command of our lord Emperor Charles, who appointed Lord Benedict as abbot there and sent his books there with him—so that it has been newly roofed and some of its walls rebuilt from their foundations. Ninety monks now appear to live there according to regular discipline.

To this abbot we also granted the power of binding and loosing, as his predecessors had possessed it: Ambrose, Maximinus, and Licinius, illustrious men who governed that place. When Eucherius, Lupus, Genesius, and the other bishops of Lyon were absent or unable to be present, they sent these men to investigate whether the Catholic faith was being rightly believed, lest heretical deceit should grow.

Such care had been entrusted to them that, if the Church of Lyon were deprived of its own patron, they themselves would serve in every respect as its rulers and comforters until the Lord might enlighten the Church with a most worthy shepherd. We have likewise handed this authority down to their successors.

Moreover, we ordered the decrees of the ancient kings of France to be drawn up, so that, just as those kings had established, the charters for purchasing and enlarging the property might possess, without any complaint, throughout the ages, all the things they now appear to have or may in the future, with God’s help, acquire.

[Note: [Col. 0873D] This should be regarded as a second part of the preceding treatise on Baptism.]

## LETTER II. [Note: [Col. 0874D] From Mabil­lon’s *Analecta*.] ALSO TO EMPEROR CHARLES

To the most glorious and truly devout emperor, victorious in Christ and most invincible in triumph, ever august: Leidrad, though unworthy, yet by divine dispensation and through your mercy bishop of the Church of Lyon.

### I.

Your most Christian and admirable religion, and your most ardent faith in God, touched by divine inspiration and moved by most devout concern, recently commanded us to answer your most penetrating inquiries concerning the sacraments of our renewal.

We understood that we could give no answer worthy of them, except that we recognized that neither was it within our capacity to answer readily nor within our ability to conceal the matter. Finally, although fit for neither task, in accordance with the smallness of our little intellect we confidently disclosed to you the account of our faith according to what we understand, to you who are most prudent, just, and devout in judging what is said.

But you, with your customary goodness, after hearing our answers—which we certainly could not give without fault—deigned, in accordance with your kindness, by which you surpass all mortals, to praise them as though they were pleasing to you. Yet even amid this praise you did not withhold your abundant learning from us, so as to judge that in these matters, which you had prepared to hear more eagerly, our ignorance had not at all satisfied you.

Then, with an admonition that was imperial but rather paternal, you deigned to make it known to us that we had said less about renouncing the devil and the things that belong to him than your piety desired. After your most gracious admonition, therefore, we understood that we ought to give a fuller answer about the works and pomps of the devil than about the other matters.

For through these desires, and through desires, the scandals of the world increase daily; and, what is worse, disagreements arise among the rulers of the Church and the administrators of the commonwealth; and, worse still, hatred insinuates itself among teachers and hearers, enmities are stirred up, and slanders are practiced.

[Col. 0874A]

### II.

Having therefore embraced your most wise admonition with every affection, we greatly admired the depth of your holy consideration. Meanwhile, because the slowness that hindered our small intellect prevented us from sufficiently discerning whether this praiseworthy admonition of yours wished us to give you an answer or merely commended to us the recognition of our own ignorance, we remained suspended in uncertainty.

We could find no more probable counsel, as it seemed to us, than first to explain, according to the poverty of our understanding and insofar as it appeared possible, those matters which we learned through you had not been properly answered by us; and then to indicate in this letter to your most serene clemency what doubt—or rather what necessity—had compelled us to write what, as we learned from you, had been lacking in our previous answers.

We have then sent these matters to your most glorious presence, so that, whether we have acted according to your command or not, there may appear before your glorious majesty both what was lacking in our earlier answers and the reason why we have now dared—or rather been compelled—to write and send these things.

If you judge them in any measure acceptable to your will, you do so according to the unfailing treasury of your goodness. But if they are vain and of little use, as perhaps they are, we know and confess that their multitude has been deserved by our ignorance, since we have been unable sufficiently to attend to your will and to the tenor of our service.

Even if we do attend to them, we are in no way simultaneously capable of answering your most lofty and incomparable inquiry. Nevertheless, we ask that it not be hidden from you what cause compelled us to write concerning those things which, under the admonition of your clemency and paternal concern, we learned had been insufficient in those earlier answers.

### III.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, whose going forth was from the summit of heaven, after he proceeded like a bridegroom from his chamber, marked by the humility and weakness of our nature, was to wage war against the prince of this world and conquer the world as the strong and mighty Lord, the Lord mighty in battle for his future soldiers, who were fleeing the dominion of the world and its prince.

Setting forth—or rather presenting—the beginnings of his covenant and campaign, he said: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.”

When someone heard this, he said to him: “I will follow you, Lord; but first allow me to renounce those who are at home.”

But holy Mother Church universal receives those who turn to her into her bosom only after they have first renounced the devil and all his angels, as well as his works and all his pomps.

### IV.

These two things must therefore be distinguished: what difference there is between *renuntiare* (“to renounce”) and *abrenuntiare* (“to repudiate” or “renounce utterly”).

Their difference appears especially in this: we renounce lawful things, but we repudiate unlawful things; we renounce attachments, but we repudiate enticements; we renounce parents, but we repudiate the devil.

He therefore renounces all that he possesses who holds the things of the world in such a way that he is not held by the world through them. He possesses temporal things for use and eternal things in desire; and once worldly greed has been excluded, divine love in him grows and reaches perfection.

Therefore, whoever wishes to possess God renounces the world. But he does not renounce the world who, out of delight, yields to earthly resources. Whoever, then, wishes to be a disciple of Christ disdains, for love of him, all that is in the world, even if he possesses it, so that they may be as having, yet not having.

Such people learn not to think proudly, nor to set their minds on uncertain riches, but on the living God, who provides us with all things. Thus they possess earthly resources for their support, while nevertheless serving God through them, whose eternal goods they desire.

And because greed, not possessions, is condemned in the divine writings, they carefully consider that they should not have what they have through love of possessing, but through the necessity of living.

Those things that must be repudiated, however, are granted no place in our possession, because they cannot in any way be possessed together with God. The devil, his works, and his pomps must be repudiated with the whole heart, so that no fellowship with them may remain for us, lest through their activity we should again be compelled to slip into the kingdom of him through whose envy death entered the world, who was a murderer from the beginning, the instigator of evil, and the bestower of sin.

### V.

For he first granted the first man the loan of sin, intending to exact daily interest from him. The wicked creditor made the human race liable to interest; and the wretched debtor paid by sinning not only what he had learned at the creditor’s prompting, but also his own inventions, which he added to the accumulation of crimes.

Therefore, when through the grace of him who redeemed our souls from interest and iniquity we are rescued from the power of the evil creditor, and thus from the wicked exactor, we must repudiate him and declare that henceforth we owe him nothing.

### VI.

What the origin and beginning of the devil’s works and pomps are, Scripture teaches most plainly when it says: “The beginning of every sin is pride” (*Ecclesiasticus* 10:15).

What could be said more clearly or more convincingly? “The beginning,” it says, “not of some sin but of every sin is pride,” so that it might plainly show that pride itself is the cause of all sins.

For pride is not only itself a sin, but no sin could have been, can be, or will be committed without it. It is therefore called the beginning of every sin because it first arose in the devil, and through it the human being was overthrown.

He would not have eaten from the forbidden tree unless he had desired it; he would not have desired it unless he had been tempted; he would not have been tempted unless he had been abandoned; he would not have been abandoned by God unless he himself had first abandoned God; and he would not have abandoned God unless he had grown proud and damnably desired equality with God.

Thus God made the human being upright, as it is written (*Ecclesiasticus* 7:30), and therefore of good will. For he would not be upright if he did not possess a good will.

Good will, therefore, is God’s work, for the human being was made by him with it. But evil will, because it preceded all evil works in the human being, was rather a falling away from God’s work toward the human being’s own works than a work of God.

The evil works are therefore evil because they are according to the human being, not according to God; and the will itself is like an evil tree producing those works as evil fruits.

### VII.

The Apostle also says: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6:10).

We must therefore carefully consider why pride is called the beginning of sin, while greed is called the root of all evils. Or perhaps the Apostle Paul, as he often does, explained the prophetic saying, since whether one says “the beginning of every sin” or “the root of all evils,” the meaning is one and the same.

Moreover, greed and pride are so much one evil that pride cannot be found without greed, nor greed without pride. For the devil, in whom pride holds the dominant place, was greedy for his own power and for the destruction of the human race; and the human being himself, through his appetite for the forbidden tree and his diseased desire to attain likeness to God, displayed the affection of greedy desire.

No one doubts that the devil fell through the evil of pride. Concerning the first human beings, however, careful consideration reveals that they first became evil in secret, so that they might fall into open disobedience. For one would not reach an evil deed unless an evil will had preceded it.

What, then, could be the beginning of an evil will except pride? What is pride except a desire for perverse exaltation? Exaltation is perverse when, having abandoned the one to whom the mind ought to cling as its principle, the mind in some way makes itself its own principle and becomes so.

This happens when the mind takes pleasure in itself. It takes pleasure in itself when it falls away from that unchangeable good which ought to have pleased it more than it pleased itself.

That falling away is voluntary. For if the will had remained steadfast in the love of the higher unchangeable good—from which it was illuminated so that it might see and inflamed so that it might love—it would not have turned away from that good toward pleasing itself, and from this it would not have become darkened or grown cold, so that either she might believe the serpent to have spoken the truth, or he might place his wife’s will before God’s command and think himself a transgressor excused by pardon if he did not abandon the companion of his life even in fellowship of sin.

The evil deed, then—that transgression by which they ate the forbidden food—was not committed except by those who were already evil. It is therefore most plainly evident that, not only in the devil but also in the first human beings, the evil of pride had secretly preceded, so that the evil perpetrated openly might follow.

True indeed is what is written: “The heart is exalted before destruction” (Proverbs 16:18), and “before glory it is humbled” (Luke 14:11).

The destruction that occurs in secret unquestionably precedes the destruction that occurs openly, although that secret destruction is not thought to be destruction. For who regards exaltation as destruction, when the falling away has already occurred by which the exalted one has been abandoned? But who does not see destruction when there is an evident and undeniable transgression of the command?

### VIII.

If we divide the transgression of the first human beings, as it were, into its individual components, it is not absurd to believe that the other sins were also committed there.

First, there is pride, because the human being preferred to exist under his own power rather than under God’s power. Then there is greed, because he desired more than should have been sufficient for him; sacrilege, because he did not believe; murder, because he plunged himself into death; spiritual fornication, because the integrity of the human mind was corrupted by the serpent’s persuasion; theft, because the forbidden food was seized; and whatever else careful consideration may discover in that single offense.

This first evil of the rational creature was followed by ignorance of what ought to be done and desire for harmful things. Error and grief accompany these; and when these two evils are felt to be impending, the movement of the fleeing mind is called fear.

When the mind attains what it desires, however harmful or empty it may be, because it does not recognize this through error, it is either overcome by diseased pleasure or carried away by empty joy.

From these sources—fountains not of abundance but of need—every misery of rational nature pours forth, in which nature lies or even rolls about, and is hurled from evils into evils.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] Saint Augustine, in the *Enchiridion*.]

### IX.

Behold the tree of evil will, which arises from the seed of pride and grows strong in the root of greed: what kinds of fruit it multiplies!

Therefore, if we wish to complete the course of our contest, let us first beware of greed and pride—not two evils, but one, from which every evil act takes its beginning.

For without pride, what sins could even be begun, since it is said that pride is the beginning of every sin? Or without greed, the root of all evils, what evils could be committed, since without a root they are either considered nonexistent or dead?

Furthermore, if no one can perpetrate any sin unless he consents to his own pleasure—which is greed’s particular character—and despises God’s commandments—which is the evil of pride—how can every sin not proceed from greed, which is called the root of all evils, and from pride, which is called the beginning of every sin?

All evils, therefore, which arise through the seedbed of pride from the root of greed are contained in these two things: works and pomps. No sin can be found that is not counted among one or the other of them.

For this reason, those who approach baptism for cleansing are declared to renounce these things.

[Col. 0877D]

### X.

Since there is an easy understanding of the works of the devil, we must first say which evils are recognized as belonging to the devil’s pomps: namely, everything that arises from wantonness and luxury, and also certain things that arise from lust.

For there are many and varied lusts. Some of them even have their own names, while others do not. Who could easily say what the lust for domination is called?

There is therefore the lust for revenge, which is called anger; the lust to possess money, which is avarice; the lust to win by any means, which is obstinacy; and the lust for glory, which is called boasting.

There is also the lust to cause harm, whether through insult or injury. Each of these may arise from the desire for revenge, as when an enemy acts against an enemy; from the desire to obtain some external advantage, as a robber acts against a traveler; from the desire to avoid an evil, as when one acts against someone who is feared; from envy, as when a wretched person acts against someone more fortunate, or against someone whose success he fears may make that person his equal, or whose equality he regrets; or from the mere will that another should suffer evil, as with spectators at gladiatorial games, or mockers and jeerers of any kind, who rejoice when they have done wrong and exult in the worst deeds, having broken through the boundaries of human society.

For nothing is more wretched than the happiness of sinners, by which punitive impunity is nourished and evil will is strengthened, so that the inner enemy may grow strong.

### XI.

All things also that charm the bodily senses and through them break in to ravage the mind, allowing it to enter by the broad and spacious road that leads to death while seeking to seize bodily pleasures, belong to these pomps.

This occurs, for example, when massive theaters are built and the foundations of virtues are dug up; when the madness of lavish expenditure is celebrated and works of mercy are mocked; when actors luxuriate in what the rich possess in abundance while the poor scarcely have what is necessary.

Through the five bodily senses the capital and citadel of the mind are captured: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

If someone delights in circus games, in athletic contests, in the movements of actors, in women’s beauty, in the brilliance of gems, clothing, metals, and other such things, the soul’s freedom is captured through the windows of the eyes.

### XII.

Again, it is captured through hearing when it is soothed by the varied music of instruments and the modulations of voices, by the poetry of poets, by the urbanities and artifices of comedies and mimes, and by whatever enters through the ears and makes the strength of the mind effeminate.

It is captured through the sweetness of fragrances, through the variety of incense, through amomum, and through the skin of a foreign mouse—things suited to the dissolute and to lovers.

As for touch: contact with other people’s bodies, and the more ardent desire for women, are a notorious disgrace [perhaps: “are a shameful vice”].

### XIII

Therefore, when certain wedges of disturbances have entered the citadel of our mind, as though through these gates, where will its freedom be? Where its strength? Where the thought of God? Especially since touch also paints for itself pleasures already past, and by recalling vices compels the soul to suffer and, in a certain sense, to practice what it is not doing. For the sins known to pertain to wantonness the prophet Isaiah recalls from the voice of the Lord threatening, saying:

“Because the daughters of Zion have become haughty, and have walked with outstretched necks, casting glances with their eyes, and going along with mincing steps, making a tinkling with their feet, walking with measured tread: the Lord will make bald the crown of the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the Lord will lay bare their hair. On that day the Lord will take away the ornament of their shoes, and the little crescents, and the necklaces, and the pendants, and the bracelets, and the headdresses, the hair-clasps, the anklets, the scent-boxes, the earrings, the rings, and the jewels hanging upon the forehead” (Isaiah 3:16).

All these things are said because of the proud brow and the shameless, luxurious actions of people who, dispersed through every desire, lead an impure life. Isaiah likewise threatens the display of the wanton, saying:

“All who rejoice in their hearts have groaned; the joy of tambourines has ceased, the sound of those who rejoice has fallen silent, the sweetness of the lyre with its song has become mute; they will not drink wine: the drink will be bitter to those who drink it; the city of vanity has been crushed” (Isaiah 24:7–10).

### XIV

The word “display” (*pompa*) is also found in the sacred writings, as in the following passage of Psalm 39, according to the Hebrew translation, however:

“Blessed is the man who placed the Lord as his confidence and did not turn aside toward the proud displays of falsehood.”

Another translation from the Greek expressed it thus:

“Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who did not look toward vanities and false insanities.”

Here it certainly signifies the vain delights of the bodily senses themselves. The prophet Amos likewise says:

“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in the mountain of Samaria, you nobles, the chiefs of the nations, entering the house of Israel with pomp; you who are set apart for the evil day and draw near to the seat of iniquity; you who sleep on ivory beds and live wantonly upon your couches; you who eat lambs from the flock and calves from the midst of the herd; who sing to the sound of the psaltery like David. They thought they had vessels for song, drinking wine from bowls, anointing themselves with the finest oil, and suffering nothing over the ruin of Joseph” (Amos 6:1–6).

### XV

The displays of the devil make a person wanton and vain. Through them he becomes changeable toward what is good, tenacious of evil, weighty in speech, foul in mind, deceitful everywhere, cheerful in prosperity, fragile in adversity, puffed up toward services, anxious before insults, immoderate in pleasures, compliant toward human beings, and resistant to what is honorable. Inflamed by the desire to acquire a reputation, he devotes himself to those actions by which human favor is purchased, and despises the goodness of character. The ardor of human praise so enkindles him that he willingly undertakes laborious works which the people admire and through which fame is spread, so that outwardly, wherever he can, he shines as a great man, while inwardly, where God alone sees, he is filthy.

### XVI

There are also people whose life is inflamed by a foul tongue, who either willingly utter or willingly listen to shameless speech. They speak what they love, and listen with delight to what they turn over in their constant thoughts, thereby revealing their foul conscience. Scripture introduces such people, saying:

“For they said, thinking wrongly within themselves.”

And shortly afterward:

“Come, therefore, and let us enjoy the good things that exist, and let us use creation as though in youth with speed. Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let not the flower of the season pass us by. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither; let there be no meadow which our wantonness does not pass through. Let none of you be excluded from our wantonness; everywhere let us leave signs of joy, for this is our portion and this is our lot” (Wisdom 2:1 ff.).

Solomon likewise displays the enticement of such people under the figure of an adulterous woman. Of her he says that she meets a foolish young man in the attire of a prostitute, prepared to capture souls, talkative and wandering, impatient of quiet. She says that she has prepared a bed woven with cords, spread with embroidered coverings from Egypt, and sprinkled the couch with myrrh, aloe, and cinnamon. These and other similar things are found written concerning the displays of the devil.

### XVII

Regarding the other vices—whether spiritual, such as heresies, schisms, boasting, envy, hostility, arrogance, and hatred; or bodily, that is, those committed not only in the mind but also with the body, such as greed, drunkenness, intemperance, fornication, and adultery—the teachers of the Church say that they proceed from seven principal vices: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. These vices have pride as their mother and queen, and they serve her like commanders with their armies.

These seven vices were signified by those nations which the Lord wished to be destroyed by the children of Israel: the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. Indeed, through various kings and peoples the Lord transferred, devastated, and destroyed many different nations. But he wished these nations to be extinguished by the children of Israel in order to signify, by the number seven, that these vices must be conquered and trampled down by his chosen ones.

For this reason Samson also broke the seven cords with which he was thought to be bound, so that these vices might be signified by the number seven; and through these vices, all the sins of the human race, which our Lord Jesus Christ bore in his body upon the wood, might be healed and broken in us by his wound. Accordingly, let us say to him: “You have broken my bonds; to you I shall sacrifice an offering of praise.” Since he grieved that we had been taken captive by these seven vices of pride, our Redeemer therefore came to the spiritual battle of liberation, filled with the Spirit of sevenfold grace.

### XVIII

Each of these vices has its own army against us.

From *cenodoxia*, that is, vainglory, arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations.

From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing at one’s neighbor’s misfortunes, and distress at his prosperity.

From anger proceed quarrels, swelling of the mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies.

From sadness arise malice, rancor, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness regarding the commandments, and wandering of the mind toward illicit things.

From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, restlessness, violence, and the hardening of the heart against mercy.

From gluttony arises foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding.

From lust are generated blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and fear or despair of the future.

Of these seven, two are carnal—gluttony and lust—while five are spiritual. Yet each is so closely joined to the others that one proceeds only from another. Vainglory, the first, gives birth to envy: while it seeks the power of an empty reputation, it wastes away lest anyone else be able to attain it. Likewise anger is generated from envy, while sadness derives from avarice. Regarding the two that are carnal, it is clear to everyone that lust arises from gluttony: while one is indulged immoderately, the other is unquestionably aroused toward insults.

### XIX

Others, especially the holy Egyptian Fathers, said that there were eight principal vices. They placed first those which are called carnal here: *gastrimargia*, which means gluttony, and fornication, which here is called lust by the general name. Third they placed *philargyria*, that is, love of money, which we call avarice; fourth, anger; fifth, sadness; sixth, acedia, that is, anxiety or weariness of heart, which our writers commonly call inconstancy or restlessness; seventh, *cenodoxia*, which we call vainglory; and eighth, pride.

They omitted envy, the greatest offspring and companion of pride, but added acedia, which the teachers of the Church did not place among the principal vices. Rather, they said that it arose from sadness or lust, because it seems, in a certain sense, to be peculiar to monks. For generally among all the faithful it appears much less evil than envy, since in the sacred writings envy is found marked with much greater abhorrence than wandering of the mind.

They placed pride last, although others have said that it is the cause and origin of all vices. Indeed, it is evident that pride is not generated from vainglory, but vainglory from pride. With equal agreement they distinguished both groups by a twofold division, namely, carnal and spiritual, although the Apostle said that all the works of the flesh are manifest together.

They also say that the operation of all vices is fourfold. Some can be completed only through bodily action, such as gluttony and fornication. Others are completed without any bodily action, such as pride and vainglory. Others receive the causes of their agitation from outside, such as avarice and anger. Still others are aroused by internal movements, such as acedia and sadness.

### XX

These and many similar vices are divided into the works and displays of the devil, who is the author and prince of the sins which we renounced in baptism. Worse still, when we return to them again, we are defiled by their pollution and weighed down by their burdens, so that we may rightly say:

“They have weighed upon me like a heavy burden. My scars have festered and become corrupt because of my foolishness. I am afflicted with miseries to the end.”

By their corruption we are torn apart, and yet we rejoice as though we were healthy. On account of these things God, the just, strong, and patient judge, threatens us with eternal punishments unless we repent: there “our worm does not die, and the fire is not extinguished.”

On account of these things we are worn down and afflicted by temporal scourges in human affairs: wars, captivities, pestilences, famine, and sickness. On account of these things come the inconveniences of the seasons, drought, excessive rains, the severity of cold, the intensity of heat, and the failure of assistance.

Because of these things we are not only rebuked and chastised from heaven, but God also places authorities over us, to whom we must be subject, not only because of wrath but also for the sake of conscience. On account of these things they promulgate laws, administer justice, impose punishments, chains, tortures, scourging, exile, mutilation of limbs, confiscation of possessions, and deaths of various kinds; and these cannot be removed from the world.

On account of these things there are ecclesiastical discipline, correction, excommunication, exclusion from the Church, penitential laws, and anathema; and these cannot be removed from the Church. Judges are appointed, officials carry out their duties, and avengers are sent so that these things may be corrected. Yet, as a further accumulation of the miseries with which mortal life is filled, when justice has been established and wickedness is thought to be condemned while innocence is acquitted, ignorance often causes the opposite to occur: evil returns victorious, and innocence is punished.

### XXI

This prohibition and instruction keep watch against the darkness with which we are born and are set against these impulses, although they themselves are also full of labors and sorrows. For what do the many kinds of fear mean, which are employed even to restrain the vanities of little children? What of pedagogues? What of teachers? What of the rods? What of the hour [perhaps, straps]? What of the discipline by which Holy Scripture says that the sides of a beloved son must be struck, lest he grow up untamed and, once hardened, either scarcely be subdued or perhaps not be subdued at all?

What is accomplished by all these punishments except that ignorance is defeated and perverse desire is restrained—those evils with which we entered this age?

### XXII

Who could recount in any speech, or comprehend in any thought, the number and magnitude of the other punishments by which the human race is harassed—punishments that do not pertain to the malice and wickedness of the unjust, but to the condition and common misery of humanity?

How great is the fear arising from human deceptions and lies, from false suspicions? How great, how miserable, how lamentable do we suppose it to be? For those who judge cannot see the consciences of the people whom they judge. When someone is investigated to determine whether he is guilty, he is tortured, and an innocent person pays the most certain penalties for an uncertain crime—not because he is discovered to have committed it, but because it is not known that he did not commit it.

Thus the judge’s ignorance is often the calamity of the innocent. And what is more intolerable and more worthy of lamentation—and, if possible, of being watered by fountains of tears—is that, when a judge tortures the accused so that he may not unknowingly kill an innocent person, the misery of ignorance causes him to kill the very man as both tortured and innocent—the man whom he had tortured so as not to kill him while innocent.

For often those who are accused, overcome by the force of pain, confess false things about themselves and are punished even though innocent; and the judge does not know whether he has killed an innocent or a guilty person.

True is what Scripture says: “The life of a human being upon earth is a trial.” And again: “Because of iniquity you have chastised a person and made his soul waste away like a spider.”

Countless disputes arise between the rulers of the Church and the administrators of the commonwealth. Instigated by pride, desire, and envy, and with our eyes closed, we strive zealously and wage war against one another as neighbors, to whom [lacuna] “Owe no one anything except to love one another.” And we consent to so many and such great evils threatening us, although our struggle ought not to be against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

Countless wars have been declared against us by the prince and power of this air, who works in the children of disobedience and rages against us with all his strength.

### XXIII

The terrors of divine threats also thunder over us. The severity of the laws and the strictness of kings keep watch to restrain us, yet we pay attention to none of these things except how to bite and devour one another, so that we may be consumed by one another.

Alas, what grief! So confidently we proceed toward the outer darkness, as though bedrooms were being built for us there, beds spread, pleasures prepared, servants provided, treasures heaped up, and ornaments multiplied, although Scripture says:

“Whatever your hand is able to do, do it diligently, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, to which you are hastening.”

Whence comes to us such shameless pride, such importunate desire, such senseless wantonness? Is it not because we foolishly return to those things which we renounced in baptism? Thus what the true proverb says happens to us: “The dog has returned to its vomit, and the washed sow to its wallowing in the mud.”

“From where,” says the Apostle, “do wars and quarrels arise among you? Is it not from this—from your desires which wage war in your members?”

### XXIV

It is therefore clear that every quarrel among us arises from desire, since there is no such good that we love here as to cause no distress to those who love it. For this reason we are often divided in quarrels, seeking victories that are deadly or at least mortal; and when someone has conquered, he is lifted up in pride.

If, however, he considers the condition of life and the common lot, he is more distressed by the adversities that may occur than he is inflated by the prosperity that has come to him. For no earthly possession can be held by many people at the same time: if one person possesses it, another is excluded from its possession.

Divine things, however, which God commands us to love, are possessed by many in such a way that nothing is diminished for anyone as the number of possessors increases. The possession of goodness in no way becomes smaller when a companion joins or remains in possession. Indeed, goodness is possessed more fully when the undivided love of the companions possesses it more broadly and more harmoniously.

The person who does not wish to possess it in common will not possess it at all; and he will find it more abundant in proportion as he is able to love his companion there more greatly. Therefore, because we love in disordered fashion the things that we ought to love, wars and quarrels arise within us from our desires.

### XXV

But we must know that we cannot in any way pass into the kingdom of eternal peace unless here we have held the peace which this war seeks through many and varied struggles—a war in which the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.
