This war would never have existed if human nature had remained, through free choice, in the upright condition in which it was made. But now the unhappy nature that did not wish to have peace with God fights against itself; and although this is …, it is nevertheless better than the earlier conditions of this life.

It is better to struggle against vices than to have them rule without any struggle. Better, I say, is war with the hope of eternal peace than captivity without any thought of liberation. We indeed desire also to be free from war, and we are kindled by the fire of divine love to attain that perfectly ordered peace in which inferior things are subjected to superior with the firmest stability. But if—God forbid—there were no hope of so great a good, we ought to prefer remaining in the distress of this conflict to allowing the vices to rule over us by failing to resist them.

### XXVI

War must therefore be undertaken against the vices and waged fiercely, lest they lead us to damnable sins. If they have not yet been strengthened by the habit of victory, they are conquered and yield more easily. But if they have become accustomed to conquering and ruling, they are overcome only with laborious difficulty.

This is accomplished through faith in Christ. For if the law that commands is present while the Spirit who assists is absent, then, as desire for sin increases and prevails through the very prohibition, the guilt of transgression is also added.

Sometimes, indeed, the most obvious vices are conquered by hidden vices that are thought to be virtues—vices in which pride and a ruinous elevation of self-satisfaction reign. Vices are to be considered conquered only when they are overcome through the love of God. God alone bestows that love, and he bestows it only through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who became a participant in our mortality in order to make us participants in his divinity.

[Note: [Col. 0883D] From a second text of Baluze.]

## LETTER III. TO HIS SISTER

To the dearest and most highly esteemed holy sister in Christ, Leidradus, although unworthy, bishop of the Church of Lyon, sends everlasting salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

May the prudence of your graciousness know that, according to the gift of the giving God, we are for a little while somewhat strong in bodily strength; and since, given the uncertainties of this life’s dangers, our health is uncertain, we ought to give thanks to God for our health. Furthermore, according to the strength of the spirit, know that we remember your temporal and eternal salvation in our prayers.

If you are also well, and, as we trust you do, remember us in your prayers, we offer immense thanks to God, since it is evident that you are as we desire you to be.

I know that your spirit was recently struck by vehement grief, first after the death of your son and afterward of your brother. Certainly, the loss of such great comfort cannot affect us without deep sorrow, since we necessarily grieve over the death of those whose life brings us joy; and the death of each person presses upon our heart with sadness proportionate to the joy with which his life had lifted it.

We cannot entirely extinguish the laws of nature so as not to grieve; but perhaps, through better counsel, we can lessen our grief so that we may endure it. Otherwise it may happen that, while the spirit, following affection, grieves tenderly for a neighbor, it becomes hostile to the divine judgments.

Great discernment is needed so that, in losses of this kind, we do not abandon the path of justice between God who judges and the neighbor who dies. Thus we may neither prove ungrateful toward the most just Judge nor fail to show, according to due measure, the sorrow of compassion for our dead neighbor.

The advice of blessed Paul the Apostle must certainly be heard:

“I do not want you, brothers, to grieve concerning those who sleep”—that is, those who have died—“as do the others who have no hope of resurrection.”

It is one thing for an unbeliever to mourn a dead person unbelievingly, as though he were completely lost and could not be expected to live again; it is another thing for a believer to grieve faithfully for a believer who has died, whom he does not doubt will rise again.

Although, as was said above, it is impossible for the death not to be bitter to us of one whose life is sweet, and although this grief is the wound or sore of a human and affectionate heart, appropriate consolations are nevertheless rightly applied for its healing. There is something to be healed; and the better the condition of the soul, the more quickly and easily it is healed.

Thus, although mortal life is sometimes afflicted more gently and sometimes more harshly by the deaths of those we love—especially those whose services are necessary to human society—we more rightly rejoice with those we love when they die than we tolerate their falling away from faith or good morals. For “human life upon earth is a trial.” And again: “Woe to the world because of scandals.”

When their death grieves us, it also consoles us, because they have escaped the evils by which good people in this life are either crushed, corrupted, or placed in danger of both. Believe me, for it seems to me that, in one respect, we ought to rejoice over every person who dies, lest, if he had lived, he might have died worse.

But since this cannot be persuaded to human beings, we must carefully consider that, although we are all born mortal and destined to die, some die in their mothers’ wombs, others immediately after being brought into this light; and thereafter no day or year can be found in which death does not arrive and cut short the life of someone who still wished to live and thought that he was living.

Since these things are so, careful reflection changes our outlook: we ought to render daily thanks to God because he gave us whatever time we have lived, for as long as we have lived, and we should not grieve that we are dying beyond the time that we were never given in order to live.

Who, I ask, does not die? If the Savior, the giver of salvation and life, died, who is so foolish as always to wish to live, when he knows that the Savior tasted death for us? We are born equal in life; equally we all die. The reward after death is different, but death itself is one for all.

We weep and groan, but we cannot benefit one another. Grief is present in the eyes, but there is no fruit of action, because nothing is disclosed when we weep. Death is deaf and hard: it neither hears nor feels compassion. No power can render it aid.

The Potter who fashioned everyone from one earth knows when and how to break the vessel. Yet none is lost to him, because he who made it from dust will restore it from dust. No one can rebel against the command of the Almighty.

Let the person who still lives consider how he may benefit the dead. The dead do not need fruitless mourning, but fruitful assistance. It is enough now to have wept over past losses. Let us work to make our future death lighter. What cannot be avoided should not be greatly feared.

Rather, those evils should be feared which we can avoid while living and which remain evils after death. For death, which is evil in itself, is evil for the wicked because through it they pass to worse things; but it is good for the good because through it they pass to better things.

“No one lives for himself, and no one dies for himself. If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. Christ died and rose again so that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living.”

Therefore, in thought, speech, and action, let us strive for those things by which we may please him whose power it is to condemn those who live wickedly and glorify those who die well; and he grants those who live wickedly to die well through amendment, but never grants those who die well to live wickedly.

# In the Year of the Lord 815. Amalarius, Archbishop of Trier

## HISTORICAL NOTICE ON AMALARIUS

*(From Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

Amalarius Fortunatus, a Benedictine monk and, from the year of Christ 810, archbishop of Trier, was sent by Charlemagne into Saxony in the year 811, where he consecrated the church of Hamburg in honor of the blessed Virgin; he died three years later.

His life was written by Constantine Gaetanus and published at Rome in 1612, quarto. He maintained that the book *On the Divine Offices* should be attributed not to the Amalarius of Metz but to this Amalarius. In addition to the Anonymous of Melk, chapter 71, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Alberic, monk of Trois-Fontaines, explicitly says the same in his *Chronicle* under the year 810, page 155:

“Wasco, abbot of Mediolanum, was archbishop of Trier, and after him Amalarius Fortunatus, a cardinal, who composed the book of the ecclesiastical Offices. But the books *On the Offices*, addressed to the most glorious emperor Louis the Pious, as he calls him, were written after the year 819 [Note: [Col. 0887A] Blondellus maintains that he was neither the bishop of Metz nor the bishop of Trier, but a third Amalarius, who wrote *On Ecclesiastical Offices* around the year 827; see his book *On Bishops*, page 80. The *Eclogues of Amalarius the Abbot* were published by Mabillon, volume II of the *Musei Italici*, pages 549–550.], when Hettius had succeeded Amalarius of Trier, who was already dead.”

Compare what Sirmond wrote on Gaetanus, in Labbe, *de S. E.*, volume I, page 692 and following, and in volume IV of Sirmond’s works, page 643 and following.

The six letters also published by Dacherius in volume VII of the *Spicilegium*, page 164, and in volume III of the new edition, page 330—of which the last is *On the Observance of Lent*—have as their author not the Amalarius of Trier but the same Amalarius who wrote *On the Offices*.

The earlier letters, which treat of the name of Jesus, constitute the final chapter of book III, *On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, which is missing in the editions but is noted in the table of contents. See B. Ittigius, *On the Libraries of the Fathers*, page 213.

As for Amalarius of Trier, the codex of Petavius vindicates to him the letter *On the Ceremonies of Baptism*, published by Canisius under the name of Alcuin in volume VI of the *Antiquae Lectiones*, page 366, and in volume II of the new edition, page 543, as well as among Alcuin’s works, page 1151; Sirmond bears witness to this in his notes on Theodulf of Orléans’ book *On the Order of Baptism*, volume II of his works, page 943.

## LETTER OF AMALARIUS TO CHARLEMAGNE THE EMPEROR: ON THE CEREMONIES OF BAPTISM

*(In Frobenius, Works of Blessed Alcuin.)*

### PRELIMINARY NOTICE

The celebrated writer Henricus Canisius first published in print, in volume VI of the *Antiquae Lectiones*, from a manuscript codex of the Weingarten library, a letter *On the Ceremonies of Baptism* to the emperor Augustus Charles. It lacked the author’s name, but Canisius nevertheless suspected that it was by our Alcuin, both because its style was not unlike Alcuin’s and because the person to whom the letter was sent appeared to him to have been Charlemagne, who was accustomed to set Alcuin to work on questions of this kind.

Following this judgment, or conjecture, of Canisius, the learned Quercetanus borrowed the letter from him and arranged for it to be published among Alcuin’s works, pages 1151 and following.

But the celebrated investigator of antiquity Jacques Sirmond detected the error of both writers after learning from the Petavian codex that the author of the letter was named Amalarius, bishop. He rightly judged that this could be none other than Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, who at the time when the questions concerning the ceremonies of baptism answered in this letter were sent by Emperor Charles in an encyclical letter to all the archbishops of his kingdom—that is, around the year 812—held that see.

Sirmond strengthened his opinion from the very text of the reply, at whose conclusion the writer professes himself to be a bishop in these words:

“You said, most serene emperor, that you wished to know how we and our suffragans teach the people about the sacrament of baptism.”

Since Alcuin was neither a bishop nor an archbishop with suffragan bishops under him, and since he had died at least seven years before the emperor Charles’s encyclical was written, all learned men subscribed to Sirmond’s judgment concerning the author of this letter.

But we will no longer need these arguments after this letter *On the Ceremonies of Baptism*, together with Charlemagne’s encyclical expressly addressed to Amalarius, bishop of Trier, and also another letter from the same emperor replying to and praising Amalarius’s letter, was discovered in an eight-hundred-year-old manuscript codex from Zurich and communicated to me by the most learned Dom Martin Gerbert. At that time he was a religious of the celebrated monastery of St. Blaise in the Black Forest, distinguished by many literary labors; now, on account of his outstanding gifts, he is the prelate of that illustrious abbey and a prince of the Holy Roman Empire.

For in that reply-letter of Charles, Amalarius is explicitly called bishop of Treveri, or Trier.

Therefore, without any hesitation concerning the true author, we now publish under the name of the distinguished Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, the letter *On the Ceremonies of Baptism* which Quercetanus falsely attributed to Alcuin.

We thought it worthwhile also to append to it the writings which, in the aforementioned Zurich codex, are connected with it as a single booklet and are addressed by Amalarius to Peter, abbot of Nonantola, formerly his companion on the embassy to Constantinople.

From these learned men will observe that Amalarius, bishop of Trier, wrote and allegorically interpreted certain other works concerning the divine office, or ecclesiastical liturgy—namely, “concerning agreement,” or conformity, as he explains it, “in all our office,” as he writes in his letter to Abbot Peter, “which is performed in the Mass, whether in singing, in posture, in quality, or in quantity, with our authentic texts, which the whole Church venerates.”

And also: “concerning the nocturnal offices and the other things performed during the day”; and “concerning the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday.”

This may have been the cause of the confusion between the two Amalariuses—the bishop of Trier, that is, and the deacon of Metz—because they had the same name and the same scholarly interest.

I do not wish here to revive the controversy over whether there was one Amalarius or two, a controversy which the distinguished Jacques Sirmond appears to have settled very well in his learned letter opposing the opinion of Dom Gaetanus. It is found in volume IV of Sirmond’s works, Venetian edition of 1728, page 461.

Nevertheless, I suspect that the other Amalarius, of Metz, borrowed several things from the earlier writings of his namesake bishop and transferred them into his own works. Many things that belong to Amalarius of Trier are also contained in the chapters of the book *On the Divine Offices*, likewise falsely attributed to Alcuin.

This suspicion arises because in both works the ceremonies of the divine office are for the most part explained through mystical reasons, the method which Amalarius of Trier professes to have used in his letter to Abbot Peter.

But these matters must be left aside until, perhaps, a greater light may be shed upon this darkness by other codices still lying hidden somewhere.

Moreover, concerning this Amalarius of ours, Pagius says under the year 814, number 31:

“Many fictitious things are circulated about this Amalarius; at least, much concerning his dignity or metropolitan authority, the year in which he obtained the episcopate, and the day and year of his death still lie in obscurity.”

It is certain from the records of that time that in the year 813, at the beginning of spring, he was sent by Emperor Charles Augustus to the East with Peter, abbot of Nonantola, to confirm peace with Emperor Michael, as is clear from the consistent account of contemporary annalists and especially from a recently discovered letter of Charles to Emperor Michael.

Pagius further declares that it can certainly be asserted, both in the place cited and under the year 811, number 10, that this same Amalarius of Trier instructed Saxony beyond the Elbe, having been sent there for this purpose by Charlemagne in the year 811.

Amalarius’s episcopate is placed by Browerus in the year 810; the most illustrious D. von Hontheim, volume I of his *History of Trier*, p. 163, note, judges that from the decree of Louis the Pious of the year 834, in Lindenbrog, *Northern Writers*, p. 125, recent edition, it appears that Amalarius was already archbishop in 809. Concerning the year of Amalarius’s death, likewise we possess nothing certain. Masenius, in note 16 to Browerus’s *Annals of Trier*, records his death in the year 814 and praises and approves the highly authoritative “*Annals of the Treveri*, which three hundred years ago Archbishop Baldwin ordered to be collected from the principal archive with great care.” Mabillon agrees with this opinion in book XVII of the *Benedictine Annals*, no. 26, and Pagius does not contradict it in his entry for this year, no. 31. There are nevertheless those who believe that the Amalarius who in 825 brought to the emperor Louis, together with Haltigarius, bishop of Cambrai, the proceedings of the Council of Paris concerning images, was the bishop of Trier, and consequently that this Amalarius prolonged his life until that year 825. (D. Bouquet, volume VI of the *Gallic Historians*, p. 341, note.) This opinion, however, is opposed by the fact that before that year—namely, at least in 816 or 817—Amalarius’s successor Hetti already held the see of Trier, as is clear from his letter to Frotharius, bishop of Toul, which D. Bouquet himself presents in the same place, p. 395, and which he considers to have been written in 817, when Bernard, king of Italy, attempted to stir up disturbances against Louis the Pious. See also another letter of the same man to the same person in the same place, p. 397, assigned by D. Bouquet himself to the year 819. We adhere to Masenius’s calculation until better evidence comes to light.

As regards the metropolitan authority of Amalarius of Trier, he himself modestly indicates at the end of his letter on the ceremonies of baptism to the emperor that no authority over the suffragan bishops had so far been granted to him. The emperor replies that, just as Amalarius had hitherto awaited the imperial order and disposition concerning this matter, so he should continue to await it until he came to the emperor’s conference. From this I infer that at that time the metropolitan authority of the bishop of Trier had been disturbed, for reasons unknown to me. Certainly several bishops of Metz—Chrodogangus, Angilramus, and Drogo—also enjoyed archiepiscopal honor. Perhaps the question then concerned transferring the metropolitan dignity from Trier to Metz? [Col. 0889D] But let others attend to this matter. For us it is enough to have suggested some points that we judged worthy of more extensive investigation by learned men of Trier.

Accordingly, we present the materials that we here share with scholars in the following order. First we place the hitherto unpublished letter of Peter, abbot of the monastery of Nonantola, to Amalarius, in which he requests that the book of the *Exposition* composed during the sea voyage—namely, during the Constantinopolitan embassy—be sent to him, together with the *Exposition on the Faith and on the Scrutiny, or Baptism*. This is followed by Amalarius’s replying letter to the former, indicating the papers to be sent to Peter. The chief of these is the inquiry of the emperor Charles, which we append, wishing to know how Amalarius himself and his suffragans teach and instruct the priests and [Col. 0890A] people entrusted to them concerning the sacrament of baptism. This letter will be followed by Amalarius’s reply to each of the questions concerning the various ceremonies of baptism; it is the very letter that Canisius, as we have said, attributed to Alcuin on a false conjecture. To this we add Charlemagne’s reply, sent to Amalarius after he had read the preceding letter, likewise hitherto unknown; in it the emperor praises Amalarius’s ready diligence and sound teaching and encourages him to undertake greater things.

## I. [Note: [Col. 0889D] This letter was written after the return of Amalarius and Peter from the Constantinopolitan embassy, in the year 814, after the death of the emperor Charles. Peter succeeded Anselm in the abbacy; Anselm died on 3 March 803. (Mabillon, book XXVII of the *Benedictine Annals*, no. 22.) Peter himself died in the year 821. (Mabillon, book 29, no. 15.)] LETTER OF THE VENERABLE ABBOT PETER

To my lord Amalarius, venerable and beloved prelate, whose name I pronounce with the greatest affection, Peter, an unworthy abbot, sends greetings in the Lord.

Let it be known to your venerable holiness that, through God’s mercy, we are well; and that we are continually present in prayers [Col. 0890B] [Perhaps, “we are continually praying”] for your health and that of your people. In humble prayer we ask your blessedness to be an intercessor for us before God. We also beseech your beloved and inviolable charity to deign to send us that book of the *Exposition* which, with the Holy Spirit dictating it to your heart, you composed during the sea voyage, for the growth and stability of our holy Church, so that those who read it and are edified may pour out prayers to the Lord for you, most blessed shepherd.

Again I beseech you concerning that *Exposition* which you yourself composed on the Faith and on the Scrutiny, or Baptism, at the command of the lord Charles, of pious memory: please send that also. When this request of ours [Perhaps, “by this request of ours”] has been fulfilled, believe that you will find great reward with God, as well as many intercessors for you—including me, unworthy as I am, and our brothers, servants in all things, whatever your venerable holiness may command us. And please deign to send us news of your health.

## II. AMALARIUS’S REPLY TO THE PRECEDING LETTER OF ABBOT PETER

To the most longed-for, most revered, and most holy Father and brother Peter, advanced in years and therefore deservedly praised, venerable abbot of the monastery of Nonantola, Amalarius, the least of men, sends perpetual greetings in the Lord.

Very recently I received a letter sent by your holiness, full of charity and humility. Among other things it contained the request that I write for your highness my work—not merely mine, but also yours, although a small work—which we fashioned amid the threats of the sea. If anything worthy, honorable, or rational is found in it, it should certainly be attributed not to my teaching but deservedly to your holy prayers.

Therefore I ask, most holy Father, that whatever has been written irrationally through my rashness and foolish presumption may, through your prudence, merit correction, and that we may receive indulgence from all teachers. For I wrote whatever seemed to me just and honorable, not with the intention of claiming that I had investigated every aspect of the work’s correctness [Col. 0891A], but so that by my undertaking I might touch upon those industrious men [Perhaps, “those men of ability”] who could most easily clarify the truth of the matter, which I ardently desired.

As you know, I wrote that I supposed myself to be imitating those who stand in the choir and sing when the bishop enters the church. In the work that follows it will be demonstrated what agreement there was throughout our entire office, which is performed in the Mass—whether in singing, position, quality, or quantity—with our authoritative sources, which the whole Church venerates. I reasoned within myself that nothing had been established in the Church, either among the ancient Fathers or among more recent writers, that lacked a rational basis.

For if pagans argue [Perhaps, “make an ingenious argument”] that some of their games have allegorical significance—for example, gamblers claim that their three dice signify the three times, present, past, and future, and they distinguish their paths by the number six because of the six ages of humanity—how much more should Christian diligence and reason, granted by God, in no way go beyond what is proper by establishing something needlessly? I did not give the example of the pagans so that we might imitate them; but if they argue [Perhaps, “make an ingenious argument”] rationally for this or that, how much more should a Christian follow everything that belongs to reason, since he makes himself a pledge to God, the supreme Reason.

The Lord does not say that the unjust steward was praised so that we might imitate him; but if he prudently provided for his future from his unjust stewardship, how much more ought a Christian to acquire, from just revenues, what will receive him into eternal dwellings? I ask, Father, that our little book not be sent to public ears, lest it fall into the teeth of detractors, nor resound through the air amid the laughter of the proud against the very humble teaching of our poverty. For I do not set myself forward as a teacher in this writing, but as a disciple seeking to learn what I love to know.

Your holiness also adds in the letter mentioned the sheets that you read, which our smallness sent to the lord emperor Charles concerning the Scrutiny and the Baptistery. You ask that they be attached to the work mentioned above. I did not delay doing this, placing them at the beginning, since everyone is catechized and baptized before reaching the holy orders. I also added the letters that the most glorious emperor mentioned sent to us: in the first he urges us to undertake this task; in the second he provides authority for the work once completed.

Likewise I ask you not to be unwilling to read through what we now add, which he did not read, so that just as the things he himself read, so also these things that are read to you may be corrected, where correction is needed, and confirmed, where confirmation is needed, by your holy authority. I also wished to place your letter at the beginning of the work specially addressed to you, together with certain verses about the sea. I do not want anything of mine to remain hidden from you.

After we had been separated bodily, I undertook to investigate certain matters concerning the Offices of the Night and the other things performed during the day, as well as the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday. If your prayers bring me to this task, I believe that the Lord’s mercy will attend and assist my efforts. Farewell in Christ!

## III. [Note: [Col. 0891D] This letter was sent in approximately the year 812, in the same terms, to other archbishops of the kingdom as well; the replies of some of them are still preserved in Baluze, Mabillon, Martène, and Pez. We have drawn variant readings from these. See, however, Pagius for the year 812, nos. 12 and 13.] EMPEROR CHARLES’S INQUIRY

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, the Great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, who by the mercy of God is also king of the Franks and Lombards, sends perpetual greetings in the Lord to Amalarius, venerable bishop.

[Col. 0892B] We would often have wished to hold a familiar conversation with you, and indeed with your other colleagues [Pez adds: “your colleagues”], concerning the welfare of God’s holy Church, if this could have been accomplished without bodily inconvenience. But although we do not fail to recognize that your holiness keeps watch over divine matters with complete devotion, nevertheless we cannot refrain from urging and reminding your devotion, through our written words and with the Holy Spirit’s prompting, that you should strive to labor more and more diligently and vigilantly in God’s holy Church through holy preaching and saving instruction, so that through your most devoted industry the Word of eternal life may grow and run its course, and the Christian people may multiply to the praise and glory of our Savior God.

For we wish to know, through your writings or from you personally, how you and your suffragans teach and instruct the priests of God [and] the people entrusted to you concerning the sacrament of baptism: namely, why an infant is first made a catechumen, or what a catechumen is; then, in order, everything that is done. Concerning the Scrutiny: what is the Scrutiny? And concerning the Creed: what is its interpretation according to the Latins? Concerning belief: how one ought to believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ his Son, born and having suffered; and in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, and the other things that follow in the same Creed?

Concerning the renunciation of Satan and all his works and pomps: what is renunciation, and what are the devil’s works and pomps? Why is he exsufflated (blown upon) [Alcuin: “insufflated,” or “breathed upon”], and why is the exorcism performed? [Col. 0892D] Why does the catechumen receive salt? Why are the nostrils touched, and the breast anointed with oil? Why are the shoulder blades [Manuscript: “spatulas”] signed [Alcuin: “the shoulder blades are washed”]? Why are the breast and shoulders smeared with oil? Why is the catechumen clothed in white garments? Why is the head anointed with sacred chrism and covered with a mystical veil, or confirmed with the Lord’s body and blood?

Strive to report all these things to us, written down with careful investigation, as we have said; or tell us whether you actually hold and preach these things, and whether you observe them yourself in what you preach. Fare well [Alcuin: “Farewell”], and pray for us.

## IV. AMALARIUS, BISHOP: REPLY

[Col. 0893A]

To the most glorious and excellent Augustus, crowned by God, Charles the most serene, perpetual life and salvation.

My most Christian lord emperor, you have sent to your servant questions concerning holy baptism, asking in order why each thing is performed in the baptistery and in the Scrutiny. Just as in all things you follow Christ’s example, so also in this: he asked Philip this question in order to teach him, saying, “Where shall we buy bread, so that these people may eat?” (John 6:5). Yet, as the Evangelist says, “He himself knew what he was going to do.”

Although I am not qualified to answer your question [Col. 0893B], nevertheless I ought not to be disobedient, but must obey your holy commands with all my senses and understanding. Therefore we have written what we are able to conjecture [Alcuin: “what we have been able to conjecture”] concerning the matters your lordship asked about, and we have directed the focus of our mind especially toward what we found readily available in the sayings of the holy Fathers, selecting from them whatever seemed suitable to your admonition.

Although we are ignorant, we nevertheless do not cease to give thanks to God for you and for your mercy, which you exercise toward all worshipers of God, and to pray for stability and wisdom for your rule. The first of these questions is as follows: Why is an infant made a catechumen before baptism?

### Concerning Catechumens

We know, most excellent emperor, that all human beings are held under the yoke of sin from the very moment of their birth until their second birth, and that the Psalmist’s truthful statement is valid: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother conceived me in sins” (Psalm 50:7). This is because of the disobedience and transgression of the first man, from whom we derive our bodily origin. We cannot be re-formed according to the image of the one who created us except through saving baptism, which we have not yet received; nor is the entrance to the kingdom of heaven open unless we are born again from water and the Holy Spirit (John 3:5).

Before baptism we are in the darkness of ignorance. Walking in the desires of the flesh, we do things that are unfitting; we live according to the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error. Therefore anyone who desires to be re-formed according to the new man must be instructed by the teachers of the Church regarding what he is before baptism and what, by God’s grace, he will be after baptism, so that he may be converted from the darkness of sins to the light of truth. Having abandoned the name of false gods, he must worship the one living and true God. After he has received this instruction from a catholic teacher, he is called a catechumen—that is, instructed or a hearer.

We cannot know the truth before we know what is false. Therefore we must teach him from whom he has departed by sinning and in what error he remains; and afterward, in whom he ought to believe and maintain the faith through works of charity.

As Augustine says in his book *On Faith and Works* (chapter 27, no. 49):

> “They who seek baptism should be catechized in such a way that they not only hear and receive what they ought to believe, but also how they ought to live. Eternal life should be promised to the faithful in such a way that no one imagines he can reach it merely through dead faith, which cannot save without works, but through that faith of grace which works through love.”

Anyone who wishes can find sufficient material concerning this instruction in Augustine’s *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*. Let them pray over the little ones, so that blindness of heart may be driven from them, the snares of Satan by which they had been bound may be broken, and they may become capable, through the growth and functioning of their limbs [Col. 0894B], of recognizing what must be abandoned and what must be retained.

### Concerning the Scrutiny

In the Scrutiny we make the sign of the cross over the children, as we find written in the Roman Order, and perform genuflection and adjuration [printed edition: “admiration”]. We teach the Lord’s Prayer to the godfathers and godmothers, so that they may likewise recite it for those whom they are to receive from holy baptism.

Similarly, we teach the Creed, whose name in our language is translated as “sign” or “knowledge.” When the apostles were dispersed throughout the whole world for the sake of preaching, they gave this [sign] of preaching, so that if someone confessed things such as are said there, he would give knowledge that he had learned them from Christ’s apostles or their successors.

### Why We Make the Sign on the Forehead

[Col. 0894C]

The seat of shame is customarily on the forehead. The Jews are ashamed in their foreheads to believe in the one whom they know was crucified, as the apostle Paul says: “But we preach Christ crucified, to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the gentiles foolishness” (1 Corinthians 1:23).

But we believe that we are saved through the Crucified One, whose name the Jews are ashamed of; we believe that we are protected by his name. Therefore we make the sign of the cross on the forehead, where the seat of shame is, as we have already said.

### With What Sign We Sign Ourselves

We sign ourselves with no other sign than the sign of the cross. For the Lord, born in the flesh, brought the banner of the cross with which he would mark the foreheads of his own [Col. 0894D], in order to destroy the dominion of death. Through this sign the opposing power recognizes that it is losing its authority over those whom God has called to the grace of baptism.

The priests, acolytes, godfathers, and godmothers make this sign on their foreheads. In the description of the temple that Ezekiel saw, it is written that there were specially slanted windows in the chambers and on the foreheads of those who were inside the gate, all around its circuit (Ezekiel 40:16). Blessed Gregory explains this as follows (*Book II on Ezekiel*, homily 5, no. 19):

> “It should indeed be noted that slanted windows are said to be within the gate, all around its circuit. For the gift of contemplation is not given to the great while it is denied to the least; rather, it is often received by the great, often by the least, more often by those who are remote, and sometimes even by married people.”

### Why the Scrutiny Is Performed Seven Times

The Scrutiny is performed seven times before Easter. The number seven often signifies totality, just as John writes to the seven Churches (Revelation 1:4) that are in Asia. Through these seven Churches he writes to the whole Church.

They are scrutinized seven times—that is, they are scrutinized perfectly—to determine whether they firmly hold in mind what they have heard from their teacher. In a certain sense, darkness is driven away from the catechumen, so that as the Scrutiny progresses the catechumens themselves may be illuminated. Hence in the Scrutiny greater service is assigned to the acolytes, who are the bearers of lights.

For this reason, in the preceding prayer we thought it appropriate to say, “Drive all blindness of heart [Col. 0895B] from him”; and in the prayer that is said in the Scrutiny, “Your eternal and most just mercy,” we say, “That you may deign to illuminate them with the light of your understanding.”

### Concerning Genuflection

We genuflect for those who have not yet been baptized, just as Stephen did, saying: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59), because they do not know what they are doing. Likewise we pray for these people, asking that God not reckon against them the fact that they have wandered and lain in sins for so long, but that according to his great mercy he may bring them to the grace of baptism.

### Concerning the Lord’s Prayer

We teach the Lord’s Prayer in this way. The Lord taught his disciples this prayer so that they would not ask for superfluous things or for things that do not pertain to their salvation.

There are seven petitions in this Lord’s Prayer. Three pertain to eternity, and four to our necessities in the present time, which are contained in this world [Manuscript: “mode,” perhaps “world”]:

“Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.”

We invoke you as Father and God, who willed to make us your adopted children and desire to have your dwelling in righteous souls, so that the holiness of your name, which is with you, may remain in our breast.

“Thy kingdom come.”

May the kingdom of the devil diminish daily, and may yours increase. Or in the manner in which they cry out in the Apocalypse: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” (Revelation 6:10).

We see this explained in the book of the lord Bede (*Bede on Revelation 6*):

> “They do not pray this out of hatred for their enemies, for whom they prayed in this world, but out of love for justice, by which, standing as it were near the Judge, they agree with him; they pray that the day of judgment may come, when the reign of sin will be destroyed, and that the resurrection of dead bodies may come. For even in the present, when we are commanded to pray for our enemies, we nevertheless say to the Lord in prayer: ‘Thy kingdom come.’”

“Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.”

By heaven we understand the spiritual creation; by earth, the bodily creation. Thus may your will be done, God the Father, so that the good things we conceive in our minds may be brought to completion in bodily action.

“Give us this day our daily bread.”

As long as we are in this world, deign always to provide us with all necessities [Col. 0896A].

“And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

We sin daily, and therefore we must say daily: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” By your giving, O God, may our heart be made gentle, so that we may quickly forgive, and may you forgive us.

“And lead us not into temptation.”

Do not allow us to be tempted by the devil in such a way that we are overcome.

“But deliver us from evil”—that is, from the sins we have committed.

### Concerning the Creed

The Creed is as follows:

“I believe in God the almighty Father.”

In the living and true Lord, the eternal Father of the eternally begotten.

“Almighty,” who will repay sinners with punishments according to their merits, and the righteous with rewards.

“Creator of heaven and earth”—that is, of spiritual and bodily creation [Col. 0896B].

“And in Jesus Christ, his Son.”

In the Savior, the Anointed One.

“His Son” [“the Only-Begotten, our Lord”].

Because he alone redeemed us with his precious blood. Through Isaiah he said: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me” (Isaiah 63:3).

“Born in the last age, from the virgin Mary.”

“He suffered for our salvation under Pontius Pilate”—that is, under the governor Pilate, who was from the island of Pontus.

“Crucified”—suspended on the cross.

“Dead”—by bodily death; and buried bodily for three days.

“He descended into hell”—in soul alone.

“On the third day he rose from the dead”—he rose bodily, with death destroyed.

“He ascended into heaven,” with the apostles looking on, in the form in which he will come to judgment.

“He ascended into heaven,” although he had never been absent from the heavenly dwellings.

“He sits at the right hand of almighty God”—that is, he reigns in the kingdom of his Father, in which nothing sinister remains or will remain [Col. 0896C].

“From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.”

He will display to the wicked and the righteous the form that the Jews crucified; to the righteous, however, he will display only that form which the unbelieving Jews did not recognize.

“To judge the living and the dead”—the righteous and sinners, each according to his deeds.

“I believe in the Holy Spirit,” who in some manner [Manuscript: “at some time”] is called the gift of God, and the love of the Father and the Son, or their communion; in this gift the forgiveness of all sins takes place. Therefore whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come (Matthew 12:32; Mark 3:29).

“I believe in the holy catholic Church,” the universal assembly of the righteous, and I believe that it is the unity of faith [Col. 0896D].

“I believe in the communion of the saints,” that it preserves the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace.

“I believe in the forgiveness of sins,” which, as we have said, takes place in the gift of the Holy Spirit.

“I believe in the resurrection of the flesh.” I believe that on the seventh day of the week the righteous, freed from the earthly body, will receive [the object is unstated in the source] and will be in great joy according to each one’s dwelling; and that they will await the eighth day, on which they will receive their bodies whole and perfect: the wicked for punishment, the righteous for eternal life [Truly and without doubt we believe this].

### Concerning Exorcism

The devil is exorcized—that is, adjured or rebuked—under whose power are all who are born with sin, so that he may depart from God’s creature [Printed edition: “from God’s nature”].

### Concerning Exsufflation (Blowing Upon)

[Col. 0897A]

He is blown upon, therefore, because the ancient deserter is worthy of such disgrace.

### Concerning Salt

During the Scrutiny, after the first prayer, we place blessed salt in the mouth. That prayer says:

“Almighty and everlasting God, deign to look upon this servant of yours, whom you have deigned to call to the beginnings of faith,”

and so forth.

After he has been instructed by an ecclesiastical teacher, he must recognize that his words ought to be seasoned with the salt of wisdom, as the apostle Paul writes to the Colossians: “Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt, that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Colossians 4:6).

### How the Final Scrutiny Is Performed

[Col. 0897B]

The Scrutiny ends on the Saturday before Easter. On that day we perform the seventh Scrutiny, as we find written in the Roman Order, and we read over them: “Nor are you unaware, Satan.”

### Concerning the Touching of the Nostrils and Ears

After this reading we touch their ears and nostrils and say to them: “Ephphatha, for a fragrance of sweetness.”

We touch the nostrils so that they may be reminded, as long as they draw the breath of this life, always to persevere in the things that they have already learned and are still learning from the mouths of catholic men. For this reason they are touched with the priest’s spittle.

Likewise we speak concerning the ears, as though the priest were saying: “Remember always to hold fast the faith that you learned from this mouth and that entered your soul through your ears, as long as you draw the breath of this life through your nostrils, so that you may be able to say with the apostle Paul: ‘We are the good fragrance of Christ’” (2 Corinthians 2:15).

And again he should say to the ears: “May these ears, by God’s mercy, always be open to understanding the words of God’s discipline, so that he may be able to say: ‘At the hearing of the ear I obeyed you’” (Psalm 17:45).

### Concerning the Anointing of the Shoulder and Breast

Afterward we touch the shoulders and breast with holy oil, saying to them: “Do you renounce Satan?” and the other words that follow.

Through oil we understand the mercy of God to be signified. For whom do we understand by the olive tree except the merciful? In Greek, *eleos* [ἔλεος] is interpreted in Latin as *misericordia*, “mercy.”

In the shoulders, or upper arms, we place the strength of the earthly person’s arm. The arms work, as do the hands that are attached to the arms. Therefore we judge that strong human works are signified by the shoulders, and good thoughts by the breast, where, in a certain sense, the chamber of thoughts is situated.

They are anointed with holy oil—that is, with God’s mercy—so that they may know that they must always implore God’s mercy, asking that he direct their hearts and works in the love of God and the patience of Christ, and so that they may recognize that they can neither do nor desire good in any other way than through God’s mercy.

### Concerning Renunciation

We question those whom we previously instructed in the faith and afterward scrutinized, asking whether they have remained in the things they first learned, and whether they have recognized themselves as blind and now advanced toward the light, since we have scrutinized them perfectly—that is, seven times.

We ask whether they renounce—that is, contradict—the opposing power of Satan, all his works, and all his pomps.

We say to the person: “Contradict Satan, with the prophet David: ‘Forget your people and your father’s house’” (Psalm 44:11).

Then we ask about all his works, which include fornication, the service of idols, sorcery, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and similar things. Although these pertain to the pleasures of the flesh, they are nevertheless works of Satan, whose hidden counselor and instigator he is.

These are the things that reign in the devil without flesh: pride, envy, enmities, quarrels, jealousies, anger, strife, dissensions, sects, and the rest. Although the Apostle calls these “works of the flesh” (Galatians 5:19 ff.), they reign in the devil without flesh. They are, in a certain way, works of the flesh because they are human works; and by living according to himself—that is, according to man—a human being has become like the devil, because the devil too wished to live according to himself.

We call these the works of Satan. For some of them he is the counselor and instigator; of others he is the head and origin.

Finally, we ask concerning all his pomps, which include empty boasting, earthly people, and melodious music, through which Christian strength is often dissolved and softened; disgraceful or superfluous spectacles; and the rest.

Then we examine the godfathers and godmothers to see whether they can recite the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, as we previously instructed. Afterward, in order, as it is written in the Roman Order, we perform the sacred office up to the most sacred work of baptism.

### Recapitulation

[Col. 0898C]

The person who is to be baptized is already a catechumen—that is, instructed [Perhaps, “must be instructed”], so that he may recognize his former error and understand the light of truth.

He has received the salt of wisdom, so that he may avoid shameful speech. The devil who was in him has been adjured, with the sign of the cross, to depart from God’s servant. Then genuflection is performed before God, so that God may drive him out from the one he has called.

He has already been taught to pray for himself in the Lord’s Prayer. He has heard in the Creed how he ought to believe. Through the priest’s spittle he has been admonished that, as long as he draws the breath of this life through his nostrils, he should hold fast the faith he heard through his ears.

After hearing the faith, he is anointed between the shoulders and on the breast, so that through God’s mercy good thoughts and works may be strengthened in him, and so that he may depart from every evil belonging to the members of Satan [Col. 0898D], do good, and confess that he believes in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ his Son, born from the Father before all ages and made from a woman in the last age; and in the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

Thus he is joined [Perhaps, “to the Church” is missing] to the sacred font of baptism.

### Concerning the Anointing of the Head

After this saving washing, his head is smeared with sacred chrism. From the Old Testament we know that priests and kings were anointed with it. The baptized person is to understand that he has received a royal and priestly ministry, because he has been united to the one who is the supreme King and true Priest. He ought to hope for an everlasting kingdom and always offer God sacrifices of blameless conduct.

### Concerning the Covering of the Head

Afterward the head is covered with a linen cloth. This too is taken from the Old Testament, for it is written in Exodus:

> “You shall also bring forward his sons, namely Aaron’s sons, and clothe them in linen tunics; you shall gird Aaron and his sons with a belt, and you shall place mitres on them” (Exodus 29:8–9).

Having received the grace of holy baptism, the person must not place confidence again in his own strength, but must always pray to be protected by heavenly assistance. We wish the Lord’s splendid protection to be understood through the linen cloth with which the head is covered.

### Concerning the Garment

He is clothed in white garments so that he may know that he possesses an inviolate body and a heart illumined by the love of the Holy Spirit; or so that he may recognize that he possesses righteousness and a nuptial garment.

By garments the works of righteousness are understood, whence it is said to them: “Let the priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131:9).

### Concerning Confirmation with the Body and Blood

Afterward he is confirmed with the Lord’s body and blood, so that he may know that through such mysteries the devil has been driven from his heart and Christ dwells within him. Thus we may confidently say: “All you who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27).

### Concerning Little Children Who Do Not Speak  
[Note: [Col. 0899D] In the manuscript of St Gall the title is: “Concerning little children who do not understand and yet have faith.”]

Although, because of their age, little children cannot understand the conversion itself toward God or belief, nevertheless we believe that they are converted to the Lord because of the sacrament of conversion, and that they possess faith because of the sacrament of faith.

Thus we read in Augustine’s letter to Bishop Boniface, who was asking about little children. Augustine says:

> “The response itself belongs to the celebration of the sacrament, just as the Apostle says concerning baptism itself: ‘We have been buried with Christ through baptism into death’ (Romans 6:4). He does not say, ‘We have signified a burial,’ but plainly says, ‘We have been buried.’ Therefore he named the sacrament of so great a thing by the name of that very thing. Thus, although the faith that consists in the will of believers is not yet present in a little child, the sacrament of that faith already makes him faithful. For just as the response is ‘to believe,’ so also he is called faithful—not by assenting to the reality itself with his mind, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality.

> “When a person begins to possess understanding, he will not repeat that sacrament, but will understand it, and his will will be conformed to it by a will agreeing with it. As long as he cannot do this, the sacrament will avail for his protection against opposing powers. It will avail so greatly that, if he should depart from this life before reaching the use of mature age [Alcuin: “before reaching the use of mature age,” or “before reaching the use of reason”], through that sacrament, with the charity of the Church commending him, he will be freed by Christian assistance from the condemnation that entered the world through one man.”

Thus far Augustine on little children who do not speak. [Col. 0900A] It may happen that those who are bound by another’s sin are released by another’s profession of faith.

Because of this, most pious Emperor, we have submitted these matters out of obedience, since it is fitting to obey your will with all our strength. Nevertheless, in all that we have said, we are ready to be corrected and amended by learned teachers [MS: illustrious teachers], with ears inclined to them. Concerning our faith, we say and accept what Isaiah said: “The Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Rom. 9:28).

We believe that the one living and true God is always immutable, yet works mutable things; that he is never without his Wisdom, that is, without his Son, nor without his will, that is, without the Holy Spirit. God the Father created all things in his good will through Wisdom. We believe in the three persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, [Col. 0900B] and we accept Sedulius’s verse:

> Not because he who is the supreme Father is also the Son,

but:

> Because what the supreme Father is, the Son also is.

We believe that the Son alone assumed human flesh, so that he might be visible to human beings; that he was baptized because it was necessary for us to be baptized; that he died bodily to the world, so that we might die to sins; that he rose from the dead, so that we might hope for the resurrection; that he will come at the final judgment, when he will separate the sheep from the goats, and afterward the wicked alone will live in hell, that is, in punishments, while the just alone will reign blessedly in the kingdom of God.

This is our faith, most just Emperor; this is our firm hope. We love this God, whom we desire to love ever more ardently.

[Col. 0900C] [Note: [Col. 0900D] See what we said in the Preliminary Notice.]

You said, most serene Emperor, that you wished to know how we and our suffragans teach the people of God concerning the sacrament of baptism. We have briefly set this out as best we could. “Suffragan” is a term of intermediate meaning; therefore we do not know what fixed designation we ought to attach to it—whether that of priests, abbots, deacons, or the other lower orders. If perhaps we ought to add the title of bishops, who were once subject to your city, I beg that the Lord will not charge this to his servant, because until the present time I have not dared to touch upon matters that were not entrusted to us. I am nevertheless ready to follow the footsteps of all Christ’s servants.

And if the reference is perhaps to priests, we have taught and admonished them according to the order stated above, [Col. 0900D] so that they may often teach the people of God to abandon the vanities of this world and seek the true things of heaven. Since your command compels me to answer concerning whether I myself observe what I preach, I reply: “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 24:15).

Let your most holy governance know, my lord, that I preach to no one that he should sin. Nevertheless, I recall the blessed James’s statement, where he says: “For we all offend in many things” (Jas. 3:2). When the supreme apostle of Christ spoke, he prefaced the statement with “in many things” and added “all,” so that even imperfect people might watch themselves in speech and action with the greater care, the more certainly they understood that not even good people who are perfect, and who walk under the guidance of the grace of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0901A] could in any way pass through this life without the offense of some sin. Therefore we teach as follows:

> “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” (1 John 1:9),

because we cannot be without sin in this life. The first hope of salvation is confession; no one should consider himself just and raise his neck before the eyes of God. Next comes love, because “the love of God covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

## V. CAROLUS THE GREAT’S REPLY TO THE PRECEDING LETTER

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great [Col. 0901B] and peaceful emperor, governing the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards, to Amalarius, venerable bishop: greetings in the Lord.

We have received with grateful hand the writing sent to us by your holiness; for this we offer you praise and thanks [Col. 0902A], especially because, when we had it read through in our presence, we found it Catholic and worthy of every commendation. We also give you thanks for having obeyed us and hastened to carry out our commands.

Although we are not unaware that your holiness is diligent in spiritual matters and Christian teaching, we nevertheless admonish and exhort you to take ever greater care to instruct in Christian doctrine and holy preaching all who are under your governance and belong to your diocese.

[Note: [Col. 0901] It is now clear that the clause of the preceding letter beginning “You said, most serene Emperor” truly belongs to this matter, about which Canisius had doubted.]

Concerning the suffragan bishops of the Church of Trier [MS thus, in place of “of the Treverians”], in which, with the Lord’s assent, we wish you to be bishop: just as hitherto [source reading: antenus; emended reading: hactenus] you have awaited our appointment, arrangement, and command, so we wish you meanwhile [Col. 0902B] to await it until you come to our conference [variant: “when you come to our conference”]. As for the other orders—that is, priests, deacons, and all the clergy—as well as the people entrusted to you who dwell inter [intra, within] your parish, strive with complete devotion to preach and teach them the way of truth.

Farewell, and pray for us.

## THEODORUS, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY

[Note: [Col. 0901B] Theodorus flourished toward the end of the seventh century; therefore, according to chronological order, this is not his proper place. Let the indulgent reader forgive this, however, for although we had long sought the book of the holy archbishop everywhere, it came into our hands only later. EDITOR.]

## THE PENITENTIAL OF THEODORE

Enlarged with all the chapters of the same author that could be found; set forth through selected canons from a very ancient manuscript Collection of Canons, together with numerous excerpts from various Penitentials hitherto unpublished; and confirmed by splendid monuments of ecclesiastical discipline selected from the best manuscript codices. James Petit first published it; he compared it with numerous canons of councils and illustrated it with dissertations and notes.

[Col. 0901]

### Dedicatory letter

TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND LEARNED MAN, MOST BENEVOLENT OF ALL, A MOST CAREFUL AND SUCCESSFUL SEEKER OF ANCIENT MANUSCRIPT BOOKS, A MOST ZEALOUS ADVOCATE OF THE LAW, OR LIBERTY, OF THE GALLICAN CHURCH, ANTHONY VYON, LORD D’HEROUVAL.

I owe you so much, most illustrious man, that I can never repay it. Yet your benefits are such as the Roman orator once praised: it is the mark of a noble spirit, when much is owed to someone, to wish to owe him still more. The poet’s statement is also certain:

> I do not at all consider it the duty of a free man,

when one who has deserved nothing asks that it be credited to him as a favor.

Accordingly, when several years ago I observed, most illustrious man, that many of the finest books of our time were being adorned by your public beneficence, and since I was a participant both in your learning and in your generosity, I wished in some way to discharge my obligation. But what could I contribute from my own resources? Should I have followed the advice of the comic poet?

> Since what you wish cannot be done, wish what you can.

[Col. 0903] Rather, like an anxious debtor who lacks the means but not the will, I searched everywhere for a gift not unworthy of being offered to you. At last, fortune, favoring my ardor, brought into my hands the Penitential of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, so highly praised by the Fathers and councils. To whom should I offer it, most illustrious man, except to you, the most careful, successful, and benevolent seeker of ancient manuscript books?

How diligently this distinguished monument of ecclesiastical discipline was sought by learned men, they themselves plainly declare. Antonius Augustinus, most illustrious and learned archbishop of Tarragona, states in his preface to the Roman Penitential that he had never read Theodore’s Penitential, but had found certain fragments of it in the collections of Burchard of Worms and Ivo of Chartres. Joannes Morinus, a man of the highest learning, declares in the appendix to his books on Penance that no one had read it who professed to have seen it, except Henry Spelman, the collector of the English councils, who testifies that a manuscript was preserved in the library of St Benedict at Cambridge, from which he copied only the titles of the chapters. Finally, Lucas Acherius, a man of the greatest learning, piety, and authority, whom the diligence of his friends allows scarcely anything to escape, affirms from letters he had received that it was no longer to be found even among the English.

But now that which had so long been sought has happily been found in two manuscript codices of the Thuana Library. To whom could I offer it, most illustrious man, except to you? Moreover, your reputation for learning is so great among all, as is your skill in distinguishing genuine from false manuscript codices, that your name alone will add great weight to so many splendid monuments of ecclesiastical discipline appended to Theodore’s Penitential. These have been selected from your innumerable notes and from the many documents of the most celebrated churches of France, which you have generously and munificently shared with me, and they ought to be brought to light under your auspices.

Finally, it is to my advantage that you kindly receive my dissertations, notes, and observations. For the greatest benevolence with which you embrace all lovers of truth will forgive much in my first efforts. If, therefore, I have not reached the truth in every respect, at least you will not despise the love of truth with which you know me to burn. If my efforts should perhaps seem ungrateful and ill-starred to you, I nevertheless hope that this testimony of a grateful spirit will not be displeasing, since I wish you to know, most illustrious man, that as long as the memory of the ancient monuments of ecclesiastical discipline and of the law or liberty of the Gallican Church lives in me, the magnificence of your benefits can never be erased by any forgetfulness.

[Col. 0903]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0903A] Among the many and great monuments of ecclesiastical discipline that are being brought to light in our time, scarcely any has been sought more diligently or desired more earnestly by learned men than the Penitential of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. For it is the oldest and most celebrated of all the Penitentials that existed in the West; after its model were composed the Penitentials of the venerable Bede, the Roman Penitential, that of Egbert of York, and finally the others.

Let it not therefore be rejected among the common penitential booklets that the synods decreed should be examined, since, as the Fathers of the Second Council of Chalon say, chapter 38: “Their errors are certain, their authors uncertain.” Theodore himself is a very well-known author: he was born at Tarsus in Cilicia and was a most holy monk, who, because of his outstanding reputation for virtue and learning, was ordained bishop of the Church of Canterbury by Pope Vitalian, as Bede testifies in book IV, chapters 1 and 2, of the Ecclesiastical History of the English People.

He was the first archbishop to whom the whole English Church consented to give its allegiance. He presided over several councils for the establishment of the churches; he stabilized the canonical manner of celebrating Easter; and he established a proper order of life not only in the Church but also in many other matters, as Bede records in book IV, chapters 2 and 5. Hence, according to that same author, book V, chapter 8, he was regarded as:

> Chief of pontiffs, blessed and highest priest.

Nothing brought Theodore greater praise or authority than his Penitential, proposed to all the churches as an outstanding model of the whole of ecclesiastical doctrine and discipline. For, in accordance with the decrees of the synods, bishops were particularly instructed to inquire of their priests whether they diligently read and understood Theodore’s Penitential, as Regino reports in book II of Ecclesiastical Discipline, inquiry 105.

For this reason, one scarcely finds a Father or council more frequently commended by the Fathers and councils themselves. [Col. 0903C] This will become clear if you compare the Penitential itself with the testimonies of ecclesiastical authors and with numerous canons of councils. We have shown that these were taken from the Penitential and later praised by more recent authors, after Isidore [Col. 0904A] Mercator—or “the merchant,” or “the sinner”—under the titles of the Fathers, saints, and synods, as well as of the ancient Roman pontiffs.

From this it may be inferred that this Isidore was not Isidore of Seville, who died in the year 636. Theodore flourished after that year, namely in 680.

But since Theodore’s Penitential embraces very many Greek and Roman rites, it is not surprising if certain practices of particular churches are found in it that are unusual, or others that the Fathers, out of great indulgence toward the weakness of many, wished to make more tolerable. So that no one may abuse these provisions, we shall at least briefly indicate in the preface how they should be understood.

Let the reader therefore be warned that the practice of rebaptizing those whom a fornicating priest had baptized, if this became known, must be considered wholly unusual after the condemnation of the Donatist schism. Since the Donatists abused such a custom in defending their position, the Church wisely judged that it should be abolished.

[Col. 0904B] Next, let him observe that permission to marry after divorce on account of fornication, prolonged absence, captivity, or any other cause arose from the great indulgence of certain leaders of the Church. Origen speaks of this as follows in volume XIV of his Commentary on Matthew, edited by Huet, volume I, page 363:

> Ἤδη δὲ παρὰ γεγραμμένα καὶ τινὲς τῶν ἡγουμένων τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἑπέτρεψάν τινα, ὣστε ζῶντος τοῦ ἀνδρὸς, γαμεῖσθαι γυναῖκα, παρὰ τὸ γεγραμμένων μὲν ποιοῦντες ἐν ῷ λέλεκθαι, κ . τ. λ.· οὐ μὴν πάντη ἀλόγως, εἰκὸς γὰρ τὴν συμπεριφορὰν ταύτην συγκρίσει χειρόνων ἐπιτρέπεσθαι παρὰ τὰ ἀπ` ἀρχῆς νενομοθετημένα καὶ γεγραμμένα

That is:

> Already, contrary to what has been written, some leaders of the Church permitted a woman to marry while her husband was still alive, acting contrary to what is written in the passage, and so forth; nevertheless, not entirely without reason, for it is likely that this concession was permitted in comparison with worse alternatives, contrary to what had been legislated and written from the beginning.

Furthermore, no one should be troubled by Theodore’s statement [Col. 0904C] that, concerning a woman married after taking a vow, it is in the husband’s power whether she fulfills her vows or not. This can be understood according to the ancient distinction between a veiled and an as-yet-unveiled girl, introduced by Innocent I in his letter to Victricius, chapters 12 and 13, and reported in the canons of the Romans to the Gallic bishops, chapter 1:

> “The question [Col. 0905A] concerns veiled virgins who have changed their intention: what judgment has consequently been rendered? If a veiled virgin, already consecrated to Christ, who had publicly professed her chastity before a priest and, after pouring forth prayers, had received the veil of blessing, whether she committed incest or, wishing to conceal her crime, gave an adulterer the name of husband—thereby taking the members of Christ and making them members of a prostitute, so that she who had been Christ’s bride might be called the wife of a man.”

And chapter 2:

> “A girl who has not yet been veiled but had decided to remain so, although she has not been veiled in Christ, nevertheless, because she had made that decision and has not been veiled in marriage, is said to have contracted a clandestine marriage.”

Finally, Saint Augustine testifies that the practice of not eating birds and animals if they were strangled in nets or killed by a hawk was changed for the better, in these words from book XXXII, chapter 13, Against Faustus the Manichaean:

> “But when the Church of the Gentiles had become such that no carnal Israelite appeared in it, who would then refrain from touching thrushes or smaller [Col. 0905B] birds, except those whose blood had been poured out?”

Since, therefore, the English Church had recently been converted to the faith of Christ and had not yet been so established that no carnal Israelite appeared within it, consideration of its weakness still required this practice. Even after Saint Augustine, the Fathers of the Second Council of Orléans ordered that it be observed under penalty of anathema, canon 20:

> “Let them be barred from the gatherings of the Church. Likewise, those who eat animals killed by the bites of beasts, or suffocated by any disease or accident.”

These, then, are customs once permitted by way of dispensation, which the Church no longer tolerates. If anyone thereafter wishes to oppose Theodore’s authority to the definitions of the Catholic Church, let him hear, in defense of so great an archbishop, what Saint Augustine once said [Col. 0905C] in praise of blessed Cyprian in a similar case, book I, chapter 30, On Baptism against the Donatists:

> “But lest I seem to say these things in praise of the most blessed martyr in order to avoid the proof, and so forth. The uninstructed object his authority, so that they may appear to be acting rightly—wretched men, and, unless they correct themselves, utterly condemned by themselves—who choose to imitate this in so great a man.”

Before I come to Theodore’s chapters, several of which perhaps belong to the Penitential, it must be acknowledged that what we present from two ancient manuscript codices of the Thuana Library—one of which is joined to a codex of canons and constitutions of the apostolic see, and the other to other collections of canons—we call the Penitential itself, not because it presents the Penitential book in its entirety, but because it appears to omit none of its principal contents.

Thus the Penitential copied by Halitgarius from the archive of the Roman Church bears the title of the Roman Penitential, although very many chapters are missing from it that ancient authors praised under the title of the Roman Penitential. In the same way, the Penitential of Egbert of York is so called, although it is nothing more than a very brief abridgment [Col. 0905D] of the vast work preserved in the Oxford Library and divided into four books, containing countless judgments [Col. 0906A] concerning individual sins, as J. Morinus testifies after Bale and Henry Spelman in the appendix to his book On Penance.

Therefore, to state my opinion of these copies briefly: along with the learned, I believe that the Penitential itself is displayed in them, but arranged in excellent order for presenting the discipline of either the Greeks or the Romans, with many commonplace matters omitted. No older monument exists in which the particularly difficult rites of the Greeks are explained more clearly.

Three things especially prove the antiquity of this monument. First is the accurate reading of the two manuscript codices. Although their readings vary somewhat, as we have noted, they nevertheless agree almost everywhere with the many testimonies transmitted by ancient authors and plainly correct much that later writers—especially collectors of canons—have excessively corrupted.

Second, nothing foreign or extraneous has been mixed into them. Nor should it be objected that Theodore is cited in these copies, since Theodore himself sometimes cites himself. Thus, in the chapters edited by the reverend and learned D. Luca Acherius in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*, chapter 12, Theodore says: “But we, through mercy,” and so forth. Likewise, in the Council of Herford, in Bede, book IV of the History, chapter 3, and in Burchard, book XVI, chapter 39. Moreover, the circumstances required him to distinguish what he himself had decreed from the decrees of others.

Finally, both manuscript codices of Theodore’s Penitential are neatly written. Men highly experienced in judging manuscript codices declare this to be evidence of antiquity.

Since Theodore’s chapters either belong to his Penitential or greatly illuminate it, and since they are found scattered through various books, I have undertaken to collect them as far as possible, both those already published and those not yet published. The most extensive collection of Theodore’s chapters has not yet [Col. 0906B] appeared in print. Nicholas Favier, a lawyer in the Parisian senate, highly skilled in both ecclesiastical and civil law and especially devoted to ancient matters, kindly shared it with me after returning from Flanders. He had diligently examined the libraries of the most celebrated churches and monasteries of Flanders and had plucked choice items from them like a bee gathering flowers from a rich meadow.

Whoever observes that certain chapters are praised now under Theodore’s name and now under the title of other Fathers or councils—not specifically, but generally—should apply to them the judgment expressed by Blessed Peter Damian in chapter 12 of the little work entitled *Gomorrhianus*.

Some chapters are Theodore’s—for example, those concerning the number of witnesses against clerics—which are commonly said to have been fabricated under the name of Pope Sylvester by Isidore Mercator. But we have observed that they were described by ecclesiastical authors before Isidore’s time and shortly after Theodore. In the same [Col. 0906C] chapters are found several provisions concerning the redemption of penances. Although Regino and the other collectors of canons greatly commended these under Theodore’s name, J. Morinus considers them interpolated and blameworthy. Yet, although we do not deny that certain things were added, we do not entirely agree with that learned man.

To these chapters we append others collected from various places. First come the ten chapters presented by Theodore, as presiding officer, to the Fathers of the Council of Herford. One of them has been terribly corrupted in a way hostile to the dignity of bishops. We have restored its genuine meaning on the authority of Egbert of York and the best manuscript codices, together with notes indicating the sources from which these chapters may have been taken.

Others were published by the reverend and learned D. Lucas Acherius in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*. Since he unquestionably used manuscript codices that had been worn away and obscured, he was able to present much only imperfectly and defectively [Col. 0906D], despite all the diligence of so experienced a scholar. Several passages are reported fully and completely in the Penitential; omitting these, we present only the fragments absent from it.

The remainder consists of fragments from canons, Penitentials, collectors of canons, and certain manuscript codices. To all these, so that nothing may appear to be missing from Theodore’s Penitential, we add the titles of the chapters of the Penitential book, which Henry Spelman copied alone from the manuscript codex of the library of St Benedict at Cambridge, in volume I of the English Councils.

Let no one read these fragments unless fortified by blessed Paul’s judgment: “Test everything; hold fast what is good.” For they contain many things falsely attributed to Theodore—namely, those matters that Peter Damian thoroughly refutes in chapters 10, 11, 12, and others of the work entitled *Gomorrhianus*, as apocryphal canons, as dirges mixed into the sacred canons, or as spurious offshoots of the canons.

There he expressly proves that they are neither Theodore’s nor in any way related to the canons of councils, in these words:

> “These matters of which we speak are recognized as spurious offshoots of the canons, excluded by the sacred councils, and entirely foreign to the decrees of the Fathers. It follows, therefore, that those things should in no way be counted among the canons which appear to proceed neither from the decretal edicts of the Fathers nor from sacred councils. For whatever is not numbered among the species is unquestionably judged to be alien to the genus. [Col. 0907A]
>
> “If the author’s name is sought, it cannot be stated with certainty, because it could not be found uniformly in the various codices. In one place it is written, ‘Theodore says’; elsewhere, ‘The Roman Penitential says’; elsewhere, ‘The Canons of the Apostles’; [Col. 0908A] elsewhere it is titled one way, elsewhere another. And since they do not deserve to have one author, they undoubtedly lose all authority. For whatever wavers under so many uncertain authors confirms nothing with certain authority.”

We have proved sufficiently and more than sufficiently in our notes that all these and similar matters, opposed to the decretal edicts of the Fathers and to the sacred canons, are far removed from our two copies of Theodore’s Penitential.

To explain the ecclesiastical discipline proposed in the preceding monuments, we present other splendid monuments selected from many manuscript codices, of which we shall speak in their proper place.

[Col. 0907]

## TESTIMONIES OF ANCIENT AND RECENT WRITERS CONCERNING THEODORE’S PENITENTIAL

[Col. 0907B] From the canons of the venerable priest Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*, chapter 1:
