> “Then the holy Fathers and Saint Paphnutius; then the canons of the holy Fathers; then others, one after another, such as Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, and Theodore. From the sayings and judgments of all these we have faithfully transcribed these matters, so that all may be saved,” and so forth.

### An excerpt published by blessed Pope Gregory III from the sayings of the Fathers and the judgments of the canons

In the preface:

> “Therefore, from the many flowers of allegory, from the treatises and published discourses of great men, from the sayings of the Fathers and the judgments of the canons—that is, of Isidore, Augustine, Gregory, Bede, Gelasius, Innocent, Theodore, Cassian, Egbert, and the others—we have endeavored to gather and compile this little Penitential book from the whole body, and together [Col. 0907C] for the use of our fellow priests. It is rightly called a Penitential, because it is appropriate to penance.”

### From Rabanus’s letter to Bishop Humbert, volume VI of Rabanus’s works, page 165

> “Likewise, in the chapters of Theodore, archbishop of the English people, which he wrote concerning necessary matters, we find that according to the Greeks it is permitted to marry within the third degree of blood relationship, and according to the Romans within the fifth. Yet they would not dissolve marriages contracted within the third degree if they had previously been joined unknowingly; and a man would be joined in marriage equally to those related to him by blood and to his wife’s blood relatives after his wife’s death.
>
> “This Theodore, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, was ordained bishop at Rome by Pope Vitalian and sent to Britain. Thus he had been fully instructed in the customs of both the Eastern and Western Churches. Nothing that the Greeks or Romans of that time observed according to law could escape him, especially since he was perfectly instructed in both languages [Col. 0907D], and so forth.
>
> “Therefore, since you wished me, in my humble capacity, to write to you what I think about this matter, I believe that, given the weakness of the present age, we should follow what Bishop Theodore, standing between Gregory and Isidore, defined in his chapters: that marriage should become lawful in the fifth degree, because neither divine law contradicts this nor do the sayings of the holy Fathers prohibit it.”

[Col. 0908B] From Regino’s book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, inquiry 95:

> “Whether he has the Roman Penitential, or that issued by Bishop Theodore, or that composed by the venerable priest Bede.”

### Note of the most learned Joannes Morinus, book IV of the *Penitential*, chapter 18

> “For priests everywhere were commanded diligently to observe the ancient forms of penance. Therefore he inserted into his collection a Penitential composed from the Penitentials of Theodore and Bede.”

### From Burchard, book XIX, chapter 8

> “Now therefore, brothers, whoever wishes first of all to bear the name of priest should consider, for God’s sake, that he must learn the things necessary for him before the bishop’s hand touches his head: namely, the Psalter, and so forth. In addition, he should have his own Penitential, arranged both according to the authority of the canons and according to the judgments [Col. 0908C] of three Penitentials: those of Bishop Theodore, the Roman pontiffs, and Bede.”

[Note: [Col. 0907D] Here I could list very many testimonies drawn from Theodore’s Penitential and praised by most councils, Penitentials, and all the collectors of canons. But I shall review them when they are compared with the Penitential itself. I shall therefore proceed to the judgments of several recent, but highly learned, writers.]

[Col. 0908D]

### Rhenanus, in the argument of the book *On Penance*, in Tertullian

> “Theodore’s Penitential was imitated by Betanus the priest, Rabanus, and other ancient writers, whose works on a similar subject are found here and there in ancient libraries and are by no means unworthy of being read, especially by those who are curious investigators of Christian antiquity.”

### Antonius Augustinus, most illustrious archbishop of Tarragona

In the preface to the Roman Penitential:

> “Three Penitential books are mentioned: that of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury; that of Bede the priest; and the one called the Roman Penitential. Theodore was a Greek by nationality and was sent by Pope Vitalian to the island of Britain, where, among many other things, he established these rules of penance. Bede followed him after a short interval; he is also said to have seen the Roman book and to have enlarged Theodore’s book from it, adding other material received from elsewhere.
>
> “I confess that I have never read these books, but have found only certain fragments of them in the collections of Burchard of Worms and Ivo of Chartres.”

### Joannes Morinus, book VII, *On Penance*, chapter 1, no. 15

Theodore was a Greek monk, born at Tarsus in Cilicia, whom Pope Vitalian ordained bishop [Col. 0909A] in the year of Christ 668. He sent him to Britain, which Theodore reached in the second year after his ordination. He occupied the see of Canterbury for 21 years, 3 months, and 26 days, as Bede writes in book IV, chapters 1 and 11, of the History of the English. He died in the year 690.

Therefore, during that period Theodore composed his Penitential, in which he assigned penances individually to each sin and described the rites of confession and absolution. It is praised as the first of all the penitential books among the Latins. Many were later composed in imitation of it, among which the most celebrated were the Roman Penitential and the one that bears Bede’s name, and so forth.

### The same work, no. 16

The origin and first occasion of the innovation that took place in the Latin Church, which I intend to describe here, was that book, Theodore’s Penitential, composed in imitation of the Greeks, published in England twenty-five years or somewhat less before the year 700, and soon afterward disseminated and celebrated throughout the Latin Church.

I think no one will be surprised at its prompt and rapid dissemination who carefully considers the difference between a Penitential and a Collection of Canons, together with certain other circumstances connected both with Penitentials and with the hypothesis under discussion, and so forth.

### The same work, no. 17

The reader will easily judge from this how suitable and convenient that new composition of penitential booklets was for individual priests. Each priest had at hand a little index, as though displayed on a tablet, according to which penances were to be assigned for individual sins and adjusted, exchanged, or redeemed according to the differing conditions, ages, disabilities, and illnesses of the persons involved.

It is therefore not surprising that the Penitential of Theodore, an archbishop highly learned for his age and most acceptable to all because of the authority of the supreme pontiff by whom he had been consecrated and sent to England, spread throughout nearly the entire [Col. 0909B] West within a short time. Nor is it surprising that many other bishops imitated it—not merely approving Theodore’s Penitential, but also [Col. 0909C] composing other books modeled on it, more convenient and more extensive. Nor is it surprising that councils and synodal assemblies held every year after the seventh [Col. 0910A] century consistently decreed with severity that every priest should have Theodore’s Penitential at hand, in order to impose penances on sinners according to its prescriptions.

### In the appendix to the book *On Penance*

Three of these penitential booklets were especially celebrated in the West. The first of all is that of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. Next comes Bede’s Penitential, entitled *On Remedies for Sins*. It is nevertheless usually cited by the ancients under the title “Penitential.” In reality it is a penitential book, for penitential books chiefly contain remedies for sins.

The third is the Roman Penitential. These are the most ancient Penitentials, celebrated and praised by all the collectors of canons and by most councils. They frequently ordered that penances be imposed for sins according to the definitions of these Penitentials.

That much-praised Penitential of Theodore has not yet been published. Many passages from it are cited by Burchard, Ivo, Gratian, and the manuscript collection of Regino. Until now I have not been able to read anyone [Col. 0910B] who professed to have seen Theodore’s Penitential except Henry Spelman, the collector of the English councils, who testifies that a manuscript is preserved in the famous library of St Benedict at Cambridge, from which he copied only the titles of the chapters.

There are very many titles that present material most suitable and useful for our purpose, and which, both because of their subject matter and because of their antiquity, are most worthy of being made public by someone. It would nevertheless be worthwhile to examine the character of the script, whether ancient or more recent, and then compare with it the passages cited by the ancients. For, as we have often noted, books of this kind commonly receive additions adapted to the use of the period in which they are copied [Col. 0910C].

[Col. 0909]

## CHAPTER ONE

## ON THE CONSTRUCTION AND CONSECRATION OF CHURCHES — ON THE ESTABLISHMENT OF CHAPELS AND THE GRANTING OF PREBENDS

1. Charter granting permission to a certain faithful man named Frodar to build an oratory, issued by Alexander, Bishop of the Church of Vienne. It explains the original institution of the consecration of churches and the reasons that moved bishops to permit laymen of means to build churches. (From the cartulary of the Church of Vienne.)

2. Charter of the Church of St Stephen of Lyon, written in the time of St Bernard, Archbishop of Vienne, who preceded St Ado and was a contemporary of Agobard, Archbishop of the Church of Lyon. It establishes that a church may not be built without the archbishop’s permission. (From the cartulary of the Church of Lyon.)

3. Charter concerning the monastery of St Peter of Clairvaux, in which it is declared that, for donations to be properly made for the building and consecration of churches, the bishop’s consent and authority are necessarily required. (From the cartulary of the monastery of Conques.)

4. Judgment delivered concerning a church built by the monks of St Praejectus without consulting the bishop of the place. For that reason the bishop claimed it as his own and granted it to the Church of Cluny for the use of the monks. (From the cartulary of the monastery of St Praejectus.)

[Col. 0912D] 5. Charter granting permission to build a basilica in the village called Blaneda and to dedicate that church. From it one may gather everything pertaining to the construction and dedication of churches: the bishop’s permission, the endowment granted, the solemn dedication, and the bishop’s right over the consecrated church. (From the cartulary concerning the honors granted to St Julian in the county of Brioude.)

6. Authentic instrument of the abbot and convent of St Denis concerning the church of Neuville, in which they declare that the Bishop of Paris kindly granted them permission to build a church, and concerning the bishop’s right over the church once built. (From the cartulary of the Church of Paris, as reported in the papers of the distinguished Antonius Vyon, lord of Hérouval.)

7. Moral exposition of the dedication of a church, from an ancient codex on blessings and consecrations [Col. 0913A] for the use of the Church of England, by the learned Philastrius, librarian of the library of the metropolitan church of Rouen.

8. Charter of a donation made by the Bishop of Limoges in a full synod, in which it is declared what is necessary for a chapel to be consecrated and established according to the canons. (From the cartulary of the monastery of Beaulieu.)

9. The patronage of the chaplaincy of Lemigniato belongs to the bishop; and concerning the oath that the chaplain instituted by the bishop is required to swear, so that the rights of the parish church may be preserved in every respect. (From the cartulary of the Church of Meaux.)

10. Concerning the count’s chapel at Tretiacum, which the bishop permits to be built, without prejudice to the rights of the mother church. (From the same cartulary.)

11. Donation of the chaplaincy of Troyes, founded with the bishop’s consent; it belongs to him. (From the same cartulary.)

12. Donation of two prebends in the church of Oissery [Col. 0913B], founded with the consent of the Bishop of Meaux; they belong to him. (From the same cartulary.)

13. Concerning an oratory erected in the house of the lady of Plessis-Placy with the bishop’s permission, with the parish rights preserved in every respect. (From the same cartulary.)

14. The patronage of the chaplaincy founded at the altar of Blessed Mary Magdalene belongs perpetually to the bishop. (From the same cartulary.)

15. Text of the letter by which Lord Simon was instituted master of the house of St Lazarus; it declares that provision and administration belong entirely to the bishop. (From the cartulary of the Church of Paris.)

16. Letters of the Bishop of Paris by which Sanson of Cristolio, a priest, was instituted master of the lepers of St Lazarus. (From the same cartulary.)

17. The establishment of the chapel of Blessed Bachina in the church of Chora, and of its chaplain, belongs to the lord bishop. (From the cartulary of the Church of Langres.)

[Col. 0913C] 18. Establishment of two chapels by the bishop, with all the rights of the parish church preserved. (From the cartulary of the Church of Langres.)

19. The chapel of Dry Rock is under the institution of the lord bishop; and homage is owed to the lord bishop for the presentation. (From the same cartulary.)

20. Letter concerning the altars founded in the Church of St Peter of Tournus, to be conferred by the chapter through the collation and grant of the lord bishop. (From the same cartulary.)

21. Letter of Innocent II concerning the presentation of the rector of the church of Grand-Château. (From the cartulary of the Church of Toulouse.)

22. Form of the second oath taken in chapter. (From the same codex, from the necrology of the Church of Chartres, and from another manuscript codex *On the Dignities of the Church of Chartres*.)

23. Oath taken by the count’s canon of Chartres. (From the same codex *On Dignities*, etc.)

[Col. 0917A] 24. Oath that every canon of Boulogne is required to take upon his first reception. (From the cartulary of the Church of Boulogne, communicated to me by D. Favier.)

25. Form of the oath that a canon who is newly received by proxy is required to take.

26. Oath that a chaplain appearing in person is required to take upon his first reception.

27. Oath that a chaplain acting by proxy is required to take. (From the same cartulary.)

28. Concerning the oath to be taken by those being released for clerical tonsure. (From the manuscript codex of the Church of Chartres, *On Oaths*.)

29. Oath that every abbot of the diocese of Thérouanne must render to the mother church. (From the cartulary of the Church of Thérouanne, communicated to me by D. Favier.)

30. Oath of a Cistercian abbot concerning the obedience and reverence established by the holy Fathers, which he is required to render to the bishop. [Col. 0917B] (From the papers of the Church of Paris.)

31. Oath of the abbot and convent of Blessed Mary of Cagia in the Diocese of Meaux concerning the obedience and reverence that they promised the bishop regarding the correction or reform of the said monastery. (From the cartulary of the Church of Meaux.)

32. Charter concerning the oath that the vicar of the abbot of Beaulieu owes to that abbot regarding the observance of the statutes. (From the cartulary of the monastery of Beaulieu.)

33. Oath that the *condonati* (“given”) brothers of the House of God and Almsgiving of Chartres are required to make in chapter upon their reception. (From the manuscript codex of the Church of Chartres, *On Oaths*.)

34. Excerpt from the oath sworn on the holy Gospels by the procurator of the Hermits of St Augustine of the Paris convent: the donation of the house called La Motte, situated near the bridge of Lagny, made to them, shall become void, invalid, and null if they fail in the work of piety [Col. 0917C] for which it was established. (From the charter of donation itself for that house, communicated to me by D. de Trechi, an exceptionally upright deputy substitute of the procurator general.)

35. Ancient charters concerning the offering of children by their parents to monasteries, in which mention is made of the oath that parents once took, namely, that their children, consecrated to God in monasteries, would observe the holy institutions. (From the cartulary of the monastery of Beaulieu.)

### ARTICLE THREE

That bishops and others may not disregard rightful constitutions and privileges properly granted to churches — how many evils arise from the failure to observe the statutes, according to which obedience alone may be demanded.

1. Letter of Paschal II to L., Bishop of Viviers, instructing him not to violate the rightful constitutions concerning the donation of the Church of St Andeolus made by that bishop to the brothers of St Rufus. (From the cartulary of the Church of St Rufus.)

2. Mandate of R., Bishop of Alba and legate of the Apostolic See, addressed to L., Bishop of Viviers, instructing him that the latter’s constitution concerning the donation should remain undisturbed. (From the same cartulary.)

3. Letter of Celestine III to the dean and chapter of Chartres, in which he declares that no one may violate privileges reasonably granted to churches—that is, properly and according to the canons, statutes, and liberties of the Church of Gaul. (From the manuscript codex on the privileges of the Church of Chartres.)

4. Charter concerning the church of Rignhago, in which it is declared, by order of Peter, Bishop of Rodez, that the rightful constitution concerning the donation of the church of Rignhago to the monks of Conques cannot be violated. (From the cartulary of the monastery of Conques.)

5. Letter . . . of the lord of Lisieux to Louis [Col. 0918A], King of the Franks, in which he declares how many evils arise from failure to observe the canons, and prescribes the form that the king may use, according to the statutes and rights of the Church of Gaul, in writing to Paul II. (From the papers of the distinguished Antonius Vyon, lord of Hérouval.)

6. Diplomas of Henry II, in which it is shown that apostolic letters, bulls, or provisions are neither approved nor received unless they agree with the canons and decrees of the Holy See, as well as with the privileges, rights, and liberties of the Church of Gaul. (From a copy of various diplomas of Henry II, etc., supplied to me by Charles Caesar Baudelot, an advocate at the Paris Senate and a most inquisitive investigator of beautiful and ancient things.)

### ARTICLE FOUR

Letters of the supreme pontiffs in which they declare that their statutes, authoritative letters, and privileges granted by them can never be set against the decrees of the canons and the rights of the churches; and councils in which these constitutions and privileges are revoked.

[Col. 0918B]

1. Letters of Urban II, together with the councils in which his privileges, extorted by fraudulent concealment against ecclesiastical rights, were rescinded, arranged in this order by Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, at Urban’s own command. (From the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble.)

2. Mandate of Paschal II by which the dispute concerning the parish of Salmorac between Guido, Bishop of Vienne, and Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble, debated for many years and in many councils, is settled, notwithstanding the aforesaid privileges. (From the cartulary of the Church of Vienne.)

3. Letter of Pope Callistus III to the Archbishop of Tours, in which he informs him that his statutes concerning the citation [Col. 0918C] of the procurator general of Charles, King of the Franks, since they were contrary to the rights and privileges of the Church of Gaul, must be considered to have no force or validity. (From the authentic instrument of the distinguished Antonius Vyon, lord of Hérouval.)

4. Letter of John, Archbishop of Tours, to William, Bishop of Nantes, concerning the execution of the aforesaid sentence by which the supreme pontiff revoked his own constitutions and ordinances, since they were contrary to the privileges of the Church of Gaul. (From the papers of the distinguished Antonius Vyon, lord of Hérouval.)

### ARTICLE FIVE

Sentences issued by supreme pontiffs, bishops, and kings, and by the court of the Parliament of Paris, against all violators of ecclesiastical statutes.

### I

Sentences pronounced by bishops and supreme pontiffs.

1. Sentence delivered by the bishops in the Council of Paris concerning the church of Orengi, which was adjudicated to the monks of Longpont against the usurpation of the monks of Gyvisi. (From the cartulary of the monastery of St Mary of Longpont in the Diocese of Paris.)

2. Sentence of Paschal II against sacrilegious usurpers of the property of a deceased bishop or of ecclesiastical rights. (From the manuscript codex of the privileges of the Church of Chartres.)

3. Sentence of Ivo of Chartres against extortionate provosts. (From the same codex.)

4. Sentence of Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, concerning the church of Hienville in the parish of Puteaux and the rights of that church, against the monks of the Greater Monastery and in favor of the monks of St Martin-des-Champs. (From the cartulary of St Martin-des-Champs.)

5. Excommunication imposed upon St Theobald, Archbishop of Vienne, and Isarnus, Bishop of Grenoble, on account of the unjust possession of the Church’s property. (From the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble.)

6. Excommunication imposed by Mainard, Archbishop of Sens, and Imbert, Bishop of Paris, on account of contempt for ecclesiastical authority; it ought to appear no less terrifying than an extraordinary absolution. (From the cartulary of the Church of Paris.)

7. Concerning the case between the monks of Resbac and the monks of the Church of St Faith of Conques, over the church of Colombier, debated for a long time in several councils and before the Archbishop of Lyon, legate of the Roman See, and finally decided in a synod against the monks of Resbac, who had seized the church of Colombier contrary to the canons and ecclesiastical statutes. (From the cartulary of the Church of Conques.)

8. Indulgence of Lucius III against priests who had concubines and were abusing the remedy of appeal contrary to the decrees of the canons and ecclesiastical statutes. (From the papers of the Church of Paris.)

[Col. 0919B] 9. Sentence of Lucius III against sacrilegious usurpers of ecclesiastical rights, from whom every remedy of appeal is removed. (From the manuscript codex of the privileges of the Church of Chartres.)

10. Judgments of Lucius III and Urban III against robbers who were abusing the remedy of appeal contrary to ecclesiastical statutes. (From the manuscript codex of the privileges of the Church of Chartres.)

11. Indulgence of Clement III against the Archbishop of Sens, who had violated ecclesiastical statutes. (From the papers of the Church of Paris.)

12. Sentence of excommunication issued by Celestine III against violators of the privileges and liberties of the Church of Chartres; he entrusts its execution to the archbishop . . . . . and the archdeacon of Sens. (From the manuscript codex of the privileges of the Church of Chartres.)

13. Sentence of the Archbishop of Sens against the Countess of Blois, confirmed by Celestine III, for the protection of the rights and liberties of the Church of Chartres. [Col. 0919C] (From the manuscript codex of the privileges of the Church of Chartres.)

### II

Royal diplomas, commands, or sentences for the best ecclesiastical discipline, against all violators of ecclesiastical statutes.

1. Command of Louis the Pious concerning the reform of the monks of the Church of St Denis, carried out in a synod. (From the cartulary of St Denis; the papers of the distinguished Antonius Vyon, lord of Hérouval, present it corrected, volume VII, *Councils*, latest edition, p. 1674.)

2. Concerning the command or sentence of Louis, son of Boso, confirming the lawful restoration, made in a synod, of Villeneuve to St Apollinaris. It had been taken away in contempt of all the statutes and rights of the churches. This is the charter in which Alexander, Archbishop of Vienne, and Isaac, Bishop of Grenoble, were approving parties. (From the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble.)

[Col. 0919D] 3. Command of Louis VI, surnamed the Fat, concerning the authority to pronounce a sentence of excommunication against those who refuse to admit, against free men, the testimony of ecclesiastical servants granted by royal authority. (From the lesser *Pastoral* of the Church of Blessed Mary of Paris.)

4. Command of Louis VI, surnamed the Fat, providing that the transgressor of the royal decree concerning the reception of the testimony of ecclesiastical servants shall be subject to excommunication. (From the cartulary of St Martin-des-Champs.)

5. Command of Louis VII, surnamed the Younger, confirming the sentence issued by the Bishop of Paris against those who violate the freedom of the house of a deceased bishop. (From the *Pastoral* of Blessed Mary of Paris.)

6. Constitutions of Charles VI, published by order of Charles VII against certain clerics who, abusing apostolic letters, were violating the rights of the Church of Gaul. (From the authentic instrument of the distinguished Antonius Vyon, lord of Hérouval.)

[Col. 0920A] 7. Several notable judgments of the court of the Parliament against the Cardinal Bishop of Constance, who, by rashly excommunicating certain persons and disregarding judgments that had been issued, had violated the statutes, rights, and liberties of the Church of Gaul; they were confirmed by Louis XI against every appeal. (From the original document belonging to the distinguished Antonius Vyon, lord of Hérouval.)

## CHAPTER THREE

## ON THE AUTHORITY OF BISHOPS AND ON THE OBEDIENCE OWED BY CLERICS AND MONKS ALIKE

### ARTICLE ONE

Public monuments concerning the obedience and reverence that clerics and regulars, as well as monks and abbots, owe to bishops, and which they solemnly promised in synods.

[Col. 0920B]

1. Charter of St Martin concerning the obedience that the regular canons promised to their bishop. (From the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble.)

2. Charter concerning the obedience and subjection that the monks of Beaulieu owe to Ivo, Bishop of Chartres, and to his successors. Ivo permitted them to build and consecrate the monastery only on this condition. (From the manuscript codex of the privileges of the Church of Chartres.)

3. Charter by which Radbod, Bishop of Noyon, grants the altar of Cappy to the Church of St Peter of Cluny. It declares the bishop’s authority over the monks who govern churches and over abbots. (From the cartulary of St Martin-des-Champs.)

4. Charter of St Donatus concerning the obedience that the regular canons of St Donatus are required to promise to Nantelmus, provost of the Church of Uzes, without prejudice to the privilege of the Apostolic See, and with the obedience, reverence, subjection, and power of the Bishop of Grenoble always preserved, both in spiritual and temporal matters. (From the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble.)

5. Charter of Chignin concerning the obedience that those who have renounced the world owe to bishops, as canons owe obedience to their own bishop. (From the cartulary of the Church of Grenoble.)

6. Charter concerning the obedience and fidelity which Theobald, canon of Saint Genevieve, promised to the bishop of Paris, in the presence of the most holy Gospels and on his priestly word, when he was presented to undertake the care of souls in the parish of Mont. (From the charters of the church of Paris.)

7. Concerning the canonical and due obedience which the abbess of the monastery of Faremoutiers promises to the bishop of Meaux, by whom she is blessed according to the statute of the synod of Soissons. (From an ancient charter of the monastery of Faremoutiers, which the most illustrious Joanna de Plas, abbess of this flourishing monastery, had copied by a learned man and sent to me. Her extraordinary piety and remarkable charity toward all the poor of the surrounding region are such that she is accustomed to be called the mother of the poor.) [Col. 0920D]

8. Concerning the canonical obedience and subjection which the brothers of the Holy Trinity, who are in the House of God, are bound to promise to the bishop of Meaux and his successors. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

9. A charter especially worthy of note concerning the authority and diligence of the archbishop of the church of Vienne in restoring the discipline of churches and monasteries; concerning the privilege granted by the Fathers of the Council of Vienne; concerning the canonical election of the provost; concerning certain warnings against simony; and concerning the observance of the statutes of the Fathers. (From the chartulary concerning the honors granted to Saint Julian in the county of Brioude.)

10. A charter by which Dalmatius, abbot, commends the monasteries to Bishop Stephen as their administrator and lord, so that the integrity of the rule may remain unimpaired. (From the same chartulary.)

[Col. 0921A] 11. Mandate of Pope Alexander III stating that, if the convent does not agree in the election of an abbot, it belongs to the bishop to confirm as abbot the man on whom the larger and sounder part has agreed. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

12. That, if a chapter disagrees among itself, the bishop may adjudicate the matter. (From the same chartulary.)

## ARTICLE TWO. Privileges granted to monasteries by the supreme pontiffs, with the canonical reverence always preserved that is owed to the bishop.

1. Privilege granted by Urban II to the monastery of Saint Nicholas, with the canonical reverence of the bishop of Angers preserved. (From the register of the county of Angers.)

2. Privilege granted by Urban II to the church of Saint Ruffus, with the canonical reverence of the bishop of Avignon preserved in all respects. (From the chartulary of the church of Saint Ruffus.)

[Col. 0921B] 3. Privilege of Pope Calixtus II concerning the obedience and reverence which all clerics and abbots are bound to show to the bishop, as members adhering to the head. (From the charters of the church of Paris and from the Lesser Pastoral.)

4. Privilege granted by Innocent III to the abbot of Saint Ruffus, with the authority of the Apostolic See preserved and the canonical right of the diocesan bishops maintained. (From the chartulary of the church of Saint Ruffus.)

## ARTICLE THREE. Donations made to churches and monasteries with the counsel and consent of the bishop, and with the reverence always preserved that is owed to the episcopal see.

1. The altar of the village called Orceacus, donated to the church of Blessed Mary of Longpont by Gaufridus, bishop of Paris, with all the reverence owed to him by ecclesiastical subjection preserved in every respect, and with all his rights preserved. (From the chartulary of Blessed Mary of Longpont.)

2. The altar situated in the village called Bonduflum, donated to the church of Blessed Mary of Longpont, with all the rights of the bishop preserved, as well as the obedience owed to him. (From the same chartulary.)

3. The church of Bains, donated to Saint Savior with the counsel and authority of Bishop Pontius. (From the chartulary of the monastery of Conques.)

4. The churches of Saint Faith of Castellet and Saint Victor, donated by Hugh, archbishop of Lyons, to the church of Saint Faith of Conques, with the obedience always preserved that must be shown to the bishop and the archpriests. (From the same chartulary.)

5. The church of the Blessed Virgin Mary founded within the walls of Besalú is donated to the church of Saint Ruffus with the counsel and consent of Lord Berengarius, prelate of Girona. (From the chartulary of the church of Saint Ruffus.)

6. The same church is restored and donated to the aforesaid [Col. 0921D] church of Saint Ruffus with the pontifical favor and canonical approval of the see of Girona. (From the same chartulary.)

7. The same donation is confirmed by Raimundus, bishop of Girona, with the reverence and obedience preserved that are owed to the episcopal see. (From the chartulary of Saint Ruffus.)

8. The church of Saint Andeolus is donated to the church of Saint Ruffus in a full synod, on this condition: that the prior may not be changed except with the counsel of the bishop of Viviers; and if any dispute should arise, it shall be resolved by the canonical judgment of that bishop and the common chapter. (From the same chartulary.)

9. Confirmation by the archbishop of Vienne of the donation to the church of Saint Ruffus of the churches of Saint Martin of Vienne, Saint Nicetius, and others, with every right, while preserving the obedience and reverence owed to the most holy mother, the episcopal church. (From the chartulary of the church of Vienne.)

10. Confirmation of the church of Tauliniacum, donated to the church of Saint Ruffus, with the reverence and obedience preserved that [Col. 0922A] are owed to the episcopal church. (From the chartulary of the church of Saint Ruffus.)

11. Confirmation of the same donation, with the episcopal right and census preserved. (From the same chartulary.)

12. The church of Ordinat is donated to the church of Saint Ruffus with the permission and grant of the bishop of Belley, but on this condition: that the prior promise canonical reverence and obedience to the bishop. (From the same chartulary.)

13. Authentic instrument concerning the settlement made with the prior of Saint Martin of Terra, called Aulnay, in which it is declared that the gift is valid in no respect unless it is confirmed by the authority of the bishop of Paris. (From the charters of the church of Paris.)

14. Indulgence of Lucius III providing that the fiefs of the bishop of Paris may not be pledged or sold without his consent. (From the same charters.)

15. Authentic instrument of William, archbishop of Sens, concerning the revenues of the deanery of Paris while it is vacant. From this it is evident that the bishop is the principal dispenser of the goods [Col. 0922B] of the church. (From the same charters.)

16. Confirmation by Clement III concerning the bishop’s right over the revenues of the deanery. (From the same charters.)

17. Letter stating that the master and brothers of Morment cannot remove any house from their control without the will of the bishop, who, according to the canons, is the first dispenser of the goods of churches. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

## ARTICLE FOUR. Letters concerning the non-election of an abbot without the permission of the bishop, who also has the right to confirm and bless the person elected.

1. Letter concerning the abbey resigned by the abbot of Molesme into the hands of the lord bishop, as is customary; and stating that permission to elect another abbot must be requested from that same bishop. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

[Col. 0922C] 2. Petition made to the bishop concerning the election of an abbot in the monastery of Saint Peter of Melun. (From the same chartulary.)

3. Petition made to the bishop that the person elected abbot of Saint Michael of Tonnerre be confirmed by him. (From the same chartulary.)

4. Petition made to the bishop concerning the abbot of the monastery of Molesme. (From the same chartulary.)

5. Petition made to the bishop concerning the abbot of Saint Stephen of Dijon. (From the same chartulary.)

6. Petition of the people of Cagia for the confirmation and blessing of the person elected. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

7. How the people of Cagia committed themselves to the will of the bishop concerning the provision of an abbot for their monastery. (From the same chartulary.)

8. Petition of the monks concerning the blessing by the bishop of Meaux of the abbot of Cagia; to that bishop they declare their due obedience and subjection. (From the same chartulary.)

[Col. 0922D] 9. Concerning the blessing of the abbot of Saint Faron by the bishop of Meaux. (From the same chartulary.)

10. Concerning the abbot of Saint Faron after the resignation of another. (From the same chartulary.)

11. Petition made to the bishop concerning the election of an abbot of the monastery of Reome. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

12. Petition made to the bishop that the election of the prior of Val Caulum be confirmed by him. (From the same chartulary.)

13. Petition made to the bishop concerning the abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Melun. (From the same chartulary.)

14. Petition of the chapter of Saint Machutus of Bar-sur-Aube made to the bishop, asking him to pardon it for having elected a dean without his permission. (From the same chartulary.)

15. How the convent of Old Nealpha announced to the chapter the death of its abbot and requested permission to elect another. (From the chartulary of the church of Chartres.)

[Col. 0923A] 16. Procuration from Old Nealpha to present to the chapter the person elected for that place, so that he might be confirmed and receive the gift of blessing from the bishop. (From the same chartulary.)

17. Election of the abbot of Old Nealpha, permission to elect having first been requested, as is customary; and stating that he is to be confirmed by the chapter of Chartres and receive the gift of blessing from the bishop. (From the same chartulary.)

18. Grant made by William, bishop of Langres, to the great claustral prior and to all and each of the priors and other monks of the monastery of Molesme, permitting them to elect an abbot according to the canonical sanctions. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

## ARTICLE FIVE. Concerning the right of institution, deposition, correction, reform, visitation, and procuration which bishops possess over monasteries, notwithstanding any privilege, whether already obtained or yet to be obtained.

[Col. 0923B]

1. Union of the hospital of Brochon with the church or monastery of Saint Stephen of Dijon; and the right of institution, deposition, correction, reform, visitation, and procuration which the bishop possesses over that house, which, under a religious vow, must renounce every privilege, whether already obtained or yet to be obtained. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

2. Charter concerning the right of institution, deposition, procuration, correction, and so forth, which the bishop of Avranches fully retained over the monastery of Saint Michael, its abbot, and twelve canons. (From the Pontifical Book of the church of Avranches, preserved in the library of Saint Victor.)

3. Charter of settlement between the bishop of Autun and the Cluniac monks, in which the jurisdiction of the bishop of Autun over the priests of the Cluniac churches is declared. [Col. 0923C] (From the archive of the priory of Saint Peter of Paredo.)

4. Charter by which Galo, bishop of Paris, grants the monastery of Saint Eligius, after the monks had been expelled because of the disgraceful depravity of their lives, to the church of Blessed Peter of Fosses. From this it is clear that the bishop possesses the right of deposition, correction, reform, and so forth, over monasteries. (From the Lesser Pastoral of the church of Blessed Mary of Paris.)

5. Stephen, bishop of Paris, grants the same monastery to the church of Saint Peter of Fosses at the petition of Pope Innocent and so forth, with his right preserved in all respects. (From the same Pastoral.)

6. Settlement made by Hugh, bishop of Auxerre, and Gaufridus of Châlons, at the command of Innocent II, between the church of Meaux and the monastery of Faremoutiers; in it the rights of the bishop over the priest of the monastery of Faremoutiers and several privileges of the abbess are observed. (From the authentic charters of the monastery of Faremoutiers, which the most illustrious abbess Joanna de Plas had copied.)

[Col. 0923D] 7. The aforesaid settlement is confirmed by Manasses, bishop of Meaux. (From the same authentic charters.)

8. The same settlement is confirmed by Innocent II and Lucius II. (From the same authentic charters.)

9. The first institution of the succentor, in which mention is made of the right of institution and deposition that the bishop possesses over the succentor just as over the cantor. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

10. Authentic instrument concerning the settlement made between Bishop Maurice and the abbot of Coulombs concerning the church of Saint Germanus at Lée, in which several matters concerning the bishop’s right over the abbot and monastery are noted. (From the charters of the church of Paris.)

11. Concerning the right of procuration which the bishop possesses over the house of Saint Celinia, subject, however, to the evangelical saying: “Whoever does not work, let him not eat.” (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

12. Concerning the bishop’s procuration in the church of Saint Exuperius of Corbeil. (From the charters of the church of Paris.)

[Col. 0924A] 13. Authentic instrument of the chapter of Paris concerning the same procuration.

14. Privilege concerning the archdeacon’s procuration and the bishop’s jurisdiction in the church of Sées. (From the same charters.)

15. Letter of Innocent III concerning the bishop’s right of procuration, which cannot be extinguished by prescription. (From the same charters.)

16. Letter of the chapter of Tonnerre stating that it is bound to swear canonical subjection and obedience to the bishops of Langres upon their taking office, and that it can neither obtain privileges nor use those already obtained. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

17. Confirmation of the statute of the entire chapter, requiring the prior of the Friars Preachers to swear to the chapter of Chartres that neither personally nor through another may he obtain a privilege or indulgence against the rights and liberties of the church, nor use privileges already obtained or yet to be obtained. (From the chartulary of the church of Chartres.)

[Col. 0924B] 18. Whoever is prior of the Friars Preachers must swear in the chapter that he will observe the church’s interdicts and will not be able to use privileges against the said church.

19. Letter of the prior of the Friars Preachers in France stating that the prior and brothers of the Dominican convent of Chartres are bound to observe the interdict; and confirming what had been done by them. (From the same chartulary.)

20. Letter concerning the jurisdiction which the lord bishop of Langres possesses over the hospital of Morment, in its head, members, and persons residing there; and stating that the hospital house may not obtain any indulgences or privileges, or in any way use those already obtained. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

21. Letter concerning the jurisdiction and correction which the lord bishop possesses over the monastery of Pelungero. (From the same chartulary.)

22. Letter concerning the subjection and reverence of the hospital of Norges toward the bishop of Langres; and stating that it is not permitted to obtain any exemption or to use one already obtained. (From the same chartulary.)

23. That the prior of the house of Saint Lazarus of Meaux is bound to promise canonical obedience to that bishop and his successors; and concerning the right of correction, visitation, and so forth, which the bishop possesses over the same house. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

24. Union of the hospital of Chilicasti with the church or monastery of Saint Stephen of Dijon; and the right of institution, deposition, and correction which the bishop possesses over it because of the care of souls, for which he must render an account to God. Hence the hospital house, like a monastery, is bound under a religious vow to renounce every privilege, whether already obtained or yet to be obtained. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

25. Letter concerning the jurisdiction of the bishop of Langres, to whom belong the institution, deposition, and correction of the prior of the monastery of Morment; so that the aforesaid monastery [Col. 0924D] must renounce every privilege or grant, whether already bestowed or yet to be bestowed. (From the same chartulary.)

## ARTICLE SIX. Letters declaring that, for proceedings of correction, expenses must be made by the bishops from the goods of the monastery, and that no one is permitted to defend monks against the authority of the bishops.

1. Letter stating that, in promoting the proceedings for the correction of the monastery of Bézu, the bishop is to pay and administer expenses from the goods of that monastery. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

2. Royal letter ordering the duke of Burgundy not to support or defend the abbot and convent of Bézu against the bishop. (From the same chartulary.)

[Col. 0925A] 3. Charter concerning Nojaret, by which the monks are bound to pay to the bishop the tithe that had been unjustly given to them; and in which Guilisius of Veracen promises that he will never be a helper of the monks against the bishop. (From the chartulary of the church of Grenoble.)

## ARTICLE SEVEN. Letters showing how an abbot’s appeal to the Apostolic See against the authority of the bishop is rendered void.

1. Royal letter addressed to the supreme pontiff concerning the temporal justice and jurisdiction of the monastery and town of Bézu, which belongs directly to the bishop of Langres; hence the abbot’s appeal to the Apostolic See is wholly void. (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

2. Letter of the abbot and convent, in which, among other things, they declare that they cannot appeal anywhere except to the bishop’s court. (From the same chartulary.)

[Col. 0925B] 3. Royal letter concerning the foregoing. (From the same chartulary.)

## ARTICLE EIGHT. Judgments issued in support of the bishop’s authority, and letters declaring their execution.

1. Sentence issued by Innocent II in favor of the bishop of Meaux against the clerics and laypeople of the village of Rebais, with the avenue of appeal removed. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

2. Letter of Hugh, archbishop of Sens, concerning the obedience and subjection that the abbot of the monastery of Rebais promised to the bishop of Meaux after the sentence issued by Alexander III. (From the same chartulary.)

3. Letter of Baldwin, bishop of Noyon. (Concerning the same matter.)

4. Letter of Peter, bishop, and Hugh, dean of Paris, concerning the execution of the sentence of Innocent III [Col. 0925C] in support of the bishop’s authority over the abbot and monastery of Rebais.

5. Sentence issued by Innocent II against the priest of Jort, who, after hearing the bishop’s order, broke out into an appeal. (From the charters of the church of Meaux.)

6. Sentence issued by Innocent II in support of the bishop’s authority against the abbess, clergy, and people of Jort, with the avenue of appeal removed. (From the same chartulary.)

7. Letter of William, archbishop of Reims, concerning the honor and reverence, and concerning every right, which Eustachia, abbess of the church of Jort, promised always to show to the bishop of Meaux. (From the same chartulary.)

8. Privilege of Eugenius III against the archdeacons of Paris, in support of the bishop’s authority. (From the charters of the church of Paris.)

9. Privilege of Adrian IV against the archdeacons, containing nothing other than what is contained in the preceding privilege of Eugenius.

10. Privilege of Alexander III in the same form against the archdeacons; and providing that the archdeacons are not to burden the priests subject to them with excessive frequency of lodging demands. (From the same charters.)

11. Privilege of Clement III against the archdeacons, containing the same provisions as Alexander’s privilege. (From the same charters.)

12. Privilege of Clement III against the archdeacons [Col. 0926A] who impede the ordinations of churches, and in support of the bishop’s authority. (From the same charters.)

13. Execution of the sentence issued by Innocent III in support of the bishop of Meaux against the dean and archdeacons, and settlement made in accordance with that sentence. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

14. Definitive sentence issued against the church of Cala by the bishops of Amiens and Tournai and other judges, in support of the bishop’s authority. (From the same charters.)

15. Sentence issued by Celestine III in support of the bishop’s authority in the church of Cala, and indeed against a privilege previously granted by him himself. (From the charters of the church of Paris.)

16. Sentence issued by William, canon of Meaux, and Peter, canon of Jort, in support of the bishop’s authority against the abbess and convent of Jort. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

17. Sentence issued by Peter, bishop of Thérouanne and dean of Saint-Omer, concerning the observance by the chapter of the bishop’s sentences. (From the same chartulary.)

18. Letter of Rainaud of Saint Faron, Albert of Blessed Mary at Caen, and John of Fontenay abbots. (Concerning the same matter.)

19. Letter of William, archbishop of Sens. (Concerning the same matter.)

20. Sentence issued by Peter, bishop of Meaux, against the chapter concerning his jurisdiction over the priest of Givry. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

21. Sentence issued by Gregory IX against the master and brothers of the leper house of Saint Lazarus of Meaux, who refused to show obedience and reverence to their bishop. (From the same chartulary.)

22. Concerning the same matter.

23. Sentence issued in defense of episcopal rights against the abbess and convent of the monastery of Faremoutiers of the Order of Saint Benedict, and against the clergy and people [Col. 0926C] of the same place in the diocese of Meaux. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

24. Letters of Innocent IV confirming the same sentence. (From the same chartulary.)

25. Sentence issued concerning the election of the master of the house of Saint Lazarus near Paris, which belongs to the bishop, as does its confirmation. (From the charters of the church of Paris.)

26. Sentence of excommunication issued by the bishop of Meaux against the master of the Great House of God of Meaux and the sisters who refused the bishop’s visitation, which they finally accepted after first taking an oath. (From the chartulary of the church of Meaux.)

27. The jurisdiction of the bishop of Meaux over the archdeacons, confirmed by the metropolitan authority of Philip, archbishop of Sens, and ratified by letters of Philip and John, kings of France. (From the register of the Chamber of Accounts, which contains the letters of John, king of France, for the years 1351, 1352, [Col. 0926D] and 1353.)

28. Sentence of the Court of Requests against the abbot of Saint Michael of Tonnerre and the priors dependent upon it, concerning the visitation. [Note: [Col. 0925D] Thus it is read in the chartulary.] (From the chartulary of the church of Langres.)

## ARTICLE NINE.

Conclusion against privileges that exempt monks not only from the vigilance of bishops but also from royal authority.

[Col. 0927]

# THE PENITENTIAL OF THE MOST HOLY AND MOST LEARNED THEODORE, ARCHBISHOP OF CANTERBURY [Note: [Col. 0927C] See the fuller observations and notes at the end of the volume.] (C)*

## CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the church, or concerning what takes place inside it.

[Col. 0927A]

[Note: [Col. 0927C] Theodore, chapter 68, from volume IX of the *Spicilegium* of the Reverend and Most Illustrious Lord Luc d’Achery; the Capitularies of Charlemagne, book V, chapter 49; Burchard, book III, chapter 38; Ivo, part III, chapter 43; Gratian, *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter “The Church,” from the Council of Agrippina.] In a church where the corpses of unbelievers have been buried, it is not permitted to celebrate the sacrifice [Alternative: to sanctify]; but, if it seems suitable for consecration, it should be taken down and rebuilt after its timbers have been scraped or washed. If it was previously consecrated, it is permitted to celebrate Masses in it if religious persons have been buried there. [Note: [Col. 0927C] Burchard, book III, chapter 13; Ivo, part III, chapter 15; *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter 27, from the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.] But if a pagan has been buried there, it is better to cleanse it in this way and cast him out. We must not make steps before the altar where the relics of the saints are to be venerated. [Note: [Col. 0927C] Here chapter 25 begins in the chapters of Theodore edited in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*.] If it can be done [Alternative adds: *fieri*, “be done”], let a candle burn there every night; but if the poverty of the place does not permit this, it does them no harm. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Another version in Theodore, chapter 27.] Let the incense of the Lord be burned on the feasts of the saints out of reverence for the day, because they, like lilies, gave forth the fragrance of sweetness and sprinkled the Lord’s Church, just as incense is first sprinkled beside the altar [Alternative: “the incense sprinkles the church”]. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Charlemagne’s Capitularies, book V, chapter 49; chapter 136 of Herard of Tours; Burchard, book VIII, chapter 87; Ivo, part VII, chapter 109, from the Council of Mainz, chapters 9 and 18.] A layman ought not to recite a reading in churches or say “Alleluia,” but only psalms or responsories without “Alleluia.” Those who live in them may sprinkle holy water whenever they wish. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Council of Nantes, chapter 4; Regino, book I, *On Church Discipline*, chapter 105; Burchard, book XVIII, in the heading.] And when someone consecrates water, let him first offer a prayer.

## CHAPTER TWO. Concerning the three principal orders of the Church

A bishop may confirm in the open country if necessary; likewise a priest may perform the rite if the deacon or the priest himself [Alternative adds: “or”] holds the chalice and offering in his hands. [Note: [Col. 0927D] Burchard, book IV, chapter 68, from the Council of Reims, chapter 10.] A bishop ought not compel an abbot to go to a synod unless there is also some reasonable [Col. 0927C] cause. The bishop shall adjudicate the cases of the poor up to fifty solidi; the king, if the amount is greater.

[Note: [Col. 0928C] Council of Orléans III, chapter 13; Orléans IV, chapter 30.] A bishop and an abbot may possess a wicked enslaved person if he has no price with which to redeem himself. A bishop may release a vow if he wishes. [Note: [Col. 0928C] Theodore, chapter 49, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*.] A priest alone may celebrate Masses, bless the people on Good Friday, and sanctify the cross. [Note: [Col. 0928C] Chapter 24.] A priest is not compelled to pay tithes. [Note: [Col. 0928C] Chapter 120; Charlemagne’s Capitularies, book V, chapter 51.] A priest may not expose the sin of a bishop, because he is above him. [Note: [Col. 0928C] Ivo, part II, chapter 44, from the decretals of Pope Fabian, chapter 10.] The sacrifice must not be received from the hand of a priest who cannot complete the offerings or readings according to the rite. If a priest sings responsories at Mass, or any other chant, he must not remove his vestment, but, when reading the Gospel, he must place it over his shoulders. [Note: [Col. 0928C] Another version in Theodore, chapter 110.] If a fornicating priest baptizes after this has become known, those whom he baptizes are to be baptized again. [Note: [Col. 0928C] Charlemagne’s Capitularies, book VI, chapter 93; Burchard, book IV, chapter 100, from the sayings of Saint Isidore, bishop; Ivo, part I, chapter 268, from the Council held at Compiègne, chapter 5.] If an ordained priest discovers that he has not been baptized, he is to be baptized and ordained again, as are all those whom he previously baptized. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Theodore, chapter 5, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*.]

Deacons are not to break the holy bread with the Greeks, nor say the Collect, “The Lord be with you,” or the dismissal. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Theodore, chapter 43; Regino, book I, *On Church Discipline*, chapter 295, from the Roman *Penitential*; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 110.] A deacon may not give penance to a layman; bishops or priests must give it. Deacons may baptize and bless food and drink, but may not distribute the bread. Monks and clerics may likewise bless food.

## CHAPTER THREE. Concerning the ordination of various persons

[Note: [Col. 0928D] Theodore, chapter 1, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*; Burchard, book I, chapter 225; Ivo, part V, chapter 338, from the sayings of Theodore the archbishop.] At the ordination of a bishop, Mass must be sung by the bishop who ordains him. At the ordination of a priest or deacon, the bishop ought to celebrate Masses, just as the Greeks customarily do at the election of an abbot or abbess. At the ordination of a monk, however, the abbot must celebrate Masses and complete three prayers over his head; and for seven days he must veil his head with his cowl, [Col. 0928C] and on the seventh day the abbot must remove his veil. Just as a priest customarily removes it from infants at baptism, so the abbot must remove it from the monk, because, according to the judgment of the Fathers, this is a second baptism, in which all sins are forgiven. A priest may consecrate an abbess with the celebration of Mass. [Note: [Col. 0928D] Theodore, chapter 3, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*; Roman Order, from Theodore, title “The Ordination of an Abbot.”]

At the ordination of an abbot, [Col. 0929A] the bishop must celebrate Mass and bless him with bowed head, in the presence of two or three witnesses from among his brothers, and give him a staff and sandals. Holy nuns, for their part, must always consecrate the basilicas entrusted to them. The Greeks bless a widow and a virgin together, and always have both consecrated. They elect an abbot. The Romans do not veil a widow. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Theodore, chapter 20, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*.] According to the Greeks, a priest may consecrate a virgin with the sacred veil, reconcile a penitent, prepare exorcised oil, and provide chrism to the sick if necessary. According to the Romans, this is not permitted except to a bishop alone.

## CHAPTER FOUR. Concerning the confirmation of baptism

In baptism, the marriages of women are not dissolved, [Col. 0929B] for children who are born before baptism become children likewise afterward. But if the woman is not considered a wife [Alternative adds: “therefore”], the children previously born are not considered children, nor can they call one another brothers or become heirs together. If a pagan has given alms [Alternative adds: “and practiced abstinence, and so forth”] and performed other good works which we cannot enumerate, did he lose them in baptism? He does not lose any good, but washes away evil. Pope Innocent, citing the case of a catechumen as an example, affirmed this. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Pope Innocent I, letter 2, chapter 6; letter 4, chapter 2; letter 22, chapter 2; letter 23, chapter 6.] Gregory of Nazianzus says that the second baptism is that of tears. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 39.] We do not consider anyone perfect in baptism. We do not dispute the bishop’s confirmation; [Note: [Col. 0929D] Theodore, chapter 4.] nevertheless, chrism was established at the Council of Nicaea. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Burchard, book IV, chapter 94, from the Council of Beauvais, chapter 8.] It is not absurd to place chrismated cloths again upon another baptized person. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Burchard, book IV, chapter 26, from the Council of Mainz, chapter 2; Ivo, part I, chapter 218, from the decretals of Pope Hyginus, chapter 10, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, in the catechism.] At the catechumenate, baptism, and confirmation, there may be one sponsor if necessary; this is not, however, the custom. For each rite, they receive one sponsor each. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Burchard, book IV, chapter 26, from the Council of Mainz, chapter 2; Ivo, part I, chapter 220, *On Consecration*, distinction 4, chapter “In Baptism.”] It is not permitted to sponsor another person who has not been baptized. A man may sponsor a woman at baptism, and likewise a woman may sponsor a man. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Theodore, chapter 86, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*; Charlemagne’s Capitularies, book VI, chapter 92; Burchard, book IV, chapter 95.] The baptized may not eat with catechumens [Alternative adds: “nor give them a kiss”], and all the more not with pagans.

## CHAPTER FIVE. Concerning the Mass for the deceased and the dead

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Theodore, chapter 90, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*.] According to the Roman Church, it is customary to carry deceased monks or religious persons into the church, anoint their breasts with chrism, and celebrate Masses for them there; then to carry them with chanting to the burial places; [Col. 0930A] and, when they have been placed in the tombs, a prayer is poured out for them. Finally, they are covered with earth or stone. Mass is to be celebrated for them on the first, third, and ninth days, and also on the thirtieth day. Thereafter, after a year, the practice may be continued if they wish. [Note: [Col. 0929D] Theodore, chapter 19, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*.]

For deceased laypeople, however, Masses are celebrated three times a year: on the third, ninth, and thirtieth days, because the Lord rose on the third day, gave up his spirit at the ninth hour, and the children of Israel mourned Moses for thirty days. At the Mass of monks, it is also customary to recite their names every week. For a deceased monk, Mass is to be celebrated on the day of his burial and on the third day; afterward, as much as the abbot wishes. For a good layman, on the third or seventh day [Alternative adds: “after the fast”; for a penitent, on the thirtieth day]; and his relatives ought to fast for seven days and offer an offering at the [Col. 0930B] altar, as is read in Jesus son of Sirach; and for Saul the children of Israel fasted, afterward for as long as the priests wish.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Theodore, chapter 69, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*.] Many say that it is not permitted to celebrate Masses for children before the age of seven. But it is permitted. [Note: [Col. 0930D] *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, chapter 7; Theodore, chapter 56, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*; response 3 of Gregory III, letter 1, to Boniface; Burchard, book III, chapter 65; Ivo, part III, chapter 67, from the sayings of Dionysius the Areopagite.] Dionysius the Areopagite says that whoever offers Masses for an evil person commits blasphemy against God; [Note: [Col. 0930D] Saint Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 10, and *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 4; Amalarius, book IV, chapter 42; *On Consecration*, distinction 1, “It Has Been Seen,” from the Second Council of Chalon-sur-Saône, chapter 39.] nevertheless Augustine says that this should be done for all Christians, because it benefits either them, or those who offer, or those who request it. Nor is it lawful for a priest or deacon to celebrate Mass if he is not permitted, or does not wish, to receive communion.

## CHAPTER SIX. Concerning abbots, monks, and monasteries
[Note: [Col. 0930D] Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 86, from the Council of Mainz, chapter 18.] An abbot may, out of humility and with the bishop’s permission, relinquish his position; nevertheless, the brothers should choose an abbot for themselves from among their own number, if they have one; otherwise, from outsiders. [Note: [Col. 0930D] Theodore, chapter 46, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*. *Penitential*, with the corresponding chapter.] Nor ought the bishop forcibly to retain the abbot in his position. The community ought to choose an abbot for itself after his death, or while he is alive, if he departs or sins. He himself may appoint no one from among his relatives, nor from among outsiders, nor appoint another abbot without the consent of the brothers. [Note: [Col. 0930D] See the letter of Pope Agatho to Æthelred, king of the Mercians, and to Theodore, archbishop. Theodore, chapter 47, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 87, from the Council of Mainz, chapter 10.] But if the abbot has sinned, the bishop may not take away the monastery’s property, even though the abbot has sinned; rather, he should send him to another monastery under the authority of another abbot. It is not permitted to an abbot or to a bishop to transfer the land of one church to another, even though both are under his authority. [Note: [Col. 0930D] Theodore, chapter 48. See the *Penitential*, together with the corresponding chapters of Theodore, collated in the *Spicilegium*. Burchard, Book III, chapter 28.] If he wishes to transfer the land of a church, he should do so with the counsel of the bishop and of his brothers [Another reading: “with the consent of both”], [Another reading adds: “if anyone wishes to move his monastery to another place”], and he should leave in the former place a presbyter for the church’s ministries. Men are not permitted to have women as nuns, nor women to have men; nevertheless, let us not abolish what is customary in this land. [Note: [Col. 0931D] Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 42; Ivo, Part VIII, chapter 32, Cause 20, Question 4, from the sayings of Basil, *To the Monk*.] A monk may not make a vow without the abbot’s consent; otherwise, it must be annulled. If the abbot has a monk whom the community has chosen to be ordained to the priestly rank, he must not abandon his former manner of life. But if afterward he is found to be proud or idle [Another reading: “vicious”], and seeks his former life in a higher rank, let him be deposed and placed in the lowest position, where he shall make amends through satisfaction. The reception of the sick into the monastery is within the monastery’s authority and freedom. It is likewise within the monastery’s freedom to wash the feet of laypeople [Note: [Col. 0931D] Theodore, chapter 38, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*]; except that they are not compelled to do so on Maundy Thursday. [Note: [Col. 0931D] Council of Toledo XVII, chapter 3; Council of Aachen under Louis IV, chapter 23.] Nor is it within the monastery’s freedom to judge the penance of laypeople [Note: [Col. 0931D] See Theodore, chapter 43, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*], since that properly belongs to clerics.

## CHAPTER VII. On the conduct of women in church or in a monastery

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 84, from the Council of Rheims, in the presence of Emperor Louis, chapter 5.] Women should not veil the altar with the corporal, nor place offerings upon the altar, nor place the chalice there; nor should they stand among the ordained in church, nor sit among priests at a feast. A woman is not permitted to impose penance on anyone, because according to the canon this is permitted to no one except priests. Women may receive the sacrifice under a black veil [Another reading adds: “as Basil judged”].

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Theodore, chapter 28, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*.] According to the Greeks, a woman may make offerings; according to the Romans, she may not.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the customs of the Greeks and Romans

On Sunday the Greeks and Romans neither sail nor ride; they do not bake bread, nor travel by cart, except only to church; nor do they bathe themselves. The Greeks do not write in public; nevertheless, when necessity requires, they write privately at home. Greeks and Romans provide clothing for their servants [Note: [Col. 0931D] Chapter 8, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 81; Regino, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 372, from the capitularies of Charlemagne], and they work even on the Lord’s Day. The monks of the Greeks do not have servants; those of the Romans do. On the day before the Nativity of the Lord, after the ninth hour, when Mass has been completed—that is, the vigil of the Lord—the Romans eat; but the Greeks dine after Vespers and Mass have been celebrated. [Note: [Col. 0931D] Theodore, chapter 23, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*.]

Concerning the plague of mortality, the Greeks and Romans say [Col. 0932A] that the sick themselves ought to be visited [Another reading adds: “and other sick people”], as the Lord commands (Matthew 25:43). The Greeks do not give the flesh of animals that have died of themselves to pigs; nevertheless, it is permitted to take their hides for footwear, as well as their wool and horns, provided they are not used for anything holy [Another reading: “or hides and footwear are permitted, and wool and horns may be taken, but not for anything holy”]. A head-washing [Another reading adds: “may be”] is permitted on Sunday, and feet may be washed in lye [Note: [Col. 0931D] Another reading: “in Theodore, chapter 29”]; but this washing of the feet is not customary among the Romans.

## CHAPTER IX. On communion with the Scots and Britons who are not united with the Catholic Church in the celebration of Easter and in tonsure

[Note: [Col. 0931D] See Bede in the notes and selected chapters of the canons of the Irish, from Book I of the collection, chapter 6, edited by the Reverend and distinguished Dom Luc d’Achery in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*.] Those who have been ordained bishops among the Scots or Britons, who are not united with the Catholic Church in the celebration of Easter or in tonsure, should again be confirmed by the laying on of hands by a Catholic bishop. [Another reading adds: “Likewise, the churches ordained by those bishops should be sprinkled with exorcised water and confirmed with some form of collection.”] We do not have permission to give them chrism or the Eucharist when they ask for it unless they have first confessed that they wish to be with us in the unity of the Church. Whoever likewise comes from their people, or anyone at all who has doubts about his baptism, should be baptized.

## CHAPTER X. On those afflicted by the devil and on those who kill themselves

If a man is afflicted by the devil and knows nothing except to run about everywhere, and kills himself for whatever reason [Col. 0932C], [Note: [Col. 0932D] Halitgar, Book IV, chapter 6; Rabanus, *Penitential*, Book III, chapter 6; Regino, Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 92, from the Council of Braga, chapter 15; see also the Council of Braga I, chapter 16; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 130; Book VII, chapter 384], it is beneficial to pray for him if he had previously been a religious person. But if he did so out of despair, or from some fear, or for unknown reasons, let us leave the judgment to God, and let us not dare to pray for him. For one who kills himself of his own will, [Note: [Col. 0932D] Rabanus, *Penitential*, Book III, chapter 6] it is not permitted to celebrate Masses, but only to pray and give alms. [Note: [Col. 0932D] Theodore, chapter 64, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*.] If someone has fallen from his senses through a sudden temptation, or has killed himself through lack of self-control, some people celebrate Masses for him.

## CHAPTER XI. On questions concerning marriage

[Note: [Col. 0932D] Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*, chapter 10; Regino, Book I, chapters 328–329; Burchard, Book V, chapter 22, from the Council of Elvira, chapter 3.] Married people should abstain from sexual intercourse for three nights before receiving communion. A man should abstain from his wife for forty days before Easter and until the octave of Easter; hence the Apostle says, “that you may devote yourselves to prayer” (1 Corinthians 7:5).

[Col. 0932D] [Note: [Col. 0932D] *Penitential of Egbert, Archbishop of York*.] A woman who has conceived should abstain from her husband for three months, before childbirth and after the period of purification—that is, for forty days and nights—[Note: [Col. 0932D] Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 141, from Theodore; Ivo, Part XV, chapters 150–151] whether she has given birth to a male or a female. A woman is also permitted to receive communion at any time before childbirth, when she is due to give birth. [Note: [Col. 0933D] Theodore, chapter 116, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; Council of Compiègne, chapter 8; *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, Book V, chapter 19; Council of Tribur in the time of Pope Formosus, chapter 41.]

If someone’s wife has committed fornication, it is permitted to divorce her and take another; that is, if a man has divorced his wife because of fornication, and she was his first wife, he may lawfully take another wife. But if she wishes to repent of her sins after two years, she may take another husband. [Note: [Col. 0933D] Basil, in his letter to Amphilochius, chapter 9; Council of Compiègne, chapter 16.] A woman is not permitted to divorce her husband, even if he is a fornicator [Another reading adds: “unless perhaps for the sake of entering a monastery”]. Basil judged this to be so.

A lawful marriage may not be dissolved without the consent of both parties, [Note: [Col. 0933D] *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, Book VI, chapter 206] though one may give the other permission to enter God’s service in a monastery [Note: [Col. 0933D] Theodore, chapter 13, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; *Excerpta of Egbert of York*, chapter 118, from the African canons; Council of Compiègne, chapter 13; Regino, Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 107, from the sayings of Jerome] and to marry, if according to the Greeks the person was in a first marriage; nevertheless, this is not canonical. But if the person was in a second marriage, it is not permitted [Col. 0933B] a third time [Note: [Col. 0933D] *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, Book VI, chapter 316] while the husband or wife is alive.

If a husband makes himself a slave through theft or fornication, or through any other sin, the woman, if she had not previously been married, has the power to take another husband after a year. But a deacon’s widow is not permitted [Another reading: “But a bigamist is not permitted…”]. After a woman’s death, a man may [Note: [Col. 0933D] *Excerpta of Egbert of York*, chapter 116; the Synod said this] take another wife after a month. After a man’s death, a woman may take another husband after a year.

If a woman is an adulteress and her husband does not wish to live with her, then, if she wishes to enter a monastery, she should receive a quarter of her inheritance; if she does not wish to do so, she should receive nothing. Whatever woman has committed adultery is within her husband’s power, if he wishes to be reconciled with the adulterous woman. If she has been reconciled to the clergy, her punishment is of no benefit; it pertains to her own husband.

If a husband and wife are married, and he wishes to separate while she does not, or if he becomes ill [Note: [Col. 0933D] Theodore, chapter 76, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; *Capitularies*, Book VI, chapter 206] or she becomes ill, nevertheless they must separate only with the consent of both.

A woman [Note: [Col. 0933D] *Roman Penitential*, title 8] who has made a vow after her husband’s death should not take another husband. If, after his death, she violates the vow by taking another, [Note: [Col. 0933D] Distinction 24, chapter “If a Husband”] and, having married him, is moved to repentance and wishes to fulfill her vows, it is within her husband’s power to decide whether she fulfills them or not.

Thus Theodore granted one permission [Note: [Col. 0933D] Theodore, chapter 12, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*. See the notes] to a woman who, after confessing her vow, married that man eleven years later. If someone in secular clothing makes a vow without the bishop’s consent, [Note: [Col. 0933D] *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, Book V, chapter 50] the bishop himself has the power to change his judgment, if he wishes.

A lawful marriage is permitted equally by day and by night, as it is written: “The day is yours, and the night is yours” (Psalm 73:16). [Note: [Col. 0933D] Theodore, chapter 13, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; Burchard, Book IX, chapter 59, from the decree of Pope Eutychian.]

If someone divorces a pagan wife after baptism, it is within his power to keep her or not. Likewise, if one of them is baptized and the other is a pagan, as the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 0934D] Theodore, chapter 45, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; Burchard, Book IX, chapter 60]: “But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart” (1 Corinthians 7:15). Therefore, if someone’s wife is an unbeliever and a pagan and cannot be converted, she should be changed [Another reading: “dismissed”].

If a woman departs from her husband, despising him, and refuses to return and be reconciled to her husband, he may, after five years [Note: [Col. 0934D] *Excerpta of Egbert of York*, chapter 122, the canon “It Says”; Regino, Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 124; Burchard, Book IX, chapter 54], with the bishop’s consent, take another wife. If she has been carried away by force into captivity and cannot be ransomed, he may take another wife after a year. Likewise, if her husband has been carried away into captivity, she should wait five years; and the same applies conversely if such things happen to a woman.

If, therefore, he has taken another wife, [Note: [Col. 0934D] *Excerpta of Egbert of York*, chapter 125, the canon “It Says] he should receive the first wife when she returns from captivity and dismiss the later one. Likewise, she should act as we said above if such things happen. If an enemy carries off someone’s wife and he cannot recover her, he may take another; it is better to do this than to commit fornication. If that wife later returns to him, he should not receive her [Another reading adds: “from him”] if he has another wife; rather, she should take another husband, if she previously had one. The same judgment [Another reading adds: “stands”] applies to overseas slaves.

[Note: [Col. 0934D] Theodore, chapter 84, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; Rabanus, in his letter to Bishop Humbert; Regino, Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 200, from a letter of Rabanus.] According to the Greeks, it is permitted to marry within the third degree of blood relationship, as it is written in the Law; according to the Romans, within the fifth. Nevertheless, they do not dissolve a marriage within the third degree once it has taken place. Therefore, they should be joined in the fifth generation. If they are found to be related in the fourth degree, they are not separated. Yet within the third degree of relationship it is not permitted to take another man’s wife after his death.

[Col. 0934C] [Note: [Col. 0934D] Rabanus in his letter to Bishop Humbert; Regino, Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 200, from a letter of Rabanus; Cause 35, Question 3, from Fabian.] A man may equally enter into marriage with women related to him by blood and with his wife’s blood relatives after his wife’s death.
