Two brothers may also have two sisters; [Note: [Col. 0934D] Theodore, chapter 75. See the *Penitential*, together with the corresponding chapters and canons, collated] and a father and son may have a mother and daughter.

A husband who has slept with his wife should wash himself before entering the church. [Note: [Col. 0934D] Theodore, chapter [number omitted], vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*.] A husband ought not to see his wife naked.

If someone has an unlawful wedding or marriage, nevertheless it is permitted to eat the food they have, because the Prophet said: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness.” [Note: [Col. 0934D] Council of Verberie, chapter 17; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 29; Regino, Book II, chapters 32 and 242, from Rabanus, Book VI, chapter 55; Burchard, Book IX, chapters 40–41; Ivo, Part VIII, chapter 76.]

If a man and a woman have joined themselves in marriage, and afterward the woman says of her husband that she cannot [Another reading adds: “marry him”], if someone can prove that this is true, she should take another husband. [Note: [Col. 0934D] Theodore, chapter 102; *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, Book VI, chapter 91; Burchard, Book IX, chapter 40; Ivo, Part VII, chapter 40.]

Parents may not give a betrothed girl to another man unless she wholly resists; nevertheless, she may go to a monastery if she wishes. But if the betrothed girl does not wish to live with the man to whom she is betrothed, [Note: [Col. 0935C] *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, Book VI, chapter 25] the money he gave should be returned to him, with a third part added; but if she refuses, she should forfeit the money he gave for her.

A girl of thirteen years has control of her own body. [Note: [Col. 0935C] Theodore, chapters 86, 116, and 118, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; Council of Toledo X, chapter 6; *Excerpta of Egbert of York*, chapters 90–91; Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapters 46 and 115; Regino, Book II, chapter 177; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 18.] A boy remains under his father’s authority until the age of fifteen. Then he may make himself a monk. A girl of sixteen or seventeen remains under her parents’ authority. After this age, however, a father may not give his daughter in marriage against her will.

## CHAPTER XII. On male and female slaves

[Col. 0935B] A father, compelled by necessity, has the power to hand his son over into servitude for seven years; afterward he has no right to hand him over without the son’s consent. A person of thirteen years may make himself a slave. A slave is not permitted to take away money that he himself has acquired. [Note: [Col. 0935C] Theodore, chapter 71, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; *Excerpta of Egbert of York*, chapter 124, the canon “It Says”; Burchard, Book IX, chapter 19.]

If a master has joined a male and female slave in marriage, then, after a male or female slave has been freed, if the woman who remains in servitude cannot be ransomed, the freed man may marry a freeborn woman. [Note: [Col. 0935C] From the Council of Mâcon, *Capitularies*, Book VI, chapter 94.]

If a free man has taken a female slave in marriage, he may not have permission to divorce her if they were previously joined with the consent of both. If a free person purchases a pregnant free woman, the child born from her is free. [Note: [Col. 0935C] Another reading: Theodore, chapter 74, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*.] Whoever frees a pregnant female slave, the child she bears is a slave.

## CHAPTER XIII. On various questions

[Col. 0935C]

[Note: [Col. 0935C] Theodore, chapter 109, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; *Capitularies*, Book VI, chapter 184.] There are three customary fasts in the year [Another reading: “for the people”]; in addition, there are forty days before the Nativity of the Lord and forty days after Pentecost [Addition: “nights”].

Laypeople should not delay fulfilling their promise, because death does not delay. [Note: [Col. 0936C] Theodore, chapter 39, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*.] A servant of God is in no way permitted to fight, even though many servants of God may advise it. [Note: [Col. 0936C] Chapter 42. See the notes.]

An infant may be given to God in a monastery in place of another infant, even though someone had vowed another; nevertheless, it is better to fulfill the vow. Likewise, animals [Note: [Col. 0936C] Theodore, chapter 22, vol. IX of the *Spicilegium*; Burchard, Book VIII, chapter 6] may be exchanged at equal value if necessary.

If a king possesses another king’s land, he may donate it for the sake of his soul. Anything found on the road should be taken up; if its owner is discovered, it should be returned to him. [Note: [Col. 0936C] See Augustine, sermon *On the Words of the Apostle*, chapter 6.]

The church’s tribute should be according to the custom of the province, so that the poor alone do not suffer coercion in tithes or in other matters. It is not lawful to give tithes except to the poor and to strangers.

Out of reverence for regeneration, one should pray in white garments at Pentecost; on the fiftieth day one prays. Prayer may be offered under a veil when necessity compels it. Whoever fasts for a dead person helps himself. As for the dead, knowledge belongs to God alone. [Note: [Col. 0936C] Burchard, Book XVIII, chapter 20; Ivo, Part XV, chapter 42; from the Council of Mainz, chapter 20.]

The sick are permitted to take food and drink at any hour, whenever they desire or are able, provided they can do so at a suitable time.

## CHAPTER XIV. On reconciliation

The Romans reconcile a person inside the apse; the Greeks do not wish this. The reconciliation of penitents on Maundy Thursday belongs only to the bishop, and it is completed [Note: [Col. 0936C] Halitgar, preface to the *Roman Penitential*; Regino, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 296; *Constitutions of Edmund, Archbishop of Canterbury*, chapter 12].

But if it is difficult for the bishop, he may, out of necessity, grant authority to a presbyter to complete it. [Col. 0936C] There is no reconciliation in this province, because there is no public penance either.

[Col. 0935]

# THE CAPITULA OF THEODORE (C)*

## FIRST CHAPTER. The manner in which the one-year penance, during which one must fast on bread and water, should be observed

[Col. 0935D]

[Note: [Col. 0935D] Ancient *Penitential* of Angers, chapter “On the Remedy of the Penitent.”] The one-year penance during which one must fast on bread and water should be as follows each week. For three days—that is, Thursday and Saturday—one should abstain from wine, mead, mulled honey-drink, and beer; from meat and fat; from cheese and eggs; and from every fatty fish. One should eat small fish, if one can obtain them. If one cannot, one should eat only one kind of fish, as well as legumes, vegetables, and fruit, if one wishes, and drink beer.

On Sundays and on the Nativity of the Lord, for those four days; on Epiphany, for one day; at Easter, until the eighth day; at the Ascension of the Lord and at Pentecost, for four days; [Note: [Col. 0936D] Council of Tribur under Pope Formosus, chapters 56–58] and on the feast of Saint John the Baptist, of Saint Mary, of the twelve holy Apostles, of Saint Michael, of Saint Remigius, of All Saints, of Saint Martin, and of that saint whose feast is celebrated in that bishopric,

[Col. 0937A] let him show charity with the other Christians on the days mentioned above—that is, let him use the same food and drink as they do—yet let him always beware of drunkenness and gluttony in all things.

This is the second year after the year during which one fasts on bread and water. It is to be fasted after that year, and it is also to be imposed on those who kill ecclesiastical persons, who habitually commit the crime of sodomy, who habitually sin against nature, who deliberately commit murders in churches, who burn churches, who commit adulteries in churches, and who have perpetrated other such acts.

The penance of this year should be as follows: on two days—that is, Monday and Wednesday—he should fast until evening each week; then he should refresh himself with dry food, that is, bread and dry but cooked legumes, or fruit, or raw vegetables. He should choose one of these three and eat it, and drink beer, but moderately. On the third day, Friday, he should observe a fast on bread and water.

He should also fast for three Lents: one before the Nativity of the Lord, the second before Easter, and the third before the Mass of Saint John. During these three Lents, he should fast two days each week until the ninth hour and eat dry food, as noted above; on Friday he should fast on bread and water; and on Sundays, on the Nativity of the Lord, for those four days, on Epiphany for one day, at Easter until the seventh day, at the Ascension of the Lord, at the Mass of Saint John the Baptist, [Col. 0937C] and on the feasts of Saint Mary, of the twelve Apostles, of Saint Michael, of Saint Remigius, of All Saints, of Saint Martin, and of that saint whose feast is celebrated in that bishopric.

On the days mentioned above he should show charity with the other Christians, but should always beware of drunkenness and the distension of the belly in all things.

## CHAPTER II. On those who cannot fast and fulfill what is written in the *Penitential*

[Note: [Col. 0937D] Bede’s canons on remedies for sins, chapter 14, “On Various Causes”; Regino, Book II, chapter 444.] Whoever can fast and fulfill what is written in the *Penitential* should do so and give thanks to God. But whoever cannot, to him we offer this counsel through God’s mercy, so that neither he nor anyone else need despair or perish.

## CHAPTER III. On the redemption of the year during which one must fast on bread and water

[Col. 0937D]

On the first day during which he ought to fast on bread and water, he should chant fifty psalms in the church, if possible, on bended knees. If this cannot be done, let him do the same in a suitable place; let him feed one poor person; and on that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, let him eat whatever he wishes.

But if he is such a person that he cannot remain on his knees for so long, let him do the following in the church, if possible: standing attentively in one place, let him chant seventy psalms [Col. 0938A] in order, feed a poor person, and on that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, eat whatever he wishes.

Whoever bends his knees one hundred times in church—that is, if he asks forgiveness one hundred times—should do so in church, if possible; this is most just. If it cannot be done, let him do it privately in a suitable place. If he does this, he may on that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, eat whatever he likes.

Whoever does not know the psalms may redeem one day of penance on bread and water by three denarii if he is rich, or by one denarius if he is poor. On that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, he may eat whatever he likes. Some say alternatively that twenty prostrations are equivalent to one day.

## CHAPTER IV. On the redemption of one week during which one must fast on bread and water

[Col. 0938B]

[Note: [Col. 0937D] Regino, Book II, chapter 440; Burchard, Book IX, chapter 18.] For one week during which he ought to fast on bread and water, he should chant three hundred psalms on bended knees in the church. If he cannot do this, he should chant three psalters attentively in the church or in a suitable place; and after chanting the psalms, except for wine, meat, and fat, he may eat whatever he wishes.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] Regino, Book II, chapter 439; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 19.] For one month during which he ought to do penance on bread and water, he should chant twelve hundred psalms on bended knees. Each day, if he wishes and does not want to abstain, he may refresh himself at the sixth hour, except that on Wednesday and Friday he should fast until the ninth hour. He should abstain from meat, fat, and wine for the entire month. After he has chanted the psalms mentioned above, he may eat other food. The whole year should be redeemed in this manner.

## CHAPTER V. On those who cannot fast and do not know how they can redeem the one-year penance, which must be observed on bread and water

[Col. 0938C]

[Note: [Col. 0938D] Regino, Book II, chapter 441; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 20.] Whoever does not know the psalms and cannot fast should, for one year during which he ought to fast on bread and water, give twenty-two [twenty-six] solidi to the poor as alms, and should fast every Friday on bread and water, as well as during three Lents: forty days before Easter, forty days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist—and if anything remains before the feast, he should complete it afterward—and forty days before the Nativity of the Lord.

During these three Lents, whatever is prepared for his mouth as food or drink, of whatever kind it may be, he should estimate how much it is worth or might be worth; half of that value he should distribute as alms to the poor. He should pray and entreat the Lord continually that his prayer and his alms may be acceptable to God.

## CHAPTER VI. On the redemption of one year during which one ought to do penance on bread and water

[Note: [Col. 0938D] *Roman Penitential*, title 9, chapter 28; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 21; Ivo, Part XV, chapter 201; from Theodore.] Likewise, whoever cannot fast and observe what is written in the *Penitential* should do what Pope Saint Boniface established for one day of penance on bread and water.

Let him ask a presbyter to sing Mass for him [Col. 0939A], unless there are capital crimes, which, once confessed, must first be washed away with tears. Then he himself should be present and listen. Devoutly, with his own hands, let him offer bread and wine into the priest’s hands; let him answer attentively, as far as he understands, the priest’s greetings and exhortations; and let him humbly beseech the Lord that God Almighty may graciously deign, through his angel, to receive the offering that he and the presbyter have offered to God for him and for his sins.

On that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, he may eat whatever he wishes, and in this way redeem the remaining days of the year.

## CHAPTER VII. On those who cannot fast but have the means by which they can redeem their penance

[Col. 0939B] [Note: [Col. 0939D] *Roman Penitential*, title 9, chapter 29; Halitgar; Regino, Book II, chapter 438; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 22; Ivo, Part XV, chapter 202.] If someone is perhaps unable to fast but has the means by which he can redeem his penance, then, if he is rich, he should give twenty solidi for seven weeks. If he does not have enough to give that much, he should give ten solidi. If he is extremely poor, he should give three solidi.

Let no one be troubled that we have ordered twenty solidi or less to be given, because it is easier for a rich person to give twenty solidi than for a poor person to give three. But let each person consider to whom he ought to give it: whether for the redemption of captives, upon the holy altar, to servants of God, or to the poor as alms.

## CHAPTER VIII. On those who cannot fulfill what is written in the *Penitential*

[Note: [Col. 0939D] *Roman Penitential*, title 9, chapter 30; Regino, Book II, chapter 445; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 23; Ivo, Part XV, chapter 203.] Those who cannot perform penance in the manner described above [Col. 0939C] should act as follows. If someone ought to fast for three continuous years and cannot fast, he can redeem it in this way.

In the first year he should distribute twenty [six] solidi as alms. In the second year he should distribute twenty solidi, and in the third year eighteen solidi—that is, sixty-four solidi. But powerful people ought to give more, because from the one to whom more is entrusted, more will be demanded. Those who commit unlawful acts should also abstain from lawful things, and they ought to afflict the body with fasts, vigils, and frequent prayers. For cheerful flesh draws one toward guilt, but afflicted flesh brings one back to pardon.

## CHAPTER IX. On those who cannot fast and have no means by which they can redeem their penance

Whoever cannot fast and has no means by which to redeem his penance [Col. 0939D], if he knows the psalms, should, for one day during which he ought to fast on bread and water, chant “Blessed are the undefiled” (*Beati immaculati*) through “To the Lord when I was afflicted” (*Ad Dominum cum tribularer*) three times, and “Have mercy on me, O God” (*Miserere mei, Deus*) six times; and he should prostrate himself on the ground seventy times, chanting the *Our Father* at each genuflection.

But whoever does not know the psalms should, for one day during which he ought to fast on bread and water, prostrate himself on the ground one hundred times, chanting the *Our Father* at each genuflection.

## CHAPTER X. On the redemption of seven years

[Col. 0940A]

Again, in another manner, twelve three-day periods, each completed with three psalters and three hundred prostrations for each psalter, release one year of penance. Twenty-four two-day periods, likewise with completed psalters and three hundred prostrations for each psalter, release two years. [Note: [Col. 0939D] These statements are cited by no ancient ecclesiastical author, but are attributed to Theodore.] Seventy-five psalms with three hundred prostrations release a two-day period. One hundred psalms with three hundred prostrations release a three-day period. One hundred and twenty special Masses, each with three psalters and three hundred prostrations, release one year. One hundred solidi given as alms release one year.

## CHAPTER XI. On penitents

[Col. 0940B]

[Note: [Col. 0940D] Regino, Book I, chapter 291, from the Council of Agde; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 36.] At the beginning of the fast, let all public penitents come in the city before the doors of the church barefoot and clothed in sackcloth, and present themselves to their bishop.

At the beginning of Lent, let all penitents who are undertaking or have undertaken public penance present themselves before the doors of the church to the bishop, clothed in sackcloth, with their faces prostrate on the ground, proclaiming by their clothing and countenance that they are guilty.

The archpresbyters of the parishes—that is, the priests of the penitents—must be present there. They should carefully examine the penitents’ conduct and impose penance according to the degree of their guilt and according to the prescribed stages.

Afterward, let the bishop introduce them into the church and, prostrate on the ground with all the clergy, chant the seven penitential psalms with tears [Col. 0940C] for their absolution. Then, rising from prayer, let him impose hands upon them, as the canons command; let him sprinkle blessed water over them, having first cast ashes upon them. Then let him cover their heads with sackcloth and, with groaning and frequent sighs, declare to them that, just as Adam was cast out of paradise, so they too are cast out of the church because of their sins.

After this, let him order the ministers to drive them outside the church door. The clergy, however, should accompany them with the responsory: “In the sweat of your face,” etc., so that, seeing the holy Church shaken and moved by their crimes, they may not make light of penance. At the Lord’s sacred Supper, however, they should again be presented to the church by their priests, with lights.

## CHAPTER XII. On the warning concerning the principal vices and their varieties

[Col. 0940D]

[Note: [Col. 0940D] Regino, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 300; capitulary of Theodulf, chapter 31; Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 6.] Now I will explain to you the eight principal sins. If you feel that you have been struck, touched, or wounded by them, take care not to conceal it from me: pride, vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. If you recognize yourself as guilty of these, accept penance. For all vices arise from them. [Note: [Col. 0940D] See Saint Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXXI, chapter 17.]

From pride, which is the beginning of every sin [Col. 0941A] and the queen of all evils, arise disobedience, presumption, obstinacy, quarrels, heresies, and arrogance.

From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing at one’s neighbor’s misfortunes, and distress at his prosperity.

From vainglory arise boasting, arrogance, indignation, discord, desire for empty glory, and hypocrisy.

From anger arise quarrels, swelling of the mind, insults, shouting, indignation, presumption, blasphemies, bloodshed, murders, desire for vengeance, and remembrance of injuries.

From sadness arise malice, resentment of spirit, faintheartedness, bitterness, despair, torpor, wandering of the mind, and often even the greatest delight in the present life.

From avarice arise envy, thefts, robbery, murders, lies, perjuries, plunder, restlessness, violence, unjust judgments, [Col. 0941B] contempt for truth, forgetfulness of future blessedness, and hardness of heart.

From gluttony spread foolish joy, buffoonery, frivolity, empty talk, bodily impurity, instability of mind, drunkenness, lust, and dullness of perception.

From lust are generated blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, precipitous conduct of the eyes or of the whole body, immoderate self-love, hatred of God’s commandments, attachment to the present age, and dread and despair concerning the future.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the virtues by which these same vices can be overcome, and on the conclusion of penance
Therefore, if you have been proud until now, humble yourself in the sight of God. If you have loved empty glory, consider whether, for the sake of passing praise, you may lose your eternal reward [Col. 0941C]. If the rust of envy has consumed you until now—which is the greatest sin and detestable above all, because the envious person is compared with the devil, who envied the first human being what he himself had lost through his own fault—do penance, and count the progress of others as your own. If sadness overcomes you, meditate on patience and steadfastness. If the disease of avarice weighs upon you, consider that it is the root of all evils and is compared with idolatry; therefore you must be generous. If anger troubles you—which rests in the bosom of fools—you must rule your spirit, and drive it away from you through peace of mind. If gluttony of the belly draws you toward devouring, pursue sobriety. If lust does so, vow chastity.

After he had confessed these deeds, the priest should then say [Col. 0941D]:

“Do you acknowledge that you are guilty of all your sins which, after baptism, you remember having committed, knowingly or unknowingly, in word, deed, or thought, against the commandment of God?”

**Response:** “I do.”

**Question:** “Do you promise to amend your past faults and renounce all the devices of the devil?”

**Response:** “I promise.”

**Question:** “Do you hold the faith you have confessed, and the sins you have confessed to God and to his priest, so that your sins may be forgiven? Do you believe this?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

**Question:** “Are you willing to amend what you have done against the commandments of God?”

**Response:** “I am.”

[Col. 0942A] **Question:** “Since you have confessed these things, do you wish to receive penance, to observe it faithfully, to renounce all the devices of the devil, and to believe in the holy Trinity?”

**Response:** “I do.”

Then let the penitent prostrate himself on the ground and say with tears:

“Both in these and in whatever other vices human frailty can commit against the Lord and its Creator—whether by thinking, speaking, acting, taking pleasure, or desiring—I acknowledge and confess that I have sinned in all things and am guilty in the sight of God above all human beings. I humbly beseech you also, priest of God, to intercede for me and my sins with the Lord and our Creator, so that I may deserve to obtain pardon and forgiveness for these and all my crimes [Col. 0942B].”

## PRAYER

Then the priest should say:

“May Christ, the Son of God, have mercy on you. May God grant you to do true penance, to have right faith, sure hope, perfect charity, true humility and wisdom, sobriety and endurance, a good end, and good perseverance. May God forgive you all your past, present, and future sins [Note: [Col. 0941D] See Regino, in the same place; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 7]. May the Holy Spirit enlighten you, direct your understanding, save your soul, inspire holy thoughts in you, and lead you to eternal life.”

Then the priest should prostrate himself on the ground with the penitent and chant these psalms:

“Have mercy on me, O God,” up to “blot out all my iniquities.”

“Bless the Lord, O my soul,” up to “it shall be renewed.”

“Save your servant, O Lord.”

“May he send you help from the sanctuary.”

“May the Lord guard you from every evil,” etc.

## PRAYER

“May Christ, the Son of the living God, cause you to persevere in good works throughout all the days of your life and lead you into eternal life. Amen.”

## PRAYER

“O God, whose forgiveness no one fails to need, remember your servant, who has been stripped bare by the slippery frailty of the earthly body. We ask you: grant pardon to the one who confesses; spare the suppliant, so that the one accused by his own sins may be saved through your mercy.”

## PRAYER

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God [Col. 0942D], who through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, have deigned to heal our wounds, we humbly beg and ask you to incline the ear of your compassion to our prayers. You also forgive all crimes and pardon every sin. Grant this servant of yours, O Lord, forgiveness for his sins, joy for his sorrow, and life for his death; and, trusting in your mercy, may he deserve to attain eternal life.”

## PRAYER

“Almighty and merciful God, who have placed the forgiveness of sins in the confession of crime, come to the aid of the fallen and have mercy on the one who confesses, so that the one whom the chain of offenses binds may be released by the greatness of your compassion.”

## PRAYER

“Almighty and everlasting God, in your mercy release the sins of this servant of yours, N., who confesses, so that the guilt of conscience may not harm him more toward punishment than the forgiveness of your compassion toward pardon.”

## PRAYER

“I beseech, O Lord, the majesty of your clemency and mercy: deign to grant your servant N., who confesses his sins and crimes, due release and pardon, and forgive the guilt of his former offenses. You who brought back the lost sheep upon your shoulders, who were appeased by the prayers and confession of the tax collector, deign also, O Lord, to be appeased toward this servant of yours. Look favorably upon him in his prayers, so that you may remain appeasable toward him in his confession. May his tears and petition swiftly obtain your perpetual clemency, and, restored to the holy altars, may he again be devoted to eternal hope and heavenly glory. You who live and reign, etc.”

## PRAYER

“May almighty God be your helper and protector, and grant forgiveness for your past, present, and [Note: [Col. 0943D] Regino, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 300; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 17] future sins.”

## CHAPTER XIV. That no bishop or priest should receive another’s penitent without letters from his bishop

The greatest care must be taken, and every precaution must be provided, lest any of our brothers and fellow bishops, or even priests, in another’s city or diocese receive a penitent, or one placed under the hand [Col. 0943C] of a priest, or one who says that he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or priest to whose parish he belongs.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning those who eat animals torn apart by beasts or strangled by snares

[Note: [Col. 0943D] Gregory III, *Judgments*, chapter 29; Bede’s canons, *On Various Matters*, chapter 14. Ancient Roman Penitential copied by Halitgar, chapter 10; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 85; Ivo, part XV, chapter 97, from the Penitential of Theodore.]

Animals that have been torn apart by wolves or dogs must not be eaten; nor should a raven or a stag be eaten if found dead, unless it is first killed by a human being while still alive; but they should be given to pigs and dogs. Birds and other animals, if strangled in nets, must not be eaten, nor if a hawk has crushed them, nor if they are found dead in this condition, because in the Acts of the Apostles abstinence is commanded from fornication, blood, what has been strangled, and idolatry.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning bees, if they have killed human beings

[Col. 0943D]

[Note: [Col. 0943D] Burchard, book XIX, chapter 86; Ivo, part XIV, chapter 98, from the Penitential of Theodore.]

If bees kill a human being, they too must be hastily killed, but the honey may be eaten.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning pigs and hens, if they eat human blood

[Note: [Col. 0943D] Burchard, book XIX, chapter 88; Ivo, part XV, chapter 99.]

If pigs or hens eat human blood, they must immediately be killed and thrown away, while the rest of the meat may be eaten. If the killing is delayed, they must not be eaten. But if they have torn apart the corpses of the dead, they must be [macerentur: literally, “macerated”; the precise practical sense is uncertain], and after a year’s interval they may be eaten. If pigs kill a human being, they must immediately be killed and buried.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning those who have eaten carrion or unclean meat

[Note: [Col. 0944D] Theodore, chapter 83; Bede’s canons, *On Various Matters*, chapter 14; Regino, book II, chapter 399; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 88; Ivo, part XV, chapter 100, from the Penitential of Theodore.]

Whoever eats unclean meat, carrion, or meat torn apart by beasts shall do penance for forty days. If it happens through the necessity of hunger, the penance is much lighter.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning those who are polluted by blood or some other unclean thing

[Col. 0944B] [Note: [Col. 0944D] Burchard, book XIX, chapter 90; Ivo, part XV, chapter 102.]

Whoever is polluted by blood or by any unclean thing: if he eats it unknowingly, it is a light matter. But if he knows, let him do penance according to the degree of the pollution.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning those who eat or drink something touched or contaminated by unclean animals

[Note: [Col. 0944D] Bede’s canons for remedies for sins, chapter 14, *On Various Matters*.]

Whoever knowingly eats or drinks something contaminated by a domestic animal, that is, a dog, etc., shall chant one hundred psalms. If he does not know, let him fast for two days; or, if he wishes to redeem it, let him chant fifty psalms. Whoever gives someone a liquid in which a dead mouse or weasel has been found shall do penance for seven days if he is a layman. If it happens in a monastery, let him chant three hundred psalms. Whoever later learns that he drank such a beverage shall chant one hundred and fifty psalms. If someone unknowingly eats something half-cooked, let him do penance for three days or chant the Psalter; if knowingly, let him do penance for seven days. For a small theft, let him do penance for twenty days. A ten-year-old child who commits a theft shall do penance for seven days. If someone dips his hand into liquid food with an unsuitable hand, let him be cleansed by one hundred strokes. If a dead mouse or weasel is found in flour, dry food, porridge, or curdled milk, everything around it shall be thrown out; what remains may be eaten.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning those who conceal their sins for a long time

[Note: [Col. 0944D] Regino, book II, chapter 136; Burchard, book IX, chapter 68.]

It must be understood that the longer someone persists in sins by his actions, the more penance he must perform.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning those who strike someone in anger

[Col. 0944D]

[Note: [Col. 0944D] Regino, book II, chapter 435.]

If someone strikes another person in anger and sheds blood, let him do penance for twenty days if he is a layman, and thirty if he is a cleric. Those who hold an ecclesiastical rank must suffer more: a deacon six months, a priest one year, and a bishop two years and six months.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Second Council of Braga, chapter 16; Halitgar, book IV, chapter 6; Regino, from the Council of Braga, chapter 15; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 130.]

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning those who have mutilated limbs

[Col. 0945A]

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Regino, book II, chapter 54, from a Penitential.]

Whoever, in a quarrel, renders a person crippled or deformed by a blow shall pay the physician’s expenses [Note: [Col. 0945D] “Let him pay the physicians’ expenses, and restore the price of the injury and his labor until he is healed, and let him do penance for half a year, etc.”], and do penance for half a year. If he has nothing with which to pay, let him do penance for one year. If a layman sheds blood by deceit, let him repay the injured person as much as he has harmed him. If he has nothing with which to repay him, let him serve in the work of his neighbor for as long as that man is ill. Afterwards let him do penance for forty days on bread and water.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The same matter

Whoever strikes his neighbor and does not injure him shall do penance for three days on bread and water. If he is a cleric, for one year or half a year. If someone deliberately cuts off any limb of another, let him do penance for three years on bread and water. Children striking one another shall do penance for three days; adolescents, however, for twenty days.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning those who rise to strike someone, wishing to kill him, but are unable to do so

Whoever rises to strike a person, wishing to kill him, shall do penance for three weeks. If he is a cleric, for six months. If he wounds him, for forty days. If a cleric wounds another cleric, for a full year; he must also pay money according to the degree of the wound he inflicted.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning those who inflict death upon themselves

It has been decreed that whoever voluntarily brings death upon himself by a weapon, poison, falling, hanging, [Col. 0945C] or by any other means shall not be commemorated in the offering, nor shall his corpse be brought to burial with psalms. Many usurp this right for themselves through ignorance; it has likewise been decreed concerning those who are punished for their crimes. Whoever, of his own will, throws himself into water, ties a rope around his neck, casts himself from a tree, strikes himself with a weapon, or gives himself over to any voluntary death—his offering shall not be accepted.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That menstruating women should not make offerings

[Note: [Col. 0945D] See the Penitential of Theodore, chapter “On Questions Concerning Marriage.”]

Women during menstruation should not make offerings, whether nuns or laywomen; if they presume to do so, let them do penance for three weeks.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning women who enter the church before the cleansing of their blood, and those who marry during these days

[Col. 0945D]

[Note: [Col. 0945D] See the notes on this chapter.]

A woman who enters the church before the purification of her blood after childbirth: if she has borne a male child, thirty-three days; if a female, fifty-six. If anyone presumes to enter the church before the appointed time, let her do penance on bread and water for as many days as she should have remained absent from the church. Whoever has intercourse with her during these days shall do penance for ten days on bread and water.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning those who lustfully insult a girl or woman

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Regino, book II, chapter 251; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 42.]

If someone indecently handles a girl’s or woman’s breast or private parts, let him do penance for five days if he is a cleric, and three days if a layman. A monk or priest suspended from divine ministry, if he does anything of this kind, shall do penance for twenty days. For it is written: “Neither touch nor insult the shameful parts of women.”

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning those who bathe with women in a bathhouse

[Col. 0946B]

[Note: [Col. 0946D] Roman Penitential, title 3, chapter 28; Burchard, book XVI, chapter 138; Ivo, part XV, chapter 148.]

If anyone presumes to bathe with women in a bathhouse, let him do penance for three days, and let him not presume to do so again.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That no one other than a bishop or priest should presume to impose penance or hear confession

[Note: [Col. 0946D] Halitgar, preface to the Penitential; Regino, book I, chapter 296; Burchard, book XIX, chapters 153–154.]

Just as no one except bishops or priests, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted, should offer the sacrifice, so no others should usurp judgment over penitents. But if necessity arises and no priest is present, a deacon may receive a penitent for holy communion.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The times during which married people must abstain

[Col. 0946C]

[Note: [Col. 0946D] Regino, book I, chapter 328, from the Council of Elvira; Burchard, chapter 19, chapter 155. See the chapter of Theodore’s Penitential, *On Questions Concerning Marriage*, and the notes.]

During the three Lents of the year, on Sunday, and on Wednesday and Friday, married people must abstain; nor should they have intercourse on those days while the wife is pregnant—that is, from the day when the child first moves in the womb until childbirth, and after childbirth for thirty-three days if the child is male, but fifty-six if female.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the woman who voluntarily kills her child

[Note: [Col. 0946D] Regino, book I, chapter 300; book II, chapters 66–67.]

If a mother voluntarily kills her child, let her do penance for fifteen [ten] years, and let her never change this except on Sunday. But if a poor woman does this because of the difficulty of raising the child, let her do penance for six years.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning those who do not honor their parents

[Col. 0946D] [Note: [Col. 0946D] Roman Penitential, title 4, chapters 11–12.]

If anyone dishonors his father or mother, let him do penance for three years. If he raises his hand against them or strikes them, let him do penance for seven years.

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning those who marry on Sunday

[Note: [Col. 0946D] Council held at Theodonis Villa, canon 4.]

If anyone marries on Sunday, let him seek pardon from the Lord and do penance for four days. If it pleases the princes and their other faithful men, let us ask that it be approved and subscribed. And it was approved and subscribed both by the prince and by all the others.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the man who kills a priest

[Note: [Col. 0947D] Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 24; Regino, book XX, chapter 43; Burchard, book VI, chapter 7.]

Whoever kills a priest shall be assigned twelve years of penance according to the canons, even if he denies it. If he is a free man, let him fast for seventy days. If he is a slave, let him purify himself over twelve burning plowshares. Once convicted of the offense, let him lack the military belt until the end of his life and remain without hope of marriage.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The same matter

[Col. 0947B] [Note: [Col. 0947D] Council of Worms, chapter 26; Council of Tribur, chapter 5; Regino, book II, chapter 42; Burchard, book VI, chapter 8.]

Whoever voluntarily kills a priest shall not eat meat or drink wine, and shall fast until evening throughout all the days of his life, except on feast days. He shall not take up weapons or mount a horse. For five years he may enter the church, but he shall not yet receive communion, remaining among the hearers. When the course of the twelfth year has ended, permission to receive communion shall be granted him, and the restriction on riding shall be remitted. In the remaining observances, however, he shall continue for three days each week, so that he may deserve to be cleansed more fully.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. That priests should not be appointed to or received by churches without the consent of bishops

[Note: [Col. 0947D] Third Council of Tours, chapter 15; Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 12; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 19; Regino, book I, chapter 338.]

Whoever obtains a church by payment must be completely deposed, since he is known to hold it contrary to the discipline of ecclesiastical rule. Whoever expels another priest legitimately ordained to a church by means of money and claims the church entirely for himself commits a vice that has spread widely and must be corrected with the utmost diligence. Likewise, clerics and laypeople must be forbidden to presume to give any church to a priest without the permission and consent of his bishop.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. By how many witnesses clerics must be bound

[Note: [Col. 0947D] See the council commonly called the Second Roman Council, under Sylvester, chapter 111. The chapters of this council that Isidore inserted into his collection appear to have been attributed to Hincmar, etc. [Col. 0948D] Cited by Egb. Eb., chapter 142; book V of the Capitularies, chapter 159, C. M.]

A priest shall not bring an accusation against a bishop; a deacon against a priest; a subdeacon against a deacon; an acolyte against a subdeacon; an exorcist against an acolyte; a reader against an exorcist; or a doorkeeper against a reader. A prelate shall not be condemned except by thirty-two [witnesses], nor shall the highest be judged by anyone, since it is written: “The disciple is not above his teacher.” A priest established in the cardinal rank shall not be condemned except by forty-four witnesses. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, or doorkeeper shall not be condemned except, as it is written, by seven witnesses. The witnesses must be free from any infamy, have wives and children, and openly preach Christ.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning fugitive clerics

[Note: [Col. 0948D] From a decree of Leo I, chapter 39; Regino, book I, chapter 421.]

Each bishop shall diligently inquire in his parish who the priests and clerics are. If he finds a fugitive, he shall make him return to his own bishop.

## CHAPTER XLI. Concerning those who are hanged on the gallows

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Council of Mainz under Rabanus, chapter 27; Regino, book II, chapter 93; Burchard, book XI, chapter 76.]

Some brothers asked about those who are hanged on the gallows for their crimes, after confession has been made to God: whether their corpses should be brought to the church, offerings made for them, and Masses celebrated, or not [Col. 0948B]. We answer them: If communion is to be given at the end, according to canonical command, to all who make a pure confession of their sins and perform worthy penance, why should it not be given to those who pay the final penalty for their sins and confess, or desire to confess? For it is written: “The Lord will not judge the same thing twice.” The Lord himself says: “On whatever day the sinner turns, his sins shall not be counted against him.” And again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” [Note: [Col. 0948D] Celestine, letter 2 to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, chapter 2.] Therefore, whoever denies penance to a person at the time of death deprives that person of salvation.

## CHAPTER XLII. Concerning thieves and robbers

[Col. 0948C]

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Council of Tribur, chapter 31; Regino, book I, chapter 94; Burchard, book XI, chapter 59.]

Concerning thieves and robbers, it is decreed that if they are killed during the very act of plunder, no prayer should be offered for them. But if, after being wounded, they fall into despair, repent of their wickedness, and, if they survive, promise God and the priest that they will amend, we do not refuse to give them communion.

## CHAPTER XLIII. Concerning homicides committed unintentionally

[Note: [Col. 0948D] Theodore, chapter 111; Roman Penitential, title 1, chapter 1, from Theodore’s Penitential; Council of Tribur, chapter 53.]

As for homicides committed unintentionally, what penance those who committed them should undergo shall remain in the bishop’s judgment. After he has seen their worthy penance, let him act toward them with greater clemency. If someone unintentionally kills his son, let him do penance according to the rule for unintentional homicide.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Concerning the continence of priests

A bishop, priest, or deacon who has fallen into fornication, perjury, or theft shall be deposed, but shall not be deprived of communion. For Scripture says [Col. 0949A] [Note: [Col. 0949D] Canon under the name of the Apostles, chapter 34; Basil, canon 3, canonical letter to Amphilochius; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 39]: “The Lord will not judge the same thing twice.”

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning bishops and clerics

[Note: [Col. 0949D] From the decrees of Leo I, chapter 17; Rabanus, letter to Heribald, chapter 11; Regino, book I, chapter 96.]

The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and priests who, while they were laymen or readers, were lawfully able both to marry wives and to beget children. But when they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been permitted to them began no longer to be permitted. Thus a carnal marriage becomes a spiritual one. They ought not to dismiss their wives, but to have them as though they did not have them, so that the affection of marriage is preserved while marital intercourse ceases.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning a crime committed in the church courtyard

[Col. 0949B] If anyone injures a priest in the courtyard of a church, or commits any sacrilege there, he shall make compensation to the altar and to the Lord [Note: [Col. 0949D] Council of Tribur, chapters 4 and 6; Regino, book II, chapter 37; Burchard, book III, chapter 195].

## CHAPTER XLVII. Concerning a freeborn faithful man accused

If a freeborn faithful man is marked by a crime, he may clear himself by oath. But if any freeborn man is publicly branded with serious infamy, so that the people have sworn against him that he is to be regarded as a criminal, and if he wishes to clear himself, let him undergo examination by iron [Note: [Col. 0949D] Rabanus’s Penitential, book III, chapter 6, from Theodore’s Penitential. For this proof, see the notable example in Aimoinus, book V, *On the Deeds of the Franks*, chapter 34; Regino, book XI, chapter 43, from the Council of Mainz, chapter 24; Burchard, book VI, chapter 7].

## CHAPTER XLVIII. Concerning married people who cannot have intercourse

[Note: [Col. 0949D] See Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, chapter 29; Regino, book II, chapter 242, cited from Rabanus’s letter.]

As for what you asked about those who are joined in marriage but cannot have intercourse—whether the man may take another wife, or the woman another husband—it is written: “If a man and a woman have joined themselves, and afterward the woman says of the man [Col. 0949C] that she cannot have intercourse with him, if she can prove by a just judgment that this is true, let her take another husband.” [Note: [Col. 0950D] See above, chapter 11 of the older Penitential code, *On Questions Concerning Marriage*; Council of Compiègne, chapter 17.] Likewise: “If someone takes a wife and has her for some time, and the woman says that she has not had intercourse with him, while the man says that he did so against her will, the man’s case is established, because the man is the head of the woman.”

## CHAPTER XLIX. Concerning the ordained, if they are found to have committed criminal sins before or after ordination

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Rabanus’s Penitential, chapter 1; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 150; from the Council of Lleida, although this canon is not found there. Ivo, part VI, chapter 400.]

It has therefore seemed good to us to write concerning those who hold sacred orders and profess that they were contaminated by capital crimes before or after ordination. In their case, as it seems to me, the following distinction must be maintained: if they are publicly caught or exposed in perjury, [Col. 0949D] theft, fornication, or other crimes of this sort, they must be deposed from their rank according to the institutions of the sacred canons, since it is a scandal for the people of God to have such persons placed over them when they are clearly excessively vicious. Indeed, through such men people are drawn away from the sacrifice, just as once the sons of Eli, rebelling against sinners and standing opposed on every side, became daily worse through their evil examples. But those of the aforementioned men who, through secret confession, confess before the eyes of God—also in the presence of the priest who is to assign them penance—the sins they secretly committed, and accuse themselves of having grievously offended, should, if they truly repent and strive to cleanse themselves through fasts, almsgiving, vigils, and holy prayers with tears, be promised hope of pardon through the mercy of God, while retaining their rank [Note: [Col. 0950D] See Isidore of Seville’s letter to Bishop Massona]. He wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, and does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.

## CHAPTER L. Concerning the one who vomits the Eucharist through drunkenness or gluttony

[Col. 0950B]

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Regino, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 149; Burchard, book V, chapter 46.]

If anyone vomits the Eucharist through drunkenness or gluttony, let him do penance for forty days if he is a cleric, monk, or deacon; a priest, for seventy days; a bishop, for ninety. If he vomits it because of illness, let him do penance for seven days.

## CHAPTER LI. If anything drips from the chalice of the sacred blood

But if, through negligence, something drips from the chalice onto the ground, the board shall be scraped. If there is no board, so that it may not be trodden upon, the place shall be scraped, consumed in fire, and the ashes stored beneath the altar; and the priest shall do penance for forty days. If the chalice drips upon the altar [Note: [Col. 0950D] See the *Judgments of Gregory III*, chapter 28], the minister shall lap up the drop and do penance for three days; if it reaches a third of the way, for nine days; if a quarter, for fifteen days. The linens that touched the drop shall be washed three times by the minister, with the chalice placed beneath them; the washing water shall be collected and stored beside the altar.

## CHAPTER LII. Concerning one who vomits the sacrifice and it is consumed by dogs

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Ivo, part II, chapter 57.]

Whoever vomits the sacrifice and it is consumed by dogs shall do penance for one year. Otherwise, let him do penance for forty days. If he vomits the sacrifice on the day when he receives communion, then, if before midnight, let him make three superpositions; if after midnight, two; if after matins, one.

## CHAPTER LIII. The same matter

[Col. 0950D]

[Note: [Col. 0950D] Roman Penitential, title 5, chapter 8; Burchard, book V, chapter 49; Ivo, part II, chapter 58.]

If he vomits the sacrifice, let him do penance for forty days. If because of illness, for seven days. If he throws it into the fire, let him chant one hundred psalms. But if dogs lick such vomit, let the one who vomited it do penance for one hundred days.

## CHAPTER LIV. Concerning the Eucharist grown old for fifty days

[Note: [Col. 0951C] Ivo, part II, chapter 59; from the Third Council of Arles, chapter 5.]

Every sacrifice ruined by foul age must be burned in fire, and the ashes buried beside the altar.

## CHAPTER LV. Concerning those who have not properly guarded the body and blood of the Lord

[Note: [Col. 0951C] Ivo, part II, chapter 60; *On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Qui bene non.”]

Whoever does not properly guard the sacrifice, so that a mouse or some other animal eats it, shall do penance for forty days. Whoever loses it in the church, or if a portion of it falls and is not found, shall do penance for twenty days [Col. 0951B]. Whoever spills something from the chalice upon the altar during the offering shall do penance for six days; if more is spilled, for seven days. Whoever spills the chalice while the solemnity of Mass is being celebrated shall do penance for forty days. Whoever receives the sacrifice while polluted by a nocturnal emission shall do penance for seven days. A deacon who forgets to offer the oblation until the cloth is offered, when the names of the departed are recited, shall likewise do penance. Whoever shows such negligence toward the sacrifice that it is consumed by worms and reduced to nothing shall do penance for three Lents on bread and water [Note: [Col. 0951C] *Judgments of Gregory III*, chapter 28]. If it is found intact, the worm shall be burned in it, and the ashes placed beneath the altar.

## CHAPTER LVI. The same matter

[Col. 0951C]

[Note: [Col. 0951C] Ivo, part II, chapter 60.]

If the sacrifice falls from the hands of the one offering it all the way to the ground and is not found, everything found in the place where it fell shall be burned; and the ashes shall be hidden as above. The person to whom this happened shall do penance for half a year. But if the sacrifice is found, the place shall be cleaned with brooms and burned as above [Col. 0952A]; the ashes shall likewise be stored, and the priest shall do penance for twenty days.

## CHAPTER LVII. The same matter

If someone loses the Eucharist through negligence, let him do penance for one year, or three Lents, or forty days. If he loses the sacrifice on the ground through negligence, let him chant forty psalms. Whoever neglects the sacrifice so that worms are in it and it has neither its color [Note: [Col. 0951C] *Judgments of Gregory III*, chapter 28] nor its taste shall do penance for twenty, thirty, or forty days.

## CHAPTER LVIII. That no one should presume to give false measures or false weights for the sake of profit

[Note: [Col. 0952C] Capitularies of Aachen, chapter 74; Sixth Council of Arles, chapter 14; Third Council of Tours, chapter 45.]

Let measures and weights be made just, as prescribed in the divine laws [Col. 0952B]; therefore we decree that this be observed by all. If anyone presumes to alter just measures and just weights for the sake of profit, let him do penance for twenty days on bread and water.

## CHAPTER LIX. Concerning the mother who placed her infant beside the fire and it died through her negligence

[Note: [Col. 0952C] Council of Tribur in the time of Pope Formosus, chapter 37.]

A mother, if she has placed her infant beside the hearth. If a man puts water into a cauldron and, when the water boils, the infant is scalded and dies, let the mother do penance for negligence; and let that man be free of blame.

## CHAPTER LX. Concerning ordained men whose sins are secret

[Note: [Col. 0952C] Rabanus’s Penitential, chapter 1. See Isidore of Seville’s letter to Bishop Massona.]

Concerning ordained men whose sins are secret and cannot be openly charged by anyone: if, being salutarily contrite, they secretly confess their sins to a bishop or priest, it seems good to me that they should do penance according to what the bishop or priest has decreed—not lukewarmly or slowly, but fervently and diligently. Thus let them trust that they will receive forgiveness of sins from the Lord and retain their rank.

[Col. 0951]

# Chapters Presented to the Fathers of the Council of Herford, with Theodore Presiding, Compared with Three Manuscript Codices of the *History of the English* of the Venerable Bede (C)*

[Col. 0951D] “Then,” says Theodore, “I immediately brought out the same book of canons, and from that book I showed them ten chapters that I had marked in various places, because I knew that they were especially necessary for us; and I asked that they be received more carefully by everyone.”

## I. Concerning Easter

[Note: [Col. 0951D] First Council of Arles, chapter 1; decree of the Council of Nicaea. In Eusebius, book III of *The Life of Constantine*, chapter 18; Athanasius, *On the Councils*; Theodoret, book I of the *History*, chapter 8; see the canon under the name of the Apostles, chapter 7.]

Let us all together keep the holy day of Easter on the Sunday after the fourteenth day of the first month’s moon.

## II. Concerning bishops

[Note: [Col. 0952D] Council of Antioch, chapter 3.]

Let no bishop invade another’s parish, but let each be content with governing the people entrusted to him.

## III. Concerning monasteries

[Col. 0953A]

[Note: [Col. 0953C] Council of Lleida, chapter 3.]

Let no bishop be permitted to disturb monasteries consecrated to God in any way or to seize anything of their property by force.

## IV. Concerning monks

[Note: [Col. 0953C] Council of Chalcedon, chapter 4; Council of Angers, chapter 8; Council of Vannes, chapter 6; Council of Agde, chapters 27 and 38; First Council of Orléans, chapter 19; Second Council of Tours, chapter 15.]

Let monks [Note: [Col. 0953C] Here the printed editions commonly read, “Let bishops who are monks …” The words *episcopi monachi* are more correctly absent from two excellent codices of the Thuane Library and from another very ancient manuscript that the most learned Jesuit Chifflet shared with me, and also from excerpts of Egbert, archbishop of York, chapter 66, where it reads: “Theodore says: Let monks not migrate from place …” Otherwise this chapter would agree with no canon of any preceding synod.] not move from place to place—that is, from monastery to monastery—except by dismissal from their own abbot; rather, let them remain in the obedience that they promised at the time of their conversion.

## V. Concerning clerics
[Note: [Col. 0953C] Council of Arles I, canon 21; Council of Nicaea, canons 15, 16; Council of Antioch, canon 3; Council of Laodicea, canons 41, [Col. 0953D] 42; canon under the name of the Apostles, 14; Council of Carthage IV, [Col. 0954C] canon 5; African Church Code, canon 71; Council of Toledo I, canon 12; Council of Angers, canon 1; Council of Épaone, canon 6; Council of Valence, canon 5; Council of Toledo II, canon 2.] No cleric, abandoning his own bishop, shall wander about indiscriminately wherever he pleases; nor shall anyone arriving anywhere be received without letters of recommendation from his bishop. If, after being received, he refuses to return when invited, both the one who received him and the one received shall be subject to excommunication.

VI. On Foreign Bishops and Clerics

[Note: [Col. 0954C] Synod of Saint Patrick, canon 30. Cited in the Capitula, book VI, canon 86.] Foreign bishops and clerics shall be content with the hospitality offered to them, and none of them may perform any priestly office without the permission of the bishop in whose diocese he is known to be staying.

VII. On Synods

[Note: [Col. 0954C] Council of Nicaea, canon 5, and several other canons derived from the Council of Nicaea.] A synod shall be convened twice a year; but because various circumstances prevent this, it was agreed by all in common that it should be convened once a year, on the Kalends of August, at the place called Clofeshooth.

VIII. On the Primacy of Bishops

[Note: [Col. 0954C] Council of Milevis II, canons 13, 14; in the complete African Church Code, canon 86; from the African Council, canon 53; Council of Carthage, no. 19, under Bishop Aurelius; Council of Agde, canon 23.] No bishop shall, through ambition, place himself before another: [Col. 0954A] let all acknowledge the time and order of their consecration.

IX. On the Number of Bishops

[Note: [Col. 0954C] Council of Carthage II, canon 5.] It was discussed in common that, as the number of the faithful increases, more bishops should be appointed; but for the present we remain silent on this matter.

X. On Marriage

[Note: [Col. 0954C] Council of Milevis, canon 17; Innocent I, letter to Bishop Exuperius, canon 6. — Cited in the Capitula, book VI, canon 87.] Concerning marriages: no one may have any union except a lawful marriage. No one shall commit incest. No one shall abandon his own spouse except, as the holy Gospel teaches, on account of fornication. If anyone expels his own spouse, lawfully joined to him in marriage, then, if he wishes rightly to remain a Christian, he shall not be joined to another; but shall remain in that state or be reconciled with his own wife.

[Col. 0954B] Since, therefore, these chapters, as Theodore continues, had been discussed and defined in common, so that henceforth no contentious scandal might arise among any of us, nor might some matters be publicized in preference to others, it was agreed that each of us should confirm what had been defined by the subscription of his own hand. I dictated this decision of the definition to the notary Titillo to be written down. Done in the month and indiction stated above. Whoever, therefore, in any way attempts to act against this decision, confirmed according to the decrees of the canons and also by our common agreement and the subscription of our hands, and to violate it, shall know that he is to be separated from every priestly office and from our fellowship. May divine grace preserve you unharmed, living in the unity of His holy Church.

[Col. 0953]

OTHER CHAPTERS COLLECTED FROM FRAGMENTS

Fragments from chapters edited by the Reverend Father Luca d’Achery in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*. (C)*

Here are omitted the matters noted above concerning Theodore’s Penitential.

[Col. 0953D] CHAPTER VI

[Note: [Col. 0953D] Burchard, book IV, chapter 51; Ivo, part I, chapter 145; Gratian, *De consecratione*, distinction 4, chapter “Quibus”.] Those who have been baptized twice in ignorance do not require penance, except that according to the canons they may not be ordained, unless in a case of great necessity. But those who were not ignorant of what they were doing have, as it were, crucified Christ again; let them do penance for seven years, on Wednesdays and Fridays, and during the three Lents.

[Col. 0954D] FROM CHAPTER VII

[Note: [Col. 0954D] See the notes to Theodore’s Penitential, concerning the work that is forbidden.] Those who work on Sunday are admonished by the Greeks the first time; the second time they have something taken from them; the third time a third part of their possessions is taken, and they are beaten, or they shall do penance for seven days.

FROM CHAPTER IX

A church may be established in another place if necessary, [Col. 0955A] and it must then be consecrated again, not merely sprinkled with holy water.

CHAPTER XII

The Greeks receive Communion every Sunday, whether clerics or laypeople, and those who do not receive Communion for three Sundays shall be excommunicated. The Romans likewise receive Communion if they wish; but those who do not wish to do so shall not be excommunicated. [Note: [Col. 0955D] See Egbert of York’s Excerpts, chapter 39.] Penitents, however, according to the canons, ought not to receive Communion before completing their penance. Theodore says: We, however, out of mercy, grant permission after a year or six months. The penance of a widow and of a maiden is the same; a greater penance is deserved by a woman who has a husband if she has committed the crime of fornication.

CHAPTER XIV

[Note: [Col. 0955D] See the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 7; Council of Laodicea, canon 1; Saint Basil, letter to Amphilochius, canon 4.] A bigamist shall do penance for the first year on Wednesdays and Fridays; during the three Lents he shall abstain from meat and be separated.

CHAPTER XVI

In a first marriage, a priest ought to celebrate Mass and bless both parties; afterward they shall abstain from the church for thirty days. When these have passed, they shall do penance for fifteen days and devote themselves to prayer; afterward they may receive Communion with an offering.

CHAPTER XVII

A free man ought to be joined to a free woman.

CHAPTER XVIII

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Roman Penitential, title 8, chapter 11; Gratian, distinction 27, chapter “Si vir”.] If a husband who has made a vow of virginity is joined to a wife, he shall not afterward dismiss his wife, but shall do penance for three years. Foolish and unbearable vows must be broken, and [Col. 0955C] a woman ought not to make a vow without her husband’s permission; but if she makes one, she may be dismissed.

CHAPTER XXXI

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Capitula, book VI, chapter 206.] Animals that have been joined in intercourse with human beings shall be killed, and the meat thrown to dogs; and where there is doubt, it must not be eaten.

CHAPTER XXXII

[Note: [Col. 0955D] The first part is from Theodore’s Penitential, Saint-Germain manuscript.] It is permitted to celebrate two Masses at one altar; and the one who is known to have eaten first is not permitted to give the kiss.

CHAPTER XXXIV

The children of the monastery eat meat until they are fourteen years old.

[Col. 0955D] CHAPTER XXXV

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Ivo, part XIII, chapter 135; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 146.] If necessary, confession may be made to God alone.

CHAPTER XL

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Roman Penitential, title 3, chapter 30.] Whoever fornicates with his sister shall do penance for fourteen years.

[Col. 0956A] CHAPTER XLI

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Chapters 22 and 27.] A priest who has been defiled by touching a woman shall do penance for forty days.

FROM CHAPTER XLIV

A husband ought not to see his wife naked.

CHAPTER L

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Ivo, part II, chapter 45, from Eutychian.] Whoever receives the sacrifice after eating shall remain under the judgment of the bishops for seven days.

CHAPTER LI

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*, chapter 15; the C. M. Capitula, book VI, chapter 9; Gratian, distinction 17, question 4, chapter “Qui”.] Whoever kills a monk or cleric shall lay down his weapons and serve the Lord, or do penance for seven years.

CHAPTER LII

[Note: [Col. 0956D] See Gregory III’s *Judgments*, chapter 1.] Whoever kills a bishop or priest shall be handed over to the king for judgment.

[Col. 0956B] CHAPTER LIII

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*, chapter 15.] If a layman kills another out of a settled hatred, then, if he does not wish to lay down his weapons, he shall do penance for seven years without meat; if it happened through sudden anger, for three years; but if by accident or chance, for one year.

CHAPTER LIV

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*, chapter 2.] Money stolen or forcibly taken from the church shall be repaid fourfold; money belonging to the laity, twofold.

CHAPTER LV

If anyone fornicates with a virgin, let him do penance for one year; with a married woman, for three years: one full year, and two further periods of forty days.

CHAPTER LVII

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Roman Penitential, title 3, chapter 15; Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*; Burchard, book XVII, chapter 27; Ivo, part 9, chapter 85.] A woman who, out of love of fornication, joins herself to another woman shall do penance for seven years. So also the other woman who, mixing her husband’s semen into food, seeks thereby to gain more of his love. [Col. 0956C] [Note: [Col. 0956D] Burchard, book XIX, chapter 91.]

CHAPTER LVIII

A consecrated virgin who fornicates shall do penance for seven years.

CHAPTER LIX

[Note: [Col. 0956D] C. M. Capitula, book III, chapter 20.] Whoever has committed homicide or theft and has not made compensation to those whom he injured, when he confesses his sins to a bishop or priest, must either return what belongs to them or make compensation; but if he has no property with which to make compensation, or does not know whom he injured, his penance shall be increased.

CHAPTER LX

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Capitula 68, book V.] Whoever has eaten sacrificial food and afterward confessed it, the priest shall consider the person involved and the age at which it occurred; and thus priestly authority shall moderate its judgment concerning the infirm person.

CHAPTER LXI

[Note: [Col. 0956D] Roman Penitential, title 1, chapter 26.] A woman who has killed her offspring shall do penance for seven years.

CHAPTER LXII

If a layman secretly departs from a monastery of monks, [Col. 0957A] let him either enter a monastery to serve the Lord or undergo a human [lacuna]. [Note: [Col. 0957C] Something is missing here; it may be supplied from the Capitula, book IV, chapter 61.]

CHAPTER LXV

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Roman Penitential, title 1, chapter 17.] Whoever kills a man at the command of his master shall fast for forty days.

CHAPTER LXVI

Before the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Greeks celebrate Mass late in the day and the Latins at the ninth hour.

CHAPTER LXX

Whoever turns money into booty shall distribute a third part and fast for forty days.

CHAPTER LXXIII

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Roman Penitential, title 3, chapter 20.] Whoever dismisses his wife and joins himself to another shall do penance for seven years.

CHAPTER LXXV

[Col. 0957B] A father and son may have a mother and daughter in marriage.

CHAPTER LXXVII

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Bede, *On Remedies for Sins*, chapter 3.] A woman who voluntarily destroys her pregnancy shall do penance for one year if it occurred before forty days of conception; but if afterward, she shall do penance for three years.

FROM CHAPTER LXXX

Likewise, those who are consecrated by the persons mentioned above shall be sprinkled with exorcised water and strengthened with some collect.

CHAPTER LXXXVIII

If a priest is traveling and a woman meets him, asking that her sick son be baptized, but he neglects this because of the urgency of his journey; and likewise, whoever in his own province, another’s, or wherever he may be found, presumes not to baptize a sick person entrusted to him, and that person dies without baptism, let him be deposed. Likewise, if he kills a man or commits fornication, let him be deposed.

CHAPTER XCI

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Egbert, *Excerpts*, chapter 31.] Whoever takes a widow as his wife, whether after baptism or before baptism, cannot be a priest.

CHAPTER XCII

[Note: [Col. 0957D] *Summary*: If anyone, 32, question 1, from Theodore’s Penitential.] A man shall not communicate with his adulterous wife; likewise, a wife shall not enter into communion of peace with an adulterous husband.

[Col. 0958A] CHAPTER XCIV

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Canon under the name of the Apostles, 9.] If any bishop or priest, after the offering has been broken, does not receive Communion, let him state a reasonable cause; otherwise, let him be deposed.

CHAPTER XCV

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Canon under the name of the Apostles, chapter 14; Council of Antioch, chapter 2; Second Council of Braga, chapter 83.] All the faithful who enter the church but do not dare to approach the holy offering, nor receive the sacrifice, should be deprived of Communion.

CHAPTER XCVI

A bishop shall not go out to another diocese and abandon his own, unless he is advanced through the judgment of many and especially through their petition. [Note: [Col. 0958C] “May advance.” See the Council of Antioch, canon 3.]

CHAPTER XCVII

[Note: [Col. 0958D] Canon under the name of the Apostles, chapters 21, 22, 23, 24; Council of Nicaea, canon 1.] If a eunuch was made so through the plotting of men, or if his genitals were cut off during persecution, or [Col. 0958B] if he was born so, and is worthy, let him become a bishop. If anyone cuts off his own genitals, he absolutely cannot be a cleric. If anyone cuts off his genitals after ordination, let him be utterly condemned. If anyone castrates himself, let him be deprived of Communion for three years.

CHAPTER XCIX

[Note: [Col. 0958D] Canon under the name of the Apostles, 30.] No one shall obtain an ecclesiastical rank through money; otherwise both he and the one who ordained him shall be expelled from Communion in every way.

CHAPTER CI

Those who eat unclean meats, and vegetables cooked together with meat, must cease from ministry.

CHAPTER CVI

[Note: [Col. 0958D] Gregory III’s *Judgments*, chapter 30.] A bishop, priest, or deacon must confess his sin. If necessary, confession may be made to God alone. [Col. 0958C]

CHAPTER CVII

[Note: [Col. 0958D] Ivo, part XI, chapter 75, from the sayings of Jerome.] A person afflicted by a demon may use stones and vegetables without incantation.

CHAPTER CVIII

[Note: [Col. 0958D] Roman Penitential, title 2, chapter 4.] Perjurers shall do penance for three years. Sodomites, seven years; effeminate men, one year.

CHAPTER CXIV

[Note: [Col. 0958D] See Tertullian, *On the Military Crown*, chapter 9, and the book *On Prayer*.] One ought to pray standing, out of reverence for God.

FROM THE LAST CHAPTER

[Note: [Col. 0958D] See the *Rule*, questions 7 and 15, discussed more fully in the longer rules.] Basil judged that boys might marry before the age of sixteen if they were unable to abstain, even if they had been monks.

[Col. 0957]

FRAGMENTS FROM THE CANONS (C)*

I. From the canons collected by García de Loaysa under the title *Councils of Toledo*

[Col. 0957D]

CHAPTER XVII.— [Note: [Col. 0957D] Regino, book II, chapter 362; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 152.] Concerning those matters about which you also asked, namely, concerning the woman who mixed her menstrual blood into food or drink and gave it to her husband to eat, and concerning the woman who drank her husband’s semen in a drink, and concerning the woman who burned a human skull in the fire [Col. 0959A] and gave it to her husband to avert illness—by what penance should they be punished? In our view, they should be sentenced in the same manner as magicians and diviners, because they are known to have practiced magic. For concerning those known to have practiced magic and to have observed omens and divinations, we possess the constitutions of Theodore, archbishop of the English people, in which it is written. [Note: [Col. 0959C] Regino, book II, chapters 360, 361; Burchard, book X, chapter 13.] Whoever sacrifices to demons in small matters shall do penance for one year. Whoever does so in great matters shall do penance for ten years. Rabanus cites the same passage from Theodore’s constitutions, but presents it in full in his letter to Heribald as follows.

We possess the constitutions of Theodore, archbishop of the English people, in which it is written: Whoever sacrifices to demons in small matters shall do penance for one year. [Col. 0959B] Whoever does so in great matters shall do penance for ten years. [Note: [Col. 0959C] Bede’s canons concerning remedies for sins, chapter 11.] If a woman places her daughter on a roof or in a furnace for the sake of curing a fever, she shall do penance for seven years. [Note: [Col. 0959C] Regino, book II, chapter 357; Burchard, book X, chapter 24.] Whoever causes grain to be burned where a man has died, for the health of the living and of the house, shall do penance for five years. If a woman performs incantations or divinations, she shall do penance for one year, or three Lents, or forty days, according to the nature of the offense. See also Rabanus, book III, *On the Satisfaction of Penitents*, chapter 48.

II. From the excerpts of Egbert, archbishop of York

CHAPTER LVI.—Theodore says: It has been established that priests shall neither be appointed in any churches nor expelled from them without the authority or consent of the bishops; and if anyone attempts to do this, let him be struck by synodal judgment.

CHAPTER LXVI.—Theodore says: Monks shall not move from place to place, [Col. 0960A] but shall remain in the obedience that they promised at the time of their conversion.

III. From the canons of the venerable Bede concerning remedies for sins

FROM CHAPTER VIII.—Theodore said: A monk committing [Note: [Col. 0960C] “Seeking,” in the old Penitential of Angers and in the manuscript of the distinguished Sir Antoine d’Hérouval.] fornication, and not finding [a partner], shall do penance for one and a half years. Likewise, a monk committing fornication with a girl shall do penance for six years.

IV. From selected chapters of the Irish canons, edited by the Reverend Father Luca d’Achery in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*

BOOK LII, CHAPTER 14.—Concerning dead pigs, animals that consume human blood, and meat eaten by wolves; concerning fish and strangled animals; concerning what has been eaten by a hawk, and concerning the horse.—Bishop Theodore says: The Greeks do not give carrion meat to their pigs. [Note: [Col. 0960C] Ivo, part XIV, chapter 97, from Theodore’s Penitential.] The hides of dead animals may indeed be taken for footwear, wool, and horns, but not for anything sacred. Nevertheless, if pigs happen by chance to eat the flesh of dead animals or human blood, we do not believe that they should be discarded; nor do we believe this concerning hens. Animals that have been eaten by wolves or dogs are not to be eaten, unless they are thrown to pigs and dogs; nor are deer or boars, if found dead. Fish, however, may be eaten, since they are of another nature. Birds and other animals, if strangled in nets, are not to be eaten. For Paul says: “Abstain from things strangled, blood, and idolatry” [Col. 0960C] (Acts XXI, 25). The same applies to animals killed by a hawk. They do not prohibit the horse; nevertheless, it is not customary to eat it.

[Col. 0959]

FRAGMENTS FROM PENITENTIAL BOOKS (C)*

I. FROM THE ROMAN PENITENTIAL

[Col. 0959C]

TITLE I, CHAPTER X. Concerning those who commit homicide in vengeance for their relatives. [Col. 0959D] (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

[Note: [Col. 0959D] Regino, book II, chapter 23; Burchard, book VI, chapter 32; Ivo, part X, chapter 16.] Whoever kills a man in vengeance for a brother or other relative shall do penance in the same manner as for voluntary homicide, since Truth itself says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.”

TITLE II, CHAPTER IV. Concerning those who knowingly commit perjury. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

[Note: [Col. 0959D] Rabanus, in his letter to Heribald, chapter 18; Regino, book II, [Col. 0960D] chapter 326; Burchard, book XII, chapter 11; Ivo, part LXII, chapter 68.] If anyone suspects that he is being led into perjury and nevertheless swears with consent, let him do penance for forty days and for the following seven years, and let him never be without severe penance.

[Col. 0960C] TITLE III, CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning those who have committed fornication as the Sodomites did. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

[Note: [Col. 0960D] Anselm, book XI, chapter 97.] If anyone has fornicated as the Sodomites did, then, if he is a bishop, let him do penance for twenty-five years: five of these on bread and water; let him be deposed from every office and end his days in exile. A priest shall do penance for fifteen years, five of them on bread and water, and shall be deposed according to the preceding sentence. A deacon and a monk shall do penance for twelve years, three of them on bread and water, and shall be deposed. Anselm adds: But if he is old or sick, let him do penance shut up in dark prisons for all the days of his life.

TITLE III, CHAPTER XXV. Concerning one who wishes to fornicate but cannot

[Note: [Col. 0960D] Anselm, book XI, chapter 129.] If anyone desires to fornicate but cannot, or if the woman does not receive him, then, if he is a bishop, let him do penance for seven [Col. 0961A] years; a priest, five; a deacon or monk, three—one of these years on bread and water. Clerics or laypeople shall do penance for two years.

CHAPTER XXIX. How a woman who practices procuring prostitution ought to do penance

THEODORE
