[Note: [Col. 0961D] Burchard, book XIX, chapter 278.] You have practiced procuring prostitution, either with yourself or with others—that is, in the manner of a prostitute, you have handed over your body to your lovers to handle and defile for payment; or, what is more cruel and dangerous, you have sold or granted another’s body—by which I mean the body of a daughter, granddaughter, or some Christian woman—to lovers, or acted as an intermediary, or given advice so that some violation might be perpetrated in this manner. You shall do penance for two years on the appointed weekdays. Nevertheless, the Council of Elvira [Col. 0961B] [Note: [Col. 0961D] Council of Elvira, canon 12.] prescribes that a woman who has perpetrated these acts shall not receive Communion except at the end.

TITLE IV, CHAPTER IV. Concerning theft committed out of necessity

THEODORE

[Note: [Col. 0961D] Burchard, book XI, chapter 58; Ivo, part XIII, chapter 4; Anselm, book XI, chapter 109.] If anyone has stolen food, clothing, or livestock because of hunger or nakedness, let him do penance for three weeks. If he makes restitution, he shall not be compelled to fast.

CHAPTER V. Concerning capital theft

[Note: [Col. 0961D] The Roman Penitential, copied by Halitgar from the Roman Church archive; Regino, book II, chapter 268; Burchard, book XI, chapter 59.] If anyone commits capital theft—that is, takes four-footed animals or breaks into houses—let him do penance for seven years and return what was stolen. If anyone commits lesser theft once or twice, let him return what he took and do penance for one year. Regino [Col. 0961C] and Burchard add: or if anyone violates a tomb, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.

CHAPTER XI. That one who expels his father or mother is to be judged a sacrilegious person

THEODORE

[Note: [Col. 0961D] Anselm, book XI, chapter 112.] If anyone expels his father or mother, he is to be judged impious and sacrilegious. Let him do penance for as long a time as he persisted in that impiety.

CHAPTER XII. On the same matter

THEODORE

[Note: [Col. 0962D] Burchard, book XIX, chapter 270.] You have cursed your father or mother, or flogged them, or dishonored them in any way: do penance for forty days on bread and water, followed by seven years, because the Lord said: “Whoever curses his father or mother shall surely be put to death.”

TITLE V, CHAPTER III. Concerning gluttony and drunkenness

THEODORE

[Note: [Col. 0962D] Burchard, book XIV, chapter 8; Ivo, part XIII, chapter 76.] If any priest becomes drunk through ignorance, let him do penance for seven days on bread and water. If through negligence, fifteen days; if through contempt, forty days. A deacon or monk shall do penance according to his order, as it is written; and the remaining clerics, as ministers, [Col. 0962A] shall do penance according to their order, at the priest’s judgment. Laypeople, since they have no vows, if they become drunk, shall be admonished by the priest that drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God, and that drunkenness leads to destruction; and he shall compel them to do penance. Whoever compels a person to become drunk shall be sharply reprimanded for his lack of humanity and shall do penance for seven days. If through contempt, thirty days. No Christian shall compel another to drink more than is sufficient for nature. If he does so, let him do penance according to what is contained in the Penitential.

TITLE VII, CHAPTER XXX. Concerning those who have taken Christian slaves captive. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

[Note: [Col. 0962D] Burchard, book V, chapter 49; Ivo, part XV, chapter 149.] If anyone captures or transports any person by any means whatsoever, let him do penance for three years.

[Col. 0962B] CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the administration of a hospice

(From Theodore’s Penitential.)

[Note: [Col. 0962D] Burchard, book V, chapter 139; Ivo, part XV, chapter 149.] If anyone administers hospices for the poor, or receives the tithes of the people, and takes anything from them for his own worldly profit or that of his secular associates, let him, as one guilty of seizing property, restore the damage, be corrected according to canonical judgment, and do penance for three years. For it is written: “The Lord seeks such a steward as will appropriate nothing of His for himself.”

TITLE VIII, CHAPTER XI. Those who marry after a vow are not to be separated from one another

THEODORE

If a man who has made a vow [Note: [Col. 0962D] In Gratian (*Decree*, part I, distinction 27, chapter 3), “a simple vow” is added, but this word is absent from all manuscript codices; and likewise below, in 27, question 1, chapter “Si quis votum”, even from the printed editions, as Gratian’s correctors observe.] of virginity is joined to a wife, he shall not afterward dismiss his wife, but shall do penance for three years.

II. FROM THE PENITENTIAL OF RABANUS MAURUS, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

BOOK III, CHAPTER VI. On the penances of laypeople

Likewise, in the Penitential that Theodore, archbishop of Britain, established with the other bishops, the following is contained: If a man is tormented by the devil and knows nothing except to wander everywhere, and kills himself for whatever reason, it is beneficial to pray for him if he had previously been religious. If he did so out of despair, or from some fear, or for unknown reasons, we leave this judgment to God, and we have not dared to pray for one who has killed himself by his own will. It is not permitted to celebrate Masses for him, but only to pray and give alms. If a Christian has fallen from his senses through sudden temptation or has killed himself through madness, some people celebrate Masses for him.

Likewise, in the same book: If anyone kills a man in vengeance for a relative, let him do penance as a homicide for seven or ten years; if, however, he wishes to pay the relatives the assessed compensation, his penance shall be lighter, namely, half the period. Whoever kills a man in vengeance for a brother shall do penance for three years. In another place it is said that he shall do penance for ten years; a homicide, however, for ten or seven years. If a layman kills another out of a settled hatred, then, if he does not wish to lay down his weapons, let him do penance for seven years, three of them without meat and wine. If anyone kills a monk or cleric, let him abandon his occupation, serve God, and do penance for seven years, subject to the bishop’s judgment. Whoever kills a priest shall be assigned twelve years of penance according to the canons; or, if he denies it, if he is free, let him swear with twelve [men]. But if he is a slave, let him purge himself by twelve red-hot plowshares; once convicted of the offense, let him lay aside the military belt until the end of his life and lose his wife. Whoever kills a man at the command of his master shall do penance for forty days, [Col. 0963B] and whoever kills a man shall abstain from the Church for forty days; [Col. 0964A] whoever kills a man in a public war shall do penance for forty days; if through anger, three years; if by accident, one year; if through the people or by some art, seven years or more; if through a quarrel, let him do penance for ten years. If anyone destroys someone by his sorcery, let him do penance for five years, two of them on bread and water. If anyone becomes a sorcerer through love and destroys no one, then, if he is a cleric, let him do penance for one year on bread and water; if a priest, for five years, two of them on bread and water. If a deacon, three years, one of them on bread and water; and a layman shall do penance for half a year. Especially if by this means someone has deceived a woman concerning her pregnancy, let each person add three years on bread and water, lest he be guilty of homicide.

[Col. 0963]

FRAGMENTS FROM COLLECTORS OF CANONS (C)

I. FROM REGINO’S TWO BOOKS ON ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE [Note: [Col. 0963D] The learned Baluze accurately emended these against a very ancient manuscript.]

[Col. 0963B]

ON RECEIVING CONFESSION

(From the Penitential of Theodore, archbishop, or of Bede the priest [Col. 0963C])

BOOK I, CHAPTER CCXCVI [Note: [Col. 0963D] Halitgar, in the preface to book VI; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 2.] When bishops or priests receive the confessions of the faithful, they ought to humble themselves and pray with a mournful groan and tears, not only for their own sins but also for the brother’s fall. For the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (II Corinthians X).

Hence the following.

CHAPTER CCXCVIII [Note: [Col. 0963D] Halitgar, in the same place; Burchard, book XIX, chapter 2.] When someone comes to a priest to confess his sins, the priest should tell him to wait a little until he enters the church or his own room for prayer. If there is no suitable place for this, let him say the following prayer in his heart.

PRAYER

[Col. 0963D] CHAPTER CCXCIX [Note: [Col. 0963D] Halitgar, in the same place; Burchard, in the same place, chapter 3.] Almighty Lord God, be merciful to me, a sinner, so that I may be able to give You worthy thanks: You who, because of Your mercy, have made me, though unworthy, a minister of the priestly office, and have appointed me, small and humble, as an intermediary to pray and intercede with our Lord Jesus Christ, Your Son, for sinners and for those returning to penance. Therefore, ruling Lord, You who desire all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth, who do not desire the death of sinners but that they should turn and live, receive my prayer, which I pour out before the sight of Your mercy for Your male and female servants who have come to penance. Grant them the spirit of compunction, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by which they are held bound, [Col. 0964C] and return to You through worthy satisfaction, through the same Lord.

When the person who has come to penance sees the priest sorrowful and weeping for his sins, he himself, struck more deeply by fear of God, will be more sorrowful and dread his sins more greatly. [Note: [Col. 0963D] This passage appears as follows in an old manuscript codex of the monastery of Ripoll: “When that brother who has come to penance sees this humility of the priest, he dreads his sins more and fears his crimes more. After this, the priest should receive him charitably, make him sit humbly beside him, and gently draw him on with words such as these: Brother, do not be ashamed to confess your sins.” [Col. 0964D]]

ORDER FOR GIVING PENANCE

Hence the following.

CHAPTER CCC [Note: [Col. 0964D] Burchard, in the same place. See the ancient Penitential of Angers, edited by J. Morin in the appendix to his book *On Penance*.] After this, question him gently and kindly. Do you believe in God the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit? Answer: I believe. — Do you believe that these three persons are one God? Answer: I believe. — Do you believe that in this very flesh in which you now are, you will rise on the day of judgment and receive either the good or the evil that you have done? Answer: I believe. — Are you willing to forgive the sins of those who have sinned against you, since the Lord says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins” (Matthew VI)? Answer: I am willing. — And inquire carefully whether he is incestuous or faithless to his lord. If he does not wish to abandon incest, you cannot give him penance. But if he wishes to do so, you may. After these questions, the priest ought to address the penitent affectionately in these words:

[Col. 0965A] Brother, do not be ashamed to confess your sins. For I too am a sinner, and perhaps I have committed things worse than those you have done. I give this admonition because, as blessed Gregory says (*Moralia*, book XXII, chapter 9), it is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and, after committing it, not to disclose it by confessing but to defend it by denial, and, when convicted, to multiply it by defending it. Although we do not fear perpetrating abominable crimes at the devil’s instigation, we are ashamed, at his prompting, to confess in words the same things that we accomplished in deeds without shame; and before a human being, who is like us and perhaps subject to the same passions, we are embarrassed to say what we feared to commit before the Lord, who sees all things, without any shame of mind, as a detestable act. Let us therefore freely confess what we committed under no compulsion. But if we conceal our crimes, they will be revealed by the one who is both the accuser and instigator of sin. He himself incites us here to sin; and when we have sinned, he accuses us. If, therefore, in this life we forestall him and become accusers of our own crime, we shall escape the wickedness of the devil, our enemy and accuser, as Paul testifies when he says: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged” (I Corinthians II).

When the priest sees him ashamed, he should continue again: Perhaps, dearest one, not everything you have done now comes to mind. I shall question you. Take care, lest, persuaded by the devil, you presume to conceal anything. — Then he shall question him in order.

[Col. 0965C] Have you committed homicide, whether by accident, intentionally, in vengeance for relatives, at the command of your master, or in a public war? If you did it voluntarily, you must do penance for seven years; if unwillingly or by accident, five years. If in vengeance for a relative, one year, and during the following two years three periods of Lent and the appointed weekdays. If in war, forty days. If you are free and killed a slave at your master’s command, one year, and during the following two years three periods of Lent and the appointed weekdays. If the slave killed deserved death, do penance for forty days.

Have you cut off someone’s hands or feet, torn out a person’s eyes, or wounded a man? For amputation, you must do penance for one year; for a wound, do penance for forty days.

[Col. 0965D] Have you committed perjury, whether out of worldly greed, under compulsion and necessity, through obstinacy, on account of relatives, in ignorance, or have you knowingly led others into perjury? If you knowingly committed perjury and led others into perjury, you must do penance for seven years. If in ignorance, one year and three periods of Lent.

Have you committed theft, sacrilege, breaking and entering, or robbery, taking what was not yours? If you broke into houses at night and took four-footed animals, or a more serious amount worth forty solidi, you must do penance for one year and return the value. If you do not return it, do penance for two years. If you committed a greater theft, you must do penance for three years. And if you did it repeatedly, seven years. For a small theft, twenty days; for a child, ten days.

You have committed adultery with another man’s wife or betrothed, or corrupted a virgin, whether with a nun or one dedicated to God, or with an unmarried woman, that is, without a husband, or with your own female slave. If you have committed adultery with another man’s wife or with a nun, do penance for seven years; with a virgin, for two years; with a widow, for one year. If you have dismissed your own wife and taken another, do penance for seven years. If with an unmarried woman, for three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast days. If with your own female slave, you must do penance for forty days.

You have had intercourse with your wife or female slave from behind. If you have done this, you must do penance for forty days.

[Col. 0966B] You have had intercourse with your wife forty days before childbirth; you must do penance for forty days.

You have married on the Lord’s Day; you must do penance for three days.

You have abducted a virgin or widow; you must do penance for three years.

You have committed fornication as the Sodomites did, with animals, or with your mother or sister; you must do penance for fifteen or twelve years.

You have defiled yourself with your wife during Lent. If you have done this, you must do penance for one year, or give twenty-six solidi as alms. If it happened through drunkenness, do penance for forty days.

This too must be observed: twenty days before Christmas and Pentecost, on every Sunday [Col. 0966C], and after the pregnancy has become apparent, a man must abstain from his wife.

You have given false testimony out of greed or unknowingly; do penance for one year.

You have amputated a limb; do penance for three years.

You have hated your brother. For as long as you remained in that hatred, do penance on bread and water for the same length of time.

You have slandered someone to his superior or to his peers out of envy; do penance for forty days.

You have violated a tomb in committing theft; do penance for two years.

Some negligence concerning the Lord’s sacrifice has happened to you; do penance for one hundred and forty days.

You have consulted magicians, soothsayers, enchanters, or diviners, or have made vows at trees or springs [Col. 0966D]; do penance for three years.

You have taken some money from a church. Either restore fourfold, or do penance for three years.

You have caused someone’s ruin through an unjust denunciation; do penance for three years.

You have led or sent someone into captivity; do penance for three years.

The Helmstedt edition reads: “You have led or sent any Christian man into captivity; three years.” Burchard, in Book XIX, gives a somewhat fuller version, with some difference: “You have led, sent, or sold someone into captivity, except for the sake of the common peace. If you have done this, bring him back [Col. 0967A] if you can. If not, do penance for two years with the prescribed fast days.”

You have burned another person’s house or threshing floor; do penance for three years.

You have vomited through drunkenness; do penance for fifteen days. If through strife, forty days. If unknowingly, six days.

The Helmstedt edition reads: “You have vomited through drunkenness; do penance for fifteen days. If through strife, forty. If unknowingly, seven days. Likewise if you have eaten blood.”

You have eaten carrion or flesh torn by beasts; do penance for forty days. Likewise if you have eaten blood.

You have drunk from a liquid in which a mouse or weasel was found dead [Col. 0967B]; do penance for forty days.

You have despised a fast proclaimed by the Church or decreed by superiors; do penance for forty days. If during Lent, for one year.

You have suffocated your infant; you must do penance for five or three years.

You have drunk some harmful potion—that is, herbs or other substances—so that you could not have children, or you gave it to another, or wished to kill someone with a deadly potion, or taught another to do this, or tasted a man’s semen so that he might burn with love for you, or drank chrism, or gave it to another to overturn God’s judgment, and so forth. If you have done anything of this kind, do penance for seven years.

You have deliberately killed your unborn children; do penance for ten years. [Col. 0967C] If you killed a son or daughter, for twelve years. If the child was not yet conceived, for one year. If conceived, for three years. If your infant died without baptism through your negligence, do penance for one year, and never be without some form of penance.

You have done or said something in any undertaking that you began through divination or magic; do penance for one year.

You have placed your child on a roof or upon a furnace for some healing purpose, or burned grain where a dead person had been; do penance for five years.

You have sung diabolical songs over the dead; do penance for twenty days.

You have joined yourself to a woman during her menstruation; do penance for forty [Col. 0967D] days.

You have had intercourse with your wife after she gave birth, before forty days had been completed; do penance for thirty days.

You have received the Lord’s sacrifice without first abstaining from your wife’s embrace for five or seven days; do penance for twenty days.

You have done some work on Sunday; do penance for seven days.

You have slandered or cursed someone out of envy; do penance for seven days. See above what follows.

[Col. 0968A] Concerning the periods during which married people must abstain from their wives. (From the same Penitential.)

CHAPTER 329. A married man shall abstain for forty days before Easter and Pentecost, or before Christmas, and throughout every Sunday night, and on Wednesday and Friday, and from the time the pregnancy becomes apparent until after the child is born. After the child is born, the wife shall abstain from church: thirty days if the child is a boy, forty days if it is a girl. A woman shall abstain from her husband for three months before childbirth and for forty days afterward. Whoever has intercourse during these days shall do penance for twenty days.

On the same matter.

CHAPTER 330. [Note: [Col. 0967D] Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 76.] Whoever has intercourse with his wife during Lent before Easter [Col. 0968B] and refuses to abstain from her shall do penance for one year [Helmstedt edition: fifteen years], or shall pay its price—namely, twenty-six solidi—to the church, or distribute it among the poor. If it happened through drunkenness and without habitual practice, he shall do penance for forty days.

That one must abstain from his spouse before Communion.

CHAPTER 331. [Note: [Col. 0967D] Burchard, Book I, chapter 22.] Every man must abstain from his own wife for seven, or five, or three days before holy Communion.

FROM BOOK II OF REGINO, ON ECCLESIASTICAL DISCIPLINE. Whoever kills a man in a feud.

(From the Penitential mentioned above.)

CHAPTER 23. [Note: [Col. 0967D] Burchard, Book VI, chapter 32.] Whoever kills a man in revenge for a brother or other relative shall do penance for one year [Col. 0968C] [Note: [Col. 0967D] “Let him do penance as for voluntarily committed homicides, since Truth itself says: ‘Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.’” [Col. 0968D] The Roman Penitential from Theodore contains the same provision. See above.] and observe three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast days during the following two years—that is, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

On the same matter. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 24. Whoever suddenly kills a man through anger, quarrelling, and drunkenness shall do penance for four years.

On the same matter. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 25. If a free man, at the command of his master, kills a slave, he shall do penance for forty days. If a free man, at the command of his master, kills an innocent man, he shall do penance for one year and, during the following two [Col. 0968D] years, observe three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast days.

If an ordained person commits homicide. (From the Penitential mentioned above.)

CHAPTER 46. [Note: [Col. 0968D] Halitgar, Book VI, chapter 1.] If a bishop or any ordained person commits homicide, he shall do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water.

If anyone consents or gives counsel that a man be killed. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 47. [Note: [Col. 0968D] Halitgar, ibid.] If anyone consents to a killing and gives counsel for it, and the deed is carried out, [Col. 0969A] he shall do penance for seven years. But if it is not carried out, he shall do penance for three years.

If anyone kills his kinsman or superior. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 48. If anyone kills his neighbor and kinsman, he shall do penance for ten years. Likewise, if anyone treacherously slaughters his superior and master.

Concerning those who consider homicide committed in war to be nothing. (From the Penitential mentioned above.)

CHAPTER 51. If anyone kills a man in a public war, he shall do penance for forty days.

Concerning a cleric who kills his neighbor. (From the same work.)

[Col. 0969B] CHAPTER 52. If a cleric commits homicide and kills his neighbor out of deliberate hatred, he shall do penance in exile for seven years.

Concerning parricides. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 53. If anyone commits this crime, some have judged that he should do penance for seven years, or that he should have completed fourteen years of penance; others, until the end of his life, like Cain, if he has committed a similar deed.

Concerning a woman whose son dies unbaptized through negligence. (From the Penitential mentioned above, chapter 17.)

CHAPTER 62. A woman who has given birth, whose son dies unbaptized through negligence, shall do penance for one year [Col. 0969C] and shall never be without some form of penance. But if it happened through the negligence of a priest, see Book I, chapter 129.

If a woman causes her child to be expelled. (From the same Penitential.)

CHAPTER 66. If a woman voluntarily loses her child in the womb before forty days, she shall do penance for one year. But if she kills it after forty days, she shall do penance for three years. If she loses it after it has become animated, she shall do penance as a homicide. Yet it makes a great difference whether she acts as a poor woman because of the difficulty of raising the child, or as a fornicator in order to conceal her crime.

Concerning a woman who kills a man by sorcery. (From the same Penitential, chapter 15.)

[Col. 0969D] CHAPTER 82. If a woman kills anyone by magical art—that is, by a potion or by some other means—she shall do penance for seven years. If she is a poor woman, she shall do penance for four years.

What if one unmarried and the other married commit adultery? (From the Penitential cited above.)

CHAPTER 134. If an unmarried man pollutes himself with another man’s wife, he shall do penance for two years. The same is to be observed concerning women.

[Col. 0970A] If a married man keeps his own female slave.

CHAPTER 135. If a married man keeps his own female slave, he shall do penance for one year, or for three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast days during another year; and for three months he shall first abstain from his wife. But the female slave, if she suffered violence, shall do penance for forty days; if she consented, she shall do penance for three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast days in one year.

If a layman has fornicated with a laywoman. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 136. [Note: [Col. 0969D] Burchard, Book IX, chapter 68.] If a layman has fornicated with a laywoman—that is, if both are unmarried and free from the law of marriage—they shall do penance for three years; and the more frequently and negligently they committed these sins, the more time and severity shall be added to their penance.

[Col. 0970B] On the fornication of various persons. (From the Roman Penitential [Note: [Col. 0969D] This is the same as the inquiry above, number 65, which reads: “The Roman Penitential, or one issued by Theodore the bishop or by the venerable priest Bede.”], of Theodore the bishop and Bede the priest.)

CHAPTER 246. If a young man sins with a virgin, he shall do penance for one year. If it happened once and by accident, his penance shall be lightened, but he shall do penance up to a full year. If a young man under thirty commits fornication, he shall do three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast days. If on account of this sin they have been reduced to human servitude, they shall do penance for forty days. If a married man has fornicated with a virgin, he shall do penance for two years, provided above all that he abstain from his wife. If his wife consented to it, an additional measure of penance shall also be imposed upon her. If a layman has fornicated with a laywoman, he shall do penance for three years; and the more frequently it occurred, the more time shall be added. A layman who defiles himself with a handmaid of God shall do penance for two years. If he has fathered a child by her, he shall do penance for three years. If he is unmarried, he shall do three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast days. If they are canons and commit fornication, one year; if frequently, two. Whoever is in orders shall do penance for three years. A monk without orders, or a canon who possesses orders, if they have fornicated with a lay girl, shall do penance for three years. If with a nun, they shall do penance for seven years. Monks who commit fornication while in orders shall do penance for seven years. If a monk takes a laywoman as wife, he shall do penance for three years, and she for two years and the prescribed fast days. If it continues as far as the begetting of a child, he shall do penance for four years. If he kills [someone], for seven years. If a bishop has committed fornication, he shall do penance for eight years. Others have judged twelve years of penance. After the third year he shall do lighter penance. A priest who fornicates with a girl shall do penance for four years, with three forty-day periods each year, and on Wednesday and Friday on bread and water. [Note: [Col. 0970D] Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 39.] If he has fornicated with a handmaid of God, he shall do penance for seven years. A bishop, priest, or deacon, if involved in fornication, perjury, and so forth. [Note: [Col. 0970D] As above in the first collection of Theodore’s chapters.]

Also concerning incest.

CHAPTER 247. If a young man takes his sister as wife, he shall do penance for five years. If his mother, for seven [Col. 0971A] years. And for as long as he lives, he shall never be without continence [penance].

Also another provision.

Whoever has fornicated with his mother shall do penance for fifteen years. Whoever has fornicated with his daughter or sister shall abstain from all flesh and do penance for fifteen years. If a mother has fornicated with her young son, she shall abstain from flesh for three years and fast until evening one day each week.

Another provision.

Whoever has a mother and daughter, two sisters, his father’s or brother’s wife, a paternal or maternal uncle’s wife, a niece or cousin, or whoever is joined in the first, second, or third degree of kinship, we wish to declare to such people that [Col. 0971B] they must separate. And, because of the Church’s new planting, they shall perform penance for seven years: during the first three years, three days each week—that is, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—forty days before Easter and twenty before the Mass of Saint John, and twenty before Christmas. During the remaining four years, on Wednesday and Friday, and for fourteen nights before the Mass of Saint John and the same number before Christmas. If one wishes to redeem this obligation, one shall give one denarius, or the value of one denarius, for each day. If poor, one shall give half a denarius.

On the defilement of boys.

CHAPTER 248. Boys who defile one another with their hands shall do penance for forty days, but older persons for one hundred days. Boys who defile one another between the thighs shall do penance for one hundred days, but older persons for three forty-day periods and the prescribed fast days. A small child oppressed by an older person shall do penance for seven days. If he consented, twenty days. A boy who voluntarily pollutes himself shall do penance for thirty days, but a young man for forty days.

On abstaining during menstruation, etc.

CHAPTER 249. Whoever has intercourse with a menstruating woman shall do penance for forty days. If anyone has intercourse with his wife from behind, he shall do penance for forty days. If from the rear, for three years, because it is a Sodomitic crime. Men who fornicate between the thighs shall do penance for one year. If from behind, for three years. If they are boys, they shall do penance for two years.

On women’s fornication.

CHAPTER 250. [Note: [Col. 0971D] Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 27, from Theodore’s Penitential alone.] A woman who fornicates by any device, whether with herself or with another woman, shall do penance for three years.

As above.

[Note: [Col. 0971D] Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 28, from Theodore’s Penitential.] If a nun fornicates with another nun by some contrivance, she shall do penance for seven years.

On lustful embracing.

CHAPTER 251. [Note: [Col. 0971D] Burchard, Book VII, chapter 42.] Whoever is polluted through lustful embraces of a woman or through a kiss shall do penance for thirty days. Whoever touches the flesh of the same woman immodestly shall do penance for three months. Whoever is polluted through obscene speech shall do penance for seven days. If a priest has kissed a woman through impure desire, he shall do penance for twenty days. If he has been polluted, he shall do penance for forty days. Whoever is polluted in a church during sleep shall do penance for three days. Whoever is polluted in sleep voluntarily shall rise, sing the seven penitential psalms, and do penance for thirty days. Whoever wished to sin in sleep but was not polluted shall sing thirty-four psalms.

On emission of semen.

CHAPTER 252. [Note: [Col. 0972D] Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 43.] If a cleric emits semen without touching himself, he shall do penance for seven days. If he touches himself with his hand, twenty days. If he is a deacon, thirty days. If a priest, four weeks. If a priest emits semen [Col. 0972B] through thought, he shall do penance for seven days. A monk likewise. Whoever voluntarily emits semen in a church shall do penance, if he is a cleric, for fourteen days; if a monk or deacon, thirty days; if a priest, forty; if a bishop, fifty days.

On fornication with quadrupeds.

CHAPTER 253. [Note: [Col. 0972D] Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 32.] Whoever sins with an animal shall do penance for one year. Some judge ten years, some seven, some four, and some one hundred days. If a cleric has fornicated with a quadruped, he shall do penance for two years; a subdeacon, three; a deacon and monk, five; a priest, seven; a bishop, ten.

On Sodomites.

CHAPTER 254. [Note: [Col. 0972D] Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 34.] Whoever fornicates as the Sodomites did: some have judged ten years, some seven, others one. Boys, one hundred days. Others have judged that, if it is habitual, a layman shall do penance for five years, a cleric for seven, a subdeacon and monk for eight, a deacon for ten, a priest for twelve, and a bishop for thirteen.

FROM THIS POINT, ON THEFT AND ROBBERY.

(From the Penitential mentioned above.)

CHAPTER 265. Whoever, overcome by greed, commits theft shall return what he took and do penance for five years.

On the same matter. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 267. Whoever has committed theft repeatedly shall do penance for seven years.

[Col. 0972D] As above.

CHAPTER 268. If anyone violates a tomb, he shall do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.

On the same matter. (From the same Penitential.)

CHAPTER 275. If anyone steals anything in any way from the church’s ministry, he shall do penance for seven years.

On perjury. (From the same Penitential.)

CHAPTER 324. [Note: [Col. 0972D] Burchard, Book XII, chapter 8.] Whoever knowingly commits perjury [Col. 0973A] shall do penance for seven years and afterward receive Communion.

From the Penitential mentioned above.

CHAPTER 325. If anyone commits perjury, he shall not afterward be admitted to an oath.

On the same matter. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 326. [Note: [Col. 0973D] Burchard, Book XII, chapter 1.] If anyone suspects that he is being induced to commit perjury, yet swears with consent, he shall do penance for two years [Note: [Col. 0973D] He shall do penance for sixty days and, in the following years, shall never be without severe penance.]

As above.

CHAPTER 327. [Note: [Col. 0973D] Burchard, Book XII, chapter 3.] If anyone commits perjury out of greed, he shall sell all his possessions and distribute them to the poor, and, entering a monastery, submit himself to perpetual penance.

[Col. 0973B] As above.

CHAPTER 328. If anyone commits perjury, laymen shall do penance for three years, clerics for five, subdeacons for six, deacons for eight, priests for ten, and bishops for twelve years.

On enchanters, sorcerers, and diviners. (From the Penitential mentioned above.)

CHAPTER 355. [Note: [Col. 0973D] Burchard, Book X, chapter 31.] Those who perform nocturnal sacrifices to demons or invoke demons through incantations shall be punished by death.

CHAPTER 356. Those who serve auguries or divinations shall do penance for five years. Those who raise storms shall do penance for seven years.

CHAPTER 357. If a woman performs diabolical divinations or incantations [Col. 0973C], she shall do penance for one year, or three forty-day periods, or forty days, according to the character of the offense.

CHAPTER 358. [Note: [Col. 0973D] Burchard, Book X, chapter 9.] All who observe auguries, or lots called false “saints,” or divinations, or who consult any kind of Scripture by lot, or make or fulfill vows at a tree, stone, or any object except a church, shall be excommunicated. If they come to penance, clerics shall do penance for three years, laymen for one and a half years.

On carrion. (From the Penitential mentioned above.)

CHAPTER 369. [Note: [Col. 0973D] Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 88.] Whoever eats unclean meat, [Col. 0973D] or carrion, or flesh torn by a beast, shall do penance for forty days. If anyone has eaten it under the compulsion of famine, let him do much lighter penance.

CHAPTER 370. Whoever knowingly eats food obtained by fraud, seizure, or theft shall do penance, if poor, for seven days; if powerful, for forty days. The sick, if they know what they are eating, shall do penance for fifteen days.

CHAPTER 371. [Note: [Col. 0973D] Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 106.] Whoever eats or drinks something contaminated [Col. 0974A] by a domestic animal—that is, by a dog or cat—shall do penance for two days.

On liquid. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 372. [Note: [Col. 0974D] Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 106.] If anyone gives someone a liquid in which mice or weasels have died, he shall do penance, if a layman, for seven days. But if they are in a monastery, they shall sing two hundred psalms. Whoever afterward learns that he drank such a beverage shall sing one psalter.

On blood. (From the same work.)

CHAPTER 373. If anyone eats the blood of an animal, he shall do penance for forty days.

Also, that no one should eat blood.

[Col. 0974B] CHAPTER 374. The faithful must be admonished that no one should presume to eat blood. For at the beginning, when we read that God gave human beings permission to eat flesh, blood was forbidden. For the Lord says to Noah and his sons: “Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you, except that you shall not eat flesh with its blood. For I shall require your blood, the blood of your lives, from the hand of every beast and from the hand of man.” (Genesis 9:3–5.) This is forbidden not only very frequently in the Old Law, but also in the New Testament the apostles, after extensive deliberation, wrote to the gentiles of the primitive Church that they should abstain from the pollutions of idols and from fornication, from things strangled, and from blood. Explaining this, Jerome says: “According to the literal sense [Note: [Col. 0974D] ‘And according to the literal sense, these precepts apply to every chosen, royal, and priestly race, which properly refers to Christians, who have been anointed with spiritual oil, concerning which it is written: “Your God has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions”: these precepts, and so forth.],” he says, “these precepts [Col. 0974C] apply to every Christian: that he should not eat carrion, whether of birds or of cattle whose blood has not been poured out. The letter sent by the apostles from Jerusalem necessarily commands that these things be observed. And flesh seized by a beast, because it too has likewise been strangled. [Note: [Col. 0974D] Saint Jerome, On Ezekiel, chapter 45.] And ‘blood,’ that is, not eating it with the blood. If, then, these things were written for those coming from gentile life, as the first beginnings of faith and because of their long-established gentile custom—as though these things alone were sufficient for their salvation—what transgressor would consider these things trivial? It must also be considered that strangled flesh and blood are equated with idolatry and fornication. Therefore let everyone be informed how great a sacrilege it is to eat blood, since it is compared with idols and fornication. If anyone violates these commands of the Lord and the apostles, let him be suspended from ecclesiastical communion until he does worthy penance.”

On liquid into which a mouse has fallen. (From the Penitential mentioned above.)

CHAPTER 434. If a mouse falls into a liquid, it shall be removed, the liquid sprinkled with blessed water, and it may be consumed. But if the mouse is found dead, the entire liquid shall be discarded [Col. 0975A]. If there is a large quantity of liquid, let it be purified, sprinkled with holy water, and consumed if necessary. If a dead mouse is found in flour, curdled milk, or honey, whatever surrounds it shall be thrown out; the remainder may be consumed.

If anyone violates a tomb, and so forth. (As above.)

CHAPTER 435. If anyone violates a tomb, he shall do penance for seven years, three on bread and water. If anyone makes amulets or magical bindings, which is detestable, he shall do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. If anyone eats carrion or anything sacrificed to idols, he shall fast for twelve weeks. If anyone voluntarily amputates any limb from himself, he shall do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water [Col. 0975B]. If anyone exacts usury of any kind, he shall do penance in the same way. If anyone violently or by any evil device improperly invades or takes another’s property, he shall do penance in the same way. If anyone improperly sells a human being, he shall do penance in the same way. If anyone voluntarily burns another’s threshing floor or house, he shall do penance in the same way. If anyone strikes someone in anger and sheds his blood or makes him disabled, he shall do penance for forty days on bread and water.

If an excommunicated person dies. (As above.)

CHAPTER 436. If an excommunicated person dies, having already confessed, and was unable to come to the priest because death overtook him [Col. 0975C] at home or on the road, his relatives shall make an offering for him at the altar and give a ransom for captives [Note: [Col. 0975D] The remaining provisions concerning one who has stolen out of necessity and concerning the price of ransom are given above in the first collection of Theodore’s chapters (Burchard, Book XI, chapter 51).].

II. FROM BURCHARD, omitting the chapters already cited above.

Concerning those who seek the future in books. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

BOOK X, CHAPTER 26. The future must not be sought by lot in tablets or books; and no one should presume to cast lots in the Psalter, the Gospel, or other things, nor observe any divinations in any matter. If anyone does so, he shall do penance for forty days.

Concerning those who have been licentious in speech. [Col. 0975D] (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

CHAPTER 56. If anyone has been licentious in speech, let him be cleansed by a three-day penance.

Concerning those who swear falsely on the hand of a bishop, or on a consecrated or unconsecrated cross. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

BOOK XII, CHAPTER 5. Whoever swears falsely on the hand of a bishop or on a consecrated cross shall do penance for three years. But if on an unconsecrated cross, he shall do penance for one year. Whoever has been deceived and, unaware, has sworn falsely, and later recognizes this, shall do penance for three forty-day periods.

[Col. 0976A] Concerning a bishop who has committed natural fornication and others. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

BOOK XVII, CHAPTER 39. If a bishop commits natural fornication, the synod has judged that he shall do penance for ten years and seek forgiveness from the Lord with many tears and almsgiving. A priest who is not bound by a monk’s vow and sins with a girl or prostitute shall do penance for three years, and during three Lents shall observe Wednesday and Friday, and always Saturday, on dry food. If with a handmaid of God or with a male, additional fasting shall be imposed—namely, seven years, if it is habitual. Likewise, deacons who are not monks shall do penance for two years, as shall monks without orders. If the deacons are monks, seven years; monks in orders, seven years [Col. 0976B]. Likewise, a bishop without a monk’s vow who sins with a girl or prostitute shall do penance for ten years. A cleric without a monk’s vow who fornicates with such a girl shall do penance for one year; if frequently, two years. If with a canoness, two years; if frequently, three years. If he fathers a child by her, four years; others say seven. Theodore said: A monk who commits fornication shall do penance for seven years.

That whenever anyone approaches penance, others ought to share in his fasts and prayers. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

BOOK XIX, CHAPTER 33. [Note: [Col. 0976D] Ivo, Part XV, chapter 36.] Whenever Christians [Col. 0976C] come to penance, we impose fasts; and we too ought to share their fast by fasting with them for one or two weeks, or as much as we can, lest what the Lord said to the Jewish priests be said to us: “Woe to you lawyers, who burden people and place heavy and unbearable burdens on their shoulders, while you yourselves do not touch those burdens with even one finger.” For no one can lift up one who is falling under a burden unless he bends down to extend his hand; nor can any physician heal the wounds of the sick unless he has shared in their foulness. Likewise, no priest or bishop can heal the wounds of sinners or remove sins from souls unless he does so with devoted care and tearful prayer. Therefore, dearest brothers, you must be concerned for sinners, since we are members of one another. And so, if we see someone lying in sins, let us hasten to call him to penance through our instruction. Whenever you give counsel to a sinner, immediately give him penance as well, telling him how much he must fast or redeem his sins by almsgiving, lest you forget what you have already told him and need to ask him again; perhaps he will be ashamed to confess his sins again, and it will be found that he is judged more severely.

[Col. 0977A] Concerning those who eat food touched by an unclean hand, or when a dog or another unclean animal has touched food. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

CHAPTER 89. If by chance someone touches food with an unclean hand, or if a dog, mouse, or unclean animal eats human blood, it does no harm; and whoever, driven by the necessity of hunger, eats an animal that seems unclean, whether bird or beast, shall do penance mercifully.

Concerning those who conceal a brother’s sin that leads to death. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

Whoever conceals a brother’s offense that leads even to death and does not rebuke him according to the evangelical rule—first between himself and the man alone, then before others, and then, if necessary, bringing the matter before the church—shall do penance for as long as the offense lasted.

Concerning those who come to confession: they must first be questioned about the resentment of envy and greed.

CHAPTER 144. Since homicide arises, as has been arranged above, from the resentment of envy, anger, and also greed, we have rightly, I think, judged that it should first be shown how this particular vice is to be completely corrected according to canonical priestly judgment; thereafter, according to the order of the vices, let the remedy follow, so that the penitent may find without delay, in each chapter, the means by which he wishes to be cleansed from whatever source.

III. FROM IVO.

Concerning those who become sorcerers through love. [Col. 0977C] (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

Part XV, chapter 116. If anyone becomes a sorcerer through love and harms no one: if he is a cleric, he shall do penance for one year on bread and water; if a subdeacon, two years; if a deacon, three, one of them on bread and water; if a layman, one and a half years. Especially if by this means someone has caused a woman to lose her child, each person shall add three years on bread and water, lest he be guilty of homicide. [Note: [Col. 0977C] The remaining provisions are noted above.]

IV. FROM GRATIAN.

[Col. 0978A]

What penalty should be imposed on one who commits perjury under compulsion. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

Cause 22, question 5, chapter 3. If anyone commits perjury under compulsion, to save his life, or for any cause or necessity, because he loved the body more than the soul, he shall do penance for three forty-day periods. Others, however, judge three years, one of them on bread and water.

Whoever has intercourse with an adulterous wife shall do penance for three years. (From Theodore’s Penitential.)

Cause 32, question 1, chapter 7. If anyone knows that his wife is adulterous and does not wish to dismiss her but keeps her in marriage [Col. 0978B], he shall do penance for three years and, for as long as she is doing penance, abstain from her.

Sufficient is the confession that is first offered to God and then to the priest.

Therefore Theodore of Canterbury says in his *Penitential*:

“Some say that sins ought to be confessed to God alone, as do the Greeks. Others judge that they ought to be confessed to priests, as does almost the whole holy Church. Both practices are carried out within the holy Church, and not without great benefit—provided only that we confess our sins to God, who remits sins. This is the practice of the perfect, so that with David we may say: ‘I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said: I will confess my iniquity against myself,’ and you forgave the guilt of my sin. Yet we must follow the institution of the Apostles, so that we confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, that we may be saved.

“Confession, therefore, which is made to God alone—the practice of the righteous—purifies sins.”  
[Note: Burchard too, and Ivo, cite this chapter from Theodore. The words “as do the Greeks,” as well as “as does almost the whole holy Church,” “this is the practice of the perfect,” and “the practice of the righteous,” are absent, just as they are absent from the added capitularies, canon 58, and likewise from the Council of Chalon II, canon 33. What the discipline in Theodore’s church actually was is sufficiently and abundantly declared by these final words of the old codex concerning the *Penitential*: “Reconciliation therefore does not exist in this province, because public penance does not exist.” Hence one may judge what ought to be thought concerning the many chapters attributed to Theodore. Corrected by Gratian.]

“But confession made to a priest teaches how those sins themselves are cleansed. For God, the author and giver of salvation and holiness, often provides this medicine of his penance through invisible administration, and often through the work of physicians.”  
[Note: The remainder has been reported above.]

[Col. 0977]

# FRAGMENTS FROM CERTAIN MANUSCRIPT CODICES (C)

## I. From the *Penitential* of Master Bartholomew, Bishop of Oxford, whose copy was communicated to me by Mr. Tonelerius, the most vigilant custodian of the library of Saint Victor

### Concerning the Sick Who Are in Danger of Death

(From Theodore’s *Penitential*.)

[Col. 0977D]

### Chapter XLVIII

From sick persons placed in danger of death, priests must diligently seek a pure confession of sins. The amount of penance, however, is not to be imposed upon them, but is to be made known to them; and, with the prayers of their friends and their efforts at almsgiving, its burden is to be lightened, lest, if they should die, they become excluded from communion or from the fellowship of forgiveness because they remain bound by it.

If, having been rescued from this danger by divine providence, they recover, they must carefully observe the measure of penance imposed by their confessor. Therefore, in accordance with canonical authority, lest the door of mercy seem closed to them, they are to be strengthened by ecclesiastical prayers and consolations with the sacred anointing of oil, and, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers, refreshed with communion as viaticum.  
[Note: Up to this point, Burchard, book XVIII, chapter 14.]

If, however, the sin was mortal but hidden, the penance that would be imposed if the sin were public is to be made known to them. Nothing is to be imposed that cannot be observed without making the sin public, such as doing penance outside the church, and similar practices that are to be enjoined only upon laypersons who sin publicly. From this they should understand what they are bound to do by merit, or how much leniency is shown them, since through secret confession they have become their own first accusers; and, in place of the shame they would have endured in public penance, they should compensate with more abundant contrition and devotion of heart, together with works of charity.

## II. From the interrogations to be given for confession, which are appended to the most ancient Collection of Canons in the codex of the illustrious Antonius Vion, Lord of Hérouval

Theodore said:

“If a monk commits fornication with a girl, let him do penance for three years. If with a nun, let him do penance for seven years. A layman who defiles himself with a servant of God, for two years. If he has a son by her, for three years. If without intercourse, for three Lents. Some judge forty days.”  
[Note: See Bede’s canons concerning remedies for sins, *Penitential*, book I, in the Angers edition of J. Morin, in the appendix to the book on Penance.]

## III. From the Collection of Canons Preserved in the Library of Saint Victor

### Chapter Concerning Simony

(From Theodore.)

No ordained person shall presume to sell anything belonging to the ministries of the Church.

If any priest or deacon is found to have sold something belonging to the ministries of the Church, since he has committed sacrilege, it has been decided that he is not to be retained in the order of the Church. Nevertheless, it is to be left to the judgment of the bishop—whether he is worthy or unworthy—whether he is to be restored to his rank.

[Col. 0979]

# TITLES OF THE CHAPTERS OF THEODOR​E’S *PENITENTIAL*

Published by Henry Spelman in *Concilia Anglicana*, volume I. (C)

He says:

“This book, the *Penitential* of Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, is held in the celebrated library of Saint Benedict at Cambridge. But since it is too extensive to be conveniently inserted here, and permission to transcribe the entire codex is not easily obtained, we shall append only the chapters, or rather the headings of the chapters.”

V. According to Luke.

VIII. Concerning the moderation of penitents.  
IX. Concerning various homicides.  
X. Also concerning penance.  
XI. Concerning penitents, that they are not to be reconciled by priests unless the bishop orders it, according to the African Council.

XIII. Concerning capital crimes.  
XIV. The chapters concerning vices begin.  
XV. Concerning vainglory.  
XVI. Concerning envy.  
XVII. Concerning anger.  
XVIII. Concerning worldly sorrow.  
XIX. Concerning avarice.  
XX. Concerning gluttony.  
XXI. Concerning lust.

XXXIII. Concerning idolatry and sacrilege; and those who worship angels; and magicians, diviners, sorcerers, lot-casters, fortune-tellers, and those who fulfill vows except at the church of God; and those who go at the January Kalends to the “little deer” and the “old woman”; and astrologers and senders of storms.

# CERTAIN CHAPTERS PUBLISHED BY THE MOST REVEREND AND LEARNED LUCA DACHERIUS IN *SPICILEGIUM*, VOLUME IX, COLLATED WITH AND CORRECTED ACCORDING TO THEODORE’S *PENITENTIAL*

[Col. 0981B]

In Theodore’s chapters, chapter VIII reads: “They work except on the Lord’s Day.” In the *Penitential*: “And they work even on the Lord’s Day.” See the notes.

In chapter XIII: “In the third proximity of the flesh, according to the Greeks, it is permitted to marry.” In the *Penitential*: “In the third degree of kinship of the flesh.”

In the same chapter: “In the third province it is not permitted to take another man’s wife after his death.” In the *Penitential*: “Nevertheless, in the third degree of kinship it is not permitted.”

In chapter XIX: “And his relatives ought to fast on the fifth day.” In the *Penitential*: “And his relatives ought to fast for seven days.”

In chapter XXIII: “Likewise livestock, if necessary, for an equal [price].” In the *Penitential*: “Likewise livestock may be exchanged for an equal price, if necessary.”

In chapter XXV: “At the Lord’s Supper, incense is burned at the Nativity of the saints out of reverence for the day.” In the *Penitential*: “The Lord’s incense is to be burned at the Nativity of the saints out of reverence for the day.”

[Col. 0981D]

In chapter XXIX: “On that day before the Nativity of the Lord, etc., the Romans eat; when evening has been announced, the Greeks sing Mass.” In the *Penitential*: “The Romans eat; but the Greeks, when evening has been announced, dine after Mass.”

In chapter XLII: “Clerics are in no way permitted to fight, except in a multitude or by the counsel of the servants of God.” In the *Penitential*: “Although it belongs to many, it is permitted by the counsel of the servants of God.” See the notes.

In chapter XLVI: “Nor ought a bishop to use force in the place.” In the *Penitential*: “Nor ought a bishop forcibly to retain an abbot in his place.”

In chapter XLVIII: “And let him leave the priest in the former place.” In the *Penitential*: “And let him leave him in the former place.”

In chapter LXXIV: “If someone buys a pregnant woman who was previously free, he is free; the one who is born is a slave.” In the *Penitential*: “If someone buys a pregnant woman, the one born from her is free.” See the notes.

In chapter LXXVI: “If he is ill, or if she is ill, let them be separated entirely by the consent of both.” In the *Penitential*: “Whether he is ill or she is ill, nevertheless they are not to be separated except by the consent of both.”

In chapter LXXXIX: “A bishop and an abbot may have a wicked man as a slave.” In the *Penitential*: “Wicked men may have a slave.”

In chapter XC: “And there celebrate Masses for them; then, with singing, to the burial places.” In the *Penitential*: “Then carry them with singing to the graves.”

In chapter CII: “Parents are not permitted to give a betrothed girl to anyone unless she entirely resists; nevertheless, she may go to a monastery.” In the *Penitential*: “Parents are not permitted to give a betrothed girl to another man unless she entirely resists; nevertheless, she may go to a monastery if she wishes.”

In chapter CX: “He who reads only the Gospel places the *culpa* (‘fault’) on his shoulder, but not in the other readings.” In the *Penitential*: “If a priest sings the responsories at Mass, he is not to remove his *cappa*; but when reading the Gospel, he is to place it upon his shoulders.”

Thus chapters that could scarcely be understood are corrected, with the aid of ancient codices of the *Penitential*, so that their true and certain meaning can now easily be discerned.

[Col. 0983]

# OUR *PENITENTIAL*

Collated with certain chapters and canons excerpted from Theodore’s own *Penitential*, from which are gathered not only variant readings but also authorities of the greatest importance, by which the truth and authority of the *Penitential* itself are confirmed. (C)

## CHAPTER I OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

[Col. 0983A]

In a church in which the corpses of unbelievers are buried, it is not permitted to celebrate the sacrifice.

Alternatively, in the chapters published by the Reverend Luca Acherius, chapter LXVIII reads:

“No dead persons are to be buried in a consecrated church. But if dead persons were buried there before it was consecrated, it is not to be consecrated.”

But if it appears suitable for consecration, it is to be pulled down from there and rebuilt after its timbers have been scraped or washed. If it had previously been consecrated, Masses may be celebrated in it if religious persons were buried there.

Otherwise, from the same chapter cited above:

“If it has been moved from there to another place, or if its boards have been washed, whatever church has been moved to another place is to be consecrated again. But if it has been moved within the same place, holy water is to be sprinkled upon it.”

But Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian, from the Council of Agrippina, report the passage, as it is read in the *Penitential*, with only a few changes:

Burchard, book III, chapter 38, from the Council of Agrippina, canon 23: “after the bodies have been removed from there and the walls scraped, etc.”

Gratian, *Decree*, part III, distinction 50, chapter 28: “and after the walls or timbers of the place have been scraped.”

But if it is pagan, it is better to cleanse it in this way and throw [the pagan body] outside.

Alternatively, chapter XXXVI:

“The dead Gentiles are to be expelled from holy places.”

Burchard, book III, chapter 13; Ivo, part III, chapter 15; Gratian, *Decree*, part III, distinction 1, chapter 27, from the Council of Orléans, canon 3:

“It is not permitted to consecrate a church in which a pagan has been buried, nor to celebrate Masses in it; rather, [the body] must be thrown outside and the church cleansed.”

A layman ought not to read a lesson in churches, nor say “Alleluia,” but only psalms or responsories without “Alleluia.”

In chapter XXVII the words are transposed. In Burchard, however, book VIII, chapter 87, and Ivo, part III, chapter 105, they are read in the same order in which they lie in the *Penitential*, and are cited from the Council of Mainz, canon 18.

## CHAPTER II OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

A bishop may confirm in the countryside if necessary.

Burchard, book IV, chapter 68, from the Council of Rheims, canon 10:

“A bishop may confirm in the countryside if necessary.”

A bishop ought not to compel an abbot to go to a synod unless there is also some reasonable cause.

Burchard, book VIII, chapter 73, from the Council of Tours, canon 2:

“A bishop ought not to compel an abbot to go to a synod unless some reasonable cause exists.”

[Col. 0983D]

If a priest who has been ordained discovers that he has not been baptized, he is to be baptized and ordained again, together with all those whom he previously baptized.

Chapter LXVII:

“Whoever is uncertain about baptism is to be baptized again.”

Burchard, book IV, chapter 74; Ivo, part I, chapter 268; Gratian, *Decree*, part II, cause 1, question 1, canon 9:

“If an ordained priest discovers that he has not been baptized, he is to be baptized and ordained again.”

Ivo, from the Council at Compiègne, canon 5, adds what is found in the old codex of the *Penitential*:

“And all those whom he previously baptized.”

A deacon is not permitted to assign penance to anyone. Bishops or priests must assign it.

Chapter XLIII:

“A deacon is not permitted to judge penance for anyone, but only bishops or priests.”

In the margin, for the purpose of correction, is placed: “to impose.” Theodore nevertheless uses the expression “to judge penance” elsewhere, in the chapter concerning abbots:

“Nor is it the freedom of a monastery to judge penance for secular persons.”

After Theodore, the First Council of Germany, canon 2, says:

“And let each prefect have one priest who can judge and impose penance upon those who confess their sins.”

The Council of Vermer, canon 1:

“But we judge his penance.”

Regino, book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 95:

“Thus others ought not to usurp the judgments concerning penitents.”

[Col. 0984B]

This is repeated by Burchard, book XIX, chapter 153. The same wording is found in the most ancient codex of the Roman Order in the library of Abbot Constantine Goetanus, from which the distinguished J. Morin reported these quoted words in book IV of his *Penitential*, chapter 18.

## CHAPTER III OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

At the ordination of a bishop, Mass ought to be sung by the bishop who ordains him.

Theodore, chapter I:

“At the ordination of a bishop, or priest, or deacon, or subdeacon, the bishop ought to celebrate Mass.”

Burchard, book I, chapter 225; Ivo, part IV, chapter 338, from the sayings of Theodore the Archbishop:

“At the ordination of a bishop, the one who ordains ought to celebrate Mass, and the one who is ordained likewise.”

## CHAPTER IV OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

[Col. 0984C]

We believe no one to be perfected in baptism without the bishop’s confirmation; nevertheless, we do not dispute the bishop’s confirmation. Yet chrism was established at the Council of Nicaea.

Chapter IV:

“We believe no one to be perfected in baptism without the bishop’s confirmation; nevertheless, we do not despair.”

It is not absurd for chrism-soaked cloths to be placed again upon another baptized person.

Burchard, book IV, chapter 94, from the Council at Beauvais, canon 8:

“If someone wishes to anoint a chrism-cloth again and place it upon another baptized person, this is not absurd.”

Gratian, *Decree*, part II, distinction 4, canon 121:

“A cloth with chrism.”

At the catechumenate, at baptism, and at confirmation, one person may serve as sponsor if necessary. This is not, however, the custom. At each rite, individual sponsors are received.

Burchard, book IV, chapter 24, from the Council of Mainz:

“At the catechumenate, at baptism, and at confirmation, one sponsor may be appointed if necessity compels it. Yet this is not the Roman custom. Rather, at each rite, individual sponsors are received.”

It is not permitted to receive as a sponsor someone who has not been baptized.

Burchard, book IV, chapter 26, from the Council of Mainz, canon 2:

“In baptism or chrismation, someone who has not been baptized or confirmed cannot receive another as a son.”

The same appears in Ivo, part I, chapter 220.

The baptized are not permitted to eat with catechumens, and even less with Gentiles.

Burchard, book IV, chapter 95:

“Catechumens ought not to eat with the baptized, nor give them a kiss, and even less ought a Gentile do so.”

## CHAPTER V OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

Although Dionysius the Areopagite says that one blasphemes God who offers Masses for an evil man, Augustine nevertheless says that this ought to be done for all Christians, because it benefits either them, or those who offer, or those who ask.

Chapter LVI:

“He blasphemes the Lord who offers Masses to the Lord for an evil man.”

Augustine says that what benefits either him, or the one offering, or consoles the living, ought to be done for all Christians.

Burchard and Ivo read the text found in the old codex of the *Penitential*, with only these changes:

“Because it will benefit either them, or those who offer, or those who ask.”

In Burchard, book III, chapter 65, and in Ivo, book III, chapter 67:

“Because it benefits either them, or will benefit those who offer.”

## CHAPTER VI OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

A monk is not permitted to make a vow without the consent of his abbot; otherwise, it must be broken.

Burchard, book VIII, chapter 9; Ivo, part VII, chapter 32; and Gratian, *Decree*, part II, cause 20, question 4, canon 2, from the sayings of Basil:

“A monk, etc. If, however, he has made a vow, it must be broken.”

## CHAPTER VII OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

Women are not to veil the altar with a corporal, nor place offerings or a chalice upon the altar; nor are they to stand among the ordained in church; nor are they to sit among priests at a banquet.

Burchard, book VIII, chapter 84, from the Council of Rheims in the presence of Emperor Louis, canon 5:

“A woman is not to give penance, nor place a corporal with an offering or a chalice upon the altar; she is not to stand among the ordained in church, nor sit among priests at a banquet.”

## CHAPTER VIII OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

The Greeks do not give the flesh of animals that have died naturally to their pigs. Nevertheless, it is permitted to take their hides for footwear, and wool and horns, but not for anything sacred.

Chapter X:

“But the Greeks do not give carrion to their pigs. The hides of carrion may be taken for footwear, etc.; but not for anything [sacred], etc.”

## CHAPTER XI OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

A woman who has conceived is to abstain from her husband for three months before giving birth, and after the period of purification—that is, forty days and nights—whether she has borne a male or a female child.

Chapter XXI:

“Women during their menstrual period are not to enter the church, nor receive communion—neither nuns nor laywomen. If they presume to do so, let those who enter the church before the blood after childbirth has been cleansed do penance for three weeks, that is, forty days.”

A legitimate marriage may not be dissolved without the consent of both. One spouse may, however, give the other permission, with the advice of the bishop, to enter the service of God in a monastery; and the other may marry if, according to the Greeks, they were in their first marriage.

Regino, book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 107, from the sayings of Jerome. A fifth case is added: when either the man or the woman, with the other’s consent, has embraced the religious life, the other may enter a new marriage, but only with a boy or girl. See the excerpts of Egbert, Archbishop of York, chapter 118.

Also the African canon:

“Therefore a legitimate marriage may not be dissolved without the consent of both. One spouse may nevertheless, with the advice of the bishop, give the other permission to enter the service of God.”

Some also say:

“Whether a man or a woman has embraced the religious life with the other’s consent, the other may enter a new marriage, but only with a girl or boy, if he or she is unable to remain continent—a view I do not approve.”

Theodore adds the same in other words:

“And yet this is not canonical.”

Whoever reads Jerome and the canons of the African Council attentively will not deny that these passages cited from Jerome and from the canon of the African Council belong to Theodore rather than to those authorities.

After his wife’s death, a man may take another wife after one month. After her husband’s death, a woman may take another husband after one year.

Excerpt of Egbert of York, chapter 116:

“The synod said: After a woman’s death, a man may take another wife after one month; but after one year a woman may take another husband.”

If a woman leaves her husband, despising him, and refuses to return and be reconciled with him, then after five years, with the consent of the bishop, he may take another wife.

Excerpt of the Archbishop of York, chapter 122:

“The canon says: If a woman leaves her husband, etc., after five or seven years, with the consent of the bishop, he may take another wife if he cannot remain continent; and let him do penance for three years, or even for as long as he lives, because according to the Lord’s judgment he is proved an adulterer.”

If a woman has been carried away captive by force and cannot be ransomed, [the man may] take another after one year. Likewise, if her husband has been carried into captivity, let the woman wait five years. The same applies to a woman if such things happen to her.

Excerpt of Egbert, Archbishop of York, chapter 122:

“The canon says: If someone’s wife has been carried into captivity and cannot be ransomed, let him take another after the seventh year. If afterward his own wife—that is, the former wife—returns from captivity, let him take her back and dismiss the later wife. Likewise, she is to act in the same way, as we said above, if such things happen to her husband.”

Two brothers may also marry two sisters; and a father and son may marry a mother and daughter.

Chapter LXXV:

“A father and son may have a mother and daughter in marriage.”

[Col. 0986D]

If a man and woman have joined themselves in marriage, and afterward the woman says that she cannot [have intercourse] with her husband, and someone can prove that this is true, let her take another husband.

Rabanus, in his letter to Heribald, chapter 29:

“We respond, not with authority, but from the statutes of certain persons, in which it is written: If a man and woman have joined themselves in marriage, and afterward the woman says of her husband that she cannot marry him, if she can prove by a just judgment that this is true, let her take another.”

Regino, book XI, chapter 242:

“that she cannot have intercourse with him.”

Burchard adds, book IX, chapter 40:

“But if he has taken another, let them be separated.”

Ivo, part VIII, chapter 79:

“Let her take another, because, according to the Apostle, her husband was unable to render the marital debt to her.”

A betrothed girl may not be given by her parents to another man unless she entirely resists; nevertheless, she may go to a monastery if she wishes.

If the betrothed woman does not wish to live with the man to whom she is betrothed, the money he gave is to be returned to him, with one-third added.

Chapter LXXXI:

“A woman betrothed to a man; afterward she does not wish to live with him: let her return the money that was given to her, and let her add one-third of her property.”

The earlier words, as they are read in the old codex of the *Penitential*, appear in Burchard, book VIII, except for the words omitted there: “unless she entirely resists.”

## CHAPTER XII OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

If a master joined his male and female slaves in marriage, then, after the male or female slave has been freed, if the one who remains in servitude cannot be ransomed, the free person may marry a freeborn woman.

Chapter LXXI:

“If he is a slave, and the master does not wish that slave to marry the maidservant with him, let him allow him to take another, if she could not come to him.”

These words, which are excessively corrupt, are restored to their genuine and clear meaning by the preceding reading of the old codex of the *Penitential*. Their correctness is confirmed by the excerpts of Egbert of York, chapter 124:

“The canon says: If a master joins a male and female slave in marriage, then, after the male or female slave has been freed, if the one who remains in servitude cannot be ransomed, the free person may, as some judge, marry a freeborn person; nevertheless, according to the Lord’s judgment, he is proved an adulterer.”

## CHAPTER XIII OF THE *PENITENTIAL*

There are three proper fasts in the year: forty days before the Nativity of the Lord, and forty days after Pentecost.

Chapter 109:

“The proper fasts are three Lents.”

The sick may take food and drink at any hour, whenever they desire or are able, provided they can do so at a suitable time.

Burchard, book XVIII, chapter 20, from the Council of Mainz, canon 20:

“The sick may take food and drink at any hour, whenever they desire.”

[Col. 0987]

# THEODORE’S *PENITENTIAL*

Collated with certain testimonies excerpted from it and praised under the spurious names of Pope Hyginus, Fabianus, and others. These testimonies are restored to their true and certain author, Theodore.

[Col. 0987B]

Since all learned men agree that the works commonly cited by more recent authors under the names of Pope Hyginus, Fabianus, Eutychianus, and others are spurious, being composed from various excerpts gathered here and there, it is sufficient to restore to Theodore himself, as their true and certain author, those passages that belong to him, just as many works have already been restored to other Fathers by highly learned men.

Gratian, *Decree*, part II, cause 27, question 2, canon 27:

“Betrothed girls are not forbidden to choose a monastery.”

This is likewise proved by the authority of Pope Eusebius, who says:

“Parents are not permitted to give a betrothed girl to another man; nevertheless, she may choose a monastery.”

This is taken from Theodore’s *Penitential*, in the questions concerning marriage, where it reads:

“A betrothed girl may not be given by her parents, etc.”

*Decree*, part II, cause 28, question 1, canon 2.  
[Note: Burchard, book IX, chapters 59–60.]

“It is within the faithful person’s power, after baptism, to take back the wife whom he had dismissed before baptism.”

From the decree of Pope Eutychianus:

“If a Gentile has dismissed his Gentile wife before baptism, after baptism it will be within his power to have her or not to have her.”

This belongs to Theodore, who says the following in the questions concerning marriage:

“If someone has dismissed his Gentile wife, etc.”

In Gratian there follows chapter 3:

“A faithful person is not compelled to follow an unbeliever who departs.”

Pope Eutychianus likewise says:

“In the same way, if one of a married couple has been baptized and the other is a Gentile and does not wish to follow, as the Apostle says: ‘If the unbeliever departs, let him depart.’”

This too belongs to Theodore, who adds:

“In the same way, if one of them has been baptized and the other is a Gentile, etc.”

[Col. 0988C]

*Decree*, part II, cause 35, question 2, canon 3:

“Persons related by affinity may marry in the fifth generation; if they are found to have married in the fourth, they are not to be separated.”

Also Pope Fabianus:

“Concerning relatives who become related by affinity through a husband and wife: after the wife or husband has died, let them marry in the fifth generation; if they are found in the fourth, let them not be separated. But in the third degree of kinship it is not permitted to take another’s wife after her husband’s death. A man may equally marry those who are related to him by blood and those related by blood to his wife after his wife’s death.”

The same is cited shortly afterward under the name of Pope Julius, in the same cause and question, chapter 13.

But these matters belong to Theodore, who says in the questions concerning marriage:

“In the third degree of kinship of the flesh, it is permitted to marry according to the Greeks, as it is written in the law; in the fifth, according to the Romans. Nevertheless, in the third degree they do not dissolve the marriage if it has taken place afterward. Therefore let them marry in the fifth generation. And so with the rest.”

From all this it is evident that Theodore’s *Penitential*, and the excellent manuscript codex that we used, possess the greatest authority.

[Col. 0989]

# SELECTED CANONS FROM THE MOST ANCIENT COLLECTION OF CANONS IN THE CODEX OF HÉROUVAL

Concerning ecclesiastical teaching and discipline, which has been set forth in the foregoing monuments.

## PREFACE

For explaining the ecclesiastical discipline set forth in the foregoing monuments, the most suitable collection is the Collection of Canons that the distinguished Antonius Vion, Lord of Hérouval, generously supplied to me from his treasury, together with several ancient manuscript codices. Everything we have selected from it clearly demonstrates that the various rites found in Theodore’s *Penitential* and in its chapters—even those that seem most unusual—agree entirely with the testimonies of the Fathers and with the ancient canons of both Churches, Eastern and Western.

Concerning this collection, which is divided into ninety-two titles and is followed by a *Penitential*, John Morin testifies in the appendix to his book on Penance that he saw only a copy, in these words:
