“We cite three Angevin codices that may reasonably be called little *Penitentials*, etc. The first *Penitential* among the three that we present is found at the end of an ancient Collection of Canons, of which we have seen and possess only a copy. It is divided into ninety-two titles. The canons of councils, decrees of pontiffs, and sayings of the Fathers from which it was compiled are all ancient.”

Since this most learned man said this only in general and in passing, we shall, by gathering together whatever is most important in this collection, demonstrate its antiquity and excellence by several very powerful arguments.

### I

The Collection of Canons in the codex of Hérouval is not defiled by any letters of Pseudo-Isidore. Hence every learned person can easily understand that it is older not only than the collections of Gratian, Ivo, and Burchard, but also than those of Regino and even the Isidorian collection, since the later collections have been disfigured by the false wares of that collection, and increasingly shamefully so as they approach later times.

But what we noted concerning Theodore’s *Penitential*—namely, that the author of the Isidorian collection was not Isidore of Seville—is likewise confirmed by the ancient Collection of Canons in the codex of Hérouval. Although it reports certain letters of Isidore of Seville in full, it nowhere mentions the letters of the Isidorian collection.

Hincmarus, therefore, and those who follow his authority, wrongly attribute this collection to Isidore, Bishop of Seville. It ought to be attributed to Pseudo-Isidore; Riculfus, Bishop of Mainz, first made it public after it had been brought from Spain into Gaul. Christophorus Justellus explicitly proves this on Hincmarus’s own authority, in his preface concerning the ancient codex of the canons of the universal Church and its authority, in Hincmarus’s letter against Hincmarus, Bishop of Laon.

### II

The Collection of Canons in the codex of Hérouval is not only free from the letters fabricated by Pseudo-Isidore; it also presents genuine letters—which were later corrupted by countless errors and interpolations—complete and uninjured.

The only possible explanation for this is its extreme antiquity. Lest this claim seem to be made without evidence, it should be noted that, although Peter Gussanvillaeus used very many manuscript codices in correcting the letters of Saint Gregory, because the oldest codices are exceedingly rare, much remained that he rightly declared, by the sole discernment of his intellect and without the authority of any manuscript codex, not to belong to Gregory.

These same passages, with only two exceptions whose explanation we provide, are absent from the letters of Gregory included in the Collection of the codex of Hérouval. Everything foreign to Gregory I and to the other Roman pontiffs is absent from that collection. Thus this extremely ancient collection does not admit certain formulas of speech that became customary in later times.

For example, when the Church is described as “the Catholic, Apostolic, and Roman Church,” wherever the word “Roman” is found in the letters of Roman pontiffs of the fourth and fifth centuries, it is absent from those same letters when cited in the Collection of the codex of Hérouval. Indeed, we have clearly shown from this collection that not merely certain words or lines, but many incongruous passages extending over entire pages, were added to the letters of the Roman pontiffs.

Furthermore, the Collection of the codex of Hérouval vindicates certain books, cited by later—though ancient—authors under spurious names, for their certain and genuine authors. For example, the book *On the Contemplative Life*, commonly attributed to Prosper by authors of the ninth century, is correctly ascribed in this collection to Julianus Pomerius as its true and certain author, in agreement with Isidore of Seville.

All these facts most clearly prove that the Collection of the codex of Hérouval is extremely ancient and of the highest quality.

### III. The Collection of the Herovallian Codex Uses a Very Ancient Interpretation of the Greek Canons

The collection of the Herovallian codex uses a very ancient interpretation of the Greek canons, namely, Rufinus’s interpretation of the Nicene canons, which presents the sense rather than the actual wording, briefly and aphoristically, in almost the same manner in which they are cited in the ancient canons of the synods of the Gallican Church.

Thus Nicene canon 1 is reported summarily by the Fathers of the Second Synod of Arles, canon 7; Nicene canon 2 in the same Synod of Arles, canon 1; Nicene canon 3 in the same Synod of Arles, canon 3; and Nicene canon 4 in the same Synod of Arles, canon 5. Nicene canon 9 appears in the same Synod of Arles, canon 10, where it agrees so closely with Rufinus’s interpretation that, although the Greek text, Isidore, and Dionysius say “three years,” the Synod of Arles reads “five years,” using precisely the same words as Rufinus’s interpretation.

It is therefore surprising that the learned Christophorus Justellus, in the preface *On the Ancient Codex of the Universal Church*, when attempting to prove that the Nicene canons and others were customarily cited in the ancient synods of the Gallican Church according to the interpretation found in Isidore Mercator, refers the reader to the Second Synod of Arles. That synod follows Rufinus’s interpretation everywhere so fully that it does not even omit his errors.

The most learned Jacobus Sirmondus observed this in his notes on canon 15 of that synod, in these words:

> “This canon is wholly taken from Nicene canon 18—not as the synod itself reads it, but as canon 20 was interpreted by Rufinus, etc. Yet the Nicene Synod, according to the Greek copies, does not forbid deacons to distribute the Eucharist when presbyters are present; it forbids them to hand it to the presbyters themselves.”

And in his notes on canon 16:

> “This too is again a feature of Rufinus’s edition, canon 21: ‘And the Paulianists, who are Photinians, are to be rebaptized.’ For the Nicene Synod could not legislate concerning the Photinians, who had not yet arisen; it mentions only the Paulianists in canon 19, from which this passage is excerpted.”

The collection likewise frequently uses, for the canons of other councils, an interpretation similar to Rufinus’s interpretation of the Nicene council’s canons. This interpretation is often found in the Councils of Valence, Riez, Angers, the First Council of Tours, Agde, Epaon, and others, as well as in Gregory of Tours—namely, in connection with canons that at that time were regarded as almost apostolic.

It must not be denied that the ancient interpretation found in Isidore’s collection was used by the ancient synods of the Gallican Church, nor that the Dionysian interpretation was used as well. In these places we observe that the very ancient collection of the Herovallian codex differs little from the ancient canons of the Gallican Church in this kind of interpretation.

From these facts two conclusions may be drawn. First, that this very ancient collection was composed for the use of the Gallican Church. Second, whatever judgment one may form of the indiscriminate use of the various interpretations employed by the collection of canons in the Herovallian codex, it is at least earlier than the time of Charlemagne. After Pope Hadrian I brought the Dionysian copy to him, the Gallican Church thereafter used that Dionysian interpretation of the Greek canons continuously. Thus it came about that in the Latin Church not only was the meaning of the ecclesiastical canons everywhere almost identical, but their wording also was nearly everywhere the same. This has been clearly demonstrated by the most distinguished Christophorus Justellus in the preface *On the Ancient Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church*, by Jacobus Sirmondus in the preface to the *Ancient Councils of Gaul*, and more recently by the most learned Paschasius Quesnel in his excellent dissertation on this subject, found in volume II of the works of Saint Leo.

### IV. On the Title of the African Canons

Regarding the title of the African canons and their number or era, the collection of the Herovallian codex often agrees with the manuscript codex of the canons in the Barberini Library, which is praised in the latest edition of the Councils, and by several very learned men, as being extremely ancient.

### V. The Antiquity of the Collection

Finally, the fact that everything in this collection is ancient is demonstrated by the index of the canons and by the other list of bishops who subscribed the canons below them; all of these bishops lived before the time of Charlemagne.

Lest we seem to be presenting anything extraneous or useless, and omitting many matters as the index of chapters of the collection of the Herovallian codex makes clear, we have selected from this collection only those materials that pertain to the exposition of the Penitential of Theodore and that especially deserve attention: first, because of the various numbers, some of which indicate that many canons are missing from the printed editions; second, because of the canons themselves that are absent from the printed editions; and finally, because of the various readings by which the new edition of the Councils is illuminated.

In collecting these materials, and likewise in noting the other matters, let it be certain to you, reader, that if I have been unable to occupy the first place in wisdom, I shall at least occupy the second place in modesty. I may speak here, as it were, with the most wise and most modest Augustine, who says the following about his own works in the preface to the *Retractations*:

> “No one, unless he is foolish, will dare to criticize me merely because I criticize my own errors. But if he says that I ought not to have said things which later displeased even me, he speaks truly and agrees with me: for he is criticizing things of which I too am the critic. Nor ought I to criticize them if I ought to have said them. But whoever was unable to occupy the first place in wisdom should occupy the second place in modesty.”

## CHAPTER I. ON THE CATHOLIC FAITH AND THE CREED

[Col. 0991A]

### Canon of Autun, no. 1

If any presbyter, deacon, [Vulgate adds: subdeacon] or cleric has not recited the Creed of the Apostles and the faith of Saint Athanasius, let him be condemned by the bishop.

[Note: In the latest edition of the Councils this canon is appended to the other canons of the Council of Autun, as though it were an appendix. The very ancient collection of the Herovallian codex nevertheless confirms what is reported from another collection of canons in the library of Saint Benignus at Dijon, and from other sources in which it is cited and called the first canon of Autun.]

### Canon of Toledo, no. 2

[Note: *Council of Toledo III*, chapter 2.]

For the reverence of the most holy faith, and to strengthen the feeble minds of human beings, [Vulgate adds: “At the counsel of our most pious and glorious lord, King Reccared”] the holy synod decreed that throughout all the churches of Spain, Gaul, [Note: The word “Gaul” is absent from the edition. Yet both words—Gaul and Gallaecia—are required: Gaul, namely Narbonensis, on the one hand only; and Gallaecia because of the Suebi who had been converted to the faith. See the note in the margin of the latest edition of the Councils.] or Gallaecia, according to the practice of the Eastern churches, the Creed [Note: Another reading: “the Creed of the Council of Constantinople, that is, the Creed of the one hundred and fifty bishops”; in the edition the words “on every Sunday” are absent.] issued at Constantinople by the 150 holy bishops should be recited [preached] on every Sunday, before the Lord’s Prayer is said, and should be sung aloud by the entire people, so that the faith may possess true testimony [manifest testimony] and so that the hearts of the people, purified by faith, may approach to partake of the body and blood of Christ.

## CHAPTER III

### Pope Leo’s Judgment on Apocryphal Scripture

[Note: Letter of Pope Leo to Turibius, bishop of Astorga, chapter 15.]

It must therefore be taken care of, and provided for with the greatest priestly diligence, that false [Vulgate: corrupted] books, at variance with sincere truth, be used in no way for reading, because they contain the seeds of falsehood. Not only must these be prohibited, [Note: In the edition this is explained as follows: “But apocryphal writings, which under the names of the apostles contain much seed of falsehood, must not only be prohibited, etc.”] they must also be entirely removed and burned in the fire. For although there are certain things in them that may seem to possess an appearance of piety, they are never free from poisons. Through the allurements of fables they secretly bring it about that people, led astray by admiration for marvelous narratives, become entangled in the snares of every kind of error. Therefore, if any bishop has not prohibited apocryphal books from being kept [in private houses], or has permitted in the church books corrupted by heretics [Note: The edition reads: “Or if he has permitted in the church, under the name of canonical books, those books which have been corrupted by the adulterous revision of Priscillian.” The collection of the Herovallian codex is more correct, since Saint Leo is speaking generally of books corrupted by any heretics.] to be read, let him know that he is to be judged a heretic; for whoever does not recall others from error demonstrates that he himself is in error.

[Note: The following words are absent from the edition.]

The treatises of Saints Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and the other holy Fathers, and the expositions of the New and Old Testaments composed by the most renowned orthodox teachers, should be read in the church as the order of things requires.

## CHAPTER IV

[Note: In another collection of the Herovallian codex the title is: “In the name of Christ begin the decrees concerning books to be received and not to be received, written by Pope Gelasius together with seventy most learned bishops.”]

### Decretal Concerning Books to Be Received and Not to Be Received

[Col. 0993B]

These things were written by Pope Gelasius together with seventy learned bishops.

[Note: Some manuscript codices attribute this to Hormisdas. But since both collections of the Herovallian codex attribute it to Gelasius, in agreement with the most ancient and best manuscripts, and since Nicholas I also praises the same decrees under Gelasius’s name in Letter 42 to all the bishops of Gaul, Gelasius’s authorship is preferable.]

After the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures, upon which the Catholic Church has been founded by the grace of God, [Note: Here the edition inserts nearly an entire page of additional material that has no relevance to the matter. Why so much concerning the primacy of the Church, and indeed against heretics, when the question concerns books to be received and not to be received? Moreover, are not the following words wholly unrelated to the subject? “We also think it should be made known that, although the universal Catholic Church throughout the world is one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman, Catholic, and Apostolic Church has not been placed above the other churches by any synodal decrees, but has obtained primacy through the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior.” These same words are also falsely attributed to Pope Sylvester in the preface to the Council of Nicaea by certain authors, such as Aeneas, bishop of Paris, in book 6 of his work *Against the Greeks*. See volume VII of L. d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*. The same applies to the remaining material up to the words “these it receives.” Binius notes this: “This decree appears in distinction 15, canon 13. Its reading differs so greatly from the original that it cannot be established with sufficient certainty which is the true and pure text of Gelasius; nor is it greatly surprising if there are some passages that cause difficulty.”]

the same Church does not prohibit the following from being received: I. the holy Synod of Nicaea, the Synod of Constantinople, the First Synod of Ephesus, and the Synod of Chalcedon, which is the fourth synod.

### Continuation of the Decretal

[Col. 0994A]

Likewise, the works [Note: In another collection of the Herovallian codex these are listed in a different order, as follows: “The works of blessed Athanasius, Saint Basil, etc.; of John of Constantinople, etc.; of Caecilius Cyprian, etc.; of Gregory of Nazianzus, etc.; of Theophilus of Alexandria, etc.; of Hilary of Poitiers, etc.; of Ambrose of Milan, etc.; of Augustine of Hippo, etc.; of Jerome the presbyter; of Prosper, a most religious man, etc. Likewise, the letters of blessed Pope Leo,” etc.] of Saint Cyprian, martyr of Carthage; the works of blessed Gregory of Nazianzus; the works of Saint Basil of Cappadocia; the works of Saint John of Constantinople; the works of blessed Theophilus of Alexandria; the works of Saint Athanasius of Alexandria; the works of Saint Hilary of Poitiers; the works of Saint Augustine of Hippo; the works of Prosper; the works of blessed Pope Leo. [Note: The other collection of the Herovallian codex adds nearly the same words as the edition: “Likewise, the letter of blessed Pope Leo addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople: if anyone disputes its text down to a single iota and does not receive it reverently in every respect, let him be anathema.”]

We also receive the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect deviated from the holy Roman Church. [Note: The edition reads: “who in no respect deviated from communion with the holy Roman Church.” After these words the following are redundant: “Nor were they separated from her faith or preaching, but by the grace of God they remained participants in that communion until the last day of their lives.”]

Likewise, we decree that the decretal letters which the most blessed popes, at various times and from the city of Rome, issued in response to various consultations [Note: Another collection of the Herovallian codex reads: “consolations.”] are to be received with reverence.

We venerate in every way the acts of the holy martyrs, which shine with marvelous tortures and triumphs [Col. 0994B] and were written by Catholic men. [Note: The edition continues with other material which, since it was added to explain the same points stated above, is absent from the more accurate collections.]

But writings composed or falsified by heretics or ignorant persons are in no way to be received; such corruption can readily be detected in their very statements by ecclesiastical men. [Note: The edition reads: “And we receive with every honor the lives of all hermits, which the most blessed man Jerome wrote”; but it wrongly omits the indispensable words “or other orthodox Fathers.” Jerome wrote the lives of only a few hermits.]

We receive with every honor the lives of the Fathers—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed Jerome or other orthodox Fathers wrote.

### Continuation of the Decretal

[Col. 0995A]

Many churches imitate and venerate the acts of blessed Pope Sylvester on account of their ancient use. Some Catholics read the writings concerning the discovery of the holy cross and the discovery of the head of John the Baptist. [Note: In the edition these writings are called “recent narratives.” In another collection of the Herovallian codex they are called “recent accounts concerning the discovery of the Lord’s cross,” of which Eusebius makes no mention at all, although later authors reported the matter in different ways from doubtful accounts that subsequently emerged.]

But when these writings have come into the hands of Catholics, the saying of blessed Paul should precede them: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good.”

Concerning Rufinus, who published many works [the edition adds: “an exposition”], Saint Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning freedom of choice. We hold those views which we know the aforesaid Jerome to have held, and not only concerning Rufinus but also concerning all those whom he himself, out of zeal for God and devotion to the faith, criticized. [Here too: “as above.”]

### Canon of Carthage, dating 24

[Note: *Council of Carthage III*, canon 47.]

[Col. 0995B]

It is also permitted to read the passions of the martyrs when their anniversaries are celebrated.

[Note: This canon is commonly appended in the edition as an appendix to canon 44 of the Third Council of Carthage. But the ancient collection of the Herovallian codex confirms what learned men have already observed: in certain books of the councils it is called the twenty-fourth chapter of the Council of Carthage.]

## CHAPTER V. THAT A SYNOD BE HELD TWICE EACH YEAR, AND HOW IT IS TO BE ANNOUNCED

### Canon of the Nicene Council

[Note: Canon 5 of the Council of Nicaea, according to Rufinus’s interpretation.]

Each year, in every province, councils are to be held twice by all the bishops [addition: “a second time”], and matters of this kind are to be judged by the bishops of the same province, so that if anything has perhaps been handled unjustly by one, it may be corrected by the others, and if correctly, may be confirmed by all.

[Note: This canon is Rufinus’s interpretation, found in book II, chapter 6 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. The Council of Riez, canon 8, uses the same interpretation of the canon. From this the antiquity of the collection of the Herovallian codex may be inferred, as we showed in the preface.]

### Canon of Chalcedon, no. 20

[Note: Canon 19 in the other interpretations of the Council of Chalcedon, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.]

[Note: This interpretation is unique when compared with the common interpretation and those of Dionysius Exiguus and Isidore, from which it differs considerably. It resembles, however, the interpretation of the canons of the Council of Nicaea given by Rufinus—that is, one that represents the sense rather than the actual words. The Gallican councils used these and similar interpretations before the time of Charlemagne, when the Dionysian interpretation was adopted among the Gauls.]

In every province, councils of bishops are to be celebrated once during the third week of the Paschal festival, and a second time on the fifteenth day of October, every year.

### Canon of Orléans, no. 1

[Note: Council of Orléans III, canon 7.]

But if, within two years, divine tranquility having been granted, the metropolitan has not called a synod after notifying the bishops of the same province, the metropolitan himself, because of the delay in summoning it, is not to presume to celebrate Mass for an entire year. If those who have been summoned neglect to attend, although not prevented by any bodily illness [alternative: “have refused through their own abuse”], they shall be subject to a similar sentence.

[Note: In the synodal text, “and the rest” are missing from the editions. Other words are substituted for them, as follows: “Yet he should know that this excuse has also been taken away from him if they believe that their absence may be excused by the division of the lot.” But since the distinguished J. Sirmondus, who carefully noted the smallest verbal discrepancies in other canons, made no observation concerning this one, it is clear that he had not examined this very ancient collection.]

At the synodal assembly, matters belonging to God are to be defined first, and human matters afterward.

### Canon of Orange, no. 28

[Note: First Council of Orange, canon 29.]

No synodal assembly is to be dissolved without the announcement of another assembly.

[Note: In the editions, *synodalis* is absent.]

### Canon of Clermont, 1

[Note: The title shows that the council was celebrated in the year of Christ 805.]

Whenever a holy synod is assembled, no bishop should presume to undertake any other business [Note: The edition reads: “to propose any other matter beforehand”] until those matters that pertain to the amendment of life, the strictness of the rule, or the remedy of souls have been settled. [Note: *Fiant*; read Ivo, part VIII, chapter 168.]

## FROM CHAPTER VI. WHO CANNOT ENTER THE SACRED ORDERS

### Canon of Nicaea, no. 1

[Note: This is Rufinus’s interpretation, which differs from the others in its brevity; the Gallican synods used this same form. Thus the Second Synod of Arles, canon 7, similarly reports this canon from the great Council of Nicaea.]

No one who has castrated himself through impatience of lust is to enter the clergy.

[Col. 0997A]

### No. 2

No one recently taken from paganism [Note: Concerning pagan life or conduct], after receiving baptism, is to become a cleric before being more carefully examined. [Note: The Second Synod of Arles, canon 1, presents this canon with the same brevity. Accordingly, although such interpretations may appear less exact, they are not to be despised; indeed, they should be received with great veneration, since by reason of their antiquity they receive authority from the ancient Gallican councils.]

### Canon of Caesarea, no. 8

[Note: Neocaesarea. The *Prisca* interpretation; neither Dionysius nor Isidore.]

If anyone’s wife has committed adultery, that man must not be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry at all.

### Canon of Epaon, no. 26

[Note: Council of Epaon, canon 37.]

A layman is not to be ordained a cleric unless he has first embraced the religious life.

[Note: This number differs so greatly from the edition that it indicates a different order of the other canons as well. The distinguished J. Sirmondus frequently observes this in other councils and teaches that it should be carefully noted, so that other matters of greater importance may be brought to light.]

### Canon of Orléans, no. 6

[Note: Council of Orléans III, canon 7.]

Every precaution must be taken that no one from among the laity is ordained before a year of conversion has elapsed or before the lawful age—namely, twenty-five years for a deacon and thirty for a presbyter. Thus those who are to be ordained clerics must themselves observe the discipline of the rule [Note: The edition reads: “Among those who are to be ordained clerics, let the rule be observed with disciplined care”], so that neither a man with two wives, nor the husband of a remarried woman, nor one who has professed penance, nor one mutilated in body [*semi*; the edition has *semus*, elsewhere *senius*], nor anyone who has at some time been publicly seized, may be promoted to the aforementioned grades.

If a bishop knowingly thinks that action contrary to these statutes should be taken, the man who has been ordained [Note: “Let him be deprived of the office he received, according to the preceding canons,” etc.] is to be deprived of his office, and that bishop, because of the rashness of the ordination, is to be suspended from celebrating the offices for six months. If he presumes to celebrate Mass within the prescribed period, he is to be deprived for an entire year of the charity of all the brothers.

If any cleric or citizen was a witness to their promotion, he is to be excluded from communion for one year. [Note: Some material is inserted here in the edition.]

Nevertheless, if they should contract a dangerous illness [Note: The distinguished J. Sirmondus reads: “Nevertheless, if they should contract a dangerous illness.” This is found in the Lyons manuscript and the ancient collections; the Pithoean and Rheims manuscripts, like the printed editions, read: “If they should fall into illness”], the viaticum [the edition: “viatic communion”] is not to be denied them.

### Written in the Letter of Pope Zosimus, no. 7

Anyone who has married a woman other than a virgin, whether before or after baptism, is not to be admitted to the clergy. For in baptism sins are forgiven, but the union with a wife already taken is not annulled.

[Note: From Letter 1 of Innocent I to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapters 5 and 6.]

### No. 8

For it is sufficiently absurd that a wife taken before baptism should not be counted after baptism, since even in the case of a second marriage contracted after baptism the priest does not bestow a blessing. [Note: These words, cited from the letter of Zosimus, are no longer found there. It may therefore be conjectured that the letter whose fragment is reported by the collection of the Herovallian codex has been lost, unless someone should perhaps say that these words belong to the letters of Innocent I, especially the letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, where chapter 5 reads: “If anyone, even a layman, has married a woman, whether before or after baptism, he is not to be admitted to the clergy, because he appears to be excluded by the same fault. For in baptism,” and the remainder as above. And from chapter 6, after other material: “For it is sufficiently absurd for anyone to believe that a wife taken before baptism is not counted after baptism; since the blessing imposed by the priest upon those marrying is taught not to have supplied an occasion for wrongdoing, but to have preserved the form of a law instituted by God from ancient times.”]

### Canon of Arles, no. 5

[Note: This canon is taken from the Council of Orange, canon 25, like several others.]

[Note: The distinguished J. Sirmondus observes here that in the ancient collection of the Pithoean codex this is called canon 45 of the Second Council of Arles.]

[Col. 0998B]

Concerning those whom the grace of their life suggests should be bound to the clerical state: if they should happen to enter into a second or repeated marriage, they are not to receive ecclesiastical dignities beyond the subdiaconate. But if they have perhaps already done so, they are to be removed from ecclesiastical office.

[Note: No number is assigned to this canon, and it is absent from the edition, unless one prefers to refer it to canon 18, which reads according to Dionysius’s interpretation: “If anyone has taken a widow, or a divorced woman, or a prostitute, or a slave woman, or any woman devoted to public spectacles, he cannot be a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, nor one of those who serve in sacred ministry.” But if this is the same canon, it is clear, as also from several others, that the Dionysian interpretation was scarcely known to the compiler; and consequently that the collection precedes the time of Charlemagne. After Pope Hadrian I had presented Charlemagne with a copy of it, the Gauls thereafter continually used that Dionysian interpretation of the Greek canons, as the most learned Christophorus Justellus observes concerning the Gallican councils under the Emperor Louis the Pious and those that followed, in the preface *On the Ancient Codex of the Canons of the Universal Church*, and concerning the authority of that codex.]

### Canon of the Apostles

If anyone has intercourse with a slave woman, he cannot enter those orders which are called clerical.

### Neocaesarean Canon, chapter 12

[Note: The *Prisca* interpretation; neither Dionysius nor Isidore.]

If anyone has been baptized while ill, he ought not to be ordained a presbyter. For his faith is not voluntary but arises from necessity—unless perhaps a scarcity of men should compel it, or because of his good zeal and faith.

[Col. 0999A]

### Canon of the Romans, no. 5

[Note: The distinguished J. Sirmondus writes: “In the Fossatensis codex it is called ‘The Synod of the Romans to the Gallican bishops,’ and ‘the letter of the Synod,’ because it was written in the form of a letter. In the very ancient collection of the Pithoean codex they are simply called ‘the Canons of the Romans.’ Thus in some matters the Pithoean codex agrees with the Herovallian codex, while in others it differs, as can be recognized from the passages already cited above.”]

[Note: It is clear that these canons are extremely ancient. But when and by whom they were composed has not been established, as chapter 70 of the collection of the Herovallian codex indicates: there the catalogue of bishops who composed or confirmed the aforesaid canons names none of their authors. The distinguished J. Sirmondus thinks that it may perhaps not be an empty conjecture to suppose that Innocent I was their author. But if they are not by Innocent, they are at least the work of some Roman synod that took account of Innocent’s decrees. For the canon cited above agrees with chapter 40 of Innocent’s letter to Victricius; Canon 1 of the Roman Canons with chapter 12; and canon 2 of the same letter with chapter 13. The same may be said of certain others.]

It is plainly impossible for those who have acquired secular power and exercised the affairs of this world to be free from sin: while the sword is drawn, or an unjust judgment is rendered, or tortures are inflicted [the edition adds: “as the necessities of cases require”], or they give themselves over to secular pleasures. Such men do themselves a great favor if they do not aspire to the episcopate, but, by doing penance, deserve after a fixed period [the editions add: “once completed”] to be joined to the altars.

### Canon of Orange, no. 24

[Note: Council of Orange, canon 15.]

[Col. 0999B]

If men of suitable and proven character [Note: The editions add: “whom the grace of their life suggests should be bound to the clerical state.” See above, canon 45 of the Second Council of Arles] should happen to enter into a second marriage, they are not to receive ecclesiastical dignities beyond the subdiaconate.

[Note: This canon is absent from the editions.]

### Canon of Turin

Neither those who after baptism have conducted legal cases or administered them, nor those from the municipal curial class, nor those who after baptism have been crowned, nor those who have held the office called the priesthood, nor those who have celebrated public entertainments—every precaution must be taken that none of these be promoted to the ecclesiastical order.

### In a Letter of Pope Leo

[Note: Letter of Leo I to the bishops throughout Campania and Picenum.]

Nor should anyone indiscriminately admit to the sacred order those whom no dignity of birth and no dignity of character supports; and those who have been utterly unable to obtain freedom from their masters should not dare to be advanced to the height of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0999D] Added in the edition: “as though servile baseness could rightly claim this honor.” The phrase “which the oldest collection of Codex Her. cannot admit” is superfluous. Moreover, *jure* (“rightly”) is absent from the new edition of the letters of Saint Leo, from the second collection in Codex Her., and from other manuscript codices; yet, once that word is removed, scarcely any sense can be extracted from these words.] [Edd.: “are advanced”]. And how can those be believed capable of proving themselves to God who have not yet been able to prove themselves to their masters [Edd.: “to prove themselves”]? Thus there is a double guilt in this matter: both the sacred ministry is polluted by association with baseness, and the rights of masters are violated [Note: [Col. 1000B] Added in the edition: “as far as the rashness of unlawful usurpation is concerned.”]. Therefore, brothers, let all the priests of your province abstain from such men; [Note: [Col. 1000C] Editions: “And not only from these, but also from those.” In Gratian, distinction 54, chapter 31: “but also from other persons bound by origin or by some condition.”] and likewise from others who are bound by birth-status or by some condition [Note: [Col. 1000C] Added in the edition: “We wish this to be moderated.”], unless perhaps the request [Another adds: “or the will”] of those who claim some power over them has been presented. For the man who is to be enrolled in divine service ought to be free from the control of others. [Note: [Col. 1000C] Added in the edition: “So that he may not be drawn away by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s camp, to which his name is enrolled.”] And [Note: [Col. 1000C] The edition omits “And when it has been established for each person,” although these words are entirely required to complete the sense, since the passage began by saying that those should not be admitted to the sacred order who are supported by no dignity of birth or character. Thus the excellent collection of Codex H., which admits neither what is superfluous nor omits what is necessary, preserves them.] when a person’s honorable birth and character have been established, he ought to be associated with the ministry of the sacred altar.

[Col. 1000B] In the letter [Note: [Col. 1000C] Letter of Pope Innocent I to the bishops of Macedonia, chapter 11.] of Pope Innocent, chapter 2.

A catechumen who married a wife before baptism and another after baptism cannot advance to a clerical rank. But if someone objects that this, together with all other offenses, was absolved in baptism, let him be asked whether what is not a sin is washed away in baptism, since the Lord permitted a man to marry a wife, as Solomon also testifies when he says: “A wife is prepared for a man by God, and a husband for a wife.” And if he had three wives in the old man, the woman who is in baptism will be his fourth. Who, I ask, would not say that this is contrary to the Apostle’s statement, who says: “the husband of one wife” [Note: [Col. 1000C] The printed editions add so much, and in so different an order, that the extent of the divergence cannot be perceived unless everything is presented. Thus the passage reads in the edition: “Next it is stated that a man should not be called a bigamist if, while a catechumen, he had and lost a wife, and after baptism acquired another, since the woman joined to the new man is to be regarded as the first. For that former marriage was washed away, together with the other offenses, through the sacrament of baptism. Since this is said of one wife, certainly, if he had three wives while he was in the old man, the woman who is fourth after baptism will, according to such interpreters, be regarded as the first; the name of virgin will equally be given to the woman who was married fourth. Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, who says that a priest must be the husband of one wife? But it is objected that in baptism everything whatsoever was done in the old man was dissolved. Tell me, I speak with your permission: are only offenses forgiven in baptism, or also those things that are fulfilled according to the commands of the law and the institutions of God? Is marrying a wife a crime, or is it not a crime? If it is a crime”—[Col. 1001C]—“then, with the pardon already mentioned, I would say that the author is at fault, since, in order that they might commit crimes, he blessed them in paradise when he himself joined them. But if it is not a crime, because what God has joined it is impious to call a crime, and Solomon added: ‘For a wife is prepared for a man by God,’ how can it be believed to have been forgiven among offenses which is read to have been accomplished by God, its author?” However this distinction may be understood, it is nevertheless useful to have noted it, so that it may be clear in what manner the letters of the Roman pontiffs were read in the oldest collections of the Gallican Church before the Isidorian collection was received.]

## CHAPTER IV [Note: [Col. 1001D] In the edition it is not distinguished from the preceding chapter.]

[Col. 1001A]

I ask: when he was a catechumen, did the man who fathered children have children who were not his children, just as those whom he fathered after baptism were his children [Note: [Col. 1001D] Another edition: “I ask, and ask anxiously, whether the wife of the man who was first a catechumen and afterward a believer is one and the same, and whether the children whom he fathered by her while he was a catechumen, and afterward other children while he was a believer…”]? Or will the earlier and the later children themselves be brothers? Or is this also erased by baptism, and is spiritual rebirth believed to have removed the names of children and fathers [Note: [Col. 1001D] Another version: “Whether they are to be called brothers, or whether, after their father’s death, they are not to have a share in the inheritance to be claimed, since spiritual rebirth is believed to have taken away from them the name of children”]? Since it is absurd to think so, what, in heaven’s name, is the reason for counting among sins, without any authority, marriages which the law commands and God joins [Note: [Col. 1001D] Another version: “Since it is absurd to think and judge in this way, what, in heaven’s name, is the reason for defending this and proclaiming it more as an empty opinion than supporting it by any authority, when what the law commands and God joins cannot be counted among sins?” The words of the collection may suffice to have compared this passage with the printed editions. For such great variation appears that, concerning the remaining passages, it would almost be necessary to transcribe nearly every individual word. If, therefore, the places in which there is variation are indicated, the diligent reader will easily compare them himself with the edition.]

## CHAPTER V [Note: [Col. 1002D] In the edition it is not distinguished from the preceding chapter.]

But if a catechumen had devoted himself to virtue [Note: [Col. 1002D] Here and below, several things are added.], is what he had faithfully done before baptism taken away from him by baptism? Were Cornelius’s prayers and almsgiving taken away by baptism? Since what is not a sin ought not to be dissolved among sins, it will be sound to judge that the former wife’s status cannot be abolished, since it was not forgiven as a sin.

## CHAPTER VI [EDITIONS III]. ON THE MAN ORDAINED BY HERETICS

We say that a man ordained by heretics has a head wounded by that laying-on of hands, and that, after the healing brought by medicine, he cannot be without a scar [Edd. vary]; and where penance is necessary, there the place of ordination cannot exist, because what the heretic did not possess he could not confer; [Other editions add:] rather, he gave, through the laying-on of a perverse hand, the condemnation which he possessed. And since he has become a participant in condemnation [Edd. vary], I cannot discover how he ought to receive ecclesiastical honor. But [Note: [Col. 1002D] Here chapter 4 begins in the editions.] it is said [Col. 1001C] that the true and just blessing of a legitimate priest removes every defect that had been branded upon a defective man [Edd. vary].

## CHAPTER VII [EDITIONS IV]

Therefore, if this is so, let sacrilegious men, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be admitted to the order [Edd. vary]. [Other editions add:] And let there be no place for penance, because ordination can provide what prolonged satisfaction is accustomed to provide.

## CHAPTER VIII [Note: [Col. 1002D] In the editions it is not distinguished from the preceding chapter.]

[Col. 1002A]

Our rule, however, is this: to those who have been baptized by heretics, through the laying-on of hands we grant only permission to communicate [Edd. vary], and nevertheless they are not to be placed even in the least clerical honor [Edd. vary]; [Note: [Col. 1002D] Here chapter 5 begins in the editions.] but those who have passed from Catholicism to heresy are to be received only through public penance [Other editions add].

## CHAPTER XI [Note: [Col. 1002D] In the editions it is not distinguished from the preceding chapter.]

Those who have passed from Catholicism to heresy [Other editions add] will never be able to be admitted to the clergy [Note: [Col. 1002D] In the editions these words are expressed in the form of a question]; their offense can be abolished only by prolonged penance.

Canon of the Africans [Note: [Col. 1002D] The Fourth Council of Carthage in the common version; but in the monastic codex of Gembloux and that of Saint Bavo at Ghent, “Ancient Statutes of the Church.” Codex Barb. adds “of the East.”], era 42 [Note: [Col. 1002D] In the common version, chapter 54; as in Codex Barb. and Palat., 42].

A cleric who envies the advancement of his brothers is not to be promoted as long as he remains in that fault.

Era 45 [Note: [Col. 1002D] In the common version, 67; in Codex Barb. and Palat., 55].

Seditious men, usurers, and those who avenge their own injuries are never to be ordained clerics [Edd. vary].

Era 84 [Note: [Col. 1002D] In the common version, 67; in Codex Barb. and Palat., 84].

A cleric is never to be ordained from among the penitents, even if he is good. If this has been done through the bishop’s ignorance, he is to be deposed [Note: [Col. 1002D] The reason is supplied in the editions].

## CHAPTER VII. WHAT KIND OF MEN, AND IN WHAT MANNER, ARE TO APPROACH THE SACRED ORDERS, AND WHERE THEY ARE TO BE ORDAINED

In the letter [Note: [Col. 1002D] Letter 5, chapter 6.] of Pope Symmachus to Bishop Caesarius.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] These initial words are absent from the editions.] In the election of a bishop, let no one acknowledge a decree or the presence of a visitor [Edd. vary], whose testimony the unanimity of the clergy and citizens can confirm [Col. 1002C]. We therefore exhort all to observe these provisions faithfully and with devoted minds, out of regard for the Catholic religion and the peace of the Churches, because there is no doubt that transgressors of such prohibitions, according to the venerable canons, suffer the loss of their own communion. Nevertheless, we wish this to come to the knowledge of all bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] From the translation of Rufinus, chapter 7; Dionysius and Isidore, chapter 6.] Canon of Nicaea, era 11.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] The Prisca translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] Clearly, if, after the common consent of all has been reasonably obtained, and a decree has been made according to ecclesiastical rule, two or three persons should dissent, the opinion supported by the greater number of priests is to prevail.

Canon of Carthage, era 4 [Note: [Col. 1003D] Council of Carthage, chapter 40].

And this also must be established: when we have assembled to elect a bishop, if some opposition should arise, three men are not to presume to clear the man who is to be ordained; rather, one or two beyond the three are to be requested [Edd. add “beyond the three”]. First, in the same Church [Edd.: “among the people”] for which he is to be ordained, the persons of those who bring the objection are to be examined; finally, the objections themselves are also to be investigated. When he has been cleared in the presence of the people, let him be ordained.

Canon of Arles, era 21 [Note: [Col. 1003D] Second Council of Arles, chapter 54].

[Col. 1003B] In the ordination of a bishop this procedure is to be observed: first, after venality and ambition have been removed, three bishops are to be nominated [“by the bishops”], from whom the clergy or citizens are to have the power to choose one.

Second Council of Orléans, era 5 [Note: [Col. 1003D] Fourth Council of Orléans; in the editions, chapter 5].

A bishop is to be ordained in the city in which he is elected by decree [Edd. vary], and he is to be consecrated in the Church over which he is to preside. But if necessity does not permit this to be fulfilled [Some additions in the editions], he is to be ordained within the province, either in the presence of the metropolitan or with his authority, by the bishops of the province.

Canon of the Apostles, era 21.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] Not in the translation of Dionysius.] If a eunuch was made such through envy, or during persecution, or if he was born so, let him become a bishop if he is worthy.

[Col. 1003C] Canon of Nicaea, era 4.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] Translation of Rufinus. See the Second Synod of Arles, chapter 5.] A bishop is to be ordained, if possible, by all the bishops of the province. But if this is difficult, by no fewer than three [than three]; nevertheless, the presence or authority [“either presence or authority”] of the metropolitan bishop must be secured. Without him, we wish the ordination to be invalid [“they wished it to be”].

Era 7.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] Translation of Rufinus.] If two or three should dissent in the ordination of a bishop [“because of some dispute”], the authority of the others, and especially that of the metropolitan together with the rest, is to be considered stronger.

Canon [Note: [Col. 1003D] Council of Laodicea, chapter 12.] of Laodicea, era 12.

[Col. 1003D] [Note: [Col. 1003D] It does not differ greatly from the translation of Dionysius.] Bishops are to be advanced to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and of the bishops who are in the surrounding region—namely, those who for a very long time have been tested both in the word of faith and by the example of upright conduct.

[Col. 1004A] Canon [Note: [Col. 1003D] Ancient Statutes of the Church. See above.] of the Africans, era [Note: [Col. 1003D] In Codex Barb. this first chapter serves as a preface to the following chapter.] 1.

Before a man who is to be ordained bishop is examined, let it be determined whether he is naturally prudent, teachable, moderate in conduct, chaste in life, sober, always free from his own business [“avoiding his own affairs”], agreeable to people [“humble and agreeable”], learned, instructed in the law of the Lord, cautious in understanding the Scriptures, and trained in ecclesiastical doctrines. Above all, let it be determined whether he asserts the proofs of the faith in simple words—that is, affirming that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, and proclaiming the entire deity in the Trinity to be of one essence, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent; whether he confesses each individual person [Col. 1004B] in the Trinity to be fully God, and all three persons to be one God [Note: [Col. 1004D] The words “all three persons … one God” are absent from the editions]; whether he believes that the divine incarnation occurred not in the Father or in the Holy Spirit but in the Son alone [The editions add “believes”], so that he who was the Son of God the Father in divinity became the Son of a human mother in humanity—true God from the Father and true man from his mother, possessing flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational soul; with both natures together in him, that is, man and God, one Son, one Christ, one Lord, the author, Lord, and creator of all things together with the Father and the Holy Spirit; that he truly suffered in the flesh and died [“by the true death of his body”], and rose again by the true resurrection of his flesh and the true restoration of his soul, in which he will come to judge the living and the dead. He must also be asked whether he believes the New and Old Testaments—that is, the law, the prophets, and the apostles—to have one and the same author and God; whether the devil became evil not by creation but by choice; whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh which we bear, and not of another; whether he believes that judgment will take place, and that each person will receive either punishment or glory for what he has done in the flesh; whether he does not prohibit [“disapprove of”] marriage. And other matters follow, with which the edition entirely agrees. [Note: [Col. 1004D] From this and other passages it is clear that the decrees of the African Fathers, or the Ancient Statutes of the Church, were not interpolated; rather, except for certain variant readings—which in no way alter the sense—they have remained intact.]

Canon of Orléans, era 4 [Note: [Col. 1004D] Third Council of Orléans, chapter 3].

[Note: [Col. 1004D] Some additions precede this in the edition for explanatory purposes.] Let the metropolitan be ordained, if possible, with all the bishops of the province present, so that the privilege of ordaining that metropolitan himself remains with the metropolitan [Note: [Col. 1004D] “Of the metropolitan bishops” rather than “of the metropolitan.” Pithou and Lyons have the reading of the printed editions, “from the metropolitan.” See the notes of the distinguished J. Sirmond.], as the custom of ordination requires. Nevertheless, let the metropolitan himself be elected by the bishops of the province, as the decrees of the apostolic see provide, with the consent of the clergy and citizens; for, as the apostolic see itself has said, it is just that the man who is to be placed over all should be chosen by all.

Canon [Note: [Col. 1005C] Council of Orléans V, chapter 12.] of Orléans IV, era 9.

Let no other bishop be ordained while a bishop is alive.—No other bishop is to be installed or superimposed upon a living bishop [“No one is to be placed over a living bishop”], unless perhaps in the place of one whom a capital crime has cast down.

In the letter [Note: [Col. 1005D] Letter of Pope Zosimus to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, chapter 3.] of Pope Zosimus.

The following periods are to be observed for the individual ranks. If a man has given his name to the ecclesiastical mysteries or ministries from childhood, he is to remain continuously among the readers until the twentieth year of his age. If he approached at a more advanced age, already mature [“already advanced in age and elderly”], so that immediately after baptism he desired to be enrolled in divine service [Col. 1005B], he is to remain either among the readers or among the exorcists for five years; thereafter he is to serve as acolyte or subdeacon for four years [Edd. omit “he is to remain”]; and thus, if he is worthy, he is to proceed to the blessing of the diaconate. If he conducts himself blamelessly in that order for five years, then, with his merits [“services”] supporting him and with the proofs of his own faith shown through all these stages, he may earn the priesthood of the presbyterate [The editions omit “may”]. From that rank, if a more exacting life has led him to good conduct, he ought to hope for the supreme pontificate; provided, however, that this rule is observed: neither a bigamist nor a penitent [Another adds: “nor the husband of a widow”] may be admitted to these ranks. Indeed, defenders of the Church who have come from the laity are also to be held to the foregoing observance if they deserve to belong to the clerical order [Col. 1005C].

[Note: [Col. 1005D] In Codex Barb., before Ancient Statutes of the Church, chapter 90, this is prefixed as the title of the following canons: “Recapitulation of the ordination of the officials of the Church.”] CHAPTER ON THE ORDINATION OF THE MINISTERIAL OFFICIALS OF THE CHURCH

On the ordination of the bishop, presbyter, and the remaining ranks.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] This is chapter 90 in Codex Barb. and chapter 1 of the Fourth Council of Carthage.] When a bishop is ordained, two bishops are to hold the book of the Gospels over his neck, and one is to pour the blessing over him [“with one pouring it over him”]; all the others who are present are to touch his head with their hands. [Note: [Col. 1005D] Chapter 91 in Codex Barb. and chapter 2 of the Fourth Council of Carthage; the remaining chapters are distinguished in the same way.] When a presbyter is ordained, while the bishop blesses him and holds his hand over his head, all the presbyters who are present are also to hold their hands over his head beside the bishop’s hand [Col. 1006A]. We omit the rest, since the printed versions do not differ from it except in the distinction of the numbers, which the collection of Codex Her. does not have at all.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] Ancient Statutes of the Church, or Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 22. But in Codex Barb., chapter 10.] Canon of the Africans, era 10.

A bishop is not to ordain clerics without the counsel of his presbyters [“clerics”], and he is to obtain the assent and testimonies of the citizens [“seek” them] [Note: [Col. 1005D] The new edition of the Council adds material at this point that is absent from the Telerian codex, as also from the collection of Codex H.].

Era 13.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] This canon is absent from the Ancient Statutes of the Church, or the Fourth Council of Carthage. See the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 4.] Let age also be required in those who are to be ordained priests.

Canon of Orléans, era 33.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] It is absent from the Council of Orléans. But see the Second Council of Arles, chapter 54, and the era cited above, 31.] It was decided that this procedure should be observed in the ordination of a bishop: first, after venality and ambition have been removed, three are to be nominated by the bishops, from whom the clergy or citizens are to have the power to choose one.

[Col. 1006B] Canon of Chalcedon, era 12.

[Note: [Col. 1005D] Thus formerly the Gallican Church summarized the canons of the Greeks. This may be observed in the Gallican synod and in the translation of Rufinus.] A province is in no way to be divided between two metropolitans.

## CHAPTER VIII. THAT THERE ARE NOT TO BE TWO BISHOPS IN ONE CITY, AND ON THE VICARS OF BISHOPS

Canon of Nicaea, era 10.

[Note: [Col. 1006D] From the translation of Rufinus, which the Gallican Church also used similarly for other councils.] There are not to be two bishops in one city.

Canon of Orléans, era 18.

[Note: [Col. 1006D] Absent from the editions.] Vicars of bishops, whom the Greeks call *chorepiscopi*, were established after the example of the seventy elders. But, as priests, let them offer because of the care and attention they show toward the poor, and let them be held in honor [Note: [Col. 1006D] This canon is absent from the Councils of Orléans and appears to have been taken from the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 13. Its interpretation as found in Isidore Mercator is much closer to the preceding words than the Dionysian version. Thus, according to Isidore’s interpretation: “The vicars of bishops, whom the Greeks call *chorepiscopi*, were indeed established after the example of the seventy elders; but, as fellow priests, because of the care and attention they show toward the poor, let them offer [their service] and be held in honor.”].

## CHAPTER IX. ON ORDAINING A BISHOP WITHIN THREE MONTHS

[Col. 1006C]

Canon of Chalcedon, era 25.

[Note: [Col. 1006D] Translation of Dionysius.] It pleased the holy synod that the ordinations of bishops be celebrated within three months.

## CHAPTER X. ON BISHOPS WHO HAVE BEEN ORDAINED BUT NOT RECEIVED

[Note: [Col. 1006D] Neither author nor number is inscribed. See the Council of Antioch, chapters 17 and 18; the canon under the name of the Apostles, chapter 35. Prisca translation.] If a bishop does not accept the office and the care of the people entrusted to him, let him be deprived of communion until he consents to obey. The same applies to a presbyter or deacon. But if he has not been received because of the people’s malice, let him nevertheless remain bishop. The clerics of the city, however, are to be deprived of communion, because they did not instruct the disobedient people.

## CHAPTER XI. ON A BISHOP ORDAINED AGAINST HIS WILL

[Col. 1007A]

Canon of Orange, era 20 [Note: [Col. 1007D] First Council of Orange, chapter 21].

(Some additions occur in the editions.) If it should happen anywhere that two bishops make one man a bishop against his will, with the perpetrators condemned [Note: [Col. 1007D] The editions read the opposite in these words: “He who suffered the violence is to be substituted in one of their Churches.” The reading of the collection of Codex Her. is supported by Ivo, Part V, chapter 181, who reads this canon as follows: “Concerning the deposition of the man whom two bishops presumed to ordain, it was decided in our provinces concerning the presumptuous men that, if it should happen anywhere that two bishops, etc.” The same appears in Gratian, distinction 64: “Concerning the deposition,” etc.], let one of them be substituted in the Church of the very man who suffered the violence; provided that his life is worthy, and let the other be ordained in the place of the other who has been deposed [Edd. add: “nevertheless”].

## CHAPTER XII. THAT NO ONE OUGHT TO BE ORDAINED WITHOUT A SPECIFIED TITLE

Canon of Chalcedon, era 6.

[Note: [Col. 1007D] Prisca translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] No one is to be ordained to an ecclesiastical rank unless the title of the Church in which he is to serve is expressly declared. [Col. 1007B] But if someone has been ordained without a title, the holy synod decreed that this kind of laying-on of hands is to be regarded as invalid, and that he cannot minister, to the injury of the ordaining bishop.

## CHAPTER XIII. ON A SLAVE OR FREEDMAN WHO HAS BEEN ORDAINED

First Council of Orléans, era 5 [Note: [Col. 1007D] First Council of Orléans, chapter 8].

If a bishop has ordained a slave [Edd. add: “in the absence of the master, or”], while the master was unaware and the bishop knew that he was a slave, as a deacon or presbyter [Edd. vary], the man himself remaining in clerical office, the bishop is to compensate him with double satisfaction [Note: [Col. 1008D] “With double satisfaction” is found in the Corbie manuscript, the Tilius manuscript, and the collection of Saint Benignus. See the notes of the distinguished J. Sirmond.]. But if the bishop did not know that he was a slave, those who gave testimony and petitioned for his ordination [Col. 1007C] are to be liable to the same restitution [“held responsible”].

Canon of Orléans, [Note: [Col. 1008D] Fifth Council of Orléans, chapter 6.] IV, era 5.

But if he has ordained a freedman without the consent of the man whose freedman he became, the man who was ordained is to be reclaimed by his master; but his ordainer [“and the man who conferred the order”], if he is proved to have acted knowingly, is not to presume to celebrate Mass for six months [Edd.: “only”]. But if he is the slave of a layman [Some editions add], with his blessing preserved, let him render service to his master in an honorable order [Edd. vary]. But if his [“lay”] master should wish to bend him in such a way that he appears to inflict an injury upon the sacred order, the bishop who ordained him is to pay two slaves according to the ancient canons [Edd. vary] [“restore him to the lay master”], and is to have the power to reclaim him for his own Church.

## FROM CHAPTER XIV. ON PRESBYTERS WHO MINISTER IN DIFFERENT CHURCHES; THAT NO CLERIC OUGHT TO MINISTER IN TWO CITIES; AND THAT AN ABBOT OUGHT NOT TO HAVE SEVERAL MONASTERIES

[Col. 1008A]

Canon of Chalcedon, era 10.

[Note: [Col. 1008D] Prisca translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] A cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in two Churches, both in the one in which he was ordained at the beginning and in the one to which he fled as though it were the better, out of a desire for empty glory. Those who do this are to be recalled to the Church in which they were first ordained, and are to minister there alone. But if he has been transferred from one Church to another, he is not to share in any way in the property of the former Church, or of the martyrs who are under it, or of the poorhouses, or of the hostels. Those who have dared to commit any of the prohibited acts are to be expelled from their own rank [Col. 1008B].

Canon of Agde, era 36 [chapter 38].

Abbots likewise may not have separate cells [“different cells individually”] or several monasteries, except that, because of hostile invasion [“hostility”], they may establish places of refuge within walls.

## CHAPTER XV. THAT A BISHOP OR CLERIC MUST NOT PASS FROM ONE PLACE TO ANOTHER WITHOUT THE BISHOP’S COMMAND

[Note: [Col. 1008D] Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 27, or rather the Ancient Statutes of the Church. In Codex Barb., chapter 11.] Canon of the Africans, era 11.

A bishop is in no way to pass by ambition from an obscure place to a distinguished one, nor is any cleric of a lower order to do so. But if the usefulness of the Church has demanded that this be done [Some additions in the editions], let it be done by decision of the synod [Edd.: “let him be transferred in the presence of the synod”], [Col. 1008C] and let another bishop be appointed in his place [Edd. vary]. Those of the lower ranks may, with the permission of their own bishop, move to these [“other”] Churches.

Canon of Arles, era [Note: [Col. 1008D] Second Council of Arles, chapter 54.] 35 [Note: [Col. 1008D] This number is especially to be observed for this council. See the notes of the distinguished J. Sirmond.].

If any layman, out of love of religion, believes that he should entrust himself to any priest, he himself shall claim the man whom he has received for the purpose of instruction.

Canon of Nicaea, era 16.

[Note: [Col. 1008D] From the translation of Rufinus.] No one is to aspire from a lesser city to a greater Church, whether he is a bishop or another [Edd.: “even another”] cleric.

Era 17.

No cleric who, having abandoned his own Church without any plausible cause, wanders [“and roams”] through other Churches is to be received into communion.

Era 18.

[Note: [Col. 1008D] From the same translation.] No one is to steal a man who belongs to another and ordain him as a cleric in his own Church without the consent of the man to whom he belongs.

[Col. 1009A] Canon of Épaone, era 55 [Note: [Col. 1009C] In the edition the numbering does not go beyond chapter 40; hence this canon and others are absent.].

A bishop who has many clerics is to grant one to another bishop for ordination, if necessary.

Canon of Antioch, era 21.

[Note: [Col. 1009C] Differs little from the translation of Dionysius.] A bishop is in no way to move from one parish to another, neither rushing there voluntarily, nor compelled by force by the people, nor driven by necessity by the bishops. Let him remain in the Church which he first received by lot from God.

Canon of Chalcedon, era 8.

[Note: [Col. 1009C] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] Clerics who are placed over poorhouses, or who are ordained for monasteries and basilicas, are to remain under the authority of the bishop according to the traditions of the Fathers, and are not to break away from their bishop through defiance. Those who refuse to obey this rule, if they are clerics [Col. 1009B], are to be subjected to canonical correction; but if they are laymen or monks, they are to be deprived of communion.

Era 20.

[Note: [Col. 1009C] Differs little from the translation of Dionysius.] Clerics ministering in a Church, if they have been established in the Church of another city, ought to be content with the place in which they were initially required to minister, except for those who, losing their own provinces, have of necessity transferred to another Church. If any bishop, after this definition, receives a cleric belonging to another bishop, it was decided that both the one received and the one receiving are to be deprived of communion until the man who had moved returns.

Canon of Orléans, era 2.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] This canon is absent from the printed edition of the Council of Orléans.] Ministers are to remain in the very places in which they have been ordained [Col. 1009C] [Note: [Col. 1009D] The same words are cited from the Council of Arles in books of decrees preserved at Ghent and in ancient codices of the monastery of Saint Bavo.].

Era 20.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] From the First Council of Arles, chapter 21.] If they wish to transfer themselves to another place, they are to be deposed.

Canon of Nicaea, era 21 [Note: [Col. 1009D] This is canon 1 of the Council of Sardica. For why it is cited in this way, see the preface of the distinguished Justellus on the ancient code of the canons of the universal Church.].

If a bishop moves from his own city to another out of ambition, let him not even be granted lay communion.

Era 22.

[Note: [Col. 1009D] This is canon 3 of the Council of Sardica. Prisca translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] A bishop is not to pass into another province in which there are bishops, unless perhaps he is invited by the brothers.

[Col. 1010A] Canon of Hippo, era 74 [Note: [Col. 1009D] This canon is found in three places: in the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 8; in the council commonly called African, chapter 41; and in the code of the African Church, chapter 74.].

An intervening bishop [Edd.: “intercessor bishop”] is not to sit on the throne in which he is serving as intervening bishop [Edd. vary]; rather, care must be taken that a bishop be given to the people within a year. If this is neglected, after the year has elapsed the intervening bishop is to depart [the editions vary greatly], and another intervening bishop is to be given to the people, who will provide a bishop for them.

Canon of Riez, era . . . [Note: [Col. 1009D] The distinguished J. Sirmond, in his notes on this council, writes: “Riez, he says, not Regiensis, in the old books. In some, a synod held in the city. Thus Faustus, who is commonly called bishop of Riez, is called *Regensis* by ancient writers, and the territory of Riez is so called by Gregory of Tours, Book IV, chapter [Col. 1010C] 34.” Thus the ancient reading is confirmed by the oldest collection of canons, Codex Her., which everywhere agrees with the old codices.] [Note: [Col. 1010C] The era or number could not be read.].

(In the editions, chapter 7.) [Note: [Col. 1010C] The same canon is read differently in the edition, in these words: [Col. 1010D] “But he is to perform all these funeral rites until the seventh day after the deceased’s death. Thereafter, returning to the Church, he is to await the mandate of the metropolitan together with all the holy bishops. No one is to approach the Church that had lost its chief priest unless invited by letters from the metropolitan, lest he be deceived by the people and appear to have wished to suffer violence.” If our collection had been examined by J. Sirmond, the most diligent scholar would certainly not have omitted such a great discrepancy in the same canon, since he observed the smallest variations in the other canons.] If a bishop comes to bury another bishop, he may celebrate his funeral rites until the seventh day after the deceased’s death; otherwise, not except by mandate of the metropolitan. No bishop is to approach the Church that has lost its chief priest, lest he be deceived by the people.

[Col. 1010B] Canon of Arles [Note: [Col. 1010D] First Council of Arles, chapter 21], era 20.

Presbyters or deacons [“concerning presbyters or deacons”] who have left the places in which they were ordained [“habitually leave and transfer themselves to other places”] without the command of their bishop [the editions omit this] are to be deposed.

## CHAPTER XVI. ON BISHOPS OR CLERICS WHO ARE STRANGERS, OR WHO ARE GOING TO THE COURT

[Note: [Col. 1010D] From the Council of Arles I, chapter 19.] Canon of Orléans, era 19.

It was decided that when visiting bishops come into a city, a place is to be given to them so that they may offer.

[Note: [Col. 1010D] Council of Sardica, chapter 11, in the translations of Dionysius and Isidore; but in the Greek, chapter 20.] Canon of Nicaea, era 10.

[Note: [Col. 1010D] Prisca translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] When a bishop who is established at a station sees another bishop proceeding onward, he is to inquire about his route, examine his reasons, and learn where he is going. And if he is traveling out of ambition, he is neither to sign his letters nor receive him into communion.

Era 19 [Note: [Col. 1010D] Council of Sardica, chapter 12 in Greek; chapter 15 in the translations of Dionysius and Isidore].

[Note: [Col. 1010D] Old translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] Let it be permitted for a bishop to go to his own estates, so that he may arrange the fruits of his labor. And if it is necessary for him to remain for three weeks, let him stay rather in his own churches; or, if there is a nearby city, nevertheless let him not appear to spend the Lord’s Day without a church [Supplement: let him go there]. Yet the bishop should go to his estate in such a way that his household affairs do not suffer loss through his absence [Col. 1011A], and so that, by frequently coming to another city, he does not incur suspicion of ostentation or ambition.

## CHAPTER XVII. ON THE LETTERS OF TRANSIT FOR TRAVELERS, AND ON CLERICS TRAVELING WITHOUT LETTERS

Canon of Antioch, era 8.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Old translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] No traveler ought to be received without a *formata*—an official letter of authorization.

Era 9 [canon 8].

Nor should presbyters give canonical letters for distant regions, but only send ordinary letters to neighboring bishops.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] The editions do not distinguish this from the preceding canon.] Era 10.

The representatives of bishops, however, may issue *formatae*.

[Col. 1011B] Canon of Chalcedon, era 11.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Old translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] Let all the poor or needy seek aid from the apostolic see with proof of their need, or travel only with peaceful ecclesiastical letters, and not with letters of recommendation, since letters of recommendation are [intended] for persons of higher standing.

Canon of Laodicea, era 28 [canon 41].

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Old translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] It is not proper for ministers of the altar, or even for a layman, to go anywhere without canonical letters, that is, a *formata*.

Canon of Chalcedon, era 13.

[Note: [Col. 1011D] Old translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] Traveling clerics must nowhere exercise ministry in another city except with letters of recommendation from their own bishop.

Canon of Agde, era 26 [canon 38].

Clerics, or even monks [the editions omit “monks”] [Col. 1011C], must not be allowed to wander about without letters of recommendation from their own bishop. [Note: [Col. 1011D] See the First Council of Vannes, canons 5 and 6.] But if correction by words does not reform them, they are also to be restrained by beatings [we decree that they be restrained].

Canon of Epaon, era 5 [Note: [Col. 1011D] Council of Epaon, canon 6.]

Let no one grant communion to a presbyter or deacon traveling without letters from his bishop. [Note: [Col. 1011D] Variant editions. But see the Third Council of Orléans, canon 15, where this canon is cited just as it is read in the collection.]

Canon of Orléans, era 18.

Clerics residing in the cities or territories of others must not be promoted to any clerical rank without the consent of their own bishop. [Note: [Col. 1011D] This canon belongs to the Third Council of Orléans, canon 15, or to the Fifth Council, canon 5, where the same meaning is reported with a few altered words. Thus, in the Council of Orléans, canon 15, it reads: “Concerning those clerics who, under any pretext or condition, have decided to remain in the cities or territories of others, they must not be promoted to any clerical rank without the written authorization and consent of their own bishop” [Col. 1012D]. Likewise, in the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 5: “No one shall dare either to promote a foreign cleric or lector without the cession of his bishop, or to claim him for himself under any conditions.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. HOW, AND FOR WHICH OFFENSES, EACH PERSON IS TO BE DEGRADED

[Col. 1011D] Canon of Nicaea, era 11.

[Note: [Col. 1012D] Rufinus’s translation. See the sixth letter of Pope John II.] And if it should happen that men indiscreetly advanced to the priesthood later either confessed some criminal matter against themselves or were convicted by others, let them be removed [from office].

Canon of Epaon, era 19.

If an abbot is found guilty [or guilty of fraud] and, asserting his innocence, refuses to accept a successor from his bishop, let him be brought before the judgment of the metropolitan.

Era 22.

[Note: [Col. 1012D] See the titles of the Gallican canons following the letter of Pope John II.] If a deacon or presbyter commits a capital crime, let him be deposed [from the honor of office] and confined in a monastery, where alone he is to receive communion for as long as he lives.

Canon of Orléans, era 6 [Note: [Col. 1012D] First Council of Orléans, canon 9. See the titles of the Gallican canons, distinction 81, from the First Council of Arles, canon 11.]

If a deacon or presbyter commits a capital crime, let him be deprived both of office and of communion.

[Col. 1012B] Era 8 [Note: [Col. 1012D] Third Council of Orléans, canon 8. See the same titles.]

[Addition in the editions.] If any cleric is either confessed or convicted of adultery, let him be deposed from office and, communion having been granted [in the monastery], confined for the whole time of his life.

Era 9 [Note: [Col. 1012D] The same Third Council, canon 8.]

If any cleric commits theft or forgery, since these are capital offenses [the crimes themselves], let him be degraded from his order, communion having been granted.

Era 2 [Note: [Col. 1012D] The same council, canon 2.]

Let no cleric, from subdeacon upward, have intercourse with the wife whom he had previously taken [the editions add certain words; variant editions]. If he does so, let him be deposed from office, after being granted lay communion [and being content with it] [the editions add certain words]. If his bishop knowingly [variant editions] permits him to act in this way and afterward admits him to office, let the bishop be suspended from his office for three months, with penance [to perform penance].

Era 7 [Note: [Col. 1012D] The same Third Council of Orléans, canon 7.]

If clerics [the editions add “who had no wives”], after receiving the blessing, decide to choose marriage—men who, willingly and without any protest, were ordained at the lawful age—let them be expelled from communion together with the women whom they have taken [the editions add “whom they take”]. But if a man was ordained unwillingly or while protesting, let him be deposed from office, but not expelled from communion. Let a bishop who has ordained [or presumed to ordain] a man unwillingly or while protesting be subject to a year of penance and not presume to celebrate Masses.

[Col. 1012D] Era 17 [Note: [Col. 1012D] The same Third Council of Orléans, canon 15.]

Concerning those who ordain clerics in another diocese.—If a bishop has ordained foreign clerics in another person’s diocese or consecrated altars, then, after removing those whom he ordained, while the consecration of the altar nevertheless remains, let the transgressor of the canons abstain from celebrating Mass for a year.

[Col. 1013A] [Note: [Col. 1013D] The editions read: “He must not invade foreign dioceses to ordain foreign clerics or consecrate altars; but if he does so . . .” The remainder is as in the collection.]

Canon of Caesarea, era 1.

Concerning presbyters who fornicate.— [Note: [Col. 1013D] Old translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] Let a presbyter who marries be deposed. If he has fornicated or committed adultery, let him be expelled from the church among the laity to perform penance.

Canon of Ancyra, era 20.

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Old translation, neither Dionysius nor Isidore.] If anyone commits adultery, then, after completing seven years of penance, let him be restored to the communion of the laity if he is a presbyter or deacon.

Canon of Valence, era 3 [Note: [Col. 1013D] Council of Valence, canon 4. See the titles of the Gallican canons appended to the letter of John II.]
