[Col. 1013B] [Some material is added in the editions.] If a deacon [variant editions: presbyter or bishop] has said that he is polluted by a mortal crime, let him be deposed [removed from the offices mentioned above], whether he has made a true confession or a false one. For in such matters there can be no acquittal [the editions lack this phrase] if they say of themselves what would be punished if said of others, since anyone who is the cause of his own death is a greater murderer.

Canon of Africa, era 44 [Note: [Col. 1013D] The Council of Carthage, called the Fourth, canon 57, or rather the Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes; in the Barberini manuscript, canon 44.]

A malicious cleric, especially among priests, must be compelled to ask forgiveness. If he refuses, let him be degraded, and never be restored to office without satisfaction.

Era 43 [Note: [Col. 1013D] The number is the same in the Barberini manuscript; Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 56.]

[Col. 1013C] Let a cleric who is discovered to be wandering about through flattery and treachery be deposed from office [degraded].

Era 84 [Note: [Col. 1013D] The same number in the Barberini manuscript; Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 68.]

If a bishop knowingly ordains a penitent, let both be degraded, the ordainer and the one ordained [another reading: let him also be deprived, at least, of the power to ordain within his own episcopate].

Era 85 [Note: [Col. 1013D] The same number in manuscript B; Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 69.]

Similarly [“he shall be subject to the same sentence”], if a bishop knowingly ordains [as a cleric] a man who has or has had a widow, a divorced woman, or a second wife.

Canon of Arles, era 7 [Note: [Col. 1013D] Fifth Council of Arles, canon 7.]

If a bishop ordains another bishop’s cleric without the consent [or letter] of his own bishop [some additions in the editions], let the one ordained be deposed, and let the ordaining bishop be deprived of communion for three months.

[Col. 1014A] Canon of the Apostles, era 30 [Note: [Col. 1013D] Canon 19 in Greek; canon 31 in Dionysius.]

[Note: [Col. 1013D] Translation other than Dionysius.] If any bishop uses secular power and, through it, obtains a church, let him be deposed; and let all who communicate with him be separated.

Era 45.

A cleric who gives himself to drunkenness must either desist or be deposed.

Canon of Mâcon [Note: [Col. 1014D] Second Council of Mâcon, canon 5.]

If [“Likewise we decree that no one,” etc.] a presbyter, stuffed with food or drunk with wine, presumes to handle the sacrifices or celebrate Mass [to concelebrate on private and feast days] [variant and other additions in the editions], let him lose the dignity of his rank according to the African canons.

Canon of the Apostles, era 40 [Note: [Col. 1014D] Canon 41 in Greek; canon 42 in Dionysius. It differs slightly from Dionysius’s translation.]

[Col. 1014B] If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon gives himself to dice, that is, board games, or to drunkenness, he must either desist or certainly be condemned.

Canon of Nicaea, era 18 [Note: [Col. 1014D] Canon 19 in Rufinus’s translation.]

[Note: [Col. 1014D] Singular translation.] Let clerics who lend money at interest and those who demand one-percent monthly interest or other interest from any transaction be expelled from the clergy.

Canon of the Apostles, era . . . [Note: [Col. 1014D] Canon 6 in Greek; canon 7 in Dionysius’s translation.]

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon must never undertake secular concerns. Otherwise, let them be deposed.

Canon of Caesarea, era 8 [canon 9].

[Note: [Col. 1014D] Translation neither by Dionysius nor Isidore.] If a presbyter confesses that before his ordination he fell into bodily sin, let him not offer the sacrifice, but let him remain in the other offices for the sake of his usefulness.

Letter of Pope Hormisdas to all the provinces [Note: [Col. 1014D] This title appears to have been written later in the manuscript. In any case, as the letter itself shows, it is wrongly attributed to Hormisdas.]

[Col. 1014C] If [Note: [Col. 1014D] First Council of Orange, canon 23; Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 4.] a deacon or presbyter is found incontinent with his wife after receiving the Levitical blessing, let him be expelled from office. It is therefore most clearly established that, according to the titles of the ancient Fathers [written at the prompting of the Holy Spirit] transmitted by holy Pope John, the Gallican canons appear to contain the judgments of 318 bishops: clerics discovered in adultery, whether they themselves confess or are convicted by others, cannot return to office. And since perhaps there are some to whom, out of excessive piety, the severity of the holy Fathers written above is not at all pleasing, let them know that they are criticizing or condemning the judgments both of the 318 bishops [addition in the edition: “the commands and authority of the holy pope, and of those bishops who, etc.”] and of those who established or decreed the remaining canons. But perhaps their piety is greater than that of the aforementioned 318 bishops, their mercy greater than that of holy [apostolic] Pope John, and their charity greater than that of the other holy priests who, by their definitions, deliberated upon these examples or remedies [“this as an example or remedy”] for the churches?

Therefore, let them either willingly consent to the commands of those men [variant editions], or recognize that they are opposed and hostile to all of them. What kind of kindness hostile to justice is it to stroke criminals and preserve their wounds unhealed until the day of judgment? If we saw them performing the most severe penance for many years, we ought in this way both to care for their salvation and to observe the statutes of the canons. But when in some of them there appears neither the compunction of humility nor perseverance in prayer or lamentation, nor do they imitate blessed David, who said: “Every night I will wash my bed; with my tears I will drench my couch.” And: “I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with weeping.” And when we do not see them devoting themselves to fasting or reading, we can recognize how negligently, how sluggishly [or: apathetically], and with what security hostile to the soul they would remain if they returned to their former office, believing that God had forgiven them without their having performed worthy penance, just as the priests also appear to have indulged them.

I speak truly: those very men whom, through a dangerous and false mercy, we seem to indulge, when they come to be condemned before Christ’s tribunal for such great sins, will bring charges against us ourselves, saying that, while we feared the harshness of their speech or gladly accepted false flatteries and dangerous adulation, we allowed them, by uselessly indulging them, to remain in their sins or even to increase those sins, not remembering what is written in the Old Testament: “When one person sins, the anger of God rages against all” [Note: [Col. 1015D] Up to this point in Gratian.]

O piety! O mercy! To spare one person and bring everyone into danger by a bad example. Saint Cyprian, in *On the Lapsed*, does not advise this, saying: “He who strokes the sinner with flattering words supplies fuel for sin; he does not suppress crimes but fosters them.” And again: “An inexperienced physician is one who, before removing the corruption, places a scar over the wound” [the editions vary greatly].

Therefore, carefully consider whether it can or ought to be done that, while despising the canons of such great and such men as those mentioned above, we presume to observe or practice something different from what they established—especially since, if we neglect the holy decrees of those 318 bishops who ordered councils to be held throughout all the churches [variant], we shall not only despise them [some additions in the editions], but also the African [bishops] and all the others who, under their direction, established something throughout the world for ecclesiastical discipline, thereby despising them with the sin of our own souls.

I altogether dare not place myself in this danger, because my own merits are not such that I should presume to take upon myself the sins of others, nor do I possess such eloquence that I could plead before Christ’s tribunal against so many and such holy priests who established the canons. Let each person who decides to think or observe otherwise see how he can render an account on the day of judgment.

For my part, insofar as God deigns to grant me strength, I wish to obey [or: strive to obey] their commands, because I desire not quarrels but peace with them, and to have whatever share I may have with them. This too must be carefully observed: those clerics who return to their own wives are to be entirely suspended from office.

Likewise, bigamists and husbands of women who have remarried [Col. 1016B]—who certainly do something lawful—nevertheless cannot be ordained clerics; and if they have been ordained, let them be deposed. Concerning such men Saint Faustus also said in his letter: “He loses the grace of the consecrated man who still wishes to exercise the office of a husband” [Note: [Col. 1015D] Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*, book I: “As long as I perform the office of a husband, I do not perform that of a Christian.” And in the defense of the books against Jovinianus: “When I perform the office of a husband, I do not perform that of one who practices continence.” See the note on the penance of Theodore.]

Since these matters have been established by such great and such men, with what conscience can anyone say that a man who has committed adultery can return again to office?

But if someone says, “Then you deny the mercy of God, who said: ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.’ And also: ‘If someone falls, will he not rise again?’ And: ‘On whatever day a sinner turns, all his iniquities will be consigned to oblivion’” [variant], we can and must answer this objection with a free voice.

Far be it from us to appear even slightly to doubt these judgments. We most firmly believe that anyone who performs worthy penance until the end of his life will receive not only forgiveness but also reach eternal life [eternal rewards]. Nevertheless, because of the ecclesiastical rule and the statutes of the ancient Fathers—which, far be it from us, we should presume either to criticize or to examine—we believe that the person whom we believe will come to eternal life after completing his penance must not return to the honor of the clergy, according to the commands of such great Fathers. Indeed, it is written in the canons: [Note: [Col. 1016D] Council of Rome under Pope Hilary, canon 3; Council of Agde, canon 43.] “Let no penitent ever be ordained a cleric.”

If a man who voluntarily seeks penance, even if he performs it perfectly, cannot be ordained bishop or presbyter—and if he is ordained through ignorance, he is to be deposed—then with what conscience may a man who is sent unwillingly to a monastery to perform penance be permitted to return to the priesthood? [Note: [Col. 1016D] The passage is corrupt in the edition.] What else, indeed, should he be called except a penitent?

Let no one bring against me any other argument contrary to the authority of the apostolic see, or contrary to the commands of the 318 bishops, or contrary to the statutes of the remaining canons. For whatever is said against the definition of those in whom we believe the Holy Spirit spoke, I do not doubt that accepting it would be not only rash but also dangerous.

I greatly fear and tremble at the condemnation which the priest Eli deserved because of his foolish indulgence. Because he chastised his sons negligently and was unwilling either to strike them or to excommunicate them, the sons themselves were killed on one day, and thirty thousand of the people were slain. The ark of the covenant was captured, and he himself, falling backward with his neck broken, died; his name was blotted out of the book of life. By contrast, Phinehas, because he was moved by zeal for God and killed two adulterers [together], delivered the whole people from God’s wrath [variant].

I do not say this so that, as he did, the priests of the Lord should now also be punished by bodily death. Rather, it is better for each person to endure shame and disgrace in this world for a short time [“as long as he lives”] than afterward to reach eternal punishments. It is much more beneficial for him, for the sake of the example of others, to remain removed from office and perform penance as long as he lives, thereby obtaining a remedy for himself on the day of need.

Whoever wishes to burden my littleness in this matter, I have decided to give him no other answer than what the canons mentioned above appear to contain. [Note: [Col. 1017D] The Corbie and Pithou manuscripts contain nothing more; the remainder was copied from a single Rheims manuscript, as the distinguished J. Sirmond observed.]

In the letter of Pope Siricius to Bishop Genesius, era 13.

[Note: [Col. 1017D] This letter is missing.] [Note: [Col. 1017D] See the letter to Himerius, in which the meaning, though not the actual wording, is found. But Pope Stephen II, in his response to various questions of the British monks, chapter 10, cites Siricius’s letter as it is read in this collection.]

A presbyter who says that he does not know whether the man who ordained him was a bishop, and who celebrated Masses for some time and afterward, abandoning his office, married a wife—who could doubt that this man is a detestable false presbyter? [Col. 1017C] On his account he must be altogether expelled and confined in a monastery to perform penance for the whole time of his life.

## CHAPTER XIX. ON ONE EXPELLED FROM THE CHURCH, AND ON ONE EXCOMMUNICATED OR CONDEMNED TO DEPOSITION FROM OFFICE

Canon of Antioch, era 2.

[Note: [Col. 1017D] Translation neither by Dionysius nor Isidore.] Whoever from the clergy is found to communicate with excommunicated persons must be deprived of communion.

Canon of Orléans, era 3 [Note: [Col. 1017D] First Council of Orléans, canon 6.]

If anyone believes that something is to be recovered from a bishop, or from the rights of the Church or of a private person, and makes no accusation of insult or crime, he must not be removed from communion merely for bringing the action [Col. 1017D].

Era 9 [Note: [Col. 1018D] The same council, canon 12.]

If a deacon or presbyter, on account of his offense, has withdrawn himself from communion at the altar under a profession of penance, then, if others are unavailable and a case of definite necessity arises, he may baptize [“the person requesting baptism”].

Era 22 [Note: [Col. 1018D] Third Council of Orléans, canon 20.]

If any cleric considers the discipline [or treatment] imposed upon him by his bishop unjust [“which cleric concerning himself”], let him appeal to a synod.

Canon of Epaon, era 28.

If a bishop dies before absolving a condemned person [“is carried off by death”], his successor may absolve the corrected or penitent person.

Canon of Arles, era 4 [Note: [Col. 1018D] Fifth Council of Arles, canon 4.]

Let a presbyter not presume, without the knowledge of his bishop, to depose a presbyter [the editions omit “a presbyter”], deacon, or subdeacon from his order. If he does so, let the person be restored to office or communion, and let the other be deprived of communion [variant and some additions in the editions] and office for a full year.

Era 29 [Note: [Col. 1018D] Second Council of Arles, canon 49.]

It has been decided that those suspended from communion are to be excluded not only from the company of clerics but also from the conversation and meals of the entire people. [Some variants and additions in the editions.]

Canon of the Apostles, era 9 [Note: [Col. 1018D] Canon 25 in Dionysius’s translation, from which this translation differs.]

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon, if condemned for crimes, must by no means be deprived of communion.

Canon of Nicaea, era 26 [Note: [Col. 1018D] Council of Sardica, canon 5, according to the Greek.]

[Note: [Col. 1018D] Translation neither by Dionysius nor Isidore.] If a degraded bishop wishes to appeal and takes refuge with the bishop of the Roman Church, and the latter writes on his behalf to the bishops in the neighboring province, they must carefully investigate everything and decide according to the truth of the faith [Col. 1018C]. But if the Roman bishop sends a presbyter from his own side on behalf of the accused, that presbyter is to possess the authority of the one by whom he was sent.

## ON THOSE UNDER INTERDICT

Canon of the Apostles, era 28 [Note: [Col. 1018D] Canon 29 in Dionysius’s translation, from which this translation differs.]

If anyone deposed for certain crimes dares to take up the ministry forbidden to him, let him be expelled from the Church.

Canon of Antioch, era . . . .

[Note: [Col. 1018D] Translation neither by Dionysius nor Isidore.] If anyone deposed from the clergy presumes to assume the rank forbidden to him, both he and those who communicate with him, knowing his sentence, ought to be expelled from the Church.

Canon of Arles, era 46.

Those who are separated from communion for their offense [Col. 1018D] are to receive communion in the same places from which they were excluded [“in the same place”].

## CHAPTER XX. ON THE ECCLESIASTICAL ORDER AND THE OFFICE OF THE MASS

Canon of Epaon, era 27.

For the celebration of the divine offices, the provincials must observe the order maintained by their metropolitans [Col. 1019A]. [Note: [Col. 1019D] Almost all manuscripts read this way; some, however, read “their fellow provincials.” See the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.]

Letter of Pope Innocent to Decentius, Bishop of Capua [Note: [Col. 1019D] Another form: “Innocent to Decentius, bishop . . . of Eugubium.”]

If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, there would be no diversity or variation in those orders and consecrations. But because each person considers not what was handed down but what seems right to himself to be what must be observed, different practices appear to be maintained [or celebrated] in different places [or churches] [variant editions]. Hence scandal arises among the people. Since they do not know that the ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, they think either that the churches do not agree among themselves or that the apostles or apostolic men held contradictory views [or that contradiction was introduced by the apostles or apostolic men].

Who, then [“for who does not know”], is unaware [“or does not perceive”] that what was handed down by the chief of the apostles, Peter, and is observed down to the present day, ought to be observed by all, and that nothing should be superimposed or introduced that does not possess his authority [variant]? [Note: [Col. 1019D] Some additions in the editions are superfluous.] This is especially clear since throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one is found to have established churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Or let them read whether in these provinces another bishop is found to have taught [Note: [Col. 1019D] The edition incorrectly reads “another of the apostles,” since the reference is not to the apostles but to those whom the successors of the apostles appointed as priests.]

And since they will never find one, they ought to follow what the Roman Church observes, from which they unquestionably received their beginning, lest, while striving after foreign assertions, they appear to lose [or omit] the source of their institutions.

There is no doubt that Your Charity has often come to the city and assembled with us [variant] at the church, and that you have learned what custom it maintains both in consecrating the mysteries and in other matters to be done [“sacred matters”]. [Note: [Col. 1019D] From this point to the words “For this reason,” the passage is so corrupt in the edition that it cannot be understood at all.]

I would consider that sufficient for the instruction or reform of your church, unless your predecessors, the priests, observed something less or otherwise. Or perhaps there are some who say that these matters ought to be observed differently from the practice of the Roman Church. We would not have known of them if you had not said that we should be consulted about certain matters.

For this reason we answer them—not because we believe that you are ignorant of anything, but so that you may instruct your own people with greater authority, or, if some are departing from the institutions of the Roman Church, admonish them or not delay in identifying them, so that we may know who they are who introduce novelties or consider the customs of a church other than the Roman Church worthy of observance. [Note: [Col. 1020D] Here the edition begins chapter 1.]

You state, then, that some command the people to exchange the peace before the mysteries have been completed, or that the priests pass it among themselves [the word “among themselves” is absent], whereas after everything—which I ought not to disclose—the peace must be declared necessary [or: prescribed]. Through it, it is shown that the people have given their consent to everything that is done in the mysteries and celebrated in the Church, and that, once everything is finished, it is demonstrated by the seal of the concluding peace.

(Chapter 2.) As for reciting the names, before the priest commends in his prayer the peace [or prayers] and the offerings of those whose names are to be recited, you yourself recognize through your prudence how superfluous it is to announce beforehand the name of the one whose offering you have not yet offered to God, since nothing is unknown to Him [variant]. First the offerings must be commended, and then the names of those to whom they belong must be declared, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries, not among the other things that we introduce beforehand in order to open a way for the prayers that will follow in the mysteries themselves. [Col. 1020B]

(Chapter 3.) As for signing infants, it is clear that this may be done by no one other than a bishop. For although presbyters are secondary priests [the words “secondary priests” are absent], they do not possess the fullness of the episcopate. This episcopal office belongs to bishops alone: to sign them or impart the Spirit, the Paraclete [variant: “This belongs to bishops alone”].

Ecclesiastical custom demonstrates this, and so does that apostolic reading which states that Peter and John were sent so that they might impart the Holy Spirit only to those who had already been baptized. For presbyters, whether outside the presence of a bishop or in the presence of a bishop, when they baptize [the editions omit “when they baptize,”] may anoint the baptized with chrism, but with chrism that has been consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil [Col. 1020C], since this belongs to bishops alone when they impart the Spirit, the Paraclete. I cannot state the actual words, lest I appear to disclose them rather than answer the inquiry.

Canon of Nicaea, era 19 [Note: [Col. 1020D] In the Greek, and in Dionysius’s translation, canon 18; in Rufinus, canon 20; in Isidore, canon 14.]

[Note: [Col. 1020D] Singular translation.] Those who have the power to offer the sacrifice shall distribute the body of Christ. Let deacons remain within their proper measure and receive the Eucharist in due order after the presbyters. If anyone does not wish to be subject, let him cease to be a deacon. But if neither a bishop nor a presbyter is present, then let the deacons give the Eucharist to the people.

Canon of Carthage, era 59 [Note: [Col. 1020D] Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes in the Barberini manuscript, canon 18; Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 38.]

Let a deacon, in the presence of a bishop [presbyter], distribute the Eucharist [the body of Christ] to the people, if necessary, when ordered to do so [variant].

Era 6 [Note: [Col. 1020D] Second Council of Carthage, canon 3; in the African Ecclesiastical manuscript, canon 6.]

The consecration [preparation] of chrism, the reconciliation of penitents except in danger of death [the editions omit “except in danger of death”] [variant], and the consecration of virgins must not be performed by presbyters.

[Col. 1021A] [Note: [Col. 1021D] The rationale of the preceding canon, which is absent from the edition.] Concerning reconciliation of penitents not to be performed by presbyters.—Presbyters and deacons must attempt nothing apart from the bishop. For the people of the Lord have been entrusted to him, and he himself will render an account for their souls.

Canon of Carthage, era 2 [Note: [Col. 1021D] Third Council of Carthage, canon 23.]

No one in the prayers should name the Father in place of the Son or the Son in place of the Father. And whenever they stand at the altar [or: whenever the altar is attended], the prayer must always be directed to the Father.

Era 3 [Note: [Col. 1021D] The edition distinguishes this from the preceding canon.]

Whoever writes prayers for himself from elsewhere [variant] must not use them until he has first discussed them with more instructed [or: better-instructed] brothers.

[Note: [Col. 1021D] Second Council of Mâcon, canon 4.] Canon of Mâcon concerning the offering of the people, era 6.

[Col. 1021B] [Some additions occur in the editions.] We decree that on every Sunday the sacred offering of the altar be presented by all men and women, both bread and wine, so that through these offerings [sacrificial offerings] [some additions in the editions] they may be freed from the burdens of sins and may be worthy to share with Abel and the other righteous [who offer]. But let all who strive through disobedience to nullify our definition be struck with anathema.

Era 8 [Note: [Col. 1021D] The same council, canon 6.]

[Some material precedes this in the editions.] The remains of the sacrifices that are left in the sacristy after the Masses [after the Mass has been completed]—on Wednesday and Friday a fast is announced for the innocent [“let the innocent be brought to the church by the person concerned, and let a fast be proclaimed for them”], and let all receive those same remains sprinkled with wine [and with the fast imposed on them]. [Col. 1021C]

Canon of Orléans II, era 14 [Note: [Col. 1021D] Orléans III, canon 14.]

[Some material precedes this in the editions.] Let the celebration [celebration] of the Mass on the principal feast days begin at the third hour, so that, once that office has more easily been completed, the other offices may be performed at the appropriate hours. [Note: [Col. 1021D] The editions explain this more fully.]

Canon of the Apostles, era 51 [Note: [Col. 1021D] Canon 9 in Greek; canon 10 in Dionysius’s translation, from which this translation differs slightly.]

Those who do not persevere in prayer and do not receive holy communion are to be deprived of communion as people who stir up disturbances in the Church.

Canon of Agde, era 44.

A presbyter may not give a blessing over the people in the church [“pour it out”], or bless a penitent in the church [Col. 1021D] [“must absolutely not do so”].

## CHAPTER XXI. ON THE RELICS OF THE SAINTS AND ON ORATORIES

Canon of Epaon, era 26 [canon 25].

Relics of the saints must not be placed in rural oratories [Col. 1022A], unless it happens that clerics of the neighboring parish are present, who may serve the sacred pledges [ashes] through frequent psalmody. [Note: [Col. 1021D] On this appended clause, which is absent from Burchard and Ivo, see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.] If such clerics are lacking, local clerics [the editions lack “clerics”] must not be ordained until adequate resources for their food and clothing have been assigned to them.

## CHAPTER XXII. ALTARS MUST NOT BE CONSECRATED UNLESS THEY ARE OF STONE

Canon of Epaon, era 25 [canon 26].

Altars must not be consecrated by anointing with chrism [Note: [Col. 1022D] “With ointment” in the Lyon manuscript, as also in Ivo, part III, chapter 30. See the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.] unless they are made of stone.

## CHAPTER XXIII. ON BAPTISM

Canon of Mâcon, era 3 [Note: [Col. 1022D] Second Council of Mâcon, canon 3.]

From the report of certain persons [the editions omit the second *quosdam*, “certain”] we have learned that some Christians do not observe lawful baptism. They baptize their sons almost every day and on the feast days of the martyrs, so that scarcely two or three are found at holy Easter to be regenerated through water and the Holy Spirit. Therefore we have decreed that from this time onward no one shall be permitted to do such a thing, except those whom extreme illness or the final day compels [addition: to have their sons receive baptism]. Accordingly, having been recalled from their errors or ignorance by the present admonitions, we command everyone without exception to observe Lent at church with their infants, so that, having received the laying on of hands on the appointed days and having been anointed with the liquid of the sacred oil, they may enjoy the celebration of the appointed day and be regenerated by holy baptism. Thus, if life accompanies them, they may both perform priestly duties and enjoy the solemn celebration of the singular festival [the solemnity of the celebration].

Canon of Laodicea, aera 45.

[Note: It differs slightly from the translation of Dionysius.] No one ought to be admitted to baptism after two weeks of Lent.

Aera 46.

[Note: Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] Those who come to baptism ought to learn the faith and recite it from memory to the bishop or priest on Thursday of Holy Week.

Aera 47.

[Note: Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] Those who receive baptism while ill ought to learn the faith thoroughly and know of what gift they have been made participants.

Canon of Africa, aera 23.

[Note: The Ancient Church Statutes; in the Barbet manuscript, chapter 23; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 84.] Those to be baptized shall give their names and, under a long period of abstinence from wine and meat [the edition omits “under”], and having been frequently examined by the laying on of hands, shall receive baptism.

Aera 24.

[Note: Ancient Church Statutes; in the Barbet manuscript, chapter 24; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 86.] Neophytes shall for some time abstain from richer banquets, spectacles, and spouses [the editions omit “and”].

Aera 41.

[Note: Ancient Church Statutes; in the Barbet manuscript, chapter 41; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 100.] A woman must not presume to baptize.

Canon of Orange, aera 2.

[Note: The distinguished Fronto Ducaeus: “In the Tilian manuscript this is the second canon; the first is the one that follows.”]

No minister who has undertaken the duty of baptizing ought ever to proceed without chrism, because it has been agreed among us that he be chrismated once. [Note: The distinguished J. Sirmond: “To be chrismated once; the commonly circulated manuscripts, Gratian, and other collectors read: to be chrismated once in baptism. It is indeed certain that baptism is meant. But since these words are not found in the ancient copies and have the appearance of a gloss, scruple prevented their retention.” From this it is clear that the collection of the Herovall manuscript agrees everywhere with the ancient copies.]

But if, necessity having compelled it, someone has been [variant: is] baptized without chrism, the priest shall remind him at confirmation [Note: In Burchard and Ivo: “he shall be perfected in the priest’s confirmation.”].

Canon of Neocaesarea, aera 6.

[Note: Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] Pregnant women ought to be baptized if necessary. Nothing, however, in this sacrament belongs in common to the child being born, because will and free choice are declared in the confession.

Canon of the Apostles, aera 48.

[Note: In the Greek text, 48. Column 1023B: Canon 49 in the translation of Dionysius, from which this differs.]

If anyone, contrary to the Lord’s command, does not baptize in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but in three principles without a beginning, or in three sons, or in three paracletes, let him be deposed.

Aera 49.

[Note: In the Greek text, 49. The translation of Dionysius differs from this.] If anyone does not celebrate the threefold immersion of the one mystery, let him be deposed.

Canon of Orange, aera 11.

[Note: The twelfth canon of the Council of Orange.] A person who suddenly becomes insensible [variant: according to his condition] may be baptized or receive penance, if there are proper testimonies concerning his former will [variants and additions in the editions].

Aera 12 [canon 13].

Whatever belongs to piety shall be conferred upon the insane [variant: shall be conferred].

In the letter of Pope Siricius, aera 14.

[Note: Absent from the edition of Siricius’s letter.] If a presbyter baptizes in wine because of an immediate necessity, so that the sick person may not perish, no fault shall be attributed to him for this. But if water was available and such necessity did not press, he shall be deprived of communion and subjected to penance. But if that infant was baptized in the holy Trinity, let him remain in that baptism.

[Note: The same matter, with a few words changed, is cited from Siricius’s letter to Bishop Himerius of Tarragona by Pope Stephen II in his responses to various questions of the British monks, chapter 11, as follows: “If someone baptized an infant in wine because he could not find water, while the infant was altogether in danger, no fault is attributed to him on that account. Let infants remain in that baptism. But if water was present, let that presbyter be excommunicated and subjected to penance, because he presumed to act contrary to the judgment of the canons.” The following words are rightly noted in the margin of the new edition of the Councils: “Let infants remain in that baptism” is a gloss, or was rashly introduced from the margin into the text by a scribe, or was transferred through carelessness from the immediately preceding canons. Therefore this passage must be corrected by the most accurate reading of the Herovall manuscript.]

Aera 15.

[Note: Absent from the edition of Siricius’s letter.] If anyone, because of an immediate necessity, baptizes an infant placed in danger with a vessel or with his hands, using water in the name of the holy Trinity, the baptism shall remain fully valid, especially when necessity demands it.

[Note: The same matter is read in the responses of Stephen II, chapter 12, as follows: “Whether, in necessity, it is permitted to pour water over the head of an infant placed in illness with a bowl or with the hands, and thus to baptize him. If this baptism was performed in the name of the holy Trinity, it shall remain fully valid, especially when necessity demands it.”]

Aera 16.

Concerning the presbyter who does not know the Lord’s Prayer.—

[Note: Absent from the edition of Siricius’s letter. See the response of Pope Stephen II, chapter 13.] If a presbyter does not know the Lord’s Prayer, nor the Creed, nor the psalms, and the one who ordained him was a bishop, let him first of all lose the dignity that he unlawfully presumed to take; and under strict penance let him live in a monastery for the whole of his life. But the infants whom he baptized in the holy Trinity shall remain baptized.

Aera 17.

[Note: Absent from the edition of Siricius’s letter. Response of Pope Stephen II, chapter 14.] Those who baptize in such a way as to say: “In the name of the Father I immerse; in the name of the Son I immerse; and in the name of the Holy Spirit I immerse”—those who have been baptized in this way, although rudely, have nevertheless been baptized in the name of the holy Trinity.

## Concerning repeated baptism

Aera 24.

[Absent from the editions.] Those who have undertaken to receive repeated baptism, whether compelled by fear or deceived by error, and who acknowledge that they have not acted outside the sacrament of the Catholic faith, shall not receive communion in our fellowship except through the laying on of the bishop’s hands. The period shall be determined by the bishop’s judgment, according as he sees or perceives the dispositions of those who have converted to be devout, taking into account also their advanced age, their circumstances, and the illnesses that place them in danger. If any of them is so severely pressed that his salvation is despaired of, let him be assisted with the grace of communion.

Canon of the Apostles, aera 46.

[Note: A translation, but not that of Dionysius.] If anyone knowingly rebaptizes one who has been rightly baptized, let him be deposed.

## Chapter XXV. Concerning confirmation; that meals must not be held in church; and that the knee must not be bent on Sunday

In the letter of Pope Innocent I.

[Note: Chapter 3. See above.] The Book of the Acts of the Apostles asserts that Peter and John were sent so that they might give the Spirit only to those who had already been baptized. For presbyters, whether outside the presence of the bishop or with the bishop present, may anoint with chrism when they baptize—but with chrism consecrated by the bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same [oil], since this belongs only to bishops when they impart the Paraclete Spirit.

Canon of Orange, aera 2.

[Note: In the commonly circulated copies, this is numbered 1, but in the Tilian manuscript and all the ancient copies, 2.]

Since there is only one blessing of the chrism itself, without prejudicing anything, repeated chrismation should not be regarded as necessary.

[Note: This reading of the canon, concerning which a very sharp dispute was waged among learned men, confirms the correctness of the opinion of the distinguished and most learned J. Sirmond; see his posthumous notes.]

Canon of Arles, aera 26.

[Note: Council of Orange I, chapter 1; Council of Arles II, chapter 26.] It has been decided that a heretic [variant: heretics] placed in danger of death, if he desires to be Catholic and a bishop is absent, shall be signed by a presbyter with the blessing of chrism.

Canon of Epaon, aera 16.

[Addition in the editions: “presbyters, for the salvation of souls, which we desire in all things.”] We permit heretics who are in desperate condition and bedridden, if they suddenly request conversion, to be assisted by a presbyter with chrism [variant in the editions]. Let all converts who are healthy know that they must seek this from the bishop.

[Note: Innocent I, Letter to Recentius, chapter 8.] But the anointing of chrism cannot be given to penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For those to whom the other sacraments are denied—how can this kind [one] be thought capable of being granted?

Canon of Laodicea, aera 28.

Concerning meals in churches.— [Note: Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] Meals must not be held in church.

Canon of Nicaea, aera 20.

[Note: Rufinus omits this canon, and it is absent from the Roman Church manuscript. See the note of the distinguished Sirmond on that manuscript. Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] On Sunday and during the days of Pentecost, so that all things may be observed consistently in every place, the holy council has decided that prayers should be offered to the Lord while standing.

## Chapter XXVI. Concerning Easter, Sunday, and the remaining festivals

Canon of Arles, aera 1.

[Variant in the editions.] Therefore we have decreed that the Lord’s Easter be observed throughout the whole world on one day.

Canon of Orléans, aera 22.

[Note: Council of Orléans I, chapter 25.] No citizen may celebrate the solemnities of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Pentecost in the countryside, except one who is demonstrably kept there by illness.

Canon of Mâcon, aera 2.

[Note: Council of Mâcon II, chapter 2.] Therefore we must all celebrate our Easter—the feast in which the highest Priest and Pontiff was sacrificed for our sins [another copy adds: “having no liability for sin”]—with festal joy [variant: with the greatest festal joy], and venerate it in all things with the sincerity of diligent observance. Thus, during those seven most holy days, no one should dare to perform servile work; rather, all gathered together and devoting themselves to the paschal hymns, let us steadfastly display through our daily sacrifices the devotion of our presence, praising our Creator and Regenerator in the evening, morning, and midday.

Canon of Mâcon, aera 1.

[Note: Council of Mâcon II, chapter 1. Much precedes this in the canon.] Keep Sunday, which has given us birth anew and freed us from every sin. Let none of us [variant: of you] be occupied with the fuel of lawsuits; let no one conduct legal actions; let no one impose upon himself such necessity that he is forced to place a yoke upon the necks of young oxen. Let all of you be attentive in mind and body to the hymns and praises of God.

Canon of Orléans, aera 21.

[Note: Council of Orléans III, chapter 28.] Since it has been established that on Sunday one ought not to travel with horses, oxen, or vehicles, nor in any way perform any task of preparing food or pertaining to the cleanliness of the house or of a person—something that appears to belong more to Jewish than to Christian observance—we decree that on Sunday whatever was previously permitted may be done. As for agricultural work, that is, plowing, working the vineyard, cutting, threshing, clearing, or making fences, we have decreed that people abstain from these activities [note: there are many variants; see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond], so that those who come more readily to church may devote themselves to prayer. If anyone is found engaging in the works written above, which are forbidden, the manner in which he is to be corrected shall rest not with lay discipline but with priestly correction.

Canon of Orléans concerning waiting for Mass, aera 24.

[Note: Council of Orléans I, chapter 26.] When the people gather [in the name of God] to celebrate Masses, no one shall depart before the Masses are completed [variant: before the solemnity of the Mass is completed]. And when a bishop is present, let them receive the bishop’s blessing.

[Note: The distinguished J. Sirmond: “By the agreement of all the books, the negation that appeared in the commonly circulated copies has been deleted; it still remains in Gratian: ‘If there is no bishop,’ instead of which Burchard, book III, chapter 29, and Ivo, part III, chapter 34, read: ‘If a bishop is absent.’ The error arose because they thought that the priest in this passage was different from the bishop, whereas he is the same.” What this most learned man observed is also made entirely clear by the very similar canon 29 of the Third Council of Orléans: “Concerning Masses, no layperson shall depart before the Lord’s Prayer has been said; and if a bishop is present, his blessing shall be awaited.”]

Aera 28.

[Note: Council of Orléans I, chapter 31.] If the bishop is not prevented by illness, he must not be absent on Sunday from the church nearest to him [variant: it shall not be permitted].

Canon of Africa, aera 77.

[Note: Council of Carthage IV, chapter 64; but more likely according to the Ancient Church Statutes, in the Barbet manuscript, chapter 77.] Anyone who deliberately fasts on Sunday must not be considered Catholic.

Aera 78.

[Note: Council of Carthage IV, chapter 64; but more likely according to the Ancient Church Statutes, in the Barbet manuscript, chapter 78.] The solemnity of Easter must be celebrated on one day and at one time.

## Chapter XXVII. Concerning the fast of Lent and the Litanies

Canon of Orléans, aera 21.

[The editions add: “This was decreed by all the priests.”] Before the solemnity of Easter, let not a fiftieth-day period but a fortieth-day period be observed.

Canon of Agde, aera 12.

Let it be decided that all the children of the churches shall fast during Lent, except on Sundays [and, in the added reading, also on Saturday], under priestly direction and the threat of discipline.

Canon of Mâcon, aera 9.

Concerning the canon to be read from the Mass of Saint Martin until the Nativity of the Lord. [Note: The editions omit “Concerning the canon … until the Nativity of the Lord.”] From the Mass of Saint Martin until the Nativity of the Lord, let them fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday [variants in the editions here and below], and let the sacrifices be celebrated according to the Lenten order. For these days we have decreed that the canons be read [with a special definition] to correct the ignorance of the people.

Canon of Orléans, aera 24.

[Note: Council of Orléans I, chapter 27.] Litanies [variant: “Rogations, that is”] have been decreed to be celebrated by all churches before the Ascension of the Lord, so that the three-day fast previously undertaken may be ended on the day of the Lord’s Ascension [festival]. During those three days, male and female servants shall be released from every service, so that the entire people may gather more readily and use Lenten foods [variant: so that all may abstain during the three days].

Aera 25.

[Note: Council of Orléans I, chapter 28.] Clerics who disdain to come to this holy work, or to be present, shall receive ecclesiastical discipline [addition and variant in the editions].

Canon of Lyon, aera 6.

[Note: Council of Lyon, celebrated in the year of Christ 567.] In the first week of the new month—that is, before the Sunday that first dawns in that month—let litanies, as the holy Fathers decreed should henceforth be held before the Ascension of the Lord, be celebrated by all churches [or parishes].

Canon of Gangra, aera 19.

[Note: Council of Gangra. Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] If anyone among those able to practice continence, without bodily necessity, proudly dissolves the common fasts that have been handed down and observed by the whole Church, let him be anathema.

## Concerning the Friday fast

In a decretal of Pope Innocent, aera 3.

[Note: Letter of Innocent I to Decentius, chapter 4.] The reason demonstrates with the greatest clarity that one ought to fast on Saturday. For if, throughout the recurring cycle of weeks, we commemorate the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ by the image of that day, and we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we ought not to pass over Saturday, which appears to be enclosed between the sorrow and joy of that time. For it is certainly established that during those two days either the apostles [something is missing] or the elders were in mourning [variant: and that they fasted to such an extent that they did not celebrate the sacraments at all].

## Chapter XXIX. Concerning what is offered at the altar, what is offered to the priest’s household, and offerings

Canon of Mâcon, aera 4.

[Note: Council of Mâcon I, chapter 4. Much precedes this in the editions.] On every Sunday, an offering of both bread and wine shall be presented in the church by all men and women. Whoever, through disobedience, despises this, let him be anathema [variant: “they strive to empty … let them be …”].

Canon of Gangra concerning offerings on Sundays, aera 8.

[Note: Council of Gangra, chapter 7. Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] If anyone wishes to receive or give outside the church the offerings, fruits, or firstfruits owed to the church, without the knowledge of the bishop, let him be anathema.

Canon of Hippo, aera 38.

[Note: Council of Carthage III, chapter 24; in full in the African Church manuscript, chapter 37.] No more of the firstfruits shall be offered on the altar [as sacrifices] than grapes and grain. [There are many variants in the editions.] Everything else shall be carried to the priest’s house to be blessed.

## Chapter XXX. Concerning communion, and that the people should attend Mass

Canon of Antioch, aera 2.

[Note: Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] All who enter the church but do not commune in prayer with the people, and through some intemperance turn themselves away from receiving holy communion, shall be removed from the church for as long as it takes them to obtain pardon through confession and penance.

Canon of Agde, aera 14 [canon 18].

Concerning the communion of laypeople.—Laypeople who do not receive communion at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, or Pentecost shall not be regarded as Catholics [variant: shall not be believed to be Catholics].

Canon of Mâcon, aera 6.

[Note: Council of Mâcon II.] No presbyter who is filled with food or drunk with wine shall presume to handle the sacrifices or celebrate Mass [variant: concelebrate on private and feast days]. If he presumes to do so, let him lose his honor [variants and additions in the editions].

Canon of Laodicea, aera 13.

[Note: Council of Laodicea, chapter 19.] [Note: It differs slightly from the translation of Dionysius.] Only those devoted to the ministry shall be permitted to enter the altar area and commune there.

Aera 44.

[Note: Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] Women ought not to enter the altar area.

Aera 57.

[Note: Chapter 58. Neither the translation of Dionysius nor that of Isidore contains this.] Offerings ought not to be consecrated by priests in private houses.

Canon of Nicaea, aera 14.

[Note: The number is the same in the translation of Rufinus, from which this passage differs, as it also differs from Dionysius and Isidore.] In general, communion should properly be given by the bishop from the offering to anyone who, placed at the point of death, requests it.

## Chapter XXXI. Concerning preaching

Canon of Arles, aera 2.

[Note: See something of this ancient canon in the Council of Arles VI, chapter 10.] For the edification of all the churches and the benefit of the whole people, it has also been decided that we grant presbyters authority to preach the word not only in the cities but also in all the parishes. If a presbyter is unable to preach because of illness, let the homilies of the holy Fathers be read by a deacon. If deacons are worthy to read what Christ spoke in the Gospel, why should they appear unworthy publicly to recite the explanations of the holy Fathers?

Canon of Africa, aera 30.

[Note: In the Barbet manuscript, Ancient Church Statutes, chapter 31; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 24.] If a priest is preaching in church, anyone who leaves the congregation shall be excommunicated.

Aera 33.

[Note: Ancient Church Statutes, chapter 33; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 88.] Whoever, on a solemn day, neglects the church assembly and goes to spectacles shall be excommunicated.

Aera 34.

[Note: Ancient Church Statutes, chapter 37; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 99.] A woman, however learned and holy, must not presume to teach men in the assembly.

Aera 38.

[Note: Ancient Church Statutes, chapter 38; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 98.] A layman must not presume to teach in the presence of clerics unless they themselves command him to do so.

## Chapter XXXII. Concerning hospitality

Canon of Africa, aera 56.

[Note: Ancient Church Statutes; in the Barbet manuscript, chapter 56; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 33.] If bishops or presbyters come to visit another bishop’s church [variant: for the purpose of visiting another bishop’s church], they shall be received according to their rank and invited both to preach the word and to consecrate the offering.

Canon of Nicaea, aera 20.

[Note: Council of Sardica, chapter 17; in Greek, chapter 21 in the translations of Dionysius and Isidore, from which this translation differs.] If anyone has suffered violence and been unjustly expelled and comes to another city, he must not be prevented from staying there as long as he is able either to return or to obtain a remedy for his wrong; even generous goodwill and humanity must be shown to him.

Canon of Mâcon, aera 11.

[Note: Council of Mâcon II, chapter 11. Much precedes this in the editions.] If any one of us fails to urge reconciliation through hospitality, either by the example of his exhortation or fails to demonstrate that he himself first puts it into practice [variant: does not demonstrate it by deed], he undoubtedly incurs the indignation of the majesty of the Lord. Let this be preached, according to the capacity of our modest ability [variant: modesty], in the ears of all Christians.

## Chapter XXXIII

Canon of Mâcon, aera 12.

[Note: The same council, chapter 5. Much precedes this in the editions.] We decree that the ancient custom be restored among the faithful, and that the entire people bring tithes to those serving the ecclesiastical rites. Let the priests, extending these either for the use of the poor or for the redemption of captives, obtain peace and salvation for the people by their prayers. But if anyone is obstinate toward our most salutary statutes, let him be separated from the members of the Church [the editions add: “at all times”].

## Chapter XXXIV. Concerning widows, orphans and the poor, the sick and prisoners, and lepers

[Note: Ancient Church Statutes; in the Barbet manuscript, chapter 32; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 83.]

The poor and the old of the church are to be honored more than others. [Note: In the Barbet manuscript, chapter 36; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 101.] Widows who are physically disabled shall be supported at the expense of the church of which they are widows.

Aera 58.

[Note: Ancient Church Statutes, chapter 68; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 102.] The bishop or presbyter who presides over the parish is liable to guilt if younger widows or consecrated women are placed under the familiar associations of clerics for the sake of maintaining their livelihood.

Aera 19.

[Note: In the Barbet manuscript, chapter 69; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 94.] The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected by priests.

Canon of Mâcon, aera 7.

[Note: Council of Mâcon II, chapter 12.] We decree that judges must not first summon widows and orphans until they have notified the bishop under whose protection they live. If the bishop is not present, the matter shall be reported to the archdeacon or to some presbyter [the editions omit “some”], so that, sitting together [variant: seated], they may settle their cases by common deliberation [variant: set limits to their cases], justly and rightly, so that thereafter the persons mentioned above may not be harassed in such matters. [Note: The distinguished J. Sirmond: “The Divion manuscript reads ‘may not be harassed’; the Angers manuscript, ‘may not be accused.’ From this it is clear that the Angers collection seen by J. Sirmond is different from ours, of which J. Morin spoke. See our preface.”] If the person who is judge, or the plaintiff, inflicts an injury upon them or transgresses the decision of so great a council, let him be suspended from communion.

Canon of Orléans, aera 12.

[Note: Council of Orléans I, chapter 16.] Let bishops provide food and clothing, as far as their means allow [variant: as much as their ability has], for the poor or sick who, because of weakness, cannot work with their own hands.

Canon of Lyon, aera 6.

[Note: Council of Lyon III.] It has been decided [also by the whole council] that the lepers of each city who are within the territory of that city [variants: are born there or are visibly residing there] shall receive sufficient food and clothing from the bishop of that church [variant: food and clothing shall be adequately provided]. Thus they shall be denied permission to wander through other cities. [The editions omit the following continuation.] Let the bishop govern the community of widows, orphans, and strangers not by himself but through the archdeacon or archpresbyter.

Canon of Orléans, aera 17.

[Note: Council of Orléans V, chapter 20.] Those who are confined in prisons [variant: for whatever offenses] shall be visited every Sunday by the archdeacon or the head of the church, so that the necessities of the bound may be mercifully relieved according to the divine command. By the bishop’s appointment [variant: in the Lyon manuscript; see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond], let a faithful and diligent person provide what is necessary, so that suitable food may be supplied from the church’s household.

Aera 20.

[Note: The same council, chapter 21.] Let provision be made in every way that mercy [variant: care for mercy] not be lacking to those whom unbearable poverty constrains through severe illness [additions and variants in the editions].

## Chapter XXXV. How the bishop should distribute or administer the property of the church; concerning what is given at the altar; and concerning basilicas throughout the parishes

Canon of Orléans, aera 10.

[Note: Council of Orléans I, chapter 14.] Of what is contributed at the altar [variant: from the offerings of the faithful], let the bishop claim half for himself, and let the clergy receive half [variant: one half], to be distributed according to the rank of each person, while estates of every kind remain under the authority of the bishops.

Aera 11.

[Note: The same council, chapter 15.] Concerning whatever the faithful have offered in the parishes—lands, vineyards, slaves, and livestock [variant]—the statutes of the ancient canons shall be observed, so that everything remains under the bishop’s authority. Of whatever has been added at the altar, however, let one third be faithfully delivered [to the bishops].

Aera 14.

All basilicas that have been built in various places [or are built each day; it has been decided, according to the rule of the earlier canons] shall remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated.

Canon of Africa, aera 4.

[Note: In the Barbet manuscript, chapter 4; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 15.] Let the bishop have inexpensive furniture, a table, and modest food, and seek the authority of his office [variant: the authority of his dignity] through the merits of faith and life.

Aera 15.

[Note: In the Barbet manuscript, chapter 15; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 31.] Let the bishop use the property of the Church as something entrusted to him, not as something belonging to him personally.

## Chapter XXXVI. Concerning property that a priest has given to his clerics

Canon of Lyon, aera 5.

[Note: Council of Lyon II. Certain material precedes this in the editions.] Property or any gifts that a priest has given to the clerics or servants of his church [variant: whether from church property for use or from his own property as ownership] shall not be taken away by succeeding bishops [variant: they must in no way presume to take them away]. If, however, some fault has occurred, let discipline be applied according to the character of the persons or the rule of the preceding canons, against the person, not against the property.

## Chapter XXXVII. Concerning property given to churches

Canon of Orléans, aera 5.

[Note: Council of Orléans III.] If any offerings consisting of any kinds of property and persons have been contributed to basilicas established in the cities, they shall be placed under the authority of the bishop; and it shall be at his discretion what is assigned for the repair of the church or for the support of those serving there. As for the resources of parishes or basilicas established in villages [of the cities], the custom of each individual place shall be observed in every respect [a verb is missing].

Canon of Agde, aera 6.

Bishops [who have been established in the highest priesthood], whenever something is left or donated by outsiders alone, either to the church or separately [whether it is left or donated], shall count it among the church’s resources—not as their own property but as property left to the church—because the donor is shown to offer it for the redemption of his soul, not for the priest’s advantage. For just as priests have what has been donated [left] to the church, so the church should have what is left to the priest.

Canon of Epaon, aera 14.

Any cleric who, after obtaining something from the generosity of the church he served, is ordained to the highest priesthood of another city [variant: is or has been ordained] shall return what he received as a gift; what he is shown to have possessed by use or ownership, according to the wording of the document [variant: to have purchased], he may retain.

## Chapter XXXVIII. Concerning church property taken away and withheld

Canon of Africa, aera 50.

[Note: In the Barbet manuscript, chapter 50; Council of Carthage, chapter 32.] Any donation, sale, or exchange by a bishop of church property without the assembly [variant: consent] and subscription of the clergy shall be void.

Aera 86.

[Note: In the Barbet manuscript, chapter 86; Council of Carthage IV, chapter 95.] Those who deny the offerings of the dead to the churches, or return them only with difficulty, shall be excommunicated as murderers of the needy.

Canon of Orléans, aera 26.

[Note: Council of Orléans III, chapter 23.] Abbots, presbyters, and other ministers may not alienate or pledge property assigned to ecclesiastical goods or to the sacred ministry without the subscription of their bishop. Whoever presumes to do so shall be degraded from the communion granted [to him], and whatever has been rashly alienated [variant: attempted] shall be restored by order of the bishop.

Aera 13.

[Note: The same council, chapter 12.] When church property has been alienated in any manner to the detriment of the church [variant: documents are known to have been uselessly pledged to the detriment of the church], if recovery is available within a period of thirty years [variant: if the acts can be challenged], let it be restored through public [variant: or elected] judgment, with justice supporting the claim. If the person who holds the church’s property, after being admonished, avoids judgment, let him be deprived of communion until he comes to an examination of the matter or restores the church’s property.

Aera 25.

[Note: The same council, chapter 22.] If anyone, prompted by dreadful greed [variant: “by the priest’s dreadful greed”], seizes or retains property owed to the Church, or its own property [many additions and variants occur throughout the editions], or for this reason delays coming before the judgment of the elect, let him be deprived of communion until the property itself has been restored. Likewise, the person who has retained offerings of the dead that were lawfully [variant: legally] left, or has presumed to assign them, shall be subject to the same judgment [variant: “those who retain or presume …”]. The person who has presumed to reclaim what he gave to the church [variant: “out of his devotion”] shall likewise be subject to the same sentence.

Canon of Lyon, aera 2.

[Note: Council of Lyon II, chapter 11.] It has been agreed that this be inviolably observed: wills that clerics [bishops, presbyters, or clerics of a lower order] have drawn up of their own free will, as well as donations and every kind of legal document, shall remain fully effective [variant: secure]. We decree especially that if the will of any religious person, through necessity or simplicity, has departed from the order of secular laws [variant: has appeared to depart], nevertheless the will of the deceased must remain undisturbed. [Some additions occur in the editions.] If anyone presumes to alienate anything from such property, let him be regarded as a stranger [variant: alien] to the ecclesiastical fellowship and to the company of all Christians [variant: the fellowship of the meal] until the donated property has been restored [variant: until the time of his correction or restoration].

Canon of Orléans, aera 19.

[Note: Council of Orléans IV.] Whoever is shown to have given something out of devotion [variant: with zeal for an offering], in fields or vineyards, even without writing [variant: without a written document], if he himself or anyone else alienates it, shall be deprived of communion until he restores what has been seized [the latest edition erroneously reads “perverted”].

Canon of Epaon, aera 7 [canon 8].

While a presbyter holds a diocese, he shall either draw up a document concerning what he has purchased in the name of the church, or depart from the administration of the church that he holds [variant: held].

Aera
17.

If a bishop has assigned something from the property belonging to ecclesiastical right by testament [after drawing up a testament, something from the ownership subject to ecclesiastical law], it shall otherwise have no validity unless he has supplied it only from the resources belonging to his own right.

**Aera 18.**

Clerics who, even without any petitions, have possessed property received as ecclesiastical remuneration for a long period [for any length of time], shall not be summoned into proprietary ownership by prescription of time [with the authority of our most glorious lord prince], provided that it is clear that the property belonged to the Church.

**Canon of Agde, aera 4.**

Let no one [whether clerics or laymen who] take away offerings of parents, whether donated or left by testament, or anything that he himself donated [if they have persisted in retaining them] [which they have believed ought to be taken away from churches or monasteries]. Those who do so shall be excluded from the Church until they return them.

**Aera c. 32 [Canon 33].**

A bishop who has no sons or grandsons [variant] shall leave no other heir than the Church. Whatever he has taken away from the Church without its own cause [if he has presumed to take anything from the Church for a purpose or necessity not belonging to the Church] shall be considered void. But whoever has sons shall ensure that, from the goods he has left, the Church’s indemnities are made good [provision shall be made for the Church’s indemnities] by his heirs.

**Canon of the Apostles, aera 38** [Note: Canon 39 in Dionysius’s translation, from which it differs slightly.]

The bishop shall possess the rights over all ecclesiastical affairs and shall administer them as though God were watching. He may not presume to take anything from them or grant anything to his own relatives. If they are poor, he shall supply them as poor persons, lest, on account of relatives, they plunder the Church.

**In a letter of Pope Symmachus** [Note: To Caesarius, bishop of Arles, chapter 1.]

Let bishops not presume to alienate Church possessions [which each person has given or left at the disposal of the Church] by any title or contract [nor do we permit this under any pretext whatsoever], except perhaps to clerics [variant], when merit, consideration for a monastery or religious purpose, or necessity among pilgrims should urge that they be granted something. Even so, they shall hold these things not perpetually but only for as long as they live.

**Canon of Ancyra, aera 16.**

[Note: Neither Dionysius nor Isidore’s translation.] If a presbyter has sold Church property, the contract being rescinded, let it be restored to ecclesiastical ownership. It shall be for the bishop to decide whether the buyer ought to recover the price, since it often happens that the revenues of property sold have repaid a greater sum than the price received.

**Canon of Agde, aera 6.**

Whatever is left to the Church by a trust [whether in the name of a priest or of the Church] or to a custodian shall not be counted among the Church’s assets [the Church will not be able to count or retain it].

**Aera 7.**

Small houses, or slaves [the Church’s small slaves], and vessels used in the Church’s ministry [many additions and variants in the editions and in what follows] may in no way be alienated. But if necessity compels that something be sold for the Church’s definite benefit, the necessity of the case must be confirmed before two or three provincial bishops, so that the sale may be strengthened by them; otherwise it shall have no validity.

**Canon of Orléans, aera 15** [Note: Council of Orléans IV, canon 25.]

If a cleric or layman, under the patronage [or in the name] of powerful persons, has sought or possessed Church property [property belonging to the Church’s jurisdiction], with contempt for the bishop [has presumed to seek or possess it], he shall first be admonished to restore civilly what he has taken. [Some editions add:] If he shows contempt, he shall be restrained from the thresholds of the Church until he restores it with satisfaction.

**In a letter of Pope Siricius, aera 2.**

[Note: Missing from the editions.] If Church property has been lost through a simple bishop, access to presenting the matter to his successor shall not be denied; and, according to the judgment of the canons, no prejudice shall at any time be done to the Church, since it is one Church spread throughout the whole world.

**Canon of Militene, aera 13.**

[Note: See the Council of Auvergne, canon 14.] If anyone defrauds, seizes, retains, or secretly appropriates gifts of any kind that have been conveyed to the Church by any written instrument, and, when admonished by the priest, does not immediately return what was conveyed, let him be expelled from communion.

**Canon of Agde, aera 26.**

If any cleric [anyone among the clerics] has suppressed, denied, or handed over to adversaries documents by which he possessed a church [by which the Church’s possession is secured], whatever loss has been inflicted on the Church through the withholding [absence] of the documents, he shall repay from his own resources and be deprived of communion. He also who has solicited instruments to the Church’s detriment [through wickedly solicited betrayers], or has received them, shall suffer the same sentence.

**Canon of Orléans, aera 33** [Note: Council of Orléans IV, canon 24.]

Whoever has received a small field of the Church from a priest to possess [during his lifetime, for whatever act of mercy, from a priest who has authority], whatever he has produced there shall have no power to alienate. Nor shall his relatives [themselves] consider anything from it [from that property] claimable for themselves.

**Canon of Carthage, aera 32** [Note: Council of Carthage III, canon 49.]

Clerics who acquire anything in their own name shall be held as invaders of the Lord’s property [liable under the charge of invasion], unless they have transferred those things to their own church [when admonished, they have transferred those very things to the Church]. But if something comes to them as their own through someone’s generosity or through inheritance from their family, let them do with it whatever accords with their profession. If they deviate backward from their profession, let them be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, as reprobates.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. ON LITIGANTS AND JUDGES

**African Canon, aera 3** [Note: Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes in the Barb. manuscript, chapter 14; Council of Carthage IV, canon 22.]

A bishop shall hear no one’s case without the presence of his clerics, because the bishop’s sentence will be invalid unless confirmed by the presence of the clerics.

**Aera 10** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 17; Council of Carthage IV, canon 55.]

A bishop shall excommunicate those who accuse their brethren. If they correct their fault, they shall be received into communion, but not into the clergy.

**Aera 30** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 30; Council of Carthage IV, canon 87.]

A Catholic who appeals his case [whether just or unjust] to the judgment of a judge of another faith shall be excommunicated.

**Aera 42** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 53; Council of Carthage IV, canon 96.]

At trial it must be investigated of what nation the accuser and the accused are, and what their faith is. A false accuser shall be placed outside the Church until he reforms himself through repentance.

**Aera 52** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 53; Council of Carthage IV, canon 31.]

Let the judges of the Church beware lest they pronounce sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being argued, for their sentence will be invalid; indeed, they will certainly have to give an account of the matter in a synod.

**Aera 53** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 54; Council of Carthage IV, canon 26.]

A bishop [variant] shall urge persons who are at odds to peace rather than to judgment.

**Canon of Chalcedon, aera 4 [Canon 9].**

[Note: Neither Dionysius nor Isidore’s translation.] Clerics who have business against one another ought not to abandon their own bishop and rush to secular courts; rather, they shall be judged before a synod.

## ON CLERICS WHO RUSH TO SECULAR JUDGMENT

**Canon of Agde, aera 31 [Canon 32].**

No cleric shall presume to summon anyone before a secular judge without the bishop’s permission. If he is summoned, let him answer, but not initiate proceedings; nor shall he dare to bring a criminal matter before a secular court [to present it in secular judgment]. If any layman has harassed [or attempted to harass, and has been defeated] a church or cleric by calumny, let him be kept from the thresholds of the Church and from communion [of Catholics] until he performs worthy penance [unless he has worthily repented].

**Canon of Orléans, aera 35** [Note: Council of Orléans III, canon 32.]

No cleric [of whatever rank] shall presume to drag anyone before a secular court without the permission of his bishop. Nor may a layman [without consulting the priest] bring a cleric before a secular court.

**Canon of Mâcon, aera 10** [Note: Council of Mâcon I, canon 7, and II, canon 10.]

A cleric must not be taken away from the Church or suffer any injury without the bishop’s knowledge. If anyone has anything against clerics, let him bring it to the bishop’s notice, and let the bishop himself, with justice leading the way, examine the cases.

**Aera 22** [Note: Council of Mâcon I, canon 7.]

Nor shall a judge drag a cleric to court without a criminal charge—that is, homicide, theft, or wrongdoing. If he does so, let the judge be kept from the Church [the thresholds of the Church] and deprived of communion for as long as the bishop [of that place] determines.

**Aera 18** [Note: Of the same council, canon 18.]

Those who accuse the innocent [Note: Variant; see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.] before princes or judges shall be degraded if they are clerics [removed from the order of their office]; but if they are laymen, they shall be deprived of communion.

**Canon of Carthage, aera 12.**

[Note: See Council of Carthage IV, canon 59.] If a dispute over earthly matters arises between bishops, within the space of a year they shall hasten, after being admonished by letters from their brethren, to settle the matter either among themselves or in the presence of chosen persons. Whoever delays doing so until the litigation itself is withdrawn shall be regarded as a stranger to the charity of the brethren.

**In a letter of Pope Siricius, aera 52.**

A dispute arising over Church property shall be brought before the metropolitan. Nothing may for any reason be suspended before the prince; it shall be settled by the judgment of the bishops.

## CHAPTER XL. ON BISHOPS OR CLERICS WHO ARE ACCUSED, AND ON THEIR ACCUSERS

**Canon of Nicaea, aera 14** [Note: Council of Sardica, canon 3.]

[Note: Variant in Dionysius and Isidore.] If a bishop has been judged in another case, and he himself wishes it, the council shall be renewed. The bishops who examined the case shall write to the Roman bishop, and whatever he judges shall be carried out.

**Aera 3** [Note: Council of Sardica, canon 4.]

[Note: Variant in Dionysius and Isidore.] Another bishop shall not be ordained in his place, since he has appealed to the Roman bishop, before the case has been examined.

**Canon of Antioch, aera 16 [Canon 14].**

[Note: Neither Dionysius nor Isidore’s translation.] If it happens that a bishop is accused of a criminal matter and differing judgments are pronounced against him by bishops, it has been decided that the metropolitan of another province, together with several bishops, should be summoned, so that they themselves may settle the questions and the judgment may be established as firm.

**Aera 14 [Canon 15].**

[Note: Neither Dionysius nor Isidore’s translation.] Whoever has received a concordant sentence from all the bishops of his province cannot be judged further by others unless he has appealed to the bishop of the Roman Church, so that the examination may be renewed.

**Canon of Carthage, aera 2** [Note: Council of Carthage III, canon 7; Code of the African Church’s Canons, canon 19.]

Whoever accuses one of the bishops shall bring the case to the primate of that province. The person against whom the charge is made shall not be suspended from communion unless, summoned by the primate’s letter to state his case [to the judgment of the chosen persons on the appointed day], he has altogether failed to appear—that is, within the space of a month from the day on which it is established that he received the letter. But if he proves [some] true causes of necessity [additions and variants], on account of which he did not appear, he shall have the opportunity to state his case [fully] within another month. After the second month, however, he shall not communicate until he has cleared himself. If he also fails to appear at the annual council [variant], so that his case may at least be settled there, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself. During the period in which he does not communicate, he shall not communicate even among his own people [in his own church or parish].

But if his accuser has never failed to appear on the days appointed for stating the case, he shall not be removed from communion. If, however, he has at some time failed to appear [withdrawing himself], after communion has been restored to the bishop [variant], the accuser himself shall be removed [from communion]; nevertheless, he shall retain [shall not be deprived of] the opportunity to carry through the case if he proves that he wished to appear on the appointed day but was unable to do so. [Many variants and some additions.]

No one shall be admitted to accuse or arraign another unless he is willing to state his own cases, though not ecclesiastical cases.

[Note: Council of Carthage III, canon 8; Code of Canons, canon 20.] If presbyters or deacons have been accused, the legitimate number of colleagues from neighboring places having been joined to them [with their own bishop]—six bishops in the case of a presbyter, three in the case of a deacon, chosen by the accused themselves—the bishops shall examine their cases, preserving the same procedure concerning days and postponements, removal from communion, and examination of the persons, between the accusers and those accused. The cases of the remaining [clerics] may be heard and concluded by the local bishop alone.

**Aera 79.**
