If a bishop has charged a cleric or layman with a crime, he shall bring the matter to proof.

**Canon of Hippo, aera 67** [Note: Council of Carthage V, canon 12; African Council, canon 46.]

Clerics accused of a crime, if they wish to assert their innocence, shall do so within a year of excommunication. If they do not clear their case within a year [if they contemptuously refuse to clear it], no statement of theirs concerning this case shall afterward be heard [at all].

**Canon of Carthage, aera 1** [Note: Council of Carthage III, canon 2; Code of Canons, canon 15.]

If any bishop or cleric, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, wishes to clear himself before public courts, he shall lose his place, even if a sentence has been pronounced in his favor. This applies to a criminal case. In ordinary legal titles, however, he shall lose what he has won, so that the authority of the Church may everywhere be evident [so that the person who has the right to choose judges may be known]. He judges himself unworthy of fellowship with the brethren who, thinking ill of the universal Church, seeks aid from a secular court, although the Apostle commands that the cases of private Christians be brought before the Church [and determined there].

[Canon 10.] If an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to a higher court, this shall not prejudice those whose sentence has been dissolved, unless they can be convicted either of having judged with hostile intent or of having been corrupted by some desire for gain [or by some form of greed or favor]. But if judges have been chosen by agreement of the parties, even if fewer judges are present [even if fewer than the established number are present, no appeal is permitted], one who is excommunicated is rightly not admitted to accuse.

**Aera 2** [Note: Council of Carthage VII, canon 2; African Council, canon 96; Code of the African Church, canon 119.]

Freedmen shall not be admitted to accuse their masters, nor shall all those whom the public laws do not admit to accuse crimes be admitted, nor all those stained by an infamous mark—that is, actors [persons subject to shameful occupations]; nor heretics, pagans, or Jews. Nevertheless [variant], everyone is permitted to accuse in his own cases, even those to whom the opportunity of accusing is denied on other grounds.

[Canon 3.] Whenever many crimes are brought against clerics [by accusers], and the accusers cannot prove one of them [the first matter they brought forward, the one they addressed first], they shall not be admitted to the others at all [any longer]. Those witnesses shall not be received who are forbidden [or not authorized] to be admitted to an accusation; nor those whom the accuser has brought from his own household to give testimony; nor those who are under fourteen years of age.

**Aera 3** [Note: Code of the African Church’s Canons, canon 30.]

If the accused or the accuser fears some force [a rash crowd] in the place where the case is being heard, he shall choose a nearby place where it will not be difficult to produce witnesses, and the case shall be concluded there.

**Aera 30** [Note: The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 87.]

A Catholic who appeals his case [addition: whether just or unjust] to the judgment of a non-Catholic judge [of another faith] shall be excommunicated.

**Aera 46** [Note: The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 58.]

No one shall receive the testimony of a person who litigates frequently and is quick to accuse [to bring suit] without a serious examination [investigation].

**Aera 8.**

[Note: See chapter 17 of Adrian I’s letter to Ingelramnus, with slight variation.] Whoever is entangled in greater crimes shall not have the right to bring an accusation against one older than himself.

**In a letter of Pope Sylvester.**

[Note: This passage is also cited by Egbert, archbishop of York, in excerpt 142, and in the manuscript of Theodore’s chapters. See above, Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 139, and chapter 72 in the chapters sent by Adrian I to Ingelramnus. See Hincmar.]

Pope Sylvester, standing in the midst of the synod, said: A presbyter shall not bring an accusation against a bishop, a deacon against a presbyter, or lower orders against higher orders. [Slightly variant.] The chief prelate shall not be condemned except by seventy-two witnesses; a presbyter shall not be condemned except by forty-three witnesses; a deacon established in the Roman city’s cardinal order shall not be condemned except by thirty-six witnesses; subdeacons or other minor orders shall not be condemned except on the testimony of seven.

**Canon of Chalcedon, aera 32.**

[Note: Slightly different from Dionysius’s translation.] Clerics or laymen accusing bishops or clerics must not be admitted indiscriminately and without proof; first, the reputation and standing of the accuser must be examined.

[Note: The remainder is missing.] It has been decided that in every accusation of clerics the faith and life of those who make the accusation must be scrutinized. For faith ought to precede every act of a person, since one who is uncertain in faith is an unbeliever. Those who either do not know the faith of truth or do not lead a proper way of life must not be believed at all, since such persons easily and indiscriminately tear apart and slander those who live rightly and devoutly.

**Aera 33.**

[Note: See Council of Arles V, canon 14.] No judge shall personally restrain or presume to condemn a presbyter, deacon, cleric, or junior member of the Church without the knowledge of the bishop. If he does so, he shall be separated from the Church to which he is known to have inflicted an injury for as long as it takes him to correct and amend the rashness of his guilt.

## CHAPTER XLI. ON CLERICS WHO TAKE INTEREST, ON DRUNKARDS AND SURETIES; AGAINST BANQUETS, SHAMEFUL SONGS, AND MANY OTHER SIMILAR MATTERS

**Canon of Nicaea, aera 19.**

[Note: Rufinus’s translation.] Let no cleric receive interest, or receive back a sixfold or twofold increase of grain or wine [as is customary], given as a new loan. If he does so, he is to be expelled as guilty of disgraceful profit.

**Canon of Arles, aera 19** [Note: Council of Arles I, canon 12.]

Concerning ministers who lend at interest, it has been decided that they shall be kept from communion according to the rule divinely given.

[Note: Missing from the editions.] **Canon of Caesarea, aera 9.**

[Note: See Council of Carthage III, canon 16.] No cleric shall receive more than he has entrusted, whether money or any kind of property.

**Canon of Sardica, aera 18.**

[Note: See the Council of Nicaea, canon 18, from the old translation read in Isidore Mercator.] Clerics who lend at interest and those who demand one-percent monthly interest, or interest from any transaction, shall be removed from the clergy.

**Canon of Arles, aera 14** [Note: Council of Arles II.]

If any cleric has lent money at interest, or has been [or wished to be] the tenant of another’s property, or has practiced any kind of commerce for the sake of disgraceful profit, he shall be deprived both of office and communion [deposed and made an outsider from communion].

**Canon of Agde, aera 39** [Note: Canon 41. Some matters precede this in the editions.]

A cleric who is established to have been drunk, as the order [or rule] declares [allows], shall either be suspended from communion for thirty days [variant editions] or subjected to corporal punishment.

**Canon of Laodicea, aera 24.**

[Note: Neither Dionysius nor Isidore’s translation.] Presbyters, monks, and ascetics ought not to enter taverns.

**Aera 52 [Canon 55 in Dionysius’s translation].**

[Note: It differs from Dionysius’s translation, as it does from Isidore’s.] Priests and clerics ought not to hold banquets from contributions or at drinking parties; this is not suitable even for laymen.

**Canon of Agde, aera 39.**

Presbyters or [deacons or subdeacons, or the remaining ministers] who are not permitted to have wives shall avoid the wedding banquets of others [some editions add a clause], lest hearing or sight, appointed for the sacred mysteries, be polluted by the contagion of shameful spectacles and the entanglement [contagion] of words.

**Canon of Caesarea, aera 7.**

[Note: Neither Dionysius nor Isidore’s translation.] Presbyters ought not to attend the banquets of secular weddings, especially since it is appropriate to impose penance for second marriages.

**Canon of the Africans, aera 73** [Note: Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes, chapter 73; Council of Carthage IV, canon 60.]

A cleric who is buffoonish and makes jokes with obscene words shall be removed from office.

**Aera 74** [Note: Ancient Ecclesiastical Statutes; in the Barb. manuscript, chapter 74; Council of Carthage IV, canon 61.]

A cleric who swears by created things shall be rebuked most severely; if he persists, he shall be excommunicated.

**Aera 75** [Note: The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 62.]

A cleric who sings amid banquets shall be restrained by the severity of the sentence stated above [of the sentence stated above].

**Aera 79** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, the same; Council of Carthage IV, canon 51.]

A cleric, though instructed in the word of God [variant editions], shall seek his livelihood by his craft.

**Aera 70** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, 80; Council of Carthage IV, canon 70.]

A cleric shall avoid the banquets and associations of heretics and schismatics.

## CHAPTER XLII. THAT CLERICS MUST NOT NEGLECT THEIR OFFICE, AND MUST NOT BE TENANTS, CONTUMACIOUS, OR INVOLVED IN SECULAR AFFAIRS

[lacuna]

[Note: Council of Chalcedon, canon 3. The translation differs slightly from Dionysius’s.] No bishop, cleric, or monk may lease possessions or involve himself in secular business. [The exception concerns] the unavoidable care of orphans, if circumstances should impose such duties, or when the bishop of the city commands that he attend to ecclesiastical affairs, or to orphans and widows who have no provider; and the fear of the Lord requires it.

**Canon of Orléans, aera 13** [Note: Council of Orléans IV, canon 13.]

[Note: More fully in the editions.] A bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall not become entangled in the administration of guardianships.

**African Canon, aera 27** [Note: See Council of Orléans V, canon 14.]

No cleric, or any other person whatsoever, shall seek or presume to receive the property of another church. If he does so, he shall be considered suspended from communion until the property is restored to its own church.

**Aera 11** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 28; Council of Carthage IV, canon 48.]

A cleric shall not walk through streets and passageways [variant editions] without a definite necessity connected with his office.

**Aera 9** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 52; Council of Carthage IV, canon 29.]

A cleric shall provide himself with food and clothing by a craft or by agriculture, provided only that this does not impair his office.

[lacuna]

[Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 29; Council of Carthage IV, canon 48.] A cleric who walks about in marketplaces or the forum for no purpose of buying anything shall be degraded from office.

**Aera 25** [Note: In the Barb. manuscript, chapter 35; Council of Carthage IV, canon 49.]

A cleric who is absent from vigils without bodily weakness shall be deprived of his stipend.

**Aera 21** [Note: Council of Carthage IV, canon 50.]

A cleric who withdraws from his office amid temptations, or acts negligently, shall be removed from office.

**Canon of Carthage, aera 71** [Note: The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 42.]

A cleric who applies himself to his office amid temptations shall be advanced in rank.

[Notes: Slightly different from Dionysius’s translation. The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 14. The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 17.]

**Canon of Agde, aera 8.**

[“It was also decided that”] If a cleric, abandoning his office because of discipline, has fled to a secular [judge], and [the person to whom he has fled] has provided him the assistance of defense, both he and that person shall be expelled from the Church’s communion.

**Canon of Mâcon, aera 10.**

[Note: Council of Mâcon I, canon 10.] Ecclesiastical orders [presbyters, deacons, or clerics of any order] shall be so subject to their bishop in the devotion of obedience that they may not observe holidays elsewhere except in his service. Whoever delays doing this shall be degraded.

**Aera 11.**

All clerics [bishops, presbyters, or all clerics of higher rank] who are elevated by the dignity of exalted wisdom shall renounce entirely the activities of the world and, chosen for sacred ministry, reject sexual partnership [variant editions: see the notes of the same author].

## CHAPTER XLIII. THAT A CLERIC MUST NOT LIVE WITH OUTSIDER WOMEN; AND ON A PRIEST’S WIDOW

**Canon of Nicaea, aera 3.**

[Note: Rufinus’s translation.] Let no bishop or other cleric live with women [various editions and additions], except his mother or any persons of this kind.

**Canon of the Africans, aera 27** [Note: The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 46.]

A cleric shall not live with outsider women.

**Canon of Arles, aera 4.**

No bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall admit a female into the privacy of his storeroom [a girl, whether freeborn or enslaved].

**Canon of Agde, aera 11.**

It has been decided that women [female slaves or freedwomen] shall be removed from the storeroom, the private ministry, or the dwelling in which the cleric lives.

**Canon of Mâcon, aera 4** [Note: Council of Mâcon I, canon 3.]

No woman shall be permitted to enter the bishop’s bedroom without two presbyters, or certainly deacons.

**Canon of Orléans, aera 4** [Note: Council of Orléans III, canon 4.]

We decree that no bishop or cleric shall have permission to keep any woman within his house, except those whom the preceding canons mention. If any cleric incurs an adverse suspicion [variant: suspicion] or slander concerning any woman [perhaps], he shall immediately cast her out [if she is certainly an outsider and legally independent] and shall take care to avoid her in every respect, so that the infamy that has arisen may be removed. Whoever does not avoid these things shall be punished with three years’ excommunication for his disobedience.

[Note: Variant editions; see the note of the distinguished Sirmond.] In these admonitions the metropolitan shall be disciplined by the provincial bishops, and the provincial bishops by the metropolitan together with the remaining provincial bishops.

**Canon of Epaon, aera 32.**

Whoever marries the widow of a presbyter or deacon [“the widow, etc., if she marries anyone”] shall be expelled from the Church together with her [to that extent], until they separate from the unlawful union.

**Canon of Orléans, aera 9** [Note: Council of Orléans I, canon 13.]

[Note: Some variants and additions in the editions.] The widow of a presbyter or deacon, if she joins herself to anyone, shall be punished by the same excommunication.

**Canon of the Apostles, aera 6.**

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon shall not in any way cast away his own wife under pretext of religion. If he casts her away, he shall be excommunicated; if he persists, he shall be deposed.

## CHAPTER XLIV. ON BISHOPS, OR THE RULES FOR CLERICS, AND THEIR CLOTHING, ETC.

**African Canon, aera 1.**

A bishop shall have a small lodging not far from the church.

**Aera 2** [Note: The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 34.]

In the church, in the assembly of presbyters, the bishop shall sit in a higher place; but within the house he shall recognize himself as a colleague of the presbyters.

**Aera 3** [Note: The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 20.]

A bishop shall not take upon himself the administration of household affairs; rather, he shall devote himself only to reading and prayer, the word of God [variant editions], and preaching.

**Aera 4** [Note: The same in manuscript B; Council of Carthage IV, canon 15.]

A bishop shall have inexpensive furnishings and a table [variant editions], and poor food; he shall acquire [seek] the authority of his dignity through the faith [faithfulness] and merits of his life.

**Aera 5** [Note: The same in manuscript B; Council of Carthage IV, canon 16.]

A bishop shall not read the books of pagans, but may read those of heretics when necessity and the occasion require [another reading: “when necessary,” omitting “and of time”].

**Aera 6** [Note: The same in the Barb. manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 18.]

A bishop shall not undertake the guardianship of testaments.

**Aera 7.**

A bishop shall administer the affairs of widows, orphans, and pilgrims not personally, but through the archpresbyter or archdeacon.

**Aera 8** [Note: The same in manuscript B; Council of Carthage IV, canon 19.]

A bishop [variant editions], even when provoked, shall not litigate over transitory matters.

**Aera 12** [Note: The same in manuscript B; Council of Carthage IV, canon 34.]

A bishop, wherever he is sitting, shall not allow presbyters to stand.

**Canon of Nicaea, aera 36** [Note: Council of Sardica, canon 17.]

[Note: Reading found neither in Dionysius nor Isidore.] If a bishop, as ought not to happen, is irascible and, angered against his cleric, wishes to expel him from the Church quickly or harshly, that cleric shall have the right to appeal to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be carefully treated and the matter examined, and so that the bishop’s sentence may either be proved or corrected.

**Canon of Vaison** [Note: Council of Valence I, canon 8.]

[lacuna]

If a bishop alone knows of someone’s crimes [is privy to another’s crime], he shall correct him through private reproofs [additions and variants in the editions]. But if, after being chastised, he becomes more obstinate and thrusts himself into public communion, and even if the bishop lacks proof when reproving the man whom he judges guilty, let the man, although not condemned, be ordered—because of the greater authority of the person—to withdraw for a time from those who know nothing, while, for as long as the bishop can prove nothing, he remains in communion with everyone except the bishop who judges him guilty.

**Canon of Orléans 2, aera 36** [Note: See Council of Orléans IV, canon 36, where this canon appears to be cited.]

If a bishop gives property from his own Church’s resources to the clergy of another Church, it shall have no validity.

**Canon of Chalcedon, aera 23 [Canon 26].**

[Note: Neither Dionysius nor Isidore’s translation.] It has been decided that every Church having a bishop shall also have a steward from its clergy to administer the Church’s property according to the bishop’s arrangement, so that the administration of the Church may not be without testimony. If a bishop neglects to have such a steward, he shall be subject to the divine ordinances.

**Canon of the Romans, aera 3** [Note: Canon 7. See above.]

At Eastertide, presbyters and deacons have been accustomed to grant remission of sins through the parishes [the editions incorrectly read “promise”] and to fulfill the ministry. They have even been accustomed to descend into the font when the bishop is present. But the supreme authority is granted in the bishop’s name [variant editions, incorrectly]. At other times [additions and variants in the editions], in the necessity of illness, a presbyter may grant forgiveness of sins through the grace of the saving water, since he is also permitted to offer a gift for the purpose of cleansing. No permission, however, is found to have been granted to deacons. But what may once have been usurped is said to be excused on grounds of necessity [through necessity] [variant editions], lest afterward it be committed through presumptuous security.

**In a letter of Pope Celestine, aera 1** [Note: Letter of Celestine I to the bishops of Apulia and Calabria, chapter 1.]

No priest may be ignorant of his own canons, nor do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers. [Addition in the editions.]

**Canon of Agde, chapter 10.**

No cleric shall join himself to the familiarity of outsider women [to an outsider woman] [for any consolation and] for any reason whatsoever.

**Canon of Orléans, chapter 13** [Note: Council of Orléans IV, canon 23.]

The Church’s servants and the priests’ servants may not engage in raiding or taking captives. [Additions and variants in the editions.] But it is just that their masters provide assistance for their ransom.

**Canon of Laodicea, aera 10** [Note: Council of Laodicea, canon 13.]

[Note: Neither Dionysius nor Isidore’s translation.] The people must not be permitted to choose those who are to be appointed to the ministry of the altar.

[Canon 15.] No one other than the canonical chanters (psaltes), who ascend the pulpit and read from the book, may sing.

[Canon 25.] Ministers ought not to give the bread or bless the chalice.

**Aera 21 [Canon 54].**
[Note: [Col. 1046D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this interpretation.] Clerics ought not to attend spectacles; but before the performers enter, they are to rise and depart.

**Canon of the Apostles, canon 24** [Note: [Col. 1046D] In the Greek text, canon 22; in Dionysius, canon 23.]

[Note: [Col. 1046D] Interpretation not found in Dionysius.] A cleric who castrates himself is to be utterly condemned.

**Canon 26** [Note: [Col. 1046D] Canon 23 in the Greek text; canon 24 in Dionysius’s interpretation.]

A layman who castrates himself is to be deprived of communion for three years.

[Col. 1046C] [lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 1046D] In Greek, canon 25; in Dionysius’s interpretation, canon 27, from which this differs.] Only clerics, lectors, and cantors may have wives.

**Canon 42**

[Note: [Col. 1046D] Interpretation not found in Dionysius.] Subdeacons, lectors, or cantors who devote themselves to drunkenness must either desist or be deprived of communion; and likewise laymen.

[Note: [Col. 1046D] See a similar canon shortly below.] **Canon of Carthage, canon 2**

Lectors are to read until they reach the age of puberty. Thereafter, unless they have either guarded their chastity or taken wives, they are not to be permitted to read. Lectors, however, shall retain the designation “clerics.”

**Canon of Laodicea, canon 12** [Note: [Col. 1046D] Council of Laodicea, canon 19.]

[Note: [Col. 1046D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this interpretation.] Only ministers of the altar may enter the altar area and communicate there.

[Col. 1046D] **Canon of Arles, canon 13** [Note: [Col. 1046D] Council of Orléans IV.]

If anyone presumes to involve in public activities a cleric who has come from any occupation [from any condition], and, after being admonished by a priest, does not reform, let him know that he does not possess the peace of the Church.

**Canon of Carthage, canon 16** [Note: [Col. 1047D] Council of Carthage III, canon 19; canonical code, canon 16. See above.]

[It was decreed that] when lectors reach the age of puberty, they must either take wives or profess continence.

**Canon of Hippo, canon 9** [Note: [Col. 1047D] Council of Carthage V, canon 1.]

So that clerics may not be compelled to give testimony publicly concerning matters within their jurisdiction [according to variant editions], and so that no ecclesiastical person may be summoned to give testimony.

**Canon of Lyons, canon 19** [Note: [Col. 1047D] See Council of Mâcon II, canon 19.]

No cleric is to approach or be present at the place where defendants are examined. But if he is present, deprived of the more honorable stole, he is to be associated with those groups of examiners whom he has preferred to the divine mysteries.

**Canon of Agde, canon 55** [Note: [Col. 1047D] The same in the Barberini manuscript of the *Ecclesiastical Statutes*; Council of Carthage IV, canon 53.]

All clerics who are fit for work [who are more capable] are to learn crafts and letters.

**Canon 58** [Note: [Col. 1047D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 38.]

A deacon, in the presence of a presbyter, may distribute the Eucharist of Christ’s body to the people if necessity compels him and he is ordered to do so. [Note: [Col. 1047D] Barberini manuscript, canon 50; Council of Carthage IV, canon 39.] A deacon is to sit wherever a presbyter orders him to sit.

**Canon 60** [Note: [Col. 1047D] The Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 41.]

A deacon is to wear the white garment only at the time of the offering and the reading.

**Canon 61** [Note: [Col. 1047D] The Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 1.]

A deacon is to speak when questioned in an assembly of presbyters.

[Col. 1047C] **Canon of Laodicea, canon 25**

[Note: [Col. 1047D] The same interpretation is found in Dionysius.] Subdeacons ought not to give the bread or bless the chalice.

**Canon 26**

[Note: [Col. 1047D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this interpretation.] Those who have not been ordained by a bishop cannot perform exorcisms.

**African canon, canon 25** [Note: [Col. 1048D] Council of Carthage IV, canon 44.]

A cleric is not to grow either his hair [Note: [Col. 1048D] Variant editions; see the note in the latest edition of the Council.] or his beard.

**Canon 26** [Note: [Col. 1048D] The Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 45.]

A cleric is to demonstrate his profession also by his clothing and manner of walking; therefore he is not to seek elegance in either garments [variant editions] or footwear.

**Canon of Agde, canon 20**

Clerics who grow their hair are to be shorn against their will [by the archdeacon; even if they refuse, they are to be shorn against their will]. [Col. 1047D] They may not possess garments or footwear except such as are suitable for religious life [the editions omit “for”].

**Canon of Mâcon, canon 5** [Note: [Col. 1048D] Council of Mâcon I.]

No cleric is to presume to wear a cloak or secular clothing [Col. 1048A] except such as is suitable for religious life. If, after this decree, a cleric is found either in unsuitable clothing or with weapons [he is to be disciplined by his superior so that], after being confined for thirty days, he is sustained each day only by water and the consumption of a small amount of bread. [Note: [Col. 1048D] Variant; see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.]

**Canon of Laodicea, canon 20**

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this interpretation.] A deacon is to sit when ordered to do so by a presbyter. Honor is likewise to be shown to deacons and to those in the grades below them.

**Canon 21**

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this.] Subdeacons and those in the lower orders ought not to touch the Lord’s vessels.

**Canon 22**

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this.] No one except subdeacons ought to use the stole [Col. 1048B] and leave the door.

**Canon 23**

Lectors and cantors ought not to use stoles.

**Canon of Caesarea, canon 14**

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore.] There are to be seven deacons, even if the city is large, in accordance with the rule of the Acts of the Apostles.

**Canon of Nicaea, canon 20**

[Note: [Col. 1048D] Rufinus’s interpretation.] And so that deacons are not placed above presbyters, they are neither to sit in the company of presbyters nor, when presbyters are present, distribute the Eucharist to them; rather, while the presbyters are officiating, they are only to minister. If no presbyter is present, then and only then may they themselves do so. Those who act otherwise [by distributing it] are to be expelled [the reading is “are ordered to be expelled”].

# CHAPTER XLV. ON HUNTING AND HOSPITALITY

[Col. 1048C]

**Canon of Mâcon, canon 13** [Note: [Col. 1048D] Council of Mâcon II.]

We therefore wish the episcopal residence—which was established so that it might receive everyone in hospitality without respect of persons—not to have dogs, lest those who trust that they will find in it relief from their hardships should be torn by the bites of savage dogs [additions and variants]. The episcopal dwelling must therefore be guarded by hymns, not barking; by good works, not poisonous bites. Where there is the continual song of God, it is monstrous and disgraceful that dogs and hawks should dwell there.

**Canon of Epaon, canon 7** [Note: [Col. 1048D] Council of Epaon, canon 4.]

Bishops, presbyters, and deacons may not possess dogs for hunting or hawks. If [If anyone of such persons is discovered to have this inclination, if he is a bishop] a bishop presumes to do this, he is to suspend himself from communion for three months; a presbyter is to abstain for two months; and a deacon is to cease from every office and from communion for one month.

# CHAPTER XLVI. THAT SINNING BELIEVERS MAY NOT BE BEATEN INDISCRIMINATELY

[Col. 1049A]

**Canon of the Apostles, canon 28** [Note: [Col. 1049D] In Greek, canon 26; canon 28 in Dionysius’s interpretation.]

We decree that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who strikes believers or unbelievers indiscriminately, and by such means [lacuna] wishes to be feared, is to be deposed from office, because the Lord has nowhere taught us this.

# CHAPTER XLVII. ON PARISHES AND THE CONSTRUCTION OF ORATORIES

**Canon of Toledo, canon 29** [Note: [Col. 1049D] Council of Toledo III, canon 19.]

Whoever builds a church contrary to the statutes of the canons and has not lawfully sought its consecration from the bishop [many variants], must either demolish it or regard the endowment that he made for that church as belonging to the bishop’s disposition. Such an act [both in the past] displeases us in the present and is prohibited for the future; but everything [addition] is to belong to the bishop’s disposition [and authority].

**Canon 7** [Canon 20]

But bishops must not oppress the parishes. [Many variants.] Let them hear the Scripture: “Be examples to the flock, not lording it over the clergy.” Therefore, except for what the institutions of the ancients command bishops to receive from the parishes, everything else [that has hitherto been presumed] is to be denied. That is, neither presbyter nor deacon is to be wearied by forced labor [variant: “wearied by levies”], lest bishops in the Church of God appear to be called exactors rather than pontiffs. Those clerics, both local and diocesan, who discover that they are being burdened by a bishop are to bring their complaints to the metropolitan [they are not to delay bringing them]. The metropolitan [addition and variants] is to restrain such presumption.

**Canon of Toledo, canon 4**

If a bishop wishes to dedicate one of the parishes [one of the parish churches] as a monastery [additions and variants], he is to have permission. The goods [many variants] that he gives there from the Church for the support of monks or nuns are to remain there perpetually; that is, he is to give them reasonably.

**Canon of Orange, canon 8** [Note: [Col. 1049D] Council of Orange I, canon 10.]

If a bishop wishes to build a church on the estate of his own church [in the territory of another city] and in the parish of another bishop [he intends to do so], he is not to be prohibited [additions and variants]; but the consecration is to be reserved entirely to the bishop in whose territory the church rises. The bishop who built it [variant] is himself to ordain clerics there; or, if they have already been ordained, he is to retain them. Nevertheless, the entire administration of that church is to belong to the bishop in whose territory it is situated [the church has risen].

**Canon of Orléans, canon 26** [Note: [Col. 1049D] Council of Orléans IV.]

If any parishes have been established in the houses of powerful persons [many variants], the clerics who are there are to be disciplined by the city’s archdeacon, according to the rank of their order [Col. 1050A] and ecclesiastical discipline [addition]. But if they are prevented in any way from performing the church’s office by agents of the powerful, or by the owners themselves [additions and variants], the authors of the wrongdoing are to be deprived of communion until they make amends.

**Canon of Toledo, canon 15** [Note: [Col. 1049D] Council of Toledo III.]

If a fiscal slave [one of the fiscal slaves] builds a church and endows it [from his poverty] [variants and additions], the bishop is to arrange through his petition that this be confirmed by the authority of the prince [the king].

# CHAPTER XLVIII. ON THE ANNIVERSARIES OF MARTYRS

**Canon of Laodicea, canon 22** [Note: [Col. 1049D] Council of Laodicea, canon 51. It does not differ from Isidore’s interpretation.]

[Col. 1050B] The anniversaries of martyrs ought not to be celebrated during Lent; rather, their memory is to be commemorated only on Saturday and Sunday.

# CHAPTER XLIX. ON SPURIOUS MARTYRS AND PLACES VAINLY VENERATED

[lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Council of Laodicea, canon 9. Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore.] Cemeteries, or places called martyria belonging to heretics, are not to be granted access, nor is one to enter them for the sake of prayer. Whoever does so is to be made incapable of communion and reduced to penance for a certain period; and if he confesses that he was in error, he ought to be received.

**Canon 16** [Canon 35]

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore.] Whoever abandons the Church of God and goes to pray in secluded corners or to hold gatherings—all of which are forbidden—and devotes himself to this idolatry, let him be anathema.

**Canon 21** [Canon 34]

[Note: [Col. 1050D] Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore.] A Christian ought not, after abandoning the martyrs, to go to false martyrs; for these are alien to God and are to be struck with anathema.

**Canon 22** [Note: [Col. 1050D] Council of Arles I, canon 22.]

Those who apostatize, never come to church [present themselves], and do not seek penance, but later request communion during illness [variant], are not to be given it before they have performed worthy penance.

**Canon of Epaon, canon 32**

We disdain that the basilicas of heretics [addition] should be applied to holy uses [Col. 1050D]; nevertheless, those that they violently took from us may be reclaimed.

**Canon of Hippo, canon 82** [Note: [Col. 1050D] Council of Carthage V, canon 14; African Council L.]

Altars that are erected through fields and vineyards [roads] as memorials of martyrs [are established] [additions] are to be overturned by the bishops who preside over those places [if this can be done]. If popular disturbances do not permit this, however, the people are nevertheless to be warned not to frequent those places. [Addition.] And absolutely no memorial of martyrs [probably] is to be accepted unless there is a body or some relics there, and the existence of some dwelling or passion is handed down on the authority of a most trustworthy source [variant]. For altars established through dreams and through the empty, so-called revelations of human beings are forbidden [rejected] in every way.

# CHAPTER L. ON LOTS AND AUGURIES

**Canon of Arles, canon 24** [Note: [Col. 1051D] Council of Arles II, canon 23.]

Those who light torches or venerate trees, stones, or springs: if the bishop of that place neglects to uproot this practice [variant], let him recognize that he is guilty of sacrilege. The person who established the practice, if admonished and unwilling to reform, is to be deprived of communion.

**Canon of the Africans, canon 74** [Note: [Col. 1051D] *Ecclesiastical Statutes* in the Barberini manuscript, canon 83; Council of Carthage IV, canon 89.]

[Col. 1051B] Anyone devoted to auguries or incantations is to be separated from the church’s assembly.

**Canon of Agde, canon 40** [Canon 42]

If anyone possesses lots that are called “of the saints” [variant], or professes knowledge of divination, or promises the future through examination of any writings, whoever [cleric or layman] is discovered presuming to consult or teach these things is to be regarded as an outsider by the Church.

**Canon of Orléans, canon 26** [Note: [Col. 1051D] Council of Orléans I, canon 30.]

If anyone believes that divinations or auguries are to be observed, or lots falsely claimed to have belonged to the saints [addition], he is to be expelled from communion with the Church, together with those who believe in them.

**Canon of Ancyra, canon 24** [Note: [Col. 1051D] The same in Greek, canon 23, and in the interpretations of Dionysius and Isidore, from which this differs.]

Those who observe auguries, omens, or any sort of divinations, or purify their houses with ritual observances, are, after confessing, to perform penance for five years.

# CHAPTER LI. ON CLERICS, MONKS, AND ABBOTS

[lacuna]

[Note: [Col. 1052D] Council of Chalcedon, canon 7. Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore. See the Council of Angers, canon 7.] Those who have once been assigned to the clergy or have chosen the life of monks are not to presume to enter military service or any worldly dignity. Those who attempt such things and do not perform penance, so that they do not return to what they first chose for the Lord’s sake, are to be anathematized.

[Col. 1051D] **Canon of Orléans, canon 9** [Note: [Col. 1052D] Council of Orléans I, canon 11.]

Those who, after undertaking penance, forget their religious profession and relapse into secular life are to be separated from communion and from the table of all Catholics [it was decreed, etc., that they be suspended]. [Variant.] If, after the prohibition, anyone presumes to eat with such a person, he too is to be deprived of communion.

**Canon 15** [Note: [Col. 1052D] Council of the same, canon 19.]

For the sake of the humility of religious life, abbots are to remain under the authority of bishops. If they do anything contrary to [outside] the rule, they are to be corrected by the bishops, who are to assemble once a year at the place selected by the bishop, after receiving a summons. Monks, however, are to submit to their abbots with complete obedience [Note: [Col. 1052D] Variant; see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.] and devotion. If anyone proves disobedient through obstinacy, or presumes to wander through various places or to possess private property, everything he acquires is to be taken from him and given to the abbots, for the benefit of the monastery according to the rule. Those who have wandered are to be brought back under guard wherever they are found, with the assistance of the bishop, as fugitives. Let that abbot recognize that he will be guilty who does not restrain such persons with regular discipline, or who receives another man’s monk.

[Col. 1052B] **Canon of Chalcedon, canon 4**

[Note: [Col. 1052D] It differs slightly from Dionysius’s interpretation.] Monks in each province or city are to be subject to the bishop; they are to love quiet and devote themselves only to fasting and prayer, remaining in the places in which they renounced the world. They are not to participate in ecclesiastical or secular business, nor to be troublesome in any way by abandoning their own monasteries, unless perhaps the bishop of the city orders them to do so for some necessary work. No one is to receive a slave into a monastery under the pretext of monasticism, against the knowledge of his master. We decree that anyone who transgresses this definition is excommunicated, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed. Nevertheless, it is the bishop’s duty to exercise appropriate oversight of the monasteries.

[Col. 1052C] **Canon of Agde, canon 19** [Canon 27]

No one is to presume to begin or establish a new monastery without the bishop’s permission [or approval]. Wandering monks are not to be ordained in cities or parishes for clerical office unless their abbot has given them a testimonial. No abbot is to presume to receive or retain a monk who migrates to another monastery without his abbot’s permission [or will]; wherever he is found, he is to be recalled to his own abbot by the authority of the canons. If it is necessary for a clerical office [for a cleric to be ordained from among the monks], the bishop may presume to ordain a monk with the abbot’s consent and will. (Canon 28.) Monasteries of women are to be located at a greater distance from monasteries of men, because of the devil’s snares and the slanders [Col. 1052D] [calumnies] of human beings.

**Canon 38**

Care must also be taken concerning monks: they are not to be permitted to withdraw from the community into solitary cells [or “by means of solitary cells”], unless, after tested labors have been completed, or because of the necessity of illness, the abbots relax the stricter rule. [Additions and variants.] Nevertheless, within the same enclosure of the monastery, they may be permitted to have separate cells under the abbot’s authority.

[Note: [Col. 1054D] Council of Arles V, canon 5.]

[Col. 1053A] **Canon of Orléans, canon 18** [Note: [Col. 1053D] Council of Orléans I, canon 20.]

A monk may not use a stole [in the monastery] or possess [Note: [Col. 1053D] Variant; see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.] a *cianga* [a term of uncertain meaning].

**Canon of Arles, canon 2** [Note: [Col. 1053D] Council of Arles V, canon 2.]

The monasteries and the discipline of monks are to belong to the bishop in whose territory they have been established.

**Canon of Chalcedon, canon 24**

[Note: [Col. 1053D] Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore.] Monasteries once dedicated with the counsel of the bishops are to remain monasteries perpetually. The properties belonging to them ought to be reserved for the monasteries, and they may no longer be made into secular dwellings. Those who permit this to happen will be subject to the penalties of the canons.

**Canon of Autun, canon 1**

[Col. 1053B] [Note: [Col. 1053D] Additions and variants.] Abbots and monks may not possess private property; monks are to receive their customary food and clothing from the abbot.

**Canon 8**

Monks are to be obedient to their abbot or superior.

**Canon 6**

Monks are not to be found wandering in cities [variant], unless they are sent there by chance for the sake of humility; and then they are to be sent with letters from their abbot to the archdeacon.

**Canon 5** [Canon 10]

No monk is to dare to have co-godparents (*compatres*), or to maintain familiarity with strange women. Whoever is found doing so is to be corrected more severely.

**Canon 10**

[Col. 1053C] Women are in no way permitted to enter a men’s monastery. We decree that no one is to presume to retain another man’s monk without his abbot’s permission; when he is found wandering, he is to be recalled to his own cell and there disciplined according to the measure of his offense.

**Canon 15**

Concerning abbots and monks, it is appropriate to observe the following: whatever the canonical order and the rule of Saint Benedict teach, they must keep [and fulfill] in every respect. For if all these things are lawfully observed by abbots and monks in every monastery, both the number of monks will increase, with God’s favor, and the whole world, through their continual prayers, will be free from every contagion of evil. [Note: [Col. 1053D] Many additions and variants. On these canons, see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.] But if anyone attempts by some transgression to nullify what has been instituted by us with God’s favor [Col. 1053D], if he is an abbot, communion is to be suspended from him for three years; if a superior, for two years; if a monk, he is either to be beaten or deprived for three years of communion and participation in the table.

**Canon of Agde, canon 36** [Canon 38]

Monks [clerics] are not to be free to wander without letters of recommendation from the bishop or permission from their abbot. [Col. 1054A] [Additions and variants.] If they do not reform through verbal reprimands, they are to be restrained by blows.

**In a letter of Pope Siricius** [Note: [Col. 1054D] To Himerius of Tarragona, chapter 13.]

We both desire and wish that monks whom the seriousness of their character and holy life [and the holy formation of their life and faith] commend be joined to the offices of the clergy. If any are under thirty years of age, they are to advance through the individual grades, with the required periods of time increasing in each order [variant], and thus reach the orders [insignia] of the diaconate or presbyterate when mature [through consecration at a mature age], so that they may not leap to the summit of the episcopate unless [variant] both the order and the requisite periods have been observed at every grade.

**In a letter of Pope Innocent** [Note: [Col. 1054D] To Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapter 10], **canon 11**

[Col. 1054B] Monks [additions and variants] who attain the clerical order ought not to deviate from their former purpose; nor, when placed in a higher grade, ought they to abandon what they long preserved. A man who was corrupted before baptism, if he marries after baptism, can in no way be admitted to the clergy.

**In the Synod of Nicaea** [Note: [Col. 1054D] See the Second Council of Nicaea, canon 21.]

If anyone was raised in a monastery up to the highest level of study and afterward departs, he is to be condemned with the guilt of desertion unless he returns. If anyone receives another man’s monk, both are to be excommunicated. [Note: [Col. 1054D] See the ancient penitential book of Theodore, chapter 11.] A boy is to remain under his father’s authority until the age of twelve. Then and thereafter he may make himself a monk. (Chapter 13.) A child may be offered to a monastery in place of another child, even if someone else had made a vow concerning him; nevertheless, it is better to fulfill the vow, lest you be found guilty in relation to it. Observe what has once gone forth from your lips, just as you promised the Lord your God.

# CHAPTER LII. ON WOMEN CONSECRATED TO GOD AND THEIR MONASTERIES

**African canon, canon 38** [Note: [Col. 1054D] The same in the Barberini manuscript, canon 39; Council of Carthage IV, canon 97.]

The man who is to be placed over religious women must be approved by the bishop of the place.

**Canon of Orléans, canon 6**

The bishop is to take care of the monasteries of women [established in his city]; nor is an abbess permitted to do anything contrary to the rule.

**Canon of Agde, canon 9** [Canon 19]

Even if their life is proven [however exemplary their life and conduct may be], religious women are not to be veiled before the age of forty [Col. 1054D].

**Canon of Epaon, canon 20**

[For a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or other clerics.] We prohibit men from visiting women after the appointed hours, that is, at midday or in the evening. Nevertheless, if there is a reason for them to be seen by the bishop, they may be seen in the presence of presbyters and clerics.

[Note: [Col. 1056D] Canon 2. See Innocent I’s letter to Victricius, chapter 13.]

[Col. 1055A] **Canon 35** [Canon 38]

Only women of proven life and advanced age [Note: [Col. 1055D] Variant; see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.] are to be permitted to enter the monasteries of women for any of their needs [or services]. Those who enter to celebrate Mass are to leave immediately and quickly once the ministry has been completed. Otherwise, neither a cleric nor a young monk is to have access to the communities of women, unless kinship on the father’s or mother’s side, or that of a sister, is proven to justify admission.

**Canon of Mâcon, canon 2** [Note: [Col. 1055D] Council of Mâcon I, canon 2.]

No cleric or layman [certain additions] is to presume to reside in monasteries of women, or to have private conversations there, for any utility or repair, unless he is of proven character and advanced age [variant]; nor are they to be permitted to enter the guest room or the oratory [Note: [Col. 1055D] Variant: “outside”; see the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond].

**Canon 11** [Canon 12]

We decree that if a girl who has voluntarily professed religious life, or done so at the request of her parents, or has received the blessing, afterward turns to marriage or to the allurements of the world [addition], she is to be deprived of communion until death with the man to whom she has joined herself [variant]. But if, moved by penance, they separate themselves, they are to be suspended from communion for as long as the bishop deems appropriate; and if they fall into danger from illness [additions and variants], the viaticum is not to be denied them.

**Canon of Chalcedon, canon 16**

[Note: [Col. 1055D] Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore.] A virgin who has consecrated herself to God, if she contracts a marriage, is to be excommunicated.

[Col. 1055C] **Canon of Orléans, canon 18**

[Note: [Col. 1055D] See Council of Orléans II, canon 17.] Both girls and widows who, after changing their clothing, convert themselves in their own homes are to be deprived of communion with the Church, together with those who join themselves to them in marriage, until separation and penance.

**Canon 19** [Note: [Col. 1055D] Council of Orléans III, canon 16.]

If anyone presumes to impose himself upon a consecrated virgin [or a devoted woman, that is, one who has professed religious life], or upon one living under a vow of devotion, he is to be expelled from communion until death [the end]. If a woman who has been abducted consents to live with her abductor [variant], she too is to be excommunicated. The same procedure is to be observed, under ecclesiastical discipline, concerning penitents and widows who remain under a vow. If a priest knowingly communicates with such persons, he is not to have the peace of the Church for a full year [Col. 1055D].

**Canon of Ancyra, canon 19**

[Note: [Col. 1055D] Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore.] Those who violate a promise of virginity are to live among bigamists, who have entered into a second marriage. But we prohibit virgins and girls who wish to live with men as sisters from associating with them.

[Col. 1056A] **Canon of Carthage, canon 68** [Note: [Col. 1055D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 102.]

The bishop or presbyter who presides over a parish will be guilty if, for the sake of providing sustenance [of sustaining their present life], younger widows or religious women are subjected to the familiarity of clerics.

**Canon of Orange, canon 26** [Note: [Col. 1055D] Council of Orange I, canon 27.]

After a profession to preserve widowhood has been made before the bishop in the secretarium [additions and variants], and the woman has been clothed by the bishop in widows’ dress, she is rightly to be condemned as one who has deserted her profession.

**Canon of Orléans IV, canon 16** [Note: [Col. 1056D] Council of Orléans V.]

Girls who seek the monastery of their own will, or are offered there by their parents, are to remain for one year in the very clothing in which they entered. In monasteries where they are not kept enclosed perpetually, they are to remain for three years [addition].

**Canon of Carthage, canon 3** [Note: [Col. 1056D] African Council, canon 2; canonical code of the African Church, canon 44.]

When sacred virgins are deprived of their parents’ guardianship, they are to be entrusted to the care of older women by the bishops or presbyters [where the bishop is absent], so that, living together, they may guard one another.

**Canon of Rome, canon 1**

A girl who has not yet been veiled, but who has nevertheless decided to remain so, if she marries, these are called clandestine marriages [addition]. A period for performing penance is to be assigned to them.

**Canon of Arles, canon 26** [Note: [Col. 1056D] Council of Arles II, canon 52.]

A girl who has vowed herself to God [addition], if after the age of fifteen [twenty-five] she turns to marriage, is to be deprived of communion together with the man to whom she has bound herself.

[Col. 1056C] **In a letter of Pope Symmachus** [Note: [Col. 1056D] To Caesarius, bishop of Arles, chapter 5.]

We do not permit widows [variant] who have persevered for a long time in religious purpose to turn to marriage. Likewise, we prohibit virgins from marrying, even if it is established that they have spent many years in monasteries [passed their years there].

**Canon of Lyons, canon 12** [Note: [Col. 1056D] Council of Lyons III, canon 3.]

Girls who, with the agreement [connivance] of their parents, have voluntarily dedicated themselves to a monastery [certain additions] and afterward withdraw from that monastery [additions and variants] are to be deprived of communion until they return there; nevertheless, the viaticum is not to be denied them.

**Canon of Epaon, canon 16** [Canon 21]

We entirely abolish the consecration of widows whom they call deaconesses [Col. 1056D] [Note: [Col. 1056D] “From every region of ours.” Another reading: “from every religion.” See the note of the distinguished J. Sirmond.] Only the blessing of penance is to be imposed upon them if they wish to convert.

# CHAPTER LIII. ON ABDUCTED WOMEN

**Canon of Chalcedon, canon 27**

[Note: [Col. 1056D] Interpretation found neither in Dionysius nor in Isidore.] The holy synod decreed that those who abduct women [Note: [Col. 1058D] But see the Council of Gangra, canon 14, with a few changes.] [Col. 1057A] are to be deprived of their proper rank if they are clerics; but if they are laymen, they are to be anathematized.

**Canon of Ancyra, canon 12**

It was decreed that betrothed girls who have been abducted by others are to be rescued and restored to those to whom they had been betrothed, even if it should happen that they have lost the flower of their chastity through the abductors.

**In a letter of Pope Siricius** [Note: [Col. 1057C] To Himerius of Tarragona], **canon 4**

We prohibit in every way that anyone else should take a betrothed woman [additions and variants], because such women cannot be blessed, and a union without priestly blessing is tantamount to sacrilege.

**Canon of Orléans, canon 11**

If an abductor takes refuge in a church with the woman he has abducted, even if it should happen that the woman herself has suffered violence, she is immediately to be freed from the abductor’s power [Col. 1057B]. The abductor, with immunity from death or punishment granted, is to be subjected to servitude, or is to have the power to redeem himself [freely]. But if the abducted woman has a father, she is to be returned to him, excused [from blame] [to the father’s authority].

**Canon 23** [Note: [Col. 1057C] Council of Carthage IV, canon 24.]

Slaves who take refuge in a church [within the precincts of a church] under the pretext of marriage are to be returned to their masters after the masters have given an assurance of pardon, on a promise of reconciliation [separation] [many additions and variants], with the masters retaining the freedom to unite them afterward if they wish.

# CHAPTER LIV. ON INCEST, ADULTERY, AND THOSE WHO DIVORCE THEIR WIVES

**Canon of Orléans, canon 11** [Note: [Col. 1057D] Council of Arles I, canon 10.]

[Col. 1057C] Those who catch their wives in adultery and [Note: [Col. 1057D] This negative particle, which is lacking in the printed editions, is correctly supplied by the Herovallian manuscript. For if they are prohibited from marrying, why is advice subsequently given not to marry? “Where advice is given,” says Jerome in book I *Against Jovinian*, “there is the freedom of the one offering it; where there is a command, there is the necessity of the one obeying. ‘I have no command from the Lord,’ he says, ‘but I give advice, as one who has received mercy from the Lord.’” And Augustine says: “Advice is one thing, command another. Advice is given so that virginity may be preserved, and so forth. A command, however, is given so that justice may be maintained, and so forth. Whoever willingly hears and follows advice will have greater glory. Whoever does not fulfill a command cannot escape punishment unless penance comes to his aid.” Yet the Fathers of this celebrated council impose no punishment; they give advice alone. Therefore the Fathers say that the matter is not prohibited—a matter that Theodore later permitted, along with several other Fathers, in his *Penitential*.] are not prohibited from marrying, let them be given as much advice as possible not to take other wives while their first wives are alive, even if the latter are adulteresses.

**In a letter of Pope Innocent** [Note: [Col. 1058C] Letter of Innocent I to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse], **canon 6**

Whoever, while his wife is alive [variant], even though separated from her, takes another wife commits adultery and is an adulterer [Note: [Col. 1058D] Many variants and additions; see R. V. Stephen II, *Responses to the Questions of the British Monks*]. He is to be deprived of communion, together with the woman whom he has taken; likewise their parents, who consented to such unions.

**Canon of Agde, canon 17** [Note: [Col. 1058D] Missing from the Council of Agde.]

If a woman wishes to leave her husband, condemning the marriage, let her be anathema.

[Col. 1058A] **Canon of Neocaesarea, canon 2**

[Note: [Col. 1058D] It differs slightly from Dionysius’s interpretation.] If a woman marries two brothers, she is to be expelled until death. Nevertheless, if at the time of death she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bond of this union, she is to receive the fruit of penance. But if the woman dies in such a marriage, penance will be difficult for one who remains alive.

**Canon of Agde, canon 19** [Canon 25]

Those who have dismissed their spouses without plausibly stating any grounds for separation, in order to pursue illicit or alien relationships, are to be excluded from communion with the holy Church and from the holy people [Note: [Col. 1058D] Addition: “because they stain faith and marriages”] if, before stating the grounds for separation before the bishops of the province, they have cast away their wives before being condemned in court.

[Col. 1058B] **Canon of Orléans** [Note: [Col. 1058D] See Council of Orléans II, canon 10; Council of Orléans III, canon 10], **canon 12**.

[Note: [Col. 1058D] In many variants, only the sense, not the wording, can be discerned.] If anyone violates by carnal intercourse his brother’s widow, his wife’s stepdaughter—that is, his stepdaughter—or his widowed cousin or niece—that is, the daughter of his paternal or maternal uncle—let him be struck by the sentence of apostolic discipline; and for as long as he remains in so great a crime, let him be deprived of the Christian assembly and of communion with the holy Church.

Canon of Epaon, Aera 16 [Note: [Col. 1058D] Council of Epaon, canon 30.]

No forgiveness whatsoever is to be reserved for incestuous unions, unless they have been cured by separation from adultery. (Some copies add:) If anyone violates carnally [by a carnal union] his brother’s widow, who had previously almost become his sister; if anyone violates his brother’s full sister, anyone his wife’s full sister, anyone his stepmother, anyone his cousin, anyone his maternal or paternal uncle’s widow, or his stepdaughter, by sexual intercourse. (Addition:) Certainly, those to whom an illicit union is forbidden shall have the freedom to enter into a better marriage. [Note: [Col. 1058D] See the Council of Agde, canon 61.] If anyone takes as a wife a woman from his own kinship, or one whom a kinsman had as a wife, let him be anathema.

Likewise Gregory, in the *Book of Pastoral Care* [Note: [Col. 1058D] See Gregory the Great, Letter 32 to Bishop Felix, Book XII; the *Excerpta* of Egbert of York, canon 137; and the canons of Isaac, bishop of Langres, title IV, “On Incest,” chapter 19.]

[Note: [Col. 1058D] Several additions occur in Gregory’s letter to Bishop Felix that are absent from the testimonies cited by the authors, as in the collection of the Herford manuscript.] He commits incest who joins himself, within the degree of affinity, to a woman related to him by blood, or to one whom a blood-relative had as a wife. For none of the faithful may take as wife, as far as the degree of affinity extends—that is, through the seventh generation—a woman related to him by blood, or one who is in any way polluted by the stain of incest. For as long as incestuous persons remain in their crime, let them occupy not the place of faithful Christians, but only that of pagans, catechumens, or the possessed. And if they are unwilling to separate themselves from that most abominable crime and return to public penance, let them be counted among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit—or even among those of whom Truth itself says: “If he does not listen to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.”

Canon of Ancyra, Aera 6.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] The translation belongs neither to Dionysius nor to Isidore.] Those who have had intercourse with animals, or who, like animals, have committed incest with blood-relatives, or who have had intercourse with males—if they committed such a crime before reaching twenty years of age—after completing fifteen years in penance, let them begin to participate only in prayer. Thereafter, remaining for five years in simple communion, let them be received into communion with the offering after twenty years. Their way of life during penance must also be examined, and accordingly let them receive this indulgence. But those who have persisted more obstinately in this crime shall receive only penance for twenty years. Those who, after reaching twenty years of age, or even while having wives, have fallen into this crime shall, after completing thirty-one years of penance, be admitted only to communion; after remaining in that communion for five years, let them receive full communion with the offering. But if, while having wives and after reaching fifty years of age, they have fallen into this crime, let them communicate only at the hour of death. These people, who have lived like dumb animals and have polluted both themselves and others with such a sin, ought to pray among those who are tossed about by the storm, whom we understand to be possessed.

Aera 19.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this.] Those who have committed adultery ought to attain perfection over seven years, according to the former stages.

Aera 20.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this.] Women who commit fornication and kill their offspring, or cause what they have conceived to be expelled, are to be removed from the Church until the hour of death, according to the former stages. But now we determine more humanely that ten years of penance be assigned to them.

Aera 24.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] It differs slightly from Isidore’s translation.] If anyone who has a fiancée violates her sister, and afterward marries the woman to whom he had been betrothed, and the woman who suffered the violation kills herself by hanging, let all who were advisers in this deed be placed under penance for ten years.

Canon of Orléans, Aera 2 [Note: [Col. 1059D] Council of Orléans IV, canon 29.]

If any women are discovered in adultery with clerics, disciplinary measures are to be applied to the clerics [Note: [Col. 1059D] These words are absent, but other additions and variants occur in the editions.] and also to the women; and the women themselves are to be expelled from the cities.

In Pope Leo’s letter to Rusticus, Aera 10 [canon 6].

A man ought to dismiss a female slave from his bed and take a freeborn wife [of established free status]. This is not a duplication of marriage but an advancement in respectability.

In the same letter, chapter 2.

[Note: [Col. 1059D] This and what follows are absent from the edition. See, however, Pope Stephen II’s *Responses to the Questions of the British Monks*, chapter 4, from the same letter of Leo I.] If a father or mother has received his or her own child from the sacred baptismal font, these persons must be separated entirely from marriage.

In the same letter, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 1060D] *Capitularies*, Book V, chapter 5.] If any man or woman has received a stepson or stepdaughter from the sacred font, or held one during confirmation, such persons must be separated from marriage in every way.

In the same letter, chapter 4.

[Note: [Col. 1060D] See Stephen II, *Responses*, chapter 3.] If a man carried into captivity there took a female slave as his wife, and afterward, having returned to his own country, married a freeborn woman; and if he is again taken to the place mentioned above, where he had the slave, and finds that same slave with another husband, he may join himself to another woman, provided that the freeborn woman whom he subsequently married has died.

In the same letter, chapter 6.

[Note: [Col. 1060D] See Stephen II, *Responses*, chapter 2.] If either spouse becomes seriously ill, so that the marital debt cannot be rendered by that person, they may never on that account be separated.

In Pope Innocent’s letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, chapter 6.

[Note: [Col. 1060D] There are many variants in the edition. See rather Stephen II, *Responses*, chapter 5.] If, after a divorce—even when the wife was dismissed on account of adultery—one person joins himself to another, it is clear that both parties are adulterers, according to the saying: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.” Likewise, whoever marries a dismissed woman commits adultery; and therefore all such persons are to be deprived of communion.

In the same letter, chapter 10.

[Note: [Col. 1060D] Absent.] If one spouse has received the other’s son or daughter from the sacred font, or held the child for chrism or for the mystery of Christianity, both wife and husband become godparents to the child’s parents, because husband and wife have become one flesh.

In Pope Siricius’s letter to Bishop Genesius, chapter 12.

[Note: [Col. 1060D] See Stephen II, *Responses*, chapter 9, from Pope Siricius’s letter to Bishop Himerius.] If a healthy man marries a leprous woman, or if leprosy subsequently comes upon her, they are to separate, lest the children conceived be stained by leprosy. For it is right that a clean person be joined to a clean person.

In Pope Leo’s letter to Bishop Nicetius [Note: [Col. 1060D] To Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia], chapter 1.

[Col. 1060D] When marriages are separated by the calamity of war, and the women who remain behind, deprived of their husbands, believe that they have been killed or will never return, and, compelled by [anxiety] solitude, enter into another marriage, while those who were thought to have perished return, then, once the evils inflicted by hostility have been removed, let each person be restored to what he or she had lawfully possessed. [Col. 1061A] (Chapter 2.) Yet the man who assumed the place of the husband who was believed no longer to exist is not to be judged culpable [or as an invader of another’s legal rights]. [Note: [Col. 1061D] Several additions occur here, and here chapter 4 begins. Much of what follows is variant. See Stephen II, *Responses*, chapter 19.] But if some women prefer to remain with the men here rather than return to their lawful marriage, they are rightly to be condemned and deprived of communion, because they show that they did this not from necessity but from their own incontinence, and that they were not pleased that this excuse could offer atonement. Let them therefore return voluntarily to their proper marriage, without any reproach; for just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands are to be regarded as impious, so those who return to the affection established by God are rightly to be judged praiseworthy.

In Pope Innocent’s letter.

[Col. 1061B] [Note: [Col. 1061D] See Innocent I’s letter to Exuperius, chapter 4, where many additions and variants occur.] Just as women, if convicted of adultery, are deprived of communion by priestly judgment, so we decree that men too, if discovered to have committed adultery, are in every way to be removed from communion.

## CHAPTER LV. ON THOSE WHO RETURN TO SECULAR LIFE AFTER LAYING ASIDE THE MILITARY BELT, AND ON THOSE WHO HAVE ADMINISTERED AFTER BAPTISM

Canon of Nicaea, Aera 18 [Note: [Col. 1061D] Canon 12 in the Greek; canon 11 in the translations of Dionysius and Isidore.]

[Note: [Col. 1061D] Isidore’s translation differs slightly.] If any, after laying aside the military belt, return to their former vomit, so as to lend money at interest and go back again to military service, let them remain among the penitents for ten years, after the first three years during which they were among the hearers. Above all, let this be observed: that their disposition and the fruit of their penance be examined. And whoever perseveres in tears and good works and demonstrates good work with sincerity, when, after the appointed period, he begins to participate in prayer, the bishop may deal with him somewhat more humanely. But those who have treated their fall indifferently and think that it is enough for them to have entered the church shall complete all the appointed periods.

Letter of Pope Innocent to Bishop Exuperius [Chapter 3].

[Note: [Col. 1061D] Some additions occur.] Concerning those who have administered after baptism and inflicted tortures, or even pronounced a capital sentence, we read nothing defined by our predecessors. For they remembered that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that the minister of God was appointed as an avenger in such matters. Concerning these things, therefore, we maintain the practice observed until now, lest we appear either to overturn discipline or to act against the Lord’s authority. Their deeds, however, will all be taken into account when they render their account. (Chapter 5.) You also wished to inquire whether, after baptism, it is permissible to request from rulers the death [or blood] of someone on account of guilt. Rulers never grant this without deliberation [knowledge], but always refer the crimes themselves to judges, so that the case may be judged after examination. Once the matter has safely been entrusted to the investigator [inquirer], either acquittal or condemnation is to be pronounced according to the nature of the case; and while the authority of the laws is exercised against the wicked, the one who pronounces [the dictator] will remain immune.

## CHAPTER LVI. ON FORGERS, PERJURERS, AND MURDERERS, AND ON CAPTIVITY AND DISCORD

Canon of Orléans, Aera 15 [Note: [Col. 1061D] Council of Arles I, canon 14.]

Those who falsely accuse their brothers [“it was decreed,” etc.] are not to communicate until the hour of death.

Canon of Mâcon, Aera 17.

[Col. 1062B] If anyone induces others to give false testimony or commit perjury, or solicits them [by any form of bribery], he himself is not to communicate until the hour of death; and those who followed him are to be prohibited from giving any testimony and branded with infamy.

Canon of Agde, Aera 36 [Canon 37].

Murderers and false witnesses [Note: [Col. 1061D] Variant. See the Council of Venice, canon 1] are to be deprived of communion until they perform penance and make satisfaction.

Canon of Lyon [Note: [Col. 1062D] Council of Lyon II, canon 3], Aera 3.

[Note: [Col. 1062D] Many variants and additions occur.] If anyone takes a person captive or hands him over, let him be deprived of communion until he has restored him to his own place.

Canon of Ancyra, Aera 21.

[Note: [Col. 1062D] The interpretation belongs neither to Dionysius nor to Isidore. See the Council of Epaon, canon 31.] If anyone commits deliberate murder, let him submit himself to penance and communicate only at the hour of death.

Aera 22 [Note: [Col. 1062D] Isidore’s translation does not distinguish this from the preceding canon; but the Greek and Dionysius do.]

[Note: [Col. 1062D] The interpretation belongs neither to Dionysius nor to Isidore.] But whoever commits murder by accident shall communicate after seven years of penance, according to the established stages. This more humane definition is contained within a period of five years.

Canon of Epaon, Aera 24 [Canon 24].

If anyone kills his own slave without the judge’s knowledge, let him be punished by excommunication for two years [he shall expiate the shedding of blood].

Canon of Arles [Note: [Col. 1062D] Council of Arles II], Aera 53.

If any servant [of whatever condition or status], as though to aggravate his master’s severity, strikes himself [filled with diabolical fury], the injury will in no way attach to the master on account of another’s crime.

In Pope Leo’s letter [Note: [Col. 1062D] To Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia.]

Captives who have been polluted by sacrificial foods are to be cleansed by the satisfaction of penance; this is to be assessed not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart, whether hunger or terror extorted the act [addition].

Canon of the Africans, Aera 47 [Note: [Col. 1063D] The same in the Barberini manuscript. Council of Carthage IV, canon 25.]

If bishops are at variance, let the fear of God—or a synod—reconcile them.

Aera 48 [Note: [Col. 1063D] The same in the Barberini manuscript. Council of Carthage, canon 59.]

If clerics are in disagreement, let the bishop, by reason or by authority, draw the disobedient toward concord; let a synod condemn them for their boldness [hearing].

Aera 49 [Note: [Col. 1063D] The same in the Barberini manuscript, canon 69. Council of Carthage, canon 99.]

The offerings of brothers who are at odds with one another are not to be received either in the sacristy or in the treasury.

Canon of Arles, Aera 80 [Note: [Col. 1063D] Council of Arles II, canon 50.]

Those who burn with public hatred against one another are to be removed from the church [from ecclesiastical assemblies], until they return [come back] to peace.

Canon of Agde, Aera 30.

Whoever are divided by hatred or by a prolonged dispute are to be rebuked by the priests. (Addition and variant:) And if they are unwilling to reform, let them be expelled from communion.

Canon of Carthage, Aera 79 [Note: [Col. 1063D] The same in the Barberini manuscript. Council of Carthage IV, canon 94.]

The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected by the priests.

## CHAPTER LVII. ON EXPOSED CHILDREN

Canon of Orléans, Aera 31 [Note: [Col. 1063D] Council of Orléans II, canon 51.]

If an exposed child is taken up before a church through anyone’s compassion, let the finder deposit a written statement. And if the child who has been taken up is not sought out and identified within ten days, let the person who collected the child possess him securely. [Note: [Col. 1063D] See the Council of Vaison I, canon 10.] But if, after the stated period, some accuser appears, let him be judged a murderer.

## CHAPTER LVIII. ON FREEDMEN

Canon of Toledo, Aera 7 [Note: [Col. 1064D] Council of Toledo III, canon 6.]

Freedmen who have been made free by the bishop from the Church’s slaves are to remain in freedom; yet they, and those descended from them [both they themselves and their offspring], are not to withdraw from the Church’s patronage. Freedmen also handed over to or commended to other churches are to be governed by episcopal patronage [addition].

Canon of Agde, Aera 27 [Canon 29].

The Church is to protect those who have been lawfully made freedmen [if necessity demands it]. But if anyone before a hearing presumes either to seize or despoil them [or them], let him be expelled from the church.

Canon of Orange, Aera 6 [Note: [Col. 1064D] Council of Orange I, canon 7.]

If anyone attempts to force those manumitted in a church, or commended to the Church by testament, back into slavery, servitude, or the status of tenant farmers, let him be restrained by ecclesiastical punishment.

[Col. 1064A] Canon of Epaon, Aera 8.

Slaves given to monks may not be manumitted by the abbot. We consider it unjust that, while monks perform rural labor [daily rural work], their slaves should enjoy the leisure of freedom.

Canon of Agde, Aera 6 [Canon 7].

Those whom the bishop has freed from the Church’s slaves [variants and additions] are to be protected by his successors, together with whatever their liberator granted them in freedom. Yet we order that they retain no more than twenty solidi [the amount and] of land, vineyards, or a small lodging; (addition and variant) for we permit small properties, or those less useful to the Church, to be assigned for the use of foreigners or clerics, without prejudice to the Church’s rights.

Canon of Orléans II, Aera 32 [Note: [Col. 1064D] Council of Orléans IV.]

[Col. 1064B] The ashes [variants and additions] of slaves, and likewise their descendants, are to remain in the place where their founder [Note: [Col. 1064D] Variant. See the note of the illustrious J. Sirmond] has been laid, under the status established by the deceased through the care of the priest. But whoever believes that this should be opposed [if any secular person, driven by human greed, resists this command] is to be suspended from the church until true correction.

Canon of Orléans IV, Aera 6 [Note: [Col. 1064D] Council of Orléans V, canon 7.]

All who have been made freedmen [variants and additions], if they are assaulted by anyone, are to be defended by the Church, except for those offenses for which the laws have ordered the freedom granted to slaves to be revoked.

Canon of Arles [Note: [Col. 1064D] Council of Arles II], Aera 34.

If anyone believes that a person manumitted in a church ought to be recalled as ungrateful [under the designation “ungrateful”], this is not permitted unless official municipal records establish him to be guilty.

Canon of Lyon, Aera 7.

Whoever has a legal action against freedmen commended to the Church must not dare to hand them over to a magistrate; rather, the matters at issue are to be heard in the bishop’s court according to the truth. For it is just that those who desire the patronage of the immortal Church be defended against the schemes of accusers. Whoever attempts to violate what we have decreed is to be struck by an irrevocable sentence of condemnation.

## ON THOSE WHO FLEE TO THE CHURCH

Canon of Orléans [Note: [Col. 1064D] Council of Orléans I], Aera 1.

Murderers, adulterers, and thieves, if they flee to a church, are to be treated according to the earlier canons and what Roman law has established: they are not to be dragged from the church atria or the bishop’s house. Rather, once oaths have been given upon the Gospels [nor are they to be surrendered in any other way except upon the Gospels], they are to be secure from death, mutilation, and every kind of punishment, so that the person against whom the criminal is liable may negotiate satisfaction. But if anyone violates his oath [if anyone is convicted of violating it and is guilty of perjury] (addition and variant), let him be separated from every Christian fellowship [Col. 1065A] and communion. If the accused flees from the church, he is not to be sought by the clergy of the church.

Aera 3 [Note: [Col. 1065D] Council of Orléans I.]
