But if, in the case of a slave, he is unwilling to leave because of the oath of immunity given by his master [many variants], it is permissible for the master to seize him.

Canon of Epaon, Aera 39.

If a slave guilty of a grave offense flees to a church, he is excused only from bodily punishments. Concerning cutting his hair [Note: [Col. 1065D] See the note of the illustrious J. Sirmond], or any work whatsoever, it has pleased the council that an oath not be demanded from the master.

Canon of Orléans, Aera 39 [Note: [Col. 1065D] See the Council of Orange I, canon 5; Council of Arles II, canon 30.]

Those who flee to a church ought not to be handed over, but defended out of reverence for the place and through intercession. [Col. 1065B] [Note: [Col. 1065D] Here begins canon 6 in the Council of Orange and canon 32 in the Council of Arles.] But if anyone believes that the slaves of clerics are to be seized as though they were his own slaves who had fled to the church [throughout all the churches], let him be struck by the strictest condemnation.

## CHAPTER LIX. ON THE JEWS

Canon of Laodicea, Aera 39 [Note: [Col. 1065D] Council of Laodicea, canon 29.]

[Note: [Col. 1065D] The interpretation belongs neither to Dionysius nor to Isidore.] Those who have become Christians from among the Jews, if afterward they are found to be Judaizing or observing the Sabbath, are to be anathema from Christ.

Canon of Mâcon, Aera 16 [Note: [Col. 1065D] Council of Mâcon I, canon 13.]

Jews are not to be appointed judges or tax collectors over Christians [Christian peoples], lest Christians, God forbid, appear to be subject to them.

[Col. 1065C] Aera 15.

No Christian is to participate in Jewish banquets [or presume to participate]. Whoever does so is to be separated from all Christian fellowship [let him know that he must be restrained], if he has been defiled by their impieties.

Aera 16.

No Christian is to serve a Jew. Rather, upon payment of twelve solidi for each healthy slave, any Christian who wishes [variant] is to have permission to redeem the slave, either into freedom or for service; for it is impious that those whom Christ redeemed with his own blood [by the pouring out of his blood] should remain entangled in the bonds of persecutors. If the Jew is unwilling to agree to this, the slave himself may return to the Christians and live wherever he wishes [Note: [Col. 1065D] Addition, but see the note of the illustrious J. Sirmond].

Canon of Agde, Aera 40.

From now on, all Christians [clerics and laypeople] are to avoid Jewish banquets, because, since they do not partake of Christian [common] foods, it is unworthy and sacrilegious for Christians to consume their food; for the things we consume with the Apostle’s permission are judged by them to be unworthy [unclean].

Aera 34.

If Jews [whose perfidy frequently returns to its vomit] wish to come to the Catholic law, let them remain among the catechumens for seven [eight] months (variant). And if they are known to profess a pure faith, let them merit the grace of baptism. But if they contract a dangerous illness within the prescribed period, let them be baptized.

Canon of Orléans, Aera 30.

Jews must not dare to go out among Christians from the Lord’s Supper [from the day of the Lord’s Supper] until the second day of the week at Easter [that is, during those four days themselves], nor on any occasion whatsoever.

[Col. 1066B] Canon of Mâcon, Aera 14 [Note: [Col. 1066D] Council of Mâcon I.]

From the Lord’s Supper until the second day of the week at Easter [the first Easter], Jews are to be denied permission to walk through the streets and marketplaces [addition], and are to show respect to all [the Lord’s priests or] clerics. (Addition and variant:) Otherwise, they are to be disciplined by the local judges according to the status of the person involved.

## CHAPTER LX. ON CLERICS WHO ABSTAIN FROM MEAT

Canon of Ancyra, Aera 13.

[Note: [Col. 1066D] It differs slightly from Dionysius’s translation.] Concerning those who are in the clergy: if they abstain from meat, it has been decreed that they should indeed touch it and then abstain if they wish. But if they abominate it so greatly that they consider even vegetables cooked with it inedible, they must withdraw from their order as persons who do not conform to the rule.

## CHAPTER LXI. ON HERETICS AND PAGANS

Canon of Nicaea, Aera 21.

[Note: [Col. 1066D] Rufinus’s translation. See the Council of Arles II, canon 16, and the note of the illustrious J. Sirmond on this canon.] Let the Paulianists and those who are Photinians be rebaptized.

Aera 22.

[Note: [Col. 1066D] Rufinus’s translation.] But deaconesses, since they do not receive the laying on of hands, are themselves also to be among the laity.

Canon of Arles, Aera 9 [Note: [Col. 1066D] Council of Arles I, canon 8.]

If someone from the heresies comes to the church, let them question him concerning the Creed. And if they ascertain that he was baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let hands alone be laid upon him, and let him receive the Holy Spirit. But if, when questioned, he does not profess this Trinity, let him be baptized.

Canon of the Africans, Aera 16 [Note: [Col. 1066D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 84.]

Let the bishop prohibit no one from entering the church and hearing the word of God, whether pagan, heretic, or Jew, until the dismissal of the catechumens.

[Col. 1067A] Aera 82 [Note: [Col. 1067D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 72.]

One must neither pray nor sing psalms with heretics.

Canon of Arles, Aera 11 [Note: [Col. 1067D] Council of Arles I.]

Faithful girls who join themselves to pagans are to be separated from communion for some period of time.

Canon of Miletus, Aera 5.

If anyone joins himself to a woman, or anyone joins himself in marital union to Jewish depravity, let him be separated from the Christian assembly and communion.

Canon of Gangra, Aera 14 [Note: [Col. 1067D] Council of Gangra.]

[Note: [Col. 1067D] The interpretation belongs neither to Dionysius nor to Isidore.] If any woman uses men’s clothing in order to alter her feminine appearance, let her be anathema.

Aera 15.

[Note: [Col. 1067D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this.] If anyone abandons his own children in order to alter his masculine appearance [Col. 1067B], let him be anathema.

Aera 16.

[Note: [Col. 1067D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this.] If any children despise their parents, especially faithful parents, or, under the pretext of religion, fail to render them the honor owed to them, let them be anathema.

Aera 17.

[Note: [Col. 1067D] Neither Dionysius nor Isidore has this.] Let a woman who, as though contemplating religion, cuts off her hair be anathema.

Canon of Laodicea, Aera 17 [Note: [Col. 1067D] Council of Laodicea, canon 30.]

[Note: [Col. 1067D] The interpretation belongs neither to Dionysius nor to Isidore.] No Christian is to share baths with women, because this is also censured among the pagans.

Aera 31 [Note: [Col. 1067D] Canon 44 in Isidore’s translation.]

Women ought not to enter the altar area.

## CHAPTER LXII. ON CATECHUMENS

[Col. 1067C]

Aera 18 [Note: [Col. 1067D] Council of Orange I, canon 19.]

Catechumens are never to frequent the baptistery.

Canon of Orange, Aera 19 [Canon 20].

They are to be separated and instructed so as to withdraw from the blessing of the faithful, even during domestic prayers, insofar as this can be avoided [or can be guarded against]. And (these words are absent) if they are adults, they are to be blessed [variant] and offered separately.

Canon of Carthage, Aera 24 [Note: [Col. 1067D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 86.]

Neophytes are to receive baptism and for some time abstain from richer banquets and spectacles [the editions omit “free”], and from their spouses.

## CHAPTER LXIII. ON CONSPIRACIES

[Col. 1067D]

Canon of Chalcedon, Aera 18.

[Note: [Col. 1068D] It differs slightly from Dionysius’s translation.] If clerics or monks are found swearing conspiratorial oaths, conspiring, or laying snares for bishops or clerics, let them be deposed from their own rank.

[Col. 1068A] Canon of Orléans [Note: [Col. 1068D] Council of Orléans III], Aera 21.

If any clerics [addition and variants in the editions] have given one another rebellious oaths or written a document, once the matter has come before a synod, let punishment be imposed according to the rank and status of the persons involved [by the bishops who have then gathered together].

## CHAPTER LXIV. ON THE POSSESSED

Canon of the Africans, Aera 62 [Note: [Col. 1068D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 90.]

Every day exorcists are to lay hands on the possessed.

Aera 63 [Note: [Col. 1068D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 91.]

The possessed are to clean the floors of God’s houses with brooms [are to sweep them].

Aera 64 [Note: [Col. 1068D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage, canon 92.]

When the possessed are present [seated] in the house of God, their daily food is to be supplied by the exorcists at the appropriate time.

Canon of Orange, Aera 13 [Note: [Col. 1068D] Council of Orange I, canon 14.]

Baptized possessed persons, if they [attend to their cleansing and] entrust themselves to the care of the clergy and obey their admonitions, are to receive communion in every way, whether they are to be fortified against demonic attacks or cleansed.

Aera 14 [Note: [Col. 1068D] Council of Orange, canon 15.]

As opportunity permits [or necessity requires], the possessed and catechumens are to be instructed concerning baptism.

Aera 19 [Canon 18].

It has been decreed [variants and additions] that the Gospels be read to catechumens.

## CHAPTER LXV. ON CHRISM

[Col. 1068C]

Canon of the Africans, Aera 87 [Note: [Col. 1068D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 36.]

Presbyters who are in the dioceses [who govern the churches] are to request chrism before the solemnity of Easter not from just any bishops but from their own, and not through a neighboring [junior] cleric, but either personally or through the person who keeps the sacristy.

## CHAPTER LXVI. ON THE FUNERALS OF THE DEAD AND TOMBS, AND THAT PALLS NOT BE PLACED OVER BODIES

Canon of Toledo, Aera 21 [Note: [Col. 1068D] Council of Toledo III, canon 22.]

The bodies of religious persons [addition and variants in the editions] are to be carried to the tombs with psalms alone and the voices of those singing psalms. For we entirely prohibit funeral songs [which are customarily sung for the dead] and beating the breast [variant].

Canon of Auvergne, Aera 4 [Note: [Col. 1068D] Council of Auvergne, celebrated in the year 835, canon 3.]

Care must be taken concerning palls [lest palls], or divine furnishings, so that the bodies of the dead are not wrapped in them [Note: [Col. 1068D] Variant in the editions. See the note of the illustrious J. Sirmond.]

[Col. 1069A] Aera 8.

Let divine furnishings not be provided for the adornment of weddings [addition in the editions].

Canon of Mâcon, Aera 18 [Note: [Col. 1069D] Council of Mâcon II, canon 17.]

We have learned that, before the bodies of the dead have yet decayed [variant in the editions], tombs are opened or other bodies placed upon them [addition and variant]. Therefore we decree that no one henceforth presume to do this.

## CHAPTER LXVII. ON READING AT TABLE

Canon of Toledo [Note: [Col. 1069D] Council of Toledo III], Aera 7.

Because idle stories are often inserted at tables [variant and addition in the editions], we therefore decree that in every banquet of priests or religious persons, this reading [of the divine Scriptures] prohibit them.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. ON THE FALLEN AND PENITENTS

[Col. 1069B]

[Note: [Col. 1069D] *Ancient Church Statutes*; canon 18 in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 85.] Let the priest impose penance on those who implore it, without respect of persons [the laws of penance]; and let more negligent penitents be received more slowly. [Note: [Col. 1069D] This begins at canon 19 in the Barberini manuscript and Council of Carthage IV, canon 75.]

Chapter 19 [Note: [Col. 1069D] Chapter 20 in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 76.]

If someone requests penance during illness, and the priest, having been summoned, comes to him, but the sick person [if by chance] becomes speechless [overcome by illness] or is turned into delirium, let those who heard him testify, and let him receive penance. And if he is immediately believed to be dying, let him be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and let the Eucharist be poured into his mouth [to his mouth]. If he survives, let the aforementioned witnesses inform him that his request was fulfilled; [Col. 1069C] and let him be subjected to the appointed period [laws] of penance for as long as the priest who granted the penance approves.

Chapter 20 [Note: [Col. 1069D] Chapter 21 in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 78.]

Penitents who received the Eucharist as viaticum during illness are not to consider themselves absolved if they survive, without the laying on of hands.

Aera 21 [Note: [Col. 1069D] The same in the Barberini manuscript; Council of Carthage IV, canon 79.]

If penitents die before completing their legitimate penance [carefully carry out the laws of penance], should they happen to die [on a journey or at sea] where a priest could not assist them [variant in the editions], let their memory be commended in prayers and offerings.

Canon of Hippo, Aera 42 [Note: [Col. 1069D] Council of Africa, canon 10; from the canonical collection of the African Church, canon [Col. 1070D] 43; Council of Carthage III, canon 31.]

[Col. 1069D] According to the distinction among sins, let the periods of penance be determined at the bishop’s discretion. [Note: [Col. 1070D] Canon 32.] And let a presbyter not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop [without the bishop’s knowledge], unless the bishop is absent [in the absence of the bishop and when necessity compels it]. Whoever’s crime is widely known is to be subjected to public penance [Col. 1070A] before the apse [before the apse], with the laying on of hands, lest the Church be disturbed [variant in the editions].

In Pope Innocent’s decretal [Note: [Col. 1070D] To Decentius, canon 7], Aera 6.

The custom of the Roman Church shows that penitents, whether for grave or lesser sins, are to be absolved on the Thursday before Easter if no illness intervenes. As for assessing the weight [to be assessed] of offenses, it belongs to the priest to judge, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession and to the tears [and weeping] of the one who is correcting himself; and then let him dismiss him when he sees that suitable satisfaction has been made. But if the penitent falls ill [variant and addition in the editions], [before the time of Easter] he is to be released, lest he depart [from the world] without communion. [Note: [Col. 1070D] Chapter 8.] The anointing with chrism [variant] cannot be administered to penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. [Col. 1070B] For to those to whom the other sacraments are denied, how can one suppose that a single kind can be granted?

Canon of Nicaea, chapter 13 [Note: [Col. 1070D] The same in the Greek and in Dionysius’s translation; Rufinus, chapter 14; Isidore’s translation, chapter 12. This text differs from all of them.]

The Eucharist is not to be denied to the dying and to those who desire it, but on this condition: if they survive, they are not to communicate before the appointed period of penance or the bishop’s approval.

Canon of Orange, Aera 3.

Those who are departing from the body [variant], after receiving penance, are to be admitted to communion without the reconciliatory laying on of hands; this is sufficient consolation for the dying. [Note: [Col. 1070D] The addition appears to be a gloss.] But if they survive, let them remain in the order of penitents, so that they may receive legitimate communion with the reconciliatory laying on of hands.

[Col. 1070C] Aera 4.

Penance is not to be denied even to clerics who desire it [the editions omit “even”].

Canon of Arles, Aera 12 [Note: [Col. 1070D] Council of Arles II.]

If those who, placed under penance, have departed this life, it was decided that none should be dismissed without Communion [should be dismissed without having received Communion]; but, because he honored penance, his offering should be accepted.

## In the Letter of Pope Innocent, chapter 15

[Note: See the Council of Agde, canon 15.]

Those doing penance, at the time when they request penance, shall receive from the priest the imposition of hands and sackcloth upon their head [as has been established everywhere]. And if they have either not cut their hair or not changed their clothing, [let them be cast out; and unless they have done penance worthily] let them not be [Col. 1070D] [received]. But penance should not easily be entrusted to the young, because of the frailty of their age. Nevertheless, the viaticum shall be given to all [who are] at the point of death.

## Council of Epaon, canon 23

(Additional material and variants in the editions.) Those who, after having received penance, relapse again into secular affairs will not be able to communicate [Col. 1071A] unless their profession has been confirmed [unless the profession which he had illicitly neglected is restored].

## Canon 35 [canon 36]

No one should be driven away from the Church without remedy and hope of life, since, if anyone repents or reforms, the way of returning to pardon is closed to no one. But if, when the danger of death has arisen, the periods of penance are relaxed, and he recovers after receiving the viaticum, the prescribed periods of penance must be observed.

## Ancient Statutes of the Church, chapter 65

[Note: The same in the Barbé codex; Council of Carthage IV, canon 80.]

Throughout the entire time of fasting, priests shall impose hands upon those doing penance.

## The same, chapter 68

[Note: Canon 66 in the Barbé codex; Council of Carthage IV, canon 82.]

Those doing penance shall also kneel on days of remission.

## Council of Carthage, canon 28

[Note: Council of Carthage V, canon 11; canonical codex, chapter 27.]

[Col. 1071B] If a presbyter or deacon is degraded, hands shall not be imposed upon him as upon one doing penance [or as upon a faithful layman].

## Council of Arles, canon 22

[Note: Council of Arles II, canon 21.]

A penitent woman [any woman], whether she has married another man after her husband’s death or has lived with a stranger in a suspect or prohibited intimacy, shall be kept away from the thresholds of the church; the same shall be observed concerning men.

## Chapter 23

[Note: Of the same council, canon 22.]

Penance should not be given to married persons except with their consent.

## Council of Orléans, canon 23

[Note: Council of Orléans III, canon 24.]

No one should dare to give the blessing of penance to young people [persons] or to married persons, unless it is with the consent [of both parties] [Col. 1071C] and when they have reached full age.

## Council of Orange, canon 11

[Note: Council of Orange I, canon 12.]

A person who has suddenly become mute [according to his condition] may be baptized or receive penance, if evidence of his previous will is available.

## Canon 12

[Note: Of the same council, canon 13.]

Whatever acts of piety are appropriate should be bestowed upon the insane.

## Decrees on Penance in a Letter of Pope Leo

[Note: Alternatively, Leo I, to all the bishops established throughout Campania, Samnium, and Picenum.]

(Additional material and variants in the editions.) In the penance which is requested by the faithful, let it not be the case that a written declaration concerning each kind of sin is publicly read out, since it is sufficient for the guilt of consciences to be disclosed to priests alone by secret confession. For although the fullness of faith seems praiseworthy, since, out of fear of the Lord, it does not blush to be ashamed before human beings, nevertheless, because not everyone’s sins are of such a kind that those seeking penance are unafraid to make them public, let this [so] objectionable custom be removed, lest many be kept from the remedies of penance while they either blush or fear that their deeds may be exposed to their enemies, by whom they can be struck down through the provisions of the laws.

For that confession is sufficient which is first offered to God and [alternatively: then; elsewhere: at that time] also to the priest, who approaches as intercessor for the offenses of those confessing and [the offenses of] those doing penance. For then more people will be able to be summoned to penance, if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people.

## In a Letter of Pope Innocent

[Note: To Exuperius, bishop, chapter 2.]

Those who, after baptism, have devoted themselves at all times to the pleasure of sexual excess and, at the end [at the final moment] of their life, ask simultaneously for penance and reconciliation [to Communion]. Former custom had prevailed, so that penance was granted [to them] but Communion was denied. For when persecutions were extremely frequent in those days [at that time], and the availability of Communion did not keep people, secure of reconciliation, from falling, Communion was rightly denied while penance was granted, so that everything might not be entirely refused; and the circumstances of the time made remission more severe. But after our Lord restored peace to the churches [once fear had been driven away], it was decided that Communion should be given to those departing, and [because of the Lord’s mercy] as a kind of viaticum to those setting out.

Therefore, Communion shall be granted together with final penance, so that people of this kind, at their last moments, with our Savior permitting [the penitents, in his mercy], may be rescued from everlasting destruction.

## Council of Toledo, chapter 8

[Note: Council of Toledo III, canon 12.]

Whenever a priest grants penance to anyone, he shall observe this: he must first shave him; or, if the person is a woman, she must change her clothing, lest she relapse after penance into the practices which she again has cause to lament.

## In a Letter of Pope Leo, chapter 8

[Note: In reply to the inquiries of Rusticus of Narbonne.]

[Col. 1072C] (Variants and additions in the editions.) Those who receive penance when already at the point of death and die before Communion must be left to God’s judgment. But we, to whom we do not give Communion while they are alive, cannot give Communion to them when dead.

## The same, chapter 10

(Many additions and variants in the editions.) Those who have professed penance are not permitted to litigate in the public forum. If, however, they have something which they ought not to neglect, they should seek ecclesiastical judgment, not civil litigation.

## The same, chapter 11

(Variant.) A penitent, whether a merchant after penance. The quality of the profit either excuses the merchant or condemns him, for there is honorable gain and dishonorable gain. Nevertheless, for a penitent it is more useful to endure losses than to be bound by the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene among those selling and buying [in the commerce of buyer and seller].

## The same, chapter 13

Those who, fearing a relapse into youthful sexual incontinence on account of penance, have preferred intercourse with their wife [so as not to incur the crime of fornication] seem to have done something venially wrong, if they have known no other woman [Col. 1073A] [at all] besides their wife. Yet we do not establish a rule in this matter; we judge only what is more tolerable, since nothing else is appropriate for one who has performed penance than perseverance in chastity [persevering chastity of both mind and body].

## The same, chapter 19

Those who have been captured by pagans, if they have merely used sacrificial foods at a pagan banquet, may be cleansed by fasts and the imposition of hands (additional material and variants) and may receive Communion. But if they have worshiped idols or have been defiled by murders or fornications, they are not to be admitted to Communion except through [public] penance.

## In the Book [of] Saint Pomerium

[Note: Book II, On the Contemplative Life, chapter 7. The three books On the Contemplative Life are commonly, but falsely, attributed to Prosper in Gratian’s Decree and in the Works of Saint Prosper. Isidore of Seville testifies in chapter 12 of his book On Ecclesiastical Writers that the author of these books was Julianus Pomerius; the oldest manuscript codices also identify him as their author. Among these we count as excellent the codex of the chapter-house of Beauvais, as the most learned Louis Hasle, doctor of the Paris faculty and associate of the Sorbonne, wrote to me.]

[Col. 1073B] Concerning those who sin secretly and do penance secretly. Those, however, who hold some rank and secretly commit a crime will more easily appease the Lord, since, without being convicted by human judgment, they acknowledge their crime: either they disclose it through their own confessions, or, while others do not know what they themselves are in their hidden affairs, they pronounce upon themselves a sentence of voluntary excommunication. Separated from the altar at which they ministered, not in spirit but in office, they mourn their life as though it were dead, confident that, once reconciled to God through the fruits of effective penance, they will not only recover what they have lost but, having become citizens of the heavenly city, will also attain everlasting joys.

## In the Council of Pope Celestine, chapter . . . .

[Note: Celestine I, Letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne and Narbonne, chapter 2.]

[Col. 1073C] We have learned that some deny penance to the dying and refuse to grant the requests of those who, at the time of their death, desire this remedy for their souls. Horrible, I confess; and no one ought to be found so impious as to despair of the mercy of God—God forbid—as though he could not come to the aid of one who hastens to him at any time, and free a man imperiled beneath the weight of sins by the burden from which he desires to be released.

What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying and, by one’s cruelty, to kill his soul so that it cannot be set free? God, who is most ready to help, invites people to penance and thus promises the sinner: “On whatever day the sinner turns, [his sins] shall not be reckoned against him.” And: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

Therefore, whoever denies the hoped-for penance at the time of death deprives a person of salvation and despairs of the clemency of God, because he does not believe that God is sufficient—or able [in a moment]—to help the dying. The thief hanging on the cross at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the penance of a single hour had not helped him. While he was suffering punishment, he repented; and through the promise of a single utterance, he merited, with God’s promise, a dwelling in paradise.

Therefore, the true conversion of those placed at the end of life must be judged by the mind rather than by the passage of time, as the Prophet testifies [asserts in these words]: “When you have turned and groaned, [then] you will be saved.” Since, therefore, the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance must not be denied at any time to the penitent [to one requesting it], since he binds himself to the Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things are revealed.

# CHAPTER LXIX. CONCERNING THOSE WHO ACT AGAINST THE CANONS

## Council of Chalcedon, canon 1

[Col. 1074B] [Note: Dionysius’s translation.] We have decreed that the rules established by the holy Fathers in each council up to the present shall retain their proper force.

## Canon 10

[Note: It differs little from Dionysius’s translation.] Those who dare, after the definition of this great and universal synod, to perpetrate anything among the things that are prohibited shall withdraw from their own rank.

## Council of Epaon, canon 40

Therefore, if any of the holy prelates who confirmed these present statutes with their own subscriptions, or any of those whom God may appoint as their successors, departs from the integrity of observance of what has been approved by common judgment [consent] through heavenly inspiration, let him know that he will be liable alike to the judgment of the Godhead and to the judgment of the brotherhood.

## Council of Orléans, canon 26

[Note: Council of Orléans III, canon 33.]

Whoever, abandoning the integrity of observance, neglects to guard [and fulfill] these things established by divine inspiration (variant), let him know that he is liable to divine judgment, since no one is permitted either to be ignorant of or to disregard his canons.

## Council of Mâcon, canon 4

[Note: Council of Mâcon II.]

Let all [however] who strive through disobedience to nullify our definitions be struck with anathema.

## Canon 5

[Note: Of the same council, the same canon.]

But if anyone is stubborn toward our most salutary statutes, let him be separated from the members of the Church for all time.

## Council of Lyon, canon 50

[Note: Council of Lyon I, canon 5.]

Whoever transgresses these things which have been defined by us through divine inspiration [which have been treated or concluded], let him know that he will be liable to the examination of the Godhead as a transgressor of divine commandments and liable to the council of the brotherhood.

# CHAPTER LXX. CONCERNING THE BISHOPS WHO CONFIRMED THE CANONS MENTIONED ABOVE

[Note: We have often noted above the various readings and numbering of these councils as they are found in the latest edition.]

[Note: This is Dionysius’s title, although he himself admits in his letter to Bishop Stephen, or in the preface to the book of ecclesiastical canons, that many did not readily give their assent to them, in these words: “At the beginning, therefore, we translated from Greek the canons which are called apostolic. Since very many did not readily give their assent to them, we did not wish your Holiness to be unaware of this, although afterward certain decrees of pontiffs seem to have been taken from these canons.” The index of synods found at the beginning of the collection indicates the same thing. Since that chapter either illustrates or explains this one, it seems appropriate to refer it here.]

In the name of the Lord, the chapters of the Greek canons begin.

[Col. 1075D] Canons of Nicaea, of 318 bishops. Canons of Ancyra, of 12 bishops. These canons are said to have been Nicene. Canons of Ephesus, of the first synod, of 200 bishops. Canons of Neocaesarea, of 18 bishops. Canons of Gangra, of 15 bishops. Canons of Antioch, of 32 bishops. Canons of Laodicea, of 22 bishops. Canons of Constantinople, of 150 bishops. Canons of Chalcedon, of 630 bishops. Canons of the Apostles, which Bishop Dionysius translated from Greek into Latin at the request of Bishop Stephen. Canons of Nicaea, of 20 bishops. This canon is not found among the Greeks, and by some it is called Sardican. Canons of Hippo, of 12 bishops. [Col. 1076C] Canons of Milan, of 18 bishops. Also, canons of the Latins. Canons of Carthage, of 218 bishops. Also canons of the second Council of Carthage. Canons of Toulon, of 33 bishops. Canons of Rome. Also canons of the Romans under Pope Saint Sylvester. Also canons of the Romans under blessed Gregory I, II, and III. Canons of Angers, of 33 bishops. Canons of Orléans, of 21 bishops. Also canons of Orléans, of 35 bishops. Also canons of the third and fourth councils of Orléans. Canons of Arles, of 600 bishops. Canons of Orange, of 18 bishops. Canons of Valence, of 19 bishops. Canons of Riez, of 12 bishops. Canons of Vaison, of 108 bishops. [Col. 1076D] Canons of Arles, of 15 bishops; 5 presbyters and 16 deacons. Canons of Auvergne, of 15 bishops. Canons of Mâcon, of 21 bishops. Canons of Lyon, of 8 bishops. Canons of Epaon, of 27 bishops. Canons of Orange, of 35 bishops. Canons of Caesarea, of 36 bishops. Canons of Lumnatium, of 37 bishops. Canons of Agde, of 22 bishops. Canons of Vienne, of 28 bishops. Canons of Urbicum, of 15 bishops. Canons of Toledo, of 10 bishops. Canons of Autun of Saint Leodegarius, bishop.]

[Col. 1075A]

I. Ecclesiastical rules of the holy Apostles, issued through Pope Clement, which are placed first in order in the Greek copies.

II. Canons of Nicaea, of 318 bishops.

III. Canons of Chalcedon, of 230 bishops.

IV. Canons of Ancyra, [Note: Concerning this synod, see Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 73,] to which Bishop Hosius and twelve others, together with the remaining bishops, gave their assent.

V. Canons of Sardica, of 20 bishops: Hosius, Gaudentius, Januarius, Aetius, and others.

VI. Canons of Antioch, of 22 bishops: Eusebius of Palestine, Theodotus, and others.

VII. Canons of Laodicea, of 22 bishops: Theodosius, [Col. 1075B] Nicetas, Anatolius, and others.

VIII. Canons of Neocaesarea, of 17 bishops: Basil, Gregory, Lupus, Justus, and others.

IX. Canons of Orange, of 16 bishops: Hilary, Eucherius, and others.

X. Canons of Arles, of 200 bishops: Pope Sylvester, Marinus of Arles, Reticius, called of the Aedui, of Lyon, in the time of the consuls Volusianus and Anianus. Also, canons of Arles, of 19 bishops: Caesarius of Arles, Cyprian. Also, canons of Arles in the village of Vaison, of 11 bishops: Caesarius, Cyprian, Prosper, Eucherius.

XI. Canons of Epaon, of 24 bishops: Avitus, Viventiolus, and others.

[Col. 1075C] XII. Canons of the African bishops, of 24 bishops.

[Col. 1076A] XIII. Canons of Arles, of 19 bishops: Sabaudus of Arles, and others.

XIV. Canons of Agde, of 34 bishops: Caesarius, Sophronius, and others.

XV. Canons of Orléans, of 21 bishops: Aurelianus, Agrestarus, and others. Also, canons of Orléans, of 21 bishops: Melanius, Lupus, and others. Also, canons of Orléans, of 25 bishops: Albinus of Angers, Lupus of Lyon.

XVI. Canons of Auvergne, of 20 bishops: Honoratus, Gallus, and others.

XVII. Canons of Mâcon, of 63 bishops: Priscus of Lyon, Siagrius of the Aedui, Sulpitius of Bourges, Eusebius of Mâcon, and others.

XVIII. Canons of Lyon, of 13 bishops: [Col. 1076B] Nicetius of Lyon, Siagrius of the Aedui. Also, canons of Lyon, of 20 bishops: Priscus of Lyon, Siagrius of the Aedui.

XIX. Agreement and confirmation of Leodegarius, bishop of Autun.

# CHAPTER LXXI. CANONS OF POPE SAINT GREGORY, CHAPTER XII

[Note: These are missing from the editions.]

1. How a bishop ought to conduct himself with his clergy.

2. Concerning the stipends of clerics who take wives.

3. Concerning communal life or almsgiving.

4. Concerning the celebration of Mass.

5. Concerning thefts from the Church.

6. Concerning marriage contracted with relatives.

7. Concerning ordinations to be performed.

[Col. 1076C] 8. Concerning the bishops of Gaul and Britain.

[Col. 1077A] 9. Concerning baptism, women in danger, and their childbirth.

10. Concerning a woman who has given birth or is menstruating.

11. Concerning intercourse with one’s own wife.

12. Concerning the pollution that occurs in dreams.

[Note: Variant in the editions. See Letter 31 of Book XII of the *Register*, the last letter of the edition.]

## RESPONSES OF BLESSED POPE GREGORY TO AUGUSTINE, WHOM HE SENT IN HIS PLACE TO SAXONY TO PREACH

[Note: Some additions occur in the editions, namely Augustine’s questions and other material, etc., in the Responses.]

The Letters of blessed Paul to Timothy bear witness to how he endeavored to instruct him concerning the manner in which he ought [should] to conduct himself in the house of God. It is the custom of the apostolic see to give instructions to bishops after their ordination, so that from every income which comes in, four portions should be made: one, namely, for the bishop and his household, on account of hospitality [and reception of guests]; another for the clergy; a third for the poor; and a fourth for the repair of churches.

[Col. 1077B] But your Fraternity, instructed in the rules of a monastery, ought not to live apart from your clergy in the Church of the English, which, by God’s agency, has recently been brought to the faith. You ought to establish the manner of life which existed among our fathers at the beginning of the nascent Church, when no one among them said that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was held in common.

[Note: Petrus Gussanvillaeus correctly observed that certain things in that letter seem foreign to the character of Saint Gregory. Accordingly, those things especially should be noted which are not received by the oldest and most accurate collection of the Herovall codex, since from these it becomes clear which things are redundant in the edition.]

## 2. Concerning the stipends of clerics who take wives

If there are some who, established outside [within] the sacred orders, cannot remain continent, they ought to take wives and receive their stipends externally, because it is written: “It was distributed to each person according as each had need.” Their stipend must also be considered and provided for, and they must be held under the rule of the Church, so that they may live with good morals, devote themselves to the singing of psalms, [Col. 1077C] and, with God as their author, preserve heart, tongue, and body from everything illicit. (Additional material in the editions.)

## 3. Concerning communal life or almsgiving

[Note: In the latest edition this is not distinguished from the preceding chapter.]

[Note: A learned man expresses the following view in his notes: “In the first response,” he says, “the matter of the four portions has already been dealt with, and communal life has been prescribed; there was therefore no reason to answer about these matters when they had not been asked.” The observation is correct, if the text is read as in the edition, since the same thing has already been said above. But that this is an entirely different question and one of the greatest importance is proved by the variant reading of the Herovall codex.]

Now that the portions are failing [concerning the making of the portions], what shall we have to say about providing hospitality and fulfilling mercy? Everything that remains is to be expended for pious and religious causes [needs], since the Lord and teacher of all says: “What remains, give as alms, and behold, everything is clean.”

## 4. Concerning the celebration of Mass

(Variant in the editions.) (Additional question.) Your Fraternity should know the custom of the Roman Church in which you were brought up. But it pleases me that, whether in the Roman Church, in the churches of Gaul, [Col. 1077D] or in any church, you have found something which can please almighty God more, you should carefully select it and pour into the Church of the English, which is still new in the faith, as a special institution whatever you have been able to gather from many churches.

For things are not to be loved on account of places, but places on account of good [the editions omit “good”] things. Therefore, from each of the various churches let your Fraternity select what is pious, religious, and right. And, gathering these things together as though into a bundle, establish them as a custom in the minds of the English.

## 5. Concerning thefts from the Church

(Variants and additions occur throughout the editions.) It is necessary to consider, from the person of the thief, how he can be corrected. For some commit theft although they possess the means [of support], while others commit it because of poverty [transgress]. Hence it is necessary to correct some by losses, some by words, some more lightly, and others more strictly [Col. 1078B]. And when one proceeds somewhat more strictly, it must be done out of charity, not fury, since this is done for the one being corrected, so that he may not be handed over to the fires of Gehenna.

We ought to maintain discipline among the faithful in the same way that good fathers customarily do with their physical children: they strike them with blows on account of their faults, yet they seek to have as heirs those whom they afflict with pain, and they preserve what they possess for those whom they appear to be pursuing.

Therefore, this charity must be kept in mind, so that the mind does absolutely nothing outside the rule of reason. But how should stolen property be returned? Far be it from the Church to receive with increase what it appears to have lost from earthly goods and to seek profits from empty [losses].

## 6. Concerning marriage contracted with relatives

(Variant.) Indeed, a certain law of the Romans [in the Roman republic] permits the son and daughter of a brother and sister, or of two brothers or two sisters, to be joined in marriage. But experience has taught us that offspring cannot grow up from such a marriage.

Therefore, it is necessary to permit the faithful to marry even in the third or fourth generation. For the second degree, which we mentioned above, must abstain entirely from such unions. To have intercourse with a stepmother, however, is a grave crime, because [also in the Law] it is written: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father.” And whoever uncovers the nakedness of his stepmother uncovers his father’s nakedness, since she was once one flesh with him.

(Additional material and variant.) A woman related by marriage has become your sister through the union with your brother.

[Note: Here the seventh response begins, but it is more correctly joined to this passage because it concerns the same question. See the note of Petrus Gussanvillaeus. The edition adds other material, namely from the words “has become your sister” up to “but if,” concerning which the learned man says in his notes: “For this reason John the Baptist, etc.; Saint Gregory would not have mixed these disparate matters, he says. For it is one thing to have intercourse with the wife of a living brother and another with that of a dead brother, as is clear from the ancient law, etc. I think that this entire appendix was placed in the margin by some preacher and later slipped into the text. Saint Gregory does not usually jump outside the chorus and mix in matters unrelated to the subject so coldly.” Although this learned man advances the point without the authority of any codex, relying only on his own perspicacity, the most exacting collection of the Herovall codex confirms it: nothing of this kind is found there, nor are any of the other things foreign to Gregory. From this it may likewise be inferred that many other passages are not Gregory’s, as the marginal notes indicate.]

But if, among the English people, while they were still in unbelief, some entered into this abominable marriage, they must be admonished to abstain and repent. Nevertheless, they must not be deprived of Communion for something which they committed unknowingly before baptism.

[Note: Much additional material is present, bearing the character of a gloss.]

## 7. Concerning ordinations to be performed

(Some material precedes.) Bishops should not be separated from one another by a long interval, so that three or four may be able to assemble for the ordination of a bishop, since it ought not to be done otherwise.

For even in spiritual matters, so that they may be arranged wisely and maturely, we can take an example from bodily matters. Certainly, when marriages are celebrated [in the world], married people are summoned so that those who have already gone before on the path of marriage may share also in the subsequent joy.

Why, then, should not such men assemble with us in this spiritual ordination, through which a human being is joined to God by a sacred mystery—men who may rejoice in the advancement [in the progress of the one ordained] of the bishop and together pour out prayers to almighty God for his protection?

[Note: This chapter is marked as chapter 10 in the edition, because a different passage concerning the relics of Saint Sixtus precedes it. That passage conflicts with the genuine and certain Letter 30 of Book IV and is therefore absent from the Herovall collection, as it is from the Tell and Carn manuscripts, etc., as Gussanvillaeus observed in his notes.]

## 9. Concerning baptism, women in danger, and childbirth

[Note: From the words “I do not doubt this” up to “a pregnant woman,” the learned man suggests that the passage is not Saint Gregory’s, because, he says, it does not sufficiently reflect Gregory the Great’s character. Although he says this without relying on the authority of any codex, we confirm it through the Herovall collection, in which nothing of this kind is read.]

A pregnant woman may be baptized, since fertility [of the flesh] is not a fault before the eyes of almighty God. For when our first parents had sinned in paradise, by the just judgment of God they lost the immortality which they had received. Since almighty God did not wish to extinguish the human race completely in its guilt, he took immortality away from humanity because of its sin [for its sin], but in the fertility of offspring he reserved for them the kindness of his mercy.

Therefore, how can that which has been reserved not by human nature [Col. 1079C] but by the gift of almighty God be barred from the grace of sacred baptism? For in that mystery, in which every fault is completely extinguished, it is exceedingly foolish to suppose that the gift of grace can be denied.

But when she has given birth, after how many days a woman ought to enter the church—you have learned from the command of the Old Testament [by the precept of the Old Testament]: she must abstain for 33 days in the case of a male child and 66 days in the case of a female child.

(Variant.) But these things are understood mystically. For if she enters the church at the very hour in which she has given birth, to give thanks, she is burdened by no weight of sin. Sexual pleasure, not pain, is culpable.

(Additional material.) For if we forbid a woman who has given birth to enter the church, we assign her own punishment to her as a fault. Nor is a woman who has given birth, or the child she has borne, to be prevented from being baptized if threatened by the danger of death [without delay], whether at the very hour in which she gives birth or, in the case of the child, at the very hour in which it is born.

For just as the grace of the sacred mystery must be provided with great discernment to the living who are capable of understanding, so it must be offered without any delay to those whom death threatens, lest, while time is still being sought to provide the mystery of redemption, a slight delay intervening [or, according to a faulty reading, “death intervening”], no one who can be redeemed be found.

## 10. Concerning a woman who has given birth or is menstruating

[Col. 1080B] [Note: In the edition this is not distinguished from the preceding chapter.]

[Note: Petrus Gussanvillaeus considers the following proposition suspect: “because,” he says, “of the words that follow, ‘until the child is weaned.’ For who among men would believe that they are bound by this law? Which prelate would dare to impose such a yoke? See John Gerson, *On Preparation for Mass after Nocturnal Pollution*, considerations 7 and 8.” This is the learned man’s first reason. Although it seems true to me, three things stand in the way. First, he uses the testimony of no codex. Second, the Herovall codex, which often confirms his sound conjectures, disproves this one as false. Third, it would follow from this reasoning that certain very certain testimonies of the Fathers ought to be expunged; for example, when Saint Clement of Alexandria speaks in Book III of the *Stromata* as follows:

“Therefore, you will show from Scripture no one among the ancients who had intercourse with a pregnant woman; but after she had carried the child in the womb, and after she had weaned the child that had been born, wives were again known by men. You will find Moses’ father observing this principle and practice, since, after an interval of three years following the birth of Aaron, he fathered Moses. And again, the tribe of Levi, observing this law of nature handed down by God, entered the promised land smaller in number than the others. For a race is not easily multiplied when men who enter a lawful marriage sow seed but await not only the carrying of the womb but also the weaning from milk.”

[Col. 1080D] Greek: *Ἀναμενόντων δὲ οὐ τὴν κυοφορίαν μόνον, ἀλλα καὶ τὴν γαλακτουχίαν*—“awaiting not only pregnancy but also suckling.”

Some other Fathers commend and prescribe the same thing: Saint Ambrose, Pope Gregory III, and nearly all the authors of penitentials. But see the notes to the chapter of the Penitential of Theodore concerning questions of marriage.]

With regard to a woman who has given birth [but in the variant, with regard to intercourse with her], her husband must not approach her for intercourse until the child that has been born has been weaned.

A wicked custom has arisen in the conduct of married people: women give their infants to other women to be nursed. This seems to have been devised solely because of incontinence, since, unwilling to abstain, they disdain to nurse the children they have borne.

Therefore, women who, because of this wicked custom, give their children to others to be nursed must not have intercourse with their husbands until the period of purification has passed. For even apart from the cause of childbirth, when they are confined by their unaccustomed [customary] menstruation, they are forbidden to have intercourse with their husbands, so that the sacred law strikes with death any husband who approaches a menstruating woman.

Nevertheless, a woman must not be forbidden to enter the church while she is undergoing her customary menstrual period, because the natural excess which occurs in her cannot be reckoned as guilt. Since she suffers it unwillingly, it is not just that she should be deprived of entry into the church.

For we know that the woman who suffered from a flow of blood came humbly from behind the Lord, touched the fringe of his garment, and immediately her illness departed from her. If, therefore, while placed in a flow of blood, she could laudably touch the Lord’s garment, why should it not be permitted to a woman suffering the flow of menstrual blood to enter the Lord’s church?

[Note: Much material is inserted here which bears the character of a gloss.]

She must not be prohibited from receiving the mystery of holy Communion during those same days. But if, out of great reverence, she does not presume to receive it, she is to be commended; if she receives it, she is not to be judged.

It is characteristic of good minds to acknowledge their faults in some manner even where there is no fault, because often something is done without fault which arises from fault. Thus, when we are hungry, we eat without fault, although the fact that we are hungry came about through the fault of the first human being.

The menstrual cycle is not any fault of women, since it occurs naturally. Yet the fact that nature itself has been so corrupted that it appears to be polluted even without the impulse of pleasure arises from fault; it is a defect proceeding from fault [from the defect of fault], in which human nature recognizes what it has become through judgment. The human being who willingly committed the fault bears the guilt of the fault unwillingly.

Just as external actions are observed in the Old Testament, so in the New Testament attention is directed not so much to what is done externally as to what is thought externally, so that it may be weighed [punished] by a subtle judgment.

# FROM CHAPTER LXXV. IN THE LETTER OF JEROME

[Note: Jerome to Oceanus, asking whether a man who remarries after baptism can become a priest.]

Concerning what the Apostle says: “The husband of one wife.”

I never thought, son Oceanus, that a prince’s indulgence could be made to suffer the reproach of the guilty. [Note: [Col. 1081D] Much of this is redundant in the edition.] The Cainite [Caina] heresy rises [Col. 1081C] up against me, and the dead viper lifts its crushed head, saying that there are some things which Christ cannot cleanse. [Note: [Col. 1081D] Much is redundant.] Cartarius, a bishop of Spain, married one wife before he was baptized and another after baptism, the first having died; and do you think that he acted against the Apostle? [Note: [Col. 1082D] An excessively excited and false argument is inserted here. See the letter of Innocent and the testimonies of others in the note on *Penance*.]

At Rome I endured from a most eloquent man a “horned,” as they say, syllogism. He asked me: “Is it a sin to marry?” I answered simply: “It is not a sin.” And he said: “In baptism evil deeds are forgiven, not good ones. Therefore, what is not forgiven remains.” And I said: “Does baptism make the whole man new?” I asked the question in full: “Then nothing of the old man is retained in baptism? What was once in the old man cannot be imputed to the new?” He fell silent. [Col. 1081D] But although he did not know how to speak, he could not remain silent. He began to sweat, grow pale, and tremble with his lips. At last he burst out and said: “Have you not read that a man who has one wife must be made a priest, and that the matter, not the times, is defined?” [Note: [Col. 1082D] Several pages are filled with further statements irrelevant to the subject.]

I replied: “A baptized man is chosen for the episcopate. What is asked is what he is, not what he was. Since, therefore, there was nothing to be forgiven, it was not forgiven in baptism; and because it was not a sin, will it be reckoned as a sin?” All harlotry, parricide, and incest are cleansed in the font; shall the stains of a wife remain, and shall brothels be preferred to marriage chambers? Let pagans and catechumens hear this and enter into dishonorable marriages; let them, in the manner of the Scots and Athenians, have promiscuous wives and children in common. Indeed, let them beware of any designation of spouse, lest, after they have believed in Christ, it harm them that they had wives rather than concubines and prostitutes. The misfortune of a dead wife will be imputed, while a prostitute’s lust will be crowned; and if you had entered into marriage, you could never afterward be ordained a cleric.

They served the Lord’s blessing, “Increase and multiply,” and concealed with modest shame what was permitted. You acted shamelessly in doing what was not permitted. To them it is written, “Marriage is honorable”; to you it is read, “The Lord will destroy fornicators and adulterers.” All these crimes were pardoned in baptism, as the Apostle says: “Such indeed were you, but you were washed.” But I ask how your filth was washed away and my purity defiled. If they had been filth, they would certainly have been washed away. But if they are not filth, how are they imputed as filth? What sort of evasion is this, and what acumen more blunt than any pestle? For what is not a sin is sin because the Lord does not forgive it, since he had nothing to forgive; and for that reason what was not forgiven remains.

But concerning the statement “a man of one wife”: the first Church of Christ, which was taught by the Apostle, came from Israel. It was customary for the Israelites, by the law and by the example of the patriarchs, even for priests, to have children by many wives. He therefore commanded that the priests should not claim the same license for the Church, but that each should have one at a time.

Let me ask something else. If someone had a concubine before baptism, and, after she died, was baptized and married a wife, ought he to become a cleric? You will answer that he may, because he had a concubine, not a wife. Therefore, [marriage contracts and] dowry rights are condemned by the Apostle, not intercourse. [Note: [Col. 1082D] Several things concerning concubines are inserted here.] Hence, when he says “a man of one wife,” intercourse with one woman may be understood.

The holy Scriptures ought not to be forced into the terms of dowry contracts; rather, they should be understood as they stand. Nor should the Savior’s baptism be emptied of its meaning, for in it all sins are submerged. [Note: [Col. 1082D] Here the discourse runs through entire pages on cold water and matters wholly irrelevant to the subject.] And if all sins are submerged, how does one wife float above them?

[Col. 1082D] “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven.” I think that we too may add something to this song: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin.” [Note: [Col. 1082D] Much is inserted over several pages that is wholly unrelated to the purpose.]

I cannot sufficiently marvel at the great blindness of human beings: they dispute about wives taken before baptism and drag into accusation what died in baptism—or rather, what was brought to life with Christ—while no one observes the other commands of the Apostle, so exceedingly clear, in which he speaks about the life of priests. The one who said “a man of one wife” also commanded that he be blameless, and so forth in what follows; yet we close our eyes to everything and see only wives. Therefore, when someone brings against us a wife taken before baptism, let us require from him all the things commanded after baptism. They pass over what is forbidden and object to what is permitted. [Note: [Col. 1083A] In the edition this letter is everywhere swollen with so many digressions that one must say, “What purpose do these things serve?” And after a long discourse: “The day would fail me if I were to recount everything,” and below: “Before I finish dictating—for I already understand [Col. 1084A] that I am exceeding the length of the letter.” All these things are far removed from the collection of the oldest Herovallian codex, since they are wholly foreign to the subject, even though they are not entirely inconsistent with his style.]

[Col. 1083]

73. Likewise, fourteen chapters of the same.

91. That *vallematia* and obscene songs be prohibited.  
92. That the ordinations of presbyters and deacons be celebrated at appointed times.

# Extracts from the Penitential of Master John of God, Doctor of Decretals

[Col. 1085]

## Notice concerning the following extracts

[Col. 1085A]

When most of the monuments of ecclesiastical discipline had already been printed, I received from the very learned D. Feronius, canon of Chartres and associate of the Sorbonne, the *Penitential of John of God*. Therefore, what we excerpted from it had to be placed here, outside its proper location, as an appendix.

Although this author, a doctor of the decretals, never rises above the level of a decretal, nevertheless he arranges the matters scattered through the body of the Decretals and Decrees so suitably for completing his *Penitential* that it ought to seem useful to many. It contains several distinctive opinions. For example, in the chapter on the pope’s penance and confession he says:

> “The question is to whom he ought to confess, and it seems that to no one except God, as the Greeks do; as is proved in *On Penance*, distinction 1, final chapter.”

Similar adaptations are found in this *Penitential*. It was composed for the use of the Bolognese school, for the benefit of the whole Church, and for the honor of God and of the Roman Church and its venerable prelate Innocent IV, as is declared at the beginning of the book in these words:

> “For the honor of the supreme Trinity and the undivided unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; of the blessed Virgin and all the angels; [Col. 1086A] and of all the saints, and especially of blessed Vincent; and for the honor and name of the venerable Fathers, the bishop and chapter of the city of Bologna; and for the benefit of the entire school; and for the honor of the Roman Church and its venerable prelate Innocent IV.”

John of God privately dedicates his work to the bishop and chapter of Bologna. His preface begins as follows:

> “To the venerable Father and lord, by divine providence bishop of the city of Bologna, and to the venerable men, the dean, archdeacon, cantor, treasurer, and master of the schools, and to the entire chapter of that same church, [Col. 1086B] Master John of God, doctor of the decretals, their canon and servant at their disposal, sends greetings in him who is the true salvation of all, with reverence as dutiful as it is devout, etc.”

First he discusses generally the vices of persons of every condition and confession; then, specifically and chiefly, the penance and confession of prelates, such as the supreme pontiff, cardinals, and others. Omitting much, we have selected what is most important in this *Penitential*, and what explains the chapters of Theodore concerning penance.

## On the confession and penance of the sick

*(From Book I, chapter 1.)*

[Col. 1085C]

Understand this carefully: you must inquire of the sick, subtly and astutely, how they conducted themselves when they were in good health, speaking to them as follows:

“My son, confess, for we are human beings and cannot be without sin. If you confess, are contrite, and resolve not to sin, God will undoubtedly forgive your fault, and I will absolve you from the penalty, if you entrust yourself wholly to my judgment or that of another priest. That this is true is proved by these words, and so forth: ‘At whatever hour the sinner groans and turns back, I will remember his sins no more.’ But if you do not wish to confess in this life, you will confess unwillingly in the next, in the sight of all angels, friends, and enemies, and you will be condemned forever, and so forth.

“That priests can remit the penalty from those who are truly contrite is proved by the fact that priests are said to be vicars of Jesus Christ and to possess the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and that they absolve before the day of judgment. But if someone is not truly contrite, priests cannot absolve him, because when guilt has not been forgiven, the penalty cannot be diminished, and so forth.”

## What the priest does after hearing the sick person’s penance

*(From chapter 2.)*

After you have learned the sick person’s confession, [Col. 1086C] you ought not impose penance on him, but merely make it known to him, saying:

“If you were healthy, you would have to do penance for so many years. But because you are sick, I do not impose penance on you. I enjoin you that, if you die, you have this much given on your behalf for that penance. And I absolve you by the authority of our Lord God Jesus Christ, of blessed Peter the Apostle, and of our office. I also enjoin you that, as soon as you are well, before you turn to other services, you come to me or to another priest, confess again in the same manner, and devoutly receive the penance that had been imposed on you,” and so forth.

## On the confession of the healthy and the penance to be imposed on them

*(From chapter 3.)*

[Col. 1086D]

If the person who confesses to you is healthy, first determine whether he is free or enslaved. If he is enslaved, inquire whether he sinned out of fear of his master or of his own will.

If he sinned out of fear of his master, although he was not permitted to obey him by force against God, nevertheless the slave is to be punished more mildly, and so forth. But if the slave sinned of his own will, without fault on the part of his master, in that case the slave is to be punished more severely in his body, and so forth; consideration nevertheless being given to the journey of pilgrimage, so that a burden is not imposed on the slave by which the master would suffer loss because of the slave’s absence, and so forth.

But if he is free, he ought to be punished more severely if he sinned of his own will. For he ought to undergo the entire penance imposed by the canon, if this can be done, and so forth.

## On the penance of the rich

*(From chapter 5.)*

[Col. 1087A]

If the person who confesses to you is rich, inquire subtly and astutely what caused him to fall into that sin, and always promise forgiveness if he confesses to you, and so forth. Impose penance on him in these three things: fasting, prayer, and almsgiving. Take care, however, if he is delicate; do not give him a harsh fast, and so forth.

## On the confession of children

*(From chapter 6.)*

Proceed as follows concerning the confession of children capable of deceit. First ask in general whether he has committed any sin, soothing him with heavenly rewards if he has truly confessed, and frightening him with eternal punishments if he has not truly confessed. Ask about the circumstances—namely, the cause, place, and time—as we shall say in the title on circumstances. Impose on him a somewhat lesser penance than if he were an adult. But if he is not capable of deceit, he ought to be punished more mildly, because such children do not know what they are doing, and so forth.

## On the penance of the elderly

*(From chapter 7.)*

If the person who confesses to you is old, consider whether he is in extreme old age, the condition of the very aged, after eighty years. Then burden him with prayers and lighten his fasts, and so forth.

But if he is an old man—that is, established in old age and not in extreme old age, from sixty up to eighty—then punish him more severely than if he were in extreme old age, because such old men, when they sin, draw the young to destruction.

## On the penance of prelates in general

*(From chapter 8.)*

If those who confess to you are prelates, and the sin is manifest, punish them more severely because of the evil example they have given. What is done by prelates is easily followed by their subjects as an example, and so forth; for sin extends farther and spreads among subjects when a sinful prelate is tolerated by his subjects out of reverence for his order, and so forth.

But if the sin is hidden, punish him more mildly, because where evil arises, there it ought to die, and so forth.

## On the penance of minor clerics in general

*(From chapter 9.)*

[Col. 1087D]

Proceed as follows concerning the penance of other clerics. Consider whether the person is a priest, and punish him more severely than a deacon; punish a deacon more severely than a subdeacon; and punish a subdeacon more severely than others established in the minor orders. For a Christian falls gravely into sins in two ways: either because of the magnitude of the sin or because of the height of his dignity.

## On the penance of monks and other religious in general

*(From chapter 10.)*

Proceed as follows concerning religious persons who confess to you in some measure: impose on them, in place of penance, that henceforth they observe the rule to which they have bound themselves, because this will be the highest penance, and so forth.

## On the penance of women in general

*(From chapter 11.)*

[Col. 1088A]

Proceed as follows concerning the penance of women. First, if the person is a girl, especially a virgin under her parents’ authority, afflict her with penance according to the canons, chiefly with fasts, so that she may subdue her flesh and prevent it from indulging in lust. For the lust of women is foul and more intense than that of a man; therefore it ought to be subdued more severely by abstinence from food, and so forth.

Also determine whether she is married. In that case impose penance on her without causing her husband scandal, so that, if her husband is absent, she fast and afflict herself as far as she can before God, according to the judgment God has given you. This applies especially if she has defiled her husband’s marriage bed through adultery, to which she ought under no condition to have been led, and so forth.

## On the penance of widows in general

*(From chapter 12.)*

[Col. 1088B]

If she is a widow, inquire carefully about the circumstances and punish her with fasting more severely than other women, for by their prayers and merits they ought to assist the churches. Nevertheless, consider whether she is an old woman unable to fast. In that case lighten her fast and increase her prayers, since it is her duty always to pray until the end of her life, and so forth.

## On the penance of the *pyrocaræ*

*(From chapter 13.)*

If there are *pyrocaræ*—women who have only recently risen from the dust—burden them with fasts and prayers, enjoining them henceforth not to cloak the impiety of their religious profession under an appearance of piety, but to take husbands if they have not made a solemn vow, or to preserve the chastity they promised to the Lord. For, as Saint Jerome says, it would have been better to enter marriage and walk on level ground than to strive toward higher things and fall into the depths of hell, and so forth.

## On circumstances that aggravate sins

*(From Book III, chapter 6.)*

The sinner ought to consider these things when making confession: sorrow because he has sinned against the Lord; age; wisdom; consideration of those who do not sin; the cleansing of tears; sorrow for the virtue that has been lost; sorrow because he does good; sorrow because in so short a life he has not acted rightly. Whoever offends in one matter becomes guilty of all. He should feel sorrow because he did not fear the Lord, who was full of wisdom; the more acceptable a person was to God, the more culpable he is when he sins.

Adam sinned more because he abounded in every good. Every virtue suffers injury from one vice. Love of money diminishes chastity. Every virtue fails in whatever crime is committed. All these matters are proved by the authorities of Augustine, Pope Alexander, and Gregory.

## What the priest must consider in the person confessing

*(From chapter 7.)*

Sorrow for the evil examples given to one’s neighbors; sorrow for the grief inflicted on the good; sorrow for the joy not brought to the good; and greater sorrow for an offense against God. No one can serve two masters, but love of persistence in one sin means the loss of all good things.

The penitent should place himself entirely under the judgment of the priest and do for the salvation of his soul whatever he would do for his temporal life, whose enjoyment he is certain of. Because he sinned voluntarily, he should abstain from what is permitted in order to obtain forgiveness. God looks to the heart, not only to the hands.

Confession must not be divided among different priests. Let the corrupted man and the corrupted woman fear being corrupted again, following the example of Dinah, daughter of Jacob.

These things also must be considered: age, place, order, wisdom, and time. The sinner ought to consider them in his confession. The priest, however, must take account of the penitent’s tears, groans, and the circumstances just mentioned, and should say to him:

“My son, consider that these are the circumstances which keep a person in sin: namely, an evil habit, which becomes a second nature. For through depraved habit a person can no longer resist. Another cause is that a person who does not confess a sin easily falls into another sin. As Saint Gregory says, a sin that is not cleansed by penance, by its own weight, drags a person into another sin.

“There is also another cause: sin comes upon a person secretly, like death, and suddenly. Another cause prevents the sick person from coming to penance, namely, the distress of illness. There is also another cause that hinders the penitent: shame at confessing and avoidance of punishment, and so forth.

“You, priest, must strengthen the penitent so that he does not despair, even if he confesses late, because God is powerful enough to convert and save a person in a single moment, preferring to bring him to penance rather than condemn him according to justice, and so forth.”

## How confession ought to be made

*(From chapter 8.)*

[Col. 1089C]

Confession, according to the authority of the holy Fathers, ought to be made simply: one should accuse oneself and not another, in accordance with the words, “Incline not my heart to words of wickedness, to excuse excuses in sins.”

It should be humble, with a pure intention and without hypocrisy. Hence Solomon says: “From fear of you, Lord, we conceived and brought forth.”

It should be faithful, under hope of forgiveness, not like Judas, who said, “I have sinned in betraying innocent blood,” and afterward went away and hanged himself.

It should be frequent. Hence Gregory says: “The sooner you confess in hope of forgiveness, the more easily you obtain forgiveness of your fault.”

It should be bare. Hence Jeremiah says that there is no one who performs penance for his sins and says what he has done.

It should be discerning. Thus Augustine says: “Seek a priest who knows how to loose and bind.”

It should be voluntary, not like the confession of Achan, but like the confession of the thief on the cross.

It should be modest. Thus Gregory says: “Modesty is the greatest part of satisfaction.”

It should be secret. Hence John Chrysostom says: “I do not tell you to expose yourself publicly.”

It should be prompt. Hence Ecclesiasticus says: “Do not delay turning to the Lord.”

It should be obedient. Hence Augustine says: “Do everything for the gaining of the soul’s life that you would do for the life of the body,” and so forth.

## On the penance of the lord pope and to whom he ought to confess

*(From Book V, chapter 1.)*

The matter of the lord pope’s penance must be discussed. Perhaps some people think that the pope does not sin, as the Julian law says that simony is not committed at Rome; hence it seems that he is permitted to do whatever he wishes.

But I, John of God, together with other doctors, hold the contrary view. I say that if the pope sins, he offends more grievously than another person, because the higher the rank, the more serious the fall, as Gregory proves in *On Penance*, distinction 2, chapter “The Beginning, he says, of the ways.”

John Chrysostom proves the same in distinction 40, “A Christian,” and Pope Hilary in 25, question 1, “No one may,” where it is said that the person who enjoys greater honor sins with greater guilt, and that the exaltation of sinners produces more serious offenses.

If someone should say that the canons mentioned above concern others, not the pope, we prove that they are understood of the pope as well, as Saint Boniface, pope and martyr, proves in distinction 40, “If the pope.” There it is said that if the pope is wicked, even though he drags many peoples along with him, he himself will nevertheless be tormented perpetually with the devil in hell.

Pope Symmachus proves the same in 9, question 3, chapter “Of other men,” where it is said that he will have no assistance before God from the splendor of his defense, since he will use his own deeds as both witness and judge. It is added that to whom more is entrusted, more is demanded.

The reason is that, as the gloss on the Psalter says concerning the psalm beginning “The hungry,” and so forth, the pope’s vicious life is an image of future death, as is proved in 19, distinction 1, chapter “Anastasius.”

Once it has been proved that the pope can sin, the question is to whom he ought to confess. Some think that he should confess to no one but God, as the Greeks do, as is proved in *On Penance*, distinction 1, final chapter.

Others think that he ought to confess to the bishop of Ostia, who consecrates him. In this respect the bishop appears to be greater, as is proved in distinction 33, chapter “Our Lord,” where it is said that the one who ordains is greater than the one who is ordained.

Others think that he ought to confess to the cardinals by whom he is elected, especially to the bishops, who at the election of the lord pope exercise metropolitan rights, as is proved in distinction 23, “In the Name of the Lord,” where it is said: “The cardinal bishops undoubtedly exercise metropolitan authority, since they raise the elected man to the summit of dignity.”

Others say that he ought to confess to a monk, because Pope Silverius renounced the papacy and was a monk.

But hold most firmly, and do not doubt at all, that he may confess to whomever he wishes. Since he himself grants indulgence to all exempt persons so that they may choose suitable confessors, he will grant it to himself, since there is no superior from whom he can ask. This is proved in distinction 30, “If the Romans,” where it is said that if the pope grants authority to others, much more does he grant it to himself.

That this jurisdiction is voluntary—that is, that the pope may submit himself to the jurisdiction of an inferior—is proved in 2, question 5, “By commands,” and in the chapter “It has been heard,” and in 2, question 7, chapter “With Balaam.” These say that Sixtus, Leo, Damasus, and Symmachus submitted themselves to the judgment of inferiors in a contentious dispute; much more, therefore, may he do so in the penitential forum.

For, insofar as this matter is concerned, every priest occupies the place of the living God and can absolve the penitent in God’s place; in this respect he is the greater, as is proved in 2, question 3, chapter, and so forth.

The section on the pope ends here.

## On the penance of cardinals and to whom they ought to confess

*(From chapter 2.)*

[Col. 1091A]

The question is raised concerning the penance of cardinals. Say that the greater they are, the more severely they ought to be punished if they sin, following the example of Adam, who sinned the more because he was nearer to God, as Saint Augustine proves.

Adam therefore sinned more because he abounded more in virtues. Since cardinals are closer to the pope, they ought to fear a fall all the more, as Saint Gregory proves in his commentary on Ezekiel concerning the cause of Lucifer: “The beginning of the ways of God,” he says, “is Behemoth.”

They ought to be pure like glass, white in conduct, and red through remembrance of Christ’s Passion, like snow and ancient ivory. They ought to be clouds of heaven, bringing spiritual waters, as Isaiah proves when he says:

[Col. 1091B]

“Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?”

They are called doves because of their simplicity. They ought to be whiter than snow, redder than ancient ivory, and purer than glass. This was said of them because of their various virtues.

Cardinals are the doors of the holy Church, just as a door is governed by hinges. If the hinge is broken—that is, if a cardinal is deposed—as Pope Leo proves, it is never read that it was restored thereafter, just as he speaks of the angel who fell and was never recalled to his former state, as is proved in *On Penance*, distinction 2, “The Beginning.”

Therefore they ought to guard themselves from sins with all the greater care, lest they be Dagons standing beside the ark of the Lord, as is read in the Book of Kings concerning the sons of Eli.

In distinction 28, “Let the bishops read,” they are warned not to be clouds and mists without water, driven about by the whirlwinds of demons, as blessed Peter proves in his Epistle and Jerome in his canon on *Penance*, distinction “If, he says,” and so forth. Bede proves the same in 2, question 7, “They followed the way of Balaam.”
