Thus not only are bishops destroyed, but they lead many peoples and clergy with them in a crowd to hell, as in distinction 40, “If the pope,” and distinction 19, “No one may.”

They must not be seized by pride, because it is the mother of all vices; they must not be seized by vainglory, because it empties every virtue; they must not be seized by money, because it is to be fled like poison; they must not be seized by love of relatives, who consume them during life like dying flies and despise them after death, saying, “He did well by me, but he could have done better.” Let us say nothing of the other carnal vices, but let them cease neither day nor night from devoting themselves to the virtues.

All these matters are proved by the authority of Isaiah in distinction 23, “To these,” and by the authority of Ambrose in 12, question 1, chapter “He whose portion is God,” and in distinction 86, “It is not enough.”

Having considered the penance of cardinals, we must now see to whom they ought to confess. They ought specifically to confess to the supreme pontiff, without whose permission they cannot make an alteration or draw up a will. This is not proved by written law but is confirmed by custom.

Others say that a cardinal deacon ought to confess to a cardinal presbyter, a cardinal presbyter to a cardinal bishop, and cardinal bishops to the supreme pontiff, and so forth.

A third group says that they ought to confess to the lord pope’s principal penitentiary, because he acts as the pope’s representative, as is proved in distinction 23, final chapter, and distinction 23, chapter 1.

But hold most firmly that, if a cardinal is absent on some legation, he may confess to whomever he wishes, according to the decretal in *Extra*, *On Penance*, final chapter.

If he is present, however, and the sin is notorious or manifest, he ought to confess to the pope and ought to be punished more severely than another sinner because of the pernicious examples, as Nicholas and Gregory prove in 2, question 3, especially.

But if the sin is hidden, it is sufficient for him to confess to the principal penitentiary.

## On the penance of the pope’s chaplains and to whom they ought to confess

*(From chapter 3.)*

The chaplains and other members of the pope’s court ought to confess to the principal penitentiary, because they cannot be absolved or bound by anyone except the pope himself or someone acting under his mandate, since they reside at the church. Anyone who thinks otherwise is a brute, as is proved in *On Penance*, distinction 6, “It has pleased,” and in 6, question 3, chapter 1.

## On the penance of patriarchs and to whom they ought to confess

*(From chapter 4.)*
## On the Penance of the Patriarch, and to Whom He Ought to Confess

In speaking of the penance of a patriarch, and to whom he ought to confess, one must first distinguish whether the patriarch’s crime is public or hidden. If it is public, notorious, or manifest, he ought to be punished more severely than other offenders because of the pernicious examples that they transmit to posterity; for prelates are worthy of as many deaths as the pernicious examples they transmit to posterity, as the holy Fathers prove, 2, q. 3, because what is done by prelates is easily imitated by their subjects as an example. [Col. 1092C] In that case they ought to be punished by the pope alone, as blessed Gregory says concerning Clementius the primate, 2, q. 7, c. *Sicut*, where he says so.

Thus Innocent III punished the patriarch of Antioch because he reduced an archbishop to the rank of a non-archbishop and made him a bishop. Likewise, Gelasius and Felix condemned Acacius, patriarch of Constantinople, 23, q. 1, *Acacius*, and c. *Minores*. Likewise, Pope Nicholas corrected the patriarch of Bourges because he judged the clerics of the bishop of Narbonne contrary to the canons. This is proved at 2, q. 3, c. *Conquestus*. Likewise, Leo the Great repeatedly rebuked Dioscorus, patriarch of Alexandria, because he did not observe the canons concerning the times for ordaining clerics, 75 dist., c. *Similiter*. [Col. 1092D] Likewise, Alexander III rebuked the patriarch of Jerusalem for the falsehood he committed by placing the names of absent brothers in privileges. Likewise, Gregory XI rebuked the patriarch of Grado because he had exacted an oath from the bishop of Castello contrary to the canons.

Confession and punishment for such and similar sins therefore belong to the lord pope. But if the sins are hidden and not enormous, so that after completing his penance he may remain in his order, he may choose a confessor for himself and confess to whomever he wishes, and so forth.

## On the Confession of Archbishops, and to Whom They Ought to Confess  
*(From chapter 5)*

[Col. 1093A] In speaking of the confession of archbishops, and to whom they ought to confess, a multiple distinction first presents itself: namely, whether the archbishop is subject to a patriarch, or whether he belongs immediately to the lord pope. Also, if he belongs to a patriarch and is nearby, he ought to confess to that patriarch, since he could do so without danger.

For one who is healthy ought not to remain in sin for even one hour of the day, as is proved in *On Penance*, distinction [uncertain reference], c. *Et veniet*, where it says: “Moses will come.” The same is proved in *On Penance*, distinction 3, c. *Ille*. King David, though so great and powerful, did not allow the consciousness of sin to remain within him even for a brief moment; rather, through prompt confession and heartfelt sorrow, he returned his sin to the Lord.

The same is likewise proved in *On Penance*, distinction 3, c. *Septies in die cadit justus et resurgit*: “Seven times a day the righteous person falls and rises again.” But if the righteous person falls, how is he righteous? [Col. 1093B] The designation “righteous” does not exclude the one who always rises again through penance.

A prelate ought in no way to judge others while he has within himself something for which he should be condemned, as is proved at 3, q. 7, c. *Judicet ille*, and c. *In gravibus*, and c. *Postulatus Dominus*. Gregory proves the same, [reference uncertain], q. 3, c. *Plerumque*; and Augustine proves the same in *On Penance*, distinction 6, *Qui vult confiteri*.

This is to be understood not only of an archbishop but of every other prelate, whether superior or inferior. For, as Ambrose says, “When those who are sent to intercede are displeasing, the angry mind is provoked to worse things,” as is proved at 3, q. 7, c. *In gravibus*. Gregory the Great proves the same in his *Pastoral Rule*, distinction 49, c. 1.

[Col. 1093C] But if the metropolitan is ill, then he may confess to whatever priest he wishes, provided that the priest is Catholic. This is proved at 26, q. 6, c. *Si presbyter*, and in *On Penance*, distinction 6, *Qui vult confiteri*.

If the metropolitan is far removed from the primate, distinguish in that case whether the crime is notorious or hidden. If it is notorious, he ought to confess to the patriarch and be corrected by him, as is proved at 3, q. 5. But if the crime is hidden, distinguish further whether it is enormous or not. If it is enormous, because it requires dispensation, he ought to confess to the patriarch or to the supreme pontiff, since no one else can dispense, as is proved at 21, *Inferior sedes*. But if it does not require dispensation, he may confess to whomever he wishes, provided that the person is a Catholic priest. This accords with the decretal *On Penance and Remission*, chapter [reference], and [another] chapter.

If he belongs immediately to the lord pope and is nearby, or within Italy, and is in good health, he ought to have confessed to him, [Col. 1093D] since he is required by necessity to visit the Roman Church once a year, as is proved at 23 dist., c. and c.

But if he is ill, he may confess to whomever he wishes, provided that the person is a Catholic priest, lest, if even a little delay intervenes, no one who can redeem him be found. This is proved at 5 dist., c. *Baptizari*. Pope Leo proves the same in *On Penance*, distinction [reference], c. 1, *Multiplex*; 26, q. 6, c. *Qui recedunt*, and c. *Is qui in tempore*.

But if he is far away, beyond Italy, or if the matter is enormous, he ought to confess to the lord pope and be corrected by him, as Pope Innocent proves at 9, q. 2, c. *Si autem aliquis*. Gregory proves the same at 74 dist., c. *Honoratur*, and at 2, q. 5, *Quanto* and *Se, qua de causa*; and at 43 dist., c. *Salomitanae*. [Col. 1094A] Pope Simplicius proves the same at 74 dist., c. and c.

But if the sin is hidden and does not require dispensation, he may confess to whomever he wishes, by Gregory’s decretal *On Penance*, c. *Ne pro dilatione*, and by Innocent III’s decree at the general council, *On Elections*.

## On the Confession of Bishops, and to Whom They Ought to Confess  
*(From chapter 6)*

Concerning the confession of a bishop, hold this most firmly and do not doubt at all: an exempt bishop is under the same law as a metropolitan who is not subject to a patriarch. But if he is not exempt, he ought to confess to the metropolitan, at least when he comes to the provincial council, which ought to be held, as is proved at 18 dist., c. and c.

[Col. 1094B] But if he is ill or very far away, necessity compelling him, he may confess to whomever he wishes—unless the crime is notorious, the correction and punishment of which belong to his superior.

Although there are many offenses that lead bishops, archbishops, and the greater patriarchs and lesser primates to disgrace and shame, let us nevertheless briefly reduce a few of them, according to the authority of the holy Fathers, to serve as a reminder, so that those who have offended may be corrected and those of the future may already be cautious and instructed to fear committing similar acts.

The first is that they confer benefices indiscriminately upon relatives, led by carnal affection to bestow such benefices, as Innocent proves in *On Ecclesiastical Benefices*, c. *Ut vestrum*.

[Col. 1094C] The second is that they indiscriminately ordain an unlearned man in the place of a learned one, one who keeps one foot in worldly affairs and the other in ecclesiastical affairs, contrary to divine law, as is proved at [possibly “lege”] 48 dist., final chapter.

The third is when they knowingly intercede for the unworthy, and so forth.

The fourth is when they ordain bigamists, illiterate men, and those physically impaired, contrary to the judgment of Pope Gelasius, 50 dist., c. *Non confidat*.

The fifth is that they ordain men bound to the court, jesters, and advocates in cases involving bloodshed, contrary to the judgment of Saint Innocent, 51 dist., c. *Aliquantos*.

The sixth is that they ordain slaves and unmanumitted *originarii*, contrary to the judgment of Pope Gelasius, 54 dist., *Frequens*, and c. *Ex antiquis*, and c. *General*. [Col. 1094D] The Council of Arles proves the same concerning bigamists, solemn penitents, and other ordained persons who ought not to be promoted. This is proved at 51 dist., c. 1.

The seventh is that they promote demoniacs and epileptics, contrary to the judgment of Pope Gelasius, 23 dist., *Usque adeo*, and contrary to the judgment of Gregory, [reference], c. *Maritum*.

The eighth is that they promote sons of priests and others born illegitimately, contrary to the judgment of Pope Urban, 56 dist., c. 1.

The ninth is that they draw religious men out of monasteries against the will of their abbots, as is proved at 58 dist., c. 1 and 2, and 18, q. 2, *Quam sit*, and c. *Luminoso*.

[Col. 1095A] The tenth is that they promote many clerics where there is a need for laymen; and when they cannot give them benefices, they give them orders, contrary to the judgment of Urban, 58 dist., *Si officia saecularia*, where it is said that the conferral of orders must always be governed by discerning judgment, because everything great is rare.

The eleventh is that the bishops themselves are indiscriminately promoted from among laymen, since this ought not to happen, as the holy Fathers prove at 58 dist., c. *Hoc ad nos*, and c. *Ordinatos*. There Pope Celestine says that they ought first to be disciples before being teachers, for every formation of life shapes itself toward that which it seeks.

The twelfth is that they promote clerics without a title, contrary to the Council of Chalcedon, as is proved at 70 dist., c. *Neminem*, and c. *Sanctorum*. The same is proved in *On Benefices*, c. *Episcop*.

[Col. 1095B] The thirteenth is that they receive clerics belonging to another bishop without letters of release from their own bishops, as is proved at 71 dist., c. *Illud*, and c. *Si quis*, and c. *De aliena*, and c. *Clericos*. The same is proved in *On Clerics from Abroad*, and at 7, q. 1, c. *Non oportet*, and c. *Placuit*. The same is proved at 28 dist., c. 1.

The fourteenth is that they neglect their own clerics and leave them like wandering sheep, contrary to the judgment of Pope Leo, as is proved at 77 dist., c. *Episcopus*.

[Col. 1095C] The fifteenth is that they promote certain unwilling men without any necessity, solely out of resentment, contrary to the authorities of the holy Fathers, as is proved at 74 dist., c. *Episcopus*, and c. *Gesta*, where it is said that no one is compelled to rise against his will.

The sixteenth is that they promote some men to sacred orders outside the appointed times, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved at 75 dist., c. *Ordinationes*, and c. *Quia patribus*, and in the same distinction, final chapter, and in *On the Time [of Ordination]*, and so forth.

The seventeenth is that they confer sacred orders upon minors who are unworthy by age, without observing the intervals between orders, contrary to the authority of the saints, as is proved throughout 77 dist. and throughout 78 dist.

The eighteenth is that they tolerate clerics in their wickedness, having been corrupted by their service, as is proved at 73 dist., *Si quis episcopus*, and c. *Error*, and c. *Consentire*.

[Col. 1095D] The nineteenth is that they are idle and negligent and cling more to the counsels of laymen than to those of clerics, as is proved at 83 dist., c. *Nihil pastore miserius*: “Nothing is more wretched than a shepherd who glories in the praises of wolves.”

The twentieth is that they refuse to give to the poor; and because of this they bear the name of bishop in vain, as at 26 dist., *Fratrem*, and c. *Non satis est bene velle*.

The twenty-first is that they negligently defend pitiable persons who belong to the forum of the Church—namely, wards, widows and orphans, freedmen and foundlings—contrary to the authority of Gelasius and the other saints, as is proved throughout 87 dist.

The twenty-second is that they involve themselves in secular affairs that do not belong to them, as is proved at 80 dist., c. *Perlatum est*, and c. *Episcopus tuitionem*, and c. *Episcopi nullam rei familiaris curam ad se provocent*: [Col. 1096A] “Let bishops not draw any concern for household affairs to themselves, but devote themselves only to reading, prayer, and the word of preaching.”

The twenty-third is that they confer several ecclesiastical benefices upon one person, contrary to the authority of the Apostle and Gregory, 88 dist., c. *Singula*. There it is said: “If the whole body were an eye, where would the foot be?” For the sacred diversity of the members preserves the strength of the body.

The twenty-fourth is that they refuse to have stewards under whose testimony the affairs of the Church may be administered, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved at 89 dist., c. *Volumus*; and if they do have stewards, they wish to have relatives, contrary to the Council of Toledo.

[Col. 1096B] The twenty-fifth is that bishops are hostile to one another, strive for one another’s downfall, and disagree in the sacraments, as at 93 dist., penultimate and final chapters.

The twenty-sixth is that they appropriate all ecclesiastical goods to themselves, as Saint Jerome proves at 23 dist., c. *Diaconi*. There it is said that, each one through the power of the episcopal name that he has illicitly claimed for himself without the Church, they apply everything belonging to the Levites to their own uses, saying:

“The wretched cleric begs in the streets, enslaved to servile work and asking alms from anyone. The bishop alone is concerned with the goods; he alone claims everything for himself; he alone seizes the portions of others; he alone kills everyone. This is the beginning of litigation and division, and the origin of crime.”

[Col. 1096C] And therefore they are accused by the clerics and condemned by the Lord Jesus Christ, because their cry enters the ears of the Lord of Hosts.

The twenty-seventh is that bishops despise priests; and when the bishops themselves are present, they do not permit the priests to perform their office, as though they envied them, contrary to the authority of Saint Jerome, as is proved at 95 dist., c. *Olim*. There it is said that bishops were made for this purpose: so that schisms might be removed.

You should say that, just as priests know themselves by custom to be subject to bishops, so bishops should know that they are greater than priests more by custom than by the truth of the Lord’s dispensation, and that together they ought to govern the Church of God. This is proved at 95 dist., c. *Ecce ergo*.

[Col. 1096D] The twenty-eighth is that they are ordained through money; such men receive leprosy and give leprosy, as is proved at 1, q. 1, c. *Cum ordinatur episcopus*, where it is said: “To receive is to receive anything, and to give is to give anything.” The same question, c. *Fertur*, says that good fruit cannot come from an infected root.

Therefore, if such a man wishes to be saved, let him renounce his office and perform severe penance; otherwise he cannot be saved, as Saint Gregory proves at 1, q. 1, c. *Si quis neque*.

The twenty-ninth is that they demand money for balsam, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, 1, q. 1, *Placuit ut nullus*, and c. *Dictum est*, and c. *Statuimus*.

The thirtieth is that they condemn clerics without investigation, as is proved at 2, q. 1, *Nos*, and so forth.

[Col. 1097A] The thirty-first is that they do not respect legitimate appeals, and therefore ought to have been punished, 2, q. 7, c. and so forth.

The thirty-second is that they are lay shepherds and not priests, such as they are inwardly, as at 2, q. 7, *Pervenit*.

The thirty-third is that they allow themselves to be promoted though insufficient, contrary to the Council of Carthage, as is proved at 23 dist., c. *Quod episcopi*. The same is proved at 38 dist., c. *Omnes psallentes*, where it is said that it belongs to the substance of a bishop that he be well educated.

Therefore the Prophet says: “You have rejected knowledge, and I will reject you, so that you may not serve as a priest.” For this reason a certain bishop was deposed by Pope Honorius.

[Col. 1097B] The thirty-fourth is that, after being promoted, they neglect to continue learning, contrary to the judgment of Gregory, 22 dist., where it is said that he is foolish who considers himself greater because he scorns to learn the good things he has heard.

The thirty-fifth is that they do not wish, or do not know how, to obey the canons. Therefore they ought to have been removed from administration until they had performed worthy penance, as Pope Damasus proves at 25, q. 1.

The thirty-sixth is that they are too credulous to the detriment of others, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as Gregory proves at 11, q. 3, c. *Grave nimis est et indecens*: “It is very serious and improper that, in a doubtful matter, a certain judgment should be pronounced.”

The same Father Gregory attests to the same at 32 dist., c. *Habuisse te concubinam*, where it is said that in a doubtful matter an absolute judgment ought not to be rendered.

[Col. 1097C] Augustine likewise proves the same at 11, q. 3, where it is said that although certain things may be true, they ought not to be believed judicially unless they are demonstrated by certain judgments. Pope Sixtus and Pope Victor prove the same at 30, q. 5, c.

The thirty-seventh is that they do not wish to raise as pillars in the Church those whom they know to be better, but rather those whom they themselves love more or whose services they prefer, contrary to the sacred canons, 8, q. 1, c. *Moyses*, and 12, q. 2, *Gloria episcopi*, where it is said that many build walls but remove the pillars of the Church. Hence hatreds often arise.

[Col. 1097D] The thirty-eighth is that they usurp ecclesiastical goods, especially those of parish churches, every year, appropriating more and more to themselves; yet they ought not to presume anything from parish churches except what the canon permits them, as the Council of Toledo proves at 10, q. 3, c. *Quod cognovimus*. Among other things, this is also proved at 16, q. 1, c. *Constitutum est nulli*.

The thirty-ninth is that they indiscriminately avenge their own injuries, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved at 5, q. 7, c. *Si quis communem traditionem*, and 46 dist., c. *Seditionarios*, and so forth. On their account they indiscriminately inflict injuries and excommunicate, as is proved at 23, q. 4, *Inter querelas*. Therefore such men possess nothing spiritual.

[Col. 1098A] The fortieth is that, when angered, they easily excommunicate the innocent and the guilty for minor matters, even when they are prepared to be corrected, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, 2, q. 3, *Episcopi*, where it is said that no one ought to be excommunicated except for grave sins and when he cannot otherwise be corrected.

The forty-first is that, in their own cases, they wish to be both judges and parties, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as at 2, q. 1, where it is said that when the role of plaintiff is assumed, judicial power is admitted. The same is proved at 3, q. 4, c. 1 and 2.

The forty-second is that they expel those who have faithfully grown old in service with their predecessors, as at 6, q. 2, c. *Hujus placiti*. And what is worse, they strip them of the reward for their service that the preceding bishops gave them, contrary to the authority of Pope Gelasius, 16, q. 6, c. *Illud*.

[Col. 1098B] The forty-third is that they wish to keep promises concerning rewards for learned or serving men, contrary to the authority of the saints, 22, c. *Quicunque*.

The forty-fourth is that they wish to be believed to the detriment of others, which ought not to happen, as is proved at 6, q. 2, *Episcopus si clerico*, and c. *Si tamen episcopus*, and c. *Placuit*, 25, q. 5, c. 2.

The forty-fifth is that they alone wish to depose clerics, contrary to the sacred canons. For at the deposition of a priest six bishops and his own bishop as the seventh ought to be present; and in the case of a deacon and subdeacon, three bishops together with his own bishop, as is proved by these laws: 1 dist., c. *Studeat*, and 15, q. 1, c. *De crimine*, and 15, q. 7, c. *Felix*, and so forth.

[Col. 1098C] The forty-sixth is that they attack exempt persons, as the holy Fathers prove at 16, q. 1, and elsewhere.

The forty-seventh is that they bind and loose indiscriminately, which ought not to happen. For this reason they are suspended for up to thirty days, as the holy Fathers prove at 23, q. 3, c. *De illicita*, and in *On the Sentence of Excommunication*. For just as they exalt some through the favor of partiality, so they humble others through hatred and envy. This is proved at 15, q. 7, c. 1, and elsewhere.

The forty-eighth is that at banquets they do not have sacred reading recited. In this they sin against the Council of Toledo, 44 dist., c. *Pro reverentia*. The reason is that, while the body is refreshed by various dishes, the tongue is loosened into detraction, as Gregory proves in the first book of his *Moralia*.

[Col. 1098D] The forty-ninth is that they do not care about the divine offices because of their banquets, contrary to Gregory’s authority, 44 dist.; and they have Mass sung beside the bed in a house where there are many impurities, thereby provoking divine patience to anger. For Mass ought never to be celebrated in a house.

This is proved in *On Consecration*, distinction 1, c. *Sicut non alibi*, where it is said: “It is holier not to sing Mass than to sing it in places where it ought not to be performed.” At the end of the chapter it adds that Mass ought in no way to be celebrated in houses.

The fiftieth is that they do not preserve the goods of the Church, contrary to the authority of the canon, 16, q. 1, c. [reference], and they squander [Col. 1099A] those same ecclesiastical goods through themselves and their associates, contrary to the authority of the Fathers, 28 dist., c. *Etsi se non corrigunt*. They ought to be deposed, as at 12, q. [reference], c. *Apostolicas*. And because they usurp the property of others, this is proved at 16, q. 6, c. *Placuit*.

The fifty-first and final matter is that they glory in their seats and do not know themselves. For if they had known themselves, they would not have despised their lesser subjects. This is proved at 12, q. 2, c. *Gloria episcopi*, and elsewhere.

If the bishops had attended to this, they would not have permitted lesser priests to sit beside the footstool of their feet, as the Council of Carthage proves. The reason is that, as blessed Gregory testifies, “When there is no fault, we are all equal according to the measure of humility,” as is proved at 22 dist., c. [reference].

[Col. 1099B] Such and similar matters, if they are notorious, so that they could not have been committed without great scandal, must be confessed to the metropolitan, and indulgence must be sought from him, so that the medicine of penance may be effective, as is proved at distinction 1, c. and c.

But if the crime is not known and there is no scandal concerning it, and in other bodily sins—except simony and homicide—they may choose a discreet priest for themselves as confessor. This is proved in *On Penance*, and elsewhere.

These things have been said for the honor of bishops, not in order to rebuke them but to admonish them. Some are holy, but let each person examine his own conscience.

Here ends the section on bishops.

## On the Confession of Abbots, and to Whom They Ought to Confess  
*(From chapter 7)*

[Col. 1099C] Concerning the confession of abbots, distinguish as follows. Either the abbot is exempt and has no other greater exempt abbot over him, or he does not.

If he is in the Roman Curia, he ought to confess to the lord pope or to his general penitentiary, as was said concerning the archbishop. But if he is far from the Roman Church, he may confess to whomever he wishes, provided that the priest is faithful and discreet, as is proved in *On Penance*, final chapter.

But if he has another greater abbot over him, whether that abbot is exempt or not, he ought to confess to him. If he has no other abbot over him and he himself is not exempt, he ought to confess to his own bishop, because the bishop is his prelate, as is proved at 41 dist., c. *Obitum*, and 12 dist., final chapter; or, with the bishop’s permission, he may choose a confessor for himself, as is proved in *On Penance and Remission*, and in *On Penance*, distinction 16, c. *Placuit*.

For otherwise he cannot be bound or loosed, according to the aforesaid laws, [Col. 1099D] unless perhaps there were a contrary rule approved by the supreme pontiff, as the Cistercian brothers have: according to their rule, they appoint a confessor for themselves.

Although there are many vices of abbots that could be counted, let us briefly touch upon a few of them, so that more secure precaution may be prepared for those of the future.

The first principal vice is that, in order to become abbots, they assume the monastic rule, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved at 16, q. 7, c. *Per laicos*, where it is said that no one should take the habit while having the hope or promise of becoming abbot. For such men do not intend to flee the world but to change it, as is proved at 53 [dist.].

[Col. 1100A] There is also a second principal vice: they hold five abbacies through simony. Such men cannot remain in administration, as is proved in *On Simony*, c. *Pervenit*. If they are accused, they ought rightly to be deposed, *On Simony*, *Dilectus filius*. Otherwise they are punished at the discretion of the judge, as in *On Simony*.

There is a fourth mortal vice, although not as great as one of those mentioned above: they neglect their fugitive monks, as is proved at 18, q. 2, *Abbates*, and in *On the Rule*, c. *Ne religiosi*.

There is a fifth vice: they receive foreign monks without letters of recommendation, as is proved at 28, q. 2.

There is a sixth vice: they indiscriminately expel their monks, as in *On the Rule*, final chapter.

[Col. 1100B] There is a seventh vice: they issue letters of release indiscriminately and believe that monks or regulars are by such letters absolved from their first obedience, unless they have first been received by that abbot through letters of release, as is proved at 71 dist., *Illud quoque*, and c. *De aliena*, and c. *Clericos*. The same is proved at 7, q. 1, c. *Non oportet*, and c. *Pervenit*, and at 21, q. 2, c. and 2.

For Pope Leo says that letters of release ought not to be issued unless it is first clear why they are being issued, lest the lost sheep be found without a shepherd, as at 72 dist., c. *Episcopus*.

The eighth vice is that, after a monk resists their vices, they punish him.

There is also a ninth vice: [Col. 1100C] if someone appeals on this account to a judgment, they immediately beat him, excommunicate him, or seize him, although the abbots ought to be punished for this.

The tenth vice is that abbots exalt certain monks out of carnal affection and depress others out of hatred and envy, as is proved at 15, q. 7, c. 1.

There is an eleventh vice: under the appearance of piety they conceal impiety. For example, on the pretext of hospitality they eat meat inadequately outside the refectory, do not come to Matins or to the Office, and the monks die of hunger while bearing the burden of the day’s duties and heat.

There is a twelfth vice: they permit certain monks to have money, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved in *On the State of a Monk*.

[Col. 1100D] There is a thirteenth vice: they do not fear usurping episcopal rights, as is proved at 16, q. 1, c. *Pervenit*.

If these matters are notorious, they ought to be confessed to the bishop. Other matters—leaving aside a fall of the flesh—if they are secret, may be confessed to one’s own confessor, according to the distinction noted above.

## On the Confession of Monks, and to Whom They Ought to Confess  
*(From chapter 8)*

It was said above concerning monks and their confessions; now it must be explained more fully to whom they ought to confess. It must be held that they ought to confess to their own abbot, who ought to know their oppositions [Col. 1101A] and what they are inwardly, as in [the decretal], because their abbot has charge of their willing and unwilling, whom they have placed over their heads in the place of God, as is proved at 12, 1, c. *Nolo*, and c. *Non dicatis*, and 13 dist., c. *Nervi testiculorum*.

It is evident that they ought to confess to the abbot in the place of God. Although there are many vices of monks, there are nevertheless certain principal ones from which they ought to abstain, which the holy Fathers detest exceedingly.

The first is that they conspire against the abbot if he attempts to correct them, wish to depose him, and make another who can foster their foolishness, as is proved at 18, q. 2, c. [reference], where it is said that no authority would remain with the abbot if he began to be subject to the monks.

The second vice is that they also conspire in order to kill, like those who conspired to kill Saint Benedict; [Col. 1101B] such men are infamous, as is proved at 11, q. 1, c. *Conspirationum*.

The third vice is that they have imprudent familiarity with women, whom they make their “co-mothers” (*commatres*), contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, and so forth.

The fourth vice is that they associate carelessly with nuns, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, 18, q. 2, c. *Monasteria*.

The fifth vice is that they are not ashamed to contract marriage, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is clear at 27, q. 1, c. *Ut lex continet*, and c. *Impudicus*.

[Col. 1101C] The sixth vice is that they wish to wander outside the monastery without the abbot’s permission, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved at 16, q. 1, c. *Cum quidam monachi*.

The seventh vice is that they wish to be idle, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, because idleness and pleasure are the weapons of the ancient enemy, as is proved in *On Renunciation*, and elsewhere.

The eighth vice is that, while healthy and without any necessity, they wish to eat meat, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved in *On Consecration*, distinction 5, c. *Carnem*, where a penance of six months is imposed upon them.

[Col. 1101D] The ninth vice is that they wish to dominate their companions, saying that they are noble and learned, which is very far from the monastic rule, as is proved in *On the State of Religious Life*, c. [reference].

The tenth vice is that they wish to have separate cells and to practice abstinence contrary to the common rule, as is proved at 20, q. 4, c. *Monachis*.

The eleventh vice is that they wish to possess personal property, which is in no way permitted to them. At death they ought to be buried in a dung heap, as is proved in *On the State of Religious Life*, c. *Monachi*.

The twelfth vice, and the more serious one, is that monks slander one another so that they may bring one another down; and thus they are spiritual murderers.

Monks ought therefore to avoid these and similar things. If they fall into them or into any of the matters mentioned above, they ought to confess to the abbot or to someone acting in his place, and they ought to be punished more severely. [Col. 1102A]

But if these matters were hidden, gather the life of monks from these verses:

> As you enter the cloister, remember to meditate on sacred things.  
> Carry nothing mortal, but always be sober.  
> Count nothing as accomplished if, at the time of the vow,  
> It proves deadly—the thing that removes the rewards of the vow.  
> Perhaps it does no good to strive if you relapse.

## On the Penance of the Dean  
*(From chapter 9)*

Concerning the penance of the dean, hold this: although the archdeacon is, according to the common law, greater after the bishop, as is proved in *On Appeals*, c. *Constitutis*, nevertheless he ought to confess to the bishop, or with the bishop’s permission choose another confessor for himself, even if the archdeacon were a priest.

[Col. 1102B] Deans sin gravely in these three matters.

First, because they are hostile to their bishops, and so forth.

Second, because they wish to be promoted to the priesthood, although they themselves ought to be priests, and so forth.

Third, because they are very proud and trample upon others, both simple and learned. Hence hatred often arises today, and homicides are committed; these require no proof from the law, because they have very often been established as matters of fact.

If they have sinned in such things or in other similar matters, leaving aside sins of the flesh, then if the matter is notorious they ought to be corrected by the bishop and perform suitable penance. But if it is hidden, they ought to repent and confess to the bishop or to someone acting in his place, as is proved in *On Penance*, distinction 1, c. [reference].

## On the Penance of the Archdeacon, and to Whom He Ought to Confess  
*(From chapter 10)*

[Col. 1102C]

Concerning the penance of the archdeacon, hold this: according to the common law he ought to confess to his bishop, since the bishop is his superior.

Archdeacons sin especially in these six matters.

First, because they wish to impose collections upon priests, contrary to the authority of the saints, as is proved at 24 dist., final chapter.

Second, because they wish to have money or a white cow for the investiture of churches or benefices, or for installing abbots or abbesses in office, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, and so forth.

Third, when they excommunicate someone for an offense, they do not wish to absolve him without money. [Col. 1102D] This is simoniacal, as is proved at 1, q. 1, c. *Quilibet ergo*, and c. *Nullus episcopus*.

Fourth, because they sell their jurisdiction to others, who extort money from priests through injury and simoniacal depravity, as is proved in *Not to Delegate the Duties of Prelates*, c. *Praeterea*, and c. *Cum*.

Fifth, because they do not wish to be promoted to the diaconal order, contrary to the Lateran Council, in *On Elections*, and elsewhere.

Sixth—and this disfigures their good character—because they associate with women, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved at 81 dist., c. *Archidiaconatuum*, and c. *Clericus solus*, where it is said that, under the pretext of humility, an archdeacon ought not to frequent the homes of married women.

They ought therefore to abstain from such and similar things; and if they have sinned, they ought to make satisfaction to the Creator through humble and discerning penance.

[Col. 1103A]

## On the Confession of Archpriests  
*(From chapter 11)*

The office of archpriests is twofold. Some are archpriests of cathedral churches; these ought to confess to the bishop, especially if they have no one greater over them, since according to the common law they perform the duties of an absent bishop in singing Masses and reciting collects, as is proved at 25 dist., c. [reference], and in *On the Office of an Archpriest*.

They sin especially in this: they are negligent in caring for cardinal priests, including the imposition of penances upon both clerics and laymen. [Col. 1103B] To say nothing of other matters, they deny justice and issue judgments in exchange for money; when the hope of money is removed from them, they immediately depart from the path of justice, as Saint Gregory testifies and as is proved at 11, q. 3.

Such and similar excesses, if they are publicly notorious, ought to be confessed to the bishop and punished by him. Otherwise, with the bishop’s permission, they may choose a discreet confessor for themselves; this is also proved in *On Penance*, distinction 6, final chapter.

There are other archpriests in rural areas, whom some call deans, sometimes parish priests, and sometimes abbots, although improperly. That they are called deans is established in *On the Office of an Ordinary*. That they are called abbots is established in *On Renunciation*. That they are called parish priests is established in *On the Office of an Ordinary*, and c. [reference].

Such men ought to confess to the bishop, and to another person with the bishop’s permission. [Col. 1103C] Yet they sin especially in this: they are negligent in correcting priests who reside in their parish under lesser titles, whose life and condition they ought to report to the bishop or archdeacons, as is proved in *On the Office of an Archdeacon*.

## On the Confession of the Treasurer, Chamberlain, or Sacristan  
*(From chapter 12)*
The treasurer or sacristan—though the names are different, the office is the same—must confess to his own bishop, or, with the bishop’s permission, choose another prudent confessor. Their principal fault in this matter is that they negligently perform their duty concerning the custody of the sacred vessels or ecclesiastical vestments, because they have the vessels or vestments handled, and handled dishonorably, by laymen or minor clerics, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved in Distinction 23, chapters *Non liceat* and *Non oportet*. They also sin concerning the church lights, the appointment of the doorkeeper, the preparation of incense, and the care of the baptistery, as is proved in Distinction 25, chapter, and so forth. Such matters and similar ones, if they are burdened by public infamy, they must confess to the bishop; otherwise, with his permission, they may choose a prudent confessor.

## On the penance of the provost, and to whom he ought to confess  
*(From chapter 13.)*

The provost is correctly so called because he has charge over others. If he is a religious, he must confess to his superior and be corrected by him, as is proved in *Extra*, “On Appeals,” and *Extra*, “On Right.” If he is not a religious, he must confess to his superior or to another with his superior’s permission.

## On the penance of the master of schools, and to whom he ought to confess  
*(From chapter 14.)*

The master of schools must confess to the bishop, to whom he is immediately subject. They sin especially in various ways. First, because they sell licenses to teach, as is proved in *Extra*, “On Masters.” Second, because they deny a license to those who deserve it. If such men were directly accused, they ought to be removed from their office permanently, as is proved in 1, question 7, and elsewhere. They also sin—and gravely—in allowing the untrained and ignorant, who could examine others, to be elevated to such an office. Likewise, when they are conspirators against their own bishops, as is proved in *Extra*, “On Calumny.” They sin in the very knowledge in which they ask that licenses be granted to them. For such men, promoted in this ambitious manner, will be cruelly punished by the devil. “The mighty will suffer mighty torments”; a person ought to measure himself against the office he desires to attain, and, if he is inferior, desist; but if he is equal to it, let him approach with fear. Such matters and similar ones, if he is burdened by infamy on their account, he must confess to the bishop if he wishes to be saved; otherwise, with his bishop’s permission, he may choose a prudent confessor.

## On the penance of the cantor, and to whom he ought to confess  
*(From chapter 15.)*

[Col. 1104C] The cantor must confess to the bishop to whom he is known to be immediately subject, or, with his permission, choose a prudent confessor. The cantor sins especially in this matter, to say nothing of others: he admits into the choir those who are unworthy, who neither know how to read nor to sing, and sometimes rejects those who are worthy. This can be established more by custom than by law. They also sin for another reason: they grant certain persons, out of favor, daily meals, although those persons negligently perform their ecclesiastical office, while they withhold them from others because they were unable conveniently to attend the office.

## On the penance of canons, and to whom they ought to confess  
*(From chapter 16.)*

Concerning the penance of canons, hold this most firmly and do not doubt at all: by common law they ought to have confessed to the dean, or to the bishop, or to some provost of the church, if he were a priest; or at least they ought to have asked the bishop’s permission to confess to others, or to establish a general penance for themselves. The aforesaid canons seriously offend in these four matters, to say nothing of others.

First, because in a time of necessity they wish to be promoted to sacred orders, as is proved in Distinction 74, chapters *Si quis clerici* and *Placuit*.

Second, because some of them, through ambition, succeed to the place of a living man; and therefore they are perpetually infamous. *Extra*, “On Benefices,” and elsewhere.

Third, because they are excessively delicate and wish to attend offices. Therefore they ought to have been suspended from their prebends until correction, though only after a warning had been given, as is proved in *Extra*, “On Clerics.”

Fourth, because they accumulate money from their prebends and refuse to distribute it to the poor, contrary to the sacred canons, as is proved in 7, question 1, final chapter. For where the canons of a cathedral church live badly, the entire city hangs head downward, and the whole condition of the city is thrown into disorder, especially because they refuse to obey their superior.

If, therefore, they have offended in the matters mentioned, or in any one of them, whether in lesser or greater matters, then, if they wish to be saved, by true penance they must satisfy their creditor, who always awaits their return, as is proved in Distinction 93, chapter *Diaconi*.

## On the penance of doctors and masters, and to whom they ought to confess  
*(From chapter 17.)*

[Col. 1105B] Doctors, if they are residenters (*inquilini*), must do penance before the priest in whose parish they live, or, with his permission, choose a confessor. But if they are *castrenses* [belonging to a court or household], they must confess to their prelate, in whose parish they live, or to someone in his place, since no other person can loose or bind them, as is proved in 8, part 2, chapters 1, 2, and 3. Understand this with the qualification that a superior can always absolve; his authority is understood as excepted.

Doctors, and especially doctors of canon law, seriously offend the Lord in many ways.

First, because they are not worthy of the mastership and arrange to be promoted to it through money, sordid entreaties, fraudulent little gifts, or otherwise unworthily.

Second, because they despise their subjects who occupy the chairs. Such men do injury to the chair, since they sit badly upon it, like Dagon upon the ark of the Lord. Hence there are many priests, but few priests.

Third, because they despise well-behaved simple people, who have preferred to renounce moral vices rather than verbal ones. As in Distinction 39, chapter *Sedulo*, they involve themselves in certain questions and subtleties in order to appear to know much, and thus confuse their hearers for their own ostentation, not for the benefit of their students.

Fourth, because they teach in the chairs whatever may please. These are the doctors of whom the Council of Constantinople says: “The doctrine of evil doctors is evil.” 1, question 7, chapter *Convenientibus*.

Fifth, because, although they themselves live badly, they dare to criticize such things, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, and so forth.

## On the confession of advocates, and to whom they ought to confess  
*(From chapter 18.)*

Advocates must confess to their own priest, or, with the permission of their own priest, to another who is more discerning; otherwise they cannot be absolved or bound by another. It would be very difficult to recount all the excesses of advocates. Nevertheless, I, John of God, an ancient doctor of Decretals, will mention a few and report them to posterity as things to be avoided.

First and chiefly, advocates sin because they deceitfully assist the adversary, thereby destroying their own client. Such men are traitors and infamous, as is proved in 2, question 3, and elsewhere.

Second, because they knowingly defend bad causes, contrary to the authority of the holy Fathers, as is proved in 11, question 3.

Third, because under the appearance of piety they conceal impiety by prolonging their client’s cases.

Fourth, they sin because, where there are no other advocates, they accept a large fee, to the serious detriment of the litigant. For this reason they ought to be removed from advocacy.

Fifth, they sin because, when they do not know the law, they disparage the advocates of the opposing party, as is proved in 3, question 7.

Sixth, they sin and are like murderers when they make their clients and witnesses utter disgraceful statements against the opposing party.

These are the principal matters about which a confessor ought to question them. If advocates wish to be saved, they must make satisfaction to those whom they have harmed, and through true penance satisfy their Creator.

## On the penance of the legal expert, and to whom he ought to confess  
*(From chapter 19.)*

A legal expert is one who resolves questions proposed concerning legal experts. Understand, therefore, that the same law applies as in the case of advocates: namely, that they must return what they wrongfully acquired, confess to their own priest, and, following his counsel, satisfy their Creator.

## On the penance of priests, and to whom they ought to confess  
*(From chapter 20.)*

Although the penance of priests has been discussed above, some matters remain, which I shall briefly set forth. A priest must confess to his superior; and lesser priests, under a prelate, may confess to one another with the prelate’s permission, or, if they wish, to the bishop. Although the wickedness of clerics, especially priests, is so great that it could scarcely be contained within a number, let us nevertheless briefly recall a few vices, for their correction and caution.

First, they sin because they allow the unworthy to be promoted to ecclesiastical offices, contrary to the ecclesiastical canons.

Second, because they are sometimes promoted through simoniacal depravity.

Third, because they live with extreme incontinence.

Fourth, because they involve themselves in spectacles and the pageants of women, receive gifts, and engage in usury; because they love the hair of laymen more than the tonsures of clerics; because they involve themselves in commerce; because they frequent the homes of widowed women; because they keep women in their households whom the canons forbid them to keep; because they frequent taverns and games of dice and hazard; because they refuse to attend the divine offices; because they love woodland and field hunts; and because, at the peril of their souls and to the scandal of many, contrary to ecclesiastical ordinances, they give more freely to hunters, prostitutes, or jesters than to the poor from the patrimony of the Crucified.

Fifth, because prelates envy their subjects, and subjects their prelate, although they ought to love one another, so that charity might be established between prelates and subjects.

Sixth, because they conceal many vices under the appearance of virtue. For although they are avaricious, they wish to appear temperate; and although they are cruel, they wish to appear compassionate.

Seventh, because the subjects themselves consume one another; and therefore they are murderers, and worse than robbers.

Eighth, because they are extremely fickle, uttering dishonorable and useless words.

Ninth, because they sin in sacrifices when they offer a broken host, or wine without water, or water without wine; when they celebrate twice in one day; when they fail to guard the chrism or Eucharist as they ought; or when they do not properly clean the vessels, altars, and vestments according to the canons.

Tenth, because they overthrow others and, in every place, as Jerome testifies, lay stumbling blocks and become a twisted snare.

These matters and similar ones, to say nothing of others, clerics must confess and henceforth avoid, unless they wish to be tormented forever with the devil. Here ends the section on priests.

## Solution to objections  
*(From chapter 21.)*

Perhaps someone might say: What does this mean—that Master John of God has listed certain vices committed by both subjects and prelates? To this I, John of God, reply: You, priest, who hear confessions in God’s place, ought to use various methods to drive out the disease of sin, and you ought generally to inquire of every penitent about each matter, according to the method, order, and condition set out above.

Likewise, if you ask whether those who have until now failed to observe these rules in making confessions will be saved, I answer according to the apostolic rule: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ”; and according to the rule of the apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

## Whether a priest may receive money or other gifts for singing Masses and for other prayers  
*(From chapter 22.)*

It seems that a priest may not receive money for singing the Masses that he has imposed as penance upon a penitent. He knew well that a layman could not sing a Mass; therefore it would be presumed that the priest had imposed such a burden fraudulently, contrary to the canon, so that afterward, once he had received the money, he might relieve him of that burden. Since this is a form of evil, it must therefore be avoided according to the Apostle. The priest ought instead to impose another penance upon him, and so forth.

## Whether a bishop or another prelate may exact or spend the monetary penalties of sinners, or ought to distribute them to the poor  
*(From chapter 24.)*

[Col. 1108B] On this matter, hold firmly and do not doubt at all: although certain bishops and other prelates exact such money in cases of homicide, the prelates themselves ought not to spend that money for their own use, but must distribute it to the poor. For such judges are not moved by love of justice but by love of money, as is proved in 11, question 3, chapter *Qui recte judicat*. Thus they become wolves as guardians, as in 4, question 4, chapter *Contra ritum*. I, John of God, testify to such prelates, under peril to their souls and in dread of the fearful judgment, that they should not exact such money; and if they do exact it, they should not spend it, but distribute it to lepers and other poor people, since the law has not granted it to them but has wholly forbidden it in the canons, as Pope Alexander proves in *Extra*, “On Penalties,” chapter.

And after many other matters, the following is read at the end:

Here ends the *Penitential Book*, composed by Master John of Spain, doctor of Decretals and canon of the city of Bologna, to the honor of the supreme Trinity and the indivisible unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; and to the honor and name of the venerable bishop and chapter of the city of Bologna and of the universal Studium of Bologna; and wherever the Church extends, in which falsehood is overcome and truth shines forth; in the year of the Lord 1247, the fifth indiction, in October, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

[Col. 1107]

# OBSERVATIONS AND NOTES ON THE PENITENTIAL OF THEODORE  
[Note: [Col. 1107D] See col. 927 of this volume.]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the church and on what takes place inside it

[Col. 1107D]

“In a church . . . it is not permitted to sacrifice.” The honor of martyrs must not be bestowed on unbelievers or on passive corpses. This is forbidden by the Fathers of the Council of Carthage, called the First and held under Julius, chapter 2, in these words:

“Let no profane person disgrace the dignity of the martyrs, nor call by the name of martyrs passive bodies which have been commanded to be entrusted to burial solely through ecclesiastical mercy—whether those driven to it by madness, or those separated by some such circumstance or by another form of sin—at a time or in a manner unsuited to the celebration of martyrdoms, and so forth.”

The Fathers of the Second Council of Braga also prohibit this, chapter 18; the Capitula of Martin of Braga, chapter 68; the synod of an uncertain place, which the distinguished J. Sirmond found appended to the Council of Paris; canon 2 of the Council of Nantes, chapter 6; the Synod of Saint Patrick, chapter 23; Saint Gregory in his letter on the exposition of various matters to Augustine, in his response to question 9; and the *Excerptions* of Egbert, archbishop of York, chapters 9–52, who cites it from canon 56 of the Council of Epaon. See Book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 159; Book II, chapter 47; the Sixth Council of Arles, chapter 21; the Capitula of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, chapter 11; and the Council of Mainz, chapter 52. In all these, the same practice is forbidden for the same reason.

### Once they have been torn down

For this reason such altars were commonly demolished, as is evident from the Fifth Council of Carthage, chapter 14:

“Let them be demolished by the bishops who preside over those places, if this can be done. But if popular disturbances prevent it, nevertheless let the people be warned not to frequent those places, so that those who think correctly may not be held there in the bonds of any superstition.”

This canon is reproduced in full in the code of the canons of the African Church, chapter 83, and in the capitulary of Aachen, chapter 42. It cannot be repeated often enough that those who think correctly should not be held in the bonds of any superstitious error.

Sulpicius Severus provides us with an excellent example of the demolition of such altars in his *History*, chapter 8: “And thus,” he says at the end of the chapter, “he freed the people from the error of that superstition.”

### But if it seems suitable for consecration, let it be rebuilt

The Christians also converted temples of the gods into churches of God after they had been demolished. So testifies Sozomen, Book VI of his *History*, chapter 20. Sometimes they hated them with such great execration that they did not consider their pollution capable of being cleansed and disdained applying them to sacred uses, as the Fathers of the Council of Epaon say, canon 33. At other times they did not destroy them but consecrated them to God in honor of a particular martyr.

“But when,” says Saint Augustine in Letter 154, “they are converted to common uses, not to private and personal uses, or to the honor of the true God, what happens to them is what happens to people themselves when they are changed from sacrilegious and wicked persons into the true religion.”

A notable example of this is found in Evagrius, Book I of his *History*, chapter 16. He relates that Theodosius, wishing to honor the divine martyr Ignatius with greater honors, consecrated in his honor a temple formerly dedicated to demons, which the inhabitants called the Temple of Fortune.

From this we learn that great regard must be paid to circumstances and that the one thing to be considered is whatever removes all scandal and serves the edification of the many.

### If this was consecrated beforehand

Athanasius was charged with what was treated almost as a capital crime: that he had held a synaxis in a church that had not yet been dedicated. But in his *Apology to the Emperor Constantius* he easily dispels this charge by the examples of his fathers and the testimonies of Scripture.

“Moreover,” he says, “because they fabricate a charge concerning the great church, namely that a synaxis was held there before it was dedicated, come, let us also give your Piety an answer concerning this matter; for those who heap hatred upon us lead us to it. It happened—I acknowledge it.”

He then presents the examples of the Fathers:

“Especially since I was not unaware that examples of this kind remained among the Fathers. The blessed Alexander, when other places were too confined, wished synaxes to be celebrated in the greater church at the Ihaeon, which he was building. The presence of the people required this, and when he gathered the people he did not consider that it had not yet been completely built. Indeed, your brother, of blessed memory, when a synaxis was being held in such a church at Aquileia, went there himself. In the same way, I too acted.”

Finally, he proves that he had acted correctly by the very words of Christ:

“It remains, therefore, that I anticipate the point at which he might sink his tooth. In his accusations he objects that the building had not yet been dedicated and that prayers had therefore been uttered there unlawfully. Yet the Lord commands the opposite when he says: ‘But when you pray, enter into your inner chamber and shut your doors.’ What, then, does the slanderer say to me? Rather, we must consider prudently and truthfully what Christians should say: regard these men as advisers to be consulted and questioned, not the detractors, since it is written of the latter: ‘A foolish man will speak foolish things to you’; but of the former it is commanded: ‘Take counsel from every wise man.’”

Once the necessity has been removed, however, Saint Basil teaches, in *On Baptism*, chapter 8, that the suitability of the place where the synaxis is held must not be neglected:

“For us too there is danger of having carried out the command badly if we neglect the character of the place, especially if we celebrate the mysteries of the priesthood in profane places; for that matter would bear the judgment of contempt in the celebrant and would also generate an occasion of offense, because of the differing dispositions and the differing weakness of many in knowledge of divine things”—διὰ τὴν τῶν πολλῶν ἐν τῇ γνώσει διάφορον ἀσθένειαν, “because of the differing weakness of the many in knowledge.”

For when Christians were full of grace and strength, as John Chrysostom says in Homily 34 on Matthew, the very houses themselves were churches in those ancient times. But when charity grew cold, and in view of the evident weakness of many, the Fathers decreed that nothing should be offered in a church before it had been consecrated.

See the Synod of Saint Patrick, chapter 23; the *Excerptions* of Egbert of York, chapter 9; *Capitularies*, Book VI, chapter 307; and the Council of Tribur, chapter 4, whose words are found in the Council of Mainz under Arnulf, chapter 9. We have already reported above, from various manuscript codices in which this first chapter of the *Penitential* is explained, much material concerning the consecration of a church. Here too it will not be out of place to add the questions that Peter the Cantor raises on the same subject in his book *On the Sacraments*.

## Selections from chapter 33 of the manuscript of *On the Sacraments* by Peter the Cantor of Paris

It is asked what the bishop means when he says, “I anoint you,” to a basilica constructed of insensate (inanimate) stones.

**Answer:** The meaning of these words is this: “Through you I signify the Church of the faithful, anointed in the sacrament of faith and in the future to be more fully anointed.”

It is also asked what is meant by the words, “Let this house be firmly built,” when perhaps the masonry itself will soon collapse.

**Answer:** This refers to that spiritual Church which is signified by it.

It is also asked whether, through the sacramental anointing and the many blessings performed at the dedication—such as when prayer is offered that whoever enters that place to ask for something may rejoice in obtaining everything—this place acquires some efficacy and an increase of grace, so that it confers something upon those praying there, namely greater devotion and a readier hearing of their prayers. Could someone not pray elsewhere with equal charity and devotion? Why, then, would his prayer not have an equal disposition?

[Note: [Col. 1111] This author often does not define his propositions.]

## From chapter 34. On the reasons for repeating the consecration of an altar

Various reasons are usually distinguished for the repetition of an altar’s consecration. Among them one reason is given: the moving of the altar table.

Before discussing this, let us ask whether, if an altar is consecrated whose support is a great mass of stones—not fixed into the earth, but entirely movable, so that the whole material may be carried from there to some profane place—it would be possible to celebrate there. One may say that nothing prevents it, provided that the altar itself is not moved by being transported. From this it is even clearer that one may celebrate upon an altar brought into a church that has not been dedicated.

To proceed to another case, let us suppose that upon a certain table, whether of stone or wood, a stone is placed, as is customary in a portable altar, and that this table is joined by cement to a large heap of stones. If, then, the stone inserted into the table has been consecrated, and the table is moved away from the heap, is the altar to be consecrated again, as though it had been moved from its support, since that heap is understood to be its support?

Some wish to distinguish whether the altar in the table was consecrated before the table was joined to the stone heap with cement, or afterward. If before, only the table is understood to have been its support; therefore, if the table is later separated from the heap, the altar is not understood to have been moved, and it need not be consecrated again. But if the consecration was performed after the table had been joined to the heap, the heap itself also seems to have served as its support; and then the altar is judged to have been moved when the table was separated.

Nevertheless, I think that in such a case one must investigate what the bishop intended to consecrate: the table, or the altar fixed into the table. But where the table is placed on top without cement or any intervening adhesive, I consider there to be no question.

## From chapter 35. Whether, once the church building has been destroyed, it may be used for common purposes

[Col. 1111D] The question then arises concerning the stones or timbers that formed part of the structure of the church building: once the building has been destroyed, may they be used for common purposes? Pope Clement and Pope Eugenius seem to lay down laws on this matter, from which the conclusion is almost that they may not.

But it is questioned whether they may be used for the necessary workshops of the brothers—for example, the chapter house, dormitory, or refectory. At first this does not seem correct, because those stones and timbers are sacred, whereas such places are either not profane or are entirely sacred in this way.

### We ought not to make steps before the altar where there are relics

For relics were not raised up high but hidden in the earth. Saint Athanasius explains this in the *Life of Saint Antony*, where he does not approve the other practice.

“For it is the custom among the Egyptians,” he says, “to wrap the bodies of noble persons, and especially of blessed martyrs, in linen, and not to deny them the customary care of burial; but not to hide them in the earth. Instead, they place them at home upon couches and preserve them. The vanity of an old custom has handed down the practice of paying this honor to the dead.

“Antony often pleaded with the bishops about this, asking them to correct the people by ecclesiastical custom. He himself rebuked laymen and women more sternly, saying that this was neither lawful nor pleasing to God, since the tombs of the patriarchs and prophets, which remain to our own time, proved the contrary. He directed them to consider the example of the Lord’s body, which, after being placed in a tomb, was enclosed by a stone until the third day of the resurrection.

“In these ways he exposed the Egyptian error concerning the dead, even when the bodies were holy, saying: ‘What can be greater or holier than the Lord’s body, which we know to have been buried in the earth according to the custom of all other peoples?’ This just persuasion tore out the deeply rooted error of many, and, when they had returned the corpses to the earth, they gave thanks to the Lord for the good instruction.”

That Saint Antony rejected this as an error and empty superstition, while testifying that the custom was deeply rooted among weaker believers, is shown by the author of the book *On the Resurrection*, which the distinguished J. Sirmond published under the name of Eusebius of Caesarea:

“For he did not cast away the tongue that the physician had cut out; rather, he received it as a medicine for the healing of the sin he had committed by denying it, and, taking it home, kept it there, as weaker, though nevertheless faithful, people are accustomed to honor whatever they have received from martyrs.”

But whether it is permitted to expose holy relics in order to collect offerings for the construction of a church is explained by Master Robert of Courson in his *Summa*.

## Selections from question 2 of chapter 12 of the manuscript of the *Summa* of Master Robert of Courson, illustrious cardinal

The question is whether a prelate ought to permit preachers, for the sake of profit and while inserting so many abominations, to carry about reliquaries and relics of the saints together with the aforesaid written notices, collecting offerings indiscriminately for the construction of a church.

It seems that he should in no way permit this, because to hand such things over to the aforesaid men is nothing other than to entrust swords to madmen. It is therefore unbecoming and contrary to the authority and honor of the saints for a bishop to make them beg from the dead and, after death, seek what they despised as dung during life.

This is evident in the case of a saint whose body, after it had been placed in Paris in a silver reliquary, immediately broke it, and likewise the golden one. At last he came to rest in a wooden one, thereby teaching, after death, that silver is to be despised, as he had despised it while alive.

This was also attested by blessed Firmin of Amiens. When collectors wished to carry his body from the place of his martyrdom in order to beg in this way, they could not move it from that place by any means.

Thus it is clear that holy relics ought not to be exposed for begging.

### Let a candle burn there

The testimonies of the Fathers prove that this was not yet customary in the first centuries of the Church.

Tertullian, in the *Apology*, says:

“Why do we not shade our doorposts with laurel on a joyful day? Why do we not diminish the daylight with lamps? And so forth. For who compels a philosopher either to sacrifice or to display useless lamps at midday?”

And in his book *On Idolatry*:

“They light lamps every day, though they have no light.”

Lactantius, Book VI of *On True Worship*, says:

“They light lamps as though for one living in darkness, and so forth. Or if they wish to contemplate the heavenly light that we call the sun, let them now understand that God has no need of their lamps, since he himself has given human beings such a bright and radiant light for their use, and so forth. Is one who offers the light of candles and wax tapers as a gift to the author and giver of light to be considered in possession of his mind?”

Around this time, between Tertullian and Lactantius, the Fathers of the Council of Elvira forbade—or rather, prohibited the abuse of—the use of candles during the day. Canon 34 says:

“It has been decided that candles should not be burned in the cemetery during the day, and so forth.”

And canon 37:

“It must also be prohibited that they light lamps publicly,” and so forth.

Later, however, the practice began. When Vigilantius condemned it most vehemently as a kind of idolatry, Jerome refuted him in the letter he wrote against him:

“We do not light candles in broad daylight, as you falsely accuse us; rather, we temper the darkness of night with this consolation and keep watch by the light, lest we sleep with you, blind, in darkness.

“But if some, through the ignorance and simplicity of secular people—or indeed of devout women, concerning whom we can truly say, ‘I testify that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge’—do this in honor of the martyrs, what do you lose by it? The apostles once complained that the ointment was being wasted, but they were corrected by the Lord’s voice. Christ did not need the ointment, nor did the martyrs need the light of candles; nevertheless, that woman did this in honor of Christ, and her devotion of mind is accepted.

“And whoever lights candles receives his reward according to his faith, as the Apostle says: ‘Let each one abound in his own judgment.’ Do you call such people idolaters? I do not deny that all of us who believe in Christ came from idolatry. We are not born Christians, but reborn as Christians. And because we once worshiped idols, must we now not worship God, lest we seem to honor him with the same honor as idols? This was done to idols, and therefore it must be detested; this is done to martyrs, and therefore it must be accepted.

“For even without the relics of martyrs, throughout the churches of the East, when the Gospel is to be read, lights are lit while the sun is already shining—not to drive away the darkness, but to display a sign of joy. Hence those evangelical virgins always have their lamps lit. And to the apostles it is said: ‘Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands,’ and so forth.”

It must be noted very carefully that Jerome says that each person receives his reward according to his faith and abounds in his own judgment. This means, as Augustine explains most excellently in Letter 120, chapter 18, that one especially salutary rule must be retained: whatever is not contrary to the faith or to good morals, and has something that promotes a better life, wherever we see it being established or learn that it has been established, we should not merely refrain from condemning it but should also pursue it with praise and imitation, provided that the weakness of some people does not make this so obstructive that the harm becomes greater.

Thus one should understand the lamps that are lit while the sun is shining: not to drive away darkness, but to display a sign of joy.

But Saint Gregory of Nazianzus and Saint John Chrysostom explain with great distinction by what lights the Church ought especially to shine. The former says in Oration 4, *Against Julian*:

“Let houses not shine with visible light, nor resound with the music and applause of flute players; for the pagans celebrate the feast of the new moon in this manner. But let us not allow ourselves to honor God in this way, nor exalt the present time with things that are wholly unfitting. Rather, let us do so with purity of soul, cheerfulness of mind, and lamps illuminating the entire body of the Church—that is, with divine contemplations and thoughts, set upon the holy lampstand and pouring light over the whole world.”

See John Chrysostom, Homily 20, *To the People of Antioch*.

Incense is sprinkled throughout the church. The judgment concerning frankincense and incense should be the same as that concerning lamps. The ancient Fathers, [Col. 1114C] especially the Latins, so scrupulously avoided rites used by pagans in their sacrifices that some abstained from practices which later Christian good intention introduced. Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus*, chapter 30:

> “I offer him a rich and greater victim than he himself commanded: prayer proceeding from chaste flesh, an innocent soul, and a holy spirit—not grains of incense costing an as, nor the tears of an Arabian tree,” etc.

And in chapter 41:

> “We certainly do not buy incense.”

Arnobius, book VII *Against the Pagans*:

> “But if in ancient times neither human beings nor the gods sought the substance of this incense, it is also proved that today it is offered vainly and uselessly: antiquity did not consider it necessary, while novelty pursued it without any reason,” etc. “Perhaps someone will say: [Col. 1114D] ‘We honor the gods with these things,’” etc. “And piety! What kind of honor is this, or how great, which is made from the smell of fire and purchased with tree resin? For, lest you perhaps be ignorant what this incense is or from where it comes: it is sap flowing from the bark,” etc.

Nevertheless, one may gather that among the Greeks there was anciently a practice of burning incense from the old canons issued under the name of the apostles. Canon 3 states:

> “No one may offer anything else upon the altar except oil for the lamp, and incense at the time of the holy offering”—*καὶ θυμίαμα τῷ καιρῷ τῆς ἁγίας προσφορᾶς*—“and incense at the time of the holy offering.”

And this is certainly a praiseworthy practice, signifying that our prayer ought to be incense in the sight of God. John Chrysostom and other Greek Fathers frequently repeat this. Therefore, if greater gains from these endeavors are [Col. 1115A] to be hoped for than losses from accusers are to be feared, it must be done without hesitation, as Saint Augustine says in his letter to Januarius.

A little later, however, Saint Augustine censures an excessive abundance of such rites, in chapter 19 of the same letter, in these words:

> “But this grieves me greatly: that many things most profitably commanded in the divine books are neglected,” etc. “For although one cannot find even this to be contrary to the faith, nevertheless they oppress the religion itself—which God’s mercy willed to be free through very few and clearly evident celebrations of the sacraments—with servile burdens, so that the condition of the Jews is more tolerable: although they did not recognize the time of freedom, they are nevertheless subjected to legal burdens, not to human presumptions.”

See also [Col. 1115B] the letter of Leo I to all the bishops established throughout Sicily, chapter 2.

A layman ought not to read a lesson in the churches. That this order had already been established in his own time is clearly declared by the most ancient Latin Father, Tertullian, who condemns the contrary practice in the church of the heretics, chapter 41:

> “Thus today one is bishop, tomorrow another; today a deacon who will be a reader tomorrow; today a presbyter who will be a layman tomorrow. For they also impose sacerdotal functions upon laymen.”

Among the Greeks, the earlier Justin seems likewise to indicate this order in the *First Apology*—which is therefore wrongly entitled the *Second* in the printed editions—according to Eusebius. He says:

> “Then, when the reader has ceased, the presider … and the people acclaim auspiciously … but when they are absent, it is sent through the [Col. 1115C] deacons,” etc.

Thus he seems to distinguish the reader from the presider, the deacons, and the people. Whether, however, there might have been a deacon who performed the office of reader, I would not categorically deny. For when he first describes the assembly, he speaks only of the presider, the deacons, and the people. Saint Clement of Alexandria, too, when presenting the ecclesiastical hierarchy in book VI of the *Stromata*, mentions only bishops, presbyters, and deacons.

Whatever the case may be, it is sufficiently and abundantly clear that this reader was not a layman. That is enough to prove that, in the early centuries of the Church, laymen likewise did not recite the lessons at the assembly.

Nor may he say the *Alleluia*. Saint Augustine, in his letter to Januarius:

> “It is sung differently in one place [Col. 1115D] and differently in another. This hymn was held in such esteem at Rome that it was sung only once each year, if we believe Sozomen, book VI, chapter 19. Moreover, at Rome the *Alleluia* is sung once each year, on the first day of the Paschal festival, so much so that many Romans are accustomed to use this oath: that they may be granted to hear and sing this hymn.”

Cassiodorus bears witness to the same in the *Tripartite History*; he could scarcely have been ignorant of this custom. Yet Jerome, in his work *Against Vigilantius*, lists among Vigilantius’s delusions the belief “that the *Alleluia* ought never to be sung except at Easter.” In the epitaph of Fabiola he reports that the *Alleluia* was sung even at her funeral in Rome. He says:
