> “How great a wonder the living Fabiola was to Rome, she demonstrated when dead. She had not yet breathed out her spirit, nor had she [Col. 1116A] returned her soul, owed to Christ; yet already flying rumor, herald of so great a grief, was gathering the people of the whole city for the funeral. Psalms resounded, and the golden roof of the temples, roaring, shook the *Alleluia* aloft.”

And whenever anyone consecrates water, let him first offer a prayer. For without prayer, according to Tertullian, the waters are widows—that is, widows of the Holy Spirit, who, when invoked over the waters, marries them to the heavenly spring, as Saint Paulinus says in letter 12 to Severus:

> The Holy Spirit descended from heaven upon this stream,  
> and from the heavenly spring married the sacred waters.

## CHAPTER II. On the Three Principal Orders of the Church

[Col. 1116B] A bishop may administer confirmation, etc., and likewise a presbyter. See below, chapter 4 of the *Penitential*, on Baptism and Confirmation.

If the deacon or presbyter himself has held the chalice and the offering in his hands. Theodoret likewise testifies that he himself did this, in the *Religious History*, chapter 20:

> “I gladly obeyed,” he says, “and ordered the sacred vessels to be brought—for the place was not far away—and, using the hands of the deacons as an altar, I offered the mystical, divine, and saving sacrifice.”

A bishop ought not to compel an abbot to go to a synod—unless, as he adds, there is also some reasonable cause. The most reasonable cause is when they are summoned by the bishop because they have acted outside the rule. The First Council of Orléans, canon 19:

> “Let abbots, on account of the humility proper to [Col. 1116C] religion, remain under the authority of the bishops; and if they do anything outside the rule, let them be corrected by the bishop. Once a year, upon receiving a summons, let them assemble at the place chosen by the bishop.”

The Council of Auxerre under Pelagius II, canon 7:

> “Let all presbyters come to the synod in the middle of May, and let all abbots assemble at the council on the Kalends of November.”

But the king, if he is superior. For the king, established by God, is the bishop of external affairs—a title which the emperor Constantine rightly claimed when addressing the bishops:

> “You,” he says, “are bishops in matters within the Church; but I have been established by God as a bishop in matters conducted outside.”

These words are found in Eusebius, book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 24. Leo I, in his letter to the emperor Theodosius:

> “How much [Col. 1116D] protection the Lord has prepared for his Church in the faith of your Clemency is shown also by the letter which you sent to me, so that we may rejoice that you possess not only a royal but also a priestly spirit.”

Agapitus, bishop of Rhodes, to the emperor Leo:

> “We all pray that you may be preserved for countless ages. For truly you are both a priest by nature and an emperor.”

Gregory II therefore does not deny that all good emperors may be called priests. Thus he replies to the emperor Leo the Isaurian in the second letter which he writes to him:

> “You have written: ‘I am emperor and priest.’ Indeed, the emperors who preceded you demonstrated this by their deeds and words: they founded churches and cared for them together with the pontiffs, inflamed by zeal and [Col. 1117A] desire,” etc.

And below:

> “These are the priests and emperors who demonstrated this by their deeds.”

If he does not have the price with which to redeem himself. See the Third Council of Orléans, canon 13; the Fourth Council of Orléans, canon 25; and Saint Gregory, book III, letter 9.

A bishop may release someone from a vow. Saint Ambrose clearly demonstrates that this is not to be censured, supported by examples from Scripture, in book III of *The Duties*, chapter 12:

> “Finally, in Isaac we have an example: on his account God appointed a ram to be sacrificed to him. Not every promise, therefore, must always be fulfilled. Finally, the Lord himself frequently changes his decision, as Scripture indicates.”

When Theodorus adds, “If he wishes,” he declares the authority of the bishop: [Col. 1117B] whoever makes a vow without his consent makes it, as it were, from another’s property and usurps what belongs to another. For, as Saint Cyprian says in letter 27:

> “The order of the Church proceeds in such a way that the Church is established over the bishops, and every act of the Church is governed by those same superiors.”

Hence Theodorus says below, in the chapter *Questions Concerning Marriage*:

> “And if someone in secular dress makes a vow without the bishop’s consent, the bishop himself has the power to change the decision, if he wishes.”

Master Robert of Flamesbure teaches the same thing in his *Penitential*.

### Selections from chapter 4 of book II of the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbure, canon of Saint Victor and penitentiary

Likewise, although with his wife’s permission he entered religious life [Col. 1117C] in the presence of monks and a priest, and the man gave himself into the hands of the abbot while the bishop was unaware of it: if the woman neither vowed perpetual continence nor entered religious life with her husband, the bishop can recall him, as stated in the decretal *Propterea*, under the title *On the Conversion of Married Persons*.

I understand this as follows: the bishop may and must recall the man at the woman’s request if, when her husband entered religious life, she declared that she did not wish to remain continent. For when it is said that the vow is solemnized when someone gives himself into the hands of an abbot, this is understood of persons who are free, not of subjects—whether married persons or others—for neither husband nor wife may enter religious life without the bishop’s authority. Therefore this married man, who gave himself into the hands of the abbot without the bishop’s authority, did nothing.

[Col. 1117D] Only a presbyter may celebrate Masses. Therefore deacons may not. The First Council of Arles, canon 15:

> “Concerning the deacons whom we have learned to offer in many places, it has been decided that this must by no means be done.”

The Council of Ancyra, canon 2:

> “Likewise, as for those deacons who have sacrificed but afterward resisted, let them retain another honor, but let them cease from every priestly ministry and, according to the rule of the universal Church, from every sacred ministry, and from offering bread or the chalice or preaching.”

For at one time the consecration of the Lord’s blood was entrusted to them, as Saint Ambrose testifies concerning Saint Lawrence the deacon, book I of *The Duties*, chapter 41:

> “Certainly, test whether you have chosen a suitable minister to whom you entrusted the consecration of the Lord’s blood. [Col. 1118A]”

Hence in former times deacons governed certain churches. The Council of Elvira, canon 77:

> “If a deacon governing a people,” etc.

Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 30:

> “After a long succession of years, Cautinus, who was appointed bishop of the city of Clermont, governed the Church in his diaconate in his place.”

And to bless the people. The Fathers of the Council of Riez permit presbyters to bless privately, but not publicly in the church:

> “Amid these minor disputes and indefinite matters, it seemed good to open to every presbyter the opportunity of blessing, according to the desire of the faithful, among families, in the fields, and in private houses. It occurs to us that some provinces already possess this practice.”

Thus, as the distinguished J. Sirmond correctly observes in [Col. 1118B] his notes on this canon, before this time presbyters in these provinces of Gaul did not give blessings even privately. At the Synod of Agde they are prohibited only from giving public blessings, not private ones. Canon 44:

> “A presbyter shall in no way be permitted to pour a blessing upon the people in the church.”

Nor is this permitted even to chorepiscopi, according to the ecclesiastical capitularies of Charlemagne, title IV, chapter 2:

> “It has been decided—as we decreed by the general and synodal counsel of Pope Leo, all our bishops, and the rest of the faithful—that no chorepiscopus presume to give a blessing to the people in the public Mass,” etc.

All these things belong to the supreme pontiffs—that is, to cathedral bishops—and not to chorepiscopi or presbyters, whose form chorepiscopi [Col. 1118C] represent according to the decrees of the holy canons. If they should attempt to perform any of these acts, whatever they do shall be invalid, and they themselves shall be entirely deprived of every ecclesiastical honor.

In the East, however, it may be inferred that both kinds of blessing were granted to presbyters from the words of Saint Basil to Amphilochius, canon 27, concerning a presbyter unknowingly involved in an impious marriage:

> “Let him bless neither publicly,” he says, “nor privately.”

The same follows from homily 34 of John Chrysostom on chapter 9 of Matthew. Theodorus plainly declares and confirms this below, at the end of chapter 3 of the *Penitential*.

A presbyter is not compelled to give tithes. For, says Gregory, it is unworthy that tithes should be demanded from clerics who become poor for the sake of him to whom the tithes belong. [Col. 1118D] See the appendix to the Third Lateran Council, chapter 9. Hence it is said below, chapter 13:

> “It is not lawful to give tithes except to the poor and to pilgrims.”

See the book of John Launoy, the most renowned doctor, *On the Definition of the Goods of the Church*, in which he proves by innumerable testimonies of the Fathers that the goods of the Church are the goods of the poor. I add the opinion of Master Robert of Courson in his *Summa*, where, in question 13 on tithes, chapter 3, he treats the question whether clerics are bound to pay tithes.

### Selections from the manuscript *Summa* of Master Robert of Courson, question 13 on tithes, chapter 3

We say that the case is different with a layman who owns property and with a cleric who is not the possessor [Col. 1119A] of what he has, but merely its steward, according to the Apostle, who says: “A stewardship has been entrusted to us.” And according to Jerome, who says in Distinction 16, question 1, in the final chapter:

> “Whatever clerics possess belongs to the poor, and therefore their houses ought to be common.”

Thus a cleric may receive from the goods of the Church, as steward and servant, what is sufficient for himself and his immediate household, and what is honestly necessary for food, drink, and clothing. With these things, as the Apostle says, let us be content; and the entire remainder, by strict right, belongs to the poor.

Therefore, in place of the tithes which laymen give, clerics are bound to distribute among the charitable needs of the poor and the Church whatever remains after what is sufficient for themselves and their immediate household. For if they retain more than is necessary, they are robbers, as Jerome testifies. Hence he says:

> “Whoever attempts to retain [Col. 1119B] more than is necessary is convicted of stealing what belongs to another.”

And Gregory says:

> “When we give goods to the poor, we do not give them what is ours but return to them what is theirs. Therefore it is not called merely mercy, since we distribute goods to the poor, but justice.”

Hence in the Psalm:

> “He scattered, he gave to the poor; his righteousness,” etc.

For we clerics are bound by strict right to give to the poor everything left over after what is necessary for ourselves and our immediate household has been taken. Hence in the Gospel:

> “Give as alms what remains, and behold, everything is clean for you.”

The same is also said in Distinction 16, question 1.

A presbyter may not expose the sin of a bishop, because the bishop is above him. Abundius, bishop, judged in the same way at the Roman council under Sixtus III:

> “He replied and said: No one is permitted to accuse [Col. 1119C] his own pontiff, since the judge will not be judged—unless, however, he has deviated from the true faith.”

Thus Charisius, presbyter and steward of Philadelphia, writes to the universal Council of Ephesus:

> “It is indeed the prayer of all who think rightly that honor and proper reverence should always be shown, especially to spiritual Fathers and teachers. But if it should happen somewhere that those who ought to teach utter to their subjects things concerning the faith that wound everyone’s ears and hearts, it is necessary that the order be changed, and that those who attempt to teach wrongly be rebuked by their inferiors.”

At the fifth Roman synod, Symmachus says that this was decreed and confirmed by many of his predecessors:

> “It is not necessary, therefore, to forge new rules about these matters, but to reconcile and confirm the old ones. For it was synodally decreed and confirmed by many [Col. 1119D] of our predecessors that the sheep entrusted to their shepherd should not presume to rebuke him, unless he has deviated from the true faith.”

They may, however, accuse him for his injustice, as the synod continues:

> “Nor may they dare to accuse him for any other matter whatsoever except his injustice,” etc.

The Fathers of the Council of Epaon grant laymen an even broader power, canon 24:

> “We permit laymen to bring an accusation against a cleric of any rank if they are prepared to charge him with a criminal offense, provided that they allege what is true.”

But how far the offenses of bishops ought to be concealed is taught most wisely by the emperor Constantine, whose words Theodoret reports in book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 10.

[Col. 1120A] A sacrifice must not be received from the hand of a priest who is unable to perform the offerings or readings according to the rite. The Roman Council held under Pope Hilary, canon 3:

> “Those who are ignorant of letters must not dare to aspire to sacred orders. Whoever is their consecrator shall undo his own act.”

The Second Council of Orléans, canon 16:

> “A presbyter or deacon without letters, or one who does not know the order of baptizing, shall in no way be ordained.”

See Regino, book *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, inquiry 83, and the notes of the most learned Étienne Baluze, who, concerning the same matter, cites Charles the Bald in his letter to Pope Nicholas, the Council of Valence, and Hincmar in chapter 36 of his later work *Against Gottschalk*.

Of the priest who reads the lessons. In certain churches priests [Col. 1120B] read the sacred Scriptures. Concerning this Sozomen, book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 19, reports a varied discipline: among the Alexandrians only the archdeacon read the sacred book; elsewhere, deacons; in many churches, only presbyters; and in some places, bishops read on the principal feasts, as at Constantinople, where on the first day of Easter they especially read the Gospel.

Presbyters are afterward addressed as follows:

> “If a presbyter sings the responsory at Mass or anything else, let him not remove his cape; but when reading the Gospel, let him place it upon his shoulders.”

His cape. That clerics used a cape different from that of the other monks and others is declared by the assembly of Aachen, chapters 12–61, and by the Council of Vaison, canon 46, where it is forbidden that church capes be worn [Col. 1120C] by laymen at the festivals of confraternities.

In Theodore’s time, and long before it, clerical garments were distinctive in most churches, as is proved by the testimonies of Gregory of Tours, book V of his *History*, chapter 14; the Third Council of Carthage, canon 41—or rather 60, according to the order of the codex of the ancient statutes of the Church; Jerome, in his commentary on book XIII of Ezekiel, chapter 44; and the Council of Laodicea, canon 22.

But the very learned Henri Valois indicates in his notes on chapter 19 of book VI of Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* that before this time such a thing appeared nowhere:

> “It is evident,” he says, “that at that time the clerics still had no distinctive clothing.”

For Heraclas, presbyter of the Alexandrian Church and afterward bishop of the same place, always retained it [the object is omitted in the supplied text]. Saint Clement of Alexandria commends white garments, but, as simple garments, for all Christians. [Col. 1120D] As he himself says in book II of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 10, it is most fitting for those who are white and not adulterated within to use white garments that are neither elaborate nor ornate.

Hegesippus speaks of James’s linen garment in Eusebius, chapter 23. Polycrates speaks of John’s *lamina* in Eusebius, book V of the *History*, chapter 23. Saint Epiphanius likewise reports the same concerning James in *Heresy* 28 and *Heresy* 78.

But by what distinctive ornaments were they distinguished not only from laymen but from all the other priests of the Church? Hence perhaps John Beleth, highly skilled in ecclesiastical matters, moved by this question, says the following in his chapter on the sacrifice of the Mass:

> “And note that in the primitive Church the apostles and apostolic men performed the sacrifice [Col. 1121A] in wooden vessels and ordinary garments. At that time there were wooden chalices and golden priests.”

In former times there were people who wished to prove from the very words of the Gospel that a distinctive use of priestly vestments was extremely ancient. Pope Celestine refutes them excellently in his letter to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne, chapter 1:

> “For we say,” he writes, “that some priests of the Lord serve a superstitious form of worship rather than purity of mind or faith. But it is not surprising that they act against ecclesiastical custom, since they did not grow up in the Church but came by another path, bringing into the Church with them those practices which they had possessed in another way of life. Wrapped in a cloak and girded about the loins, they believe that they fulfill Scripture not according to the spirit but according to the letter. For if these commands were given [Col. 1121B] so that they might be observed in this manner, why are the things that follow not done likewise—why are burning lamps not held in the hands together with a staff? These things possess their own mystery, and to those who understand they are so clear that they should be observed according to the meaning that is fitting: in the girding of the loins, chastity is indicated; in the staff, pastoral governance; in the burning lamps, the splendor of good works, of which it is said, ‘Let your works shine.’ Perhaps those who live in more remote places and dwell far from others should retain this manner of dress, following custom rather than reason. But how has this garment arisen in the Gallican Churches, so that, after so many years and so many bishops, custom should be changed into another dress? We must be distinguished from the common people and from others by teaching, not by clothing; by conduct, not by dress; by purity of mind, not by [Col. 1121C] adornment. For if we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by the Fathers and make room for unnecessary superstitions. We must not therefore lead the inexperienced minds of the faithful toward such things. They should be taught rather than mocked. Such things should not be imposed upon their eyes; precepts should instead be poured into their minds. This is how clerics, especially, are to be distinguished from the common people. And this is what Saint Basil says the Apostle commanded, in the book of the *Longer Rules*, response to question 22.”

And below:

> “Let this canon be observed perpetually.”

See Gregory of Nazianzus, oration 19; Isidore of Pelusium, book I, letter 45; the *Book of the Sacraments* of Saint Gregory, in the prayer for the consecration of a bishop; and Fortunatus, book II, epigram 10, concerning [Col. 1121D] Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris:

> Yet he proceeds gently, like another Aaron,  
> not resplendent in clothing, but pleasing in piety.  
> Stones, scarlet, bright gold, purple, and fine linen  
> do not adorn his shoulders; rather, living faith shines.

For this reason the author of the *Life of Saint Fulgentius* testifies concerning him:

> “In the tunic in which he slept, he also celebrated the sacrifice; and at the time of the sacrifice he used to say that hearts, rather than garments, ought to be changed.”

Let those whom he baptized be baptized again: a fornicating presbyter, after his crime has become known, if he has baptized them. It is surprising that anything of this kind should be read after the question had been discussed so extensively by the Fathers against the Donatists.

Earlier, certain Fathers spoke more freely. Saint Clement of Alexandria, book VII of the *Stromata*: [Col. 1122A]

> *ἐμφανῶς, παρούσης τῆς γραφῆς … οὐκ οἰκεῖον καὶ γνήσιον ὕδωρ λογιζομένη*  
> “Plainly, with the Scripture present … reckoning it not to be proper and genuine water.”

Tertullian, book *On Modesty*, chapter 21. Origen, in his commentaries on Matthew:

> *Εἰ δὲ σειραῖς τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων αὐτοῦ ἐσφίγκτο, μάτην καὶ δεσμεῖ καὶ λύει*  
> “But if he was bound by the chains of his sins, he binds and looses in vain.”

Concerning this the distinguished Pierre-Daniel Huet made the following observations in book II of the *Origeniana*, p. 176:

> “In this passage,” he says, “Sixtus of Siena notes that Origen alludes to the error later defended by the Hussites, who wished the power of the pope and bishops to depend upon moral holiness,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

> “I agree with Sixtus, and I say that Origen is in error and appears to embrace the heresy in which the Donatists later became involved, when they made the power of the Church depend upon the holiness of its priests.”

[Col. 1122B] Those who are mentioned by Dionysius of Alexandria in his letter to Philemon, written to the Roman Church, embraced the same opinion as Tertullian and Origen. Eusebius preserves their most distinguished fragments in book VII of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 7. Among the other defenders, the principal ones were Saint Cyprian, in his letter to Magnus concerning the baptism of the Novatians and in letters 74, 76, and 78, and Saint Firmilian in his letter to Saint Cyprian.

Saint Basil speaks of them as follows in his canonical letter to Amphilochius, canon 1:

> “Indeed, it seemed good to the ancients—I mean Cyprian and our Firmilian—to subject all these people to a single judgment,” etc., “since they can no longer bestow upon others the grace of the Holy Spirit, from which they themselves have fallen.”

The most learned Rigaltius explains the reasoning behind these doctrines in his notes on Cyprian’s letter 64, in these words:

> “Pamelius opposes [Col. 1122C] to Cyprian’s opinion the opinion of Augustine, who holds that sacraments administered by impious and wicked bishops or presbyters remain valid. This matter requires a distinction concerning the fact brought into controversy.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Cyprian and the others throughout Africa, Numidia, and Mauretania appear to have established and confirmed such doctrines in an age most afflicted by the attacks of secular powers and the factions of the ministers of the Church, so that they might make the people steadfast in the Christian faith and have ministers more devoted to the peace and unity of the Church.”

Thus the most learned men judge this opinion of certain Fathers, which Theodorus followed together with the author of the book *On Those Who Are Initiated into the Mysteries*, cited by Saint Ambrose, chapter 4:

> “The baptism of the faithless does not heal,” he says; “[Col. 1122D] it does not cleanse but pollutes.” he says; “it does not cleanse but pollutes.”

It should be noted that the phrase “after his crime has become known” introduces a distinction. Master Robert of Courson likewise made the same distinction much later concerning the power of absolving sins in his *Summa*.

### Selections from the manuscript *Summa* of Robert of Courson, question 3, chapter 5

The question is whether a priest who is in mortal sin possesses the aforesaid keys by which he may bind or loose. It seems that he does not, etc. Gregory says:

> “Who is weighed down by his own sins does not wash away those of another.”

Therefore an unclean man does not wash away the sins of another. Gregory also says elsewhere:

> “Only those placed in this flesh possess the power of binding and loosing who hold the apostles’ doctrine and life.”

Therefore, since an unclean priest does not [Col. 1123A] possess these, he neither binds nor looses, etc.

What, then, should be said about this? It seems to us that a distinction must be made. The priest is either notorious or secret. If he is notorious, he ought to bind or loose neither on the basis of the merit of his life nor by virtue of his office; indeed, he ought to be entirely barred from exercising the keys. Likewise, we say that such a man must be barred from the office of public representation, preaching, and celebrating Masses. The authorities cited above speak of such a case.

But if he is secret, he may be tolerated; and if he binds or looses, his binding or absolution is valid. Just as, if an evil man consecrates, the consecrated thing is consecrated; if he baptizes, the person is baptized. But such absolution and binding takes place to the destruction of the man who binds or looses. For he does not bind by the merit of his life, but by virtue of the office entrusted to him.

[Col. 1123B] He discovers that he has not been baptized. Dionysius of Alexandria, questioned about nearly the same matter, replied as follows in his letter to Xistus, bishop of the city of Rome, which Eusebius reports in book VII of his *History*, chapter 9:

> “For a man who has frequently heard the thanksgiving and answered ‘Amen’ with the others; who has stood at the sacred table and extended his hands to receive the holy food; who has received it and for a very long time has partaken of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—I would not dare to renew him from the beginning. But, so that he might be of good courage and approach participation in the Lord’s body with firm faith and full of good hope, I gave this command.”

Later, however, the Fathers of the fifth Council of Carthage decided otherwise: he ought to be baptized, without that hesitation. See [Col. 1123C] canon 6, which is reproduced in full in the complete codex of the canons of the African Church, chapter 72; and the abridged statutes of the Council of Hippo, chapter 40.

Saint Leo likewise gives the same ruling in his letter to Leo, bishop of Ravenna, and in his replies to the inquiries of Rusticus of Narbonne, response 16:

> “If,” he says, “there are no indications among relatives or members of the household, nor among clerics or neighbors, by which those in question can be shown to have been baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn. lest those plainly perish in whom what is not shown to have been done cannot, since reason does not permit it, be regarded as repeated.”

Bishop Trojanus, replying to Bishop Eumerius, likewise declares that he unhesitatingly judges according to what was established by his predecessors. He therefore concludes:

> “[Col. 1123D] Know that it has been established that whoever does not remember having been baptized, and for whom it is not proved that this was done by another person, should receive baptism without any delay, lest, if his soul is separated from the baptized, it be required of us.”

See Gregory II, letter 13, chapter 9; the *Excerptions* of Egbert of York, chapter 41; and Gregory III, letter 1, chapter 5.

At that time, therefore, no condition was inserted. For lawful acts, as the jurists say, do not admit a condition. Nevertheless, they sometimes tacitly admit one; when it is expressly included, it introduces a defect. The statutes of Saint Boniface of Mainz, however, prescribe baptism under a condition, chapter 28, with these words:

> “I do not baptize you again; but if you have not yet been baptized, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, [Col. 1124A] and of the Holy Spirit.”

From the Roman *Spicilegium* of Dom Luc d’Achery, volume IX.

Master Robert of Flamesbure, in his *Penitential*, thinks that the opinion of Dionysius of Alexandria should not be condemned, although he considers the more common judgment of the others safer.

### Selections from the manuscript *Penitential* of Robert of Flamesbure, book III

Baptism also belongs to the substance of order, because baptism is the gate and foundation not only of the orders but of all the sacraments. Therefore, without baptism, no order and no sacrament is received.

Nevertheless, Lord Innocent says that if someone has faith, then—even if he has been baptized neither with water nor with his own blood, as occurs in martyrdom—he receives order. For a person is baptized in the Spirit; and from the moment he has faith, he has Christ. Thus he has been baptized in Christ, who is the foundation of all good things.

Nevertheless, he caused an unbaptized priest to be baptized and [Col. 1124B] ordained again, because his predecessors had held this view; and this is the safer course.

And all those whom he had previously baptized: the presbyter who discovers that he has not been baptized. There were indeed those who thought that persons who had become laymen no longer possessed the power either to baptize or to ordain, as Saint Basil testifies in his canonical letter to Amphilochius, canon 1:

> “Those who have been cut off and made laymen possess the power neither of baptizing nor of ordaining,” etc.

For this reason they ordered those baptized by such men—regarding them as baptized by laymen—to come to the Church and be cleansed by the baptism of the Church.

Moreover, the question whether baptism can be given by those who have never been [Col. 1124C] Christians is so significant that Saint Augustine does not dare affirm anything about it in book II *Against the Letter of Parmenian*, chapter 12:

> “This is indeed another question,” he says: “whether baptism can also be given by those who have never been Christians. Nothing should be rashly affirmed about it without the authority of so great a council as is sufficient for so great a matter.”

Not long afterward the Fathers of the Council of Compiègne defined the question, canon 9:

> “If someone has been baptized by an unbaptized presbyter, and the Holy Trinity was invoked in that baptism, he has been baptized, as Pope Sergius said.”

Hence Master Robert of Courson does not hesitate to assert that baptism truly given by an unbeliever is valid, provided that he intends to immerse the person in the manner taught by the Church, even though he does not intend to confer the fruit [Col. 1124D] of baptism and regards it as a joke.

### Selections from the manuscript *Summa* of Master Robert of Courson, question 38, chapter 10

If the one who immerses intends to do what the Church does, and to do it for the purpose for which the Church does it, there is no doubt that he baptizes. But if he intends to immerse in the manner taught by the Church, yet does not intend to confer the fruit of baptism, it may be doubted whether he baptizes someone.

For example, suppose a believer, when going abroad, entrusts his little child to an unbeliever, adding the condition that, if he sees the child laboring at the point of death, he should baptize him with a triple immersion according to the form of words stated above. In such a case we say that, since the man seriously intends [Col. 1125A] to baptize in the manner in which the Church baptizes, he undoubtedly baptizes, even though he does not direct his mind toward the fruit of baptism and indeed regards the entire fruit as a joke.

It is not permitted for a deacon to administer penance to a layperson. The Council of Elvira says that this is permitted only under compelling necessity, canon 32:

> “If anyone, after a serious fall, has come into the peril of death, it has been decided that he should not perform penance before a presbyter, but rather before the bishop. Yet, when illness compels it, the presbyter must necessarily provide Communion, and the deacon also, if the priest orders him to do so.”

Saint Cyprian, in Epistle 12:

> “If they have been seized by some misfortune and danger of illness, without waiting for our presence, they may make confession of their sin before any presbyter who happens to be present; or, if no presbyter is found and death begins to press upon them, they may also do so before a deacon, so that, after the hand has been laid upon them in penance, they may come to the Lord in peace.”

Indeed, according to Optatus and Jerome, deacons belong to the third degree of the priesthood. See Halitgar in the preface to the *Roman Penitential*; Regino, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, §295, from the *Roman Penitential*. For just as no one except bishops and presbyters, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted, ought to offer the sacrifice, so others ought not to usurp the judgments of penitents. Section 296:

> “If necessity should arise, and no presbyter be present, let the deacon receive the penitent for holy Communion.”

Theodore adds:

> “But bishops or presbyters ought to administer it; if presbyters have the authority, nevertheless they should not do so without the bishop’s command, as the authorities of the Fathers cited above make clear.”

Master Robert of Courson confirms this in his *Summa*.

### Selections from the manuscript *Summa* of Master Robert of Courson, on the Question of Penance, chapter 46

We say that the two matters stated above—namely, giving counsel and imposing penance—belong to any priest belonging to another jurisdiction, provided that he has received this authority by a special mandate from a superior, such as the local bishop or the papal legate. Thus the monks of Saint Victor would possess this authority only by mandate of the Bishop of Paris. Therefore neither they nor anyone else may intrude upon this function without the mandate of the lord bishop.

Deacons may baptize. The right is granted to them, but they possess it only by the authority of the bishop, for the honor of the Church. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 17:

> “The chief priest, who is the bishop, certainly possesses the right of giving it; thereafter, the presbyters and deacons—but not without the bishop’s authority, for the honor of the Church. When that is preserved, peace is preserved.”

Saint Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*:

> “The safety of the Church depends upon the dignity of the chief priest. If a certain power, exempt and eminent above all others, is not given to him, as many schisms will arise in the Churches as there are priests. Hence it follows that without chrism and the bishop’s command neither presbyter nor deacon possesses the right to baptize.”

Pope Gelasius I, *To the Bishops of Lucania*, Epistle 9, chapter 7:

> “We have also established that deacons must observe their proper measure, and we do not permit them to attempt anything beyond the scope assigned to them by the canons of the Fathers: they must apply absolutely none of those functions to their ministry which antiquity decreed to belong properly to the first orders. They must not dare to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless extreme necessity perhaps compels it, when the aforesaid ministers are situated at a considerable distance—a practice which is also often permitted to Christian laypeople.”

[Col. 1125B]

They may not give the bread. Council of Laodicea, canon 25:

> “Ministers ought not to give the bread or bless the cup.”

That deacons did give the bread in which thanksgiving had been offered and distribute the cup is demonstrated clearly and abundantly by the Fathers of earlier centuries of the Church. Saint Justin, in the *First Apology* according to Eusebius:

> “The deacons distribute to each of those present the bread over which thanks have been given, and so forth. Moreover, this food is called Eucharist among us.”

Saint Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*:

> “When the solemn rites had been completed and the deacon began to offer the cup to those present, and so forth.”

Nevertheless, Tertullian, Cyprian’s teacher, testifies that the sacrament of the Eucharist was not to be received from the hand of anyone other than the presiding ministers, in *On the Crown*, chapter 2. Later Saint Athanasius, speaking of distributing the blood of Christ, asserts that this is permitted to no one except priests:

> “It belongs to you alone,” he says in the *Second Apology*, “to distribute the blood of Christ to the people, and to no one else.”

John Chrysostom agrees with Athanasius in Homily 46 on chapter 13 of Matthew:

> “Do you not see that it is lawful for the priest alone to hand you the cup of the blood?”

[Col. 1126C]

In such rites, however, one must always consider not only the times but also the places. For around the time of John Chrysostom, in whose Church only priests distributed the cup, Ambrose testifies that in the Church of Milan even widows administered the body and blood of Christ, in *On Widows*:

> “At the same time it is shown what she who ministers to Christ ought to be like. She must first be free from the allurements of various pleasures and avoid the inward weakness of body and soul, so that she may minister the body and blood of Christ, and so forth.”

Dionysius of Alexandria, in his letter to Fabius, preserved by Eusebius, Book VI of the *History*, chapter 44, writes that a priest gave the Eucharist to a boy so that he might administer it to Serapion:

> “But since I had given instructions that, if the dying requested it—and especially if they had previously begged for it earnestly—forgiveness should be granted to them, so that they might depart this life full of good hope, he gave a small portion of the Eucharist to the boy and ordered him, after dipping it in water, to let it drip into the old man’s mouth.”

[Col. 1126D]

All these practices were subsequently prohibited altogether by the Synod of Rheims, canon 2:

> “It has come to our knowledge that certain presbyters hold the divine mysteries in such little regard that they entrust the sacred body of the Lord to a layman or woman to carry to the sick; and those who are forbidden to enter the sanctuary or approach the altar are entrusted with the holy of holies. Every religious person’s prudence recognizes how horrifying this is. Therefore the synod absolutely forbids such rash presumption from occurring hereafter. Rather, in every case, the presbyter must communicate the sick person himself. If he acts otherwise, he shall be subject to the peril of his rank.”

[Col. 1127A]

### Monks and clerics may bless food

Virgins also used to bless it, as the author of the book *On Virginity*, which is read among the works of Saint Athanasius, testifies:

> “If three virgins are present with you, let them pronounce the blessing over the bread and pray with you, and so forth. For you are holy to the Lord, and your food and drink are sanctified. Through prayers and more sacred words it is sanctified.”

Saint John Chrysostom, in Homily 32 on chapter 19 of Matthew, shows that no Christian ought to consume food unless it has been blessed and sanctified by prayer and thanksgiving. For, he says, if someone does not offer his food to God through prayer, he eats it in defilement. Referring to such food, the Apostle says:

> “For every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.”

He shows by this that all food is defiled unless it has been cleansed and sanctified through prayer. That Christians should make the sign over bread before blessing it is indicated by the unknown author of the *Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew*, among the works of John Chrysostom, Homily 18:

> “For example, you make the sign over your bread, which you eat, as Paul says: ‘For it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.’”

See Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 19, where he relates that he nourished his sick mother with blessed bread marked with the cross, and that she thereby recovered, regained her strength, and was restored.

## CHAPTER III. On the ordination of various persons

[Col. 1127C]

### For seven days he shall cover his head with his cowl

Council of Aachen, chapter 35:

> “After making his profession, a monk shall keep his head covered with his cowl for three days.”

### According to the second baptism and the judgment of the Fathers

That is, on account of penance, which the Fathers very often call a baptism more severe and more laborious. Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 39:

> “The fifth place is held by the baptism of tears. It is indeed harsher and more laborious: by it is immersed the person who washes his bed and couch with tears every night, whose very scars of vice stink, who enters mourning and sorrow, who imitates the repentance of Manasseh and the humility of the Ninevites, upon whom mercy was bestowed, and so forth.”

[Col. 1127D]

John Climacus values this baptism so highly that he seems to prefer it to baptism by water:

> “After baptism,” he says in Step 8, “the fountain of tears is a baptism more powerful than baptism, if one may speak so. Baptism cleanses only the former filth of sins, whereas mourning washes away the offenses contracted after baptism. The baptism by which we were immersed as infants we all later defiled; but through the fountain of tears we restore even baptism to its own purity. If the most merciful God had not granted this to humanity, very few indeed would attain salvation.”

[Col. 1128A]

### A presbyter may consecrate an abbess

But the Fathers of the Third Council of Carthage prescribe that he must not do so without consulting the bishop, canon 36:

> “A presbyter shall not consecrate virgins without consulting the bishop, and he shall never prepare chrism.”

Holy nuns, however, ought always to consecrate basilicas through continual sacrifices of prayers and thanksgivings. Hence the Fathers frequently call them the pure altars and altars of God. Tertullian, Book I *To His Wife*, chapter 7:

> “For a pure altar of God ought to be set forth; that whole radiant priesthood of widowhood and celibacy is inscribed with holiness.”

Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 103. The ancient author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book II, chapter 26:

> “Also honor virgins, as representing the censer and the incense.”

[Col. 1128B]

See Book III, chapter 6, and Book IV, chapter 2.

### The Greeks bless a widow and a virgin together

See the Fourth Council of Carthage, canons 12 and 13, or rather the *Ancient Statutes of the Church*, canon 99:

> “When a consecrated virgin comes for consecration, and so forth.”

And canon 100:

> “Widows or consecrated women who come for ministry, and so forth.”

### The Romans do not veil a widow

This is likewise confirmed by the Fathers of the Council of Tours, canon 20, in these words:

> “As for what some say—why should a widow who has not been blessed not be permitted to take a husband?—everyone knows that a widow’s blessing is never read of in the canonical books. Her purpose alone ought to suffice, as was written in the Epaon canons by Bishop Avitus or by all the bishops: ‘We altogether abolish throughout our region the consecration of widows whom they call deaconesses,’ and so forth.”

[Col. 1128C]

And the Council of Tribur, canon 22:

> “Let no bishop attempt to veil widows, as was established in the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 13, since neither divine authority nor the form of the canons has prescribed this.”

See below, chapter 7.

### According to the Greeks, a presbyter may consecrate a virgin with the sacred veil, reconcile a penitent during a public Mass, prepare exorcised oil, and, in the bishop’s absence, do whatever he could have done had the bishop been present

This custom was widely observed in Alexandria and throughout Egypt, as many writers affirm. The author of the *Commentary on the Epistle of Paul to the Ephesians*, chapter 3, preserved by Ambrose:

> “Finally, in Egypt presbyters confirm when the bishop is not present.”

The author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, preserved by Saint Augustine:

> “For in Alexandria and throughout Egypt, if the bishop is absent, the presbyter consecrates.”

See Jerome, in his letter to Evagrius; Rabanus, in his letter to Regimbaldus.

The reason which these same writers propose is summarized briefly by Hilary the deacon, preserved by Ambrose in his commentary on the First Epistle to Timothy:

> “Because bishops and presbyters have one ordination. Both are priests, but the bishop is first.”

[Col. 1128D]

See the same author in the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, preserved by Augustine, Question 101; Jerome in his letter to Oceanus, in his letter to Evagrius, and in his *Commentary on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus*, where he speaks as Tertullian does in *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 7; and Saint Augustine in his letter to Jerome. Not to omit the Greek Fathers, consult John Chrysostom on chapter 1 of Paul’s Epistle to the Philippians, and Theodoret on chapter 3 of Paul’s First Epistle to Timothy and on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus.

### Chrism for the sick, if necessary

According to the Greeks and the Fathers of the Council of Toledo, canon 20, and of the Council of Orange, canon 1:

> “It has been decided that heretics who are placed in danger of death, if they desire to be Catholics, should be marked by presbyters with chrism and a blessing when no bishop is present.”

You will find the same in the Second Council of Arles, canon 26, and the Council of Epaon, canon 16.

[Col. 1129A]

### According to the Romans, however, this is not permitted except to the bishop alone

That is: consecrating a virgin with the sacred veil, reconciling a penitent during a public Mass, and preparing exorcised oil. Thus prescribe the Fathers of the Second Council of Carthage, canon 3, which is reproduced in full in the code of canons of the African Church, canon 36; Pope Gelasius, in his letter to the bishops of Lucania, chapter 6; the Fathers of the Council of Agde, canon 44; and the Fathers of the Second Council of Seville, canon 7, in these words:

> “For although they share with bishops in the administration of very many mysteries, they should know that certain things have been prohibited to them by the newer ecclesiastical rules. Such things include the consecration of presbyters, deacons, and virgins; the establishment, blessing, or anointing of an altar. For they are not permitted to consecrate a church or altars, nor through the laying on of hands to impart the Paraclete Spirit to baptized believers or to converts from heresy; nor to prepare chrism, nor to mark the foreheads of the baptized with chrism; nor indeed publicly to reconcile any penitent during Mass; nor to send letters of commendation to anyone.”

[Col. 1129C]

This Roman practice, differing from the rites of the Greeks, also has its own explanations, which the Fathers set forth in various ways. Some think that this was done because all the orders are contained in the bishop, and because it would seem a common and utterly insignificant thing if everyone could perform the same functions. Hilary the deacon, in his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians*, chapter 4:

> “For all the orders are contained in the bishop, because he is the first priest—that is, the chief of the priests—and also a prophet, an evangelist, and everything else required for the ministry of the faithful in the Church, and so forth.”

[Col. 1129D]

And below:

> “So that the people might grow and multiply, everything was initially permitted to all, and so forth. But once the Church had encompassed all regions, assemblies had been established, rulers appointed, and the other offices arranged in the Churches, and so forth, the Church began to be governed by another order and plan. For if everyone could do the same things, it would be irrational, and the matter would appear common and utterly insignificant. Hence it is that now no one, and so forth.”

Others say that this decree was made in order to eliminate schisms. Saint Jerome, in his commentary on chapter 1 of the Epistle to Titus:

> “A presbyter, therefore, is the same as a bishop. Before rivalries arose in religion at the instigation of the devil and people said among themselves, ‘I belong to Paul,’ ‘I to Apollos,’ and ‘I to Cephas,’ the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters. But after each person began to regard as his own, rather than Christ’s, those whom he had baptized, it was decreed throughout the world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and placed over the others, so that the entire care of the Church might belong to him and the seeds of schisms might be removed, and so forth. This was said to show that among the ancients presbyters and bishops were the same; but gradually, so that the shoots of dissension might be uprooted, all responsibility was transferred to one.”

[Col. 1130A]

Finally, for the honor of the Church—“when that is preserved, peace is preserved,” as Tertullian says in *On Baptism*, chapter 17, and as Saint Cyprian frequently commends in his letters—they established that all the aforesaid functions belong to the right of the bishop alone, and that all these things are unlawful for presbyters. For, as the Fathers of the Second Council of Seville say, canon 7:

> “They do not possess the height of the episcopate, which the authority of the canons prescribes as belonging to bishops alone, so that through this both the distinction of ranks and the summit of the highest dignity may be demonstrated.”

[Col. 1130B]

## CHAPTER IV. On the confirmation of baptism

### In baptism, marriages are not dissolved

For, as he adds, baptism washes away evil, not good. Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 80:

> “For just as a bath has the power to erase sins, so it does not extinguish rightly performed deeds.”

### This is Pope Innocent’s position

Pope Innocent used this argument in his letters, namely in his letter to Victricius, Bishop of Rouen, chapter 6; his letter to the bishops of Macedonia, chapter 2; his letter to the synod assembled in the city of Toledo, canon 6; and Epistle 23 to the bishops of the Council of Toledo.

The argument which Innocent repeats so often, by which he proves that even those who married a second time after baptism, following the death of their first wife, are bigamists, was brought against Jerome by a highly eloquent man, as Jerome himself reports in his letter to Oceanus. Among other things, the man said that a man is “the husband of one wife” if he has had wives one at a time.

[Col. 1130D]

> “The phrase ‘the husband of one wife’ can also be explained in another way. The Apostle was a Jew, and the first Church of Christ was gathered from the remnants of Israel. He knew that the Law permitted, and that the example of the patriarchs and of Moses had made it familiar to the people that children could be begotten from many wives. Even the priests themselves had the discretion to exercise this permission. He therefore commanded that the priests should not claim this same permission for the Church, nor take two or three wives at the same time, but should have one wife at a time.”

The bishops whom Tertullian criticizes rather harshly in *On Monogamy*, chapter 12, evidently did not reject this interpretation:

> “The Holy Spirit foresaw that some would say: ‘Everything is permitted to bishops,’ just as your man of Utica did not even fear the Scantinian vice (*scantinia*). For the fact that bigamists also preside among you, openly insulting the Apostle and certainly not blushing, is clear when these things are read under their authority.”

[Col. 1131A]

Nevertheless, he had earlier said in Book I *To His Wife*, chapter 7:

> “How greatly second marriages conflict with holiness is shown by the discipline of the Church and the Apostle’s prescription, since it does not permit bigamists to preside.”

And in *On the Exhortation to Chastity*, where he discourages second marriages, he mentions that certain bigamists had been removed from office. But he reports this as something altogether unusual:

> “Indeed,” he says in chapter 7, “I remember that certain bigamists were removed from office.”

It is likely that many more had presided in the Church, since Saint Jerome asserts that the whole world was full of such ordinations. As he says in his letter to Oceanus:

> “I do not speak of presbyters, nor of the lower orders; I come to bishops. If I wished to name them individually, such a number would be assembled that the multitude of the Council of Ariminum would be surpassed. But it is unbecoming to defend one in such a way that you seem to accuse many, and to defend by association with sinners one whom you cannot defend by reason.”

[Col. 1131B]

Who would believe Jerome if one reads what Saint Epiphanius, following Origen, says in Heresy 59: that, after Christ’s coming, the holy preaching of God does not admit those who, after their wives’ death, have entered a second marriage, on account of the exceptional honor and dignity of the priesthood?

One should observe, however, that testimonies of other Greek Fathers support Jerome’s opinion: Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 10 on the First Epistle of Paul to Timothy, chapter 3, and Theodoret. The latter, commenting on chapter 3 of the First Epistle to Timothy, reports the opinion of those who thought that a man who lives chastely with one wife alone is worthy to be ordained bishop, and that the Apostle did not reject second marriages. He then endeavors to confirm this by the authority of Saint Paul and finally declares that he prefers this interpretation to the others, in these words:

[Col. 1131C]

> “Ταῦτα καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα σκοπούμενος, ἀποδέχομαι τῶν οὕτω νενοηκότων τὴν ἑρμηνείαν.”
>
> “Considering these and similar matters, I accept the interpretation of those who have understood them in this way.”

The Latin Fathers who preceded Jerome themselves testify that many such bigamists had been ordained. For this reason the Fathers of the Council of Valence decided, canon 1, that nothing should be changed concerning the status of those who had previously been ordained.

Saint Ambrose, in Book I of *The Duties*, chapter 50, says that many people find it surprising that a second marriage before baptism should create impediments to election to office and to the privilege of ordination, when even crimes ordinarily do not hinder a person if they have been remitted through the sacrament of the bath. Nevertheless, he embraces the contrary opinion:

> “We must understand,” he says, “that guilt can be forgiven in baptism, but the law cannot be abolished. In marriage there is not guilt but law. Therefore whatever belongs to guilt is released in baptism; whatever belongs to law is not dissolved in marriage.”

[Col. 1131D]

Afterward nearly all the others spoke in the same way: Pope Siricius, in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona, chapters 9 and 10; Innocent I, in all the passages cited above; the Council of Carthage called the Fourth, canon 69; and Saint Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 18, whose words deserve attention:

> “Therefore the sacrament of marriage in our time has been restricted to one husband and one wife, so that no one may be ordained as a steward of the Church unless he is the husband of one wife. Those who judged that even a man who had taken another wife while still a catechumen or pagan should not be ordained understood this more acutely. For the matter concerns a sacrament, not a sin. In baptism all sins are forgiven.”

[Col. 1132A]

See Pope Leo I, in his letter to Anastasius, Bishop of Thessalonica, chapter 3; in his letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne, chapter 1; the Council of Orange, canon 25; the Council of Angers, canon 11; the Roman Council under Pope Hilary, canon 2; the Council of Agde, canon 1; and the Fourth Council of Arles, canon 3.

### We believe that no one is perfected in baptism

That is, one who is not completed by the other sacraments. Here Theodore speaks especially in agreement with the Latin Fathers. Tertullian, *On Baptism*, chapter 6:

> “Not that we receive the Holy Spirit in the waters, but, having been cleansed in the water, we are prepared for the Holy Spirit under the angel.”

[Col. 1132B]

Cornelius, in his letter to Fabius concerning Novatian, preserved by Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 63:

> “While he was lying on the bed on which he had been drenched, he received baptism—if indeed one should say that he received baptism of this kind. But after he had recovered from his illness, he did not receive the remaining things which, according to ecclesiastical rule, ought to be received; nor was he confirmed by the bishop. Since he had not received this seal, how could he possibly receive the Holy Spirit?”

Saint Cyprian, Epistle 74 to Pompey. An ancient author, whom the distinguished N. Rigaltius published together with Cyprian after the cited letter.

Cyprian and Jerome nevertheless do not deny that, when necessity compels it, divine concessions confer everything. Saint Cyprian says this also concerning those baptized while bedridden, in his letter to Magnus on the baptism of the Novatians, and concerning those who receive grace while confined to bed:

[Col. 1132C]

> “In the saving sacraments, when necessity compels and God grants his indulgence, divine concessions confer everything upon believers.”

What Cyprian says about those baptized while bedridden, Jerome affirms concerning those who had been baptized by presbyters or deacons in more remote places and had died before being confirmed by the bishop. Thus Saint Jerome speaks excellently in *Against the Luciferians*:

> “If you ask at this point why someone baptized in the Church does not receive the Holy Spirit unless through the hands of the bishop, although we assert that the Spirit is given in true baptism, learn that this observance derives from the authority of the fact that, after the Lord’s ascension, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. We find the same thing practiced in many places, more for the honor of the priesthood than from the necessity of the law. Otherwise, if the Holy Spirit descends only at the bishop’s invocation, we should mourn for those who, having been baptized by presbyters and deacons in prisons, fortresses, or more remote places, died before bishops could visit them.”

[Col. 1132D]

Therefore Theodore says in chapter 4:

> “We believe that no one is perfected without the bishop’s confirmation; nevertheless, we do not despair.”

### We do not dispute the bishop’s confirmation

Here Theodore, a Greek by nation, appears to indicate the opinion of the Greek Fathers, who say that baptism signifies three things: immersion, by which a person is imbued with faith; submersion, by which he is cleansed of filth and stains; and emergence, by which he rises again. Accordingly, they call it illumination, washing, perfection, and “perfect,” since nothing is lacking from it.

After Saint Justin, at the end of the *Second Apology* in the printed editions—which is the first according to Eusebius; Saint Theophilus of Antioch, *To Autolycus*, Book II, against the detractors of the Christian religion; and Saint Irenaeus, Book II *Against Heresies*, chapter 19—Saint Clement of Alexandria explains this most clearly in Book I of the *Pedagogue*, chapter 6:

[Col. 1133A]

> “This same thing happens to us also, whose model was the Lord. Having been immersed, we are illuminated; having been illuminated, we are adopted as sons; having been adopted, we are perfected; having been perfected, we are made immortal. This work is called by many names: grace, illumination, perfection, and washing. It is called washing because through it we wash away sins; grace because through it the punishments due to sins are remitted; illumination because through it we behold that holy and saving light—that is, through it we perceive what is divine; and perfection because we call that perfect which lacks nothing.”

Many other Greek Fathers agree with these statements: Origen, *Commentary on John*, volume II of Huet’s edition, page 124; Saint Athanasius, in the *Oration against the Arians*, in the words “God is the Word”; Saint Basil, in his homily on baptism and in Sermon 2, chapter 1; Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, in his oration on holy baptism; and others.

It must nevertheless be admitted that the Fathers of the Council of Laodicea appear to speak differently in canon 48.

### Nevertheless, chrism was established at the Council of Nicaea

This is not found among the decrees of the Council of Nicaea. There are, however, certain matters that are not found among the twenty canons, such as the decree concerning the feast of Easter, preserved by Eusebius and Athanasius, and the decree concerning the acts of the earlier synod being examined in a later synod, which Pope Julius mentions in a letter reported by Saint Athanasius in the *Second Apology*.

[Col. 1133C]

These decrees, commended by Fathers who attended the synod or who lived at nearly the same time, possess the greatest authority. Those supported only by later testimony have less authority, or almost none, such as the decrees found in Gregory of Tours and others—for example, the decree concerning the letters of commendation, reported by more recent writers. It is very uncertain from whom they received these materials.

But it is difficult to determine to what class of decrees this establishment should be assigned. For how could chrism have been established at the Council of Nicaea when Tertullian, the most ancient author, speaks of it in *On Baptism*, chapter 7, and in other places?

[Col. 1133D]

I therefore do not see what Theodore means here, unless perhaps he understands it as what was established by Pope Sylvester around the time of the Council of Nicaea, described in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*:

> “He also established that the presbyter should anoint with chrism the baptized person raised from the water, on account of the danger of death.”

The meaning would therefore be this: “We do not dispute the bishop’s confirmation; nevertheless, Pope Sylvester established, and the Council of Nicaea did not reject, that presbyters should anoint the baptized with an anointing of chrism”—an anointing which the Fathers of the Council of Orange decided should not be repeated.

[Col. 1134A]

Hence perhaps certain people, prompted also by the authority of Saint Gregory, said that in cases of necessity, and in certain places, the power of confirmation had been granted to presbyters.

### Selections from the manuscript book *On the Sacraments* by Master Peter the Chanter of Paris, on confirmation, chapter 30

After baptism, which is the gateway of the sacraments, confirmation follows. Concerning this the first question is how, since it belonged specifically to the disciples alone and afterward to their successors, and is therefore numbered among the sacraments of dignity, Gregory permitted simple priests to celebrate it because of urgent necessity arising from a shortage of bishops.

[Note: Gregory I, Book III, Epistle 26, to Januarius, Bishop of Cagliari: “But if some are altogether troubled about this matter, where bishops are lacking we grant that presbyters too should touch those who have been baptized on the forehead with chrism.”]

For we have neither heard nor believed that, in the case of the other sacraments, the power to celebrate them can be extended or restricted according to the rank and condition of the persons who confer them. How, then, could an extension beyond the aforesaid limits, followed later by a return to the original state, have occurred uniquely in this sacrament?

[Col. 1134B]

Again, one must consider that when this one change was made, it was made for an evident and certain reason. But suppose that today the presbyters of some region or province, lacking access to a bishop, should demand such a concession from the supreme pontiff and obtain it, while others allege an equal or somewhat greater necessity and do not obtain it. I therefore ask whether, in this matter, the authority of the one granting the dispensation should prevail or be taken into account, or the reason for the dispensation, or both equally.

### Selections from the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbure, Book III, chapter 1

[Col. 1134C]

Ministers of the Church are instituted not by just anyone but by their own bishop or by a priest—for example, the order of psalmist, or the person called a *corona* among us and a *clericus* among the Lombards. Formerly this office was conferred by a simple priest, and even today it is conferred in Alemannia. In former times simple priests also administered confirmation.

### Individuals may act as sponsors

Tertullian calls those who receive children at baptism sponsors, in *On Baptism*, chapter 17:

> “For what need is there to expose sponsors also to danger?”

This authority demonstrates that the use of sponsors in baptism is extremely ancient in the Church.

What the duty of sponsors is, however, is taught by the Fathers of the Council of Calchuth, canon 2, and of the Sixth Council of Paris, canon 7:

[Col. 1134D]

> “How those who receive others from the sacred font ought to instruct them is shown by blessed Augustine in a sermon delivered to the people, where he says: ‘Therefore, whatever men and whatever women have spiritually received children from the sacred font should recognize that they have become their guarantors before God. It is necessary, therefore, that they always show them the concern of true charity, admonish them, discipline them, and correct them, so that they may preserve chastity, keep virginity until marriage, and devote themselves to the other good works. In this matter, which is under discussion, it must not be ignored how far the practice has departed from the Christian religion.’”

## CHAPTER V. On the Mass for the dead

[Col. 1135A]

### According to the Roman Church

So that I may not be more prolix in reviewing the rites of the Roman Church concerning burials, and of the African Church, which followed the Roman Church in most matters, see Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 40; *On Idolatry*, chapter 11; the letter of the Roman clergy to the Carthaginian clergy concerning Cyprian’s withdrawal, which is numbered 2 among his letters; Cyprian’s Epistle 37 in Rigaltius’s edition; the acts of Cyprian’s martyrdom, which Pontius mentions; Saint Ambrose, at the end of *On Widows*, in Epistle 85 to his sister, and in *On Tobit*, chapter 1; Saint Jerome, at the end of the epitaph for his mother Paula, addressed to the virgin Eustochium; at the end of the epitaph for Fabiola, addressed to Oceanus; and at the end of the *Life of Paul the Hermit*; the Council of Valence, canon 4; and the Second Council of Orléans, canon 6.

### Although Dionysius the Areopagite says this

The meaning of the words can be gathered from chapter 7 of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. Although Theodore cites it under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, one might rightly doubt whether he considered it to be by Dionysius himself, since he prefers the opinion of Saint Augustine to that of this author.

Whatever the case may be, as soon as these books appeared, they were brought forward against the Catholics by the Severians and were rejected by the Catholics as wholly unknown to antiquity. This is clear from the conference held at Constantinople between the Catholics and the Severians in the time of the Emperor Justinian:

[Col. 1135C]

> “Those testimonies which you call the writings of Dionysius the Areopagite—how can you show that they are genuine, as you suppose? If they were his, they could not have remained unknown to blessed Cyril. But why do I speak of blessed Cyril? If blessed Athanasius had known with certainty that they were his, he would have brought forward these testimonies above all at the Council of Nicaea concerning the consubstantial Trinity, against the blasphemies of Arius concerning a different substance. But if none of the ancients remembered them, how can you now show that they are his? I do not know.”

See the book of John Launoy, the most learned doctor of Paris, *On the Two Dionysiuses*.

### Augustine nevertheless says that prayers are to be made for all Christians

In *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, chapter 4:

[Col. 1135D]

> “But even if some necessity permits bodies to be buried, or to be buried in such places, when no opportunity is given [for the customary arrangements], prayers for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted. These prayers are to be made for all the deceased within the Christian and Catholic fellowship, even without mentioning their names, whom the Church has received under a general commemoration.”

The reason for this can be drawn from what Saint Augustine says elsewhere, in Book XXI, chapter 27 of *The City of God*, addressed to Marcellinus:

> “What this mode is, and what those sins themselves are which so impede entry into the kingdom of God that nevertheless forgiveness may be obtained through the merits of holy friends, is extremely difficult to discover and most dangerous to define. For my part, although I have labored over this matter up to the present, I have not been able to reach a determination concerning it.”

And it is not lawful for a presbyter or [Col. 1136A] deacon to celebrate Mass if he is not permitted, or does not wish, to receive Communion. Canon 8 of the Canons under the name of the Apostles states: “If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or anyone listed among the priests, after making the offering does not communicate, let him state his reason, etc.” At that time it was not only unlawful for a presbyter to celebrate Mass; the other faithful were likewise forbidden to attend the divine mysteries unless they intended to receive Communion. See Saint Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*; canon 9 of the Canons under the name of the Apostles; the Council of Antioch, canon 2; and the Council of Toledo, canon 13: “Concerning those who enter the church and are found never to communicate: they shall be admonished, so that, if they do not communicate, they may approach penance; if they do communicate, they shall not be kept from it; if they do not comply, they shall be excluded.”

[Col. 1136B] Some interpret these canons as referring to those who, for a definite reason—namely, because of some superstition or erroneous opinion—shrank from Communion in the sacraments. But every semblance of such a distinction is dispelled by John Chrysostom, who speaks as follows in homily 3 on chapter 2 of Paul’s Epistle to the Ephesians: “Are you unworthy of the sacrifice and of participation? Then you are unworthy also of prayer. Do you hear the herald standing and saying: ‘All of you who are doing penance, depart’? All who do not participate are doing penance. For whoever does not participate is doing penance.”

## CHAPTER VI. On abbots, monks, and monasteries

The community must choose its own abbot. Gregory [Col. 1136C] I, book IV, letter 43: “We wish you to appoint as abbot of that monastery not someone else, but the man whom the entire community, by common consent, has demanded as worthy in character and conduct of monastic discipline.” And book VII, letter 18: “When the abbot of any community has died, let no outsider be appointed, unless he belongs to the same way of life, but let the united brotherhood freely choose for itself someone whom it wishes; and let the man who has been chosen be appointed without fraud or any form of bribery. If they are unable to find a suitable person among themselves, let them diligently choose someone from another monastery for appointment in the same manner.” See the Council of Aachen, chapter 32. That Louis the Pious issued the same command is reported by the charters of the monastery of Piscaria, or the Abbey of Saint Clement, which are now preserved in the Royal Library: “The emperor issued [Col. 1136D] an ordinance concerning the election of the abbot, that no one should be chosen from an outside community; but whenever the abbot who presides has died, the brothers shall have permission to choose an abbot from their own community. Whoever violates this shall know that he is appointing not a shepherd but a wolf, and that punishment awaits him at the final judgment.”

An abbot or bishop may not alienate the church’s land. Except with the counsel of the brothers, as he adds below. The same rule concerning the Church’s property is prescribed in the Fourth Council of Carthage, or rather in the ancient statutes of the Church. This is the title borne by the codices of the monastery of Gembloux, of Saint Bavo at Ghent, and by several manuscripts of excellent quality. Canon 32 reads as follows [Col. 1137A]: “A donation, sale, or exchange of ecclesiastical property by bishops without the concurrence and subscription of the clergy is invalid.” See the letter of Pope Hilary to the bishops of the various provinces of Gaul, chapter 5; the Council of Agde, canon 45; and the Council of Hertford, presided over by Theodore, canon 3, in Bede, book IV, chapter 3. What the ancient statutes of the Church determine concerning church property applies equally to other matters. For just as the clergy ought to do nothing without the bishop, so the bishop did nothing without the clergy, to such an extent that a bishop’s judgment was invalid unless it was confirmed by the presence of the clergy, in accordance with the same ancient statutes of the Church, canon 14.

Men may not keep women as nuns. The Fathers very frequently prohibited this, both in their writings [Col. 1137B] and in the decrees of councils. Thus the Fathers of the Second Council of Seville say, canon 11: “Far be it from us to wish monks—even the thought is unspeakable—to be intimate with Christ’s virgins. Rather, in accordance with what the commands of rules and canons prescribe, we assign them to their care while keeping them far apart and separated, establishing that one of the most approved monks should be chosen to be responsible for them, etc.” And Egbert, archbishop of York, says: “The holy Fathers Augustine, Jerome, Basil, Gregory, and many others prohibited this by their decrees.”

Nevertheless, let us not abolish what is customary in this land. The Council of Valence explains through several [Col. 1137C] examples how matters are to be handled which cannot be accepted because of the holiness of the Church, yet cannot be condemned merely because they have become customary: “Therefore,” say the Fathers in their synodal letter to all the bishops of Gaul, “after long and carefully balanced deliberation, a precautionary course was maintained which would both remove scandals and preserve the holiness of the Church.”

A monk may not make a vow without the abbot’s consent; otherwise the vow must be broken. Saint Basil gives the reason in his *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 27, in these words: “A monk ought not to possess even for a moment the power of himself by which he may conduct his private affairs. For just as, when the craftsman is absent, an instrument would not move of its own accord, and just as a limb could not be separated or moved, even for the briefest moment, from a body without the will of the craftsman within it and of the governor of the whole body [Col. 1137D] of the whole body, so likewise it is not lawful to do or carry out anything pertaining to the observance of religion without the judgment of one’s superior.” Therefore those vows of a monk are invalid which do not lie within his own jurisdiction but depend upon the abbot’s authority. Master Robert of Flamesbury judged in the same way in his *Penitential*.

### Selections from the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbury, book II, chapter 4

Anyone who has jurisdiction over himself may make a vow—and, as I think, as soon as he is capable of deceit. A person subject to another cannot make a vow without that person’s consent: thus a monk cannot vow without the consent of his abbot, nor a woman without the consent of her husband, nor a daughter, while she is under her father’s authority, without his [Col. 1138A] consent; perhaps a slave likewise cannot vow without his master’s consent, nor can he make any vow to the master’s prejudice. Nevertheless, every such person has some member of his own body concerning which he can make a vow without another’s consent: thus a woman may vow that she will not demand her marital debt from her husband. If, however, any of the persons mentioned, or anyone similar to them, makes a vow with the consent of his or her superior, that superior, after considering the matter, can revoke the vow. Thus, if a woman makes a vow with her husband’s consent, the husband can revoke it after considering the matter, and she is bound to obey. The same applies to a monk and his abbot; concerning others, the matter is not equally certain.

It is also within the monastery’s liberty to wash the feet of laypeople; except that they are not compelled to do so on Maundy Thursday. And below: The Roman custom does not include this washing of feet. Saint Augustine explains why some did not adopt this custom and others removed it. Thus, in letter 119, chapter 18 [Col. 1138B]:

“Concerning the washing of feet, since the Lord commended this as an example of humility, which he had come to teach, just as he subsequently explained it himself, the question arose at what time so great a matter could most suitably be taught also by an action, and at what time the commendation itself might take deeper religious root. But, lest it appear to pertain to the sacrament of baptism itself, many refused to adopt it as a custom. Others did not hesitate to remove it from customary practice.”

And in the *Exposition of the Gospel of John*, tractate 58:

“Wherever this custom does not exist among holy people, what they do not perform with the hand, they perform in the heart.”

The ancient author of the *Book of the Sacraments* [Col. 1138C], cited under Ambrose, book III, chapter 1, praises this practice of washing to the greatest extent and reproaches the Roman Church for not having it:

“We are not unaware,” he says, “that the Roman Church does not have this custom, although in everything we follow its model and pattern. Yet it does not have the custom of washing feet. Consider, therefore, whether perhaps it has departed from it because of the multitude.” And shortly afterward: “What does the Roman Church answer to this?”

But the Roman Church’s answer is ready. For whoever this author may be, he must be counted among the simple and more rustic people who cling too closely to the letter. Origen speaks of such people in his *Commentary on John*, tome II of Huet’s edition, page 331:

“So much so that for this reason the Lord himself also comes to wash the feet of a believing servant [Col. 1138D], etc. This practice is now observed only among the exceedingly simple and rustic.”

And in homily 6 on Isaiah:

“No one who takes up a towel for just anyone who comes—whether deacon, presbyter, or bishop—washes his feet.”
