Nevertheless, afterward the Fathers of the Seventeenth Council of Toledo decreed that Christ’s example should be observed as though it were a chief Gospel command, to such an extent that “if,” they say in canon 3, “any priest should delay fulfilling this decree of ours, let him know that he will be deprived of receiving holy Communion for two months.” And earlier in the same canon:

“Finally, although the example of holy action shines forth, in some churches the priests do not wash the feet [Col. 1139A] of the brothers on Maundy Thursday, partly through negligence and partly through custom. They offer no other excuse than the custom of tradition alone, although Truth rebukes them, saying: ‘Why do you transgress God’s commandment because of your tradition?’”

See the Council of Aachen, canon 23.

Nor is it within the monastery’s liberty to judge the penance of secular people, since this properly belongs to the clergy. The Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon forbid monks to involve themselves in ecclesiastical or secular affairs. Canon 4:

“Monks in every region and city are to be subject to the bishop, to embrace quiet, to devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer, and to persevere firmly in the places where they have been established; they are not to involve themselves in either ecclesiastical or secular affairs, etc.”

The Council of Tarragona, canon 11:

“We forbid monks leaving the monastery [Col. 1139B] to presume to perform any ecclesiastical ministry, except perhaps by the command of the abbot.”

## CHAPTER VII. On women’s conduct in church and in ministry

Women shall not veil the altar, etc. Saint Epiphanius, against the Collyridians, heresy 79:

“If women had been commanded to sacrifice to God or to perform any administrative function in the Church, then Mary herself ought rather to have performed the sacrifice in the New Testament—she who was made worthy to receive within her own womb the King and God of all things, the heavenly Son of God, whose womb became a temple and dwelling place [Col. 1139C], prepared by God’s goodness for the Lord’s dispensation in the flesh and for the wondrous mystery. But this was not pleasing to him; nor was she entrusted with administering baptism. Otherwise Christ could have been baptized by her rather than by John.”

The ancient author of the *Constitutions* uses a similar argument, book III, chapter 4.

Women may receive the offering under a black veil. Therefore they were not permitted to receive the Eucharist with an uncovered hand, nor even to place their hand upon the Lord’s cloth. The Council of Auxerre, canon 36: “A woman may not receive the Eucharist with an uncovered hand.” And canon 37: “A woman may not place her hand upon the Lord’s cloth.” Earlier, too, the Fathers of the Council of Laodicea had decreed, canon 19, that only those who had been consecrated might approach the altar and communicate.

Nevertheless, testimonies of the Fathers prove that in most places the Eucharist was commonly received with the uncovered hand. [Col. 1139D] They frequently admonish the faithful to recognize that the right hand which is brought near Christ’s body is consecrated, as are the tongue and the heart. See Clement of Alexandria, book I of the *Stromata*; Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 7; Saint Cyprian, letter 56, to the Thibaritans, *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, and *On the Good of Patience*; the outstanding fragment of letter 5 of Dionysius of Alexandria to Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome, in Eusebius, book VII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 9; Saint Cyril of Jerusalem, in the *Catechetical Lectures*; Saint Gregory Nazianzen, oration 11, in praise of Gorgonia; Saint John Chrysostom, homily 21, to the people of Antioch; and Ambrose, in the oration in which he rebukes the emperor Theodosius, reported by Theodoret, book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17. See also above, the notes on chapter 3.

[Col. 1140A] A woman may make offerings according to the Greeks, but not according to the Romans. This is not to be understood of the offerings of all the faithful—that is, alms, among which were loaves intended to be consecrated for the Eucharist—as the distinguished N. Rigalt observed in Saint Cyprian’s *On Works and Almsgiving*. The same is clear from Saint Augustine’s letter 122. Rather, it refers, as the title indicates, to a certain ecclesiastical ministry to which the Greeks admitted women and from which the Romans at that time excluded them.

The Council of Orange, canon 26:

“Deaconesses are in no way to be ordained; if any already exist, let them bow their heads to the blessing bestowed upon the people.”

The Council of Epaon, canon 21:

“We completely abolish throughout our entire region [Col. 1140B] the consecration of widows whom they call deaconesses.”

Some codices read: “from every religious order.”

The Second Council of Orléans, canon 18:

“It has also seemed good that henceforth no woman should be entrusted with the diaconal blessing, because of the weakness inherent in this condition.”

The Council of Tours, canon 20, proves the same by the authority of the Fathers of Epaon already cited. Nevertheless, in the earliest centuries the discipline of the entire Church enrolled them in an order, as Tertullian testifies in book I *To His Wife*, chapter 7:

“The discipline of the Church and the Apostle’s prescription make this clear: it does not permit a bigamist to preside, and it does not allow a widow to be enrolled in the order unless she has had one husband.”

See also the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 12, or rather the ancient statutes of the Church, canon 100. Furthermore, the Fathers explain what sort of ecclesiastical order [Col. 1140C] and honor women were admitted to. See Clement of Alexandria, book III of the *Stromata*; Origen, *Commentary on John*, tome II, page 90, Huet’s edition; and the Council of Nicaea, canon 19, where Gabriel Albaspinaeus, the distinguished bishop of Orléans, proves against Baronius that they had been properly and regularly consecrated:

“For when,” he says, “the synod judges that certain women who had been instituted less properly and outside the order are to be counted among the laity, it plainly leaves it to be understood that there were some who had been consecrated properly and according to due order.”

Saint Basil, canonical letter to Amphilochius, canon 44; Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *Life of Saint Macrina*. Saint Epiphanius, cited above, does not contradict their opinion; indeed, in the same passage he openly affirms it when he says: “And there is an order of deaconesses in the Church, etc.” The ancient author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* holds the same view, book VIII, chapter 19, where he declares that presbyters, deacons, and deaconesses are ordained by the laying on of the bishop’s hands. See the Council of Chalcedon, canon 15, δεξαμένη τὴν χειροθεσίαν [Col. 1140D] (“having received the laying on of hands”); the Council of Trullo, or Quinisext Council, canon 40; and Sedulius, on chapter 16 of the Epistle to the Romans. This author, writing around the ninth century, testifies that only in the Eastern regions did deaconesses minister. From this the various rites reported everywhere by Theodore can be recognized.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the customs of the Greeks and Romans

And they work even on Sunday. They worked on Sunday [Col. 1141A], including nuns, as Jerome testifies in his letter to the virgin Eustochium, concerning the epitaph of Paula, her mother:

“Only on Sunday did they go forth to church, which stood beside their dwelling, and each group followed its own mother; then, returning together from there, they applied themselves to the work assigned to them, making clothing either for themselves or for the others.”

Work which distracted people from prayer and the worship of God was prohibited by Constantine, who was the first to order a day of rest, as Eusebius reports in book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 18. This was later confirmed by several synodal decrees, though in such a way that Christians would not Judaize, as the Fathers of the Third Council of Orléans admonish, canon 28:

“Since the peoples have been persuaded that on Sunday they ought not to travel with horses, oxen, or vehicles, nor engage at all in preparing anything for food [Col. 1141B] or anything pertaining to the cleanliness of the house or of a person—which practice is shown to belong more to Jewish than to Christian observance—we decree that on Sunday whatever was previously permitted shall remain permitted, etc.”

The same is read in the Council of Vernus, canon 14. Those who defended this Jewish observance are so thoroughly refuted by Saint Gregory the Great that he attacks them as though they were preachers of Antichrist, book XI, letter 3:

“It has come to my attention,” he says, “that certain men of perverse spirit have sown among you various things that are wrong and contrary to the holy faith, so that they forbade working on the Sabbath. What else should I call them but preachers of Antichrist? For when he comes, he will cause both the Sabbath and Sunday to be kept from all work.”

See book I of the *Capitularies*, chapter 71 [Col. 1141C], and Regino, book I *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 372, from a capitulary of Charles:

“Three kinds of cart-work may be done on Sunday: military wagons, provisions, or transport service; and, if it should happen to be necessary, the body of anyone may be carried to the grave.”

Hence it is clear that the better reading is “even on Sunday,” rather than “except on Sunday.”

Greek monks do not have slaves; Roman monks do. Concerning the slaves of Roman monks, see the Council of Agde, chapter 56, and the Council of Epaon, canon 8.

Romans eat; Greeks, after Mass has been said in the evening, dine. Saint Augustine provides a particularly notable rule concerning this differing custom when consulted in letter 118, chapter 5 [Col. 1141D]:

“To this I answer as follows: if the authority of divine Scripture prescribes what is to be done in any of these matters, there must be no doubt that we ought to do what we read, so that the question is no longer how it is to be done, but how the sacrament is to be understood. Likewise, if something is practiced by the whole Church throughout the world, then it is the height of insane arrogance to debate whether it ought to be done. But neither the one nor the other applies to what you are asking. It remains, therefore, that it belongs to that third category which varies according to places and regions. Let each person do what he finds practiced in the Church to which he has come. None of these things is done contrary to the faith or to better customs on either side. For these are the reasons—namely, faith or morals [Col. 1142A]—for correcting what was wrongly done or instituting what was not done. For a change in custom, even one that is beneficial, disturbs by its novelty. Consequently, what is not beneficial is, through its fruitless disturbance, harmful as well.”

## CHAPTER IX. On the communion of the Scots and Britons, who are not Catholic in Easter and tonsure

Those who are not united with the Church in the Catholic observance of Easter or tonsure. Bede describes the origin and cause of this schism at length in book II of his *History*, chapter 25. Among many passages, the following few may be cited:

“When the dispute had ended and the assembly had been dismissed, Agilbert returned home. Colman, seeing that his teaching had been rejected [Col. 1142B] and his party despised, took with him those who wished to follow him—that is, those who refused to accept the Catholic Easter and the tonsure in the form of a crown, for there was also a considerable dispute concerning this—and returned to Scotland to discuss with his people what ought to be done about these matters, etc.”

This dispute occurred in the year 664 of the Lord’s incarnation, which was the twenty-second year of King Oswiu; the episcopate of the Scots, however, which they held in the province of the English, had lasted thirty years. See also the selected chapters from the ancient Collection of Irish Canons, published by R. D. Luc d’Achery in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*. There the following is extracted from book I, chapter 6:

“Concerning the tonsure of the Britons, Gildas says [Col. 1142C]: ‘The Britons, contrary to the whole world and hostile to Roman customs, serve the shadows of things to come rather than the truth, according to the Romans, not only in the Mass but also in their tonsure, like the Jews. The Romans’ tonsure touched only from ear to ear; in the excellence of that very form, it was the tonsure of the magicians, by which only the front of the forehead used to be covered, according to the earlier practice. But the author of this tonsure in Ireland was Subulcus, son of King Loigaire, as Patrick’s statement testifies; from him nearly all the Irish took this tonsure.’”

But Bede, book V, chapter 21, reports the letter of Abbot Ceolfrid to Naiton, who judges the question of the tonsure as follows:

“But if we are free to confess this, the difference in tonsure does no harm to those whose faith in God is pure and whose charity toward their neighbor is sincere—especially since we never read that the Catholic Fathers had any controversy about the difference in tonsure comparable to their disputes concerning the difference in Easter [Col. 1142D] or in the faith.”

The same was once the judgment of many ancient Fathers concerning the question of Easter, as their writings sufficiently and abundantly show, especially those of Irenaeus preserved in Eusebius, book V, chapter 24, and the letter of Firmilian to Saint Cyprian, published among Saint Cyprian’s letters. That question, however, was settled by the decree of the Council of Nicaea, which thereafter all Catholics embraced with unanimous agreement. See Eusebius, book III of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 19; Saint Athanasius, *On the Councils* and *To the Africans*; Saint Epiphanius, heresy 70; Saint John Chrysostom, oration 52, tome V; and Theodoret, book I, chapter 8.

## CHAPTER X. On those afflicted by the devil

[Col. 1143A]

And we did not dare to pray for him. The Second Council of Orléans, canon 15:

“We decree that the offerings of the dead who were killed while involved in some crime ought to be received, provided that they are not shown to have inflicted death upon themselves with their own hands.”

The Second Council of Braga, canon 16:

“It has likewise seemed good that for those who inflict violent death upon themselves, whether by the sword, poison, falling, hanging [Col. 1143B], or any other means, no commemoration be made for them in the offering, nor should their bodies be carried to burial with psalms. For many have presumed to do this through ignorance.”

The Council of Auxerre, canon 17:

“Whoever by his own will throws himself into water, ties a noose around his neck, casts himself from a tree, strikes himself with iron, or by any voluntary occasion gives himself over to death, such a person’s offering shall not be received.”

The same judgment is found in the *Judgments of Gregory III*, chapter 32, and in the *Capitularies*, book VII, chapter 334. See Halitgar, book IV, chapter 6; Regino, book II *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*, chapter 92. Shortly afterward Theodore adds:

“Masses may not be celebrated for one who has killed himself by his own will; one may only pray and distribute alms for him.”

Master Robert of Flamesbury follows this judgment in his *Penitential*.

### Selections from the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbury, book IV

Concerning one who kills himself or hangs himself by a noose. [Col. 1143C] It must be considered that, if a relative wishes to give alms, he should give them and offer prayers in the recitation of the psalms; but he should refrain from offerings and Masses.

“Whoever by his own will throws himself into water, ties his neck, casts himself from a tree, strikes himself in a frenzy, or by any voluntary occasion gives himself over to death, such a person’s offering shall not be received. You said: ‘The betrayer perished by a noose and left a noose for such people.’ This does not concern us at all; for we do not venerate as martyrs those who have tied a noose around their own neck. It has been decided that for such people, etc.”

From canon 16 of the Second Council of Braga.

If someone, overcome by a sudden temptation, loses control of his mind or kills himself through insanity, some celebrate Masses for him. Theophilus of Alexandria, in his canonical responses, to question 14 [Col. 1143D]:

“If someone, while not in possession of his faculties, lays hands upon himself or even throws himself from a height, is an offering to be made for him or not?

“Answer: The cleric must discern whether he truly did this while his mind was disturbed. Often those connected with the person to whom this happened, wishing to obtain an offering and prayer for him, lie and say that he was not himself. Sometimes, however, he may have done it because of people’s insults or in some other way through negligence. In that case an offering must not be made for him, for he is his own murderer. The cleric must therefore inquire carefully, lest he fall under judgment.”

The Council of Orange, canon 13 [Col. 1144A]:

“Whatever belongs to piety is to be granted to the insane.”

The distinguished J. Sirmond observed that an offering could be made for one who had taken his own life through insanity, and confirms this by the response of Timothy of Alexandria, canon 13. Since the question here concerns the sin of a madman, it will not be out of place to present the opinion of Master Praepositivus, a man who in his time stood among the scholastics at the highest rank, who resolves the entire difficulty in his *Summa* by the authority of Gregory I.

### Selections from the manuscript *Summa* of Praepositivus, on the sin of a madman

“As inquiry is made concerning offenses, so inquiry is made concerning things done while the mind is alienated, or in nocturnal sleep, as to whether they are imputable. It seems that they are not, because Augustine says: ‘We know that some people, suddenly becoming insane, overwhelmed many with sword, club, and stones, and killed some; but when captured and brought before a judge [Col. 1144B], they were not made guilty, because they had done this not by their own will but under the impulse of some force I know not what.’ Likewise Augustine says: ‘Who sins in what he cannot avoid?’—as though he were saying, ‘No one.’ Again: ‘If concupiscence, which dwells in the dying members, is without guilt in the mind or body of one who sleeps, how much more is it without guilt in the body of one who does not consent.’ Therefore, whether someone was mentally deranged or acted in a dream, it is not imputed. But the answer is that these statements are to be understood when someone has not come into this necessity through his own fault.”

And below:

“It is the common opinion of the masters that those things are imputed in which a person comes into the situation through his own fault. This is proved by the authority of blessed Gregory, who distinguishes nocturnal illusion: if it comes to you from an excess of nature [Col. 1144C] or from weakness, it is not to be feared; if it comes from guilt, the priest is barred from consecrating the sacrament, though not from receiving it, unless necessity requires that divine services be celebrated by him.”

[Col. 1144D]

## CHAPTER XI. On questions concerning marriage

Those who are married shall abstain for three nights. Saint Augustine, book II *Against Julian the Pelagian*, drawing from Saint Ambrose’s book *On Philosophy*:

“Self-indulgence is the mother of all vices, and it turns even lawful things into vice. Therefore the Apostle not only withdraws us from fornication but also teaches a certain restraint within marriage and prescribes times for prayer. For one who is excessive in marriage is nothing other than a kind of adulterer against his wife.”

The *Excerpta* of Egbert, archbishop of York, canon 110:

“Those who are married shall abstain for three nights before they communicate, and for one night after they have communicated. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Do not defraud one another, except by agreement, for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.’”

Bede, *Remedies for Sins*, chapter 10:

“Those who are married shall abstain for three Lents, and on Sunday night, Saturday, Wednesday, and Tuesday, if they are lawfully married; and they shall abstain for three nights before they communicate.”

See Regino, book I *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*, chapter 331, from a *Penitential*. See also the ancient *Penitential* books, especially the Second and Third of Angers, in the appendix to the learned J. Morin’s book *On Penance*. To these I shall add what I selected from an old manuscript belonging to the distinguished Wion, lord of Hérouval, concerning penalties to be imposed for sins, and from the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbury.

[Col. 1145A]

### Selections from the old manuscript of the distinguished Wion, lord of Hérouval, concerning penalties to be imposed for sins

“Those who have wives shall abstain from them for forty days before Easter and Christmas, and every Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday. Whoever does not abstain on Sunday shall do penance for seven days.”

### Selections from the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbury, book IV, chapter 6

“If a wife is taken for the purpose of having children, not much time seems to have been granted for the act itself [Col. 1145B], since feast days and procession days, as well as the very nature of childbirth and conception, show according to the law that it ought to cease during those periods.”

And below:

“Let the husband not use force against his wife, thinking that intercourse is permitted at every time during marriage. Whoever renders the marital debt to his wife cannot devote himself to prayer, nor eat of the flesh of the Lamb. If the loaves of the Presence could not be eaten by those who had touched their wives, how much more may that bread which descended from heaven not be violated or touched by those who shortly before had clung to marital embraces. This is not because we condemn marriage, but because at the time when we are going to eat the flesh of the Lamb, we ought to abstain from fleshly intercourse.”

Forty days before Easter. John the Faster, bishop of Constantinople, in his *Penitential* booklet [Col. 1145C], exceedingly famous among the Greeks, published by the learned J. Morin in the appendix to his book *On Penance*:

“When,” he says, “there are some who, because of the violence of long-established habit, cannot restrain themselves from sins even during the great Lent—as is often the case even with those who have wives—it is necessary that they, after completing their penances, even if many years pass and they have no way to communicate because they continually fall into sins, should restrain themselves from sin at least throughout the whole holy Lent, and communicate with fear and trembling on the three days of Easter. We say this hesitantly because they cannot abstain from carnal defilements, not because this is done according to some other distinction concerning Communion. If, however, during the great Lent such people fall into self-indulgence [Col. 1145D], they should not communicate even then. For if the holy Fathers decreed that those who are subject to that pitiable sickness and disorder of the soul which dominates everyone and is exceedingly difficult to abandon should be barred from Communion for only forty days, how much more must this be observed during Lent, since they prescribed it concerning the other ordinary days of the year?”

Bede, *Remedies for Sins*, chapter 2:

“A married man shall abstain for forty days of the year before Easter and Christmas, and every Sunday, etc.”

And chapter 10:

“Whoever has intercourse with his wife during Lent before Easter and refuses to abstain shall do penance for one year, or pay his fine to the church, or distribute it among the poor, or pay twenty-six solidi.”

The capitulary of Theodulf of Orléans, chapter 143 [Col. 1146A]:

“For one must abstain from one’s spouse during these most sacred days and live chastely and piously, so that these holy days may be passed with heart and body sanctified, and so that one may reach the holy day of Easter. For a fast polluted by marital intercourse is almost worthless, and neither prayers, vigils, nor almsgiving commend it.”

Hence Master Robert of Flamesbury says in his *Penitential* that it is not lawful to contract marriage during Advent or Lent.

### Selections from the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbury, book II, chapters 4 and 13

“The time of festivals and an ecclesiastical interdict impede marriage, because during Advent, Lent, and an ecclesiastical interdict [Col. 1146B] people do not contract marriage—that is, marriages ought not to be contracted. Nevertheless, whatever marriages have been contracted shall stand.”

And chapter 13:

“Whoever has intercourse with his wife during Lent and refuses to abstain from her shall do penance for one year, or give the equivalent—namely, twenty-five solidi—to the church, or distribute it among the poor. If it occurred through drunkenness and without habitual practice, he shall do penance for forty days.”

Hence the Apostle says, “so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.” On the authority of this testimony of Paul, many Fathers proved that married persons ought for a certain period to abstain from intercourse before they participate in the Church’s prayers, the Eucharist, or other sacraments. Tertullian, *On Prayer*, chapter 14; Origen, *Homily VI on Matthew*; Peter of Alexandria, in his canonical epistle; Gregory of Nyssa, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, oration 1; Hilary the deacon, in his *Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, chapter 7, among the works of Saint Ambrose; Saint John Chrysostom, on Matthew 6, homily 19, and on chapter 15, homilies 42 and 57.

Theophilus of Alexandria, in his *Canonical Responses*, question 5, asks:

“If a wife has slept with her husband at night, or a husband with his wife, and they have also had intercourse, ought they to communicate, or not?”

**Answer:** “They ought not, since the Apostle cries out: ‘Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.’”

For this reason, shortly afterward he answers question 13, which is proposed as follows:

**Question 13:** “On which days of the week should those joined in the marital partnership be instructed to abstain from intercourse with one another? And on which days may they have intercourse?”

**Answer:** “What I said before, I say now also. The Apostle says: ‘Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control.’ It is necessary, however, to abstain on Saturday and Sunday, because a spiritual sacrifice is offered to the Lord on those days.”

You will find the same teaching in Saint Ambrose, *Apology of David*, chapter 11; in Pope Siricius, in his letter to the brothers and fellow bishops throughout Africa; in Saint Jerome, in his letter to Pammachius, *On the Apology for the Books against Jovinian*; and in Saint Augustine, *On Faith and Works*, chapter 6. The same is the judgment of Veranus, bishop of Cavaillon, in a certain synod held around the year 183.

Nevertheless, Gregory the Great holds that a person may receive the sacraments who, being placed in fire, does not know how to burn. “Legitimate intercourse,” he says in his response to Augustine’s tenth question, “ought to be for the sake of offspring, not pleasure; and the mingling of bodies ought to be for the purpose of generating children, not the satisfaction of vice. Therefore, if someone uses his wife not seized by the desire for pleasure, but solely for the generation of children, he must certainly be left to his own judgment, whether concerning entrance into the church or reception of the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood; for he ought not to be prohibited by us, since, being placed in fire, he does not know how to burn.”

Among the Greek Fathers, Saint Clement of Alexandria likewise says in book 7 of the *Stromata*:

> Διό καὶ ἐστίων, καὶ πίνων, καὶ γαμῶν, ἐάν ὁ λόγος ἔρῃ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ὀνείρους βλέπων, τὰ ἅγια ποιεῖ, καί νοεῖ. Θαῦτη καταρός εἰς εὐχὴν πάντοτε.

“Therefore, eating, drinking, and marrying, if reason (ὁ λόγος) directs, and even seeing dreams, he does and thinks holy things. The final printed clause is corrupt or uncertain: ‘Thus [καταρός?] unto prayer always.’”

Master Robert of Flamesbure holds the same opinion in his *Penitential*, on the authority of Saint Gregory.

## Selections from the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbure, book 4, chapter 6

“Legitimate intercourse ought to be for the sake of offspring,” and so forth, as above. Shortly afterward:

“Likewise, when someone has washed with water after intercourse with his wife, he may also receive the mystery of Holy Communion, since, according to the judgment defined above, he was likewise permitted to enter the church.”

## Before childbirth and after the period of purification

Saint Clement of Alexandria, book 2 of the *Stromata*:

“Man, who is sown, is nobler and more precious than the seeds of wheat and barley, which are cast down at suitable times; for him all things are brought forth by nature. Those seeds, indeed, are cast down by sober farmers. If, therefore, there is any filthy and unclean practice, it is to be purged from marriage, lest it be charged against us as a reproach that the intercourse of irrational animals is more in accordance with nature than human union in the very heat of Venus.”

And in book 3 of the *Stromata*:

“Thus you will show from Scripture no one among the ancients who had intercourse with a pregnant woman. But after she had carried the child in her womb, and after she had weaned the infant once it was born, wives were again known by men. You will find Moses’s father observing this purpose and ordinance: after an interval of three years following the birth of Aaron, he begot Moses. And again, the tribe of Levi, observing this law of nature handed down by God, entered the promised land smaller in number than the others.”

Saint Ambrose, book 1 of his *Commentary on Luke*, chapter 1:

“And what wonder is it concerning human beings, if even beasts, by a certain mute act, express that their purpose is to generate, not a desire to copulate? For when they have once felt their bellies grow heavy and have received seed in their generative womb, they no longer indulge in intercourse or assume the wantonness of lovers, but take up the care of parents. Human beings, however, spare neither what has been conceived nor God: they defile the former and provoke the latter.

“‘Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and in your mother’s womb I sanctified you.’ To restrain your wantonness, consider the hands of your Creator forming a human being in the womb. He is the craftsman, while you defile the secret place of the sacred womb with lust. Either imitate the beasts or revere God.

“And why should I speak of beasts? The earth itself often rests from the work of generation. If the impatient eagerness of human beings frequently occupies it with seeds cast into it, the farmer’s shamelessness is punished and fertility is changed into barrenness. Thus, even among the elements and the beasts, it is a shame before nature not to cease from the use of generation.”

Saint Gregory the Great, book 12, letter 30, in his response to Augustine’s tenth question:

“Her husband ought not to approach her in intercourse until the child who is born has been weaned. A depraved custom, however, has arisen in the conduct of married people, so that women refuse to nurse the children whom they bear and hand them over to other women to be raised. This was evidently devised solely because of lack of self-control: since they do not wish to exercise continence, they disdain to nurse the children they have borne. Therefore, women who, because of this depraved custom, hand their children over to others for nursing ought not to have intercourse with their husbands until the period of purification has passed.”

Accordingly, following the tradition of the Fathers, Theodore judged that one ought to abstain from embraces before childbirth and after the period of purification. Hence Gregory III later defined in his *Judgments*, chapter 25: “If anyone does this, let him perform penance for forty days.”

See the ancient *Penitentials* in the appendix to the *Book of Penance* of the most learned J. Morin, especially the *Penitential Book* of John the Faster, bishop of Constantinople, and that of Egbert, archbishop of York. I shall add what I selected from an old codex concerning penalties to be imposed for sins, and from the *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbure.

## Selections from an old manuscript codex of the distinguished Wion, lord of Herouvall, concerning penalties to be imposed for sins

“From the manifestation of conception until after the child has been born, the husband shall abstain from his wife—that is, for three months. After the child has been born, the wife shall abstain from the church: if the child is a boy, for thirty days; if a girl, for forty. For if anyone has intercourse during the time of menstrual blood, he shall perform penance for thirty days.”

## Selections from the manuscript *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbure, book 4, chapters 6 and 14

“Every month women’s heavy and sluggish bodies are relieved by the discharge of unclean blood. If, at that time, a man has intercourse with a woman, they are said to draw the corruption of the seed along with them, so that lepers and elephantine sufferers are born from such a conception; and health is corrupted in both bodies by foul depravity or deformity of the limbs. Therefore it is prescribed that they should know fixed times for intercourse not only with other men’s wives but also with their own, with whom they appear to unite: when intercourse is to take place and when they are to abstain from their wives.”

And chapter 14:

“If anyone has intercourse with a woman during her lying-in after childbirth, let him perform penance for ten days on bread and water.”

If someone’s wife has committed fornication, he may dismiss her and take another.

## [Col. 1149A]

The discipline prescribed by the Fathers of the Council of Trent must be followed in every respect. The most distinguished Joannes Launoy has shown that it was excellently explained by the most eminent Cardinal Pallavicino, in his outstanding book *On the Royal Power over Marriage*. Moreover, the most ancient Fathers—especially those who did not even permit remarriage after the death of a spouse—undoubtedly judged that this discipline was to be strictly observed after divorce, as they plainly declare in the same places.

Athenagoras, in his *Legation for the Christians*:

“Therefore, either let each of us remain as he was born, or let him be joined in a single marriage; for second marriages are, in a certain sense, a respectable adultery. ‘Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery,’ says our Lord, neither allowing him to dismiss the woman whose chastity has been violated nor to marry another. For whoever deprives himself of his first wife, even though she has died, is an adulterer, though secretly so, and transgresses God’s command, since in the beginning God created one man and one woman, and separated flesh from flesh and the union of the two sexes.”

Clement of Alexandria, book 3 of the *Stromata*:

“‘Let him who can receive it receive it.’ They do not understand what follows after he had spoken about divorce, when some asked whether, if such were the case concerning a wife, ‘it is not expedient for a man to marry’; then the Lord said: ‘Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given.’ Those who asked this wanted to know whether, when a wife had been condemned and dismissed on account of fornication, he permitted the man to marry another.”

To Saint Clement of Alexandria I shall add Blessed Hermas, whose book, *The Shepherd*, was praised so highly by him that it may rightly be said to have been made his own in a certain sense. To the question, “What then, if the woman persists in her vice?” he presents an angel answering in book 2, commandment 4:

“Let the husband dismiss her and remain by himself. But if he dismisses his wife and marries another, he too commits adultery.”

Tertullian, *On Monogamy*, chapter 9:

“For us, even if we divorce, it will not be permitted to marry. I already see that we are being referred to the Apostle. To understand his meaning more easily, it must be impressed upon us with all the more insistence that a woman is all the more bound, by the claim of the deceased husband (*defuncto merito*), not to admit another man.”

Accordingly, the distinguished N. Rigaltius made the following observation on this passage:

“‘For us,’ he says, that is, for the *Paracletics* (*paracleticis*). For among the ‘psychics’—that is, the less rigorous Christians—he indicates that other marriages after divorce had been permitted, at the beginning of book 2 of *To His Wife*, in these words:

“‘Now we shall turn to the second counsels, out of regard for human weakness, admonished by the examples of certain women who, when an opportunity for continence had been offered through divorce or the death of a husband, not only rejected the opportunity for so great a good, but did not even wish to remember discipline in marrying, so that they might marry, above all, in the Lord.’”

Origen asserts that certain rulers of the Church permitted this contrary to the law of Scripture, in his *Commentary on Matthew*, p. 363, Huet’s edition:

“Now, he says, certain rulers of the Church have permitted a woman to marry while her husband is alive, acting contrary to what is written: ‘A woman is bound as long as her husband lives’; and contrary to this: ‘Therefore, while her husband lives, she will be called an adulteress if she is with another man.’ Nevertheless, they apparently did not act entirely without reason. For, in order to avoid worse things, they probably permitted these women, following a custom established by human judgment, to act contrary to the law laid down and written at the beginning.”

Thus formerly certain bishops permitted remarriage after divorce in order to avoid worse things. See the Council of Elvira, canon 9; the First Council of Arles, canon 10, as it is read in the very ancient collection of the Herouvall codex; the Council of Laodicea, chapter 1; Lactantius, book 6 of *The True Worship*, chapter 23; Saint Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, *Commentary on Matthew*, chapter 6; Saint Basil, in his canonical letter to Amphilochius, canon 9; Saint Epiphanius, *Heresy* 59:

“Yet he tolerates it because of weakness: Οὐδὲ ἀπὸ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας καὶ τῆς ζοῆς ἀποκηρύπτει, ἀλλὰ διαβαστάζει διὰ τὸ ἀσθινὲς.”

“He does not exclude him from the Church or from life, but bears with him because of weakness.” [The supplied Greek contains an apparent textual corruption.]

Also Innocent I, letter 9, to Probus; the synod of Saint Patrick, canon 26; and the Council of Vannes, canon 2. Therefore the other matters that follow in Theodore concerning questions of marriage must be understood in the same way, since shortly afterward he says that it is better to act in this manner than to fornicate.

## If a man dismisses his wife because of fornication

And below:

“If the husband himself makes himself a slave through theft, fornication, or any other sin, then, if the woman previously had no marriage, she has the power, after one year, to take another husband.”

Certain Fathers understood the term “fornication” broadly, so that they considered the gravest crimes a legitimate cause for divorce. Therefore Blessed Hermas, in book 2 of *The Shepherd*, commandment 4, judges that a wife ought to be dismissed on account of idolatry:

“Not only is it adultery,” he says, “for those who defile their flesh, but also he who makes an idol commits adultery. If she persists in these deeds and does not repent, withdraw from her and do not live with her; otherwise you too will be a participant in her sin.”

Saint Clement of Alexandria appears to have spoken in the same sense in book 3 of the *Stromata*, saying that the Apostle uses “fornication” in three ways. Origen discusses the same question at greater length, as one involving the greatest difficulty, in his *Commentary on Matthew*, tome 1, p. 365, Huet’s edition.

Saint Epiphanius, however, has no doubt about this, *Heresy* 59: “Or on account of another cause,” he says.

But Saint Augustine, after considering all aspects on both sides, admits in book 1 of the *Retractions*, chapter 19, that this is a most obscure question:

“But what sort of fornication,” he says, “the Lord wishes to be understood as the reason for which it is permitted to dismiss a wife—whether that which is condemned in adulteries, or that of which it is said, ‘You have destroyed everyone who fornicates away from you’—is very obscure.”

And shortly afterward:

“But how this fornication is to be understood and removed, and whether it is also permitted to dismiss a wife on account of it, is a most obscure question.”

Nevertheless, the Fathers of the Council of Verberie, chapter 5, grant a man permission to dismiss his wife completely because she gave counsel concerning his murder:

“If a woman has plotted the death of her husband with other men, and the husband, defending himself, has killed one of them, and he can prove this, that man may dismiss his wife; and, if he wishes, he may take another.”

She, however, if she wishes to repent, may take another husband.

The Council of Tribur, canon 41:

“If anyone has taken a legitimate wife and, because of some domestic infirmity, is unable to perform the marital act with her, and his brother, persuaded by the devil and loved by her, secretly violates her and returns her violated, they shall be separated completely, and that woman shall thereafter be touched by neither of the two. Thus the marriage that was legitimate has been polluted by brotherly defilement, and what was lawful has become unlawful. As Jerome says: ‘A woman shall not ascend the bed of two brothers; but if she does ascend it, she will commit adultery.’

“Since human weakness, however, is prone to fall, it must somehow be fortified for standing. Therefore, after considering their mental weakness and after the penance imposed by his direction has been completed, the bishop may, if they are unable to remain continent, console them with a legitimate marriage, lest, while they are hoped to be lifted to lofty things, they fall into the mire.”

Thus Burchard, drawing on the Council of Tribur, book 9, canon 43:

“If a man has taken a wife but is unable to have intercourse with her, and his brother has secretly violated her and made her pregnant, they shall be separated. But, considering their weakness, mercy shall be granted to them, for marriage only in the Lord.”

And from the Roman *Penitential*, Burchard, book 19, chapter 4:

“But if your wife can prove that, through your fault and at your command, although she refused and resisted, she was made an adulteress, then, if she cannot remain continent, let her marry whomever she wishes, only in the Lord.”

Almost all the other Fathers deny this. Indeed, the Fathers of the Council of Compiègne, canon 8, say:

“If a man has a legitimate wife and his brother has committed adultery with her, neither the brother nor the woman who committed the adultery shall ever, as long as they live, have a marriage. The man whose wife she was has the power, if he wishes, to take another.”

## A woman may not dismiss her husband, even if he is a fornicator

Basil judged this. In his letter to Amphilochius, canon 9:

“But if he himself lives in fornication, we do not have this custom in the ecclesiastical constitution. Even the wife of an unbelieving husband is commanded not to separate from him, but to remain because the outcome is uncertain. ‘For what do you know, woman, whether you will save your husband?’ Therefore the woman who leaves him is an adulteress if she goes to another husband. But the man who is left is worthy of pardon, and the woman who lives with him is not condemned for that reason.”

The author found in Ambrose’s *Commentary on the Epistle to the Corinthians*, chapter 7, holds the same view.

Other Fathers condemned this inequality, such as Gregory of Nazianzus in oration 31:

“What was the reason that he restrained the woman but indulged the husband and left him free, and so forth? I do not approve this law at all; I do not praise this custom in the least. Men were the ones who enacted this law.”

For this reason Saint Epiphanius admits no discrepancy in *Heresy* 59:

> Συναφθέντα δευτέρᾳ γυναικὶ, ἢ γυνὴ δευτέρᾳ ἀνδρὶ· οὖκ αἱτιᾶται ὁ θεῖος λόγος.

“The divine Word does not condemn a man joined to a second wife, or a woman joined to a second husband.”

Saint Jerome, in the *Epitaph of Fabiola*:

“Whatever is commanded to men consequently applies to women. For an adulterous wife is not to be dismissed while an adulterous husband is retained. … The laws of the Caesars are one thing, the laws of Christ another; Papinian prescribes one thing, our Paul another. Among them the reins of sexual immorality are loosened for men. … Among us, what is not permitted to women is equally not permitted to men, and the same servitude is judged under equal conditions.”

And Saint Augustine, after treating this question at length and in detail, concludes in book 2 of *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapter 20:

“Remember that I say these things concerning both sexes, but especially because of men, who think themselves superior to women for this reason: that they do not deign to be equal to them in chastity, in which they ought even to take the lead, so that women might follow them as their heads.”

## “A legitimate marriage may not be separated without the consent of both”

Saint Basil discusses this at greater length in his *Book of Rules*. He answers differently the question proposed as follows:

**Question:** “How should those who are joined in marriage be received?”

**Answer:** “Those who are joined in marriage and approach this way of life must also be asked whether they are doing so with the consent of the other party, in accordance with the Apostle’s command. For, he says, a man does not have authority over his own body. If it is discovered that they are acting in this way, the person who approaches must then be admitted with many witnesses present, since nothing ought to be regarded as more important than God’s commands.

“But if the other party dissents and continually contends against the first, being less concerned with how to please God, then this person ought to remember what the Apostle said: ‘God has called us to peace.’ And thus one must obey the Lord’s command, who said: ‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, and brothers, he cannot be my disciple.’ For nothing ought to be considered more important than obeying God’s commands.”

Other Fathers disagree, and with them Theodore holds that a legitimate marriage cannot be separated without the consent of both parties.

Saint Augustine, letter 46:

“Such vows ought not to be made by married people except with mutual consent and agreement. Even if something has been done rashly, the rashness ought rather to be corrected than the promise fulfilled. For God does not require someone to vow something belonging to another; rather, he forbids the usurpation of what belongs to another.”

Saint Gregory the Great, book 9, letter 39:

“For if they say that marriages ought to be dissolved for the sake of religion, it must be known that, even if human law has permitted this, divine law has nevertheless forbidden it.”

See Egbert of York, *Excerptions*, chapter 119; the Council of Verberie, canon 4; the Council of Compiègne, canon 3:

“If a woman, without her husband’s permission, places a veil on her head, he shall, if it pleases her husband, receive her again into marriage.”

This agrees with what Theodore says in chapter 18:

“Vows that a husband makes to God without his wife’s consent are foolish and burdensome and must be broken.”

## One may nevertheless give the other permission to enter the service of God in a monastery and to marry

See the various readings in which this passage is cited and explained by Egbert and Regino.

Theodore adds: “Yet it is not canonical.”

Nevertheless, the Council of Compiègne confirmed this not long afterward, canon 13:

“If a man dismisses his wife and gives her permission, for the sake of religion, to serve within a monastery, or gives her permission to take the veil outside a monastery, as we have said, for God’s sake, then her husband may take a legitimate wife; likewise, the woman may do the same. George consented.”

## A deacon’s widow may not remarry

The First Council of Toledo, chapter 18:

“If any widow of a bishop, presbyter, or deacon takes a husband, no cleric and no religious person shall share a meal with her; she shall never communicate, and only when she is dying shall the sacrament be given to her.”

The First Council of Orléans, chapter 13:

“If the widow of a presbyter or deacon joins herself to any man in a second marriage, either let them separate after correction, or, if they persist in their criminal purpose, let them be punished with equal excommunication.”

The Council of Epaon, canon 32:

“If the widow of a presbyter or deacon remarries anyone, let her be expelled from the Church until she separates from the illicit union; her husband too must be punished with similar severity until correction.”

The Council of Auxerre has the same provision, chapter 22; likewise the Second Council of Mâcon, canon 14.

## But if he, or she, has been weakened by illness

If they separate with mutual consent, what should be done by the one who cannot remain continent?

Gregory II answers in letter 13 to Bishop Boniface, canon 2:

“For concerning what you proposed—if a woman, overcome by illness, is unable to render the marital debt to her husband, what should her spouse do? It would be good if he remained in this state, so that he might devote himself to abstinence. But because this is a matter for the great, the one who cannot remain continent should rather marry; nevertheless, he must not withdraw every form of assistance from the woman whom illness prevents, and whom no detestable fault excludes.”

Egbert of York, in his response to question 13:

“No one acts against the Gospel or against the Apostle without punishment; therefore we give no approval to adulterers. Yet we impose on no one burdens that cannot be borne without danger, while we confidently proclaim the commands that belong to God. But concerning one whom illness prevents from fulfilling them, we leave much, certainly, to the judgment of God.

“Therefore, lest we appear by our silence to encourage adulterers, or lest the devil, who deceives adulterers, exult over adulterers, hear the words of the avenger: ‘What God has joined, let no man separate’; and again: ‘Let him who can receive it receive it.’ For often, when circumstances change, necessity breaks the law. What did David do when he was hungry? And yet he was without sin.

“Therefore, in doubtful matters no sentence should be imposed; rather, counsels must be risked for the salvation of others, on this condition: that the person who has devoted himself to continence may in no way enter a second marriage while the first spouse is alive.”

The Council of Compiègne, canon 16:

“If a leprous man has a healthy wife, and wishes to give her permission to take a husband, the woman may, if she wishes, take one; likewise, the man may do so.”

But the Fathers of the Second Council of Orléans show no indulgence, in agreement with Augustine in several places, especially book *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 15, and book 2 of *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapter 11. Thus canon 11 says:

“Marriages that have been contracted are not to be dissolved because illness has intervened, against the will of either party. If any married persons do this, they shall know that they are to be deprived of communion.”

## A woman who vowed after her husband’s death and then married again

Saint Basil testifies in his letter to Amphilochius, canon 18, that the Fathers dealt mercifully with fallen virgins who had professed a life of chastity to the Lord:

“Concerning fallen virgins who had professed a life of chastity to the Lord but had violated their agreements and covenants, the Fathers, acting mercifully and gently toward the weakness of those who fall, judged that they should be admitted after one year, assigning them the status of bigamists.”

Among those Fathers of whom Saint Basil speaks, Saint Cyprian must be numbered. He writes in letter 62 to Pomponius:

“If they have devoted themselves to Christ in faith, let them persevere modestly and chastely, without any scandal, strong and steadfast, awaiting the reward of virginity. But if they do not wish or are unable to persevere, it is better that they marry than that they fall into the fire through their sins.”

The Fathers of the Council of Ancyra must especially be counted among these, and Saint Basil appears to have had their words in view. Thus canon 19 says:

“Those who profess virginity but make their profession void shall fulfill the definition concerning bigamists.”

Saint Basil says, however, that when the number of virgins devoted to God increased, and the vow had already become solemn and public, the earlier discipline had to be changed. Accordingly, in canon 18 he declares that he had first established another rule:

“It seems to me,” he says, “that, since the Church advances by God’s grace and becomes stronger, and the order of virgins increases, attention must be given to what is discerned through understanding and to the judgment of Scripture that can be found by logical consequence. … A virgin is subjected to the judgment of an adulteress if we call a man who lives with another man’s wife an adulterer and do not admit him to communion until he has ceased from sin. In the same way, then, we shall regard the man who has a virgin.”

He had already decreed in canon 6 that such unions were fornications which, as he says, could not be regarded as marriages and had to be completely dissolved.

The Fathers of the First Council of Valence, canon 2, support this judgment; likewise the *Ancient Statutes of the Church*, canon 103:

“For if adulterous wives are bound to their husbands by the guilt of adultery, how much more will widows who have changed their religious profession be branded with the crime of adultery if, after having voluntarily and without compulsion offered their devotion to God, they corrupt it with lustful pleasure and pass to a second marriage!”

Also the First Council of Toledo, canon 19; Siricius, in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona, canon 6; and Saint John Chrysostom, in book 2 *To Theodore after His Fall*, where he says:

“But it is no longer permitted for you to preserve the rights of marriage. For to leave the heavenly bridegroom to whom one has once been joined and to become entangled in the bonds of a wife is to incur the crime of adultery. Although you may call this a marriage a thousand times, I nevertheless affirm that it is worse than adultery, inasmuch as God is greater and better than mortal beings.”

Innocent I, in his letter to Victricius, bishop of Rouen, chapter 12, indeed calls those women adulteresses who had been veiled by a priest. But in chapter 13 he decrees only that those who have promised always to remain in the virginal vocation, but who have not yet been covered with the sacred veil, must perform penance for some time if they marry.

The ancient Roman canons that the distinguished J. Sirmond appended to the letters of Innocent I make the same ruling. See canons 1 and 2.

Saint Augustine treats this question wonderfully in his book *On the Good of Widowhood*. He appears, however, not to consider sufficiently sharply and carefully what those people are saying who would raise the following argument:

“If a woman who marries another man while her husband is alive is an adulteress, as the Lord himself defines in the Gospel, then, since Christ is alive and death no longer rules him, a woman who had chosen his marriage is an adulteress if she marries a man.”

Saint Augustine says:

“Those who say this are indeed moved by an acute argument, but they pay too little attention to how great an absurdity in other matters follows from it. For since a woman may laudably vow continence to Christ, with the consent of her husband, even while he is alive, then, according to their reasoning, no one ought to do this, lest she make Christ himself—something wicked even to think—an adulterer, by marrying him while her husband is alive, and so forth.”

After Saint Augustine, see Saint Leo in his responses to inquiry 15 of Rusticus of Narbonne; the First Council of Orange, canons 24–28; the synod of Saint Patrick, canon 17; the Council of Chalcedon, canon 16; the Second Council of Arles, canon 51; the Council of Angers, canon 5; the First Council of Tours, canon 6, from chapter 7; the Fourth Council of Arles in Ivo, book 3; Gratian, 27, question 1; Pope Symmachus, letter 7 to Caesarius, bishop of Arles, canons 4 and 5; the Third Council of Paris, canon 5; and the Second Council of Tours, canons 15 and 20, where several of the canons cited above are repeated.

## Therefore Theodore granted one permission

Thus Theodore cites himself in chapter 12:

“Theodore says: ‘But we, through mercy,’” and so forth.

And in the Council of Hertford, in Bede, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 4, chapter 3, and in Burchard, book 17, chapter 39.

## The bishop himself has the power to change this

Especially if the vow is foolish or harmful.

Saint Basil, concerning foolish vows, in his letter to Amphilochius, canon 28:

“It seemed ridiculous to me that anyone should vow to abstain from pork. Therefore deign to teach them to abstain from foolish vows and promises, while allowing the use of indifferent things. For no creature of God is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving. Therefore the vow is ridiculous; abstinence is not necessary.”

Thus Saint Basil urges Bishop Amphilochius to change and release such foolish and ridiculous vows.

Concerning harmful vows, Saint Ambrose says in book 1 of *The Duties*, chapter 50:

“It is also sometimes contrary to duty to fulfill a promise and to keep an oath, as Herod did.”

See above.

## Therefore, if someone’s wife is an unbeliever and a pagan and cannot be converted, he may change his marriage

Saint Ambrose, book 8 on Luke, chapter 16:

“To the others I speak,” he says, “not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and so forth. Therefore, where there is an unequal marriage, the law of God does not apply.”

And he added:

“But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart, and so forth.”

Saint Augustine, book 1 of *On Adulterous Marriages*, chapter 13:

“Because the faithful spouse could lawfully leave an unbelieving spouse, the Lord does not prohibit this, but the Apostle does. What the Lord prohibits is altogether unlawful. … You, however, seem to think that unbelievers may not be dismissed by believers, because the Apostle forbids this; whereas I say that it is permitted, because the Lord does not forbid it—not, however, that it is expedient, because the Apostle urges that it not be done. He also gives the reason why it is not expedient, although it is permitted.”

The author of the *Commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, found among the works of Ambrose, chapter 7:

“He preserves the religious vocation by commanding Christians not to leave their marriages. But if the unbeliever departs out of hatred for God, the believer is not guilty of dissolving the marriage, and so forth. For a marriage that exists without devotion to God is not binding; therefore it is not a sin for one who is dismissed on God’s account if he joins himself to another. The insult against the Creator dissolves the marital right for the one who remains, so that he is not accused when joined to another.”

## [Col. 1156C] If a woman departs from her husband, despising him and unwilling to return … he may take another wife

The *Excerptions* of Egbert, archbishop of York, chapter 122, contain the same rule; likewise the Council of Verberie, canon 11:

“If anyone, compelled by unavoidable necessity, flees to another duchy or province, or follows his lord, to whom he could not refuse his loyalty, and his wife, although she is able and capable, refuses to follow him because of her parents or her possessions, she shall remain unmarried for all time, as long as the husband whom she did not follow remains alive. For that husband of hers who fled to another place under the compulsion of necessity may, if he cannot remain continent, take another wife with penance.”

The reason Egbert of York gives in the canon cited above is this:

“With the consent of the bishop,” he says, “let him take another wife if he cannot remain continent, and let him perform penance for three years, or even for as long as he lives, because according to the Lord’s judgment he is proved an adulterer.”

## If she has been taken captive by force and cannot be ransomed, he may take another after one year

This is confirmed by the *Excerptions* of Egbert of York, canon 122. Several Fathers, however, disagree with it: Saint Basil, in his canonical letter to Amphilochius, chapter 31; Theophilus of Alexandria, in his response to question 15; Saint Augustine, book 2 of *On Adulterous Marriages*; and the Second Council of Orléans, canon 11.

## Let him dismiss the later wife

Innocent I, in his letter to Probus:

“When the woman Ursa was being held in the captivity mentioned above, it became known that the aforesaid Fortunius had contracted another marriage with Restituta.” But, by the Lord’s favor, when Ursa returned, she approached us and, with no one denying it, clearly proved that she was the wife of the aforesaid man. Therefore, illustrious son, we rightly establish, with the Catholic faith supporting us, that the marriage which had first been founded by divine grace was the true marriage; and that the union with the second woman, while the first survived and had not been expelled by divorce, could in no way be legitimate.”

Leo I supports this response in his letter to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, chapters 1–4.

In the third degree of blood relationship. Rabanus explains this passage excellently in his letter to Bishop Humbert, in these words:

> “Similarly, in the acts of Archbishop Theodore, in the chapters concerning the English which he composed on necessary matters, we find that, according to the Greeks, marriage is permitted in the third degree of blood relationship, and in the fifth according to the Romans. Nevertheless, they would not dissolve marriages contracted in the third degree if they had previously been entered into unknowingly; and a man would likewise be joined in marriage to those related to him by blood, and, after his wife’s death, to his wife’s blood relatives, etc. Therefore, since you wished me, in my humble capacity, to write back to you what I thought about this matter, I believe that, given the frailty of the present age, what Bishop Theodore—proceeding midway between Gregory and Isidore—defined in his chapters should rather be followed: namely, that marriage should already be permitted in the fifth generation. For divine law does not contradict this, nor do the statements of the holy Fathers prohibit it. But if a union has been contracted unknowingly even in the fifth degree, it seems better to me that, with the humility of penance, the man should satisfy God if he does not wish to remain continent while married.”

See Regino, book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 200. But above all consult Hugh of Saint-Victor, book II of the *Sacraments*, part XI, where he proves the same question by numerous testimonies of the Fathers, the Roman pontiffs, and others. To these may be added what Master Robert of Flamesbure teaches in his *Penitential*.

## Excerpts from the *Penitential* of Master Robert of Flamesbure, book II

Kinship prevents and invalidates marriage, not in the ascending or descending line, which is the same without limit—for if Adam were alive today, no woman could marry him. In the collateral line, however, marriage is invalidated even in the seventh degree. A dispensation may nevertheless be granted, but only by the pope, and only beyond the third degree, because the law prohibits unions in the first, second, and third degrees. The pope, however, cannot dispense against the law and the Gospel, as stated above.

He should wash before entering the church. Gregory I, in his tenth response to Augustine’s question:

> “A man who has slept with his own wife should not enter the church unless he has washed with water; but even after washing he should not enter immediately, etc.”

A little later he declares that this was a Roman custom received from earlier times:

> “Nevertheless, it was always the custom of the Romans, received from their forebears, after intercourse with one’s own wife, to seek purification by washing and reverently to abstain for a little while from entering the church. In saying this, we do not consider marriage itself to be a fault; but because this lawful intercourse of husband and wife cannot take place without carnal pleasure, one must abstain from entering the sacred place, since pleasure itself can in no way be without fault.”

And afterward the woman says that she cannot have intercourse with her husband. See the Council of Verberie, canon 17; the Council of Compiègne, canon 17; and Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, chapter 29:

> “You asked concerning those who are joined in marriage but cannot have intercourse, whether the man may take another wife or the woman another husband. It is written: If a man and woman have joined themselves, and afterward the woman says of her husband that he cannot have intercourse with her, then, if she can prove by a proper judgment that this is true, she may take another.”

See Regino, book II, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 242; book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 55.

Parents may not give a betrothed girl to another man. Council of Elvira, canon 54:

> “If any parents break faith with respect to an engagement, they shall abstain for a period of three years. Nevertheless, if the same bridegroom or bride is discovered to have committed a grave crime, the parents shall be excused. If the fault is in the parties themselves and they have defiled themselves, the preceding judgment shall remain in force.”

Pope Siricius gives the following reason for this in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona, canon 4:

> “You have also asked about the violation of a marriage contract: whether another man may take a girl who has been betrothed to someone else. We absolutely forbid this, because the blessing which the priest bestows upon a woman about to marry would, among the faithful, be like a sacrilege if it were violated by any transgression.”

But if she does not wish to live with the man to whom she is betrothed, the money he gave shall be returned to him, and a third part shall be added. Nevertheless, Saint Gregory the Great teaches in book VI, letter 20, that a betrothed woman who enters a monastery is not to be punished by any loss:

> “For,” he says, “the legal decrees have determined that a betrothed woman who wishes to convert should not be punished by any loss whatsoever, in the Code, *On Bishops and Clerics*, law 36. What has seemed contrary to our religious gentleness?”

A boy up to the age of fifteen is to be …; then he may make himself a monk; but a girl [may do so at] sixteen or seventeen.

Saint Basil, in his letter to Amphilochius, canon 18:

> “We judge professions to be valid from the time when the age of reason has reached maturity. For childish utterances should not be considered fully valid in these matters. Rather, a girl who is more than sixteen or seventeen years old, who possesses reason, and who has persevered after prolonged examination and testing, and who insists through her prayers on being admitted, ought then to be enrolled among the sacred virgins, her profession ought to be confirmed, and her renunciation ought to be punished without mercy if she abandons it. For many parents and brothers offer girls, and some of their relatives present them, not because they have themselves been moved to celibacy before the proper age, but while seeking to secure something for their livelihood; such girls ought not readily to be admitted until we have clearly examined their own judgment.”

This canon is cited by the Quinisext Council, canon 40.

Saint Ambrose, book III, *On Virgins*:

> “Many also say that virgins of more mature age ought to be veiled. Nor do I deny that priestly caution should be exercised, so that a girl is not veiled rashly. Let the priest certainly examine her age—but also her faith and modesty; let him examine the maturity of her reserve; let him test the gray hairs of her seriousness, the old age of her character, and the years of her chastity and courage for continence. Yet if the secure guardianship of her mother and the sober diligence of her companions are present, the virgin does not lack long-standing maturity; if these are absent, let the girl be deferred because of her character rather than her years. Thus it is not a more flourishing age that is rejected, but the mind that is examined.”

Council of Zaragoza, canon 8:

> “It was likewise read that virgins who have dedicated themselves to God are not to be veiled unless they have been proven at forty years of age, which the priest has confirmed.” All the bishops replied: “It is approved.”

Third Council of Carthage, canon 3:

> “It was likewise approved that neither deacons should be ordained nor virgins consecrated before the age of twenty-five.”

Second Council of Milevis, chapter 26:

> “It was likewise approved that if any bishop, because of the danger threatening a virgin’s chastity—when either a powerful suitor or some abductor is feared, or when she has been struck by some perilous fear of death lest she die without being veiled, or at the demand of her parents or of those responsible for her care—has veiled, or does veil, a virgin under the age of twenty-five, this council’s decree concerning that number of years shall not prejudice him.”

This canon is reproduced in full in the code of the African Church, canon 126.

Council of Agde, canon 19:

> “Nuns, however approved their life and conduct may be, are not to be veiled before the fortieth year of their age.”

Saint Gregory, book III, letter 11:

> “Therefore let your fraternity permit no virgin to be veiled unless she is sixty years old and her age and conduct require it.”

From all these statements it can clearly be concluded that such matters must be judged religiously according to the various circumstances. Above all, care must be taken that girls of childish age are not veiled before they know how to choose what they wish, as prescribed by the ecclesiastical chapters of Charlemagne, chapter 14, and by Emperor Louis the Pious’s *Capitulary* I, chapter 26, where some of the canons cited above are reproduced.

After this age, a father may not give his daughter in marriage against her will. Therefore, before this age he was permitted to do so. Theodoret seems to indicate this discipline, for he explains these words of the First Epistle to the Corinthians as follows:

> “But if anyone thinks that he is acting improperly toward his virgin because she is past the age of maturity, and it ought to happen in this way, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if she marries. He who,” he says, “regards celibacy as dishonorable and for that reason wishes to join his daughter to a husband may do what seems good to him.”

Others, however, explain the passage differently.

Hilary the Deacon, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter VII:

> “Therefore, if any girl desires marriage and is already mature for its use, it is better that she marry publicly according to the permission granted by the law than that she secretly and shamefully commit this act, and be put to shame, etc.”

A little later:

> “He says this so that a man who has a virgin whose mind is not inclined toward marriage may preserve her and not impose the fuel of marriage upon one whom he sees to have no desire to marry. For if benefits are to be bestowed, how much more should they not be taken away.”

Saint Jerome, on the same words:

> “Here he is not speaking of the parents of virgin daughters; for the decision concerning another person’s continence cannot be within their power. Rather, each person has the disposal of his own flesh, to keep it undefiled, etc. He makes a firm decision when the consent of his girl confirms the father’s will.”

Synod of Saint Patrick, canon 27:

> “Let the virgin do what her father wishes, because the husband is the head of the woman. But the father must seek the virgin’s will, since God has left human beings in the hand of their own counsel.”

# CHAPTER XII. On Male and Female Slaves

If a woman in servitude cannot be redeemed, a free man may marry a freeborn woman. Council of Verberie, canon 6:

> “If a freeborn man has taken a female slave as his wife, believing her to be freeborn, and afterward the woman has been reduced to servitude, then, if she cannot be redeemed, he may, if he wishes, take another wife. Likewise, if a freeborn woman takes a male slave believing him to be freeborn, and afterward he is enslaved for any reason—unless he sold himself because of poverty, compelled by hunger, and she consented to this and was freed from hunger by the price paid for her husband—then, if she wishes, she may dismiss him; and if she cannot remain continent, she may take another husband. The same applies to a woman if she sells herself and her husband consents to it: they may remain in this condition if they separate. Nevertheless, penance is necessary for both. For one who has been freed from such necessity by the price paid for his partner ought to remain in such a marriage and not separate.”

Council of Compiègne, canon 5:

> “If a Frankish man takes a woman, supposing her to be freeborn, and afterward discovers that she is not freeborn, he may dismiss her if he wishes and take another.”

A child born from her is free. For, according to Justinian’s *Institutes*, book I, title 4:

> “It is sufficient that the mother was free at the time when the child is born, even if she conceived while a slave.”

The laws, as far as possible, favor natural right, because, as it is said in title 2, “by natural law all human beings were born free from the beginning.” And in title 3 slavery is defined as follows:

> “It is an institution of the law of nations by which one person is subjected to a master contrary to nature.”

Therefore the contrary reading is not correct in chapter 74, which was published by the Right Reverend Luca Acherius as follows: “he who was born is a slave.”

# CHAPTER XIII. On Various Questions

The prescribed fasts … before the Nativity of the Lord. See the *Dialogue* of Egbert, Archbishop of York, who, in his response to question 16, testifies that this custom had arisen in the English Church from the time of Pope Vitalian and Theodore:

> “For this custom,” he says, “thanks be to God, arose in the English Church from the time of Pope Vitalian and Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, and was regarded as almost obligatory: not only clerics in monasteries, but also lay people with their wives and families, would come to their confessors and, with the distribution of alms, cleanse themselves through tears from participation in carnal desire during these twelve days, so that they might receive the Lord’s Communion at the Nativity in a purer state. Besides these established fasts, many fasted on Wednesday and Friday because of Christ’s Passion, and on Saturday because on that day he lay in the tomb.”

A servant of God is in no way permitted to fight, even if it is with the counsel of many servants of God. This is certainly more correct than the reading found in chapter 42, published by the Right Reverend Luca Acherius as follows: “Clerics are in no way permitted to fight except in a multitude or with the counsel of servants of God.” This reading is wholly at odds with the canons of the councils, both those preceding and those following it.

Council of Chalcedon, chapter 7:

> “We decree that those who have once been ordained into the clergy, and likewise monks, may not enter military service or attain secular rank. Those who dare to do this, and who return to what they had previously chosen for God’s sake without being moved to repentance, are to be anathematized.”

Council of Angers, canon 7:

> “Clerics who, having abandoned the clergy, have turned to secular military service and to the laity are justly removed by the Church which they abandoned.”

Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 4:

> “If clerics are found to have willingly taken up arms in any sedition, or to have taken them up, they shall lose their rank and be delivered to a monastery of penance.”

First Council of Mainz, chapter 2:

> “We have altogether prohibited servants of God from carrying weapons, fighting, or going to the army and into battle.”

Synod of Metz, canon 16:

> “That clerics shall not carry weapons.”

The ecclesiastical chapters of Charlemagne, chapter 4:

> “For the second time, instructed by apostolic authority and by the admonition of many bishops, and taught by the rules of the holy canons, with the counsel, namely, of all our nobles, correcting ourselves and giving an example to our successors, we wish no priest to go into battle, etc.”

A little later:

> “They are not to carry weapons, go to battle, or become shedders of blood or instigators; rather, they are to carry only the relics of the saints and the sacred ministries, and devote themselves earnestly to prayers, so that the people who must fight may, with the Lord’s help, be victorious, and so that the priest may not be like the people.”

If Charlemagne says that he is correcting himself, instructed by the rules of the canons, for having ordered something contrary to them—namely, that priests should fight—how could Theodore, who was deeply devoted to the rules of the canons, have decreed that clerics were permitted to fight with the counsel of many servants of God?

Finally, it is clear from the chapters of Herard of Tours that such men were to be deposed so that they would not even possess lay communion. Chapter 50:

> “If priests and deacons go forth into war with weapons, they are to be deposed in such a way that they may not even receive lay communion.”

Therefore the text must be read as it appears in two manuscripts of Theodore’s *Penitential*:

> “A servant of God is in no way permitted to fight, even if it is with the counsel of many servants of God.”
