An infant may be given to God in place of an infant. That it is sufficiently ancient in the Church to dedicate infants to perpetual virginity is shown by the example which Sulpicius Severus reports in the *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 20:

> “This event,” he says, “so affected Arborius that he immediately vowed the girl to God and dedicated her to perpetual virginity, etc.”

Saint Augustine, *On the Quantity of the Soul*, chapter 36:

> “But how much the consecration of infant children benefits them is a very obscure question; nevertheless, it must be believed that it benefits them to some extent. Reason will discover this when it is necessary to inquire into it, although I have already presented many other matters to you as subjects for inquiry rather than as things to be known. This will be done most profitably if they are sought under the guidance of piety.”

After Saint Basil, Theodore judged that consecrations of this kind could easily be dissolved. Thus, in chapter 120, Basil judged that boys were permitted to marry before the age of sixteen if they could not remain continent, even though they had been monks. See also what we related above.

Concerning the dead, knowledge belongs to God alone. Anastasius II, in letter 1 to Anastasius Augustus, chapter 2:

> “Therefore, since the most blessed Apostle Paul warns us not to create any stumbling block in the Church by attempting to judge those who have already passed away concerning matters which belong to God alone, let your Serenity know that this must be observed. For he says concerning those who presume to judge matters belonging to God alone: ‘None of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself,’ etc.”

Other testimonies of the Fathers on this matter may be read in Pope Vigilius’s decree concerning the Three Chapters. But the same question was discussed at length by the Fathers of the Second Council of Constantinople. See the Emperor Justinian’s letter to the Second Council of Constantinople; Cyril’s letter to Saint Proclus; Proclus’s letter to John of Antioch; the Eighth Session of the Second Council of Constantinople; Pope Pelagius II’s letter to Elias of Aquileia and the other bishops of Istria; and Emperor Justinian’s edict against the Three Chapters.

# CHAPTER XIV. On Reconciliation

[Col. 1162D]

The Romans reconcile a person within the apse. Second Council of Carthage, canon 32:

> “If the public and notorious crime of any penitent is known throughout the whole Church, hands are to be imposed upon him before the apse.”

Since Theodore says “within the apse,” the apse must necessarily be understood not merely as the bishop’s seat or throne, but rather as that space near the high altar which is separated from the rest of the church by screens, as Stephanus Baluzius learnedly observes in his notes on Regino and proves by the testimony of Anastasius in the *Life of Leo III*.

[Col. 1163]

# The Doctrine on Penance of Theodore, Most Holy and Most Learned Archbishop of Canterbury, Vindicated from Every Suspicion of Novelty

[Col. 1163A]

Joannes Morinus, a most learned man, in book X of *Penance*, chapter 17, presents Theodore as an innovator in ecclesiastical discipline concerning penance, as follows:

> “Once this has been granted,” he says, “the first foundations of this custom were laid in England around the year 680, and Theodore, a Greek who was the first openly to abolish the practice of doing public penance for secret crimes, etc.”

He professes that this custom was sanctioned by very many canons of the councils, in book V, chapter 9, in these words:

> “There are almost as many arguments for this ancient practice as there are canons enacted against those guilty of crimes a thousand years ago.”

Morinus himself asserts the same thing by several other arguments, which must be examined in their proper place. But to prove that Theodore could not have introduced anything novel in this matter contrary to the canons, I shall first demonstrate three points:

1. That the Fathers plainly deny that the practice of doing public penance for secret sins was established by a decree of the Church;
2. That the same Fathers affirm that the Church’s practice was to do penance secretly for secret sins;
3. That public penance was instituted by the Church only for public crimes.

## CHAPTER I. The Fathers Deny That the Church Established by Decree the Practice of Doing Public Penance for Secret Sins

Origen, *Homilies on Leviticus*, homily 3:

> “Do you wish to know that these things also agree with the evangelical commandments? The Lord himself says: ‘If you see your brother sinning, rebuke him between yourself and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others. But if he does not listen to them either, tell it to the Church. But if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.’  
> 
> “But the evangelical commandment was given in a more perfect form in that it established the method and discipline for reporting a sin. For it does not wish you, if you happen to see your brother’s sin, immediately to fly into public view, proclaim it everywhere, and spread another person’s sins abroad; that would certainly be not correction but rather defamation. ‘Between yourself and him alone,’ he says, ‘rebuke him.’ For when the one who has sinned sees that he may keep the matter secret, he will also preserve the shame of correction. But if he sees himself being defamed, he will immediately turn to the shamelessness of denial; and you will not only fail to correct the sin, but will also double it.  
> 
> “Learn, therefore, the order from the Gospels. First, he says, alone between yourself and him; second, take with you one or two others. Why one or two? ‘For in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.’ Since he commands that the correction be brought to the Church the third time, he wishes one or two witnesses to be brought the second time. If, in their presence, the person rebuked does not wish to amend himself, then, when his sin has been brought before the Church, it can be refuted by the witnesses who were brought.”

There are as many arguments here as there are statements, by which Origen plainly denies that it was the Church’s practice to do public penance for secret sins.

1. He says that the evangelical commandment was given in a more perfect form because it established the method and discipline for reporting a sin. Yet it is clear that this method and discipline completely overturn public penance for secret sins.

2. He asserts that Christ’s evangelical commandment forbids secret sins from being made public. But what makes secret sins more public than public penance, which is for that reason called *exomologesis* by the Fathers? Although they distinguish public penance from public confession, public penance nevertheless brought the accused so fully into public view that at that time anyone was permitted to judge him to have been stained by murder, adultery, or idolatry.

3. He says that this is certainly not correction but rather defamation. But who would believe that in Origen’s time it was the Church’s custom not to correct sinners but rather to defame them—or at least that Origen believed this?

4. “When,” Origen says, “the one who has sinned sees that he may keep the matter secret, he will also preserve the shame of correction.” But where is the secrecy of sins, and what shame of correction is preserved by public penance?

5. Origen declares that when the secrecy of sins and the shame of correction are not preserved, the sinner turns to shamelessness. Thus, he says, “you will not only fail to correct the sin, but will also double it.”

6. Finally, he sets out the order of charity prescribed by Christ in the Gospels: if a person corrected by one individual concerning a secret sin amends himself, he ought not to be corrected by two; and if, after being corrected by two, or indeed by three, he amends himself, he ought not to be accused before the Church, expelled from the Church, or consequently punished by public penance.

It is therefore clear that Origen, by several arguments, denies that it was the Church’s practice to do public penance for secret sins.

Origen, *Commentary on Matthew*, edited by Huet, volume I, page 335:

> “After declaring that the words ‘You have gained your brother’ apply only to the one who obeyed, he did not repeat the same expression concerning the one who had been rebuked twice or three times, etc.  
> 
> “‘But if he does not listen to you, take with you one or two others, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand.’ What, then, will happen to the one rebuked twice, after every word has stood in the mouth of two or three witnesses? He leaves us to consider this. And again: ‘But if he does not listen to them’—that is, the witnesses previously brought—‘tell it,’ he says, ‘to the Church.’ He did not add what would happen if he did not listen to the Church, but taught that henceforth he was to be regarded as a pagan and a tax collector by the one who had rebuked him three times and had not been heard, if he did not follow the custom of the Church.”

If the words “You have gained your brother” apply to the one who obeyed, and that person ought not to be accused before the Church or expelled from the Church, it is evident that by this interpretation Origen completely denies that it was the Church’s practice to do public penance for secret sins.

An ancient author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, whom Eusebius mentions in book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 25, reports the discipline of the Church instituted by Christ in book II, chapter 37, as follows:

> “You, therefore, examine the one who has been accused, wisely observing what his life and character are. If you discover that the accuser is speaking the truth, do as the Lord taught should be done: meet the accused privately and rebuke him in the presence of no one, so that he may repent. But if he does not obey, bring one or two others, disclose his error to him, and admonish him with gentleness and discipline, since wisdom rests in a good heart, but in the heart of fools it is recognized.”

And chapter 38:

> “If, therefore, he trusts you three, all is well. But if someone is harsh and obstinate, tell it to the Church. If he despises the Church and refuses to listen, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector, and do not admit him to the Church as a Christian; rather, avoid him as a tax collector.”

A sinner is to be corrected privately by one person, with no one else present. If he does not obey, two or three are brought in; if he trusts them, all is well. It is not necessary to accuse him before the Church or expel him from the Church, unless afterward he becomes harsh and obstinate and makes the crime public. This is the Church’s discipline—one cannot set it forth without plainly denying that it was the Church’s practice to do public penance for secret sins.

[Col. 1165D]

Hilary, Bishop of Poitiers, *Commentary on Matthew*, canon 18:

> “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him, etc. The Lord imposed upon us this order for preserving charity, the same order which he himself had observed in preserving Israel. For he commands that the brother who has sinned be corrected and rebuked by the one against whom he has sinned. He himself rebuked the Jewish people when they sacrificed to foreign gods, by the majesty of his coming and by all the terror of his present power. Then, when that same people could not endure the approaching presence of God, although it was stationed outside the mountain, he ordered one or two to be brought in, so that by the testimony of two witnesses the reliability and truth of the word might remain.  
> 
> “Because Israel was insolent, the Law, the Prophets, and John were sent to it, and through these witnesses it was summoned to cease sinning. At the Lord’s third coming itself, it was admonished as though under the scrutiny of the assembly of the Church; and when these rebukes had been disregarded in vain, it was neglected with the contempt due to tax collectors and pagans.  
> 
> “For the terror of the greatest fear, by which all might then be restrained, he set forth beforehand the unalterable judgment of apostolic severity: that those whom they bind on earth—that is, whom they leave tied by the bonds of sins—and those whom they loose, receiving them into salvation through the confession, namely, of forgiveness.”

Saint Hilary affirms that this is the order for preserving charity which God observed toward the people of Israel and which Christ prescribed in the Gospel: sinners are to be corrected privately, then before two or three witnesses; they are not to be rebuked publicly unless, after being accused before the assembly of the Church, they are condemned as obstinate.

Therefore Hilary plainly denies that it was established by a decree of the Church that public penance should be done for secret sins.

John Chrysostom, in Homily 61 on Matthew, chapter 18:

> “But if your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone; if he listens to you, you have gained your brother. Since he had used vehement language against those who cause scandal, terrifying them with many arguments lest those who suffer scandals become sluggish and careless on this account; and lest, thinking that all the blame had been shifted onto others, they fall into softness and, imagining themselves worthy of every favor, lapse into arrogance: observe how he also restrains and checks the offenders themselves, and commands that the rebuke take place between two alone, lest, when the accusation appears more serious because of the testimony of the multitude, the person who has been rebuked disdainfully present himself as more difficult to correct. Therefore he says, ‘between you and him alone’; and, ‘if he listens to you, you have gained your brother.’ What does ‘if he listens to you’ mean? If, persuaded by you, he condemns himself for his sin, you have gained your brother, and so forth.

> “But what, you ask, shall I do if he is hard and obstinate? ‘Take with you,’ he says, ‘one or two others, so that every word may stand upon the mouth of two or three witnesses.’ For the more shameless and obstinate he is, the more diligently we must strive for his correction without anger or distress. A physician, too, when he sees that the illness is more serious, does not desist or, overwhelmed by difficulty, give up; rather, he prepares himself more carefully to apply remedies. This is what he also commands us to do, and so forth.

> “And if he has been hardened by obstinacy, let him also bring the Church to this sick man: ‘Tell it to the Church,’ and so forth. You see that this is done not for punishment but for correction. For this reason he does not bring anyone forward at the beginning; and when he himself has accomplished nothing, even then he does not order the matter to be entrusted to the multitude, but adds one person, or at most a second. If the offender despises these because of his insolence, only then does he decide that the matter should be brought before the Church. Thus great is his concern that the offenses of one’s neighbors should not be exposed until after a first and a second admonition.

> “What, then, does ‘every word shall stand upon the mouth of two or three witnesses’ mean? ‘You now have witnesses,’ he says; your work has been completed by you in such a way that nothing which pertains to you appears to remain. But if he does not listen to them, tell it to the Church—that is, to the bishops and those who preside—and so forth. ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven,’ and so forth. For when he knows this, although at the first stage he may have accomplished little, yet, convicted by the multitude of judgments, he may perhaps lay aside his anger. For this reason he does not cut him off immediately, but proceeds as far as a third judgment, so that, if he has not obeyed the first, he may obey the second.”

Thus Saint John Chrysostom denies that it was a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church to do public penance for hidden sins; he rejects such a practice as wholly contrary to charity:

> “‘Even then,’ he says, ‘he does not command the matter to be entrusted to the multitude. For this reason he does not cut him off immediately, but proceeds as far as a third judgment, lest, when the accusation appears more serious because of the testimony of the multitude, the person rebuked disdainfully present himself as more difficult to correct.’”

John Chrysostom, in Homily 29 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

> “‘This is the third time I am coming to you: in the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word stand.’ From many other considerations, and especially from this passage, one may perceive Paul’s wisdom and fatherly affection: namely, how abundant and vehement he is in announcing punishments, but how slow and reluctant in inflicting them. For he did not immediately punish those who were sinning, but admonished them once and again. Nor did he even then take action against the disobedient; rather, he admonishes and warns them again, saying, ‘This is the third time I am coming to you’; and, ‘before I come, I write again.’ Then, lest delay produce sluggishness in them, see how he corrects them here also, continually threatening and holding out blows, using these words: ‘If I come again, I will not spare.’ And lest, when I come, I should mourn over many.

> “He does and says these things in order to imitate the Lord of all even in this respect. For God continually threatens and often announces punishments, but does not often punish or inflict torment. This, therefore, he also does. For that reason he had said earlier, ‘Sparing you, I did not come again to Corinth.’ What does ‘sparing you’ mean? This: lest, finding you bound by crimes and persisting in them without any correction, I should afflict you with punishment and torment, and so forth.

> “What he says has this meaning: ‘Once I told you, and again when I came to you; and now I say the same thing by letter. If you listen to me, what I desired has happened. But if you despise my words, it will henceforth be necessary for me to do what I said and impose punishment,’ and so forth. Do you see fatherly care and concern? Do you see a prudence fitting for a teacher? He neither remained silent nor again inflicted punishment. Rather, he repeatedly foretells it, remains constant in his threats, and postpones the punishment. But if they remain obstinate in their sins, then at last he threatens that he will in fact inflict punishment.

> “What did you foretell, and what do you now write while present? ‘If I come again, I will not spare.’ After he had shown above that he could not do this unless compelled by necessity, and had called it mourning and humiliation, he says: ‘Lest, when I come, God should humble me before you, and I should mourn over those who sinned before and did not repent.’ Excusing himself to them, he asserts that he had warned them once, twice, and three times; and that he does and attempts everything possible to avert punishment and correction and to make them better through fear of his words. Then he places before them that grave and dreadful threat, saying: ‘If I come again, I will not spare.’

> “He did not say, ‘I shall punish and avenge myself and exact penalties’; rather, in fatherly language he sets forth the punishment, thereby showing his own inward affection and his heart suffering with them, since out of his indulgence toward them he continually deferred inflicting punishment. But lest they should now think that he was again using delay and employing only verbal threats, for this reason he had previously said, ‘In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word stand,’ and, ‘If I come again, I will not spare.’ What he says is this: ‘I shall delay no longer if, God forbid, I find you without correction; rather, I shall undoubtedly inflict punishment and carry out what I have said.’”

Since Saint Paul, imitating the Lord, did not immediately punish the impurity, fornication, and unchastity committed by many, but admonished them once and again; and since he issued so many threats that they might correct their vices and that their obstinacy would not compel him to expel them from the Church or subject them to punishment—is it not clear that he offered all the prelates of the Church an outstanding example of patience? This passage, so brilliantly explained by John Chrysostom, sufficiently demonstrates that it was not a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church to do public penance for hidden crimes, or for those which the obstinacy of the sinners did not make public.

Jerome, on the same words of Matthew, “Rebuke him,” and so forth:

> “A brother should be rebuked privately, lest, if he once loses his sense of shame and modesty, he remain in sin. If he listens, we gain his soul, and through the salvation of another our own salvation is also acquired. But if he refuses to listen, a brother should be brought in. If he does not listen to him either, a third should be brought in, either with the intention of correcting him or of confronting him in the presence of witnesses. But if he refuses to listen to them also, then it must be told to many, so that they may hold him in detestation; and he who could not be saved by shame may be saved by disgrace. When it is said, ‘Let him be to you as a heathen and a publican,’ it is shown that the person who, under the name of a believer, performs the works of unbelievers is more deserving of detestation than those who are openly gentiles, and so forth.

> “‘Amen, I say to you: whatever you bind,’ and so forth: he gives the apostles authority, so that they may know that those condemned by such persons are confirmed by divine judgment in their human judgment; and that whatever is bound on earth is likewise bound in heaven.”

If, then, according to Jerome’s opinion, when the offender refuses to listen to the testimony of three, it must be told to many, so that he who could not be saved by shame may be saved by disgrace, then undoubtedly, if he had been corrected under the testimony of three, it would not have been necessary to tell it to many; and he who could have been healed by shame would not have been healed by the disgrace of public penance. Jerome therefore denies that it was a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church to do public penance for hidden sins.

Bacchiarius, in his letter to Januarius on receiving back the lapsed:

> “Behold, it is forbidden that the fall or ruin of a brother should be scattered within the boundaries of Geth or the borders of Ashkelon—that is, into the knowledge of secular or worldly people. Yet we have endured that not only the city in which he lives, but the whole world, should be filled with despair concerning his reputation. Does not that evangelical saying also agree with this command, which says: ‘If your brother sins against you, rebuke him alone; but if he does not listen to you, take with you two or three witnesses,’ and the rest contained in the wording of the command, and so forth?”

Since Bacchiarius censures the recklessness of certain people who had made hidden sins public, he plainly denies that it was a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church to do public penance for hidden crimes.

Augustine, Sermon 16 on the Words of the Lord:

> “Therefore rebuke him between you and him alone, looking to his correction and sparing his shame. Perhaps, because of embarrassment, he begins to defend his sin, and you make the person whom you wish to make better worse. Rebuke him, therefore, between you and him alone. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother, because he would have perished unless you had acted. But if he does not listen to you—that is, if he defends his sin as though it were righteousness—bring two or three to him, because ‘in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.’ If he does not listen even to them, report it to the Church; if he does not listen to the Church either, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican. Do not count him any longer among the number of your brothers; nevertheless, his salvation must not for that reason be neglected,” and so forth.

And below:

> “‘If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between you and him alone.’ Why? Because he sinned against you. What does ‘he sinned against you’ mean? You know that he sinned. Since it was secret when he sinned against you, seek secrecy when you correct what he did against you. For if you alone know that he sinned against you, and you wish to accuse him before everyone, you are not a corrector but a betrayer, and so forth.

> “Therefore those things should be rebuked before everyone which are committed before everyone; but those things should be rebuked more privately which are committed more privately.”

Certainly, by these words Saint Augustine denies that it was a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church to do public penance for hidden sins.

Julianus Pomerius, Book II of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 5:

> “Moreover, if the weak are deprived of communion with the Church—those who cannot be cured when rebuked, or who, overwhelmed beyond measure by an unbearable weight of sorrow, collapse and turn away from the faces of all the saints through whom they might be restored to God—or if, once embittered, they rush into every shamelessness of sin and publicly perpetrate whatever evil they had done secretly, and through despair of recovering salvation fall into such madness that they turn the serious words of those rebuking them into deadly jokes with shameless wit, and by the very boasting of their disgraceful behavior feed the malicious joy of those who live wickedly—then, for this reason, those who cannot be rebuked because of their weakness must be borne with gentle compassion.

> “And indeed, if, while you blush for the sinner, you instill in him a salutary shame, and by pious compassion transfer to him the embarrassment which you assume on account of his sins, you easily suppress in him every license to sin and remove from him all the shamelessness that encourages wanton disgrace. Then shame, the guardian of integrity, will adorn his conduct, so that he will come to like what previously disgusted him when he was living in filth, and what previously pleased him will disgust him when he himself displeased all good people. He will lovingly follow holy men, and by following them will gradually be formed in their likeness through the correction of his former life. What was laborious for him when he rose to the heights of virtue will become as deformed to him when he descends again into the vices which he rejoices to have abandoned. For just as virtue is burdensome to the vicious, so vicious pleasure is bitter to the friend of virtue.

> “Behold how he treats or rebukes all sinners gently, considering nothing except the salvation of those whom he wishes to benefit.”

Julianus Pomerius first shows how harmful public rebuke is to the weak, so much so that one must fear that they may publicly perpetrate whatever evil they had done secretly; then he declares how useful and entirely necessary secret penance is for hidden sins. Therefore, like the other Fathers, he plainly denies that it was a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church to do public penance for hidden sins.

## Chapter II. The Fathers affirm that secret penance suffices for hidden sins, and that the Church’s custom was to do penance for them secretly

The arguments by which the Fathers deny that it was a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church to do public penance for hidden sins prove the same thing: that secret penance suffices for hidden sins. For if someone, having been rebuked by one person, corrects himself, he ought not to be rebuked by two or three; and if someone who did not obey at first nevertheless obeys two or three, he ought not to be expelled from the Church—that is, punished with public penance. Since penance is altogether necessary, it must also be the case that secret penance suffices for him. Hence it is clear that the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden sins. We shall nevertheless demonstrate the same question by other evident arguments, so that every doubt may be removed.

Origen, Homily 2 on Psalm 38:

> “But if he himself becomes his own accuser, accusing and confessing himself, he simultaneously vomits out the offense and digests the entire cause of the illness. Only take careful thought about to whom you ought to confess your sin. First test the physician to whom you should disclose the cause of your sickness, one who knows how to be weak with the weak and to weep with those who weep, who knows the discipline of grieving and compassion. Then, if he proves himself both an educated and merciful physician, do whatever advice he gives and follow it. If he understands and foresees that your illness is of such a kind that it ought to be disclosed and cured in the gathering of the whole Church, from which perhaps the others may also be edified and you yourself easily healed, this must be undertaken only after much deliberation and with the sufficiently expert advice of that physician.”

Here are three arguments by which Origen affirms that the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden sins.

1. Origen does not approve of confessing oneself guilty before everyone, but only before an expert and tested physician. Would a physician need to be tested? Would a sinner need to consider carefully to whom he should confess his sin, unless the custom of the Church had been to do penance secretly? It is useless to reply that public confession is distinct from public penance. Public penance would not spare shame any more, since at that time anyone would have been able to judge that the crime committed was homicide, adultery, or idolatry.

2. This tested physician gives advice to do public penance, not a command. Therefore public penance for hidden crimes had not yet been sanctioned by a decree of the Church; rather, the custom was to do penance secretly. For, as Jerome says in Book I *Against Jovinianus*: “Where advice is given, the choice belongs to the one who offers it; where a command is given, necessity belongs to the one who obeys.”

3. Advice to do public penance is given only in an exceptional case. But just as an exception confirms the rule, so this exceptional case demonstrates that the Church’s custom was to do penance secretly for hidden crimes.

The Fathers of the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 4:

> “If someone resolves to desire a woman in order to sleep with her, but his desire does not proceed to the act, he appears to have been freed by grace.”

Adultery committed in the heart is a serious crime, and yet the Fathers declare that secret penance suffices; consequently, the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden crimes.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, in his exposition of Psalm 51:

> “For confession of sins exists only during the time of this age, while each person is left to his own will and, through the freedom of life, has the choice of confession,” and so forth.

He added the reason for confession, saying, “because you have done it”: that is, confessing the Lord as the author of all things, he teaches that confession should be made to no one other than the one who made the fruitful olive of hope through the mercy that endures forever.

Basil the Great, in his homily on Psalm 37:

> “It is characteristic of prudent people, on account of what they have committed through sin, whether by some presumptuous thought or by the enemy’s deception, not to exalt themselves, but rather to be covered with shame and blush, and, as though pricking their conscience with goads, to conduct themselves more humbly and abase themselves. David therefore says afterward: ‘I roared from the groaning of my heart,’ or, according to Aquila, ‘I groaned from the groaning of my heart.’ I do not confess with my mouth in order to become known to many; rather, with my eyes closed, roaring within myself in my heart, I show you alone, who behold hidden things, my groans. For I do not need many words for confession; the sighs of my heart and the complaints sent to you, my God, from the deepest recesses of my soul are sufficient.”

Basil, in the *Shorter Rules*, response to question 229:

> “The same principle applies altogether to the confession of sins as to the disclosure of bodily illnesses. Therefore, just as people do not recklessly disclose bodily illnesses to everyone, but only to those who can treat them, so confession of sins should be made only to those who can cure them. This agrees with what is written: ‘You who are stronger, bear the weaknesses of the weak’—that is, remove them through your diligence and care.”

Thus Saint Hilary and Basil wish confession and penance to be so secret that they say it should be performed before God alone and before those who are able to cure. They therefore openly affirm that the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden sins.

Gregory of Nyssa, in his canonical letter to Letoius, bishop of Melitene:

> “But whoever secretly appropriates what belongs to another, if afterward he discloses his sin to a priest by confession, will cure his illness by changing the tendency of his vice into its opposite. I mean by giving away what he has, so that, while he pours out what he possesses, he may openly show himself freed from the disease of greed. But if he has nothing except his body, the Apostle commands him to cure that disease through bodily labor. The wording of the passage is as follows: ‘Let the one who stole steal no longer, but rather let him labor, doing what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one in need.’”

Saint Gregory of Nyssa testifies that in this canonical letter he reports not his own judgment but that of his fathers and the canonical judgment. Why, then, is the person who secretly appropriated what belonged to another not punished according to the canons with public penance, but is considered sufficiently punished by secret penance, unless the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden sins?

Hilary the deacon, author of the work composed under Pope Damasus, *Questions from the Old and New Testaments Mixed Together*, question 52:

> “There is still something which Novatian discovers. ‘Why,’ he says, ‘do they give the Lord’s body to those whom they know to be sinners?’ As though those who are judges could themselves become accusers. But if they had been accused and exposed, they could have been expelled. For what judge would assume the role of an accuser? If the Lord himself tolerated Judas, whom he knew to be a thief and to carry away what was put into the common purse, and did not expel one who had not been accused, this example must be followed, so that one who has not been publicly exposed may not be expelled.

> “Nor is it fitting for a righteous man to accuse anyone. Hence Matthew says: ‘Joseph, being a just man and unwilling to expose her, wished to dismiss her secretly.’ Judas, therefore, while he was among the disciples, did not defile them by his contamination, since they certainly dissented from his thefts; and, receiving the Eucharist among them, he did not pollute the innocent. The Lord did not deny his body to the one whom he knew to be a thief, because, according to the Apostle, ‘the one who receives it unworthily receives a sword for himself.’”

Hilary the deacon, against the Novatians, confirms the custom of the Catholic Church by Christ’s example: one who has not been publicly exposed may not be expelled. Therefore the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden sins.

Ambrose, in his exposition of Psalm 37:

> “She was accused and remained silent. She was led to death and concealed herself in silence, lest she expose her shame. Yet within herself she spoke to God, who heard her more readily while she was silent. If she had wished to speak, perhaps she would not have been heard. And so you, who have resolved to make satisfaction for your offenses to the Lord your God, cleanse yourself before him alone in your inmost heart; look to him who can wash away sins.”

Saint Ambrose could not use this exhortation without affirming that the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden sins. The author of his life therefore testifies that he observed this custom so carefully that he left the other priests a good example:

> “Whenever someone who had fallen confessed his sins to him in order to receive penance, he wept in such a way that he compelled the other person also to weep. He seemed to himself to lie together with the one lying prostrate. But the causes of the crimes which they confessed to him he spoke of to no one except the Lord alone, before whom he interceded—leaving a good example to later priests, that they should be intercessors before God rather than accusers before human beings.”

For, according to the Apostle, charity must be confirmed toward such a person, because he is his own accuser and does not wait for an accuser, but forestalls one, so that by confessing he may himself lighten his offense and leave nothing for an adversary to accuse. Therefore Scripture says: “The righteous man is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech.” He takes away the voice of the adversary and, like teeth prepared for prey, breaks the hostile accusation by confessing his sins, giving honor to God, before whom all things are naked and who desires the sinner’s life more than his death.

John Chrysostom, in Homily 20 on Genesis, chapter 5:

> “For the fornicator, or adulterer, or one who has committed anything of that kind, even if he can escape the notice of everyone, nevertheless never lives in tranquility, and so forth. Yet if the person who has done these things wishes to use the aid of conscience as he ought, and hastens to confess his crimes, and shows the wound to a physician who will cure him and not reproach him, and receives remedies from him, and speaks to him alone, with no one else aware, and tells him everything carefully, he will easily correct his sins. For confession of sins is also the abolition of offenses.”

What could be clearer than these words, by which Saint John Chrysostom affirms that any crimes—such as fornication, adultery, and other things of the same kind—which are hidden from others are abolished by secret penance?

Some think that John Chrysostom speaks in this way because they believe that public penance was abolished by his predecessor, Nectarius, bishop of Constantinople. But first they are refuted by Chrysostom’s own testimonies, since in his homilies delivered at Constantinople he preached public penance, as is demonstrated most effectively in his life written in French by Godefridus Hermantius, a most learned theologian and associate of the Sorbonne.

Second, this objection is entirely without force, since there is no doubt that he delivered the homilies on Genesis at Antioch, just as he delivered the homilies on the Epistle to the Corinthians, in which he declares that public penance for public sins was in force. Thus, in Homily 28 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, he says:

> “Again, when we exclude those who cannot participate in the sacred table, another prayer must be made, and all must likewise lie prostrate on the ground,” and so forth.

Saint Chrysostom, in Homily 21 to the people of Antioch:

> “Our Agonothete (president of the games) does the opposite. He does not take the person up and lead him around saying, ‘Does anyone accuse this man?’ Rather, he cries out: even if the demons, standing with the devil, accuse him of the foulest and most hidden crimes, I neither reject nor abhor him; instead, freeing him from his accusers and absolving him from iniquity, I lead him to the contests—and not without reason, and so forth.

> “Nor is this alone admirable: that he forgives us our sins, but also that he does not reveal them or make them public, and does not compel those who approach him to declare in the midst of the assembly what they have done. Rather, he commands them to render an account to him alone and confess to him. For if, among secular judges, someone were to say to one of the imprisoned robbers or graverobbers that he should confess his sins and be released from punishment, they would certainly accept this with complete readiness, disregarding shame out of desire for salvation. Here, however, it is not merely that he forgives sins; he also does so without compelling them to declare them in the presence of others. He requires only this one thing: that the person who receives forgiveness should learn the greatness of the gift.”

John Chrysostom, in Homily 8 on Penance:

> “Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink from that cup. He did not expose the wound or bring the accusation into the public theater. He did not appoint witnesses of his sins. Rather, within his conscience, with no one present except God, who sees all things, who searches and judges sins, and who weighs everyone’s life as though on a balance, let him establish judgment concerning his sins and bring his whole life before the judgment of his mind; reform what you have done wrong, and then approach the sacred table with a pure conscience and become a participant in the holy sacrifice. Keeping these things in mind, and remembering all that we have said about lust, and the punishment appointed for those who gaze immoderately and immodestly upon a woman’s face, and keeping before our eyes fear of God and love of him, let us cleanse ourselves in every way and so draw near to the sacred mysteries, lest they become for us judgment and condemnation, but that we may receive them for salvation, the healing of the soul, and the continual assurance of this salvation.”

In Homily 10 on Penance, which in published editions is incorrectly entitled 9:

> “Even if you have sinned in extreme old age, enter and do penance. This is a place of medicine, not of judgment; it does not exact punishments but grants forgiveness of sins. Tell your sin to God alone: ‘Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you,’ and your sin is forgiven.”

In the sermon on the Pharisee and the Publican:

> “Therefore I urge you to confess your sins. For I neither bring you into the theater of your fellow servants nor compel you to declare them to human beings. Lay your conscience open before God; show him your deeds and wounds, and ask him for medicine. Show yourself to one who does not reproach but cures.”

In Homily 31 on the Epistle to the Hebrews:

> “Let us not merely call ourselves sinners, but also enumerate our sins, listing each one. I do not tell you to bring them into public or accuse yourselves before others, but to obey the Prophet who says: ‘Commit your way to the Lord’; confess your sins to God.”

In Homily 36 on the Acts of the Apostles:

> “What, then, if I have grievously offended? Cease offending, shed tears, and then approach; immediately you will find him especially favorable. Say only, ‘I have offended’; say it from the heart and with a pure mind, and everything is forgiven. You do not desire your sins to be forgiven as greatly as he desires your sins to be forgiven.”

See the same things in Homily 5 on the Incomprehensible Nature of God; Discourse 4 on Lazarus; Homily 2 on Psalm 50; and in the homily entitled *That Sins Must Not Be Made Public*. See also Cassian, the disciple of John Chrysostom, in Conference 20, chapter 8. All these passages demonstrate that the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden sins.

Innocent I, in his letter to Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, chapter 4:

> “It has also been desired that it be known why married men who communicate do not remain with adulterous wives, whereas wives seem to remain in the company of adulterous husbands. On this matter Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and hidden sins do not receive punishment; men, however, are accustomed to report adulterous wives more freely to priests, and therefore communion is denied to women when their crime has been exposed, whereas, when the offense of men remains hidden, scarcely anyone is withheld on the basis of suspicions. He will indeed be removed if his crime is uncovered. Since, therefore, the case is equal, when proof is lacking the administration of punishment sometimes comes to an end.”

Why, then, are many adulterous men not punished with public penance? “Because,” he says, “hidden sins do not receive punishment,” when the offense of men remains hidden. Therefore the custom of the Church was to do penance secretly for hidden sins.

Bacchiarius, in his letter to Januarius:

> “But, leaving these matters aside, let the deceased be mourned and the dead buried—that is, let his sin be concealed and removed from public view, partly by our labor and partly by the confusion of his own shame. Let us provide the linens of consolation and the perfumes of heavenly hope. But let him, confused within the tomb of his secrecy by shame over his sin, restrain himself there; let him be torn by the worm of his conscience, which binds within him all the putrefactions of sins.”

Is this not penance performed secretly? Nevertheless, Bacchiarius considers it sufficient even for the unspeakable crime of adultery; his little works are praised by Gennadius in the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*.

Augustine, on Psalm 31:

> “‘I shall declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my heart. ‘I said.’ What did you say? He does not yet declare it, but promises that he will declare it, and God already forgives. Pay attention, brothers: a great thing is this—‘I said, I shall declare.’ He did not say, ‘I declared, and you forgave’; for by saying, ‘I shall declare,’ he shows that he had not yet declared with his mouth, but had declared in his heart. To say this very thing, ‘I shall declare,’ is to declare it; therefore you also forgave the wickedness of my heart. My confession had not yet come to my mouth. I had said, ‘I shall declare against myself,’ yet God heard the voice of my heart. My voice was not yet in my mouth, but the ear of God was already in my heart.”

No penance can be imagined more secret than this; nevertheless, Saint Augustine considers it sufficient, since he acknowledges that the sin was forgiven by God.

In Sermon 44 on the Gospel of John:

> “‘Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.’ He has not yet approached her bodily; he consented in his heart. He has a dead man within, but has not yet carried him outside. And it happens, as we know and as people experience daily, that at times, when they hear the word of God—as though the Lord were saying, ‘Arise’—their consent to iniquity is condemned, and they breathe again into salvation and righteousness. The dead man rises within the house; he comes back to life in the secrecy of thought. This is the resurrection of the soul that was dead within, within the hiding places of the conscience, as though within the walls of the household.”

He speaks in the same way in many other places. For example, in Sermon 44 on the Words of the Lord:

> “But if the sin has still been conceived and has not proceeded into action, let the person repent, let the thought be corrected, and let the dead man rise within the house of conscience.”

How does this resurrection of the soul that was dead within take place—in the secrecy of thought, within the house of conscience, within the hiding places of conscience, as though within the walls of the household—unless by penance performed secretly? And why is public penance not applied? Because, Augustine says, “he has the dead man within and has not yet carried him outside”—that is, the crime is not yet public.

In Sermon 15 on the Words of the Lord:

> “Rebuke sinners before everyone, so that the others may have fear. Certainly, if someone distinguishes the times—which alone is correct—he resolves the question. If the sin is secret, rebuke secretly. If the sin is public and open, rebuke publicly, so that the offender may be corrected and the others may fear.”

And in the following sermon he clearly declares what the discipline of the Church is in these words:

> “Therefore those things should be rebuked more privately which are committed more privately. Distinguish the times, and Scripture agrees. Let us act in this way, and this is how we ought to act—not only when someone sins against us, but when someone sins in such a way that another person does not know: rebuke him secretly, lest, by wishing to rebuke him publicly, we betray the man. We wish to rebuke and correct him; but what if an enemy is seeking to hear something for which he can punish him? The bishop knows someone to be a murderer, and no one else knows it. I wish to rebuke him publicly, and you seek to bring an accusation. Certainly I neither betray nor neglect him. I rebuke him secretly; I place the judgment of God before his eyes; I terrify his blood-stained conscience; I persuade him to repent. We ought to be endowed with this charity.

> “For this reason people sometimes criticize us, saying that we do not rebuke, or they suppose that we know what we do not know, or that we remain silent about what we know. Perhaps you know it and I know it too, but I do not rebuke him in your presence, because I wish to cure, not accuse. There are adulterers in their homes who sin secretly. Sometimes their wives expose them to us, often out of jealousy, sometimes seeking their husbands’ salvation. We do not expose them publicly, but rebuke them secretly. Where the evil occurred, there let the wound die.”

Thus Saint Augustine frequently teaches that the Church’s custom was, with respect to hidden crimes, secretly—
of repenting.

[Col. 1177A] Cassian, *Collation* XX, “On the End of Penance,” chapter 5: “Therefore the truest examiner of penance and judge of pardon resides in our conscience: while we are still dwelling in this flesh, before the day of knowledge and judgment, he reveals to us the absolution of our guilt and discloses the grace of satisfaction and remission.”

Peter Chrysologus, sermon 24: “Peter and Paul, the princes of the Christian faith, spread knowledge of the name of Christ throughout the whole world. A woman was the first to teach the practice of approaching Christ; a woman was the first to provide the model of how a sinner may, through silent confession, erase sin without shame; how one who has done wrong, known only to God, need not be compelled by a conscience made ashamed to lay bare his guilt before human beings; how a person may anticipate judgment through pardon.” [Col. 1177B] This is the discipline of the Church: to do penance secretly for hidden sins. A woman first provided its model, and thereafter the Fathers proclaimed it with unanimous agreement.

The Fathers of the Council of Vaison II, canon 8: “If, however, a bishop knows himself to be aware only of another person’s crime, as long as he cannot prove it, let him say nothing; but together with that person let him work toward his repentance through private admonitions.”

Leo I, in his letter to all the bishops established in Campania, Samnium, and Picenum: “I also decree that the presumption against apostolic rule which I have recently learned is being committed there by certain persons through unlawful usurpation must be removed by every means—namely, the practice concerning penance which is imposed on the faithful in such a way that a written declaration listing the kind of each person’s sins is read publicly, when it is sufficient for the guilt of consciences to be disclosed to priests alone by secret confession. For although that fullness of faith seems praiseworthy which, out of fear of God, does not hesitate to be ashamed before human beings, nevertheless, since not everyone’s sins are of such a kind that those requiring penance do not fear to make them public, let so unreasonable a custom be removed, lest many be kept from the remedies of penance because they are either ashamed or afraid that their deeds might be disclosed to their enemies, for which they could be punished under the provisions of the law. That confession is sufficient which is first offered to God and then also to the priest, who comes as an intercessor for the offenses of the penitents. [Col. 1177C] For then more people will be able to be called to penance if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people.”

Although Saint Leo speaks of public confession, this must also be understood at the same time of public penance, which spared modesty no less than public confession and which made crimes from hidden offenses so public that those who had reason to fear that their deeds would be disclosed to their enemies—and for which they could be punished under the provisions of the law—were exempted from it. This is demonstrated by canon 34 of Saint Basil’s letter to Amphilochius. Since, therefore, exactly the same evils arise from public confession and public penance, it must be admitted that Saint Leo calls public penance for hidden crimes “a presumption against apostolic rule” and “an unreasonable custom,” one that was never confirmed by any decree of the Church. Accordingly, it is clear that penance performed secretly for hidden crimes is sufficient, and that it was the custom of the Church to do penance for them secretly.

Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 53: “Nor do we deny that mortal crimes may be absolved through secret satisfaction.”

Julianus Pomerius, *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 7: “Moreover, those whose sins are hidden from human knowledge, neither confessed by themselves nor made public by others, if they refuse either to confess or to amend them, will have as their avenger the God whom they have as their witness. And what does it profit them to avoid human judgment, when, if they persist in their evil, they are destined to undergo eternal punishment, by God’s assignment? But if they become their own judges and, as avengers of their own wickedness, willingly impose upon themselves here the punishment of the severest correction, they will exchange eternal punishments for temporal ones; and tears flowing from true contrition of heart will extinguish the flames of the eternal fire.” Since, if they become their own judges, they anticipate the Church’s judgment concerning public penance, it is evident that penance performed secretly is sufficient for them. This is also perfectly clear from the fact that afterward he joins to the penance of clerics—whom everyone knows not to have practiced public penance at that time—their penance as well, and describes both in the same way:

“Accordingly, they will more readily appease God who, not convicted by human judgment, but voluntarily, acknowledge their crime: either they disclose it by their own confessions, or, while others do not know what they secretly are, they themselves pronounce upon themselves a sentence of voluntary excommunication and, separated from the altar at which they ministered—not in spirit but in office—mourn their life as though it were dead, confident that, once God has been reconciled to them through the fruits of effective penance, they will recover not only what they have lost but will also, having become citizens of the heavenly city, attain everlasting joys.” Thus it was the custom of the Church to do penance secretly for hidden sins.

Caesarius, bishop of Arles, in homily 44, volume II of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 349: “I admonish you, brothers, in the sight of God . . . . . But if he does penance with all his heart—provided that he truly does penance—[Col. 1178D] when God saw a heart like David’s, when, rebuked by the prophet, he cried out with deep anguish and after God’s terrible threats, saying: ‘I have sinned,’ he immediately heard: ‘The Lord has taken away your sin.’ How much can three syllables accomplish? For there are three syllables: ‘I have sinned.’ But in those three syllables the flame of the sacrifice of his heart rose to heaven.”

In some manuscript codices this homily is attributed to Augustine, and in others to Ambrose. But whoever its Catholic author may have been, these words signify that penance performed secretly is sufficient even for the gravest crimes.

Laurentius, bishop of Novara, in a homily on penance: “If you possess prudence, if you have counsel and the proper judgment of your mind, God is in you. [Col. 1179A] He himself will be your penance, your fountain, your baptism, and your remission; he never ceases or fails within you. Why do you struggle in uncertainty? Why are you troubled in mind and, wearied by the foolish burdens of your conscience, grow numb? You sinned after the fountain; you fell after baptism; you committed a crime after universal pardon. Why has hope now perished? Has the reward perhaps been cut off? . . . From the day and hour when you came out of the bath, you yourself are a perpetual fountain and enduring remission. You have no need of a teacher or of the priest’s right hand. As soon as you came up from the sacred font, you were clothed in a white garment and anointed with mystical ointment; the invocation was made over you, and the threefold power came upon you, filling this new vessel with this new teaching. From then on he appointed you yourself as your own judge and arbiter, and gave you knowledge [Col. 1179B] so that you could learn from yourself good and evil—that is, the difference between merit and sin. And because, while remaining in the members and structure of the body, you could not exist free from sin and immune from guilt, after baptism he established your remedy within yourself and placed remission at your own disposal, so that you need not seek a priest when necessity demands it. Rather, like a knowledgeable and clear-sighted teacher, correct your error within yourself and wash away your sin through repentance. Therefore let hardness cease, let despair cease, let sloth cease. The fountain never fails; the water is within; cleansing lies at your own disposal; sanctification lies in diligence; remission lies in the dew of tears. Do not collapse into sluggishness: a perpetual fountain of repentance has been preserved in the human being. There is penance there in response to the voice of the Baptist, who cries out in the wilderness and, with penetrating proclamation, rouses the desolate minds of human beings, saying: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near.’ No one can possess the summit or height of the heavenly realm unless he has been supported by the aid of repentance. No one reaches the innermost places of the heavenly kingdom unless he does penance. The Baptist repeats again: ‘I baptize you with water for repentance; but another is coming after me who will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.’ Do not now seek either John or the Jordan. Be your own Baptist. Have you been polluted after the washing? Have your inward parts been corrupted? Has your soul been defiled? Dip yourself in the water of repentance; wash yourself with an abundance of tears; let the fountain of contrition overflow [Col. 1179D] in your inward parts; let living waters surge through your fibers. Prepare yourself for the coming Lord, and he himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire, holding the winnowing shovel in his hand. This signifies the examination or weighing of repentance and sin. He himself weighs both burdens in you; he himself sees in you the mass and the mass: one of repentance, the other of corruption. The fruit of repentance, like wheat, he gathers for your progress; but your sins, like the chaff of corruption, he burns with unquenchable fire. This is private remission, summoned from the innermost heart and acquired through repentance.”

How many words, so many arguments proving that penance performed secretly for hidden crimes is sufficient and that it was the custom of the Church to do penance secretly for hidden sins.

[Col. 1180A] Gregory, *Moralia*, book IV, on chapter 3 of Blessed Job, chapter 15: “We therefore turn day into darkness when, punishing ourselves strictly, we torment through the severe lamentations of penance the very enticements of wrongful pleasure, and when, with tears, we pursue whatever we silently sin in our hearts through pleasure. For since every faithful person knows that thoughts will be examined with subtlety at the judgment—as Paul attests when he speaks of ‘thoughts accusing or even defending one another’—he examines himself inwardly with great rigor before the judgment, so that the strict Judge may come all the more peacefully, seeing that the guilt he wishes to examine has already been punished for the offense.”

Then, the comparison which Saint Gregory establishes in the entire following chapter between the penance that will be made especially public on the day of the final judgment and the other voluntary penance practiced here in this life by many who judge themselves within the hiding places of conscience sufficiently and more than sufficiently confirms that penance performed secretly is sufficient, so that they will certainly not be judged by the Lord on the day of manifestation.

Gregory, *Pastoral Care*, part III, admonition 8: “The shameless must be admonished in one way, and the modest in another. The former are restrained from the vice of shamelessness only by harsh rebuke. The latter, however, are generally brought to better conduct by a measured exhortation. The former do not know that they are doing wrong unless they are rebuked by many; for the latter, it is generally enough for conversion that their teacher gently recalls their sins to their memory. The one who reproves them by attacking them corrects the former more effectively; but the latter make greater progress if what is reproved in them is touched, as it were, obliquely. He later demonstrates this by the example of God and Paul, and gives this reason: harsh speech would expose the faults of the former, while gentler speech would conceal the negligence of the latter.”

Therefore public penance is necessary for the shameless, whose crimes are exposed by harsh rebuke; but hidden penance suffices for the modest, whose sins are covered by gentler speech.

In admonition 30: “For the merciful God often washes away the sins of the heart more quickly by not allowing them to proceed into actions; and the sooner a contemplated wickedness is released, the less strictly it is bound by the accomplishment of the deed. Hence the Psalmist rightly says: ‘I said: I will declare my injustices against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.’ For the one who brought forward the wickedness of his heart indicated that he wished to declare the injustices of his thoughts. Finally, he says: ‘I will declare my injustices against myself.’ And when he says, ‘I said, I will declare,’ and immediately adds, ‘and you forgave,’ he shows how easy forgiveness is in this matter. While he still promises to ask, he obtained what he promised to ask for: because the fault had not yet reached the deed, repentance did not reach torment, but the affliction conceived in thought cleansed the mind which conceived in thought alone had defiled.”

In admonition 32: “Again, they must be admonished that, if they are not afraid to be evil, they should at least be ashamed to appear what they are. For often a fault is driven away while it is hidden, because when the mind is ashamed to be seen as what it nevertheless was not afraid to be, it eventually becomes ashamed to be what it wished to avoid appearing to be.”

Thus, through numerous testimonies, Saint Gregory makes clear that penance performed secretly is appropriate and sufficient for the modest whose sins are hidden, and therefore that it was the custom of the Church to do penance secretly for hidden sins.

John, abbot of Raithu, to whom John Climacus wrote a letter, in his scholia on the fifth step of Climacus, on the words, “and the secure care of each person for himself”: “Because,” he says, “he cares for nothing earthly, but is concerned for himself, he hastens to reconcile God to himself and to recover the salvation lost through sin by doing penance and mourning. He is concerned for himself and judged by himself, because, punishing himself and despising all that belongs to the world and himself, he is penitent and vigilantly recognizes himself as worthy of every judgment. His thought, therefore, has been judged by himself, because he does not need someone else for judgment; rather, the penitent person is himself his own judge and avenger.”

Eligius, bishop of Noyon, in a homily on the prodigal son: “You also, brothers, after the exhortation we have given to penitents, I admonish together with myself: let each of us return to the secrets of his conscience and ask himself how he has conducted himself throughout the year, especially during these holy days. And if he finds in his heart thorns and thistles of sins, let him strive, with God’s help, to uproot them as quickly as possible [Col. 1181C] and, by uprooting them, eradicate them; once they have been eradicated, let him dig with the saving plow and put in manure—that is, good works—so that he may produce fruit. And if even today he has confessed purely and lived devoutly, so that he may be worthy to take part in the solemnity of this present day—which is called the Supper because on it the Lord supped with his apostles—let him take the greatest care to be able to receive worthily the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood, so that he may obtain salvation rather than condemnation, and so forth. Therefore let us not shun these penitents on account of the magnitude of their crimes, for it may be that many among us have committed worse things.”

Why, then, would one who perhaps committed worse things than the public penitents, and who found in his heart thorns and thistles of sins, be able, if he had even today confessed purely and lived devoutly, to take part worthily in the solemnity, indeed in the Lord’s Supper—unless it was the custom of the Church to do penance secretly for hidden sins?

In homily 15, “On the Eating of Both Paschal Lambs”: “Whoever among you, therefore, recalls that during these observances of forty days he has practiced penance and fulfilled the obligation of his confession, let him give thanks to the Lord; and whatever he has destroyed within himself by violating the temple of God, let him not despair, but quickly rise from the evil of his iniquity. For it is not the fact that he sins, but the fact that he persists in sin, that is hateful to God. Therefore, to use the words of the Lord according to Mark, when he says, ‘What I say to all I say: Watch,’ similarly, what I say to all of you I say: to clerics, laypeople, and holy women: whatever he recalls himself to have been touched by through the contagion of envy, slander, hatred, fornication or incest, perjury, or other vices, let him at least today strive to purify himself, insofar as he can, through the medicine of divine salvation. Let him confess his injustice against himself to the Lord, so that he may forgive the wickedness of his heart, and the remnants of his thoughts may keep a feast for the Lord. The remnants of one’s thoughts keep a feast for the Lord when any sinner, after having previously made confession, promises to restrain himself from his iniquity and pours himself out entirely in tears and heartfelt affection, because God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart. Such a festivity is made for rejoicing angels, as the Truth bears witness, saying: ‘There is joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner.’”

Since Saint Eligius immediately turns his discourse to public penitents, it is clear that he was addressing hidden sinners, including perhaps those whom he notes to have committed the crime of incest. Nevertheless, he affirms that they can quickly rise from the evil of their iniquity, so that, if they confess their injustice against themselves to the Lord, he will forgive the wickedness of their hearts; the remnants of their thoughts will keep a feast for the Lord; this festivity will be celebrated by rejoicing angels; and on that very day they will purify themselves through the medicine of divine salvation.

These are the testimonies of the Fathers, brought down through the succession of times as far as Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury. All of them demonstrate that penance performed secretly for hidden sins is sufficient, and that it was the custom of the Church to do penance secretly for them.

## CHAPTER III. The Fathers testify that public penance was canonically established by the Church only for public crimes.

It is unnecessary to show that Tertullian, in his book *On Penance*, and Cyprian, in his letters, spoke of public penance as something imposed only on account of public crimes. Nicolaus Rigaltius, a most learned man who illuminated those Fathers with his notes, has made this more than sufficiently clear.

Origen, *Homilies on Joshua*, homily 21: “But just as it is said concerning the weeds, ‘lest, while gathering the weeds, you also uproot the wheat with them,’ so too it can be said concerning those in whom there are either doubtful or hidden sins. For we are not speaking about those who are manifestly and evidently guilty, so that they should not be expelled from the Church.” [Col. 1182D] And shortly afterward: “Therefore, since we cannot expel those who trample upon us, let us at least expel those whom we can—those whose sins are manifest. For where sin is not evident, we can expel no one from the Church, lest, while uprooting the weeds, we also uproot the wheat with them.”

If, where sin is not evident, prelates cannot expel anyone from the Church, it is clear from what Origen said above that only those who are manifestly and evidently guilty [Col. 1183A] are expelled from the Church, and therefore that public penance was established by the Church only for public crimes.

Origen, *Homilies on Judges*, chapter II, homily 2: “And, as it seems to me, even now people are delivered into the power of the devil in two ways. In the first way, as we said above, when a person’s offense becomes manifest to the Church and he is expelled from the Church by the priests, so that, marked by everyone, he may be put to shame, and so that what follows may happen to him: that his spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the other way, someone is delivered to the devil when his sin is not made manifest to human beings, but God, who sees in secret, observes his mind and soul serving vices and passions; and when he sees in his heart not only love of the world but also greed, lust, boastfulness, or other things of this kind, the Lord himself delivers such a person to Satan.”

This clear distinction between public and hidden excommunication plainly shows that public penance was established only for public crimes.

Origen, *Commentary on Matthew*, tractate 35: “For this reason such a custom has also prevailed in the Church of Christ: those who are manifest in great offenses are excluded from common prayer, lest a little leaven from the unclean heart of those praying corrupt the whole mixture of unity and agreement. Such, then, is the custom in the Churches of Christ: sinners are expelled from the Church and perform public penance—not because they have committed great offenses, but because they are manifest in great offenses.”

Thus Origen repeatedly declares that public penance was established by the Church only for public crimes.

The Fathers of the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 9: “But if he has not confessed it himself and cannot be openly convicted, let him be left to the judgment of his own power.”

Basil, letter 246: “It is necessary to hand him over according to the canons sanctioned by the Lord. For it is written: ‘If your brother sins, rebuke him between yourself and him; but if he does not listen to you, take another with you; and if he still does not listen, tell the Church; but if he does not listen even to the Church, let him thereafter be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.’ This very procedure was carried out in his case. He was accused and denounced at the same time; he was rebuked before one and another; thirdly, he was rebuked in the presence of the Church. Therefore, since we ourselves have testified against him and he did not submit to us, let him henceforth be excommunicated, and let him be denounced to the entire Church, so that they may not admit him.”

He was not handed over according to the canons sanctioned by the Lord until his obstinacy had brought his crime into public view; and Saint Basil affirms that this could not otherwise have been done. Since, therefore, the canons of the Church do not differ from the canons of the Lord, everyone must admit that public penance was established by the Church only on account of public crimes.

Hilary the deacon, on Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, chapter V: “Once this deed was known, he had to be expelled from the assembly of the brethren. For everyone knew of his crime and did not rebuke him; publicly he had his stepmother [Col. 1184A] in place of a wife. In this matter there was no need either of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.”

And in *Questions from the Old and New Testaments*, mixed together, question 102: “This is why the Apostle rebukes the people of Corinth: because they did not rebuke or avoid the man who publicly had his father’s wife, so that he might amend himself, saying: ‘Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?’ Since there was no leader or superior of the Church, it was the people’s responsibility to rebuke the man whom they saw behaving so shamefully and obscenely among them. Accordingly, the Apostle rebukes them as though they were consenting to his crime. For in this matter there was no need of an accuser or witnesses. Publicly he had his stepmother [Col. 1184B] in place of a wife.”

The reason for public penance is stated here with complete clarity, as Hilary reports it: “Everyone,” he says, “knew of his crime. Publicly he had his stepmother in place of a wife. In this matter there was no need either of witnesses, nor could the crime be concealed by any evasion.”

John Chrysostom, on Matthew 12, homily 82: “But someone may say that it is very easy to accuse the envious; rather, it must be explained how we may be freed from this disease. How, then, shall we prevent it from infecting us with its poison? If we take care that, just as it is unlawful for a fornicator to enter the church, so it should also be unlawful for an envious person.”

John Chrysostom maintains that envy which infects others with its poison—that is, envy which is public and a source of scandal to others—must be punished with public penance. Yet, as we showed above, he does not judge public penance necessary for hidden fornication and adultery. Therefore he plainly testifies that public penance was established by the Church only for public crimes.

Augustine, in his final homily: “Let a person therefore judge himself willingly in these matters while he can, and turn his conduct toward what is better, lest, when he can no longer do so, he be judged by the Lord even against his will. And when he has pronounced upon himself the sentence of the severest medicine, let him come to the bishops, through whom the keys are administered to him in the Church; and, like a good son who is already beginning to be, while preserving the order of the mother’s members, let him receive from the overseers of sacred things the measure of his satisfaction, so that, in offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart, devout and suppliant, he may do what benefits not only himself in receiving salvation but also the others by his example. Thus, if his sin consists not only in grave harm to himself but also in scandal to others, and if the bishop judges it beneficial to the welfare of the Church, he should not refuse to do penance before many people or even before the entire congregation. Let him not resist; let him not add swelling, through shame, to a lethal and deadly wound.”

Thus, when the bishop prescribes public penance to a sinner, it is not sufficient that his sin consist in grave harm to himself; it must also consist in scandal to others—that is, it must be public.

Augustine, *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, book III, chapter 2: “For this reason the Apostle himself also says, ‘If anyone is named a brother.’ In what he says, ‘if anyone,’ he seems to have wished to signify nothing other than that a person who sins among dissimilar people can be corrected in this way to his salvation—that is, among those whom the contagion of similar sins does not corrupt. But in saying ‘is named,’ he surely wished it to be understood that it is not enough for someone to be such unless he is also named—that is, unless he appears notorious—so that the sentence of anathema pronounced against him may seem entirely deserved to everyone. In this way he is corrected without violating peace, struck without destroying him, and burned medicinally.”

Augustine, sermon 41, *On the Saints*: “But for capital crimes this alone is not sufficient; tears, groans, and sighs must be added, together with fasts continued and prolonged for a long time, more generous almsgiving, our voluntarily withdrawing ourselves from communion with the Church, remaining for a long time in mourning and sadness, and even performing public penance. For it is just that the one who destroyed himself along with the destruction of many should redeem himself through the edification of many.”

Augustine, *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 65: “But because one person’s sorrow is often hidden from another and does not come to the knowledge of others through words or any other signs, although it is before the one to whom it is said, ‘My groaning is not hidden from you,’ those who preside over the Church rightly establish periods of penance, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church, in which the sins themselves are forgiven.”

Public penance is performed so that satisfaction may be made to the Church. But no one is considered to make satisfaction unless he has inflicted an injury, and unless the satisfaction is proportionate to the injury. If, therefore, the satisfaction must be public, it is likewise necessary that the injury was public.

Augustine, *On Correction and Grace*, chapter 16: “Rebuke those who sin before everyone, so that the others may have fear.” This must be understood of sins that are not hidden, lest he be thought to have spoken contrary to the Lord’s judgment. Thus Saint Augustine frequently testifies that public penance was established by the Church only for public crimes.

Julianus Pomerius, *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 7: “But whatever crimes of any persons, if they become known by any means while the guilty themselves refuse to confess them, and if they have not been healed by the gentle medicine of patience, must be burned and treated, as it were, by the fire of pious rebuke.
