But if even then the remedy of one who patiently bears with them and piously rebukes them has no effect on those who, though long tolerated and salutarily reprimanded, refuse to be corrected, they must be cut off by the sword of excommunication like rotten parts of the body. For just as dead flesh, if it is not cut away, infects at least the remaining flesh with the contagion of its rottenness, so these people, who disdain amendment and persist in their disease, will infect others by the example of their destruction if they remain among the holy in their depraved conduct.”

They are expelled from the Church because of the scandal they inflict on others. Therefore their crime was public. And since he declares that they must not be excommunicated until, after being tolerated for a long time and salutarily rebuked, they refuse to be corrected and infect others by the example of their destruction, he clearly shows that public penance was established by the Church only for public crimes.

Caesarius of Arles, homily 1: “But if anyone, questioning his own conscience, has committed some capital offense; or if he has attacked and betrayed his faith by false testimony; or has violated the sacred name of Truth; or, having stained the true baptismal garment and the beautiful silk robe of virginity, has polluted it with the filth of defiled modesty; or, by killing a human being, has killed the new person within himself; or, through augurs, diviners, and enchanters, has handed himself over as a captive to the devil—these and similar offenses cannot be completely expiated by ordinary and moderate satisfaction, even if it is secret. Rather, grave cases require more serious and harsher public remedies, so that the one who destroyed himself along with the affliction of many may redeem himself in like manner through the edification of many.”

This is the most certain rationale for public penance, which the Fathers repeat very frequently: the one who destroyed himself along with the affliction and destruction of many should redeem himself in like manner through the edification of many. Thus they testify that public penance was established by the Church on account of public crimes.

Gregory the Great, book XII, letter 32, to Felix, bishop of Messana: “Manifest sins must not be cleansed by hidden correction; those who do harm openly must be rebuked openly, so that, while they are healed by open reprimand, those who sinned by imitating them may be corrected. When one person is rebuked, many are amended. It is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through the license of one.”

Isidore of Seville, *Rules for Monks*, chapter 15: “A sin committed openly must be rebuked openly; and while the one who sins manifestly is corrected, those who imitated him in evil may be corrected.”

Eligius, bishop of Noyon, homily 16: “Moreover, my brothers, we address two men whom a public criminal accusation has compelled to perform public penance.”

Since these same Fathers, as we showed above, affirm that it was the custom of the Church to do penance secretly for hidden sins, they cannot introduce this rationale for public penance without plainly declaring that public penance was established by the Church only for public crimes.

But if the Fathers affirm that public penance was established by the Church only for public crimes; if the Fathers testify that, for hidden sins, it was the custom of the Church to do penance secretly; and if, finally, the Fathers plainly deny that it was a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church to do public penance for hidden sins, it is astonishing how J. Morinus could say that Theodore was the first person openly to abolish the practice of doing public penance for hidden crimes, and that there are so many proofs of this ancient practice—almost as many as there are canons enacted against criminals a thousand years ago. To prove this, he employs three principal arguments, which must now be examined and weighed according to their importance.

## CHAPTER IV. J. Morinus’s first argument is presented and refuted.

Joannes Morinus, a most learned man, in order to prove that, when confession of hidden capital crimes was made secretly to a priest, penance was nevertheless performed publicly according to the canons, first presents this argument in book V of *The Administration of the Sacrament of Penance*, chapter 9:

“There are,” he says, “as many proofs of this ancient practice as there are almost canons enacted against criminals a thousand years ago. For what else is it—or rather, what else can be imagined in the mind—than public penance when the canons decree that whoever has committed murder, [Col. 1187B] whoever has committed fornication, adultery, or incest, or has consulted magicians and enchanters, and so forth, should remain among the hearers for so many years, among those prostrated for so many years, among those standing for so many years, and then become a participant among the good, the perfect, and those in communion? In ancient times these and other terms were customarily used for reconciliation with God and the Church.

“Perhaps someone will object that there is no way to deny that these punishments were public. For who in his right mind could deny this? But they are to be understood as applying only to public sins. I would ask the person who makes this objection to consider three things.

“First, as Bishop Albaspinaeus of Orléans rightly also noted in canon 32 of the Third Council of Carthage, none of these canons distinguishes between public and hidden crime: ‘The one whose fornication is public shall stand among the hearers,’ [Col. 1187C] and so forth; but they speak absolutely: ‘whoever has fornicated,’ ‘whoever has committed murder.’ The canons often distinguish intentional murder from accidental murder; fornication from adultery; adultery against nature from human adultery; and various kinds of incest, with punishments appropriate to each. But they always impose public punishments. Yet never do the laws say, ‘If this crime is public, it shall be punished in this way; but if it is hidden, in that way.’”

**Response.**—But do not the Fathers clearly distinguish between public and hidden crimes, and between the penance appropriate to each—public penance for public crimes, secret penance for hidden ones—whenever they deny that it was the custom of the Church to perform public penance for hidden sins, as we showed in the first chapter; whenever they affirm that it was the custom of the Church to perform secret penance for hidden crimes, as we declared in the second chapter; [Col. 1187D] and whenever, finally, they assert that public penance was established by the Church only for public crimes, as we proved in the third chapter? What else is it to distinguish? Thus, for example, when Saint Augustine says in his sermon *On the Words of the Lord*: “Certainly, if someone distinguishes the times—which is the only true course—and thereby resolves the question, the matter is clear. If the sin is secret, rebuke him secretly. If the sin is public and openly known, rebuke him publicly, etc.” And in the following sermon: “Therefore, the things which are committed before everyone should be rebuked before everyone; but the things which are committed more secretly should be rebuked more privately.”

Could a clearer distinction be produced than that offered by the Fathers of the Council of Neocaesarea, [Col. 1188A] who decree that adultery committed in the heart is not to be punished by any form of public penance; and by the Fathers of the Second Council of Vaison, who in canon 8 forbid a bishop, when a hidden crime has been disclosed to him, to expel the guilty person from the Church and punish him publicly, but require him, as the Fathers say, to labor through secret reproofs? The Fathers of the Third Council of Carthage also plainly distinguish the matter in canon 3. Perceiving the difficulty of this canon, J. Morinus proposes to resolve it as follows:

“Immediately,” says J. Morinus, “the reader may perhaps object with canon 3 of the Third Council of Carthage: ‘If the crime of any penitent is public and most widely known, so that the whole Church is aware of it, hands shall be laid upon him before the apse.’ There is a different reading in this canon, but it contributes nothing to the present question. Yet, as Dionysius Petavius—whom we commended in the preceding chapter—rightly observed, [Col. 1188B] a strong argument for our position is drawn from this canon when it is compared with the preceding one. For the preceding canon says: ‘A presbyter shall not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when the bishop is absent and necessity compels it’; then comes: ‘But if the crime of any penitent is public, etc.’ It most evidently establishes two classes of public penitents: one whose crime is public, and another whose crime is not public, that is, hidden.”

But if, when these passages are compared, the canon establishes two classes of public penitents—one whose crime is public, and another whose crime is not public, that is, hidden—[Col. 1188C] it necessarily follows that anyone whose crime is public and widely known cannot be reconciled by a presbyter without consulting the bishop, even when the bishop is absent and necessity compels it. This conflicts with African discipline, even in the time of Saint Cyprian. In Letter 12, according to Rigalt’s edition, Cyprian writes to the clergy that those who have lapsed should not depart without reconciliation—that is, those who, through the crime of idolatry, had stirred the whole Church against themselves:

“If they are overtaken by some misfortune or danger of illness,” he says, “then, without awaiting our presence, they may make confession of their offense before any presbyter who is present; or, if no presbyter can be found and death begins to press upon them, they may make confession even before a deacon, so that, when hands have been laid upon them in penance, they may come to the Lord in peace.”

[Col. 1188D] Subsequently, this was established by several canons, so that no one might depart from life without reconciliation. Therefore J. Morinus’s interpretation is far removed from the true meaning. The true and genuine sense of this canon can easily be understood as follows: a presbyter, without consulting the bishop, shall not reconcile a penitent except when the bishop is absent and necessity compels it; but whenever the penitent’s crime is public, hands are to be laid upon him before the apse, except in a case of necessity. The *Penitential of Theodore* proves that this is unquestionably the meaning. It testifies that among the Romans the reconciliation of penitents took place within the apse, on Maundy Thursday, only by the bishop and after the penance had been completed; and that, if it was difficult for the bishop to do so, he could, for the sake of necessity, grant a presbyter authority [Col. 1189A] to complete the rite. Halitgar likewise bears witness to this in the preface to the *Roman Penitential*, as does Regino, Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*, chapter 296.

Since, then, among the Romans the reconciliation of all public penitents, except in cases of necessity, took place within the apse, and since the Fathers of the Third Council of Carthage assert that the reason for this public reconciliation was a public crime, it is clear that public penance was imposed by the Church only on account of public crimes. Consequently, they distinguished public crimes from hidden ones, for which all the Fathers, with unanimous agreement, judged secret penance sufficient.

This is the order for maintaining charity which God maintained toward the people of Israel, which Christ commanded in the Gospel, [Col. 1189B] and which the entire tradition of the Fathers confirms. Finally, it is the law of public equity and of the common law praised by all wise men: that each person should be loosed in the manner in which he has been bound by the cords of his sins.

## CHAPTER V

The second argument is refuted; and it is shown that, although nearly all the ancient canons are to be understood as referring to public crimes, J. Morinus nevertheless cannot rightly conclude from this that the ancient Fathers entirely neglected the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul. For, besides public penance of the sort described by J. Morinus, the ancient Fathers proposed many other remedies which they judged entirely sufficient for the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul.

“Secondly,” says J. Morinus, “it will follow that the ancient Fathers concerned themselves only with public crimes [Col. 1189C] and none at all with hidden ones. For if those canons are to be understood of public sins, no provision remains for hidden murders, fornications, and so forth. Yet crimes of this kind are secretly committed, while only one or another person is publicly detected. It would therefore follow that the ancient Fathers entirely neglected the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul—something which it is impious even to think, much less to say. If they regarded penance merely as punishment, this might perhaps be tolerated. But since they chiefly present it as a medicine, and since the Fathers give particular attention to this medicinal aspect, it cannot be said that they abandoned or treated with complete indifference the healing of ulcers so deadly that they would spread only if they appeared publicly and openly—a condition that occurs extremely rarely, scarcely ever—and that they were concerned only with curing light [Col. 1189D] and venial sins.”

**Response.**—Although the ancient Fathers did not explain, in the canons—which are public laws governing ecclesiastical judgment—the remedies by which hidden crimes are cleansed, J. Morinus nevertheless cannot rightly conclude from this that the ancient Fathers entirely neglected the healing of the gravest [Col. 1190A] diseases of the soul. For elsewhere, besides the public penance which J. Morinus describes in Book IV, chapter 7, *On the Administration of the Sacrament of Penance*, and which he says was established from the very beginnings of the Church in manifest afflictions and mortifications of the body, the ancient Fathers proposed many other remedies which they judged entirely sufficient for the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul.

Therefore, to make clear that the ancient Fathers did not neglect the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul, even though the canons are to be understood as referring to public crimes—and indeed that they exercised the greatest care concerning their healing—we shall set forth these remedies from the most ancient Fathers.

Clement, the disciple of the apostles, in the letter which he wrote in the name of the Roman Church to the Church of the Corinthians—a letter which Eusebius, Book III of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 16, testifies was accepted by all with unanimous agreement as eminent and wholly admirable—proposes the following remedies for sins:

“Ministers of divine grace, inspired by the Holy Spirit, spoke of repentance. The Lord himself, the Lord of all things, also spoke of repentance under oath. [Col. 1190B] ‘As I live,’ he says, ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner,’ adding this excellent statement concerning repentance: ‘Repent, house of Israel, from your iniquity.’ Say to the children of my people: ‘Even if your sins are multiplied from earth to heaven, even if they are redder than scarlet and blacker than sackcloth, and if you turn to me with your whole heart and say, “Father,” I will listen to you as to a holy people.’ And in another place he says: ‘Wash yourselves; be clean. Remove the evils from your souls before my eyes. Cease from your wickedness. Learn to do good; seek justice; deliver the oppressed; judge the orphan; and justify the widow. Come, let us reason together, says the Lord. Even if your sins are like crimson, I will make them white as snow; and if they are like scarlet, I will make them white as wool.’ [Col. 1190C] These are the remedies of repentance which the ministers of divine grace, inspired by the Holy Spirit, taught, and which the Lord himself, the Lord of all things, taught.”

Who, then, will deny that Saint Clement judged these remedies, drawn from Scripture, sufficient for the remission of the gravest crimes?

Justin Martyr, in his dialogue with Trypho the Jew, says:

“This is not where the good pleasure of our God consists. If there is among you a perjurer or a defrauder, let him cease from sinning. If there is a fornicator, let him turn away from evil and keep God’s true and joyful Sabbaths. If anyone has unclean hands, let him wash them and become pure.”

Saint Justin appears to have had in mind the words of Saint Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians, chapters IV and V, where the Apostle proposes suitable remedies for nearly every kind of sin: [Col. 1190D] for the sins of lying, truthfulness: “Therefore, putting away falsehood, let each of you speak the truth with his neighbor, because we are members of one another.” For the sins of anger and revenge, gentleness, mercy, and the remission of debts: “Be angry and do not sin. Do not let the sun go down upon your anger. Do not give place to the devil. Let all bitterness, anger, wrath, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice. Be kind to one another, compassionate, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.” For the crime of theft, almsgiving: “Let the one who stole steal no longer; rather, let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give [Col. 1191A] to the one in need.” For the sins of fornication, impurity, and greed: “Let fornication and every impurity or greed not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints.”

Then the Apostle describes the fruits of this penance: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light—for the fruit of light consists in all goodness, justice, and truth—proving what is pleasing to God. Do not participate in the unfruitful works of darkness; instead, expose them.”

And in the Letter to the Galatians, chapter V, he describes all the vices and immediately supplies suitable remedies:

“The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, shamelessness, debauchery, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, [Col. 1191B] anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, long-suffering, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, and chastity.”

These are the remedies which Saint Justin Martyr, following the Apostle, sets forth; and since he mentions no others, he judged these, together with Saint Paul, sufficient.

Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, Book I: “To do penance is to recover from illness.”

In Book II of the *Stromata*, the same teacher also says that repentance is great understanding:

“For the one who is led by repentance for what he has done no longer does or says such things, etc. [Col. 1191C] Repentance is a belated recognition, but recognition is the first cessation from sin. Repentance is therefore also the duty and work of faith. Unless a person believes that the thing by which he was previously held is sin, he will not withdraw from it; and unless he believes that punishment awaits the one who sins, while salvation is prepared for the one who lives according to the commandments, he will not change even then.”

Book IV of the *Stromata*:

“It is sufficient, as I believe, for a person’s purification to have complete, firm, and steadfast repentance: when we have condemned ourselves for our former actions, we should move forward, afterward understanding and raising up the mind, immersed in the love of God, both from the things that please the senses and from our former offenses.”

Book VI of the *Stromata*:

“There are two kinds of repentance: one is common, [Col. 1191D] because a person has sinned; the other arises when, having learned the nature of sin, a person is persuaded by the governing reason to desist from sin, with the consequence that he no longer sins.”

In *Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?*, chapter 38:

“If anyone receives that [teaching] into his mind, even though he is burdened with sins and has committed many unlawful deeds, he can correct his errors by increasing love and practicing pure repentance.”

The definitions of repentance which Saint Clement of Alexandria reports contain the greatest remedies, which he himself declares sufficient for the remission of the gravest sins. Among them, however, he in no way includes that public penance which J. Morinus says was established from the very beginnings of the Church through manifest afflictions [Col. 1192A] and mortifications of the body.

Tertullian, Book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 24:

“For even in the Greek expression, the name of repentance is formed not from confession of sin but from a change of mind, which we show before God as circumstances of various kinds present themselves.”

Origen, Book III *Against Celsus*:

“We do not teach unjustly that this is sufficient for a person to be received by God: that he should acknowledge his own misery, condemn his former life, and turn himself toward better fruit, for God receives the one who does so.”

Lactantius, Book VI *On True Worship*, chapter 13:

“To do penance is nothing other than to profess and affirm that one will sin no further.”

In the same book, chapter 24:

“For the one who repents of his deed understands his former error. [Col. 1192B] Therefore the Greeks more accurately and expressively call it *metanoian* (μετάνοιαν, ‘repentance’), which we might call a change of mind, etc. Let us therefore cleanse the conscience, which is open to the eyes of God; and, as the same writer says, let us always live as though we believed that we must give an account. Let us think that at every moment we are watched—not by human beings in some theater of the world, as he put it, but from above by the one who will at once be judge and witness, before whom, when he demands an account of our life, it will not be possible to deny our deeds. Therefore it is better either to escape the accusation of conscience or voluntarily to open our hearts and pour out the destruction by cutting open the wounds. No one can heal them except the one who makes the lame walk, restores sight to the blind, cleanses defiled limbs, and raises the dead.” [Col. 1192C]

Book *On the Anger of God*, chapter 21:

“Therefore God is appeased not by incense, sacrifice, or costly gifts—all of which are perishable—but by the amendment of conduct; and the one who ceases to sin makes God’s anger mortal. For this reason he does not punish every wrongdoer immediately, so that a person may have the opportunity to change his mind and correct himself.”

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, on Psalm II:

“But this vessel of irrational matter has also been adapted, under another interpretation, to the reason of the human will: human beings fall through these vices of theirs; but if they repent of them—that is, if they cease from them—God also will repent of the things which he has established as punishment for this fall.”

[Col. 1192D] Athanasius, in his letter *On the Interpretation of the Psalms*:

“There are also in other Scriptures prohibitory statements which forbid evil things; but in this book it is explained how one should abstain from evil: elsewhere it is declared that one must do penance, and that penance consists in ceasing from sins.”

What could be more effective than these remedies for the remission of hidden crimes? Since neither Tertullian, Origen, Lactantius, Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, nor Athanasius mentions public penance in any way among them, are we therefore to say that all these Fathers entirely neglected the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul? Far be such an insult from us.

Basil, in a homily on various passages of Scripture, where he discusses [Col. 1193A] different vices:

“One person is chaste, another lustful. Which of these two is richer: the one who preserves chastity, or the one who possesses money obtained through injustice? Certainly, the chaste person. The memory of the one is everlasting; the other’s riches are fragile. No thief will dig out the treasure of the former; the wealth of the latter flourishes today and withers tomorrow. Therefore, look upon things as equal and level, assigning each its proper honor; value the rational faculty more highly, so that you may find mercy.

“Tell me, then: is there among you anyone who desires empty glory but is not irascible? You desire empty glory? You do not see what is level. Are you irascible? Do not live with an irascible person. Do you see how our vices are corrected through brevity of speech, etc.?

“Receive the remedy. If you summon a physician and see various medicines contained in various compartments [Col. 1193B] before him, you will consider what is suitable for your illness. For the person who has injured his foot does not seek treatment for the eye; rather, the one whose eye is affected seeks suitable assistance for the eye. Therefore, let each person take from Scripture what corresponds to his illness. Are you irascible? Restrain your anger. ‘An irascible person,’ says Scripture, ‘is disgraceful.’ Learn this from Scripture.”

Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 15:

“One of us oppressed a poor man and took away part of his land, transgressing the boundary wickedly, either by fraud or by force, and joining field to field in order to deprive his neighbor of something, etc. Another polluted the land with usury and interest, etc. Another sacrificed to his net, which gathered much, and, having the poor man’s spoil in his house, either forgot God entirely or at least remembered him wickedly, etc.”

[Col. 1193C] After other remarks, he exhorts the priest to teach his people these remedies, by which their vices may be cured and God’s anger restrained:

“Instruct your people in these things. Teach them to break bread for the hungry, to bring the poor who lack shelter into their homes, to clothe the naked, and not to despise their kindred; especially now, so that our goodness may arise from poverty, not from abundance. By this God is more delighted than by many offerings and great gifts.”

Gregory of Nyssa, in his oration against those who condemn others too harshly:

“But you, whose soul is sick, why do you not hasten to the physician? Why do you not reveal your illness to him by confessing it? Why do you allow it to feed, prevail, and become inflamed? [Col. 1193D] At last, repent and know yourself. You have offended God; you have provoked your creator, the one who has power over the present life and is Lord and judge of the future.

“You have fallen ill through indulging in pleasures: cure it by abstinence and fasting. Your soul suffers from lack of self-control: apply the medicine of temperance. You have fallen into a fever through a manifold and excessive desire for money: let generosity and almsgiving drive it away. For this is the cure of a mind that has been overfilled.

“The seizure of another’s property has harmed you: let what was taken return to its proper owners. Falsehood has led you close to destruction—‘You will destroy all who speak falsehood,’ Scripture says—let the danger be avoided through devotion to truth, etc.

“For what else is repentance than the dissolution and overthrow of past things which have been committed either in deed or in thought? etc. [Col. 1194A] Show me your bitter and abundant tears, so that I too may mingle mine with them. Take the priest as a participant and companion in your affliction, as a father, etc. Therefore let your confidence in the one who begot you in God be greater than in those from whom you were begotten bodily. Boldly show him what is hidden. Reveal the secrets of your soul to the physician as hidden wounds. He himself will take care both of your honor and of your health.”

[Col. 1194B] Ambrose, Book II, Letter 7:

“For as soon as someone has confessed, he is absolved. Thus I said: ‘I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my heart. The delay of absolution lies in confessing; the remission of sins follows confession.”

The Fathers describe many grave diseases of the soul and set many remedies against them, which they profess to be supremely suitable for salvation. But if the canons concerning public penance are to be understood of hidden crimes as well as public ones, why did the Fathers not mention this most salutary remedy? It is impious even to think, much less to say, that the Fathers omitted it through such great carelessness.

John Chrysostom, in his homily on Psalm I, translated by James Billy, abbot:

“You have disgraced and dishonored your entire youth; you have wasted the whole period of your life. First you were a fornicator, afterward you robbed and deprived another of what was his, and bound yourself by perjury and blasphemy. What hope of salvation can remain for you? It is all over with you. Nothing remains but to enjoy at least the pleasures of this present life. [Col. 1194C]”

“These are the devil’s words. But mine are the opposite: You have been ruined, but you can attain salvation. Have you devoted yourself to fornication and lust? You can devote yourself to chastity. Have you committed adultery? You can be freed from this stain. Have you fallen? You can rise again. Is your repentance slight? The Lord’s kindness is great. Have you committed murder or taken another person’s property? Put on a better mind. Have you bound yourself by adultery? Withdraw from it. Are you wounded? Apply medicine, etc.

“You have no time during the day to do this, because fear of the authorities, conversations with companions, the care of business, concern for raising children, the management of your wife, anxiety about preparing the table, and finally countless affairs distract your mind. [Col. 1194D] If you are in bed and the memory of your sins comes to you, weep with it; by this means you can erase them. Entreat and beseech your God. Then surrender your body to sleep, after first confessing your sins and demanding an account from yourself. In this way you will obtain rest from God.

“Is it troublesome and burdensome, while lying in bed, to reckon up your daily sins? When you reckon them, lift up your mind, strip it bare, open it through fear of Gehenna, and apply to it an incision that causes no pain. Set before yourself a fearful tribunal; make your mind gentler, so that on the following day you may approach the commission of sins more hesitantly.”

John Chrysostom, in Homily 10 on Matthew 3:

“By repentance I mean not only that we cease from our former evils, but also that we are filled with the fruits of good works. [Col. 1195A] ‘Produce,’ he says, ‘fruits worthy of repentance.’ But how can we bear fruit unless we do things opposed to our sins? For example, have you taken what belongs to another? Begin now to give away what is your own. Have you fornicated for a long time? Abstain even from the lawful use of marriage, and repeatedly treat yourself for lasting chastity with a few days of continence. Have you injured someone by deed or word? Return words of blessing for insults, and strive to appease those who strike you, now by services and then also by benefits. For it is not enough for the wounded person’s salvation merely to pull the arrows from the body; remedies must also be applied to the wounds.

“Did you previously overflow with luxury and drunkenness? Counterbalance both through fasting and drinking water, so that you may overcome the hunger that threatens. [Col. 1195B] Have your eyes looked upon another person’s beauty with immodesty? Do not look at a woman at all; after your wounds, be drawn to greater caution. ‘Turn away from evil,’ Scripture says, ‘and do good.’”

In Homily 43 on Matthew 12:

“Who is free from the crime of greed? Do not tell me that you touched what belonged to another moderately and cautiously; instead, consider that because of this small thing which you stole, you are to be punished eternally with no small torment. Consider this, I say, and repent.

“Who is free from insult and slander? Yet this vice certainly insinuates itself. Who has not secretly slandered his neighbor? Who has not swollen with pride? Such a person is more impure than all the others. Who has restrained his eyes from a lustful gaze—someone whom we do not hesitate to say has sinned through adultery? Who has been angry with his brother without becoming liable to judgment and punishment? [Col. 1195C] Who has not sworn falsely? What can I say about this? You see that I assert that the one who swears is guilty of evil. Who has not at some time been a slave of Mammon, thereby ensuring that he is not a servant of Christ?

“I could list other things greater than these, but I have considered these sufficient to move you to compunction, unless someone is utterly stony and senseless. For if each of these individually leads to Gehenna, what will happen when they all come together in one person?

“‘How, then,’ you ask, ‘is it possible to be saved?’ If we apply remedies opposed to these things: mercy toward the poor, prayer, compunction, repentance, humility, an especially contrite heart, and contempt for present things. For God has set before us a thousand paths of salvation, provided that we are willing to attend carefully. Let us therefore recognize our condition and receive the medicine, [Col. 1195D] so that through every remedy we may heal our wounds and wipe away our stains.

“We can do this easily if we are merciful; if we are not angry at those who have caused us pain; if we give thanks to God in all things; if we fast according to our strength, pray continually, and make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity. In this way we shall certainly be able both to obtain forgiveness of our sins and to attain future blessings.”

In his homily on Blessed Philogonius:

“Therefore, you too should now make him propitious by the very things through which you provoked him. You provoked him by the theft of money: reconcile him through that same money. When you have restored what was stolen to those whom you injured, and have added something more, say with Zacchaeus: ‘I restore fourfold everything that I have stolen.’ [Col. 1196A]

“You provoked him with your tongue and cursing, having treated many people insultingly: appease him in turn with your tongue by uttering pure prayers, blessing those who curse, praising those who criticize, and giving thanks to those who inflict injury. These things do not require many days or years; they are accomplished by the mere purpose of the mind and in a single day.

“Depart from evil, embrace virtue, cease from wickedness. Promise that you will not commit these things again, and that will be sufficient for your defense. I testify and pledge that, if each of us who are burdened with sins departs from his former evils and truly promises God from the heart never afterward to return to them, God requires nothing else for a greater defense, etc.

“It is not necessary to cross the sea or climb over the summits of mountains. [Col. 1196B] Sitting at home, if you show devotion and great compunction of heart, you can see him; you can tear down the entire wall, remove every obstacle, and shorten the length of the road.”

[Col. 1196C] John Chrysostom assigned to each crime its own appropriate remedy, among which public penance is nowhere found. When he speaks of tears, it is immediately clear that he means tears shed in the privacy of one’s home and poured out at night in bed, by which sins are erased. When he speaks of fasts, he does not declare that they are imposed for every kind of crime, as in public penance, but only for the sins of luxury and drunkenness. Finally, he asserts that the remedies he proposes, although they require neither many days nor much labor, are nevertheless entirely sufficient, and that God requires nothing else for a greater defense.

Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus:

“When David went in to Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and was rebuked by the prophet Nathan, he replied, ‘I have sinned,’ and immediately deserved to hear: ‘The Lord has taken away your sin,’ etc. ‘The righteousness of the righteous shall not deliver him on whatever day he sins; and the wickedness of the wicked shall not harm him on whatever day he turns back.’ He judges each person as he finds him. He does not consider past things but present ones—provided that ancient crimes are changed by a new conversion.”

Sulpicius Severus, in the *Life of Saint Martin*, chapter 24:

“Some of the brothers also testified that they had heard a demon rebuking Martin with insolent words, asking why he had received within the monastery certain brothers who, having formerly lost their baptism through various errors, had afterward been converted, [Col. 1196D] and recounting the crimes of each. Martin, resisting the devil, replied firmly that ancient offenses are cleansed by a better way of life, and that through the mercy of the Lord those who cease to sin are to be absolved from their sins.”

Augustine, Book *On Faith and Works*, chapter 26:

“But unless there were certain sins so serious that they should even be punished by excommunication, the Apostle would not say: ‘When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, deliver such a person to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus.’ Hence he also says: ‘Lest, when I come, God should humble me before you, and I should mourn over many of those who sinned previously and have not repented of the impurity, fornication, and shamelessness which they committed.’

“Again, unless there were certain sins which were not to be healed [Col. 1197A] by the humility of penance as it is given in the Church to those who are properly called penitents, but by certain medicines of reproof, the Lord himself would not say: ‘Reprove him between yourself and him alone; and if he listens to you, you have gained your brother.’

“Finally, unless there were certain sins without which this life is not lived, he would not have placed a daily remedy in the prayer which he taught, etc.”

Thus the remedies for hidden crimes are distinguished no less clearly from the remedies for public crimes—that is, crimes involving public scandal—than they are distinguished, in the same manner, by Saint Augustine in the final homily of the fifty, chapter 11, from the remedies for those sins without which this life is not lived and whose remedy is daily. [Col. 1197B]

Cassian, *Conferences* XX, “On the End of Penance,” chapter 10:

“Let us understand, as we said above, that we have finally made satisfaction for past sins when the very impulses and affections through which we committed the things requiring repentance have been cut away from our hearts. Yet no one should think that he can attain this unless he first cuts away, with all the fervor of his spirit, the causes and materials through which he fell into those crimes.

“For example, if he fell into fornication or adultery through a destructive intimacy with women, let him with the utmost haste avoid even the sight of them. Or if he was inflamed by an excess of wine and banquets, let him punish with the utmost strictness his gluttony in tempting foods. Again, if he fell into perjury, theft, murder, or blasphemy, [Col. 1197C] through desire for and love of money, let him cut away the seductive material of greed, the source of his deception. If he is driven into the vice of anger by the passion of pride, let him tear out the fuel of arrogance through the supreme virtue of humility, etc.”

Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and Grace of Christ*:

“When our Savior himself, by the command of his own voice, addressed the human will, saying, ‘Repent and believe in the Gospel,’ it nevertheless becomes clear that, in order for a human being to begin believing in God, he receives from God repentance leading to life, so that he cannot believe at all unless he has received repentance as a gift from the merciful God. But what is human repentance other than a change of will?”

Book I, *On the Remission of Sins*, chapter 13: [Col. 1197D]

“Concerning those who, situated within the Church, persisted in evil works, he speaks to the Corinthians in medicinal language: ‘Lest, when I come again, God should humble me before you, and I should mourn over many of those who sinned previously and have not repented of the impurity, fornication, and shamelessness which they committed.’

“The Apostle would not grieve sorrowfully over these people, nor would he grieve in humiliation over those others, if he believed that remission of sins would be granted to the impious and wicked while they continued to provoke divine justice without a conversion of heart; for remission of sins itself takes effect only in the conversion of the heart.”

Chapter 15:

“For the effect of remission itself consists in the conversion of the heart, etc. For what else is it to obtain remission of sins than to be freed from the domination of sin?” [Col. 1198A]

Chapter 16:

“Conversion is then proved to be genuine in a person when impiety and iniquity are driven from the heart.”

Chapter 17:

“That conversion, therefore, is pleasing and acceptable in God’s sight in which both the soundness of faith is preserved and the rule of a good life is maintained; that is, first, that a right judgment concerning God be held in principle, and then that the charity commanded by God be shown toward one’s neighbor.”

Eligius, bishop of Noyon, in Homily 2:

“But if someone is so poor that he cannot offer true innocence together with simplicity of a pure heart and chastity of mind and body, let him at least offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons—that is, the two kinds of compunction, namely fear and love. Let him offer one, namely fear, because of sin, [Col. 1198B] for which he fears and groans lest he be dragged into the punishments of Tartarus. Then let him offer the other as a burnt offering, namely love, because of his desire for the heavenly homeland, when, already presuming upon pardon, he does not groan on account of punishment but because he is delayed so long from the kingdom of God which he desires.”

In Homily 11:

> “For there are two kinds of compunction by which the faithful sacrifice themselves to the Lord in the ark of the heart: namely, when the soul, sensing the Lord, is first pierced by fear, or afterward by love. At first it afflicts itself with tears, because, when it remembers its sins, it fears enduring eternal punishments for them. But when the long anxiety of death has been consumed by fear, a certain security arising from the presumption of pardon is born, and the mind is inflamed with love for heavenly joys. Thus the one who first wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is delayed from the kingdom. For the mind contemplates what the choirs of angels are like, what the fellowship itself of the blessed spirits is, and what the majesty of the eternal vision of God is; and it laments more because it is deprived of everlasting blessings than it had previously wept when it feared eternal evils. May Christ graciously deign to accept both sacrifices of our compunction: he who mercifully forgives the errors of those who mourn and are afflicted for sin, and who refreshes with the eternal light of his vision those who burn with the whole attention of their minds for entry into heavenly life—Jesus Christ our Lord.”

And lest anyone suppose that these two kinds of compunction comprise public penance, he himself afterward, turning his discourse to public penitents, testifies that he had first spoken of another kind, namely secret penance, which applies to hidden crimes.

From all this it is clear that, besides public penance of the kind J. Morinus describes, the ancient Fathers taught that there were as many other remedies entirely sufficient for the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul as there are hidden crimes. I therefore cannot sufficiently wonder that a man of the highest learning should have asserted that, if the canons are to be understood of public crimes, it follows that the ancient Fathers wholly neglected the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul and took no care concerning hidden crimes. For this argument proves too much not only concerning public penance for hidden crimes, but also concerning public crimes, since the Fathers testify that the ancient canons of public penance are not to be understood of all public crimes, and that there was another kind of penance sufficient for the remission of certain crimes, even public ones, as we demonstrate in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER VI

J. Morinus’s same argument is refuted. It is demonstrated that the Fathers testify that the ancient canons of public penance are not to be understood of all public crimes, and that they held another kind of penance sufficient for the remission of lesser public crimes. From this it becomes clear which public crimes were subject to public penance.

Origen, in his *Commentaries on Matthew*, edited by Huet, vol. I, p. 334:

> “Accordingly, just as the person who declares that such statements were made concerning every sin—whether that sin be murder, poisoning, the defilement of boys, or something similar—provided an opportunity for us to grasp in our minds the greatness of Christ’s patience and delay; so, conversely, the person who distinguished a brother from one who is called a brother teaches that the man who, on account of the lesser sins to which human beings are liable, has not been converted after a rebuke is to be regarded as a gentile and a publican. This concerns sins which are not unto death, or which, as the Law calls them in Numbers, are not deadly; and this certainly seems excessively cruel. For I do not think it easy to find anyone who has not been rebuked three times for the same kind of offense—for example, for cursing, by which people become abusive; or for those who flare up in anger and slander the name of their relatives; or for drunkenness; or for false and idle speech; or for some other fault among those which commonly cling to many people.”

According to the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 6: “Neither the effeminate, nor the covetous, nor the drunkards shall possess the kingdom of God.” Yet Origen testifies that it was not the custom of the Church to punish with public penance those who cursed—not even those who slandered the name of their relatives—and drunkards. If someone objects that Origen calls these things “lesser,” let him observe that the Fathers of those times spoke in no other way. Thus, in Saint Cyprian, the crime of idolatry is the supreme, gravest, and ultimate offense, whereas adultery and murder are lesser offenses.

Cyprian, in his book *On the Lapsed*:

> “Each person was intent on increasing his wealth; and, forgetting what believers had done either in the time of the apostles or what they ought always to have done, they devoted themselves with the insatiable ardor of desire to enlarging their possessions. There was no devoted religious observance among the priests, no unimpaired faith among the ministers, no mercy in works, no discipline in conduct. Men’s beards were disfigured; women’s appearance was painted. After God’s hands had fashioned them, their eyes were adulterated; their hair was colored with falsehood. Crafty deceits were devised to deceive the hearts of the simple, and deceitful intentions to ensnare the brethren. They joined themselves in marriage with unbelievers; they prostituted Christ’s members to the gentiles. They not only swore rashly, but even perjured themselves. They despised their superiors with arrogant pride; they cursed them with poisoned mouths; they were divided from one another by obstinate hatred. Many bishops—who ought both to be an encouragement and an example to the rest—despising divine stewardship, became administrators of worldly affairs, abandoning their chairs and deserting their people. Wandering through foreign provinces, they pursued the profitable markets of commerce. They did not assist their hungry brethren in the Church; they desired to possess silver in abundance; they seized estates by treacherous frauds; they increased interest-bearing loans through multiplying usury.”

From these words of Saint Cyprian I conclude, together with Saint Augustine in Book III *Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, that the covetous and rapacious—who will not possess the kingdom of God—were tolerated in the Church in Saint Cyprian’s time, and that it was not the custom of the Church for crimes of avarice, theft, and perjury to be punished by public penance.

Pacianus, in his *Exhortation to Penance*:

> “Let us therefore, as I have said, first reconsider the condition of sinners, carefully inquiring which things are sins and which are crimes, lest anyone suppose that, on account of the countless offenses from whose deceits no one is immune, I intend to bind the whole human race under an indiscriminate law of penance. Among Moses and the ancients, even those guilty of the smallest sin—of a single quadrans, so to speak—were rolled about in the same torrent of misery. Those who violated the Sabbaths, those who touched unclean things, those who presumed upon forbidden foods, those who murmured, those who entered the temple of the supreme King with a corrupted wall and a stained garment, and those who touched the altar with their hands or contacted it with their clothing while subject to these offenses—all of them found it sooner preferable to ascend to heaven or to die than to observe all these things. From all these and many other carnal vices, therefore, the blood of the Lord has liberated us, the redeemed, so that each person might more quickly reach his appointed destiny; he has emancipated us from slavery to the Law and given us the freedom of faith. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: ‘You have been called to freedom.’ This is that freedom: we are not bound by everything to which the ancients were subject. Rather, with the forest of offenses, so to speak, forgiven and indulgence appointed for remedies, we have been confined to a few necessary things which would be very easy for believers both to observe and to avoid. Thus, with the greatest justice, he would not refuse Tartarus who, ungrateful for so great a gift, had not observed even these few things. Let us see what they are.

> “After the Lord’s passion, the apostles, having considered and examined everything, delivered a letter to be brought to those who had believed from the gentiles. The judgment of the letter was this: ‘The apostles and presbyters, brothers, to the brothers who are in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, who are from the gentiles, greetings. Since we have heard that some who came out from us have troubled you with words.’ And below: ‘It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you except these things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from fornication. If you observe yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.’ This is the entire conclusion of the New Testament. The Holy Spirit, despised in many things, bequeathed these to us under the condition of capital danger. The remaining sins are cured by compensation through better works; but these three crimes are to be feared like the breath of some basilisk, like a cup of poison, like a deadly arrow, for they know how not merely to wound the soul but to destroy it. Thus graspingness will be redeemed by generosity, abuse will be balanced by satisfaction, sadness by joy, harshness by gentleness, levity by seriousness, perversity by integrity, and all things that are improved by their opposites will advance.

> “But what will the despiser of God do? What will the bloodstained man do? What remedy will the fornicator take? Will the deserter of the Lord be able to appease him? Or will he preserve his own blood who shed another’s? Or will he restore the temple of God who violated it by fornication? These are the capital offenses, brothers; these are the deadly ones, and so forth. Receive the remedy, if you have begun to despair; if you recognize that you are wretched; if you are afraid.”

Much in this testimony deserves particular consideration:

1. Pacianus declares that he is being asked which crimes are to be punished by public penance, lest anyone suppose that he wishes to bind the whole human race under an indiscriminate law of penance.

2. He says that the faithful of the new law have been freed from slavery to the ancient law and reduced to a few necessary things which would be very easy both to observe and to avoid.

3. He says that these things which must be avoided were identified by the apostles in these words: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you except these things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from fornication,” and so forth.

4. He calls these three crimes capital and deadly, and says that they alone require the remedy of public penance.

5. He says that the remaining sins are cured by compensation through better works.

J. Morinus therefore does not correctly conclude that the crimes of which the ancient canons of penance cannot be understood to speak were wholly neglected by the ancient Fathers.

Basil, in his canonical letter to Amphilochius, canon 30:

> “Concerning those who carry off others, we have no ancient canon, but we give our own judgment, that they themselves and those who carry off others with them should remain outside the prayers for three years.”

Since Saint Basil declares that he is the first to impose public penance upon those who carry off others, does it therefore follow that the ancient Fathers wholly neglected this crime and took no care concerning it? But see Origen’s third homily on Leviticus, chapter 6, where he asserts that all who carry off—whether women or other things—cannot possess the kingdom of God unless they have done penance for these offenses.

Basil, in the preface to his *Ethics*:

> “Without doubt, a most evil custom has deceived us; without doubt, a perverse human tradition has become the cause of great evils among us. It has turned away from some sins, while accepting others without making any distinction; and although it pretends to be vehemently angry with certain sins, such as murder, adultery, and others of the same kind, it judges other things not even worthy of a simple rebuke, such as anger, abuse, drunkenness, avarice, and anything similar. Yet elsewhere he from whose mouth Christ spoke, Paul, pronounced judgment against all these things when he said that those who do such things are worthy of death.”

At least Saint Basil himself bears witness to the custom that he condemns. But whether the practice which Saint Pacianus testifies to have descended from the tradition of the apostles is rightly to be criticized, his brother Saint Gregory of Nyssa explains as follows.

Gregory of Nyssa, in his canonical letter to Letoius, bishop:

> “It remains for us to propose an examination of the irascible part of the soul, when, having fallen away from the proper use of anger, it has fallen into sin. Since many sins and evils of every kind are committed through anger, it pleased all our Fathers not to act with excessive precision in certain matters, nor to expend excessive effort and labor in treating all the offenses that arise from anger, although Scripture prohibits not only wounding but also every insult or curse, and anything else of this kind that anger produces. They introduced penalties only for the prevention of murder, and so forth.

> “The other form of idolatry—for the divine Apostle calls avarice by this name—I do not know how it has been passed over by the Fathers without any remedy of punishment. Yet this evil appears to be an affection of three dispositions of the soul, and so forth. To speak generally, this disease agrees with the Apostle’s definition of avarice. For the divine Apostle declared it not only idolatry but also the root of all evils, and so forth.

> “Since, then, these matters were passed over by the Fathers, I think it sufficient to cure them by the means provided through public instruction, insofar as this can be done—for example, by cleansing through prayer certain diseases arising from overindulgence, the affections of insatiable avarice. We regard only theft, the opening of graves, and sacrilege as vices, because this has been handed down to us by the succession of the Fathers. Yet in divine Scripture both interest and usury are prohibited, as is transferring another’s property to one’s own possession through a kind of power, even if this has perhaps been done under the appearance of a contract or transaction. Since we are not considered trustworthy enough to attain the authority of the canons, we shall now add the canonical judgment to what has already been said concerning those things that are expressly prohibited.”

Saint Gregory of Nyssa does not criticize the custom of the Church concerning public penance for only the three crimes noted above by Saint Pacianus. Indeed, he considers it sufficient to cure by other remedies the remaining sins, which, although they exclude people from the kingdom of God, may be cleansed like certain diseases arising from overindulgence—namely, the affections of insatiable avarice.

But lest someone perhaps object to the opinion of Saint Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus, who speaks as follows in Oration 39:

> “Why should I regard Novatian’s cruelty as law? He punished avarice—which is another form of idolatry—with no penalty, but condemned fornication so harshly and bitterly as though he himself consisted only of an exposed part of flesh and body.”

As though anticipating objections, Gregory admits that he thinks this way because, as he says, “we are not considered trustworthy enough to attain the authority of the canons.”

Ambrose, Book II *On Penance*, chapter 10:

> “For if they truly did penance, they would not think it necessary to repeat it afterward, because, just as there is one baptism, so there is one penance, which is nevertheless performed publicly. For we ought to repent of our daily sin. But the former concerns more serious offenses, the latter lesser ones.”

He explains which offenses are lesser in his *Exhortation to Perform Penance*:

> “What does it mean to live well after penance? Teach us. I say to you: abstain from drunkenness, from lust, from theft, from evil speech, from immoderate laughter itself, and from idle speech, concerning which people will have to give an account on the day of judgment. These are the things I have called lesser, so that I might remain silent about the grave and destructive ones.”

Saint Ambrose therefore asserts that it was not the custom of the Church to do public penance for every public sin, namely drunkenness, theft, and other such offenses. And what sins are called lesser and minor except those compared with the greatest and more serious offenses, as we have already observed from Saint Cyprian?

John Chrysostom judged that not only the gravest crimes—adulteries, murders, and others of the same kind—but also envy and anger, and indeed even swearing, ought to be punished by public penance. Yet he openly declares that he himself first established this by private, noncanonical authority in his forty-second homily on Matthew 12, concerning envy, in these words:

> “How, then, shall we prevent envy from infecting us with its poison? If we take care that, just as it is forbidden for a fornicator to enter the church, so also it should be forbidden for the envious person—indeed, the envious person should be expelled from the assembly of the faithful much more than the fornicator. For if, since this evil now appears almost insignificant, it is despised by some, then surely, if the atrociousness of its malignity were evident to all, we would easily recoil from it. Therefore fountains of tears ought to flow from the eyes in weeping. You should pray to God and learn that envy is the most shameful offense. Thus, as though fleeing from a dangerous disease, you will quickly escape from this disposition and do penance.

> “But who does not know, you will say, that envy is a vice? No one, as you say, is ignorant of that. Yet they do not regard it as abominable in the same way as fornication or adultery. To make you believe this, tell me, I ask: when has anyone ever wept bitterly because he had fallen into envy? When has anyone prayed that God be propitious to him because he had sinned through envy? Certainly no one ever has. Yet although he is more envious than all other human beings, he thinks that he has made amends by some fasting or by giving a small amount of silver to the poor, so that he appears to have done no evil, even though he is afflicted by the worst and most criminal passion of all.”

The same Saint Chrysostom testifies concerning anger and oaths in his homily on quarrelsomeness, or anger:

> “For just as it is impossible for a fornicator or blasphemer to participate in the sacred table, so also the person who nurses enmity or persists in anger cannot enjoy holy communion. And rightly so. For the one who has committed fornication or adultery, as soon as he has satisfied his desire, has put an end to his sin; and if, repenting, he wishes to raise himself from his fall and shows great repentance, he will undoubtedly obtain no ordinary consolation. But the person who persists in quarrelsomeness sins every day and never brings the sin to an end. In the case of adultery, the sin is completed together with the offense; here, the same crime is attempted every day. What pardon, then, shall we hope for, when we have voluntarily surrendered ourselves to such a beast?”

And in the same homily, concerning oaths:

> “Forty days have already passed; if the holy Easter season also passes, I shall thereafter grant pardon to no one. I shall employ not admonition but the force of authority and a severity that must not be disregarded. For this is not a valid excuse: the thief does not plead custom and thereby escape punishment; why does not the murderer or adulterer do the same? I therefore now announce and declare that, if I meet individuals and catch them, I shall certainly catch them. And if I discover that some have not corrected these vices, I shall impose a penalty and order them to remain outside, beyond the sacred mysteries.”

Similarly, concerning spectacles, John Chrysostom judges in several places—and especially in his seventh homily on the first chapter of Genesis—that not mild medicines but astringent and biting remedies of public penance ought to be applied. He says:

> “For it is not always beneficial to use mild medicines. But when an ulcer resists treatment, astringent and biting remedies must be applied so that the disease may be confronted more quickly. Let all who are subject to these crimes know, therefore, that if they remain in this negligence after our present admonition, we shall not tolerate them but shall use the ecclesiastical laws and teach them with great severity, so that they may not henceforth neglect such things or listen to the divine utterances with such contempt.”

Since John Chrysostom declares himself to be the first author of these decrees—about which many people complained—he sufficiently shows that he established them by private, noncanonical authority. Consequently, it had not been established as the custom of the Church that, at least at that time, these public crimes were subject to public penance.

Jerome, in Book III of his *Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter 5:

> “Therefore, in the soul in which sin has reigned, the kingdom of God cannot reign. For what fellowship is there between righteousness and iniquity? What communion between light and darkness? What agreement between Christ and Belial? And do we think that we shall attain the kingdom of God if we are free from fornication, idolatry, and sorcery? Behold, enmities, contention, anger, quarrels, dissension, drunkenness, and the other things that we regard as small exclude us from the kingdom of God. It makes no difference whether one is excluded from blessedness by a single thing or by many, since all exclude in the same way.”

And, commenting on these words of the later Epistle, chapter 13—“For I fear that, when I come, I may not find you as I wish, and that I may be found by you as you do not wish; lest perhaps there be among you contentions, rivalries, hostilities, dissensions, slanders, whisperings, conceits, and seditions”—he says:

> “On account of these things he said that he would exact punishment with the greatest severity. What would he do if he came in our times, when, in comparison with other crimes, these things are not even thought to be sins?”

This false persuasion had undoubtedly arisen from the fact that these sins, although they exclude people from the kingdom of God, were nevertheless customarily cured not by public and arduous penance but by other very easy remedies.

Augustine, in his book *On Faith and Works*, chapter 19:

> “Those who think that the remaining sins can easily be compensated for by almsgiving nevertheless do not doubt that three things must be punished by excommunication until they are healed by more humble penance: unchastity, idolatry, and murder. For there is no need now to investigate what their opinion is, or whether it should be corrected or approved, lest we prolong the work we have undertaken, and so forth.”

Although Saint Augustine elsewhere seems to say that all crimes are subject to the penalties of public penance, but only after many conditions have been met, which we shall report below, he nevertheless testifies here that there were many in the Church who, undoubtedly moved by the same considerations that had moved the ancient Fathers—including Saint Pacianus and Gregory of Nyssa—believed that these three crimes, unchastity, idolatry, and murder, were the only ones requiring the remedies of more humble penance, while the remaining offenses could easily be compensated for by almsgiving and other such means.

Finally, in order to trace the tradition of the Fathers down to Theodore, I shall present the outstanding testimony of Eligius, bishop of Noviomagus, from his sixteenth homily:

> “That penance is true which means that a person no longer commits the evils he has committed, but repents of the past, guards against the future, and does not return again to the same things. Therefore, beloved, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words, let us turn away from evil and do good. And so that you may know how this ought to be done, listen more attentively to what we are about to say.

> “Whoever was proud or arrogant should restrain his pride and be humble and simple, because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Whoever was angry, or, what is worse, furious and threatening, insolent and cruel, should restrain his savagery and the cruelty of his mind and be patient, gentle, and devout, because the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God; and no one can attain the kingdom of God without patience and devotion.

> “Whoever was a marauder, even an executioner, or, what is worse, a murderer, should turn and perform worthy penance and be gentle and devout. For just as murderers cannot attain eternal life unless they perform worthy penance, so neither can marauders who, without pity for the wretched, tear apart or cut off their limbs.

> “Whoever was envious or hateful should, having turned from his wickedness, be kind and merciful and learn to love the brother whom he previously hated.

> “Whoever was a fornicator, adulterer, or incestuous person, unclean, should turn and do penance and thereafter live soberly and chastely, and so forth.

> “Whoever was a buffoon—that is, one who threatened, pursued shameful things, and spoke obscenely—should correct himself and cease to be what he was. Let him learn to speak what is good, since previously, by speaking vain and shameful things, he polluted both himself and his hearers.

> “Whoever was avaricious or grasping—that is, one who desired what belonged to others and was not at all generous with what was his—should be content with his own possessions and be generous and beneficent. That is, he should not covet what belongs to others, should not seize it, should not defraud anyone, and, insofar as his strength permits, should give.

> “Whoever stole should steal no longer, but should rather labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need.

> “Whoever was a glutton, that is, a voracious eater or drunkard, should be moderate and sober.

> “Whoever was accustomed, for the sake of human reputation, to squander his possessions indiscriminately and excessively on food and drink should learn to distribute them rationally. For just as avarice—that is, graspingness—is an abomination before the Lord, so indiscriminate extravagance is a sin. God does not want us to be grasping or wasteful—that is, extravagant.

> “Whoever was a liar or falsifier should correct his evil and cease to be as he was; let him be a lover of truth and uprightness.”

Thus, except for the crimes of adultery, murder, and others for which worthy penance was appropriate—such as was then publicly performed in the Church—Saint Eligius testifies that the remaining sins, such as pride, anger and savagery, which exclude people from the kingdom of God; envy and hatred; the pursuit of shameful and unclean things; avarice, which is the service of idols; drunkenness, extravagance, and lying, can easily be cured by other remedies.

It is therefore clear that public penance was not imposed for all public crimes. If J. Morinus’s argument proves too much concerning public crimes, it proves much more concerning hidden crimes. And since an argument that proves too much, according to the laws of dialectic, proves nothing, everyone must admit that the argument J. Morinus uses to demonstrate that it was the ancient practice of the Church to do public penance for hidden crimes is entirely without force.

## CHAPTER VII

J. Morinus’s third argument is refuted, and Augustine’s testimony is explained.

J. Morinus says:

> “Third, if someone had voluntarily disclosed his crimes, he would remain for a shorter time in prostration, hearing, and so forth than if he had been accused and convicted. For most of the canons and many statements of the Fathers prescribe this rule for those accused of crimes; you can read many testimonies to this effect in Book II, chapter 6. If you posit public crimes as the subject to be explained by these laws, what explanation can be invented for this distinction? If the crime is public, conviction has already taken place by itself; the notoriety of the deed, so to speak, was equivalent to conviction. The person denounced cannot evade the matter. Indeed, the bishop does not even need an accuser when the crime is assumed to be public and notorious, but only someone to bring it to his attention—and not even such a person, since in that case the bishop, stimulated solely by his awareness of the duty he must perform, can discipline the public sinner who has repented by means of penance.”

**Response.** Even if I were to grant that the crime was hidden, what follows from that if it later becomes public through a voluntary disclosure before the judges of the Church? For no injury is done to one who is willing. Moreover, this disclosure—which was made before the judges of the Church for various reasons, and especially so that persons accused and convicted of a crime already known to some would not be punished with more severe penance—cannot be understood as secret confession. On account of secret confession, no one was ever permitted, according to the canons, to impose public penance, as we have demonstrated above through so many testimonies of the Fathers. Therefore J. Morinus’s third argument cannot have any force.

J. Morinus continues:

> “Saint Augustine, in Homily 49 of the collection of 50, chapters 3 and following, teaches this very clearly. He addresses the baptized and the faithful: ‘If you could not or would not have conjugal chastity or continence, and you departed from your purpose, whether from the marriage bond or from the devotion to continence, let there be in you the sorrow and humility of penance.’ Since it might perhaps be unclear to someone what kind of sin he meant and what kind of penance he understood, he immediately explains it: ‘I speak more openly: let no one say, “I did not understand.” You who have defiled yourselves by unlawful intercourse after your marriages, if you have had intercourse with someone besides your wives, do penance of the kind performed in the Church, so that the Church may pray for you.’

> “The question concerns adultery committed, and above all adultery committed secretly. For he addresses adulterers generally, whoever they may be, and by an equal and undiscriminating necessity, and by hypothetical words concerning the crime—words which would foolishly be spoken of a public offense—he exhorts and binds them to public penance, namely penance of the kind performed in the Church, so that the Church may pray for them.”

**Response.** Since Saint Augustine very often declares elsewhere that public penance was imposed only for public crimes, and that secret penance was sufficient for hidden crimes, as we have shown above, everyone can see that when Saint Augustine speaks generally of crimes punished by public penance, only public crimes can be understood. For example, when someone says that civil laws punish adulterous women, he speaks only of those who have been convicted of adultery in a secular court.

Saint Augustine affirms that the same must be understood of ecclesiastical judgment in his final homily from the collection of fifty, chapter 12:

> “We cannot prohibit anyone from communion, although this prohibition is not yet deadly but medicinal, unless the person has either confessed voluntarily or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment. For who would dare to assume both roles for himself, so that he might be both accuser and judge of another? The Apostle Paul is also understood to have briefly indicated such a rule in the same Epistle to the Corinthians, when, after mentioning certain crimes, he provided from them a model of ecclesiastical judgment for all similar cases.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For he did not wish a person to be judged by another according to the discretion of suspicion or even by an extraordinary judgment usurped for the occasion, but rather according to the law of God and the order of the Church, whether the person had confessed voluntarily or had been accused and convicted. Otherwise, why did he say, ‘If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator or an idolater,’ and so forth, unless he wished the naming to be understood as that which occurs when a sentence is pronounced against someone according to judicial procedure and integrity? For if naming alone were sufficient, many innocent people would have to be condemned, since crimes are often falsely attributed to someone by name.”

J. Morinus continues:

> “Moreover, it is wholly improbable that they insisted that secret penance should be performed for a public sin, as those whom he refutes insisted. For he immediately addresses the objection of certain people who, in order to avoid the disgrace of public penance, claimed that they were doing penance privately and secretly, as though private penance were sufficient to cleanse their crime. But Augustine denies this and gives the reason for his denial: ‘Let no one say to himself, “I am acting secretly; I am acting before God. God knows, who forgives me, because I act in my heart.” Then it was said without reason: “Whatever you shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven”? Then the keys were given to the Church of God without reason? Do we frustrate the Gospel of God? Do we frustrate Christ’s words? Do we promise you what he denies? Are we not deceiving you? Whoever wishes to do penance secretly for a sin for which the Church has imposed public penance frustrates the Gospel of Christ and regards as superfluous those words by which he grants the Church the power of binding, since that person does not submit to the Church and its decrees. He thinks that the Church is deceiving him and mocking him with an empty promise of the remission of sins if he carries out what has been commanded.’”

**Response.** But this is not wholly improbable, since shortly afterward Saint Augustine testifies that the sin could not have been concealed. Could they not have said that they were doing penance secretly for public sins? This is what many people did not long afterward, as Anastasius of Sinai reports at the end of his *Oration on the Holy Synaxis*:

> “Suppose that your brother is a sinner. How do you know the rest of his actions? For many are frequently found who have sinned openly but have performed great penance secretly and privately. We know when they sin, but we do not know their penance and conversion; and although they are judged sinners by us, they have been justified before God.”

Joan. Morinus:

“Having removed this support for hidden penance, he removes another obstacle to the performance of public penance [Col. 1208D], namely, shame—not shame concerning public confession, for he would not have been more ashamed to confess secretly than to do penance secretly, and one readily follows from the other. Furthermore, it seems probable, indeed certain, that those of whom he speaks had confessed their sins privately but refused public penance, and had put forward the performance of private penance as a pretext. For Saint Augustine is wholly concerned with establishing the necessity of public acts. Hence it must necessarily be inferred that those against whom he argues had either already confessed privately or had raised no dispute about private confession, but had merely shrunk from public penance. Whatever the case may be, Augustine did not have hidden acts in view, but public ones alone, with regard to which he attempts to lessen shame [Col. 1209A]. ‘The son of pestilence resists me and is ashamed to bend his knee beneath God’s blessing? What an emperor is not ashamed of, a senator is not ashamed of; only a member of the curia is ashamed, and so forth. Therefore God willed that the emperor Theodosius should perform public penance in the sight of the people, especially because his sin could not be concealed; and the senator is ashamed of what the emperor is not ashamed of,’ and so forth.

This is what they were especially ashamed of: bending their knees in the church together with the penitents, placing their heads beneath the hands and blessings of the priests, and consequently being expelled from the Church’s sacrifice and from the assembly of the faithful. To enable them to endure these things modestly and humbly, he exhorts them by the example of the emperor Theodosius.
