When Saint Augustine notes that Theodosius performed public penance especially because his sin could not be concealed [Col. 1209B], he confirms by this new statement that public penance was to be performed for a hidden crime. For it necessarily follows from this that penance was publicly performed both for a hidden and for a public crime, but especially for a public crime, or for one that could not be concealed.”

**Response.** Who would think that Saint Augustine, skilled in dialectic, was exhorting any hidden adulterers to perform public penance by this argument: “God willed that the emperor Theodosius should perform public penance in the sight of the people, especially because his sin could not be concealed; therefore God wills that you, whose sins are hidden, should perform public penance”? Would the excuse be ready? Rather, God does not wish us to perform public penance, especially when our sin could have been concealed. Therefore, for Saint Augustine’s exhortation to have some validity, we must say that the sins of those whom he urges to perform public penance were public.

Moreover, these words—“especially”—do not confirm by any new statement that public penance should be performed for hidden sins; they merely indicate that it could be imposed for certain other reasons, which Origen explained above. The chief reason for public penance, and the only one sanctioned by the Fathers, was a public crime.

J. Morinus adduces several other testimonies of the Fathers. Since the same points need not be repeated, it is sufficient to respond as follows: I. No testimony has been produced that clearly proves that, according to the canons, public penance was to be performed for hidden sins. II. What the Fathers say about expiating capital sins through public penance can be understood only of public crimes, since elsewhere the Fathers most clearly distinguish between public and hidden crimes, and between the penance appropriate to each: hidden penance for hidden crimes, public penance for public crimes.

## CHAPTER VIII

Certain words of the *Penitential* are explained; and it is shown that public penance, of the kind described by Joan. Morinus, was not absolutely necessary even for the gravest public crimes, and why several Fathers exempted many public sinners from it.

Someone may perhaps object to the words of the *Penitential*, where [Col. 1210A] Theodore reports that in his province there is no reconciliation because there is no public penance; and he may maintain that Theodore changed public penance not only for hidden sins but also for public ones. It must, however, be observed that Theodore could not have changed, contrary to the canons, something that had never been established by any decree of the Church—namely, public penance for hidden crimes.

With regard to public crimes, one must consider that Theodore is presenting the discipline of the whole Church, both Eastern and Western; and that, having regard to the weakness of many, he preferred to tolerate the custom which he had found established in his province rather than remove it by private authority, to the scandal of others. Therefore, lest some lover of stricter discipline criticize Theodore, whom the Fathers praised in synods as both devout and learned [Col. 1210B], it is necessary to show:

I. That public penance of the kind which J. Morinus describes in Book IV of *De Poenitentia*, chapter 7, and which many say was established from the Church’s beginnings in manifest and prolonged afflictions and mortifications of the body, is not altogether necessary for the remission even of the gravest public crimes.

II. For what reasons the Fathers were moved to exempt many public sinners from that penance.

Justin, in the *Apology*, which according to Eusebius is the first and is therefore wrongly entitled the second in printed editions:

“The Prophet, speaking in the person of the Father, says: ‘I will not endure a day of great fasting and idleness, nor, when you come to appear before me, will I hear you. Your hands are full of blood. And when you offer fine flour or incense, it is an abomination to me. I do not want the fat of lambs or the blood of goats. For who has required these things from your hands? Rather, dissolve every bond of iniquity; break apart the bundles of violent contracts; cover the naked and wandering person; break your bread for the hungry.’ From these examples you can understand what things God commanded through his prophets.”

In the *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*:

“‘Why do you fast for me, so that your voice may be heard today in shouting? I did not choose this fast, that a man should humble his soul on the day. Even if you bend your neck like a circle and spread beneath you sackcloth and ashes, you will not call this a fast and an acceptable day to the Lord. I did not choose such a fast,’ says the Lord, ‘but dissolve every bond of iniquity; release the obligations of violent contracts; send away the broken in freedom and tear up every unjust document; break your bread for the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise anyone of your own household.” Then your light will break forth like the morning, and the healing of the sinner will quickly arise; your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of God will embrace you. Then you will call, and God will hear you; while you are still speaking, he will say: “Here I am.” If you remove from yourself the bond, the entanglement of hands, and the word of murmuring, and if you give your bread to the hungry from your heart and fill the humbled soul, then your light will rise in darkness and your darkness will be like midday.’”

Saint Justin speaks of a penance that is entirely sufficient for the remission of the gravest and public crimes. Yet it is not the penance that J. Morinus describes, and that many learned men have said was established from the Church’s beginnings in manifest and prolonged bodily afflictions and mortifications. Thus Saint Justin judged that such penance was not absolutely necessary for the remission of the gravest and public crimes.

Theophilus of Antioch, *To Autolycus*, Book III:

“Moreover, the prophet Isaiah addresses everyone in general, but especially the Jews, urging them to hasten to repentance, saying: ‘Seek the Lord when he may be found; call upon him when he is near. Let the impious man abandon his way and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness.’ Another prophet, Ezekiel, says: ‘But if the impious man turns away from all his sins which he has committed, and keeps all my statutes and does judgment and righteousness, he shall surely live and shall not die. None of all his iniquities which he has committed shall be remembered against him, but in the righteousness which he has done he shall live. Do I desire or wish the death of the impious man, says the Lord God, rather than that he should turn from his ways and live?’ Isaiah again, insisting on repentance, says: ‘Turn back, you who devise profound and wicked counsel, so that you may be saved.’ Likewise Jeremiah: ‘Turn back to the Lord your God, as a grape-picker turns to the basket, and you shall obtain mercy.’ There are very many passages, almost beyond counting, contained in Holy Scripture concerning the performance of repentance, and so forth.

“The ministers of both Testaments, inspired by one and the same Spirit, have spoken. Isaiah cries out: ‘Remove the wickedness of your endeavors from before my eyes; cease to do evil; learn to do good; seek justice; rescue the oppressed; defend the cause of the orphan and the widow in judgment.’ The same prophet says elsewhere: ‘Dissolve impious bonds; release burdensome bundles; set the broken free, and break every burden. Is it not to share your bread with the hungry and bring the homeless poor into your house? If you see the naked, cover him, and do not hide yourself from your own kinsman.” Then your light will break forth like the dawn, and your healing will quickly grow, and your righteousness will go before you.’

“Jeremiah agrees with this, saying: ‘Stand beside the roads and look around; ask about the ancient paths, and whatever way is better, walk in it, so that you may find rest for your souls. Judge with just judgment, for in these things consists the will of the Lord your God.’ Moses agrees with him, saying: ‘Keep judgment and draw near to the Lord your God, who established the heavens and founded the earth.’ Zechariah does not disagree, saying: ‘Judge with the judgment of truth, and let each one practice piety and mercy toward his brother. Do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the stranger, or the poor; and let none of you devise evil in his heart against his brother.’”

Saint Theophilus describes, through numerous and principal testimonies of Scripture, true repentance, which is entirely sufficient for the remission of public and gravest crimes. Since it is not the penance which many have said was established from the Church’s beginnings in manifest and prolonged bodily afflictions and mortifications, it is certain that Saint Theophilus judged this penance not absolutely necessary for the remission of public and gravest crimes.

Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, Book IV, chapter 32:

“But, taking pity on their blindness and indicating the true sacrifice by which those who offer it will propitiate God and receive life from him, he says elsewhere: ‘A sacrifice to God is a contrite heart’; a fragrant offering to God is a heart that glorifies the one who formed it, and so forth. Zechariah also, among the Twelve Prophets, signifying God’s will to them, says: ‘Thus says the almighty Lord: Judge with just judgment; practice piety and mercy, each toward his brother. Do not oppress the widow, the orphan, the proselyte, or the poor; and let none of you recall the wickedness of his brother in his heart; do not love a false oath. For I hate all these things,’ says the almighty Lord.

“David likewise says: ‘Who is the man who desires life and loves to see good days? Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.’”

Through other testimonies of Scripture, Saint Irenaeus describes perfect repentance for crimes, whether public or most grave, which nevertheless does not consist in manifest and prolonged bodily afflictions and mortifications.

Clement of Alexandria, in the book entitled *Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?*, relates the repentance of a young man who, having joined a band of robbers and readily becoming their leader, surpassed them all in violence, slaughter, and cruelty:

“And when the old man—that is, the apostle John—came near, he embraced him. With groans and lamentations, as much as he could, he begged for pardon, and was cleansed by his tears as by a second baptism, hiding only his right hand. Then the apostle promised and solemnly swore that he had obtained pardon for him from the Savior; praying and falling upon his knees, he kissed the young man’s right hand, which had been cleansed by repentance, and brought him back into the church. From that time, partly by frequently beseeching God in prayer, partly by striving continually together with the young man, and finally by soothing his mind with every kind of persuasive speech, he did not depart until he had restored him to the Church and had displayed to everyone a great example of sincere repentance, an immense proof of renewed regeneration, and a trophy of manifest resurrection.”

Behold a great example of repentance, showing that public and most serious crimes can be washed away without prolonged bodily afflictions and mortifications.

Thus far the testimonies of the Fathers clearly demonstrate that public penance consisting in manifest and prolonged bodily afflictions and mortifications was not absolutely necessary. It will also be clear that, even when this penance was most prevalent, if we show for what reasons the Fathers were moved to exempt many public sinners from public penance.

The Fathers of the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 9:

“If a presbyter, overtaken by carnal sin, is advanced [to ordination] and confesses that he sinned before ordination, he shall not consecrate the offerings, but shall remain in the other duties, because of his good zeal.”

For many have said that the remaining sins can be forgiven through the laying on of hands. A hidden crime becomes public through confession itself. Yet the person who committed it is freed from public penance because of the laying on of hands which he received at ordination.

This reasoning Innocent I appears later to refute in his letter to the bishops of Macedonia, chapter 4, in these words:

“Therefore, if this is so, let sacrilegious persons, adulterers, and those guilty of every crime be admitted to ordination, since the crimes or vices are thought to be removed by the blessing of ordination. Let there be no place for penance, because ordination can provide what prolonged satisfaction customarily provides.”

Basil, in his canonical letter to Amphilochius, canon 32:

“Clerics who commit a sin unto death are indeed deposed from their rank, but they are not excluded from communion with the laity. For you shall not punish twice for the same offense.”

Although there are very ancient examples of another discipline, this practice is itself ancient and highly approved. Saint Basil reports it as already established in his own time, and later Fathers bear witness to it and defend it: Optatus of Milevis at the end of Book II; Siricius in his letter to Himerius of Tarragona, chapter 14; the Fathers of the Fifth Council of Carthage, canon 11—which canon is reported in full in the code of the African Church, canon 27; Jerome in his letter to Sabinian; Augustine, Book I of *On Baptism Against the Donatists*, chapter 1; and Leo I in his letter to Rusticus of Narbonne, response II:

“This,” he says, “without doubt descends from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: ‘If a priest has sinned, who will pray for him?’ Therefore, for such fallen persons to obtain the mercy of God, private withdrawal must be sought, where, if their satisfaction is worthy, it may also be fruitful.”

The Fathers of the Council of Epaon, canon 22:

“If a presbyter or deacon commits a capital crime, he shall be deposed from the honor of his office and confined in a monastery; there alone, for as long as he lives, shall he receive communion.”

And Isidore of Seville, Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 16:

“Only the distinction of ranks being preserved, so that it be done by priests and Levites with God alone as witness, but by the rest with the priest solemnly standing before God.”

Basil, in the same canonical letter, canon 34:

“Our fathers forbade adulterous women who confessed, or who were convicted in any manner, to be publicly exposed, lest we provide the convicted with a cause of death. But they ordered them to remain without communion until the period of penance had been completed.”

Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 39:

“Since they showed no repentance at all, he rightly rejected them; for I myself do not receive those who are either in no way humbled or not humbled sufficiently, and who do not bring a correction of life proportionate to the crime committed. When I do receive them, I assign them an appropriate place; but those who have been worn down by tears I will by no means imitate.”

John Chrysostom, in his homily on David and Saul:

“The publican did not utter any such cold words as those we use every day, covering one another with insults and curses. Rather, sighing bitterly and beating his breast, he said only this: ‘Be merciful to me, a sinner,’ and he went down justified. Do you see the speed? He accepted reproach and washed away reproach; he acknowledged his sins and laid down his sins; the accusation of his crimes became for him the remission of his crimes; and the enemy, unknowingly, became a benefactor.

“How many labors would the publican have had to undertake—fasting, sleeping on the ground, keeping watch, distributing his possessions to the needy, sitting for a long time in sackcloth and ashes—in order to lay down so many sins? But now, without doing any such thing, he laid aside all his iniquity with a simple word. The insults and reproaches of the Pharisee, who seemed to be abusing him, brought forth for him the crown of righteousness, and this without sweat, without labor, and without the delay of a long period.”

In Homily 1 *On Repentance*:

“Why did he reduce the prescribed period to so short a time? So that you might learn the virtue of the barbarians—I mean the Ninevites, who were able in only three days to avert the wrath provoked by their sins—and so that you might admire God’s clemency, since they were content with three days of repentance for so many sins; and so that you might not collapse into despair, even if you have sinned a thousand times.

“For just as a sluggish and negligent soul, even if it is given much time for repentance, accomplishes nothing great and does not reconcile God to itself because of its laziness, so one who burns with an awakened purpose and displays repentance with great diligence can erase sins accumulated over a long period in a brief moment of time.

“Did Peter not deny him three times? And three times with an oath? And did he not do so because he feared the words of a lowly servant girl? What then? Was it necessary to frighten him with many years of penance? Certainly not. He fell and rose again that same night; he received both the wound and the medicine; he became ill and returned to his former health.”

In the homily on Blessed Philogonius:

“Let no one say to me: ‘I am afraid; my conscience is filled with sins; I carry an exceedingly heavy burden.’ The period of these five days is sufficient, if you are sober, attentive, and watchful, to make the multitude of your sins smaller. Do not consider that the time is short; consider instead that the Lord is benevolent. The Ninevites, too, drove away such great wrath of God within three days. The shortness of the time did not hinder them; rather, readiness of spirit, embracing the Lord’s benevolence, enabled them to accomplish everything.

“That prostitute, too, in a brief moment of time, when she approached Christ, washed away all her reproaches. When the Jews criticized him for admitting her and granting her such confidence, Christ silenced them; and, having freed her from all her evils and approved her zeal, he sent her home. Why was this? Because she approached with fervent spirit, burning heart, and ardent faith; she touched those holy and sacred feet, with her hair loosened, streams of tears pouring from her eyes, and perfume lavishly poured out.”

[Col. 1215B] Bacchiarius, in his letter to Januarius concerning the reception of the lapsed:

“How, I ask, can we despair of the Lord’s mercy, when he even rebuked Pharaoh because he was unwilling to repent, and so forth? That remarkable Solomon, who deserved to be joined to God’s attendant—that is, to wisdom—fell into the embraces of foreign women and, ensnared by the bond of lust, polluted himself also with the error of sacrilege, because he fashioned an image of Chemosh, the Moabite idol. But since, through the prophet, he acknowledged the guilt of his error, is he excluded from heavenly mercy?

“Perhaps you will say: ‘Nowhere in the canon do I read that he repented or obtained mercy.’ Listen, then, brother. His repentance, which is not recorded in public laws, is perhaps judged more acceptable for this reason: he repented not before the face of the people, but in the secrecy of his conscience, with God as witness.

“We recognize that he obtained pardon from this fact: when he had been released from the body, Scripture records that he was buried among the bodies of the kings of Israel. Yet we know that this was denied elsewhere to sinful kings who remained in the perversity of their purpose until the end of their lives. Therefore, because he deserved to be buried among righteous kings, he was not excluded from pardon. But he could not obtain that pardon without repentance.”

Augustine, in the last homily from Psalm 50, chapter 11:

“Let no one, brothers, suppose that he ought to despise the counsel of this saving repentance because he has perhaps observed and knows that many approach the holy altar, whose such crimes he is not unaware of. For many are corrected like Peter.”

This is why the canons allow bishops to make the punishments of penance lighter and less severe in proportion as contrition of heart increases; and the Fathers teach that the measure of time should not be considered so much as the measure of sorrow.

Augustine, in the *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 65:

“In the practice of penance, when such a crime has been committed that the one who committed it is separated even from the body of Christ, the measure of time should not be considered so much as the measure of sorrow. God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.”

Leo I, in his letter to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, chapter 5:

“We have thought that this also should be answered to the consultation of your charity: it is not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart that the matter must be weighed.”

Pope Vigilius I, in his letter to Caesarius of Arles:

“But since, as we confidently believe your charity well knows, the measure of penance in present cases is entrusted rather to the judgment of priests, so that, in accordance with the merit of contrition, the remedy of pardon may also be granted, we think that this should rather be left to your judgment.”

Hence Gennadius testifies in the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chapter 53, that all who gave the clearest signs of true and perfect repentance were entirely exempt from public penance:

“We do not deny that mortal crimes may also be absolved through secret satisfaction, but only after the secular habit has first been changed, and after a profession of religious devotion has been made through correction of life and continual, indeed perpetual, mourning, provided only that the penitent performs actions contrary to those for which he repents, and receives the Eucharist on every Sunday, in supplication and humility, until death.”

Finally, the Fathers unanimously declare that God requires nothing other than charity from sinners, who departed from him only through desire; that this is what the whole law and the prophets consist in; and therefore that the yoke is easy and the burden light, to which Christ calls all who labor and are burdened by crimes.

I could produce almost countless testimonies of the Fathers on this subject, but the testimony of Salvian will stand for all of them. He speaks thus in Book VII of *On the True Judgment and Providence of God*:

“Especially since God demands nothing burdensome, nothing grievous, from us, and so forth. For what does he say? ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light.’

“The Lord therefore does not call us to labor but to refreshment. What does he demand of us, what does he command us to provide for him, except only faith, chastity, humility, sobriety, mercy, and holiness? None of these burdens us; rather, they adorn us. Not only that: they so adorn the present life that they can adorn the future life even more.”

Not only were those who were converted like Peter not subjected to public penance; many who were tolerated like Judas, or as being excessively weak, were treated likewise. [Col. 1216D] This is the second reason Augustine gives in the homily from Psalm 50, chapter 11:

“For many are corrected like Peter; many are tolerated like Judas.”

Saint Augustine explains the same reason elsewhere, in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 3:

“Both things must be done, as the diversity of weakness also teaches us. We have undertaken the care of those whom we certainly ought not to destroy but to correct and heal, and one must be healed in one way, another in another. So there is also a reason for overlooking and tolerating the wicked in the Church; and there is again a reason for chastising and rebuking, for not admitting or for removing from communion. But people err when they do not preserve the proper measure. Once they begin to incline readily toward one side, they do not attend to the other testimonies of divine authority [Col. 1217A], by which they could be recalled from that position and established in the truth and moderation tempered from both sides.”

Augustine, in Letter 48 to Vincentius, against Donatus and Rogatus, concerning the correction of heretics:

“For the sake of the good, the wicked must be tolerated. Thus the prophets tolerated those against whom they uttered such great denunciations, nor did they abandon communion in the sacraments with that people. Thus the Lord himself tolerated the guilty Judas until his fitting end, and allowed him to share the sacred supper with the innocent. Thus the apostles tolerated those who preached Christ out of envy, which is a vice of the devil himself. Thus Cyprian tolerated the avarice of his colleagues, which, according to the Apostle, he calls idolatry.”

[Col. 1217B] Augustine, Book III against the letter of Parmenianus, chapter 4:

“Isaiah said: ‘Depart, go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean.’ But why did he himself touch the uncleanness of that people, which he severely rebuked, by gathering together with them, and so forth? David said: ‘I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not enter with the wicked; I have hated the assembly of the most evil, and I will not sit with them.’ Let them read what kind of persons he tolerated in that people in his own time, who showed such honor to the mystical sacrament of anointing that he did not despise it even in the most wicked Saul; rather, he revered it so greatly that he could do nothing more, and so forth.

“Will they say that in those times the righteous were not permitted to withdraw from the evil people, but that they are permitted to do so in these times? What could be said more perversely? At that time, the good supposedly could not be separated bodily from the wicked, when many sacraments appeared to be observed bodily; but now bodily separation is supposedly necessary, when those things are already observed spiritually? Woe to the blind who lead the blind, and to the blind who follow.”

Augustine, in Tractate 50 of his *Exposition of the Gospel of John*:

“What, then, did our Lord Jesus Christ wish to teach the Church, my brothers, when he wished to have one lost man among the twelve, except that we should tolerate the wicked, lest we divide Christ’s body? Behold, Judas is among the saints; behold, Judas is a thief—and do not disregard the fact that he is a sacrilegious thief, not an ordinary thief. He is a thief of the money-box, but of the Lord’s money-box; of the money-box, but of the sacred one.

“If crimes are distinguished in court according to ordinary theft and embezzlement—for embezzlement is theft of public property, and theft of private property is not judged in the same way as theft of public property—how much more severely must the sacrilegious thief be judged, who dared not to take from just anywhere, but to take from the Church? Whoever steals something from the Church is compared with the lost Judas.

“Such was this Judas, and yet he entered and went out with the eleven holy disciples; he approached the Lord’s supper together with them; he was able to live among them, though he could not defile them. Peter and Judas both received from the one bread, yet what share does the faithful have with the unfaithful? Peter received it for life; Judas for death, and so forth.

“Why did he admit the thief, unless so that his Church might patiently tolerate thieves? But he who had been accustomed to take money from the money-box did not hesitate, after receiving money, to sell the Lord himself. Let us see what the Lord answers to these things. See, brothers: he does not say to him, ‘You say these things because of your thefts.’ He knew the thief but did not wish to expose him; rather, he tolerated him and showed us an example of patience for enduring the wicked in the Church.”

Augustine, Book III against the letter of Parmenianus, chapter 2:

“But when the same disease has seized very many, nothing remains for the good except sorrow and groaning, so that, through the sign revealed to the holy Ezekiel, they may deserve to escape unharmed from their devastation. Therefore, when the same Apostle had discovered that many had been defiled by unclean lust and fornications, writing to those same Corinthians in his second letter [Col. 1218B], he did not likewise command that they should not even eat with such persons. There were many of them, and it could not be said of them: ‘If anyone is named a brother who is a fornicator, or a servant of idols, or avaricious, or anything of that kind, do not even eat with such a person.’ Rather, he says: ‘Lest, when I come again, God should humble me, and I should mourn over many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the uncleanness, lust, and fornication which they committed.’ Through his mourning, he threatened that they would be restrained by divine punishment, rather than through that correction by which the others were to refrain from association with them.

“Accordingly, he says: ‘Behold, this is the third time I am coming to you; by the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand. I have already said, and I now say in advance, as when I was present the second time and now absent, to those who sinned before and to all the others: if I come again, I will not spare, because you seek proof of Christ speaking in me.’”

Chapter 4 of the same book:

“Finally, if the prophets warned their descendants to separate themselves bodily from the chaff before the time of the final winnowing, and by such separation to avoid touching what was unclean and not to enter with the wicked, why did the Apostle Paul not do this? Were they not chaff who preached Christ not from truth but from envy? Were they not unclean who did not preach the Gospel chastely? The Church testifies that such persons existed in those times, and later generations likewise imitated its most excellent charity, which tolerates all things.”

Chapter 2 of the same book:

“Let the eyes of the heart be opened, lest the eyes of the body be open in vain, and let them read the preacher of truth writing in that very First Letter to the Corinthians: ‘Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor servants of idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the avaricious, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers shall possess the kingdom of God.’

“How, then, did Cyprian and the other grains of the Lord, in that Church of unity at that time, eat the Lord’s bread and drink the Lord’s cup with avaricious and rapacious persons, with those who will not possess the kingdom of God—not merely with laymen or clerics of whatever rank, but even with the bishops themselves—when the same Apostle commands that they should not associate with such persons and cries out that they should not even eat with them?

“Was it because they could not be separated bodily from them without uprooting the wheat as well? Was it sufficient for them to be separated from such persons in heart, distinguished from them in life and conduct, for the sake of preserving peace and unity, for the salvation of the weak and, as it were, of the infant grains, lest the members of Christ’s body be torn apart by sacrilegious schisms?”

And below, chapter 4:

“Was it uncleanness, or even avarice? Cyprian did not touch it in his heart, and yet he lived most peacefully among the avaricious. For he had not become deaf to the words of the Psalms, so as to sit in the assembly of vanity and enter with the wicked, or fail to hate the assembly of the malicious and sit with the impious.

“Was there not an assembly of vanity among those who, while their brothers in the Church were hungry, desired to glitter with the most lavish silver? Were there not wicked men who treacherously seized estates from their brothers? Were they not most evil and impious who increased interest through multiplying usury? Yet he washed his hands with the innocent and surrounded the altar of the Lord.

“For this reason he tolerated the guilty, so that he would not abandon the innocent with whom he washed his hands, because he loved the beauty of the house of the Lord; and that beauty was found in honorable vessels.”

Moved by all these examples, Saint Augustine judges that drunkards and gluttons, of whom there was such a great multitude, ought rather to be tolerated than excluded from the Church and punished with severe penance. Thus he writes in Letter 64:

> “When the Apostle placed together in one passage three brief categories of vices to be detested and avoided, from which the harvest of countless sins arises, one of these, the second in his list, is punished most severely in the Church; but the other two, namely the first and the last, seem tolerable to human beings. Thus it may gradually happen that they are no longer even considered vices. For the Chosen Vessel says: ‘Not in revelries and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and indecencies, not in strife and deceit; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires.’ Of these three, bedrooms and indecencies are regarded as so great a crime that no one who has defiled himself with this sin seems worthy not only of ecclesiastical ministry but even of communion in the sacraments. And entirely rightly. But why only this? Revelries and drunkenness are considered so permitted and lawful that they are celebrated even in honor of the most blessed martyrs—not only on feast days, which anyone who observes these things with anything other than bodily eyes must surely see is deplorable, but also every day, etc.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Therefore these things are not removed harshly, as I think, nor severely, nor by an authoritarian command; they are removed more by teaching than by ordering, more by admonishing than by threatening. For this is how one must deal with a multitude of sinners: severity, however, must be exercised against the sins of the few.”

Augustine himself could have learned this reason for such great indulgence—which he frequently employs here and elsewhere, especially in Book III Against the Letter of Parmenian—from Innocent I, who writes in this way in his letter to the bishops of Macedonia, chapter 6:

> “Therefore let your Charity understand that such things have been tolerated up to this point, and consider that, as you say, necessity required that the Churches, once established in peace, should not presume to undertake this; but, as often happens, whenever a people or crowd sins, because punishment cannot be exacted against everyone on account of their number, it is customary for the matter to pass unpunished. The earlier matters should be left to God’s judgment, while for the future the greatest care must be taken to prevent them.”

And in his letter to the synod assembled in the city of Toledo, chapter 1:

> “We criticize their deed in such a way that, because of the number of those who must be corrected, we do not call into question what was done in whatever manner, but rather leave it to God’s judgment.”

Salvian reports, for the same reason, that almost countless wicked people were tolerated in the Church, in Book III of *On the True Judgment and Providence of God*:

> “For whom will you find in the Church who is not either a drunkard, or a glutton, or an adulterer, or a fornicator, or a robber, or a wastrel, or a bandit, or a murderer? And, what is worse than all these things, nearly all of them without end, etc. For almost the entire populace of the Church has been reduced to this disgrace of morals, so that among the whole Christian people it is, in a way, a kind of holiness to be less vicious, etc. But into the temples—or rather, into the altars and sanctuaries of God—all the filthy and shameful rush indiscriminately, with absolutely no reverence for sacred honor, etc. Finally, if someone wishes to know what such people had in mind in the temple, let him observe what follows. For as soon as the solemn sacred rites have been completed, they immediately hurry off to their customary pursuits: some, of course, to steal; others, to get drunk; others, to fornicate; others, to engage in banditry. Thus it plainly appears that, while they are inside the temple, they are contemplating what they carry out after they have gone forth.”

Finally, I shall produce the testimonies of Julianus Pomerius and Anastasius Sinaita. The former was a Latin, while the latter was a Greek; both report the discipline of their respective Churches and testify how great the Church’s indulgence toward public sinners was on account of the multitude and weakness of sinners.

Thus Julianus Pomerius writes in Book II of *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 5:

> “In another place the same Apostle says: ‘You who are stronger must bear the weaknesses of the weak.’ He therefore bears patiently, as weak persons, those whom he has been unable to correct even after chastising them. Accordingly, because it is neither expedient to rebuke everyone nor to treat everyone gently, holy priests know and discern whom they ought to correct with measured severity and whom they ought to bear with priestly magnanimity. Therefore, in regard to all whom they care for by God’s grace, they look not to their wishes but to their welfare. In the end, they pass over some who ambitiously seek honor in an unbecoming manner, knowing that it would not benefit them—not out of anyone’s envy, but by the counsel of profound prudence. They honor others who wish to remain hidden, so as to open for them a path toward greater progress. Those whom they judge able to endure reprimand they discipline; those unable to bear reproof they handle gently, like the sick—not flattering them because they are such, but having compassion on their weaknesses, if perhaps they cannot be healed in any other way.”

Anastasius Sinaita, at the end of his *Discourse on the Holy Synaxis*:

> “Suppose your brother is a sinner: how do you know the rest of his actions? For many are often found who have sinned openly but have secretly and privately performed great penance. We know when they sin, but we do not know their penance and conversion; and in our judgment they are sinners, while before God they have been justified.”

Public penance, therefore, is not absolutely necessary, since the Church exempted so many public sinners from it for many and various reasons. If these reasons are to be praised in the Fathers, they certainly cannot be condemned in Theodore, whose holiness and teaching have so often been praised by synods.

## CHAPTER IX. Defense of the Redemptions of Penance Which Joannes Morinus Condemns and Therefore Excludes from Theodore’s and the Roman Penitential

Joannes Morinus, Book X of *On the Administration of the Sacrament*, chapter 17:

> “Three things remain for us to demonstrate concerning these redemptions of penances, which seemed best to explain separately: when this kind of redemption began in the Church; when it ceased; and in what way it provided an occasion for diminishing the ancient penances. The first point is easily inferred from what was said in the preceding chapter. For we have produced no testimony more than eight hundred and some years old; therefore this period cannot precede that date by a considerable length of time. Certainly no testimony of this matter is ever encountered before the year of Christ 700, and such testimonies are rare until one reaches the year of salvation 900. Read the capitularies and laws of Charles the Great, Louis, and Charles the Bald, as well as the councils celebrated under their reigns: nowhere is there mention of redemptions of penance. The oldest is that of Isaac of Langres, which he says he excerpted from the capitularies, although, as I think, that canon is not now found among them. Whatever the case may be, it contains a particular circumstance that does not properly concern the redemption of which we are speaking. The Council of Tribur is directly relevant, but it was held in the year 895. The councils preceding it under the Carolingian emperors and kings make no mention of these matters. It may be objected that Burchard, Ivo, and the Penitential called Roman by Antonio Agustín report certain chapters from these formulas of penitential redemptions as though they came from Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury, etc.”

He later reports the testimony of the synod of Clovesho in articles 3 and 4, from which he argues as follows:

> “Having considered these matters, I can scarcely be brought to believe that Theodore of Canterbury was the author of this penitential redemption. For this council was presided over by Cuthbert, Theodore’s successor but one, and that synod was held in the fifty-first or fifty-second year after Theodore’s death. Who could believe that Theodore’s successor would so easily derogate from a man as renowned throughout the Christian world as Theodore, tear at his constitutions, accuse them of novelty, and have the other bishops approve these things by unanimous consent? Since, therefore, this depraved custom was gaining strength, certain writers inserted such laws of redemption into Theodore’s Penitentials; afterward, copies transcribed from them and disseminated everywhere imposed upon many people, so that they believed them to belong to Theodore, although they had merely been stuffed into his writings. The same should apparently be said of the Roman Penitential, which Halitgarius published eight hundred years ago and added at the end of his books *On Remedies for Sins*.”

### Response

Before we examine J. Morinus’s arguments, we must understand what the redemptions of penances are that authors cite from Theodore’s and the Roman Penitential. Anyone who carefully reads those that we have reported under Theodore’s name from a manuscript codex, as well as those found in the Roman Penitential, will recognize that they are nothing other than exchanges of one kind of penance for another, and indeed on account of necessity. Moreover, this penance has always been valid before the Lord, who never commanded what cannot be done.

It is therefore surprising that J. Morinus asserts that no testimony of this matter is encountered before the year of Christ 700, that such testimonies are rare until the year of salvation 900, and that the synod of Clovesho condemned these redemptions and therefore they cannot belong to Theodore’s Penitential. For it is clear that the synod of Clovesho condemned only the abuse of redemptions—namely, when people sin more freely because they give larger alms. For the Fathers speak in this way in canon 26:

> “And they are certainly not to be given for this purpose: that anyone may act with greater license in committing even the smallest sins, in proportion as either he himself or anyone else gives alms on his behalf.”

These words are wholly unrelated to the redemptions of penances cited from Theodore’s and the Roman Penitential. In those texts, redemptions of penances are not commended as a means of sinning more freely, but of obtaining the easier remission of sins; not for changing, without any necessity, the penalties imposed by canon law, but only on account of necessity, when penance cannot otherwise be performed; and in accordance with the canons, which permit the bishop to increase or diminish them as the present circumstances require.

Yet, however the matter may be understood, whether with reference to good or bad use, J. Morinus has not identified the true period. If the bad use is meant, the ancient Fathers had reproved it long before.

Lactantius, Book VI of *On True Worship*, chapter 13:

> “Whenever, therefore, you are asked, believe that you are being tested by God to see whether you are worthy to be heard. Examine your conscience, and as far as you can, heal its wounds; but do not suppose that, because sins are removed by generosity, permission to sin has been granted you. For they are abolished if you give generously to God because you have sinned. But if you sin in the confidence that you can give generously, they are not abolished.”

Augustine, Book XXI of *The City of God* addressed to Marcellinus, chapter 27:

> “They try to use the prayer taught by the Lord both as an advocate for themselves and as a witness, so that they may suppose that their daily sins—whatever and however great they may be, provided only that they do not cease committing them—can be forgiven through alms, etc. Whatever and however great these sins may be, even if they are committed daily and their life does not depart from them through a change for the better, they presume that forgiveness may not be denied them through almsgiving. It is good, however, that these people insist that alms worthy of their sins must be given; for if they were to say that any sort of alms could obtain divine mercy for daily and great sins and for any continual practice of wickedness, so that daily remission would follow, they would see that they were saying something absurd and ridiculous. For they would then be forced to admit that a very wealthy man could redeem murders, adulteries, and every kind of nefarious deed by spending ten small coins a day on alms, etc. Therefore alms must be given so that, when we ask forgiveness for past sins, we may be heard—not so that, while persisting in those sins, we may believe that we can purchase permission to do evil through alms.”

Caesarius of Arles, Homily 17:

> “By giving alms we feed another person’s flesh, while by committing crimes we slaughter our own soul. Therefore, as I have frequently warned, let us give alms for our greater sins in such a way that we never return to those crimes.”

Eligius of Noyon, Homily 8:

> “But concerning the person who preserves the evils mentioned above in his heart and believes that he can redeem his many sins through alms, let us hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: ‘If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, go first to be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift.’”

This statement clearly shows that offering sacrifice or giving alms will be of no benefit unless reconciliation with one’s enemy has first taken place. Thus the Fathers who preceded the periods fixed by J. Morinus condemned the abuse of redemptions of penances.

But if the redemptions of penances, as they are read under Theodore’s name and in the Roman Penitential, are understood—as they ought to be—as exchanges of certain kinds of penance for others that are easier, namely, perfect conversion of the heart, almsgiving, prayer, and so forth, and indeed on account of necessity, then the ancient character of these forms of penance, and the fact that they are true practices everywhere celebrated in the Holy Scriptures—and therefore the principal and superior means by which sins are more easily forgiven—are made entirely clear by the ancient Fathers.

Origen, Homily 2 on Leviticus:

> “Hear now how many remissions of sins there are in the Gospels. The first is that by which we are baptized for the remission of sins. The second remission is in the passion of martyrdom. The third is given through almsgiving. For the Savior says: ‘Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.’ The fourth remission of sins comes through our forgiving the sins of our brothers. For the Lord and our Savior himself says that if we forgive our brothers their sins from the heart, our Father will also forgive us our sins; but if we do not forgive our brothers from the heart, neither will our Father forgive us. Thus he taught us to say in prayer: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’ The fifth remission of sins occurs when someone converts a sinner from the error of his way. For the divine Scripture says that whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way saves his soul from death and covers a multitude of sins. The sixth remission also comes through an abundance of love, as the Lord himself says: ‘Truly I tell you, her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much’; and the Apostle says that love covers a multitude of sins. There is still a seventh remission, although it is harsh and laborious: the remission of sins through penance, when the sinner washes his bed with tears.”

But someone may say that all these things are required. Let whoever raises this objection listen to John Chrysostom.

John Chrysostom, in the homily entitled the ninth, *On Penance*:

> “What does this mean? We began speaking about penance and said that there are many different paths of penance by which salvation is made easy for us. For if he had given us only one, we would certainly have rejected it, saying: ‘We cannot enter upon this path; we cannot be saved.’ But now, cutting off this objection of yours, he has given you not one, nor a second, nor a third, but many and diverse paths, so that by their number your ascent to heaven may be easy for you.
>
> “We said that penance is easy and imposes no burden: you are a sinner; enter the church; say, ‘I have sinned,’ and you have dissolved your sin. We brought forward David as one who sinned and dissolved his sin. Then we proposed a second path: weeping over one’s sin, and we said: ‘What labor is this? There is no need to spend money, to travel long roads, or to say anything of that sort; one need only weep over the sin.’ We drew this from Scripture, where God changed his decision concerning Ahab because he wept and was sorrowful: he forgave him his sin. He himself said this to Elijah: ‘Have you seen how Ahab has humbled himself before me, weeping and sorrowful? I will not act according to my anger.’
>
> “Then we gave a third path of penance and brought forward from Scripture the Pharisee together with the publican: the Pharisee, lifted up in pride, fell away from righteousness, while the publican, consenting to humility, received the fruit of righteousness. He was not burdened by any labor; he gave words and received the reality.
>
> “Come, then, let us follow what we have begun and bring forward a fourth path. And what is it? Almsgiving, that queen of virtues, brings people most swiftly to the heavenly heights and acts as an excellent advocate.”

And somewhat later:

> “For this reason he also gave us many other different paths of penance, so as to remove every occasion for our indolence. For if we had only one path, we might be unable to follow it; the devil always flees from this sword.
>
> “You have sinned: enter the church and erase your sin. Whenever you fall in the marketplace, so often you rise again; likewise, whenever you sin, repent of the sin and do not despair. Even if you have sinned a second time, repent a second time, and do not, disheartened, fall away from hope of the good things prepared. Even if you have sinned in extreme old age, enter and do penance: this is a place of healing, not of judgment; it does not exact punishments but grants the remission of sins. Tell your sin to God alone.
>
> “You have another penance that is not difficult but entirely suitable. What is it? This: weep over your sin; and this too is taught from the sacred Gospels.”

Saint Augustine, Book II *Against Cresconius the Grammarian*, chapter 12:

> “They are cleansed also by the word of truth, by him who says: ‘Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.’ They are cleansed also by the sacrifice of a contrite heart, by him of whom it is said: ‘A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.’ They are cleansed also by alms, by him who says: ‘Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you.’ They are cleansed also by love, which surpasses all things, by him who said through the Apostle Peter: ‘Love covers a multitude of sins.’ When this alone is present, all those things are rightly done; but if it is absent, all are done in vain.”

Cassian, a disciple of John Chrysostom, in Conference XX, chapter 8:

> “After that general grace of baptism and that most precious gift of martyrdom, which is acquired by the washing away of blood, there are many fruits of penance through which the expiation of crimes is attained. Eternal salvation is not promised merely under that single name of penance concerning which the blessed Apostle Peter says: ‘Repent and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out’; and John the Baptist, or the Lord himself: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.’
>
> “The mass of sins is also overwhelmed through the affection of love. For love covers a multitude of sins. Likewise, through the fruit of almsgiving, healing is provided for our wounds, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin. The washing away of sins is likewise acquired through the outpouring of tears: ‘For every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears.’
>
> “Finally, he adds, showing that they were not poured out in vain: ‘Depart from me, all you who practice iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.’ The abolition of sins is also granted through confession of crimes: ‘I said,’ he says, ‘I will declare my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin.’ And again: ‘Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified.’
>
> “Through affliction of heart and body, remission of committed crimes is likewise obtained. For he says: ‘See my humility and my labor, and forgive all my sins.’ Above all, it is obtained through amendment of morals: ‘Take away,’ he says, ‘the evil of your thoughts from my eyes; cease to act perversely; learn to do good; seek judgment; assist the oppressed; judge the orphan; defend the widow; and come and accuse me, says the Lord. And if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow; and if they are red like crimson, they shall become white like wool.’
>
> “Sometimes forgiveness of sins is also obtained through the intercession of the saints. ‘Whoever knows his brother to be committing a sin not unto death, let him ask, and God will give life to the one whose sin is not unto death.’ And again: ‘Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.’
>
> “Sometimes, too, the stain of vices is burned away through the merit of mercy and faith, according to the saying: ‘Sins are cleansed by mercy and faith.’ Often it is accomplished through the conversion and salvation of those who are saved by our admonitions and preaching, since whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way saves his soul from death and covers a multitude of sins.
>
> “Through our indulgence and forgiveness likewise, we attain forgiveness of our own crimes: ‘For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your offenses.’
>
> “You see, therefore, how many entrances to mercy the Savior’s clemency has opened, so that no one who desires salvation may be crushed by despair, when he sees himself invited to life by so many remedies. If you claim that, because of bodily weakness, you cannot abolish your sins through the affliction of fasting, you cannot say: ‘My knees have grown weak through fasting, and my flesh has been changed because of oil’; or: ‘I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with tears.’ Redeem them, then, by the abundance of almsgiving.
>
> “If you have nothing to distribute to the needy—for no necessity of want or poverty excludes anyone from this work, since even the widow’s two coins are preferred to the great gifts of the wealthy, and the Lord promises to repay a cup of cold water—then surely you can be cleansed through the amendment of your morals without those things.
>
> “If you cannot attain the perfection of virtues by eliminating all vices, devote pious concern to the welfare of another’s salvation. If you complain that you are not fit for this ministry, you can cover your sins through the affection of love. If any indolence of mind has made you weak even in this, at least through prayer and the intercession of the saints, humbly submit yourself and ask for remedies for your wounds.
>
> “Finally, who cannot humbly say: ‘I have made my sin known to you, and I have not hidden my injustice’? Through this confession he may confidently add: ‘And you forgave the wickedness of my heart.’ If shame restrains you and you are embarrassed to reveal these things before human beings, do not cease confessing them in continual supplication to the one from whom they cannot be hidden, saying: ‘I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me. Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you.’ He is accustomed to heal without publicizing that shame and to forgive sins without reproach.
>
> “After this so ready and certain aid, divine kindness has also granted us another, even easier resource: it has placed the power of the remedy itself within our discretion, so that we may presume upon the forgiveness of our crimes according to our own disposition, saying to him: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’”

Caesarius of Arles, Homily 9:

> “Consider, dearest brothers, and see that no excuse can remain for us by which we may say that we have been unable to redeem our sins. Perhaps you can say that you are unable to afflict your flesh with fasts and vigils, or that you cannot abstain from wine or meat. But surely you cannot say that you are unable to give to the poor, for your sins, what God has given you in greater abundance than was necessary?
>
> “There is still another kind of almsgiving through which we can redeem our sins without any labor. If someone is so poor that he has neither gold, nor grain, nor wine or oil with which to give bodily alms, since it is impossible for someone not to suffer injury from other people, let him forgive all his enemies with his whole heart. Then no sin will remain to gnaw at his conscience, and he may confidently say in the Lord’s Prayer: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.’
>
> “In him will be fulfilled what Christ deigned to promise in the Gospel, saying: ‘If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will forgive you your sins’; and also: ‘Give, and it will be given to you; forgive, and you will be forgiven,’ etc.
>
> “Behold, you have said that you can neither gather grain in abundance, from which you might give food or clothing to the poor, nor endure an injury that you ought to forgive your enemies; and therefore you doubt that you have nothing with which you can redeem your sins. Receive, then, and faithfully hold to the distinguished and principal third kind of almsgiving.
>
> “Let there be good will in your life: love all people as yourself; pray for everyone; desire for them what you desire for yourself. Then the words proclaimed to you by the angels will be fulfilled: ‘Peace to people of good will.’
>
> “And because good will itself is love, if you wish to possess it, what is written will be fulfilled in you: ‘Love covers a multitude of sins.’ Recognize, then, that every excuse for and objection against your sins has been removed. For you cannot say that you are unable to have good will, since it may happen that you do not wish to have it; but you will never be able to prove that you cannot have it.
>
> “Therefore, with the help of the Lord, let us labor to receive and preserve faithfully—not negligently—the benefits and such distinguished remedies of our Lord and Savior, so that we may deserve not only to receive the forgiveness of sins but also to attain eternal rewards.”

In Homily 38:

> “The first remission of sins is that by which we are baptized in water, according to what is written: ‘Unless someone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’
>
> “The second remission is the affection of love, as in the saying: ‘Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much.’
>
> “The third remission is the fruit of almsgiving, according to this: ‘Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.’
>
> “The fourth remission is the outpouring of tears, the Lord saying: ‘Because he wept in my sight and walked before me sorrowfully, I will not bring evil upon him in his days.’
>
> “The fifth remission is the confession of crimes, as the Psalmist testifies: ‘I said, I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my sin.’
>
> “The sixth remission is affliction of heart and body, as the Apostle consoles us: ‘I handed such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.’
>
> “The seventh remission is amendment of morals, that is, renunciation of vices, as the Evangelist testifies: ‘You have been healed; do not sin any longer, lest something worse happen to you.’
>
> “The eighth remission is the intercession of the saints, as in the saying: ‘If anyone is sick, let him call for the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray for him.’ And the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power before the Lord.
>
> “The ninth remission is mercy, the merit of faith, according to this: ‘Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.’
>
> “The tenth remission is the salvation of others, as the Apostle James affirms: ‘Whoever converts a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins.’
>
> “The eleventh remission is indulgence and our forgiveness, as the Truth permits: ‘Forgive, and you will be forgiven.’
>
> “The twelfth remission is the passion of martyrdom, the unique hope of salvation and forgiveness, with the Lord responding to the bloodstained thief: ‘Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in paradise.’”

Eligius of Noyon, Homily 4:

> “If there are among you some who, God forbid, have pretended until now to perform penance rather than truly performing it, we say that even they should not despair of God’s mercy if today they turn to him at least with their whole heart. With him true conversion suffers no delay, as the Spirit of God says through the prophet: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved’; and elsewhere: ‘Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified.’ Likewise, ‘With the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.’
>
> “Finally, his manifold mercy has bestowed upon us, for the expiation of crimes, manifold fruits of penance. Eternal salvation is not promised only under that single name of penance concerning which the Apostle Peter says: ‘Repent, therefore, and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out’; nor only in the words of John the Baptist: ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.’
>
> “The forgiveness of sins is also accomplished through the affection of love, through the fruit of almsgiving, through the outpouring of tears, through confession of crimes, through affliction of heart and body, and especially through amendment of morals. Sometimes it is also accomplished through the intercession of the saints, and through our indulgence and forgiveness, by which we forgive those who sin against us. Divine Scripture testifies that sins can be abolished by all these means.
>
> “Since, therefore, the ineffable power of our God has opened for us salutary entrances to forgiveness, who, in misery and desiring mercy and salvation, would be broken by any despair, when he is invited to forgiveness by so many remedies?”

The redemptions of penances, therefore, as they are read under Theodore’s name and in the Roman Penitential, are excellent and most ancient. The ancient Fathers show that they are everywhere approved in the Holy Scriptures. J. Morinus therefore strayed far from the truth when he condemned them and maintained that no testimony concerning them could be produced that was more than eight hundred and some years old. Although I have reported the redemptions of penances under Theodore’s name alone, without affirming that they belong to his Penitential, I can nevertheless rightly and justly conclude that the arguments J. Morinus employs to deny this have no weight.

## CHAPTER X. It Is Demonstrated That Joannes Morinus Did Not Set Forth Sound Arguments and True Causes Concerning Theodore’s Penitential

Let us now set forth what arguments and reasons J. Morinus has advanced concerning the Penitential of Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury.

> “But,” he says in the appendix to his book *On Penance*, “when the discipline was changed in the East and West at the periods noted, the matter took a different course. At that time penance for every kind of hidden crime was imposed secretly; once it had been performed secretly, reconciliation too was carried out secretly. Therefore the imposition of this canonical penance, and canonical absolution after that penance had been completed, was also permitted to any presbyters.
>
> “From that time it was judged that the canons were insufficient, but that books had to be composed in which an appropriate penance would be assigned to each sin, since much was superfluous and much lacking in the canons for this purpose. There remain many canons, to be sure, that say nothing about imposing penances for crimes, and their number greatly exceeds the others. But much more is lacking in them.
>
> “I. The canons often define one and the same crime in different ways. This diversity easily disturbs simple presbyters, to whom that private imposition of penance belongs. Moreover, it is inconvenient and contrary to good administration that crimes in the same province should be punished in different ways, with some following one canon and others another.
>
> “II. Sometimes the canons are obscure to simple presbyters and therefore require clearer expression.
>
> “III. The canons do not explain the manner or ritual of making confession, imposing penance, and granting reconciliation.
>
> “IV. They contain neither admonitions and exhortations to be given to penitents nor instruction for them concerning virtues and vices.
>
> “V. There are many specific crimes for which the canons impose no penance, although many bishops judged that penance for them ought not to be entrusted to the discretion of simple presbyters.
>
> “Therefore, after punishment for all hidden crimes had been granted to any presbyters, penitential books were composed in addition to the canons. In these books all these matters were distinctly explained for the benefit and necessary instruction of simple presbyters, so that they might be able to discharge the duty of imposing penances.
>
> “Previously this had not been so necessary, because penances for many of these crimes were public and were imposed by bishops and chief priests, who could easily supply what was lacking in the canons. Of these penitential books, three were most renowned in the West. The very first was that of Theodore, Archbishop of Canterbury.”

The foundation of J. Morin’s principal arguments is a proposition whose falsity we have demonstrated above from the entire tradition of the Fathers down to Theodore. Once the foundation has been overthrown, the principal arguments likewise collapse. Accordingly, it has not been established that the changed discipline permitted reconciliation and absolution to any presbyters whatsoever; indeed, the contrary is read in the Penitential in these words:

“Reconciliation of penitents on the Lord’s Supper [Maundy Thursday] is performed only by the bishop and after penance has been completed. But if it is difficult for the bishop, he may, on grounds of necessity, grant a presbyter the authority to complete it.”

We have shown in the notes, with the most certain evidence, that this discipline agrees entirely both with what precedes and with what follows. Finally, the difference in discipline which J. Morin thought could easily disturb simple presbyters is not the reason that moved Theodore to compose his Penitential, since, on the contrary, he sets forth the varying practice of the whole Church, both Eastern and Western.

All this I have judged worth noting against J. Morin. Although I cannot help admiring his varied and extensive learning, I have been impelled solely by love of the truth and by zeal for the glory of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, from whom, insofar as I could, I have removed every suspicion of novelty.

## SUPPLEMENT TO AUTHORS OF UNCERTAIN DATE FROM THE EIGHTH CENTURY. ASCARICUS AND TUSAREDUS

*(In Gotth. Heine, Bibliotheca Anecdotorum.)*

[Col. 1231]

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTERS OF ASCARICUS AND TUSAREDUS

The letters of Ascaricus and Tusaredus, which I here offer you, benevolent reader, I found in a codex dated 1085 of the era, that is, written in the year 1047. Formerly preserved among the books of the church of Zaragoza, it is now held in the Escorial library under the number J. I. 3.

The manuscript contains various materials. It begins with those letters that contain Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologies*. Then follows, written by another hand, a section of Gregory’s commentary composed on Isaiah. This is followed, without any other heading, by: “Here begins the prologue. Sibyls are generally called all women,” and so forth—that is, the well-known little book on the Sibyls, at the end of which are written the words: “The book ends happily; thanks be to God. The presbyter Dominicus made it on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, in the era 1305.” Finally, there is again, written by another hand, a book on the seven planets of heaven.

Tusaredus, to whom the first letter is written and who replies in the second, is otherwise unknown. Ascaricus, however, who writes to him and receives a letter from him, is none other than the bishop of the Astures who is mentioned when the Adoptianist controversies broke out. Pope Adrian, in a letter addressed to the bishops of Spain (letter 97), complains that among them, besides the errors which Egila—about whom, he says, he had already spoken several times—had disseminated under the leadership of Migetius, Elipandus and Ascaricus too were spreading heretical opinions concerning the adoption of the Son of God. In a letter addressed to the abbot Fidelis [another reading: Fidelem], Elipandus proposes this Ascaricus as an example to follow, praising him because he had approached him not with the arrogance of a teacher assumed by himself, but with the modesty of one who asks questions.

But since the letters which I have arranged to publish here contain no discussion of the actual controversy concerning Adoption, and since it cannot be supposed that another period and another Ascaricus, bishop of the Astures, whom we do not know, are meant, we must conclude that these letters were written before the true controversy had broken out. In them we recognize men carefully investigating the opinions of the Astures, as well as those of the Nestorians—opinions which could, and ought to, lead rapidly to an open outbreak of controversy. Thus they fill a great gap that had existed until now in the history of Adoptianism. For the rest, I present them in the same faulty Latin in which the author wrote them, hoping that I shall thereby gratify investigators of languages.

[Col. 1231]

## [LETTERS OF ASCARICUS AND TUSAREDUS]

### I. ASCARICUS TO TUSAREDUS

Ascaricus, bishop, sends to Tusaredus, servant of God, concerning the bodies of those holy sleepers who rose with Christ—what the account of these events contains, namely, concerning their glory.

Although discordant mourning, intolerable grief, and my vehement sorrow were sounding forth while the funeral uproar of the crowd announced that you had fallen into the destruction caused by the darts of your ambushers, nevertheless, because in a calm reversal another report thundered to me that your kindly spirit remained safe, every shadow of agitation was immediately wiped away from me, and the joy of the revived news caused my heart to pass everywhere from sadness to gladness.

Therefore, stretching out my arms and voice toward heaven, with complete exultation I blessed the power of Christ, unworthy though I am, who thus protects and delivers his own amid the snares of the ungodly. Finally, I know that after imprisonment, after expulsion, after lamentation, and after countless insults, I was sending you, in accordance with the Apostle, words of consolation; but from the wisest and bravest of men I know that he has now been calmed both by time and by reason.

There are only the shoots of the schisms that have recently sprung up in these regions that I have taken care to report to your Reverence. For almost all those from here among the Asturians to the coast, who persist in the offices of the clergy, strive, as though with one mouth—or nearly so—to spread shamelessly disgraceful statements about him from whose body the bodies of the holy sleepers rose—indeed, about bodies made alive . . . .  

[Note: [Col. 1231A] It seems that *spargere errores*—“to spread errors”—should be read.]

Although all of them do not flee into one and the same understanding, their collective interpretation can nevertheless be summed up in a single statement. For most of them do not believe that those bodies rose glorified, but corrupted; nor that they were raised to live perpetually with Christ among human beings, but so that they might show Christ’s glorious resurrection to unbelieving human beings. They say that they appeared not in the heavenly Jerusalem, as blessed Jerome relates, but in that earthly Jerusalem of the Jews. And just as Lazarus and the other bodies raised by the Lord himself before the Lord’s Passion returned to their former condition, then went back to their own tombs, and rested there until the Lord’s coming, so, they say, those bodies are to be raised.

They bring forward, as though incidentally, an edict of blessed Isidore concerning Adam and the three patriarchs, saying that he relates that they rest in tombs in the place of their own city. They do not understand that such men are foolish and raving, as though he could know whether their bodies had been raised at the Lord’s command, or whether he had seen with his own eyes that they were or were not in their tombs. Rather, Genesis merely relates the ancient life or death of the fathers.

Some, however, not knowing the difference between body and soul, miserably assert that the soul was raised because it is written that the Lord “bit” hell and rescued only the souls of the righteous, not those of sinners. Others believe that the bodies truly rose and affirm that they live to this day, but they abominate the idea that they are in heaven. They bring forward that most sacred evangelical oracle: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.” They say that no human being’s flesh can be in heaven except that flesh which the Lord deigned to assume for salvation.

These men also wish to add the statement of the blessed Isidore mentioned above: that after the resurrection an abode in heaven has been promised to the saints in the flesh. They recognize that this applies to the resurrection that will occur once, at Christ’s second coming, as the resurrection of all human beings, and not to that of which John speaks in the Apocalypse: “This is the first resurrection.”

Besides these, they bring forward many other nonsensical and childish ravings, which ought rather to be laughed at than repeated in order. Nor must I keep silent about the fact that they shamelessly and fearlessly utter weak and foolish things concerning Mary, the glorious and ever-virgin mother of our Lord Jesus Christ—things which I am ashamed to report: that she suffered the common death before the eyes of men, and that her body has until now been seen by many people resting in a tomb.

And because they do not cease to pierce me daily with fiery darts, not even with the smallest ones, I beg you—since some person who wishes or is able to help me may do so for this reason—and, as though you were present, I humbly entreat you; I appeal to you through the peace of the Lord Jesus Christ, which surpasses all understanding, to write down whatever your blessedness thinks or recalls having read concerning this matter and to send it to me without long delay.

May you thus possess the kingdom without end. Let your Holiness arrange to compose such a letter, supported by the testimonies of many, which may both instruct me and openly refute the contentious—for if your prudent counsel does not come to my aid quickly, I think I shall be utterly devoured by their bites.

Imitate, imitate, my lord, the patriarch Abraham. With three times six and three times a hundred servants, conquer in famous battle, and rescue your captured brother from Sodom, so that Solomon’s truthful saying may be fulfilled in you: “A brother helped by a brother is like a fortified city.” For a double or triple cord is difficult to break, and if there are two, one is placed beneath the other; just so, a shield formed by a mass of combatants easily escapes the arrows.

I know, indeed I know, that anxieties very often beset you from every side. But if anyone should wish to impede you, let those difficulties be overcome by that charity which conquers all things and which seeks not what is its own, but what belongs to another.

Come, come, my lord; come, do not delay writing, and rescue me from the troops of so many barking men and from their bites on every side, bringing me back to the right path. May your Holiness always have Christ as your helper in all things.

[Col. 1234A]

After these expressions of greeting, I send you my salutations and disclose to your sacred ears the remembrances of the saints. I beg you to deign to pray for me, so that my sins may be cleansed and I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judea. Through you I earnestly ask those lords and our common, most beloved sons who are to be saved.

### II. TUSAREDUS TO ASCARICUS

When I had reviewed the series of your letter, the Lord made my spirit joyful, because the signs of your safety were revealed to me. For if I had a more eloquent tongue, I could not express the joy that illumined my heart or the jubilation with which it exalted me—so much so that even the fear revived after a long time caused tears of love to flow and renewed the old sorrow.

As soon as the report itself had been read, like John raised from a charnel house, I immediately cast away anxieties, outward and inward, with the hands of my heart, right and left. I ran swiftly to the tower of David, which the *Song of Songs* celebrates—namely, to the strength of the Scriptures—in which a thousand shields hang, and every weapon of the strong, so that I might take from it even one shield and sword, by which I could safely rescue you, my dear brother, from Sodom and restore you to prosperity.
