For this reason, beloved one, sweeter to me than honey, since I did not have all the books I wanted at hand, relying with great confidence on your prayers, I seized from that same tower one shield first—Gregory—and from it I gathered a brief summary, which may be sufficiently opposed to the controversy of those men. A contemptuous dispute, as the Apostle says, is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear. These men who contradict wisdom would do better, if they were wise, to be wise unto sobriety, rather than generate schism in the Church among the simple-minded.

They ought to have acted most beautifully if, together with the Apostles, they had remained in the city until they were clothed with power from on high; and if they had hidden the Lord’s words in their hearts so that they would not sin. We do not say this to prevent them from investigating, but so that they may leave the higher mysteries to the Holy Spirit.

It would be enough for them, together with Rahab the prostitute in Jericho, to let down the scarlet thread through the window—that is, through the confession of the mouth, to believe in Christ crucified and to be saved. They would also hear Paul, the chosen vessel, saying: “I do not confess to know more than Christ, and him crucified.”

With what confidence, then, do these men already strive toward more exalted journeys among the dwelling places—namely, toward the tenth, in which manna flows, the twentieth, the thirtieth, and the other two, through which greater mysteries are understood? They wish to ascend or descend the ladder that Jacob saw, although they have not yet learned the narrowest path through the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth stages.

Having gone out from Egypt, let them first labor in the wilderness through many winding paths and narrow places. Let them fight with the kings Sihon and Og—that is, with vices or with the devil, through whom schism and heresy arise in the Church—and then let them approach to eat the manna. For it is commanded that no more manna be gathered than suffices; if anything extra was stored, it boiled with worms.

Let them understand what we say. We, however, ought not to follow the madness of those who labor vainly in the Church through schism and disputes, wishing to make themselves appear learned when they are ignorant. Rather, we must avoid them; and when we ought not answer their questions craftily or adulterate the word of God, we must speak what is known in the manifestation of truth and leave what is unknown to the Holy Spirit, so that, according to Isaiah, our faithful things may remain until we deserve to see our king in beauty.

Since the foregoing has been said, and since your letter mentioned those saints whom Christ, the mediator of God and humanity, deigned to rescue from the prison of hell, I have drawn from the books of our predecessors the statements that I have gathered for this page, just as your Holiness wished me to do—although not as I wanted, but as I was able.

1. That before the coming of the mediator of God and humanity, both the good and the wicked descended to the prison of hell.

2. That although the souls of the good descended into hell, they did not suffer punishments.

3. That the Lord rescued only the souls of the elect from the prison of hell, not those of the reprobate.

4. That the saints who rose gloriously with Christ received spiritual bodies of the kind that we expect to receive in the future resurrection.

5. That the glorified bodies of those saints of whom we are speaking rose.

6. That we ought to understand the Jerusalem in which they were seen as the heavenly Jerusalem.

7. Concerning that same Jerusalem, so that we may understand both the heavenly and the earthly.

8. That not all the saints whom Christ rescued from the prisons of hell rose in the flesh, but many did, as the holy Gospel says.

9. Concerning what is said in the Apocalypse: “This is the first resurrection,” and so forth.

10. Concerning what the Gospel says: “No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.”

11. Concerning glorious Mary: that no account teaches that she suffered the Passion or any kind of death.

### 1. That before the coming of the mediator of God and humanity, both the good and the wicked descended to the prison of hell

Gregory speaks as follows in his books of the *Moralia*:

“It is beyond doubt that every human being, however pure and approved his life may have been, descended to the prison of hell before the coming of the mediator of God and humanity. For the human being who fell by himself could not by himself return to the rest of paradise, unless he came who, through the mystery of his incarnation, opened for us the way to that same paradise. Hence blessed Job rightly asks the Lord, saying: ‘Who will grant me that you may protect me in hell?’ The Psalmist likewise says: ‘You have rescued my soul from the lower hell.’”

Again, Gregory himself says:

“All the elect who came into this world before the coming of our Redeemer, however much they possessed virtue and righteousness, could not, once they had been led out of their bodies, immediately enter into the bosom of the heavenly homeland, because he had not yet come who, by his descent, would open the prison of hell and place the souls of the righteous in an eternal dwelling.”

Again, in the same works:

“The earlier saints could not be freed from the places of hell, because he had not yet come who would descend there without guilt, in order to free from guilt those who were held there because of original sin.”

### 2. That although the souls of the good descended into hell, they did not suffer punishments

The same teacher says in those treatises:

“Before the incarnation of our Redeemer, the souls of the righteous are believed to have descended into hell, but not in such a way that they were held in places of punishment.”

[Note: [Col. 1235] A note added in the margin says: “It must be believed that the upper places of hell are one thing and the lower places another.”]

“Rather, the righteous rested in the upper regions, while the unjust were tormented in the lower.”

Again, he says:

“The souls of the righteous were at some time to be freed by the coming of the mediator from the places of hell, although they were not places of punishment. For this reason blessed Job says: ‘Appoint me a time when you will remember me.’ Augustine likewise says: ‘Before our Redeemer paid the penalty of the human race by his death, those who followed the ways of the heavenly homeland remained, after leaving the flesh, in the prison of hell—not so that punishment might chastise them as sinners, but so that, through the mediator’s entrance, he might absolve them from the guilt of the first sin.’”

### 3. That the souls of the elect alone were rescued from the prison of hell, not those of the reprobate

The holy Gregory himself speaks in these words from the *Moralia*:

“For the Lord, returning from hell, did not draw out the elect and the reprobate together; rather, he removed from it everything that he knew had clung to him.”

Through the prophet Hosea the Lord says:

“I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O hell.”

For what we kill we act so as to make it wholly cease to exist; but from what we sting, we remove one part and leave another. Therefore, because the Lord utterly killed death in his elect, he became the death of death. But because he removed one part from hell and left another, he did not utterly kill it, but stung hell.

Thus he says: “I shall be your death, O death”—that is, “In my elect I utterly destroy you.” “I shall be your sting, O hell,” because, after taking them away, I pierce you in part.

### 4. That the saints who rose gloriously with Christ received spiritual bodies of the kind that we expect to receive in the future resurrection

Every Catholic does not hesitate to believe and proclaim this. For when the most blessed Gregory was instructing the holy Roman Church, and through it the whole Church, concerning the resurrection itself, he addressed it in the first homily of the second book as follows:

“Perhaps someone may rightly say to himself: Christ rose because, being God, he could not be held by death. Therefore, to instruct our ignorance and strengthen our weakness, he did not wish the example of his resurrection to be sufficient for us. He alone died at that time, and yet he did not rise alone. For it is written: ‘Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose.’ Thus every argument of unbelief has been removed.

“For let no one say that a human being ought not to hope for himself for what God, in his flesh, displayed in a human being. Behold, we know that human beings rose with God—human beings whom we do not doubt were merely human. If, therefore, we are members of our Redeemer, let us presume in ourselves what is known to have occurred in the head. If we have cast ourselves down greatly, we ought to hope in ourselves, the lowest members, for what we have heard concerning his higher members.”

These are the words of that most holy man. When he says that we are the lowest members and should hope for a resurrection like theirs, he clearly teaches us that they received glorified—that is, spiritual—flesh, such as we shall receive in the future. For he was speaking only of the future resurrection.

### 5. That the glorified bodies of those saints of whom we speak rose

In the seventh oracle of the Sabbath, that is, in the Easter hymn, he addressed the Lord as follows:

“The bodies of the saints rise, made alive; the dwelling that had lain for a little while rises gloriously.”

Again, in the fourth Sabbath of the same week:

“Just as once, when you died, dead bodies rose, so now, at this festival of your resurrection, those buried are transferred to eternal rest.”

And if bodies rose, with what face do they assert that souls rose, since the soul is a spiritual and incorporeal substance? Or if bodies rose but were not glorified, how can he assert that they will rise again, like Lazarus who was to die?

Similarly, in the sixth Sabbath of the same week, he recalls the one whom I have just mentioned:

“May concord of charity flourish in us, through the merits of those who, together with your only Son, deserved to rise from the tombs—those glorified and made-alive bodies that will reign forever.”

And if they intercede for us, and if they were raised by him, why are the wicked not ashamed to say that they tasted the second death?

### 6. That the Jerusalem in which those who rose with Christ were seen must be understood as the heavenly Jerusalem

In the same week already mentioned, on the third Sabbath, he addressed that petition which is said as the Lord’s Prayer, as I stated above:

“Rushing swiftly to the dreadful throne of the altar, we ask you, almighty Father, that all sins may be washed away and that they may be made firm in the anointing of indulgence within the ecclesiastical body, so that we may breathe with our reborn infants and enter Jerusalem, the heavenly city, carrying offerings rich in marrow with the dead who have been raised.”

Again, the most blessed Jerome, in his letter to Heliodorus on the death of the presbyter Nepotianus, which is also called an epitaph, began among many other things as follows:

“Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose and appeared in the holy heavenly Jerusalem. Then that blessing was fulfilled: ‘Rise, you who sleep, and Christ will enlighten you.’”

There are many other statements of various teachers on this subject, which have not now been brought before us. But let us produce at least a few testimonies from those that we have presently found. Blessed Rufinus the presbyter, in his commentaries, after explaining the Creed, says among other things:

“When Christ rose, the tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep rose and appeared to many; and they entered the holy city.”

[Note: [Col. 1237] A later hand added in the margin: “Without doubt, [the] entry into the holy city of which the Apostle says…”]

“That city,” the Apostle says, “which is above is the true Jerusalem, free, which is the mother of us all.”

Hence the prophet Hosea, speaking in their person, says:

“He healed us after two days; on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight.”

### 7. Concerning that same Jerusalem, so that we may understand both the heavenly and the earthly

The holy Jerome, teacher and presbyter of the church at Bethlehem, says in the fourth book of his commentaries on Matthew:

“Let us understand the holy city in which they were seen rising either as the heavenly Jerusalem or as this earthly one, which had previously been holy and was called holy because of the temple and the Holy of Holies. But when he says, ‘They appeared to many,’ it is shown that this was not a general resurrection that would appear to everyone, but a special one, directed to many, so that those who deserved to see might behold it.”

These are the words of blessed Jerome. Since, therefore, he wished us to understand that in both Jerusalems—the earthly and the heavenly—we would see them, why do these men contemptuously deny that they ascended to the heavenly Jerusalem? He would certainly not have said that we should understand the heavenly Jerusalem if he denied that they had risen in glorified flesh.

### 8. That not all the saints whom Christ rescued from the prisons of hell rose in the flesh, but many did, as the holy Gospel says

Ambrose, Augustine’s teacher, speaks as follows in the *Hexaemeron* homilies, in the dogma of Christ:

“A certain portion of the ancient fathers rises in the flesh with Christ, so that our resurrection may be hoped for without ambiguity when he comes again.”

### 9. Concerning what is said in the Apocalypse: “This is the first resurrection,” and so forth

Jerome and Victorinus say:

“The first resurrection now takes place through faith in the soul, by which one arrives at baptism, having been absolved from original sin and entering the kingdom of God. The kingdom, certainly, is not only that which will be everlasting without end for the saints, but also that in which Christ now reigns in the Catholic Church. This resurrection does not permit human beings to pass into the second death.”

The Apostle speaks of this resurrection when he says:

“If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above.”

### 10. Concerning those who say, “No one ascends into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man”

Let those who contradict this read the book of blessed Julian—not of Pomerius, but of Toledo—which is called the *Anticimena*. It was composed concerning those matters that sound contrary in Scripture, although they are not contrary for those who, with vigilant understanding, investigate Scripture in its purity. There are many such matters concealed from these men. Let them then strive to keep silent and not speak about what they do not know.

If the *Anticimena* is unavailable, let them turn to Augustine and consult him in his book of homilies on John; let them hear him investigating this very passage. He says:

“Lest anyone be terrified at what is understood concerning God, we believe that Christ said this: ‘No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man’—namely, Christ, God and human being, one person.”

If anyone desires to know more, let him return to the text of this work and also read the commentaries of Eucherius or Niceta. Among other things, Saint Eucherius says:

“For this reason he himself ascended who descended: although he assumed a human being, nevertheless the human being . . . that is, Christ is one person.”

And since he is the head while the saints are members, the members must necessarily follow where the head has gone before, so that Christ may be the fullness of the body in heaven.

### 11. Concerning glorious Mary, whom no account teaches to have suffered the Passion or any kind of death

You will find this at the end of this work.

[At this point Isidore’s books of the *Etymologies* are inserted, followed, unless I am mistaken, by a treatise on heaven excerpted from Bede’s *On Times*. Finally, Tusaredus’s letter continues as follows:]

[Col. 1239B]

Concerning the glorious virgin Mary, whom no account teaches to have suffered the Passion or any kind of death, Isidore says:

“Mary, whose name is interpreted as ‘Lady’ or ‘Enlightener,’ is signified by the enclosed garden, the sealed fountain, and the shoot arising from the root of Jesse. She is the mother of the Lord, the temple of God, the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, a virgin who bore a child, a virgin before childbirth, and a virgin after childbirth. She receives the greeting from the angel and recognizes the mystery of the conception. She inquires into the nature of the birth and does not refuse, contrary to the law of nature, to obey in faith.

“When the Lord himself, hanging on the cross, commended the virgin to the disciples through the testament of his blood, he did so that the virgin might have as her companion in life the one whom the Son knew to be the guardian of virginity.””

Some, because of bodily bonds, assert that she departed this life through the Passion, on the grounds that the righteous Simeon, embracing Christ in his arms, had prophesied to the mother, saying: “And your own soul a sword will pierce.”

It is uncertain, however, whether he spoke of a material sword or of the word of God, powerful and sharper than every two-edged sword.

Yet no account specifically teaches that Mary’s soul was slain by the sword’s piercing, since her death is nowhere read of, although her tomb is found.

Omitting these matters, I sweetly send you an abundance of greetings, and I urge you to refresh me again and again with your letters, and in any event to lift me up—or at least sustain me—amid my sorrows.

Christ is to be loved above one’s parents, 31. He is peace, and his place is in peace, 33. He is the head of the body, and his members are one’s neighbors, 44. He went before by example, 54. He is the shepherd, 114. He is the rock, 176. Although he is one thing by which he is God and another by which he is man, he is not another person but is always God-man, 107. He suffered by will, not by necessity, 110. He is not divided into a nominal and a proper Christ, 111. He is one thing in relation to the Father and another in relation to his mother, but is not another person, 112. Redeemer, Savior, and so forth—not redeemed, saved, and so forth, 115. Adoptive in the active sense, not adopted, 116. He prays for us, the head for the members, when he asks to be delivered, ibid. Christ troubled himself when he wished, 117. He did not pray from necessity, 118. He called God “the Father,” or “my Father,” never “our Father,” 120. In what sense he was predestined the Son of God, 138. He alone is called the Son of God in Scripture in a singular sense, 142. He sometimes speaks of his members as of himself, the head, 149. How he is subject and to be subjected to the Father, and how all things are subject and to be subjected to him, 158. How he is called a servant in Scripture, 210. - Felix of Urgell, a Spanish, not a Gallic, bishop, 214, 225 and 227. He first teaches adoptionism concerning Christ, 214. How eager he was to disseminate his error, 215. He leaves the Council of Narbonne more insolent, 216. He is brought to the Council of Regensburg, ibid. He is brought to Rome by Angilbert, 217. While imprisoned at Rome, he writes an orthodox booklet, ibid. He repudiates his error, ibid. He is absolved and sent back to his own country, ibid. — He returns to his vomit, ibid. Perjured, 102 and 216. A deserter from the battle, 102. At one time a follower of Arius, at another of Nestorius, 104. Inconsistent with himself, 105. He divides the Son of God into one proper and one adoptive, 106. He divides Christ’s person and confuses his natures, 106, 107 and 108. Properly, a delirious and obstinate old man, 113. Supinely ignorant, 213. Blasphemous with Macedonius against the Holy Spirit, 115. A corrupter of the Scriptures, 117 and 140. He misunderstands them, 118. He posits four persons, 123. He assigns two sons to Christ, 144. He constitutes the true God in a titular God, and the true Son in an adoptive one, 145. He accuses Peter, disparages Paul, and mutilates the Evangelists, 159. He is represented by the wounded man of Jericho, 190. In what he agrees with Macedonius, 207. In what with Arius, ibid. and 208. In what he disagrees with Arius, 307. He comes closer to Nestorius, ibid. and 209. His fraud, lest he be detected as a Nestorian, 210. How he corrupted a passage of Hilary, 211. He writes at length against Alcuin, 217. He does not attend the Council of Frankfurt, 219. He composed a dialogue with a Saracen, which Charlemagne wishes to see, 220, 227, 228 and 245. How humanely he was treated at the Council of Urgell by bishops sent by Charlemagne, 223. He is brought to the Council of Aachen, and what was done there, ibid. At the Council of Aachen he comes to his senses with his disciples and sends a profession of faith to those absent, 224. He is stripped of his bishopric and sent into exile, 224. In exile at Lyons he resumes his errors and teaches them, ibid. He was regarded by some as a saint, ibid. He dies in his error, ibid. Defended by Jacques Basnage, 227.

## H

- The distinction between clerical and lay dress, 44.
- The heresies that troubled the Church in Paulinus’s time, 77 and 221.
- Heretics abuse the Scriptures, 69. They adhere to foreign doctrines, ibid. They are serpents, 100. They are represented by lamiae, 154. The death of P. Antonio Pagi, 235. What wrestling schools (*palaestrae*) were and what purpose they served, 102. What the *palaestric* style of speaking was, ibid. The death and praise of Palladia de Olivis (Venilia), IV. Francis Palladius more accurate than Candidus, XVI. How *palliare* is to be understood, 182. *Palmulae* are the palm’s dates, 194. *Palpare* and *palpitare* said of one who is uncertain, 108. The origin of *palpebrae* (“eyelids”), 113. How *palpetrae* differ from *palpebrae*, ibid. Dry bread, 20. The pomp of the world is the devil’s clothing, 58. The Paraclete is the same as the advocate, 4. Whether one should say *Paracletus* or *Paraclitus*, 11. Parents are to be loved if they do not hinder one from following Christ, 31. The bishopric of Parenzo, 205. The virtues and duties of children, 47. Paschal II did not open the door to dispensations granted on account of marriage, 85. Dominicus Passioneus is praised, V. Christ the shepherd, 56. The pastoral staff given to the chapter of Udine, 280. How far the life of pastors ought to excel that of the flock, 73. How the bishopric of Padua was made subject to Aquileia, 206. Why we say “Our Father,” not “My Father,” 120. The holy Fathers, when citing Scripture, often followed not the order of the words but the meaning, 112. The patriarch of Aquileia was to be ordained by the archbishop of Milan, XI.—Whether the patriarch of Grado communicated with Photius concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, 231. See “Patriarch of Aquileia.” The patriarchal rite, 279. It continued longer in the church of Como, 206, 280. Patrick, bishop of Emona, 204. The Patripassians deprived the Son of divinity, 70. Their author was Sabellius, 173 and 234. The error of Paul the Deacon, who calls Paulinus I, the schismatic patriarch of Aquileia, blessed, X. His reading is sometimes inconsistent, ibid. The rhythm on the destruction of Aquileia is not his, 186. Paulinus I, schismatic patriarch of Aquileia, XI. Saint Paulinus II, Italian by birth, patriarch of Aquileia, XII. Originally from Forum Julii, ibid. In what sense he was called Austrian, ibid. Saint Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, was born in the village of Premariacco, XIII. He was made a grammarian by Charlemagne, XIV and 258. He became patriarch of Aquileia after Siguald, XXII. He foretold the imperial dignity to Louis, son of Charlemagne, XXIV. He attended the Council of Regensburg [Col. 1258] and obtained for his clergy the freedom to choose their patriarch thereafter, XXV and 258. He held the first place at the Council of Frankfurt, XXVIII and 218. After the council he wrote books, XXIX. He held the Council of Forum Julii, XXIX, 65 and 201. He brought Carinthia back to the faith, XXIX. He was called the apostle of the Hungarians, XXXII. It is probable that he was present at Rome for Charlemagne’s coronation as emperor, XXXIV and 258. Its gifts, ibid.—What the virtues of the soul are, ibid. Force and fraud, and how they injure contracts, 86. Canonical life, XXVI and 80. Vitellian, patriarch of Grado, 205. Remedies for vices, 29. The exiled sons of King Vitiza, blinded by Roderic, 212. One should live according to the customs of the past but speak with the words of the present, XLIII.—To live according to the flesh, 29. The voices of animals, 12. Udalric I, patriarch of Aquileia, executor of Cacellinus’s will, founded the monastery of Mosac, 262 and following. Woldaric II established the celebration of the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene, 264 and following. Self-will cast down angels and human beings, 153.—How unity of will in Christ is to be understood in Paulinus’s rejection of the Monothelite error, 152.—How Christ does not act according to his own will, 153. Vulfad searches out Paulinus’s opinion on wife-killers as an example, XLIII and 16. The difference between *vulnus* (“wound”) and *ulcus* (“ulcer”), 103. Antonius and Cajetanus Vulpes, brothers, wrongly attribute Paulinus’s hymn to Elpidius, 177. Who the *togati vulturii* (“robed vultures”) are, 135.

## W

Walgand, rebellious against Charlemagne, XV. His possessions were given to Paulinus, XVI and 258. Waldo, bishop of Freising, XIX. Whether Walpert, patriarch of Aquileia, communicated with Photius concerning the Spirit, 231.

[Col. 1265]

Westremirus, bishop of Toledo, 225. Wicthpert, bishop of Augsburg, 205.

## X

What fasts *xerophagia* (“dry eating”) imply, 1.

## Z

Pope Zacharias at the consecration of the chapel of Saint Peter at Lubiana, XIX.—Pope Zacharias translated the *Dialogues* of Saint Gregory the Great into Greek, 230. How the Greeks corrupted his passage concerning the [Col. 1266] Holy Spirit, ibid. He was treated unfairly by Basnage, 231. The heretical imitators of the adulterer Zimri, 69. Zancto, or Anto, founded the monasteries of Sesto and Salt with his brothers, 255. Nicolaus Zani, 278. Antonius Zanoni, VII. How one should understand that it is not Christ’s role to give the kingdom to the sons of Zebedee, 156. The Apostle Zeno is praised, IV. The tares are an evil thought, 41.

SAINT PAULINUS’S THREE BOOKS AGAINST FELIX, BISHOP OF URGEL. 343  
Letter of Saint Paulinus to King Charles concerning the following books. Ibid.  

BOOK ONE. 349  
CHAPTER I.—He sets forth the laments of the grieving Church. Ibid.  
CHAPTER II.—Heretics are enemies of the Church, sons of the devil. 350  
CHAPTER III.—The Church triumphs over the heretics. 353  
CHAPTER IV.—Heretics are serpents. 354  
CHAPTER V.—He complains of Felix as a violator of the agreements of the councils attended by Charlemagne and Paulinus himself. 355  
CHAPTER VI.—He attacks Felix as a deserter from battle and as lukewarm and vomited out. 356  
CHAPTER VII.—Felix must be struck down like Goliath by a stone and consumed by fire like the hydra. 358  
CHAPTER VIII.—Felix, departing from the opinion of the Fathers, follows sometimes Arius and sometimes Nestorius. Ibid.  
CHAPTER IX.—Felix, inconsistent with himself, calls Jesus Christ at one time true God and Son of God, and at another an adoptive and titular god. 360  
CHAPTER X.—Paulinus does not intend to examine Felix’s heart and intention, but his words. 362  
CHAPTER XI.—He teaches that Felix thinks wrongly about God and speaks still worse, dividing the Son into a proper son and an adoptive son. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XII.—Felix, like the Jews and Arius, introduces division in the person and confusion in the natures of the Son of God; Paulinus rejects this. 363  
CHAPTER XIII.—Although one thing belongs to Christ by virtue of his being God and another by virtue of his being man, there is not another Christ, but always God-man. 364  
CHAPTER XIV.—The Word was not changed into flesh and suffered neither division nor mixture. 365  
CHAPTER XV.—Paulinus proves from the Apostle that Christ is Son of God and son of man; otherwise Mary, who nevertheless truly bore the Most High God, would have to be called only a titular, not a true, mother. 366  
CHAPTER XVI.—By bringing together the testimonies of John and Paul, he says that Christ’s glory is truly that of the Son of God, not of a titular son. 367  
CHAPTER XVII.—He accuses Felix of corrupting a passage of the Apostle; he teaches that Christ suffered, was buried, and so forth in his own flesh. 368  
CHAPTER XVIII.—Christ suffered by his will, not by necessity. 370  
CHAPTER XIX.—Testimonies from the Psalms and the Prophets show that Christ is not divided into a titular and a proper son. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XX.—Christ is one way in relation to the Father and another in relation to his mother, but he is not another Christ. 373  
CHAPTER XXI.—He reproaches Felix for his long-standing obstinacy. 374  
CHAPTER XXII.—He rebukes the yawning Felix, blindly ignorant of the difference between what is assumed and what is adopted. 375  
CHAPTER XXIII.—He refutes Felix’s error concerning the difference between advocate and mediator. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XXIV.—The Holy Spirit, although the Paraclete, that is, the Advocate, is nevertheless God. 377  
CHAPTER XXV.—Christ Jesus is Redeemer, not redeemed; Savior, not saved; Liberator, not liberated. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XXVI.—Jesus is the adopter, not the adopted; we, however, are adopted. 378  
CHAPTER XXVII.—Although Christ is not adoptive, he is nevertheless man. 379  
CHAPTER XXVIII.—When Christ prayed in Scripture to be saved, redeemed, and liberated, he did not speak for himself but for us; he spoke as the head for the members. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XXIX.—Christ troubled himself when he willed it. The Father’s voice glorifying him, and his prayer to the Father, were both uttered not for his own benefit but because of the circumstances. 380  
CHAPTER XXX.—Felix’s corruptions of Scripture: Christ prayed not for himself but for us, just as he was born, died, and was buried not for himself but for us. 381  
[Col. 1268] CHAPTER XXXI.—Christ did not pray out of necessity; Felix misunderstands a passage of Paul. 382  
CHAPTER XXXII.—Paul asserts Christ to be not an adoptive but a proper Son, not a titular but the true God: in Scripture he is recognized by the Father as the true Son, and in turn the Father as the true Father by the Son; he calls the Father not “our” but “my” Father. 384  
CHAPTER XXXIII.—How Israel, God’s firstborn, is to be understood; and why Christ taught us, when praying, to say “Our Father,” not “My Father.” 385  
CHAPTER XXXIV.—The text “God was with him,” misunderstood by Felix, is explained by Paulinus, who teaches through several passages of Scripture that Christ is the true Son of God. 386  
CHAPTER XXXV.—There are other titular christs; Jesus Christ is the proper one. The Apostle says that he suffered in the flesh, not together with the flesh. 388  
CHAPTER XXXVI.—He demonstrates from Scripture that Christ is true God. 389  
CHAPTER XXXVII.—He reproaches Felix for introducing a division of four persons in Christ, whom he nevertheless proves to be inseparable. 390  
CHAPTER XXXVIII.—Martha, the thief, the centurion, and Gabriel confess Christ to be the true Son of God; Felix calls him adoptive. 393  
CHAPTER XXXIX.—Scripture contains neither a titular god nor an adoptive son, but, to the contrary, the true God and the proper Son. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XL.—Emmanuel, Jesus, Redeemer, and Christ are names of the Son of God in Scripture, not of a titular or adoptive son. 394  
CHAPTER XLI.—What a titular god is, and why the term does not apply to Christ. 395  
CHAPTER XLII.—He explains by example and analogy that one person cannot be both an adoptive son and a proper son. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XLIII.—Adoption, because it applies to us, does not apply to Christ. 396  
CHAPTER XLIV.—Since God makes adoptive sons from sons of wrath through baptism, he argues that Felix ought either to have called Christ a son of wrath or ought not to call him adoptive through baptism. Christ did not need baptism; rather, by submitting to it, he sanctified it for us. 397  
CHAPTER XLV.—The Apostles, baptizing and performing miracles in the name of Jesus, prove that he himself is God. 400  
CHAPTER XLVI.—Jesus is the author of life, life itself, and the resurrection; therefore he is not a titular but the true God. 401  
CHAPTER XLVII.—Paulinus understands the repeated scriptural statement that the Lord is God as though it said that Jesus Christ is God. 402  
CHAPTER XLVIII.—He explains Isaiah’s passage concerning Jesus, who, although a man from the earth, is nevertheless, by the unity of his person, true God, not a titular god. 403  
CHAPTER XLIX.—The altar of earth, to which ascent by steps is forbidden, is Christ in the Incarnation; his person is nevertheless not multiplied. 404  
CHAPTER L.—The Word became flesh, yet there was not another Son, but always the same one who existed previously. Jesus was never merely an earthly man, since he was always also heavenly. 405  
CHAPTER LI.—Jesus, who descended, ascended to where he was before; for the Son of God is less than the Father according to human nature, but the Son is not thereby lesser, although he is man. Hence, too, the man inherited a name above every name. 406  
CHAPTER LII.—David and Paul confess Christ to be God without the addition “titular,” and the Son of God without the addition “adoptive.” 408  
CHAPTER LIII.—Christ is from the fathers according to the flesh, and according to divinity from God the Father; he is true God, not a titular god, a term unknown to the Catholic faith. He is the proper and only-begotten Son of the one Father. 409  
CHAPTER LIV.—The Apostle testifies that Christ is the Son of God, and the Father himself does so at the Jordan. 411  
CHAPTER LV.—He responds to Felix’s objections, showing Christ, God and man, to be the only-begotten one in the singularity of his person. 412  
CHAPTER LVI.—Paul’s passage explained: Christ, insofar as he is God, raised himself; insofar as he is man, it was nevertheless not one who raised and another who was raised. 413  
CHAPTER LVII.—He proves that Christ’s sitting at the right hand of the Father means that he is not a titular god but the true God, and not an adoptive son but the proper Son. 415  

BOOK TWO. 417  
CHAPTER I.—Jesus was predestined Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, as Paul says, not through adoption, as the heretics claim. Ibid.  
CHAPTER II.—He confirms by the testimony of Paul and Ezekiel that Christ is God over all. 419  
CHAPTER III.—He accuses Felix of misunderstanding Paul’s statement, “God was in Christ”; according to Paul himself, Christ, though existing in the form of God, was true God. 420  
CHAPTER IV.—By a popular example he declares that Christ, in assuming the form of a servant, did not lose the name of true Son, nor duplicate it into an adoptive son, nor change it into a titular son. 421  
CHAPTER V.—The name above every name and every genuflection do not belong to a titular god but to the true God; Jesus, therefore, is God, since these belong to him. 423  
CHAPTER VI.—In Scripture no one is called the Son of God except Christ; he explains the statement, “No one has ascended into heaven except …” 424  
CHAPTER VII.—He continues to explain what is meant by the Son of Man who is in heaven. 427  
CHAPTER VIII.—From Felix’s confession he argues that Felix admits two sons. 428  
CHAPTER IX.—He accuses Felix of error for saying that Jesus, the Son of Man who is the Son of God, was not in heaven before he was born on earth. He would excuse the error, but doubts Felix’s repentance. 429  
CHAPTER X.—He reproaches Felix for inconsistency, since he sometimes calls the Son God and sometimes denies it, asserting that the true God dwells in the titular god and the proper Son in the adoptive son. From the Gospel he proves that the Son of Man is the Son of God. 430  
CHAPTER XI.—From the testimonies of John the Baptist and the Apocalypse he shows that the Lamb of God is the Son of God. 432  
CHAPTER XII.—He accuses Felix of lying when he says that Scripture asserts that the Son of Man was delivered up for us, not the Son of God. He reproaches Felix for misunderstanding the name “servant,” which is identical with “Son of Man.” Ibid.  

BOOK THREE. 433  
CHAPTER I.—The testimonies of John the Baptist and John the Evangelist concerning the divinity of Christ Jesus. Ibid.  
CHAPTER II.—Jesus alone is the true Son, in whom the Father was well pleased; in the others he was not well pleased, since they are from the mass of perdition, and therefore they are not true sons but adoptive sons. 434  
CHAPTER III.—Felix’s misunderstanding of Scripture concerning the beloved Son of God the Father: in Scripture Christ sometimes speaks as the head concerning the members, and the members sometimes speak concerning Christ the head. 435  
CHAPTER IV.—He rejects Felix’s opinion that, because Jesus was a titular god, it was not his will to suffer or die, and that therefore he prayed the Father to take the cup away from him. 436  
CHAPTER V.—He shows from Christ’s voluntary submission to the Passion that he prayed and sweated in the garden for his own people and as an example. 437  
CHAPTER VI.—He addresses Jesus so that he may understand what it means for him to have descended from heaven, not to do his own will but that of the Father who sent him. 439  
CHAPTER VII.—He continues to address Jesus, teaching the distinction between the persons of the Father and the Son, not a distinction of wills, since the Father and the Son have one will. 440  
CHAPTER VIII.—By the similarity of the speech and teaching belonging to Christ and the Father, he confirms what precedes. 441  
CHAPTER IX.—He teaches that Christ descended from heaven as an example of humility and obedience, not to do his own will but the Father’s. Ibid.  
CHAPTER X.—The will to save human beings, which is in the Father, is also in the Son. And how the statement “No one is good except God alone” is to be understood. 442  
CHAPTER XI.—He shows that Christ does not deny that he is good, but replies that no one is good except God, to the one who believed that he was merely a good man. 443  
CHAPTER XII.—How is the Son said not to know the day of judgment, when judgment pertains to him? Paulinus modestly refrains from settling the controversy, although in the authoritative copies of his own Church, and in Jerome and Ambrose, the word *Son* (*Filius*) is not found in the cited statement. 444  
CHAPTER XIII.—He refers the question concerning the mother of the sons of Zebedee to Hilary and Ambrose. 445  
CHAPTER XIV.—He explains in two ways that it is not Christ’s to give the kingdom to the sons of Zebedee, but to those for whom it was prepared by the Father. 446  
CHAPTER XV.—He raises, from the Apostle, the difficulty of how Christ was or is to be subject to the Father. 448  
CHAPTER XVI.—He appeals to the Apostle concerning his meaning regarding the difficulty raised. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XVII.—Solution of the difficulty proposed: all things were subjected to Christ through the power of his divinity; all things are to be subjected through the obedience of his servants. And then God will be all in all. 449  
CHAPTER XVIII.—He begins to cite the opinions of teachers, first those of the Apostles Peter and Paul, showing that Felix misunderstood them. 450  
CHAPTER XIX.—He accuses Felix of misusing Hilary’s meaning, which he explains. 452  
[Col. 1270] CHAPTER XX.—He presents various statements of Hilary supporting his Catholic position. 452  
CHAPTER XXI.—He cites and explains Ambrose’s authority; he accuses Felix of corrupting Ambrose’s reading. 454  
CHAPTER XXII.—He adduces Jerome in support of his position. 455  
CHAPTER XXIII.—He presents testimonies from the books of Augustine. 456  
CHAPTER XXIV.—He teaches that Felix’s heresy had already been struck down by the anathema of Pope Damasus. He cites certain passages of Athanasius altered by Felix himself and explains how they are to be understood. 460  
CHAPTER XXV.—He examines and praises the teaching of Cyril of Alexandria. 462  
CHAPTER XXVI.—Testimonies of Pope Leo. Ibid.  
CHAPTER XXVII.—He discusses at length the authorities of Pope Gregory. 463  
CHAPTER XXVIII.—He explains the authority of Fulgentius. Paulinus’s confession and thanksgiving to God for the work he has completed. 466

## OBSERVATIONS AND NOTES ON THEODORE’S PENITENTIAL

## THEODORE’S DOCTRINE OF PENANCE, VINDICATED FROM EVERY SUSPICION OF NOVELTY

1163

### CHAPTER ONE

The Fathers deny that it was a custom sanctioned by a decree of the Church that people should do public penance for hidden sins. Ibid.

### CHAPTER II

The Fathers affirm that secret penance was sufficient for hidden sins, and that the custom of the Church was to do penance for them secretly. 1170

### CHAPTER III

The Fathers testify that public penance was canonically established by the Church only for public crimes. 1182

### CHAPTER IV

J. Morin’s first argument is presented and refuted. 1187

### CHAPTER V

The second argument is refuted. It is shown that, although almost all the ancient canons are to be understood as concerning public crimes, J. Morin nevertheless does not rightly conclude that the ancient Fathers therefore wholly neglected the healing of the gravest diseases of the soul, since, in addition to public penance and the form described by J. Morin, the ancient Fathers proposed numerous other remedies which they judged entirely sufficient for healing the gravest diseases of the soul. 1189

### CHAPTER VI

J. Morin’s same argument is refuted. It is demonstrated that the Fathers testify that the ancient canons concerning public penance are not to be understood as applying to all public crimes, and that there was another form of penance which they considered sufficient for the remission of lesser public crimes. From this it becomes clear which public crimes were subject to public penance. 1199

### CHAPTER VII

J. Morin’s third argument is refuted, and Augustine’s testimony is explained. 1207

### CHAPTER VIII

Certain words of the Penitential are explained. It is shown that public penance of the kind described by John Morin was not absolutely necessary even for very serious public crimes, and why the Fathers exempted many public sinners from it. 1210

### CHAPTER IX

A defense of the redemptions of penances that J. Morin condemns and therefore excludes from Theodore’s and the Roman Penitentials. 1221

### CHAPTER X

It is demonstrated that J. Morin did not set forth the certain reasons and true causes of Theodore’s Penitential. 1229
